summary: On a September evening in 1985, armed pirates stormed the Sabah town of Lahad Datu, killing at least 21 people in a raid that exposed the region's vulnerability to cross-border violence.

subject: 1987 America's Cup
summary: The 1987 America's Cup off Fremantle became the most internationally charged sailing event ever held, as Dennis Conner completed a stunning comeback to reclaim the trophy Australia had wrested from the New York Yacht Club in 1983, transforming a quiet Western Australian port city in the process.

subject: 1987 Burkina Faso Coup d'État
summary: On 15 October 1987, Thomas Sankara - the revolutionary who renamed his country 'the Land of Upright People' - was killed alongside twelve others in a coup that haunts Burkina Faso still.

subject: 1987 Forsyth County protests
summary: In January 1987, a small civil rights march of 75 people in Georgia's all-white Forsyth County was met with Klan violence -- and one week later, 20,000 marchers returned in one of the largest civil rights demonstrations in American history.

subject: 1987 Mecca incident
summary: On 31 July 1987, more than 400 people died in Mecca when Iranian pilgrim demonstrators and Saudi security forces collided at the edge of the hajj, in a confrontation that ruptured Iran-Saudi relations for years.

subject: 1987 Superstition Hills earthquakes
summary: A seismic one-two punch on November 24, 1987, when a magnitude 6.2 foreshock and magnitude 6.5 mainshock struck the Imperial Valley, triggering the largest ground acceleration ever recorded at the Superstition Mountain station in 55 years of monitoring.

subject: 1988 Summer Olympics opening ceremony
summary: Seoul's 1988 Olympic opening ceremony marked South Korea's arrival on the world stage -- and became infamous as the last time doves were released, after some burned alive in the Olympic cauldron.

subject: 1989 Paraguayan coup d'état
summary: On the night of February 2, 1989, tanks rolled through Asunción to end thirty-four years of dictatorship in a single bloody evening known as La Noche de la Candelaria.

subject: 1989 Sudanese coup d'état
summary: The coup that brought Omar al-Bashir to power on 30 June 1989 - launching a 30-year rule that would include the Darfur genocide and the largest sustained Sudanese emigration in living memory.

subject: 1990 British Army Gazelle shootdown
summary: On a February morning in 1990, heavy machine-gun fire from across the Irish border brought down a British Army Gazelle helicopter near Augher, marking a shift in how the IRA's East Tyrone Brigade fought.

subject: 1991 Haitian coup d'état
summary: The 1991 military coup that overthrew Haiti's first democratically elected president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, unleashing three years of violence, refugee crisis, and international intervention before Operation Uphold Democracy restored him to power.

subject: 1991 Los Angeles Runway Collision
summary: On February 1, 1991, a USAir Boeing 737 landed on top of a SkyWest commuter plane at LAX, killing 35 people and exposing critical failures in runway control procedures.

subject: 1991 Miaoli Train Collision
summary: On 15 November 1991, two passenger trains collided near Zaoqiao Station in Miaoli County, killing 30 people and injuring 112 — the deadliest railway disaster in Taiwan since 1948.

subject: 1992 Gothenburg tram derailment
summary: A cascading chain of small decisions transformed a routine power outage into Sweden's deadliest tramway disaster.

subject: 1992 Summer Olympics opening ceremony
summary: The night a flaming arrow lit the Olympic cauldron over Montjuïc and Barcelona announced itself to 3.5 billion people.

subject: 1993 Finisterre Earthquakes
summary: Three major earthquakes struck Papua New Guinea's Finisterre Range in October 1993, killing at least 65 people and remaking the terrain through 4,700 landslides that damned rivers and buried villages.

subject: 1993 Perth tank rampage
summary: In the early hours of 27 April 1993, a 27-year-old man with a history of mental illness stole an armoured personnel carrier from an army barracks and drove it through the streets of Perth, Western Australia.

subject: 1995 Airstan Ilyushin Il-76 hijacking
summary: In 1995, the Taliban forced a Russian cargo plane carrying weapons to land at Kandahar, holding its seven-man crew captive for over a year -- until the crew overpowered their guards and flew their own aircraft to freedom.

subject: 1995 Borodianka Mid-Air Collision
summary: On a winter afternoon in 1995, two Antonov aircraft flying in formation collided over the fields near Borodianka, and the first prototype of a new transport plane fell with all seven of its crew.

subject: 1995 British Isles heatwave
summary: The summer the lawns turned brown and the reservoirs revealed their ghosts - 1995 still ranks among the warmest and driest the British Isles have ever recorded.

subject: 1995 Rugby World Cup
summary: When Nelson Mandela walked onto the Ellis Park pitch wearing a Springbok jersey, he transformed a rugby final into the most powerful act of reconciliation in South Africa's young democracy.

subject: 1995 Rugby World Cup Final
summary: When Nelson Mandela walked onto Ellis Park wearing a Springbok jersey - the very symbol of the apartheid regime that had jailed him for 27 years - a divided nation held its breath, and then roared as one.

subject: 1995 San Diego tank rampage
summary: On the afternoon of May 17, 1995, a 35-year-old Army veteran named Shawn Nelson stole a 57-ton M60 tank from a San Diego National Guard armory and drove it through residential streets for 25 minutes — crushing cars and fire hydrants but somehow injuring no one else — before police shot him dead through the open hatch.

subject: 1996 Pat Sin Leng Wildfire
summary: On February 10, 1996, a wildfire on the Pat Sin Leng ridgeline in Hong Kong's New Territories killed five people — three students and two teachers who gave their lives trying to help others escape.

subject: 1997 Central European flood in Wrocław
summary: When the Oder swallowed forty percent of Wrocław in July 1997, half a million sandbags and a city full of volunteers held the line around the medieval Old Town.

subject: 1997 Lego Spill
summary: A rogue wave off Land's End in 1997 spilled nearly five million Lego pieces into the Atlantic; they are still washing up on Cornish beaches today.

subject: 1997-98 UEFA Champions League
summary: The season Real Madrid ended a 32-year drought - and a one-goal moment in Amsterdam that reset European football's balance of power.

story.title: 1998 Winter Olympics: Nagano's Moment on the World Stage

subject: 1998 Winter Olympics
summary: The 1998 Winter Olympics brought 2,176 athletes from 72 nations to Nagano, Japan, introducing snowboarding and women's ice hockey to the Games while transforming the mountain city with a bullet train line that cut the journey from Tokyo in half.

subject: 1LIVE
summary: Every other person under thirty in North Rhine-Westphalia tunes in at least once a day. From a Cologne studio, 1LIVE has spent three decades figuring out what public broadcasting sounds like when the audience does not want to feel like it is being broadcast at.

subject: 2000 Sipadan Kidnappings
summary: On April 23, 2000, six Abu Sayyaf militants seized twenty-one hostages from one of the world's premier dive resorts, turning a tropical paradise into the stage for a months-long crisis that reshaped security across maritime Southeast Asia.

subject: 2001 Bradford Riots
summary: Two nights of rioting in Bradford in July 2001 that came at the end of a summer of unrest across northern England and led to the largest mass riot prosecution in English legal history.

subject: 2001 United Kingdom foot-and-mouth outbreak
summary: An eleven-month epidemic that began with a single pig in an Essex abattoir, spread through swill from a Northumberland farm, and ended with six million slaughtered animals and the smoke of pyres rising over the British countryside.

subject: 2003 Dutch TT
summary: On a rain-slicked Saturday at Assen in June 2003, Valentino Rossi raised his arm and rode into the pit lane - and the rest of the MotoGP grid followed him, delaying the start of their own Grand Prix.

subject: 2003 Standoff in Abbeville, South Carolina
summary: A ten-foot strip of highway right-of-way became the spark for a fourteen-hour gun battle that killed two South Carolina lawmen in December 2003.

subject: 2004 Boscastle flood
summary: On a summer Monday in 2004, a freak stationary thunderstorm dumped seven inches of rain on the Cornish village of Boscastle, sending a wall of water carrying 50 cars into the sea -- and remarkably, not a single person died.

subject: 2004 Summer Olympics closing ceremony
summary: Under a full moon over Marousi, Athens said farewell to the Games it had waited a century to host, then handed the flame east toward Beijing.

subject: 2006 Southeast Asian Haze
summary: A man-made atmospheric catastrophe that blanketed Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for months, grounding flights, closing schools, and igniting a diplomatic crisis across half a dozen nations.

subject: 2007 Alderney UFO Sighting
summary: On a clear April afternoon in 2007, a veteran Channel Islands pilot saw something over Alderney he could not explain - and another pilot, miles away, saw it too.

subject: 2007 Bengkulu earthquakes
summary: A magnitude 8.4 megathrust earthquake off Sumatra's coast on September 12, 2007, one of the twenty largest ever recorded, followed by two more magnitude 7+ quakes within hours, triggering tsunami warnings across the Indian Ocean.

subject: 2007 Guatemala City sinkhole
summary: A ruptured sewer pipe quietly dissolved the volcanic rock beneath a poor neighborhood in Guatemala City until, on February 23, 2007, the ground opened into a nearly perfect 100-meter-deep shaft that swallowed homes and killed five people.

subject: 2007–2008 Kenyan crisis
summary: A disputed election plunged one of Africa's most stable democracies into two months of ethnic violence that killed more than a thousand people, until a former UN chief brought the rivals to share power.

subject: 2008 Chatsworth Train Collision
summary: The deadliest US rail accident in fifteen years, caused when a Metrolink engineer ran a red signal while texting, killing 25 people in the hills above the San Fernando Valley.

subject: 2008 Irish Pork Crisis
summary: A single feed plant near Fenagh, County Carlow contaminated nearly every Irish pork product on sale in December 2008, triggering a worldwide recall across 23 countries.

subject: 2008 Santa Catarina floods
summary: In November 2008, two months of relentless rain culminated in catastrophic floods and landslides across Brazil's Santa Catarina state, killing at least 135 people and forcing nearly 80,000 from their homes.

subject: 2008 Summer Olympics closing ceremony
summary: Directed by Zhang Yimou, the Beijing Olympics closing ceremony traded the opening's solemnity for celebration, featuring a handover to London and performances by artists from Placido Domingo to Jimmy Page.

subject: 2008 Summer Olympics opening ceremony
summary: Watched by over a billion people worldwide, Zhang Yimou's opening ceremony for the 2008 Beijing Olympics featured 2,008 drummers, movable-type printing performed by human blocks, and fireworks that traced the path of footsteps across Beijing's sky.

subject: 2008 Vintage Yachting Games
summary: Sixty-six sailors in forty-seven boats from seventeen countries gathered at Medemblik for the first multi-class regatta dedicated entirely to Olympic sailing classes the Olympics had abandoned.

subject: 2008 invasion of Anjouan
summary: An African Union amphibious assault on the Comoran island of Anjouan to depose a renegade colonel who declared independence after a disputed election -- dubbed the strangest invasion in history.

subject: 2009 Bank of Ireland Robbery
summary: A 24-year-old bank clerk, three hostages, and 7.6 million euro in cash carried out of a Dublin bank in broad daylight - the largest bank robbery in Irish history.

subject: 2009 CPISRA Football 7-a-side International Championships
summary: For ten days in 2009, Papendal in Arnhem hosted the cerebral palsy football world's qualifier for Beijing's successor tournament. Iran's Abdolreza Karimizadeh scored thirteen goals.

subject: 2009 Gerry Weber Open
summary: The week Tommy Haas, ranked 39th and on a wildcard, beat Novak Djokovic for his first title in two years - on grass in a Westphalian town of 22,000.

subject: 2009 Sumatra earthquakes
summary: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake off the coast of Padang in September 2009 killed over 1,100 people and triggered landslides, fires, and a massive international relief effort across West Sumatra.

subject: 2009–10 Belgian Pro League
summary: The season a sixteen-year-old striker named Romelu Lukaku finished as top scorer of Belgium's top division — while Anderlecht clinched another league title at home.

subject: 2010 FIFA World Cup
summary: The first World Cup ever held on African soil, a month-long roar of vuvuzelas in which South Africa proved the doubters wrong and Nelson Mandela took the field one last time.

subject: 2010 Hebei tractor rampage
summary: A workplace grievance escalated into mass murder in rural Hebei when a coal yard worker turned a bucket loader into a weapon, killing 11 and injuring 20 before bystanders stopped him.

subject: 2010 Thai political protests
summary: Bangkok's commercial heart became a battleground when tens of thousands of Red Shirt protesters occupied the Ratchaprasong intersection for weeks, ending in a military crackdown that killed more than eighty people.

subject: 2010 Winter Olympics
summary: Vancouver had to truck in its own winter, lost a young athlete before the flame was lit, and still ran one of the most warmly remembered Games in Olympic history.

subject: 2010 Yeonpyeongdo bombardment
summary: On November 23, 2010, North Korea shelled the inhabited South Korean island of Yeonpyeongdo with 170 artillery rounds, killing soldiers and civilians alike in the most serious military attack on South Korean territory since the Korean War armistice.

subject: 2010-2011 Queensland Floods
summary: Over the summer of 2010-2011, floods drowned much of Queensland, killing 33 people, including those swept away when an inland tsunami tore through Toowoomba and the Lockyer Valley.

subject: 2011 CPISRA Football 7-a-side World Championships
summary: Sixteen national football teams gathered in the Netherlands for two weeks in the summer of 2011 to play the world championship of their sport - and to qualify their countries for the London 2012 Paralympic Games.

subject: 2011 Egyptian revolution
summary: Eighteen days in Tahrir Square toppled a thirty-year presidency and shook the Arab world, though the revolution's promise of bread, freedom, and dignity proved far harder to deliver than the protest that demanded it.

subject: 2011 England Riots
summary: Five days in August 2011 when looting, arson, and grief spread from a police shooting in Tottenham across cities and towns the length of England.

subject: 2012 Malian coup d'état
summary: A soldiers' mutiny at the Kati barracks near Bamako spiraled into a coup that toppled Mali's president weeks before an election, and inadvertently handed the country's north to the rebels the soldiers had been fighting.

subject: 2012-13 Belgian Second Division
summary: The season KV Oostende, a club from a seaside town with no real footballing tradition, climbed out of Belgium's second tier and changed what the league looked like for a decade.

subject: 2012-13 Hoofdklasse
summary: The Dutch amateur football season nobody remembers, except for one ugly fight after a playoff game that rewrote the rules for an entire division.

subject: 2013 Lahad Datu Standoff
summary: A 2013 military conflict in which followers of a Sulu sultan claimant invaded eastern Sabah, triggering weeks of standoff, airstrikes, and a permanent reshaping of the region's security landscape.

subject: 2013 National Scout Jamboree
summary: The first Scout jamboree at the Summit Bechtel Reserve - a stress test of a new venue, a culture in transition, and the future of American scouting.

subject: 2013 Santa Monica Shootings
summary: On June 7, 2013, 23-year-old John Zawahri killed five people across nine crime scenes in a 13-minute rampage through Santa Monica, beginning with his own family.

subject: 2013 Shahbag protests
summary: A massive popular uprising at a Dhaka intersection demanding justice for war crimes committed during the 1971 Liberation War.

subject: 2013 UEC European Track Championships
summary: Three days in October when Apeldoorn's Omnisport hosted a world record-shattering team pursuit by Laura Trott's Britain, a hat-trick of medals from sprinter Kristina Vogel, and Ireland's first ever European track cycling medal.

subject: 2014 Badulla landslide
summary: On an October morning in 2014, monsoon-saturated hillside collapsed onto a Sri Lankan tea estate, burying the homes of plantation workers in Koslanda and exposing the deadly intersection of deforestation, poverty, and extreme rainfall.

subject: 2014 IPC Swimming European Championships
summary: Three hundred and seventy-five Para swimmers from 35 countries gathered in Eindhoven for a week in August 2014, and the records they broke - in classes from S1 to S14 - still anchor the sport's modern history.

subject: 2014 Nuclear Security Summit
summary: For two March days in 2014, fifty-eight world leaders converged on The Hague to discuss how to keep the most dangerous materials on Earth out of the wrong hands.

subject: 2014 Thai coup d'état
summary: Thailand's twelfth coup since 1932 saw General Prayut Chan-o-cha seize power from a caretaker government in May 2014, reshaping Thai politics for years to come.

subject: 2014-15 Belgian Second Division
summary: On a Sunday in December, with four months still to play, Sint-Truiden effectively wrapped up the title. The rest of the season was a long, careful coast.

subject: 2015 Shenzhen Landslide
summary: On 20 December 2015, a mountain of excavated soil and construction debris that had been accumulating for two years collapsed onto the Hengtaiyu industrial park in Shenzhen, killing 73 people in a man-made disaster born of negligence and inadequate oversight.

subject: 2015 Tianjin explosions
summary: On August 12, 2015, a series of catastrophic explosions at a chemical storage facility in the Port of Tianjin killed 173 people and exposed systemic failures in industrial safety oversight.

subject: 2015 Yuen Long Protest
summary: On March 1, 2015, thousands of protesters descended on Yuen Long to challenge a practice — parallel trading — that had reshaped everyday life in Hong Kong's border towns, closing shops and straining public transport.

subject: 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires
summary: On November 28, 2016, mountain wave winds gusting to 87 mph drove a smoldering fire out of Great Smoky Mountains National Park and into the tourist towns of Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge, killing 14 people and destroying over 2,000 buildings in the deadliest wildfire in the eastern United States in nearly 70 years.

subject: 2016 Waroona-Yarloop bushfire
summary: A lightning-sparked bushfire in January 2016 that burned from the Darling Scarp to the Indian Ocean, destroying the historic town of Yarloop and killing two people in one of Western Australia's worst fire disasters.

subject: 2017 Barcelona attacks
summary: On August 17, 2017, a van driven into pedestrians on La Rambla killed 14 people and injured over 130, making it the deadliest attack in Spain since the 2004 Madrid train bombings.

subject: 2017 Payson flash floods
summary: On a summer afternoon in 2017, a six-foot wall of black water swept through a popular Arizona swimming hole, killing ten people at a family birthday celebration in one of the state's deadliest flash flood events.

subject: 2017 U.S. Women's Open
summary: Park Sung-hyun's stunning comeback victory at the 72nd U.S. Women's Open at Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, turned a seven-stroke deficit into a historic first major title.

subject: 2017 Zimbabwean coup d'état
summary: In November 2017, the Zimbabwean military seized control of Harare and forced the resignation of Robert Mugabe after 37 years in power, replacing him with Emmerson Mnangagwa.

subject: 2017-18 Belgian Second Amateur Division
summary: The season RFC Liege - one of the oldest football clubs on the continent - clawed its way back up Belgian football's fourth tier and out of it.

subject: 2017-18 FIBA Europe Cup
summary: In a season most basketball fans missed entirely, a small club from Venice quietly outran continental giants while a team from the cold north of the Netherlands made the deepest European run in its history.

subject: 2018 Attica wildfires
summary: In July 2018, a wind-driven firestorm overran the seaside town of Mati near Athens in minutes, killing 104 people and becoming one of the deadliest wildfire disasters in modern Greek history.

subject: 2018 Hong Kong Bus Accident
summary: On the evening of February 10, 2018 — the eve of Lunar New Year — a Kowloon Motor Bus double-decker flipped on a curve on Tai Po Road, killing 19 people and injuring 65 in Hong Kong's second-deadliest road accident on record.

subject: 2018 Winter Olympics
summary: PyeongChang's 2018 Winter Games brought the first Winter Olympics to mainland Asia, set a record with 102 medal events, and saw North and South Korean athletes march together.

subject: 2018 Yilan Train Derailment
summary: On a Sunday afternoon in October 2018, a Puyuma Express train entered a curve in Yilan County at nearly twice the speed limit with its safety system switched off, killing 18 passengers and reshaping Taiwan's approach to rail safety.

subject: 2019 Amazon rainforest wildfires
summary: On August 19, 2019, smoke from fires thousands of kilometers away turned the São Paulo afternoon dark and the world finally paid attention to the Amazon.

subject: 2019 Iranian shoot-down of American drone
summary: The June 2019 shoot-down of a $130 million US Global Hawk drone over the Strait of Hormuz that nearly triggered a war -- until the president changed his mind with planes already in the air.

subject: 2019 Northeast Brazil oil spill
summary: The worst oil spill in Brazilian history, origin still unknown, cleaned up in large part by volunteers with plastic bags.

subject: 2019 Open Championship
summary: Sixty-eight years after Max Faulkner's win at Portrush, the Claret Jug came home to an Irish hand and a Northern Irish links - and Shane Lowry walked the eighteenth fairway in a roar that hadn't been heard on this coast in a long time.

subject: 2019 Reed Bank incident
summary: In June 2019, a Chinese steel-hulled vessel rammed and sank a Philippine wooden fishing boat at Reed Bank in the South China Sea, abandoning its twenty-two crew members in open water -- an incident that crystallized the human cost of competing sovereignty claims.

subject: 2019 Sudanese coup d'état
summary: After four months of sustained street protest in temperatures sometimes dropping below freezing at night, Sudanese civilians and their military finally dislodged Omar al-Bashir after thirty years in power.

subject: 2020 Gjerdrum landslide
summary: In the predawn darkness of December 30, 2020, a quick clay landslide devoured part of Ask village in Gjerdrum, Norway, killing ten people and exposing decades of ignored warnings about building on unstable ground.

subject: 2020 Malian Coup d'État
summary: In August 2020, soldiers at the Kati garrison outside Bamako rose up, arrested President Keïta, and ended his rule — Mali's second coup in less than a decade, born of protest, war-weariness, and a region sliding toward instability.

subject: 2021 Henan floods
summary: In July 2021, a year's worth of rain fell on Zhengzhou in three days, killing 398 people and revealing both the power of extreme weather and a government cover-up of the true death toll.

subject: 2021 Northern Ireland riots
summary: Eleven nights in spring 2021 when Northern Ireland's youngest generation, born after the Good Friday Agreement, threw petrol bombs at police in scenes that looked uncomfortably familiar.

subject: 2021 Sudanese coup d'état
summary: Two years after the revolution that deposed al-Bashir, the same general who had helped manage the transition turned on it - and ordinary Sudanese went back into the streets by the hundreds of thousands.

subject: 2022 Chinese Military Exercises Around Taiwan
summary: When Nancy Pelosi stepped off a plane in Taipei in August 2022, China responded by encircling Taiwan with the largest live-fire military exercises since the 1996 crisis, firing eleven ballistic missiles into surrounding waters.

subject: 2022 Denbighshire Urdd National Eisteddfod
summary: After a three-year COVID pause, Europe's largest youth festival returned in 2022 to a farm field outside Denbigh - 118,000 visitors, free entry, three pavilions, a 12-year-old composer winning her first major prize.

subject: 2022 FIVB Women's Volleyball World Championship
summary: On 15 October 2022 in Apeldoorn, Serbia swept Brazil to win a second straight Women's Volleyball World Championship — and Tijana Bošković collected her second consecutive MVP.

subject: 2022 Leicester Unrest
summary: In August and September 2022, sectarian tensions between parts of Leicester's Hindu and Muslim communities erupted into street disorder, fanned by social media misinformation and outside agitators in a city long held up as a model of multicultural cohesion.

subject: 2022 Winter Olympics
summary: Beijing became the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics when it staged the XXIV Olympic Winter Games in February 2022, an event shaped as much by geopolitics and a global pandemic as by athletic competition.

subject: 2022 Winter Olympics opening ceremony
summary: On February 4, 2022, the Bird's Nest stadium hosted a Winter Olympics opening ceremony that wove ancient Chinese calendar traditions into the world's largest LED display, marking Beijing's unprecedented double as both Summer and Winter Olympic host city.

subject: 2023 Herat earthquakes
summary: Four magnitude 6.3 earthquakes struck Herat Province in October 2023, killing nearly 1,500 people -- 90 percent of them women and children trapped inside their mud-brick homes -- and leaving over 100,000 in need of humanitarian aid.

subject: 2023 Nottingham attacks
summary: In the early hours of 13 June 2023, three people in Nottingham were killed by a man whom mental-health services had failed to detain; their families are still pressing for accountability.

subject: 2023 Odisha train collision
summary: On a June evening in 2023, a signaling error sent a speeding passenger train onto the wrong track near Bahanaga Bazar station in Odisha, triggering a three-train collision that killed 296 people.

subject: 2023 Stenungsund landslide
summary: When construction companies illegally dumped 170,000 tons of excavated soil on unstable quick clay, Sweden's main highway to Norway collapsed in less than a minute.

subject: 2023–2025 Manipur violence
summary: Beginning in May 2023, ethnic violence between the Meitei majority and Kuki-Zo tribal minority tore through Manipur, displacing tens of thousands and exposing deep fractures in India's northeastern frontier.

subject: 2024 Baltic Sea submarine cable disruptions
summary: A Chinese cargo ship anchored in the Kattegat became the center of an international standoff after two critical undersea cables were severed in the Baltic Sea within hours of each other.

subject: 2024 Bangladesh anti-Hindu violence
summary: In the chaotic aftermath of Sheikh Hasina's resignation in August 2024, Bangladesh's Hindu minority faced a wave of targeted attacks - more than 2,000 incidents in 16 days by one Hindu advocacy group's count, including assaults on temples, homes, and businesses, though the true scale and how much was religious rather than political remain disputed.

subject: 2024 Dutch Masters of Motocross
summary: Jeffrey Herlings collected a fifth title and a place in series history; a separate twenty-five-point class went to the wire and was decided by one.

subject: 2024 Finneidfjord train derailment
summary: A rockslide on the Nordland Line in October 2024 killed the train driver, severed Norway's only continuous north-south road and rail links, and effectively cut the country in two for weeks.

subject: 2024 Iranian missile strikes in Pakistan
summary: In January 2024, Iran launched missile and drone strikes into Pakistan's Balochistan province, triggering retaliatory Pakistani airstrikes into Iran -- the first known attacks on Iranian soil since the Iran-Iraq War and a crisis that was resolved within days through urgent diplomacy.

subject: 2024 New York City Subway derailment
summary: A chain of human errors turned a pulled emergency brake on Manhattan's Upper West Side into a train collision and derailment that disrupted subway service for three days in January 2024.

subject: 2024 Solingen Stabbing
summary: Solingen was celebrating its 650th birthday when an attacker walked into the crowd and changed the city's anniversary forever.

subject: 2024 United Kingdom Riots
summary: A week of far-right riots in English and Northern Irish towns in summer 2024, triggered by the murder of three children at a Southport dance class and amplified by online disinformation falsely identifying the attacker as a Muslim asylum seeker.

subject: 2024-25 Belgian Division 3
summary: A coastal Belgian club that played in the Europa League just six years earlier collapsed into bankruptcy. The fifth tier absorbed what was left, attached to a small West-Flemish town's matricule.

subject: 2025 Cambodian–Thai border crisis
summary: In mid-2025, a series of border incidents between Cambodia and Thailand escalated into the worst armed confrontation between the two nations in over a decade, involving airstrikes, rocket barrages, and tens of thousands of displaced civilians before a fragile peace accord was signed in Kuala Lumpur.

subject: 2025 Louvre heist
summary: On a Sunday morning in October 2025, thieves disguised as construction workers stole eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels from the Louvre in under eight minutes, exposing security failures that had been warned about for over a decade.

subject: 2025 North Sea Ship Collision
summary: A Filipino sailor lost his life when a Portuguese container ship struck a US fuel tanker at anchor off the Yorkshire coast on a foggy March morning in 2025.

subject: 2025 Northern Ireland riots
summary: Two weeks of anti-immigrant violence across Northern Ireland in June 2025, beginning in Ballymena - homes burned, families forced to barricade themselves in attics, and a community of Roma neighbours largely driven out by the end.

subject: 2025 Open Championship
summary: Scottie Scheffler buried the field at Royal Portrush with four sub-70 rounds and a four-stroke win - the third Open in the dunes of the North Antrim coast, and the first in this century that Portrush hosted as a returning regular.

subject: 2025 Taipei Stabbings
summary: On 19 December 2025, a planned attack at Taipei Main Station and Zhongshan Station killed three people and injured eleven others; a bystander named Yu Chia-chang died trying to stop the assailant.

subject: 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference
summary: COP30 came to Belem in November 2025, pulling 56,118 delegates into the mouth of the Amazon for the first time, and left with a compromise that did not mention fossil fuels.

subject: 24th World Scout Jamboree
summary: Forty thousand Scouts from 152 nations on a reclaimed West Virginia mountain - the only World Scout Jamboree the United States has hosted in the 21st century.

subject: 25 August 2019 Hong Kong Protest
summary: On 25 August 2019, a sanctioned march through Tsuen Wan and Kwai Tsing escalated into running confrontations between police and protesters — the day water cannons were deployed in Hong Kong for the first time, and a 12-year-old boy became the youngest person arrested in the protest movement.

subject: 27 Brigade
summary: In the chaos following Taiwan's February 28 Incident of 1947, students, workers, and former soldiers in Taichung formed the 27 Brigade to defend their communities — and paid a devastating price.

story.title: The Perfect Crime on a Fuchu Side Street

subject: 300 million yen robbery
summary: On December 10, 1968, a fake motorcycle cop stopped a bank car on a quiet Tokyo street, shouted 'Bomb!', and drove off with 294 million yen -- the largest heist in Japanese history, still unsolved.

subject: 32 Demands
summary: On the evening of March 7, 1947, Taiwanese representatives delivered 32 demands for democratic reform to their governor, knowing that troops from mainland China were already on the way to crush them.

subject: 39th G8 Summit
summary: In June 2013, eight world leaders met behind four miles of razor wire on the shore of Lough Erne. It was the first G8 summit in Northern Ireland and the last summit Russia ever attended.

story.title: 3rd National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party

subject: 3rd National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party
summary: In June 1923, more than thirty delegates representing 420 Communist Party members gathered at a modest address in Guangzhou and made a decision that would reshape the course of Chinese history.

subject: 47th G7 summit
summary: In June 2021 the leaders of the world's seven richest democracies met on the sand at Carbis Bay to argue about pandemics, climate, and how to handle China.

story.title: 7 March Speech of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman

subject: 7 March Speech of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman
summary: The speech that launched a nation -- Sheikh Mujib's 1971 address to a million people at the Ramna Race Course, now a UNESCO-recognized documentary heritage.

subject: 700,000 People Looking Up
summary: Once a year, Marine Corps Air Station Miramar opens its gates and San Diego pours in.

subject: 7000 Oaks
summary: Joseph Beuys dumped seven thousand basalt columns on Kassel's main square in 1982 and made a rule: a stone could only leave when someone planted an oak to go with it. It took five years and outlived him.

subject: 798 Art Zone
summary: Inside decommissioned military factories designed by East German architects in the 1950s, Beijing's 798 Art Zone has grown from a cluster of underground studios into China's most influential contemporary art district.

subject: 826 Valencia
summary: A writing center for young people in San Francisco's Mission District, founded by Dave Eggers and disguised as a pirate supply store because zoning required a retail frontage.

subject: 9 O'Clock Gun
summary: A naval cannon cast at Woolwich in 1816 has been Vancouver's official time signal from Brockton Point for more than a century - and it has the ransom note, the paint job and the powder shortages to prove it.

subject: 9th Military Region (Brazil)
summary: In Campo Grande, a barracks more than 126 meters long still anchors a military presence that has shaped this city since the Brazilian army made it a frontier capital.

subject: A Symphony of Lights
summary: Every evening at 8 pm, the skyscrapers lining Victoria Harbour ignite in a coordinated display of lasers, searchlights, and LED colour — the world's largest permanent light and sound show, certified by Guinness World Records.

subject: A-Z West
summary: An 80-acre desert compound in Joshua Tree, California, where artist Andrea Zittel spent two decades turning daily life into art — and the weaving studio, ceramics workshop, and chicken coop into subject matter.

subject: A. J. Meerwald
summary: New Jersey's official tall ship - a 1928 gaff-rigged oyster schooner that dredged, smuggled, and now teaches schoolchildren about the Delaware Bay.

subject: A. Lange & Söhne
summary: A Dresden watchmaker talked the Saxon government into funding a watch industry in a played-out mining valley, and Glashütte has been making movements ever since — through nationalisation, forty-two years of erasure, and a re-founding staged on the exact anniversary of the first.

subject: A. P. Carter Homeplace
summary: The half-dovetailed log cabin where A.P. Carter was born in 1891 - now relocated to stand beside the Carter Family Fold.

subject: A12 blockade
summary: The protest is simple - sit down on a section of highway in The Hague and do not move. The argument behind it has split the Netherlands.

subject: A31 motorway (Netherlands)
summary: A short Frisian motorway whose stop-start lanes tell the story of a region the Dutch state never quite committed to connecting.

subject: A4 motorway (Netherlands)
summary: A 119-kilometer ribbon of Dutch motorway that took eighty years to finish - and still has gaps.

subject: ACE Basin
summary: Three rivers, 350,000 acres of untouched Lowcountry, and a thirty-year conservation effort that saved one of the Atlantic Coast's largest undeveloped estuaries from disappearing under asphalt.

subject: ACX1 Studios
summary: An Atlantic City pier built in 1906 for a million dollars, reinvented as a 1980s ocean liner mall, a 2010s ghost mall, and finally a 2023 film studio betting on the Hollywood of the East.

subject: AFC Ajax
summary: How a club in Amsterdam reinvented football twice - once with Cruyff and total football in the 1970s, once with a youth academy that gave the world a generation in 1995.

subject: AFL Grand Final
summary: On the last Saturday of September, more than a hundred thousand people fill the Melbourne Cricket Ground for the single biggest day in Australian sport, the match that decides the football premiership.

subject: AMD
summary: The scrappy Silicon Valley chipmaker that spent decades as Intel's underdog before its processors powered the world's fastest supercomputers and transformed the AI revolution.

subject: AMORC
summary: The Ancient and Mystical Order Rosae Crucis, a Rosicrucian organization headquartered in San Jose since 1927, whose Egyptian Museum and park campus create one of the city's most unexpected landmarks.

subject: AVUS
summary: Widely regarded as the world's first road built for cars alone — a toll route through the Grunewald that doubled as a race track for seventy-seven years, complete with a 43-degree brick banking that had nothing at the top of it.

subject: Aalborg
summary: Denmark's fourth city grew up at the one place where the Limfjord pinches narrow enough to cross — and has spent thirteen centuries making a living from that fact.

subject: Aalto Centre, Seinäjoki
summary: Six buildings by Alvar Aalto that transformed a small Finnish city's civic core into one of the most complete modernist architectural ensembles in Scandinavia.

subject: Aarhus
summary: Denmark's second city grew from a Viking harbour called Aros into a young, student-heavy port that has spent two decades converting its container quays into a new district.

subject: Abadia de Goiás
summary: A small municipality on the edge of Goiânia became the permanent resting place for six thousand tonnes of waste from Brazil's worst radiological accident — and for the memory of the four people it killed.

subject: Abadiânia
summary: A highway town in Goiás that built its entire economy around one man's healing centre, and had to work out what it was after he was convicted of raping dozens of women.

subject: Abae
summary: The Phocian sanctuary of Abae housed one of the ancient world's most respected oracles of Apollo — consulted by Croesus of Lydia before his fateful war with Persia — and was burned by the army of Xerxes in 480 BCE, then burned again more than a century later, and eventually rebuilt by the Emperor Hadrian.

subject: Abaetetuba
summary: An island-laced city at the mouth of the Tocantins that carves the Amazon's lightest wood into the painted toys carried by pilgrims at Brazil's largest religious procession.

subject: Abandonment of Buffaloes in Brotas
summary: An anonymous tip in November 2021 led police to a farm outside Brotas where more than a thousand buffaloes had been left without pasture or water, in a case Brazilian animal-welfare groups came to describe as one of the worst in the country's history.

subject: Abasto de Buenos Aires
summary: For ninety years the great Art Deco hall on Avenida Corrientes fed Buenos Aires its fruit and vegetables - and gave tango its most beloved voice, the boy the city still calls the Songbird of the Abasto.

subject: Abbeyfeale
summary: A Limerick market town built around a medieval abbey that has all but vanished, holding fast to the memory of Father Casey, the priest who fought landlords for tenant farmers.

subject: Abbeyleix
summary: A Cistercian-named Laois town the Viscount picked up and moved to higher ground - and where the carpets on the Titanic were woven.

subject: Abbotsford, British Columbia
summary: British Columbia's largest city by area sits on a drained lakebed at the US border — and in 2021 and again in 2025, the lake came back.

subject: Abdul Sattar Edhi
summary: A man who owned two sets of clothes and lived in a room attached to his office built the world's largest private ambulance network and became the guardian of nearly 20,000 adopted children.

subject: AbeBooks
summary: Two couples in Victoria launched a website in 1996 listing the stock of exactly four bookstores; twelve years later Amazon bought it, and a single ornithology book on it sold for $191,000.

subject: Abel Tasman Coast Track
summary: New Zealand's most popular tramping track hugs 60 kilometres of golden-sand coastline through Abel Tasman National Park, where the tides dictate the schedule and a moss-lined natural waterslide waits at the end of a side trail.

subject: Aberaeron
summary: A whole Regency town invented from scratch by a single clergyman in 1807, painted in pastel candy colours, and now famous for honey ice cream made on the harbour where ships were once built.

subject: Aberarth
summary: A small Ceredigion village where Cistercian monks landed Bath Stone for an inland abbey, and where the only Viking hogsback stone in Wales is bolted to a churchyard wall.

subject: Abercych
summary: A tiny Pembrokeshire village in the Cuch valley with two chapels, two pubs, a care farm with two royal awards, and a river that in medieval Welsh legend was a doorway to the otherworld.

subject: Aberdaron
summary: The last village on the medieval pilgrim road to Bardsey - where R.S. Thomas was vicar for eleven years and pilgrims still wait for the weather to cross.

subject: Aberdeen
summary: Scotland's granite city gleams silver in the northern light, its grand Victorian architecture built on fishing and farming, then transformed by North Sea oil into Europe's offshore energy capital.

subject: Aberdeen Typhoon Shelters
summary: Two sheltered channels between Hong Kong Island and Ap Lei Chau where breakwaters carved out a refuge for fishing fleets — and where the Tanka boat-dwelling community made their floating home.

subject: Aberdeen, Hong Kong
summary: A fishing harbour on Hong Kong's southern shore where the Tanka boat-dwelling community gave the city its original name, and where sampans still weave between the hulls of junks.

subject: Aberdeenshire
summary: Scotland's granite north-east corner, where red sandstone cliffs meet a coastline farther north than Newfoundland and castles sprout from every glen.

subject: Aberdyfi
summary: A small Welsh seaside village at the mouth of the Dyfi estuary that built 45 ships in 40 years, gave its name to one of the most beloved Welsh songs, and where Jimmy Page wrote much of Led Zeppelin's third album in a nearby cottage with no electricity.

subject: Abereiddy
summary: A coastal hamlet on the wild north Pembrokeshire coast, Abereiddy is home to the Blue Lagoon - a flooded Victorian slate quarry whose 27-metre cliff platform hosts the Red Bull Cliff Diving World Series.

subject: Aberfan
summary: A village in the Taff Valley whose name became inseparable from the morning a colliery tip slid down the mountain and into a school full of children.

subject: Aberfeldy
summary: A Highland town on the River Tay where General Wade's most expensive bridge crosses, Robert Burns wandered the birch glens, and the nearby village of Dull markets itself to tourists alongside Boring, Oregon and Bland, New South Wales.

subject: Aberffraw
summary: For 800 years this small Anglesey village was the capital of the Kingdom of Gwynedd - the seat from which the medieval Princes of Wales ruled, until an English king demolished it for stone.

subject: Aberglaslyn Pass
summary: A narrow gorge where the Devil was once cheated of a human soul by a magician with a loaf of bread, and where a steam train now threads three tunnels through the rock.

subject: Abergwili
summary: A quiet Carmarthenshire village where the Bishops of St Davids lived for four centuries and where, in 1567, the first Welsh New Testament was finished.

subject: Aberlemno sculptured stones
summary: A collection of Pictish carved stones in an Angus village that may preserve the only contemporary depiction of one of Scotland's most decisive battles.

subject: Abermawr
summary: A storm-swept shingle beach in Pembrokeshire that, for a few decades, was the place where Britain first heard what North America had to say.

subject: Abernethy, Perth and Kinross
summary: A small Perthshire village whose Pictish past, Irish-style round tower, and Roman fort make it one of the most layered historical landscapes in Scotland.

subject: Abersoch
summary: A Llyn Peninsula fishing village turned premier yachting resort, now contending with second-home pressures that have priced out the families and closed the Welsh-language school.

subject: Abersoch Lifeboat Station
summary: More than 150 years of volunteer sea rescue on the southern Llyn Peninsula, run today out of a smart 1994 boathouse on the south side of Abersoch bay.

subject: Aberystwyth
summary: The unofficial capital of mid-Wales — a university town and seaside resort on Cardigan Bay that holds the National Library of Wales, Wales's first English-language university, and a 130-year-old funicular railway up its northern headland.

subject: Aberystwyth Lifeboat Station
summary: A Welsh lifeboat station, working continuously since 1843, that in 1964 became the first RNLI station in the country to switch from offshore lifeboats to inshore lifeboats only — a quiet revolution in coastal rescue.

subject: Abidjan
summary: West Africa's second-largest city, where the ghosts of colonial grandeur haunt modernist towers along the Ebrie Lagoon and the midnight curfew reminds visitors that peace here remains a work in progress.

subject: Abingdon-on-Thames
summary: An Iron Age oppidum, an abbey founded around 676, the MG sports car factory, and the rock band Radiohead — Abingdon-on-Thames claims to be the oldest continuously occupied town in England, and throws thousands of buns from its rooftop to prove it.

subject: Abiquiu
summary: The red-rock country that captivated Georgia O'Keeffe - a tiny New Mexico village where painted desert cliffs rise from the Rio Chama valley, and one of America's greatest artists found her spiritual home.

subject: Abisko and Björkliden
summary: A tiny Arctic village where the northern lights are so reliable that a sky station was built on a mountaintop to watch them, and where three of Europe's great long-distance trails converge.

subject: Abitibi gold belt
summary: Stretching from Wawa, Ontario to Val-d'Or, Quebec, the Abitibi gold belt has produced over 170 million ounces of gold from more than 100 mines since 1901, making it one of the richest mineral districts on the planet.

subject: Abkhazia
summary: A subtropical Black Sea paradise caught between empires, where snow-capped Caucasus peaks meet palm-lined beaches in a territory recognized by almost no one but visited by millions.

subject: Aboriginal Shire of Hope Vale
summary: The Guugu Yimithirr community north of Cooktown - whose language gave the world the word 'kangaroo,' who were torn from their country during the war, and who came home to govern their own land.

subject: Aboriginal Shire of Kowanyama
summary: On the wetlands of the Mitchell River delta, an Aboriginal community whose name means 'place of many waters' has become one of the nation's leaders in taking back control of its own land and rivers.

subject: Aboriginal Shire of Mapoon
summary: In 1963 the Queensland government burned this community to the ground to clear the way for bauxite. The Tjungundji and their neighbours fought their way home — and Mapoon stands today because they refused to disappear.

subject: Aboriginal Shire of Pormpuraaw
summary: A Thaayorre and Wik-Mungkan community on the Gulf coast of Cape York, where artists weave the deadly fishing nets that wash up on their beaches into luminous sculptures of the sea creatures those nets kill.

subject: Abrau-Dyurso
summary: On the shore of a mysterious mountain lake near the Black Sea, a village built to pour sparkling wine for the Tsar still fizzes with the bubbles French winemakers taught it to make.

subject: Abric Romaní
summary: A rock shelter near Capellades where mineral-rich water turned Neanderthal wooden tools to stone, preserving a record of their craft found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Abu 'Arish
summary: A city in southwestern Saudi Arabia that began as a medieval teaching post under a makeshift wooden pergola, flourished on the old pilgrim route, and now serves as a transportation hub in Jizan Province.

subject: Abu Dhabi
summary: The UAE's federal capital rises from Persian Gulf islands like a fever dream of marble mosques, Formula 1 circuits, and world-class museums, where the desert meets unlimited ambition.

subject: Abu Simbel
summary: A traveler's guide to the temples saved from drowning and reassembled inside an artificial mountain.

subject: Abu Simbel
summary: The colossal temples of Ramses II, sawed into numbered blocks and moved sixty meters uphill to save them from a rising reservoir.

subject: Abu Simbel (village)
summary: A village of 2,600 people built from scratch in the 1960s to serve a relocated temple and the tourism that now sustains it.

subject: Abu Simbel Phoenician graffiti
summary: Two and a half thousand years ago, Phoenician sailors stopped at Ramses's colossal statues and carved their names into the stone.

subject: Abujhmarh
summary: A 4,000-square-kilometer wilderness in Chhattisgarh, larger than Goa, where tribal communities and Maoist insurgents coexist in one of India's most inaccessible landscapes.

subject: Abushneib
summary: A Gezira farming town where the canals, the trucks, and the tomb of Sheikh al-Tayyib have shaped everyday life for nearly a century.

subject: Abydos, Egypt
summary: At the desert's edge above the Nile, Abydos held the tombs of Egypt's first kings and became the holy ground where pilgrims sought Osiris, lord of resurrection.

subject: Abyei
summary: A 10,546-square-kilometer area on the Sudan-South Sudan border that belongs simultaneously to both nations and neither - where Ngok Dinka farmers and Misseriya nomads have shared land for centuries while governments fight over the oil beneath it.

subject: Acacus Mountains
summary: In the most arid corner of the Sahara, the painted walls of the Tadrart Acacus remember a Libya of rivers, giraffes, and herders - a green world that the sand swallowed whole.

subject: Academy of Fine Arts Vienna
summary: One of Europe's oldest art schools, the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna has shaped centuries of artistic talent -- and is forever linked to its most infamous rejection letter.

subject: Academy of Light
summary: Sunderland AFC's UEFA five-star training ground sits on 220 acres of contested green belt north of the city - a facility that took two public inquiries, a Sven-Goran Eriksson ceremony, and a decade of legal wrangling to complete.

story.title: Academy of Music (Atlantic City, New Jersey)

subject: Academy of Music (Atlantic City, New Jersey)
summary: A theater built and rebuilt three times by the salt water taffy king of Atlantic City, with each successive building destroyed by a different boardwalk fire.

story.title: Acadia: Where America Sees the First Sunrise

subject: Acadia
summary: The Maine park where Cadillac Mountain catches the first rays of sun to touch the United States - where rocky coastline meets the Atlantic, where Rockefeller's carriage roads wind through forest, and where the rugged beauty that summer 'rusticators' discovered became the first national park east of the Mississippi.

subject: Acadiana
summary: The sprawling Cajun Country of southwest Louisiana, where French-speaking exiles from Nova Scotia built a culture of boudin, zydeco, and crawfish boils unlike anything else in America.

subject: Acapulco
summary: Mexico's original resort town where galleons once sailed from Manila and cliff divers still plunge into the Pacific, Acapulco remains a sun-drenched testament to glamour, grit, and the enduring pull of its legendary bay.

subject: Acarnania
summary: Greece's westernmost ancient region — rugged, lake-threaded, perpetually embattled — whose slingers, mountaineers, and stubborn league outlasted every empire that tried to absorb them.

subject: Access to Medicine Index
summary: An Amsterdam nonprofit ranks the world's twenty largest pharmaceutical companies by what they actually do for the poorest patients - a quiet idea that turned shame into spreadsheets.

subject: Accomack County, Virginia
summary: The largest Virginia county by total area and the easternmost, Accomack covers more water than land — and carries the most towns of any county in the Commonwealth, fourteen of them.

subject: Accompong
summary: A Maroon village in Jamaica's Cockpit Country that won its autonomy from the British in 1739 and has governed itself ever since.

subject: Accra
summary: Where Ghana's capital grows along the Gulf of Guinea, where slave castles remember Africa's wounds, where independence began and the diaspora returns.

subject: Aceh Sultanate
summary: For two centuries, the kingdom at the northern tip of Sumatra controlled the pepper trade, challenged Portuguese warships, and earned the title 'Porch of Mecca' -- before a brutal Dutch war ground it into submission.

subject: Acehnese language
summary: Spoken by millions on the northern tip of Sumatra, Acehnese is a linguistic survivor whose 'funny nasals,' split ergativity, and three tiers of politeness encode centuries of trade, war, and fierce independence.

subject: Achaea
summary: Modern Achaea, the regional unit around Patras in the northwestern Peloponnese, is where the Peloponnese meets the mainland across the Rio–Antirrio Bridge — a region of dramatic mountains, ancient history, and Greece's third-largest city.

subject: Achaea (Ancient Region)
summary: Ancient Achaea was the mountainous coastal strip along the northern Peloponnese whose twelve cities formed the celebrated Achaean League — a political confederation that was part of the Greek world for centuries before Rome absorbed it in 146 BC.

subject: Achaia (Roman province)
summary: When Rome conquered Greece in 146 BC, it inherited a civilisation it could not master — so captive Greece captured its conquerors instead, turning the province of Achaia into the cultural heartland of the empire's eastern half.

subject: Achaia Clauss
summary: A Bavarian merchant came to Patras for the blackcurrant trade, planted a few vines as a hobby, and built a winery that would outlast empires — Achaia Clauss, founded in 1861, and still pouring its celebrated Mavrodaphne dessert wine from the hillside above the Gulf of Corinth.

subject: Acharnae
summary: The largest deme of ancient Attica, whose charcoal-burners supplied Athens with fuel and whose stubborn fury Aristophanes turned into comedy.

subject: Acheron
summary: The Acheron is a real river in northwestern Greece — cold, clear, and turquoise — that the ancient Greeks believed was the threshold between the living and the dead, the water across which Charon ferried souls into the underworld.

subject: Achilles '29
summary: A village football club from the Dutch-German border climbed all the way to professional football, then fell from the second tier to the seventh in just six years.

subject: Achnacarry
summary: The seat of Clan Cameron on an isthmus between two lochs, burned by the Duke of Cumberland after Culloden, host to the Commando Basic Training Centre in the Second World War, and signatory of a 1928 oil cartel agreement.

subject: Achterhoek
summary: The Dutch region whose name literally means 'back corner', where bike paths thread between castles, peat bogs, and the slow rhythm of a dialect outsiders barely understand.

subject: Aclare
summary: A Sligo village on a tributary of the River Moy, in the shadow of the ruined Belclare Castle - site of a battle in 1512 between two of the great Gaelic Irish clans - and birthplace of the singer Tommy Fleming.

subject: Acle
summary: A Norfolk market town whose name means 'clearing in the oaks' - oaks that built Elizabeth I's warships and left the village to tell the story.

subject: Acoma Pueblo
summary: Perched atop a sandstone mesa for over 2,000 years, Acoma Pueblo is one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in North America, a sky city whose people turned sheer cliffs into an impenetrable fortress.

subject: Aconcagua
summary: At 6,961 meters, Aconcagua is the highest peak in the Americas and one of the deadliest, a former volcano thrust skyward that the Inca held sacred and modern climbers still underestimate at their peril.

subject: Acraman Impact Structure
summary: A faint ring of salt and rock in the Gawler Ranges marks where an asteroid struck South Australia some 580 million years ago, scattering debris that still lies in the Flinders Ranges 300 kilometres away.

subject: Acronicta rumicis
summary: The knot grass moth - a Linnaeus-described, hedgerow-loving night-flier whose wing colour darkened with the soot of Europe's industrial revolution and is now slowly turning grey again as the air clears.

subject: Action of 18 June 1793
summary: A dawn frigate duel off Start Point gave Britain the first major French warship captured in the Revolutionary Wars - and made Edward Pellew a national hero.

subject: Action of 18 November 1809
summary: A Napoleonic-era naval clash in the Bay of Bengal where a lone East Indiaman captain charged a French frigate -- only to be abandoned by his own convoy, hunted for five days, and then asked to save his captor's ship from a cyclone.

subject: Active Pass
summary: A 5.5-kilometre dog-leg between two Gulf Islands, so narrow that full-size ferries pass within shouting distance of the shore, and so busy that its accidents have their own dates.

subject: Ad's Path
summary: A 25-kilometer loop through the beech forests south of Leuven, scattered with sculptures by the artist whose construction-site fall sent him in search of a second life.

subject: Adam's Peak
summary: A conical sacred mountain in central Sri Lanka where Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and Christians have climbed for centuries to venerate a mysterious footprint near the summit, each faith claiming it as their own.

subject: Adamantina Formation
summary: The red sandstones of western Sao Paulo hold one of the richest records of Late Cretaceous life in Gondwana - dinosaurs, strange armored crocodiles, and a vanished world.

subject: Adamawa Wars
summary: Between 1899 and 1907, Germany's colonial army fought its way across the Adamawa Plateau, toppling Fulani emirates and Mahdist movements alike to extend Kamerun from the Atlantic to the shores of Lake Chad.

subject: Adams Morgan
summary: A Washington neighborhood named for two elementary schools - one Black, one white - that merged after desegregation in 1955. Birthplace of Toys R Us, the D.C. hardcore scene, and the jumbo slice.

subject: Adams Morgan and Columbia Heights
summary: Named for two formerly segregated elementary schools that were forced to merge, Adams Morgan stretches between Florida Avenue and Columbia Road - the loudest, jumbo-slice-eating, most genuinely cosmopolitan corner of Washington, where Salvadoran pupuserias share blocks with Ethiopian coffee houses.

subject: Adana
summary: Eight thousand years of civilization converge in Turkey's fourth-largest city, where a Roman bridge still spans the Seyhan River and the local kebab has conquered the world.

subject: Adare
summary: Ireland's prettiest village prepares to host golf's greatest rivalry, where thatched cottages line the main street, medieval friaries crumble picturesquely in the manor grounds, and traffic congestion threatens to overwhelm the pastoral charm.

subject: Addis Ababa
summary: Founded in 1886 by a king and queen who looked down from a mountain and chose a spot for a new capital, Addis Ababa grew into Africa's diplomatic hub, hosting the African Union and more than 120 international missions while keeping its identity as a city where injera, coffee, and centuries of layered history shape daily life.

subject: Adega
summary: San Jose's first Michelin-starred restaurant, a Portuguese fine dining establishment in the Little Portugal neighborhood that earned its star in 2016, closed in 2023, and reopened under new ownership in 2024.

subject: Adelaide
summary: Australia's wine capital blends colonial grace, multicultural flavour, and a festival spirit that transforms its wide boulevards into stages for the world's second-largest fringe festival each March.

subject: Adelaide Fringe
summary: For one month each summer the world's second-largest fringe festival turns Adelaide's parks and laneways into a sprawling open-access carnival of more than 7,000 artists.

subject: Adelaide Oval
summary: One of the world's last hand-operated scoreboards still clatters above this parkland ground, where Don Bradman batted and Bodyline nearly sparked a riot.

subject: Aden
summary: Where Marco Polo witnessed the transfer of Eastern treasures and the British built an empire's coaling station, this ancient port city guards the entrance to the Red Sea.

subject: Aden Colony
summary: For 128 years, Britain held Aden as a strategic coaling station and military outpost -- a colony whose story encompasses imperial ambition, labor unrest, the displacement of an ancient Jewish community, and a messy retreat that left the region's fault lines deeper than ever.

subject: Adinkerke
summary: A small Belgian village three kilometres from the French border that quietly became Europe's tobacco capital, with more tobacconists per capita than anywhere on the continent.

subject: Adirondacks
summary: America's first protected wilderness - six million acres of lakes, peaks, and old-growth forest in upstate New York where Gilded Age tycoons built 'Great Camps,' two Winter Olympics played out, and the cure for tuberculosis was cold mountain air.

subject: Adkins Arboretum
summary: A 400-acre native garden tucked inside Tuckahoe State Park - five miles of paths through the indigenous plant communities of the Delmarva Peninsula.

subject: Administrative Zone 3 (Gambela)
summary: A former Ethiopian zone along the Sudan border where ninety-eight percent of inhabitants were Nuer, and where the rainy season transformed the grasslands into a seasonal sea.

subject: Admiraliteitslijnbaan, Amsterdam
summary: The Amsterdam ropewalk that armed the Dutch fleet, hosted a future tsar, and survived as a 500-meter ghost in the modern street grid of Oostenburg.

subject: Admiralty Inlet
summary: The six-kilometer-wide strait that serves as Puget Sound's front door, where Spanish explorers, British admirals, and six-knot tidal currents have shaped two centuries of Pacific Northwest history.

subject: Adobe Inc.
summary: The San Jose software giant that gave the world Photoshop, PDF, and the creative tools that define digital media, named after a creek that ran behind its founders' Los Altos home.

subject: Adolfström
summary: A Lapland village built to smelt silver, burned in a suspected arson, abandoned for decades, and restarted in 1840 by one family - now a lifeline on the loneliest stretch of the King's Trail.

story.title: Adonara: The Five Shores and the Feuding Brothers

subject: Adonara
summary: An Indonesian island where coastal Muslims and mountain Catholics divided the landscape into rival halves, forged alliances with competing European empires, and maintained a dynasty of rajas whose line stretches back to the 1600s.

subject: Adramyttium
summary: For more than fifteen centuries, the ancient city of Adramyttium changed hands between empires — Persian, Macedonian, Roman, Byzantine, Crusader, Nicaean — and still the place endured, until it simply picked itself up and moved thirteen kilometres down the road.

subject: Adrar Region
summary: A Mauritanian region the size of a small country, home to around seventy thousand people, four caravan cities, and a way of life upended by drought.

subject: Adrar, Algeria
summary: The red-earth capital of the Touat oasis country, where caravans once unloaded gold and salt and an ancient network of underground water channels still keeps the date palms alive.

subject: Adria Downs
summary: A family cattle station the size of a small country, holding the towering Big Red dune and a river that floods 20 kilometres wide but runs only ankle-deep.

subject: Adrigole
summary: A Beara Peninsula village at the foot of the Healy Pass, remembered in a 1929 play about a family that starved to death long after the Famine was supposed to have ended.

subject: Adulis
summary: On Eritrea's Red Sea coast, the ruins of Adulis preserve an African port city that connected Aksum to the Mediterranean for a thousand years, trading ivory and war elephants with pharaohs, Ptolemies, and emperors.

subject: Advanced Light Source
summary: Inside a 1930s dome built for a Nobel Prize-winning cyclotron, electrons circle a storage ring 1.4 million times per second, producing some of the brightest beams of ultraviolet and soft X-ray light on Earth for 2,000 researchers a year.

subject: Adventure Way
summary: An 1,152-kilometre touring route that carries travellers from Brisbane to the far south-western corner of Queensland and on to the South Australian border, where the bitumen runs out and the desert begins.

subject: Aeron Express
summary: A hand-cranked aerial cable car that once shuttled workers across Aberaeron's harbour, vanished in 1994 to satisfy health-and-safety officials, and refuses to be forgotten by the town.

subject: Aerospace Walk of Honor
summary: On Lancaster Boulevard, granite monuments honor the test pilots who flew the experimental aircraft of Edwards AFB — Neil Armstrong, Jimmy Doolittle, Jacqueline Cochran among them — in a walk that ran from 1990 to 2009 before quietly concluding.

subject: Aetolia
summary: Ancient Aetolia — the rugged, mountainous region of western Greece above the Gulf of Corinth — was home to warrior tribes ancient historians called semi-barbaric, yet it produced one of the most powerful confederacies in the Greek world and gave mythology its most famous boar hunt.

subject: Af Chapman (ship)
summary: A 19th-century sailing ship that circled the globe as a cargo vessel, trained Swedish naval cadets, and now serves as one of the world's most unique youth hostels.

subject: Afar triple junction
summary: Three tectonic plates meet in the Afar region at a unique ridge-ridge-ridge triple junction, where the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and East African rifts all tug Africa apart in different directions.

subject: Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman
summary: Five ancient water channel systems dating to AD 500, part of a 5,000-year-old irrigation tradition, still deliver water across Oman by gravity alone -- despite being deliberately bombed by the British in 1957.

subject: Afon Marlais, Pembrokeshire
summary: A small Pembrokeshire river whose Welsh name promises a stagnant stream - but which has been carrying angular grains of gold through the Vale of Lampeter for centuries.

subject: Afonso Gonçalves Baldaia
summary: A royal cup-bearer with no sailing experience pushed a small ship past the edge of the known world and named a barren inlet the River of Gold.

subject: Africa (Roman province)
summary: Rome's North African breadbasket stretched from Tunisia through Algeria to the Libyan coast, feeding the empire for eight months of every year and producing a civilization that lasted eight centuries.

subject: Afrika Festival Hertme
summary: A village of 500 in the eastern Netherlands has spent over three decades hosting one of Europe's best world music festivals, run by 400 volunteers.

subject: Afrikanisches Viertel
summary: A working-class Berlin neighbourhood laid out as a map of the German colonial empire — where, in December 2022, a street named for Adolf Lüderitz was renamed for a man who died in a concentration camp in the town that bears Lüderitz's name.

subject: Afsluitdijk
summary: A 32-kilometre wall of clay and basalt that ended the existence of an entire sea - and turned the Netherlands' deadliest neighbour into a freshwater lake.

subject: After the Navy Left
summary: For most of the twentieth century, the Naval Training Center occupied 361 acres of San Diego's Point Loma peninsula, turning generations of American sailors into the Navy's enlisted force.

subject: Afterburn
summary: Six inversions, 62 miles per hour, and a name that survived a corporate divorce - Carowinds' inverted coaster keeps its Top Gun pedigree under a quieter title.

subject: Afterglow Vista
summary: A lime baron built his family a stone dinner table in the woods above Roche Harbor, seated them around it in limestone chairs holding their own ashes, and left one column deliberately broken.

subject: Aftermath Clubhouse
summary: A women's reading circle in a raw Washington port town raised its own money, bought its own land, and built what is believed to be the first women's clubhouse in the state.

subject: Agats
summary: A town built on stilts above a tidal swamp, where every road is a wooden walkway and the tide reaches five meters above the sea.

subject: Agbekoya
summary: In 1968, Yoruba cocoa farmers near Ibadan rose up against corrupt tax collectors and broken government promises, winning a revolt that remains the most celebrated example of peasant collective action in western Nigerian history.

subject: Agbokim Waterfalls
summary: Seven separate streams plunge off a single cliff near the Nigeria-Cameroon border, creating a seven-part cascade hidden in tropical rainforest that was discovered by a hunter in the early 1900s.

subject: Aggersborg
summary: Denmark's largest Viking ring fortress swallowed a village, consumed five thousand oak trees, and stood empty within a generation.

subject: Aghaboe
summary: A small Laois village where a sixth-century saint, a Norman tower, and a Dominican ruin share a single quiet field west of Abbeyleix.

subject: Aghada
summary: A quiet civil parish on the eastern shore of Cork Harbour, where a Victoria Cross recipient is buried, an American naval air station once operated, and the local women's football team won the county title.

subject: Agia Anna (Evvia)
summary: Seven kilometers of sand, a watchtower hidden in the bushes, and a horizon scattered with islands - the traveler's Agia Anna, on the wild green north coast of Evvia.

subject: Agia Anna, Euboea
summary: A northern Euboean village born from a survived pirate raid and a vision of Saint Anne, whose winter population of a thousand swells sevenfold under the summer sun.

subject: Agia Paraskevi
summary: A northeastern Athens suburb where Greece's only nuclear reactor once operated beside the country's oldest American college, on a mountainside locals once defended from bulldozers.

subject: Agia Paraskevi, Lesbos
summary: An inland village above Kalloni Bay nicknamed the Little Paris of the Aegean for its mansions and agora, home to the Bull Festival, an ox-sacrifice whose roots reach back to ancient Greece.

subject: Agios Andreas, Katakolo
summary: A small coastal settlement near Katakolo that sits on the ruins of ancient Pheia — a Homeric port city swallowed by the sea in a 6th-century earthquake, later rebuilt as a Frankish castle called Beauvoir.

subject: Agios Dimitrios
summary: Once an Ottoman pasha's estate called Brahami, this southern Athenian suburb reinvented itself in the 20th century — trading its agricultural roots for metro lines and neighborhood sports clubs.

subject: Agios Georgios Nileias
summary: A Pelion village said to have been founded by shepherds who found a holy icon in a bush, scattered across the mountain by the rhythm of the seasons.

subject: Agios Ioannis Renti
summary: Wedged between Athens and Piraeus along the ancient Cephissus river, this industrial suburb hosts Greece's largest food market, the Athens School of Fine Arts, and the training ground of Olympiacos — an unlikely combination that captures the layered character of the Greek capital's western edge.

subject: Agios Isidoros, Lesbos
summary: A village two kilometers from the ouzo town of Plomari, fronted by one of the longest pebble beaches on Lesbos and a strip of clear Aegean water that keeps earning its Blue Flag.

subject: Agios Kirykos
summary: The capital and southern port of Ikaria, named for a three-year-old martyr, where storm-battered winters give way to summers beside some of the most radioactive healing springs on Earth.

subject: Agios Panteleimonas, Athens
summary: A central Athens neighborhood built around one of the Balkans' largest churches, and a place where the strains of a changing city became sharply, painfully visible.

subject: Agios Sostis
summary: A small Arcadian border village where a church built on Byzantine monastery ruins became a gathering point for the whole region — founded, legend says, after a vision led to the discovery of 60 monastic cells beneath the earth.

subject: Agios Stefanos, Attica
summary: A high northern suburb in the Attic hills where the river Kifisos is born, an Arvanite town now crowned by a 210-metre radio mast.

subject: Agios Thomas Tanagras
summary: A walkable Boeotian olive village where the sights are chapels, caves, and an ancient necropolis - and the only way to stay overnight is to leave.

subject: Agios Thomas, Boeotia
summary: A Boeotian olive village built where Byzantine farmers once worshipped beside ancient Tanagra, renamed three times, and declared a martyr village in 2020.

story.title: Agios Vasileios — Mycenaean Palace of Laconia

subject: Agios Vasileios
summary: A Linear B tablet found by accident on a hillside near Sparta in 2008 led to excavations that have uncovered a major Mycenaean palatial complex at Agios Vasileios — the first palace-level site discovered in Laconia, rewriting what we know about Bronze Age power in the region.

subject: Agios Vasileios, Corinthia
summary: A small Greek village in the Chouni Pass that has served as a crossroads, fortress, and frontier since the Bronze Age.

subject: Agistri
summary: A small pine-clad hook of an island just west of Aegina in the Saronic Gulf, named for the fishing hook shape that frames its quiet beaches, feral peacocks, and Arvanite heritage.

story.title: Agnes Chow: Arrest Under the National Security Law

subject: Agnes Chow
summary: On 10 August 2020, Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Agnes Chow was arrested under the newly enacted National Security Law — one of a wave of arrests that drew condemnation from governments and citizens across Asia and beyond.

subject: Agnew Gold Mine
summary: A northern Goldfields gold mine where six men once drowned underground in a desert flash flood - and which now draws much of its power from one of Australia's largest renewable microgrids.

story.title: Agon Shu: The Fire Festival on the Mountain

subject: Agon Shu
summary: A Japanese new religion headquartered in Kyoto's Yamashina district, founded by a man who nearly took his own life in jail, now known for its massive Hoshi Matsuri fire festival where twin pyres consume millions of prayer sticks in flames visible across the city.

subject: Agop Batu Tulug Caves
summary: Limestone caves in Sabah's Kinabatangan district where 125 carved wooden coffins, some shaped like crocodiles and birds, have rested for up to 900 years.

subject: Agost
summary: An inland Alicante town that makes more clay water jugs than anywhere in Spain, where porous earthenware keeps water cold without a scrap of ice.

subject: Agounit
summary: A small desert settlement deep in the Polisario-controlled Free Zone of Western Sahara, Agounit holds a hospital, a school, and a quiet claim to statehood in disputed land.

subject: Agra
summary: Where the Taj Mahal stands as love's monument in white marble, where Mughal emperors ruled India from red sandstone forts, where one building eclipses the city that holds it.

subject: Agria
summary: A Pelion port town that once called itself the largest in the world for olives, and gave the world the composer who scored Chariots of Fire.

subject: Agrinio
summary: Agrinio, the largest city of Aetolia-Acarnania in western Greece, has reinvented itself repeatedly across three millennia — as an ancient Aetolian town, an Ottoman administrative hub, a city citizens burned rather than surrender, and the tobacco capital of modern Greece.

subject: Agrour Amogjar
summary: On a rocky peak near Mauritania's Amogjar Pass, small shelters hold thousands of years of painted memory: cattle, dancers, giraffes, and a vanished green Sahara.

story.title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians

subject: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians
summary: The Cahuilla people who named these hot springs 'agua caliente' have lived in the Coachella Valley for over 7,000 years, and their checkerboard reservation now underlies some of Palm Springs' most valuable real estate.

subject: Agua Hedionda Lagoon
summary: The Spanish named it 'stinking water,' and for most of the twentieth century an industrial dredging cycle was the only thing keeping the coastal lagoon between Carlsbad and the Pacific from silting shut.

story.title: Aguateca: The Maya Pompeii on the Cliff's Edge

subject: Aguateca
summary: Perched atop a 90-meter limestone bluff overlooking Guatemala's Petexbatun Lagoon, Aguateca was a fortified Maya capital that fell so suddenly around 830 CE that its residents left tools, ceramics, and valuables scattered on the floors - a frozen moment of daily life that archaeologists call the Maya Pompeii.

subject: Ahafo mine
summary: One of the largest gold mines in Ghana, where billions of dollars in extracted wealth have collided with displacement, pollution, and a community of subsistence farmers fighting for their land.

subject: Ahakista
summary: A wooded coastal village on the Sheep's Head peninsula whose sundial garden marks the morning a bomb killed 329 people in the Atlantic sky above.

subject: Ahascragh
summary: A village of 186 in east Galway that produced an English baronet's estate, an Irish saint, a hat-maker to the world, and two future Tánaistí.

subject: Ahenny
summary: A tiny Tipperary village whose 8th-century stone high crosses are believed to be among the oldest in Ireland -- carved to imitate wooden crosses they remember.

subject: Ahmadnagar Sultanate
summary: Founded by a falconer's son who defeated three armies and declared independence in 1490, the Ahmadnagar Sultanate endured for 146 years as a Deccan power whose architecture and painting rivaled the great Persianate cities.

subject: Ahmed Baba Institute
