summary: Timbuktu's modern home for tens of thousands of medieval manuscripts, named for the city's greatest scholar and tested by fire in 2013.

subject: Ahoghill
summary: A small County Antrim town named for a vanished yew forest, where three Presbyterian churches face a Roman Catholic chapel across streets still shaped by the Troubles.

subject: Ahousaht First Nation
summary: The largest Nuu-chah-nulth nation, a confederation of seven peoples whose territory encompasses much of Clayoquot Sound, governed by hereditary chiefs with oral histories stretching back 17 or 18 generations.

subject: Ahrensburg
summary: A Hamburg commuter town with a white Renaissance water castle bought by Denmark's biggest slave trader - and a boggy valley on its edge that gave its name to the Ice Age reindeer hunters who left the earliest clear evidence of the bow and arrow.

subject: Ahvaz
summary: Split by Iran's mightiest river, Ahvaz is a city of oil wells, ancient scholarship, and extreme heat where Arab and Persian cultures have blended for millennia.

subject: Ai-Petri
summary: A Crimean summit whose height reads like a countdown and whose winds can flatten a standing person, crowning the coast above Alupka.

subject: Aigaleo
summary: A western Athens suburb on the mountain from which Xerxes watched his fleet destroyed at Salamis, later a powder-town of dangerous factories, refugees, and rebetiko nights.

subject: Aigeira
summary: Above the Gulf of Corinth on the northeastern Achaean coast, modern Aigeira sits near one of Greece's most continuously occupied sites — a settlement whose story stretches from Neolithic cheese-makers through Mycenaean warriors, Hellenistic theatregoers, and Roman traders, all the way to Austrian archaeologists who have been digging here since 1916.

subject: Aigosthena
summary: An ancient fortified port city at the foot of Mount Cithaeron on the Gulf of Corinth, whose spectacularly preserved Hellenistic walls and towers — some of the tallest surviving in Greece — guard a tiny modern beach village called Porto Germeno.

subject: Ailsa Craig
summary: A volcanic plug rising abruptly from the Firth of Clyde, Ailsa Craig is the world's primary source of curling-stone granite, a former refuge for persecuted Catholics, and a bird sanctuary whose puffins returned only after rats were eradicated in 1991.

subject: Ain Farah
summary: Perched 100 meters above a Darfur spring, a long-vanished sultan built a stone city on a ridge so steep it reminded travelers of eagles' nests.

subject: Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations
summary: The only port mortuary in the continental United States - where the remains of American war dead return home, and where scandals exposed how easily that sacred work can be mishandled.

subject: Ait Benhaddou
summary: Hollywood's favorite stand-in for ancient Jerusalem rises from the Moroccan desert, a mud-brick fortress city that has starred in more blockbusters than most actors while its few remaining residents carry on traditions unchanged for centuries.

subject: Aitoliko
summary: Built on an island in a lagoon near Messolonghi, Aitoliko — called 'the little Venice' — is an ancient island town surrounded by some of the richest fishing waters in Greece, a wetland world of wooden huts on stilts and 170 species of birds.

subject: Ajana
summary: A railhead built at the edge of a rabbit fence, where the wheat belt runs out and the long road to Kalbarri begins.

subject: Ajanta Caves
summary: Thirty Buddhist caves carved into a horseshoe-shaped gorge over seven centuries, then abandoned to the jungle for a thousand years until a British hunting party stumbled upon the greatest ancient picture gallery in the world.

subject: Ajax Youth Academy
summary: At a training complex called The Future, on the southeastern edge of Amsterdam, a single football method has produced more world-class players than almost any place on Earth.

subject: Ajuran Sultanate
summary: A medieval Somali empire that ruled the rivers themselves, the Ajuran built wells and dams across the Horn of Africa, traded with Ming China, and turned back the Portuguese fleets of the Age of Discovery.

subject: Akaa
summary: A Pirkanmaa town that was abolished in 1946 and reassembled in 2007, built on a railway junction, a vanished timber industry, and twenty million bees.

subject: Akal Takht
summary: The highest seat of Sikh temporal authority, the Akal Takht has been built, destroyed, and rebuilt across four centuries, embodying the faith's insistence that spiritual life and political sovereignty are inseparable.

story.title: Akatsuchiyama Kofun: The Keyhole in the Hills

subject: Akatsuchiyama Kofun
summary: A 110-meter keyhole-shaped burial mound in Nara Prefecture, believed to be the grave of a powerful Wani clan leader, where rows of clay sentinel figures still stand after sixteen centuries.

story.title: Akihabara: From Ashes to Electric Town

subject: Akihabara
summary: A Tokyo neighborhood born from a fire-prevention shrine became the world's most famous electronics bazaar, then reinvented itself again as the beating heart of otaku culture.

subject: Akjoujt
summary: Its name means 'wells', but this desert town in Mauritania has spent three thousand years digging for something harder to reach: the copper and gold beneath it.

subject: Akobo (woreda)
summary: The westernmost point of Ethiopia lies within a Nuer woreda where the name translates to I say - a swampy borderland where cattle, rivers, and the rainy season dictate every rhythm of life.

subject: Akra, Crimea
summary: A Greek city that once anchored ships and traded goods now lies beneath the waves of the Kerch Strait, its Classical streets preserved intact under the sea like a drowned time capsule.

story.title: Akron: The Rubber City That Lost Its Bounce

subject: Akron
summary: The Ohio city where tires were made for America - where Goodyear, Firestone, and Goodrich concentrated before the industry left, where LeBron James grew up, and where polymer science continues what rubber began.

story.title: Akron: The Rubber Capital That Bounced Back

subject: Akron
summary: The city where Goodyear, Firestone, General, and Goodrich made America roll on rubber, where the All-American Soap Box Derby still races down Derby Downs, and where LeBron James grew up shooting hoops in housing projects.

subject: Al Amarat, Khartoum
summary: Khartoum's first high-rise neighborhood laid out its streets in odd numbers, ran 1st through 61st, and never quite shed the name that meant simply: the Buildings.

subject: Al Nasla
summary: A remote mountain village in Ras Al Khaimah where 40 houses built by a Dubai ruler sit mostly empty except during Eid, when families return to a settlement that time has nearly abandoned.

subject: Al Naslaa
summary: A freestanding desert boulder split down the middle by a fissure so straight and clean it looks machine-cut, though the explanation is pure geology.

subject: Al Qadarif State
summary: Sudan's granary state of Al Qadarif feeds the country from 7.1 million hectares of rainfed sesame and sorghum - and now shelters the people displaced by the war that broke Sudan in 2023.

subject: Al-Baha
summary: A Saudi mountain city at 2,500 meters where juniper forests grow, fog rolls in from the Red Sea, and a 400-year-old marble village still glows at sunset.

subject: Al-Baha Province
summary: Saudi Arabia's smallest province hides forests in the clouds, terraced villages on cliff tops, and stone towers whose purpose still puzzles historians.

subject: Al-Balad, Jeddah
summary: Jeddah's historic heart - a UNESCO-listed quarter of coral-stone houses, carved roshan windows, and alleyways older than most of the modern kingdom.

subject: Al-Hallaniyah
summary: The largest of Oman's remote Khuriya Muriya Islands, where a tiny fishing community speaks an ancient language and a Portuguese shipwreck yielded the world's oldest known marine astrolabe.

subject: Al-Okhdood
summary: An ancient ruined town in southern Saudi Arabia where, in the 520s, a king burned the Christians of Najran in trenches - a massacre the Quran later named.

subject: Al-Ula
summary: A northwest Arabian oasis where seven thousand years of caravans, kingdoms, and carved sandstone meet beneath towering cliffs.

subject: Ala Kahakai National Historic Trail
summary: A 175-mile network of ancient Hawaiian coastal trails that once connected communities, fishponds, and temples along the Big Island's western shore.

subject: Alagoas
summary: Brazil's second-smallest state gave the republic its first two presidents, sheltered the country's greatest act of self-liberation, and still runs on sugarcane and the sea.

subject: Alamance County, North Carolina
summary: A Piedmont county named for the blue mud of Great Alamance Creek, host to a pre-Revolutionary battle, the Kirk-Holden War of Reconstruction, the textile boom that built Burlington, and the modern lynching of Wyatt Outlaw - a place where the long arc of Carolina history is still legible.

subject: Alamo Square, San Francisco
summary: The hilltop park whose view of Victorian 'Painted Ladies' against the downtown skyline is one of the most photographed scenes in San Francisco.

subject: Alamor
summary: A small highland town at the edge of Peru where the Puyango River becomes the Tumbes, Alamor holds the quiet rhythm of coffee harvests, cane rum, and saints' days.

subject: Alang Ship Breaking Yard
summary: On a 14-kilometer stretch of Gujarat's coast, the world's largest ship breaking yard dismantles supertankers and ocean liners by hand at the edge of the tide.

subject: Alaró
summary: A quiet Mallorcan wine town beneath a mountain-top fortress so well sited that armies broke against it for centuries — and where two defenders burned for their loyalty became folk heroes.

subject: Alausi
summary: The traveler's Alausí - a five-hour ride from Quito to reach the station for the Devil's Nose, where a tourist train zigzags down the steepest mountain descent of any railway in the world.

subject: Alausí
summary: Founded in 1534 on the lands of the Lausí people, this Ecuadorian highland town preserves its colonial streets, 18th-century churches, and a railway heritage built on the graves of Jamaican laborers.

subject: Alausí Canton
summary: A canton stretched across 1,288 square kilometers of Chimborazo Province, where altitude swings from 1,225 meters in Huigra to 3,340 at Achupallas and thirty mountain lakes wait in the páramo.

subject: Alaçatı
summary: Stone houses with lilac shutters, old windmills on the ridge, and steady Aegean wind: a Turkish town built by a vanished Greek community, now famous for windsurfing.

subject: Alban Square, Aberaeron
summary: A modest grass square in west Wales lined with Grade II* listed Regency townhouses, painted in unauthentic pastel colours that nobody plans to repaint.

subject: Albanian Riviera
summary: Europe's last undiscovered coastline - where turquoise coves hide beneath Ottoman castles, mountain villages overlook beaches Julius Caesar once walked, and Mediterranean beauty comes without Mediterranean prices.

story.title: Albany: Where the Erie Canal Changed America

subject: Albany
summary: New York's capital since 1797, where Dutch traders established a fur trading post in 1614, where the Erie Canal's eastern terminus transformed commerce, and where five centuries of architecture stand against the Hudson River.

subject: Albany Bulb
summary: A former landfill peninsula jutting into San Francisco Bay that became an anarchic commons of art, ecology, and homelessness before the city reclaimed it as parkland.

subject: Albany Mudflats Ecological Reserve
summary: A 160-acre stretch of tidal flats on the East Bay shoreline where thousands of migratory shorebirds refuel each winter, protected since 1982 as one of the San Francisco Bay's last intact intertidal ecosystems.

subject: Albemarle County, Virginia
summary: The Piedmont Virginia county that produced Thomas Jefferson, Meriwether Lewis, James Monroe, and Jack Jouett, and that until the Civil War was majority enslaved.

subject: Albemarle Sound
summary: A vast brackish estuary behind the Outer Banks where the first English settlements in Carolina rose - and where the fisheries have been collapsing for decades.

subject: Alberni Inlet
summary: A 54-kilometre fjord that cuts nearly through Vancouver Island, Alberni Inlet is a glacier's trench, a shipping channel, and a funnel that turns distant earthquakes into waves at Port Alberni's doorstep.

subject: Albert Goodwin
summary: A red-haired coal miner turned union firebrand whose death in the Vancouver Island bush in 1918 sparked Canada's first general strike and whose grave still draws mourners every year.

subject: Albert Square, Manchester
summary: When Prince Albert died of typhoid in 1861, Manchester wanted a memorial — and built an entire civic square around it, anchored by Alfred Waterhouse's Gothic town hall that has presided ever since.

subject: Albion, British Columbia
summary: A Fraser River neighbourhood whose train stop was won by one heavy man on a stormy night, and whose orchards and ferry have since given way to subdivisions.

story.title: Albuquerque: Where Hot Air Balloons Fill the October Sky

subject: Albuquerque
summary: The New Mexico metropolis at the crossroads of Route 66 and the Rio Grande - where the Balloon Fiesta attracts 500 balloons annually, where Breaking Bad filmed its meth empire, and where Spanish, Native, and Anglo cultures layer atop each other.

story.title: Albuquerque: The Duke City Where Balloons Fill October Skies

subject: Albuquerque
summary: The high desert city where 500 hot air balloons launch each October, where Route 66 runs through downtown, where Breaking Bad was filmed, and where Spanish colonial, Native, and Anglo cultures layer atop one another.

subject: Alcalà de Xivert
summary: An inland Valencian town crowned by a soaring church tower, where astronomers once gathered to watch a total eclipse and a Templar castle still guards the ridge.

story.title: Alcatraz: The Prison No One Could Escape

subject: Alcatraz
summary: The San Francisco Bay island that held America's most dangerous criminals for 29 years - where Al Capone and Machine Gun Kelly served time, where 36 men tried to escape and officially none succeeded, and where three disappeared in 1962 in a mystery still unsolved.

subject: Alcazaba of Mérida
summary: The first Muslim alcazaba ever built on the Iberian Peninsula, Merida's 9th-century fortress was constructed from the recycled stones of the Roman city it was meant to suppress.

subject: Alcoy
summary: An industrial mountain city where velvet-clad armies refight a 13th-century siege each spring, and where factory workers once invented a coffee liqueur to keep warm.

subject: Alcântara Space Center
summary: Brazil's equatorial launch base in Maranhão - a spaceport whose geographic advantage is inseparable from the painful history of the quilombola communities displaced to build it.

subject: Alcúdia
summary: A walled medieval town at Mallorca's northeastern tip, built on a failed Roman city and now flanked by a fourteen-kilometer beach.

subject: Aldeburgh
summary: A Suffolk coast town that built the flagship of the Virginia Company, inspired Britten's Peter Grimes, elected Britain's first female mayor, and is now slowly losing itself to the North Sea.

subject: Aldeburgh Festival
summary: An English classical music festival founded by Benjamin Britten and Peter Pears in 1948, centred on a converted Victorian malthouse on the Suffolk marshes.

subject: Aldercrest Sanatorium
summary: A tuberculosis sanatorium that served Snohomish County for 36 years before transforming into a brain injury facility and ultimately disappearing beneath a suburban housing development.

subject: Alderley Edge
summary: A wooded sandstone escarpment guards a Cheshire village where copper miners worked since the Bronze Age and a sleeping king is said to wait.

subject: Alderney Lifeboat Station
summary: From a battered breakwater on the northernmost inhabited Channel Island, a volunteer crew launches into some of Europe's most violent tidal water - and has been doing it, on and off, since 1869.

subject: Aldo Leopold Wilderness
summary: New Mexico's wildest wilderness honors the father of conservation while hiding the scars of Apache battles and forest fires in its rugged Black Range.

subject: Alexander L. Kielland (platform)
summary: A 6mm weld on a sonar bracket cracked, and 123 men died in the North Sea -- the worst offshore disaster in Norwegian history.

subject: Alexander Pantages
summary: A Greek runaway who dug the Panama Canal, survived the Klondike, built 84 theaters across North America, and was ultimately brought down by a scandal that may have been engineered by Joseph Kennedy.

subject: Alexander S. Onassis Foundation
summary: A grieving shipping magnate turned a father's loss into one of Europe's largest philanthropic engines, and its boldest mark is a glowing marble box on a busy Athens avenue.

story.title: Alexandria: George Washington's Hometown on the Potomac

subject: Alexandria
summary: The colonial port surveyed in 1749 where George Washington worshipped and Robert E. Lee grew up, where nearly 4,000 18th-century buildings line cobblestone streets, and where Old Town's brick sidewalks preserve Virginia's past just outside the nation's capital.

subject: Alexandria Carmania
summary: One of Alexander the Great's lost cities, founded in 324 BC where his army reunited after the desert crossing of Gedrosia, and still unlocated.

subject: Alexandria in Orietai
summary: One of seventy cities Alexander the Great founded or renamed during his conquests, this lost settlement in Balochistan was meant to control the spice trade between India and Kandahar -- but its exact location has never been found.

subject: Alexandria in the Caucasus
summary: An ancient city founded by Alexander the Great at a crossroads beneath the Hindu Kush, where Greek, Persian, and Indian civilizations collided and fused for centuries.

subject: Alexandrowka (Potsdam)
summary: Twelve Russian soldiers taken prisoner in 1812 never went home; a Prussian king built them a village of log houses north of Potsdam and gave each household a cow.

subject: Alexânia
summary: A Goiás town born from a 1957 land giveaway on the highway between Brasília and Goiânia, now known for its artisanal cachaça and weekend ranches.

subject: Alfenas
summary: A landlocked coffee city in southern Minas Gerais that calls itself the gateway to the sea — a sea that engineers made in 1963 and that changed everything about the place.

subject: Alfred Lämmerhirt
summary: A Harz-born engineer who helped dig the Gotthard Tunnel, founded a mining-machinery factory, and ended his career running an iron foundry in the small German town of Warstein.

subject: Alfred Nobel
summary: The Swedish inventor who created dynamite and left behind the world's most prestigious prizes was born in this Stockholm neighborhood, his legacy forever split between destruction and enlightenment.

subject: Alfred Wallis
summary: A St Ives marine stores dealer who never picked up a brush until his seventieth year, Alfred Wallis painted the vanished world of sail from memory onto torn cardboard, and accidentally helped invent British modernism.

subject: Alfsee
summary: A reservoir built to tame the flood-prone Hase that became Lower Saxony's unlikely sailing destination.

subject: Alhambra
summary: The last great palace of Islamic Spain, a fortress city on a hill above Granada where Nasrid rulers created some of the most refined architecture in human history.

subject: Alhambra Decree
summary: The 1492 edict signed in the Alhambra that expelled unconverted Jews from Spain, scattering the Sephardic diaspora across the Ottoman Empire, North Africa, and beyond.

subject: Alicante
summary: A Mediterranean port crowned by a castle on a white crag, where a Carthaginian general's fortress became a Roman town, a medieval trading city, and the capital of the Costa Blanca.

subject: Alice Springs
summary: Fifteen hundred kilometres from the nearest city in any direction, Alice Springs sits in the Red Centre of Australia -- an outback town of 25,000 where Arrernte culture stretches back 50,000 years and the Todd River almost never flows.

subject: Alice Springs
summary: Australia's most famous outback town, a settlement of around 28,000 in the geographic center of the continent where Arrernte culture, frontier history, and modern desert life converge.

subject: Alice Springs Telegraph Station
summary: The stone buildings beside a waterhole sacred to the Arrernte people mark the birthplace of European settlement in Central Australia -- a telegraph relay station built in 1872 that gave Alice Springs its name.

subject: Alimos
summary: On the shore where Thucydides was born, this seaside suburb of Athens has been reimagining itself for 2,500 years — from ancient fishing deme to Olympic venue to one of Greece's largest marinas.

subject: Alishan
summary: Taiwan's most-visited national park is a mountain range where 2,000-year-old cypress trees, a century-old narrow-gauge railway, and a sea of clouds at sunrise have made Alishan the island's most iconic highland destination.

subject: Alishan National Scenic Area
summary: At dawn, visitors ride a narrow-gauge train to the summit to watch the sun rise over Yushan and a sea of clouds -- a ritual that has made Alishan, alongside Taroko Gorge and Sun Moon Lake, one of Taiwan's three most iconic landscapes.

subject: Aliwal Shoal
summary: Five kilometers off the KwaZulu-Natal coast near Umkomaas, an ancient fossilized sand dune rises from the seafloor to create one of South Africa's premier dive sites -- a reef teeming with ragged tooth sharks, soft corals, and the rusting hulk of a Norwegian cargo ship.

story.title: Alkali Sink Ecological Reserve: Holding Ground for a Ghost

subject: Alkali Sink Ecological Reserve
summary: A 930-acre patch of salt-crusted earth near Fresno where the last known Fresno kangaroo rat was captured in 1992 - and where biologists still search for a species that may already be gone.

subject: All Together Now (festival)
summary: Each August Bank Holiday, an 18th-century estate in County Waterford transforms into Ireland's most ambitious boutique festival, mixing the Prodigy with poetry on a landscaped demesne.

subject: Alladale Wilderness Reserve
summary: A 23,000-acre highland estate in Sutherland where a furniture-industry heir is trying to bring back wolves and the forest Britain lost three centuries ago.

subject: Alleghany County, Virginia
summary: On Virginia's far western edge, where the Cowpasture meets the Jackson to form the James, a paperboard mill town anchors a county built first on rope, then on rail, and held together by the Allegheny ridge.

subject: Allegheny Front
summary: The geological wall that kept the American colonies hemmed against the Atlantic for a century, where no river crosses east to west and 132 wind turbines now line a single ridge.

subject: Allegheny Mountains
summary: A 300-mile run of quartzite ridges from Pennsylvania to West Virginia that once stopped westward travel cold and still makes its own weather.

subject: Allende meteorite
summary: At 1:05 AM on February 8, 1969, a car-sized rock from the birth of the Solar System exploded over the Chihuahuan desert, scattering over two tonnes of the oldest solid matter ever held in human hands.

subject: Allenheads
summary: A former lead-mining village 1,325 feet up in the North Pennines, now home to a hydraulic engine, a contemporary arts centre, and a dark-sky observatory.

story.title: Allentown: The Steel Town Billy Joel Made Famous

subject: Allentown
summary: The Pennsylvania city that became Billy Joel's metaphor for industrial decline - where Bethlehem Steel once employed 30,000, where the Lehigh Valley anchors economic recovery, and where the anthem of deindustrialization still plays.

subject: Allihies
summary: A copper-mining village at the western tip of the Beara Peninsula whose Cornish-built engine houses, abandoned in the 1880s, sent generations of Irish families to Butte, Montana.

subject: Alloway
summary: A former village turned suburb where ruined kirks glow green at night, where a national poet was born in a four-room cottage, and where a haunted bridge is also a real bridge.

subject: Alma (1891)
summary: Built in 1891, the scow schooner Alma is the last surviving vessel of the flat-bottomed workboat fleet that hauled hay, grain, and lumber across San Francisco Bay.

subject: Almenum
summary: The Frisian village that started a century-long blood feud over who got to give alms first - and was eventually swallowed by the city next door.

subject: Almere City FC
summary: A club whose first name meant 'The Black Sheep' - and which spent sixty-five years trying to make the label obsolete.

subject: Almere Haven
summary: When the first families moved into the oldest district of Almere in 1976, the planners had built canal houses inside the shopping mall to make them feel at home.

subject: Almere Poort
summary: The newest district of the Netherlands' newest city was never in the original plan: Almere Poort grew up between a beach and an Olympic-themed station, on streets named for Homer and Columbus.

subject: Almorada
summary: The Omdurman neighborhood whose name means "the Anchorage," where Mahdist sailboats once unloaded firewood and where Sudan's first woman physician grew up.

subject: Almyros
summary: A Thessalian farming town in a plain of tomatoes and almonds, heir to an ancient port and a medieval trading hub fought over by Sicilians, Venetians, and crusaders.

subject: Alness
summary: An Easter Ross town that reinvented its high street through flowers, won a Scottish championship for it, and sits in the shadow of two distilleries and a folly that mimics an Indian gatehouse.

subject: Alnmouth Lifeboat Station
summary: A Duke's experiment with a self-righting lifeboat in 1852 spawned a rescue station that saved fifteen lives before quietly closing in 1935.

subject: Alnwick
summary: A Northumberland market town built around the most besieged castle of the Wars of the Roses, the seat of the Percy family, and the stand-in for Hogwarts.

subject: Alodia
summary: A medieval Christian kingdom in central Sudan whose capital Soba prospered on Nile trade for nearly a thousand years before vanishing in the 16th century.

subject: Alonissos
summary: The least-touristed island in the Sporades, where the cleanest water in the Aegean laps against a hilltop village reached on foot up an hour of switchbacks.

subject: Alonnisos
summary: An Aegean island that lost its old name, its vineyards, and its hilltop capital in turn, yet rebuilt itself each time around the sea that defines it.

subject: Alotenango
summary: Nestled between two volcanoes in Guatemala's Sacatepequez department, Alotenango is an ancient town whose name means 'in the wall of the parrots,' where award-winning coffee and centuries of volcanic exploration define daily life.

subject: Alpha Ventus Offshore Wind Farm
summary: Germany's first offshore wind farm — twelve turbines in 30 metres of North Sea, built as a national experiment and run, briefly, at world-record efficiency.

subject: Alphen aan den Rijn
summary: A Dutch town whose name comes from Albaniana, a Roman fort on the empire's northern frontier that still lies buried beneath its city centre.

subject: Alpheus (deity)
summary: The Alpheus — greatest river of the western Peloponnese — was worshipped as a god and immortalized in myth as a hunter who pursued the nymph Arethusa beneath the sea from Greece to a sacred spring in Sicily.

subject: Alquezar
summary: A medieval village of 300 clinging to a limestone spur above the Rio Vero canyon in Aragon, where vultures nest on the cliffs and canyoners set out into the gorges of the Sierra de Guara.

subject: Alsace
summary: The wine road between two worlds - a strip of France that has been German four times, where half-timbered villages climb vineyard slopes beneath ruined castles, and the cuisine tastes like both countries invented it together.

subject: Alsdorf
summary: A former coal-mining town northeast of Aachen where the second-worst mining accident in German history took 271 lives, the last pit closed in 1992, and Continental now builds fuel tanks where the Anna mine once stood.

subject: Alston Moor
summary: England's highest civil parish, anchored by its highest market town - a remote North Pennines upland of lead mines, Quaker industry, and W. H. Auden's secret love.

subject: Alta Gracia
summary: A Córdoba hill town whose dry air healed a sick boy named Che, sheltered an exiled Spanish composer, and grew up around a 400-year-old Jesuit estancia.

subject: Altaelva
summary: The third-longest river in Finnmark carved one of Europe's largest canyons, hosts world-class Atlantic salmon, and sparked Norway's most consequential indigenous rights battle.

subject: Altamira, Para
summary: Brazil's largest municipality by area, where a highway, a dam and a decade of boom rearranged a Xingu river town and moved a quarter of its people away from the water.

subject: Altamont Free Concert
summary: The December 1969 concert that became rock music's darkest day, when a free Rolling Stones show devolved into chaos and violence in the California hills.

story.title: Altar de Sacrificios: Where Rivers Meet and Civilizations End

subject: Altar de Sacrificios
summary: Sitting on a small island at the confluence of the Pasion and Salinas Rivers in Guatemala's Peten department, Altar de Sacrificios was one of the earliest settlements in the Maya lowlands - predating Tikal - and one of the last to flicker out as strangers took over the dying trade routes.

subject: Altar of the Twelve Gods
summary: For ancient Athens this small marble enclosure was point zero - the spot from which every road's length was measured - and today almost all of it lies hidden beneath a working railway.

subject: Altavista (Zacatecas)
summary: The northernmost ceremonial center of ancient Mesoamerica, where Chalchihuites astronomers aligned their buildings to the summer solstice and controlled the turquoise trade from New Mexico to the Valley of Anahuac.

subject: Altea
summary: A few miles from Benidorm's skyscrapers, Altea kept its whitewashed old town, its blue-domed church and its artists, a Costa Blanca town that chose character over concrete.

subject: Alter do Chao, Para
summary: A Tapajos River village where the dry season uncovers white-sand freshwater beaches The Guardian once called the most beautiful in the world, and where a Catholic festival still argues the case for pink dolphins.

subject: Altes Rathaus (Bonn)
summary: A small pink Rococo town hall closes one end of Bonn's market square. From its gilded staircase, JFK, de Gaulle, and Gorbachev addressed the people of West Germany's capital.

subject: Alto Loa National Reserve
summary: Chile's largest natural reserve at 300,000 hectares, Alto Loa protects the source of the Loa River in the Atacama Desert, a landscape of salt flats, high-altitude wetlands, and wildlife negotiated into existence between mining companies and Quechua communities.

subject: Alto Maués Ecological Station
summary: Larger than the U.S. state of Delaware, this strictly protected ecological station between the Madeira and Tapajos rivers shelters 14 primate species, over 600 bird species, and jaguars in one of the Amazon's richest biological sanctuaries.

subject: Alto Paraíso de Goiás
summary: The 14th parallel crosses this high-plateau town, and something about the crossing draws dozens of mystical communities, hundreds of waterfalls, and a steady stream of travelers hunting the cerrado's edge.

subject: Alto Paraíso de Goiás
summary: A municipality founded as a 1750s cattle ranch in cerrado highlands, now an ecotourism hub for Chapada dos Veadeiros and home to a rural Esperanto school.

subject: Alton Downs Station
summary: A remote cattle run in the far northeast corner of South Australia, abandoned twice to drought and rabbits, where the Warburton River carries water all the way to Lake Eyre.

subject: Altona Bloody Sunday
summary: On 17 July 1932 an SA march through working-class Altona ended with eighteen dead - sixteen of them residents shot by police - and gave Franz von Papen his pretext to destroy the government of Prussia three days later.

subject: Altos de Lircay National Reserve
summary: An eleven-hour climb up the Lircay ends at a vast plateau of brick-shaped stones that has fueled UFO legends for decades.

subject: Alviso, San Jose
summary: San Jose's only waterfront district, a former independent town founded in 1852 that once served as the South Bay's primary port before railroads made its harbor obsolete and flooding made its streets a recurring challenge.

subject: Ama Site
summary: An ancient Yayoi settlement discovered beneath a Kyoto University farm in 1928, revealing the earliest evidence of rice cultivation in Japan's Kinai heartland -- a community that grew, flooded, shrank, and vanished over centuries.

subject: Amagasaki derailment
summary: A 2005 commuter train disaster in Hyogo Prefecture where a toxic workplace culture of punitive retraining pushed a young driver to fatal excess speed, killing 107 people and forcing Japan to confront the human cost of its railroad punctuality obsession.

subject: Amager Bakke
summary: A working incinerator that burns 400,000 tonnes of Copenhagen's rubbish a year, with three ski pistes, a hiking trail and the world's tallest climbing wall on its roof.

subject: Amaicha del Valle
summary: A Diaguita-Calchaquí community in Tucumán's high valleys that has held title to its ancestral land since a 1716 royal decree, and each February honors Mother Earth in one of Argentina's most enduring festivals.

subject: Amalfi Coast
summary: Vertical Italy - where pastel villages cling to cliffs above the Tyrrhenian Sea, lemon groves terrace impossible slopes, and a single winding road connects some of the Mediterranean's most dramatic scenery.

subject: Amaliapolis
summary: A seaside village that carries a queen's name and a frontier's memory, where Athenians vanish after August and the sea urchins keep the rocks honest.

subject: Amanã Sustainable Development Reserve
summary: Connecting the Mamirauá reserve to Jaú National Park, Amanã completes one of the largest contiguous tracts of protected rainforest on Earth.

subject: Amarna
summary: On a virgin stretch of desert by the Nile, the pharaoh Akhenaten built a brand-new capital for a brand-new god - a city of the sun that flourished for barely a generation before it was abandoned and erased.

subject: Amarynthos
summary: For over a century scholars hunted for a lost sanctuary of Artemis somewhere near this Euboean beach town. In 2017, the inscriptions finally gave it up.

subject: Amazon (Ecuador)
summary: The eastern third of Ecuador, spread across six provinces of lowland rainforest where canoe travel remains the most reliable road and jungle lodges are the only safe way for strangers to move through.

subject: Amazon Basin
summary: Seven million square kilometers of South America drained by one river system that once flowed the other way, fertilized by dust from the Sahara, and still holding more freshwater fish species than any other basin on Earth.

subject: Amazon biome
summary: Nine countries, 6.7 million square kilometers, and one of the densest concentrations of life on Earth - stitched together by rivers that carry 16 percent of the planet's freshwater.

subject: Amazonas (Brazil)
summary: Brazil's largest state by area, where 98 percent of the land remains tropical rainforest and most travel still happens by boat.

subject: Amazonas (Brazilian state)
summary: The ninth-largest country subdivision on Earth, named for warrior women a Spaniard claimed to have fought on a river in 1541.

subject: Ambalat
summary: A deep-sea oil block in the Celebes Sea where Indonesia and Malaysia have both awarded drilling rights to competing companies -- and where warships have nearly opened fire over who owns the seabed.

subject: Ambalavao
summary: A highland market town where thousands of zebu cattle change hands each week and paper has been pressed from tree bark with embedded flowers for centuries.

subject: Ambatovy mine
summary: Madagascar's largest mine and biggest-ever foreign investment, Ambatovy pulls nickel and cobalt from a lateritic deposit carved out of one of the island's richest rainforests, an experiment in whether a mine can offset what it destroys.

story.title: Ambelau: The Spice Island the Empire Forgot

subject: Ambelau
summary: A volcanic island in Indonesia's Banda Sea where wild pigs defeat rice farmers, seven villages cling to the coast, and four centuries of colonial neglect produced a community that outlasted every empire that claimed it.

subject: Amble
summary: A small Northumberland coal port at the mouth of the Coquet that exchanged friendly telegrams with the Mauretania and styled itself the kindliest port in England.

subject: Amble Lifeboat Station
summary: A lifeboat station at the mouth of the Coquet whose history runs through Victorian shipwreck associations, an upside-down RAF pinnace, and four medals won in a single dawn.

subject: Ambleside
summary: A small Cumbrian town at the head of England's largest natural lake, where Roman walls, Wordsworth's stamp office, and modern climbing shops sit within a few hundred yards of each other.

subject: Ambleston
summary: A bilingual Pembrokeshire village named after a Norman-French farmer called Amlot, sitting astride the Landsker Line - the medieval boundary between Welsh-speaking Wales and Little England beyond Wales.

subject: Ambohimanga
summary: Madagascar's only UNESCO cultural World Heritage Site, the sacred Blue Hill served as the spiritual capital of the Merina Kingdom for over four hundred years -- and pilgrims still come.

story.title: Ambon: Indonesia's City of Music on the Spice Islands

subject: Ambon
summary: A tropical island where Portuguese forts vanish beneath banyan roots, sectarian scars give way to tolerance awards, and the locals named the place for the morning dew that clings to its mountains.

subject: Ambositra
summary: In the woodcarving capital of Madagascar's highlands, Zafimaniry artisans turn endemic timber into geometric patterns that UNESCO recognizes as a living heritage of humanity.

subject: Amboy Crater
summary: A dormant Mojave cinder cone whose 70-square-kilometer lava field last erupted roughly 10,000 years ago, briefly hosted Hollywood film crews who lit fires inside the crater to simulate a journey to Earth's core, and served as a training ground for Apollo 15 astronauts.

subject: Ameland
summary: A long ribbon of sand that ruled itself for nearly three centuries, where ferries still carry the names of villages the sea swallowed.

story.title: American Bank Note Company Printing Plant

subject: American Bank Note Company Printing Plant
summary: A mammoth Bronx printing plant where engravers once crafted stock certificates featuring half-naked figures to foil counterfeiters has reinvented itself across three centuries of New York commerce.

subject: American Samoa
summary: The only US territory south of the equator - where Pago Pago's dramatic harbor cuts into volcanic mountains, ancient Polynesian traditions trump constitutional norms, and one of America's least-visited national parks protects pristine Pacific ecosystems.

subject: American Tobacco Company
summary: The Durham, North Carolina tobacco giant that once controlled 90% of America's cigarette production, was broken by the Supreme Court, and found new life as a revitalized campus of offices and restaurants.

subject: American Tobacco Trail
summary: A 22-mile rail-trail that traces the path tobacco once took to Durham, now carrying cyclists, walkers, and horses through the Research Triangle.

subject: Amerikamura
summary: Osaka's 'American Village' began in the 1970s when a shopkeeper filled a converted warehouse with imported West Coast jeans and vinyl records, accidentally creating the city's restless epicenter of youth culture and street fashion.

subject: Amersfoort
summary: A medieval city named for a ford that no one needs anymore, where a single church tower defines the origin of every map in the Netherlands.

subject: Ames Research Center
summary: NASA's Silicon Valley outpost has been testing the boundaries of aeronautics and space science since 1939, from supersonic wind tunnels to astrobiology and autonomous drones.

subject: Amethyst Gas Field
summary: A North Sea gas field named after a Royal Navy frigate, drilled into Permian sandstone 2,700 metres below the seabed, now being slowly unbolted from the sky.

subject: Amgen
summary: Amgen, founded in 1980 in Thousand Oaks, California, grew from a small applied science startup into one of the world's largest biotechnology companies — pioneering medicines derived from living cells rather than chemistry.

subject: Amhara Region
summary: The highland heartland of Ethiopia - source of the Blue Nile, home of Ras Dashen, and the landscape that shaped an empire.

subject: Amherst County, Virginia
summary: A rolling Piedmont county where the Blue Ridge meets the James River, home to the Monacan Nation, Sweet Briar College, and a quiet history that produced explorers, judges, and one of the men who opened the Santa Fe Trail.

subject: Amherst, Virginia
summary: A small Virginia town at the intersection of two old federal highways, set against the Blue Ridge and surrounded by Monacan country, Sweet Briar College, and the Appalachian Trail.

subject: Amlwch
summary: A quiet harbour town on Anglesey's north coast that was, for a few decades in the late 1700s, the world's largest copper port - and the second-largest town in Wales after Merthyr Tydfil.

subject: Amman
summary: Where ancient Philadelphia became modern Jordan's capital, where seven hills hold millennia of civilization, where refugees found shelter and created home.

subject: Ammarnäs
summary: A village of about a hundred people in the Swedish mountains grows almond potatoes above the cultivation limit, on a gravel hill divided into 23 shares and worked for more than 150 years.

subject: Ammoudia
summary: At the mouth of the mythological Acheron River, where ancient Greeks believed souls crossed into Hades, Ammoudia is a small fishing village where the river's cold blue-green water meets the warm shallows of the Ionian Sea.

subject: Amnat Charoen
summary: A quietly proud capital of Thailand's Isan region, Amnat Charoen holds the country's largest community of mor lam musicians, a Buddha image that serves as the province's logo, and a way of life still shaped by Lao and Phu Thai roots.

subject: Amoeba Music
summary: The largest independent record store in the world, a Haight Street institution where vinyl still outsells downloads and the listening stations never close.

subject: Amorgos
summary: The easternmost of the Cyclades is a long, lean island of donkey paths and cliffside chapels that a single French film turned into a worldwide synonym for the blue.

subject: Amos Norcott
summary: A British officer who fought through the Peninsular War with the 95th Rifles and commanded a battalion at Waterloo, before dying in command of the Cork District in 1838.

subject: Amphiareion of Oropos
summary: A wooded ravine in the Attic hills where ancient pilgrims slept on ram fleece to be healed by a hero who was swallowed by the earth.

subject: Amposta
summary: The gateway city to the Ebro Delta, whose very name means 'placed on the river,' known for a Brooklyn-inspired suspension bridge, a medieval Hospitaller past, and a landscape of rice, salt, and flamingos.

subject: Ampthill
summary: A Bedfordshire market town whose vanished castle once held Catherine of Aragon during Henry VIII's divorce - and whose great park later hid a golden hare for a famous treasure hunt.

subject: Amroth
summary: A Welsh coastal village where, at extreme low tide, the petrified stumps of a 7,000-year-old forest emerge from the sand alongside Neolithic flints.

subject: Amrum
summary: A ten-kilometre island in the North Sea where more people speak Oeoemrang in Iowa than in some Amrum villages - and where the largest dune in northern Europe shifts a little further every winter.

subject: Amrumbank West
summary: Eighty turbines stand in the open North Sea, their foundations sunk through sandbags the size of small cars - a wind farm built on engineering nobody had tried before.

subject: Amstelveen
summary: A leafy Amsterdam suburb where KLM keeps its headquarters, sixteen 'wild gardens' redefined Dutch landscape design, and one of Europe's largest Japanese expat communities settled in among the polders.

subject: Amsterdam
summary: Venice of the North - where 17th-century traders dug concentric canals around their medieval core and created the world's first global financial center, and where the complicated legacy of that wealth still shapes the city today.

subject: Amsterdam Binnenstad
summary: Inside the medieval core of Amsterdam, a UNESCO-listed canal ring wraps around an old city that was already old when Rembrandt painted it, and which still looks remarkably like his canvases.

subject: Amsterdam Derby
summary: Long before Ajax dominated Dutch football alone, Amsterdam had four serious clubs and a city rivalry that filled the Olympic Stadium with blue-and-white zebra stripes and Louis Davids cabaret songs.

subject: Amsterdam Westerpark Train Collision
summary: A red signal misread on a Saturday evening sent two trains onto the same track west of Amsterdam Centraal, killing one passenger and injuring 117 others.

subject: Amsterdam-Noord
summary: Across the IJ from the postcard city - a borough of gallows fields, shipyards, Fokker factories, wartime bombs, and creative reinvention now reachable by free ferry every two minutes.

subject: Amsterdam-Oost
summary: The Amsterdam most tourists never see, where Surinamese roti shares a market stall with Moroccan olives and the city's data still flows through old port land.

subject: Amsterdam-Zuid
summary: Amsterdam's wealthiest borough — three world-class museums, a working-class market that fed a neighborhood, and a financial district inspired by Paris.

subject: Amsterdam-Zuidoost
summary: An exclave of Amsterdam built as a 1960s modernist dream, repopulated by Surinamese, Ghanaian, and Caribbean Amsterdammers, and home to the Netherlands' largest Rastafarian community.

subject: Amsterdamsche Droogdok Maatschappij
summary: For more than a century, ADM lifted ships out of the IJ on iron docks named for queens — until a forced merger and a workforce it could not afford brought it down in 1985.

subject: Amtrak Cascades
summary: A 460-mile rail corridor threading through the Pacific Northwest, the Amtrak Cascades connects 18 cities from Vancouver to Eugene while the snow-capped peaks of its namesake range keep watch.

subject: Amur
summary: The Black Dragon River forms the border between Russia and China for over 1,600 kilometers, shelters the world's largest freshwater fish, and carries more contested history per mile than almost any waterway on Earth.

subject: Amuri, Tampere
summary: Finland's first purpose-built workers' district, where four families shared a single kitchen and each was allotted its own corner of it — one block of which still stands as a museum.

subject: Amy of Garmoran
summary: A 14th-century Gaelic noblewoman who brought the lands of Garmoran and the North Isles to her marriage with John of Islay, the first Lord of the Isles.

story.title: Amykles — The Throne of Apollo and the Tomb of Hyacinthus

subject: Amykles
summary: Six kilometers south of Sparta, the village of Amykles sits near the ruins of ancient Amyclae — once the site of one of the most extraordinary religious monuments of the ancient Greek world: the Throne of Apollo, which enclosed the burial mound of Hyacinthus and was decorated with a vast encyclopedia of mythological imagery.

subject: An Giang province
summary: Roman gold in a rice field, a border cut by hand with eighty thousand shovels, and a goddess who may once have been Shiva.

subject: An Teallach
summary: A mountain whose Gaelic name means 'the forge,' An Teallach hammers together some of the most demanding ridge scrambling in Scotland.

subject: An Triúr Deirféar
summary: Three small peaks on the northwestern lip of the Dingle Peninsula are called the Three Sisters in Irish - although, awkwardly, none of them carries a woman's name.

subject: Anaconda Smelter Stack
summary: The 585-foot smokestack in Montana that's the tallest surviving masonry structure in the world - built to disperse the toxic fumes from copper smelting that poisoned the surrounding valley for decades.

subject: Anacortes
summary: Gateway to the San Juan Islands - a working waterfront town where ferry horns punctuate the day and adventure awaits just across the water.

subject: Anacostia
summary: The neighborhoods east of the Anacostia River - home to Frederick Douglass, Marvin Gaye, Kenilworth Aquatic Gardens, and a complicated history of segregation, demographic shift, and chronic federal neglect.

subject: Anadoluhisarı, Beykoz
summary: A small Bosphorus village in the Beykoz district of Istanbul, Anadoluhisarı grew up in the shadow of a medieval Ottoman fortress and remains one of the strait's most atmospheric waterfront communities.

subject: Anagyrous
summary: An ancient Attic deme near the Saronic coast whose very name was a punchline in Aristophanes — and whose hillsides, archaeologists believe, hid a Mycenaean cemetery, a nymphs' cave, and the fields where Plato's parents once lulled their infant son to sleep.

subject: Analavelona
summary: A green island of cloud-fed forest rising from the arid plains of southwestern Madagascar, held sacred by the Bara people and home to lemurs, endemic plants, and a bird found almost nowhere else.

subject: Anamã
summary: A small rubber-era town on the Solimoes River whose Nheengatu name translates as thick, dense, or possibly a breed of duck.

subject: Anandpur Sahib
summary: The holy city where Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa in 1699, Anandpur Sahib pulses every spring with the martial spectacle of Hola Mohalla.

subject: Anau, Turkmenistan
summary: Named 'new water' in Persian, Anau has been continuously inhabited since roughly 5500 BC, making it one of Central Asia's oldest known settlements and a key site for understanding the origins of agriculture in the region.

subject: Ancaster, Lincolnshire
summary: A Lincolnshire village where two Roman roads crossed, where Roman ghosts still surface in fields, and where the limestone underfoot built Lincoln Cathedral.

story.title: Anchorage: Alaska's Gateway City at the Edge of Wilderness

subject: Anchorage
summary: Alaska's largest city where urban sprawl meets wilderness at the Chugach Mountains, where summer brings 19 hours of daylight and moose wander suburban yards, and where half of Alaska's population lives within a city that insists it's not the 'real' Alaska.

subject: Ancient Agora of Athens
summary: The marketplace at the foot of the Acropolis where Athenian democracy was argued, voted on, and shopped around; uncovered by archaeologists who demolished a working neighborhood to find it.

subject: Ancient Carthage
summary: Founded by Phoenician exiles in 814 BC, Carthage grew from a trading post on the Tunisian coast into the dominant power of the western Mediterranean -- until Rome decided it could not be allowed to exist.

subject: Ancient Chernihiv
summary: A protected reserve gathering thirty-four monuments of one of the oldest cities of Kievan Rus', from pagan burial mounds to golden-domed cathedrals.

subject: Ancient City of Tabran
summary: The ruined heart of ancient Tus, birthplace of the poet Ferdowsi, where clay walls and a ninth-century dome still mark the city that shaped Persian literature.

subject: Ancient Corinth
summary: A city-state on the narrow neck of land between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, rich enough to invent the Corinthian column, demolished by Rome, and rebuilt by Julius Caesar.

subject: Ancient Elis
summary: The city-state that ran the ancient Olympic Games for centuries, policed the sacred truce, and produced a philosopher who founded skepticism — all from a fertile plain in the northwestern Peloponnese.

story.title: Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy Sites of Burkina Faso

subject: Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy Sites of Burkina Faso
summary: Some of Africa's oldest iron furnaces - towering clay chimneys that pulled iron from the earth nearly 2,800 years ago.

story.title: Ancient Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata

subject: Ancient Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata
summary: Four medieval Saharan trading towns - Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt, and Oualata - jointly inscribed by UNESCO in 1996 as the surviving record of a vanished caravan world now fighting the encroaching sand.

subject: Ancient Linzi
summary: Capital of the ancient Qi state and home to China's earliest academy, where Mencius debated philosophy and 600 horses were sacrificed for a duke's burial.

subject: Ancient Mediterranean Religions
summary: Across the ancient Mediterranean, religion meant doing rather than believing - and nowhere is that older world easier to read than in Athens, where altars, processions, and ruined sanctuaries still mark the rhythm of a sacred year.

subject: Ancient Mesopotamia
summary: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers gave humanity its first cities, its first writing, and the blueprint for civilization itself.

subject: Ancient Messene
summary: Built in 85 days to give liberated helots a capital city, ancient Messene is one of the most remarkable acts of political architecture in Greek history — and one of the best-preserved archaeological sites in the Peloponnese.

subject: Ancient footprints of Acahualinca
summary: Preserved in volcanic mud on the shore of Lake Managua, the footprints of up to 15 people walking over 2,100 years ago are the oldest known human tracks in Central America.

subject: Ancoats
summary: Called the world's first industrial suburb, Ancoats packed the planet's largest cotton mills, an Irish population, a Little Italy and the Avro aeroplane factory into a square mile of Manchester — then was very nearly knocked flat in the 1960s.

subject: Ancon Hill
summary: A jungle-covered hill rising 199 meters above Panama City, Ancon Hill spent decades under American control and became a potent symbol of Panamanian sovereignty when its flag finally flew at the summit.

subject: Andalusia (Milledgeville, Georgia)
summary: The 544-acre Georgia farm where Flannery O'Connor, battling lupus and isolation, wrote nearly all of the dark, funny, unforgettable fiction that made her one of the greatest American short story writers of the twentieth century.

subject: Andean Highlands (Ecuador)
summary: Alexander von Humboldt called the central plateau of Ecuador the Avenue of the Volcanoes, and the name stuck - a 400-kilometer corridor where the country's culture, language, and food all feel the pressure of altitude.

subject: Anderlecht
summary: A Brussels district stitched together from a medieval village, an Industrial Revolution boom town, and the most successful football club in Belgium.

subject: Anderson County, South Carolina
summary: Named for a Revolutionary War general, ringed by Lake Hartwell's nearly 1,000 miles of shoreline, and home to 27 BMW suppliers, Anderson County is the corner of South Carolina where Carolina backcountry history collides with the global auto industry.

subject: Anderson, South Carolina
summary: The hometown of Chadwick Boseman, James 'Radio' Kennedy, and a hospital network named AnMed sits in the South Carolina upstate, where Sunbrella fabric is made and the 'Electric City' nickname dates to the 1890s.

subject: Andingmen
summary: Where one of Beijing's Ming-dynasty city gates once controlled access to the imperial capital, a modern traffic overpass now carries the 2nd Ring Road -- a transformation that encapsulates the city's fraught relationship with its own walls.

subject: Andratx
summary: At Mallorca's southwestern tip, where the Serra de Tramuntana dives into the sea, an old inland town looks out over a coast of yachts, dragon-shaped islands, and dry-stone trails.

subject: Andravida
summary: A quiet town in the plains of Elis whose name may derive from a Slavic word for 'otters,' but whose Gothic cathedral ruin and medieval history as capital of the Frankish Principality of Achaea give it weight far beyond its modest size.

subject: Andreas, Isle of Man
summary: A quiet village in the Manx northern plain whose parish church holds eleven medieval stone slabs, including a cross that shows Odin being eaten by Fenrir at the end of the world.

subject: Andrew Ball (Townsville pioneer)
summary: The man credited with founding Townsville named it after a granite hill and the Isle of Man - but the city carries another man's name, and the country was never empty when he arrived.

subject: Andrew Johnson National Historic Site
summary: A sixteen-acre site in Greeneville, Tennessee, where every May 26 visitors vote on whether the seventeenth president should have been removed from office.

subject: Andrew Leon
summary: A Cantonese migrant who planted the first cane of the Cairns sugar industry and led its Chinese community - then watched a new nation turn its laws against his own family.

subject: Andriivskyi Descent
summary: Kyiv's steepest, most storied cobblestone street has a baroque church with no bells, because legend says the first toll would wake a buried sea and drown half the city.

subject: Android Lawn Statues
summary: Giant foam dessert sculptures at Google's campus mark each Android release -- from Cupcake to the present -- creating Silicon Valley's most whimsical outdoor gallery.

subject: Andros
summary: The greenest and most well-watered of the Cyclades, Andros has been home to wealthy shipowning families for generations, and its neoclassical capital Chora remains one of the archipelago's most elegant towns.

subject: Andros, The Bahamas
summary: Bigger than all 700 other Bahamian islands combined yet home to fewer than 8,000 people, Andros is a labyrinth of mangroves, blue holes, and the world's third-longest barrier reef.

subject: Androy
summary: Madagascar's driest, southernmost region, where the Tandroy people have endured recurring famine for centuries in a thorny landscape shaped by wind, water scarcity, and a resilience that outsiders have often underestimated.

subject: Angastaco
summary: Where red rock canyons meet some of the highest vineyards on Earth, a tiny Calchaquí village pours wine grown in light so clear it seems to come from the moon.

subject: Angel Mounds
summary: A thousand-person Mississippian culture city flourished on Indiana's Ohio River from AD 1100 to 1450, leaving behind thirteen earthen mounds and 2.4 million artifacts that make it one of the best-preserved prehistoric sites in the United States.

subject: Angel Oak
summary: A Southern live oak on Johns Island that has been growing for roughly five centuries, its massive limbs so heavy they rest on the ground and burrow beneath the earth before rising again, sheltering 17,200 square feet beneath its canopy.

subject: Angeln
summary: A quiet hilly peninsula in Germany's far north whose people left in the fifth century, took the name with them, and gave it to England.

subject: Angels Flight
summary: Angels Flight, the world's shortest railway in Bunker Hill, has operated fitfully since 1901 — surviving a 27-year storage, a fatal accident, a brake bypass involving a tree branch, and four separate reopenings.

subject: Angkor
summary: Once the largest city on Earth, the Khmer capital of Angkor supported a million people through an intricate hydraulic network before falling to invasion and drought in the 15th century.

subject: Angkor Borei and Phnom Da
summary: A living Cambodian market town sits on top of what may be the country's oldest city - and on the granite hill three kilometres away stands the sculpture that begins the history of Khmer art.

subject: Angkor Thom
summary: The last great capital of the Khmer Empire, Angkor Thom enclosed nine square kilometers of temples, canals, and monumental gateways behind walls that were meant to represent the mountains at the edge of the world.

subject: Angle Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station founded in 1868 to guard the entrance of the Milford Haven Waterway, financed by the son of the man who built Saltaire and tied forever to the wreck of the Loch Shiel.

subject: Angle, Pembrokeshire
summary: A small Pembrokeshire village at the very tip of the Milford Haven peninsula, where a 1405 French invasion, a Victorian estate village, and a 1996 oil spill all left marks on the same shoreline.

subject: Anglesey
summary: The largest island in Wales and the seventh largest in Britain, Anglesey is where Druids made their last stand against Rome, medieval Welsh kings held court, and over half the population still speaks Welsh as a daily language.

subject: Anglesey Aluminium
summary: For thirty-eight years the biggest single user of electricity in Britain ran an aluminium smelter on the edge of Holyhead, powered by Wylfa nuclear station fifteen miles away. The power contract ended in 2009. Five hundred and forty people lost their jobs.

subject: Anglesey Circuit
summary: A 2.1-mile motor racing circuit on the southwest coast of Anglesey - Trac Môn - widely regarded as the most scenic in Britain, with straights that run along the cliffs above the Irish Sea.

subject: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
summary: For 57 years, two countries officially governed Sudan together. In practice, one did the ruling, the other took the blame, and the Sudanese ran out of patience with both.

subject: Angourie, New South Wales
summary: A tiny village at the edge of Yuraygir National Park that became a surfing legend - home to one of the country's first National Surfing Reserves, the cult film Morning of the Earth, and a pair of spring-fed pools born from an old quarry beside the sea.

subject: Angurugu
summary: An Anindilyakwa community on Groote Eylandt that grew from a 1940s mission into the home of one of Australia's most distinctive Aboriginal languages.

subject: Anicuns
summary: A small Goias town named for a vanished bird and the people who hunted it, Anicuns outlasted gold, survived a name change, and held on through shoe factories and sugarcane.

subject: Anindilyakwa Indigenous Protected Area
summary: Ten thousand square kilometres of land and sea country off Arnhem Land, looked after by Anindilyakwa rangers blending ancient knowledge with modern conservation.

subject: Anja Community Reserve
summary: A tiny forest among giant boulders where villagers reversed a wildlife collapse and now protect Madagascar's densest gathering of ring-tailed lemurs.

subject: Anjouan
summary: A volcanic island in the Comoros archipelago where ylang-ylang perfume, pirate history, and over twenty coups have shaped a fiercely independent culture in the Mozambique Channel.

subject: Anjudan
summary: A small Iranian village of fewer than 500 people that served as the secret seat of the Nizari Ismaili Imamate for centuries, surviving Tamerlane's siege and shaping one of Islam's most resilient minority traditions.

story.title: Ankarana Special Reserve: Madagascar's Limestone Labyrinth

subject: Ankarana Special Reserve
summary: A 150-million-year-old limestone massif in northern Madagascar where razor-sharp tsingy formations guard over 100 kilometers of caves, a dozen lemur species, and blind fish that have never seen daylight.

subject: Anlong Veng
summary: Anlong Veng is a small Cambodian town in the Dângrêk Mountain foothills where the Khmer Rouge leadership spent its final years, leaving behind graves, ruins, and an eerie man-made lake that now draws the curious to one of Southeast Asia's most unsettling historical landscapes.

story.title: Ann Arbor: Tree Town and the Big House

subject: Ann Arbor
summary: The Michigan college town where the University of Michigan dominates everything, where 100,000 fans fill the Big House on football Saturdays, and where bookstores and coffee shops outnumber chain restaurants.

subject: Anna Creek Station
summary: The largest working cattle station on Earth sprawls across nearly 24,000 square kilometres of South Australian desert, a property bigger than Israel run on the country of the Arabana people.

subject: Annaglogh Lead Mines
summary: A Victorian-era lead mining district near Castleblayney, run by a Scots captain, whose collapsed shafts still open without warning in farmers' fields.

subject: Annandale Station
summary: The first cattle run in the country west of Birdsville, where droughts killed thousands of cattle and even Australia's 'Cattle King' could not always win against the Channel Country.

subject: Annapolis
summary: Maryland's capital, briefly the capital of the United States, home of the Naval Academy and the largest wooden dome built without nails in the country - all packed into the smallest land area of any state capital.

story.title: Annapolis: The Sailing Capital Where Congress Once Met

subject: Annapolis
summary: The colonial town that served as the nation's capital in 1783-84, where the Naval Academy has trained officers since 1845, and where more sailboats per capita dock than anywhere in America.

subject: Annapolis Convention (1786)
summary: Only twelve delegates from five states showed up to a meeting about trade disputes in September 1786 -- but one of them was Alexander Hamilton, and the report he drafted from that failed convention led directly to the writing of the United States Constitution.

subject: Annascaul
summary: A small Dingle Peninsula village that sent Tom Crean to Antarctica three times and now keeps his pub, his statue, and his memory.

subject: Anne Beadell Highway
summary: A 1,350-kilometer dirt track through the Great Victoria Desert, built for Cold War nuclear testing and now one of Australia's most remote and punishing overland routes.

subject: Anne Frank tree
summary: A horse chestnut tree glimpsed through a hidden window gave hope to a girl in hiding, and now its offspring grow at Holocaust memorials around the world.

subject: Anne Springs Close Greenway
summary: Twenty-one hundred acres of forest, lake, and pasture donated to Fort Mill by the family whose textile mills built the town - a complicated gift, fully given.

subject: Annet, Isles of Scilly
summary: On a kilometre of granite and storm-beach a kilometre west of St Agnes, more seabirds nest than anywhere else in Scilly, and no human is allowed to land.

subject: Annette McGavigan
summary: A fourteen-year-old Bogside schoolgirl killed by gunfire on 6 September 1971; her ice cream still in her hand, her family still without justice, her face still painted on a Derry gable wall.

story.title: Annexation of Dadra and Nagar Haveli

subject: Annexation of Dadra and Nagar Haveli
summary: In 1954, a coalition of freedom fighters, tribal activists, and nationalist volunteers liberated two tiny Portuguese enclaves in western India through a swift and largely bloodless campaign.

subject: Annexation of Tibet by China
summary: In October 1950, the People's Liberation Army crossed into eastern Tibet; within months, a document signed under duress ended centuries of de facto Tibetan self-rule and set in motion one of the 20th century's most enduring political disputes.

subject: Anniston and Birmingham bus attacks
summary: On May 14, 1961, Ku Klux Klan mobs firebombed a Greyhound bus and beat Freedom Riders in Anniston and Birmingham, Alabama, in attacks that shocked the nation and helped end segregation in interstate transportation.

subject: Anno Domini (gallery)
summary: A contemporary art gallery in San Jose's SoFA district that championed street art, zine culture, and tattoo art before the mainstream art world acknowledged them.

subject: Annobón
summary: A tiny volcanic island 335 km off the African coast where residents speak a Portuguese creole, endemic birds share space with toxic waste, and an exile movement has petitioned to join Argentina.

subject: Anosy
summary: A southeastern Madagascar region whose name means 'islands' in Malagasy, where Portuguese shipwrecks, French colonial ambitions, uranium mining, and extraordinary biodiversity have collided for five centuries.

subject: Anseba region
summary: A highland region of Eritrea named for the river that drops from Asmara's outskirts into the Sudanese lowlands, centered on the ancient trading town of Keren.

subject: Anshan
summary: China's self-proclaimed capital of iron and steel, where a Japanese-built industrial empire became the backbone of Communist-era heavy industry, and where a jade Buddha weighing 260 tons sits inside a city trying to reinvent itself.

subject: Anson Street African Burial Ground
summary: A construction crew's backhoe unearthed 36 forgotten graves in downtown Charleston, launching a decade-long journey to name, honor, and reinter the enslaved Africans buried beneath what is now the Gaillard Center.

subject: Antalya
summary: Where Turkey's turquoise coast meets ancient ruins, where resorts line beaches that civilizations have enjoyed for millennia, where tourism has transformed fishing town to gateway.

subject: Antananarivo
summary: Madagascar's highland capital, the City of a Thousand, sprawls across terraced ridges at 1,280 meters where rice paddies glow green between pastel terracotta buildings.

subject: Antandrus
summary: On a hill above the Gulf of Adramyttium, the ancient city of Antandrus guarded the timber of Mount Ida, sheltered Trojan refugees according to Virgil, and minted its own coins for seven centuries — yet its very origins remained a matter of fierce scholarly disagreement for more than two thousand years.

subject: Anthedon (Boeotia)
summary: On the Euboean Gulf, where a fisherman was said to have tasted an herb and become a sea-god, the ancient port of Anthedon traded in fish, purple dye, and sponges at the very edge of Boeotia.

subject: Anthochori, Arcadia
summary: Anthochori — 'flower village' — was a settlement in the Arcadian valley of the Alpheios that was demolished between 2006 and 2008 to make way for a lignite mine, leaving only its church standing on a column of soil before that too collapsed.

subject: Antigua Guatemala
summary: The earthquake-ruined colonial capital - where Spanish baroque churches crumble photogenically beneath three volcanoes, cobblestones ring with Holy Week processions, and Central America's most beautiful city refuses to stay abandoned.

subject: Antikyra
summary: A small Greek port on the Gulf of Corinth whose ancient fame rested on hellebore — the plant the ancients believed cured madness — giving rise to the saying 'sail to Antikyra' as a way of telling someone they were out of their mind.

subject: Antiparos
summary: A small Cycladic island separated from Paros by a shallow strait, Antiparos offers a laid-back alternative to its famous neighbours, with wind-swept beaches, a spectacular stalactite cave, and an unhurried pace of life that once drew hippies and now draws anyone looking to exhale.

subject: Antissa
summary: An ancient city on the wild western tip of Lesbos, birthplace of the lyre's inventor and, by legend, the resting place of Orpheus's singing head, now a village beside the ruins of a medieval castle.

subject: Antofagasta
summary: Chile's copper capital wedged between the Atacama Desert and the Pacific, a working city whose contested history and stark natural monuments reward travelers willing to look past its industrial edges.

subject: Anton-Wilhelm-Amo-Straße
summary: A central Berlin street that carried a contested name for 318 years now honours the man who, in 1729, wrote a dissertation on the legal rights of Africans in Europe — a text that has since been lost.

story.title: Antonin Dvorak: The New World Symphony Was Written Here

subject: Antonín Dvořák
summary: A Czech composer lived on East 17th Street in Manhattan for three years and wrote one of the most famous symphonies ever composed, drawing on African American spirituals and the sounds of a city that was nothing like Bohemia.

subject: Antsirabe
summary: Norwegian missionaries founded a spa town on Madagascar's high plateau, drawn by volcanic thermal springs; today it is the island's rickshaw capital, where thousands of hand-pulled pousse-pousse glide through cool mountain air.

subject: Antsiranana
summary: At Madagascar's northern tip lies one of the finest natural harbours on Earth, a vast sheltered bay said to be second only to Rio de Janeiro.

subject: Antwerp
summary: Where Rubens painted and diamonds trade, where Europe's second port loads container ships, where Belgian pride has Flemish accent.

subject: Antwerp diamond heist
summary: Over the weekend of February 15-16, 2003, Italian thieves defeated ten layers of security to empty 109 safe deposit boxes in the world's diamond capital, pulling off what investigators called 'the heist of the century.'

subject: Antônio Prado historic center
summary: A highway built somewhere else in the 1930s left Antônio Prado behind - and in doing so saved the largest surviving ensemble of Italian-immigrant timber architecture in Brazil.

subject: Anubanini rock relief
summary: A rock relief carved around 2300 BC on a cliff face in western Iran, showing a Lullubi king trampling a defeated enemy beneath the gaze of the goddess Ishtar -- a composition that may have inspired the far more famous Behistun Inscription two thousand years later.

subject: Anuradhapura
summary: Sri Lanka's most ancient city -- a UNESCO World Heritage site where white-clad pilgrims still circumambulate 2,000-year-old stupas, and the world's oldest historically documented tree grows behind a golden railing.

subject: Anza, California
summary: A Riverside County valley community at 3,921 feet where the Cahuilla have lived for over 2,000 years, where Red Skelton kept horses, and where the Pacific Crest Trail passes through a valley renamed from Cahuilla to Anza in 1926.

subject: Anzali Lagoon
summary: A 15,000-hectare Ramsar-listed lagoon on Iran's Caspian coast that once supplied 70% of Gilan Province's commercial fish catch -- now shrunk to a quarter of its former size but still sheltering 243 bird species and nine endangered ones.

subject: Anápolis
summary: A Goiás industrial hub of nearly 400,000 people that grew from a mule train miracle into Brazil's largest generic drug plant and a Hyundai assembly line.

subject: Aoudaghost
summary: A vanished caravan city on the edge of the Sahara, once so rich a single merchant might own a thousand servants, now a silent mound of sand called Tegdaoust.

subject: Aouelloul crater
summary: A near-perfect 390-meter circle gouged into the Mauritanian Sahara roughly three million years ago, when a meteorite struck the Akchar Desert hard enough to fuse sand into glass.

subject: Aoukar
summary: A vast dry basin in southeastern Mauritania, once a lake big enough to feed an early civilization and later the cradle of the Ghana Empire, now sand, salt, and the last refuge of a vanishing antelope.

subject: Ap Chau
summary: Smaller than many city blocks and home to only three permanent residents, Ap Chau is Hong Kong's tiniest inhabited island — a 0.04-square-kilometre speck in Crooked Harbour where Tanka fishermen once built a community that sent emigrants to cities across Britain.

subject: Ap Lei Chau
summary: A duck-tongue island off Aberdeen that Guinness World Records once called the most densely populated island on Earth — and whose early fishing village gave Hong Kong its name.

subject: Apache Pass
summary: A mountain pass where water scarcity, Apache resistance, and American expansion collided to shape the fate of the Southwest.

subject: Apache Trail
summary: A supply road carved through Arizona's Superstition Mountains became one of America's first scenic highways.

subject: Apalachicola, Florida
summary: A tiny Gulf Coast town where the inventor of air conditioning fought yellow fever, where 90% of Florida's oysters once grew, and where the third-busiest cotton port on the Gulf now sleeps under Spanish moss.

subject: Aparecida de Goiânia
summary: What started in 1922 with a donated plot for a Marian chapel grew into Goiás's second-largest city, a 600,000-person industrial suburb on the edge of the capital.

subject: Apeldoorn
summary: A city engineered to grow - and the royal hunting palace, ape forest, and waterfall it grew around.

subject: Apollo 9
summary: The overlooked Apollo mission that proved humans could fly the lunar module, gave spacecraft nicknames like Gumdrop and Spider, and cleared the path to the Moon four months before Apollo 11.

subject: Apollonia (Illyria)
summary: A Greek colony founded around 600 BC on Illyrian soil became one of the ancient world's great centers of learning, where the young Octavian studied before becoming Augustus Caesar.

subject: Apostolic Vicariate of Istanbul
summary: The Latin Catholic presence in Istanbul stretches from Ottoman Constantinople to the present day — a small but diplomatically significant community that has served for nearly three centuries as a bridge between the Roman Catholic Church and the city where Eastern Christianity still finds its spiritual center.

subject: Appalachia
summary: A cultural region named for the Apalachee people of Florida, sprawling across 13 states and 26 million people, defined as much by stereotype as by geography.

subject: Appalachian League
summary: Founded in 1911 as a Class D circuit of mill-town nines, the Appalachian League has reinvented itself four times in a century and still plays summer baseball in towns named for moonshiners, Civil War boosters, and one whistling marmot.

subject: Appalachian Mountains
summary: The oldest mountains in North America, the Appalachians have spent 480 million years being worn down into the gentle, forested ridges that define the eastern edge of the continent.

subject: Appalachian String Band Music Festival
summary: Each summer at Clifftop, thousands of fiddlers, banjo players, and dancers turn a Fayette County camp into the global headquarters of old-time music.

subject: Appalachian Trail
summary: A 2,198-mile footpath threading the spine of eastern America, from Georgia's red-clay hills to a granite summit in Maine.

story.title: The Appian Way: Queen of Roads

subject: Appian Way
summary: Rome's first strategic military highway, built in 312 BC to move legions south during the Samnite Wars, stretched 560 km to Brindisi on the Adriatic coast - its original paving stones still intact in places after 2,300 years, earning it the ancient title 'regina viarum,' queen of the long roads.

subject: Apple Daily Raids and Arrests
summary: In 2020 and 2021, Hong Kong police raided the offices of Apple Daily — the city's largest pro-democracy newspaper — arrested its executives, froze its assets, and forced the 26-year-old paper to close forever.

subject: Appleby Horse Fair
summary: Each June for nearly 250 years, Romani and Traveller families have gathered on a Cumbrian hill outside Appleby for the largest traditional Gypsy fair in Europe.

subject: Appleby-in-Westmorland
summary: A market town that refused to let its county die: when Westmorland was abolished in 1974, Appleby added the words to its own name and held on.

subject: Applecross
