summary: A remote Wester Ross peninsula that an Irish monk named The Sanctuary in 673, reachable today only by Scotland's steepest road or a 1975 coast road.

subject: Appledore Lifeboat Station
summary: On 28 December 1868, the Appledore lifeboat went out three times in a single storm, lost its rudder, capsized once, and pulled nine people from a wreck. Two hundred years of rescues are layered on a sandy estuary in north Devon.

subject: April 2018 inter-Korean summit
summary: On April 27, 2018, Kim Jong Un stepped across the military demarcation line into South Korea, the first North Korean leader to do so since the Korean War ended in 1953, and shook hands with President Moon Jae-in in a summit that produced bold pledges of peace and denuclearization.

subject: Apuan Alps
summary: A 55-kilometer mountain chain in northern Tuscany that formed from Triassic sea sediments, gave the world Carrara marble, and sustains over 300 bird species while its quarries reshape its peaks.

subject: Apuseni Mountains
summary: A Carpathian mountain range in western Transylvania riddled with 400 caves, shaped by geological forces spanning from the Precambrian to the Ice Age, and home to wolves, bears, and some of the oldest cave art in Central Europe.

subject: Aq Qaya
summary: A sheer white cliff rising a hundred meters above a Crimean valley, sculpted from ancient chalk into pillars, grottoes, and niches.

subject: Aquarius Festival
summary: The ten-day 1973 counterculture festival that turned a dying dairy village into Nimbin and staged what is widely called Australia's first Welcome to Country.

subject: Arabat Spit
summary: A pencil-thin ribbon of sand and shell, 112 kilometers long, that walls off a poisonous salt lagoon from the open sea.

subject: Aracaju
summary: Sergipe's capital did not grow into its shape — an engineer drew it as a chessboard in 1855, and the grid still runs straight down to the river.

subject: Aracati
summary: A colonial port on the Rio Jaguaribe that got rich salting beef, lost the trade to a drought in 1777, and kept the town the money built.

subject: Arachosia
summary: An ancient Persian satrapy centered on the Arghandab River in modern Afghanistan, where Kandahar predates Alexander the Great and empires rose and fell for over a thousand years.

subject: Araguainha crater
summary: A 40-kilometer impact crater on the Mato Grosso-Goiás border, dated to roughly 254 million years ago and possibly linked to the worst mass extinction in Earth's history.

subject: Araguari
summary: In the Triangulo Mineiro, a cattle-ranch outpost called Brejo Alegre became a city the moment the trains arrived in 1896 - and it has been running to catch up ever since.

subject: Arai Barrier
summary: The last surviving Edo-period checkpoint on Japan's great Tokaido highway, battered by tsunamis and earthquakes yet still standing after four centuries.

subject: Araioses
summary: The easternmost city in Maranhão, a gateway to the Parnaíba Delta, where a labyrinth of river channels, mangroves, and islands spills into the Atlantic at the edge of two Brazilian states.

subject: Aramac Station
summary: A vast central-western Queensland sheep run named for three letters a pastoralist once carved on a tree, established on Iningai country in 1863 amid the violence and ambition of the pastoral frontier.

subject: Arapahoe, North Carolina
summary: Named for a postmaster's old white horse after the U.S. Postal Department rejected the first two name choices, this Pamlico County town is the unlikely home of four summer camps and a Methodist environmental center.

subject: Arapiraca
summary: Tobacco made Arapiraca and then unmade it; the second city of Alagoas rebuilt itself on a street market and a stubborn talent for creating jobs.

subject: Araraquara
summary: A city of a quarter million in central São Paulo state whose Tupi name means lair of the macaws, built by railway workers and orange growers, and known across Brazil as the Abode of the Sun.

subject: Araripe Geopark
summary: The first UNESCO geopark in the Americas covers 3,796 square kilometres of southern Ceará, six towns, the world's densest concentration of pterosaur fossils, and a bird that breeds in a single square kilometre.

subject: Arasbaran
summary: A UNESCO biosphere reserve in northwestern Iran where 72,460 hectares of ancient forests, oak woodlands, and mountain meadows shelter species found nowhere else, on land shaped by Medes, Persians, Armenians, and Turks.

subject: Arastradero Preserve
summary: is in the background

subject: Araxa
summary: Almost everything known about this inland Lycian city comes from a single inscription honouring one man who spent his life defending it.

subject: Araçatuba
summary: For three decades the price of Brazilian beef was set in pencil in a public square in Araçatuba, a railway camp of 1908 that grew into the northwest of São Paulo's largest city and still answers to the name Capital of Fat Cattle.

subject: Araçuaí
summary: The hottest temperature ever recorded in Brazil was measured here - 44.8°C - in a town founded by prostitutes who fled a priest's rules.

subject: Arbroath
summary: A small Angus fishing port where a 1320 declaration of independence, a 36-0 football match, and a delicacy called the smokie all somehow share the same coastline.

subject: Arcadia (region)
summary: The rugged highland heart of the Peloponnese — home of Pan, Hermes, and the Arcadian League — became, in the imagination of Renaissance Europe, the very name for pastoral paradise, a place that never quite existed the way poets described it.

subject: ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih
summary: Ukraine's largest steelworks was built on one of the richest iron seams on Earth - a city-sized furnace that has fed empires, changed hands in a scandal, and kept its fires lit through war.

subject: Arch of Cabanes
summary: A lone Roman arch standing in an open Castellón plain for some eighteen centuries, likely built to mark a grave rather than a victory.

story.title: Arch of Dignity, Equality, and Justice

subject: Arch of Dignity, Equality, and Justice
summary: A pearlescent Mayan-style arch in downtown San Jose honoring Cesar Chavez and the farmworkers' movement, standing in the plaza named after the labor leader who organized in the surrounding valley.

subject: Arch of Hadrian (Athens)
summary: A marble gateway where two inscriptions argue over who really founded Athens: the hero Theseus, or the Roman emperor who loved the city enough to claim it.

subject: Arch of Trajan (Timgad)
summary: A triple-arched Roman gateway rising 12 meters above the Algerian desert, marking the western entrance to a city buried for centuries under Saharan sand.

story.title: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn

subject: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
summary: Five-thousand-year-old beehive tombs and mysterious circular buildings that traded copper with the Sumerians, protected for centuries not by guards but by sheer remoteness.

subject: Archaeological Society of Athens
summary: A learned society founded in 1837, just years after Greece won its independence, to dig up and protect the ancient past of a brand-new nation.

subject: Archaeology of Igbo-Ukwu
summary: Ninth-century bronze castings of astonishing virtuosity, unearthed from a backyard in southeastern Nigeria, overturned colonial assumptions about African art and revealed trade networks stretching to Mesopotamia.

subject: Archaic Greece
summary: Between roughly 800 and 480 BC, the Greeks invented the city-state, the alphabet, coined money, monumental sculpture, lyric poetry, and the Olympic Games — a compressed revolution that set the terms for everything that followed.

subject: Archdiocese of Beijing
summary: One of the oldest Catholic dioceses in Asia, established in 1307 when a Franciscan friar reached the court of the Mongol Khan, suppressed, revived, and still navigating the complex space between Rome and Beijing.

subject: Archdiocese of Mechelen-Brussels
summary: The primatial see of Belgium, founded in 1559, governed from two cathedrals and shaped by archbishops who became cardinals, resisters, and reformers.

story.title: Archdiocese of Naxos, Tinos, Andros and Mykonos

subject: Archdiocese of Naxos, Tinos, Andros and Mykonos
summary: The Roman Catholic archdiocese spanning the central Cyclades — a living vestige of Venetian rule that has persisted in these Greek Orthodox islands for eight centuries.

subject: Archdiocese of Shenyang
summary: A Catholic archdiocese whose roots trace to 1838, when the Vatican carved a vicariate from the 'vast Tartar province called Leao-Tung' and sent French missionaries into Manchuria.

story.title: Arches: The Stone Windows That Frame the Desert

subject: Arches
summary: The Utah park containing over 2,000 natural stone arches - where Delicate Arch stands alone against the sky, where the geological processes that created the formations continue to destroy them, and where what seems permanent is merely the pause between transformations.

subject: Archie Barton
summary: Taken from his mother as a small child, Archie Barton found his way back to his people and led the campaign that won the Maralinga lands home.

story.title: Arctic Village and the Gwich'in People

subject: Arctic Village and the Gwich'in People
summary: The Alaska village 100 miles above the Arctic Circle where the Gwich'in people have followed caribou for 20,000 years - fighting oil drilling in the calving grounds they call 'the sacred place where life begins,' defending a way of life against the modern world.

subject: Ardashir-Khwarrah
summary: An ancient circular city in Fars province designed with compass-like precision, Ardashir-Khwarrah was the birthplace of the Sasanian Empire and the seat of its founder's glory.

subject: Ardclough
summary: A small village in County Kildare on the Grand Canal - probable birthplace of Arthur Guinness, third-worst rail accident in Irish history, and granite for Nelson's Pillar.

subject: Ardenwood Historic Farm
summary: A working Victorian-era farm in Fremont where visitors can still see crops harvested the 19th-century way, managed by the East Bay Regional Park District.

subject: Ardfert
summary: The birthplace of St. Brendan the Navigator - the Irish monk who, according to legend, sailed west and may have reached North America a thousand years before Columbus.

subject: Ardgay
summary: A small Sutherland village whose Gaelic name translates as 'high wind', and which has been the postal town for a vast wedge of empty country ever since.

subject: Ardglass
summary: A fishing village on the Lecale coast that holds more medieval tower houses than any town in Ireland.

subject: Ardgraigue Bog
summary: Ireland holds half the Atlantic region's active raised bog—and this 177-hectare hummocked basin near Portumna is one of the last places it is still alive.

subject: Ardgroom
summary: A Beara peninsula village named for two glacial hills, where an eleven-stone Bronze Age circle still stands a mile off the old Kenmare road.

subject: Ardmore Lifeboat Station
summary: A Waterford lifeboat station that ran for 37 years, earned four Silver Medals in a single rescue in 1860, and was closed in 1895 when the rescue economy had moved on.

subject: Ardmore, County Waterford
summary: A County Waterford seaside village where a 5th-century saint, a Michelin-starred restaurant, and the rusted hulk of a 1980s crane ship all share the same mile of cliff.

subject: Ardnamurchan
summary: The westernmost tip of mainland Britain, where a 60-million-year-old volcano left a perfect ring in the rock and a single-track road runs out at the edge of the Atlantic.

subject: Ardnamurchan
summary: The remote 50-square-mile peninsula at the westernmost point of mainland Britain, accessed by single-track road and home to a Gaelic-speaking community, golden eagles, and an extinct volcano.

subject: Ardrossan
summary: A North Ayrshire harbour town on the Firth of Clyde, gateway to Arran, with a ruined castle, a radio-history first, and a railway-age origin story.

subject: Ardrossan Lifeboat Station
summary: From 1807 to 1930, the lifeboat at Ardrossan answered distress calls on the Firth of Clyde - including the terrible night the Fair Maid of Perth capsized.

subject: Ardwell
summary: A 'high town' named in Gaelic, Ardwell tucks a walled garden, a swan pond, and the bones of three lost castles into one fold of Scotland's western shore.

story.title: Area 51: Where America Keeps Its Secrets (and Maybe Aliens)

subject: Area 51
summary: The Nevada military base so classified the government denied its existence until 2013 - where U-2 spy planes were really tested, where conspiracy theorists insist alien bodies are really stored, and where the truth remains classified enough to fuel both possibilities.

subject: Areguá
summary: A sleepy Paraguayan town where colonial buildings and ceramic workshops line the road to a once-beloved lake, and where strawberry festivals draw crowds every winter.

subject: Arem language
summary: In the mountains along the Laos-Vietnam border, a language built almost entirely out of half-syllables has come down to a number of fluent speakers you can count on your fingers.

subject: Arend Petroleum Company
summary: A Royal Dutch Shell subsidiary that transformed Aruba from a quiet island into an oil-refining hub in 1927, survived a German U-boat attack in 1942, and left behind an Eagle Village whose colonial architecture still echoes the Dutch East Indies.

subject: Areopagus
summary: The bare rock northwest of the Acropolis where Athenians tried murderers, where myth tried a god, and where the Apostle Paul preached to a city full of altars.

subject: Argentine Confederation
summary: For nearly a decade the river city of Paraná served as capital of a breakaway Argentina, the Argentine Confederation, a name still written into the country's constitution.

subject: Argolis
summary: A compact peninsula of the northeastern Peloponnese where Bronze Age citadels, ancient theatres, Venetian fortresses, and hidden coves stack atop each other like the layers of its long story.

subject: Argon Pedion
summary: The Argon Pedion — the "untilled plain" — is a closed karst basin in the Arcadian highlands where winter rains can turn the 4-by-2-kilometer grassland into a temporary lake, with water draining underground through limestone fissures and re-emerging nearly 200 hours later as a submarine spring in the Argolic Gulf.

subject: Argos, Peloponnese
summary: Argos has been continuously inhabited for at least 7,000 years, making it one of the oldest cities in the world — and the city keeps the receipts: Bronze Age citadels, a democracy older than Athens's, and the grave where a tile dropped from a rooftop killed a conquering king.

subject: Argyll's Lodging

story.title: 2207 Seymour Avenue: Cleveland's House of Horrors

story.title: Arima Onsen: Where Warlords Came to Soak

subject: Arisaig

story.title: Arjuno-Welirang: The Hero and the Sulfur

subject: Arkiko

subject: Armidale

summary: How travelers actually reach the Adrar - by paved highway, by bush taxi, or by climbing into the dusty ore wagons of one of the longest trains on Earth.

summary: The Georgia capital that rose from Sherman's ashes to become the capital of the New South - where Coca-Cola was invented, where Delta built a hub, and where the civil rights movement found both leadership and resistance.

summary: The New Jersey shore town that invented the boardwalk, inspired Monopoly, became the East Coast's answer to Las Vegas, and still draws millions to its casinos and beaches despite decades of boom and bust.

summary: A sprawling 4,142 km² cattle station on the Victoria River frontier, where a card game ended in the Northern Territory's first legal execution and a riverbank yielded a prehistoric giant in 2010.

subject: Auyán-tepui
summary: The largest tepuy in Venezuela's Guiana Highlands, a flat-topped mountain whose 667-square-kilometer summit hosts species found nowhere else -- and from whose cliffs the world's tallest waterfall plunges.

subject: Avalon Ballroom
summary: The Polk Gulch venue where the San Francisco counterculture found its sound from 1966 to 1969, hosting the Grateful Dead, Big Brother, and Janis Joplin under psychedelic light shows.

subject: Avalon, New Jersey
summary: A four-mile sliver of barrier-island affluence named for King Arthur's burial place, where 1,243 year-round residents swell to 45,000 every July.

subject: Avaya
summary: A telecommunications company born from the breakup of AT&T's Lucent Technologies, headquartered in New Jersey, whose business communications systems connect millions of offices worldwide.

subject: Avebury
summary: The largest megalithic stone circle in the world -- so vast that a village was built inside it. Unlike Stonehenge, you can walk among these Neolithic standing stones, touch them, and grasp the scale of what prehistoric Britain achieved.

subject: Avenida Corrientes
summary: Buenos Aires' answer to Broadway - the street that never sleeps, where neon marquees, all-night pizzerias, secondhand bookshops, and tango lyrics all crowd together after dark.

subject: Avenue Habib Bourguiba
summary: Tunis's grand central boulevard -- compared to the Champs-Elysees and renamed for the father of independence -- has witnessed colonial ambition, revolution, and the daily life of a capital for over a century.

subject: Avenue of Stars, Hong Kong
summary: A 440-metre waterfront promenade in Tsim Sha Tsui that pays tribute to a century of Hong Kong cinema across nine red pillars and the permanent gaze of a 2.5-metre Bruce Lee.

subject: Avenue of the Baobabs
summary: A grove of ancient Grandidier's baobabs lining an unpaved road in western Madagascar -- the last survivors of a dense tropical forest, now towering alone over rice paddies in one of the island's most iconic landscapes.

subject: Avery County, North Carolina
summary: The youngest county in North Carolina is also one of its highest, a fir-scented highland where wooly worms predict winters and Scottish bagpipes echo off Grandfather Mountain.

subject: Aviemore
summary: The Speyside ski town that became a year-round outdoor capital — Britain's most accessible base for Munro climbing, steam railways, and Bronze Age stone circles.

subject: Avion Pirata
summary: A Lockheed Constellation forced down by P-51 Mustangs over Santa Cruz in 1961 became Bolivia's most famous urban legend and an unlikely city landmark.

subject: Avoca, County Wicklow
summary: Thomas Moore wrote his most famous lyric here under a tree by a river junction, copper miners worked these hills for two and a half centuries, and a 1990s BBC drama gave the village a second life as a film set.

subject: Avrupa Pasajı
summary: Built after a devastating fire swept through Beyoğlu in 1870, the Avrupa Pasajı is Istanbul's elegant 19th-century arcade — mirrors, chandeliers, female statues representing the crafts, and arches between every shop.

subject: Aweil West County
summary: On the agricultural lands of the Lol River, a Dinka county has produced generals, sultans, and the quiet farmers who kept feeding everyone between the wars.

subject: Aweil, South Sudan
summary: The capital of Northern Bahr el Ghazal sits where two rivers meet in Dinka country - a town shaped by slave raiders, civil war, famine, and the Lost Boys who came from here.

subject: Axum
summary: For 800 years Aksum ruled a kingdom ranked among the great powers of the ancient world, and its granite stelae still rise over the Tigray highlands.

subject: Axum
summary: The sacred city of Ethiopia - capital of an ancient empire, keeper of granite obelisks, and home to a chapel that Ethiopians say holds the Ark of the Covenant.

subject: Ayakapı
summary: A Golden Horn quarter in Istanbul's walled city where a gate named for a female saint stands near one of the finest surviving Byzantine churches and a bathhouse built by the great Mimar Sinan.

subject: Aylvapoldermolen
summary: The windmill standing in the Frisian village of Burgwerd is not the one that used to stand there. It was carried, piece by piece, from another town fifty kilometers away, to fill a hole left by fire forty years earlier.

subject: Ayod County
summary: In a Gawaar Nuer county of Jonglei State, a 1994 health study found that twenty percent of the people examined had Guinea worm lesions - and the story only gets more complicated from there.

subject: Ayr
summary: The sugar capital of the Burdekin delta - one of Australia's most productive irrigated cane districts - a town built on sweet underground water and on a hard, human history of South Sea Islander labour.

subject: Ayr Lifeboat Station
summary: For more than a century, men rowed out of Ayr harbour into North Atlantic gales to bring sailors home. The motor engine ended that.

subject: Ayrshire
summary: A crescent of fertile coast and rugged hill country on the Firth of Clyde - a county that no longer exists administratively but still defines how its 366,800 residents see themselves.

subject: Ayu-Dag
summary: A great domed headland on the Crimean coast whose profile looks so much like a bear stooping to drink from the sea that three languages named it for the animal.

subject: Ayvalık
summary: An Aegean port where Greek churches became mosques and Cretan refugees made a new home, Ayvalık is a town built on olives, fish, and the layered memory of two displaced peoples.

subject: Ayvansaray
summary: A historic Golden Horn neighbourhood in Istanbul where the ancient land walls meet the sea, the Byzantine palace quarter of Blachernae once stood, and companions of the Prophet are said to lie buried beneath a wall that survived the fall of Constantinople.

subject: Azawad
summary: For ten months in 2012, Tuareg rebels declared an independent state across northern Mali - a nation no country recognized and that has since vanished from the map.

subject: Azougi
summary: A small oasis village seven kilometers from Atar, Azougi pairs ancient rock paintings and Almoravid ruins with the kind of unhurried Saharan hospitality that turns a day trip into a memory.

subject: Azov Upland
summary: A low tableland of feather-grass steppe in eastern Ukraine, crowned by burial mounds that have watched over the land for thousands of years.

subject: Azul
summary: A cattle town born from a frontier fort on the pampas became UNESCO's official 'City of Cervantes' and home to some of Argentina's most startling Art Deco architecture - a soaring white cemetery gate built for the dead.

subject: Azusa Street Revival
summary: Beginning April 9, 1906 in a small former livery stable in downtown Los Angeles, the Azusa Street Revival launched the global Pentecostal movement — one of the most consequential religious events in modern American history.

subject: Açu, Rio Grande do Norte
summary: A sunbaked river town in Brazil's semi-arid northeast, where carnauba palms, salt flats, and the waters of a great reservoir meet on the dry hinterland of Rio Grande do Norte.

subject: Ağva
summary: Ağva — whose very name means 'between the rivers' — is a tiny Black Sea resort where two rivers meet the sea, where Istanbulites have escaped city noise for generations, and where hand-loomed Şile cloth is still woven on wooden frames.

subject: Aṉangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara
summary: In the remote northwest of South Australia, the APY Lands form one of the country's largest Indigenous governance areas -- a place where Aboriginal law, language, and culture persist across 103,000 square kilometers of desert.

subject: BARD Offshore 1
summary: Germany's first far-offshore wind farm — 80 turbines, two workers' lives, a €3 billion bill, and the bankruptcy of the company that built it. A pioneer that almost broke its pioneers.

story.title: BRIDEX: Brunei's Window on the World's Arsenals

subject: BRIDEX
summary: A purpose-built defence exhibition in the jungles of Brunei that drew warships, fighter jets, and Ospreys from a dozen nations before quietly ending after just four editions.

subject: BRP Sierra Madre
summary: Built in Indiana in 1944, the BRP Sierra Madre has served three navies across three wars and now rusts on a reef in the Spratly Islands as the Philippines' most improbable military outpost.

subject: BTS Skytrain
summary: Bangkok's elevated railway turned a city strangled by traffic into one threaded with steel rails above the chaos, reshaping how millions move through the Thai capital.

subject: BUTEC
summary: A submarine listening range in the Inner Sound between Skye and Applecross, where every Royal Navy boat has to pass a sound test before going to sea.

subject: Baarle
summary: A single village split into 22 enclaves where the international border crosses through houses, cafes, and even one front door.

subject: Baarle-Hertog
summary: A Belgian municipality scattered into 26 pieces of land, 22 of them stranded inside the Netherlands by a 700-year-old land dispute that nobody has gotten around to fixing.

subject: Baarle-Nassau
summary: The Dutch town that wraps around 22 pieces of Belgium, with iron pins in every street to show where one country ends and the next begins.

subject: Baarn
summary: A Utrecht railway town where Dutch monarchs raised their children, M.C. Escher drew his impossible staircases, and a quiet forest still hides the palace where Queen Juliana lived for sixty years.

subject: Bab Bou Jeloud
summary: The ornate blue-and-green gate that serves as the grand entrance to the world's oldest continuously inhabited medieval city was not built by any sultan but by French colonial administrators in 1913.

subject: Bab-el-Mandeb
summary: The narrow strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa - one of the busiest shipping chokepoints on earth and, quite possibly, where our species first left Africa.

subject: Babahoyo
summary: Where three rivers converge in the Ecuadorian lowlands, the capital of Los Ríos province has been moved, renamed, rebuilt from fires, and flooded routinely - and once, in 2023, held a woman who was wrongly pronounced dead.

story.title: The Bacardi Buildings: Miami's Modernist Jewel Box

subject: Bacardi Buildings (Miami)
summary: Two bold Modernist buildings on Biscayne Boulevard - one sheathed in blue Brazilian tile, the other wrapped in hammered-glass mosaics - tell the story of Cuban exile, corporate ambition, and Miami's identity as a tropical city.

subject: Bach Dancing & Dynamite Society
summary: A beachfront jazz club in Half Moon Bay where Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, and Count Basie performed, born from a night when guests danced to Bach while someone lit dynamite on the beach.

subject: Bacolod
summary: The City of Smiles, where sugar wealth built Millionaires' Row, revolutionaries bluffed their way to freedom with bamboo rifles, and the annual MassKara Festival turns grief into dance.

subject: Bad Dürrenberg burial
summary: Nine thousand years ago a woman was buried sitting upright in red ochre with an infant in her lap and a headdress of antlers - and her community still remembered the spot six centuries later.

subject: Bad Iburg
summary: The Teutoburg Forest spa town where the first Queen of Prussia was born, six Anabaptists were tortured in a tower, and a Zeppelin airship crashed in 1910.

subject: Badab-e Surt
summary: Iran's answer to Turkey's Pamukkale, Badab-e Surt is a mountainside of orange, red, and yellow travertine terraces formed over thousands of years by two mineral hot springs with radically different chemical compositions.

subject: Badaguan
summary: A seaside neighborhood in Qingdao where streets named after ancient military fortresses are lined with European-style villas from the German colonial era, each avenue canopied by a single species of tree.

subject: Badak LNG
summary: In 1973, Indonesia signed a contract to export liquefied natural gas to Japan from a field near the Mahakam River delta -- and built one of the largest LNG plants on Earth to do it.

subject: Badaling
summary: The most visited section of the Great Wall of China, where Richard Nixon walked in 1972 and Olympic cyclists raced through ancient gates in 2008.

subject: Badawi Tekke of Beylerbeyi
summary: A Sufi lodge on Istanbul's Asian shore that has survived republican-era suppression, decades of neglect, and careful restoration to continue its original mission: feeding the hungry and gathering the faithful for the practice of remembrance.

subject: Baekje Historic Areas
summary: Eight archaeological sites across three Korean cities preserve the legacy of Baekje, an ancient kingdom that shaped the culture of East Asia for nearly seven centuries.

subject: Baeza (Ecuador)
summary: An Ecuadorian mountain town where Andes meet Amazon, whitewater kayakers gather from around the world, and Spanish Quito's eastern outpost still watches over the Quijos River valley.

subject: Bafoulabé
summary: The Malian town whose name means "meeting of two rivers" - the place where the black Bafing and the white Bakoy join to become the Sénégal, and where a hippopotamus once befriended a girl.

subject: Bagamoyo
summary: A faded coastal town 70 kilometres north of Dar es Salaam where German colonial architecture crumbles alongside Arabic-carved doorways, and where David Livingstone's body made its last stop on African soil before sailing to Westminster Abbey.

subject: Bagamoyo Historic Town
summary: A Swahili stone town whose name means 'take a load off your heart' -- the final stop for thousands of ivory porters who trekked for months from Lake Tanganyika, and a place whose real history is more nuanced than the slave-trade mythology that modern tourism has built around it.

subject: Bagan
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where over two thousand Buddhist temples and pagodas rise from a dusty plain along the Irrawaddy River, Bagan is the architectural legacy of a medieval kingdom that built with an intensity unmatched in Southeast Asia.

story.title: Bagby Stationhouse, Water Tanks and Turntable

subject: Bagby Stationhouse, Water Tanks and Turntable
summary: The last surviving station of the Yosemite Valley Railroad, rescued from a drowning town and reassembled at the gates of Yosemite, where the last manually operated gallows-frame turntable in America still stands.

subject: Bagdad-Chase Mine
summary: The largest single gold and copper producer in San Bernardino County history — discovered in 1898, peaked between 1904 and 1916, survived the Panic of 1907 and the Great Depression, operated through World War II, and produced $6 million in gold from the Mojave Desert before closing in the early 1950s.

subject: Bagé
summary: Born from soldiers who couldn't keep up with the march, Bagé became the 'Queen of the Frontier' - a gaucho city forged on the contested seam between Brazil and Uruguay.

subject: Bahadur Shah Zafar grave dispute
summary: The last Mughal emperor died in exile in Rangoon in 1862, and the British deliberately erased his grave to prevent it from becoming a site of pilgrimage -- but the earth remembered what the empire tried to forget.

subject: Bahama Banks
summary: Vast submerged limestone platforms built over 150 million years, visible from space as swirls of turquoise against the dark Atlantic.

subject: Bahia
summary: The Brazilian state where Portugal first landed in 1500 - and where African, Indigenous, and European cultures braided into something unmistakably Bahian.

subject: Bahia de Caraquez
summary: Where the Chone River meets the Pacific on the Ecuadorian peninsula, a resort town has declared itself an eco-city and preserved a heart-shaped mangrove island full of frigate birds.

subject: Bahir Dar
summary: The capital of Ethiopia's Amhara Region, where the Blue Nile begins its journey out of Lake Tana - a palm-lined city that won a UNESCO peace prize.

subject: Bahía Blanca
summary: A port city on the salt-rimmed bay that gave it its name, built as a frontier fort and grown into Patagonia's gateway by rail and sea.

subject: Bahía Bustamante
summary: A remote Patagonian hamlet born from the hunt for hairspray ingredients, once the world's only seaweed-harvesting village, now an unlikely wildlife haven dubbed Argentina's private Galapagos.

subject: Bahía Negra
summary: A remote Paraguayan settlement at the tri-border with Bolivia and Brazil, where centuries of colonial fortifications, territorial wars, and indigenous resilience converge at a bend in the Paraguay River.

subject: Bahía Wulaia
summary: A sheltered bay on Isla Navarino where the Yámana lived for ten thousand years, where Darwin walked ashore, and where a mission ended in bloodshed in 1859.

subject: Bailiwick of Guernsey
summary: The last surviving fragment of the medieval Duchy of Normandy, where England's claim to French soil quietly endures eight centuries after the rest of Normandy was lost.

subject: Baixada Maranhense Environmental Protection Area
summary: A vast seasonal wetland where 32 municipalities share the same floodplain, where buffalo wade through flooded meadows, and where the Amazon and Cerrado biomes dissolve into each other under Brazilian monsoon rains.

subject: Bajo Nuevo Bank
summary: A barely-there reef in the western Caribbean claimed by four nations and inhabited by none, Bajo Nuevo Bank has been fought over by mapmakers, pirates, guano speculators, and international courts for nearly four centuries.

subject: Bakassi conflict
summary: A mangrove peninsula at the border of Cameroon and Nigeria became one of Africa's longest-running territorial disputes, leaving hundreds of thousands of people caught between nations.

story.title: Bakersfield: The Oil Town Where Country Music Got Its Sound

subject: Bakersfield
summary: The California city that's culturally Oklahoma - where Dust Bowl refugees created the Bakersfield Sound, where oil derricks dot the hills, and where conservative values persist in liberal California.

subject: Bakhchysarai
summary: The old capital of the Crimean Tatar Khanate, a valley town of palaces and cliff cities that lost its people to deportation in 1944 and has been reclaiming its heritage ever since.

subject: Bakouma
summary: Beneath a small Central African town sits the largest uranium deposit in sub-Saharan Africa. Four nations have tried to mine it. None has succeeded.

subject: Bakr Awa
summary: A 40-meter-high settlement mound near Halabja holds seventeen layers of continuous human occupation spanning from the Uruk period to the present day, its history scarred by modern looting.

story.title: Bakuya Kofun: A Prince's Tomb in the Clay Hills

subject: Bakuya Kofun
summary: A massive 6th-century burial mound in western Nara Prefecture holds one of the region's largest stone chambers -- built from sixty-ton granite monoliths hauled into hills that produce no stone -- and over 20,000 grave goods that suggest it entombs a son of an emperor.

subject: Bala Hissar, Kabul
summary: Kabul's ancient fortress, dating to at least the 5th century, served Kushans, Mughals, and Durrani kings before British forces destroyed it in 1880 -- and its ruins still anchor the city's southern skyline.

subject: Baladityapura
summary: A seventh-century Khmer capital known almost entirely from a scholarly argument — the vanished city of Water Chenla, somewhere in the lower Mekong, between the fall of Funan and the founding of Angkor.

subject: Balat, Fatih
summary: For centuries Balat was home to Jewish, Greek, and Armenian communities who built synagogues, churches, and hospitals along the Golden Horn — and whose descendants were largely driven out through violence and expulsion across the twentieth century.

subject: Balberta
summary: A Maya trading city on Guatemala's Pacific coastal plain that rose to power through obsidian trade with distant Teotihuacan -- then was abandoned almost overnight around AD 400 when its patron decided to build a rival colony next door.

story.title: Baldwin Locomotive Works: The Engine That Built America

subject: Baldwin Locomotive Works
summary: For over a century, the Baldwin Locomotive Works in Philadelphia produced more than 70,000 locomotives that hauled freight, passengers, and munitions across six continents, only to be undone by the very industrial revolution it had helped to power.

subject: Baleshare
summary: A tidal island so flat it barely lifts above the Atlantic, where storms can swallow fifty metres of coast in a single night and a 1962 causeway changed everything.

subject: Bali
summary: An island where Hindu temples rise from volcanic slopes, rice terraces encode a thousand-year-old irrigation philosophy, and the world's tourists have remade paradise in their own image.

subject: Bali District
summary: Across the Tamsui River from Taipei's tourist crowds, this quiet New Taipei district hides an Iron Age archaeological site, a folk hero's temple, and a riverfront cycling path with one of the best views in northern Taiwan.

story.title: Bali Strait: The Narrowest Gap Between Two Worlds

subject: Bali Strait
summary: A 2.4-kilometer channel where six British merchant ships once bluffed a French naval squadron into retreat, and where Java and Bali -- geologically joined until the last ice age -- remain tantalizingly close but culturally distinct.

subject: Baliceaux
summary: A small, uninhabited island in the Grenadines where British colonial forces imprisoned nearly 5,000 Garifuna people after the Second Carib War -- a place of immense suffering now being reclaimed as sacred ground.

subject: Balivanich
summary: The Town of the Monk became the unlikely Cold War nerve centre of the Outer Hebrides, where Gaelic, Catholic faith, and military rocketry share a single runway.

subject: Balkh
summary: Once called the 'Mother of Cities,' Balkh was the capital of ancient Bactria, visited by Alexander the Great, Marco Polo, and Ibn Battuta before an epidemic emptied it in the nineteenth century.

subject: Ballabeg
summary: A small Manx village in the parish of Arbory, southern Isle of Man, whose churchyard holds the man who steered HMS Victory at Trafalgar.

subject: Ballabeg station
summary: A request stop on the Isle of Man Steam Railway - one small wooden hut, a half-height platform, and 148 years of continuous service.

subject: Ballachulish
summary: A Highland village at the narrows of Loch Leven whose slate roofed Edinburgh and Glasgow, whose ferry crossing was essential for two and a half centuries, and whose most famous monument honours a man hanged for a murder he did not commit.

subject: Balladonia, Western Australia
summary: A lonely roadhouse on the Nullarbor that briefly became the place where America's falling space station came down, and then fined NASA for the mess.

subject: Balladoole
summary: A small green hilltop above the southern coast of the Isle of Man holds eleven thousand years of ritual, ending with a Viking ship buried over the graves of Christians.

subject: Ballaghaderreen
summary: A Roscommon town that was part of Mayo until 1899, opened its great Cathedral of the Annunciation in 1860, became an Emergency Reception Centre for Syrian refugees in 2017, and was honoured a year later with a People of the Year Award for how it welcomed them.

subject: Ballana
summary: A Nubian royal cemetery of 122 tombs where kings were buried with crowns, horses, and sacrificed servants between the fall of Meroe and the rise of Christian Nubia.

subject: Ballantrae Lifeboat Station
summary: For 48 years from 1871, a lifeboat named after a widow's husband sat on the rocky south-west Scottish coast waiting to be needed — its most famous service the 1909 rescue of eight men from a grounded steamer in a blizzard.

subject: Ballarat
summary: Gold turned a sheep run into a boomtown that once rivalled Melbourne. Ballarat spent its fortune on grand architecture and wide boulevards, and the wealth of 'The Golden City' is still standing.

subject: Ballasalla
summary: A Manx village grown from the stones of a dissolved twelfth-century abbey, threaded by the Silverburn river and shadowed by the runways of the island's only airport.

subject: Ballast Point Brewing Company
summary: What began as a home-brew supply shop in a San Diego strip mall became one of the most celebrated craft breweries in America — and then sold for one billion dollars to a company that makes Corona.

subject: Ballaugh
summary: In 1819 two men dug a nearly complete Irish Elk skeleton out of the bog beside this Manx village. The skeleton went to Edinburgh. The bog stayed where it was.

subject: Ballaugh (Parish)
summary: A Manx parish named for a vanished lake holds the island's first internationally protected wetland, the largest winter roost of hen harriers in Western Europe, and one of the last breeding sites of the corn crake.

subject: Ballera gas plant
summary: The remote outback gas hub that gathers fuel from 130 wells across the Cooper Basin and pipes it 755 kilometres to the cities of the east coast.

subject: Ballina, New South Wales
summary: A town where a nine-metre concrete prawn shares the skyline with the river mouth that has welcomed aviators, raftsmen and the Bundjalung for thousands of years.

subject: Ballinasloe
summary: Béal Átha na Sluaighe—'the ford-mouth of the crowds'—has been a meeting point on the Suck since the Bronze Age, and still draws 80,000 people each October for Europe's oldest horse fair.

subject: Ballincollig Royal Gunpowder Mills
summary: A 435-acre industrial complex near Cork that manufactured gunpowder for over a century, where explosions killed workers by the dozen and a pilferer's carelessness levelled a city street.

subject: Ballingarry Coal Mines
summary: For 150 years anthracite was hauled out of the hills above Ballingarry by miners with names for everything -- 'banshee,' 'cane,' 'jigger' -- in pits now drowned beneath their own water.

subject: Ballinrobe
summary: A 3,148-person market town where Lithuanian transatlantic pilot Feliksas Vaitkus crash-landed in 1935, Harry Clarke's stained glass fills the parish church, and Mayo's only racecourse runs nine times a year.

subject: Ballintaggart Ogham Stones
summary: Nine sandstone boulders arranged in a circle outside Dingle preserve some of Ireland's earliest written language - personal names in ogham script, carved into stone in the centuries when Patrick was still alive.

subject: Ballintemple
summary: A Cork suburb where George Boole walked himself into pneumonia, the Duke of Grafton's intestines were buried, and Boolean logic met a graveyard mistaken for the Knights Templar.

subject: Ballintubber
summary: An 800-year-old abbey in County Mayo where Mass has been celebrated without interruption since 1216, even through Cromwell, the Penal Laws, and the priest hunters.

subject: Ballona Wetlands
summary: The Ballona Wetlands near Marina del Rey — second-largest open space within Los Angeles city limits — are a 577-acre remnant of a marshland that once stretched for 1,800 acres, now protected as an ecological reserve but caught in a decades-long battle over restoration.

subject: Ballum
summary: The smallest village on Ameland was once the most powerful, where a Renaissance castle ruled a free lordship until its stones became too expensive to keep.

subject: Ballybeg Priory
summary: A 13th-century Augustinian priory near Buttevant whose nesting holes for pigeons - three hundred and fifty-two of them, stacked eleven tiers high - rank as the finest medieval dovecot in Ireland.

subject: Ballybough
summary: Mud Island, where Ulster refugees built a kingdom on Dublin's marsh, then guarded it as Ireland's first Jewish cemetery quietly took root next door.

subject: Ballycastle
summary: A traveller's gateway to the top of County Antrim: ferries to Rathlin and Scotland, climbing on Fair Head, the Lammas Fair, and a coast most tour buses speed past.

subject: Ballycastle, County Antrim
summary: A 5,600-person port town at the top of County Antrim where Marconi made his first commercial wireless transmission and where the Lammas Fair has been held every August since 1606.

subject: Ballycastle, County Mayo
summary: A small north Mayo village seven kilometres from the Ceide Fields - the oldest known stone-walled farmland on the planet - and home to one of Gaelic football's greatest forwards.

subject: Ballyconneely
summary: A west Connemara village where legend claims the famous Connemara pony breed began with Arabian stallions swimming ashore from a Spanish shipwreck.

subject: Ballyconnell
summary: A Cavan border town that gave its name to a colonial settlement in Maryland, hosted the first GAA club in Ulster, and produced both a billionaire cement magnate and Ireland's most successful golfing twins.

subject: Ballycotton
summary: A fishing village on a cliff above the Atlantic, home to the most famous lifeboat rescue in Irish history, a black lighthouse on an offshore island, and a ninth-century Celtic cross with an Arabic inscription that confused historians for a century.

subject: Ballycroy
summary: A scattered village at the edge of Wild Nephin National Park, where the last commercial dance hall in rural Ireland still stands derelict at a crossroads, and the Mayo Dark Sky Festival celebrates the country's most pristine night skies.

subject: Ballydavid
summary: A Gaeltacht village on the Dingle Peninsula whose official Irish name, Baile na nGall, translates as 'town of the foreigners.'

subject: Ballydehob
summary: A West Cork village with a twelve-arch railway bridge to nowhere, a turnip race, an annual gathering of working boats, a 1930s world wrestling champion, and a 1960s artists' colony all squashed into a population of 350.

subject: Ballygar
summary: A planned 19th-century market town in County Galway where the landlord gave prizes for cleanliness and birthed the songwriter of 'When Johnny Comes Marching Home'.

subject: Ballygilgan
summary: Every October about 3,000 barnacle geese arrive at a 73-acre field on the Maugherow Peninsula - the largest mainland flock of the species in Ireland - and stay until the spring carries them back to Greenland.

subject: Ballyglass Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI lifeboat named Clann Lir, for the four cursed swans of Irish legend, launches from a peninsula where two stations close a gap on the west coast that had stood open since 1927.

subject: Ballygroll Prehistoric Landscape
summary: Eleven acres of peat-covered hillside in County Londonderry hold cairns, standing stones, three different types of grave, and an entire Neolithic-to-Bronze-Age field system, mostly still unexcavated.

subject: Ballyhale
summary: A small Kilkenny village that produced both the most successful hurling club in All-Ireland history and a sandstone quarry containing 400-million-year-old fossil ferns.

subject: Ballyhornan
summary: A County Down coastal village that became a 'lost village' when the airbase next door closed.

subject: Ballyliffin
summary: At the windswept north-western tip of Inishowen, two links courses Nick Faldo calls among his favourites unfold between Pollan Strand and the green-cloaked island of Glashedy.

subject: Ballymacoda
summary: A village of fewer than 200 people in East Cork that produced a Hiberno-Norman war poet, an Irish-language poet who continued writing in America, and a Fenian leader killed in 1867.

subject: Ballymena
summary: A market town on the River Braid in County Antrim, founded by Scottish settlers on land granted by Charles I in 1626, that has spent four centuries being many different things to many different people - and is now confronting what it became in June 2025.

subject: Ballymoney
summary: A County Antrim market town that has sent Scots-Irish emigrants to America since 1718 and produced the Dunlop motorcycle dynasty - and where three Catholic children were murdered in 1998.

subject: Ballymore
summary: A small village in the centre of Great Island where Sonia O'Sullivan first ran, a 9th-century church once stood, and the Normans planted a family that's still here.

subject: Ballymote
summary: A Sligo market town built around the last and mightiest Norman castle in Connacht, where a medieval scribe compiled one of Ireland's great manuscripts and where a piece of the World Trade Center now anchors a memorial to The Fighting 69th.

subject: Ballymun
summary: Seven tower blocks named for the executed leaders of 1916, built in a single year as Ireland's bold answer to inner-city slums - and called the worst planning disaster in the state's history.

subject: Ballynavenooragh
summary: A stone cashel on the western slopes of Mount Brandon where archaeologists found apple, blackberry, hazelnut and grape seeds alongside silver pennies of Henry III.

subject: Ballysadare
summary: A Sligo town on the Owenmore River that Ptolemy may have noted on his second-century map, where Saint Columba came to meet the prelates of Ireland in 575 AD, and which still carries the bones of an early monastic church beneath modern housing estates.

subject: Ballyshannon
summary: Donegal's oldest town once held burials with quartz crystals placed in the dead's hands, lent its river to a secret WWII air corridor, and produced the guitarist Rory Gallagher.

subject: Ballyvourney
summary: An Irish-speaking village where a sixth-century saint followed nine white deer to a sheltered valley and stayed.

subject: Ballywalter Lifeboat Station
summary: For forty years a small Ards Peninsula village ran a sailing lifeboat into Irish Sea gales - until a single Boxing Day capsize and a coxswain's drowning began a chain of decisions that ended the station's life.

subject: Ballywiheen
summary: An early medieval Christian site on the Dingle Peninsula where an ogham stone was once broken open by treasure hunters searching for gold.

story.title: Balmorhea: The West Texas Oasis Where You Can Swim With the Endangered

subject: Balmorhea
summary: The spring-fed swimming pool in the middle of the desert - where 15 million gallons of 72-degree water flow daily, creating a 1.3-acre pool that's also habitat for two endangered species that somehow coexist with cannonballing teenagers.

subject: Balmy Alley
summary: A one-block alley in the Mission District that holds the most concentrated collection of murals in San Francisco, painted by neighbors since 1973 as political protest and community art.

subject: Balneario El Cóndor
summary: Where the Río Negro meets the Atlantic, a wall of sandstone cliffs holds tens of thousands of parrot nests — the largest colony of its kind on Earth.

subject: Balsall Heath
summary: A Birmingham inner-city neighbourhood at the heart of the Balti Triangle, shaped by Yemeni migration in 1940, redefined by residents' street patrols in the 1990s, and home to Cluedo's inventor.

subject: Balseiro Institute
summary: From the wreckage of a notorious fusion hoax, a lakeside Patagonian campus grew into one of the world's most selective physics schools, training the mind behind string theory's most-cited paper.

story.title: Baltimore: The Charm City Where the Star-Spangled Banner Survived Dawn

subject: Baltimore
summary: The Maryland port city that inspired the national anthem and perfected the crab cake - where Fort McHenry flew a flag through bombardment, where Edgar Allan Poe died mysteriously, and where The Wire told uncomfortable truths.

story.title: Baltimore: Birthplace of the Star-Spangled Banner

subject: Baltimore
summary: The gritty seaport city where Francis Scott Key watched bombs burst in air over Fort McHenry in 1814, where Edgar Allan Poe died mysteriously in 1849, and where blue crabs and The Wire define local identity.

subject: Baltimore Convention Center
summary: Built in 1979 as the centerpiece of Baltimore's post-industrial tourism strategy, the Inner Harbor convention center has spent the last decade fighting an increasingly difficult battle to keep its biggest conventions from leaving for newer halls in Washington and Philadelphia.

subject: Baltimore Lifeboat Station
summary: Founded after a local archdeacon improvised a wartime sea rescue, the Baltimore lifeboat has been hauling people out of the Fastnet's weather for over a century -- including, in 1985, a future Taoiseach.

subject: Baltimore Symphony Orchestra
summary: Founded in 1916 as a branch of Baltimore's municipal government - the only major American orchestra to begin that way - and led for 14 years by Marin Alsop, the first woman to head a major U.S. orchestra.

subject: Baltimore, County Cork
summary: A pirate-haven, a fort of jewels, and the site of the largest Barbary slave raid ever launched on Ireland -- Baltimore is a village that has carried more history per acre than almost anywhere on the Cork coast.

subject: Baltimore-Washington Parkway
summary: A forty-mile parkway through wooded median between the country's capitals of government and steel - built in part to evacuate Washington in a nuclear emergency, and run for sixty years by the National Park Service.

subject: Baltrum
summary: On the smallest of the East Frisian Islands, there are no street names - houses are numbered in the order they were built, so the address is a kind of date.

subject: Baltusrol Golf Club
summary: Named for a murdered farmer and built on land shaped by glaciers and ancient lava, Baltusrol Golf Club in Springfield, New Jersey has hosted more major championships than almost any course in America.

subject: Balvanera
summary: A dense Buenos Aires barrio where tango was born in the markets of Abasto, Yiddish theater once filled the houses of Once, and a single neighborhood holds the Congress, the city's Jewish heart, and a kilometer-zero monolith from which all Argentine roads are measured.

subject: Balıkesir
summary: A provincial capital in Turkey's Southern Marmara region where Roman hunting lodges, Ottoman mosques, and abandoned French-era mining towns layer over each other in a hilly, agricultural landscape that has always sat at the crossroads of Istanbul and Izmir.

subject: Bam, Iran
summary: An ancient Silk Road oasis city in southeastern Iran whose 2,000-year-old adobe citadel was devastated by a catastrophic earthquake in 2003 and is now slowly rising from its own dust.

subject: Bamako
summary: A traveler's Bamako runs on negotiation and rhythm: motorcycle taxis threading the dust, baguettes on every corner, grilled Niger fish, and live music that spills into the weekend nights.

subject: Bamako
summary: Where the Niger River breaks into rapids, Mali's capital grew from a fishing settlement of a few thousand into one of West Africa's great cities, a place of music, museums, and relentless reinvention.

subject: Bamberton
summary: A cement company built a town on Saanich Inlet with a dance floor to rival the Empress Hotel's — and its sister plant across the water is now Butchart Gardens.

subject: Bamboo Brook Outdoor Education Center
summary: A botanical garden and public park in Morris County, New Jersey, Bamboo Brook preserves the landscape artistry of pioneering American landscape architect Martha Brookes Hutcheson at her historic Merchiston Farm.

subject: Bamburgh
summary: A Northumbrian village in the lee of a vast red sandstone castle, where an Anglo-Saxon queen, a Victorian heroine, and a Tyneside industrialist all left their marks on the same long beach.

subject: Bamfield
summary: A village of 179 people on Vancouver Island's Barkley Sound whose history spans Indigenous habitation, a global telegraph hub, and the gateway to one of the world's great hiking trails.

subject: Bampur
summary: A small Baloch city in southeastern Iran whose archaeological layers connect the Helmand culture of Afghanistan to the Jiroft civilization and the Umm an-Nar culture of Oman.

subject: Ban Chiang
summary: A Harvard student tripped over a tree root in a Thai village and landed face-first on pottery that rewrote the prehistory of Southeast Asia.

subject: Ban Nahin
summary: A three-thousand-person village with three names, wedged between limestone towers on the highway that runs from the South China Sea to the Thai interior.

subject: Ban Nakasang
summary: The plain little Lao river town that every visitor to the Four Thousand Islands passes through, and almost nobody remembers.

subject: Ban Singh Tha
summary: A mythical lion once guarded the pier where Chinese merchants docked — and the neighborhood named for that legend became the cradle of the city that is now Yasothon.

subject: Banco Central Burglary at Fortaleza
summary: In August 2005 a crew tunneled eighty meters under downtown Fortaleza and carried three and a half tonnes of banknotes out of the Central Bank vault - and then the money started killing them.

subject: Banco Palmas
summary: The first community bank in Brazil, founded in 1998 by residents of a displaced fishing community on the outskirts of Fortaleza - and the spark for a nationwide network of more than fifty neighborhood-run banks issuing their own social currency.

subject: Bandai-Azuma Roadway
summary: A 29-kilometer alpine road that climbs to 1,622 meters through Fukushima's volcanic Azuma Mountains, passing crater rims, sulfurous moonscapes, and springtime corridors carved through walls of snow.

subject: Bandar Torkaman
summary: A Caspian Sea port where half of Iran's caviar is harvested, Turkmen horse races thunder across hundred-hectare fields, and women still sing the centuries-old Laleh lament for brides separated from their homeland.

subject: Bandiagara
summary: The dusty gateway town where every journey into Dogon Country begins - last stop for supplies before the great sandstone cliff that has sheltered cultures for a thousand years.

subject: Bandiagara
summary: The plateau town whose name means 'large eating bowl' - once capital of a West African empire, now the gateway to the great Dogon cliffs.

subject: Bandiagara Escarpment
summary: A 150-kilometer wall of sandstone in Mali where the Tellem buried their dead in caves above the floods and the Dogon, arriving centuries later, built a world clinging to the cliff.

subject: Bandra–Worli Sea Link
summary: Mumbai's cable-stayed bridge across Mahim Bay took a decade of legal battles and engineering feats to build, cutting a 30-minute commute to 10 minutes while becoming the city's most photographed modern landmark.

subject: Banff and Macduff Lifeboat Station
summary: A small granite boathouse on the Aberdeenshire coast that for 64 years sent volunteers into North Sea storms to pull strangers from drowning.

subject: Banff, Scotland
summary: A medieval royal burgh on the Moray Firth coast whose name confused even its naming committee, and whose William Adam mansion gave the Canadian Rockies their most famous town.

subject: Bang Rachan
summary: Thailand's Alamo: the village of eleven leaders and four hundred farmers who defeated the Burmese army seven times before falling to a siege their own capital refused to relieve.

subject: Bangalore
summary: Where India's Silicon Valley transforms traditional capital, where startups meet temples, where the garden city vanishes under tech-driven growth.

subject: Bangalow
summary: A heritage-listed village in the green dairy hills behind Byron Bay, Bangalow trades on its preserved main street, its monthly markets, and a name that once briefly belonged to an Irish pirate queen.

subject: Bangor
summary: A small cathedral city on the Menai Strait that serves as the practical gateway to Snowdonia and the ferry routes for Ireland - 1,500 years of Welsh history packed into a short walk.

subject: Bangor Erris
summary: A north Mayo town in remote Erris where a 1934 road crew unearthed pikes from the 1798 Rebellion, where a great flood drowned seventeen people on one stormy December night, and where the Crying Stone now stands beside the N59 in memory of those who sailed away.

subject: Bangor, County Down
summary: Northern Ireland's newest city, a Viking burial site, a sixth-century missionary centre, and the place where Eisenhower addressed Allied troops bound for D-Day.

subject: Bangor, Gwynedd
summary: Founded in the sixth century by Saint Deiniol, the only Welsh city to hold city status by ancient prescriptive right today has 15,000 residents, the longest high street in Wales, and a 1,500-foot pier reaching out into the Menai Strait.

subject: Bangui
summary: The capital of the Central African Republic sits on the Ubangi River just below the rapids that block shipping, a city founded in 1889 atop at least 26 ancient Iron Age sites, where French expats keep one of Africa's best ice cream parlors running and the KM-5 district is best avoided entirely.

subject: Bangweulu Wetlands
summary: Nine thousand square kilometers of floodplain where the horizon disappears, shoebills stalk the shallows, and the only remaining significant population of black lechwe still runs.

subject: Banjawarn Station
summary: A vast, remote cattle run on the edge of the Great Victoria Desert became, for one strange year, the secret outback laboratory of a Japanese doomsday cult that would go on to gas the Tokyo subway.

subject: Bank of Greece
summary: Greece's central bank, born from a League of Nations bailout, whose governors fled to London with the nation's gold as the Axis closed in.

subject: Banlung
summary: A red-dust town of 17,000 that governs a province the size of a small country, named for the gems in its mountains.

subject: Bannockburn
summary: A town south of Stirling famous for one of the most decisive battles in Scottish history — and for a quieter legacy of weaving the tartans the world now thinks of as ancient.

subject: Bansha
summary: A small Tipperary village famous as 'The Model Parish,' birthplace of a rural revival and unlikely refuge of soldiers, poets, and exiled French counts.

subject: Bant (Omdurman)
summary: An affluent Omdurman district whose name may come from a phrase meaning "only a brave man builds here," or from the eagles that once gathered along its ridges.

subject: Bant's Carn
summary: A Bronze Age entrance grave on the high ground of St Mary's, dug into a hillside above the ruins of an Iron Age village that came nearly two thousand years later.

subject: Bantry
summary: A West Cork market town at the head of a 30-kilometre bay, where French invasion fleets, pilchard fisheries, oil tankers, and an Air India disaster have each in turn shaped a single, deeply remembering place.

subject: Banyalbufar
summary: A village of two thousand stone terraces climbing straight out of the sea, built by Moorish hands for a sweet wine that kings coveted, and watered by aqueducts still running a thousand years on.

subject: Banzhuang
summary: A border town in northern Jiangsu whose administrative identity has been reshaped by imperial collapse, Japanese occupation, civil war, and the displacement caused by reservoir construction.

subject: Bao Loc
summary: A highland rest stop with more character than its reputation suggests — a city built around a lake, strung along the road between Ho Chi Minh City and Da Lat, where local life unfolds at a cooler, slower altitude.

subject: Baoding Military Academy
summary: One of the 'three great strategist cradles' of modern China, this academy trained 11,000 cadets -- including Chiang Kai-shek -- and shaped the military history of the Republic.

subject: Baotou
summary: The Steel City of the Grassland straddles the Yellow River in Inner Mongolia, where Tibetan Buddhist monasteries overlook industrial plains rich with rare earth minerals.

subject: Baotu Spring
summary: An emperor named it the finest spring in all of China, and for over two thousand years, poets, painters, and pilgrims have agreed.

subject: Bar Abanicos police raid
summary: On a June night in 1997, police raided a Cuenca bar hosting Ecuador's first gay queen pageant and tortured the people they arrested - triggering the movement that, five months later, decriminalized homosexuality in Ecuador.

subject: Bar U Ranch
summary: Canada's greatest cattle kingdom - where George Lane built an empire of 50,000 cattle in Alberta's foothills, supplied beef to two world wars, and created the ranch that defined the Canadian West.

subject: Barawa
summary: An ancient coral-stone town on Somalia's Indian Ocean coast, Barawa was once a great center of Islamic learning whose people still speak a thousand-year-old language found nowhere else.

subject: Barbastro
summary: An Aragonese river town whose cathedral bell tower hides a scorched Muslim minaret, wrapped in a thousand years of concentric walls.

subject: Barberton Greenstone Belt
summary: The Makhonjwa Mountains of Mpumalanga hold some of the oldest exposed rock on the planet - a 3.6-billion-year-old archive of a younger, stranger Earth, complete with the scars of meteorites that boiled the seas.

subject: Barbican Centre
summary: Europe's largest performing arts centre, hidden inside a concrete brutalist ziggurat that Londoners once voted their city's ugliest building.

subject: Barcelona
summary: Where Antoni Gaudi bent stone into dreams, where anarchists and artists shaped a city that refuses to be Spanish or French but fiercely, defiantly Catalan.

subject: Barcelona, Venezuela
summary: Founded in 1671 as a colonial trading port on the Neveri River, Barcelona has weathered earthquakes, independence wars, and centuries of reinvention to become the vibrant capital of Anzoategui state.

subject: Barendrecht
summary: A Rotterdam suburb whose name means 'muddy river crossing', and whose modern fame rests on swimming gold medals, vegetable wholesale, and one famous rejection of underground carbon dioxide.

subject: Barichara
summary: A Colombian town carved from golden stone, where 18th-century streets inspired Disney's Encanto and an ancient indigenous path connects two worlds frozen in time.

subject: Barisan Mountains
summary: A 1,700-kilometer volcanic spine running the entire length of Sumatra, home to 35 active volcanoes including the supervolcano that created Lake Toba -- the largest volcanic eruption in the past two million years.

subject: Barkley Sound
summary: A sprawling inlet on Vancouver Island's wild west coast where the Nuu-chah-nulth have fished for millennia, European empires competed for naming rights, and a ghost ship's lifeboat drifted for 27 years.

subject: Barlovento, Venezuela
summary: A windward region of Venezuela where the rhythms of West African drumming, the aroma of cacao, and the legacy of enslaved Kongolese and Yoruba people shape a culture unlike anywhere else in South America.

subject: Barmouth
summary: The Victorian seaside town at the mouth of the Mawddach estuary, where Wordsworth came for the view and the first piece of land ever donated to the National Trust still sits above the rooftops.

subject: Barmouth Lifeboat Station
summary: One of the oldest lifeboat stations in Wales, established at the mouth of the Mawddach in 1828 - and named for a Princess of Wales on a cold, wet day in 1982.

subject: Barnes Point
summary: A landslide delta on Lake Crescent that became a trailhead, a plant nursery, and a refuge for a Dutch resistance fighter the war had nearly killed.

subject: Barney and Betty Hill incident
summary: The first widely reported alien abduction claim in American history unfolded on a lonely New Hampshire highway in September 1961, transforming a quiet interracial couple into reluctant icons of UFO culture.

subject: Baroda State
summary: A Maratha kingdom turned princely state in Gujarat, where the Gaekwad dynasty ruled for over two centuries through poisoning scandals, progressive reforms, and a collection of gold cannons and pearl carpets before merging into independent India in 1949.

story.title: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians

subject: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians
summary: In a highland valley of good farmland east of San Diego, the Kumeyaay people have built a community that blends traditional governance with modern enterprise since establishing their reservation in 1932.

subject: Baronscourt
summary: The Tyrone seat of the Dukes of Abercorn - four centuries of Hamilton family power, one famous architect's reversed floor plan, and a 1918 IRA raid that left only six rusty swords behind.

subject: Barony of Arcadia
summary: Born from the wreckage of the Latin Empire in 1262, the Barony of Arcadia — centred on Kyparissia — survived two centuries of Frankish intrigue, Byzantine reconquest, and dynastic turmoil to become the last Frankish foothold in the Peloponnese.

subject: Barony of Geraki
summary: Perched on a rocky spur above the Laconian plain, the Barony of Geraki was one of the original twelve Frankish fiefdoms carved from the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade — a frontier stronghold built to hold down a region that refused to be tamed.

subject: Barony of Gritzena
summary: The Barony of Gritzena was one of the original twelve secular baronies of the Frankish Principality of Achaea, yet it vanished so completely from the historical record that scholars cannot even say with certainty where it stood.

subject: Barony of Nikli
summary: One of the twelve original Frankish baronies carved from the conquered Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade, centered on the ancient city of Tegea — renamed Nikli — and remembered today chiefly as the site of the 1261 Ladies' Parliament.

subject: Barony of Patras
summary: After the Fourth Crusade carved up the Byzantine world, Frankish knights turned Patras into a barony — but the city's bishop eventually outmaneuvered every secular lord, building an independent ecclesiastical domain that balanced popes, Venetians, and Byzantine emperors for two centuries.

subject: Barony of Polop
summary: An 800-year-old feudal lordship whose castles El Cid once held, and whose 17th-century baroness brought water to a ruined village called Benidorm and set the seed of the modern resort.

subject: Baroque Churches of the Philippines
summary: Four Spanish colonial churches scattered across the Philippine archipelago earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 1993 for their unique fusion of European Baroque, Chinese, and indigenous Filipino design.

subject: Barotse Floodplain
summary: Each year the Zambezi floods a plain 500 kilometers across, and each year the Litunga of the Lozi people moves his court to higher ground - a ceremony older than any modern border.

subject: Barra (neighborhood)
summary: The tip of Salvador where Brazil began - and one of the rare places on Earth where you can watch both sunrise and sunset from the same beach.

subject: Barra Head
summary: The southernmost island of the Outer Hebrides, where eighty-three archaeological sites tell five thousand years of human story and the Atlantic still rules absolutely.

subject: Barra do Garças
summary: At the confluence of the Garças and the Araguaia, beneath a mountain range named for the noise it makes, a Brazilian river town built a landing pad for flying saucers — and waits.

subject: Barranca
summary: A Peruvian coastal port 190 kilometers north of Lima, base camp for visiting Caral and three other Norte Chico sites - and home to the most underrated swimming beach on the central coast.

subject: Barranca Yaco
summary: A bend in an old colonial road in the Córdoba hills where, in 1835, an assassination launched a thousand pages of Argentine literature.

subject: Barranquilla Carnival
summary: The second-largest carnival in the world transforms Colombia's Caribbean port city into four days of cumbia, costumes, and collective joy, culminating in the mock funeral of a character who dies of too much fun.

subject: Barreira do Inferno Launch Center
summary: Fishermen named the red cliffs south of Natal the Barrier of Hell; in 1965 Brazil put its first rocket range behind them, and kept the name.

subject: Barreiras
summary: A river town in western Bahia that grew from 20,000 people to 157,000 in a single generation - built on soybeans, cotton, and the highway that came just in time.

subject: Barreirinhas
summary: The main gateway to Lençóis Maranhenses, a river town where Toyota 4x4s depart daily for the world's strangest desert and where the Rio Preguiças still serves as the region's main highway.

subject: Barriles
summary: On the volcanic slopes of western Panama, a row of stone statues depicting figures riding on the shoulders of other men hints at a pre-Columbian society whose hierarchies archaeologists are still working to understand.

subject: Barrio Puerto
summary: The salt-stained heart where Valparaíso began, a tangle of cobblestones between the wharf and the sea that the world once called the Jewel of the Pacific.

subject: Barrio Sur, Montevideo
summary: On the southern edge of Montevideo, between the old city and the sea, the drums of candombe still call every weekend from the neighborhood where the rhythm was born.

subject: Barry Docks
summary: In 1913 a small Welsh town shipped more coal than any port on Earth - 11 million tons in a year - then watched its trade vanish, its scrapyard become a graveyard for steam locomotives, and its quays become a supermarket.

subject: Barton Springs
summary: Austin's sacred swimming hole - where 68-degree water has flowed from limestone aquifers for thousands of years, survived damming, development battles, and endangered salamanders to remain the soul of the city.

subject: Barton Springs Pool
summary: Fed by ancient springs sacred to the Coahuiltecan people and home to an endangered salamander found nowhere else on Earth, this spring-fed pool in the heart of Austin has been a gathering place for centuries.

subject: Barunga, Northern Territory
summary: A small Jawoyn community 80 km southeast of Katherine where, in 1988, a painted statement handed to a prime minister launched Australia's long, unfinished conversation about a treaty with Indigenous peoples — and where every June, thousands gather for a music and cultural festival that still carries that political weight.

subject: Barus
summary: A Sumatran port town whose camphor once sold for its weight in gold, attracting traders from Greece, India, Arabia, and China across two millennia of recorded history.

subject: Barvas
summary: A road-junction village on the west coast of Lewis that still holds one of Scotland's highest concentrations of Gaelic speakers, with an archaeological record running from the Bronze Age to a buried medieval church.

subject: Basankusu
summary: Deep in the Congolese rainforest, a town reachable only by a weeks-long river journey from Kinshasa serves as a staging post for bonobo conservation, the ancestral home of the barkless Basenji dog, and the place where monkeypox was first recorded in humans.

subject: Basilan
summary: The largest island of the Sulu Archipelago, where rubber plantations once rivaled those of Malaya, three ethnolinguistic groups share a multilingual culture, and a decades-long insurgency reshaped everything.

subject: Basra
summary: Founded in 636 at the dawn of the Islamic era, Iraq's third-largest city was once called the Venice of the East for its network of canals and Ottoman mansions, but decades of war, rebellion, and climate extremes have stripped away much of that heritage.

subject: Bassett Road machine gun murders
summary: In 1963, two men were shot dead with a submachine gun in a quiet Auckland suburb, exposing a hidden world of illegal drinking houses where beatnik poets, rugby league players, and hardened criminals crossed paths in the shadow of New Zealand's six o'clock closing laws.

subject: Bastar State
summary: A princely state founded around 1324 CE in the forested heart of central India, where Kakatiya dynasty descendants ruled for over six centuries under the protection of the goddess Danteshwari.

subject: Bastos
summary: A Japanese colony founded in 1928 on a São Paulo cattle farm became first Brazil's silk capital and then its egg capital — a town of 21,000 people and millions of hens.

subject: Basutoland
summary: Completely encircled by South Africa, Basutoland survived decades of colonial neglect and apartheid-era pressure to emerge as the independent Kingdom of Lesotho -- one of the few African territories never absorbed by its powerful neighbor.

subject: Bat Masterson
summary: The Wild West gunfighter and Dodge City sheriff who reinvented himself as a New York sportswriter, died at his desk in 1921 composing a column about economic inequality, and is buried in the Bronx.

subject: Batalla de Santa Clara
summary: A rural Cuban ward named for the revolution's final battle, where farmland and scattered villages carry the weight of a nation's turning point.

subject: Batang, Sichuan
summary: A Tibetan caravan town on the Tea Horse Road where the sound of sheep gave the place its name, empires drew their furthest boundaries, and gold dust once washed from every stream in eastern Tibet.

subject: Batatais
summary: A sugarcane-belt city in São Paulo named — possibly — for a fire-snake, holding the largest collection of sacred art Cândido Portinari ever painted.

subject: Batavia, Dutch East Indies
summary: For 320 years, the Dutch colonial city of Batavia served as the hub of European trade in Asia - a canal-laced port built on the ruins of Jayakarta that would eventually become Jakarta, Indonesia's sprawling capital.

subject: Batavian Republic
summary: For eleven years the Netherlands experimented with democracy at the point of French bayonets - and almost made it work.

subject: Bath County Pumped Storage Station
summary: One of the world's largest pumped-storage hydroelectric facilities - two reservoirs separated by 1,260 feet of vertical drop, capable of generating 3,003 megawatts when the eastern U.S. grid needs them.

subject: Bath County, Virginia
summary: A Virginia mountain county named for an English spa town, with 4,209 residents, 89 percent forest cover, and the distinction of being the only county in Virginia without a traffic signal.

subject: Bath, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's oldest town has survived pirates, plagues, wars, and a preacher's curse -- yet stubbornly refuses to grow beyond the 71 lots its founder laid out in 1705.

subject: Bathonea
summary: On the shores of Lake Küçükçekmece, 20 kilometers west of Istanbul, archaeologists have been excavating a site that may — or may not — be the ancient harbor settlement known as Bathonea, uncovering harbors, a lighthouse, an olive oil workshop, and traces of Vikings, all beneath what was once a submerged lakebed.

subject: Baths of Antoninus
summary: The largest Roman bathhouse ever built in Africa -- and among the three largest in the entire Roman Empire -- the Baths of Antoninus in Carthage had to be designed taller than any other because the Mediterranean clay beneath them would not support a basement.

story.title: Baton Rouge: The Red Stick Capital on the Mississippi

subject: Baton Rouge
summary: Louisiana's capital city where French explorers found the red stick marking tribal boundaries, where Huey Long built America's tallest state capitol and was assassinated inside it, and where LSU Tigers football is religion.

subject: Batopilas, Chihuahua
summary: A silver town at the bottom of a canyon so deep it was the second city in Mexico to get electricity -- and then lost it for 49 years when a flood destroyed the hydroelectric plant.

subject: Battlefields (KwaZulu-Natal)
summary: A landscape in northern KwaZulu-Natal where the Zulu, Boers, and British clashed across seven decades of the nineteenth century, leaving battle sites that now stand as memorials to all who fought and died.

subject: Battles of Saratoga
summary: Two clashes on the same ground eighteen days apart that shattered a British invasion army, launched Benedict Arnold into legend, and convinced France to bet on American independence.
