subject: Batu Caves
summary: A 400-million-year-old limestone mogote north of Kuala Lumpur where Hindu temples share ancient caves with endemic spiders, 21 species of bats, and the largest Thaipusam celebration on Earth.

subject: Batuan, Bali
summary: A Balinese village where painters fill every inch of canvas with sorcery, daily life, and hidden humor, and where an 11th-century temple inscription anchors a thousand years of artistic tradition.

subject: Baturyn
summary: The lost capital of the Cossack Hetmanate on the Seym River, razed to a ghost town in 1708 and reborn around a palace designed by a Scottish architect for Catherine the Great's court.

subject: Bauhaus Center Tel Aviv
summary: A cultural hub on Dizengoff Street dedicated to the world's largest collection of Bauhaus-style buildings, preserved in Tel Aviv's UNESCO-listed White City.

subject: Baumberg
summary: A Rhine-bank village of fishermen and goat farmers became one of the Rhineland's most surprising experiments in Brutalist church architecture.

subject: Bauru
summary: The interior city where three railroads met, where Pele kicked his first professional ball, and where Brazil's first astronaut grew up - Bauru is where inland Sao Paulo learned to be a crossroads.

subject: Bauru Group
summary: A red sandstone stack beneath southeastern Brazil holds the country's richest record of the last dinosaurs — and of the strange land-running crocodiles that outnumbered them.

subject: Bauru station (NOB)
summary: For most of the twentieth century, this was where Brazil's inland frontier began - the departure point of the Northwest Railroad that stitched Sao Paulo to Cuiaba and, eventually, to the Bolivian border.

subject: Bawnboy
summary: A small Cavan village named for a yellow cattle stronghold, with a derelict Victorian workhouse, a county's first farming society, and a writer who turned a six-figure children's book deal into a literary career.

subject: Bawomataluo village
summary: A hilltop megalithic village on Nias Island where 500 traditional houses line stone-paved roads leading to the chief's palace, and young men still leap over two-meter stone walls in an ancient rite of passage.

subject: Baxian Caves
summary: The Baxian Caves on Taiwan's east coast are sea caves carved by an ocean that no longer reaches them — the cliff has risen, the waves have retreated, and the hollows left behind contain some of the oldest evidence of human habitation in Taiwan.

subject: Baxter Cliffs
summary: A 190-kilometre rampart of limestone where the Nullarbor simply ends, named for a man who died on the great crossing and the loyal companion who survived it.

subject: Baxter Clock
summary: A 20-foot four-faced street clock that watched over Pollock Street, was smashed in 1977, spent fourteen years in pieces in a basement, and was reassembled in 1991.

subject: Baynes Sound
summary: A 40-kilometre sliver of protected water between Denman and Vancouver Island that grows a startling share of British Columbia's shellfish - and carries the name of an admiral famous for refusing to start a war.

subject: Bayocean, Oregon
summary: Once marketed as the 'Atlantic City of the West,' Bayocean was a planned resort community on Oregon's Tillamook Spit that the Pacific Ocean slowly reclaimed, earning it the nickname 'the town that fell into the sea.'

subject: Bayshore Cutoff
summary: The 1907 rail line along San Francisco Bay's western shore that cost $7 million to build and still carries Caltrain commuters past the industrial waterfront.

subject: Baños
summary: Ecuador's adventure capital sits in the shadow of an active volcano, where hot springs, waterfalls, and a taffy-pulling tradition coexist with bungee jumping and class IV rapids.

subject: Beacon Hill (Hong Kong)
summary: A 457-metre sentinel above Kowloon whose name preserves the memory of a 17th-century dynastic upheaval — and whose summit still serves as a silent guardian of Hong Kong's skies.

subject: Beadnell
summary: A Northumbrian fishing village named for Bede, fronted by the only west-facing harbour on the English east coast, and quietly stitched into the medieval landscape that runs from Lindisfarne to the Farnes.

subject: Beagle Channel
summary: The strait at the bottom of the world where Darwin first saw glaciers, where two nations nearly went to war, and where the southernmost towns on Earth face each other across the water.

subject: Bealach na Bà
summary: The UK's steepest road - a single-track Highland pass that drovers used for cattle and that Top Gear and the Daily Telegraph have both, separately, made famous.

subject: Beale Street
summary: The birthplace of the blues runs barely two miles through downtown Memphis, but its influence stretches across the entire history of American music -- from W.C. Handy's 'Beale Street Blues' through Elvis Presley's formative years to its designation as a National Historic Landmark in 1966.

subject: Bear (barony)
summary: An administrative ghost in modern Ireland, the medieval barony of Bear still defines two thirds of the Beara peninsula, with Hungry Hill at its heart and Dursey Island at its tip.

subject: Beartooth Mountains
summary: Ancient peaks guarding Yellowstone's northern frontier, where four-billion-year-old rocks meet one of America's last wild ecosystems.

subject: Beating of Ken Tsang
summary: In the early hours of 15 October 2014, seven Hong Kong police officers beat handcuffed social worker Ken Tsang in a dark corner of Tamar Park — caught on camera, debated for years, and tried in court.

subject: Beaufort County, North Carolina
summary: Founded in 1705 as Pamptecough Precinct and split in half by the wide Pamlico River, Beaufort County is the fifth-largest county in North Carolina by area and home to the country's first town named for George Washington.

subject: Beaufort's Dyke
summary: A glacial trench at the bottom of the North Channel where Britain dumped more than a million tons of conventional and chemical munitions, and where bombs still occasionally wash ashore.

subject: Beaufort, North Carolina
summary: The third-oldest town in North Carolina, where Blackbeard's flagship lies just offshore and where Budget Travel readers voted it America's Coolest Small Town in 2012.

subject: Beaufort, South Carolina
summary: A Lowcountry town where a former slave hijacked a Confederate warship, a heavyweight champion learned to fight, and Spanish moss still drapes the live oaks along antebellum streets.

subject: Beauly
summary: A queen looked out of a priory window on a bright August morning in 1564 and exclaimed in French, "What a beautiful place" - and a Highland village got its name.

subject: Beaumaris Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station on the Menai Strait that began in 1891 with a near-fatal capsize on its first major rescue and now operates a Blue Peter-funded inshore lifeboat.

subject: Beaver (steamship)
summary: The first steamship to work the North Pacific coast spent fifty years serving fur posts and charting fjords, ended as a Burrard Inlet tugboat, and was slowly carried away by souvenir hunters after running aground below Stanley Park.

subject: Bebedouro
summary: Named for a stream where 19th-century drovers watered their cattle, Bebedouro traded coffee for oranges and became a research capital of Brazil's citrus belt.

subject: Bebek, Beşiktaş
summary: A small, affluent neighbourhood cupped in a Bosphorus bay, Bebek has been Istanbul's most coveted address since Ottoman times—a place where Egyptian royalty summered, American missionaries founded a college, and the water is always in view.

subject: Beberibe
summary: The name means 'where the sugar cane grows' - and for a century it did, spinning a backwater farming community into a town that once called itself Vila Rica.

subject: Beccles
summary: A Suffolk market town on the River Waveney where Horatio Nelson's parents were married in 1749, the Nobel laureate Dorothy Hodgkin was born, and a 97-foot Perpendicular Gothic bell tower stands detached from the church it served.

subject: Bechuanaland Protectorate
summary: The colonial territory that became Botswana survived eighty-one years of empire largely because its Tswana chiefs kept saying no.

subject: Beckley, West Virginia
summary: A southern West Virginia city built on coal that now invites visitors underground - voluntarily - to feel what the seams really meant.

subject: Bed Burial
summary: For a brief period in seventh-century England, high-status women were buried lying in their beds — a rare and deeply symbolic practice that blurred the line between sleeping and dying in ways that still fascinate archaeologists today.

subject: Beddgelert
summary: An 18th-century innkeeper invented a fake grave for a faithful hound, and the village named after a forgotten Welsh saint became one of the most-visited spots in Snowdonia.

subject: Bedekaspel
summary: An East Frisian village whose name means "penitence church," rebuilt from the rubble of the deadliest flood in North Sea history.

subject: Bedford
summary: A market town on the River Great Ouse where John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress in jail, where a postwar wave of Italian brickworkers transformed the cultural fabric, and where the gardens of the Embankment still line one of England's least known but most photographed urban rivers.

subject: Bedourie
summary: A town of 150 people on the edge of the Simpson Desert whose name means dust storm, where a steel camp oven, a thermal bore, and July camel races define life in the Channel Country.

subject: Beechworth
summary: A gold-rush boomtown in Victoria's high country, preserved in granite, where Ned Kelly stood trial, a candidate's horse wore golden shoes, and a future Governor-General learned his letters.

subject: Beehive Works
summary: An eighteen-bay Victorian cutlery works in Sheffield's Devonshire Quarter, purpose-built so that scores of independent craftsmen - the city's famous little mesters - could rent space, share power, and forge their own knives.

subject: Beelitz
summary: A Brandenburg asparagus town whose sanatorium in the pines became a Great War hospital, a Soviet military clinic, and finally one of Europe's most photographed ruins - with a forest growing inside it.

subject: Beemster
summary: The world's first lake-drained polder, laid out in 1612 as a Renaissance grid - and still farmed to that grid today.

subject: Beeston, Nottinghamshire
summary: A Trent-side town where silk-weavers, telephone-makers, bicycle pioneers and the world's largest pharmacy all built something — and where bees keep turning up in the brickwork.

subject: Beethovenhalle
summary: Three concert halls in Bonn have carried Beethoven's name. The first lasted two months. The second was bombed in 1944. The third is the one with the copper-green wave-shaped dome on the bank of the Rhine.

subject: Begho
summary: Founded in the 11th century at the edge of Ghana's forest-savanna transition, Begho grew into one of West Africa's great trading cities, linking Akan goldfields to Timbuktu before the Ashanti Empire destroyed it in the mid-18th century.

subject: Behistun Inscription
summary: Carved high on a limestone cliff in western Iran, this trilingual inscription by Darius the Great served as the Rosetta Stone for cuneiform -- the key that unlocked the written languages of ancient Mesopotamia.

subject: Behkadeh Raji
summary: The world's first self-sufficient leper village, built in 1961 in northeastern Iran on royal land, where patients received not just treatment but sheep, farmland, and the dignity of economic independence.

subject: Beidou, Changhua
summary: A former harbor town on the Zhuoshui River plain that gave Taiwan its beloved ba-wan dumpling and raised the father of an NBA star.

subject: Beifudi
summary: A Neolithic village in Hebei where a dozen carved clay masks -- the oldest engraved clay artifacts ever found -- reveal ritual life and ceremonial practices dating back over 7,000 years.

subject: Beigang, Yunlin
summary: Every year, more than a million pilgrims converge on this small Yunlin township to honor Mazu, the goddess of the sea — making Beigang one of Taiwan's most spiritually charged places despite being nowhere near the ocean.

subject: Beijing Central Axis
summary: A 7.8-kilometer line through the heart of Beijing connecting the Drum Tower to the Yongdingmen Gate, threading through the Forbidden City and Tiananmen Square along a spine of imperial power dating to the thirteenth century.

subject: Beijing Film Academy
summary: With an acceptance rate below two percent, the Beijing Film Academy has shaped every generation of Chinese cinema -- from the fifth-generation directors who redefined art film to the stars who dominate streaming platforms today.

subject: Beijing Financial Street
summary: The nerve center of China's financial system sits inside Beijing's innermost ring road, where the central bank and top regulators occupy towers designed around the ancient courtyard principles of the hutong neighborhoods they replaced.

subject: Beijing Shejitan
summary: A Ming dynasty altar where emperors once prayed for bountiful harvests, the Shejitan stands as a quiet counterpart to the Forbidden City's grandeur.

subject: Beijing Subway
summary: The world's busiest rapid transit system by annual ridership, Beijing's subway has grown from a single Cold War-era line into a sprawling network carrying billions of passengers each year.

subject: Beijing city fortifications
summary: The most extensive defense system in Imperial China -- 60 kilometres of walls, towers, barbicans, and moats that protected Beijing through six centuries of Mongol invasions, the Boxer Rebellion, and the Eight-Nation Alliance, only to be demolished by the city's own government for a subway line.

subject: Beinan, Taitung
summary: A rural township in southeastern Taiwan named in the Puyuma language for chief Pinara, where the Puyuma and Rukai peoples have made their home for centuries.

subject: Beinn Eighe
summary: Britain's first national nature reserve, where Cambrian quartzite catches the light like snow and a Lancaster bomber sleeps beneath the ridge.

subject: Beipu
summary: Beipu is a small Hakka town in Hsinchu County where a 19th-century frontier settlement survives as a living heritage site — walled ancestral homes, fragrant tea houses, and traditions that have outlasted the dynasty that once granted this land.

subject: Beira
summary: Mozambique's second city, Beira is a crumbling, resilient Indian Ocean port that survived colonial exploitation, civil war, and a catastrophic cyclone -- and keeps rebuilding.

subject: Beira, Mozambique
summary: Mozambique's second-largest port, a cosmopolitan colonial city built on the convergence of two rivers, that was nearly erased when Cyclone Idai made landfall in March 2019.

subject: Beirut
summary: Where the Paris of the Middle East has rebuilt itself repeatedly, where nightlife thrives despite everything, where resilience defines a city that refuses to die.

subject: Beiyang government
summary: The military-backed government that ruled China from Beijing during the chaotic Warlord Era, dissolved in 1928 when Zhang Xueliang raised the Nationalist flag and unified the country under one banner.

subject: Belcoo
summary: A Fermanagh border village where Saint Patrick's holy well still draws pilgrims, the ford between two loughs once carried a Cromwellian fort, and a hound's mouth gave the place its name.

subject: Belfast City Council
summary: Sixty councillors meet in a 1906 Edwardian city hall to govern Belfast - a council whose century-long unionist majority ended in 1997 and whose 2011 census made Catholic backgrounds the city's largest.

subject: Belfast Grand Central station
summary: At eight hectares, the largest integrated transport facility on the island of Ireland - and the buses began running before the trains did.

subject: Belgian Colonial Empire
summary: A small kingdom in Western Europe once controlled a territory in central Africa seventy-six times its own size — first as one man's private estate, then as a state colony, and the human cost is still being reckoned with.

subject: Belgian Congo
summary: From Leopold II's private horror to a paternalistic colony that produced uranium for the atomic bomb, the Belgian Congo's 52-year history shaped central Africa and haunts it still.

subject: Belgian Pro League
summary: Starting on Christmas Day 1932, a Brussels club called Union Saint-Gilloise went sixty league matches without losing — a Belgian record that stood untouched for ninety years and bookended a league older than most.

subject: Belgium
summary: A small federal kingdom at Europe's crossroads where three languages, dozens of beers, and centuries of compromise produced one of the continent's strangest and most rewarding countries.

subject: Belgradkapı
summary: A gate in Istanbul's ancient Theodosian walls carries the name of a city conquered half a millennium ago—and the neighbourhood around it preserves the memory of the Belgraders who were brought here by Ottoman decree.

subject: Belknap Crater
summary: The youngest shield volcano in the entire Cascade Range, Belknap's barren lava fields stand in stark contrast to the forested slopes of its older neighbors.

subject: Belkıs Tombolo
summary: The Belkıs Tombolo is the double sandbar that binds the Kapıdağ Peninsula to the Turkish mainland — a 1,700-meter-wide strip of sand, dune, and marsh that was once open sea, and upon which one of the ancient world's great cities rose and fell.

story.title: Bell Centre: Where Montreal's Heart Beats Loudest

subject: Bell Centre
summary: Home to the Montreal Canadiens and the site of the infamous 1997 Montreal Screwjob, the Bell Centre is Canada's largest indoor arena -- a 21,000-seat cathedral to hockey, music, and the city's fierce sense of identity.

subject: Bell Labs
summary: The Murray Hill, New Jersey research campus where scientists invented the transistor, the laser, Unix, the C programming language, and earned eleven Nobel Prizes - the most prolific industrial laboratory in history.

subject: Bell of Chersonesos
summary: A bronze bell cast from captured cannon, carried off to Notre-Dame as spoils of war, and returned decades later as a gift of friendship - all before it spent forty years warning ships off the rocks.

subject: Bellanagare Bog
summary: Twelve hundred hectares of raised bog west of Castlerea, slowly being unlocked from centuries of turf-cutting and quietly trying to remember how to grow.

subject: Belle Air Plantation
summary: A rare seventeenth-century timber-frame house standing on the north bank of the James — and a reminder that Charles City County's wealth was built by enslaved labor that outnumbered the free population.

subject: Belleek, County Fermanagh
summary: The westernmost village in the United Kingdom, famous for the translucent parian china produced here for over 165 years and counting.

subject: Bellingen, New South Wales
summary: A lush riverside town in Gumbaynggirr country where a misread letter split a name in two, and where cedar money, heritage verandahs and an enduring counterculture all share the same valley.

subject: Bellingham (Washington)
summary: The City of Subdued Excitement - America's northernmost major city, where the North Cascades rise from waterfront doorsteps and adventure waits in every direction.

subject: Bellingham waterfront
summary: A 137-acre pulp and chemical complex on Bellingham Bay changed hands for ten dollars - and the buyer took on a century of mercury with it.

subject: Bellingwedde
summary: A Dutch municipality of fewer than 10,000 people that existed for almost exactly fifty years, formed by merging two villages in 1968 and dissolved into a larger merger in 2018 — leaving behind a portmanteau name, five windmills, and a fortified borg in the village of Wedde.

subject: Bellingwolde
summary: A quiet Groningen border village that built itself on a sand ridge between clay and peat, flooded for five centuries, and turned out to be the birthplace of the man who invented the cassette tape.

subject: Belmullet
summary: A planned 1820s town squeezed onto an isthmus between two bays in Irish-speaking Mayo, where Synge wrote, fairies bent a fence in 1958, and a famine workhouse held three thousand starving people at its peak.

subject: Beloyarsk, Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug
summary: A Nenets ethnic village above the Arctic Circle where reindeer herding, indigenous language preservation, and Soviet-era collective farming collide in the frozen expanse of western Siberia.

subject: Beltana Station
summary: From this remote Flinders Ranges sheep run, camels and the Afghan cameleers who handled them set out to open the heart of a continent.

subject: Belterra, Pará
summary: Henry Ford's second attempt to grow American rubber in the Amazon—a flat-topped plateau of transplanted Michigan, complete with bungalows, rubber trees, and fire hydrants.

subject: Belvoir, Leicestershire
summary: A Leicestershire village whose Norman-French name is pronounced 'Beaver' - sitting on the spur of land that gives Belvoir Castle its panoramic view.

subject: Bemidji, Minnesota
summary: A northern Minnesota lumber town where the Mississippi River flows through a lake, early settlers misnamed an Ojibwe chief, and a Depression-era Paul Bunyan statue became the second most photographed sculpture in America.

subject: Ben Alder
summary: A remote Munro where a Jacobite chief hid for nine years, Stevenson set a chapter of Kidnapped, and one of Britain's richest lichen floras clings to a band of ancient limestone.

subject: Ben Amera
summary: A 633-meter granite dome rising from the empty Sahara, Ben Amera is Africa's largest monolith and the second largest on Earth, trailing only Australia's Uluru.

subject: Ben Franklin (PX-15)
summary: A 130-ton Swiss-built submarine designed not to steer - it drifted 1,444 miles inside the Gulf Stream with six men aboard while NASA watched to see what a month in a sealed tube does to people.

subject: Ben Lomond
summary: The most southerly Munro in Scotland, rising 974 metres above the eastern shore of Loch Lomond, climbed by about thirty thousand people every year and named in one of the most famous songs in the Scottish songbook.

subject: Ben Lomond (Otago)
summary: A 1,748-metre peak named by a homesick Scottish shepherd that now offers Queenstown's defining day hike and a 360-degree panorama of the Wakatipu Basin.

subject: Benagil
summary: A tiny Algarve fishing village whose sea cave, with its cathedral-like ceiling opening to the sky, has become one of Portugal's most photographed natural wonders.

subject: Benbecula
summary: Bonnie Prince Charlie hid here. A grizzly bear named Hercules went missing here. In between, Benbecula has been many things, but never quite a tourist destination.

subject: Benbecula
summary: Twelve kilometres of low, loch-pocked machair between two larger islands, Benbecula is a Catholic Gaelic enclave whose history runs from Pictish missionaries to a community buyout.

subject: Benbulbin
summary: Yeats lies buried in its shadow, fighters were hunted across its slopes during the Civil War, and tiny alpine plants that survived the Ice Age still cling to ledges nowhere else in Ireland.

subject: Bendigo
summary: A central Victorian city whose deep-reef gold built grand Victorian boulevards and a thriving Chinese community, remembered today in a surviving temple and the world's longest ceremonial dragon.

subject: Benelux
summary: Three small kingdoms, three official languages too few for the region's many tongues, and one shared instinct - learned the hard way - to build something larger than themselves.

subject: Bengal Sultanate conquest of Orissa
summary: In 1568, a military campaign by the Bengal Sultanate ended five centuries of Odishan independence - and the commander who won the war became infamous for the temples he destroyed.

subject: Bengali language movement
summary: The 1952 protest in Dhaka where students died defending their right to speak Bengali, an act that eventually led to the birth of Bangladesh and inspired the world's only international holiday honoring a language.

subject: Benicarló
summary: A Valencian port town proud enough of its artichoke to give it a protected name, layered over an Iberian settlement, an Arab farmhouse, and centuries of war.

subject: Benicàssim
summary: A Costa del Azahar beach town where 19th-century summer villas share the shoreline with some of Spain's biggest music festivals.

subject: Benidorm
summary: A mayor's mid-century dream to build upward turned a small Alicante fishing village into Spain's skyscraper-lined beach city, where a Manhattan skyline meets four kilometres of Blue Flag sand.

subject: Benidorm International Song Festival
summary: The seaside contest that launched Julio Iglesias and gave Spain its answer to Sanremo, before returning decades later as the country's road to Eurovision.

subject: Bennekom
summary: A quiet Gelderland village whose Old Church has stood since around 1015, watched over a 1944 winter as forbidden territory, and still falls silent every May 4th.

subject: Bennettsville, South Carolina
summary: Marian Wright Edelman grew up here, in a Pee Dee cotton town that later named its library for the woman who founded the Children's Defense Fund.

subject: Bentiu
summary: Capital of Unity State in South Sudan, a city destroyed and rebuilt by civil war, now home to one of the world's largest displacement camps - where over 100,000 people shelter behind UN perimeters while oil pipelines run through the surrounding countryside.

subject: Bentumersiel
summary: A river-marsh settlement where Germanic potsherds mingle with Roman amphorae and legionary gear - the Empire's farthest-flung trading post in the Frisian lowlands.

subject: Bequia
summary: The 'island of the clouds' in the Grenadines where Alexander Hamilton's father lived in exile, Blackbeard may have hidden his ships, and whalers still hunt humpbacks from open sailboats with hand-thrown harpoons.

subject: Berat
summary: Albania's 'City of a Thousand Windows' layers Ottoman and Byzantine heritage across a dramatic riverside hillside beneath the sacred slopes of Mount Tomorr.

subject: Berdychiv
summary: Once a great crossroads of trade and one of the world's most vibrant centers of Jewish life, this Ukrainian city gave the world Joseph Conrad, a beloved rabbi, and a phrase that meant 'send it to nowhere.'

subject: Bere Ferrers Rail Accident
summary: On 24 September 1917, ten New Zealand soldiers fresh off the troopships at Plymouth stepped down on the wrong side of their train at a small Devon station and were killed by an oncoming express.

subject: Berengo
summary: The crumbling village palace where a self-crowned emperor staged his fantasies of Napoleon, and where his unmarked grave now sits tiled like a bathroom floor.

subject: Berenty Reserve
summary: A private nature reserve in southern Madagascar where ring-tailed lemurs roam freely among visitors, protected by the same family since 1936.

subject: Berezan' Runestone
summary: A single carved stone found on a Black Sea island records a Viking merchant's grief for a business partner who died two thousand miles from home, the only runestone ever found in southern Ukraine.

subject: Berg concentration camp
summary: A Norwegian-run concentration camp near Toensberg where 280 Jewish prisoners were deported to Auschwitz -- only seven survived -- making it one of the darkest chapters of Norway's wartime collaboration.

subject: Berg en Bos
summary: An Antwerp timber merchant bought wasteland, planted pines for the mines, and accidentally created one of the Netherlands' most distinctive residential neighborhoods.

subject: Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe
summary: Europe's largest hillside park, where 750,000 litres of water are released down a wooded slope above Kassel on summer afternoons and travel the whole way by gravity, exactly as an eighteenth-century landgrave intended.

subject: Beriev
summary: For nearly a century, a design bureau on the shore of the Sea of Azov has built aircraft that blur the line between airplane and boat.

subject: Berkeley Marina
summary: Built on decades of garbage and landfill, Berkeley Marina transformed from a city dump into one of the Bay Area's most beloved waterfronts, though what lies buried beneath its park may yet complicate that story.

subject: Berkeley Square
summary: The plane trees at the center of Berkeley Square were planted in 1789, the year of the French Revolution, and have watched prime ministers, robbers, nightingales, and hedge funds come and go ever since.

subject: Berkelland
summary: An Achterhoek municipality born in 2005 from four small towns, three of which were torn apart by tornadoes in the 1920s, and one of which still holds a working 1748 water mill.

subject: Berkshire
summary: The Royal County of Berkshire holds Windsor Castle, Reading, the Thames Valley, Ascot's racing week, the Berkshire Downs where King Alfred grew up, and the headquarters of half the British technology industry.

subject: Berlin Marathon
summary: A baker started it in 1974 with 244 finishers. Fifty years later it is the flattest, fastest marathon course in the world and has broken the world record thirteen times.

subject: Berlin, Maryland
summary: An Eastern Shore town pronounced 'Burl'in,' where Julia Roberts left a wedding twice and Man o' War spent his foal years on a nearby farm.

story.title: Bermuda Triangle: The Mystery That Wasn't There

subject: Bermuda Triangle
summary: The Atlantic region where ships and planes allegedly vanish without explanation - where Flight 19 disappeared in 1945, where the legend grew through magazines and movies, and where the mystery dissolves when you check the Coast Guard statistics that show nothing unusual at all.

subject: Bernal Heights, San Francisco
summary: A hilltop neighborhood in southeastern San Francisco where a microwave tower crowns a windswept summit and the views stretch from downtown to the bay.

subject: Bernera Barracks
summary: An eighteenth-century redoubt built to subdue Jacobite Glenelg, abandoned within seventy-four years of completion, and now a roofless ruin staring across the Kyle Rhea narrows toward Skye.

subject: Bernward Doors
summary: Two bronze door leaves at Hildesheim, each nearly five metres tall and cast in a single pour around 1015 — the oldest monumental figural bronze doors north of the Alps.

subject: Bertie County, North Carolina
summary: Established in 1722 between the Roanoke and Chowan rivers, Bertie is one of North Carolina's oldest counties and one of its most rural - one hundred percent of the population now lives outside any urban area.

subject: Berwick-upon-Tweed
summary: The northernmost town in England changed hands more than a dozen times before settling in 1482 - and its identity has been negotiated ever since.

subject: Berwick-upon-Tweed
summary: The northernmost town in England sits on the wrong side of its own river, in a county named after a town in another country, with Elizabethan walls that are among the finest of their kind in Europe.

subject: Berwick-upon-Tweed Lifeboat Station
summary: From a citizens' subscription after a fatal 1834 wreck to today's modern Atlantic 85, lifeboats have launched from the Tweed estuary for nearly two centuries.

subject: Bessarabskyi Market
summary: At the head of Kyiv's grandest avenue stands a covered market a sugar tycoon paid for from beyond the grave, where light pours through a glass roof onto stalls of salo, honey, and fruit.

subject: Bessborough Mother and Baby Home
summary: For 76 years a Cork institution stripped women of their names, took their children, and buried more than 900 infants in unmarked graves.

subject: Beth Sarim
summary: In 1929, the Watch Tower Society built a ten-bedroom mansion in a San Diego neighborhood and deeded it in trust for the expected resurrection of Abraham, Moses, David, and other biblical princes — a house literally built for the dead, used for decades by the living.

subject: Beto Carrero World
summary: Built by a self-made cowboy entertainer from upstate Sao Paulo, Beto Carrero World opened in 1991 on the coast of Santa Catarina and grew into the largest theme park in Latin America, spanning seven themed worlds across 14 square kilometers.

subject: Betoota, Queensland
summary: A town with an official population of zero, a single pub, a racetrack and a runway, marooned on a stony desert plain in the heart of the Channel Country.

subject: Better Place
summary: Better Place raised and spent about $850 million to make electric cars refuel like petrol ones. Denmark was one of its two real markets. In the end the receivers sold everything for $450,000.

subject: Bettyhill
summary: A north-coast village of 576 named for the countess who cleared the Strathnaver glens - and home to the museum that preserves the memory of the people forced out.

subject: Beulaville, North Carolina
summary: Once called Snatchet, this tobacco-and-moonshine town in Duplin County was so rowdy locals called it Tearshirt.

subject: Bevatron
summary: The particle accelerator in the Berkeley Hills that proved antimatter exists, earned two Nobel Prizes, and wailed like a ghost for nearly four decades before falling silent forever.

subject: Beverley
summary: A Yorkshire market town named for the beavers in its river, parent of Beverly Hills, with a Gothic Minster, a medieval brick gate, and the easy walkability that has kept its centre intact since the 14th century.

subject: Beverley
summary: The county town of East Yorkshire, founded in the 7th century around the church of St John of Beverley, was once England's eleventh-largest settlement and now lends its name to a Hollywood neighbourhood.

subject: Beverley Bar
summary: Built in 1409 as Beverley's North Gate and toll-house, the brick-built Bar is the only surviving entrance to a town that never quite walled itself, and it still funnels traffic single-file under medieval rib vaulting.

subject: Beverley Uranium Mine
summary: Australia's first in-situ leach uranium mine, where the ore is dissolved underground and the controversy ran deep.

subject: Bewdley
summary: A Georgian river town on the Severn where Thomas Telford's bridge spans the water, Stanley Baldwin was born, Robert Plant performs in a pub upstairs, and the river still floods most winters.

subject: Bezerros
summary: An 1881 prank involving masks and a bowl of cornmeal porridge became Pernambuco's most famous carnival tradition — in the same town where a cordel poet taught himself woodcut.

subject: Bezymianny
summary: A Kamchatka volcano so unremarkable it was never given a proper name -- until 1956, when it produced one of the most violent eruptions of the twentieth century and has refused to stay quiet since.

subject: Beşiktaş Mevlevihanesi
summary: Founded in 1613 on the Bosphorus shore and demolished three times before vanishing entirely, the Beşiktaş Mevlevi lodge embodied both the spiritual richness and the institutional fragility of Ottoman Sufi culture.

subject: Bhaja Caves
summary: Twenty-two rock-cut caves carved into a Western Ghats hillside over 2,200 years ago, where ancient Buddhist monks worshipped in horseshoe-arched halls and a stone carving of a woman playing tabla rewrites the history of Indian music.

subject: Bheemunipatnam
summary: A coastal town north of Visakhapatnam where Buddhist monasteries from the 3rd century BCE, Dutch colonial trading posts, and British clock towers share the same stretch of shoreline.

subject: Bi'r Tawīl
summary: A traveler's guide to the 2,060 square kilometers of desert that no country wants.

subject: Biak
summary: At a festival called Munara Wampasi, people in Biak walk barefoot across rocks heated red in open fires - a tradition that survives alongside dive resorts and World War II wrecks.

subject: Biar
summary: A small, remarkably intact medieval town in northern Alicante where two Christian kingdoms once drew the border between them, its name a memory of the wells that made life here possible.

subject: Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica
summary: Behind a facade of carved stone heads on the Keizersgracht sits one of the world's strangest libraries - and the story of how Dan Brown helped save it.

subject: Bibra Family
summary: The name of a 900-year-old German noble family of prince-bishops and barons travelled, by an unlikely path, to one of the most remote stretches of the Western Australian coast, where a younger son grazed sheep and traded guano on a windswept island in Shark Bay.

subject: Bicolline
summary: Deep in the Quebec countryside, over 4,000 people gather each summer to inhabit a persistent medieval world complete with its own economy, politics, and massive foam-weapon battles.

subject: Bidibidi Refugee Settlement
summary: In north-west Uganda, a stretch of scrubland that filled in months with a quarter-million South Sudanese, and then began, against the odds, to become a home.

subject: Bielefeld conspiracy
summary: In 2019 a German city of 330,000 people offered a million euros to anyone who could prove it did not exist. The offer was entirely serious, and so, for twenty-five years, had been the joke.

subject: Big Banana
summary: A banana grower's roadside gimmick in 1964 Coffs Harbour became Australia's first Big Thing and launched a national craze for giant novelty landmarks that now numbers in the thousands.

subject: Big Bell, Western Australia
summary: A planned 1930s gold town southwest of Cue whose grandest ruin, the art deco Big Bell Hotel, was said to hold one of the longest bars in Australia.

story.title: Big Bend: The Borderland That Both Countries Forgot

subject: Big Bend
summary: The Texas wilderness where the Rio Grande carves canyons at the bend that names it - where the nearest traffic light is 100 miles away, where you can wade to Mexico for a beer and walk back, and where isolation preserved something both nations' governments barely notice.

story.title: Big Bone Lick: The Birthplace of American Paleontology

subject: Big Bone Lick
summary: The Kentucky salt lick where mammoths came to die - where colonists found bones so large they thought giants had walked the earth, where Thomas Jefferson sent an expedition to prove America still had mastodons, and where American vertebrate paleontology began.

subject: Big Burro Mountains
summary: A 35-mile mountain range where the Continental Divide crosses ancient island-arc granite and turquoise veins that Native Americans mined long before copper prospectors arrived.

subject: Big Muddy Badlands
summary: Where outlaws once hid and ancient floods carved a haunting landscape, the Big Muddy Badlands hold secrets in stone.

subject: Big Pineapple
summary: A 16-metre fibreglass pineapple beside the old Bruce Highway became the most recognisable roadside giant in Queensland, and you can still climb the stairs inside it.

subject: Big Red Bash
summary: Billed as the world's most remote music festival, the Big Red Bash plants a stage and thousands of people at the foot of a 40-metre desert dune west of Birdsville.

subject: Big Stone Gap, Virginia
summary: A coalfield town that John Fox Jr. made famous, where Elizabeth Taylor once choked on a chicken bone and the lonesome pine still stands in popular memory.

subject: Big Tex
summary: Born as a 49-foot Santa Claus in the small town of Kerens, rebuilt as a 52-foot cowboy for the State Fair of Texas, burned to his iron skeleton on his 60th birthday, and resurrected the following year -- Big Tex has had more lives than most Texans.

subject: Big White
summary: British Columbia's third-largest ski resort delivers 7.5 meters of annual snowfall, western Canada's largest night skiing operation, and a slopeside village where you can literally ski to your hotel door.

subject: Biga Çayı
summary: The Biga Çayı — the ancient Granicus River — is a modest stream in northwestern Turkey that flows from the slopes of Mount Ida to the Sea of Marmara, carrying with it the memory of one of history's most consequential river crossings.

subject: Bigfork
summary: A small art town where the Swan River meets Flathead Lake - named one of the hundred best small art towns in America, surrounded by cherry orchards, and close enough to Glacier National Park to share its visitors.

subject: Bijlmerbajes
summary: Six identical towers, opened in 1978 as the Netherlands' most enlightened prison and closed in 2016, now being torn apart and reassembled as a green residential neighborhood called Bajeskwartier.

subject: Bijlmermeer
summary: Amsterdam's grand modernist experiment was supposed to be the city of the future. Then the future arrived and rewrote the script.

subject: Bijvoet Centre for Biomolecular Research
summary: Named for the Dutch chemist who first proved which way a molecule actually turns, this Utrecht institute now runs one of the world's strongest magnets - and uses llama antibodies to deliver chemotherapy.

subject: Bila Tserkva
summary: A thousand-year-old Ukrainian city named for a vanished white church, birthplace of a storyteller who inspired Fiddler on the Roof and a sniper who became a legend.

subject: Bilbao
summary: Where a museum changed a city's destiny, where Basque identity runs deep, where industrial decline became cultural rebirth through titanium curves.

subject: Bilinarra language
summary: The Bilinarra language of the Victoria River District carries a name meaning 'rock' or 'hill' and has survived massacres, cattle station displacement, and colonial erasure — though by 2013, only one person still spoke it as their primary tongue.

subject: Billown Circuit
summary: A 4.25-mile motorcycle road race course on public Manx roads, threading through Castletown's lanes and farm hedges since 1955 - and home to the Southern 100.

subject: Bilohirsk
summary: For centuries the great market town of inland Crimea under the name Karasubazar, this city carries layers of Tatar, Cossack, and imperial history beneath the white cliffs that gave it its modern name.

subject: Bilsk Hillfort
summary: The largest fortified settlement of the Scythian age in Eastern Europe, its ramparts running for thirty-three kilometers, and possibly the wooden city Herodotus called Gelonus.

subject: Bimbo's 365 Club
summary: One of San Francisco's oldest nightclubs, Bimbo's 365 Club on Columbus Avenue has hosted live entertainment since the 1930s in an Art Deco interior that time forgot.

story.title: Binalud Mountains: Where Turquoise Grows in Ancient Rock

subject: Binalud Mountains
summary: A mountain range in northeastern Iran whose Eocene volcanic rocks produce the world's most famous turquoise, mined for at least five thousand years from the foothills between Nishapur and Mashhad.

subject: Bindal People
summary: The Bindal are the Aboriginal people of Thul Garrie Waja - some 2,600 square kilometres of coastal country from the Burdekin River to Cape Cleveland - Traditional Owners who have belonged to this place for hundreds of generations and belong to it still.

subject: Bingara
summary: A small Gwydir River town where orange trees grow as a war memorial, a 1936 Greek-built Art Deco cinema still glows, and the riverbed once gave up gold and diamonds.

subject: Bingham, Nottinghamshire
summary: A market town in the Vale of Belvoir where Roman fort, Anglo-Saxon hill court, and modern housing estates layer over the same patch of east Nottinghamshire fields.

subject: Binghamstown
summary: A landlord village built in 1796 by Major Denis Bingham, who set up a toll gate on the road to charge anyone who tried to take their cattle to the rival fair in Belmullet; the gate failed but its Irish name, the Big Gate, lasted.

subject: Biniai Nou hypogea
summary: Near Mao lie two rock-cut tombs holding the oldest known human remains on Menorca, and the story of the first farmers who reached the island by boat with their herds aboard.

subject: Binibeca Vell
summary: A whitewashed Menorcan fishing village so photogenic that visitors assume it is centuries old, Binibeca Vell was in fact designed from scratch in the 1960s and is now nearly loved to death.

subject: Binissafullet
summary: A Bronze and Iron Age settlement near Sant Lluis whose fallen T-shaped taula was the only one on Menorca ever lifted back upright, part of the island's 2023 UNESCO World Heritage prehistory.

subject: Binnendieze
summary: A medieval river system that disappeared under 's-Hertogenbosch as the city built itself on top, was nearly buried for parking lots, and now carries tourist boats through dim stone tunnels under houses.

subject: BioCurious
summary: A community biology lab in Sunnyvale where citizen scientists, entrepreneurs, and hobbyists share equipment and knowledge, pioneering the biohacker movement in Silicon Valley.

subject: Bir Lehlou
summary: A small desert oasis where, by radio on a February night in 1976, a people without a state declared one into being.

subject: Bir Tawil
summary: A colonial surveyor's paperwork mismatch created the only habitable land on Earth that no recognized government claims.

subject: Birao
summary: The northernmost outpost of French colonial Ubangi-Shari, Birao has been burned, exiled to, contested between militias, and occupied by Russian mercenaries - a town whose history reads like a warning about what remoteness can mean.

subject: Birds' Paradise
summary: A small island in Tianma Village covered by an ancient banyan forest — born from a single inserted branch, made famous by writer Ba Jin in 1933, and now home to nearly 40 bird species in the heart of the Pearl River Delta.

subject: Birdsville
summary: At the lonely edge of the Simpson Desert, a town of about a hundred swells to thousands for the races, sells the outback's most famous curried camel pie, and offers travellers one last cold beer before the dunes.

subject: Birdsville Races
summary: Each September a desert town of about 100 swells to some 7,000 people for two days of horse racing, dust and revelry - the 'Melbourne Cup of the outback,' run since 1882 to raise money for the Royal Flying Doctor Service.

subject: Birdsville Track
summary: A 520-kilometre stock route through three deserts, where cattle once walked to the railhead and a mailman became a legend.

subject: Birdwatching in Costa Rica
summary: In a country smaller than West Virginia, over 800 bird species thrive across cloud forests, coastal mangroves, and volcanic highlands - making Costa Rica one of Earth's supreme birdwatching destinations.

subject: Birigui
summary: The city named after a biting fly became Brazil's children's shoe capital - producing 57 million pairs a year from a town that started as a railway clearing.

story.title: Birmingham: The Steel City That Shook the World

subject: Birmingham
summary: The Alabama industrial city that named itself for England's steel capital, where Bull Connor's fire hoses shocked the nation in 1963, and where the civil rights movement won its most important battles in streets now lined with memorials.

story.title: Birmingham: The Steel City Where the Civil Rights Movement Found Its Voice

subject: Birmingham
summary: The Alabama city that was the most segregated in America - where Bull Connor's fire hoses horrified the nation, where the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing killed four girls, and where the steel industry rose and fell.

subject: Birmingham
summary: Britain's second-largest city, the Workshop of the World, where Black Sabbath and HP Sauce and the Spitfire were all invented, and where the canals outnumber Venice's by a wide margin.

subject: Birmingham
summary: Britain's second city, with a population of 1.14 million and more listed buildings than anywhere outside London -- a thousand trades, hundreds of canals, and one of Europe's most diverse migrant populations.

subject: Birmingham Civil Rights Institute
summary: A museum built directly across from the church where four girls died and the park where children faced fire hoses -- the Birmingham Civil Rights Institute preserves the city's hardest truths as a living memorial to the movement that changed America.

subject: Birmingham District
summary: The rare geological convergence where limestone, iron ore, and coal lie side by side in central Alabama -- the foundation that made Birmingham 'The Magic City' and the third-largest pig iron exporter in the world by the end of the 19th century.

subject: Birr, County Offaly
summary: A Georgian town where the world's biggest telescope sat for seventy years, the world's first traffic fatality occurred in 1869, and one Catholic Carrollton's descendant signed the American Declaration of Independence.

story.title: Bisbee: The Copper Town That Refused to Die

subject: Bisbee
summary: The Arizona mining town that extracted $6 billion in copper, deported 1,200 workers during WWI, then reinvented itself as an artist colony - where Victorian architecture clings to canyon walls and the massive Lavender Pit reminds everyone what built the town.

subject: Bisbee Deportation
summary: On a single July morning in 1917, a copper company used 2,200 armed deputies to round up 1,300 striking miners and deport them by cattle car across the desert -- and no one was ever convicted.

subject: Bishopwearmouth
summary: The 10th-century settlement King Aethelstan granted to the Bishop of Durham, now the west side of Sunderland - birthplace of Joseph Swan, inventor of the incandescent light bulb.

story.title: Bisti Badlands: New Mexico's Alien Landscape

subject: Bisti Badlands
summary: The New Mexico wilderness of hoodoos, petrified wood, and otherworldly erosion - no trails, no signs, no water, just 45,000 acres of formations that look like another planet and will swallow hikers who don't pay attention.

subject: Bitcoin City
summary: El Salvador's planned cryptocurrency utopia at the base of a volcano -- announced in 2021, modeled on special economic zones, and still largely a set of renderings and promises years later.

subject: Bitung
summary: North Sulawesi's second city is a port town where sea slugs attract more international visitors than the shipping containers do, and a ferry route to the Philippines opened and closed within two years.

subject: Blachernae
summary: For a thousand years, Blachernae was the sacred northwest corner of Constantinople — home to the empire's most venerated shrine of the Virgin Mary, a succession of imperial palaces, and walls that held off sieges when the rest of the city could not.

subject: Black Combe
summary: Standing in isolation at the south-west corner of the Lake District, Black Combe gave William Wordsworth what he called 'the amplest range of unobstructed prospect' in Britain — and gave Ordnance Survey one of its five Cumberland triangulation stations in 1809.

subject: Black Creek, British Columbia
summary: Mennonite families fleeing the Soviet Union were handed a stump field on Vancouver Island where some of the world's largest Douglas firs had stood, and turned it into dairy farms.

subject: Black Diamond Mines Regional Preserve
summary: Five ghost towns sleep in these East Bay hills, where California's only coal mines once fueled the railroads and ships of a young state, and where a cemetery holds more children than miners.

subject: Black Grave
summary: A towering tenth-century burial mound in Chernihiv where two Norse warriors were cremated with their armor, their idol of Thor, and their ornamented drinking horns.

subject: Black Hawk (nightclub)
summary: The Tenderloin jazz club where Miles Davis recorded, Johnny Mathis was discovered, and teenagers sat behind wire mesh just to hear the music.

subject: Black Isle
summary: It is not black and it is not an island - it is a fat green peninsula between three Highland firths where bottlenose dolphins surf the tide at Chanonry Point and the Brahan Seer was supposedly murdered for telling the wrong truth.

subject: Black Mountains (North Carolina)
summary: A fifteen-mile crest in western North Carolina holding eighteen peaks above 6,300 feet — the highest mountains east of the Mississippi, named for the dark spruce-fir forest crowning their summits.

story.title: Black Rock City: The World's Most Temporary Metropolis

subject: Black Rock City
summary: The Nevada playa where 80,000 people build a city every August, burn it, and leave no trace - the world's largest annual experiment in radical self-reliance, radical self-expression, and radical impermanence.

subject: Black Sea Biosphere Reserve
summary: Ukraine's largest biosphere reserve, a wetland world of shifting bays and sandbars where more than 300 kinds of birds gather and roughly half of all Black Sea fish species have been recorded.

subject: Black Sea Shipyard
summary: The Mykolaiv yard that built every aircraft carrier the Soviet Union and Russia ever launched, from Belgian founding to bankrupt silence in a single century.

subject: Black Stone
summary: A fragmented, silver-framed rock in the eastern corner of the Kaaba - touched, kissed, and prayed toward by more than a billion people.

subject: Black Tiger Spring
summary: Water roars through three stone tiger mouths into Jinan's old city moat -- the second-ranked spring in China's Spring City, and the most dramatically named.

story.title: Black Volta: The River That Draws Nations' Borders

subject: Black Volta
summary: A 1,352-kilometer river that rises near Burkina Faso's highest peak and carves its way south through gorges and floodplains, tracing the boundaries of three West African nations before joining the Volta system.

subject: Blackall Woolscour
summary: The last steam-driven wool-washing works in Australia, where a 1908 engine still hisses to life and artesian water from a mile underground once scrubbed the grease from outback fleece.

subject: Blacklion
summary: A Cavan border village named for a coaching inn, sitting at the meeting point of three counties and the home of chef Neven Maguire's renowned MacNean Bistro.

subject: Blackpool
summary: A working-class holiday capital whose ballrooms launched ballroom dancing as we know it, whose grime scene became a Channel 4 controversy, and whose football team won the 1953 FA Cup with Stanley Matthews on the wing.

subject: Blackpool Illuminations
summary: Over a million bulbs, six miles of seafront, and an autumn season-saving tradition that began with eight arc lamps in 1879 and has been blinking on every year since.

subject: Blackrock, Cork
summary: A Cork fishing village that grew into a suburb, kept its castle and its hurling club, and buried George Boole in the churchyard on Church Road.

subject: Blacksburg
summary: A college town built around Virginia Tech, anchored to Hokie Stone buildings, the Drillfield, and a Pylon memorial that begins with World War I.

subject: Bladensburg Dueling Grounds
summary: A small grove along Dueling Creek near Washington, D.C. witnessed approximately fifty duels between 1808 and 1868, earning the nickname "The Dark and Bloody Grounds" and claiming the lives of congressmen, a naval hero, and the son of Francis Scott Key.

subject: Blaenau Ffestiniog
summary: A Welsh slate town surrounded by black mountains of its own waste, where the National Gallery hid its paintings from Hitler and where tourists now bounce on giant trampolines underground.

subject: Blaenavon
summary: The Welsh hill town built around three blast furnaces and a name that means river's source, now a UNESCO World Heritage town of just over six thousand people.

subject: Blaenavon Industrial Landscape
summary: The South Wales hillside where the modern world was forged, now the United Kingdom's first cultural landscape recognized by UNESCO.

subject: Blaenavon Ironworks
summary: The Welsh ironworks where two cousins solved a problem that had stumped European metallurgy for a century, then watched their own works die because they had solved it.

subject: Blaine, Washington
summary: A town of fewer than six thousand people sits where Interstate 5 runs out of country, guarding a monument to peace and a border that has always leaked in both directions.

subject: Blakeney Lifeboat Station
summary: For over seventy years, a succession of lifeboats launched from the shingle spit at Blakeney Point on the Norfolk coast, saving 65 lives across eight decades before the station was quietly closed in 1935.

subject: Blakeney Point
summary: A 6.4-kilometre shingle spit on the north Norfolk coast where 500 seals haul out at the tip and four thousand pairs of Sandwich terns nest in the dunes.

subject: Blankenese
summary: Hamburg's steepest quarter climbs the Elbe bank on some five thousand steps - a fishing village turned villa district where the rubbish still has to be carried out by hand.

subject: Blantyre
summary: Named for a Scottish missionary's hometown, Blantyre is Malawi's commercial heart -- a city where Indian-run shops, bustling open-air markets, and the country's oldest church sit side by side in the Shire Highlands.

subject: Blarney
summary: A small Cork village whose entire identity hinges on a single stone, a single legend, and the millions of visitors who have hung upside-down to kiss it.

subject: Blauw-Wit Amsterdam
summary: Before Ajax became Ajax, Amsterdam had three top football clubs. Two of them are gone. This is the story of one.

subject: Bleikvasslia
summary: A Nordland village where water built the economy twice over and then drowned half of it - a hydroelectric powerhouse next door to a mine that flooded shut.

subject: Blennerhassett
summary: A small suburban community south of Parkersburg, West Virginia, named for the Ohio River island that lies just across the floodplain from it.

subject: Blessing from the Hilltop
summary: In a land famous for its elaborate funeral rites, a 40-meter bronze Christ stands on a hilltop 1,700 meters above sea level, arms outstretched over the mountains of Tana Toraja.

subject: Block 5A, South Sudan
summary: Of 240,000 people who lived in this South Sudanese oil concession, an estimated 12,000 were killed or died of starvation and 160,000 were forcibly displaced - a war for oil whose criminal charges reached a Swedish courtroom two decades later.

subject: Blockade of Soyapango
summary: In December 2022, 10,000 Salvadoran soldiers and police encircled an entire city to root out gang members, in one of the most dramatic operations of President Bukele's controversial anti-gang campaign.

subject: Bloedel Reserve
summary: A lumber baron's 140-acre meditation on nature and impermanence, where Western landscapes meet Japanese philosophy on Bainbridge Island.

subject: Bloemfontein
summary: South Africa's judicial capital gave the world both the man who imagined Middle-earth and the movement that ended apartheid, yet the city itself remains a quiet place where people eat dinner early and roses bloom everywhere.

story.title: Blok M: Jakarta's Quarter That Refused to Die

subject: Blok M
summary: A shopping quarter born from a Dutch colonial master plan, Blok M rose to become Jakarta's pop-culture heartbeat in the 1980s, crashed with the Asian financial crisis, and is now reinventing itself as a creative hub with underground malls and viral street food.

subject: Bloody May Day (1977)
summary: On 1 May 1977, tens of thousands gathered in Taksim Square to celebrate International Workers' Day — and at least 34 of them did not go home.

subject: Bloomfield Track
summary: A rough coastal 4WD route through the Daintree, the Bloomfield Track was bulldozed in 1983 against a wall of protesters — a battle that helped win World Heritage protection for one of the oldest rainforests on Earth.

subject: Blowing Rock
summary: A North Carolina mountain village that triples in size every summer, where a bubble machine on Main Street pours soap into the air and an actual rock formation blows wind upward.

subject: Blue City, Oman
summary: A $20 billion planned city on the Omani coast that was supposed to redefine the Gulf's future -- until the 2008 financial crisis reduced it to empty coastline and cautionary tale.

subject: Blue Grotto (Capri)
summary: A sea cave on Capri's coast where sunlight filtering through an underwater opening turns the water an otherworldly blue, drawing writers, painters, and choreographers since its modern rediscovery in 1826.

subject: Blue Ledge Mine
summary: An abandoned copper mine in the Siskiyou Mountains whose toxic legacy poisoned Joe Creek for decades until EPA Superfund cleanup buried 70,000 tons of waste underground.

subject: Blue Mountains (Jamaica)
summary: Jamaica's highest and steepest mountain range shelters the world's second-largest butterfly, communities of Maroon descendants who won their freedom by treaty, and the high-altitude coffee that commands some of the highest prices on earth.

subject: Blue Nile
summary: From a spring called Gish Abay to a silt-laden confluence at Khartoum, a 1,450-kilometre river carries Ethiopia's soul, Sudan's cotton, and 85 percent of Egypt's water.

subject: Blue Peter
summary: The world's longest-running children's television programme, broadcasting from London since October 1958 with badges, pets, appeals, and the immortal phrase 'Here's one I made earlier.'

subject: Blue Ridge Mountains
summary: Five hundred and fifty miles of ancient Appalachian crest from Pennsylvania to Georgia, named in Cherokee for the haze that drifts off its forests and once stood as tall as the Alps.

subject: Blue Ridge Parkway
summary: A 469-mile scenic motor road built across half a century along the crest of the Blue Ridge, connecting Shenandoah and Great Smoky Mountains National Parks and now the most-visited site in the entire National Park System.

subject: Bluefield, Virginia
summary: The Virginia twin of Bluefield, West Virginia, was originally called Pin Hook, then Graham, and only became Bluefield in 1924 by referendum — celebrated with a mock wedding between two cities of the same name.

subject: Bluefield, West Virginia
summary: The 'Air-Conditioned City' where Nobel laureate John Nash grew up, free lemonade flows whenever the thermometer hits 90, and a railroad boomtown is still finding its second act.

subject: Blumenau
summary: Founded by a German pharmacist with 17 settlers in 1850, Blumenau grew into a Brazilian city where fachwerk architecture lines the streets, craft breweries pour Dunkel and Weizenbock, and the world's second-largest Oktoberfest draws over half a million revelers each October.

subject: Blyth Lifeboat Station
summary: Twenty-five lifeboatmen died in the early years of Blyth's lifeboat service - a cost that built one of Northumberland's most decorated rescue stations.

subject: Blåmannsisen
summary: Norway's fifth-largest glacier holds a lake shut behind a wall of ice, and roughly every other summer the wall lets go.

subject: Bo
summary: A traveler's waypoint in southern Sierra Leone - more crossroads than destination, where Star beer is cold and the heat is relentless.

subject: Bo'ness
summary: A 15,000-strong Scottish town on the Firth of Forth where Romans built the eastern end of the Antonine Wall, James Watt tinkered with steam engines, and ironworkers cast the panels of Westminster Bridge.

subject: Bo, Sierra Leone
summary: Sierra Leone's second city, born of a railway and a famous school for chiefs' sons, where resolve carried it through war untouched.

subject: Boa Esperança, Minas Gerais
summary: Lamartine Babo wrote a song about this mountain range, and it became one of the definitive melodies of Brazilian popular music - all about a town built on coffee, a river, and a lake.

subject: Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary
summary: In the twin villages of Boabeng and Fiema in Ghana's Bono East Region, some 700 Campbell's mona monkeys and 300 Geoffrey's pied colobus live among humans as sacred beings, protected by traditional law and buried in coffins when they die.

subject: Bobiri Butterfly Sanctuary
summary: West Africa's only butterfly sanctuary, a 55-square-kilometer forest reserve near Kumasi where over 600 species have been documented amid endangered timber and ongoing climate research.

subject: Bobo (gorilla)
summary: A western lowland gorilla who became Seattle's biggest celebrity in the 1950s and 60s, raised as a human child in Anacortes before drawing millions to Woodland Park Zoo, and whose missing skull sparked a decades-long mystery not resolved until 2007.

subject: Bocas de Ceniza
summary: Where Colombia's mightiest river meets the Caribbean, a pair of massive jetties engineered in the 1930s force the Magdalena's ash-colored waters through a narrow throat -- creating the port that made Barranquilla.

subject: Bocas del Toro
summary: A Caribbean archipelago town in western Panama where bars perch on stilts over turquoise water and water taxis are the primary mode of transit between islands.

subject: Bocchoris (city)
summary: One of Mallorca's oldest cities, a mostly unexcavated ruin near Port de Pollença that Rome once honored as a formal ally.

subject: Bochum
summary: A Ruhr city of 362,000 that traded coal mines for cinemas and the longest-running musical in Germany, but kept the soundtrack Herbert Groenemeyer wrote for it.

subject: Bode (crater)
summary: A small lunar crater named after the German astronomer who gave Uranus its name, sitting at a celestial crossroads between three of the Moon's most distinctive features.

story.title: Bodega Head: Where Two Plates Meet

subject: Bodega Head
summary: A wind-scoured headland on the Sonoma Coast that straddles the San Andreas Fault, shelters a storied bay, and sits at one corner of the Red Triangle -- the Pacific's most concentrated great white shark feeding ground.

subject: Bodie Ghost Town
summary: The town that time preserved - California's best-preserved ghost town, where 10,000 people once dug gold and 'the bad man from Bodie' became a byword for frontier lawlessness.

subject: Bodmin Moor
summary: A 208-square-kilometre slab of Permian granite where Cornwall hides its highest hills, its only natural lake, and a big-cat legend that still hasn't been settled.

subject: Bodorgan
summary: A scattered Welsh-speaking village on Anglesey's south-west, named for the great country estate that dominates it - and where a 21-year-old councillor first elected in the 1950s is still in office seven decades later.

subject: Boeing Plant 1
summary: The birthplace of the Boeing Company, where a bankrupt boatbuilder's shed became the cradle of American aviation and the Red Barn that survived demolition became Seattle's most famous industrial relic.

subject: Boekentoren
summary: Ghent built three medieval towers for bells. In the 20th century, it built a fourth - for books.

subject: Boeng Tonle Chhmar
summary: For half the year this Ramsar wetland on the Tonlé Sap is a forest. For the other half you can paddle a boat through the tops of its trees.

subject: Boeotia
summary: The broad agricultural heartland of central Greece — land of Thebes, Hesiod, Pindar, and Epaminondas — long mocked by the Athenians as dull, and long revenging itself on that reputation.

subject: Boesmansgat
summary: One of the world's deepest freshwater sinkholes, a flooded shaft in the Kalahari that has drawn record-breaking divers - and claimed lives in its black water.

subject: Bogenfels
summary: A 55-metre arch of dolomite leaps straight out of the Atlantic surf on one of the most forbidden coastlines on Earth, guarded for a century by the diamond police of Namibia's Sperrgebiet.

subject: Bogensee
summary: A small forest lake north of Berlin that the city cannot give away, because on its shore stand Joseph Goebbels's country house and the Stalinist campus East Germany built to train its youth cadres.

subject: Bogota
summary: Where Colombia's capital spreads across an Andean plateau, where street art covers walls and violence has given way to transformation, where 8 million people build Latin America's unexpected success story.

subject: Bogue Banks
summary: A 21-mile barrier island off North Carolina that runs east to west instead of north to south, where European contact with the state began in 1524 and where Verrazzano's name still marks a historic boundary.

subject: Bohai Shipyard
summary: China's first and only nuclear submarine shipyard, the Bohai Shipbuilding Heavy Industry Company in Huludao has expanded from a small 1954 slipway to a facility with 20 submarine construction bays and capacity to build ships up to 400,000 deadweight tons.

subject: Bohemian Caverns
summary: A basement speakeasy turned legendary jazz club on U Street where Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, and John Coltrane played beneath plaster stalactites in Washington's Black Broadway.

subject: Bohemian Club
summary: San Francisco's most exclusive private club began as a gathering of journalists and artists in 1872, then attracted the industrialists the artists had hoped to avoid.

subject: Bohemian Switzerland
summary: The Czech half of the Elbe sandstone country - arches, gorges and rock castles, a national park argued into existence over nine years, and a 2022 fire that burned an eighth of it.

subject: Boho, County Fermanagh
summary: A tiny Fermanagh hamlet sits atop a 4,000-year-old Neolithic site, gave the world a Procter and Gamble founder, and may harbor an antibiotic that fights MRSA in its blessed soil.

subject: Boiling Down Works, Burketown
summary: On the banks of a Gulf river, a frontier industry once rendered tens of thousands of cattle into tallow and brined beef — until drought, fire, disease and white ants ate it back into the ground.

subject: Boipeba
summary: The Tupi called it flat snake for the way the island curls between ocean and estuary - a no-cars, three-tractors Bahian refuge where the Atlantic rainforest meets reef-sheltered beaches.

subject: Bois Forte Indian Reservation
summary: Spread across three separate parcels in northern Minnesota's deep woods and lake country, the Bois Forte reservation is home to the Zagaakwaandagowininiwag -- the 'Men of the Thick Woods' -- whose 7,300-acre Nett Lake produces more hand-harvested wild rice than any other body of water in the United States.

story.title: Boise: The Idaho Capital Where California Refugees Landed

subject: Boise
summary: The Idaho capital suddenly becoming something - where Californians fled high prices, where the Boise River runs through downtown, and where a sleepy Western town is learning to handle growth it never expected.

story.title: Boise: The City of Trees at the Edge of Everywhere

subject: Boise
summary: Idaho's capital where the Boise River runs through downtown, where the foothills rise directly behind the city, and where a blue football field put the Broncos on the map.

subject: Bojjannakonda
summary: Twin hillocks near Visakhapatnam where rock-cut caves and monolithic stupas preserve over seven centuries of Buddhist worship, from the 2nd to the 9th century AD.

subject: Bokoni
summary: Across thousands of square kilometres of the Mpumalanga escarpment, stone circles, terraces, and linking roads trace a sophisticated farming society that colonial writers refused to believe Africans had built.

subject: Bokor, Cambodia
summary: Nine hundred people died building a mountain resort so the French could escape the heat; a century later the same plateau is becoming Cambodia's newest city.

subject: Bolan Pass
summary: The southern twin of the Khyber Pass, Bolan Pass is a narrow defile through Balochistan's mountains that has funneled invaders, traders, and railway engineers between the Indian subcontinent and Central Asia for centuries.

subject: Bolayır
summary: A small village at the neck of the Gallipoli Peninsula holds the tombs of an Ottoman prince who helped found an empire and a poet whose words lit the fuse of Turkish nationalism.

subject: Boldyni Hory
summary: A green ridge above the Desna in Chernihiv where pagan burial mounds, a hermit's caves, and the graves of Ukraine's writers layer a thousand years of the dead into one hillside.

subject: Bolinas Lagoon
summary: A 1,100-acre tidal estuary on the San Andreas Fault, Bolinas Lagoon is a marine sanctuary where harbor seals haul out on mudflats that shift with every earthquake.

subject: Bolinas, California
summary: A famously reclusive coastal village in Marin County where residents tear down road signs to discourage visitors, Bolinas exists at the intersection of the San Andreas Fault and Pacific counterculture.

subject: Bolsón de Mapimí
summary: A vast endorheic basin in northern Mexico where rivers flow inward and vanish, the Bolsón de Mapimí has swallowed the waters of the Nazas and Aguanaval rivers for millennia while serving as a crossroads for nomadic peoples, Comanche war parties, and the largest private landholding in the Americas.

subject: Bolívar Square (Caracas)
summary: The political and spiritual heart of Caracas, where executions, revolutions, and the remains of a liberator have defined a single city block for over four centuries.

subject: Bom Despacho, Minas Gerais
summary: The German immigrants who came here in the 1920s left behind a cemetery and a handful of descendants who still speak the language - all that remains of a forgotten settlement experiment.

story.title: Boma, Democratic Republic of the Congo

subject: Boma, Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary: Once the capital of Leopold II's Congo Free State, Boma is a port town on the Congo River whose old piers, colonial governor's residence, and oldest church in the country quietly testify to a history both consequential and cruel.

subject: Bombardment of Barcelona (1842)
summary: The day the guns on Montjuïc turned inward, and a government shelled its own rebellious city into submission.

subject: Bombardment of Chios (1681)
summary: A French admiral chasing pirates anchored under friendly flags in Chios harbor in 1681, then suddenly hoisted his colors of war and fired four thousand cannonballs into a town full of civilians.

subject: Bombardment of Tangier
summary: On August 6, 1844, a French naval fleet commanded by a prince of the Orleans dynasty shelled the Moroccan city of Tangier, opening the First Franco-Moroccan War and dragging North Africa into Europe's colonial ambitions.

story.title: Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home

subject: Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home
summary: On a quiet edge of Tuam, a local historian uncovered what an entire country had agreed not to see: 796 children buried in a disused septic tank.

subject: Bonaire
summary: A Caribbean island where license plates read 'Diver's Paradise,' flamingos outnumber expectations, and the entire coastline is a legally protected marine park.

story.title: Bonampak: The Painted Walls That Survived a Thousand Years

subject: Bonampak
summary: A small Maya site in the Chiapas jungle, Bonampak is home to the best-preserved murals in the ancient Maya world - three rooms of vivid paintings depicting royal ceremony, brutal warfare, and ritual sacrifice that transformed scholars' understanding of Classic Maya society.

subject: Bonanza Creek Discovery
summary: The Yukon creek where three men found gold in 1896 and sparked the last great gold rush - where you can still pan for gold on the actual Discovery Claim that sent 100,000 people racing to the frozen North.

subject: Bonanzaville, USA
summary: Forty historic buildings relocated to a single site in West Fargo form a reconstructed prairie village where visitors can make telephone calls between buildings on working vintage equipment and explore several hundred thousand artifacts of Northern Plains life.

subject: Bonn
summary: For forty-one years a German city of three hundred thousand was the capital of one of the most consequential nations on Earth - and then, almost overnight, it wasn't.

subject: Bonn-Oberkassel Dog
summary: Fourteen thousand years ago, a sick puppy in the Rhine valley was nursed for weeks by humans who had nothing to gain from saving it - and buried alongside them when they all died.

subject: Bonneville Salt Flats
summary: The fastest place on earth - where ancient Lake Bonneville left a perfectly flat salt plain where land speed records have been set since 1914, and where the annual Speed Week draws racers chasing 500 mph.

subject: Bono Manso
summary: Once the capital of the earliest Akan state, Bono Manso linked the gold of the southern forests to Timbuktu and Djenne for seven centuries -- until the Asante destroyed it in 1723.

subject: Bonthe
summary: A sleepy fishing town on Sherbro Island where weathered colonial villas remember a busy port long gone, and the only traffic is the slap of paddles against the tide.

subject: Bonthe District
summary: A scatter of low islands and mangrove-fringed mainland where the Sherbro people built one of West Africa's oldest crossroads of trade, faith, and titanium-rich earth.

subject: Bonwire
summary: A small Ashanti town where two hunters watched a spider weave its web and invented Kente cloth, the vibrant textile that became a symbol of royalty, identity, and African heritage worldwide.

subject: Booger Hole, West Virginia
summary: A Clay County hollow in the Rush Fork Valley with one of the most unusual place names in West Virginia, and a violent year in 1917 that locals tried to solve themselves.

subject: Boolardy
summary: A remote Murchison cattle station became one of the radio-quietest places on Earth, so astronomers could listen to the first stars switching on.

subject: Boone, North Carolina
summary: The highest-elevation city in the Eastern US over 10,000 people, where Doc Watson learned guitar, Eric Church and Old Crow Medicine Show grew up, and an outdoor drama has run every summer since 1952.

subject: Boot Düsseldorf
summary: The world's largest boat show happens 600 kilometers from the open sea, indoors, in a Rhineland trade fair complex — every January, with 180-tonne yachts wheeled in whole.

subject: Boquete
summary: A sleepy Panamanian farming village that reinvented itself as the coffee capital of Central America and a magnet for North American retirees, all while keeping its cloud-forest charm intact.

subject: Bor, South Sudan
summary: A river town at the southern edge of the Sudd, Bor has been an ivory depot, a mission cradle, a battlefield, and - throughout - the cultural heart of Dinka country.

subject: Bora Bora
summary: A volcanic remnant rising from an impossibly turquoise lagoon - the South Pacific island that defined the word paradise and invented the overwater bungalow.

subject: Borbeck-Mitte
summary: The old center of a Ruhr district that was once nearly a city in its own right, ruled for centuries by princess-abbesses from a moated castle.

subject: Bordeaux
summary: Where wine became religion and region became brand, where the Garonne curves through golden limestone facades, where France's sixth-largest city cultivates its liquid heritage.

subject: Border Region
summary: Five Irish counties along the partition line with Northern Ireland — Cavan, Donegal, Leitrim, Monaghan and Sligo — making up Ireland's only region without a motorway, holding the source of the Shannon and the Erne, and ranked Europe's most Brexit-exposed economy.

subject: Boreraig
summary: A green and sheltered glen on Loch Eishort where a hundred and twenty people lived in 22 households until they were forced out in 1853 - the ruined walls still standing as a quiet record.

subject: Boring
summary: Twinned with Dull, Scotland and part of the League of Extraordinary Communities where place names became a tourism strategy.

subject: Borja, Peru
