summary: A Spanish colonial outpost founded in 1619 just past the Pongo de Manseriche gorge, where a Jesuit mission once sought to Christianize the Maina people and where the Andes give way to the Amazon.

subject: Borkum
summary: Germany's westernmost East Frisian island, where whaling captains once fenced their gardens with whale jaws and the salt air itself became a cure.

subject: Borne
summary: A small Twente town whose people are still called the flour-bag people, and whose ground holds Charlemagne-era silver and a buried warrior.

subject: Borneo's Dayak Heartland
summary: Indonesia's largest province by area is a world of longhouses, peat forests, and rivers that serve as roads -- where Dayak culture endures against the pressures of modernity.

subject: Borneo's Oil Capital
summary: A Bugis fishing village that became the financial heart of Kalimantan, Balikpapan has survived Japanese occupation, Allied bombing, a secret CIA air raid, and oil spills -- all because of what lies beneath its bay.

subject: Borra Caves
summary: India's deepest caves, carved into the Ananthagiri hills of the Eastern Ghats, where 30,000-year-old stone tools share space with living sulfur springs, orange microbial mats, and a stalagmite worshipped as Shiva.

subject: Borrego Sink
summary: The lowest point of the Borrego Valley at 455 feet, where Juan Bautista de Anza's 1775 expedition dug wells for 140 horses, and where Coyote Creek — the valley's only perennial stream — finally comes to rest.

subject: Borroloola
summary: A small town on the McArthur River where four Aboriginal nations hold the law, a courthouse once overflowed with 3,000 donated books, and the longest land-rights fight in the country finally came home.

subject: Borrowdale
summary: A green valley in the central Lake District where a unique deposit of pure graphite, discovered around 1500, gave the world the modern pencil.

subject: Borth
summary: A narrow Cardigan Bay village strung along three miles of sand, where black tree stumps emerge from the tide and a drowned kingdom is said to lie just offshore.

subject: Boryspil
summary: The gateway city to Kyiv, named for a murdered prince, birthplace of the man who wrote Ukraine's national anthem, and home to the country's busiest airport.

subject: Borá
summary: Brazil's second-smallest municipality, a São Paulo farm town of roughly 900 people that has more registered voters than residents, once led the country in Facebook signups, and waited 44 years for its first robbery.

subject: Bosawás Biosphere Reserve
summary: The second-largest rainforest in the Western Hemisphere covers 15 percent of Nicaragua, shelters harpy eagles and jaguars, and sits at the center of an ongoing struggle between indigenous communities and illegal settlers.

subject: Boscastle
summary: A North Cornwall harbour village remembered for two stone walls built by Sir Richard Grenville in 1584, and the August 2004 flash flood that became Britain's largest peacetime rescue operation.

subject: Bosporan Kingdom
summary: Its rulers wore two crowns at once, calling themselves modest magistrates to their Greek citizens and outright kings to the Scythian tribes; for eight centuries this half-Greek, half-nomad realm grew rich feeding Athens its daily bread.

subject: Bosporus
summary: The 31-kilometer strait dividing Europe from Asia has shaped the fate of empires, sparked myths of clashing rocks, and may have triggered the flood stories of the ancient world.

subject: Bostadh (Iron Age settlement)
summary: A January storm in 1993 stripped a sand dune off Bosta Beach and exposed the stone walls of a village that had been buried for fifteen hundred years.

story.title: Boston: The City Built on Landfill and Revolution

subject: Boston
summary: The Massachusetts capital where the Revolution began and the Big Dig buried an expressway - where half the city is artificial land, where Harvard and MIT shaped American education, and where the accent remains defiantly incomprehensible.

story.title: Boston: The Freedom Trail Through Revolution's Birthplace

subject: Boston
summary: The Massachusetts city where American independence was conceived and launched - where the Tea Party wasn't polite, where Paul Revere rode, where the shot heard round the world was fired, and where 2.5 miles of painted red line connects the sites where tyranny became intolerable.

subject: Botallack
summary: A small Cornish village whose Manor Farm became Poldark's Nampara, and whose seventeenth-century manor still stands in the lanes above the cliffs.

subject: Botallack Mine
summary: The most photographed mine in Britain, where Cornish miners crawled out under the Atlantic seabed to chase tin and copper through tunnels half a mile long.

subject: Botetourt County, Virginia
summary: Once stretching from the Blue Ridge to the Mississippi, Botetourt County is named for a colonial governor who died young - and is the place where the James River first becomes itself.

subject: Bothwell
summary: A genteel conservation village on the Clyde where Henrik Larsson once kept a house, where scarecrows take over Main Street in autumn, and where mining money built the most expensive street in the West of Scotland.

subject: Botswana
summary: A landlocked southern African nation where a river vanishes into the Kalahari to create the world's largest inland delta, where currency is named for rain because rain is that precious, and where diamonds and good governance transformed one of the poorest countries on Earth into a model of stability.

subject: Bougainville
summary: An autonomous region on the verge of nationhood - rugged volcanic interior, some of the Pacific's best undived reefs, and a welcome that has to be earned the slow way.

subject: Bougainville Conflict
summary: A decade-long civil war ignited by the world's largest copper mine, leaving as many as 20,000 Bougainvilleans dead and a path to independence in its wake.

subject: Bougainville Copper Limited
summary: The Australian-registered mining company that extracted billions from a Bougainvillean hillside, paid the island less than two percent of the profits, and became the corporate face of a ten-year civil war.

subject: Bougouni
summary: A southern Malian cotton town whose name means 'small house' in Bambara, Bougouni grew from a quarantine outpost into the bustling administrative heart of its cercle.

subject: Boulia Camel Races
summary: Every July, a tiny Channel Country town ten times its size for a weekend as camels thunder around a dirt track in the self-styled Melbourne Cup of camel racing.

subject: Boulmer Lifeboat Station
summary: In a Northumberland village of perhaps 150 people, four out of every five residents were involved in launching the lifeboat, and the women hauling ropes earned an institutional vellum.

subject: Boulogne-sur-Mer
summary: On the narrowest stretch of the English Channel, France's largest fishing port wraps a medieval walled city around the spot where Claudius launched the Roman conquest of Britain.

subject: Boulonnais
summary: A curved belt of chalk downs, wooded hills, and a coastline that finally turns its back on the rest of France - the northernmost west-facing shore in the country.

subject: Boundaries of Hong Kong
summary: Hong Kong's borders were drawn by treaties, closed by politics, and renegotiated by history — a 30-kilometre land fence and 733-kilometre maritime line that mark one of the world's most unusual constitutional arrangements.

subject: Boundary Street
summary: A three-lane Kowloon street that was once an international frontier — the line between British Hong Kong and Qing China, held in place by bamboo fences and two empires' competing interests.

story.title: Boundary Waters: A Million Acres of Silence

subject: Boundary Waters
summary: The Minnesota-Ontario wilderness where motors are banned and portage trails connect a thousand lakes - the most visited wilderness in America, yet still wild enough that wolves hunt moose and paddlers can travel for weeks without seeing another soul.

subject: Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness
summary: Over a thousand lakes stitched together by portage trails form the largest wilderness east of the Rockies -- a million-acre canoe country on the Minnesota-Ontario border where motors are banned, roads do not exist, and the only soundtrack is loon calls echoing off boreal forest.

subject: Bourke
summary: Where the Darling River meets the red dirt and the saying goes that if you know Bourke, you know Australia.

subject: Bournville
summary: The model village built by George Cadbury in 1879 for the workers at his chocolate factory -- a Quaker experiment in dignified housing that became one of the most influential pieces of urban planning in British history. Still a dry estate.

subject: Bourtange
summary: A village of about 430 people lives inside a perfectly preserved star fort, where the year is forever 1742.

subject: Boutilimit
summary: A modest desert town southeast of Nouakchott, Boutilimit holds an outsized place in Mauritania's life of the mind: a center of Islamic scholarship whose famous family library preserved four generations of learning in the sand.

subject: Boven-Digoel Concentration Camp
summary: Four hundred and fifty kilometers up the Digul River, in malaria-ridden swampland, the Dutch colonial government built a camp to exile the people it feared most — and inadvertently created a nursery for Indonesian independence.

subject: Bovenkarspel
summary: A West Frisian flower town that learned, in the spring of 1999, how silently a hot tub can kill.

subject: BowMac sign
summary: Vancouver's biggest piece of 1950s neon survived the wrecking crew by agreeing to be hidden behind a toy company's logo.

subject: Bowen
summary: North Queensland's first town wears its quiet on the outside and its drama on the walls: 27 murals, a ten-metre mango, and a stretch of beaches that doubled for wartime Darwin on the silver screen.

subject: Bowen Road
summary: Bowen Road traces the contour of Hong Kong Island's Mid-Levels above Central and Wan Chai — a quiet, shaded path built over Victorian water infrastructure, beloved by joggers, and haunted by a decades-long mystery of poisoned dogs.

story.title: The Bowery: Manhattan's Oldest Road and Its Many Lives

subject: Bowery
summary: Before it was a synonym for skid row, before the elevated train darkened its streets for seventy-seven years, before CBGB and before luxury condos, the Bowery was a Lenape footpath -- and it has reinvented itself with every generation of New Yorkers since.

subject: Bowness-on-Windermere
summary: The 'Rio' of Arthur Ransome's Swallows and Amazons, this lakeside town has been waterfront tourism's English capital for almost two centuries.

subject: Bowra Sanctuary
summary: A former cattle station turned wildlife refuge near Cunnamulla, where more than 200 bird species - roughly a quarter of all the birds in Australia - gather on the Warrego River plains.

subject: Boxhole Crater
summary: A perfect bowl gouged into the desert north-east of Alice Springs, where an iron meteorite struck somewhere between five thousand and thirty thousand years ago - young enough that people may have watched it fall.

subject: Boyington Oak
summary: A live oak tree that grew from the grave of a man hanged for murder in 1835, who swore the tree would spring from his heart to prove his innocence.

subject: Boyle
summary: A small Roscommon town at the foot of the Curlew Mountains - home to a Cistercian abbey, a Georgian mansion called King House, and the actress Maureen O'Sullivan.

subject: Braak Bog Figures
summary: Two oak figures, a man and a woman with open mouths, pulled from a Schleswig-Holstein peat bog in 1947 — and an argument about whether they are gods, ancestors, or a restorer's invention.

subject: Bradford
summary: A West Yorkshire city of half a million people that built itself on wool, weathered industrial decline, and reinvented itself around film, food and its 2025 turn as UK City of Culture.

subject: Bradford
summary: The Woolopolis of the Industrial Revolution became the UK's first UNESCO City of Film and the 2025 City of Culture.

subject: Bradford Murders
summary: Three Bradford women lost between 2009 and 2010 became the centre of a case that exposed how easily society can fail those at its margins.

subject: Bradshaw Field Training Area
summary: A former cattle station south of Darwin transformed into Australia's premier joint military training area, where US Marines and Australian soldiers exercise alongside — and increasingly with — the Ngaliwurru, Jaminjung, and Nungali traditional owners of the land.

subject: Braemar
summary: The Highland village where the A93 begins its climb over Cairnwell, home to Scotland's most famous Highland Games and a regular stop on the royal autumn calendar.

subject: Braemar
summary: A village of 808 people that shares the UK record for lowest temperature ever recorded, attended every September by the British royal family for the Highland Games.

subject: Brakna region
summary: Where the Sahara runs out of sand and the Senegal River draws a green line through Mauritania, the Brakna region holds the country's hardest contrast: desert above, river valley below.

subject: Bramble Cay
summary: Australia's northernmost point of land, a 3.6-hectare sand cay at the end of the Great Barrier Reef, where the first mammal extinction caused by climate change was recorded and green turtles still come to nest.

subject: Brandberg
summary: Namibia's highest mountain -- a granite massif that glows red at sunset, shelters over a thousand San rock paintings, and is surrounded by 4x4 tracks so remote that a tourist couple once died of thirst five kilometres from a farmhouse.

subject: Brandon, County Kerry
summary: A Gaeltacht village at the foot of Ireland's holiest mountain, host to a pre-Christian harvest festival, and one of the country's premier wave-sailing destinations.

subject: Brasilia
summary: A city built in four years on an empty plateau, shaped like an airplane and designed as a monument to the future.

subject: Brawley, California
summary: A city built for extremes — where the temperature once hit 122°F, where 177 summer afternoons each year bake above 90°F, and where César Chávez's wife, two professional wrestlers, and a World Series pitcher all grew up.

subject: Brazil
summary: A continent-sized country of rainforests, beaches, favelas, and colonial towns - the only place in the Americas where Portuguese is the official language.

subject: Brazil
summary: A country named for a red-dyewood tree, home to more than 213 million people and the planet's largest rainforest.

subject: Brazilian Air Force Academy
summary: East of Pirassununga, the largest air force academy in Latin America turns 650 cadets a year into pilots and officers - and eliminates a third of them before they ever finish the second year.

subject: Brazzaville
summary: The Republic of Congo's capital sits directly across the Congo River from Kinshasa, making them the world's closest pair of national capitals -- twin cities divided by water, history, and colonial legacy.

subject: Breadalbane Hydro-Electric Scheme
summary: Seven power stations, sixty miles of tunnels bored through Highland rock, and a postwar promise that electricity would lift the glens out of poverty.

subject: Breagh Gas Field
summary: Discovered in 1997, on production since 2013 - a relatively young North Sea gas field whose 100-km export pipeline crosses to Coatham Sands and feeds gas into Teesside's industrial heart.

subject: Brechin
summary: A small Angus town that insists on calling itself a city, anchored by an eleventh-century round tower of a kind Scotland kept only two of.

subject: Breda
summary: A Dutch city of nearly 185,000 people whose history runs through a famous painting, a peat-boat ruse, and the exiled English king who wrote his way back to the throne.

subject: Brejo da Madre de Deus
summary: A town whose name means marsh sits in the dry middle of Pernambuco, holding an island of Atlantic Forest above the caatinga — and, out in its Fazenda Nova district, the vast open-air stage of Nova Jerusalém.

subject: Bremen
summary: A twelve-hundred-year-old Hanseatic port on the Weser that governed itself for most of its history, and put a ten-metre stone knight in the market square to make the point.

subject: Bremen Roland
summary: An archbishop's soldiers burned Bremen's wooden Roland in 1366, so the city carved a ten-metre replacement in stone and pointed its inscription straight at the cathedral.

subject: Bremerhaven
summary: A city bought and built from scratch in 1827 because a river was silting up — and the quay through which roughly seven million people left Europe.

subject: Bremerton
summary: A Navy town on Puget Sound where aircraft carriers dock at the shipyard and a ferry ride brings you from Seattle to a waterfront of fountains and maritime history.

subject: Brevard, North Carolina
summary: A small Blue Ridge town at the entrance to Pisgah National Forest, famous for white squirrels, a world-class summer music festival, and a Windows XP wallpaper photographer.

subject: Brick Lane
summary: One street in east London has been, in sequence, a brick-making track, a Huguenot weaving district, a Jewish neighborhood, a Bangladeshi quarter, and a global arts destination — each wave of arrivals leaving traces that the next found already there.

subject: Bridalveil Fall
summary: A 620-foot waterfall the Ahwahneechee called Pohono - Spirit of the Puffing Wind - where gusts routinely blow the falling water sideways and the mist never quite reaches the ground.

subject: Bride's Pool
summary: A waterfall and plunge pool deep in Hong Kong's Plover Cove Country Park, carrying a name from a legend that has haunted this forested corner of the New Territories for generations.

subject: Bridges of Edirne
summary: A loop of the Tundzha River nearly encircles Edirne, and seven Ottoman stone bridges - some six centuries old - still carry the city's traffic across it.

story.title: Bridgetown: The Capital Built on a Bridge the Arawaks Left Behind

subject: Bridgetown
summary: Barbados's only city grew from a swampy river crossing where English colonists found an Arawak bridge, drained the estuary, and built a harbor that became the hub of Caribbean trade.

subject: Bridlington
summary: The largest lobster port in Europe, a Yorkshire coast town that lands over 300 tonnes of lobster a year and remembers Wallace Hartley conducting on the Titanic.

subject: Brig o' Balgownie
summary: A single gothic arch built around 1320 still spans the River Don in Old Aberdeen - and for five centuries, whoever held it controlled the road north.

subject: Brigade Speciale Beveiligingsopdrachten
summary: From a wooded base outside Utrecht, the Netherlands' elite Marechaussee brigade guards diplomats in Kabul, watches gold leave the central bank, and rides hidden among passengers on flagged flights.

subject: Bright Angel Trail
summary: The Grand Canyon's most storied descent, where a Havasupai footpath became a toll road, a photography studio, and eventually America's most famous inner-canyon trail.

subject: Brighton
summary: A Sussex fishing village turned Regency pleasure dome, where the Prince of Wales built a pavilion in the style of a Mughal palace and the Lanes still smell of fish-and-chips and weed.

subject: Brindleyplace
summary: Birmingham's most ambitious experiment in canalside city-making, where derelict Victorian factories became seventeen acres of squares, restaurants, and offices linked by water.

subject: Bringewood Ironworks
summary: A vanished charcoal ironworks on the River Teme in north Herefordshire, where the Knight family turned wood and ore into iron renowned for its toughness across two centuries.

subject: Brisbane Arcade
summary: A glass-roofed avenue of jewellers and milliners, cut through a city block in 1924 and still trading a century later, all on a fortune left to a medical school.

subject: Brisbane Baylands Development
summary: A 660-acre former railyard and landfill just south of San Francisco that spent two decades in planning limbo before voters finally agreed to let people live there.

subject: Brisbane Showgrounds
summary: Every August the country comes to the city here for the Ekka, on grounds that were a Turrbal camping place, then a colonial garden, then the stage for everything from Bradman's debut to Saturday-night speedway.

subject: Bristol, Virginia
summary: Where two states share a single Main Street, country music was born in a 1927 recording session, and a 50-dollar paycheck to A.P. Carter and his family launched an entire genre.

subject: British Bencoolen
summary: A 140-year saga of pepper, disease, and imperial miscalculation on Sumatra's southwest coast, where the East India Company built a colony nobody wanted -- and from which Stamford Raffles launched Singapore.

subject: British Camp
summary: An Iron Age hillfort terraced like a wedding cake atop Herefordshire Beacon, where the diarist John Evelyn found one of the godliest vistas in England.

subject: British Central Africa Protectorate
summary: The colonial entity that became Malawi began as a scramble between missionaries, merchants, and European empires over the lands David Livingstone described beside Lake Nyasa.

subject: British Empire
summary: At its peak the largest empire in history, covering a quarter of the world and ruling some 412 million people. A story of trade, conquest, slavery, famine, resistance, and the long, painful work of decolonisation.

subject: British Empire Exhibition
summary: A vast and contradictory imperial showcase staged at Wembley in 1924-25, where twenty-seven million visitors saw the empire reduced to butter sculptures, fairground rides, and colonised peoples put on display as exhibits.

subject: British Hong Kong
summary: For 156 years, a rocky harbour island became one of history's most improbable transformations — from a place a British diplomat described as 'barren' to a city that remade the global financial order, built by Chinese hands and shaped by two cultures neither willing to fully let go.

subject: British Kaffraria
summary: Between the Keiskamma and Great Kei rivers, the Xhosa people fought nine wars over a century to hold land that the British Empire kept annexing, renaming, and reorganizing -- but never managed to fully control.

subject: British New Guinea
summary: The British didn't really want it. Queensland pushed them into it. For eighteen years, southeastern New Guinea was an empire's reluctant afterthought.

subject: British Weihaiwei
summary: Britain's forgotten colony on the Shandong coast, leased from China in 1898 as a counterweight to Russian expansion, administered for 32 years, and returned with barely a trace.

subject: British West Indies
summary: An arc of Caribbean islands where sugar and slavery built an empire, federation attempts collapsed under island pride, and six territories chose to remain British long after their neighbors walked away.

subject: British concession in Tianjin
summary: Established in 1860 after the Convention of Peking, the British Concession became Tianjin's economic heart -- until a 372-day Japanese blockade in 1939 and the upheavals of World War II ended eight decades of colonial commerce.

subject: British nuclear tests at Maralinga
summary: Between 1956 and 1963, Britain detonated seven nuclear weapons in the South Australian desert, irradiated its own soldiers, poisoned the traditional lands of the Maralinga Tjarutja people, and then spent decades trying to clean up what could not be cleaned.

subject: Brixton
summary: South London's Caribbean heart, birthplace of David Bowie, scene of the 1981 and 1985 uprisings, and a community whose music, market, and political memory shaped modern Britain.

subject: Brixworth
summary: A Northamptonshire village where one of the oldest Anglo-Saxon churches in England stands a short walk from the factory that builds Formula One engines.

subject: Broby bro Runestones
summary: Six Viking Age runestones stand as a family chronicle carved in granite, telling the saga of a matriarch named Estrid and her husband Osten who journeyed to Jerusalem and died in the Byzantine Empire.

subject: Brodowski, São Paulo
summary: A small coffee town on São Paulo's red earth where Cândido Portinari was born, painted his family's walls, and left behind a house that is now a museum of frescoes.

subject: Broek in Waterland
summary: A pastel-painted Dutch village so notoriously tidy that Napoleon took off his shoes before walking inside.

subject: Broeksterwâld
summary: A Frisian village that became official only in 1964, born from turf huts on the edge of a swampy peatland whose names kept shifting across the centuries.

subject: Broetje-Automation GmbH
summary: Every time a riveting head punches an Airbus wing or a Boeing fuselage joins on the line, a machine designed in a quiet Lower Saxon town called Rastede is probably doing the work.

subject: Broken Hill
summary: Australia's Silver City rose from a single broken ridge of ore in the outback, became the cradle of BHP and a militant union stronghold, and is now the first whole city on the nation's National Heritage List.

subject: Broken Hill Ore Deposit
summary: A boundary rider mistook the world's richest silver-lead-zinc orebody for tin, staked it anyway in 1883, and the buried boomerang of metal beneath Broken Hill gave birth to the company that became BHP.

subject: Bronckhorst
summary: A Dutch municipality named after the smallest city in the country - and built around a town with eight castles.

subject: Bronze Head from Ife
summary: A 14th-century copper alloy portrait head from Ife, Nigeria, whose lifelike artistry shattered Western assumptions about African civilization and sparked a repatriation debate that continues today.

story.title: Brooketon Colliery: Brunei's Forgotten Black Gold

subject: Brooketon Colliery
summary: Long before oil made Brunei one of the wealthiest nations on Earth, a coal mine near Muara fueled a colonial power struggle between a Scottish merchant and the White Rajah of Sarawak.

subject: Brooklyn Heights
summary: New York City's first designated historic district, a neighborhood of pre-Civil War brownstones perched on a bluff above the East River where abolitionist Henry Ward Beecher auctioned enslaved people to freedom and literary luminaries from Walt Whitman to Truman Capote found refuge from Manhattan.

story.title: Brooklyn Navy Yard: The Can-Do Shipyard

subject: Brooklyn Navy Yard
summary: A shipyard on Wallabout Bay that built the USS Monitor, employed 75,000 workers during World War II, and reinvented itself as one of New York City's largest industrial parks after the Navy left in 1966.

subject: Broome
summary: A remote Kimberley town reinvented from pearling port to beach resort, Broome carries the weight of its multicultural past in its cemeteries, its sunsets, and its name.

subject: Brough, Cumbria
summary: A Pennine village split in two by a dual carriageway, watched over by a ruined castle and a church whose four bells are the heaviest full-circle ring in the world.

subject: Bruges
summary: Where medieval Flanders froze in amber when the river silted, where belfries and canals create the fairy-tale city that tourism relentlessly promotes.

subject: Brumado
summary: A Bahian mining town named for the morning fog that drifts down Serra das Eguas, sitting on one of Brazil's richest seams of magnesite and talc.

subject: Brunei's Billion-Dollar Bet on Urea
summary: In the jungles of Belait District, Brunei built one of Southeast Asia's largest fertilizer plants -- a B$1.8 billion wager that the country's future lies not just in pumping oil, but in transforming it.

subject: Brunette Downs Station
summary: On the Barkly Tableland sprawls a cattle station larger than some countries, where the year's biggest event is a bush race meeting that draws crowds from across Australia.

subject: Brunswick County, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's southernmost county turned 47 percent more populous in a decade, trading rice plantations for retiree subdivisions while its barrier islands quietly anchor the Cape Fear coast.

subject: Brunswick Heads
summary: A relaxed coastal village at the mouth of the Brunswick River, where a fishing fleet, timber footbridges and an old-fashioned seaside calm have outlasted the development all around it.

subject: Brunswick Lion
summary: A hollow bronze animal twelve millimetres thick, cast in the 1160s or 1170s as a duke's claim to authority — and moved indoors in 1980 because modern air was doing what eight centuries of weather could not.

subject: Bruntsfield
summary: The Edinburgh district where golfers have teed off for centuries on a former plague burial ground, now lined with elegant tenements and Muriel Spark's childhood haunts.

subject: Brussels and the European Union
summary: Brussels never officially became the capital of the European Union. It just kept hosting more institutions until everyone treated it as one.

subject: Bryher
summary: On the smallest inhabited island of Scilly, a farmer once turned up an Iron Age sword - and the woman buried with it had been waiting two thousand years.

subject: Brühl Train Derailment
summary: On 6 February 2000, the Amsterdam-Basel night train entered a 40 km/h switch at 122 km/h. Nine people who had gone to sleep expecting to wake up in Switzerland never woke up at all.

subject: Brühl's Terrace
summary: A Saxon minister was handed Dresden's ramparts as a personal reward for inventing a tax; an occupying Russian general gave them back to the public, and the result became the Balcony of Europe.

subject: Buan
summary: Thirty-four listed buildings and four hundred eighty-four people across a quiet farming community on the Llŷn Peninsula.

subject: Bucegi Mountains
summary: An ancient Dacian holy mountain where wind-carved rock formations resemble a sphinx and old women, rising to 2,505 meters above Romania's most popular ski valleys.

subject: Buchanan County, Virginia
summary: The only county in Virginia that touches both Kentucky and West Virginia - so far back in the mountains that locals pronounce its name differently from the president it was named for.

subject: Buchanan Street
summary: Glasgow's premier shopping thoroughfare was carved out of a tobacco fortune, repaved in granite, and now ranks among Britain's most expensive retail addresses outside London.

subject: Bucharest
summary: A capital of belle epoque elegance, Stalinist concrete, and Ceausescu's bulldozers - Bucharest carries every chapter of the twentieth century in its skyline.

subject: Buckhannon
summary: An Upshur County seat of about 5,700, named for a Lenape chief whose English-mispronounced name became the town - home to West Virginia Wesleyan College and a strawberry festival that draws tens of thousands every May.

subject: Buckingham
summary: The old county town that gave its name to a palace, lost its primacy to Aylesbury in the eighteenth century, and rebuilt itself in Georgian brick after a 1725 fire.

subject: Buckinghamshire
summary: An English county where Roald Dahl wrote in a garden shed, codebreakers cracked Enigma in a manor house, and beech woods cover the chalk hills the Romans called the Chilterns.

subject: Budapest
summary: Where Buda and Pest merged across the Danube, where thermal baths steam beneath Habsburg palaces, where Hungary's heart beats in a city of imperial grandeur and turbulent history.

subject: Buddhas of Bamiyan
summary: Two colossal Buddha statues carved into Afghan cliffs in the 6th century stood for nearly 1,500 years before the Taliban dynamited them in March 2001, turning empty niches into monuments to cultural destruction.

subject: Bude
summary: A north Cornish surf town where a Victorian inventor lit a thousand stages and tarot's most famous artist quietly died.

subject: Budva
summary: Montenegro's busiest resort town wraps a walled medieval old town in a tangle of beach bars, promenades, and high-rise hotels -- ancient and brash in equal measure.

subject: Buena Fe Canton
summary: A canton in Ecuador's Los Rios province named, literally, Good Faith - born as a roadside shop in 1943, now the agro-industrial heart of palm oil, cocoa, and coffee country.

subject: Buena Vista, Virginia
summary: An independent city in the Blue Ridge that took its Spanish name from a battle in Mexico, boomed on iron and railroad money, and learned what hurricanes upstream can do to a downstream town.

subject: Buenos Aires
summary: Where tango was born in the brothels and bars, where European immigrants built a Paris of the South, where economic crisis and cultural brilliance define the Argentine capital.

subject: Buenos Aires Underground
summary: On a December day in 1913, Buenos Aires sent the first subway in the Southern Hemisphere rumbling beneath its streets, and for a full century the original wooden cars never stopped running.

story.title: Buffalo: The Queen City That Rose and Fell and Rises Again

subject: Buffalo
summary: The city that was America's eighth-largest in 1900, where Frank Lloyd Wright built houses, where chicken wings were invented in 1964, and where abandonment is slowly yielding to rebirth.

subject: Buffalo Bill
summary: William F. Cody earned his nickname by killing 4,282 buffalo in eighteen months, then became the most recognizable celebrity on Earth through his Wild West show.

story.title: Buffalo Bill Center of the West

subject: Buffalo Bill Center of the West
summary: Five museums spanning seven acres house 50,000 artifacts of the American West in the town Buffalo Bill founded, from 16th-century hand cannons to the Winchester factory collection to replicas of Frederic Remington's studio.

subject: Buffalo Creek flood
summary: On a Saturday morning in 1972, a coal slurry dam in Logan County, West Virginia, collapsed and sent 132 million gallons of black waste water through 16 communities, killing 125 people and exposing the human cost of unchecked coal mining.

subject: Bujumbura
summary: Burundi's former capital and largest city sits on the shore of Lake Tanganyika, the world's second deepest lake, where wind off ancient water cools a tropical city that lost its capital status but not its pulse.

subject: Bukchon Hanok Village
summary: Nestled between two royal palaces in Seoul, Bukchon Hanok Village preserves hundreds of traditional Korean houses in a neighborhood that has been home to the elite since the Joseon dynasty.

subject: Bukittinggi
summary: A highland city in West Sumatra that once served as Indonesia's emergency capital, where Minangkabau tradition, Dutch colonial history, and Japanese wartime tunnels converge beneath the shadow of an active volcano.

subject: Bulawayo
summary: Zimbabwe's second city, built over the ruins of the last Ndebele king's capital, where wide colonial boulevards, World Heritage sites, and a subtropical climate converge.

subject: Bulbjerg
summary: A 47-metre limestone bluff over the Skagerrak — the only cliff in Jutland, the only bird cliff on mainland Denmark, and the place where a legend about the end of the world came true in 1978.

subject: Bull Ring, Birmingham
summary: Eight hundred and seventy years of selling things in the same patch of Birmingham, from a 1154 cloth market to a Selfridges clad in fifteen thousand aluminium discs.

subject: Bullring by the Sea
summary: Standing 60 meters from the U.S.–Mexico border and one block from the Pacific Ocean, the Plaza Monumental de Tijuana is one of the world's most improbably situated bullrings — and the site of a 1968 rock festival that became a legendary disaster.

subject: Bulolo
summary: A Morobe highlands town where eight 2,000-tonne gold dredges were flown in piece by piece and assembled in the jungle, some still rusting by the river today.

subject: Bunaken
summary: A banana-shaped island off northern Sulawesi where vertical coral walls plunge into 1,500-meter depths, harboring 70% of the Indo-Western Pacific's fish species in waters so clear you can see 35 meters down.

subject: Bunburra Rockhole Meteorite
summary: A stone that fell on the Nullarbor in 2007 became the first meteorite ever found by tracing its fireball through the sky - and the first whose orbit around the Sun could be wound backwards.

subject: Buncrana
summary: On the eastern shore of Lough Swilly, a small Donegal town with the oldest nine-hole links course in Ireland and a long memory of rebellions, rail lines, and lost industry.

subject: Bunda Cliffs
summary: Where the treeless Nullarbor Plain reaches the sea, it simply ends, dropping in a sheer limestone wall that runs for hundreds of kilometres along the Great Australian Bight.

subject: Bundesautobahn 30
summary: A west-east motorway that took eighty-five years to finally close its last ten-kilometer gap - the only piece of highway in Germany famous for what was missing.

subject: Bundian Way
summary: An ancient Aboriginal pathway runs 265 kilometres from Australia's highest summit to the whale-watching coast at Eden, carrying thousands of years of journeys, gatherings, and obligation to Country.

subject: Bundoran
summary: The County Donegal seaside town that National Geographic named one of the world's top 20 surf towns, where Victorian gentry once hired bathing boxes on wheels to change in.

subject: Bunhill Fields
summary: In a small unconsecrated burial ground just north of the City of London, Daniel Defoe, William Blake, John Bunyan, and approximately 123,000 others found their final rest — mostly because the Church of England refused to bury them.

subject: Bunker Hill, Los Angeles
summary: Bunker Hill in downtown Los Angeles was once a Victorian residential neighborhood housing 22,000 people; the city declared it blighted in 1955 and spent 40 years demolishing it, displacing its residents, and replacing it with the cultural institutions and towers that define downtown today.

subject: Bunkeya
summary: Once the capital of Msiri's vast central African trading empire, Bunkeya witnessed the collision of indigenous power, European ambition, and colonial violence on a remote Congolese plain.

subject: Bunny Man
summary: Northern Virginia's most enduring urban legend began with two real police reports in 1970, a hatchet through a car window, and a man in a rabbit costume who has haunted the Colchester Overpass ever since.

subject: Bunschoten
summary: A medieval Utrecht town twinned with the fishing village of Spakenburg, where flat-bottomed botters still moor in the old harbor and a handful of women still wear a costume their grandmothers wore.

subject: Bunyoro
summary: Bunyoro-Kitara, once the most powerful kingdom in the East African Great Lakes region, survived colonialism, dictatorship, and abolition to endure as one of Uganda's five constituent kingdoms.

story.title: Buraco das Araras Private Natural Heritage Reserve

subject: Buraco das Araras Private Natural Heritage Reserve
summary: A massive sinkhole in Brazil's Cerrado that was once used as a dumping ground for stolen cars and, according to local legend, inconvenient people is now a protected reserve teeming with macaws, caimans, and toucans.

subject: Burcht
summary: The village of Burcht takes its name from an Old Germanic word for birch, not for the fortress its name now suggests - a small linguistic accident that hides 800 years of Flemish history under a single misleading syllable.

subject: Burdaard
summary: A Frisian canal village so small the Elfstedentocht skaters pass through it twice - and where a long-distance swimmer once became its newest landmark.

subject: Bureau of Engraving and Printing
summary: Behind a neoclassical limestone facade on the Tidal Basin, every dollar bill in America is born.

subject: Buren, Friesland
summary: The easternmost village on Ameland keeps the memory of a witch who tied lanterns to cows to lure ships onto the sandbars - until the storm brought her own son home.

subject: Burgazada
summary: The third largest of Istanbul's Princes' Islands, Burgazada carries ancient Greek, Byzantine, and Ottoman layers beneath its pine-forested hill — and was home to one of Turkey's most celebrated short-story writers.

subject: Burhanpur
summary: The Mughal outpost on the Tapti River where Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 -- Shah Jahan originally planned to build the Taj Mahal here before choosing Agra, and the royal bath he built for his wife still bears its intricate ceiling paintings.

subject: Burke and Hare murders
summary: In 1828 Edinburgh, sixteen people, most of them poor and easily overlooked, were murdered and sold to an anatomy school by two lodgers who exploited a city that had stopped seeing them.

subject: Burketown
summary: A tiny, flood-prone town on the Gulf of Carpentaria, Burketown is the Barramundi Capital of Australia and the one place on Earth where pilots come to surf a rolling cloud the length of a small country.

subject: Burkeville, British Columbia
summary: A wartime village of 328 identical small houses on Sea Island, built for Boeing's aircraft workers in 1944 and now the only neighbourhood inside Vancouver International Airport.

subject: Burke–Gilman Trail
summary: A 42-mile rail trail threading through Seattle's neighborhoods and eastside suburbs, following the abandoned corridor of a railroad founded in 1885 by a judge and a lawyer who dreamed of connecting Puget Sound to the transcontinental lines.

subject: Burleigh H. Murray Ranch
summary: A Gold Rush-era dairy ranch with California's only English-style bank barn, built with Italian masonry techniques dating to Roman times, now preserved as a 1,325-acre state park.

story.title: Burlington: Vermont's Lakefront City Where Bernie Became Mayor

subject: Burlington
summary: The college town on Lake Champlain where Church Street Marketplace pioneered pedestrian malls, where Ben & Jerry's was born, and where Bernie Sanders's political career began with an upset mayoral victory in 1981.

subject: Burnham Market
summary: Three medieval Burnhams merged into one Norfolk village so picturesque that Conde Nast Traveler put it in the UK and Ireland's top 20.

subject: Burnham Thorpe
summary: The Norfolk village where Horatio Nelson was born in 1758, baptised in the parish font that still stands, and toasted by his neighbours at the pub he renamed himself.

subject: Burns Bog
summary: A rain-fed peat dome the size of a small city, wedged between Vancouver's highways and its landfill, still doing the work of a wilderness.

subject: Burns Howff
summary: For a few crucial decades, an upstairs lounge at 56 West Regent Street was where Scottish rock and roll learned to play loud.

story.title: Burren and Cliffs of Moher Geopark

subject: Burren and Cliffs of Moher Geopark
summary: A UNESCO Global Geopark on Ireland's Atlantic coast where 340-million-year-old limestone pavements meet vertical sea cliffs rising over 200 metres from the ocean.

subject: Burringurrah Aboriginal Community
summary: A Wajarri community in the Gascoyne, living at the foot of the mountain that bears its name and its oldest story - the boy Burringurrah, whose body, in Wajarri tradition, became the rock itself.

subject: Burry Port Lifeboat Station
summary: The Carmarthenshire lifeboat station that closed for sixty years, reopened in 1973 after a swimming club fundraiser, and looks out on the inlet where Amelia Earhart unexpectedly landed in 1928.

story.title: The Burr-Hamilton Duel: Dawn at Weehawken

subject: Burr–Hamilton duel
summary: On the morning of July 11, 1804, the sitting Vice President of the United States shot and killed the former Secretary of the Treasury on a narrow ledge above the Hudson River in Weehawken, New Jersey.

subject: Bursa
summary: The first Ottoman capital, the great Silk Road exchange, the green city under Mount Uludag - Bursa was where the empire learned to be an empire.

subject: Burscough Priory
summary: Two stone piers in a Lancashire field are all that's left of the Augustinian priory where the Stanley earls of Derby buried their dead and where eight medieval bells once hung.

subject: Bury St Edmunds
summary: The Suffolk market town built around the shrine of a Saxon king the Vikings killed, where medieval barons swore the oath that produced Magna Carta and a sugar factory now powers 110,000 homes.

subject: Busan
summary: South Korea's second city is a port metropolis where mountains plunge into the sea, fish markets rival any on earth, and a world-class film festival fills the beaches every October.

subject: Bushmills, County Antrim
summary: A village of twelve hundred on the north coast of County Antrim, named for a watermill on the River Bush and famous for a distillery whose royal licence dates to 1608.

subject: Butjadingen
summary: A North Sea peninsula whose name and shape were both written by storms - the lands beyond the Jade, once cut adrift by medieval floods.

subject: Butte
summary: The 'richest hill on Earth' where copper built a cosmopolitan boomtown, miners ate pasties underground, and the Berkeley Pit now fills with toxic water as a reminder of extraction's cost.

subject: Buttevant
summary: The Norman market town that gave the world the steeplechase, named for the de Barry war cry 'Butez en avant' - Bash your way forward.

subject: Buttevant Franciscan Friary
summary: Six centuries of friars under one roof in a Cork market town - from David Og de Barry's 1251 foundation to the last gout-stricken Franciscan in Bishop Coppinger's obituary list around 1820.

subject: Buôn Hồ
summary: A coffee town on Đắk Lắk's northern basalt, promoted to township, then to town, then abolished as a town in the sweeping 2025 reform that erased an entire tier of Vietnamese government.

subject: Buôn Ma Thuột
summary: A highland city built on red basalt and robusta, where a tank sits on the central roundabout, Ede longhouses have become suburbs, and almost nobody comes for the sights.

subject: Buôn Đôn
summary: On the Srepok River, Lao traders, Ede farmers and Mnong elephant catchers built a village unlike anywhere else in Vietnam - and buried its most famous son under a tomb that borrows from all three cultures.

subject: Bwana Mkubwa
summary: The oldest mine on Zambia's Copperbelt, named in Swahili for the big boss - a place where copper has been dug since the fourteenth century and where one colonial company's accounting disaster became another century's footnote.

subject: ByWard Market
summary: Ottawa's oldest and liveliest district takes its name from the surveyor who laid it out in the 1820s, and nearly two centuries later still operates as the beating commercial heart of Canada's capital.

subject: Byerstown
summary: A Palmer goldfield boomtown that lived and died in a single decade, undone the moment the road shifted and the coaches stopped coming.

subject: Bywell
summary: A tiny Tyne-valley village with two churches, a Palladian hall, and an unfinished castle gatehouse - a complete medieval settlement preserved in working order.

subject: Byzantine Empire
summary: The Byzantine Empire left a trail of surviving monuments across Turkey, Greece, Bulgaria, Italy, and beyond — a traveler's circuit through mosaic floors, sea walls, and churches that outlasted the empire itself by centuries.

subject: Byzantine Empire
summary: For over a thousand years, the Eastern Roman Empire — which called itself Rome — held together an unlikely civilization at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, outlasting plagues, invasions, and the Fourth Crusade before finally falling on May 29, 1453.

story.title: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos Dynasty

subject: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty
summary: Two centuries of slow contraction, civil war, plague, and final fall - and a quiet artistic flowering that helped seed the Italian Renaissance.

subject: Byzantium
summary: Long before Constantinople, long before Istanbul, there was Byzantium — a Greek colonial city perched on the tip of a peninsula between two seas, whose strategic location at the Black Sea's only entrance made it one of the most contested pieces of ground in the ancient world.

subject: Byōbugaura
summary: A 10-kilometer wall of striped sea cliffs on Chiba's Pacific coast, nicknamed the 'Dover of the East,' where volcanic ash from Mount Fuji and Mount Hakone has been sculpted by centuries of relentless ocean erosion.

subject: Bäniyala
summary: A tiny Yolngu homeland on Blue Mud Bay whose people won the High Court case that returned the tidal waters of Australia's coast to their traditional owners.

subject: Béryl Incident
summary: On 1 May 1962, a French atomic test deep inside a Saharan mountain failed to stay contained — and a cloud of radioactive gas swept over the soldiers, officials, and Tuareg villagers below.

subject: Béthanie (Hong Kong)
summary: Tucked into the pine-covered hills of Pok Fu Lam, Béthanie is Hong Kong's oldest surviving sanatorium — a French neo-Gothic complex built in 1875 that has outlasted empires, occupation, and the threat of the wrecking ball.

subject: Börger
summary: A Lower Saxon village whose name means high birch, founded by Charlemagne's era and so poor that for centuries its men crossed the Dutch border each spring to dig peat for other people.

subject: Böttcherstraße
summary: One hundred metres of expressionist brick in Bremen, built on a decaffeinated-coffee fortune by a patron who courted the Nazis - and whose street they condemned as degenerate.

subject: Børsen
summary: Christian IV's 17th-century bourse, whose spire of four twisted dragon tails was meant to guard it against fire — until 16 April 2024, when the roof burned and the spire came down.

subject: Búng Bình Thiên
summary: The Mekong runs the colour of milky tea past a lake that refuses to go brown - which is why the Cham and Vietnamese who live on its banks call it the lake from the sky.

subject: Büyükada
summary: The largest of Istanbul's Princes' Islands, Büyükada earned its silence through centuries of exile, pilgrimage, and reinvention — and for most of its modern life, the loudest thing you heard was hooves.

subject: Bābā Jān Tepe
summary: A multi-period archaeological mound in Iran's Lorestan Province, Baba Jan Tepe preserves 4,000 years of settlement from the Chalcolithic through the Achaemenid period, including a painted ceremonial hall destroyed by fire in the 8th century BC.

subject: Bạc Liêu
summary: A childless marriage ended here in 1916, and the song the husband wrote about it became the backbone of southern Vietnamese opera - one of several improbable legacies left by a coastal province that no longer exists.

subject: C. Louis Leipoldt
summary: Poet, doctor, war correspondent, yacht physician to Joseph Pulitzer, and cookbook author -- the polymath C. Louis Leipoldt is buried beneath San rock art in the Cederberg mountains he loved most.

subject: C. W. Parker Carousel No. 119
summary: A 1912 Kansas carousel that toured Texas with a circus, spent half a century on Vancouver midways, and was nearly auctioned off one horse at a time before its neighbours bought it back.

subject: C.A. Thayer (1895)
summary: Built in 1895 near Eureka, the schooner C.A. Thayer is one of the last survivors of the Pacific lumber trade, now preserved at San Francisco's Maritime National Historical Park.

story.title: CBGB: The Dive Bar That Invented Punk Rock

subject: CBGB
summary: A former biker bar on the Bowery that was supposed to be a country and bluegrass club but instead became the birthplace of American punk rock, launching the Ramones, Blondie, Talking Heads, and an entire musical revolution.

story.title: COVID-19 Pandemic in the Isle of Man

subject: COVID-19 Pandemic in the Isle of Man
summary: How a small island Crown Dependency closed its borders, lost its lifeline events, and briefly became the only place in the British Islands without social distancing.

subject: COVID-19 protests in the Netherlands
summary: The Netherlands had not imposed a nationwide curfew since the German occupation. When one returned in January 2021, three nights of rioting tore through dozens of Dutch cities and towns.

subject: CSA Mine
summary: Three initials, three nationalities, and a copper shaft that drops nearly two kilometres into the earth beneath Cobar - one of the deepest mines in Australia.

subject: CSS Virginia
summary: Built from the burned-out hull of a scuttled Union frigate, the CSS Virginia became the Confederacy's fearsome ironclad warship and fought the USS Monitor in the first battle between armored ships, forever changing naval warfare.

subject: Ca Mau
summary: Mainland Vietnam's southernmost city carries a Khmer name meaning black water, moves most of its freight by boat, and sits at the end of the country's road network.

subject: Ca Na
summary: A quiet fishing village on Vietnam's south-central coast where the best salt in the country dries in flat pans under a relentless sun.

subject: Caacupé
summary: Each December 8, a quiet hill town in Paraguay swells to nearly a million pilgrims, drawn to a small wooden Virgin a Guaraní convert is said to have carved from the tree that saved his life.

subject: Cabazon Dinosaurs
summary: Two enormous concrete dinosaurs loom over Interstate 10 in the California desert, the eleven-year obsession of a sculptor who wanted drivers to remember his diner.

subject: Cabezo Redondo
summary: A Bronze Age regional capital on a round hill near Villena, where archaeologists found a gold treasure, the weights of a 3,000-year-old loom, and the outline of a real town.

subject: Cabo Blanco, Peru
summary: The Peruvian fishing village where Hemingway hunted marlin for a month while filming Old Man and the Sea, and where a surfer in 1979 found a wave the world now calls the Peruvian Pipeline.

subject: Cabo Wabo
summary: A rock-and-roll cantina born from a Van Halen song that became a tequila empire worth $80 million.

subject: Cabo de Santo Agostinho
summary: A volcanic headland south of Recife that marks the last place South America and Africa were joined - and that a Spanish captain reached three months before Portugal officially discovered Brazil.

subject: Cabo de la Vela
summary: A windswept headland on Colombia's Guajira Peninsula where the Wayuu people guard one of South America's first European contact points -- and the place they believe souls pass into the afterlife.

subject: Cabot Trail
summary: A 298-kilometer scenic highway looping Cape Breton Island, named not for where its namesake explorer actually landed but for a premier's vision of Scottish tourism branding.

subject: Caburé
summary: A sliver of sand between a river and the sea at the edge of the Lençóis Maranhenses, where the dunes shift, the wind carries the beach into your breakfast, and four pousadas stand in a row.

subject: Cache Creek Wilderness
summary: In the serpentine hills of Lake County, toxic soils have produced one of California's most distinctive ecosystems -- a wilderness where poison spawns rarity and bald eagles nest year-round.

subject: Cachi
summary: A whitewashed adobe town beneath a 6,380-meter snow peak in the Calchaquí Valleys, where the church is roofed in cactus wood and the vineyards climb past three thousand meters.

subject: Cachoeira
summary: A Bahian river town where Catholic spires share the skyline with candomblé terreiros, hand-rolled cigars come out of a 19th-century factory, and the Saturday market still sets the clock.

subject: Cachoeira
summary: The sugar, cotton, and tobacco town on the Paraguaçu that Brazil declared a national monument - and where Ana Nery, the mother of Brazilian nursing, was born.

subject: Cachoeira da Fumaça
summary: A 340-metre waterfall in the Chapada Diamantina where the wind takes the river apart in mid-air, so that on most days the water never reaches the ground.

subject: Cachuela Esperanza
summary: A ghost town in the Bolivian Amazon where a rubber baron built a miniature European city -- complete with an opera theater, tennis courts, and Bolivia's first X-ray machine -- only for the jungle to reclaim it all.

subject: Cactus Club (San Jose)
summary: A pioneering nightclub in San Jose's SoFA district that helped transform South First Street from a red-light strip into a cultural corridor, hosting punk, indie, and alternative acts throughout the 1990s.

subject: Cactus Hill
summary: A sandy ridge above the Nottoway River in Virginia where prickly pear cacti grow over evidence that humans lived in the Americas thousands of years before anyone thought possible.

subject: Cades Cove
summary: A limestone valley hidden deep in the Great Smokies where Cherokee trails, pioneer homesteads, moonshine feuds, and a bitter fight against the federal government wove together a century of Appalachian life before the mountains reclaimed it.

subject: Cadiz, California
summary: A railroad water stop named alphabetically by a 19th-century engineer, now the subject of a decades-long water rights battle over whether to pump billions of gallons from the Mojave Aquifer beneath its 35,000 acres to coastal California cities.

subject: Caer Bran
summary: An Iron Age hillfort named for a raven king, where Cornish folklore says the Little People still keep sanctuary among Bronze Age cairns and stolen stones.

subject: Caer Leb
summary: A double-ringed earthwork on Anglesey - possibly Iron Age, occupied through the Roman period, abandoned in the medieval, and small enough to walk around in fifteen minutes if you know where to find it.

subject: Caerleon
summary: A small Welsh town built inside the walls of a Roman legionary fortress - claimed in medieval legend as King Arthur's capital and visited by Tennyson while he wrote the Idylls of the King.

subject: Caernarfon
summary: A Royal Town on the Menai Strait built by Edward I as an English colonial garrison - and now one of the most fiercely Welsh-speaking places in Wales, where 86% of residents were born in the country.

subject: Caernarfon Town Walls
summary: Edward I built a complete medieval town wall around Caernarfon between 1283 and 1285 - eight towers, two twin-towered gateways, an 800-yard circuit, all still standing seven centuries later.

subject: Caerwent
summary: A Welsh village of 1,200 people sitting inside the walls of a Roman market town - some of the best-preserved Roman town defences in northern Europe.

subject: Caetetus Ecological Station
summary: A 2,176-hectare fragment of Atlantic forest in western Sao Paulo where rediscovered black lion tamarins prove an ecosystem can refuse to disappear.

subject: Cafayate
summary: A high-desert wine town in Salta whose very name is contested, and whose intense sun and thin air give the world its most distinctive high-altitude Torrontés.

subject: Cafe Astoria
summary: Opened in October 1949 by an 18-year-old Chinese entrepreneur and six Russian émigré partners, Taipei's Cafe Astoria became the city's first Western-style pastry shop — and for decades, the unlikely meeting ground for exiled White Russians, KMT officials, American soldiers, and Taiwan's greatest literary generation.

subject: Café Tortoni
summary: For more than a century and a half, the marble tables of Avenida de Mayo have held the coffee cups of poets, tango legends, and a young Borges who came for the conversation.

subject: Café du Monde
summary: New Orleans' oldest coffee stand has been dusting beignets in powdered sugar and pouring chicory-laced café au lait since 1862, surviving wars, hurricanes, and the relentless passage of time with a menu that refuses to change.

subject: Caguana Ceremonial Ball Courts Site
summary: In the mountains of Utuado, thirteen stone-lined courts built by the Taino more than 700 years ago remain the largest and most important pre-Columbian site in the West Indies.

subject: Caherdaniel
summary: A T-junction village on the Ring of Kerry where Bronze Age copper miners, a Liberator's family, and a Jadotville commander all left their marks.

subject: Cahersiveen
summary: The town where Daniel O'Connell was born and where a Victorian police barracks built in Bavarian Schloss style still presides over Main Street, in a sky so dark it qualifies as one of four Gold Tier Reserves on the planet.

subject: Cahir
summary: A small Tipperary heritage town built around an island castle - one of Ireland's best-preserved medieval fortresses - at the meeting point of the Galtees and the Knockmealdowns.

story.title: Cahokia: The American City Older Than London

subject: Cahokia
summary: The Illinois site where a city larger than medieval London rose and fell before Columbus - 20,000 people, a plaza bigger than five football fields, and the largest earthwork north of Mexico, built by a civilization America forgot.

subject: Cahokia
summary: The Illinois metropolis that housed 20,000 people in 1100 AD - larger than London at the time - whose massive earthen mounds still rise from the floodplain, evidence of a sophisticated civilization that vanished before Europeans arrived to wonder what happened.

story.title: Cahokia Mounds: North America's Forgotten Metropolis

subject: Cahokia Mounds
summary: The Mississippi city that was larger than London in 1100 AD - where 20,000 people built the largest earthwork in the Americas, then vanished so completely that European settlers assumed the mounds were natural.

subject: Cahokia Mounds
summary: America's forgotten city - where 20,000 people lived in 1100 AD, built a pyramid larger than any in Egypt's base, and created North America's largest pre-Columbian settlement before abandoning it for reasons still debated.

subject: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site
summary: Eight hundred years ago, a city of 20,000 people thrived on the Mississippi floodplain east of modern St. Louis, building earthen mounds taller than most buildings of medieval Europe and tracking the sun with timber circles that rival Stonehenge in sophistication.

story.title: Cahokia Woodhenge: America's Ancient Solar Observatory

subject: Cahokia Woodhenge
summary: A series of massive timber circles built between 900 and 1100 CE at the Cahokia archaeological site served as a solar calendar, discovered by accident during highway construction in the 1960s and now reconstructed at the original location.

subject: Cahora Bassa
summary: Africa's fourth-largest artificial lake, named from the Nyungwe phrase meaning "finish the job" - a 250-kilometer reservoir with a disputed colonial history and a possible population of freshwater bull sharks.

subject: Caiguna, Western Australia
summary: A lone roadhouse at the end of Australia's longest straight road, where the Nullarbor's hidden caves breathe and the unofficial clocks run forty-five minutes ahead.

subject: Caisteal Maol
summary: A ruined keep above Kyleakin harbour, traditionally founded around 900 by a MacKinnon chief and a Norse princess who hung a chain across the strait and collected tolls.

subject: Caister-on-Sea
summary: A Norfolk seaside village whose lifeboatmen drowned together in 1901 rather than turn back - and whose motto became 'Caister men never turn back'.

subject: Caithness and Sutherland Peatlands
summary: Britain's largest blanket bog, named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024 - the Flow Country of Caithness and Sutherland.

subject: Cajon Speedway
summary: A quarter-mile dirt oval that grew up beside Gillespie Field and ran for four decades before a murder and an expiring lease ended it together.

subject: Cajón del Maipo
summary: A river-carved canyon on Santiago's doorstep, the Cajón del Maipo climbs from vineyards to glaciers and the southernmost six-thousander on Earth.

story.title: Cal Orck'o: Where 68 Million Years Walked Uphill

subject: Cal Orck'o
summary: A limestone cliff near Sucre, Bolivia holds over 12,000 dinosaur footprints from nine different species - the largest such collection on Earth - preserved when tectonic forces tilted a Cretaceous lakebed nearly vertical.

subject: Cala Benirrás
summary: A pine-framed cove on Ibiza's north coast where drummers first gathered to protest a war in 1991, and where the sunset drumming ritual has never truly stopped.

subject: Cala Comte
summary: A west-facing pair of beaches on Ibiza's quiet southwest shore, famous for glass-clear turquoise water and a sunset staged behind a chain of offshore islets.

subject: Cala Galdana
summary: A shell-shaped cove on Menorca's south coast, reached by a single road, where a river meets the sea and some of the island's wildest beaches lie a short walk away.

subject: Cala Morell Settlement
summary: A Bronze Age village clinging to a Menorcan clifftop whose people, though they lived above the sea, seem never to have eaten a single fish.

subject: Cala d'Albarca
summary: A wild, hard-to-reach horseshoe cove on Ibiza's north coast, where a cracked natural arch and turquoise water reward only the most determined visitor.

subject: Calabar
summary: One of Nigeria's oldest trading centers, Calabar rose from a slave port to a colonial capital and reinvented itself as the country's tourism hub, where Efik heritage meets December carnival fever.

subject: Calais
summary: France's busiest passenger port and the closest mainland to England - a town shaped by two centuries of English rule, a Tudor reconquest, a Jacquard loom, and a refugee crisis that the world watched and forgot.

subject: Caldas Novas
summary: A cerrado city in Goias where the world's largest hydrothermal complex pumps 1,200 cubic meters of warm water an hour from rock beneath a plateau.

subject: Caldbeck
summary: A Cumbrian village whose name simply means cold stream in Old Norse, Caldbeck holds the grave of John Peel the huntsman, the boyhood home of an American Shakespearean actress, and a 1,106-foot transmitter that beams television across two countries.

story.title: Caldeirão de Santa Cruz do Deserto

subject: Caldeirão de Santa Cruz do Deserto
summary: A thousand peasants built a cooperative farming community on the Chapada do Araripe under a Black lay holy man born to freed parents. In May 1937 the Brazilian state bombed it, and has never said where the dead were buried.

subject: Caldercruix
summary: A North Lanarkshire village whose name comes from a bend in the river, whose 19th-century paper mill closed in 1970, and whose railway station took 54 years and bad weather to reopen.

subject: Caldwell Parsonage
summary: An 18th-century parsonage in Union Township, New Jersey, tied to one of the Revolution's most tragic family stories - a minister whose wife was killed by the British and who was later shot by his own side.

subject: Caldy
summary: A red-sandstone village on the Wirral's western flank, Caldy was a working farm parish until the Caldy Manor Estates Company turned it into one of the most exclusive addresses in the north of England.

subject: Calf of Man
summary: How to visit a one-square-mile bird sanctuary off the southwest tip of the Isle of Man - boat trips, three hours ashore, no shops, no signal, and the chance to walk among the seals.

subject: Calf of Man
summary: A 618-acre island off the southwest tip of the Isle of Man, where Manx shearwaters take their scientific name from these waters - and where a generation of conservationists has fought to bring them back.

story.title: Calgary: The Oil Capital That Plays Cowboy Once a Year

subject: Calgary
summary: The Alberta metropolis where petroleum built skyscrapers and the Stampede builds myth - where oil booms and busts define the economy, where the Rockies rise an hour west, and where Texas-style ambition meets Canadian restraint.

subject: Calgary (Scotland)
summary: A tiny west-coast Mull village reached by a winding B-road, with a sculpture trail through Calgary Farmhouse woods and the beach that named a Canadian city.

story.title: Calgary Stampede: The Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth

subject: Calgary Stampede
summary: The Alberta rodeo that started as a rancher's farewell to the dying frontier - now ten days of chuck wagons, bucking broncos, and pancake breakfasts where a modern city pretends to be a cowtown for over a million visitors.

story.title: Calgary Stampede: The Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth

subject: Calgary Stampede
summary: The Alberta rodeo that became the world's richest and rowdiest - where cowboys and oilmen drink together, where chuckwagon races kill horses controversially every year, and where a city of skyscrapers and petroleum puts on boots and pretends it's still the Wild West for ten days each July.

story.title: Calico: The Ghost Town Walter Knott Saved

subject: Calico
summary: The California silver town that Walter Knott (of Knott's Berry Farm) restored as a 1950s theme park before theme parks existed - part genuine ruin, part reconstruction, now a county park where history and entertainment merge in the Mojave Desert sun.

subject: California Historical Society
summary: California's official historical society survived 154 years of earthquakes, fires, and financial crises before dissolving in 2025 and sending its half-million photographs to Stanford.

subject: California's Great America
summary: A theme park in Santa Clara that has survived ownership changes from Marriott to Kings Entertainment to Paramount to Cedar Fair to Six Flags, sitting on land so valuable that its future has been debated since the day it opened in 1976.

subject: Calipatria, California
summary: A small Imperial Valley city that holds the distinction of being the lowest incorporated city in the Western Hemisphere, sitting 180 feet below sea level in the shadow of two state prisons.

subject: Callanish
summary: A linear village along a Hebridean sea loch, home to one of the most spectacular Neolithic monuments in Europe and a constellation of smaller circles scattered across the moor.

subject: Calle Real, Iloilo
summary: A historic street in downtown Iloilo City where neoclassical, beaux-arts, and art deco buildings line a thoroughfare that has been the commercial heart of the city since the Spanish era.

subject: Caloric ship Ericsson
summary: A revolutionary paddle steamer designed by John Ericsson to run on hot air instead of steam, she survived sinking in New York Harbor only to end her days wrecked at the entrance to Barkley Sound.

subject: Calpe
summary: A Costa Blanca town shaped by two thousand years of watching the sea, for the fish it fed them and the raiders it carried.

subject: Calpe (Bithynia)
summary: Calpe was the ancient Greek harbor on the Black Sea coast where Xenophon's Ten Thousand — ten thousand mercenaries trying to walk home from Persia — paused, debated building a city, and wrote one of history's most vivid accounts of a place seen through the eyes of exhausted soldiers.

subject: Calton Hill
summary: The volcanic crag at the east end of Princes Street where Edinburgh built a half-finished Parthenon, holds an annual fire festival, and tried to argue itself into being Athens.

subject: Calvià
summary: One of the Mediterranean's busiest holiday coasts hides behind an unremarkable name: a municipality whose tiny inland town has been eclipsed by the resorts strung along its shore.

subject: Calydon
summary: Calydon in ancient Aetolia was Homer's 'lovely' city of fertile plains and mythic heroes — home to Meleager, the Calydonian Boar hunt, and the goddess Artemis Laphria — before Augustus dismantled it to populate his new city of Nicopolis.

subject: Cam Ranh
summary: A port city whose ancient Champa roots, colonial fortifications, and 20th-century military history all converge on one of Southeast Asia's great natural harbors.

subject: Cam Ranh Base
summary: Few places in Southeast Asia have been claimed by more flags than Cam Ranh Bay — French, Japanese, American, Soviet, Russian, and finally Vietnamese — each leaving layers of concrete, steel, and history on one of the finest natural deep-water harbors in Asia.

subject: Camanche Reservoir
summary: A 7,700-acre foothill lake built over drowned Gold Rush towns, now stocked with 50,000 pounds of trout annually and surrounded by California oak woodland that shelters bobcats, deer, and one of the state's key salmon hatcheries.

subject: Camas
summary: A paper mill town on the Columbia River where the industrial past meets the Gorge and an extinct volcano provides the foundation for hilltop neighborhoods.

subject: Cambará do Sul
summary: A small, frost-bitten town on Brazil's southern highlands that guards the entrance to some of the deepest canyons in the Americas.

subject: Cambois
summary: A coal village at the mouth of the Blyth that became a notorious gigafactory failure - and where a choreographer is now reviving the old Miners Welfare Institute as a theatre.

subject: Cambridge
summary: An English university city where cattle still graze a few hundred yards from the market square, punts drift past medieval colleges, and eight centuries of world-changing ideas are written into the stone.

subject: Cambuquira
summary: A small hydromineral town in the Circuito das Aguas of Minas Gerais where three sisters left a farm to the enslaved people who worked it, and the mineral springs later made the town.

subject: Camden Market
summary: What began in 1974 as a temporary Sunday crafts market on a disused canal wharf became the fourth most visited tourist attraction in London — a 16-acre sprawl of 1,000 stalls where coffin-shaped handbags and organic kimchi coexist without apparent difficulty.

subject: Camden Town
summary: Once dismissed as unfashionable, Camden Town remade itself into one of London's most vivid neighbourhoods — where canal horses once hauled freight, railway engines transformed the city, and Amy Winehouse found her home.

subject: Camelford water pollution incident
summary: In July 1988 a relief driver poured 20 tonnes of aluminium sulphate into the wrong tank on Bodmin Moor, poisoning the water supply for 20,000 people in Britain's worst mass-poisoning event.

subject: Camera Obscura, Edinburgh
summary: Edinburgh's oldest purpose-built attraction began in 1835 when a woman fought to claim a telescope she said was her inheritance, and it has been projecting real-time images of the city ever since.

subject: Caminito
summary: A hundred-meter alley in the old port of Buenos Aires, painted every color at once by a man who grew up carrying coal there, and set forever to the melody of a tango.

subject: Caminito del Rey
summary: Once called the world's most dangerous walkway after multiple fatalities, this narrow path pinned to gorge walls 100 meters above the river was rebuilt and reopened in 2015 as one of Spain's most thrilling hikes.

subject: Camino Primitivo
summary: The oldest pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, first walked by a king in 814 and still drawing tens of thousands of hikers each year across the mountains of Asturias and Galicia.

subject: Camino Real de Tierra Adentro
summary: The 2,560-kilometer Silver Route that connected Mexico City to New Mexico for nearly three centuries, carrying silver south, settlers north, and shaping the identity of an entire continent's interior.

subject: Camino del Cid
summary: A 1,500-kilometre route across Spain that follows a medieval warlord into exile - not by history exactly, but by the epic poem that immortalized him.

subject: Camocim
summary: A Ceará port named for a burial urn, built up by a railway and undone when the river moved its own mouth.

subject: Camondo Stairs
summary: An elegant Art Nouveau staircase in Istanbul's Galata quarter, built circa 1870–1880 by Sephardic Jewish banking patriarch Abraham Salomon Camondo — a family whose Istanbul legacy endures even as its Paris branch was murdered in Auschwitz.

subject: Camp 4
summary: A dusty campground beneath Yosemite's granite walls where a generation of misfits, dirtbags, and visionaries invented modern rock climbing - and then fought the government to keep their home.

subject: Camp Armen
summary: On a hillside near Tuzla, an Armenian summer camp built by children's hands in 1962 — including those of a young Hrant Dink — was seized by the state, nearly demolished, and then reclaimed through a 175-day act of communal resistance that became one of modern Turkey's most remarkable civil-rights stories.

subject: Camp Bird Mine
summary: A prospector's discovery in the San Juan Mountains produced 1.5 million ounces of gold, funded the purchase of the Hope Diamond, and inspired a country song.

subject: Camp Cady
summary: A forgotten Army outpost on the Mojave Road where soldiers guarded a water hole, Paiute raids shaped its brief history, and California declared it a landmark a century after it was abandoned.

story.title: Camp David: Where Presidents Escape and History Gets Made

subject: Camp David
summary: Hidden in the wooded hills of Maryland's Catoctin Mountain Park, the presidential retreat that FDR named Shangri-La has hosted Cold War summits, Middle East peace accords, and post-9/11 war councils - all from a compound so secret it does not appear on park maps.

subject: Camp Dunlap
summary: A 250,000-acre World War II Marine Corps training base in the California desert that trained artillery regiments for the Pacific — and whose concrete slabs became the foundation of Slab City.

subject: Camp Fuji
summary: A U.S. Marine Corps combined arms training center at the base of Mount Fuji, where samurai once drilled and where American and Japanese forces now share a military landscape with centuries of martial history.

subject: Camp Holloway
summary: A helicopter field three kilometers east of Pleiku, named for a warrant officer killed three days before Christmas 1962, that grew from a transport company's dirt strip into the aviation hub of Vietnam's Central Highlands.

subject: Camp Joe Scherman
summary: Perched at 5,500 feet in the San Jacinto Mountains on land that was Cahuilla homeland for millennia, Camp Joe Scherman was named for California's first state park ranger and woven through with Cahuilla language in the names of its units.

subject: Camp Jones Gulch
summary: Camp Jones Gulch is a YMCA summer camp in La Honda, California, in the Santa Cruz Mountains of the San Francisco Bay Area. It was founded in 1934 and

subject: Camp Lockett
summary: A US Army post in Campo, California where the Buffalo Soldiers of the 10th and 28th Cavalry served during World War II — stationed on the border they were sent to defend, while being refused service at restaurants in the nearby town of Jacumba.

subject: Camp Mather
summary: San Francisco's secret Sierra hideaway, where repurposed city polling booths became cabins, a gravel pit became a swimming lake, and generations of urban families discovered the mountains - all because one determined woman on the Playgrounds Commission refused to wait another year.

subject: Camp Pilot Knob
summary: A World War II Army training camp near the Mexico border that prepared infantry divisions for combat in Italy and the Pacific, operating for barely a year before being closed and largely forgotten.

subject: Camp Salvation
summary: On September 23, 1849, Lieutenant Cave Johnson Couts pitched camp on the edge of the Sonoran Desert and began pulling Gold Rush emigrants back from the brink of death — creating a refugee center that California later marked as Historical Landmark #808.

subject: Campbeltown
summary: A 4,600-person town near the southern tip of the Kintyre Peninsula, Campbeltown once called itself the whisky capital of the world with over 30 distilleries — three survive today, including Springbank, and the town remains one of Scotland's five protected whisky regions.

subject: Camper and Nicholsons
