summary: Founded in Gosport in 1782, Camper and Nicholsons built five J-class yachts for the America's Cup, ferries that helped evacuate Dunkirk, and the largest wooden sailing yacht in the world.

subject: Campina Grande
summary: A cotton town on the edge of the dry country that renamed itself the Queen of Borborema, bought northeastern Brazil's first computer, and throws a June festival that swallows the whole city.

subject: Campine
summary: A vast sandy heath stretching across the Belgium-Netherlands border, the Campine was for centuries a backwater that monks, smugglers, and folk legends made their own.

subject: Campo Bahia
summary: Fourteen brightly painted houses built in a Bahian fishing village as Germany's 2014 World Cup base, finished days before the team arrived and now running as a beach hotel that barely mentions it.

subject: Campo Grande
summary: The capital of Mato Grosso do Sul, a state carved out of Mato Grosso in 1977, where an Okinawan community, a vast urban forest, and a Brazilian Air Force base share the cerrado plateau.

subject: Campo de Perizes
summary: Between São Luís and the Maranhão mainland lies a salt-soaked floodplain that engineers had to reinvent the ground itself to build across.

subject: Campo de Provas Brigadeiro Velloso
summary: The largest military testing range in Brazil, the size of a small country, where a secret parallel nuclear weapons program once came within a year or two of producing a bomb.

subject: Campo del Cielo
summary: Around 4,000 years ago a fireball broke apart over the Chaco and rained iron across the plain; the people who lived there knew the metal as a gift from the sky long before any European arrived.

subject: Campo, California
summary: A small census-designated place in eastern San Diego County near the Mexican border — the southern terminus of the Pacific Crest Trail, home to a railway museum, and historically a stagecoach stop, cavalry post, and gateway to the backcountry.

subject: Campos Belos
summary: A border town in northeastern Goiás where cerrado meets caatinga, built from a chapel donated by cattle ranchers in 1881.

subject: Campos do Jordão
summary: Perched at 1,628 meters in the Serra da Mantiqueira, Campos do Jordao is Brazil's highest city -- a mountain retreat where Bavarian-style architecture, winter frost, and rare snowfall create something that feels nothing like the tropics.

subject: Camí de Cavalls
summary: An ancient coastal path that rings the whole of Menorca, once ridden by island cavalry guarding the shore and now a 185-kilometre walking route linking its most hidden beaches.

story.title: Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Ranges

subject: Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Ranges
summary: A joint Canadian-American torpedo and sonar testing facility at Nanoose Bay, where the deep, obstacle-free mud bottom of the Strait of Georgia creates ideal conditions for underwater weapons trials.

subject: Canals of Amsterdam
summary: A hundred kilometers of water, ninety islands, fifteen hundred bridges - and the seventeenth-century city planners who imagined the whole thing on paper before a single shovel went in.

subject: Canary Wharf
summary: A cluster of skyscrapers rising from the old West India Docks - built on a marsh, bankrupted in 1992, rescued by a tube line, and now the second financial centre of London and home to 105,000 workers.

subject: Canatuan Mine
summary: An open-pit gold, silver, copper, and zinc mine carved into Mount Canatuan -- a mountain sacred to the Subanon people -- that operated from 2004 to 2014, producing roughly 100,000 ounces of gold while igniting a fierce debate over indigenous rights, environmental justice, and economic development in Mindanao.

subject: Canaveral National Seashore
summary: Twenty-four miles of undeveloped Atlantic coastline where rockets launch over nesting sea turtles and place names date to the age of Spanish explorers.

subject: Cancer Alley
summary: The 85-mile stretch of the Mississippi River between Baton Rouge and New Orleans lined with over 200 petrochemical plants, where pollution and environmental justice collide.

story.title: Cancun: The Mexican Beach Resort Built from Nothing for American Tourists

subject: Cancun
summary: The Quintana Roo city that didn't exist until computers selected it - where Mexican planners created a tourist paradise from jungle and sand, where spring break became an industry, and where the Maya pyramids are just a day trip away.

subject: Candangolândia
summary: The first camp built for the workers who raised Brasília, and the neighbourhood that kept their name after the city they made had moved on without them.

subject: Candeias Oil Well (C-1)
summary: The Bahian well that turned Brazilian oil from a rumour into an industry, and gave Getúlio Vargas the stage for the campaign that created Petrobras.

subject: Candlestick Point State Recreation Area
summary: California's first urban state park was born from a Navy shipyard plan abandoned after World War II and a landfill that the state spent $10 million to reclaim.

subject: Canela, Rio Grande do Sul
summary: Named for cinnamon and famous for snow, this highland town pairs a 65-meter Gothic stone church with a 130-meter waterfall in the Serra Gaúcha.

subject: Canike
summary: A 15th-century Crimean princess and kingmaker who made the pilgrimage to Mecca with 300 horsemen, helped birth the Crimean Khanate, and lies buried as "Great Empress" in the cliff city of Chufut-Kale.

subject: Canindé, Ceará
summary: A semi-arid town of 74,000 absorbs roughly 2.5 million pilgrims a year — the largest Franciscan romaria in Latin America.

subject: Canlis
summary: A family-owned fine dining landmark that has shaped Pacific Northwest cuisine from its perch above Lake Union since 1950.

subject: Canna
summary: A small island given to the Scottish nation by a Gaelic folklorist, where fifteen people live, the compass points the wrong way, and the rats are gone.

subject: Canna, Scotland
summary: The westernmost of the Small Isles, where Compass Hill bends ships' needles, a medieval abbot begged the Pope for protection from pirates, and 10,000 rats were eliminated to save the seabirds.

subject: Cannich wildfire
summary: A fortnight-long blaze in the Highlands in 2023 grew large enough to be photographed from space by NASA, destroyed half of an RSPB nature reserve, and triggered an emergency appeal that raised £200,000 for replanting.

subject: Canning Stock Route
summary: The longest historic stock route in the world stretches 1,850 kilometres through three Australian deserts, built by a surveyor who chained Aboriginal men by the neck and forced them to reveal their water sources.

subject: Cannington Mine
summary: Hidden beneath a featureless Queensland plain lies one of the world's single largest sources of silver and lead - the ore body that medalled two Olympic Games.

subject: Canoa
summary: A laid-back Ecuadorian fishing village with sixteen kilometers of mostly empty beach, gentle learner surf, and a Hotel Bambu tradition of trading a cocktail for a bag of beach trash.

subject: Canoa Quebrada
summary: Red sandstone cliffs, a moon-and-star symbol carved above the beach, and a hippie village that tried - and mostly failed - to stay off the tourist map.

subject: Canouan
summary: A 7.6-square-kilometer Grenadine island where Arawak canoe-builders preceded luxury resorts by two millennia, and where an NBA player grew up before a golf course did.

subject: Canovee
summary: A rural parish in the Lee valley that locals still call an island, bounded by rivers on three sides and shaped by the Long family who held it through the Civil Survey of 1656.

subject: Canteen Kopje
summary: A rocky hillside near Barkly West holds up to 2.3 million years of stone tool technology and sparked South Africa's first alluvial diamond rush, creating a site where human prehistory and colonial fortune-hunting collide.

subject: Canterbury
summary: A small Kent city has spent 2,000 years being the most consequential 55,000 people in England - the seat of an archbishop, the destination of Chaucer's pilgrims, the place where a murder in a cathedral changed the church.

subject: Canterbury, Queensland
summary: A pastoralist's carved initials at a desert waterhole grew into a Channel Country township, then a pub, then a ghost town of crumbling earthen walls.

subject: Canton Fair
summary: Twice a year, Guangzhou becomes the trade capital of the world — the Canton Fair has brought buyers and sellers together every spring and autumn since 1957, making it the oldest and largest trade fair in China.

subject: Cantre'r Gwaelod
summary: Welsh legend tells of a fertile kingdom drowned beneath Cardigan Bay — and at low tide on the beach at Borth, the petrified stumps of a real submerged forest emerge from the sand to keep the story alive.

subject: Cao (state)
summary: A small Zhou dynasty vassal state on the North China Plain survived five centuries of fratricidal politics before a fatal diplomatic miscalculation brought it to extinction in 487 BC.

subject: Cape Agulhas
summary: Named 'Cape of Needles' by Portuguese navigators who noticed compass needles aligned with true north here around 1500, Cape Agulhas is Africa's southernmost point and a graveyard of some 150 ships.

subject: Cape Alava
summary: The westernmost point in the contiguous United States, reached by a three-mile boardwalk through old-growth rainforest, where petroglyphs mark a coastline that received Japanese castaways in 1834 and glacial sediments older than civilization.

subject: Cape Aya
summary: A holy headland of grottoes and blue cliffs where the Crimean Mountains make their final plunge into the Black Sea, wild enough that the great marine painter Aivazovsky set a storm against it.

subject: Cape Bedford Mission
summary: The oldest surviving mission in north Queensland, where the Guugu Yimithirr built a community over half a century - until 1942, when the army removed them all and a quarter never came home.

subject: Cape Blomidon
summary: A red-cliffed headland on Nova Scotia's Bay of Fundy coast, sacred in Mi'kmaq tradition as the home of the culture hero Glooscap, and renamed so many times that its final name is a corruption of what the wind does to anyone standing on top.

subject: Cape Byron
summary: The easternmost point of mainland Australia, named by Captain Cook for a storm-cursed admiral, and known to its Arakwal custodians as Walgun, the Shoulder.

story.title: Cape Canaveral: America's Doorstep to the Stars

subject: Cape Canaveral
summary: The Florida cape where America launched its space age - where Shepard became the first American in space, where Apollo departed for the Moon, where Challenger and Columbia broke the nation's heart, and where SpaceX now lands rockets that once would have crashed into the ocean.

subject: Cape Canaveral
summary: The third oldest European place name in the United States, Cape Canaveral has been a landmark for shipwrecked Spanish sailors, a hunting ground for Harvard graduates, a Cold War missile range, and the launchpad for humanity's journey to the Moon.

story.title: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station: America's Oldest Launch Site

subject: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station
summary: The military installation on Florida's Atlantic coast that has launched nearly every American spaceflight first -- from Explorer 1 in 1958 to the Voyagers that left the solar system -- and now serves as the busiest commercial launch site in the nation.

story.title: Cape Cod: The Flexed Arm That Pilgrims First Touched

subject: Cape Cod
summary: The Massachusetts peninsula where the Mayflower first landed in 1620 - where the Cape's distinctive shape bends 65 miles into the Atlantic, where summer people and year-rounders have coexisted uneasily for a century, and where the National Seashore protects 40 miles of beach from the development that consumed the rest.

subject: Cape Columbine
summary: The most westerly point in South Africa's Western Cape province, where a lighthouse named after a shipwreck stands guard over a coastline that has claimed at least nine vessels since 1829.

subject: Cape Cornwall
summary: The headland that was once believed to be the westernmost point of England, before the Ordnance Survey moved the title four miles south to Land's End.

subject: Cape Correntes
summary: A Mozambican headland so feared by sailing ships that nearly a third of all Portuguese India Armada losses happened here, and the sea is named after the killing current that did it.

subject: Cape D'Aguilar
summary: The southeastern tip of Hong Kong Island carries the name of a Victorian general and the memory of a battle, a whale, and a sea cave called the Crab's Eye — a headland where colonial history and wild coastline meet.

subject: Cape D'Aguilar Marine Reserve
summary: Hong Kong's only Marine Reserve, at the island's far southeastern corner, is home to some of the territory's most diverse marine life — and to the skeleton of a fin whale calf that died in Victoria Harbour in 1955, whose flesh fed refugees before its bones became a symbol of conservation.

subject: Cape Disappointment (Washington)
summary: One of the foggiest places in America, this headland got its name from a British fur trader who sailed right past the mouth of the Columbia River and never realized it.

subject: Cape Fiolent
summary: A wall of ancient volcanic cliffs plunging into water so clear it seems lit from below - and the mythic shore where the Greeks imagined Iphigenia was carried.

subject: Cape Flattery
summary: The northwesternmost point of the contiguous United States, named by Captain Cook in 1778 for a harbor that did not exist, where Japanese castaways washed ashore in 1834 and a rectangular sea stack named for a Greek sailor still defies the Pacific.

subject: Cape Floristic Region
summary: The smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms packs over 9,000 plant species into a strip of South African coast, with 69 percent found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Cape Fold Belt
summary: A 1,300-kilometre chain of folded mountains that once stretched from Argentina through Africa to Antarctica, now defining South Africa's western and southern coastlines.

subject: Cape Fugui
summary: Taiwan's northernmost point carries a name that means 'rich and noble' in Mandarin but actually transcribes a Dutch word for 'hook' -- a linguistic fossil from 400 years of colonial layering.

subject: Cape Henry
summary: The sandy headland where 104 weary Englishmen waded ashore on April 26, 1607, becoming the first permanent English colony in North America.

subject: Cape Kiwanda State Natural Area
summary: A sandstone headland on the Oregon Coast where the Pacific is slowly winning a geological war - carving arches, chasms, and tide pools into rock that was never hard enough to resist.

subject: Cape Lookout National Seashore
summary: Fifty-six miles of undeveloped barrier islands along North Carolina's Crystal Coast - home to wild horses on Shackleford Banks, an abandoned village at Portsmouth, and the diamond-patterned Cape Lookout Light.

subject: Cape Maclear
summary: A fishing village on Lake Malawi where 10,000 people, a handful of dive shops, and one dirt road create the kind of place travelers check into and forget to leave.

subject: Cape Maobitou
summary: A headland at the western entrance to South Bay in Kenting National Park, Taiwan, whose Mandarin name — Cat Nose Head — captures the shape that sailors and speakers of several languages have been trying to describe for centuries.

subject: Cape Martian Reserve
summary: A small protected headland where a stray piece of the Mediterranean somehow survives on the Crimean coast, cradling evergreen trees found nowhere else on the peninsula.

subject: Cape May County, New Jersey
summary: A peninsula county where 900,000 birds pass through in a single year, 49% of the land is preserved open space, and storms have shaped the coastline for centuries.

subject: Cape May Point, New Jersey
summary: A tiny borough at the southern tip of New Jersey where a president once kept a cottage and a concrete ship still rests offshore.

subject: Cape May, New Jersey
summary: America's oldest seaside resort sits at the southernmost tip of New Jersey, where a five-day fire in 1878 accidentally created the nation's second-largest collection of Victorian homes and earned the entire city designation as a National Historic Landmark.

subject: Cape May–Lewes Ferry
summary: The only ferry crossing on U.S. Route 9, connecting New Jersey and Delaware across the mouth of the Delaware Bay -- a fleet of vessels that began as castoff steamships from Virginia and evolved into floating attractions with pizza ovens and cocktail bars.

subject: Cape Melville
summary: A headland built of giant tumbled granite boulders on Cape York, where in 2013 scientists climbing into a hidden rainforest found animals new to science - a true lost world above the saltwater country of the Yiithuwarra.

story.title: Cape Mesurado: The Headland Where Liberia Began

subject: Cape Mesurado
summary: The rocky promontory where Portuguese sailors, slave traders, freed African Americans, and the birth of an entire nation all converged on the same stretch of West African coast.

subject: Cape Nome
summary: An Alaska headland where a cartographer's mistake became a Gold Rush legend and an Inuit village faded into history.

subject: Cape Palos
summary: A volcanic headland on the Murcian coast where a Carthaginian god was once worshipped, four naval battles were fought, and a marine reserve now guards the water.

subject: Cape Point
summary: The dramatic promontory at the southeastern corner of the Cape Peninsula, where two lighthouses stand watch over the collision zone of Atlantic and Indian Ocean currents.

subject: Cape Reinga
summary: At the tip of New Zealand's North Island, where the Tasman Sea collides with the Pacific Ocean, an ancient pohutukawa tree marks the place where Maori spirits leap into the underworld.

subject: Cape San Blas Light
summary: Four lighthouses built, four lighthouses claimed by the sea -- the Cape San Blas Light spent over 160 years in a losing battle against coastal erosion before finally being carried to safety on the back of a flatbed truck.

subject: Cape Sao Roque
summary: The point where Brazil's coast turns west and comes closest to Africa - named in 1501 for whichever saint the calendar happened to offer.

subject: Cape Sarych
summary: The southernmost tip of Crimea, named by the Greeks for a ram's forehead, marks the narrowest crossing of the Black Sea and the site of a brief, misty battle between empires in 1914.

subject: Cape Town
summary: Where Table Mountain watches over the collision of two oceans, where Dutch settlers became Afrikaners, where Mandela was imprisoned and apartheid finally died.

subject: Cape Winelands
summary: Northeast of Cape Town, a patchwork of over 500 wine estates spreads across valleys and mountain slopes where European vines have grown since the 1650s, producing world-class wines from Pinotage to Cap Classique.

subject: Cape Wrath
summary: The most north-westerly point of mainland Britain - a Norse "turning point" where 50,000 seabirds nest in cliffs that double as a live-firing range.

subject: Cape York Telegraph Line
summary: Completed in 1887 after years of hacking through some of Australia's most hostile terrain, the Cape York Telegraph Line connected Brisbane to Thursday Island and the wider world -- then quietly disappeared into stockyard fences and shed walls.

subject: Cape of Good Hope
summary: The rocky headland where Africa bends eastward, named the Cape of Storms by the explorer who found it and renamed by a king who saw opportunity -- a place that has shaped global trade routes for over five centuries.

subject: Capilla del Monte
summary: A small mountain town in Córdoba that quietly reinvented itself as Argentina's capital of the unexplained after a single strange night in 1986.

subject: Capital Cafe
summary: A cha chaan teng in Wan Chai that is really a love letter to a vanished record label, where scrambled eggs made with Hokkaido milk sit beneath concert posters for singers who co-own the place, and a piece of toast has been named for Alan Tam.

subject: Capitan Grande Reservation
summary: A 15,753-acre reservation created in 1875 whose heart was flooded by California in 1931 to make a reservoir, forcing two tribes to abandon it — and leaving an uninhabited mountain landscape held jointly by both.

subject: Capitán Pastene
summary: A village of cured ham, dialect, and homesickness, founded by families from the Modenese Apennines who were promised farmland and handed a forest instead.

subject: Capitólio
summary: The self-proclaimed Queen of the Lakes in Minas Gerais - a small town on the Furnas reservoir where tourists flock to canyons and in 2022 a 20-meter rock wall collapsed onto pleasure boats.

story.title: Cappadocia: The Underground Cities That Hid 20,000 People

subject: Cappadocia
summary: Where ancient Anatolians carved entire cities into soft volcanic rock, creating underground labyrinths eight stories deep that sheltered thousands during invasions for millennia.

subject: Capri
summary: The island that emperors and celebrities have sought for two millennia - where the Blue Grotto glows with impossible light, limestone cliffs plunge into azure waters, and day-trippers share space with the ghosts of Tiberius.

subject: Captain Thunderbolt's Death Site
summary: A quiet paddock near Uralla where a single constable ended the long career of bushranger Captain Thunderbolt in 1870.

subject: Captain Thunderbolt's Grave
summary: In a corner of Uralla's old cemetery lies the bushranger Frederick Ward, beneath a headstone a town paid for decades after his death.

subject: Captain Thunderbolt's Rock
summary: A granite outcrop south of Uralla where Australia's longest-roaming bushranger began and very nearly ended his career.

subject: Captaincy General of Venezuela
summary: Created by royal decree in 1777, the Captaincy General of Venezuela stitched six scattered provinces into a single administrative unit — inadvertently drawing the borders of a nation that would rebel against Spain within a generation.

subject: Captaincy of São Paulo
summary: A colonial territory that was carved apart over two centuries, losing Minas Gerais, Goiás, Mato Grosso, Santa Catarina, and Paraná before becoming the Brazilian state that today anchors South America's largest economy.

subject: Capture of Abbasabad
summary: In July 1827, a six-day siege and a decisive cavalry battle in the Nakhichevan Khanate broke Persian resistance and opened the road to peace negotiations that would redraw the map of the Caucasus.

subject: Capture of Abimael Guzmán
summary: On September 12, 1992, a small team of Peruvian intelligence agents tracked the leader of the Shining Path to an upstairs room in a Lima dance studio, ending a manhunt that had consumed Peru for over a decade.

subject: Capture of Lubumbashi
summary: In April 1997, fewer than 300 rebels seized Zaire's second-largest city in a battle that lasted barely two days, ending Mobutu's grip on the mineral-rich Katanga province and setting the stage for his regime's final collapse.

subject: Capture of Minorca (1798)
summary: In eight days of November 1798, a British force seized Menorca from Spain with barely a shot fired, all to win one magnificent harbour.

subject: Capture of Montserrat
summary: In February 1782, a French naval squadron seized the Caribbean island of Montserrat from the British in a swift wartime capture tied to the American Revolution's ripple effects across the West Indies.

subject: Capture of Muscat (1507)
summary: The brutal Portuguese conquest of Muscat in 1507, when Afonso de Albuquerque's seven ships and 500 men burned the principal trading port of the Kingdom of Hormuz to the ground.

subject: Capture of Port Egmont
summary: In 1770 a handful of British troops on a fogbound Falklands shore faced 1,400 Spanish soldiers, surrendered without a death, and nearly dragged three empires into war.

subject: Capture of Sint Eustatius
summary: A British admiral's greed on a tiny Caribbean island may have cost Britain the American Revolution.

subject: Capture of St. Lucia
summary: In December 1778, a British expeditionary force seized the French island of St. Lucia in a ten-day campaign that featured a naval battle, a lopsided land engagement, and a regimental tradition born from white feathers plucked off fallen enemies.

subject: Capture of the Bahamas (1783)
summary: In April 1783, a Loyalist officer named Andrew Deveaux sailed from Saint Augustine with seventy men, bluffed and stormed his way past a Spanish garrison of over 600, and recaptured Nassau for Britain -- only to learn the peace treaty had already made the whole adventure unnecessary.

subject: Caputh
summary: A lakeside village south of Potsdam where Albert Einstein built a small wooden summer house in 1929, used it for four seasons, and left it forever - the only home of his that still stands in Germany.

subject: Caracas helicopter incident
summary: In June 2017, a police investigator and film actor flew a stolen helicopter over central Caracas, dropping stun grenades on the Supreme Court and Interior Ministry in a dramatic one-man protest against the Maduro government.

subject: Caracas-La Guaira highway
summary: The audacious 1950s highway that punched through mountains to connect Caracas to the sea in 20 minutes - a showcase of oil-wealth engineering that earthquakes and landslides have been trying to undo ever since.

subject: Caraíva
summary: A roadless Bahian village where you arrive by canoe, walk on sand streets, and meet the Pataxó whose ancestors greeted the first Portuguese ships five centuries ago.

subject: Cardamom Mountains
summary: Cambodia's largest mountain range shelters one of Southeast Asia's most intact tropical rainforests, harboring at least 62 globally threatened species alongside ancient rock art, jar burial sites, and indigenous communities whose traditions predate the Angkor empire.

subject: Cardamom Mountains rain forests
summary: A 44,000-square-kilometre ecoregion across Thailand, Cambodia and Phu Quoc island where the rainforest runs from waist-high conifer bog to thirty-metre tropical oak canopy, and where science still has not finished the inventory.

subject: Cardamom and Elephant Mountains
summary: Eight Cambodian provinces wrapped around two mountain ranges you can drive around but barely across - a region where the coast reinvented itself in five years and the interior has scarcely changed in fifty.

subject: Cardia (Thrace)
summary: For two centuries Cardia played every great power in the ancient Aegean against the others — until the general who won the whole board decided the city itself was more useful as building material.

subject: Cardiff Docks
summary: At its 1913 peak, the seven-mile dock system on the south side of Cardiff was one of the world's largest ports, exporting more coal than anywhere on earth - a place where 122 shipping companies operated, and from which the modern city sprang.

subject: Cardiff-by-the-Sea
summary: A Welsh immigrant named Esther Cullen reached California in 1911, looked at the new coastal subdivision her husband was developing, thought of the town in Wales where she was born, and gave it a name that has stuck for more than a century.

subject: Cardigan Lifeboat Station
summary: Volunteers have launched from Cardigan since 1849, including the first all-female lifeboat crew in Wales — answering calls from a sandbar that has wrecked ships for centuries.

subject: Cardigan Priory
summary: A Benedictine priory founded around 1115 became home to a brilliant 17th-century poet, then vanished as a monastic institution at the Dissolution.

subject: Cardigan, Ceredigion
summary: A small Welsh town at the mouth of the Teifi that once owned seven times as many ships as Cardiff — and now makes denim that ended up on a duchess.

subject: Cardona
summary: A Catalan town beside a genuine mountain of translucent rock salt, guarded by a fortress whose dukes grew so rich on the mineral they were called kings without crowns.

subject: Cardwell UFO Festival
summary: Australia's only UFO festival turns a sleepy tropical town into a gathering place for believers, sceptics and the merely curious - all of it rooted in a banana farmer's strange morning in 1966.

subject: Carew
summary: A Pembrokeshire village with an 11th-century Celtic cross marking a forgotten Welsh king, a Norman castle that became an Elizabethan mansion, and a cricket scandal serious enough to make the BBC.

subject: Caribbean
summary: Hundreds of islands strung between two continents, shaped by sugar and slavery, colonized by six empires, and home to a musical and culinary culture found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Caribbean English
summary: The oldest export of the English language from Britain - a family of dialects shaped by Elizabethan settlers, enslaved West Africans, Irish indentured servants, and Indian laborers, spoken across more than 20 territories where 'Where is that boy?' becomes a different sentence on every island.

subject: Carihuairazo
summary: An eroded Ecuadorian stratovolcano whose Quichua name means 'man of ice and wind' - according to Andean legend, destroyed by Father Chimborazo himself in a fight over the love of Mama Tungurahua.

subject: Cariló
summary: A resort town where the streets are still made of sand, the houses hide inside a forest that humans planted, and the road names spell out, alphabetically, the local trees and birds.

story.title: Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site

subject: Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site
summary: A 264-acre estate in the Blue Ridge foothills of North Carolina where America's beloved poet Carl Sandburg spent his final 22 years, writing among bookshelves, goats, and the quiet rhythms of mountain life.

subject: Carlingford
summary: A medieval walled town on the Cooley Peninsula whose narrow lanes, ruined castle, town gate, and Mint townhouse still stand beneath Slieve Foy mountain.

subject: Carlisle
summary: Cumbria's only city - a compact red-sandstone cathedral town ten miles from the Scottish border, where Romans, Reivers and railways all converged, and most travellers still treat as a one-night stop on the way north.

subject: Carlisle
summary: The most besieged place in the British Isles - a Roman garrison that became a Norman castle town, a Reiver stronghold, a Jacobite trophy, and the largest cotton-mill city in Cumberland, all within walls that still half-stand on a slight rise above the Eden.

subject: Carloway
summary: A crofting district on the west coast of Lewis built around one of Scotland's finest Iron Age brochs, where football, Gaelic and an annual Highland Games still hold a small community together.

story.title: Carlsbad Caverns Bat Flight: 400,000 Wings at Sunset

subject: Carlsbad Caverns Bat Flight
summary: The New Mexico cave where hundreds of thousands of Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral out at dusk - a vortex of wings discovered by ranchers who thought the rising column was smoke from a fire.

subject: Carlsbad by the Sea
summary: A well-driller discovered mineral water in 1882 that tasted like the famous springs of Karlsbad, Bohemia — and the name of a European spa town crossed an ocean to become a California city.

subject: Carlsbad, California
summary: Named for a Bohemian spa town by way of a mineral spring discovered in 1882, Carlsbad grew from a railroad stop into one of the more deliberately planned cities on the Southern California coast.

subject: Carlsberg District
summary: The Copenhagen brewery grounds where a scientist defined the pH scale and another isolated pure lager yeast, now 33 hectares of ornate industrial architecture turning into a neighbourhood.

subject: Carmarthen
summary: Wales's claimant to oldest-town status, founded as Roman Moridunum, named for Merlin in Welsh, and built around a castle, an Augustinian priory, and a vanishing oak.

subject: Carmarthenshire
summary: Wales's largest historic county, the 'Garden of Wales' - a stretch of green hills, drowned estuaries, ruined castles, and Dylan Thomas's last writing shed.

subject: Carmel Head
summary: The northwest tip of Anglesey, where three white pillars known locally as the White Ladies line up across the headland and an offshore island to mark a reef that has been wrecking ships for two hundred years -- and where the rocks themselves are the oldest in Wales.

subject: Carmen de Andacollo
summary: A copper mine carved into hills that have drawn gold seekers and pilgrims to a dark-faced Madonna for four centuries.

subject: Carmen de Patagones
summary: The oldest town in Patagonia, founded by settlers from northern Spain whose descendants are still called maragatos, and the place where armed townsfolk once captured a Brazilian fleet's battle flags.

subject: Carn Fadryn
summary: A 1,217-foot conical hill in the centre of the Llyn Peninsula, fortified in the Iron Age, refortified by the sons of Owain Gwynedd, and offering one of the great views in Wales.

subject: Carnaby Street
summary: A Soho backstreet of sweatshops and a Central Electricity Board depot that became, in fifteen years, the most photographed shopping street on Earth - and the place where a Victorian doctor first proved how cholera moved.

subject: Carnarvon
summary: A banana-growing town at the mouth of a river that is usually dry, where a giant Cold War dish still points at the sky and the night reveals a southern firmament most northerners have never seen.

subject: Carnarvon Tracking Station
summary: For twelve years, a cluster of antennas in the Western Australian scrub was NASA's eyes and ears on spacecraft bound for the Moon — and often the last station to hear from them before they vanished over the Pacific.

subject: Carnaval de Ponce
summary: Puerto Rico's oldest and largest carnival, dating to 1858, where papier-mache vejigante masks with multiple horns transform Ponce's streets into a week-long collision of Spanish, African, and Antillean traditions.

subject: Carncastle
summary: A tiny County Antrim village above the sea where Ned Stark filmed an execution, a Spanish Armada sailor sprouted a chestnut tree, and a Bronze Age fort still stands.

subject: Carndonagh
summary: The market town of Inishowen's north, anchored by a seventh-century high cross, and the gateway to Malin Head, the northernmost point on the Irish mainland.

subject: Carnedd Llewelyn
summary: At 1,064 metres, the second-highest summit in Wales carries the name of the last independent Welsh prince - and the wreckage of a 1950 RAF bomber on its boulder plateau.

subject: Carneddau
summary: The largest unbroken expanse of high ground in Wales and England - eighteen peaks, a herd of feral ponies, and the bones of Iron Age villages still visible from the air.

subject: Carnewas and Bedruthan Steps
summary: Slate stacks rise like islands stranded on Cornwall's north coast, a procession of giant stepping stones that no human foot has ever crossed.

subject: Carnival of Vinaròs
summary: For eleven days each winter, a small fishing town on the Castellón coast throws one of Spain's liveliest carnivals, complete with flour battles, secret queens' costumes, and a giant effigy burned on the beach.

subject: Carnoustie Golf Links
summary: Scotland's most punishing championship course, where the wind off the North Sea and the Barry Burn have humbled the world's best golfers for nearly two centuries.

subject: Carolina Sandhills
summary: A belt of wind-blown ancient dunes across three states, once carpeted in longleaf pine and now reduced to a fragile one percent of what it was.

subject: Carolinas
summary: Two states named for a single king, sharing tobacco fields, hurricane coasts, and an argument about what the South means.

subject: Carowinds
summary: The amusement park that opened in 1973 straddling the Carolinas line - now Six Flags' Carolinas flagship and home to one of the tallest roller coasters in the world.

subject: Carrara
summary: The town whose very name means 'quarries' has supplied white marble to sculptors from Michelangelo to the present day -- while its quarry workers built one of the most enduring anarchist movements in Europe.

subject: Carrboro, North Carolina
summary: A former mill town that became one of the South's most progressive municipalities, while still bearing the name of a Confederate veteran and white supremacist.

subject: Carretera Austral
summary: Chile's Route 7 stitches together a thousand kilometers of fjords, glaciers and rainforest that no road had ever reached - the highway built to claim a corner of the world.

subject: Carriacou
summary: Grenada's quiet second island, Carriacou was named 'surrounded by reefs' by its earliest inhabitants -- and those reefs, once obstacles to commerce, are now the main reason visitors come.

subject: Carrick-on-Shannon
summary: The county town of Leitrim straddles the Shannon at one of its oldest fording points - a small inland river port that grew from castle to charter to canal to capital of Ireland's narrowboat fleet.

subject: Carrick-on-Suir
summary: A Norman-Butler town on the tidal Suir that gave Ireland its first GAA president, a cycling world champion, and the Clancy Brothers.

subject: Carrickfergus
summary: The Norman castle on the rock of Fergus made this Belfast Lough town the only English foothold in Ulster for four hundred years.

subject: Carrickmore
summary: A small Tyrone village that is the ancestral home of Kurt Cobain, the site of a 6,000-year-old neolithic tomb, and home to a stand pulled out of Croke Park itself.

subject: Carrigeenamronety Hill
summary: A 401-metre Ballyhoura hill where Brian Boru's brother was murdered, millstones were once quarried, and a rare fern still hides among the heath.

subject: Carrigrohane Straight
summary: Cork's flat-as-a-table 2.75 miles of road - a 19th-century engineering exercise that turned into one of Europe's most famous makeshift race circuits, drawing 70,000 spectators in 1938.

subject: Carrizo Creek Station
summary: Carrizo Creek Station served as the first source of flowing water for exhausted Gold Rush emigrants after the Colorado River crossing — and its first keeper committed murder and vanished into the desert.

subject: Carrizo Impact Area
summary: For seventeen years, the Navy dropped bombs on 45 square miles of California desert. They stopped in 1959, but the bombs — some buried 30 feet deep — are still there.

subject: Carrizo Plain
summary: The California valley so remote that pronghorn antelope still run and the San Andreas Fault carves visible scars - empty most of the year, then carpeted in wildflowers during rare superblooms that turn the plain into a painting.

subject: Carrowmore
summary: One of the largest megalithic cemeteries in Ireland and among the oldest, with thirty surviving dolmens older than the pyramids and contemporary with the very first farming communities to settle these islands.

subject: Carsaig Arches
summary: On the wild southern coast of Mull, the sea has cut two enormous arches through cliffs of ancient lava, reachable only by a four-mile scramble at low tide.

subject: Carshalton
summary: A south London village built around chalk springs that fed lavender fields, watercress beds and the River Wandle — and somehow still keeps two ponds in its high street.

subject: Cartagena
summary: Where colonial walls protected Spanish treasure and now embrace Caribbean color, where Colombia's coast offers the romance that Gabriel García Márquez immortalized.

subject: Cartagena (Spain)
summary: A working seaport that has been the prize of nearly every empire to reach the western Mediterranean, Cartagena stacks three thousand years of history around one of the world's great natural harbors.

subject: Carter Family Fold
summary: An 842-seat concert venue in Poor Valley where the daughter of A.P. and Sara Carter kept the family's music alive - and where Johnny Cash gave his last public performance.

subject: Carter's Grove
summary: A National Historic Landmark on the James River, Carter's Grove plantation hides beneath its Georgian mansion the archaeological remains of Wolstenholme Towne, a 1620 settlement devastated in one of colonial Virginia's earliest and most violent encounters.

subject: Carteret County, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's third-largest county by area, where 62 percent of the territory is water, where Blackbeard once owned a house, and where the first English-parentage male was born in 1629.

subject: Carthaea
summary: Karthaia, one of the four ancient city-states of Kea, slept undisturbed for fifteen centuries above a remote Aegean bay — its temples still standing, its theater still intact, its silence broken only by seabirds and the footsteps of those willing to walk an hour to find it.

subject: Carthage Punic Ports
summary: Two small lagoons in a Tunisian suburb -- one circular, one rectangular -- are all that remain of the harbor that sheltered the most feared navy in the ancient Mediterranean and fueled an empire built on trade.

subject: Carthage tophet
summary: Near the ancient Punic ports, a sacred enclosure holds 20,000 urns containing the cremated remains of children -- whether they were sacrificed to the gods or buried after natural deaths remains the most divisive question in Mediterranean archaeology.

subject: Carthago Nova
summary: The ancient city beneath modern Cartagena was Hannibal's springboard toward Rome, a silver mine that made empires rich, and a capital that outlasted the Roman world itself.

subject: Cartier-Brébeuf National Historic Site
summary: At the confluence of the Saint-Charles and Lairet rivers in Quebec City, a small park marks the spot where Jacques Cartier's crew nearly perished in the winter of 1535 and where the first Jesuit mission in Quebec took root a century later.

subject: Cartmel
summary: A medieval Augustinian priory anchors this Cumbrian village, now also celebrated for a three-Michelin-star kitchen drawing on its surrounding farmland.

subject: Cartmel Racecourse
summary: A tiny national hunt course in a Cumbrian village that draws crowds of 20,000, sends every winner home with a sticky toffee pudding, and was once at the centre of British racing's most audacious betting coup.

subject: Caruaru
summary: The agreste capital where a street market became a national hit song, a clay sculptor founded an artisan dynasty, and June runs for thirty days.

subject: Cary, North Carolina
summary: A railroad village that quintupled, then quintupled again - a planned Triangle suburb that became the largest privately held software company's headquarters and, somehow, one of the safest places in America to live.

subject: Carystus
summary: An ancient city at the foot of Mount Oche on southern Euboea, named in Homer's Iliad and in Bronze Age Linear B tablets, Carystus gave Rome its prized green cipollino marble and paid a hard price for sitting between Persia and Athens.

subject: Casa Milà
summary: The rippling limestone apartment block Barcelona mocked as "the quarry" became Antoni Gaudí's last private commission and a UNESCO-listed marvel.

subject: Casa Vicens
summary: Gaudí's first major commission, a riot of marigold-tiled walls and palm-leaf ironwork in Gràcia, born from the wildflowers he found growing on the empty lot.

subject: Casa de Estudillo
summary: Built in 1827 by one of California's most prominent Spanish colonial families, the Casa de Estudillo in Old Town San Diego became both a landmark of Mexican California and, a century later, a tourist site reimagined as the setting for a fictional romance — a layering of real history and invented legend that defines the place to this day.

story.title: Casa del Fundador Gonzalo Suarez Rendon

subject: Casa del Fundador Gonzalo Suárez Rendón
summary: The only surviving residence of a city founder anywhere in Latin America, this Andalusian-style house on Tunja's central plaza was built by 3,000 Muisca laborers for the conquistador who established Colombia's second-most important colonial city.

subject: Casablanca
summary: Where Morocco meets the Atlantic and modernity meets tradition, where the Hassan II Mosque rises from the ocean and a film gave a city immortal romance it never quite possessed.

subject: Casals Festival
summary: Born from a cellist's exile and a government's ambition, San Juan's Casals Festival brought world-class classical music to Puerto Rico -- and ignited a decades-long struggle over who the music was really for.

subject: Casco Viejo, Panama
summary: Panama City's UNESCO-listed historic quarter was built in 1673 after pirates destroyed the original city, and its layered architecture tells three centuries of reinvention.

subject: Cashel, County Tipperary
summary: A small town in the Golden Vale dwarfed by the limestone bluff that gave Ireland its City of the Kings.

subject: Cashew of Pirangi
summary: A single cashew tree in Rio Grande do Norte that two genetic quirks turned into something the size of a city block — and that you walk through rather than stand beside.

subject: Cashtal yn Ard
summary: A four-thousand-year-old Neolithic chambered tomb that crowns a hill in Maughold, with views across the Irish Sea to the Lake District.

story.title: Caspian Iran: Where the Desert Nation Turns Green

subject: Caspian Iran
summary: The lush northern coast of Iran, where ancient Hyrcanian forests meet the Caspian Sea and the Alborz Mountains rise abruptly from forested plains - a region so unlike the rest of the country it feels like a different world entirely.

subject: Casquets Lighthouses
summary: Three coal-fired stone towers, built together on a rock west of Alderney in the 1720s, were once lit simultaneously - and a single keeper's family lived among them, growing vegetables in imported soil.

subject: Cassadaga, Florida
summary: A tiny Florida community where mediums and psychics have practiced Spiritualism since 1894, earning Cassadaga the title of 'Psychic Capital of the World.'

subject: Cassidy, British Columbia
summary: A coal company built a model town here in 1919 — paved streets, a theatre, sidewalks with grass verges — and seventeen years later it was auctioned off and carted away.

subject: Castalian Spring
summary: The sacred spring of Delphi, fed by a cleft in the Phaedriades cliffs, where pilgrims, athletes, and the Pythia herself washed before approaching the oracle — and where Roman poets believed the waters gave the gift of verse.

subject: Castellón
summary: A calm, flat provincial capital on the Coast of Orange Blossom, where a lone bell tower presides over a bilingual city you can cross by bicycle.

subject: Castilletes Formation
summary: A 440-meter-thick geological formation in Colombia's Cocinetas Basin preserves a Middle Miocene world of giant crocodilians, ancient turtles, boa constrictors, and hundreds of marine invertebrate species from 14 to 17 million years ago.

subject: Castillo San Cristóbal (San Juan)
summary: The largest fortification Spain ever built in the New World began as a single sentry box on a hill called 'gallows hill' -- and its most famous legend involves a soldier who vanished not to the devil but to his girlfriend.

subject: Castillo Serrallés
summary: A 1930s hilltop mansion built by Puerto Rico's most powerful rum dynasty, purchased by the city of Ponce for a fraction of its value and transformed into a museum chronicling the sugar and rum industries that shaped the island's economy.

subject: Castlebay
summary: Barra's only village wraps a sheltered Atlantic bay around a castle on a rock, served by ferry, school, lifeboat, and a Catholic church on the hill above.

subject: Castlebellingham
summary: A Louth village where a Cromwellian cavalry officer's reward became three centuries of Bellingham residence, marked by biblical verses cut into the window sills.

subject: Castleblayney
summary: A Monaghan market town whose castle was once owned by the family that sold the Hope Diamond and burned down in a 2010 arson attack.

subject: Castlecaulfield
summary: A County Tyrone village where a Plantation-era English manor house disguised as an Irish castle was burned by rebels, and where a young Oxford poet wrote a famous elegy in 1816.

subject: Castlecomer
summary: A Yorkshire planter's coal town in north Kilkenny, designed in the seventeenth century to look like an Italian island, that ran on anthracite for three hundred years.

subject: Castledawson
summary: A County Londonderry village on the River Moyola where Seamus Heaney spent his childhood, founded in 1710 by an Irish Chief Secretary who built the country's largest single-span stone bridge.

subject: Castlederg
summary: A Tyrone border town that holds both Northern Ireland's coldest and hottest temperatures on record - and a Bronze Age cauldron pulled out of its peat in 2011.

subject: Castlefield
summary: On a red sandstone bluff where the Romans built Mamucium, the Industrial Revolution arrived by canal in 1761 and the world's first passenger railway terminated in 1830.

subject: Castlegregory
summary: A small village at the foot of the Maharees sandspit on Ireland's wildest coast, where seventh-century monastic ruins, mutton pies, and one of the world's strangest GAA pitches all coexist.

subject: Castleisland
summary: A Kerry town built around a 13th-century moated castle, famous for the widest main street in Ireland and the cave system that opens beneath it.

subject: Castlemartin Training Area
summary: A British Army tank range on the South Pembrokeshire coast, established in 1938, shared with German armoured units for 35 Cold War years, and the site of three live-fire deaths between 2012 and 2021.

subject: Castlemartyr
summary: A County Cork village where the Dogs of Blood once ruled, the Rolling Stones once took tea, and a five-star hotel now occupies the lands Walter Raleigh once owned.

subject: Castlepollard
summary: A Georgian estate town in north Westmeath built around a triangular green, with a sculpture of the Children of Lir at its centre and the seat of the Pakenham family two kilometres west — and on its edge, the former Mother and Baby Home that has only recently begun to be discussed.

subject: Castlepollard Mother & Baby Home
summary: Between 1935 and 1971, almost five thousand unmarried Irish women were sent to a former manor house in County Westmeath to give birth in secret. The buildings still stand, mostly empty now, holding the memory of one of the largest of Ireland's Mother and Baby Homes.

subject: Castlerea
summary: Birthplace of Ireland's first president Douglas Hyde and of Oscar Wilde's surgeon father, this Roscommon town also produced the O'Rourke sisters - boxers who have collectively brought home World and European gold - and was once home to a distillery making 20,000 gallons of whiskey a year.

subject: Castlerock
summary: A seaside village on the basalt cliffs of County Londonderry where C.S. Lewis took childhood holidays that may have shaped Narnia.

story.title: Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd

subject: Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd
summary: Four fortresses -- Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, and Beaumaris -- form a UNESCO World Heritage Site recognised as the finest examples of late 13th-century military architecture in Europe, and together they tell the story of one king's obsessive campaign to subdue Wales permanently.

subject: Castleskreen
summary: A County Down drumlin with 1,200 years of intermittent human occupation - an early medieval ringfort overlaid by a fifteenth-century tower house, excavated in the 1950s and still legible in the landscape.

subject: Castletown
summary: A compact Manx harbour town that wears its long stint as the island's capital lightly, where the day begins around Castle Rushen and ends in a pub by the railway tracks.

subject: Castletown Civic Centre
summary: A 1980s civic complex on Farrants Way that ended Castletown's century-long search for a permanent town hall, gathering library, police and commissioners under one quietly modern roof.

subject: Castletown Cox
summary: A Georgian Palladian mansion in County Kilkenny commissioned by an archbishop, designed by an Italian-born architect, and famously called 'the most beautiful house in Ireland.'

subject: Castletown Lifeboat Station
summary: A former RNLI lifeboat station that operated from Castletown harbour for almost a century, launching pulling-and-sailing boats into the Irish Sea to save merchant crews from shipwreck.

subject: Castletownbere
summary: Ireland's biggest white-fish port, tucked into the second-safest natural harbour in the world, and the town where the most famous pub on the Wild Atlantic Way still sells eggs and prosecco from the same shelf.

subject: Castletownbere Lifeboat Station
summary: The Atlantic west coast was largely uncovered by lifeboats until the 1990s. In Castletownbere, the new station has been pulling boats off the rocks ever since.

subject: Castletownroche
summary: A North Cork village named for the rock its lords were named for - and the only place in Ireland where, a few days before Christmas 1942, a stranger with a Luger turned up out of nowhere.

subject: Castlewellan
summary: A French architect's vision of tree-lined squares, set between two mountains, gave Castlewellan a streetscape unlike anywhere else in Ireland.

subject: Castro
summary: On Chiloé's eastern shore, Chile's third-oldest city balances a hillside of bright wooden houses against rows of palafitos that stand in the tide on stilts.

subject: Castro District, San Francisco
summary: One of the first gay neighborhoods in the United States, transformed from a working-class Irish enclave into a symbol of LGBTQ identity that reshaped American civil rights.

subject: Caswell County, North Carolina
summary: Bright leaf tobacco was perfected here in 1839, made the county briefly rich, and built one of the state's most haunted political histories along the Virginia border.

subject: Catacombs of Rome
summary: Beneath Rome's sunlit streets, over 150 kilometers of underground tunnels hold the remains and artwork of the city's earliest Christians, Jews, and pagans -- a subterranean world that debunks Hollywood myths while preserving some of Western civilization's oldest sacred art.

story.title: Catalan Romanesque Churches of the Vall de Boi

subject: Catalan Romanesque Churches of the Vall de Boí
summary: Nine Romanesque churches in a remote Pyrenean valley, whose medieval frescoes were so extraordinary that art dealers tried to sell them to American museums before Catalonia intervened.

subject: Catalão
summary: A prosperous phosphate and auto-assembly city in southern Goias, named after a Catalan chaplain and home to Brazil's largest Congadas festival.

subject: Catanduva
summary: A city of 115,000 in northern São Paulo state that grew out of a settlement called Cerradinho and became the place where a startling share of Brazil's electric fans are built.

subject: Cataraqui
summary: Within sight of the new life they had crossed the world to reach, nearly 400 emigrants drowned in the dark off King Island in Australia's deadliest shipwreck.

subject: Catatumbo lightning
summary: The most electrically active place on Earth, where lightning strikes up to 40 times per minute over Lake Maracaibo for up to 300 nights a year, producing over 1.2 million bolts annually.

subject: Cataviña
summary: A remote desert oasis in central Baja California, Cataviña sits amid a surreal boulder field scattered with cave paintings and giant cardon cacti, a lonely waypoint on the long road south.

subject: Catawba people
summary: The Iswa - People of the River - once dominated the Carolina Piedmont, survived smallpox and federal termination, and fought for decades to reclaim sovereignty along the same waterway that gave them their name.

subject: Cateura
summary: On the edge of Asunción's largest landfill, a community of recyclers built an orchestra from the trash they sort, sending children's music made on oil-drum cellos around the world.

subject: Catharine Macaulay
summary: The first Englishwoman to publish a history of her country, the only published female historian in the world during her lifetime, and the radical thinker Mary Wollstonecraft called her hero — Catharine Macaulay dined with George Washington and quietly outlived her own fame in Berkshire.

subject: Catlettsburg, Kentucky
summary: The Boyd County seat at the mouth of the Big Sandy River, once the largest hardwood timber market in the world - and home to the clown who revamped Ronald McDonald.

subject: Catrine
summary: An East Ayrshire village built around two iron water wheels of unprecedented scale, where Scotland's first cotton mills turned out fabric and a moral philosopher hosted Robert Burns over dinner.

subject: Cattle Depot Artist Village
summary: A Grade II historic slaughterhouse in Kowloon's Ma Tau Kok, operating from 1908 to 1999, reborn in 2001 as a community of artists who make art inside red-brick pens that once held cattle.

subject: Catí
summary: A stone village on a mountain balcony in the Alt Maestrat, remembered for a coat of arms bearing a loyal dog, a lawsuit against a neighbor that ran for four centuries, and the healing springs of L'Avellà.

subject: Cauberg
summary: A 1,200-metre limestone ramp out of Valkenburg, the Cauberg is the most famous climb in Dutch cycling - and the hill that made the town a tourist destination long before bicycles arrived.

subject: Caucaia
summary: A Jesuit mission that became a suburb, an industrial port and a kitesurfing coast - and the home of the Tapeba, who spent twelve years being asked to prove they were Indigenous.

subject: Cavalcante
summary: An old gold-mining town in northern Goiás, now surrounded by the largest Kalunga quilombola territory in Brazil.

subject: Cavan
summary: The county town founded by an O'Reilly chieftain whose family name became a byword for prosperity itself.

subject: Caverna Aroe Jari
summary: Brazil's largest sandstone cave runs 1,550 meters through 400-million-year-old rock, and the Bororo who named it called it the dwelling of souls.

story.title: Caverna do Maroaga Environmental Protection Area

subject: Caverna do Maroaga Environmental Protection Area
summary: A 374,700-hectare preserve of caves, waterfalls and rainforest named for a Waimiri-Atroari leader who took shelter in the cave during highway construction.

story.title: Caves of the Tullybrack and Belmore Hills

subject: Caves of the Tullybrack and Belmore Hills
summary: Hidden under two unassuming Fermanagh hills lies one of the most important underground karst landscapes in Northern Ireland, with the longest cave pitch in Ireland and a 50-metre shaft where a diver lost his life.

subject: Caxias do Sul
summary: Italian farmers fleeing hunger crossed an ocean and climbed a mountain to build, out of nearly nothing, the industrial heart of the Serra Gaúcha.

subject: Cayastá
summary: A quiet riverside town built beside the buried bones of the original Santa Fe, the first planned city of the Río de la Plata.

subject: Cayo Coco
summary: A former buccaneer hideout off Cuba's north coast where Hemingway set his fiction, flamingos wade beside a controversial causeway, and resorts rose from what charcoal burners left behind.

subject: Cayo Guillermo
summary: A sliver of sand off Cuba's northern coast where Hemingway once hunted marlin, fishermen and charcoal-burners preceded the resorts, and Playa Pilar remains one of the Caribbean's finest beaches.

subject: Cağaloğlu
summary: A historic Fatih quarter whose name comes from a Sicilian-born Ottoman admiral of Genoese family, and whose streets have hosted ink and steam in equal measure — the newspaper publishers of Istanbul and the glorious 1741 hamam that still bathes visitors today.

subject: Ceará
summary: A state of sertão and coastline in Brazil's Northeast - once among the country's poorest, now a kitesurfing and beach-buggy destination that still serves crab with a wooden hammer.

subject: Ceará
summary: The state that abolished slavery four years before Brazil did - a land of jangada fishermen, carnauba palms, and droughts so severe they rewrote half a million lives.

subject: Cebu
summary: The oldest city in the Philippines and birthplace of Christianity in the archipelago, Cebu is a province of 168 islands whose history stretches from a pre-colonial lion kingdom through Magellan's arrival to a modern hub of commerce and coral reefs.

story.title: Cedar Point: America's Roller Coast on Lake Erie

subject: Cedar Point
summary: A narrow Lake Erie peninsula that has hosted thrill-seekers since 1870, Cedar Point packs 18 roller coasters into 364 acres and holds claim as the second-oldest operating amusement park in the United States.

subject: Cederberg
summary: A rugged sandstone wilderness 300 km north of Cape Town where wind-sculpted rock formations, endangered cedar trees, and San rock art share a landscape shaped by 450 million years of geology.

subject: Ceduna
summary: Last real town before the Nullarbor: shuck a just-harvested oyster on the jetty, fill the tank, and look west - because after Ceduna, the road goes very quiet for a very long way.

subject: Ceduna, South Australia
summary: A Wirangu word for a resting place became the name of South Australia's far-western frontier town - where the sky once carried half the nation's phone calls and a total eclipse darkened the afternoon.

subject: Ceilândia
summary: The largest city in the Federal District began as a campaign - three capital letters stamped on a problem Brasília's planners preferred not to see.

subject: Celbridge
summary: A Liffey-side Kildare town with five thousand years of habitation, an Arthur Guinness boyhood, a Swift love affair, a notorious Famine workhouse and a mill that briefly was the largest wool factory in Ireland.

subject: Celebration, Florida
summary: Disney's real-world utopia: a master-planned town of 11,000 built from scratch in the 1990s, where starchitects designed the post office and the first homeowners were chosen by lottery.

subject: Celle State Stud
summary: In 1735 Hanover decided to manufacture a better horse by putting good stallions within reach of ordinary farmers — and nearly three centuries later the breed that resulted is still named after the electorate.

subject: Cemaes
summary: The northernmost village in Wales - a small fishing harbour on a sheltered bay, with a 5th-century church on the headland that may have been founded by Saint Patrick himself.

subject: Cemaes Head
summary: The northernmost point of Pembrokeshire Coast National Park, where 470-million-year-old mudstones rear up in tortured folds and the cliffs reach 175 metres above the Atlantic.

subject: Cemaes Lifeboat Station
summary: Opened in 1872 with a transferred lifeboat from the failing Cemlyn station, run for sixty years from a cliff cove at Wylfa Head, and home to four boats with very specific donors and very specific names.

subject: Cemlyn Lifeboat Station
summary: The first lifeboat station on Anglesey - founded in 1828 by a Welsh clergyman and his wife after they watched 140 people drown - which closed, reopened, and finally closed again in 1919.

subject: Cemoro Lawang
summary: A tiny hamlet perched at 2,217 meters on the rim of the Tengger Caldera, Cemoro Lawang is the last outpost before the vast volcanic sand sea and the smoking cone of Mount Bromo.

subject: Cenarth
summary: A small Carmarthenshire village beside one of the most famous salmon-leap waterfalls in Wales, home to the National Coracle Centre and a perforated-spandrel bridge built in 1787.

subject: Centenary Square
summary: A century of civic ambition compressed into one stretch of Birmingham paving, where 525,000 bricks were once laid out in the pattern of a Persian rug.

subject: Centenary, Zimbabwe
summary: A tobacco-farming township in Mashonaland Central that made the eclipse-chaser pilgrimage list on 21 June 2001, when its skies fell dark in one of Zimbabwe's narrow paths of totality.

subject: Central African Republic
summary: A landlocked nation in the heart of Africa where over 80 ethnic groups share a land of dense rainforests and ancient megaliths, yet decades of coups, civil war, and a self-declared emperor have made it one of the most turbulent countries on Earth.

subject: Central African Republic–Chad border
summary: A 1,556-kilometer border stitched together from a dozen rivers and three short straight lines, drawn by French colonial cartographers through country people had been crossing for centuries.

subject: Central African Republic–Sudan border
summary: Just 174 kilometers long, this short border roughly follows the watershed between the Nile and Congo basins - a continental divide that British and French commissioners demarcated on foot in the 1920s.

subject: Central Amazon Ecological Corridor
summary: An experiment in connected conservation, the corridor links protected areas across 52 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, spanning two major river basins and multiple ecosystem types.

subject: Central Bank of Venezuela
summary: For nearly 50 years the Central Bank of Venezuela kept inflation at 2-3%, but the bolivar's collapse into hyperinflation and US sanctions have made it a symbol of the country's economic unraveling.

subject: Central Boulevards of Brussels
summary: Brussels buried its river to build these grand 19th-century boulevards — and a century and a half later, fought to take them back from the cars.

subject: Central Coast (Vietnam)
summary: Vietnam's Central Coast is the narrow bamboo pole connecting the nation's two baskets — a 1,000-kilometer spine of beaches, imperial capitals, ancient trading ports, and cave systems that have shaped the country's identity for centuries.

subject: Central District, Seattle
summary: The neighborhood that William Grose built -- from a 12-acre land purchase in 1882 to the heart of Black Seattle, through redlining and civil rights, to a 21st-century reckoning with gentrification.

subject: Central European Hockey League
summary: The name overstates the geography by a wide margin. Two German clubs joining a Dutch-Belgian merger were enough to relabel the whole league.

subject: Central Freeway
summary: The elevated highway that the 1989 earthquake damaged, the city twice voted to tear down, and whose removal created one of San Francisco's most desirable neighborhoods.

subject: Central Highlands (Vietnam)
summary: The plateau country Vietnamese lowlanders once refused to enter, and which now grows most of the nation's coffee on the ground its first peoples farmed in common.

subject: Central Kalahari Game Reserve
summary: The second-largest wildlife reserve on Earth sprawls across central Botswana, where fossilized rivers cut through sand-covered plains and the San people's ancient connection to the land remains a contested chapter in modern history.

subject: Central Marshes
summary: Once covering 3,000 square kilometers of wetland between the Tigris and Euphrates, the Central Marshes were nearly annihilated by deliberate drainage in the 1990s and are now struggling to return.

subject: Central Papua
summary: An Indonesian province born in 2022, stretched from Cenderawasih Bay to Puncak Jaya - from coastal mangroves to the equator's last glacier.

subject: Central Province, Zambia
summary: 94,394 square kilometers of farmland, national parks, and the Mulungushi Rock of Authority - the open-air site in Kabwe where the chant for Zambian independence first went up in the early 1960s.

subject: Central Queensland
summary: Straddling the Tropic of Capricorn from sapphire fields to coal ports, Capricornia is a region so vast and so far from its own capital that it once petitioned Queen Victoria to let it become a state of its own.

story.title: Central Sulawesi: Where the Earth Remembers

subject: Central Sulawesi
summary: A province shaped by ancient stone carvers, volcanic fury, and one of the deadliest earthquakes of the 21st century, Central Sulawesi sits at the crossroads of Asia and Oceania.

subject: Central Zambezian miombo woodlands
summary: A ragged arc of dry tropical woodland that drapes across six countries - home to Jane Goodall's chimpanzees, some of Africa's last black rhinos, and a canopy that burns and regrows every year.

subject: Central Zambia
summary: The country's beating middle - Lusaka Province with the capital, Central Province with Kabwe and TAZARA, and a string of national parks where elephants outnumber traffic lights.

subject: Central and Western District
summary: The administrative district that contains all of colonial Hong Kong's original bones — the first land sale, the first banks, the oldest streets — spread across 12.4 square kilometres where the city's European and Chinese commercial worlds long ran parallel before finally merging.

subject: Central region (Eritrea)
summary: Eritrea's smallest region is also its most important - a highland plateau where Italian colonial architects built a capital that still looks like 1930s Rome.

subject: Central, Hong Kong
summary: The square kilometre where Hong Kong was decided — where the British built their first city in 1841, where the banks and the government have been ever since, where protests have repeatedly gathered, and where the view across Victoria Harbour still anchors everything.

subject: Central-West Region, Brazil
summary: The Brazilian interior that feeds the world - a cerrado breadbasket of soy, cattle, and cotton spread across the plateau between the Amazon and the Atlantic forest.

subject: Central–Mid-Levels Escalator
summary: The world's longest outdoor covered escalator system threads 800 metres up Hong Kong's vertiginous hillside, reversing direction with the morning commute and incidentally creating one of the city's most distinctive neighbourhoods.

story.title: Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona

subject: Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona
summary: A former almshouse that once sheltered Barcelona's poorest children is now the CCCB, a museum devoted to the idea of the city itself, crowned by a glass wall that mirrors the rooftops.

story.title: Centre for Research on Multinational Corporations

subject: Centre for Research on Multinational Corporations
summary: A small Amsterdam research office, born from outrage over a 1973 coup, has spent half a century reading corporate annual reports the way detectives read confessions.

story.title: Centre for Underground Physics in Pyhäsalmi

subject: Centre for Underground Physics in Pyhäsalmi
summary: A particle physics laboratory buried 1,430 meters underground in Europe's deepest base metal mine, where Finnish scientists hunt for cosmic rays and neutrinos beneath a shield of ancient rock.

subject: Centro Histórico, Porto Alegre
summary: Three hundred Azorean colonists landed on a lake-edge peninsula in 1752, and the parish they founded grew into the political and architectural heart of southern Brazil.

subject: Century Mine
summary: From a hole in the Gulf hinterland, batches of zinc travel 304 kilometres underground to the sea - the longest single-pump slurry pipeline on Earth.

subject: Ceredigion Coast Path
summary: Sixty-five miles of footpath along the cliffs and coves of Cardigan Bay, opened in 2008 and now woven into the eight-hundred-and-seventy-mile loop of the Wales Coast Path.

subject: Ceres, Goiás
summary: A Brazilian farm colony founded in 1941 on promises of free land - where a Syrian ex-president was assassinated in exile and where the population later emptied out.

subject: Cerrejón
summary: One of the world's largest open-pit coal mines, spanning over 690 square kilometers of Colombia's La Guajira desert, Cerrejon is both an industrial colossus and a flashpoint for indigenous rights and environmental justice.

subject: Cerro Ballena
summary: A hillside in the Atacama Desert holds the remains of over 40 whales that died in repeated mass strandings millions of years ago -- a graveyard revealed by highway construction in modern Chile.

subject: Cerro Baúl
summary: A flat-topped mountain in Peru's Moquegua Valley where two rival pre-Incan empires -- the Wari and the Tiwanaku -- coexisted for four centuries, brewed ceremonial beer together, and left behind evidence of a dramatic final feast before the Inca siege ended it all.

subject: Cerro Champaquí
summary: Córdoba's highest peak takes its name from a tiny lake near its summit - water at the top of the hill, in the language of the Comechingones.

subject: Cerro Chato
summary: A cattle town split between three Uruguayan departments holds an outsized place in history: in 1927 its women cast the first female votes in Latin America - eleven years before the rest of the country caught up.

subject: Cerro El Plomo
summary: The snow peak that watches over Santiago kept a five-century secret near its summit: an Inca boy, sent up the mountain to die as an offering, and found frozen and almost untouched in 1954.

subject: Cerro Gordo Mines
summary: A ghost town perched 8,500 feet above Owens Valley where silver and zinc booms created California's most productive 19th-century mine, now being restored by a YouTuber living alone among the ruins.

subject: Cerro Rico
summary: The 'mountain that eats men' -- a Bolivian peak whose silver built empires and cathedrals while consuming the lives of countless indigenous and enslaved workers across five centuries of mining.

subject: Cerro Tuzgle
summary: A near-perfect volcanic cone rises alone from the Argentine Puna, hundreds of kilometers from where volcanoes are supposed to be.

subject: Cerro de los Santos
summary: An Iberian hilltop sanctuary where worshippers left some three hundred carved stone figures — mostly women holding offering cups — to keep praying in their place.

subject: Cerro de los Siete Colores
summary: A wall of striped rock above a tiny Andean village, where 600 million years of sediment stand exposed like the pages of an open book.

subject: Cervera
summary: A hilltop Segarra town where a king's marriage terms and a monopoly university twice put the whole of Spain's history through its narrow medieval streets.

subject: Cha Kwo Ling
summary: One of Hong Kong's last squatter villages clings to its hillside, named for the leaves used to make a Hakka snack, its granite quarry once feeding the foundations of a colonial city.

subject: Chad–Sudan border
summary: From the Libyan tripoint 423 kilometers down the 24th meridian, then a wandering 980 kilometers to the CAR corner - a 1,403-kilometer line that has been war zone, refugee corridor, and caravan route in turn.

subject: Chaeronea
summary: The Boeotian village where Philip II of Macedon crushed the allied armies of Athens and Thebes in 338 BC, ending the era of the independent Greek city-states — and where a colossal stone lion still stands over the grave of the Sacred Band of Thebes, who died together rather than surrender.

story.title: Chaharbagh: Isfahan's Avenue of Four Gardens

subject: Chaharbagh, Isfahan
summary: Shah Abbas the Great bought four vineyards and built an avenue that visitors have compared to the Champs-Elysees for four centuries - a boulevard designed not for traffic but for pleasure, where water once cascaded down stone channels beneath rows of plane trees and cypresses.

subject: Chai Wan
summary: At the eastern end of Hong Kong Island, Chai Wan wears its past lightly — a bay once named for firewood, shaped by wartime execution, reclaimed land, and the world's 11,000th McDonald's.

subject: Chain of Craters Road
summary: A 19-mile road through Hawaii Volcanoes National Park that has been buried by lava in 41 of the past 53 years -- a drive where the destination is the road itself and the volcanic forces that keep erasing it.

subject: Chaine des Puys
summary: A chain of 48 cinder cones, eight lava domes, and 15 maars marching across the Massif Central -- volcanoes so perfectly preserved that 18th-century locals mistook them for Roman slag heaps.

subject: Chalandri
summary: A northern Athens suburb built over the ancient deme of Phlya, where marble cutters once served the Parthenon and rock bands later played to a weekend crowd.

subject: Chalandriani
summary: More than 600 Early Bronze Age tombs on the northeastern coast of Syros — the largest Early Cycladic cemetery ever found, and the site where Christos Tsountas coined the term 'Cycladic culture' in 1898.

subject: Chalcedon
summary: Before Byzantium, there was Chalcedon — the city the ancient world called blind for choosing the wrong shore, yet which gave its name to a gemstone, hosted the council that divided Christianity, and now lives on as Kadıköy.

subject: Challenger mine
summary: Named after a geologist's dog and found almost by luck, this remote gold mine chased coarse gold deep into rock nearly three billion years old.

subject: Chama (Zambia)
summary: A remote district seat in Zambia's Eastern Province where the power is sporadic, the rice is famous, and the only road out is notoriously bad in the best of weather.

subject: Chamberlain Square
summary: The Birmingham square named for the city's most famous mayor, where a bronze statue of an economist sits on the steps with his pages scattered beside him.

subject: Chambishi
summary: A Zambian mining town whose name means 'place of zebras,' Chambishi traces its copper story from an 1899 prospector killed by a lion to a 21st-century Chinese economic zone.

subject: Chamonix
summary: The birthplace of mountaineering sits at the foot of Mont Blanc, where the first Winter Olympics were held in 1924 and alpinism became a sport.

subject: Champa
summary: For sixteen centuries an Austronesian, Indic, seafaring civilisation held the coast of what is now Vietnam — and its Cham descendants are still here.

subject: Champasak
summary: A southern Lao province layered with Khmer temple ruins, royal Lao history, and a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, anchored by the Mekong River and the ancient temple-mountain of Vat Phou.

subject: Champion-Providence Mine
summary: A decades-long legal war between two rival gold mines on Deer Creek ended only when one bought the other, creating one of the most productive mining operations in California's Nevada City District.

subject: Chanco, Chile
summary: A neo-colonial coastal town on Chile's Maule shore that a German forester saved from being buried alive by sand.

subject: Chang and Eng Bunker
summary: The original 'Siamese twins' who transformed from sideshow curiosities into North Carolina plantation owners, forever linking Mount Airy to one of the 19th century's most extraordinary lives.

subject: Chang'an Avenue
summary: Beijing's central boulevard, named after the ancient capital, is paved in reinforced concrete to support tank parades and has witnessed some of the most consequential moments in modern Chinese history.

subject: Changdao County
summary: An archipelago of 32 islands strung across the Bohai Strait, the Changshan Islands served as a military-restricted zone until 2008 and still guard the only sea passage between the Bohai and Yellow Seas.

subject: Changhua
summary: Changhua is Taiwan's most populous county-administered city, a place where a 26-meter Great Buddha watches over an ancient settlement that has been home to aboriginal tribes, Dutch merchants, Chinese immigrants, Japanese colonists, and a modern Taiwanese metropolis — all layered onto the same patch of fertile western plain.

subject: Changhua Roundhouse
