summary: Built because a farmer refused to sacrifice his fishing pond, Darlington Raceway's lopsided egg shape has been humbling NASCAR's best drivers since 1950.

subject: Darnall Works
summary: The last surviving large complex of crucible furnaces in the world, where 132 melting holes once turned scrap into the steel that built modern Sheffield.

subject: Darra Adam Khel
summary: A single main street in Pakistan's tribal frontier where every shop sells handmade firearms, from pen guns to anti-aircraft weapons, crafted by artisans whose skills have passed from father to son since 1897.

subject: Darrynane Beg Ogham Stone
summary: A weathered sandstone slab beside a Kerry road that has carried one man's name in Ireland's earliest script for fifteen hundred years.

subject: Dartmoor Crosses
summary: Around 132 stone crosses still stand on Dartmoor, some nearly a thousand years old, raised to keep medieval travellers from dying in the bogs.

subject: Dartmoor Kistvaens
summary: Bronze Age stone burial chests scattered across Dartmoor, their slabs facing the sun and their contents long since pillaged by treasure hunters.

subject: Dartmouth Friary
summary: An Augustinian friary that lasted only sixteen years on the Dartmouth waterfront, undone by jurisdictional warfare between bishops, abbeys, and a wealthy local burgess.

subject: Daru
summary: The remote capital of Papua New Guinea's Western Province, founded by Yam Islanders centuries ago, where barramundi swim the Gulf of Papua and the nearest commercial flight connects to a world most residents rarely see.

subject: Darunta training camp
summary: A complex of military camps near Jalalabad whose disputed ties to al-Qaeda reveal how murky the lines between insurgent factions, Cold War legacies, and the war on terror truly were.

subject: Darvel
summary: A small Ayrshire town where Alexander Fleming was born, the SAS trained for D-Day, and a small Junior football club beat Aberdeen 1-0 in the Scottish Cup.

subject: Das Buddhistische Haus
summary: Europe's oldest Theravada Buddhist centre stands in a pine wood at the top of Berlin, built by a German doctor in 1924 and rescued from demolition by monks from Sri Lanka.

subject: Dascylium
summary: Dascylium was the capital of the Persian satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia for two centuries — until Alexander the Great marched past on his way to conquer the world — and archaeologists are still finding the evidence of that vanished court in the fields near Ergili.

subject: Dashilan Subdistrict
summary: A 275-meter lane south of Tiananmen Square where century-old shops still sell silk, shoes, and herbal medicine, Dashilan is Beijing's oldest commercial street and the birthplace of Chinese cinema.

subject: Daule, Esmeraldas
summary: A seven-hundred-resident fishing and shrimp-farming village on the Esmeraldas coast, built on sand three meters above the Pacific, where every tropical storm is an existential question.

subject: Davenport Downs Station
summary: Queensland's largest cattle station, a Mitchell-grass empire on the Diamantina floodplain where army snipers once shot feral cats to save the bilby.

subject: David Berkowitz
summary: The apartment building at 35 Pine Street in Yonkers became ground zero for one of New York City's most notorious criminal cases when police arrested David Berkowitz, the 'Son of Sam,' on August 10, 1977.

subject: David C. Broderick
summary: The anti-slavery U.S. Senator from California who was killed in a duel by a former friend at Lake Merced in 1859, the last sitting senator to die in a duel.

subject: David Malo
summary: A Native Hawaiian who witnessed the collapse of ancient traditions and spent his life writing them down, David Malo became the first Hawaiian historian to preserve his people's culture in their own language.

subject: Davis
summary: The highest incorporated town in West Virginia, with 595 people, four ski slopes, surprisingly good restaurants, and the Eastern Continental Divide zigzagging through its outskirts.

subject: Davis Mountains
summary: A volcanic sky island in West Texas where ancient forests cling to peaks above the desert, and where America's darkest skies reveal the cosmos from one of the highest roads in the state.

subject: Davleia
summary: The modern village of Davleia stands in the narrow valley below the acropolis of ancient Daulis, its name an unbroken thread connecting a living community to three thousand years of Phocian history.

subject: Dawenkou culture
summary: A Neolithic civilization that flourished in Shandong from 4300 to 2600 BC, the Dawenkou people practiced trepanation, beat drums made of alligator hide, and carved signs on pottery that may be ancestors of Chinese writing.

subject: Dawesville Channel
summary: An artificial channel carved through the Western Australian coast in the 1990s to rescue a dying estuary from decades of toxic algal blooms, transforming it into one of the region's great environmental success stories.

subject: Dawson City
summary: The Yukon boomtown where 100,000 people rushed in 1898 to find gold - now a perfectly preserved frontier town of 1,300 where the permafrost kept buildings intact and where the dirt streets still freeze in perpetual twilight through winter.

story.title: Dawson City: The Gold Rush Town Built on Melting Ground

subject: Dawson City
summary: The Yukon town where buildings lean like drunks because the permafrost is thawing - gold rush architecture sinking into ground that's been frozen for 10,000 years, giving way as climate change redefines what's solid.

subject: Dawson City
summary: The Paris of the North - the Yukon boomtown that held 30,000 gold seekers in 1898, became the largest Canadian city west of Winnipeg, and nearly vanished when the gold ran out.

story.title: Dawson Creek: Where the Alaska Highway Begins

subject: Dawson Creek
summary: The British Columbia town where Mile Zero of the Alaska Highway marks the start of 1,500 miles of road built in eight months during World War II - a wartime miracle of engineering that now draws travelers beginning or ending the last great North American road trip.

subject: Daxi Old Street
summary: A colonial-era street in Taoyuan where Baroque facades built by Japanese-era merchants still stand above shops selling Taiwan's most celebrated dried tofu, fragrant and dark, braised in sweet soy sauce for a century.

subject: Daxinzhuang
summary: A Shang dynasty outpost in Shandong where oracle bones bearing a regional variant of the earliest Chinese writing were found in a farming field beside a railway.

subject: Day Dawn Mine Remains
summary: A fenced-off shaft and a scatter of foundations are all that mark the Day Dawn - the reef that gave Charters Towers its first great fortune.

subject: Day Dawn, Western Australia
summary: Three thousand people once lived in this scrap of red dirt south of Cue; today a single stone office is all that proves they were here.

subject: Day Dream Smelter
summary: A lonely stone chimney on a bare hill marks a silver boomtown that burned bright, ran for barely ten months, and was eclipsed by the riches at Broken Hill nearby.

story.title: Dayton: The Birthplace of Aviation Where the Wright Brothers Built

subject: Dayton
summary: The Ohio city where two bicycle mechanics invented powered flight - where the Wright Brothers built their flyer, where the Air Force Museum preserves aviation history, and where industrial decline followed invention.

subject: De Bilt
summary: When a Dutch newspaper prints tomorrow's weather, the numbers came from here - a suburban town on a low ridge east of Utrecht that has measured the Netherlands' sky since 1897.

subject: De Boom Die Alles Zag
summary: A grey poplar in Amsterdam carries dark eye-shaped scars on its trunk. The neighborhood that lost forty-three people in a 1992 plane crash decided those eyes had watched.

subject: De Fryske Marren
summary: Eighteen months after it was created, the new Frisian municipality officially changed its name from Dutch to Frisian, a small act of linguistic insistence in a country still arguing about its own languages.

subject: De Marne
summary: A Wadden Sea municipality of 21 villages where pilgrims swap handkerchiefs with a crying Virgin and a salt sea became fresh countryside in a single act of engineering in 1969.

subject: De Panne
summary: The westernmost town in Belgium and the only patch of unoccupied Belgian soil during the First World War, where King Albert I and Queen Elisabeth lived out four years in a seaside villa while the rest of their country was held by Germany.

subject: De Stijl
summary: Founded in a Leiden studio in 1917 by a stubborn art critic with a borrowed 600 guilders, De Stijl reduced art to red, yellow, blue, black, and straight lines, and changed how the world looks at almost everything.

subject: De Verwachting, Hollum
summary: The windmill at Hollum is not the original windmill at Hollum - it was disassembled in another province, hauled across the country, and rebuilt on a foundation that had been empty for 42 years.

subject: De Wallen
summary: Amsterdam's oldest neighborhood is also its most contested - a place where sex workers, residents, tourists, and city hall have been negotiating the meaning of public space for seven hundred years.

subject: Dead Birds (1963 film)
summary: Robert Gardner's 1963 documentary filmed the Dani of the Baliem Valley - and Michael Rockefeller was there with a microphone, months before he vanished in Asmat country.

subject: Dead Man's Curve
summary: A notorious bend on County Road 492 in Marquette County, Michigan, where so many drivers crashed that a road engineer named Kenneth Sawyer invented something the entire world now takes for granted: the painted center line.

subject: Dead Sea
summary: The lowest point on Earth's land surface, where water nearly ten times saltier than the ocean is shrinking before our eyes.

subject: Deadvlei
summary: On a cracked white pan ringed by the world's tallest red dunes, a stand of camel thorn trees has stood dead for six centuries, too dry even to rot.

story.title: Deadwood: Where Wild Bill Hickok Drew the Dead Man's Hand

subject: Deadwood
summary: The South Dakota gold camp where Wild Bill Hickok was shot holding aces and eights - now a gambling town again, its Victorian Main Street preserved, its violent past memorialized in museums and the graves of legends who died young in a lawless gulch.

story.title: Deadwood: Wild Bill's Town in the Black Hills

subject: Deadwood
summary: The illegal gold rush town where Wild Bill Hickok was shot holding aces and eights, where Calamity Jane lived and lied, and where legalized gambling saved a dying historic town in 1989.

subject: Deal, Kent
summary: A small Kent town with no harbour grew rich serving the ships that anchored off its shingle beach - and produced the most famous boatmen in 19th-century England.

subject: Dean Village
summary: An 800-year milling village hidden in a wooded gorge a few minutes' walk from Princes Street, where eleven waterwheels once turned the grain of Edinburgh.

story.title: Death and Funeral of Lee Teng-hui

subject: Death and Funeral of Lee Teng-hui
summary: When Taiwan's "Mr. Democracy" died in 2020 at age 97, his funeral united rival political camps, drew tributes from Japan's former prime minister and the Dalai Lama, and became the island's reckoning with the man who ended authoritarian rule.

story.title: Death and Legacy of Tom Thomson

subject: Death and legacy of Tom Thomson
summary: A painter's mysterious drowning on Canoe Lake in 1917 became one of Canada's most enduring enigmas, transforming Tom Thomson from talented artist into national myth.

subject: Death of Chan Yin-lam
summary: Chan Yin-lam was a fifteen-year-old student in Hong Kong whose death in September 2019 — during the citywide protests — could not be explained to anyone's satisfaction, leaving an open verdict and a city left to carry unanswered questions about a girl who should still have been in school.

subject: Death of Chow Tsz-lok
summary: Chow Tsz-lok was a twenty-two-year-old computer science student at HKUST who fell from a car park in Tseung Kwan O on the night of 4 November 2019 and died four days later — his death, amid Hong Kong's unresolved protests, drawing thousands to mourn and leaving a question the courts could not finally answer.

subject: Death of Harry Dunn
summary: On an August evening in 2019, a nineteen-year-old motorcyclist was killed outside an RAF base in Northamptonshire. The fight his parents waged for the next three years changed how Britain treats the families of foreign intelligence officers stationed on its soil.

subject: Death of Marilyn Monroe
summary: Marilyn Monroe died on the evening of August 4, 1962, at her home at 12305 Fifth Helena Drive in Brentwood — found unresponsive before dawn by her housekeeper, at 36, with a bottle of barbiturates nearby.

subject: Death of Santiago Maldonado
summary: A 28-year-old craftsman vanished during a Mapuche land protest in 2017, and for 77 days a grieving family and a divided nation asked the same question: where is Santiago Maldonado?

story.title: Deaths of Kris Kremers and Lisanne Froon

subject: Deaths of Kris Kremers and Lisanne Froon
summary: In April 2014, two young Dutch women vanished on a hiking trail near Boquete, Panama, leaving behind phone records and jungle photographs that would fuel one of the decade's most haunting unsolved cases.

subject: Debert Palaeo-Indian Site
summary: The most northeasterly Palaeo-Indian site in North America, where stone tools dating back 10,500 to 11,000 years reveal the earliest known human presence in eastern Canada -- discovered by accident beneath a World War II military base.

subject: Debre Tabor
summary: Named for the Mount of the Transfiguration, fed by 48 springs, this Ethiopian highland town served as imperial capital under two emperors who both died failing to hold it.

subject: Deccan Traps
summary: One of the largest volcanic features on Earth, where flood basalts more than two kilometers thick once covered half of India - erupting right around the time the dinosaurs vanished 66 million years ago.

subject: Decorated Farmhouses of Hälsingland
summary: Seven painted timber farmhouses where Swedish peasants created interior decorations rivaling European aristocracy now hold UNESCO World Heritage status.

subject: Deebing Creek Mission
summary: On a creek south of Ipswich, Aboriginal people from across Queensland were gathered, controlled and buried in unmarked graves - and their descendants are still fighting to protect the ground that holds them.

subject: Deep Cove, North Vancouver
summary: Whales were butchered on this beach; a century later the same shoreline launched Vancouver's first mountain bikes and rents kayaks by the hour.

subject: Deep Ellum, Dallas
summary: A Dallas neighborhood born where two railroad lines crossed in the 1870s, built by freed people, shaped by Blind Lemon Jefferson and Lead Belly, nearly erased by freeways, and revived by artists who moved into its abandoned warehouses.

subject: Deep Navigation Colliery
summary: For nearly 120 years, the deepest pit in the South Wales coalfield raised the steam coal that drove Cunard's record-breaking liners across the Atlantic - and is now a park where children feed ducks on the lakes built over its slag.

subject: Deepwater Horizon oil spill
summary: The largest accidental marine oil spill in petroleum industry history, the Deepwater Horizon disaster released millions of barrels of crude into the Gulf of Mexico over 87 days, devastating ecosystems from the seafloor to the shoreline and costing over $54 billion.

subject: Deia
summary: The cliffside Tramuntana village where poet Robert Graves, once reported dead in the war, spent most of his long life.

subject: Deir el-Medina
summary: The walled village where the artisans who carved the pharaohs' tombs left behind the most intimate record of ordinary life anywhere in the ancient world.

subject: Del Amo Superfund Site
summary: For thirty years, a synthetic rubber plant dumped benzene and carcinogens into unlined pits between Torrance and Carson — and when it closed, the poison stayed, spreading slowly through the ground beneath people's homes.

subject: Del Mar Fairgrounds
summary: Bing Crosby helped open the Del Mar Racetrack in 1937, and the 370-acre fairgrounds that grew around it became one of California's premier entertainment complexes — hosting county fairs, thoroughbred racing, and enough other events to fill a calendar all year.

subject: Del Mar, California
summary: A small California beach city famous for its racetrack and its bluff-top views — and home to the rarest native pine tree in the United States, a species that exists naturally in only two places on earth.

subject: Delaware
summary: The second-smallest U.S. state, where more than three-fifths of the Fortune 500 incorporate themselves - and where Caesar Rodney's overnight ride decided American independence.

subject: Delft
summary: A small Dutch city that gave the world a painter, a porcelain, and a prince - and still floats on canals dug nearly a thousand years ago.

subject: Delft Aerospace Rocket Engineering
summary: A student rocket club that has been quietly trying to fly an amateur-built vehicle into space, and breaking European altitude records along the way.

subject: Delfzijl
summary: A Groningen port city on the Ems estuary where the Belgian novelist Georges Simenon was holed up with a broken-down boat in the winter of 1929 when, depending on which version you believe, he invented Inspector Maigret.

subject: Delos
summary: The tiny, uninhabited island that myth made the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis — a sacred sanctuary for a thousand years before it became one of the ancient world's busiest ports.

subject: Delphi
summary: The Greek sanctuary on the slopes of Mount Parnassus where city-states built treasuries, athletes won crowns of laurel, and three short maxims were carved into the temple wall.

subject: Delphi (Modern Town)
summary: The modern town of Delphi exists because archaeologists needed a village moved — and the 2,373 people who live there today occupy a hillside that was empty as recently as 1893, beside the ruins of the place the ancient world called the centre of the earth.

subject: Delta Downs Station
summary: A vast Gulf cattle station that the Kurtijar people bought back on their own Country - one of the first cattle stations in Australia run by its Traditional Owners.

subject: Delta Force
summary: Born from a Special Forces colonel's conviction that America needed a unit not just of teachers but of doers, the 1st SFOD-D became the most secret tier-one special mission unit in the U.S. military.

subject: Delta Works
summary: The Netherlands' monumental forty-year battle against the North Sea, recognized as one of the Seven Wonders of the Modern World.

story.title: Delta do Parnaíba Marine Extractive Reserve

subject: Delta do Parnaíba Marine Extractive Reserve
summary: A protected area created so that people can keep taking things out of it - 27,000 hectares of channel and mangrove where the law protects a way of working, not a view.

subject: Demak Sultanate
summary: Java's first Islamic state rose from a swampy port village to dominate the island's north coast, bridging the Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit empire and the Muslim kingdoms that followed.

subject: Demetrias
summary: A king named a brand-new royal city after himself, filled it with people emptied from eight surrounding towns, and made it one of the three fortresses that chained Greece to Macedonian power.

subject: Den Gamle By
summary: A schoolteacher saved a condemned mayor's house in 1908, and Aarhus ended up with the world's first open-air museum of town life — seventy-five relocated buildings that now run from 1550 to the 1970s.

subject: Den Hulst
summary: An Overijssel hamlet that grew up on a 19th-century peat canal, gave the Netherlands its Union bicycle, and ended up as a long ribbon of houses along a motorway.

subject: Denbigh
summary: A Welsh hilltop market town beneath an Edwardian castle ruin - birthplace of Henry Morton Stanley, Beatrix Potter's holiday inspiration for Peter Rabbit, and home to a Boxing Day barrel-rolling competition that has run for over fifty years.

subject: Denbigh Plantation Site
summary: A half-timbered manor house, a vanished colonial port town, and 350 years of enslaved labor compressed into a Newport News neighborhood park.

subject: Dendermonde
summary: A Flemish city where a wooden horse and four brothers ride into a roaring crowd once every ten years - and the rest of the time, two rivers do the quieter work of holding a town together.

subject: Dendra Panoply
summary: Unearthed in a warrior's grave in the Argolid in 1960, the Dendra panoply is the oldest known complete bronze plate armour in the world — fifteen interlocking pieces of beaten metal that encased a Mycenaean fighter from neck to knee around 1400 BC.

story.title: Denver: The Mile High City Where the Mountains Begin

subject: Denver
summary: The city exactly one mile above sea level where the Great Plains meet the Rocky Mountains, where Coors was born, and where the 13th step of the State Capitol sits at exactly 5,280 feet.

subject: Denver Union Station
summary: A grand Beaux-Arts landmark where presidents once arrived by rail, now reborn as Denver's living room connecting trains, buses, and light rail beneath historic chandeliers.

subject: Deoksugung
summary: The smallest of Seoul's five grand palaces blends Western neoclassical and traditional Korean architecture, a physical record of Korea's fraught attempt to modernize before colonization swallowed it whole.

subject: Deolali transit camp
summary: The British Army transit camp in Maharashtra that gave the English language the word 'doolally,' where soldiers waiting months for ships home lost their minds to heat, boredom, and despair.

subject: Depaldo Stairs
summary: A dying Greek merchant left his fortune to build a grand staircase down to the sea - and its clever optical trick would later make Odessa's Potemkin Stairs famous.

subject: Department of Ancash
summary: A land of contrasts where the White Range crowns Peru with its highest peak while the Black Range shadows a valley that has survived earthquakes, empires, and the rise of civilization itself.

subject: Department of La Libertad
summary: The department named for freedom was once called Trujillo, home to the largest pre-Columbian city in South America and the stage where Peruvian independence first declared itself.

subject: Department of Loreto
summary: Peru's largest and most remote department - a slice of Amazonia the size of Germany, centered on Iquitos, the largest city on Earth that cannot be reached by road.

subject: Department of Piura
summary: Where the tropics meet the desert in northern Peru: algarrobo forests, Peru's hottest days, and the first Spanish city in Peru.

subject: Department of Tumbes
summary: Peru's smallest department holds mangroves, tropical dry forests, black scallops, and the first drop of oil ever drilled on the continent.

subject: Deptford Dockyard
summary: Founded by Henry VIII in 1513 as the Royal Navy's first dockyard, where Drake was knighted, Marlowe was killed nearby, and Peter the Great spent six chaotic months learning to build ships.

subject: Derby (Western Australia)
summary: A remote Kimberley town where a 1,500-year-old hollow boab tree once served as an Aboriginal ossuary and nearly 12-metre tides turn the sea into cold brown cocoa.

story.title: Derby Lane: America's Oldest Greyhound Track and the End of the Dogs

subject: Derby Lane Greyhound Track
summary: The oldest continuously operating greyhound track in America ran its last race on December 27, 2020, after 95 years of white sand, mechanical hares, and million-dollar purses in St. Petersburg, Florida.

subject: Derby, British Columbia
summary: A crossroads in a Langley farm field is all that remains of the townsite that was briefly meant to be the capital of British Columbia.

subject: Deriivka
summary: For decades this drowned village on the Dnieper was hailed as the place humans first climbed onto a horse's back, until a single radiocarbon date rewrote the story and sank the claim.

subject: Deroche
summary: A crossing on Nicomen Slough that has been a meeting place for far longer than it has been a village - and which now holds fewer people than it did in 1951.

subject: Derry City Council
summary: The local authority that ran Derry from 1973 until 2015, took its present name in 1984, and put a skeleton on its coat of arms.

subject: Derrynane
summary: A small village on Derrynane Bay where Bronze Age miners, an early Christian saint, the Liberator, and a French feminist novelist all left layered traces.

subject: Derrynane Inshore Rescue
summary: Born from grief after a 1991 drowning, this volunteer rescue station now scrambles a 43-knot RIB across the Kenmare River on the south-west coast of Ireland.

subject: Derrynane RNLI Lifeboat Station
summary: A short-lived nineteenth-century lifeboat station whose existence may have owed more to a political feud between an English shipping reformer and Daniel O'Connell than to actual maritime need.

subject: Derwentwater
summary: A scenic Lake District lake surrounded by wooded fells, dotted with seven islands, and pressed into service as a stand-in for everything from Silent Hill's Toluca Lake to Star Wars' planet Takodana.

subject: Derybasivska Street
summary: Odesa's beloved pedestrian promenade, named for the Spanish-born admiral who built the city, where a fountain, a bronze chair, and a river of April jokers converge.

story.title: Des Moines: The Iowa Capital Where Presidential Campaigns Begin

subject: Des Moines
summary: The Iowa capital that matters every four years - where insurance companies cluster, where the Iowa caucuses launch presidential campaigns, and where a Midwestern city of 215,000 briefly becomes the center of American politics.

subject: Des Voeux Road
summary: Hong Kong's great northern commercial artery, built on reclaimed land in the 1850s and carrying trams, buses, and the city's financial pulse along the edge of what was once the harbour shoreline.

subject: Deserts of Australia
summary: Ten great deserts cover nearly a fifth of Australia and feel like another fifth more, a red interior of dune seas and gibber plains that has been home to Aboriginal peoples for at least 50,000 years.

subject: Desfina
summary: A mountain town on the Desfina Peninsula between Delphi and the Gulf of Corinth, set on a plateau at 680 meters with views of Parnassus, its ancient ruins, revolutionary martyrs, and quiet square encircled by cafes looking out toward the sea.

subject: Desilu Productions
summary: Founded by Desi Arnaz and Lucille Ball in 1950, Desilu invented the multi-camera sitcom, produced I Love Lucy and Star Trek, and made Ball the first woman to run a major Hollywood studio.

subject: Desolation Sound
summary: George Vancouver found nothing here that pleased his eye and named it accordingly; the Tla'amin, Klahoose, and Homalco peoples had been living in it for thousands of years, and it is now one of the most sought-after cruising grounds on the Pacific coast.

subject: Despotate of the Morea
summary: From its fortified capital at Mystras, the Despotate of the Morea ruled the Peloponnese as the last expression of Byzantine power — a realm where emperors-to-be governed, philosophers wrote, and the end came slowly, then all at once in 1460.

subject: Despotiko
summary: A tiny uninhabited islet southwest of Antiparos in the Cyclades, Despotiko is where archaeologists since 1997 have been uncovering one of the most significant sanctuaries of Apollo in the Aegean — a site that was, in antiquity, a major religious centre drawing pilgrims from across the Mediterranean world.

subject: Destruction of Neuss
summary: In July 1586, the Duke of Parma's army surrounded a Rhineland town of 4,500 people. When it was over, eight buildings stood and most of the inhabitants were dead.

story.title: Detroit: The Motor City That Keeps Reinventing Itself

subject: Detroit
summary: The city that put the world on wheels, that gave America Motown and techno music, that filed the largest municipal bankruptcy in history, and that refuses to stop rebuilding itself.

subject: Deutschlandfunk
summary: Germany's national public radio for news and current affairs, born of the Cold War to broadcast across the Iron Curtain and headquartered in Cologne.

subject: Deventer
summary: On the east bank of the IJssel, a Hanseatic merchant city kept its medieval bones and gave the Netherlands its oldest stone house, oldest scientific library, and a spice cake still baked after five centuries.

story.title: Devil's Golf Course: Where Salt Grows in Silence

subject: Devil's Golf Course
summary: The Death Valley salt flat where crystals grow upward like frozen chaos - so jagged that early surveyors said only the devil could play golf here, so quiet you can hear the salt crackle as it expands in the sun.

subject: Devil's Millhopper
summary: The 120-foot-deep sinkhole in Gainesville where a pocket rainforest grows - complete with waterfalls, ferns, and temperatures 20 degrees cooler than the Florida surface, formed when a limestone cavern collapsed thousands of years ago.

subject: Deziwa mine
summary: East of Kolwezi in Lualaba Province, Deziwa is an open pit holding an estimated 4.6 million tonnes of copper and 420,000 tonnes of cobalt - and a dossier of deals that has drawn scrutiny from Global Witness and RAID.

subject: Dhar Tichitt
summary: Along a 4,000-year-old escarpment in the Sahara lie the oldest stone settlements south of the desert, where West Africa first built towns and a civilization rehearsed the rise of an empire.

subject: Dharavi
summary: Once a mangrove island inhabited by Koli fishermen, Dharavi grew into one of the world's most densely populated neighborhoods -- and one of its most productive, generating an estimated billion dollars in annual economic output from 15,000 single-room factories.

subject: Dhimurru Indigenous Protected Area
summary: Across 5,500 square kilometres of Yolngu land and sea around Nhulunbuy, Dhimurru's rangers manage Country the way their ancestors did - pulling drowning turtles from drifting ghost nets and guarding sacred places.

subject: Dhofar
summary: The southernmost region of Oman, where monsoon rains turn barren mountains emerald green and the world's finest frankincense still grows on gnarled trees clinging to limestone slopes.

subject: Dhofar Mountains
summary: A mountain range in southern Oman where the Indian Ocean monsoon transforms barren Arabian desert into a green, fog-draped landscape each summer, sheltering some of the world's last Arabian leopards.

subject: Di Linh
summary: A highland district town carrying two names and two centuries of history — from the Mạ people's 'Djiring' to a French administrative center to a modern Vietnamese commune on the road between Bảo Lộc and Da Lat.

subject: Di'anmen
summary: The northern gate of Beijing's Imperial City was demolished in 1954 to improve traffic flow, but its materials were recycled into the Temple of Heaven, giving ancient stones a second sacred life.

subject: Dia, Mali
summary: Before Timbuktu, before the empires, before even famous Djenné-Jeno, people were building a city here in the Niger's floodwaters - nearly three thousand years ago.

subject: Diamantina Lakes Station
summary: The Channel Country cattle run that helped build - and nearly broke - Australia's Cattle King, Sidney Kidman, now reborn as one of Queensland's largest national parks.

subject: Diamond Head, Hawaii
summary: A volcanic tuff cone on Oahu whose Hawaiian name, Leahi, describes a ridgeline shaped like a tuna's dorsal fin, and whose English name comes from British sailors who mistook calcite crystals for diamonds.

subject: Diamond Hill
summary: A Kowloon hill whose name is a mistranslation of a stone quarry, whose slopes once housed 50,000 squatter residents, and whose reinvention — from shantytown to Buddhist garden to film mythology — mirrors Hong Kong's own restless transformation.

subject: Diamond Rock
summary: A million-year-old volcanic plug off Martinique that the Royal Navy once commissioned as a warship, Diamond Rock now shelters endangered snakes, nesting seabirds, and a deep underwater cave beloved by divers.

subject: Diamond-Star Motors
summary: A former joint-venture sports car plant in Illinois evolved from a symbol of international cooperation into a hub for electric vehicle manufacturing.

subject: Diaolou
summary: The fortified watchtowers of Kaiping, Guangdong — built by emigrants' remittances during dangerous times, fusing Chinese structure with Western ornament — are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most unusual architectural landscapes in China.

subject: Diaoyutai State Guesthouse
summary: An 800-year-old royal garden turned ultra-secure state guesthouse where Nixon stayed during his historic China visit, where Kissinger held secret negotiations, and where heads of state still reside behind walls few citizens ever see beyond.

subject: Dibba
summary: A coastal town divided between three governments -- two UAE emirates and Oman -- that was the site of one of Islam's bloodiest early battles and sits atop a major active earthquake fault.

subject: Dibulla, La Guajira
summary: A Caribbean town at the foot of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta whose name means 'lagoon by the sea' in the Guanebucan language, Dibulla carries five centuries of layered history -- from Tairona descendants to escaped enslaved Africans to a violent marijuana war that shook La Guajira.

subject: Dick King
summary: In 1842, Dick King and his servant Ndongeni rode 960 kilometers through wilderness to save a besieged British garrison at Port Natal -- a journey that shaped the colonial future of KwaZulu-Natal.

subject: Diederichs's stone
summary: A German imperial monument on a Qingdao hillside that was overwritten by Japanese conquerors, then dismantled entirely when China reclaimed the city -- a five-meter-tall stone chronicle of colonialism's impermanence.

subject: Diemen
summary: Six kilometers southeast of Amsterdam sits a town that has spent centuries quietly insisting it is not Amsterdam, even as Amsterdam slowly grew around it on three sides.

subject: Diemerpark
summary: Joggers, dog walkers and nesting kingfishers move freely across ninety hectares of Amsterdam parkland. About a meter below their feet, sealed in clay and plastic, is one of the most polluted sites in Dutch history.

story.title: Dieng Temples: Java's Oldest Stone Shrines, Named for Heroes Nobody Built Them For

subject: Dieng temples
summary: Eight surviving Hindu temples from the 7th-8th century stand on a misty volcanic plateau in Central Java - the oldest stone structures in the region, named by local villagers after Mahabharata characters because no one remembered who actually built them.

subject: Diepholz
summary: A small Lower Saxon capital where two rivers meet, a medieval county once governed itself, and a Diepholz-born chemist accidentally launched the modern plastics age.

subject: Diepkloof Rock Shelter
summary: Sixty thousand years ago, people living in a sandstone shelter above the Verlorenvlei River engraved geometric patterns on ostrich eggshell containers -- among the earliest known examples of human symbolic expression anywhere on Earth.

subject: Diest
summary: The small Brabant city where the House of Orange-Nassau held court for nearly three centuries - the family that would later supply kings to the Netherlands, and whose pious eldest son chose to be buried here.

subject: Different Fur
summary: A Mission District recording studio named by a Beat poet in 1968, where Grammy and Oscar winners have tracked alongside independent artists for more than five decades.

subject: Digbeth
summary: Birmingham's first industrial quarter, named for an old path or possibly a duck's bath, where the River Rea was buried, Italians were interned, and Peaky Blinders came home to film.

subject: Dihua Street
summary: Taipei's oldest street has been a commercial artery since the Dutch colonial era, named after a distant city in Xinjiang, and still draws three-quarters of a million shoppers each Lunar New Year to buy dried goods from stores that have operated for generations.

subject: Diksmuide
summary: The Belgian town that drowned the German advance in 1914 by opening the floodgates - and rebuilt itself, brick by brick, from total ruin.

subject: Dikulushi Mine
summary: A remote copper and silver mine west of Lake Mweru whose concentrate once crossed a lake by pontoon ferry, and whose nearby town of Kilwa became the site of a massacre that still shadows the operation.

subject: Dillalah
summary: A vast cattle run on the Warrego River near Charleville, named for the galah at a waterhole, whose 150-year story of booms, busts and ever-changing owners traces the making of the Queensland outback.

subject: Dillenburg
summary: A small Hessian town on the river Dill where William the Silent was born in 1533 - and from whose hilltop the Dutch revolt against Spain was directed.

subject: Dimini
summary: Six concentric stone walls, a pottery painted in spirals, and a Mycenaean palace that may be Homer's Iolcos make this Thessalian village one of Europe's deepest archaeological dives.

subject: Din Lligwy
summary: A 4th-century defended Welsh village near Moelfre, where the foundations of stone roundhouses and barns survive almost intact - and where the iron-working pots they used were patched, in their day, with iron clamps.

subject: Dinas Dinlle
summary: An Iron Age hillfort on the Welsh coast that the sea is slowly devouring, revealing the largest known roundhouse in Wales before it disappears forever.

subject: Ding Family Murders
summary: On 29 April 2011 — the day of the Royal Wedding — four members of the Ding family were murdered at their home in Wootton, Northampton, a crime that led to a worldwide manhunt and a moment of profound failure in emergency response.

subject: Ding ware
summary: The most celebrated white porcelain of Song dynasty China, produced for six centuries in Hebei kilns whose innovations in glaze, mould-work, and firing technique laid the groundwork for the global dominance of Chinese ceramics.

subject: Dingle
summary: The fishing town on Ireland's Dingle Peninsula where a wild bottlenose dolphin named Fungie courted human company for thirty-seven years before vanishing in 2020.

subject: Dinguiraye
summary: From this small Guinean town, a scholar named El Hadj Umar Tall built a fortress, gathered an army, and launched a jihad that would carve an empire across West Africa.

subject: Dingwall
summary: A Viking assembly site, a former seaport that lost its sea, and the small Highland town that gave Shakespeare's Macbeth his Thane of Cawdor - Dingwall has been at the centre of northern Scotland for a thousand years.

subject: Dinh III
summary: Built between 1933 and 1938 on a pine-forested hilltop, Dinh III was the summer retreat of Bao Dai, Vietnam's last emperor — a place where imperial family life continued in quiet until abdication ended it in 1945.

subject: Dinklage
summary: A small Catholic town in Lower Saxony's Oldenburg Münsterland, where a moated castle became a Benedictine abbey and produced one of the few German bishops who openly defied Hitler.

subject: Dinópolis
summary: In one of Spain's emptiest provinces, the largest dinosaur ever found in Europe anchors a paleontology empire spread across eight towns of Teruel.

subject: Diocese of Amyclae
summary: A bishopric named for the wrong city, the Diocese of Amyclae spent nearly a millennium in the wrong place — yet outlasted empires, crusades, and exile to survive as a metropolis of independent Greece.

subject: Diocese of Cloyne
summary: A Catholic diocese founded by the 6th-century poet-monk Colman, devastated seven times by Vikings, suppressed under Penal Laws, merged with Cork and then with Ross, and rebuilt with about a hundred plain churches between 1800 and 1850.

story.title: Diocese of Galway, Kilmacduagh and Kilfenora

subject: Diocese of Galway, Kilmacduagh and Kilfenora
summary: A Roman Catholic diocese in western Ireland whose curious tripartite name reflects 275 years of papal compromises between archbishops, baronies, and the Burren.

subject: Diocese of Lincoln
summary: Once the largest diocese in England, stretching from the Humber to the Thames and covering eight counties, now reduced to the flat lands of modern Lincolnshire.

subject: Diocese of Mendi
summary: A Catholic diocese carved out of Papua New Guinea's Southern Highlands, born from a French missionary's refusal to leave in 1954 and grown in seventy years to serve 75,000 Catholics across 31 parishes.

subject: Diocese of Rotterdam
summary: A young Catholic diocese carved out of older territory in 1956 - a minority church in a stubbornly secular country, governed from a cathedral named for two saints in a city famous for trade.

subject: Diocese of Rumbek
summary: A Catholic diocese larger than Switzerland, held together for decades by a handful of priests through two civil wars, two ethnic cleansings, and the razing of its cathedral town.

subject: Diocese of St Davids
summary: An Anglican diocese centred on the smallest city in Britain, holding together the religious life of three Welsh counties from a cathedral begun in 1181 on the site of a sixth-century monastery.

subject: Diolkos
summary: For nearly a millennium, the Diolkos — a paved limestone trackway across the Isthmus of Corinth — allowed whole ships to be hauled overland between two seas, a feat of ancient engineering that the comic poet Aristophanes made proverbial.

subject: Disappearance of ARA San Juan
summary: In November 2017, an Argentine submarine vanished beneath the South Atlantic with forty-four people aboard, beginning a search that gripped a nation and ended a year and a day later, almost a kilometer down.

subject: Disappearance of Frederick Valentich
summary: A young pilot flying to King Island reported a strange craft circling above him, said "It's not an aircraft," and vanished into Bass Strait, never to be found.

subject: Disappearance of Michaela Garecht
summary: On November 19, 1988, nine-year-old Michaela Garecht was abducted in broad daylight from a Hayward parking lot. Her case remains one of California's most haunting unsolved disappearances.

subject: Disappearance of Natalee Holloway
summary: The 2005 disappearance of an 18-year-old Alabama high school graduate from Aruba's tourist district became one of the most heavily covered missing-person cases in American media history, reshaping how the public thinks about crime coverage and justice across borders.

subject: Disappearance of Simon Cheng
summary: In August 2019, Simon Cheng — a Hong Kong employee of the British Consulate — was detained in Shenzhen for fifteen days; his account of torture and coerced confession, and the Chinese authorities' denial, became one of the defining human stories of Hong Kong's political crisis.

subject: Discovery Passage
summary: The most important natural waterway for vessels entering or leaving the Salish Sea from the north, Discovery Passage funnels shipping traffic through a 25-kilometre corridor that narrows to just 750 metres at its most treacherous point.

subject: Discovery of Nuclear Fission
summary: In December 1938 a laboratory in Berlin-Dahlem produced barium out of uranium, and the one person who could explain why had been driven out of the country five months earlier.

subject: Disney utilidor system
summary: Beneath the Magic Kingdom lies a hidden network of utility tunnels -- the utilidors -- where trash vanishes through pneumatic tubes, costumed characters travel unseen, and the entire illusion of the park is maintained from below.

subject: Disputation of Barcelona
summary: In July 1263, the rabbi Nachmanides was summoned to defend Judaism before the King of Aragon in a debate he could neither safely win nor afford to lose.

subject: Dissen, Lower Saxony
summary: A small Teutoburg Forest town first mentioned in 822, with a coat of arms whose meaning nobody can fully decode and a name that may mean 'misty'.

subject: District Six
summary: A vibrant multiracial neighborhood destroyed by apartheid's bulldozers, whose 60,000 displaced residents left behind a legacy of jazz, literature, and unfinished restitution.

subject: District of West Augusta
summary: For two years before the Revolution, Virginia claimed Pittsburgh - and a vast wedge of what is now southwestern Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia - as part of a colonial district called West Augusta.

subject: Dithmarschen
summary: For three centuries the farmers of this North Sea marsh governed themselves without a lord, running courts, armies and a Hanseatic trade network from their parish churches.

subject: Diving in South Africa/Sardine run
summary: Each winter, billions of sardines migrate up South Africa's east coast in one of the planet's greatest wildlife spectacles, drawing thousands of dolphins, sharks, whales, and diving gannets into a feeding frenzy visible from the air.

story.title: Diy-Gid-Biy: Where Chiefs Called the Rain

subject: Diy-Gid-Biy
summary: High in the Mandara Mountains along the Cameroon-Nigeria border, sixteen dry-stone terrace complexes stand as the oldest coherent archaeological sites in the range - built by the Mafa people possibly as ritual structures to summon rain, and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025.

subject: Dizin
summary: One of the 40 highest ski resorts in the world sits in the Alborz Mountains north of Tehran, where wealthy Iranians show off designer gear, couples chat openly, and Mount Damavand looms on the horizon.

subject: Diễn Châu
summary: A coastal strip of Nghệ An that drowned a Tang poet, buried a legendary king, produced mandarins by the generation, and gave every village its own trade.

subject: Djabugay
summary: The rainforest people of the Barron Gorge near Kuranda, whose country is written into the land itself by the ancestral beings of bulurru.

subject: Djenné
summary: Home to the largest mud-brick building on Earth, the island city of Djenné is one of sub-Saharan Africa's oldest, rebuilt by its own hands every single year.

subject: Djenné
summary: A river-island town of mud palaces and Quranic schools that once made caravans cross the Sahara to reach its Monday market.

subject: Djerba
summary: North Africa's largest island has been a crossroads for three millennia, from its legendary association with Homer's lotus-eaters to its 2,500-year-old Jewish community and its 2023 designation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Djibo
summary: A dusty Sahelian market town in northern Burkina Faso, capital of Soum province, where cattle herders, fresh milk, and famously good bread define daily life.

subject: Djibouti
summary: A small nation at the Horn of Africa's hinge point - 157 meters below sea level in places, ringed by volcanic chimneys, and the base of military installations for half a dozen foreign powers.

subject: Djibouti
summary: A small nation at the mouth of the Red Sea where five armies rent basing rights and 1,066,809 people speak Somali, Afar, Arabic, and French.

subject: Djibouti City
summary: Founded in 1888 on an uninhabited stretch of coast, this Red Sea port now hosts bases from six nations and calls itself, with characteristic bluntness, the French Hong Kong in the Red Sea.

subject: Djiboutian–Eritrean border conflict
summary: A four-day shootout over a hill at the edge of the Red Sea in June 2008, and the decade of tense silence that followed.

subject: Djurs Sommerland
summary: A hotelier and a music agent opened an amusement park in a Djursland field in 1981; their sons now run the most-visited summer park in the Nordic countries.

subject: Dnieper Hydroelectric Station
summary: A curving concrete wall on the Dnieper drowned a hundred kilometers of ancient rapids to power a young Soviet Union, and has been fought over ever since.

subject: Dnieper Rapids
summary: For thousands of years the Dnieper thundered over nine great cataracts that swallowed ships, killed a Viking-age prince, and gave a city its name, until a Soviet dam drowned them all in a single decade.

subject: Dnipro
summary: A Ukrainian city closed to the outside world for decades, where Soviet rockets were built in secret beside a river that has carried three different names for the same place.

subject: Dockery Plantation
summary: A cotton plantation in the Mississippi Delta where Charley Patton, Robert Johnson, and Howlin' Wolf forged the sound of Delta blues, Dockery Plantation is widely regarded as the birthplace of an art form that changed American music forever.

subject: Doctor Moisés Bertoni
summary: A quiet railway town in Caazapá that traded its old name for the memory of a Swiss naturalist who gave the world stevia and died poor in the Paraguayan jungle.

subject: Documenta
summary: Every five years Kassel hosts one of the most consequential exhibitions in contemporary art - founded in 1955 to put back on German walls the modern art the Nazi state had driven out of them.

subject: Dodan Barracks
summary: Named after a World War II battle in Burma, this Lagos military compound served as Nigeria's seat of power through six coups, a civil war, and a visit from an American president.

story.title: Dodge City: The Wickedest Little City in America

subject: Dodge City
summary: The Kansas cattle town that earned its Wild West reputation honestly - where Wyatt Earp and Bat Masterson kept order, where cowboys blew off steam after months on the trail, and where 'get out of Dodge' entered the American lexicon as an escape from trouble.

subject: Dodge City
summary: The wickedest city in America - where cattle drives, buffalo hunters, and the railroad created a frontier boomtown so lawless that Wyatt Earp and Bat Masterson had to clean it up, and where Boot Hill got its name.

subject: Dodona
summary: The oldest oracle in the Greek world, where for over two thousand years pilgrims traveled to a remote valley in Epirus to hear the voice of Zeus in the rustling of a sacred oak tree.

subject: Dogon Country
summary: A traveler's guide to hiking the Bandiagara Escarpment - the cliff-clinging villages, the trek between them, and the courtesies that make a visit worthwhile.

subject: Dogon Country
summary: A 150-kilometer wall of sandstone in central Mali, where the Dogon built granaries into a cliff that had already sheltered people for two thousand years.

subject: Dokk1
summary: Scandinavia's largest public library sits on the Aarhus waterfront under a hovering metal disc, and rings a three-tonne bronze gong every time a baby is born in the city.

subject: Dokkum
summary: A small fortified Frisian city where an Anglo-Saxon missionary was killed in 754 - and where, more than a millennium later, exhausted skaters of the Elfstedentocht still turn for home.

subject: Dolfinarium Harderwijk
summary: Europe's largest marine mammal park, where a 1960s vision of bottlenose dolphins as wonders to be displayed has run headlong into a twenty-first-century conversation about what we owe the animals we keep.

subject: Dollart
summary: Folklore says the bells still ring beneath the bay — a memory of the Cosmas flood of 1509, which drowned somewhere around two dozen villages in a single storm.

subject: Dolores mine
summary: A controversial silver and gold mine in Mexico's Tarahumara highlands where environmental justice, indigenous rights, and the Mexican drug war collide.

subject: Dolphin and Walrus
summary: Two diesel locomotives that worked a Twickenham gravel pit, became a pleasure-park dragon, and ended up rescuing the Groudle Glen Railway from ruin.

subject: Domfelsen
summary: A Permian sandstone reef breaks the surface of the Elbe below Magdeburg Cathedral — long credited, wrongly, with deciding where both the city and the cathedral stand, and a rock the locals learned to dread the sight of.

story.title: Dominica: The Caribbean Island That Refused to Be Tamed

subject: Dominica
summary: The most mountainous island in the Lesser Antilles, where volcanic peaks hide a boiling lake, 365 rivers carve through primordial rainforest, and the Kalinago people who resisted European colonization longest still call home.

subject: Dominical
summary: A scruffy Pacific surf town where donation-funded lifeguards patrol one of Costa Rica's most powerful beach breaks, humpback whales from both hemispheres converge offshore, and the nightlife runs on a rotating schedule between a handful of bars.

subject: Dominican Republic–Haiti border
summary: A 391-kilometer line drawn across Hispaniola where colonial rivalry, economic disparity, and deforestation create one of the most visually dramatic international borders on Earth.

subject: Don Det
summary: A farming island seven kilometres around that became Southeast Asia's most famous place to do nothing, where the boats leave when they are full and the electricity only recently stopped going off.

subject: Don Kho
summary: A small Mekong River island north of Pakse where roughly 450 people fish, weave silk, and live largely outside the tourism economy — a place where months can pass without a foreign visitor.

subject: Don Khon
summary: A Mekong island carrying the trackbed of a seven-kilometre colonial portage railway, built so French gunboats could be taken apart, carried past the falls, and put back together on the other side.

subject: Don Pedro Reservoir
summary: Named for a Gold Rush prospector and built to water California's agricultural heartland, Don Pedro Reservoir submerges 26 miles of the Tuolumne River beneath a lake that also quenches the thirst of San Francisco.

subject: Don Som
summary: The second largest of the Four Thousand Islands has seven thousand residents, twelve villages and one guesthouse - and once sheltered a French painter who came for three months and stayed forty years.

subject: Donaghadee
summary: A small Ulster harbour town where eloping couples once caught the Scotland ferry, lifeboat heroes pulled survivors from the Irish Sea, and Johnny Cash once mispronounced its name in song.

subject: Donaghadee Lifeboat Station
summary: On a January night in 1953, the Donaghadee lifeboat brought back 33 of the 44 survivors of the worst British civilian maritime disaster since the war - the loss of the MV Princess Victoria.

subject: Donald Morrison (outlaw)
summary: A Scottish-Gaelic-speaking cowboy from Quebec's Eastern Townships who triggered Canada's longest manhunt in 1888 after a land swindle stole his family farm -- and became a folk hero whose story is still celebrated in Gaelic song.

subject: Donar Groningen
summary: Named for the Norse god of thunder, born from a gymnastics-and-fencing club founded in 1881, seven-time Dutch champion, bankrupt and reborn in 2023 - the basketball club of Groningen has more lives than the cat on its city's coat of arms.

subject: Donemana
summary: A cricket-mad Tyrone village at the foot of the Sperrins, founded in 1609 by a Scottish planter, where the local team has won four successive Senior Cup finals in modern times.

story.title: Dong Ampham National Biodiversity Conservation Area

subject: Dong Ampham National Biodiversity Conservation Area
summary: Two hundred thousand hectares of Laotian highland forest on the western slope of the Annamite Range — among the last intact lowland tropical forests in mainland Southeast Asia, sheltering clouded leopards, Siamese crocodiles, and primates found almost nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Dong Ap Bia
summary: The Montagnard people called it 'the mountain of the crouching beast' long before American soldiers gave it a name that stuck: Hamburger Hill.

subject: Donggang, Pingtung
summary: A working fishing port on Taiwan's southern coast where bluefin tuna season draws sashimi pilgrims and a triannual King Boat ceremony lights up the harbor with fire.

subject: Donghe, Taitung
summary: A coastal township on Taiwan's eastern seaboard where Amis indigenous culture runs deep, surfers chase Pacific swells, and one particular steamed bun has achieved island-wide fame.

subject: Donglü
summary: A small village in Hebei where nearly 80% of residents are Catholic, home to a Marian apparition during the Boxer Rebellion and a pilgrimage site the Chinese government has repeatedly tried to suppress.

subject: Dongmen, Shenzhen
summary: Shenzhen's oldest commercial district — a 300-year-old market town now known as Laojie, Old Street, where the city's first McDonald's opened in 1990 and the pedestrian lanes still bustle.

subject: Dongo conflict
summary: A dispute over fish ponds that had simmered since 1946 exploded in 2009 into a conflict that displaced 168,000 people along the Ubangi River, turning a small Congolese town into a ghost town and triggering one of the UN's largest peacekeeping deployments in the DRC.

subject: Dongola
summary: The capital of Sudan's Northern State inherited its name from a word meaning red brick, and its identity from a medieval kingdom, a Mamluk retreat, and a colonial war.

subject: Dongola Reach
summary: A 160-kilometer stretch of the Nile between cataracts that cradled the Kerma culture, the Kingdom of Kush, and the Christian kingdom of Makuria.

subject: Dongshi District
summary: Dongshi is Taichung's easternmost district — a Hakka enclave pressed between the Dajia River and the Xueshan Range, where spherical pears ripen in mountain orchards and a converted railway station keeps the community's cultural memory alive.

subject: Dongzhimen
summary: A former city gate turned transportation hub, Dongzhimen connects three subway lines, hundreds of bus routes, and a street nicknamed Ghost Street where over 150 restaurants blaze with red lanterns until dawn.

subject: Donna Nook Air Weapons Range
summary: An MOD bombing range on the Lincolnshire coast that doubles as a seal colony - the only national nature reserve in the UK on Ministry of Defence land.

subject: Donna Nook Lifeboat Station
summary: For 102 years a lifeboat crew launched from this Lincolnshire saltmarsh to save sailors from the shifting sands offshore.

subject: Donner Pass
summary: Where pioneers ate their dead - the Sierra Nevada crossing where the Donner Party became trapped by early snow in 1846-47, and survivors resorted to cannibalism to endure the deadliest winter in American frontier history.

subject: Donuzlav
summary: The deepest lake in Crimea, split from the Black Sea by a thin bar of sand until 1961, when a single canal turned a lake into a bay overnight.

subject: Dooagh
summary: The Achill village whose beach disappeared in a 1984 storm, stayed gone for 33 years, then returned overnight on a freak high tide in April 2017 - only to vanish again in early 2019.

subject: Doohoma
summary: The Erris peninsula village where families once dug mass graves in the sandbanks after the Famine - and where, in 1926, three hundred men built a wall by hand to give the dead a proper cemetery.

subject: Doolin
summary: A Clare fishing village that became the capital of Irish traditional music - and the gateway to the Cliffs of Moher.

subject: Doolough
summary: The Erris townland where, in the 1950s, the wind exposed the bones of children buried in the sandbanks during the Famine - and where, since 1605, the people have been remembering exactly who their landlords were.

subject: Doon, County Limerick
summary: Eight ring forts, a name that means "fort of the harlot", and the first All-Ireland hurling title in 2024 - a small east Limerick village with a remarkable history.

subject: Dooniver
summary: A Gaeltacht village on Achill Island's eastern shore where one of the strongest tidal currents in Europe rips through the narrow channel of Bullsmouth - and where the boxer Johnny Kilbane's people came from.

subject: Dorasan station
summary: South Korea's northernmost train station sits 650 meters from the DMZ, its platforms gleaming and its destination boards pointing toward Pyongyang -- a city no train from here has reached in decades.

subject: Dorchester Square
summary: Built over a cholera cemetery and framed by cathedrals, railway stations, and skyscrapers, Dorchester Square has served as the crossroads of Montreal for over a century -- a green oasis where Victorian statues face off against modern towers and every layer of the city's history is visible at once.

subject: Dordrecht
summary: The oldest city in Holland sits on an island it did not used to be on, hosted the meeting that started the Dutch Republic, settled a theological war that nearly tore the country apart, and lost its trade to Rotterdam without ever quite forgetting that it had once mattered most.

subject: Dorestad
summary: For two centuries it was the busiest port in northwest Europe - then the Vikings came, and the river itself walked away.

subject: Dori, Burkina Faso
summary: The hottest place a thermometer has ever measured in Burkina Faso - and a Sahel crossroads where Fulani emirs, Tuareg traders, and camel caravans still meet on market day.

subject: Doris (Greece)
summary: A tiny mountain valley between Oeta and Parnassus that tradition called the cradle of the Dorian Greeks — a place so small it seems impossible that it could have seeded Sparta, Corinth, and Syracuse.

subject: Dornoch
summary: A former royal burgh on the Sutherland coast where Britain's last legal witch execution happened in 1727, and where one of the world's great golf links was carved from the dunes.

subject: Dornum
summary: A village in East Frisia that gave the world the mother of the Marx Brothers and still keeps the only surviving synagogue building in the region.

subject: Dornumersiel
summary: Two harbor villages built side by side in 1653, divided only by a narrow channel that was once an international border.

subject: Dorothea Quarry
summary: A 106-metre-deep slate pit pumped dry for a century by a Cornish beam engine, now a flooded lake that has drowned more than twenty divers.

subject: Dorrigo, New South Wales
summary: A cool, rain-soaked timber-and-dairy town perched 731 metres up on its own plateau above the Bellinger Valley, gateway to one of the wettest, greenest corners of New South Wales.

subject: Dortmund
summary: Once Westphalia's medieval beer capital, then a smoking citadel of coal and steel, Dortmund is now a city that learned how to outlive its own purpose.

subject: Dortmund Sparkassen Chess Meeting
summary: For half a century, a Ruhr savings bank has paid the world's strongest grandmasters to play summer chess in Dortmund. The 2002 edition crowned a challenger for the world title.

subject: Dos Palmas Spring
summary: An artesian spring at the foot of the Orocopia Mountains that sustained Native Americans, Gold Rush travelers, and the man who gave Ehrenberg, Arizona its name — until a murder ended one chapter of its history.

subject: Dos Pilas
summary: Founded in AD 629 as a Tikal outpost to control Peten trade routes, Dos Pilas betrayed its parent city within two decades, launching a century of dynastic warfare that reshaped the Maya lowlands before the city's own vassals turned on it in 761.

subject: Dosan Seowon
summary: A 16th-century Confucian academy in Andong where the scholar Yi Hwang taught, planted apricot trees, and shaped Korean philosophical thought for four centuries.

subject: Dotawo
summary: The indigenous name for Christian Nubia's central kingdom, Dotawo persisted from at least the 1180s into the 17th century, one of the last Christian states in the region.

subject: Double Haven
summary: A sheltered harbour of deep-red rocks and ancient seagrass beds in Hong Kong's northeast corner, where Jurassic geology meets one of the territory's most quietly protected marine parks.

subject: Double-headed eagles derby
summary: AEK Athens and PAOK wear the same Byzantine eagle and carry the same refugee story, a football rivalry born from one of the great upheavals of the 20th century.

subject: Doubtful Sound
summary: Captain Cook looked at this fiord and decided not to enter - he doubted he could sail back out. The name stuck, and so did the isolation that inspired it.

subject: Dougga
summary: UNESCO calls Dougga the best-preserved Roman small town in North Africa -- a 75-hectare site where a Numidian mausoleum, Roman capitol, and Byzantine fort chart two thousand years of continuous habitation.

subject: Douglas
summary: A Cork suburb that produced Cillian Murphy, Ronan O'Gara, and Joffrey Baratheon - where woollen mills once spun, the N40 now hums, and Nemo Rangers keep winning football.

subject: Douglas
summary: The Manx capital wears its two-mile promenade like a wide-brimmed hat against the Irish Sea, complete with horse-drawn trams that still plod the same route they pioneered in 1876.

subject: Douglas Southern Electric Tramway
summary: For forty-three years, double-deck trams clattered along cliff-edge viaducts between Douglas Head and Port Soderick on a line described by passengers as a white-knuckle ride.

subject: Douglas, Isle of Man
summary: From thirteen households to a Crown Dependency capital, Douglas grew on smuggling, lifeboats, internment camps, and the Bee Gees.

subject: Douglas, Wyoming - Jackalope Capital
summary: The small Wyoming town where two teenage taxidermist brothers invented America's favorite imaginary animal in 1932 - and then leaned all the way in, with an eight-foot statue, official hunting licenses, and zero embarrassment.

subject: Doukissis Plakentias Station
summary: An Athens metro hub carries the name of a Philadelphia-born duchess who poured her fortune into Greek independence and is buried in the hills above the line.

subject: Doun Kaev
summary: The quiet provincial capital of Cambodia's silk country, where two-thirds of the nation's weavers work beneath their houses and an hour's drive away lies the delta that produced the first Khmer kingdoms.

subject: Doune
summary: A Perthshire burgh of fairy hills, racing engines and pistols that allegedly fired the first shot of the American Revolution.

subject: Dounreay
summary: A white golf ball on the Caithness coast was where Britain tried to crack the fast breeder reactor - and where it now spends decades undoing what it built.

subject: Dover
summary: Twenty miles from France, twenty centuries deep, Dover is the town that has always been Britain's front door - and the place where the channel itself was born from a flood.

subject: Dover Motor Speedway
summary: The Monster Mile - a one-mile concrete oval banked at 24 degrees, where NASCAR Cup cars hit 175 miles per hour and the harness horses race inside the same circle.

subject: Dover, Delaware
summary: The state capital where Jell-O is made, NASCAR races, the country's only continental military mortuary operates - and a volunteer fire department staffs the only volunteer-fire-departmented capital in America.

subject: Dovrefjell
summary: The mountain range so central to Norwegian identity that the nation's founders swore their constitutional oath upon it -- and where musk oxen, wild reindeer, and the Mountain King of Peer Gynt still roam.

subject: Dowlais Ironworks
summary: Founded in 1759 and at one point the largest steel producer in the United Kingdom, Dowlais helped invent the railway age and then helped trigger a royal abdication crisis.

subject: Downtown Eastside
summary: Vancouver's oldest neighbourhood was once the centre of the city; a century of removals, closures and policy reversals left it carrying burdens the rest of the city set down.

subject: Downtown Norfolk, Virginia
summary: A waterfront downtown that nearly killed itself with a pedestrian mall in the 1970s, was saved by a battleship, an upscale shopping center, and a forty-year urban-renewal effort, and is now reinventing itself again.

subject: Downtown Oakland
summary: Oakland's downtown core defies every stereotype about the city, layering 19th-century Victorian remnants, Art Deco theaters, and vibrant cultural traditions beneath its modern skyline.

subject: Dr Ludwig Becker's Grave
summary: On a lonely stock route by the Bulloo River lies the last grave of the Burke and Wills expedition, where a brilliant German artist who painted the desert that killed him was finally allowed to rest.

subject: Dr Sun Yat-sen Historical Trail
summary: Sixteen bronze markers embedded in the pavements of Central and Sheung Wan trace the places where Sun Yat-sen plotted the end of imperial China, turning an ordinary walking route through Hong Kong's oldest districts into a map of revolution.

subject: Dracena
summary: Four men laid a foundation stone in the forest in 1945, held a contest to name the place, and a houseplant won.

subject: Drachten
summary: Friesland's second-largest town tore out its traffic lights and watched the accidents almost disappear.

subject: Dragon and Tiger Pagodas
summary: At Lotus Pond in Kaohsiung's Zuoying District, the Dragon and Tiger Pagodas invite visitors to enter through the dragon's open mouth and exit through the tiger's — a walk-through ritual meant to transform bad fortune into good.

subject: Dragon's Back
summary: A narrow mountain ridge in southeastern Hong Kong Island, Dragon's Back offers one of Asia's most celebrated urban hikes — where paragliders drift above the South China Sea and city skylines appear around every bend.

story.title: Dragão do Mar Center of Art and Culture

subject: Dragão do Mar Center of Art and Culture
summary: A Fortaleza cultural complex named for the Black jangadeiro whose 1881 refusal to ferry enslaved people helped push Ceará to abolish slavery four years before the rest of Brazil.

story.title: Draining and Development of the Everglades

subject: Draining and development of the Everglades
summary: The century-long saga of how politicians, developers, and engineers tried to transform a vast subtropical wetland into farmland and cities -- and how nature fought back with hurricanes, drought, and vanishing topsoil.

story.title: Drakes Estero: The Hand That Holds the Tide

subject: Drakes Estero
summary: A tidal estuary shaped like a human hand, where Sir Francis Drake may have beached his ship in 1579, and where a bitter fight between oyster farmers and conservationists played out across decades.

subject: Dreamland Margate
summary: On the Margate seafront, the oldest amusement park in continuous use in the United Kingdom has been a salt marsh, a Victorian pleasure garden, a circus, a wartime requisition, a Bembom Brothers white-knuckle theme park, a derelict ruin, and now itself again.

subject: Dreamworld
summary: Australia's largest theme park rose from coastal scrub at Coomera on one man's stubborn vision, and across four decades it has held the country's joy, its thrills, and one of its deepest sorrows.

subject: Drenthe
summary: The Netherlands has 54 prehistoric stone tombs. Fifty-two of them are in Drenthe, a quiet northeastern province whose name means 'three lands' and whose richest export, for thousands of years, has been silence.

subject: Drenthse Veenkolonien
summary: A quiet corner of Drenthe where, in 1818, a Dutch general tried to fix poverty by moving 52 families to the moors, handing them a plot of land, and grading them on their behaviour.

subject: Drogheda
summary: The walled port at the mouth of the Boyne where Cromwell came in 1649, where Saint Oliver Plunkett's head sits behind glass, and where 44,000 people now live above 800 years of history.

subject: Droitwich Spa
summary: A town floating on brine ten times saltier than the sea, where Romans built saltworks, Victorians floated in baths, and a longwave radio mast broadcast the nation to itself.

subject: Dromore, County Down
summary: A small Down market town with a sixth-century saint, a Norman motte, a rare set of stocks, the inventor who made the tractor practical - and the bypass it has been on the receiving end of for half a century.

subject: Drumheller
summary: Where the Red Deer River carved a striped canyon through the Alberta prairie, a small town has built itself around 75-million-year-old bones - and an 86-foot fiberglass T. rex you can climb inside.

story.title: Drumheller: The Town the Dinosaurs Built

subject: Drumheller
summary: The Alberta badlands where so many dinosaur bones emerge from the eroding hills that they built a town around them - the Royal Tyrrell Museum holds 160,000 specimens, and new fossils still wash out with every rain.

subject: Drummore
summary: Scotland's southernmost village - a harbour, a hotel, and the start of a 26-mile coastal path.

subject: Drummore
summary: The southernmost village in Scotland, where a community is still trying to buy back the harbour their forebears built for lime ships.

subject: Drumnadrochit
summary: The Highland village at the foot of Glen Urquhart sits where the River Enrick meets Loch Ness, anchoring the monster-hunting economy, two long-distance footpaths, and the only lifeboat station on a freshwater loch.

subject: Drumshanbo
summary: A small Leitrim town at the lower tip of Lough Allen, in the shadow of the Iron Mountain - now home to one of Ireland's fastest-growing craft distilleries.

story.title: Dry Creek Rancheria Band of Pomo Indians

subject: Dry Creek Rancheria Band of Pomo Indians
summary: Descendants of the Mihilakawna and Makahmo bands, the Dry Creek Pomo hold 75 acres near Geyserville -- a fraction of the land they once knew -- where they operate a casino, navigate internal political upheaval, and guard a cultural identity that predates every vineyard in Sonoma County.

subject: Dubai
summary: Where desert became skyline in a single generation, where the Burj Khalifa pierces the clouds, where ambition built an oasis of commerce from sand and oil.

subject: Dublin
summary: From Viking longphort to literary capital - where raiders became traders, where an illuminated manuscript became Ireland's greatest treasure, and where writers invented streams of consciousness on Georgian streets.

subject: Dublin International Film Festival
summary: Dublin watches more films per head than almost any other European city, yet the capital had no international film festival until 2003 -- when critic Michael Dwyer and a Trinity undergraduate decided that absurdity had gone on long enough.

subject: Dubrovnik
summary: The Pearl of the Adriatic - where medieval walls embrace a marble-paved old town that survived centuries of maritime rivalry, earthquakes, and war to become Croatia's most spectacular destination.

subject: Duchess of Richmond's Ball
summary: On the night of 15 June 1815, Brussels danced. By dawn the next morning, the officers in dress uniform were riding south to Quatre Bras. Some never came back.

subject: Duchy of Berg
summary: For seven centuries, a red double-tailed lion ruled the east bank of the Rhine - until Napoleon gave the duchy to a five-year-old boy.

subject: Duchy of Brabant
summary: For six centuries a medieval duchy ruled the heart of the Low Countries from Leuven and Brussels; modern Belgium still flies its gold lion on a black field.

subject: Duchy of Neopatras
summary: A Catalan mercenary state carved out of medieval central Greece, the Duchy of Neopatras existed for seventy years before Florentine ambition and Ottoman expansion erased it from the map.

subject: Duchy of Oldenburg
summary: Created in 1774 as the byproduct of a Russian-Danish horse-trade brokered by Catherine the Great, the Duchy of Oldenburg lasted barely four decades before Napoleon dissolved it from the map.

subject: Duchy of Warsaw
summary: Eight years of hope. A Napoleonic client state that briefly returned Poland to the map after the partitions had erased it - then disappeared again at the Congress of Vienna, leaving a generation of Poles to mourn what might have been.

subject: Dudley
summary: The Black Country market town that smelted iron with coke before Coalbrookdale, lost its shops to Merry Hill, and gave the world Lenny Henry, James Whale, and Duncan Edwards.

subject: Dudleytown
summary: The abandoned Connecticut settlement where legend claims demonic activity drove residents mad - a 'village of the damned' protected by a forest trust that forbids visitors, ensuring the mystery stays mysterious and the curse remains unchallenged.

subject: Dudleytown, Connecticut
summary: The abandoned Connecticut village where legends say every family met tragic ends - demonic possession, madness, murder, suicide - now closed to visitors by landowners tired of paranormal enthusiasts, but the curse stories persist.

subject: Dueholm Priory
summary: A house of the Knights Hospitaller on the island of Mors that ran the town's hospitals, fought the townspeople for control of them, and survives as one wing and two copied books.

subject: Dufftown
summary: A 19th-century planned town in Moray that became the whisky capital of the world, producing more malt whisky than any other Scottish town from its six working distilleries.

subject: Dugort
summary: The planned 19th-century Protestant mission village on the slopes of Slievemore that grew, during the Famine, into a refuge of last resort - and a place where the religious history of West Mayo became unbearably complicated.

subject: Duin en Kruidberg
summary: A Dutch country estate where the invasion of England was planned in 1688, later rebuilt as one of the Netherlands' grandest Renaissance Revival mansions.

subject: Duisburg
summary: Where the Ruhr meets the Rhine, a Frankish royal court grew into the world's largest inland port.

subject: Duisburg Hauptbahnhof
summary: A Ruhr Valley railway hub where three rival companies once built three competing stations side by side - and where one of Europe's busiest stretches of track still passes under a fading 1930s shed.

subject: Dulan Site
summary: A 3,000-year-old megalithic site on Taiwan's southeast coast where stone coffins and ancient walls reveal the deep roots of the Amis people in Dulan.

subject: Dulan, Taiwan
summary: Dulan — A'tolan to the Amis people who have called it home since at least 1500 BC — is a Pacific coast village where indigenous culture, surf breaks, and a repurposed sugar factory art scene coexist on Taiwan's southeast shore.

subject: Duluth lynchings
summary: On the night of June 15, 1920, a mob of thousands dragged three African-American circus workers from the Duluth city jail and lynched them on a downtown street corner -- an act of racial terror that prompted Minnesota's anti-lynching law and, a century later, a memorial of bronze statues across from the site where they died.

subject: Dumaguete
summary: A seaside university city on Negros Island, Dumaguete blends colonial heritage, marine ecosystems, and a thriving academic culture that has earned it the nickname 'City of Gentle People.'

subject: Dumbarton Oaks
summary: The Georgetown estate where Stravinsky's concerto premiered, the United Nations was sketched out, and Beatrix Farrand designed her masterpiece.

subject: Dumfries
summary: A red sandstone market town where Robert Burns spent his final years, repeatedly sacked by invaders yet endlessly rebuilt on the Nith.

subject: Dumfries
summary: A former royal burgh on the Nith where Robert the Bruce committed murder, Robert Burns died, and Norwegian soldiers waited out a war.

subject: Dunaff
summary: A coastal townland of cliffs and Mesolithic flint, where Ireland's oldest known campsite faces six hundred feet of sheer rock at the eastern entrance to Lough Swilly.
