subject: Dunbar
summary: An East Lothian seaside town that gave the world John Muir, and the conservation movement that created America's national parks.

subject: Dunbar Lifeboat Station
summary: A volunteer maritime rescue station whose 1808 founding makes it one of the oldest lifeboat stations in Britain.

subject: Duncan
summary: The City of Totems where over forty poles line the streets and Cowichan artisans craft the world-famous sweaters that carry their name.

subject: Duncan Cedar
summary: The largest known Western redcedar in the world, a thousand-year-old giant saved from the chainsaw by the loggers who found it, standing alone in a clearcut on Washington's Olympic Peninsula.

subject: Duncan Dunbar (ship)
summary: A clipper bound for Sydney struck an unlit coral atoll in the South Atlantic in 1865 — and all 117 people aboard came home alive.

subject: Dundee
summary: Scotland's fourth city, reinvented from its industrial past of jute, jam, and journalism into a design capital anchored by the V&A museum -- all set on the north bank of the Tay where the river meets the sea.

subject: Dunedin
summary: New Zealand's Edinburgh of the South, where Scottish settlers, Maori heritage, a 19th-century gold rush fortune, and the world's steepest street converge at the edge of a wild peninsula.

subject: Dungannon
summary: From the hilltop seat of the O'Neill kings to a 21st-century mosaic of Polish, Brazilian and East Timorese voices, this Tyrone town has reinvented itself again and again.

subject: Dungiven
summary: A small town at the foot of Benbradagh in the Sperrin Mountains, where three rivers meet and a 12th-century priory still guards the tomb of an O'Cahan chief.

subject: Dunmore Head
summary: The westernmost point of mainland Ireland, where Old Red Sandstone cliffs face the Atlantic and Luke Skywalker once stood in a Star Wars film.

subject: Dunnichen Stone
summary: A 7th-century Pictish symbol stone discovered in 1811 near the site of one of Scotland's most important early battles, bearing rare symbols that scholars have yet to fully decipher.

subject: Dunquin
summary: The westernmost village in Eurasia, where Peig Sayers told stories, David Lean filmed Ryan's Daughter, and CAMRA was founded in a bar called Kruger's.

subject: Dunster
summary: A medieval Somerset wool village beneath a Norman castle, where a thousand years of buildings - yarn market, dovecote, tithe barn, watermill - still cluster around a single steep main street.

subject: Dunwich
summary: Once the medieval capital of East Anglia and an international port the size of fourteenth-century London, now a Suffolk village of fewer than 200 residents, with its eight churches lying under the North Sea and the largest medieval underwater site in Europe just offshore.

subject: Dunwich Benevolent Asylum
summary: On the western shore of Minjerribah, an island institution sheltered Queensland's aged and destitute for eighty years, sustained throughout by the labour of the Quandamooka people whose Country it occupied.

subject: Dunwich Convict Causeway
summary: A low wall of red stone, laid without mortar by convict hands in 1827, is the only convict-built sea structure left in Queensland, and the doorway to two centuries of arrivals and departures on Minjerribah.

subject: Duplin County, North Carolina
summary: Duplin County raises more hogs than any other county in America and is the birthplace of the man who invented Pepsi.

subject: Dupont Circle
summary: A roundabout L'Enfant drew, mansions a Gilded Age built, and a neighborhood that became one of America's first gay enclaves.

subject: Durango, Colorado
summary: A railroad town built from scratch in 1880 when nearby Animas City refused the Denver and Rio Grande Railway, Durango became the gateway to Colorado's San Juan mining district and a Hollywood filming location that launched Marilyn Monroe.

subject: Durban
summary: Africa's busiest port and South Africa's third-largest city, where Zulu heritage, Indian cuisine, and a subtropical coastline collide in a place Vasco da Gama first spotted on Christmas Day, 1497.

subject: Durham Downs Station
summary: A sprawling Cooper Creek cattle station that helped build the legend of the Cattle King and now anchors one of the world's great pastoral empires.

subject: Durham, North Carolina
summary: The Bull City - tobacco capital turned research and university town, home of Duke, the Hayti district once called Black Wall Street, and the first sit-in of the modern civil rights movement in North Carolina.

subject: Durness
summary: A village of 347 perched on a patch of limestone in Scotland's far north - home to Smoo Cave, the country's most northerly chocolatier, and a Cold War craft village.

subject: Duroville
summary: On tribal land near Mecca, California, a community of roughly 4,000 residents — most of them farmworkers from Michoacán — built their lives in a mobile home park that the government spent years trying to close, and a federal judge ruled that forcing them out would constitute one of the largest forced migrations in California history.

subject: Durrie Station
summary: A vast cattle run on the Diamantina in Queensland's Channel Country, Durrie Station rides the floods that turn desert to grassland, on land taken from the Karuwali through frontier violence and held since by some of Australia's biggest pastoral names.

subject: Dusseldorf
summary: Capital of North Rhine-Westphalia, home to the largest Japanese community in Germany, the world-changing electronic band Kraftwerk, and an Altstadt that locals call the longest bar in the world.

subject: Dusseldorf-Unterbach
summary: In a Dusseldorf neighborhood whose carnival call is I-A and whose mascot is a donkey, the locals still remember when their sand built half the city.

subject: Dust Bowl Region
summary: When the earth blew away - where drought and overfarming stripped the Southern Plains of topsoil in the 1930s, creating black blizzards that buried farms, killed livestock, and drove 2.5 million people from their homes.

subject: Dutch Basketball League
summary: The Dutch Basketball League ran from 1960 to 2021 as the country's top tier of professional basketball, never quite breaking through internationally except for one remarkable 2018 run by Donar Groningen.

subject: Dutch Brazil
summary: For twenty-four years a Dutch republic governed the richest sugar coast on earth from a city called Mauritsstad, importing painters and naturalists along with the guns, and then lost the whole thing in a planters' war.

subject: Dutch Cape Colony
summary: What began in 1652 as a small refreshment station for ships grew into a settler colony built on enslaved labor, reshaping the language, demographics, and power structures of southern Africa.

subject: Dutch Ceylon
summary: For 156 years, the Dutch East India Company controlled Sri Lanka's coastline through a tangled web of treaties, betrayals, and cinnamon profits -- never conquering the Kandyan kingdom that watched from the interior.

subject: Dutch Empire
summary: An empire run by accountants - and the people across four continents who paid the bills.

subject: Dutch Grand Prix
summary: Formula One left the Dutch dunes in 1985 because the company running the circuit went broke; it took thirty-six years and one orange-clad national hero to bring it back.

subject: Dutch Language
summary: A West Germanic tongue caught between English and German that somehow ended up giving the world Afrikaans, Suriname's official language, and a fifth of the Indonesian vocabulary.

subject: Dutch Loango-Angola
summary: For seven years in the mid-seventeenth century, the Dutch West India Company seized Portugal's most valuable African colony -- not to build an empire, but to feed Brazil's insatiable demand for enslaved labor.

subject: Dutch Malacca
summary: For 183 years the Dutch held Malacca not to grow rich from it, but to make sure nobody else could -- a colonial possession defined more by strategic denial than by trade.

subject: Dutch New Guinea
summary: For thirteen years after Indonesian independence, the Netherlands held onto the western half of New Guinea, preparing Papuans for nationhood that was instead handed to Jakarta in 1963.

subject: Dutch Republic
summary: From 1588 to 1795, a confederation of seven small provinces ran a global trading empire, financed the Enlightenment, sheltered religious refugees, and rewrote what a state could be.

subject: Dutch Slave Coast
summary: The network of Dutch West India Company trading posts along the coast of present-day Ghana, Togo, Benin, and Nigeria that funneled enslaved Africans to plantations in the Americas from 1660 to 1760.

subject: Duyfken Point
summary: A low sandy point on the Gulf of Carpentaria named for the little Dutch ship whose 1606 voyage brought the first recorded, and violent, meeting of Europeans and Aboriginal Australia.

subject: Dwarka
summary: One of Hinduism's holiest cities, where the mythic kingdom of Krishna meets underwater archaeology and pilgrims descend 56 steps to bathe at the confluence of river and sea.

subject: Dwight Baldwin (missionary)
summary: A Connecticut minister who became Maui's de facto doctor during devastating epidemics, Dwight Baldwin founded a family dynasty that grew into one of Hawaii's most powerful business empires.

subject: Dyea Ghost Town
summary: The Alaska boomtown that exploded to 10,000 people during the Klondike Gold Rush then vanished completely within two years - now a ghost town where foundations disappear into the forest at the start of the infamous Chilkoot Trail.

subject: Dykanka
summary: The village Gogol immortalized in his first great book, where a horror tale set on St John's Eve rippled outward into one of the most famous pieces of Russian music.

subject: Dyrehavsbakken
summary: Nobody founded Bakken - it grew, unplanned, around a spring a woman found in the royal forest in 1583, and it has been entertaining Copenhagen ever since.

subject: Dzanga-Sangha Special Reserve
summary: A lowland rainforest reserve in the southwestern Central African Republic where three nations' protected areas converge into a UNESCO World Heritage Site, harboring western lowland gorillas, forest elephants, and the indigenous Ba'aka people who have lived among them for millennia.

subject: Dzharylhach
summary: A shape-shifting Black Sea sandbar that the ancient Greeks called the Course of Achilles, part island and part spit depending on the water.

subject: Dzogchen Beara
summary: A Tibetan Buddhist retreat centre on a cliff above the Atlantic in West Cork - one of the most westerly seats of Tibetan Buddhism on earth.

subject: Dâmrei Mountains
summary: The Elephant Mountains take Cambodia's heaviest rain on one flank and a quarter of it on the other, and the pepper grown on their skirts went from a million poles to four tonnes a year and back again.

subject: Dédougou
summary: A quiet Burkinabè provincial capital that becomes, every other year, the masked heart of West Africa.

subject: Dénia
summary: A Costa Blanca port crowned by a castle and named a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, home of the hundred-euro red prawn, three Michelin stars, and twenty-six kilometres of beaches.

subject: Döberitzer Heide
summary: Three centuries of soldiers never ploughed this sandy heath west of Berlin, and the unexploded shells they left behind kept everyone else out — which is why wild bison graze it now.

subject: Dún Laoghaire
summary: Dublin's coastal twin -- named for a 5th-century High King, briefly Kingstown after a George IV visit, terminus of Ireland's first railway, home of the world's first one-design yacht race, and the spot where Samuel Beckett claimed to have his life-changing artistic epiphany.

subject: Dülken
summary: A 1554 fools' academy in a windmill grants honorary doctorates to popes, astronauts, and Dali. The town joke that became Dülken's most enduring institution.

subject: Dümmer
summary: A shallow, ancient lake in southern Lower Saxony whose name appears in a tenth-century document and whose shoreline has been settled since the Stone Age.

subject: Dōgo Onsen
summary: Japan's oldest hot spring has been healing bathers for over a thousand years, from legendary princes to the novelist who immortalized it in fiction.

subject: Dōjima Rice Exchange
summary: Established in 1697, Osaka's Dojima Rice Exchange operated as the world's first organized futures market, where samurai wages were converted to coin, paper money was invented by merchants, and the modern concept of derivatives trading was born centuries before Wall Street existed.

story.title: Dotonbori: Osaka's Neon-Drenched Canal of Appetite

subject: Dōtonbori
summary: A 400-year-old canal district in Osaka where a mechanical crab waves its legs, a drumming clown greets sumo wrestlers, and the local proverb warns visitors to eat until they go bankrupt -- Dotonbori is Japan's most exuberant celebration of food, spectacle, and illuminated excess.

subject: Dōyamachō
summary: Tucked 500 meters east of Osaka Station, Doyamacho is a compact entertainment district where salarymen unwind at ten-seat bars, jazz clubs gave way to izakaya after Japan's bubble burst, and a quietly significant LGBTQ community has taken root in the narrow streets north of the tracks.

subject: E11 hiking trail
summary: A footpath invented in 1980 to link two sister cities on opposite sides of a divided Europe - and then, once the Iron Curtain fell, pushed straight through it and kept going east.

story.title: ELDYK - The Hellenic Force in Cyprus

subject: ELDYK - The Hellenic Force in Cyprus
summary: Born in an Athens suburb and shipped to Cyprus as part of the island's independence settlement, the small Greek garrison known as ELDYK fought one of the last desperate battles of the 1974 Turkish invasion.

subject: ERT - The Hellenic Broadcasting Corporation
summary: Greece's state broadcaster was switched off by government decree on a single night in 2013 - but its journalists refused to go dark, broadcasting on through the small hours in one of Europe's most dramatic media standoffs.

subject: Eagle Ranger Station
summary: A 1930s Forest Service outpost in the Sol Duc valley where Depression-era craftsmanship and CCC labor created a small compound that outlasted the agency that built it.

subject: Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: A Himalayan biodiversity hotspot in Arunachal Pradesh where a new bird species was discovered, elephants climb to 11,000 feet, and a single unpaved road spans an entire altitudinal range of life zones.

subject: Earliest known life forms
summary: The Pilbara region of Western Australia holds the oldest direct evidence of life on Earth — 3.48 billion-year-old stromatolites in the Dresser Formation, fossils of the microbes that first filled the atmosphere with oxygen.

story.title: Earth Simulator: The Machine That Modeled a Planet

subject: Earth Simulator
summary: Built in Yokohama for 60 billion yen, the Earth Simulator was the fastest supercomputer on the planet from 2002 to 2004 -- a massive machine purpose-built to simulate global climate at a resolution no one had achieved before, now in its fourth generation and still running.

subject: Easdale
summary: One of Scotland's smallest inhabited islands, where flooded slate quarries host the annual World Stone Skimming Championship.

subject: Easington Lifeboat Station
summary: A short-lived RNLI station at the end of Seaside Road that closed after just twenty years, leaving only a foundation and a story of one dramatic February rescue.

subject: Easky
summary: A Sligo surf village on the Wild Atlantic Way whose name in Irish means abounding in fish, where two world-class reef breaks draw international competitions, and whose 1207 castle still stands beside the pier.

subject: East Bergholt
summary: The Suffolk village where John Constable was born in 1776, where a Tudor bell cage still rings five enormous bells by hand because Cardinal Wolsey's downfall stopped the tower.

subject: East End of London
summary: The working-class heart of London - shipbuilders, dockers, Huguenot weavers, Jewish refugees, Bangladeshi grocers, and a century of arrivals that made the most layered, polyglot, fought-over neighbourhood in the city.

subject: East Frisia
summary: A historic region on the Lower Saxony coast where 469,000 people drink 300 liters of tea each per year and pour cream on top in clouds that mustn't be stirred.

subject: East Fuji Maneuver Area
summary: An 88-square-kilometer military training ground in Mount Fuji's foothills where samurai once drilled, the Imperial Army fired artillery, and today the JGSDF stages its largest annual firepower demonstration beneath the volcano's gaze.

subject: East Kilbride
summary: Scotland's first new town, designated 1947, where workers at the Rolls-Royce factory refused to service engines for Pinochet's air force - and where Glaswegians call it Polo Mint City for its 199 roundabouts.

subject: East Malaysia
summary: Malaysian Borneo -- where Sabah, Sarawak, and Labuan hold 60% of Malaysia's land but a fraction of its people, guarding the world's largest cave chamber, its third-largest island, and a political autonomy that requires West Malaysians to show their passports at the border.

subject: East Palo Alto, California
summary: Separated from its wealthy neighbor by a creek and a freeway, East Palo Alto has been shaped by redlining, the crack epidemic, and gentrification -- a small city where Silicon Valley's extremes collide.

story.title: East Patagonia, Tierra del Fuego and Strait of Magellan Dispute

subject: East Patagonia, Tierra del Fuego and Strait of Magellan Dispute
summary: For decades Chile and Argentina contested the windswept ends of the continent, fighting with maps, flags, and gifts to indigenous chiefs over who would hold the Strait of Magellan, until a treaty in 1881 drew the line that still divides Patagonia.

story.title: The Iron Heart of the Illinois River

subject: East Peoria, Illinois
summary: East Peoria evolved from swampy settlements like Bluetown and Coleville into a global industrial hub anchored by Caterpillar Inc., eventually transforming its industrial legacy into modern community spaces like the Levee District.

subject: East Texas Oil Field
summary: Discovered in 1930 by a persistent wildcatter and a widow's farm well, the East Texas Oil Field stretches across five counties and ranks as the largest oil field ever found in the lower 48 states by total production.

subject: East Wheal Rose
summary: On a July afternoon in 1846, a sudden cloudburst flooded this Cornish lead mine and trapped the men below ground. Thirty-nine drowned, and the story still hangs over the valley.

subject: EastEnders
summary: Britain's most-watched soap opera, launched on the BBC on 19 February 1985, set in a fictional East End square and filmed continuously for forty years on an outdoor lot in Hertfordshire.

subject: Eastern Cordillera Real montane forests
summary: A narrow band of cloud forest along the eastern Andes that may hold more plant species than the entire Amazon basin - and is disappearing fastest.

subject: Eastern Docklands
summary: Four artificial peninsulas in Amsterdam - Borneo, Sporenburg, KNSM, Java - built in the late 1800s for ships bound to the Dutch East Indies, abandoned by containerization, and reinvented in the 1990s as one of Europe's most studied experiments in dense modern housing.

subject: Eastern Ghats
summary: Older than the Himalayas and fragmented across five Indian states, the Eastern Ghats are an ancient mountain chain born when supercontinents collided over a billion years ago.

subject: Eastern Market, Detroit
summary: The largest historic public market district in the United States, where 40,000 Detroiters crowd open-air sheds each Saturday to buy produce from the same site their city has used since 1891.

subject: Eastern North Carolina
summary: The 41-county coastal plain where North Carolina began - pirate haven, colonial capital, military backbone, and the state's most-overlooked region.

subject: Eastern Province, Zambia
summary: Zambia's breadbasket and cultural crossroads - a Chewa, Tumbuka, and Nsenga heartland that was almost absorbed into Malawi, where festivals of masked dancers still draw people from three countries.

subject: Eastern Scheldt
summary: The Netherlands' largest national park is a 370-square-kilometre body of salt water that, by every strict definition, is no longer an estuary at all.

subject: Eastern Shore of Virginia
summary: Seventy miles of flat farmland and barrier marsh, cut off from the rest of Virginia by the Chesapeake Bay, the Eastern Shore has been a place apart since the colonial Accawmacke word meant exactly that: the other shore.

subject: Eastern Taiwan
summary: Taiwan's east coast—covering Yilan, Hualien, and Taitung counties—is the island's dramatic, less-travelled side, where the Central Mountain Range drops almost directly into the Pacific and indigenous cultures remain at the centre of everyday life.

subject: Eastgate, Chester
summary: Built in 1768 as an elegant sandstone arch and crowned with an ironwork clock for Victoria's diamond jubilee, the Eastgate at Chester is said to be the most photographed clock in England after Big Ben.

subject: Eastsound
summary: The village at the head of the horseshoe where Orcas Island's artists and artisans gather around a waterfront that once welcomed the Mosquito Fleet.

subject: Eastwood, Nottinghamshire
summary: A coal town on the edge of Sherwood Forest where ten pits surrounded a collier's cottage — and the collier's son grew up to be D. H. Lawrence.

subject: Eatonville, Florida
summary: Incorporated in 1887, Eatonville is one of the oldest self-governing all-Black municipalities in the United States, the childhood home of Zora Neale Hurston, and a community still fighting to preserve the land that defines it.

subject: Ebano Verde Scientific Reserve
summary: A Dominican cloud forest named for an endangered magnolia, where a president once ordered a tractor set on fire to stop logging, and where the only way in is on foot.

subject: Ebeltoft
summary: A cobbled Danish port town of 7,400 with the world's longest surviving wooden warship parked in a dry dock at the end of the street.

subject: Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve
summary: The first National Historical Reserve in the United States, where 1850s farmland patterns survive intact on a Puget Sound island bluff.

subject: Ecbatana
summary: The first capital of the Median Empire, ringed by seven concentric walls painted in the colors of the planets, now buried beneath the modern city of Hamadan in western Iran.

subject: Ecclefechan
summary: A tiny Dumfriesshire village whose tongue-twisting name produced one of Scotland's best-loved philosophers and a Christmas tart that conquered Sainsbury's.

story.title: Echigo-Tsumari: Where Snow Country Became an Art Gallery

subject: Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennial
summary: Every three years, 750 square kilometers of depopulating Japanese snow country transforms into one of the world's largest outdoor art exhibitions, scattering hundreds of installations across rice paddies, abandoned schools, and mountain tunnels in a radical experiment to revive rural life through contemporary art.

subject: Echinades
summary: Named for the sea urchin's sharp spine, these scattered Ionian islets have been slowly merging with the Greek mainland for millennia — a geological process that Herodotus watched, Thucydides predicted, and the river Achelous has still not finished.

subject: Echizen Province
summary: The ancient province where Lady Murasaki found inspiration, warriors burned castles, and paper-makers perfected their craft over twelve centuries.

subject: Echuca
summary: On the bend of the Murray where it runs closest to Melbourne, an ex-convict's punt grew into Australia's greatest inland port, and the world's largest fleet of paddle steamers still works the river.

subject: Eco-Runner Team Delft
summary: A rotating team of TU Delft students who build a new hydrogen car every year - and in June 2023 drove one of them 2,488 kilometers on less than a kilogram of fuel.

subject: Ecuador
summary: A small country that fits four worlds - Andean peaks, Amazon jungle, Pacific coast, and the Galapagos - into an area smaller than Nevada.

subject: Ecuador
summary: The first country to grant legal rights to nature in its constitution - a megadiverse republic whose four regions squeeze Andean peaks, Amazon rainforest, Pacific coast, and the Galapagos Islands into a single small country.

subject: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
summary: In the Fener district of Istanbul, the Church of St. George houses the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople — the spiritual center of Eastern Orthodox Christianity worldwide, a see that has endured conquest, exile, and centuries of constraint while remaining the first among equals of world Orthodoxy.

subject: Ed Dubeibat
summary: A small-hills town in South Kordofan whose roads made it useful to traders and, later, to armies.

subject: Edam
summary: The Dutch town whose name became a cheese - and whose hidden shipyards once rivalled Amsterdam.

subject: Edenton National Fish Hatchery
summary: A 70-acre federal hatchery on Pembroke Creek that has been raising striped bass, shad, and endangered Cape Fear shiners for the better part of 125 years.

subject: Edenton, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's first colonial capital, where women staged America's earliest female political protest and an enslaved woman hid in a crawl space for seven years before writing a masterpiece.

subject: Edgbaston
summary: A Birmingham suburb whose 19th-century landlords refused factories and warehouses, leaving room for towers, gardens, and a J. R. R. Tolkien childhood that left its mark on Middle-earth.

subject: Edgbaston Cricket Ground
summary: On a Birmingham meadow the Calthorpe estate dismissed as rough grazing, Warwickshire built a cricket ground that grew into one of the loudest, most consequential stadiums in the English game.

subject: Edgbaston Reserve
summary: A cluster of desert springs north-east of Longreach shelters more than two dozen creatures found nowhere else on Earth, including the tiny, critically endangered red-finned blue-eye.

subject: Edgefield County, South Carolina
summary: A rural county on the Savannah River that gave South Carolina ten governors, the potter Dave Drake, and a long, hard chapter of Reconstruction violence.

subject: Edgefield, South Carolina
summary: A small county seat near the Savannah River whose clay produced Dave Drake's signed stoneware and whose politics produced ten governors and a long shadow of violence.

subject: Edgemoor Farm Dairy Barn
summary: A prize-winning Guernsey dairy became San Diego County's poor farm, and the Dutch gambrel barn that survived both uses now houses a historical society.

subject: Edhi Foundation
summary: Born from one man's experience caring for his disabled mother, the Edhi Foundation grew from a single free dispensary in Karachi into the world's largest volunteer ambulance organization.

subject: Ediacara Hills
summary: Low hills in the Flinders Ranges where a young geologist found the fossil impressions of Earth's first complex life.

subject: Edifício Copan
summary: Oscar Niemeyer's sinuous, S-shaped residential tower in downtown São Paulo houses over 1,100 apartments, 72 businesses, and its own postal code — a concrete wave that has defined the city's skyline since 1966.

subject: Edinburgh
summary: Scotland's capital on its volcanic throne - where a medieval Old Town and Georgian New Town created a UNESCO masterpiece, and where the Enlightenment was born in tavern conversations.

subject: Edinburgh City Bypass
summary: A dual-carriageway arc around the south of Edinburgh, built piece by piece across the 1980s, where one stubborn roundabout has held up the rest of Scotland's traffic for forty years.

subject: Edinburgh East
summary: The eastern districts of Edinburgh, where a sailor named a hamlet for a Panamanian battle, a minister skated into immortality, and a railway claimed it had never had an accident.

subject: Edinburgh International Festival
summary: Funded by the winnings of a wartime racehorse and built to heal Europe's cultural wounds, the August festival has hosted every major classical name from Furtwangler to Pavarotti since 1947.

subject: Edinburgh New Town
summary: James Craig's 1767 Georgian grid laid out atop a drained loch, where Robert Adam's Charlotte Square anchors a UNESCO World Heritage masterpiece of Enlightenment urban planning.

subject: Edinburgh Town Walls
summary: Three successive walls built to defend Edinburgh against English invasion, easily breached every time but useful for collecting smugglers' taxes, with fragments still standing in the Vennel, Greyfriars Kirkyard and Drummond Street.

subject: Edinburgh Trams
summary: A 776-million-pound modern light rail line that took twelve years and a public inquiry to deliver, finally reaching Newhaven in 2023 to restore the link severed when the old tram network was scrapped in 1956.

subject: Edinburgh Vaults
summary: Hidden beneath South Bridge in Edinburgh's Old Town, a warren of nineteen brick arches sheltered tradesmen, then the city's poorest residents, then nothing at all - until 1985, when archaeologists found the toys they had left behind.

subject: Edirne
summary: The Ottoman capital before Istanbul, where three rivers meet, oil-slick wrestlers grapple, and Sinan built his masterpiece.

subject: Edirnekapı, Fatih
summary: At the highest point of Constantinople's ancient walled city, the Gate of Charisius — now called Edirnekapı — is where Mehmed II entered in triumph on May 29, 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire and beginning the Ottoman age.

subject: Edison and Ford Winter Estates
summary: The adjacent winter retreats of Thomas Edison and Henry Ford on the Caloosahatchee River, where two of America's greatest inventors tested 17,000 plant samples in search of domestic rubber and planted a botanical garden that still flourishes over a century later.

subject: Edith Thompson and Frederick Bywaters
summary: On 9 January 1923, in two London prisons half a mile apart, the British state hanged a 29-year-old woman and her 20-year-old lover at nine in the morning. A century later, lawyers and historians still call it a miscarriage of justice.

subject: Edmonds
summary: The Puget Sound ferry town charming enough for Rick Steves - where ferries depart for the Kitsap Peninsula, trains roll through on their way to everywhere, and a walkable downtown faces the water that defines Pacific Northwest life.

subject: Edo Wonderland Nikko Edomura
summary: A theme park in the mountains of Tochigi where the Edo period never ended -- visitors dress as samurai, ninja perform on rooftops, oiran parade through the streets, and the film studios behind it all double as sets for historical dramas.

subject: Edremit
summary: Edremit, on the Gulf of Edremit in Turkey's Northern Aegean, sits above the buried remains of ancient Adramyttium, flanked by olive groves and the forested slopes of Mount Ida — and its modern story is as layered as its ancient one, shaped by expulsion, migration, and the slow return of tourism.

subject: Eduard Bohlen
summary: A German steamship that ran aground in fog in 1909 and now sits marooned in the dunes, roughly half a kilometre from the sea that wrecked her.

story.title: Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve

subject: Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve
summary: Bolivia's most visited protected area sprawls across 714,745 hectares of high altiplano where flamingos wade through rainbow-colored lagoons, geysers erupt at dawn, and wind-carved rock formations rise from desert sand beneath volcanoes topping 5,900 meters.

subject: Edward Harland
summary: A Yorkshire physician's son became manager of a Belfast shipyard at twenty-three, bought it at twenty-seven, and his name now sits on the firm that built the Titanic.

subject: Edward R. Madigan State Fish and Wildlife Area
summary: A conservation area in Logan County, on land once managed by the Department of Mental Health, encircles two state prisons.

subject: Edward Youde Aviary
summary: Walk through 600 birds representing 80 species inside the largest walk-through aviary in Southeast Asia, tucked into a natural valley at the heart of Hong Kong Park.

subject: Edwards Air Force Base
summary: Where humanity first broke the sound barrier and where the Space Shuttle came home, Edwards Air Force Base remains the crucible where experimental aircraft earn their wings.

subject: Edwin Fox
summary: Built of teak in Calcutta in 1853, the Edwin Fox carried troops to the Crimean War, convicts to Australia, and settlers to New Zealand before being abandoned to rot -- then rescued for one shilling.

subject: Eersel
summary: A small Kempen town in North Brabant where Bronze Age burial mounds, a 712 charter to Saint Willibrord, a 1464 Gothic chapel, and a tradition of cigar-making all line up around a single protected market square.

subject: Efteling
summary: Europe's third-largest theme park, built in a real forest of North Brabant, drawn by an illustrator who looked nothing like Walt Disney.

story.title: Egmond aan Zee Offshore Wind Farm

subject: Egmond aan Zee Offshore Wind Farm
summary: Thirty-six turbines standing in the North Sea ten kilometres off a Dutch beach town - the country's first offshore wind farm, and the proving ground for everything that came after.

subject: Egremont, Cumbria
summary: A Cumbrian market town beneath a Norman castle, where the World Gurning Championships descend from a 13th-century crab apple charter.

subject: Egremont, Merseyside
summary: A Wallasey suburb named for a Cumberland village by the captain who built the first house there, Egremont once had the longest pier on Merseyside and now has a quiet promenade where the ferry used to land.

subject: Egtved Girl
summary: A teenage girl buried in an oak coffin in Jutland in the summer of 1370 BC, whose hair, cord skirt and bronze belt disc survived to become the best-preserved outfit of the Nordic Bronze Age.

subject: Egyptian pyramids
summary: At least 138 pyramids dot the Egyptian landscape, from the stepped experiments at Saqqara to the perfected geometry at Giza, monuments that took millennia to build and that no one has managed to destroy.

subject: Eigg
summary: A small Hebridean island where 395 people were suffocated in a cave during a clan feud, a dinosaur bone was discovered in 2020, and the residents bought their own island for 1.5 million pounds.

story.title: Eight Acres for a Plant That Exists Almost Nowhere

subject: Eight Acres for a Plant That Exists Almost Nowhere
summary: A tiny nature reserve in California's Lake County protects one of the rarest plants on Earth - the Loch Lomond button celery, an endangered species that went undiscovered at any second location for over fifty years.

subject: Eight-Nation Alliance
summary: In 1900, an unprecedented coalition of eight rival powers invaded China to relieve their besieged diplomats, then stayed to loot Beijing's cultural treasures on an industrial scale.

subject: Eilean Chaluim Chille
summary: A small uninhabited island at the mouth of Loch Erisort where, according to tradition, Columban monks first carried Christianity ashore on Lewis.

subject: Eilendorf (Aachen)
summary: An Aachen borough that began as Erlendorf - the village of the alder trees - grew up around a zinc-ore mine, and still carries crossed mining hammers on its coat of arms.

subject: Eirunepé
summary: On a bend of the Juruá River, 2,400 kilometers by water from Manaus, a rubber-era town drowsing in the Amazon's deepest southwest dreams occasionally of becoming a state capital.

subject: Eisenhower Tree
summary: A loblolly pine on the 17th fairway at Augusta National that so tormented President Eisenhower he demanded it be cut down -- only to have the club chairman adjourn the meeting rather than refuse a sitting president.

subject: Eisenhüttenstadt
summary: East Germany built a steel mill on the Oder and then built a town beside it to prove a point about how people should live - and for eight years that town was called Stalinstadt.

subject: Eisenstück affair
summary: A family quarrel in 1876 Nicaragua escalated into a German naval blockade, a $30,000 forced indemnity, and what one historian called a classic example of gunboat politics.

subject: Eisleben
summary: Martin Luther was born in this Saxon copper town and died in it sixty-two years later - and spent almost none of the time in between here.

subject: Eixample
summary: The clipped-corner grid that defines Barcelona from the air was a 19th-century social utopia by Ildefons Cerdà, half-built into the city's most elegant district.

subject: Ekbatan
summary: Named after the ancient Median capital and built by an American company before the 1979 revolution, Ekbatan is a massive planned town in western Tehran that became a self-contained universe of 15,500 apartments, graffiti art, underground music, and revolutionary protest.

subject: Ekel (Norden)
summary: A neighborhood of Norden whose name means "acorn" and whose boundaries have never been properly drawn.

subject: Ekenäs, Finland
summary: A Swedish-speaking coastal town whose founding king spent the next four years trying to move its inhabitants somewhere else, and whose wooden old town survived because nobody could afford to replace it.

subject: Eko Atlantic
summary: A city being built on nine square kilometers of land reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean off Lagos, designed to house 250,000 residents and shield the eroding coastline from the sea.

subject: Ekom-Nkam Waterfalls
summary: Twin waterfalls in Cameroon's Northwest Highlands where the Nkam River drops 80 meters through jungle that once doubled as Tarzan's Africa.

subject: El Airo, Loja
summary: A southern Ecuadorian parish of 1,093 people where organic coffee grows between 1,600 and 3,200 meters, and spectacled bears still wander the paramo.

subject: El Boleo
summary: A copper mine in the Baja California desert that built a French colonial town, created a harbor from its own slag, and has lured investors from four nations across 150 years of booms and busts.

subject: El Bolsón
summary: A hop-growing, beer-brewing valley town where 1970s counterculture put down roots beneath a peak the Mapuche named 'hanging from the clouds.'

subject: El Cabanyal
summary: A grid of tile-clad fishermen's houses beside Valencia's main beach, El Cabanyal survived a two-decade demolition plan to become one of the coolest neighbourhoods in Europe.

subject: El Calafate
summary: Gateway to the Perito Moreno Glacier and Los Glaciares National Park, this Patagonian town on the shores of glacial Lake Argentina serves as base camp for some of Earth's most spectacular ice.

subject: El Capitan
summary: A 3,000-foot granite monolith in Yosemite Valley whose Miwok name honors a humble inchworm, and whose sheer face has driven climbers to madness, glory, and one unforgettable morning without a rope.

subject: El Castell de Guadalest
summary: A village of fewer than two hundred people, reached only through a tunnel carved in solid rock, whose white bell tower on a crag became the emblem of the Costa Blanca.

subject: El Castillo, Nicaragua
summary: A Nicaraguan river village built around a 17th-century fortress where a 19-year-old woman helped repel a British siege and a young Horatio Nelson fought one of his earliest battles.

subject: El Chal
summary: A Maya city that outlasted its neighbors for over 1,600 years, now half-buried under a modern Guatemalan village whose streets cut through ancient pyramids.

subject: El Chaltén
summary: Argentina's trekking capital - a frontier village of hostels and gear shops huddled beneath the impossible granite spires of Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre, where world-class trails start from the edge of town.

subject: El Chiflón del Diablo
summary: One of Chile's oldest coal mines burrowed beneath the floor of the Pacific, and the men who worked it gave the writer Baldomero Lillo the material for his unflinching portrait of life underground.

subject: El Dorado
summary: What began as a Muisca coronation ritual on a Colombian lake became the most persistent treasure hunt in history, luring conquistadors, bankers, and English knights into the South American interior for over a century.

subject: El Guabo Canton
summary: A banana canton in Ecuador's El Oro Province, named for a tree that once lined a riverbank where canoes tied up to load cocoa and coffee.

subject: El Khandaq
summary: On the left bank of the Nile, 423 km north of Khartoum, a medieval Christian fortress anchors a Nubian river town whose two-story mud-brick houses have stood empty since the 1970s.

subject: El Mozote
summary: A small village in El Salvador's Morazan Department where, on December 11, 1981, soldiers of the Atlacatl Battalion killed nearly 1,000 civilians in the worst massacre of the Salvadoran Civil War -- a crime denied for years until forensic evidence and one survivor's testimony forced the world to reckon with what happened.

subject: El Nido, Palawan
summary: A municipality on the northern tip of Palawan whose limestone cliffs, hidden lagoons, and marine sanctuary have earned it recognition as one of the most beautiful island destinations in the world.

subject: El Opeño
summary: The oldest known tombs in Mesoamerica, dating to around 1600 BCE, quietly challenge the assumption that the Olmec were the mother culture of all civilization in the region.

subject: El Oro Province
summary: Ecuador's southernmost coastal province traded one yellow commodity for another: gold for bananas, and became one of the world's great fruit ports.

subject: El Ostional
summary: A small Nicaraguan fishing village on a crescent-shaped Pacific bay, El Ostional holds layers of indigenous archaeology, revolutionary history, and fragile coastal ecosystems -- all within 10 kilometers of the Costa Rican border.

subject: El Palo Alto
summary: A thousand-year-old coast redwood on the banks of San Francisquito Creek gave Palo Alto its name, its city seal, and its identity -- though the tree lost one of its two trunks in a 19th-century storm.

subject: El Paraíso Verde
summary: A gated colony of German-speaking emigrants in rural Paraguay, founded as a refuge from modern Europe and now entangled in lawsuits over the money that was meant to build it.

subject: El Paraíso, Peru
summary: One of the largest Preceramic settlements in the Americas, El Paraiso's monumental stone architecture rose on the Peruvian coast more than 4,000 years ago, built by a people who drew over 90 percent of their protein from the sea.

story.title: El Paso: The Border City Where Texas Meets Mexico

subject: El Paso
summary: The Texas city inseparable from its Mexican twin - where Ciudad Juárez is visible from every hilltop, where the border divides what geography unites, and where cultures blend in ways the rest of America doesn't understand.

story.title: El Paso: The Sun City at the Pass of the North

subject: El Paso
summary: The Texas border city where the Rio Grande divides two nations, where Spanish explorers named the 'Pass of the North' in 1581, and where Fort Bliss guards the largest military installation in the United States.

subject: El Paso, Texas
summary: At the crossroads of three states and two nations, El Paso has been a vital mountain pass for Native peoples, Spanish conquistadors, Mexican settlers, and American pioneers for over 10,000 years.

subject: El Peñón de Guatapé
summary: A 65-million-year-old granite monolith rising 200 meters from the Colombian highlands, scaled by 740 steps built into a crack in its face, with an unfinished graffiti war painted on its western wall.

subject: El Portal
summary: A tiny Merced River canyon community that serves as Yosemite's front porch, where wildflower trails lead to abandoned gold mines and historic railroad equipment rusts beside the road to the valley.

subject: El Raval
summary: Barcelona's most contradictory neighborhood packs a Gaudi palace, the city's best food market, a Keith Haring mural, a giant bronze cat, and a serial killer's legacy into a few dense blocks.

subject: El Salt
summary: At a limestone shelter near Alcoy, layers of ancient campfires and the oldest known human excrement reveal how Neanderthals lived, cooked, and finally vanished from Iberia.

subject: El Tatio
summary: The third-largest geyser field on Earth and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere, El Tatio erupts at 4,320 meters in Chile's Atacama highlands, where dawn turns columns of steam into gold against a ring of Andean volcanoes.

subject: El Teniente
summary: High in the Chilean Andes, the world's largest underground copper mine hides more than 3,000 kilometers of tunnels inside a single mountain - a hollow city of rock built over more than a century.

subject: El Torcal de Antequera
summary: A surreal karst landscape in Andalusia where 150-million-year-old seabeds have been sculpted by erosion into towers, corridors, and shapes resembling everyday objects.

subject: El Toro (Menorca)
summary: Menorca's highest point is named 'the Bull' by accident; the word really means hill, and from its 358-metre summit you can see the whole island at once.

subject: El Valle
summary: A village inside a volcanic crater that has been continuously inhabited for 11,000 years, where the soil is so rich it is sold in bags across Panama and fence posts sprout leaves.

subject: El Walamo
summary: A small agricultural town south of Mazatlan named for a vanished tree, built around a sugar mill that boomed and collapsed, now sustained by some of Mexico's finest chili peppers.

subject: El-Gadarif
summary: Sudan's breadbasket city where 70 percent of the country's mechanized farming happens and a town of 269,395 grew up around the sorghum harvest.

subject: El-Kurru
summary: The first royal cemetery of Kush's Napatan kings, where the Black Pharaohs who conquered Egypt were buried beneath Nubian pyramids starting around 850 BC.

subject: Elche
summary: A shoemaking city of a quarter-million that lives inside Europe's only great date-palm oasis, planted by Phoenicians, watered by Arab engineers, and honored twice over by UNESCO.

subject: Elche Palm Sunday Procession
summary: On Palm Sunday, tens of thousands of people fill the streets of Elche carrying not green fronds but the intricate bleached-white palms for which this palm-grove city has been famous for six centuries.

subject: Eldorado (Berlin)
summary: A Schöneberg nightclub that issued coins entitling the holder to dance with someone of the same sex — the emblematic queer room of Weimar Berlin, closed by the police weeks before Hitler took power and then handed to the SA.

subject: Eldoret
summary: Once called 'Farm 64' for its distance from the nearest railhead, Kenya's fifth-largest city became the world's running capital -- a highland training ground that has produced more Olympic and World Championship distance medals than any comparable place on Earth.

subject: Electorate of Hanover
summary: For 123 years the King of Britain was also a north German prince-elector who mostly wasn't there - and the arrangement ended not in revolution but on a point of inheritance law.

subject: Elefsina
summary: The gritty industrial port city west of Athens that was, in antiquity, the home of the Eleusinian Mysteries — the most sacred secret rites of the ancient Greek world — and which became a European Capital of Culture in 2023.

subject: Elem Indian Colony
summary: A 50-acre Pomo reservation on the shore of Clear Lake sits atop one of California's most toxic superfund sites, where a century of mercury mining contaminated the land, the water, and the people who never left.

subject: Eleuthera
summary: A 110-mile Bahamian island so narrow it pinches to 30 feet wide, where English settlers attempted the Western Hemisphere's first democracy, the U.S. Navy secretly hunted submarines, and pink sand beaches meet the open Atlantic.

subject: Eleutherae
summary: A border town that bought its freedom by giving it away, Eleutherae left Greece a wine god, the theatre, and one of antiquity's best-preserved fortresses.

subject: Elfstedentocht
summary: A 200-kilometre skating race past eleven Frisian cities - last held in 1997, and likely never again.

subject: Elgin
summary: The Moray county town built on Triassic sandstone, ruined cathedral country, midpoint between Inverness and Aberdeen, and a working base for exploring Speyside whisky.

subject: Elis
summary: The region of Elis in the western Peloponnese wielded an authority far exceeding its size — as the state that owned and administered ancient Olympia, it held the sacred franchise of the Games for over a millennium.

subject: Elis (city)
summary: The ancient Greek city of Elis served as the administrative capital of the polis of Elis and the headquarters for judging the Olympic Games — yet it left so little behind that by the 19th century only scattered stone and tile marked where it had stood.

subject: Elizabeth City
summary: The Harbor of Hospitality - a Pasquotank River town that hosts the Coast Guard's biggest air base, raised Alex Haley, and invented the Moth Boat.

subject: Elizabeth Klarer
summary: A Cambridge-educated meteorologist and pilot who became one of South Africa's most famous UFO contactees, claiming interstellar love from a hilltop in the Natal midlands.

story.title: Elizabeth Saunders Home: The Mother of Two Thousand Children

subject: Elizabeth Saunders Home
summary: A Christian orphanage in Oiso, Kanagawa, founded by a Mitsubishi heiress who sold everything she owned to shelter the biracial children abandoned by postwar Japan -- and named for an Englishwoman she never met.

subject: Elkington Silver Electroplating Works
summary: On Newhall Street, a Birmingham factory used electricity to plate silver onto cheaper metals and accidentally hosted the invention of the first plastic before becoming the city's science museum.

subject: Elkins
summary: A West Virginia mountain town that smells like ramps in spring and pulls visitors from Seneca Rocks, Spruce Knob, and the Monongahela National Forest.

subject: Ellendale Diamond Field
summary: The Kimberley diamond field that rewrote geology textbooks by proving lamproite could produce diamonds, supplied half the world's fancy yellow stones to Tiffany & Co., and still guards a geological mystery known as the Lost Alluvials.

subject: Ellensburg
summary: A college town on the dry side of the Cascades where Labor Day brings one of America's oldest rodeos and the Mountains to Sound Greenway crosses the state.

subject: Ellesmere Port
summary: An industrial town built where a canal ended at the wrong river, Ellesmere Port now anchors Cheshire's industrial heart with the Stanlow oil refinery, a Vauxhall plant that has built cars since 1962, and the largest canal boat collection in the world.

subject: Ellicott's Stone
summary: A rough sandstone block on the banks of the Mobile River marks where the United States ended and the Spanish Empire began -- placed by surveyor Andrew Ellicott in 1799 using nothing but stars and rudimentary instruments.

subject: Elliott Key
summary: The northernmost true Florida Key - a sliver of ancient coral reef where pirates hid, pineapple farmers prospered, and developers bulldozed a spite highway that the tropical forest quietly erased.

subject: Elliott Knob
summary: The highest peak in northern Virginia at 4,463 feet - high enough to support a small ice-age relict stand of red spruce on its summit, surrounded by oak and hickory in the valleys below.

subject: Ellisland Farm
summary: The riverside farm where Robert Burns wrote Tam o' Shanter and Auld Lang Syne, struggled with stony soil, and ultimately turned to the Excise.

subject: Elliston
summary: A tiny town on a wine-glass bay, where a clifftop sculpture trail draws visitors to the same headlands that hold the memory of an Aboriginal massacre long denied and now, at last, acknowledged.

subject: Elm Hill, Norwich
summary: A cobbled Tudor-era lane in central Norwich that the city nearly demolished for a swimming pool in 1926 - and that now plays itself in Stardust and Jingle Jangle.

subject: Eloise Copper Mine
summary: An underground copper mine southeast of Cloncurry that has died and been reborn more than once - now expanding again on the back of the world's rising hunger for copper.

subject: Els Quatre Gats
summary: The café whose name is Catalan slang for "hardly anyone" became the beating heart of Barcelona's Modernisme and hosted a teenage Picasso's first solo show.

subject: Else (Werre)
summary: A river with no source - born from a bifurcation where the Hase splits, and a third of its water turns east instead of north.

subject: Elsey Station
summary: A vast Northern Territory cattle property named after an explorer's surgeon, immortalised in a beloved 1908 novel, shaped by violence and grief, and eventually returned to the Mangarrayi people whose country it has always been.

subject: Elstow
summary: A small Bedfordshire village with a 15th-century timber Moot Hall on its green, the remains of a Benedictine nunnery founded in 1078 by William the Conqueror's niece, and a May Day festival tradition older than the village itself.

subject: Elstree
summary: A small village in Hertfordshire that gave its name to the film studios where Star Wars, the Indiana Jones films, The Shining, and EastEnders were made - and where, in 1779, a Norfolk rector shot dead the mistress of the Earl of Sandwich.

subject: Ely and Littleport Riots of 1816
summary: In May 1816, desperate fenland labourers, their children starving after the Napoleonic Wars, rose up in Littleport and marched on Ely — a rebellion that ended with five hangings, transportation to Australia, and the silence that follows suppressed hunger.

subject: Elysian Fields (Hoboken, New Jersey)
summary: The vanished pleasure grounds on Hoboken's Hudson River waterfront where New Yorkers escaped the city, cricket flourished, the New York Yacht Club was born, and baseball evolved from gentlemen's pastime to national obsession.

subject: Embleton, Northumberland
summary: A Northumberland coastal village whose son went down with the Titanic and whose Victorian vicar later ran the Diocese of London.

subject: Emboaca
summary: A 500-person fishing village on the Ceará coast where men still sail to sea on balsa-log rafts the size of a kitchen table.

subject: Emden
summary: When a German light cruiser raided Madras in 1914, her name entered the Tamil language — and to this day, an Emden in Tamil is a person who dares and acts with precision.

subject: Emerald Isle
summary: A family-vacation beach town at the western end of Bogue Banks where bike paths trace the dunes, fighter jets pass overhead, and the Point's currents stay dangerously fast.

subject: Emerald Mound site
summary: The second-largest Mississippian earthwork in North America, an eight-acre ceremonial platform built by the ancestors of the Natchez people along what is now the Natchez Trace Parkway.

subject: Emirate of Asir
summary: A Sufi-founded, Idrisi-led state that flickered on the Red Sea coast of Yemen and southern Arabia from 1907 to 1934, caught between the Ottomans, the British, the Hashemites, and the rising Saudis.

subject: Emirate of Trarza
summary: For two centuries the Emirate of Trarza ruled the desert north of the Senegal River, growing rich on the sap of acacia trees before its wars with France ended an independence that had outlasted empires.

subject: Emirgan
summary: A leafy Bosphorus village north of central Istanbul, Emirgan carries the name of a Safavid commander, holds the oldest surviving yalı on the European shore, and sustains itself on tea gardens, tulips, and the particular light off the strait.

subject: Emlagh East Ogham Stone
summary: Ireland's first recorded ogham stone, carved around 1,600 years ago as a grave marker for Bruscus son of Cailech and noted by an antiquarian in 1702.

subject: Emlyn
summary: One of the seven cantrefi of medieval Dyfed, the ancient Welsh district whose name survives in Newcastle Emlyn and whose territory traced the Teifi valley between the Preselis and the Cambrians.

subject: Emmen
summary: Most visitors come for the zoo and then discover the rest: Stone Age tombs inside the city limits, a famous American earthwork in a former sand pit, and the southernmost tip of the wooded Hondsrug ridge.

subject: Emmen, Netherlands
summary: A planned Dutch city of 107,000 grown out of peat-cutters' hamlets, where a Nobel-winning chemist grew up next door to a Stone Age dolmen and the Robert Smithson earthwork that helped invent land art.

subject: Emperor Norton
summary: The self-proclaimed Emperor of the United States who ruled San Francisco by decree for twenty years, abolishing Congress, ordering a bridge across the bay, and dying beloved by the entire city.

subject: Emperor Norton's San Francisco
summary: The bankrupt rice merchant who declared himself Emperor of the United States in 1859 - and San Francisco played along for 21 years, accepting his self-printed currency and following his imperial decrees.

subject: Empire Polo Club
summary: A thousand-acre polo facility in Indio that in 1993 began leasing its grounds to a music promoter named Goldenvoice — launching what became the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival and, eventually, a 28-year deal that closed the polo fields permanently.

subject: Empire of China (1915–1916)
summary: In late 1915, President Yuan Shikai attempted to restore the Chinese monarchy with himself as emperor -- an 83-day reign that collapsed under the weight of its own absurdity and plunged the nation into the Warlord Era.

subject: Empire of Great Fulo
summary: The Denanke Kingdom, a Fulani empire of the Senegal valley that rose on a cavalry migration, toppled an older empire, and fell at last to a holy war.

subject: Empresa de Ferrocarriles Ecuatorianos
summary: Ecuador's state railway climbed the Andes, stitched the country together, and then died twice in a century - by mudslide, then by pandemic.

subject: Empress Market
summary: Built on the ground where British forces executed rebellious sepoys in 1857, Karachi's Empress Market was named for Queen Victoria and remains one of the city's most chaotic and beloved shopping destinations.

subject: Emu Field, South Australia
summary: The remote desert clay-pan where Britain detonated its first atomic bombs on the Australian mainland in 1953, and where a black mist of fallout rolled over Anangu people who were never warned.

subject: Enchanted Rock
summary: A billion-year-old dome of pink granite in the Texas Hill Country that groans and creaks at night -- sounds that convinced the Tonkawa people ghost fires burned on its summit and that led Spanish explorers to call it enchanted.

subject: Encinitas Boathouses
summary: Two houses built to resemble ocean vessels in Encinitas, California — the S.S. Encinitas and S.S. Moonlight — stand as the city's most photographed buildings and a testament to one builder's whimsical tribute to the sea.

subject: Encinitas, California
summary: A coastal city in northern San Diego County where surf culture, flower farming, and Kumeyaay history weave together along a stretch of Pacific shoreline shaped by centuries of human aspiration and salt air.

subject: End of the World Turn
summary: An almost-half-circle bend in the Elk River, where cliffs rise 1,100 feet and pioneer raftsmen named the place for the dead-end they thought they had reached.

subject: Enets language
summary: Spoken by fewer than 100 people along the Lower Yenisei, the Enets language preserves a way of understanding the Arctic world that no other tongue can replicate.

subject: Enga Province
summary: Enga is the one province in Papua New Guinea where everyone speaks the same language - about half a million highland farmers sharing sweet potatoes, pig exchanges, and a landscape of ridges steep enough to collapse without warning.

subject: English Riviera Geopark
summary: An urban UNESCO Global Geopark in Torbay where 400-million-year-old reefs, a Permian desert, and the cave that gave its name to a geological period are all within walking distance of an ice cream stand.

subject: English ship Dartmouth (1655)
summary: A 22-gun Commonwealth fifth-rate that fought the Dutch, the Barbary pirates, and the Jacobites before a storm drove her onto rocks in the Sound of Mull in 1690.

subject: Enkapune Ya Muto
summary: A rock shelter on Kenya's Mau Escarpment where ostrich eggshell beads dated to nearly 40,000 years ago represent some of the earliest known personal ornaments made by humans.

subject: Enkhuizen
summary: Once one of the Netherlands' wealthiest VOC ports, Enkhuizen now wears its Golden Age silt as a kind of preservation - 360 monuments held in amber.

subject: Ennedi Est (province)
summary: A Chadian province wedged against the Libyan and Sudanese borders, where the longest runway in the country sits beside a refugee camp of nearly 68,000 people fleeing Sudan's civil war.

subject: Enniskillen
summary: The county town of Fermanagh sits on a single island between the two halves of Lough Erne, a fortress passage that Maguires built, English captains seized, and 14,000 people now call home.

subject: Enniskillen Lifeboat Station
summary: The RNLI's first ever inland lifeboat station was opened in 2001 on the shore of Lough Erne, after two visitors drowned the weekend before its official launch.

subject: Ennistymon
summary: A market town on the Cascades, where a 1848 famine note pinned to an orphan's shirt is now carved in stone.

subject: Enomoto Takeaki
summary: A samurai who became an admiral, fought a losing war, declared an independent republic in Hokkaido, was convicted of treason, pardoned, and then rose higher in the new government than anyone who had fought against it.

subject: Enon Formation
summary: The rubble of a supercontinent's breakup, scattered in reddish conglomerate patches across the southern Cape, recording the moment Gondwana tore apart.

subject: Enoshima
summary: A tiny sacred island off the coast of Kanagawa where an ancient goddess, a Victorian-era British botanist, and two Olympic Games collide in one of Japan's most beloved day trips from Tokyo.

subject: Enriqueta Martí
summary: The 1912 case that Barcelona remembers as "the Vampire of the Raval" is really the story of poor children who vanished while a whole city looked away.

subject: Enschede
summary: A Dutch textile city undone by Asian competition, leveled in part by a 2000 fireworks disaster, and rebuilt - especially the Roombeek neighborhood - as a quiet international showcase of modern architecture and remembrance.

subject: Entebbe
summary: A lakeside town on a peninsula jutting into Lake Victoria serves as Uganda's international gateway, forever linked to a 1976 hostage rescue that became one of the most audacious military operations of the twentieth century.

subject: Entrepotdoksluis
summary: A small 1903 drawbridge in Amsterdam's old warehouse district still tilts up for passing boats more than a century after it was built.

subject: Eora
summary: The saltwater people of the Sydney coast, whose bark canoes once crowded the harbour and whose descendants carry a culture the colony tried to erase.

subject: Epcot
summary: Walt Disney's utopian city became a permanent world's fair instead, where a geodesic sphere and eleven nation pavilions draw 12 million visitors a year to central Florida.

subject: Epe, North Rhine-Westphalia
summary: A small village on the German-Dutch border sits above one of Europe's largest underground gas storage facilities - roughly 75 caverns dissolved out of an ancient salt bed nearly a mile below.

subject: Epidaurus Limera
summary: A sea-city born from a divine omen, Epidaurus Limera stood for centuries on the Laconian coast before its people abandoned it to build something more defensible — a fortress-town on a rock that would become Monemvasia.

story.title: Equal Justice Initiative: Naming the Dead, Freeing the Living

subject: Equal Justice Initiative
summary: A Montgomery-based legal organization founded by Bryan Stevenson in 1989 that has saved more than 125 people from the death penalty and built the nation's first memorial to lynching victims -- 800 steel columns hanging like bodies, each bearing the name of a county where racial terror occurred.

subject: Equality Colony
summary: A socialist colony founded near Edison in 1897 by people who intended to convert Washington State — and then the continent — and who lost it to an argument, a barn fire, and a court order.

story.title: Equally Low: Samarinda and the Mahakam

subject: Equally Low
summary: Borneo's most populous city began as a Bugis refugee settlement where every house floated at the same height, embodying an ideal of equality that shaped the city's name and character.

subject: Equatoria
summary: On the upper White Nile, Egypt once tried to build a model province in the African interior - and left behind a name, a memory of isolated outposts, and a region that would fight for decades to govern itself.

subject: Equinoctial France
summary: The short-lived 1612 French colony that founded São Luís - three years of Capuchin friars, Tupinambá alliances, and a Portuguese military expedition that ended it all.

subject: Erdek
summary: Erdek is a small Turkish resort town on the Kapıdağ Peninsula, five kilometers from the ruins of ancient Cyzicus, where seasonal tourists now swim in the same waters that once carried Greek and Spartan war fleets.

subject: Eredivisie
summary: Dutch top-flight football was an amateur affair until a charity match in 1953 changed everything. Three years later the Eredivisie was founded, and Ajax, PSV, and Feyenoord have spent nearly seven decades dividing the spoils.

subject: Eredivisie (women)
summary: The Netherlands' top women's football league started in 2007 with six clubs and a national team that could not qualify for anything. Within a decade the Oranje Leeuwinnen were European champions. The league itself is still figuring out what it wants to be.

subject: Eresos
summary: On the volcanic southwest coast of Lesbos lies the birthplace of Sappho, antiquity's greatest lyric poet, and of Theophrastus, the father of botany.

subject: Eretria
summary: A Greek city-state that defied the Persian Empire, paid for it with everything, and left its ruins beneath a modern beach resort.

subject: Erfurt
summary: Thuringia's capital grew rich on a dye plant, kept nearly all of its medieval centre, and has been quietly consequential ever since.

subject: Erg Amatlich
summary: A narrow river of sand 130 kilometers long, trapped between desert mountains - a dune sea so confined it reads less like a wasteland than a deliberate brushstroke across the Sahara.

subject: Erg Chech
summary: A sand sea the size of a country, almost entirely empty - and the place where someone found the oldest piece of volcanic rock in the solar system.

subject: Erg Iguidi
summary: A 400-kilometer sea of linear dunes straddling Algeria and Mauritania, where dry winds comb the sand into endless parallel ridges.

subject: Eridu
summary: Traditionally the first city on the Sumerian King List and among the oldest settlements in southern Mesopotamia, Eridu was the holy city of Enki, god of water and wisdom, where eighteen temples were built one atop another over thousands of years.

subject: Eriskay
summary: A three-mile-long island where a French privateer landed Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1745 and a freighter dropped 264,000 bottles of whisky in 1941, with a critically endangered pony breed still grazing the hillsides in between.

subject: Eriskay
summary: From the Old Norse for Eric's Isle, a Hebridean island of 160 people, a 1745 royal landing, a 1941 whisky wreck, and a song that asks 'sad am I, without thee'.

subject: Eritrea
summary: One of the most closed countries in the world, with some of the most spectacular modernist architecture, pristine Red Sea reefs, and friendly people travelers ever meet.

subject: Eritrea
summary: A Horn of Africa republic of nine recognized peoples, a 1,200-kilometer Red Sea coastline, and one of the longest independence struggles in modern history.

subject: Eritrea–Sudan border
summary: A 686-kilometer line through desert and highland that has been a war front, a refugee corridor, and a colonial fault line for over a century.

subject: Erkelenz
summary: A thousand-year-old Rhineland town that has been losing its outlying villages, one by one, to the slow advance of an open-pit brown-coal mine.

subject: Erligang culture
summary: Beneath modern Zhengzhou lie the remains of a 3,600-year-old Bronze Age metropolis whose massive walls and sophisticated bronze workshops reveal one of the earliest urban civilizations in China.

subject: Erlitou
summary: The archaeological site in Henan's Yiluo Basin that may be the oldest capital city in Chinese history, where palace complexes, bronze workshops, and the earliest known Chinese road grid emerged around 1700 BC.

subject: Erlitou culture
summary: China's earliest Bronze Age civilization, flourishing from roughly 1900 to 1500 BC in the Yellow River valley -- possibly the legendary Xia dynasty, though proof remains tantalizingly out of reach.

subject: Ermelo, Netherlands
summary: A Veluwe town with Roman ruins under its hills, a windmill named The Cow, and the Amazon CTO's hometown - all named for a god of woods.

subject: Ernest Henry Mine
summary: A copper-gold mine northeast of Cloncurry, named for the restless prospector whose 1867 strike on the Cloncurry River opened up the whole mineral district.

subject: Eromanga Sea
summary: The driest heart of Australia was once an ocean floor: a vast, cold, shallow inland sea where plesiosaurs and giant marine reptiles swam, leaving their bones in the desert that took its name from the town furthest of all from the modern sea.

subject: Erongo
summary: A Namibian region where the Namib Desert meets the Atlantic, home to desert elephants that roam dry riverbeds, a 1,500-year-old welwitschia plant, and a night train that stops at every rock because there are no trees.

subject: Erris
summary: A north Mayo barony of two hundred thousand acres of blanket bog, sea cliff, and Atlantic emptiness, where the Children of Lir are said to be buried and where geological time is written into rocks that once belonged to Canada.

subject: Ershui
summary: A small Changhua township whose name — "Two Waters" — tells the story of the ancient irrigation canals that transformed a mountain frontier into the breadbasket of central Taiwan.

subject: Ervia
summary: The semi-state company that built Ireland's national gas network, briefly held the national water utility, lost its famous name in a bailout sale, and was finally dissolved into its own subsidiary.

subject: Erythrae
summary: On a quiet Turkish peninsula opposite Chios stand the walls of an ancient Ionian city whose prophetess once told kings their futures.

subject: Es Baluard
summary: Palma's museum of modern and contemporary art fills the great stone bastion of the city's old sea walls, tracing a century of Balearic art from the painters who chased the island's light to Miró, Picasso, and Barceló.

subject: Es Castell
summary: The easternmost town in Spain, founded by the British as Georgetown at the mouth of Port Mahon, where black-and-white riders still rear their horses through the summer crowds.

subject: Esbjerg
summary: Denmark lost a war in 1864 and lost its North Sea port with it, so in 1868 the state decided to build a new one on an empty stretch of Jutland coast — and a city grew up around it.

subject: Escalante, Negros Occidental
summary: A northeastern Negros city whose ancient burial grounds, Spanish-era sugar mills, and rich coastal ecosystems trace a history stretching from twelfth-century traders to the youngest chess FIDE Master in the world.

subject: Escondida
summary: The world's largest copper mine hides in plain sight at 3,100 meters in the Atacama Desert, producing enough copper each year to wire entire nations while reshaping Chile's economy and forcing hard questions about water in the driest place on Earth.

subject: Escondido, California
summary: The Spanish called it 'hidden' — a valley tucked behind a coastal ridge that shielded it from the marine layer and gave it a climate suited to avocados, citrus, and, eventually, craft beer.

subject: Esh Shaheinab
summary: A Mesolithic and Neolithic site on the west bank of the Nile north of Omdurman where hunter-gatherers made shell fishhooks and argued, it seems, about the color of their tools.

subject: Eshowe
summary: The oldest British settlement in KwaZulu-Natal was once home to four Zulu kings and endured a ten-week siege in the Anglo-Zulu War, and today sits wrapped in one of the last coastal scarp forests in the province.

subject: Eski Kermen
summary: Some four hundred rooms carved straight into the rock of a lonely Crimean plateau - all that remains of a fortress-town that outlived the empires that built and conquered it.

subject: Eski Yurt
summary: Beneath the cottages and streets of western Bakhchysarai lies a vanished medieval town whose dragon-slaying saint, khan tombs, and sacred cemetery were nearly paved over by history.

subject: Esmeraldas
summary: The warm, salty, marimba-soaked Pacific capital where Afro-Ecuadorian coastal culture meets cheap ceviche, long waves, and a travel advisory that asks you to pay attention.

subject: Esmeraldas, Ecuador
summary: The Pacific port capital of Afro-Ecuadorian Ecuador - where a 1553 shipwreck turned into centuries of Black self-rule, and where the country's main oil pipeline now ends at the sea.

subject: Esna
summary: A Nile town where conservators spent years scrubbing centuries of soot from a temple ceiling - and found a painted heaven of gods, planets, and the zodiac waiting underneath.

subject: Espacio Lejano Station
summary: A 35-meter Chinese antenna rises from the empty Patagonian steppe, listening to spacecraft on the far side of the Moon and stirring a quiet international argument.

subject: Esperanza, Santa Fe
summary: Two hundred European families landed on the Santa Fe pampas in 1856 and planted the first organized farming colony in Argentina, a town whose very name means hope.

story.title: Esplanade of Sacrifice to the Heaven and Earth

subject: Esplanade of Sacrifice to the Heaven and Earth
summary: South of Huế, a three-tiered imperial altar where Vietnamese emperors once rode elephants in grand procession to pray to Heaven — a UNESCO-protected site where the ancient rite of Nam Giao still echoes every two years.

subject: Esplanade, Penang
summary: The seafront field where Captain Francis Light fired silver coins into the jungle to entice workers to clear Penang's first British settlement.

subject: Esquel (meteorite)
summary: A Patagonian farmer digging a hole for a water tank struck one of the most beautiful objects ever to fall from space, a meteorite full of glowing olivine crystals.

subject: Esquimalt Lagoon Migratory Bird Sanctuary
summary: A shallow tidal lagoon behind a driftwood-strewn sand spit outside Victoria, protected since 1931, where more than 190 bird species stop over on a shoreline the Esquimalt and Songhees Nations have used for thousands of years.

subject: Esquimalt Royal Navy Dockyard
summary: Britain's only naval base in western North America began as three wooden huts built to receive casualties from a Crimean War battle fought on the Kamchatka Peninsula, and is still a working dockyard after 180 years.

subject: Esquipulas
summary: A small Guatemalan town where millions of pilgrims journey each year to venerate a dark wooden Christ sculpted in 1594, making Esquipulas the most important Catholic pilgrimage site in Central America.

subject: Essakane
summary: A scatter of settlements in the dunes west of Timbuktu, Essakane became, for seven improbable years, the stage for one of the most remote music festivals on Earth.

subject: Essen
summary: From a women's abbey ruled by Ottonian princesses to the Armory of the Reich to a UNESCO-listed monument of post-industrial reinvention, Essen has been remade more often than almost any city in Germany.

subject: Essen, Belgium
summary: A small Belgian municipality that sticks like a thumb into the Netherlands, where the only border that ever really mattered was the one drawn by a railroad in 1854 and a 2,000-volt fence in 1915.

subject: Essex Skating Club
summary: From an outdoor rink in suburban New Jersey, a figure skating club has sent athletes to the Olympics, produced national champions, and built one of America's most successful synchronized skating programs.

subject: Estancia Harberton
summary: Patagonia's oldest farm, founded by a missionary who learned a language no one else recorded and saved it from vanishing.

subject: Estate Rust Op Twist
summary: A former Danish colonial sugar plantation on St. Croix whose name -- Dutch for 'Rest After Struggle' -- became an unintended epitaph for the enslaved people who built its wealth and the industry that consumed them both.

subject: Esterwegen concentration camp
summary: One of the first camps the Nazi state built, set in the Emsland bogs, where prisoners were handed spades and called themselves peat bog soldiers.

subject: Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic
summary: Half a century of Soviet annexation that Estonia never legally accepted, marked by deportations, occupation, and finally a singing revolution that restored independence in 1991.

subject: Estrela do Sul
summary: A town that renamed itself after a diamond an enslaved woman pulled from the Bagagem River in 1853 - and the last place in the Triângulo Mineiro where colonial houses still stand.

subject: Estremoz
summary: A small Portuguese city in the Alentejo where marble is so abundant that even doorsteps, cobblestones, and house paint are made from it -- the stone that built the Monastery of Jeronimos begins here.

subject: Estância
summary: The Sergipe town an emperor called the garden of his province, where street after street of Portuguese-tiled facades is still standing and slowly coming apart.

subject: Eswatini
summary: A landlocked kingdom the size of a small US state, Eswatini is the last absolute monarchy in Africa, where reed-dancing maidens and a thatched cattle byre still sit at the center of national life.

subject: Etak
summary: Before GPS, before Google Maps, Etak built the first practical automotive navigation system in 1985 -- a Silicon Valley startup that invented digital mapping.

subject: Ethiopian Empire
summary: A Christian African empire that lasted 700 years, defeated a European colonial power at Adwa, and fell only in 1974 with the deposition of Haile Selassie.

subject: Etowah Indian Mounds
summary: The most intact Mississippian culture site in the Southeast, where massive earthen mounds on the Etowah River tell the story of a civilization that thrived for five and a half centuries.

subject: Euboea
summary: Greece's long second island, where a strait reverses direction many times a day, a whistled language survives, and Aristotle came home to die.

subject: Eucla
summary: Halfway across the Nullarbor, Eucla is the fuel stop where you reset your watch by 45 minutes, walk out to a buried telegraph station, and remember that the desert meets the sea.

story.title: Eugene: Tracktown USA and the Hippie Mecca

subject: Eugene
