summary: The Oregon college town where Nike was born, where the University of Oregon's Ducks became a football dynasty, and where Ken Kesey and the counterculture found a permanent home in the Willamette Valley.

subject: Eulo
summary: A speck of a town on the Paroo River, Eulo gave Australia an opal queen who wore nautilus shells, a champion racing cockroach with his own monument, and mud springs that bubble up from the Great Artesian Basin.

subject: Euonymeia
summary: A quiet residential neighborhood in south Athens carries five thousand years of continuous history beneath its limestone hills — Mycenaean workshops, a theatre that predates the Parthenon's completion, and a connection to the trial of Socrates.

subject: Eurardy Reserve
summary: A former sheep station turned wildflower sanctuary, where some 700 plant species and two dozen orchids bloom on the edge of one of Earth's great botanical hotspots.

subject: Eureka Diamond
summary: A fifteen-year-old boy picked up a shiny pebble on the banks of the Orange River in 1867, and that single stone launched South Africa's diamond rush, its mineral revolution, and a century of fortunes won and lost.

subject: Euripus Strait
summary: A narrow channel in Greece whose current reverses several times a day, a riddle that may have driven Aristotle to despair.

subject: Euronext
summary: The story of how five rival European stock exchanges put aside centuries of competition to become one company - and what they had to survive to stay that way.

subject: European Capital of Culture
summary: An actress-turned-minister from Athens conceived one of Europe's most enduring cultural programmes in 1983 — and her own city became its first laureate in the summer of 1985.

subject: European Classical Music
summary: Four centuries of Europe's high musical tradition, viewed from the city whose Concertgebouw has the legendary acoustic and whose canals once funded the patrons who paid the composers.

subject: European Committee of the Regions
summary: Three-quarters of EU laws are implemented by mayors, councillors and regional presidents. This Brussels assembly is where they get to argue back.

subject: European Cooperation for Space Standardization
summary: In a Dutch beach town, a small secretariat writes the 139 standards that decide whether European spacecraft fly straight or fall apart.

subject: European External Action Service
summary: How do you build a foreign ministry for 27 countries from scratch? Catherine Ashton tried, starting in a leased triangle of glass on Brussels' Schuman roundabout.

subject: European Marine Energy Centre
summary: The world's only accredited open-sea test bed for wave and tidal power, where engineers from a dozen countries park experimental machines off the Orkney coast to find out whether their ideas can survive the North Atlantic.

subject: European Professional Basketball League
summary: American investors thought they could shove pro basketball down Europe's throat in 1975. The Brussels-based Belgium Lions lasted ten weeks before the whole league collapsed.

subject: European Structural and Investment Funds
summary: Five financial instruments, governed by a common rulebook in Brussels, move hundreds of billions of euros from Europe's wealthier regions toward its poorer ones, aiming to narrow the gaps a single market would otherwise widen.

subject: Eurosonic Noorderslag
summary: Every January, Europe's music industry descends on a small Dutch city to discover who will matter next year.

subject: Eurovision Song Contest 1993
summary: On a May evening in 1993, a Cork town of fifteen hundred people hosted the largest entertainment broadcast in Europe and refused to apologize for any of it.

subject: Eurovision Song Contest 1997
summary: Ireland's fourth Eurovision in five years -- the seventh and so far last to be staged in Dublin -- saw televoting tested, Iceland's Paul Oscar become the first openly LGBT contestant, and Katrina and the Waves walk away with 227 points for the United Kingdom.

subject: Eveleth, Minnesota
summary: A tiny mining town on Minnesota's Mesabi Range that became the unlikely cradle of American hockey -- home to the United States Hockey Hall of Fame, the world's largest hockey stick, and the landmark sexual harassment case that inspired the film North Country.

subject: Everett
summary: Where Boeing builds the world's widebodies in the world's largest building, a working waterfront city at the northern edge of Seattle's sprawl.

subject: Evopod
summary: A tethered floating tidal turbine prototype that ran for years in the Strangford Narrows, generating electricity from one of the strongest tidal flows in the British Isles.

subject: Evvia
summary: The big windy island Athenians keep to themselves - hot springs in the north, wind farms in the south, and a coast road that punishes the impatient.

subject: Ewenny Priory
summary: A 12th-century Benedictine priory in the Vale of Glamorgan whose military-style defences have puzzled historians for centuries -- fortifications built not for war, but for show.

subject: Ex-Sham Shui Po Service Reservoir
summary: A Romanesque brick-vaulted underground reservoir completed in 1904 on Bishop Hill in Sham Shui Po — hidden for a century, nearly demolished in 2020, saved by a citizen who stood in front of the drilling machine.

subject: Exarcheia
summary: A small Athens neighborhood that became the conscience of a nation, where students faced tanks, where a teenager's death sparked the largest uprising in a generation, and where ordinary people still argue about how to live.

subject: Exercise Frisian Flag
summary: Every spring, more than seventy NATO fighters turn the skies above Leeuwarden into a two-week war.

story.title: Exhumation and Reburial of Richard III

subject: Exhumation and Reburial of Richard III
summary: The improbable story of how a Scottish screenwriter's hunch led archaeologists to dig in a Leicester car park, find the bones of England's most controversial king on day one, and trigger a five-year legal and ceremonial drama that ended with Richard III reburied in 2015.

story.title: Exhumation and Reburial of Francisco Franco

subject: Exhumation and reburial of Francisco Franco
summary: It took Spain eight years of parliamentary debates, court challenges, and one beauty queen's funeral request to move Franco's remains from the Valley of the Fallen to a municipal cemetery in 2019.

subject: Exmoor
summary: Europe's first International Dark Sky Reserve covers 692 square kilometres of moorland, sea cliffs, and red deer above the Bristol Channel. The geological period called Devonian gets its name from these hills.

subject: Exmouth (Western Australia)
summary: A small town at the tip of North West Cape that exists because of a submarine communications station and survives on whale sharks, pristine reef, and the kind of isolation that reminds visitors how far from anywhere a person can get.

subject: Exorcist steps
summary: A steep concrete staircase in Georgetown that became one of cinema's most iconic filming locations after its starring role in the 1973 horror classic The Exorcist.

story.title: Experiment to Detect the Global EoR Signature

subject: Experiment to Detect the Global EoR Signature
summary: A table-sized radio antenna in the Murchison desert claimed in 2018 to have heard the first stars switch on, a stunning result that remains fiercely disputed.

subject: Experimental Lakes Area
summary: Fifty-eight pristine boreal lakes in northwestern Ontario were set aside in 1968 as living laboratories -- and the experiments conducted here changed global water policy, banned phosphates in detergents, and survived an attempt by the Canadian government to shut them down.

subject: Expo 2000
summary: Hanover won the world's fair by a single vote, expected forty million visitors, drew twenty-five, and ran up a deficit of roughly 600 million dollars.

subject: Expo 2005
summary: Japan's 2005 World Exposition in Aichi Prefecture drew over 22 million visitors to a forest east of Nagoya, then left behind a park that would one day become the home of Ghibli Park.

subject: Expo 2025
summary: Held on the artificial island of Yumeshima in Osaka Bay from April to October 2025, Expo 2025 drew over 29 million visitors beneath the Grand Ring -- the world's largest wooden architectural structure -- for a six-month showcase of global ambition built on reclaimed land.

subject: Expo 67
summary: The world's fair that defied a computer's verdict of 'impossible' - built on islands conjured from the St. Lawrence River, Expo 67 drew over 50 million visitors to Montreal and became the defining moment of Canadian national pride.

subject: Expo 86
summary: The last world's fair held in North America turned a derelict rail yard into modern Vancouver — at a cost counted in dollars, and in the homes of more than a thousand people who were put out to make room for the visitors.

subject: Extension, British Columbia
summary: A Vancouver Island coal town born from a Black pioneer's unsolved death, scarred by an explosion that killed thirty-two and a strike that brought in troops, now a quiet Nanaimo bedroom community with a slag heap hidden in the trees.

subject: Externsteine
summary: Thirteen sandstone pillars in the Teutoburg Forest that the Nazi state dug up looking for an ancient Germanic sanctuary - and where the diggers found nothing of the kind.

subject: Extreme Points of Europe
summary: From a frozen Russian archipelago at nearly 82 degrees north to a Greek island barely above the Tropic of Cancer, Europe's geographic extremes span a continent whose very borders remain a matter of debate.

subject: Exuma
summary: A chain of over 365 Bahamian islands where Lucayan history, pirate lore, and Hollywood glamour drift across waters so clear they barely seem real.

subject: Eye, Suffolk
summary: A Suffolk market town named for the island it once was - a borough whose Norman castle was attacked twice, whose Speaker of the Commons later became Prime Minister, and whose 'borough' charter turned out to belong to Hythe.

subject: Eyemouth Lifeboat Station
summary: A small fishing town on the Berwickshire coast has been launching lifeboats since 1876, and the names on its boats trace a path through Victorian Africa to Antarctic disaster.

subject: Eyeries
summary: A village of painted houses on Ireland's south-western edge, where Coulagh Bay glints below and a cheesemaker once changed a country's food.

subject: Eylesbarrow Mine
summary: A 19th-century tin mine on the southern shoulder of a Bronze Age burial hill, whose 50-foot waterwheel was the biggest on Dartmoor and whose owner used to row guests across his reservoir.

subject: Eyre Highway
summary: Australia's loneliest road runs 1,668 kilometers across the southern edge of the Nullarbor Plain, where roadhouses are the only punctuation in a sentence that never seems to end.

subject: Eğlenhoca
summary: A small vineyard village on Turkey's Karaburun peninsula where brides once wore gilded bay leaves and rubble-stone houses have weathered five centuries of earthquakes.

subject: F.L.Y.
summary: The world's first flying launched coaster threads through a steampunk city built around it, with riders pinned face-down to the air at 48 miles per hour.

subject: FANUC
summary: Hidden in a forest at the foot of Mount Fuji, the secretive FANUC corporation builds the yellow robots that assemble much of the modern world, commanding 65% of the global CNC market from a campus where everything -- buildings, machines, uniforms -- is painted the same shade of yellow.

subject: FC Viktoria Köln
summary: Cologne's other football club went bankrupt in 2010 and was forced to restart in the lowest amateur league. A decade later, they were back in the professional ranks.

story.title: FESPACO: The Panafrican Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou

subject: FESPACO
summary: Every two years, the largest film festival in Africa fills a dusty Sahelian capital with cinema - and crowns its best film with a golden stallion named for a warrior princess.

subject: FSO Nabarima
summary: A floating oil storage vessel abandoned with 1.3 million barrels of crude aboard, tilting in the Gulf of Paria while governments, sanctions, and neglect conspired to prevent its rescue.

subject: Facundo Astudillo Castro
summary: A 22-year-old vanished on a lockdown road in 2020 after a police stop; the search for him and the questions about how he died moved a nation.

subject: Fageda d'en Jordà
summary: A rare lowland beech forest that grows almost flat on a cooled lava flow in the Garrotxa volcanic zone, immortalized by a Catalan poet and tended by a cooperative that employs people others overlooked.

subject: Fahamore
summary: A windswept fishing village on the Maharees with fifty houses, a pub, and a working currach yard where wood-and-canvas boats are still built and raced.

subject: Fahan, County Kerry
summary: A stretch of coast below Mount Eagle holding 460 ancient stone structures - including 414 beehive-shaped huts - that make up one of the densest archaeological landscapes in Ireland.

subject: Fair Head
summary: A three-mile wall of dolerite columns rising up to 300 feet above the sea at the top of County Antrim, regarded by climbers as the finest single trad-climbing crag in the world.

subject: Fairbridge, Western Australia
summary: A former farm school near Pinjarra where thousands of British children were sent under migration schemes that promised opportunity but often delivered abuse, now a heritage village confronting its painful past.

subject: Fairfield County, South Carolina
summary: A rural Piedmont county named (it is said) by a passing British general, anchored by a 19th-century town clock modeled on Independence Hall, and grounded in blue granite that built half the world's monuments.

subject: Fairhaven, Bellingham, Washington
summary: A town founded by a man called Dirty Dan, inflated from 150 people to 8,000 in a single year by railroad speculators, left stranded when the tracks went to Seattle, and now legally required to keep looking like 1890.

subject: Fairy Creek old-growth logging protests
summary: The largest act of civil disobedience in Canadian history unfolded in a remote Vancouver Island watershed, where 1,188 people were arrested defending old-growth forest.

subject: Fairy Pools
summary: A chain of cyan plunge pools at the foot of the Cuillin where 180,000 visitors a year wade into mountain water that hurts.

subject: Fairy circle (arid grass formation)
summary: Mysterious circular patches of barren earth scattered across the Namib grasslands have baffled scientists for a century, spawning theories from termites to self-organizing mathematics -- and myths about dragon breath.

subject: Falcarragh
summary: The largest Gaeltacht village along the road to Tory Island, where seventy per cent of the population speaks Irish and the wind never stops.

subject: Falcón
summary: Venezuela's northwestern corner where Saharan-scale sand dunes meet Caribbean coastline, a state named for a revolutionary general whose capital city is one of South America's oldest European settlements and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Falkirk
summary: A central Scottish town of 34,000 with a 600-year-old mansion at its heart, a pair of monumental horse-head sculptures at its edge, and a rotating boat lift connecting two of Britain's great canals.

subject: Falkirk Wheel
summary: The world's only rotating boat lift, the Falkirk Wheel reconnects two Scottish canals with an engineering solution so elegant it uses less energy than boiling eight kettles of water.

subject: Fall of Constantinople
summary: On 29 May 1453, after a fifty-three-day siege, the Ottoman army broke through the walls of Constantinople, ending eleven hundred years of Roman and Byzantine imperial continuity — a morning that brought triumph to some and catastrophe to many, and permanently changed the shape of the world.

subject: Fall of Gwoza
summary: In August 2014, Boko Haram militants disguised in Nigerian military uniforms stormed the border city of Gwoza, declaring it the capital of their caliphate - the first time the insurgent group claimed sovereign territory.

subject: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: In 1521, a Spanish-led coalition besieged and destroyed the Aztec island capital of Tenochtitlan, ending one of the largest civilizations in the Americas and erasing a city of 200,000 people from the map.

subject: Fall of Tripoli (1289)
summary: The Mamluk destruction of the Crusader County of Tripoli in 1289 ended 180 years of uninterrupted Christian rule -- the longest of any major Frankish conquest in the Levant -- and set the stage for the final collapse of the Crusader states.

subject: Falles of Alzira
summary: Seventy satirical monuments rise in the streets of Alzira each March, sculpted over months by professional artists, and by the last night every one is deliberately set on fire.

subject: Falling Creek Ironworks
summary: North America's first iron production facility, established in 1619 on the James River and destroyed in the coordinated Powhatan attack of 1622, its exact location lost for nearly four centuries.

subject: Falmouth Lifeboat Station
summary: Since 1867, the lifeboat crews of Falmouth have launched into the Western Approaches in every weather from gale to hurricane, including the catastrophic Fastnet storm of 1979.

subject: Falmouth, Cornwall
summary: A 17th-century planned town on the third-deepest natural harbour in the world, born of royalist politics, raised on the mail trade, and quietly the place where The Wind in the Willows began.

subject: Falun Mine
summary: A millennium-old Swedish copper mine that funded an empire, birthed the world's oldest corporation, discovered multiple chemical elements, and inspired Carl Linnaeus to compare it to hell itself.

story.title: Famous Views of the Sixty-odd Provinces

subject: Famous Views of the Sixty-odd Provinces
summary: Hiroshige's monumental series of 70 ukiyo-e prints capturing a famous view from each of Japan's 68 provinces -- completed just as Commodore Perry's Black Ships arrived to change the country forever.

subject: Fan District
summary: Named for the fan-shape of streets spreading west from Monroe Park, Richmond's Fan District contains one of the longest continuous stretches of Victorian and Edwardian architecture in America - and a Monument Avenue from which the Confederate generals have all come down.

subject: Fan Lau
summary: The southwestern tip of Lantau Island — where Pearl River meets South China Sea — holds five thousand years of human presence in a single peninsula: a Neolithic stone circle, an imperial fort, a nearly empty village, and a lighthouse that still guides ships through the channel.

subject: Fangliao
summary: An American consul's 1867 dispatch, a Japanese landing force in 1895, and a Hollywood game show crew in the 2000s: Fangliao township, at the tail end of Taiwan's western plains, has attracted an improbable cast of outsiders across the centuries.

subject: Fanling
summary: A New Territories town that grew from a market village into a city, Fanling holds walled clan settlements, a Taoist temple, and a landscape poised between Hong Kong's past and its next wave of development.

subject: Fanling Lodge
summary: Hidden inside a Hong Kong golf club, this colonial country retreat served governors, sheltered teachers, housed soldiers — and may yet survive the bulldozers.

subject: Fanling Wai
summary: A walled village built during the Ming dynasty, Fanling Wai is the ancestral stronghold of the Pang Clan — a family whose migration from Gansu to Hong Kong spanned a thousand years.

subject: Fantagraphics
summary: The scrappy comics publisher that moved from Maryland to Seattle in 1989 and spent five decades championing alternative artists, preserving Peanuts and Krazy Kat, and proving that comic books could be literature.

subject: Far Hills Races
summary: A century-old steeplechase in the Somerset Hills where top-tier horse racing, elaborate tailgating, and millions raised for charity converge each October.

subject: Faras
summary: A Nubian city now drowned under Lake Nasser, Faras produced some of the greatest surviving Christian frescoes of Africa - 169 paintings saved from rising water in a four-year Polish rescue.

subject: Farellones
summary: An hour above Santiago by a road of forty hairpin turns, a 1930s ski village clings to the Andes within sight of a peak where the Inca once climbed to bury a child.

subject: Farewell Spit
summary: New Zealand's longest sand spit stretches 30 kilometres into Golden Bay - a Ramsar wetland hosting 29,000 shorebirds in summer and a 'whale trap' where pilot whale herds tragically beach themselves.

subject: Farhād Tarāsh
summary: A massive smoothed cliff face on Mount Behistun whose true purpose remains one of ancient Iran's great unsolved mysteries.

subject: Farnham
summary: A Surrey market town where the Bishops of Winchester held court for a thousand years, William Cobbett was born above a pub, and J. M. Barrie thought up Peter Pan.

story.title: Farnsworth Onshore and Farnsworth Offshore State Marine Conservation Areas

subject: Farnsworth Onshore and Farnsworth Offshore State Marine Conservation Areas
summary: Off the southwest coast of Catalina Island, two contiguous marine protected areas shelter rare purple hydrocoral, dense kelp forests, and a deepwater pinnacle that draws advanced divers from around the world.

subject: Farringdon Station
summary: Farringdon opened on 10 January 1863 as the terminus of the world's first underground railway — and 160 years later it became the only station in Britain connecting both the north-south Thameslink line and the east-west Elizabeth line.

subject: Farsala
summary: Farsala, the modern Thessalian town built on the site of ancient Pharsalos, carries millennia of history — from the legendary birthplace of Achilles to a decisive Roman battle — and today is famous across Greece for its halva.

subject: Fasil Ghebbi
summary: A 17th-century royal compound in the highlands of northern Ethiopia where Indian masons, Ethiopian architects, and Beta Israel craftsmen built castles for emperors.

subject: Fasilides
summary: The 17th-century Ethiopian emperor who founded Gondar, expelled the Jesuits, built castles that earned the city its reputation as 'Africa's Camelot,' and isolated his empire from Europe for two centuries.

subject: Fat Tong Chau
summary: Once a small island in Junk Bay with a village of fewer than forty people and a Qing dynasty customs post collecting taxes on opium, Fat Tong Chau no longer exists as an island — Hong Kong's relentless land reclamation swallowed it into the peninsula — but its ruins, and its story, remain.

subject: Father Damien
summary: A Belgian farm boy who became a priest, volunteered to live among people exiled with leprosy on Molokai, contracted the disease himself, and was canonized as a saint more than a century after his death.

subject: Faubourg Marigny
summary: A former plantation turned bohemian neighborhood, the Marigny is where Jelly Roll Morton first snuck out to play piano and where Frenchmen Street became New Orleans' living room for live music.

subject: Fayette County, West Virginia
summary: A coal-and-gorge county in southern West Virginia, named for Lafayette, shaped by the New River, and now living its second act as the country's newest national park.

subject: Fayetteville, West Virginia
summary: Once called Vandalia, now the gateway to America's newest national park - a coal-era county seat that has reinvented itself as the climbing, rafting, and BASE-jumping capital of West Virginia.

subject: February 26 incident
summary: An attempted coup d'etat in 1936 Tokyo where young Imperial Japanese Army officers assassinated government leaders and occupied the capital's center for four days before the Emperor himself ordered their surrender.

subject: February 28 Incident
summary: A cigarette vendor's beating in 1947 Taipei ignited an island-wide uprising that the Kuomintang crushed with military force, killing an estimated 18,000 to 28,000 people and shaping Taiwan's political identity for generations.

subject: Federación
summary: An Argentine town that drowned beneath a dam reservoir and was rebuilt, street by street, on higher ground a few kilometers away.

story.title: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution

subject: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution
summary: Germany built a domestic intelligence agency designed to spy on its own democracy's enemies, then spent the next 75 years arguing about whether the BfV was the cure or part of the disease.

subject: Federal Public Service Foreign Affairs
summary: Belgium has been a state for less than two centuries and a federal one for less than fifty years, yet its foreign ministry now coordinates the diplomatic life of the most internationalized capital city on Earth.

subject: Federal Republic of Central America
summary: For sixteen turbulent years, five newly independent nations tried to govern themselves as one country — modeling their constitution on the United States, fighting two civil wars, and ultimately proving that shared geography does not guarantee shared politics.

story.title: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

subject: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: The most powerful of the twelve Federal Reserve Banks sits at 33 Liberty Street in Lower Manhattan, housing the world's largest gold vault 80 feet below street level and implementing the monetary policy that shapes the American economy.

subject: Federal Territory of Ponta Porã
summary: For three years Brazil governed its Paraguayan frontier as a federal territory — long enough to move the capital twice, burn through four governors, and vanish from the map.

subject: Federation Square
summary: Melbourne's most divisive landmark - a fractured, sandstone-clad civic square built on a deck above live railway lines, hated and then loved by the city it serves.

subject: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
summary: A colonial experiment in Central African unity lasted exactly ten years before African opposition and political reality tore it apart, leaving three territories on sharply divergent paths toward independence.

subject: Fehmarn
summary: Germany's sunniest island, its third largest, and the field where Jimi Hendrix played his last full concert twelve days before he died.

subject: Feira de Santana
summary: A city of more than 600,000 that began as a place where cattle drovers stopped to trade, and has never stopped being a crossroads.

subject: Feira do Açaí
summary: Around a hundred tons of açaí change hands here between one and five in the morning, hauled off river boats by hand and sold by shout - the market that feeds Belém before Belém wakes up.

story.title: Feliciano Miguel Abdala Private Natural Heritage Reserve

subject: Feliciano Miguel Abdala Private Natural Heritage Reserve
summary: A Lebanese immigrant's son kept his promise to preserve a forest, and in doing so saved a monkey species that once numbered a million and almost disappeared.

subject: Felicity, California
summary: A 2,600-acre desert community in Imperial County that bills itself as the Official Center of the World and is home to a pyramid, a church on a hill, and a granite-slab Museum of History in Granite being assembled piece by piece.

subject: Felling mine disasters
summary: Four explosions at Felling Colliery between 1812 and 1847 killed over one hundred people and drove the invention of the miners' safety lamp that would save countless lives.

subject: Fen Skating
summary: When the Fenland froze hard enough, the flat flooded meadows of East Anglia became a racing circuit — and agricultural labourers with remarkable names like Turkey Smart, Gutta Percha See, and Fish Smart flew across the ice in front of crowds of ten thousand.

subject: Fenambosy Chevron
summary: A vast arrowhead of sediment on Madagascar's tip that some scientists read as the scar of an ancient ocean-spanning wave, and others read as nothing more dramatic than wind.

subject: Fener
summary: On the southern shore of the Golden Horn, the Phanar — Istanbul's historic Greek-Orthodox quarter — has been the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate since 1602, keeping alive a community that has endured conquest, fire, and centuries of change.

subject: Feng Yuxiang
summary: A Chinese warlord who converted to Christianity, banned opium in his territories, drove the Japanese out of Chahar Province, and died under mysterious circumstances in a shipboard fire on the Black Sea.

subject: Fengbin
summary: Where Taiwan's east coast meets a line drawn by the sun: a small township of indigenous peoples, crashing Pacific surf, and one of the island's most dramatic coastal highways.

subject: Fengbitou
summary: At the southern tip of Kaohsiung's Siaogang District, Fengbitou shelters one of Taiwan's richest prehistoric archaeological sites — a 9.7-hectare plateau where human culture has layered itself for more than five thousand years.

subject: Fengjian Village
summary: Fengjian Village in Shunde, Foshan, is a Lingnan water town of stone-arch bridges, ancestral halls, and imperial gifts — with roots back to the Western Han dynasty and three dynasties' worth of monuments still standing among its waterways.

subject: Fengyuan District
summary: Fengyuan District in north-central Taichung traces its roots to the Pazeh people who called it Haluton, became famous for imperial-quality rice and a thriving bakery trade, served as capital of Taichung County for decades, and now navigates a new chapter as a district within Taiwan's third-largest city.

subject: Fenian Ram
summary: The world's first practical submarine was built in 1881 by an Irish immigrant schoolteacher, funded by Irish-American revolutionaries, and stolen before it ever saw combat.

subject: Fenian Rising
summary: The 1867 Irish uprising that failed everywhere it tried to start—and changed Irish politics forever by failing in interesting ways.

subject: Fenit Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI rescue station first established in 1879, closed for decades, reopened in 1994, and quietly funded by - among others - the legacy of a beloved British comedy actress.

subject: Fenqihu
summary: A lunch box changed the fate of a mountain railway town: when steam locomotives stopped at Fenqihu to take on coal and water, local vendors fed the passengers, and a tiny settlement halfway up the Alishan line became one of the most visited stops on the most scenic railway in Taiwan.

subject: Fentons Creamery
summary: California's longest continually operating creamery has survived arson, invented rocky road ice cream, and earned a cameo in a Pixar film -- all from a corner of Oakland's Piedmont Avenue.

subject: Feodosiya
summary: A faded Black Sea resort where twenty-six centuries of Greeks, Genoese, Ottomans, and Russians have layered a small town with an outsized past.

subject: Ferriter's Cove
summary: A small bay at the westernmost edge of Ireland where Mesolithic foragers left human teeth dating to 4,250 BC - and Norman knights named le Fereter arrived 6,000 years later.

subject: Ferrocarril de Sóller
summary: The wooden electric train that a citrus boom paid for, still tunneling through Mallorca's mountains a century later.

subject: Ferry Farm
summary: The boyhood home where George Washington grew up, told tall tales, and learned to survey the land -- saved from becoming a Walmart parking lot.

subject: Ferryside
summary: A Carmarthenshire estuary village where Dylan Thomas spent his childhood holidays, the first community in Britain to switch off analogue television, and a place that may have helped inspire Under Milk Wood.

subject: Ferryside Lifeboat
summary: An independent volunteer lifeboat charity on the Tywi estuary, operating a Ribcraft RIB called The Freemason and answering 999 calls in waters with the second-largest tidal range in the world.

subject: Ferryside RNLI Lifeboat Station
summary: A century of RNLI lifesaving on the Tywi estuary, from 1860 to 1960, including a silver-medal rescue in 1905 when the crew of the City of Manchester were washed overboard saving a Norwegian barque.

subject: Fes
summary: Where Morocco's oldest imperial city holds the world's oldest university, where the medina swallows visitors in labyrinthine souks, where tanneries have dyed leather the same way for a millennium.

subject: Festa da Uva
summary: Every other February, Caxias do Sul fills its pavilions with grapes, wine, and parades - a harvest festival that became a defiant celebration of who its people are.

subject: Festa do Peão de Barretos
summary: A dare between exhausted cattle drovers in a São Paulo slaughterhouse town grew into the largest rodeo in the Southern Hemisphere, staged in an arena designed by Oscar Niemeyer.

subject: Festival Internacional de Benicàssim
summary: A Spanish beach festival famous for running its stages through the night, where headliners can take the stage closer to dawn than to dinner.

subject: Festival Western de Saint-Tite
summary: A small Quebec leather-working town that reinvented itself as the rodeo capital of Eastern North America, drawing 600,000 visitors each September to streets transformed into a Wild West village.

story.title: Festival d'ete de Quebec: Canada's Biggest Stage on a Battlefield

subject: Festival d'été de Québec
summary: Every July, the Plains of Abraham -- where the battle that decided the fate of French North America was fought in 1759 -- transforms into Canada's largest music festival, with a main stage holding 100,000 people and eleven days of performances spanning every genre imaginable.

subject: Festival de Gramado
summary: Every August, the trophy that crowns the best of Brazilian cinema is a grinning little sun called the Kikito, and every filmmaker in the country wants one.

subject: Fethard, County Tipperary
summary: One of the best-preserved medieval walled towns in Ireland -- where 13th-century defenses still rise nearly eight metres high and the Coolmore Stud horses graze nearby.

subject: Feyenoord
summary: The dockworkers' football club that became the first Dutch side to conquer Europe and the world, then spent half a century defining Rotterdam's stubborn identity.

subject: Fez
summary: Where the world's largest car-free urban zone holds Morocco's spiritual capital, where medieval lanes confuse and tanneries stink and crafts survive unchanged.

subject: Fforest Fawr Geopark
summary: The first UNESCO-recognised Geopark in Wales, covering 300 square miles of the western Brecon Beacons and seven thousand years of human and geological story.

subject: Fianarantsoa
summary: A highland city whose name means "good education," built as a colonial capital over a conquered kingdom and now the cultural and wine heart of southern Madagascar.

story.title: Field of the Cloth of Gold

subject: Field of the Cloth of Gold
summary: In June 1520, two young kings pitched a city of gold-cloth tents in a Picardy field and tried to outshine each other for seventeen days.

subject: Fiji
summary: An archipelago of 332 islands scattered across the South Pacific - a place where volcanic peaks meet coral reefs, where Indian and Melanesian cultures blend, and where the world's new day begins.

subject: Fike Chemical
summary: A small Nitro chemical plant so badly run that Lesley Stahl called it 'the messiest place we've ever been' on 60 Minutes - and the EPA still monitors the groundwater.

subject: Filadelfia
summary: Deep in Paraguay's arid Chaco, a German Mennonite colony founded in 1930 built a cooperative-run city where Low German, Spanish, Guarani, and indigenous languages mix on the same dusty streets.

story.title: Filatov Institute of Eye Diseases and Tissue Therapy

subject: Filatov Institute of Eye Diseases and Tissue Therapy
summary: The Odesa institute where Vladimir Filatov turned a bold idea into restored sight for hundreds of thousands, and where Ukraine still trains its eye surgeons today.

subject: Filey Brigg
summary: The narrow rock finger pointing a mile out into the North Sea, where Romans built a signal station and the Devil, according to legend, named the haddock.

subject: Fillmore Counterbalance
summary: A gravity-powered streetcar system that used descending cars to pull ascending ones up a 25% grade -- and produced some of San Francisco's most spectacular transit disasters.

subject: Filoli
summary: A 654-acre Gilded Age estate in Woodside with 16 acres of formal gardens, whose name encodes its original owner's philosophy: FIght, LOve, LIve.

subject: Filoti
summary: The largest mountain village on Naxos, spilling across two hills below the peak of Zeus, where shepherds, feudal towers, and a fiercely loved church have shaped a thousand years of stubborn island life.

subject: Finca Vigía
summary: Ernest Hemingway's hilltop home outside Havana, where he lived for over two decades, wrote The Old Man and the Sea, kept a colony of cats, and left behind a life he could never reclaim.

subject: Findhorn Ecovillage
summary: A pioneering experiment in sustainable living on Moray's coast, claimed to have the lowest ecological footprint of any community in the industrialized world.

subject: Findhorn Foundation
summary: A Scottish spiritual community founded in 1962 in a caravan park, famous for huge vegetables, New Age teachings, and a half-century of ecological experimentation.

subject: Fine Gold Creek
summary: A creek in Madera County's Sierra foothills where gold rush miners named the landscape for what they pulled from it - and where Mono, Chukchansi Yokuts, and Dumna Yokuts peoples had lived for centuries before the prospectors arrived.

subject: Fingal
summary: A north Dublin county whose name comes from the Old Norse for foreigners - and where the locals once spoke a language that mixed English, Norse, and Irish until the mid-19th century.

subject: Finger Lakes
summary: Eleven glacial lakes stretching like fingers across upstate New York, where ancient ice carved valleys deep enough to sink below sea level, and where the Iroquois Confederacy held power for centuries before vineyards took root on the same slopes.

subject: Finn Slough
summary: Thirty people live in wooden houses on the marshy edge of the Fraser River in Richmond, some on pilings and some afloat, in a Finnish fishing settlement that has been quietly refusing to disappear since the 1880s.

subject: Finnish Institute at Athens
summary: Tucked into a neoclassical townhouse in the shadow of the Acropolis, the Finnish Institute at Athens has been Finland's outpost for Greek archaeology and cultural exchange since 1984 — one of 19 foreign institutes that make Athens the most internationally excavated city in the world.

subject: Fintona
summary: A Tyrone village whose road signs still feature a horse named Dick - because Fintona kept the British Isles' last working horse-drawn tram until 1957.

subject: FiraTàrrega
summary: Every September a small Catalan town hands its medieval streets over to street theatre, in a festival born from the reclaimed public space of a new democracy.

subject: Firland Sanatorium
summary: Seattle's tuberculosis treatment center operated for 62 years, evolving from open-air cottages where patients couldn't cough to locked wards that drew ACLU investigation.

subject: First BHP Offices Chimney Ruin
summary: A lone stone chimney on the common is all that survives of the hut where one of the world's largest mining companies was born in 1885.

subject: First Brazilian Republic
summary: The Old Republic of 1889 to 1930, when Brazil was ruled by cafe com leite politics, coffee-rich Sao Paulo alternating with dairy-rich Minas Gerais, until the Revolution of 1930 installed Getulio Vargas.

subject: First Republic of Venezuela
summary: The first Spanish American colony to declare independence, Venezuela's First Republic lasted barely a year before earthquakes, economic collapse, and civil war brought it down -- but the precedent it set changed a continent.

subject: First indoor ice hockey game
summary: On March 3, 1875, eighteen men, sticks imported from Nova Scotia, and a flat block of wood instead of a ball launched organized ice hockey inside Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink - and the game ended in a fight that had nothing to do with the sport.

subject: Fish Creek Mountains Wilderness
summary: A 21,388-acre desert wilderness in the Colorado Desert where limestone outcrops hold ancient water tanks and the ghost of a massive lake lingers in the rocks.

subject: Fisherman's Wharf, San Francisco
summary: San Francisco's most visited neighborhood began as a working fishing port in 1884 and still has family restaurants going back three generations.

subject: Fishguard Lifeboat Station
summary: A Welsh lifeboat station since 1822, built by a Royal Navy lieutenant on his own dime, later funded by children watching Blue Peter on the BBC.

subject: Fiskardo
summary: Fiskardo is the only village in Cephalonia to survive the 1953 earthquake intact — a jewel-like harbour village named for a Norman warlord who died on its shores in 1085 and whose legacy turns out to be a remarkable Roman grave opened for the first time in 2,000 years.

subject: Fiskars, Finland
summary: A village of fewer than a thousand people on a small Finnish river, where a 1649 blast furnace grew into an industrial dynasty, emptied out, and came back as one of Europe's densest concentrations of working craftspeople.

subject: Fitzgerald Marine Reserve
summary: A 402-acre marine reserve on the San Mateo coast where 5,800 years of human history meet some of Northern California's richest tide pools, all perched atop an active earthquake fault.

subject: Fitzrovia
summary: London's most creatively misnamed neighbourhood — a place that didn't officially exist until a bohemian poet invented it during a wartime pub crawl.

subject: Five Great Avenues
summary: A neighborhood of over 230 Western-style buildings in downtown Tianjin where Renaissance, Gothic, and Romantic architecture lines five parallel streets that once housed China's wealthiest refugees from political upheaval.

story.title: Five Points: America's Most Notorious Neighborhood

subject: Five Points, Manhattan
summary: The 19th-century Manhattan slum where Irish and Black communities forged the first large-scale voluntary racial integration in American history, inventing tap dance and influencing jazz before reformers razed it all.

subject: Flag Fen
summary: A Bronze Age timber causeway of more than 60,000 posts, driven into the fenland east of Peterborough between 1365 and 967 BC, with swords and gold offerings still emerging from the peat.

subject: Flagstaff, Arizona
summary: The world's first International Dark Sky City, where astronomers, elite runners, and Route 66 travelers share a mile-high mountain town at the doorstep of the Grand Canyon.

subject: Flambeau Mine
summary: Wisconsin's only metallic mine to be permitted, operated, and reclaimed under modern state law, the Flambeau Mine near Ladysmith extracted 181,000 tons of copper, 334,000 ounces of gold, and 3.3 million ounces of silver in just four years -- then became a cautionary tale about the gap between reclamation promises and water quality reality.

subject: Flamborough Head
summary: An eight-mile chalk promontory where 200,000 seabirds nest, John Paul Jones fought the Royal Navy, and a lightning bolt sent 100 tonnes of cliff into the sea in 2006.

subject: Flanders
summary: The Dutch-speaking northern half of Belgium, where medieval wool weavers built one of Europe's first urban civilizations and a federal state is still negotiating what it wants to be.

subject: Flatwoods Monster
summary: A 1952 night-time encounter on a Braxton County hilltop became one of America's most famous monster stories - though the leading explanation involves a meteor, an aircraft beacon, and a startled barn owl.

subject: Fleetwood
summary: A Victorian planned town designed by Decimus Burton, built around a sand dune by an ambitious landowner who went broke, that became one of England's great fishing ports - and is still home to Fisherman's Friend.

subject: Fleetwood Lifeboat Station
summary: Founded in 1859 after a coastguard captain wrote a letter, Fleetwood's RNLI lifeboats have spent 166 years answering distress calls at the mouth of the River Wyre.

subject: Fleishhacker Pool
summary: One of the largest outdoor swimming pools in the world when it opened in 1925, a thousand-foot-long saltwater basin next to the San Francisco Zoo that entertained a city for forty-six years before closing in 1971.

subject: Flevopolder
summary: The largest artificial island on Earth — 970 square kilometers of farms, forests, and cities built on what was a sea less than a lifetime ago.

subject: Flight of the Earls
summary: On 14 September 1607, two of Ireland's most powerful Gaelic lords boarded a French ship at Rathmullan and sailed away forever, taking with them the old order of Gaelic Ireland.

story.title: Flin Flon: The Mining Town Named After a Science Fiction Character

subject: Flin Flon
summary: The Manitoba mining city named after Josiah Flintabbatey Flonatin, protagonist of a 1905 pulp novel - where the hero supposedly inspired the city's discoverer, where a 24-foot statue now honors the fictional explorer, and where the name has confused visitors for over a century.

subject: Flinders Ranges
summary: South Australia's greatest mountain range is a worn-down giant of folded ancient rock, the homeland of the Adnyamathanha people, and the ground where Earth first recorded complex life.

subject: Floralis Genérica
summary: An eighteen-ton steel flower in a Buenos Aires plaza was built to close its petals at dusk and open them again at dawn, a daily rebirth that storms have lately interrupted.

subject: Florence County, South Carolina
summary: Carved out of older counties at the end of the 19th century and named for a general's daughter, Florence County is the modern heart of the Pee Dee region.

subject: Florence Hutchings
summary: The first non-Ahwahneechee child born in Yosemite Valley, who greeted tourists in boots and trousers, played with lizards instead of dolls, and died at seventeen guiding a party to Glacier Point.

subject: Florence, South Carolina
summary: Built where three railroads met, halfway between New York and Miami at the crossroads of I-20 and I-95, Florence is the Pee Dee region's modern heart and an unexpected birthplace of national figures.

story.title: Flores: The Island That Named Itself in Flowers

subject: Flores
summary: A volcanic island in eastern Indonesia where Portuguese missionaries, Komodo dragons, hobbit-sized human ancestors, and tri-colored crater lakes share a landscape of improbable wonders stretching 360 kilometers across the Lesser Sunda chain.

subject: Floriade 2022
summary: A green-utopian world expo that lost more than 100 million euros, sank a centuries-old tradition, and is now being quietly converted into apartments.

subject: Florianopolis
summary: An island city of 42 beaches and Azorean roots, Florianópolis remade itself from a contested state capital into southern Brazil's most coveted coastal escape.

subject: Florida Keys
summary: A 120-mile arc of coral and limestone islands curving from Miami toward Cuba, the Florida Keys are the southernmost point of the continental United States and home to the only barrier reef in North America.

subject: Florida Street
summary: A one-kilometer pedestrian street in the heart of Buenos Aires that has carried foot traffic since the city's founding in 1580, lined with the ghosts of grand department stores, gilded shopping arcades, and the writers who walked it at dawn.

subject: Floridablanca (Patagonia)
summary: A model Enlightenment colony of farming families, planted on the Patagonian coast in 1780 and erased four years later - now an archaeological window into a Spanish experiment that failed.

subject: Florisbad Skull
summary: A partial skull found at a hot spring bath in the Free State has been reclassified for nearly a century, its identity shifting from 'lowly race' to proto-Australian to early Homo sapiens as science evolved faster than the fossil itself.

subject: Flow Country
summary: The largest blanket bog in Europe sprawls across northern Scotland, locking up centuries of carbon and now, finally, recognized by UNESCO for what it actually is.

story.title: Floyd Bennett Field: New York's Forgotten Runway

subject: Floyd Bennett Field
summary: New York City's first municipal airport was built by connecting Barren Island to Brooklyn with sand pumped from Jamaica Bay, became a launchpad for aviation's golden age record-breakers, then served as a naval air station during World War II before transforming into a national park where grasslands now grow between cracked runways.

subject: Floyd County, Virginia
summary: A high Blue Ridge plateau where no streams flow in, where Confederate deserters became permanent Republicans, and where Friday nights still mean old-time music at the country store.

subject: Fo Guang Shan
summary: From a single hillside purchased in 1967, Fo Guang Shan grew into a global Buddhist organization spanning 173 countries with 3,500 monastics, driven by a philosophy that insists Buddhism must serve the living world.

subject: Fo Tan
summary: A Hong Kong industrial district whose empty factory floors became artist studios — Fo Tan reinvented itself from light manufacturing hub to one of the territory's most unexpected creative communities.

subject: Foam Fotografiemuseum Amsterdam
summary: Inside three knitted-together canal houses on the Keizersgracht, Foam runs four shows at a time - from Cartier-Bresson retrospectives to debut work by photographers under thirty.

subject: Foggy Bottom
summary: Marshy German Hamburgh became Foggy Bottom, a riverside slum that became the State Department, the Kennedy Center, and a metonym for American foreign policy.

subject: Foja Mountains
summary: When scientists finally helicoptered into the Foja Mountains in 2005, they landed on a boggy lakebed and found echidnas that let themselves be picked up - an animal that had never learned to fear people.

subject: Fokker
summary: The Dutch aircraft manufacturer that armed Germany in one world war, dominated global airliner sales in the next decade, and went bankrupt in 1996.

subject: Folkestone
summary: Once the most fashionable resort in Edwardian England, then a Channel Tunnel town that lost its ferries - Folkestone has spent two decades reinventing itself around a creative quarter, a saint's bones in the parish church, and the cliffs that William Harvey grew up beneath.

subject: Folsom Street Fair
summary: The world's largest leather event, California's third-biggest single-day outdoor spectacle, and the annual culmination of San Francisco's Leather Pride Week since 1984.

subject: Fond du Lac Indian Reservation
summary: The Ojibwe called this place Nagaajiwanaang -- 'where the current is blocked' -- and for centuries the Fond du Lac Band has held fast to the land at the head of Lake Superior, surviving allotment, dispossession, and federal policy to rebuild a sovereign nation across the forests of northern Minnesota.

subject: Fongyi Tutorial Academy
summary: Built in 1814 during Qing Dynasty rule, the Fongyi Tutorial Academy in Fengshan is the largest preserved Confucian academy in Taiwan — a 37-room complex where ambitious young scholars once prepared for the imperial examinations that could transform their lives.

subject: Football at the 1928 Summer Olympics
summary: The Olympic football tournament that delivered Uruguay's second world title in four years, killed itself in the process, and convinced FIFA the next event needed to be its own.

subject: Foothills Nature Preserve
summary: Foothills Nature Preserve (formerly named Foothills Park) is a 1400 acres park and nature preserve in the Santa Cruz Mountains of California, United S

subject: Forbidden City (nightclub)
summary: The Chinatown nightclub where Chinese American performers headlined floor shows from the 1930s, inspiring The Flower Drum Song and challenging the era's racial boundaries in entertainment.

story.title: Ford Hunger March: The Day Dearborn Opened Fire

subject: Ford Hunger March
summary: On March 7, 1932, unemployed auto workers marched one mile through bitter cold toward the Ford River Rouge plant to deliver their demands -- and were met with tear gas, fire hoses, and machine gun fire that killed five.

subject: Fordow Uranium Enrichment Plant
summary: An Iranian uranium enrichment facility buried deep inside a mountain near the holy city of Qom, whose secret construction, cyberattack sabotage, and ultimate destruction by American bunker busters trace the arc of Iran's nuclear ambitions.

subject: Foreign Cattle Market
summary: From 1872 to 1913, half of London's freshly killed meat passed through a quarantine market on the old Deptford Dockyard — cattle brought by steamer from the American plains, the Argentine pampas, and the Russian steppe.

subject: Foreign Correspondents' Club (Hong Kong)
summary: Founded in wartime Chongqing and now occupying one of Central's last colonial buildings, the FCC has been the nerve center of Hong Kong journalism for decades — and a test case for press freedom.

subject: Foreign concessions in Tianjin
summary: Nine foreign nations carved self-governing enclaves from a single Chinese port city, creating a five-square-mile patchwork of European architecture, extraterritorial law, and imperial ambition that shaped Tianjin for nearly a century.

subject: Forfar
summary: The county town of Angus, home of the Forfar bridie, the witch trials of 1661–62, and the fourth-oldest 18-hole golf course in the world.

subject: Forges du Saint-Maurice
summary: North America's first successful ironworks spent 150 years burning through private fortunes and royal treasuries near Trois-Rivieres, forging everything from cooking pots to steamship parts before the furnaces finally went cold in 1883.

subject: Forks, Washington
summary: A small logging town on the Olympic Peninsula that reinvented itself twice: first as a gateway to the rainforest, then as an unlikely literary pilgrimage site for Twilight fans.

subject: Forlorn Hope (boat)
summary: In May 1865, seven men set sail from Adam Bay in the Northern Territory in an open boat they named Forlorn Hope, rowing and sailing 2,000 miles down the Western Australian coast to Geraldton — a feat of improvised seamanship that no one at either end knew was happening.

subject: Formby
summary: A Sefton coast town of pinewoods, red squirrels, and ancient human footprints — some up to nine thousand years old — emerging from the eroding sand.

subject: Former Central Magistracy
summary: Built in 1913–14 on the site of Hong Kong's first magistracy, this Greek Revival courthouse at the top of Arbuthnot Road now forms part of Tai Kwun, the city's flagship heritage complex.

subject: Former Shawinigan Aluminium Plant
summary: The birthplace of Canadian aluminium production, this 1900-era industrial complex on a plateau above the Saint-Maurice River is now a National Historic Site and cultural venue.

subject: Former Tangrong Brick Kiln
summary: Established in 1899 in Kaohsiung's Sanmin District, the Former Tangrong Brick Kiln once produced roughly 70 percent of all bricks in Taiwan — a Hoffmann continuous kiln complex that shaped a city, then went silent, and now stands as a protected industrial heritage site.

subject: Formosa (Brazil)
summary: A city in Goias named for its beauty, founded by leather-tent traders after malaria drove people from the Parana valley, now best known for Itiquira Falls and rock art dating back 4,500 years.

subject: Formosa, Goiás
summary: A Goias municipality where waters from three continental river basins (Amazon, Plata, Sao Francisco) have their headwaters, earning it the title Cradle of the Waters of Brazil.

subject: Formula Student Team Delft
summary: How twenty Delft students rewrote the rules of student racing by deciding that lighter, not louder, was the way to win - and ended up holding a Guinness World Record.

subject: Fornalutx
summary: A tiny stone village in Mallorca's Tramuntana mountains that stripped its own walls bare to look more beautiful, and won national prizes for it.

subject: Foros
summary: The southernmost resort in Crimea, a quiet seaside town where, in one August week of 1991, the fate of the Soviet Union hung in the balance.

subject: Forres
summary: A small Moray town where Shakespeare set Macbeth, Ptolemy charted the estuary, and three witches are reputedly still imprisoned in a 10th-century stone.

subject: Forrest
summary: A near-empty settlement on the world's longest straight railway, where a once-vital outback airfield and weather station now wait, mostly in silence, for planes that rarely come.

subject: Forssa
summary: A Finnish-speaking mill town with a Swedish name, built around one waterwheel on the Loimijoki - birthplace of the Social Democrats' 1903 programme and, later, of the protest that started Finland's green movement.

subject: Fortaleza
summary: A 25-kilometer strip of urban beach, sandy-footed forró nights, and traditional jangada rafts sailing home at dawn.

subject: Fortaleza
summary: Brazil's fourth-largest city grew out of a Dutch fort, abolished slavery four years before the empire did, and now anchors the cultural and economic weight of the northeast.

subject: Fortaleza do Monte
summary: Macau's Fortaleza do Monte fired its cannon in anger exactly once — and won — before spending four centuries as governor's palace, weather station, and finally, a hilltop museum with panoramic views over the city it once defended.

subject: Forteviot
summary: A whisky baron's 1920s model village sits atop a vanished Pictish royal capital where Kenneth mac Alpin died and Bronze Age kings were buried with golden daggers.

subject: Fortifications of Den Helder
summary: A ring of fortresses Napoleon ordered built to guard the Dutch fleet - a 19th-century coastal defence network that British, French, German, and Dutch armies all garrisoned in turn.

subject: Fortifications of Guernsey
summary: Four thousand years of nervous coastline - from Iron Age earth ramparts through fifteen Napoleonic loophole towers to the 616,000 cubic meters of German concrete poured between 1941 and 1943.

story.title: Fortifications on the Caribbean Side of Panama: Portobelo-San Lorenzo

subject: Fortifications on the Caribbean Side of Panama
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, the Spanish colonial fortifications at Portobelo and San Lorenzo guarded the Caribbean chokepoints of Panama's treasure route for over two centuries -- and their crumbling walls still bristle with spiked cannons.

subject: Fortified granaries of Aures
summary: Multi-storied stone fortresses in Algeria's Aures Mountains, used for centuries as grain stores and refuges, described by both Sallust in antiquity and French anthropologists in the 19th century as 'eagle nests.'

subject: Fortingall
summary: A tiny Highland village whose legends include the birthplace of Pontius Pilate and a tree that may be older than recorded history.

subject: Fortingall Yew
summary: An ancient yew in a Perthshire churchyard, possibly five thousand years old, that began producing berries on a single branch in 2015.

subject: Fortnum & Mason
summary: London's grandest grocer was built on used candle wax, royal connections, and 318 years of stocking everything from Scotch eggs to Heinz baked beans.

subject: Forty Mile Point Light
summary: Built to fill a deadly gap in the chain of lighthouses along Lake Huron, Forty Mile Point Light still shines through the last working classic Fresnel lens on the lake -- a patchwork of glass panels made in Paris over 150 years ago.

subject: Forty Thousand Hills
summary: A UNESCO Global Geopark of roughly 40,000 conical limestone hills, 119 stalactite-filled caves, and underground rivers stretching along Java's southern coast -- with human fossils dating back 1.8 million years.

subject: Forty-Five Names on a Constitution
summary: The Cachil DeHe Band of Wintun Indians, once reduced to just 45 members on a small rancheria in Colusa County, formalized their sovereignty in 1941 and built a community that endures in California's Sacramento Valley.

subject: Forum of Arcadius
summary: Built in 403 CE on Constantinople's seventh hill, the Forum of Arcadius held one of the ancient world's great commemorative columns — a towering spiral of carved reliefs that stood for over a thousand years before it was pulled down in 1715.

subject: Forum of Constantine
summary: The oval forum that Constantine the Great laid at the heart of his new capital in 330 CE, centered on a column that still stands today — though everything else the Crusaders got to in 1203–1204 was either burned or melted down.

subject: Forum of Theodosius
summary: Once the largest public square in Constantinople, the Forum of Theodosius was the beating civic heart of a Roman empire reborn in the East — now buried beneath Istanbul's Beyazıt Square.

subject: Forum of the Ox
summary: One of Constantinople's monumental public squares — built along the Mese in the valley of the Lycus creek, used for commerce, procession, and executions, and erased so completely that its location had to be deduced from road-construction rubble in 1956.

subject: Forze Hydrogen Racing
summary: The only student team in the world racing high-powered hydrogen fuel cell cars - and the first to ever beat petrol-powered cars in an official race.

subject: Foshan
summary: With nearly nine and a half million people and a thousand years of history, Foshan is simultaneously China's ceramic and martial arts capital, the birthplace of Cantonese opera, and the city that locals describe as simply being the same city as Guangzhou.

subject: Fossar de les Moreres
summary: An eternal flame beside Santa Maria del Mar burns over the mass grave of Barcelona's defenders of 1714, marking not a victory but the defeat that forged Catalan identity.

subject: Foster City, California
summary: A master-planned city built on reclaimed bayshore land in the 1960s, Foster City was engineered from scratch -- from its lagoon system to its street grid to its place in Silicon Valley.

subject: Fotheringhay
summary: A Northamptonshire village of around 120 people whose tall-towered Yorkist church and quiet river bank carry the weight of a royal dynasty that began and ended here.

subject: Four Million Second Chances
summary: A hatchery on the American River that raises four million baby salmon each year to replace the 125 miles of spawning habitat that the dams above it destroyed.

story.title: Four Sails in the Selayar Strait

subject: Four Sails in the Selayar Strait
summary: In the waters off southern Sulawesi, a small Royal Navy squadron mistook a merchant ship for a warship, hesitated overnight, and then won a decisive engagement that opened Britain's campaign to seize the Dutch East Indies.

subject: Four Sephardic Synagogues
summary: Four interconnected synagogues in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter tell the story of a displaced community that built, lost, and rebuilt its houses of prayer across five centuries.

subject: Fourni
summary: A scattered archipelago of more than twenty barren islets in the eastern Aegean, once a notorious pirates' lair and now a quiet fishing haven ringed by one of the richest concentrations of ancient shipwrecks in the world.

story.title: Fourth Ward: Freedmen's Town and the Battle for Houston's Soul

subject: Fourth Ward, Houston
summary: Once the center of Black life in Houston, the Fourth Ward's Freedmen's Town was built by formerly enslaved people who paved their own streets when the city refused -- then spent a century fighting to keep what they had built.

subject: Fowey Lifeboat Station
summary: A volunteer lifeboat station guarding the Cornish coast since 1859, where William Rashleigh's 50-pound donation after a fatal shipwreck launched 165 years of rescues.

subject: Foxdale Mines
summary: A belt of lead, silver, and zinc workings that ran east to west across the Isle of Man, once among the richest ore mines in the British Isles, killed not by depletion but by cheap imports.

subject: Foxhol
summary: A potato, a paint factory, and a transatlantic shipping line all trace back to a single Groningen village that most maps barely bother to name.

subject: Foyers hydropower schemes
summary: Two power stations sit on the south-east shore of Loch Ness—one a Victorian aluminium smelter, the other a 300 MW pumped-storage giant whose turbines run forward by day and backward by night.

subject: Foyleside Shopping Centre
summary: Northern Ireland's second-largest shopping centre, built into the steep banks of the Foyle and stitched together so cleverly that three of its four levels each have their own ground-floor entrance.

subject: Fragrant Hills
summary: Every autumn, the smoke trees of Fragrant Hills turn the Western Hills crimson, drawing thousands of visitors to a park that has survived the Second Opium War, the Boxer Rebellion, and eight centuries of dynastic change.

subject: Framlingham
summary: The Suffolk town where Mary Tudor was proclaimed Queen of England in 1553, where Ed Sheeran grew up and wrote 'Castle on the Hill' about, and where the two oldest pillar boxes in Britain still take post.

subject: Franca
summary: Brazil's National Capital of Footwear, where Italian immigrants turned a cattle-trail rest stop into the country's leather-goods engine and its premier basketball city.

subject: Frances Street Squats
summary: Six condemned houses in East Vancouver held thirty-six people for nine months in 1990, and ended with a police operation that brought a helicopter and a bomb squad to a street of wooden bungalows.

story.title: Francis E. Warren AFB: From Cavalry Post to Nuclear Arsenal

subject: Francis E. Warren Air Force Base
summary: The oldest continuously active military installation in the Air Force began as a frontier cavalry post protecting railroad workers in 1867. Today it controls 150 Minuteman III nuclear missiles scattered across three states.

subject: Francis X. Prefontaine
summary: A French Canadian priest who arrived in Seattle in 1869 speaking no English, built the city's first Catholic church in a rented two-room house, and left $5,000 in his will for a public fountain that still bears his name.

subject: Francisco's Fight
summary: A towering Revolutionary War soldier, unarmed and outnumbered nine to one, allegedly snatched a dragoon's own sword and turned the tables on Tarleton's cavalry at a Virginia plantation in 1781.

subject: Francke Foundations
summary: A Halle pastor emptied his parish poor box in 1695, found four thalers and sixteen groschen, and started a school - which by his death had 2,300 pupils and a half-timbered city of its own.

subject: Franja Transversal del Norte
summary: A 15,750-square-kilometer strip across northern Guatemala where land, oil, and timber fueled decades of military corruption, guerrilla warfare, and indigenous displacement during the Guatemalan Civil War.

subject: Frank H. Ogawa Plaza
summary: Oakland's civic heart -- named for the city's first Japanese American council member -- has served as a stage for speeches, protests, and public art for over a century.

subject: Frank Hann
summary: Explorer, pastoralist, and perpetrator of colonial violence — Frank Hann's life across Australia's remote north contains discovery, atrocity, and an unsettling friendship, all within a single generation.

subject: Franklin County, Virginia
summary: The Moonshine Capital of the World, where Booker T. Washington was born enslaved, where the Bondurant brothers ran illegal liquor through Prohibition, and where Smith Mountain Lake now draws weekenders from Roanoke and Lynchburg.

subject: Franschhoek
summary: A tiny valley town founded by French Huguenot refugees makes a serious case for being South Africa's food and wine capital, where a single road in and spectacular mountains on every side create a feeling of delicious isolation.

subject: Fraser Mills
summary: A sawmill on the north bank of the Fraser imported its workforce from Quebec and Punjab, became its own municipality, then a landfill, then a retail strip - and is now slated to be a waterfront town again.

subject: Fraserburgh Lifeboat Station
summary: The first Scottish station of the RNLI, founded 1858 - twice scarred by lifeboat disasters in 1953 and 1970 that took eleven of its own.

subject: Fray Bentos
summary: A small Uruguayan river town that once fed armies and earned the nickname 'the kitchen of the world,' now a UNESCO landscape of brick, machinery, and memory.

subject: Freckleton's Stores, Camooweal
summary: For generations of drovers heading into the outback, this pair of corrugated-iron stores at the edge of Camooweal was the last place to load up on flour, fuel, and everything else before the long ride west.

subject: Fred Korematsu
summary: The Oakland-born welder who refused to report to a Japanese American internment camp, lost his case before the Supreme Court, then spent forty years waiting for justice to catch up with his courage.

subject: Fredensborg (slave ship)
summary: A Danish slave ship that sank off Norway in 1768, whose wreck and remarkably preserved logbooks became the most thoroughly documented slave vessel ever found.

subject: Fredvang Bridges
summary: Two matching cantilever bridges that leap across Arctic straits to connect the fishing village of Fredvang with the rest of Lofoten, creating one of Norway's most photographed road crossings.

subject: Free Acres, New Jersey
summary: An Irish-born Tolstoy follower founded a utopian community in New Jersey in 1910 based on a radical land-tax philosophy — it still exists today, 85 households in the woods.

subject: Free Derry
summary: For three years between 1969 and 1972, a corner of Derry declared itself outside British control - and painted those words on a gable wall that still stands.

subject: Free Republic of Wendland
summary: For thirty-three days in 1980, a hut village of anti-nuclear protesters at Gorleben declared itself a country, issued passports valid for the entire universe, and was carried away one person at a time.

subject: Free State of Galveston
summary: The satirical 'nation' that ran on rum, roulette, and celebrity entertainment - how Galveston Island became America's most flamboyantly lawless city during Prohibition and the Depression, thriving while the rest of the country went broke.

subject: Free and Real
summary: An experimental eco-community on a Euboean mountainside, built around yurts and natural farming, that tries to live in deliberate harmony with the land.

subject: Freedom Square, Kharkiv
summary: One of Europe's largest city-center squares, whose changing names, from Veterinary to Dzerzhinsky to Freedom, trace a century of who ruled Kharkiv.

subject: Freemasonry in Venezuela
summary: Founded in 1824, just three years after Venezuela's independence, the Grand Lodge in Caracas reveals how deeply Freemasonry shaped the young republic's political class -- its first Grand Master was a former vice president.

subject: Freeport of Monrovia
summary: Liberia's main commercial port, built on Bushrod Island in 1948 by American wartime engineers, has witnessed palm oil booms, civil war sieges, and a presidential capture.

subject: Freer Gallery of Art
summary: A Detroit industrialist's gift of 8,000 Asian art objects to the Smithsonian, anchored by Whistler's Peacock Room and 26,000 things since.

subject: Freetown
summary: Sierra Leone's capital climbs from one of West Africa's great natural harbors into forested peninsula mountains, fringed by some of the finest beaches on the continent.

subject: Freetown
summary: A city founded by the formerly enslaved, where the descendants of London's Black Poor, Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia, Jamaican Maroons, and tens of thousands of Africans freed from slave ships built a home and a language of their own.

subject: Freetown Christiania
summary: For fifty years the residents of Christiania governed themselves on a strip of old Copenhagen rampart - and in 2024 they tore up their own most famous street to take it back.

subject: Freixenet
summary: Founded in 1914 from the marriage of two ancient Catalan wine families, the Sant Sadurni cellar of Freixenet grew into the world's largest maker of traditional-method sparkling wine and heralded Spanish Christmases with Hollywood stars.

subject: Fremont Older Open Space Preserve
summary: Fremont Older Open Space Preserve is a 739 acres regional park located in Santa Clara County, California and operated by the Midpeninsula Regional Ope

subject: Fremont Troll
summary: An 18-foot concrete troll clutching a real Volkswagen Beetle beneath Seattle's Aurora Bridge, born from a 1990 art competition and now one of the city's most visited landmarks.

subject: French Algeria
summary: For 132 years, Algeria was not merely a French colony but an integral part of France itself -- a legal fiction that made decolonization all the more violent when it finally came.

subject: French Cameroon
summary: A mandate territory born from the ashes of German colonialism, French Cameroon's path to independence was marked by a forgotten war that cost tens of thousands of lives.

subject: French Guinea
summary: For sixty years a French colony ruled from Dakar, Guinea made history in 1958 as the only African territory to vote 'No' to de Gaulle and choose immediate independence, a defiance France punished by stripping the country bare on its way out.

subject: French Madagascar
summary: For six decades, France ruled Madagascar as a colony, suppressing a sovereignty that the Merina monarchy had maintained for centuries -- and provoking resistance that cost tens of thousands of Malagasy lives.

subject: French Pass
summary: New Zealand's fastest tidal strait, where 8-knot currents have drowned a mythical shag, nearly wrecked a French corvette, and attracted a dolphin so famous he became the first in the world protected by law.

subject: French Polynesia
summary: A scattered constellation of 118 volcanic and coral islands sprawled across 4 million square kilometers of the South Pacific, where turquoise lagoons, black pearls, and ancient Polynesian traditions blend with French sophistication.

story.title: French Quarter: Where America Invented Jazz

subject: French Quarter
summary: The New Orleans neighborhood where French colonial architecture survived, where jazz emerged from the collision of African, Caribbean, and European music traditions, and where the party has been continuous since before the United States existed - 300 years of drinking, dancing, and defying death.

subject: French Quarter
summary: The oldest neighborhood in New Orleans is an architectural paradox: called the French Quarter, nearly every building standing was built by the Spanish.

story.title: French Quarter: Where America Learned to Party

subject: French Quarter
summary: The New Orleans neighborhood that survived fires, hurricanes, and urban renewal - where jazz was born in brothels, voodoo queens held court, and the ironwork balconies are actually Spanish because the French Quarter burned twice before the Spanish rebuilt it.

subject: French Upper Volta
summary: A colony drawn on a map in 1919, erased to save money in 1932, and resurrected by Mossi persistence in 1947 - Upper Volta was a country that France kept inventing and abolishing.

subject: French West Africa
summary: For sixty years, eight colonies and millions of people across an area eight times the size of France were governed from a single city in Senegal - until the whole federation came apart in a span of two years.

subject: French Western Australia
summary: For a few hours in 1772, and again under Napoleon a generation later, the western third of Australia very nearly became French.

subject: French frigate Surveillante (1778)
summary: A 32-gun French frigate that survived one of the most savage sea battles of the American Revolutionary War, then sank itself in Bantry Bay nearly two decades later during a doomed invasion of Ireland.

subject: French protectorate of Cambodia
summary: For ninety years, Cambodia existed under French colonial control -- a protectorate born from a king's desperate gamble to escape Siamese domination, which reduced the monarchy to ceremonial figureheads while reshaping the nation's economy, borders, and identity.

subject: Fresnillo
summary: A silver mining city founded in 1554 beside a freshwater spring and a small ash tree, where one of the world's richest silver mines still operates and pilgrims flock to pray to the Holy Child of Atocha.

story.title: Fresno: The Agricultural Capital Nobody Visits

subject: Fresno
summary: The California city feeding America from the valley everyone drives through - where the Central Valley produces more food than entire states, where the air quality ruins the view, and where the cheap housing attracts those priced out of the coast.

subject: Fridericianum
summary: One of the first purpose-built public museums in Europe, opened in Kassel in 1779 - and paid for with the money Britain handed over for Hessian soldiers.

subject: Friedrichsruh
summary: The forest estate Kaiser Wilhelm I gave Bismarck in 1871, where the chancellor spent his exile from power, died in 1898, and lies buried under an epitaph that pointedly names the wrong emperor.

subject: Friedrichstadt
summary: Founded in 1621 for Dutch religious refugees who had lost an argument about predestination, Friedrichstadt is a grid of canals and gabled brick houses on the Eider - a duke's experiment in buying prosperity with tolerance.

subject: Friendship Oak
summary: A 500-year-old live oak on the Mississippi Gulf Coast that was already a sapling when Columbus sailed, and whose shade is said to bind visitors in lifelong friendship.

subject: Friesland
summary: The Dutch province that kept its own language, its own freedom, and a horse, a sport and a skating tour all its own.

subject: Friesland (district)
summary: The German district called Friesland insists, with unshakeable patience, that it is not part of East Frisia - even though geography places it squarely east of East Frisia.

subject: Frigorífico Anglo del Uruguay
summary: The riverside meatpacking giant that fed Allied soldiers through two world wars, and the multinational company-town of workers who made it run.

subject: Frisia
summary: A cross-border cultural region stretching along the Wadden Sea from the Netherlands into Germany, named after a Proto-Germanic word that may have meant 'curly' - a description of hair.

subject: Frisian Lakes
summary: Twenty-four lakes stitched together by canals, bridges, and Frisian names that quietly insist this is its own country.

subject: Frodsham
summary: Daniel Craig grew up in the pub. Gary Barlow was born here. The Beatles played the cliff-top above town. Frodsham is a Cheshire market town that has been quietly producing famous people for centuries.

story.title: From Ammunition Bunkers to Cattle Country

subject: From Ammunition Bunkers to Cattle Country
summary: A sprawling weapons depot that armed four American wars became a Superfund site, a self-driving car test track, and eventually one of the largest urban parks in the Bay Area.

story.title: From Buffalo Field to Freedom Square

subject: From Buffalo Field to Freedom Square
