summary: Jakarta's 100-hectare central square has cycled through colonial names, occupying armies, and independence rallies to become Indonesia's symbolic heart.

story.title: From Wartime Runways to Racing Legends

subject: From Wartime Runways to Racing Legends
summary: A World War II naval airfield in Sonoma County that flooded out of military service and found an improbable second life as a celebrity-studded sports car racing circuit.

story.title: Fromm Brothers Fur and Ginseng Farm

subject: Fromm Brothers Fur and Ginseng Farm
summary: Four Wisconsin farm boys read about a $1,200 fox pelt, called themselves 'The Company,' and built the world's largest silver fox and ginseng operation from the fields of Marathon County.

subject: Frontier Closed Area
summary: A restricted border zone along Hong Kong's northern boundary with mainland China, established in 1951 to control migration and smuggling — and accidentally preserved as one of the territory's wildest natural landscapes.

subject: Frutal
summary: A Minas Gerais town named for its jabuticaba-like wild fruit, now a soy and cattle giant anchoring the Triangulo Mineiro between the Grande River and the state line.

subject: Frutillar
summary: A tiny German town on a Chilean lake that built a glass concert hall on stilts over the water and turned itself into one of South America's great stages for classical music.

subject: Fryske Akademy
summary: Twenty-five volumes of dictionary, three thousand donors, one mission: keep the Frisian language alive on its own terms.

subject: Ftelia
summary: A windswept Mykonos beach hiding the most important Late Neolithic settlement in the Cyclades, where farmers worked gold seven thousand years ago and the Aegean's oldest securely dated gold object was found.

subject: Fugumba
summary: In a highland river valley stood the spiritual heart of the Imamate of Futa Jallon, the town where a jihad was declared, rulers were consecrated, and a council of elders held kings in check.

story.title: Fuji Five Lakes: The View on the Thousand-Yen Note

subject: Fuji Five Lakes
summary: Five lakes born from Mount Fuji's own lava flows cradle the mountain's northern base -- and the view from one of them has appeared on Japan's banknotes since a photographer captured it in 1935.

subject: Fuji Rock Festival
summary: Japan's largest outdoor music festival, born from a typhoon-struck disaster at the base of Mount Fuji and reborn among the mountains of Niigata, where forest trails connect seven stages and the world's longest gondola lift carries fans to the summit.

story.title: Fujiwara-kyo: Japan's First Planned Capital, Abandoned Before It Was Finished

subject: Fujiwara-kyō
summary: For sixteen years between 694 and 710 AD, Fujiwara-kyo served as Japan's imperial capital -- the first city in Japanese history laid out on a Chinese-style grid, larger than the capitals that followed it, and abandoned before its palace corridors were even complete.

subject: Fukuhara-kyō
summary: In 1180, the most powerful man in Japan forced the entire imperial court to relocate to his seaside estate near modern Kobe -- and within six months, the experiment collapsed in rain, resentment, and civil war.

subject: Fulong
summary: A northeast coast village where a legendary bento box, a rock festival, and a white-sand beach divided by a river mouth draw Taipei day-trippers to Taiwan's Pacific edge.

subject: Fulton Bag and Cotton Mills
summary: A German Jewish immigrant's bag-making enterprise grew into one of Atlanta's largest industrial complexes, survived labor strikes, fire, and a tornado, and was reborn as the loft apartments of Cabbagetown.

subject: Fulton Fish Market
summary: America's most important wholesale fish market for nearly two centuries, surviving fires, Mafia control, and a controversial relocation from the South Street Seaport to the Bronx.

subject: Fulwell, Sunderland
summary: The affluent northern Sunderland district that absorbed its farming roots into urban sprawl, but kept its 1808 working windmill - the only one in the UK with a stone reefing stage.

subject: Funeral Composition
summary: A 1958 painting by Yiannis Moralis that channels Athens' ancient grave reliefs into modern form, won the eye of an Italian master, and now hangs in the National Gallery.

story.title: Funerary Naiskos of Demetria and Pamphile

subject: Funerary Naiskos of Demetria and Pamphile
summary: Two sisters in marble, separated by decades in life and reunited in death, on one of the last great tombstones Athens allowed before the law silenced such grief.

subject: Funicular de Santiago
summary: A century-old cable railway that hauls passengers up San Cristóbal Hill, carrying everyone from Sunday picnickers to a visiting pope toward the Virgin watching over Santiago.

subject: Funj Sultanate
summary: Founded in 1504 between the Blue and White Niles, the Funj Sultanate ruled much of what is now Sudan for more than three centuries, balancing Islam, indigenous traditions, and a court where political standing ran through women.

subject: Furong Street
summary: A 432-meter lane with a creek running through it has been the commercial heart of Jinan for over two thousand years -- and the water lilies that gave it its name still bloom.

subject: Further Confusion
summary: One of the longest-running furry conventions in the United States, Further Confusion has gathered thousands of anthropomorphic art enthusiasts in San Jose every January since 1999, raising over $100,000 for charity along the way.

story.title: Furuichi Kofun Cluster: The Imperial Tombs You Cannot Open

subject: Furuichi Kofun Cluster
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site of ancient burial mounds in Osaka Prefecture, where keyhole-shaped tombs up to 425 meters long have stood for over 1,500 years -- and 27 of them remain sealed by imperial decree, forbidden to archaeologists.

story.title: Futazuka Kofun: The Tomb That Carved Into a Mountain

subject: Futazuka Kofun (Katsuragi)
summary: A 6th-century keyhole-shaped burial mound at the foot of Mount Katsuragi in Nara, built by excavating directly into the mountainside, containing three separate burial chambers -- one of which was never looted, yielding 118 grave goods packed tightly inside.

subject: Future of Life Institute
summary: A nonprofit founded by cosmologists and a Skype co-founder to steer powerful technologies away from catastrophic risk, best known for its 2023 open letter calling for a pause on advanced AI development.

subject: Fyre Festival
summary: A luxury music festival promised paradise on a Bahamian island but delivered disaster relief tents and cheese sandwiches, becoming the defining cautionary tale of influencer-era fraud.

subject: Föhr
summary: A green North Frisian island whose churchyards are full of gravestones that tell the whole life of the whaling captains beneath them, and whose grandchildren opened delicatessens in New York.

subject: Fürstenzug
summary: Dresden's mural of eight hundred years of Saxon rulers failed within a generation as plaster, so the city rebuilt it out of 23,000 porcelain tiles — and that is why it survived 1945.

subject: Făgăraș Mountains
summary: Romania's highest mountains, where glacial lakes sit in ancient amphitheaters and the Transfăgărășan highway twists through one of Europe's most dramatic alpine passes.

subject: Fındıklı, Beyoğlu
summary: Wedged between the Bosphorus and the hills of Beyoğlu, Fındıklı is a slim waterfront district where a Sinan mosque, a grand vizier's fountain, two imperial palaces turned art school, and a tram line all share the same stretch of Istanbul's European shore.

subject: G-Land
summary: Hidden in the jungle of a Javanese national park, G-Land offers one of the longest and most perfect left-hand barrel waves on Earth -- a surf break so remote it was only discovered in 1971.

subject: GEO600
summary: A gravitational wave detector in a field south of Hannover that never detected a gravitational wave - and proved almost every technique the detectors that did rely on.

subject: GLBT Historical Society
summary: The first full-scale, stand-alone LGBTQ history museum in the United States — and only the second in the world after Berlin's Schwules Museum — preserving the archives of San Francisco's queer community in the heart of the Castro District.

subject: Gaberoun
summary: A salt lake cupped in the towering dunes of Libya's Ubari Sand Sea, ringed by palms and the ruins of a village whose people once ate the shrimp of its briny water.

subject: Gabon
summary: One of Africa's wealthiest and least visited nations, Gabon protects 85% of its rainforest across 13 national parks where elephants walk on beaches and leatherback turtles nest by the thousands.

subject: Gaborone
summary: A capital city conjured almost from nothing in the 1960s, named after a chief and built on the promise of a new nation.

subject: Gad, West Virginia
summary: A small Nicholas County community drowned in 1966 when the US Army Corps of Engineers closed the gates on Summersville Dam - now visible only when the winter pool is drained.

subject: Gadani Ship Breaking Yard
summary: On a ten-kilometer stretch of beach northwest of Karachi, workers dismantle the world's ships by hand, cutting through steel hulls with blowtorches for as little as twelve dollars a day.

subject: Gaelic Ireland
summary: For roughly 1,500 years -- from before the Romans named the island Hibernia until the last Gaelic lords fled north in 1607 -- Ireland was a patchwork of warring kingdoms whose lawyers wrote the most sophisticated legal code in medieval Europe and whose monks reintroduced literacy to half a continent.

subject: Gaeltacht na nDéise
summary: Munster's only Gaeltacht: the small Irish-speaking community on the Waterford coast where, against every demographic odds, the language is still gaining ground.

subject: Gaineswood
summary: A cotton planter with no formal training in architecture spent nearly two decades transforming a frontier log cabin into one of the most ambitious Greek Revival mansions in the American South.

subject: Gair Loch
summary: An Geàrr Loch, 'the short loch,' a six-mile sea inlet on the Wester Ross coast lined with villages and one inhabited island.

subject: Gairloch
summary: A scattered village on the North Coast 500 where seals, minke whales, and one Russian Arctic Convoy memorial all share the same patch of coast.

subject: Gairloch
summary: The Wester Ross village whose lairds refused to evict a single tenant during the Highland Clearances.

subject: Galashiels
summary: A Borders mill town where a 1337 raid for plums became a coat of arms, the Romans destroyed a broch, and a £6.7 million tapestry centre now tells Scotland's whole history in 160 stitched panels.

subject: Galataport
summary: A US$1.8 billion reinvention of Istanbul's historic Bosphorus waterfront, Galataport transformed a kilometre of derelict port warehouses into a cruise terminal, cultural campus, and public square that now defines how the city meets the sea.

subject: Galatasaray Islet
summary: A small private island in the Bosphorus, Galatasaray Islet holds an unexpected history: a sultan's gift to an Armenian architect, a celebrated painter's studio, and now a members-only retreat for one of Turkey's most famous football clubs.

subject: Galatzó
summary: Named for the highest mountain in Calvià, this modest settlement was built in the late 1970s not for tourists but for the working families who keep Mallorca's resort coast running.

subject: Galax, Virginia
summary: Named for a Blue Ridge groundcover plant and home since 1935 to the oldest fiddlers' convention in the United States, Galax sits on a 2,500-foot plateau where Appalachian old-time music never went away.

subject: Galaxidi
summary: Galaxidi is a handsome sea-captains' town on the Gulf of Corinth — built on a double natural harbour, rich with the memory of the sailing fleet that once made it a seafaring power, and famous every Clean Monday for the Flour Wars that fill its streets with coloured clouds.

subject: Galaxy SOHO
summary: Zaha Hadid's sinuous, aluminum-clad complex in central Beijing reimagines the traditional Chinese courtyard as four flowing domes fused together, provoking both architectural acclaim and fierce heritage controversy.

subject: Galle
summary: A Sri Lankan port city where Persian traders, Portuguese storms, Dutch engineers, and British administrators each left their mark inside the same UNESCO-listed walls.

subject: Galle Face Green
summary: A five-hectare strip of ocean-side green in Colombo that has served as a colonial cannon field, horse racing course, golf links, cricket pitch, and protest camp since the Dutch first cleared it for a line of fire.

subject: Gallery of Modern Art, Brisbane
summary: Australia's largest gallery of modern and contemporary art, a long white pavilion on the Brisbane River that turned a subtropical city into an unlikely crossroads of Asia-Pacific art.

subject: Gallery of Modern Art, Glasgow
summary: A neoclassical mansion built by a tobacco merchant in 1778 became Glasgow's contemporary art gallery, and the Duke of Wellington outside became the city's most famous joke.

subject: Gallia Belgica
summary: Before there was Belgium, there was Belgica - a Roman province carved out of land Julius Caesar said held the bravest people in Gaul.

subject: Gallipolis
summary: An Ohio River town founded in 1790 by French aristocrats fleeing the Revolution - who bought their land from a company that did not own it, and most of whom did not survive the first winters.

subject: Galloping Goose Regional Trail
summary: Fifty-five kilometres of abandoned railway turned into Victoria's busiest commuter route, named after a rattling gas-powered railcar and ending at a locked gate in front of a gold-rush ghost town nobody is allowed to visit.

subject: Gama, Federal District
summary: A satellite city in the Federal District designed in the shape of a beehive in 1960 to house construction workers who built Brasilia, now home to 137,000 and anchoring an engineering campus.

subject: Gambaga Witch camp
summary: For over two centuries, women accused of witchcraft in northern Ghana have been banished to Gambaga, where a cluster of mud huts offers the only alternative to execution or mob violence.

subject: Gamboa, Panama
summary: A former Canal Zone township at the end of a single-lane road, Gamboa was built for dredge workers and their families and is now one of Central America's premier birdwatching destinations.

subject: Gamcheon Culture Village
summary: A hillside neighborhood in Busan transformed from a poverty-stricken settlement into a vibrant open-air gallery, earning nicknames like 'Korea's Santorini' and sparking debate about art, gentrification, and community.

subject: Gamelan From Heaven
summary: Indonesia's first record label, founded in 1956 to press vinyl for state radio, launched the careers of the nation's most beloved musicians -- then went bankrupt and rented out its studio as a futsal court.

subject: Gamescom
summary: In 2008, the German games industry walked out on Leipzig, started a rival show in Cologne, and won. Gamescom is now the largest gaming event on the planet.

subject: Gamkaskloof
summary: An isolated Swartberg valley where a handful of families lived cut off from the world for over a century, only to leave when the road they begged for finally arrived.

subject: Gamla Stan
summary: Stockholm's medieval heart, where a legend of gold-filled logs, a royal massacre, and 800 years of cobblestone history converge on a tiny island.

subject: Gamla Uppsala
summary: Sacred burial mounds and the last bastion of Norse paganism in Sweden, where kings were crowned and sacrifices made to Odin, Thor, and Freyr.

subject: Gandhara
summary: For nearly a thousand years, the ancient kingdom of Gandhara fused Greek aesthetics with Buddhist devotion to create an art tradition unlike anything else in history, then vanished so completely that its rediscovery required Chinese travelogues and 19th-century coin hunters.

subject: Gandía
summary: A Valencian city that keeps its working life and its holiday beaches four kilometers apart, so neither one swallows the other.

subject: Ganges, British Columbia
summary: Salt Spring Island's only town: settled in 1859 by Black families leaving California, named for a teak warship, and reachable only by ferry or floatplane.

subject: Gangō-ji
summary: One of Japan's earliest Buddhist temples, Gangō-ji once rivaled Tōdai-ji in scale before centuries of decline splintered it into three separate temples hidden within Nara's old town.

subject: Ganh Da Dia
summary: Roughly 35,000 dark basalt columns — polygonal, stacked like dinner plates, fractured by ocean waves into stepped terraces — make Gành Đá Đĩa one of Southeast Asia's most striking geological formations and a site now recognized as a Vietnamese National Special Relic.

subject: Ganos
summary: For a thousand years, the monks and winemakers of Ganos supplied the Byzantine Empire's finest sweet wine — and the amphorae to ship it — from a clifftop town on the Thracian shore of the Sea of Marmara.

subject: Gao
summary: Once the capital of the largest empire in West African history, Gao still sits where the desert meets the Niger, a city that has been a metropolis, a ruin, and a metropolis again.

subject: Gao-Saney
summary: A vanished trading town near the Niger Bend whose buried mounds and Spanish marble tombstones reveal medieval Gao's astonishing reach across the Sahara and beyond.

subject: Gaomei Wetlands
summary: Gaomei Wetlands, a 300-hectare tidal preserve on Taiwan's western coast, is famous for its migratory birds, offshore wind turbines, and sunsets that draw visitors from across Asia — a place where the Taiwan Strait turns the color of embers at dusk.

subject: Gapuwiyak
summary: Beside a brackish lake in north-east Arnhem Land, the Yolngu community of Gapuwiyak is renowned for the clever hands of its weavers, who turn pandanus and bush string into living art.

subject: Garda Emergency Response Unit
summary: The armed tactical unit of an otherwise unarmed police force, the Garda ERU was created in 1977 after Irish officers studied Germany's GSG 9 -- and is now considered one of the most respected counter-terror units in Europe.

subject: Gardenstown
summary: The largest of a string of cliff-clinging fishing villages on Aberdeenshire's north coast - locally known as Gamrie, neighbour to Crovie and to Local Hero's Pennan.

subject: Gardenstown
summary: Founded in 1720 by Alexander Garden, a fishing village 8.7 miles east of Banff - in the parish of Gamrie, with a 1513 ruined kirk above and the threat of the sea always close.

story.title: Gare du Palais: The Station That Died and Came Back

subject: Gare du Palais
summary: Quebec City's chateauesque railway station, built in 1915 to echo the Chateau Frontenac, was expropriated and stripped of its rails in 1976 to build a highway -- then reopened nine years later after a remarkable restoration, earning heritage designation as the eastern anchor of Canada's busiest rail corridor.

subject: Garibaldi, Rio Grande do Sul
summary: Named for an Italian revolutionary who once fought in these southern lands, this hill town became the place where Brazil first made sparkling wine - and never stopped.

subject: Garrett County, Maryland
summary: Maryland's only county west of the Eastern Continental Divide, sitting entirely in the Appalachian Mountains, where the highest point in the state rises to 3,360 feet at Hoye-Crest.

story.title: The Garrison: Where Barbados Raised Its Own Flag

subject: Garrison Historic Area
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage military district south of Bridgetown where British regiments drilled, George Washington convalesced, and Barbados declared independence on a parade ground turned racecourse.

subject: Garth Newel Music Center
summary: A 114-acre Allegheny mountainside estate built by two American painters in the 1920s for their Arabian horses and small concerts - now the home of a piano quartet that has performed on five continents.

subject: Garvagh
summary: A County Londonderry Plantation village on the Agivey River, immortalised in a Protestant ballad about an 1813 sectarian skirmish that became the founding myth of Orange Garvagh.

subject: Gas Street Basin
summary: Two rival canal companies once built a seven-foot stone wall through this Birmingham basin to keep each other from stealing water; today narrowboats moor against both sides of what remains.

subject: Gascoyne Junction
summary: A tiny outback town where two rivers meet, holding Australia's record for the hottest Christmas, repeatedly drowned by floods on a river that is usually bone dry, and serving as the gateway to Mount Augustus.

subject: Gash-Barka region
summary: Eritrea's southwestern breadbasket - a 33,200 square kilometer region of bananas, sorghum, gold mines, and 700,000 people farming the country's most fertile ground.

subject: Gaskill Brothers' Stone Store
summary: A California Historical Landmark in Campo built in 1868 by two brothers who came west in the Gold Rush — the site of a bloody bandit raid in 1875 that left eight dead and brought the US Army to the border country.

subject: Gaspra
summary: A white-named spa town on the Crimean coast that gave the world an asteroid, sheltered Leo Tolstoy in his final years, and raised one of the most influential Crimean Tatar thinkers of the modern age.

subject: Gastonia, North Carolina
summary: A Piedmont mill town where Ella May Wiggins was killed during the 1929 Loray strike, and where today's headquarters of the world's largest spun-yarn maker still anchors a region remaking itself.

subject: Gastown
summary: Vancouver began as a saloon that sawmill workers built in exchange for all the whisky they could drink in one sitting - and the city is still arguing about the man who bought the round.

subject: Gastown Steam Clock
summary: Vancouver's most photographed antique was built in 1977 to cover a sidewalk vent, and an electric motor has been doing most of the work since 1986.

subject: Gastown riots
summary: A two-minute ultimatum in Maple Tree Square turned a marijuana smoke-in into what a Supreme Court justice would call a police riot.

subject: Gateshead
summary: A town of 196,151 on the Tyne's south bank, historically part of County Durham, whose industrial decline gave way to the most ambitious post-millennial cultural transformation in the English North.

subject: Gatún
summary: A small Panamanian town that has been reinvented by every transit scheme to cross the isthmus -- pirate stopover, gold rush waystation, French construction camp, American canal town -- and is now a ghost town administered by the Panama Canal Authority.

subject: Gavà Mines
summary: Six thousand years ago, Neolithic people tunneled deep beneath what is now Gavà to reach variscite, a green gem worn as jewellery, leaving behind the oldest known mines of their kind in Europe and, in their exhausted shafts, their dead.

subject: Gdansk
summary: Where World War II began and Solidarity ended communism, where Hanseatic wealth built amber-trading magnificence, where Poland meets the Baltic.

subject: Gebel Adda
summary: A table mountain and fortified city occupied from Roman times to the 18th century - likely the late capital of Christian Dotawo - now mostly submerged beneath Lake Nasser.

subject: Gedser Odde
summary: A boulder on a low clay cliff marks the last of Denmark, the last of Scandinavia and the last of the Nordic countries - and on a good March morning forty thousand eiders go past it in a single day.

subject: Geel
summary: For more than seven centuries, this Flemish town has welcomed people with mental illness into ordinary households, treating them not as patients but as neighbors.

subject: Geelong
summary: Once the wool-and-manufacturing pivot of western Victoria, Geelong has reinvented itself from a factory town into a waterfront city of design — Australia's second-fastest-growing city, on the shores of Corio Bay.

subject: Geevor Tin Mine
summary: When Geevor's pumps fell silent in May 1991, eighty years of underground labor flooded with seawater, drowning a way of life that had defined this stretch of Cornish cliff for centuries.

subject: Geirangerfjord
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage fjord where seven waterfalls plunge past abandoned cliff farms, a mountain slowly prepares to collapse, and Disney found the landscape for Arendelle.

subject: Gelders Arcadië
summary: A railway turned a wealthy Dutch retreat into a public park - the country estates of the Veluwezoom that anyone can now walk through.

subject: Gelgel
summary: For nearly two centuries, this quiet Balinese village was the seat of a kingdom that ruled Bali, Lombok, and parts of Java, preserving the Hindu-Javanese civilization that the fallen Majapahit empire left behind.

subject: Gelonus
summary: A wooden city Herodotus described 2,400 years ago, burned before an invading Persian army could reach it, and still being searched for on the Ukrainian forest-steppe.

subject: Gemini 11
summary: The Gemini mission that docked on its first orbit, climbed higher than any crewed spacecraft would for decades, spun two vehicles on a tether to create artificial gravity, and was born from Pete Conrad's thwarted dream of flying to the Moon.

subject: Gemini 12
summary: The final Gemini mission proved that astronauts could work in the void of space, clearing the last hurdle before Apollo could aim for the Moon.

subject: Gemini Wind Farm
summary: A pair of 75-turbine arrays spinning fifty-five kilometers off the Dutch coast, briefly the second-largest offshore wind farm on Earth.

subject: Genbikei
summary: A volcanic gorge in Iwate Prefecture praised by shoguns and emperors, now famous for its 'flying dango' -- sweet rice dumplings sent sailing across the ravine on a rope from a shop that has been doing it since 1878.

subject: General Atomics
summary: Founded in 1955 by nuclear physicists who wanted to make peaceful use of atomic energy, General Atomics became San Diego's largest defense contractor — developing both the fusion reactor technology of tomorrow and the armed drones reshaping warfare today.

subject: General Cliff Rock Paintings
summary: Neolithic petroglyphs carved into a cliffside near Lianyungang, dubbed the 'Oriental Book from Heaven' for their undeciphered symbols that may date to 8000 BC.

subject: Geneva
summary: Where Calvin reformed Christianity and diplomats negotiate everything, where the lake reflects Alps that money can almost buy, where Swiss neutrality becomes international institution.

subject: Genipabu
summary: A dune field north of Natal where the sand physically relocates itself, the buggy drivers ask whether you want emotion, and the camels that made it famous are gone.

subject: Genk
summary: A village of 2,000 farmers turned into a coal-mining boomtown of 70,000 - Italian, Turkish, Greek, Polish - and then had to figure out what to do when both the coal and Ford left.

subject: Genoese Gazaria
summary: For two centuries a merchant republic ruled a scattered empire of Black Sea ports from a single Crimean capital, governed by law codes and a bank rather than a king.

subject: GeoMôn
summary: A UNESCO Global Geopark spanning the entire island of Anglesey, where rocks from nearly every chapter of Earth's history surface within a 720-square-kilometre area.

story.title: Geography of the Isle of Man

subject: Geography of the Isle of Man
summary: The whole island, all 572 square kilometres of it plus its seas and skies, is a single UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, an honour granted to no other entire jurisdiction on Earth.

subject: George
summary: South Africa's sixth-oldest town sits between the Outeniqua Mountains and the Indian Ocean, serving as the Garden Route's main gateway while keeping the small-town character that world-class golf courses and a working airport have not managed to erode.

subject: George Alonzo Johnson
summary: George Alonzo Johnson arrived in California during the Gold Rush, built a steamboat empire on the Colorado River that transformed military supply costs, married into a San Diego ranching dynasty, served in the California Assembly, and then lost almost everything — a life that traced the arc of nineteenth-century California ambition.

story.title: George C. Reifel Migratory Bird Sanctuary

subject: George C. Reifel Migratory Bird Sanctuary
summary: A family farm in the Fraser delta that was handed to the government with two conditions attached - and became a refuge of hemispheric importance.

subject: George Fisher mine
summary: Twenty kilometers north of Mount Isa, one of the largest zinc, lead and silver mines on Earth pulls ore from more than a kilometer underground, fighting water every meter of the way.

story.title: George Floyd protests in the Netherlands

subject: George Floyd protests in the Netherlands
summary: In June 2020, an American police killing forced the Netherlands to look at its own reflection — colonial, Surinamese, Moluccan, Indo — and ask harder questions than it had asked in decades.

subject: George Reeves
summary: The actor who played Superman on television in the 1950s, beloved by millions of children and trapped by the role — his death at 45 from a gunshot wound in his Benedict Canyon home was ruled suicide but has never stopped being questioned.

story.title: George Washington and Jefferson National Forests

subject: George Washington and Jefferson National Forests
summary: 1.8 million acres of Appalachian forest stretching across Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky - a single managed unit since the late 1990s that includes the first Civilian Conservation Corps camp ever built.

subject: Georges Le Marinel
summary: Born on an Iowa farm, educated at a Belgian military academy, Georges Le Marinel spent his career in service of King Leopold's Congo Free State - drawing the borders that still divide Central Africa today.

story.title: Georgetown: The Piece of North America in the Outback

subject: Georgetown
summary: A tiny gold town on the Etheridge goldfield that happens to sit on a 1.7-billion-year-old fragment of ancient North America - and now keeps a collection of 4,500 mineral specimens in the savannah, a long way from anywhere.

subject: Georgetown
summary: Older than the city around it, built on a tobacco and slave trade economy, ruined by the Civil War, gentrified by John and Jacqueline Kennedy and the federal civil servants who wanted to live near them - Georgetown is what survives when a colonial port town becomes the most expensive neighborhood in Washington.

subject: Georgetown (Washington, D.C.)
summary: A Maryland tobacco port older than the federal city, swallowed into Washington in 1871 and now one of the wealthiest neighborhoods in the United States.

subject: Geothermal areas of Yellowstone
summary: Yellowstone contains half the world's active geysers, with over 10,000 thermal features scattered across nine distinct basins above an ancient supervolcano.

subject: Gerakas
summary: A booming northeast Athens suburb built on the ancient deme of Gargettus, ancestral home of Epicurus, where farmland turned to apartment blocks in a single generation.

subject: Germa
summary: The mud-brick ruins of Garama, capital of the Garamantian kingdom, where a desert civilization built its largest city in the Libyan Fezzan.

subject: German Air Force
summary: Disbanded in 1946 and rebuilt from scratch a decade later, the postwar Luftwaffe learned to fly the F-104 the hard way and now anchors NATO's air defense from the Lower Rhine.

story.title: German Colonization of Valdivia, Osorno and Llanquihue

subject: German Colonization of Valdivia, Osorno and Llanquihue
summary: In the 1850s, six thousand Germans crossed the world to settle Chile's Lake District, reshaping its towns, its breweries, and even the words children used to play marbles.

subject: German South West Africa
summary: Germany's only settler colony in Africa lasted just three decades, but its legacy of genocide, forced labor, and racial segregation cast a shadow that stretches from 1884 to the present day.

subject: German Submarine U-1109
summary: A Type VIIC/41 U-boat that surrendered at Loch Eriboll in May 1945 and was torpedoed off Ireland eight months later as part of Operation Deadlight.

subject: Germanna
summary: A forgotten colonial settlement where German miners and a scheming lieutenant governor planted the seeds of Virginia's iron industry along the Rapidan River.

subject: Gettysburg, Washington
summary: A logging town at the mouth of the Lyre River that burned in 1927 and left behind nothing but a name and one very strange prison sentence.

subject: Gezira State
summary: The island between the Blue and White Niles grew cotton for the British empire, staples for modern Sudan, and, in 2023, hosted an exodus of 250,000 people in four days.

subject: Ghaba
summary: A Neolithic cemetery mound near Shendi on the middle Nile whose graves quietly rewrote when Africans began eating domesticated wheat and barley.

subject: Ghadir Khumm
summary: At a desert pool in 632 CE, the Prophet Muhammad spoke of Ali ibn Abi Talib in words Sunni and Shia Muslims have read, with deep respect, in different ways ever since.

subject: Ghana Empire
summary: The first great empire of the Sahel grew rich not on gold it owned but on gold it taxed - and its king sat in court so splendid that Arab geographers called him the wealthiest ruler on earth.

subject: Ghent
summary: The medieval Flemish city whose nobles once had to walk barefoot wearing nooses for defying their emperor.

subject: Gholhak
summary: One of Tehran's oldest neighborhoods, Gholhak was once the first village of Shemiran -- a place of aqueducts, sycamore trees, and a British Embassy garden where Freemasons reportedly shaped Iran's political future.

subject: Gia Lai province
summary: A plateau province named for the Jarai people who have lived on it for centuries, now doubled in size and reaching all the way to the sea.

subject: Gia Nghia
summary: The provincial capital of Vietnam's Dak Nong Province, Gia Nghia is a clean and unhurried Central Highlands town where nineteen ethnic groups share a landscape of waterfalls, plateaus, and highland rivers.

subject: Giant Rock
summary: A seven-story freestanding boulder in the Mojave Desert that has served as a home, a UFO convention site, an FAA-certified airstrip, and a launching pad for scientific balloons — sometimes simultaneously.

subject: Giant Swing
summary: A towering teak frame where Brahmin priests once swung for bags of coins in a ceremony reenacting Shiva's descent to earth, silenced by fatal accidents in 1935 but still standing as Bangkok's most distinctive landmark.

subject: Giant's Causeway
summary: Forty thousand basalt columns, mostly hexagonal, stepping down into the North Atlantic - and a giant called Fionn whose wife is the reason he won.

story.title: Gibsonton: The Town That Didn't Stare

subject: Gibsonton
summary: The Florida town where carnival and sideshow performers built a community on their own terms - where neighbors understood, zoning allowed backyard elephants, and nobody gawked.

subject: Gibsonton, Florida
summary: A tiny Florida community south of Tampa where carnival performers have wintered since the mid-20th century, earning it the nickname 'Carnie Town' and making it home to the largest showmen's association in the United States.

subject: Giethoorn
summary: A village in Overijssel with 2,620 residents, 176 bridges, no roads in its centre, and a tourism problem so acute that the bus signs are now in Mandarin.

subject: Gifford, East Lothian
summary: An East Lothian village whose ruined Goblin Ha inspired Walter Scott and whose minister, John Witherspoon, was the only clergyman to sign the American Declaration of Independence.

subject: Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg
summary: Ten European countries competed for Tesla's first European plant — one of them lobbied in Minecraft — and Brandenburg won it, along with the bombs, the protest camps and the fight over water.

subject: Gigha
summary: A six-mile sliver of land off the west coast of Kintyre, ancestral home of Clan MacNeill and one of the first islands in Scotland to be bought by the people who live on it - in 2002, for four million pounds, after a succession of private landlords had run the population down to 98.

subject: Gila City, Arizona
summary: A gold rush boomtown on the Gila River that appeared in 1858, disappeared in 1862, and left so little behind that its site has been entirely reclaimed by the river and the desert — the complete story of a frontier community from discovery to erasure in four years.

subject: Gillespie Field
summary: A Marine parachute training base from World War II became San Diego County's busiest general aviation airport — and now displays the F-14 Tomcat that appeared in Top Gun: Maverick.

subject: Ginza
summary: Tokyo's most famous shopping district, built on a 16th-century swamp and named for a silver mint, where weekend streets close to traffic and pedestrians stroll past luxury boutiques, Michelin-starred sushi bars, and a clock tower that has marked time since 1894.

story.title: Ginzan Onsen: Where Silver Became Steam

subject: Ginzan Onsen
summary: A narrow mountain valley in Yamagata Prefecture where a failed silver mine gave way to one of Japan's most atmospheric hot spring towns -- wooden ryokan from the Taisho era lining a central river, lit by real gas lamps after dark.

subject: Gion
summary: Kyoto's legendary geisha district, where wooden teahouses along cobblestone lanes preserve a world of art, dance, and ritual hospitality that has survived since the Sengoku period -- though the women who practice this tradition call themselves not geisha but geiko.

story.title: Giri Kedaton: Java's Pope on the Hilltop

subject: Giri Kedaton
summary: For over a century, the rulers of this small hilltop principality near Gresik held the power to legitimize every Muslim sultan in Java - a spiritual authority so potent that even the mighty Mataram Sultanate needed an army and a bloodline argument to finally break it.

subject: Girl with a Pearl Earring
summary: In 1881, an Hague collector bought a small, damaged, unsigned tronie at auction for two guilders and thirty cents. It is now one of the most recognisable paintings on Earth, and we still do not know who the girl was.

subject: Girnar
summary: Sacred to Jains, Hindus, and history itself, Girnar's ancient peaks near Junagadh hold 2,300-year-old Ashoka edicts, exquisite medieval temples, and Asia's longest ropeway.

subject: Girón, Azuay
summary: A small Andean town named for a Spanish conqueror, where a treaty once ended a war and a crucifix is still asked to bring rain.

subject: Giá Rai
summary: A shrimp-farming town on Highway 1 whose fields hosted the most famous peasant land case of French Cochinchina, and whose parish church became a pilgrimage site for the whole delta.

story.title: Glacial Erratic Boulders of the Puget Sound Region

subject: Glacial Erratic Boulders of the Puget Sound Region
summary: Boulders the size of houses, carried hundreds of kilometres by ice and dropped across the Puget lowland, where they now sit in back yards, parks, and second-growth forest.

subject: Gladbeck
summary: A young coal-and-steel Ruhr town with a thousand-year history and a name that German journalism has not quite been able to live down.

subject: Glamaig
summary: A near-perfect cone of red scree above Sligachan, climbed in barefoot record time by a Gurkha in 1899 and almost never beaten since.

subject: Glandore
summary: A West Cork sailing village on a harbour guarded by two rocks called Adam and Eve, where the local rule is simple: avoid Adam, hug Eve.

subject: Glanfahan
summary: A townland on the southern slopes of Mount Eagle containing 417 drystone structures, 19 souterrains and 18 standing stones - an abandoned village of beehive huts that may have been a stop on the pilgrimage to Skellig Michael.

subject: Glangevlin
summary: A Cavan glen where the last Irish glacier persisted and Irish was still spoken into the 1930s, the legendary home of a magical cow whose milk signalled prosperity itself.

subject: Glarentza
summary: For two centuries, Glarentza was the chief port and mint of the Frankish Principality of Achaea — the gateway through which Mediterranean commerce flowed into the Peloponnese. Today it is a swamp and a few scattered stones near the modern village of Kyllini.

subject: Glasgow
summary: Scotland's largest city scrubbed off a century of industrial soot to reveal red-sandstone Victorian streets, a riverside reinvention, and a music scene that punches well above its weight.

subject: Glasgow
summary: Once called the Second City of the Empire, Glasgow built more than half of Britain's ships, a quarter of the world's locomotives, and now writes its next act on the same riverbank.

subject: Glasgow City Chambers
summary: The Victorian seat of Glasgow's city government on George Square, inaugurated by Queen Victoria in 1888 and topped by a figure locals call Glasgow's Statue of Liberty.

subject: Glasgow Subway
summary: The world's third-oldest underground metro, opened in 1896, a 4-foot-gauge circular loop under the Clyde that Glaswegians still call the Subway and almost no-one calls the Clockwork Orange.

story.title: Glaspaleis: A Glass Palace Built for Miners

subject: Glaspaleis
summary: In 1935 a fabric merchant and a young architect built Heerlen a department store so transparent it had to be propped against thirty mushroom-shaped pillars. Patton used it as a headquarters, a supermarket nearly killed it, and a city's stubbornness brought it back as a cultural center.

subject: Glasserton
summary: A windswept parish of Bronze Age stones, a saint's cave, and a bronze otter that remembers the naturalist who wrote Ring of Bright Water.

subject: Glastonbury
summary: A small Somerset town where Neolithic trackways, Joseph of Arimathea, King Arthur, Holy Thorns, ley lines, and the world's largest music festival all somehow coexist.

subject: Glastonbury Festival
summary: The five-day Somerset arts festival that grew from 1,500 hippies on a dairy farm in 1970 to 200,000 attendees and a national institution, still run from the same family farm in the Vale of Avalon.

subject: Glastonbury Thorn
summary: A hawthorn tree that flowers twice a year - once at Christmas - and the legend, propagation, and acts of vandalism that have kept it alive for centuries.

subject: Glen Affric
summary: Often called Scotland's most beautiful glen, Glen Affric holds the third-largest surviving fragment of the ancient Caledonian Forest, a recreated tartan, and the birthplace of the golden retriever.

subject: Glen Coe
summary: A U-shaped valley carved by ice-age glaciers from the remains of a 420-million-year-old supervolcano, haunted by the memory of a 1692 massacre and prized by climbers worldwide.

subject: Glen Helen, Isle of Man
summary: A Victorian-planted wooded glen at the foot of Lambfell Mountain that became part of the most famous racing road on Earth.

subject: Glen Innes Showground
summary: One of the oldest and most complete country showgrounds in New South Wales, where a ring of Federation timber pavilions has hosted the same agricultural show every year since the 1870s.

subject: Glen Innes, New South Wales
summary: A New England tableland town that answers to two pasts: the Aboriginal country of Gindaaydjin, and a Celtic identity it built from scratch, complete with thirty-eight standing stones and street signs in Gaelic.

subject: Glen Shiel
summary: A nine-mile Northwest Highland glen lined by the Five Sisters of Kintail and the South Cluanie ridge, and the site in 1719 of the last close engagement between British and foreign troops on mainland British soil.

subject: Glenamaddy
summary: The crossroads town that gave the world Four Country Roads, lost a priest to penal-era hangmen at a place still called the Priest's Valley, and once filled the Esker Ballroom with showband fans until the marquees took the dancers away.

subject: Glenbeigh
summary: A Ring of Kerry village in the valley of the birch tree, where prehistoric rock art, mythological lovers, and a Victorian folly all share the same view.

subject: Glencoe
summary: A Highland village and valley where glacial geology, a 1692 massacre, world-class mountain scrambles, and coach-tour commerce converge under a single name.

subject: Glencolmcille
summary: A scatter of Gaeltacht villages on Donegal's wildest coast, where barefoot midnight pilgrims still walk a 5-km circuit of fifteen holy sites every June 9th.

subject: Glencolmcille
summary: A Gaeltacht parish on Donegal's Atlantic coast where Christian saints layered themselves onto sites already sacred for three thousand years.

subject: Glenelg
summary: A scattered West Highland community with a palindromic name, the world's last hand-operated turntable car ferry, the best brochs on mainland Scotland, and an official twinning with a crater on Mars.

subject: Glenfiddich
summary: The world's best-selling single malt whisky began as one man's Christmas Day gamble in 1887, and its family has never let go of the stills.

subject: Glenfinnan
summary: A tiny Highland village where a doomed prince launched a rebellion, a viaduct became a film star, and 139 residents endure the consequences of global fame.

subject: Glenlivet
summary: A remote highland glen whose name became shorthand for legitimate Scotch whisky, born from a Protestant-Catholic battle, a hidden seminary, and a license that changed the industry forever.

subject: Glenmoriston
summary: A Highland glen where a preacher's footprints will not grow back, wild boar were recently reintroduced, and Bonnie Prince Charlie hid for a week.

subject: Glenorchy
summary: A small town at the head of Lake Wakatipu where the road ends and New Zealand's most famous tramping tracks begin - gateway to the Routeburn, Greenstone-Caples, and Rees-Dart.

subject: Glenridding
summary: A small village at the southern foot of Ullswater, born of the largest lead mine in the Lake District, now the launching point for ascents of Helvellyn and trips on the Ullswater Steamers.

subject: Glenrowan, Victoria
summary: A small town on the Hume Freeway where, at dawn on 28 June 1880, Ned Kelly walked out of the mist in homemade iron armour and into Australian legend.

subject: Glenville, West Virginia
summary: A central West Virginia county seat of about 1,100 people, anchored by a hilltop university with more students than residents, a Little Kanawha River bend, and a federal prison on the outskirts.

subject: Glikson Crater
summary: A 19-kilometre wound from deep time, ground almost flat by erosion and buried under dunes, betrayed only by a ghostly magnetic ring that no eye can see.

subject: Glodok
summary: Jakarta's Chinatown was born from a massacre -- forced into existence when the Dutch confined surviving Chinese residents outside the city walls in 1740, and it has endured violence, discrimination, and reinvention ever since.

subject: Glossa
summary: A whitewashed hill village on Skopelos, hung with bougainvillea and twinkling lights, gazing across the water to Skiathos from above its little harbor at Loutraki.

subject: Gloucester
summary: A cathedral city on the River Severn where Edward II is buried, Harry Potter's school corridors were filmed, and Britain's first jet engine took to the air.

subject: Gloucester County, Virginia
summary: Where Werowocomoco rose, where daffodils bloom each April, and where Walter Reed grew up - a Middle Peninsula county quietly carrying centuries of Virginia.

subject: Glyder Fach
summary: Wales' sixth-highest peak crowns its summit chaos with a 25-tonne stone slab that juts out into thin air - the Cantilever, easily Snowdonia's most photographed boulder.

subject: Glyder Fawr
summary: Until 2010 it was measured at 999 metres; a more careful survey added 1.8 metres and quietly promoted Wales' fifth-highest mountain into the four-figure club.

subject: Glyderau
summary: Eleven peaks, five of them over 3,000 feet, and a botanic refuge that keeps Britain's only Snowdon lily - the Glyderau are the mountain range that punctures Snowdonia between Snowdon and the Carneddau.

subject: Glyfada
summary: Glyfada is the glossy coastal suburb that anchors the Athens Riviera — a place where the Saronic Gulf meets European boutiques, seafront clubs, and a golfing strip that owes its particular character partly to an American airbase that closed in the early 1990s.

subject: Gnaraloo
summary: A remote pastoral station at the wild southern end of the Ningaloo coast, where one of the planet's heaviest left-hand surf breaks shares the shore with one of its largest loggerhead turtle rookeries.

subject: Goa
summary: Where Portuguese India survives in churches and cuisine, where beaches draw seekers of all kinds, where India's smallest state punches above its weight.

story.title: Goa Gajah: The Demon Mouth at the Bottom of the Stairs

subject: Goa Gajah
summary: A thousand-year-old cave sanctuary near Ubud where a carved demon's mouth swallows visitors into a space sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, lost for centuries before Dutch archaeologists stumbled upon it in 1923.

subject: Goat Fell
summary: The highest peak on the Isle of Arran at 875 metres, with views to Northern Ireland on a clear day - and the dark history of an 1889 murder that still haunts its summit.

subject: Goathland
summary: A North York Moors village whose railway station played Hogsmeade in the Harry Potter films, whose pubs and shops served as Heartbeat's Aidensfield, and whose sheep still graze the green by ancient right.

subject: Gocta
summary: A waterfall hidden in Peruvian cloud forest that the outside world only measured in 2006, though local villagers had always known the siren who cursed it.

subject: Goddard Institute for Space Studies
summary: A NASA laboratory above a Seinfeld-famous diner where scientists coined the term 'quasar,' helped birth plate tectonics, and shaped the world's understanding of climate change.

subject: Godin Tepe
summary: A 7,000-year-old trading outpost in western Iran where archaeologists found some of the earliest evidence of wine and beer production, along with clay tablets linking the site to the Uruk commercial networks.

subject: Godmanchester
summary: A Roman crossroads town with a neolithic sun temple buried in its gravel pits, a Chinese bridge held together by a stubborn myth, and 2,000 years of continuous occupation along the River Great Ouse.

subject: Goes
summary: A medieval salt-and-cloth town on Zuid-Beveland where Spanish tercios once arrived by wading across the Scheldt, now the fourth-largest economic center in Zeeland.

subject: Gogo Station
summary: Once Western Australia's largest cattle station with 90,000 head, Gogo Station on the Fitzroy River tells the story of the Kimberley's pastoral frontier from the 1880s land rush to modern-day Aboriginal communities.

subject: Goguryeo tombs
summary: North Korea's first UNESCO World Heritage site preserves thirty ancient tombs whose vivid wall paintings are nearly all that survives of the Goguryeo kingdom -- a civilization that once stretched from Manchuria to central Korea.

subject: Goiatuba
summary: A south-central Goias town whose name means 'big Goias' in Tupi-Guarani, and whose dairy quietly supplies most of the ice cream in Brazil's McDonald's stores.

subject: Going-to-the-Sun Road
summary: Fifty miles of engineering audacity carved into Montana's most dramatic peaks - America's most spectacular mountain road crosses the Continental Divide through Glacier National Park.

subject: Goiás
summary: The central Brazilian state whose name comes from a word meaning "people of the same origin" - a high, flat land of cerrado savanna, colonial gold towns, river beaches, and pequi fruit you cannot bite.

subject: Goiás (city)
summary: The colonial gold-rush capital that UNESCO recognized in 2001 for preserving 18th-century Brazil almost accidentally - because the state capital moved away and left it alone.

subject: Goiás, Goiás
summary: Also called Goiás Velho, the former colonial capital shrunk by nearly half after the government moved away - and in losing its importance preserved its 18th-century architecture well enough to become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Goiânia
summary: A city drawn on paper in 1933 and built from scratch for 50,000 people that now holds over a million and a half, Goiânia is Brazil's capital that nobody saw coming.

subject: Goiânia
summary: Goiânia is Brazil's great planned city that nobody planned for - a 1930s art-deco experiment that grew wildly past its blueprint and became the green capital of the Central-West.

subject: Goiânia accident
summary: In September 1987, a stolen radiotherapy capsule released caesium-137 into a working-class neighborhood in Goiânia, killing four people - including a six-year-old girl - and contaminating hundreds.

subject: Gokayama
summary: A secluded mountain valley in Toyama Prefecture where steep-roofed gasshō-zukuri farmhouses have stood for centuries, hidden from the outside world by the gorges of the Shōgawa River.

subject: Gokstad Mound
summary: A 50-meter burial mound in Vestfold that yielded one of the finest Viking ships ever found -- a 23.8-meter oak vessel built around 890 AD, buried with its chieftain, twelve horses, and sixty-four shields.

subject: Gold Coast
summary: Australia's glittering holiday city, where a wall of high-rises faces 52 kilometres of surf beach, the rainforest hides in the hills behind, and the Kombumerri have been the Salt Water people for millennia.

subject: Gold Country
summary: Where the world changed in 1848 - the Sierra Nevada foothills where James Marshall's gold discovery sparked the largest migration in human history, transforming California from backwater to phenomenon.

subject: Golden Bauhinia Square
summary: A gilded six-metre flower, officially a symbol of Hong Kong's 1997 handover and the site of daily flag-raising ceremonies, but affectionately nicknamed the 'Golden Pak Choi' by locals who see something a little absurd in its grandeur.

subject: Golden Ears
summary: The twin summit that dominates the Lower Mainland skyline owes its name to a mishearing, its official name to a governor who lasted a year, and its forest to a fire that burned 60,000 hectares.

subject: Golden Gumboot
summary: A 7.9-metre fibreglass rubber boot stands in Tully as the trophy in a friendly war between three Queensland towns over which is the wettest in Australia.

subject: Golden Hind
summary: Francis Drake sailed a 120-ton galleon around the world between 1577 and 1580, returned with so much Spanish treasure that he paid off England's national debt, and made a deer the most famous ship in Tudor history.

subject: Golden Horn
summary: Istanbul's great horn-shaped harbor inlet has sheltered empires and fleets for millennia — the same sheltered water that defeated the Kievan Rus', tempted Leonardo da Vinci, and witnessed the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople.

subject: Golden Horns of Gallehus
summary: Two fifth-century gold horns, found a century apart in a Jutland field, melted down by a thief in 1802 — and known today only through the drawings made before they vanished.

subject: Golden Triangle (Southeast Asia)
summary: The mountainous borderland where Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos converge has been one of the world's largest narcotics-producing regions since the 1950s, shifting from opium empires to synthetic drug factories while impoverished farmers remain trapped in between.

subject: Golden Village, Richmond
summary: Four streets in suburban Richmond holding a dense cluster of Asian shopping malls - built by the people who shop in them, ten minutes from the runways of YVR.

subject: Golden lancehead
summary: A critically endangered pit viper found nowhere on Earth except a single forbidden island off the Brazilian coast, where its venom evolved to be five times deadlier than its mainland relative's.

subject: Goldeneye (estate)
summary: The Jamaican cliffside estate where Ian Fleming wrote every James Bond novel, later owned by Bob Marley and then Island Records founder Chris Blackwell, now operating as one of the Caribbean's most storied luxury resorts.

subject: Golders Green Crematorium
summary: London's first crematorium, opened in 1902, has since performed more than 323,500 cremations — more than any other British crematorium — for a guest list that includes Peter Sellers, Marc Bolan, T.S. Eliot, and Sigmund Freud.

subject: Goldfish Street
summary: A single block of Tung Choi Street in Mong Kok where hundreds of plastic bags filled with fish hang like ornaments in shop windows, making it one of Hong Kong's most visually distinctive markets — and one that carries concerns about endangered species.

subject: Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: A tropical fjord on Costa Rica's southern Pacific coast where scalloped hammerhead sharks raise their young in warm mangrove nurseries, humpback whales from both hemispheres come to breed, and half the country's biodiversity crowds into three percent of its land area.

subject: Golspie
summary: A planned Sutherland coastal village where the seat of Clan Sutherland watches the North Sea from beneath Ben Bhraggie.

subject: Gomantong Caves
summary: A vast limestone cave system in Sabah, Malaysia, where centuries-old traditions of harvesting edible swiftlet nests meet nightly spectacles of 275,000 bats pouring into the tropical dusk.

subject: Gondar
summary: A traveler's guide to the royal city of Ethiopia, where 17th-century castles rise above a modern highland town that still celebrates the emperors' Timkat each January.

subject: Gondar
summary: Ethiopia's royal capital from 1636 until the late 18th century, city of 44 churches, emperors, empresses, and two hundred years of Ethiopian political power.

subject: Gondrani
summary: A mysterious cave city carved into rock near Bela in Balochistan, believed to be the remains of an eighth-century Buddhist monastery, whose exact builders and purpose remain unknown to this day.

subject: Gonzanamá
summary: A southern Ecuadorian mountain town whose name splices an Indigenous chieftain with a sacred valley, and whose biggest festival burns castles in the night.

subject: Goodwick
summary: A Welsh coastal town whose Norse name means good bay, where 1,400 French invaders surrendered on the sands in 1797 and the first ever flight from Britain to Ireland took off in 1912.

subject: Goodwin Sands
summary: Ten miles of shifting sand off the Kent coast that has swallowed more than two thousand ships - and, on the right summer afternoon at low tide, hosted a cricket match.

subject: Goodwood Plantation
summary: A cotton plantation in Leon County, Florida, built on land the Marquis de Lafayette never visited, shaped by a shipwreck that killed an entire family, and transformed across two centuries from slave labor to lavish entertaining to public museum.

subject: Gooi
summary: A medieval commons that survived until 1972, a Bronze Age culture that left its name in pottery, and a ridge of dry sand that made the Netherlands' most famous suburb possible.

subject: Gooi en Vechtstreek
summary: Half an hour from Amsterdam by Sprinter, a region where Dutch broadcasting was born, the country's richest families built villas in the woods, and the Vecht winds past 17th-century country estates.

subject: Gooise Meren
summary: Three towns with separate histories — a fortress, a commuter village, and a castle harbor — merged into one municipality in 2016, and an unlikely roster of Olympic swimmers, Golden Age painters, and a Dutch Resistance hero now share a town hall.

subject: Goonhilly Satellite Earth Station
summary: On a treeless heath in Cornwall, an antenna nicknamed Arthur caught television out of the sky for the first time and changed how the world saw itself.

subject: Goostrey
summary: A Cheshire farming village that grew up around a thousand-year-old yew and now hosts the world headquarters of humanity's most ambitious radio telescope.

subject: Gordale Scar
summary: A vertical limestone ravine in the Yorkshire Dales where Wordsworth saw lions and Hollywood filmed Skeksis.

subject: Gorg Blau
summary: A mountain reservoir in Mallorca's highest country that drowned a celebrated beauty spot once painted by poets and artists.

story.title: Gorgan: The Yellow City at the Caspian Gate

subject: Gorgan
summary: Capital of Iran's Golestan Province, Gorgan has endured under a dozen names across three millennia - from the ancient Hyrcanian capital Zadracarta to the medieval stronghold of Astarabad to the modern city that guards the southeastern corner of the Caspian Sea.

subject: Gorleben
summary: A village of 614 people on the Elbe gave its name to Germany's nuclear waste argument — and after more than two billion euros and forty years of drilling, the salt dome beneath it was ruled out and is now being filled back in.

subject: Goroka
summary: A highland city in Papua New Guinea that becomes the stage for one of the world's greatest tribal gatherings every September.

subject: Gorom-Gorom
summary: A Sahel crossroads in northern Burkina Faso whose great Thursday market gathers Fulani, Tuareg, Songhai and Bella traders beneath the desert sun.

subject: Gorontalo
summary: A province on Sulawesi's Minahasa Peninsula where Islamic tradition runs so deep the region earned the nickname 'Porch of Medina,' and where whale sharks visit a fishing village every summer.

subject: Gorredijk
summary: A Frisian peat-trading town that an 1823 traveller described as a place where one in three Frisian criminals lived in half-buried houses, and which became respectable enough to brew its own jenever.

subject: Gort
summary: A south Galway market town where Brazilian meatpackers, W.B. Yeats's tower house, and Lady Gregory's Coole Park share the same few square kilometres.

subject: Gortin
summary: A village of 374 people under the Sperrins, where a workhouse stood, a brewery vanished, and the landlord could ride around his estate in a single day.

subject: Goryeo
summary: The medieval Korean dynasty that gave the world the name 'Korea' also produced jade-green celadon ceramics, the world's oldest movable metal type, and 80,000 wooden printing blocks carved to summon Buddhist protection against Mongol invaders.

subject: Goseck Circle
summary: A wooden enclosure raised around 4900 BC with gates open to the midwinter sun - found from the air in a dry summer, and still argued over.

subject: Goshiki-numa
summary: Five volcanic lakes born from a catastrophic 1888 eruption, each shimmering a different color -- from cobalt blue to reddish green -- that shifts mysteriously with the seasons.

subject: Goslar
summary: Silver from the Rammelsberg made Goslar rich enough to build in timber and slate for five hundred years, and poor enough afterwards to leave more than 1,500 of those houses standing.

subject: Gotham, Nottinghamshire
summary: The Nottinghamshire village whose feigned medieval madness gave New York and Batman their nickname.

subject: Gothenburg
summary: Sweden's gateway to the world, a city built by Dutch engineers on marshy ground where Scandinavian ambition meets Atlantic commerce.

subject: Gothic Quarter, Barcelona
summary: Barcelona's Gothic Quarter is a labyrinth of medieval streets built on Roman foundations, except that much of the 'medieval' architecture was actually constructed in the 20th century.

subject: Gotland
summary: Sweden's largest island holds more Viking silver than anywhere else on Earth, a testament to its role as the crossroads of medieval trade.

subject: Gouda
summary: The city that made the world's most famous cheese without actually making it, and whose stained-glass windows have been pulling tourists in since the 1600s.

subject: Gouda
summary: A traveler's guide to a 76,000-person Dutch city that delivers more on a one-day visit than most capitals deliver in three.

subject: Goudi Coup
summary: On a August night in 1909, a few hundred junior officers gathered at the Goudi barracks and, without firing a shot, cracked open the old order of Greek politics.

subject: Gourmet Ghetto
summary: A few blocks of North Berkeley where specialty coffee, California cuisine, farm-to-table dining, and the sourdough baguette all took root -- before the neighborhood retired its own nickname.

subject: Gourock
summary: A town whose name means 'pimple' in Gaelic - from a fishing village on the upper Firth of Clyde to a Victorian seaside resort to a residential commuter base with one of Scotland's last outdoor seawater pools.

subject: Governador Valadares, Minas Gerais
summary: A Brazilian gem-trading city in the Rio Doce valley, famous equally for its paragliding peak and for the Framingham and Newark addresses of residents who left.

subject: Government Camp
summary: Mount Hood's alpine village where ski lifts run through September and the Oregon Trail once forced emigrants to abandon their wagons in the snow.

subject: Government Dockyard
summary: On Stonecutters Island, Hong Kong's Government Dockyard quietly keeps the territory's entire fleet of public-service vessels afloat — a place where the Royal Navy once anchored its final chapter in Hong Kong waters.

subject: Government of Rotterdam
summary: Three months after Pim Fortuyn's party swept Rotterdam's 2002 elections, he was assassinated - and the city's politics has never quite recovered from the question of what comes next.

subject: Gowran
summary: A small Kilkenny town built around a medieval church, a Butler castle, and a racecourse where Arkle won - and the place from which Walt Disney's ancestors set sail in 1801.

subject: Graaff-Reinet
summary: The Karoo town with more national monuments than any other in South Africa sits in a horseshoe bend of the Sundays River, surrounded by the eerie stone pillars of the Valley of Desolation.

story.title: Grace Quan: The Junk That Remembers

subject: Grace Quan
summary: A reconstructed Chinese shrimp-fishing junk that sails San Francisco Bay twice a year, retracing the routes of an immigrant fishing fleet that once dominated the bay's shrimp industry before being erased from memory.

subject: Grace Sherwood
summary: The last person convicted of witchcraft in Virginia was a farmer, healer, and midwife who wore trousers, grew herbs, and refused to stop being herself.

subject: Gracias
summary: A colonial-era town in western Honduras whose name comes from exhausted Spanish explorers thanking God for flat land, now a gateway to the country's highest peak and its soothing hot springs.

subject: Graduate Theological Union
summary: A consortium of theological schools on Berkeley's 'Holy Hill' where Baptist ministers, Dominican friars, Buddhist monks, and Islamic scholars study side by side.

subject: Grafton (New South Wales)
summary: For two weeks each spring, this Clarence River city vanishes beneath a haze of purple as 1,700 jacarandas bloom at once - the heart of Australia's oldest floral festival.

subject: Grafton Street
summary: Dublin's most famous shopping street started as a lane shaped by a buried river and is now scored by buskers, neon, and the ghost of Bewley's coffee.

subject: Grahamstown
summary: A city with more than 40 churches and Africa's largest arts festival carries two names that tell the story of colonial conflict and cultural reclamation on the Eastern Cape frontier.

subject: Grainthorpe
summary: A Domesday Book village on the Lincolnshire marsh where a medieval harbour once silted into oblivion and a 13th-century church still keeps watch over the flat coast.

subject: Gramado
summary: In a country famous for beaches and heat, Gramado sells snow, chocolate, and a Christmas that never really ends.

subject: Gran Colombia
summary: Bolivar's republic of 2.6 million people stretched from the Caribbean to the Amazon for twelve years before it came apart over whether a continent could be governed from a single capital.

subject: Gran Pajatén
summary: A ruined city of twenty-six circular stone buildings on a cloud forest ridge, which the government of Peru protects by refusing to let anyone visit it.

subject: Granada
summary: Where the Alhambra crowns Moorish Spain's final kingdom, where the Reconquista ended in 1492, where flamenco echoes through cave dwellings on the Sacromonte.

subject: Grand Central, Birmingham
summary: Built atop the rebuilt New Street Station, this Birmingham shopping centre has been three different things in fifty years and recently turned up in a Mission: Impossible film.

subject: Grand Concourse (Bronx)
summary: The Bronx's 5.2-mile answer to the Champs-Elysees, a boulevard whose Art Deco apartments, devastating decline, and slow revival tell the full arc of twentieth-century New York.

subject: Grand Duchy of Finland
summary: The autonomous Russian-ruled predecessor state of modern Finland, which existed from 1809 to 1917 and forged a national identity that would survive empire, revolution, and civil war.

subject: Grand Portage, Minnesota
summary: A tiny Ojibwe community at Minnesota's northeastern tip where a grueling nine-mile portage once made this the crossroads of the North American fur trade, linking Lake Superior to the continental interior.

subject: Grand Raid
summary: Réunion's Diagonale des Fous - the Madmen's Diagonal - drags runners 165 kilometers across a volcanic island, with enough climbing to summit Everest from sea level and back.

story.title: Grand Rapids: The Furniture City That Became Beer Capital

subject: Grand Rapids
summary: The Michigan city that reinvented itself from furniture to beer - where the craft brewery boom created 'Beer City USA,' where the Christian Reformed Church shapes culture, and where Gerald Ford came from.

story.title: Grand Staircase-Escalante: The Last Wilderness in the Lower 48

subject: Grand Staircase-Escalante
summary: The Utah wilderness so vast it has its own staircase - five geological levels stepping down from Bryce to the Grand Canyon, slot canyons no one has named, and terrain so rugged that it was the last place mapped in the contiguous United States.

story.title: Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians

subject: Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians
summary: A federally recognized tribe on Michigan's Leelanau Peninsula whose centuries-long fight for sovereignty became a landmark in Native American self-determination.

subject: Grand Trianon
summary: Built as Louis XIV's escape from his own creation, the Grand Trianon traded the gilded excess of Versailles for pink marble and white walls, then went on to host Napoleon, imprison a marshal for surrendering his army, and redraw the map of Central Europe.

subject: Grand-Place
summary: The heart of Brussels where opulent Baroque guildhalls rise from cobblestones, rebuilt in defiant splendor after French bombardment in 1695 and now recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Grandma Prisbrey's Bottle Village
summary: A woman who had survived six of her seven children's deaths began, at age 60, to build a village of colored glass and salvaged objects in a Simi Valley lot—and created one of California's most remarkable works of folk art.

subject: Grange
summary: A North Sligo village where three Spanish Armada ships went down, and where the dancer who toppled a Bavarian king was born.

subject: Grangetown, Sunderland
summary: The southern Sunderland suburb where Hendon Beach meets the North Sea, where local rumour insists a Roman road lies under St Aidan's Avenue, and where the city's only eye infirmary has stood for over a century.

subject: Granite outcrops of Western Australia
summary: Rising abruptly from farmland and coastal scrub, Western Australia's granite outcrops are ecological islands hosting over 1,300 plant species, ancient lichen crusts possibly a billion years old, and rainwater pools that sustain life found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Granite-Steppe Lands of Buh
summary: Where the Southern Buh saws through the roots of mountains two billion years old, a Ukrainian steppe park hides rapids, rare wildflowers, and the drowned home of the Zaporizhian Cossacks.

subject: Granitschale im Lustgarten
summary: Berliners call it the soup bowl: seventy-five tonnes of Swedish granite, nearly seven metres across, cut from an erratic boulder an ice sheet left in the Brandenburg woods and polished for two and a half years to a mirror finish.

subject: Granja Comary
summary: The mountain training center in Teresópolis where every Brazil national team since 1990 has prepared for the World Cup, except once.

subject: Grantham
summary: A Lincolnshire market town that produced a prime minister, a scientific revolution, the world's first diesel engine, and a curious gingerbread biscuit.

subject: Grantham Rail Accident
summary: On a clear night in September 1906, an express train ran through Grantham station instead of stopping, killing fourteen people for reasons no inquiry could ever explain.

subject: Grantown-on-Spey
summary: A planned Highland holiday town laid out on a grid in 1765, surrounded by Caledonian pinewoods, glacial 'sheep' boulders, and a Speyside valley that contains heritage steam, capercaillie, and the route of a final Jacobite rout.

subject: Grantown-on-Spey
summary: An 18th-century planned town founded by Sir James Grant in 1765 as part of post-Jacobite Highland economic improvement - now a Cairngorms regional centre with listed Georgian hotels, Victorian tourism heritage, and an unusual list of notable former residents.

subject: Granville County, North Carolina
summary: A tobacco county on Virginia's border where more than 10,000 enslaved people worked the bright-leaf fields before the Civil War, and where federal eviction created the town of Butner during World War II.

story.title: Grasslands Wildlife Management Area: The Pacific Flyway's Great Rest Stop

subject: Grasslands Wildlife Management Area
summary: The largest concentrated easement program for wildlife in California, where 1.5 million ducks and geese descend on privately managed wetlands each winter along the Pacific Flyway.

story.title: Graton Rancheria: Declared Dead, Very Much Alive

subject: Graton Rancheria
summary: A tiny plot of hilly, waterless land in Sonoma County became the unlikely seed of one of California's most remarkable stories of tribal persistence -- from termination and erasure to federal recognition and a $600 million casino.

subject: Grauballe Man
summary: The best-preserved bog body ever found kept his hands intact — which is why a man who died in the third century BC has a set of recorded fingerprints.

subject: Gravatá
summary: Eight degrees south of the equator, a Pernambuco hill town serves fondue — and Recife drives up the escarpment for the cold.

story.title: Grave Stelai from Grave Circle A, Mycenae

subject: Grave Stelai from Grave Circle A, Mycenae
summary: The carved limestone grave markers that stood above Mycenae's royal shaft graves — depicting chariot races, hunting scenes, and swirling spirals — are among the earliest narrative relief sculptures from ancient Greece.

subject: Grave of David Lloyd George
summary: A wartime Prime Minister chose to be buried under a boulder by his childhood river - and his friend the architect of Portmeirion designed the enclosure.

subject: Gravity Hill
summary: The Pennsylvania road where cars appear to roll uphill - one of dozens of 'gravity hills' across America where optical illusions make slight downhill grades look like impossible ascents.

subject: Gray Fossil Site
summary: A road construction crew in Tennessee accidentally uncovered a 4.5-million-year-old sinkhole pond where red pandas, rhinoceroses, mastodons, and the world's largest known population of fossil tapirs once lived and died.

subject: Great Australian Bight
summary: Born 50 million years ago when Gondwana split apart, this vast oceanic bay along Australia's southern coast shelters migrating whales, sustains extraordinary marine biodiversity, and has repeatedly resisted the oil industry's ambitions.

subject: Great Beguinage, Leuven
summary: A UNESCO-listed medieval sanctuary where unmarried religious women lived independently for 700 years, now preserved as one of the largest and most complete beguinages in the Low Countries.

subject: Great Bernera
summary: A small Hebridean island where 252 people, four Iron Age brochs, an Iron Age village, a deliberate semicircle of standing stones and the site of a famous nineteenth-century crofters' rebellion all share roughly five miles by two.

subject: Great Cobar mine
summary: The copper mine that built a town, led Australia in production, raised the nation's mightiest chimney - and then collapsed so completely that 700 houses were carted away.

subject: Great Colonnade at Palmyra
summary: Stretching over a kilometer through the ancient desert city, the Great Colonnade at Palmyra linked the Temple of Bel to the western gates along an avenue once lined with bronze statues of queens and kings.

subject: Great Depression in Latin America
summary: When Wall Street crashed in 1929, Latin America burned coffee, abandoned nitrate fields, and watched regimes rise and fall in the economic aftershock.

subject: Great Dismal Swamp
summary: A vast wetland straddling the Virginia-North Carolina border, the Great Dismal Swamp sheltered maroon communities of escaped enslaved people for generations and remains one of the East Coast's most ecologically significant refuges.

subject: Great Dyke
summary: A 2.575-billion-year-old band of mineralized rock stretching 550 kilometers through Zimbabwe - the planet's second-largest known reserve of platinum group metals, hidden in plain sight.

subject: Great East Road
summary: The strategic thread of pavement that knits Zambia's Eastern Province to the rest of the country, crossing wilderness where no other road dares.

subject: Great Famine (Ireland)
summary: Between 1845 and 1852, blight, politics, and exported food turned an island of eight and a half million into a place of one million dead and two million emigrants.

subject: Great Fingall Mine office
summary: An elegant Italianate stone office, built to run a goldfield empire, now stands alone at the lip of an open pit - the last building of a town that no longer exists.

subject: Great Flood (China)
summary: The foundational myth of Chinese civilization, in which the hero Yu the Great tamed a catastrophic flood that may have been real, founding the Xia dynasty and establishing the principle that rulers earn their mandate by mastering nature.

subject: Great Glen Fault
summary: A 400-million-year-old crack across Scotland that holds Loch Ness, ran under the Atlantic, and now lives on as the Cabot Fault in Newfoundland.

subject: Great Highway
summary: The 3.5-mile road along San Francisco's Pacific edge, running from the Cliff House to Lake Merced, where the city ends and the ocean begins.

subject: Great Indian Bustard Sanctuary
summary: A drought-prone stretch of Deccan grassland near Solapur is one of the last refuges for the critically endangered great Indian bustard, a bird whose survival depends on keeping the landscape open and wild.

subject: Great Lakes Aquarium
