subject: Helltown, Ohio
summary: The abandoned Ohio village where the government bought up every house and left them to decay - spawning legends of Satanic churches, mutants from chemical spills, and a slaughterhouse road that grows longer as you drive.

subject: Helmand Province
summary: Afghanistan's largest province by area, where a Bronze Age civilization, Zoroastrian scripture, Ahmad Shah Durrani's tribal land grants, and twenty years of NATO combat all converge along the valley of the Helmand River.

subject: Helmond
summary: An East Brabant city built around a moated castle, the Zuid-Willemsvaart canal, and centuries of weaving - now best known for one of Europe's most coherent New Urbanist neighbourhoods.

subject: Helmsdale
summary: A Sutherland fishing village built to absorb the Highland Clearances, watching its emigrants depart from a stone monument by the harbour.

subject: Helsby
summary: Look at Helsby Hill from the right angle and a man's face stares back. The 'Old Man of Helsby' has weathered the same sandstone cliff since the Vikings named the village beneath it 'the place on the edge.'

subject: Helsinki
summary: A city founded in spite, made capital by accident, and turned by the twentieth century into one of the world's most quietly confident urban experiments.

subject: Helston
summary: Every May 8th, the most southerly town in mainland Britain dances itself through its own streets in one of the oldest surviving folk traditions in the country.

subject: Helvellyn
summary: The Lake District's most-climbed mountain, England's third-highest, where a young artist's death and his dog's three-month vigil made the peak famous in 1805 - and where a biplane somehow landed and took off again in 1926.

subject: Helvetia, West Virginia
summary: Thirty-eight residents, one apple butter tradition, one Swiss cheese recipe, and a winter Fasnacht parade keep this 1869 settlement going in a back hollow of Randolph County.

subject: Hemavan
summary: A village of a couple of hundred people that serves as the southern terminus of Sweden's 467-kilometre King's Trail and, with Tärnaby, its biggest downhill skiing centre.

subject: Hemel Hempstead
summary: A medieval market town reborn as one of Britain's first post-war New Towns, marked forever by the largest peacetime explosion in European history.

subject: Hemerdon Mine
summary: The fourth-largest tungsten deposit in the world sits in a Devon hillside, opened twice for war and closed three times for economics.

subject: Henbury Meteorites Conservation Reserve
summary: Roughly 4,200 years ago a meteor broke apart over the Australian outback, punching 13 to 14 craters into the desert floor -- craters the local Aboriginal people remembered as the work of a fire-devil from the Sun.

subject: Hendersonville, North Carolina
summary: An apple-growing Blue Ridge town with a marble angel that inspired Thomas Wolfe, a Sierra Nevada brewery, and an unhurried Main Street.

subject: Hendon, Sunderland
summary: Sunderland's East End - shipbuilding's birthplace, the football club's birthplace, and the site of Britain's worst stampede.

subject: Hengchun
summary: Taiwan's southernmost town has kept its ancient walls standing for nearly 150 years — and true to the name a Qing viceroy gave it in 1875, it stays green and warm all year long.

subject: Hengelo
summary: The Dutch metaalstad - metal city - where Stork built locomotives and a garden village, where Allied bombs flattened the old center, and where postwar Dutch planning rebuilt one of the country's most studied modern cities.

subject: Henichesk
summary: A small Azov port whose very name means narrow, guarding the strait where the open sea slips into a maze of salt lagoons.

subject: Henry County, Virginia
summary: A Virginia county named for the firebrand orator Patrick Henry, who lived here, and home today to NASCAR's shortest oval, a fossil-filled state museum, and an unusual jurisdictional puzzle.

story.title: Henry Morgan's Raid on Porto Bello

subject: Henry Morgan's raid on Porto Bello
summary: In July 1668, Welsh privateer Henry Morgan led 470 men against one of Spain's most fortified Caribbean ports, capturing three castles, extracting a 100,000-peso ransom, and returning to Jamaica with plunder worth more than the island's entire annual agricultural output.

subject: Henry Nicholas Greenwell
summary: A fourth son from County Durham with no inheritance, Henry Nicholas Greenwell crossed four continents before landing injured on Hawaii's Kona Coast, where he built a coffee empire that still shapes the landscape today.

subject: Henry Perrine Baldwin
summary: A one-armed missionary's son who built a 17-mile irrigation ditch across Maui's canyons, co-founded one of Hawaii's Big Five corporations, and transformed the island's dry central plains into one of the world's great sugarcane empires.

subject: Henry Street Settlement
summary: A pioneering social service agency born from one nurse's encounter with poverty on the Lower East Side, still operating from its original 1830s row houses after more than 130 years.

subject: Heraea (Arcadia)
summary: The chief city of western Arcadia in antiquity, positioned on the Alpheios river where roads from Olympia, Megalopolis, and Messene converged — now a scatter of ruins on a fertile hillside.

subject: Heraion of Argos
summary: The great sanctuary of Hera in the Argolid — older than the Parthenon by centuries, positioned between Mycenae and Midea, and once the religious center of an entire civilization's plain.

subject: Heraklion
summary: Crete's capital has been called Chandax, Candia, Megalo Kastro, and Kandiye - a city whose names track every empire that ever wanted it.

subject: Herat
summary: Called the 'Diamond of Asia,' Herat has been destroyed and rebuilt so many times across its 2,500-year history that resilience itself became the city's defining trait.

subject: Herborn Academy
summary: For two and a half centuries, a small Calvinist school in a Hessian timber-frame town quietly trained the minds that built modern education, Reformed theology, and a printing press that shaped the German Bible.

subject: Herborn, Hesse
summary: A bear-marked town of timber-framed houses on the Dill river, Herborn earned the nickname Nassauisches Rothenburg through centuries of fire, war, scholarship, and quiet survival.

subject: Herculaneum
summary: Where the same eruption that buried Pompeii preserved a smaller Roman town even more perfectly - including charred scrolls that scientists are still learning to read.

subject: Hereford
summary: A small, walkable cathedral city on the bend of the River Wye where the Mappa Mundi lives, the SAS trains, and the cider is taken seriously.

subject: Hereford
summary: A small cathedral city on the Wye that has been a Mercian capital, an SAS regimental town, the home of the Hereford cow, and the unofficial capital of English cider.

subject: Hereke
summary: A small coastal town on the Gulf of İzmit whose imperial weaving factory, founded in 1843, gave the world a category of carpet — and whose name is now synonymous with the finest Turkish textile tradition.

subject: Heriot Row
summary: A Second New Town terrace built from 1802 onward, virtually unchanged in 200 years, where Robert Louis Stevenson grew up looking at a small pond and wrote Treasure Island - the most distinguished single street in Edinburgh, and perhaps Scotland.

story.title: Heritage Exhibition of a Traditional Pawnshop Business

subject: Heritage Exhibition of a Traditional Pawnshop Business
summary: A 1917 pawnshop in Macau's Sé district — where families once surrendered belongings to survive — has been preserved as a museum documenting the human economy of last resort.

subject: Herm
summary: A mile-and-a-half-long island east of Guernsey with no cars, sixty-five residents, and a hereditary herd of escaped wallabies that a Prussian prince once decided it needed.

subject: Hermanus
summary: A seaside town on Walker Bay where southern right whales come so close to shore that the town employs a whale crier -- a man who roams the streets blowing a kelp horn to announce sightings.

story.title: Hermione: The City at the Edge of the World

subject: Hermione
summary: On a small Argolic peninsula overlooking the sea toward Hydra, the ancient city of Hermione accumulated three thousand years of history — Homer named it, the Dryopes built it, the Argives took it, and modern archaeologists are only now beginning to read what it left behind.

subject: Heroon at Nemea
summary: A sacred mound beside the Nemea river where ancient Greeks mourned a murdered infant, founded games in his honor, and, centuries later, left lead tablets inscribed with curses against their rivals in love.

subject: Herrnhut
summary: A village of religious refugees in Upper Lusatia that kept a prayer going around the clock for a hundred years, sent missionaries to four continents, and joined the World Heritage list in 2024.

subject: Hertfordshire
summary: An East of England home county where deer cross old fords, Roman ruins sit under medieval streets, and the world's first garden city sits twelve miles from the world's first New Town.

subject: Hertogin Hedwigepolder
summary: A 295-hectare polder reclaimed from the sea in 1907, given deliberately back to the tides in 2022 - the Netherlands' most controversial de-poldering.

subject: Hervanta
summary: A whole town was drawn on paper in 1967, built in a forest ten kilometres from Tampere, spent thirty years as Finland's byword for a concrete suburb - and then won.

subject: Herzogin Cecilie
summary: A four-masted German grain windjammer ran onto Devon rocks in fog in 1936 and never sailed again - one of the last great square-riggers, beached at Salcombe.

subject: Heshigten Global Geopark
summary: Eight landscapes crammed into one UNESCO Geopark -- stone forests, glacial potholes, volcanic plugs, hot springs, and a canyon carved through the homeland of the Khitan people.

subject: Hesquiaht First Nation
summary: A Nuu-chah-nulth community of about 100 people at Hot Springs Cove on Vancouver Island's remote west coast, governed by a hereditary system where four chiefs sit hierarchically like the four fingers of a hand.

subject: Hessel
summary: Six centuries of owners, one catastrophic fire, oak felled in 1600, and a parlour that has not been redecorated since the year Napoleon crossed the Alps.

subject: Heswall
summary: An affluent Wirral town that grew when railways let Liverpool's merchants commute from the Dee shore, Heswall sits on a high ridge looking across the estuary to Wales, with John Peel, Ian Botham, and the McCartneys among its former residents.

subject: Hewitt Avenue Trestle
summary: A causeway that has terrified commuters and confounded engineers for nearly a century, the Hewitt Avenue Trestle carries U.S. Route 2 across the Snohomish River floodplain between Everett and Lake Stevens.

subject: Hewlett-Packard
summary: A coin flip in a Palo Alto garage in 1939 decided whose name came first, launching a company that would define Silicon Valley itself.

subject: Hexham
summary: A Tyne Valley market town so often raided, burned and contested that locals once used its name as a euphemism for Hell.

subject: Heybeliada
summary: The second largest of Istanbul's Princes' Islands, Heybeliada carries centuries of Greek, Ottoman, and republican history in a compact two and a half square miles — from a naval academy founded in 1773 to a seminary that still waits to reopen.

subject: Heysham
summary: A coastal village of rock-cut graves, Viking hogbacks, an ancient labyrinth, and two nuclear reactors — Heysham layers thirteen centuries on a single Lancashire headland.

subject: Heysham Port
summary: Built by the Midland Railway in 1904 to challenge Liverpool and Fleetwood, Heysham Port still runs the only mainland passenger service to the Isle of Man.

subject: Heyuan
summary: A city in northern Guangdong where Hakka culture, ancient dynasties, and one of China's richest concentrations of dinosaur fossils converge along the banks of the Dong River.

subject: Heʻeia Fishpond
summary: An 88-acre walled fishpond on Oahu's windward coast, built between the 1200s and 1400s using mortarless stonework, and the only Hawaiian fishpond fully encircled by a wall.

subject: Hibbing, Minnesota
summary: The town that picked up and moved two miles south when miners discovered iron ore beneath its streets -- birthplace of Greyhound bus lines, childhood home of Bob Dylan, and gateway to the world's largest open-pit iron mine.

subject: Hickman Crater
summary: A geologist spotted this near-perfect meteorite scar on his computer screen in 2007, hiding in plain sight for 50,000 years in the iron country north of Newman.

subject: Hickory Ground
summary: The last capital of the Creek Nation before removal, Hickory Ground is a 33-acre archaeological site near Wetumpka, Alabama, where 10,000 years of human history collide with a modern fight over sacred land.

subject: Hickory, North Carolina
summary: A Catawba Valley city of 44,000 that built a hospital in 54 hours during the 1944 polio epidemic and now houses Apple and Google data centers in former furniture country.

subject: Hida Mountains
summary: When an English geologist first called these peaks the 'Japanese Alps,' he meant only the Hida range -- the original and grandest of the three mountain chains that would eventually share the name.

subject: Hierakonpolis
summary: The City of the Falcon - one of Egypt's oldest cities, where the Narmer Palette, the oldest painted tomb, and the world's first zoo reveal how a civilization was born.

subject: Hierve el Agua
summary: Petrified waterfalls in Oaxaca's highlands where mineral-laden springs have spent millennia painting white cascades down valley cliffs -- frozen rivers of calcium carbonate that fooled early travelers into believing the water was boiling.

subject: High Hills of Santee
summary: A twenty-five-mile ridge of sandy uplands where wealthy planters built summer retreats to escape Lowcountry malaria, leaving a landscape of plantations, graveyards, and a future First Lady's birthplace.

subject: High Junk Peak
summary: At 344 metres, High Junk Peak is not Hong Kong's tallest mountain — but its near-vertical summit cone earns it a place among the city's three legendary sharp peaks, with views that stretch from Lobster Bay to Kowloon.

subject: High Point, North Carolina
summary: The Furniture Capital of the World - 12 million square feet of showroom, twice a year filled with the people who decide what America's living rooms will look like.

subject: High Road to Taos
summary: A winding scenic byway threads through centuries-old Spanish land grant villages, Pueblo communities, and mountain forests on its climb from Santa Fe to Taos.

subject: Highgate
summary: North London's hilltop village — where Samuel Taylor Coleridge recovered from opium addiction, Karl Marx is buried, and the first cable car in Europe once hauled passengers up the steepest street in London.

subject: Highland County, Virginia
summary: Virginia's least populous county - 2,232 people scattered across mountain valleys called Bluegrass, Monterey, Bullpasture, and Cowpasture, with one annual maple festival that brings in 60,000 visitors.

subject: Highland Papua
summary: Indonesia's only landlocked province - founded in 2022, peopled for millennia, and reachable mostly by air.

subject: Highlands (Papua New Guinea)
summary: A plateau of over two million people, five provinces, hundreds of languages, and the only UNESCO World Heritage Site in Papua New Guinea - a region the outside world did not know existed until 1933.

subject: Highlands Highway
summary: The Highlands Highway is Papua New Guinea's main road - a single two-lane ribbon that climbs from the coast at Lae to the 2,478-metre Daulo Pass and on to the gold mines of Porgera, feared as often as it is used.

subject: Hijr Ismail
summary: A semi-circular white marble wall beside the Kaaba - low enough to step over, hallowed enough that no pilgrim may enter. The reason why is a story about money, humility, and a Roman shipwreck.

subject: Hilden
summary: An ordinary Rhineland industrial town with an extraordinary native son — the man who invented modern scientific surgery.

subject: Hilina Slump
summary: The south flank of Kilauea is sliding into the Pacific at 10 centimeters per year, a slow-motion landslide that has triggered tsunamis, killed dozens, and fueled debate about whether Hawaii could one day generate a megatsunami.

subject: Hill Cumorah
summary: The New York drumlin where Joseph Smith claimed to find the golden plates that became the Book of Mormon - site of annual pageants with cast of 700 until 2019, now a quiet pilgrimage destination for Latter-day Saints.

subject: Hillbilly Hot Dogs
summary: A roadside hot dog stand in Lesage, West Virginia that turned a 15-inch deep-fried Homewrecker into national fame - and a Fallout 76 cameo.

subject: Hillegersberg
summary: The leafy lake-side village in Rotterdam's north that the German bombers missed in 1940 - leaving intact a thousand-year-old church, the dungeon of a destroyed castle, and a legend about a giant.

subject: Hilliers, British Columbia
summary: A quiet crossroads on Vancouver Island that hosted a fall fair, a wetland worth saving, and one of the province's strangest six-year experiments in communal living.

subject: Hillside Club
summary: A Berkeley neighborhood social club born from the Arts and Crafts movement in 1898, whose campaign to protect the hills from ugly development created an entire architectural tradition -- and whose clubhouse has been built, burned, and rebuilt.

subject: Hilversum
summary: A town that was never granted city rights, built its identity in 1918 around a radio factory, became the broadcasting capital of the Netherlands, and was given its modern face by an architect named Dudok who built schools and a town hall like sculpture.

subject: Himmelbjerget
summary: Denmark spent decades convinced this 147-metre hill was its highest point, found out in 1847 that it wasn't, and went on loving it anyway.

subject: Himmerland
summary: A Jutland peninsula that may be named after the tribe that terrified Rome, and that gave Danish literature its most famous fictional parish.

subject: Hindenburgdamm
summary: An eleven-kilometre causeway across the Wadden Sea with rails and no road — which is why every car going to Sylt has to ride a train.

subject: Hindustan Shipyard
summary: India's second-largest shipyard, born from one industrialist's determination to build ships on Indian soil, launched the country's first post-independence vessel in 1948.

subject: Hinemoa
summary: A sacred virgin of the Te Arawa people who strapped calabash gourds to her body and swam 3.2 km across Lake Rotorua in darkness to reach the man she loved on Mokoia Island -- a story so enduring it inspired New Zealand's first feature film.

subject: Hingol mud volcanoes
summary: A complex of bubbling mud volcanoes in Balochistan where geological forces and Hindu devotion intersect -- pilgrims confess sins at the rim of 300-foot cones of warm mud, reading the earth's bubbling response as divine judgment.

subject: Hinoki Village
summary: Twenty-eight Japanese-era cypress-wood dormitories, restored and reopened as a living cultural village in the heart of Chiayi City, where the scent of old hinoki still drifts through the corridors.

story.title: Hinokuma-dera: The Temple Built by Immigrants

subject: Hinokuma-dera
summary: The ruins of a seventh-century Buddhist temple in the village of Asuka reveal how Korean immigrants shaped the birth of Japanese architecture -- and how a building's unusual layout can rewrite history.

subject: Hippo Regius
summary: An ancient port city in Algeria where Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Byzantines all left their mark -- and where Saint Augustine spent his final decades shaping Western thought.

subject: Hiraab Imamate
summary: A Somali kingdom that overthrew the Ajuran Sultanate, repelled European warships, and governed Mogadishu and its hinterlands for three centuries before colonial partition carved it apart.

subject: Hiraizumi
summary: A tiny Tohoku town that once rivaled Kyoto in splendor, Hiraizumi preserves the remnants of a golden Buddhist civilization and the ghosts of warrior dreams that moved Japan's greatest poet to tears.

subject: Hirtshals
summary: A harbour was built where there was no bay, a town was designed on paper to go with it, and the North Sea now runs through a four-and-a-half-million-litre tank in the middle of it.

subject: Historic Areas of Istanbul
summary: Four UNESCO-protected zones on Istanbul's historic peninsula hold 1,500 years of imperial ambition in stone, tile, and dome.

subject: Historic Buildings in Ramsgate
summary: A town where Augustus Pugin built his ideal community, the Royal Harbour was carved by hand, and a tomb copies one in Bethlehem.

story.title: Historic Center of Caxias do Sul

subject: Historic Center of Caxias do Sul
summary: Around Dante Alighieri Square, the old core of Caxias do Sul still holds the grid laid for Italian colonists in 1879 - and the scars of a century that nearly forgot them.

subject: Historic Centre of Lima
summary: The grid Francisco Pizarro scratched into the Rímac Valley in 1535 became the political and religious capital of Spanish South America, and today its concentration of colonial churches, convents, and palaces makes it one of the most intact viceregal city centers on the continent.

subject: Historic Centre of Macau
summary: More than twenty sites across the Macau Peninsula preserve the longest continuous East-West encounter in history — a UNESCO World Heritage collection where Chinese temples and Portuguese churches share the same streets.

subject: Historic Centre of Odesa
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage city built by Catherine the Great as a warm-water port, whose grand nineteenth-century streets now carry both the glory of a cosmopolitan boom and the scars of war.

story.title: Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments

subject: Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments
summary: A city built on swampland by imperial decree, inscribed by UNESCO across 126 separate sites that together form one of Europe's most ambitious urban experiments.

story.title: Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca

subject: Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca
summary: Two UNESCO World Heritage cities on the Strait of Malacca preserve five centuries of cultural collision between Malay, Chinese, Indian, Portuguese, Dutch, and British worlds.

subject: Historic Downtown San Salvador
summary: The Spaniards called it the Valley of the Hammocks for its ceaseless earthquakes, and after nearly five centuries, the historic center of San Salvador keeps rebuilding itself around the same colonial grid.

story.title: Historic Monuments and Sites of Hiraizumi

subject: Historic Monuments and Sites of Hiraizumi
summary: Five linked sites in a quiet Tohoku valley form one of Japan's most extraordinary UNESCO World Heritage designations -- a twelfth-century attempt to build the Buddhist paradise on earth.

story.title: Historic Monuments of Novgorod and Surroundings

subject: Historic Monuments of Novgorod and Surroundings
summary: Medieval Russia's only republic, where citizens gathered in the public square to elect princes - and where the Mongols never came.

subject: Historic Tennis Club
summary: Palm Springs' oldest neighborhood began with a father's desperate gamble — bringing his tubercular son to the desert for clean air in 1884 — and grew into a district where Albert Einstein once rested, and where the city's oldest surviving hotel still operates.

story.title: Historic Villages of Shirakawa-go and Gokayama

subject: Historic Villages of Shirakawa-gō and Gokayama
summary: Three mountain villages in central Japan where centuries-old thatched farmhouses survive as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, their steep prayer-hand roofs engineered to shed four meters of winter snow.

story.title: Historical Archive of the City of Cologne

subject: Historical Archive of the City of Cologne
summary: At 1:58 on a Tuesday afternoon, a thousand years of Cologne's memory fell into a hole. Two neighbors died. The recovery will take generations.

subject: Historical capitals of China
summary: Beijing is only the latest in a chain of Chinese capitals stretching back over three thousand years -- a list that includes Xi'an, Luoyang, Nanjing, Kaifeng, and Hangzhou, each one a mirror of the dynasty that chose it.

subject: History of Ecuador (1830-1860)
summary: Thirty years of coups, exile, and treachery that forged a republic from the wreckage of Gran Colombia.

subject: History of El Paso, Texas
summary: From Franciscan friars founding missions along the Rio Grande to the railroads transforming a frontier crossing into Texas's westernmost city, El Paso's history spans empires, revolutions, and the complex interweaving of American and Mexican destinies.

story.title: History of New Italy, New South Wales

subject: History of New Italy, New South Wales
summary: Swindled into a phantom Pacific paradise and left destitute, a band of Venetian families was resettled on poor scrub here - and against every odds built a thriving community of silk and wine.

subject: History of Seattle
summary: A city defined by cycles of boom and bust, Seattle rose from a muddy logging camp on Elliott Bay to become the Pacific Northwest's dominant metropolis through gold rushes, great fires, wartime industry, and tech revolutions.

story.title: History of the Isle of Man TT Races 1920–1929

subject: History of the Isle of Man TT Races 1920–1929
summary: The decade after the Great War transformed the Isle of Man TT from a daring road race into a modern motorsport, complete with named corners, scandals, fatalities, and the first 70 mph lap.

story.title: History of the Jews in Arta

subject: History of the Jews in Arta
summary: For nearly a thousand years, Romaniote Jewish families built a community in Arta — scholars, weavers, cantors, merchants — until German forces deported almost the entire population to Auschwitz in 1944.

story.title: History of the Jews in Guernsey

subject: History of the Jews in Guernsey
summary: Three Jewish women were registered, deported, and murdered at Auschwitz with the cooperation of the Channel Islands authorities. Their names are Therese Steiner, Marianne Grunfeld, and Auguste Spitz.

story.title: History of the Nuclear Program of Iran

subject: History of the nuclear program of Iran
summary: From an American-supplied research reactor in 1967 to underground centrifuge halls and international crisis, Iran's nuclear program has shaped global diplomacy for more than half a century.

subject: Hitis
summary: A Swedish-speaking Finnish archipelago of more than two thousand islands, built around a sheltered strait that has been an anchorage since the Viking age and a municipality that lasted just 108 years.

story.title: Hiyoshi Taisha: The Mountain God's Shrine at the Foot of Hiei

subject: Hiyoshi Taisha
summary: Guarding the spiritually vulnerable northeast of the ancient capital, Hiyoshi Taisha has stood at the base of Mount Hiei for over two millennia -- its distinctive Sanno torii now the symbol of nearly 3,800 shrines across Japan.

subject: Hjortspring Boat
summary: The oldest plank-built boat ever found in Scandinavia, sunk in a bog on Als around 350 BC with the drowned weapons of a defeated army heaped around it.

subject: Hjørring
summary: Vendsyssel's oldest market town has three medieval churches, a coin bearing its Latin name, and no settled explanation of what that name means.

subject: Hluhluwe
summary: A small town wedged between two of South Africa's wildest reserves, where the road to the saved white rhino runs through pineapple fields and thornveld.

subject: Hlukhiv
summary: For half a century this small town on the Esman River was the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate, a Baroque city of hetmans, composers, and a triumphal arch that still stands.

subject: Hoba meteorite
summary: Sixty tonnes of iron and nickel sit in the exact spot where they landed less than 80,000 years ago on a Namibian farm, making the Hoba meteorite the largest known meteorite on Earth -- and a gift, as the Khoekhoegowab name suggests.

subject: Hobart
summary: Australia's second-oldest city guards the edge of the world, where Antarctic expeditions once departed and the Southern Lights still dance above a harbour ringed by colonial warehouses and crowned by snow-dusted Mount Wellington.

subject: Hobbiton Movie Set
summary: Where a New Zealand sheep farm became Middle-earth's most beloved village, and the temporary film set that rain saved from demolition became a permanent pilgrimage for Tolkien fans worldwide.

subject: Hobcaw Barony
summary: A 16,000-acre peninsula estate in Georgetown County, South Carolina, that evolved from an 18th-century royal land grant to a dozen rice plantations, then became Wall Street financier Bernard Baruch's hunting retreat before his daughter Belle preserved it as a research reserve.

subject: Hobet Coal Mine
summary: For four decades, draglines flattened mountains here for five million tons of coal a year - and then the bottom fell out of an entire industry.

story.title: Hoboken: Where Baseball Began and Sinatra Was Born

subject: Hoboken
summary: The square-mile New Jersey city across the Hudson from Manhattan where the first organized baseball game was played in 1846, where Frank Sinatra grew up, and where 'On the Waterfront' was filmed among the longshoremen.

subject: Hochelaga
summary: Somewhere beneath modern Montreal lies Hochelaga, a thriving St. Lawrence Iroquois village of 3,000 people that Jacques Cartier visited in 1535 -- and that had vanished without explanation by the time he returned six years later.

story.title: Hochschule für Musik und Tanz Köln

subject: Hochschule für Musik und Tanz Köln
summary: Karlheinz Stockhausen learned to bend electronic sound here, and so did the jazz students Kurt Edelhagen brought in when no other German conservatory would teach it.

subject: Hoedjiespunt
summary: A fossilized hyena lair on a peninsula near Saldanha Bay yielded the teeth and bones of a young Homo heidelbergensis individual who lived roughly 280,000 years ago.

subject: Hoendiep
summary: A canal whose name probably means 'muddy water' carried a quarter of Groningen's sugar beet barges in 1898, then quietly retired when a wider rival opened upriver.

subject: Hof te Dieren
summary: The favourite hunting lodge of King-Stadtholder William III on the wooded edge of the Veluwe, lost to fire in the war's last winter and remembered now as a shallow depression in a public park.

subject: Hof van Cleve
summary: For nearly two decades, the only three-Michelin-star restaurant in Belgium sat in a converted farmhouse in a village of 8,000 people, an hour from anywhere - until Peter Goossens decided that was the problem.

subject: Hofje Codde en Van Beresteijn
summary: A Haarlem almshouse founded in 1598 for poor Catholic women, made wealthy in 1882 by the sale of a Frans Hals portrait, and still housing devout Catholic women over sixty rent-free today.

subject: Hofvijver
summary: A rectangle of dark water in the middle of The Hague that began as a dune lake, ended up as a city's mirror, and is now patrolled by an underwater gate to keep swimmers away from the prime minister.

subject: Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation
summary: A Georgia rice plantation that cycled through three distinct lives -- forced-labor rice empire, modest dairy farm, and state historic site -- tracing the full arc of the antebellum South's rise, collapse, and uneasy reckoning along the Altamaha River.

subject: Hog Hammock, Georgia
summary: The last intact Gullah-Geechee community in the United States clings to its patch of Sapelo Island with fewer than fifty residents, two churches older than most American cities, and a centuries-long fight to keep land their ancestors were forced to work as enslaved people.

subject: Hogan's Alley, Vancouver
summary: For six decades an alley off Union Street held Vancouver's only concentrated Black neighbourhood, until a freeway that was never finished took it down anyway.

subject: Hogeland
summary: In a country where two meters above sea level counts as a highland, the Hogeland is exactly that - clay-built ground reclaimed from the Wadden Sea, dotted with mound villages and crossed by some of the oldest sea dikes in Europe.

subject: Hogganvik runestone
summary: A fifth-century runestone bearing one of Norway's oldest known inscriptions lay face-down in a garden in Mandal for over 1,500 years before a resident turned it over in 2009.

subject: Hoggar Mountains
summary: A volcanic island of rock and cold air in the middle of the Sahara, the Hoggar holds Algeria's highest peak, a famous sunrise plateau, and a refuge for creatures the desert nearly erased.

subject: Hohaiyan Rock Festival
summary: For two decades, Fulong Beach rang every July with the sound the indigenous Taiwanese gave a name to: ho-hai-yan — the melody of waves, now the anthem of Taiwan's beloved summer rock festival.

subject: Hoi An
summary: Where Vietnam's ancient trading port preserves lantern-lit streets and tailors who sew silk suits overnight, where the Thu Bon River meets the South China Sea.

subject: Hoi Ha
summary: A Hakka village tucked at the innermost shore of Hoi Ha Wan, where two 19th-century lime kilns still stand as quiet proof that coral and shells once fuelled an entire industry.

story.title: Hokenoyama Kofun: The Tomb That May Belong to Himiko's Age

subject: Hokenoyama Kofun
summary: A scallop-shaped burial mound from around 250 AD in the Makimuku Kofun Cluster yielded bronze mirrors depicting divine beasts, a vermillion-painted cedar coffin, and artifacts that place it squarely in the era of Japan's most mysterious queen.

subject: Hokitika
summary: A West Coast town that was briefly New Zealand's busiest port during the 1860s gold rush - now a quiet gateway to glaciers, gorges, and greenstone, with a crooked main street that still follows the sand dunes.

subject: Holborn Tube Station
summary: Beneath the junction of High Holborn and Kingsway, a station with ghost platforms that once stored the Elgin Marbles during the Blitz, and where a Nobel Prize-winning physicist once planned to build a particle detector underground.

subject: Holetown
summary: The first English settlement in Barbados, Holetown began as a windswept landing site named for a stream called 'The Hole' and became the birthplace of a colonial society that would shape the Caribbean for centuries.

subject: Holkham
summary: A tiny Norfolk village dominated by a Palladian estate, an agricultural revolution, and a beach so wide it stages films from Shakespeare in Love to The Eagle Has Landed.

subject: Hollandia (1742 ship)
summary: A brand-new Dutch East India ship sailed for Batavia on her maiden voyage in July 1743 and struck Gunner Rock off Annet ten days later, taking 306 lives - including thirty passengers who never reached the East.

story.title: Hollandse Kust West Offshore Wind Farm

subject: Hollandse Kust West Offshore Wind Farm
summary: The Dutch wind zone fifty-three kilometers offshore where green hydrogen ambitions meet ecology-first turbine design - and where you can no longer see land.

subject: Hollow Tree
summary: A dead western red cedar in Stanley Park, big enough inside to hold an elephant, kept upright by a steel frame and the stubbornness of the people who refused to let the city take it down.

subject: Hollyford Track
summary: A 56 km track through Fiordland that traces a river valley from the mountains to a wild Tasman Sea coast - one of the few major Fiordland trails that stays low, stays flat, and stays open year-round.

story.title: Hollywood Boulevard Commercial and Entertainment District

subject: Hollywood Boulevard Commercial and Entertainment District
summary: Twelve blocks of Art Deco theaters, Spanish Revival hotels, and movie palaces that defined Hollywood's golden age and still host film premieres today.

subject: Hollywood Freeway chickens
summary: A colony of feral chickens has thrived under a Los Angeles freeway off-ramp since around 1970, defying multiple relocation efforts and inspiring a Terry Pratchett short story.

subject: Hollywood Walk of Fame
summary: More than 2,800 coral-pink terrazzo stars line fifteen blocks of Hollywood Boulevard, honoring entertainers from Mickey Mouse to Muhammad Ali in one of the world's most-visited monuments.

subject: Hollywood's Favorite Gold Rush Town
summary: A Mother Lode mining settlement turned railroad town where the most filmed steam locomotive in history still runs, and where Marty McFly once outran a speeding train.

subject: Holmes's Bonfire
summary: In two days of August 1666, an English raid destroyed 130 Dutch merchant ships in the Vlie estuary and burned the pacifist Mennonite town of West-Terschelling to the ground — an act of war the Dutch would not forget, and one year later, would answer.

subject: Holstebro
summary: A west Jutland market town decided in the mid-1960s to buy its way into cultural significance — starting with a Giacometti in the square — and largely got what it paid for.

subject: Holsworthy
summary: A Devon market town where one secret woman is named the Pretty Maid every July and a 1614 charter is still proclaimed in the street.

subject: Holtville, California
summary: The Carrot Capital of the World — a small Imperial Valley city with Swiss-German roots, a linguist who decoded an Amazonian language, and a cameo in a Bugs Bunny cartoon.

subject: Holy Blood of Wilsnack
summary: A knight burned a village to spite his bishop in 1383 and accidentally created one of medieval Europe's great pilgrimage destinations — three scorched communion wafers that drew crowds for 170 years until a local pastor burned them himself.

subject: Holy Infant of Atocha
summary: A medieval devotion born from prisoners' desperation in Moorish Spain that crossed the Atlantic to become the protector of Mexican miners and one of the most beloved folk-Catholic images in the Americas.

subject: Holy Week in Popayan
summary: Every year for more than four centuries, the White City of Colombia carries its saints through cobblestone streets on the shoulders of men.

subject: Holyhead
summary: The largest town on Anglesey, built around a three-walled Roman fort that became St Cybi's churchyard, and grown rich on three centuries of being the place where Britain reaches for Dublin.

subject: Holyhead Breakwater
summary: Britain's longest breakwater, 1.7 miles of Holyhead Mountain quartzite hand-placed over twenty-eight years by Victorian divers in submarine bells, blasting foundations with gunpowder sealed in tin pipes.

subject: Holyhead Lifeboat Station
summary: Nearly two hundred years of rescues on one of the most dangerous stretches of the Irish Sea, with three Gold Medals, dozens of Silver and Bronze, and a Manchester industrialist's inheritance paying for the boats.

subject: Holywell
summary: The Lourdes of Wales - a market town built around a spring that has welcomed pilgrims continuously since the seventh century.

subject: Hombori
summary: An ancient stone-built town in central Mali, set beneath the country's highest peak amid desert towers that recall Monument Valley.

subject: Hombourg, Belgium
summary: A trilingual Walloon village where a procession mishap split the parish for a century — and where the first shot of World War I in Belgium echoed through a railway tunnel.

subject: Homeboy Industries
summary: Founded in 1992 by Father Greg Boyle, Homeboy Industries is the largest gang intervention and rehabilitation program in the world, offering employment, training, and tattoo removal to formerly incarcerated men and women in East Los Angeles.

subject: Homestake Mine (South Dakota)
summary: From ruthless gold baron to Nobel Prize physics, this mile-and-a-half deep hole in South Dakota has witnessed both frontier violence and humanity's quest to understand the universe.

subject: Honeymoon Uranium Mine
summary: A uranium mine with no pit and no headframe, where the ore is dissolved underground and pumped to the surface - twice abandoned, and in 2024 brought back to life in the South Australian desert.

subject: Hong Kong
summary: The Fragrant Harbor - where opium wars gave Britain a trading post, where 156 years of colonial rule ended at midnight on July 1, 1997, and where seven million people squeeze into one of the world's most vertical cities.

subject: Hong Kong / Central
summary: Central is where Hong Kong's financial ambition and colonial history meet the harbor — a district of glass towers, Victorian lanes, hilltop neighborhoods, and the world's longest escalator system.

subject: Hong Kong 12
summary: In August 2020, twelve young Hong Kongers were intercepted at sea while attempting to flee to Taiwan, then held for months in a mainland Chinese detention facility — setting off an international legal and diplomatic crisis.

subject: Hong Kong Arts Centre
summary: Built on reclaimed land after years of advocacy by local arts groups, the Hong Kong Arts Centre became the city's first independent home for contemporary art — and remains the institution that dares to set the terms of cultural discourse.

subject: Hong Kong Cultural Centre
summary: A landmark performing arts complex on the Kowloon waterfront, housing Asia's largest pipe organ and the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra beneath its distinctive tilted roof.

subject: Hong Kong Disneyland
summary: Built on reclaimed land in Penny's Bay after SARS devastated Hong Kong's economy, this Disneyland adapted ancient principles of feng shui — including a bend in its entrance walkway — to welcome Chinese visitors while growing into a globally ranked theme park.

subject: Hong Kong Eastern District
summary: The eastern shore of Hong Kong Island runs from the notorious nightlife of Wan Chai through the shopping frenzy of Causeway Bay and out to quieter neighbourhoods where wet markets, historic cemeteries, and the world's most sought-after egg rolls share the same tram line.

subject: Hong Kong Express Rail Link
summary: The underground high-speed rail corridor linking Hong Kong to mainland China cut travel time to Guangzhou roughly in half — and came with a legal anomaly: the passenger compartments are officially Chinese territory, even while the train is still in Hong Kong.

subject: Hong Kong Federation of Students
summary: Founded in 1958 by four university student unions, the Hong Kong Federation of Students became the city's most visible student voice — marching over island disputes, boycotting classes during Tiananmen, and leading street occupations during the 2014 Umbrella Movement before losing most of its membership.

subject: Hong Kong Film Archive
summary: A five-storey vault in Sai Wan Ho where the fragile celluloid memory of an entire cinematic culture is kept alive, screened, and shared.

subject: Hong Kong Golf Club
summary: Founded in 1889 by thirteen enthusiasts who barely knew the game, the Hong Kong Golf Club at Fanling has survived two world wars, a Japanese occupation, and a protracted battle over public housing to become one of Asia's most storied private clubs—and an unlikely ecological refuge.

subject: Hong Kong Observation Wheel
summary: A 60-metre Ferris wheel on reclaimed land at the Central Harbourfront, the Hong Kong Observation Wheel survived a near-demolition, attracted a million riders in seven months, and was later destroyed — onscreen at least — by Godzilla.

subject: Hong Kong Tramways
summary: Since 1904, Hong Kong's double-decker trams have threaded the northern shore of Hong Kong Island for HK$3.30 a ride — the world's largest operational double-decker tram fleet, and the city's most democratic form of transport.

subject: Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark
summary: A 150-square-kilometre UNESCO-listed geopark spanning the eastern New Territories, where hexagonal columns of ancient volcanic rock line sea cliffs and 400-million-year-old sediment tells the full geological history of Hong Kong.

subject: Hong Kong/Kowloon
summary: Kowloon — the peninsula of nine dragons — is one of the most densely packed places on Earth, where the neon-lit waterfront faces Hong Kong Island across Victoria Harbour.

subject: Hong Kong/Lamma
summary: Lamma Island — car-free, low-rise, and laced with seafood restaurants — offers a pace of life that feels impossible to find just a short ferry ride from one of the world's most intense cities.

subject: Hong Kong/Lantau
summary: Lantau, Hong Kong's largest island, holds an airport, a Disney park, a 34-metre bronze Buddha, and enough wild mountain country to make you forget the city is only 30 minutes away.

subject: Hong Kong/Southern District
summary: On the wrong side of the hills for a century, Hong Kong's Southern District has quietly become one of the most enviable addresses in Asia — a world of secluded bays, typhoon-hardened villages, and ocean-view mansions where city and sea meet.

subject: Hongan-ji
summary: A Buddhist institution that survived siege by warrior monks, ten years of bombardment by Oda Nobunaga, and a deliberate political split -- only to emerge as the largest Pure Land sect on Earth, anchored by twin temples that dominate the skyline south of Kyoto Station.

subject: Hongkong United Dockyards
summary: Formed in 1973 from the merger of two Victorian-era shipyards, Hongkong United Dockyards on Tsing Yi Island keeps Hong Kong's maritime fleet seaworthy using one of the few floating dry docks still operating in Asia.

subject: Hongshan culture
summary: Spanning 4700 to 2900 BC across the West Liao River basin, the Hongshan culture produced some of the world's earliest jade carvings, built underground goddess temples, and may have shaped the foundations of Chinese civilization itself.

subject: Hongō Haniwa Kiln Site
summary: An ancient kiln complex in Gunma Prefecture where a hereditary caste of potters mass-produced haunting clay figures for the tombs of Japan's Kofun-era elite.

subject: Honister Slate Mine
summary: The last working slate mine in England, where Westmorland green slate has been cut since the 17th century and a local businessman bet his life on its revival.

story.title: Honolulu: The Pacific Capital Where Paradise Has Traffic Jams

subject: Honolulu
summary: The Hawaiian capital where Waikiki's towers crowd the shore - where Pearl Harbor changed history, where the price of paradise includes $8 milk and $1 million condos, and where East meets West in every aspect of life.

subject: Hoogeveen
summary: In the fall of 1883, a depressed thirty-year-old Vincent van Gogh stepped off the train at Hoogeveen and walked into the peat bogs - the place his Dutch period would never quite leave behind.

subject: Hoogstraten
summary: A Belgian town stranded in a Dutch embrace, where a sixteenth-century brick tower still rules the skyline and strawberries quietly rule the economy.

subject: Hooiberg
summary: A 165-meter conical hill at the heart of Aruba, Hooiberg has served as beacon, watchtower, agricultural anchor, and national symbol for centuries -- its silhouette appears on the country's coat of arms, and a 900-step staircase built without blueprints leads to its summit.

subject: Hoorn
summary: A West Frisian port that named Cape Horn, raised the man who massacred Banda, and is now arguing about both.

subject: Hope Cement Works
summary: A 132-metre chimney rises out of a national park - the UK's largest cement plant, sitting where the limestone meets the shale.

subject: Hope Cove Lifeboat Station
summary: A Devon lifeboat funded by the Freemasons and named for a princess saved sixty-four lives in fifty-two years - and pulled a Russian crew off a burning oil tanker in 1896.

subject: Hope Downs Mine
summary: A mother's name on a vast Pilbara iron mine, where a prospector's improbable bet finally paid off three decades after he placed it.

subject: Hope Plantation
summary: A Palladian timber masterpiece built by North Carolina's 15th governor, Hope Plantation was declared 'hopeless' before a grassroots campaign saved it from ruin.

subject: Hope Town
summary: A Bahamian village on Elbow Cay where cars are banned, streets are too narrow for golf carts, and one of the last hand-cranked kerosene lighthouses on Earth still flashes five times every fifteen seconds.

subject: Hopi Reservation
summary: An island of ancient pueblo culture entirely surrounded by the Navajo Nation, where three mesas hold villages that have been continuously inhabited for over three centuries.

subject: Hopkins (Belize)
summary: A Garifuna village on Belize's Caribbean coast where drumming traditions, coconut-milk fish stews, and barrier reef diving coexist on three miles of unhurried beachfront.

subject: Horch
summary: Thrown out of the company that carried his own surname, August Horch translated it into Latin and started again down the road - which is why the world drives Audis.

subject: Horinouchi Shell Mound
summary: A horseshoe-shaped heap of ancient shells in suburban Tokyo that rewrote the understanding of Japan's earliest settled communities and gave its name to an entire style of prehistoric pottery.

subject: Horn of Africa
summary: The great peninsula jutting into the Indian Ocean where Africa nearly touches Arabia -- a crossroads of ancient trade, competing empires, and some of the oldest evidence of human migration on earth.

subject: Horning
summary: An ancient Norfolk Broads village where King Canute gave the manor to St Benet's Abbey in 1020, where Arthur Ransome wrote Coot Club, and where 21 of 24 drinkers in the Ferry Inn died in a single Luftwaffe raid in 1941.

subject: Horry County, South Carolina
summary: Surrounded by rivers and swamps, Horry County declared itself an 'Independent Republic' and kept the silent-H pronunciation of a French-Huguenot Revolutionary War hero.

subject: Horse Guards Parade
summary: London's great ceremonial parade ground has hosted jousting tournaments for Henry VIII, beach volleyball for the 2012 Olympics, and centuries of military pageantry — and for most of the late 20th century, it was a car park.

subject: Horseley Ironworks
summary: A Tipton ironworks that built the world's first iron steamship in pieces, then shipped it to France for assembly, before going on to cast canal bridges for half of England.

subject: Horseshoe Pass
summary: A turnpike road from 1811 climbs to 417 metres in a long curve around the side of a Denbighshire valley - the most famous drive in north-east Wales.

subject: Horsetail Fall (Yosemite)
summary: A seasonal waterfall on El Capitan's eastern face that, for ten minutes on certain February evenings, catches the setting sun and glows like liquid fire - nature's accidental replacement for the manmade Firefall that Yosemite banned in 1968.

subject: Horta de Sant Joan
summary: The hilltop village where a young Pablo Picasso claimed he learned everything he knew, watched over by the great pale forms of Benet's Rocks.

story.title: Horton and Port Eynon Lifeboat Station

subject: Horton and Port Eynon Lifeboat Station
summary: On New Year's Day 1916 the lifeboat Janet went out from Port Eynon, was capsized twice, and three of its crew did not come home.

subject: Hortus Botanicus (Amsterdam)
summary: The 1638 Amsterdam herb garden that propagated a single coffee plant whose descendants now grow on every coffee farm in South America.

subject: Hortus Botanicus Leiden
summary: The oldest botanical garden in the Netherlands, where a Flemish botanist planted the tulip bulbs that would remake the country.

subject: Hoshigatō obsidian mine site
summary: High on the slopes of Mount Kirigamine, 193 interconnected pits mark where Jomon-era miners extracted volcanic glass that traveled 300 kilometers across ancient Japan.

subject: Hosmer's Grove
summary: A century-old forestry experiment gone wrong on the slopes of Haleakalā, where imported trees became invaders and the native shrubland fights for survival alongside honeycreepers found nowhere else on Earth.

story.title: Hosokawa Gracia: The Samurai's Wife Who Refused to Be a Hostage

subject: Hosokawa Gracia
summary: A traitor's daughter who became a Catholic convert in feudal Japan, Hosokawa Gracia chose death over captivity in 1600 -- and her defiance changed the course of the Battle of Sekigahara.

subject: Houdaille Quarry
summary: Bisected by Interstate 78 and closed since the 1970s oil shock, this former basalt quarry in New Jersey's Watchung Mountains has become an accidental nature preserve — and home to one of the finest greenockite crystal localities in the United States.

subject: Houhai
summary: An artificial lake built for Mongol emperors in the thirteenth century is now the center of Beijing's most atmospheric nightlife district, where centuries-old hutong alleys meet lakeside bars and cafes.

story.title: Houston: The Space City That Air Conditioning Made Possible

subject: Houston
summary: The Texas megacity built on oil, humidity, and sheer will - where Mission Control guides astronauts, where the lack of zoning creates controlled chaos, and where 7 million people live in a swamp because the AC never stops.

subject: Houston Ship Channel
summary: A dredged bayou that turned a landlocked prairie city into one of the busiest seaports on Earth, carrying oil tankers past the battlefield where Texas won its independence.

subject: Houthi insurgency
summary: What began in 2004 as a Zaidi religious rebellion in Yemen's forgotten north grew, across six phases of war and one 2014 takeover of Sana'a, into the Arab world's worst humanitarian catastrophe.

subject: Houtong Cat Village
summary: A former coal mining village in northern Taiwan that was saved from irrelevance by stray cats, becoming one of the world's most famous feline destinations after a 2008 online photo campaign went viral.

subject: Howard County, Maryland
summary: Founded in 1851 and reshaped by James Rouse's 1967 planned community of Columbia, Howard County has become one of the wealthiest, most educated, and most racially diverse jurisdictions in the United States - with no incorporated cities anywhere within its borders.

subject: Howden
summary: A Vale of York market town where William the Conqueror gave the manor to the Bishops of Durham, where Nevil Shute helped design an airship, and where the minster's tower has kept time since 1932.

subject: Howgill Fells
summary: Smooth, rounded uplands of ancient slate and gritstone between the Lake District and the Yorkshire Dales, finally added to a national park in 2017.

subject: Howmore
summary: A South Uist village of thatched cottages, medieval church ruins, and one of Scotland's strangest small churches - white-harled, central-tabled, used by fishermen as a daymark.

subject: Howth
summary: A peninsular fishing village at the northern hook of Dublin Bay, where Vikings were defeated, rifles were landed for revolution, and the seafood is still pulled in fresh each morning.

subject: Hoxne Hoard
summary: In November 1992, a metal detectorist searching a Suffolk field for a lost hammer uncovered the largest collection of late Roman gold and silver ever found in Britain — a treasure buried in the ground nearly 1,600 years earlier and never reclaimed.

subject: Hoy
summary: The second-largest of the Orkney Islands - hilly, sparsely populated, home to the Old Man of Hoy sea stack and the lonely wartime anchorage of Scapa Flow.

subject: Hoylake
summary: The Wirral seaside town where William of Orange sailed for the Boyne, the Open Championship returns to Royal Liverpool, and Daniel Craig grew up.

subject: Hoành Sơn Range
summary: Fifty kilometres of sideways mountain that walled two kingdoms apart, carries a thirty-kilometre rampart of dry-stacked red stone, and once launched a dynasty on the strength of eight words of advice.

subject: Hoʻokipa
summary: Maui's north shore beach where four distinct reef breaks, relentless trade winds, and winter swells up to 30 feet created the birthplace of competitive windsurfing.

subject: Huaca de Chena
summary: On a hill south of Santiago, the Inca laid out stone walls in the shape of a great cat, marking the farthest edge of their empire with the same sacred geometry they used in distant Cusco.

subject: Huacachina
summary: A tiny oasis village built around a blue-green lagoon in Peru's desert, where sand dunes tower overhead and dune buggies replace taxis.

subject: Huacho
summary: The Pacific port city where guinea pigs dress up for festival parades each year, and where electric trams once hummed through streets just a few years after Lima's.

subject: Huacrachuco
summary: A town in central Peru whose people once wore deer antlers on their heads, worshipped thunder gods, and held out against Tupac Yupanqui's Inca army through an entire summer campaign.

subject: Hualapai Smith's
summary: A forgotten steamboat landing and ferry crossing on the Sonora bank of the Colorado River, named for a prospector who explored the Hualapai Valley before any other in the early 1860s.

subject: Huamachuco
summary: A northern Peruvian town called the Land of Falcons, where pilgrims once traveled for centuries to consult a thunder-god oracle that outlasted the collapse of the Wari Empire.

subject: Huambo
summary: Once named Nova Lisboa and designed to replace Luanda as Angola's capital, Huambo carries the architectural ambitions of its Portuguese founders alongside the bullet scars of a civil war that nearly erased them.

subject: Huanbei
summary: A Bronze Age walled city buried eight feet underground near Anyang, burned to the ground after just fifty years, whose destruction may have prompted the founding of Yinxu, China's most famous archaeological site.

subject: Huanghuacheng
summary: At Huanghuacheng, sections of the Great Wall disappear beneath a turquoise reservoir, creating one of Beijing's most surreal and least-visited landscapes.

subject: Huangya Pass
summary: Perched on a steep mountain ridge 78 miles north of urban Tianjin, Huangya Pass is a section of the Great Wall that has guarded northern approaches for over 1,400 years.

subject: Huaqiangbei
summary: Shenzhen's Futian District subdistrict that became one of the world's largest electronics markets, where 38,000 businesses pack a single square kilometer with every component, gadget, and circuit board imaginable.

subject: Huaraz
summary: The basecamp town where the Cordillera Blanca, the highest tropical mountain range on Earth, begins at the end of the street.

subject: Huaricanga
summary: Established around 3500 BC, this dusty site in the Fortaleza Valley may be the oldest city in the Americas - older than the pyramids of Giza.

story.title: Hubbell Trading Post National Historic Site

subject: Hubbell Trading Post National Historic Site
summary: The oldest continuously operated trading post on the Navajo Nation, where a trilingual young man built a commercial empire from sandstone and trust, and where Navajo rugs are still sold across the same wooden counter they were a century ago.

subject: Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve
summary: A 241-acre pocket of ancient California hides in the Oakland Hills, where plants that vanished from the rest of the Bay Area thousands of years ago still thrive in quiet defiance of the modern world.

subject: Huddersfield
summary: A West Yorkshire town with the third largest collection of listed buildings in England, the birthplace of rugby league, and a railway station that poet John Betjeman called the finest in the country.

subject: Huddersfield
summary: A West Yorkshire mill town that grew on Pennine water and Victorian wool money, became the birthplace of rugby league, and is the only English town to have outright bought itself from its aristocratic landlord.

subject: Hufeisensiedlung
summary: Bruno Taut bent a 350-metre apartment block into a horseshoe around an ice-age pond in Neukölln, painted the working-class terraces deep blue and ochre, and put a bathroom in every flat — a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.

story.title: Huffman Prairie: The Cow Pasture Where Flight Became Real

subject: Huffman Prairie
summary: An 84-acre cow pasture outside Dayton where the Wright brothers transformed a twelve-second novelty at Kitty Hawk into a practical, controllable airplane - the field where powered flight truly grew up.

subject: Hugh Town
summary: The tiny capital of the Isles of Scilly, where a thousand people live on a sandy isthmus joining a granite headland to the rest of St Mary's, and where rowing races finish at the harbour quay each May Day.

subject: Huittinen
summary: A flat Satakunta farming town that produced Finland's oldest stone sculpture, its wartime president, and a working gold mine.

subject: Huizhou (Guangdong)
summary: A mid-sized Guangdong city that surprised the world by transforming from a sleepy Pearl River Delta town into a major industrial hub, all while retaining scenic lakeside streets and a distinctly Hakka character.

subject: Huizum
summary: A 900-year-old Frisian village swallowed by suburban Leeuwarden, still keeping a poet's grave plate propped at the door of its church.

subject: Hulao Pass
summary: Named 'Tiger Cage' after a Zhou king trapped a tiger here, this mountain pass between Mount Song and the Yellow River has guarded the approach to Luoyang for over two thousand years.

subject: Huldremose Woman
summary: An Iron Age woman recovered from a Jutland bog in 1879, unique among Denmark's bog bodies because she was found still dressed — and her clothes survive nearly complete.

subject: Hull–Rust–Mahoning Open Pit Iron Mine
summary: The largest open-pit iron mine in Minnesota -- a terraced chasm stretching over three miles long that supplied one-fourth of all U.S. iron ore during two world wars and forced an entire town to pick up and relocate.

subject: Hulme
summary: An inner-city Manchester ward that gave birth to Rolls-Royce, raised Morrissey, and outlived the brutalist concrete crescents that once tried to redefine it.

subject: Hulst
summary: A Dutch town shaped like a holly leaf - or maybe the leaf is shaped like the town - where Sebastien de Vauban came knocking in 1702 and went home empty-handed.

subject: Humahuaca
summary: A high-desert town named for the people who lived here long before Argentina, where a nine-meter bronze figure keeps watch over a valley of cactus and colored stone.

subject: Humber Forts
summary: Two concrete drum-shaped sea forts planted in the mouth of the Humber Estuary in 1915 - one finished a year after the war it was built for had ended.

subject: Humber Lifeboat Station
summary: For over two centuries the only full-time paid RNLI lifeboat crew in the United Kingdom lived at the end of a moving spit of sand - until the spit started to break.

subject: Humberston Fitties
summary: A century-old plotland of 330 wooden chalets where families still vacate every winter to keep the camp from becoming a town.

story.title: Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works

subject: Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works
summary: Two abandoned saltpeter refineries in the Atacama Desert preserve the entire world of Chile's nineteenth-century nitrate boom -- theaters, churches, swimming pools, and crushing plants -- as a UNESCO World Heritage Site slowly dissolving in the driest air on Earth.

subject: Hundested
summary: A Danish harbour town at the tip of the Halsnæs peninsula that began as a pilots' house, grew into Zealand's busiest fishing port, and keeps the cliff-top home of Arctic explorer Knud Rasmussen.

subject: Hung Hom
summary: On the southeast tip of the Kowloon Peninsula, Hung Hom has been reclaimed from the harbour, renamed by occupiers, and stitched into the city by tunnel, rail, and ferry — a neighborhood that connects Hong Kong to itself and, historically, to mainland China.

subject: Hungry I
summary: The North Beach nightclub where Lenny Bruce, Barbra Streisand, Bill Cosby, and the Kingston Trio launched their careers against a bare brick wall.

subject: Hunstanton Lifeboat Station
summary: The only east-coast lifeboat station in England that faces west — positioned on The Wash where launching a boat means crossing miles of mud flat at low tide — and the place that pioneered tractor-launched lifeboats before any other station had tried it.

subject: Hunt family murders
summary: On 9 July 2024 in Bushey, Hertfordshire, Carol Hunt and her daughters Hannah and Louise were killed by an ex-boyfriend - and a country was forced to look at what crossbow law had not done.

subject: Hunteburg
summary: A village south of the Dümmer that grew up around a fourteenth-century bishop's castle and still uses a stone arch bridge built in 1424.

subject: Hunters Point Naval Shipyard
summary: A 638-acre former Navy shipyard at San Francisco's southeastern tip, contaminated by decades of military and industrial use, whose cleanup and redevelopment has been plagued by scandal.

subject: Huntingdon
summary: A Saxon river town that grew into a coaching post, a parliamentary seat, and the birthplace of Oliver Cromwell - now home to about 24,000 people, an RAF intelligence hub, and a 14th-century medieval bridge that survived a Civil War.

subject: Huntington, West Virginia
summary: The Jewel City - West Virginia's second-largest city, built by railroad money in 1871, named for the man who built it, home to Marshall University and the world's largest rotating root beer mug.

subject: Huntly
summary: The Aberdeenshire town that the Gordons renamed in 1508 after their Berwickshire seat - a market burgh, a regimental cradle, and now a quietly internationally-minded centre of contemporary art.

story.title: Huntsville: Where Rocket City Built the Machines That Reached the Moon

subject: Huntsville
summary: Alabama's largest city where Wernher von Braun and his team of German rocket scientists created the Saturn V, where the U.S. Space & Rocket Center displays machines that carried astronauts to the moon, and where 'Rocket City' still builds the vehicles taking humanity to space.

subject: Hunze
summary: A small Dutch river that was straightened, redirected, and renamed half a dozen times over six hundred years is now being slowly unstraightened - the meanders restored, one bend at a time, on a thirty-year timeline.

subject: Hupacasath First Nation
summary: Stewards of 229,000 hectares in the Alberni Valley, the Hupacasath have governed their territory according to the seasons for millennia, following deer migrations and salmon runs across five reserves on Vancouver Island.

subject: Hurghada
summary: A sleepy Red Sea fishing village that became one of Egypt's biggest dive resorts - where the real attractions lie a boat ride offshore, beneath the surface.

subject: Husab Mine
summary: One of the world's largest uranium mines, carved into the Namib's ancient granite, where a Chinese-financed megaproject meets thousand-year-old plants.

subject: Hussain Sagar
summary: A 460-year-old heart-shaped lake at the center of Hyderabad, where a colossal Buddha rises from the water and 34 bronze statues line the shore, telling the story of Telugu civilization.

subject: Hutchinson Internment Camp
summary: A wartime British internment camp on the Isle of Man became known as 'the artists' camp' because so many of those interned, many of them Jewish refugees from Hitler, happened to be among Europe's leading creative minds.

subject: Hutton-le-Hole
summary: A stream-cut village green where sheep keep the grass short, Quakers wove cloth for two centuries, and the world championship of Nine Men's Morris was contested each year until 1997.

subject: Huu-ay-aht First Nations
summary: A Nuu-chah-nulth nation on Vancouver Island's Pachena Bay whose oral history of a catastrophic 1700 tsunami helped scientists pinpoint one of North America's largest earthquakes.

subject: Huwei, Yunlin
summary: Huwei, Yunlin County's largest urban township, carries centuries of layered identity — from the powerful Babuza people who once dominated this plain to the glove-puppet tradition that still defines the town's cultural life.

subject: Huánuco
summary: The city the conquerors moved when the first location was too cold - and where two Peruvian rivers meet beneath some of the best weather in the Andes.

subject: Huánuco Pampa
summary: A mountaintop city of 4,000 buildings where the Inca Empire flexed its architectural muscle - then abandoned the effort almost as quickly as they raised it.

subject: Hvar
summary: A Croatian island where ancient Greek colonists carved fields still farmed today, where Benedictine nuns weave lace from agave leaves, and where lavender blooms color hillsides purple every summer.

story.title: Hyakusai-ji: The Temple That Burned Three Times and Still Stands

subject: Hyakusai-ji
summary: One of the Three Great Temples east of Lake Biwa, Hyakusai-ji traces its legendary founding to a glowing cedar tree discovered in 606 AD -- and across fourteen centuries of fires, wars, and Oda Nobunaga's wrath, has never stopped rising from its own ashes.

subject: Hyampolis
summary: A Phocian city that guarded a mountain pass, beaten by Xerxes, besieged by Boeotians, torched by a tyrant, and captured by Rome — and mentioned by Homer before any of it happened.

subject: Hyde Street Studios
summary: The Tenderloin recording studio that was Wally Heider's before it was Hyde Street, where Creedence Clearwater Revival, Santana, and generations of Bay Area artists have tracked.

subject: Hyderabad
summary: Where Nizams built palaces and biryani became legend, where tech parks rise beside ancient monuments, where Telugu and Urdu cultures meet.

subject: Hyderabad State
summary: A princely state that once sprawled across the Deccan, ruled for over two centuries by the Nizams, whose wealth became legendary and whose final act of defiance against independent India ended in a military operation that redrew the subcontinent's map.

story.title: Hydra: The Island That Refused the Car

subject: Hydra
summary: Hydra is the Saronic island where wheeled vehicles are banned by law, donkeys do the carrying, and visitors who stay past the last ferry discover that one of Greece's most-visited places becomes, after dark, one of its most peaceful.

subject: Hymettus
summary: Hymettus — the long blue ridge east of Athens — has been famed since antiquity for its thyme-scented honey, its violet-tinted marble, and its monasteries clinging to the rock above the city.

subject: Hyperion Water Reclamation Plant
summary: For sixty years, the city of Los Angeles dumped its raw sewage directly into Santa Monica Bay — and the plant that finally stopped the practice became the largest sewage treatment facility west of the Mississippi.

subject: Hyrcania
summary: The ancient 'Wolf-land' south of the Caspian Sea, a province that passed through Median, Achaemenid, Seleucid, Arsacid, and Sasanian hands over a millennium of revolt, conquest, and literary legend stretching from Virgil to Shakespeare.

subject: Hà Tiên
summary: At the far western end of the Mekong Delta, a small Vietnamese seaside town keeps a Chinese founder's tombs on its hillside, a tidal lagoon at its back, and Cambodia seven kilometres up the road.

subject: Hà Tiên Province
summary: A Ming refugee built a port on the Gulf of Siam, gave it to the Vietnamese lords, and founded a frontier state that ran a poetry society and once owned what is now the Cambodian coast.

subject: Hälsingland
summary: A forested Swedish province where medieval Vikings once gathered their shipping fleets and farmers built three-story mansions to declare their independence.

subject: Hämeenkyrö
summary: A cottager's son born in a rented hut here became the only Finn ever to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, and the landscape he wrote about is now one of twenty-seven chosen to stand for the whole country.

subject: Hümmling
summary: A low, wooded ridge in Lower Saxony where Neolithic dolmens, Baroque hunting lodges, and a defiant peasant lawsuit all share the same patch of sandy ground.

subject: Hürth
summary: Both Schumacher brothers learned to race here, on the kart track that helped turn a thirteen-village Cologne suburb into a Formula One pipeline.

subject: Hālona Blowhole
summary: A volcanic lava tube on Oahu's southeast coast that shoots sea spray up to thirty feet high, set beside the tiny cove made famous by the beach scene in From Here to Eternity.

subject: Hēmeroskopeion
summary: An ancient Greek daytime watchtower on the Spanish coast, most likely beneath modern Dénia, a lost Massaliot city of tuna, iron, and a temple to Artemis whose exact site still eludes historians.

subject: Hōlei Sea Arch
summary: A 90-foot basalt arch carved by Pacific waves at the end of a road buried by lava, the Holei Sea Arch is where Kilauea's creative and destructive forces meet in a single frame.

subject: Hải Vân Pass
summary: The Hải Vân Pass — 'ocean cloud pass' — has divided kingdoms, climates, and armies across two thousand years of Vietnamese history, and remains one of the most dramatic coastal mountain crossings in Southeast Asia.

subject: Hậu Giang province
summary: A Mekong Delta province that existed for twenty-one years, kept a floating market where seven rivers meet, and sits so low that half a metre of sea-level rise would put four-fifths of it under water.

subject: Hội An wreck
summary: Twenty-two nautical miles off the Vietnamese coast, a 15th-century merchant ship carrying a quarter-million pieces of fine Vietnamese ceramics lay undisturbed for five centuries — until fishermen found it, looters nearly gutted it, and a $14 million salvage operation saved what remained.

subject: I Know Where I'm Going!
summary: The 1945 Powell and Pressburger film that taught British cinema the Hebrides were not a backdrop but a subject - a romance about a woman who learns she is going the wrong way.

subject: IBGE Ecological Reserve
summary: A 1,300-hectare research reserve 25 km south of Brasília preserving one of the world's richest and most threatened savannas.

subject: IJburg
summary: Amsterdam voted against it. The threshold was 155,000 votes; the no campaign only delivered 133,000. So the city built six artificial islands in the IJmeer anyway, and is now raising three more.

subject: IJssel
summary: A small Dutch branch of the Rhine - probably hand-dug by Roman soldiers around 12 BCE - that built the Hanseatic cities of Arnhem, Zutphen, Deventer, Zwolle and Kampen along 125 quiet kilometres.

subject: IJtunnel
summary: Twenty metres below sea level, a 1968 concrete tube under the IJ river ties central Amsterdam to the city's north, the engineering answer to a watery line on the map.

subject: INS Dega
summary: India's eastern naval air station in Visakhapatnam, named for the Telugu word for a great eagle, grew from four helipads into a sprawling base guarding the Bay of Bengal.

subject: IR-40
summary: Iran's 40-megawatt heavy water reactor near Arak became a focal point of nuclear diplomacy, surviving redesign under the 2015 Iran nuclear deal before sustaining damage in a 2025 Israeli airstrike.

subject: IRT Powerhouse
summary: A massive Renaissance Revival power station designed by Stanford White's firm to electrify New York's first subway, now a city landmark that still feeds Manhattan's steam network after more than 120 years of continuous operation.

subject: Ibbenbüren
summary: A Westphalian town whose golden anchor on a blue shield hints at a strange inland identity built around coal, canal, and counts.

subject: Iberá Wetlands
summary: One of the world's largest wetlands, where jaguars and giant otters have returned to waters whose name means 'bright water.'

subject: Ibirité
summary: A Minas Gerais dormitory city of 182,000 that hosts a Petrobras refinery, the legacy of a Russian educator, and a state park named for a rolling girl.

subject: Ibiza
summary: The island where electronic music became a way of life - but beyond the superclubs and sunset strips lies a UNESCO-protected landscape of pine forests, hidden coves, and a history stretching back to the Phoenicians.

subject: Ibn Battuta
summary: A 21-year-old Moroccan judge set out for Mecca in 1325 and did not come home for 24 years. When he finally wrote it down, his Rihla described a journey of roughly 75,000 miles across three continents - more than any pre-modern traveler.

subject: Ibra
summary: One of Oman's oldest and most culturally rich cities, where the country's only women-only market day draws traders in silver and halwa, and where the Bait al Kabir has stood as a seat of power since 1650.

subject: Ichiriki Chaya
summary: Behind a vermilion-walled entrance in the heart of Gion, a 300-year-old teahouse has served as the stage for samurai revenge plots, the secret planning room for the overthrow of the shogunate, and one of Kyoto's most exclusive invitation-only establishments.

subject: Icoaraci
summary: In a district whose Tupi name means 'sun of the river,' some eighty workshops reproduce vessel forms the Marajoara made centuries before Europeans reached the Amazon.

subject: Ictíneo II
summary: Launched in Barcelona harbour in 1864, Narcís Monturiol's Ictíneo II was the first submarine that could make its own air and burn fuel underwater, decades before the rest of the world caught up.

subject: Idanre
summary: A Yoruba town at the foot of spectacular inselbergs in southwestern Nigeria, Idanre is the country's largest cocoa-producing area and the gateway to a hill settlement where people lived among boulders for nearly a thousand years.

subject: Idanre Hill
summary: A 3,000-foot inselberg in southwestern Nigeria where the Yoruba people of Idanre lived for nearly a millennium, Oke Idanre shelters ancient palaces, shrines, unique wildlife, and the only known habitat of Perret's toad.

story.title: Iditarod: The Last Great Race to the End of the Road

subject: Iditarod
summary: The Alaska dog sled race following a trail forged in the 1925 serum run - where mushers drive teams 1,000 miles from Anchorage to Nome, where the wilderness between checkpoints is exactly as harsh as advertised, and where the tradition that saved children from diphtheria became the world's most famous endurance race.

subject: Idyllwild–Pine Cove
summary: A mile-high mountain village flanked by two famous rock formations, Idyllwild began as the summer refuge of Cahuilla people escaping desert heat and became, over a century, a refuge for climbers, artists, writers, and anyone else who needed a mountain to think by.

subject: Ifaty
summary: A pair of former fishing villages on Madagascar's Baie de Ranobe, where octopus trees and squat baobabs crowd a spiny forest behind beaches that front one of the longest coral reefs in the western Indian Ocean.

subject: Iga ikki
summary: Before they became pop-culture legends, the ninja of Iga Province governed themselves through a written constitution, a parliament of warrior-farmers, and an alliance with neighboring Koka -- a mountain republic that defeated one of Japan's greatest warlords before being crushed by his father.

subject: Igarassu
summary: A Pernambuco town named after a canoe, holding the building that Brazil's heritage institute recognises as the oldest Catholic church in the country.

subject: Igbo Landing
