summary: A marshy bend in Dunbar Creek on St. Simons Island where, in 1803, a group of captive Igbo people seized control of their captors' vessel and chose death over slavery, inspiring one of the most enduring legends in African American folklore.

story.title: Iglesia de La Merced, Antigua Guatemala

subject: Iglesia de La Merced, Antigua Guatemala
summary: One of the few churches in Antigua Guatemala that survived the catastrophic 1773 earthquakes, La Merced endured thanks to cutting-edge construction techniques -- and then watched as colonial authorities forcibly removed its most sacred sculpture to compel the faithful to abandon the ruined city.

subject: Iglesias, Sardinia
summary: Named for its abundance of churches, this medieval Sardinian mining town preserves centuries of Pisan and Aragonese influence in its walled historic center while grappling with the legacy of an industry that shaped and scarred the surrounding landscape.

subject: Iipay Nation of Santa Ysabel
summary: A federally recognized Kumeyaay tribe whose 15,000-acre homeland in the mountains east of Julian sustains seven species of oak and a tradition of governance stretching back long before California statehood.

subject: Iizaka Onsen
summary: One of the three great hot springs of Oshu, where a legendary prince was healed, Japan's most famous poet soaked after weeks on the road, and a riotous fighting festival takes over every October.

subject: Ikaalinen
summary: Finland's first market town, founded in 1858, spent its entire existence being taxed by the parish around it — and got exactly five years of independence before the whole category was abolished.

subject: Ikaria
summary: A rugged Aegean island named for a boy who flew too close to the sun, where one in three residents reaches their 90s and a history of exile shaped a culture of solidarity.

subject: Ikebukuro
summary: A Tokyo district whose name means 'pond bag,' built on the site of a wartime prison, anchored by the third-busiest train station on Earth, and quietly home to both a Frank Lloyd Wright school and a yakuza headquarters.

subject: Ikegami-Sone Site
summary: A 2,000-year-old Yayoi settlement sprawling across 600,000 square meters of Osaka suburbia, where dendrochronology dated a massive pillar building to exactly 52 BC and 1,300 stone knives revealed an ancient industrial economy hidden beneath modern Japan.

subject: Iklaina
summary: A small Greek village sitting atop a once-powerful Mycenaean city, Iklaina yielded what may be the oldest Linear B tablet ever found on the Greek mainland — a scrap of clay that rewrote the early history of Bronze Age writing.

subject: Ikogosi Warm Springs
summary: In the forested hills of Ekiti State, a warm spring and a cold spring flow side by side and meet at a single confluence -- each somehow maintaining its own temperature, a geological phenomenon that has drawn pilgrims, missionaries, and tourists for generations.

story.title: Ikuno Korea Town: Where Kimchi Tells a Complicated Story

subject: Ikuno Korea Town
summary: One of Japan's largest Koreatowns, Osaka's Ikuno district is a vibrant neighborhood where two million visitors a year come for the food -- and where the history of Korean forced labor, discrimination, and resilience simmers beneath every storefront.

subject: Ilakaka
summary: A village of 40 people that exploded to 60,000 after the discovery of one of Earth's largest sapphire deposits, becoming Madagascar's Wild West overnight.

subject: Ile des Cendres
summary: A group of submarine volcanoes in the South China Sea — active since the Holocene, known to have erupted as recently as 1923, and capable of generating tsunamis in future eruptions.

subject: Ilemi Triangle
summary: A wedge of dry rangeland where Kenya, South Sudan, and Ethiopia meet - claimed, patrolled, and grazed, but never settled on any agreed map.

subject: Ilercavonia
summary: A region with no capital, borders, or parliament that its people have recognized as home for more than two thousand years.

subject: Ilfracombe Lifeboat Station
summary: Three lifeboats with the same name, a Spanish freighter rescued in a 1949 gale, and a defunct outpost whose boathouse became a beach cafe. Ilfracombe's rescue station has been running since 1828.

subject: Ilha da Queimada Grande
summary: A 43-hectare island off the coast of São Paulo that is home to the world's only population of golden lancehead pit vipers and has been closed to the public since the Brazilian Navy deemed it too dangerous for human visitation.

story.title: Ilha do Bananal / Cantão Environmental Protection Area

subject: Ilha do Bananal / Cantão Environmental Protection Area
summary: A 1.7 million hectare mosaic in Tocantins where four of Brazil's major biomes meet, stitched together around one of the most biodiverse inland river deltas on Earth.

subject: Ilha do Caju
summary: A privately held island in the Parnaíba delta that will refuse you entry unless you book a bed, hire a boat, and give it five days' notice.

subject: Ilhabela
summary: An archipelago off the northern coast of Sao Paulo state, Ilhabela earns its Portuguese name -- 'beautiful island' -- with rainforest-draped mountains, wild eastern beaches, and a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve that covers most of its territory.

subject: Ilhéus
summary: The Bahian port city that Jorge Amado turned into literature, where cocoa barons once killed over land, and where travelers now walk the same streets his characters did.

subject: Ilhéus
summary: Once Brazil's cocoa capital, where barons killed each other for plantations and Jorge Amado turned the bloodshed into world literature. Today a tourism center facing decisions about its own coast.

subject: Ilisos
summary: The Ilisos River once flowed through a sacred landscape on the edges of ancient Athens, where Socrates walked and gods were worshipped — now buried beneath the city's streets, it survives as a ghost haunting the modern pavement.

subject: Ilkley Moor
summary: A wind-scoured Pennine moor full of Bronze Age rock carvings, mythical giants, and the song that became Yorkshire's unofficial anthem.

subject: Ilkurlka Community, Western Australia
summary: A tiny roadhouse at the heart of the Spinifex People's country - the place a desert people came home to, on land they won back by painting it.

subject: Illa Conillera
summary: A low, rabbit-covered islet off Sant Antoni that legend claims as Hannibal's birthplace and whose stony ground once hid the tortured bones of executed pirates.

subject: Illa Grossa
summary: A tiny volcanic island off the Valencian coast, once burned to rid it of snakes and later shelled by two navies, now a strictly protected marine reserve.

subject: Illa de Tagomago
summary: A mile-long private island off Ibiza's east coast whose ancient name links a Carthaginian warrior, a Muslim-era rechristening, and a landmark 1970s rock album.

subject: Illa de l'Aire
summary: A small islet off Menorca's southeast tip, home to an endemic black lizard found nowhere else and once the site of a pioneering field trial of a self-spreading vaccine.

subject: Illa de la Discòrdia
summary: On one block of Passeig de Gràcia, Barcelona's greatest Modernista architects built houses that clash on purpose, giving the city its famous Block of Discord.

subject: Illa de s'Espartar
summary: A bare, uninhabited rock west of Ibiza that shelters the western Mediterranean's largest storm-petrel colony and a wall lizard found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Illerup Ådal
summary: A drainage crew in 1950 cut into the bed of a vanished Iron Age lake and found the equipment of a destroyed army — more than 15,000 objects, deliberately wrecked before being thrown into the water.

subject: Illiniza
summary: Two peaks that were once one volcano, two kilometers apart and over 5,100 meters tall, named for a Colorados legend about lovers turned to stone.

subject: Illinois State Fair
summary: A look at the Illinois State Fair's journey from a nomadic agricultural exposition to a permanent spectacle of pop culture and high-stakes livestock auctions.

subject: Illumina, Inc.
summary: Founded in San Diego in 1998, Illumina built machines that made reading the human genome affordable and fast — and in doing so, became responsible for generating 90 percent of all DNA data ever produced.

subject: Iloilo City
summary: Once the Philippines' second city after Manila, Iloilo blends Spanish colonial grandeur with a modern rebirth as a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy and the cultural capital of the Western Visayas.

subject: Iloilo City Proper
summary: The historic downtown core of Iloilo City, established in 1602 and once honored as the last capital of the Spanish Empire in Asia, where heritage architecture and modern governance share 45 barangays on the coast of Panay Island.

subject: Iluka, New South Wales
summary: On the quiet north bank of the Clarence, a village of trawlers guards the largest surviving stand of coastal rainforest in New South Wales.

subject: Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká
summary: The Casa Branca - widely considered Brazil's oldest Candomblé terreiro, founded around 1830 by three African-born freedwomen in Salvador, Bahia.

subject: Imamate of Oman
summary: For 1,200 years, the interior of Oman elected its own rulers through a system of governance older than most European monarchies, until British-backed forces ended the tradition by military force in 1959.

subject: Imatong Mountains
summary: South Sudan's highest range, an island of montane forest rising from savanna, holding species found nowhere else in the country and a recent history scarred by war.

subject: Imperial Arsenal
summary: The Ottoman Empire's great naval shipyard on the Golden Horn — the Tersane-i Amire — built the warships that projected Ottoman power across the Mediterranean for five centuries, and one of its successor facilities is still in operation today.

subject: Imperial City of Huế
summary: Three nested walls, a moat fed by the Perfume River, and the memory of thirteen emperors — the Imperial City of Huế is Vietnam's answer to the Forbidden City, built in 1804 on geomantic principles and still bearing the scars of a century of war.

subject: Imperial City, Beijing
summary: The walled zone of gardens, shrines, and lakes that surrounded the Forbidden City, once accessed through seven gates and forbidden to commoners, now fragments into parks, government compounds, and remnant walls beneath modern Beijing.

subject: In Amenas Hostage Crisis
summary: In January 2013, militants seized a remote Algerian gas plant and hundreds of workers; four days later the siege ended with about 40 hostages from across the world dead - and one Algerian guard remembered as a hero.

subject: Ina Coolbrith
summary: Born the secret niece of Mormon prophet Joseph Smith, Ina Coolbrith reinvented herself in San Francisco and became America's first state poet laureate - mentoring Jack London and Isadora Duncan along the way.

story.title: Inaja Band of Diegueno Mission Indians

subject: Inaja Band of Diegueno Mission Indians
summary: The Inaja and Cosmit Reservation near Julian, California, holds land claimed by the Kumeyaay Nation in the San Diego backcountry — land that census records show as unpopulated even as the tribe maintains its sovereign presence.

subject: Inal, Mauritania
summary: A small rail town in the Mauritanian desert whose name belongs forever to the men hanged at its military base on the night of independence, and to the families still demanding their names be answered for.

subject: Inariyama Kofun
summary: A 5th-century keyhole-shaped burial mound in Saitama whose excavated iron sword -- inscribed with 115 gold-inlaid characters -- rewrote scholars' understanding of how far the ancient Yamato court's power reached across Japan.

subject: Inca road system
summary: A 40,000-kilometer network of engineered highways that stitched together the largest empire in pre-Columbian America, from Colombia to central Chile.

subject: Inca-Caranqui
summary: At the northern edge of an empire that spanned the Andes, a sacred water pool still waits on a vacant lot in an Ecuadorian village.

subject: Inchcailloch
summary: An 85-metre-high oak-covered island on Loch Lomond, named for an Irish nun, used by Clan MacGregor for sacred oaths and grown into a quiet nature reserve.

subject: Inconfidência Mineira
summary: In 1789, Brazilian intellectuals plotted independence from Portugal and lost. Tiradentes hanged for it; his body was quartered and displayed across Minas Gerais.

subject: Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong)
summary: In 1974, Hong Kong created an anti-corruption agency unlike any that had come before it — one that took on its own police force and, in doing so, changed the city forever.

subject: India Basin, San Francisco
summary: A bayshore neighborhood in southeastern San Francisco where waterfront access, industrial legacy, and community gardens meet in one of the city's least-known corners.

subject: Indian Arm
summary: A twenty-kilometre glacial fjord with no bridges and almost no roads, running north out of Burrard Inlet into wilderness that begins within sight of a major city.

story.title: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

subject: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science
summary: India's oldest research institute, founded by a private medical practitioner in 1876, is the place where C.V. Raman discovered the Raman effect -- the light-scattering phenomenon that won him the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics and changed spectroscopy forever.

subject: Indian Point Energy Center
summary: A shuttered nuclear power plant on the Hudson River that once supplied 25% of New York City's electricity, whose closure replaced clean energy with fossil gas and made the city's climate goals harder to reach.

subject: Indian Wells Open
summary: The BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells has grown into the best-attended tennis tournament outside the four Grand Slams — but it took Venus and Serena Williams fourteen years to return after racial slurs drove them away in 2001.

story.title: Indiana Dunes: Where the Sand Sings and Steel Mills Smoke

subject: Indiana Dunes
summary: The Indiana shore where 15,000 years of glacial sand meets century-old steel mills - singing dunes that hum when you walk on them, surrounded by smokestacks and refineries in America's strangest national park.

subject: Indiana Dunes
summary: The birthplace of ecology between the smokestacks - where Henry Cowles invented the science of ecological succession in 1899, studying sand dunes that survived a century of pressure from steel mills and Chicago suburbs.

story.title: Indianapolis: The Crossroads of America Where They Race 500 Miles

subject: Indianapolis
summary: The Indiana capital built at the geographic center of nowhere important - where the Indianapolis 500 is the world's largest single-day sporting event, where the soldiers' monument anchors a city designed on a grid, and where flyover country embraces being flown over.

story.title: Indianapolis: The Racing Capital of the World

subject: Indianapolis
summary: Indiana's capital where the Indianapolis 500 has drawn hundreds of thousands since 1911, where more interstate highways converge than anywhere in America, where the NCAA makes its home, and where a planned city on the White River became the Crossroads of America.

subject: Indianapolis 500
summary: The Greatest Spectacle in Racing, held annually at the Brickyard since 1911, where 33 cars hurtle 500 miles around a track built from 3.2 million bricks before crowds that can exceed 350,000.

story.title: Indianapolis Motor Speedway: The Brickyard Where Speed Was Born

subject: Indianapolis Motor Speedway
summary: Built in 1909 on Indiana farmland as a proving ground for the automobile industry, the Indianapolis Motor Speedway became the world's largest spectator sporting venue and the spiritual home of American racing, where a yard of original bricks still marks the start-finish line.

subject: Indigenous Ketagalan Boulevard Protest
summary: An ongoing indigenous rights encampment on Taipei's most politically charged boulevard became a rallying point for land rights, environmental justice, and unlikely alliances.

subject: Indigenous Taiwanese Culture
summary: Taiwan's sixteen officially recognized indigenous peoples — Amis, Puyuma, Paiwan, Bunun, Atayal, and eleven more — are Austronesian communities whose ancestors may have seeded the entire Pacific, from Madagascar to New Zealand, some 6,500 years ago.

subject: Indische Buurt
summary: An Amsterdam neighborhood whose streets carry the names of a vanished empire - and whose residents now speak roughly a hundred languages of their own.

subject: Indonesia–Papua New Guinea Border
summary: A straight line drawn by European powers in the 19th century slices the world's second-largest island in half, separating peoples, languages, and ecosystems that have been connected for millennia.

subject: Indrapura (Champa)
summary: Indrapura — the City of Indra — was the Cham Buddhist capital that flourished for a century beginning in 875 CE, only to be bombed into rubble by American aircraft in 1969.

subject: Industrial Heritage Trail
summary: A 400-kilometer loop of dead factories, drained canals, and silent pit-heads, signposted and turned into a tourist circuit. The Ruhr decided that the dignity of its industrial wreckage was worth preserving instead of erasing.

subject: Indústrias Reunidas Fábricas Matarazzo
summary: The largest business group in Latin America at its peak, built by a destitute Italian immigrant whose first shipment of lard sank in the harbor.

subject: Ine-ura
summary: A fishing village on the Sea of Japan where 230 wooden boathouses line the shore of a sheltered bay, their ground floors open to the water so boats could be pulled inside, earning Ine the nickname 'the Venice of Japan.'

subject: Inga Stone
summary: A forty-six-metre wall of gneiss in a Paraiba riverbed, carved in low relief with animals, human figures and forms nobody has ever read - Brazil's most famous unsolved sentence.

subject: Inga dams
summary: Two Cold War-era hydroelectric dams on the Congo River that operate at a fraction of their capacity, sitting atop rapids with enough potential energy to power the entire African continent.

subject: Inge Lehmann
summary: From a small office in Copenhagen, a Danish seismologist read a New Zealand earthquake wrong-side-out and found the solid iron heart of the planet - then spent the rest of a 104-year life being slowly given her due.

subject: Inglewood Oil Field
summary: The Inglewood Oil Field is the largest urban oil field in the United States, covering roughly 1,000 acres in Los Angeles County. Discovered in 1924, it produced around 400 million barrels of crude oil before Los Angeles County voted to close it in 2021.

subject: Ingombe Ilede
summary: An archaeological site on a hill above the Zambezi, Ingombe Ilede reveals a 15th- and 16th-century trading community that connected the copper mines of Central Africa to the Indian Ocean world.

subject: Inhambane
summary: Vasco da Gama named it Terra de Boa Gente -- Land of the Good People -- when he stopped here in the late 1400s, and this sleepy Mozambican port on its bay-side peninsula has been quietly charming visitors ever since.

subject: Inis Beag
summary: The pseudonym an American anthropologist gave to Inisheer in 1959 - and the contested portrait that followed him into the journals.

subject: Inis Mór
summary: The largest of the Aran Islands packs prehistoric forts, sea-carved blowholes, and a thousand kilometres of dry stone wall into 31 square kilometres of limestone pavement.

subject: Inis Oirr
summary: The smallest Aran island, where a 1940 minesweeper-turned-cargo-ship still rusts on the shore - the wreck that opens every Father Ted.

subject: Inishbiggle
summary: The 650-acre Mayo island whose population had dropped to eight people by 2023, separated from Achill by one of the strongest tidal currents in Europe - and where the cable car to fix the problem has been argued about since 1996.

subject: Inishcoo
summary: A small granite island in the Donegal Rosses, once a coast-guard station, now holiday homes in the channel between Burtonport and Arranmore.

subject: Inishfree
summary: Two small Donegal islands where a primal-scream commune called The Screamers settled in 1980 and one man held out alone until 2013.

subject: Inishmaan
summary: The middle Aran island - 184 people, a chair on a cliff where Synge dreamed up Riders to the Sea, and a parkrun that starts at 11am.

subject: Inishowen
summary: Ireland's most northerly peninsula, the Island of Eoghan, where high kings ruled from a ringfort that still stands and where Ireland's mainland ends in Atlantic cliffs at Malin Head.

subject: Inishtooskert
summary: Seen from the mainland, this northernmost Blasket island looks like a recumbent figure - the Sleeping Giant - and on its grey cliffs more than 27,000 pairs of storm-petrels nest in Ireland's largest colony.

subject: Inishturk South
summary: A small uninhabited island off the Connemara coast whose Irish name means Wild Boar Island, whose hilltop wears a radio mast, and whose stone cottages now serve as holiday lets for visitors content with no electricity and the ferry coming when the swell allows.

subject: Inishvickillane
summary: Sometimes called the last parish before America, this Blasket island was bought in 1974 by a future Taoiseach and became the most politically eccentric retreat in modern Ireland.

subject: Inkerman
summary: A small Crimean town whose name means 'cave fortress,' quarried for the white stone that built a peninsula and remembered for a fog-bound battle that made it briefly famous across the world.

subject: Innamincka Station
summary: On the banks of Cooper Creek, where Burke and Wills died, a cattle station the size of a small country has weathered floods, droughts and an underground sea of gas.

subject: Inner Mongolia
summary: China's third-largest region stretches 2,400 kilometers across grasslands, deserts, and mountains, where nomadic Mongol traditions persist alongside coal mines, rare-earth deposits, and rocket launch pads.

subject: Inner Tay Estuary
summary: The inner, western reach of the Firth of Tay - a 20-kilometre stretch of intertidal mudflats, reedbeds, and salt marsh that hosts the largest continuous Phragmites reedbed in the United Kingdom.

subject: Innerleithen
summary: A small Tweeddale town where a pilgrim monk arrived by coracle in 737, the oldest sports meeting in Scotland still runs every July, and downhill mountain bikers now plummet the same hillsides.

subject: Innisidgen
summary: Four thousand years ago, Bronze Age islanders built stone chambers on a Scilly hillside to hold their dead, and the chambers are still there.

subject: Innovative Genomics Institute
summary: The Berkeley research institute where Jennifer Doudna and her colleagues are turning CRISPR gene editing from a Nobel Prize-winning discovery into cures for genetic disease, tools for climate resilience, and a commitment to making it all affordable.

subject: Innsbruck
summary: An Alpine city wedged between 2,000-meter peaks that has hosted two Winter Olympics and served as an imperial capital, where Roman roads, Habsburg palaces, and snowboard culture coexist.

story.title: Inouchi Inarizuka Kofun: A Tomb Between Traditions

subject: Inouchi Inarizuka Kofun
summary: A sixth-century keyhole burial mound in Nagaokakyo, Kyoto, where an innovative horizontal stone burial chamber coexists with a traditional nailless wooden coffin -- revealing a local power caught between old ways and new influences along the Katsura River.

subject: Insite
summary: North America's first supervised injection site, opened in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside in 2003 - and kept open by a unanimous Supreme Court of Canada that told the federal health minister he had no choice.

subject: Institut Pasteur de Dalat
summary: Founded in 1936 by Alexandre Yersin, the Dalat Pasteur Institute spent decades producing vaccines against cholera, plague, and typhoid for populations across Indochina — and in 1956, its scientists discovered a new strain of salmonella isolated from a gecko.

subject: Institut der Wirtschaftsprüfer in Deutschland
summary: How a 1929 insurance collapse led Germany to invent the modern public auditor — and why the rules still come out of Düsseldorf.

story.title: Institute for Astronomy, Astrophysics, Space Applications and Remote Sensing

subject: Institute for Astronomy, Astrophysics, Space Applications and Remote Sensing
summary: On Mount Penteli, a research institute watches both the faintest galaxies and the wildfires burning across Greece, scanning the country from space every five minutes.

story.title: Institute for International Research in Glass

subject: Institute for International Research in Glass
summary: Where Sunderland's thousand-year glassmaking tradition became a global research enterprise on the bank of the Wear.

story.title: Institute of Contemporary Art San Jose

subject: Institute of Contemporary Art San Jose
summary: A free-admission nonprofit gallery in San Jose's SoFA District, the ICA has championed contemporary art in Silicon Valley since 1980, offering site-specific installations and rotating exhibitions in a city better known for its tech campuses than its art scene.

subject: Institute of Contemporary Arts
summary: Tucked inside a Nash terrace steps from The Mall, the ICA has spent eight decades as Britain's most reliably provocative cultural institution — launching Pop Art, hosting early computers alongside Adam Ant's debut, and preserving a bloodstain on its wall as an unofficial exhibit.

subject: Instituto Butantan
summary: Born from a plague outbreak in 1901, São Paulo's Instituto Butantan became Latin America's largest vaccine producer -- a place where venomous snakes save lives and a catastrophic fire could not destroy a century of purpose.

subject: Integratron
summary: A 38-foot wooden dome built in the California desert to specifications allegedly provided by Venusian visitors, funded partly by Howard Hughes, and now used for sound bath sessions with 22 quartz crystal bowls.

subject: Intel
summary: The semiconductor company that put a processor in every personal computer, shaped Silicon Valley's identity, and gave the world a five-note jingle it cannot forget.

subject: Inter-American Court of Human Rights
summary: The hemispheric human rights court in San Jose, Costa Rica, where seven judges hold governments accountable for violations across the Americas.

subject: Intercity Experimental
summary: A prototype built to settle an argument about whether German trains should ride on rails or float above them. It hit 406.9 km/h in 1988, fathered the entire ICE fleet, and now sits behind a fence in Minden.

subject: International Criminal Court
summary: A permanent court for the worst crimes humans can commit took the world a century to build. It has stood in The Hague since 2002 - hopeful, controversial, indispensable, contested.

subject: International Criminal Court investigations
summary: Every file in the ICC's case index is a place. Bogoro. Barlonyo. Darfur. Benghazi. Behind every docket number is a village, and behind every village is a list of people the prosecutors keep counting.

subject: International Financial Services Centre, Dublin
summary: Eleven derelict acres on the Dublin docklands became Europe's quietest financial powerhouse, a special economic zone that grew, controversies and all, into 7% of Irish GDP.

story.title: International Habaneras and Polyphony Contest of Torrevieja

subject: International Habaneras and Polyphony Contest of Torrevieja
summary: Every July, choirs from around the world gather on Torrevieja's old salt-loading grounds to sing a Cuban song that this town's own sailors carried home across the Atlantic.

subject: International Institute of Space Commerce
summary: A small Isle of Man think-tank built around the unexpected idea that a Crown dependency in the Irish Sea could quietly position itself at the centre of the new commercial space economy.

subject: International Istanbul Film Festival
summary: Turkey's oldest and most prestigious international film festival, held every April in Istanbul since 1982, has championed world cinema on the Bosphorus — and once fought off government censors with a protest march led by Elia Kazan.

story.title: Nichibunken: The Library That Holds Japan's Reflection

subject: International Research Center for Japanese Studies
summary: Tucked into the western hills of Kyoto, the International Research Center for Japanese Studies houses nearly half a million volumes, thousands of rare photographs, and an Edo-period Who's Who -- all dedicated to understanding what it means to be Japanese.

subject: International Settlement (San Francisco)
summary: A six-block stretch of Pacific Street that was San Francisco's most infamous entertainment district from the 1930s to the 1960s.

subject: International Short Film Festival Oberhausen
summary: Founded in 1954 as a West German educational-film showcase, the Oberhausen festival became the world's oldest short film festival - and in 1962 launched a one-page document that ended an entire era of German cinema.

subject: Intersection for the Arts
summary: San Francisco's oldest alternative nonprofit art space, established in 1965, home to the longest continuous reading series outside academia in California.

subject: Interurban Trail (King County)
summary: Two rail trails following the ghost corridors of early 20th-century electric railways stitch together Seattle's suburbs, connecting a string of valley towns from Shoreline to Fife along paths where commuter trains once hummed.

subject: Intuit
summary: The company that made tax software unavoidable began in 1983 when its founder watched his wife struggle to balance their checkbook and thought there had to be a better way.

subject: Inuvik
summary: The town built on stilts at the end of the road - where the Canadian government created an Arctic community from scratch in 1958, perching buildings on pilings above permafrost in a place with 56 days of midnight sun.

subject: Invasion of Algiers (1775)
summary: An Irish-born Spanish general, a Tuscan admiral, 20,000 soldiers, and 304 ships sailed to Algiers in 1775 to demonstrate Spanish power -- and walked into one of the most humiliating defeats in Mediterranean military history.

subject: Invasion of Algiers (1830)
summary: A fly-whisk, a diplomatic insult, and 567 ships launched 132 years of French rule in Algeria -- a conquest that began with a king's distraction from domestic trouble and ended with the fall of an Ottoman-era state.

subject: Invasion of Cuba (1741)
summary: A British fleet of warships and 4,000 soldiers landed at Guantanamo Bay in 1741 to capture Santiago de Cuba - then spent four months doing nothing while fever killed more men than the Spanish ever could.

story.title: The Invasion of Dominica, 1778: When the American Revolution Reached the Caribbean

subject: Invasion of Dominica (1778)
summary: On September 7, 1778, French forces invaded British-held Dominica before the island's defenders even knew France had entered the American Revolutionary War - a surprise attack that launched years of Caribbean island-swapping between European empires.

subject: Invasion of Guadeloupe (1810)
summary: In early 1810, a British amphibious force took France's last colony in the Americas in just nine days — the final act of a Caribbean campaign that had systematically dismantled Napoleon's presence in the Western Hemisphere.

subject: Invasion of the Cape Colony
summary: In 1795, a British fleet sailed into False Bay and seized the Dutch Cape Colony -- a port of no economic value but enormous strategic importance on the sea road to the East Indies.

subject: Inver, County Mayo
summary: A Gaeltacht village on Broadhaven Bay, birthplace in 1648 of the prophet Brian Rua U'Cearbhain, with a ruined castle that passed from Clan Barrett to Munster newcomers after a revolt, and a stained glass window from Dublin's Earley Studios.

subject: Inveraray
summary: A planned eighteenth-century town built around five herrings on a coat of arms, a duke's ambition, and one of the best-preserved Georgian townscapes in Scotland.

subject: Inverbervie
summary: A small Kincardineshire coastal town that once spun Scotland's first flax mill into existence and still has Scotland's reigning chip shop on the high street.

subject: Invercargill
summary: New Zealand's southernmost city trades in Scottish street names, record-breaking motorcycles, and summer sunsets that stretch past 9:30 PM - earning its title as the City of Water and Light.

subject: Inverell
summary: Known as the Sapphire City, Inverell sits on the Macintyre River in northern New South Wales, its name meaning 'meeting place of swans' - a prosperous gem-and-farming town whose surrounding district holds both rich blue sapphires and one of Australia's most consequential reckonings with frontier violence.

subject: Inveresk
summary: The East Lothian village built on a Roman cavalry fort, called the Montpellier of Scotland, with a churchyard holding a Waterloo hero, two Open Champions, and a slave-owner's son.

subject: Inverkip
summary: A small Inverclyde village on the Firth of Clyde that has been a witch-hunt town, a smuggler's coast, a tourist resort, and home to Scotland's first marina across nearly a thousand years of recorded history.

subject: Inverness
summary: Inverness -- 'Mouth of the River Ness' in Gaelic -- is the Highland capital, a compact Victorian city where the North Coast 500 begins and Macbeth's shadow still falls across a castle that has nothing to do with him.

subject: Inverness-shire
summary: Scotland's largest historic county, stretching from Ben Nevis to St Kilda and including a contested rock 230 miles out in the Atlantic.

subject: Inverurie
summary: Where the Ury joins the Don and the imposing hill of Bennachie watches over the Garioch, a market town carries three battles, a Pictish stone, and the memory of locomotive workshops in its centre.

subject: Inō Tadataka
summary: A retired sake brewer who, at age 55, began walking the entire coastline of Japan -- 34,913 kilometers over 17 years -- to produce maps so accurate they were still in use a century after his death.

subject: Iochdar
summary: A crofting hamlet at the top of South Uist, Iochdar grew an outsider artist who wove grass and a football club that keeps winning the Uist and Barra league.

subject: Iona
summary: St Columba's island, three miles long, where the only village is a straggle of cottages and the eighteen-hole golf course's main hazard is a bull.

subject: Iona Nunnery
summary: One of only three medieval houses of Augustinian women in Scotland, founded around 1203 by Bethoc, daughter of Somerled, and now the most complete nunnery ruin in the country.

subject: Ionian Village
summary: Since 1970, Ionian Village — the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America's summer camp on the Elis coast — has brought more than 20,000 Greek-American teenagers to Greece for an immersive blend of Orthodox faith, Greek culture, and Ionian Sea swimming.

subject: Ios
summary: On a windswept hill at the northern tip of Ios, a stone marker claims to cover Homer's grave - while down in Chora, the music thumps until dawn.

subject: Ipameri
summary: A southeastern Goias town whose Tupi name means 'between the rivers,' and where legend says a rancher, bitten by a snake, promised the land to heaven in exchange for his life.

subject: Iporá
summary: A west-central Goiás city nicknamed for its abundance of streams, wrapped by the Serra do Caiapó and built on cattle, corn, and nickel.

subject: Ipswich
summary: The county town of Suffolk, one of Saxon England's busiest ports, now a 133,000-person town where 1960s tower blocks share streets with half-timbered Tudor cottages and a Norman Foster skyscraper.

subject: Ipswich Blackfriars
summary: Founded by King Henry III in 1263, the Dominican friary of Ipswich Blackfriars was dissolved in 1538 and its buildings gradually disappeared — but excavations in the 1970s and 1980s revealed the footprint of a substantial medieval complex that is now preserved and explained on the ground.

subject: Ipswich Martyrs
summary: Nine Protestants burnt alive in Ipswich between 1515 and 1558 for their beliefs, ordinary East Anglian people whose names a Suffolk schoolteacher rescued from obscurity four centuries later.

subject: Ipswich Minster
summary: The civic church of Ipswich, where the town's charter was written in 1200, redesignated as a minster in 2025 after nearly a millennium of continuous worship.

subject: Iquique
summary: A Chilean port city wedged between the Atacama Desert and the Pacific, Iquique rose on saltpeter wealth, bore witness to war and massacre, and reinvented itself as a duty-free beach resort.

subject: Iquitos
summary: A city of 380,000 people unreachable by road, where motorcycles outnumber cars, the Amazon rises and falls eleven meters a year, and Gustave Eiffel designed a house that was carried through the jungle in pieces.

subject: Iquitos
summary: In the Peruvian Amazon, an isolated city built by rubber money became the birthplace of Amazonian pop art, Werner Herzog's Fitzcarraldo, and a community of Moroccan Jewish descendants who eventually migrated to Israel.

subject: Iquitos várzea
summary: A flooded forest ecoregion where fish swim between tree trunks to eat fruit, the river changes course overnight, and 624 bird species share space with pink dolphins.

subject: Iraft
summary: A small, unregulated lake in Swedish Lapland where the King's Trail meets a river delta, and where the water level still sits roughly where the retreating ice left it.

subject: Iran Khodro
summary: The Middle East's largest automaker built its empire on a British car from the 1960s, survived revolution and sanctions, assembled Mercedes-Benzes in Tehran, and put 65 percent of Iran's cars on the road.

subject: Iranian Azerbaijan
summary: A divided homeland where more Azeris live on the Iranian side of the border than in the entire Republic of Azerbaijan, shaped by the 1828 Turkmanchay Treaty that split a people along the Aras River.

subject: Iranian National Jewels
summary: A dazzling treasury of crowns, thrones, and gemstones spanning five centuries of Persian empire, now locked in a bank vault where they back Iran's currency.

story.title: Iranian Space Agency: Reaching Orbit Against the Odds

subject: Iranian Space Agency
summary: Iran's national space agency, which turned the country into the ninth nation to launch a domestically built satellite on its own rocket - a journey from 1960s satellite receivers in rural Hamedan to orbital capability achieved under international sanctions.

subject: Ireby
summary: A small Cumbrian village just outside the Lake District National Park, in the area locals call Back o'Skiddaw, with a thirteenth-century market charter and a pub that was once a haunt of John Peel.

subject: Ireland Cricket Team
summary: The team that beat Pakistan on St Patrick's Day, scored the fastest century in World Cup history, and waited 102 years between its first match and its first Test cap.

subject: Irish Defence Forces
summary: A small neutral state's military - two army brigades, an air corps based at Baldonnel, a navy at Haulbowline - with the southern brigade headquartered at Collins Barracks in Cork.

subject: Irish Free State
summary: The fifteen-year experiment in dominion status between empire and republic, born of treaty and civil war, that finally let Ireland write its own constitution.

subject: Irish Open (golf)
summary: Ireland's national golf championship, first played at Portmarnock in 1927 in rain that knocked down the press tents, revived in 1975, and now one of the most heavily attended events on the European Tour.

subject: Irish Sea
summary: A shallow, much-crossed inland sea between Britain and Ireland - corridor of invaders, ferries, U-boats, gas fields and wind farms.

subject: Irish Whiskey
summary: The water of life nearly died: from twenty-eight distilleries to two, then back to thirty-two, the story of Irish whiskey is a near-extinction and a slow, stubborn return.

subject: Irminsul
summary: A wooden pillar the Saxons worshipped, torn down by Charlemagne in 772 — and then reinvented in 1929 by a man who wanted the Germans to have a native religion, with consequences he lived to see.

subject: Iron Gates
summary: Where the Danube knifes through the Carpathian and Balkan mountains, two 20th-century dams turned a legendary gorge into a reservoir and drowned an island that had been Turkish for three centuries.

subject: Iron Ore Line
summary: The northernmost railway in Western Europe hauls 8,600-tonne ore trains from Arctic mines to the sea -- and the trains going downhill generate more electricity than they consume.

subject: Iron Quadrangle
summary: A 7,000-square-kilometer mineral province in central Minas Gerais has produced roughly 40% of all the gold mined in Brazil since 1500. In 2015 and 2019, it produced two of the worst mining disasters in the country's history.

subject: Iron Range
summary: Minnesota's Arrowhead Region holds some of the richest iron deposits on Earth -- a chain of mining districts around Lake Superior where immigrants from over 23 countries built a culture of pasties, potica, hockey, and fierce union solidarity.

subject: Ironbridge
summary: A Shropshire village that grew up around the world's first cast iron bridge and became the commercial heart of an industrial revolution, now preserved as a quiet riverside settlement within a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Ironton, Ohio
summary: The Ohio River town that forged iron for the USS Monitor, helped enslaved people escape on the Underground Railroad, and accidentally invented the NFL's Thanksgiving Day game.

subject: Iruya
summary: A village of stacked stone houses clings to a cliff at the bottom of an Andean canyon, reachable only by crossing a 4,000-meter pass.

subject: Irvine Burns Club
summary: Founded in 1826 by a circle of Robert Burns's personal friends, this Ayrshire club holds six original Kilmarnock Edition manuscripts and is one of the world's longest-running Burns societies.

subject: Irvine Lifeboat Station
summary: For 80 years a lifeboat answered distress calls on Irvine Bay - including the hurricane rescue of the Norwegian Frey, for which a 71-year-old coxswain won the Silver Medal.

subject: Irvine's Landing
summary: A Latvian sailor and a Madeiran stowaway bought a trading post at the mouth of ḵalpilin in 1898 and turned it into the Sunshine Coast's first real port of call.

subject: Irvine, North Ayrshire
summary: A Royal Burgh since 1372, designated Scotland's last new town in 1966 - Burns worked here as a flax-dresser, and Mary Queen of Scots is said to have slept nearby.

subject: Irving Whale
summary: A fuel barge that sank off Prince Edward Island in 1970 and spent 26 years leaking oil on the Gulf floor, becoming a case study in corporate responsibility and the true cost of marine pollution.

subject: Isaac N. Ebey
summary: The first permanent white settler of Whidbey Island, whose violent death at the hands of northern raiders in 1857 became one of Puget Sound's most haunting frontier stories.

subject: Isabel Luberza Oppenheimer
summary: Born in Ponce's poorest neighborhood, Isabel Luberza Oppenheimer became one of Puerto Rico's most storied figures, inspiring novels, films, and a street named in her memory.

subject: Isabela, Basilan
summary: The former provincial capital of Basilan, a port city where rubber processing plants still hum, ferries arrive every 30 minutes from Zamboanga, and the diverse communities of a multilingual island converge.

subject: Isaris
summary: A fortress-named mountain village in western Arcadia whose fewer than one hundred defenders held off 3,500 soldiers in 1825, and whose sons went on to guard the Guggenheim and act in Hollywood.

story.title: Ishinohoden Kofun: The Stone Chamber That Outlasted Its Mountain

subject: Ishinohōden Kofun
summary: A seventh-century burial mound near Osaka whose earthen shell eroded away centuries ago, leaving behind a remarkable granite burial chamber carved from two massive monoliths -- a rare construction method that still puzzles archaeologists.

subject: Ishirō Honda
summary: The son of a Buddhist monk who survived six years of war, then channeled his nightmares about nuclear destruction into Godzilla -- creating the longest-running film franchise in history and defining the kaiju genre.

story.title: Ishiyama Hongan-ji: The Warrior Temple That Became Osaka Castle

subject: Ishiyama Hongan-ji
summary: A retired priest built a small temple at the mouth of the Yodo River in 1496 and inadvertently founded Japan's second-largest city -- then warrior monks held its fortress against Oda Nobunaga for eleven years in the longest siege in Japanese history.

subject: Isis Downs Station
summary: Named for a tributary of the Thames, this vast Barcoo River run grew into one of Australia's great sheep stations - 200,000 sheep, a famous round woolshed, and a harder history beneath the wool.

subject: Isisford, Queensland
summary: A 200-person town on the Barcoo gave its name to the 98-million-year-old ancestor of every crocodile alive today, and lent its sun-baked country to Banjo Paterson's verse.

subject: Isla Espíritu Santo
summary: An uninhabited island in the Sea of Cortez where 9,000-year-old fishhooks, endemic black jackrabbits, and a dramatic conservation battle converge.

subject: Isla Mocha
summary: A small green island off the Chilean coast, where the Mapuche sent their dead and where a white whale named Mocha Dick gave Moby-Dick his legend.

subject: Isla Suárez
summary: A river island in the Amazon where two nations have quietly disagreed about sovereignty for over 150 years, Isla Suarez sits in the Mamore River between Bolivia and Brazil -- claimed by both, settled by neither.

subject: Isla de Cabras
summary: Goat Island sits in the mouth of San Juan Bay -- a small islet that has served as a Spanish gun emplacement, a place of isolation for people with leprosy, a World War II coastal battery, and today a national park with gazebos and a swimming beach.

subject: Isla del Sol
summary: The largest island in Lake Titicaca, where Inca mythology says the sun itself was born -- a sacred place still contested by the communities who live on it.

subject: Islas Marías
summary: A Pacific archipelago that spent over a century as Mexico's most notorious penal colony before its 2019 closure transformed it into a UNESCO biosphere reserve open to visitors.

subject: Islay
summary: The southernmost Inner Hebridean island - capital of the medieval Lordship of the Isles, home to nine working distilleries and roughly 3,000 people, where Gaelic is still spoken, geese spend the winter in tens of thousands, and the air smells of peat smoke and rain.

subject: Islay Lifeboat Station
summary: The RNLI station at Port Askaig that has answered calls in the rough waters around Jura and the Sound of Islay since 1934, including the catastrophic day in 1953 when 133 people drowned in the North Channel and the Islay crew launched twice in a single full gale.

subject: Isle Maree
summary: A small wooded island in Loch Maree where an Irish saint lived as a hermit, where pilgrims once sought cures for madness, and where the wish tree died of copper poisoning.

subject: Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana
summary: A narrow ridge of land in Terrebonne Parish where a Native American tribe has watched 98 percent of their island vanish, becoming America's first climate refugees.

subject: Isle of Arran
summary: Often called 'Scotland in miniature,' Arran is the Firth of Clyde's largest island - a geologist's paradise split by the Highland Boundary Fault, with stone circles, Bronze Age cairns, and the silhouette of a sleeping warrior.

subject: Isle of Doagh
summary: The Isle of the Dune, an island no longer, where five thousand years of rock art weather the same Atlantic that wrecked the ships and starved the families whose names fill the records.

subject: Isle of Lewis
summary: The largest island in the Outer Hebrides, where Neolithic stone circles, Norse place names, Sabbath observance, and peat cutting exist in the same landscape -- a place that has kept its own time for five thousand years.

subject: Isle of Man Government
summary: From medieval Lord of Mann through 18th-century smuggling raids to a 21st-century Council of Ministers, the Isle of Man Government quietly evolved its own self-rule next to its much larger neighbour.

subject: Isle of Portland
summary: A four-mile slab of limestone tethered to Dorset by a single beach, Portland has quarried itself into half the great buildings of London.

subject: Isle of Skye
summary: Scotland's most celebrated island, where the jagged Cuillin ridge meets Norse history, Gaelic culture, and landscapes that have drawn artists, climbers, and fugitive princes.

subject: Isle of Whithorn
summary: A former island, now joined by a causeway, where pilgrims once stepped ashore, smugglers later landed, and The Wicker Man chose its final scenes.

subject: Isle of Wight
summary: A diamond-shaped island off England's south coast, where fossil cliffs, royal retreats, and one of the largest rock festivals in history all share a single 380-square-kilometre stage.

subject: Isle of the Dead
summary: A one-hectare island off Port Arthur where more than a thousand convicts and colonists were buried, most of them in unmarked graves.

subject: Isles of Scilly
summary: An archipelago of 140 granite islets 45 kilometres beyond Land's End, where palm trees grow at the latitude of Winnipeg and a 335-year war with the Netherlands quietly persisted.

story.title: Isleton: The Half-Square-Mile Town That Made Perry Mason Famous

subject: Isleton
summary: A tiny delta town of fewer than 800 people, Isleton holds a National Register historic district, a gambling case that inspired a Perry Mason novel, and the birthplace of Pat Morita -- all squeezed onto an island in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta.

subject: Isleworth
summary: A Thames-side town in west London where Henry V planted a Bridgettine monastery, the Percys built Syon, Vincent van Gogh briefly taught Sunday school, and David Attenborough was born in 1926.

subject: Islington
summary: North London's most densely populated borough has been a market garden, a pleasure ground, a byword for poverty, and a laboratory for gentrification — and somehow, all of it ended up in novels by Dickens, Trollope, Neil Gaiman, J.K. Rowling, and Douglas Adams.

subject: Isohama Kofun Cluster
summary: Over 4,100 grave goods buried with ancient kings who ruled from a hilltop overlooking the Pacific -- a cluster of burial mounds in Ibaraki Prefecture that hints at a forgotten maritime power in eastern Japan.

subject: Issaquah
summary: Seattle's gateway to the Issaquah Alps - where hikers flock to Tiger, Squak, and Cougar mountains, where salmon return each October to streams that run through the historic downtown, and where tech wealth meets trail town character.

subject: Issaquah Alps
summary: A chain of forested highlands east of Seattle, playfully named 'Alps' by conservationist Harvey Manning to shame developers into preserving them, these modest peaks guard some of the most accessible wilderness in the Pacific Northwest.

subject: Issaquah Highlands
summary: A planned community born from coal mines and conservation battles, Issaquah Highlands rose on Grand Ridge through a decade of political compromise between developers, environmentalists, and county government.

story.title: Istana Darussalam: Where a Sultan Was Born on a Riverbank

subject: Istana Darussalam
summary: A modest wooden palace on the Kedayan River where Brunei's current sultan was born in 1946, now protected as a national heritage site amid the village homes it once towered over.

subject: Istanbul
summary: A city of roughly sixteen million people that has been Byzantium, Constantinople, and Istanbul, straddling Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus.

story.title: Istanbul's New City: Beyoğlu to Maslak

subject: Istanbul's New City
summary: North of Taksim Square, Istanbul's New City layers Art Nouveau neighborhoods, upscale Nişantaşı boutiques, and a soaring business district where some of Europe's tallest towers now crowd the Bosphorus skyline.

subject: Istanbul/Asian Bosphorus
summary: The Asian shore of the Bosphorus — from ancient Üsküdar to the forested heights of Beykoz — offers a quieter, greener Istanbul: Ottoman mosques, waterfront mansions, fish sandwiches on the quay, and the shimmer of the strait itself dividing two continents.

subject: Istanbul/Asian Side
summary: Across the Bosphorus from Istanbul's famous skyline lies a half-city of 5.6 million people—ancient Chalcedon and Scutari reborn as Kadıköy and Üsküdar—where ferries still carry the city's daily rhythms between two continents.

subject: Istanbul/Eastern Suburbs
summary: Beyond Kadıköy, Istanbul's eastern districts—Maltepe, Kartal, Pendik, Tuzla and the rest—trace an arc from ancient salt flats and Greek villages to a sprawling modern city that is still figuring out what it wants to be.

subject: Istanbul/European Bosphorus
summary: The European shore of the Bosphorus—village after village strung along the world's most storied waterway—blooms pink with Judas trees each May and carries the memory of six Ottoman palaces, two medieval castles, and a strait that has never stopped mattering.

subject: Istanbul/Golden Horn
summary: The Golden Horn—Istanbul's ancient harbor—spent much of the twentieth century as an industrial sewer before a late-1980s reclamation restored its waters and parks, and today it carries both the city's Ottoman memory and the Greek Orthodox Epiphany back to its shores.

subject: Istanbul/Kadıköy
summary: Kadıköy on Istanbul's Asian shore began as Chalcedon — the city the Delphi oracle called 'the land of the blind' — and has spent two and a half millennia turning that slight into one of the liveliest, most creative districts on either side of the Bosphorus.

subject: Istanbul/Western Suburbs
summary: West of Istanbul's ancient walls lies a vast, varied fringe that serves as the city's gateway to Europe — from Marmara lagoons to Black Sea beaches, transit hubs to quiet farms.

subject: Isthmian Games
summary: One of the four great Panhellenic festivals of ancient Greece, the Isthmian Games gathered athletes, musicians, and politicians at the Sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus of Corinth every two years — a gathering so politically charged that the Roman general Flamininus used it to announce the liberation of all Greece.

subject: Isthmus of Corinth
summary: A narrow neck of land dividing two seas, the Isthmus of Corinth has been the hinge of Greek geography for three millennia — and the setting of one of antiquity's most relentless engineering ambitions.

subject: Isthmus of Panama
summary: A narrow ribbon of land that stitched two continents together, rerouted the world's ocean currents, triggered an ice age, and then let humans carve it open again with a canal.

subject: Isturitz and Oxocelhaya caves
summary: Paleolithic caves in the French Basque foothills where Neanderthals lived 80,000 years ago and early modern humans carved bone flutes, painted cave walls, and fashioned spear points across seventy millennia of nearly continuous occupation.

subject: Itaboraí Formation
summary: A one-square-kilometer quarry near Rio de Janeiro is the richest Cenozoic fossil site in Brazil. Cement workers dug up marsupials, a ratite ancestor, and the namesake mammal age itself.

subject: Itabuna
summary: Bahia's sixth-largest city, named by the Tupiniquim for a father-sized stone in a river, grown rich on cocoa and then forced to reinvent itself when the fungus came.

subject: Itacaré
summary: A fading cocoa port on the Bahian coast that found a second life as a surf town, set against one of the last large stretches of Atlantic rainforest in Brazil.

subject: Itaipé
summary: A small municipality in the rugged northeast of Minas Gerais, named in Tupi for the path of stones that defines its landscape. Its most dramatic rock, Pedra do Chifre, stands 1,100 meters above surrounding hills.

subject: Itaituba
summary: Nugget City on the Tapajos: a gold-rush town that became a soy port, where the mercury from half a century of mining now shows up in Munduruku bloodwork.

subject: Itajubá
summary: A Minas Gerais valley town home to Brazil's federal engineering university, a helicopter factory, and the national armaments plant that makes the army's assault rifles.

subject: Italian Eritrea
summary: Italy's First-Born Colony (1890-1941) - a Red Sea outpost that became a showpiece of modernist architecture, a racialized colonial society, and a launchpad for the invasion of Ethiopia.

subject: Italian Somaliland
summary: Italian Somaliland was Italy's colonial possession in present-day Somalia, lasting from the 1880s through 1941 and revived as a UN trust territory from 1950 to 1960 -- a period that saw fierce Somali resistance, plantation exploitation, fascist expansion, and ultimately independence.

subject: Italian concession of Tianjin
summary: For forty-two years, a 46-hectare slice of Tianjin operated as an Italian colony -- complete with its own barracks, football team, and Mediterranean architecture -- making it one of the most improbable outposts of European imperialism in Asia.

subject: Italica
summary: The first Roman settlement in Spain, founded in 206 BC by Scipio Africanus, birthplace of emperors Trajan and Hadrian, with an amphitheater that seated 25,000 in a city of 8,000.

subject: Itapira
summary: An interior Sao Paulo town once renamed to bury a shameful history, now known as the City of the Mad for its three major psychiatric hospitals and the World Cup captain it buried with honors.

subject: Itapuranga
summary: A northern Goiás farming town that began with a Dominican mass under a Xixá tree and grew into the capital of the Vale do São Patrício.

subject: Itauguá
summary: Half an hour from Asunción, Itauguá is the world capital of ñandutí, the radiant 'spider-web' lace in which two cultures meet on a single circular frame.

subject: Itaúnas
summary: A beach village in northern Espírito Santo where dunes swallowed the old town in the 1960s and the new town dances forró on the sand.

subject: Itelmen language
summary: The last surviving Kamchatkan language clings to existence with fewer than a hundred elderly speakers, carrying the deep history of a people who inhabited the peninsula for thousands of years before Russian contact.

subject: Ituiutaba
summary: In this Minas Gerais cattle town, a rejected Afro-Brazilian festival marched itself into the church at five in the morning and made history.

subject: Iturup
summary: The largest of the disputed Southern Kuril Islands, where volcanic fire meets geopolitical fault lines between Russia and Japan.

subject: Ituxi Extractive Reserve
summary: A vast 776,940-hectare extractive reserve along a blackwater river in the deep Amazon, where twenty communities harvest Brazil nuts, rubber, and acai under the protection of the Chico Mendes Institute.

subject: Ivanhoe
summary: A remote crossing point on the Cobb Highway and the transcontinental railway, where horses once changed for the Darling and trains still pass in the night.

subject: Ivlia (ship)
summary: In 1989, a team of Ukrainian archaeologists and shipwrights built an ancient Greek bireme from Durmast oak and Siberian larch — then sailed it more than 3,000 nautical miles to prove what the ancient mariners had always known.

subject: Ivybridge
summary: A hump-backed bridge wrapped in ivy gave this Devon town its name, its identity, and seven centuries of history at the southern edge of Dartmoor.

subject: Iwajuku Site
summary: A natto seller's stubborn curiosity at a roadside cutting in Gunma Prefecture overturned all of Japanese archaeology in 1949, proving that humans had lived on the islands tens of thousands of years before anyone thought possible.

subject: Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine
summary: Japan's largest silver mine operated for nearly four centuries and at its peak produced a third of the world's silver, fueling global trade and sparking fierce battles among warlords for its control.

story.title: Iwase-Senzuka: Nine Hundred Graves on a Mountainside

subject: Iwase-Senzuka Kofun Cluster
summary: Spread across the Ryumon Mountains east of Wakayama, over 900 ancient burial mounds mark three centuries of power held by the provincial lords of Kii -- one of the largest concentrations of kofun in all of Japan.

subject: Iwayayama Kofun
summary: A seventh-century burial mound in Asuka village whose granite chamber was first reported to Western scholars by the 'father of Japanese archaeology' -- and whose occupant remains an imperial mystery.

subject: Ixelles
summary: Karl Marx wrote here. Lenin lived here. Audrey Hepburn was born here. Puccini died here. One Brussels municipality, fewer than seven square kilometers, has accumulated more world-changing residents than most countries.

subject: Iximche
summary: The Kaqchikel Maya capital whose name became 'Guatemala' itself - a ridgetop fortress city of pyramid-temples and ballcourts that briefly served as the first Spanish colonial capital before its own allies turned against the conquistadors.

subject: Izapa
summary: The largest ancient site in Chiapas, Izapa produced an art style so distinctive it became a category unto itself, bridging the gap between the Olmec world and the Maya.

subject: Izhma
summary: A village founded in 1567 on the subarctic Izhma River, where the Komi-Izhemtsy people have kept their reindeer-herding traditions and wooden architecture alive for centuries.

subject: Izki
summary: Legendarily Oman's oldest city, Izki may have been mentioned in Assyrian cuneiform texts from 640 BC, and contains twin walled towns, 142 towers, and a cave said to hide a golden calf guarded by magical incantations.

subject: Izmir
summary: Where ancient Smyrna became modern Turkey's most liberal city, where the Aegean coast offers Greek islands without crossing borders, where secular culture thrives.

subject: Izu Ōshima
summary: Tokyo's largest outlying island, a volcanic outpost where camellias bloom in the shadow of an active crater, rare birds nest in subtropical forests, and Godzilla met his cinematic match.

subject: Izumi Koganezuka Kofun
summary: A keyhole-shaped burial mound from the fourth century AD that yielded a bronze mirror inscribed with a date corresponding to 238 AD -- possibly one of a hundred mirrors a Chinese emperor sent to the legendary Queen Himiko of Japan.

subject: J-PARC
summary: On the Pacific coast of Ibaraki Prefecture, one of the world's most powerful proton accelerator complexes fires beams of neutrinos through 295 kilometers of solid earth toward detectors buried in a mountain on the other side of Japan.

subject: J. & K. Smit Shipyard
summary: Two brothers, a Frisian sailor brother-in-law, and a worldwide dredging empire built from the riverbank at Kinderdijk.

subject: JOS Watergraafsmeer
summary: An amateur Amsterdam football club where Rinus Michels learned to coach - and where, half a century later, his old apprentices' grandsons played Ajax in front of the cameras.

subject: Jabal al-Nour
summary: On a stark mountain above Mecca, a cave barely twelve feet long became the birthplace of a faith that would reshape the world.

subject: Jaboticabal
summary: A São Paulo town named for a tree that fruits directly on its trunk, founded on a donated inheritance, and now Brazil's leading peanut producer and home to one of the country's most important agricultural science campuses.

subject: Jaci Paraná Extractive Reserve
summary: A rubber-tapper reserve in Rondônia where 44,000 illegally grazed cattle nearly outnumbered the people, and the state legislature tried to simply erase the protected area from existence.

subject: Jacinth-Ambrosia Mine
summary: On a buried beach in the empty heart of South Australia, the world's largest zircon mine digs ancient sand for tiny crystals that outlast continents.

subject: Jack Daniel's
summary: In a Tennessee hollow where limestone-filtered spring water flows from a cave, the world's most recognized whiskey has been distilled since 1866, in a dry county where you still cannot legally buy a bottle.

subject: Jack Hills
summary: A low range of hills in outback Western Australia that contains the oldest material ever found on Earth: zircon crystals 4.4 billion years old, formed when the planet was barely 150 million years young.

subject: Jack Kerouac Alley
summary: A one-block alley connecting Chinatown and North Beach, renamed for the Beat author whose work defined the neighborhood.

subject: Jack London Square
summary: Oakland's waterfront district honors the adventure writer who once drank at its saloon -- and still keeps a presidential yacht, a Klondike cabin, and freight trains running through the middle of the street.

story.title: Jackson: The Mississippi Capital Where Civil Rights Were Won and Lost

subject: Jackson
summary: The Mississippi capital where Medgar Evers was assassinated - where the civil rights movement faced its fiercest resistance, where white flight hollowed the city, and where the infrastructure crisis reveals ongoing inequality.

subject: Jackson
summary: The Jackson County seat in southeast Ohio, where the water tower is painted to look like an apple and the town builds its identity around the autumn Apple Festival.

subject: Jackson Ward
summary: Once called the 'Harlem of the South,' Jackson Ward in Richmond was the cradle of Black enterprise, entertainment, and civil rights in Virginia, its streets walked by everyone from Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson to the lawyers who helped dismantle segregation.

story.title: When the Taps Ran Dry: Jackson's Water Crisis

subject: Jackson, Mississippi water crisis
summary: A decades-long spiral of neglect, underfunding, and demographic upheaval culminated in 2022 when 150,000 residents of Mississippi's capital lost access to safe drinking water.

story.title: Jacksonville: The City So Big It Swallowed Its County

subject: Jacksonville
summary: The Florida megacity few tourists visit - where the consolidated city-county covers 875 square miles, where the Navy dominates the economy, and where the Jaguars play in a stadium that's usually half-empty.

subject: Jade Bight
summary: A 180-square-kilometer bay carved out by medieval storm floods - and the deep natural channel that turned a quiet marsh into a German naval power.

subject: JadeWeserPort
summary: Germany's only deep-water container port - opened the year the global container market went sideways, and built for ships that hadn't quite arrived yet.

subject: Jaduguda uranium mine
summary: India's first uranium mine, buried 640 meters beneath Jharkhand, has fueled the nation's nuclear ambitions since 1967 while leaving the tribal communities above it to wrestle with questions no one in power seems eager to answer.

subject: Jaeger City, California
summary: A ghost town that briefly became the largest settlement near Fort Yuma after Louis Jaeger established a ferry crossing in 1851, only to be erased entirely by the Great Flood of 1862 — leaving nothing behind but its name.

subject: Jaffna
summary: The cultural capital of Sri Lankan Tamils, Jaffna is a city shaped by ancient kingdoms, colonial fortifications, devastating civil war, and a resilient people rebuilding their identity at the northern tip of the island.

subject: Jagdgeschwader 72
summary: The Westphalia Wing's final Phantom was painted entirely black, with the leaping Westphalian horse on its flanks, and flew away from Hopsten one last time on 20 December 2005.

subject: Jaguar Land Rover Gaydon Centre
summary: The principal engineering centre of Jaguar Land Rover, built on the runways of a Cold War V-bomber base, where almost every Range Rover, Defender and Jaguar of the last forty years has been designed, tested or proven.

subject: Jaguarão
summary: Walk across one bridge here and you change countries, no passport required, into a frontier town whose 300 protected buildings make it one of Brazil's most complete colonial townscapes.

subject: Jaipur
summary: Where the Pink City's uniform facades create India's most planned urban space, where Rajput forts crown every hill, where the Golden Triangle begins or ends.

subject: Jakarta MRT
summary: It took thirty-four years from the first proposal to the first train -- Jakarta's MRT fought through an economic crisis, a revolution, and the world's worst traffic before finally breaking ground on a system that may eventually span ten lines and 122 kilometers.

subject: Jakobsbakken
summary: A mining village above the tree line in Arctic Norway that once held 350 people, a school and a shop — and today holds no one permanently at all.

story.title: Rancho Izaguirre: The Recruitment Trap in Teuchitlan

subject: Jalisco extermination camp
summary: A cartel-operated forced recruitment site in rural Jalisco, discovered by volunteer searchers in March 2025, where the Jalisco New Generation Cartel lured people with fake job ads and left behind hundreds of shoes, clothing, and charred human remains.

subject: Jama-Coaque Ecological Reserve
summary: A 2,100-acre remnant of forest where clouds drip water to the ground and six species of wild cats still move through the trees.

subject: Jamanota
summary: Aruba's highest point at 188 meters, where the Arawak people once sought the Source of Great Spirits and where endemic rattlesnakes, wind-bent trees, and freely roaming goats share an ancient volcanic landscape.

subject: Jambi Sultanate
summary: A pepper-trading Sumatran sultanate that defied the Dutch East India Company, played Chinese and Thai merchants against European monopolists, and held on for nearly three centuries before falling in 1904.

subject: James City County, Virginia
summary: America's oldest surviving English county, where Jamestown took root in 1607 and four centuries of history layer beneath the Tidewater forests.

subject: James Colnett
summary: A Royal Navy officer whose arrest by the Spanish at Nootka Sound in 1789 nearly ignited a war between two empires over the fur-rich Pacific Northwest.

subject: James Venture Mulligan's Grave
summary: In a small bush cemetery at Mount Molloy lies the prospector whose 1873 gold strike opened North Queensland - and who died defending the peace he had spent his life trying to keep.

story.title: Jamestown: The Colony That Nearly Starved to Death

subject: Jamestown
summary: The Virginia settlement where England's first permanent American colony almost failed entirely - where 'Starving Time' killed 80% of colonists, where cannibalism has been archaeologically confirmed, and where the myths of Pocahontas and John Smith began.

subject: Jamestown
summary: The real first - England's first permanent American settlement, founded in 1607, where colonists starved, fought, and somehow survived to plant the seeds of a nation built on tobacco and enslaved labor.

subject: Jamestown Settlement
summary: A Virginia living history museum that reconstructs the 1607 James Fort, a Powhatan town, and replicas of the Susan Constant, Godspeed, and Discovery alongside the actual archaeological site of the first lasting English colony in North America.

subject: Jamiat Kheir
summary: Founded at a mosque in Jakarta's Pekojan district in 1901, Jamiat Kheir -- 'The Association of Goodness' -- was an Arab-Indonesian educational society that predated Indonesia's most celebrated nationalist organizations and became the unlikely flashpoint for a bitter conflict over equality, lineage, and who gets to define Islam.

subject: Jan van Eyck Academie
summary: Founded in 1948 to train Catholic artists for restoring war-damaged churches, the Jan van Eyck Academie evolved into one of Europe's most respected post-academic art institutes - and added female names to its all-male labs in 2017.

subject: Janaúba
summary: A cattle and banana town in the dry north of Minas Gerais, 692 meters above sea level, where the rains come in five months and stay away for seven.

subject: Janszoon Voyage of 1605–1606
summary: In 1606 a small Dutch ship named the Little Dove brushed the western coast of Cape York, and two worlds met for the first time on record — a meeting that turned to bloodshed.

subject: Januária
summary: A river town on the left bank of the São Francisco named for an emperor's daughter, producing some of the best cachaça in Brazil and guarding one of the country's most dramatic limestone caves.

story.title: Japan Mint: Where a Nation Forged Its Modern Identity in Metal

subject: Japan Mint
summary: Established in Osaka in 1871 as one of the Meiji government's first modernization projects, the Japan Mint transformed Japan's chaotic feudal currency into a unified national coinage -- and its Hiroshima branch survived an atomic bomb.

subject: Japanese Alps
summary: Three vast mountain ranges bisect Honshu, named by an Englishman who saw echoes of Europe in peaks that Buddhist monks and samurai surveyors had known for centuries.

subject: Japanese Gulch
summary: A 1,071-acre drainage basin in Mukilteo where Japanese immigrant lumber workers once lived in company housing, Japanese Gulch survived a century of industry, war, and development threats to become a protected urban wilderness.

subject: Japanese Migration to Indonesia
summary: From 17th-century mercenaries enforcing Dutch colonial rule to post-war soldiers who chose Indonesia over surrender, the Japanese presence in the archipelago has been shaped by trade, exploitation, war, love, and the unlikely persistence of communities that kept forming even when history tried to pull them apart.

subject: Japanese Village (Ayutthaya)
summary: The forgotten settlement where masterless samurai became Siam's elite warriors, rising to the third-highest rank in the kingdom before a king burned their village to the ground.

subject: Japanese cruiser Naniwa
summary: A British-built protected cruiser that fought in two wars, fired the opening shots of the First Sino-Japanese War, and ended her career on a reef in the Kuril Islands.

subject: Japanese cruiser Takachiho
summary: A British-built protected cruiser that fought in two wars and three decades of service before being torpedoed off Qingdao in 1914, taking most of her crew down with her.

subject: Japanese imperial tombs
summary: Scattered across the Kansai plain, 124 imperial burial mounds hold the remains of Japan's emperors -- and the Imperial Household Agency guards them so fiercely that most have never been excavated.

subject: Japantown, San Jose
summary: One of only three surviving Japantowns in the United States, San Jose's Nihonmachi has persisted through internment, redevelopment, and demographic change since the late 1800s.

subject: Japantown, Vancouver
summary: Paueru-gai, the Japanese Canadian neighbourhood on Powell Street that was emptied by government order in 1942 and never allowed to come back - and the single building in Canada that was.

subject: Jaraguá, Goiás
summary: An 18th-century gold town in central Goiás that reinvented itself as Brazil's capital of clothing manufacturing.

subject: Jardin
summary: An Antioquian town that has barely changed in a hundred and sixty years, still painting its balconies by hand and serving coffee on the main plaza.

subject: Jardin
summary: Three priests fleeing a civil war founded a town in a valley of white snakewood. A hundred and sixty years later, the paint still gets touched up every year.

subject: Jardin Exotique de Monaco
summary: A cliffside botanical garden in Monaco where thousands of succulents from five continents cling to engineered rock terraces above the Mediterranean.

subject: Jardine's Lookout
summary: A 433-metre hilltop above Happy Valley where trading empire lookouts once scanned the sea for clipper sails, Canadian soldiers fought Japanese forces in 1941, and today some of Hong Kong's most expensive houses perch in quiet seclusion.

subject: Jarlshof
summary: A single archaeological site in Shetland containing 4,500 years of continuous human habitation, from Bronze Age smithies through Iron Age brochs and Pictish wheelhouses to Viking longhouses.

subject: Jarrell Plantation
summary: A remarkably preserved middle-class cotton plantation in Georgia's red clay piedmont, where one family's 140-year farming legacy reveals the brutal economics of forced labor and the gritty self-sufficiency of Southern agriculture.

subject: Jarrow
summary: A small town on the south bank of the Tyne whose name carries two of England's defining stories: the scholar Bede and the 1936 hunger march.

subject: Jask
summary: An Iranian port town on the Gulf of Oman where the East India Company first traded and where modern heat records approach the limits of human survival.

story.title: Jasper Dark Sky Preserve: The Universe Above the Rockies

subject: Jasper Dark Sky Preserve
summary: The Alberta national park where darkness is protected - the second-largest Dark Sky Preserve on Earth, where light pollution regulations let visitors see the Milky Way so clearly that the ancient light seems touchable.

subject: Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve
summary: Stanford's 1,200-acre outdoor laboratory sits where serpentine rock meets chaparral, hosting experiments on climate change, invasive ants, and the ancient geology of the San Andreas Fault zone.

subject: Jataí
summary: Where cattle once stopped moving and stayed, a Goiás town now feeds nearly 2.5 million chickens and the world's appetite for soybeans.

subject: Jatun Sacha Foundation
summary: An Ecuadorian conservation NGO whose name means big forest in Kichwa - and whose reserves now stretch from the Amazon to the Galapagos.

subject: Jazan Province
summary: On Saudi Arabia's tropical southwestern coast, the kingdom's smallest-by-density province grows coffee at 3,000 meters, mangoes in the lowlands, and an archipelago of two hundred islands in the Red Sea.

subject: Jbilet Winselwan Meteorite
summary: A scatter of dark stones found in the Western Sahara in 2013 turned out to be one of the most useful carbonaceous chondrites on Earth - a cheap, plentiful stand-in for the asteroids spacecraft fly billions of miles to sample.

subject: Jebel Akhdar (Oman)
summary: Oman's 'Green Mountain' rises to 3,018 meters from surrounding desert, supports rose gardens, pomegranate orchards, and olive groves at altitude, and was the site of a guerrilla war that drew in the British SAS.

subject: Jebel Barkal
summary: A sandstone mountain the Kushites believed was the home of the god Amun - sacred to Egyptian pharaohs and to the Black Pharaohs who conquered them, crowned with temples and flanked by pyramids.

subject: Jebel Moya
summary: A granite outcrop 250 km south of Khartoum holds the largest burial complex yet found in sub-Saharan Africa, and the people in it kept cattle, pulled teeth ritually, and grew sorghum earlier than anyone thought they did.

subject: Jebel Sahaba
summary: A prehistoric Nile Valley cemetery holding some of the world's earliest evidence of organized human conflict - 64 skeletons, many bearing the marks of arrows and spears, buried around 13,000 years ago.

subject: Jedburgh
