summary: A Scottish Borders town where Mary Queen of Scots nearly died in 1566, where a kaleidoscope was invented, and where men were once hanged first and tried afterwards.

subject: Jeddah
summary: Saudi Arabia's second-largest city and its main gateway for Hajj pilgrims, where multi-story coral houses crumble in the old town and Formula One cars tear along the world's longest street circuit.

subject: Jeddah
summary: The city motto translates as Jeddah is different, and the claim holds: on a coast that is supposed to be Saudi Arabia, here is a Red Sea port with coral-stone houses, Henry Moore sculptures in the roundabouts, and a fountain 312 meters high.

subject: Jelling stones
summary: Two 10th-century runestones in a Jutland churchyard where a Viking king carved his claim to have won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.

subject: Jena
summary: A Thuringian valley town where students once had to recite seven local wonders in the correct order to prove they had studied here - one of them a seven-headed dragon made of bones and papier-mâché.

subject: Jenner Headlands Preserve
summary: A 5,630-acre preserve where coastal prairie, redwood forest, and raptor flyways converge above the Sonoma Coast -- and where endangered coho salmon returned in 2025 after a sixty-year absence.

subject: Jens Olsen's World Clock
summary: A Copenhagen locksmith taught himself astronomy and spent the rest of his life designing a clock with 15,448 parts and a gear that turns once every 25,753 years - then died ten years before it started.

subject: Jeonju Hanok Village
summary: A village of over 800 traditional Korean houses in the heart of Jeonju, where the spiritual capital of the Joseon Dynasty meets International Slow City status and nearly eight million annual visitors.

subject: Jequitinhonha
summary: A town founded in 1811 to guard a river rumoured to hold diamonds, at the downstream end of a valley whose women turned clay into one of Brazil's great art traditions.

subject: Jerome, Arizona
summary: A billion-dollar copper town that slid down Cleopatra Hill, died with 50 residents, and reinvented itself as Arizona's most spirited ghost town.

subject: Jerusalem
summary: Where three faiths claim the same stones, where David built his capital and Christ was crucified, where holiness and conflict have been inseparable for three millennia.

subject: Jessop's Clock
summary: Jessop's Clock stood outside a San Diego jewelry store for more than a century — 22 feet tall, 300 moving parts, 17 faces showing the time in 13 cities around the world, built by a man who rowed out to ships to check their chronometers, and now destined for Balboa Park after a decade in storage.

subject: Jesuit Missions of Chiquitos
summary: Six former Jesuit settlements in Bolivia's remote eastern lowlands survived the order's expulsion intact, preserving a baroque-mestizo architectural style found nowhere else on Earth and a musical heritage that still fills their churches.

subject: Jesuit Missions of the Chiquitos
summary: A traveler's circuit through six UNESCO-listed Jesuit mission towns in remote eastern Bolivia, where baroque churches rise from red-earth tracks and bus schedules depend on the driver's mood.

story.title: Jesuit Missions Among the Guaraní: Utopia, Refuge, and Ruin

subject: Jesuit missions among the Guaraní
summary: For 150 years, some 30 Jesuit mission towns sheltered up to 141,000 Guaraní people across the borderlands of Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay -- communities that were praised as socialist utopias, condemned as theocratic prisons, and ultimately abandoned when Spain expelled the Jesuits in 1767.

subject: Jesús María, Argentina
summary: A quiet Córdoba farming town that holds a UNESCO Jesuit estate and erupts each January into Argentina's most famous festival of gauchos and bronco-busting.

subject: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
summary: Founded by Caltech researchers in 1936 in the Arroyo Seco foothills, JPL now operates under NASA as the primary center for planetary robotic spacecraft — the place that put rovers on Mars, sent probes to Jupiter, and manages the Deep Space Network that keeps humanity in contact with the edges of the solar system.

subject: Jetnamsklumpen
summary: A 1,513-metre granite-gneiss dome in Børgefjell that held a county record until the county itself was abolished — and that watches over a point where four provinces of two nations meet.

subject: Jeunesses Musicales International
summary: A young Brussels lawyer walked the beams of a half-built concert hall in 1928, imagining audiences of young people he could not yet see - and seventeen years later, in a city still rebuilding from war, the dream became a worldwide youth music movement.

subject: Jever
summary: The small Friesian market town that locals call Marienstadt - Mary's City - in honour of Maria of Jever, the unmarried woman who ruled it for sixty years and outwitted everyone who tried to take it.

subject: Jeverland
summary: A vanished sea-state on the North Sea coast, knit together in the 15th century from older Frisian tribal districts, fed by a chain of sluice-ports that no longer have a port to fall into.

subject: Jewish quarter (Barcelona)
summary: In the narrow lanes of El Call, Barcelona's medieval Jewish community thrived for centuries as physicians and financiers, until the violence of 1391 erased it from the city.

subject: Jiadong
summary: A small Pingtung township called Katangkha by its first inhabitants, the Makatao people — later the site of a decisive 1895 battle that marked the end of the short-lived Republic of Formosa, and today the birthplace of one of Taiwan's most celebrated film directors.

subject: Jiangmen
summary: Jiangmen is the Pearl River Delta city whose five counties — the Sze Yup heartland — sent hundreds of thousands of emigrants to build overseas Chinese communities across North America and Southeast Asia, while filling the countryside with ornate watchtowers bought with foreign gold.

subject: Jiankou
summary: The wildest section of the Great Wall near Beijing, Jiankou is a 20-kilometer stretch of crumbling Ming-era fortification that draws hikers willing to risk its unrestored, unmaintained trails.

subject: Jiaoxi
summary: A rare ground-level hot spring town tucked in Yilan County, where steaming mineral waters rise naturally from the earth and soothe weary travellers just an hour from Taipei.

subject: Jicarilla Apache
summary: The Jicarilla Apache, named for the small sealed baskets they crafted as drinking vessels, survived centuries of displacement to build a sovereign nation on a reservation rich in oil, gas, and cultural resilience.

subject: Jicheng (Beijing)
summary: Before Beijing was Beijing, it was Ji -- an ancient city dating to 1045 BC that served as capital of the states of Ji and Yan, survived conquest by every major dynasty, and became the foundation beneath the modern capital.

subject: Jiddat al-Harasis
summary: A stony desert in south-central Oman where fragments of the Moon and Mars lie scattered across the ground, and the last wild Arabian oryx fight for survival among acacia shade trees.

subject: Jigalong
summary: A Martu community on the desert's edge, and the place three Aboriginal girls walked roughly 1,600 kilometres to come home to in 1931, following a fence across the heart of the continent.

story.title: Jigokudani Stone Buddhas: Hell Valley's Hidden Shrine

subject: Jigokudani Stone Buddhas
summary: Six Buddhist figures carved into a volcanic cliff along an ancient mountain road near Nara have weathered over a thousand years of rain and silence, their gold leaf fading but their stone faces still watching over a path that once connected the imperial capital to the Yagyu valley.

subject: Jijoca de Jericoacoara
summary: The municipality that contains Jericoacoara, the gateway where paved roads end and the sandy, carless village begins.

subject: Jikmir, South Sudan
summary: A Nuer Payam fifteen miles from the Ethiopian border, Jikmir has been an SPLA command post, a displacement shelter, and a football-winning town - all while sitting quietly across the Sobat from an Ethiopian village whose residents it still considers neighbors.

subject: Jingjintang Expressway
summary: Once celebrated as China's 'golden expressway,' this 143-kilometer link between Beijing and Tianjin earned a grimmer nickname as traffic overwhelmed its two-lane design: the 'road of death.'

subject: Jinguashi
summary: A mountainside gold-mining village in northern Taiwan where waterfalls run golden with dissolved pyrite, a ruined smelter echoes Pompeii, and the sea itself splits into yellow and blue at the shore.

subject: Jingzaijiao Tile-paved Salt Fields
summary: Taiwan's oldest surviving salt fields, established in 1818 in Beimen District, where workers laid broken pottery shards across crystallizing ponds to keep the salt pure — a 200-year-old technique that still glitters in the Tainan sun.

subject: Jinja
summary: The Ugandan town at the source of the Nile, where the world's longest river begins its journey north and adventurers gather to raft its rapids.

subject: Jinniushan
summary: A limestone hill near Yingkou, Liaoning, yielded one of the most significant archaic human fossils ever found in East Asia -- a specimen that blurs the boundary between Homo erectus and Homo sapiens.

subject: Jinshanling
summary: A 10.5-kilometer stretch of the Great Wall with 67 watchtowers, Jinshanling is where Ming dynasty military engineering meets wild mountain scenery in one of the wall's most photogenic sections.

subject: Jinzhou
summary: An ancient city guarding the narrow corridor between North China and Manchuria, Jinzhou has spent a thousand years as the strategic hinge where empires and armies pass through.

subject: Jirisan
summary: The tallest mountain on the Korean mainland, Jirisan anchors seven Buddhist temples on its slopes and carries legends of serpent-dragons in its valleys.

subject: Jiufen
summary: A former gold mining town in the hills of northern Taiwan whose narrow lantern-lit streets and Pacific Ocean views made it a film location, a Studio Ghibli rumor, and the most popular day trip from Taipei.

subject: Jiujiufeng
summary: The Ninety-Nine Peaks of central Taiwan — jagged, closely packed, and unlike almost anything else in the landscape — owe their strange silhouette to Pleistocene gravel and the erosive patience of rain.

subject: Jiumenkou
summary: The only section of the Great Wall built directly over a river, Jiumenkou spans the Jiu River in Liaoning Province with a unique engineering feat that earned it UNESCO World Heritage status in 2002.

story.title: Jo-an: A Warlord's Brother and the Art of Tea

subject: Jo-an
summary: Built around 1618 for Oda Nobunaga's younger brother, the Jo-an teahouse is one of Japan's three finest surviving chashitsu and a National Treasure -- a tiny structure where samurai once knelt to enter through a crawling door.

subject: Joan Gamper
summary: A Swiss athlete turned away from one Barcelona club founded his own on the opposite principle, giving FC Barcelona its identity as a club open to everyone.

subject: Joara
summary: Decades before Roanoke's Lost Colony or Jamestown, Spanish soldiers built Fort San Juan at the Mississippian chiefdom of Joara in the North Carolina foothills -- the first European settlement in the interior Southeast, destroyed by a Native uprising within eighteen months.

subject: Jockey Club Creative Arts Centre
summary: Hong Kong's first adaptive reuse of a former factory into an arts village, the JCCAC transformed a 1977 nine-storey flatted factory in Shek Kip Mei into 140 working studios where painters, ceramicists, dancers, and photographers make their practice visible.

subject: Jockey Hollow
summary: The Continental Army's winter encampment at Jockey Hollow in 1779-1780 was worse than Valley Forge -- colder, hungrier, and largely forgotten by the nation that survived because of the soldiers who endured it.

subject: Jodenbuurt
summary: For four centuries this quarter east of the Amstel was Amsterdam's Jewish heart - the home of Spinoza, a neighborhood that Rembrandt walked through every day, and a community of 80,000 that the Nazi occupation reduced to roughly 5,000.

subject: Jodhpur
summary: Where the Blue City spreads beneath an impregnable fortress, where Rajput warriors built defenses that never fell, where indigo paint colors entire neighborhoods.

subject: Joggins
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Bay of Fundy where 310-million-year-old fossils from a vanished tropical rainforest tumble from coal-seamed cliffs with every tide, including some of the earliest known reptiles in Earth's history.

subject: Johannesburg
summary: Where gold built a city from nothing in 1886, where apartheid's injustice concentrated and collapsed, where South Africa's largest city struggles with its past and builds its future.

subject: Johannesburg/Soweto
summary: Soweto -- South Western Townships -- was built by apartheid as a mechanism of racial separation, then became the crucible of resistance that helped topple the system that created it.

subject: John Joseph Montgomery
summary: A California professor who made controlled heavier-than-air flights two decades before the Wright Brothers, then died testing the very machines he pioneered.

subject: John Melton Black
summary: The Scottish-born pastoralist who founded Townsville in 1864 for the merchant Robert Towns, then lost everything to a theatre, his name now scattered across the city in roads, rivers and a hilltop.

subject: John Palmer Parker (rancher)
summary: A Massachusetts sailor who arrived in Hawaii around 1809, married into Kamehameha I's royal family, and founded Parker Ranch -- one of America's oldest and largest cattle operations.

subject: John Singer Sargent
summary: Born in Florence to wandering American parents, John Singer Sargent painted nearly 900 oils and 2,000 watercolours, scandalised Paris with one bare shoulder, and died at 31 Tite Street in Chelsea in 1925 — the unrivalled portraitist of his age.

subject: John o' Groats
summary: A tiny village at the north end of the British road network, famous mostly for being the start (or end) of the long walk to Land's End.

subject: Johnnie Walker
summary: The world's best-selling Scotch whisky began as a grocery shop on Kilmarnock's High Street, run by a teetotaller who never distilled a drop himself.

subject: Johnson County, Kentucky
summary: U.S. 23 runs through here - the highway country music historians call the Country Music Highway, where Loretta Lynn and Crystal Gayle and Chris Stapleton all grew up within a few hollers of each other.

story.title: Johnson Space Center: Where Houston Heard the Words From the Moon

subject: Johnson Space Center
summary: The Texas complex where NASA controls human spaceflight - where 'Houston, we have a problem' was first spoken, where 'The Eagle has landed' was first heard, and where the consoles that directed Apollo now sit preserved as monuments to the mission that defined what humans could achieve.

subject: Johnson Space Center
summary: Built on former cattle-grazing land donated through Rice University, NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston has been the headquarters of American human spaceflight since 1963, earning Houston its official nickname 'Space City.'

subject: Johnstown Inclined Plane
summary: The world's steepest vehicular funicular -- built in 1891 as an escape route from the flood-prone valley that had just killed 2,209 people, and pressed into exactly that service twice more in the century that followed.

subject: Johor Sultanate
summary: Born from the ashes of fallen Malacca in 1528, the Johor Sultanate fought Portuguese invaders, Acehnese rivals, and Dutch opportunists across three centuries of struggle for control of the Strait of Malacca.

subject: Joint Genome Institute
summary: A federal facility at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory where scientists decode the DNA of everything from cottonwood trees to soil microbes, reshaping humanity's understanding of the living world one genome at a time.

subject: Jolo Group of Volcanoes
summary: A cluster of active volcanoes on a figure-eight-shaped island in the Sulu Archipelago, where crater lakes still steam and a submarine eruption once triggered a tsunami.

subject: Jolo, Sulu
summary: The capital of Sulu province, a town defined by centuries of resistance, clan politics, and a slow emergence from decades of conflict toward fragile peace.

subject: Jomfru Ane Gade
summary: Denmark's most concentrated stretch of bars and discotheques is named after a sixteenth-century nun.

subject: Jon Brower Minnoch
summary: A Bainbridge Island taxi driver who became the heaviest person ever documented, whose story is one of human struggle, medical extremes, and a life lived against extraordinary physical odds.

subject: Jonas Bronck
summary: A Swedish immigrant who settled on 274 hectares along the Harlem River in 1639 and died just four years later gave his name to an entire New York City borough -- the Bronx.

subject: Jones County, North Carolina
summary: With 9,172 people spread across 470 square miles of swamp and pine, Jones County is one of the smallest and quietest in eastern North Carolina.

subject: Jorvik Viking Centre
summary: Built directly over the Coppergate archaeological dig that yielded 40,000 Viking artefacts, Jorvik reconstructs a 10th-century York street as it would have looked, sounded and smelled in 975 AD.

subject: Jose Maria Alviso Adobe
summary: The last Monterey Colonial adobe in the Santa Clara Valley, built in 1837 for an early alcalde of San Jose and still standing with original walls, 1853 hardware, and an intact 1920s kitchen.

subject: Jose Rizal's Farm
summary: A 40-hectare farm in Zamboanga del Norte that the Philippines' national hero acquired during his exile -- payment for curing a man's blindness, purchased with lottery winnings.

subject: Joseon
summary: For 505 years, the Joseon dynasty shaped Korea's language, culture, and bureaucracy, rising from a military coup to become one of the longest-ruling dynasties in world history.

subject: Josep Maria Jujol
summary: The overlooked genius behind the color and mosaic of Antoni Gaudí's masterpieces, whose own spiky hilltop sanctuary at Montferri was finished half a century after his death.

subject: Joseph Hanks
summary: Abraham Lincoln's maternal great-grandfather, a Virginia tenant farmer who moved his family to what is now Mineral County, West Virginia, before joining the great migration to Kentucky.

subject: Josephine Earp
summary: The woman behind Wyatt Earp ran away from San Francisco as a teenager, lived through the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral, and spent her final decades trying to rewrite her own history.

subject: Joshua Slocum
summary: The Nova Scotia farm boy who ran away to sea at sixteen, commanded eight vessels across the Pacific, survived shipwrecks and pirates, then rebuilt a derelict oyster boat and sailed it alone around the world - becoming the first person in history to complete a solo circumnavigation.

subject: Joshua Tree
summary: Where the deserts meet and the rocks tumble - where two desert ecosystems collide among surreal boulder piles, creating a landscape so alien that rock climbers, spiritual seekers, and U2 all found what they were looking for.

subject: Joure
summary: Where Egbert Douwes opened a small shop in 1753 that became one of Europe's great coffee houses, and where residents are still nicknamed Calf's Legs after a pastry offered to a water spirit.

subject: Joy Hing's Roasted Meat
summary: A Teochew family's char siu shop that survived the Qing Dynasty, two world wars, and an avian flu pandemic to become Wanchai's most beloved queue — and one of Hong Kong's Michelin-recognized treasures.

subject: Joya de Cerén
summary: A Maya farming village frozen in volcanic ash around AD 600 -- the 'Pompeii of the Americas' -- where sleeping mats were still rolled up, hearths still burning, and a ceremony may have been interrupted mid-ritual when everyone fled into the night.

subject: João Pessoa, Paraíba
summary: A city founded in 1585 that has been called Nossa Senhora das Neves, Filipeia, Frederikstad and Parahyba, and finally took the name of a governor shot dead in a Recife sweet shop.

subject: Juan de Fuca Channel
summary: A hidden submarine canyon that acts as an underwater Amazon River, pumping nutrient-rich deep ocean water into Puget Sound and fueling one of the Pacific Northwest's richest marine ecosystems.

subject: Juan de Fuca Ridge
summary: A 500-kilometer submarine mountain range off the Pacific Northwest coast where the Earth is literally pulling itself apart, feeding underwater volcanoes and hydrothermal chimneys that sustain life in total darkness.

subject: Juba
summary: The capital of the world's youngest nation began as a Bari village on the White Nile and grew into a city that has carried both the hope of independence and the wounds of civil war.

subject: Juba–Terekeka–Rumbek Road
summary: A 392-kilometer highway being paved with money borrowed against 30,000 barrels of South Sudanese crude oil a day.

subject: Juchitán de Zaragoza
summary: An indigenous Zapotec city on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec that earned the title 'Heroic' for defeating the French army, where the traditional culture of muxes has made it a remarkable oasis of gender fluidity in southern Mexico.

subject: Juist
summary: A 17-kilometer slip of sand off the German coast where motor traffic is mostly illegal and the locals call the place 'Magic Land.'

subject: Juiz de Fora
summary: A Minas Gerais city in a deep river valley halfway between Rio, Belo Horizonte, and São Paulo, known for its gay-friendly ordinance, colonial music festival, and Paraibuna riverside street food.

subject: Juiz de Fora
summary: A Minas Gerais city that was once Latin America's industrial frontier, built the first hydroelectric plant on the continent, and reinvented itself three times across 175 years.

subject: Julfa, Azerbaijan (city)
summary: A border city on the Aras River, Julfa has been destroyed and rebuilt across millennia -- from a thriving medieval Armenian trading hub to a scorched-earth wasteland under Shah Abbas, and from a World War II supply corridor to a modern border crossing between Azerbaijan and Iran.

subject: Julia Robinson Mathematics Festival
summary: Born from a Bay Area woman's memory of a math contest that no longer existed, the Julia Robinson Mathematics Festival has grown from a single 2007 event at Google's Mountain View campus to nearly 500 events across 25 states and 15 countries, all free and all named for a mathematician who broke barriers.

subject: Julian, California
summary: A gold rush mountain town east of San Diego where Black pioneers were among the earliest and most prominent settlers, the apples still come in October, and the Milky Way is visible on clear nights.

subject: Juliana Republic
summary: For 109 days in 1839, a breakaway republic flew its own flag over the Brazilian port of Laguna, with Giuseppe and Anita Garibaldi among its defenders.

story.title: Juliana's Tokyo: The Dance Floor Where Japan's Bubble Burst

subject: Juliana's
summary: A British-Japanese mega-disco in Tokyo's Shibaura district that burned bright from 1991 to 1994, Juliana's became the defining nightlife symbol of Japan's bubble-era excess -- where office ladies in skin-tight bodycon dresses danced on elevated stages as techno thundered and a nation's economic dream began to unravel.

subject: Julius Caesar's Invasions of Britain
summary: In 55 BC, Caesar tried to invade Britain with two legions and almost lost everything. He came back the next year with 800 ships - and Britain entered written history.

subject: Juma Sustainable Development Reserve
summary: A pioneering Amazon reserve where 157 families of small farmers became Brazil's first community to be funded through a REDD carbon credit program, proving that standing forests can be worth more than cleared land.

subject: Jumilla
summary: A dry-country wine town in the hills of northern Murcia where people have lived for nearly half a million years and a Gothic castle crowns a hill that has been fortified since the Bronze Age.

story.title: Juneau: The Capital That No Road Can Reach

subject: Juneau
summary: The Alaska capital connected to the world only by sea and air - where the Mendenhall Glacier descends to suburban proximity, where state legislators arrive by ferry or floatplane, and where the isolation that preserved it from development may also preserve it from remaining the capital.

subject: Jupiter Mosman
summary: An Aboriginal boy of about twelve found the gold that built one of Australia's richest cities - and the place still carries his name.

subject: Jura, Scotland
summary: An island in the Inner Hebrides with about 200 residents, 6,000 deer, one road, three quartzite peaks, and the remote farmhouse where George Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four.

subject: Juruá–Purus moist forests
summary: 242,000 square kilometers of road-less Amazonian rainforest in northwest Brazil, where rivers function as barriers and the highway extension everyone fears has not yet arrived.

subject: Jussara
summary: A cattle town in the Vale do Araguaia, renamed in 1950 for Jussara Amorim, the first woman from Goiás to be crowned Miss Brasil.

subject: Jussarö
summary: Finland's only ghost town sits on an outer-archipelago island where iron was dug by prisoners, a village was built and abandoned twice, and the army practised street fighting in the ruins.

subject: Juye Incident
summary: The 1897 murder of two German missionaries in rural Shandong that gave the German Empire its pretext to seize Chinese territory, triggering the Scramble for China and helping ignite the Boxer Uprising.

subject: Juyong Pass
summary: One of the Great Wall's three legendary mountain passes, Juyong Pass has guarded the northern approach to Beijing since the Qin dynasty first named it over two thousand years ago.

subject: Jwaneng diamond mine
summary: In the dry heart of Botswana, an ancient volcanic pipe yields the richest haul of diamonds on Earth - and helped turn one of the world's poorest nations into one of Africa's success stories.

subject: Jægersborg Dyrehave
summary: A UNESCO-listed forest north of Copenhagen whose roads were cut in a star pattern so that a seventeenth-century king could watch dogs run down deer from a single point.

subject: Jümme
summary: An East Frisian collective municipality between two tidal rivers - locals call it Mesopotamia - where Central Europe's oldest hand-worked ferry still pulls passengers across.

subject: K computer
summary: Once the fastest supercomputer on Earth, the K computer consumed enough electricity to power 10,000 homes and was named for a number so large most languages lack a word for it.

subject: K'gari
summary: The world's largest sand island grows towering rainforest out of pure sand, cradles mirror-clear lakes, and carries its true name again: K'gari, paradise.

story.title: KEK: Japan's Atom Smasher That Launched the Country's First Website

subject: KEK
summary: Japan's largest particle physics laboratory sits in a Tsukuba campus where 3-kilometer accelerator rings hunt for asymmetries in the universe, a Nobel laureate solved one of physics' deepest puzzles, and someone plugged in the country's first web server in 1992.

subject: KPFA
summary: The first listener-funded radio station in America, KPFA 94.1 FM has been broadcasting dissent, poetry, and experimental sound from Berkeley since 1949.

subject: Ka Lae
summary: The southernmost point of the fifty United States, Ka Lae is a windswept headland where ancient Hawaiian fishermen drilled mooring holes into lava rock and modern wind turbines harvest the same relentless gusts.

subject: KaZantip
summary: The legendary Crimean dance festival that began as windsurfers partying on the sand and grew into a self-declared republic of 100,000 revelers, born inside an abandoned nuclear plant.

subject: Kaaba
summary: A cuboid of stone and marble in the heart of Mecca orients the prayers of nearly two billion people, five times a day, from every continent on Earth.

subject: Kaatsheuvel
summary: The North Brabant town of about 16,600 where a 1935 Catholic recreation field grew into Efteling - a fairytale theme park that now draws 5.3 million visitors a year and quietly outranks more famous neighbours.

subject: Kabadougou Kingdom
summary: Founded by a trader who became a warlord, the Kabadougou Kingdom reshaped the social order of northwest Ivory Coast around a slave-based military economy before falling to French colonial forces in 1898.

subject: Kabara, Mali
summary: Timbuktu's river port on the Niger, the desert city's hard-won link to the water that fed its golden age and witnessed its sorrows.

subject: Kabataş, Beyoğlu
summary: Kabataş is the Beyoğlu shore's great transit crossroads — where the T1 tram meets the funicular to Taksim, ferries depart for Asia and the islands, and the Bosphorus opens wide before you.

subject: Kabompo
summary: A town of six languages and miles of teak forest in northwestern Zambia, where a future president once lived under colonial house arrest.

subject: Kabul–Kandahar Highway
summary: Afghanistan's most important road -- a Cold War-era highway linking the country's two largest cities -- has been built, destroyed, rebuilt, and fought over for more than sixty years.

subject: Kabwe
summary: A Zambian city where independence found its voice and lead dust found its way into the blood of children.

subject: Kabwe mine
summary: A former lead mine near Kabwe, Zambia, that yielded one of the most important fossils in human evolution and left behind one of the most toxic landscapes on Earth, where 140,000 women and children may have been poisoned by its legacy.

subject: Kaditz Lime Tree
summary: There are iron rings buried in the bark of this tree, left over from the centuries when it served as the village pillory — and the two halves of the collar have been pulled apart by a thousand years of growth.

subject: Kaesong
summary: Once the glittering capital of the Goryeo dynasty, Kaesong now sits just north of the world's most heavily armed border -- a UNESCO World Heritage city frozen between two Koreas.

subject: Kafa Biosphere Reserve
summary: The word 'coffee' traces back to this corner of Ethiopia, where wild Coffea arabica still grows beneath the canopy of a UNESCO biosphere reserve sheltering 300 mammal species and the genetic birthplace of the world's most popular beverage.

subject: Kafouri
summary: A Beirut-born farmer named Aziz Kafouri took over failed English irrigation land in 1899 and built a dairy empire; the neighborhood that grew around it became Khartoum's wealthiest suburb, and then a battlefield.

subject: Kafue Flats
summary: Zambia's vast seasonal floodplain once supported a quarter-million lechwe antelope and thousands of wattled cranes, but two dams and a rising human population have fundamentally altered its ancient flood rhythms.

story.title: Kahrizak: The Detention Center That Broke Iran's Silence

subject: Kahrizak Detention Center
summary: An underground detention facility south of Tehran became a symbol of state brutality after the disputed 2009 presidential election, when detainees were beaten to death, a whistleblower physician died under mysterious circumstances, and even the Supreme Leader was forced to order it closed.

story.title: Kaibara Domain: The Cursed Inheritance of the Oda Clan

subject: Kaibara Domain
summary: A feudal domain in central Japan passed down through a bloodline of madness, rebellion, and ruin -- where descendants of the great Oda Nobunaga struggled for centuries against floods, droughts, and their own misfortune.

subject: Kaikoura
summary: A small New Zealand coastal town whose name means 'eat crayfish' in Maori, squeezed between snow-capped mountains and a Pacific Ocean so deep that sperm whales hunt within sight of the shore.

subject: Kaikōura Dark Sky Sanctuary
summary: A 2,039-square-kilometre sanctuary where the town dimmed its lights not just for the stars but to save a seabird that breeds nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Kainantu
summary: A Papua New Guinea highland town where coffee, gold, and one of the Pacific's oldest golf courses share a single ridge.

subject: Kaiping
summary: In the rice-farming countryside of Guangdong, hundreds of fortified watchtowers rise above the paddies — built by emigrant families who sent money home and feared the bandits who knew it.

subject: Kairaku-en
summary: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens, Kairaku-en was built in 1842 by a feudal lord who insisted that beauty should belong to everyone -- and planted 3,000 plum trees to prove it.

subject: Kaiser-Wilhelmsland
summary: For thirty-six years, the northeastern quarter of New Guinea was called Emperor William's Land and claimed for the German Empire, though Germany never really knew what it owned.

subject: Kaiserkeller
summary: A St. Pauli basement with a stage made of planks on beer crates, where two Liverpool bands played themselves into shape in 1960 and then broke it on a bet.

subject: Kajabbi
summary: A near-empty railway town on the Leichhardt River that stands as the gateway to Battle Mountain, where the Kalkadoon made their stand in 1884.

subject: Kakaban
summary: An uninhabited island in Indonesia's Derawan archipelago whose name means 'hug' -- because it wraps around a prehistoric marine lake filled with stingless jellyfish found almost nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Kakuda Space Center
summary: A quiet facility in rural Miyagi Prefecture where JAXA engineers have tested the rocket engines that lifted Japan into space for over half a century.

subject: Kakuma
summary: What began in 1992 as an emergency shelter for thousands of children who had walked out of Sudan's war has become a city of the displaced in the Kenyan desert, home to people from across a continent.

subject: Kalakla
summary: A 450-year-old neighborhood on the west bank of the White Nile south of Khartoum, founded by a scholar from Al-Azhar and home to a Qur'anic school established in 1885 that outlasted empires, independence, and, so far, a civil war.

subject: Kalalau Trail
summary: Eleven miles of narrow, cliff-hugging path along Kauai's Na Pali Coast, named one of America's most beautiful and dangerous hikes, connecting Ke'e Beach to the remote Kalalau Valley.

subject: Kalaloch, Washington
summary: A windswept coastal enclave within Olympic National Park where annual rainfall is measured in feet, a famous Sitka spruce clings to life over an eroding creek, and the Quinault word for this place means 'a good place to land.'

subject: Kalamata
summary: Kalamata is a seaside city famous for its black olives and its place in history as the first town liberated in the 1821 Greek War of Independence — and one rebuilt twice over, after Ibrahim Pasha's army destroyed it in 1825 and the 1986 earthquake killed 20 people and damaged much of the city again.

subject: Kalambo structure
summary: At Kalambo Falls on the Zambia-Tanzania border, two interlocking logs dated to at least 476,000 years ago may be the oldest known wooden structure on Earth - built by hominins who predate Homo sapiens by more than 100,000 years.

subject: Kalapodi
summary: A small Greek village in Phocis that sits above one of the ancient world's longest-lived sanctuaries — an altar to Apollo and Artemis used without interruption from the Mycenaean Bronze Age through Imperial Roman times.

subject: Kalasha Valleys
summary: Deep in the Hindu Kush, three narrow valleys shelter the Kalasha -- Pakistan's smallest ethnoreligious group, who have practiced their ancient animist traditions for centuries amid an overwhelmingly Muslim nation.

subject: Kalaupapa, Hawaii
summary: A flat peninsula beneath the world's tallest sea cliffs, where more than 8,000 people were exiled with leprosy over a century and where a handful of former patients still live in one of Hawaii's most remote communities.

subject: Kalaureia
summary: On a hilltop of this ancient island, Greece's greatest orator chose poison over surrender — inside the very sanctuary that had sheltered generations of fugitives.

subject: Kalawao County, Hawaii
summary: The smallest county in the United States by land area and the second smallest by population, a place with no elected government where freight arrives once a year and the 2016 Republican presidential candidate received exactly one vote.

subject: Kalbarri
summary: A coastal town where 420-million-year-old sandstone meets the Indian Ocean, Kalbarri guards a serpentine river gorge carved through rock that once teemed with the earliest land spiders.

subject: Kalemba Rockshelter
summary: A granite overhang above the Chipwete valley that sheltered people for 37,000 years and still holds their paintings on the rock.

subject: Kalemie
summary: A lakeside port on the western shore of Lake Tanganyika where flights from Kinshasa arrive twice a week, trains creep in from Lubumbashi, and the N5 is mostly a rumour - a traveller's view of a town that rewards persistence.

subject: Kalemie
summary: Capital of Tanganyika Province, founded in 1891 as an anti-slavery outpost under Captain Alphonse Jacques, renamed from Albertville in 1971, and still the junction where rail, road and 673 kilometres of lake meet.

subject: Kalinago Territory
summary: The only indigenous territory in the Eastern Caribbean - 3,700 acres on Dominica's windward coast where the Kalinago people have maintained their land, governance, and cultural identity for over a century against colonial pressure, isolation, and natural disaster.

subject: Kalinga (region)
summary: An ancient coastal kingdom whose bloodiest defeat changed the course of world religion - Kalinga stretched along India's eastern seaboard for millennia, defying empires until one emperor's remorse gave birth to Buddhist compassion.

subject: Kalkriese
summary: A quiet strip of farmland north of Osnabrück where a British major with a metal detector reopened Rome's oldest missing-persons case, and where archaeologists are still arguing about the answer.

subject: Kallithea
summary: A densely built southern suburb of Athens whose name means 'beautiful view' — a district shaped by Olympic history, waves of refugee settlement, and the haunting melodies of rebetiko.

subject: Kalloni
summary: A market town at the head of a shallow, bird-thronged gulf on Lesbos, where Aristotle once studied the first animals and where the sardine still rules the summer table.

subject: Kalos Limen
summary: The stone bones of a Greek harbor town that changed hands between Hellenes and Scythians for two centuries before the steppe swallowed it whole.

subject: Kalukundi mine
summary: A copper-cobalt deposit 65 kilometres from Kolwezi whose development stalled for years behind an ownership dispute and an international bribery scandal that ended with a $412 million US settlement.

subject: Kalulushi
summary: A planned company town named for a hare, built for copper, reshaped by mine closures, and remade by a university that took its place.

subject: Kam Tin
summary: On a flat alluvial plain north of Hong Kong's tallest peak, Kam Tin has been the heartland of the Tang clan for more than a thousand years — a landscape of walled villages, ancestral halls, and a communal grave inscribed with six days of outstanding bravery.

story.title: Kamagasaki: The Neighborhood That Doesn't Officially Exist

subject: Kamagasaki
summary: Home to Japan's largest concentration of day laborers, Kamagasaki is an Osaka neighborhood so inconvenient to the city's image that the government erased its name from official maps -- yet 30,000 people continue to live within its unmarked borders.

story.title: Kamaishi: Steel, Tigers, and the Kannon's Gaze

subject: Kamaishi
summary: A former steelmaking capital squeezed into a narrow Pacific valley, Kamaishi is home to a UNESCO World Heritage iron mine, a giant goddess watching over fishermen, and Tiger Dance troupes that bless businesses with taiko drums and bamboo flutes.

story.title: Kamakura: Japan's Fortress Capital Between Mountains and Sea

subject: Kamakura
summary: Once the fourth-largest city in the world and seat of Japan's first military government, Kamakura hides a millennium of samurai history, Zen temples, and an outdoor Great Buddha behind the hills that made it an impregnable fortress.

subject: Kamaran
summary: A low, flat island in the Red Sea that once grew rich on the business of pilgrimage - and went to ghost almost overnight.

subject: Kamatanda
summary: A region north of Likasi where the Sanga people mined copper for centuries, where Belgian Union Miniere took over in 1906, and where in 2010 some 400 children were working among 2,000 artisanal diggers in open pits up to 25 metres deep.

subject: Kamatero
summary: A small village of grain and wine on the western edge of Athens that became a dense working-class suburb - and twice found itself in the path of history, from a doomed 1827 battle to the 1999 earthquake's epicenter.

subject: Kamchatka
summary: A 1,250-kilometer peninsula larger than California with only 315,000 inhabitants, 160 volcanoes, and no road connecting it to the rest of Russia -- Kamchatka is one of the most geologically violent and biologically rich places on Earth.

subject: Kamchatka earthquakes
summary: The Kamchatka Peninsula sits above one of Earth's most violent subduction zones, producing magnitude 9-class earthquakes and devastating tsunamis in a pattern that has repeated for centuries.

subject: Kamehameha III
summary: Born on a rock at Keauhou Bay and revived by a prophet's prayer, Kauikeaouli became Hawaii's longest-reigning king, transforming an absolute monarchy into a constitutional democracy while fighting to keep his island nation sovereign.

subject: Kamiesberge
summary: A 140-kilometer mountain range of granite inselbergs in Namaqualand that harbors one of Earth's 25 plant biodiversity hotspots, where predictable rainfall and desert fog produce spring wildflower displays of global significance.

subject: Kaminaljuyu
summary: Buried beneath Guatemala City's western suburbs, Kaminaljuyu was a Maya metropolis of 200 temple mounds that thrived for nearly three thousand years — and now survives as fewer than 35 eroding remnants surrounded by strip malls and traffic.

subject: Kamioka Liquid Scintillator Antineutrino Detector
summary: Buried deep inside a former zinc mine in the Japanese Alps, KamLAND is a 1,000-ton antineutrino detector that proved neutrinos change identity as they travel, and now listens for ghost particles rising from the Earth itself.

subject: Kamishichiken
summary: Kyoto's oldest geisha district grew from seven teahouses built with leftover materials from the reconstruction of Kitano Shrine during the Muromachi era -- a quiet neighborhood of dark wooden buildings in the Nishijin textile quarter where roughly 25 geisha and apprentices maintain traditions that the busier, more famous Gion has long since packaged for tourists.

story.title: Kamo Aquarium: The Jellyfish That Saved Everything

subject: Kamo Aquarium
summary: A small-town aquarium on the verge of bankruptcy reinvented itself as the world's greatest jellyfish museum, earned a Guinness World Record, and then a Nobel laureate called to help make the jellyfish glow again.

subject: Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: A troubled big-cat sanctuary near Whangarei whose two decades of ownership disputes, regulatory battles, and animal welfare scandals ended with the euthanasia of its last elderly lions.

story.title: Kamo Shrines: Kyoto's Shield Against Demons

subject: Kamo shrines
summary: Two ancient Shinto shrines flanking the Kamo River were positioned to guard Kyoto's cursed northeast corner from demonic infiltration -- and their primeval forest, called the Forest of Truth, has survived wars, fires, and twelve centuries of urban growth.

subject: Kamo site
summary: A Yayoi-period village buried beneath the southern edge of Kawanishi city, where a single bronze bell discovered in 1911 led to 225 excavations revealing a moated settlement spanning thousands of years.

subject: Kamoto mine
summary: An underground copper and cobalt mine near Kolwezi whose ore helps power the world's electric vehicles, and whose tailings have poisoned a river.

subject: Kamp Amersfoort
summary: A Dutch town's residents watched silhouettes of prisoners march from the railway sidings to the camp, and when their children waved through the lace curtains, the children were pulled back.

subject: Kampala
summary: Uganda's capital began as a royal hunting ground full of antelope and grew across seven green hills into a city of markets, motorbikes, and the famous street-food Rolex.

subject: Kampen, Overijssel
summary: A Hanseatic port at the mouth of the IJssel where the medieval city wall still stands, the bishop got a fish made of eggs, and three centuries of trade left a town that decided to stop growing.

subject: Kampong Thom
summary: A twenty-minute bus stop halfway between Phnom Penh and Siem Reap that turns out to be the doorway to Cambodia's oldest capital and one of its last great grasslands.

subject: Kampong Thom province
summary: A province named for a pair of vanished serpents, holding Indochina's last great lowland forest, two cores of the Tonle Sap biosphere, and a roll of names Cambodia would rather not claim.

subject: Kampot
summary: A river town that was once Cambodia's only door to the sea, now better known for salt, pepper and a roundabout with a giant concrete durian in it.

subject: Kampot province
summary: A province of pepper vines, salt pans and a mountain whose abandoned French resort cost nine hundred lives to build.

subject: Kamunting
summary: A Malaysian tin-mining town whose founding legend involves a runaway elephant, Kamunting grew from jungle wilderness into a garrison town and industrial satellite of Taiping.

subject: Kamunting Detention Centre
summary: Malaysia's most notorious detention facility held political prisoners, opposition leaders, and alleged terrorists under the Internal Security Act for decades.

subject: Kan'ei-ji
summary: A Tendai Buddhist temple in Tokyo's Ueno district, once a sprawling 30-building complex and funeral temple for six Tokugawa shoguns, destroyed in a single afternoon during the Battle of Ueno in 1868.

subject: Kananaskis Country
summary: The alternative to Banff that nobody knows about - where Alberta created a provincial park system to relieve pressure on the national parks, offering the same Rocky Mountain scenery without the crowds, fees, or reservations.

subject: Kanapoi
summary: A sun-cracked fossil ground southwest of Lake Turkana where the bones of Australopithecus anamensis - among the earliest known members of the human lineage - emerged from four-million-year-old mud.

subject: Kandahar
summary: Afghanistan's second-largest city has been conquered, destroyed, and rebuilt so many times that its ruins form geological strata of empire, from Alexander the Great to Ahmad Shah Durrani to the Taliban.

subject: Kandahar Greek Edicts of Ashoka
summary: A fragmentary Greek inscription found in Old Kandahar reveals that an Indian emperor once used the language of Aristotle to preach Buddhist compassion to Alexander the Great's descendants.

subject: Kandovan, Osku
summary: An Iranian village where families still live inside cone-shaped volcanic rock formations carved out over centuries, a living Cappadocia that refuses to become a ruin.

subject: Kandy
summary: Where Buddha's tooth relic draws pilgrims to Sri Lanka's hill capital, where the last kingdom fell to the British and where Sinhalese culture finds its center.

subject: Kandy Esala Perahera
summary: A sacred Buddhist procession over 1,500 years old that unites fire dancers, caparisoned elephants, and the Sacred Tooth Relic in ten nights of devotion through the streets of Kandy.

subject: Kanesatake
summary: The oldest continuing Mohawk community in existence, Kanesatake sits where the Ottawa and St. Lawrence rivers meet -- a place whose 300-year land dispute erupted into the 1990 Oka Crisis, a 78-day armed standoff that forced Canada to confront Indigenous land rights.

subject: Kangaba
summary: In a small town on the upper Niger stands a round mud sanctuary that has been re-roofed by hand every seven years since 1653, its rethatching a five-day ceremony where griots recite the founding story of the Mali Empire.

subject: Kanheri Caves
summary: A complex of 109 Buddhist caves carved into a single basalt hill near Mumbai, spanning a thousand years of monastic life, trade, and worship.

subject: Kanlıca
summary: A quiet Bosphorus village on Istanbul's Asian shore, Kanlıca is famous across Turkey for one thing: a thick yogurt dusted with powdered sugar that locals have been making and selling from its waterfront cafés for generations.

subject: Kanmon Straits
summary: The narrow channel where Honshu and Kyushu nearly touch has shaped the fate of empires, from the drowning of a child emperor to the opening of Japan to the modern world.

story.title: Kansas City: Where Barbecue Is Religion and the Chiefs Finally Won

subject: Kansas City
summary: The Missouri metropolis that straddles two states and invented a barbecue style - where Boss Pendergast ran an open city, where jazz flourished under corruption, and where the Chiefs ended 50 years of Super Bowl futility.

story.title: Kansas City: Where Barbecue Is Religion and Jazz Never Stopped

subject: Kansas City
summary: The city that straddles Missouri and Kansas, where over 100 barbecue joints smoke meat with local distinction, where Charlie Parker learned to fly, and where a corrupt political machine built a surprisingly beautiful city.

subject: Kansas City Jazz
summary: How a corrupt political machine, an all-night liquor economy, and a generation of Black musicians at 18th and Vine invented the sound that would become bebop.

subject: Kansas City, Missouri
summary: Born at the confluence of two rivers where three westward trails converged, Kansas City grew from a fur trading post into a metropolis of fountains, jazz, and barbecue straddling the Missouri-Kansas border.

subject: Kanyika mine
summary: A Malawian niobium deposit that promised 1,200 jobs, drew Chinese investment, and left 243 households in court over compensation.

subject: Kaohsiung
summary: Taiwan's Harbor Capital reinvented itself from a gritty industrial port into a subtropical city of bike paths, night markets, and glittering waterfront art—all while keeping one of Asia's busiest seaports humming behind the scenes.

subject: Kaokoland
summary: Namibia's most remote and untouched region, where the OvaHimba people maintain a traditional way of life in a landscape of desert valleys, fairy circles, and crocodile-haunted rivers bordering Angola.

subject: Kapellen
summary: When the Antwerp-Rotterdam railway sliced through this sleepy Campine parish in 1854, the rich citizens of Antwerp climbed aboard and built villas. Today Kapellen is a green Voorkempen suburb of 27,000 people, liberated in 1944 by Quebec's Fusiliers Mont-Royal.

subject: Kapenguria
summary: A small Kenyan town that became a crucible of independence when Jomo Kenyatta and the 'Kapenguria Six' were tried here in 1953, and later produced marathon world-record holder Tegla Loroupe.

subject: Kapiʻolani (chiefess)
summary: A Hawaiian high chiefess who walked sixty miles to descend into the fiery crater of Kilauea, defying the goddess Pele to prove the power of her new Christian faith.

subject: Karako-Kagi Site
summary: A 420,000-square-meter Yayoi village site in Nara where archaeologists found painted pottery depicting a multi-story tower, upending assumptions about what prehistoric Japan could build.

subject: Karakoram Pass
summary: At 5,540 meters, the Karakoram Pass once connected the silk routes between Ladakh and the Tarim Basin -- a crossing so barren that caravans marked their progress by the bones of pack animals that had died on earlier journeys.

subject: Karaköy
summary: At the foot of the Galata Tower where the Golden Horn meets the Bosphorus, Karaköy has been Istanbul's gateway to the world for eight centuries — a district where Genoese merchants, Sephardic Jews, White Russian exiles, and Mediterranean cruise ships have all made landfall.

subject: Karangetang
summary: The locals call it Api Siau -- the Fire of Siau. With 41 eruptions since 1675, Karangetang is one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes and the tallest peak in offshore North Sulawesi.

subject: Karditsa
summary: Flat as a tabletop and proud of it, Karditsa in western Thessaly has turned its topography into a civic identity — roughly 40 percent of all trips in this city of 40,000 are made by bicycle.

subject: Karelia
summary: A borderland divided between Finland and Russia, where Europe's two largest lakes anchor a region shaped by centuries of war, displacement, and cultural resilience.

subject: Karema, Tanzania
summary: A fishing village on Lake Tanganyika where a Belgian fort, a mission founded by freed captives, and a 1913 steamship converged into one unlikely history.

subject: Karenni States
summary: The Karenni States occupied a strange legal limbo for over a century -- recognized as belonging neither to Burma nor to Britain -- and their people have been fighting for autonomy ever since.

subject: Kargopol
summary: A once-prosperous medieval Russian trading town that rejected the railroad and drifted into beautiful obscurity, preserving centuries of white-stone churches and a living tradition of clay toys.

story.title: Karimunjawa: The Convict Islands That Became Paradise

subject: Karimunjawa
summary: A 27-island archipelago in the Java Sea whose unlikely history winds from pirate haven to penal colony to one of Indonesia's most treasured marine national parks.

subject: Karl Guthe Jansky
summary: The 27-year-old Bell Labs radio engineer whose merry-go-round antenna on four Model-T wheels first heard the Milky Way's whisper in 1932 - and who was told there was no money to pursue what he had found.

subject: Karoi
summary: A Zimbabwean tobacco town whose Shona name means "little witch" and whose highway carries half the country's traffic to Zambia.

subject: Karonga District
summary: A Malawian border district on the northern tip of Lake Malawi where dinosaur bones, a uranium mine, and ancient trade routes share the same red earth.

subject: Karoo
summary: South Africa's vast semi-desert heartland, a Khoikhoi-named landscape of extremes where 250-million-year-old fossils lie beneath flat-topped koppies, mountain zebras were saved from extinction, and the night sky is dark enough for the Square Kilometre Array.

subject: Karpenisi
summary: Nestled below Mount Tymfristos in the heart of Greece's wildest mountain region, Karpenisi has been a town of strategic importance, athletic achievement, and surprising culture — and its very name is a small puzzle that scholars are still untangling.

subject: Karratha
summary: Karratha is a city assembled from scratch in 1968 to service the Pilbara's mineral wealth, built on land where the Yapurarra people lived for tens of thousands of years before dispossession.

subject: Karuizawa, Nagano
summary: A highland resort town born when a Scottish-Canadian missionary recognized its Scottish-like landscape in 1886 -- a place where emperors fell in love on tennis courts and John Lennon spent quiet summers with his family.

subject: Karumba
summary: At the mouth of the Norman River, Karumba is the only Gulf town where the road reaches the sea - Queensland's prawn and barramundi capital, famous for the way the sun drops straight into the water.

subject: Karuo culture
summary: Tibet's oldest permanent settlement, where Neolithic farmers grew foxtail millet at 3,100 meters until a cooling climate drove them away around 1750 BC.

subject: Karyes
summary: A mountain village on Mount Parnon in Laconia whose ancient dancing maidens — young women performing the ritual of caryatis for the goddess Artemis — gave their name to the caryatids, the stone figures that hold up the Erechtheion on the Athenian Acropolis.

subject: Karystos
summary: A Bavarian-planned grid town beneath Mount Ochi, where Roman emperors quarried green-veined marble and a red castle still guards the bay.

subject: Kasaï-Oriental
summary: A Congolese province that holds the world's densest known concentration of industrial diamonds - and whose capital, Mbuji-Mayi, grew from a refuge into a city of millions.

subject: Kashan
summary: A 7,000-year-old oasis city on the edge of Iran's central desert, Kashan enchants with merchant palaces, Persian gardens, rose water distilleries, and an underground city built to hide from the Mongols.

subject: Kaskaskia, Illinois
summary: Once the first capital of Illinois with 7,000 residents, Kaskaskia was swallowed by the Mississippi River and now sits as a ghost village of 21 people on the wrong side of the state line.

subject: Kassala
summary: A Sudanese market town at the base of the Taka Mountains where coffee is served with incense, fruit grows on the Eritrean border, and a legend says drinking from the well of Totil will bring you back.

subject: Kassbet Lahrar
summary: A string of palm-shaded ksour in the Touat oasis country, where dates once served as wages and underground water channels still decide what grows.

subject: Kastro-Kyllini
summary: A Crusader fortress crowns the Kyllini peninsula where ancient thermal baths, a medieval port town, and layers of Frankish history meet the Ionian Sea.

subject: Kasubi Tombs
summary: On a hill above Kampala stand the tombs of four Buganda kings, sheltered under one of Africa's great thatched domes - burned in 2010, and rebuilt by the hands of a kingdom.

subject: Kasungu
summary: A tobacco town in central Malawi with a Cambridge-style boarding school founded by the country's first president, famines in its recent memory, and a hospital that makes do with almost nothing.

subject: Kat Hing Wai
summary: Iron gates, seven-meter walls, and a story of resistance: Kat Hing Wai is a walled village in Hong Kong's New Territories where about 400 Tang clan descendants still live inside fortifications their ancestors built to outlast empires.

subject: Kata Tjuta
summary: Thirty-six ancient domes rise from the red desert of central Australia, their Pitjantjatjara name meaning 'many heads' -- a sacred landscape 600 million years in the making.

subject: Katanga
summary: A traveler's guide to the southeast corner of the Democratic Republic of the Congo - copperbelt, Lubumbashi, and the long horizon where the plateau meets Zambia.

subject: Katas Raj Temples
summary: A complex of ancient Hindu temples on Pakistan's Potohar Plateau whose sacred pond is said to have formed from the tears of Shiva, surviving centuries of empires, Partition, and modern industrial encroachment.

subject: Katavi Region
summary: One of Tanzania's newest and most forested administrative regions, nearly the size of Estonia, where miombo woodland covers more than two-thirds of the land.

subject: Kate Sessions
summary: Katherine Olivia Sessions spent sixty years working twelve-to-fourteen-hour days as a botanist, horticulturalist, and landscape architect in San Diego — importing plants from around the world, planting trees in Balboa Park in exchange for a nursery lease, and transforming the look of an entire city.

subject: Katherine
summary: The third-largest town in the Northern Territory, 300 km south of Darwin, where a river carved 13 separate gorges through ancient sandstone and an adventure playground of canoeing, bushwalking, and barramundi fishing spreads out in every direction.

subject: Kathiri
summary: A sultanate in Yemen's Hadhramaut valley that lasted nearly six centuries, whose diaspora shaped politics from East Timor to Indonesia long after the kingdom itself vanished.

subject: Kati, Mali
summary: A market town and garrison just northwest of Bamako, Kati has worn many uniforms — colonial barracks, independent Mali's military school, and the launch point of the coups that have repeatedly reshaped the nation.

subject: Kattegatcentret
summary: A Danish aquarium built on the argument that the cold grey sea outside its own door deserves the same wonder as a coral reef — and that you should be allowed to swim in it.

subject: Katutura
summary: Named in Otjiherero for 'the place where people do not want to live,' this Windhoek township was born from forced removal in 1961 and became the crucible of Namibia's independence movement after police killed 11 protesters in 1959.

subject: Katwe
summary: A working neighborhood near central Kampala where metalworkers improvise machines from scrap - and where a girl who sold maize became a world-traveling chess champion.

subject: Katz's Delicatessen
summary: A Lower East Side kosher-style deli founded in 1888 that serves 15,000 pounds of pastrami a week, survived subway construction and neighborhood transformation, and became an unlikely movie star.

subject: Katzie First Nation
summary: Their name means land of the moss, and it comes from an instruction: pile up moss, and build the village on that.

subject: Kauhakō Crater
summary: A volcanic crater at the center of the Kalaupapa Peninsula whose lake holds the world's greatest depth-to-surface-area ratio and once suffered a mysterious overturning event that killed everything living in it.

subject: Kaunas
summary: For two decades between the world wars, Kaunas was Lithuania's improvised capital and built the modernist architecture that earned it UNESCO World Heritage status nearly a century later.

subject: Kaurareg
summary: The traditional owners of Thursday Island, the Kaurareg people survived massacres, forced relocations, and a century of displacement before winning back their ancestral islands in a landmark court ruling.

subject: Kavieng
summary: At the northern tip of New Ireland, a small tropical port trades quiet streets for world-class surf, coral-fringed wrecks, and the slow rhythm of a town that most travelers never reach.

story.title: Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology

subject: Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology
summary: Where Stanford meets SLAC, a Norwegian philanthropist's gift funds scientists probing dark matter, dark energy, and the fundamental structure of the universe.

subject: Kawachi Kokubun-ji
summary: The vanished provincial temple of Kawachi Province, ordered built by Emperor Shomu in 741 AD after a devastating smallpox epidemic, where a massive pagoda base is all that remains of a seven-story tower that once proclaimed imperial Buddhist authority across the Yamato River plain.

subject: Kawah Putih
summary: A volcanic crater lake 50 km south of Bandung where the water shifts between bluish, white-green, and brown depending on sulfur concentration -- so acidic at pH 0.5 that it has bleached the surrounding rocks white and kept birds away for centuries.

subject: Kay Moor, West Virginia
summary: An abandoned coal town stacked vertically in the New River Gorge - mine on the bench, processing plant 560 feet below, conveyors connecting the two.

subject: Kaya
summary: The leather capital of Burkina Faso, where artisans have turned hide into craft for generations on the road toward the Sahel.

subject: Kayoa
summary: A 66-island archipelago straddling the equator that was once the only place on Earth where cloves grew, with archaeological evidence of spice trade stretching back two thousand years.

subject: Kaʻahumanu
summary: Born in a Maui cave to a fugitive chief, Kaʻahumanu became the most powerful woman in Hawaiian history, abolishing the ancient kapu system and reshaping the kingdom from within.

subject: Kaʻula
summary: A shrinking volcanic crescent in the remote Hawaiian chain, Ka'ula is simultaneously a sacred island of Hawaiian mythology, a seabird sanctuary, and a U.S. Navy bombing target.

subject: Kaʼapor Sign Language
summary: In the forests of northwestern Maranhão, a Kaʼapor community built a sign language that hearing and deaf people share — a language with no relatives anywhere on earth, in which the past sits in front of you.

story.title: Kebayoran Baru: The Garden City That Swallowed Its Plan

subject: Kebayoran Baru
summary: Conceived in 1948 as a Dutch colonial garden city and designed by the first native Indonesian urban planner, Kebayoran Baru was supposed to be a self-sufficient satellite town 15 kilometers from the capital -- but Jakarta grew to meet it, and now this planned utopia is the beating center of South Jakarta.

subject: Kebnekaise
summary: Sweden's highest peak is losing a race against its own glacier, as climate change slowly reshapes which of its twin summits holds the crown.

subject: Kechries
summary: The eastern harbour of ancient Corinth, where the Apostle Paul once set sail and where archaeologists found glass panels packed in their original crates two millennia after they were made — part of a city now partly swallowed by the sea.

subject: Keegan Field
summary: A modest Yuma softball park that briefly hosted the San Diego Padres' first-ever spring training in 1969, including a game witnessed by Willie Mays, Willie McCovey, and Juan Marichal.

subject: Keeling Curve
summary: A single graph, plotted from data gathered on a Hawaiian volcano since 1958, provided the first undeniable proof that humanity was altering the composition of Earth's atmosphere.

subject: Keelung
summary: Taiwan's 'Rainy Port' - a city shaped by Spanish forts, British bombardments, French invasions, Japanese industry, and an annual Ghost Festival born from a clan war truce in 1855.

subject: Keelung Islet
summary: A volcanic island five kilometers off Keelung that locals once considered haunted, the military used for training, and typhoons keep trying to reclaim.

subject: Keepers of the Royal Genealogy
summary: Established by Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah in 1982, the Brunei History Centre houses the nation's archival memory -- including a replica of the Batu Tarsilah, the stone tablet tracing the royal lineage back to 1363.

subject: Keesler Air Force Base
summary: Named for a World War I aerial observer who fought until his final breath, this Biloxi installation has trained generations of airmen and is home to the legendary Hurricane Hunters.

subject: Kefalari (Argolis)
summary: A small Greek village whose very name comes from the mythic severed head of the Hydra — and whose ancient spring, sacred cave, and Orthodox chapel layer three thousand years of worship atop the same gushing water.

subject: Keighley
summary: A West Yorkshire mill town that signed the world's first recorded twinning agreement, lost a Hindenburg parcel down its high street, and gave its name to a market chartered in 1305.

subject: Keith, Moray
summary: A small town on the Isla where two grieving parents built a bridge so no one else would lose a child to the river, and where the Malt Whisky Trail begins.

subject: Kejetia Market
summary: West Africa's largest single market, where 20,000 vendors and 50,000 daily visitors sustain a century of Ashanti commerce beneath a ceiling woven with Adinkra symbols.

subject: Kelabit Highlands
summary: A remote plateau in Borneo's interior where one of Southeast Asia's smallest indigenous groups has cultivated wet rice for millennia, accessible only by small aircraft or multi-day jungle trek.

subject: Kelin
summary: An Iberian city that minted its own coins and may have ruled a whole plateau - and whose name still echoes, reshaped, in the town below.

subject: Kellogg (Idaho)
summary: A Silver Valley mining town that transformed from hosting the world's largest smelting complex to operating one of Idaho's premier ski resorts - but not before tragedy and toxic legacy reshaped its identity forever.

subject: Kelly Mine, Devon
summary: A Dartmoor mine that produced not iron ore but "shiny ore" - the flaky stuff used to make rust-resistant paint for the industrial age.

subject: Kelok 9
summary: A century-old mountain road of nine hairpin turns in West Sumatra, now spanned by a modern overpass that soars above the original switchbacks carved through the Barisan Mountains.

subject: Kelowna
summary: British Columbia's wine capital on Okanagan Lake, where summer brings beach crowds and water sports, winter brings world-class skiing at Big White, and vineyards cover the surrounding hills.

subject: Kelso Depot
summary: A 1923 Spanish Colonial Revival railroad depot in the Mojave Desert that Union Pacific tried to demolish in 1985, survived through preservation advocacy, and became the visitor center for Mojave National Preserve — now temporarily closed for renovation with a 2026 reopening expected.

subject: Kelso, California
summary: A desert ghost town whose name was chosen by hat draw from three railroad workers, which boomed to 2,000 people during World War II, was known in the 1970s as the town with no television signal, and whose Spanish Colonial Revival depot now serves as the Mojave National Preserve visitor center.

subject: Kempische Vaart
summary: A 19th-century Belgian canal built to turn heath into farmland - replaced by a bigger canal, mostly filled in, occasionally resurfacing.

subject: Kendal
summary: The Auld Grey Town - gateway to the Lake District, birthplace of Kendal Mint Cake, and the seat of Catherine Parr's family for generations.

story.title: Kendari: The Bay That Built a City

subject: Kendari
summary: A sheltered bay on Sulawesi's southeastern peninsula gave rise to a trading post, a colonial outpost, and eventually a provincial capital where the Tolaki people's rattan-bound traditions still shape civic life.

subject: Kenilworth
summary: A Warwickshire market town of 22,500 most famous for the ruined castle on its edge -- besieged for six months in 1266, host to Elizabeth I's most extravagant Tudor entertainment in 1575, and slighted by Parliament in 1649 because it was too powerful to leave intact.

story.title: Kennedy Space Center: Where Humanity Left Earth

subject: Kennedy Space Center
summary: The Florida launch complex where every American crewed spaceflight began - from Mercury through Apollo through the Shuttle, the place where rockets still rise and tourists can stand where astronauts walked to the Moon.

story.title: Kennesaw: The Town That Requires Gun Ownership

subject: Kennesaw
summary: The Georgia city that passed an ordinance in 1982 requiring every household to own a gun - a symbolic response to a Chicago suburb's handgun ban, unenforceable by design, yet still on the books 40 years later as America's strangest gun law.

subject: Kennywood's Thunderbolt
summary: The wooden roller coaster that drops into a ravine - built in 1924, radically redesigned in 1968 by burying the first drop in a hillside, and still one of the world's most terrifying rides because it uses terrain in ways modern coasters can't.

subject: Kenroku-en
summary: A garden that took thirteen generations to perfect, where feudal lords pursued the impossible: six contradictory qualities of landscape beauty in a single space.

story.title: Kensington Market: The Neighbourhood That Refused to Be Tamed

subject: Kensington Market
summary: A designated National Historic Site of Canada since 2006, Kensington Market has cycled through waves of Irish, Jewish, Portuguese, Caribbean, East Asian, and Latin American immigrants - each one layering its shops, flavors, and politics onto a few narrow blocks of Victorian row houses in downtown Toronto.

subject: Kensington Oval
summary: Barbados's premier cricket ground has hosted Test matches since 1930, three World Cup finals, and a Rihanna concert, all on an outfield built over ancient coral reef limestone in the heart of Bridgetown.

subject: Kent
summary: England's garden county has stood as the gateway to Europe for two millennia, its white cliffs facing the Continent across twenty miles of often-troubled water, its orchards and hop gardens feeding a nation.

subject: Kent County, Delaware
summary: Delaware's middle county - where Neil Armstrong's moonwalking suit was made, the state capital sits, and 33,000 acres of tidal marsh shelter the East Coast's largest snow goose flock.

subject: Kentucky Appalachians
summary: The mountains that gave America Loretta Lynn, Chris Stapleton, and a poet laureate who wrote about hill country with the precision of a botanist.

subject: Kep
summary: A small Cambodian seaside town where lunch is still swimming when you buy it, and the crab comes cooked in green Kampot pepper.

subject: Kep province
summary: Cambodia's smallest province holds the ruins of its most glamorous resort - and the truth about how those ruins were made is not the one usually told.

subject: Kepler Track
summary: A 60-kilometer circuit through Fiordland named after the astronomer Johannes Kepler, crossing lakeshores, ancient beech forests, and exposed alpine ridgelines where kea parrots shred the boots of anyone careless enough to leave them outside.

subject: Kepoi
summary: A small Greek colony on the Taman Peninsula whose name simply meant "the Gardens," and whose most famous connection runs, improbably, back to the greatest orator of ancient Athens.

subject: Kerameikos
summary: Northwest of the Acropolis lies the ancient potters' quarter and chief cemetery of Athens, where the word 'ceramic' was born and the city buried its dead along the Sacred Way.

subject: Kerkouane
summary: The only Phoenicio-Punic city to survive intact, a UNESCO World Heritage Site whose ancient name has been completely lost.

subject: Kerma culture
summary: One of Africa's oldest urban civilizations, centered in Upper Nubia from 2500 to 1500 BC - a populous, wealthy kingdom with its own architecture, metallurgy, and beliefs that rivaled Egypt on its own terms.

subject: Kermanshah
summary: An ancient city in the western Zagros where Sasanian kings carved their triumphs into cliff faces and Paleolithic humans left tools in caves, Kermanshah bridges deep time and Kurdish modernity.

subject: Keros
summary: On an uninhabited, off-limits island in the Cyclades, someone deliberately smashed hundreds of marble figurines four and a half thousand years ago - and carried the broken pieces here from across the Aegean.

subject: Kerr-Addison Mine
summary: Once the largest gold producer in North America, the Kerr-Addison Mine began with an Indigenous chief's stolen claim and ended with an environmental legacy that owners spent decades trying to avoid.

subject: Kerry Bog Village
summary: An open-air museum on the Ring of Kerry that recreates a 19th-century thatched village and helped save a small native pony from extinction.

subject: Kesh Ambush
summary: On a December morning in 1984, an SAS ambush near Kesh in County Fermanagh killed two IRA volunteers and one SAS soldier - and left a third volunteer to drown in the swollen Bannagh River.

subject: Kesh, County Fermanagh
summary: A small Fermanagh village named for a wicker bridge, where Iron Age ringforts, Lough Erne marina life, and a 1984 SAS ambush all share the same crossroads.

subject: Keswick
summary: The market town at the northern end of Derwentwater where the world's pencil industry was born, where Coleridge and Southey lived at Greta Hall, and where mountaineering quietly took its modern shape.

subject: Keta Taisha
summary: The foremost shrine of Noto Province, where a cormorant released at three in the morning on December 16 foretells the harvest, and a forest behind the sanctuary has been left untouched for centuries.

subject: Ketagalan Boulevard
summary: A 400-meter road in Taipei that has been renamed, protested on, and fought over more than any street in Taiwan -- because it leads straight to the seat of power.

subject: Keti Bandar Port
summary: A once-thriving port in the Indus delta, Keti Bandar has sunk three times, lost its river, and watched the sea swallow its land -- yet its fishermen still push their boats into the Arabian Sea each morning.

subject: Kettering
summary: A Northamptonshire shoe town from which an American pilot would later fly to Hiroshima, where Britain's second-oldest theme park has been spinning since 1921 and Weetabix has its global headquarters.

subject: Ketton Cement Works
summary: A Rutland quarry village where Jurassic limestone has been dug for five centuries first as building stone for Cambridge colleges and now as one-tenth of the United Kingdom's Portland cement supply.

subject: Keukenhof
summary: Seven million flower bulbs bloom each spring in what began as a medieval kitchen garden, now one of the world's largest flower displays.

subject: Keumalahayati
summary: A sixteenth-century Acehnese woman commanded a fleet, killed a Dutch expedition leader, forced the Netherlands to pay reparations, and negotiated with an envoy of Queen Elizabeth I -- though the details of her life remain tangled between history and legend.

subject: Keutsang Hermitage
summary: A hillside hermitage above Lhasa where a cave-dwelling abbot's retreat grew into the institution that identified the 14th Dalai Lama.

subject: Keweenaw Copper Country
summary: The first American mining boom - where prehistoric copper had been worked for 7,000 years before miners blasted the Keweenaw Peninsula in the 1840s, creating company towns, millionaires, and the deadliest disaster in Michigan history.

subject: Key Marco
summary: A shell mound island near Marco Island where a Smithsonian expedition in 1896 unearthed more than a thousand wooden artifacts from a muck pond -- including the famous Key Marco Cat -- the largest collection of prehistoric wooden objects ever found in the eastern United States.

story.title: Key West: The End of the Road and the Beginning of Everything

subject: Key West
summary: The Florida island where the United States runs out - ninety miles from Cuba, famous for sunsets, Hemingway's cats, and the tolerance that attracted everyone from pirates to presidents - where the Overseas Highway ends and Caribbean culture begins.

story.title: Key West: The End of the Road

subject: Key West
summary: The island at mile marker zero where Hemingway wrote, where Tennessee Williams lived, where Cuban cigar makers settled, and where being weird was normal before Austin discovered the concept.

subject: Keyport, Washington
summary: A tiny Kitsap Peninsula community of 554 people nicknamed 'Torpedo Town USA,' home to a Navy torpedo depot since before World War I and the Naval Undersea Museum.

subject: Keystone (Berkeley, California)
summary: A small Berkeley music club where Jerry Garcia played 206 times, punk found its East Bay foothold, and future legends performed before anyone knew their names.

subject: Khabarovsk
summary: At the confluence of the Amur and Ussuri rivers, where Manchu emperors, Cossack adventurers, and Japanese occupiers once contested the same ground, Khabarovsk has become the unlikely cultural capital of the Russian Far East — a city that wears its layered history gracefully and rewards visitors who make the journey.

subject: Kham
summary: The wild eastern frontier of Tibet -- a patchwork of warrior kingdoms, monastic centers, and trading routes through the Hengduan Mountains that may have inspired the legend of Shangri-La.

subject: Khammouane Province
summary: A Lao province built almost entirely of limestone, where rivers run underground for kilometres and a rodent family thought extinct for eleven million years turned up on a butcher's table.

subject: Khantia-Mansia
