summary: A vast Siberian territory that produces the majority of Russia's oil, while sheltering the ancient Khanty and Mansi cultures -- the closest living relatives of the Hungarians, separated by four thousand miles and a millennium.

subject: Khanty-Mansiysk
summary: A subarctic Siberian city of 100,000 that has hosted Chess Olympiads, Biathlon World Championships, and Deaflympics -- all funded by the oil wealth flowing beneath its frozen ground.

subject: Khaosan Road
summary: Khaosan Road is a 410-meter street in Bangkok's Bang Lamphu neighborhood that transformed from a rice market into the world's most famous backpacker strip, drawing up to 50,000 visitors daily.

subject: Kharga Oasis
summary: The southernmost of Egypt's New Valley oases was the last shaded stop on the Forty Days Road, a caravan route that carried gold, ivory, and enslaved human beings out of Africa.

subject: Khari Baoli
summary: Asia's largest wholesale spice market has operated in Old Delhi since the 17th century, built over a vanished stepwell whose salty water gave the street its name.

subject: Kharkiv
summary: Ukraine's second city rose at the meeting of three rivers, served as the country's first capital, and became a place where jazz festivals, sci-fi conventions, and one of Europe's grandest squares define a stubbornly living culture.

story.title: Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology

subject: Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology
summary: On the wooded northern edge of Kharkiv, a Soviet-era institute split its first atomic nucleus, nurtured a Nobel laureate, and then watched the secret police come for its finest minds.

subject: Kharkiv Philharmonic Society
summary: The grand hall where Rachmaninov played, where Ukraine saw its first movie and heard its first radio broadcast, and where an orchestra a century old still holds the city's musical memory.

subject: Khartoum
summary: Three cities fused at the place where two Niles meet, stitched together by bridges and the patience of people who keep showing up.

subject: Khartoum
summary: A city founded for war and remade for trade, where every generation rebuilds on the rubble of the last.

subject: Khartoum North
summary: The industrial third of Sudan's triangular capital, Khartoum North sits on the east bank of the White Nile at its confluence with the Blue, and held more than a million people before war remade it.

subject: Khartoum State
summary: Sudan's smallest state by area and its most populous holds eight million people, three rivers, two national museums, and a name that may come from the Arabic word for an elephant's trunk.

subject: Khatumo State
summary: Born from the Dhulbahante clan's refusal to be governed by either Somaliland or Puntland, Khatumo State is one of the most contested political entities in the Horn of Africa -- a story of clan politics, armed resistance, and the search for self-determination.

subject: Khaybar
summary: An ancient date-palm oasis ringed by black lava fields, whose buried Bronze Age town is rewriting the early history of Arabia.

subject: Khe Sanh Combat Base
summary: Built on a plateau where a French-era airstrip met ancient red clay, Khe Sanh became the most watched piece of ground in the Vietnam War — and today it grows coffee.

subject: Khiyaban
summary: One of Tabriz's oldest neighborhoods shelters the Blue Mosque, a revolutionary heritage, and streets once lined with poplars and water canals -- a district where the Iranian Constitutional Revolution found its fiercest fighters.

subject: Khlong Yai
summary: A Thai town on a two-kilometre sliver of coast that takes nearly five metres of rain a year - and for seven years sheltered more Cambodian refugees than it had residents.

subject: Khmer Empire
summary: For six centuries, the Khmer Empire dominated mainland Southeast Asia from its hydraulic capital at Angkor, building the largest pre-industrial city on Earth before drought and invasion brought it down.

subject: Khmer Rouge Tribunal
summary: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia spent over two decades pursuing justice for the Cambodian genocide, ultimately convicting only three senior Khmer Rouge leaders before closing in 2022.

subject: Khok Phanom Di
summary: A prehistoric mound in central Thailand where 20 generations of coastal dwellers left behind seven meters of cultural material -- including a master potter buried with over 120,000 shell beads.

subject: Kholodnyi Yar
summary: An ancient oak forest in central Ukraine hides more than 150 archaeological sites - and a memory of rebellion so persistent that a self-declared republic once made its stand beneath these trees.

subject: Khor Fakkan
summary: The 'Creek of Two Jaws' -- an exclave of Sharjah on the UAE's east coast with 3,000 years of settlement, a Portuguese fortress, a drowned village beneath a dam, and the region's only natural deep-sea port.

subject: Khorasan
summary: Iran's northeastern frontier - where the name itself means 'where the sun arrives from' - is a crossroads of Persian, Turkmen, Afghan, and Arab cultures, home to the holy city of Mashhad and the ancient Silk Road corridor that connected Iran to Central Asia.

subject: Khortytsia
summary: The largest island on the Dnieper has been home to people for five thousand years and became the legendary heartland of the Zaporozhian Cossacks.

subject: Khotiv Hillfort
summary: On a plateau south of Kyiv, a rampart raised 2,500 years ago by Scythian-era farmers still traces the outline of a town that traded with the ancient Greek islands.

subject: Khreshchatyk
summary: Kyiv's main street was blown apart by some of the longest-range radio-controlled bombs used in the war, rebuilt from rubble, and has since become the stage where the whole nation gathers.

story.title: Khudafarin Bridges: The Crossing God Created

subject: Khudafarin Bridges
summary: Two ancient arch bridges straddling the Aras River at the Iran-Azerbaijan border, whose origins are so old and so often destroyed and rebuilt that legend says only God could have made them.

subject: Khunjerab Pass
summary: The highest paved international border crossing on Earth, where the Karakoram Highway threads between Pakistan and China at 4,693 meters and drivers switch from the left side of the road to the right.

subject: Khyber Pass
summary: The most famous mountain pass in the world has funneled conquerors, traders, and refugees between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent for over two millennia -- and the Pashtun clans who guard it have charged every one of them a toll.

subject: Kibiro
summary: Clinging to the shore of Lake Albert at the bottom of the Western Rift Valley, the village of Kibiro has sustained itself for centuries through a singular craft: women extracting salt from the earth itself.

subject: Kick 'em Jenny
summary: The Caribbean's most active submarine volcano lurks 185 meters beneath the waves north of Grenada, erupting at least fourteen times since 1939 and capable of sinking ships with nothing more than bubbles.

subject: Kidd Mine
summary: The world's deepest base metal mine plunges over 3,000 meters below the surface near Timmins, Ontario, where it holds two astonishing records: the deepest accessible non-marine point on Earth and the oldest known flowing water on the planet.

subject: Kidderminster
summary: The Worcestershire carpet town that produced the Penny Black, Led Zeppelin's frontman, and one of the first Black African autobiographies published in Britain.

subject: Kidman's Tree of Knowledge
summary: A single coolibah on Glengyle Station, said to be where a runaway boy named Sidney Kidman dreamed up a cattle empire that would one day cover 3.5 percent of Australia.

subject: Kidwelly
summary: A Carmarthenshire town anchored by one of the best-preserved Norman castles in Wales, and a field where in 1136 a Welsh princess led an army against the Normans.

subject: Kielder Water
summary: The largest artificial lake in the United Kingdom, built in the 1970s for an industrial future that never arrived, and now surrounded by Europe's largest planted forest.

subject: Kievan Rus'
summary: A thousand years ago Kyiv was the seat of a medieval superpower whose princesses became queens across Europe and whose choice of faith still echoes today.

subject: Kifissia
summary: Athens has always escaped its own summers by fleeing north to Kifissia - a green, well-watered suburb of belle-epoque villas, old-money families, and the city's natural-history museum.

subject: Kigali
summary: Rwanda's capital city sprawls across a constellation of green hills, a place where one of Africa's darkest chapters has given way to one of its most ambitious urban reinventions.

subject: Kiix-in
summary: An ancient Huu-ay-aht village whose name echoes the waves that have crashed against its rocky shore since time immemorial.

subject: Kilbirnie
summary: A small Garnock Valley town that grew from three houses to a steel-making centre, gave the Kilbirnie 'blasties' nickname to a Burns poem, and once hosted Gerry and the Pacemakers.

subject: Kilbrittain
summary: A West Cork village with a castle dated to 1035, the skeleton of a 59-foot fin whale in its park, and a 15th-century manuscript that once contained Marco Polo's travels translated into Irish.

subject: Kilcommon
summary: A north Mayo parish of two peninsulas named for giant brothers in folktale, where two-billion-year-old gneiss meets blanket bog at the Atlantic's edge, and where Ireland's last red-necked phalaropes still breed.

subject: Kilcrea Friary
summary: A roofless 15th-century friary in the Bride valley where the body of Art O Laoghaire lies - the man whose murder produced the greatest lament in the Irish language.

subject: Kilcullen
summary: On the River Liffey in County Kildare - where Vikings raided in 936 and 944, the Gordon Bennett Cup ran through in 1903, and a six-arch bridge from the 1310s still spans the river.

subject: Kildonan Lifeboat Station
summary: On the south-east shore of Arran, a Victorian-era lifeboat station saved sailors from the gales of the Firth of Clyde for thirty-one years before falling quiet as steam replaced sail.

subject: Kilgarvan
summary: A Kerry village of 264 souls beside the Roughty River, home to a famous political dynasty, a vintage motor museum, and the largest onshore wind farm in Ireland.

story.title: Kilimanjaro: The Snows That Hemingway Wrote About Are Disappearing

subject: Kilimanjaro
summary: Where Africa's highest peak rises 19,341 feet from tropical savanna, its glaciers shrinking 80% since 1912 - the iconic snows that inspired Hemingway may vanish entirely by 2040.

subject: Kilkee
summary: A Clare seaside town with a horseshoe bay, a tradition of cliff-diving, and the shipwrecks of three ships that sank within fifty years of each other.

subject: Killaloe
summary: A Shannon-side village where a thirteen-arch bridge has stood since 1825 and where Brian Boru, High King of Ireland, was likely born.

subject: Killalpaninna Mission
summary: On the Dieri homelands near Cooper Creek, a remote Lutheran mission produced the first complete Bible translation into an Australian Aboriginal language, even as it reshaped the lives of the people it set out to convert.

subject: Killarney
summary: Where Brian Boru learned to read, Queen Victoria came to gawk, and the lakes still turn impossibly blue beneath the Reeks.

subject: Killeshandra
summary: A Scottish Plantation linen town with Huguenot weavers, a 17th-century church called "arguably the finest Restoration building in Ulster," and the founding creamery of what is now Lakeland Dairies — Ireland's second largest dairy co-operative.

subject: Killin
summary: A historic conservation village at the head of Loch Tay, where the Falls of Dochart tumble through a stone-arched bridge and the last native speakers of Perthshire Gaelic recently fell silent.

subject: Killing of Alex Nieto
summary: A security guard eating dinner on a Bernal Heights bench was shot by police who mistook his taser for a firearm, igniting a citywide reckoning with gentrification, policing, and who belongs in San Francisco's changing neighborhoods.

subject: Killing of Alfred Olango
summary: Alfred Okwera Olango had survived the Lord's Resistance Army and years in refugee camps before arriving in the United States. He was shot and killed by El Cajon police in September 2016 while holding an e-cigarette.

subject: Killing of Amadou Diallo
summary: In 1999, four NYPD plainclothes officers fired 41 shots at an unarmed Guinean immigrant reaching for his wallet on a Bronx doorstep, igniting a national reckoning over racial profiling and police use of force.

subject: Killing of Banko Brown
summary: The fatal shooting of a homeless transgender man over suspected candy shoplifting outside a San Francisco Walgreens exposed the city's intersecting crises of homelessness, policing, and justice.

subject: Killing of Brenda Sue Brown
summary: An eleven-year-old girl was murdered in Shelby, North Carolina in 1966. Her sisters spent forty years pushing for the case to be reopened, and their persistence eventually broke it.

subject: Killing of Eleanor Bumpurs
summary: In 1984, NYPD officers sent to evict a 66-year-old mentally ill woman from her Bronx public housing apartment shot and killed her with a 12-gauge shotgun, sparking reforms in how police handle encounters with emotionally disturbed people.

story.title: Killing of João Alberto Silveira Freitas

subject: Killing of João Alberto Silveira Freitas
summary: On the eve of Black Consciousness Day in 2020, a Black man named João Alberto Freitas was beaten to death by security guards in a Porto Alegre supermarket, and a nation that had long denied its racism was forced to look.

subject: Killing of Keith Lamont Scott
summary: On September 20, 2016, Keith Lamont Scott - a 43-year-old Black father of seven waiting for his son's school bus - was shot and killed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg police, igniting days of protests that demanded the city see what it had done.

subject: Killing of Lasa and Zabala
summary: Two young Basque men were seized in France, tortured, and buried in quicklime in the hills of Alicante - among the first killings by a death squad later traced to figures inside the Spanish state.

subject: Killing of Mark Duggan
summary: On a summer evening in Tottenham in 2011, two police shots ended the life of a young father — and the questions that followed have never fully been answered.

subject: Killing of Marvin Gaye
summary: On April 1, 1984 — the day before his 45th birthday — soul legend Marvin Gaye was shot and killed by his father, Marvin Gay Sr., at the family home in Los Angeles. The killing ended the life of one of American music's most transformative artists.

subject: Killing of Muammar Gaddafi
summary: On 20 October 2011, Muammar Gaddafi was dragged from a drainage pipe in his hometown of Sirte and killed by rebel fighters, ending 42 years of authoritarian rule and raising difficult questions about justice and vengeance in revolutionary Libya.

subject: Killing of Pro-Biafra Protesters (2015–2016)
summary: Between 2015 and 2016, Nigerian security forces killed scores of unarmed protesters across southeastern Nigeria who were demanding the restoration of the Republic of Biafra, drawing international condemnation from Amnesty International and the European Union.

subject: Killing of Rayshard Brooks
summary: A routine DUI stop at a Wendy's drive-through in south Atlanta escalated into a fatal police shooting that reignited national protests in the summer of 2020.

subject: Killing of Robert Hamill
summary: A 25-year-old Catholic man beaten to death in Portadown in 1997 while four armed police officers sat in a Land Rover twenty feet away.

subject: Killing of Trayvon Martin
summary: The 2012 shooting of a 17-year-old in a Sanford, Florida gated community became a national reckoning on race, self-defense law, and policing, and gave rise to the phrase 'Black lives matter.'

subject: Killingworth
summary: A North Tyneside town where George Stephenson built his first locomotive in 1814, launching the age of steam from a colliery workshop behind his cottage on Lime Road.

subject: Killybegs
summary: Ireland's largest fishing port, where Spanish Armada survivors were repaired and resupplied in 1588 before sailing to disaster off Antrim.

subject: Kilmainham
summary: A Dublin suburb built on layers - an early Christian monastery, the largest Viking cemetery in western Europe outside Scandinavia, a Knights Hospitaller priory, and the gaol where the 1916 leaders were shot.

subject: Kilmarnock
summary: An Ayrshire town that taught the world to drink Scotch, gave it penicillin, and quietly produced two Nobel laureates from a single school.

subject: Kilmarnock
summary: The Ayrshire town that printed the first collection of Robert Burns's poetry in 1786, then spent two centuries inventing, building and losing the industries that defined it.

subject: Kilmaurs
summary: An Ayrshire village whose coat of arms tells the story of forks - the cutlery once made here, and the hay-fork that allegedly saved a future king of Scots.

subject: Kilmovee
summary: A County Mayo parish where a saint's staff is said to have struck three wells from the earth, and where a flat ten-kilometre race draws runners from across Ireland.

subject: Kilnsea
summary: A tiny village at the base of Spurn Head whose church, public houses and graveyard have repeatedly fallen into the North Sea, and whose name in Old English means kiln by the lake.

subject: Kilrush
summary: A Clare port town built by a Dutch-Irish landlord family, scarred by Famine evictions, and now watched over by a resident pod of bottlenose dolphins.

subject: Kiltimagh
summary: The Oxford English Dictionary credits this small Mayo town with giving Ireland the word "culchie" - and the closed railway station has been reborn as a museum, a sculpture park and a velorail that lets visitors pedal seven kilometres of disused track.

subject: Kilwa Sultanate
summary: A medieval East African trading empire whose coins reached Australia, whose pilots outnavigated the Portuguese, and whose coconut-coir ships carried gold across the Indian Ocean for five centuries.

subject: Kilwinning
summary: An Ayrshire town that claims the founding seat of Scottish Freemasonry, an annual medieval archery contest, and the ruins of one of Scotland's most extravagant nineteenth-century castles.

subject: Kilyos
summary: A Black Sea beach village at Istanbul's northern edge, where a 14th-century Genoese castle watches over sand dunes and breaking waves just 40 kilometers from one of the world's greatest cities.

subject: Kim Bồng woodworking village
summary: Across the Thu Bon River from Hội An's lantern-lit streets, Kim Bồng village has shaped wood into art, boats, and imperial palaces since the 15th century.

subject: Kimbe
summary: A young oil palm town rides the crescent of a coral-rich bay, where more than sixty percent of the Indo-Pacific's coral species crowd into the water offshore.

subject: Kimberley (Western Australia)
summary: Australia's last great wilderness — a region the size of California where 65,000 years of Aboriginal culture, billion-year-old rocks, and one of the most dramatic monsoon climates on Earth come together in the remote north of Western Australia.

subject: Kimitoön
summary: An island municipality of some three thousand islands in the Archipelago Sea, where an ironworks ran for 326 unbroken years, a newspaper baron planted fifty thousand apple trees, and a closed military skerry reopened as a national park.

subject: Kimmeridge Lifeboat Station
summary: A wooden boathouse, three boats named Mary Heape, eighteen lives saved across twenty-seven years, and one death that started it all.

subject: Kimmerikon
summary: On the flank of a lonely Crimean mountain stood a Greek fortress city with walls thick enough to stop the Scythians, until Goths, pirates, and time reduced it to stones on a hillside.

subject: Kimolos
summary: Kimolos is a small chalk-white Cycladic island whose silver-tinted cliffs gave the ancient world its finest fuller's earth, and whose mushroom-shaped volcanic stone and unhurried pace make it one of the Aegean's most quietly remarkable places.

subject: Kinburn Spit
summary: A ten-kilometer ribbon of sand and salt marsh where seven million birds pass each year and orchids grow a hundred to the square meter, a fragile wilderness at the mouth of the Dnieper.

subject: Kinclaven Station
summary: A cattle run the size of a small country, stitched together from older leases on the dry western rim of the Nullarbor, and named for a Scottish village half a world away.

subject: Kinderdijk windmills
summary: Nineteen historic windmills stand sentinel along the Dutch waterways, a testament to centuries of human ingenuity battling an unrelenting sea.

subject: Kindia
summary: A railway town at the foot of the Fouta Djallon, Kindia gathers waterfalls, banana plantations, and one of colonial science's most unsettling experiments.

subject: King George Square
summary: Brisbane's grand civic forecourt, where bronze lions guard City Hall and a century of protests, processions, and royal visits has crossed the paving.

subject: King Street Station
summary: Seattle's King Street Station survived decades of botched modernizations that buried its grand interior under drop ceilings and Formica, only to be reborn in a $55 million restoration that revealed the beauty hidden beneath.

subject: King's Lynn
summary: The Hanseatic port where Tuesday and Saturday markets still trade in brown shrimp the way they have for seven centuries.

subject: King's Lynn
summary: England's most important port in the 14th century, the first English town bombed from the air, and the place where Margery Kempe wrote the first autobiography in English.

subject: Kingdom of Afghanistan
summary: From 1926 to 1973, Afghanistan's monarchy navigated modernization, Cold War rivalries, and tribal resistance -- until a cousin's bloodless coup ended centuries of royal rule.

subject: Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia
summary: In 1860 a French lawyer declared himself king of the Mapuche, a story usually told as farce, but for the Mapuche leaders who backed him it was a serious gamble to keep their land.

subject: Kingdom of Ardra
summary: The kingdom that gave birth to three nations -- Allada, Dahomey, and Porto-Novo -- still maintains a non-sovereign monarchy in modern Benin, a living thread connecting 12th-century Aja migrations to the Haitian Revolution.

subject: Kingdom of Chiang Mai
summary: For over a century, the Kingdom of Chiang Mai navigated between Burmese invaders and Siamese overlords -- a teak-rich northern polity whose rulers forged dynasties, repelled armies, and ultimately lost their autonomy to Bangkok's centralizing ambitions.

subject: Kingdom of Corsica (1736)
summary: A German adventurer talked Corsican rebels into crowning him king, ruled for eight months, fled his creditors across Europe, and eventually died penniless in London -- bequeathing his kingdom to the men he owed money.

subject: Kingdom of Dagbon
summary: Ghana's oldest traditional kingdom, founded by the Dagomba people in the 15th century, spanning 8,000 square miles of savannah and preserving its history through the rhythmic drumming of the Lunsi court historians.

subject: Kingdom of Derge
summary: A Tibetan kingdom in Kham that traced its lineage to the 7th century and became a major center of Buddhist scholarship, printing, metalwork, and the ecumenical Rime movement before falling to Chinese control in the early 20th century.

subject: Kingdom of Greece
summary: For most of 140 years Greece was a kingdom ruled by imported royalty - a state born in 1832, driven by the dream of reuniting the Greek world, and ended at last by a referendum in 1974.

subject: Kingdom of Hormuz
summary: A medieval maritime kingdom so wealthy it inspired Milton, Marvell, and Marco Polo -- built on salt and sea trade at the mouth of the Persian Gulf.

subject: Kingdom of Kandy
summary: The last independent Sinhalese kingdom survived over three centuries of European colonialism through guerrilla warfare, mountain fortification, and sheer defiance before falling to internal betrayal in 1815.

story.title: Kingdom of Kubang Pasu Darul Qiyam

subject: Kingdom of Kubang Pasu Darul Qiyam
summary: A short-lived Malay kingdom born from one nobleman's refusal to become a Siamese puppet, Kubang Pasu existed for just twenty years in northern Kedah before vanishing back into the state that created it.

subject: Kingdom of Kurdistan
summary: A short-lived Kurdish state declared in Sulaymaniyah after the Ottoman collapse, where a Sufi sheikh crowned himself king and defied the British Empire from 1921 to 1924.

subject: Kingdom of Loango
summary: A pre-colonial Central African state that controlled trade on the coast north of the Congo River for three centuries, resisting European encroachment through shrewd diplomacy and commercial competition.

subject: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang
summary: Born from the fracture of the great Lao kingdom of Lan Xang in 1707, Luang Phrabang endured two and a half centuries as a small monarchy caught between Burmese, Siamese, and French ambitions before merging into the modern nation of Laos.

subject: Kingdom of Majorca
summary: Stitched together from islands and distant mainland scraps, wedged between France and Aragon, the Kingdom of Majorca was built to be awkward — and its long, precarious life is the real surprise.

subject: Kingdom of Mapungubwe
summary: Southern Africa's first state, a thousand-year-old kingdom at the confluence of the Shashe and Limpopo rivers where gold-adorned elites ruled from a hilltop, trade routes reached the Indian Ocean, and the discovery was suppressed because it contradicted apartheid mythology.

subject: Kingdom of Mrauk U
summary: A kingdom on the Arakan coast that flourished from 1429 to 1785, where Buddhist kings bore Islamic titles, Portuguese pirates served as mercenaries, and a capital city of 160,000 rivaled the splendor of Venice.

subject: Kingdom of Murcia
summary: For nearly six centuries there was a Kingdom of Murcia, a realm that stretched well beyond today's region yet never crowned a king of its own, existing as one of the many kingdoms folded inside the Crown of Castile.

subject: Kingdom of Nagpur
summary: A Maratha kingdom built on Gond foundations, where Bengali mothers still sing lullabies about the terror of the Bargi cavalry raids three centuries later.

subject: Kingdom of Nicoya
summary: An indigenous Chorotega kingdom on Costa Rica's Nicoya Peninsula that flourished for over a millennium before Spanish contact, leaving behind polychrome ceramics and jade that define the region's identity today.

subject: Kingdom of Pajang
summary: A short-lived but pivotal 16th-century Javanese sultanate whose eighteen years of existence bridged the fall of Demak and the rise of Mataram, the greatest Islamic kingdom in Java.

story.title: Kingdom of Polonnaruwa: The Island Empire That Reached Across the Sea

subject: Kingdom of Polonnaruwa
summary: From 1070 to 1232, the Kingdom of Polonnaruwa unified Sri Lanka and projected military power across the Indian Ocean, reaching its zenith under the builder-king Parakramabahu I before collapsing into faction and foreign invasion.

subject: Kingdom of Prussia
summary: For 217 years a sandy north German state with a disciplined army outmanoeuvred its larger neighbours, unified Germany behind it — and then, in 1918, vanished.

subject: Kingdom of Saxony
summary: Saxony chose Napoleon. Saxony chose Austria. Twice the kingdom backed losing sides — and twice it survived, by being too rich and too cultured to dismantle.

subject: Kingdom of Sefwi
summary: In Ghana's western forests, refugees from Akan wars built a kingdom whose very name means 'the war is over' -- and whose rivalries have never quite ended.

story.title: Kingdom of Tallo: Two Kings, One People

subject: Kingdom of Tallo
summary: For four centuries, the Kingdom of Tallo stood as the quieter half of a formidable dual monarchy in South Sulawesi -- the voice behind the throne that helped build an empire stretching from Sulawesi to Timor, before the Dutch shattered it all.

subject: Kingdom of Tungning
summary: Born from a pirate lord's defiance of the Qing dynasty, the Kingdom of Tungning became the first ethnic Han Chinese state in Taiwan and held the island for twenty-two years before falling to an admiral with a personal vendetta.

subject: Kingdom of Vientiane
summary: Born from the fracture of the great Lan Xang empire in 1707, the Kingdom of Vientiane endured as a pawn between Siam, Burma, and Vietnam until its obliteration in 1828.

subject: Kingdom of Warri
summary: Founded around 1480 by a Benin prince who escaped his father's court inside an iroko-wood ark, the Kingdom of Warri became one of West Africa's earliest Christian monarchies and a major Niger Delta trading power whose Itsekiri rulers dealt with Portuguese merchants a full century before the British arrived.

subject: Kingdom of Whydah
summary: A powerful West African coastal kingdom whose name endures in a bird, a pirate ship, and the Beninese city of Ouidah -- but whose deepest legacy is the more than one million enslaved people shipped from its shores to the Americas.

subject: Kingdome
summary: Seattle's ill-fated concrete dome stood for just 24 years before becoming the largest building ever demolished by implosion, and King County kept paying for it fifteen years after it was gone.

subject: Kingsport, Tennessee
summary: America's only planned industrial city designed by John Nolen in 1916, built around Eastman Chemical and the place where Daniel Boone began the Wilderness Road, the Long Island iced tea may have been invented, and the Santa Train has run for over eight decades.

subject: Kingston upon Hull
summary: A Yorkshire port city of 800 years of seafaring, civil-war defiance, abolitionist conscience, and a stubborn cultural rebirth that earned it UK City of Culture in 2017.

subject: Kingswear
summary: The village across the river from Dartmouth - a steam railway terminus, a medieval pilgrim landing, and the launch point for a Maine fishing town.

subject: Kinlochbervie
summary: A small fishing village at the end of a single-track Highland road, where Sandwood Bay, a Spitfire wreck, and a Victoria Cross winner all share the same windswept parish.

subject: Kinlochleven
summary: The first village in the world to have every house wired for electricity, built around an aluminium smelter at the head of Loch Leven, and now a centre for ice climbing and West Highland Way walkers.

subject: Kinlochleven Hydroelectric Scheme
summary: An early-twentieth-century hydro scheme built by three thousand Irish navvies in squalid conditions to power an aluminium smelter, still generating electricity into the National Grid more than a century later.

subject: Kinsale
summary: A sheltered Cork harbour where Spanish armies landed, kings fled in disgrace, and the man who inspired Robinson Crusoe set sail for the Pacific.

subject: Kinsale Lifeboat Station
summary: The RNLI lifeboat at Adams Quay carries the longest name in the British and Irish fleet, given by an English donor with bowel cancer who liked to remind everyone: better a bag than a box.

subject: Kinsevere
summary: A Congolese copper mine whose 61 million dollars bankrolled a governor's 2007 election and whose current owners are now investing 600 million more to extract cobalt for the world's batteries.

subject: Kinshasa
summary: The largest city in Africa by population, Kinshasa is a sprawling, chaotic capital where Congolese rumba spills from nightclubs, traffic jams last hours, and the Congo River separates two national capitals by barely a kilometer.

subject: Kintampo waterfalls
summary: A three-stage waterfall on the Pumpum River in Ghana's Bono East Region, once called Sanders Falls, that drops 70 metres through dense forest and reopened in 2019 with canopy walkways after a deadly tree collapse.

subject: Kinvara
summary: A Galway Bay sea-port village watched over by a 16th-century tower house, with Cromwellian massacres, agrarian rebels, and John Prine in its history.

subject: Kirikongo
summary: On a bend of the Mouhoun River in Burkina Faso, thirteen earthen mounds hold seventeen centuries of one community's life, death, and quiet revolutions.

subject: Kirjurinluoto
summary: An island the Kokemäenjoki built after Pori was founded, which went from tar-barrel yard to English landscape park to a delta that holds eighty thousand people for a jazz festival.

subject: Kirk Michael
summary: A west-coast agricultural village in the Isle of Man, once host to early Tynwald sittings, later patronised by Fletcher Christian, and today briefly the fastest place on the TT course.

subject: Kirkcaldy
summary: The Fife coastal town where Adam Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations, where linoleum once perfumed the streets, and where a four-mile esplanade earned the nickname Lang Toun.

subject: Kirkcudbright
summary: The Artists' Town of Galloway: a former royal burgh where the Glasgow Boys and Scottish Colourists settled, the saint's bones once rested, and brown road signs proudly announce the trade.

subject: Kirkcudbright Lifeboat Station
summary: A Galloway lifeboat station founded in 1862, where crews once rowed sixteen hours through Solway swell to collect a new motorised boat.

subject: Kirkcudbright Tolbooth
summary: A 17th-century Scottish tolbooth that held witches, Covenanters and John Paul Jones, now an art gallery on the Artists' Town's high street.

subject: Kirkcudbrightshire
summary: The Stewartry: a historic Scottish county of granite hills, smuggling coast and one of the world's first integrated sewer engineers - administered by a steward, not a sheriff, for 600 years.

subject: Kirkinner
summary: A quiet Machars village whose 10th-century carved cross and macabre wedding-night tragedy gave the world the plot of Walter Scott's Bride of Lammermoor.

subject: Kirkkokari
summary: A third of a hectare of stone barely a metre above the water, reached by rowboat — and the only Roman Catholic pilgrimage destination in modern Finland.

subject: Kirkland
summary: Once dreaming of being the 'Pittsburgh of the West,' this lakeside city reinvented itself as an art-filled waterfront community where the Seattle skyline glitters across the water.

subject: Kirkmaiden
summary: The most southerly parish in Scotland, Kirkmaiden stretches from Iron Age ramparts at the Mull of Galloway to a saint whose name, gender and origin remain in dispute.

subject: Kirkwall
summary: The capital of Orkney, a working port town built around a red sandstone cathedral and the ruins of palaces, with two whisky distilleries and a Norse soul.

subject: Kirthar Mountains
summary: The mountain range that divides Sindh from Balochistan holds 21 prehistoric sites, rare Chinkara gazelles, and a peak named after a man who buried his loyal dog at the summit.

subject: Kiruna mine
summary: The largest underground iron ore mine in the world has produced over 950 million tonnes since 1898 -- and forced an entire Arctic city to relocate to avoid falling into the hole.

subject: Kisangani
summary: At the end of the navigable Congo, a million-person city sits stranded in the rainforest - a place of ancient fishing weirs, colonial ghosts, and wars that scarred its streets.

subject: Kisenge
summary: A small village in the far south of Lualaba Province, once a manganese-mining town on the Benguela Railway, now a quieter place at the Congolese-Angolan frontier.

subject: Kiso Mountains
summary: Japan's Central Alps, where a ropeway with the greatest height difference in the country lifts visitors to a glacial cirque carved 20,000 years ago, and where cutting a single cypress tree once carried a death sentence.

subject: Kitadani Formation
summary: Japan's primary source of Cretaceous-aged dinosaur fossils, a layer of 115-to-127-million-year-old rock near Katsuyama that has yielded everything from raptor teeth to the country's first pterosaur footprints.

subject: Kitezh
summary: Russia's Atlantis: a legendary city said to have sunk beneath Lake Svetloyar rather than fall to the Mongol invasion, its bells still ringing under the water for those pure enough to hear them.

subject: Kittelfjäll
summary: A Swedish Lapland ski village of sixty-odd residents where the finest descents were carved not by machines but by a mountain slowly falling apart.

subject: Kitterland
summary: A small uninhabited islet in the Calf Sound, remembered in Manx folk memory for the salvage explosion of 1852 that left twenty-two widows and seventy-seven children.

story.title: Kitty Hawk: Where Humans First Flew

subject: Kitty Hawk
summary: The North Carolina beach where the Wright Brothers achieved powered flight on December 17, 1903 - 12 seconds that changed human history, witnessed by five men and preserved in a photograph that became the world's most important aviation image.

subject: Kitwe
summary: Zambia's second city, a Copperbelt mining town founded in 1936 that produced two presidents, a Pritzker Prize-winning architect, and the deepest cobalt mine in the country.

subject: Kiyamachi Street
summary: A Kyoto street born from a 1611 canal excavation that evolved from lumber warehouses to samurai hideouts to one of the city's liveliest nightlife corridors.

subject: Kiên Giang province
summary: Vietnam abolished Kiên Giang in 2025, but the name still runs along its coast, its islands and every bottle of Phú Quốc fish sauce.

subject: Kladas
summary: A small village five kilometers north of Sparta, Kladas takes its name from a medieval Greek military hero and sits quietly between Taygetos and Parnonas, where olive groves, bicycle lanes, and the occasional fog define daily life on the Spartan plain.

subject: Klahoose
summary: Descendants of the Great Flood survivors in Coast Salish oral tradition, the Klahoose people have maintained their connection to Cortes Island and the deep mainland inlets for millennia, anchoring their modern community at Squirrel Cove.

subject: Klamath Basin
summary: A watershed spanning Oregon and California where an ancient lake three times larger than the Salton Sea once spread across the high desert, and 3.7 million birds still migrate through its remnant wetlands each year.

subject: Klein Constantia
summary: A Cape Town wine estate whose famous dessert wine was praised by Jane Austen, rhapsodized by Baudelaire, and reportedly served to Napoleon on his deathbed -- all from vines first planted in 1685.

subject: Klein-Venedig
summary: A German banking dynasty bought a colony in Venezuela from the Holy Roman Emperor to settle a debt, then spent eighteen years chasing El Dorado through jungles and mountains until betrayal and execution ended the strangest chapter in the colonization of the Americas.

subject: Kleine Dommel
summary: A modest Brabant brook that Van Gogh painted twice, that Dutch engineers straightened in the 1960s and lovingly un-straightened in the 2000s, and that now floods on purpose to save Geldrop.

subject: Klitmøller
summary: Three watermills gave this village its name and a century of trade with Norway; when the sea took the trade away, the wind eventually brought the world back as "Cold Hawaii".

subject: Klondike Gold Rush Sites
summary: The last great gold rush - where 100,000 prospectors headed for Canada's Yukon in 1897-98, climbing the Chilkoot Pass with a year's supplies on their backs, only to find most claims already staked.

story.title: Kluane: Canada's Secret Everest Training Ground

subject: Kluane
summary: The Yukon wilderness where Canada's highest peak hides behind other mountains - Mount Logan rises 19,551 feet but remains invisible from any road, protected by the largest non-polar ice field on Earth.

subject: Klyuchevskaya Sopka
summary: The highest active volcano in Eurasia, Klyuchevskaya Sopka has erupted 110 times in the Holocene and remains so dangerous that its first successful ascent was not repeated for over a century.

story.title: Knights Ferry: Murder, a President's Brother, and the Town That Refused to Disappear

subject: Knights Ferry
summary: A Gold Rush town founded by a man killed in a gunfight months after establishing its ferry, Knights Ferry survived murder, flood, and the loss of the county seat to preserve a remarkable collection of 1850s buildings.

subject: Knights of Saint Columbanus
summary: An Irish Catholic fraternal order founded in 1915 Belfast that wielded quiet influence in twentieth-century Irish public life - sometimes for the poor at Christmas dinner, sometimes for tighter laws on contraception.

subject: Knightstown, County Kerry
summary: A planned 19th-century village at the eastern tip of Valentia Island, where 244 people now live in the place that once received the first transatlantic telegraph.

subject: Knock (Ireland)
summary: A village of 1,000 people in County Mayo where Mary Bryne saw three silent figures on a wet August evening in 1879 - and where a priest later argued Ireland into building an international airport.

subject: Knock, County Mayo
summary: A village whose Irish name changed after 1879 from "the hill" to "hill of the Virgin Mary," and which a determined parish priest named Monsignor James Horan transformed in the late 20th century by building a 10,000-seat basilica and lobbying an international airport into existence.

subject: Knockando Woolmill
summary: A working Speyside woolmill operating since at least 1784, saved from collapse by a £3.3 million heritage restoration, where the same Victorian machinery still spins yarn into tartan.

subject: Knocktopher
summary: A small Kilkenny village whose Carmelite friars were dissolved in 1542 and then quietly came back in 1735 -- and have stayed ever since.

subject: Knossos
summary: The labyrinth of myth was real - and the man who excavated it poured concrete walls back into the Bronze Age, in choices archaeologists are still arguing about.

story.title: Knoxville: Gateway to the Smokies Where Cormac McCarthy Grew Up

subject: Knoxville
summary: Tennessee's third-largest city where the Tennessee River bends beneath the Great Smoky Mountains, where the 1982 World's Fair left a golden Sunsphere, where Neyland Stadium holds 103,000 screaming in orange, and where Cormac McCarthy and Quentin Tarantino were raised.

subject: Knoydart
summary: Britain's last roadless peninsula, where Highland Clearances emptied the land and returning war veterans seized it back in a defiant 1948 land raid.

subject: Knuthenborg Safaripark
summary: Northern Europe's largest safari park sits inside a Victorian botanical garden ringed by a 7.4 km wall built from stones dredged out of the sea.

subject: Knutsford
summary: King Canute may have forded the river here a thousand years ago; today Elizabeth Gaskell's old market town still sands its streets in patterns for May Day.

subject: Knysna
summary: The oyster capital of South Africa's Garden Route, where a lagoon guarded by sandstone cliffs hides ghost elephants, indigenous forests, and a Khoi name that means 'hard to reach.'

story.title: The Fishing Village That Launched a Revolution

subject: Kobe Naval Training Center
summary: A defiant samurai bureaucrat bankrolled a rogue naval school in a tiny fishing village, training the very revolutionaries who would topple the government that employed him -- and accidentally planting the seed that became Mitsubishi.

subject: Kobe child murders
summary: In 1997, a series of attacks on schoolchildren in Kobe's Suma ward shocked Japan when the killer turned out to be a 14-year-old boy -- a case that rewrote the country's juvenile justice laws and still haunts the city's quiet residential hills.

subject: Kodok
summary: Capital of the Shilluk Kingdom, sacred coronation city of a monarchy older than sixteen centuries, and the place where Britain and France nearly went to war in 1898.

subject: Koegas mine
summary: Once the world's largest blue asbestos mine, Koegas left behind a legacy of disease, a landmark House of Lords ruling, and a town whose streets were paved with the mineral that killed its workers.

subject: Koffiefontein mine
summary: A diamond mine in the Free State that produced gems of legendary clarity but treated its workers with legendary cruelty, leaving behind skeletons buried in mine tailings and a graveyard discovered a century later.

story.title: Kofun: The Keyhole Tombs That Shaped a Nation

subject: Kofun
summary: Over 161,000 ancient burial mounds dot the Japanese landscape -- some shaped like giant keyholes visible only from the air, built by rulers whose empire was literally measured in earth moved.

subject: Koh Ach Seh
summary: A small island in the Kep Archipelago where an old Khmer Rouge outpost became the base for Cambodia's most stubborn experiment in marine protection.

subject: Koh Kong
summary: A Cambodian border town that spent a century under Siamese rule, kept by France in a 1907 treaty swap, and still takes payment in three currencies.

subject: Koh Kong province
summary: Siam ran this coast until 1904, France kept it in a 1907 swap, and a century later Chinese investors began rebuilding it from the shoreline inward.

subject: Koh Puos
summary: The bridge to Snake Island was finished in 2011; the city it was meant to serve is still being argued over.

subject: Koh Rong
summary: Cambodia's second-largest island has 23 beaches, four villages, water that glows at night, and a ninety-nine-year lease hanging over all of it.

subject: Koh Russei
summary: Bamboo Island is a 1.4-square-kilometre crescent off Sihanoukville with sand coarse enough to need shoes - a navy outpost that became a ten-dollar-a-night beach and then found itself in the path of Cambodia's biggest boom.

subject: Koh Sdach
summary: King's Island: a bean-shaped fishing settlement of Khmer and Chinese families, named for a spring a king is said to have opened with his sword.

subject: Koh Seh
summary: Horse Island: uninhabited, mangrove-ringed, the far southeastern corner of Ream National Park — and routinely confused with a more famous island sixty kilometres away.

subject: Koh Thmei
summary: Three hundred metres from the Cambodian mainland and reachable only the long way round, Koh Thmei is the island Ream National Park was meant to protect — and the one being sold.

subject: Koijärvi
summary: A shallow bird lake north of Forssa, a municipality erased from the map in 1969, and the drainage dispute that gave Finland its green movement.

subject: Kokemäenjoki
summary: The river that keeps outrunning its own harbours: 121 kilometres draining 27,100 square kilometres of southwestern Finland into the largest river delta in the Nordic countries.

subject: Kokopo
summary: When Rabaul's volcanoes buried a capital in 1994, the old colonial town of Herbertshoehe down the coast quietly became New Britain's new one.

subject: Koksilah Ridge
summary: A plough-shaped ridge south of the Cowichan Valley - Hwsalu'utsum to the Quw'utsun people, the place where the first man fell from the sky, and now a logged watershed at the centre of British Columbia's first water sustainability plan.

subject: Koktebel
summary: A Crimean seaside town where the poet Maximilian Voloshin gathered the great writers of his age, beneath the black volcanic cliffs of Kara Dag.

subject: Kola Superdeep Borehole
summary: The deepest hole ever drilled by humans, a Soviet scientific borehole on the Kola Peninsula that reached 12,262 meters and overturned fundamental assumptions about what lies beneath the Earth's crust.

subject: Kolindsund
summary: A twenty-five-kilometre lake on Djursland was pumped dry in 1874 to make farmland, and a century and a half later Denmark is seriously debating whether to let the water back in.

subject: Kolkata
summary: Where the British built their Indian capital before Delhi, where Mother Teresa served the dying, where Bengali culture and communist politics shaped the City of Joy.

subject: Kolmanskop
summary: A diamond-rush boomtown that once boasted Africa's first tram and the southern hemisphere's first X-ray station, now a ghost town where Namib sand pours through Edwardian doorways.

subject: Kolnisches Stadtmuseum
summary: Cologne's city history museum holds 350,000 objects and somewhere to put almost none of them - a seven-year wander from flooded armoury to repurposed fashion house.

subject: Kolobeng Mission
summary: The ruined mission where David Livingstone made his one and only convert - and where the African chief he baptized went on to spread Christianity further than Livingstone ever did.

subject: Kolomoki Mounds
summary: Georgia's largest and oldest Woodland-era mound complex, where astronomically aligned earthworks and effigy pottery reveal a civilization that thrived for centuries in southwest Georgia.

subject: Kolponomos
summary: Twenty million years ago, a bear-like carnivore hunted shellfish along the shores of the ancient Olympic Peninsula, feeding like a sea otter and biting like a sabertooth -- and it took paleontologists two decades just to free its skull from stone.

subject: Kolwezi
summary: A mining city in southern Congo created by colonial extraction and scarred by a 1978 battle, Kolwezi sits atop some of the richest copper-cobalt deposits on Earth and has a rare mineral named in its honor.

subject: Komi Republic
summary: A vast subarctic region of Russia where Europe's largest virgin forests meet the western slopes of the Urals — and where the beauty of the wilderness stands in permanent contrast to the brutal gulag history buried beneath it.

subject: Komsomolsk-on-Amur
summary: A Soviet dream city in the Russian Far East, built in the 1930s by Komsomol youth — and by nearly a million prisoners — on the banks of the Amur River, its wide boulevards and Stalin-era architecture now serving as monuments to a story far more complicated than its founding mythology.

subject: Kona Coffee Living History Farm
summary: On 5.5 acres of the Kona hillside, a Japanese immigrant's coffee farm preserves the daily rhythms of early 20th-century Hawaii, where over 140,000 workers from Japan remade their lives one cherry at a time.

subject: Konar Sandal
summary: Twin Bronze Age mounds in the Halil River valley of southeastern Iran, where a 13.5-hectare citadel, mysterious undeciphered inscriptions, and city seals matching those of ancient Ur suggest a civilization that rivaled Mesopotamia's earliest urban centers.

subject: Kong Empire
summary: A decentralized West African trading state founded by warrior-scholar Seku Watara in 1710, centered in present-day northeastern Ivory Coast, that controlled trade routes across four modern countries before Samori Ture burned its capital in 1898.

subject: Kongsberg Silver Mines
summary: Norway's largest pre-industrial workplace, where over 450,000 man-years of labor across 335 years extracted more than 1.3 million kilograms of silver from over 80 mines beneath the hills of Buskerud.

subject: Konotop
summary: A northeastern Ukrainian city whose very name means the marsh where horses drowned, site of a great Cossack victory in 1659 and of a mayor's defiant vote in 2022.

subject: Konso
summary: A UNESCO cultural landscape in southern Ethiopia where the Konso people have terraced stony hills, walled their hilltop towns, and carved wooden statues to stand watch over their heroes.

subject: Konstantin Battery
summary: A horseshoe of pale stone guarding the mouth of Sevastopol Bay, whose gates were built to become a killing zone and whose garrison was once ordered to hold to the last man.

subject: Kontoskalion
summary: Once Constantinople's second great harbor on the Marmara shore — capable of holding 300 galleys — the Kontoskalion silted up, was filled in by mosque construction debris, and vanished so completely that the neighborhood still bears its name while the harbor itself is gone.

subject: Koobi Fora
summary: On the eastern shore of Lake Turkana, a ridge of crumbling badlands has yielded more than 200 fossils of our ancestors - and the bones that named a species.

subject: Koonibba Test Range
summary: On the lands of the Koonibba Aboriginal community, the first commercial rocket left Australian soil in September 2020 - the first launch anywhere permitted by an Indigenous community on their own country.

subject: Kootenays
summary: British Columbia's mountain playground stretches from the Alberta border to the Columbia ranges - a land of deep lakes, legendary powder skiing, and communities that chose isolation over convenience and have never regretted it.

subject: Kopachi
summary: A village near Chernobyl that was not just evacuated but buried - bulldozed house by house into grassy mounds marked only by radiation signs and a lone abandoned kindergarten.

subject: Korakou Culture
summary: Named for a low mound on the Corinthian coast, the Korakou culture was an Early Bronze Age civilisation whose pottery, corridor houses, and cylinder seals reached from Crete to Thessaly — flourishing between roughly 2650 and 2200 BC before much of it ended in fire.

story.title: Korcula: Marco Polo's Island in the Dalmatian Adriatic

subject: Korcula
summary: An island of medieval stone towns, rare white wines found nowhere else on Earth, and the disputed birthplace of history's most famous traveler, floating in the crystalline waters of the Croatian Adriatic.

subject: Kordofan
summary: A vast Sudanese plain where caravans once crossed between empires and where a Mahdi's revolt began that would shake the British Empire.

subject: Korea under Japanese rule
summary: From 1910 to 1945, Japan's colonial rule over Korea transformed the peninsula through forced assimilation, economic exploitation, and resistance movements that shaped both nations for generations.

subject: Koreiz
summary: A Crimean seaside settlement of grand palaces, where Stalin kept his favorite dacha and hosted the powers dividing the postwar world.

subject: Koreshan State Historic Site
summary: A Florida state park in Estero preserving the grounds of the Koreshan Unity, a utopian community founded by Cyrus Teed who believed humanity lived on the inside of a hollow Earth.

subject: Koroni
summary: Perched on a hill above the Gulf of Messinia with its Venetian castle at its back, Koroni spent three centuries as one of the two 'eyes' of the Venetian Republic — watching over the sea lanes to the Levant and enduring conquest after conquest before finding peace as a quiet Greek coastal town.

subject: Korosten
summary: An ancient city on the Uzh River where a prince was torn apart by bent trees and a queen's revenge burned the town to the ground - a place whose motto declares it does not burn in a flame.

subject: Korouoma
summary: A 30-kilometer fracture canyon in Finnish Lapland where frozen waterfalls draw ice climbers each winter and old-growth forest carpets the surrounding hills.

subject: Korsakov (town)
summary: Sakhalin's oldest Russian settlement began as an Ainu fishing village, became a Tsarist penal outpost, served as a Japanese colonial port, and now sits at the crossroads of Pacific energy and the lingering ghosts of competing empires.

subject: Korsun-Shevchenkivskyi
summary: A thousand-year-old fortress town on the rocky Ros River, twice a battlefield and now home to one of Ukraine's most romantic riverside parks.

subject: Kortrijk
summary: A West Flemish textile city on the Lys, scene of the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302 - the day Flemish weavers and farmers slaughtered a French royal army and pulled the gilded spurs from the corpses of their knights.

subject: Kostroma Moose Farm
summary: Deep in Russia's Kostroma Oblast, a farm has spent over six decades trying to domesticate the moose, producing milk for a nearby sanatorium and challenging nearly everything we think we know about which animals can be farmed.

subject: Kota Formation
summary: A 200-million-year-old geological formation in central India that preserves a Jurassic freshwater world of dinosaurs, ancient mammals, and living fossils in the Pranhita-Godavari Valley.

subject: Kota Kinabalu
summary: Sabah's capital has been burned, bombed, renamed three times, and rebuilt from scratch -- and it still faces the South China Sea with the confidence of a city that knows how to start over.

subject: Kota Tua Jakarta
summary: Once called the Jewel of Asia by European sailors, Jakarta's Old Town spent centuries as the nerve center of the Dutch spice trade before decades of abandonment left its colonial grandeur crumbling - a decline that an ambitious restoration campaign is now fighting to reverse.

subject: Kotagede
summary: The birthplace of the Mataram Sultanate, where a forest clearing became the Great City, and where silversmiths still hammer filigree in workshops lining streets named for the kingdom's founders.

subject: Kotor
summary: A walled medieval town wedged between the Mediterranean's deepest fjord and a sheer mountain that serves as its back wall, where Venetian fortifications and Ottoman influences meet in a car-free labyrinth of stone.

subject: Koudougou
summary: Burkina Faso's third city, where the country's first president was born and an Earthen-brick architecture revolution now keeps schoolchildren cool.

subject: Koufonisi
summary: A car-free speck in the Lesser Cyclades where a single coastal path strings together cove after cove of water so clear the boats look like they are floating on air.

subject: Koufonisia
summary: Three small islands in the Lesser Cyclades, one densely populated, two nearly empty, bound together by a fishing heritage, a five-thousand-year-old culture, and a channel that once sheltered pirates.

subject: Koulikoro
summary: Where the railway from the Atlantic finally meets the navigable Niger, Koulikoro is the river town near the legendary field where Mali's empire was born.

subject: Koumbi Saleh
summary: A ruined stone city in the Mauritanian desert, widely believed to be the lost capital of the Ghana Empire - found because of a single name in a 17th-century manuscript, yet still missing the one inscription that would prove it.

subject: Kouros of Apollonas
summary: A 10.7-metre marble giant lies face-up in the Naxian quarry where it was carved, abandoned mid-cut some 2,500 years ago and never finished.

subject: Koutiala
summary: Mali's white-gold capital, where cotton built a city of factories in the heart of Minianka country.

subject: Kowloon
summary: Nine dragons, eight mountains, and one young emperor gave Kowloon its name — and the peninsula across Victoria Harbour from Hong Kong Island has been reinventing itself ever since.

subject: Kowloon City
summary: Kowloon City has been a place of refuge, resistance, and reinvention for two thousand years — from Song dynasty emperors fleeing the Mongols to the Thai community that made it Hong Kong's Little Thailand.

subject: Kowloon Cricket Club
summary: Founded in 1904, the Kowloon Cricket Club has kept willow on leather alive in Hong Kong for over a century — through colonial gentility, world war, and a city that rarely sits still.

subject: Kowloon Group of Reservoirs
summary: Carved into the hills north of Kowloon between 1901 and 1931, the Kowloon Group of Reservoirs was the infrastructure backbone of a growing colonial city — and its oldest dams are now declared monuments, quietly admired by hikers and monkeys alike.

subject: Kowloon Reservoir
summary: Built in 1910 as the first reservoir in the New Territories, the Kowloon Reservoir quietly ended a city's dependence on wells and set Hong Kong on a path toward modern urban life.

subject: Kowloon Walled City
summary: For decades, tens of thousands of Hongkongers built lives inside a six-and-a-half-acre enclave that two governments refused to claim — a place of hardship, ingenuity, community, and extraordinary human resilience.

subject: Kozmodemyansk, Mari El Republic
summary: A fortress town Ivan the Terrible planted at the confluence of the Volga and Vetluga rivers, where centuries of Mari culture survived beneath layers of Russian imperial, Soviet, and modern identity.

subject: Kraainem
summary: A bilingual commune on Brussels' eastern edge where Roman roads, Frankish fortifications, and European bureaucrats share the same 5.8 square kilometers.

subject: Krakatoa
summary: A volcanic caldera in the Sunda Strait whose 1883 eruption was the loudest sound in recorded history, killed over 36,000 people, and altered global climate for years.

subject: Krakow
summary: Where Poland's royal capital survived the wars that destroyed Warsaw, where the Main Square is Europe's largest, where history lives in every stone.

subject: Krameramtsstuben
summary: Twenty rent-free apartments built in 1676 for the widows of Hamburg's shopkeepers — a charity that was also, quite openly, a way of getting them out of their husbands' shops.

subject: Kraton Kacirebonan
summary: Built with a pension its founders once refused on principle, Kraton Kacirebonan is the youngest of Cirebon's four royal palaces -- and a living archive of the cultural crossroads where Sundanese, Javanese, Chinese, Arab, and Dutch influences all left their mark.

subject: Kraton Kasepuhan
summary: The oldest royal palace in the Indonesian city of Cirebon, built in 1447, where Sundanese brick, Javanese carving, Dutch tilework, Chinese ceramics, and French chandeliers coexist under a single roof.

subject: Krefeld
summary: In March 1945, the US Army handed administration of a recently captured German city to a 21-year-old private who happened to speak the language. His name was Henry Kissinger.

subject: Krokhino, Vologda Oblast
summary: A drowned village on the Sheksna River where only a half-ruined Baroque church still rises above the waterline, a haunting monument to the communities sacrificed for the Volga-Baltic Waterway.

subject: Kropyvnytskyi
summary: A central Ukrainian city that has changed its name three times and once cradled the first professional Ukrainian theater, still calling itself a little Paris.

subject: Krupp Steelworks
summary: For more than a century the Krupp steelworks in Essen armed Germany's wars. Behind that history are the tens of thousands of forced laborers whose work kept the furnaces lit, and whose dignity the postwar reckoning never fully restored.

subject: Kryvbas
summary: A narrow, hundred-kilometer band of ore-rich earth in central Ukraine holds one of Eastern Europe's greatest iron treasuries - the basin that gave a whole region its name and its fate.

subject: Kryvyi Rih
summary: One of the longest cities in Europe stretches for 126 kilometers along a seam of iron - a hard-working, sprawling place where trams run for free and the horizon glows at night.

subject: Ksar el Barka
summary: A ruined caravan town below the Tagant cliffs, Ksar el Barka rose as a desert way-station and a seat of religious learning - then was destroyed, rebuilt, and finally left to the sand.

subject: Kucapungane
summary: A 600-year-old Rukai aboriginal village of 163 slate houses in the mountains of southern Taiwan, abandoned since the 1970s and reachable only on foot over unstable terrain.

subject: Kudi Chin
summary: A Bangkok riverside neighborhood where a Portuguese Catholic church, a Chinese shrine, a Buddhist temple, and a mosque have shared the same few blocks since the 18th century.

subject: Kuhikugu
summary: An archaeological complex in the Xingu rainforest where up to 50,000 people once lived in a planned network of twenty towns before European diseases emptied them.

subject: Kuialnyk Estuary
summary: A hypersaline lagoon north of Odesa where the ground sinks below the sea, the water can turn saltier than the ocean, and people come to bury themselves in black healing mud.

subject: Kuk Swamp
summary: A wetland in the Wahgi Valley of Papua New Guinea where people independently invented agriculture 9,000 years ago - one of only a handful of places on Earth where farming began, and the only UNESCO World Heritage Site in the country.

subject: Kuku Nyungkal
summary: The Kuku Nyungkal are the rainforest people of the upper Annan River south of Cooktown — keepers of a deep law of country who were forced off their land by tin miners and missions, and who are now walking their way back home.

story.title: Kul Tepe Jolfa: Seven Thousand Years on a Hill

subject: Kul Tepe Jolfa
summary: Discovered in 1968, this ancient mound near the Araxes River in northwestern Iran holds 7,000 years of continuous human occupation -- from Chalcolithic potters to Bronze Age metalworkers to the Urartian kingdom.

subject: Kulb
summary: A village in the craggy Batn-El-Hajar region of Sudan, home to a rare domed Nubian church and the southernmost point where Old Kingdom Egyptian officials once searched for gold.

story.title: Kule Loklo: The Village That Keeps Returning

subject: Kule Loklo
summary: A recreated Coast Miwok village at Point Reyes National Seashore, destroyed by arson in 1992 and rebuilt by a community that refused to let it disappear.

subject: Kulubnarti
summary: A small island in the Nile where Christian Nubians held out until the fifteenth century, whose cemeteries yielded one of the best-studied bioarchaeological collections in the world.

subject: Kumkapı
summary: On Istanbul's Marmara shore, Kumkapı — the Sand Gate — has been home to the city's Armenian community for centuries and remains famous for its lively fish taverns and the seat of the Armenian Patriarchate of Constantinople.

subject: Kumzar
summary: Oman's most isolated village, accessible only by boat, where residents speak a unique language influenced by 45 others and migrate seasonally to escape summer heat that makes their home uninhabitable.

subject: Kungsleden
summary: Sweden's 450-kilometer King's Trail cuts through Europe's largest wilderness, from the birch forests of Abisko to the mountains of Hemavan.

story.title: Kuni-kyo: The Capital That Lasted Four Years

subject: Kuni-kyō
summary: The short-lived capital of Japan from 740 to 744, built by a frightened emperor fleeing rebellion, abandoned before completion, and now reduced to foundation stones in a schoolyard in Kyoto Prefecture.

subject: Kunstmann
summary: In a rainy river town settled by German immigrants, a family that started brewing in their kitchen turned Valdivia's heritage into Chile's most recognizable craft beer.

subject: Kunstmuseen Krefeld
summary: Two private villas designed by Mies van der Rohe in 1928 became, against all expectation, one of the strangest and most influential exhibition spaces in postwar European art.

subject: Kupang
summary: Indonesia's southernmost city and closest to Australia, Kupang was the improbable safe harbor where Captain Bligh ended history's most famous open-boat voyage -- and where colonial empires clashed for centuries over the island of Timor.

subject: Kuranda
summary: The village in the rainforest above Cairns, reached by a hand-built heritage railway or a gondola over the canopy, where market stalls hum beneath trees on Djabugay and Buluwai Country.

subject: Kurashiki
summary: A city whose name means 'warehouse town,' where white-walled Edo-period storehouses line a willow-draped canal and Japan's first Western art museum holds works by El Greco, Monet, and Renoir.

subject: Kuridala Township site
summary: Two thousand people, six hotels, and a cinema once filled this plain south of Cloncurry. Today Kuridala is an empty field of foundations - north-west Queensland's first boom town, and one of its first ghosts.

story.title: Kurohimeyama Kofun: The Armory Beneath the Mound

subject: Kurohimeyama Kofun
summary: A 5th-century keyhole-shaped burial mound in Sakai yielded 24 complete sets of armor standing upright in rows -- the largest cache of ancient armor ever found at a single site in Japan.

subject: Kurokawa gold mine
summary: The mountain goldfields that bankrolled one of Japan's greatest warlords, where Takeda Shingen minted coins of legendary purity before the mines fell silent and the forest reclaimed the tunnels.

subject: Kurozuka Kofun
summary: A 130-meter keyhole-shaped burial mound in Nara where 33 bronze mirrors were found exactly as they were placed around a coffin some 1,700 years ago -- the most complete in-situ mirror arrangement ever excavated in Japan.

subject: Kursk
summary: An ancient fortress city that never fell to its besiegers sits atop the world's largest iron-ore reserve, its very ground pulling compass needles askew.

subject: Kusatsu Onsen
summary: A thousand-year-old hot spring town perched at 1,200 meters in the Gunma mountains, where volcanic waters pour through wooden chutes at 32,300 liters per minute and locals still cool the scalding baths with an ancient paddle-stirring ritual.

subject: Kustavi
summary: A municipality of 972 people and more than two thousand islands, where the land is still rising out of the sea and Finland's most celebrated difficult novel was born.

subject: Kutum
summary: A market town along a seasonal riverbed in North Darfur, where the Fur, Tunjur, and Berti have made their lives for centuries and where war keeps returning.

subject: Kutupalong refugee camp
summary: The world's largest refugee camp sprawls across the hills of Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, where nearly a million Rohingya people live in a dense maze of bamboo shelters with no clear path home.

subject: Kuwait
summary: A small monarchy between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, Kuwait transformed from a pearl-diving outpost into one of the world's wealthiest nations, only to be invaded, liberated, and rebuilt within a single decade.

subject: Kuwait City
summary: A capital rebuilt from the ashes of invasion, Kuwait City pairs futuristic towers and gleaming malls with the ancient rhythms of a pearl-diving port on the Persian Gulf.

subject: Kuzguncuk
summary: Tucked into an Asian Bosphorus valley south of Beylerbeyi, Kuzguncuk spent centuries as a rare corner of Istanbul where Jewish, Greek, Armenian, and Muslim neighbors shared cobblestone streets, synagogues, churches, and mosques within a few minutes' walk of one another.

subject: Kwahu Easter
summary: Every Easter, Ghana's Kwahu Hills transform into the country's largest festival as paragliders launch from mountain ridges, carnivals fill the streets, and the Kwahu people celebrate their annual homecoming.

subject: Kwai Chung
summary: Once a tidal stream emptying into a bay that no longer exists, Kwai Chung transformed from a rural backwater into a Hong Kong district of 287,000 people — and the site of one of the world's great container ports.

subject: Kwai Tsing Container Terminals
summary: Built on the buried remains of two small islands and a reclaimed bay, the Kwai Tsing Container Terminals rose from a 1966 government committee's urgent recommendation to become one of the busiest ports on earth.

subject: Kwantung Leased Territory
summary: Passed from China to Russia to Japan to the Soviet Union and back to China, the Kwantung Leased Territory at the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula was the fulcrum around which East Asian power politics turned for half a century.

subject: Kweilin Street Night Market
summary: For three nights every Lunar New Year, when the shops close and the inspectors go home, Kweilin Street in Sham Shui Po transforms into one of Hong Kong's most cherished and contested street markets — a tradition born from necessity and kept alive by collective memory.

subject: Kwun Tong
summary: From Song dynasty salt yards to mid-century factories to a post-industrial waterfront, Kwun Tong on Kowloon's eastern edge has been remaking itself for a thousand years without ever quite leaving its working-class roots behind.

subject: Kwun Yam Shan (Yuen Long District)
summary: Named for the Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion and noted in historical gazetteers for its sharp, sky-piercing profile, Kwun Yam Shan rises 546 metres in northern Hong Kong — a sacred peak sitting atop ancient volcanic rock, with warm mist rising from the summit in winter.

subject: Kyalami Grand Prix Circuit
summary: Africa's most storied racetrack, where Niki Lauda and Jody Scheckter chased glory, where a freak accident in 1977 killed a driver and a teenage marshal, and where the roar of Grand Prix engines fell silent under apartheid sanctions.

subject: Kyiv Funicular
summary: For more than a century, a little cable railway has hauled Kyivans up a hill too steep for trams, linking the city's cathedral heights to the riverside quarter below.

subject: Kyiv Pechersk Lavra
summary: For nearly a thousand years, monks have prayed in the caves a single hermit dug into a hillside above the Dnieper, founding one of the great centers of Eastern Christianity.

subject: Kyle Rhea
summary: A narrow tidal strait between Skye and the Scottish mainland where cattle once swam roped together to market and a hand-cranked turntable ferry still runs in summer.

subject: Kyle of Lochalsh
summary: The mainland village at the narrowest point between Scotland and Skye, where centuries of ferry crossings ended in 1995 with a controversial toll bridge that took protesters a decade to defeat.

subject: Kyle of Lochalsh
summary: A small Scottish village whose Gaelic name means "strait of the foaming loch," sitting almost exactly 500 miles due north of Land's End and serving as the mainland gateway to Skye.

subject: Kymi, Greece
summary: A green hilltown perched above the eastern coast of Euboea, Kymi earned the nickname 'The Balcony of the Aegean' and gave the world the man who invented the Pap smear.

subject: Kynance Cove
summary: Turquoise water, rocks that travelled 375 million years to get here, and a beach that drew poets, princes, and a queen.

subject: Kyogle
summary: A small dairy-and-timber town named for the bush turkey, Kyogle calls itself the Gateway to the Rainforest at the foot of the Border Ranges.

subject: Kyparissia
summary: Homer knew it as Cyparissia; the Franks called it Arcadia; Ibrahim Pasha burned it in 1825. Through every name and every destruction, the town on the western Messenian coast has persisted — its castle on the hill the one constant across three thousand years of occupation.

subject: Kypseli
summary: Once the most glamorous address in Athens, this dense central neighborhood rose, faded, and is finding a third life along the palm-lined promenade of Fokionos Negri.

subject: Kythnos
summary: An island in the western Cyclades known since the Middle Ages as Thermia for its healing hot springs, dotted with more than a hundred churches, home to one of the oldest known Mesolithic settlements in the Aegean, and — quietly — one of the first places in Greece to run a wind park.

subject: Kâğıthane Creek
summary: Once the gilded pleasure-ground where Ottoman sultans picnicked and poets rhapsodized, Kâğıthane Creek has lived through empire, rebellion, and industrial ruin — and is still finding its way back.

subject: Kénédougou Kingdom
summary: For two and a half centuries the Kenedougou Kingdom held the plains of southeastern Mali, building West Africa's largest fortified city at Sikasso before its last king chose death over French surrender in 1898.

subject: Köln Messe/Deutz Station
summary: Cologne's east-bank station handles ICE trains and trade-fair crowds today; from its lower platforms, the Nazis deported almost every Jew in the city.

subject: Königsallee (Düsseldorf)
summary: Düsseldorf's most famous boulevard was renamed after a king got pelted with horse manure, then grew into one of the most expensive shopping streets in Europe.

subject: Köpenick
summary: An old town on three islands where the Dahme meets the Spree, and where in 1906 an unemployed cobbler in a second-hand uniform arrested the mayor.

subject: Köyliönjärvi
summary: Finland long called the killing on this lake's ice its first documented historical event — though almost nothing about it can be documented, and the lake itself now sits a metre lower than it did.

subject: Kīlauea
summary: One of the most active volcanoes on Earth, Kilauea has been reshaping Hawaii's Big Island for over 200,000 years, destroying towns, creating new coastline, and captivating scientists and visitors with its relentless power.

subject: Kınalıada
summary: The reddish henna island closest to Istanbul, where Byzantine emperors went into exile and Armenian families came to summer — a small island carrying centuries of layered history.

story.title: Koka Ikki: The Ninja Republic That Governed Itself

subject: Kōka ikki
summary: In the forested hills of southern Omi Province, fifty-three clans formed a self-governing confederacy of ninja warriors who answered to no feudal lord -- a shadow republic that endured for over a century during Japan's most violent age.

subject: Kōraku-en
summary: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens, built in 1700 by the lord of Okayama, whose very name encodes a philosophy: 'grieve before others, enjoy after others.'

subject: Kōrankei
summary: A river gorge in central Japan where a Buddhist monk's 1634 maple plantings have grown into one of the country's most celebrated autumn spectacles, drawing over half a million visitors each November to a valley that glows in eleven shades of red and gold.

story.title: The Place of the Rotten Cane: Rise and Fall of the K'iche' Kingdom

subject: Kʼicheʼ kingdom of Qʼumarkaj
summary: From a fortified highland capital whose name meant 'place of the rotten cane,' the K'iche' Maya built the most powerful kingdom in pre-Columbian Guatemala -- then lost it in a single act of Spanish treachery in March 1524.

subject: L'Aplec del Caragol
summary: Every May, Lleida's riverside fills with brass bands, human towers, and twelve tons of snails, in a festival that grew from eighteen clubs into one of Catalonia's great gatherings.

subject: L'Haridon Bight
summary: Too salty for almost anything to live in, this quiet bay grew a beach of shells and harbours life older than complex animals.

subject: L'Isle-aux-Coudres
summary: A St. Lawrence River island named by Jacques Cartier for its hazel trees in 1535, where beluga whale hunts once defined island life and a 450-million-year-old meteor crater shaped the very ground beneath it.

subject: L. Smit en Zoon
summary: The Kinderdijk shipyard that invented the modern long-distance ocean tug and, in 1953, launched what was then the most powerful tugboat on Earth for the Suez Canal.

subject: LAPAN
summary: Indonesia's national space agency launched its first rockets in 1962, built satellites with Germany and India, and dreamed of equatorial spaceports on remote Pacific islands -- then was quietly absorbed into a larger bureaucracy in 2021.

subject: La Amistad
summary: A Spanish schooner whose name meant 'Friendship' became the site of one of history's most consequential slave revolts, sparking a Supreme Court case that galvanized the American abolitionist movement.

subject: La Barceloneta, Barcelona
summary: A triangular neighborhood that was underwater until the 1600s became Barcelona's beach district, birthplace of its greatest flamenco dancer, and home to the city's most famous potato ball.

subject: La Bastida de les Alcusses
summary: An Iberian city on a Valencian ridge, so suddenly destroyed around 330 BC that its people left tools in their houses and a lead ledger rolled beneath a grinding stone, earning it the name a new Pompeii.

subject: La Belle (ship)
summary: A 17th-century French warship that sank in Matagorda Bay in 1686, La Belle lay forgotten for over 300 years until archaeologists recovered its hull and over a million artifacts from the Texas mud.

subject: La Boca
