summary: A working port barrio painted by a coal-hauler's son, where Italian immigrants, tango, and Boca Juniors gave Buenos Aires its loudest, most stubborn heart.

subject: La Boqueria
summary: Barcelona's most famous market has been selling food at the same spot since 1217, evolving from open-air meat tables outside the city gate to one of the world's great public markets.

subject: La Calera, Cundinamarca
summary: Eighteen kilometers east of Bogota, across a gap in the Eastern Hills, a limestone town remembers the cement factory that built it and now imagines what to become next.

subject: La Candelaria, Bogota
summary: Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada founded a city here in 1538 on land where a Muisca ruler had taken his rest. The street corners still remember.

subject: La Ceiba
summary: Honduras's carnival city and eco-tourism capital, founded under a giant ceiba tree where banana railroads once ran and half a million revelers now dance each May.

subject: La Colmena, Paraguay
summary: The first Japanese colony in Paraguay, where families who crossed an ocean in 1936 cleared the red earth at the foot of a volcanic ridge and stayed.

subject: La Conchita, California
summary: La Conchita is a tiny coastal community in Ventura County wedged between the Pacific and unstable hillsides — a place of extraordinary beauty that has twice been buried by catastrophic landslides.

subject: La Conner
summary: A tiny waterfront town in Washington's tulip country where artists have gathered since the 1940s and spring brings ribbons of color across the richest farmland in the Pacific Northwest.

subject: La Draga
summary: On the shore of Lake Banyoles, waterlogged mud preserved an entire Neolithic village for seven thousand years, from Europe's oldest known bows to four hundred thousand seeds.

subject: La Ferrería
summary: An archaeological site south of Durango where circular ritual spaces, obsidian knives, and burial pots reveal a culture that bridged Mesoamerica and the American Southwest for over five centuries.

subject: La Fonteta Phoenician Port
summary: Under the dunes of Guardamar del Segura lie the remarkably intact walls of one of the western Mediterranean's largest Phoenician cities, buried and preserved by the same sand that hid it for millennia.

subject: La Fortuna
summary: A Costa Rican town that owes its name to surviving a catastrophic volcanic eruption in 1968, La Fortuna sits in the shadow of Arenal Volcano and draws visitors to its hot springs, rivers, and rainforest trails.

subject: La Frontera (Chile)
summary: For nearly three centuries, the Bío Bío River marked the edge of the Spanish world in South America - the line where empire stopped and the independent Mapuche nation began.

subject: La Gran Sabana
summary: A vast highland savanna in southeastern Venezuela where flat-topped mountains older than complex life itself rise from ancient rock, harboring species found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: La Grande Soufrière
summary: The highest peak in the Lesser Antilles is an active volcano on Guadeloupe that once prompted the evacuation of 72,000 people — and drew Werner Herzog to film the one man who refused to leave.

subject: La Grange, California
summary: A Gold Rush boomtown turned quiet hamlet of 166 people, La Grange was once the lawless county seat of Stanislaus County and the starting point for John Muir's first summer in the Sierra.

subject: La Guajira Department
summary: Colombia's northernmost department is a land of extremes - a desert peninsula where the Wayuu people held off the Spanish Empire, where flamingos gather in coastal lagoons, and where Lebanese immigrants, African descendants, and indigenous nations share the same arid ground.

subject: La Güera
summary: At the wind-scoured tip of the Cap Blanc peninsula stands an abandoned Spanish town, its ruins half-buried in sand, watched over by a handful of fishermen and the monk seals that were once its symbol.

subject: La Haye Sainte
summary: A walled farmhouse on the Brussels road where 400 King's German Legion riflemen held the centre of Waterloo until the last cartridge was gone.

story.title: La Honda Creek Open Space Preserve

subject: La Honda Creek Open Space Preserve
summary: From Ohlone gathering grounds to Mexican rancho to logging frontier, this San Mateo County preserve holds layers of Peninsula history beneath its redwoods and grasslands.

subject: La Honda, California
summary: A fog-wrapped hamlet in the Santa Cruz Mountains where Ken Kesey launched the psychedelic counterculture, Neil Young found solitude, and landslides still rearrange the landscape.

subject: La Imperial
summary: A Spanish city named for an emperor rose on the Imperial River in 1552, then vanished into the forest when the Mapuche reclaimed their land.

subject: La Jolla Cove
summary: La Jolla Cove is a small, cliff-framed inlet on San Diego's northern coast where the Pacific meets sandstone, sea lions haul out, and snorkelers drift above orange garibaldi fish in one of California's most protected marine reserves — plus a nonprofit formed specifically to complain about the smell.

subject: La Jolla Historical Society
summary: A historic campus on Ellen Browning Scripps' former estate where rescued cottages, Irving Gill architecture, and postmodern pergolas tell La Jolla's story.

subject: La Jolla Institute for Immunology
summary: Founded in 1988 on Torrey Pines Mesa, the La Jolla Institute for Immunology has grown into one of the world's foremost independent immunology research centers, its work spanning allergies, autoimmune disease, infection, and cancer.

subject: La Macarena
summary: A tiny town in the plains of the Orinoquia, the only way into a river that blooms seven colors for four months of the year.

subject: La Manga
summary: A ribbon of sand roughly 21 kilometers long, La Manga holds two seas apart — the open Mediterranean on one side, the warm salt lagoon of the Mar Menor on the other.

story.title: La Mano de Punta del Este

subject: La Mano de Punta del Este
summary: Five colossal fingers claw up out of the sand at Brava Beach, the most photographed warning sign in South America.

subject: La Maná
summary: A canton founded on gold-rich soil where indigenous Tsachila melted metals centuries before Spanish captains knew the place existed.

subject: La Matanza
summary: In January 1932, a peasant uprising in western El Salvador was crushed in days -- the government killings that followed lasted weeks, and the silence imposed on indigenous communities lasted generations.

subject: La Merced
summary: A small town at 750 meters where the high Andes give way to the high jungle - the gateway to Peru's coffee country and Ashaninka territory.

subject: La Mercè
summary: Each September Barcelona hands its streets to giants, fire-breathing devils, human towers, and two million people for La Mercè, a festival born from a vow made during a plague of locusts.

subject: La Mulâtresse Solitude
summary: An enslaved woman of mixed heritage who joined the 1802 insurrection against Napoleon's reinstatement of slavery in Guadeloupe, fought alongside the resistance, and was executed the day after giving birth.

subject: La Muralla Roja
summary: Ricardo Bofill's crimson labyrinth on a Calpe hillside, a working apartment block reimagined as a North African casbah and now one of modern architecture's most photographed walls.

subject: La Paz
summary: The world's highest national capital, built inside a canyon where altitude maps directly onto social class -- the lower you go, the wealthier the neighborhood.

subject: La Perla, San Juan, Puerto Rico
summary: A neighborhood wedged between Old San Juan's fortress walls and the Atlantic, where community, music, and resilience have defined daily life for nearly three centuries.

subject: La Peña Cultural Center
summary: A Berkeley cultural center born from the ashes of Chile's democracy, where Latin American exiles turned art into resistance and built a community that outlasted the dictatorship.

subject: La Pita
summary: An access road exposed a yellow patch of earth in the Colombian western cordillera. The mine that followed once produced 80 percent of the world's green fire.

subject: La Plata
summary: Argentina built an entire provincial capital from nothing in 1882, drawing it as a perfect grid slashed by diagonals and laced, some say, with Masonic symbolism: the City of Diagonals.

subject: La Push, Washington
summary: The westernmost ZIP code in the contiguous United States belongs to a Quileute village at the mouth of the Quillayute River -- a community now physically moving uphill to outrun the rising sea.

story.title: La Quebrada: Where Gravity Meets the Tide

subject: La Quebrada (Acapulco)
summary: At this narrow ravine on Acapulco's coast, cliff divers leap from heights of up to 80 feet into a shallow surge channel, timing their plunge to coincide with incoming waves - a tradition formalized in 1934 but rooted in a ravine that 18th-century engineers tried and failed to carve open.

subject: La Rambla, Barcelona
summary: Barcelona's most famous street was once a seasonal streambed -- its name comes from the Arabic word for sand -- and its 1.2 kilometers have absorbed eight centuries of riots, opera, slave fortunes, and terrorism.

subject: La Redota
summary: Uruguay's founding epic - the day in 1811 when thousands of ordinary people abandoned their homes to follow Jose Artigas into exile, naming their own retreat after the word for defeat.

subject: La Serena
summary: Chile's second-oldest city wears a uniform of colonial-style stone and stucco by deliberate design, gateway to clear desert skies and a valley of pisco.

subject: La Soufrière (Saint Vincent)
summary: The highest peak in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, La Soufriere is an active stratovolcano with five explosive eruptions since 1718 -- including a 1902 blast that killed 1,680 people hours before Mount Pelee destroyed Martinique.

subject: La Tomatina
summary: The world's biggest food fight began by accident in 1945, survived a Franco-era ban with a mock funeral, and now turns the town of Buñol red every August.

subject: La Trochita
summary: A century-old narrow-gauge steam train that Paul Theroux rode to the end of the line, still hauling its 1922 locomotives across the Patagonian foothills.

subject: La Unión, Huánuco
summary: The provincial capital in the shadow of a great Inca ruin - two towns, two bridges, and the festival that returns the sun to the plateau each July.

subject: La Unión, Murcia
summary: A Murcian mining town that literally named itself for a merger — born when rival ore-rich hamlets broke from Cartagena, then crowned itself with modernist palaces and the deep laments of the cante minero.

subject: La Vall d'Uixó
summary: A workaday Castellón town whose greatest treasure runs beneath it: Europe's largest navigable underground river, threading a painted limestone cave.

subject: La Vega Central
summary: Santiago's great wholesale market has fed the city from the banks of the Mapocho for over a century, a roaring 60,000-square-meter labyrinth of fruit, fish, and Chilean life.

subject: La Vela de Coro
summary: The port where Venezuela's flag first touched its own soil - a UNESCO World Heritage town of Spanish and Dutch colonial architecture where German bankers once governed and a failed revolutionary's landing changed a nation's symbols forever.

story.title: La Ventanilla: Where Twenty-Five Families Guard a Lagoon

subject: La Ventanilla, Oaxaca
summary: A tiny Zapotec village on the Oaxacan coast where three families on a coconut plantation became twenty-five families running one of Mexico's most authentic ecotourism projects - protecting sea turtles, replanting 30,000 mangroves, and paddling tourists through a crocodile-filled lagoon.

subject: Labuan
summary: A small island off Borneo's coast that the British once hoped would become a second Singapore, Labuan instead found its own identity as an offshore financial center, wreck diving destination, and crossroads of cultures.

subject: Ladainha, Minas Gerais
summary: A small rural municipality in northeast Minas Gerais named for an old man who prayed the rosary at a railway halt - a town built by 61 houses for Bahia-Minas railroad workers in 1926.

subject: Ladby Ship
summary: Denmark's only Viking Age ship burial, where the vessel itself has rotted entirely away and what remains is its outline in the soil, drawn by two thousand iron rivets.

subject: Ladder Street
summary: Built between 1841 and 1850 to connect Hong Kong's early hillside settlements, Ladder Street is a Grade I historic stairway in Sheung Wan that has climbed through colonial history, cinema, and living neighborhood life for nearly two centuries.

subject: Ladeira da Preguiça
summary: Salvador's Slope of Laziness was named by the people who watched enslaved porters haul sixty-kilo sacks up it — a joke that outlived them and became a stereotype about all of Bahia.

subject: Lado Enclave
summary: A muddy triangle on the Upper Nile, leased to King Leopold II for his lifetime, that dissolved into a lawless no man's land where the last great elephant hunt on the continent played out.

subject: Lady Elizabeth (1879)
summary: A rusting iron barque from Sunderland, wrecked rounding Cape Horn and left to drift into a Stanley cove, the Lady Elizabeth has become the most photographed shipwreck in the Falkland Islands.

story.title: Lady Saigo: The Power Behind the Shogun

subject: Lady Saigō
summary: Nicknamed Oai -- meaning 'love' -- this concubine of Tokugawa Ieyasu shaped the policies that unified Japan, mothered the second shogun, and founded a charity for blind women, only to die under mysterious circumstances at age thirty-seven.

subject: Ladysmith, KwaZulu-Natal
summary: A KwaZulu-Natal town where the scars of a four-month Boer War siege share the streets with a celebrated mosque, a Gandhi connection, and the harmonies of Ladysmith Black Mambazo.

subject: Lagash
summary: One of the oldest city-states in Mesopotamia, where archaeologists found the earliest known depiction of organized warfare, a 5,000-year-old tavern with food still inside, and thousands of cuneiform tablets that illuminate the dawn of civilization.

subject: Lago Colony
summary: An American company town planted on the eastern tip of a Caribbean island, Lago Colony thrived for six decades around one of the world's largest oil refineries -- then vanished almost entirely when the oil stopped flowing.

subject: Lago Ranco
summary: On the shore of Chile's second-largest lake, a Huilliche homeland became a logging frontier reached by rail and crossed by steamships, all of it shadowed by the volcanoes that shape the land.

subject: Lagoa da Prata
summary: A Minas Gerais town named for sunlight hitting water, home to a World Cup champion, a sugar mill owned by Louis Dreyfus, and a lagoon that started as a Portuguese millpond.

subject: Lagos City
summary: Africa's most populous city sprawls across islands and mainland, a megacity of over sixteen million people where Nollywood was born, Afrobeat still pulses, and the traffic never fully stops.

subject: Lagos Colony
summary: Britain seized the island of Lagos in 1861 from an Oba who resisted for eleven days, turning a slave-trading port into a colonial possession that would eventually become the nucleus of Nigeria.

subject: Lagosa
summary: A tiny Tanzanian village on Lake Tanganyika's eastern shore, where a century-old German ferry is the main reason the outside world shows up.

subject: Laguna Blanca (Paraguay)
summary: A spring-fed lake in Paraguay's interior so clear you can drink from it untreated, Laguna Blanca sits atop calcareous sand in a rare patch of Cerrado ecosystem that harbors 283 bird species and carnivorous plants.

subject: Laguna Lejía
summary: A shallow salt lake at 4,325 meters in the Atacama highlands, Laguna Lejia was once five times its current size and now serves scientists as an earthly analog for ancient lakes on Mars.

story.title: Laguna Miramar: The Lake That Takes Days to Reach

subject: Laguna Miramar
summary: Hidden deep in Chiapas's Lacandon Jungle near the Guatemalan border, Laguna Miramar is one of Mexico's most ecologically untouched areas, sheltering roughly 20 percent of the country's species and guarded by Maya communities that manage all access to its warm blue waters.

subject: Laguna Negra, Catamarca
summary: A shallow, salt-heavy lake on Argentina's Puna plateau harbors living stromatolites that resemble the oldest life forms on Earth — and may offer scientists a window into what early Mars looked like.

subject: Laguna Quilotoa
summary: A volcano that erupted in 1280 and sent pyroclastic flows and lahars to the Pacific, now a turquoise crater lake 250 meters deep.

subject: Laguna Salada
summary: Laguna Salada is a vast, usually dry lake 10 meters below sea level in Baja California — a tectonic depression linked to the San Andreas Fault, site of the 2010 earthquake, and the location where Discovery Channel deliberately crashed a Boeing 727 to test aircraft survivability.

subject: Laguna de Apoyo
summary: A volcanic crater lake in Nicaragua where the water stays warm year-round, the depths plunge at a 45-degree angle from shore, and the only road in descends through the crater rim.

subject: Laguna de Rocha
summary: A brackish lagoon on Uruguay's Atlantic coast where a single ribbon of sand decides whether 7,200 hectares of water meet the sea, and where flamingos paint the shallows pink.

subject: Laguna de las Momias
summary: A cliff above a cloud-forest lake where the Chachapoya buried their dead in mausoleums the world forgot - until looters found them, and the archaeologists followed.

subject: Laguna del Desierto incident
summary: On a remote Patagonian shore in 1965, a single shot killed a young Chilean lieutenant and turned an uninhabited valley into one of the bitterest wounds between Chile and Argentina.

subject: Laguna, Santa Catarina
summary: A colonial port on Brazil's southern coast that birthed a revolutionary heroine, served briefly as the capital of a breakaway republic, and still fishes hand in hand with wild dolphins.

subject: Lahinch
summary: A Clare beach town where Old Tom Morris laid out a golf course in 1892 and surfers now ride the same Atlantic.

subject: Lai Chi Kok
summary: Named for lychee trees that once lined a bay now buried under reclaimed land, Lai Chi Kok has spent more than a century being reimagined — from a Qing customs post to a British torpedo depot to one of Kowloon's most densely populated neighborhoods.

subject: Lai Chi Wo
summary: A beautifully preserved Hakka walled village in Hong Kong's northeastern wilderness, where 300-year-old clan halls, ancient feng shui woodland, and Hong Kong's only significant seagrass bed survive together at the edge of Mirs Bay.

subject: Lairg
summary: The crossroads of the north - an inland Highland village where four roads meet, the largest sheep sale in Europe takes place each August, and an impact crater 1.2 billion years old lies beneath the moor.

story.title: Lakes Muncoonie, Mumbleberry and Torquinie Important Bird Area

subject: Lakes Muncoonie, Mumbleberry and Torquinie Important Bird Area
summary: When the rains finally reach this cluster of Channel Country salt lakes west of Bedourie, dry clay pans become shallow seas that have held more than a million waterbirds at once.

subject: Lakes State
summary: A state named for its inland waters, home to cattle camps that define Dinka life, and possibly the site of South Sudan's future capital.

subject: Lakewood Speedway
summary: For six decades, a one-mile dirt oval at Atlanta's Lakewood Fairgrounds was the 'Indianapolis of the South,' launching NASCAR legends before fading into the Georgia clay.

subject: Lalibela
summary: In the Ethiopian highlands, eleven churches were carved downward into living volcanic rock - sculpted, not built - more than nine centuries ago.

subject: Lalu Wetlands National Nature Preserve
summary: The world's largest urban wetlands, sitting at 3,646 meters in the middle of Lhasa, where bar-headed geese and black-necked cranes share space with a city that nearly destroyed them.

subject: Lam Tin
summary: A dense residential district in southeastern Kowloon that began as salt fields in the Song dynasty, was emptied by imperial decree in 1662, and was rebuilt in the twentieth century into a home for 130,000 people.

subject: Lam Tsuen
summary: A valley union of 26 villages north of Tai Po, Lam Tsuen is where Punti and Hakka settlers once built a market to break a merchant clan's monopoly — and where Hong Kong still comes every Lunar New Year to make wishes beneath two old trees.

subject: Lam Tsuen Wishing Trees
summary: Two ancient banyan trees in Hong Kong's Tai Po District have drawn wish-seekers for centuries — and a single broken branch in 2005 forced a rethinking of how faith, tradition, and living things can coexist.

subject: Lam Vien Square
summary: Da Lat's central square carries the name of the highland plateau it stands on — a gathering place where flower festivals light up the cool mountain air and the city's identity comes into focus.

story.title: Lamakera: The Village That Traded Harpoons for Snorkels

subject: Lamakera
summary: A remote Indonesian whaling village on Solor Island transformed itself from the world's largest manta ray hunting ground into a marine tourism destination after a documentary film changed everything.

subject: Lambaréné
summary: A river town 75 kilometers south of the equator where Albert Schweitzer built a hospital in 1913 that still operates today, and where the Ogooue River splits the city into three distinct districts.

subject: Lamlash
summary: A sheltered bay facing a holy island, Lamlash is Arran's quiet administrative heart - a place where Mary, Queen of Scots once anchored and where a community successfully fought to protect the seabed.

subject: Lampacau
summary: A vanished island in the Pearl River Delta that served as the Portuguese Empire's first foothold in Chinese waters — now absorbed by sediment into a larger landmass, its very name contested across a dozen spellings in two languages.

subject: Lan Kwai Fong
summary: A labyrinth of alleyways in Central Hong Kong where matchmakers once plied their trade, and where a Montreal expat's dream transformed a forgotten block into the city's most electric nightlife district — shadowed forever by the tragedy of a New Year's crowd that grew too large.

subject: Lancashire
summary: The northwest English county whose cotton mills powered an empire, whose Red Rose fought a thirty-year war, and whose moors, coast, and grit-stone fells still define a quietly distinct corner of the country.

subject: Lancaster County, South Carolina
summary: Catawba homeland, Scots-Irish backcountry, Revolutionary War battlefield country, and birthplace of Andrew Jackson - 555 square miles of South Carolina Piedmont named for an English rose.

subject: Lance's Right
summary: A legendary reef break off Sipura Island in Indonesia's Mentawai chain, named for the surfer who first rode it and feared for a section of reef so sharp locals call it the surgeon's table.

story.title: Land Between the Lakes: Where the Government Drowned America

subject: Land Between the Lakes
summary: The Kentucky-Tennessee peninsula where TVA forcibly removed 2,300 families to create a recreation area - their churches now underwater, their cemeteries relocated, their moonshine heritage drowned beneath two artificial lakes.

story.title: Land Between the Lakes and the Drowned Towns

subject: Land Between the Lakes and the Drowned Towns
summary: The 170,000-acre peninsula where the TVA relocated entire communities to create two massive lakes - former residents still gather annually at cemeteries accessible only by boat, mourning towns that now lie beneath fifty feet of water.

subject: Land Reform in Taiwan
summary: A government that had just lost an entire country to revolution arrived on a small island and did the one thing its enemies had promised but failed to deliver: it gave the land to the people who farmed it.

subject: Land in the Sea
summary: One of Bali's seven great sea temples sits on an offshore rock that visitors can reach only at low tide - and more than a third of that rock is now artificial, rebuilt with Japanese engineering after the original stone began to crumble.

subject: Land of Frankincense
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site spanning four ancient locations in Oman's Dhofar region, where the frankincense trade shaped civilizations for thousands of years.

subject: Land of Punt
summary: For three thousand years, the ancient Egyptians traded with a land they called Punt -- God's Land -- sending expeditions to bring back gold, frankincense, myrrh, and baboons. Where exactly Punt was remains one of archaeology's greatest unsolved mysteries.

story.title: Land of the Heavenly Kings: Tana Toraja

subject: Land of the Heavenly Kings
summary: In the highlands of South Sulawesi, the Toraja people keep the dead among the living for months or years, bury them in cliff faces with wooden effigies standing guard, and sacrifice water buffalo to ferry souls to the afterlife.

subject: Land's End
summary: The famous westernmost point of mainland England, where the Penwith granite finally meets the Atlantic and the long road to John o' Groats begins.

subject: Landers
summary: A Mojave Desert community of nearly 3,000 people who call themselves Landroids, organized their skies into one of the densest concentrations of amateur observatories in the United States, and built a time machine out of plywood and determination.

subject: Landsborough's Blazed Tree (Camp 69)
summary: A single coolibah south of Charleville still carries the axe-cut record of the night an exhausted expedition camped beneath it in 1862, on the first crossing of Australia from north to south.

subject: Lane Seminary
summary: A Cincinnati seminary's 18-day debate over slavery in 1834 triggered a mass student exodus, shaped the abolitionist movement, and launched the careers of Harriet Beecher Stowe and the Lane Rebels.

subject: Langalibalele
summary: King of the amaHlubi, Langalibalele refused to surrender his people's guns to colonial authorities in 1873 -- a stand that cost him decades on Robben Island and split the Colony of Natal down the middle.

subject: Langebaan
summary: A West Coast town that banned industry to protect its identity as a fishing and holiday village, Langebaan sits on a turquoise lagoon that draws kitesurfers, sailors, and mussel lovers to a coastline an hour from Cape Town.

subject: Langeberg
summary: Stretching 250 kilometers across the Western Cape, the Langeberg mountains serve as a living sundial -- local lore says the shadows of the seven Clock Peaks tell the time of day.

subject: Langeoog
summary: A car-free East Frisian island whose dune cemetery holds the singer of the most famous song of the Second World War, and the men who never came home from forced labor a few hundred meters away.

subject: Langfossen
summary: A 612-meter waterfall that slides directly into a fjord, voted the world's most beautiful in 2006 and never harnessed for hydropower -- one of Norway's last wild cascades.

subject: Langley Air Force Base
summary: The oldest continuously active air force base on Earth, established before America entered World War I, named for the aviation pioneer who almost flew first, and now home of the 1st Fighter Wing's F-22 Raptors.

subject: Langley Speedway (Virginia)
summary: The flat little Hampton short track where Denny Hamlin learned to drive, where NASCAR ran its last Grand National race before becoming the Winston Cup, and where the lights still come on every Saturday night.

subject: Langston Hughes
summary: Poet, playwright, and columnist Langston Hughes made Harlem the center of his creative life for four decades, writing jazz-inflected verse that insisted Black America's beauty and pain were worthy of literature's highest ambitions.

subject: Langweer
summary: A Frisian sailing village whose long-lost grietman locked his front door in 1829 and left the house untouched for thirty years.

subject: Lanquín
summary: A Guatemalan jungle town where turquoise limestone pools hide an underground river, millions of bats darken the sky at dusk, and the Maya once descended into caves they believed led to the underworld.

subject: Lantau Peak
summary: The Phoenix Mountain — Hong Kong's second-highest peak and the highest point on Lantau Island — rises from ancient volcanic rock to offer one of the finest dawn vistas in Asia, where on clear mornings hikers watch the shadow of the peak stretch across the South China Sea.

subject: Lantau Trail
summary: A 70-kilometre loop around Hong Kong's largest island, opened in 1984, that takes hikers from a sleepy ferry town over the island's highest peaks, past a giant Buddha, through an ancient fishing village, along wild coastline, and back — all within an hour's journey from one of Asia's greatest cities.

subject: Lanzón
summary: A fanged granite deity stands at the heart of a subterranean labyrinth in the Peruvian Andes, where worshippers met their god in darkness and altered consciousness.

subject: Lapa Terra Ronca
summary: A cave named for the sound it makes, with a mouth 96 metres tall, where every August pilgrims carry candles into the dark of the Goias cerrado.

subject: Lapidarium, Kerch
summary: One of the world's great collections of ancient carved stone, where more than two thousand Bosporan inscriptions, statues, and gravestones preserve the voices of a vanished kingdom.

subject: Laplace affair
summary: In 1839, a French warship sailed into Hawaiian waters and forced King Kamehameha III to end the persecution of Catholics -- a confrontation that reshaped religious freedom in the Kingdom of Hawaii at the point of a cannon.

subject: Lapland (Sweden)
summary: Sweden's northernmost province covers nearly a quarter of the country and holds fewer than 90,000 people — and is quietly shedding the name outsiders gave it.

subject: Lapland gold rush
summary: A desperate famine-stricken nation sent an expedition to the Arctic wilderness in 1868, and the gold they found along the Ivalo River sparked Finland's only gold rush.

subject: Laponia
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage landscape of glaciers, old-growth forests, and wetlands where Sami reindeer herders have shaped the land for millennia.

subject: Lapplandsleden
summary: A 190-kilometer wilderness trail through Swedish Lapland connecting Borgafjäll to Hemavan, offering raw subarctic solitude above the treeline where the Sami once walked.

subject: Large Helical Device
summary: The world's second-largest superconducting stellarator, hidden in rural Gifu Prefecture, where scientists achieved ion temperatures of 120 million degrees in pursuit of fusion energy.

subject: Large Latin American Millimeter Array
summary: On a wind-scoured Andean ridge nearly five kilometers high, a single white dish is learning to listen to the faint millimeter glow of the universe.

subject: Largs
summary: A Firth of Clyde seaside town where the Scots and Norwegians fought in 1263, where Allied commanders planned D-Day in 1943, and where Nardini's still serves ice cream on the Esplanade.

subject: Largs Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI inshore lifeboat station on the Firth of Clyde, established in 1964 and the site of a 1983 rescue that earned crewman Arthur Hill the RNLI Silver Medal.

subject: Larissa Cremaste
summary: A fortress city that seemed to hang from the flank of Mount Othrys, captured and recaptured by Macedonian kings and Roman legions in the wars that decided Greece.

subject: Lark Quarry Dinosaur Trackways
summary: Thousands of dinosaur footprints pressed into 95-million-year-old mud, long read as the world's only fossil stampede, now at the centre of a scientific whodunit.

subject: Larkhall
summary: A former mining and weaving town in the Clyde valley, known for the tallest viaduct in Scotland, an Olympic hurdler and a stubborn local aversion to the colour green.

subject: Larne
summary: A County Antrim ferry port of 19,000 people where Edward Bruce landed an invasion army in 1315 and where six P&O sailings a day still tie Northern Ireland to Scotland.

subject: Larung Gar
summary: Once the largest Buddhist monastic community in the world, Larung Gar became a battleground between Tibetan Buddhist devotion and Chinese state authority.

subject: Larung Gar Buddhist Academy
summary: Founded in 1980 by a single teacher and a handful of students, Larung Gar grew into the largest Tibetan Buddhist academy in the world before the Chinese government began demolishing it.

subject: Las (Greece)
summary: Las, a Homeric town on the Laconian Gulf named in the Catalogue of Ships, spent three millennia being contested, conquered, and abandoned — until only the hill of Passavas and the ruins of a medieval castle remain.

subject: Las Anod
summary: Capital of Somalia's Sool region, Las Anod has been claimed by Puntland, Somaliland, and Khatumo State in succession, making it one of the most contested cities in the Horn of Africa.

subject: Las Chinchillas National Reserve
summary: In the dry hills of north-central Chile lies the only reserve on Earth built to save the long-tailed chinchilla, a creature once hunted nearly to extinction for the softest fur in the world.

subject: Las Haldas
summary: A 4,000-year-old ceremonial complex on the driest coast of Peru that challenged everything archaeologists thought they knew about the origins of civilization.

subject: Las Leñas
summary: Argentina's most ambitious ski mountain, where a single temperamental chairlift unlocks some of the most extreme lift-served terrain on the planet.

story.title: Las Vegas: The City That Exists Because Everything Else Is Illegal

subject: Las Vegas
summary: The Nevada oasis where gambling built a neon empire in the desert - where the mob built the Strip, where Elvis performed 837 shows, and where 42 million visitors annually come to do things their home states won't allow.

story.title: Las Vegas Strip: The City That Never Stops Reinventing Itself

subject: Las Vegas Strip
summary: The Nevada boulevard where Bugsy Siegel's desert dream became America's playground - where themed megaresorts rise and implode, where excess is virtue, and where what happens stays because the city erases yesterday to build tomorrow.

subject: Las Vegas Strip
summary: The mirage in the desert - where mobsters built casinos, corporations made them respectable, and 42 million visitors annually lose money amid fake Eiffel Towers, erupting volcanoes, and the most concentrated display of neon on Earth.

subject: Las Vegas culture (archaeology)
summary: The oldest known settled culture in Ecuador, a people who domesticated squash and gourds eight thousand years before Columbus.

subject: Lascar Row
summary: A narrow alley in Sheung Wan that has been called Matchmaker Lane, Cat Street, and Antiques Street at different points in its history — a street whose many names tell the story of Hong Kong's layered, contentious relationship with the people who built it.

subject: Lascaux
summary: Discovered by four teenagers and a dog in 1940, Lascaux's six hundred Paleolithic paintings are among the most important artistic achievements in human history -- and no living person will ever see the originals.

subject: Last Exit on Brooklyn
summary: Before Starbucks made Seattle synonymous with coffee, a University District coffeehouse named after a counterculture novel served as the city's living room for chess masters, folk musicians, bohemians, and anyone willing to linger over an espresso.

subject: Lastage
summary: Amsterdam's first industrial suburb, where the city's ships were built, rope was spun, and masts were stepped - until the city walls finally caught up with the workers in the 1590s.

subject: Lathen train collision
summary: On a Friday morning in 2006, a maglev train carrying invited guests along a test track in the Emsland ran into a maintenance vehicle nobody had confirmed was clear. Twenty-three people died.

subject: Latimeria
summary: A genus of fish thought extinct for 66 million years, rediscovered off the coast of South Africa in 1938, with its largest known population living in the volcanic caves of the Comoros Islands.

subject: Lau Fau Shan
summary: For generations the small shore village of Lau Fau Shan shipped 100 tons of oysters a year from the mudflats of Deep Bay — a harvest that has largely faded, leaving behind seafood restaurants, a 1,500-year-old temple, and the widest view of the border with mainland China that Hong Kong offers.

subject: Lau Shui Heung Reservoir
summary: Tucked inside Pat Sin Leng Country Park, the small Lau Shui Heung Reservoir earned the name 'mirror of the sky' for its deep green stillness — until hikers in 2018 walked across a cracked, bone-dry lakebed and discovered how precarious that reflection really was.

subject: Laugharne
summary: The Carmarthenshire estuary town where Dylan Thomas wrote Under Milk Wood, still governed by a medieval charter and a portreeve wearing a chain of gold cockle shells.

subject: Launceston
summary: Tasmania's northern city, one of Australia's oldest, where three rivers meet, Japanese macaques chatter in a park, and a place full of firsts now calls itself a city of food.

subject: Launceston, Cornwall
summary: The gateway to Cornwall: the county's only walled town, with a Norman castle on its hill, the county town until 1838, and the local birthplace of the mathematician who predicted Neptune.

subject: Laura Plantation
summary: A Creole plantation on the Mississippi where enslaved Senegalese storytellers preserved the trickster tales that became America's Brer Rabbit.

subject: Laura Street Trio
summary: Three buildings rose from the ashes of Jacksonville's Great Fire of 1901 and brought Prairie Style architecture to the American South, only to spend decades crumbling while the city argued over how to save them.

subject: Laura to Maytown Coach Road
summary: The last brutal leg of the road to the Palmer River gold, hand-cut through stone ranges by men chasing fortunes and the Cobb & Co coaches that followed them.

subject: Laurel, Mississippi
summary: Once the yellow pine lumber capital of the world, this small Mississippi city traded sawdust for Southern charm and now stars in HGTV's Home Town.

subject: Lauwerzijl
summary: A 195-person Groningen village named for a lock that no longer exists, in a landscape where coastal land kept being reclaimed away from the sea.

subject: Lava Cap Mine
summary: An abandoned gold mine southeast of Nevada City that chronicles the transition from Gold Rush prospecting to industrial hard-rock mining, now being considered for National Historic Landmark status.

subject: Lavenham
summary: A medieval Suffolk wool town that was once richer than York or Lincoln, then froze in time when the cloth trade collapsed - now Tudor timber-framing, Witchfinder General, Twinkle Twinkle, and Harry Potter's Godric's Hollow.

subject: Lavras
summary: A Minas Gerais town whose name means 'mines' — built on gold rush excavations, now ringed by waterfalls, university campuses, and a reservoir lake that reshaped the landscape.

subject: Lavras
summary: Founded by a Paulista rebel hunting gold in 1729, Lavras later became known as the 'land of ipês and schools' — a Minas Gerais town that turned its name for mining excavations into an academic legacy.

subject: Lavrio
summary: Lavrio, at the tip of Attica, built its ancient and modern identity on silver and lead pulled from the earth — the same mines that financed Athens's navy in the 5th century BC, were abandoned for a thousand years, then reopened in the 19th century by French and Greek industrialists under conditions that ended in a violent strike.

subject: Lawn Hill crater
summary: A perfect ring of dolomite hills in the Queensland outback marks where a meteorite struck water-logged seabed nearly half a billion years ago.

subject: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
summary: A hillside laboratory founded by cyclotron inventor Ernest Lawrence that has produced sixteen Nobel laureates, discovered sixteen chemical elements, and quietly shaped the modern world from the Berkeley Hills.

subject: Laxey
summary: A small east-coast Manx village whose name means 'salmon river,' whose famous wheel pumped lead mines for 75 years, and whose station is the start of the only mountain railway in the British Isles.

subject: Laxey
summary: A Norse-named Manx village built around the world's largest working waterwheel and three vintage railways climbing the glen.

subject: Laxey Wheel
summary: The largest surviving original working waterwheel in the world - 72 feet across, named Lady Isabella - built into a Manx hillside in 1854 to drain a lead mine.

subject: Laxton, Nottinghamshire
summary: The last village in England still working the medieval open field system, where strips of land are still farmed in common and a Court Leet still meets each year to enforce the boundaries.

subject: Laynhapuy Indigenous Protected Area
summary: Across the homelands south of Yirrkala, Yolngu rangers care for more than 1.2 million hectares of land and sea as a single living Country - protecting turtles, dugongs and sacred sites under their own law.

subject: Le Pays de la Sagouine
summary: A fictional Acadian village built on an island in Bouctouche, New Brunswick, brings the literary world of Antonine Maillet to life and draws 60,000 visitors each summer to a town of 2,400.

subject: LeBreton Flats
summary: A land deal born from eavesdropping accidentally rerouted the Rideau Canal and created Parliament Hill - then the neighbourhood that started it all was bulldozed, poisoned, and left empty for forty years.

subject: Leach Pottery
summary: Founded in 1920 by Bernard Leach and the Japanese master Shoji Hamada, the Leach Pottery in St Ives launched the British studio pottery movement and built the first traditional Japanese climbing kiln in the western world.

subject: Leadville
summary: The two-mile-high city that silver built - where a mining boom created Colorado's second-largest city by 1880, made Horace Tabor a millionaire and his wife Baby Doe a legend, then collapsed when silver crashed.

subject: Leather and LGBTQ Cultural District
summary: San Francisco officially designated a South of Market neighborhood as a cultural district to preserve half a century of leather and LGBTQ history threatened by rapid development.

subject: Leavenworth (Washington)
summary: Bavaria in the Cascades - a former logging town reinvented as an Alpine village, where half-timbered facades frame views of real mountains and the Enchantments beckon climbers to world-class wilderness.

subject: Lebedyn
summary: A swan-named fortress town in the Ukrainian northeast that gave the world one of its great operatic basses, and carries the memory of a brutal reprisal ordered by a tsar.

subject: Ledesma S.A.A.I.
summary: One of Argentina's great sugar empires, rooted in the Jujuy lowlands since 1830, and forever bound to the night in 1976 when its own lights stayed on while the town around it went dark.

subject: Lee Tung Street
summary: Hong Kong's Wedding Card Street — a Wan Chai lane where printers once produced millions of wedding invitations — demolished in 2007 despite years of community resistance, its story becoming a landmark moment in Hong Kong's civic history.

subject: Leechtown, British Columbia
summary: Vancouver Island's only real gold rush town, born in 1864 on a geological fault line, now a ghost town locked inside Greater Victoria's drinking water supply.

subject: Leeds
summary: A Yorkshire market town that became a city of a thousand trades, then a financial centre, with arcades and parks among the greenest in Europe.

subject: Leeds
summary: The metropolitan district of Leeds - a city built on cloth and coal that today is the UK's largest financial centre outside London.

subject: Leeds Corn Exchange
summary: Cuthbert Brodrick's domed 1864 Italianate exchange, now a Grade I listed shopping centre and one of three working corn exchanges left in Britain.

subject: Leenane
summary: A village of about 200 at the head of Killary fjord on the Galway-Mayo border, where the 1990 film The Field was shot, where the head of the valley is a mountain the Irish call the devil's testicles, and where a Celtic cross marks the Famine deaths at Doo Lough.

subject: Leer, Lower Saxony
summary: An East Frisian port that calls itself Germany's tea capital - registering 20 percent of the country's merchant fleet and home to the Bünting tea brand sold across the country.

subject: Leer, South Sudan
summary: Birthplace of hip-hop artist Emmanuel Jal and home village of politician Riek Machar, this Unity State town has been burned and rebuilt across three decades of war.

subject: Leesburg, Virginia
summary: A Loudoun County seat founded in 1758 - briefly the safe-deposit box of the United States during the War of 1812, contested ground in the Civil War, and home to George Marshall's quiet retirement.

subject: Leesmuseum voor Vrouwen
summary: In 1877 Amsterdam, the city's reading societies were closed to women — so eight women built one of their own, and watched their husbands' colleagues panic when one woman tried to join the men's.

subject: Leeuwarden
summary: Capital of Friesland, birthplace of M.C. Escher and Mata Hari, 2018 European Capital of Culture, and finish line of the Eleven Cities skating tour.

subject: Leeward Antilles
summary: A chain of Caribbean islands slowly drifting into South America, split between Dutch territories and Venezuelan dependencies, where turquoise waters mask the grinding collision of tectonic plates beneath.

subject: Lefkandi
summary: A village on Euboea where a single buried building forced historians to rewrite the Greek Dark Ages.

subject: Legislative Assembly of Minas Gerais
summary: The 77-deputy state legislature of Minas Gerais, housed on Avenida Afonso Pena in Belo Horizonte, born from imperial decree and surviving two dictatorships.

subject: Legoland California
summary: The first Legoland outside Europe opened in Carlsbad in 1999, bringing a world built entirely from plastic bricks to the Southern California coast.

subject: Leicester
summary: An East Midlands city built on Roman foundations and knitting frames, now one of the most ethnically diverse places in Britain, where Diwali outshines the Christmas lights and the Caribbean Carnival closes August.

subject: Leicester City Centre
summary: The compact historical core of Leicester, where a Roman town named for an Iron Age tribe became a Norman castle stronghold, a medieval market, and a Victorian commercial heart - all still legible in the modern street grid inside the inner ring road.

subject: Leicester Square
summary: A 17th-century gentlemen's residential square in central London that became Britain's biggest entertainment district, home to the country's largest cinema, a Shakespeare fountain, and the Mr Bean and Iron Throne statues.

subject: Leiden
summary: A city that chose books over tax breaks, made paper money from prayer books, and built a Golden Age skyline that Amsterdam alone surpasses.

subject: Leidsche Rijn
summary: On 4 December 1997, a Dutch prime minister drove the first pile into a polder west of Utrecht. Three decades later, that polder holds 45,000 people, two new railway stations, and a covered highway - the largest planned suburb in Dutch history.

subject: Leigh Creek, South Australia
summary: A coal town in the northern Flinders that was picked up and moved so the mine could dig out the ground it stood on - and then outlived the very coal that built it.

subject: Leimebamba District
summary: A small Peruvian cloud-forest town famous for the museum that holds more than 200 Chachapoya mummies rescued from a lake hidden in the mountains.

subject: Leinster Nickel Mine
summary: One of Australia's great nickel mines, Leinster built its own town in the desert, rode decades of brutal price swings, and was paused indefinitely in 2024 as the global nickel market collapsed.

subject: Leipzig
summary: Saxony's largest city - Bach's parish, Mendelssohn's home, Wagner's birthplace, and the city whose Monday demonstrations brought down East Germany.

subject: Leith
summary: Edinburgh's historic port, where the 1920 vote against re-merger was overruled anyway, Rose's Lime Cordial saved the Royal Navy from scurvy, and gentrification finally brought trams back after almost a century.

subject: Leith
summary: Edinburgh's port for nine centuries: where Mary of Guise held court, where the rules of golf were written, where Trainspotting was set, and where the trams finally came back in 2023.

subject: Leith Walk
summary: A defensive earthwork against Cromwell became one of Edinburgh's longest streets, lined with tenements, tram history, and a public gallows whose name supposedly gave the area its drink.

subject: Leland, North Carolina
summary: In thirty years Leland went from 1,900 people to more than 23,500 - the fastest-growing town in North Carolina, born from a railroad crossing and a 1989 annexation grudge with the neighbor next door.

subject: Lelystad
summary: The Dutch capital built on a seabed, named for the engineer who spent forty years convincing the Netherlands to drain a sea.

subject: Leme, São Paulo
summary: A São Paulo sugar-cane town where August 29, 1895 is still celebrated annually, bicycles outnumber buses, and twelve chapels mark a cycling pilgrimage route.

subject: Lemmer
summary: A Frisian port town where 500 farmers with field guns once dared the British Navy to open fire — and where the world's largest still-operating steam pumping station now keeps the polders dry.

subject: Lemnian Athena
summary: Ancient writers called this bronze Athena the most beautiful thing Pheidias ever made - and then it vanished, leaving art historians to reassemble a masterpiece from scattered Roman copies.

subject: Lemvig
summary: A market town wedged between steep hills and the innermost corner of a Limfjord bay, where Denmark's first scale model of the solar system begins at a hairpin bend and ends four and a half kilometres later at the sea.

subject: Lenapehoking
summary: Before it was New York, New Jersey, or Pennsylvania, the land between the Hudson and Delaware river valleys was Lenapehoking -- homeland of the Lenape people, whose language still echoes in the place names of the region they were forced to leave.

subject: Lengo Petroglyphs
summary: A 200-meter laterite slab in the Central African Republic bush, engraved with more than 500 figures: antelope, leopards, spears, throwing knives, and a single human with a bird's head.

subject: Lennox Head
summary: A laid-back coastal village between Ballina and Byron Bay, Lennox Head is famous for one of the world's great right-hand point breaks, a tea-stained dune lake, and a Bundjalung ceremonial ring still standing among the houses.

subject: Lençóis
summary: The cobblestone diamond-era town at the gateway to Chapada Diamantina National Park, where trekkers gather before setting out into canyons, caves, and waterfalls in the Bahian interior.

subject: Lençóis Maranhenses
summary: A desert that fills with rain-fed lakes each year, turning 155,000 hectares of white sand into a moving gallery of blue and turquoise pools.

subject: Leo Petroglyph
summary: Thirty-seven carvings of humans, animals, and footprints pecked into a sandstone slab in Jackson County, Ohio - meanings still unknown - protected since the WPA built a shelter over them in the 1930s.

subject: Leonidio
summary: A 'red town' tucked between towering ochre cliffs at the mouth of a Peloponnese gorge, Leonidio is the living capital of Tsakonia — guardian of the last surviving descendant of ancient Doric Greek — and famous worldwide for its sweet purple eggplant.

subject: Leopoldina, Minas Gerais
summary: A coffee town in the Zona da Mata named for a princess, built on land once belonging to the Puri people, now a dairy municipality of 51,000.

subject: Lepreum
summary: Chief city of ancient Triphylia, Lepreum fought for centuries against Eleian domination — the only Triphylian town to send troops to Plataea — until its ruins were swallowed by the hills west of Mount Minthi.

subject: Leptis Magna
summary: Once the third-most important city in Roman Africa, Leptis Magna was buried for centuries beneath Libyan sand dunes -- preserving one of the most complete Roman cityscapes anywhere in the Mediterranean.

subject: Les Saintes
summary: A tiny French archipelago south of Guadeloupe where fishermen's wives invented the Tourment d'Amour pastry, cars are outnumbered by scooters, and the bay is ranked among the most beautiful in the world.

subject: Lesbos
summary: The third-largest Greek island, an emerald slab of olive groves and petrified stone in the northeastern Aegean, home to Sappho's poetry, the Gattilusi lords' castles, eleven million olive trees, and a recent history written on the shore where the world's displaced came ashore.

subject: Lesche of the Knidians
summary: A fifth-century BCE clubhouse at Delphi whose walls once held Polygnotos's celebrated paintings of the fall of Troy and Odysseus's descent into the underworld — the greatest lost paintings of antiquity, known only through Pausanias's detailed description.

subject: Lesvos
summary: The third-largest Greek island, shaped like a plane-tree leaf by its two deep gulfs, where ouzo flows in Plomari, flamingos wade at Kalloni, and a forest turned to stone records a volcanic past.

subject: Letcher County, Kentucky
summary: An eastern Kentucky coal county whose disasters - the 1976 Scotia Mine explosions, the 2022 Appalachian floods, the 2024 courthouse murder - keep reshaping it.

subject: Letchworth
summary: The world's first garden city, founded in 1903 to test a quiet pamphleteer's idea that cities and countryside might be combined into something better than either, and still owned today by a charity that exists for the benefit of its own residents.

subject: Leticia
summary: At the point where Colombia, Brazil, and Peru meet in the heart of the Amazon, one small port town serves as the gateway to three countries and one of Earth's greatest rivers.

subject: Leticia, Amazonas
summary: On a muddy bank of the Amazon where three nations touch, Colombia's southernmost town was named for a Peruvian engineer's wife.

subject: Letseng diamond mine
summary: Perched in the mountains of Lesotho where temperatures plunge to minus twenty and snow buries the workings in winter, the world's highest diamond mine produces the fewest stones per ton but the most valuable per carat.

subject: Letterfrack
summary: A village built by Quaker famine-relief workers that became, under different management, a site of one of Ireland's most painful chapters of institutional cruelty - and is today a furniture college, a national park gateway, and a community working to honor those it failed.

subject: Letterkenny
summary: Donegal's largest town, nicknamed the Cathedral Town, built around an early 17th-century Plantation castle and a Victorian neo-Gothic cathedral, now the commercial centre of northwest Ireland.

subject: Leuven
summary: A medieval university town where the world's largest brewery and the world's oldest Catholic university occupy the same compact center, both rebuilt twice from rubble.

subject: Levant Mine and Beam Engine
summary: On 20 October 1919, the man engine at Levant collapsed and thirty-one Cornish miners fell to their deaths in the shaft; a century later, the world's last working beam engine on its original site still breathes steam above their names.

subject: Leverburgh
summary: A South Harris ferry village renamed in 1920 for a soap tycoon who tried, and failed, to industrialise the Outer Hebrides.

subject: Leverburgh
summary: A South Harris village renamed in 1920 after the soap magnate whose ambitious herring empire collapsed with his death five years later.

subject: Levi Strauss & Co.
summary: The San Francisco company that turned riveted denim work pants into the most iconic garment in American history.

subject: Levisham
summary: A village of 70 people on the North York Moors whose 11th-century church stands abandoned in a field, the original settlement having moved uphill after the Black Death.

subject: Levy Mwanawasa
summary: Zambia's third president, whose slurred speech (the result of a 1991 crash that killed his aide) became an opposition joke and who died in office in 2008 having made anti-corruption the defining cause of his career.

subject: Lewenborg
summary: Every street in this 1970s Groningen suburb is named for a ship part - anchor, keel, crow's nest, gangway - and three apartment towers were demolished to dig a canal through the middle.

subject: Lewes (Delaware)
summary: The First Town in the First State - founded by Dutch whalers in 1631, massacred a year later, and rebuilt into a Bay-front harbor where the ferry to Cape May still leaves every two hours.

subject: Lewis
summary: The northern two-thirds of the largest island in the Outer Hebrides, low-lying and treeless, with Stornoway as its only town, Gaelic on its road signs, and a long history of land struggle behind every quiet field.

subject: Lewis Pass
summary: Long before surveyors named it, Ngai Tahu carriers crossed this saddle in the Southern Alps bearing pounamu - New Zealand's sacred greenstone - from the wild West Coast to Canterbury.

subject: Lewis Peatlands
summary: Almost 590 square kilometres of blanket bog covering more than a third of the Isle of Lewis, one of the largest and most intact peatland landscapes in the world.

subject: Lewiston (Idaho)
summary: Idaho's only seaport sits 465 miles from the Pacific, where the Snake and Clearwater rivers meet in a valley so deep that ocean-going vessels can navigate here - making this former territorial capital the most improbable port city in the American West.

story.title: Lexington: The Horse Capital of the World

subject: Lexington
summary: The Kentucky city where thoroughbreds are royalty - where the Bluegrass horse farms define the landscape, where bourbon ages in warehouses, and where the University of Kentucky basketball is religion.

subject: Lexington Market
summary: One of the longest continuously operating public markets in America - founded in 1782 on land donated by a Revolutionary War officer, and home for two centuries to Faidley's crab cakes and the everyday Baltimore that the Inner Harbor isn't.

story.title: The Town That Waited for the Rails

subject: Lexington, Illinois
summary: Founded in 1836 but slow to grow, Lexington, Illinois, transformed from a struggling prairie outpost into a bustling commercial hub following the arrival of the railroad in 1854 and later the alignment of Route 66.

subject: Leybucht
summary: A North Sea bay that was once 129 square kilometers, then was diked away to 19, and was almost erased entirely before nature conservationists made it stop.

subject: Li Yuen Street East
summary: A narrow market lane in Hong Kong's Central district that has been called 'Newspaper Street,' 'Central's Women Street,' and the first street in colonial Hong Kong named after a Chinese person — all within about 130 years.

subject: Liancourt Rocks
summary: Two volcanic islets in the Sea of Japan, known as Dokdo in Korea and Takeshima in Japan, sit at the center of one of East Asia's most enduring territorial disputes, guarded by South Korean police and home to a single civilian resident.

story.title: Liang Bua: The Cave That Rewrote Human History

subject: Liang Bua
summary: A limestone cave on Flores where archaeologists unearthed the bones of a meter-tall hominin species -- the 'hobbits' -- who hunted dwarf elephants and dodged Komodo dragons for tens of thousands of years.

subject: Liaodong Commandery
summary: An ancient Chinese administrative region east of the Liao River that endured for over a millennium, from the Warring States period through the Northern dynasties.

subject: Liaoning
summary: China's gateway between the heartland and Manchuria, Liaoning is a province where 8,000 years of human habitation, Manchu imperial legacy, and 20th-century industrial might converge along the northern shore of the Yellow Sea.

subject: Liathach
summary: Liathach's terraced sandstone flanks are built from rock a billion years old, capped with quartzite that preserves the fossilized burrows of creatures that crawled across an ancient seabed half a billion years ago.

subject: Libby Hill, Richmond
summary: Standing on Libby Hill in 1737, William Byrd II decided this view of the James reminded him of Richmond on the Thames - and named the city he was founding accordingly. The view is still there.

subject: Liberdade
summary: A cattle road renamed Freedom after the troops who won Bahia marched down it — and the Salvador neighbourhood that became the home address of Black Bahian cultural and political life.

subject: Liberdade (district of São Paulo)
summary: Once São Paulo's execution ground for enslaved people and convicts, the neighborhood renamed itself Liberty -- and became the largest Japanese diaspora community in the world.

subject: Liberec
summary: The Manchester of Bohemia, a textile city of 108,000 in a mountain basin, whose German name and German population both vanished within a decade - and whose library now stands on the site of the synagogue that was burned.

subject: Liberty Bell
summary: Cast in London, cracked in Philadelphia, recast twice by local founders, and adopted by abolitionists as a symbol of freedom, the Liberty Bell is America's most famous flawed icon.

subject: Liberty Clock
summary: A 1925 mechanical clock set into the Tudor-revival archway between Carnaby and Kingly Streets, with four winged winds at its corners and a Saint-George-and-the-dragon animation that runs every hour above the heads of the West End shoppers below.

subject: Liberty, South Carolina
summary: A small Pickens County town probably named after a Revolutionary-era congregation hearing news of Cornwallis's surrender, Liberty rode the cotton-mill century from 1901 to the 1990s and is still figuring out what comes next.

subject: Liceu
summary: Barcelona's opera house has burned twice, been bombed once, and hosted the most-performed repertoire in Europe -- each catastrophe only deepening the city's refusal to let it die.

subject: Lichfield
summary: A cathedral city of 35,000 in Staffordshire that birthed the first English dictionary, the founder of the Ashmolean Museum, and a generation of Enlightenment philosophers who turned a coaching town into a city of ideas.

subject: Lichfield
summary: A red-sandstone city where Bishop Chad of Mercia died in 672, the largest Anglo-Saxon gold hoard ever found was unearthed in a nearby field, and the last man burned at the stake for heresy in England met his end in the market place.

subject: Lida Ghetto
summary: About 8,000 Jews of Lida and the surrounding villages were forced into a few blocks between the railroad and the river in 1941; on a single morning in May 1942, more than 5,600 of them were marched into a forest and shot.

subject: Liemers
summary: A small Dutch region named, possibly, for the Roman border - where the IKEA outside Duiven sits roughly where the legions once watched the Rhine.

subject: Liepāja massacres
summary: The Latvian port city where systematic murder was documented on film, creating some of the only surviving footage of Holocaust atrocities as they occurred.

subject: Lier
summary: A small Flemish city where a 14th-century livestock-market decision still echoes in nicknames, and a 1930s clock tracks thirteen kinds of time.

story.title: Lieutenant Governor of the Isle of Man

subject: Lieutenant Governor of the Isle of Man
summary: The Crown's man on a Norse-flavoured island, whose powers have been quietly dismantled one century at a time.

subject: Lifford
summary: Donegal's county town, an O'Donnell castle, and the ancestral home of an American president - all sitting on the wrong side of the River Foyle from a Northern Irish town twice its size.

subject: Light Rail (MTR)
summary: The goldenrod-colored thread on the MTR map, Hong Kong's Light Rail carries nearly half a million passengers daily through the northwestern New Territories — a surface network born from a new town and shaped by decades of growth.

subject: Lighthouses on Lundy
summary: Three lighthouses on a Bristol Channel island — including one so tall it was capped by fog and saved nobody for sixty years.

subject: Likasi
summary: A Congolese copper city in the hills of Katanga, 120 kilometers north of Lubumbashi, built on ore and remembered for a siege.

subject: Lilaea (ancient city)
summary: Built at the very source of the Cephissus river on the north slopes of Parnassus, ancient Lilaea was a Phocian city-state whose citizens believed the sacred spring at Delphi was their river's gift to the world.

subject: Lillehammer Olympiapark
summary: The five venues built for the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer survive as an active sports complex, a rare example of Olympic infrastructure that found meaningful life after the closing ceremonies.

subject: Lilleø
summary: On a sliver of land smaller than Central Park, in a corner of the Danish Baltic that almost nobody flies over, a strange microclimate produces apples and pears so vivid that Copenhagen's best chefs build menus around them.

subject: Lilongwe
summary: Malawi's capital is so green that the city sometimes disappears behind its own trees, a place where Old Town village life and New Town government ambition exist side by side.

subject: Lily Point Marine Reserve
summary: On a bluff at the edge of a stranded piece of America, the richest reef net fishery on the Salish Sea survived a cannery, a golf course, and the border itself.

subject: Lima
summary: Where Pizarro founded Spain's South American capital on a desert coast, where fog shrouds the city eight months a year, where ceviche was perfected and the Pacific defines everything.

subject: Limavady
summary: A market town named for a leaping dog, where Jane Ross transcribed Londonderry Air and Richard Branson accidentally landed his transatlantic balloon.

subject: Limburg (Belgium)
summary: Belgium's easternmost Flemish province carries a borrowed name, an unborrowed dialect, and the quietest temperament in Flanders - shaped by coal mines that are gone and orchards that are not.

subject: Limburg (Netherlands)
summary: The southernmost Dutch province - Catholic, hilly, multilingual, mined out and now reinventing itself - the strange salient where the Netherlands meets Belgium and Germany at a single point.

subject: Limburg-Hohenlimburg
summary: A 13th-century hilltop seat above the Lenne river where one ambitious count's inheritance arithmetic split a Westphalian dynasty in two.

subject: Lime Street, Liverpool
summary: Named for the lime kilns that once stank up the neighbourhood so badly that the doctors at the infirmary complained, Lime Street became Liverpool's grandest civic boulevard -- and the favourite haunt of a folk-song prostitute who outlived the kilns by two centuries.

subject: Limehouse Cut
summary: London's oldest canal still runs in a straight line from Bow to the Thames, carrying two and a half centuries of stinking history beneath a floating towpath.

subject: Limerick
summary: Ireland's third-largest city, where Viking longships once burned and Munster rugby still answers in roar.

subject: Liming New Village
summary: A planned community built in 1970s Taichung to house government workers relocated from Taipei, Liming New Village survives today as a quiet, tree-lined enclave caught between preservation and the pressures of a fast-growing city.

subject: Limingen
summary: Norway's eighth-largest lake lies 725 metres from Sweden, drains out of both ends through tunnels, and rises and falls by ten vertical metres at the convenience of the power system.

subject: Limón
summary: Costa Rica's Caribbean port city speaks Mekatelyu as well as Spanish, throws the country's wildest carnival, and channels nearly 90% of the nation's imports and exports through its docks at Moin.

subject: Lin Ma Hang
summary: A Hong Kong border village beside the Shenzhen River where an abandoned lead and silver mine, ancestral halls, and a now-unused "international bridge" for cross-border farmers tell the layered story of life at the edge of two worlds.

subject: Linbian
summary: A quietly tropical township on the edge of Taiwan's Pingtung plains, Linbian wears summer twelve months a year and has turned that fact into a fruit.

subject: Lincoln
summary: A medieval city the railways and the A1 forgot — leaving its cathedral, its castle, and one of the steepest streets in England exactly where the Romans left them.

subject: Lincoln Colored Home
summary: Eva Carroll Monroe founded the Lincoln Colored Home in Springfield, Illinois, to provide a safe haven for African-American children excluded from segregated orphanages and for elderly women. Through an interracial partnership with Mary Lawrence, she established a brick facility that served as a beloved community center until its closure in 1933.

subject: Lindbergh kidnapping
summary: The 1932 abduction and murder of aviator Charles Lindbergh's infant son from a remote New Jersey estate became the 'crime of the century,' spawning a media frenzy, a sensational trial, and federal kidnapping laws still in force today.

subject: Linden Assembly
summary: For 68 years, General Motors' sprawling Linden plant built everything from Buicks to Wildcat fighter planes before a white Chevrolet Blazer rolled off the line as its last vehicle in 2005.

subject: Linden Lab
summary: The San Francisco company that created Second Life, one of the earliest and most ambitious virtual worlds.

subject: Lindenstraße
summary: For 34 years, German families gathered on Sunday evenings to watch their nation argue with itself through a fictional Munich street that was actually a sound stage in Cologne.

subject: Lindholm Høje
summary: A hill above the Limfjord where more than 700 graves and several hundred stone ships lay sealed under drifting sand for eight centuries.

subject: Lindis Pass
summary: The highest highway pass on New Zealand's South Island, where golden tussock grasslands roll between the valleys of the Lindis and Ahuriri Rivers in a landscape so remote that cellphones fall silent.

subject: Line 1 (Athens Metro)
summary: Athens has been riding the same rail line since 1869 - the green line locals still call the Elektrikos, the oldest urban railway in Greece.

subject: Line 3 (Athens Metro)
summary: Athens Metro Line 3 is the city's longest metro line, running 47.3 km from Piraeus port to the international airport — and its central stations double as underground museums of the antiquities unearthed during construction.

subject: Line 4 (Athens Metro)
summary: Two tunnel-boring machines named Athina and Niki are carving a U-shaped subway beneath Athens - a line that doesn't carry passengers yet, but already reshapes the city above it.

subject: Linhares
summary: The largest municipality in Espírito Santo by area, hosting 69 lakes, the country's largest private Atlantic Forest reserve, and some of Brazil's best surf breaks.

subject: Linhuangfu
summary: Founded in 918 by the Khitan emperor Yelü Abaoji and completed in just 100 days, Linhuangfu was the supreme capital of the Liao dynasty, a nomadic empire that ruled between China and the steppe for two centuries.

subject: Linked Hybrid
summary: A visionary housing complex near Beijing's old city wall that draws 70% of its heating and cooling from 655 geothermal wells drilled 100 meters underground.

subject: Linlithgow
summary: A West Lothian town of 16,500 famous for its royal palace, its loch, its loyal black bitch, the first medical chloroform, and the future birthplace of Star Trek's Mr. Scott.

subject: Lion Mountains
summary: The forested coastal range whose Portuguese name, Serra Lyoa, gave an entire nation its identity.

subject: Lion Rock
summary: A 495-metre granite peak above Kowloon whose crouching-lion silhouette became the symbol of Hong Kong's resilience, and whose trails carry a real edge of danger.

subject: Lion Salt Works
summary: The last open-pan salt works in Britain produced a flaky salt called 'Lagos Salt' that was shipped to Nigeria for nearly a century. The Biafran War helped kill the trade. The pans went cold in 1986.

subject: Liptako
summary: A hilly, gold-bearing region where Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso meet, Liptako is the heart of a 19th-century Fulani emirate whose monarchy quietly endures to this day.

subject: Lisburn
summary: Out of the fire I shall arise - Lisburn's Latin motto comes from the 1707 conflagration that levelled the linen town. The mills came back. So did the town.

subject: Lismore
summary: A resilient riverside city in the heart of the Northern Rivers, where artists, alternative culture and a community shaped by catastrophic floods all meet on Bundjalung country.

subject: Lismore Seminary
summary: After a century of fleeing soldiers, leaking roofs, and rowdy inns, the Catholic seminary of Scotland's Highland district finally settled into a Presbyterian island - and lasted exactly twenty-five years.

subject: Lismore, Scotland
summary: St Moluag cut off his own finger to win a boat race for this island in the Lynn of Lorn, and Lismore has been quietly defying expectations ever since.

subject: Lispole
summary: A small Gaeltacht village on the Dingle Peninsula whose stone railway viaduct remembers a vanished narrow-gauge line - and whose families produced one of Ireland's most consequential revolutionaries.

subject: Lisse
summary: A small town between Haarlem and Leiden whose sandy soil grew Holland's bulb empire and whose 32-hectare spring garden draws over 1.4 million visitors in eight weeks.

subject: Listowel
summary: The largest town in north Kerry, home of the world's first operational monorail and a literary tradition that fills the Kerry Writers Museum.

subject: Litherland
summary: A Sefton town whose town hall hosted some of the earliest Beatles gigs - and whose name, in Old Norse and Old English, means simply 'the land on the slope.'

subject: Little Andaman
summary: The fourth largest Andaman island sits at the archipelago's southern edge, where the Onge people's ancestral homeland meets Bengali settler villages, rainforest waterfalls, and some of India's most remote surf breaks.

story.title: Little Bighorn: The Day Custer Died

subject: Little Bighorn
summary: The Montana battlefield where George Armstrong Custer and 268 soldiers died fighting Lakota and Cheyenne warriors in 1876 - the worst military defeat of the Indian Wars, transforming a vain commander into martyr and guaranteeing vengeance that would end at Wounded Knee.

story.title: Little Bohemia Lodge: The Night Dillinger Slipped Through the FBI's Fingers

subject: Little Bohemia Lodge
summary: A rural Wisconsin lodge built in 1929 became the site of one of the FBI's most humiliating failures when John Dillinger and his entire gang escaped a botched 1934 raid, leaving behind bullet holes that remain in the walls to this day.

subject: Little Eva
summary: A B-24 bomber ran out of fuel over the Gulf Country in 1942; the men who parachuted into the dark faced a far longer ordeal than the crash itself.

subject: Little Germany, Manhattan
summary: Manhattan's vanished German neighborhood was once the third-largest German community in the world, thriving with beer gardens and shooting clubs until a steamship disaster killed over a thousand residents in a single afternoon.

subject: Little Havana
summary: Miami's vibrant Cuban exile neighborhood where domino tiles clatter daily in Maximo Gomez Park and the annual Calle Ocho Festival once produced the world's longest conga line.

subject: Little Petra
summary: A narrow canyon north of Petra hides 2,000-year-old ceiling frescoes depicting winged gods harvesting grapes -- the only surviving interior Nabataean figurative painting, and among the finest Hellenistic artworks anywhere.

subject: Little Saint James
summary: A 70-acre Caribbean island whose tropical beauty became the backdrop for one of the most extensive sex trafficking operations in modern American history.

subject: Little Salt Spring
summary: A sinkhole in North Port, Florida, that looks like an ordinary pond but drops into a cenote containing 13,000-year-old evidence of some of the earliest Americans, including a giant tortoise cooked in its own shell.

story.title: Little Sister's Book and Art Emporium

subject: Little Sister's Book and Art Emporium
summary: A Davie Street bookshop survived two bombings and then spent seventeen years suing the Canadian government over the mail it was never allowed to receive — and rewrote Charter law doing it.

story.title: Little Sisters Book and Art Emporium v Canada

subject: Little Sisters Book and Art Emporium v Canada
summary: A Davie Street bookstore spent a decade proving that Canada Customs was deciding what was obscene by looking at who had ordered it.

subject: Little Tobago
summary: A tiny Caribbean island where a British businessman tried to save the greater bird of paradise from extinction by transplanting 47 birds from New Guinea -- a bold conservation experiment undone by a hurricane a half-century later.

story.title: Little and Broad Haven Lifeboat Station

subject: Little and Broad Haven Lifeboat Station
summary: Once the RNLI's smallest station, closed in 1921 and reopened in 1967, this Pembrokeshire inshore lifeboat now covers the holiday beaches of St Bride's Bay with a single fast inflatable.

subject: Lituanica
summary: Two Lithuanian emigrants crossed the Atlantic non-stop in an orange Bellanca bought by their community, then went down in a German forest 636 kilometres short of home - and became the figures a nation carved into its largest boulder.

subject: Liubech
summary: A quiet village on the Dnieper where, in 1097, the princes of Rus' sat down to carve their world into pieces, and where the father of East Slavic monasticism was born.

subject: Liubice
summary: Four kilometres downstream from Lübeck's spires, an Obotrite prince held a fortified harbour called Liubice - the lovely place - until a Rani fleet burned its church in 1138 and left the ground clear for somebody else's city.

subject: Liulichang
summary: A Beijing street that evolved from a Ming dynasty glazed-tile factory into the city's intellectual heart -- where scholars, painters, and calligraphers gathered for centuries, and where visitors still bargain for antiques today.

subject: Livingston (Guatemala)
summary: A Caribbean town with no road access where Garifuna, Maya, and Spanish cultures blend over drums, coconut rum, and freshwater waterfalls tumbling into the sea.

subject: Lizard Point
summary: The southernmost tip of mainland Britain - 49 degrees 57 minutes 30 seconds north, a headland where ocean passages begin and where, far too often, they have ended.

subject: Lizzie Borden
summary: On August 4, 1892, Andrew and Abby Borden were hacked to death in their Fall River, Massachusetts, home. Andrew's 32-year-old daughter Lizzie was tried and acquitted, but the case -- and the children's rhyme it spawned -- has never stopped haunting American culture.

subject: Liège
summary: A French-speaking city that has rebelled against every authority that tried to rule it, and still calls itself the fervent city.
