subject: Llanaelhaearn
summary: The Llyn village named for a seventh-century saint with an iron brow, where pilgrims to Bardsey once waited beside a well that 'laughed' bubbles -- until a 1900 diphtheria outbreak locked it away from the public for good.

subject: Llanaelhaearn Lifeboat Station
summary: A Welsh lifeboat funded by a paint-and-varnish widow in Henley, named for the ship whose captain died giving his life-jacket to a stowaway.

subject: Llanbedrog
summary: A small village on the Llyn Peninsula's south coast, named for a sixth-century Cornish saint and home to Plas Glyn-y-Weddw, the oldest art gallery in Wales.

subject: Llanberis
summary: A village of 2,023 people at the foot of Snowdon, where seven in ten residents still speak Welsh, the slate museum sits in the old quarry yard, and the busiest mountain rescue team in Britain takes 150-200 calls a year.

subject: Llanberis Pass
summary: A narrow mountain road wedged between Snowdon and the Glyderau, and the cliffs lining it have been a crucible of British rock climbing for almost a century.

subject: Llandaff
summary: An unofficial city within Cardiff, where a 6th-century cathedral has been wrecked by Welsh princes, Cromwell, the Luftwaffe and a lightning strike - and rebuilt every time.

subject: Llanddwyn Lifeboat Station
summary: A lifeboat station on a tiny tidal island off Anglesey that opened in 1826, closed twice for the same reason - not enough crew - and saved dozens of lives in between.

subject: Llandudno
summary: The Queen of the Welsh Resorts - a Victorian planned seaside town between two limestone headlands, with a vintage cable tramway, wild Kashmiri goats, and Alice Liddell's childhood summers on the West Shore.

subject: Llandudno Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station founded in 1861, for over a century unique in Britain for sitting inland - so its lifeboat could be towed to whichever shore needed it.

subject: Llandysul
summary: A small Ceredigion town on the Teifi where a 6th-century saint's church anchors a community of canoeists, Welsh-language publishers, and a New Year's Day ball game that became a Sunday school.

subject: Llanerchaeron
summary: A John Nash villa of 1795 that survived intact because its owners could not be bothered to update it, complete with brewery, dairy, laundry, water-wheel electricity, and a deserted medieval village in the parkland.

subject: Llanfaethlu
summary: A small west-Anglesey village on a five-mile stretch of coast that has wrecked at least sixteen named ships - and where the Holyhead lifeboat once saved 43 lives in a single night.

subject: Llanfechell
summary: A north-Anglesey village whose 12th-century parish church carries an unusual cupola - and whose schoolboy alumnus William Jones introduced the world to the symbol pi.

subject: Llangefni
summary: Anglesey's county town, the centre of an island where four out of five people still speak the language Edward I tried to extinguish.

subject: Llangollen
summary: A Welsh town where the River Dee runs white between stone bridges, where two women lived together for fifty years in the 18th century, and where the world's choirs gather every July.

subject: Llangrannog
summary: A Ceredigion coastal village squeezed into a narrow valley above a Blue Flag beach, watched over by a sea stack called the Giant's Tooth and home to the famous Urdd Welsh-language summer camp.

subject: Llanidan
summary: A quiet south Anglesey community hiding the buried street grid of a forgotten Roman town - and the field names that may mark where Tacitus described frenzied women defending the Druid groves.

subject: Llanllyfni
summary: The Nantlle Valley slate village where the world's most famous Welsh opera singer went to primary school, 85 percent of residents still speak Welsh at home, and a fair has been held every July for at least 200 years.

subject: Llanrwst
summary: A market town in the Conwy valley where the price of British wool was once set, with an Inigo Jones bridge from 1636, the stone coffin of Llywelyn the Great, and an old joke about applying to join the United Nations.

subject: Llanthony Secunda Priory
summary: Augustinian canons fled here from Welsh raids in 1135, made the king's favourite cheese, and possibly inspired Humpty Dumpty when a Royalist cannon blew itself up on these walls in 1643.

subject: Llanystumdwy
summary: The Welsh-speaking village on the Dwyfor river where David Lloyd George grew up, returned to die, and lies buried beneath a boulder chosen by the future architect of Portmeirion.

subject: Lleida
summary: One of Catalonia's oldest cities, crowned by a cathedral on its hill and set on a foggy inland plain, Lleida has been Ilergete stronghold, Roman Ilerda, Moorish Larida, and university town.

subject: Llevant de Mallorca
summary: Mallorca's eastern face in miniature: prehistoric stone towers, wild headlands, red sausage and airy pastries, all packed into a coast where the deep past lies just beneath your feet.

subject: Llullaillaco
summary: At 6,723 meters on the Argentine-Chilean border, this dormant stratovolcano holds the world's highest archaeological site, where three Inca child mummies were discovered in 1999 -- among the best-preserved pre-Columbian remains ever found.

subject: Llyn Alaw
summary: Anglesey's largest body of water - a shallow reservoir, just 5.2 metres deep at most, that was created in 1966 by flooding a marsh and now hosts thousands of overwintering wildfowl.

subject: Llyn Cerrig Bach
summary: A small Anglesey lake where, in 1942, the head groundsman of an RAF base accidentally dug up the most important Iron Age treasure hoard ever found in Wales.

subject: Llys Rhosyr
summary: The buried royal court of the Welsh princes of Gwynedd, lost beneath drifting sand for six centuries until archaeologists uncovered it in the 1990s.

subject: Llíria
summary: A town of 25,000 north of Valencia where thousands of residents play instruments and two brass bands have been proud rivals for over a century - all built atop a buried Iberian and Roman city.

subject: Lo Wu
summary: Hong Kong's busiest land border crossing, where 85 percent of all overland departures to mainland China funnel through a single rail terminus — a crossing whose name once meant 'shell lake' and whose tiny 1911 population of eight has grown into one of Asia's most trafficked checkpoints.

subject: Lobamba
summary: A small town in a green valley, Lobamba is the spiritual and royal heart of Eswatini - home to parliament, the Queen Mother's residence, and the cattle byre where the nation was born.

subject: Lobito
summary: Angola's second port city wraps around one of Africa's finest natural harbours, where a long sandy spit called the Restinga shelters the waterfront and a war-scarred lighthouse stands restored.

subject: Lobos
summary: A modest dairy town on the Argentine pampas where, in 1953, a sitting president returned to open a museum in the small house where he was born.

subject: Loch Achray
summary: A small Trossachs loch where a pardoned exile turned hunter-keeper outwitted a raiding Argyll party, weaving the place into Scottish lore long before Walter Scott put it in print.

subject: Loch Broom
summary: The sea loch whose Gaelic name means 'loch of rain showers' - flanked by An Teallach's ten-summit ridge, threading inland from the Minch past Ullapool to the rivers of the Dirrie Mountains.

subject: Loch Coruisk
summary: The Cauldron of Waters - an inland loch hemmed by the Black Cuillin that Walter Scott called 'a scene so stern' and Tennyson failed to see through the fog.

subject: Loch Druidibeg
summary: A 1,677-hectare freshwater loch on South Uist that holds Britain's stronghold of breeding greylag geese, a strange experimental forest, and a hard-won case study in community-owned conservation.

subject: Loch Fleet
summary: A shallow sea loch on the Sutherland coast where ospreys fish, seals haul out on sandbanks, and a Telford causeway changed the tideline forever.

subject: Loch Garten
summary: The freshwater loch in the Abernethy pinewoods where ospreys returned to breed in Britain for the first time in nearly half a century, founding the conservation success story that gave Boat of Garten its nickname.

subject: Loch Katrine
summary: A serpentine Trossachs loch that Walter Scott made famous as the setting for The Lady of the Lake and that has supplied Glasgow's drinking water by gravity for over 165 years.

subject: Loch Kishorn
summary: A quiet sea loch in Wester Ross that once built the largest movable object on Earth and gave its name to a defiant folk anthem.

subject: Loch Lomond
summary: Scotland's largest loch by surface area stretches twenty-three miles across the Highland boundary fault, an inland sea of islands, songs, and wallabies.

subject: Loch Maree
summary: A 13-mile loch in Wester Ross whose largest island contains a loch that contains an island - a geographic oddity unique in Britain - and whose name remembers an 8th-century Irish saint.

subject: Loch Naver
summary: A ten-kilometre Sutherland loch at the head of Strathnaver - one of the most beautiful and most haunted glens in Scotland.

subject: Loch Ness
summary: Loch Ness holds more freshwater than all the lakes of England and Wales combined -- twenty-three miles of dark, peat-stained water along a geological fault older than most mountain ranges on Earth.

subject: Loch Ness Monster
summary: For fourteen centuries, something in Loch Ness has refused to be explained away -- from Saint Columba's encounter in 565 AD to the 2019 DNA survey that found no evidence of a large animal but plenty of eel.

subject: Loch Ròg
summary: A sprawling sea loch on Lewis's Atlantic shore where Neolithic astronomers, Iron Age villagers, and modern fish farmers all read the same patient tides.

subject: Loch Shin
summary: The largest loch in Sutherland - a 17-mile finger of water that was raised by thirty feet in the 1950s to power the Highlands.

subject: Loch Torridon
summary: A glacier-carved sea loch ringed by some of the oldest rocks in Britain, where Torridonian sandstone mountains rise above langoustine creels.

subject: Lochaber
summary: A vast western district of the Scottish Highlands, ruled by clans, raided by Vikings, and pillaged by government troops after Culloden in what Gaels still call the Year of the Pillaging.

subject: Lochaline
summary: A 200-person ferry village at the mouth of a sea loch, founded during the Highland Clearances and later home to evacuees from St Kilda.

subject: Lochalsh
summary: The Highland district facing Skye across the narrow Kyle of Lochalsh, where Picts, Norsemen, MacDonalds, Mackenzies and the Royal Navy have all left their fingerprints on a coast still defined by the bridge that arrived in 1995.

subject: Lochboisdale
summary: South Uist's ferry port and main village - a herring boom town that has reinvented itself around a new marina, a renovated pier, and the long Atlantic crossing to Mallaig.

subject: Lochearnhead
summary: A village at the head of Loch Earn where Pictish frontiers, water-horse legends, drove roads, and Victorian railways all converge beneath the Highland hills.

subject: Lochinver
summary: A small fishing village under Suilven's shadow where foreign trawlers crowd the pier and a Brutalist hermit's castle squats on the headland.

subject: Lochinver Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station founded in 1967 whose crew won a Bronze Medal for rescue in 2016 and whose boathouse was built with a Russian-born donor's £4 million bequest.

subject: Lochmaddy
summary: The capital of North Uist - a former pirate refuge and royal fishing station, now a ferry port named for rocks that early sailors thought looked like crouching hounds.

subject: Lochnagar
summary: The Munro that overshadows Balmoral - 1,155 metres of granite, Lord Byron's childhood obsession, and the subject of an unfinished Beethoven setting.

subject: Lochranza
summary: The most shaded village in Britain, set on a north-facing sea loch at the tip of Arran, where Bruce reputedly landed, James Hutton found an unconformity, and red deer share the golf course with whisky barrels.

story.title: Locke: The Town They Built But Could Not Own

subject: Locke
summary: In the Sacramento Delta, a 14-acre town built by Chinese immigrants who were legally forbidden from owning the land beneath it became America's only rural community built entirely by Chinese Americans -- and a National Historic Landmark.

subject: Lockhart Road
summary: Lockhart Road runs the full east-west length of Wan Chai on Hong Kong Island — named for the colonial secretary who signed the 1898 New Territories lease, and famous as the setting of The World of Suzie Wong.

subject: Lofoten Fishery
summary: Every winter, millions of Atlantic cod return to the frigid waters off the Lofoten Islands, drawing fishermen from across Norway into one of the world's oldest continuous fisheries.

subject: Logan County, West Virginia
summary: Named for a Mingo chief who lost his family to settler violence, Logan County is the heart of the southern West Virginia coalfield and the site of the Battle of Blair Mountain, the largest armed labor uprising in American history.

subject: Logan Rock
summary: An eighty-ton granite boulder that rocks at a touch, the lieutenant who toppled it in 1824, and the £130 bill the Royal Navy made him pay.

subject: Lohne, Germany
summary: A self-styled 'city of special industries' in Lower Saxony's Catholic Münsterland, where plastics quietly took over from feathers, brushes, and peat — and where over a hundred wayside crosses still mark the back roads.

subject: Loja Province
summary: The southern Ecuadorian province where a valley is called the Smiley Valley and a nearby town is known as the Valley of Longevity.

subject: Loja, Ecuador
summary: The first Ecuadorian city to run electric lights, founded in the Smiley Valley and known today as the country's musical capital.

subject: Lokeren
summary: The Flemish city where horse sausage is a regional product, the largest chocolate warehouse in Europe sits at the edge of town, and the locals answer to two nicknames - Lokeraars or Rapenfretters - depending on the joke.

subject: Lola ya Bonobo
summary: The world's only sanctuary for orphaned bonobos sits in 30 hectares of primary forest on the outskirts of Kinshasa, rescuing infants from the bushmeat trade and pioneering the first-ever bonobo rewilding.

subject: Lolol
summary: A village of mud-brick mansions and long shaded corridors in the Colchagua wine country, where huaso tradition and colonial architecture survived three centuries and one devastating earthquake.

story.title: The Loma Mountains: Sierra Leone's Rooftop and Last Refuge

subject: Loma Mountains
summary: Sierra Leone's highest mountain range, home to Mount Bintumani at 1,945 meters, where chimpanzees, pygmy hippos, and forest elephants survive in montane forests that have been protected since 1952 but face growing pressure from deforestation and illegal farming.

subject: Lomami Province
summary: One of the DRC's newest provinces, carved out of Kasaï-Oriental in 2015 - agro-pastoral, diamond-bearing, and wrestling with infrastructure left half-built.

subject: Lombard Street (San Francisco)
summary: The famous one-block section with eight hairpin turns that is both San Francisco's most photographed street and its most congested tourist attraction.

subject: Lombok
summary: Separated from Bali by just 25 miles of water and a biogeographic boundary that divides continents, Lombok is Indonesia's wilder sibling - an island where the second-highest volcano in the archipelago towers over rice terraces, surf breaks, and a culture that blends Islam, Hinduism, and animism into something entirely its own.

subject: Lomekwi
summary: On a dry hillside west of Lake Turkana, someone struck stone against stone 3.3 million years ago - and left behind the oldest known tools on Earth.

subject: Lon Goed
summary: A five-mile straight cart-track lined with oak and beech, planted between 1819 and 1828 by a Talhenbont estate steward -- and immortalised in R. Williams Parry's poem Eifionydd, one of the most famous in the Welsh language.

subject: London
summary: Two thousand years of civilization on the Thames - from Roman Londinium to global megacity, repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt, each incarnation larger and more stubborn than the last.

subject: London Underground
summary: The world's first underground railway, opened in 1863, still runs more than a billion passenger journeys a year and shapes how every other transit system on the planet thinks about itself.

story.title: London bid for the 2012 Summer Olympics

subject: London bid for the 2012 Summer Olympics
summary: How a derelict patch of east London beat Paris by four votes — and how the celebration lasted one day before bombs went off across the city.

subject: Londres, Catamarca
summary: A dusty Andean village named for a royal wedding in faraway England guards the southernmost capital the Inca Empire ever built.

subject: Lone Pine Koala Sanctuary
summary: The world's first and oldest koala sanctuary, opened in 1927 as a refuge from the fur trade and named for a single pine on a riverside bend.

subject: Long Ke Wan
summary: A remote bay at the edge of the MacLehose Trail in Sai Kung, where a 1918 chapel, a small village, and one of Hong Kong's finest beaches occupy a stretch of coast that takes effort to reach.

subject: Long Melford
summary: A three-mile village strung along a single Suffolk road - wool money, Holy Trinity Church, Kentwell Hall, Melford Hall and a hundred listed buildings - that made Daniel Defoe stop and remark on the wealth.

story.title: Long Ravine Trestle: Where the Railroad Crossed Itself

subject: Long Ravine Trestle
summary: A pair of steel bridges near Colfax carry Union Pacific freight and the daily Amtrak California Zephyr over Long Ravine and Interstate 80, on a site where the first transcontinental railroad once crossed above a narrow gauge line built to serve Gold Rush mining towns.

subject: Long Xuyên
summary: A Mekong city that took its name from its own marketplace, ships the delta's rice, and produced two men who ended up on opposite sides of the same war.

subject: Longanikos
summary: A mountain village at the triple border of Laconia, Arcadia, and Messinia, Longanikos has been a military transit point since Spartan times, a silk-producing town visited by Ottoman travelers, and the ancestral home of a diaspora that stretches from Lynn, Massachusetts to South Africa.

subject: Longhope, Orkney
summary: A small Orkney settlement with Napoleonic-era defences and a lifeboat station that suffered one of Britain's worst rescue tragedies when all eight crew were lost in 1969.

subject: Longju
summary: A remote outpost in the Tsari Chu valley where a line drawn on a map in 1914 met the reality of contested terrain, sparking the 1959 incident that marked the transition from verbal to physical violence between India and China.

subject: Longleat
summary: The first stately home ever opened to the public, Longleat is an Elizabethan masterpiece set within Capability Brown parkland, home to Britain's original safari park and the world's longest hedge maze.

subject: Longport, New Jersey
summary: The quiet tip of Absecon Island - a borough of fewer than a thousand year-round residents where the boardwalk ends and the inlet begins.

subject: Longreach
summary: An outback wool town on the Tropic of Capricorn that became the cradle of Qantas, where a 747 sits parked on red dirt and the Thomson River glows at sunset.

subject: Longreach Ambulance Centre
summary: A 1921 timber ambulance station on Ibis Street, built to bring skilled rescue to a district where the nearest help was hundreds of kilometres away.

subject: Longwangtang Reservoir
summary: A Japanese colonial-era reservoir in Dalian whose dam conceals one of the city's most beloved cherry blossom gardens on its opposite face.

subject: Looe
summary: Two medieval boroughs facing each other across the Looe River became one twin-village fishing port - raided by Barbary pirates in 1625, painted by an American in red in 1918, and still landing its catch on the East Looe quayside each morning.

subject: Lord of the Rings tourism
summary: How Peter Jackson's film trilogy turned New Zealand's landscapes into Middle-earth and created one of the country's most enduring tourism industries.

subject: Lordship of Argos and Nauplia
summary: For nearly two centuries, two ancient Greek cities passed through the hands of French crusaders, Italian dukes, Catalan mercenaries, and Venetian merchants — a medieval saga of absentee lords, failed invasions, and a young woman's decision to sell her inheritance to the most powerful republic in the Mediterranean.

subject: Lordship of Chios
summary: For a quarter-century, a single Genoese family ruled Chios as their private domain, one of them styling himself King of Asia Minor, until the island's own Greeks invited the emperor to take it back.

subject: Lordship of Gödens
summary: A tiny East Frisian feudal lordship that ran a side business in religious refugees - building five churches in a town of 800 to house Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, Mennonite and Jewish congregations all on the same square mile.

subject: Lordship of Utrecht
summary: On October 20, 1528, a bishop signed away centuries of temporal power, and the prince-bishopric of Utrecht ceased to exist - replaced by a Habsburg lordship that would soon spark a revolt.

subject: Lordship of Villena
summary: A medieval feudal realm that grew so powerful its lord minted his own coins and kept a thousand knights, ruling a private buffer state wedged between the crowns of Castile and Aragon.

subject: Loreto, Baja California Sur
summary: The first Spanish colonial settlement on the Baja California Peninsula, once capital of all the Californias, now a fishing town where dorado season draws anglers from across the continent.

subject: Lorrha
summary: A tiny North Tipperary village where Vikings raided in 843, where a ninth-century monk wrote the Stowe Missal, and where Cromwell allegedly stole the abbey bell and had its silver clapper replaced with base metal.

story.title: Los Angeles: The Sprawl That Invented the 20th Century

subject: Los Angeles
summary: The Southern California megalopolis that manufactured American dreams - where Hollywood created the movies, where freeways replaced trains, where 13 million people sprawl across a basin between mountains and sea.

subject: Los Angeles Basin
summary: The Los Angeles Basin is a sedimentary basin in Southern California formed millions of years ago on the Pacific Plate's edge. It is ringed by mountains, crossed by major fault systems, and underlies one of the most densely populated regions in North America.

subject: Los Angeles Metro Rail
summary: The Los Angeles Metro Rail system operates six lines and 107 stations across the greater LA region. Launched in 1990, it has grown into the largest light rail system in the United States and is continuing rapid expansion ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics.

subject: Los Angeles Opera
summary: Founded in 1986, the Los Angeles Opera is the fourth-largest opera company in the United States. Its inaugural production starred Plácido Domingo, who later served as general director for sixteen years before resigning amid misconduct allegations in 2019. Music director James Conlon led the company for twenty years starting in 2006, stepping down in 2026 as conductor laureate.

subject: Los Banos Wildlife Area
summary: One of California's oldest wildlife reserves, where the Yokuts once harvested the valley's abundance and where the Pacific Flyway's migratory birds still descend by the tens of thousands each winter.

subject: Los Dominicos Village
summary: A craft village of adobe lanes and copper-domed towers where Santiago's artisans sell their work on land first granted to a conquistadora in 1544.

subject: Los Estoraques Unique Natural Area
summary: In a quiet corner of Colombia's Norte de Santander, four million years of wind and water have sculpted sandstone into a labyrinth of towers, columns, and canyons that rise 30 meters from the dry earth -- a geological anomaly unlike anything else in the country.

subject: Los Gatos Creek (Santa Clara County)
summary: A 24-mile creek born on the slopes of Loma Prieta that flows through drowned towns, concrete channels, and salmon spawning grounds before joining the Guadalupe River in downtown San Jose.

subject: Los Llanos Region, Venezuela
summary: Venezuela's Llanos Region encompasses the states of Guarico and Apure, a vast rural expanse where seasonal floods reshape the land and cattle outnumber people.

subject: Los Organos
summary: A quiet beach town on Peru's northern coast where the fishermen still bring in mero and the waves at Punta Veleros wait mostly empty for surfers.

subject: Los Peñasquitos Lagoon
summary: A 500-acre coastal marsh in San Diego where Kumeyaay people harvested shellfish for six millennia, and where engineers now manage the lagoon's mouth with controlled breaches — one of the last remaining estuarine systems in California.

subject: Los Toldos
summary: A small pampas town founded by a Mapuche chief who chose survival over war, and the birthplace of a poor girl who became Eva Perón.

subject: Losheng Sanatorium
summary: A 1930s leprosy sanatorium in New Taipei became the center of a bitter battle between transit expansion and the rights of elderly patients who had already been confined there against their will.

subject: Losser
summary: A small town on the German border, burned by Munster's troops in 1665 and now home to the only Syriac Orthodox monastery in Europe.

subject: Lossiemouth
summary: A small fishing town on the Moray coast where Britain's first Labour prime minister was born - and from where Typhoons now scramble to intercept Russian bombers.

subject: Lost Horse Mine
summary: Johnny Lang tracked his missing horses into a valley in Joshua Tree in 1890, bought a gold claim he found there, and set in motion four decades of extraction that produced 10,000 ounces of gold and stripped the surrounding mountains bare.

subject: Lota, Chile
summary: Coal built this town on the Gulf of Arauco, sending generations of Chileans down shafts that ran beneath the sea before the mines closed and flooded for good.

subject: Lotus Hill
summary: An ancient quarry turned national park in Panyu, Guangzhou, where Western Han dynasty stone-cutters left behind dramatic cliffs that legend transformed into a mountain born from a goddess's lotus.

subject: Lotus Pond, Kaohsiung
summary: An artificial lake in Kaohsiung ringed by over a dozen ornate temples, where dragons swallow visitors whole and a 72-meter Taoist god rises from the water.

subject: Loudoun County, Virginia
summary: The wealthiest county in America by median income - 70 percent of the world's daily internet traffic passes through here, between horse farms and Civil War battlefields.

subject: Lough Corrib
summary: Ireland's largest lake by area within the Republic, holding more than 1,300 islands, the wreck of a Viking-age boat carrying battle axes, and the first canal ever cut on the island of Ireland.

subject: Lough Erne
summary: A 50-mile lake system named for a drowned goddess, dotted with 150 islands, where Catalina flying boats once slipped through a secret WWII corridor and world leaders met in 2013 behind four miles of razor wire.

subject: Lough Neagh
summary: The largest lake in the British Isles - 383 km² of shallow water at the centre of Northern Ireland, owned by one earl, drunk by half the country, and now choking on its own algae.

subject: Lough Swilly
summary: One of only three glacial fjords in Ireland, a forty-kilometre fingertip of sea that has carried away rebels, sheltered the Grand Fleet, and given its name to a many-eyed monster.

subject: Loughborough
summary: The Leicestershire market town that casts the world's biggest bells, trains its Olympic athletes, and gave Thomas Cook the idea of the package tour.

subject: Loughmore
summary: A Tipperary village whose Irish name means 'reward-field' - and whose churchyard holds the bodies of two brothers hanged for a murder they did not commit.

subject: Loughrea
summary: A medieval Norman market town on a grey speckled lake, where stilt-house dwellers, Anglo-Norman knights, Celtic revivalists, and one wandering Kiefer Sutherland all left their mark.

subject: Louisburgh, County Mayo
summary: A planned eighteenth-century town built to shelter Catholic refugees and named for a fortress in Nova Scotia, set between Clew Bay's beaches and Croagh Patrick.

story.title: Louisville: The Derby City Where Bourbon and Baseball Bats Are Born

subject: Louisville
summary: The Kentucky city that hosts the most famous two minutes in sports - where the bourbon flows, where the sluggers swing Louisville Sluggers, and where the Ohio River marks the cultural border between North and South.

story.title: Louisville: Where the Kentucky Derby Runs and Muhammad Ali Danced

subject: Louisville
summary: Kentucky's largest city where Churchill Downs has hosted the most exciting two minutes in sports since 1875, where Muhammad Ali learned to float like a butterfly, where bourbon flows freely along Whiskey Row, and where the Louisville Slugger has been swinging since 1884.

subject: Louth Navigation
summary: An eighteenth-century Lincolnshire canal with six elliptical-walled locks that nobody else built quite the same way, abandoned to navigation in 1924 but still draining the marsh today.

subject: Louth, New South Wales
summary: A tiny Darling River village where a grieving husband built a granite Celtic cross so precisely that, on the evening of his wife's death anniversary, the setting sun still flares off its polished stone toward the town below.

subject: Loutra, Kythnos
summary: Loutra on Kythnos has been drawing people to its thermal springs since at least the Roman period — two springs of volcanic origin, one reaching 52°C, housed in neoclassical spa buildings designed by the same architects who shaped modern Athens.

subject: Loutraki
summary: Greece's most famous spa resort, Loutraki has been drawing visitors to its natural mineral springs since antiquity — a town rebuilt twice from earthquake rubble, bottling its water for the whole country and running one of Europe's largest casinos beside the Corinthian Gulf.

subject: Love Parade
summary: It began in West Berlin in 1989 as a birthday party for 150 people, legally registered as a political demonstration. It ended in 2010 on a ramp in Duisburg where 21 people were crushed to death.

subject: Low Countries
summary: A name born in a duke's court that has somehow survived a thousand years of partition, war, and political reinvention to mean essentially the same thing it always did.

subject: Low-Level Radioactive Waste Storage Site
summary: Since 1982, the southeastern corner of Orchid Island has stored nearly 100,000 drums of nuclear waste from Taiwan's mainland power plants — a decision made without the meaningful consent of the indigenous Tao people, who have protested its presence for decades.

subject: Lowell Mills
summary: America's first industrial city - where power looms and 'mill girls' from Yankee farms built the nation's textile industry in the 1820s, creating both a manufacturing revolution and the first organized women workers.

subject: Lower City Mills
summary: A Category A listed Perth watermill whose 4.7-metre wheel ground oats from a 1375 royal charter until 1953.

subject: Lower Larymna
summary: Where the river Cephissus surfaced from its underground course and ran to the sea, an ancient harbor town grew rich as the gateway between landlocked Boeotia and the open eastern water.

subject: Lower Mainland
summary: Home to Greater Vancouver and stretching from the Sunshine Coast to the American border, the Lower Mainland encompasses Canada's largest metropolitan area west of Toronto.

subject: Lower Rio Negro Mosaic
summary: Eleven protected areas totaling 7.4 million hectares around Manaus, governed together as a single management mosaic after decades of conflict between conservation and the communities who live there.

subject: Lower Shawneetown
summary: A sprawling 18th-century Shawnee settlement at the confluence of the Ohio and Scioto Rivers, Lower Shawneetown became the unlikely center of imperial rivalry between France and Britain -- and a place where Native American autonomy held out until the eve of the French and Indian War.

subject: Lowestoft
summary: Britain's easternmost town, where the first light of each new day breaks over a coast shaped by herring, war, and a stubborn refusal to look away from the sea.

subject: Loweswater
summary: A quiet lake in the northwest Lake District that breaks the rules of the region by draining inward, toward the centre of the fells, rather than outward to the sea.

subject: Lowlands Festival
summary: A 60,000-person three-day music festival on a reclaimed Dutch polder where the tents are named in the NATO phonetic alphabet and everyone shouts the name of a boy who once went looking for a toilet.

subject: Lualaba District
summary: A century of shifting borders across southern Congo, traced through one administrative district that appeared, vanished, and reappeared on Belgian and Congolese maps.

subject: Luanda
summary: Angola's capital has reinvented itself from a war-scarred colonial port into a booming Atlantic metropolis, its skyline bristling with construction cranes as oil wealth funds one of Africa's most dramatic urban transformations.

subject: Luba Crater Scientific Reserve
summary: A 51,000-hectare reserve on the volcanic island of Bioko in Equatorial Guinea, the Gran Caldera de Luba shelters some of Africa's highest primate densities behind crater walls a kilometer high, even as the bushmeat trade threatens to empty it.

subject: Luba Empire
summary: For a thousand years, a sophisticated Central African state flourished in what is now the DRC, governed by sacred kings and remembered by professional historians called 'men of memory.'

subject: Lubaantun
summary: A Maya city built without mortar from black slate blocks, famous for hundreds of ceramic whistle figurines and an infamous crystal skull hoax that overshadowed its real archaeological significance.

subject: Lubango
summary: Angola's second-largest city sits at 1,760 meters on the Huila Plateau, founded by Madeiran colonists in the 1880s, battered by decades of civil war, and now rebuilding as the provincial capital of a country still finding its peacetime footing.

subject: Lubartów Ghetto
summary: In a small Polish town north of Lublin, around 3,500 Jews from Lubartów, nearby Polish villages, Slovakia, and Ciechanów were held in a few blocks around two market squares before being sent in two waves to the gas chambers at Bełżec.

subject: Lubbock, Texas
summary: Hub City of the Llano Estacado, birthplace of Buddy Holly, home to Texas Tech, and the second-most conservative city in America, where windmills and cotton fields meet a billion-dollar university economy.

subject: Lublin
summary: On June 26, 1569, in a city now of about 330,000 people in eastern Poland, the parliaments of Poland and Lithuania merged into the largest state in Renaissance Europe; Lublin still carries the layered marks of being a royal Polish city, a center of Jewish learning destroyed in the Holocaust, and now a European Capital of Culture-elect for 2029.

subject: Lublin Ghetto
summary: The first ghetto liquidated under Operation Reinhard, where in four weeks of spring 1942 some 30,000 Lublin Jews were sent to die at Bełżec; only 230 are known to have survived the German occupation of a city that had been Jewish for five centuries.

subject: Lubumbashi
summary: The mining capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Lubumbashi is a city where Swahili and French mingle in songs that switch languages mid-verse, and where a football club once reached the FIFA Club World Cup final.

subject: Lucasfilm Games
summary: The video game division of Lucasfilm, best known as LucasArts, that created some of the most beloved adventure games in history.

subject: Lucentum
summary: On a low hill above an old lagoon in Alicante lie the ruins of Lucentum - a Carthaginian citadel turned Roman town that gave the modern city its name and nearly vanished under the developers' cranes.

subject: Luckenbach, Texas
summary: A Texas Hill Country hamlet with a population of zero became one of the most famous towns in country music after Waylon Jennings sang about going back to the basics of love -- even though he had never set foot there.

subject: Luconia Shoals
summary: A vast submerged reef complex in the South China Sea where sovereignty disputes, oil wealth, and marine conservation collide far from any shore.

subject: Lucy the Elephant
summary: A six-story tin-skinned elephant stands guard on the Jersey Shore, the oldest surviving roadside attraction in America, built in 1882 to sell real estate and still drawing visitors 140 years later.

subject: Ludlow
summary: A Shropshire market town with nearly 500 listed buildings, the castle where Edward V learned he was king, and one of the best food scenes outside London.

subject: Lufilian Arc
summary: An 800-kilometre crescent of folded rock across Zambia and the Congo that holds roughly a quarter of the world's copper and most of its cobalt.

subject: Lugard Road
summary: A narrow pedestrian path 400 metres above Hong Kong on Victoria Peak, begun in 1913 and interrupted by a world war, Lugard Road circles The Peak with views across Victoria Harbour that have stopped walkers mid-stride for over a century.

subject: Lui Seng Chun
summary: A 1931 Mong Kok tong lau shophouse built by a Kowloon Motor Bus founder, its name promising to bring patients back to life — now Hong Kong's most storied Chinese-medicine clinic.

subject: Luishia Mine
summary: An open pit copper and cobalt mine in southern Congo, its century-long history shaped as much by the workers who struck in 1941 as by the ore that made it famous.

subject: Luján, Buenos Aires
summary: Argentina calls it the Capital of the Faith, but this pampas city also holds the prison cells of a captured British commander and the country's first steam locomotive.

subject: Lukang
summary: Once Taiwan's second-largest city and a thriving deer-hide port, Lukang declined when its harbor silted up and it refused the railroad -- a stubbornness that accidentally preserved one of the island's richest collections of historic temples and streetscapes.

subject: Lukanga Swamp
summary: A vast circular wetland of papyrus and lagoons in central Zambia, listed under the Ramsar Convention and still geologically mysterious.

subject: Lukttinden
summary: A 1,343-metre peak in inner Helgeland whose name looks like a joke in Norwegian and turns out to be Sami, standing just west of the glaciers it politely declines to imitate.

subject: Lulenge
summary: A mountainous sector of eastern Congo where five communities share land, a history of displacement, and the ongoing wars of the Great Lakes region.

subject: Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina
summary: The largest Native American tribe east of the Mississippi, the Lumbee people of southeastern North Carolina spent 140 years fighting for federal recognition -- a battle that ended in December 2025 with the Lumbee Fairness Act.

subject: Lumberton, North Carolina
summary: An eighteenth-century lumber-shipping town on the blackwater Lumber River, county seat of the most racially diverse rural county in North Carolina, twice nearly drowned by hurricanes.

subject: Lumwana
summary: A village that became a town in a decade, built around one of Zambia's newest copper mines in the remote North-Western Province.

subject: Lunar Landing Research Facility
summary: The gantry where 24 Apollo astronauts learned to land on the Moon still stands in Hampton, Virginia - a National Historic Landmark that served NASA for six decades across three different identities.

subject: Lund, British Columbia
summary: Where Highway 101 ends and the water begins, a tiny harbour village founded by Swedish brothers in 1889 serves as the last outpost before Desolation Sound and the islands beyond.

subject: Lundazi
summary: A small district capital in eastern Zambia best known for a Norman-style castle built with forced labour during the dying years of colonial rule.

subject: Lundy
summary: A three-mile granite island in the Bristol Channel that once printed its own postage stamps, fought as a pirate state, and gave Britain its first Marine Conservation Zone.

subject: Lung Fu Shan
summary: A 831-foot hill on Hong Kong Island whose name translates to Dragon Tiger Mountain — home to the University of Hong Kong, the boundary of the old City of Victoria, and a country park tucked between the Peak and the Mid-Levels.

subject: Lung Kwu Tan
summary: A remote Tuen Mun village on a black-sand beach where a fleeing Song-dynasty emperor once hid in a cave, and where endangered Chinese white dolphins still surface offshore.

subject: Lung Yeuk Tau
summary: A cluster of five Tang clan walled villages northeast of Fanling in Hong Kong's New Territories, preserving 600 years of ancestral heritage along a dedicated heritage trail.

subject: Lunga, Firth of Lorn
summary: An uninhabited Slate Island that disintegrates at high tide into a chain of separate islets, guarded to the south by the Little Corryvreckan tidal race.

subject: Lupah Sug
summary: The pre-Islamic predecessor state to the Sultanate of Sulu, where rajahs, mystics, and monsoon-blown seafarers built competing kingdoms on a single volcanic island.

subject: Luque
summary: For a few desperate months in 1868 this town was Paraguay's capital; today it is the country's workshop of harps, guitars, and gold filigree.

subject: Luray Caverns
summary: Discovered in 1878 by a tinsmith who felt cool air rising from a sinkhole, Luray Caverns holds formations the Smithsonian called the most profusely decorated of any cave in the world.

subject: Lurgan
summary: A Plantation-era linen town just south of Lough Neagh whose ramrod-straight main street was laid down by an English baron in 1610.

subject: Lusaka
summary: Zambia's capital is a sprawling, energetic city of 2.7 million where minibus conductors shout destinations through open windows, markets sell music from across the continent, and one in six Zambians navigates daily life.

subject: Lusaka Province
summary: Zambia's smallest but most populous province, where more than three million people live on a high plateau between the Zambezi and the Kafue.

subject: Lusaka–Livingstone Road
summary: A 430-kilometre highway linking Zambia's capital to Victoria Falls, and part of the transcontinental Cairo–Cape Town route.

subject: Lusatia
summary: A region with a name in five languages and an administrative existence in none, shredded between Bohemia, Hungary, Saxony, Prussia and finally Germany and Poland - and still, stubbornly, itself.

subject: Luss
summary: A village of 120 residents on Loch Lomond's western shore receives over 750,000 visitors a year, mostly because of a Scottish soap opera.

subject: Lustleigh
summary: A thatched Dartmoor village where the May Queen is still crowned on a granite throne, and the whole village was used as Godric's Hollow in the 2025 Harry Potter TV series.

subject: Luxor
summary: Where ancient Thebes ruled Egypt from temples that still stand, where pharaohs lie in valleys meant to hide their tombs, where the Nile divides the living from the dead.

subject: Luye
summary: A Taitung valley township where hot-air balloons drift over high-altitude tea gardens each summer, and the Huadong Valley opens into one of eastern Taiwan's most scenic highland plateaus.

subject: Luz Station
summary: Built in Glasgow, shipped in pieces across the Atlantic, and reassembled in São Paulo, this Victorian railway station has served as the city's gateway since 1901 — surviving two major fires and outlasting the coffee empire that paid for it.

subject: Luziânia
summary: A colonial-era Goiás town just south of Brasília that grew into an agribusiness power on the strength of the Corumbá River and the soy boom.

subject: Luís Eduardo Magalhães, Bahia
summary: A western Bahia city that went from a single gas station in the 1990s to Brazil's fastest-growing agribusiness hub - created by a municipal act the Supreme Court later ruled unconstitutional.

subject: Lviv
summary: A city of many names and many masters -- founded by a medieval Ukrainian king, shaped by Polish, Austrian, and Soviet rulers -- Lviv endures as the cultural heart of western Ukraine.

subject: Lycosura
summary: Pausanias called Lycosura the oldest city in the world; its sanctuary of the goddess Despoina held a colossal sculptural group whose mysteries were so secret that her true name has never been revealed.

subject: Lycée Yersin
summary: A red-brick lycée built on a Da Lat plateau in 1927 educated two future heads of state — Vietnam's Emperor Bảo Đại and Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk — even as it enforced and then slowly abandoned the racial hierarchies of French colonial rule.

subject: Lykaia
summary: The ancient Arcadian athletic festival held every four years on Mount Lykaion in honor of Zeus Lykaios — one of the oldest known Greek religious games, steeped in myths of transformation and shrouded in deliberate secrecy.

subject: Lyme Regis
summary: A small Dorset seaside town where a young carpenter's daughter changed how the world thought about time, and where a curving harbour wall has stood against the English Channel for seven centuries.

subject: Lynchburg
summary: A traveler's guide to Lynchburg, Virginia — the City of Seven Hills above the James River, where Amtrak's Crescent and Northeast Regional stop daily and a 13.5-mile paved trail follows the river through downtown.

subject: Lyon
summary: Where two rivers meet and Roman Gaul began, where silk made fortunes and gastronomy became religion, where France's second city quietly outperforms its reputation.

subject: Lyrnessus
summary: A lost Cilician city in northwest Turkey where Achilles sacked and enslaved; its most enduring legacy is Briseis — a woman whose grief, dignity, and inner life Homer captured even as war reduced her to a captive.

subject: Lysa Hora
summary: The Bald Mountain of Slavic legend, where folk tradition placed the witches' sabbath, later became a real place of executions, and is now a quiet nature reserve in Kyiv.

subject: Lysefjord
summary: A 42-kilometer gash carved by glaciers into southwestern Norway, where granite walls plunge over a thousand meters and the only roads are carved through the mountains themselves.

subject: Lysimachia (Thrace)
summary: Founded in 309 BC by one of Alexander the Great's generals as his imperial capital, Lysimachia rose to power on the Gallipoli isthmus and then endured centuries of earthquakes, sackings, and slow decay until its very name disappeared from the map.

subject: Lyttelton
summary: Christchurch's volcanic harbour town was the first foothold of Canterbury settlement, connected to the plains by tunnel and tenacity, and rebuilt after earthquakes shook it to its foundations.

subject: Lytton Quarantine Station
summary: At the mouth of the Brisbane River, this isolated station was where new arrivals were held when disease was feared, often a migrant's very first hours on Australian soil.

subject: Lyuba (mammoth)
summary: A Nenets reindeer herder found a 42,000-year-old baby mammoth on the banks of the Yuribey River in 2007 -- the most complete mammoth specimen ever discovered, named 'Love' after his wife.

subject: Læsø
summary: The Kattegat island that boiled its groundwater into salt for three centuries, burned every tree doing it, and then roofed its houses in seaweed because nothing else was left.

subject: Léon Hanolet
summary: A Belgian colonial officer whose expeditions across the upper Ubangi helped set the borders of what would become the Central African Republic and the Congo Free State.

subject: Lôn Eifion
summary: A 20-kilometre cycle path along the trackbed of a vanished Welsh railway, threading the gap between mountains and sea from Caernarfon to Bryncir.

subject: Løgstør
summary: Denmark dug a 4.4-kilometre canal past the Løgstør shoals in five years — and then a dredge cut straight through the shoals and made the whole thing pointless.

subject: Løkken
summary: A Danish west-coast town that traded with Norway, fished without a harbour, and turned nineteen kilometres of driveable beach and a row of white bathing huts into a national summer institution.

subject: Lübeck
summary: Six of Lübeck's church towers stand over a hundred metres high - more than any other city on earth - and on one night in 1942 the RAF set out to prove that the medieval town beneath them would burn.

subject: Lüderitz
summary: A German colonial town on Namibia's Atlantic coast where Art Nouveau facades face into relentless desert wind, penguins breed on offshore islands, and the road in crosses a forbidden diamond zone you cannot leave.

subject: Lüshun Port
summary: Named 'Bay of Calm Travels' by a Ming dynasty prince in 1371, Lushun Port has been anything but calm -- passing through Chinese, Russian, Japanese, and Soviet hands before returning to China in 1955.

subject: Lüshunkou, Dalian
summary: Known to the West as Port Arthur, this district at the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula has been governed by five different nations since 1894 and remains partially closed to foreigners today.

subject: Lütje Hörn
summary: A German Wadden Sea island that has crept hundreds of meters eastward in living memory - and shrunk from 61 hectares to about 6.

subject: Lăng Cô
summary: Pinched between a mountain pass and the South China Sea, Lăng Cô is a slender peninsula of white sand and fishing boats that sits at one of Vietnam's most dramatic geographic crossroads.

story.title: M-Wave: The Olympic Cathedral That Paid for Itself

subject: M-Wave
summary: Built for the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics, M-Wave is one of the world's largest hanging wooden roof structures -- and one of the rare Olympic venues that remains profitable decades after the games.

subject: M5 Motorway
summary: The motorway that carries Britain's summer to the seaside, threading from the West Midlands down to Devon along the western edge of England.

subject: MT Independența
summary: On the night of 15 November 1979, the Romanian supertanker Independența collided with a Greek freighter at the southern entrance of the Bosphorus and exploded in a catastrophe that claimed nearly all of her 44 crew members and burned for 29 days.

subject: MTS Oceanos
summary: When the captain of the MTS Oceanos fled his sinking ship in 1991, the onboard entertainers took command -- broadcasting mayday calls, launching lifeboats, and saving all 571 people aboard.

subject: Ma On Shan Iron Mine
summary: For seventy years, a workforce of hundreds bored deep into the hills of Hong Kong's New Territories, producing iron ore that Japan forged into steel — and then, in 1976, it was over in a single year.

subject: Ma On Shan New Town
summary: Built on the strip between a mountain and a harbour in Hong Kong's New Territories, Ma On Shan grew from a mining hinterland into a new town of over 200,000 people — a place that kept three treasures: iron ore, a flower found almost nowhere else on Earth, and a barking deer.

subject: Ma On Shan Peak
summary: A 702-metre saddle-shaped mountain above Tolo Harbour, Ma On Shan has spent 200 million years becoming itself — and the shape it became gave the mountain, the mine beneath it, and eventually an entire new town their name.

subject: Ma On Shan Village
summary: A mining community that rose to more than 10,000 people on the slopes of a Hong Kong hillside, Ma On Shan Village was built entirely around the iron mine above it — and when the mine closed, the village's reason for existing went with it.

subject: Ma Shi Chau
summary: Twice a day, the tide drops low enough to walk between two islands in Tolo Harbour — and the sandbar underfoot is made of rock that was already ancient when the dinosaurs appeared.

subject: Ma Wan
summary: A tiny island between two great bridges — Ma Wan carries Neolithic graves, a pirate's temples, shrimp-paste traditions, and a full-scale Noah's Ark replica, all within less than a square kilometer.

subject: Maaden El-Irvane
summary: Founded in 1975 by a Sufi sheikh as 'the deposit of knowledge,' this Mauritanian desert oasis built itself around an unusual idea: that men and women should farm, build, and live as equals.

subject: Maasai Mara National Reserve
summary: Kenya's most celebrated wildlife reserve hosts the Great Migration -- over a million wildebeest crossing crocodile-filled rivers each year -- across 1,510 square kilometers of savanna the Maasai people have called home since the 17th century.

subject: Maaseik
summary: A small Belgian border town on the Meuse, claimed as the birthplace of the Van Eyck brothers, that keeps the oldest gospel book in the Benelux in the back of a parish church.

subject: Maastricht
summary: A Roman river crossing that gave its name to a geological age, a treaty, and the euro.

subject: Mac Clark (Acacia peuce) Conservation Reserve
summary: On a wind-scoured plain at the Simpson Desert's eastern edge stands one of only three wild groves of waddywood on Earth, a tree so slow and so dense it can outlive five human lifetimes.

subject: MacArthur Maze
summary: The tangled concrete heart of East Bay traffic has been built, shattered by earthquake, melted by fire, and rebuilt in record time -- a freeway interchange whose disasters reveal as much about the Bay Area as its engineering does.

subject: Macau
summary: Half the size of Manhattan but denser than almost anywhere on Earth, Macau is the place where 400 years of Portuguese colonialism, Cantonese tradition, and the world's most lucrative gambling strip collide on a tiny peninsula in the Pearl River Delta.

subject: Macau Fisherman's Wharf
summary: A 133,000-square-metre waterfront complex where Amsterdam's gabled facades stand next to a replica Potala Palace — Macau Fisherman's Wharf tried to compress the world's great seaports into a single entertainment district built on reclaimed land.

subject: Macau Grand Prix
summary: What began in 1954 as a treasure hunt through Macau's streets became one of motorsport's most demanding proving grounds — a street circuit so narrow and unforgiving that every future Formula One champion who conquered it did so knowing the barriers left no room for error.

subject: Macau Incident (1799)
summary: On 27 January 1799, six warships of France and Spain arrived in the Wanshan Archipelago to destroy Britain's China convoy — and then, for reasons both sides would dispute for years, sailed away without firing a shot.

subject: Macaé
summary: A Rio de Janeiro coastal city nicknamed 'City of Petroleum' - the onshore base for Brazil's Campos Basin offshore oil industry, a thousand-expat town, and birthplace of a president.

subject: Macclesfield
summary: The town that once made the world's silk, gave rock music Joy Division, and runs uphill from the River Bollin to a 108-step climb that locals navigate without thinking.

subject: Macduff, Aberdeenshire
summary: A North Sea fishing town renamed in 1783 by an Earl who borrowed the name of a Shakespearean character he believed was an ancestor, and the last place in Britain to build deep-water wooden fishing boats.

subject: Mace Head Atmospheric Research Station
summary: On a Connemara headland exposed to the open Atlantic, instruments have measured the cleanest air in Europe - and, on 24 January 2025, Ireland's strongest wind gust ever.

subject: Maceió
summary: Alagoas' capital is named after a lagoon that keeps disappearing - a city of green water, sugar-money history, and a lagoon-and-ocean geography that shaped everything about it.

subject: Macha Mission
summary: A century-old mission station in Tonga country whose malaria research now collaborates with Johns Hopkins.

subject: Machala
summary: Ecuador's Banana Capital of the World, where bananas are loaded onto ships bound for North American grocery stores.

subject: Machala
summary: Ecuador's sixth-largest city, second-busiest port, and the engine room of the country's banana exports.

subject: Mache-Chindul Ecological Reserve
summary: A coastal massif in northwestern Ecuador where rainforest dissolves into dry forest, and where Chachi and Afro-Esmeraldas communities have lived for generations inside one of the last wet remnants of the Choco.

subject: Machrie Moor Stone Circles
summary: Six Bronze Age stone circles on the Isle of Arran, one of them dated to around 2030 BCE and aligned so that the rising sun at the summer solstice strikes a notch in the hills — a piece of prehistoric astronomy hidden in plain sight on a damp Scottish moor.

subject: Machu Picchu
summary: The 'Lost City of the Incas' perches on a mountain saddle 8,000 feet above sea level, its dry-stone temples and terraces overlooking the Urubamba River in Peru's Sacred Valley.

subject: Machynlleth
summary: The Dyfi Valley market town where Owain Glyndŵr held the first - and last - free Welsh Parliament, and where Laura Ashley opened the shop that became a global brand.

subject: Mackay
summary: Australia's sugar capital on the Pioneer River - an art-deco city rebuilt from a cyclone's rubble, on Yuwibara country, and home to the nation's largest Australian South Sea Islander community, whose ancestors built the cane fields under coercion and endure with dignity.

subject: Mackem Shibboleth
summary: A neon mural of a single Wearside syllable that decides whether you belong.

subject: Maclean, New South Wales
summary: A sugar town on the lower Clarence that wraps its power poles in tartan and calls itself the Scottish Town in Australia, built on a river of red cedar, cane, floods, and older histories.

subject: Macumba Station
summary: A cattle run the size of a small nation, where for a century and a half flood and drought have traded the land back and forth.

subject: Macuro
summary: The only spot on the South American mainland where Columbus set foot, Macuro is a tiny fishing village at the tip of the Paria Peninsula that has cycled through boom and abandonment for five centuries.

subject: Madagascar
summary: The world's fourth-largest island, separated from India 88 million years ago, where over 90% of wildlife exists nowhere else on Earth and Austronesian settlers built a culture unlike anything on the African mainland.

subject: Madagascar Spiny Forests
summary: A thorned, alien-looking wilderness in Madagascar's parched southwest where almost every plant grows nowhere else on Earth, and the trees only pretend to be cacti.

subject: Madang and Morobe
summary: Two provinces covering the northeastern shoulder of New Guinea, where volcanoes smoke, rivers drain a continent's worth of forest, and nearly four hundred languages share two provinces.

subject: Madeira–Tapajós moist forests
summary: Spanning nearly 72 million hectares between two of the Amazon's mightiest tributaries, this ecoregion harbors endemic primates, river dolphins, and the wild ancestor of chocolate -- while losing ground to highways, mining, and agriculture at its edges.

subject: Madha
summary: An Omani exclave completely surrounded by the UAE, containing within it a second-order enclave belonging to Sharjah -- a geographic curiosity born from a village vote in the 1930s.

subject: Madinat al-Zahra
summary: The ruined palace-city west of Cordoba that served as capital of the Caliphate of Cordoba, built to rival Baghdad and Cairo and destroyed within a single lifetime.

story.title: Madison: The Wisconsin Capital on an Isthmus

subject: Madison
summary: The Wisconsin capital squeezed between two lakes - where the university dominates everything, where liberal politics thrive in conservative Wisconsin, and where the isthmus creates a natural campus town.

story.title: Madura: Salt, Bulls, and the Island That Emptied Itself

subject: Madura
summary: An Indonesian island where bull races thunder across hundred-meter courses, salt flats shimmer under equatorial sun, and most of the Madurese people no longer live on Madura at all.

subject: Madura Station
summary: A Nullarbor sheep run larger than Brunei that began in 1876 as a horse stud, breeding cavalry remounts on the edge of the desert to be shipped across the ocean to the British Army in India.

subject: Madura, Western Australia
summary: A lone roadhouse at the foot of Madura Pass, where the Eyre Highway tips off the Nullarbor and travellers reset their clocks to a time zone that exists almost nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Madurodam
summary: The Netherlands shrunk to 1:25 scale - a beloved miniature city in The Hague founded by two grieving parents as a memorial to their son, who died at Dachau.

subject: Mae La refugee camp
summary: Thailand's largest Karen refugee camp, where tens of thousands of people displaced by decades of ethnic persecution in Myanmar have built a community in the mountains of Tak Province.

subject: Maesa Tompaso Racecourse
summary: In the volcanic highlands of North Sulawesi, a 24-hectare dirt track carries on a horse racing tradition that predates Indonesian independence and defines Minahasan culture.

subject: Maevarano Formation
summary: A band of rust-colored sandstone in northwestern Madagascar holds the densest record of latest-Cretaceous life in the southern world - including a dinosaur that ate its own kind and a frog the size of a beach ball.

subject: Mafate
summary: Named for a formerly enslaved man who fled into its volcanic walls, the Cirque de Mafate on Reunion Island has been a refuge for those escaping the world outside since the 18th century -- from maroon communities to the off-grid families who live there today.

subject: Magaliesberg
summary: Almost a hundred times older than Everest, this modest South African ridge has watched the entire span of life on Earth - from shallow ancient seas to the first humans of the Cradle of Humankind.

subject: Magaluf
summary: A stretch of drained marshland reborn as Mallorca's most notorious party strip, where cheap flights and cheaper drinks meet a bay that once sheltered a medieval king and a hillside that hides a darker past.

subject: Magdalena Festival
summary: Once a year Castellón walks back up the hill it abandoned in 1251, retracing its own founding with canes, giant paella, fireworks, and towers of pure light.

subject: Magdeburg
summary: The mayor who held two copper hemispheres together with nothing but a vacuum also rebuilt this city from a few hundred survivors — and Magdeburg has been starting over ever since.

subject: Magere Brug
summary: The skinny white drawbridge over the Amstel, lit by 1,200 bulbs at night, has been called the most romantic spot in Amsterdam since 1691.

subject: Magh Adhair
summary: An ancient mound in a Clare field where the kings of Thomond were inaugurated for at least fifteen hundred years — and where felling the sacred tree was an act of war.

subject: Maghera
summary: At the foot of the Glenshane Pass, a small town whose 10th-century crucifixion carving may be the oldest in Ireland - and whose 18th-century son signed the American Declaration of Independence.

subject: Maghery
summary: A small Armagh village on the southwest shore of Lough Neagh - where two rivers meet, a foot-and-cycle bridge replaces a vanished ferry, and the deposition of one publican still speaks across two centuries.

subject: Maghull
summary: A Sefton town strung along the Leeds and Liverpool Canal where Frank Hornby invented Meccano, John Lennon briefly lived with relatives, and the Beatles played the Albany Cinema in October 1961.

subject: Magic Kingdom
summary: Walt Disney never saw it open. Built atop a hidden network of tunnels because Florida's water table made underground construction impossible, Magic Kingdom has drawn more visitors than any other theme park on Earth for eighteen consecutive years.

story.title: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art and Life

subject: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art and Life
summary: Born from Yiddish records rescued from dumpsters and Judaica salvaged from vanishing communities across three continents, the Magnes Collection at UC Berkeley preserves 45,000 artifacts of Jewish life that nearly disappeared.

subject: Magnetic Hill (Moncton)
summary: A one-kilometer stretch of road in Moncton where cars appear to roll uphill has been confounding visitors since the 1930s -- and a young woman selling ice cream turned the illusion into a Canadian institution.

subject: Magome-Tsumago Trail
summary: An eight-kilometer preserved section of the Nakasendo highway through the Kiso Valley, the Magome-Tsumago Trail lets modern walkers experience the same forested mountain path that feudal lords, poets, and palanquin bearers traveled during the Edo period.

subject: Magome-juku
summary: An Edo-period post town on the Nakasendo highway, Magome-juku once hosted feudal lords and traveling merchants on the steep mountain road between Mino and Shinano provinces, and today survives as a beautifully restored hillside village where stone-paved lanes wind past wooden inns beneath the shadow of Mount Ena.

subject: Magong
summary: Magong is the island capital of Penghu County in Taiwan — a harbor city whose name traces back to a goddess, whose streets carry centuries of layered history, and whose subtropical shores sit at the crossroads of every power that ever wanted control of the Taiwan Strait.

subject: Magtymguly, Turkmenistan
summary: A Turkmen mountain town renamed for its national poet, where a Soviet rubber plant station ended up selling fruit jam and a saint's mausoleum supposedly cures madness.

subject: Mahabad
summary: A Kurdish city in northwestern Iran whose old name meant 'cold spring,' Mahabad served briefly as the capital of a short-lived Kurdish republic in 1946 and remains a cultural touchstone for Kurdish identity, poetry, and national aspiration.

subject: Mahabaleshwar
summary: A plateau hill station in the Western Ghats where five rivers are born, British colonists recreated England in miniature, and strawberry farms now produce 85 percent of India's harvest.

subject: Mahajanga
summary: On Madagascar's drier western coast along the Mozambique Channel, Mahajanga draws visitors with its easy-going atmosphere, red-earth landscapes, and access to some of the island's most remarkable nature reserves.

subject: Mahale Mountains
summary: One of Africa's most remote national parks, where chimpanzees inhabit forested peaks that plunge into Lake Tanganyika -- reachable only by boat, and explorable only on foot.

story.title: Mahameru: The Great Mountain That Never Sleeps

subject: Mahameru
summary: Java's highest peak and one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes, Semeru has been erupting almost continuously since 1967—a mountain named for the abode of the gods that keeps reminding the people below of its power.

subject: Maharees
summary: A five-kilometre sandy tombolo that shelters County Kerry's main fishing port and provides habitat for one of Ireland's rarest amphibians - the Natterjack toad.

subject: Mahd Al-Dhahab
summary: The "Cradle of Gold," an Arabian mine worked for nearly five thousand years and tied by legend to the riches of King Solomon.

subject: Mahendraparvata
summary: A laser mounted on a helicopter finally drew the map that a century of ground survey could not: a formally planned Khmer grid city of 40 to 50 square kilometres, lying under forest on the Phnom Kulen plateau since the ninth century.

subject: Maheshwar
summary: A small town on the Narmada River in Madhya Pradesh where a legendary 18th-century queen built temples and ghats that still stand, and where handloom weavers still produce saris using techniques dating back to the 5th century.

subject: Mahmut Pasha Hamam
summary: Built in 1466 as the bathhouse of Istanbul's first grand Ottoman külliye, the Mahmut Pasha Hamam contains the earliest surviving half-dome in the city — a ribbed scallop of stone that prefigures the great Ottoman domes to come.

subject: Mahon
summary: A peninsula on the southeast edge of Cork that went from cattle pasture to office parks to Munster's second-largest shopping centre - and still has William Penn's harbour view next door.

subject: Mai Po Marshes
summary: On the edge of one of Asia's most densely built cities, Mai Po Marshes shelters over 350 bird species, a quarter of the world's Black-faced spoonbills, and a firefly found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Maicao
summary: A border town on Colombia's Guajira desert where Wayuu resistance met Middle Eastern immigration, producing one of South America's largest mosques, a contraband economy, and a cultural mix found nowhere else on the continent.

subject: Maidan Nezalezhnosti
summary: Kyiv's Independence Square has worn seven names in a century and a half, and twice in a decade its pavement became the place where Ukraine remade itself.

subject: Maidanetske
summary: Beneath the sunflower fields of a quiet Ukrainian village lie the traces of one of the largest human settlements on Earth, built nearly 6,000 years ago.

subject: Maidstone
summary: The county town of Kent, set on the River Medway in the Garden of England - a place that has signed a king's death warrant, milled the paper of the Industrial Revolution, and given British TV its plasticine puppet.

subject: Maillardville
summary: A lumber company went shopping for workers in Quebec in 1909 and accidentally founded the largest francophone community west of Manitoba - on a slope above the Fraser River in what is now Coquitlam.

subject: Mailín
summary: A town of a few hundred people in Santiago del Estero that swells past two hundred thousand each May, when pilgrims walk for days to reach a found cross.

subject: Main Street, Letterkenny
summary: The long, hilly thoroughfare claimed to be Ireland's longest street, where Wolfe Tone was held captive in 1798 and where children were once hired by the day at the Rabble Fair.

subject: Maison Saint-Gabriel
summary: A 17th-century farmhouse in Montreal's Pointe-Saint-Charles neighborhood has survived fire, industrialization, and three centuries of urban transformation to become one of the oldest standing buildings on the Island of Montreal and a window into the lives of New France's earliest settlers.

subject: Maison de la Magie (Blois)
summary: Europe's only public museum dedicated to the art of magic, housed in the birthplace city of Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, the French illusionist who inspired Houdini's stage name.

subject: Majete Wildlife Reserve
summary: A Malawian reserve where poachers had exterminated every elephant by 1992, and where African Parks then spent two decades rebuilding -- translocating approximately 3,000 animals of 17 species, reintroducing black rhinos and lions, and proving that a devastated landscape could be brought back.

subject: Majlis al Jinn
summary: The 'Meeting Place of the Spirits' -- a single cave chamber 310 meters wide with a ceiling 120 meters high, accessible only through three holes in its roof on a remote Omani plateau.

subject: Major Oak
summary: The 800-to-1,000-year-old English oak in Sherwood Forest that has carried the weight of the Robin Hood legend, twenty-three tonnes of timber, and a steel scaffolding since the 1970s.

subject: Major film studios
summary: The Big Five studios command 80-85% of American box office revenue, their corporate headquarters scattered across Los Angeles County from Burbank to Culver City.

subject: Makah
summary: The only Wakashan-speaking people in the United States, whale hunters for millennia at the tip of the Olympic Peninsula, whose 1855 treaty is the only one in American law that explicitly guarantees the right to hunt whales.

subject: Makah National Fish Hatchery
summary: A federal fish hatchery on the Tsoo-Yess River that exists because the Makah held the United States to an 1855 treaty promise, releasing 92 million fish since 1981 to sustain the salmon runs central to tribal life.

subject: Makah Reservation
summary: A 47-square-mile reservation at the extreme northwestern tip of the Olympic Peninsula, where the Strait of Juan de Fuca meets the Pacific Ocean and the Makah people maintain a whaling culture older than written history.

subject: Makapansgat
summary: In a limestone valley in Limpopo, the bones of our three-million-year-old ancestors lie alongside a pebble one of them may have carried home simply because it looked like a face.

story.title: Makassar: The Port That Refused a Monopoly

subject: Makassar
summary: Indonesia's fifth-largest city was once a defiant free-trade port where Makassarese kings welcomed every merchant the Dutch tried to exclude -- and gave its name to the hair oil that spawned the antimacassar on Victorian armchairs.

subject: Makay Massif
summary: A 4,000-square-kilometer labyrinth of Jurassic sandstone canyons in western Madagascar so impassable and unexplored that scientists call it a lost world - and keep finding species new to science inside it.

subject: Makeni
summary: The Temne capital of Sierra Leone's north, a bauxite-and-bombali heartland that endured rebel occupation and rebuilt itself into a city of universities and hospitals.

subject: Makgadikgadi Pan
summary: One of the world's largest salt flats marks the bed of an ancient lake larger than Switzerland, where stone tools predate Homo sapiens and flamingos still breed in seasonal waters that transform the Kalahari.

subject: Makian
summary: A nearly circular volcanic island in Indonesia's Maluku archipelago whose violent eruptions have repeatedly devastated its population, yet whose people always return to the fertile slopes of Mount Kie Besi.

subject: Makran
summary: The semi-desert coast where fish eaters gave a region its name, where Alexander's army nearly perished, and where five millennia of empires from the Sumerians to the Mughals left their marks on one of the most strategically contested coastlines on Earth.

subject: Makran Coastal Highway
summary: A 653-kilometer highway along Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast that transformed a two-day ordeal over dirt tracks into a six-hour drive through some of the most dramatic coastal scenery on Earth, built by the same military engineers who carved the Karakoram Highway through the Himalayas.

subject: Maksym Zalizniak Oak
summary: A single oak in the Kholodnyi Yar forest has stood for more than eleven centuries - old enough to have shaded the rebel whose name it now carries.

subject: Makuria
summary: A Christian African kingdom centered at Dongola on the Nile that repelled Arab armies in 651, signed the extraordinary Baqt treaty, and endured as a sophisticated Nubian state for nearly a thousand years.

subject: Malacacheta
summary: A coffee and cattle town in northeastern Minas Gerais whose name comes from a local mineral and whose history includes one of Brazil's darkest crimes of religious fanaticism.

subject: Malacca Sultanate
summary: Founded by a fugitive prince who saw a mouse deer outwit a hunting dog, the Malacca Sultanate grew from a fishing village into the greatest maritime power in Southeast Asia before falling to Portuguese cannons in 1511.

subject: Malahat
summary: A sacred mountain with the Trans-Canada Highway laid over it - and the single stretch of road whose closure can cut southern Vancouver Island in half.

subject: Malahat First Nation
summary: A Coast Salish nation of roughly 350 members on the western shore of Saanich Inlet who bought a large piece of their own territory back in 2015 and built a 650-metre treetop walkway over it.

subject: Malakal
summary: The capital of Upper Nile State, changed hands twelve times in two years of civil war, and rebuilt again by the families who never left the White Nile.

story.title: Malang: The City Built on a Cursed Dagger

subject: Malang
summary: East Java's second city began as the seat of a kingdom founded by assassination, became the Dutch colonial elite's highland retreat, and now balances ancient temple ruins against a modern university culture -- all in a basin ringed by volcanoes.

story.title: Malapa Fossil Site, Cradle of Humankind

subject: Malapa Fossil Site, Cradle of Humankind
summary: A nine-year-old boy's sharp eyes led to the discovery of Australopithecus sediba at this limestone cave north of Johannesburg, reshaping the debate over humanity's direct ancestors.

subject: Malargüe
summary: A quiet town on the southern edge of Mendoza Province where ski traffic, cosmic-ray physicists, and deep-space engineers all converge under enormous skies.

subject: Malargüe Station
summary: On the high Argentine pampa, a 35-metre dish listens for whispers from spacecraft hundreds of millions of kilometres away.

subject: Malaysia–Thailand border
summary: A 595-kilometer line drawn by empires and rivers divides two nations on the Malay Peninsula, where sultans, colonial diplomats, and geography itself have shaped one of Southeast Asia's most complex borders.

subject: Malden, West Virginia
summary: A salt-making village on the Kanawha River that gave young Booker T. Washington his first classroom and his first wage.

subject: Maldonado
summary: The old garrison town behind the glamour of Punta del Este, where Artigas began his soldiering and the British once held the streets.

subject: Malecón Simón Bolívar
summary: Guayaquil's 2.5-kilometer riverfront boardwalk, reclaimed from decay in the late 1990s and now a global model for urban regeneration.

subject: Malexander murders
summary: A quiet Swedish lakeside village became the site of one of the nation's most traumatic crimes when neo-Nazi bank robbers executed two police officers in 1999.

subject: Mali
summary: Landlocked at the edge of the Sahara, Mali holds the gold-and-salt legacy of medieval empires, the mud mosques of Djenné and Timbuktu, and a musical tradition that rivals any on Earth.

subject: Maliau Basin
summary: Called Sabah's Lost World, this 588-square-kilometre basin in the heart of Borneo remained virtually unexplored until the 1980s and is now one of the planet's most pristine wilderness areas.

subject: Malibu Hydro
summary: A small but ingenious hydroelectric system that drops water 1,250 feet from an alpine lake, runs a submarine cable under a fjord, and powers a remote youth camp on Jervis Inlet.

subject: Malkastenpark
summary: Goethe walked these paths. So did Wilhelm von Humboldt. Then a worldwide lottery of paintings saved the garden from a gas company director who wanted to bulldoze it for housing.

subject: Malkheda
summary: Once the imperial capital built to rival the city of the gods, Manyakheta was so thoroughly destroyed that no one today knows exactly where its palaces stood.

subject: Mallaig
summary: A working fishing village at the end of the road - and the end of the West Highland Line, where the Jacobite Steam Train terminates and ferries fan out to Skye and the Small Isles.

subject: Mallaig
summary: A fishing port carved into Scotland's western edge, where the Road to the Isles meets the Sound of Sleat and the Hogwarts Express ends its journey.

subject: Malle
summary: A small Campine town that survived the Spanish Fury, the French Revolution, two World Wars - and then a tornado.

subject: Malpelo plate
summary: Identified in 2017, the Malpelo plate is the 57th tectonic plate on Earth - a microplate off western Colombia and Ecuador whose only emerged surface is a single lonely rock.
