subject: Malta Kiosk
summary: A neo-baroque hunting lodge tucked in the wooded heights of Yıldız Park, the Malta Kiosk carries the perfume of imperial intrigue alongside its gilded chandeliers and marble fountains.

subject: Maltby Main Colliery
summary: A deep South Yorkshire mine that produced coal for a century and was closed in 2013 because the geology below it would not cooperate any longer.

subject: Maltby Street Market
summary: Renegade traders evicted from Borough Market started a weekend food market beneath the world's first elevated railway arches - and accidentally created one of London's best.

story.title: Maluku: Where the World Went to War Over Seasoning

subject: Maluku
summary: For centuries, these scattered islands were the only place on Earth where cloves and nutmeg grew — a botanical accident that drew empires, sparked wars, and left a cultural mosaic unlike anywhere else in Indonesia.

story.title: Maluku: A Traveler's Guide to the Spice Islands

subject: Maluku
summary: The 632 islands of Maluku offer pristine reefs, volcanic peaks, crumbling colonial forts, and the lingering fragrance of the spice trade that once made these remote Indonesian islands the most coveted real estate on Earth.

subject: Malyn
summary: A paper-making town in the Polissya woods that wears a sheet of paper on its coat of arms, listens for secret nuclear tests, and may carry the name of a rebellious Drevlian prince.

subject: Mambaí
summary: The easternmost city in Goiás, surrounded by waterfalls and limestone caves carved by rivers on the edge of the Vão do Paranã.

subject: Mambwe people
summary: An ethnic group of northeastern Zambia and southwestern Tanzania whose origin stories, clan system, and long resistance to Bemba raids remain alive in memory and ceremony.

subject: Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve
summary: The world's first Sustainable Development Reserve, created in 1996 to prove that conservation and the river-dwelling ribeirinho communities who live inside it could work together.

subject: Mammen
summary: A farmer's spade in 1868 opened a Viking chamber grave here, and the silver-inlaid axe inside gave its name to an entire style of Scandinavian art.

subject: Mamoudzou
summary: The bustling capital of Mayotte, a fragment of France in the Indian Ocean, rebuilding after one of the worst cyclones in its history.

subject: Manabí mangroves
summary: A critically endangered ecoregion along Ecuador's Pacific coast, where mangrove roots hold together an ecosystem that shrimp farms nearly destroyed.

subject: Manacapuru
summary: A city of 102,000 on the Solimões known as the Land of Cirandas, where a folk festival organizes the calendar and Pope John Paul II's canoe-altar still sits in the mother church.

subject: Manacor
summary: An inland Mallorcan market town that tourists rarely stop in, yet the whole island bends toward it — birthplace of Rafael Nadal, home of Majorica pearls, and a riot of dancing demons each January.

subject: Manado
summary: The capital of North Sulawesi is a rare Indonesian city where churches outnumber mosques, the local creole borrows from Portuguese and Dutch, and the world-class reefs of Bunaken lie just offshore.

subject: Manam Motu
summary: A ten-kilometer-wide stratovolcano in the Bismarck Sea with four "avalanche valleys" that channel pyroclastic flows, evacuated in 2004 and still erupting.

subject: Manapouri
summary: A village of roughly 270 people on the shore of New Zealand's second-deepest lake, where a Maori legend of two sisters' tears meets the story of the country's first great environmental campaign.

subject: Manaure, La Guajira
summary: A salt-encrusted town on Colombia's arid Guajira Peninsula where evaporation ponds have produced treasure for centuries and the Wayuu people fought for decades to reclaim their ancestral role in the industry.

subject: Manaus
summary: A metropolis of 2.6 million at the heart of the Amazon rainforest, where Belle Epoque buildings meet jungle tours and two great rivers run side by side without mixing.

subject: Manaus
summary: Capital of Amazonas state, Brazil - once the rubber boom's Paris of the Tropics, now a 2.3-million-person metropolis at the confluence of the Negro and Amazon rivers.

subject: Manaus Air Force Base
summary: A Brazilian Air Force base nine kilometers from downtown Manaus, home to helicopters and transport planes that patrol the Amazon's vast green expanse.

subject: Manchester
summary: Once Cottonopolis, then Madchester, now a media and football capital - England's perpetually reinventing northern powerhouse.

subject: Manchester
summary: From Roman Mamucium to the world's first industrial city, Manchester's history reads as a sequence of accidents that became revolutions.

subject: Manchester Band of Pomo Indians
summary: A federally recognized Pomo tribe on California's Mendocino Coast whose 364-acre rancheria preserves the traditions of the Bokeya -- the largest Pomo tribelet by territory -- from ghost ceremonies to a constitution written in the wake of the Indian Reorganization Act.

subject: Mandalay Hill
summary: A 240-meter hill of legend, devotion, and battle, Mandalay Hill is where the Buddha is said to have prophesied the founding of a great city -- and where Gurkha soldiers fought hand-to-hand to reclaim it from the Japanese in 1945.

subject: Mandara Mountains
summary: A 190-kilometer wall of eroded volcanoes along the Cameroon-Nigeria border, where needle-sharp spires rise above hillsides terraced by hand for centuries.

subject: Mandu, Madhya Pradesh
summary: A ruined fortress city perched on the Vindhya Range where a palace floats between two lakes, India's first marble tomb foreshadowed the Taj Mahal, and a thousand years of conquest left behind some of the subcontinent's most haunting architecture.

subject: Mandø
summary: A Wadden Sea island of roughly thirty people, reached by a gravel road the North Sea covers twice a day - or by a tractor-drawn bus that runs on the tide table rather than the clock.

subject: Mangalajodi
summary: A village of former bird poachers turned conservationists, Mangalajodi sits on the northern edge of Chilika Lake and now hosts over 150,000 migratory birds each winter -- a transformation driven not by government decree but by the community itself.

subject: Mangazeya
summary: A vanished 17th-century Siberian trading city once called "the Baghdad of Siberia," whose location was deliberately erased from maps and forgotten for three centuries until archaeologists found its wooden kremlin in the tundra.

subject: Mangue Seco
summary: A dune-backed fishing village of a couple hundred people at the top of the Bahian coast, made famous nationwide by a telenovela whose town was a stage set built a thousand kilometres away.

subject: Manhattan Savings Institution robbery
summary: In 1878, a gang of thieves pulled off the largest heist in American history -- $2.7 million from a Manhattan bank -- using a full-scale replica of the vault, a bribed night watchman, and a device called the 'little joker,' all masterminded by a man who was already dead.

subject: Manhattanhenge
summary: Twice a year, the setting sun aligns perfectly with Manhattan's street grid, flooding its urban canyons with golden light -- a celestial event born from a 200-year-old surveying decision.

subject: Manicoré
summary: Founded as a colonial trading post in 1797, Manicore sits where its namesake river joins the Madeira, governing a municipality the size of Denmark from the banks of the Amazon's most commercially vital tributary.

subject: Manicoré Biological Reserve
summary: At 359,000 hectares of fully protected Amazon rainforest, the Manicore Biological Reserve forms the strictest core of a conservation shield designed to halt the advancing arc of deforestation in southern Amazonas.

subject: Manipur
summary: A northeastern Indian state where an oval valley ringed by blue mountains harbors one of the subcontinent's most complex intersections of ethnicity, language, and contested sovereignty.

subject: Manipur (princely state)
summary: An independent kingdom at the India-Burma frontier for centuries, Manipur endured Burmese invasions, British protectorate status, and a controversial merger with India that remains contested to this day.

subject: Manises
summary: The town where Valencia's airport sits was once famous across medieval Europe for golden lustreware so prized that popes and princes sought it out — and its kilns are still burning today.

subject: Manises UFO incident
summary: In November 1979, a Spanish airliner became the first ever forced to make an emergency landing because of a UFO — and the fighter jet scrambled to chase it came home with its systems jammed.

subject: Manizales
summary: A university town of 434,000 nestled on a ridgeline between a volcano and a thousand coffee farms, with eight microclimates and a cathedral third-tallest in Latin America.

subject: Mankien
summary: A Bul Nuer town in Unity State's oil belt that was bombed by Antonov aircraft, overrun by cavalry, recaptured by mutineers, and burned again in 2011.

subject: Manly, New South Wales
summary: A Sydney beach suburb that took its name from a first encounter, sold itself as an escape, and helped invent Australian surf culture.

subject: Mannaea
summary: A forgotten kingdom south of Lake Urmia that played empires against each other for three centuries before vanishing into the dust of Iranian history.

subject: Manorbier
summary: The Norman village on the Pembrokeshire coast where Britain's first travel writer was born, and the only place he ever called home.

subject: Manorhamilton
summary: A North Leitrim town named for the soldier-of-fortune who took the O'Rourke lands, sitting at the centre of a thinly populated district of dance halls, waterfalls, executed rebels and a lake monster.

subject: Manseibashi Station
summary: A phantom station in the heart of Tokyo, Manseibashi was designed by the same architect who created Tokyo Station, destroyed by earthquake, closed in 1943, and reborn in 2013 as a stylish commercial space where you can sip coffee on the original platform.

subject: Mansfield
summary: An ex-coal-mining market town in the Maun valley where Henry III granted the original royal charter in 1227 and where Rebecca Adlington learned to swim.

subject: Mansons Landing
summary: A sandspit, a lagoon and a warm freshwater lake at the south end of Cortes Island, where thousands of years of Klahoose shell midden lie under a park named for a Shetland trader's store.

subject: Manta
summary: Ecuador's second-largest seaport, a coastal city where fishing boats, surf breaks, and tagua nut carvers share a single working waterfront.

subject: Manta ray night dive
summary: Off the Kona coast of Hawaii's Big Island, divers and snorkelers shine lights into dark water to create columns of illuminated plankton, summoning manta rays with wingspans up to 16 feet for one of the ocean's most extraordinary wildlife encounters.

subject: Manta, Ecuador
summary: Ecuador's tuna capital and largest seaport, where a French equator mission once disembarked and U.S. surveillance planes once patrolled Colombian skies.

subject: Mantasoa
summary: A shipwrecked Frenchman built Madagascar's first industrial complex on this highland lakeshore for Queen Ranavalona I, using thousands of forced Malagasy laborers to forge cannons, glass, and silk.

subject: Mantinea
summary: Three of antiquity's most consequential battles were fought on the same flat Arcadian plain — where the city of Mantinea rose, fell, and rose again across eight centuries.

subject: Mantra-Rock Dance
summary: The night in 1967 when the Grateful Dead, Janis Joplin, Allen Ginsberg, and a Hare Krishna swami shared a stage at the Avalon Ballroom, and 3,000 hippies chanted Sanskrit for two hours.

subject: Manus
summary: Papua New Guinea's smallest province by land, vast by sea - where Margaret Mead returned seven times, obsidian once became trade currency, and coral atolls still hide some of the Pacific's best diving.

subject: Manus Regional Processing Centre
summary: The offshore detention facility on Manus Island became one of the most documented sites of prolonged confinement in the modern Pacific, and the men held there turned journalists, filmmakers, and witnesses against the silence meant to contain them.

subject: Manuscript 512
summary: A ten-page 1753 document found in Rio's National Library describing a lost city with Roman-style arches and Greek inscriptions somewhere in the Bahian interior, inspiring a century of expeditions and at least three novels.

subject: Manx Grand Prix
summary: An amateur road race on the same 60-kilometre Mountain Course as the TT, where ordinary riders chase the same Snaefell ghosts as world champions did before them.

subject: Manx Radio
summary: A tiny island station that beat the entire United Kingdom to legal commercial radio by nearly a decade, broadcasting since 1964.

subject: Manyikeni
summary: A mortarless stone enclosure in coastal Mozambique, built in the Great Zimbabwe tradition but constructed from limestone instead of granite, Manyikeni linked the inland empire to Indian Ocean trade networks for five centuries.

story.title: Manzanita Band of Diegueno Mission Indians

subject: Manzanita Band of Diegueno Mission Indians
summary: The Manzanita Band of Kumeyaay Indians, living near Boulevard in the southern Laguna Mountains, maintains a culture built on Bird Songs that carry collective memory, Eagle Dances that connect sky and community, and basket weaving traditions encoded with ecological knowledge.

subject: Maokong
summary: In the tea-growing hills above southern Taipei, Maokong offers tieguanyin tea, sweeping city views, and a gondola ride that turns the commute to a teahouse into something worth remembering.

subject: Maokong Gondola
summary: A cable car system that stranded a mayor in mid-air on day one, trapped hundreds of passengers on day seventeen, and nearly lost a support pillar to typhoons -- yet became one of Taipei's most beloved attractions.

subject: Maolin National Scenic Area
summary: A mountain scenic area straddling Kaohsiung and Pingtung where the western foothills of Taiwan's Central Mountain Range shelter the Rukai people's homeland and one of Asia's most spectacular butterfly wintering sites.

subject: Mapenduma Hostage Crisis
summary: A World Wildlife Fund biodiversity expedition into the Papuan highlands in January 1996 ended in a four-month hostage ordeal that tangled together insurgent politics, international diplomacy, and a controversial Kopassus rescue.

subject: Maple Ridge, British Columbia
summary: Fifty families on thirty-three thousand acres became a city of ninety thousand, and it took the paperwork exactly 140 years to catch up - to the day.

subject: Maputo
summary: Mozambique's capital wears its layered history in its architecture, its jacaranda-lined avenues, and a name that once marked the southern edge of a liberation dream.

subject: Mar Menor
summary: Spain's largest saltwater lagoon, a shallow warm-water sea shaped by Romans, pirates and pollution that became the first ecosystem in Europe granted legal rights.

subject: Mar del Plata
summary: Argentina's great Atlantic resort city - a place of 682,605 residents that swells with eight million summer visitors, where aristocratic chalets, a fishing fleet of yellow boats, and sea lions all share one shore.

subject: Mara Rosa
summary: A town that refused to die twice - once renamed, once relocated - and still grows saffron in Goiás.

subject: Marabastad
summary: On the western edge of Pretoria stands a neighborhood that apartheid emptied of its people but could not quite erase.

subject: Marabá, Pará
summary: From space the city reads as a Y, where the Itacaiúnas meets the Tocantins. On the ground it reads as five economic cycles - rubber, Brazil nuts, diamonds, gold, steel - laid on top of each other.

subject: Maracanaú
summary: An industrial satellite of Fortaleza whose Tupi name remembers the red-shouldered macaws that once flew over its lagoons.

subject: Maragheh
summary: A quiet Iranian city in the East Azerbaijan foothills that once served as the Mongol Ilkhanate's intellectual capital, Maragheh still guards medieval tomb towers whose geometric brickwork anticipated mathematical discoveries made centuries later.

subject: Maragogi
summary: Twice a day the tide falls far enough to let you stand six kilometres out to sea, in the reef pools that turned a quiet Alagoas town into the Northeast's best-known snorkelling destination.

subject: Maralinga
summary: A 3,300-square-kilometer patch of South Australian desert where British nuclear bombs poisoned the ancestral land of the Maralinga Tjarutja people, who fought for decades to get it back and now live with what remains.

subject: Maralinga to Emu Road
summary: A dead-straight dirt road bulldozed across the Great Victoria Desert in 1955 to link Britain's two mainland atomic-test sites, the work of a single dogged surveyor.

subject: Maranhão
summary: A Brazilian state where reggae echoes through colonial streets, dunes form the only desert in the world dotted with crystal lagoons, and a carnival called Açaí-Folia keeps the party going off-season.

subject: Maranhão
summary: A northeastern Brazilian state of seven million, the world's tallest mangroves, and a capital liberated in 1823 by a Scottish admiral who became 1st Marques of Maranhão.

subject: Maranhão mangroves
summary: Eleven thousand square kilometers of tidal forest along Brazil's northern coast, holding half the country's shorebirds.

subject: Marathon, Greece
summary: The town whose name became a foot race - and whose ancient burial mound still holds the bones of the 192 Athenians who died fighting Persia.

subject: Marazion
summary: The mainland anchor of St Michael's Mount, named for its Thursday market and once the busiest pilgrimage town in west Cornwall, Marazion is the small grey-stone settlement at the end of the causeway where a tidal island rises out of Mount's Bay.

subject: Marañón Dry Forests
summary: A rainshadow ecoregion in northern Peru where the Andes block the Amazon's rain, creating a dry valley forest richer in endemic plants than any other inter-Andean valley.

subject: Marburg
summary: A hillside university town of staircases and half-timbering that has spent a century making itself one of the easiest places in Germany to move through without sight.

subject: Marcardsmoor
summary: A late-nineteenth-century settler village dug straight into a raised bog north of Wiesmoor, built one drainage ditch at a time by colonists and prisoners working for the Prussian Central Moor Commission.

subject: Marchamalo salt flats
summary: At the built-up tip of La Manga, a surviving fragment of salt flats and dunes shelters flamingos, an endemic fish, and a Copper Age fishing village older than the resorts around it.

subject: Mardyke (UCC)
summary: The Cork sports ground where Ireland played Hungary in 1939, where Munster Rugby grew up, and where the River Lee burst its banks in 2009 and washed four million euro of equipment downstream.

subject: Mare aux Hippopotames
summary: A hippo-filled lake on the Black Volta floodplain - Burkina Faso's only UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.

story.title: Marfa: The Mysterious Lights No One Can Explain

subject: Marfa
summary: The West Texas town where unexplained lights have danced on the desert horizon since at least 1883 - attracting tourists, scientists, and true believers to a viewing platform where everyone sees something, though no one agrees what.

story.title: Marfa: Where Minimalist Art Colonized the Desert

subject: Marfa
summary: The West Texas town that Donald Judd transformed into an art destination - where hundred-unit concrete works dot the landscape, where mysterious lights appear in the desert, and where the population of 1,800 swells with weekenders seeking culture at the end of the earth.

story.title: Marfa: The Desert Art Town That Shouldn't Exist

subject: Marfa
summary: The tiny West Texas town where Donald Judd installed minimalist sculptures in abandoned military buildings, where mysterious lights appear on the horizon, and where art pilgrims drive 200 miles from the nearest airport.

subject: Marfin Bank Arson
summary: On 5 May 2010, three bank employees died in a firebombed Athens branch during Greece's largest anti-austerity protest, a tragedy that still marks Stadiou Street.

story.title: Marga: Where Bali's Last Stand Became Its Founding Myth

subject: Marga
summary: A quiet Balinese district of monkey forests and fruit orchards that holds the grave of I Gusti Ngurah Rai, the national hero whose fight-to-the-death against the Dutch in 1946 gave Bali's international airport its name.

subject: Margaret Thatcher
summary: Britain's first female prime minister, who transformed the British economy and society between 1979 and 1990 and remains one of the most divisive figures in modern British politics.

subject: Margariti
summary: A hilltop village in Thesprotia whose four centuries as a flourishing Muslim Albanian town ended in the violence and expulsions of the Second World War — a loss carried by real families and a community that is now gone.

subject: Margate
summary: A Kent seaside town where T. S. Eliot wrote part of The Waste Land, J. M. W. Turner painted the loveliest skies in Europe, and the Shell Grotto's four million seashells still defy explanation.

subject: Margate City, New Jersey
summary: Home of Lucy the Elephant and Marven Gardens, this small shore city has spent 140 years cultivating its peculiarities.

subject: Mari Mari Cultural Village
summary: An open-air museum in the Sabah rainforest where five indigenous tribes of northern Borneo keep their ancestral traditions alive through interactive village replicas.

subject: Mariachi Plaza
summary: In Boyle Heights, a sunlit plaza has anchored the tradition of Mexican street musicians for nearly a century — a gathering place where hireable bands wait under a hand-carved stone kiosk, and where the legacy of ranchera music echoes across generations.

subject: Mariager
summary: A cobbled town of 2,650 on Mariager Fjord that calls itself the City of Roses, sits on a salt dome, and produced the architect who gave Copenhagen its grandest façades.

subject: Marichjhanpi
summary: A mangrove island in the Sundarbans became the site of one of independent India's most suppressed tragedies, when thousands of Dalit refugees were violently expelled from a promised homeland.

subject: Marie-Galante
summary: Named after Columbus's flagship and still dotted with the towers of 72 surviving sugar mills, this round Caribbean island off Guadeloupe carries five centuries of colonial history in its landscape.

subject: Marin County Civic Center
summary: Frank Lloyd Wright's last major commission -- a sweeping pink-and-blue government complex that became a Star Wars filming location and a National Historic Landmark.

subject: Marina City
summary: A janitors' union bankrolled these twin corncob towers on the Chicago River in the early 1960s to lure white-collar workers back downtown -- and accidentally invented the template for mixed-use urban living that cities worldwide still copy today.

story.title: Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms

subject: Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms
summary: The largest Marine Corps base in the United States, covering 1,102 square miles of Mojave Desert terrain used to train every combined-arms tactic the Corps knows — including operations in a fabricated 274-acre Middle Eastern city.

subject: Marine Corps Air Station Yuma
summary: The busiest Marine Corps air station in the world, developed from a 1928 municipal field into a major WWII training installation and then the permanent home of Marine Corps aviation in the American Southwest — where F-35Bs now fly from a runway named for a man who inspired a comic strip.

story.title: Marine Corps Auxiliary Landing Field Bogue

subject: Marine Corps Auxiliary Landing Field Bogue
summary: An 875-acre patch of Bogue Sound where Marine Harrier pilots practice landing on the painted outline of a ship's deck.

subject: Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune
summary: Camp Lejeune is 246 square miles of Marine Corps training ground, fourteen miles of beach, and a forty-year reckoning with the water its families drank.

subject: Marine Institute Ireland
summary: Ireland's state marine science agency, headquartered on a Galway Bay peninsula, with three research vessels and a deepwater ROV named Holland 1.

subject: Marinekazerne Suffisant
summary: A Dutch naval barracks on Curacao born from a Venezuelan revolutionary's failed raid, now reinvented as a place where young conscripts trade six months of military discipline for an education and a diploma.

subject: Maringa-Lopori-Wamba Landscape
summary: A 74,000-square-kilometer expanse of Congolese rainforest where Japanese researchers have studied bonobos since 1973, and where the brutal legacy of King Leopold's rubber trade still echoes in a landscape that is among the poorest and most remote on Earth.

subject: Marion Downs Station
summary: One of the great Channel Country cattle runs near Boulia, watered by four rivers and the Simpson Desert, where a sheep paradise became a cattle empire and the land has killed men with both flood and thirst.

subject: Marion, North Carolina
summary: A McDowell County seat named for a Revolutionary guerrilla, scarred by mill-strike gunfire in 1929, now living on as the gateway where Main Street meets the Blue Ridge.

story.title: Mariposa Grove: Where Lincoln Drew the Line

subject: Mariposa Grove
summary: The largest giant sequoia grove in Yosemite, whose 427 ancient trees inspired Abraham Lincoln to sign the first act protecting wilderness for public benefit - and whose survival now depends on the return of the fire that humans spent a century suppressing.

subject: Maritime Guinea
summary: Where the Fouta Djallon highlands finally let go of their rivers, Guinea dissolves into a drowned coast of mangrove, mud, and tidal light.

subject: Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz
summary: On a windswept island in the Wadden Sea, a maritime academy named for an Arctic explorer who never came home has been teaching young Dutch sailors how to find their way for nearly 150 years.

subject: Maritime Quarter, Swansea
summary: The Welsh tallest tower rises over a re-excavated dock that the city had filled in, dug out again, and finally turned into a marina.

subject: Maritime Research Institute Netherlands
summary: Before a new oil platform rides a North Sea storm or a container ship cuts its first wake, a 1:50 model of it has already been pushed, tilted, and waved at in a giant indoor lake in Wageningen.

subject: Markala
summary: A 2.4-kilometer weir across the Niger turned the dry plains north of Ségou into Mali's rice basket, the centerpiece of a colonial irrigation dream.

subject: Marken
summary: A former island in the Zuiderzee where wooden houses still sit on mounds, and the sea that defined village life was sealed off in living memory.

subject: Market Bosworth
summary: A Leicestershire market town two miles from the field where Richard III lost his crown, his life, and a dynasty, where Samuel Johnson once taught school and a Formula E champion grew up.

subject: Market Square (Lviv)
summary: Rynok Square has been the center of Lviv since the 14th century -- a place where kings accepted homage, rebels proclaimed independence, and 44 tenement houses tell six centuries of architectural history.

subject: Market Street (San Francisco)
summary: The boulevard that nearly got its surveyor lynched for making it too wide became San Francisco's spine, carrying everything from cable cars to victory parades for 175 years.

subject: Market Street Chinatown
summary: Two successive Chinatowns in 19th-century San Jose, both destroyed by arson with official complicity, whose buried remains were rediscovered during 1980s construction.

subject: Market Street Depot
summary: San Jose's first intercity rail station connected the Santa Clara Valley to San Francisco for seven decades before the automobile rendered its downtown tracks untenable.

subject: Market Street subway
summary: A two-level subway built beneath San Francisco's most important street carries both BART and Muni trains in an engineering compromise born from political deal-making.

subject: Marlboro County, South Carolina
summary: Named for an 18th-century English duke, this Pee Dee county was settled by Welsh Baptists and is still home to the Pee Dee Indian Tribe, who never left.

subject: Marlborough Sounds
summary: A labyrinth of drowned valleys at the top of New Zealand's South Island, where forested ridgelines plunge into tidal water and the only way to reach most places is by boat.

subject: Marlik
summary: A 3,000-year-old royal cemetery in northern Iran's Gilan Province where 53 tombs yielded golden cups adorned with griffins, winged bulls, and gazelles -- treasures now displayed in museums from Tehran to the Louvre.

subject: Marlin Mine
summary: A gold and silver mine in Guatemala's western highlands where the clash between a Canadian mining corporation, Maya communities, international courts, and contested water samples became one of Latin America's most closely watched resource conflicts.

subject: Marlinton
summary: A small West Virginia town that doubles as the seat of "the Birthplace of the Rivers" - and once a year, the world capital of roadkill cooking.

subject: Maroon Town, Jamaica
summary: A small Jamaican settlement in the rugged Cockpit Country where formerly enslaved people fought two guerrilla wars for their freedom, then were deported across the Atlantic -- only to have some return generations later.

subject: Marqua Station
summary: On the eastern edge of the Northern Territory, a remote cattle run breeds beef beside the dunes of the Simpson Desert, hostage to fire, drought, and the occasional flood.

subject: Marrah Mountains
summary: A temperate island of rain, lakes, and pine rising three kilometers above the Sahel, the highest ground in Sudan and a refuge for the Fur people.

subject: Marrakech
summary: Where the medina maze has swallowed travelers for a millennium, where Berber dynasties built mosques that still define the skyline, where Africa meets Arabia in the Red City.

subject: Marree
summary: A tiny outback junction town where Afghan cameleers built one of Australia's first mosques and two legendary tracks meet.

subject: Marree Man
summary: A hunting figure nearly three kilometres tall appeared in the South Australian desert in 1998 - and no one has ever admitted making it.

subject: Marribank
summary: Once the Carrolup Native Settlement where Stolen Generations children were confined, Marribank became the unlikely birthplace of an internationally celebrated Aboriginal art movement created by those same children.

subject: Marringarr language
summary: Along a remote stretch of the Northern Territory's northwest coast, the Marringarr language and its close relative Mati Ke once encoded an entire way of understanding the world — a system with ten noun classes ranging from weapons to spirits — but by 2005, only three people still spoke Mati Ke.

subject: Marsabit
summary: An island of misty forest and crater lakes rising a kilometer above the deserts of northern Kenya, where herdsmen sing to their cattle and an elephant once wore the protection of a president.

subject: Marsden Rock
summary: The 250-million-year-old sea stack whose famous arch fell during one winter of storms and never came back.

subject: Marsden, Tyne and Wear
summary: The colliery village that vanished into the cliff-top wind, and the rattling pit train named after it.

subject: Marseille
summary: Where the Greeks founded France's oldest city and North Africa begins before you leave Europe, where the Vieux-Port holds 2,600 years of maritime history and bouillabaisse is sacred.

subject: Marsha P. Johnson
summary: Known as the 'Saint of Christopher Street,' Marsha P. Johnson was a transgender activist who helped ignite the Stonewall uprising, co-founded a shelter for homeless transgender youth, and became an enduring symbol of LGBTQ resistance in New York City.

subject: Martha's Vineyard
summary: An island off Cape Cod where Wampanoag heritage, whaling history, a unique sign language, presidential retreats, and the filming of Jaws converge in one of America's most storied summer destinations.

subject: Martin County coal slurry spill
summary: Just after midnight on October 11, 2000, the bottom dropped out of a Massey Energy coal slurry pond. 306 million gallons. About 28 times the Exxon Valdez. The water in 27,000 homes turned black.

subject: Martin Luther (steam locomotive)
summary: A British-built steam traction engine that broke down in the Namib in 1897 and never moved again, earning the name Martin Luther for standing its ground.

subject: Martino, Phthiotis
summary: An Arvanite village named for an Albanian chieftain, built atop a vanished ancient city, that helped turn back the Ottoman army in one of the decisive battles of the Greek War of Independence.

subject: Martinsville Speedway
summary: NASCAR's shortest oval - 0.526 miles of paperclip-shaped pavement in southern Virginia, where the first race in 1947 left every spectator coated in red clay dust and the racing has been beating and banging ever since.

subject: Martinsville, Virginia
summary: An independent Virginia city that was once the Sweatshirt Capital of the World and claimed more millionaires per capita than anywhere in America - until globalization sent the textile mills overseas and left a town reinventing itself.

subject: Marton, Middlesbrough
summary: A southern Middlesbrough suburb that was a North Riding village until the 1950s, birthplace of Captain James Cook, with a Norman church where he was baptised.

subject: Marudi
summary: A riverside town in Sarawak where headhunting feuds were ended not by force, but by boat racing -- and where crocodiles are reclaiming the quiet river.

subject: Mary Kathleen, Queensland
summary: A model uranium town rose in the Selwyn Range, thrived for three decades, then was sold for parts and erased - leaving only kerbs, slabs, and roads that lead nowhere.

subject: Mary King's Close
summary: A 17th-century lane buried under Edinburgh's City Chambers, named for a merchant woman who ran a household there, and a place where many people lived and died in confined spaces.

subject: Mary Rose
summary: Henry VIII's flagship Mary Rose sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545 with the loss of nearly 500 men, and was lifted from the seabed 437 years later in one of the most ambitious salvage projects in history.

subject: Mary, Turkmenistan
summary: Built in 1884 as a Russian military outpost thirty kilometers from the ruins of ancient Merv, Mary is an oasis city in the Karakum Desert where the Silk Road's ghosts meet Soviet-era cotton fields and twenty-first-century marble monuments.

subject: Marylebone
summary: A central London district where Sherlock Holmes never lived, Madame Tussaud finally settled, and a small stream still bends through the grid that was built over it.

subject: Marylebone Cricket Club
summary: The 1787 gentlemen's club that wrote cricket's laws and still owns the game's most famous ground.

subject: Maryport
summary: A Cumbrian harbour town where Hadrian's western frontier still slumbers beneath grassy ramparts, and a Georgian gentleman renamed an entire town for the woman he loved.

subject: Marília
summary: Named from a poet's verse on a ship to Europe, this São Paulo town gave Brazil its first Olympic swimming medal, an airline, a major bank, and the country's 'Capital of Food Processing.'

subject: Masanjia re-education through labor camp
summary: A labor camp near Shenyang where prisoners were forced to manufacture goods for export, Masanjia became an international symbol of China's laojiao system after an SOS letter was discovered hidden inside a box of Halloween decorations sold at an American store.

subject: Maschsee
summary: Designed to stop floods, dug by unemployed men for wages barely above the dole, opened by the Nazi Party in 1936, and hidden under canvas six years later.

subject: Mashhad
summary: Iran's holiest city draws nearly 30 million pilgrims a year to the golden-domed shrine of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia Imam who was poisoned here in 818 CE.

subject: Mashhad Ardehal
summary: A small Iranian city where 200,000 pilgrims gather annually to wash a sacred carpet in a centuries-old mourning ceremony for a murdered saint.

subject: Masrur Temples
summary: A group of 8th-century rock-cut Hindu temples in Himachal Pradesh, carved from a single sandstone ridge in the Kailasa style to mirror Mount Meru's cosmic geometry.

subject: Massandra Winery
summary: A cliffside cellar built for a czar, where century-old bottles have outlasted revolutions, occupations, and every leader who tried to give them away.

subject: Massawa
summary: A traveler's view of Eritrea's Red Sea port, where climb down from Asmara means shedding three layers and arriving among coral houses and causeway islands.

subject: Masters Tournament
summary: Golf's most exclusive invitational tournament, held each April at Augusta National, where the green jacket, the pimento cheese sandwich, and nearly a century of drama have made the Masters a sporting institution unlike any other.

subject: Mastichochoria
summary: In two dozen fortified villages of southern Chios, families still bleed a small tree for the resin the rest of the world cannot grow.

subject: Mata Escura Biological Reserve
summary: A strict nature reserve in the Jequitinhonha valley whose protected status sits in unresolved tension with an 81-family quilombo community that has lived on the land far longer than the decree that created the reserve.

subject: Mataderos
summary: Named for its slaughterhouses, this southwestern barrio is where the city met the pampas - the gaucho's last stop, the cattle market's beating heart, and a Sunday fair of folk and flame.

subject: Matadi
summary: The DRC's chief seaport, built on steep hills where the Congo River meets its final rapids, where a local saying insists residents must master three verbs: to go up, to go down, and to sweat.

story.title: Mataquescuintla: The Town That Made a President

subject: Mataquescuintla
summary: A quiet Guatemalan highland town whose Nahuatl name means 'net to catch dogs' served as the unlikely base from which an illiterate mestizo swineherd launched a peasant revolution, toppled a liberal government, and ruled Guatemala for a quarter century.

subject: Mataram Sultanate
summary: The last great independent Javanese kingdom, whose rise and fracture shaped the cultural heartland of Central Java for centuries.

subject: Matheran
summary: A car-free hill station perched at 800 meters in the Western Ghats, where a narrow-gauge toy train climbs through forest to reach one of India's smallest and most fiercely protected retreats.

subject: Mathews County, Virginia
summary: A county that is two-thirds water, has no traffic light, and once briefly belonged to John Lennon - the Chesapeake's quietest corner.

subject: Mathry
summary: A Welsh hilltop village named for seven Christian martyrs, with a parish register that may hold the birth record of the woman who captured a French invasion force with a pitchfork.

subject: Matias Cardoso
summary: A brick church raised on the São Francisco in the 1670s — older than the gold that made Minas Gerais — in a town still carrying the name of the bandeirante who built it.

subject: Mato Grosso do Sul
summary: A state the size of Germany where the Pantanal's flooded plains meet the cerrado savanna, and where two great river systems mark Brazil's border with three neighbors.

subject: Mato Grosso tropical dry forests
summary: A vast transitional forest between Amazon and Cerrado, now cut through by highways and shrinking by three quarters of a percent every year.

subject: Matsdal
summary: A thin ribbon of a village between two fells in Swedish Lapland, founded by a discharged soldier who walked north for twenty years and froze to death eight winters after he arrived.

subject: Matsieng Footprints
summary: On a flat sandstone outcrop near Gaborone, ancient engravings mark the spot where, by Tswana tradition, the first people stepped out of the earth.

subject: Matsqui First Nation
summary: A Sto:lo nation on the Fraser River whose name means "easy portage," whose founder was transformed into a beaver, and who speak two languages where most of their neighbours speak one.

subject: Matsu New Village
summary: A preserved military dependents' village in Zhongli District, Taoyuan — the first such settlement built for Nationalist officers after 1949 and one of Taiwan's thirteen nationally designated cultural preservation areas for juancun heritage.

story.title: Matsugaoka: Where Samurai Became Silk Farmers

subject: Matsugaoka Land Reclamation Area
summary: After losing the Boshin War, over 3,000 former samurai of Shonai Domain traded their swords for mulberry seedlings and built Japan's largest silk cooperative on reclaimed mountain land -- and 64 descendant families still work there today.

subject: Matsushima
summary: A bay scattered with 260 pine-cloaked islands so beautiful that Japan's most celebrated poet arrived, gazed out, and declared himself speechless.

subject: Matsés National Reserve
summary: A 4,200-square-kilometer Amazon reserve co-governed with the Matsés people, who refused sustained contact with outsiders until the 1960s and still shape the land's future.

subject: Matthew Flinders
summary: The navigator who first sailed right around Australia, gave the continent its name, explored Moreton Bay with the Aboriginal man Bungaree, and spent six years a French prisoner.

subject: Matthias Petersen
summary: The Föhr whaling captain known as Lucky Mathew killed 373 whales in fifty years at sea, then ran out of luck in the final year of his life.

subject: Mattru Jong
summary: A river town named for buffalo, where a mission hospital, a paramount chief, and a famous wartime memoir all converge on the slow brown water of the Jong.

subject: Maun, Botswana
summary: Botswana's tourism capital still calls itself a village despite a population of 85,000, mixing bush-plane runways and safari outfitters with free-roaming donkeys and curbside cattle markets along the Thamalakane River.

story.title: Mauna Kea: Where Sacred Mountain Meets the Stars

subject: Mauna Kea
summary: The Hawaiian peak that is the world's premier astronomical site - where thirteen telescopes scan the universe from above 40% of Earth's atmosphere, where Native Hawaiians consider the summit sacred ground, and where science and sovereignty collide in ongoing conflict.

subject: Mauna Kea Ice Age Reserve
summary: High on the slopes of Mauna Kea, a 3,894-acre reserve protects evidence of both ice ages and ancient Hawaiian industry: glacial moraines, tropical permafrost, a high-altitude lake, and the largest primitive quarry in the world.

subject: Mauna Kea Observatories
summary: Thirteen telescopes funded by eleven countries perch atop a sacred Hawaiian volcano, making it Earth's premier window on the cosmos -- and the stage for one of science's most charged cultural conflicts.

subject: Maungakiekie / One Tree Hill
summary: A 182-metre volcanic cone that once supported a thriving Māori pā of 5,000 people, One Tree Hill carries layers of history from ancient Polynesian settlement to a U2 song, all crowned by an obelisk and a complicated absence.

subject: Mavericks
summary: Named for a white German Shepherd who swam into the surf in 1967, this Half Moon Bay break produces 60-foot waves that killed one of Hawaii's greatest surfers and inspired Apple to name an operating system.

subject: Mawlamyine
summary: The old colonial port where Rudyard Kipling gazed lazily at the sea and George Orwell witnessed a hanging -- a city layered with Mon, British, and Burmese history at the mouth of the Thanlwin River.

subject: Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics
summary: The only Max Planck Institute devoted entirely to how language works in the human mind, founded by a Dutch psycholinguist in 1980 and quietly archiving the world's dying languages from a campus in Nijmegen.

subject: May 2020 Afghanistan attacks
summary: In the deadliest month since a U.S.-Taliban peace deal was signed, a wave of attacks across Afghanistan killed hundreds -- including mothers and newborns gunned down in a Kabul maternity ward.

subject: May Fourth Movement
summary: A student protest in Beijing on May 4, 1919 over the Treaty of Versailles ignited a nationwide cultural and political awakening that redefined modern China.

subject: May Fourth Square
summary: A ten-hectare public square in Qingdao dominated by a 30-meter spiraling red sculpture that commemorates the 1919 student uprising born from the city's colonial betrayal at Versailles.

subject: Maybole
summary: Once the capital of Carrick and seat of the Kennedy clan, Maybole produced the man who invented modern road surfacing, the founder of the Guinness Book of World Records, and Robert Burns's mother.

subject: Mayfair
summary: The London neighbourhood named after a disreputable spring fair that became the most expensive square on the Monopoly board.

subject: Maymont
summary: A Gilded Age railroad fortune built this hundred-acre Richmond estate, then quietly left it to the city - mansion, gardens, animals, and all.

subject: Maynas province
summary: A jungle province the size of a small country, anchored by Iquitos, the largest city in the world unreachable by road - and once the disputed prize of a war between Peru and Gran Colombia.

subject: Mayom County
summary: An administrative division in the heart of Unity State's oil belt, where a 2011 declaration by a dissident general briefly tried to declare a new transitional government.

subject: Mayom, South Sudan
summary: A Bul Nuer cattle-trading town turned garrison turned battleground, captured by Riek Machar in 1988, retaken by Paulino Matiep in 1989, and fought over continuously since.

subject: Mayombe
summary: A mountainous rainforest corridor spanning four Central African countries, where ancient Limba trees and the Yombe people endure amid dramatic deforestation and a dismantled colonial railway.

subject: Mayong, Assam
summary: Known as India's 'capital of black magic,' this village on the Brahmaputra has been associated with sorcery, tantric practice, and tales of vanishing men for centuries.

subject: Mayotte
summary: A French archipelago in the Mozambique Channel where a sultan sold sovereignty for 5,000 francs, and where the population has twice voted to remain part of France while its Comoran neighbors chose independence.

subject: Maytown
summary: The vanished capital of the Palmer River goldfield, where a 1870s rush drew tens of thousands of diggers and a vast Chinese community onto Kuku-Yalanji country, leaving a ghost town built on fortune, violence, and forgetting.

subject: Mazabuka
summary: A southern Zambian sugar town whose name, in Tonga, means "you have crossed," commemorating the river crossing that first brought people here.

subject: Mazagão Velho
summary: A Portuguese fortress town evacuated from Morocco in 1769 was rebuilt in the Amazon rainforest — and its descendants still stage the war they left behind every July.

subject: Mazamitla
summary: A highland Pueblo Magico in Jalisco whose Nahuatl name means 'place where arrows are made to hunt deer,' Mazamitla layers Aztec origins, colonial rebellion, and pine-scented mountain tourism into a small town 2,200 meters above sea level.

subject: Mazar-e Sharif
summary: A city born from a dream about a saint's hidden grave, Mazar-e Sharif grew around the Blue Mosque to become northern Afghanistan's capital after the ancient city of Balkh was abandoned to disease.

subject: Mazarrón
summary: A Murcian coastal town where two of the oldest boats in the Mediterranean were raised from the shallows, backed by mountains mined since the Carthaginians.

subject: Mazatlán
summary: A Pacific coast city whose Nahuatl name means 'place of deer,' where centuries of German immigration, carnival tradition, and seafood culture meet one of Mexico's highest natural lighthouses.

subject: Mazunte
summary: A Pacific coast village that once ran Mexico's largest sea turtle slaughterhouse and reinvented itself as a conservation hub - now home to the Mexican National Turtle Center, a Body Shop-linked cosmetics cooperative, and beaches where 900,000 olive ridley turtles arrive in a single nesting season.

subject: Maó
summary: The capital of Menorca, wrapped around one of the Mediterranean's finest natural harbours, fought over by Carthage, Britain, France and Spain, and quite possibly the birthplace of mayonnaise.

subject: Mbabane
summary: Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane is a cool, mist-prone mountain town on the Highveld - a modern commercial hub that shares the duties of a capital with the royal valley just down the road.

subject: Mbala District
summary: A Zambian district named for a spotted bushbuck, where the Great Rift Valley drops from 2,067-meter peaks to 400 meters above the sea.

subject: Mbeya
summary: A highland crossroads city in southwestern Tanzania where three countries converge, flanked by volcanic peaks and connected by the TAZARA railway to Zambia and local dalla-dallas to Malawi.

subject: Mbeya Region
summary: Tanzania's Southern Highlands country, where a collapsed volcano holds one of the world's largest rare earth deposits and eleven Bantu peoples share a region the size of Guinea-Bissau.

subject: Mbuji-Mayi
summary: A city built on top of one of the world's largest diamond deposits, Mbuji-Mayi grew from a tightly controlled mining camp into the Congo's second-largest metropolis -- and never stopped being defined by what lies beneath it.

subject: McAdam station
summary: A granite castle in the New Brunswick woods that once fed 2,000 travelers a day and now stands as the largest railway station in the province, a monument to the age when rail was king.

subject: McGulpin Point Light
summary: One of the oldest surviving lighthouses on the Straits of Mackinac, McGulpin Point Light spent a century as a private home before a community effort restored its lantern room and relit its beacon in 2009.

subject: McMartin Preschool Trial
summary: Beginning in 1983 in Manhattan Beach, California, accusations of ritual child abuse at a preschool spiraled into the longest and most expensive criminal trial series in American history — and ended without a single conviction, leaving behind lasting questions about how the justice system handles children, memory, and moral panic.

subject: McMinnville
summary: Where the Spruce Goose found its final home and Oregon's wine country spreads across the surrounding hills of the northern Willamette Valley.

subject: Mchinji
summary: A Malawian border town where a lion once stalked the streets for five months, where Madonna's adoption case sparked international controversy, and where a new railway finally linked two countries that had been talking about it since 1982.

subject: Me-no-Sen-You-no-Come
summary: A hidden village founded by enslaved people who escaped Jamaica's sugar plantations and named their refuge with a warning: if I don't send for you, don't come.

story.title: Meadows near Rijswijk and the Schenkweg

subject: Meadows near Rijswijk and the Schenkweg
summary: Vincent van Gogh's view from his rented Hague window in January 1882: a half-rural polder being eaten by a railroad, painted by an artist who had just decided to stop drawing and start painting.

subject: Measurex
summary: A Cupertino company that revolutionized paper-making with computer-controlled sensors named its street 'Results Way' -- and decades later, Apple moved in.

subject: Meat Riots
summary: In October 1905, Santiago's working poor marched to ask their president for cheaper meat. Within days, the army had killed as many as two hundred of them in the streets of the capital.

subject: Mecca
summary: Islam's holiest city and the site of the Hajj, where millions face the Kaaba in prayer five times a day and where the Saudi government's modernization has erased much of the thousand-year-old city Muhammad once knew.

subject: Mecca
summary: In a narrow valley 70 kilometers inland from the Red Sea, the holiest city in Islam is also one of the ten most-visited cities in the world, triply populated for one week each year by pilgrims from every nation on Earth.

subject: Mecca, California
summary: At 150 feet below sea level in the eastern Coachella Valley, Mecca has recorded two of the highest temperatures in California history — and its residents, mostly farmworkers growing the date palms that define the region, have lived with that heat for generations.

subject: Mechelen
summary: Briefly the capital of the Low Countries under a regent who raised the future Charles V, Mechelen lost its political center in 1530 and rebuilt itself around bells, lace, and tapestry.

subject: Mechra el Rek
summary: The only mechra, or landing place, on the northwestern edge of the Sudd, where ivory merchants disembarked and Dinka porters were hired for journeys into the interior.

subject: Mecklenburg County, North Carolina
summary: Named for a German queen, the home of the contested 1775 Mecklenburg Declaration, and now home to over 1.2 million people - Mecklenburg County is North Carolina's most populous and one of its most layered.

subject: Medellin
summary: Where Colombia's second city transformed from world murder capital to urban innovation showcase, where cable cars connect hillside barrios, where Pablo Escobar's shadow fades.

subject: Medeon (Phocis)
summary: An ancient Phocian town on the Gulf of Antikyra, destroyed by Philip II of Macedon in 346 BCE and never rebuilt — its acropolis survives on a steep coastal hill, its inscribed sympoliteia treaty a rare document of how small Greek cities negotiated survival.

subject: Medieval Europe
summary: A thousand years of European history compressed into walls and cathedrals and market squares you can still walk through, mostly because the locals never quite got around to tearing them down.

subject: Medina
summary: Al-Madinah, the city that welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and holds his tomb, is the second-holiest place in Islam and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year.

subject: Medina of Sfax
summary: Founded in 849 by order of the Aghlabid prince of Kairouan, the walled medina of Sfax remains home to 113,000 residents and preserves a thousand years of domestic architecture behind ramparts that have withstood invasions, bombardments, and the pressures of modernity.

subject: Mediumwave Transmitter Flevoland
summary: Two 195-metre steel masts stood alone on the polder for 39 years, blanketing Europe with 400 kilowatts of Dutch radio - until a January morning in 2019 when explosives folded them onto the wet grass.

subject: Medway Megaliths
summary: The only prehistoric megalithic group in eastern England - a cluster of chambered Neolithic tombs strung along the River Medway, built six thousand years ago and systematically smashed in the 13th century.

subject: Meekatharra, Western Australia
summary: A Murchison gold-and-pastoral hub whose Yamatji name means 'place of little water' - a Royal Flying Doctor base and outback crossroads where the desert and the highway have always set the terms.

subject: Megaliths in the Netherlands
summary: Fifty-four stone tombs built by Funnelbeaker farmers over five thousand years ago still cluster along a ridge in Drenthe - one of them held the broken pieces of 649 pottery vessels.

subject: Megara
summary: The ancient city on the road between Athens and Corinth that founded Byzantium, invented a school of philosophy, pioneered democracy — and is remembered by its neighbors mostly for being a difficult neighbor.

subject: Meghalaya
summary: India's 'Abode of Clouds' where matrilineal tribes, living root bridges, and the wettest places on Earth converge on ancient subtropical plateaus.

subject: Mehrgarh
summary: One of the oldest farming settlements on Earth, Mehrgarh rewrites the story of civilization on the Kacchi Plain of Balochistan.

subject: Mehri language
summary: Spoken in the mountains and wadis of Yemen's Mahra Governorate and Oman's Dhofar, Mehri is the largest surviving Modern South Arabian language -- a family older than Arabic that predates Islam on the peninsula.

subject: Mei Foo Sun Chuen
summary: When it was completed, Mei Foo Sun Chuen's 99-tower complex was considered the largest private housing development in the world — a city within a city, built on a former oil depot on the Kowloon waterfront.

subject: Meigs Field
summary: On the night of March 30, 2003, Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley sent bulldozers to carve giant X marks into the runway of Meigs Field while the city slept -- destroying the busiest single-strip airport in America and stranding planes on the ground.

subject: Meili Snow Mountains
summary: A sacred Tibetan Buddhist mountain range in Yunnan whose highest peak -- Kawagarbo at 6,740 meters -- has never been summited, protected by both deadly conditions and a climbing ban imposed after a catastrophic 1991 avalanche killed 17 mountaineers.

subject: Meinarti
summary: A Nile island village near the Second Cataract whose stratified archaeological mound held eighteen layers of human history across 1,500 years -- all of it now submerged beneath Lake Nubia.

subject: Meiringspoort
summary: A 25-kilometer road crosses the same river 25 times as it slices through the Swartberg, a UNESCO World Heritage fold mountain that once separated two worlds of the South African Karoo.

subject: Meishi Street
summary: A 2006 documentary that handed cameras to Beijing residents as bulldozers came for their neighborhood before the Olympics, capturing the raw human cost of urban renewal from the inside.

subject: Mekong
summary: Asia's third-longest river flows through six countries from the Tibetan Plateau to the South China Sea, sustaining the world's most productive inland fishery and shaping the cultures of sixty million people.

subject: Melbourne
summary: Australia's cultural capital - where gold rush wealth built a city of Victorian grandeur, street art transforms every laneway into a gallery, and coffee obsession became an identity.

subject: Melbourne Cup
summary: On the first Tuesday of November, two miles of Flemington turf hold the attention of an entire nation, and increasingly its conscience too.

subject: Melgunov Kurgan
summary: One of the oldest Scythian burial mounds ever opened gave up a hoard of gold beneath the steppe - and the eagle on one buried plate still flies on a region's flag today.

subject: Melle, Germany
summary: A long valley town wedged between the Wiehen Hills and the Teutoburg Forest, where 56 villages were stitched into one of Lower Saxony's largest cities.

subject: Meller Möbelfabrik
summary: A small-town German furniture maker that sold a study to Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, changed its founders' surname to escape Nazi persecution, and left behind a quarter of Melle in clinker brick.

subject: Melo, Uruguay
summary: The capital of Cerro Largo - cattle country near the Brazilian border, birthplace of the beloved poet "Juana de América," holder of Uruguay's coldest temperature, and the unlikely setting of a famous film about a papal visit and a toilet.

subject: Melton Mowbray
summary: Britain's self-styled Rural Capital of Food, where pork pies are protected by EU law and Stilton has been crumbling for centuries.

story.title: Memphis: Where Elvis Lived, MLK Died, and the Blues Never Left

subject: Memphis
summary: The Tennessee river city where Sun Records launched rock and roll and the Lorraine Motel witnessed assassination - where Beale Street still swings, where barbecue is religion, and where music emerged from pain that hasn't entirely healed.

story.title: Memphis: Where the Blues Were Born and Elvis Came Home

subject: Memphis
summary: Tennessee's second-largest city where Beale Street created the blues, where Sun Studio launched Elvis and rock and roll, where Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated, where FedEx invented overnight shipping, and where the barbecue is dry-rubbed or wet-sauced but always serious.

subject: Menara (tree)
summary: The world's tallest tropical tree, a yellow meranti standing nearly 100 meters in Borneo's Danum Valley, confirmed by a climber with a tape measure in 2019.

subject: Mendi
summary: The capital of Papua New Guinea's Southern Highlands, a valley town of 56,000 at 1,675 meters elevation, shadowed by Mount Giluwe and rich in coffee, clan relationships, and hard-won traditions.

subject: Mendoza
summary: Argentina's wine capital, a desert city rebuilt after a catastrophic earthquake on a grid of wide avenues and irrigation canals, in the shadow of the highest peak in the Americas.

subject: Menelaion
summary: On a low hill above the Eurotas valley near Sparta, where Mycenaean palaces once stood and where Helen of Troy was said to have been born, successive generations of ancient Greeks built shrines to two of their most famous heroes — and archaeologists are still uncovering what they left behind.

subject: Mengenlehreuhr
summary: A seven-metre column of coloured lamps on Budapester Straße tells the time in blocks of five — and eleven letters of an unsolved CIA cipher point straight at it.

subject: Menil Collection
summary: A world-class art museum hidden in plain sight among gray bungalows in a quiet Houston neighborhood, where a Renzo Piano masterpiece houses Picasso, Rothko, and stolen Byzantine frescoes - all free to enter.

subject: Menindee, New South Wales
summary: On the banks of the Darling-Baaka in far western New South Wales, Menindee is the river town where Burke and Wills slept their last comfortable night before vanishing into the inland - and where, twice in five years, the river ran with millions of dead fish.

subject: Menno Colony
summary: The first Mennonite settlement in South America, carved out of the brutal Paraguayan Chaco by Canadian farmers who crossed an ocean to keep teaching their children in German.

subject: Menoken Indian Village Site
summary: A fortified village occupied around 1100-1300 CE near Bismarck, North Dakota, the Menoken site predates the well-known Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara cultures, preserving a mystery about who these early Plains dwellers actually were.

subject: Menokin
summary: The crumbling stone plantation of a Declaration of Independence signer, now being rebuilt with glass walls in one of the most audacious preservation projects in America.

subject: Meoto Iwa
summary: Two sea stacks off the coast of Ise, bound by a sacred shimenawa rope weighing over 200 kilograms, that have embodied the Shinto concept of divine marriage for centuries -- and on summer mornings, frame the rising sun with Mount Fuji hovering behind them.

story.title: Meow Wolf: House of Eternal Return

subject: Meow Wolf
summary: The Santa Fe art installation inside a converted bowling alley where visitors climb through a refrigerator into another dimension - funded by Game of Thrones author George R.R. Martin and now the most successful immersive art experience in America.

subject: Meppel
summary: A small Drenthe canal city whose own residents once mistook a swarm of mosquitoes for a church fire, and whose 17th-century peat harbor still feeds three-thousand-ton ships into the IJsselmeer.

subject: Meppen
summary: A medieval river town at the meeting of three waterways, with a Guinness-certified world map painted on a cooling tower and the largest weapons-testing range in Western Europe at its back door.

subject: Mercado Adolpho Lisboa
summary: An 1883 Art Nouveau market on the banks of the Rio Negro in Manaus, modeled on the old Les Halles of Paris, its iron frame shipped from Europe across the Atlantic.

subject: Mercado Central de Santiago
summary: Santiago's central market, where a Victorian iron roof shipped from Glasgow shelters a century and a half of fishmongers, eel, and the country's great seafood lunch.

subject: Mercado Central, Valencia
summary: One of Europe's largest markets, Valencia's Mercat Central is an Art Nouveau palace of iron, glass and coloured light where the city has done its daily shopping for nearly a century.

subject: Mercedes, Corrientes
summary: A cattle town in the Corrientes heartland, gateway to the Iberá wetlands and home to Argentina's most beloved folk saint.

subject: Merchant City
summary: Glasgow's first planned New Town, built on the wealth of the tobacco lords and reborn in the 1980s as a cultural quarter of restored Victorian warehouses, bars, and festivals.

story.title: Mercury Control Center: The Room That Launched America Into Space

subject: Mercury Control Center
summary: The modest three-row control room at Cape Canaveral where NASA guided America's first astronauts into orbit, tracked capsules across a global network of 18 stations, and proved that humans could work in space.

subject: Merlin diamond mine
summary: In the remote Gulf country of the Northern Territory lies the source of the largest diamond ever found in Australia - a mine that has opened, closed, and tantalised for two decades.

subject: Merpati Nusantara Airlines Flight 9760D
summary: A Twin Otter bound for Oksibil in August 2009 took a pilot's shortcut through valley haze toward a mountain the crew could not see.

subject: Merrie Monarch Festival
summary: The world's most prestigious hula competition, held each spring in Hilo, honoring the king who brought the forbidden dance back into public life and transforming a struggling town into the cultural capital of Hawaiian performance.

subject: Mersa Gawasis
summary: The desert harbor where pharaonic fleets were carried in pieces across 100 miles of sand, rebuilt on the shore, and launched toward the fabled Land of Punt.

story.title: Merv: The Silk Road City That Died Twice

subject: Merv
summary: Once possibly the largest city on Earth, this Silk Road oasis in Turkmenistan's Karakum Desert flourished under the Seljuks, attracted scholars like Omar Khayyam, and was annihilated by the Mongols in 1221 - leaving ruins that span 4,000 years of human civilization.

subject: Merv
summary: Once possibly the largest city on Earth, this Silk Road oasis in modern Turkmenistan flourished for five millennia before the Mongols opened its gates and ended its story in a single week.

story.title: Mesa Grande Band of Diegueno Mission Indians

subject: Mesa Grande Band of Diegueno Mission Indians
summary: The Mesa Grande Band of Diegueño Mission Indians is a federally recognized Iipay tribe on a reservation near Santa Ysabel in eastern San Diego County — established in 1875 on a mesa in the coastal mountain range, on land that has been Iipay homeland for millennia.

story.title: Mesa Verde: The Cities Built in Cliffs

subject: Mesa Verde
summary: The Colorado plateau where Ancestral Puebloans built elaborate stone cities in cliff alcoves 800 years ago - then abandoned them within a century, leaving mysteries that archaeologists and descendants still work to understand.

subject: Mesa Verde
summary: The cliff dwellings they left behind - where Ancestral Puebloans built elaborate stone cities in Colorado's canyon alcoves, lived for centuries, and then mysteriously abandoned everything around 1300 AD.

subject: Mesabi Range
summary: The Ojibwe called it 'Giant Mountain,' and they were not exaggerating -- the Mesabi Iron Range is the largest iron ore district in the United States, a 110-mile scar across northeastern Minnesota that built America's steel industry, enriched the Rockefellers, and transformed the Great Lakes into an industrial highway.

subject: Mese (Constantinople)
summary: The great colonnaded avenue of Byzantine Constantinople — 25 meters wide, lined with porticoed shops and imperial monuments — whose ancient course still pulses under the modern streets of Istanbul.

subject: Mesopotamian Marshes
summary: A vast wetland between the Tigris and Euphrates that Saddam Hussein drained as punishment for Shia resistance, and that nature and its people have been fighting to reclaim ever since.

subject: Messe Dusseldorf
summary: Every four years, the world's printing industry converges on a single fairground on the Rhine for Drupa. In between, the largest boat show on earth and the global medical-technology fair pass through the same halls.

subject: Messenia
summary: The fertile southwestern region of the Peloponnese, where olive groves and Byzantine castles share a landscape shaped by one of antiquity's most consequential struggles for freedom.

subject: Messenia (Ancient Region)
summary: The fertile southwestern district of the ancient Peloponnese, whose people Sparta enslaved as helots for three centuries — until Theban intervention ended one of the longest occupations in Greek history.

subject: Metal Open Air
summary: The three-day São Luís festival of April 2012 promised Brazil its own Wacken Open Air and delivered one of the worst disasters in Latin American live music.

subject: Metallurgical Laboratory
summary: The secret Chicago lab where scientists built the world's first nuclear reactor under a football stadium, launching the atomic age in a city that had no idea what was happening beneath its streets.

subject: Metamorfosi, Laconia
summary: A small Greek village that spent fifteen centuries named after a hole in the ground — the sinkhole created when a catastrophic earthquake swallowed a river whole in AD 375 — before finally renaming itself for resurrection.

story.title: Meteor Crater: The Hole That Proved Impacts Happen

subject: Meteor Crater
summary: The Arizona pit so perfectly preserved that scientists refused to believe it for decades - until one geologist proved the absurd truth that a 150-foot nickel-iron boulder had slammed into the desert at 26,000 miles per hour.

subject: Meteor Crater
summary: The hole that proved impact - where a 150-foot nickel-iron meteorite slammed into Arizona 50,000 years ago, creating a crater so perfect that Daniel Barringer spent 27 years digging for the main mass that had vaporized on impact.

story.title: Meteora: The Monasteries Built on Impossible Pillars

subject: Meteora
summary: Where Byzantine monks built 24 monasteries atop 1,000-foot sandstone pillars in central Greece - accessible only by rope ladders and nets hauled up cliff faces, in deliberate isolation from the world.

subject: Methana
summary: Methana is a volcanic peninsula jutting into the Saronic Gulf, where sulphur springs, ancient history, and the latent heat of the earth's crust have drawn visitors for three millennia.

story.title: Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel

subject: Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel
summary: Fifty meters beneath the suburbs of Tokyo, fifty-nine colossal pillars hold up a cathedral-like chamber that exists for one purpose: swallowing floodwater before it swallows the city above.

subject: Metropolitan Opera
summary: The largest classical music organization in North America, the Met has staged opera in New York City since 1883, moving from its gilded Broadway house to Lincoln Center in 1966.

subject: Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority
summary: The independent authority created by Virginia and D.C. in 1986 runs Reagan National and Dulles on a 50-year lease from the federal government - and now operates the Silver Line, the Dulles Toll Road, and its own police force.

subject: Mettmann
summary: In the summer of 1856, quarry workers at a limestone cave near Mettmann threw aside some old bones. Those bones turned out to be the first scientifically recognized Neanderthal, and rewrote what humans thought they were.

subject: Mexican Heritage Plaza
summary: A Chicano and Mexican-American cultural center in San Jose's Mayfair neighborhood where mosaic portraits of Carlos Santana, Los Tigres del Norte, and Linda Ronstadt guard the entrance.

subject: Meyer Werft
summary: A 230-year-old family shipyard in a Lower Saxon peat town builds some of the world's largest cruise liners indoors, then walks them stern-first down 36 kilometers of river too narrow to turn around in.

subject: Mezine
summary: On a quiet bank of the Desna River, Ice Age hunters left behind mammoth-bone houses and a carved ivory bird bearing what may be humanity's oldest known meander pattern.

subject: Mfuwe
summary: A one-road village in eastern Zambia where elephants raid after dark, the primary means of communication is radio, and the entire settlement exists because a national park full of leopards and lions lies just across the bridge.

story.title: Miami: The City Where Latin America Meets America

subject: Miami
summary: The Florida metropolis that's more Latin American than American in character - where Cuban exiles built a city within a city, where Art Deco hotels line South Beach, and where the sea is rising faster than the politicians admit.

subject: Miangas
summary: A tiny Indonesian island whose very name means 'exposed to piracy,' Miangas became the subject of a landmark international arbitration case that redrew colonial boundaries in the Pacific.

subject: Miaoli
summary: Miaoli is the cultural heartland of Taiwan's Hakka people, where a distinct language, cuisine, and way of life have endured for generations in the rolling hills of central Taiwan.

subject: Micanopy, Florida
summary: The oldest continuously inhabited community in interior Florida, where Seminole War battlefields, a Hollywood film set, and Tom Petty lyrics converge in a town of 648 people that calls itself 'The Town that Time Forgot.'

subject: Michael (parish)
summary: An Isle of Man parish where Bishops once held court, a French privateer was defeated nearby, and the Manx Tynwald may have first convened.

subject: Michael Healy (artist)
summary: Born in a Dublin tenement, trained at the Accademia in Florence, Michael Healy spent forty years at An Tur Gloine making some of the finest stained glass of the twentieth century.

subject: Michael Reardon (climber)
summary: An American free-solo climber who once made 1,000 solo ascents in 30 days, Michael Reardon was swept from a sea cliff at Dohilla on Valentia Island in July 2007.

subject: Michelham Priory
summary: An Augustinian priory founded in 1229 and surrounded by England's longest filled medieval moat, where a 15th-century gatehouse still guards a working watermill and eight acres of moated gardens.

subject: Michigan Central Station
summary: For thirty years the gutted shell of Detroit's grandest train station stared out over Roosevelt Park as the city's most photographed ruin - then Ford spent nearly a billion dollars putting it back together.

story.title: Michigan Central Station: Detroit's Phoenix in Beaux-Arts Stone

subject: Michigan Central Station
summary: The tallest rail station in the world when it opened in 1914, Michigan Central Station spent three decades as the most photographed ruin in America before Ford Motor Company poured over $740 million into bringing it back to life.

subject: Michigan Territory
summary: Before Michigan was a state, it was a diplomatic chess piece -- traded between France, Britain, and a fledgling republic that could not even deliver its own mail to Detroit.

subject: Mickey Marcus
summary: Born on Hester Street, a Brooklyn kid became a West Point graduate, gangster prosecutor, war planner, and Israel's first modern general -- killed by friendly fire hours before a ceasefire.

subject: Microsoft
summary: Two childhood friends from Seattle wrote a BASIC interpreter for a computer they had never touched, parlayed it into a software empire that put a PC on nearly every desk in the world, and built a Redmond campus so large it functions as its own small city.

subject: Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport
summary: A state-owned commercial spaceport on the southern tip of Wallops Island where Antares rockets carry Cygnus cargo modules to the International Space Station and Rocket Lab launches Electrons from a pad called Virginia is for Launch Lovers.

subject: Mid-Levels
summary: Halfway up Victoria Peak, Hong Kong's Mid-Levels has drawn the ambitious and the well-heeled for over 160 years — connected to the city below by the longest outdoor escalator in the world.

subject: Middelaldercentret
summary: A trebuchet built for a town's 700th birthday drew tens of thousands of visitors and was never taken down - it became the seed of Denmark's most uncompromising experiment in living medieval technology.

subject: Middelburg, Zeeland
summary: The 17th-century capital of Zeeland was, after Amsterdam, the second-most powerful chamber of the Dutch East India Company, the home of the spectacle-makers who may have invented both the telescope and the microscope, and the city Chaucer name-checked in the 1380s.

subject: Middelfart
summary: A Funen town at the narrowest point of the Little Belt that spent five centuries hunting porpoises for lamp oil, then became the hinge between Denmark's two halves.

subject: Midden-Groningen
summary: Twenty villages stitched into one municipality, sitting atop Europe's largest gas field, and quietly shaking from the consequences.

subject: Middle Road, Hong Kong
summary: A street in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, whose gentle curve traces the ghost of a vanished beach — and whose underground corridor now carries thousands of pedestrians a day.

subject: Middlesbrough
summary: An industrial port on the Tees that grew from a hamlet of 25 to a steel city in a single century, now reinventing itself after the heavy industries fell silent.

subject: Middlesbrough
summary: Once the steel capital that built the Sydney Harbour Bridge, Middlesbrough is a Tees-side town learning to live without the industries that made it.

subject: Middleton Place
summary: Home to the oldest landscaped gardens in America and birthplace of a Declaration of Independence signer, Middleton Place survived British ransacking, Union fire, and a devastating earthquake -- only the south flanker still stands along the Ashley River.

subject: Midleton
summary: A monastery at a weir became a Williamite plantation town, then a distillery town, and is now where Jameson, Powers and Paddy whiskeys are made - alongside a sculpture thanking the Choctaw Nation.

subject: Midnight Sun Film Festival
summary: Every June in the tiny Finnish town of Sodankyla, above the Arctic Circle, films screen around the clock while the sun never sets -- drawing legends like Coppola, Kiarostami, and Forman to one of cinema's most improbable gatherings.

subject: Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District
summary: A voter-created special district that has permanently preserved over 70,000 acres of foothills, baylands, and redwood forests across 26 preserves on the San Francisco Peninsula.

subject: Miedenmolen, Holwerd
summary: Built in 1855 to drain the Dwergsmear Polder, the Miedenmolen still lifts 1,667 litres of water per turn - the muscular cousin of Friesland's polder mills.

subject: Miguel Pereira
summary: A cool mountain getaway 150 km from Rio, where locals swear they have the third-best climate in the world and where Lake Javary's pedal boats have become the town's unofficial mascot.

story.title: Miharu Takizakura: The Thousand-Year Waterfall of Blossoms

subject: Miharu Takizakura
