summary: A single weeping cherry tree over a thousand years old draws 300,000 visitors each spring to the farming town of Miharu in Fukushima -- a living national treasure whose cascading pink blossoms have survived earthquakes, nuclear fears, and heavy snow.

subject: Miho funerary couch
summary: A sixth-century stone funerary couch from northern China that tells the story of a Sogdian nobleman through carved reliefs blending Zoroastrian, Turkic, and Chinese artistic traditions.

subject: Mikindani
summary: Once the most important port in southern Tanzania and the launching point for David Livingstone's final expedition, Mikindani has settled into a quiet second act as a fishing village where centuries of Swahili, Arab, German, and British history crumble photogenically in the salt air.

subject: Mikura-jima
summary: A tiny volcanic island south of Tokyo where two million streaked shearwaters nest in old-growth forests, dolphins patrol the surrounding waters, and one in ten residents descends from political exiles of the Tokugawa shogunate.

subject: Milagra Ridge
summary: A decommissioned coastal artillery battery turned island ecosystem, where endangered butterflies and garter snakes survive on a ridge between Pacifica and Daly City.

subject: Mile End, Montreal
summary: A crossroads tavern a mile north of 19th-century Montreal evolved through railway booms, immigrant waves, and a legendary bagel rivalry into the neighborhood that launched Arcade Fire and became Canada's indie-culture capital.

subject: Mileura Station
summary: A Murchison sheep station that became an unlikely cradle of science, hosting research into Earth's oldest minerals and the first site tests for the Square Kilometre Array.

subject: Milford Haven
summary: Founded in 1790 by Nantucket Quakers fleeing American taxes, Milford Haven planted a New England whaling colony on the Welsh coast - and has been navigating boom and bust ever since.

subject: Milford Haven Waterway
summary: A drowned valley flooded by the last ice age, Milford Haven became one of the world's deepest natural harbours - and the doorway through which kings, conquerors, refineries, and Qatari LNG tankers have all entered Wales.

subject: Milford Mine
summary: The site of Minnesota's worst mining disaster, where a flooded shaft killed 41 men on February 5, 1924, leaving behind more than 80 children and a community that still remembers.

subject: Milford Road
summary: New Zealand's most dramatic highway, carved through Fiordland's mountains by pick and shovel, threading 119 kilometres of ancient beech forest, mirror lakes, and avalanche country to reach the country's most famous fiord.

subject: Milford Sound
summary: A glacier-carved fiord at the edge of New Zealand's South Island where 6,400 mm of annual rain feeds hundreds of waterfalls down sheer cliff faces, and the Maori name Piopiotahi mourns an extinct bird that flew here in grief.

subject: Milford Track
summary: A 53.5 km trail through Fiordland that books out within minutes each year - four days of rainforest, avalanche chutes, and a 1,069-metre alpine pass, ending at the edge of New Zealand's most famous fiord.

subject: Military Sealift Command
summary: The Navy's quiet workhorse: civilian-crewed ships in haze gray paint with blue-and-gold stack bands, hauling 90 percent of the equipment America's military needs to fight overseas.

subject: Millbillillie Meteorite
summary: A fireball trailing sparks crossed the outback sky in October 1960, and a piece of the asteroid Vesta came to rest on the red dirt of a Western Australian cattle run.

subject: Mille Lacs Indian Reservation
summary: Established by the Treaty of Washington in 1855 and reaffirmed by federal courts as recently as 2022, the Mille Lacs Indian Reservation anchors a sovereign Ojibwe nation across 61,000 acres of central Minnesota lakeland.

subject: Millennium Dome
summary: Tony Blair called it a beacon to the world. The press called it a white elephant. Then a billionaire bought it, renamed it the O2, and turned it into one of the busiest entertainment venues on the planet.

subject: Miller Arcade
summary: A Preston dentist held a design competition in 1895 and got back a glass-roofed Victorian shopping arcade modelled on London's Burlington, complete with pepper-pot turrets and a Geisha Ballroom upstairs.

subject: Millisle
summary: An Ards Peninsula village best known for its eighteenth-century windmill and for sheltering Jewish children rescued from the Reich on a small farm called Magill's.

subject: Millom
summary: Built in a hurry around the Hodbarrow iron mines in the 1860s, Millom grew to 11,000 people, lost its ironworks in 1968, and survives as the lifelong home of poet Norman Nicholson and the oldest amateur rugby league club in the world.

subject: Millungera Station
summary: A million-acre cattle run in Queensland's Gulf Country, where mitchell-grass plains, flooding rivers, and 160 years of pastoral survival meet under an enormous tropical sky.

subject: Millwood, South Africa
summary: A gold rush town that flared to life in the indigenous forests near Knysna, drew fortune-seekers from three continents, and collapsed within five years -- leaving a ghost town in the trees.

subject: Milly Milly
summary: A vast sheep station on the Murchison River whose history runs through pioneers, floods, drought, two unsolved deaths, and a stallion bred from a Melbourne Cup champion.

subject: Milos
summary: Milos is a volcanic Cycladic island whose obsidian-rich shores fed the ancient Aegean world, whose soil yielded the Venus de Milo, and whose lunar-white beaches and mineral-painted cliffs draw visitors from across the globe.

subject: Milton Blockhouse
summary: The forgotten twin of Gravesend Blockhouse, built on a dissolved chantry's field, demolished after just eighteen years and ground over by a Victorian canal basin.

subject: Milton Keynes
summary: A city most people pass through without stopping - and the visitors who actually get out and look around discover concrete cows, world-changing codebreakers, and pubs called The Cock & Bull.

subject: Milton Keynes
summary: The most ambitious experiment in British urban planning - a city designed from scratch on twenty-two thousand acres of Buckinghamshire farmland, built grid square by grid square, and still arguing about whether it worked.

story.title: Milwaukee: The Beer City That Sobered Up and Found Itself

subject: Milwaukee
summary: The Wisconsin lakefront city where German brewers built empires and cheese curds come fried - where the Fonz stands in bronze, where Harley-Davidsons are still assembled, and where the drinking culture survived the brewery consolidations.

story.title: Milwaukee: The Beer City That Built America's Beverage

subject: Milwaukee
summary: The city where German immigrants invented America's brewing industry, where Pabst, Schlitz, and Miller once dominated, and where the Calatrava-designed Art Museum now defines the lakefront.

subject: Min Ping Yu No. 5540 Incident
summary: On July 21–22, 1990, twenty-five people from Fujian suffocated in the sealed hold of a fishing boat while being repatriated by Taiwan authorities — a tragedy that forced both sides of the strait to reckon with the human cost of policies that treated people as a security problem.

subject: Mina Clavero
summary: A mountain town with river beaches, a saint's road, and a rally legend - the gateway to Córdoba's Traslasierra valley.

subject: Mina, Saudi Arabia
summary: Eight kilometers southeast of Mecca lies the largest tent city in the world: 100,000 fireproof tents that house millions of Hajj pilgrims for five days a year and then stand empty until the next season.

subject: Minahasa Regency
summary: An Indonesian regency whose founding date was reverse-engineered from a national hero's birthday and a famous congress, Minahasa blends volcanic highlands, Dutch colonial history, and tribal alliances centuries old.

subject: Minas
summary: An inland town cradled by hills, birthplace of an independence hero and source of the water that the whole country drinks.

subject: Minas Gerais
summary: General Mines. The Brazilian state where a dentist led a revolution, where the cuisine is rich enough to be a religion, and where the mineiro accent turns train into thing and why into a form of punctuation.

subject: Minas Gerais
summary: Brazil's fourth-largest state by area, second-largest by population, and first in mines. Home to 20 million mineiros, more baroque churches than anyone has counted, and a state flag whose Latin motto means liberty though it be delayed.

subject: Minas Novas
summary: A gold town founded by accident in 1730 when a bandeirante took a wrong turn. Three centuries later its Baroque wattle-and-daub Sobradao still stands, four stories tall, on a hill in the Jequitinhonha backlands.

subject: Minas de Corrales
summary: Gold fever built this small Uruguayan town in the 1870s, and to chase it, European engineers raised what is remembered as South America's first hydroelectric dam.

subject: Minaçu
summary: A Goias town built on two things the rest of the world is walking away from - asbestos and a river dam.

subject: Minden
summary: A cathedral town on the Weser that Prussia fortified so thoroughly it could not grow for sixty years, and where an astronomer's son learned to look up.

subject: Minden, West Virginia
summary: A coal village along Arbuckle Creek where decades of PCB contamination have left residents fighting both cancer and bureaucracy - a story documented in the film Impossible Town.

subject: Mindo
summary: A cloud forest town two hours from Quito, home to 450 bird species and one of the planet's densest concentrations of hummingbirds.

subject: Mine Howe
summary: An Iron Age underground chamber dug six metres into an Orkney mound, rediscovered by a farmer in 1999, with twenty-nine drystone steps descending into the dark.

subject: Minehead Lifeboat Station
summary: A small stone boathouse on the Somerset coast that has been launching volunteers into the Bristol Channel since 1901 - and where two men died in 1941 going out to check what turned out to be a German mine.

subject: Mineiros
summary: A westernmost-in-Goiás farm town named for the explorers from Minas Gerais who settled here in 1873, now a gateway to one of Latin America's most biodiverse cerrado reserves.

subject: Mineirão
summary: Belo Horizonte's Pampulha Giant - a false ellipse of concrete built in eight months of round-the-clock shifts, where Germany put seven goals past Brazil in the worst 90 minutes of Brazilian football history.

subject: Mines of Laurion
summary: The silver mines that bankrolled the Athenian Golden Age were worked by tens of thousands of enslaved people in brutal, lethal conditions — a debt of suffering that the marble city above rarely acknowledged.

subject: Minesto
summary: A Swedish company that spun out of Saab's wind division and built tidal turbines shaped like underwater kites, flown in figure-eight loops through the currents of the Holyhead Deep.

subject: Ming tombs
summary: Thirteen Ming dynasty emperors rest in a feng shui-chosen valley north of Beijing, guarded by a seven-kilometer Spirit Way lined with larger-than-life stone guardians.

subject: Mingo County, West Virginia
summary: West Virginia's youngest county, carved from secessionist Logan County in 1895, holds the Tug Fork border with Kentucky, the town of Matewan, and a labor and political history as steep as its hills.

subject: Mingo Oak
summary: For roughly 582 years the world's largest and oldest white oak stood in a Mingo County cove until the sulfur fumes of a burning coal spoil tip killed it in 1938.

subject: Mingulay
summary: The Lost Island. Two thousand years of continuous habitation ended in 1912, when the last Gaelic-speaking residents of Mingulay carried what they could to the boats and left for the mainland.

subject: Mingun Bell
summary: Cast in 1808 from an alloy of five metals and weighing over 90 tons, the Mingun Bell held the title of world's largest ringing bell for nearly two centuries.

subject: Miniatur Wunderland
summary: Two brick warehouses in Hamburg's Speicherstadt hold more than sixteen kilometres of model railway, roughly 290,000 tiny people, and a night that falls every fifteen minutes.

subject: Mining in Papua New Guinea
summary: A nation of extraordinary mineral wealth and extraordinary cost - where the rivers have been poisoned, the landowners have sometimes won, and the question of who benefits has never been settled.

subject: Ministry of Migration and Asylum
summary: Greece's Ministry of Migration and Asylum, headquartered in the Agios Ioannis Rentis district of western Athens, manages one of Europe's most complex migration challenges — processing asylum claims, receiving arrivals, and protecting unaccompanied children, all at the edge of the EU's external border.

subject: Minka
summary: Japan's vernacular folk houses, built for farmers, artisans, and merchants across centuries, showcase eight distinct structural forms and regional adaptations to climate that range from bamboo-clad Shizuoka dwellings to the towering prayer-hand roofs of Gifu.

story.title: Minneapolis: The City That Turned Flour Into Fortune

subject: Minneapolis
summary: The Minnesota metropolis built on milling and Scandinavian determination - where waterfalls powered industry, where skyways connect buildings so you never face winter, and where a murder sparked global protests.

story.title: Minneapolis: City of Lakes Where Prince Was King

subject: Minneapolis
summary: Minnesota's largest city where 13 lakes lie within city limits, where Prince created his Minneapolis Sound, where flour mills made it 'Mill City,' and where 11 miles of skyways let you walk all winter without ever going outside.

subject: Minoan palaces
summary: Across Bronze Age Crete, six massive courtyard buildings shaped a civilization that wrote in scripts we still cannot read and vanished in fires we cannot fully explain.

subject: Minsener Oog
summary: A North Sea island that humans built on purpose - twice - to keep the channel to Wilhelmshaven open.

subject: Minsk
summary: The capital of Belarus, rebuilt from rubble after 80 percent of the city was destroyed in World War II, Minsk today is a Soviet-monumental capital of about two million people, governed since 1994 under the authoritarian rule of Alexander Lukashenko.

subject: Minsk Ghetto
summary: One of the largest Nazi ghettos and the largest in the occupied Soviet Union, the Minsk Ghetto held close to 100,000 Jews; most were murdered, but roughly 10,000 escaped to the partisans - the highest rate of escape from any ghetto in occupied Europe.

subject: Minton's Playhouse
summary: The Harlem jazz club where bebop was born in late-night jam sessions that rewrote the rules of American music.

subject: Miquel Capllonch Rotger
summary: A fisherman's town on Mallorca's northern shore sent one of its sons to the courts of Berlin, and welcomed him home with a bronze bust in the square.

subject: Mir Ghetto
summary: A Nazi ghetto in the small Belarusian shtetl of Mir, where roughly 2,900 of the 3,000 Jewish inhabitants were murdered between 1941 and 1942 - and where Oswald Rufeisen, infiltrating the local police as a Wehrmacht translator, warned the ghetto in time for hundreds to escape into the partisan forests.

subject: Mir Jumla's invasion of Assam
summary: The Mughal Empire's most ambitious push into northeast India seized the Ahom capital in 1662 but ended in retreat, disease, and a treaty that dissolved within four years.

subject: Miracle Mile, Los Angeles
summary: In the 1920s, a real estate developer named A.W. Ross reimagined a stretch of Wilshire Boulevard as the world's first car-oriented commercial street — complete with parking lots, timed traffic signals, and storefronts engineered to be read at 30 miles per hour. He called it the Miracle Mile, and it changed how cities thought about the automobile.

subject: Mirassou Winery
summary: Founded in 1854 by French immigrants in what would become Silicon Valley, the Mirassou Winery endured six generations before the land was sold and the vineyards paved over for housing developments.

subject: Mirbat
summary: A quiet Omani fishing town that was once the capital of Dhofar and the site of a dramatic 1972 battle that helped turn the tide of a Cold War insurgency.

subject: Miri
summary: A Bornean fishing village that struck oil in 1910 and transformed into Sarawak's second-largest city, gateway to the oldest human remains in Southeast Asia and four national parks.

subject: Misfat al Abriyeen
summary: A 2,000-year-old village perched on a rock in the Western Hajar mountains, where an ancient falaj irrigation system still feeds terraced gardens of mangoes, pomegranates, and figs.

subject: Mishima Taisha
summary: The paramount Shinto shrine of ancient Izu Province, where a wandering deity came to rest after island-hopping across the volcanic chain, where samurai prayed for victory before battle, and where a 1,200-year-old osmanthus tree still perfumes the autumn air.

subject: Mishmi Hills
summary: Where the Himalayas make a sharp turn to meet the Indo-Burma ranges, the Mishmi Hills shelter one of Asia's richest and least-explored biodiversity hotspots.

story.title: Misión San Fernando Rey de España de Velicatá

subject: Misión San Fernando Rey de España de Velicatá
summary: The only Franciscan mission ever founded in Baja California, established by Junípero Serra on Pentecost Day 1769 as the launching point for Spain's push into Alta California.

story.title: Misión San Pedro Mártir de Verona

subject: Misión San Pedro Mártir de Verona
summary: A Dominican mission founded high in the Sierra de San Pedro Mártir in 1794 to bring the independent Kiliwa people within the mission system — and abandoned within a generation.

story.title: Misión Santa María de los Ángeles

subject: Misión Santa María de los Ángeles
summary: The last mission the Jesuits ever founded in Baja California, established in 1767 just months before the entire order was expelled from New Spain.

story.title: Mision Santa Rosa de las Palmas

subject: Misión Santa Rosa de las Palmas
summary: A Jesuit mission in Baja California where European ambition collided with indigenous resistance, disease, and the slow erasure of the Guaycura people.

story.title: Mision de Nuestra Senora de Loreto Concho

subject: Misión de Nuestra Señora de Loreto Conchó
summary: The first successful Spanish mission in Baja California, founded in 1697 on a patch of stunted shrubbery beside the only freshwater spring for miles, launched an enterprise that would eventually reach San Francisco Bay.

subject: Misool
summary: One of the four great islands of Raja Ampat, Misool sits at the heart of the Coral Triangle, where sultanates once competed for influence and reefs still hold the richest marine biodiversity on Earth.

subject: Miss Macao
summary: On 16 July 1948, four men boarded a Cathay Pacific–owned seaplane operated by Macau Air Transport Company on what should have been a routine 20-minute flight from Macau to Hong Kong — and changed the history of aviation by committing the world's first hijacking of a commercial aircraft.

subject: Mission Estate Winery
summary: New Zealand's oldest surviving winery began in 1851 when French Marist missionaries planted vines in Hawke's Bay to make sacramental wine, and has been producing ever since.

story.title: Mission Puerto de la Purísima Concepción

subject: Mission Puerto de la Purísima Concepción
summary: A Spanish mission established in Quechan territory in October 1780 that lasted less than a year before the Quechan people — their lands seized and their crops consumed by Spanish livestock — rose up and destroyed it, killing Father Francisco Garcés and more than a hundred colonists.

subject: Mission San Buenaventura
summary: The ninth and final mission founded by Junipero Serra, San Buenaventura has endured fires, earthquakes, pirates, and wars across nearly 250 years of continuous worship.

story.title: Mission San Fernando Rey de Espana

subject: Mission San Fernando Rey de EspaÃ±a
summary: The seventeenth California mission, founded in 1797, survived secularization, earthquakes, and a stint as a hog farm to become the namesake of the San Fernando Valley.

story.title: Mission San Fernando Rey de España

subject: Mission San Fernando Rey de España
summary: Founded September 8, 1797 as the seventeenth of twenty-one Alta California missions, Mission San Fernando sits on land the Tongva called Achooykomenga — a place where thousands of Indigenous people lived and died under the mission system before secularization, earthquakes, neglect, and restoration successively remade it across two centuries.

subject: Mission San Francisco Solano
summary: The 21st and final California mission, built after Mexican independence as a strategic bulwark against Russian expansion.

subject: Mission San Francisco de AsÃ­s
summary: The oldest intact structure in San Francisco, this 1791 adobe chapel and its 1918 basilica stand as the city's founding site, where Ohlone hands shaped 36,000 bricks and Spanish missionaries named a city.

subject: Mission San José de Tumacácori
summary: A weathered Spanish mission in southern Arizona whose roofless walls have witnessed Jesuit founders expelled by royal decree, O'odham farmers granted then betrayed of their land, and Apache raids that finally emptied its congregation in 1848.

subject: Mission, British Columbia
summary: A Fraser Valley city built on cedar and hydroelectricity, holding a five-thousand-year-old Stó:lo village site, a modernist Benedictine abbey, and a name it inherited from a residential school.

subject: Missoula
summary: Montana's most unconventional city where you can take a city bus to wilderness, climb to the M overlooking town, then soak in natural hot springs an hour away.

subject: Mitchell Caverns
summary: The only limestone caves in the California State Park system, set at 4,300 feet in the Providence Mountains, where the Chemehuevi called them 'eyes of the mountain,' a couple ran them as a Route 66 tourist stop for twenty years, and Shasta ground sloth remains were found inside.

subject: Mitchell County, North Carolina
summary: The Mineral City of the World, home to Penland School of Craft and the world's largest natural rhododendron garden, named for the professor who fell to his death proving Mount Mitchell was the tallest peak in the East.

subject: Mither Tap Hillfort
summary: A Pictish stronghold on a granite outcrop above Aberdeenshire, possibly the royal seat of the lost kingdom of Ce and a candidate for the site of Tacitus's Mons Graupius.

subject: Mithymna
summary: A Genoese-castled town tumbling down a green hillside to the sea on the north coast of Lesbos, where stone mansions and a tangled bazaar street recall its long centuries as the island's proud second city.

subject: Miyake-jima
summary: A volcanic island southeast of Tokyo where residents once carried gas masks daily, Miyake-jima has erupted 13 times in 890 years and hosts rare bird species found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Mo Tat
summary: Three villages on a quiet spur of Lamma Island, facing Aberdeen across the water — a place where fewer than 40 permanent residents have chosen to stay precisely because the world hasn't followed them here.

story.title: Moab: Where Red Rock Became the Adventure Capital

subject: Moab
summary: The Utah town between Arches and Canyonlands that transformed from uranium bust to adventure boom - where slickrock became the proving ground for mountain biking, where the Colorado carves through red towers, and where too much love threatens to love the desert to death.

story.title: Moba, Democratic Republic of the Congo

subject: Moba, Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary: On a narrow shelf between Lake Tanganyika and the Marungu highlands, the Tabwa town of Moba endures in a region soldiers once called the Triangle of Death.

story.title: Mobile: The Port City Where Mardi Gras Actually Began

subject: Mobile
summary: The Alabama port city older than New Orleans - where Mardi Gras started before spreading to Louisiana, where the azaleas bloom in antebellum gardens, and where the Gulf Coast shipbuilding tradition persists.

story.title: Mobile: Where Mardi Gras Began in America

subject: Mobile
summary: The Alabama port city founded as the capital of French Louisiana in 1702, where America's first Mardi Gras celebration predates New Orleans by 15 years, and where the Battle of Mobile Bay gave Admiral Farragut his famous battle cry.

subject: Mochrum
summary: A 22,000-acre Galloway parish whose Cumbric name translates as 'pig ridge' and whose fields hide one of the oldest settlements in Scotland.

subject: Moclips, Washington
summary: Once a booming beach resort town with a 270-room hotel that loomed from the dunes, Moclips was washed away by storms, burned by fire, and reduced to 211 residents -- but its Quinault name endures, and so does a surprising connection to grunge rock.

subject: Modbury
summary: A small Devon town with a Domesday-era market charter, a steam-pump inventor, and the woman who taught Elizabeth I to read.

subject: Model Housing Estate
summary: Hong Kong's oldest surviving public housing estate, built between 1951 and 1953 by a voluntary organisation — not the government — and still occupied today, with a mystery at its heart: in 1979, the manager disappeared.

subject: Modelo Market
summary: A busy handicraft market in Salvador's Comércio district, housed in a 19th-century customs house whose flood-prone basement is widely remembered as a place where enslaved Africans were held upon arrival in Bahia.

story.title: Modern Buildings on Zhongshan Square in Dalian

subject: Modern Buildings on Zhongshan Square in Dalian
summary: Ten buildings encircle a round plaza in Dalian, each one a former Japanese colonial institution now housing Chinese banks and offices, forming a miniature Bund.

subject: Modern history of Knossos
summary: Knossos was rediscovered twice: once by a Cretan merchant the Ottomans imprisoned, and again by an English heir who poured his fortune into rebuilding what he thought he saw.

subject: Modernist architecture of Kaunas
summary: Between 1919 and 1940, when Kaunas served as Lithuania's temporary capital, roughly 12,000 modernist buildings transformed a Russified fortress town into a Bauhaus-influenced European capital - work that UNESCO inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2023 as 'Modernist Kaunas: Architecture of Optimism.'

subject: Moelfre, Anglesey
summary: A fishing village on Anglesey's east coast whose lifeboat crews, in two storms a century apart, performed two of the most celebrated rescues in RNLI history.

subject: Moeraki Boulders
summary: Giant spherical concretions that took millions of years to form on a Paleocene seafloor, now scattered across a New Zealand beach where Maori tradition sees the cargo of a wrecked voyaging canoe.

subject: Moerdijk
summary: A village of 1,205 people whose bridges are so famous the Dutch use the place name as shorthand for the entire country to its north.

story.title: Mogadishu: Four Thousand Years on the Horn of Africa

subject: Mogadishu
summary: One of Africa's oldest continuously inhabited cities, where medieval merchants traded gold and ivory with the kingdoms of Arabia and India, where Italian colonists laid boulevards over ancient quarters, and where decades of civil war have not extinguished one of the continent's most resilient urban cultures.

subject: Moghalmari
summary: Beneath a village mound in West Bengal, archaeologists have unearthed a Buddhist monastery complex dating from the 6th to 12th century -- a place the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang may have visited fourteen centuries ago.

subject: Mogi Mirim
summary: A bandeirante waystation named for a small river of snakes, now an auto-parts town in São Paulo's interior — and the club where Rivaldo returned at 43 to play alongside his son.

subject: Mogilev Ghetto
summary: A Nazi ghetto in eastern Belarus established in August 1941, the Mogilev Ghetto held the city's prewar Jewish community of nearly 20,000; about 10,000 were murdered, most in the second half of 1941 by units of the Einsatzgruppen, Sicherheitsdienst, and Belarusian Auxiliary Police.

subject: Mohsen Fakhrizadeh
summary: The quiet Tehran suburb of Absard became the site of one of the most technologically sophisticated assassinations in history when Iran's top nuclear scientist was killed by a remote-controlled weapon in November 2020.

subject: Moidart
summary: An almost-island peninsula in the Scottish Rough Bounds, road-free until 1966, where Catholicism, Gaelic, and a Norse name meaning 'muddy loch' all survived together through three centuries of isolation.

subject: Moisés Ville
summary: On the Santa Fe pampas stands the first Jewish farming colony in South America, founded by refugees who buried their children before they ever broke the soil.

subject: Mojeños
summary: The Mojeños are an Arawak-descended people of Bolivia's Beni Department whose ancestors engineered thousands of artificial hills and hydraulic systems across the Amazon lowlands centuries before European contact.

subject: Mokha
summary: The Yemeni port that gave its name to mocha coffee, built a five-hundred-year trade, and then watched the world move on.

subject: Moldavanka
summary: A working-class Odesa neighborhood older than the city itself, immortalized by Isaac Babel as the raffish heart of Jewish Odesa and its legendary underworld.

subject: Mole Hill
summary: A 1,893-foot wooded knob west of Harrisonburg that is, geologically, one of the youngest volcanoes on the East Coast of North America - extinct for 47 million years.

subject: Molenbeek-Saint-Jean
summary: A Brussels canal commune named after a millstream - Riffian Moroccan in the lower town, Art Deco in the upper, and ninety-eight thousand people who would like the world to remember the rest of their story.

subject: Molenbeek-Ter Erpenbeek
summary: A modest 25-kilometer Flemish brook whose banks once powered eight water mills, most of them still standing - a small drainage carrying the name of a vanished labor.

subject: Molly Maguires Region
summary: Where miners hanged for fighting back - the Pennsylvania coal region where Irish immigrant workers were executed in the 1870s for alleged terrorism, in trials orchestrated by mine owners using Pinkerton spies.

subject: Molo, Iloilo City
summary: Called the 'Athens of the Philippines' for producing an extraordinary concentration of chief justices, senators, and revolutionary generals, Molo began as a Chinese Chinatown in 1637 - and even its name is a mispronunciation.

subject: Molokaʻi
summary: The most Hawaiian of the Hawaiian Islands, where residents chose subsistence and tradition over tourism and development, and where the world's highest sea cliffs guard a history of exile, devotion, and resilience.

subject: Molokini
summary: A crescent-shaped volcanic crater rising from the channel between Maui and Kahoolawe, Molokini shelters 250 marine species inside its natural breakwater and carries the scars of World War II target practice on its outer rim.

subject: Moltkeviertel
summary: An entire neighbourhood of mansions and garden streets planned as a single artwork on the eve of the First World War, then preserved by its descendants for a century.

subject: Mompiche
summary: A small Pacific beach town in Ecuador's Esmeraldas province where black iron-titanium sand, artisanal fishing, and a thin tourism economy coexist in uneasy balance.

subject: Mona Mona Aboriginal Mission
summary: A mission in the rainforest near Kuranda where Aboriginal families were gathered against their will, closed in 1962 and scattered, yet never wholly let go.

subject: Monaco
summary: A sovereign city-state smaller than Central Park - where Formula 1 cars race through casino-lined streets, superyachts crowd the harbor, and the world's wealthiest residents enjoy the world's most favorable tax regime.

subject: Monaco Grand Prix
summary: The world's most prestigious Formula One race, threaded through Monaco's streets since 1929, where glamour meets punishing hairpins and the harbor waits for anyone who gets it wrong.

subject: Monadhliath Mountains
summary: The grey mountain range west of the Cairngorms — an ancient, rounded moorland plateau with four Munros and a remote, sinuous river valley running through its centre.

subject: Monasterevin
summary: The Venice of Ireland - a Kildare town of bridges, aqueducts, and a sixth-century saint with the political instincts of a modern spin doctor.

subject: Monchengladbach
summary: The only German city with two main railway stations both called Hauptbahnhof, where a postmodern museum on an abbey hill watches over a football town built on cotton and beer.

subject: Monemvasia
summary: The "Gibraltar of the East" — a fortress-town clinging to a great sea-rock by a single causeway, birthplace of the poet Yannis Ritsos and source of a wine that gave its name to courts across medieval Europe.

subject: Mong Kok
summary: Once named for its ferns, now named for its prosperity — the densest neighbourhood on Earth by one measure, a maze of specialist markets, tong-lau shophouses, and the kind of street-level intensity that Hong Kong cinema has returned to again and again.

subject: Mong La
summary: A remote village that reinvented itself as the Golden Triangle's answer to Las Vegas, Mong La sits on the Myanmar-China border -- a town that runs on Chinese electricity, Chinese currency, and trades in everything from casino chips to pangolin scales.

subject: Moniaive
summary: A festival village on the Cairn Water where Covenanters once hid, Glasgow Boys painted, and four Andy Goldsworthy arches stride across the hills.

subject: Monkey Jungle
summary: At this South Florida wildlife park, humans walk through caged tunnels while 300 primates roam free overhead -- a concept born in 1933 when the monkeys kept attacking the guests.

subject: Monkey Mia
summary: On a shallow beach in Shark Bay, wild dolphins have swum into the laps of waves to meet people for generations, turning a remote pearling camp into one of the world's great windows onto the minds of another species.

subject: Monkey Selfie Copyright Dispute
summary: A macaque in a Sulawesi nature reserve pressed a shutter button in 2011, and the resulting grin launched a seven-year legal battle that redefined who -- or what -- can own a photograph.

subject: Monkwearmouth
summary: The north bank of the Wear has been a centre of learning, glassmaking, shipbuilding, and now glass-roofed reinvention since the monks arrived in 674.

subject: Monmouth
summary: A small Welsh market town that gave its name to a king, a county, a hat, and Charles Rolls, anchored by Britain's only surviving medieval fortified bridge.

subject: Monowi
summary: The Nebraska town where Elsie Eiler serves as mayor, clerk, and sole taxpayer - granting herself a liquor license, holding elections where she is the only candidate, and maintaining America's smallest incorporated municipality out of pure stubbornness.

subject: Monroe County, West Virginia
summary: A rural West Virginia county whose claims to fame include the largest alluvial diamond in North America, the birth of American paleontology, and the nation's first federal women's prison.

story.title: Monroeville Mall: Where Zombies Conquered America

subject: Monroeville Mall
summary: The Pennsylvania shopping center where George Romero filmed 'Dawn of the Dead' in 1978 - turning a suburban mall into horror-movie history, creating the zombie-apocalypse-in-consumer-spaces genre, and leaving fans making pilgrimages to buy sneakers where the undead once shuffled.

subject: Monroeville, Alabama
summary: A small Alabama county seat where two childhood neighbors -- Harper Lee and Truman Capote -- grew up to become two of the most celebrated American writers of the 20th century, leaving a literary legacy that draws 30,000 visitors a year to a town of fewer than 6,000 people.

subject: Monsaraz
summary: A hilltop village above the Guadiana River in Portugal's Alentejo where megalithic monuments, Roman roads, Visigoth traces, and a medieval castle compress five thousand years of habitation into a parish of fewer than 800 people.

subject: Monserrat, Buenos Aires
summary: Buenos Aires began on these muddy shores in 1580, and Monserrat has kept the city's oldest streets, its first church, and the plaza where a nation declared itself free.

subject: Mont-Sainte-Anne
summary: A Laurentian mountain northeast of Quebec City where volunteers hand-cut the first ski trail in 1943, now home to 71 runs, the tallest night-skiing vertical in Canada, and the country's largest cross-country ski network.

story.title: Montagne des Francais: Where Baobabs Guard a Colonial Ruin

subject: Montagne des Français
summary: A karst mountain overlooking Diego Suarez Bay in northern Madagascar, where some of the world's rarest trees grow among French colonial fortifications and an extraordinary density of endemic species found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Montagu
summary: A small Western Cape town where over 400 rock climbing routes scale the surrounding mountains, hot mineral springs steam in the valley below, and Route 62 leads onward into the Klein Karoo.

story.title: Montara State Marine Reserve and Pillar Point State Marine Conservation Area

subject: Montara State Marine Reserve and Pillar Point State Marine Conservation Area
summary: An 18-square-mile underwater park off the San Mateo coast, designed by local divers, fishermen, and scientists to protect six species found nowhere else in the world.

subject: Montara oil spill
summary: For 74 days in 2009, oil and gas gushed from an uncontrolled well in the Timor Sea off northern Australia — spreading across 6,000 square kilometres of ocean, killing marine life, and setting off a political dispute between Australia and Indonesia that lingered for years.

subject: Montañita
summary: A village on Ecuador's Pacific coast that went from fishing huts to international surf-and-party destination in roughly two decades.

subject: Montañita
summary: A cluster of fishermen's huts on Ecuador's Pacific coast became an international surf capital when foreigners arrived in 1960 and never left.

subject: Montblanc
summary: A walled medieval town in inland Catalonia that claims to be where Saint George slew the dragon, ringed by 14th-century ramparts and crowned by an unfinished Gothic cathedral.

subject: Monte Alegre de Goiás
summary: A poor Goias municipality with fifty caves, nine rivers, and a Kalunga quilombo community whose ancestors escaped enslavement.

subject: Monte Arabí
summary: A lone limestone mountain above the vineyards of Yecla, marked with ten thousand years of rock art, foot-shaped carvings and prehistoric shrines.

subject: Monte Bello Open Space Preserve
summary: Named 'beautiful mountain' by Italian winemakers who settled its slopes, this 3,100-acre preserve sits atop the San Andreas Fault rift valley and once harbored a commune of 100 people.

subject: Monte Dourado
summary: A planned company town on the Jari River, built from 1967 for Daniel K. Ludwig's attempt to turn a piece of the Amazon the size of a small country into the world's pulp supply - a venture whose pulp mill arrived from Japan already assembled, floating.

subject: Monte Pissis
summary: The world's second-tallest volcano and third-highest peak in the Western Hemisphere stands in the Atacama Desert, so dry it holds no permanent glacier yet so massive it was climbed only twice in its first fifty years of mountaineering history.

subject: Monte Verde
summary: A creek-side bog in southern Chile preserved the campsite of people who lived here roughly 14,500 years ago—and in doing so, overturned everything science thought it knew about who first reached the Americas.

story.title: Monterrey: Mexico's Industrial Capital Where Mountains Meet Money

subject: Monterrey
summary: The Nuevo León capital where Mexican industry was born and billionaires are made - where dramatic mountains frame a city of factories and corporate headquarters, where NAFTA made fortunes, and where the work ethic resembles Texas more than Mexico City.

subject: Montes Claros
summary: The capital of northern Minas Gerais sits on a fault that never fully stops moving, above a cave system with its own underground river, in a sertão that grew a city out of a 1707 cattle grant.

subject: Montes Claros de Goiás
summary: A 1956 settlement in the far west of Goias where one farmer's donated land became a town.

subject: Monteverde
summary: A community in Costa Rica's cloud forest founded by American Quaker pacifists who left Alabama in 1950 rather than submit to military service, Monteverde became one of the world's great ecotourism destinations -- home to 500 orchid species and the extinct golden toad.

subject: Montevideo
summary: Where Uruguay's capital holds half the nation on the Rio de la Plata, where tango was born alongside Buenos Aires, where South America's most progressive society quietly thrives.

story.title: Montgomery: Where Rosa Parks Sat Down and the Confederacy Stood Up

subject: Montgomery
summary: Alabama's capital where the Confederacy was born and the civil rights movement took flight, where Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, where Martin Luther King Jr. launched the bus boycott, and where the Selma marchers finally arrived.

subject: Montgó Massif
summary: A 753-metre limestone giant shaped like an elephant, guarding the Marina Alta coast with a botanical treasury found almost nowhere else on Earth.

story.title: Monticello: The Town Beneath the Water

subject: Monticello
summary: A small California farming town that was deliberately drowned in the 1950s to create Lake Berryessa, documented in its final days by photographer Dorothea Lange.

story.title: Monticello: The Genius Estate Built on Contradiction

subject: Monticello
summary: The Virginia mountaintop where Thomas Jefferson designed his ideal home while owning over 600 enslaved people - where architectural innovation met moral failure, where the author of 'all men are created equal' kept Sally Hemings in bondage, and where America's founding hypocrisy is made visible.

subject: Montjuïc
summary: The broad hill over Barcelona's harbour where the city was born, quarried, fortified, executed upon, and finally crowned with Olympic glory.

subject: Montjuïc circuit
summary: A breathtaking street circuit threaded through Barcelona's parkland, remembered for beauty, danger, and the only World Championship points ever scored by a woman.

subject: Montpelier (Orange, Virginia)
summary: James Madison's Virginia plantation tells the intertwined stories of a Founding Father's constitutional vision, the enslaved community whose labor sustained it, and a landmark reckoning with shared governance.

story.title: Montreal: The French City That's Not Quite France

subject: Montreal
summary: The Quebec metropolis where French is defended by law and joie de vivre survives the winter - where bagels are better than New York's, where underground tunnels make -20°C bearable, and where the separatist question never quite dies.

story.title: Montreal Central Station: The Invisible Hub Beneath the City

subject: Montreal Central Station
summary: Nearly 11 million passengers a year pass through a train station that is almost invisible from the street -- swallowed over the decades by skyscrapers, hotels, and the underground city that it helped to create.

story.title: Montreal International Jazz Festival: The World's Largest Stage

subject: Montreal International Jazz Festival
summary: Holder of the Guinness World Record as the world's largest jazz festival, the Festival International de Jazz de Montreal draws over 2 million visitors each summer to more than 650 concerts across 20 stages, transforming downtown Montreal into ten days of music that spills from concert halls onto cordoned-off streets and terraced parks.

subject: Montrose (Scotland)
summary: A small Angus port that the modern world never quite swept away, watched over by a bronze St Bernard and ringed by one of the best birding basins in Britain.

subject: Montsec Range
summary: A 40-kilometer limestone wall of the Pre-Pyrenees, cut by river gorges, packed with Cretaceous fossils, and crowned by some of the darkest skies in Europe.

subject: Montseny Massif
summary: A forested massif near Barcelona that stacks Mediterranean, temperate, and near-alpine worlds in a single ascent, a UNESCO biosphere reserve and home to a newt found nowhere else.

subject: Montserrat
summary: Called the 'Emerald Isle of the Caribbean' for its Irish heritage, Montserrat is an island split in two -- lush tropical green in the north, ash-buried ghost town in the south -- where a volcano reshaped everything.

subject: Monumental Arch of Palmyra
summary: A masterwork of Roman engineering that solved an awkward 30-degree bend in Palmyra's Great Colonnade, the Monumental Arch stood for nearly two millennia before ISIS destroyed it in 2015 -- yet most of its stones survived, and restoration is underway.

subject: Mook en Middelaar
summary: A small Dutch municipality at the northern tip of Limburg whose heath saw a Nassau prince killed by Spanish tercios in 1574, and whose villages were liberated, lost, and liberated again in 1944.

subject: Moonah Creek Hanging Tree
summary: A ghost gum on the Barkly Tableland is remembered by the Waluwarra people as the place where their kin were hanged, a heritage-listed witness to the violence of the Queensland frontier.

subject: Moonhole
summary: A private community on Bequia where a retired New York ad couple built open-air homes from whalebones, driftwood, and native stone beneath a massive volcanic arch through which the moon sometimes sets.

subject: Moonville
summary: A Vinton County ghost town remembered mostly for the dark railroad tunnel it left behind - where at least 21 people died on the tracks and four named ghosts are still said to walk.

subject: Moorefield
summary: A poultry-and-cattle town at the center of West Virginia's South Branch Valley, founded in 1777 and largely overlooked until U.S. 48 turned it into a four-lane gateway.

subject: Moorgate Station
summary: Moorgate is one of London's oldest Underground stations, opened in 1865 and still carrying four tube lines through the City — but it is defined by a single morning in February 1975, when a southbound train failed to stop and 43 people were killed in the worst peacetime accident in the history of the London Underground.

subject: Mopti
summary: Where the Niger meets the Bani, a town once dismissed as a 'miserable village' grew into the great river port of inland Mali, salt slabs from the Sahara stacked beside fish from the floodplain.

subject: Moraira
summary: A Costa Blanca fishing village that refused to become Benidorm, keeping its pines, its low skyline and an 18th-century gun fort right on the sand.

subject: Moramanga
summary: A railway town between the highlands and the coast, Moramanga is where the 1947 Malagasy Uprising against French rule began, and where colonial soldiers later machine-gunned detainees locked in railway wagons.

subject: Morar
summary: A small village beside Britain's deepest freshwater loch, where Bonnie Prince Charlie passed through, SOE agents trained in secret, and the White Sands stretch toward the islands.

subject: Moray Firth
summary: The largest sea inlet in Scotland - 800 kilometres of coastline, a resident population of bottlenose dolphins, North Sea oilfields turned wind farms, and a name older than Scotland itself.

subject: Morea
summary: For nearly a millennium the Peloponnese was known as Morea — a name derived, most likely, from the mulberry tree whose leaf-shaped silhouette matched the peninsula's outline — and under that name it passed through Frankish crusaders, Byzantine despots, Ottoman sultans, and Venetian admirals before becoming the cradle of Greek independence.

subject: Morecambe Lifeboat Station
summary: Home to the RNLI's first life-saving hovercraft and the most decorated helm in its history — Morecambe's lifeboats answer to a bay that has never been forgiving.

subject: Morelia
summary: A colonial city built almost entirely of pink cantera stone, Morelia has preserved its original 1541 street plan so faithfully that UNESCO designated the entire historic center a World Heritage Site.

subject: Morella
summary: A walled hilltop town of barely 2,500 in the mountains of Castellón, fought over for millennia and still making wool, truffles, and honey beneath its castle.

subject: Mori Point
summary: A Prohibition-era speakeasy bluff turned national parkland, where endangered frogs share the wetlands with wildflowers and a Jaguar hearse once flew off the cliff in Harold and Maude.

subject: Moria refugee camp
summary: Built for three thousand people and holding far more, Moria on Lesbos became Europe's largest refugee camp, a place where families fleeing war waited for years until fire destroyed it in September 2020.

subject: Morila Gold Mine
summary: Nicknamed 'Morila the Gorilla' for its astonishing grades, this open-pit mine in southern Mali yielded over 7.5 million ounces of gold before foreign owners walked away — and the Malian state bought it back for a single symbolic dollar.

subject: Mormond Hill
summary: A broad Buchan hill that is Scotland's only home to hill figures: a 38-metre white horse laid in quartz around 1820 and a white stag added a century later, both still visible from the air.

subject: Morney Plains Station
summary: On 6,240 square kilometres of Channel Country floodplain, a cattle station the size of a small nation rides the brutal rhythm of drought and flood.

subject: Morningside, Edinburgh
summary: The Edinburgh suburb that gave Britain a famous accent, an Art Deco cinema run by one family since 1938, and the schoolgirl who became Miss Jean Brodie.

story.title: Morningstar Commune: The Land That Belonged to God

subject: Morningstar Commune
summary: A 31-acre ranch in Sonoma County where a folk musician tried to give the land to everyone -- and then to God -- becoming ground zero for California's open-land commune movement in the late 1960s.

subject: Mornington
summary: A small Meath village at the mouth of the Boyne, with an Elizabethan watchtower, a strange folk tale about a wife thrown from its top, and a family name that became one of the great titles of the British peerage.

subject: Morobe Province
summary: Papua New Guinea's most populous province, where 101 languages are spoken, German plantations once ringed the coast, and Lyndon Johnson once flew thirteen minutes of combat.

subject: Morondava
summary: A dusty, unhurried coastal town in western Madagascar that serves as the gateway to the Avenue of the Baobabs and the wildlife-rich Kirindy Forest, where lemurs outnumber tourists by a comfortable margin.

subject: Morongo Basin
summary: A High Desert basin in the Mojave that holds Joshua Tree National Park, a massive Marine base, an alien-contact dome, and a handful of communities where artists, veterans, and desert eccentrics have built lives far outside the California mainstream.

subject: Morrison Hill
summary: A hill between Wan Chai and Bowrington that was quarried away to build Hong Kong's waterfront, leaving behind a name — and a neighbourhood — that outlasted the hill itself.

subject: Morro Velho
summary: For thirteen years this Brazilian gold mine was the deepest hole humans had dug on the planet - a British-owned shaft descending 7,126 feet into the red Minas Gerais earth, worked first by enslaved Africans and their descendants, then by generations of Brazilian miners, and still pulling gold today after three centuries of continuous operation.

subject: Morro da Igreja
summary: On a summit that froze to nearly minus eighteen degrees, Brazil keeps its coldest record and a stone window carved clean through the rock.

subject: Morro de São Paulo
summary: A car-free village on the northern tip of Tinharé Island in Bahia, guarded by a 1630 fortress built against pirates, reached only by boat or small plane and known for beaches numbered First through Fourth.

subject: Morro do Careca
summary: Natal's great bare dune was the city's favourite ride until 1997, when it was closed to save it — a landmark you can only photograph.

subject: Mortimer L. Schiff Scout Reservation
summary: For nearly five decades, a 500-acre tract in the hills of Mendham, New Jersey, served as the Boy Scouts of America's national training center -- the place where American scouting learned how to be itself.

subject: Morvern
summary: A 250-square-mile Highland peninsula whose name means 'the sea-gap', with 320 residents now where 2,500 once lived before the Clearances.

subject: Moscow
summary: A classic college town in the rolling Palouse where the University of Idaho anchors a community surrounded by the most beautiful wheat country in America.

subject: Moscow
summary: Where Ivan the Terrible crowned himself Tsar, where Napoleon burned his ambitions, where Stalin built a socialist metropolis and the Soviet empire rose and fell.

subject: Moseley Bog
summary: A Bronze Age sweat lodge site, a Victorian millpond reservoir, and the patch of woodland that a Birmingham boy named Ronald Tolkien turned into Middle-earth.

subject: Mosjøen
summary: An aluminium town on a Nordland fjord that once voted to bulldoze its own historic waterfront for parking — and was talked out of it by about a hundred neighbours.

subject: Moss Side
summary: Once Manchester City's home, then the heart of Manchester's Caribbean community, Moss Side has spent forty years being labelled by outsiders and rebuilt by the people who actually live there.

subject: Mossgiel
summary: A vanished coaching town on the lonely Hay plains, named for a Scottish poet's farm and finished off by drought, sand, and a railway that ran somewhere else.

subject: Mossoró
summary: A traveler's guide to Rio Grande do Norte's second city - salt flats, cashew groves, a petroleum museum, and the biggest June festival in the Brazilian northeast.

subject: Mossoró
summary: The northeastern Brazilian city that freed its slaves five years before the rest of the country and beat back the most feared bandit of the sertão.

subject: Mossâmedes
summary: A 1755 mission village where a chief's granddaughter negotiated between Portuguese and Kayapo - and where the forest they once lived in is now a state park.

subject: Motherwell
summary: Once nicknamed Steelopolis and home to one of Europe's largest steel mills, Motherwell rebuilt itself after the 1992 closure of Ravenscraig and remains the heart of North Lanarkshire.

subject: Mothman Festival
summary: An annual September festival in Point Pleasant, West Virginia built around a 1960s cryptid sighting - drawing over 15,000 paranormal enthusiasts a year to a town of 4,000 for cosplay, lectures, and red-eyed plush dolls.

subject: Motion Raceway
summary: Once a high-octane haven for nitro-burning legends, Motion Raceway transitioned from a professional drag strip to a makeshift grain depot before fading into a rural ruin.

story.title: Moulin Rouge: The Red Windmill That Invented Parisian Nightlife

subject: Moulin Rouge
summary: A cabaret at the foot of Montmartre that opened in 1889, burned down in 1915, rebuilt itself, survived two world wars and the Nazi occupation, and still draws a thousand spectators nightly.

subject: Mountaineer Wind Energy Center
summary: The first wind farm in West Virginia and once the largest east of the Mississippi - 44 turbines on a coal-state ridge in 2002.

subject: Mountbellew
summary: Founded by the Bellew family, planned around a triangular square that still hosts a Tuesday market, and home to Ireland's first agricultural college - this east Galway town also has a monument to a steeplechaser who won the Grand National in 1999.

subject: Movie Colony East
summary: Renamed from 'Ruth Hardy Park' to 'Movie Colony East' by a neighborhood vote in May 2012, this Palm Springs district is defined by Frank Sinatra's Twin Palms estate — a 1947 E. Stewart Williams design where the Chairman of the Board lived the first chapter of his Palm Springs life.

story.title: Movimiento de Arte y Cultura Latino Americana

subject: Movimiento de Arte y Cultura Latino Americana
summary: A Chicano and Latino contemporary arts space in downtown San Jose that fought to stay in the heart of the city's art district rather than be relegated to the margins.

subject: Moyobamba
summary: A cloud-forest city founded in 1540 as the first Spanish town in the Peruvian Amazon - now known for 3,500 native orchids and a saint-day dish shaped like a severed head.

subject: Mozarlândia
summary: A Goias town named for a surveyor who gave away land, now home to a slaughterhouse that ships beef to Egypt and Iran.

subject: Mozes en Aaronkerk
summary: A Catholic church that began life as a hidden parlor in a Jewish neighborhood, run by Franciscans behind a pair of houses called Moses and Aaron, and grew into the neoclassical landmark that anchors Waterlooplein today.

subject: Mozu Tombs
summary: A sprawling cluster of ancient keyhole-shaped megalithic tombs in suburban Osaka, where Japan's largest burial mound -- attributed to the semi-legendary Emperor Nintoku -- sits ringed by three moats and buried under fifteen centuries of forest growth, invisible at street level but unmistakable from the air.

subject: Moçâmedes
summary: A Portuguese fishing port wedged between the Namib Desert and a cold Atlantic current, Moçâmedes has worn two names and outlasted both colony and war.

subject: Moše
summary: A Slovenian village whose very name means 'the people by the bridge,' Moše has anchored life on the banks of the Sava River since medieval records first noted it in 1334.

subject: Mpala
summary: A lakeside mission station in the Congo where a Belgian officer, Catholic priests, and a French soldier tried to build a Christian kingdom in the 1880s -- only to spend a decade fighting slavers before the dream collapsed into colonial reality.

subject: Mpanda
summary: A Tanzanian frontier town where sleeper trains arrive twice a week, gold prospectors pass through, and the rice harvest meets its buyers.

subject: Mpanda
summary: Capital of Tanzania's newest region, Mpanda juggles four ethnic groups, five denominations, rice exports, and a railhead at the end of the line from Tabora.

subject: Mpande kaSenzangakhona
summary: Dismissed as a simpleton by his brothers and spared when they killed everyone else who might threaten the throne, Mpande became the longest-reigning Zulu king -- a master of survival in a dynasty that devoured its own.

subject: Mpimbwe District
summary: A Tanzanian district where elephants and lions still walk near farms, where livestock losses to predators are falling, and where a small college teaches Bee Resources Management.

subject: Mponeng Gold Mine
summary: The deepest mine on Earth, where humans dig for gold nearly four kilometers below the South African highveld and scientists have discovered bacteria that live without sunlight, inspired by a line from Jules Verne.

subject: Mpulungu
summary: Zambia's only port on Lake Tanganyika, founded because a colonial commissioner tricked a governor into approving a harbour over champagne and fishing, and still the southern terminus of one of Africa's most storied ferry routes.

subject: Mrauk U
summary: Once a cosmopolitan kingdom rivaling Venice in its network of canals, Mrauk U ruled from the Ganges to the Ayeyarwady before falling silent among its own temples.

subject: Mt. Rich Petroglyphs
summary: Deep in a Grenadian ravine, boulders carved by Amerindian shamans over a thousand years ago bear more than sixty faces - some human, some animal, some something else entirely - still watching the river flow past.

subject: Much Wenlock
summary: A small Shropshire market town whose surgeon William Penny Brookes started the Wenlock Olympian Games in 1850 and inspired Pierre de Coubertin to revive the modern Olympics.

subject: Muchinga Province
summary: Zambia's newest province straddles the Great North Road and the TAZARA Railway, connecting the copperbelt to the Tanzanian coast across 88,000 square kilometers of rural uplands.

subject: Mud Caves of Anza-Borrego
summary: In the Carrizo Badlands of Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, more than 22 mud caves have formed where erosion carved passages through ancient marine sediments — some stretching 1,000 feet long and 80 feet high, and accessible only by crawling.

subject: Mudan Incident
summary: In December 1871, Ryukyuan sailors shipwrecked on Taiwan's coast wandered into Paiwan territory and fifty-four of them were killed; three years later, Japan used their deaths to launch an invasion that would reshape the political map of East Asia.

subject: Mudéjar architecture of Aragon
summary: The Muslim craftsmen who stayed on under Christian kings left Aragon more than a hundred brick-and-tile buildings so beautiful the conquerors kept them.

subject: Mui Ne
summary: A fishing village turned kite-surfing capital, Mui Ne sits where the South China Sea winds and Vietnam's most dramatic sand dunes converge on a 15-kilometer crescent of coast.

subject: Mui Wo
summary: A rural town on Lantau Island where a Song dynasty emperor died in exile, a silver mine opened and closed before 1900, and Japanese soldiers committed a massacre days after the war had already ended.

subject: Muirfield
summary: The East Lothian golf course where Jack Nicklaus completed his first career grand slam, where the wind hits every hole differently, and where in 2017 the club finally admitted women.

subject: Muizenberg
summary: Cape Town's original surf town, where a row of candy-colored beach huts frames one of South Africa's best beginner waves and a seaside walkway leads past Victorian bathing pools toward the Cape Peninsula.

subject: Mukdahan
summary: A Thai city named 'moonstone' by its 18th-century founder, sitting on the Mekong River across from Laos and home to eight ethnic minorities who have traded across this border for centuries.

subject: Mukurob
summary: A 450-ton sandstone pillar that balanced on a narrow base for 50,000 years in the Namib Desert collapsed one night in 1988, fulfilling -- to the week -- a Nama prophecy about the end of colonial rule.

subject: Mulanje Massif
summary: A 130-million-year-old granite island rising abruptly from the plains of southern Malawi, the Mulanje Massif holds the country's highest peak, its critically endangered national tree, and a human history stretching from Stone Age tool-makers to Scottish missionaries to armed forestry patrols fighting illegal loggers.

subject: Mulga Lands
summary: A vast inland bioregion of dry red plains and silver-green acacia woodland, where a single tree species has engineered survival across a quarter-million square kilometres of outback Australia.

subject: Mulga Queen Community
summary: A small Aboriginal community in the northern Goldfields, on Wongatha country, where people gathered through generations of upheaval and now govern their own place far out in the mulga.

subject: Mull
summary: A large, thinly populated Inner Hebridean island built from 60-million-year-old lava, where colourful Tobermory anchors a landscape of single-track roads and shaggy Highland cattle.

subject: Mull of Kintyre
summary: At the southwestern tip of the long Kintyre peninsula, the Antrim coast of Northern Ireland sits twelve miles across open water — and Paul McCartney's farm sits just over the hill.

subject: Mullaghmore
summary: A North Sligo harbour village shadowed by Benbulben, where coffin ships sailed during the Famine and a 1979 IRA bomb killed Louis Mountbatten.

subject: Mullingar
summary: The county town of Westmeath is named for a mill that ran backwards — a 7th-century miracle that gave Mullingar its name and the kind of self-deprecating humour that has carried it from medieval abbeys through canal-age prosperity to its current life as Niall Horan's home town.

subject: Mullion Cove
summary: A Cornish fishing harbour built by a lord to feed his fishermen, now caught in a slow argument with a rising sea.

subject: Mullion Lifeboat Station
summary: Forty-one years, fourteen launches, three lives saved - and a lifeboat named for a Methodist preacher who drowned in the Bay of Biscay.

subject: Mullumbimby
summary: A lush Byron-hinterland town below the sacred peak of Mount Chincogan, Mullumbimby trades on a slogan as outsized as its reputation: "The Biggest Little Town in Australia."

subject: Munakata Taisha
summary: Three Shinto shrines stretched across mainland Kyushu and two islands guard the sea lanes between Japan and Korea, protecting 80,000 ritual artifacts and an island where no woman may set foot.

subject: Mundafan
summary: A vanished lake in Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter that once stretched 300 square kilometers, where hippos waded and early humans hunted aurochs on savannas that are now buried under sand.

subject: Mundi Mundi
summary: From a lookout in the Barrier Ranges, the land falls away into a plain so vast and flat you can see the curve of the Earth - the place where Mad Max raced into legend and where 10,000 people now camp for the Mundi Mundi Bash.

subject: Mundigak
summary: A Bronze Age city northwest of Kandahar that flourished for three thousand years, featuring a palace with painted white pilasters and a monumental temple -- one of the earliest urban centers in Central Asia.

subject: Mundo Novo, Goiás
summary: A 1960 cattle ranch that became a municipality, still growing slowly in an emptying corner of northwestern Goias.

subject: Mundrabilla, Western Australia
summary: A roadhouse and pioneer sheep station on the Nullarbor where geologists stumbled on the largest meteorite ever found in Australia, a 12.4-tonne iron mass that fell from the sky a million years ago.

subject: Munduruku Indigenous Territory
summary: Home to more than 6,500 Munduruku and members of five other indigenous groups, this 2.38-million-hectare territory along the upper Tapajos River has become a flashpoint in Brazil's struggle between hydroelectric development and indigenous constitutional rights.

subject: Mungana Archaeological Area
summary: Among the limestone towers near Chillagoe, a vanished mining town and far older galleries of rock art record two very different ways of belonging to this country.

subject: Munro's Books
summary: A 1909 bank on Government Street, a 24-foot coffered ceiling, a future Nobel laureate behind the counter in 1963, and an owner who handed the whole thing to his staff.

subject: Munster Blackwater
summary: A 169-kilometre river that drains three Irish counties, ends at Youghal, and in August 2025 suffered the worst fish kill in the history of the State.

subject: Muntendam
summary: For most of the twentieth century, this small Groningen village was officially the reddest place in the Netherlands - until a right-wing minister picked its mayor.

subject: Murano
summary: The island where Venice banished its glassmakers in 1291 to prevent fires -- and where those glassmakers became aristocrats, prisoners, and keepers of secrets that shaped European luxury for centuries.

subject: Murchison Widefield Array
summary: A field of hundreds of spider-like antennas in the Western Australian outback, listening for the echo of the first stars that ever shone.

subject: Murcia
summary: A baroque garden city on the Segura, founded by a Moorish emir, famous for its huerta, its Holy Week sculptures, and the giant Christ crowning a Moorish castle.

story.title: Murders of Alison Parker and Adam Ward

subject: Murders of Alison Parker and Adam Ward
summary: Two young Virginia journalists — Alison Parker, 24, and Adam Ward, 27 — were shot and killed on live television at Bridgewater Plaza on Smith Mountain Lake on the morning of August 26, 2015.

story.title: Murders of Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner

subject: Murders of Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner
summary: On June 21, 1964, three young civil rights workers were murdered by Klansmen and local law enforcement in Neshoba County, Mississippi, a crime that shocked the nation and helped propel passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

story.title: Murders of Jan Pietrzak and Quiana Jenkins-Pietrzak

subject: Murders of Jan Pietrzak and Quiana Jenkins-Pietrzak
summary: The 2008 murders of a Marine sergeant and his wife by four fellow Marines — two of them serving under his command — resulted in one of the most severe criminal sentences in California military history.

story.title: Murders of Kate Bushell and Lyn Bryant

subject: Murders of Kate Bushell and Lyn Bryant
summary: Two women, walking their dogs along quiet West Country lanes thirteen months apart, were killed in 1997 and 1998. Both cases are still open, and a DNA profile waits patiently in an evidence locker for a match.

story.title: Murders of Katherine and Sheila Lyon

subject: Murders of Katherine and Sheila Lyon
summary: Two sisters, ages 10 and 12, vanished from a suburban Maryland shopping center in 1975, launching one of the largest investigations in Washington-area history and a cold case that would take forty-two years to crack.

subject: Muriaé
summary: The name means the taste of sweet sugarcane in an indigenous language, and the city that earned the name sits at a highway crossroads in southeastern Minas Gerais - a 1817 trading post that grew into a river-fed municipality of 104,000 people along the Muriaé River valley.

subject: Murin-an
summary: A Meiji-era garden in Kyoto built by a two-time prime minister and samurai-born military reformer who modeled Japan's army on Prussia but modeled his private retreat on the sound of flowing water from Lake Biwa.

subject: Murphy's Haystacks
summary: A cluster of wind-sculpted pink granite pillars on an Eyre Peninsula farm, older than complex life on Earth - and named because a passing traveller mistook them for an impossibly good crop of hay.

subject: Murrawarri Republic
summary: On the red-soil country of the Culgoa River, the Murrawarri people made a declaration the rest of the world had stopped expecting: that their sovereignty was never given away.

subject: Murray Barracks
summary: For over a century, Murray Barracks anchored British military life in the heart of Hong Kong's Central district — until the city's skyline consumed every trace of it.

subject: Murray Battery
summary: Built in 1841 as Hong Kong's first coastal defence, Murray Battery trained its guns over Victoria Harbour for decades before land reclamation stranded it inland and redevelopment erased it entirely.

subject: Murwillumbah
summary: An art-deco river town in the green caldera of an ancient volcano, beneath the sacred peak of Wollumbin and famous for Australia's largest unsolved bank robbery.

subject: Musasir
summary: An ancient holy city of the Urartian kingdom whose name means 'Exit of the Serpent,' Musasir housed the great temple of the god Haldi until Assyrian king Sargon II sacked it in 714 BC.

subject: Museo Juan Manuel Fangio
summary: In the potato-farming town where a bandy-legged mechanic's son grew up, a six-level museum holds the cars and trophies of the greatest racing driver of his age.

story.title: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (Buenos Aires)

subject: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (Buenos Aires)
summary: Argentina's national art museum holds Goya, Rembrandt, Van Gogh and Manet inside a building that once pumped the city's storm water.

subject: Museo Nao Victoria
summary: On the shore of the Strait of Magellan, full-size replicas of the boats that opened the bottom of the world stand rebuilt plank by plank.

subject: Museo Torres García
summary: The Old Town museum to the painter who turned the map of South America upside down and declared that our north is the south.

subject: MuseuMAfricA
summary: Housed in Johannesburg's 1913 fruit and vegetable market, MuseuMAfricA holds the continent's cultural memory in collections ranging from African musical instruments to the documentary record of the Rivonia Trial.

subject: Musgrave Telegraph Station
summary: The last survivor of seven fortified telegraph stations that once carried Morse code up the spine of Cape York is now a roadhouse on a long, lonely peninsula road.

subject: Musiktheater im Revier
summary: Yves Klein covered the lobby wall with a twenty-meter blue sponge relief. The blue is not his patented International Klein Blue - he had to mix a new one for the wall, because the acetone in the original kept evaporating off the sponges. The replacement was named Gelsenkirchen Blue.

subject: Muskerry East
summary: An Irish barony west of Cork that traces its territory back to a 5th-century Gaelic kingdom and witnessed the moment in 1171 when an Irish king's submission cost his dynasty their lands.

subject: Muskerry West
summary: A medieval Irish barony, second only to Ibane and Barryroe for spoken Irish in 1871, whose history is a millennium of clan war between the Eoganacht, the O'Flynns, the de Cogans and the MacCarthys.

subject: Musqueam First Nation
summary: The people of xʷməθkʷəy̓əm have lived at the mouth of the Fraser for thousands of years, hold three small reserves inside a city built on their unceded territory, and are buying pieces of it back.

subject: Mussel Point
summary: A massive shell midden on South Africa's West Coast preserves 2,500 years of San hunter-gatherer ingenuity in layers of mussel, bone, and stone.

subject: Mustique
summary: A private Caribbean island named after mosquitoes, bought for 45,000 pounds in 1958, that became the most exclusive retreat in the West Indies after a Scottish baron gave Princess Margaret a plot of land as a wedding gift.

subject: Mutianyu
summary: Older than Badaling and better built than any other section, Mutianyu's Great Wall packs 22 watchtowers into a single 2,250-meter stretch of granite fortification.

subject: Mutitjulu
summary: A small Aboriginal community at the base of Uluru whose people are the traditional owners of Australia's most sacred monolith.

subject: Mutoshi mine
summary: A cobalt and copper mine in the Congolese Copperbelt where thousands of artisanal miners worked by hand, and where global supply chains for electric-vehicle batteries pass through a dusty, disputed pit near Kolwezi.

subject: Muttrah
summary: Oman's most densely populated district and historic commercial heart, where a labyrinthine souq so dark it earned the name Market of Darkness has traded frankincense, silver daggers, and dishdashas for centuries.

subject: Mutum, Minas Gerais
summary: Pedra Invejada rises above a Minas Gerais municipality where the Rio Doce lowlands collide with the foothills of the Serra do Caparaó, where a holy spring at the top of a rock never dries up, and where coffee farmers wake every morning to golden mist on the ridges.

subject: Mutunópolis
summary: A small Goias town named for a ground-dwelling Amazonian bird - and slowly shrinking like the cerrado habitat the bird needs.

subject: Mwela Rock Paintings
summary: More than 1,000 ancestral paintings on granite outcrops near Kasama, made by hunter-gatherer ancestors of modern Africans two millennia ago, form one of the densest rock art concentrations in Africa.

subject: Myklebust Burial Mound
summary: One of Norway's seven great Viking burial mounds and its only cremation grave, hiding the remains of what may be the largest Viking ship ever built and a message left by a 19th-century archaeologist.

subject: Mykolaiv
summary: A shipbuilding city on a river peninsula in Southern Ukraine, planned from its first day around the vessels it would send to sea.

subject: Mykolayiv Shipyard
summary: For more than two centuries, this admiralty on the Ingul River launched the warships of three different states, until bankruptcy finally silenced its slipways.

subject: Mykonos Windmills
summary: A row of white, round, thatch-capped windmills built by the Venetians to grind grain for passing ships, now the most photographed silhouette in the Cyclades.

subject: Mynydd Bodafon
summary: A small heathland hill near the east coast of Anglesey - the island's highest natural point, with a spring-fed lake that local legend insists is bottomless.

subject: Myrmekion
summary: An ancient Greek town on the Kerch shore named perhaps for ants, where wine flowed for centuries and a shattered marble sarcophagus carved with the life of Achilles came to light.

subject: Mystery Hole
summary: A 1973-vintage Appalachian gravity-hill attraction beside US Route 60, where balls roll uphill, a hippie VW Beetle crashes into the wall, and the rules of physics politely take a break.

subject: Mystery Play of Elche
summary: For more than five centuries, the city of Elche has staged a sung medieval drama of the Virgin's death and assumption inside its basilica, complete with angels who descend from the dome on flying machines.

subject: Mystery Spot
summary: California's original gravity-defying tourist trap, where a tilted shack in the Santa Cruz redwoods has been making visitors question their senses since 1941.

subject: Mystras
summary: Mystras was the last great city of Byzantine civilization — a fortified hilltop capital in the Peloponnese where the final emperor was crowned, Plethon dreamed of a new philosophy, and frescoes of extraordinary beauty were painted even as Constantinople prepared to fall.

subject: Mytilene
summary: The capital of Lesbos was Sappho's city, a poet's harbor of five anchorages and neoclassical mansions that has watched Romans, Genoese, Ottomans, and refugees pass through its twin ports for three thousand years.

subject: Máncora
summary: Peru's northernmost beach town, where Lima weekenders, international surfers, and humpback whales converge along a single stretch of Pacific coast.

subject: Märchenbrunnen
summary: A city architect built Berlin a fountain of fairy tales because he watched children playing on the site — then spent twelve years arguing about it with the Kaiser.

subject: Médio Purus Extractive Reserve
summary: A 604,000-hectare extractive reserve stretching along the Purus River in western Amazonas, where ninety-two riverine communities harvest Brazil nuts, rubber, and acai from forests surrounded by indigenous territories.

story.title: Mérida: The White City Gateway to Mayan Civilization

subject: Mérida
summary: The Yucatán capital where Mayan heritage meets Spanish colonial elegance - where cenotes dot the landscape, where Chichén Itzá is a day trip, and where the heat slows everything to a sensible pace.

subject: Mérida cable car
summary: The world's highest cable car climbs 12.5 kilometers from the city of Merida to Pico Espejo at 4,765 meters, a feat of mid-century engineering rebuilt in the 21st century as the Mukumbari system.

subject: Mêdog County
summary: Tibet's last roadless county, a sacred Buddhist refuge where monsoon rains from the Indian Ocean create a subtropical paradise at the foot of the Himalayas.

subject: Møn
summary: A chalk-soiled Danish island that kept its darkness, its Neolithic graves and a nameless painter's sleepy-eyed saints.

subject: Møns Klint
summary: Six kilometres of Cretaceous seafloor shoved 128 metres into the air by ice, and still falling into the Baltic.

subject: Mülheim an der Ruhr
