summary: A Ruhr city where a Nobel-winning chemist transformed twentieth-century plastics, two brothers founded the world's biggest discount supermarket, and a young woman drove an open-top car around the planet.

subject: Münster
summary: A Westphalian city of 320,000 where the Thirty Years' War was ended by treaty in 1648, where three iron cages still hang from a church tower commemorating an apocalyptic Anabaptist theocracy that briefly seized the town in 1534, and where there are now more bicycles than people.

subject: Măng Đen
summary: Perched at 1,200 meters in Vietnam's Central Highlands, Măng Đen is a town that has been renamed by a typo, nearly capital of a separatist state, abandoned for decades, and is now being reinvented as the country's next great eco-tourism destination.

subject: Mỹ Sơn
summary: For nine centuries, Cham kings built temples in a mountain valley 68 kilometers from Da Nang — a sacred landscape that survived fire, invasion, and the fall of a civilization, only to be largely destroyed in a single week of bombing in 1969.

subject: NAC Breda
summary: A Dutch football club born from a 1912 merger argument, named for two phrases meaning 'Never Give Up' and 'Pleasant Through Entertainment', and famous for its electrifying evening home matches.

story.title: NALF Santa Rosa: From Torpedo Bombers to Die Hard

subject: NALF Santa Rosa
summary: A World War II naval airfield in Sonoma County that trained 21 squadrons of fighters, dive bombers, and torpedo planes, then spent its final years as a civilian airport doubling as a Hollywood film set before closing for good in 1991.

subject: NAN Ranch Ruin
summary: A thousand-year-old Mimbres village along the Mimbres River reveals the art, architecture, and daily lives of a people who mysteriously vanished around 1140 CE.

subject: NASA Advanced Supercomputing Division
summary: NASA's primary supercomputing facility sits at Ames Research Center in Mountain View, modeling everything from space shuttle aerodynamics to hurricane formation to planetary atmospheres.

subject: NATO Enhanced Forward Presence
summary: Multinational NATO battlegroups deployed across Europe's eastern flank serve as a military tripwire -- small enough to avoid provocation, large enough that no invasion could avoid engaging the flags of a dozen allied nations.

subject: NS Savannah
summary: The first nuclear-powered merchant ship ever built, NS Savannah was Eisenhower's gleaming ambassador for the Atoms for Peace program -- and she now rests in Baltimore Harbor, a National Historic Landmark awaiting her next chapter.

subject: Naches Trail
summary: The pioneer wagon route that crossed the Cascades before any road existed, where settlers lowered their wagons down near-vertical cliffs by rope to reach Puget Sound.

subject: Nadir Crater
summary: A nine-kilometer scar buried beneath the Atlantic seafloor off Guinea, the Nadir Crater may mark a second asteroid strike at the very moment the dinosaurs vanished.

subject: Nadym
summary: An Arctic gas town in Western Siberia where Nenets etymology, Soviet industrial ambition, and Gazprom's empire converge on the frozen banks of the Nadym River.

subject: Nafpaktos
summary: Nafpaktos — ancient Naupactus, medieval Lepanto — is a small Greek harbor town on the north shore of the Gulf of Corinth whose perfectly round Venetian port, castle-crowned hillside, and layered two-and-a-half millennia of history make it one of the most quietly astonishing places on the Greek mainland.

subject: Nafusa Mountains
summary: A mountain escarpment in northwestern Libya where Berber identity, Ibadi Islam, and a thousand years of resistance have survived against every force that tried to erase them.

subject: Naga Army
summary: Founded in 1952, the Naga Army has fought one of South Asia's longest insurgencies, a seven-decade struggle for self-determination that spans the India-Myanmar border and defies every attempt at resolution.

subject: Nagaland
summary: India's most Baptist state is also its most linguistically diverse, where 15 Naga ethnic groups maintain distinct identities across a landscape of rugged hills and terraced valleys.

subject: Nagashima Spa Land
summary: Japan's fourth-most-visited amusement park pairs a legendary steel roller coaster with ancient hot springs and eight million LED lights.

subject: Nagoya
summary: Japan's fourth-largest city balances samurai-era craftsmanship with industrial might, from the golden dolphins atop its castle to the factories that build the world's best-selling cars.

subject: Nahavand
summary: Continuously inhabited since at least 5,000 BC, this Iranian city on the fertile Nisaean plain was where the Sasanian Empire made its last stand in 642, a battle that opened the Iranian plateau to Arab conquest.

story.title: The Kantei: Japan's Haunted Seat of Power

subject: Naikaku Sōri Daijin Kantei
summary: Japan's Prime Minister's Office stands in the Nagatacho political district of Tokyo -- a modern five-story building beside a much older residence where a prime minister was assassinated, renegade soldiers killed six people, and multiple occupants have reported seeing ghosts in military uniforms.

subject: Nairobi
summary: Where the railway built a city from nothing, where lions still roam within sight of skyscrapers, where East Africa's hub grew faster than anyone planned.

subject: Najd
summary: The high desert heartland of Arabia, where a limestone escarpment, a string of mudbrick oasis towns, and the dynasty that became Saudi Arabia all rose from the same dry plateau.

subject: Najran Province
summary: At the southern edge of Saudi Arabia, in a fertile valley that has sheltered Christians, Jews, Ismaili Muslims, and Sunni Muslims in succession, lies a corner of the kingdom that has always been its own.

subject: Nakatajima Sand Dunes
summary: One of Japan's three great sand dune systems, slowly vanishing as dams upstream starve the coast of the sediment that built it over millennia.

subject: Nakazato Shell Mound
summary: Buried beneath bullet train tracks in northern Tokyo, Japan's largest shell midden reveals a 4,700-year-old Jomon industrial complex where oyster cultivation may have predated ancient Rome by millennia.

subject: Nakhchivan (city)
summary: The capital of Azerbaijan's landlocked exclave, Nakhchivan is a city of mausoleums, lavash bread, and geopolitical isolation -- separated from the rest of its country by Armenian territory and connected to the outside world by flights to Baku and border crossings to Iran and Turkey.

subject: Nakhon Phanom
summary: A quiet riverfront town where a Vietnamese exile once kept a garden, an American air war was run by computer, and burning boats still float down the Mekong once a year.

subject: Nakhon Phanom Province
summary: A long ribbon of Thailand pressed against the Mekong, where the culture is Lao, the map is Thai, and the province rebuilt its holiest tower out of small donations.

subject: Nam Sang Wai
summary: A photogenic wetland in Hong Kong's New Territories — home to migratory birds, reeds, and mangroves — that has spent decades holding off developers through courts, planning boards, and community resistance.

story.title: The Namamugi Incident: The Murder That Started a War

subject: Namamugi Incident
summary: On a road near Yokohama in 1862, a British merchant refused to dismount before a Japanese lord's procession and was cut down by samurai -- an act of cultural collision that triggered the Bombardment of Kagoshima and helped crack open Japan's feudal order.

subject: Namaqualand
summary: A 440,000-square-kilometer desert that erupts into one of Earth's most spectacular wildflower displays each spring, Namaqualand spans the border of Namibia and South Africa along the Atlantic coast.

subject: Namasia District
summary: In the mountain valleys of northeastern Kaohsiung, Namasia District is home to the Bunun, Kanakanavu, and Saaroa peoples — indigenous communities who have lived in these highlands for generations, survived catastrophic floods, reclaimed their district's name, and built a future rooted in their own languages and governance.

subject: Namdaemun
summary: South Korea's National Treasure No. 1, a 14th-century city gate built to keep out Siberian tigers and greet foreign emissaries, was destroyed by arson in 2008 and painstakingly rebuilt over five years.

subject: Namib
summary: The world's oldest desert, arid for some 55 million years, where Atlantic fog feeds a parade of creatures and one of the strangest plants on Earth.

subject: Namsskogan Familiepark
summary: A wildlife park beside a pond on the E6 that drew more than sixty visitors for every resident of its municipality, went bankrupt in 2025 with the animals still in their enclosures, and reopened in 2026 under a new name.

subject: Namsskogan Municipality
summary: A municipality the size of a small county with the population of a village, whose coat of arms is a pair of moose antlers and whose newest export is electricity sold to a cryptocurrency mine.

subject: Namsvatnet
summary: A 17-kilometre lake at the doorstep of Børgefjell, source of the river Namsen, dammed in 1959 and now rising and falling through fourteen metres a year.

subject: Nan MacKinnon
summary: A Vatersay singer who recorded over a thousand traditional Gaelic songs and stories, preserving an oral tradition that would otherwise have been lost when the last native speakers died.

subject: Nanaimo
summary: Vancouver Island's Harbour City, built on Snuneymuxw ground and a century of coal, where the most famous mayor raced bathtubs dressed as a pirate.

subject: Nanao (Taiwan)
summary: At the southern edge of Yilan County, Nan'ao is a largely Atayal township where the mountains drop suddenly to the Pacific — a place of hot springs, waterfalls, a mysterious gravel beach, and one of Taiwan's deepest alpine lakes.

subject: Nandigram
summary: A small Bengali town between two rivers that was freed from British rule before the rest of India, Nandigram became a flashpoint in 2007 when villagers resisted industrial land acquisition at the cost of fourteen lives.

subject: Nanfeng Kiln
summary: Built during the Ming Dynasty's Zhengde period (1506–1521), the Nanfeng Kiln in Shiwan has fired ceramics without interruption for over 500 years — making it one of the longest continuously operating dragon kilns in China.

story.title: Nangu Taisha: The Shrine of Metals at the Foot of the Sacred Mountain

subject: Nangū Taisha
summary: The highest-ranked Shinto shrine in old Mino Province has stood at the foot of Mount Nangu for over a millennium, dedicated to the kami of mining and metals -- burned to the ground during the Battle of Sekigahara, then rebuilt by a shogun whose 1642 structures still stand as designated Important Cultural Properties.

subject: Nanih Waiya
summary: Deep in the pine forests of Winston County, Mississippi, an ancient earthen mound has served as the sacred origin place of the Choctaw people for centuries, surviving removal, private ownership, and erasure before returning to tribal hands.

subject: Nanjie
summary: A tiny village in Henan province that reversed China's market reforms, Nanjie is widely reported as the last Maoist collective in the country.

subject: Nanjing (Liao dynasty)
summary: Before it was Beijing, the city was called Nanjing -- the southern capital of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, a predecessor identity buried beneath centuries of imperial reinvention.

subject: Nankin-machi
summary: Kobe's Chinatown has been destroyed twice -- by wartime bombs and by earthquake -- and rebuilt both times by a Chinese community that has called this neighborhood home since the port opened in 1868.

subject: Nanluoguxiang
summary: An 800-meter hutong alley dating to the Yuan Dynasty, where traditional courtyard homes now share space with coffee shops, live music venues, and crowds of tourists navigating one of Beijing's oldest neighborhoods.

subject: Nannine, Western Australia
summary: The first town of the Murchison goldfield, raised on the shore of a salt lake and now almost entirely vanished - its grandest hall carried away to a neighbour, its name older than gold itself.

subject: Nanny Town
summary: High in Jamaica's Blue Mountains, a village founded by people who escaped enslavement held off the British Empire for over a decade, led by an Ashanti woman whose name now graces the Jamaican $500 bill.

subject: Nant Ffrancon Pass
summary: A U-shaped valley so textbook-perfect that geography teachers point at aerial photographs of it - and the road Thomas Telford carved across its eastern flank as he built the London-to-Holyhead trunk road.

subject: Nant Gwrtheyrn
summary: A quarry village abandoned in World War II at the foot of a single-track road called 'Climbing the Unclimbable' -- reborn in 1978 as a residential Welsh language centre that takes its name from the British king who invited the Saxons in.

subject: Nantou (historic town)
summary: A walled town in Shenzhen whose history reaches back to 331 CE — once the administrative capital of a region spanning what is now Shenzhen, Hong Kong, and Macau, it survives today as a layered urban village.

subject: Nantucket
summary: A crescent-shaped island thirty miles off Cape Cod that rose from a Wampanoag homeland to the world's whaling capital, burned in catastrophic fire, and reinvented itself as one of America's most exclusive destinations.

subject: Nantwich
summary: An old Cheshire salt town with one of the densest collections of listed buildings in England, rebuilt after a great fire by Queen Elizabeth I and still wearing the bones of medieval and Tudor streets.

subject: Nanuque
summary: A three-state corner of Brazil tucked against the boundaries of Bahia and Espírito Santo, Nanuque sits in the Mucuri River valley where the inselbergs of the Serra dos Aimorés rise like stone islands - including Fritz's Stone, a kilometer-tall granite wall where climbers and skydivers work the edge.

subject: Nanxiong Formation
summary: A vast layer of Late Cretaceous red rock in northern Guangdong that has yielded some of China's richest dinosaur fossils — including oviraptorid eggs with embryos still inside.

subject: Nanzhuangtou
summary: One of northern China's earliest Neolithic settlements, where 10,000-year-old pottery, domesticated dogs, and some of the world's first cultivated millet reveal the dawn of agriculture on the North China Plain.

subject: Naoshima
summary: A tiny fishing island in Japan's Seto Inland Sea transformed into one of the world's most extraordinary open-air art destinations, where Yayoi Kusama's polka-dotted pumpkins sit on piers and entire abandoned houses have become installations.

subject: Napata
summary: The Kushite royal capital at the foot of Jebel Barkal, where African pharaohs of the 25th Dynasty ruled over all of Egypt and built the first pyramids the Nile had seen in a thousand years.

subject: Naples
summary: Where Vesuvius looms over pizza's birthplace, where chaos and beauty share every street, where Italy's most intense city refuses to be tamed.

subject: Napo moist forests
summary: One hectare of this western Amazonian ecoregion contains more than 310 species of trees - more tree species than in all of continental North America combined - and that is just the beginning of what the Napo holds.

subject: Nappa Merrie
summary: The cattle station on Cooper Creek where the Burke and Wills Dig Tree still stands, marking one of the cruelest near-misses in exploration history.

subject: Naqa
summary: A Kushite city in the Butana where a lion-headed warrior god, an Egyptian pantheon, and a Roman kiosk all stand on the same sandstone floor.

subject: Naqada culture
summary: A thousand years before the first pharaoh, a wealthy town on the Nile they called the Golden Town was quietly inventing the civilization Egypt would become.

story.title: Nara Dreamland: Japan's Bootleg Magic Kingdom

subject: Nara Dreamland
summary: A brazen Disneyland imitation built in 1961 after its founder's licensing deal with Walt Disney fell apart, Nara Dreamland drew 1.6 million visitors a year before the real thing arrived in Tokyo and competition slowly killed it -- leaving behind a decade-long afterlife as Japan's most famous urban exploration site.

subject: Narai-juku
summary: Japan's longest surviving post town stretches one kilometer through the Kiso Valley, its Edo-period wooden buildings preserved exactly as they stood when samurai, merchants, and monks walked the Nakasendo highway.

subject: Narberth
summary: A small Welsh market town that hosted Elton John's first headlining gig, jailed the leaders of the Rebecca Riots, and served as the court of Pwyll in the oldest stories in Welsh literature.

subject: Naryan-Mar
summary: The Arctic capital of the Nenets Autonomous Okrug, where midnight sun meets petroleum industry on the banks of the Pechora River.

subject: Nasa silver mine
summary: A 17th-century silver mine on the Swedish-Norwegian border produced little precious metal but left deep scars -- forced labor, exploited Sami reindeer herders, and a corrupt foreman imprisoned by royal commission.

story.title: Nascentes da Serra do Cachimbo Biological Reserve

subject: Nascentes da Serra do Cachimbo Biological Reserve
summary: A strict nature reserve of 342,192 hectares where the headwaters of the Xingu and Tapajós rivers emerge, hyacinth macaws still fly, and squatters arrived fifteen years before protection did.

story.title: Nashville: Where Country Music Lives and Bachelorette Parties Never Die

subject: Nashville
summary: The Tennessee capital where the Grand Ole Opry invented country radio and honky-tonks line Broadway - where everyone's a songwriter, where the hot chicken burns, and where the pedal taverns full of bachelorettes have become their own musical genre.

story.title: Nashville: Where Country Music Became an Industry

subject: Nashville
summary: The Tennessee city where the Grand Ole Opry made country music a national phenomenon - where Hank Williams and Patsy Cline became legends, where Music Row transformed songs into commerce, and where every tourist with a guitar dreams of discovery on Broadway's neon strip.

story.title: Nashville: Where Country Music Became America's Soundtrack

subject: Nashville
summary: The city where the Grand Ole Opry has broadcast every Saturday since 1925, where honky-tonks line Lower Broadway, and where bachelorette parties now outnumber aspiring songwriters on any given weekend.

subject: Nasir, South Sudan
summary: A Sobat River town where a British aid worker married a rebel commander, where a Sudanese vice president died in a plane crash, and where South Sudan's peace process has repeatedly nearly broken down.

subject: Nassau, Bahamas
summary: The Bahamian capital began as a pirate stronghold called Charles Town, burned to the ground and renamed for a Dutch prince, and grew into a Caribbean crossroads where colonial history, Junkanoo rhythms, and cruise ship tourism collide on a single small island.

subject: Natal
summary: A capital named Christmas that cannot agree on who founded it, wrapped around a river mouth, a colonial fort and 1,172 hectares of dunes inside the city limits.

subject: Natal Air Force Base
summary: The Americans called it the vertex of a triangle reaching to Africa and Europe — the Trampoline of Victory — and the name stuck to the city as well as the airfield.

subject: Natalia Republic
summary: The Natalia Republic lasted barely four years, but its violent birth at Blood River and its absorption by Britain set the pattern for a century of conflict between Boer, Briton, and Zulu in southern Africa.

subject: Nataruk
summary: On a vanished lakeshore west of Lake Turkana, twenty-seven people died together some ten thousand years ago - a discovery that forced a hard question about how old human violence really is.

story.title: Natchez: The Antebellum City That Cotton Built and Time Preserved

subject: Natchez
summary: Mississippi's oldest city on the bluffs above the river, where more antebellum mansions survive than anywhere in America, where the Natchez Trace began its 440-mile journey, and where Cotton Kingdom wealth is preserved in Greek Revival splendor.

subject: Natchez slave market
summary: The Forks of the Road in Natchez was the second-largest slave market in the United States, where more than four thousand enslaved people were bought and sold annually during the 1830s before Union soldiers and Black troops tore the pens down in 1863.

subject: Natchez, Mississippi
summary: The oldest settlement on the Mississippi River, Natchez holds the largest collection of antebellum homes in the United States, a legacy of the cotton wealth that once made it home to more millionaires per capita than any other American city.

subject: Natchitoches, Louisiana
summary: The oldest permanent settlement in the Louisiana Purchase territory, Natchitoches is a city of wrought iron, brick streets, and French colonial charm on the banks of Cane River Lake.

subject: Nathan Cooper Gristmill
summary: A four-story fieldstone gristmill on the Black River in Chester Township, New Jersey, has been grinding grain -- or standing ready to -- since a retired Revolutionary War general rebuilt it in 1826.

subject: Nathan Road
summary: Kowloon's main artery runs 3.6 kilometres from the harbour's edge to Boundary Street, threading through five distinct neighbourhoods and a century and a half of urban history.

subject: National Association of Music Merchants
summary: What started in 1901 as a piano dealers' alliance fighting knockoff manufacturers has grown into a global trade organization that invested over $200 million in music education and now calls Carlsbad, California home.

subject: National Bank of Greece
summary: Founded in 1841 by a Swiss philhellene and a Greek merchant, the National Bank of Greece printed the young nation's money, financed its refugees, survived occupation and crisis, and still anchors a city block in the heart of Athens.

subject: National Bank of Romania
summary: Romania's central bank, founded in 1880, occupies two grand palaces on Lipscani Street in old Bucharest and is still owed the gold reserve it sent to Moscow in 1916.

subject: National Coal Heritage Area
summary: A federally designated heritage area covering eleven southern West Virginia counties that fueled the American twentieth century with smokeless bituminous coal.

subject: National Coracle Centre
summary: In a small Welsh village beside the falls of the Teifi, a 17th-century mill houses the only museum in the world devoted to the round, skin-covered boat that nine civilisations independently invented.

subject: National Documentation Centre (Greece)
summary: Established in 1980 with United Nations funding, Greece's National Documentation Centre (EKT) has grown into the country's central nerve system for scientific knowledge — gathering, preserving, and opening up research for anyone who needs it.

subject: National Eisteddfod of Wales
summary: Europe's largest music and poetry festival - traced to a bardic competition in 1176 and held in Welsh since 1861 - travels each August to a different corner of Wales, dressing its winners in robes and crowning its poets in stone circles.

subject: National Hellenic Research Foundation
summary: Born of Cold War optimism and a 100-million-drachma American gift, Greece's flagship research foundation gathers Byzantine historians and laser physicists under one modernist roof.

subject: National High Magnetic Field Laboratory
summary: The only facility of its kind in the United States, the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory in Tallahassee holds world records for the strongest magnets ever built -- and locals joke that its 45.5-tesla fields are what deflect hurricanes from the city.

subject: National Japanese American Historical Society
summary: A nonprofit in San Francisco's Japantown preserving the full arc of Japanese American history, from immigration and internment to military service and cultural achievement.

story.title: National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts

subject: National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts
summary: Built on a former military training ground, Weiwuying is the world's largest performing arts center under a single roof, its wave-shaped canopy inspired by the banyan groves that once shaded soldiers.

subject: National Liberal Club
summary: Gladstone's Liberal redoubt off Whitehall, built for six thousand members in a Victorian pile by Alfred Waterhouse, with a wine cellar excavated for a railway that never ran.

story.title: The Mint That Made the World's Money

subject: National Mint of Bolivia
summary: The Casa de la Moneda in Potosi once produced so many silver coins that Cervantes immortalized the city's name as a synonym for fortune - and the building itself became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: National Museums Scotland
summary: Dolly the sheep, a Concorde, the Lewis chessmen, and a complete ancient Egyptian royal burial - the spread of objects gathered under one Scottish institution defies easy summary.

subject: National Portrait Gallery, London
summary: The world's first public gallery dedicated to portraits selects its subjects for who they were, not who painted them.

subject: National Redoubt (Belgium)
summary: A 95-kilometer double ring of 28 forts built around Antwerp between 1859 and 1914 to make the city impregnable - destroyed in six weeks by German howitzers that outranged everything inside.

subject: National Route 40 (Argentina)
summary: Argentina's legendary Ruta 40, a more than 5,000-kilometer road running the entire length of the country along the spine of the Andes, from Patagonian steppe to the Bolivian border.

story.title: National Space Facilities Control and Test Center

subject: National Space Facilities Control and Test Center
summary: For twenty years, every Soviet spacecraft bound for another planet was flown from this coastal plain near Yevpatoria, until an institution outgrew the ground it was born on.

subject: National Sports Centre (Isle of Man)
summary: Built on the site of an old Douglas park, the Isle of Man's National Sports Centre has hosted the Island Games, the Commonwealth Youth Games, and the everyday training of an entire island of athletes.

subject: National Steel and Shipbuilding Company
summary: NASSCO is the last major new-construction shipyard on the U.S. West Coast — a San Diego institution that built the Exxon Valdez, survived corporate consolidation, and today builds cargo ships and Navy vessels on the same bay it has occupied since 1960.

subject: Nationalmuseum robbery
summary: A daring 2000 heist that saw three masterworks worth up to $45 million escape Stockholm's Nationalmuseum by speedboat, only to be recovered across three continents over five years.

subject: Natirar
summary: A 491-acre Somerset County estate whose name spells 'Raritan' backwards has passed from a whaling heiress to the King of Morocco to a county park and luxury resort -- each owner reimagining the same rolling landscape.

subject: Natural Chimneys
summary: Seven 500-million-year-old limestone towers near Mt. Solon, Virginia - and the home of the oldest continuously held jousting tournament in the United States, dating to 1821.

story.title: Nauvoo: The Mormon City That Had to Be Abandoned

subject: Nauvoo
summary: The Illinois city that Joseph Smith built into America's tenth-largest before a mob murdered him and drove his followers into the wilderness - now restored as a pilgrimage site by descendants of the people who fled.

subject: Naval Air Facility El Centro
summary: A remote desert air base that has trained elite naval aviators since World War II and serves as the winter home of the Blue Angels.

subject: Naval Air Station Key West
summary: America's southernmost naval air station has trained combat aviators since World War I, launching everything from Curtiss biplanes hunting German U-boats to F/A-18 Super Hornets sharpening their dogfighting skills over the turquoise waters between Florida and Cuba.

subject: Naval Amphibious Base Coronado
summary: Commissioned in 1944 on the Silver Strand between San Diego Bay and the Pacific, Naval Amphibious Base Coronado is the home of Navy SEALs, BUD/S training, and a set of barracks that, from above, form an uncomfortable shape.

subject: Naval Consolidated Brig, Miramar
summary: Built in 1989 to consolidate all Department of Defense corrections facilities in the western United States, the Naval Consolidated Brig at Miramar has held some of the most controversial military prisoners in recent American history.

subject: Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific
summary: The Navy's first West Coast laboratory evolved from radio research in 1940 to become a global center for cyber warfare, autonomous systems, and C4ISR.

subject: Naval Radio Section Aldergrove
summary: Twelve hundred acres of Fraser Valley farmland kept deliberately empty so the Royal Canadian Navy can hear its Pacific fleet - the listening half of a station that once needed 130 people and now needs about sixteen.

subject: Naval Radiological Defense Laboratory
summary: An early Cold War military lab at Hunters Point studied the effects of nuclear weapons and radiation, leaving a legacy of contamination that San Francisco is still cleaning up.

subject: Naval Special Warfare Center
summary: The crucible where ordinary sailors are transformed into Navy SEALs, this Coronado facility runs one of the most demanding military training programs in the world.

subject: Naxos
summary: The largest and greenest of the Cyclades, where a marble doorway to nowhere frames the sunset, long sandy beaches run for miles, and mountain villages hide in valleys few tourists ever find.

subject: Naxos (city)
summary: The main town of Naxos greets arriving ferries with a giant marble doorway that frames the sea, and climbs behind it through a Venetian castle that is still a living medieval town.

subject: Naypyidaw
summary: Myanmar's purpose-built capital -- a city four times the size of London with a fraction of the population, where 20-lane boulevards sit largely empty and apartment roofs are color-coded by ministry, all shaken by a devastating 2025 earthquake.

subject: Nazca culture
summary: An ancient Peruvian civilization that carved enormous geoglyphs into the desert floor, engineered underground aqueducts to farm an arid landscape, and left behind some of the most vivid pottery in the pre-Columbian world.

subject: Nazinga Game Ranch
summary: A 94,000-hectare conservation experiment in southern Burkina Faso proved that wildlife management could lift communities out of poverty -- until politics destroyed what science had built.

subject: Nchanga Copper mine
summary: Africa's largest copper mine is a four-mile gash in the Zambian earth, and the story of the 1,800 villagers who sued their way into a British Supreme Court ruling that reached far beyond its fence line.

subject: Ndola
summary: On September 18, 1961, a UN plane carrying Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold went down outside this Zambian mining city, and the peace talks he was flying to never happened. Ndola has been living with the weight of that missing conversation ever since.

subject: Ndola
summary: Zambia's third-largest city is a mosaic of limestone, copper, railways, and memory - founded in 1904 by a trader nicknamed Chiripula, anchored by a slave-market fig tree that has now fallen to termites, and shaped by the railhead that still runs through its center.

subject: Nduga Hostage Crisis
summary: A New Zealand pilot named Phillip Mehrtens was taken captive in the Papuan highlands in February 2023 and held for nineteen months in a crisis that reopened decades-old fault lines across West Papua.

subject: Nea Anchialos
summary: A seaside town of red-sand beaches and tsipouro tables, founded by refugees who carried the name of a lost Black Sea home and built it again above an ancient harbor.

subject: Nea Peramos
summary: A coastal town on the Bay of Megara whose residents include the descendants of Greek families expelled from Asia Minor in 1922, who built a new life here, named their town for the home they had lost, and brought with them an icon from a church they would never see again.

subject: Neale, County Mayo
summary: A small Mayo village holding a 1760 step pyramid built as famine relief, the parish priest who coined the word 'boycott,' and a stone said to mark the grave of an Irish god.

subject: Neanderthal 1
summary: In August 1856, quarrymen in a limestone cave near Dusseldorf threw out bones they took for ancient bear. Sixteen pieces survived, and one of them belonged to a man who had broken his arm.

subject: Nebel
summary: A village in the middle of Amrum where a windmill stands on a Bronze Age grave mound, a church holds a baptismal font from Roman times, and 152 sandstone slabs in the churchyard tell the lives of the people buried beneath them.

subject: Nebra sky disc
summary: Looted from a hilltop in 1999 and recovered in a Basel sting operation, the Nebra sky disc is the oldest concrete depiction of the heavens known anywhere on Earth.

subject: Nechells
summary: An inner Birmingham ward where Britain's first all-petrol car was built, the country's first trolleybus replaced its first tram, and a wall collapse killed five men in 2016.

subject: Nechung
summary: The seat of Tibet's State Oracle, where a monk channels the spirit of Pehar to advise the Dalai Lama on matters of state, and where pre-Buddhist shamanic traditions survive within Gelug orthodoxy.

subject: Necromanteion of Acheron
summary: On a hill above the mythic rivers of the underworld in Epirus, the ancient Greeks built a place where the living came to speak with their dead — the Necromanteion, Oracle of the Dead.

subject: Neder-Betuwe
summary: A narrow strip of orchard country squeezed between the Rhine and the Waal, where 250,000 people once fled a wobbling dike and a decommissioned nuclear reactor waits out its half-life in silence.

subject: Needham Market
summary: A Suffolk town that chained itself shut against the plague in 1665 and lost two-thirds of its people - the surviving street names still trace the routes the corpses took.

subject: Nefyn
summary: The Llyn town where Edward I held a tournament in 1284 to celebrate conquering Wales, herrings were called 'Nefyn beef,' and a golf course runs along cliffs above the bay where Welsh emigrants left for Argentina.

story.title: Negishi Racecourse: Where East Met West at the Starting Gate

subject: Negishi Racecourse
summary: Japan's first European-style racecourse transformed a Yokohama swamp into a crossroads of cultures, drew Emperor Meiji fourteen times, survived the Great Kanto Earthquake, and now stands as a haunting Art Deco ruin at the edge of a public park.

subject: Negril
summary: Jamaica's westernmost beach town grew from a place where visitors once waded ashore from ferries into one of the Caribbean's most famous resort destinations, anchored by its seven-mile stretch of white sand.

subject: Negros Occidental
summary: The 'Sugarbowl of the Philippines,' Negros Occidental produces more than half the nation's sugar -- a sweet dominance that has shaped its politics, culture, and tragedies for over a century.

subject: Neiwan
summary: A Hakka railway village in Hsinchu County that slept through three decades of economic decline and woke up as one of Taiwan's most charming heritage destinations, reached by a slow mountain train that is half the point.

subject: Nelson
summary: The Queen City of the Kootenays where heritage buildings from the silver rush line Baker Street and Steve Martin filmed Roxanne in a mountain town reborn as an arts community.

subject: Nelson's Column
summary: A 169-foot tribute to the admiral who died winning Britain's most decisive naval victory, watched over by four bronze lions cast from melted French cannon.

subject: Nemean Games
summary: Every two years, in a sacred valley between Cleonae and Phlius, Greeks from across the ancient world gathered to race, wrestle, and compete in honour of Zeus — crowned not with gold but with a wreath of wild celery.

subject: Nenagh
summary: A North Tipperary market town in the shadow of a thirty-metre Norman keep - the first stronghold of the Butlers, who would later move to Kilkenny and rule there for five centuries.

subject: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
summary: Russia's least populous federal subject, where Nenets reindeer herders and petroleum giants share 177,000 square kilometers of Arctic tundra.

subject: Nenetsia
summary: A vast, roadless Arctic region where reindeer sleighs remain a practical mode of transport and the only way in is by air or river.

subject: Nenthead
summary: One of England's highest villages and one of its earliest purpose-built industrial settlements - a Quaker company town set down on a Pennine moor in 1737 to mine the lead beneath it.

subject: Neom
summary: Saudi Arabia's $500-billion bid to build a futuristic city from bare desert, and the people whose homes stood in its way.

subject: Nerópolis
summary: A small town twenty-five kilometers outside Goiânia became Brazil's unofficial capital of garlic, then pivoted to sweets and tomato paste when Chinese imports crushed the garlic market.

subject: Neshoba County Fair
summary: Every July, more than 600 hand-built cabins come alive near Philadelphia, Mississippi, as the nation's largest campground fair hosts a week of horse racing, political speeches, and front-porch fellowship stretching back to 1889.

subject: Ness of Brodgar
summary: A 2.5-hectare Neolithic complex on the isthmus between two Orkney lochs, excavated from 2003 to 2024 and then deliberately reburied to save what remained from the air.

subject: Ness, Lewis
summary: The northernmost district of Lewis, sixteen Gaelic-speaking villages where each year ten men sail to Sula Sgeir to hunt gannets - the only such legal seabird harvest in Britain.

subject: Neston
summary: A Wirral market town with a Viking name, a vanished port, underwater coal mines, and the unlikely distinction of being the birthplace of Lord Nelson's Emma, Lady Hamilton - all where the silted Dee Estuary meets Cheshire.

subject: Netherlands
summary: A country that decided the sea was negotiable, and built a civilization on the terms.

subject: Netherlands Film Festival
summary: Every autumn for forty-odd years, Utrecht has turned itself into the country's screening room, where Dutch cinema gathers to hand out a small bronze cow.

subject: Netherlands Institute for Space Research
summary: SRON builds superconducting detectors so cold they catch X-ray photons one at a time, and methane-tracking spectrometers that just helped one Dutch researcher win the Stevin Prize.

subject: Netherlands national cricket team
summary: The Flying Dutchmen play cricket on grounds reclaimed from polder farmland, beat England at Lord's as 500-to-1 outsiders, and once recruited their first international team from interned British officers.

subject: Neuenhaus
summary: In a Lower Saxon town just over the Dutch border, the official language was Dutch until barely a hundred years ago. The shield over the door still shows a Dutch baron's war tent.

subject: Neugrund crater
summary: Estonia's largest and oldest impact crater lies invisible under the Gulf of Finland - but you can walk up and touch the rock it threw out, sitting in the surf on Osmussaar.

subject: Neuland Colony
summary: The youngest of Paraguay's Mennonite colonies, founded in 1947 by war-broken refugees from the Soviet Union whom no wealthier country would take.

subject: Neuquén
summary: Patagonia's largest city sits on a strip of green where two rivers meet, riding a shale boom that has made the arid steppe one of the most coveted energy frontiers on Earth.

subject: Neuruppin
summary: A town that burned to the ground in 1787 and rebuilt itself as a grid of neoclassical calm — birthplace of the architect who shaped Berlin and the novelist who wrote Brandenburg into literature.

subject: Neuss
summary: In 1984, Neuss threw itself a two-thousandth birthday party. Romans founded it in 16 BCE, and unlike most settlements that age, it never stopped being a city.

subject: Neuss Hauptbahnhof
summary: Four rail lines converge here on a platform island in the Rhineland - a station built in 1853 that quietly stitches the Lower Rhine together one timetable at a time.

subject: Neuwesteel
summary: A 1934 polder village built where a 14th-century village drowned, with a spade on its coat of arms and a raft instead of a bridge.

subject: Nevada City, California
summary: A Gold Rush boomtown that became California's most important mining center in 1850, then reinvented itself as a Victorian arts colony twinned with Cornish mining towns an ocean away.

subject: Nevada Fall
summary: A 594-foot waterfall with a distinctive bent shape where water strikes a granite shelf mid-fall, creating the snowy turbulence that inspired its Spanish name and has drawn - and killed - visitors for over a century.

subject: Neville Ranch raid
summary: The last serious Mexican raid on Texas soil ended a bloody chapter of the Bandit War, but its roots lay in the horrors of the Porvenir Massacre.

subject: New Australia
summary: A utopian socialist colony of Australian idealists who sailed to Paraguay in 1893 to build a world without bosses — and discovered they had brought their human flaws along with them.

subject: New Bern, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's first colonial capital, founded in 1710 by Swiss and German settlers, and the place where Pepsi-Cola was invented in 1898.

subject: New Brighton Lifeboat Station
summary: On Kings Parade at the mouth of the Mersey, one of Britain's oldest lifeboat stations has stood watch over Liverpool Bay since the days when ships emptied their gunpowder before entering port.

subject: New Cumnock
summary: An Ayrshire mining village in the upper Afton Water valley with deep Wallace connections, a tragic colliery, and Burns's Parnassus Hill.

subject: New Echota
summary: The last capital of the Cherokee Nation before the Trail of Tears, where a people built a government, published a newspaper in their own syllabary, and signed a treaty that sealed their exile.

subject: New France
summary: A sprawling colonial empire built on fur and rivers rather than gold and conquest, New France stretched from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to the Mississippi Delta for over two centuries before vanishing almost entirely from the map.

subject: New Georgia
summary: The largest island in Solomon Islands' Western Province is a volcanic slab of jungle where medieval Roviana shrines, colonial missionaries, and the bloodiest jungle fighting of the Pacific war all left their marks within a single stretch of coast.

subject: New Guinea
summary: The world's second-largest island shelters more plant species than Madagascar, more languages than any other place on Earth, and a rainforest older than anyone can remember.

subject: New Guinea Highlands
summary: A 1,600-kilometer spine of mountains rising from Wondama Bay to Milne Bay, the Central Cordillera harbors birds of paradise, intermountain civilizations thousands of years old, and the last equatorial glaciers in Asia.

subject: New Guinea Mangroves
summary: Covering 26,800 square kilometers of coastline, the New Guinea mangroves harbor the greatest diversity of mangrove species on Earth — an underwater forest that breathes through snorkels and gives birth to live young.

subject: New Hanover County, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's second-smallest county by land area is also one of its most populous, most consequential, and most haunted - home to Wilmington, the Cape Fear River, and the only successful coup in American history.

story.title: New Harmony: Where Utopia Went to Die (Twice)

subject: New Harmony
summary: The Indiana town where two separate utopian communities collapsed in spectacular fashion - first the German Rappites who fled, then Robert Owen's socialist experiment that imploded in two years, leaving America's most educated ghost town.

subject: New Harmony
summary: The town two utopias built - where German pietists created a communal society in 1814, then sold it to Robert Owen for a socialist experiment in 1825, leaving behind Indiana's most architecturally significant village and a trail of failed idealism.

subject: New Harmony and America's Utopias
summary: The Indiana town that hosted two utopian experiments - first the German Harmonists building a perfect religious community, then Robert Owen's secular socialist experiment that failed in two years but seeded American reform movements.

story.title: New Haven: The Yale Town Where Pizza Became Apizza

subject: New Haven
summary: The Connecticut city dominated by Yale - where the university and the city have uneasy coexistence, where 'apizza' developed its own tradition, and where the Elm City struggles despite Ivy League presence.

story.title: New Haven: Yale's City and America's Pizza Capital

subject: New Haven
summary: The city that's been synonymous with Yale since 1718, where the New Haven pizza style rivals New York and Chicago, and where town and gown have coexisted uneasily for three centuries.

story.title: New Hellenic Radio, Internet and Television

subject: New Hellenic Radio, Internet and Television
summary: Born from the most controversial broadcasting blackout in modern European history, NERIT lasted barely thirteen months before the screens it replaced flickered back to life.

subject: New Ireland
summary: A long, narrow island where shark callers still sing their catch to the canoe, northern swells draw surfers, and cyclones never arrive because the equator is too close.

subject: New Ireland Province
summary: Formerly Neu-Mecklenburg under German rule and Nova Hibernia before that, this province of Papua New Guinea spans around 230,000 square kilometers of ocean and a scattering of islands where teak, gold, and Malagan carvings still define the land.

subject: New Jersey Audubon Society
summary: Founded in 1897 and fiercely independent from its national namesake, New Jersey Audubon runs hawk watches, nature centers, and the World Series of Birding from its headquarters in the Somerset County hills.

subject: New Jersey Brigade Encampment Site
summary: In the brutal winter of 1779-80, about 1,300 soldiers of the New Jersey Brigade camped separately from the main Continental Army at Jockey Hollow -- their fireplace remains still visible in the Bernardsville woods.

subject: New Lanark
summary: A cotton-mill village on the Clyde, founded in 1786 and transformed by Robert Owen into a working experiment in industry without misery — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: New Madrid seismic zone
summary: A buried ancient rift beneath the Mississippi Valley that produced four of the largest earthquakes in North American history, made the river flow backwards, and still threatens seven states today.

subject: New Mexico Pueblos
summary: Living history in adobe and stone - where nineteen Native American communities have continuously occupied their mesa-top villages since before Columbus, survived Spanish conquest and American expansion, and still practice traditions a thousand years old.

subject: New Moor
summary: An island born from a cyclone and claimed by two nations vanished beneath rising seas before either could settle the dispute, becoming a stark symbol of climate change.

story.title: New Orleans: The Crescent City Where Death Is a Party and the Party Never Ends

subject: New Orleans
summary: The Louisiana port city built below sea level - where jazz was born, where funerals become parades, where Hurricane Katrina killed 1,800 people, and where the good times roll despite everything that says they shouldn't.

story.title: New Orleans: The City That Care Forgot

subject: New Orleans
summary: The city where jazz was invented, where the dead are buried above ground, where Mardi Gras never really ends, and where Katrina's floodwaters couldn't drown a 300-year-old culture.

subject: New Providence
summary: The island the Lucayan people called Nema - 'middle-water' - became a pirate republic, a blockade-runner's haven, a rum-smuggling depot, and finally a tourist paradise holding nearly three-quarters of the Bahamas' population on 80 square miles of coral limestone.

subject: New Quay
summary: The pastel-painted Ceredigion town where Dylan Thomas drafted half of Under Milk Wood from a wooden bungalow with no running water.

subject: New Quay Lifeboat Station
summary: Born of one terrible October night in 1859, the New Quay lifeboat has answered the sea's calls for more than 160 years.

subject: New Rome
summary: When Constantine the Great refounded Byzantium as his imperial capital in 330 CE, he called it Nova Roma — New Rome — planting the idea that an empire's center of gravity could shift, and history could begin again.

subject: New Spitalfields Market
summary: Europe's leading horticultural wholesale market, New Spitalfields Market moved from its ancient East London home to a purpose-built site in Leyton in 1991, keeping London fed with exotic produce from around the world.

subject: New Territories
summary: Leased from Qing China for 99 years in 1898, the New Territories make up 86 percent of Hong Kong's land area — a landscape of walled villages, mountain country parks, and new towns that tells the whole arc of colonial and post-colonial history.

subject: New Territories, Hong Kong
summary: Leased from China in 1898 and often overlooked by visitors rushing between Hong Kong Island and Kowloon, the New Territories is where the colony's rural past still breathes—in walled villages, mountain trails, seafood harbors, and country parks that dwarf anything on the island.

subject: New Town, Edinburgh
summary: Edinburgh's New Town was built on drained swampland to stop wealthy Scots from fleeing to London -- and was partly funded by the profits of slavery in the Caribbean.

subject: New Westminster Salmonbellies
summary: A lacrosse club born on a cricket ground in 1888, named after an insult, and holder of more national championships than any team in the sport.

subject: New Xade
summary: The G/ui and G//ana San who were moved here named their new home Kg'oesakene - "looking for life" - after the government relocated them out of the Central Kalahari.

story.title: New York City: The Capital of Everything Except America

subject: New York City
summary: The five-borough metropolis that was bought for beads and became the world's capital - where Ellis Island processed millions, where Wall Street crashed civilization, and where 8 million people living atop each other created a culture unlike anywhere else on Earth.

subject: New York City Subway
summary: The world's largest subway system by station count, running 472 stations across four boroughs around the clock since 1904 -- a city beneath a city, carrying billions of riders through a labyrinth of tunnels that never sleeps.

subject: Newark Light Rail
summary: Buried beneath Newark's streets runs a rail line born from a filled-in canal, adorned with Art Deco murals, and stitching together a city's past and present.

subject: Newark water crisis
summary: When Newark's aging lead pipes began poisoning the city's drinking water in 2016, more than 200,000 residents faced contamination levels that exceeded federal safety limits -- and the contractor hired to fix the problem faked the work at 1,500 properties.

subject: Newbattle
summary: A Midlothian village whose name means 'new building' in Old Scots - and which has been rebuilding itself, sometimes from the ground up, since King David I planted Cistercian monks here in 1140.

subject: Newberry Springs, California
summary: A Route 66 desert community where summer temperatures average 107°F, the Bagdad Café became an international film location, and one of the largest aquifers in the American West runs deep beneath the sand.

subject: Newbiggin Lifeboat Station
summary: The oldest boathouse still operated by the RNLI, on the Northumberland coast - founded in 1851 after a storm drowned fourteen fishermen, manned by miners and dragged into the sea by 25 women in waders.

subject: Newborough Warren
summary: One of the largest dune systems in the British Isles, half-buried under a Corsican pine plantation that may be slowly drying out the very wetlands it was planted to protect.

subject: Newborough, Anglesey
summary: A planted town founded in 1303 by exiled Welsh families forcibly relocated by Edward I - now a quiet village beside the largest dune system in the British Isles.

subject: Newcastle Emlyn
summary: A small market town on a loop of the Teifi where, in 1718, the first permanent printing press in Wales started turning out books, and where local legend insists a wyvern was once shot down with the help of a red cloak.

subject: Newcastle West
summary: A 13th-century Earl of Desmond's banqueting hall still stands in the middle of a Limerick market town whose crest carries a wild boar - and where the river Arra runs past a stone bridge known as the Bridge of Tears.

subject: Newcastle upon Tyne
summary: A Geordie city on the north bank of the Tyne where Roman supply trains, medieval coal cartels, Victorian shipyards and Saudi-owned football collide in a single street grid.

subject: Newcastle upon Tyne
summary: The Tyneside city whose international ties reach from Atlanta to Bergen to Haifa, and whose sister-city ledger stretches back to a 1948 agreement with Gelsenkirchen.

subject: Newhall Incident
summary: In less than thirty minutes on a spring night in 1970, four young California Highway Patrol officers were killed in a Valencia shootout that permanently changed how police are trained across America.

subject: Newman
summary: A town built from scratch by a steel company beside the world's largest iron pit - named for a surveyor who died young, on land the Martu have known for 45,000 years.

subject: Newmarket, Suffolk
summary: The global headquarters of thoroughbred racing, Newmarket hosts more than 3,500 racehorses, 50 miles of turf gallops, and a history of royal obsession stretching back to James I — who first arrived in 1605, described it as a 'poor little village,' and immediately saw its potential.

subject: Newmilns
summary: A small Ayrshire weaving village whose emigrant lace workers helped introduce football to Sweden by founding Örgryte IS - and which still holds a Covenanter memorial in its parish churchyard.

subject: Newport Lifeboat Station
summary: A lifeboat station that operated for just ten years at the mouth of the River Nevern, dispatched only a handful of rescues, and closed in 1894 with a one-line entry in the minutes of an RNLI committee meeting.

subject: Newport Medieval Ship
summary: A 15th-century Basque-built merchant ship, lost while being repaired at Newport in 1469, rediscovered in June 2002 when construction workers dug into the riverbank to build an arts centre.

subject: Newport News Shipbuilding
summary: The sole builder of America's nuclear aircraft carriers and one of only two submarine manufacturers for the U.S. Navy, Newport News Shipbuilding has launched more than 800 vessels since delivering its first tugboat in 1891.

subject: Newport News, Virginia
summary: The city built by a California railroad magnate to load coal onto ships, that now builds every nuclear aircraft carrier in the U.S. Navy and probes the fundamental structure of matter at the Thomas Jefferson Lab.

subject: Newquay
summary: A medieval fishing harbour on the Cornish north coast that became Britain's surfing capital, and is now also trying to be its spaceport.

subject: Newry
summary: An Irish border city whose Gaelic name means "the yew tree at the head of the strand," and which still draws euro-armed shoppers north through what locals call the Newry effect.

story.title: Newton Burial Ground: The Lives Beneath the Cane Fields

subject: Newton Slave Burial Ground
summary: An unassuming site beside a former sugar plantation in Barbados holds the remains of more than 570 enslaved people, whose burial practices reveal the African cultural traditions they sustained across generations of bondage.

subject: Newtown Creek
summary: A 3.5-mile estuary between Brooklyn and Queens that went from pastoral waterway to petroleum capital to one of America's most contaminated Superfund sites.

subject: Nexus Instituut
summary: A small Dutch think-tank that has somehow persuaded Susan Sontag, Jurgen Habermas, Mario Vargas Llosa, Patti Smith, and Emmanuel Macron to come argue about Europe in front of an audience.

subject: Neßmersiel
summary: A small East Frisian harbor village whose port has been rebuilt and relocated three times as the sea retreated and the silt closed in.

subject: Ng Tung Chai
summary: A small Hakka village on the slopes of Hong Kong's highest peak is the gateway to a cascade of waterfalls — including the Main Fall, considered the highest in Hong Kong at 35 metres — set inside one of the territory's most botanically rich ravines.

subject: Nga Tsin Wai Tsuen
summary: Kowloon's last walled village — a settlement tracing its roots to the 14th century and its walls to 1724 — was cleared of its final residents in January 2016 to make way for two high-rise towers, ending more than six centuries of continuous habitation.

subject: Ngarrabullgan
summary: An immense sandstone mesa west of Cairns, sacred to the Djungan people and home to some of the oldest evidence of human life in Australia, where the archaeological record and Aboriginal tradition tell the same story of a mountain left to its spirit.

subject: Ngga Pulu
summary: For most of human memory this ice-capped summit was the highest point between the Himalaya and the Andes. The glacier melted. The title moved.

subject: Ngoc Hoi
summary: A small Vietnamese border town at the junction of three nations — the last stop before Laos, with buses to Hanoi and Attapeu and the unhurried pace of a place that has always been a gateway rather than a destination.

subject: Ngorongoro Conservation Area
summary: The world's largest unbroken caldera -- 21 kilometers across and 600 meters deep -- where lions prowl at the highest density on Earth and the Leakeys unearthed fossils that rewrote human origins.

subject: Ngualla
summary: A billion-year-old collapsed volcano in remote southwest Tanzania holds 1.6 million tonnes of rare earth oxides - enough to matter to the global battery and wind-turbine economy.

subject: Ngukurr
summary: On the banks of the Roper River in southern Arnhem Land, Ngukurr holds the weight of eight endangered languages, a century of mission history, and a remarkable community that turned survival into culture.

subject: Ngwenya Mine
summary: On a hematite ridge in western Eswatini lies Lion Cavern, where people dug red ochre out of the rock more than 40,000 years ago - making Ngwenya the oldest known mine on Earth.

subject: Ngọc Linh
summary: At 2,598 metres, Ngọc Linh is the highest point of southern Vietnam — a summit that harbors a rare ginseng found nowhere else on earth, two frog species unknown to science until this century, and a name that the Jeh-Tariang people gave long before any map was drawn.

subject: Nha Trang
summary: Vietnam's most celebrated seaside city — a bay shaped by Cham civilization, adopted by French colonists, R&R'd by American soldiers, and now claimed simultaneously by Russian retirees, Vietnamese families, and the country's entire scuba diving industry.

subject: Nhialdiu
summary: A Leek Nuer village at a strategic crossroads in Unity State, Nhialdiu has absorbed wave after wave of displaced neighbors while its own farmlands went quiet under the shadow of oil-road warfare.

subject: Nhulunbuy
summary: The largest town in east Arnhem Land, built in the 1970s for a bauxite refinery on Yolngu land, named for a sacred hill, and now reinventing itself after the refinery closed and rockets began flying from the country next door.

subject: Niagassola
summary: A small Guinean town with no electricity and three water pumps guards one of West Africa's most precious objects: the Sosso-Bala, the sacred balafon of the Mali Empire, named a UNESCO Masterpiece of human heritage.

subject: Niani, Guinea
summary: A quiet village on the Sankarani River that many scholars believe was the capital of the medieval Mali Empire, the seat of Mansa Musa, the richest man the world had ever seen.

subject: Nibe
summary: Nibe put three herring on its coat of arms, built a town on them for five centuries, and lost them completely by 1828.

subject: Nice
summary: Where the Riviera invented itself for tourists and artists chased the light, where the Promenade des Anglais curves along azure water and the Old Town hides Italianate lanes.

story.title: Nichelini Winery: Bootleggers, Miners, and Seven Generations of Wine

subject: Nichelini Winery
summary: Napa Valley's oldest continuously family-owned winery has survived Prohibition through bootlegging, outlasted every industry trend, and is now in its seventh generation of winemakers.

subject: Nickel mining in Western Australia
summary: From a 1966 discovery near Kambalda to the most notorious share bubble in Australian history and the modern battery-metal bust, the story of an industry built on boom and reckoning.

story.title: Nicky Verstappen: Twenty Years on the Brunssummerheide

subject: Nicky Verstappen
summary: An eleven-year-old boy vanished from a summer camp tent on the Brunssummerheide in 1998. The Limburg heath kept the secret for two decades until the largest DNA screening in Dutch history finally produced an answer for his family.

subject: Nicopolis
summary: Augustus built Nicopolis — the City of Victory — on the Epirote shore where he had defeated Antony and Cleopatra, and for eight centuries it stood as a Roman capital, a philosophical school, a Christian see, and a crossroads of the Mediterranean world.

subject: Niederfinow Boat Lift
summary: Germany's oldest working boat lift has been carrying barges 36 metres straight up a Brandenburg hillside since 1934 — and since 2022 it has had a much larger successor standing beside it.

subject: Niemba ambush
summary: On 8 November 1960, an Irish UN patrol was ambushed near Niemba in the Congo, killing nine soldiers and marking Ireland's bloodiest day in peacekeeping history.

subject: Nieuwe Vaart
summary: A canal dug in 1649 to stop Amsterdam's eastern harbor from silting up - and the waterway where, a hundred and fifty years later, ship's carpenters raised a drawbridge against their own government.

subject: Nigg Stone
summary: One of the finest Pictish carved stones in Europe, shattered in the eighteenth century and pieced back together with a fragment recovered from a stream.

subject: Nii-jima
summary: A volcanic Tokyo island of white rhyolite cliffs, exile cemeteries, world-class glass art, and a hot spring built like a Greek ruin -- all two hours by jet boat from Shibuya.

subject: Niigata-Yakeyama
summary: One of Japan's youngest volcanoes, only 3,100 years old, whose lava dome sits so close to the Sea of Japan coast that pyroclastic flows from its major eruptions have reached the shoreline.

subject: Nijkerk
summary: A small Gelderland town that exported governors to New Netherland, tobacco merchants to Amsterdam, and a Nobel laureate to medical history.

subject: Nijmegen
summary: Holland's oldest city, where Roman legionaries once watched the Waal, now hosts the largest walking march on Earth.

story.title: Nikko: Where a Shogun Became a God

subject: Nikko
summary: A mountain town north of Tokyo where the dying wish of Japan's most powerful shogun created one of the world's most ornate sacred complexes -- and where three small carved monkeys upstage it all.

subject: Nikolaiviertel
summary: East Germany rebuilt Berlin's medieval heart for the city's 750th birthday — part salvaged fact, part concrete panel, and entirely honest about neither until you look closely.

subject: Niland, California
summary: A small community near the Salton Sea whose proximity to Slab City, Salvation Mountain, and a wandering mud geyser has made it an unlikely landmark in California's off-grid geography.

subject: Nile
summary: The river along which civilization invented itself - 6,695 kilometers from Lake Victoria and the Ethiopian highlands to Rosetta on the Mediterranean, crossing eleven nations and five thousand years of human history.

subject: Nim Li Punit
summary: A Maya city named 'Big Hat' after the towering headdress on one of its carved stelae, where astronomers tracked solstices and jaguars still roam the surrounding jungle.

subject: Nimba Range
summary: A narrow Precambrian ridge straddling three nations, the Nimba Range is home to the world's only truly viviparous toad and one of West Africa's richest concentrations of endemic species.

subject: Nimbin
summary: A tiny dairy village reborn as Australia's countercultural capital, Nimbin trades in rainbow murals, hemp activism and the lush caldera country of the Rainbow Region.

subject: Nimbin Rocks
summary: Dramatic volcanic spires rising from the valley floor near Nimbin, the Nimbin Rocks are a deeply sacred site of the Bundjalung people, associated with the Clever Men.

subject: Nindowari
summary: An archaeological site in the hills of Balochistan where the Harappan and Kulli civilizations overlapped, offering evidence that one of South Asia's earliest cultures may have branched from the Indus Valley tradition.

subject: Nine Standards Rigg
summary: Nine stone cairns of mysterious origin crown a Pennine summit above the watershed where England's rivers split toward two seas.

subject: Ninepin Group
summary: A cluster of 29 uninhabited islands in Hong Kong's easternmost waters, the Ninepin Group's towering hexagonal rock columns were shaped by a volcanic eruption 140 million years ago and are now protected as part of Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark.

subject: Ningaloo Coast
summary: Australia's largest fringing reef hugs the remote Gascoyne coast so closely that visitors wade in from the beach to swim alongside whale sharks.

subject: Ningaloo Coast
summary: A 705,015-hectare World Heritage Site where Australia's largest fringing coral reef meets one of the continent's most remote and pristine coastlines.

subject: Ningaloo Station
summary: The remote sheep station that lent its name — an old Aboriginal word for the land jutting into the sea — to one of the world's great fringing reefs, and whose campers later rallied to keep its coastline in local hands.

subject: Ninhue
summary: A quiet farming commune in the hills of Ñuble that gave Chile its greatest naval hero — and a phrase about courage that the whole country still repeats.

subject: Niono
summary: A town built by water that was engineered to flow there, Niono is the hub of the Office du Niger - a colonial-era irrigation scheme that turned dry plains into the rice basket of Mali.

subject: Nioro du Sahel
summary: A Sahelian town that was once the capital of a Bambara kingdom and is now one of West Africa's great Sufi pilgrimage centers, drawing thousands each year to the seat of the Hamawiyya brotherhood.

subject: Nipissing First Nation
summary: At the crossroads of two great watersheds on the north shore of Lake Nipissing, the Nbisiing Anishinaabeg have been master traders, diplomats, and survivors for centuries -- from fur-trade wars to the first Aboriginal constitution in Ontario.

subject: Nipponbashi
summary: Osaka's Den Den Town, where Edo-period merchant streets transformed into a neon-lit paradise for electronics haggling, anime shopping, maid cafes, and one of Japan's largest cosplay festivals.

subject: Nippur
summary: The sacred city where Sumerian kings came to legitimize their rule, Nippur held no armies and conquered no territory -- yet no monarch could claim to be king without its blessing.

subject: Niquelândia
summary: In 1938 a German miner panning for gold stumbled onto the second-largest nickel deposit in the world, and a small town founded in the bandeirante era became Brazil's Nickeland.

story.title: Nisa: The Forgotten Capital of the Parthian Empire

subject: Nisa, Turkmenistan
summary: Founded around 250 BC as the first seat of the Arsacid dynasty, the fortress city of Nisa blended Greek art with Iranian tradition at the crossroads of the ancient world before an earthquake erased it from the landscape -- only for archaeologists to uncover its ivory rhytons and Hellenistic treasures two millennia later.

subject: Nishan Reservoir
summary: Known as Confucius Lake and Sacred Water Lake, this reservoir southeast of Qufu was built in under two years during the Great Leap Forward and remains the largest in the Jining region.

subject: Nishapur
summary: Once among the greatest cities on the Silk Road, Nishapur gave the world Omar Khayyam, Attar's mystical poetry, and turquoise mined from the earth for seven millennia.

subject: Nitro, West Virginia
summary: An entire West Virginia town built in 1918 to make gunpowder for World War One - then handed to the chemical industry, with consequences that lasted a century.

subject: Niuheliang
summary: A 5,500-year-old Neolithic ceremonial complex in Liaoning Province, Niuheliang holds the remains of the Hongshan culture's Goddess Temple, jade-eyed clay figurines, and a pyramid that predates Egypt's by millennia.

subject: Niujie
summary: Beijing's oldest Muslim quarter, where Hui culture has thrived since the armies of Genghis Khan brought Islam to the capital eight centuries ago.

subject: Niumatou Site
summary: Where Taiwan's oldest known central civilization left stone hoes in the earth 4,000 years ago — a Neolithic settlement that gave its ancient indigenous name to the coast of Taichung.

subject: Niyamgiri
summary: Where a tribal community told a multinational mining corporation no - and where India's Supreme Court said the hills belonged to the people who worship them.

subject: Nizhny Novgorod Cableway
summary: Stretching 3,660 meters across the Volga River on 82-meter masts, the Nizhny Novgorod Cableway is one of Europe's longest gondola lifts over water, carrying nearly two million passengers in its first year alone.

subject: Nizhny Novgorod Fair
summary: Once the largest marketplace in the Russian Empire, the Nizhny Novgorod Fair drew merchants from India, Iran, and Central Asia to the banks of the Volga for nearly four centuries.

subject: Nizhyn
summary: A Cossack trading town on the Oster where a young Gogol went to school, a Greek merchant colony grew rich, and the pickle became a point of pride.

subject: Nişantaşı
summary: Istanbul's most elegant uptown quarter takes its name from Ottoman archery targets — stones that once marked where sultans' arrows landed — and has been a crossroads of writers, exiles, diplomats, and fashion ever since.

subject: Niʻihau
summary: Hawaii's 'Forbidden Isle' is a privately owned island where 84 residents speak Hawaiian as their first language, live rent-free, and have maintained a way of life largely unchanged since the 19th century.

subject: Noah's Ark (Hong Kong)
summary: A full-size replica of Noah's Ark on Ma Wan Island — an evangelical theme park built by Hong Kong's most powerful property developers that became the centerpiece of a landmark corruption scandal.

subject: Nob Hill, San Francisco
summary: The San Francisco neighborhood that was once home to the railroad barons and is now defined by luxury hotels built on the ruins of their mansions.

subject: Nobatia
summary: A Christian Nubian kingdom in what is now southern Egypt whose archers shot with thumb rings like their Persian and Chinese counterparts, whose temples were converted to churches painted with new saints, and whose cavalry king rode into battle spearing Blemmyes.

subject: Nobel Foundation
summary: The institution born from dynamite profits that has honored humanity's greatest minds for over a century.

subject: Nobles Emigrant Trail
summary: A carpenter from Minnesota stumbled onto a better route to California while searching for a legendary gold lake that did not exist.

subject: Noisebridge
summary: An anarchist hackerspace in the Mission District where anyone can walk in and use the tools, the network runs on consensus, and the only rule is be excellent to each other.

subject: Nokia, Finland
summary: The town that gave the world's most famous Finnish brand its name is itself named after a fur animal that probably never lived here — and has always refused to put up a monument to the company.

subject: Nome and the Iditarod Finish
summary: The remote Alaska town where mushers finish the 1,000-mile Iditarod sled dog race - the same town saved from diphtheria in 1925 by relay dog teams whose desperate run inspired the race, including the famous lead dog Balto.

subject: Nonesuch Mine
summary: A ghost town in Michigan's Porcupine Mountains where millions of pounds of copper lay trapped in sandstone that no one could profitably extract - until someone finally did, three miles away and forty years too late.

subject: Nooitgedacht Glacial Pavements
summary: Between Kimberley and Barkly West, ancient rock pavements scoured smooth by 300-million-year-old glaciers became canvases for Stone Age artists, then yielded 80,000 diamonds from their gravels.

subject: Nooksack Giant
summary: A Douglas-fir felled near Maple Falls in 1896 taped out at 465 feet - eighty-five feet taller than the tallest tree alive today, and the measurement has been argued over ever since.

subject: Nooksack, Washington
summary: A small Whatcom County city named for a river it does not sit on, where a logging photographer met his wife and where both are buried.

subject: Noonkanbah Station
summary: A Kimberley cattle station where a 1980 convoy of drilling rigs escorted by hundreds of police forced its way onto Aboriginal sacred land, making Noonkanbah a turning point in Australian land rights history.

subject: Noordhollandsch Kanaal
summary: When silt strangled Amsterdam's harbor, the Dutch dug a 75-kilometer detour for ocean-going ships - and twelve horses towed a 44-gun frigate inland to prove it worked.

subject: Noormarkku
summary: A former Satakunta municipality, swallowed by Pori in 2010, where three generations of the Ahlström family built three houses — the last of them now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Nootka Sound
summary: The waterway between Vancouver Island and Nootka Island where four empires collided over fur, sovereignty, and the future of the Pacific Northwest -- and where a lonely orca once captivated a nation.

subject: Nora, Italy
summary: On a narrow peninsula near Cagliari, the ruins of Nora tell a story spanning Phoenician traders, Carthaginian power, and Roman ambition -- while the Mediterranean slowly reclaims the city from below.

subject: Norddeich Radio Station
summary: For 91 years the call sign DAN carried voices across the world's oceans, from spark-gap transmitters in 1907 to its final shutdown on New Year's Eve 1998.

subject: Norddorf
summary: A North Frisian village that lost its harbour to drifting sand and its thatched roofs to a single fire, and somehow became one of Schleswig-Holstein's busiest resorts.

subject: Norden, Lower Saxony
summary: The oldest town in East Frisia made its name on a grain spirit so smooth it became a household word - and on a 17th-century organ heard around the world.

subject: Nordhorn
summary: A border town on the Vechte that turned itself, in a single century, from inland port to textile boomtown to handball arena and bike-trail capital.

subject: Nordkalottleden
summary: An 800-kilometer hiking trail threading through three countries above the Arctic Circle, where the path crosses borders more often than it crosses roads.

subject: Nordnorsk Kunstmuseum
summary: Norway's Museum of the Year 2017 began as a telegraph office, became a police station, and now houses the art of a region where the light itself is the first masterpiece.

story.title: Norfolk: The Navy's Capital Where the Fleet Calls Home

subject: Norfolk
summary: The Virginia port city that hosts the world's largest naval base - where aircraft carriers line the waterfront, where the Navy has been present since 1917, and where sea level rise threatens everything the military built.

subject: Norfolk
summary: The English county where Boudica raised her revolt, where the wool trade built medieval cathedrals, and where the USAAF Eighth Air Force fought half its war from quiet farms.

subject: Norfolk, Virginia
summary: A 1682 seaport at the mouth of the Chesapeake became the world's largest naval base and a city whose downtown sits inches above an ocean that keeps rising.

subject: Norham
summary: A Northumbrian border village beneath a famous ruin, where Edward I once decided the future king of Scotland and J. M. W. Turner found the subject that made his career.

subject: Norilsk
summary: A closed city above the Arctic Circle where gulag prisoners built one of the world's largest nickel mines, and where 175,000 people live surrounded by chemical smog, frozen tundra, and some of the highest salaries in Russia.

subject: Norilsk
summary: The world's northernmost major city, built by gulag prisoners on top of vast nickel deposits, where 176,000 people endure polar night, extreme pollution, and total isolation from Russia's road network.

subject: Norman Studios
summary: The last surviving silent film studio from Jacksonville's forgotten era as America's original movie capital, where a white filmmaker from rural Florida produced groundbreaking films with all-Black casts.

subject: Norman's Cay
summary: A tiny Exuma island that served as the Medellin Cartel's Caribbean transshipment hub, where a sunken drug plane still rests in the shallows and the Fyre Festival's promotional lies began.

subject: Normanton
summary: The largest town in Queensland's Gulf Country, where a life-size replica of the biggest crocodile ever shot guards the park, a purple pub anchors the main street, and the one-of-a-kind Gulflander rolls out across flood-proof steel.

subject: Norra Storfjället
summary: The highest ground in Västerbotten, split by a glacial valley that is one of Swedish Lapland's landmarks — and whose South Sámi name became the title of a film about what Sweden did to Sámi children.

subject: Norrard Rocks
summary: A scatter of granite islets west of Bryher where storm-petrels nest in burrows and humans are forbidden to land.

subject: Norris Wright Cuney
summary: Born enslaved on a Texas plantation, Norris Wright Cuney rose to become the highest-ranking Black federal appointee in the post-Civil War South, transforming Galveston's docks and the Texas Republican Party from the inside out.

subject: North Bend Rail Trail
summary: Seventy-two miles of converted Baltimore and Ohio rail bed unwind across north-central West Virginia, threading hikers and cyclists through thirteen tunnels and over thirty-six bridges between Parkersburg and Wolf Summit.

subject: North Bend, Washington
summary: A small Cascade foothills town where David Lynch found the otherworldly backdrop for Twin Peaks, and weekend hikers find the first serious mountains within reach of Seattle.

subject: North Berwick
summary: A medieval royal burgh on the Firth of Forth that became Scotland's most expensive seaside town, famous for witch trials, gannet colonies, and golf courses older than most countries.

subject: North Berwick Lifeboat Station
