summary: A small inshore lifeboat station on Victoria Road, founded after a Victorian shipwreck and reborn in 1967 thanks to around 250,000 paperback books donated by Blue Peter viewers.

subject: North Borneo
summary: A territory carved from the concessions of two sultans, administered by a chartered company, occupied by Japan, and finally absorbed into Malaysia as the state of Sabah.

subject: North Brabant
summary: The Catholic, Burgundian-flavored Dutch province where Carnival is sacred, Van Gogh learned to draw, and five big cities anchor an economy that quietly punches third in the Netherlands.

subject: North Cape (New Zealand)
summary: New Zealand's true northernmost point -- a volcanic headland where serpentine cliffs host plants found nowhere else on earth, guarded by an electrified fence against introduced predators.

subject: North Cape (Norway)
summary: A 307-meter cliff on the island of Mageroya where the Atlantic meets the Arctic Ocean, the North Cape has drawn travelers to Europe's symbolic northern edge since an English sea captain named it in 1553.

subject: North Carolina Mountains
summary: The southern Blue Ridge — the highest, deepest, and oldest mountain country east of the Mississippi, with more plant diversity per acre than all of Europe.

subject: North Channel Naval Duel
summary: On 24 April 1778, John Paul Jones captured the Royal Navy sloop Drake in the waters off Belfast Lough in the first American naval victory in British home waters.

subject: North China Plain
summary: China's largest alluvial plain and the cradle of Chinese civilization -- 409,500 square kilometers of fertile flatland shaped by the Yellow River's silt, floods, and millennia of human ambition.

subject: North Coast 500
summary: A 516-mile loop around Scotland's northern Highlands - a route that has always existed in pieces but only became a brand, and a problem, in 2015.

subject: North Coast 500
summary: A 516-mile scenic route around the north Highlands of Scotland, launched in 2015 and quickly reshaping the economies and traffic patterns of every village it touches.

subject: North Cotes
summary: A Lincolnshire coastal village whose thirteenth-century church is best known across the English-speaking world as the name of a hymn tune by its long-serving Victorian rector.

subject: North Cowichan
summary: A district municipality of 32,000 that owns six mountains and a logging operation, and whose best-known town answered a mill closure by covering itself in paintings.

subject: North Darfur
summary: The largest state of Sudan's Darfur region, former seat of the Sultanate of Darfur, now the epicenter of RSF atrocities in the current civil war after the fall of El Fasher in October 2025.

subject: North Devon Coast
summary: Designated in 1959, England's first AONB in Devon: 171 square kilometres of cliffs, dunes, surf beaches, and a UNESCO biosphere from Combe Martin to the Cornish border.

subject: North Frisian language
summary: A severely endangered language of Germany's North Sea coast, spoken by a few thousand people across ten dialects so distinct that neighbours a ferry ride apart can struggle to understand each other.

subject: North Halmahera Regency
summary: A regency of white beaches, coral reefs, and active volcanoes on Indonesia's most oddly shaped island, where a centuries-old pact between Muslims and Christians shattered in 1999.

subject: North Holland
summary: The province that gave the world tulips, Edam, Vermeer's hometown country, and a Manhattan-shaped polder - all packed onto a peninsula reclaimed from a lost inland sea.

subject: North Hollywood shootout
summary: The 1997 gunbattle between two heavily armored bank robbers and LAPD officers transformed American law enforcement, as news helicopters broadcast 44 minutes of sustained combat that outgunned every officer on scene.

subject: North Iceland
summary: Iceland in miniature - a region of volcanic craters, whale-filled fjords, and the Arctic Circle's edge, where Icelandic horses gallop across lush valleys beneath glacier-capped peaks.

subject: North Maluku
summary: An Indonesian province built on the ruins of four spice sultanates, where Portuguese forts crumble beside volcanic peaks and the Coral Triangle's richest waters lap at shores that once drew empires.

subject: North Nicosia
summary: The capital of an unrecognized country, divided by a UN buffer zone since 1974, where two communities still measure daily life against what they lost.

subject: North Point
summary: A dense, layered district on Hong Kong Island's northeastern shore that reinvented itself twice — first as a Shanghai-in-exile, then as a Fujianese enclave — and was briefly the most densely populated place on Earth.

subject: North Queensferry
summary: A Fife village a thousand years old, the world's smallest working lighthouse, and three of the great bridges of British engineering meeting the shore at the same point.

subject: North Sea Flood of 1953
summary: On the night of 31 January 1953, a spring tide and a North Sea hurricane drowned 1,836 people in the Netherlands, 307 in England, and hundreds more at sea — and changed how a country lives with water.

subject: North Shields
summary: A North Tyneside town that grew on a narrow riverside ledge and a high plateau, where Stan Laurel grew up, the herring fleet docked, and the Meadow Well riots changed council housing.

subject: North Shields Fish Quay
summary: A fishing port founded in 1225 as a cluster of shielings beside the mouth of the Tyne, today the largest English port for prawns.

subject: North Shore (British Columbia)
summary: Where Vancouver's glass towers meet dramatic mountains, the North Shore offers suspension bridges over canyon depths, Olympic ski venues, and the infamous Grouse Grind.

subject: North Shore, California
summary: A small community on the Salton Sea's northeastern shore where two centuries of California history converge — from Spanish expeditions to WWII training grounds to a 100-megawatt solar farm.

subject: North Somercotes
summary: A Lincolnshire marsh village whose name still records its Anglo-Saxon function - summer pasture - and whose nearest neighbour is a beach where grey seal pups are born each winter.

subject: North Star Mine and Powerhouse
summary: The second-largest gold producer of California's Gold Rush era pioneered hydroelectric power with the world's largest Pelton wheel, now preserved as a California Historical Landmark.

subject: North Sulawesi
summary: A province where two-thirds of the population is Christian in a Muslim-majority nation, where 30,000-year-old cave sites sit alongside world-class dive reefs, and where the northernmost island of Indonesia stares across at the Philippines.

subject: North Uist
summary: Twenty miles by twenty-five of low boggy land scattered with hundreds of lochans, where the wind ruffles the marram grass on summer beaches and the winter sky goes wild with stars.

subject: North West 200
summary: Three Northern Irish towns become a closed-roads racing circuit one weekend a year, where motorcycles touch 208 mph past front gardens lined with hay bales.

subject: North West Highlands Geopark
summary: Scotland's first UNESCO geopark contains rocks three billion years old, the first thrust fault ever discovered, and caves that have sheltered humans since the Mesolithic.

subject: North Wilkesboro Speedway
summary: An asymmetrical 0.625-mile oval where Enoch Staley built NASCAR's spiritual home in 1947, watched the sport leave for Texas in 1996, and where a 2023 All-Star Race brought Cup cars back after 27 years of abandonment.

subject: North York Moors
summary: An English national park holding one of the largest expanses of heather moorland in the United Kingdom, carved by Jurassic seas, glacial meltwater, and centuries of monastic sheep.

subject: North-Western Province, Zambia
summary: The emptiest province in Zambia - 20 people per square kilometer across an area larger than Greece - where the continental watershed splits rivers between the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean, and where the Luvale still make fire each July at a UNESCO-recognized ceremony.

subject: Northampton
summary: The town the British call The Shoe Town, where Doctor Martens were born, the Beatles played twice, and the football club is called The Cobblers.

subject: Northamptonshire
summary: The English county called 'the rose of the shires' for its stately homes, country churches and rolling middle-country landscape, where George Washington's ancestors farmed and Formula One engines are now built.

subject: Northeast (Brazil)
summary: Nine states of sunny beaches, colonial cities, Afro-Brazilian culture, and dry sertão interior - the region where Portuguese colonization began and where the modern country most visibly carries its roots.

subject: Northern Aegean
summary: The Northern Aegean — Kuzey Ege — is where olive groves climb to pine forests, ancient city-states gave way to Greek and Ottoman shoreline towns, and Mount Ida still watches over a gulf that Homer knew.

subject: Northern Bahr el Ghazal
summary: A Dinka heartland of floodplains and tropical savanna, Northern Bahr el Ghazal carries the scars of the Sudanese railway raids and annual floods, yet remains fiercely defined by the resilience of Aweil's people.

subject: Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation
summary: Home to over 6,000 Cheyenne people who walked a thousand miles to reclaim their homeland, this Montana reservation stands as testament to a nation that refused to die in exile.

subject: Northern Circars
summary: A narrow coastal strip along the Bay of Bengal that passed through Mughal, Golconda, and British hands, the Northern Circars shaped the map of southern India for centuries.

subject: Northern Dvina
summary: One of Russia's great northern rivers, the Northern Dvina flows 744 kilometers from Veliky Ustyug to the White Sea at Arkhangelsk, draining a basin the size of Germany and carrying eight centuries of trade, exploration, and conflict in its current.

story.title: Northern Dynasties Tombs of Ci County

subject: Northern Dynasties tombs of Ci County
summary: A cluster of royal tombs near Handan containing thousands of pottery figurines reveals the artistic ambition and political complexity of China's Eastern Wei and Northern Qi dynasties.

subject: Northern Ireland
summary: A territory of 1.9 million people, drawn from two communities that for a century could not agree on what to call the place they shared - now finding a complicated peace.

subject: Northern Ireland Assembly
summary: The 90-seat devolved legislature created by the Good Friday Agreement that meets at Stormont, requires power-sharing by design, and has spent more than seven of its first 28 years suspended.

subject: Northern Ireland Executive
summary: The mandatory power-sharing cabinet that runs Northern Ireland - eight ministers drawn from across the unionist and nationalist blocs, designed so that no community can be excluded and any party can collapse the whole thing by walking out.

subject: Northern Netherlands
summary: Three provinces - Friesland, Groningen and Drenthe - that the rest of the Netherlands considers remote, where a once-a-generation ice-skating marathon binds eleven cities together and the entire country waits all winter to see if the canals will freeze.

subject: Northern Oregon Coast
summary: Where the Pacific meets the Cascades - a dramatic coastline of sea stacks, haystack rocks, and misty headlands stretching from the Columbia River to the Cape Perpetua wilderness.

subject: Northern Red Sea region
summary: Eritrea's coastal province stretches along three quarters of the Red Sea's western shore, cradling the ancient port of Massawa and the 209 islands of the Dahlak Archipelago.

subject: Northern Sudan
summary: The three northern states of Sudan -- Northern, Red Sea, and River Nile -- encompass the ancient Kerma, Napata, and Meroe heartlands plus the Red Sea coral reefs of the Sanganeb Marine National Park.

story.title: Northern Territories of the Gold Coast

subject: Northern Territories of the Gold Coast
summary: A British protectorate covering present-day northern Ghana from 1901 to 1957, administered from Gambaga under treaties that would dissolve on the day Ghana became a nation.

subject: Northwestern Andean Montane Forests
summary: Three hundred species of flowering plants can crowd into a single hectare of these Andean cloud forests - half of them growing nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Norwich
summary: The capital of Norfolk, a two-cathedral medieval city with a tradition of political radicalism, the largest permanent outdoor market in Europe, and an unfair reputation as a Norfolk backwater.

subject: Norwich Market
summary: One of the largest and oldest outdoor markets in Britain, Norwich Market has operated on the same site for over 900 years — surviving the Black Death, royal transfers, and a controversial 2003 rebuilding proposal — its brightly coloured stalls flanked by a 15th-century guildhall and a 1930s city hall.

subject: Nos. 600–626 Shanghai Street
summary: Ten pre-war shophouses in Mong Kok, built in the 1920s and 1930s, that survived colonial redevelopment and carry the architectural logic of an older Hong Kong — narrow-fronted, arcade-covered, still occupied.

subject: Nosy Be
summary: Madagascar's premier resort island, where chameleons outnumber tourists, the main town is named Hell-Ville, and a constellation of satellite islands offers everything from lemur encounters to world-class diving.

subject: Nosy Boraha
summary: A narrow island off Madagascar's east coast where pirate captains once anchored between raids on East Indies treasure ships, and where humpback whales now breach in the warm channel waters each winter.

subject: Nosy Komba
summary: A volcanic island off Madagascar's northwest coast where black lemurs are protected by villagers, a colonial sanatorium once treated malaria-stricken troops, and shade-grown coffee plantations have accidentally become wildlife refuges.

subject: Nosy Mangabe
summary: A tiny rainforest island in Antongil Bay became a last refuge for the aye-aye - the lemur many feared as an omen of death - and keeps four centuries of Dutch sailors' graffiti carved into its shoreline rocks.

subject: Nosy Tanikely
summary: A tiny uninhabited island off Madagascar's northwest coast where a marine sanctuary protects some of the Indian Ocean's healthiest coral reefs, and where sea turtles swim close enough to touch.

story.title: Nothing, Arizona: The Town Named for What It Has

subject: Nothing, Arizona
summary: The Arizona desert outpost named with brutal honesty - founded on stubbornness and a dark joke, abandoned to the sand, where a gas station once promised travelers 'Nothing' and delivered exactly that.

subject: Notre-Dame de Paris
summary: A medieval cathedral that survived revolution, war, and a catastrophic fire, Notre-Dame de Paris anchors the heart of the city on an island in the Seine.

subject: Nottingham
summary: The 'Queen of the Midlands' built on lace, coal and caves - a Robin Hood city of trams, pub crawls, sandstone basements, and the Goose Fair.

subject: Nottingham Contemporary
summary: Verdigris concrete panels embossed with traditional Nottingham lace, wrapped around 3,000 square metres of gallery built on the oldest site in the city.

subject: Nottinghamshire
summary: The East Midlands county defined by the River Trent, Sherwood Forest, the Robin Hood legend, the Pilgrim Fathers' Scrooby and Babworth, four ducal estates of the Dukeries, and a coal industry that shaped two centuries of working life.

subject: Nouadhibou
summary: Mauritania's second city runs on iron ore and fish, sends out one of the longest trains on Earth, and looks out over a bay full of rusting shipwrecks toward a peninsula where monk seals still haul ashore.

subject: Nouadhibou
summary: Mauritania's iron-ore and fishing capital, built on a desert headland where three-kilometre freight trains meet the Atlantic and the world's largest ship graveyard rusts in the bay.

subject: Nouakchott
summary: Mauritania's capital rewards the traveler who arrives without expectations: a low desert city where the day's best hours happen at the fishing wharf and over endless glasses of sweet tea.

subject: Nouakchott
summary: A capital conjured almost from nothing on the edge of the Sahara, Nouakchott grew from a fishing village of a few thousand into a sprawling Saharan metropolis of more than a million in a single lifetime.

subject: Nouakchott fish market
summary: The Port de Peche, where hundreds of hand-painted wooden pirogues storm a single Atlantic beach each afternoon to land Mauritania's daily catch in a riot of colour, salt, and shouting.

subject: Nouamghar
summary: In this coastal village at the edge of the Banc d'Arguin, fishermen once called wild dolphins to the surf to help them herd the mullet ashore - one of the world's rarest partnerships between people and the sea.

subject: Nouvelle Route du Littoral
summary: A highway built on stilts out over the Indian Ocean to escape a killer cliff - and at well over two billion euros, among the most expensive roads ever built.

subject: Nova Andradina
summary: The "Capital of the Ivinhema Valley" was the planned creation of one farmer with extraordinary vision, who acquired five farms and a river port before laying out the city in 1957.

subject: Nova Crixás
summary: In a municipality the size of a small European country, 12,603 people share space with 690,665 head of cattle - fifty-four cows for every person.

subject: Nova Friburgo
summary: In 1819, a royal decree transplanted a hundred Swiss families from the Canton of Fribourg to the mountains of Rio de Janeiro - the only planned Swiss colony in Brazilian history - and the Alpine architecture, cheese schools, and mountain-climate nostalgia of that settlement still shape a city that grew from 1,458 immigrants into a municipality of 190,000.

subject: Nova Lima
summary: The town that a British gold mine built - a hilly suburb 20 kilometers south of Belo Horizonte where the Saint John Del Rey Mining Company brought 150 British families in the 1830s, founded the oldest Anglican congregation in Minas Gerais, and built one of the oldest football clubs in the state.

subject: Nova Olinda, Ceará
summary: A Cariri town of under 16,000 people where a museum, a library, a theatre and a cultural foundation are run by the local children — beneath a sandstone escarpment that UNESCO counts as a geopark.

subject: Nova Petrópolis
summary: Half-timbered houses, hydrangea-lined roads, and the smell of streuselkuchen mark this German-founded town in the Brazilian highlands as a transplanted corner of old Europe.

subject: Novaya Zemlya
summary: A remote Arctic archipelago where the Ural Mountains sink beneath the sea, Novaya Zemlya carries the scars of Cold War nuclear testing alongside glaciers, polar bears, and centuries of polar exploration.

subject: Novgorod Oblast
summary: Birthplace of the Russian state, medieval republic, UNESCO heritage city, and a region whose population still has not recovered from the German occupation of 1941-1944.

subject: Novgorod Republic
summary: For three centuries, a medieval Russian city-state governed itself through popular assemblies and elected officials, building a trading empire that stretched from the Gulf of Finland to the Ural Mountains before Moscow crushed it in 1478.

subject: Novhorod-Siverskyi
summary: A thousand-year-old city on the Desna where a doomed medieval campaign inspired the most famous poem in East Slavic literature and monasteries still crown the river bluffs.

subject: Novo Airão
summary: A small municipality 180 km up the Rio Negro from Manaus, gateway to the Anavilhanas archipelago and the Jau National Park - a place where pink river dolphins swim up to floating cafes.

subject: Novo Cruzeiro
summary: A northeastern Minas Gerais town named for a vanished currency, born as a ranch on the banks of a small stream in 1917, sitting at 980 meters in the Jequitinhonha Valley - one of Brazil's poorest regions, where most of the 31,335 residents still farm beans and coffee on family plots.

subject: Novy Urengoy
summary: Russia's gas capital above the Arctic Circle, a Soviet-planned city born from one of the world's largest gas fields, connected to the outside world by a railway that once carried a grimmer name.

subject: Novyi Svet
summary: A wind-sheltered cove where Crimea's first great sparkling wine was born, ringed by rocky peaks that seal it off from the rest of the world.

subject: Novyi Svit Winery
summary: The Crimean cellars where a Russian prince spent a decade perfecting a sparkling wine that would be poured at a tsar's coronation and crowned in Paris.

subject: Nowshahr
summary: Once the unofficial summer capital of Iran, this Caspian port city blends Mazandarani culture with a Dutch-built harbor and the lush forests of Mazandaran province.

subject: Nozawaonsen
summary: A tiny hot spring village in Nagano Prefecture where every January 15, men build a three-story wooden shrine and then spend two hours trying to burn it down in a centuries-old fire festival that doubles as a mandatory rite of passage.

subject: Nsimbo District
summary: A young Tanzanian district born in 2012 where protected forests cover more land than farms, and seven ethnic peoples share 272 hamlets on the edge of Katavi National Park.

subject: Ntawere Formation
summary: A 245-million-year-old Middle Triassic rock formation in Zambia's Luangwa Valley, preserving the ancestors of mammals and dinosaurs in red floodplain mudstones.

subject: Ntonso
summary: A small Ashanti town that has been the birthplace of Ghana's Adinkra cloth for centuries, where symbols encoding proverbs and philosophy are still stamped by hand onto fabric.

subject: Ntusi
summary: Two grassy mounds in southwestern Uganda hold the remains of the oldest known town in the region - a thousand-year-old society of cattle and trade that legend credits to a vanished race of demigods.

subject: Nubia
summary: The ancient African civilization of the Nile between Khartoum and Aswan, home to Kerma, Kush, the 25th Dynasty pharaohs who ruled Egypt, and the medieval Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria, and Alodia.

subject: Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System
summary: The world's largest known fossil water aquifer, holding roughly 150,000 cubic kilometers of groundwater beneath two million square kilometers of the eastern Sahara -- water deposited tens and hundreds of thousands of years ago that four modern countries now draw on.

subject: Nubian pyramids
summary: More than 200 steep, narrow pyramids spread across four Sudanese sites -- the royal tombs of Kushite kings and queens who built the last great pyramids in Africa, some of them deliberately demolished by a single Italian looter in 1834.

subject: Nuclear Power in Taiwan
summary: For nearly half a century, Taiwan generated electricity from nuclear fission -- at its peak, more than half the island's power. Then came Fukushima, a fierce anti-nuclear movement, and a political reckoning that shut every reactor by 2025.

subject: Nuclear facilities in Iran
summary: Scattered across Iran's mountains, deserts, and cities, a network of nuclear facilities has been at the center of one of the most consequential geopolitical standoffs of the 21st century.

story.title: Nucleus, the Nuclear and Caithness Archives

subject: Nucleus, the Nuclear and Caithness Archives
summary: Britain's national civil nuclear archive shares a silver-clad Caithness building with county records dating back to 1589.

subject: Nueva Cádiz
summary: The ruins of Spain's first city in Venezuela lie partly submerged off the coast of Cubagua, a ghost town that rose and fell with the pearl oyster beds it was built to exploit.

subject: Nueva Germania
summary: Founded in 1887 as an antisemitic utopian colony by Nietzsche's sister and her husband, Nueva Germania outlived its hateful origins to become a quiet Paraguayan farming town where residents call themselves 'Germanino' and speak Guarani, Spanish, and German.

subject: Nueva Helvecia
summary: A slice of Switzerland transplanted to the Uruguayan countryside, where the houses wear Alpine cantonal shields and the cheese still carries the colony's name.

subject: Nueva Imperial
summary: A colorful river town in the heart of Mapuche country, where a 1989 agreement between a presidential candidate and indigenous leaders briefly seemed to promise a different future.

subject: Nuevo Rocafuerte
summary: At the Ecuador-Peru border, reachable only by an eight-hour boat ride down the Rio Napo, sits the last town before one of the last great stretches of uncut Amazon rainforest.

story.title: Nuggety Gully Water Race and Chinese Camp

subject: Nuggety Gully Water Race and Chinese Camp
summary: Deep in a remote Queensland ravine, dry-stone walls built by Chinese miners in the 1880s survive as the finest example of Chinese stonework on the old Palmer goldfield.

subject: Nuis, Netherlands
summary: A 670-person Groningen village whose archaeology depot holds millions of artifacts from across the north, on land that once was a wartime labor camp.

subject: Nullarbor Plain
summary: The world's largest single exposure of limestone bedrock stretches treeless across 200,000 square kilometers of southern Australia, where the land itself remembers being ocean floor.

subject: Nullarbor Regional Reserve
summary: A vast protected sweep of the treeless Nullarbor, hollowed below by the world's largest semi-arid cave system and bounded by the longest straight railway on Earth.

subject: Numbulwar
summary: A remote Nunggubuyu community at the mouth of the Rose River on the Gulf of Carpentaria, born of a mission the people themselves asked for, now fighting to keep its ancient language Wubuy alive.

subject: Numidia
summary: An ancient North African kingdom that fed Rome's armies, fused Berber and Punic cultures, and shaped Mediterranean history from its capital at Cirta.

subject: Nundroo, South Australia
summary: A lone roadhouse on the Eyre Highway marks the spot where South Australia's wheat country runs out of road and the long, empty crossing of the Nullarbor truly begins.

subject: Nuneaton
summary: A market town named for the nunnery that anchored it, the birthplace of George Eliot, and the home of a roundabout whose fountain throws fifty thousand gallons of water an hour.

subject: Nunnery Colliery
summary: A 500-yard underground rope, ninety men and thirty boys riding in a tub-and-bar train, and a December morning in 1923 that Sheffield mining never forgot.

subject: Nunuk Ragang
summary: Where the rivers meet in Borneo's interior, a legendary red banyan tree once sheltered the ancestors of the Kadazan-Dusun people -- until something drove them away and peopled an entire island.

subject: Nuri
summary: Eighty Kushite royals sleep beneath pyramids whose shadows once touched Jebel Barkal at sunrise on Egyptian New Year's Day.

story.title: Nusa Ceningan: The Smallest Sister Between the Seaweed and the Cliffs

subject: Nusa Ceningan
summary: A tiny island between Nusa Lembongan and Nusa Penida where seaweed farmers, mangrove forests, and a 13-meter cliff jump coexist in the waters southeast of Bali.

story.title: Nusa Penida: Bandit Island Turned Bali's Last Refuge

subject: Nusa Penida
summary: Once called 'Bandit Island' by the Dutch for its role as a place of exile, Nusa Penida now shelters the critically endangered Bali starling, speaks a dialect incomprehensible to mainland Balinese, and hides one of the largest coral colonies ever discovered.

subject: Nushabad
summary: An Iranian desert city built above a vast underground labyrinth of tunnels, trap doors, and ambush corridors where residents hid from invaders for centuries.

subject: Nutibara Hill
summary: An 80-meter rocky hill in the geographic center of Medellin named for an indigenous chief, crowned by a replica village and studded with sculptures -- one of the Aburra Valley's seven guardian hills.

subject: Nuttallburg, West Virginia
summary: A West Virginia ghost town in the New River Gorge whose post office closed in 1955 and whose long Ford-built conveyor still descends the cliff face toward the empty railroad below.

subject: Nuwara Eliya
summary: A colonial hill station at 1,868 meters in Sri Lanka's highlands, where British-era architecture, manicured gardens, and tea plantations coexist with the complicated legacy of the labor that built them.

subject: Nuwekloof Pass (Western Cape)
summary: Three centuries of ox-wagons, botanists, and pass builders carved a route through the Obiqua Mountains where the Klein Berg River had already done most of the work.

subject: Nuyorican Poets Café
summary: Born in a professor's apartment on Halloween 1973, the Nuyorican Poets Cafe became the epicenter of Puerto Rican literary identity in New York and helped launch the slam poetry movement.

subject: Nuʻuanu Pali
summary: A windswept cliff pass on Oahu where Kamehameha I drove 400 warriors to their deaths in 1795, now a scenic lookout where trade winds can knock visitors off their feet.

subject: Nyal, South Sudan
summary: A swamp-edge town in Panyijar County that has sheltered tens of thousands fleeing South Sudan's civil wars, Nyal survives on mango trees, relief flights, and a stubbornness that goes back to the Nuer-British War.

subject: Nyamata
summary: A quiet Rwandan town of rolling hills and fertile valleys, Nyamata carries one of the country's most harrowing memorials inside a church where thousands sought refuge during the 1994 genocide.

subject: Nyamina
summary: A Niger River trading town that watched empires rise and fall, Nyamina became the upstream edge of safe travel during a century of war along the river.

subject: Nyarong
summary: A remote Tibetan river valley whose very isolation bred one of 19th-century Kham's most audacious rebel leaders.

subject: Nyasaland
summary: The British protectorate that became Malawi, Nyasaland's six decades of colonial rule were shaped by land seizures, a preacher's doomed rebellion, and a generation of educated Africans who ultimately won their country back.

subject: Nyboder
summary: Christian IV built rows of small yellow houses for the sailors who crewed his navy - and nearly four centuries later, Danish service families still live in them.

subject: Nydam Mose
summary: A Danish farmer once handed his children Iron Age swords to play with; the bog he pulled them from held a 23-metre oak warship and the wrecked equipment of defeated armies.

subject: Nyenchen Tanglha Mountains
summary: A 700-kilometer mountain range containing nearly 3,000 glaciers, peaks called the Alps of Tibet, and summits that defeated some of the world's best climbers for decades.

subject: Nyero Rock Paintings
summary: Concentric circles painted in red ochre on granite in eastern Uganda, made centuries ago by hunter-gatherers whose names the rock no longer remembers.

subject: Nyhavn
summary: Denmark's most photographed row of houses spent three centuries as a working sailors' canal that respectable Copenhagen preferred to walk around.

subject: Nymagee
summary: A central-western copper town that swelled to thousands then emptied to a ghost town, near the real sheep run that gave Banjo Paterson his most famous bush ballad.

subject: Nymphaeum of Herodes Atticus
summary: When a Roman billionaire's wife attended the ancient Olympics and found thousands of athletes and spectators dying of thirst, her husband promised to fix it — and built one of the ancient world's great feats of hydraulic engineering.

subject: Näsijärvi
summary: Pirkanmaa's largest lake, whose 18-metre drop built the city of Tampere and whose worst September storm produced Finland's deadliest inland shipwreck.

subject: Näsinneula
summary: Finland's tallest free-standing structure doubles as a public weather forecast, spelled out in coloured bars above Lake Näsijärvi.

subject: Nærøyfjord
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage fjord so narrow that its rock walls seem close enough to touch from a boat, the Naeroyfjord is Norway's most dramatic branch of the mighty Sognefjord.

subject: Néma
summary: Where the great trans-Mauritanian Road of Hope finally runs out of pavement, a desert town of plateaus and palm-cart traffic marks the far eastern edge of a country - and the threshold of the open Sahel.

subject: Năm Căn district
summary: Named for five stilt houses raised on the mud two centuries ago, Năm Căn straddles the only river in Vietnam that both begins and ends at the sea — and it was struck off the map in 2025.

subject: O Homem da Meia-Noite
summary: A giant puppet that opens Olinda's carnival at the stroke of midnight, invented in 1931 by six men who had been blackballed from another club's board and decided to get out in front of it.

subject: O'Connell Street
summary: Dublin's grand 150-foot-wide boulevard, named for the Liberator, stage for the 1913 lockout, the 1916 Rising, the 1922 Civil War, the 1966 bombing of Nelson's Pillar, and the 2003 Spire.

subject: O.K. Corral
summary: Thirty seconds in Tombstone - where Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday faced the Clanton and McLaury gang on October 26, 1881, in the most famous gunfight in Western history.

subject: OK Mine & Smelter
summary: An octagonal brick chimney and a perfectly symmetrical mountain of slag are all that remain of a short-lived copper boom in the bush behind Chillagoe, where a mine named after a jam tin briefly led North Queensland.

subject: OLT Express Germany
summary: A modest fifty-year-old East Frisian island-hopper was bought by a Polish Ponzi scheme in 2011 — fourteen months later, it was finished.

subject: OTC Satellite Earth Station Carnarvon
summary: A strange scoop-shaped antenna in the Western Australian desert carried Australia's first satellite television, reunited migrant families across the world by live link, and relayed humanity's first steps on the Moon — and it may soon watch deep space again.

subject: Oadby
summary: A Leicestershire town with a Danish name, an Anglian burial ground, a racecourse on its northern edge, and the schoolboy who would become the bass player for Queen.

subject: Oak Hill, West Virginia
summary: The largest city in Fayette County, the place Hank Williams was pronounced dead on New Year's Day 1953, and a town still negotiating with its coal past.

subject: Oakham
summary: The county town of England's smallest historic county, where over 200 ceremonial horseshoes line the walls of a 12th-century Norman hall and royal visitors still pay the forfeit demanded by a tradition older than the Tudors.

subject: Oakland Army Base
summary: For nearly six decades, the Oakland Army Base funneled millions of tons of cargo and hundreds of thousands of soldiers through the East Bay waterfront -- from World War II through Vietnam -- before closing in 1999 and slowly becoming a shoreline park.

subject: Oaksterdam, Oakland
summary: A few blocks of downtown Oakland where AIDS patients, cannabis activists, and city politicians built America's first openly operating medical marijuana district -- and named it after Amsterdam.

subject: Oamaru
summary: A small New Zealand port town that accidentally preserved the finest Victorian streetscape in the country because it went broke at exactly the right time, then reinvented itself around penguins and steampunk.

story.title: Oaxaca: The Cultural Capital Where Mezcal and Mole Meet

subject: Oaxaca
summary: The southern Mexican city preserving indigenous heritage - where Day of the Dead is celebrated most authentically, where mezcal is made in ancestral ways, and where seven moles define a cuisine found nowhere else.

subject: Obelisco de Buenos Aires
summary: A 67.5-meter concrete needle thrown up in just 31 days, the Obelisco has become the place where an entire nation gathers to grieve, protest, and celebrate.

subject: Oberhausen
summary: A Ruhr city named after a railway station, where Europe's largest mall, a 117-meter gas tower, and an underground wrestling scene now occupy the space coal used to fill.

subject: Oberhausen Hauptbahnhof
summary: The Ruhr's first railway station predates the city it serves - and the modernist building that replaced it once had a cinema hidden behind a false ceiling.

subject: Oberliga (ice hockey)
summary: Germany's oldest continuously operating ice hockey league has been the top tier, the second tier, and the third tier - sometimes all in the same decade.

subject: Obuse
summary: A tiny Nagano town where the great ukiyo-e master Hokusai spent his final creative years, leaving behind ceiling phoenixes and a 600-year tradition of chestnuts.

subject: Occoneechee Speedway
summary: The only dirt track surviving from NASCAR's inaugural 1949 season, killed off by Sunday-racing protests and now slowly being reclaimed by pine forest outside Hillsborough.

subject: Occupy Central (2011–2012)
summary: For nearly eleven months, a small encampment beneath HSBC's headquarters in Hong Kong's financial district embodied the global Occupy movement — until court bailiffs spent eight hours dismantling what protesters had built.

subject: Occupy Oakland
summary: Frank Ogawa Plaza became ground zero for one of the most confrontational chapters of the Occupy movement, where tear gas, mass arrests, and a fractured skull turned a protest encampment into a national flashpoint.

subject: Ocean (train)
summary: North America's oldest continuously operated named passenger train has run between Montreal and Halifax since 1904, surviving wars, budget cuts, pandemics, and the loss of its turnaround loop to keep rolling through the night.

subject: Ocean City (Maryland)
summary: A ten-mile beach with 6,800 year-round residents and eight million summer visitors - Maryland's only Atlantic Ocean city, packed onto a narrow strip of sand.

subject: Ocean City (New Jersey)
summary: A dry town founded by Methodist ministers, now "America's Greatest Family Resort," where 2.5 miles of boardwalk meet 8 miles of guarded beach.

subject: Ocean City, Maryland
summary: The Ladies' Resort to the Ocean became Maryland's biggest summer city - and the White Marlin Capital of the World - after a hurricane cut its harbor in 1933.

subject: Ocean City, New Jersey
summary: A barrier-island city founded by Methodist ministers as a Christian seaside retreat, where alcohol has been prohibited since 1879 and the boardwalk runs 2.5 miles.

subject: Ocean Observatories Initiative
summary: An NSF-funded network of over 900 ocean sensors in the Atlantic and Pacific, the Ocean Observatories Initiative has been continuously measuring the sea from seafloor to surface since 2016 — with Scripps Institution of Oceanography in La Jolla managing its global arrays.

subject: Ocean Shores, New South Wales
summary: A quiet coastal town north of Brunswick Heads began as a 1960s dream sold by an American developer and a crooning celebrity: a resort city for 22,000 people, named after a beach in Washington State.

subject: Ocean Shores, Washington
summary: A planned beach resort city on Washington's coast, Ocean Shores was built from bare sand in the 1960s, attracted celebrity investors, and now faces the existential challenge of preparing for a Cascadia earthquake and tsunami.

subject: Oceanside, California
summary: North County San Diego's largest city grew from a Spanish mission founded in 1798 into a coastal community of 174,000 — shaped by Marines, surfers, artists, and the long pier that has been rebuilt six times.

subject: Ocetá Páramo
summary: Called the most beautiful paramo in the world, this high-altitude ecosystem in Colombia's Eastern Andes holds ancient Muisca birthing pools, stone monoliths, and forests of frailejones that grow just one centimeter per year.

subject: Ochakiv
summary: A small Black Sea town that has been Greek, Roman, Tatar, Ottoman, and Ukrainian in turn, guarding the narrowest gate to two of Europe's great rivers.

subject: Ochil Hills
summary: A Devonian lava plateau north of the Forth valley whose southern escarpment marks the geological fault between Highland and Lowland Scotland, topped by Ben Cleuch at 721 metres.

subject: Octopus Tree (Oregon)
summary: A 250-to-300-year-old Sitka spruce on Cape Meares with no central trunk and a 46-foot circumference, whose massive limbs radiate outward like tentacles -- shaped, according to historians, by the hands of local Tillamook tribes who trained the tree for ceremonial use.

subject: Odaiba
summary: An artificial island in Tokyo Bay that began as a chain of cannon batteries built in eight desperate months to repel Commodore Perry's Black Ships, then lay dormant for over a century before reinventing itself as Tokyo's futuristic waterfront playground.

subject: Odanak
summary: Odanak, an Abenaki word meaning 'in the village,' is a First Nations reserve on the Saint-Francois River that has survived raids, relocations, and centuries of colonial warfare to become a living centre of Abenaki culture and identity.

subject: Odense
summary: Denmark's third city spent eleven years cutting a motorway through its medieval heart, then spent a fortune taking it out again.

subject: Odesa
summary: A cosmopolitan Black Sea port dreamed up by an empress and built by four foreigners, whose graceful grid of the old town is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Odesa Film Studio
summary: One of the oldest film studios in the former Russian Empire, where Dovzhenko learned to make cinema and a Soviet detective drama became a national obsession.

subject: Odesa International Film Festival
summary: Each July, silent classics flicker across the Potemkin Stairs to a live orchestra, in the city whose most famous staircase was made immortal by a silent film.

subject: Oea
summary: Beneath the streets of modern Tripoli lies Oea, a Phoenician city founded in the 7th century BC that survived Greeks, Romans, Vandals, and Byzantines before becoming the capital of Tripolitania.

subject: Oeiras, Piauí
summary: Piauí's first capital lost the seat of government to Teresina in 1852 and stopped growing at a capital's pace — which is precisely why its colonial center is still standing.

subject: Oeniadae
summary: Ancient Oeniadae on the Achelous River survived siege by Pericles, defied Athens through most of the Peloponnesian War, and left behind stone ship-sheds carved from the rock that still stand near the modern village of Trikardo.

subject: Oerol Festival
summary: Once a year for ten days every June, the entire island of Terschelling becomes a stage — fifty-five thousand visitors, performances in dunes and farm sheds, and a name borrowed from a vanished tradition of letting cattle roam everywhere.

subject: Office du Niger
summary: Mali's rice belt was carved from the Sahel by tens of thousands of forced laborers, who paid for a French colonial dream of cotton in lives no one counted.

subject: Offside (2006 Iranian film)
summary: To film a movie about women banned from Iranian football stadiums, director Jafar Panahi submitted a fake script to government censors and shot key scenes at a real World Cup qualifier -- creating a Silver Bear-winning film that remains banned in the country where it was made.

subject: Ofoten Line
summary: A 43-kilometer railway connecting the ice-free port of Narvik to the Swedish border, the Ofoten Line has hauled iron ore across the Arctic since 1902 and remains one of the heaviest-trafficked freight corridors in Scandinavia.

subject: Ogbunike Caves
summary: A sacred labyrinth of tunnels beneath the Nigerian rainforest, where warm underground streams meet cold rivers and bat colonies fill chambers that have held spiritual significance for centuries.

subject: Ogden Point
summary: Canada's busiest cruise port sits on a granite breakwater built for a canal 6,000 kilometres away - and some of the world's best cold-water diving lies directly beneath it.

subject: Ohio Brew Week
summary: A nine-day craft beer festival held each July in Athens, Ohio, that turns a college-town downtown into a statewide brewing showcase.

subject: Ohne, Germany
summary: A village whose name is also the German word for 'without' - and which in 2022 received a new road sign that was entirely blank, because a factory worker took the instructions literally.

subject: Ohrid
summary: A lakeside town in North Macedonia where the Cyrillic alphabet was born and three million years of natural history meet fifteen centuries of human civilization.

subject: Oi! (Hong Kong)
summary: A former Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club clubhouse built in 1908 now serves as the government's boldest experiment in community art-making.

subject: Oiapoque
summary: A Brazilian border town where French citizens drive across a 2017 bridge to buy tobacco, and where Brazil's northernmost coastline begins.

subject: Oil City, Washington
summary: A town platted in 1911 for a deepwater oil port that never materialized, Oil City spent a century as a real estate fraud before reinventing itself as an off-grid community at the mouth of the Hoh River.

story.title: Oil Springs: The Place That Changed Everything

subject: Oil Springs
summary: The Ontario town where James Miller Williams drilled North America's first commercial oil well in 1858 - a year before Drake's more famous well in Pennsylvania, launching the petroleum age in a quiet Canadian village that the world forgot.

subject: Oil Street
summary: A short street in North Point that has carried successive identities — yacht club, artist village, ghost-story circuit, and one of Hong Kong's most storied cultural corridors.

subject: Ojuela
summary: A ghost town perched atop a mountain in Durango, Ojuela is connected to the world by a suspension bridge designed by the same engineers who built the Brooklyn Bridge -- a bridge that has outlasted the mines, the town, and the entire reason it was built.

subject: Ok Tedi Mine
summary: A mountain once described as a gold cap on a copper core has become a deep pit in the ground — and a cautionary tale about what extracting it cost.

subject: Oka-dera
summary: A hillside temple in Asuka village houses the largest clay Buddhist statue in Japan and carries the formal name 'Dragon Lid Temple' -- from the legend that its founder sealed an evil dragon beneath a pond of stones.

subject: Okadaira Shell Mound
summary: Japan's first archaeological site excavated by Japanese scientists, this 7,000-year-old ring-shaped shell midden on the shores of Lake Kasumigaura survived both millennia of burial and a 1970s real estate developer's bulldozer.

subject: Okahandja
summary: Where the Okakango and Okamita rivers meet, Okahandja has served as the administrative heart of the Herero people for two centuries -- a town whose graves hold the leaders who shaped Namibian history.

subject: Okanagan
summary: Canada's fruit basket and wine heartland, where a 135-kilometer lake anchors a sun-drenched valley that contains the country's only true hot desert and over a hundred wineries.

subject: Okapi Wildlife Reserve
summary: In the depths of the Ituri Forest lives an animal so elusive that science only confirmed it a century ago - and a reserve where rangers have died defending it.

subject: Okavango Delta
summary: A river that never reaches the sea instead fans out across the Kalahari Desert, creating one of Earth's largest inland deltas -- a UNESCO World Heritage Site where mokoro canoes glide through channels older than the last ice age.

subject: Okefenokee Swamp
summary: Four hundred thirty-eight thousand acres of blackwater swamp where the peat islands literally tremble underfoot - the Hitchiti word for it means just that - and where, in 2025, a six-year campaign finally bought out the titanium mine that would have drained it.

subject: Okefenokee Swamp
summary: North America's largest blackwater swamp spans 438,000 acres across the Georgia-Florida border, where 6,500 years of accumulated peat create a trembling landscape that has defied every human attempt to tame it.

subject: Okhtyrka
summary: A Cossack fortress town turned oil capital in Ukraine's Sumy Oblast, home to a Baroque cathedral, a famous miraculous icon, and a hard-won reputation for resilience.

subject: Oksskolten
summary: At 1,916 metres, Oksskolten is the highest mountain in Northern Norway - and the ice on its flank has outlasted every warm spell of the past nine thousand years.

subject: Okstindan
summary: North Norway's highest summit stands not in Lofoten or Lyngen but in a glaciated massif on the Swedish border that most Norwegians have never heard of.

subject: Oktonia
summary: A scattered hill village on eastern Euboea where ruined castles once signaled each other by torchlight, and where the wars of Greek independence left scars still visible on the bare flank of a mountain.

subject: Old Aberdeen
summary: Through harmony, small things increase - Old Aberdeen kept its Latin motto, its medieval bridge, its 1495 university, and its independence from the larger granite city next door until 1891.

subject: Old Aberdeen Police Station
summary: Built in 1891 to keep order in Aberdeen's fishing community, this Neo-Classical colonial station outlasted its original purpose by more than a century — bombed, repurposed, and now alive again as a youth centre.

subject: Old Bahama Channel
summary: The treacherous strait between Cuba and the Bahamas that funneled Spanish treasure fleets, swallowed warships, and still divides two worlds separated by barely 14 miles of water.

subject: Old Bailey
summary: England's most storied criminal court, the Old Bailey has occupied its spot beside the ancient city wall since the 16th century, witnessing more than 100,000 trials, public executions, and the drama of London's darkest cases.

subject: Old Central Government Offices
summary: Laid in 1847 at a cost of £14,393, Hong Kong's first purpose-built seat of government housed the colony's entire administration for over a century before white ants and timber rot ended its tenure.

subject: Old City of Jerusalem
summary: Less than one square kilometer of walled city contains sites sacred to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, layered atop three thousand years of continuous habitation and contested sovereignty.

subject: Old City of Zuoying
summary: A Qing-era walled city in Kaohsiung whose stone gates have survived rebellions, invasions, superstition, and the Japanese military to become first-class historic sites.

subject: Old Course at St Andrews
summary: The world's oldest golf course, where the game was first played in the fifteenth century, where the standard of 18 holes was invented by accident, and where Bobby Jones said he could take everything out of his life except St Andrews and still have lived fully.

subject: Old Dhaka
summary: The Mughal-era heart of Bangladesh's capital, founded in 1608 as Jahangirabad, where centuries of Hindu, Muslim, Armenian, and colonial history compress into narrow lanes famous for biriyani, kite festivals, and crumbling palaces.

subject: Old Dongola
summary: For a thousand years, the Makurian capital of Tungul stood against armies and empires on the Nile's east bank - until its court finally walked away in 1364.

subject: Old Firm
summary: The rivalry between Celtic and Rangers, two Glasgow football clubs whose 449-match history and combined trophy haul have shaped Scottish sport, culture and division.

subject: Old Great Square (Turku)
summary: Finland's oldest public square has proclaimed Christmas Peace for 700 years, witnessed fire and rebirth, and now anchors Turku's historic heart with neoclassical mansions and medieval festivals.

subject: Old Havana
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage district where five centuries of colonial architecture line narrow streets once enclosed by fortress walls, and a nightly cannon ceremony still marks the closing of gates that no longer exist.

subject: Old Location
summary: When Windhoek's Black residents refused to be moved from their homes, the police opened fire — and the eleven who died on 10 December 1959 became the reason Namibia now marks Human Rights Day.

subject: Old Mackinac Point Light
summary: Built from Cream City brick and Indiana limestone in 1892, Old Mackinac Point Light grew out of a fog station that once burned 52 cords of wood in a single fortnight -- and went dark the same day the Mackinac Bridge opened.

subject: Old Man of Coniston
summary: A volcanic fell rising above Coniston village, the highest point in the historic county of Lancashire, whose slopes have been worked for copper and slate for eight hundred years.

subject: Old Man of Hoy
summary: A 137-metre sea stack that did not exist 250 years ago, the Old Man of Hoy has become one of Britain's most iconic climbing destinations -- and it may collapse into the ocean at any time.

subject: Old Mobile Site
summary: The forgotten first capital of French Louisiana, founded in 1702 on the Mobile River, where a fragile colony of soldiers, priests, and casquette girls struggled to survive at the edge of a continent.

subject: Old Muscat
summary: The original walled city of Muscat, where gates once closed three hours after dusk and anyone caught on the streets without a lantern risked arrest -- a district where centuries of Omani history compress into a few hundred meters of waterfront.

subject: Old Oakland
summary: A cluster of Victorian-era commercial buildings that survived earthquake, decline, and demolition to become downtown Oakland's most atmospheric block -- where cast-iron columns and plate-glass storefronts from the 1870s now frame farmers' markets and bistros.

subject: Old Parish
summary: An Irish-speaking Waterford parish where the local council taught Mayor Daley's father's father his alphabet - and where all education is still delivered through Irish.

subject: Old Plank Road
summary: A 6.5-mile road of 13,000 interlocking wooden planks built in 1915 across the Algodones Dunes of Imperial County — the only way to cross the dunes before the age of pavement — where the planks had to be moved aside when two cars met going opposite directions.

subject: Old Quebec
summary: The only fortified city north of Mexico, where 1,400 buildings within stone ramparts earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 1985 -- a living district split between the clifftop Upper Town and the river-level Lower Town connected by a funicular.

story.title: Old Rauma: Six Hundred Wooden Houses, Still Occupied

subject: Old Rauma
summary: The largest coherently preserved wooden town centre in the Nordic countries is not a museum - roughly 800 people sleep in its 600-odd houses every night, which is precisely the thing UNESCO listed in 1991.

story.title: Old Saint Hilary's Open Space Preserve

subject: Old Saint Hilary's Open Space Preserve
summary: A Marin County park in Tiburon featuring a restored 1888 church and rare wildflowers found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Old Salem
summary: A meticulously preserved 18th-century Moravian settlement in the heart of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, where living-history interpreters practice centuries-old trades among buildings that are 70% original.

subject: Old San Francisco Mint
summary: The Granite Lady survived the 1906 earthquake and fire to save a third of the nation's gold reserves, then spent a century looking for a second act.

subject: Old San Juan
summary: The oldest European settlement in Puerto Rico, where five centuries of colonial fortifications, cobblestone streets, and Caribbean life pack into a seven-block islet that has outlasted every empire that tried to claim it.

subject: Old Spitalfields Market
summary: Old Spitalfields Market has traded on the same patch of East London ground since 1638, surviving plague, fire, the Commonwealth, the Blitz, and a bitter 20th-century redevelopment fight to emerge as one of London's most beloved covered markets.

subject: Old Stanley Police Station
summary: Constructed in 1859 and now the oldest surviving police station building in Hong Kong, this declared monument in Stanley has lived many lives — colonial outpost, Japanese Gendarmerie headquarters, restaurant, and today a supermarket inside walls that have witnessed 165 years of the city's most turbulent history.

subject: Old Store at La Honda
summary: A California Historical Landmark since 1939, this corner store at the crossroads of La Honda Road and Sears Ranch Road has served the mountain community since the stagecoach era.

subject: Old Tai O Police Station
summary: Built in 1902 to fight pirates on the Pearl River, the Old Tai O Police Station stands on Hong Kong's westernmost hill — now a nine-room heritage hotel where the stilt village below it still fishes at dawn.

subject: Old Towns of Djenné
summary: Beneath and beside the living town lie four ancient sites, including one of sub-Saharan Africa's oldest cities, settled before Rome ruled the Mediterranean.

subject: Old Tucson Studios
summary: A Depression-era movie set built in 40 days that became the enduring backdrop for Hollywood's Western mythology.

subject: Old Wenchi
summary: An ancient Akan state in Ghana's Bono Region, whose people trace their origins to a sacred hole in the ground at Bonoso -- and whose archaeological record reaches back to the 7th century.

subject: Oldambt
summary: Farmers got rich here on land the sea once owned — and built mansions to prove it, while the laborers who pulled the harvest in slept in row houses behind the dairy.

subject: Oldenburg
summary: A small ducal capital that survived World War II almost intact, then absorbed 42,000 refugees and became, briefly, the seat of a state that no longer exists.

subject: Oldenburg
summary: A traveller's Oldenburg: pedestrian Old Town, free buses on Saturdays, cheap rental bikes, and a horse market that sells no horses.

subject: Oldenzaal
summary: For one weekend each year, this medieval Hanseatic city of 32,000 swells to over 100,000 people who come to celebrate its self-given nickname: Cabbage-town.

subject: Olinda
summary: The colonial capital that lost its port, its trade and eventually its status to Recife next door - and kept, in exchange, one of the best-preserved eighteenth-century townscapes in the Americas.

subject: Olst-Wijhe
summary: A Salland municipality where the IJssel river hides medieval mansions, working windmills, a stone cross marking a 1493 murder, and the birthplace of New York's literary Knickerbocker.

subject: Olvera Street
summary: Olvera Street in downtown Los Angeles is the oldest surviving pedestrian block in the city, home to buildings dating to 1818, and a contested site where Mexican cultural heritage has been both preserved and, some argue, carefully packaged for tourist consumption since the 1920s.

subject: Olympia
summary: Birthplace of the Olympic Games - where athletes competed for Zeus for over a thousand years, where the flame is still lit for each modern Games, and where fallen columns mark humanity's oldest sporting tradition.

subject: Olympia (Washington)
summary: Washington's unconventional capital - a small city of artists, activists, and alternative culture at the southern tip of Puget Sound, where the State Capitol dome rises above an unexpectedly bohemian downtown.

subject: Olympiacos–PAOK Rivalry
summary: The rivalry between Olympiacos of Piraeus and PAOK of Thessaloniki is considered the fiercest intercity football rivalry in Greece — a contest that goes beyond sport to reflect the long, unresolved argument between the two great cities of the Greek nation.

subject: Olympias (trireme)
summary: A 1987 reconstruction in the Hellenic Navy tested whether ancient historians had exaggerated trireme speeds. They had not.

story.title: Olympic: Where Rainforest Meets the Wild Pacific

subject: Olympic
summary: The Washington wilderness where three ecosystems collide - where temperate rainforests drip with moss, where glaciated peaks rise above alpine meadows, and where the wildest coastline in the Lower 48 crashes uninterrupted against sea stacks and tidepools.

subject: Olympic Club
summary: The oldest athletic club in the United States, founded during the Gold Rush, has hosted five U.S. Open golf championships on its lakeside course near the Pacific.

subject: Olímpia
summary: A coffee-era farm town turned "Brazilian Orlando," where the Thermas dos Laranjais water park draws nearly two million visitors a year in the highlands of São Paulo state.

subject: Omagh
summary: The county town of Tyrone where rivers meet, history runs deep, and a Saturday afternoon in August 1998 changed everything forever.

story.title: Omaha: The Beef Capital Where Buffett Still Lives

subject: Omaha
summary: The Nebraska city where Warren Buffett chose to stay - where the stockyards built fortunes, where the College World Series draws baseball, and where a modest Midwestern city hosts one of the world's richest people.

story.title: Omaha: Warren Buffett's Town and the College World Series

subject: Omaha
summary: Nebraska's largest city where Warren Buffett still lives in his original house, where the College World Series has crowned baseball champions since 1950, and where the Henry Doorly Zoo ranks among the world's best.

subject: Omani ship Al Munassir
summary: An 84-meter Omani warship built to defend the Strait of Hormuz that now serves as an artificial reef off Muscat, where yellowbar angelfish patrol corridors once walked by sailors.

subject: Ombilin Coal Mine
summary: Southeast Asia's oldest coal mine, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built on the backs of chained prisoners in a remote Sumatran valley, now preserves the dark legacy of colonial extraction alongside surprising natural beauty.

subject: Omdurman
summary: The Mahdi's capital, Kitchener's target, the Mother of Durman whose identity has been forgotten but whose city keeps holding on.

subject: Ometepe
summary: Two volcanoes joined by a narrow isthmus rise from the middle of Lake Nicaragua to form an island that has been continuously inhabited for 4,000 years, earning recognition as one of 100 geological heritage sites worldwide.

subject: Ommen
summary: A Hanseatic city on the Vecht where bells from 1517 still ring at nine, an Indian philosopher founded a religious order, and thousands died in a 19th-century paupers' colony.

subject: Ommoord
summary: A 1970s Rotterdam high-rise district where the streets are named for plants and a giant wooden chicken became an accidental monument.

subject: Omo remains
summary: Near the Omo River in Ethiopia lie the oldest known fossils of our own species - the face of Homo sapiens, more than 230,000 years deep in time.

subject: Omoa
summary: A Caribbean fishing village in Honduras that guards one of Central America's largest and best-preserved Spanish colonial fortresses, built to protect silver shipments from pirates.

subject: Omonoia Square
summary: Named for an oath of peace between bitter rivals, Athens' most restless square has been torn up and rebuilt so many times it has become a mirror of the city itself.

subject: Omugulugwombashe
summary: In a quiet forest in northern Namibia, the first shots of the war for independence were fired in 1966 - and the small settlement where they rang out became sacred ground for a nation.

subject: Once Brewed
summary: A Northumberland hamlet where the village sign tells one story driving east and a different story driving west, just south of Hadrian's Wall.

story.title: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo: The Prints That Changed Western Art

subject: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
summary: A series of 119 ukiyo-e woodblock prints by Hiroshige that mapped every corner of old Tokyo between 1856 and 1859, inspired Vincent van Gogh to copy them in oil, helped launch European Art Nouveau, and profoundly influenced the development of modernism.

subject: One Stove, Three Stones
summary: In a remote Papuan port town where limestone hills force the streets to twist and turn, a centuries-old cooking philosophy teaches Muslims and Christians that they are still family.

subject: Onehunga Ironworks
summary: A colonial-era ironworks in Auckland that spent twelve years trying to smelt New Zealand's volcanic black iron-sands, failing repeatedly but pioneering the direct-reduction process that would eventually build the nation's modern steel industry.

subject: Oneida Community
summary: A 19th-century utopian commune in upstate New York that practiced free love, communal child-rearing, and selective breeding -- then dissolved into one of America's most famous silverware companies.

subject: Onslow County, North Carolina
summary: Onslow County is the Carolina Coastal Plain wrapped around the largest Marine Corps base east of the Mississippi.

subject: Onstwedde
summary: An eleven-hundred-year-old esdorp on top of an Ice Age moraine, where the Westerwold dialect still survives and salt domes lie hidden in the bedrock.

subject: Onzole Formation
summary: An Early Pliocene rock unit in northwestern Ecuador's Borbon Basin whose shales and sandstones hold the teeth of megalodon and a menagerie of vanished marine fish.

subject: Oodnadatta
summary: A bright-pink roadhouse blazing out of the red desert marks one of the hottest, driest towns in Australia, set on an ancient water road that became the route of the Overland Telegraph and the old Ghan railway.

subject: Oodnadatta Track
summary: A 617-kilometer gravel road through the South Australian outback that traces the routes of Afghan camel trains, the old Ghan railway, and the Overland Telegraph.

subject: Ooldea, South Australia
summary: For thousands of years a hidden soak gave water and gathering to the Anangu at the desert's edge; then a railway, a mission and a nation's machinery drew it dry and dispersed the people from their country.

subject: Oontoo, Queensland
summary: A vanished customs town on the Queensland-South Australia border, built to tax passing cattle and gone within a generation.

subject: Oosterbeek
summary: A painters' village turned into a battlefield, where one of Europe's most beautiful nineteenth-century landscapes became, for nine days in 1944, the perimeter where a British airborne division died.

subject: Oosterdok
summary: Amsterdam's eastern harbor was built in 1828 to save a silted port - and two centuries later it carries the city's libraries, museums, and the spiked green roof of NEMO.

subject: Oosterenkstadion
summary: Johan Cruijff played the last official match of his career here, against FC Zwolle, and the main stand carried his name until the day the wreckers arrived.

subject: Oostvaardersplassen
summary: An accidental wilderness on reclaimed seabed that became the most contested rewilding experiment in Europe.

subject: Operation Big Bang
summary: The Royal Navy stacked 6,700 tonnes of leftover war on a German island and lit the fuse. The island declined to disappear.

subject: Operation Clean-up
summary: A brutal 1992-1994 military operation in Karachi that targeted ethnic political movements and left thousands dead or missing in what became the bloodiest chapter of the city's modern history.

subject: Operation Delaware
summary: In April 1968 — weeks after the Tet Offensive — the 1st Cavalry Division and 101st Airborne plunged into the A Shau Valley for the first time in two years, meeting a fortified enemy on its own ground.

subject: Operation Donnerkeil
summary: The Luftwaffe umbrella that protected the Channel Dash - three German capital ships running the English Channel in broad daylight in February 1942.

subject: Operation Dwarka
summary: In September 1965, the Pakistan Navy shelled the ancient pilgrimage town of Dwarka in its first-ever naval engagement -- a raid that exposed India's coastal vulnerability and reshaped the subcontinent's naval balance.

subject: Operation Green Sea
summary: The 1970 seaborne raid on Conakry, when Portuguese forces and Guinean exiles tried and failed to topple Sékou Touré, with consequences that haunted Guinea for years.

subject: Operation Helsby
summary: In February 1952, British special forces launched Operation Helsby in Malaya's Belum Valley -- the first recorded use of helicopters in direct support of a special forces ground operation.

subject: Operation Hot Rock
summary: In 1992, U.S. Marines flew helicopter loads of concrete blocks into the lava tubes of erupting Mount Etna to save a Sicilian town -- an unprecedented military operation against a volcano.

subject: Operation Jaque
summary: On July 2, 2008, Colombian soldiers wearing Che Guevara T-shirts flew into the jungle, convinced FARC commanders to hand over fifteen hostages - and rescued them without firing a shot.

subject: Operation Moses
summary: The seven-week covert airlift that carried roughly 8,000 Ethiopian Jews out of Sudanese refugee camps to Israel in 1984-85, after thousands had died on the walk from Ethiopia.

subject: Operation Serval
summary: In January 2013, with armed groups advancing on Mali's south, France launched a swift intervention that drove the jihadists from the northern towns, at a cost in soldiers' lives and amid a crisis that was far from over.

subject: Operation Stack
summary: When the Channel closes, the M20 becomes a lorry park. For three decades, that was Britain's contingency for keeping freight moving between Dover and the continent - until 2019, when Operation Brock replaced it.

subject: Opfermoor Vogtei
summary: A shallow Thuringian bog where people brought offerings - and sometimes people - to the same patch of water for a thousand years, now the largest known Iron Age cult site in Central Europe.

subject: Opitsaht
summary: The ancient seat of the Tla-o-qui-aht chief Wickaninnish on Meares Island, destroyed by American cannons in 1792 and still home to the First Nation whose name means 'different people.'

subject: Oppikoppi
summary: For more than two decades, tens of thousands of South Africans drove into the dust of a Limpopo cattle farm each August to camp in the thorn scrub and chase music across the bushveld night.

subject: Opéra de Monte-Carlo
summary: Built in eight and a half months by the architect of the Paris Opera, the Salle Garnier seats just 524 but has hosted 45 world premieres and the voices of Caruso, Melba, and Chaliapin.

subject: Orange County Regional History Center
summary: Housed in Orlando's 1927 neoclassical courthouse -- where a jail once occupied the top floor -- the Orange County Regional History Center traces 12,000 years of Central Florida life, from Paleo-Indian settlements to the theme park age.

subject: Orange County Speedway
summary: A 3/8-mile asphalt oval near Rougemont where Dale Jarrett got his first NASCAR win, Jeff Gordon took his first pole, and a small-town track has refused to stay closed.

subject: Orange Lawn Tennis Club
summary: Founded in 1880 in South Orange, the Orange Lawn Tennis Club helped create the United States Tennis Association, hosted the U.S. National Championship, and survived into the 21st century as one of the last grass court clubs in America.

subject: Orangozinho
summary: Little Orango is a flat island of mangroves and rice paddies where 700 Bijagó people live by the tide, in a society run by women.

subject: Orania
summary: A small Afrikaner settlement in the Northern Cape Karoo, founded in 1991 as a self-determined ethnic community, where the contradictions of post-apartheid South Africa are lived out in miniature.

subject: Oranjemund
summary: A Namibian diamond town where oryx have the right of way and honking is forbidden, Oranjemund spent eight decades as a private company settlement before opening its gates to the public in 2017.

subject: Oranjestad
summary: Aruba's capital began as a scattered heap of houses around a horse bay, was named for a Dutch king during a gold rush, and reinvented itself through oil wealth and cruise ship tourism -- all while keeping its Papiamento soul.

subject: Oranjewoud
summary: A Frisian forest village where a Princess of Orange built a summer palace in 1676, and where four generations of Dutch monarchs kept coming back long after the palace itself was gone.

subject: Oratory of the Borgias
summary: A modest Gothic chapel in the Valencian town of Canals marks the ancestral cradle of the Borgias, the family that rose from these fields to seize the papacy and scandalize Renaissance Rome.

subject: Orcadian Basin
summary: Beneath the gray North Sea waters between Caithness and Shetland lies the buried memory of Lake Orcadie, a Devonian inland sea whose fish fossils and flagstones still surface 400 million years later.

subject: Orchomenus (Arcadia)
summary: A hill-city in ancient Arcadia whose acropolis commanded two mountain-ringed plains, whose kings were twice stoned to death by their own people, and whose theatre still gazes across a karst basin where a lake once swallowed the plain.

story.title: Ordinary Hunger: Life on Savu Island

subject: Ordinary Hunger
summary: On this remote Indonesian island between Sumba and Timor, the Savunese have survived centuries of drought, colonial exploitation, and tectonic upheaval through an intimate relationship with the lontar palm and the rhythms of monsoon rain.

subject: Oregon Shakespeare Festival
summary: A remarkable theatrical tradition born from an abandoned Chautauqua dome, boxing matches, and a $400 gamble in Depression-era Oregon.

subject: Oregon Trail
summary: The 2,200-mile route from Independence, Missouri to Oregon City carried 400,000 settlers westward between the 1830s and 1869 -- then was immortalized by a computer game where everyone died of dysentery.

subject: Oreus
summary: An ancient Euboean city Homer praised as rich in grapes, where a six-ton marble bull rose from the sea and a Venetian fortress still guards the strait.

story.title: Organ at the Dorpskerk at Noordbroek

subject: Organ at the Dorpskerk at Noordbroek
summary: Arp Schnitger built it in 1696 as his first major Dutch commission - a baroque organ that has been rebuilt, restored, and re-voiced for more than three centuries and still speaks in the voice he intended.

story.title: Organ in the Jacobikerk at Uithuizen

subject: Organ in the Jacobikerk at Uithuizen
summary: Arp Schnitger built the Jacobikerk organ in 1701 and complained bitterly about his workmen there - but he also built one of the most beautifully preserved baroque organs in Europe, hidden in a village church on the Groningen coast.

story.title: Organ in the Martinikerk at Groningen

subject: Organ in the Martinikerk at Groningen
summary: An organ in northern Netherlands whose oldest pipes were cast in the late fifteenth century and still speak today, layered with five hundred years of rebuilds.

subject: Orgreave rail accident
summary: A foggy December morning in 1926. Three trains, around 800 miners on the workmen's express, and the safety rules that should have prevented a collision.

subject: Oriental, North Carolina
summary: A village of 880 people on the Neuse River named for a Civil War steamship whose nameplate washed up on the Outer Banks - and grew up to become the Sailing Capital of North Carolina.

subject: Orihuela
summary: A historic cathedral city cradled between a mountain and the Segura River, ringed by one of Europe's great palm groves, birthplace of the poet Miguel Hernandez, and now split between an ancient inland town and a booming stretch of coast.

subject: Orinoco
summary: South America's third-largest river drains a basin the size of France and Germany combined, harboring over 1,000 fish species, the world's rarest crocodile, and one of the planet's largest petroleum deposits.

subject: Orinoco Basin
summary: South America's third-largest watershed drains nearly a million square kilometers through Venezuela and Colombia, feeding a river whose volume dwarfs the Danube fivefold.

subject: Orinoco Delta swamp forests
summary: Covering nearly 28,000 square kilometers of permanently flooded rainforest, the Orinoco Delta swamp forests are one of Earth's largest intact wetlands -- and home to jaguars, harpy eagles, and the critically endangered Orinoco crocodile.

subject: Oriximina
summary: An Amazon municipality larger than most countries, straddling the Equator, where descendants of people who escaped slavery hold the first quilombo land title Brazil ever granted.

subject: Orizona
summary: A "Region of Rice" named by public vote in 1943 that became a cachaça capital, with about thirty small sugarcane distilleries shipping the traditional Brazilian spirit abroad.

subject: Orkney
summary: An archipelago where Norse earls, Neolithic farmers, and two world wars left their marks on seventy islands at the edge of the North Atlantic.

story.title: Orlando: The City Walt Disney Bought in Secret

subject: Orlando
summary: The Florida city transformed by a mouse - where Disney secretly purchased 27,000 acres, where theme parks became the economy, and where the real Orlando hides behind tourism that draws 75 million visitors annually.

subject: Ormskirk
summary: A West Lancashire market town named for a Norse warrior's church, famous for gingerbread once eaten by a future king and for a parish church that has both a tower and a spire because, the legend goes, of two sisters who could not agree.

subject: Oronsay
summary: A two-mile tidal island reached on foot at low water across The Strand, home to seven people, the ruined Augustinian priory of 1380, two of Scotland's finest medieval Celtic crosses, and a grass airstrip that, as one writer noted, fights a losing battle with the rabbits.

subject: Oropus
summary: A coastal town caught for centuries between Athens and Boeotia, ancient Oropus changed hands so often it became a byword for a border that would not stay put.

subject: Orpheum (Vancouver)
summary: Canada's largest theatre when it opened in 1927, saved from becoming a multiplex by a public campaign and a city cheque in 1974, and restored by the same decorator who had chosen its colours fifty years earlier.

subject: Ortaköy
summary: A lively Bosphorus village that has sheltered British writers, German architects in exile, and NATO summits — Ortaköy thrives today as one of Istanbul's most atmospheric waterfront neighborhoods.

subject: Oseberg ship
summary: A Viking burial ship from 834 CE, exquisitely carved and entombing two mysterious women, stands as one of the finest artifacts ever recovered from the Norse world.

subject: Oshino Hakkai
summary: Eight crystalline spring-fed ponds in the shadow of Mount Fuji, where snowmelt filtered through volcanic rock for 80 years emerges as some of Japan's purest water.

subject: Oslo
summary: Where Vikings built a kingdom and oil built a sovereign wealth fund, where the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded and nature begins at the city limits, where Norway governs its quiet prosperity.

subject: Osnabrück
summary: The Westphalian city where peace was negotiated in 1648 - and where, two and a half centuries later, a boy named Erich was born who would teach the world what war really cost.

subject: Osnabrück (district)
summary: The rural ring around the city of Osnabrück - 2,122 square kilometers that almost perfectly preserve the borders of a 600-year-old prince-bishopric.

subject: Osnabrück Garrison
summary: For sixty-three years the British Army's largest base outside the United Kingdom occupied a German city the RAF had bombed - and in 1996 the IRA followed them there.

subject: Osteel
summary: Father and son trained telescopes on the sky from this Frisian village and changed astronomy - then died, almost together, in the same impossible year.

subject: Ostend
summary: Belgium's most-bombed city became a king's resort, an artist's haunt, and the studio where Marvin Gaye reinvented himself.

subject: Oster
