summary: A river town at the meeting of the Oster and Desna, guarding the last surviving church of a vanished medieval principality and a fresco that has watched for nine centuries.

subject: Osterburg (Groothusen)
summary: The last survivor of three medieval moated castles in a long-warft village that once welcomed Frisian trading ships.

subject: Osterby Man
summary: A man of about sixty, struck on the head and beheaded some nineteen centuries ago, whose hair is still knotted exactly as someone tied it on the last morning of his life.

subject: Ostfriesland-Stadion
summary: An almost entirely standing-room football ground in Emden where the East Stand is nicknamed after the sailor caps its older fans still wear.

subject: Ostia Antica
summary: Rome's ancient port city, buried under sand dunes for centuries, preserves a vivid cross-section of daily life in the Roman Empire -- from its pirate-sacked harbor to Europe's earliest known synagogue.

subject: Osun-Osogbo
summary: One of the last surviving sacred forests that once bordered every Yoruba city, the Osun-Osogbo Grove shelters centuries-old shrines along the Osun River and hosts a 700-year-old festival honoring the river goddess Yeye Osun -- earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 2005.

subject: Oswestry
summary: A Shropshire market town five miles from the Welsh border with an Iron Age hillfort on its northern edge, a name derived from a slain king's tree, and Wilfred Owen's birthplace.

subject: Ota Benga
summary: A Mbuti man from the Congo was put on display in a cage at the Bronx Zoo in 1906, sparking outrage -- and then spent his final years in Lynchburg, Virginia, unable to return home.

subject: Otago gold rush
summary: New Zealand's biggest gold strike transformed Central Otago from empty backcountry into a frenzy of 18,000 prospectors, turned Dunedin into the country's largest city, and left behind ghost towns, scarred riverbeds, and a university.

subject: Otavalo
summary: At the foot of three volcanoes in northern Ecuador, the Otavaleño people have built one of Latin America's most successful indigenous economies on a foundation of woven textiles.

subject: Otavalo
summary: Two hours north of Quito, Otavalo is the Andean town travelers plan a weekend around - Saturday market, Peguche Waterfall, Cuicocha Lake, and a skyline of volcanoes.

subject: Otis Redding
summary: Born in Dawson and raised in Macon, Georgia, the "King of Soul" burned through 26 years with a voice so raw and honest it redefined American popular music—then fell silent over a frozen Wisconsin lake.

subject: Otjimbingwe
summary: Once the de facto capital of German South West Africa, Otjimbingwe rose on copper, missionaries, and Herero political unity before the railway bypassed it into quiet obscurity.

subject: Otlu Qaya
summary: A pierced Crimean cliff surrounded by a scatter of boulders that local legend remembers as a petrified flock of sheep, frozen in stone by a shepherd's disgrace.

subject: Otrobanda
summary: The 'other side' of Willemstad, where coral-walled forts and pastel colonial buildings tell three centuries of Caribbean history shaped by trade, slavery, and reinvention.

story.title: Ottawa: The Capital Nobody Visits Except on Business

subject: Ottawa
summary: The Ontario-Quebec border city that became Canada's capital because everywhere else was too controversial - where Parliament's Gothic Revival towers anchor the nation, where the Rideau Canal freezes into the world's largest skating rink, and where bureaucracy is the primary industry.

subject: Otter Point, Greater Victoria
summary: A rural forestry district west of Sooke where the arbutus reaches its western limit and the sheltered half of Vancouver Island hands off to the wild one.

subject: Otter Trail
summary: South Africa's most celebrated five-day hike, a 44-kilometer coastal route through the Tsitsikamma National Park named for the elusive Cape clawless otter.

subject: Otterburn Training Area
summary: Britain's largest live-fire range covers 242 square kilometres of the southern Cheviots, the only place in the UK where multiple launch rockets can be fired in anger.

subject: Ottery St Mary
summary: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was born here in 1772. On Guy Fawkes Night the residents carry flaming tar barrels through the streets. A 14th-century cathedral-in-miniature anchors the town that gave the Romantic age one of its founding poets.

subject: Ottoman Empire
summary: For six centuries, the Ottoman Empire ruled from Constantinople over three continents — rising from a small Anatolian principality to a global power, and falling to revolution, war, and the forces it could no longer contain.

subject: Ottoman Public Debt Administration
summary: A European-controlled financial bureaucracy installed inside a bankrupt empire, the Ottoman Public Debt Administration was, at its peak, larger than the empire's own finance ministry.

subject: Ottoman Tunisia
summary: For three centuries, the Regency of Tunis operated as a semi-autonomous Ottoman province where corsairs, janissaries, and local dynasties shaped a North African power that defied easy classification.

subject: Ottoman conquest of Adrianople
summary: Sometime in the 1360s the Greek Byzantine city of Adrianople fell to the Ottomans and became Edirne, capital of an empire that would soon swallow Constantinople itself.

subject: Otuzco
summary: A small La Libertad mountain town where thousands of pilgrims walk 73 kilometers from Trujillo every December to reach the Virgin of the Gate, and racing donkeys become the local sport.

subject: Ouadane
summary: A ruined medieval caravan city on the edge of the Adrar escarpment in Mauritania - once the richest town of the Adrar, fought over by Portuguese and Moroccans for its salt and gold, and the nearest settlement to the great Eye of the Sahara.

subject: Ouagadougou
summary: A traveler's Ouaga: green taxis you haggle into, a clean grid of streets where drivers actually stop at red lights, and a Friday-morning royal ceremony you can watch for free.

subject: Ouagadougou
summary: The capital of Burkina Faso is a Sahelian metropolis of over two million where an emperor still holds weekly court - and where, every Friday, a centuries-old ceremony chooses peace over war.

subject: Ouahigouya
summary: The capital of the Yatenga kingdom and the last Burkinabè city before Mali - a dusty crossroads where the Sahel begins to win.

subject: Oualata
summary: The easternmost of Mauritania's ancient ksour, a caravan terminus where women paint the houses and family libraries still guard centuries of manuscripts.

subject: Ouanda Djallé
summary: A tiny sub-prefecture in the remote northeast of the Central African Republic, Ouanda Djallé sits below Mont Toussoro in a region repeatedly shaken by rebels, the LRA, and the advancing Sahel.

subject: Oude IJsselstreek
summary: A Dutch municipality where iron foundries became a cultural center, and where one small village raised a football manager who would coach four countries to World Cup glory.

subject: Oude Kerk, Amsterdam
summary: Amsterdam's oldest building - a 13th-century church that now stands at the heart of the Red Light District, surrounded by the city's longest argument with itself.

subject: Oude Pekela
summary: A peat-colony town that built ships, made cardboard, survived the Holocaust with twelve Jewish residents, and in 1987 became the centre of a moral panic that never had any evidence behind it.

subject: Oudenaarde
summary: A small Flemish city with three claims to international fame: master tapestry weavers, a famous 1708 battle, and the finish line of the Tour of Flanders.

subject: Oudlajan
summary: Once Tehran's wealthiest neighborhood, Oudlajan was home to Jewish and Zoroastrian communities, Qajar-era politicians, and a language older than Persian itself.

subject: Oudtshoorn
summary: The self-proclaimed ostrich capital of the world, where feather fortunes once rivaled diamond wealth and 200,000 ostriches still outnumber the human population three to one.

subject: Oundle
summary: An ironstone market town on a horseshoe bend of the River Nene, with a tower the height of a fifteen-storey building, a hotel built from the rubble of Mary Queen of Scots' execution site, and a school that has been here since the fifteenth century.

story.title: Our Lady of the Rosary Parish (Pirenópolis)

subject: Our Lady of the Rosary Parish (Pirenópolis)
summary: A parish founded in 1736 in a gold-rush town that wanted to be the capital of Goiás - built on Sundays off by enslaved laborers, burned to the ground in 2002, rebuilt and still active today.

subject: Ouray, Colorado
summary: A former gold mining town of 898 people that calls itself the Switzerland of America, where frozen waterfalls in the Uncompahgre Gorge created the world's first ice climbing park and Ayn Rand found inspiration for Galt's Gulch.

subject: Ouro Preto
summary: Brazil's first UNESCO World Heritage Site, where steep cobbled streets and Baroque churches mark the capital of an 18th-century gold boom that briefly made it larger than New York.

subject: Ouro Preto
summary: Officially, 800 tons of gold left this Minas Gerais town for Portugal in the 18th century. Today it is frozen in baroque stone - Brazil's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Outeniqua Choo Tjoe
summary: Africa's last scheduled steam train ran 67 kilometers along the Garden Route coast until floods silenced it -- but a revival is now underway.

subject: Outeniqua Mountains
summary: The mountain range the Khoikhoi named for honey, the Portuguese called the Mountain of the Star, and generations of road-builders cursed as impassable.

subject: Outer Hebrides
summary: A 130-mile chain of windswept islands off Scotland's west coast where Gaelic survives, gneiss is older than oxygen, and the sabbath still stops the clock.

subject: Ovamboland
summary: A Bantustan in northern Namibia where more than half the country's people were confined to just six percent of its land, Ovamboland was both a tool of apartheid control and the heartland of Namibian resistance.

subject: Ovelgönne Bread Roll
summary: Half a charred bread roll, weighing two and a half grams, dropped into a rubbish pit near Buxtehude some 2,500 years ago - and the oldest shaped baked good surviving anywhere in Europe.

subject: Overland Track
summary: Australia's most famous alpine walk: six days and 65 kilometres on foot from Cradle Mountain to Lake St Clair, across glacial peaks, buttongrass plains, and rainforest older than the continent's separation.

subject: Overseas Chinese Town
summary: Shenzhen's culture-and-tourism flagship, built on farmland that predates the city itself — OCT is home to Window of the World, Happy Valley, and the companies like Konka and ZTE that helped define China's economic opening.

story.title: Overtown: The Harlem of the South

subject: Overtown (Miami)
summary: Once the vibrant cultural heart of Black Miami where Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday found refuge after performing on whites-only Miami Beach, Overtown was gutted by interstate highways in the 1960s and is now fighting its way back.

subject: Ovruch
summary: A thousand-year-old Rus town in the Polissya woods, home to a rare surviving church of colored stone and brick that a prince built, a siege toppled, and a famous architect resurrected.

subject: Oxapampa
summary: A Peruvian high-jungle town founded in 1891 by Austrian and Tyrolean colonists whose descendants still build in Alpine style and raise cattle on coffee slopes halfway up the Andes.

story.title: Oxford: Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha and Ole Miss Football Saturdays

subject: Oxford
summary: The North Mississippi college town where William Faulkner wrote his Nobel Prize-winning novels at Rowan Oak, where Ole Miss tailgating in The Grove is a Southern religion, where James Meredith integrated the university amid riots, and where 'the Square' anchors a literary tradition that continues today.

subject: Oyapock
summary: A 403-kilometer river that marks the edge between France and Brazil, settled by an Englishman in 1608 and settled into its current name by Swiss arbitration in 1900.

subject: Oybin
summary: A Holy Roman Emperor put a monastery on top of a sandstone dome in 1369; the Romantics painted its ruin, and the village below still runs torchlit processions up the rock.

subject: Oyotunji
summary: Deep in the South Carolina Lowcountry, a Yoruba kingdom has existed since 1970 -- the first African-inspired village in North America, transplanted from Harlem to the backroads of Beaufort County.

subject: Oysterville, Washington
summary: A twenty-person village on Willapa Bay that was once the seat of Pacific County, Oysterville boomed on oyster harvests in the 1850s, lost its county records to a raid in 1893, and survives today as a National Historic District of pre-1880 buildings slowly yielding to the sea.

subject: Ozegahara
summary: A 6,000-year-old peat bog cradled between two volcanoes at 1,400 meters, where wooden boardwalks wind through Japan's largest highland marsh and its astonishing carpet of seasonal wildflowers.

subject: Ozette Indian Village Archeological Site
summary: A Makah village buried by a mudslide around 1560 and preserved for centuries, yielding 55,000 artifacts when a 1970 storm revealed the site -- the Pacific Northwest's answer to Pompeii.

subject: P. O. Box 1142
summary: A nondescript mailing address concealed one of World War II's most productive intelligence operations, where Jewish refugees who had fled Nazi Germany interrogated over 3,400 German prisoners -- including Wernher von Braun -- without ever raising a fist.

subject: PNS Hangor (S131)
summary: The French-built diesel-electric submarine that achieved the first submarine kill since World War II, sinking an Indian frigate during the 1971 war and forcing the cancellation of India's planned third missile attack on Karachi.

subject: PS Rodney
summary: The charred remains of a paddle steamer lie in the bed of the Darling River, the only Australian vessel ever destroyed in an industrial dispute, burned by striking shearers in the bitter winter of 1894.

subject: PS Speicher
summary: Einbeck gave the world bock beer and a nearly complete half-timbered old town. Its 1898 grain silo now holds several hundred motorcycles and cars, stacked six floors deep in reverse chronological order.

subject: Paakantyi
summary: The river people of the Darling, the Baaka, whose language was called sleeping and is now being woken, and who in 2015 won legal recognition of country they never left.

subject: Paarl
summary: South Africa's third-oldest town sits beneath one of the world's largest granite outcrops, a massive dome of rock that glows like a pearl after rain -- which is how the town got its name.

subject: Pabbay
summary: An island named for its long-vanished monks, emptied in a single storm in 1897 that killed most of its working men, now one of the finest sea-cliff climbing venues in the United Kingdom.

subject: Paccha
summary: Founded in 1582 as one of Cuenca's original parishes, Paccha is a Kichwa-named highland town where twenty small villages weave ancient Inca history into Andean Catholic tradition.

subject: Pachacamac
summary: A 1,300-year-old sanctuary where the creator god Pacha Kamaq held sway over Peru's central coast, surviving conquest by the Inca and destruction by the Spanish.

subject: Pachmarhi
summary: Central India's only hill station, where Pandava-legend caves, British-era cantonments, waterfalls, and a UNESCO biosphere reserve share a single valley in the Satpura Range.

story.title: Pacific Biological Station: A Century of Counting Fish

subject: Pacific Biological Station
summary: The oldest fisheries research centre on the Pacific coast, established in Departure Bay in 1908 with one employee, now a designated National Historic Event site that discovered Pacific ocean perch can live to 100 years and has been measuring Departure Bay's water temperature every single day since 1914.

subject: Pacific High Recording
summary: An independent San Francisco recording studio that captured the sound of the Bay Area's rock, jazz, and folk scenes from the late 1960s through the era's creative peak.

subject: Pacific Missile Range Facility
summary: On Kauai's remote western shore, the world's only military range capable of simultaneously tracking submarines, ships, aircraft, and space vehicles stretches across thousands of square miles of ocean and sky.

subject: Pacific Northwest
summary: A region defined by volcanoes, rain, coffee, and contradictions - where the wettest rainforests in the lower 48 lie within hours of high desert, and tech giants share geography with some of America's last true wilderness.

subject: Padrão
summary: Carved from Portuguese limestone and planted on African headlands, the stone pillars called padroes were the fifteenth-century equivalent of planting a flag -- monuments that said 'we were here first, and this land is ours.'

subject: Padstow Lifeboat Station
summary: Thirteen volunteer crew have died trying to save lives at the mouth of the River Camel, where a sandbar called the Doom Bar earns its name in every gale.

subject: Paestum
summary: An ancient Greek colony in southern Italy whose three Doric temples -- built between 550 and 450 BC -- survive in such extraordinary condition that for centuries travelers visited Paestum instead of Greece to see what classical architecture actually looked like.

subject: Paga Crocodile Pond
summary: A sacred pond in northern Ghana where children swim alongside wild crocodiles believed to carry the souls of their ancestors.

subject: Pagan kingdom
summary: On the banks of the Irrawaddy, over 2,000 Buddhist temples rise from the plains of Bagan -- the remnants of a medieval empire that unified Burma and gave Theravada Buddhism its greatest stronghold.

subject: Pagaruyung I inscription
summary: A 14th-century stone inscription in the Minangkabau highlands where King Adityawarman declared himself founder of a new dynasty, blending Sanskrit, Old Malay, Buddhism, and Hinduism into 21 lines of carved sandstone that still stand today.

subject: Paiján Culture
summary: Peru's earliest known culture, whose slender fishtail points tell the story of the first people to make a living along the Pacific coast eleven thousand years ago.

subject: Pailón del Diablo
summary: A priest excommunicated a man for insisting this 80-meter waterfall be called the Devil's Cauldron - and the name stuck anyway.

subject: Paimio
summary: A quiet town on Finland's largest Archipelago Sea river, where Alvar Aalto designed a sanatorium so carefully that even the washbasins were engineered to be silent.

subject: Paimio Sanatorium
summary: Alvar and Aino Aalto designed a tuberculosis sanatorium from the point of view of someone lying on their back — and built one of modern architecture's landmarks in the process.

subject: Paint Bank, Virginia
summary: An unincorporated Craig County village named for the red clay that the Cherokee mined here for paint, later a Civil War Union sympathizer enclave, now a quiet trout-hatchery hamlet between two mountains.

subject: Painted ladies
summary: The row of colorful Victorian houses at Alamo Square became San Francisco's most photographed postcard image, but the term describes a citywide revival that rescued thousands of buildings from drab conformity.

subject: Paintsville, Kentucky
summary: Named for the tribal art Shawnee hunters painted on debarked trees by the salt lick. Loretta Lynn grew up just up the holler.

subject: Paithan
summary: Ancient capital of the Satavahana dynasty, whose silk saris once drove Rome to ban luxury imports, and whose saints shaped the soul of Maharashtra.

subject: Paiyun Lodge
summary: Perched at 3,402 meters on the slopes of Taiwan's highest mountain, Paiyun Lodge is the last place to sleep before the Yushan summit — and the hardest bed in the country to book, with lottery odds sometimes as low as 1%.

subject: Pak Nai
summary: A wetland coastline at Hong Kong's western edge where horseshoe crabs older than the dinosaurs share mudflats with the ghost of Sun Yat-sen's revolution — and where the sunsets over Shenzhen Bay draw photographers from across the city.

subject: Pak Sha O
summary: A Hakka hamlet in Sai Kung's hills, dating to the 17th century, where a Catholic chapel, two Grade I clan houses, and the ghost of a water-diverted river tell the story of a village that chose faith over tax collectors — and ultimately lost its farmland to a reservoir.

subject: Pakke Tiger Reserve
summary: In the Eastern Himalayan foothills of Arunachal Pradesh, a tiger reserve thrives because village chiefs and their communities decided to make conservation their own tradition.

subject: Pakse
summary: The French-founded hub city of southern Laos, where the Xe Don meets the Mekong and the roads to ancient temples, highland plateaus, and island river life all begin.

subject: Palacio Taranco
summary: A French belle epoque palace rises from the old heart of Montevideo, built atop the city's first theatre by the architects who shaped Paris itself.

subject: Palacio de los López
summary: Built for a son who never lived in it, looted by invaders, and restored to become Paraguay's seat of government, the Palacio de los López has witnessed nearly every chapter of the nation's turbulent history.

subject: Palaio Faliro
summary: Old Phalerum — Athens' southern seaside suburb on Faliro Bay — layers ancient harbour history beneath a sun-drenched promenade lined with warships, a marina, and the Stavros Niarchos cultural complex.

subject: Palais Jacques Coeur
summary: A masterpiece of fifteenth-century Flamboyant Gothic architecture in Bourges, built by a merchant prince who was arrested before he could live in it.

subject: Palais des Beaux-Arts de Lille
summary: Napoleon sent Lille a Donatello, two Goyas, and the spoils of Revolutionary war — and the city has been arranging the loot in ever-grander buildings ever since.

story.title: Palatine Hill: The Birthplace of the Word 'Palace'

subject: Palatine Hill
summary: The centremost of Rome's seven hills, where Romulus legendarily founded the city and murdered his brother, where Augustus built the first imperial residence, and whose very name gave the world the word 'palace.'

story.title: Palauet de la muralla de Balaguer

subject: Palauet de la muralla de Balaguer
summary: A Balaguer manor built into the medieval city wall above the Segre, with a Jewish cellar below and a thousand books once saved by a bricked-up door.

subject: Palawan
summary: Stretching 450 kilometers between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea, Palawan is the Philippines' largest province, its last biodiversity frontier, and home to the world's largest pearl.

subject: Paldi, British Columbia
summary: A Sikh-founded mill town on Vancouver Island where a Gurdwara, a Buddhist temple, and a one-room school once anchored one of Canada's earliest multicultural communities.

subject: Pale Male
summary: A red-tailed hawk who nested on a Fifth Avenue apartment building for over three decades, Pale Male became New York City's most famous wild animal and the founder of an urban raptor dynasty.

subject: Palenque
summary: A Maya city-state in the jungles of Chiapas whose ruins -- spanning 226 BC to 799 AD -- produced one of the richest royal tombs in the ancient Americas and some of the longest hieroglyphic texts in the Maya world.

subject: Paleo Trikeri
summary: A green island with no cars and no roads, where thousands of women and their children were once exiled for the politics of their families.

subject: Paleontological Sites of Santa Maria
summary: Beneath a Brazilian city sleeps one of the oldest chapters in the story of dinosaurs, written in stone 230 million years before anyone thought to read it.

subject: Palermo, Buenos Aires
summary: Buenos Aires' largest barrio is really a dozen neighborhoods in one, sprawling from Borges's childhood streets to vast French-inspired parks, polo fields, and the city's most restless nightlife.

subject: Palestina Canton
summary: A nineteenth-century traveler named an Ecuadorian estate after the Holy Land, and today that same name marks a canton along the Daule River where mango and rice grow in the lowland heat.

subject: Palingsound
summary: A fishing village on the IJsselmeer produced a disproportionate share of Dutch pop stars, and the music they made together earned a name borrowed from the eels they once caught.

subject: Palitana temples
summary: Nearly 900 Jain temples crowding the twin peaks of Shatrunjaya hill in Gujarat, built and rebuilt over a thousand years by devoted merchants and pilgrims who believed that climbing to the summit was climbing toward liberation itself.

subject: Pallasca District
summary: A high Andean district in northern Ancash where Inca memory, Spanish conquest, and Chilean war folded themselves into a single stubborn mountain town.

subject: Pallene (Attica)
summary: Beneath a modern Athenian suburb lies a lost ancient deme where, by legend, Athena killed a giant - and where a real tyrant once won an empire in a midday ambush.

story.title: Palm Springs: The Desert Oasis of Midcentury Dreams

subject: Palm Springs
summary: The California desert city where Hollywood stars escaped and midcentury modern architecture bloomed - where hot springs drew the Cahuilla for centuries before Sinatra built his compound, where every swimming pool represents defiance of the desert, and where retirement and revival coexist in perpetual sunshine.

subject: Palm Springs International Film Festival
summary: Mayor Sonny Bono launched the festival in 1989 to give a small desert city an outsized cultural voice — and it grew into the largest world cinema festival in the United States, drawing 135,000 people and 134 films from 64 countries at its 34th edition.

story.title: Palm Springs Walk of the Stars

subject: Palm Springs Walk of the Stars
summary: Established in 1992 with nearly 480 stars across seven categories — from Entertainment to Military to Architect/Artist/Designer — Palm Springs' version of Hollywood's famous Walk covers the boulevard where celebrities once strolled without being noticed because everyone around them was also famous.

subject: Palm Springs, California
summary: The Cahuilla people called it Séc-he; the celebrities called it their desert retreat; in January 2018 it became the first city in America with an entirely LGBTQ-comprised city government — and through all of it, the San Jacinto Mountains kept watch from the west.

subject: Palma de Mallorca
summary: An ancient Mediterranean capital and a summer playground at once, stacked with two thousand years of conquest behind its old walls.

subject: Palmares (quilombo)
summary: For most of the seventeenth century, a self-governing confederation of people who had freed themselves held the palm-covered hills of Pernambuco against everything Portugal and the Dutch could send at it.

subject: Palmas, Tocantins
summary: Brazil's youngest state capital, designed from scratch in 1989 and modeled on Brasília, where a symmetrical park centers a grid of avenues on one of the hottest capital cities in the country.

subject: Palmeiras
summary: A former diamond town in the Chapada Diamantina that now lives on trekking, and the gateway to the Vale do Capão beneath Morro do Pai Inácio.

subject: Palmelo
summary: Goias's smallest municipality grew outward from a single Spiritist meeting hall founded in 1929, and it remains the only town in Brazil where the census finds Spiritists to be the largest religious group.

subject: Palmeral of Elche
summary: A living oasis of some 200,000 date palms grows on the coast of Spain, the only North African-style palm grove in Europe, engineered over two thousand years by Carthaginians, Romans, Arab hydraulic masters, and Christian settlers.

subject: Palmyra
summary: Once the richest caravan city between Rome and Persia, Palmyra rose from a desert oasis to challenge an empire under Queen Zenobia, fell to ruin, and endured destruction by ISIS -- yet its columns still stand.

subject: Palo Alto Art Center
summary: A community art hub housed in Palo Alto's former City Hall, where glass pumpkin patches and woven willow sculptures have turned a civic building into one of Silicon Valley's most surprising creative spaces.

subject: Palo Alto Baylands Nature Preserve
summary: The largest tract of undisturbed marshland remaining in San Francisco Bay, where 1,940 acres of tidal habitat host one of the West Coast's premier birdwatching destinations just minutes from Silicon Valley.

subject: Palouse
summary: The rolling wheat hills of southeastern Washington where wind-blown loess creates one of America's most photographed agricultural landscapes.

subject: Palparara
summary: A Channel Country cattle run that passed through the hands of Australia's greatest pastoral empire-builder, Sidney Kidman, before vanishing into ever-larger aggregations.

subject: Pambamarca
summary: An eroded stratovolcano 25 miles from Quito holds the greatest concentration of pre-Columbian fortresses in Ecuador - evidence of a 17-year war that nearly stopped the Incas.

subject: Pamir Mountains
summary: Known as the 'Roof of the World,' this ancient crossroads where Central Asia's greatest mountain ranges converge has drawn explorers, empires, and pilgrims for over two millennia.

subject: Pampa de Achala
summary: A high granite tableland at the heart of the Sierras de Córdoba where Andean condors ride the updrafts and nearly every stream in the province is born.

subject: Pampilla Festival
summary: Every September, hundreds of thousands of Chileans camp on a Coquimbo hillside for La Pampilla, the country's largest Independence celebration.

subject: Pan American Unity
summary: Diego Rivera painted his last great American mural at a World's Fair on Treasure Island, working in public view while the world around him marched toward war.

subject: Pan-STARRS
summary: From a volcanic summit on Maui, two telescopes armed with the world's largest astronomical cameras scan the entire visible sky every few nights, hunting for asteroids that could threaten Earth and cataloging the cosmos on an unprecedented scale.

subject: Panaga
summary: A Brunei village shaped by Shell petroleum, where a golf course once served as a wartime airstrip, a police station withstood a rebel siege, and oil company infrastructure now coexists with solar panels and lagoon picnics.

subject: Panagia Marmariotissa, Chalandri
summary: A wealthy Roman's marble tomb in the Athens suburb of Chalandri became, centuries later, a tiny Christian chapel - its name a memory of the precious stone it was built from.

subject: Panagia Tourliani
summary: The richly ornamented patron monastery of Mykonos in the inland village of Ano Mera, home to a miraculous icon and a Baroque altarpiece carved by Florentine artists in 1775.

subject: Panajachel
summary: A small town on the north shore of Lake Atitlan that evolved from a hippie enclave into Guatemala's premier lakeside tourist hub, where tuk-tuks circle cobbled streets, Mayan textiles line the main drag, and spectacular sunsets light up three volcanoes.

subject: Panam Nagar
summary: A haunting ghost city near Dhaka where 19th-century merchant mansions with Mughal arches, cast-iron columns, and mosaic floors line a single street flanked by canals -- the last visible fragment of ancient Sonargaon.

subject: Panama-Pacific International Exposition
summary: The 1915 world's fair that celebrated San Francisco's recovery from the 1906 earthquake and the opening of the Panama Canal.

subject: Panamá Viejo
summary: The oldest continuously occupied European settlement on the Pacific coast of the Americas, founded in 1519 and burned to the ground in 1671 by the privateer Henry Morgan.

subject: Pancake Rocks and Blowholes
summary: A 30-million-year geological marvel where limestone stacked like enormous flapjacks meets the Tasman Sea, sending plumes of seawater skyward through vertical blowholes.

subject: Pandie Pandie Station
summary: South Australia's northernmost cattle station sits where the Birdsville Track begins and the Diamantina runs - and its founder is the man who gave Birdsville its name.

subject: Pando Department
summary: Bolivia's most remote and least populated department, Pando is a densely forested Amazonian frontier shaped by rubber booms, territorial wars, and a capital city named in mourning for a lost Pacific coastline.

subject: Panduranga (Champa)
summary: For more than two centuries after the fall of their kingdom, the Cham people of Panduranga kept their language, faith, and royal lineage alive in the shadow of expanding Vietnamese power.

subject: Pangrati
summary: Named after the ancient sanctuary of Hercules Pancrates, Pangrati is a lively central Athens neighbourhood of writers, Nobel laureates, and neighbourhood cafés — and the home of the Panathenaic Stadium.

subject: Panguna Mine
summary: A mile-wide hole in the mountains of central Bougainville that produced one of the world's largest copper reserves, a ten-year civil war, and a scar visible from orbit.

subject: Panjiayuan antique market
summary: Beijing's largest flea market began as a pre-dawn ghost market in the 1980s and grew into a 48,500-square-meter bazaar where folk art from every province in China changes hands.

story.title: Panoche Hills: California's Last Desert Refuge

subject: Panoche Hills
summary: A fossil-rich badlands in the Inner Coast Ranges where ancient ocean floors meet California's most endangered desert species, and where hot springs steam beside 65-million-year-old cold seeps.

story.title: The Pantheon: Two Thousand Years Under an Open Sky

subject: Pantheon, Rome
summary: Built by Emperor Hadrian around AD 126, the Pantheon's unreinforced concrete dome remains the largest of its kind nearly two millennia later - its oculus open to the rain and sun, its interior a perfect sphere where the height equals the diameter at 142 feet.

subject: Pantikapaion
summary: The greatest Greek city of the Black Sea's far shore, whose name meant 'fish-path' and whose gold coins and grain harbors made it the capital of a kingdom between two worlds.

subject: Papar
summary: The Irish monks who left bells, books, and crosiers across the North Atlantic before the Vikings arrived - and left their name on islands all the way from Iceland to South Uist.

subject: Papenburg
summary: Germany's southernmost seaport sits forty kilometers inland, threaded with canals dug by peat cutters and dominated by a shipyard that builds some of the largest cruise liners on Earth.

subject: Papua
summary: The Indonesian half of New Guinea - six provinces stretched across the world's second-largest island, where tree-kangaroos share rainforest with the world's largest reef system.

subject: Papua New Guinea
summary: A country of over 800 languages, roadless mountains, and the shortest cultural learning curve in human history, occupying the eastern half of the world's largest tropical island.

subject: Paraburdoo Mine
summary: Deep in the iron heart of the Pilbara, an open pit named for 'feathered meat' feeds a railway to the sea and helps supply the ore that built modern Australia.

subject: Paracas National Reserve
summary: Where the Atacama Desert meets the cold Humboldt Current, a Peruvian reserve protects both ancient textiles and the richest marine ecosystem on the South American Pacific coast.

subject: Paracatu
summary: A colonial gold town in northwestern Minas Gerais where a national heritage centre and one of Brazil's largest open-pit gold mines share the same hillside.

subject: Paradise, New Zealand
summary: A remote valley at the head of Lake Wakatipu where beech forests stood in for Middle-earth, paradise shelducks may have inspired the name, and the landscape remains as cinematic as anything Peter Jackson put on screen.

subject: Paraguayan Chaco
summary: Sixty percent of Paraguay's territory but home to barely three percent of its people, the Chaco is a vast, thorn-studded wilderness where jaguars, rheas, and a peccary once thought extinct share the landscape with Mennonite colonies and indigenous nations.

story.title: Paraiba do Sul, Rio de Janeiro

subject: Paraiba do Sul, Rio de Janeiro
summary: A backwater in the river, discovered by a 20-year-old in 1681, became the pioneer town of the Serra Fluminense and the burial place of the arm of Tiradentes.

subject: Paramaribo swamp forests
summary: A narrow belt of peat-laden freshwater swamp along Suriname's coast where most of the country lives, where peat fires smolder underground, and where scarlet ibis stop to rest on their migrations.

subject: Paramushir
summary: A volcanic island of 23 volcanoes in the northern Kuril Islands, where Ainu heritage, imperial ambitions, wartime fortifications, and a devastating 1952 tsunami shaped a remote landscape now inhabited by a dwindling population and thriving wildlife.

subject: Paranapiacaba
summary: A Victorian railway village planted in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest by British engineers, where timber cottages that could pass for Surrey sit beneath a clock tower modeled on Big Ben, and the Tupi name means 'where you will find the sea.'

subject: Paraná, Entre Ríos
summary: Capital of Entre Ríos and, for eight years, capital of an entire breakaway nation, this river-bluff city has spent its history looking out over the great Paraná toward Santa Fe on the far shore.

subject: Paraopeba
summary: A small Minas Gerais town of 24,700 on BR-040 north of Sete Lagoas, where citrus groves and cattle pastures meet one of Brazil's main interior highways.

subject: Paraíba
summary: The Brazilian state where the day begins carries a single word on its flag — nego, I refuse — and runs from the easternmost cape in the Americas up onto a plateau of stone, drought and dinosaur tracks.

subject: Parbold
summary: A West Lancashire village in the valley of the River Douglas, marked by a 19th-century stone bottle on the hill and a windmill that has stood beside the Leeds and Liverpool Canal since 1794.

subject: Pardee Home
summary: A Victorian time capsule in downtown Oakland where three generations of a politically powerful California family left every knick-knack, elk head, and piece of scrimshaw exactly where Helen Pardee placed them.

subject: Parga
summary: A luminous terraced town on the Ionian coast, Parga spent four centuries under Venetian protection before its people chose exile rather than surrender — and when they left in 1819, they carried their ancestors' bones.

subject: Parihaka
summary: A small settlement on the western slopes of Taranaki Maunga where two Maori chiefs pioneered nonviolent resistance decades before Gandhi, and where 2,500 unarmed people sat in silence as 1,600 colonial troops invaded on 5 November 1881.

subject: Parintins
summary: An island city of 115,000 in the Amazon River, famous for the Boi-Bumba festival each June - when the population swells by tens of thousands for a three-night competition of dance, story, and rivalry.

subject: Paris
summary: The City of Light - where a single prefect demolished medieval Paris to create the modern metropolis, where revolution and culture shaped a capital that believes it invented beauty.

subject: Parium
summary: Founded in 709 BC on the Hellespont, Parium was an ancient Greek city that served as the customs gateway to Constantinople — a crossroads of empires whose coins, saints, and buried children's toys still speak across millennia.

subject: ParkShuttle
summary: A 1.8-kilometre driverless shuttle in suburban Rotterdam that has been quietly carrying paying passengers since 1999 - longer than almost any autonomous vehicle anywhere.

subject: Parker Ranch
summary: Founded in 1847 by a New England sailor who married into Hawaiian royalty, Parker Ranch became one of the largest cattle operations in America on land where paniolos predated Texas cowboys by decades.

subject: Parkersburg
summary: A West Virginia city of 30,000 at the confluence of the Little Kanawha and Ohio rivers, founded as Newport in 1773, renamed in 1810, and famously documented as the first place to commercialize petroleum in the United States.

subject: Parksville, British Columbia
summary: A Vancouver Island beach city where the tide walks a kilometre out, comes back warm over sunbaked sand, and has drawn a higher concentration of retirees than anywhere else in Canada.

subject: Parktown Mansions
summary: On a wooded ridge above Johannesburg, the gold-rush millionaires built their palaces in stone, and a handful of them still stand.

subject: Parnaíba
summary: Most travelers pass through Parnaíba without pausing - which is exactly why those who linger discover a Piauí coast unlike any other in Brazil.

subject: Parnaíba
summary: In the 18th century, Parnaíba's warehouses shipped carnauba wax to Germany and cotton to England - and for a time the port city mattered more than Piauí's capital.

subject: Parnitha
summary: The highest mountain ringing Athens, Parnitha is the city's green lung, its ancient watchtower, and the scene of a 2007 wildfire whose scars a century may not erase.

subject: Parque Bicentenario de Quito
summary: For 53 years planes roared over Quito's rooftops. When the airport finally moved, the city turned its runway into its biggest park.

subject: Parque El Ejido
summary: On 28 January 1912, a mob dragged the body of Ecuador's liberal president through Quito's streets and burned it where this park now stands.

story.title: Parque Nacional de las Cavernas del Río Camuy

subject: Parque Nacional de las Cavernas del Río Camuy
summary: One of the world's largest cave systems hides beneath the green hills of northwestern Puerto Rico, carved by the third-largest underground river on Earth.

subject: Parque Tantauco
summary: At the wild southern end of Chiloe Island, a privately owned wilderness shelters one of South America's rarest foxes and some of the last untouched temperate rainforest on Earth.

subject: Parque Tres de Febrero
summary: Buenos Aires turned a dictator's confiscated estate into its grandest public park, 400 hectares of rose gardens, lakes, and groves laid out by the French-Argentine landscaper Carlos Thays.

subject: Parque de la Independencia
summary: In the green heart of Rosario, gardeners have spelled out the day's date in living flowers every evening since 1946.

subject: Parral, Chihuahua
summary: The city that Philip IV of Spain crowned Capital of the World of Silver in 1640, where Pancho Villa was assassinated in 1923, and where a hill of ore still anchors the identity of a Mexican mining town.

subject: Parral, Chile
summary: A railway town in Chile's Maule Region where a stationmaster's son was born and grew up to become Pablo Neruda.

subject: Parramatta
summary: The eel place the Burramattagal named, where a starving colony staked its survival on a farm, and where Western Sydney now raises its skyline.

subject: Partenit
summary: A seaside settlement in the shadow of a mountain shaped like a sleeping bear, where olive trees have stood for five centuries and Greeks, Goths, and Genoese all left their mark.

subject: Pará
summary: Everything the world has ever wanted from the Amazon has left through Pará - rubber, iron, bauxite, beef, soy - and in November 2025 the world came to Belém to argue about it.

subject: Pasages (steam trawler)
summary: A Canadian-built minesweeper that survived the First World War, became a herring trawler, and ran aground off the Isle of Man in 1931 - where her rusted ribs still show at low tide.

subject: Pasaje Canton
summary: Twice driven from its original settlements by a river the Quechua called 'devourer of men,' the town of Pasaje took three tries to find a spot it could keep.

subject: Pasaquan
summary: In the rural backwoods of Marion County, Georgia, a self-proclaimed saint built a psychedelic compound of painted concrete walls, sculptures, and totems -- a visionary folk art environment unlike anything else in the American South.

subject: Pascagoula incident
summary: On an October evening in 1973, two shipyard workers went fishing on the Pascagoula River and came back with a story that turned a quiet Mississippi port town into the center of America's UFO obsession.

subject: Pascha (brothel)
summary: Twelve storeys of rented rooms on the Hornstraße housed Europe's largest brothel for nearly fifty years, until COVID-19 closed it down and a money-laundering investigation reopened the case.

subject: Pascua Lama
summary: High in the Andes, above glaciers that feed a farming valley, sits one of the largest gold deposits ever found and one of the most contested mining projects in the Americas, now ordered shut.

subject: Paseo de la Princesa
summary: A 19th-century promenade along Old San Juan's southern wall that began as a cleared field of fire for cannons and became the city's most beloved public gathering place.

subject: Paseo de la Reforma
summary: Built by an Austrian emperor to connect his castle to downtown, Mexico City's grandest boulevard outlasted its creator and became the stage on which the nation celebrates, protests, and reinvents itself.

subject: Paso de la Amada
summary: Home to the oldest known ballcourt in Mesoamerica, Paso de la Amada preserves evidence of the moment egalitarian villages began producing rulers.

subject: Pass of Brander stone signals
summary: In 1881, a falling boulder hit a train in a Highland gorge. The Victorian engineer's response - a four-mile fence of wires that trips signals when rocks break them - still works in 2026.

subject: Pass of Drumochter
summary: The highest point on Britain's longest road, this glacial U-shaped gap between the rivers Spey and Tay is the only practical road crossing of the Grampian Watershed for nearly 100 kilometres.

subject: Passat (ship)
summary: A four-masted Hamburg barque that rounded Cape Horn thirty-nine times, nearly capsized off Portugal seven weeks after her stablemate Pamir went down with eighty men, and has been tied up at Travemünde ever since.

subject: Passing Mother's Grave
summary: An 1856 oil painting by Groningen-born Jozef Israels of a widowed fisherman walking past his wife's grave with his two children, all three of them barefoot.

subject: Passo Fundo
summary: A cattle-trail town on the high plateau became the only city in Brazil declared National Capital of Literature by federal law.

subject: Passos
summary: A southwestern Minas town whose name means "steps" and whose motto turns that into a promise — the way through, rather than the destination.

subject: Pasteur Institute of Iran
summary: Founded in 1920 through a partnership between Paris and Tehran, the Pasteur Institute of Iran has spent over a century fighting rabies, cholera, plague, and tuberculosis -- saving millions of lives across the Middle East and beyond.

subject: Patagonia
summary: The end of the world begins here - where granite towers pierce the sky, glaciers calve into turquoise lakes, and the wind never stops blowing across the most dramatic landscapes in South America.

subject: Patalkot, India
summary: A horseshoe-shaped valley so deep and remote that its indigenous Bharia and Gond communities lived in near-total isolation for centuries, developing their own herbal medicine tradition.

subject: Patani Kingdom
summary: For over a century, this Malay sultanate on the Gulf of Thailand was ruled by four queens named for colors, fought off Siamese invasions, and drew merchants from China, Portugal, Holland, England, and Japan to its port.

subject: Paternoster
summary: A whitewashed fishing village on the West Coast of South Africa where fishermen still sell their catch on the beach and the smell of crayfish defines the local economy.

subject: Paternoster Midden
summary: A massive ancient refuse heap on South Africa's West Coast reveals thousands of years of human coastal life, from tortoise bones and seal remains to elephant ivory and ostrich eggshell beads.

subject: Paternoster Square
summary: Shadow of St Paul's Cathedral, Paternoster Square has cycled through meat market, publishing district, bombing rubble, architectural disgrace, and finally a polished redevelopment that houses the London Stock Exchange — all within a single city block.

subject: Paterson, New Jersey
summary: Alexander Hamilton's experiment in American industrial independence became the Silk City, then a beacon for immigrants from around the world, its Great Falls still thundering through a landscape of reinvention.

subject: Path of 100 Towers (Sardinia)
summary: Italy's longest trek -- 1,284 kilometers circling Sardinia's entire coastline -- follows a chain of 105 watchtowers built by the Spanish to repel Saracen raids, connecting medieval fortifications with wild beaches, lagoons, and Mediterranean scrub.

subject: Patmos
summary: A small, quiet Dodecanese island that mythology says rose from the sea and Christian tradition holds as the birthplace of the Book of Revelation - now both a pilgrimage destination and one of the Aegean's most tranquil retreats.

subject: Patraeus
summary: Half of an ancient Greek farming colony still stands above the fields of the Taman Peninsula; the other half lies drowned beneath Taman Bay.

subject: Patras
summary: Greece's third-largest city and its gateway to the West, Patras is a port where four millennia of history stack up between the Byzantine castle on the acropolis and the ferry terminals pointing toward Italy — with Europe's most exuberant carnival in between.

subject: Patrick County, Virginia
summary: Birthplace of Confederate cavalryman J.E.B. Stuart, home to Mabry Mill and the legendary Wood Brothers NASCAR team, and the Blue Ridge county where six rock churches still preach the gospel of a mountain pastor named Bob Childress.

subject: Patrocínio
summary: A Minas Gerais town whose name means "protection" after a landowner's legendary vow, now one of Brazil's largest hog producers and home to a suspected impact crater visible from space.

subject: Patum de Berga
summary: A UNESCO-honored Corpus Christi festival in the Catalan city of Berga where costumed giants, an eagle, mules, and fire-covered devils dance to the beat of a great drum.

subject: Paul Gauguin Interpretation Centre
summary: At Le Carbet in Martinique, a small interpretation centre marks the six months in 1887 when Paul Gauguin painted a dozen canvases that transformed his art and pointed him toward Tahiti.

subject: Paulet affair
summary: In 1843, a rogue British naval captain seized the Hawaiian Islands without authorization from London, triggering a five-month crisis that ended with American warships, a diplomatic race across two oceans, and the motto Hawaii still uses today.

subject: Pauline Epistles
summary: The letters Paul the Apostle wrote to early Christian communities — including two to the fractious port city of Corinth — are among the oldest surviving Christian documents and have shaped Christian theology for two millennia.

subject: Paulino Neves
summary: The paved road almost killed Paulino Neves as a destination - then locals rediscovered that their dunes are easier to reach than the famous ones next door.

subject: Paulista Avenue
summary: The 2.8-kilometer spine of Sao Paulo's ambition, where coffee barons' mansions gave way to glass towers, and where the city gathers to celebrate, protest, and simply be seen.

subject: Pavonia, New Netherland
summary: The first European settlement on the west bank of the Hudson River, Pavonia became a flashpoint of colonial violence when a Dutch massacre of Lenape refugees ignited a devastating war across New Netherland.

subject: Pawnee Rock, Kansas
summary: A tiny Kansas town of 193 people takes its name from the sandstone bluff that marked the approximate halfway point of the Santa Fe Trail -- a landmark so significant that travelers carved their names into it for decades before settlers built a community in its shadow.

subject: Paxos
summary: Greece's smallest main Ionian island, draped in ancient olive groves, riddled with sea-caves, and carrying a history that stretches from Phoenician traders to Venetian fleets to British aristocrats.

subject: Paysandú
summary: On the banks of the Uruguay River, this northern Uruguayan city wears the title 'La Heroica' and serves a meringue dessert whose recipe one family has guarded for three generations.

subject: Peace Arch
summary: A white arch straddling the exact line between Canada and the United States, with a box of relics sealed in its cornerstone and two iron gates deliberately left open.

subject: Peak Hill, Western Australia
summary: A Murchison gold town that boomed, emptied to a single resident, and then was dug up entirely - its old streets swallowed by four open-cut pits.

subject: Peak Tram
summary: Asia's first funicular railway, the Peak Tram has hauled passengers up Hong Kong's Victoria Peak since 1888, carrying colonial governors, commuters, and millions of tourists along one of the world's most dramatic urban ascents.

subject: Pearl S. Buck Birthplace
summary: In the hills of Pocahontas County, West Virginia, a three-story house built by Dutch refugees became the birthplace of the first American woman to win both the Pulitzer Prize and the Nobel Prize for Literature.

subject: Pearl Spring
summary: Bubbles rising through a square stone pool gave this spring its name -- and for centuries, the most powerful officials in Shandong built their offices around it.

subject: Pechora Sea
summary: A shallow, river-fed Arctic sea that defies its latitude with temperate characteristics, supporting the Barents Sea's highest biomass and one of Northern Europe's largest salmon migrations.

subject: Pedder Street
summary: The short, storied spine of Hong Kong's Central district, Pedder Street was named for the harbour master of Britain's first iron warship and has served as the commercial heart of the colony since the earliest days of British rule.

subject: Pederneiras
summary: A São Paulo farm named for the flint stones scattered on its land became a geographic center of the state and a truck-parts manufacturing hub when Volvo arrived in 1974.

subject: Pedra Azul
summary: The world's largest cut aquamarine came out of the ground here, in a Jequitinhonha town founded on the ashes of a fire that burned for sixty days.

subject: Pedra Furada
summary: A rock shelter in Piaui holds either the oldest evidence of humans in the Americas or a pile of rocks that fell off a cliff — and after fifty years, archaeology still cannot agree which.

subject: Pedro Carbo
summary: The town of Pedro Carbo sits at the 63-kilometer marker on the road north from Guayaquil, where woodworkers and hat weavers keep traditional crafts alive amid the tropical heat.

subject: Peduase Presidential Lodge
summary: A hilltop presidential retreat on Ghana's Akuapem Ridge, built under Kwame Nkrumah in 1959, where Nigerian leaders gathered in 1967 for peace talks that failed to prevent the Biafran War.

subject: Peebles
summary: A royal burgh on the River Tweed where three salmon, a Latin motto about swimming against the stream, and a 1629 witch trial all share the same square mile.

subject: Peel
summary: The Manx fishing port called the sunset city and the rose red city, built of red sandstone facing west across the Irish Sea, home to a Viking-age burial that produced grave goods unequalled in the British Isles.

subject: Pegu Club
summary: A Victorian gentlemen's club in colonial Rangoon that gave the world a famous cocktail, hosted Rudyard Kipling and Paul Theroux, survived military rule and socialist nationalization, and is now being coaxed back to life as a heritage venue.

subject: Pei County
summary: The hometown of Liu Bang, the peasant who overthrew the Qin dynasty and founded the Han, one of the most transformative dynasties in Chinese history.

subject: Peirópolis
summary: A Minas Gerais lime village where a railway cut exposed the bones of the last dinosaurs in Brazil — and where the old station now houses the museum built to hold them.

subject: Peking Man
summary: The Homo erectus subspecies that inhabited caves near Beijing for half a million years, reshaping the study of human evolution -- until the fossils vanished during World War II and became one of science's greatest missing treasures.

subject: Pelindaba
summary: On a quiet farm west of Pretoria, apartheid South Africa secretly built six atomic bombs - then became the only nation in history to construct its own nuclear arsenal and voluntarily destroy it.

subject: Pellana
summary: A small hill village 27 kilometers north of Sparta, Pellana carries a disputed claim as the Mycenaean capital of Laconia — and possibly as the legendary seat of Menelaus — while a Hellenic retaining wall and ancient fountains still survive along the Eurotas riverbank below.

subject: Pellene
summary: The easternmost of the twelve ancient Achaean cities, Pellene sat on a fortified hill in the northern Peloponnese, produced Olympic champions including an athlete who made himself tyrant, and is mentioned in Homer's Iliad.

subject: Peloponnese
summary: The great mountainous southern peninsula of Greece — joined to the mainland only by the Isthmus of Corinth — is the land of Sparta and Olympia, Mycenae and Mystras, the Mani and the ancient world's most contested battlegrounds.

subject: Pelotas
summary: Brazil's National Capital of Sweets built its neoclassical grandeur on dried beef and the labor of enslaved people, leaving a city of mansions, markets, and quindim.

subject: Pembina, North Dakota
summary: The oldest European-American settlement in the Dakotas sits at the confluence of the Red and Pembina rivers, just south of the Canadian border -- a tiny city of 512 people whose five competing fur-trading posts, Metis buffalo hunts, and frontier fort tell the story of how empires carved up the northern plains.

subject: Pembroke Dockyard
summary: From 1814 to 1926, Pembroke Dockyard built 263 Royal Navy ships and five royal yachts on the south shore of Milford Haven - then closed in interwar austerity and was reborn as a flying boat base.

subject: Pembroke, Pembrokeshire
summary: The Welsh town where a 13-year-old widow gave birth to a future king of England, founding the Tudor dynasty in a castle that no army ever took.

subject: Pembrokeshire Coast Path
summary: A 186-mile cliff-top trail through Britain's only coastal national park, threading volcanic headlands, smugglers' coves, and ancient pilgrim ground.

subject: Pen-yr-Orsedd Quarry
summary: The last working slate quarry in the Nantlle Valley, opened 1816 and finally closed in 1979 -- a vast staircased pit whose steam-era locomotives now run on tourist railways across Wales and England.

subject: Penang Hill
summary: A cluster of forested peaks rising 833 meters above Penang Island, connected to the lowlands since 1923 by Malaysia's only funicular railway and recognized by UNESCO as a Biosphere Reserve.

subject: Penang Strait
summary: An 11-kilometer channel between Penang Island and the Malay Peninsula that has served as a strategic shipping lane, wartime battleground, and engineering canvas since the British established George Town in 1786.

subject: Penang ferry service
summary: Malaysia's oldest ferry service has connected George Town to the mainland since 1894, surviving Japanese occupation, the opening of the Penang Bridge, and a 2020 suspension before reinventing itself with a modern catamaran fleet.

subject: Penbryn
summary: A National Trust beach below a circular Druidic churchyard, a sixth-century inscribed stone in a nearby field, and a wooded valley once known to smugglers as Robbers Valley - all wrapped into one small Ceredigion village.

subject: Pendeen
summary: A Cornish village built by miners on the cliff above the Atlantic, granite from its own hill in its church walls, and the birthplace of the antiquary who first taught Britain to see its prehistory.

subject: Pendle Hill
summary: The 557-metre Lancashire hill linked to three transformative events of the 17th century: the trial of ten people accused of witchcraft, George Fox's vision that founded the Quakers, and Richard Towneley's pioneering barometer experiment.

subject: Pendleton County, West Virginia
summary: A 700-square-mile West Virginia county with 6,143 residents, the state's highest peak, an NSA listening post, the world's largest Virginia big-eared bat hibernaculum, and a maple syrup industry.

subject: Penedo
summary: A colonial port stacked up a bluff above the lower São Francisco, where ocean-going ships once tied up and gilded rococo churches still look out over the water.

subject: Peng Chau
summary: Hong Kong's smallest inhabited outlying island, where no cars roam and eight temples stand within a single square kilometre of sedate, unhurried life.

subject: Penglipuran
summary: A traditional Balinese village where 112 hectares of ancestral architecture and sacred bamboo forest are both preserved and threatened by the 3,500 daily tourists who come to admire them.

subject: Penicuik
summary: A papermaking town on the North Esk whose name means 'hill of the cuckoo' in old Brythonic, where 309 French prisoners died, a Nobel laureate was born, and Sherlock Holmes' real-life model trained.

subject: Peninsular Ranges
summary: A single mountain chain stretching 1,500 kilometers from the San Jacinto Mountains of Southern California to the southern tip of Baja California, the Peninsular Ranges are geology made visible at continental scale.

subject: Penlee Lifeboat Station
summary: Moved to Newlyn after the catastrophic loss of the Solomon Browne and her entire crew on 19 December 1981, Penlee Lifeboat Station carries one of the most consequential names in British maritime memory - and the only RNLI gold medal awarded posthumously to a coxswain.

subject: Penmon Lifeboat Station
summary: Founded in 1831 by a Welsh clergyman and his wife who had witnessed 140 souls drown, Penmon Lifeboat Station saved hundreds of lives before motor lifeboats made it obsolete in 1915.

subject: Penmynydd
summary: The small Anglesey village whose name means 'top of the mountain' was the cradle of the Tudor dynasty - the ancestral seat of the family that would put Henry VII on the English throne.

subject: Penn Quarter
summary: Once the dead heart of downtown Washington, the blocks between the FBI Building and Capital One Arena were revitalized in the 1990s into a 24-hour neighborhood of theaters, restaurants, and condos.

subject: Pennan
summary: A single row of houses, a harbour, and a red phone box - the Aberdeenshire fishing village that played Ferness in Local Hero.

subject: Pennine Way
summary: Britain's first and most demanding national trail - 268 miles of windswept moors, ancient peat bogs, and wild uplands tracing the spine of England from the Peak District to Scotland.

subject: Penrhyn Du Mines
summary: A cluster of lead, zinc, and copper mines on the Llyn Peninsula's Black Headland, worked sporadically since at least the sixteenth century and intensively in the Victorian era.

subject: Penrhyn Quarry
summary: The world's largest slate quarry at its peak, built on Jamaican slave wealth, scarred by the longest strike in British history, and now spanned by a zip line above its flooded floor.

subject: Penrhyndeudraeth
summary: A Welsh-speaking town that grew from a malarial swamp, made explosives for 130 years, and gave Bertrand Russell a quiet view of the estuary in his last years.

subject: Penrith
summary: A red sandstone market town at the crossroads of the Eden Valley, where Anglo-Saxon kings, Vikings, Richard III and the Beacon Hill bonfires of 1804 all left their mark.

subject: Pentagon City
summary: From empty fields in 1946 to Amazon's HQ2 eight decades later - the 190-acre stretch of southeast Arlington has become one of the most consequential mixed-use districts in the country.

subject: Pentland Firth
summary: The strait that separates Orkney from mainland Scotland, where some of the fastest tidal currents on Earth squeeze between two oceans and Norse sailors named whirlpools after the witches who turn the millstone of the sea.

subject: Pentland Hills
summary: A twenty-mile range of volcanic and sedimentary hills rising southwest from Edinburgh, where Iron Age forts, a 1666 battle, a poet's garden, and a triple murder all share the same upland pasture.

subject: Pentland Skerries
summary: A scatter of four uninhabited rocky islets in the middle of the Pentland Firth, marked by a pair of lighthouses lit in 1794 and home to seabird colonies that fill the wind for half the year.

subject: Pentonville
summary: A quiet North London district built in the 1770s on what was open countryside, Pentonville gave its streets to Georgian development and its corner rooms to some remarkable tenants — including the birthplace of John Stuart Mill and a lodging shared by Lenin and Trotsky.

subject: Penwith
summary: The far western tip of Cornwall - a granite peninsula of cliffs, neolithic stones, last Cornish speakers, and tin mines that fed half the world - reaches further into the Atlantic than anywhere else in England.

subject: Penzance
summary: The southernmost and westernmost railway terminus in England, Penzance is the working harbour town that gave Gilbert and Sullivan their pirates, the Bronte sisters' mother her childhood, and Cornwall its principal port for nearly five hundred years.

story.title: People From the Top of the Land

subject: People From the Top of the Land
summary: The Kashaya Pomo of Stewarts Point Rancheria are the only California tribe never removed from their ancestral territory, and in 2015 they reclaimed 688 acres of coastline after a century of forced separation from the sea.

story.title: People's Liberation Army Support Base in Djibouti

subject: People's Liberation Army Support Base in Djibouti
summary: China's first overseas military base sits on 0.5 square kilometers of Djiboutian coast, sharing the country with American, French, Japanese, and Italian forces along the most contested strait in world shipping.

subject: Peperbus
summary: A hexagonal stone building in the Karoo town of Fraserburg, designed in 1861 by a pastor and built by a Baster craftsman, that has served as market house, library, magistrate's office, and symbol of a town's stubborn identity.

subject: Peplos Kore
summary: We picture ancient Greek statues as serene white marble, but the Peplos Kore was once a riot of color, her hair red, her lips painted, her gown patterned bright.

story.title: Pepper, Copper, and the Edge of the Known World

subject: Pepper, Copper, and the Edge of the Known World
summary: The Dutch East India Company ship Vianen survived a grounding on the Australian coast in 1628 -- an accident that produced one of the earliest European charts of Western Australia and the first recorded European sighting of Indigenous Australians there -- before sinking in the Sunda Strait on her second voyage.

subject: Peralta (Mesoamerican site)
summary: A 150-hectare pre-Hispanic city in Guanajuato with 22 pyramids, sunken ceremonial plazas, and trade goods from Guatemala to New Mexico -- part of the enigmatic Bajio tradition that flourished while Teotihuacan declined.

subject: Peralta Adobe
summary: Built in 1797 by one of San Jose's founders, the Peralta Adobe is the oldest standing building in the city, its two-foot-thick walls a physical link to California's Spanish colonial past.

subject: Perchem
summary: A Crimean mountain that was once a living coral reef on the floor of a vanished ocean, now a wooded massif guarding the western edge of the Sudak valley.

subject: Percy Fawcett
summary: A British artillery officer who believed in Atlantis-style lost cities disappeared into the Mato Grosso in 1925 with his son and his son's friend - and his disappearance became one of the twentieth century's most durable mysteries.

subject: Percé Rock
summary: A 400-million-year-old limestone monolith pierced by the sea, standing sentinel at the tip of Quebec's Gaspé Peninsula amid one of the world's largest gannet colonies.

subject: Pereiaslav
summary: One of the oldest cities of Kievan Rus, now an open-air treasury of more than twenty museums, and the birthplace of the beloved Yiddish writer Sholem Aleichem.

subject: Pergamon Altar
summary: A Hellenistic altar that ancient writers almost entirely ignored became Berlin's most famous possession - and has now been out of public view for over a decade.

subject: Perim
summary: A small volcanic island in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait that has served as British coaling station, Soviet listening post, Yemeni outpost, and, most recently, the site of a mysterious airbase built during the Yemeni civil war.

subject: Pernambuco
summary: A narrow blade of a state running from Atlantic reef to the São Francisco River, Pernambuco built Brazil's sugar economy, broke with the empire twice, and turned both into music.

subject: Perth
summary: Where Australia's most isolated major city watches sunsets over the Indian Ocean, where mining wealth builds skylines, where the distance from everywhere else becomes identity.

subject: Perth (Scotland)
summary: Scotland's ancient 'Fair City' at the gateway to the Highlands, where the River Tay turns tidal, medieval kings held court, and Walter Scott found the setting for one of his greatest novels.

subject: Perth Basin
summary: The hidden rift beneath Western Australia's cities -- a sedimentary basin born from the breakup of Gondwana that now supplies the water Perth drinks and the coal that powers its grid.

subject: Peru
summary: A republic of 34 million spanning Pacific desert, Andean sierra, and Amazon rainforest - heir to one of the longest continuous histories of civilization on Earth.

subject: Peruvian Amazonia
summary: Sixty percent of Peru lies under Amazon rainforest - a region larger than Spain where only five percent of Peruvians live, and where the fight over who owns the trees has turned deadly.

subject: Pete Dye Golf Club
summary: A 7,308-yard Pete Dye-designed course built on a former coal mine outside Bridgeport, West Virginia - ranked among America's top 100 golf courses and the only one Pete Dye agreed to put his own name on.

subject: Peter O'Neill Crowley
summary: A Fenian leader from Ballymacoda who died in Kilclooney Wood in March 1867, the failed rising made him a folk hero - and put his name on terraces, quays, and street corners across County Cork.

subject: Peter O'Reilly (civil servant)
summary: From a verandah on the Gorge Waterway, an Irish immigrant spent eighteen years drawing the lines that became British Columbia's Indian reserve system - and his lawn became a rescue station on the worst day in Victoria's history.

subject: Peterborough
summary: A Cambridgeshire cathedral city of 200,000, an hour from King's Cross on the East Coast Main Line, with a striking twelfth-century cathedral, two royal burials, an industrial-meets-New-Town fringe, and the Fens at its back door.

subject: Peterborough
summary: A Fenland cathedral city built on Anglo-Saxon foundations, Roman pottery, and a 20th-century empire of bricks.

subject: Peterhead
summary: The Bloo Toon: easternmost town on the Scottish mainland, the UK's busiest whitefish port, and a place where the fish supper still arrives the same day it was caught.

subject: Petra
summary: The Nabataean capital carved from rose-red sandstone controlled ancient trade routes for centuries, was lost to the Western world for nearly a millennium, and remains one of the most astonishing archaeological sites on Earth.

subject: Petrobras 36
summary: When P-36 sank off the Brazilian coast in March 2001, it was the largest oil platform in the world. Eleven Petrobras workers died. The cause was a valve that should not have leaked.

subject: Petroglyphs of Sikachi-Alyan
summary: On basalt boulders along the Amur River near the Nanai village of Sikachi-Alyan, someone carved mammoths, shamans, horses, and spirals into stone — some of the carvings up to 14,000 years old, made when ice-age megafauna still walked this valley.

subject: Petrolina
summary: In the one corner of Brazil's drought-stricken sertao that people move to rather than away from, irrigated vineyards and mango orchards feed supermarkets on two continents.

subject: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky
summary: The capital of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, a port city of 180,000 ringed by snow-capped volcanoes, geographically closer to San Francisco than to Moscow, and one of the most isolated large cities on Earth.

subject: Petticoat Lane Market
summary: Petticoat Lane Market on Middlesex Street has traded clothing and goods at London's eastern boundary since Tudor times, absorbing wave after wave of immigrants — Huguenots, Jews, South Asians — each leaving their mark on one of Britain's oldest surviving street markets.

subject: Pettigo
summary: A small village bisected by an international border, briefly invaded by the IRA in 1922 and shelled by British field guns, today best known as the gateway to one of Christianity's oldest pilgrimages.

subject: Pewsum
summary: An East Frisian warft village whose chieftain dynasty ended in 1565, leaving behind the Manningaburg castle — built in 1458 and the emblem of Pewsum — and a 19th-century tower mill housing a craft museum.

subject: Peñíscola
summary: A whitewashed town clinging to a rocky headland thrust into the Mediterranean, crowned by the last castle the Knights Templar ever built and defended, once, by a pope who refused to quit.

subject: Peʻahi, Hawaii
summary: Maui's deep-water reef break where waves exceeding 60 feet attract the world's best big-wave surfers to a coastline so rugged there are no beaches -- only cliffs, a dirt road, and the open Pacific.

subject: Pfaueninsel
summary: A 67-hectare island in the Havel where a 17th-century chemist made ruby glass, a Prussian king kept nine hundred animals, and the peacocks still have the run of the place.

subject: Phaeno Science Center
summary: Zaha Hadid's concrete science centre in Wolfsburg, propped on ten hollow cones so that the city can walk underneath it.

subject: Phan Ngọc Hiển
summary: A blacklisted young schoolteacher was posted to the last village in Vietnam to keep him quiet; eighty years later the district, the commune and the school all carry his name.

subject: Phan Rí Cửa
summary: Phan Rí Cửa is a coastal port town in southern Vietnam whose Cham name — Panrik — echoes a civilization that thrived here for nearly two millennia before the modern town took its place.

subject: Phanagoria
summary: Founded by refugees fleeing a Persian conqueror, the greatest Greek city of the Taman Peninsula later sheltered an exiled emperor and, buried in its soil, one of the oldest synagogues ever found.

subject: Phantasialand
summary: A theme park hemmed in by its own small footprint has spent six decades reinventing itself, tearing down rides to make room for ever more detailed worlds.

subject: Pharaohs' Golden Parade
summary: On 3 April 2021, twenty-two royal mummies traveled through Cairo in nitrogen-filled capsules, escorted by a philharmonic orchestra, ancient Egyptian hymns, and a 21-gun salute.

subject: Pheneus
summary: An ancient Arcadian city enclosed in a mountain-ringed plain riddled with sinkholes, where myth credited Heracles with digging the drainage channels, Pliny counted five catastrophic floods, and the plain itself was still washing away into the underground as recently as 1821.

subject: Phigalia
summary: This rugged ancient city above the Neda gorge commissioned the Temple of Apollo at Bassae — built by the architect of the Parthenon, and still among the best-preserved temples in Greece — after the gods delivered them from plague.

story.title: Philadelphia: America's First City, Second-Guessed Ever Since

subject: Philadelphia
summary: The Pennsylvania city where the nation was founded and then immediately left behind - where the Liberty Bell cracked and the cheesesteaks divide loyalties, and where a Rocky statue gets more visitors than the art museum it stands beside.

subject: Philadelphia
summary: The city where the Declaration of Independence was signed, where the Constitution was debated, where the Liberty Bell cracked, and where they still boo Santa Claus at Eagles games.

subject: Philippine Air Lines Flight F26
summary: On May 20, 1964, a De Havilland Canada DHC-3 Otter flying Philippine Air Lines' rural route struck a hill at Sibuco Point in near-zero visibility, killing all aboard and ending the airline's use of the rugged bush plane that had connected Mindanao's remote communities.

subject: Philips Natuurkundig Laboratorium
summary: For most of the twentieth century, the world's first compact disc, the audio cassette, and a stream of fundamental physics breakthroughs all came out of one campus on the southern edge of Eindhoven.

subject: Philips Stadion
summary: What is now the third-largest football ground in the Netherlands began life in 1910 as a village green for Philips factory workers, with a korfball field and a bandstand.

story.title: The Philosopher's Path: Two Kilometers of Thought

subject: Philosopher's Walk
summary: A narrow stone path along a cherry-tree-lined canal in Kyoto's Higashiyama district, named for the philosopher who walked it daily while developing ideas that bridged Eastern and Western thought.

subject: Phlius
summary: Perched in its own upland plain at 900 feet above sea level in the northeastern Peloponnese, the ancient city-state of Phlius was small, fiercely independent, and the unlikely birthplace of both satyr drama and a student of Plato.

subject: Phnom Kulen
summary: Angkor was quarried out of this mountain and the Khmer Empire was proclaimed on top of it, which is why Cambodians still come up Phnom Kulen in pilgrimage to a reclining Buddha carved from a single sandstone boulder.

subject: Phnom Santuk
summary: A 207-metre rise in the paddy country of Kampong Thom where Buddhas sleep inside the boulders, kings once rehoused relics carried from Angkor, and a doomed 1971 offensive reached its furthest point before it broke.

subject: Phnom Sorsia
summary: A limestone hill east of Kampot where a stalagmite is revered as a white elephant and several thousand bats leave through a chimney in the rock each evening.

subject: Phnom Thnout-Phnom Pok Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: A couple moved into a patch of northern Cambodian forest in 2014; three years later a government sub-decree turned 42,097 hectares of it into a wildlife sanctuary.

subject: Phocis (Ancient Region)
summary: A small mountain state in central Greece whose lack of material wealth was more than compensated by its possession of Delphi — the sanctuary that the ancient world treated as the center of everything.

subject: Phoenician shipwrecks of Mazarrón
summary: Two small Phoenician trading vessels, sunk by a freak storm and sealed in sand for some 2,600 years, are among the best-preserved ancient ships ever found.

story.title: Phoenix: The City That Shouldn't Exist But Won't Stop Growing

subject: Phoenix
summary: The Arizona metropolis built in a desert that reaches 115 degrees - where ancient irrigation canals were rediscovered and rebuilt, where air conditioning made life possible, and where water borrowed from elsewhere sustains a city of 5 million.

story.title: Phoenix: The Desert City That Shouldn't Exist

subject: Phoenix
summary: The city that rose where ancient Hohokam canals once irrigated the desert, now America's fifth-largest metropolis where summer highs regularly exceed 110°F and air conditioning is not optional.
