subject: Phoenix, Arizona
summary: America's fifth-largest city rose from the ruins of the Hohokam civilization, transforming ancient irrigation canals into a modern metropolis where five million people thrive in the Sonoran Desert.

story.title: Phou Hin Poun National Biodiversity Conservation Area

subject: Phou Hin Poun National Biodiversity Conservation Area
summary: A rodent bought at a Thakhek market turned out to belong to a family absent from the fossil record for eleven million years - and the limestone it came from has an annual protection budget of about five hundred dollars.

subject: Phthiotic Thebes
summary: A Thessalian harbor city that outlived its conquerors, traded its name for a king's, and left nine Early Christian basilicas paved in mosaic floors.

subject: Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt
summary: Germany's legal second is counted by four caesium clocks on the western edge of Braunschweig, then broadcast at 77.5 kilohertz to every radio-controlled clock in Central Europe.

subject: Phú Ninh Reservoir
summary: Called 'the blue pearl of Quảng Nam,' Phú Ninh Reservoir is a vast artificial lake surrounded by protected forest, 15 scattered islands, and hot mineral springs — a working water resource that has quietly become one of central Vietnam's most important natural sanctuaries.

subject: Phú Xuân
summary: Before it was Huế, it was Phú Xuân — a city that changed hands six times in two centuries of Vietnamese dynastic warfare and became the capital of a unified Vietnam under the very dynasty that almost destroyed it.

subject: Piauí
summary: Brazil's eleventh-largest state has 66 kilometres of coast, an inland capital drawn on paper in 1852, and a history that runs the wrong way - inland to outward, cattle before towns.

subject: Piazza San Marco
summary: The only space in Venice deemed worthy of the title 'piazza,' where Napoleon saw the drawing room of Europe and where the Adriatic now floods the floor.

subject: Piazza dei Cavalieri, Pisa
summary: Pisa's second great square began as the political heart of the medieval republic, was remade by Vasari for the Medici crusading knights, and now houses one of Italy's most prestigious universities.

subject: Piccadilly
summary: Less than a mile long but carrying centuries of London life, Piccadilly has been a road to Reading, a row of aristocratic palaces, a Rothschild enclave, the cradle of British bookselling, and — in its darker chapter — the centre of London's illegal drug trade.

subject: Piccadilly Circus
summary: The London junction named for seventeenth-century collars, lit by neon since 1908, and so reliably crowded that the British use 'like Piccadilly Circus' as shorthand for chaos.

subject: Piccadilly line
summary: The deep-level London Underground line that opened in 1906 with ox-blood terracotta stations, was extended to Heathrow in stages from 1975, and carried 218 million journeys in 2019.

subject: Picchetti Brothers Winery
summary: Italian immigrants Secondo and Vincenzo Picchetti named this ridge 'Monte Bello' and planted some of the first grapevines in the Santa Cruz Mountains, where their winery still operates.

story.title: Picher: America's Most Toxic Ghost Town

subject: Picher
summary: The Oklahoma mining town so contaminated it had to be erased - where lead and zinc mining poisoned the children, undermined the ground, and created America's largest Superfund site until the government paid everyone to leave.

subject: Pickens County, South Carolina
summary: A South Carolina county where the Blue Ridge falls to the Piedmont, Clemson orange runs through every conversation, and the most famous son was a barefoot kid from Brandon Mill named Shoeless Joe.

subject: Pickerill and Juliet Gas Fields
summary: Two unmanned steel platforms, 66 km off Spurn Head, that quietly produced North Sea gas for a quarter-century - and then were dismantled so thoroughly that nothing above the seabed remains.

subject: Pickfair
summary: For two decades, a Beverly Hills estate called Pickfair was the closest thing Hollywood had to a royal court — a place where Charlie Chaplin and Albert Einstein shared the same table, and where Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks presided over the golden age of silent film.

subject: Picnic Point, Toowoomba
summary: Where Toowoomba runs out of land, the city stops at a cliff edge and hands you 180 degrees of the Lockyer Valley.

subject: Pico Cristóbal Colón
summary: Colombia's highest peak rises nearly 5,700 meters just 42 kilometers from the Caribbean shore, making it the tallest coastal mountain on Earth and one of the most difficult summits in South America to reach.

subject: Pico do Jaraguá
summary: The highest point in the city of Sao Paulo, where a 16th-century gold rush, Tupi heritage, and television broadcasting towers share a single Atlantic Forest peak at 1,135 meters.

subject: Picton (New Zealand)
summary: A small harbor town that stitches New Zealand's two islands together, where ferries, fishing boats, and cruise ships converge in the sheltered waters of Queen Charlotte Sound.

subject: Picton, Lennox and Nueva
summary: Three windswept islands at the bottom of the world that, in 1978, brought Chile and Argentina within hours of war.

subject: Picts
summary: The pre-Gaelic people of northern Scotland who left no written language, only stones carved with serpents and combs, and a kingdom that became Alba.

subject: Pictured Rocks
summary: The painted cliffs of Lake Superior - where 200-foot sandstone bluffs streak with mineral stains of red, green, and yellow along 42 miles of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, America's first designated national lakeshore.

subject: Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore
summary: America's first National Lakeshore, where 500-million-year-old sandstone cliffs paint Lake Superior's shore in streaks of iron red, manganese black, and copper green across 42 miles of Michigan's Upper Peninsula coastline.

subject: Piedmont Atlantic Megaregion
summary: The sprawling Sun Belt megaregion that follows I-85 from Birmingham through Atlanta and Charlotte to the Research Triangle, home to 12 percent of Americans.

subject: Piedmont Triad
summary: Three cities, one metro - Greensboro, Winston-Salem, and High Point bound together by interstates, by textiles and tobacco and furniture, and by a long civil rights history.

subject: Piedra Movediza
summary: For decades a 300-ton granite boulder teetered on a single point above Tandil, smashing bottles wedged beneath it - until one summer afternoon in 1912 it finally let go.

subject: Pierre Charles L'Enfant
summary: The French-born artist and engineer who designed America's capital city, then was fired before seeing it built, and died penniless -- only to be reburied with honors overlooking the city he imagined.

subject: Piet Retief
summary: Voortrekker leader Piet Retief wrote the manifesto that launched the Great Trek, negotiated a land treaty with the Zulu King Dingane, and was murdered -- along with his entire delegation -- at the moment of its ratification.

subject: Pietermaritzburg
summary: KwaZulu-Natal's capital city, where Voortrekker history, Victorian red brick, and an 89-kilometer ultramarathon converge in the 'Place of the Elephant.'

subject: Pieterpad
summary: Two women in 1983 mapped a 492-kilometer walking route from a Wadden Sea village to a hill outside Maastricht. It is now the most famous long-distance walk in the Netherlands.

subject: Pietà (Michelangelo)
summary: Michelangelo's only signed work depicts a young Mary cradling her dead son, carved from a single block of Carrara marble by a 24-year-old sculptor who had to sneak back at night to chisel his name onto it.

subject: Pigüé
summary: A Pampas town founded in 1884 by 165 poor French farmers from Aveyron, who crossed an ocean on the promise of land and built a stubborn outpost of Occitan language and culture that survives to this day.

subject: Pike Place Market
summary: Seattle's century-old public market where fishmongers hurl salmon over the counter, the original Starbucks still pours coffee, and nearly 500 residents call the bustling arcades home.

subject: Pike's Peak gold rush
summary: The rallying cry that launched 100,000 fortune seekers across the Great Plains and gave birth to Denver, Boulder, and the Colorado Territory.

subject: Pikes Creek Tragedy
summary: On October 2, 1884, a work train sent to repair washed-out track along Wisconsin's Lake Superior shore plunged into rain-swollen Pikes Creek, killing ten men in a disaster that made coast-to-coast headlines before fading into near-total obscurity.

subject: Pikes Peak
summary: The fourteener that inspired 'America the Beautiful' - a 14,115-foot Front Range summit where the Ute people traced their creation, gold seekers fixed their hopes, and doughnuts collapse if you carry them downhill.

subject: Pikes Peak International Hill Climb
summary: Since 1916, drivers and riders have raced 156 turns up Pikes Peak in the oldest and most dangerous hill climb in America.

subject: Pikeville, Kentucky
summary: The town that moved a mountain to save itself, deep in the country where the Hatfields and McCoys fought their famous feud.

subject: Pikworo Slave camp
summary: A haunting rock formation in northern Ghana where enslaved people were held, auctioned, and forced to begin a 150-kilometer march toward the Atlantic coast.

subject: Pilar de Goiás
summary: A town that began as a settlement of escaped enslaved people in 1736, grew rich on gold, produced a 900-kilo bell cast with an arroba of gold, and is slowly emptying out.

subject: Pilar, Paraguay
summary: A river town where Paraguay's only authorized foreign trade port once funneled yerba mate to the world, and where church bells rang for hours when Brazilian occupiers finally left.

subject: Pilbara
summary: An ancient craton larger than California, the Pilbara holds some of Earth's oldest rocks and Australia's largest iron ore reserves beneath a punishing sun.

subject: Pilgrim's Rest
summary: A gold-rush town in Mpumalanga that the diggers never quite left, preserved corrugated-iron and all as a living museum to South Africa's first great rush.

subject: Pillar Point Bluff
summary: A coastal bluff trail on the San Mateo coast offering views of Mavericks surf break, migrating gray whales, and the working harbor below.

subject: Pillars of Hercules
summary: The two promontories flanking the Strait of Gibraltar -- the Rock of Gibraltar and a disputed peak in North Africa -- marked the edge of the known world for ancient Greeks and Romans, and their name still echoes in the coat of arms of Spain.

subject: Pilungah Reserve
summary: A conservation reserve on the Queensland edge of the Simpson Desert, named for a Wangkamadla spring, where Devonian fish fossils, ancient trade routes, and rare desert wildlife meet on country recently returned under native title.

story.title: Pilón Lajas Biosphere Reserve and Communal Lands

subject: Pilón Lajas Biosphere Reserve and Communal Lands
summary: Where the Andes break apart into Amazon rainforest, the Tsimané and Mosetén peoples won legal title to an ancestral homeland that is also a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

subject: PinchukArtCentre
summary: A steel fortune built one of Eastern Europe's boldest contemporary art centers in the heart of Kyiv, where admission is free and a global prize hunts for the next generation of artists.

subject: Pindaya Caves
summary: Hidden inside a limestone ridge in Shan State, Myanmar, the Pindaya Caves shelter more than 8,000 Buddha images spanning nearly three centuries -- a gilded labyrinth where Theravada and Mahayana traditions once converged.

subject: Pine Ridge Indian Reservation
summary: One of America's largest reservations, home to the Oglala Lakota Sioux, where the echoes of Wounded Knee and a century of resistance still resonate across the windswept prairie.

subject: Ping An Finance Centre
summary: At 599.1 metres, Ping An Finance Centre lords over Shenzhen's skyline — a needle of glass and steel so tall that its designers abandoned plans for an antenna because it would have disrupted flight paths.

subject: Ping Kong
summary: A walled village in Hong Kong's North District where a once-a-decade Taoist festival still brings the Hau clan home from Europe and the Americas, and the old name — Lucky Dragon Wall — has never entirely been forgotten.

subject: Pinglin
summary: A mountain district where more than 80% of residents earn their living from tea, and where the world's largest tea museum stands as testament to one variety's quiet dominance.

subject: Pingxi
summary: A mountain district in northeast Taiwan where coal-mining history, paper sky lanterns, and waterfall trails converge in the narrow valley of the upper Keelung River.

subject: Pingxi District
summary: Taiwan's smallest New Taipei district, where the coal miners who built a mountain economy are now honored in museums and sky lanterns carry their descendants' wishes into the dark above the Keelung River valley.

subject: Pingxi Line
summary: A 12.9-kilometer single-track branch railway through the mountain valleys of northeast Taiwan, built in 1921 to haul coal and now carrying tourists past waterfalls, old mining towns, and the headwaters of the Keelung River.

subject: Pingüino de Humboldt National Reserve
summary: Three desert islands off Chile's coast shelter most of the world's Humboldt penguins, plus whales, dolphins, and sea otters in some of the richest cold water on Earth.

subject: Pinksterlanddagen
summary: Every Pentecost since 1924, anarchists from across Europe have gathered in a Frisian forest at a campsite literally called For Freedom of Mind - making it one of the longest-running anarchist events on earth.

subject: Pinnacle Point
summary: A series of caves on a rocky headland south of Mossel Bay holds evidence that humans were harvesting shellfish, using fire to improve their tools, and painting their bodies 170,000 years ago.

subject: Pinson Mounds
summary: The largest Middle Woodland mound complex in the United States, where 17 prehistoric earthworks rise from a Tennessee plateau, aligned to the movements of the sun.

subject: Pinto Mountains
summary: A range of dark gneiss running east-west across the north-central portion of Joshua Tree National Park, topped at 1,403 meters, flanked by wilderness established by Congress in 2009, and dominated by creosote bush rather than the Joshua trees that give the park its name.

subject: Pioneer Square totem pole
summary: A Tlingit totem pole carved around 1790 to honor a woman called Chief-of-All-Women was stolen by Seattle businessmen in 1899, sparking indictments, rival newspaper warfare, and a century of complicated civic pride.

subject: Pioneer Square, Seattle
summary: Seattle's oldest neighborhood rose from ashes and landfill, where a stolen totem pole stands in a triangular plaza above buried storefronts, and the term 'Skid Row' was born on the very street that once hauled logs to Henry Yesler's mill.

subject: Pioneertown Mountains Preserve
summary: A 25,500-acre wild corridor in the Little San Bernardino Mountains where granite domes, volcanic mesas, and perennial streams stitch together two distinct desert worlds.

subject: Pioneertown and Pappy & Harriet's
summary: The California desert town built as a 1940s movie set - where the fake Old West buildings became a real community and a roadhouse bar became one of America's best live music venues, hosting Paul McCartney in a 200-person room.

subject: Pioneertown, California
summary: Built in 1946 as a live-in Western movie set where actors could reside while filming, Pioneertown never stopped playing its part and remains a functioning community where Mane Street still bans automobiles.

subject: Piper Alpha
summary: The world's deadliest offshore oil platform disaster, in which 167 workers lost their lives on a single night in the North Sea, reshaping safety regulation for the global oil industry.

subject: Piraeus
summary: The mighty port of Athens — the busiest passenger port in Europe and the busiest container port in the Eastern Mediterranean — has been the maritime gateway of Greece for 2,500 years, bound to its city by walls, by history, and by the sea.

subject: Piraeus Station
summary: Two stations side by side at the edge of the sea: Piraeus is the terminus of Athens Metro Line 1 — Greece's oldest railway — and a suburban rail hub that has carried the city's traffic through wars, collapse, and renewal since 1869.

subject: Pirajá, Salvador
summary: A neighborhood on the northern edge of Salvador whose Tupi name means 'full of fish' - and whose hills were the site of the 1822 battle that secured Bahia's independence from Portugal.

subject: Piranguinho
summary: A railway village in the Sapucaí valley that turned rapadura and roasted peanuts into an identity, and once a year builds a slab of candy longer than a swimming pool.

subject: Piranhas
summary: A whitewashed river town wedged into the canyons of the lower São Francisco, once the head of navigation, the start of a railway to nowhere, and the place where the cangaço came to a public end.

subject: Pirapora
summary: A river port on Brazil's mightiest inland river, where paddle steamers once ran to Bahia and where fish still jump in the spawning season.

subject: Pirassununga
summary: The Tupi named this place for the noise migrating fish make fighting upriver; today the same town trains every officer in the Brazilian Air Force and distils the country's most famous cachaça.

subject: Pirca Pirca
summary: A hilltop archaeological site in Peru's La Libertad region where Chavín, Wari, and Chimú builders each left their stones.

subject: Pirenópolis
summary: Stone-paved streets, 18th-century churches, and a three-day cavalry battle against the Moors - an 18th-century gold town that refused to disappear.

subject: Pirenópolis
summary: The Greek-named gold town that homesick Catalans christened after the Pyrenees, where Charlemagne's knights still ride every Pentecost.

subject: Pires do Rio
summary: A Goiás town that sprang up around a railway station and still honors the engineer-minister who ordered its steel to be laid.

subject: Piriápolis
summary: A quieter alternative to Punta del Este, built from scratch by an alchemist who wanted his seaside city to mirror the constellation of Aquarius.

subject: Pisa, Greece
summary: Long before Italy's famous leaning tower, there was another Pisa — a fierce Greek city-state that founded the Olympic Games, fought Elis for control of the sanctuary for centuries, and was ultimately erased so completely that later historians questioned whether it had ever existed.

subject: Pisagua, Chile
summary: Once Chile's third-largest port, this isolated coastal village rose on nitrate wealth, fell when the boom ended, and served as a prison camp under three different regimes.

subject: Pisco Elqui
summary: A village so important to Chile's claim on pisco that the country renamed it after the drink — anchoring the mystical, star-filled upper Elqui Valley.

subject: Pispala
summary: A working-class district built without a plan on Finland's highest gravel esker, saved from the bulldozers by its own residents, and still holding the country's oldest working public sauna.

subject: Pitinga mine
summary: An open-pit tin mine 300 km from Manaus, reputed to hold the world's largest undeveloped tin deposit - and the source of a 1981 federal decree that shrank the Waimiri-Atroari indigenous reserve to make mining possible.

subject: Pitlochry
summary: A Victorian resort town in the heart of the Scottish Highlands where the railway, the hills, and the river still set the rhythm of the day.

subject: Piton de la Fournaise
summary: One of the most active volcanoes on Earth, Piton de la Fournaise erupts two to three times a year, reshaping the landscape of southeastern Reunion with rivers of fluid lava that occasionally cut across the coastal highway.

subject: Piton des Neiges
summary: At 3,069 meters, Piton des Neiges is the highest point in the entire Indian Ocean - a dead volcano that built an island and then collapsed into three vast valleys around itself.

subject: Pitons (Saint Lucia)
summary: Two volcanic spires rising nearly 800 meters from the Caribbean Sea, the Pitons of Saint Lucia are a UNESCO World Heritage Site where rare elfin woodland clings to summits, the Arawak saw a stone family, and the island named its beer.

subject: Pitt Meadows
summary: A farming city of 19,000 boxed in by three rivers, with 86 per cent of its land legally forbidden to be anything but farmland - and the ninth-busiest airport in Canada sitting in the corner of it.

story.title: Pittsburgh: The Steel City That Cleaned Up Its Act

subject: Pittsburgh
summary: The Pennsylvania city where three rivers meet and steel made America - where Carnegie built libraries with fortunes from mills, where the skyline was once invisible through smoke, and where tech and medicine replaced the industry that left.

story.title: Pittsburgh: The City of Bridges Where Three Rivers Meet

subject: Pittsburgh
summary: The city where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers merge to form the Ohio, where Andrew Carnegie built steel and libraries, and where 446 bridges connect neighborhoods divided by water and hills.

subject: Pittston Coal Strike
summary: When a coal company stopped paying for retired miners' health care, 2,000 workers and their families turned a hollow in southwest Virginia into Camp Solidarity and held the line for ten months.

subject: Pittsylvania County, Virginia
summary: Virginia's largest county by land area, named for the British Prime Minister who opposed harsh colonial policies — and sitting on the largest undeveloped uranium deposit in the United States.

subject: Pituba (neighbourhood)
summary: A large upper-class Salvador neighborhood planned in 1919 on the model of Belo Horizonte, now roughly 250,000 people between beach and avenues, home to northeastern Brazil's first shopping mall.

subject: Piumhi
summary: A Minas Gerais town whose river once teemed with so many fish that engineers redirected the entire watercourse into a different basin.

subject: Piura
summary: Peru's city of eternal heat serves ceviche you remember for years and sends buses north, south, and east to cloud forests, colonial churches, and the pilgrimage statue of Ayabaca.

subject: Piura
summary: Francisco Pizarro founded Piura in 1532 as the first Spanish city in Peru, and its streets have been absorbing empires, rebellions, floods, and El Niño seasons ever since.

subject: Pixieland (Oregon)
summary: A fairy-tale amusement park on the Oregon Coast that opened to a governor's dedication in 1969 and collapsed into bankruptcy four years later, its 57-acre site now returned to the Salmon River estuary it once displaced.

subject: Place Ville Marie
summary: A cruciform skyscraper built over a railway trench became the birthplace of Montreal's Underground City and announced to the world that a Canadian metropolis could reshape modern urbanism.

subject: Place du Général-de-Gaulle (Lille)
summary: A medieval marsh canalised, paved over by aldermen, ringed with seventeenth-century Flemish brick, crowned with a bronze goddess — and renamed in 1944 for the local boy who walked away to London.

subject: Placencia
summary: A sliver of sand at the tip of a Belizean peninsula where the world's narrowest main street leads past dive shops and rum bars to the longest barrier reef in the northern hemisphere.

subject: Plaka
summary: In the shadow of the Acropolis lies the oldest continuously inhabited neighborhood in Athens, a labyrinth of lanes that locals call the Neighborhood of the Gods.

subject: Planaltina, Federal District
summary: Before Brasília existed, Planaltina did - the oldest city in the Federal District, where the foundation stone of the future capital was placed in 1922.

subject: Planaltina, Goiás
summary: The half of Planaltina that Brasília left behind - a municipality born twice, once as an 18th-century mule stop and again as a city built from scratch on a cleared farm.

subject: Plas Mawr
summary: The finest surviving Elizabethan town house in Britain, built by a self-made Welshman whose hospitality - and tangled will - preserved it through four centuries.

subject: Plas Menai
summary: Wales's national watersports centre on the mainland shore of the Menai Strait - a purpose-built launch pad for sailors, paddlers, and windsurfers, set against a backdrop of mountains and tidal currents.

subject: Plataea
summary: A small Boeotian city that helped save Greece from Persia, then spent two centuries being destroyed, exiled, and rebuilt for the crime of choosing the wrong friends.

story.title: Playa Zipolite: Beach of the Dead, Beach of the Free

subject: Playa Zipolite
summary: Mexico's only legal nude beach earned its Zapotec name - 'beach of the dead' - from treacherous currents that have claimed swimmers for generations, but its reputation was built by counterculture travelers who arrived in the 1960s and never quite left.

story.title: Playland: Fresno's Scrappy Little Amusement Park

subject: Playland
summary: A community-built amusement park that opened six weeks before Disneyland, survived seven decades on dime-a-ride charm and Rotary Club devotion, and finally closed its gates in 2025.

subject: Playland (San Francisco)
summary: For nearly half a century, a ten-acre amusement park at Ocean Beach gave San Francisco its thrills, from the Big Dipper coaster to Laughing Sal's mechanical cackle, before falling to wrecking balls in 1972.

subject: Playland (Vancouver)
summary: Vancouver's amusement park runs a 1958 wooden roller coaster that was its designer's last work, on grounds that held Japanese Canadian families in livestock barns sixteen years earlier.

subject: Plaza Huincul
summary: This small Patagonian oil town sits atop two kinds of buried treasure: the petroleum that built it, and the bones of the largest dinosaurs the world has ever known.

subject: Plaza Independencia
summary: Montevideo's central square is a hinge between the old walled city and the new, guarding the underground tomb of the national hero Jose Gervasio Artigas beneath his bronze likeness.

subject: Plaza Indonesia
summary: Jakarta's first luxury mall rose on the ruins of a journalists' hostel built for the 1962 Asian Games, survived a nine-year construction freeze during the Asian financial crisis, and anchored a corner of Jalan Thamrin where the Selamat Datang Monument welcomes visitors to a city that never stops rebuilding itself.

subject: Plaza de Armas (Santiago)
summary: Pedro de Valdivia laid out this square in 1541 as the heart of a new colonial capital, never knowing he was building on top of an Inca settlement that had been there first.

subject: Plaza de España, Seville
summary: A sweeping half-circle of tile, brick, and ambition built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition, where every province of Spain claims its own ceramic alcove and Hollywood keeps returning to film.

subject: Plaza de la Diversidad Sexual
summary: In Montevideo's Old City stands the first public square in Latin America dedicated to sexual diversity, marked by a granite triangle that turns a symbol of persecution into one of pride.

story.title: Plaza de toros de las Arenas

subject: Plaza de toros de las Arenas
summary: A grand 1900 Barcelona bullring whose brick shell was jacked into the air and rebuilt as a domed shopping complex after Catalonia turned against the bulls.

subject: Pleasley Colliery
summary: Two Victorian headstocks still rise above the Meden valley, where volunteers spent decades restoring the steam winders that once raised coal from a thousand feet below.

subject: Pleasurewood Hills
summary: A 59-acre Suffolk theme park born in 1983 as an American-themed family attraction, where Mr Blobby once held court and roller coasters now roar between the Suffolk woods.

subject: Pleistos
summary: The Pleistos valley below Delphi holds the largest continuous olive grove in Greece — a sea of silver-green trees that has carpeted this ancient rift since prehistoric times.

subject: Plered
summary: A Javanese royal capital that rose in brick, fell to rebellion and war, and now lies beneath rice paddies along the Opak River, its walls traced only by archaeologists and old Dutch maps.

subject: Plisskën Festival
summary: Athens's genre-defying underground music festival, born in the depths of the Greek financial crisis and named for a fictional outlaw, has become one of Europe's most distinctive indie showcases.

subject: Plockton
summary: A planned 1810s fishing village where palm-like trees grow in the Scottish Highlands and the cast of Hamish Macbeth once filmed at every corner.

subject: Plockton
summary: A planned Highland village on Loch Carron where palm-like trees grow, Hamish Macbeth was filmed, and Gaelic remains stubbornly alive.

subject: Plopsaland Belgium
summary: It started in 1935 as a roadside honey stand. Ninety years and one talking gnome later, it has seven roller coasters and 55 attractions.

subject: Plovdiv
summary: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, where eight thousand years of life have stacked themselves twelve meters deep on seven syenite hills.

subject: Plover Cove
summary: A sheltered cove in Hong Kong's Tai Po District where eleven Hakka villages, a dammed freshwater reservoir, and an annual open-water swim across 2,600 metres of tidal water converge in an unlikely corner of one of the world's densest cities.

subject: Plover Cove Reservoir
summary: Engineers sealed a sea inlet with dams, pumped out the saltwater, and filled it with rain — creating the world's first freshwater coastal lake and solving a water crisis for one of the world's most densely populated cities.

subject: Pluckemin Continental Artillery Cantonment Site
summary: Before West Point existed, General Henry Knox ran America's first military academy from a cantonment nestled against the Watchung Mountains in Pluckemin, New Jersey, during the winter of 1778-1779.

subject: Plymouth Breakwater
summary: A mile-long stone wall built in the English Channel to shelter the Royal Navy, requiring four million tons of rock, two engineers' lifetimes, and Napoleon's grudging admiration.

subject: Plymouth Brethren
summary: Born in a Dublin drawing room in 1825 and named for an English port city they reached six years later, the Plymouth Brethren built a quiet, scripture-only Christianity that would splinter into rival movements still arguing today.

story.title: Plymouth Rock: The Small Stone That Bore a Great Myth

subject: Plymouth Rock
summary: The Massachusetts boulder that allegedly received the Pilgrims' first steps - where the Mayflower passengers actually landed at Provincetown first, where the rock was first identified 121 years after 1620, and where American origin mythology congealed around a stone that may or may not have been there at all.

story.title: Plymouth Rock: America's Most Overrated Landmark

subject: Plymouth Rock
summary: The Massachusetts boulder that supposedly welcomed the Pilgrims in 1620 - identified 120 years after the fact, broken and moved multiple times, now weighing one-third its original size, yet somehow remaining an icon of American founding despite thin evidence it mattered at all.

subject: Plymouth Sound
summary: The deep-water inlet that launched the Mayflower, sheltered captive Napoleon, sent Darwin to the Galapagos, and is now being shaped into Britain's first National Marine Park.

subject: Plympton
summary: The town that gave Plymouth its name, then watched its river silt up and the world move downstream.

subject: Po Hing Fong
summary: A short cul-de-sac in Sheung Wan, Po Hing Fong has sheltered revolutionaries plotting the fall of a dynasty, a colonial governor, and nearly eighty people who died on a July morning when a rain-soaked hillside gave way.

subject: Po Nagar
summary: Standing on Cù Lao Mountain above the Cái River since before 781 CE, the Cham towers of Po Nagar have survived raiders, conquerors, and centuries of spiritual reinvention to remain an active place of worship today.

subject: Poarch Creek Indian Reservation
summary: The only federally recognized tribe in Alabama, the Poarch Band of Creek Indians survived forced removal, a century of marginalization, and segregated schools to win federal recognition in 1984 and build a self-governing community in Escambia County.

subject: Pocomoke City, Maryland
summary: An Eastern Shore river town named for the black water that flows past it - and the subject of a documentary called The Friendliest Town that was not friendly.

subject: Podil
summary: Kyiv's Lower City, where potters, tanners, and tar-workers once crowded a riverside floodplain, remains the neighborhood where the capital first learned to trade, learn, and rebuild.

subject: Poeppel Corner
summary: Deep in the Simpson Desert, three states meet at a single point - a place where you can celebrate New Year three times in one evening.

subject: Poeppel Corner Survey Marker
summary: A weathered desert post marks the spot where three Australian states meet - and where a surveyor's slightly-too-long chain put the corner in the wrong place.

subject: Poilão
summary: A tiny, sacred, uninhabited island at the southern tip of Guinea-Bissau - and one of the most important green sea-turtle nurseries on Earth.

subject: Point Culver
summary: A headland where a homesick English navigator saw the white cliffs of his own coast, marking the start of one of the longest cliff lines on Earth.

subject: Point Grenville
summary: A windswept Washington headland where Spanish explorers first stepped ashore in 1775, sea otters were brought back from the brink, and the Quinault Nation has reclaimed both the land and its name.

subject: Point Isabel Regional Shoreline
summary: A 50-acre park on San Francisco Bay built atop landfill and industrial waste, Point Isabel is now one of America's most celebrated dog parks — a place where broken porcelain washes up on the beach, monarch butterflies overwinter in the eucalyptus, and 1.5 million visitors a year come to walk the shoreline.

subject: Point Labatt
summary: On a clifftop above the Eyre Peninsula coast lies the only place on mainland Australia where one of the world's rarest sea lions comes ashore to breed.

subject: Point Molate Naval Fuel Depot
summary: A decommissioned Navy fueling station on the western shore of Richmond with a history that includes bootlegging and fuel storage.

story.title: Point Pleasant: Where the Mothman Watches

subject: Point Pleasant
summary: The West Virginia town where a winged creature appeared before the bridge collapsed - 46 people died when the Silver Bridge fell in 1967, and witnesses swore they'd seen something watching in the months before.

subject: Point Pleasant
summary: A small West Virginia town at the confluence of the Ohio and Kanawha rivers, famous for the Mothman sightings of 1966-67 and for the 1774 battle some historians call the first of the Revolution.

subject: Point Reyes National Seashore
summary: A peninsula severed from the continent by the San Andreas Fault, Point Reyes is the only park on Earth where breeding elk and elephant seals share the same coastline.

subject: Point Roberts, Washington
summary: Five square miles of the United States hanging below the 49th parallel, reachable from the rest of America only by crossing Canada twice - a town whose entire character was set by a survey line nobody checked.

subject: Point of Air Lifeboat Station
summary: The first Welsh lifeboat station on the Prestatyn coast - founded 1826, lost thirteen men to one terrible morning in 1857, transferred to the RNLI in 1894 and closed weeks later.

subject: Pointe-Noire
summary: Congo's oil capital on the Atlantic coast, where French colonial architecture meets a booming petroleum economy and a fishing culture fighting to survive alongside it.

subject: Pok Fu Lam
summary: A valley between Victoria Peak and the sea, Pok Fu Lam holds Hong Kong's oldest village, its first reservoir, its first dairy farm — and a Fire Dragon that has danced through Mid-Autumn nights for generations.

subject: Pol'and'Rock Festival
summary: For sixteen summers a free festival named after a dubbed American television series turned the fields outside Kostrzyn nad Odrą into one of the largest gatherings on Earth — up to 750,000 people, none of whom paid to get in.

subject: Polabian Language
summary: A Slavic language spoken along the Elbe for a thousand years, recorded almost too late by a village pastor and a farmer, and possibly the reason Berlin is called Berlin.

subject: Polaria
summary: The world's most northerly aquarium sits on the Tromsoe waterfront, its architecture mimicking Arctic ice floes tumbling ashore.

subject: Polesie State Radioecological Reserve
summary: Belarus fenced off its most contaminated corner after Chernobyl, emptied the villages, and unintentionally created one of Europe's richest wildlife sanctuaries.

story.title: Politics and Government of the Dutch Republic

subject: Politics and Government of the Dutch Republic
summary: For two centuries, a confederation of seven Dutch provinces ran a global commercial empire without a king, governed instead by merchant regents who met daily in The Hague.

subject: Pollentia (Mallorca)
summary: A wealthy Roman city on Mallorca whose theater and forum survive at Alcúdia, even as its name migrated ten kilometers inland to Pollença.

subject: Pollença
summary: A preserved medieval town in Mallorca's northeastern mountains, famous for the 365 steps that climb to its hilltop Calvary.

subject: Polonezköy
summary: Thirty kilometers from the minarets of Istanbul, a village founded by Polish exiles in 1842 still holds its church services in Polish, buries its dead with Polish inscriptions, and hosts folk musicians from Warsaw every summer — a living fragment of one nation's diaspora, planted in the forest of another.

story.title: Polonnaruwa: Sri Lanka's Second Kingdom, Frozen in Stone

subject: Polonnaruwa
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage city where the ruins of a medieval Sinhalese capital sit compactly together amid the dry zone landscape, more accessible and better preserved than the older Anuradhapura.

subject: Polperro
summary: A fishing village of tightly-packed cottages climbing a narrow combe to a tidal harbour, where smuggling reached its zenith under a local merchant who became known as the Smugglers' Banker.

subject: Poltava
summary: A green, hilly city on the Vorskla where modern Ukrainian literature was born, and where, one summer morning in 1709, a battle rearranged the map of Europe.

subject: Pompeia, São Paulo
summary: A São Paulo coffee town named for a senator's wife, reshaped by Japanese immigrants whose family company, Jacto, became a global leader in agricultural machinery.

subject: Pompeii
summary: When Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it buried a thriving Roman city under meters of ash -- preserving everything from bakery ovens to the final postures of people who could not escape.

story.title: Pompeii's Graffiti: The Bathroom Walls of Ancient Rome

subject: Pompeii's Graffiti
summary: Where volcanic ash preserved not just buildings but over 11,000 pieces of Roman graffiti - crude jokes, love declarations, political slogans, and profanity that prove humans haven't changed in 2,000 years.

subject: Ponce Historic Zone
summary: Puerto Rico's southern jewel preserves over a thousand historic structures in a unique architectural style found nowhere else in the Caribbean.

subject: Pondicherry
summary: France's most charming colonial footprint in India, a coast where Sri Aurobindo's ashram draws seekers and Tamil and French cultures fuse into something entirely their own.

subject: Poniatowa Concentration Camp
summary: A small SS labour camp near Lublin where, on 4 November 1943, around 14,000 Jewish prisoners were shot in a single day as part of Aktion Erntefest — Operation Harvest Festival — the largest German massacre of Jews in the entire war.

subject: Ponta d'Ouro
summary: Mozambique's southernmost beach town, Ponta d'Ouro is a sandy outpost famous for wild dolphins, year-round shark dives, and turquoise water just across the border from South Africa.

subject: Ponta do Seixas
summary: A survey in 1941 settled it by 1,683 metres: the easternmost corner of the continental Americas is not a cliff or a cape but an ordinary Paraiba beach.

subject: Pontefract
summary: A West Yorkshire market town named for a broken bridge, famous for liquorice cakes, three Civil War sieges, and the longest continuous horse racing circuit in Europe.

subject: Pontianak Sultanate
summary: A Hadrami Arab dynasty ruled western Borneo for nearly two centuries, surviving Dutch colonialism only to face destruction under Japanese occupation and a turbulent path into Indonesian independence.

subject: Pontic Olbia
summary: The ruins of a Greek city named 'the wealthy one,' where merchants once cast coins in the shape of leaping dolphins on the far edge of the classical world.

subject: Poochera, South Australia
summary: A tiny wheat-belt town that became a place of pilgrimage for the world's ant scientists, after a broken-down truck led to the rediscovery of a 'living fossil' ant on the night of 22 October 1977.

subject: Pooncarie
summary: A tiny Darling River wharf town where paddle-steamers once loaded outback wool, now the road gateway to ancient Lake Mungo.

subject: Popayán
summary: Seventeen Colombian presidents and the country's first UNESCO City of Gastronomy emerged from a white colonial city where cargueros still carry Passion floats through cobblestone streets each Holy Week.

subject: Poppit Sands
summary: A wide Welsh Blue Flag beach at the mouth of the River Teifi — backed by the highest cliffs in Pembrokeshire and concealing a 1,000-year-old submerged fish trap offshore.

story.title: Population Transfer in the Soviet Union

subject: Population transfer in the Soviet Union
summary: Between 1930 and 1952, the Soviet government forcibly relocated at least six million people -- entire ethnic groups, social classes, and political undesirables -- to remote regions of Siberia, Central Asia, and the Far East.

subject: Poquoson, Virginia
summary: Poquoson means 'great marsh' in Algonquian. Four centuries later, in an independent city of 12,460 Bull Islanders, the marshes still rule everything.

subject: Porangatu
summary: A Tupi-Guarani name meaning "beautiful landscape," a cattle town at the crossroads of northern Goiás, and an old gold rush that barely survived the local resistance.

subject: Porbandar
summary: The birthplace of Mahatma Gandhi on Gujarat's Arabian Sea coast, where ancient port traditions meet wildly unpredictable monsoons and rare dugong sightings.

subject: Porgera Gold Mine
summary: Sixteen million ounces of gold pulled from a rainforest valley at 2,500 meters, shut down in 2020, reopened in 2024 — and shadowed by some of the most serious human rights allegations associated with any mining operation in the world.

subject: Pori
summary: A Finnish port city founded in 1558 because the sea kept retreating, burned down nine times, rebuilt on boulevards, and now known for a jazz festival, a grieving father's mausoleum and the night Finnish-language theatre began in a hotel dining room.

story.title: Pori Jazz: From 600 People to a Third of a Million

subject: Pori Jazz
summary: A handful of local jazz fans staged a two-day festival on a Finnish park island in July 1966 and drew 600 people to the main concert. By 2019 the festival's own count was 349,518 visitors.

subject: Porlock
summary: A submerged forest at low tide, a poem ruined by an unwelcome visitor, and a hill so steep it has its own toll road. The Somerset village of Porlock has been small and significant for over a thousand years.

subject: Poros
summary: Henry Miller called it 'sailing through the streets' — the channel between Poros and the mainland is so narrow that arriving feels like threading a needle through three thousand years of Greek history.

subject: Port Alberni
summary: Named for a Spanish military officer who never saw it become a city, Port Alberni sits at the head of Vancouver Island's longest inlet -- a twin-city-turned-one where tsunami scars, residential school history, and world-class salmon fishing coexist in a valley ringed by mountains.

subject: Port Alice
summary: A rain-soaked pulp mill village on Vancouver Island named after its founder's mother, where the ground has been sliding out from under the town for a century and Canada's largest sinkhole lurks in the nearby forest.

subject: Port Augusta
summary: At the head of Spencer Gulf, where every highway and railway in southern Australia converges, a coal city is teaching itself to run on sun.

subject: Port Chalmers
summary: Once the third-largest port in Australasia during the gold rush, this compact harbor town on Otago Harbour reinvented itself as a container terminal, cruise ship destination, and artists' colony.

subject: Port Douglas
summary: A 19th-century gold port that withered to a fishing village and was reborn in the 1980s as a tropical playground - the rare place where the Great Barrier Reef and the world's oldest rainforest sit an hour apart.

subject: Port Elizabeth
summary: South Africa's fifth-largest city, known as the Friendly City, sits where the Indian Ocean meets Algoa Bay with dolphins, diving reefs, and layers of contested history.

subject: Port Erin
summary: A small Manx seaside village at the western end of the steam railway, with a white-sand bay, a cliff path called The Way of the Gull, and a cylindrical sauna midway along the beach.

subject: Port Erin Lifeboat Station
summary: Since 1883 a small RNLI station on Breakwater Road has been the answer to bad weather in the south-west of the Isle of Man, named lifeboats funded by named donors saving named lives.

subject: Port Hammond
summary: For a few months it was the western end of the Canadian Pacific Railway; a century later Hammond is a riverside mill village of cottages, ballfields and film crews.

subject: Port Hedland
summary: A town built on iron ore and Dreaming stories, Port Hedland ships half a billion tonnes of red dust annually while flatback turtles nest on its beaches.

subject: Port Kenny
summary: A tiny town on the sheltered shore of Venus Bay that once shipped a district's wheat to the world and now lives on fish, farms, and a jetty full of anglers.

subject: Port Logan
summary: A planned village built by a Galloway laird in 1818 with a quay by Thomas Telford, Port Logan went on to play a Hebridean island on BBC television and a haunted Scottish coast in Gerard Butler's lighthouse thriller.

subject: Port Logan Lifeboat Station
summary: From 1866 to 1932, a small RNLI station on the Rhins coast launched a rowed-and-sailed lifeboat into hurricanes to rescue strangers - and once, a captain whose own wife had donated to the boat that saved him.

subject: Port Madison Indian Reservation
summary: Home of the Suquamish Tribe and the grave of Chief Seattle, the Port Madison Indian Reservation has endured systematic land loss to become a walkable cultural district on Puget Sound.

subject: Port Moody
summary: For one spectacular year the head of Burrard Inlet was the western end of Canada. Then the railway laid twelve more miles of track, and Port Moody had to become something else.

subject: Port Qasim
summary: Pakistan's second-busiest port sits where an ancient channel of the Indus meets the Arabian Sea, surrounded by one of the world's largest arid-climate mangrove forests.

subject: Port St Mary
summary: A small Manx harbour village that exists mainly as the trailhead for one of the best coastal walks in the British Isles.

subject: Port Townsend
summary: Victorian seaport preserved in amber - a town of towered mansions and waterfront warehouses where the 19th century never quite ended and the maritime arts still thrive.

subject: Port Vell
summary: Barcelona's ancient harbor spent centuries battling sand, storms, and obsolescence before the 1992 Olympics transformed it from derelict warehouses into the city's glittering waterfront.

subject: Port William, Dumfries and Galloway
summary: A planned 18th-century fishing village built where 'The Church on the Beach' once stood, home to one of Scotland's oldest community lifeboats.

story.title: Port an Eilean Mhòir boat burial

subject: Port an Eilean Mhòir boat burial
summary: The first fully intact Viking boat burial ever found on the UK mainland - a 10th-century warrior laid in a five-metre vessel with his sword bent S-shaped beside him.

subject: Port-Gentil
summary: Gabon's oil capital and economic engine, an island city on the Atlantic coast where petroleum wealth collides with crumbling infrastructure and Time Magazine once named it the world's most expensive city.

subject: Portadown
summary: The Hub of the North, a Victorian railway junction town on the River Bann where four lines once met, and where the Drumcree parade dispute became one of the defining flashpoints of the Troubles.

subject: Portaferry
summary: Where the Vikings once measured a tide-race fierce enough to deserve its own name, a small County Down village now hosts the world's longest-running experiments in turning that current into electricity.

subject: Portaferry Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station at the mouth of the largest sea inlet in the British Isles, funded for forty years by the children of the BBC's Blue Peter and the tide that runs at its door.

subject: Portage and Main
summary: Where an ox cart merchant set up shop in 1862, Winnipeg's most famous intersection became the self-proclaimed 'crossroads of Canada' -- a corner so iconic it has its own Monopoly square, its own beer, and a decades-long fight over whether pedestrians should be allowed to walk across it.

subject: Portarlington, County Laois
summary: On the banks of the River Barrow, a town where French was spoken from the pulpit until the 1820s and where Jonathan Swift wrote much of Gulliver's Travels.

subject: Portavogie
summary: Ireland's easternmost settlement built itself around prawns and herrings, and its primary school wall tells the entire story in three murals.

subject: Porte des Morts
summary: The treacherous strait between Door Peninsula and the Potawatomi Islands gave Door County its name and earned its fearsome reputation through centuries of shipwrecks and an ancient battle between nations.

subject: Portendick
summary: On a waterless stretch of Mauritanian coast, two empires once fought a slow war over tree sap - the gum arabic that thickened ink, set dyes, and built fortunes.

subject: Porth Dafarch
summary: A hundred-metre sandy beach below Precambrian cliffs, used as the back-up port for Holyhead in bad weather for two centuries, now a Blue Flag swimming spot with a transatlantic fibre-optic cable buried under the sand.

subject: Porth Hellick
summary: A tidal inlet on the south coast of St Mary's where the body of Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell washed ashore in October 1707 after the worst peacetime disaster in Royal Navy history.

subject: Porth Nanven
summary: A Cornish cove where the rounded boulders on the beach are not the work of today's Atlantic but of a sea that retreated 120,000 years ago, leaving its cobbles fossilised in the cliff above.

subject: Porth Ruffydd Lifeboat Station
summary: A short-lived RNLI station built in response to one catastrophic 1889 wreck, it launched fourteen times in thirteen years and saved no one before closing forever.

subject: Porth Wen Brickworks
summary: Three beehive kilns, a tall chimney and a tramway descending to the sea - an abandoned Victorian brickworks perched on cliffs above a remote Anglesey cove.

subject: Porthall
summary: A Donegal village on the Foyle whose mid-18th-century Georgian house was once owned by a junior counsel at the Nuremberg Trials, near a 1611 stone house and the ruined castle of Red Hugh O'Donnell's mother.

subject: Porthcurno
summary: The Cornish village whose white-shell beach served as the eastern terminus of the all-red telegraph network, the granite cable hub of the British Empire.

subject: Porthdinllaen Lifeboat Station
summary: The only RNLI station in Britain where Welsh is the crew's first language, founded 1864, with an 8-million-pound boathouse built using materials delivered entirely by sea because there was no road in.

subject: Porthmadog
summary: William Madocks reclaimed a tidal estuary in 1811 to build himself a port - and a town grew up around it, shipping Welsh slate to roof the empire and three different heritage railways into the present day.

subject: Porthmion
summary: A tiny Greek fortress-town named for the very act of crossing, built to guard an ancient ferry over the Kerch Strait, whose ruins preserve everything from ash-buried disaster to a dog buried inside a watchtower.

story.title: Portland: The City Where Weirdness Became Municipal Policy

subject: Portland
summary: The Oregon city where 'Keep Portland Weird' is a bumper sticker and a way of life - where the food carts number in the hundreds, where the strip clubs outnumber any American city, and where environmental consciousness became culture before it was cool.

story.title: Portland: Where Weird Became Municipal Policy

subject: Portland
summary: The Oregon city that branded itself on weirdness before Austin did - where strip clubs outnumber any American city, where Powell's Books fills a city block, and where 'Keep Portland Weird' reflects not aspiration but description of what the city had already become.

subject: Portland Bill
summary: The southernmost point of Dorset, where three lighthouses, a tidal race, and a sandbank have been killing ships for centuries.

subject: Portland Place, Aberaeron
summary: Seven Regency townhouses that form the most ambitious terrace in a planned Welsh port - and an inscription dated 1855 that tells you who built them.

subject: Portland Street
summary: Named after an 18th-century British Prime Minister, Portland Street cuts through the densest district in Kowloon — neon signs, noodle shops, chess players at dusk, and a Langham Place tower that tried, and largely failed, to change the street's character.

subject: Portland Works
summary: Where stainless steel cutlery was first made in 1914 - and where, a century later, nearly five hundred Sheffielders bought back their own heritage in one of Britain's largest community share issues.

story.title: Portland, Maine: The Working Waterfront That Became Foodie Heaven

subject: Portland, Maine
summary: The peninsula city destroyed four times by fire and war, where lobster boats still work the harbor, and where more restaurants per capita than San Francisco made Portland America's unexpected food destination.

subject: Portland, Oregon
summary: The City of Roses where the Willamette meets the Columbia - a fiercely independent metropolis of food carts, craft beer, and urban wilderness, with snow-capped volcanoes framing every horizon.

subject: Portlaoise
summary: The county town of Laois - once Maryborough, now Ireland's fastest-growing midland commuter hub, with the country's first aeroplane and its maximum-security prison.

subject: Portmagee
summary: A Kerry fishing village named for an 18th-century smuggler, Portmagee is the boat launch for Skellig Michael and the home of an old folk drama that resurrects the year every December.

subject: Portman Square
summary: Built between 1765 and 1784 in Marylebone, Portman Square was designed for the Georgian aristocracy, housing dukes, earls, and at least one royal princess — and conceals within its elegant townhouses some extraordinary architectural and social history.

subject: Portmeirion
summary: A surreal Italianate village on the Welsh coast, built by one architect over 50 years, immortalized as 'The Village' in the cult television series The Prisoner.

subject: Portmán
summary: The Romans called it Portus Magnus, the Great Port; three decades of toxic mining waste filled its bay with sediment until the harbor became dry land, one of the Mediterranean's worst ecological disasters.

subject: Porto
summary: Where port wine was born in riverside cellars, where the Douro meets the Atlantic, where Portugal's second city refuses to be second to Lisbon in beauty or spirit.

subject: Porto Alegre
summary: Brazil's southernmost state capital, where five rivers meet, citizens once helped write the budget, and the water of 2024 broke an eighty-year record.

subject: Porto Alegre Public Market
summary: Porto Alegre's oldest market has survived floods and four fires - and in 2024 watched the Guaiba climb higher than it ever had before.

subject: Porto Digital
summary: Pernambuco privatised its electricity company and put the money into a technology park inside Recife's derelict old port quarter - a regeneration bet that took twenty-five years to pay out, and did.

subject: Porto Flavia
summary: A unique harbor carved into Sardinian sea cliffs in 1924, where two superimposed tunnels and nine vertical ore reservoirs replaced an entire fleet of sailing boats -- and where a 'Death Squad' of workers dangled into the reservoirs to keep the ore flowing.

subject: Porto Seguro
summary: A traveler's guide to the Bahian coast where Brazil begins: historic hilltop churches, ferry crossings to Arraial d'Ajuda, and some of the Atlantic's best-rated beaches.

subject: Porto Seguro
summary: The Bahian coastal town where Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet made landfall in April 1500, now a palimpsest of first-contact history, Pataxó indigenous territory, Atlantic Forest reserves, and Brazilian Carnival.

subject: Porto de Galinhas
summary: Brazil's most-voted beach carries a cheerful name that came out of the illegal slave trade: word that new chickens had arrived at the port.

subject: Porto do Itaqui
summary: A deepwater channel 23 meters deep and a 1.8-kilometer-wide entrance made Itaqui one of Brazil's most strategic cargo ports - it just took 27 years from the idea to the first ship.

subject: Portobello Road
summary: A Notting Hill street named after a 1739 naval battle in Panama, now host to the largest antiques market in the United Kingdom.

subject: Portobello, Dublin
summary: A Dublin quarter named for a Panamanian harbour, where Lithuanian Jews built Little Jerusalem and George Bernard Shaw learned to write.

subject: Portobelo
summary: Once the third-richest city on the Spanish Main, Portobelo is now a sleepy Caribbean town of around 4,500 people where treasure fleet ruins, a World Heritage fortress complex, and the lead coffin of Sir Francis Drake all share the same deep natural harbor.

subject: Portofino
summary: Pliny the Elder called it Portus Delphini -- the Port of the Dolphin. Two thousand years later, this tiny Ligurian fishing village has become one of the most exclusive addresses on Earth, with a bronze Christ standing guard on the seabed below.

subject: Portoviejo
summary: An Ecuadorian city that rebuilt itself around its kitchen after a 2016 earthquake leveled its center, earning UNESCO Creative City status for its gastronomy.

subject: Portree
summary: The colourful harbour capital of Skye, a tight bowl of pastel cottages around a sheltered bay where Bonnie Prince Charlie said farewell to Flora Macdonald in 1746.

subject: Portrush Lifeboat Station
summary: Since 1860, the boats out of Portrush Harbour have answered calls in the worst weather on the north Antrim coast - and on at least one night in November 1889, they paid for it.

subject: Portsmouth
summary: The historic seaport where 400-year-old houses line brick streets, where the Naval Shipyard built America's first submarine, and where New Hampshire's 18 miles of coastline concentrate into one compact, beautiful town.

subject: Portsmouth
summary: A faded Ohio River industrial city that once led the nation in shoe and brick manufacturing, hosted the original Detroit Lions, and now stages its complicated history on 2,000 feet of floodwall murals.

subject: Portsmouth Historic Dockyard
summary: Three warships spanning 400 years of naval warfare -- the Mary Rose, HMS Victory, and HMS Warrior -- all anchored in one extraordinary dockyard on Portsmouth harbour.

subject: Portsmouth Square
summary: San Francisco's original public square, where the American flag was first raised in 1846, the Gold Rush was announced in 1848, and Chinatown's elders now practice tai chi each morning.

subject: Portsmouth, North Carolina
summary: Founded in 1753 as the busiest port south of Norfolk, Portsmouth is now an empty ghost village on the Outer Banks, its weathered houses standing watch over silent sand flats.

subject: Portsoy
summary: A 17th-century fishing harbour eight miles west of Banff, famous for green serpentinite jewellery, the 2016 remake of Whisky Galore, and a saithe-named cove that filmmakers cannot resist.

subject: Portsoy
summary: A burgh of barony since 1550, a Peaky Blinders filming location, and the place a herring fleet of fifty-seven boats once called home.

subject: Portstewart
summary: A Victorian seaside town on the Atlantic edge of County Londonderry, where Sabbatarian convictions kept the railway out and a Dominican convent crowns the cliff.

subject: Portuguese Angola
summary: Five centuries of Portuguese rule shaped Angola from a slave-trading outpost into Africa's second-largest white settler colony, until a Lisbon revolution and guerrilla war brought independence in 1975 and sent hundreds of thousands of settlers fleeing.

subject: Portuguese Macau
summary: For 442 years, a tiny peninsula on the South China Sea was simultaneously Chinese territory and a Portuguese city — the world's longest-running experiment in coexistence.

subject: Portumna
summary: Where the Shannon widens into Lough Derg, a 1611 castle, a 1911 swing bridge, and a 17th-century Irish Wolfhound's bones make a market town that took its name from an oak.

subject: Positano
summary: A pastel-colored village spilling down steep cliffs to two beaches on the Amalfi Coast, where the only way through town is a single winding road and hundreds of ancient stairways.

subject: Posse, Goiás
summary: The town named "possession," founded by malaria refugees from Buenos Aires, now a border commerce hub trading with the soy fields of western Bahia.

subject: Possession Street
summary: On 26 January 1841, Britain raised its flag on a rocky promontory above Hong Kong harbour — a moment that founded a city. The street that marks the spot is now landlocked, surrounded by buildings, the original coastline long since buried under reclaimed earth.

subject: Potato Chip Rock
summary: Balanced at the summit of Mount Woodson, a thin cantilever of granite juts 14 feet into the air — and thousands of hikers per weekend queue up to stand on it and pretend the world is about to crack.

subject: Potato Germans
summary: In 1759 a Danish king promised German families land, livestock and twenty tax-free years on the Jutland heath. What most of them found was heather to the waist.

subject: Potemkin Stairs
summary: Odesa's great staircase to the sea is an optical trick in stone, so cleverly built that the steps vanish from above and the landings vanish from below.

subject: Potomac Highlands
summary: An eleven-county slice of West Virginia where mountain roads outnumber interstates, cell signals fade for federal reasons, and Devonian fossils sit waiting in roadside cuts.

subject: Potosi (barque)
summary: One of the largest and fastest windjammers ever built, the five-masted Potosi outran every Cape Horn storm for nineteen years, then burned and was sunk by gunfire off the coast of Patagonia.

subject: Potosí
summary: One of the highest cities in the world, built on silver wealth and colonial suffering, where baroque churches rise at 4,000 meters and the shadow of Cerro Rico falls across every street.

subject: Potrero Generating Station
summary: A natural gas power plant that generated electricity and controversy for decades on San Francisco's southeastern waterfront before being demolished to make way for the neighborhood it had long burdened.

subject: Potrero Hill
summary: A sunny hilltop neighborhood where the crookedest street in San Francisco (not Lombard) zigzags between Victorian houses and views of the downtown skyline draw engagement photographers.

subject: Potsdam
summary: A city of 190,000 that arranged its tram network around the leisure architecture of dead kings, and spent forty years as the far side of a closed border.

subject: Pottinger Street
summary: A cobblestone ladder street in Hong Kong's Central district that once divided Chinese and European neighbourhoods, survived Japanese bombing in 1941, and still carries the name of the colony's first governor.

subject: Poté
summary: A small municipality in northeast Minas Gerais named for an indigenous Botocudo leader, where coffee grows and ox-carts outnumber tractors.

subject: Pouldergaderry Sinkhole
summary: An 80-metre-wide hole in the County Kerry karst, marked on Irish maps since 1829 and still slowly eating itself.

subject: Pouso Alegre
summary: A Minas Gerais city literally named "Joyful Stay" after a colonial governor was so charmed by its horizons that he ordered it renamed.

story.title: Poverty Point: The 3,400-Year-Old City Nobody Expected

subject: Poverty Point
summary: The Louisiana earthworks older than the Egyptian pyramids at Giza - built by hunter-gatherers who weren't supposed to have the organization for monumental construction, who moved 1.5 million cubic yards of earth without wheeled vehicles or metal tools.

subject: Poverty Point
summary: A 3,700-year-old complex of earthen ridges and mounds in northeastern Louisiana, built by hunter-gatherers who created the largest Late Archaic earthwork in North America and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Poços de Caldas
summary: A Brazilian spa town built inside an extinct volcanic caldera, where sulphurous springs, Murano-descended glassblowers, and Alcoa's bauxite pit share the same geological inheritance.

subject: Prado, Montevideo
summary: Montevideo's oldest public park anchors a leafy neighborhood of mansions, rose gardens, and old villas that grew from the country estate of a nineteenth-century French entrepreneur.

subject: Praia Grande (Macau)
summary: Once the most painted bay in Asia, Praia Grande was Macau's grand colonial promenade — and its slow disappearance beneath land reclamation is its own kind of history.

subject: Praia de Pipa
summary: Eleven beaches under forty-metre cliffs where a fishing village discovered by surfers in the 1970s became one of Brazil's most cosmopolitan addresses — and is still working out the bill.

subject: Praia do Cassino
summary: A beach so long that no one can agree how long it is, running for as much as 254 unbroken kilometers from a Brazilian seaport to the Uruguayan border.

subject: Praia do Forte
summary: The Bahian beach village that became national headquarters for Projeto TAMAR, Brazil's sea-turtle conservation program, and a gentler counterpoint to Salvador's relentless rhythm.

subject: Prainha Historic Site
summary: The small beach in Vila Velha where the Portuguese first landed in Espírito Santo on May 23, 1535, and where one of Brazil's oldest churches still stands.

story.title: Prainha do Canto Verde Extractive Reserve

subject: Prainha do Canto Verde Extractive Reserve
summary: For two decades, fishers on this strip of Ceará coast held off real estate speculators with lawyers and courage - and in 2009 they won themselves a reserve.

subject: Prater
summary: Vienna's six-square-kilometer green heart began as a royal hunting ground, hosted a World's Fair, witnessed a revolution, and became the place where a Kenyan runner first broke the two-hour marathon barrier.

subject: Pravčická brána
summary: Europe's largest natural sandstone arch is not one rock but two leaning against each other, and it has been closed to feet since 1982 because visitors wore most of a metre off the top.

subject: Praça da Sé
summary: Every road in São Paulo is measured from this square — the city's geographic and symbolic heart, where a Marco Zero monument marks the point from which all distances begin and where, in January 1984, 300,000 Brazilians gathered to demand democratic elections.

subject: Praça dos Três Poderes
summary: An open triangle where Brazil's three branches of government face each other as equals — and where, on 8 January 2023, that arrangement was physically attacked.

subject: Preah Khan Kompong Svay
summary: The largest thing the Khmer ever built is a hundred kilometres east of Angkor, swallowed by forest, and on most days almost nobody is there.

subject: Preah Sihanouk province
summary: Cambodia's smallest coastal province carries two names — Port of the Moon and Holy Sihanouk — and twenty-two islands between them.

subject: Preah Vihear province
summary: Cambodia's third-largest province holds an abandoned imperial capital, a clifftop temple two nations have argued over for a century, and one of the last great lowland forests in Indochina.

subject: Preesall
summary: A Viking named Haakon, a Norman crossbowman, and a salt mine that swallowed itself — Preesall has worn many lives on the eastern bank of the Wyre.

subject: Prehen
summary: An estate above the Foyle where the rope broke twice for a man called Half-Hung MacNaghten, a one-eyed marksman shot a French officer across a river, and a Prussian baron lost everything to the Great War.

subject: Prehistoric Cornwall
summary: Two hundred thousand years of human presence are written across the granite of this small peninsula, from flint handaxes to the tin that reached the Eastern Mediterranean.

subject: Prehistoric Europe
summary: Deep time you can actually visit - a traveler's guide to the European continent before writing, when the maps were drawn by glaciers and the cities were carved from stone.

subject: Prehistory of Iran
summary: The Iranian plateau holds a continuous record of human presence stretching back a million years, from the earliest stone tools to the rise of cities and the invention of writing.

subject: Prek Sbauv
summary: Ten houses of fishermen on the Sen River, a kilometre off the highway — and the birthplace of the man whose government killed roughly a quarter of Cambodia.

subject: Premier Mine
summary: From this carrot-shaped volcanic pipe east of Pretoria came the Cullinan - the largest rough gem diamond ever found, now split between the British Crown Jewels.

subject: Presaddfed Burial Chamber
summary: Two Neolithic chamber tombs hunch in an Anglesey field, the surviving capstone still resting on stones placed there more than five thousand years ago.

subject: Prescott, Arizona
summary: Arizona's original frontier capital where Doc Holliday drank, fires forged a brick downtown, and the self-proclaimed World's Oldest Rodeo has run every year since 1888.

subject: Preseli Transmitting Station
summary: A 235-metre broadcasting mast on the eastern Preseli ridge that carried colour ITV into Wales, was climbed by Welsh-language protesters jailed for trespass, and bounced television signals across the Irish Sea into Dublin and Wicklow for half a century.

subject: Presencia de América Latina
summary: A 300-square-meter mural in Concepción reads like an epic poem in paint, telling the story of Latin America from Aztec gods to a single woman cradling a map of the continent.

subject: Presidente Epitácio
summary: The last stop on the Sorocabana railway, where São Paulo runs out of land and a dam turned a working river port into a beach town.

subject: Presidente Prudente
summary: Named for São Paulo's first republican governor, this cotton-and-cattle city of western São Paulo state became a surveillance nerve center after Brazil closed its most infamous prison.

subject: Prestbury, Cheshire
summary: A priest's fortified enclosure on the River Bollin grew into a silk-weaving village, then a footballer's enclave still wrapped around a Saxon cross.

subject: Preston
summary: A Lancashire mill city that Karl Marx once called the St Petersburg of England, Preston still makes aircraft, gave the world Wallace and Gromit, and holds a civic festival once every twenty years.

subject: Preston Bus Station
summary: A 1969 Brutalist masterpiece with curving concrete balconies and bays for eighty double-deckers, Preston's bus station was twice voted the city's favourite building and twice condemned to demolition before being saved.

subject: Preston Minster
summary: An ancient site that has been a church for at least 930 years has worn three saints' names, lost six bells to Pittsburgh, and has rung twelve new ones since Preston became a city.

subject: Prestwich
summary: The priest's farm on the old Roman road north of Manchester — once seat of the largest asylum in Europe, now the 'new Didsbury' of Bury, and the patch of north Manchester that produced Mark E. Smith, Victoria Wood, Guy Garvey and Howard Jacobson.

subject: Prestwick
summary: A South Ayrshire coastal town whose airport once welcomed Elvis to Britain, whose old course staged the very first Open Championship, and whose well water was said to have cured a king of leprosy.

subject: Pretoria
summary: South Africa's administrative capital turns purple each spring, a city of jacarandas, embassies, and the sandstone seat of a nation's power.

subject: Prey Lang Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: The last great lowland evergreen forest on the Indochinese peninsula is named, in Kuy, for the idea that it belongs to everyone - and the Kuy have spent two decades documenting who keeps taking it.

subject: Primate Research Institute
summary: A pioneering Japanese research center in Inuyama where scientists revolutionized our understanding of primate intelligence and animal culture.

subject: Prime Meridian (Greenwich)
summary: A brass strip on a Greenwich hillside marks the line that the world agreed in 1884 would be zero - the place where east and west begin.

subject: Prince Albert (South Africa)
summary: A Karoo village of 7,000 where thirteen National Monument buildings line the streets, the wool commands premium prices, and ghost tours run after dark.

subject: Prince-Bishopric of Liège
summary: For 810 years a Belgian state existed that had no king, no duke, and no count, only a bishop who happened to be a prince.

subject: Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück
summary: An ecclesiastical state whose 1648 treaty invented an extraordinary solution to religious civil war - bishops who alternated, by law, between Catholic and Protestant.

subject: Princely Beguinage, Bruges
summary: A medieval sanctuary where unmarried women once lived in spiritual independence, now home to Benedictine nuns preserving centuries of contemplative tradition.

subject: Princes Street
summary: King George III vetoed its original name, Charles Darwin named a Falkland Islands rockfield after it, and one of the world's great urban views runs the length of its south side.

subject: Princess of Hope
summary: A natural rock formation in Hingol National Park that resembles a crowned woman gazing toward the horizon, named by Angelina Jolie during a 2002 UN visit and sculpted over millennia by nothing more than wind and waves.

subject: Principality of Chernigov
summary: The second power of Kievan Rus', born of a rare peace between warring brothers, ruling a vast domain across today's Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia for half a millennium.

subject: Principality of Novgorod-Seversk
summary: A medieval frontier realm of the Rus', ruled by an ambitious branch of the Rurik dynasty, whose most famous prince rode to a defeat that became immortal verse.

subject: Principality of Theodoro
summary: A tiny Greek principality in the Crimean mountains that outlived the Byzantine Empire itself, becoming the very last territorial remnant of the Roman world before it fell to the Ottomans in December 1475.

subject: Principality of Thuận Thành
summary: The Principality of Thuận Thành — known to the Cham as Panduranga — was the last surviving fragment of the ancient Champa civilization, enduring as a semi-sovereign client state until Emperor Minh Mang finally extinguished it in 1832.

subject: Principality of Tver
summary: A medieval Russian principality that nearly became the center of a unified Russian state before Moscow crushed its rival on the Upper Volga.

subject: Prins Hendrik Barracks
summary: A colonial barracks in Nijmegen-Oost where soldiers trained for service in the East Indies, and where, by accident, the largest walking event on Earth was born.

subject: Prins Plantation
summary: A ruined coconut plantation in Aruba's Arikok National Park, named for a Swedish gold prospector who spent two fruitless years searching for treasure on behalf of the Dutch West India Company.

subject: Printers Inc. Bookstore
summary: Palo Alto's beloved independent bookstore fought chain competition and Amazon for years, surviving a 1998 closure scare through community protest before finally closing in 2001.

subject: Priobskoye field
summary: Russia's largest oil field sprawls across 5,466 square kilometers of Western Siberian wetland along the Ob River, where corporate power struggles mirror the scale of the petroleum buried beneath the permafrost.

story.title: Pripyat: The City That Died Overnight

subject: Pripyat
summary: Where 49,000 Soviet citizens were evacuated in 36 hours after the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, leaving behind a perfectly preserved ghost city frozen in time with Ferris wheels, schools, and apartments full of abandoned possessions.

subject: Prittlewell Priory
summary: A small Cluniac priory in Essex where an internal feud once ended with a prior struck dead at the altar, now a public park gifted to Southend by the town jeweller.

subject: Proconnesus
summary: The ancient Greek city of Proconnesus on Marmara Island produced the famous Proconnesian marble that built the columns of Hagia Sophia, the floors of the Roman Forum, and countless monuments across the ancient world — and sent to exile those whom the empire wished to forget.

subject: Professorville
summary: A historic neighborhood in Palo Alto where Stanford's founding professors built their own homes rather than lease university land, creating a district of gambrel-roofed houses that now sits at the heart of Silicon Valley.

subject: Prome kingdom
summary: For sixty years, a minor Burmese kingdom at Prome played its larger neighbors against each other -- sacking the capital of one, betraying the alliance of another -- until its luck ran out in a five-month siege.

subject: Prominent Hill mine
summary: A copper-gold mine in the ancient Gawler Craton south-east of Coober Pedy, hidden beneath a barren plain inside one of the world's most secretive stretches of desert.

subject: Promontory Summit
summary: Where America was joined - the Utah hilltop where the golden spike connected the transcontinental railroad on May 10, 1869, uniting a nation still healing from Civil War and shrinking a continent to a week's journey.

subject: Promontory forts of Cornwall
summary: Cornish call them cliff castles, scattered along headlands where Iron Age builders cut off a piece of the world with a wall, a ditch, and the sea on three sides.

subject: Proserpine
summary: A working sugar town on a crocodile river, Proserpine is the unglamorous gateway most Whitsunday holidaymakers pass through on their way to the postcard islands - and it has been growing cane since the 1880s.

subject: Protestant Reformation
