summary: A Phu Thai district in Nakhon Phanom province whose hand-dyed indigo ends up on the shelves of a Premier League club shop in England, and whose people were marched here across the Mekong in the 1830s.

subject: Reposaari
summary: An island of wooden houses and stowaway Mediterranean plants at the outer edge of the Kokemäenjoki delta, where Finland's busiest export harbour once stood and fifty-three sailors are still remembered.

subject: Republic of Afghanistan (1973–1978)
summary: Afghanistan's first republic lasted just five years, as Mohammad Daoud Khan's ambitious modernization and military buildup ended when the communist revolution he helped enable consumed him.

subject: Republic of Cabinda
summary: A tiny territory on Africa's Atlantic coast that declared independence in 1975 and was absorbed by Angola the same year -- its government still operates in exile from Paris, and its oil still fuels the nation that claims it.

story.title: Republic of China Air Force Academy

subject: Republic of China Air Force Academy
summary: Founded in Nanjing in 1928, Taiwan's air force academy has been relocating ahead of wars and revolutions for nearly a century before settling in Kaohsiung.

subject: Republic of Genoa
summary: For seven centuries, the Republic of Genoa projected power from a cramped strip of Ligurian coast to the Black Sea, the Crusader ports, and the counting houses of Europe -- a maritime empire built on commerce, banking, and ruthless pragmatism.

subject: Republic of Hawaii
summary: The Republic of Hawaii lasted just four years, a transitional government engineered by American-descended sugar planters who overthrew the queen and waited for Washington to annex the islands.

subject: Republic of Indian Stream
summary: For three years in the 1830s, about 300 people at the headwaters of the Connecticut River declared themselves an independent republic because neither the United States nor Britain could agree on which country they belonged to.

subject: Republic of Negros
summary: In 1898, Filipino revolutionaries bluffed the Spanish garrison on Negros Island into surrendering by marching with rifles carved from palm fronds and cannons made of rolled bamboo painted black.

subject: Republic of San Marco
summary: For 17 months in 1848-49, Venice resurrected its republic in defiance of the Habsburg Empire -- a doomed revolution that became a founding myth of Italian unification.

subject: Republic of Sudan (1985–2019)
summary: Thirty-four years of political history - from the 1985 coup that removed Nimeiry, through three decades of Omar al-Bashir, to the revolution in 2019 - seen from the streets of the country it reshaped.

subject: Republic of Swellendam
summary: In June 1795, sixty disgruntled Cape farmers stormed the local magistrate's office and declared their own republic -- inspired by the French Revolution and gone within five months.

subject: Republic of Upper Volta
summary: For twenty-four years a landlocked West African nation was named for a river - until a revolutionary captain gave it a name that meant 'Land of Upright People.'

subject: Republic of West Papua
summary: A state that does not exist on any recognized map - declared by exiles, backed by two Pacific nations, and waiting to be more than a claim.

subject: Republic of the Congo
summary: A sparsely populated Central African nation where dense jungle canopy meets political complexity, Congo-Brazzaville hides some of the continent's last great wilderness areas behind a turbulent modern history.

subject: Requena
summary: A Valencian wine town that speaks Castilian, ringed by Bobal vineyards below a Moorish citadel that once grew rich on silk.

subject: Reric
summary: A planned Viking-age trading town on the Baltic whose merchants a Danish king carried off to Hedeby in 808 — lost for a thousand years, and found again in a field near Gross Stroemkendorf.

subject: Reserva Provincial La Payunia
summary: In southern Mendoza, more than 800 volcanic cones crowd a black-and-red wilderness - one of the densest concentrations of volcanoes anywhere on Earth, roamed by wild guanacos and the source of the planet's longest recent lava flow.

subject: Resistencia
summary: The capital of Chaco turned its streets into an open-air museum, scattering more than 600 sculptures across sidewalks and plazas until the whole city became a work of art.

subject: Reston, Virginia
summary: The planned community Robert E. Simon built on a Fairfax County whiskey farm in 1964 - 63,000 people, four lakes, 55 miles of trails, and a virus that scared the world in 1989.

subject: Rettendon murders
summary: Three drug dealers shot dead in a Range Rover on an Essex farm track in December 1995 - a triple murder that became a film franchise.

subject: Reus
summary: A Catalan market town that once set the world price of grape spirit alongside Paris and London, went on to invent Spain's vermouth, and claims Antoni Gaudi as its native son.

subject: Revash
summary: A row of painted stone mausoleums tucked into a limestone cliff in the Peruvian cloud forest - the Chachapoya built their dead a neighborhood with a view.

subject: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
summary: For nearly three decades a small Greek terrorist group murdered 23 people on the streets of Athens - diplomats, officers, businessmen, a politician - before a botched bombing in 2002 finally unraveled it and brought its members to trial.

subject: Reykjavik
summary: Europe's northernmost capital clings to a volcanic island at 64°N, its streets warmed by geothermal heat, its 130,000 people facing the North Atlantic with surprising swagger.

subject: Rhamnous
summary: On a lonely headland above the Euboean Strait stands the best-preserved town site in Attica, built around the sanctuary of Nemesis, the goddess who punished pride, and home to a statue the Persians unwittingly supplied the marble for.

subject: Rheiderland
summary: In winter, 120,000 wild geese descend on this flat strip of land between two countries — and the Netherlands once tried, briefly and unsuccessfully, to claim the whole thing.

subject: RheinEnergieStadion
summary: A 50,000-seat football stadium on the western edge of Cologne has hosted three World Cup tournaments across a century — and stands on ground that became available only when the Treaty of Versailles ordered the city's fortifications torn down.

subject: Rheindahlen
summary: A small Lower Rhine town with Neanderthal tools in the soil and a half-empty British military headquarters in the woods.

subject: Rheine
summary: A Westphalian crossroads on the Ems whose history reads like a ledger of fires, floods and rebuilds.

subject: Rheinisches Braunkohlerevier
summary: Europe's largest lignite mining region - holes deep enough to be visible from orbit, villages erased to reach the coal beneath them, and an industry now planning its own twilight.

subject: Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region
summary: Ten million people, no obvious center, and a fifteen-percent share of German GDP - the largest metropolitan area in Germany is a city that refuses to be one.

subject: Rhodes
summary: Greece's largest Dodecanese island wears its name like a flower, born of Helios and the nymph Rhodos in myth and shaped by every empire that ever wanted the eastern Aegean.

subject: Rhodes (city)
summary: Layer upon layer, Rhodes' old city preserves Hospitaller fortifications, Ottoman minarets, and Italian-era reconstructions inside the most complete medieval town wall in Europe.

subject: Rhodes blood libel
summary: In 1840, the Jewish community of Rhodes was falsely accused of ritual murder, tortured under interrogation, and besieged in their own quarter for twelve days before international protest forced their acquittal.

subject: Rhoscolyn
summary: A village on the southwest tip of Holy Island, named for a Roman boundary pillar -- with a sixth-century saint's church on the cliffs, a holy well a mile inland, and the memory of five lifeboat men still in the churchyard.

subject: Rhoscolyn Lifeboat Station
summary: Founded in 1830 by an Anglesey rector who had watched 140 people drown -- and closed in 1929 after the loss of its own coxswain and four crew in the storm that took the coaster Timbo down the Welsh coast.

subject: Rhosneigr
summary: A west Anglesey seaside village where kite-surfers race across Traeth Llydan, the clock tower frames a view of Snowdonia, and the name remembers a fifth-century Welsh leader almost no one remembers anything else about.

subject: Rhosneigr Lifeboat Station
summary: A small Anglesey RNLI station that closed in 1924 - but whose name was forever marked by a 1942 tragedy in which eleven men died trying to save the crew of a crashed Blackburn Botha.

subject: Rhumsiki
summary: A Kapsiki village in Cameroon's Mandara Mountains where volcanic plugs rise like stone sentinels around thatched-roof homes, creating scenery that travel guides call breathtaking -- even as they warn that tourism is changing what it celebrates.

subject: Riau-Lingga Sultanate
summary: A Malay maritime kingdom caught between British and Dutch colonial ambitions, the Riau-Lingga Sultanate endured from 1824 to 1911 before its rulers chose exile over submission.

subject: Ribe
summary: Denmark's oldest town began as a Viking trading post minting Frisian pennies around 700, then stopped growing - which is exactly why its medieval streets are still standing.

subject: Ribeirão Preto
summary: The city they called the Brazilian California built itself first on coffee, then on sugarcane - and every boom left behind mansions, opera houses, and more immigrants than the land could initially hold.

subject: Richard Hawkins
summary: An Elizabethan seaman whose raid on the Pacific coast of Spanish America ended badly in 1594 off what is now Ecuador - and whose eight-year Spanish imprisonment produced one of the period's most vivid sea memoirs.

subject: Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility
summary: Sitting on 780 acres of mesa just 1.5 miles from Mexico, Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility is California's southernmost state prison — and the only one in San Diego County, home to some of the most high-profile inmates in American criminal history.

subject: Richard Trevithick
summary: The Cornish mining engineer who invented the high-pressure steam engine and, in 1804 at Merthyr Tydfil, drove the world's first railway locomotive.

subject: Richmond County, North Carolina
summary: A county of longleaf pine, peach orchards, and the great Sandhills classification yard — home to The Rock, the railroad town of Hamlet, and a saxophonist named John Coltrane.

subject: Richmond Olympic Oval
summary: An Olympic speed skating rink built on 300 metres of river silt, roofed with beetle-killed pine, and backed by a contingency plan to fly the whole competition to Calgary if an earthquake moved the floor.

subject: Richmond Raceway
summary: What started as a horse track at the 1946 Virginia State Fair grew into one of NASCAR's most beloved short tracks - then quietly shrank again.

subject: Richtersveld
summary: The only arid biodiversity hotspot on Earth, where the Nama people still practice transhumant herding among half-human trees, 53-degree summers, and nearly 5,000 plant species -- 40 percent of them found nowhere else.

subject: Richwood, West Virginia
summary: The self-proclaimed Ramp Capital of the World, a former timber boomtown in the West Virginia mountains that throws an annual festival for a pungent wild leek.

subject: Rico Harris
summary: A former Harlem Globetrotter who vanished in the hills of Yolo County during an October 2014 road trip, leaving behind a car, a backpack, and a mystery that remains unsolved.

subject: Riga
summary: Where Art Nouveau facades line streets in unprecedented concentration, where Hanseatic history meets Baltic independence, where Latvia's capital displays architectural ambition.

subject: Rigopiano avalanche
summary: On 18 January 2017, an avalanche containing up to 60,000 tonnes of snow struck the Hotel Rigopiano in Italy's Abruzzo region at 100 km/h, killing 29 people in the deadliest avalanche in Italy since 1916.

subject: Rimba
summary: Born from a mission to fly doctors into Borneo's roadless interior, Rimba Air Force Base grew from three borrowed RAF helicopters into the operational heart of one of Southeast Asia's smallest but most meticulously equipped air forces.

subject: Rimutaka Incline
summary: A Victorian-era railway line that defied New Zealand's Remutaka Range with a radical third-rail system, climbing grades so steep that trains needed five locomotives and a top speed of just 8 km/h.

subject: Rinca
summary: An island where Komodo dragons outnumber the humans who share its scorched hills, guarded by whirlpool straits and currents that have swallowed divers whole.

subject: Rincon (surfspot)
summary: Called the Queen of the Coast, Rincon is one of the most celebrated surf breaks in California — a right-point wave at the Ventura–Santa Barbara county line with a lineage stretching back to Chumash villages and Spanish explorers.

subject: Rincon, Bonaire
summary: The oldest settlement in the Dutch Caribbean, founded in 1527 in a hidden valley to outsmart pirates, where the annual Dia di Rincon draws twelve thousand people to a town of fewer than two thousand.

subject: Rincón de Ademuz
summary: A Spanish-speaking scrap of Valencia stranded in the highlands between Cuenca and Teruel - one of the country's oddest jurisdictional survivals, threaded by the young river Turia.

subject: Ring of Brodgar
summary: The finest truly circular Neolithic stone ring in Britain, standing on a narrow isthmus between two lochs in Orkney as part of a UNESCO World Heritage ceremonial landscape.

subject: Ring of Gullion
summary: A ring of ancient volcanic hills in County Armagh that was the first ring dyke ever mapped on Earth and known in Irish tradition as the District of Poets.

subject: Ring of Kerry
summary: A 179-kilometer ribbon of road wraps the Iveragh Peninsula in scenery so dense it has become one of Ireland's defining drives.

subject: Ringaskiddy
summary: A County Cork fishing village that became Ireland's main pharmaceutical hub, where most of the world's Viagra is manufactured, and where the National Maritime College sits next to the naval base at Haulbowline.

subject: Ringstrasse
summary: Vienna's grand circular boulevard replaced medieval walls with opera houses and parliaments, turning a military defensive perimeter into Europe's most celebrated urban showcase.

subject: Rio Branco, Acre
summary: The capital of a state that only exists because a rubber boom and an improvised war made it Brazilian.

subject: Rio Grande
summary: The fourth longest river in the United States -- a waterway so over-claimed that it now fails to reach the sea, while two nations, three states, and centuries of history fight over what remains.

subject: Rio Madeira HVDC system
summary: Once the world's longest HVDC power line, this 2,375-kilometer line from the Amazon rainforest to southeastern Brazil delivers 7,100 megawatts of hydroelectric power.

subject: Rio Ouro Preto Extractive Reserve
summary: One of the first four extractive reserves created in Brazil, Rio Ouro Preto was born from the movement Chico Mendes died for -- a place where rubber tappers live on stilts above the floodwaters and harvest the forest without destroying it.

subject: Rio Quente
summary: A Goiás town of three thousand people sits on a river that runs at body temperature, fed by rain that fell on a plateau and came back up a kilometre later, warm.

subject: Rio São Francisco mangroves
summary: A 500-kilometer ecoregion of broken, river-mouth mangrove forests along eastern Brazil - three mangrove species, migratory shorebirds, and the tangled roots that protect estuaries from Alagoas to Salvador.

subject: Rio Verde, Goiás
summary: Goiás's grain heartland, where 250,000 hectares of soybeans, the state's largest cattle herd, and a cooperative among the country's three biggest all drive toward the port of Santos.

subject: Rio Vista, California
summary: A Sacramento River Delta town that moved itself to higher ground after a flood, became famous when a lost humpback whale swam 60 miles upstream, and now watches Silicon Valley billionaires buy up the farmland around it.

subject: Rio de Janeiro
summary: Where Christ the Redeemer opens his arms above the bay, where favelas climb the hillsides, where Carnival transforms the city that defines Brazilian dreams.

subject: Riobamba
summary: A sleepy Andean city of 150,000 nicknamed the Sultan of the Andes, ringed by snowcapped volcanoes and seven daily markets that spill into the streets.

subject: Riohacha
summary: A Caribbean port city born from pearls and pirate raids, where the Wayuu people endure, Gabriel Garcia Marquez found literary inspiration, and three competing legends explain an axe that gave the place its name.

subject: Rioja DOCa
summary: Spain's premier wine region, where Phoenician-era vineyards meet modern winemaking under the highest classification in Spanish wine law.

subject: Ripple Rock
summary: An underwater mountain that sank over 100 vessels and killed at least 110 people before Canada blew its top off in 1958 -- one of the largest non-nuclear explosions in history, broadcast live on national television.

subject: Ritan (Beijing)
summary: Built in 1530 as a Ming dynasty altar for imperial sun-worship rituals, this park has transformed from a sacred ceremonial site into a 24-hour public oasis in Beijing's embassy district.

subject: Rivera
summary: On Uruguay's northern frontier, Rivera shares a single open plaza with a Brazilian city across the street, a border so soft you can stand with one foot in each country.

subject: Riversleigh World Heritage Area
summary: A weathered limestone plateau in north-west Queensland holds 25 million years of Australian mammal evolution, including marsupial lions and toothed platypuses found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Rivierenland
summary: Wedged between the Waal, the Rhine, and the Maas, this Dutch fruit basket spends three weeks each spring under a roof of pink and white blossom.

subject: Riñihuazo
summary: After the largest earthquake ever recorded sealed a lake behind a wall of fallen mountainside, a month-long race with shovels and bulldozers kept 4.8 cubic kilometers of water from drowning Valdivia.

subject: Rjukan–Notodden Industrial Heritage Site
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where the landscape itself tells the story of how two Norwegian scientists turned waterfalls into fertilizer, transforming remote Telemark valleys into the cradle of Norway's industrial age.

subject: Road of the Seven Lakes
summary: A 107-kilometer ribbon of Argentina's Route 40 strings together seven Andean lakes between two Patagonian towns, threading through two national parks on one of South America's great scenic drives.

subject: Roan Antelope copper mine
summary: A Zambian copper mine born from a hunter's lucky kill in 1902, Roan Antelope has weathered malaria, labor strikes, nationalization, flooding, and four changes of ownership across more than a century of booms and busts.

subject: Roanoke Colony
summary: Two English attempts to plant a colony on Roanoke Island ended in abandonment and mystery -- the second group of 115 settlers vanished without a trace, leaving behind only the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a post.

subject: Roanoke Region
summary: Once Big Lick — a hamlet under five hundred named for the salt marshes that drew wildlife — Roanoke became the railroad's Magic City and now anchors a metropolitan region of nearly half a million.

subject: Roanoke, Virginia
summary: A Blue Ridge boomtown that grew 22-fold in a decade after the railroads arrived, Roanoke wears a giant illuminated star atop Mill Mountain - and earned its other nickname, The Magic City, the hard way.

subject: Roatán
summary: Honduras's largest Bay Island, built on an ancient coral reef, where the world's second-largest barrier reef meets backpacker dive culture and cruise ship economics.

story.title: Robert Burns and the Eglinton Estate

subject: Robert Burns and the Eglinton Estate
summary: The Ayrshire woodlands where a struggling flax-dresser was persuaded by a sea captain friend that he might be a poet worth printing.

subject: Robert Quayle (1814 ship)
summary: A 356-ton Liverpool merchant ship that stowed three convicts, chased whales through the Derwent, and ended her days in the Canadian timber trade.

subject: Robert Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve
summary: A 928-acre preserve in the Berkeley Hills built around a 10-million-year-old volcano tilted on its side, where hikers leave talismans in a stone labyrinth and geologists read the earth's deep past.

subject: Robert Towns
summary: The merchant who named a city after himself also opened the door to Queensland's South Sea Islander labour trade - a legacy the city is still reckoning with.

subject: Roberto-Sunol Adobe
summary: An 1836 adobe built by a Tamien Ohlone man on his own Mexican land grant, passed through debt to a Spanish merchant, then through a Dalmatian sea captain, Italian orchardists, and a determined restorer -- the oldest surviving home in San Jose.

subject: Robertsport
summary: A faded Americo-Liberian town on Liberia's Cape Mount, where plantation-style houses crumble above some of West Africa's finest surf breaks.

subject: Robeson County, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's largest county by area and one of the most racially diverse rural counties in the United States — Lumbee, Black, white, and Latino in close to equal parts.

subject: Robin's Nest (Hong Kong)
summary: Known in Chinese as Hung Fa Leng — Red Flower Ridge — this Hong Kong border mountain spent decades as an off-limits military zone before becoming the territory's 25th country park in 2024.

subject: Robins Air Force Base
summary: Georgia's largest industrial complex began as a whistle-stop depot in dairy-farm country, named for a spy-turned-pilot who invented Air Force logistics.

subject: Robson Bight
summary: The world's first ecological reserve designated for killer whales, where northern resident orcas practice a behavior found nowhere else on Earth: deliberately rubbing their bodies against smooth pebble beaches.

story.title: Rochester: The Kodak City Where Photography's Capital Lost Its Film

subject: Rochester
summary: The Western New York city that Kodak built and Kodak's bankruptcy devastated - where George Eastman democratized photography, where Frederick Douglass published his newspaper, and where the Genesee Falls powered an empire.

subject: Rochester, Kent
summary: A Roman bridge town turned Norman cathedral city turned Dickens stomping ground - the only place in British history to have lost its city status by paperwork oversight.

subject: Rock Art of Hail Province
summary: On two sandstone outcrops in Saudi Arabia's Hail Province, tens of thousands of carvings record ten thousand years of human life, hunters, herders, vanished wildlife, and the people who watched their world turn to desert.

story.title: Rock Art of the Iberian Mediterranean Basin

subject: Rock Art of the Iberian Mediterranean Basin
summary: Across more than 700 rock shelters in eastern Spain, prehistoric painters left the largest concentration of such art in Europe - hunters, dancers, warriors, and one immortal figure raiding a wild bees' nest.

subject: Rock Creek and Potomac Parkway
summary: Five Park Police on motorcycles flip the entire direction of a federal parkway every morning and every afternoon - a Washington commuter ritual hidden inside a National Register landscape.

subject: Rock Hill, South Carolina
summary: On a January day in 1961, nine Black students walked into a Rock Hill lunch counter, were jailed for sitting where they were told they couldn't, and refused bail - a small Carolina city's permanent contribution to American conscience.

subject: Rock carvings at Alta
summary: More than 6,000 prehistoric carvings spanning nearly 5,000 years line the rocky shores near Alta in Arctic Norway, a UNESCO World Heritage Site revealing a lost world of hunters, shamans, and bear worshippers.

subject: Rock of Monaco
summary: A 62-meter monolith on the Mediterranean coast that has anchored human settlement from prehistoric times through the Grimaldi dynasty's seven-century reign.

subject: Rocket sled
summary: The high-speed test track at Holloman Air Force Base, where scientists pushed humans and machines to the edge of destruction, achieving Mach 8.5 and giving the world Murphy's Law.

subject: Rockingham County
summary: An 853-square-mile Virginia county named for the British prime minister who supported American independence - the birthplace of Abraham Lincoln's father and the unlikely landing place of the first German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley.

subject: Rockingham, Northamptonshire
summary: A tiny village of 113 people where a Norman king once tried to depose an Archbishop of Canterbury, where a Norman castle still stands above the Welland valley, and where a vast medieval royal forest took its name.

subject: Rocky Boy's Indian Reservation
summary: Montana's smallest reservation holds a complex story of landless Chippewa, Cree refugees, and a chief who died months before Congress granted his people a home.

subject: Rodeo Lagoon
summary: A brackish coastal lagoon in the Marin Headlands separated from the Pacific by a sand bar, where freshwater creeks and ocean tides create a liminal ecosystem.

subject: Roe Plains
summary: A low coastal plain along the Great Australian Bight that was once the floor of an ancient sea, left stranded beneath towering limestone cliffs when the ocean withdrew.

subject: Roebourne, Western Australia
summary: The oldest gazetted town in Western Australia's North West, Roebourne carries the layered history of gold rush prosperity, colonial violence against Aboriginal people, and a present-day transformation led by its Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi traditional owners.

subject: Roermond
summary: The Limburg city that produced the architect of the Amsterdam Rijksmuseum, hosted Europe's largest Dutch witch trial, and now draws six million shoppers a year to a designer outlet.

subject: Roeselare
summary: Rebuilt from rubble after WWI, the West Flanders city is a brewing capital, a UNESCO belfry town, and the spiritual home of Belgian cycling.

subject: Rogers Pass
summary: The Canadian Rockies mountain pass where avalanches killed hundreds of railroad workers - now crossed by the Trans-Canada Highway protected by the world's largest avalanche control program, with artillery firing into the mountains.

subject: Rohingya genocide
summary: In Rakhine State, Myanmar, a people denied citizenship in their own land have endured decades of persecution that erupted into one of the 21st century's gravest humanitarian catastrophes.

story.title: Rokatenda: The Volcano That Is the Island

subject: Rokatenda
summary: Nearly ten thousand people share a roadless island in the Flores Sea with one of Indonesia's most active stratovolcanoes, living on the flanks of a mountain that has killed their neighbors within living memory.

subject: Rold Skov
summary: Denmark's second-largest forest, notorious for centuries as robber country, hiding chalk springs, five thousand species of fungi, and a Cold War government bunker.

subject: Roman Baths (Bath)
summary: Rain falling on the Mendip Hills today will rise as hot water in Bath in around ten thousand years - which is roughly how long humans have been bathing here.

subject: Roman Baths, Strand Lane
summary: Dickens called it Roman in David Copperfield. The wall plaque insists it dates to Vespasian. The truth is stranger: a Tudor cistern reinvented as antiquity by a Victorian shopkeeper looking for paying customers.

subject: Roman Catholic Diocese of Killala
summary: A small Catholic diocese spanning the northernmost parts of Mayo and Sligo, created in 1111 AD, whose bishops have hidden from Cromwell in mice-infested rooms, lived in poverty in the mountains, and as of 2024 sit vacant for the first time in nearly four centuries.

subject: Roman Polanski Sexual Abuse Case
summary: In 1977, celebrated director Roman Polanski drugged and sexually assaulted a 13-year-old girl at a Bel Air home; he pleaded guilty, then fled the United States before sentencing — and has never returned.

subject: Roman Road, London
summary: An East End market street where suffragettes printed newspapers, socialists held lectures over public baths, and grime music found its first audience at 391 Roman Road.

story.title: Roman and Medieval Aqueducts of Patras

subject: Roman and Medieval Aqueducts of Patras
summary: Two aqueducts built a thousand years apart — one Roman, one Ottoman — now stand side by side in a small archaeological park in Patras, where stone arches that once carried water across ancient valleys are visible in residents' back gardens.

subject: Roman conquest of Anglesey
summary: Two Roman invasions of the Welsh island of Mona, separated by seventeen years, broke the Druids' last sanctuary in Britain — and the only account that survives was written by the conqueror's son-in-law.

subject: Roman walls of Barcelona
summary: Beneath Barcelona's Gothic Quarter, the bones of Roman Barcino survive -- 2,000-year-old walls, towers, and gates woven so tightly into the medieval city fabric that buildings literally grew on top of them.

subject: Romanesque Road
summary: Eighty-eight buildings in sixty-five places, strung along 1,200 kilometres of road shaped like a figure of eight that crosses itself at Magdeburg — Saxony-Anhalt's inventory of the centuries when this was the frontier of Christian Europe.

subject: Romanisches Café
summary: Weimar Berlin's central artists' café sorted its customers into a swimmers' pool and a non-swimmers' pool — and was erased so completely that a shopping centre now stands where it was.

subject: Romaria
summary: A diamond camp once called Dirty Water renamed itself Pilgrimage, and every August a town of 3,500 people disappears beneath one of the largest religious gatherings in Minas Gerais.

subject: Rome
summary: The Eternal City - where the Roman Empire shaped Western civilization, where the Vatican still draws pilgrims, and where 2,800 years of history layers beneath every street.

subject: Romeral fault system
summary: A 700-kilometer scar through western Colombia marks where oceanic crust met continent 200 million years ago - and where, in 1983 and 1999, two modern cities were leveled in seconds.

subject: Romney
summary: The oldest town in West Virginia, named in 1762 by Lord Fairfax after a Cinque Ports city on the English Channel, with a Civil War history of changing hands more than fifty times.

subject: Romsdalen
summary: A 60-kilometer Norwegian valley where waterfalls rank among the world's tallest, the Troll Wall defies climbers, and wartime gold once fled toward the sea.

subject: Roncador Field
summary: Three billion barrels of oil beneath 1,500 meters of Atlantic water - and the platform that sank in 2001, killing eleven men, before production could really begin.

subject: Roncevaux Pass
summary: A Pyrenean mountain pass at 1,057 metres where Charlemagne's rearguard was destroyed in 778, inspiring The Song of Roland and marking this crossing between France and Spain as one of Europe's most storied passages for over a millennium.

subject: Ronda
summary: Perched above a gorge so deep it once inspired Hemingway's darkest fiction, this Andalusian hill town has been fought over by Celts, Phoenicians, Romans, and Moors -- and still divides old from new with a single bridge.

subject: Rondonópolis
summary: Mato Grosso's third-largest city grew from a telegraph route into the place where Brazil's soybean frontier meets the rails.

subject: Ronse
summary: For a thousand years, families across Europe brought their mentally ill relatives to Ronse, hoping a Roman saint named Hermes could cure them.

subject: Roodeplaat Research Laboratories
summary: On a quiet farm north of Pretoria, apartheid's scientists built a laboratory whose purpose was to kill the regime's enemies in ways no autopsy could detect.

subject: Roomade
summary: A Brussels arts organisation that once locked a hundred people inside the Atomium for twenty-four hours - and made a habit of staging exhibitions where the art was hard to find on purpose.

subject: Roosendaal
summary: A North Brabant railway hub that hosts the world's only official ABBA Fan Club, trains the Dutch special forces, and has a name that means the valley of roses.

subject: Rosalind Franklin
summary: An English X-ray crystallographer whose Photo 51 made the double helix visible, and whose contribution was acknowledged only after she could no longer answer for herself.

subject: Rosario
summary: Argentina's third city - cradle of the national flag, birthplace of both Che Guevara and Lionel Messi - was never officially founded by anyone at all.

subject: Roscommon
summary: An Irish county town where a 13th-century king of Connacht lies in his abbey, a female executioner once worked the gaol, and the last High Kings of Ireland are buried.

subject: Rosewood, Florida
summary: A once-thriving Black community in rural Levy County wiped from the map by racial violence in 1923, Rosewood endures as a ghost town and a Florida Heritage Landmark bearing witness to one of America's most painful chapters.

subject: Rosguill
summary: A Donegal peninsula whose Irish name remembers a killing in legend, where roughly a third of residents still speak Irish and bluefin tuna boats launch from a quiet harbour each autumn.

subject: Rosh Haniqra
summary: Where chalk cliffs meet the Mediterranean in a dazzling display of white stone, sea grottoes, and geopolitical tension at Israel's northernmost point.

subject: Roskilde Festival
summary: Europe's largest non-profit music festival, run by volunteers since 1971 and permanently marked by the 30 June 2000 crowd crush in which nine young men died.

subject: Ross Alley
summary: A narrow Chinatown alley where the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory still hand-folds cookies on vintage machines, carrying forward a tradition that dates to the neighborhood's earliest decades.

subject: Rossbeigh
summary: A two-mile Kerry sandspit that the Atlantic broke in half during a single storm in 2008 - and may yet rebuild from the sediment it scattered offshore.

subject: Rosscarbery
summary: A West Cork village that was once one of the major cities of Europe, where pilgrims studied in the School of Ross and where the Fenian leader Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa was born.

subject: Rostock
summary: A Baltic port that has been trading since 1218 and teaching since 1419, rebuilt after four nights of bombing in 1942 and still reckoning with a week in August 1992.

story.title: Roswell: Where America's UFO Obsession Began

subject: Roswell
summary: The New Mexico town where something crashed in 1947 and the Army briefly announced it was a 'flying disc' before changing the story to weather balloon - spawning decades of conspiracy theories, a tourism industry, and America's most persistent belief that the government hides alien contact.

story.title: Roswell: Where a Weather Balloon Became an Alien Spaceship

subject: Roswell
summary: The New Mexico town where something crashed in 1947 and conspiracy never died - where the official story changed three times, where the Air Force eventually said it was a balloon (a secret one), and where alien gift shops now outnumber gas stations.

subject: Roswell
summary: Where something crashed in 1947 - the New Mexico ranching town that became synonymous with UFOs after the Army announced it had recovered a 'flying disc,' then changed the story to a weather balloon, sparking decades of conspiracy theories.

subject: Rosyth Dockyard
summary: Built in 1909 because Britain feared the German navy, Rosyth Dockyard now dismantles nuclear submarines and assembles the Royal Navy's largest-ever aircraft carriers.

subject: Rote Flora
summary: Hamburg tried to put The Phantom of the Opera into a derelict Schanzenviertel theatre; the neighbourhood took the building instead, and has held it since 1989.

subject: Roter Faden
summary: Told it was the most boring city in Germany, Hanover painted a red line on its own pavement in 1971 and dared visitors to follow it for 4.2 kilometres.

subject: Roter Kamm crater
summary: A 2.5-kilometer scar punched into the Namib Desert nearly five million years ago by a meteorite the size of an SUV, now half-buried in migrating dunes inside one of the most restricted zones on Earth.

subject: Rothbury
summary: An ancient Coquetdale town transformed by Victorian industry, royal visits, and an industrialist's fairy palace on the hill above.

subject: Rothensee boat lift
summary: To dig its two sixty-metre shafts the builders froze the ground to minus forty; the machine they installed in them lifts a ship and 2,600 tonnes of water on under 500 kW, because buoyancy does the rest.

subject: Rotselaar
summary: A Flemish municipality where three rivers meet, a 14th-century knight's keep sits on a Greek-cross floor plan, and a neighboring field hosts one of the largest music festivals in Europe.

subject: Rotterdam
summary: Where World War II bombs created blank canvas for bold architecture, where Europe's largest port shapes a working city, where Dutch pragmatism builds futures.

subject: Rotterdam Centraal station
summary: An angular steel and glass roof points at the city like a paper plane; below it, 112,000 people a day pass through what is officially recognized as a world station.

subject: Rotterdam Feijenoord
summary: A south-bank island where a disgraced army officer built Rotterdam's harbor empire, and where a hundred years of European emigrants boarded ships for New York.

subject: Rotterdam Kralingen-Crooswijk
summary: Over six days in June 1970, a park reclaimed from a peat lake and built on bomb rubble hosted what the Dutch press called the European Woodstock.

subject: Rotterdam Metro
summary: When it opened in 1968, the Netherlands' first metro was barely six kilometers long. Today its yellow trains run from the North Sea coast to the Hague city centre.

subject: Rotterdam Northern Rotterdam
summary: Four villages, a castle that fell in 1426, a 1920s garden city, and a polder so chewed up by peat-cutting that its airport now sits below sea level.

subject: Rotterdam-The Hague Metropolitan Region
summary: On 1 January 2015, two Dutch cities that had spent four centuries deliberately ignoring each other agreed to share a government for transport, economy and waste collection.

subject: Rough (facility)
summary: An exhausted offshore gas field converted into Britain's largest underground gas vault, closed in 2017 and reopened against the clock in October 2022 as Europe braced for an energy crisis.

subject: Round Oak Steelworks
summary: For 125 years a steelworks the size of a town stood at Brierley Hill. Now a shopping mall stands where it stood.

subject: Roundstone, County Galway
summary: A Connemara fishing village built by a Scottish engineer in the 1820s - the name is a translation mistake, but the painters and filmmakers who came afterward stayed for what's actually here.

subject: Rourkela Steel Plant
summary: One of Nehru's 'temples of modern India,' this steel plant was built with West German aid on tribal land in Odisha, growing from Cold War geopolitics into a cornerstone of Indian industrial self-reliance.

story.title: Route of the Castles of Vinalopó

subject: Route of the Castles of Vinalopó
summary: A 75-kilometer trail up one of Spain's most heavily fortified valleys, linking a chain of frontier castles raised when this corridor was the seam between rival kingdoms and rival faiths.

subject: Rovos Rail
summary: From a private siding in Pretoria, the self-styled "most luxurious train in the world" sets out across Southern Africa at a deliberately unhurried pace.

subject: Royal Arcade, London
summary: Completed in 1880 and earning its royal name when Queen Victoria patronised a shirtmaker there, the Royal Arcade in Mayfair is one of the best-preserved Victorian shopping arcades in Britain — its saddled glass roof, Ionic columns, and curved shop fronts barely changed in 145 years.

subject: Royal Arsenal
summary: For three centuries the secret weapons works of the British state. At its First World War peak it covered 1,285 acres and employed 80,000 people. Today the same site is luxury flats, a Crossrail station, and one of London's newest cultural districts.

subject: Royal Aruba Aloe
summary: Founded in 1890 by Cornelis Eman, Royal Aruba Aloe is one of the few companies on Earth that grows, harvests, and processes aloe on a single site -- and in 2021, it became the first business outside the Netherlands to earn a Royal Predicate.

subject: Royal Avebe
summary: A century-old farmer-owned cooperative in Veendam that turned a Groningen potato into the largest source of food-grade potato starch on Earth.

subject: Royal Bafokeng Nation
summary: A Tswana community that bought its own land in the 1800s later found the world's richest platinum reef beneath it, and turned the windfall into a future.

story.title: Royal Brunei Airlines: The Sultan's Flag in the Sky

subject: Royal Brunei Airlines
summary: Brunei's government-owned flag carrier turned two Boeing 737s and four regional routes into a 32-destination network spanning Southeast Asia, Europe, and Oceania -- breaking a world record along the way.

subject: Royal Charter (ship)
summary: A gold-laden steam clipper wrecked off Anglesey in 1859, killing about 450 people and inspiring both Charles Dickens and the creation of Britain's first gale warning service.

subject: Royal Charter Storm
summary: On the night of 25-26 October 1859, the worst storm to hit the Irish Sea in the nineteenth century killed more than 800 people around the British Isles. More than 450 of them died within sight of land at Moelfre, on the east coast of Anglesey.

subject: Royal Court of Tiébélé
summary: A five-hundred-year-old Kassena royal compound in Burkina Faso where women paint elaborate symbolic murals on adobe walls using earth pigments and guinea fowl feathers.

subject: Royal Dornoch Golf Club
summary: Golf has been played on the linksland at Dornoch since 1616, and the course shaped by Old Tom Morris remains one of the world's most revered -- despite never hosting a major professional tournament.

subject: Royal Geographical Society
summary: Founded as a London dining club in 1830, the RGS sent Darwin, Livingstone, Scott, and Shackleton into the world and now holds one of the largest private map collections on Earth.

subject: Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club
summary: A sailing club that began in 1849, earned its royal warrant in 1894, excluded women until 1977, and solved the problem of its own name after the 1997 handover through a quiet compromise: English and Chinese say different things.

subject: Royal Ice Cream sit-in
summary: The June 23, 1957 protest at a Durham ice cream parlor by Reverend Douglas E. Moore and six other African Americans - the Royal Seven - two and a half years before Greensboro and almost entirely forgotten by history.

subject: Royal Institute of British Architects
summary: Since 1834, the RIBA at 66 Portland Place has been the custodian of British architecture — holding the world's largest collection of Palladio drawings, sheltering Adolf Loos's archives during World War II, and wrestling with its own long exclusion of women from the profession.

subject: Royal Kurgan
summary: A colossal 4th-century BC burial mound near Kerch whose long stone corridor and vaulted chamber are a masterwork of ancient engineering - and whose king was carried off by grave robbers long ago.

subject: Royal Leamington Spa
summary: A Regency boomtown built on the dubious promise of sodium-chloride springs, where Queen Victoria's 1838 visit added the word Royal to the name and where, in 1872, four players invented the modern sport of lawn tennis on a croquet lawn.

subject: Royal Mews
summary: The name comes from the French word for moulting - because in 1377 these stables in central London were a place where the king's hawks lost their feathers.

subject: Royal Mile
summary: A glacier-carved ridge between castle and palace, the Royal Mile threads almost exactly one Scottish mile through Edinburgh's Old Town.

subject: Royal Mint
summary: The maker of Britain's coins has lived in the Tower of London, on Tower Hill, and - since 1968 - on a 38-acre site outside the small Welsh town of Llantrisant, where every penny in the country is struck.

subject: Royal Palaces of Abomey
summary: Twelve palaces spread across 40 hectares in the heart of Benin tell the story of the Kingdom of Dahomey, a West African power that rose in 1625, dominated the slave trade, survived colonial conquest, and is now reclaiming its looted treasures from European museums.

subject: Royal Square (Barcelona)
summary: A palm-shaded arcaded square off La Rambla where a young Gaudi got his first public commission, and where Barcelona still gathers to drink, dance, and see in the new year.

subject: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
summary: The institution that decides who wins the Nobel Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, and Economics was founded in 1739 by Carl Linnaeus and five colleagues determined to make science accessible.

subject: Royal Swedish Naval Academy
summary: For 231 years, Sweden trained its naval officers through an institution that survived fires, relocations, and even a brief stint as a reformatory before closing in 1987.

story.title: Royal Tombs of the Goryeo Dynasty

subject: Royal Tombs of the Goryeo Dynasty
summary: Scattered across the hills near Kaesong, the burial places of the Goryeo kings span five centuries and hold murals, star charts, and 158 painted dogs -- a constellation of royal graves shaped by Confucian rites and Korean geomancy.

subject: Royal Troon Golf Club
summary: An Ayrshire links course where the Postage Stamp and the Railway hole still humble the world's best, and where the Open Championship has been contested ten times since 1923.

subject: Royal Tunbridge Wells
summary: An ailing 17th-century baron drank from a Wealden spring, felt better, and built a fashion industry around it. Three centuries later the spa is gone but the Pantiles, the gardens and the 'Royal' prefix remain.

subject: Royal Turf Club of Thailand
summary: A Bangkok racecourse where aristocrats, generals, and political schemers gathered for a century before the Crown took it back and planted a park.

subject: Royal United Services Institute
summary: The Duke of Wellington founded RUSI in 1831 as a place where soldiers and sailors could study the science of war — making it the world's oldest defence think tank, and one now deemed so consequential that Russia declared it an undesirable organization in 2025.

subject: Royal Welsh Yacht Club
summary: The fourteenth Royal Yacht Club in Britain, founded in 1847 in Caernarfon and housed in a medieval tower at the foot of the town walls - one of the oldest yacht clubs still operating anywhere in the world.

subject: Royal William Victualling Yard
summary: The Royal Navy's vast Georgian supply complex - a 16-acre granite-and-limestone city of bakeries, breweries, and slaughterhouses, built by convict labour and named for a sailor king.

story.title: Royston: Where Warships Go to Die and Rhododendrons Bloom

subject: Royston, British Columbia
summary: A small Comox Valley community that grew from a chance meeting between a Scottish settler and a coal baron, served as a logging port for a century, and is now known for its eerie breakwater of sunken warships and its legacy of rhododendron cultivation.

subject: Ru ware
summary: The rarest of China's imperial ceramics, Ru ware was produced for barely a generation around 1100 AD -- fewer than 90 complete pieces survive, each worth tens of millions of dollars.

subject: Rua do Cunha
summary: A narrow food street in Taipa named after a Portuguese governor who died of cholera 37 days after arriving — now the most fragrant lane in Macau, stacked with almond cakes, egg rolls, and restaurants that have been feeding the neighborhood for decades.

subject: Rub' al Khali
summary: The largest continuous sand desert on Earth, where 650,000 square kilometers of dunes conceal lost cities, the world's biggest oil field, and centuries of human defiance.

subject: Rub' al Khali Basin
summary: Beneath the world's largest sand desert lies a sedimentary basin spanning four nations, holding billions of barrels of undiscovered oil locked in rocks older than complex life itself.

subject: Rubha an Dunain
summary: An uninhabited peninsula south of the Cuillin where archaeologists found a Viking-era harbour complex, complete with stone quays and a canal to the sea.

subject: Rubislaw Quarry
summary: Six million tonnes of granite were dug out of the west end of Aberdeen over two centuries, leaving one of Europe's biggest man-made holes - now a 142-metre-deep flooded pit ringed by suburban houses.

subject: Rudd Concession
summary: On 30 October 1888, a Ndebele king signed away mineral rights he did not fully understand to agents of Cecil Rhodes -- a single document that became the legal foundation for the colonization of an entire country.

subject: Rudolf Virchow
summary: The pathologist who founded cellular medicine, built Berlin's sewers, and then measured the hair and eye colour of nearly seven million German schoolchildren to prove that the German race did not exist.

subject: Rugby, North Dakota
summary: A tiny North Dakota prairie town built its identity around being the geographic center of North America -- except modern calculations prove the real center is 105 miles away, in a town literally called Center.

subject: Ruisui
summary: A township where the Tropic of Cancer crosses an east coast river valley, the Amis people hold harvest festivals older than the railways, and golden hot springs have been drawing visitors since a Japanese bathhouse first opened its doors in 1919.

subject: Rukwa Region
summary: A Tanzanian region the size of Haiti, bordered by Lake Tanganyika to the west and named for an ancient alkaline lake to the south, where the Fipa people farm a fertile plateau rising 1,700 meters above the lakes below.

subject: Rum Jungle, Northern Territory
summary: A place whose name comes from a gold theft and a cask of spilled rum in 1873, Rum Jungle became the site of Australia's first uranium mine — and then one of its most contaminated environments, a legacy still being addressed today.

subject: Rumbek
summary: The capital of Lakes State in South Sudan, Rumbek briefly served as the administrative center of the entire south before Juba took that role -- a town rebuilding from civil war in one of the world's youngest nations.

subject: Rumelifeneri, Istanbul
summary: At the European mouth of the Bosphorus where the strait meets the Black Sea, Rumelifeneri is a fishing village named for its ancient lighthouse — a place that sailors have used as their last landmark or first landfall for at least six hundred years.

subject: Rumelikavağı
summary: A Bosphorus village whose Ottoman name means 'control post,' Rumelikavağı has served as a fortress, a fishing harbor, and a refuge — its medieval castle ruins and waterfront fish restaurants coexisting beside one of the world's great suspension bridges.

subject: Runcorn
summary: An Anglo-Saxon queen built a fort here in 915 to fight the Vikings. A thousand years later, Runcorn built the world's first bus rapid transit system. The town has always been an experiment.

subject: Runestones of Högby
summary: A thousand-year-old stone in a Swedish village tells the fate of five Viking brothers who died across the known world, from Byzantine Greece to the shores of Denmark.

subject: Rungholt
summary: A North Frisian settlement drowned by the storm tide of January 1362, mythologised for centuries as a rich city punished for its sins - until magnetic surveys of the tidal flats found its dike, its harbour and the footprint of its church.

subject: Rupiah Banda
summary: The fourth president of Zambia was born in a Zimbabwean town where his parents had gone to find work, educated by a Dutch Reformed preacher and an Indian family, and served as UN ambassador before winning the Zambian presidency by two percentage points in 2008.

subject: Ruskin, British Columbia
summary: A co-operative sawmill village at the mouth of the Stave River, named for a Victorian social critic, undone first by a drought and later by a government order.

subject: Russell Books
summary: Three generations, two cities and more than a million used volumes - and in 2019, half a million of them carried across a Victoria street by hand.

subject: Russian Battleship Rostislav
summary: The world's first capital ship to burn oil instead of coal, commanded by a Russian grand duke and dogged by disaster, now lies half-buried in the silt of the Kerch Strait where she was scuttled in 1920.

subject: Russian frigate Alexander Nevsky
summary: The Tsar's flagship went aground off Thyborøn in 1868 with a Russian grand duke aboard; Danish fishermen took nearly everyone off, five men drowned, and the survivor with the best story told it for the rest of his life.

subject: Rutherford County, North Carolina
summary: The most important gold-producing county in America for fifty years before the California Gold Rush, where a German immigrant minted the first US gold dollars and Dirty Dancing was filmed at Lake Lure.

subject: Ruthin
summary: A medieval market town where Owain Glyndŵr lit the fuse of a Welsh rebellion - and where the oldest dated timber-frame house in Wales still leans into Castle Street.

subject: Rutland
summary: Multum in parvo: England's smallest historic county, abolished in 1974 and resurrected by stubborn residents, with a horseshoe for an emblem and a habit of getting its way.

subject: Rutland Water
summary: Britain's largest reservoir by surface area drowned two Rutland villages in the 1970s, and what was lost has become, over fifty years, an unlikely sanctuary for ospreys, sailors, and a Jurassic sea dragon.

subject: Ruweng Administrative Area
summary: An oil-rich Dinka homeland in northern South Sudan that produces roughly 80 percent of the nation's petroleum, Ruweng is also the land of the Panaruu and Biemnom Dinka and two lakes where the Bahr el Ghazal meets the White Nile.

subject: Rwenzori Mountains
summary: The legendary Mountains of the Moon, Africa's highest non-volcanic range, where equatorial glaciers are vanishing, giant heathers grow six meters tall, and streams from the snowfields feed one of the sources of the Nile.

subject: Rybinsk
summary: A Volga River city that has been renamed four times, drowned a neighboring town beneath a reservoir, and gave Hollywood two of its most powerful studio executives.

subject: Rydal Water
summary: A small, quiet lake in the Rothay Valley between Grasmere and Ambleside, fed and drained by the same river, and walked past by William Wordsworth almost daily for nearly forty years.

subject: Ryhope
summary: A coastal village on the southern edge of Sunderland whose name means rough valley in Old English, where a stolen bronze pony was replaced with rocking horses and the world watched.

subject: Ryojun Guard District
summary: The Imperial Japanese Navy's base at Ryojun was activated, deactivated, upgraded, and deactivated again over four decades -- a naval installation whose status rose and fell with the tides of Pacific geopolitics.

story.title: Ryujin Onsen: The Dragon God's Hot Spring

subject: Ryujin Onsen
summary: Hidden deep in the mountains of Wakayama Prefecture along the upper reaches of the Hidaka River, Ryujin Onsen is one of Japan's three legendary Bijin-no-yu -- 'beautiful women hot springs' -- where sodium bicarbonate waters have been smoothing skin and drawing pilgrims, monks, and shoguns for over 1,300 years.

subject: Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster
summary: The largest concentration of ancient burial mounds in the Kanto region -- 114 tumuli stretched across a narrow plateau in Chiba Prefecture, including a square-sided step pyramid with a double moat that has been open and empty since the Edo period.

subject: Ryūsen-ji
summary: A 1,200-year-old Buddhist temple in Tokyo whose black-eyed guardian statue gave the entire Meguro district its name, and whose grounds hold the graves of doomed lovers, a sweet potato evangelist, and a pre-war revolutionary.

subject: Råbjerg Mile
summary: Denmark's last free-moving dune walks northeast across the top of Jutland at roughly fifteen metres a year, and everything in its path has a deadline.

subject: Réunion
summary: A French overseas department in the Indian Ocean where Creole culture, volcanic landscapes, a troubled colonial history, and some of the best hiking on Earth coexist on an island smaller than Rhode Island.

subject: Río Gallegos, Santa Cruz
summary: One of the windiest cities on Earth, this Patagonian port built itself on sheep, sovereignty, and the relentless gale that never stops blowing.

subject: Río Grande (Argentina)
summary: Argentina's northernmost Fuegian city is a working town of factories and fishing rivers, built on land taken from the Selk'nam, where a hesitant prosperity rises and falls on the wind off the Atlantic.

subject: Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage rainforest in Honduras's Mosquitia region -- the largest contiguous forest north of the Amazon, where indigenous communities navigate by dugout canoe.

subject: Rössing uranium mine
summary: The longest-running open-pit uranium mine in the world sits in the Namib Desert, 70 kilometers from the coast, producing yellowcake under an ownership structure that links China, Iran, South Africa, and Namibia in a single operation.

subject: Rømø
summary: A Danish Wadden Sea island with a beach wide enough to drive on, a fence made of whale jawbones, and the whaling-captain fortunes that built both.

subject: Røros Copper Works
summary: For over three centuries, this mining operation in the Norwegian mountains produced 110,000 tonnes of copper, shaped a town now recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and left scars in the landscape that tell their own story.

subject: Røstvangen Mines
summary: A complete mining town -- bakery, movie theater, post office, and 260 workers -- appeared in Norway's remote Osterdalen district in 1904, extracted copper for seventeen years, and then vanished almost overnight when the company went bankrupt.

subject: Røsvatnet
summary: Norway's second-largest lake earned that rank by drowning 23 farms — a reservoir whose superlative is also a record of what the water took.

subject: Røyrvik Municipality
summary: Norway's third-smallest municipality by population — 423 people spread across 1,585 square kilometres of lake, border mountain and South Sami reindeer country.

subject: Rùm
summary: The largest Small Isle has been inhabited since 8000 BC, evicted in the 1820s, run as a sporting estate complete with alligators, and is now a nature reserve outnumbered ten to one by mountain goats.

subject: Rạch Giá
summary: The first place in Vietnam to manufacture its own land out of the sea, Rạch Giá became a provincial capital in the same year it stopped being a city.

subject: S'Espalmador
summary: A private, uninhabited island you can wade to at low tide, bought for 252 euros in 1932 and sold for 16 million pounds in 2018.

subject: S4C
summary: Wales's Welsh-language public broadcaster, launched in 1982 only because Gwynfor Evans threatened to starve himself to death until Margaret Thatcher kept her party's manifesto promise.

subject: SAS Saldanha
summary: South Africa's primary naval training base occupies a harbor that has been fortified since World War II, when anti-submarine nets and coastal guns turned Saldanha Bay into an Allied stronghold.

subject: SAS Transvaal
summary: A World War II-era frigate built for the Royal Navy but transferred to South Africa, the SAS Transvaal spent three decades annexing islands, rescuing sailors, and surveying volcanoes before being scuttled as an artificial reef in False Bay.

story.title: SCMaglev: The Train That Floats at 603 km/h

subject: SCMaglev
summary: Deep in the mountains of Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan's superconducting maglev has spent decades perfecting the art of levitation -- setting a world speed record of 603 km/h and inching closer to a commercial line that will connect Tokyo and Nagoya in under 40 minutes.

subject: SM U-27
summary: A German submarine that made naval history by sinking another submarine - then went to the seabed in an incident so ugly that German propagandists called it a cowardly murder for the rest of the war.

subject: SOHAR Port and Freezone
summary: A deep-sea port and free zone on Oman's northern coast, strategically located outside the Strait of Hormuz, handling over a million tonnes of cargo weekly as part of Oman's economic diversification.

subject: SRI International
summary: A Menlo Park research institute that separated from Stanford in 1970 after inventing the computer mouse, helping create the internet, and developing Siri, becoming one of the most prolific innovation engines in American history.

subject: SWIFT
summary: In a wooded suburb south of Brussels, a postmodern fortress quietly routes half the world's high-value cross-border payments.

subject: Sa Caleta Phoenician Settlement
summary: On a rocky headland ten kilometers west of Ibiza Town, the foundations of a 7th-century BC Phoenician settlement reveal the island's oldest urban experiment -- a four-hectare town that thrived for fifty years and then vanished.

subject: Sa Calobra
summary: A tiny Mallorcan cove reached by one of Europe's most theatrical roads, a ribbon of asphalt that famously ties itself into a knot and passes beneath its own carriageway.

subject: Sa Cudia Cremada
summary: A remarkably preserved Talaiotic settlement on the edge of Mahón, where Bronze Age towers, a hidden sanctuary, and rock-cut tombs have outlasted every empire that followed.

subject: Sa Talaiassa
summary: Ibiza's highest peak, whose name means 'the great watchtower' - a summit that has surveyed the island for centuries and bears the memory of a 1972 tragedy.

subject: Saalfeld Fairy Grottoes
summary: A Thuringian alum mine abandoned in 1850 that spent the next sixty years quietly growing what Guinness calls the most colourful show grottoes in the world.

subject: Saanich Inlet
summary: A 226-metre-deep fjord outside Victoria whose bottom water has been oxygen-free for roughly seven thousand years - which is precisely why oceanographers have wired it for live video.

subject: Saaremaa
summary: Estonia's largest island was once home to Viking pirates who terrorized Scandinavia, a meteorite impact that burned forests for miles, and Soviet military secrets hidden from the outside world for forty-three years.

subject: Saatchi Gallery
summary: The London gallery where an advertising magnate's restless eye turned British art upside down, launched Damien Hirst's shark into history, and made shock and spectacle into a movement.

subject: Sabana Formation
summary: Under Bogotá lies the bed of a vanished Ice Age lake - where mastodons once walked, early humans built the first camps in Colombia, and modern skyscrapers now tilt on 320 meters of unconsolidated clay.

subject: Sabang, Aceh
summary: Indonesia's northernmost city occupies a volcanic island at the mouth of the Strait of Malacca, where four centuries of colonial ambition, wartime destruction, and geopolitical maneuvering have shaped a place that still lives by its harbor.

subject: Sabetta
summary: An Arctic industrial port carved from frozen tundra on the Yamal Peninsula, where ice-breaking LNG tankers load year-round at 71 degrees north and fly-in workers maintain one of the most remote energy facilities on Earth.

subject: Sabi Sand Game Reserve
summary: The private reserve where the fence to Kruger came down and the leopards learned to ignore the Land Rovers, now the most reliable place on Earth to watch a leopard at close range.

subject: Sabina Shoal
summary: Sabina Shoal, a submerged atoll 75 nautical miles from Palawan, became the South China Sea's newest flashpoint in 2024 when Philippine and Chinese coast guard vessels repeatedly collided over its coral waters.

subject: Sabratha
summary: One of the three ancient cities of Roman Tripolis, this UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Libyan coast has endured Phoenician traders, Roman emperors, Vandal conquerors, and a bid to host the Beatles' final concert.

subject: Sabu-Jaddi
summary: More than 1,600 rock drawings across 6,000 years record the moment the Sahara was green - and the long slow afternoon when it wasn't.

subject: Sack of Barcelona (985)
summary: In the summer of 985 the feared general Almanzor stormed and razed Barcelona, slaughtered its garrison, and carried its people into slavery in a single devastating week.

subject: Sack of Baturyn
summary: In a single November morning in 1708, the Cossack capital fell and thousands of its people died, an event Ukraine now remembers with a day of national silence.

subject: Sack of Constantinople
summary: In April 1204, soldiers of the Fourth Crusade — Christian warriors who had set out to reclaim Jerusalem — instead stormed and plundered Constantinople, killing, enslaving, and brutalizing the city's Christian inhabitants and leaving a wound between Eastern and Western Christianity that has never fully healed.

subject: Sack of Cullera
summary: In May 1550 the Ottoman corsair Dragut sacked Cullera and carried off nearly the whole town into slavery in Algiers - a raid the coast has never quite forgotten.

subject: Sack of Damietta (853)
summary: A Byzantine naval raid on the undefended Egyptian port of Damietta in 853 CE shocked the Abbasid caliphate into rebuilding Egypt's long-neglected navy, catalyzing a maritime renaissance that would culminate under the Fatimids three centuries later.

subject: Sack of Mahón
summary: In 1535 the corsair Hayreddin Barbarossa sailed into Mahón's harbor flying false imperial colors, and turned a homecoming into one of the darkest nights in Menorca's memory.

subject: Sack of Surat
summary: In January 1664, Maratha leader Shivaji attacked the wealthy Mughal port of Surat with four thousand soldiers, plundering the city for days while an English factory held out behind its own walls with artillery.

subject: Sack of Torreblanca
summary: A 1397 corsair raid on a Valencian coastal village that carried off 108 captives and a sacred vessel, igniting a crusade against the North African coast.

story.title: Sacramento: The California Capital in Gold Rush Country

subject: Sacramento
summary: The California capital that most Californians forget about - where Sutter's Fort preceded the Gold Rush, where the Transcontinental Railroad began, and where the politicians gather in a city that isn't LA or San Francisco.

story.title: Sacramento: Where the Gold Rush Ended and California Began

subject: Sacramento
summary: California's capital where the Gold Rush created a city overnight, where the transcontinental railroad began its westward push, where the Sacramento and American rivers converge, and where Old Sacramento preserves the Wild West waterfront that supplied the Sierra mining camps.

story.title: Sacramento Mountains: Sky Islands of the Desert

subject: Sacramento Mountains (New Mexico)
summary: Rising sharply from the Tularosa Basin, the Sacramento Mountains form a dramatic forested escarpment that splits New Mexico's desert landscape and feeds the otherworldly white dunes below.

subject: Sacramento's First Post-Prohibition Pour
summary: The first bar to get a liquor license in Sacramento after Prohibition ended in 1934, Old Ironsides spent ninety years as a family-run dive where future rock stars played their earliest gigs.

subject: Sacramento, Minas Gerais
summary: A coffee-and-cattle municipality in the Triângulo Mineiro whose old schoolhouse, founded by a teacher who died at 38, still draws visitors from across Brazil.

subject: Sacromonte
summary: Granada's hillside neighborhood of whitewashed cave dwellings, where Romani culture, flamenco tradition, and centuries of legend are carved into the rock itself.

subject: Sado mine
summary: For nearly four hundred years, the Sado gold and silver mines bankrolled shoguns, modernized Japan's mining industry, and left behind a legacy that remains diplomatically contested to this day.

subject: Sadri Alışık
summary: Born Mehmet Sadrettin Alışık in Istanbul in 1925, Sadri Alışık became one of the most beloved figures in Turkish cinema — a comedian who made audiences laugh at poverty without ever mocking the poor, and whose greatest character, the bumbling wanderer Turist Ömer, followed Turks to movie theaters for over a decade.

subject: Safavid capture of Tabriz (1603)
summary: Shah Abbas the Great recaptured Tabriz from the Ottoman Empire in September 1603 through deception, perfect timing, and a city that had no walls to defend it.

subject: Sagaing
summary: A city of golden spires and monastic devotion on the Irrawaddy, Sagaing has served as a royal capital, a center of Buddhist learning, and a place where Myanmar's layered history of faith, resistance, and catastrophe converges on a single ridge of hills.

subject: Sagara Oil Field
summary: Japan's only Pacific coast oil field, where crude so pure it could fuel a car without refining once drew 600 workers to a tiny Shizuoka village -- now a quiet park preserving the nation's petroleum origins.

subject: Sagastad
summary: A Viking knowledge center in Nordfjordeid housing the full-scale reconstruction of Norway's largest Viking ship, built from the evidence of a cremation grave that burned a thousand years ago.

subject: Sagunto
summary: A Mediterranean city where a single hilltop stacks Iberian, Roman, Moorish and medieval empires above thirteen kilometres of beach.

subject: Sahara International Film Festival
summary: The only film festival on earth held in a refugee camp, where the grand prize is a live white camel and the screen stands against the desert night.

subject: Sahrawi refugee camps
summary: On a desert plain so harsh it was called the Devil's Garden, a displaced people built schools, hospitals, and a government - and have waited there for half a century to go home.

subject: Sai Kung District
summary: Called the 'back garden of Hong Kong,' Sai Kung District is one of the city's least urbanized corners — a patchwork of country parks, ancient fishing villages, UNESCO-recognized geology, and one of Asia's great new university campuses, all packed into a peninsula jutting into the South China Sea.

subject: Sai Kung Town
summary: Sai Kung Town is the seafood-famous, waterfront market town at the heart of the Sai Kung Peninsula — a place that expanded not through industry or finance but because a reservoir forced fisherfolk from their villages, and yet somehow stayed exactly itself.

subject: Sai Wan
summary: The westernmost reach of Hong Kong Island, Sai Wan has been plague ground, pleasure district, colonial frontier, and — after 1997 — a quiet metonym for political power in the city.

subject: Sai Wan Ho
summary: A working-class dockyard neighborhood on Hong Kong Island's northeastern shore that housed 10,000 Taikoo workers in 1909, watched the sea recede northward through decades of reclamation, and quietly became one of the island's most livable corners.

subject: Sai Yeung Choi Street
summary: A street named for watercress fields that were paved over a century ago, Sai Yeung Choi Street South became Mong Kok's most crowded pedestrian strip — then lost that status to noise complaints and a culture war fought in decibels.

story.title: Sai-ji: The West Temple That Lost the Centuries

subject: Sai-ji
summary: One of two grand guardian temples built at the gates of eighth-century Kyoto, Sai-ji was the mirror image of the surviving To-ji -- until poor drainage, court politics, and fire erased it from the landscape, leaving only foundation stones beneath a neighborhood park and an elementary school.

subject: Saighir
summary: A clapperless bell rang itself in the Slieve Blooms, and where it sounded Ciarán built one of Ireland's oldest Christian sites—older than Patrick's mission, older than the parchment that records it.

story.title: Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage: Thirty-Three Temples, One Promise

subject: Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage
summary: Japan's oldest pilgrimage route threads through seven prefectures across the Kansai region, connecting thirty-three temples dedicated to Kannon -- born from a monk's encounter with the King of Hell, who promised that those who complete the circuit will not fall into the underworld.

subject: Saikazaki
summary: A weathered cape on Wakayama's coast where Japan's most feared gunners once held off Oda Nobunaga, now a quiet fishing village called 'Japan's Amalfi' for its houses tumbling down hillsides toward the Kii Channel.

subject: Sail and Life Training Society
summary: A Victoria charity that builds its own tall ships - one of them assembled in public at Expo 86 - and puts 1,700 teenagers a year on their decks.

subject: Sainsbury's
summary: From a single Drury Lane dairy in 1869 to a household name with six hundred stores, Sainsbury's traces the arc of how Britain learned to shop.

subject: Saint Anne, Alderney
summary: The pastel-painted capital of Alderney is the only town on an island that was emptied of its people in 1940 and forced to start its civic life over from baptism registers and family memory.

subject: Saint Augustin, Madagascar
summary: A sheltered bay at the mouth of the Onilahy River where a 1645 English colony starved within a year, then became a pirate haven, and today survives on fishing and outrigger canoes.

subject: Saint Croix
summary: The largest U.S. Virgin Island has been claimed by seven flags, sustained by sugarcane and enslaved labor, scarred by hurricanes and economic collapse, and shaped by waves of migration that made it one of the most culturally layered places in the Caribbean.

subject: Saint John City Market
summary: Canada's oldest continuously operated farmer's market has been feeding Saint John since 1785, housed beneath a roof built by shipwrights who shaped its trusses like an inverted keel.

story.title: Saint John d'El Rey Mining Company

subject: Saint John d'El Rey Mining Company
summary: A British gold-mining firm that brought Cornish miners to Brazil, held enslaved people in defiance of its own contract, and dug the world's deepest mine into the Minas Gerais hills.

subject: Saint Laurent Boulevard
summary: Montreal's great dividing line -- known simply as 'The Main' -- has served for over three centuries as the seam where languages, cultures, and immigrant dreams collide along a single 11-kilometer artery.

subject: Saint Lucia
summary: A volcanic Caribbean island fought over fourteen times between France and Britain, where twin volcanic peaks called the Pitons rise from the sea and a drive-in volcano steams beside rainforest-covered mountains.

subject: Saint Malo, Louisiana
summary: The first Filipino settlement in North America -- a hidden fishing village in the Louisiana marshes, founded by sailors who jumped ship from Spanish galleons as early as 1763, and erased by a hurricane in 1915.

subject: Saint Martin
summary: The smallest inhabited island shared by two nations, where French boulangeries and Dutch casinos coexist without a border fence.

subject: Saint Peter Port Lifeboat Station
summary: From a 170-pound boat bought by twelve men in 1803 to a 17-meter all-weather lifeboat answering its 1,500th call, the Guernsey lifeboat service has saved over 600 lives in some of Europe's worst tides.

story.title: Saint-Denis: The Capital Named for a Lost Ship

subject: Saint-Denis (Réunion)
summary: The largest city in all of France's overseas departments, Saint-Denis owes its name to a tiny 60-ton vessel that went missing in the Canary Islands and found its own way across the Indian Ocean to Reunion.

subject: Saint-Georges, French Guiana
summary: On the Oyapock River, a tiny French town faces Brazil across the only land border France shares with another South American country.

subject: Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni
summary: A pretty tropical town whose elegant colonial streets were swept clean by the convicts the town existed to imprison.

subject: Saint-Leu
summary: A west-coast town in Réunion famous for one of the finest left-breaking waves in the world - and for the 1811 slave revolt that began in the ravines above it.

subject: Saint-Paul, Réunion
summary: Réunion's oldest town, where French settlement on the island began in 1663 - and where a notorious pirate's tomb still draws treasure hunters to a seaside cemetery beneath the cliffs.

subject: Saint-Paul-de-Vence
summary: A medieval hilltop village above the French Riviera where Picasso painted, Sartre philosophized, James Baldwin wrote, and Chagall chose to be buried -- all drawn by the same ancient light.

subject: Saint-Pierre, Martinique
summary: Once called 'the Paris of the Caribbean,' Saint-Pierre was Martinique's cultural capital until the morning of May 8, 1902, when Mount Pelee erupted and killed nearly 28,000 people in minutes.

subject: Sainte Claire Club
summary: Founded in 1888 with just twenty members, the Sainte Claire Club is one of California's oldest private gentlemen's clubs, housed in a Mission Revival building designed by A. Page Brown in San Jose's St. James Square Historic District.

subject: Sainte Luce Reserve
summary: A sliver of intact coastal rainforest in Madagascar's far southeast, where a lemur found nowhere else clings on between the Indian Ocean and the bulldozers of a titanium mine.

subject: Sainte-Rose, Réunion
summary: On Réunion's storm-lashed eastern coast, the village of Piton Sainte-Rose watched a 1977 lava flow swallow its streets and stop at the door of its church.

subject: Sajama Lines
summary: A vast web of thousands of perfectly straight paths etched into Bolivia's Altiplano over three millennia, covering an area fifteen times larger than the Nazca Lines.

story.title: Sak Tz'i': The Kingdom Found in a Farmer's Backyard

subject: Sak tzʼi (Maya site)
summary: For decades, scholars knew the ancient Maya kingdom of Sak Tz'i' - 'White Dog' - only from inscriptions at rival cities that described capturing its lords. In 2020, researchers finally identified its capital at a site called Plan de Ayutla, in the backyard of a Mexican rancher in Chiapas.

story.title: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro: The Shogun Who Became a Legend

subject: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro
summary: The second person to hold the title of Sei-i Taishogun, Sakanoue no Tamuramaro served Emperor Kanmu in the early Heian period, conquered the Emishi peoples of northern Honshu, funded the construction of Kiyomizu-dera, and after death transformed into a mythic demon-slayer whose legacy still lights up Japan's greatest summer festivals.

subject: Sakhalin
summary: Russia's largest island, a 1,000-kilometer sliver of taiga, mountains, and oil wealth wedged between the Sea of Japan and the Sea of Okhotsk -- fought over by empires, home to indigenous Nivkh and Ainu peoples, and still one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth.

subject: Sakhalin Ainu language
