summary: An extinct language once spoken across Sakhalin Island, Sakhalin Ainu vanished in 1994 with the death of its last speaker -- carrying with it millennia of oral tradition from one of Northeast Asia's oldest indigenous cultures.

subject: Sakitama Kofun Cluster
summary: Nine ancient keyhole-shaped burial mounds on the Kanto Plain gave their name to an entire prefecture -- and one yielded a gold-inlaid iron sword that rewrote the history of 5th-century Japan.

subject: Sakon Nakhon
summary: A lakeside Isan town where Thai and Lao blur into each other, and where every Christmas Eve the largest Catholic community in Thailand fills the roads with illuminated stars.

subject: Sakon Nakhon province
summary: The province whose name means "city of cities" is better known in Thailand for what happens outside its cities: the forest monasteries of the Phu Phan hills.

subject: Saky
summary: A small Crimean town built around a healing salt lake, where mud from the lakebed has drawn the sick and the curious for nearly two centuries.

subject: Sala Silver Mine
summary: A five-century Swedish silver mine where visitors can now sleep 155 meters underground, surrounded by rock that turned green from the minerals that once made kings wealthy.

story.title: Salaga: The Timbuktu of the South

subject: Salaga
summary: Once West Africa's greatest inland market and a hub of the trans-Saharan slave trade, Salaga's hundred wells and baobab-shaded market square hold the memory of a town where fortunes and human lives changed hands.

subject: Salalah
summary: Oman's second city and the birthplace of Sultan Qaboos, where ancient frankincense souqs meet monsoon-soaked summers and a two-thousand-year trading history.

subject: Salar de Atacama
summary: Chile's largest salt flat fills a closed basin between the Andes and the Cordillera de Domeyko, harboring flamingos, ancient geology, and the lithium brines that power the world's batteries.

subject: Salar de Pedernales
summary: Chile's largest salt flat in the Atacama Region holds eleven thousand years of human history, dark slope streaks that scientists compare to Mars, and a modern fight between copper mining and the wetlands it is slowly draining.

subject: Salar de Uyuni
summary: The world's largest salt flat transforms between seasons from an endless white desert of hexagonal patterns into the planet's biggest mirror, reflecting the Bolivian sky so perfectly that the horizon disappears.

subject: Salar del Huasco
summary: A high-altitude salt flat in northern Chile where three thousand flamingos nest among spring-fed lagoons, ice age archaeology sits beside cutting-edge microbiology, and copper mining threatens the water that sustains it all.

subject: Salcombe
summary: A Devon harbour town built by fruit-trade schooners now floats a thousand yachts on the drowned valley that inspired Tennyson's most famous goodbye.

subject: Salcombe Lifeboat Station
summary: The Salcombe lifeboat was capsized on the bar at the mouth of its own harbour in 1916, taking thirteen of its fifteen-man crew - and went back to work after.

subject: Saldanha man
summary: A half-million-year-old skull found among shifting sand dunes near Hopefield, South Africa, reshaped our understanding of early human migration across the African continent.

story.title: Salem: The Witch City That Turned Tragedy Into Tourism

subject: Salem
summary: The colonial town where 20 people were executed for witchcraft in 1692, where October transforms streets into costumed celebration, and where America confronts its history of deadly hysteria.

subject: Salem witch trials
summary: In 1692, a fractious Massachusetts village became the site of colonial North America's deadliest witch hunt, where more than 200 people were accused and 20 were executed before reason finally prevailed.

subject: Salem, Virginia
summary: A small city of 25,000 in the Roanoke Valley that quietly hosts more NCAA championship events than seems mathematically possible - and was once Virginia's largest town before deciding it had to become a city to survive.

subject: Salesforce Transit Center
summary: A $2.2 billion transit hub topped by a 5.4-acre rooftop park that was closed for emergency repairs within six weeks of opening, then reopened as San Francisco's grand central station.

subject: Salford
summary: A separate city facing Manchester across the Irwell, where industrial collapse and 21st-century media regeneration sit a few streets apart - and L.S. Lowry still defines how the world pictures it.

subject: Saliagos
summary: A tiny islet between Paros and Antiparos holding the earliest known farming settlement in the Cyclades, where people lived, fished for tuna, traded obsidian across 200 kilometers of open sea, and carved marble figurines between 5000 and 4500 BC.

subject: Salinas Grandes
summary: A blinding white salt desert at 3,450 meters in the Argentine Andes, patterned in perfect hexagons and now a battleground over the lithium buried beneath it.

subject: Salinas and Steinbeck Country
summary: The California agricultural valley John Steinbeck immortalized in 'East of Eden' and 'The Grapes of Wrath' - where the Nobel laureate grew up among lettuce fields and migrant workers, observing the stories that would define American literature.

subject: Salinas de Guaranda
summary: An Andean Ecuadorian town that reorganized itself as a cooperative in the 1970s and now produces premium cheese, chocolate, and a blue liquor called Pajaro Azul.

subject: Salinas, Ecuador
summary: The westernmost point of mainland Ecuador, where the Humboldt Current keeps a tropical beach town cool and where silver coins from a 1654 shipwreck rest beside pre-Columbian figurines.

subject: Salinas, Minas Gerais
summary: A town named for rock salt that Brazil's Congress declared, by federal law, the national capital of cachaça.

subject: Salinópolis
summary: Pará's headline beach town was founded on salt and dried fish, and now empties and fills with the Amazon's rain calendar.

subject: Salisbury, Maryland
summary: The capital of the Eastern Shore is the home of Perdue chicken, the world's first Kindness USA city, and a courthouse lawn that has reckoned with three lynchings.

subject: Salish Sea
summary: An 18,000-square-kilometre inland sea shared by British Columbia and Washington, holding 400 islands, living glass sponge reefs and 8.76 million people - and carrying a name that is barely older than the internet.

subject: Salish Sea Human Foot Discoveries
summary: Twenty detached feet in running shoes have washed up around the Salish Sea since 2007, and the answer turned out to be less a mystery than a story about drowning, grief, and what a foam sole does in saltwater.

subject: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
summary: Jonas Salk founded this research institute above the Pacific in 1960 — and Louis Kahn's campus design, with its travertine plaza pointing toward the ocean, became one of the most admired buildings of the twentieth century.

subject: Salme ships
summary: Two Viking-era ship burials discovered on an Estonian island containing 41 warriors killed in battle, pushing back the dawn of the Viking Age by decades.

subject: Salo
summary: A Finnish town that spent ninety years making the future — radios, colour televisions, then the mobile phone — and then had to work out what it was without it.

subject: Salo
summary: Ten municipalities became one, so Salo is less a town than 2,000 square kilometres of manor country, ironworks villages and castle ruins with a market square in the middle.

subject: Salt Reservations
summary: An 18th-century federal anti-monopoly experiment that locked salt springs out of private sale to keep frontier meat preservation affordable - a Founders-era policy now nearly forgotten.

subject: Salta
summary: A colonial jewel cradled in an Andean valley, where Spanish facades, gaucho tradition, and the preserved bodies of three Inca children give the city its haunting beauty.

subject: Saltaire
summary: A Yorkshire wool baron built an entire village in 1851 so his workers could escape the slums of Bradford, and a century and a half later the whole thing became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Saltcoats
summary: An Ayrshire seaside town named for the small cottages where seawater was once boiled down to salt, and later a Glasgow Fair holiday resort whose decline is the story of cheap European flights.

subject: Salthill
summary: Galway's seaside suburb, with a two-kilometre promenade, a 19th-century tramway, Christmas Day swims at Blackrock Tower, and a name-drop in a Steve Earle song.

subject: Salto, Uruguay
summary: Uruguay's second city went looking for oil and found hot water instead. The wells that disappointed prospectors gave Salto its thermal springs and a new identity.

story.title: Salton City: The Beach Resort That Became a Wasteland

subject: Salton City
summary: The California development where investors built streets and yacht clubs for a desert sea that was slowly dying - where subdivided lots still wait for buyers, where dead fish coat the shore, and where the American dream of waterfront living curdled into environmental disaster.

subject: Salton Sink
summary: The lowest trough in the western United States, where tectonic forces are slowly pulling California apart and ancient lakes have come and gone for tens of thousands of years.

subject: Saltstraumen
summary: A narrow strait near Bodø where 400 million cubic meters of seawater surge through every six hours, creating one of the world's strongest tidal currents and whirlpools up to 10 meters wide.

subject: Salvador
summary: Salvador rewards visitors who learn its rhythm - the cliff-divided geography, the beach-by-beach calibration, the Pelourinho-after-dark versus Pelourinho-in-daylight calculus - more than any Brazilian city except maybe Rio.

subject: Salvador Metro
summary: Brazil's fifth-largest city got its subway eleven years late and just in time for the 2014 World Cup - a two-line system whose brevity tells the story of how hard it is to build anything underground in a Brazilian capital.

subject: Salvador, Bahia
summary: Brazil's first capital and the largest landing point for enslaved Africans in the Americas, Salvador turned four centuries of forced migration into the most densely African city outside Africa itself.

story.title: Salzburg Residenz: Where Prince-Archbishops Ruled Like Kings

subject: Salzburg Residenz
summary: The palatial seat of Salzburg's prince-archbishops since the 12th century, redesigned in the early 1600s by the Venetian architect Vincenzo Scamozzi and now housing the Residenzgalerie - a collection assembled to replace the art lost during the Napoleonic Wars.

subject: Sam Phan Bok
summary: Three thousand shallow pools carved into the Mekong's rocky riverbed in northeastern Thailand, revealed each dry season like a submerged canyon rising to the surface.

subject: Samad al-Shan
summary: An oasis cemetery of 260 excavated graves spanning the Bronze Age to Late Iron Age, whose dead reveal a society of date farmers who buried men with weapons and women without them, and whose origins remain one of Arabian archaeology's deepest puzzles.

subject: Samana Cay
summary: An uninhabited Bahamian island at the center of a centuries-old debate over where Columbus first set foot in the Americas, Samana Cay holds Lucayan artifacts, abandoned settlement ruins, and groves of cascarilla bark.

subject: Samar
summary: A Cossack river town that outlived three names, Samar reclaimed its oldest one in 2024 after two and a half centuries as Novomoskovsk.

subject: Samarai
summary: Once the second-largest town in the Territory of Papua and a trading port three times wealthier than Port Moresby, Samarai today is a 29-hectare island of 460 people and the ghosts of its own former importance.

subject: Samatya
summary: A layered Marmara-shore quarter of Istanbul where Armenians and Greek Orthodox communities built lives across centuries, leaving churches, schools, and names that outlasted empires.

subject: Sambava
summary: On Madagascar's northeast coast, a beach town where much of the world's vanilla is cured by hand, bean by fragrant bean.

subject: Sambor Prei Kuk
summary: More than a hundred brick sanctuaries in a Cambodian forest, ten of them eight-sided and found nowhere else on earth - carved with palaces that fly, cratered by American bombs, and mined until 2008.

subject: Samborondón
summary: A peninsula between two rivers became Ecuador's wealthiest suburb, named for an Irish monk who sailed into medieval legend and a city thousands of miles from Guayaquil.

subject: Samburu National Reserve
summary: A semi-arid reserve along the 'brown water' river in northern Kenya, named for the Samburu people, where doum palms shade a special cast of desert-adapted animals - and a lioness once adopted a baby antelope.

story.title: Sammallahdenmäki: Graves Built for a Shoreline That Left

subject: Sammallahdenmäki
summary: For some 1,500 years, Bronze Age families carried their cremated dead up a ridge in Satakunta and raised granite cairns meant to be seen from the sea. Land uplift has since moved the water fifteen kilometres away.

subject: Sammamish, Washington
summary: A wealthy plateau city east of Seattle where the 'Willow People' once lived in longhouses, and where America's highest-earning families now grapple with the tension between growth and preservation.

subject: Sammy Marks
summary: A Lithuanian tailor's son who became the industrialist nicknamed the "uncrowned king of the Transvaal," Sammy Marks left his mark on Pretoria in brick, bronze, and a grand Victorian house east of the city.

subject: Samoa
summary: Where Polynesia began - volcanic islands wrapped in three thousand years of unbroken culture, where Robert Louis Stevenson found his final rest and villages still gather for the 'ava ceremony as their ancestors did.

subject: Samorian state
summary: A twenty-year empire built on horseback, gunpowder, and sheer defiance, Samori Ture's Wassoulou state waged one of the longest resistance campaigns against French colonialism in West African history.

subject: Sampson County, North Carolina
summary: North Carolina's second-largest county by land area produces more turkeys, hay, and flue-cured tobacco than any other in the state - and on a 947-square-mile patchwork of farmland it raises some two million hogs.

subject: Samson, Isles of Scilly
summary: The largest uninhabited island in the Isles of Scilly, abandoned in 1855 when its starving families were finally evicted to the mainland.

subject: Samsø
summary: A Danish island that dug a canal through its own middle in the 8th century and rebuilt its entire energy supply in the 21st.

story.title: Samuel Elmore Cannery: The Bumble Bee That Burned

subject: Samuel Elmore Cannery
summary: The longest continuously operated salmon cannery in America stood on Astoria's waterfront for 82 years, birthed the Bumble Bee tuna brand, and ended not with a whimper but with a fire that stripped it of its National Historic Landmark status.

subject: Samuel Morse
summary: The painter-turned-inventor who wired the world for instant communication lived his final years in a Manhattan brownstone, leaving behind a legacy measured in dots and dashes.

subject: Samuel Pepys
summary: A tailor's son from Fleet Street who buried his parmesan in the garden to save it from the Great Fire, and along the way wrote the most important diary in English.

subject: Samuraizuka Kofun
summary: A pair of fifth-century burial mounds on the Kanto Plain that became the site of Japan's earliest recorded archaeological excavation, ordered by a Tokugawa lord in 1692 who believed the tombs held the remains of ancient rulers named on a nearby seventh-century stone stele.

subject: Samus culture
summary: Four thousand years ago in Western Siberia, Bronze Age people cast metal, carved human faces into pottery, and built fortified settlements along the Ob River, leaving behind an archaeological puzzle that still connects modern Siberian peoples to their deep past.

subject: San Agustín culture
summary: More than 300 stone giants stand on the green hills of southern Colombia, carved by a culture that flourished 2,000 years ago and then vanished - leaving behind Latin America's largest group of pre-Columbian megalithic statues.

subject: San Antonio
summary: The Texas city where 200 defenders died at the Alamo in 1836, where the River Walk transformed urban renewal into tourism gold, and where Mexican and Texan identities blend in the oldest major city in the state.

story.title: San Antonio Missions: The Churches That Built Texas

subject: San Antonio Missions
summary: The chain of five Spanish colonial missions including the Alamo - where Franciscans converted and congregated Indigenous peoples, where thick stone walls defended against raids, and where the oldest surviving European structures in Texas still hold Mass 300 years after construction.

subject: San Antonio de Areco
summary: On the banks of the Areco River, Argentina's National Capital of Tradition keeps the gaucho alive in silver, leather, and the cadence of a horse at walk.

subject: San Antonio de los Cobres
summary: Nearly 3,800 meters up in the Argentine Puna, a windswept mining town is the high point of one of the world's most spectacular railways.

subject: San Antonio, Baja California Sur
summary: A tiny mining town in the mountains of Baja California Sur that witnessed conquistadors, Dutch pirates, and a filibuster's short-lived republic.

subject: San Basilio de Palenque
summary: Founded around 1603 by formerly enslaved Africans who fought their way to freedom, San Basilio de Palenque is the first free African town in the Americas and a UNESCO-recognized living monument to resistance.

subject: San Bernardino County, California
summary: The largest county in the contiguous United States, where over 80 percent of the land is federally owned, more wilderness areas exist than in any other U.S. county, and a population of over two million people lives almost entirely in a narrow strip along one edge.

subject: San Bernardino Ranch
summary: The legendary home of lawman John Slaughter, who tamed Tombstone after the O.K. Corral and built a ranch that straddled two nations.

subject: San Blas, Nayarit
summary: A small Pacific port that once rivaled Acapulco as a shipbuilding center, supplied Spain's California missions, and launched expeditions to Alaska -- now a Pueblo Mágico where the bells that inspired Longfellow still echo in ruin.

subject: San Borja
summary: A Jesuit mission town on the Maniqui River that grew into the cattle gateway between the Andes and the Amazon, where vaqueros and the rhythms of the Beni still set the pace.

subject: San Carlos Apache Indian Reservation
summary: Once called 'Hell's Forty Acres' for its brutal conditions, the San Carlos Apache Indian Reservation is now home to sacred lands under threat, world-class peridot mines, and a people fighting to preserve their language and sovereignty.

subject: San Carlos Institute
summary: Founded by Cuban exiles in 1871 and beloved by Jose Marti as 'La Casa Cuba,' the San Carlos Institute on Duval Street survived fires, hurricanes, and decades of neglect to remain the heart of Key West's deep Cuban heritage.

subject: San Carlos, Chile
summary: A market town in Chile's orchard country that claims the cradle of the woman who reinvented Latin American folk song.

subject: San Carlos, Salta
summary: A small Calchaquí Valley village that swallowed four failed Spanish cities and once lost the chance to become Salta's capital by a single vote.

subject: San Cosme y Damián
summary: At a Jesuit mission on the Paraná, a priest built telescopes from bamboo and river quartz and charted Jupiter's moons - work that made this small Paraguayan town the cradle of South American astronomy.

subject: San Cristobal (Galapagos)
summary: The easternmost Galapagos island, where Darwin first set foot on the archipelago in 1835 and where the only large freshwater lake feeds a town of sea lions, frigatebirds, and giant tortoises.

subject: San Cristóbal Hill
summary: Spanish conquistadors renamed this hill — known by its Quechua name Tupahue — for the patron saint of travelers, and ever since it has been Santiago's great landmark, crowned by a luminous Virgin who watches the whole city.

story.title: San Cristobal de las Casas: The Highland City Where Rebellion Simmers

subject: San Cristóbal de las Casas
summary: A colonial highland city in Chiapas designated a Pueblo Magico, where Tzotzil and Tzeltal Maya artisans sustain centuries-old craft traditions, the Zapatista uprising of 1994 reshaped Mexican politics, and the local drink is a cane liquor called posh.

story.title: San Diego: The City Where California's History Actually Began

subject: San Diego
summary: The California city where the Spanish first landed and the Navy never left - where the zoo became world-famous, where the weather is impossibly consistent, and where Tijuana is close enough to walk to.

subject: San Diego
summary: The Southern California city with near-perfect weather, where the Navy dominates the harbor, where the Zoo became world-famous, and where California began when Junipero Serra founded the first mission in 1769.

subject: San Diego (ship)
summary: A Spanish galleon that sank without firing a shot in 1600, then yielded over 34,000 artifacts when rediscovered nearly four centuries later off the Philippine coast.

subject: San Diego County, California
summary: No county in the United States contains more Native American reservations than San Diego — 18 of them, scattered across a terrain that runs from Pacific beaches to Sonoran desert in fewer than 70 miles.

subject: San Diego Ostrich Ranch
summary: A South African family sailed to California to raise ostriches, built a 35-acre ranch near Escondido, and ended when the owner was arrested in 1992 for smuggling eggs hidden in chocolate boxes.

subject: San Diego Supercomputer Center
summary: One of five original NSF supercomputing centers founded in 1985, SDSC at UC San Diego maintains the Protein Data Bank and has pushed the boundaries of scientific computing from early grid networks to flash-memory supercomputers.

subject: San Elijo Lagoon
summary: One of the largest remaining coastal wetlands in San Diego County, San Elijo Lagoon has been used by humans for 8,500 years and is now bisected by three transportation corridors — yet it still draws 40 percent of all North American bird species.

subject: San Felipe 250
summary: A 250-mile off-road race through the Baja California Peninsula that has tested motorcycles, trucks, and drivers against the desert every spring since 1982.

subject: San Felipe Municipality, Baja California
summary: Mexico's newest municipality as of 2022, San Felipe is home to barely 18,000 people on the Gulf of California shore, where the Kiliwa people once fished and Jesuit explorers mapped a world they did not understand.

subject: San Francisco Armory
summary: A Moorish Revival fortress in the Mission District that served as a National Guard armory, a boxing venue, a film studio, and a community center, its uses as diverse as the neighborhood around it.

subject: San Francisco Art Institute
summary: One of America's oldest art schools, founded in 1871, which trained generations of artists before financial pressures forced its closure after 150 years.

story.title: San Francisco Cable Cars: The World's Last Moving Landmarks

subject: San Francisco Cable Cars
summary: The only mobile National Historic Landmarks in America - Victorian-era transit cars still climbing San Francisco's impossible hills, pulled by underground cables, operated by gripmen whose skill keeps the 19th century alive in a city that invented the future.

subject: San Francisco Jazz Festival
summary: An annual three-week celebration produced by SFJAZZ, the San Francisco Jazz Festival has hosted decades of performances by jazz legends from Keith Jarrett to Ornette Coleman.

subject: San Francisco LGBT Community Center
summary: Housed in a Victorian landmark and a modern solar-powered addition on Market Street, the SF LGBT Center has served as a hub for queer community life since 2002.

subject: San Francisco Symphony
summary: Founded in 1911 and saved from Depression-era bankruptcy by a public bond measure, the San Francisco Symphony became one of America's most decorated orchestras under a succession of transformative music directors.

subject: San Francisco Zen Center
summary: Founded in 1962 by Shunryu Suzuki and his American students, the San Francisco Zen Center grew from a beatnik sitting group into the largest Soto Zen organization in the Western world.

subject: San Francisco, Cundinamarca
summary: A hummingbird sanctuary, a parish priest's vision, and two landowners named Francisca and Francisco - how a Colombian mountain village got its name in one winter afternoon in 1857.

subject: San Gimignano
summary: A Tuscan hill town frozen in medieval amber, San Gimignano's fourteen surviving towers once numbered seventy-two -- stone declarations of wealth in a city that the Black Death stopped in time.

subject: San Gorgonio Pass Wind Farm
summary: One of California's first three major wind farms, developed in the 1980s at the natural wind funnel of San Gorgonio Pass, the farm peaked at over 4,200 turbines in 1987 and has since undergone decades of repowering — replacing many aging smaller turbines with fewer, larger ones that generate more energy.

subject: San Gregorio, California
summary: A 214-person hamlet where the Portola expedition camped for three days in 1769, wealthy San Franciscans once arrived by stagecoach, and seven cheese factories once thrived.

subject: San Ignacio Miní
summary: A Jesuit mission that survived Bandeirante raids, colonial suppression, and military destruction, now stands as one of South America's most intact monuments to the Guaraní people who built it.

subject: San Ignacio de Moxos
summary: In this small Beni town, the Moxeño people transform a colonial saint's day into the Ichapekene Piesta, a UNESCO-honored festival where feathered warriors dance their own myth back to life.

subject: San Ignacio de Velasco
summary: A frontier town built around a Jesuit dream, where Chiquitano craftsmen still carve cedar and the music of the missions has never quite stopped playing.

subject: San Ignacio, Paraguay
summary: The first Jesuit reduction in Paraguay and the mother of all the rest, San Ignacio Guazú still guards a baroque legacy carved by Guaraní hands - and on Good Friday it becomes a stage of living paintings.

subject: San Jacinto Mountains
summary: The San Jacinto Mountains rise from the desert floor in one of the most abrupt fault-scarp escarpments in North America, lifting San Jacinto Peak to 10,834 feet within miles of sea-level Palm Springs — and their granite faces gave birth to the Yosemite Decimal System for rock climbing.

subject: San Javier (Spain)
summary: A Mar Menor town where summer jazz shares the sky with the fighter jets of Spain's air force officer academy, once home to its famous aerobatic team.

subject: San Javier, Uruguay
summary: A town on the Uruguay River where Russian religious refugees planted sunflowers in 1913, kept their language for a century, and remember a doctor the dictatorship tortured to death.

subject: San Javier, Ñuflo de Chávez
summary: The first of the Chiquitos missions, founded in 1691, where a Swiss Jesuit's baroque church and the music it sheltered survive in a town the rainforest nearly reclaimed.

subject: San Joaquin Experimental Range
summary: A 1,800-hectare outdoor laboratory in the Sierra Nevada foothills where scientists have studied the relationship between cattle, grass, and fire for nine decades, producing one of the longest continuous ecological records in the American West.

subject: San Joaquín
summary: A small town on a seasonal road through the Bolivian Amazon lowlands, where life moves at the pace of the rivers and the rhythm of the fiesta.

story.title: San Jose: The Capital of Silicon Valley

subject: San Jose
summary: America's tenth-largest city and the Bay Area's largest, where garage startups became tech giants, where Cisco, Adobe, and eBay are headquartered, and where the 'orange sauce' was invented at taquerias serving the nation's second-largest Vietnamese community.

subject: San Jose Flea Market
summary: A 120-acre bazaar in San Jose's Berryessa district where more than 2,000 vendors have drawn millions of visitors since 1960, creating a self-contained world of commerce, food, and community that even found its way into American literature.

subject: San Jose Grand Prix
summary: A short-lived Champ Car street race that threaded through downtown San Jose from 2005 to 2007, where light rail tracks launched cars airborne and the shortest circuit on the schedule tested the limits of what a city street could endure.

subject: San José del Palmar
summary: On the wettest slope in the Americas, where the Pacific forest meets the Andes, a tiny 1938 frontier town guards an ecological corridor connecting two oceans of biodiversity.

subject: San Juan Bautista (ship)
summary: Built in just 45 days by 4,500 workers in 1613, this Japanese-built Spanish galleon carried samurai across the Pacific on a doomed diplomatic mission to the Vatican.

subject: San Juan Chamula
summary: A fiercely independent Tzotzil Maya town in the Chiapas highlands where Christianity and ancient traditions merge inside a candle-lit church that operates beyond the reach of Mexican law.

subject: San Juan Hill, Manhattan
summary: Before Lincoln Center's marble plazas and concert halls, these six blocks between 59th and 65th streets were San Juan Hill -- a vibrant African-American, Afro-Caribbean, and Puerto Rican neighborhood that gave birth to the Charleston and nurtured jazz legends like Thelonious Monk.

subject: San Juan Mountains
summary: A volcanic mountain range in southwestern Colorado where gold and silver mining towns cling to rugged slopes, ancient calderas hide beneath alpine meadows, and a narrow gauge railway still threads through canyons it first entered in the 1880s.

subject: San Juan Spruce
summary: Once the second-largest known Sitka spruce on Earth, the San Juan Spruce was struck by lightning in July 2016 and lost much of its height and mass in a single violent moment.

story.title: San Juan del Sur: Vanderbilt's Shortcut to California

subject: San Juan del Sur
summary: A sleepy Nicaraguan fishing village that became a key stop on the Gold Rush transit route from New York to San Francisco, San Juan del Sur has reinvented itself as a Pacific coast surf and beach town where the name itself is a geographical riddle.

subject: San Juan, Argentina
summary: A desert oasis city in the Cuyo region, rebuilt on a modern grid after the catastrophic 1944 earthquake that launched Perón's national career, and birthplace of Argentina's schoolmaster-president Domingo Sarmiento.

subject: San Juancito, Honduras
summary: A Honduran mountain town that once rivaled the capital in size and technology, powered by gold and silver mining, now a quiet gateway to La Tigra cloud forest.

subject: San Luis
summary: Named for a point of land where deer once gathered, San Luis is a sun-baked provincial capital at the foot of the Sierras Grandes, where independence-era monuments share the horizon with one of Argentina's largest solar parks.

subject: San Luis de Pambil
summary: A laidback Andean foothills town on the edge of Ecuador's vanishing rainforest, where backpackers find waterfalls, aguardiente distilleries, and a community quietly guarding what remains.

subject: San Marcos, California
summary: San Marcos was named on St. Mark's Day 1797 when Spanish soldiers chasing livestock thieves stumbled into a fertile valley — and it has been reinventing itself ever since, growing from a farming town to a city of nearly 95,000 anchored by two colleges.

subject: San Martín de los Andes
summary: Argentina planted this lakeside town in 1898 to win a border argument, and it grew into a shingle-roofed mountain village of immigrants that is now one of Patagonia's most beloved year-round resorts.

subject: San Miguel (Ecuador)
summary: An Afro-Ecuadorian village reachable only by riverboat, where rainforest begins behind the community hotel and the Cayapas River serves as the only road.

subject: San Miguel de Tucumán
summary: Argentina's largest northwestern city, where the nation's independence was declared in 1816, sits in a lush subtropical plain at the foot of the Andes, blending colonial gravitas with the noise and energy of nearly a million inhabitants.

subject: San Miguel de Velasco
summary: A baroque mission church glowing with ochre and gold rises from a small Bolivian town where prayers are still spoken in a language nearly lost.

subject: San Miguel del Bala
summary: A 32-family Tacana indigenous community on the Beni River that built its own eco-lodge at the doorstep of Bolivia's Madidi National Park, becoming a model for community-run rainforest tourism.

subject: San Nicolás de los Arroyos
summary: A steel city on the Paraná where Argentina's provinces once agreed to become a nation, and where pilgrims now walk for days to reach the riverbank shrine of Our Lady of the Rosary.

subject: San Pablito, Puebla
summary: A remote Otomi village in Mexico's Sierra Norte mountains where women and children keep alive the pre-Hispanic craft of amate bark paper, once restricted to shamans, now sustaining an entire economy.

story.title: San Pasqual Band of Diegueno Mission Indians

subject: San Pasqual Band of Diegueno Mission Indians
summary: A federally recognized Kumeyaay tribe whose history runs from their pueblo's founding in 1835 through eviction in 1878 and return to their homeland in the San Pasqual Valley — home to the San Diego Zoo Safari Park.

subject: San Pedro Square
summary: San Jose's oldest neighborhood, where a 1797 adobe stands within walking distance of craft cocktail bars, anchoring a district that bridges the city's Spanish colonial origins and its modern downtown nightlife.

subject: San Pedro de Atacama
summary: A dusty oasis town of 3,900 people in northern Chile that serves as the gateway to salt flats, geysers, flamingo-filled lagoons, and some of the clearest night skies on Earth.

subject: San Pedro del Pinatar
summary: At the northern tip of the Mar Menor, San Pedro del Pinatar has lived off salt and sea since Roman crews mined its pans to make garum.

subject: San Pedro la Laguna
summary: A laid-back backpacker town on Lake Atitlan's western shore where Tz'utujil Maya culture meets Spanish language schools, volcano hikes, and lakeside bonfires -- unless you visit during the last week of June, when simulated artillery shells go off day and night.

story.title: San Pedro y San Pablo Asistencia

subject: San Pedro y San Pablo Asistencia
summary: A sub-mission established in 1786 at an Ohlone village where disease collapsed the population from 300 to 25 in two years, leaving only roof tiles salvaged for a Burlingame train station.

subject: San Rafael, Mendoza
summary: Born as a frontier fort on a contested river, this orchard city grew on snowmelt, immigrant labor and dammed Andean torrents into the heart of southern Mendoza.

subject: San Salvador de Jujuy
summary: The capital of Argentina's northernmost province, where the Argentine flag was first shown to the public in 1813, and where Andean indigenous culture meets colonial history on streets still anchored by a cathedral with an 18th-century cedar pulpit.

subject: San Telmo, Buenos Aires
summary: Buenos Aires' oldest barrio, where cobblestones, a Sunday antiques fair, and the ghost of early tango fill the streets that survived plague and exodus.

subject: San Tin
summary: A marshland hamlet in Yuen Long District whose name means 'new fields,' San Tin has been home to the Man clan for over six centuries — yet today it also hosts the only 24-hour border crossing between Hong Kong and mainland China.

subject: San Uk Ling Holding Centre
summary: A remote Hong Kong detention facility near the mainland border — built in 1979 to hold illegal immigrants, it gained painful prominence in 2019 when arrested protesters were held there and allegations of mistreatment sparked a controversy the authorities disputed and an oversight body found warranted concern.

subject: San Vicente del Caguán
summary: A livestock town at the edge of the Colombian Amazon that became the center of a peace process - and the center of its collapse.

subject: San Vicente, Palawan
summary: Home to the Philippines' longest white sand beach -- a 14.7-kilometer ribbon of shoreline nearly three times the length of Boracay's famous White Beach -- San Vicente is Palawan's emerging frontier of tourism and transformation.

subject: San'ya
summary: A Tokyo neighborhood that officially ceased to exist in 1966 persists as the city's most storied district of day laborers, drifters, and quiet resilience -- a place the government tried to rename out of existence.

subject: San, Mali
summary: A market town that grew up at a river crossing, San has spent six centuries trading gold, cloth, and grain at the place where the delta meets the road south.

subject: SanDisk
summary: Born from a refugee scientist's breakthrough in semiconductor memory, SanDisk grew from a Milpitas startup into the company that put flash storage in every pocket on the planet.

subject: Sana'a
summary: A traveler's view of one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, where jambiya daggers and qat afternoons shape daily life in a highland capital that predates recorded history.

subject: Sanaa Governorate
summary: The administrative region surrounding - but not including - Yemen's capital, home to the highest mountain in the Arabian Peninsula and nearly three million people spread across 16 districts of ancient villages and fortified hill towns.

subject: Sanam, Sudan
summary: A modern Sudanese village sits atop the remains of a Kushite city - and one of the very few ancient cemeteries we have that belonged to ordinary people.

subject: Sanandaj
summary: Capital of Iran's Kurdistan Province and a UNESCO Creative City of Music, Sanandaj sits in a fertile Zagros valley where Kurdish culture thrives in sound, craft, and stone.

subject: Sanctuary of Aphrodite Urania
summary: Archaeologists knew this Athenian altar belonged to Aphrodite before they read a single inscription - the bones gave it away, because only she received doves.

subject: Sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas
summary: The older hilltop shrine above Epidaurus where the region's healing cult began, dedicated to Apollo Maleatas on Mount Kynortion — centuries before Asclepius arrived below.

subject: Sanctuary of Asclepius, Epidaurus
summary: The most celebrated healing sanctuary of the ancient Greek world, where the desperately sick came from across the Mediterranean to sleep in the abaton and hope that the god Asclepius would visit them in dreams.

story.title: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Fuensanta

subject: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Fuensanta
summary: A hilltop Baroque sanctuary above Murcia, built where a spring is said to have appeared, home to the patron of the city and its fertile plain.

subject: Sanctuary of St. Paschal Baylon
summary: In an orange-growing Castellón town, the world's largest swinging bell hangs above the tomb of a shepherd-turned-saint, in a shrine rebuilt from the ashes of the Civil War.

subject: Sandbach
summary: An ancient Cheshire market town built around two Saxon crosses, a Royal Charter from Elizabeth I, a brass band of national renown, and a name pronounced 'sand-batch' by anyone who lives there.

subject: Sandbach Crosses
summary: Two ninth-century Anglo-Saxon stone crosses, thrown down by reformers or civil-war soldiers and pieced back together in 1816, still standing where Mercian carvers raised them.

subject: Sandhorst
summary: A district on the northern edge of Aurich where a windmill from 1908, the Bluecher Barracks of the Luftwaffe's 4th Division, and the factories of wind-turbine maker Enercon share the same flat horizon.

subject: Sandia Peak Tramway
summary: The longest aerial tram in the Americas, built by a balloonist and the father of a Nobel laureate using 5,000 helicopter trips to string cables across the rugged face of the Sandia Mountains.

subject: Sandimen
summary: A Paiwan and Rukai indigenous township in Pingtung County where the name itself has been claimed, translated, renamed, and reclaimed across a century of colonial and postcolonial history.

subject: Sandpoint
summary: Where timber and fishing roots meet world-class tourism on the shores of Idaho's largest lake - a small mountain town that earned recognition as both USA Today's top summer vacation destination and Sunset Magazine's best small Western town.

subject: Sands Street, Hong Kong
summary: A short, steep street in Kennedy Town named for a Victorian-era ship captain who built a dock here, Sands Street connects the harbour waterfront to a set of hillside terraces that have barely changed in a century.

subject: Sandstone Gold Mine
summary: A modern open-pit gold operation that has changed hands eight times in a century, working the same auriferous ground that built and then nearly buried a Western Australian town.

subject: Sandstone Trail
summary: A 55-kilometre footpath threads the length of the Mid Cheshire Ridge, marked by yellow discs with footprint logos and bookended by sandstone monuments at each end.

subject: Sandstone, Western Australia
summary: A gold-rush town of fewer than a hundred souls, guarding a natural basalt arch, an underground brewery cut into a cliff, and the memory of the eight thousand who once lived here.

subject: Sandton
summary: Built from horse trails and farmland in a single generation, Sandton became the richest square mile in Africa, the glass-towered financial heart that pulled Johannesburg's money north.

subject: Sanford, North Carolina
summary: A Lee County railroad town named for a civil engineer, famous for brick and pottery, that solved its two-towns problem by putting the courthouse in a field between them.

subject: Sangha, Mali
summary: A cluster of villages on the lip of the Bandiagara cliff, a heartland of Dogon religion and the place where a French ethnographer spent decades trying to understand a people's vision of the cosmos.

subject: Sangin
summary: A small town in Afghanistan's Helmand River valley that became the deadliest place in the country for coalition forces, consuming a decade of British and American lives before the Taliban reclaimed it in 2017.

subject: Sangiran
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in Central Java where more fossils of early humans have been unearthed than at any comparable site on Earth, reshaping our understanding of Homo erectus across more than a century of discovery.

subject: Sangkulirang-Mangkalihat Karst
summary: Deep in Borneo's limestone towers, 40,000-year-old paintings of wild cattle mark the oldest known figurative art ever found -- older than any cave painting in Europe.

subject: Sangre de Cristo Mountains
summary: Named for the blood-red alpenglow that paints their snowy peaks at dawn and dusk, the Sangre de Cristo Mountains form the Rocky Mountains' southernmost wall, stretching from central Colorado to the outskirts of Santa Fe.

subject: Sanhe Tile Kiln
summary: The last surviving kiln in what was once Taiwan's most prolific tile-making district, a historic factory in Dashu, Kaohsiung, founded in 1918 and now reinvented as a cultural hub producing eco-friendly bricks.

subject: Sanisera
summary: A Roman city on Menorca's wild north coast, born as a military camp among the famed Balearic slingers and layered over by Christians, Muslims, and the sea.

subject: Sanju Pass
summary: Once the most-used caravan crossing between Ladakh and the Tarim Basin, the Sanju Pass carried centuries of Silk Road trade across the Kunlun Mountains at 5,364 meters before geopolitics and newer roads left it behind.

story.title: Sanjusangen-do: One Thousand and One Golden Faces

subject: Sanjūsangen-dō
summary: A 120-meter-long hall in Kyoto's Higashiyama district houses 1,001 gilded statues of the Thousand-armed Kannon, built by a samurai who traded temple construction for a noble title, and for centuries served as the arena for Japan's most grueling archery contest.

subject: Sankt Peter-Ording
summary: A village that could never build a harbour because the sand would not stay still - and so ended up with a twelve-kilometre beach, houses on stilts out in the tidal flat, and the second-highest overnight-stay count of any North Sea resort in Schleswig-Holstein.

subject: Sankyo Warehouses
summary: Twelve dark-roofed rice warehouses, shielded by a canopy of zelkova trees and built with salt-hardened floors, have stored grain on the banks of Sakata's rivers since 1893.

subject: Sanlitun
summary: Named for its distance from a city gate -- 'three li away' -- this neighborhood transformed from a quiet embassy zone into Beijing's most famous nightlife district, home to 70% of the capital's bars.

subject: Sansanding
summary: A walled market town on the Niger that grew rich on long-distance trade, twice held off a besieging empire, and once hosted the doomed explorer Mungo Park.

subject: Sant Antoni de Portmany
summary: A two-thousand-year-old fishing village on Ibiza's western bay that reinvented itself, in a single generation, as a global capital of sunsets and all-night clubbing.

subject: Sant Carles de la Ràpita
summary: A neoclassical port town a Spanish king began and never finished, now a working fishing harbor at the edge of the Ebro Delta.

subject: Sant Llorenç de Balàfia
summary: A fortified hamlet of seven huddled houses and refuge towers in the heart of Ibiza, built shoulder to shoulder against centuries of pirate raids.

subject: Sant Lluís
summary: A grid-planned village on Menorca's southeast tip, built by French soldiers, named for a French saint, and flavored by the British gin that outlasted them all.

subject: Sant Mateu
summary: A well-preserved medieval town at the heart of the Maestrat, whose arcaded stone square and archpriest's church recall its wealthy past, and whose most famous son drew tiny jokes in the margins of MAD magazine.

subject: Sant Miquel de Balansat
summary: The largest village in northern Ibiza's Sant Joan municipality, crowned by a hilltop church that was built as much for defence as for worship.

subject: Santa Ana (La Florida)
summary: An archaeological site on the Andean slope of Ecuador holds the earliest known evidence of cacao use in the Americas - 5,300 years ago, rewriting the map of chocolate's origins.

subject: Santa Barbara
summary: The Spanish colonial coastal city rebuilt in white stucco after the 1925 earthquake, where the mountains meet the sea, where wine country begins, and where California dreams come with ocean views.

subject: Santa Bárbara, Minas Gerais
summary: A baroque gold town founded in 1704, birthplace of Brazil's sixth president, sheltered under the ridges of the Serra do Caraça.

subject: Santa Claus Village
summary: Straddling the Arctic Circle near Rovaniemi, Finland, Santa Claus Village turned a Cold War diplomatic visit and a Finnish folk legend into one of Europe's most unusual tourist destinations.

subject: Santa Cruz (city, Bolivia)
summary: Bolivia's largest and most prosperous city exploded from a sleepy lowland outpost into a tropical boomtown once a paved road finally connected it to the rest of the country.

subject: Santa Cruz de Goiás
summary: One of the oldest towns in Goiás once administered a judicial district nearly the size of Portugal; today its countryside holds twice as many people as its streets.

subject: Santa Cruz de Mompox
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage colonial town on Colombia's Magdalena River that was the first in the country to declare independence from Spain, preserved in amber by the river's silting that killed its commerce but saved its architecture.

subject: Santa Cruz de Nuca
summary: The only verified Spanish settlement in what is now Canada, Santa Cruz de Nuca was founded at Friendly Cove in 1789 as Spain's northernmost colonial outpost on the Pacific -- and nearly started a war between two empires.

subject: Santa Cruz del Islote
summary: A three-acre artificial island off Colombia's Caribbean coast where roughly 500 people live without police, without crime, and without locked doors -- often called the most densely populated island on Earth.

subject: Santa Cruz do Sul
summary: A bilingual Brazilian city where German is still spoken in the Hunsrückisch dialect, Oktoberfest fills the streets each spring, and the world's tobacco capital hides beneath a tunnel of seventy-year-old trees.

subject: Santa Cruz, Chile
summary: The capital of Chile's most famous wine valley, where a single ambitious museum turned a quiet farm town into the gateway of the Colchagua wine route.

subject: Santa Elena, Ecuador
summary: Two bodies buried embracing each other, 8,000 years ago, have made a provincial Ecuadorian capital the country's most important archaeological site - and given a name to the Las Vegas culture, Ecuador's first.

subject: Santa Eulària des Riu
summary: The only Ibizan town named for the island's only river, guarded by a fortress church and remembered for the fishermen who saved a shipwreck's survivors in 1913.

story.title: Santa Fe: America's Oldest Capital Where Adobe Is Religion

subject: Santa Fe
summary: The New Mexico capital where Pueblo Revival architecture is mandatory - where the oldest capital in North America cultivates antiquity, where art galleries outnumber residents' needs, and where the high desert light draws painters and prices out tourists.

story.title: Santa Fe: The Oldest Capital City in America

subject: Santa Fe
summary: The New Mexico city founded in 1610 - a decade before the Pilgrims landed - where adobe architecture and turquoise jewelry define an aesthetic copied worldwide, where three cultures blended into something unique, and where altitude and light attract artists who never leave.

subject: Santa Fe (city, Argentina)
summary: The provincial capital where thirteen quarreling Argentine provinces finally agreed on a constitution that still governs the country today.

subject: Santa Fe Depot (San Diego)
summary: San Diego's Spanish Colonial masterpiece opened in 1915 as the city's bold bid to become the Pacific terminus of a transcontinental railroad — a race it lost to Los Angeles, but won in architecture.

subject: Santa Fe Institute
summary: Born from a group of Los Alamos scientists who wanted to think beyond nuclear weapons, the Santa Fe Institute has spent four decades pioneering the study of complex systems -- from scaling laws in cities to the evolution of human language -- in a small hilltop campus above New Mexico's capital.

subject: Santa Fe Opera
summary: A world-class opera company perched on a New Mexico mesa, where open-air theaters frame sunsets and thunderstorms as part of the performance.

subject: Santa Fe Plaza
summary: The oldest public gathering place in the United States, where four centuries of Spanish, Mexican, and American history converge around a single adobe square.

subject: Santa Fe Trail
summary: The highway that built the Southwest - 900 miles from Missouri to Mexico where traders, soldiers, and settlers forged an international trade route that brought American commerce to Spanish territory before the first shot was fired.

subject: Santa Fe Trail
summary: For nearly sixty years, the Santa Fe Trail connected Missouri to New Mexico across 900 miles of prairie, desert, and mountain pass -- a commercial highway that reshaped the American West and left wagon ruts still visible from the air today.

subject: Santa Fe, New Mexico
summary: The oldest state capital in the United States, Santa Fe blends over four centuries of indigenous, Spanish, Mexican, and American heritage into a city where adobe architecture, world-class art, and high-desert light converge at 7,000 feet.

subject: Santa Inês
summary: A western Maranhão crossroads where every Belém-to-Fortaleza bus stops, where Carnival fills the streets with 20,000 revelers, and where out-of-season mango rains arrive with lightning.

subject: Santa Justa Lift
summary: A 45-meter iron elevator in Neo-Gothic style, built in 1902 to solve Lisbon's vertical geography, and now the last surviving conventional lift among the city's famous urban elevators.

subject: Santa Lucía Hill
summary: A 15-million-year-old volcanic core in the heart of Santiago, this hill is where Pedro de Valdivia founded the city in 1541 and where a 19th-century mayor turned bare rock into an ornate garden using prison labor.

story.title: Santa Maria, Rio Grande do Sul

subject: Santa Maria, Rio Grande do Sul
summary: A university town in the exact geographic heart of Brazil's southernmost state, where students, soldiers, and 230-million-year-old dinosaurs all share the same red ground.

story.title: Santa María la Antigua del Darién

subject: Santa María la Antigua del Darién
summary: The first permanent European settlement on the American mainland, founded by a stowaway hiding in a barrel with his dog, and swallowed by jungle within fourteen years.

subject: Santa María, Paraguay
summary: A Jesuit mission town that gave Paraguay an independence hero, sheltered a famous French botanist as a prisoner, and saved its baroque sculptures from the fire that took its church.

story.title: Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area

subject: Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area
summary: The largest urban national park in the world, stretching from Griffith Park to the Pacific coast, holding 10,000 years of human history and the last significant Mediterranean ecosystem in North America.

subject: Santa Olga
summary: A Maule town of five thousand that, in a single night in 2017, was erased by the worst wildfire in Chile's modern history.

subject: Santa Pola
summary: A Costa Blanca fishing town where a 16th-century anti-pirate fortress, a Roman harbor, flamingo-filled salt pans, and a six-million-year-old fossil reef meet the working Mediterranean.

subject: Santa Ponsa
summary: The beach where a young king landed in 1229 to conquer Mallorca is now a sun-and-golf resort that restages the invasion every September — a town that trades on history and holidays in equal measure.

subject: Santa Rosa Mountains
summary: Rising from the floor of the Coachella Valley to a summit above 8,700 feet in less than twenty miles, the Santa Rosa Mountains were among the last ranges in the Southwest to receive a permanent Spanish name — and the first in the region to receive federal protection for their endangered bighorn sheep.

subject: Santa Rosa Wilderness
summary: Carved from the Coachella Valley's southwestern wall by two major fault systems, the 72,259-acre Santa Rosa Wilderness shelters one of the last viable populations of Peninsular Range bighorn sheep along trails that have served as pathways through these mountains for thousands of years.

subject: Santa Rosa de Tastil
summary: A village of eleven people guards the stone ruins of what was once the largest pre-Columbian city in present-day Argentina, abandoned before the Spanish ever arrived.

subject: Santa Rosa, Paraguay
summary: A small Misiones town whose Jesuit past survives in a chapel of indigenous frescoes and a 20-meter bell tower of red stone.

subject: Santa Tecla Festival
summary: Every September, Tarragona hands its streets to giants, devils, and human towers in a festival whose backbone was fixed in 1370 and whose relic arrived by sea from Antioch in 1321.

subject: Santa Vitória do Palmar Meteorite
summary: A man searching for ancient arrowheads on the Brazilian plains instead picked up a rock that had been falling toward Earth for four and a half billion years.

subject: Santa Ysabel Asistencia
summary: Founded in 1818 as a satellite of Mission San Diego, Santa Ysabel Asistencia housed 450 native neophytes, camped General Kearny before his ill-fated battle, and lost its bells to thieves who stole them in the summer of 1926.

subject: Santana Group
summary: A rift lake in northeastern Brazil fossilized with such fidelity that feathers, insect wings, and dinosaur skin survive from 113 million years ago in the rocks below the Chapada do Araripe.

subject: Santana do Livramento
summary: A Brazilian frontier city whose streets flow directly into Uruguay, Santana do Livramento has become the official symbol of Brazil's integration with its neighbors.

subject: Santarém
summary: Midway between Manaus and Belém on a 36-hour boat ride, Santarém sits where the Tapajós meets the Amazon and the waters refuse to mix.

subject: Santarém, Pará
summary: Founded by Jesuits in 1661 where two great rivers meet, Santarém is 360 years of Amazon history layered along a waterfront of white beaches and soybean terminals.

subject: Santiago
summary: Where the Andes rise like a wall behind Chile's capital, where Pinochet's coup still shadows democracy, where South America's most stable economy concentrates in a valley between mountains and sea.

subject: Santiago de Bolivar
summary: A colonial Ecuadorian town on the Route of the Saints, where carnival parades, aguardiente called Blue Bird, and one of the last high-altitude subtropical forests shape everyday life.

subject: Santiago del Estero
summary: Argentina's first and oldest Spanish city, the 'Mother of Cities' on the Dulce River, and the birthplace of its national folk music.

subject: Santiago, Paraguay
summary: A small hilltop town in the Misiones Department that keeps Paraguay's only complete Jesuit altarpiece and a wooden St. James riding through the centuries - mission art that survived where the missions themselves did not.

subject: Santo Antônio de Matupi
summary: Known simply as Km 180, this Trans-Amazonian Highway boomtown grew from nothing into the largest timber producer in Amazonas state, where certified logging, cattle ranching, and frontier lawlessness coexist in equal measure.

subject: Santo Antônio do Rio Abaixo
summary: A tiny Minas Gerais town, 1,760 people, founded along a gold-bearing river, where waterfalls still do most of the work of drawing visitors.

subject: Santo Ângelo
summary: The last of the seven Guaraní-Jesuit missions to be founded, Santo Ângelo grew into a city that still carries the missions' memory in its cathedral, its university, and the airport named for the Guaraní who died defending this land.

subject: Santos Dumont, Minas Gerais
summary: A Minas Gerais town renamed in 1934 after the aviation pioneer born in its hills - the man Brazil remembers as the father of powered flight.

story.title: Santuario de la Virgen de la Nube

subject: Santuario de la Virgen de la Nube
summary: A Franciscan sanctuary carved from stone quarried from the hill above it, built over 42 years through community labor, and the focus of an Ecuadorian Marian devotion dating to a 1696 vision in Quito.

subject: Sanxia Old Street
summary: Minquan Street in Sanxia, New Taipei, preserves a remarkable 200-meter stretch of Baroque-influenced red-brick arcaded shophouses from the Japanese colonial era, recently restored to their early twentieth-century grandeur.

subject: Sanxiantai
summary: A coastal islet off Chenggong Township in Taitung County, reached by an eight-arched footbridge shaped like a sea dragon, where three massive rocks give the "Platform of the Three Immortals" its name.

subject: Sanyi, Miaoli
summary: Sanyi Township in Miaoli earned the title 'Woodcarving Kingdom of Taiwan' because at its peak, over 80% of local families made their living with a chisel — and the workshops lining its main street still fill the mountain air with the smell of camphor shavings.

subject: Sanzhi UFO Houses
summary: A cluster of futuristic pod-shaped vacation homes on Taiwan's northern coast was abandoned before anyone ever moved in, haunted by rumor and superstition until demolition crews erased them from the landscape in 2010.

subject: Sao Miguel
summary: The Azores' green heart pulses with volcanic fury and subtropical beauty, where twin crater lakes shimmer in impossible colors and locals cook traditional meals in the steaming earth itself.

subject: Sao Paulo
summary: Where South America's largest city sprawls endlessly, where Japanese and Italian communities thrive, where Brazil's economy pulses through concrete canyons.

subject: Sappho, Washington
summary: A Kansas homesteader hauled his family twenty miles into Olympic Peninsula rainforest and named the clearing after an ancient Greek poet; the logging camp that followed is now a junction in the wettest corner of the Lower 48.

subject: Saraguro people
summary: A Kichwa nation in the southern Ecuadorian Andes, the Saraguro kept their land, their language, and their distinctive black-and-white dress - and built a modern presence that carries the old symbols into new forms.

subject: Sarah Knox-Goodrich
summary: A Virginia-born suffragist who founded San Jose's first Women's Suffrage Association in 1869, hosted Susan B. Anthony in her home, and left her mark on downtown in Romanesque sandstone.

subject: Sarat Chandra Kuthi
summary: On the banks of the Rupnarayan River, the house where Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Devdas and other masterpieces of Bengali literature still stands, preserved as a museum in the village he renamed Samtaber.

subject: Sarawak Chamber
summary: The world's largest cave chamber by area lies beneath the rainforest of Borneo, so vast that one of its discoverers felt agoraphobia -- underground.

subject: Sarayburnu
summary: The promontory at the tip of Istanbul's historic peninsula where the Golden Horn, the Bosphorus, and the Sea of Marmara converge — one of the most consequential pieces of geography in the history of civilization.

subject: Sari
summary: Capital of the ancient Hyrcania civilization and twice the capital of Iran, Sari sits between the Alborz Mountains and the Caspian Sea with caves dating to the 7th millennium BC and travertine terraces that rival Pamukkale.

subject: Sarina, Queensland
summary: A sugar town at the foot of the Connors Range south of Mackay, watched over by a giant fibreglass cane toad and built around a mill that has crushed cane since 1896.

subject: Sark
summary: A two-square-mile Channel Island governed by a hereditary Seigneur until 2008, with no cars, no streetlights, dark enough skies to see the Milky Way, and a causeway built by German POWs.

subject: Sassenpoort
summary: Zwolle's last surviving medieval city gate, built in 1409 from volcanic stone, with thirteen coats of arms in its windows and a missing fourteenth.

subject: Sastamala
summary: Finland's self-declared Book Capital: a river municipality stitched together from a string of older ones, where 15,000 people arrive each summer for a festival about secondhand books.

subject: Saterland Frisian language
summary: Saterland Frisian - Seeltersk - is the last surviving East Frisian language, kept alive by roughly 2,000 speakers in three small villages on what used to be islands of sand in a vast Lower Saxon bog.

subject: Satpura Range
summary: The ancient mountain range that divides the Indian subcontinent in two, gives the Narmada and Tapti rivers their courses, and provided Rudyard Kipling with the setting for The Jungle Book.

story.title: Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute

subject: Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute
summary: Named after the filmmaker whose Apu Trilogy brought Indian cinema to the world, this Kolkata institute trains the next generation of directors, cinematographers, and editors -- and has produced alumni behind some of India's most acclaimed films.

subject: Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site
summary: The first integrated ironworks in North America, where a 500-pound trip hammer and seven massive waterwheels forged the raw materials of a new industrial civilization on the banks of the Saugus River.

subject: Saundersfoot
summary: A Pembrokeshire seaside village whose three Victorian coal-railway tunnels - the only tunnels on the entire 870-mile Wales Coast Path - now carry walkers along the seafront where anthracite once moved by horse-drawn tram.

story.title: Sausapor: Where Turtles Nest and Empires Landed

subject: Sausapor
summary: A small town on the Bird's Head Peninsula where sea turtles have nested for millennia, where Dutch colonialism met local resistance through religion, and where an American amphibious assault in 1944 met almost no opposition at all.

subject: Sauteurs
summary: A quiet Grenadian fishing village whose French name -- 'Leapers' -- remembers the Kalinago people who chose death over subjugation on its clifftop in 1651.

subject: Sauvo
summary: A peninsula of manors, summer cottages and one very old church, where farmers once sailed their own cargo to Stockholm and a vanished village still lends its name to a fifth of Finland's electricity grid.

story.title: Savannah: The Haunted City Sherman Spared

subject: Savannah
summary: The Georgia port city preserved by accident and cultivated as art form - where Sherman ended his March to the Sea, where the moss hangs from oaks in perfect squares, and where the ghost tours never stop.

story.title: Savannah: The Most Haunted City in America

subject: Savannah
summary: The Georgia city planned around 22 elegant squares - where Spanish moss drapes live oaks, where the walking dead tours never end, and where General Sherman's army paused to appreciate what they might have burned, sparing America's most beautiful urban landscape.

story.title: Savannah: The City Built on Squares and Secrets

subject: Savannah
summary: The Georgia port where Oglethorpe's original grid of shaded squares survives - where Spanish moss drapes live oaks, where Forrest Gump's bench sat, and where the city Sherman spared became the South's most haunted, most beautiful, most unrepentant destination.

story.title: Savannah: The Belle of the South

subject: Savannah
summary: The city Sherman spared on his March to the Sea, where Spanish moss drapes over 22 perfect squares, where 'Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil' made murder literary, and where ghosts are a tourist attraction.

subject: Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art
summary: A 900-square-metre art space in Tamale, Ghana, founded by internationally acclaimed artist Ibrahim Mahama, transforming northern Ghana into an unlikely epicenter of contemporary African art.

story.title: Savannah Cotton Exchange: The Building That Floats on Iron

subject: Savannah Cotton Exchange
summary: A Romanesque Revival building raised thirty-five feet on iron pillars above a city ramp, where brokers once set the world price of cotton and Freemasons now keep the oldest lodge in the Western Hemisphere.

story.title: Savannah's Underground: Pirates, Plague, and Prohibition Tunnels

subject: Savannah's Underground
summary: The Georgia port city built atop a maze of tunnels - allegedly used by pirates to smuggle, by doctors to move plague victims, and by bootleggers to deliver whiskey during Prohibition, though historians question how much is truth and how much is tourist legend.

subject: Savannakhet
summary: Laos's second-largest city, where French colonial architecture survives alongside dinosaur fossils and a Mekong riverfront that connects east to Vietnam and west to Thailand.

subject: Savassi
summary: Belo Horizonte's trendiest neighborhood, named for the Italian family bakery that once stood at its central square.

subject: Save the Redwoods League
summary: Since 1918, the Save the Redwoods League has protected over 200,000 acres of ancient coast redwood and giant sequoia forests, helping create 66 parks and reserves across California.

subject: Sawahlunto
summary: A Dutch colonial coal town in the West Sumatran highlands that nearly became a ghost town when the mines closed, Sawahlunto reinvented itself as a UNESCO-recognized heritage destination built atop its own painful history.

subject: Sawtelle Veterans Home
summary: In 1887, a senator and a real estate developer donated three hundred acres of West Los Angeles land to create a home for the disabled veterans of the Civil War. What grew from that gift became the largest VA healthcare campus in the United States.

subject: Sawtooth Wilderness
summary: Idaho's serrated granite skyline, where 50 peaks pierce the clouds above hundreds of glacial lakes frozen in a landscape of Pleistocene memory.

subject: Sawyer Camp Trail
summary: A six-mile paved trail through the San Andreas Fault rift valley where 300,000 annual visitors jog, walk, and cycle alongside the reservoir that provides San Francisco's drinking water.

subject: Saxmundham
summary: A small Suffolk market town in the valley of the River Fromus, holding a market charter since 1272 and an East Anglian patrimony that runs from Domesday Book through a 1990s NBA All-Star's childhood years.

subject: Saxon Switzerland
summary: A Cretaceous seabed cut into towers and table mountains by the Elbe, named after a country six hundred kilometres away by two homesick painters, and laced with four hundred kilometres of marked trail.

subject: Saxon Switzerland climbing region
summary: Germany's oldest non-Alpine climbing region, where chalk, nuts and cams are banned, protection means knots tied into slings, and a rulebook printed in 1913 still governs 17,000 routes.

subject: Sbeitla
summary: A small Tunisian town guards the best-preserved Roman forum temples in the country, standing where the Muslim conquest of North Africa began at the ancient city of Sufetula.

subject: Scafell
summary: England's second-highest mountain, often more prominent than its taller neighbour, with a spelling history as tangled as its crags.

subject: Scarborough Shoal
summary: A barely-visible coral atoll in the South China Sea that became the most contested piece of rock in Southeast Asia, fought over by nations with water cannons, fishing boats, and international tribunals.

subject: Scarborough Shoal standoff
summary: The 2012 naval confrontation between China and the Philippines over a tiny coral reef that redrew the power map of the South China Sea and led to landmark international arbitration.

subject: Scary, West Virginia
summary: An unincorporated community along the Kanawha River with one of America's better place names - and a small Civil War battlefield to match.

subject: Schaerbeek
summary: Brussels's city of donkeys is a working-class commune where Belgian Turkish bakeries line the Chaussee de Haecht, sour cherry trees still mark the avenues, and Art Nouveau houses survive on side streets the guidebooks rarely mention.

subject: Scharnebeck Twin Ship Lift
summary: Two counterweighted troughs that carry barges 38 metres straight up in three minutes - once the largest ship lift in the world, now too short for the boats it was built to serve.

subject: Scheunenviertel
summary: Berlin's barn quarter became the address the state assigned to Jews in 1737, the landing place for Eastern European Jewish families after 1918, and the scene of a pogrom on 5 November 1923.

subject: Schevenhutte Quarry
summary: An abandoned slate quarry on the edge of the Eifel exposing 490-million-year-old rock - the oldest in North Rhine-Westphalia - and quietly slipping away.

subject: Schiedam
summary: Five windmills tower over a small Dutch town because the gin warehouses underneath them grew so tall the wind couldn't reach the sails.

subject: Schiermonnikoog
summary: The smallest inhabited Wadden island has fewer than a thousand residents, no cars for tourists, and a coastline that has crept far enough east that the provincial border has been redrawn twice this century.

subject: Schinkel (Osnabrück district)
summary: An Osnabrück working-class district named for a hill, mistaken for a Prussian architect, and bombed for its copper.

subject: Schnoor
summary: Bremen's last medieval quarter survived into the present for an unglamorous reason: for four centuries its residents were too poor to modernise it.

subject: Schoonhoven
summary: Holland's Silver City: a fortified town on the Lek where silversmiths have worked since the 17th century and a single medieval gate still holds back the river.

subject: Schortens
summary: A Frisian town that grew up around a typewriter factory, a victory church, and a naval base that never seems to fade.

subject: Schramsberg Vineyards
summary: A Napa Valley winery founded in 1862 by a German immigrant barber, immortalized by Robert Louis Stevenson, abandoned for half a century, then revived to become America's premier sparkling wine producer.

subject: Schull
summary: A small West Cork harbour town beneath the radar masts of Mount Gabriel, with a planetarium, a pirate history, and a 1996 murder that has never been solved.

subject: Schwartz's
summary: A Romanian immigrant's tiny smoked-meat counter on The Main has outlasted nearly a century of rivals, language wars, and ownership dramas to become Montreal's most stubbornly authentic culinary landmark.

subject: Schöningen spears
summary: Ten wooden throwing spears, the oldest complete hunting weapons ever found, pulled out of a lignite mine in Lower Saxony and still arguing with archaeologists about their own age.

subject: Schüttorf
summary: The oldest town in the County of Bentheim - electrified the same year as Berlin's Unter den Linden, and once hosted David Bowie, Frank Zappa, and the Rolling Stones in its meadows.

subject: Scia'new First Nation
summary: The name means salmon place. In 1850 the people who held it signed away nearly everything for a stack of blankets, and they are still at the negotiating table.

subject: Science World
summary: It began in 1977 with hands-on exhibits hauled around the Lower Mainland in a truck, and ended up inside the geodesic dome Expo 86 left behind at the head of False Creek.

subject: Scotland County, North Carolina
summary: A county carved from another county in 1899 for the sake of party politics, where high school marching bands still wear kilts and the school song is older than the United States.

subject: Scott Circle
summary: Despite the name, Scott Circle is not a circle - it is a bow-tie of pavement holding a bronze general, hiding a buried creek, and split in half by a 1941 underpass that two rival neighborhoods spent years fighting over.

subject: Scott County, Virginia
summary: A far-southwestern Virginia county on the Tennessee line, where Daniel Boone built forts, the Wilderness Road carried settlers west, and the Carter Family invented country music.

subject: Scott's Head
summary: A tiny village on a volcanic isthmus at Dominica's southwestern tip, where the Caribbean Sea meets the Atlantic and divers explore a submerged crater 160 meters deep.

subject: Scottish Association for Marine Science
summary: In 2024 a Scottish marine institute founded in 1884 after the Challenger expedition published the first evidence that the deep ocean floor produces oxygen in total darkness - a finding that may rewrite biology.

subject: Scottish National Gallery
summary: Scotland's national collection of Western European art, holding works from Raphael and Titian to a skating minister and Monet's haystacks.

subject: Scottish National Portrait Gallery
summary: The world's first purpose-built portrait gallery, a red sandstone Gothic Revival landmark on Edinburgh's Queen Street holding portraits of Scots from 1507 to today.

subject: Scourie
summary: A tiny village on Scotland's wild northwest coast where Cordyline palms thrive against all expectation and a Mackay general once raised forces for William III.

subject: Scripps Institution of Oceanography
summary: Founded in 1903 on a La Jolla bluff above the Pacific, Scripps Institution of Oceanography grew from a one-man marine biology station into one of the world's preeminent centers for understanding the ocean, the atmosphere, and the planet itself.

subject: Scripps Research
summary: Founded in 1924 by Ellen Browning Scripps in the weeks after insulin was announced to the world, Scripps Research has grown into the most influential research institution in the world by some measures — with three Nobel laureates, eleven FDA-approved drugs, and 1,100 patents.

subject: Scythian Neapolis
summary: On a rocky plateau at the edge of Simferopol lie the ruins of a Scythian royal capital, where nomadic horsemen built a walled city of Greek columns and buried their kings beneath gold.

subject: Sea Isle City
summary: A five-mile barrier island town built around a single promenade, a single main avenue, and the kind of summer rhythm that lets you park your car for a month.

subject: Sea Isle City, New Jersey
summary: A barrier-island city founded by a Vineland developer with a Mediterranean dream, now a Polar Bear Plunge town with an Italian fishing enclave called Fish Alley.

subject: Sea Lion (steam locomotive)
summary: A narrow-gauge Manx engine built in 1896 and once stripped for scrap, rescued in pieces, restored by nuclear apprentices, and now running again in her original gold-leaf livery.

subject: Sea World (Australia)
summary: The Gold Coast marine park that grew out of a water-ski show, ran Australia's first monorail, and quietly built one of the country's busiest marine-rescue operations.

subject: Sea of Abaco
summary: A 62-mile saltwater lagoon in the Bahamas where crystal-clear shallows hide the third-largest barrier reef on Earth, and a phenomenon called 'Abaco Rage' turns calm channels into chaos without warning.

subject: Sea of Marmara
summary: Turkey's inland sea — named for a single marble island — links the Black Sea to the Aegean, separates Europe from Asia, and sits atop a fault line that has repeatedly remade its shores.

subject: Sea to Sky Gondola
summary: The Squamish gondola that rises 2,900 feet from sea level to mountain summit in 10 minutes - sabotaged twice by cable cuts that sent 30 cabins crashing down, rebuilt both times as a symbol of resilience on the road to Whistler.

subject: SeaGen
summary: The world's first commercial tidal stream generator spent eleven years feeding electricity into Northern Ireland's grid from a single point in a Viking-named channel - and proved a renewable industry could exist.

subject: Seaburn Dene
summary: A Sunderland suburb where every street name borrows from the Lake District and the Peak District, mapping Cumbria and Derbyshire onto a corner of the Durham coast.

subject: Seacombe
summary: The Wallasey district where the Mersey Ferry lands, a giant Art-Deco tunnel ventilator faces the river like stereo speakers, and Olaf Stapledon - the man who imagined the next two billion years of human evolution - was born on Falkland Road.

subject: Seaham
summary: A County Durham coastal town where Lord Byron married, where Ada Lovelace was conceived, and where beach-walkers still find sea glass dumped by a Victorian bottle works.

subject: Seahouses
summary: The Northumberland harbour where kippers were reportedly born, lifeboats still honour Grace Darling, and boats leave each morning for the seal-strewn Farne Islands.

subject: Seahouses Lifeboat Station
summary: The Northumberland lifeboat station that didn't quite reach the Forfarshire in 1838 - but whose modern inshore boat is named for the young woman who did.

subject: Seal Rocks
