summary: A cluster of rocky islets at the edge of Lands End where Steller's sea lions and California sea lions have hauled out for centuries, Seal Rocks marks the wild Pacific boundary of San Francisco.

subject: Sealand of the Pacific
summary: For twenty-three years an aquarium at Oak Bay Marina kept killer whales in netting hung in the open sea, a few hundred metres from the waters they came from. It closed after the death of a young trainer, and almost nothing of it remains.

subject: Sean Kelly (cyclist)
summary: The Carrick-on-Suir farm boy who became the world's number-one ranked cyclist for five straight years and one of the greatest Classics riders in history.

subject: Searsville, California
summary: A logging town founded in 1854 that thrived for four decades before being drowned by the dam that bears its name -- now submerged beneath Searsville Reservoir in the Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve.

subject: Seascale
summary: A small Cumbrian seaside village whose history is interwoven with Norse settlers, Victorian holiday ambitions, and the long shadow of Britain's nuclear age.

subject: Seascale Lifeboat Station
summary: A short-lived RNLI station whose only successful rescue required a hastily-arranged special train and twenty years of waiting.

subject: Seaside Aquarium
summary: A 1920s saltwater swimming pool that reinvented itself as one of the oldest aquariums on the West Coast, where the same ocean pipe that once filled a natatorium now sustains 100 species of marine life - and where visitors still line up to feed the harbor seals.

subject: Seaside, Florida
summary: A tiny planned community on the Florida Panhandle that launched the New Urbanism movement, became the set of a Hollywood blockbuster, and proved that how you arrange buildings can change how people live.

subject: Seaside, Oregon
summary: A small Oregon beach town where Lewis and Clark boiled seawater for salt, a French war veteran gifted a mile-and-a-half promenade, and residents stockpile emergency barrels against the tsunami they know is coming.

subject: Seaton Carew Wreck
summary: An eighteenth- or nineteenth-century collier brig of the same type Captain Cook took to the Pacific, slowly emerging from a Durham beach.

story.title: Seattle: The Emerald City That Rebuilt Itself on Top of Itself

subject: Seattle
summary: The Pacific Northwest port city where Amazon and Microsoft tower over former timber town - where the city literally raised its streets one story after the Great Fire, where grunge was born, and where it rains less than you think.

subject: Seattle Fault
summary: An invisible seismic threat running directly beneath Seattle's most populated corridors, the Seattle Fault last produced a magnitude 7 earthquake around 923-924 CE -- an event so devastating it entered Native American oral traditions as the work of a spirit called a'yahos.

subject: Sebbe Als
summary: Denmark's oldest sailing Viking-ship replica, built by scouts and volunteers in an Augustenborg lumber yard in 1969 — and still sailing every summer.

subject: Sechelt
summary: A Sunshine Coast town pinched between Trail Bay and Sechelt Inlet, where the shishalh Nation's cultural center stands beside drag races at the local airport and old-growth forest hides just minutes from downtown.

subject: Sechelt Inlet
summary: A fjord that nearly severs the Sechelt Peninsula into an island, connected to the open sea through rapids so violent they rage like waterfalls even in calm weather.

subject: Second Garrotte
summary: A Gold Rush ghost town near Groveland named for a hanging tree that may or may not have killed anyone -- where legend, frontier justice, and California history tangle in the Sierra foothills.

subject: Second Ostend Raid
summary: Three weeks after Zeebrugge, the same battered cruiser HMS Vindictive limped back to the Belgian coast to be sunk on purpose.

subject: Second Thomas Shoal
summary: A rusting World War II-era ship deliberately grounded on a submerged reef has become the Philippines' most defiant symbol of sovereignty in the South China Sea.

subject: Secunda CTL
summary: On the Mpumalanga Highveld, a sprawling plant turns coal into petrol and, in the process, emits more carbon dioxide than the whole of Portugal.

subject: Sedniv
summary: An ancient fortress town on the River Snov, home of the Cossack Lyzohub family and beloved of the poet Taras Shevchenko, that survived the Mongols but was gutted by famine.

story.title: Sedona: Where Red Rocks Meet New Age Believers

subject: Sedona
summary: The Arizona town where dramatic red rock formations attract both hikers and spiritual seekers - where 'vortexes' allegedly channel earth energy, where psychics outnumber gas stations, and where geology inspires metaphysics in ways that science cannot explain or explain away.

story.title: Sedona Vortexes: Where Red Rocks Channel the Cosmos

subject: Sedona Vortexes
summary: The Arizona town where New Age seekers claim to feel Earth's spiritual energy swirling from the red rock formations - a phenomenon dismissed by geologists but felt by millions, turning a desert art colony into America's metaphysical capital.

subject: Sedona, Arizona
summary: A red rock desert city where Hollywood once filmed westerns disguised as Texas, spiritual seekers hunt invisible vortices, and 270-million-year-old sandstone glows pink at sunset.

subject: Seeley, California
summary: A small Imperial Valley community where Juan Bautista de Anza stopped at an ancient desert well in 1774, now honored as California Historical Landmark No. 1008.

subject: Segeberger Kalkberg
summary: A gypsum hill in the middle of Bad Segeberg that people quarried down by two-thirds, leaving a cave where 25,000 bats hibernate and a pit where Apache warriors ride every summer.

subject: Sehome, Bellingham, Washington
summary: The first town on Bellingham Bay began when two loggers tipped over a tree and found coal in its roots; the mine is long gone, but the street grid, the hill and the name remain.

story.title: Seibal: The City That Outlived Its Own Destruction

subject: Seibal
summary: Conquered in AD 735 and its written history literally chopped off its monuments, Seibal rose again a century later under foreign-backed rulers who blended Maya and Mexican art styles - becoming the last major city to erect dated monuments before the Classic Maya collapse swallowed the Peten.

story.title: Sekigahara: Japan's Gettysburg in a Valley of Rice Fields

subject: Sekigahara
summary: A quiet rural town of 7,000 people in Gifu Prefecture where 195,000 samurai clashed on a single October morning in 1600 -- the battle that created the Tokugawa Shogunate and reshaped Japan for 260 years, now walked by visitors who follow marked paths past memorial posts and through forests where bears still roam.

subject: Sekiu, Washington
summary: A fishing village of twenty-four year-round residents on the Strait of Juan de Fuca, where the summer swells the population and the salmon decide the calendar.

subject: Selima Oasis
summary: The last salt caravan to Selima Oasis left in 1980, closing a trade that had moved through this Saharan crossroads for more than a millennium.

subject: Sellafield
summary: Europe's largest nuclear site, the diverse heart of Britain's atomic age, and the workplace of around ten thousand people now devoted to dismantling the past.

subject: Selly Oak
summary: A Birmingham suburb that holds the oldest pottery yet found in the city, a Roman fort site, the workhouse-turned-hospital that became a military trauma centre, and the stump of the oak tree that gave the place its name.

subject: Selma to Montgomery march campsites
summary: The places where civil rights marchers slept along the 54-mile route from Selma to Montgomery in March 1965 tell their own story of courage, community, and the Black families who risked everything to shelter a movement.

subject: Selous Game Reserve
summary: Africa's largest game reserve -- twice the size of Switzerland -- named for a hunter killed within its borders during World War I, now split between a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage site battling a poaching crisis.

subject: Selymbria
summary: The ancient Greek city of Selymbria — now Silivri on the Marmara coast — accumulated more than two thousand years of history, emperors, bishops, and curious literary footnotes without ever quite becoming famous, which may be why it has survived so completely into the present.

subject: Semiahmoo First Nation
summary: A small Coast Salish nation on 312 acres at the Canada-US border, where an international line, a municipal landfill, and sixteen years without drinkable tap water all landed on the same shore.

subject: Semiahmoo Spit
summary: A mile-and-a-quarter finger of drifted sand where a cannery town, an ancient village, and an international border all crowd onto the same narrow beach.

subject: Semna (Nubia)
summary: At the narrowest point of the Nile valley, four Egyptian fortresses held a frontier for centuries - before Lake Nasser swallowed all of them in 1971.

subject: Semnan, Iran
summary: An ancient Silk Road city where windcatchers still rise above pomegranate gardens and a thousand-year-old mosque stands on the foundations of a Zoroastrian fire temple.

subject: Sen Monorom
summary: Perched 733 meters above sea level at the edge of Cambodia's least-visited province, Sen Monorom is a highland town where rolling grasslands meet deep jungle and the indigenous Bunong people have called these hills home for generations.

subject: Senado Square
summary: Macau's central public square, paved in hand-laid Portuguese calçada stone and ringed by colonial-era buildings, has served as parade ground, film set, and the site of a murdered soldier for over four centuries — and today appears on Macau's currency.

subject: Sendai
summary: Japan's 'City of Trees' was named after a mythical Chinese palace in the mountains by the one-eyed warlord who founded it in 1600 -- today it is the million-strong capital of the Tohoku region, famous for grilled beef tongue, spectacular festivals, and wide zelkova-lined boulevards.

subject: Sendai Daikannon
summary: A 100-meter-tall white statue of the bodhisattva Kannon that briefly held the title of tallest statue on Earth, rising above a quiet Sendai neighborhood with 108 Buddhas spiraling through her hollow interior.

subject: Sendai Mediatheque
summary: A radical glass cube on a Sendai boulevard dissolves the boundaries between library, gallery, and city street -- its twisting steel tubes and transparent floors rewriting the rules of what a public building can be.

subject: Seneca Caverns
summary: The Ohio cave system discovered by two boys chasing a rabbit in 1872 - now offering tours 110 feet underground where visitors can see the 'Ole Mist'ry River' flowing through passages still being mapped.

subject: Seneca Caverns
summary: A West Virginia show cave first entered in 1781 by a Methodist bishop, owned by the same German farming family for 150 years, and open to visitors since 1930.

subject: Seneca Rocks
summary: A blade of 440-million-year-old quartzite rising nearly 900 feet above the Potomac headwaters in West Virginia, Seneca Rocks is the premier traditional rock climbing destination on the East Coast and a landmark whose history stretches from ancient ocean floor to World War II assault training.

story.title: Seneca Village: The Neighborhood Erased for Central Park

subject: Seneca Village
summary: In 1825, a young Black shoe shiner named Andrew Williams paid $125 for three lots in upper Manhattan and helped found a thriving community of free African American landowners -- a community that was erased by eminent domain thirty-two years later to build Central Park.

subject: Senen
summary: Founded in 1733 as a market for Batavia's colonial upper town, Senen evolved into Jakarta's most volatile district -- a place where gamblers, poets, sex workers, and dangdut musicians shared the same streets, and where a 1974 student demonstration sparked anti-Japanese and anti-Chinese riots.

subject: Sennen Cove
summary: The last village before Land's End, where granite cottages back onto a beach that hosted Britain's first canine lifeguard and the Atlantic terminus of a transatlantic telegraph cable.

subject: Sennen Cove Lifeboat Station
summary: For 173 years, volunteers have launched into the Atlantic from Sennen Cove to bring strangers home from the rocks beneath Land's End.

subject: Sen̓áḵw
summary: A Squamish village at the head of False Creek, sold out from under its residents in 1913 and burned - and now, on the 11.7 acres the courts gave back, the site of one of the largest Indigenous-led developments in Canada.

subject: Seokguram
summary: A granite grotto carved into a Korean mountainside 1,200 years ago, Seokguram houses a seated Buddha so precisely engineered that sunrise over the East Sea aligns with the entrance -- and so fragile that well-meaning restorations nearly destroyed it.

subject: Seoraksan
summary: South Korea's third-highest mountain holds granite towers, ancient Buddhist temples, and a rocking boulder that thousands have tried and failed to topple.

subject: Seoul Halloween crowd crush
summary: On October 29, 2022, a crowd surge in a narrow alley in Seoul's Itaewon neighborhood killed 159 people during Halloween festivities, most of them young adults, in a disaster that investigators attributed to inadequate crowd management despite repeated warnings.

subject: Separate Reality
summary: A 20-foot crack splitting a horizontal ceiling in Yosemite became the proving ground where rock climbing's greatest soloists tested their nerve, their skill, and their relationship with gravity.

subject: Sepik
summary: The Sepik is Papua New Guinea's Amazon - a slow brown river winding through swamp and jungle, home to crocodiles, yam-cult spirit houses, and the highest concentration of languages on Earth.

story.title: Seppuku: The Blade, the Bow, and the Code

subject: Seppuku
summary: The ritualized practice of self-disembowelment that defined samurai honor for nearly a thousand years -- from desperate battlefield acts in the Heian period to the elaborately choreographed ceremonies of the Edo era and Yukio Mishima's shocking public death in 1970.

story.title: Sequoia: Standing Among the Largest Living Things on Earth

subject: Sequoia
summary: The California park where giant sequoias reach sizes beyond comprehension - where General Sherman is the largest tree on Earth by volume, where fires the sequoias evolved to need now threaten their groves, and where standing at the base of a 275-foot tree recalibrates the human sense of scale.

subject: Sergipe
summary: Brazil's smallest state folds mangrove, sugar country and hard thorn-scrub sertão into a strip of coast the Tupi named for its crabs.

subject: Seria
summary: A Brunei oil town once known as Wild Pigeon's Field, razed in World War II, rebuilt on petroleum wealth, and home to everything from a shuttered 1950s cinema to the British Army's jungle warfare school.

subject: Seria Oil Field
summary: Northwest Borneo's largest oil field has produced over a billion barrels since 1929, surviving Japanese sabotage, rebel seizure, and a mile-long aerial cable railway called the Sky Hook -- and it still pumps 20,000 barrels a day.

subject: Serifos
summary: Serifos is a rugged, iron-rich Cycladic island where myth placed Perseus and Danaë, where ore carts once ran on iron tracks across bare hillsides, and where a whitewashed Chora above a deep harbor rewards those who make the effort to arrive.

subject: Serpent Mound
summary: The 1,348-foot earthwork snake in rural Ohio - the largest effigy mound in the world, built by Indigenous peoples around 300 BCE, its open jaws aligned to the summer solstice sunset.

story.title: Serpent Mound: The 1,400-Foot Snake Nobody Can Explain

subject: Serpent Mound
summary: The Ohio earthwork shaped like a snake swallowing an egg - built by a civilization we don't understand, for purposes we can only guess, aligned with celestial events that still draw crowds on solstice.

subject: Serpent Mound
summary: The largest serpent effigy in the world stretches 1,348 feet across an ancient meteorite crater in rural Ohio, its origins still debated after more than a century of archaeological investigation.

subject: Serpentine Lakes
summary: A winding chain of salt lakes traces an ancient river across the Great Victoria Desert, marking the border between two states in country returned to its traditional owners.

subject: Serra Calderona
summary: A coastal mountain range named after a king's runaway favourite, where a silent charterhouse, olive groves, and old bandit gorges lie an hour from Valencia.

subject: Serra Gaúcha
summary: In the highlands of southern Brazil, Germans took the valleys and Italians took the heights - and two transplanted European worlds grew side by side into a region of wine, hydrangeas, and hot springs.

story.title: Serra Geral do Tocantins Ecological Station

subject: Serra Geral do Tocantins Ecological Station
summary: One of Brazil's largest strict nature reserves, spanning 707,000 hectares of cerrado where golden grass grows and fires rage through the dry season.

subject: Serra Pelada
summary: Forty thousand men climbed ladders out of a single hand-dug pit carrying sixty-kilo sacks of ore on their backs. Sebastiao Salgado called them slaves without chains. The pit is a polluted lake now.

subject: Serra Talhada
summary: A working city of ninety thousand in the Pernambuco sertão that happens to be the birthplace of Lampião — and has spent nearly a century deciding what to do about it.

subject: Serra da Barriga
summary: The long green ridge above União dos Palmares held Macaco, the principal settlement of Palmares - and it is now Brazil's most visited site of Black memory.

subject: Serra da Ibiapaba
summary: A 200-kilometre sandstone escarpment on the Ceará-Piauí line that traps enough rain to grow a humid forest island above the thorn scrub.

subject: Serra da Mantiqueira
summary: A 500-kilometer mountain range the Tupi-Guarani called the mountain that cries - because of the springs pouring out of it.

subject: Serra da Saudade
summary: Brazil's least populous municipality is a Minas Gerais hill town of 833 people, named for a word other languages have to borrow.

story.title: Serra das Almas Private Natural Heritage Reserve

subject: Serra das Almas Private Natural Heritage Reserve
summary: A 6,137-hectare private reserve on the Ceará-Piauí border, seeded by a 1935 flight from Milwaukee in search of carnauba wax - and now one of the larger strongholds of intact caatinga in Brazil.

subject: Serra de Tramuntana
summary: The mountain range along Mallorca's northwest coast, a UNESCO cultural landscape carved by a thousand years of hand-stacked dry stone walls and terraces.

subject: Serra do Cachimbo
summary: A low Amazonian mountain range that births rivers, shelters 380 species of birds, and hides one of Brazil's most secretive military installations.

subject: Serra do Rio do Rastro
summary: A mountain wall in southern Brazil where a single highway folds back on itself again and again, climbing from coastal forest to a frost-bitten plateau.

subject: Serra dos Cocais
summary: A granite mountain range near the Steel Valley of Minas Gerais, named for the coconut palms the first clearers found on its slopes.

story.title: Serra dos Três Irmãos Ecological Station

subject: Serra dos Três Irmãos Ecological Station
summary: A shrinking sanctuary on the left bank of the Madeira River, where nine species of primates swing through a forest that dams and politics have steadily whittled away.

subject: Serra dos Órgãos
summary: The granite escarpment north of Rio de Janeiro - 620 million years of geology and one November night of landslides that closed the highway.

subject: Serra, Espírito Santo
summary: The largest city in Espírito Santo - bigger than its own state capital - named for the single mountain that stands behind it.

subject: Serranópolis
summary: Eleven thousand years ago someone here was buried wearing a necklace of human teeth and mother of pearl — among the oldest known jewelry in the Americas.

subject: Ses Feixes Wetlands
summary: A thousand-year-old Arab irrigation garden of narrow farmed strips beside Ibiza Town, now abandoned to marsh and to more than 140 species of migrating birds.

subject: Ses Païsses
summary: A Bronze Age talayotic settlement near Artà, where a three-thousand-year-old tower and eight-tonne stone walls stand overgrown by holm oak.

subject: Sesklo
summary: On a low Thessalian hill, farmers built one of Europe's first towns nine thousand years ago and left behind the continent's oldest village.

story.title: Sessho-seki: The Stone That Killed Everything It Touched

subject: Sessho-seki
summary: A volcanic boulder in the mountains of Nasu said to be the petrified corpse of a shape-shifting nine-tailed fox -- it split in half in 2022, and Japan held a ceremony to make sure the demon stayed put.

subject: Sevagram
summary: The tiny village where Mahatma Gandhi spent the last twelve years of his life, deliberately choosing a place with no post office, no telegraph, and no road -- then reshaping India's independence movement from its mud-walled huts.

subject: Sevastopol
summary: A white-stone city of thirty bays and two thousand monuments, where an ancient Greek colony, a Christian conversion, and centuries of naval history all crowd the same shoreline.

subject: Sevenoaks
summary: A Kentish commuter town whose name commemorates seven oak trees that have been replanted across the centuries, anchored by a 15th-century mansion and a railway disaster that changed British engineering.

subject: Seventh-Kilometer Market
summary: A sprawling city of shipping containers outside Odesa, possibly Europe's largest market and a world unto itself.

subject: Seymour Narrows
summary: A five-kilometre stretch of water where currents hit 15 knots and turbulence reaches Reynolds numbers of 100 million -- possibly the most extreme natural water channel on Earth.

subject: Sfax
summary: Tunisia's second city guards an ancient medina where tourists are rare and life unfolds as it has for centuries, a gateway to the Kerkennah Islands and the Star Wars landscapes beyond.

subject: Sfinks Festival
summary: A small folk gathering in a Boechout schoolyard in 1975 grew into a four-day world-music festival drawing 40,000 people - and gave Belgians their first live encounters with Manu Dibango, Nina Simone, Youssou N'Dour and Ali Farka Toure.

subject: Sha Tau Kok
summary: Hong Kong's northernmost town — a closed border settlement where a single street divides the city from Shenzhen, Hakka farmers became the ancestors of a community that has lived between two systems for more than a century.

subject: Sha Tin
summary: Once called 'Sand Fields,' Sha Tin transformed from rice paddies into one of Hong Kong's most ambitious new towns — a valley that saw the territory's first powered flight in 1911 and now shelters hundreds of thousands.

subject: Sha Tin Pass
summary: A mountain pass between Temple Hill and Unicorn Ridge that once served as the sole route between Kowloon and Sha Tin, Sha Tin Pass carried 600 people a day in 1904 — many of them porters hauling fresh fish across the hills to city markets.

subject: Sha Tin Racecourse
summary: Built on reclaimed land in 1978 and now capable of holding 85,000 spectators, Sha Tin Racecourse is the larger of Hong Kong's two horse racing venues and hosts some of the world's most prestigious international races each December.

subject: Shadah Al-asfal
summary: A granite mountain in southwestern Saudi Arabia's Sarawat range, rising above Tihamah with caves, rock art, and villages held by the Zahran tribe.

subject: Shady Rest Country Club
summary: Founded in 1921, Shady Rest was the first African-American country club in the United States — a sanctuary in Scotch Plains, New Jersey where golf pioneers, jazz legends, and tennis champions shaped history that the wider sporting world refused to acknowledge.

subject: Shah Abbasi Caravansarai, Nishapur
summary: One of the 999 roadside inns that Shah Abbas the Great built across Persia to revive Silk Road commerce, this Safavid-era caravansarai in central Nishapur now houses handicraft shops and museums within its four-hundred-year-old brick walls.

story.title: Shah Tepe: Buried Lives on the Gorgan Plain

subject: Shah Tepe
summary: A prehistoric mound in northeastern Iran where Swedish archaeologists uncovered 257 skeletons spanning from the Chalcolithic period to the Islamic era - including mothers buried with their children, mutilated bodies in collective graves, and thousands of years of human life compressed into eight meters of earth.

subject: Shahandasht
summary: A tiny village of 69 people in Iran's Mazandaran province where a 180-meter triple waterfall, a pre-Islamic mountaintop castle, and an ancient cave converge in a place whose name means 'Field of the Kings.'

subject: Shahr-e No
summary: Once Tehran's walled-off red light district, Shahr-e No housed 1,500 women behind brick walls before the 1979 Revolution erased it from the city's landscape -- and then from its maps, its books, and its official memory.

subject: Shahr-e Sukhteh
summary: A Bronze Age city that burned three times yet yielded the world's oldest artificial eye, oldest complete board game, and evidence of brain surgery -- only to be swallowed by the desert around 2300 BC.

subject: Shahr-i Gholghola
summary: Known as the City of Screams, this ancient fortress city in Afghanistan's Nimroz Province preserves the only known example of 10th-century Saffarid architecture and bears the scars of destruction by both Genghis Khan and Timur.

subject: Shahrizor
summary: A fertile plain in Iraqi Kurdistan where human settlement stretches back to the Neolithic, where empires rose and fell, and where the Yarsan faith still awaits the Last Judgement.

subject: Shai Hills
summary: A rocky landscape north of Accra where the Dangme-Shai people lived for nearly nine centuries before British colonial forces displaced them in 1892, now protected as Ghana's closest wildlife reserve to the capital.

subject: Shaigiya tribe
summary: An Arabized Nubian tribe whose horsemen once ruled the Nile between Korti and the Fourth Cataract, whose language quietly preserved Old Nobiin into the 20th century, and whose name runs through every chapter of Sudanese history.

subject: Shakadang Trail
summary: A marble canyon river trail in Taroko National Park where turquoise water winds past boulders shaped like molar teeth — a path with both breathtaking beauty and a difficult recent history.

subject: Shakespeare Institute
summary: A postgraduate research centre dedicated entirely to Shakespeare and the English Renaissance, housed in the Stratford home of a forgotten Edwardian bestseller who outsold all her contemporaries put together.

subject: Shakespeare North
summary: A 1590s playhouse stood in Prescot - the only purpose-built Elizabethan theatre outside London. No plans of it survived. In 2022 a Merseyside town built a Shakespearean playhouse where the old one used to be.

subject: Sham Chung
summary: Tucked into the southern shore of Tolo Channel, the Hakka village of Sham Chung can only be reached by ferry or on foot — and that remoteness has kept it one of Hong Kong's most ecologically and historically intact corners.

subject: Sham Shui Po District
summary: Sham Shui Po is the district where Hong Kong's public housing system was born — sparked by a catastrophic fire in 1953 that left tens of thousands homeless and forced the government to act on a scale it had never attempted before.

subject: Sham Tseng
summary: A small coastal village in Tsuen Wan District that became Hong Kong's roast goose capital, and whose shoreline views of the Tsing Ma Bridge now anchor a cluster of private housing estates built on the site of a defunct brewery.

subject: Shan State
summary: Myanmar's largest state is a highland patchwork of ethnic kingdoms, floating villages, and contested borderlands where the Golden Triangle meets ancient Tai civilization.

story.title: Shanb Ghazan: The Mongol Satellite City

subject: Shanb Ghazan
summary: A village became a Buddhist temple, then a Mongol satellite city crowned by a 135-meter dome, then a battlefield, then ruins buried by earthquakes. Today, almost nothing remains of the neighborhood that once astonished visitors to Tabriz.

subject: Shang dynasty
summary: China's first historically verified dynasty, the Shang ruled the Yellow River valley for five centuries, inventing Chinese writing on oracle bones and producing bronze work of unsurpassed sophistication.

subject: Shangdang Commandery
summary: An ancient highland fortress region in the Taihang Mountains that served as a strategic battleground for over two thousand years, from the Warring States period through the Chinese Civil War.

subject: Shangdu
summary: The real Xanadu -- Kublai Khan's summer capital on the Mongolian steppe, where marble palaces once stood and Coleridge dreamed his most famous poem.

subject: Shanghai Street
summary: Before Nathan Road existed, Shanghai Street was the commercial spine of Kowloon — 2.3 kilometres of wedding shops, pawnbrokers, and courts that defined the peninsula's daily life for nearly a century.

subject: Shanghainese People in Hong Kong
summary: When Shanghai fell, its capitalists, filmmakers, and tailors packed what they could and rebuilt their world in Hong Kong — transforming a trading outpost into an industrial powerhouse and seeding a culture that still hums beneath the city's Cantonese surface.

subject: Shangxiajiu Pedestrian Street
summary: In the old Xiguan quarter of western Guangzhou, a 1,200-meter arcade of hybrid Tong Lau buildings shelters centuries-old teahouses, legacy clock shops, and the continuous hum of Cantonese street commerce.

subject: Shanhai Pass
summary: The 'Greatest Pass Under Heaven' -- where the Great Wall of China meets the sea, and where every army that wanted to conquer China from the northeast had to either breach the walls or take the long way through the mountains.

subject: Shankill, Dublin
summary: An old church gave this Dublin coastal suburb its name, a Victorian landlord nearly emptied it, and a generous neighbour rebuilt it from scratch on quarter-acre plots.

subject: Shannan, Tibet
summary: The cradle of Tibetan civilization, where sacred lakes reveal the future of Dalai Lamas and the Yarlung Valley guards the oldest farms and palaces on the plateau.

subject: Shannon Region
summary: Ireland's mid-west: three counties along the lower Shannon, half a million people, and a landscape of castles, karst, and the airport that gave the region its name.

subject: Shapinsay
summary: A small Orkney island where Victorian fantasy meets Neolithic memory, and where a placename's lost meaning hints at shelter from the sea.

subject: Sharm el-Sheikh
summary: A barren fishing village turned world diving capital and diplomatic stage - the Sinai resort known as the City of Peace, shaped by both reefs and history.

subject: Shaw (Washington, D.C.)
summary: A neighborhood that grew out of freedmen's encampments became the pre-Harlem capital of Black America - the Shaw that produced Duke Ellington, fed Langston Hughes the 'sad songs of 7th Street,' and now wrestles with what gentrification has made of all of it.

subject: Shaw (Wikivoyage)
summary: Black Broadway, the home of Duke Ellington's first piano lessons, the place where U Street jazz predated Harlem - Shaw is the neighborhood that produced Duke Ellington, burned in 1968, lost forty years to disinvestment and crack, and reemerged in the 2010s as one of the most expensive parts of the District.

subject: Shaw Air Force Base
summary: Home of the 20th Fighter Wing's F-16s and the headquarters of U.S. Air Forces Central Command, named for a Sumter County pilot killed in a Bristol Fighter over the Western Front in 1918.

subject: Shaybah
summary: A self-contained oil settlement in Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter where summer temperatures hit 50 degrees Celsius, annual rainfall measures less than 3 centimeters, and the ground holds over 14 billion barrels of extra-light crude.

subject: Shearers' Strike Camp Site, Barcaldine
summary: On the bank of Lagoon Creek, up to a thousand striking shearers camped through the autumn of 1891 in a confrontation that helped give birth to the Australian Labor Party.

subject: Sheba
summary: The Kingdom of Sheba dominated South Arabia for over a millennium, built an empire on frankincense and conquest, and left behind a legendary queen whose story is claimed by three religions and two continents.

subject: Sheep's Head
summary: The narrowest of West Cork's three western peninsulas, with a low rugged spine, stone-age tombs in the rough fields, and an eighty-eight kilometre walking trail that helped invent a new kind of Irish tourism.

subject: Sheffield Blitz
summary: The devastating German bombing of Sheffield in December 1940, codenamed Operation Crucible, targeting the city's vital steel and armaments factories.

subject: Sheikh, Somaliland
summary: A mountain town at 1,430 meters in Somaliland's Golis Mountains, Sheikh hides medieval trading ruins, a school that produced two presidents, and the most scenic drive in the Horn of Africa.

subject: Shek Kip Mei
summary: A hillside district in Kowloon that went from near-empty farmland to one of Hong Kong's most storied neighbourhoods — shaped by waves of migrants, a catastrophic fire, and a public housing revolution that changed the city forever.

subject: Shek Kip Mei Estate
summary: Born from the ashes of a Christmas night fire that left 53,000 people homeless, Shek Kip Mei Estate became Hong Kong's first public housing estate and transformed the colony's approach to housing its most vulnerable residents.

subject: Shek Kong
summary: Shek Kong — 'rocky mount' in Cantonese — is a valley settlement north of Tai Mo Shan whose layered history stretches from Tang dynasty pottery to a clan water war, Japanese occupation, British barracks, Gurkha families, and the present-day People's Liberation Army.

subject: Shek Kwu Chau
summary: Once known as Coffin Island, this restricted speck of land south of Lantau has spent the last six decades quietly doing some of Hong Kong's most difficult work — offering people struggling with addiction a place to begin again, far from the pressures of the city.

subject: Shek O
summary: Shek O — the 'rocky bay' — is Hong Kong Island's most remote village: a 200-year-old fishing community clinging to a dramatic peninsula where surfers, prehistory, and the city's elite golf club share the same windswept coast.

subject: Shek O Peak
summary: At 284 metres, Shek O Peak crowns the Dragon's Back — the most celebrated ridge walk on Hong Kong Island, where the city meets the South China Sea.

subject: Shek Pik
summary: A drowned valley on Lantau's southwestern shore where Neolithic rock carvings, centuries of farming villages, and a reservoir built at the cost of a community all share the same stretch of coastline.

subject: Shekou
summary: The southern tip of Nanshan District that became China's first experiment in luring the outside world in — a peninsula where Chevron roughnecks, French ferries, and Pearl River Delta capitalism all collided.

subject: Shell Grotto, Margate
summary: Under a Margate back garden, 70 feet of subterranean passages and chambers are decorated with 4.6 million seashells in elaborate mosaic. No one knows who built it, when, or why.

subject: Shenkeng Old Street
summary: In the hills southeast of Taipei, Shenkeng Old Street has made itself synonymous with tofu — selling it smoked, stewed, skewered, frozen, and even as popsicles — while its restored Qing-dynasty shop-houses survive as a testament to the residents who refused to let them be demolished.

subject: Shenyang
summary: Formerly known as Mukden, Shenyang is a city of 9 million that has served as Manchu capital, Russian stronghold, Japanese industrial base, and the site of the largest battle in Asia before World War II.

subject: Shenzhen
summary: A city of 20 million that did not exist forty years ago — where electronics markets sprawl across entire city blocks, Hakka villages survive in the suburbs, and every restaurant serves food from a different Chinese province.

subject: Shenzhen Special Economic Zone
summary: The policy laboratory that turned a border market town of 310,000 into a megacity of millions — and convinced the world that China's economic opening was real.

subject: Shepshed
summary: The Leicestershire market town whose name simply means the hill where sheep graze - and whose history is largely the story of that one industry.

subject: Shergar
summary: The 1981 Epsom Derby winner, kidnapped from the Aga Khan's Ballymany Stud near Newbridge in 1983 - a ransom demanded, never paid, and a horse that was never recovered.

subject: Sheringham
summary: Norfolk's "sea enriches and the pine adorns" town was the first place in Britain bombed from the air, once housed Ernest Shackleton, and claims a distinction shared by nowhere else on earth: four of its original lifeboats, all still preserved.

subject: Sherman, Illinois
summary: A village defined by a random drawing and professional golf, and hit by a powerful tornado.

subject: Sheung Wan
summary: Sheung Wan is where Hong Kong Island's colonial history began — the 'Gateway District' where British forces first stepped ashore in 1841, now a layered neighbourhood of ancient temples, antique markets, and contemporary art.

subject: Shevchenko National Reserve
summary: A hillside sanctuary above the Dnieper at Kaniv, built around the grave of Ukraine's national poet, that draws pilgrims by the hundred thousand every year.

subject: Shibayama Kofun Cluster
summary: A cluster of 1,500-year-old keyhole-shaped burial mounds in Chiba Prefecture, renowned for a remarkable clay funeral procession frozen in time since the 6th century.

subject: Shichahai
summary: Three interconnected lakes northwest of the Forbidden City that once formed the northern terminus of the Grand Canal -- surrounded by ten temples, princely mansions, and the heartbeat of old Beijing.

subject: Shijimizuka site
summary: A four-thousand-year-old shell midden in Hamamatsu where millions of clam shells preserve the daily life of Japan's Jomon people across a millennium of continuous habitation.

subject: Shikoku Pilgrimage
summary: A 1,200-kilometer walking circuit of 88 Buddhist temples around the island of Shikoku, following in the footsteps of the monk Kukai across four provinces that symbolize the path to enlightenment.

subject: Shilin Night Market
summary: What began as a riverside wharf where Shilin farmers sold produce in the early 1900s has grown into Taiwan's largest and most famous night market, a 539-stall culinary labyrinth that peaks between 8 p.m. and midnight.

subject: Shima Onsen
summary: A centuries-old hot springs town in Gunma Prefecture whose name promises 40,000 cures, and whose oldest inn may have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away.

subject: Shimabara, Kyoto
summary: Kyoto's last surviving pleasure quarter, where sword-scarred pillars and soot-stained paintings preserve 345 years of art, intrigue, and transformation.

subject: Shimotsuke Yakushi-ji
summary: One of only three temples in ancient Japan authorized to ordain Buddhist priests, Shimotsuke Yakushi-ji was built in the 7th century with Korean engineering and survived a millennium of political upheaval before finally falling to the wars of the Sengoku era.

subject: Shinas
summary: A coastal Omani town near the UAE border where ancient forts, traditional dhow harbors, and aflaj irrigation channels preserve a seafaring and agricultural heritage stretching back to the 13th century.

subject: Shing Mun Reservoir
summary: Built in the 1930s to quench Kowloon's thirst, it drowned villages, set an engineering record, and earned a royal name that no one remembers — while the bell-shaped overflow at its heart won a prize from the Institution of Civil Engineers.

story.title: Shinjuku Golden Gai: Two Hundred Bars in Six Alleys

subject: Shinjuku Golden Gai
summary: A labyrinth of over 200 tiny bars crammed into six narrow alleys, Golden Gai survived yakuza arsonists, developers, and decades of demolition pressure to remain Tokyo's most defiant relic of postwar drinking culture.

story.title: Shinjuku Gyoen: A Feudal Lord's Gift to the City

subject: Shinjuku Gyo-en
summary: What began as a feudal lord's private estate in 1590 became an imperial garden, an agricultural laboratory, and finally a 58-hectare public oasis where three centuries of garden design converge beneath the towers of Shinjuku.

subject: Shinjuku Ni-chōme
summary: A five-block stretch of Shinjuku holds the world's highest concentration of gay bars -- roughly 300 tucked into buildings where a red-light district once thrived.

subject: Shinobazu Pond
summary: A natural pond in the heart of Tokyo that was once a cove of Tokyo Bay -- drained for wartime rice paddies, nearly paved over for a baseball diamond, and accidentally emptied by subway construction -- yet still blooms with lotus flowers every summer.

subject: Shinsaibashi
summary: Osaka's premier shopping district traces its name and soul to a 1622 wooden bridge built by merchant Shinsai Okada, whose legacy survives four centuries later beneath neon signs and luxury storefronts.

subject: Shinsekai
summary: Osaka's 'New World' was built in 1912 as a fantasy blending Coney Island and Paris, complete with a tower modeled on the Eiffel Tower and Arc de Triomphe, and has since become the city's grittiest, most characterful neighborhood.

subject: Shipai Village
summary: Surrounded on all sides by Guangzhou's modern Tianhe District, Shipai Village is a dense, labyrinthine urban village where a community with roots in the Song dynasty has adapted, negotiated, and survived seven centuries of change.

subject: Shipbourne
summary: A Kentish village of executed Parliamentarians, royal horse trainers, and a Bauhaus weather-board cottage the locals nicknamed the Chicken House.

subject: Shipbuilding in Frindsbury
summary: On the bank opposite Chatham Dockyard, private yards built warships including the Bellerophon - the seventy-four that fought the French flagship at the Nile, survived Trafalgar, and took Napoleon's surrender.

subject: Shipshewana
summary: The buggy capital of America - where the third-largest Amish settlement has transformed a northern Indiana town into a living museum of 19th-century life, with horse-drawn traffic, enormous auctions, and tourists who outnumber locals.

subject: Shirakawa-go
summary: A mountain village where steep-roofed farmhouses built to withstand crushing snowfall became a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a living window into premodern Japan.

subject: Shiraz
summary: The cultural heart of Iran, where the tombs of Hafez and Saadi anchor a 2,500-year-old city of gardens, poetry, and Persian tradition at the edge of the Zagros Mountains.

subject: Shire of Aurukun
summary: On the western shore of Cape York, the Wik and Wik-Waya peoples won a High Court case that changed Australia - and still carve, paint, and dance the country they never surrendered.

subject: Shirley, British Columbia
summary: A postmaster's wife named this stretch of the Juan de Fuca coast after her hometown near Southampton, and the homesickness stuck for more than a century.

subject: Shiveluch
summary: Kamchatka's northernmost active volcano has erupted at least 60 times in the Holocene and shows no signs of quieting -- its 2023 eruption punched ash 20 kilometers into the stratosphere and blanketed villages in gray.

subject: Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory
summary: The true birthplace of Silicon Valley: a paranoid Nobel laureate's semiconductor lab at 391 San Antonio Road, where eight young scientists walked out and spawned an industry worth trillions.

subject: Shockoe Bottom
summary: The second-largest slave-trading center in the United States is now a neighborhood of apartments and restaurants - with parts of the burial ground still buried under I-95.

subject: Shockoe Bottom African Burial Ground
summary: Beneath a Richmond parking lot lies the older of two municipal burial grounds for enslaved and free Black people, a site erased for nearly two centuries before a historian rediscovered it on a map in the 1990s.

subject: Shockoe Hill African Burying Ground
summary: Over twenty-two thousand free and enslaved Black Richmonders were buried here. The city then paved over them and forgot.

subject: Shoemaker Impact Structure
summary: Australia's oldest known impact scar, a ringed bullseye of salt lakes in the Western Australian desert, carries the name of the geologist whose own ashes were later carried to the Moon.

subject: Shompen language
summary: A language so poorly documented that linguists cannot agree whether it is one tongue or several, spoken by roughly 400 hunter-gatherers in the rainforest interior of Great Nicobar Island.

subject: Shoreditch
summary: Where Romeo and Juliet first cried out their lines, where Huguenot silkweavers built their looms, and where Silicon Roundabout now rents desks by the hour.

subject: Shotts
summary: A small Lanarkshire town that once lit the gas-lamps of the British Empire, made the world's diesel engines, and produces 16 million pies a year — and is home to the most successful pipe band on Earth.

subject: Shou Qiu
summary: A legendary hill encased in stone 900 years ago, Shou Qiu marks the mythical birthplace of the Yellow Emperor and anchors a complex where giant turtle-borne stelae from the Song dynasty still lie unfinished.

subject: Shoushan (Kaohsiung)
summary: Called Ape Hill by the Dutch, renamed for a crown prince by the Japanese, and now home to thousands of Formosan rock macaques, this coral limestone mountain has watched over Kaohsiung Harbor for five millennia.

story.title: Shreveport: The Other Louisiana Where Casinos Meet Country Music

subject: Shreveport
summary: The northwest Louisiana city culturally closer to Texas - where the Louisiana Hayride launched Elvis, where riverboat casinos line the Red River, and where Cajun culture gives way to Southern plain.

subject: Shrewsbury
summary: An almost-island town inside a tight loop of the Severn, with 660 listed buildings, a Norman castle, and the house where Charles Darwin was born.

subject: Shun Hing Square
summary: China's tallest building from 1996 to 1997 — completed in Shenzhen at a pace of four floors every nine days, using 24,500 tonnes of steel, as the city raced to prove what it had become.

subject: Shunde
summary: Shunde is a district of Foshan in Guangdong Province with an outsized reputation in Chinese cuisine — a local saying holds that when you eat in Guangdong, you are really eating food from Shunde.

subject: Shuntian Prefecture
summary: The administrative body that governed Beijing for over 500 years across the Ming and Qing dynasties, where the magistrate wielded silver seals and outranked every other prefect in the empire.

story.title: Shogo-in: The Mountain Monks' Imperial Temple

subject: Shōgo-in
summary: A Kyoto temple where 25 of 37 head priests came from the imperial family, Shogo-in served as the headquarters of Japan's mountain ascetic tradition and twice became a temporary imperial palace -- yet remains one of the city's least-visited treasures.

story.title: Shosoin: The Empress's Gift That Held the Silk Road

subject: Shōsōin
summary: A wooden storehouse built without a single nail has preserved nine thousand artifacts from across the ancient world for nearly 1,300 years -- all because an eighth-century empress could not let go of her husband's belongings.

subject: Si Phan Don
summary: An archipelago in the middle of a river, where half the islands drown every monsoon and resurface rearranged, and where the last Irrawaddy dolphin in Laos washed ashore in 2022.

subject: Siahkal
summary: A small Gilak city in the forested mountains of Gilan Province, Iran, whose ancient Jewish community -- claiming descent from King David -- scattered across the world after a pogrom, a Marxist insurrection, and the founding of Israel.

subject: Siavonga
summary: A hillside town on the Zambian shore of Lake Kariba, where most of the country comes to see what a seaside town feels like - except the sea is a reservoir, the sand is white and scalding, and the water is full of crocodiles.

subject: Siberia Governorate
summary: The largest administrative division in Russian history, stretching from the Urals to the Pacific, governed from Tobolsk and plagued by corruption so extreme its first governor was hanged.

subject: Siberian Traps
summary: Beneath the step-like plateaus of central Siberia lies the crime scene of Earth's worst mass extinction, where volcanic eruptions lasting two million years wiped out roughly 90% of all species.

subject: Siberut
summary: The largest of Indonesia's Mentawai Islands, isolated from mainland Sumatra since the Middle Pleistocene, where four endemic primate species share a rainforest island with the Mentawai people and their communal longhouse traditions.

subject: Sibiu
summary: A Transylvanian city where German, Hungarian, and Romanian cultures have layered themselves into cobblestone squares, fortified churches, and hearty food that costs a fraction of its Western European equivalents.

subject: Siby, Mali
summary: Below the Mandingue plateau, a natural sandstone arch marks the village where the kings allied with Sundiata Keita gathered before the battle that founded the Mali Empire, and where legend says one of them pierced the mountain with a sabre.

subject: Sicao Wetlands
summary: The 515-hectare Sicao Wetlands in Tainan's Annan District shelter mangrove forests, salt marshes, and one of Taiwan's most celebrated gatherings of black-faced spoonbills — a vulnerable bird that winters here by the hundreds.

subject: Sicyon
summary: Ancient Sicyon, capital of Greek painting and bronze sculpture, gave the world Lysippos, Apelles's teacher, and a city so steeped in the arts that even its tyrants competed at the Olympics.

subject: Sicyonian Treasury
summary: What stands at Delphi as the Sicyonian Treasury is actually the third building on the same spot — beneath its foundations, archaeologists found the carved metopes of two earlier structures that the city buried rather than let anyone else reuse.

subject: Sidi Bou Said
summary: A Tunisian hilltop village painted entirely in blue and white that has drawn artists from Paul Klee to Michel Foucault.

subject: Sidney-class ferry
summary: Two ships built in 1960 to end a strike became the first fleet of BC Ferries, ran for four decades almost unaltered, and ended as hulks on the Fraser River.

subject: Sieben Steinhäuser
summary: Five Neolithic tombs sitting in the middle of a live NATO artillery range, protected by earth walls the army built to keep shellfire off them.

subject: Siebengebirge
summary: Seven hills, except there are over forty of them, and the name might not actually mean seven at all.

subject: Siegburg
summary: A small Rhineland town named for the fort on the Sieg river, Siegburg gave the world a distinctive gray-and-blue stoneware so prized in the sixteenth century that the pitchers traveled as far as London.

subject: Siegelsum
summary: Watch a village's name reshape itself across five centuries of land deeds and tax registers - and behind every spelling, the trace of one early settler named Sygheld.

subject: Siegen
summary: An iron-working city in South Westphalia, birthplace of Rubens, ancestral land of the Orange-Nassau, and one of the greenest big cities in Germany.

subject: Sieges of Boulogne (1544-1546)
summary: An aging Henry VIII crossed the Channel in person to lay siege to a French port - his last great continental adventure, won in six weeks and lost in six years.

subject: Sierra (motor ship)
summary: The first motor ship built on Grays Harbor, launched in 1916 with Swedish engines, survived a collision and a fire, hauled reindeer meat from Alaska, and earned a place on the National Register of Historic Places.

subject: Sierra Leone
summary: A West African nation founded as a home for freed people, named for its lion-shaped mountains, scarred by a diamond-fueled war, and remade by a fragile, hard-won peace.

subject: Sierra Nevada
summary: California's granite backbone stretches 400 miles from north to south, holding three national parks, the tallest peak in the contiguous United States, and the gold that once drew the world to the American West.

subject: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
summary: The world's highest coastal mountain range rises from Caribbean beaches to snow-capped peaks in just 42 kilometers, sheltering four indigenous nations and one of the planet's most irreplaceable concentrations of biodiversity.

subject: Sierra Vista Open Space Preserve
summary: A 1,678-acre preserve in the eastern foothills above Silicon Valley where the Calaveras Fault Trail traces an active earthquake line and endangered red-legged frogs breed in the creeks below.

subject: Sierra de la Ventana (mountains)
summary: A range of ancient quartzite peaks rising abruptly from the flat Pampas, named for a natural window worn clean through the rock, and crowned by the highest summit in Buenos Aires Province.

subject: Sierra de las Minas
summary: A 130-kilometer mountain range in eastern Guatemala that holds Mesoamerica's largest cloud forests, 885 animal species, and the lost jade deposits that once fueled Olmec and Maya civilizations -- rediscovered only after Hurricane Mitch tore the landscape open in 1998.

subject: Sierras de Córdoba
summary: Argentina's gentlest great mountains, ancient rounded ranges where condors ride the thermals, German brewers settled the valleys, and three million tourists come every year.

subject: Sifnos
summary: A green, terraced Cycladic island that was once one of the wealthiest places in ancient Greece — punished by the gods for its greed — and later gave the world its most influential Greek cookbook writer.

subject: Signal Hill, California
summary: The Tongva lit signal fires on its summit for centuries; Buster Keaton filmed comedies on its slopes; and in 1921 a gusher erupted and turned Signal Hill into one of the most productive oil fields in history — all packed into 2.2 square miles surrounded by Long Beach.

subject: Sigri (village)
summary: A safe harbour at the western tip of Lesbos guards a fishing village built beside a forest turned to stone nearly twenty million years ago.

subject: Siguiri
summary: On the banks of the upper Niger sits a city named for the wild buffalo that once roamed here, now famous for the gold beneath its soil and the goldsmiths who work it.

subject: Sihanoukville Autonomous Port
summary: France paid twelve million dollars to build the deep-water port whose whole purpose was to end Cambodia's dependence on French-run Saigon.

subject: Sikasso
summary: Once the largest fortified city in West Africa, Sikasso grew from a small village into the proud capital of the Kénédougou Kingdom before falling to French artillery in 1898.

subject: Sikhote-Alin
summary: A 900-kilometer mountain range in Russia's Far East where Siberian tigers and reindeer share the same forests — and where a 1947 meteorite shower left craters that are still visible today.

subject: Silay
summary: Called the Paris of Negros, this Philippine city preserves over thirty heritage houses from the sugar industry's golden age and a revolutionary history that begins with a legendary warrior princess.

subject: Silbury Hill
summary: The largest prehistoric artificial mound in Europe rises from the Wiltshire plains near Avebury -- comparable in volume to the Egyptian pyramids, built with antler picks over fifteen years, and its purpose remains completely unknown.

subject: Silla
summary: The smallest and most isolated of Korea's Three Kingdoms outlasted them all, unifying the peninsula through cunning alliances with Tang China before turning on its ally to forge an independent Korean state.

story.title: Silver Centre: The Ghost Town That Rivaled Cobalt

subject: Silver Centre
summary: A ghost town in Ontario's Timiskaming District where a lumberman's misidentified silver sample sparked a legendary lost-mine story, two silver rushes built and emptied three successive town sites, and the massive 4,402-pound Keeley nugget became a symbol of the riches pulled from the Canadian Shield.

subject: Silver Islet
summary: A rock no bigger than a tennis court yielded $3.25 million in silver before Lake Superior reclaimed it, leaving behind a ghost town turned cottage community at the tip of the Sibley Peninsula.

subject: Silver Pit
summary: A drowned glacial valley on the bed of the North Sea, named in the 19th century by trawlermen who found it stuffed with winter soles.

subject: Silver Springs (attraction)
summary: Florida's oldest tourist attraction, where glass-bottom boats have revealed crystal-clear spring waters since the 1870s, and where Hollywood filmed Tarzan swinging through the jungle canopy.

subject: Silver Star
summary: A painted Victorian village perched at 1,915 meters, surrounded by four distinct mountain faces and Canada's largest network of daily-groomed Nordic trails.

subject: Silver mining in Arizona
summary: Soldiers warned Ed Schieffelin that the only stone he would find in Apache territory would be his tombstone, so when he struck silver in 1877, he named his claim exactly that, launching Arizona's wildest boom.

subject: Silver mining in Colorado
summary: From the first silver strike near Montezuma in 1864 to the Aspen district's 101 million troy ounces, Colorado's silver story reshaped the state's identity, built and bankrupted fortunes, and left ghost towns scattered across the Rockies.

subject: Silverdale, Lancashire
summary: A small Lancashire village hard against the Cumbrian border, ringed by limestone pavements, RSPB reeds, Viking silver, and the persistent literary ghost of Elizabeth Gaskell.

subject: Silverstone Circuit
summary: An abandoned wartime bomber base turned into the spiritual home of Formula One - first by twelve friends and a flock of unfortunate sheep.

subject: Silverton, Colorado
summary: A remote mining town in the San Juan Mountains where the Spanish Flu hit harder than anywhere else in America, and a narrow gauge railroad became the lifeline that refused to die.

subject: Silverton, New South Wales
summary: A silver-boom town of 3,000 that emptied almost overnight when Broken Hill struck it richer - and was reborn as an artists' colony and the most-filmed ghost town in Australia, where the Mad Max car still sits outside the pub.

subject: Silverwood Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: The 2003 Cedar Fire burned through every acre of a 757-acre nature sanctuary east of San Diego — and what grew back in the years that followed became a case study in how Southern California chaparral recovers from catastrophe.

subject: Silvio Gesell
summary: The self-taught merchant who thought money should rot like fruit, spent eight days as finance minister of a revolutionary Bavarian republic, and lived out his life in a vegetarian orchard settlement north of Berlin.

subject: Silvânia
summary: One of the oldest towns in Goiás, founded by 18th-century gold miners who arrived carrying a statue of Nosso Senhor do Bonfim and built a village that bore its name until a local Silva family earned a rename in 1943.

subject: Sima de las Cotorras
summary: A limestone sinkhole in Chiapas where thousands of green parakeets spiral up from the depths each dawn, cave paintings line the walls, and a Zoque community runs an ecotourism center that only ten to fifteen people visit per day.

subject: Simatai
summary: Clinging to the Yan Mountains at grades approaching 80 degrees, the Simatai section of the Great Wall is where the fortification becomes something closer to vertical -- and where, on clear nights, you can see Beijing's lights shimmering 120 km away.

subject: Simferopol
summary: Crimea's inland capital is a crossroads city where Scythian ruins, a Tatar market, and the world's longest trolleybus line all converge.

subject: Simien Mountains
summary: A range of 4,000-meter peaks in northern Ethiopia formed by a Hawaiian-type shield volcano 25 million years ago, home to the endemic walia ibex and gelada baboon, and one of the very few places in tropical Africa where snow falls.

subject: Simon's Town
summary: A small naval town on False Bay where African penguins nest among boulders, a Great Dane once held the rank of able seaman, and the train from Cape Town delivers you to the doorstep of Cape Point.

subject: Simonside Hills
summary: A heather-clad Northumberland ridge with Beowulf in its name, a dragon-slayer in its etymology, and a lantern-bearing dwarf in its folklore.

subject: Simpson's-in-the-Strand
summary: Simpson's-in-the-Strand began in 1828 as London's premier chess venue, became the city's temple of roast beef, inspired P.G. Wodehouse and Sherlock Holmes, and is preparing to reopen in 2026 after closing for the pandemic.

subject: Simpson, Northern Territory
summary: A locality the size of a small country, covering the Northern Territory's slice of the Simpson Desert, where the 2016 census counted not a single resident.

subject: Sinaia
summary: Named after a pilgrim's memory of Mount Sinai, this Carpathian resort town became Romania's unofficial summer capital after a king built a fairy-tale castle in its forests.

subject: Sinaw
summary: An Omani market city where Bedouin communities still trade livestock and silver on Thursdays, and where archaeologists unearthed a 2,300-year-old warrior buried with an iron sword, two daggers, leather shoes, and a sacrificed camel.

subject: Sincura
summary: A mountain range in central Bahia whose 19th-century diamond rush grew a village of 8,000 into a boomtown of 30,000 in a single year - a forgotten episode of Brazilian mining history now overshadowed by the park that protects it.

subject: Sind Club
summary: Established in 1871, this gentlemen's club in Karachi bears the design influence of Richard Francis Burton's critique of Gothic architecture and remains a bastion of colonial-era exclusivity in a city that has transformed around it.

subject: Singapore
summary: From third world to first in one generation - where an expelled city-state built itself into Asia's wealthiest nation through discipline, planning, and an obsessive attention to detail that extends from airport terminals to hawker centers.

subject: Singer Laren
summary: The Laren art museum founded on a Pittsburgh steel fortune that a son refused to inherit, and the small Dutch town that briefly held a stolen Van Gogh.

subject: Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City
summary: A 30-square-kilometer planned city built on saltpans and polluted wasteland, jointly developed by China and Singapore as a proving ground for sustainable urban development.

subject: Sinop, Mato Grosso
summary: A planned Amazon frontier city built out of raw jungle in the 1970s by a Paraná real estate company, Sinop grew in one generation into the fourth-largest city in Mato Grosso and a capital of Brazilian agribusiness.

subject: Sint Eustatius
summary: Once the richest port in the Caribbean, this tiny Dutch island fired the salute that first recognized the United States.

subject: Sint-Niklaas
summary: Belgium's largest market square belongs to a city whose 13th-century countess promised to leave the ground bare - and a town whose September festival fills that same empty space with hot air balloons.

subject: Sint-Oedenrode
summary: A market town on the Dommel that traces its name to a blind Scottish princess fleeing magpies, and its modern identity to a corridor of American paratroopers in September 1944.

subject: Sintra
summary: A mist-shrouded town of royal palaces, Romantic castles, and literary pilgrimage 28 km from Lisbon, where Lord Byron found his 'Glorious Eden' and the Portuguese court spent its summers for centuries.

subject: Sir Samuel, Western Australia
summary: Named for a South Australian judge who never saw it, this Goldfields boomtown once held three banks and a racecourse before the gold ran out and the desert took it back.

subject: Siraya Language
summary: A Formosan language dormant since the nineteenth century, now being reawakened by children in Tainan who can speak and sing in the tongue of their ancestors.

subject: Sirkeci
summary: The bustling transport-and-commerce district at the tip of Istanbul's historic peninsula — where the Orient Express ended, ferries begin, and the city's layers compress into a single, restless neighborhood.

subject: Sirpur Group of Monuments
summary: A vast archaeological complex on the banks of the Mahanadi where Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain monuments spanning eight centuries reveal the capital of the Dakshina Kosala kingdom.

subject: Sisaket
summary: A quiet Thai provincial town that guards more Khmer ruins than anywhere else in the region — and shares a contentious cliff-top temple with Cambodia.

subject: Sistan
summary: A desert region straddling Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan where Scythian warriors, Zoroastrian pilgrims, and Persian epic heroes all left their mark across five millennia of continuous conquest and reinvention.

subject: Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence
summary: Founded in 1979 when a group of gay men in San Francisco donned nun's habits, the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence combine drag, religious satire, and charitable fundraising into a movement that has spread worldwide.

subject: Sisupalgarh
summary: Near modern Bhubaneswar lie the ruins of a fortified city that predates the Mauryan Empire - once home to as many as 25,000 people, now being swallowed by illegal construction despite national protected status.

subject: Sitges
summary: A whitewashed seaside town of seventeen beaches southwest of Barcelona, Sitges is by turns a painters' haven, one of Europe's great gay resorts, and the stage for a Carnival that shakes off all its composure.

subject: Sitges Film Festival
summary: The world's premier fantasy and horror film festival, born in a sun-drenched Mediterranean beach town in 1968 and now a pilgrimage site for genre filmmakers and fans alike.

story.title: Sitka: Where Russia Sold America Its Future

subject: Sitka
summary: The Alaska town where the Russian Empire's flag came down in 1867, ending Moscow's presence in North America - where Tlingit warriors fought Russian colonizers, where onion domes still mark Orthodox churches, and where the purchase that seemed foolish made America a Pacific power.

subject: Sittwe
summary: A city whose very name means 'the place where the war meets' -- Rakhine State's storm-battered capital sits where three rivers pour into the Bay of Bengal, layering Buddhist relics, colonial ambition, political defiance, and humanitarian crisis into a single estuarial landscape.

subject: Siurana (Tarragona)
summary: A tiny stone village clinging to a cliff edge in the Prades Mountains, Siurana was the last Muslim stronghold to fall in Catalonia and is now one of the world's great rock-climbing destinations.

subject: Sivriada
summary: A barren spike of rock in the Sea of Marmara, Sivriada carries the weight of two names: one for its shape, one for a 1911 act of mass cruelty that Istanbul has never entirely shaken off.

subject: Siwash Rock
summary: A 32-million-year-old basalt stack off Stanley Park's western shore - to the Squamish, a man made permanent; to mariners, a bowling pin; and the subject of a long argument about what to call him.

story.title: Six Blocks That Bet on Walking

subject: Six Blocks That Bet on Walking
summary: Fresno's Fulton Mall was the second pedestrian mall in America and drew delegations from more than fifty cities -- then spent decades emptying out before cars were finally let back in.

story.title: Six Flags AstroWorld: Houston's Lost Kingdom of Thrills

subject: Six Flags AstroWorld
summary: The amusement park that Roy Hofheinz dreamed up as a companion to the Astrodome thrilled Houston for 37 years before corporate debt and rising land values erased it from the map, leaving nothing but asphalt and memory.

subject: Six Flags St. Louis
summary: The last park personally envisioned by Six Flags founder Angus G. Wynne opened in 1971 in Eureka, Missouri, and has spent five decades reinventing itself -- from its original six internationally-themed lands to a sprawling 323-acre playground of roller coasters, DC Comics heroes, and Looney Tunes characters.

subject: Six Gallery Reading
summary: On a single October evening in 1955, a poetry reading in a tiny San Francisco gallery ignited the Beat Generation and changed American literature forever.

subject: Six Seconds on Moorland Avenue
summary: On an October afternoon in 2013, a 13-year-old boy carrying a toy gun was shot and killed by a Sonoma County deputy in Santa Rosa, igniting months of protests and a community's reckoning with police use of force.

subject: Sixth Street (Austin)
summary: Once called Pecan Street and once nearly abandoned, Austin's Sixth Street has reinvented itself from frontier stagecoach stop to Victorian commercial hub to the live music corridor that helped earn Austin the title Live Music Capital of the World.

story.title: Sixty Thousand Experiments on Eighteen Acres

subject: Sixty Thousand Experiments on Eighteen Acres
summary: The remnants of Luther Burbank's experimental farm in Sebastopol, where the horticulturist once ran 60,000 plant experiments simultaneously and commuted 17 miles by bicycle from Santa Rosa to tend them.

subject: Sizewell Nuclear Power Stations
summary: Two generations of British nuclear engineering on a single Suffolk shingle beach: Magnox reactors that ran from 1966 to 2006, a pressurised water reactor that has supplied the grid since 1995, and the planned twin EPR reactors of Sizewell C.

subject: Sizihwan
summary: Sizihwan is Kaohsiung's legendary sunset bay — a black-sand crescent tucked between Shoushan mountain and the open Taiwan Strait, where poets have compared the view to one of China's great beauties.

subject: Sjellebro Stone
summary: A Viking Age granite face, braided and round-eyed, set at a river crossing on Djursland - the only mask stone in Scandinavia that carries no runes at all.

subject: Sjønstå
summary: For sixty-four years every ton of copper ore out of Sulitjelma had to be lifted, carried and lowered again at Sjønstå — then the railway was extended past it, and the village emptied.

subject: Skadovsk
summary: A Black Sea resort port founded by a scientist on a Crimean Tatar fishing village called the quiet harbor, once known for grain exports and an albino tigress.

subject: Skagway
summary: The Alaska boomtown that exploded from nothing to 10,000 people in 1897 - where stampeders climbed the Chilkoot Pass to reach Klondike gold, ruled by con man Soapy Smith until a vigilante shot him dead.

subject: Skagway
summary: Gateway to the Klondike - the Alaska boomtown where 20,000 stampeders landed in 1897-98, ruled briefly by con man Soapy Smith until he was killed in a gunfight on the town wharf.

subject: Skamlingsbanken
summary: The highest hill in Southern Jutland, bought outright in the 1840s so that Danes in contested Schleswig would have somewhere to stand and speak their own language out loud.

subject: Skara Brae
summary: Europe's most complete Neolithic village, older than Stonehenge and the Pyramids, preserved for millennia beneath Orkney sand and now threatened by the sea that revealed it.

subject: Skateraw Lifeboat Station
summary: A small RNLI station opened on the East Lothian coast in 1907 in response to the Alfred Erlandsen tragedy, closed in 1943, now reduced to cobbles in the shadow of Torness nuclear station.

subject: Skatopia
summary: An 88-acre skatepark in rural Ohio run as a self-declared anarchist commune by professional skateboarder Brewce Martin since 1995.

subject: Skegness
summary: A town swallowed by the sea once and rebuilt further inland, Skegness has been England's dependable seaside resort for over 150 years — sand, amusements, and a stubborn loyalty that foreign package holidays never quite displaced.

subject: Skegness Lifeboat Station
summary: Since 1830, volunteer crews at Skegness have launched into some of the North Sea's most treacherous waters — a shifting coastline of shoals and sandbanks that has claimed ships for centuries.

subject: Skeleton Coast
summary: Namibia's fog-shrouded Atlantic shore, where more than a thousand shipwrecks rust in the sand, desert elephants dig for water, and the San people named the land 'The Place God Made in Anger.'

subject: Skellig Michael
summary: A visitor's guide to reaching and exploring this extraordinary Atlantic island -- where 618 ancient stone steps, no safety rails, and a maximum of 180 visitors per day make every landing an adventure.

subject: Skiathos
summary: A small pine-cloaked island in the northern Aegean with more than sixty beaches, the birthplace of a great Greek writer, and the backdrop to Mamma Mia.

subject: Skiathos (town)
summary: The island's only town, where a Venetian fortlet guards the harbor mouth and the house of Greece's great short-story writer still stands two streets back from the sea.

subject: Skibbereen
summary: A West Cork town whose name became shorthand for the worst of the Great Famine, where eight to ten thousand of the dead lie in unmarked pits.

story.title: Skinwalker Ranch: Utah's Portal to the Unexplainable

subject: Skinwalker Ranch
summary: The Utah ranch where a billionaire funded scientific investigation of UFOs, cattle mutilations, and phenomena so strange that researchers allegedly experienced psychological trauma - a property so weird it launched TV series, government interest, and the question of what happens when science meets the inexplicable.

subject: Skinwalker Ranch
summary: America's strangest 512 acres - the Utah property where UFOs, cattle mutilations, poltergeists, and shapeshifting creatures have been reported for decades, making it a magnet for paranormal investigators and billionaire buyers.

subject: Skinwalker Ranch
summary: A 512-acre Utah ranch bordering Ute tribal lands has drawn UFO researchers, billionaire investors, and Defense Department funding despite decades of investigation yielding no conclusive evidence.

subject: Skive, Denmark
summary: A Limfjord market town chartered in 1231, with saints on its church walls, cheese ageing in limestone caves, and ten thousand bats wintering underground nearby.

subject: Skomer
summary: An island off the Pembrokeshire coast that holds roughly half the world's Manx shearwaters, Britain's largest southern puffin colony, and 5,000 years of human footprints in the soil.

subject: Skookumchuck Narrows
summary: A tidal bottleneck on BC's Sunshine Coast where currents exceeding 16 knots generate standing waves, whirlpools, and whitecaps -- even on perfectly calm days.

subject: Skopelos
summary: The greenest island in the Aegean, shaped like a saxophone and pressed with plums, that the world fell in love with as the backdrop to Mamma Mia!

subject: Skopelos (town)
summary: A whitewashed town that climbs its own hillside like a theatre, crowned by a Venetian castle and stitched with hundreds of tiny churches.

subject: Skorpios
summary: The private Ionian island Aristotle Onassis transformed from a barren rock into a forested sanctuary — site of his 1968 wedding to Jacqueline Kennedy and the resting place of three generations of his family.

subject: Skuldelev ships
summary: Five 11th-century Viking vessels scuttled around 1070 to block a channel in Roskilde Fjord, raised from the mud between 1957 and 1962, and now one of the richest sources we have on how the late Viking Age built ships.

subject: Skunk Ape
summary: Florida's contribution to North American cryptid folklore - a seven-foot, foul-smelling swamp ape that the Miccosukee and Seminole have been telling stories about for far longer than anyone has been calling it Bigfoot.

subject: SkyPoint Observation Deck
summary: Near the top of one of the world's tallest residential towers, SkyPoint hands the Gold Coast to you in a single 360-degree sweep, from Brisbane's haze to the surf-line at Byron Bay.

subject: SkyTrain (Vancouver)
summary: Vancouver's driverless elevated railway was built to show off at a world's fair in 1986 and became the spine the whole region grew along.

subject: Skye Trail
summary: 128 unwaymarked kilometres along the spine of Skye, from Rubha Hunish to Broadford, across some of the most punishing and beautiful ground in Britain.

subject: Skyline Drive
summary: A 105-mile ribbon of asphalt tracing the spine of Virginia's Blue Ridge Mountains, Skyline Drive was born from Depression-era ambition and built by the hands of the Civilian Conservation Corps.

subject: Skyrail Rainforest Cableway
summary: A 7.5-kilometre gondola that glides over the canopy of the world's oldest rainforest - built without roads, flown in by helicopter, in agreement with the Djabugay Traditional Owners.

subject: Skyros
summary: The southernmost of the Sporades hides Achilles among its myths, a poet beneath its olive trees, and a breed of miniature horse found almost nowhere else on Earth.

story.title: Slab City: The Last Free Place in America

subject: Slab City
summary: The abandoned Marine base where squatters built a desert society without rules, rent, or running water - where Salvation Mountain rises in psychedelic glory and outcasts from everywhere gather to live off the grid in 100-degree heat.

story.title: Slab City: The Last Free Place in America

subject: Slab City
summary: The California desert settlement where America's dropouts, retirees, and wanderers live rent-free on abandoned military concrete - no laws, no utilities, no running water, just the Salton Sea shimmering toxic in the distance and Salvation Mountain welcoming everyone.

subject: Slade Point
summary: A limestone headland that Matthew Flinders sailed straight past in 1802, lost in haze, leaving it nameless for another century on the wild western edge of Eyre Peninsula.

subject: Slane
summary: The Meath village on the Boyne where Saint Patrick is said to have lit the Paschal fire in defiance of the High King, where 408 bottles of Bushmills once went into the river, and where the world's biggest rock concerts now happen on a hillside.

subject: Slave Auction Block, Fredericksburg
summary: An 800-pound sandstone block that served as a platform for selling enslaved people for nearly two decades sat on a Fredericksburg street corner for 177 years before the city finally moved it to a museum.

subject: Slavutych
summary: The last city the Soviet Union ever built, raised in a hurry to rehouse the families of Chernobyl and shaped like a mosaic of eight republics.

subject: Slea Head
summary: A wind-scoured promontory of 400-million-year-old sandstone at the western tip of the Dingle Peninsula, where the road ends and the Atlantic begins.

subject: Sleaford
summary: A Lincolnshire market town whose Bishop's manor became a Bass maltings, whose canal was killed by railways, and whose population doubled when an aristocrat went broke.

subject: Slebech
summary: On the northern bank of the Eastern Cleddau, a vanished community holds the oldest Knights Hospitaller commandery in Wales, an English merchant's first New World report, and a Jamaican sugar fortune that bought a Pembrokeshire estate.

subject: Sleen
