summary: A small Drenthe village where a 450-year-old church anchors a brick-paved green, and a 498-kilometer hiking trail passes straight through the heart of town.

subject: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore
summary: A Chippewa legend turned grief into geography here, where a mother bear became a towering sand dune and her drowned cubs became islands in Lake Michigan.

story.title: Sleepy Hollow: Where the Headless Horseman Still Rides

subject: Sleepy Hollow
summary: The New York village where Washington Irving's 1820 tale became reality - where tourists seek the Headless Horseman's bridge, where the Old Dutch Church stands unchanged since colonial days, and where Halloween is less holiday than identity.

subject: Sleepy Hollow
summary: The village that embraced its headless horseman - where Washington Irving set his 1820 tale of Ichabod Crane, and where the real town now capitalizes on literary legend with Halloween tourists and a cemetery full of famous names.

subject: Slieve Gullion
summary: The highest mountain in County Armagh - a Paleocene volcano whose summit holds Ireland's highest surviving passage tomb, called locally Cailleach Beara's House.

subject: Slieve Miskish Mountains
summary: The Mountains of Malice - a low sandstone range at the tip of the Beara Peninsula, with abandoned copper mines on its western flank and four peaks small enough that everyone has climbed at least one of them.

subject: Sligo
summary: An Irish town whose name means 'abounding in shells,' where Bram Stoker's mother survived cholera, Yeats found his country, and Neolithic farmers built Ireland's oldest known monument 6,000 years ago.

subject: Slope Point
summary: The southernmost point of New Zealand's South Island, where Antarctic winds have bent entire groves of trees sideways and a lonely signpost marks the halfway point between the equator and the South Pole.

subject: Sluis
summary: Once a Hanseatic harbor that could hold five hundred ships, Sluis now sits seven kilometers from the sea, its medieval belfry watching over a town the tide forgot.

subject: Small Heath
summary: The Birmingham district where Britain's only rifle factory survived three Luftwaffe air raids in 1940, where Birmingham City FC was founded, and which Peaky Blinders has made famous to a generation that never saw the BSA works.

subject: Small Isles
summary: Four inhabited islands scattered off Scotland's west coast - Rum, Eigg, Muck, Canna - where ferries on baffling rotation are the only way in and out.

subject: Smallingerland
summary: A Friesland municipality founded on a failed peat venture that bankrupted its investor and built a city anyway.

subject: Smalls Paradise
summary: For sixty-one years, this Harlem nightclub was where waiters danced the Charleston on roller skates, Billie Holiday failed her first audition, and Malcolm X waited tables.

subject: Smangus
summary: Taiwan's most remote indigenous village - once called Black Village for its isolation - now runs as a communal society inspired by both Atayal tradition and the Israeli kibbutz.

subject: Smithfield, London
summary: A medieval meadow on the edge of London became a place of livestock, jousts, plague graves, and quiet executions, and remains today the City's last surviving wholesale market.

subject: Smithsonian Institution
summary: An illegitimate Englishman who never set foot in America left his fortune to a country he had never visited - 104,960 gold sovereigns that became the Smithsonian, 21 museums, a zoo, and the closest thing the United States has to a national attic.

subject: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute
summary: The only Smithsonian bureau outside the United States, rooted on an island that rose from the floodwaters of the Panama Canal a century ago.

subject: Snaefell Mine
summary: Twenty miners died on the morning of 10 May 1897 in the worst industrial disaster in Manx history, after an unseen fire turned a lead mine into a chamber of carbon monoxide.

subject: Snake Alley (Taipei)
summary: Once a red-light district where vendors skinned live snakes for crowds, Taipei's most infamous night market outlived its own notoriety -- its last snake restaurant closed in 2018, but the Michelin Guide came calling a year later.

subject: Sneek
summary: The sailing capital of Friesland, where 50 carillon bells ring across canals that once carried the wealth of Leeuwarden to the Zuiderzee — and where a single week each August fills the lakes with white sails.

subject: Sneem
summary: A Kerry village whose name means 'the knot', where de Gaulle holidayed, a wrestling champion learned to row, and the first head of British intelligence was born.

subject: Snohomish County Centennial Trail
summary: A 30-mile rail trail following the ghost of the Seattle, Lake Shore and Eastern Railway, the Centennial Trail threads through the farms, wetlands, and small towns of Snohomish County with a public art installation that honors a Japanese American family forced to sell their land during WWII.

story.title: Snow Ruyi National Ski Jumping Centre

subject: Snow Ruyi National Ski Jumping Centre
summary: Shaped like a ruyi scepter and nestled between two mountain ridges, Snow Ruyi hosted the 2022 Winter Olympics ski jumping events and became one of the Games' most distinctive architectural statements.

subject: Snowdon
summary: The highest peak in Wales, steeped in Arthurian legend and served by Britain's only public rack-and-pinion railway, now officially known by its Welsh name Yr Wyddfa.

subject: Snowdonia
summary: In 2022 the national park stopped calling itself Snowdonia in English. The Welsh name Eryri - which probably means 'highland', though many think it means 'place of the eagle' - had been waiting for nine centuries.

subject: Snowshoe
summary: A traveler's guide to West Virginia's largest ski destination - where the lift tickets cover three slopes, the cell signal is restricted by federal law, and AT&T is the only carrier that works.

subject: Snowy Mountains Scheme
summary: A quarter-century of tunnelling beneath the Australian Alps turned a river inside-out, generated power for three states, and built a new multicultural nation out of postwar migrants.

subject: So Lo Pun
summary: A near-abandoned Hakka village deep in Hong Kong's northeastern wilderness, where compasses reportedly stop working and more than a thousand years of history quietly crumble.

subject: SoFA District
summary: Three blocks of South First Street in downtown San Jose transformed from a 1970s red-light district into Silicon Valley's creative heart, home to galleries, theaters, and the Cinequest film festival.

subject: SoHo, Hong Kong
summary: SoHo — South of Hollywood Road — is a pocket of Hong Kong where a 1993 escalator transformed an elderly residential neighbourhood into the city's most internationally flavoured dining and nightlife district.

subject: Soba (city)
summary: The red-brick capital of the medieval Christian kingdom of Alodia, which ruled the Blue Nile for nearly a thousand years and then quietly dissolved, leaving the modern suburbs of Khartoum built on its bones.

subject: Sobral Santos II
summary: An overloaded Amazon riverboat rolled over while docking at Óbidos before dawn on 19 September 1981; 178 people were counted alive, and the number who died has never been established.

subject: Sobral, Ceará
summary: On a cloudy morning in 1919, a cattle-and-cotton town in the Ceará backlands took the photographs that made Einstein famous.

subject: Society for Creative Anachronism
summary: Born from a 1966 Berkeley backyard party where grad students fought with plywood swords, the SCA grew into a global medieval living-history organization headquartered in Milpitas, California.

subject: Soconusco
summary: A narrow tropical strip between the Sierra Madre de Chiapas and the Pacific where cacao cultivation birthed Mesoamerican civilizations -- and where German coffee barons later carved estates with names like Hamburgo and Prussia into the jungle.

subject: Socotra
summary: An isolated archipelago in the Indian Ocean where millions of years of separation from the mainland produced a landscape so alien that a third of its plant species exist nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Sofala
summary: Once the golden gateway to Great Zimbabwe and the most powerful city south of Kilwa, Sofala has been swallowed by the shifting sands of its own estuary, leaving almost no trace of a port that once held a hundred ships.

subject: Sofia
summary: Constantine the Great called Serdica his Rome, and the city he loved still sits in a valley at the foot of Vitosha mountain, layered with Roman, Byzantine, Bulgarian, and Ottoman history.

subject: Sognefjord
summary: Norway's longest and deepest fjord stretches 205 kilometers inland, carved by glaciers nearly three kilometers thick into a chasm deeper than most of the North Sea.

subject: Soho
summary: A square mile of London where John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to a single pump, where Mozart played as a child, where bebop arrived in Britain, and where the lives of immigrants, workers, and artists have been pressed together for three centuries.

subject: Sohr Damb
summary: A red-earthen mound in central Balochistan has yielded nearly six millennia of human occupation, polychrome pottery that predates the Indus Valley cities, and the oldest stratified sesame sample ever found.

subject: Sok Kwu Wan
summary: Picnic Bay on Lamma Island hides a seafood village, a green-turtle beach, and abandoned Japanese suicide boats from the final days of World War Two.

subject: Sokhta Koh
summary: A 4,500-year-old Harappan trading outpost on the Makran coast where hundreds of thousands of potsherds still litter the hillsides, silent evidence of a vast pottery industry that once packaged goods for the ancient world's maritime trade networks.

story.title: Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute

subject: Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute
summary: A NASA institute headquartered at Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley that coordinates dozens of research teams across the country and around the world, preparing the science for humanity's return to the Moon and beyond.

subject: Solar eclipse of April 8, 2024
summary: The Great North American Eclipse swept a path of totality from Mexico's Pacific coast to Canada's Atlantic provinces, with its longest darkness -- four minutes and 28 seconds -- falling near the town of Nazas, Durango.

subject: Solihull
summary: A market town that kept its identity while England's second city sprawled toward it, Solihull is where the Land Rover was born and where the parish church still gives directions across the Forest of Arden.

subject: Solimões–Japurá moist forests
summary: An Amazon ecoregion the size of Greece, threaded by three colossal rivers and crossed by only two short roads, holding one of the most diverse concentrations of life on the planet.

subject: Solingen
summary: Solingen has been forging blades for two thousand years - and almost every kitchen knife in the world has a Solingen cousin.

subject: Solitaire, Namibia
summary: A one-pump desert outpost famous for apple pie, rusting car wrecks, and being the only sign of life for a hundred lonely kilometres in any direction.

subject: Sollas
summary: A small crofting township on North Uist's northern coast - and the site, in 1849, of one of the Highland Clearances' most violent attempted evictions.

story.title: Solor: The Island That Empires Fought Over and Forgot

subject: Solor
summary: A narrow volcanic island in eastern Indonesia where Portuguese priests, Dutch soldiers, and Solorese whalers battled for centuries over sandalwood, souls, and sovereignty.

subject: Solva Lifeboat Station
summary: A widow's gift built a Victorian lifeboat station at Solva that lasted just eighteen years before the sea won.

subject: Somalia
summary: Somalia occupies the Horn of Africa with a coastline longer than any other mainland African nation, a history reaching back to the ancient Land of Punt, and a culture of fierce hospitality that persists through decades of conflict and rebuilding.

subject: Somaliland
summary: A self-declared republic on the Horn of Africa that has maintained peace, held democratic elections, and built functioning institutions for over three decades - all without international recognition as a sovereign state.

subject: Sombrerete, Zacatecas
summary: A Pueblo Magico founded in 1555 and named for a mountain shaped like a three-cornered hat, where silver mines funded a colonial dynasty, Benito Juarez sheltered during the French Intervention, and faith still places crosses on every surrounding peak.

subject: Somerset County, Maryland
summary: Maryland's southernmost county was founded in 1666 by Virginia Quakers fleeing a conversion law - and almost became Napoleon's hideout.

subject: Somorrostro
summary: A popular Barcelona beach that spent a century as a self-built shanty of fifteen thousand people, birthplace of the flamenco legend Carmen Amaya, whose old name was only restored in 2010.

subject: Son Oleza
summary: A Bronze Age village near Valldemossa whose sky-watching sanctuary tracked the Southern Cross until the stars themselves moved on.

subject: Songhai Empire
summary: From its capital at Gao on the Niger, Songhai grew into the largest empire West Africa ever saw, until a Moroccan army with gunpowder crossed the Sahara and broke it in a single afternoon.

subject: Songo
summary: A Mozambican town built from scratch in 1969 to house dam workers, Songo sits in the hills above the Cahora Bassa hydroelectric scheme, sending power as far as South Africa.

subject: Songo Mnara
summary: A 14th-century Swahili stone town on a small Tanzanian island where archaeologists found Chinese porcelain, Kilwa-minted coins, and evidence that even private houses were shared communal spaces.

subject: Songwe Region
summary: Tanzania's newest region, split from Mbeya in 2016, where coffee farmers work the Southern Highlands, the TAZARA railway crosses into Zambia, and the Nyiha people remain the largest indigenous community.

subject: Sonmiani Flight Test Range
summary: Pakistan's only rocket launch facility began in 1961 as a NASA-assisted civilian space program and has since transformed into a military missile test range on the Balochistan coast.

subject: Sonnenhügel
summary: An Osnabrück residential district with a 900-meter cave network under its monastery hill - and a former German president among its school's alumni.

subject: Sony Pictures Studios
summary: In Culver City, a studio lot founded in 1912 has hosted the filming of some of the most iconic movies ever made — from The Wizard of Oz to Gone with the Wind to Star Wars — and still produces films, television, and music recordings under its current Japanese owners.

subject: Soo Locks
summary: These parallel locks on the St. Marys River pass 10,000 ships a year between Lake Superior and the lower Great Lakes, making them one of the busiest and most critical chokepoints in North American commerce.

subject: Sooke
summary: Where Vancouver Island's road system starts to run out, a debt-ridden Scottish captain bought the colony's first private farm, three broom seeds took root, and a gold rush came and went in a single season.

subject: Sorbian Settlement Area
summary: The homeland of Germany's indigenous Slavic minority, a territory whose borders had to be fixed by law because they could never be fixed by counting.

subject: Sorbie
summary: A small Machars village whose disused creamery, T-plan kirk and ancestral tower mark the slow ebb of Galloway industry alongside the deep tide of clan history.

subject: Sorley MacLean
summary: The Raasay-born Gaelic poet whose lament for a cleared village became one of the twentieth century's great elegies.

subject: Sorrento
summary: Perched on cliffs above the Bay of Naples, Sorrento serves as the gateway to the Amalfi Coast, Capri, Pompeii, and Herculaneum — a town built on lemons, limoncello, and the art of the long evening.

subject: Sossusvlei
summary: A clay pan ringed by some of the tallest sand dunes on Earth in the world's oldest desert, where dead trees have stood perfectly preserved for centuries because there is not enough moisture for them to decompose.

subject: Soul City, North Carolina
summary: A civil rights leader's audacious attempt to build a brand-new city for Black economic empowerment on a former tobacco plantation in rural North Carolina became one of America's most ambitious and tragic experiments in planned community development.

subject: Souli
summary: High in the mountains of Thesprotia, the Souliotes built a warlike Orthodox community that resisted Ottoman rule for generations — until Ali Pasha finally broke them in 1803, forcing a tragic exodus that became one of the defining stories of Greek resistance.

subject: Sound of Mull
summary: The narrow Atlantic channel separating Mull from mainland Scotland - a corridor of ferries, lighthouses, and at least four shipwrecks that still attract divers from across Europe.

subject: Sounion Kouros
summary: Carved around 600 BCE from Naxian marble and standing over three meters tall, the Sounion Kouros is one of the earliest colossal Greek sculptures — a nude youth poised on the threshold between Egypt and something entirely new.

subject: South African Republic
summary: For fifty years a landlocked Boer republic called the Transvaal held out north of the Vaal River, growing rich on gold and ending in one of the most controversial wars of the British Empire.

subject: South Andros
summary: The remote southern third of the Bahamas' largest island, where the mail boat brings everything from milk to petrol once a week, the road ends at Mars Bay, and the world-famous bonefish flats draw anglers to one of the Caribbean's least-developed coasts.

subject: South Australia
summary: The only Australian state founded entirely by free settlers, South Australia stretches from world-class wine country and festival culture in Adelaide to some of the continent's most forbidding desert.

subject: South Bank Parklands
summary: Brisbane threw a world's fair, then refused to let the party end, turning the Expo site into a beloved riverside park with its own beach.

subject: South Bend, Washington
summary: A tiny Pacific County seat that calls itself the Oyster Capital of the World, South Bend won its courthouse by raiding the old county seat across Willapa Bay and hauling the records away by steamboat.

subject: South Bronx
summary: The neighborhood that America watched burn on live television during the 1977 World Series went on to birth hip-hop, rebuild from the ashes, and remain the poorest congressional district in the nation.

subject: South Crofty
summary: On a March afternoon in 1998, the last shift came out of South Crofty and a 400-year tradition of working Cornish tin went silent, sealed underwater for the next quarter-century.

subject: South Galway Station
summary: On a Cooper Creek cattle run where half the land floods, a 1951 pilot flew a biplane low over the water to muster a marooned herd to safety.

subject: South Kaibab Trail
summary: Built by the National Park Service in 1924 to break a toll-charging senator's monopoly, the South Kaibab Trail rewards hikers with unobstructed 360-degree views of the Grand Canyon.

subject: South Kerry Greenway
summary: A thirty-two-kilometre walking and cycling trail being built along the bed of a railway closed in 1960 - delayed by a decade of legal challenges that reached the Irish Supreme Court, with the first sections opening in late 2025.

subject: South Kordofan
summary: A Sudanese state centered on the Nuba Mountains, South Kordofan holds pro-South Sudan communities who fought alongside southern rebels and have been bombed, displaced, and targeted by the Khartoum government in the years since independence split the country in two.

subject: South Limburg
summary: The Dutch call it 'a piece of abroad in the Netherlands' — a hilly, Catholic, sweet-and-sour panhandle that quarries marl, drinks Brand beer, and looks more like Belgium than Holland.

subject: South Papua
summary: Indonesia's least populous province is a land of swamps, sago forests, and Asmat woodcarvers, where 30-meter treehouses overlook rivers choked with wild sugarcane and headhunting is still within living memory.

subject: South Queensferry
summary: A medieval royal burgh under three iconic bridges, where Queen Margaret's eleventh-century ferry crossing gave way to a town that still celebrates a man covered head-to-toe in burrs.

subject: South Rona
summary: An uninhabited Hebridean island whose tiny natural harbour was once known as Port of the Robbers and is now home to a population of one.

subject: South San Francisco Hillside Sign
summary: Giant concrete letters spelling 'SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO THE INDUSTRIAL CITY' have adorned Sign Hill since the 1920s, visible to every plane descending into SFO.

subject: South Shields
summary: A Tyne-mouth town with a Roman fort, Viking shipwrecks, the oldest Muslim community in Britain, and a Muhammad Ali wedding blessing.

subject: South Stoa I (Athens)
summary: A shabby, mudbrick building on the edge of the Athenian Agora was where the city's bureaucrats ate dinner - and one of its rooms still preserves the receipt for a set of official weights handed from one year's inspectors to the next.

subject: South Sudan
summary: The world's newest widely-recognized country is a land of Nilotic peoples, the enormous Sudd swamp, and a population that voted 98.83 percent for independence in 2011 - only to plunge into civil war two years later, and to keep rebuilding through floods, famine, and fragile peace.

story.title: South Sulawesi: Where Kingdoms Built Ships and Honor Demanded Blood

subject: South Sulawesi
summary: A province shaped by warring kingdoms, master shipbuilders, and a cultural code so fierce that its people would rather die than live without honor.

subject: South Uist
summary: A 25-mile Hebridean island with white-shell beaches, boggy mountains, a missile range, and a community-owned future - and a population that mostly still speaks Gaelic and is mostly Roman Catholic.

subject: South Uist
summary: An island built on 2.9-billion-year-old rock that holds Britain's only prehistoric mummies, the birthplace of Flora MacDonald, and a Gaelic-Catholic culture that survived clearances, conscription, and the Cold War.

subject: South West Africa
summary: The territory that became Namibia passed through German colonial rule, a League of Nations mandate, decades of illegal South African occupation and apartheid, and a protracted independence struggle before finally becoming a nation in 1990.

story.title: South of Market Leather History Alley

subject: South of Market Leather History Alley
summary: Bronze bootprints embedded in a SoMa alleyway honor 28 individuals who built San Francisco's leather community, from bar owners and publishers to the creator of the leather pride flag.

subject: Southeast (Brazil)
summary: The cultural and economic engine of Brazil, holding three of its four largest cities and the ghosts of its gold and coffee centuries.

story.title: Southeast Sulawesi: The Province That Ferries Built

subject: Southeast Sulawesi
summary: No highway connects Southeast Sulawesi to the rest of its island. Ferries, fortresses, and an archipelago of culturally distinct islands define this province on the far edge of Wallacea.

subject: Southern Court
summary: An exiled imperial court in the mountains of Yoshino that lost every battle but won the argument -- centuries later, Japan declared its defeated emperors the only legitimate rulers of the Nanboku-cho era.

subject: Southern Highlands Province
summary: Nearly a million people speaking more than eight major languages share a province that stretches from Papua New Guinea's second-tallest mountain to the volcanic lowlands of Mount Bosavi, rich in natural gas, endemic fish, and political turbulence.

subject: Southern Laos
summary: A vast, culturally layered region where the Mekong forms the western border, the Annamite mountains form the east, and thousands of islands, ancient temples, and minority communities fill the space between.

subject: Southern Marmara
summary: The great peninsula south of the Sea of Marmara — home to Troy, Bursa, Bird Paradise, and 3,000 years of Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman crossroads history.

subject: Southern Patagonian Ice Field
summary: The largest mass of ice outside the poles with land access — a 350-kilometer plateau of frozen Andes that feeds dozens of glaciers and hides volcanoes beneath its surface.

subject: Southern Patagonian Ice Field dispute
summary: On a frozen plateau where no one lives, Chile and Argentina still cannot agree where one country ends and the other begins — the last unfinished stretch of their 5,000-kilometer border.

subject: Southern Province, Zambia
summary: Home to Victoria Falls, Lake Kariba, and most of Zambia's maize, Southern Province is the country's breadbasket and its showcase - an uplifted plateau where tourism, farming, and coal dig all share the same geography.

subject: Southern Red Sea region
summary: Eritrea's hottest, driest, and most sparsely populated province stretches 500 kilometers along the Red Sea coast through the Danakil Desert, holding the port of Assab and some of the most extreme climate on the African continent.

subject: Southern Ute Indian Reservation
summary: Once given a third of Colorado, the Southern Ute people now hold a narrow strip of their ancestral homeland where forested mountains meet arid mesa, and where a modern tribe turns coalbed methane into carbon offsets.

subject: Southern region (Eritrea)
summary: The most populous region of Eritrea, formed in 1996 from the historical provinces of Seraye and Akele Guzai, containing Mount Soira at 3,018 meters - Eritrea's highest peak - and the archaeological sites of Metera, Qohaito, and Mendefera.

subject: Southorn Playground
summary: Wan Chai's main gathering ground since the 1930s, Southorn Playground was reclaimed from the harbour, named for a colonial secretary, and survived Japanese occupation, the MTR's arrival, and a World Trade Organization ministerial conference — while remaining a place where senior citizens play chess and young players build street basketball reputations.

subject: Southport
summary: A Victorian seaside town on the Lancashire coast with the longest covered shopping canopy in Britain, Royal Birkdale's championship dunes, and a habit of welcoming strangers into a tightly knit community.

subject: Southside (Richmond, Virginia)
summary: Before 1788 you needed a boat. Now four highways, two beltways, and nine bridges connect the south bank to the city - and the Southside is finally Richmond's other half.

subject: Southwick, Sunderland
summary: A former Wear-side village that made bottles, blew glass, built ships, and finally lost all three to the twentieth century's great industrial subtractions.

subject: Soutpansberg
summary: South Africa's northernmost mountain range packs more reptiles into a few ridges than most of the country combined, and shelters a sacred Venda lake guarded, the people say, by a python god.

subject: Soyo
summary: At the mouth of the Congo River, a province of the Kingdom of Kongo fought its way to independence, routed a Portuguese invasion, and five centuries later became Angola's largest oil-producing region.

subject: Spaans Lagoen
summary: Aruba's only inner bay, Spaans Lagoen is a Ramsar-designated wetland forged during the last ice age, where mangrove forests, tidal mudflats, and volcanic rock converge in a compact ecological mosaic.

subject: Space Sciences Laboratory
summary: A hilltop lab born from the Space Race that has sent instruments on more than 100 satellites, flown 150 balloons, and launched the world's largest search for extraterrestrial intelligence.

subject: Space Shuttle Endeavour
summary: The youngest of the space shuttles, built to replace Challenger, flew 25 missions before completing its final journey through the streets of Los Angeles to its permanent home at the California Science Center.

subject: Spaceship Earth (Epcot)
summary: A 180-foot geodesic sphere housing a dark ride through 40,000 years of human communication, co-designed by science fiction writer Ray Bradbury and engineered so that rainwater never touches the ground.

subject: Spaghetti Junction
summary: The world's most famous tangle of roads got its name from a Birmingham sub-editor in 1965, and the phrase has stuck to interchanges from Atlanta to Auckland ever since.

subject: Spalding, Lincolnshire
summary: A Lincolnshire market town in the heart of the Fens, where tulip petals built floats, where Dutch merchants set up a flower industry, and where the first UK barcode was scanned.

subject: Spanish Armada
summary: In 1588, 130 Spanish ships sailed to invade Protestant England. Fireships at Calais and Atlantic storms off Ireland destroyed the Enterprise of England.

subject: Spanish Town
summary: Jamaica's forgotten capital, where three centuries of colonial rule left an architectural palimpsest and a musical legacy that echoes far beyond the Caribbean.

subject: Spanish Wells
summary: A tiny Bahamian fishing community on St. George's Cay where Spanish treasure fleets once filled their water casks, shipwrecked Bermudian colonists washed ashore in 1647, and lobstermen still head out on weeks-long smack trips across the shallow banks.

subject: Spanish conquest of Guatemala
summary: A two-century campaign to subjugate Guatemala's Maya peoples, from the first Caribbean landings in 1524 to the bloody fall of the last independent Maya capital on Lake Peten Itza in 1697.

subject: Spanish missions in Baja California
summary: A chain of 30 religious outposts that stretched the length of Baja California between 1683 and 1834, where Jesuits, Franciscans, and Dominicans transformed and devastated indigenous cultures.

subject: Sparkbrook
summary: An inner-city Birmingham ward where Joseph Priestley discovered oxygen in his garden, Sampson Lloyd founded a bank, and a generation of immigrants invented the balti.

subject: Sparta, Laconia
summary: Modern Sparti was laid out on a royal decree in 1834 on the site of the ancient city — a planned town built from scratch among ruins, now the quiet capital of Laconia with a population of around 18,000.

subject: Spartanburg
summary: An Upstate South Carolina city built where six Revolutionary War engagements happened in four weeks, then reinvented as a railroad hub, then a textile capital, then BMW's American foothold.

subject: Spata
summary: A town of layered identities on the Mesogeia plain east of Athens — Mycenaean cemetery, medieval Albanian clan settlement, retsina country, and now the home of Greece's busiest airport.

story.title: Speaking in Layers: The Balinese Language

subject: Speaking in Layers
summary: Balinese is one of the few languages in the world where the words you choose depend not just on what you want to say, but on who you are saying it to -- a register system so elaborate that speaking to your priest, your friend, and your child may require three entirely different vocabularies.

subject: Spencer, West Virginia
summary: The seat of Roane County, home to the West Virginia Black Walnut Festival and the oldest continuously operating movie theater in the country.

subject: Spenceville Wildlife Area
summary: A ghost town turned wildlife preserve in the Sierra Nevada foothills, where copper mines, a vanished 19th-century community, and Maidu grinding stones share 11,448 acres of oak woodland and waterfall trails.

subject: Spenger's Fresh Fish Grotto
summary: A Berkeley seafood institution that grew from a ten-cent clam stand in 1890 into a maritime wonderland, only to close 128 years later and scatter its treasures at auction.

subject: Spetses
summary: A car-free Saronic island that threw itself into the Greek War of Independence with its merchant fleet and its extraordinary naval captain Laskarina Bouboulina, Spetses still commemorates the 1822 Battle of Spetses each September with fire on the harbor.

subject: Speyside Way
summary: A long-distance Highland trail tracing the Spey from the Moray coast up through whisky country to the Cairngorms.

subject: Spice Run Wilderness
summary: A 6,000-acre federal wilderness in the Monongahela National Forest with no road access - reachable only by fording the Greenbrier River or walking in through Calvin Price State Forest.

subject: Spicers Gap Road
summary: A hand-built mountain road over the Main Range, hacked through bog and scrub to haul Darling Downs wool to the coast, abandoned almost the moment the railway arrived, and now the best-preserved piece of 1860s road engineering in Queensland.

subject: Spindletop
summary: The gusher that changed the world - where oil exploded 150 feet into the air on January 10, 1901, launching the Texas oil boom and transforming global energy forever.

subject: Spinnenkop Wedderveer
summary: A spider-head sawmill built in 1938 to cut a man's own oak plantation, now one of only two windmills in the Netherlands that still use its peculiar winding system.

subject: Spire of Dublin
summary: A 120-metre stainless steel needle on O'Connell Street, raised in 2003 where Nelson's Pillar had stood until republicans blew it up in 1966.

story.title: Spiro Mounds: The Archaeological Crime of the Century

subject: Spiro Mounds
summary: The Oklahoma burial site where commercial looters dynamited their way into the richest undisturbed ceremonial chamber in North America - selling priceless artifacts by the truckload before outraged archaeologists could stop them, destroying context that can never be recovered.

subject: Spiro Mounds
summary: The Oklahoma site where Depression-era looters dynamited sacred Native American burial mounds to sell artifacts - accidentally destroying one of the most important pre-Columbian ceremonial centers in North America.

subject: Spitalfields
summary: For over eight centuries, Spitalfields in East London has been a landing place for people fleeing persecution — Huguenots, Irish weavers, Jewish refugees, Bangladeshi immigrants — each community leaving its mark on Brick Lane and the streets around it.

subject: Spitzkoppe
summary: Granite inselbergs nicknamed the Matterhorn of Namibia rise from flat desert plains, sheltering San rock art, rock hyraxes, and campsites run by a local women's cooperative.

subject: Splendid China Folk Village
summary: A 30-hectare park in Shenzhen where more than 100 of China's most famous landmarks have been faithfully miniaturized at 1:15 scale, letting visitors traverse the entire country in a single afternoon.

subject: Split
summary: Where Diocletian's retirement palace became a living city, where Roman walls hold medieval churches and modern bars, where Croatia's Adriatic coast concentrates.

story.title: Spokane: The Lilac City Where the Inland Northwest Meets

subject: Spokane
summary: The eastern Washington city between mountains and prairie - where the falls powered early industry, where Expo '74 cleaned the riverfront, and where the affordable alternative to Seattle attracts those priced out of the coast.

subject: Spokane
summary: The heart of the Inland Empire where waterfalls thunder through downtown and the Centennial Trail connects two states along the river that gave the city its name.

subject: Spook Hill
summary: A stretch of road in Lake Wales, Florida, where cars placed in neutral appear to roll uphill -- an optical illusion born from ancient geology, draped in ghost stories, and famous enough to land on the front page of the Wall Street Journal.

subject: Sportpark Berg & Bos
summary: An Asian longhorn beetle nearly toppled the most beautiful grandstand in Gelderland - and a striker's plea on the internet kept it standing.

subject: Sportpark De Toekomst
summary: Ajax's training complex on the southern edge of Amsterdam, literally named The Future, where the club's reserves, women's team, and amateurs share nine pitches beside the senior team's daily drills.

subject: Sportpark Het Schootsveld
summary: A modest cricket ground in the eastern Netherlands where a Scotland-Ireland tie became the international rulebook's most embarrassing footnote.

subject: Spouting Horn
summary: A natural blowhole on Kauai's south coast where ocean waves force through a lava tube to shoot spray fifty feet into the air, accompanied by a hissing roar that Hawaiian legend attributes to a trapped giant lizard.

subject: Sprague's Super Service
summary: A 1931 Tudor Revival gas station on Route 66, built to fit in with the surrounding homes.

subject: Spreepark
summary: East Germany's only permanent amusement park went bankrupt, shipped six of its rides to Peru, and ended in a cocaine conviction — then spent twenty years rusting in a Berlin forest before the city started bringing it back.

subject: Spreetshoogte Pass
summary: Namibia's steepest mountain pass plunges nearly a kilometer off the Great Escarpment in just four kilometers of road, built stone by stone by a single farmer.

subject: Spreewald
summary: An hour south of Berlin the Spree stops behaving like a river and splits into 1,300 kilometres of channels, where the post still arrives by punt and the pickles have EU protection.

subject: Spring Scream
summary: Two American expatriates started a small beach music festival in Taiwan in 1995; at its peak, Spring Scream hosted up to 300 acts on 8 stages at the edge of the South China Sea before the festival wound down around 2018–2019.

subject: Spring and Autumn Pavilions
summary: Twin octagonal towers on Lotus Pond in Kaohsiung built because the Goddess of Mercy appeared on a dragon in the clouds and told people to put her there.

subject: Springbok
summary: Namaqualand's largest town sits in a valley ringed by hills, where South Africa's first commercial copper mine turned the earth blue, and nearly half the plant species found here exist nowhere else on the planet.

story.title: Springfield: The City Where Basketball Was Invented

subject: Springfield
summary: The Massachusetts city where James Naismith hung a peach basket - where basketball began, where the armory made rifles for a nation, and where the population dropped by half.

story.title: The Magic in the Wheat Field: The Story of Springfield's Muni Opera

subject: Springfield Municipal Opera
summary: From a nomadic series of park performances to a 55-acre wheat field, the Springfield Municipal Opera overcame devastating fires and financial hurdles to become one of the Midwest's largest self-supporting community theaters.

story.title: The Land of Lincoln and the Seat of Power

subject: Springfield, Illinois
summary: Springfield, Illinois, is a city defined by its role as the state capital and its enduring connection to Abraham Lincoln. From its origins as "Calhoun" to the political lobbying of the "Long Nine," the city has evolved into a hub of government and history. While it celebrates its architectural grandeur and Lincoln's legacy, Springfield also grapples with the trauma of the 1908 race riot and seeks an equitable future through community-led redevelopment in areas like South Town.

subject: Sprogø
summary: For thirty-eight years this small island in the Great Belt was a place the Danish state sent women it had declared morally defective — roughly five hundred of them, almost all sterilised before release.

subject: Sproul Plaza
summary: The concrete stage where the Free Speech Movement found its voice and six decades of Berkeley activism have played out under pollarded plane trees.

story.title: Spruce Knob-Seneca Rocks National Recreation Area

subject: Spruce Knob-Seneca Rocks National Recreation Area
summary: The first national recreation area inside any U.S. National Forest, established in 1965 to protect West Virginia's highest peak, its most famous climbing crag, and a Potomac canyon.

subject: Spuistraat
summary: A medieval defensive canal, then a smelly ditch, then a tram line, then a punk squat. Spuistraat keeps becoming something else.

subject: Spurn
summary: A three-and-a-half-mile sand finger curling into the North Sea, where lost medieval towns sleep beneath the waves and a 213-year lifeboat tradition only just ended.

subject: Spuyten Duyvil Creek
summary: A turbulent tidal creek whose devilish name and engineered transformation reshaped the boundary between Manhattan and the Bronx.

subject: Sq'éwlets First Nation
summary: A Sto:lo community on Harrison Bay whose ancestral hill holds 198 burial mounds, and which helped change how archaeology is done on Indigenous ground.

subject: Square Peristyle
summary: An enormous, never-finished law court built for thousands of Athenian jurors - abandoned mid-construction and now buried beneath the Stoa of Attalos.

subject: Squares of Savannah, Georgia
summary: Twenty-two leafy squares form the heartbeat of Savannah's historic district, a radical 1733 urban plan born from military tactics and London's fire-scarred memory.

subject: Sri Ksetra kingdom
summary: The largest city in Southeast Asia before Angkor, Sri Ksetra was a Pyu civilization center whose monumental brick walls enclosed nearly 1,900 hectares along the Irrawaddy River -- and whose golden Pali manuscripts may be the oldest surviving texts in that sacred language.

subject: St Abbs
summary: A tiny Berwickshire fishing village that doubled as Asgard in the Marvel Cinematic Universe and shelters Britain's first marine reserve.

subject: St Abbs Lifeboat Station
summary: A Berwickshire lifeboat station founded in 1911 after the Alfred Erlandsen wreck, withdrawn by the RNLI in 2015 against community wishes, and reopened months later as an independent charity.

story.title: St Agnes Lifeboat Station, Isles of Scilly

subject: St Agnes Lifeboat Station, Isles of Scilly
summary: A thousand-foot slipway of Australian Jarrah wood and a December night in 1907 when a father drowned, a son swam after the captain, and the United States struck gold medals for the rowers of an open boat.

subject: St Andrews
summary: A small Scottish town where the world's oldest golf course, Scotland's oldest university, and the ruins of its medieval ecclesiastical capital converge on a windswept headland above the North Sea.

subject: St Bees Lifeboat Station
summary: A small RNLI station on Cumbria's westernmost headland, where a boat named for a World War widow's husband has saved 125 lives.

subject: St Bees Priory
summary: A Cumbrian priory where a 14th-century knight was found buried with his skin, nails, and stomach contents perfectly preserved after 600 years.

subject: St Conan's Kirk
summary: A lochside Scottish kirk built and rebuilt by one obsessive amateur architect, blending Roman, Norman, and Celtic styles, and housing what's said to be a fragment of Robert the Bruce.

subject: St Davids
summary: Britain's smallest city, where the patron saint of Wales was born, lived, died, and is still drawing pilgrims fifteen hundred years later.

subject: St Davids Lifeboat Station
summary: A working RNLI station at St Justinian's, founded in 1869 and credited with saving over 360 lives, including the night in 1910 that cost three crewmen their own.

subject: St Dogmaels
summary: A Pembrokeshire village where 12th-century abbey ruins, a medieval mill that still grinds flour, and the long northern terminus of the Pembrokeshire Coast Path meet at the mouth of the Teifi.

subject: St Gwenfaen's Well
summary: A medieval holy well in a cleft of rock above Hawk Bay on Holy Island -- where the offering is two white quartz pebbles, and the cure, by long tradition, is for the trouble of the mind.

subject: St Helen's, Isles of Scilly
summary: A small uninhabited island where Bronze Age cairns, an 8th-century hermitage, and a Georgian plague quarantine sit within a few hundred yards of each other.

subject: St Ives Lifeboat Station
summary: In a single year between 1938 and 1939 the St Ives lifeboat capsized twice and lost thirteen crewmen — and the Cocking family kept sending sons back to sea.

subject: St Ives, Cambridgeshire
summary: The Cambridgeshire market town that gave its name to a famous nursery rhyme - founded by Anglo-Saxons as Slepe, renamed after a saint conjured up by monks, home to Oliver Cromwell for five years, and the place where Clive Sinclair built the first pocket calculator.

subject: St Ives, Cornwall
summary: Four kinds of people came to St Ives for four different reasons, and the small Cornish fishing town let each of them believe it was theirs.

subject: St James's Square
summary: London's most powerful square, where seven dukes and seven earls once lived side by side, and where Operation Overlord was planned—a single Georgian garden holding centuries of British power.

subject: St John's, Isle of Man
summary: Every 5 July, a small Manx village holds an open-air parliament on a four-tiered grass mound, reading new laws in English and Manx to whoever shows up.

subject: St Just in Penwith
summary: The most westerly town in mainland Britain, a 19th-century mining capital that sent its sons to Bendigo and Nevada City, and whose medieval playing place is still hosting plays in the Cornish language.

subject: St Kilda
summary: Melbourne's bayside playground, where a laughing clown's mouth, a fairy penguin colony, and a hundred and fifty years of glamour and grit all share one stretch of sand.

subject: St Kilda, Scotland
summary: Britain's most remote inhabited archipelago, evacuated in 1930 after millennia of human settlement, where the highest sea cliffs in the UK guard a dual UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: St Mark's Clocktower
summary: Two bronze 'Moors' have struck the hours atop Venice's clock tower since 1499, guarding a face that tracks the sun, moon, and zodiac over the entrance to the city's most important street.

subject: St Mary Redcliffe
summary: The Bristol parish church Queen Elizabeth I called the fairest in England - a 274-foot Gothic spire, a tram rail blasted into the churchyard by the Blitz, and bells that ring across the city.

subject: St Mary's Lifeboat Station
summary: One gold medal, nine silver, sixteen bronze - the receipts of nearly two centuries spent pulling sailors out of the Atlantic off the southwestern edge of England.

story.title: St Mary's by the Sea, Port Douglas

subject: St Mary's by the Sea, Port Douglas
summary: A little white timber church on the Port Douglas foreshore, built after a cyclone, saved by its town, and now framed by a window that opens straight onto the water.

subject: St Mary's, Isles of Scilly
summary: On the largest of the Scilly Isles, an eight-pointed star castle still guards a town built for fishermen, lifeboat crews, and Admirals who washed ashore in 1707.

subject: St Neots
summary: A Cambridgeshire market town founded around the bones of a 9th-century Cornish saint, scarred by a brutal Civil War battle in 1648, and grown by London overspill into the largest town in Huntingdonshire.

subject: St Patrick's Purgatory
summary: On a small island in a Donegal lake, pilgrims have been locked in a cave for twenty-four hours, fasting and praying, since the twelfth century. The cave was sealed in 1632, but pilgrims still come.

subject: St Stephen's Green
summary: Dublin's 22-acre Georgian garden square - briefly an Irish Citizen Army trench in 1916, given to the city by a Guinness, and named for a medieval leper hospital.

story.title: St. Augustine: The Oldest City in America (That Europeans Built)

subject: St. Augustine
summary: The Florida settlement founded by Spanish conquistadors in 1565 - older than Jamestown, older than Plymouth, the longest continuously occupied European-established city in America, built on land that Indigenous peoples had occupied for thousands of years.

story.title: St. Augustine: America's Oldest City (If You Don't Count the Others)

subject: St. Augustine
summary: The Florida city that claims to be America's oldest continuously occupied European settlement - older than Jamestown, older than Plymouth, though Taos Pueblo and San Juan would like a word about who was here first.

subject: St. Augustine
summary: The city founded by Spain in 1565, 42 years before Jamestown, where the Castillo de San Marcos still guards the harbor, and where Florida's Spanish history survived even British occupation.

subject: St. Augustine, Florida
summary: The oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the contiguous United States, where Spanish conquistadors, British Loyalists, Gilded Age tycoons, and civil rights marchers have all walked the same narrow streets.

subject: St. George's
summary: Grenada's capital city wraps around a volcanic crater turned harbor, where French forts, British churches, and Caribbean color layer centuries of contested history into a few steep streets.

story.title: St. Louis: Gateway to the West

subject: St. Louis
summary: The city where the Mississippi meets the Missouri, where the Gateway Arch rises 630 feet above the riverfront, and where Eero Saarinen's gleaming monument marks where western expansion began.

subject: St. Mary's City, Maryland
summary: Maryland's first European settlement and colonial capital, founded in 1634 as a haven for persecuted Catholics, where the fourth oldest English colony in America now lies buried beneath farm fields and a college campus, slowly being pieced back together by archaeologists.

subject: St. Walfriduskerk
summary: The tower of a small church in the Groningen village of Bedum leans further forward than the Leaning Tower of Pisa - and has been doing so since the Middle Ages.

subject: Stadion An der Alten Försterei
summary: Union Berlin's supporters dug up and rebuilt their own terraces in 2008 rather than leave Köpenick, and every December they fill the ground with candles to sing carols.

subject: Stadland
summary: Four villages, a windmill, a nuclear power station, and a tunnel under the Weser. A municipality born in a 1974 reform on land mostly reclaimed from the sea.

subject: Stadsaal Caves
summary: In the Cederberg's sandstone halls, San rock paintings up to 8,000 years old share wall space with modern graffiti -- including the signatures of two future prime ministers of South Africa.

subject: Stadskanaal
summary: A town built in a straight line along a canal the city of Groningen dug in secret, starting in 1762, to mine peat out from under its neighbor.

subject: Staffa
summary: A tiny uninhabited island of hexagonal basalt columns in the Inner Hebrides, where Fingal's Cave inspired Mendelssohn's Hebrides Overture and the Vikings saw the pillars of their own buildings.

subject: Staithes
summary: A Yorkshire fishing village pressed into a narrow cleft in the cliffs, where a teenaged James Cook served a grocer's apprenticeship before running away to sea, where fishermen refuse to say the word 'pig', and where one alley is just 18 inches wide.

subject: Staley Field
summary: Staley Field served as the home for the Decatur Staleys, an industrial team that transitioned into a professional powerhouse and charter member of the NFL before relocating to become the Chicago Bears.

subject: Stamford, Lincolnshire
summary: England's first conservation area, designated in 1967 to protect a Georgian and Jacobean limestone town that the Industrial Revolution largely ignored, on the old Great North Road.

story.title: Stand-off at the Fords of Arkaig

subject: Stand-off at the Fords of Arkaig
summary: A week-long armed confrontation in September 1665 that ended a 360-year clan dispute over the lands around Loch Arkaig, settled by a cash sale instead of bloodshed.

subject: Standing Rock Sioux Reservation
summary: Straddling the border of North and South Dakota, the Standing Rock Reservation became the center of the largest gathering of Native American tribes in a century when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the Missouri River -- the reservation's sole water supply.

subject: Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource
summary: Born as a 'hole in the wall' off a particle collider in 1972, SSRL grew into a national facility where 2,000 scientists a year use light brighter than the sun to study everything from drug design to environmental cleanup.

subject: Staniel Cay
summary: A tiny Bahamian island of fewer than 120 residents where James Bond filmed underwater, loyalist settlers built a village, and the annual regatta pits visiting yachts against traditional Bahamian sloops.

subject: Stanley (Tasmania)
summary: A weatherboard fishing village in Tasmania's far northwest huddles at the foot of The Nut, a 143-metre volcanic plug that looms over every street.

subject: Stanley, Hong Kong
summary: A coastal town on southern Hong Kong Island whose Cantonese name means 'Red Pillar' — first capital of the British colony, site of a wartime massacre and internment camp, and today a market town where expats, prisoners, and hikers share an improbable peninsula.

subject: Star of India
summary: Built in 1863 and named after Euterpe, the Greek muse of music, this iron-hulled sailing ship survived a mutinous crew, cyclones, and decades of neglect to become the oldest ship in the world still sailing regularly.

subject: Star-Club
summary: A Hamburg cinema bought to satisfy a fire regulation became the loudest room in Europe - and the stage where the Beatles finished their apprenticeship.

subject: Starstreet Precinct
summary: A hilltop neighborhood in Wan Chai where Hong Kong's first power station once lit the streets, and celestial names—Sun, Moon, Star—still mark the lanes today.

subject: Staryi Krym
summary: The quiet Crimean town that once gave the entire peninsula its name, a former capital of the Golden Horde now known mostly for gardens and a beloved writer's grave.

subject: State Archives (Belgium)
summary: Three hundred and twenty-five kilometres of paper, 38,000 seal moulds, and 27,000 digitised parish registers - the Belgian State Archives is the institutional memory of a country still working through its own colonial past.

subject: State of Franklin
summary: America's 'Lost State' lasted four and a half years in the 1780s, a breakaway republic in the Appalachian Mountains that tried to become the 14th state, courted Spanish rule, and vanished into Tennessee.

subject: State of Katanga
summary: A mineral-rich breakaway state born from Cold War maneuvering and corporate greed, Katanga's three-year secession reshaped the Congo and left scars that endure.

subject: Staunton
summary: A Shenandoah Valley city of about 25,000 with a remarkably intact Victorian downtown, the birthplace of Woodrow Wilson, and one of the world's only recreations of Shakespeare's indoor theater.

subject: Stavoren
summary: The oldest city in Friesland, ruined by its own pride according to legend - and silted into obscurity according to history.

subject: Steamboat Jenny Lind
summary: A ferry named after a Swedish opera star that exploded in San Francisco Bay in 1853, killing at least 31 people and directly spurring construction of the San Francisco and San Jose Railroad.

subject: Steck-Salathe Route
summary: A sweltering five-day first ascent in 1950 opened a route up Sentinel Rock that would become one of America's fifty classic climbs - famous for its punishing chimneys, its place in big-wall history, and the tragedy that haunts it.

subject: Stedman, California
summary: A Mojave Desert ghost town where Scandinavian miners nicknamed their camp 'Copenhagen,' water was piped in from miles away, and a 1932 thunderstorm washed away nearly a mile of railroad.

subject: Steel Dragon 2000
summary: A record-shattering giga coaster at Nagashima Spa Land, built with enough steel to withstand Japanese earthquakes and named for the Year of the Dragon.

subject: Steep Point
summary: The westernmost tip of mainland Australia — a sand-track pilgrimage to the place that sees the continent's final sunset, where the open ocean has thrown up both tsunamis and an unforgettable tale of survival.

subject: Steetley Colliery
summary: A single-shaft pit on the Derbyshire-Nottinghamshire border that solved its ventilation problem by drilling tunnels to its neighbour, and gave its name to the village of Rhodesia.

subject: Stegner Fellowship
summary: Silicon Valley's most improbable export: a creative writing fellowship that has produced Ken Kesey, Raymond Carver, Larry McMurtry, and a remarkable concentration of American literary talent.

subject: Steinfurt
summary: A stony ford on the river Aa grew into a Calvinist-Mennonite island in Catholic Munsterland, ringed by four gates and crowned by one of Westphalia's loveliest moated castles.

subject: Steinsdalsfossen
summary: A 46-meter waterfall near Norheimsund where visitors walk behind the curtain of falling water -- a spectacle that kept Kaiser Wilhelm II returning every summer for twenty-five years.

subject: Steinway & Sons
summary: A charcoal burner's son from the Harz built his first piano as a wedding present, emigrated to New York, and thirty years later his family shipped the company back to Hamburg to get around a tariff.

subject: Stellenbosch
summary: South Africa's second-oldest town hides its street names in yellow paint along the sidewalk edges, lines its avenues with ancient oaks, and produces wines that rank among the best in the world -- all within 50 km of Cape Town.

subject: Stenbjerg
summary: Drifting sand buried the fields behind Stenbjerg and turned its farmers into fishermen; three centuries later the fishery is gone and the little white gear sheds on the beach are what the village kept.

subject: Stennis Space Center
summary: NASA's largest rocket engine test facility, built on the erased remains of five Mississippi communities whose sacrifice helped send humans to the Moon.

subject: Stevenage
summary: Britain's first post-war New Town, designated in 1946 over the protests of its own residents, built around six self-contained neighbourhoods and an engineer's vision of completely segregated cycle paths, and home to seven-time Formula One world champion Lewis Hamilton.

subject: Stevenson
summary: The county seat of Skamania where Beacon Rock rises from the Columbia and the Bridge of the Gods crosses to Oregon.

subject: Stevenston
summary: An Ayrshire town built on Scotland's first commercial canal, ICI's explosives factories, and the dunes where Robert Burns met the woman he called the most elegant in the world.

subject: Stewarton
summary: An East Ayrshire town once famed for bonnet-making, where Robert Burns's uncle stood guard against body snatchers and the founder of New Lanark's cotton mills was born.

subject: Steyl
summary: On the Dutch bank of the Meuse, a wine merchant's village reinvented itself as a colony of missionary monasteries, founded by a priest fleeing Bismarck's Germany.

subject: Stilbaai Tidal Fish Traps
summary: Stone walls in the surf along South Africa's Western Cape coast trap fish at low tide just as they have for thousands of years, maintained by the same hands-on method our ancestors invented.

subject: Still Hacking Anyway
summary: For five days in August 2017, a Dutch scout camp near Zeewolde hosted 3,300 hackers from 50 countries - with gigabit Ethernet plumbed into the portable toilets and Phil Zimmermann on the main stage.

subject: Stiltsville
summary: A renegade village of wooden houses perched on stilts above Biscayne Bay, where bootleggers, bikini clubs, and Florida governors once escaped the mainland for a lawless paradise on the water.

subject: Stirling
summary: He who holds Stirling holds Scotland: a city on a volcanic plug at the lowest crossing of the Forth, clasping Highlands and Lowlands together.

subject: Stoa Basileios
summary: The small Royal Stoa where Athens kept its laws on stone - and where Socrates was summoned to answer the charge that would kill him.

subject: Stockbridge, Edinburgh
summary: A New Town neighbourhood where Henry Raeburn designed streets, James Clerk Maxwell was born, the first international rugby match was played, and the Royal Botanic Garden is a few minutes' walk away.

subject: Stockholm Bloodbath
summary: A coronation feast turned execution ground in 1520 that permanently severed Sweden from Denmark and gave rise to the Vasa dynasty.

subject: Stockholm Exhibition (1930)
summary: A five-month spectacle that convinced four million Swedes to embrace modernism, transforming not just architecture but an entire society's relationship with how it lived.

subject: Stockton-on-Tees
summary: The Tees-side town where Locomotion No 1 hauled the world's first passenger railway in 1825, where the friction match was invented, and where the High Street is still the widest in Britain.

subject: Stoke-on-Trent
summary: A polycentric city where asking for the centre will get you a raised eyebrow, and where the best souvenirs are still made by hand in the factory you can tour that afternoon.

subject: Stoke-on-Trent
summary: Six towns refused to merge their identities even after they were forced into a single city, and the result is one of the strangest urban shapes in England.

subject: Stone Circles of Hong Kong
summary: Prehistoric stone circles on Lamma Island and Lantau Island reveal that Hong Kong's coastlines were sacred — or at least purposeful — to people living here thousands of years ago during the Neolithic and Bronze Ages.

subject: Stone Town
summary: The UNESCO-listed heart of Zanzibar City is a maze of coral-stone alleys where Swahili, Arab, Persian, Indian, and European influences fused into one of East Africa's most distinctive urban landscapes.

subject: Stone circles of Junapani
summary: Three thousand years ago, people arranged stones into circles on the plains near Nagpur -- burial sites that may also encode astronomical knowledge in their cup-marked stones.

subject: Stone spheres of Costa Rica
summary: Over 300 mysterious stone spheres, some weighing 15 tons and measuring more than two meters across, scattered across Costa Rica's Diquis Delta -- carved from hard gabbro rock by an extinct culture whose methods and motives remain unknown.

subject: Stonehaven
summary: A town of 11,177 people on the northeast coast of Scotland — county town of the now-abolished Kincardineshire, birthplace of the BBC's first director and the pneumatic tyre, and home to a 420-million-year-old fossil and a still-burning Hogmanay tradition.

story.title: The Stonewall Riots: The Night Greenwich Village Fought Back

subject: Stonewall riots
summary: In the early hours of June 28, 1969, a routine police raid on a Mafia-owned gay bar in Greenwich Village ignited six days of uprising that launched the modern LGBTQ rights movement worldwide.

subject: Stoning of the Devil
summary: At Mina, millions of pilgrims each year cast pebbles at three walls in a ritual thousands of years old, in a place where ancient devotion and modern crowd engineering meet.

subject: Stop Cop City
summary: A patch of urban forest southeast of Atlanta became the flashpoint for one of America's most charged conflicts over policing, protest rights, and urban green space -- culminating in a protester's death, 61 RICO indictments, and a training center that opened over the objections of tens of thousands.

subject: Stopera
summary: Amsterdam's combined opera house and city hall opened in 1986 on ground that still carries the memory of the Jewish neighborhood that once stood there.

subject: Stora Blåsjön
summary: A hamlet of seventy-odd people below the Stekenjokk plateau that once went on hunger strike to force a copper mine into existence — and won.

subject: Store Vildmose
summary: One of Denmark's last great raised bogs, half of it drained into farmland that grows a famously thin-skinned potato, half of it still wet enough for cloudberry and corn crake.

subject: Stork Farm Loburg
summary: Roughly two thousand injured white storks have come through a family's garden in a small Saxony-Anhalt town since 1979 — and the birds that can never fly again simply stay.

subject: Storm King Ranger Station
summary: A hand-hewn log cabin on the shores of Lake Crescent carries the name of the man who championed Olympic National Park's creation -- and has survived a runaway tractor, relocation, and a century of Pacific Northwest weather.

subject: Stornoway
summary: The only town in the Outer Hebrides: a working harbour, a Sabbatarian conscience, and one famous cherry brandy.

subject: Storr Lochs Hydro-Electric Scheme
summary: A 1952 hydro station on Skye, reached by a funicular railway down a 350-foot cliff, that switched on the lights for the first time across the island.

subject: Storyville, New Orleans
summary: New Orleans' infamous red-light district gave birth to jazz, immortalized vice in printed 'Blue Books,' and vanished almost entirely -- leaving behind only three buildings and a musical revolution.

subject: Stourhead
summary: One of England's finest landscape gardens, Stourhead was designed as a three-dimensional painting -- a walk around an artificial lake that recreates Aeneas's journey through the underworld in classical temples, grottoes, and perfectly placed trees.

subject: Stowmarket
summary: A Mid Suffolk market town whose name means 'principal place' in Old English, with an exploded guncotton factory, John Milton connections, two novae discovered by amateurs, and a music venue named for John Peel.

subject: Strabane
summary: A Tyrone border town that printed the U.S. Declaration of Independence, gave the world Woodrow Wilson's ancestors, and survived being the most bombed town in Europe.

subject: Strabane Ambush
summary: On a February morning in 1985, the SAS killed three IRA volunteers - one of them sixteen, the youngest to die in the conflict - in what became the most successful SAS operation of the Troubles before Loughgall.

subject: Strachur
summary: On the eastern shore of Loch Fyne, this small Cowal village holds a stone said to wander between hilltops, a Campbell stronghold, and the legacy of Sir Harry Lauder.

subject: Stradbally, County Waterford
summary: A planned 18th-century estate village on the Waterford coast with a medieval church, a mysterious gravestone, and the unsolved disappearance of a Christmas-night postman.

subject: Straffan
summary: A Liffey-side Kildare village named for a forgotten saint, home now to the Ryder Cup at the K Club, a steam museum, a Bordeaux wine dynasty's vanished estate, and one of Ireland's worst railway tragedies.

subject: Strait of Bonifacio
summary: The narrow, treacherous channel separating Corsica from Sardinia has earned a fearsome reputation among sailors for its violent currents, sudden weather, and hidden shoals.

subject: Strait of Dover
summary: The narrowest gap between Britain and continental Europe - 33 kilometers of chalk-bottomed water that was carved by two catastrophic ice-age floods and now carries over 400 ships a day.

subject: Strait of Georgia
summary: A 240-kilometre inland sea between Vancouver Island and the mainland, fed almost entirely by one river, crossed by the busiest ferries in Canada, and renamed three times in two centuries.

subject: Strait of Hormuz
summary: The world's most strategically vital maritime chokepoint, where a quarter of all seaborne oil passes between Iran and Oman.

subject: Strait of Magellan
summary: The narrow, wind-torn channel that gave the world its first sea passage from Atlantic to Pacific, named for a navigator who would not live to finish the voyage.

subject: Strait of Malacca
summary: The 900-kilometer passage between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula through which a quarter of the world's traded goods flow, shaped by empires from Srivijaya to the modern shipping industry.

story.title: The Strand Bookstore: Eighteen Miles and Counting

subject: Strand Bookstore
summary: A Lithuanian immigrant's used-book stall, founded on Manhattan's Book Row in 1927, outlasted every one of its 48 neighboring bookshops to become an institution that claims to hold eighteen miles of books -- and has survived the Depression, rent wars, Amazon, and a pandemic.

subject: Strandbad Wannsee
summary: Berlin built itself a seaside on a lake, trucking Baltic sand onto 1,275 metres of Havel shoreline so that people who could never reach the coast would have one anyway.

subject: Strandhill
summary: A village known to the Irish as Larass grew into one of Ireland's surfing capitals on a peninsula already shaped by 5,000 years of human habitation and the relentless work of shifting sand.

subject: Strangford
summary: A village of 560 people on the west bank of the Strangford Narrows that doubled as Winterfell for Game of Thrones - and still feels like it could be the gate to a kingdom.

subject: Strangford Lough
summary: The largest sea inlet in the British Isles is also one of the most biologically rich, hosting three-quarters of the world's pale-bellied brent geese each winter and over 2,000 marine species year-round.

subject: Stratford, London
summary: Six miles northeast of central London, Stratford transformed from Essex farmland to Victorian industrial powerhouse to Olympic host city—a district that has never stopped reinventing itself.

subject: Stratford-upon-Avon
summary: An 800-year-old Warwickshire market town of 30,000 that receives 2.5 million visitors a year because, in 1564, a glover's wife gave birth here to a boy who would become the most influential writer in the history of the English language.

subject: Strathallan Estate
summary: A 70-hectare housing estate in Melbourne's Macleod suburb whose boundaries trace back to a colonial land grant in 1840 and a railway corruption scandal in 1909.

subject: Strathfoyle
summary: A post-war housing village northeast of Derry, where wartime concrete bunkers still slumber in the woods and the Foyle slides past Lisahally's deep-water docks.

subject: Strathpeffer
summary: A Highland spa village built on sulphur springs, Victorian ambition, and one of the most extreme mountain bike races on Earth.

subject: Stratos
summary: Stratos was the great capital of ancient Acarnania — the most fortified city on the Achelous River, whose 7.5-kilometer walls enclosed four hills and three valleys, and whose unfinished Temple of Zeus, begun in 321 BC, still stands as one of the most important Early Hellenistic buildings in mainland Greece.

subject: Stratton
summary: The Cornish town that was once the head of its own ancient hundred — and where, on a hill above the town, the King's army won the South West.

subject: Strawberry Field
summary: A Salvation Army children's home in Woolton where John Lennon hid behind the hedge as a boy listening to the brass band - now a Beatles pilgrimage site, training centre, and the place that gave the world one of the strangest pop songs ever recorded.

subject: Streatham
summary: A South London district built along a Roman road, with mineral springs that made it fashionable, the longest shopping street in postwar south London, and a community that has rebuilt itself more than once.

subject: Streedagh Armada wrecksite
summary: Three ships of the Spanish Armada lie beneath Streedagh beach in County Sligo -- the largest concentration of Armada wrecks in the world, carrying the stories of over a thousand soldiers and sailors lost in 1588.

story.title: STAR: The Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries

subject: Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries
summary: In the wake of the Stonewall uprising, Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera founded America's first trans political organization -- and ran a shelter for homeless transgender youth out of a semi-truck trailer before scraping together rent for a crumbling four-bedroom apartment in the East Village.

subject: Stromness
summary: A flagstone harbour on Orkney's Mainland where Hudson's Bay traders, Captain Cook, and Franklin's doomed expedition all stopped for fresh water and a fair wind.

subject: Strontian
summary: A lead-mining village on Loch Sunart that gave its name to a chemical element, the only one named after a place in the United Kingdom.

subject: Struer, Denmark
summary: A Limfjord harbour town of fewer than ten thousand people that gave the world one of the most recognisable names in audio design - and is still trying to work out what that means.

subject: Strzelecki Track
summary: A 472-kilometre outback road from Lyndhurst to Innamincka with no fuel between the ends, leading to Cooper Creek and the Burke and Wills Dig Tree.

subject: Strzelecki Track
summary: A historic outback stock route in northeastern South Australia, first driven by a cattle thief in 1870 and now the access road to the Cooper Basin gas fields.

subject: Ströbeck
summary: A farming village in the Harz foothills put a chessboard on its coat of arms and chess on its school timetable - and has kept both for two centuries.

subject: Strøget
summary: The man who ordered the cars off Copenhagen's main shopping street received death threats for it. Sixty years later, half the world's cities have copied him.

subject: Stuart Range
summary: The low ridge that turned back an explorer hid a fortune he never saw - and gave the world's richest opal field its first name.

subject: Studebaker
summary: From wheelbarrows in the California Gold Rush to the last car rolling off the line in 1966, Studebaker's story is the story of American transportation itself, born in a South Bend blacksmith shop and buried in a secret graveyard of rusting prototypes.

subject: Studio City (Macau)
summary: Studio City is Cotai's Hollywood-themed resort — Art Deco towers inspired by Gotham City, a figure-8 ferris wheel boarding passengers on the 23rd floor, and a $70 million opening film directed by Martin Scorsese.

subject: Stung Treng
summary: A small Cambodian river town that France traded away from Laos in 1904, sitting where three great tributaries and the Mekong gather within a few kilometres of one another.

subject: Stung Treng Province
summary: A northeastern Cambodian province that two French administrations swapped in 1904, where the Mekong gathers three great tributaries and the last dolphin of the border pools died in 2022.

subject: Styal
summary: A planned mill village beside the River Bollin, where Samuel Greg's cottages, chapel and school still stand as the most complete factory colony of the Industrial Revolution.

subject: Stymfalia
summary: A high mountain lake in northern Arcadia where Heracles drove off the Stymphalian Birds in his sixth labour, Hera was worshipped in three phases of a woman's life, and a Canadian archaeology team has been carefully excavating the ancient city's grid-planned streets since 1982.

subject: Stymphalus (Arcadia)
summary: Pindar called it the mother of Arcadia, and Heracles once came here to drive away man-eating birds — the ancient city of Stymphalus, sealed inside its ring of mountains beside a lake that vanishes underground.

subject: Suakin
summary: On a circular island off Sudan's Red Sea coast, a ruined city built of coral blocks preserves centuries of trade, pilgrimage, and slow abandonment.

subject: Suao
summary: A working port town at the southern edge of Yilan, where carbonated cold springs, fresh seafood hauled straight off fishing boats, and a railway at the end of the line make for an honest, unhurried Taiwan day trip.

subject: Suba, Bogotá
summary: Bogotá's northwest locality where the Muisca held ground for centuries - and, after more than a hundred years of legal erasure, hold it again.

subject: Subatan-Diza (archeological site)
summary: A fortified hilltop settlement dating to the end of the second millennium BC, Subatan-Diza in Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan exclave preserves three thousand years of continuous habitation in its cyclopean walls, painted ceramics, and a name rooted in the Elamite language.

subject: Submillimeter Array
summary: Eight radio dishes arranged in a geometric pattern on a volcanic lava field helped produce humanity's first image of a black hole.

subject: Subotiv
summary: A small village on the Tiasmyn River where the founder of the Cossack state built a stone church, and where his bones are said to still rest.

subject: Suchitoto
summary: A colonial hill town of 7,700 people where cobblestone streets, a lakeside perch, and a growing arts scene have made it El Salvador's most charming small-town destination.

story.title: Sucre: Bolivia's White City and Constitutional Capital

subject: Sucre
summary: Bolivia's official capital may cede most government functions to La Paz, but Sucre keeps the title - along with a UNESCO-listed colonial center, a famously tranquil atmosphere, and the world's largest collection of dinosaur footprints just outside town.

subject: Sudak
summary: An ancient Black Sea port whose Genoese fortress still crowns the cliffs, guarding a city that has changed hands, names, and empires for nearly two thousand years.

subject: Sudan
summary: Africa's third-largest country, home to more pyramids than Egypt, some of the continent's warmest hospitality, and a present shaped by decades of conflict - approach with respect, patience, and updated travel advisories.

subject: Sudan
summary: Africa's third-largest country by area, site of the world's earliest known war and more pyramids than Egypt, home to 51.8 million people caught today in one of the worst humanitarian crises on earth.

story.title: Sudanese Style Mosques in Northern Cote d'Ivoire

subject: Sudanese style mosques in northern Côte d'Ivoire
summary: Eight mud-brick mosques scattered across northern Ivory Coast carry seven centuries of Saharan trade routes and Islamic scholarship in their sun-baked walls, earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 2021.

subject: Sudbury Basin
summary: Nearly two billion years ago, an asteroid slammed into what is now northern Ontario, creating one of the largest impact craters on Earth and depositing the mineral wealth that would build one of the world's great mining regions.

subject: Sudbury, Suffolk
summary: The Stour Valley market town that gave England Thomas Gainsborough, kept its Saxon street plan, and watched American B-24s decorated with zodiac signs lift off from its fields toward Germany.

subject: Sudwala Caves
summary: Inside one of the oldest caves on Earth, a mysterious flow of fresh air once saved a Swazi prince from suffocation and gives every visitor the same cool, breathable welcome today.

subject: Suebi
summary: A name that started on the Elbe, was applied by Romans to half of Germania, and ended up attached to both Swabia and a kingdom in northwest Iberia that outlasted Rome by a century.

subject: Suffolk
summary: An English county of pink-washed villages, ship burials, container ports and racehorses, where Anglo-Saxon kings sleep under burial mounds and 700,000-year-old hand axes still emerge from the clay.

subject: Suffolk, Virginia
summary: An Italian immigrant peanut salesman built his factory here in 1912, and ninety-four years later Suffolk - the largest city by land area in Virginia - is still the place where Mr. Peanut was born and the Joint Forces Command was housed.

subject: Sugar Hill, Manhattan
summary: A hilltop neighborhood in upper Harlem where the 'sweet life' drew W. E. B. Du Bois, Duke Ellington, and Thurgood Marshall -- and whose name echoed from jazz standards to the birth of hip-hop.

subject: Suicide of Kurt Cobain
summary: On Lake Washington Boulevard in Seattle's Denny-Blaine neighborhood, a greenhouse above a garage became the site where the voice of a generation fell silent in April 1994, leaving behind music that redefined rock and questions that have never fully subsided.

subject: Suilven
