summary: Vikings named it 'pillar mountain,' and a billion years of erosion have left Suilven standing like a sandstone sentinel above the gneiss wilderness of Assynt.

subject: Sukur
summary: On a Nigerian hilltop, a chiefdom of iron-smiths and terrace farmers became the first cultural landscape in Africa ever inscribed by UNESCO, then survived Boko Haram.

subject: Sula Vineyards
summary: A Stanford graduate quit Silicon Valley, returned to India, and built the country's largest wine brand in the unlikely terroir of Nashik, turning a region known for onions into the Wine Capital of India.

story.title: Sulawesi's Cloud Forests: Evolution's Island Laboratory

subject: Sulawesi's Cloud Forests
summary: Straddling the Wallace Line where Asian and Australian wildlife collide, Sulawesi's montane rain forests harbor an extraordinary concentration of species found nowhere else on Earth, including primates once believed extinct.

subject: Sulby, Isle of Man
summary: A village where, for one week each June, ordinary tarmac becomes the fastest stretch of road in motorcycle racing.

subject: Sulitjelma
summary: An Arctic mining village where 1,300 workers gathered on lake ice in January 1907 because it was the only ground the company did not own.

subject: Sulitjelma Mines
summary: A copper, pyrite, and zinc mining operation in arctic Norway that was once the country's second-largest industrial company, where workers held a legendary union meeting on a frozen lake in 1907.

subject: Sulphur Springs, Saint Lucia
summary: Billed as the world's only drive-in volcano, Sulphur Springs is a geothermal field near Soufriere where boiling mud pits, sulfurous steam, and tar-black water draw 200,000 visitors a year to the edge of a collapsed caldera.

subject: Sultanate of Aussa
summary: An Afar kingdom that ruled the Afar Triangle for nearly three centuries, defeated an Egyptian army in 1875, and whose last reigning sultan exiled by Haile Selassie returned triumphantly in 1991 to resume his rule.

subject: Sultanate of Cirebon
summary: A Javanese port sultanate born from shrimp paste and royal marriages, Cirebon wove Hindu, Islamic, and Chinese threads into one of Java's most culturally layered kingdoms before fracturing into four rival palaces that still stand today.

subject: Sultanate of Deli
summary: A four-century sultanate on Sumatra's east coast, born from Acehnese conquest and Batak alliance, whose tobacco wealth built the Maimoon Palace and shaped the city of Medan.

subject: Sultanate of Ifat
summary: A medieval Muslim sultanate that controlled the vital trade corridor between Ethiopia's highlands and the Red Sea coast, sparking centuries of war with the Christian Abyssinian Empire.

subject: Sultanate of Langkat
summary: Born from the Kingdom of Aru around 1568, the Sultanate of Langkat grew fabulously wealthy under Dutch patronage before a violent revolution in 1946 swept away its palaces, its privileges, and its last sultan.

subject: Sultanate of Serdang
summary: Born from a succession crisis and a mother's exile, the Sultanate of Serdang became one of Sumatra's most enduring Malay kingdoms, surviving colonial rule and revolution across more than two centuries.

subject: Sultanate of Singora
summary: A 17th-century fortified port city founded by a Persian adventurer in southern Thailand, destroyed after decades of defiance against Ayutthaya, whose inscribed cannon traveled from Siam to Burma to London's Royal Hospital Chelsea.

subject: Sultanate of Sulu
summary: A Sunni Muslim state that once controlled the Sulu Archipelago, parts of Borneo, and key maritime trade routes, defying Spanish and American colonial powers for centuries.

subject: Sultanate of Ternate
summary: One of the oldest Muslim kingdoms in Indonesia, the Sultanate of Ternate built a spice empire from a single volcanic island that drew Portuguese, Spanish, and Dutch empires into its orbit.

subject: Sultanate of the Geledi
summary: The Geledi Sultanate, ruled by the Gobroon dynasty from the late 17th century to 1911, was a powerful Somali kingdom centered on the wealthy city of Afgooye that dominated East African trade, received tribute from the Omani Empire, and maintained the institutions of a modern state.

subject: Sulu
summary: A Philippine province in the Sulu Archipelago whose capital Jolo has been the seat of sultans, the target of colonial expeditions, and the center of a separatist conflict spanning decades.

subject: Sumas
summary: The northernmost incorporated town in the lower 48 states where Cherry Street ends at Canadian customs and cross-border commerce defines daily life.

subject: Sumberawan
summary: A solitary Buddhist stupa on the forested slopes of Mount Arjuno in East Java, Sumberawan is the only shrine of its kind in the region -- a relic of the Majapahit empire once known as the Garden of the Heavenly Nymphs.

subject: Sumdorong Chu standoff
summary: In 1986, India discovered Chinese troops occupying a Himalayan pasture it claimed as its own, triggering Operation Falcon and a military standoff that brought Asia's two largest nations to the brink of war before diplomacy prevailed.

subject: Sumer
summary: The earliest known civilization, born between the Tigris and Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, where writing, cities, and mathematics first emerged over five thousand years ago.

subject: Summer Isles
summary: An archipelago in the mouth of Loch Broom where a conservationist lived alone in the 1930s and a fictional pagan island borrowed the name for cinema.

subject: Sumter, South Carolina
summary: A South Carolina city of swans and iris, named for a Revolutionary guerrilla and home to a remarkable roster of athletes, artists, and aviators - and to a 14-year-old wrongly executed in 1944.

subject: Sumy
summary: A city that Cossacks raised on the banks of the Psel, where Anton Chekhov once dreamed of settling forever among the willows and the water.

subject: Sun City
summary: A palatial casino resort built to exploit a legal loophole in apartheid South Africa, Sun City became both a pleasure dome and a moral battleground that musicians around the world refused to cross.

subject: Sun Studio
summary: The small Memphis recording studio at 706 Union Avenue where Sam Phillips recorded 'Rocket 88,' discovered Elvis Presley, and hosted the legendary Million Dollar Quartet session -- the birthplace of rock and roll.

subject: Sundarbans
summary: The world's largest mangrove forest sprawls across the Ganges Delta, where Bengal tigers swim between islands and tides erase a third of the land every day.

subject: Sunderland
summary: The Wearside city the Venerable Bede called a 'sundered land', whose Mackem dialect, glass-making heritage and recently promoted football club give the North East coast its own distinct accent.

subject: Sunderland
summary: The Wearside city that once built a quarter of all British wartime merchant tonnage, lost its shipyards and coal mines in a single generation, and is rebuilding itself on the cleared ground.

subject: Sunderland Civic Centre
summary: A pair of red-brick hexagons opened by Princess Margaret in 1970 and demolished in 2023, this Basil Spence Brutalist landmark spent its last years on the Guardian's list of buildings most at risk.

subject: Sunderland International Airshow
summary: Europe's biggest free airshow ran every July from 1989 to 2019, drawing a million spectators a year to the Roker and Seaburn seafronts - until Sunderland City Council quietly retired it in 2022.

subject: Sunderland Lifeboat Station
summary: Operating since 1800, Sunderland is the most complicated lifeboat history in the RNLI's 238-station network - thirteen different stations, thirty-five boats, and one wreck that stayed visible for seventy years.

subject: Sundial, Taganrog
summary: The oldest surviving sundial in Russia has kept an approximate watch over a Taganrog stairway since 1833, its shadow tuned precisely to the latitude of the town.

subject: Sung Wong Toi
summary: A carved boulder in a small Kowloon park holds the memory of the last boy emperors of the Song dynasty, who took refuge in Hong Kong in 1277 — and the layers of history that the stone itself has survived.

subject: Sunniside, Sunderland
summary: The Victorian business district of Sunderland that housed foreign consulates in the shipbuilding age, slid into urban decay in the 1980s, and rebuilt itself as the city's cultural quarter.

subject: Sunny South (clipper)
summary: One of the most beautiful clippers ever built, sold into the illegal slave trade and chased down by the Royal Navy with 846 captive Africans aboard.

subject: Sunset Crater
summary: A cinder cone born from a violent eruption around AD 1085 that reshaped life for the Sinagua people and was nearly destroyed by a Hollywood film studio before becoming one of Arizona's first national monuments.

subject: Sunset Peak (Hong Kong)
summary: Tai Tung Shan — the Big East Mountain — is Hong Kong's third-highest peak and Lantau Island's second-highest, where winter silvergrass turns the ridgelines gold and every clear evening earns its name.

subject: Sunshine Coast
summary: An hour north of Brisbane, a string of surf towns, jagged volcanic peaks and misty hinterland villages add up to Queensland's most relaxed coastline.

subject: Sunshine Coast (British Columbia)
summary: A populous stretch of the British Columbia mainland that no road reaches - fifty thousand people, a highway that starts and ends on a ferry, and the fastest tidal rapids on the coast.

subject: Sunshine Coast Trail
summary: Canada's longest hut-to-hut hiking trail stretches 180 kilometers through old-growth rainforest, alpine ridges, and coastal bluffs on British Columbia's upper Sunshine Coast, connecting sixteen free backcountry huts built entirely by volunteers.

subject: Super League Greece
summary: Greece's top football league: a century of passion dominated by a Piraeus port club, shadowed by violence and won, again and again, by Olympiacos.

subject: SuperFerry 9
summary: A ferry with a troubled mechanical history that capsized off the Zamboanga Peninsula in September 2009 with 971 people aboard -- 961 were rescued in a massive search operation, but ten lives were lost to seas that the vessel's operators knew were dangerous.

subject: Superior Hiking Trail
summary: Born from Appalachian Trail dreams in the mid-1980s, this 310-mile footpath traces the volcanic ridgeline above Lake Superior from the Wisconsin border to Canada, threading through boreal forest, seven state parks, and 94 backcountry campsites along Minnesota's rugged North Shore.

subject: Superkilen
summary: A wedge of Nørrebro furnished with 108 objects imported from 62 countries — swings from Iraq, a Soviet bus stop, a Moroccan fountain — and a neighbourhood that has never entirely agreed on whether it worked.

subject: Superstition Mountains
summary: Arizona's legendary range where Apache beliefs, lost gold, and volcanic spires meet at the edge of Phoenix.

story.title: Supreme Civil and Criminal Court of Greece

subject: Supreme Civil and Criminal Court of Greece
summary: Greece's highest court borrows its name from a mythic rock and counts among its founders a judge who refused to sign a hero's death sentence.

story.title: Supreme Court of Japan: Eight Strikes in Sixty Years

subject: Supreme Court of Japan
summary: In six decades, the highest court in Japan struck down just eight laws -- a record of restraint so extreme it raises the question of whether judicial review in Japan is a power exercised, or merely possessed.

subject: Supreme Federal Court
summary: Brazil's constitutional court has existed since 1808, when the Portuguese royal family arrived in Rio after fleeing Napoleon, and in 2009 The Economist called it the most overburdened court in the world.

subject: Sur, Oman
summary: An ancient Omani port city that once built ships sailing to China and Zanzibar, brought low by the abolition of the slave trade and the Suez Canal, now preserving its dhow-building heritage.

subject: Surabaya
summary: Indonesia's second city guards the Madura Strait, colonial quarters survive amid megacity sprawl, and East Java's capital hums with commerce few outsiders bother to witness.

subject: Surantih
summary: A coastal Minangkabau settlement in West Sumatra stretching 30 kilometers from the Indian Ocean into the Bukit Barisan highlands, where traditional fishing, Padang cuisine, and the cultural pull of merantau shape daily life.

subject: Surfers Paradise International Raceway
summary: For twenty-one years a fearsome racing circuit roared across the Gold Coast flats at Carrara; today its asphalt sleeps beneath the lawns and lakes of a canal estate.

subject: Surfing in Indonesia
summary: From one American surfer at Kuta Beach in the 1930s to a half-billion-dollar industry spanning thousands of islands, Indonesia became one of the world's great surfing destinations.

subject: Suriye Pasajı
summary: Tucked off İstiklal Avenue since 1908, the Suriye Pasajı — Cité de Syrie — is a six-storey neoclassical arcade that once housed the offices of Istanbul's Greek, Armenian, and French minority press, and still shelters an unlikely mix of antiques, tea, and neighborhood life.

subject: Surrey
summary: Surrey calls itself a southern region and has lived up to the name for more than a thousand years — chalk downs, stockbroker villages, the Diggers' commune at Weybridge, McLaren in Woking, and the field where Magna Carta was sealed.

story.title: Susa: The City That Outlived Its Empires

subject: Susa
summary: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, Susa served as the capital of Elam and the winter palace of Persian kings for millennia before fading into the modern Iranian town of Shush.

subject: Sussex
summary: From the South Saxons who landed in AD 477 to the cricket clubs and bonfire societies that still define it, Sussex has spent fifteen centuries cultivating a stubborn independence summed up in three words: we wunt be druv.

subject: Sussex County, Delaware
summary: The site of Delaware's first European settlement - a failed Dutch whaling colony in 1631 - and now home to the state's Atlantic beaches and the northernmost bald cypress swamp in America.

subject: Sutil Channel
summary: A broad Discovery Islands strait carrying the name of a small Spanish schooner that circled Vancouver Island in 1792 — and the site of a whaling station that emptied the Strait of Georgia in eighteen months.

subject: Sutkagan Dor
summary: The westernmost outpost of the Indus Valley Civilization, a fortified settlement near the Iranian border where massive stone citadel walls up to 7.5 meters thick guarded an ancient trade route linking the Persian Gulf to the heart of the subcontinent.

subject: Sutter Hock Farm
summary: The site of John Sutter's retirement dream on the Feather River, where California's first large-scale farm thrived and then burned, taking with it the personal records of one of the West's most consequential and tragic figures.

subject: Sutton Coldfield
summary: A medieval royal hunting chase that became one of Birmingham's most expensive suburbs, Sutton Coldfield still calls itself a Royal Town and still keeps 2,200 acres of woodland inside its own boundaries.

subject: Sutton Hoo
summary: In 1939, a self-taught archaeologist and a Suffolk widow dug into a riverside mound and found the richest Anglo-Saxon burial ever discovered in England — a ship, a king, and an entire world preserved in the sand.

subject: Sutton Hoo Helmet
summary: Forged from a single piece of iron, decorated with dragons and dancing warriors, and buried with a king somewhere between 610 and 635 AD, the Sutton Hoo helmet has become the defining image of early medieval England.

subject: Sutton, West Virginia
summary: A small Braxton County town at the geographic center of West Virginia, famous for a 1952 alien sighting that gave the world the Braxton County Monster - or, depending on whom you ask, the Phantom of Flatwoods.

subject: Sveti Stefan
summary: A fortified island village built with plunder from captured Turkish galleys, Sveti Stefan spent centuries as a fishing community before reinventing itself as one of the Mediterranean's most exclusive hotel resorts.

subject: Swakopmund
summary: Namibia's adventure capital and biggest coastal town, where German colonial architecture meets the Namib Desert and Atlantic fog creates a climate unlike anywhere else on Earth.

subject: Swanage Lifeboat Station
summary: A 150-year-old RNLI station on Peveril Point in Dorset, founded after a coal brigantine wrecked in winter 1875 and still launching all-weather rescues from a new boathouse opened in 2017.

subject: Swanlinbar
summary: Jonathan Swift mocked the name of this Cavan village, which combines four men's surnames who lost their fortunes making the worst iron in Ireland, before sulphurous springs turned it briefly into a Georgian spa town.

subject: Swansboro
summary: A small North Carolina riverfront town that built North Carolina's first steamboat, throws a festival for the mullet, and sits where the White Oak River meets the Intracoastal Waterway.

subject: Swartberg
summary: A 230-kilometer fold mountain range that forms the boundary between South Africa's Great and Little Karoo, home to the Western Cape's highest peak, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and engineering feats carved through its ancient quartzite.

subject: Swartberg Pass
summary: A 19th-century engineering marvel carved through ancient fold mountains, connecting two Karoo worlds across a UNESCO World Heritage landscape of contorted quartzite and dry-stone hairpin bends.

subject: Swash Channel Wreck
summary: In 1990 a Dutch dredger hit something in the sand outside Poole Harbour. It turned out to be 400 years of preserved 17th-century merchantman, complete with mermen carved into the rudder.

subject: Swedish Academy
summary: The arbiter of literary immortality, this eighteenth-century institution selects Nobel laureates, guards the Swedish language through monumental dictionaries, and has weathered scandal and royal intervention without abandoning its founding motto: Talent and Taste.

subject: Swedish warship Mars
summary: The largest warship of her age, nicknamed 'The Jute Hater,' exploded in battle in 1564 and lay undiscovered on the Baltic seafloor for over four centuries.

subject: Sweeney Ridge
summary: The 1,200-foot ridge where Spanish scouts first glimpsed San Francisco Bay in 1769, now home to abandoned Nike missile bunkers and one of the Bay Area's best raptor migration lookouts.

subject: Swellendam
summary: South Africa's third-oldest European settlement hides beneath ancient oaks at the foot of the Langeberg Mountains, where Cape Dutch gables and a near-extinction rescue story share the same postcode.

subject: Swift Creek Landslide
summary: For years Whatcom County dredged Swift Creek and gave the sediment away free for driveways and foundations - until testing showed what the mountain was shedding into it.

subject: Swinomish Indian Tribal Community
summary: On Fidalgo Island, a Coast Salish nation rebuilt the first traditional clam garden in the United States in two hundred years - and won a $394 million judgment against a railroad.

subject: Sword Well
summary: A small stone well in Dajia District, Taichung, where legend holds that the 17th-century commander Koxinga plunged his sword into the earth and drew forth water for his army — and where locals still come to remember him.

subject: Swords
summary: A north Dublin commuter town whose name comes from the Irish for "pure" - a holy well blessed by St Colmcille in the 6th century - and where Brian Boru's body lay after the Battle of Clontarf.

subject: Sycamore Gap Tree
summary: The most photographed tree in England, felled in a single night in September 2023 in an act of vandalism that shocked a country.

subject: Sydney
summary: Australia's Harbour City - where an unlikely opera house and a Depression-era bridge became the defining symbols of a nation, and golden beaches curve along a coastline that never seems to end.

subject: Sylacauga (meteorite)
summary: The only verified meteorite in recorded history to strike a human being crashed through a farmhouse roof in rural Alabama on a quiet November afternoon in 1954.

subject: Syntagma Square
summary: Athens named its central square for a promise extracted at gunpoint: the Constitution that soldiers forced from King Otto on a September night in 1843.

story.title: Syracuse: The Salt City That the Highway Ate

subject: Syracuse
summary: The upstate New York city built on salt and divided by interstate - where the Erie Canal brought prosperity, where I-81 sliced through downtown, and where snow falls in quantities that other cities can't imagine.

subject: Syros
summary: The unlikely capital of the Cyclades — a small Aegean island that became independent Greece's first great port city, its industrial heartland, and a showcase for neoclassical ambition, then quietly endured the world moving on.

subject: Syvash
summary: A vast, foul-smelling, pink-tinged maze of salt lagoons, so shallow armies have twice waded across it, that nearly severs Crimea from the mainland.

subject: Sánchez Navarro ranch
summary: For a century, the Sánchez Navarro family controlled 16.5 million acres of the Chihuahuan Desert -- an estate larger than West Virginia, five times the size of the biggest ranch in the United States, and ultimately impossible to hold against Comanche raiders, revolution, and a nation determined to reclaim its land.

subject: São Borja
summary: A Jesuit mission founded in 1682 on the Argentine frontier that became the oldest town in Rio Grande do Sul and the birthplace of two Brazilian presidents.

subject: São Carlos
summary: Brazil's self-declared National Capital of Technology, where one in every 135 residents holds a PhD and Faber-Castell churns out 1.5 billion pencils a year.

subject: São Domingos, Goiás
summary: A 19th-century gold-seekers' settlement at the far edge of Goiás, where a state park hides a cavern that roars like the earth itself.

subject: São Gabriel da Cachoeira
summary: The most indigenous city in Brazil, where 23 peoples speak their own languages, FOIRN authorizes visitors to traditional lands, and the highest mountain in the country rises just beyond town.

story.title: São Geraldo do Araguaia Environmental Protection Area

subject: São Geraldo do Araguaia Environmental Protection Area
summary: A buffer zone along the Araguaia River where 8,000-year-old rock inscriptions share territory with harpy eagles and the ghosts of a 1970s guerrilla war.

subject: São Gonçalo do Pará
summary: A small Minas Gerais municipality founded by a Portuguese tax rebel fleeing arrest in 1717, who built a chapel to his saint and hid his family on the Pará River.

subject: São Jorge
summary: A quartz-mining camp that ran out of buyers and reinvented itself as the front door to Chapada dos Veadeiros, where the standing advice for getting around is to walk, preferably barefoot.

subject: São João das Missões
summary: A small municipality in northern Minas Gerais where four in ten residents are Xacriabá - the largest indigenous population in the state - living on land their ancestors fought the colonial cattle trail to keep.

subject: São João del-Rei
summary: A colonial Brazilian gold town where baroque churches, steam trains, and Holy Week processions have all survived into the present tense.

subject: São Leopoldo
summary: On a July day in 1824, the first German settlers stepped ashore here - and a dialect of the Rhineland took root that still echoes across southern Brazil two centuries later.

subject: São Luís
summary: A traveler's São Luís: colonial tile streets by day, reggae bars and river-mouth beaches by night, and the jumping-off point for the otherworldly Lençóis Maranhenses dunes.

subject: São Luís de Montes Belos
summary: A 19th-century cattle ranch that grew into the self-declared industrial capital of western Goiás, where Gir and Nelore bulls graze on pasture named for beautiful hills.

subject: São Luís, Maranhão
summary: The only Brazilian state capital founded by France, São Luís wears 17th-century Portuguese bones beneath Brazil's largest collection of exterior azulejo tiles, Latin America's best-preserved colonial townhouses, and a reggae scene loud enough to rattle the sobrados.

subject: São Martinho dos Tigres
summary: Once Angola's busiest fishing port, this desert village died the day the sea cut its peninsula loose and turned it into an island.

subject: São Mateus, Espírito Santo
summary: One of Brazil's oldest continuously inhabited cities, where a Jesuit settlement, an abandoned river port, and a beach where sea turtles still nest share the same municipal boundary.

subject: São Miguel do Araguaia
summary: A frontier cattle town at Goiás's northern edge where the Araguaia River's dry season reveals kilometers of white sand beaches and a fishing village of 800 swells to 30,000.

subject: São Miguel do Guamá
summary: A Pará town of 59,000 that fires 30 million bricks and 8 million roof tiles every month, built where the Carmelite friars laid out a chapel in 1758.

subject: São Miguel dos Milagres
summary: A village of eight thousand on the Alagoas coast, named for a fisherman's healed wound, now the quiet heart of the Rota Ecológica and a place where manatees are returned to the sea.

subject: São Pedro Clock
summary: Salvador demolished the São Pedro church in 1913 to push an avenue through; three years later the city's shop and office clerks paid for a cast-iron clock to stand where it had been.

subject: São Roque de Minas
summary: A town of seven thousand sitting almost entirely inside a national park, where Brazil's greatest inland river begins as a spring and the local cheese has its own tourist route.

subject: Sädvvájávrre
summary: A hydropower reservoir in Swedish Lapland whose annual drawdown has been slowly uncovering the graveyard of Silbojokk, a parish that served the Sami for 137 years and then vanished.

subject: Särkänniemi
summary: A concrete needle went up on a sandy cape in 1971, and Finland's second-biggest amusement park grew underneath it.

subject: Sæby
summary: A Kattegat harbour town whose monks gave up in 1536, whose harbour has been silting up ever since, and whose centre survived because nobody ever got rich enough to replace it.

subject: Ségou
summary: Once the capital of a Bambara warrior kingdom and still Mali's proudest river city, Ségou pairs colonial avenues, mud-cloth artistry, and a music festival on the Niger.

subject: Ségou
summary: The four-quarters capital of the Bambara kingdom on the Niger, where a young men's drinking club became an army and an empire.

subject: Síyáh-Chál
summary: A disused cistern beneath Tehran where Baha'u'llah, founder of the Baha'i Faith, was imprisoned for four months in 1852 and experienced the revelation that launched a world religion.

subject: Sóc Trăng
summary: A delta city of fifty pagodas where the temples are Khmer, the pastry is Teochew, and one monastery is famous mainly for the thousands of fruit bats that live in its garden.

subject: Sóc Trăng Province
summary: The province's name is a Khmer phrase worn smooth by Vietnamese mouths - and the people it came from are still here, a third of the population, on land where the border moved around them.

subject: Sóller
summary: A mountain-locked valley of oranges on Mallorca's northwest coast, cut off from its own capital until a narrow-gauge railway threaded the rock in 1912.

subject: Sông Cầu
summary: A quiet coastal town on Vietnam's South Central Coast, Sông Cầu has been reorganized, merged, split, and renamed so many times since the Vietnam War that its administrative history reads like a catalog of the country's attempt to reassemble itself.

subject: Sông Đốc
summary: From this river mouth on the Gulf of Thailand, the last ships of the 1955 regroupment sailed north — and a fishing town grew up around the memory.

subject: Súdwest-Fryslân
summary: Six medieval Frisian cities, dozens of villages, and a young sportsman who taught the Netherlands to play cricket — all gathered now under one Frisian name that means simply Southwest-Friesland.

subject: Słubice
summary: A German suburb that woke up in 1945 as a Polish town, took back a thirteenth-century Slavic name, and now hosts a university building that Poland owns and Germany staffs.

story.title: Soji-ji: The Temple That Grew by Walking

subject: Sōji-ji
summary: One of only two head temples of Soto Zen Buddhism, Soji-ji began as a tiny Shingon chapel inside a Shinto shrine on the remote Noto Peninsula in 740, then spent centuries sending monks into the countryside to convert village chapels into a vast network of affiliated temples -- before relocating its entire headquarters to the port city of Yokohama in 1911.

subject: TPC at Sawgrass
summary: The golf course built to humble professionals, where a happy accident created one of sport's most feared holes and a seagull once stole a ball on live television.

subject: TRIUMF
summary: Under the forest at the edge of the UBC campus sits the world's largest normal-conducting cyclotron - a 520 MeV machine that has spent half a century making medical isotopes, rare nuclei and Canada's seat at CERN.

subject: TV Rain
summary: Russia's last independent TV channel signed off in 2022 by playing Swan Lake. Eleven months later, it was broadcasting again from a studio in Amsterdam.

subject: Ta'if
summary: High in the Hijaz mountains, a city of 690,000 escapes Arabia's summer heat with rose gardens, mountain air, and centuries of trade.

subject: Tababela
summary: The small Andean town that became Ecuador's airport village overnight when Quito's new international airport opened in 2013 eighteen kilometers east of the capital.

subject: Tabarca
summary: A tiny walled island off Alicante, resettled by ransomed Genoese captives from a Tunisian isle of the same name and now guarding Spain's first marine reserve.

subject: Tabatinga
summary: A Brazilian city on the Amazon where three countries meet, with no road connecting it to the rest of Brazil and three currencies circulating in its shops.

subject: Tabatinga
summary: An 18th-century Portuguese fort on the upper Amazon that became a Brazilian municipality only in 1983, still a National Security Area and a city accessible only by river or plane.

subject: Tabin Wildlife Reserve
summary: A vast lowland rainforest reserve on Sabah's Dent Peninsula that shelters Borneo's three largest mammals: elephants, rhinoceroses, and wild cattle.

subject: Taboga
summary: A tiny island 20 kilometers south of Panama City where pirates once hid between raids, French canal workers came to die, and the second-oldest church in the Western Hemisphere still holds Saturday mass.

subject: Tabon Caves
summary: The Philippines' 'cradle of civilization,' where 50,000 years of human habitation, elaborate jar burials, and 25-million-year-old limestone formations hide inside 215 caves on a Palawan headland.

subject: Tabor City, North Carolina
summary: A weekly newspaper in a small tobacco town won the 1953 Pulitzer Prize for taking on the Ku Klux Klan when no one else would.

subject: Tabubil
summary: Eight meters of rain a year fall on this company town in the Star Mountains, a place that didn't exist before copper drilling crews arrived in the 1970s.

subject: Tachibana-dera
summary: A temple born from legend -- named for the magical fruit of immortality and built where Prince Shotoku drew his first breath, Tachibana-dera has burned, shrunk, and endured for fourteen centuries in the ancient village of Asuka.

subject: Tacoma
summary: The City of Destiny in the mountain's shadow - a gritty port city reinventing itself with world-class glass art, while Mount Rainier looms impossibly close on the eastern horizon.

subject: Tacuarembó
summary: In Uruguay's gaucho heartland, a quiet inland town stakes one of the most stubborn claims in tango: that the genre's greatest voice was born here.

subject: Tada Silver and Copper Mine
summary: A thousand-year-old mining complex in the mountains north of Osaka whose veins once fueled samurai wars and shogunate treasuries -- and whose richest seam may have been deliberately hidden by Toyotomi Hideyoshi himself.

subject: Tadao Ando
summary: Self-taught architect Tadao Ando left boxing to pursue a career with no formal training, traveled the world studying masters like Le Corbusier, then returned to Osaka to create some of the most spiritually charged concrete structures on Earth -- earning architecture's highest honor, the Pritzker Prize, in 1995.

subject: Tadasu no Mori
summary: A primeval sacred forest in the heart of Kyoto that has survived war, fire, and centuries of urban encroachment to remain a living relic of ancient Japan.

subject: Tadjoura
summary: Djibouti's third-largest city, a whitewashed coastal town whose name means 'abundant with water' in Afar, once the main 19th-century trading port between the Ethiopian highlands and the Red Sea, and now the terminus of a newly rebuilt deep-water cargo port serving the Ethiopian potash trade.

subject: Tadlo
summary: A small village on Laos's Bolaven Plateau where three cascading waterfalls tumble through jungle, and the sound of rushing water is never far away.

subject: Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve
summary: Maharashtra's largest national park, where Bengal tigers hunt through teak forests that the Gondi people once ruled - and where a black panther appeared in habitat no one expected.

subject: Tadoussac
summary: The oldest surviving French settlement in the Americas, where the Saguenay Fjord meets the St. Lawrence and beluga whales surface year-round in waters that drew Jacques Cartier ashore in 1535.

subject: Tafjord
summary: An isolated Norwegian fjord village where a 1934 rockslide sent a 62-meter tsunami through sleeping homes, and where foehn winds still produce the country's hottest winter temperatures.

subject: Tafí del Valle
summary: A highland valley town in northwest Argentina where 7,000-year-old menhirs stand among Andean grasslands, Jesuit cheese-making traditions endure, and the landscape shifts from cloud forest to desert within a single mountain pass.

subject: Taganga
summary: One of the oldest colonial settlements in the Americas, this Colombian fishing village sits at the foot of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, where Cretaceous-era rocks meet Caribbean reef life and backpackers mingle with fishermen hauling nets at dawn.

subject: Tagant Region
summary: A high plateau of stone and oasis at the heart of Mauritania, where the rain has been retreating for sixty years and the people followed it into the towns.

subject: Taghaza
summary: A town where the houses were built of salt and the salt traded ounce-for-ounce against gold - and where enslaved miners did all the digging, hundreds of kilometers from the nearest food.

subject: Taguatinga, Federal District
summary: The satellite city that absorbed the workers who built Brasilia, Taguatinga grew from a Tupi-named clay-bank farmhouse into the economic capital of the Federal District, with 222,000 residents and a tunnel named for Pele.

subject: Taholah, Washington
summary: A Quinault village of 840 people on Washington's outer coast is doing what few communities dare: moving itself uphill, one building at a time, to escape the rising Pacific.

subject: Tahquitz Peak
summary: An 8,846-foot granite peak named for a luminous spirit-demon of the Soboba Indian tribe, Tahquitz Peak is where rock climbers in the 1950s developed the Yosemite Decimal System — the difficulty rating scale that still governs climbing worldwide.

subject: Tahrir Square
summary: Originally named after the khedive who built it as 'Paris on the Nile,' Tahrir Square became synonymous with revolution when millions gathered to topple a president in 2011.

subject: Tahsis
summary: Once a booming mill town of 2,500 on Vancouver Island's remote west coast, Tahsis has reinvented itself as a sport fishing village of under 400 people, its deep inlet still sheltering boats from Pacific storms as it has for over 4,000 years.

subject: Tai A Chau
summary: The largest of the Soko Islands once exported shrimp paste to Europe and sheltered two villages — then became a detention camp for thousands of Vietnamese refugees before returning to silence.

subject: Tai Hang (Tai Po)
summary: In the hills of Tai Po, the village cluster of Tai Hang preserves a direct connection to one of Chinese history's most celebrated scholar-heroes — and a living tradition of walled villages, Qing-dynasty temples, and the Da Jiu festival observed every five years.

subject: Tai Ho Wan
summary: A bay on Lantau's north shore where ancient villages, a fish-rich stream found nowhere else on Earth, and frozen development plans have kept one of Hong Kong's quietest corners quietly extraordinary.

subject: Tai Hom Village
summary: Once Kowloon's largest squatter village, Tai Hom sheltered 35,000 people across three centuries — from Hakka farmers and Japanese warplanes to Hong Kong movie stars — before disappearing in 2001.

subject: Tai Hong Wai
summary: Tucked into the Kam Tin plain of Yuen Long, Tai Hong Wai is one of Hong Kong's surviving walled villages — a centuries-old settlement where earth walls, watchtowers, and a seven-year ritual cycle still shape daily life.

subject: Tai Kwun
summary: A former colonial police compound in Central Hong Kong, transformed into a celebrated heritage and arts centre after a HK$1.8 billion restoration.

subject: Tai Lam Chung Reservoir
summary: Hong Kong's first post-war reservoir drowned entire villages to satisfy a thirsty, growing city — and on low-water days, the rooftops still appear beneath the surface.

subject: Tai Long Sai Wan
summary: Voted Hong Kong's most beautiful scenic site in 2006, this remote white-sand beach on the Sai Kung Peninsula earns its reputation — and its dangers — from the same relentless surf that makes it unforgettable.

subject: Tai Mo Shan
summary: At 956 meters, Hong Kong's highest peak is a Jurassic volcano that still exhales warm air, grows wild cloud tea, and vanishes inside its own weather for much of the year.

subject: Tai O
summary: A centuries-old stilt-house fishing village on western Lantau where the river divides around a small island, pink dolphins surface in the estuary, and the smell of drying fish and shrimp paste drifts through lanes that have changed less than almost anywhere else in Hong Kong.

subject: Tai Ping Shan Street
summary: A short street on the slope of Victoria Peak in Sheung Wan that has witnessed colonial displacement, a devastating bubonic plague outbreak in 1894, and reinvention as a centre of contemporary art.

subject: Tai Po
summary: From Neolithic clamming grounds to a New Territories new town of 320,000, Tai Po's history spans pearl farming under the Yuan dynasty, rival clan markets during the Qing, and a twentieth-century transformation that reclaimed the sea itself for development.

subject: Tai Po Market
summary: Tai Po Market — known in Cantonese as Tai Po Hui — has shifted location, changed names, and split into rival market towns across five centuries, its identity shaped by clan politics, colonial railways, and the perpetual reshuffling of Hong Kong's New Territories.

subject: Tai Tam
summary: Tai Tam means 'big pool' — and in January 1841, when a Royal Navy survey ship charted this triangular bay on the eastern coast of Hong Kong Island, the name proved exactly right.

subject: Tai Tam Reservoirs
summary: Four Victorian-era reservoirs tucked into Hong Kong Island's eastern hills tell the story of a colony's desperate race to quench a booming city's thirst.

subject: Tai Tau Chau (Southern District)
summary: A tiny, uninhabited island off Shek O that geology separated from the headland and history made witness to some of Hong Kong's most desperate crossings.

subject: Tai Wai
summary: A valley crossroads between Kowloon and the New Territories, where Ming dynasty walled villages survive inside a ring of country parks and the busiest rail interchange in Sha Tin District.

subject: Tai Wai Village
summary: A Ming dynasty walled village founded in 1574 that gave the entire Sha Tin area its name, where sixteen clan families built their lives behind thick walls and watch towers.

subject: Tai Wo
summary: A Tai Po area whose name has shifted more than its geography, tracing a rivalry between powerful Tang clan merchants and an alliance of smaller villages competing for control of the district's markets since 1892.

subject: Taichung
summary: Taiwan's second city lives at a gentler pace than Taipei — a place of pleasant weather, night markets, colonial architecture, mountain trails, and a cultural confidence that has been quietly building for decades.

subject: Taif
summary: The unofficial summer capital of Saudi Arabia, a mountain city of over 560,000 that has been called the Garden of the Hejaz since pre-Islamic times.

subject: Taifa of Dénia
summary: An 11th-century Muslim kingdom on the Valencian coast, founded by a formerly enslaved man who built a navy powerful enough to raid Sardinia and the shores of Italy.

subject: Taifa of Lérida
summary: A small Muslim kingdom on the Ebro frontier that survived by paying protection money to Christian counts, until the money ran out and the Aragonese advance closed in.

subject: Taifa of Majorca
summary: The island kingdom founded by a formerly enslaved man that became the last Almoravid holdout in all of Muslim Spain.

subject: Taihang Mountains
summary: A 400-kilometer mountain wall that divides China's Loess Plateau from the North China Plain, shaping the identities and very names of two provinces.

subject: Taima-Taima
summary: A pre-Clovis archaeological site in Venezuela where ancient hunters drove stone spearpoints into mastodons more than 13,000 years ago, rewriting the story of how humans settled the Americas.

subject: Taimali
summary: A small coastal township in Taitung County where the Paiwan people established a village they called 'the village of sunrise' at least a thousand years ago — and where the sun still rises from the Pacific in a way that justifies the name.

subject: Tain
summary: An Easter Ross burgh of pilgrims, silversmiths, and whisky, where Victorian streetscapes guard a thousand years of Highland history.

subject: Tain Tolbooth
summary: A Scottish baronial steeple that has marked the centre of Tain since 1708, still ringing the bell its first builders cast in Holland nearly four centuries ago.

subject: Tainan
summary: Taiwan's oldest city, where Dutch forts, Ming loyalist heroes, and the world's best street food collide in a low-rise maze of temples and alleys.

subject: Taipei Main Station
summary: Taiwan's busiest transport hub, where Qing-era railway history meets four underground levels of trains, malls, and metro lines that move millions of passengers through a building designed to be its own small city.

subject: Taipei Nan Shan Plaza
summary: A diamond-shaped skyscraper that reshaped Taipei's Xinyi District, standing as the city's third-tallest building while weaving together art, commerce, and urban connectivity.

subject: Taipei World Trade Center
summary: The four-in-one complex that helped transform Taiwan from an export-driven tiger economy into a global trade hub, hosting COMPUTEX and shaping Xinyi District since 1986.

subject: Taishan City
summary: Taishan, the 'First Home of the Overseas Chinese,' is the ancestral homeland of hundreds of thousands of ethnic Chinese in North America — a place whose most famous export has always been its people.

subject: Taishanese People
summary: From a corner of Guangdong no larger than a small American state, the Taishanese diaspora built Chinatowns across four continents, laid the western half of the first transcontinental railroad, and reshaped Asian-American history.

subject: Taitung
summary: Wedged between Taiwan's Central Mountain Range and the Pacific at the mouth of the East Rift Valley, Taitung is a subtropical city of indigenous character, Japanese-era streets, and an unhurried pace that the rest of Taiwan's boom largely passed over.

subject: Taivoan Language
summary: The Taivoan language of the Taiwanese Plains indigenous Taivoan people — a distinct Austronesian tongue with deep roots in southwestern Taiwan, documented by Dutch records and kept alive today through revitalization efforts.

subject: Taiwan Garrison Command
summary: The secret police apparatus that enforced martial law in Taiwan for nearly four decades, suppressing communists, democrats, and independence advocates alike before its quiet dissolution in 1992.

subject: Taiwan Historica
summary: Tucked inside the planned town of Zhongxing New Village, Taiwan Historica is the national institution responsible for compiling the official historical record of Taiwan Province — a mission that began in 1948 and has outlasted the government it originally served.

subject: Taiwan Strait
summary: The 180-kilometer channel separating Taiwan from mainland China is one of the most heavily contested bodies of water on Earth, where shipping lanes, fighter jets, and wind farms share the same shallow sea.

subject: Taixi, Yunlin
summary: A small coastal township in Yunlin County whose name was invented in 1941 to fill a geographic gap in Taiwan's naming system — there was a Taipei, Taichung, Tainan, and Taitung, but no Taixi, 'Taiwan-West.'

subject: Tajima Yahei Sericulture Farm
summary: A humble farmhouse in Gunma Prefecture where a self-taught silk farmer's obsessive experiments with ventilation and temperature control revolutionized Japan's sericulture industry -- earning his home a place among the UNESCO World Heritage Sites that powered the nation's leap into modernity.

subject: Takakonuma Greenland
summary: A short-lived amusement park near Fukushima that opened in 1973, closed twice, was swallowed by fog and forest, and became one of Japan's most famous internet ghost stories before being demolished and replaced by solar panels.

subject: Takalik Abaj
summary: Where the Olmec and Maya worlds overlap: Takalik Abaj was a major trading city for nearly two millennia and holds some of the earliest Maya hieroglyphic inscriptions ever found.

subject: Takarkori
summary: A rock shelter in the Libyan Sahara where the desert preserved baskets, milk-stained pottery, and the bodies of people whose DNA revealed a lost branch of humanity, hidden for fifty thousand years.

subject: Takasaki Byakue Daikannon
summary: A 41.8-meter white goddess of mercy stands sentinel over Takasaki, built in 1936 to honor fallen soldiers and now beloved for cherry blossoms, a Valentine's Day red string ritual, and a cameo in kaiju cinema history.

subject: Takayama Jin'ya
summary: The last surviving Edo-period government office in Japan, where 25 shogunal administrators ruled the timber-rich mountains of Hida Province for nearly two centuries.

subject: Takeshi Kaneshiro Tree
summary: A single bishop wood tree standing in the Chishang rice paddies became an unlikely celebrity after an EVA Air commercial in 2013 — then survived a typhoon to become one of Taiwan's most improbable pilgrimage sites.

subject: Takht Sri Damdama Sahib
summary: One of Sikhism's five Takhts -- Seats of Temporal Authority -- where Guru Gobind Singh compiled the final version of the Guru Granth Sahib in 1705 after losing all four sons to the Mughal Empire.

subject: Taksim Square
summary: The symbolic heart of modern Istanbul, Taksim Square has witnessed both the founding of a republic and some of the darkest episodes in Turkey's modern history.

subject: Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 71 "Richthofen"
summary: West Germany's first jet fighter wing, given the honorary name of the Red Baron on the forty-third anniversary of his death, and the unit that flew the German Air Force's last F-4 Phantom into retirement in 2013.

subject: Takéo province
summary: A flat, flooded province called the cradle of Khmer civilization, which produced both the man who won an Oscar for playing a genocide survivor and one of the men who ran the genocide.

subject: Talawana Track
summary: The last road Len Beadell ever cut, a 600-kilometre line scratched across the desert by one man in a Land Rover, ending eight years of survey work amid heat, dust, and flies.

subject: Talca
summary: Most travelers blow straight through Talca on the highway, never knowing Chile signed away Spanish rule here in 1818.

subject: Taleh
summary: The fortress town of Taleh in northeastern Somalia was the last capital of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan's Dervish movement -- a two-decade anti-colonial resistance that ended only when the Royal Air Force bombed it from the sky in 1920.

subject: Talgarreg
summary: A Welsh-speaking village in the hills between New Quay and Llandysul that, for its size, may have produced more bardic chairs and crowns than anywhere else in Wales.

subject: Talgua Caves
summary: A Honduran cave where 3,000-year-old skulls glow under flashlight beams, revealing a Pre-Classic civilization that traded jade with the Maya.

subject: Talia Station
summary: A sheep run on the western Eyre Peninsula whose name means 'near water', set along a coast of sea caves and a vast granite crater called The Tub.

subject: Talking Gravestones of Amrum
summary: A hundred and fifty-two sandstone slabs in a Frisian churchyard. Each one tells the life story of the person beneath it - sometimes on both sides of the stone, because the front ran out of room.

subject: Talking Gravestones of Föhr
summary: On a small Frisian island, captains who survived the Arctic carved their entire lives into stone - and their widows are remembered as star-shaped flowers beside them.

subject: Tallaght
summary: Built on what Irish legend calls a plague grave, transformed from a 4,500-person village in 1961 into a city-sized suburb of 81,000, Tallaght carries thirteen centuries of monastic, military and modern Dublin history within its sprawl.

subject: Tallinn
summary: A medieval Hanseatic port turned 21st-century tech capital, where 14th-century city walls enclose Skype's birthplace and NATO's cyber-defense brain.

subject: Talvivaara mine
summary: Finland's largest nickel mine became one of its worst environmental scandals, a cautionary tale of industrial ambition, toxic spills, bankruptcy, and reinvention under state control.

subject: Tam Giang–Cau Hai Lagoon
summary: Stretching nearly 70 kilometers along the coast of central Vietnam, the Tam Giang–Cau Hai lagoon system is the largest in Southeast Asia — a vast, shallow inland sea where the Perfume River ends and an entire fishing civilization persists.

subject: Tam Kỳ
summary: Quảng Nam Province's overlooked third city, Tam Kỳ sits on Vietnam's central coast with a fishing village full of murals, a nearly empty beach, and the quiet confidence of a place that doesn't mind being passed over.

story.title: Tama Zenshoen: The Colony That Printed Its Own Money

subject: Tama Zenshoen Sanatorium
summary: A leprosy sanatorium in Tokyo that opened in 1909 once issued its own currency, confined patients for decades under a law later ruled unconstitutional, and produced one of Japan's most celebrated works of illness literature -- recommended by a future Nobel laureate.

subject: Taman
summary: A Cossack village on the Black Sea coast built atop three thousand years of vanished cities, and the setting of one of Russian literature's most unsettling short stories.

subject: Tamandaré
summary: A reef-sheltered stretch of Pernambuco's south coast that gave its name to an admiral, to a barony, and eventually to the patron of the Brazilian Navy.

subject: Tamanrasset
summary: At 1,300 metres in the heart of the Sahara, Tamanrasset is the capital of the Hoggar and the great crossroads city of the Tuareg — a green smudge of date palms in a sea of volcanic rock.

subject: Tamar, Hong Kong
summary: The name Tamar belongs to a British naval ship that arrived in 1897 and never quite left — first as a vessel, then as a shore station, then as a metonym for the government of Hong Kong itself.

story.title: Tamarindito: The Vassal That Broke Its Master

subject: Tamarindito
summary: Once the capital of the Petexbatun region, displaced by Dos Pilas, Tamarindito struck back on January 26, 761 - defeating its overlord and setting off a chain reaction of warfare that would destroy every major city in the region, including Tamarindito itself.

subject: Tambaba
summary: A kilometre of sand in Conde, Paraíba — the first beach in Brazil where naturism was permitted by municipal law, and the first place in the Southern Hemisphere to host the world naturist congress.

subject: Tambogrande
summary: A lime-and-mango farming town in northern Peru that voted 98.72% against a Canadian gold mine in 2002, reshaping Latin American mining politics.

subject: Tambopata National Reserve
summary: A Peruvian rainforest reserve where jaguars stalk riverbanks, giant otters fish in family packs, and an unknown spider species builds miniature Stonehenges out of silk.

subject: Tamerton Foliot
summary: A quiet village on the north edge of Plymouth where a hollow oak tree marks the spot where a Lord of the Manor is said to have killed his own godson.

subject: Tammerkoski
summary: A short, steep channel of rapids that dropped eighteen metres between two lakes, powered a city into existence, and is now one of Finland's official national landscapes with tram wires strung over it.

story.title: Tampa: The Cigar Capital That Became Florida's Working City

subject: Tampa
summary: The Florida gulf city where Cuban cigar makers built a community and football finally won - where Ybor City preserves immigrant history, where the port moves more cargo than Miami, and where Florida's workaday identity survives Disney's shadow.

subject: Tampere
summary: The Manchester of the North traded its looms for laboratories, kept every brick, and now holds the official title of Sauna Capital of the World.

subject: Tampere Central Station
summary: Tampere lowered an entire street by several metres to make its 1936 station work, and the city has organised itself around which side of the tracks you are on ever since.

subject: Tampere Film Festival
summary: Every March since 1970, a Finnish mill town has handed out one of the short film world's most consequential prizes inside a converted cotton factory.

subject: Tampere Tatar Congregation
summary: Merchant families from a handful of Volga villages built a Muslim congregation in an industrial Finnish city — and have kept a language alive at 61 degrees north for a century and a half.

subject: Tamshiyacu Tahuayo Regional Conservation Area
summary: A million-acre Peruvian Amazon reserve where red bald uakaris swing through flooded forests and local communities saved the land from loggers twice.

subject: Tamsui
summary: Once the largest port in Taiwan, Tamsui reinvented itself as Taipei's favorite sunset destination -- a riverside district where Spanish forts, iron eggs, and the smell of fried tofu draw weekend crowds to the place where the river meets the sea.

story.title: Tana Toraja: The Land Where the Dead Never Leave

subject: Tana Toraja
summary: In the highlands of South Sulawesi, the Toraja people bury their dead in cliff faces, dress their ancestors' corpses in fresh clothes, and build houses shaped like boats bound for the afterlife.

subject: Tanais
summary: A Greek trading post at the edge of the known world became a medieval Venetian boomtown, twice built and twice burned where the Don meets the sea.

subject: Tandil
summary: A frontier fort founded in 1823 grew into a granite-ringed pampas city that named itself after a falling rock and produced a tennis champion the world calls the Tower of Tandil.

subject: Tandragee
summary: A small County Armagh town overlooked by a 19th-century mock castle whose grounds have been the home of the Tayto potato crisp since 1956.

subject: Tanganyika Territory
summary: A colonial territory that passed through German, British, and finally African hands over less than a century, Tanganyika's path to independence was shaped by ivory caravans, world wars, and a quiet schoolteacher named Julius Nyerere who won every seat in the first elections.

subject: Tangier
summary: Where Africa meets Europe across the Strait of Gibraltar, where Beat writers found freedom and smugglers found opportunity, where Morocco meets the world.

subject: Tangier, Virginia
summary: A vanishing Chesapeake Bay island where watermen still speak in centuries-old cadences and the roads are only wide enough for two golf carts.

subject: Tangut dharani pillars
summary: Two stone pillars discovered in 1962 in Baoding bear the latest known inscriptions in the Tangut script, evidence of a community that survived nearly 300 years after the Mongol annihilation of their homeland.

subject: Tanjay
summary: One of the oldest continuously settled places in the Philippines, Tanjay traces its origins to Boholano refugees fleeing a Portuguese-backed raid in 1563 and a parish founded before the 17th century was out.

subject: Tank Man
summary: On June 5, 1989, an unidentified man carrying shopping bags stepped in front of a column of tanks on Chang'an Avenue, creating one of the most iconic photographs of the twentieth century and an enduring symbol of individual defiance against state power.

subject: Tanzawa Mountains
summary: Tokyo's backyard wilderness -- a rugged mountain range where Japanese cedar forests give way to beech-covered ridgelines, Asiatic black bears roam the high valleys, and weekend hikers escape the world's largest metropolis in under two hours.

subject: Tao Fong Shan
summary: On a 130-metre hilltop above Sha Tin, a Norwegian missionary built a Christian centre in 1930 designed to speak the architectural language of Buddhism — and the buildings have been drawing pilgrims of all kinds ever since.

subject: Taolagnaro
summary: France's oldest foothold in Madagascar, where a doomed 17th-century fort gave way to a remote modern town hemmed by mountains, lemur reserves, and an ilmenite mine.

story.title: Taos: The Pueblo That Inspired a Thousand Artists

subject: Taos
summary: The high desert town where Taos Pueblo has stood for a thousand years, where artists from Georgia O'Keeffe to D.H. Lawrence found inspiration, and where the Sangre de Cristo Mountains meet New Age spirituality.

story.title: Taos Pueblo: A Thousand Years of Continuous Life

subject: Taos Pueblo
summary: The New Mexico adobe village continuously inhabited for over 1,000 years - where multi-story apartment buildings predate Rome's fall, where residents still live without electricity or running water by choice, and where tourists are guests in someone's actual home.

story.title: Taos Pueblo: A Thousand Years of Continuous Occupation

subject: Taos Pueblo
summary: The New Mexico adobe village that has been continuously inhabited for over a millennium - where multi-story earthen buildings predate Columbus, where residents still live without electricity by choice, and where the oldest continuously occupied dwellings in North America rise against the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

subject: Taos Pueblo
summary: The oldest continuously inhabited community in the United States - a UNESCO World Heritage Site where multi-story adobe buildings have stood against the Sangre de Cristo Mountains for a thousand years, and where the Tiwa-speaking people fought empires to keep their sacred Blue Lake.

story.title: Taos, New Mexico: A Broken Wagon Wheel's Legacy

subject: Taos, New Mexico
summary: A high desert town of 6,000 where a thousand-year-old pueblo, a famous art colony born from a broken wagon wheel, and a mysterious low-frequency hum converge beneath the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

subject: Taoudenni
summary: In the hottest reach of the Sahara, men still cut salt by hand from a dead lake bed - the same work that, under one regime, became a death sentence.

subject: Tap Mun
summary: At the mouth of Tolo Harbour, Tap Mun — Grass Island — is a 1.69 square kilometre world of feral cattle, a 400-year-old temple, and a fishing village that once fed thousands and now quietly persists.

subject: Tapajós Environmental Protection Area
summary: Nearly two million hectares of protected Amazon forest in Para that was created to defuse social tensions from crackdowns on illegal logging, then repeatedly trimmed by legislation to make room for dams, highways, and railways.

subject: Tapajós–Xingu moist forests
summary: An Amazonian ecoregion bounded by two great rivers, home to 556 bird species and a white-nosed saki monkey found only on the east side of the Tapajos.

subject: Taphians
summary: Long before the age of maps, a seafaring people called the Taphians haunted the Ionian islets off Acarnania — pirates, metal-traders, and mythmakers whose ships appear in the Odyssey itself.

subject: Taq-e Bostan
summary: Sasanian rock reliefs carved beside sacred springs in the Zagros Mountains, where kings recorded their divine right to rule along a Silk Road caravan route.

subject: Taqah
summary: A coastal Omani town where mountains meet the Arabian Sea, ancient inlets are protected by royal decree, and the mother of Sultan Qaboos rests in a quiet cemetery beside a mosque.

subject: Tarabya
summary: Named for poison by Medea and renamed for healing by a patriarch, Tarabya has been a summer refuge for Istanbul's elite since the 17th century — a sheltered Bosphorus bay where Greek aristocrats, foreign ambassadors, and Ottoman sultans all sought the same clean air.

subject: Taras Hill
summary: The riverside mound near Kaniv where Ukraine's national poet was carried home to be buried, a hill that has drawn both pilgrims and the guards sent to stop them.

subject: Tarbert (Harris)
summary: The narrow Hebridean isthmus where the ferry from Skye lands, the Golden Road starts, and a rocket once tried to deliver the mail.

subject: Tarbert, Harris
summary: A Gaelic word for portage gave its name to this Hebridean village, where two sea lochs nearly meet and an earl built a hotel for fishermen.

subject: Tarbolton
summary: A South Ayrshire village where a young Robert Burns founded a debating society in 1780, dance halls of the Bachelors' Club still stand, and football has produced a curiously large number of professionals.

subject: Tariana people
summary: The children of the blood of the thunder - an Indigenous people of the Uaupés River who have kept their own name for themselves through centuries of outside attempts to give them other ones.

subject: Tarim, Yemen
summary: A mud-brick city deep in Yemen's Hadhramaut valley, Tarim is renowned for its hundreds of mosques, towering Al-Muhdhar minaret, and centuries of Islamic scholarship that radiated across the Indian Ocean world.

subject: Tarko-Sale
summary: A small Siberian town on the Pyakupur River that serves as headquarters for Russia's largest independent gas producer, where a monument to geologists honors the people who transformed the Arctic tundra into an energy empire.

subject: Tarlabaşı
summary: A densely layered inner-city neighborhood behind İstiklal Caddesi, Tarlabaşı has sheltered successive waves of Istanbul's minorities and migrants for over a century — and is now navigating a contested transformation.

subject: Tarlair Swimming Pool
summary: An Art Deco lido tucked beneath sandstone sea cliffs east of Macduff - opened in 1931, shuttered in the mid-1990s, and slowly being coaxed back to life.

subject: Tarnak Farms
summary: A compound near Kandahar that served as Osama bin Laden's base from 1998 to 2001, and later became the site of a devastating friendly fire incident that killed four Canadian soldiers.

subject: Tarporley
summary: A Cheshire village where England's oldest surviving hunt club still gathers each Christmas, named in Domesday for a pear wood that probably never existed quite the way the scholars thought.

subject: Tarqui, Cuenca Canton
summary: A rural parish south of Cuenca, Ecuador where French geographers once measured the shape of the Earth and Peruvian armies were turned back in 1829.

subject: Tarraco
summary: The oldest Roman city on the Iberian Peninsula grew so important that a whole Roman province was named after it, and its emperors, walls, and aqueduct still shape modern Tarragona.

subject: Tarragona
summary: An hour south of Barcelona, Tarragona layers a golden-sand beach, one of Spain's biggest ports, and a UNESCO Roman city into one walkable, vermouth-loving seaside town.

subject: Tarskavaig
summary: A crofting village on Skye's Sleat peninsula said to have the finest view of the Cuillin - and a Viking-named bay that still speaks Gaelic.

subject: Tashirojima
summary: Japan's famous 'Cat Island' where a 1602 decree freed all domestic cats to protect silkworms, creating a feral colony that now vastly outnumbers the island's dwindling human population.

subject: Tasiast Gold Mine
summary: On a stretch of Saharan coast where almost nothing grows, one of Africa's largest gold mines pulls fifteen tonnes of metal a year from the bare ground.

subject: Tassili n'Ajjer
summary: A vast Algerian sandstone plateau whose name means 'plateau of rivers' - now bone dry, but carved into a stone forest and painted with one of the greatest galleries of prehistoric art on Earth.

subject: Tata Steel Netherlands
summary: The largest industrial site in the Netherlands sits at the mouth of the North Sea Canal, employing thousands while a national argument rages over what it does to the air.

subject: Tatai
summary: A truck stop where Highway 48 crosses a river in the Cardamom Mountains - and one of the last waters on Earth holding wild Siamese crocodiles.

subject: Tatai Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: Created by sub-decree in 2016 and shrunk by another one in 2021, this corner of the Cardamom Mountains is where Cambodia's conservation ambitions and its land economy meet head-on.

subject: Tateâ€“LaBianca murders
summary: The August 1969 killings orchestrated by Charles Manson's followers at two Los Angeles homes shattered the innocence of the 1960s and changed Hollywood forever.

subject: Tatun Volcanic Group
summary: A cluster of dormant volcanoes on the northern edge of Taipei, still venting sulfurous gases and heating hot springs — a reminder that one of Asia's great metropolises sits in the shadow of a volcano field nominated for World Heritage status.

subject: TauTona Mine
summary: Named 'great lion' in Setswana, TauTona was once the deepest mine on Earth at 3.9 kilometers below the South African highveld, where rock temperatures reach 60 degrees Celsius and the journey to the working face takes over an hour.

subject: Taupō Volcanic Zone
summary: A 350-kilometer volcanic corridor through New Zealand's North Island where the Earth's crust stretches thin over a film of magma, producing more explosive rhyolite eruptions than anywhere else on the planet.

subject: Tavros
summary: An industrial inner suburb of Athens that carries the name of a mountain range its founders fled, built by refugees who survived the Greek genocide in Asia Minor.

subject: Tawau
summary: Sabah's third-largest town, where cocoa plantations meet the Celebes Sea and the border with Indonesia defines daily life as much as it does geopolitics.

subject: Tawi-Tawi
summary: The Philippines' southernmost province, an archipelago of 107 islands where human habitation dates to 6,800 BC and the oldest mosque in Southeast Asia still stands.

subject: Tayma
summary: One of Arabia's oldest oases and a great caravan town, Tayma is where a Babylonian king abandoned his throne to live for a decade in the desert.

subject: Taymyr Autonomous Okrug
summary: Once Russia's northernmost federal subject, the former Taymyr Autonomous Okrug sprawled across 862,100 square kilometers of tundra and permafrost with fewer than 40,000 inhabitants.

subject: Tazewell County, Virginia
summary: A southwestern Virginia county shaped by Pocahontas coal, defined by Burke's Garden — a bowl-shaped valley carved from a collapsed anticline — and home to petroglyphs that survived 10,000 years on Paintlick Mountain.

subject: Tbilisi
summary: Where Georgia's capital tumbles down gorge walls to sulfur baths, where alphabet and wine were invented, where East meets West in a city that has been conquered and rebuilt dozens of times.

subject: Tchibanga
summary: A small Gabonese city where Bwiti ceremonies begin at midnight to the sound of drumming, where masks are carved for ritual rather than tourists, and where the Nyanga River catches fire at sunset.

subject: Tchitundu-Hulu
summary: Four rock art sites clustered within a single kilometer in Angola's Namibe desert, where thousands of engravings and paintings -- some possibly dating to the first millennium BC -- cover the slopes of a hill whose name translates as 'hill of heaven.'

subject: Te Anau
summary: A lakeside town of fewer than 3,000 people that serves as the gateway to Fiordland, where glowworm caves glow beneath the mountains and a bird once thought extinct was rediscovered just across the water.

subject: Tearing Ledge Wreck
summary: Sixty-five iron guns and a ship's bell dated 1701 lie in a granite gully on the Western Rocks - quite possibly what remains of Admiral Shovell's fleet, sunk in one of the worst peacetime disasters in Royal Navy history.

subject: Teatro Colón
summary: Singers come to Buenos Aires for the air itself - the Teatro Colón is rated among the finest opera houses on Earth, born of a construction so cursed it took twenty years and two deaths to finish.

subject: Teatro El Círculo
summary: When Enrico Caruso sang here in 1915, he said the acoustics rivaled the Metropolitan Opera in New York.

subject: Techno Viking
summary: Four minutes filmed on a Berlin street in 2000 became one of the first great internet memes - and then its subject went to court and won back the rights to his own face.

subject: Teen Talwar
summary: Three white marble swords rise from a roundabout in Clifton, Karachi, originally commissioned by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1973 as a political symbol and designed by Zoroastrian architect Minu Mistri to embody Jinnah's motto of Unity, Faith, and Discipline.

subject: Teesdale
summary: A high Pennine valley where igneous rock, sub-Arctic climate and post-glacial flora produced a unique 'Teesdale Assemblage' of plants found nowhere else together.

subject: Tefé
summary: A lakeside Amazon town with no roads in, the last outpost before the Mamiraua flooded-forest reserve, reachable only by a 50-minute flight or a three-day boat ride from Manaus.

subject: Tefé
summary: Founded by Carmelite friars in the 1690s on a lake of the Solimoes, Tefe is one of the oldest permanent European settlements on the Amazon and was once the capital of the language Henry Walter Bates heard for 2,500 miles.

subject: Tegea
summary: Tegea was the great rival city-state to Mantinea on the Arcadian plain — home to the sanctuary of Athena Alea, one of antiquity's most powerful places of asylum, and a city that fought Sparta, defied Sparta, and then outlasted nearly everything else in Arcadia.

subject: Tegelen
summary: A Limburg pottery town that lent its name to a geological epoch and still stages a passion play every five years has been quietly arguing with its neighbor Venlo for six centuries.

subject: Tehran
summary: Iran's sprawling capital of 14 million sits at the foot of the Alborz Mountains, a city of 800 parks and ancient bazaars where Qajar palaces share the skyline with modern towers and ski resorts rise within an hour's drive.

subject: Tehran Metro
summary: The largest metro system in the Middle East survived revolution, war, and decades of geopolitical isolation to become the backbone of a megacity that moves three million passengers a day.

subject: Tehuantepec
summary: The Zapotec cultural capital of Mexico's narrowest point, where women have dominated the markets for centuries and a nineteenth-century candy seller became the most powerful person in the isthmus through her alliance with a future president.

subject: Teijo, Salo
summary: An ironworks village of 370 people whose patron built Finland's smallest stone church — shaped like a pagoda — in thanks for a flood that never arrived.

subject: Tel Aviv
summary: Where Jewish refugees built a city from sand dunes, where Bauhaus became the White City, where Israel's secular heart beats faster than Jerusalem's prayers.

subject: Telangana movement
summary: A five-decade struggle for statehood that carved India's 29th state from Andhra Pradesh, rooted in broken promises and the fierce identity of the Deccan Plateau's Telugu heartland.

subject: Teleférico de Caracas
summary: A gondola lift inaugurated in 1955 carries passengers from the streets of Caracas to the summit of El Avila, where the city stretches out on one side and the Caribbean coast appears on the other.

subject: Telegraph Avenue
summary: A four-and-a-half-mile corridor connecting downtown Oakland to UC Berkeley, Telegraph Avenue has served as a telegraph route, a streetcar corridor, a counterculture battleground, and a living mosaic of immigrant communities since 1859.

subject: Telegraph Cove
summary: A former telegraph station turned sawmill village turned whale-watching capital of northern Vancouver Island, with a population of about twenty and a boardwalk that has survived fire, industry collapse, and reinvention.

subject: Telegraph, Isles of Scilly
summary: The highest point in the Isles of Scilly, named for the cable that connected the islands to London in 1869 by way of a continuous 30-mile spool of copper, hemp and iron.

subject: Tell Kunara
summary: Two ancient mounds on the banks of the Tanjaro River may hold the remains of the Lullubi capital, a Bronze Age city that used its own system of measurement and built walls with mortar made from crushed bones.

story.title: Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here

subject: Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here
summary: A 1969 film about the last great desert manhunt in American history — the 1909 pursuit of a Chemehuevi-Paiute man through the Mojave — and the two very different stories its making set in motion.

subject: Telluride, Colorado
summary: A box canyon town where Butch Cassidy robbed his first bank, Westinghouse proved alternating current could travel long distances, and hippies replaced miners to build one of Colorado's most iconic resort communities.

subject: Temagami Greenstone Belt
summary: A 2.7-billion-year-old strip of metamorphosed volcanic rock in northeastern Ontario that has witnessed the assembly and breakup of at least four supercontinents, yielded iron, copper, gold, and silver from its mines, and holds some of the oldest exposed rock on the planet.

subject: Tembagapura
summary: A company town at 1,930 meters where expatriate children attend the world's most remote international school, and the Amungme still insist the land is theirs.

subject: Temperance Wick
summary: When mutinous soldiers came for her horse during the brutal winter of 1780, Temperance Wick -- 22 years old, her father newly dead, her mother ill -- reportedly hid the animal in a bedroom of her family's farmhouse at Jockey Hollow.

subject: Templemore
summary: A Tipperary town in the shadow of the Devil's Bit, where Marian apparitions briefly drew pilgrims in 1920 and where every garda in Ireland now learns the job.

subject: Templin
summary: The Uckermark town that burned to the ground in four hours in 1735 and kept its medieval wall: 1,735 metres of fieldstone, three gates, and fifty surviving wall houses around an eighteenth-century town.

subject: Temryuk
summary: A port town at the mouth of the Kuban River where rusting war tanks sit parked on the slope of a mud volcano, named for a Circassian prince whose daughter married Ivan the Terrible.

subject: Tena
summary: Ecuador's self-styled cinnamon capital sits at a river junction in the Amazon, launching rafts, backpackers, and cave-swimmers into the jungle.

subject: Tenby Lifeboat Station
summary: The Pembrokeshire harbour where a farmer's three-million-pound legacy paid for a lifeboat named in his memory and Channel 4 filmed Grand Designs converting the Victorian boathouse next door.

subject: Tendra Spit
summary: A thread of Black Sea sand where ancient Greeks worshipped Achilles, an empire's fleet won a famous battle, and 800 buried coins finally gave up the island's oldest secret.

story.title: Tenganan: The Village That Stayed Behind

subject: Tenganan
summary: One of Bali's oldest communities has preserved pre-Hindu traditions, strict marriage laws, and a sacred double-ikat textile found in only three places on Earth.

subject: Tenham (meteorite)
summary: Stones that fell on a sheep run in 1879 hold the first natural specimens of minerals that make up most of the Earth's deep interior.

subject: Teniky
summary: Deep in the Isalo massif lie precise stone walls, terraces, and cliff niches unlike anything else in Madagascar - and a 2024 study argues their closest cousins are a thousand-year-old Zoroastrian tombs in Iran.

subject: Tenkodogo
summary: The oldest of the Mossi kingdoms, where a name that means 'ancient land' still carries the weight of nine centuries of dynasty.

subject: Tennant Creek
summary: Known as the Territory's heart of gold, Tennant Creek is a remote outback town where Aboriginal Warumungu culture, 1930s gold rush history, and the vast Barkly Tablelands converge under some of Australia's most brilliant night skies.

subject: Tennant Creek
summary: Australia's last great gold rush town sits at the crossroads of the Stuart and Barkly highways, where Warumungu country, telegraph history, and outback grit meet under skies that produce 181 clear days a year.

subject: Tenoumer Crater
summary: A near-perfect circle punched into the Mauritanian Sahara, Tenoumer is the scar left by a meteorite that struck ancient rock that had already weathered for a billion years.

subject: Tenterfield
summary: A high-country town that gave Australia a federation, a saddler's song, and a granite landscape that draws climbers to its edges.

subject: Tenterfield, New South Wales
summary: A granite-country border town where a single 1889 speech set Australia on the road to nationhood - and where a saddler's grandson turned the family shop into one of the country's best-loved songs.

subject: Teotihuacan
summary: The largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas held up to 125,000 residents, dominated Mesoamerican trade and culture for centuries, and was so thoroughly abandoned that even the Aztecs could only guess at who built it.

subject: Tepe Ghabristan
summary: A 6,000-year-old archaeological mound on Iran's Qazvin Plain that preserves some of the earliest evidence of organized copper metallurgy, with workshops, crucibles, and 20 kilograms of malachite ore left behind by its ancient craftspeople.

subject: Tepe Hissar
summary: An ancient mound near Damghan harbors nearly 4,000 years of continuous human habitation, from Chalcolithic painted pottery to Bronze Age metalworking that connected Mesopotamia to Central Asia along the Great Khorasan Road.

subject: Tepe Sialk
summary: A pair of ancient mounds near Kashan, Iran harboring 8,000 years of continuous human settlement, the world's oldest known ziggurat, and some of the earliest evidence of metallurgy.

story.title: Tepe Sofalin: Where Writing Was Born on the Tehran Plain

subject: Tepe Sofalin
