summary: A cache of extraordinary Romano-British gold and silver — spoons inscribed to a pagan woodland god, rings of dazzling filigree, a belt buckle adorned with a dancing satyr — found in failing light on a November evening in 1979, under circumstances that left its story permanently incomplete.

subject: Thetford Priory
summary: Founded in 1103 as a substitute for a pilgrimage vow, Thetford Priory became one of the most important monasteries in East Anglia — and the burial ground of dukes, earls, and royal children before it fell to the English Reformation.

subject: Thialf
summary: An ice arena in the Frisian town of Heerenveen, named for Thor's servant who outraced a giant in Norse myth, where almost every speed-skating world record was broken in a single season.

subject: Third Street, Hong Kong
summary: A single street in Sai Ying Pun that contains multitudes — a Chinese liquor factory, a chili sauce outlet, five music schools, five auto mechanics, and the quiet bones of a neighborhood that has resisted becoming something else.

subject: Third Ward, Houston
summary: Houston's Third Ward, nicknamed 'The Tre,' has evolved from a 19th-century silk-stocking neighborhood into one of the city's most culturally significant African-American communities, now navigating the pressures of rapid gentrification.

subject: Thirteen Factories
summary: For nearly a century, a strip of warehouses along the Pearl River in Guangzhou was the only place on earth where Western merchants could legally trade with China — a world of silk, tea, porcelain, and opium that burned to the ground three times before disappearing for good.

subject: This Pride of Java
summary: Scattered across 100 square kilometers of East Javanese farmland lie the ruins of Trowulan, the probable capital of the Majapahit Empire, where red-brick temples, split gateways, and a pool called 'the sea' testify to a city that once rivaled any in the medieval world.

subject: Thiseio
summary: An old Athens neighbourhood named after a temple misidentified for centuries, where pedestrian streets thread between the Agora, the Pnyx, and the finest views of the Acropolis.

subject: Thisted
summary: A Limfjord market town named for the Norse god Tyr, with an unusual habit of producing people who left and changed something somewhere else.

subject: Thomas Circle
summary: Named for the Union general known as the Rock of Chickamauga, surrounded by two churches and a tunnel that opened on the same day Hitler invaded Norway, Thomas Circle marks the line between downtown Washington and the city's gentrifying north.

subject: Thomas Cromwell
summary: A Putney blacksmith's son who rose to remake the English state, broke from Rome, and lost his head to the king he had served. Hilary Mantel made him human again.

subject: Thomas Gillespie
summary: An 18th-century North Carolina planter whose Sills Creek plantation depended on the labor of seven enslaved people, who left a paper trail of land grants stretching from the Yadkin to the Clinch, and who happened to be the great-grandfather of a future president.

subject: Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility
summary: A racetrack-shaped particle accelerator buried beneath suburban Newport News, Virginia, where 2,000 scientists probe the fundamental structure of matter using the world's most powerful continuous electron beam.

subject: Thomas L. "Pegleg" Smith
summary: A mountain man who reportedly amputated his own leg, ran the largest horse theft ring in the Southwest, and spent his later years selling maps to a gold mine that may or may not have ever existed.

subject: Thomas Petrie
summary: A settler's son who grew up among the Turrbal people, spoke their language, feasted at a bunya gathering, and through his daughter's book preserved a record of Aboriginal Brisbane before it was lost.

subject: Thomas Polk
summary: The Charlotte founder who guarded the Liberty Bell on its escape from Philadelphia, hosted George Washington overnight, and seeded a family that produced an American president.

subject: Thomas Smith (engineer)
summary: His father drowned. He became an ironmonger, then a lampmaker, then the engineer who lit Scotland's first lighthouses - and founded the Stevenson dynasty.

subject: Thomas W. Lawson
summary: The largest pure-sail vessel ever built had seven masts, no engine, and a problem: no one could agree what to call her masts. She solved the argument by sinking off the Western Rocks in 1907, killing seventeen men and creating possibly the first large marine oil spill.

subject: Thornewood Open Space Preserve
summary: A widow's bequest to the Sierra Club created this small preserve in the Santa Cruz Mountains, where second-growth redwoods surround a lake named after the Schilling spice dynasty.

subject: Thornton Peak
summary: A granite-crowned giant rising 1,374 metres straight out of the Daintree lowlands, Thornton Peak is sacred Eastern Kuku Yalanji country and a cool-climate ark for creatures found almost nowhere else.

subject: Thorsberg moor
summary: A peat bog in Angeln where, for some five centuries, people sank weapons, armour and clothing into the water - and where the acid and the airlessness preserved a pair of trousers with the feet still attached, and one of the oldest runic inscriptions ever found.

subject: Thousand Palms
summary: A quiet Coachella Valley community where the San Andreas Fault creates a hidden oasis sheltering endangered species and twenty thousand acres of protected desert.

subject: Thousand-Buddha Cliff
summary: A 63-meter cliff face bearing over 210 Tang dynasty Buddhist carvings, begun by a 70-year-old monk in 619 AD as an act of devotion during an era when Buddhism itself was politically dangerous.

subject: Three Bays Protected Area
summary: Haiti's second-largest protected area shelters 75,000 hectares of coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds along the country's northeastern coast, where Taino history and the Haitian Revolution left marks as deep as the reef systems below the surface.

subject: Three Castles
summary: Three Norman fortresses, one medieval lordship, and a 30-kilometre walk that still ties them together eight centuries after the Crown decided they should be a single thing.

story.title: Three Centuries of Spice and Subjugation

subject: Three Centuries of Spice and Subjugation
summary: For 350 years, the Dutch turned the Indonesian archipelago into one of the most profitable colonies in history - built on spice monopolies, forced labor, and a racial hierarchy that shaped the lives of millions.

subject: Three Mountains of Dewa
summary: Japan's oldest mountain worship site, where three sacred peaks represent birth, death, and rebirth -- and where the ascetic tradition of Shugendo has survived imperial bans, world war, and fourteen centuries of change.

subject: Three Names, One Town
summary: A Gold Rush settlement in the Sierra Nevada foothills has been called Summersville, Carters, and Tuolumne, each name marking a chapter in a story that runs from placer mining through lumber milling to Hollywood westerns.

subject: Three Parallel Rivers
summary: Three of Asia's mightiest rivers run side by side for over 300 kilometers through Yunnan's Hengduan Mountains before diverging to empty into three different seas thousands of kilometers apart.

subject: Thuburbo Majus
summary: A sprawling Roman city in the Tunisian countryside where mosaics of Venus, Bacchus, and fishing scenes have survived nearly two millennia of silence.

subject: Thula Thula
summary: A game reserve in Zululand where a conservationist talked a herd of condemned elephants out of running, and where those elephants later mourned him when he died.

subject: Thunder Road
summary: A racing wooden coaster themed to a Robert Mitchum moonshine film, opened 1976 with NASCAR royalty in attendance and demolished in 2015 for Fury 325 - and remembered ever since.

subject: Thunder over the Boardwalk
summary: An annual military airshow staged over the Atlantic City beach, drawing crowds of 750,000 or more to watch Thunderbirds, Blue Angels, and Golden Knights perform between the casino towers and the sea.

subject: Thung Yai Naresuan Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: Thailand's largest protected area, a UNESCO World Heritage Site where Indochinese tigers breed in Southeast Asia's most complete dry tropical forest, and where a billionaire poaching scandal exposed the country's unequal justice.

subject: Thursday Morning Club
summary: Founded in 1896 in Madison, New Jersey, the Thursday Morning Club has spent more than 125 years evolving from a women's social organization into a community services anchor that runs childcare programs, legal aid, and workforce support.

subject: Thurso
summary: Scotland's northernmost town takes its name from Thor, surfs three-metre waves at the top of mainland Britain, and grew up around a nuclear reactor.

subject: Thurstaston Common
summary: A windswept Wirral heath where Triassic sandstone breaks the surface and the Welsh hills shimmer on a clear day.

subject: Thylejren
summary: A seventy-four-day festival in the summer of 1970 that nobody ever quite ended — and the village its residents have been running on their own terms ever since.

subject: Thylungra
summary: On a remote bend of mulga country southwest of Quilpie, an Irish-Australian family built a pastoral empire on land that already belonged to the Boonthamurra people.

subject: Tiananmen Square
summary: The world's most politically charged public space has witnessed the founding of modern China, student movements that shook the nation, and a military crackdown that the government still works to erase from collective memory.

subject: Tianguá
summary: A gateway town at the top of the Serra da Ibiapaba escarpment, halfway between Teresina and Fortaleza, Tianguá trades in cooler air, improbable strawberries, and a perimeter of waterfalls that most Brazilian maps miss.

subject: Tianjin Eye
summary: The only Ferris wheel in the world built directly on top of a bridge, the 120-meter Tianjin Eye rises above the Yongle Bridge over the Hai River, offering riders a slow, thirty-minute rotation through views of a city where nine nations once flew their flags.

subject: Tianzi Wharf
summary: The oldest wharf on the Pearl River, Tianzi Wharf witnessed Lin Zexu's destruction of British opium in 1839 and Sun Yat-sen's desperate escape to Hong Kong — two scenes that helped make modern China.

subject: Tibau do Sul
summary: A Rio Grande do Norte fishing municipality reshaped by surfers, where a brackish lagoon, a mangrove river and a bay full of grey dolphins matter as much as the famous beaches.

subject: Tibet
summary: The roof of the world, where the highest plateau on Earth sustains one of civilization's most distinctive cultures beneath a sky that seems close enough to touch.

subject: Tibet Art Center
summary: A Finnish avant-garde musician spent forty-five years collecting Tibetan thangkas and gilded bronzes, and left them in a closed village schoolhouse in the middle of Loimaa's grain fields.

subject: Tibetan Empire
summary: From a valley south of Lhasa, the Yarlung dynasty built an empire that captured the Chinese capital, controlled the Silk Road, and rivaled the Tang and Abbasid caliphates before collapsing in civil war.

subject: Tibooburra
summary: The granite-strewn outback town that is regularly the hottest place in New South Wales, a gold-rush relic turned gateway to the Corner Country.

subject: Tichit
summary: A half-abandoned medieval caravan town on the Tagant escarpment, built from six colors of stone, one of the four UNESCO Ancient Ksour and one of the oldest stone settlements south of the Sahara.

subject: Tichit
summary: A stone caravan town at the foot of the Tagant Plateau, slowly disappearing beneath the dunes that once made it rich.

subject: Tidal Basin
summary: A 107-acre flushing reservoir engineered in the 1880s to clean the Washington Channel became, by an accident of diplomatic gift-giving, the most photographed body of water in the United States every spring.

subject: Tide Mills, East Sussex
summary: Founded by a future Prime Minister in 1762, run for half a century by a milling family who built cottages and a school for their workers, and then condemned in 1936 and forcibly evacuated in 1939 - Tide Mills is the abandoned village between Newhaven and Seaford.

story.title: Tides of Empire: California's Maritime Story

subject: Tides of Empire
summary: From tule reed canoes to Gold Rush ghost ships to the largest naval fleet on the Pacific coast, California's coastline has been shaped by every vessel that ever touched its waters.

subject: Tidjikja
summary: A 17th-century date-palm oasis on the Tagant plateau, once the crossroads where salt caravans from across the Sahara converged - and still a town that celebrates its dates with a festival every year.

subject: Tidore
summary: A volcanic island sultanate in the Maluku archipelago that played European colonial powers against each other for two centuries before finally succumbing to Dutch control.

subject: Tiefwasserreede
summary: A patch of open North Sea water that is legally German territory, marooned thirty kilometres beyond the usual twelve-mile limit, where freighters bound for Hamburg and Bremen drop anchor and wait.

subject: Tierpark Hagenbeck
summary: The Hamburg zoo that taught the world to replace cages with moats was built by a man who also put human beings on display - eight of whom, brought from Labrador in 1880, died within four months.

subject: Tierra del Fuego
summary: The Land of Fire was named for flames its first explorers never understood - the cooking and signal fires of people surviving naked at the bottom of the world, on an archipelago split between two nations and battered by the planet's fiercest winds.

subject: Tierra del Fuego gold rush
summary: The gold that drew fortune-hunters to the bottom of the world also funded the destruction of the people who had lived there for ten thousand years.

subject: Tifariti
summary: A bombed-out desert oasis that the Sahrawi people rebuilt brick by brick into the working capital of a republic still seeking its homeland.

subject: Tighnabruaich
summary: A Gaelic-named village on the Kyles of Bute that the steamers built, the road eventually reached, and shinty has made unusually famous for its size.

subject: Tigray Province
summary: The historical heartland of the Aksumite Empire and modern Ethiopia's most culturally dense region, home to the oldest surviving Christian churches in Africa, the battlefield of the Battle of Adwa, and the site of the catastrophic 2020-2022 war whose casualties remain incompletely counted.

subject: Tigray Region
summary: Ethiopia's northernmost region holds three thousand years of stone-carved monuments, ancient Aksum's obelisks, and the fresh wounds of a war that killed an estimated 600,000 people.

subject: Tigre
summary: Where the city meets the wild delta, Tigre offers Buenos Aires residents an escape into a labyrinth of waterways once stalked by jaguars.

subject: Tigre, Buenos Aires
summary: Where Buenos Aires runs out of streets, Tigre begins - a city of brown water and wooden boats at the doorstep of the vast Paraná Delta.

story.title: Tijuana: The Border City That Became Its Own Third Country

subject: Tijuana
summary: The Baja California metropolis where Mexico meets America and neither quite wins - where the wall divides but doesn't stop, where maquiladoras manufacture for American companies, and where a food scene emerged that rivals any city on either side.

subject: Tijuana Cultural Center
summary: Opened in 1982, the Tijuana Cultural Center — known as CECUT — anchors the Zona Río district with its striking spherical OMNIMAX cinema and stands as a symbol of Tijuana's identity as a city of culture, not just a border crossing.

subject: Tilburg
summary: The Dutch city that wove the empire's wool, mourned 145 lost mills when the industry collapsed, and quietly remade itself into a university town with Tesla on the edge of town.

subject: Tilcara
summary: The cultural heart of the Quebrada de Humahuaca, where Andean traditions, colonial stone, and the deepest archaeology in Argentina meet in one small mountain town.

subject: Tilikum (boat)
summary: A hundred-year-old Nuu-chah-nulth cedar dugout, bought for eighty dollars and rigged with three masts, sailed from Vancouver Island to the Thames — and killed one of the men aboard her.

subject: Tillamook Head
summary: A 1,200-foot basalt promontory on the Oregon coast where 15-million-year-old lava from Idaho meets the Pacific, and where William Clark once hiked to find a beached whale.

subject: Timbo, Guinea
summary: In the green highlands of the Fouta Djallon, a quiet Guinean town once held the throne of a theocratic state that ruled for nearly two centuries.

story.title: Timbuctoo: Gold Rush Ghost of the Yuba

subject: Timbuctoo
summary: A California Gold Rush boomtown named for a West African city, Timbuctoo rose on hydraulic mining wealth, fell when a federal court killed the industry, and now survives only as a fenced ruin that looters tore apart searching for hidden gold.

subject: Timbuktu
summary: The legendary desert city on the edge of the Sahara, a byword for the ends of the earth, and a place that is still genuinely hard to reach.

subject: Timeline of London
summary: Two thousand years of the city — from the Roman bridge of AD 50 to the Shard. Seven moments that turned London into itself.

subject: Timeline of Riga
summary: Riga's eight centuries — from a German bishop's outpost on a Liv river mouth to a Hanseatic port, a Russian capital, a Soviet city, and the capital of an independent Latvia.

subject: Timeline of Salvador, Bahia
summary: Five centuries of Salvador, Brazil's first capital — a walkable city of churches, rebellions, elevators, and drums built above a bay that Amerigo Vespucci named for a Florentine parish.

subject: Timgad
summary: A Roman city buried for centuries beneath Saharan sand, its perfect grid plan now the best-preserved example of Roman urban planning in the world.

subject: Timoleague
summary: An Irish village on the Argideen estuary whose name means 'Molaga's House,' where a sixth-century saint, French-speaking friars, a Maharaja of Gwalior, and a Polish-speaking 21st-century neighbourhood have all left their mark.

subject: Timoleague Friary
summary: The largest medieval ruin in West Cork rises directly out of the Argideen estuary - a Franciscan friary with a Leper's Window, a Fairy Cupboard, and a French saint's eroded head set into its outer wall.

story.title: Tin Hau Temples in Hong Kong

subject: Tin Hau Temples in Hong Kong
summary: More than 100 temples across Hong Kong honor the sea goddess Tin Hau — a network of sacred places that map the territory's maritime history from harbor to island to bay.

subject: Tin Hau, Hong Kong
summary: A district named for a goddess whose temple was once on the waterfront — now surrounded by reclaimed land and residential towers, and known as much by its MTR station as by the deity who gave it its name.

subject: Tin Pan Alley
summary: A single block on West 28th Street in Manhattan gave American popular music its industrial engine — and its name — from roughly 1885 until rock and roll made the whole machinery obsolete.

subject: Tin Shui Wai
summary: A satellite town of nearly 300,000 people built on reclaimed fishponds in the northwestern New Territories — a place that grew fast, faced real challenges, and has been telling its own story in film, music, and daily life ever since.

subject: Tin Walls and Divided Sidewalks
summary: After a fire destroyed Isleton's Asian commercial district in 1926, two communities rebuilt Main Street in pressed tin and brick -- Chinese families on one side, Japanese families on the other -- creating the only Asian-built district of its kind in California's Sacramento Delta.

subject: Tinallinge
summary: A tiny Groningen village built on a 2,500-year-old artificial mound, with a thirteenth-century church at the top and almost no construction since 1900.

subject: Tindouf
summary: An Algerian garrison town in the deep Sahara where a displaced nation outnumbers the locals two to one - and where the closest you can get to Sahrawi culture is a refugee camp.

subject: Ting Kok
summary: On the northern shore of Plover Cove, Ting Kok is a village older than most Hong Kong records — a Punti settlement that became a Catholic missionary hub, a wetland sanctuary, and one of the territory's quieter surprises.

subject: Tinos
summary: A Cycladic island of ancient pilgrimage, a thousand ornate dovecotes, and marble-carving villages — where Greek Orthodox and Catholic communities have coexisted for centuries.

subject: Tintagel
summary: The North Cornwall village where Geoffrey of Monmouth set King Arthur's conception in the 1130s - and where archaeologists later found a real fifth-century trading site with Mediterranean pottery.

subject: Tintern
summary: A village on a bend of the River Wye whose ruined Cistercian abbey has inspired poets, painters, and 70,000 visitors a year, with iron forges hidden in the valley behind it.

subject: Tip of Borneo
summary: The northernmost point of the world's third-largest island, where the South China Sea meets the Sulu Sea and where pirates, Magellan's fleet, and the Rungus people have all left their mark.

subject: Tipasa
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Algerian coast where Punic traders, Roman soldiers, and early Christians each left their mark across two thousand years, now threatened by the rising sea itself.

subject: Tiputini Biodiversity Station
summary: A remote Ecuadorian research camp at the edge of Yasuni where more reptiles, amphibians, and birds have been counted than anywhere else in South America.

subject: Tiradentes
summary: A tiny colonial town in the Minas Gerais highlands where gold-era churches still glitter and a steam train rolls in on weekends.

subject: Tiraspol
summary: The capital of a country the world does not recognize, where Soviet-era trolleybuses and Lenin statues make an isolated town on the Dniester feel like a step back in time.

subject: Tiree
summary: The flattest of the Inner Hebrides, where rebels learned golf from Royal Marines and a granite boulder rings when struck like a bell.

subject: Tireli, Mali
summary: A Dogon village pressed against the foot of the Bandiagara cliff, where market beer, tobacco grown in a dry riverbed, and the great masked Dama dances mark the rhythm of life beneath the sandstone.

subject: Tiris Zemmour
summary: Mauritania's vast northern desert region, where one of the world's longest freight trains hauls iron ore across the Sahara to the sea.

subject: Titanic Quarter
summary: Once a people's park with a zoo and Crystal Palace, then the world's most famous shipyard, Belfast's 185-acre Titanic Quarter has reinvented itself as a waterfront district of film studios, universities, and heritage sites where Game of Thrones was filmed.

subject: Titanochampsa
summary: A Cretaceous Brazilian crocodyliform so massive that paleontologists first mistook its fossil for a titanosaur - an ambush predator that rewrote what lived in the Bauru Group.

subject: Tithorea
summary: A small Phocian village on the slopes of Parnassus that has carried the same storied ground through 4,000 years of gods, soldiers, and saboteurs.

subject: Tithorea (Phocis)
summary: Perched above the gorge of the Cachales stream on the northeast flank of Parnassus, ancient Tithorea was a formidable refuge-city whose walls, sacred rites, and exceptional olive oil all bear witness to a community shaped by terrain.

subject: Titiwangsa Mountains
summary: The granite spine of the Malay Peninsula, the Titiwangsa Mountains run 480 kilometers from southern Thailand to the tip of Negeri Sembilan, dividing a subcontinent in two.

story.title: Titusville: The Best Seat for Rocket Launches

subject: Titusville
summary: The Florida Space Coast city directly across the Indian River from Kennedy Space Center, where locals gather on riverbanks to watch rockets rise, where aerospace workers live, and where every launch is a community event.

subject: Tiu Keng Leng
summary: Once called 'Little Taiwan' and sealed off from Hong Kong's own police, Tiu Keng Leng was a Cold War anomaly — a Nationalist Chinese enclave hiding in plain sight beside Junk Bay.

subject: Tiwanaku
summary: A pre-Columbian archaeological site near Lake Titicaca whose megalithic stonework and astronomical alignments mark it as the spiritual and political center of a civilization that shaped the Andes for nearly a thousand years.

subject: Tjaskers in Germany
summary: Six tiny post-mounted windmills survive in Lower Saxony - the smallest working drainage machines in Europe, each barely larger than a garden shed.

subject: Tla-o-qui-aht First Nations
summary: A confederation of Nuu-chah-nulth peoples whose name means 'different people from a different place,' forged by war, tested by colonialism, and now generating hydroelectric power on their ancestral territory.

story.title: Tlacolula de Matamoros: The Sunday Market at the Place of Abundance

subject: Tlacolula de Matamoros
summary: A Zapotec valley city whose Sunday market is one of the oldest and largest in Oaxaca, whose Dominican church hides an astonishing Baroque chapel, and whose residents have migrated in such numbers to Venice Beach, California, that Zapotec is the first language of thirty percent of schoolchildren in certain Los Angeles neighborhoods.

subject: Tlaquepaque
summary: The Guadalajara suburb where the name literally means 'place above clay land' and artisans have been shaping pottery, blown glass, and papier-mâché for centuries.

subject: Tlowitsis Nation
summary: A Kwakwaka'wakw nation whose territory spans the islands and inlets of Johnstone Strait, carrying a complicated history of forced amalgamation and a disputed relationship with the Ma'amtagila people.

subject: Tmutarakan
summary: A medieval trading city so remote its name became Russian slang for the middle of nowhere, Tmutarakan once controlled the gateway between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

subject: To Kwa Wan
summary: A low-rise Kowloon neighborhood shaped by an airport that no longer exists — To Kwa Wan kept its human scale while the city around it soared, and residents fiercely value what that means.

subject: Toamasina
summary: Madagascar's great Indian Ocean port, built on a coral reef and a sandy spit, where nearly everything the island trades with the world passes through.

subject: Toba Batak language
summary: An Austronesian language spoken by 1.6 million people around Lake Toba carries a unique verb-first grammar, an ancient script, and a naming tradition that encodes colonial and post-colonial identity.

subject: Toba Inlet
summary: A remote BC fjord whose name traces back to a Spanish bureaucratic tribute, where grizzly bears outnumber people and an 18th-century painted plank gave a waterway its first identity.

subject: Tobermory
summary: The main settlement on the Isle of Mull is a bustling Hebridean town by island standards, a small village by mainland reckoning, defined by its painted seafront and ferry-connected isolation.

subject: Tobermory Lifeboat Station
summary: A volunteer lifeboat crew on the Isle of Mull has answered emergency calls in the Sound of Mull and the wider Hebrides since 1938, with a long gap from 1947 to 1990.

subject: Tobermory, Mull
summary: The capital of the Isle of Mull is a planned 18th-century fishing port whose brightly painted seafront, Spanish-galleon legend, and TV stardom have made it one of Scotland's most photographed harbours.

story.title: Tobu World Square: The Whole Earth at Your Feet

subject: Tobu World Square
summary: A theme park in Nikko's Kinugawa Onsen where 102 of the world's most famous buildings stand at 1:25 scale -- from the Pyramids of Giza to the Tokyo Skytree -- populated by 140,000 tiny figures and tended by 20,000 bonsai trees.

subject: Tocantins
summary: Brazil's youngest state, born in 1988 from the upper half of Goias, stretching between the Amazon and the cerrado with orange-sand dunes, river islands, and a planned capital younger than most of its residents.

subject: Tochal
summary: A 3,963-meter peak rising directly above Tehran, connected to the city by one of the world's most dramatic gondola lifts -- where 15 million people can look up from their morning commute and see a ski resort.

subject: Todos Santos, Baja California Sur
summary: A small Baja California town that died when its spring went dry, came back to life when the water returned, and now wrestles with the consequences of its own charm.

subject: Tofino
summary: A surf town at the end of the road on Vancouver Island's west coast, where Hollywood films on its beaches, wild cows roam nearby islands, and Canada's first Olympic surfer learned to ride waves.

subject: Tohoku Shinseien Sanatorium
summary: The sixth of Japan's national leprosy sanatoriums, founded in 1939 in rural Miyagi Prefecture, became both a place of forced isolation and, decades later, a landmark in the legal battle that declared Japan's segregation of Hansen's disease patients unconstitutional.

subject: Toirano Caves
summary: A karst cave system in the Ligurian hills where the bones of cave bears share the darkness with spectacular stalactites and speleothems shaped over millennia.

subject: Tokatlıyan Hotels
summary: An Armenian entrepreneur from Tokat built what became one of Istanbul's grandest hotels on the Rue de Pera in 1897 — a place where Atatürk felt at home and history periodically dropped in to make a scene.

subject: Tokeh, Sierra Leone
summary: A white-sand fishing village turned celebrated beach resort, twice built and twice nearly lost.

subject: Tokugawa Ieyasu
summary: Born a hostage, raised among enemies, and forged by decades of patience, Tokugawa Ieyasu became the last of Japan's three great unifiers and founded a shogunate that ruled for over 250 years of peace.

story.title: Tokyo: A City That Keeps Rebuilding Itself

subject: Tokyo
summary: Leveled by earthquake in 1923 and firebombed flat in 1945, Tokyo rebuilt itself into the world's largest metropolitan area -- a city of 14 million where Edo-era shrines stand in the shadow of 634-meter broadcast towers and 3,000 people cross a single intersection at once.

subject: Tokyo Disneyland
summary: The first Disney theme park built outside the United States opened on a 600-acre landfill in Chiba Prefecture in 1983, and within eleven years more people had passed through its gates than the entire population of Japan.

subject: Tokyo International Forum
summary: A glass-and-steel convention hall shaped like an elongated boat -- designed by Uruguayan-American architect Rafael Vinoly on the former site of Tokyo's City Hall, completed in 1996, and host to everything from Olympic weightlifting to the World Bank's annual meetings.

subject: Tokyo Motor Show
summary: Born as a modest outdoor exhibition of commercial trucks in 1954 Hibiya Park, the Tokyo Motor Show grew into one of the world's five premier auto shows, a stage where Japan's automakers unveiled dream machines that reshaped the global automotive landscape.

subject: Tolar Grande
summary: A village of roughly 200 people stranded in the high Puna de Atacama, where salt flats stretch to the horizon and rare living stromatolites breathe in pools called the Eyes of the Sea.

subject: Toliara
summary: Madagascar's sun-scorched southwestern port city, where pousse-pousse rickshaws outnumber cars, Route Nationale 7 ends at the Mozambique Channel, and the surrounding spiny desert harbours species found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Tolima Department
summary: A Colombian department whose name means snowed in the language of the people who were here first, stretched between two ranges of the Andes and crossed by the Magdalena River.

subject: Tollygunge
summary: A jungle named after a British colonel who dredged a dead canal became the cradle of Indian cinema -- and the neighborhood whose name inspired 'Tollywood' long before Bombay ever adopted 'Bollywood.'

subject: Tombo, Sierra Leone
summary: One of Sierra Leone's great fishing towns, Tombo is a five-century-old Sherbro settlement whose harbour, mosques, and crowded boats tell a layered story of trade, faith, and a surname carried down from the slave-trade era.

subject: Tombos (Nubia)
summary: Under its mud-brick pyramids, Tombos buried not only the Egyptian elite sent to govern conquered Nubia but also the low-ranking workers who kept the colonial machine running.

story.title: Tombstone: 30 Seconds That Built a Legend

subject: Tombstone
summary: The Arizona mining town where the Earps and Doc Holliday shot it out with the Clantons in a gunfight lasting less than a minute - 30 seconds of violence that spawned a thousand movies, endless debate about heroes and villains, and a town that refuses to die.

story.title: Tombstone: The Town Too Tough to Die

subject: Tombstone
summary: The silver mining town where the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral lasted 30 seconds in 1881, where Wyatt Earp became legend, and where daily reenactments keep the Old West alive for tourist dollars.

subject: Tominian
summary: A small town on the edge of Mali's Ségou Region, Tominian is the heart of Bwa country, where masks of leaf and wood still carry the old stories.

subject: Tomohon
summary: Flanked by two active volcanoes in the Sulawesi highlands, Indonesia's 'City of Flowers' grows orchids in volcanic soil, runs horse carts through its streets, and hosts an observatory connected to NASA telescopes.

subject: Tomonoura
summary: A rare surviving Edo-period port town on the Seto Inland Sea whose circular harbor inspired Hayao Miyazaki's Ponyo and has been celebrated in Japanese poetry since the 8th century.

subject: Tomorrowland
summary: On disused clay pits south of Antwerp, two brothers built what became the largest electronic dance music festival in the world. In 2025, fire destroyed the main stage two days before opening.

subject: Tomé Tragedy
summary: On a winding coastal road above Tomé, a busload of football fans heading home from a victory plunged into a ravine; sixteen people died, and a club learned to carry its grief in silence.

subject: Tonantins
summary: A boat-only Amazon river town named after a long-ago indigenous rival, where the annual pirarucu festival draws thousands from across Amazonas state.

subject: Tonantins
summary: Born from a violent collision between missionaries and a river tribe in the 1770s, this Amazonas municipality became a reality TV footnote 243 years later.

subject: Tonbridge Priory
summary: An Augustinian priory founded in 1124 that survived 400 years and a Christmas feast of 200 loaves and three casks of beer - then died twice, once to Wolsey, once to the railway.

story.title: Tondabayashi Jinaimachi: The Temple Town That Time Forgot

subject: Tondabayashi Jinaimachi
summary: A fortified temple town from the 1550s, complete with moats, bamboo groves, and four wooden gates that closed each night, survives almost intact in southern Osaka -- overlooked by the very modernization that destroyed every town like it.

subject: Tondidarou
summary: On the bank of a small lake southwest of Timbuktu stand carved stone monoliths more than a thousand years old - one of West Africa's great megalithic enigmas, and one of its most threatened.

subject: Tong Fuk
summary: A quiet village on Lantau Island's southern coast where Chan and Tang clan descendants, offshore submarine cables, and twenty-plus nationalities share the same narrow strip of road.

subject: Tong Lau
summary: The Chinese shophouse that defined urban life across Hong Kong, Macau, and Southern China — narrow, tall, commercial at ground level and residential above, built from the late 19th century until the 1960s.

subject: Tongariro Alpine Crossing
summary: New Zealand's most popular day hike crosses 19.4 kilometers of active volcanic terrain where fumaroles vent sulphur, lakes glow emerald green, and the word 'Alpine' was added to the name in 2007 because too many casual walkers were dying.

subject: Tongeren
summary: Belgium's oldest town, where a defiant Eburones chieftain who annihilated a Roman legion now glares in bronze across a square that has hosted markets since the days of Caesar.

subject: Tongue, Sutherland
summary: A coastal village at the head of a sea loch in northern Scotland, where Clan Mackay built their seat and Bonnie Prince Charlie lost his gold.

subject: Tonj
summary: An old Dinka town in Warrap State that sent cattle to the British war effort and produced John Garang and Emmanuel Jal, Tonj carries one of the deepest claims to historical identity in South Sudan - and a reputation for student excellence that has surprised East Africa.

subject: Tonle Sap–Mekong Peat Swamp Forests
summary: Eighty-five percent farmland, fifteen percent forest, less than one percent protected — the drowned paperbark swamps of the lower Mekong are among the most completely converted landscapes on earth.

story.title: Tono: Where the Kappa Are Red

subject: Tono
summary: A small city in Iwate Prefecture where folklorist Kunio Yanagita collected 119 tales of red-skinned kappa, horse-marrying maidens, and mischievous house spirits -- stories that founded the entire discipline of Japanese folklore studies.

story.title: Tonopah: Where Stealth Aircraft Hid in Plain Sight

subject: Tonopah
summary: The Nevada test facility where F-117 Nighthawk stealth fighters flew only at night for nearly a decade - so secret that pilots lived double lives, their families unaware they were flying aircraft the world didn't know existed.

subject: Tonragee
summary: A scatter of houses on the Currane peninsula whose Irish name - 'Tóin Re Gaoith' - translates roughly as 'backside to the wind,' which is a perfect summary of life on this exposed Atlantic edge.

subject: Toorale Station
summary: A vast Darling River sheep station that once ran a quarter-million sheep was bought back by government in 2008 - not to graze it, but to let its dammed waters flow free again into a thirsty river.

subject: Toowoomba
summary: A city that started life as 'The Swamp' now calls itself the Garden City, perched 700 metres up on the rim of the range where Queensland turns cool.

subject: Top Withens
summary: A roofless farmhouse on the windswept Haworth Moor draws walkers from as far as Japan, all looking for a novel that may or may not have been born here.

subject: Topanga
summary: Topanga — in the Tongva language, 'where the mountain meets the sea' — is a canyon community in western Los Angeles County where Neil Young recorded After the Gold Rush in his basement in 1970, and where a 300-ton boulder blocked the only road for most of a week in 2005.

subject: Tophane
summary: The waterfront district that built the Ottoman Empire's cannons — including those that brought down Constantinople — is now a contested neighborhood caught between gentrification and its industrial past.

subject: Torbay Lifeboat Station
summary: Born from the storm of 1866 that killed seventy people in Tor Bay, the Brixham lifeboat crew has gone out into Force 9 seas more than a thousand times and brought back twenty-six medals for gallantry.

subject: Torihama shell mound
summary: A waterlogged Jomon-period settlement near the Mikata Five Lakes that yielded the world's oldest lacquer tree, Japan's oldest canoe, and evidence of sophisticated plant cultivation dating back 12,000 years.

subject: Toritama
summary: Roughly one in seven pairs of jeans made in Brazil comes from a town of 41,000 people that fits inside thirty square kilometres of dry agreste.

subject: Toro Peak
summary: At 8,717 feet, Toro Peak is the highest point of the Santa Rosa Mountains — a sky island where limber pines cling to survival as ice-age relics, and on a clear day the eye can reach the mountains of Nevada.

story.title: Toronto: Canada's Biggest City in Constant Search of Identity

subject: Toronto
summary: The Ontario metropolis where half the population was born elsewhere - where the CN Tower defined the skyline for 40 years, where a crack-smoking mayor became international entertainment, and where Canada's most multicultural city keeps asking what it wants to be.

subject: Torre d'en Galmés
summary: One of the largest prehistoric towns in the Balearics, this Menorcan hilltop yielded a bronze Egyptian god and a water system of startling ingenuity.

subject: Torre de San Martín
summary: A 14th-century Teruel bell tower that doubles as a city gate - built on the plan of a Muslim minaret, sheathed in glazed tile, with a street still running straight through its base.

subject: Torre del Oro
summary: A twelve-sided Almohad watchtower on the Guadalquivir whose golden shimmer gave it its name, survived an earthquake that nearly destroyed it, and anchored the chain that once blocked all river traffic to Seville.

subject: Torres Strait
summary: The 150-kilometre passage between Australia and New Guinea, where 274 islands shelter a unique Indigenous culture, 580 coral reefs make navigation treacherous, and Captain Nemo once ran aground.

subject: Torres de Quart
summary: One of two surviving gates of Valencia's medieval wall, the Torres de Quart still carries the pockmarks of French cannon fire, preserved on purpose as a memory of 1808.

subject: Torres de Serranos
summary: Valencia's grand ceremonial gate, built in the 1390s, once became a padded bunker for the Prado's masterpieces and now opens the city's Fallas festival each spring.

subject: Torres, Rio Grande do Sul
summary: The only stretch of Rio Grande do Sul's coast where ancient basalt towers meet the sea, giving this beach town its name, its drama, and a sky full of balloons each autumn.

subject: Torrevieja
summary: A Costa Blanca town that grew from a single coastal watchtower into a booming, salt-built resort ringed by pink lagoons and twenty kilometers of beaches.

subject: Torrey Pines Golf Course
summary: A public golf course on the cliffs above the Pacific that somehow became one of the most storied venues in major championship history.

subject: Torridon
summary: The mountains around Torridon rise from sea level to over 3,500 feet in a single sweep of billion-year-old sandstone -- a landscape so raw that it hosts one of the world's most punishing triathlons.

subject: Torrinha
summary: A small São Paulo municipality whose cuesta canyons hide 100-foot sandstone walls and a German-trained mining engineer once built a Presbyterian church in its founding hills.

subject: Torsåker witch trials
summary: In 1675, seventy-one people were beheaded and burned in a single day in this remote Swedish parish -- the largest mass execution in Sweden's witch trial history, carried out without legal authority.

subject: Tortel
summary: A village with no streets, only cypress boardwalks — wedged between two great ice fields at the mouth of Chile's mightiest river, with a small island of the dead in its waters.

subject: Tortosa
summary: A river city on the lower Ebro where you can sleep inside a Roman-Moorish-Christian castle, wander a medieval Jewish quarter, and eat cod fritters at the gateway to a vast biosphere reserve.

subject: Tortugas Pueblo
summary: Named for the turtles that once filled a nearby oxbow of the Rio Grande, Tortugas Pueblo preserves the living traditions of the Piro, Manso, and Tiwa peoples who were displaced from their homelands during the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, maintaining their heritage despite lacking federal recognition.

subject: Tortuguero
summary: A roadless village on Costa Rica's Caribbean coast where four of the world's seven sea turtle species return to nest each year, reachable only by boat or small plane through a labyrinth of canals the locals call 'Costa Rica's Amazon.'

story.title: Toshimaen: The Carousel That Crossed Three Continents

subject: Toshimaen
summary: A Tokyo amusement park that opened in 1926 and closed in 2020 was home to Carousel El Dorado, an Art Nouveau merry-go-round built in Munich in 1907 that traveled from Oktoberfest to Coney Island to Nerima before the site became the Warner Bros. Studio Tour Tokyo.

story.title: Totsukawa: Japan's Largest Village at the End of Every Road

subject: Totsukawa
summary: Deep in the mountains of Nara Prefecture, Japan's largest village has no flat ground, no train station, and no easy way in -- but it has suspension bridges over gorges, hand-pulled monkey gondolas, a UNESCO shrine, and a story of catastrophic exile that created a twin village 1,500 kilometers away in Hokkaido.

subject: Tottenham
summary: A north London district named for a Saxon farmer called Tota — home to Premier League football, Bruce Castle, and a community that has carried losses no neighbourhood should have to carry alone.

subject: Tottenham (1802 Indiaman)
summary: An East Indiaman launched in 1802 that spent nearly two decades sailing between Britain, India, and eventually Australia — carrying trade goods, a letter of marque, and two hundred transported convicts before being sold for breaking up in 1820.

subject: Tottori Sand Dunes
summary: Japan's largest sand dunes stretch nine miles along the Sea of Japan coast, a landscape shaped by 100,000 years of wind and river sediment that looks more like the Sahara than the country of cherry blossoms.

subject: Toucheng
summary: The oldest settlement on Yilan County's northern coast, where the Kavalan people first held this gateway between mountains and sea, and surfable waves still break at Honeymoon Bay.

subject: Toucheng Old Street
summary: Once Yilan's busiest harbor town, Toucheng Old Street traces a slow arc from commercial dominance to flood-driven decline — and a present-day revival written in 3D murals and colonial-era arcades.

subject: Toufen
summary: Taiwan's most Hakka city — with roughly 90% of its 107,000 residents tracing Hakka heritage — Toufen sits at the northern edge of Miaoli County where the hills of central Taiwan give way to the Zhunan plain.

subject: Toungoo dynasty
summary: From a remote river town in central Burma, the Toungoo dynasty built what was probably the largest empire in Southeast Asian history, stretching from Assam to the borders of Cambodia.

subject: Touros
summary: At the northeastern hinge of South America, Touros is the point where Brazil's coast makes its dramatic right-angle turn south.

subject: Town Musicians of Bremen
summary: Four discarded animals set out to become musicians in Bremen, never get there, and end up as the city's best-loved bronze anyway.

subject: Townsville
summary: The unofficial capital of northern Australia, a garrison city of pink granite, palm-lined beaches, and a reef on its doorstep - built on Wulgurukaba and Bindal country.

subject: Toyota Gazoo Racing Europe
summary: A workshop on the western edge of Cologne where Toyota fights its European motorsport wars, from Carlos Sainz's rally titles to the Hypercar that finally won Le Mans.

subject: Toyota Motor Manufacturing West Virginia
summary: A Toyota engine and transmission plant in Buffalo, West Virginia, that quietly builds nearly a million powertrains a year for North American vehicles.

subject: Toyota Research Institute
summary: A billion-dollar bet by Toyota that the future of automobiles will be decided in Silicon Valley, not Detroit -- led by a former DARPA roboticist from a lab in Los Altos.

subject: Tra Vinh
summary: A small Mekong Delta city that grew up under old trees, where Khmer pagodas outnumber landmarks and a square pond keeps a 400-year-old argument alive.

subject: Trafalgar Square
summary: London's official centre - a square named for a Spanish cape, where Norway sends a Christmas tree every year and Nelson watches over everything.

subject: Tragedy of Alpatacal
summary: In 1927, a train carrying young Chilean military cadets to a celebration in Buenos Aires collided with another train at a tiny station in the Mendoza desert, killing thirty and binding two nations in shared grief.

subject: Tragedy of Antuco
summary: In 2005, a routine training march on the slopes of the Antuco volcano became Chile's worst peacetime military disaster when a sudden blizzard killed 45 young men, most of them teenage conscripts.

subject: Trail
summary: A Kootenay smelter town where the Columbia River flows past the Teck Cominco stacks and Canadian flags mark hiking viewpoints on the surrounding peaks.

subject: Trakhtemyriv
summary: A drowned Cossack capital on the Dnieper, now a summer-only ghost village where nine people once wintered and the reservoir laps over the old town.

subject: Trams in Amsterdam
summary: From horse-drawn rails in 1875 to one of the largest tram networks in Europe, Amsterdam's blue-and-white trams have outlived empires, two world wars, snowstorms, and several attempts to replace them with buses.

subject: Trams in Berlin
summary: The world's first electric tramway ran in a Berlin suburb in 1881, and the network's modern map still traces the line of the Berlin Wall almost exactly.

subject: Trams in Brisbane
summary: For 84 years Brisbane ran on rails - one of Australia's great tram networks, beloved for its breezy open cars, ended by a single catastrophic fire.

subject: Tramvia Blau
summary: Barcelona's Blue Tram climbed the Avinguda Tibidabo from 1901 until 2018, a 1.3-kilometer heritage streetcar line that survived the death of every other tram route in the city -- though it now awaits restoration after years of suspended service.

subject: Trancoso, Bahia
summary: A fishing-village-turned-beach-retreat on the southern Bahian coast where a sixteenth-century Jesuit church still watches over a rectangular square the locals call the Quadrado.

subject: Tranquebar
summary: A Tamil fishing village reimagined as a Danish colonial outpost for 225 years, Tharangambadi -- 'the land of the singing waves' -- preserves a rare hybrid of Scandinavian and South Indian architecture on the Bay of Bengal.

subject: Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum
summary: A massive hand-cut stone asylum in Weston, West Virginia, built over 23 years starting in 1858, designed for 250 patients but swelling to 2,400, now a National Historic Landmark open for tours.

subject: Trans-Canada Highway
summary: Eight thousand kilometers of asphalt threading through six time zones - the ribbon of road that stitches together the second-largest country on Earth, from Pacific rainforest to Atlantic fishing villages.

subject: Trans-Labrador Highway
summary: Over 1,200 kilometers of sub-Arctic highway threading through one of North America's last true wildernesses, where road signs warn of 410 kilometers between services.

subject: Trans-Oconee Republic
summary: In 1794, a Revolutionary War hero marched several hundred followers into Creek territory, declared an independent republic, wrote a constitution, and built forts -- only to be surrounded by federal troops four months later.

subject: Transkei
summary: South Africa's first nominally independent Bantustan, Transkei was a state that no other nation would recognize -- a territory built on the fiction that apartheid could be rebranded as self-determination.

subject: Transportation in Richmond, Virginia
summary: In February 1888, Richmond's brutal hills became the proving ground for the world's first successful electric streetcar — a network that would shape every other American city.

subject: Transylvania
summary: Romania's largest and most storied region, where roughly 100 castles, 70 fortified churches, and the Carpathian Mountains frame a landscape shaped by centuries of Romanian, Hungarian, Saxon, and Roma coexistence.

subject: Tre'r Ceiri
summary: The name means "town of the giants" -- and on a 485-metre summit above the Llyn coast, the Iron Age built one of the best-preserved hill towns in Europe, with 150 stone houses still standing inside walls that climb four metres into the wind.

subject: Trearddur
summary: A west-coast Holy Island holiday village built around a sandy bay - with surfers, golfers, and a sailing club that operates only in August.

subject: Treasure Hill
summary: An illegal hillside settlement built by Kuomintang veterans that accidentally became an ecological model for urban living, then was transformed into an artist village at the cost of displacing its original residents.

subject: Treasure of Villena
summary: Nearly ten kilograms of Bronze Age gold pulled from a dry riverbed near Villena, second in Europe only to the royal graves of Mycenae, and containing iron that fell from the sky.

subject: Treasury of Atreus
summary: Constructed between 1350 and 1250 BC at Mycenae, the Treasury of Atreus held the world's largest dome for more than a thousand years — its corbelled vault of 33 stone courses, 13.5 meters high, exceeded by nothing until the Romans built the Pantheon.

story.title: The Treaty of Waitangi: A Document That Means Two Different Things

subject: Treaty of Waitangi
summary: New Zealand's founding document was signed in 1840 in two languages that said fundamentally different things, creating a constitutional fault line that the country has spent nearly two centuries navigating.

subject: Treaty of al-Hudaybiya
summary: In March 628, fifteen hundred unarmed Muslims camped outside Mecca and negotiated a peace treaty that historians call the most important victory without a battle in Islamic history.

subject: Trebah
summary: A sub-tropical Cornish ravine of giant gunnera and rhododendrons whose beach launched 7,500 American soldiers toward Omaha on D-Day.

subject: Tree That Owns Itself
summary: A white oak in Athens, Georgia holds a deed to itself and the land within eight feet of its trunk, a legal impossibility that the local government officially recognizes anyway.

subject: Tree of Knowledge, Camooweal
summary: A single coolibah on the Georgina River floodplain became the outback's news service - the shaded spot where generations of drovers swapped tea, gossip, and word from the road.

subject: Tref Alaw
summary: A dispersed Anglesey community wrapped around Llyn Alaw, the island's largest body of water, where Bronze Age cremation urns and a Mabinogion legend share ground with a wind farm of 35 turbines.

subject: Trefor, Gwynedd
summary: A village of about 1,000 people beneath the three peaks of Yr Eifl, where a granite quarry once supplied stone so rare it is now used for Olympic curling stones -- found in only one other place on Earth.

subject: Trefriw
summary: A Welsh village on a glaciated valley wall, with a Roman spa, a steamer quay, and the country's oldest working woollen mill in family hands.

subject: Trefriw Woollen Mills
summary: Two centuries on, the same family still cards, spins, dyes, and weaves Welsh wool on the banks of the Afon Crafnant.

subject: Treinta y Tres
summary: A city named for the number 33 - honoring the thirty-three patriots who set Uruguay's independence in motion, and improbably sitting almost exactly on the 33rd parallel south.

subject: Trelew
summary: A Welsh railhead in the Patagonian desert, Trelew carries a Celtic name and a teapot tradition half a world from Wales.

subject: Trelissick
summary: A National Trust garden above the Fal where Cornish copper money built a stately home and Spode's flower painters once came to sketch the camellias.

subject: Tremp Formation
summary: A band of Pre-Pyrenean rock that records the final chapter of the dinosaurs, with over a thousand bones, whole nests of eggs, and the extinction line itself.

subject: Tremé
summary: The oldest African-American neighborhood in the United States, where enslaved people once danced in Congo Square and brass bands forged the foundations of jazz.

subject: Tren de las Sierras
summary: A century-old mountain railway through the Punilla Valley that has died and come back to life more times than almost any line in Argentina.

subject: Tres Arroyos
summary: Argentina's largest Dutch community took root on this windswept plain, where Friesland farmers and a 9,000-year-old burial ground share the same patch of pampas.

subject: Tresaith
summary: A small cove on the Ceredigion coast where a river drops straight off a cliff into the sea, and where, in 1827, a family of innkeepers built their first ship on the beach.

subject: Tresor
summary: A bank vault under a derelict East Berlin department store became the club where Detroit techno and a newly reunified city found each other.

subject: Trevalga
summary: A North Cornwall hamlet that was preserved for sixty years by a single trust deed, and then sold in 2023 for sixteen million pounds against the wishes of its tenants.

subject: Trevelin
summary: A Welsh town in the Argentine Andes where tea houses serve black cake, a flour mill gave the place its name, and a horse named Malacara is buried with an epitaph thanking him for a life saved.

subject: Trieste
summary: An underestimated Italian city at the crossroads of Latin, Slavic, and Germanic worlds, Trieste blends Viennese grandeur with Adriatic light and a coffee culture rivaling any in Europe.

subject: Trikora
summary: On the northeast coast of Bintan, four numbered beaches carry the name of a 1961 Indonesian military campaign - and the backpacker scene that faded.

subject: Trilobite Wilderness
summary: A Mojave wilderness area in the Marble Mountains where virtually every piece of extracted Cambrian rock contains fragments of trilobite fossils from an ancient shallow sea — making it a bucket-list destination for paleontologists and a 500-million-year-old window into life before fish existed.

subject: Trim, County Meath
summary: The Meath town where Ireland's largest Norman castle stood in for medieval York in Braveheart, Wellington learned politics, and Mel Gibson rewrote the skyline.

story.title: Trinidad: The Sex Change Capital of the World

subject: Trinidad
summary: The Colorado mining town that became America's unlikely center for gender confirmation surgery - where a single surgeon performed over 6,000 operations, transforming a dying coal town into a destination for people seeking transformation themselves.

subject: Trinidad, Beni
summary: Bolivia's wettest capital city sits on the southern edge of the Amazon basin, where Jesuit mission origins, open drainage ditches, a landlocked navy, and a museum with a floating pink river dolphin define a place that defies easy categorization.

subject: Trinity (nuclear test)
summary: At 5:29 a.m. on July 16, 1945, the world's first nuclear weapon detonated in a New Mexico desert, melting sand into glass and opening an era no one could close.

subject: Trinity Alps Wilderness
summary: California's second-largest wilderness area, where Sierra Nevada species thrive just thirty miles from the Pacific Ocean in peaks of white granite, red ultramafic rock, and green forest.

subject: Trinity Royal Heritage Conservation Area
summary: Saint John's first heritage conservation area preserves a dense cluster of Victorian brick buildings raised from the ashes of the catastrophic 1877 Great Fire.

subject: Trinity Site
summary: The New Mexico desert where the atomic age began - where the first nuclear weapon was detonated on July 16, 1945, turning sand to glass and leaving a crater that's now open to visitors twice a year.

story.title: Trinity Site: Where the Nuclear Age Began

subject: Trinity Site
summary: Where the first atomic bomb was detonated on July 16, 1945, creating a flash visible 250 miles away, a mushroom cloud 40,000 feet high, and a crater of radioactive glass that marked humanity's entry into the atomic age.

subject: Tripitaka Koreana
summary: Carved onto 81,352 wooden blocks in the 13th century as a prayer against Mongol invasion, the Tripitaka Koreana contains 52 million characters and remains in pristine condition after more than 750 years.

subject: Triple Frontier
summary: Where the Iguazu and Parana rivers meet, three nations converge at the world's most populated tripoint - a place of waterfalls, hydroelectric power, shopping bazaars, and geopolitical intrigue.

subject: Tripoli (Greece)
summary: Arcadia's capital and Peloponnese crossroads, Tripoli is a city of wide squares, dramatic mountain weather, and a civic life that knits together the highland villages around it.

subject: Tripoli, Greece
summary: Three times razed and three times rebuilt, the city the Ottomans called Tripolitsa has always risen from its plateau — carrying inside it the violent pivot point of Greek independence.

subject: Tripolitanian Republic
summary: Declared in 1918 from the small town of Aziziya south of Tripoli, the Tripolitanian Republic was the first republican government in the Arab world -- and one of its most fleeting, undone by internal rivalries and Italian military power.

subject: Triunfo
summary: The highest town in Pernambuco, where the sertão turns cold, wet and green, and a 1922 cinema has been running long enough to start an argument about records.

subject: Triệu Dynasty
summary: The kingdom of Nanyue, founded by Zhao Tuo in 204 BC with its capital at Panyu (modern Guangzhou), is claimed by both Chinese and Vietnamese historiography — a dynasty that refuses to belong to just one national story.

subject: Trofors
summary: A village of 860 people where two rivers become the Vefsna, where the road to Sweden begins, and which sent a pair of twins to Eurovision under the wrong flag.

subject: Trogir
summary: A medieval town compressed onto a tiny island between the Croatian mainland and Ciovo, where 15th-century walls enclose narrow streets you can circumnavigate in twenty minutes.

subject: Trolleybuses in Solingen
summary: Solingen runs the largest of just three surviving trolleybus networks in Germany - and at one end of route 683 spins the last trolleybus turntable on Earth.

subject: Trollfjord
summary: Named for the trolls of Norse mythology, this two-kilometer crack in the rock of Austvagoya island has a mouth barely 100 meters wide -- and a history of battles, daring navigation, and regional pride.

subject: Trollstigen
summary: Eleven hairpin turns carved into a near-vertical mountainside, named for the trolls of Norse legend and opened by a king after eight years of blasting through rock.

subject: Trombas
summary: A quiet cattle municipality in northern Goiás that was, for a decade in the 1950s and 60s, the site of one of the most effective peasant land movements in Brazilian history.

subject: Tronador (rocket)
summary: On a windswept stretch of the Río de la Plata coast, Argentina has spent two decades trying to build something only a handful of nations possess: a rocket of its own design that can throw a satellite into orbit.

subject: Troon
summary: A South Ayrshire seaport with one of the first railways in Scotland, a working harbour, championship links along the coast, and a name that may simply mean the nose.

subject: Troon Lifeboat Station
summary: An Ayrshire RNLI station founded in 1871 whose crews have earned three medals across four storm rescues, and whose boathouse and harbour have anchored the community for more than a century and a half.

subject: Tropical Rainforest Heritage of Sumatra
summary: Three national parks along Sumatra's volcanic spine hold 25,000 square kilometers of rainforest -- home to the world's largest flower, its tallest flower, and critically endangered orangutans, tigers, rhinos, and elephants.

subject: Tropicana Atlantic City
summary: Built atop the old Ambassador Hotel - where Al Capone called the 1929 organized crime summit - the Trop is now Atlantic City's largest casino resort, with six towers, a Havana-themed shopping quarter, and a long history of strange ownership.

subject: Trostianets
summary: A Ukrainian town where Tchaikovsky composed by a riverside villa, a sugar baron built an estate, and a chocolate factory still perfumes the air, all shadowed and outlasted by war.

story.title: Trou de Fer: The Iron Hole

subject: Trou de Fer
summary: Six waterfalls plunge up to 300 meters into a volcanic chasm on Reunion Island, feeding a slot canyon so narrow and violent that one of its waterfalls is called the Washing Machine.

subject: Troy
summary: On a low mound near the Dardanelles, nine cities lie stacked on top of each other - and one of them was probably the place Homer wrote about three thousand years ago.

subject: Trujillo, Honduras
summary: Where Columbus first touched Central America, where pirates gathered in record numbers, and where a fugitive American mercenary met his firing squad.

subject: Trump National Golf Club Bedminster
summary: A 36-hole private golf club on the former DeLorean estate in Somerset County that became a presidential retreat, a source of aviation restrictions, and one of the most politically charged sporting venues in the United States.

subject: Trump Turnberry
summary: A links course on the Firth of Clyde, born from a Victorian railway scheme, scene of golf's famous Duel in the Sun, and - since 2014 - one of the more closely watched properties on the Trump Organization's books.

subject: Trundholm Sun Chariot
summary: On 7 September 1902, the first plough ever driven through a drained bog in Odsherred turned up a bronze horse pulling a gold-faced sun disc - a 3,400-year-old model of how the Nordic Bronze Age believed the sky worked.

subject: Truro
summary: Cornwall's only city and its administrative centre, where Tudor tin barons, Royalist refugees, and a Victorian cathedral all left their mark on a town in a steep river bowl.

subject: Tryal Rocks
summary: A reef in the Indian Ocean that sank the first known shipwreck in Australian waters in 1622, then eluded mariners and mapmakers for over three centuries before its true location was finally confirmed in 1969.

subject: Tryfan
summary: Britain's favourite mountain, a 3,010-foot pointed wedge of rock above the Ogwen valley, with two stone monoliths on its summit that you have to jump between to earn the Freedom of Tryfan.

subject: Trà Kiệu
summary: Beneath a quiet Vietnamese village lie the ramparts of Simhapura, once the royal capital of the Cham kingdom — a city whose ceramic roof tiles still bear the faces of a civilization that shaped Southeast Asia for a thousand years.

subject: Trà Vinh province
summary: Erased from the map in June 2025 after two centuries of being renamed, this delta province between two river branches still answers to the Khmer name that started it all.

subject: Três Corações
summary: The small Minas Gerais town where Pelé was born, where a two-day Brazilian president came from, and where three rivers are said to form three hearts on the land.

subject: Três Marias
summary: A Brazilian city named for three vanished waterfalls, whose name the locals filled with legend after a dam swallowed the landscape.

subject: Três Pontas
summary: A coffee town named for a three-peaked mountain where runaway slaves once built a sanctuary, and where Brazilian music found one of its most beloved voices.

subject: Ts'uubaa-asatx
summary: The People of the Lake, canoe builders at the centre of Vancouver Island, whose nation now numbers a few dozen on a reserve of forty-two hectares.

subject: Tsakonia
summary: Tucked into the eastern Peloponnese, Tsakonia harbors one of the world's most improbable linguistic survivors — a tongue descended not from common Greek but from the ancient Doric dialect of Sparta, still spoken in thirteen mountain villages where inhabitants were still being called pagans in the tenth century.

subject: Tsawwassen
summary: Its Halkomelem name means land facing the sea, but the sea in front of it is too shallow to float a ferry -- so Tsawwassen built a three-kilometre causeway, and became the gateway between Vancouver, Vancouver Island, and an American town you can only drive to through Canada.

subject: Tseshaht First Nation
summary: Created on Benson Island according to their oral history, the Tseshaht became the dominant nation of the Alberni Valley through warfare and alliance, producing whalers, artists, and one of the most important ethnographic collaborations in North American anthropology.

subject: Tseung Kwan O
summary: A city built on reclaimed water — 400,000 residents, submarine internet cables, a Kuomintang refugee village, and Hong Kong's first marine viaduct, all rising from what was a narrow bay until the 1980s.

subject: Tseung Kwan O Village
summary: Founded in the Ming dynasty, emptied by a Qing imperial edict, and then rebuilt by returning villagers, Tseung Kwan O Village has outlasted every transformation of the bay it once looked directly onto — including the reclamation that moved the ocean 100 feet further away.

subject: Tsim Sha Tsui
summary: The sharp sandspit at the tip of Kowloon Peninsula, where Hong Kong's colonial history, neon-lit commerce, and some of the world's most iconic harbour views converge.

subject: Tsing Chuen Wai
summary: A fortified walled village in Tuen Mun, built by the To Clan and already mapped by a missionary cartographer in 1866, where a surviving stretch of green-brick wall still stands at the entrance.

story.title: Tsing Yi Fishermen Village and St. Paul's Village

subject: Tsing Yi Fishermen Village and St. Paul's Village
summary: Two small villages on Tsing Yi Island — one built by American charity for fishing families displaced from Tsuen Wan, the other founded eight years later — preserve the memory of a waterborne life that modern Hong Kong has almost entirely erased.

subject: Tsing Yi Peak
summary: Known in Cantonese as Sam Chi Heung — Three Sticks of Incense — Tsing Yi Peak rises through three summits to 334 metres above Victoria Harbour, hiding a rare endemic plant, ancient burial grounds, and one of the most spectacular urban panoramas in Hong Kong.

subject: Tsleil-Waututh First Nation
summary: The People of the Inlet have governed the north shore of Burrard Inlet since long before Vancouver existed, and have spent the last half-century making the rest of the country notice.

subject: Tsodilo
summary: Four quartzite hills rise from the flat Kalahari, carrying more than 4,500 rock paintings and the prayers of the San and Hambukushu who hold them sacred.

subject: Tsuen Wan
summary: A town with two thousand years of settlement, a pirate-toll legend, and a second life as Hong Kong's first purpose-built new town, Tsuen Wan rose from fishing boats and incense-stick factories to become the textile capital of postwar Hong Kong.

subject: Tsuen Wan District
summary: One of Hong Kong's 18 administrative districts, Tsuen Wan District stretches from industrial waterfronts to the territory's highest summit, weaving together Hakka village heritage, pineapple-war folklore, and a corner of Disneyland.

subject: Tsukiji
summary: A Tokyo district literally built from nothing -- marshland filled in after a catastrophic fire in 1657, then reinvented across four centuries as a temple quarter, foreign settlement, naval academy, and the world's most famous fish market.

subject: Tsukiji fish market
summary: The world's largest wholesale fish market for over 80 years, born from earthquake rubble and shut down in 2018, its outer market stalls still draw crowds to a district whose very name means 'reclaimed land.'

subject: Tsukuba
summary: A city conjured from rice paddies by government decree, where 60 national research institutes and two Nobel laureates coexist with the ancient pilgrimage trails of Mount Tsukuba.

subject: Tsukudajima
summary: A tiny fishing island in Tokyo Bay whose Osaka transplants invented tsukudani, fed a fleeing shogun, and left a pocket of old Edo wedged between gleaming high-rises.

subject: Tsumago-juku
summary: A perfectly preserved Edo-era post town in the Kiso Valley where residents banned selling, renting, or demolishing any building, freezing an entire village in the 17th century.

subject: Tsumeb
summary: A Namibian mining town whose underground pipe has yielded 243 cataloged mineral species -- 56 of them first described here and 20 found nowhere else on Earth -- plus sinkhole lakes of unknown depth and a World War I arms cache.

subject: Tsumkwe
summary: A dusty crossroads at the heart of Nyae Nyae, the Ju/'hoansi San homeland and the site of Namibia's first community-run conservancy.

subject: Tswalu Kalahari Reserve
summary: A British businessman bought dozens of failing farms to rebuild a corner of the Kalahari from scratch — then willed it to the Oppenheimers, who pulled down the fences and let the desert come back.

story.title: Tsutenkaku: The Tower That Reached Heaven Twice

subject: Tsūtenkaku
summary: Modeled after the Eiffel Tower in 1912, scrapped for wartime steel in 1943, rebuilt by popular demand in 1956, and watched over by an American good-luck doll named Billiken -- Osaka's 'Tower Reaching Heaven' is the neon-lit heart of the Shinsekai district.

subject: Tuam
summary: Bronze Age burial mound, medieval seat of the High Kings of Ireland, Showband Capital of the 1960s, and the town that finally forced Ireland to confront the buried children of its mother and baby homes.

subject: Tucker County, West Virginia
summary: A West Virginia county where a county-seat dispute turned into an armed raid in 1893, the ground burned for six straight months in 1914, and 6,762 people now share three state parks.

subject: Tucker's Grove Camp Meeting Ground
summary: An African Methodist Episcopal Zion camp meeting ground in Lincoln County, North Carolina, gathering African American families every August on land Mary Tucker gave - continuously since 1874.

story.title: Tucson: The Desert City That Stayed Weird When Phoenix Got Corporate

subject: Tucson
summary: The Arizona university town where saguaros frame the skyline and weirdness is cultivated - where the Sonoran Desert is protected rather than paved, where boneyard aircraft rust under endless sun, and where 'Keep Tucson Shitty' is a civic slogan.

story.title: Tucson: The Old Pueblo in the Sonoran Desert

subject: Tucson
summary: The desert city surrounded by saguaro cacti, where the Mission San Xavier del Bac has stood since 1797, and where Pima and Spanish and Mexican and American layers create the authentic Old West.

subject: Tucson, Arizona
summary: Arizona's oldest incorporated city began as a Spanish presidio, became a Confederate capital for ten months, and is now America's first UNESCO City of Gastronomy -- a desert metropolis where five mountain ranges frame 4,000 years of continuous human habitation.

subject: Tudweiliog
summary: A small Welsh-speaking farming village on the Llyn Peninsula's north coast, with hidden coves, Bronze Age relics, and a place name that sparked centuries of folk-etymology debate.

subject: Tuen Mun
summary: One of Hong Kong's oldest settlements — documented from the Neolithic period and fortified by the Tang dynasty — Tuen Mun reinvented itself in a single generation as a sprawling new town of half a million people, squeezed between two mountains and Castle Peak Bay.

subject: Tuen Mun Road
summary: Hong Kong's first expressway was built fast, built cheap, and has spent decades paying the price — a winding coastal road of viaducts and tight bends that carries millions of journeys and bears the weight of one of the city's worst road disasters.

subject: Tufi
summary: A small town on Papua New Guinea's northeast coast where tropical fjords plunge 90 meters deep beneath cliffs hung with moss and orchids.

subject: Tugen Hills
summary: A line of weathered hills above Kenya's Rift Valley holds one of the oldest known members of the human family - a six-million-year-old ancestor that may have walked upright before almost any other.

subject: Tukulor Empire
summary: El Hadj Umar Tall returned from Mecca with a title and a vision, and carved a short-lived Islamic empire across the western Sudan before the French swept it away.

subject: Tukuyu
summary: A small Tanzanian highland town in a landscape of tea plantations, crater lakes, and the country's third-highest peak, sitting on the road between Mbeya and the Malawi border.

story.title: Tulip Mania: When a Flower Bulb Cost More Than a House

subject: Tulip Mania
summary: Where the Dutch became so obsessed with tulips in 1637 that single bulbs sold for more than houses, before the market collapsed and created history's first recorded economic bubble.

story.title: Tulsa: The Oil Capital's Art Deco Treasure

subject: Tulsa
summary: The Oklahoma city where oil barons built an Art Deco skyline, where the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre destroyed 'Black Wall Street,' and where Route 66 passes through a city that turned petroleum wealth into world-class art museums.

subject: Tulsa, Oklahoma
summary: Settled by the Lochapoka band of Creek Indians in the 1830s and later fueled by an oil boom that made it the self-proclaimed Oil Capital of the World, Tulsa is a city shaped equally by Indigenous heritage, petroleum wealth, art deco grandeur, and a musical tradition that gave the world Western Swing and the Tulsa Sound.

subject: Tulsk
summary: A small Roscommon village beside Cruachan - the Iron Age royal seat of Queen Medb, the cave the monks called the entrance to Hell, and the burial ground of the kings of Connacht.

subject: Tumaco
summary: Colombia's Afro-Pacific port city, birthplace of world-class footballers and heir to the ancient Tumaco-La Tolita culture, set on stilt-house neighbourhoods above the Pacific.

subject: Tumbes
summary: Peru's northernmost city, a gritty border town that guards one of South America's most unusual ecosystems: Pacific mangroves, dry forest, and the last Tumbes crocodiles.

subject: Tumblagooda Sandstone
summary: In the red rock around Kalbarri, faint parallel rows of dents record some of the first footsteps any animal ever pressed into dry land.

subject: Tumebamba
summary: The Inca northern capital built by Huayna Capac, destroyed in the civil war, and now buried under the Ecuadorean city of Cuenca.

story.title: Tumpak Sewu: A Thousand Waterfalls in the Shadow of Fire

subject: Tumpak Sewu
summary: A semicircular curtain of water plunges into a jungle gorge at the foot of Java's tallest volcano, earning its Javanese name: a thousand waterfalls.

subject: Tumu Crisis
summary: In 1449, a eunuch's vanity led the Ming emperor into a catastrophic ambush by Mongol cavalry, producing one of China's greatest military disasters.

subject: Tundavala Gap
summary: Where Angola's highlands end in a single vertical stroke, the Tundavala escarpment drops a kilometer into thin air, opening a window over 10,000 square kilometers of plain.

subject: Tung Chung
summary: A fishing village turned new town on Lantau Island's northwest shore, Tung Chung layered a thousand years of history beneath one of the world's busiest airports.

subject: Tung Chung New Town
summary: Hong Kong's youngest new town, built to serve an airport that transformed Lantau Island — and still navigating the tensions between rapid growth and the daily needs of the people who live there.

subject: Tung Lin Kok Yuen
summary: A Buddhist nunnery in Happy Valley built by a woman who turned personal grief into Hong Kong's first free school for girls, Tung Lin Kok Yuen endures as a Grade I declared monument and the city's only seminary for Buddhist nuns.

subject: Tung Ping Chau
summary: Hong Kong's most remote and geologically unique island, Tung Ping Chau is the territory's only sizeable island made of layered sedimentary rock — a flat, kidney-shaped reef of siltstones and chert that once held 3,000 people and now stands nearly empty.

subject: Tung Tak Pawn Shop
