summary: A 1930s International Modern shophouse on Wan Chai's Hennessy Road, the Tung Tak Pawn Shop survived decades as a working pawnbroker before being demolished in 2015 despite holding Grade III historic status.

subject: Tung Wah Coffin Home
summary: Perched above Sandy Bay on Hong Kong Island, the Tung Wah Coffin Home has served since 1875 as a way station for overseas Chinese awaiting repatriation to their home villages — a compassionate institution that UNESCO honored in 2005 for its architecture and the human story it embodies.

subject: Tungurahua
summary: The Throat of Fire that erupted continuously from 1999 to 2017, forcing 25,000 people to flee and burying hamlets under pyroclastic flows.

subject: Tunja
summary: The old Muisca capital of Hunza became one of Colombia's oldest Spanish cities - and today, counter-intuitively, one of its safest.

story.title: Tunjungan: The Street That Tore a Flag in Half

subject: Tunjungan
summary: Surabaya's most iconic boulevard has cycled through colonial commerce, Japanese occupation, revolutionary bloodshed, and modern reinvention - all without changing its name or losing its grip on the city's identity.

subject: Tunnsjøen
summary: A Norwegian lake with a mountain standing in the middle of it — Europe's highest island in a lake, and a Southern Sami holy place called Tjåehkere.

story.title: Tupelo: Where Elvis Was Born in a Two-Room Shotgun House

subject: Tupelo
summary: The northeast Mississippi city where Elvis Presley was born in 1935 in a shotgun house his father built for $180, where the future King of Rock and Roll sang in church and discovered the blues before Memphis, and where a tornado in 1936 shaped his family's hardscrabble life.

subject: Tureng Tepe
summary: A 5,000-year-old archaeological mound in Iran's Gorgan Plain whose name means 'Hill of the Pheasants,' concealing Bronze Age graves, gold vessels, and terracotta figurines linked to civilizations as far away as the Indus Valley.

subject: Turmi
summary: A dusty crossroads town on the savanna of Ethiopia's South Omo, where the Hamar people gather to trade gourds, herd cattle, and mark the passage from boyhood to manhood.

subject: Tursiannotko
summary: A Viking-age village in Pirkkala where Finland's acidic soil, for once, failed to eat the bones — leaving fifteen hundred fragments and possibly the country's oldest stove.

subject: Turtle Mound
summary: The largest shell midden on the U.S. mainland rises from a narrow spit between the Mosquito Lagoon and the Atlantic -- a 35-foot hill of oyster shells built by the Timucua over six centuries, now cloaked in tropical forest and managed as part of Canaveral National Seashore.

subject: Tutunendo
summary: A tiny Colombian village in the Choco rainforest that ranks among the wettest inhabited places on Earth, receiving nearly 12 meters of rain every year.

story.title: Tututepec: The Mixtec Empire on the Pacific Shore

subject: Tututepec
summary: Founded in the late 11th century by the legendary warrior-king Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, this coastal Mixtec capital grew into an empire controlling over 25,000 square kilometers of territory - a power that rivaled the Aztecs and endured until Spanish conquistadors arrived in 1522.

subject: Tutóia
summary: The guidebooks call it a stopover between the dunes and the delta - which is a strange way to describe a municipality of 53,000 people and more than eighty islands.

subject: Tuwaiq
summary: An 800-kilometer limestone wall slicing through the heart of central Arabia, the Tuwaiq Escarpment is both the geological backbone of the Najd plateau and the hidden reservoir beneath one of the world's largest oil fields.

subject: Tvind
summary: On a West Jutland farm, teachers and students built the world's largest wind turbine — and an international network whose finances put its founder in a Danish courtroom and then beyond Interpol's reach.

subject: Tvindkraft Wind Turbine
summary: Built by teachers and students in the 1970s, Denmark's Tvindkraft turbine helped launch the modern wind energy industry and still generates power with most of its original components.

subject: Tweed Regional Gallery
summary: A regional gallery above the Tweed River that rebuilt a beloved painter's gloriously cluttered Sydney studio room by room, and hosts the richest portrait prize in the world.

subject: Twente
summary: A Saxon corner of the Netherlands where Roman cavalrymen, textile barons, and ASML's chip wizards have all called home.

story.title: Twenty Rounds in a Grandmother's Backyard

subject: Twenty Rounds in a Grandmother's Backyard
summary: The 2018 police killing of an unarmed man in Sacramento's Meadowview neighborhood sparked citywide protests and rewrote California's use-of-force law.

story.title: Twenty-Nine Palms Band of Mission Indians of California

subject: Twenty-Nine Palms Band of Mission Indians of California
summary: The descendants of a Chemehuevi band who settled near Twentynine Palms in 1867, lost their homeland after the Willie Boy incident of 1909, and spent generations rebuilding their presence across two California counties.

subject: Twic East County
summary: Home to the Twi Dinka, whose origin myth involves an eight-year drought and a chieftainship earned by returning home, Twic East County is the cradle of John Garang and a surprising list of global South Sudanese celebrities.

subject: Twin Forts of Romblon
summary: A pair of coral-and-limestone fortifications built atop twin hills in the 1640s by a missionary-turned-military-commander to defend a Philippine island town from Dutch warships and Moro pirates.

subject: Twin Peaks
summary: Rising 925 feet in the geographic center of San Francisco, the Twin Peaks divide the city's fog-bound western neighborhoods from its sunlit east, offering the most commanding panorama of the Bay Area.

subject: Twist, Germany
summary: A bog village on the Dutch border, named for a centuries-long argument about where Germany ends and Holland begins, that briefly became the German Texas.

subject: Twyfelfontein
summary: On sandstone slabs in the Namibian desert, ancient artists chiseled thousands of animals through the rock's dark skin, leaving Africa's richest gallery of engravings and Namibia's first World Heritage Site.

subject: Tynaarlo
summary: A Drenthe municipality of brinkdorpen - villages built around their shared green - where megalithic tombs older than the Pyramids share the landscape with a small international airport.

subject: Tyne-Wear Derby
summary: The 12-mile-apart inter-city rivalry between Sunderland and Newcastle United, with a 9-1 record win, six consecutive Sunderland victories, and a top-flight reunion confirmed by Sunderland's 2025 promotion.

subject: Tynemouth Lifeboat Station
summary: More than two centuries of rescue at the Tyne mouth - a station whose disasters helped invent the self-righting lifeboat.

subject: Tynwald
summary: The legislature of the Isle of Man, claiming over a thousand years of continuous existence, whose name derives from the Old Norse for the meeting-field of the assembly.

subject: Typhoon Ellen (1983)
summary: In September 1983, Typhoon Ellen crossed the western Pacific and struck Hong Kong as the worst typhoon since 1979 — leaving eight people dead in the city, 2,000 homeless, and a tornado scar that entered the meteorological record books.

subject: Tyritake
summary: A small Greek town on the Kerch shore that lived on wine and salted fish for a thousand years, weathering the Goths and the Huns before slipping quietly into the Middle Ages.

subject: Tyseley Locomotive Works
summary: A Great Western Railway depot saved from demolition by one schoolteacher and one steam locomotive, now overhauling mainline steam engines for the Shakespeare Express.

subject: Tzintzuntzan (Mesoamerican site)
summary: Capital of the Purépecha Empire and home to five unique rounded pyramids called yácatas, Tzintzuntzan was a city of 30,000 that surrendered to the Spanish rather than suffer the fate of Tenochtitlan.

subject: Tây Sơn District
summary: The birthplace of Vietnam's most celebrated revolutionary dynasty, this river valley in Bình Định Province sent three brothers out to overturn a divided kingdom — and has quietly carried that identity ever since.

subject: Tåsinge
summary: A Danish island where one family owned almost everything until 1919, where sea captains built the prettiest village in Funen, and where a murder-suicide in the woods became a love story it never was.

subject: Tóin an tSeanbhaile
summary: A flat plain on Achill Island where Daniel Craig once played a fugitive who attacked his employer, where rare liverworts grow nowhere else in Ireland, and where the population has more than halved in a century.

subject: Tønder
summary: Denmark's oldest market town lost its harbour to a dyke, replaced it with twenty thousand lacemakers, hosted the target of the first carrier air raid in history, and voted to stay German in 1920 anyway.

subject: Tú Làn Caves System
summary: More than ten caves connected by underground rivers thread through 400-million-year-old limestone in one of Vietnam's most remote jungle valleys, where the youngest passages are only three million years old.

subject: Tōjinbō
summary: Dramatic volcanic sea cliffs on the Sea of Japan coast, shaped by 13 million years of geological forces and haunted by centuries of legend.

subject: Tōmei Expressway
summary: Japan's busiest expressway fuses the kanji for Tokyo and Nagoya in its name and carries over 100,000 vehicles a day through some of the country's most dramatic scenery, passing south of Mount Fuji and along the coast of Suruga Bay on the same corridor that Edo-period travelers once walked.

subject: Tịnh Biên
summary: A Vietnamese border crossing beneath the Seven Mountains, where the highway changes its number, the population is heavily Khmer, and the delta's only real hills carry both pilgrims and a very hard memory.

subject: U.S. Space & Rocket Center
summary: Wernher von Braun's dream turned Alabama cotton country into rocket country -- and the U.S. Space & Rocket Center in Huntsville houses 1,500 artifacts that tell the story of how America reached the Moon.

subject: UFO Welcome Center
summary: A 46-foot plywood flying saucer built in a Bowman, South Carolina backyard by a self-appointed ambassador to extraterrestrial life -- complete with bed, TV, and shower -- until fire claimed it in 2024.

subject: UK City of Culture
summary: A British government initiative born from the success of Liverpool's European Capital of Culture year - and the title that Derry won first, in 2013, as the United Kingdom's inaugural City of Culture.

subject: UMgungundlovu
summary: The royal capital of Zulu King Dingane, a vast kraal of up to 1,700 huts in the eMakhosini valley where diplomacy, power, and tragedy collided in the 1830s.

subject: Uan Muhuggiag
summary: In a Libyan rock shelter, archaeologists found the carefully embalmed body of a small child laid to rest some 5,600 years ago - Africa's oldest known mummy, older than the pharaohs.

subject: Ubajara
summary: A highland town named for canoes that sits 847 metres above the nearest navigable water, and whose economy hangs on a three-minute cable car ride.

subject: Ubasute
summary: A mountain in Nagano Prefecture carries the haunting name of a mythical Japanese practice of abandoning the elderly, yet today its slopes hold one of Japan's most celebrated moon-viewing sites, where the full moon reflects across hundreds of terraced rice paddies.

subject: Uberaba
summary: The zebu cattle capital of Brazil, where Cretaceous dinosaur bones emerge from red soil and a Tupi name means 'bright water'.

subject: Uberlândia
summary: Minas Gerais is famous for small colonial towns; its second-largest city is neither small nor colonial, and it moves a startling share of Brazil's freight.

subject: Ubon Ratchathani
summary: Founded by Lao princes fleeing a fallen kingdom, named the Royal City of the Lotus, and shaped by an American air war — Ubon Ratchathani is Isaan's easternmost major city, where the Mun River meets the Mekong in two different colors.

subject: Ubon Ratchathani Candle Festival
summary: Every year at the start of Buddhist Lent, the city of Ubon Ratchathani parades enormous carved candles through its streets — candles so elaborate they depict entire mythological scenes, and so sacred they are never actually lit.

subject: Ubá
summary: A city named for the reed arrows of the Coroado people, grown rich first on tobacco, then on furniture - and famous across Brazil for a single sweet mango.

subject: Ucluelet
summary: A small fishing village turned adventure-tourism hub on Vancouver Island's wild west coast, whose Nuu-chah-nulth name means 'people of the safe harbour.'

subject: Udaipur
summary: Where palaces float on lakes and Rajput romance fills the air, where James Bond found his villain's lair, where India's most picturesque city earns every superlative.

subject: Udmurt language
summary: A Uralic language with fifteen grammatical cases and its own Cyrillic characters, Udmurt connects the forests of central Russia to the linguistic family that includes Finnish, Estonian, and Hungarian.

subject: Ueno
summary: The district where northern Japan's trains once terminated is a collision of world-class museums, wartime black markets, shogunal temples, and the stubborn spirit of Tokyo's original working-class Shitamachi culture.

story.title: Ueno Station: Gateway to the North

subject: Ueno Station
summary: Opened in 1883, Tokyo's Ueno Station served for over a century as the emotional departure point for journeys to northern Japan -- inspiring famous poetry, sheltering war orphans, and launching the country's first subway line before bullet trains shifted the center of gravity south to Tokyo Station.

subject: Uglich
summary: A Volga River town whose coat of arms shows a murdered boy holding a knife, Uglich's history pivots on the death of a ten-year-old prince that plunged Russia into chaos.

subject: Uig
summary: A ferry village curled around a horseshoe bay where Bonnie Prince Charlie's rescuer is buried and the road to the Outer Hebrides begins.

subject: Uig, Lewis
summary: On a remote western shore of the Outer Hebrides, a storm uncovered a hoard of medieval chessmen carved from walrus tusks, and the world found out what Uig had been hiding.

subject: Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation
summary: The largest Ute reservation spans seven Utah counties in a legal patchwork that took over a century of court battles to define, with tribal jurisdiction still contested today.

subject: Uist
summary: Six low-lying islands threaded by causeways in the Outer Hebrides, where the Atlantic seeps inland through thousands of lochans and the line between land and water has never been simple.

subject: Ukarumpa
summary: A missionary community in the Eastern Highlands of Papua New Guinea, built on land that was once tribal war grounds, dedicated since 1956 to translating the Bible into the hundreds of languages spoken across PNG.

subject: Ukase of 1821
summary: A single Russian decree once claimed the entire Pacific Northwest down to present-day Oregon, triggering a diplomatic crisis that shaped the borders of Alaska, Canada, and the Monroe Doctrine.

subject: Ukhta
summary: A subarctic industrial town in Russia's Komi Republic, built on oil springs known since the 17th century and expanded in the 1940s through the forced labor of Gulag prisoners.

subject: Uki, New South Wales
summary: A buttery dairy hamlet in the shadow of Wollumbin that took its name from a timber stamp and became one of the Tweed Valley's most beloved village stops.

subject: Ukrainian Cruiser Ukraina
summary: A guided-missile cruiser nearly finished but never commissioned, moored for over three decades at a bankrupt shipyard as one country after another declined to claim her.

subject: Ullapool
summary: The whitewashed planned fishing village on Loch Broom that became the gateway port for Lewis ferries, the Highland Scottish Gaelic music capital, and the unofficial halfway house of the North Coast 500.

subject: Ulldecona
summary: A southern Catalan town layered with 8,000 years of history, from UNESCO-listed prehistoric rock art and monumental ancient olive trees to a frontier castle and a soaring Gothic church.

subject: Ullswater
summary: The Lake District's second-largest lake, a Z-shaped glacial ribbon carved by three Ice Age glaciers, where Wordsworth saw the daffodils that became the most-quoted poem in the English language.

subject: Ulsanbawi
summary: A six-peaked granite monolith in Seoraksan National Park, Ulsanbawi carries centuries of Korean poetry, Buddhist folklore, and one boulder nobody can push over.

subject: Ulster Folk and Transport Museums
summary: Spread across 176 acres near Belfast, these twin museums preserve a vanishing rural Ulster in reconstructed farms and cottages while housing Ireland's largest railway collection and a DeLorean straight from Belfast's brief dream of becoming a car capital.

subject: Ulster Rugby
summary: The Belfast-based provincial team that was the first Irish side ever to lift the European Cup.

story.title: Uluru: The Rock That Reaches 2.5km Underground

subject: Uluru
summary: Where a 600-million-year-old monolith rises from the Australian Outback - but the 348-meter surface dome is just the tip of a sandstone formation extending 2.5km into the Earth.

subject: Ulva
summary: A small Hebridean island off Mull's west coast where the population fell from 859 to five before the community bought itself in 2018.

subject: Uman
summary: A modest central-Ukrainian city that draws two very different pilgrimages: one to a Hasidic master's grave, the other to a count's mythological garden.

subject: Umbakumba
summary: On the north-east shore of Groote Eylandt, an Anindilyakwa community carries a name that means the lapping of waves - and a history that runs from Macassan sailing praus to wartime flying boats.

subject: Umbrella Rock
summary: A ten-tonne natural rock formation balanced on a narrow pillar in Ghana's Eastern Region, large enough to shelter fifteen people, reached by a challenging forest hike from the nearby Boti Falls.

subject: Umbrella Square
summary: For 74 days in 2014, a stretch of Admiralty's major roads became one of the most watched protest encampments in the world — a self-organized city within a city, demanding democratic elections for Hong Kong.

subject: Umm al Samim
summary: Known locally as the 'Mother of Poisons,' Umm al Samim is a vast quicksand basin on Oman's border with the Empty Quarter -- a salt crust that looks solid but swallows anything heavy enough to break through.

subject: Una Biological Reserve
summary: A strict-protection reserve in southern Bahia holding the largest wild population of the golden-headed lion tamarin, a monkey found nowhere on Earth but this stretch of Atlantic Forest.

subject: Unazuki Onsen
summary: A century-old hot spring town perched at the mouth of Japan's deepest gorge, where the water arrives through a 7-kilometer pipe from an upstream spring and the only way deeper into the mountains is aboard a tiny open-air trolley train.

subject: Unaí
summary: A Minas Gerais cerrado city with 10,000-year-old archaeological caves, the oldest ceramics found in Brazil outside the Amazon, and a 2004 labor-inspector murder that changed the country's approach to rural slave labor.

subject: Uncompahgre Peak
summary: The highest summit in the San Juan Mountains carries a Ute name meaning dirty water, set a world heliograph record in 1894, and stands as the loftiest point in the entire Colorado River drainage basin.

subject: Underground City, Montreal
summary: Beneath the glass towers of downtown Montreal lies a parallel city: 32 kilometers of climate-controlled tunnels connecting half a million daily travelers to shops, universities, concert halls, and the Bell Centre without ever stepping outside.

subject: Une
summary: A three-letter Muisca name clinging to a potato-growing municipality in the hills southeast of Bogotá - once known as the Red Star of the East for staying liberal in a sea of conservatives.

subject: Union Iron Works
summary: San Francisco's Union Iron Works built warships for the U.S. Navy and commercial vessels from the 1880s through both World Wars, anchoring the city's industrial waterfront at Potrero Point.

subject: Union Mills
summary: A Manx village named for the union of a corn mill and a cloth mill, where the TT course thunders past the old miller's house each summer.

story.title: Union Pacific Big Boy: The Locomotive That Outweighed a 747

subject: Union Pacific Big Boy
summary: Twenty-five locomotives built between 1941 and 1944, each heavier than a fully loaded Boeing 747, conquered the Wasatch Range for Union Pacific. In 2019, No. 4014 roared back to life - the largest operating steam locomotive in the world.

subject: Union Station (Ogden, Utah)
summary: Where the transcontinental railroad was truly joined, Ogden's grand 1924 station now houses museums preserving rare locomotives including one of only two surviving 'Big Blow' gas turbines.

subject: Union Stock Yards
summary: The square mile of marshland that nine railroads turned into the meat-processing center of the world, where 400 million animals were butchered in 35 years and the disassembly line inspired Henry Ford's assembly line.

subject: Union between Sweden and Norway
summary: A 91-year political marriage between two proud kingdoms, born from Napoleonic diplomacy and dissolved without a single shot in 1905, in one of history's rarest achievements: a peaceful divorce between nations.

subject: Unite the Right rally
summary: On a summer weekend in 2017, a white supremacist rally in the college town of Charlottesville, Virginia turned deadly, killing one counter-protester and forcing America into a raw confrontation with its unfinished racial history.

subject: United Auburn Indian Community
summary: A Miwok tribe in the Sierra Nevada foothills that survived Gold Rush violence, federal termination, and the loss of nearly all its land -- then rebuilt sovereignty from a 2.8-acre remnant.

subject: United Kingdom of the Netherlands
summary: A 24-year experiment, stitched together at the Congress of Vienna to fence Napoleon's France out of the Low Countries, that broke apart when its Catholic southern half rose up at the Brussels opera in 1830.

subject: United States Customhouse (San Francisco)
summary: This Beaux Arts masterpiece rests on the hull of a Gold Rush steamship and took five years to build because the 1906 earthquake destroyed the city around it.

subject: United States Grand Prix West
summary: From 1976 to 1983, Formula One's fastest cars raced through downtown Long Beach — a carnival of Ferrari red and Brabham blue that produced one record-breaking last-to-first win, one paralyzing crash, and eight years of the most glamorous motorsport California has ever seen.

subject: Unity State
summary: A South Sudanese state named for unity that has known mostly division - where Nuer cattle camps, Dinka villages, and oil rigs share contested ground along the White Nile's western reaches.

subject: Universal Studios Hollywood
summary: From a working chicken farm with five-cent tours in 1915 to a sprawling entertainment complex hosting 8.7 million visitors annually, Universal Studios Hollywood has survived nine backlot fires to become one of the world's most visited theme parks.

subject: Universal Studios Japan
summary: The first Universal theme park built outside the United States, a 54-hectare world of cinematic and gaming immersion on the shores of Osaka Bay that draws over 16 million visitors a year.

subject: Unter den Linden
summary: Prussia's grandest boulevard began as a shortcut to a hunting ground, took its name from trees that have twice been cut down, and still points ten kilometres straight across Berlin.

subject: Upington
summary: A desert oasis town on the banks of the Orange River, Upington serves as the gateway to the Kalahari and the thundering Augrabies Falls.

subject: Upingtonia
summary: A Boer republic founded on land bought for twenty-five guns, a horse, and a cask of brandy - it lasted barely two years before collapsing with its founder's murder.

subject: Uplands
summary: Canada's most carefully designed garden suburb, laid out by John Charles Olmsted in 1907 - and its finest feature is the seventy-six acres he left wild.

subject: Upper Douglas Cable Tramway
summary: A 33-year-old cable tramway that climbed the steep streets of Douglas until it closed in 1929 - and one car of which lived another life as somebody's bungalow.

subject: Upper Harz Water Regale
summary: Water flooded the Harz silver mines and drowned them. Water was also the only power available to pump them out. Four centuries of miners resolved that contradiction by re-plumbing an entire mountain range — 143 ponds, 500 kilometres of ditch, and a legal right granted by kings.

subject: Upper Larymna
summary: A small Boeotian ghost-town remembered for a river that vanished underground and surfaced again at its gates, and for a port-twin that eventually swallowed it whole.

subject: Upper Market Square (Görlitz)
summary: Görlitz laid out its largest square in 1250 to sell grain, and has spent the seven centuries since letting whoever currently governs Germany stand on it and make a speech.

subject: Upper Senegal and Niger
summary: A short-lived French colony governed from Bamako, Upper Senegal and Niger was carved up and renamed within seventeen years, but in its borders lay the outline of the future nation of Mali.

subject: Upper Teesdale
summary: A botanical refuge in the high western Durham fells where arctic-alpine flowers have survived since the last Ice Age, growing on one of only two outcrops of 'sugar limestone' in Britain.

subject: Uppingham
summary: A market town on a high Rutland ridge, named the best place to live in the Midlands in 2022, where ironstone houses cluster around a 14th-century church and the annual fatstock show is still held in the open market place.

subject: Upshur County, West Virginia
summary: Named for the U.S. Secretary of State killed in an 1844 cannon explosion on the Potomac, this 355-square-mile central West Virginia county has voted Republican for nearly every election since the Civil War - and was the site of the 2006 Sago Mine disaster.

subject: Upstalsboom
summary: The medieval gathering place outside Aurich where, every year on the Tuesday after Pentecost, representatives of the Seven Sealands of Frisia met under a tree to argue about laws, currencies, and how to remain free.

subject: Uquía
summary: A tiny Andean village whose modest church hides nine winged soldiers - angels in aristocratic finery, aiming muskets, painted three centuries ago.

subject: Uralla
summary: A high, cold goldmining-and-pastoral town on the Northern Tablelands where the road is named for a bushranger, the wool is among the finest on earth, and the grave of Captain Thunderbolt draws visitors still.

subject: Urdesa
summary: A Guayaquil neighborhood born in 1956 as a gardened suburb and grown into a multicultural commercial heart, where streets are named for trees in alphabetical order.

subject: Uribia, La Guajira
summary: Colombia's youngest municipality is also its most indigenous - a Wayuu stronghold on the Guajira Peninsula where desert, mountains, and Caribbean Sea converge at the northernmost tip of South America.

subject: Uritorco
summary: A modest Córdoba peak that became Argentina's most famous magnet for UFO seekers, New Age pilgrims, and anyone hoping the mountain hides a city of light.

subject: Urjala
summary: A municipality of four thousand people that produced Finland's greatest novelist, one of the world's first women MPs, a governor of Russian America, and 221 unbroken years of glassmaking.

subject: Urk
summary: An island that lost its sea. Urk is the Dutch town the polders left landlocked, and it speaks, votes, and fishes accordingly.

subject: Urmia
summary: The capital of Iran's West Azerbaijan Province, Urmia has been a crossroads of Azerbaijanis, Kurds, Persians, Assyrians, and Armenians for millennia -- a city whose name may mean 'City of Water' and whose identity has been shaped by the collision of empires, faiths, and ethnic communities.

subject: Urris
summary: The remote Inishowen valley that briefly became the Poitin Republic, the last Irish-speaking corner of the peninsula, and the place where Roger Casement spent six months learning Gaelic in 1904.

subject: Ursulines of Quebec
summary: The oldest institution of learning for women in North America, founded in 1639 by Ursuline nuns who crossed the Atlantic to educate Indigenous children in the wilderness of New France.

subject: Uruaçu
summary: The name is Tupi-Guaraní for large bird, and the town sits on the highway that still carries trucks between Brasília and the Amazon.

subject: Uruguaiana
summary: A Brazilian border city where three countries meet, a famous bridge crosses, and gaucho song fills the night.

subject: Uruk
summary: Once the largest city on Earth, Uruk gave humanity its first writing, its first epic literature, and the very concept of urban life.

subject: Urup
summary: An uninhabited volcanic island in the Kuril chain whose name means 'sockeye salmon' in Ainu, and whose history reads like a summary of every imperial ambition that ever reached the North Pacific.

subject: Usatove
summary: A quiet village near Odesa that gave its name to a five-thousand-year-old culture whose burial mounds still dot the Black Sea steppe.

subject: Useless Loop, Western Australia
summary: A French sailor dismissed this looping inlet as worthless for ships; two centuries later it became one of the world's great salt fields.

subject: Uspallata
summary: A high desert valley where Hollywood once built a fake Tibet, where independence armies forged their weapons, and where the road to Chile climbs into some of the Andes' most dramatic scenery.

subject: Ust-Tsilma
summary: A remote village on the Pechora River founded in 1542, where Old Believers fleeing religious persecution preserved the folk traditions of the Russian North for centuries.

subject: Ustvymlag
summary: A Gulag logging camp in the Komi forests that held over 24,000 prisoners at its peak in 1943, where journalists, diplomats, and intelligence officers felled trees alongside Volga German laborers and prisoners of war.

subject: Usuda Deep Space Center
summary: Nestled in the mountains of Nagano at nearly 1,500 meters elevation, JAXA's Usuda Deep Space Center pioneered beam-waveguide antenna technology and has been Japan's ear to the cosmos since 1984.

subject: Usui Pass
summary: A mountain pass on the border of Nagano and Gunma that has been a critical transportation corridor since the 8th century -- from the legendary hero Yamato Takeru to the rack-and-pinion railway to the drift racers of Initial D.

subject: Utamaro
summary: The ukiyo-e master whose portraits of Edo-era women crossed oceans to reshape European Impressionism, before censorship and handcuffs silenced his brush.

subject: Utersum
summary: A village on the southwest corner of Föhr that voted to be Danish in 1920, sent three sailors to the most famous ghost ship in history, and became the favorite resort of a Berlin quiz-show host.

subject: Utica, Tunisia
summary: North Africa's oldest Phoenician colony, a city whose very name meant 'the Old one' to distinguish it from upstart Carthage.

subject: Utrecht
summary: Utrecht began as a Roman fort on a bend of the Rhine in roughly 50 CE, became the religious capital of the Netherlands, lost a cathedral nave to a tornado in 1674, and now hums along as the country's quietly powerful fourth-largest city.

subject: Utrecht (province)
summary: The smallest province in the Netherlands began as a bishopric in 695 AD and now anchors a 71-billion-euro economy at the center of the country.

subject: Utrecht Centraal station
summary: Two or three times a year, a small problem at Utrecht Centraal froze the entire Dutch railway. The fix came from Tokyo.

subject: Utsalady, Washington
summary: A tiny Camano Island community that was shipping timber to France and China by 1860 -- two years before it had a telegraph office.

subject: Utzon Center
summary: Jørn Utzon's last building stands on the waterfront of the town he grew up in — and it was never meant to be a museum.

subject: Uusikaupunki
summary: A town called New Town since 1617, which gave its Swedish name to the treaty that ended the Great Northern War and then burned down and rebuilt itself in wood.

subject: Uxbridge
summary: A Middlesex market town where Charles I's failed peace talks and the Battle of Britain operations room both shaped English history.

subject: V&A Waterfront
summary: Cape Town's oldest working harbour reinvented itself as a 123-hectare precinct where Victorian grain silos house contemporary art and 24 million visitors a year walk docks that once supplied the Dutch East India Company.

subject: VLCC Metula Oil Spill
summary: In 1974 a supertanker ran aground in the Strait of Magellan and bled crude oil onto the shores of Tierra del Fuego, leaving asphalt scars that lingered for decades in one of the world's most remote seas.

subject: VLS-1 V03
summary: Three days before a planned launch at Brazil's Alcântara Space Center, one of the rocket's first-stage boosters ignited on the pad, killing twenty-one engineers and technicians.

subject: Vaals
summary: In a country defined by flatness, the southeasternmost corner of the Netherlands climbs to 322.4 meters, touches Belgium and Germany at the same point, and used to share a border with a country that no longer exists.

subject: Vaca Muerta
summary: A slab of 150-million-year-old seabed buried beneath the Patagonian steppe turned a quiet ranching province into one of the most fracked places on Earth.

subject: Val-Jalbert
summary: A pulp mill company town in Quebec that grew to 950 residents, then emptied completely when the mill closed in 1927 -- leaving behind over 70 original buildings and Canada's best-preserved ghost town.

subject: Valdivia
summary: Chile's riverside pearl where sea lions bask at the fish market, German heritage flavors the architecture, and craft breweries have earned this southern city its title as the nation's beer capital.

subject: Valdivian Temperate Forests
summary: Cut off from the rest of the continent by desert, mountains, and steppe, this dripping green ribbon of southern Chile evolved its own world of living fossils, the smallest deer on Earth, and trees that were ancient when Rome was young.

subject: Vale do Aço metropolitan area
summary: The Steel Valley of Minas Gerais, where Usiminas built Brazil's industrial backbone and four cities grew around its furnaces.

subject: Vale do Capão
summary: A single-street village deep inside Chapada Diamantina where the cell phones don't work, the supermarkets use pocket calculators, and the trails lead to some of interior Brazil's most dazzling waterfalls.

subject: Valencia
summary: Where Spain's third city reinvented itself with futuristic architecture, where paella was born, where a river became park and a city found new identity.

subject: Valencia Metro derailment
summary: On a July afternoon in 2006, a Valencia metro train took a curve at twice the safe speed and forty-three people died - then their families spent years fighting the official verdict that it was simply bad luck.

subject: Valencia, Ecuador
summary: A coastal Ecuadorean banana town named for a 19th-century sorcerer whose estuary settlement grew into a canton in the Los Rios agricultural belt.

subject: Valenciana Mine
summary: A colonial silver mine that once produced sixty percent of the world's silver, where the fortune of one man earned him a title from the King of Spain and nearly bankrupted the empire that replaced him.

subject: Valentia Lifeboat Station
summary: On the eastern tip of Valentia Island, an RNLI station that traces its founding to 1864 still launches one of the largest all-weather lifeboats in the British Isles.

subject: Valkenburg aan de Geul
summary: The Netherlands has exactly one hilltop castle ruin, and the small Limburg town beneath it has been finding new ways to make a living from that fact since 1853.

subject: Valldemossa
summary: A mountain village one famous guest scorned and an Austrian archduke loved so completely he bought the coastline around it.

subject: Valle de Cocora
summary: A Colombian cloud-forest valley where wax palms sixty meters tall rise like green-tipped masts from a carpet of pasture and mist.

subject: Valle de Las Palmas
summary: A small agricultural valley between Tijuana and Tecate in Baja California — certified as Mexico's first Integral Sustainable Urban Development, with plans to grow it to a city of one million by 2030.

subject: Valle del Cauca Department
summary: A Colombian department where sugarcane fields stretch between two ranges of the Andes and where 8.5 million tons of cargo move every year through Buenaventura, the country's busiest Pacific port.

subject: Vallecito
summary: Vallecito — the Kumeyaay village of Hawi — served as an essential oasis on the Southern Emigrant Trail, offering the salt grass and cienegas that sustained travelers and livestock through the desert crossing to California.

subject: Vallenato Legend Festival
summary: Every April in Valledupar, accordion players, singers, and lyrical combatants gather for Colombia's most revered music festival -- a celebration born in 1968 to preserve a genre that UNESCO now considers endangered.

subject: Valletta
summary: Where the Knights of St. John built Europe's first planned city on a rocky peninsula, where Baroque churches fill every street, where a tiny capital punches above its weight.

subject: Valparaíso
summary: Sailors once called this riot of cobbled hills and rattling funiculars the Jewel of the Pacific, and a wander through its painted alleys explains why.

subject: Van Diemen's Land
summary: Before it was Tasmania, this island was a name that meant terror: a place of chains, exile, and the near-destruction of its first people.

story.title: Vancouver: The Rain-Soaked Pacific City Where Real Estate Went Insane

subject: Vancouver
summary: The British Columbia metropolis where mountains meet ocean and housing costs exceed reason - where Stanley Park preserves wilderness in the city core, where film productions stand in for everywhere, and where Chinese money transformed neighborhoods overnight.

story.title: Vancouver: The Glass City That Lives Outdoors

subject: Vancouver
summary: The British Columbia metropolis where ski slopes, ocean beaches, and glass towers coexist - where mountains rise directly from the urban core, where the world's most livable city wrestles with housing costs that price out everyone who makes it livable, and where rain is simply a lifestyle choice.

subject: Vandalia
summary: An 18th-century British colony that never quite existed, named after a queen whose ancestors were thought to be barbarian invaders of Rome - and the closest the United States ever came to having a 14th original colony.

subject: Vandellòs I nuclear incident
summary: On an October night in 1989, a turbine fire at a Catalan reactor built partly to make bomb-grade plutonium came within reach of catastrophe, and the people inside held it back by hand.

subject: Vankor Field
summary: One of Russia's largest oil fields, carved from the frozen tundra of Eastern Siberia and connected to the world by a 556-kilometer pipeline through permafrost.

subject: Varel
summary: A small Frisian town on the Jade Bight that produced a countess who corresponded with Voltaire, a chemist who built the periodic table independently of Mendeleev, and one of the great altars of Northern German Mannerism.

subject: Vargem Grande do Rio Pardo
summary: A small, dry, high-plateau municipality in the far northeast of Minas Gerais where drought, cerrado, and a new sustainable-development reserve define daily life.

subject: Vargem Grande do Sul
summary: A São Paulo potato-farming town built by Italian immigrants who brought their dialect, their mutual-aid societies, and a fondness for fetta instead of pedaço.

subject: Varginha UFO incident
summary: In 1996, three young women in a Brazilian coffee town said they saw the devil. The city turned the story into a water tower, a football-jersey-wearing mascot, and a tourism industry.

subject: Varna, Bulgaria
summary: Bulgaria's third-largest city and the country's window onto the Black Sea, where Greek colonists, Roman bath-goers, Ottoman traders, and modern beach clubs have all left their layer.

subject: Vasa (ship)
summary: The world's most spectacular maritime failure became one of archaeology's greatest triumphs when this 17th-century warship rose from Stockholm's harbor after 333 years on the seafloor.

subject: Vase Rock
summary: A nine-meter column of coral limestone stands just offshore from Liuqiu Island, shaped by the sea into something between a pedestal and a ghost — and named for a history the tourism brochures get wrong.

subject: Vasilissis Sofias Avenue
summary: Athens's grand boulevard of embassies, museums, and mansions, running three kilometers from Parliament past the city's finest neoclassical houses.

subject: Vasse-Wonnerup Estuary
summary: A Ramsar-listed wetland near Busselton where 20,000 waterbirds gather each dry season -- and where floodgates installed in 1907 accidentally created an entire freshwater ecosystem.

subject: Vastas
summary: In the Arcadian village of Vastas, seventeen trees grow straight out of the stone roof of a tiny chapel — and the roots, investigated with ground-penetrating radar, run invisibly down through the walls to the earth below.

subject: Vatersay Causeway
summary: Two hundred and fifty metres of rock that ended centuries of isolation, built after a bull drowned in 1987 and the islanders demanded a permanent fix.

subject: Vaux Site
summary: The 26-acre brownfield wound at the heart of Sunderland where Vaux Breweries stood for 110 years, sat dormant for 17 more in a legal row with Tesco, and is now being rebuilt office by office.

subject: Vazante
summary: A Brazilian mining town founded on a rancher's vision of the Virgin Mary in a cave, now home to the country's largest zinc deposit.

subject: Vechta
summary: A small Lower Saxon university town whose summer fair has been running since 1298, where the highest birth rates in Germany are powered by a 700-year-old Catholic culture surrounded by Protestant neighbors.

subject: Vechtstreek
summary: The Dutch country along the river Vecht, where Golden Age merchants built rows of country estates and centuries of peat-cutting left a landscape of man-made lakes and reed-fringed water.

subject: Veendam
summary: Founded in 1648 as a peat colony, Veendam grew into the only Dutch town besides Amsterdam and Rotterdam to host a Lloyd's Register office - and lent its name to four ocean liners.

subject: Veenhuizen
summary: A Drenthe village built in 1823 as a social experiment to house and reform the poor - and inscribed by UNESCO in 2021 as testimony to one of history's most ambitious and uncomfortable attempts at engineered benevolence.

subject: Veenkoloniën
summary: A region in northeastern Netherlands where centuries of peat extraction left behind a landscape of impossibly straight canals, ruler-line villages, and farms that grew out of what used to be bog.

subject: Vefa
summary: A small inner-city quarter of Istanbul where a 150-year-old boza shop preserves the taste of Byzantine streets — and the cup Atatürk drank from is still on the wall.

subject: Vefsna
summary: Nordland's largest river was ruined by a half-millimetre parasite, poisoned from end to end to be rid of it, and declared healthy again in 2018.

subject: Veliky Ustyug
summary: An ancient merchant town at the confluence of the Sukhona and Yug rivers in Vologda Oblast, Veliky Ustyug preserves a treasury of Northern Baroque churches and doubles as the official residence of Russia's Ded Moroz -- Santa Claus.

subject: Vella Lavella
summary: An island where the language itself is a puzzle - Bilua speakers surrounded by Austronesian neighbors, descendants of a migration no one can quite trace.

subject: Velondriake
summary: A 64,000-hectare marine area in southwest Madagascar where Vezo fishing communities proved that letting octopus grounds rest for a few months could boost catches by 700 percent -- and built a conservation model that spread to ten countries.

subject: Veluwe
summary: A glacial ridge in the middle of the Netherlands that medieval iron-makers stripped to sand, the wind sculpted into dunes, and the Dutch eventually replanted into the country's largest forest.

subject: Velyki Sorochyntsi
summary: Nikolai Gogol was born in this village and its raucous market inspired one of his most beloved tales; the fair he made world-famous still fills the streets once a year.

subject: Vendsyssel
summary: Denmark's northernmost district is an island that nobody treats as one — a raised seabed still rising, with a dune walking across it at eighteen metres a year.

subject: Venetian Ghetto
summary: The neighborhood that gave the world the word 'ghetto' -- where Venice confined its Jewish population for nearly three centuries, and where a small community persists today.

story.title: Venetian Pool: The Quarry That Became a Lagoon

subject: Venetian Pool
summary: An ugly coral rock quarry in Coral Gables was transformed in 1924 into an 820,000-gallon spring-fed swimming pool with waterfalls, caves, and Venetian bridges -- the only swimming pool on the National Register of Historic Places.

subject: Venezuelan Andes
summary: Where the longest mountain chain on Earth finally ends, the Venezuelan Andes split into two branches -- the Cordillera de Merida and the Sierra de Perija -- shaped by three colliding tectonic plates and scarred by Ice Age glaciers.

subject: Venezuelan Llanos
summary: Covering over 243,000 square kilometers of central Venezuela, the Llanos are a sedimentary plain so flat that it slopes less than a meter per kilometer, hiding vast oil reserves beneath seasonal floodwaters.

subject: Venice
summary: Where refugees built a republic on mud, where merchants controlled the Mediterranean for centuries, where the lagoon that protected the city now threatens to swallow it.

subject: Venice/Lido
summary: The barrier island that shields Venice's lagoon from the Adriatic -- where Thomas Mann set Death in Venice, where the world's oldest film festival unfolds each September, and where Venetians go to feel normal.

subject: Venlo
summary: A Hanseatic river city on the German border that survived thirteen failed Allied bombing raids on its bridges, then rebuilt itself as Europe's greenest city and a horticulture capital.

subject: Ventanas
summary: The self-declared Corn Capital of Ecuador, a city on the Zapotal River named either for a 19th-century shopkeeper's many windows or for its role opening commerce between mountain and coast.

subject: Ventnor City, New Jersey
summary: Atlantic City's quieter neighbor - 1.7 miles of boardwalk, an unusually varied notable roster, and the only shore town whose name was lifted from an English village on the Isle of Wight.

subject: Ventry
summary: A Gaeltacht village on the Dingle Peninsula whose long sandy beach has hosted Iron Age forts, mythological battles, and twenty-eight shipwrecked Greek sailors.

subject: Venus State Battery
summary: For a century the stamps of the Venus Battery thundered day and night, pulverising rock into gold dust - and you can still walk the crushing floor where they fell.

subject: Verdant Works
summary: Scotland's Jute Museum occupies a rare surviving courtyard-type mill in Dundee, telling the story of an industry that once employed half the city's working population.

subject: Vergadeika
summary: A tiny Laconian village perched on the flank of Mount Taygetos, where ancient olive groves, a 15th-century church, and the slow rhythms of Greek mountain life endure above the valley Spartan armies once marched through.

subject: Vergina
summary: A small Greek town built atop ancient Aigai, the first capital of Macedon, where archaeologist Manolis Andronikos unearthed the royal tombs of Philip II and the family of Alexander the Great in 1977.

subject: Verhildersum
summary: A fourteenth-century moated borg outside Leens that survived two sackings by the city of Groningen, lost a Michelin star in 2012, and now welcomes visitors to ninety varieties of rose laid out by the golden ratio.

subject: Verlorenvlei Heritage Settlement
summary: A cluster of surviving 18th-century Langhuis farmhouses on a Ramsar wetland tells the story of Cape frontier life, from loan farms to grain booms to quiet decline.

subject: Vermilion Range (Minnesota)
summary: Minnesota's first iron range produced ore so pure that two pieces could be welded together, launched an industry that fed the nation's steel mills for eighty years, and for three decades housed a physics laboratory 2,341 feet underground where scientists hunted for dark matter shielded by ancient rock.

subject: Vernal Fall
summary: A 317-foot waterfall on the Merced River where hikers climb through drenching mist, emerald pools hide lethal currents, and a Philippine postage stamp accidentally immortalized the wrong country's waterfall.

subject: Verneukpan
summary: A 57-kilometer salt pan in South Africa whose Afrikaans name means 'to trick' -- as Malcolm Campbell learned when he tried to break the land speed record here in 1929.

subject: Versfeld Pass
summary: Built by a farmer who woke in the night and saw the shape of his road in a glinting watch face, Versfeld Pass climbs 689 meters to the fruit farms atop the Piketberg range.

subject: Versmold
summary: A small Westphalian town that turned sausage-making into a global industry - and put a bronze statue of a worker hauling six sausages in its central square to prove it.

story.title: Very Large Array: Listening to the Universe

subject: Very Large Array
summary: The New Mexico radio telescopes that look like alien technology - 27 antennas arranged in a Y-pattern across the desert, working together to hear signals from the edge of the observable universe.

subject: Vesuvio Cafe
summary: Across a narrow alley from City Lights Bookstore -- an alley now named for Jack Kerouac -- this 1948 bar was the Beat Generation's living room.

subject: Vetera
summary: At a hill above the Lower Rhine, two Roman legions held the northwest frontier of the empire for eight decades - until the winter of 69 CE, when the world around them came apart.

subject: Vettisfossen
summary: Europe's tallest unregulated free-falling waterfall, where a single column of water drops 275 meters off a cliff in the Jotunheimen mountains, unreachable except by a two-to-three-hour hike up the Utladalen valley from the nearest road.

subject: Veurne
summary: An ancient Flemish town whose central square is ringed by Renaissance brick and whose summer streets fill with hooded penitents carrying crosses, the same procession that has walked since 1646.

subject: Viborg
summary: For six centuries no Danish king was truly king until a crowd of Jutlanders in a Viborg field said so.

subject: Vic (Barcelona)
summary: A fog-wreathed Catalan market city with two thousand years of history, famous for its cured sausage, its vast medieval square, and a past that keeps demanding to be remembered.

subject: Vicente Pires
summary: An agricultural colony turned dense suburb, Vicente Pires fought for decades to become its own administrative region of Brazil's federal district.

story.title: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

subject: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata
summary: Spain's last and shortest-lived American viceroyalty was born of silver and smuggling on the muddy banks of the Río de la Plata, and it lasted barely a generation before its own capital tore it apart.

subject: Vichuquén
summary: A preserved colonial village near a brackish coastal lake where black-necked swans glide and weekend sailors chase the wind, in a corner of Chile that was already old when the Spanish arrived.

subject: Victoria
summary: British Columbia's garden capital where Edwardian elegance meets Pacific wilderness - a city of afternoon tea, orca-filled waters, and the most British corner of Canada.

story.title: Victoria: The British Outpost That Time Forgot

subject: Victoria
summary: The British Columbia capital where afternoon tea survives, where double-decker buses carry tourists past the Parliament Buildings, and where the British Empire's most distant outpost became Canada's mildest, most genteel city - 'a little bit of olde England beside the sea.'

subject: Victoria Barracks, Hong Kong
summary: For over a century the Victoria Barracks dominated the Admiralty district of Hong Kong Island; today its footprint lives on as Hong Kong Park, Pacific Place, and a handful of Grade I historic buildings that survived demolition.

subject: Victoria Peak
summary: At 552 metres, Victoria Peak is the tallest hill on Hong Kong Island — and for forty-two years, Chinese residents were legally forbidden from living there.

subject: Victoria Skating Rink
summary: On March 3, 1875, inside a Montreal rink named for Queen Victoria, nine players faced nine players with a flat wooden disc instead of a ball -- and the game that would become ice hockey was born.

subject: Victoria Square, Birmingham
summary: The geographic centre of Birmingham, where the city measures its distances from, home to the Floozie in the Jacuzzi, an Antony Gormley iron giant, and a queen whose statue was nearly forgotten.

subject: Victoria, Hong Kong
summary: The City of Victoria was Hong Kong's first urban settlement, named for Queen Victoria in 1843 and formally granted city status in 1849 — a name that quietly persists across the harbour, the peak, and the park.

subject: Vicuña
summary: The largest town of the Elqui Valley gave the world a Nobel laureate and offers some of the clearest night skies on Earth.

subject: Viedma
summary: Patagonia's oldest European settlement, twice nearly chosen as Argentina's capital and once erased by a flood, sits quietly on the Río Negro where the steppe meets the sea.

subject: Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians
summary: The Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians, whose name translates as 'Valley of the Old Women,' has built remarkable economic sovereignty including California's first Native American-owned bank and a 50% stake in a major AM radio station.

subject: Vienna
summary: The imperial city of music and coffee - where Habsburgs ruled for 650 years, where Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert composed immortal works, and where sitting in a coffee house became UNESCO-protected heritage.

subject: Vientiane
summary: Where Southeast Asia's quietest capital drowses along the Mekong, where French colonial charm meets Buddhist serenity, where Laos keeps its own pace.

subject: Vieques, Puerto Rico
summary: An island where the Spanish tried to block out the devil's glow, the U.S. Navy dropped bombs for sixty years, and the people who endured it all now welcome visitors to some of the Caribbean's most pristine beaches and the world's brightest bioluminescent bay.

subject: Viersen
summary: A small Niederrhein town where the world's three-cushion billiards championships unfold every March, and where one of Germany's largest carnival parades rolls through Dulken every February.

subject: Vietnamese National Military Academy
summary: Perched in the cool highland city of Dalat, the Vietnamese National Military Academy forged the officers of South Vietnam across three decades of colonial transition, national struggle, and cold-war entanglement.

subject: Vieux-Lille
summary: An expressway was once planned through the centre of Vieux-Lille — a working-class immigrant quarter the city wanted to bulldoze. It survived, and is now the most expensive postal code in northern France.

subject: Viikinsaari
summary: Fifteen hectares in Lake Pyhäjärvi that a confectioner turned into a restaurant, a city bought for its mill workers, and a sculptor turned from a lock-up into a chapel.

story.title: Vijaya — The Lost Capital of Champa

subject: Vijaya
summary: For three centuries, Vijaya was the heart of the Champa kingdom — a city of 70,000, towers of stone and brick, and a port that traded eaglewood to the world — until it was destroyed in 1471, leaving towers that still stand in Bình Định Province.

subject: Vijzelgracht
summary: A canal filled in 1933, a metro tunnel that twice made the monumental weaver houses above it sink as much as 23 cm in a single afternoon, and a national lesson in what happens when you build deep under a 17th-century city.

subject: Viktoriapark
summary: Berlin's most famous borough is named after a cast-iron cross on a 66-metre hill, and the waterfall running down that hill has to be switched on.

subject: Vila Bela da Santíssima Trindade
summary: Brazil abandoned its old frontier capital and the enslaved people it left behind stayed, turning a forgotten gold town into a stronghold of Afro-Brazilian culture.

subject: Vila Boa, Goiás
summary: A filling station on the highway to Salvador that soybean money turned into a municipality in a single generation — and which shares its name, confusingly, with the colonial capital of Goiás.

subject: Vila Império
summary: A small neighborhood in Governador Valadares where even the main street runs in four disconnected pieces.

subject: Vila Velha
summary: The oldest city in Espírito Santo, founded on Pentecost Sunday in 1535 and now watching the modern metropolis grow up around it.

subject: Vilafranca del Penedès
summary: The capital of Catalonia's Penedès wine country pairs deep-red local wine and a xató salad with the first Gothic parish church built in the region and streets lined with medieval manor houses.

subject: Vilcabamba
summary: A quiet Andean village near Podocarpus National Park where travelers trade city life for mountain trails, hot-oil massages, and the myth of the Valley of Longevity.

subject: Vilcabamba, Ecuador
summary: A southern Ecuadorean village celebrated as the Valley of Longevity in the 1970s - a reputation Harvard researchers eventually traced to systematic age exaggeration.

subject: Village Vanguard
summary: A wedge-shaped basement jazz club on Seventh Avenue South where Max Gordon's dream of a bohemian salon became, improbably and permanently, the most important small room in the history of jazz.

subject: Villajoyosa
summary: A Costa Blanca fishing town whose seafront was painted every color so returning sailors could find their own front door from far out at sea.

subject: Villarrica
summary: A lakeside town of German and Dutch surnames that the Spanish founded, lost to the Mapuche for nearly three centuries, and rebuilt in the shadow of a volcano that has never stopped breathing.

subject: Villarrica, Paraguay
summary: Founded in 1570 and forced to relocate seven times over a century, the 'Wandering City' finally settled near the Ybytyruzú hills and became Paraguay's cultural capital.

subject: Villena
summary: A crossroads city in the hills of inland Alicante where a single archaeologist unearthed two Bronze Age gold hoards in one astonishing year.

subject: Vilnius
summary: Where Baroque churches fill Eastern Europe's largest old town, where Jewish history was both brilliant and tragic, where Lithuania's capital hides surprising depths.

subject: Vinaròs
summary: A fishing city on the border of Valencia and Catalonia, famous for its prized prawns, a fortress-like Renaissance church, and a long past built on shipyards, wine, and the sea.

subject: Vindeby Offshore Wind Farm
summary: Eleven small turbines in four metres of water off Lolland became the world's first offshore wind farm in 1991 — and the first one taken back down again in 2017.

story.title: Vineyard Landscape of Piedmont: Langhe-Roero and Monferrato

subject: Vineyard Landscape of Piedmont
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage landscape where Etruscans, Celts, and Romans planted the roots of Italian winemaking across the rolling hills of Piedmont.

subject: Vinnytsia
summary: A central Ukrainian city on the Southern Bug that grew from a Tatar-frontier fortress into a place of chocolate factories, musical fountains, and hard-won memory.

subject: Vinpearl Cable Car
summary: Seven Eiffel-type towers planted in the South China Sea carry passengers 3,320 metres across the water from Nha Trang to Hon Tre Island — a crossing that takes about fifteen minutes and offers an unobstructed view of the bay.

subject: Violieren
summary: In 1561 five thousand performers from twelve cities walked into Antwerp for a poetry competition staged by a flower-named drama guild - a literary spectacle the size of a small army, presided over by painters and rhymers.

subject: Virgem da Lapa
summary: A municipality in Minas Gerais named for an image of the Virgin found in a cave, where eighteenth-century prospectors, the Aranã indigenous people, and an August pilgrimage still shape local life.

story.title: Virginia Air and Space Science Center

subject: Virginia Air and Space Science Center
summary: Apollo 12's Yankee Clipper splashed down in 1969 with 45 lunar orbits behind it. Today it sits in downtown Hampton, where you can also climb inside a B-24.

subject: Virginia International Raceway
summary: A 3.27-mile road course carved into Dan River bottomland with a bulldozer in 1957, abandoned for 26 years, then revived as the country club track that taught American racing how to monetize nostalgia.

subject: Virginia V
summary: The last surviving steamship of Puget Sound's Mosquito Fleet still churns through the waters of Seattle, her 1904-cast triple-expansion engine beating like a centenarian heart.

subject: Virginia, County Cavan
summary: An Ulster plantation town named for an English queen that ended up making the cream for Baileys Irish Cream.

subject: Virginia, Minnesota
summary: Named not for the southern state but for the home turf of its earliest lumber workers, Virginia anchors the Mesabi Iron Range -- a gritty Minnesota mining town where Rockefeller, Carnegie, and Hill once competed for ore, immigrants from a dozen nations built a brick downtown after fire destroyed the original, and the local kid who grew up to play Star-Lord was far from the first to leave a mark.

subject: Visbek
summary: A small Lower Saxon village whose surrounding heath holds two of the largest megalithic tombs in Germany - the Visbek Bride and Bridegroom.

subject: Visby
summary: A medieval walled city on the Baltic island of Gotland, where decline preserved architectural treasures and even inspired the animated world of Kiki's Delivery Service.

subject: Vitória
summary: Honey Island, Sun City - the third-oldest Brazilian capital, small enough to walk, close enough to reach a dozen other destinations by lunchtime.

subject: Vitória da Conquista
summary: Bahia's third-largest city sits on a thousand-metre plateau, born of eighteenth-century indigenous conquest, now the economic capital of southwestern Bahia and birthplace of filmmaker Glauber Rocha.

subject: Vitória, Espírito Santo
summary: A Brazilian state capital on an island that used to be fifty islands, named for a battle the Portuguese won 472 years ago.

subject: Vizianagaram Estate
summary: A dynasty that played the French against the British, won a title meaning 'Lord of Elephants,' and produced everyone from a chief minister to a controversial cricket captain -- all from a fort whose very name means 'city of victory.'

subject: Viçosa, Minas Gerais
summary: A Brazilian hill town that a native son turned into a university - and the university turned back into a city.

subject: Viña del Mar
summary: The Garden City of the Chilean coast trades on flowers, beaches, and a casino, but its name remembers the vineyards that a single storm destroyed.

story.title: Viña del Mar International Song Festival

subject: Viña del Mar International Song Festival
summary: Latin America's oldest and largest music festival is ruled not by judges but by a 15,000-strong crowd the press calls El Monstruo, the Monster.

subject: Vlaardingen
summary: A Dutch town that defeated a Holy Roman Emperor in 1018, lost itself to herring, smog, and the slow tide of suburbanization, and still keeps a working windmill and a museum to the boats that once filled its harbor.

subject: Vlachokerasia
summary: A mountain village in southern Arcadia that has stood since antiquity as Oeum, home of the warrior Skiritai who guarded the road between Sparta and Tegea, and has survived every empire that tried to govern it.

subject: Vlakplaas
summary: On an ordinary farm west of Pretoria, the apartheid state ran a secret death squad - and the names that matter most are those of the people it murdered.

subject: Vlieland
summary: A car-free sliver of dunes adrift in the Dutch Wadden Sea, where one village faces a vanished twin that the North Sea swallowed whole.

subject: Vlieter Incident
summary: In a tidal trench between Texel and the Dutch mainland, twelve warships of the Batavian Navy surrendered without firing a single shot - the most humiliating capitulation in Dutch naval history.

subject: Vlissingen
summary: A Zeeland port that exported its name to a Queens neighborhood, its admirals to the world's oceans, and finally itself to British commandos who came to take it back from the Germans in 1944.

subject: Voeren
summary: Six villages stranded between Flanders, Wallonia and the Netherlands — and the language fight here brought down a Belgian government in 1987.

subject: Vogelfluglinie
summary: The Copenhagen-Hamburg corridor named after migrating cranes, where express trains drove onto a ship until December 2019.

subject: Vohemar
summary: On Madagascar's northeast coast, a quiet fishing town sits atop a vanished trading civilization whose tombs once held Chinese porcelain, carved stone, and gold.

subject: Voice of Han
summary: Taiwan's armed-forces radio station, born in wartime China and carried across the strait in 1949, has broadcast across the island and toward the mainland for more than eight decades.

subject: Vojens Speedway Center
summary: A 300-metre shale oval in a small South Jutland town that Ole Olsen built in 1975 and turned into one of speedway's great world-championship venues — famous for its finals and infamous for its rain.

story.title: Vokes Hill Corner to Cook Road

subject: Vokes Hill Corner to Cook Road
summary: A lonely 1961 outback track cut by the legendary surveyor Len Beadell, running south through red desert to link the inland weapons country with a railway ghost town on the Nullarbor.

subject: Volcanoes of Kamchatka
summary: The Kamchatka Peninsula hosts around 160 volcanoes — 29 of them still active — forming one of the most geologically violent landscapes on Earth and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

subject: Volendam
summary: A Dutch fishing village that built its identity by leaning hard into being looked at - and lost fourteen of its own on a New Year's Eve that changed the country.

subject: Volimidia
summary: A hillside near Chora holds 35 Bronze Age chamber tombs used and re-used across three thousand years — the cemetery of a Mycenaean community that may have worshipped the goddess Potnia and sent forty-six "servants of the god" to a religious centre called Sphagianes.

subject: Volissos
summary: A hill village in northwest Chios crowned by a six-towered castle, where a marble plate at the entrance insists that Homer himself once lived and wrote here.

subject: Volkerakdam
summary: Three separate hydraulic structures across three bodies of water, built after the 1953 flood killed nearly two thousand Dutch citizens, and the place where a Mesolithic carved figure was unearthed in 1966.

subject: Volos
summary: The Thessalian port where Jason launched the Argo, built atop ancient Iolcos at the foot of Mount Pelion, mixing myth, steel, tsipouro, and a painter's birthplace.

subject: Volubilis
summary: A Berber-Roman city in Morocco whose mosaics, basilica, and triumphal arch still stand after two millennia, bearing witness to empires that rose and fell around it.

subject: Volunteer Point
summary: At the windswept end of a Falklands peninsula stands the largest king penguin colony in the islands, a metre-tall congregation at the very northern edge of the species' range.

subject: Vondelpark
summary: Forty-seven hectares of English-garden park in the middle of Amsterdam, opened in 1865 by a club of citizens who wanted somewhere to ride their horses.

subject: Vorden
summary: A small Dutch village in the Achterhoek surrounded by a circle of eight medieval castles, all reachable on a 34-kilometer bike route that may be the most concentrated dose of nobility in the Netherlands.

subject: Vorkutlag
summary: For thirty years, the Vorkuta Corrective Labor Camp processed roughly two million prisoners through coal mines above the Arctic Circle, where 16-hour workdays, starvation rations, and temperatures far below zero killed an estimated 200,000 people.

subject: Vorupør
summary: In 1887 the fishermen of Nørre Vorupør pooled their boats, their gear and their earnings into what is remembered as the world's first cooperative fishing company — and then built a stone mole to hold the North Sea off it.

subject: Voskhod 2
summary: The 1965 Soviet space mission in which Alexei Leonov became the first person to walk in space, then nearly died when his suit ballooned and he could not fit back through the airlock.

subject: Vossbarg
summary: A tiny East Frisian row village born from a Prussian land grant in 1780, hammered by poverty, and rescued by an industrial power station next door.

subject: Votuporanga
summary: A Brazilian furniture-making city whose Tupi name means 'soft breezes' and whose civic pride includes a champion cow, a shopping mall named after her, and a lively nightlife.

subject: Vouliagmeni
summary: The name means 'sunken' — and Vouliagmeni, the wealthy Athens Riviera suburb 18 kilometres south of the city, has a sunken lake fed by underground springs to prove it, along with ruins of a temple to Apollo, beaches that have won Olympic triathlons, and some of the most expensive real estate in the Mediterranean.

subject: Voxtrup
summary: A southeastern district of Osnabrück whose name is older than its city, whose court convened in 1088, and whose woods still hide a megalithic monument called the Devil's Stones.

subject: Vriezenveen
summary: A 6.2-kilometre-long Twente village whose tradesmen ran shops on St Petersburg's Nevsky Prospekt for two centuries, until the Russian Revolution sent them home.

subject: Vrijthof
summary: Maastricht's central square has been a Roman cemetery, a pilgrimage gathering ground, an execution site, a French parade ground, and the open-air stage where Andre Rieu plays Strauss waltzes to fifteen thousand people at a time.

subject: Vrilissia
summary: An affluent green suburb at the foot of the marble mountain that built the Parthenon, where wide straight streets feel almost un-Athenian.

story.title: Vulcan, Alberta: The Town That Became a Homeworld

subject: Vulcan, Alberta
summary: The Canadian prairie town that shared its name with Star Trek's most famous planet - and decided to embrace the coincidence so completely that Leonard Nimoy came to dedicate a starship replica.

subject: Vulcania
summary: Born from the vision of two volcanologists who died chasing eruptions, Vulcania is a theme park buried inside an extinct volcanic landscape in France's Auvergne region.

subject: Vuoggatjålme
summary: Sweden's official cold record, minus 52.6 degrees, was written down at this lakeside outpost on the Silver Road by an observer who half-suspected his thermometer had broken.

subject: Várzea Grande
summary: Across the Cuiabá River from Mato Grosso's capital sits the second-largest city in the state, home to its international airport and the Festival of Saint Peter.

subject: Vía Verde de Ojos Negros
summary: Once the longest private railway in Europe, built to haul iron ore to the sea, this 160-kilometre corridor is now the longest greenway in Spain.

subject: W. T. Preston
summary: A sternwheel snagboat built from the parts of her predecessors, who cleared the rivers of Puget Sound for half a century and once hauled a sunken bomber off the bottom.

subject: WDBJ
summary: Roanoke's CBS station has signed on the air since October 3, 1955 — known for The Andy Griffith Show, four meteorologists, and the August morning in 2015 when two of its own were murdered live on the air.

subject: Wabar craters
summary: Hidden deep in Arabia's Empty Quarter, impact craters from a meteorite strike less than 250 years old were discovered by a British explorer searching for a legendary lost city.

subject: Wachovia Tract
summary: Nearly 99,000 acres of North Carolina backcountry, purchased in 1753 by German-speaking Moravians who named it after Count Zinzendorf's family estate on the Danube.

subject: Wacken Open Air
summary: A Schleswig-Holstein village of 2,085 people hosts the world's biggest metal festival every August, when 85,000 visitors arrive and the population multiplies forty times over.

subject: Wad Madani
summary: Capital of Al Jazirah state and heart of the Gezira cotton scheme, Wad Madani grew from a 19th-century Turco-Egyptian outpost into one of Sudan's great agricultural and cultural centers - then became the Rapid Support Forces' prize in December 2023.

subject: Wadden Sea
summary: The world's largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats, stretching 500 kilometers across three countries - and recognized by UNESCO as a place worth saving.

subject: Wadebridge
summary: Where a medieval vicar built a stone bridge to stop drownings, a Cornish market town grew straddling the River Camel - and the second locomotive on its 1834 railway arrived from Wales already mistakenly named Elephant.

subject: Wadi Allaqi
summary: In Egypt's Eastern Desert, a biosphere oasis between the Nile and the Red Sea shelters Bedouin communities, ancient trade routes, and the rare Egyptian vulture.

subject: Wadi Halfa
summary: At the far northern edge of Sudan, a small town of fifteen thousand stands on the desert shore of Lake Nasser, the new Wadi Halfa - the old one lies beneath the water.

subject: Wadi Halfa Salient
summary: A finger of disputed territory juts north from Sudan into Egypt - fifty-two villages once, now mostly drowned beneath Lake Nasser, the map itself underwater.

subject: Wadi Rum
summary: Jordan's vast Valley of the Moon -- 720 square kilometers of sandstone towers, Nabataean inscriptions, and Bedouin camps -- has doubled as Mars, Arrakis, and Jedha on screen, but its real history runs deeper than any script.

subject: Wadi Tiwi
summary: A thousand-year-old inhabited canyon in Oman where ancient falaj irrigation channels sustain date palms, banana groves with 500-year-old cultivars, and pools full of 'doctor fish' that nibble on swimmers.

story.title: Wae Rebo: Seven Houses Above the Clouds

subject: Wae Rebo
summary: A Manggarai village of seven cone-shaped houses perched at 1,100 meters in the mountains of Flores, where UNESCO-recognized architecture encodes a philosophy of life in five sacred levels.

subject: Wagah
summary: The only open road crossing between India and Pakistan stages a nightly spectacle of synchronized goose-stepping, thunderous crowds, and a handshake at sunset.

story.title: Waigeo: The Island That Nearly Split in Two

subject: Waigeo
summary: The largest island in the Raja Ampat archipelago, Waigeo harbors 50,000 years of human history, endemic species found nowhere else on Earth, and an inland sea that almost cleaves it in half.

subject: Waimiri Atroari Indigenous Territory
summary: The forest between Manaus and Boa Vista where a military dictatorship tried, and failed, to erase an entire people.

subject: Wairarapa
summary: A sheltered valley on New Zealand's lower North Island where Maori legend, boutique wine, and a daily rail commute through a mountain define the character of a region that feels a world away from Wellington despite being just over the hill.

subject: Waithali kingdom
summary: An ancient Arakanese kingdom that flourished from roughly 370 to 818 AD, where Buddhist kings claimed descent from the Hindu god Shiva and ships from China, India, and Persia converged on a walled city built along a tidal creek.

subject: Waiting for the Interurban
summary: A 1978 cast aluminum sculpture of six commuters and a dog in Seattle's Fremont neighborhood, where the sculptor hid a private revenge in the dog's face and the community has been dressing the statues for nearly five decades.

subject: Wakatobi
summary: An acronym stitched from four island names, Wakatobi holds some of the richest coral reefs on Earth in waters that most divers have never heard of.

subject: Wakefield
summary: Wakefield, a cathedral city of 110,000 on the River Calder, was for centuries the administrative capital of the West Riding of Yorkshire and is now best known as the capital of the Rhubarb Triangle.

subject: Wakestock
summary: For fourteen summers, a wakeboard festival in a Welsh seaside village brought Calvin Harris and a 200,000-gallon pool gap to a peninsula better known for monasteries.

subject: Wakhjir Pass
summary: The only navigable crossing between Afghanistan and China, this remote pass at the tip of the Wakhan Corridor has been a thread between empires for centuries, yet barely a handful of Westerners have ever crossed it.

subject: Wakkanai
summary: Japan's northernmost city sits at the edge of everything: the last train station, the nearest point to Russia, and the gateway to some of Hokkaido's wildest islands.

subject: Walcha, New South Wales
summary: A small wool town on the New England Tablelands that turned its streets into Australia's densest open-air sculpture gallery.

subject: Walcheren
summary: A rhombus-shaped former island at the mouth of the Scheldt, repeatedly drowned and re-claimed, whose dykes the RAF deliberately bombed in 1944 to flush out the German army.

subject: Walden Pond
summary: A 64-acre glacial kettle pond in Concord, Massachusetts, where Henry David Thoreau lived for two years and wrote one of the most influential works in American literature.

subject: Waldomore
summary: A Clarksburg mansion whose name combines a husband and wife - now home to the city library, the West Virginia historical archive, and the papers of a UFO writer who claimed three Men in Black visited him.

subject: Waleswood Colliery
summary: A South Yorkshire coal mine whose buildings survived the pit's closure to become an industrial estate, and whose namesake locomotive is still being restored to steam.

subject: Walhalla, Victoria
summary: A town named for the Norse hall of the gods, wedged into a gorge so steep its houses cling like birds' nests, where 4,000 people once chased the richest gold reef in Victoria.

subject: Walla Walla
summary: Where sweet onions grow in volcanic soil and over a hundred wineries have transformed wheat country into Washington's premier wine destination.

subject: Wallace (Idaho)
summary: The only city in America entirely listed on the National Register of Historic Places earned that distinction by fighting three existential battles - against mining violence, the largest wildfire in U.S. history, and a federal freeway that would have erased it from the map.

subject: Wallasey
