summary: A Wirral town of merged seaside villages whose name means "island of the Britons" and whose history runs from Viking trading post to wartime bombing target.

subject: Walle Plough
summary: A 4,000-year-old oak plough surfaced from an East Frisian peat bog in 1927, preserved by the same waterlogged ground that hid it.

subject: Walled Villages of Hong Kong
summary: Scattered across the New Territories, Hong Kong's walled villages are stone-and-brick fortresses built by clans who refused to let pirates, bandits, or rival families drive them from their land.

subject: Wallops Flight Facility
summary: NASA's most prolific launch site sits not in Florida but on a narrow barrier island off Virginia's Eastern Shore, where over 16,000 rockets have roared skyward since 1945 -- and the ocean creeps closer every year.

subject: Walls of Dubrovnik
summary: Nearly two kilometers of unbroken stone encircle one of Europe's best-preserved medieval cities, walls that have repelled Saracens, Normans, and modern artillery across twelve centuries of siege.

subject: Walls of Macau
summary: Built from clay, sand, rice straw, and oyster shells in the sixteenth century, the old city walls of Macau defended Portugal's first foothold in Asia — and survived centuries of neglect to earn a place on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

subject: Walls of Old San Juan
summary: The only walled city under U.S. jurisdiction, Old San Juan's three miles of 16th-to-18th-century ramparts still encircle the islet -- a Caribbean stone embrace that survived earthquakes, empires, and the wrecking ball.

story.title: Walnut Grove: Where the Towers Touch the Clouds

subject: Walnut Grove
summary: A tiny delta town founded in 1851 became both a crossroads of Chinese and Japanese immigrant life along the Sacramento River and the unlikely home of some of the tallest structures in the Western Hemisphere -- broadcast towers rising 2,048 feet above the flat Central Valley floor.

subject: Walsall
summary: The town that made the Queen's handbags and the royal family's saddles, Walsall sits where the Black Country shades into the wooded Midlands and where the local accent is so distinctive that linguists have given it its own name.

subject: Walsingham Priory
summary: For five centuries, Walsingham was England's most sacred pilgrimage destination — visited by kings, Erasmus, and countless ordinary believers — until Henry VIII ended it all in a single act of spoliation in 1538.

subject: Walt Disney Studios (Burbank)
summary: The birthplace of animated dreams, where Snow White's success built a campus that transformed American entertainment and still houses the Disney empire today.

subject: Walter Annenberg
summary: How a Philadelphia publisher's son built a media empire worth billions, befriended presidents and a queen, and ended his life giving most of it away — all while making Rancho Mirage his desert kingdom.

subject: Walter Siepmann
summary: The third-generation engineer-inventor whose oilfield valves earned the family Westphalian forge a market in North America - and whose company prospered through both the Nazi armaments boom and the postwar recovery.

subject: Walton-on-the-Naze
summary: An Essex seaside town clinging to a crumbling clay headland, where the sea swallowed the medieval village whole and continues to advance at two metres a year.

subject: Wamena
summary: A town of 66,000 perched at 1,660 meters in a valley that was stone-age civilization when the Dutch built its first airstrip.

subject: Wan Chai
summary: Once a waterfront cove for fishermen and sailors, Wan Chai has shapeshifted across two centuries into Hong Kong's most layered neighborhood — from colonial red-light district to the stage for the handover of a city.

subject: Wan Chai District
summary: One of Hong Kong's most layered districts, Wan Chai has worn a dozen identities — colonial port, red-light notoriety, handover ceremony ground — and keeps accumulating more.

subject: Wan Chai Heritage Trail
summary: A two-hour walking trail through 15 heritage sites in Wan Chai, threading together painted shophouses, Bauhaus-inflected markets, and 19th-century temples into a single navigable story.

subject: Wanaka
summary: Queenstown's cooler little brother - a lakeside town where half of New Zealand's Olympic skiers live, a lone willow tree became the country's most photographed subject, and the locals will correct your pronunciation with a smile.

subject: Wangapeka Track
summary: A grueling backcountry route through Kahurangi National Park where gold prospectors, surveyors, and modern trampers have tested themselves against four metres of annual rainfall, unbridged rivers, and some of New Zealand's most remote wilderness.

subject: Wangerooge
summary: The easternmost East Frisian Island drifted eastward for centuries, swallowing its own villages, until twentieth-century sea defenses finally pinned it in place.

subject: Wangfujing
summary: Named for a sweet-water well discovered among Qing dynasty princely estates, Beijing's most famous shopping street has reinvented itself from imperial merchant lane to pedestrian boulevard to contested ground for democracy protesters.

subject: Warbirds over Wanaka
summary: Every second Easter, the Southern Alps become a backdrop for one of the world's great air shows - a biennial gathering born from one man's obsession with World War II fighters that has drawn 111,000 spectators, Buzz Aldrin, and aircraft from a dozen nations.

subject: Warbreccan
summary: A Channel Country sheep-and-cattle station strung along fifteen miles of the Thomson River, where the great frontage was both the asset and the reason the place endured.

subject: Warendorf
summary: A medieval Westphalian linen town on the Ems that became the equestrian capital of Germany - home to the North Rhine-Westphalian state stud, the National Olympic Committee for equestrian sport, and the Bundeswehr Sports School.

subject: Warfhuizen
summary: A village built on two earth mounds north of Groningen, home to the northernmost Marian shrine on the European mainland and one of the very few hermitages in the Netherlands still occupied by an actual hermit.

subject: Warialda
summary: Warialda - 'place of wild honey' in the Kamilaroi tongue - is a quiet northern-NSW town that was the first settlement on the North West Slopes, guarding a creek-side jumble of balancing boulders called Cranky Rock.

subject: Warm Springs Indian Reservation
summary: A sovereign nation where three tribes merged from centuries of conflict into one confederation, preserving ancient languages while pioneering drone certification and wolf conservation in Oregon's high desert.

subject: Warm Springs, Georgia
summary: A tiny Georgia town whose naturally heated springs drew a polio-stricken future president, transformed it into a center of hope and rehabilitation, and left it forever marked by Franklin Roosevelt's life and death.

subject: Warmbad, Namibia
summary: The oldest European-founded settlement in Namibia began with hot springs, survived the destruction of its first buildings by Orlam resistance, and has reinvented itself through two centuries of missionaries, colonial soldiers, and uranium prospectors.

subject: Warner Bros. Movie World
summary: Hollywood came to the Gold Coast in 1991 and never left; three decades on, Batman and Bugs Bunny still share a Main Street where Australia's tallest roller coaster looms over the back lot.

subject: Warner Bros. Studios, Burbank
summary: The 62-acre studio lot in Burbank that Warner Bros. acquired in 1928 on the strength of The Jazz Singer has produced some of American cinema's most enduring images — from Casablanca to Friends — across 35 sound stages still in active use.

subject: Warner's Ranch
summary: A pivotal waystation on the Southern Emigrant Trail where thousands of Gold Rush travelers found respite, and where the Cupeno people lost a Supreme Court battle for their ancestral homeland in 1901.

subject: Warrap (state)
summary: A South Sudanese state in the Bahr el Ghazal region that has sent a president, a basketball giant, and a supermodel to the world while rebuilding itself from decades of war.

subject: Warren County PCB Landfill
summary: The small community of Afton, North Carolina became the birthplace of the American environmental justice movement when residents lay down in front of trucks carrying PCB-contaminated soil to a landfill in 1982.

subject: Warren Magnuson
summary: An orphan from Minnesota who became Washington state's longest-serving senator, Warren Magnuson shaped twentieth-century America through 44 years in Congress, championing civil rights, public broadcasting, and the protection of Puget Sound.

subject: Warrenpoint Ambush
summary: On 27 August 1979, two bombs at Narrow Water killed eighteen British soldiers, the deadliest single attack on the British Army of the Troubles.

subject: Warrington
summary: A working town wedged between Liverpool and Manchester, with a top-tier rugby league side, a Saxon ford, a Pugin church on Smith Street, and pubs that have been pouring beer since the 1500s.

subject: Warrington
summary: A Roman crossing on the Mersey, a Saxon ford, a wire-making town that built half of Britain's chemical industry, and a 1968 New Town that doubled its population in fifty years.

subject: Warroora
summary: A working cattle station south of Coral Bay whose 50 kilometres of Ningaloo lagoon frontage has become a byword for low-key, off-grid beach camping at the edge of a World Heritage reef.

subject: Warsingsfehn
summary: An East Frisian peat colony that pivoted from cutting bog into ocean-going ships, ending up with 82 seagoing vessels and becoming the capital of its municipality.

subject: Waru Waru
summary: An ancient raised-field farming technique from the Andes that turned the harsh altiplano around Lake Titicaca into productive cropland, now being revived by modern communities.

subject: Waruga
summary: Stone sarcophagi where the Minahasan dead sat facing north, knees drawn to their chests, waiting for whatever comes next. The Dutch banned the practice in 1828, but 370 waruga still stand.

subject: Warwick
summary: The county town of Warwickshire, a market settlement of perhaps 36,000 people built around one of Britain's most-visited castles, where Aethelflaed of Mercia built a hilltop burh in 914 and the Great Fire of 1694 rebuilt the medieval centre in fine Stuart and Georgian stone.

subject: Warwick
summary: A Warwickshire county town whose history reaches from Neolithic flint pits through a Roman barn, Anglo-Saxon mint, Norman castle, medieval guild hall, Great Fire, Georgian rebuild, and the 1571 charitable foundation that still houses retired soldiers in dark-blue Elizabethan gowns.

subject: Wasdale
summary: A narrow Cumbrian valley that holds England's deepest lake, highest peak, and the birthplace of British rock climbing - all in a parish of 127 people.

subject: Wash Woods, Virginia
summary: A village built by shipwreck survivors from the cypress wood of other shipwrecks, abandoned when two 1933 hurricanes washed away the only life its people knew.

subject: Washington County, Virginia
summary: Carved out of frontier Fincastle County in 1776 and named for a sitting general fighting a war he might still lose, this county at the top of the Holston Valley has been Virginia's southwestern doorstep for two and a half centuries.

story.title: Washington DC: The City Built for Government and Nothing Else

subject: Washington DC
summary: The capital city carved from swampland that still lacks voting representation - where the monuments are free, the traffic is terrible, and 700,000 residents pay federal taxes but have no senator to show for it.

subject: Washington Metropolitan Area
summary: The DMV - District, Maryland, Virginia - is a region defined by a beltway, fueled by federal power, and shaped by some of America's most educated and affluent residents.

subject: Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority
summary: Six lines, 98 stations, an interstate compact between Maryland Virginia and the District, and a transit agency that has built one of the country's largest rapid transit networks and survived the country's most expensive transit crashes - the Washington Metro is what happens when three jurisdictions and the federal government agree to do something together.

subject: Washington Square (San Francisco)
summary: Established in 1847, this North Beach park sheltered earthquake refugees, inspired Dirty Harry's sniper scene, and anchors a neighborhood where Ferlinghetti watched the old Italians die.

subject: Washington, D.C.
summary: A capital city born of compromise in 1790, burned by the British in 1814, redesigned by Beaux-Arts planners in 1901, riot-scarred in 1968, gentrified in the 2000s - Washington holds the federal government, the Smithsonian, the largest Ethiopian community outside Africa, and a hundred miles of monumental sightlines.

subject: Washington, D.C.
summary: Three founders ate dinner in June 1790 and decided where to put the United States capital. The compromise placed it on the Potomac, near Washington's plantation, on land surveyed by a Black astronomer whose father had been enslaved.

subject: Washington, North Carolina
summary: Established in 1776 on the banks of the Pamlico River, Washington is the first town anywhere in the United States to be named after George Washington - a fact the locals defend by calling their home 'Original Washington' or, more often, 'Little Washington.'

subject: Washington, Tyne and Wear
summary: A coal-and-chemical town that gave its name to a continent, then reinvented itself as a Nissan-fuelled new town between Sunderland and Gateshead.

subject: Wasson Bluff
summary: A mile-long stretch of 200-million-year-old cliffs on Nova Scotia's Minas Basin that yielded more than 100,000 bones from Canada's oldest known dinosaurs, marking the exact moment one geological age gave way to another.

subject: Watauga County, North Carolina
summary: A North Carolina High Country county once called one of the Lost Provinces, where Calloway Peak crowns the skyline at 5,946 feet and Beech Mountain holds the title of highest incorporated town east of the Mississippi.

subject: Watchet
summary: An ancient Somerset harbour where Alfred the Great defended his kingdom against the Vikings, Coleridge dreamed up the Ancient Mariner, and a colour called Watchet Blue still streaks the cliffs.

subject: Watchet Lifeboat Station
summary: From 1875 to 1944 a Somerset harbour town launched its own pulling-and-sailing lifeboat into the Bristol Channel - and when the station closed, its boathouse became the town library, which it still is.

subject: Watchung Reservation
summary: A 1,945-acre wilderness nestled between volcanic ridges in suburban New Jersey, where Jurassic fossils, a ghost town, hidden murals, and Cold War missile silos share space with ancient Lenape campsites.

subject: Water Cube
summary: Designed using the mathematics of soap bubbles and clad in a material thinner than a credit card, Beijing's National Aquatics Center saw 25 world records fall during the 2008 Olympics before transforming into an ice rink for the 2022 Winter Games.

subject: Waterberg Biosphere
summary: A 654,000-hectare massif of red sandstone cliffs and dry bushveld in northern Limpopo, the Waterberg holds rock art, rhinos, and rock 2.7 billion years old — and is one of the few corners of the Lowveld where malaria barely reaches.

subject: Waterford
summary: Ireland's oldest city, founded by Vikings in 914 AD, where Reginald's Tower has guarded the same corner for a thousand years and the surviving city walls run longer than any in Ireland except Derry.

subject: Waterland
summary: The pastoral municipality just north of Amsterdam where below-sea-level dairy farms, former Zuiderzee fishing villages, and a centuries-old cycling network all share the same flat horizon.

subject: Waterloo, Belgium
summary: The town whose name became a synonym for total defeat is, in person, a leafy commuter suburb where Wellington once prayed and Mastercard now runs Europe.

subject: Waterloo, Sierra Leone
summary: A crossroads city built by freed Africans and Caribbean soldiers, where the Krio language and culture took root.

subject: Waterville, County Kerry
summary: A Kerry village on an isthmus between a lake and the sea, where Charlie Chaplin took eleven family holidays and the world's transatlantic cables once came ashore.

subject: Watts Riots
summary: Six days of uprising in August 1965, ignited by a traffic stop and sustained by decades of segregation, police brutality, and economic exclusion, that left 34 dead and changed Los Angeles forever.

subject: Wau, South Sudan
summary: A trading hub on the Jur River where French colonials, slave-traders, British administrators, and multiple civil wars have layered themselves onto the same riverbank in northwestern South Sudan.

subject: Wave Hill
summary: A 28-acre Bronx estate overlooking the Hudson River and the Palisades that passed through the hands of a publisher, a J.P. Morgan partner, and Mark Twain before becoming one of New York's most treasured public gardens.

subject: Wave Hill Station
summary: One of Australia's great pastoral leases, Wave Hill Station was established in 1883 on Gurindji land and became the scene of a seven-year Indigenous walk-off that transformed Australian land rights law.

subject: Wave Hill walk-off
summary: In August 1966, 200 Gurindji stockmen and their families walked off Wave Hill Station and refused to return for seven years, transforming a labor dispute into Australia's most consequential Indigenous land rights movement.

subject: Wave-Gotik-Treffen
summary: Every Pentecost, twenty thousand people in black take over Bach's city - a festival that began as an illegal gathering of 150 in a Potsdam park and survived its own bankruptcy without a single arrest.

subject: Waverly Fairgrounds
summary: A vanished fairground on the Newark-Elizabeth border where the worst team in 19th-century baseball played its doomed home games, state fairs drew crowds for three decades, and a racing oval outlasted them all.

subject: Wearside
summary: Named for the river that carved it, Wearside is the corner of north-east England where shipyards and collieries once defined a way of life - and where the people they shaped are still figuring out what comes next.

subject: Webster Marble
summary: A timber cruiser who spent twenty years hauling surveying equipment through Michigan's Upper Peninsula forests invented the outdoor tools that Teddy Roosevelt carried to Africa and Charles Lindbergh carried across the Atlantic.

subject: Webster Sycamore
summary: A 500-year-old sycamore tree on the Back Fork of the Elk River, briefly the largest of its species in the United States, killed by a 17-year-old arsonist in 2007.

subject: Wedgwood
summary: Josiah Wedgwood mixed 3,000 batches of clay to invent the colour now called Wedgwood blue, and the firm he founded in 1759 has been working out what to do with his ambitions ever since.

subject: Wedgwood Institute
summary: A slice of the Doge's Palace landed in a Staffordshire pottery town, encrusted with terracotta zodiac panels, and then waited 150 years for someone to figure out what to do with it.

subject: Wedgwood Rock
summary: A 700-metric-ton glacial erratic carried 55 miles by ice 14,000 years ago, Wedgwood Rock sits in a Seattle residential neighborhood where it trained some of America's greatest climbers before the city council made climbing it a crime.

subject: Weeki Wachee Springs
summary: Where mermaids have performed underwater since 1947, breathing through hidden air hoses in a spring that sits atop the deepest known freshwater cave system in the United States.

subject: Weesp
summary: A tiny medieval town overbuilt with fortifications it never needed, famous for almond cakes and gin, swallowed by Amsterdam in 2022 and still refusing to disappear.

subject: Weeze
summary: When the Royal Air Force left Weeze in 1999 it took 5,000 people with it. Twenty-five years later, the abandoned airbase is one of Europe's busiest discount-airline hubs.

subject: Wei (state)
summary: One of the seven major powers of China's Warring States period, Wei rose from the ashes of a partitioned Jin dynasty to become the dominant state of its era -- before a rival's engineers turned the Yellow River against its capital.

subject: Weipa
summary: A company town built on one of the world's largest bauxite deposits, on the Western Cape country of the Alngith, Thanikwithi and other peoples, whose displacement cleared the way for the mine.

subject: Welch, West Virginia
summary: Once called "The Heart of the Nation's Coal Bin," Welch built the country's first municipal parking garage, hosted the first federal food stamps, and watched the coalfield empty around it.

subject: Welkait
summary: A fertile lowland district that has changed hands between empires, rebels, and rival ethnic administrations for four centuries, and whose Tigrayan inhabitants were driven from their homes in 2020.

subject: Wellcome Trust
summary: Born from the fortune of an American-born pharmaceutical entrepreneur, the Wellcome Trust grew into one of the world's most powerful biomedical research funders — shaping global health from its twin buildings on London's Euston Road.

subject: Wellingborough
summary: A Northamptonshire market town surrounded by five medicinal wells - one of which drew Charles I's queen and her physician in 1627 - and built on a Jurassic ironstone deposit that powered the British steel industry for a hundred years.

subject: Wellington
summary: New Zealand's capital clings to hills above Cook Strait, battered by winds that never stop, powered by film industry magic, and defined by government and coffee culture in equal measure - the coolest little capital.

subject: Wellington Barracks, Hong Kong
summary: A British military complex that stood between Central and Wan Chai for over a century, Wellington Barracks gave Hong Kong's Admiralty MTR station its Chinese name — 'Golden Clock' — before disappearing entirely to become a park.

subject: Wellington Cable Car
summary: Wellington's beloved funicular railway has been climbing 120 meters from Lambton Quay to Kelburn since 1902, surviving fires, safety crises, and privatization debates to carry its millionth passenger each year.

subject: Wellington station (British Columbia)
summary: A humble flag stop on the E&N Railway that was once the northern terminus and the epicenter of Vancouver Island's coal empire -- built on the wealth of Robert Dunsmuir and the grievances of the miners who made him rich.

subject: Wellington, British Columbia
summary: A fishing trip at Diver Lake in 1869 turned into the richest coal seam on Vancouver Island, a company empire, and one of Canada's worst mine disasters.

subject: Wells, Somerset
summary: The second-smallest city in England by area, named for three holy springs, dominated by a 13th-century cathedral whose carved west front survived a Civil War and a Monmouth Rebellion.

subject: Wells-next-the-Sea
summary: A North Norfolk port town named for its springs, made rich by malt, defended by tides, and now a seaside resort fighting siltation, storms, and second homes.

subject: Wells-next-the-Sea Lifeboat Station
summary: Nearly two centuries of lifeboat service at Wells-next-the-Sea, where volunteer crews have launched into the North Sea's worst storms from a station that has relocated twice to keep pace with the tide.

subject: Wellshot Station
summary: A vast sheep run south of Ilfracombe that by 1892 carried more sheep than any station on Earth, gave the town of Ilfracombe its first name, and helped give birth to the Australian shearers' union.

subject: Welsh 1000 m Peaks Race
summary: An annual mountain endurance race that climbs every Welsh peak over 1,000 metres in a single morning, from the Conwy Bay shoreline to the summit of Snowdon.

subject: Wenatchee
summary: The self-proclaimed 'Apple Capital of the World' sits where the Wenatchee River meets the Columbia, offering 300 days of sunshine on the dry side of the Cascades.

subject: Wendy Yoshimura
summary: Born in the Manzanar internment camp during World War II, Wendy Yoshimura later joined the Symbionese Liberation Army before reinventing herself as a still life watercolor painter.

subject: Wenlock Goldfield
summary: An Aboriginal woman carting wash discovered the nugget that built Cape York's richest goldfield, now a ghost of mango trees and rusting boilers on the Wenlock River.

subject: Werder (Havel)
summary: A Havel island town of 27,000 that swells to half a million visitors every spring, when Brandenburg's orchards bloom and the fruit wine comes out of the garden sheds.

subject: Werderaner Wachtelberg
summary: The vines on this glacial hill above the Havel froze to death in the winter of 1955/56 and stayed dead for nearly thirty years - until a Brandenburg town decided to plant 17,200 of them again.

subject: Werowocomoco
summary: The lost capital of the Powhatan Confederacy, where Wahunsenacawh ruled over dozens of Algonquian tribes and where John Smith was brought as a captive in 1607 - rediscovered on the York River after centuries of misidentification.

subject: Wesleydale Mission
summary: New Zealand's first Wesleyan mission, founded in 1823 beside the Kaeo River and destroyed by warriors in 1827 -- a brief, desperate experiment in faith on a contested frontier.

subject: West Coast (New Zealand)
summary: New Zealand's last frontier - a narrow strip of wild coast squeezed between the Tasman Sea and the Southern Alps, where glaciers descend toward rainforest, Pancake Rocks blow spray skyward, and 33,000 hardy 'Coasters' live by their own rules.

subject: West Coast Trail
summary: A 75-kilometer lifesaving trail turned legendary backpacking route along Vancouver Island's shipwreck-haunted southwest coast.

subject: West Coast Treetop Walk
summary: A steel canopy walkway threads through ancient rimu forest near Hokitika, lifting visitors 20 meters into the crowns of trees that have watched over New Zealand's West Coast for centuries.

subject: West Cork
summary: Three rocky peninsulas reach into the Atlantic, carrying stone circles, pirate harbours, and the last green edge of Ireland.

subject: West Cork Oil Spill
summary: In February 2009, a European satellite spotted oil where no oil should be off the south coast of Ireland - and a long awkward conversation began between Dublin, Moscow, and the crew of a Russian aircraft carrier that had not bothered to mention the spill.

subject: West Darfur
summary: Historically known as Dar Masalit - the Masalit homeland - West Darfur state sits on the Chadian border, and its capital Geneina has been the site of some of the worst ethnic violence of the 2023-present Sudanese civil war.

subject: West End Gasworks
summary: For more than a century a gasworks on a Brisbane River bend lit the city's southern suburbs - and the great cylindrical gasholder it left behind is the last of its kind in Queensland.

subject: West Highland Way
summary: Ninety-six miles from Glasgow's suburbs to the foot of Ben Nevis - Scotland's first long-distance path, treading drovers' trails and military roads through the wildest landscapes in Britain.

subject: West Kilbride
summary: An Ayrshire village turned Craft Town Scotland, looking across the Firth of Clyde to Arran, where a Celtic brooch surfaced from a drain in 1826 and a Neolithic stone still carries three carved spirals.

subject: West Kirby
summary: The Wirral seaside village where the tide retreats a mile twice a day, exposing a path of stepping-stone islands all the way to Hilbre.

subject: West Kowloon
summary: A vast district conjured from the harbour itself, West Kowloon transformed reclaimed seabed into one of Hong Kong's most ambitious urban canvases — skyscrapers, rail terminals, and a cultural district rising where ships once anchored.

subject: West Siberian Plain
summary: The world's largest unbroken flatland, stretching 2,500 kilometers from the Arctic Ocean to the Altai foothills, harboring vast swamps, eight vegetation zones, and the petroleum reserves that fuel modern Russia.

subject: West Sole Gas Field
summary: The first offshore gas field Britain ever produced - struck in 1965, flowing by 1967 - and the moment a coal nation began its hurried turn to North Sea gas.

subject: West Stow Anglo-Saxon Village
summary: On a sandy hillside in Suffolk, archaeologists uncovered a complete early Anglo-Saxon village — and then rebuilt it, creating one of Britain's most unusual open-air museums where the early medieval past is not just displayed but reconstructed.

subject: West Virginia
summary: The only American state lying entirely within a mountain range, born of a Civil War split from Virginia and shaped by coal, ramps, and pepperoni rolls - the Mountain State has the highest mean elevation in the East and the best-kept tourism secret in Appalachia.

subject: West Virginia Colored Children's Home
summary: For more than a century, this Huntington institution sheltered Black orphans and elders in a segregated state - and then, in 2011, it was demolished.

story.title: West Virginia Industrial Home for Boys

subject: West Virginia Industrial Home for Boys
summary: For 92 years near Grafton, West Virginia, a state institution held boys aged 12 to 20 sentenced for crimes ranging from felonies to 'incorrigibility' - language that meant whatever the courts wanted it to mean.

subject: West Virginia Italian Heritage Festival
summary: Every Labor Day weekend since 1979, downtown Clarksburg has hosted a three-day Italian-American street festival that draws more than 100,000 visitors - born when Joe DiMaggio rode in a parade through the streets of north-central West Virginia.

subject: West Virginia State Wildlife Center
summary: A 1923 state game farm in French Creek that became a wildlife sanctuary - now home to 29 species of West Virginia wildlife along a wooded mile-and-a-quarter trail, including the bison, elk, wolves, and cougars the state lost long ago.

subject: West Wales
summary: A region that meant Cornwall before it meant Wales, that no two organisations can agree on the boundaries of, and that everyone agrees is one of Britain's most beautiful corners.

subject: Westelijke Eilanden
summary: Three artificial islands at the western edge of Amsterdam's harbor, built from floating peat in the 1610s to store herring, tar, tobacco, and cat skins.

subject: Westerbork
summary: A quiet Drenthe village of 4,700 whose name became inseparable from one of the darkest chapters in Dutch history - a weight it now carries with a kind of stubborn ordinariness.

subject: Westerkwartier
summary: A thousand years before the Dutch had dikes, the people of this quiet corner of Groningen piled earth into mounds and lived on the high ground. Many of those mounds are still inhabited.

subject: Westermarsch I
summary: A polder village whose history was kept in a school chronicle started in 1622 - a four-hundred-year record of cattle plagues, broken dykes, and brickyards.

subject: Westermarsch II
summary: The mounds beneath these fields are a thousand years older than the village that sits on them - and today a North Sea spa rises on the same earth.

subject: Western Australia
summary: A state the size of a continent in itself, where three million people occupy the western third of Australia and most of the land remains untouched desert.

subject: Western Bahr el Ghazal
summary: A state at South Sudan's northwestern edge where the Sahel meets the equatorial rivers, and where the 19th-century slave trade cut a demographic wound that the land still shows.

subject: Western Cape Karoo
summary: A semi-desert valley between mountain ranges where ostrich feather millionaires built red-stone palaces, Khoisan heritage lingers in place names, and the only way in or out is through gorges cut by ancient rivers.

subject: Western Market
summary: Hong Kong's oldest surviving market building has been feeding and supplying the neighbourhood since September 1844 — a redbrick Edwardian survivor that outlasted demolition, MTR construction, and more than 180 years of a city reinventing itself around it.

subject: Western Netherlands
summary: The Randstad is a city in the shape of a ring, and the empty middle is the point.

subject: Western Nghệ An Biosphere Reserve
summary: Southeast Asia's largest biosphere reserve protects an animal that no one has photographed since 2013, and a community of a few hundred people whose language is nearly gone.

subject: Western North Carolina
summary: The mountain region of North Carolina holds 125 peaks above 5,000 feet, the tallest summits in eastern North America, and the cultural homeland of the Cherokee who never left.

subject: Western Papua New Guinea
summary: Two vast provinces where crocodile farming, birdwatching for Birds of Paradise, and the mighty Fly River define life in one of the most sparsely populated corners of the Pacific.

subject: Western Rocks, Isles of Scilly
summary: A granite archipelago that includes the most southerly point of the United Kingdom, has wrecked ships for centuries, and now shelters England's only colonies of European storm petrel.

subject: Western Zone, Tigray
summary: The fertile zone between the Tekezé River and the Sudanese border, now occupied by Amhara forces, was the site of one of the largest documented ethnic cleansing campaigns of the twenty-first century.

subject: Westerwolde
summary: A border region in the southeast corner of Groningen, defined for centuries by raised peat bogs that were political as much as geographic.

subject: Westfalenstadion
summary: Germany's biggest football ground packs 81,365 fans around a single yellow terrace of 24,454 standing supporters, the largest free-standing grandstand in European football.

subject: Westhoek
summary: The far corner of Flanders where Dutch dialect, French citizenship, and North Sea sand have spent twelve hundred years refusing to pick a side.

subject: Westmorland, California
summary: One of Imperial County's smallest cities, with a police department of six officers and a community shaped by desert agriculture and the earthquakes that periodically shake the valley floor.

subject: Weston, West Virginia
summary: A central West Virginia town of about 3,900, anchored by an enormous sandstone hospital that for 130 years held the state's mental patients - and now welcomes paying visitors to the largest hand-cut sandstone building in North America.

subject: Westover Plantation
summary: The Georgian masterpiece of the Byrd family on the James River, built by enslaved labor in the 1750s and later borrowed by Hollywood as the West Wing.

subject: Westport
summary: A planned Georgian town built in 1780 on the banks of the Carrowbeg River, where pilgrims still climb Croagh Patrick barefoot, traditional music spills out of pubs, and 141 drumlin islands wait offshore in Clew Bay.

subject: Westport, Washington
summary: A small fishing town on the Point Chehalis Peninsula, Westport operates the largest marina on the Pacific Northwest's outer coast and has become a national leader in tsunami preparedness.

subject: Westray Mine
summary: A methane explosion killed twenty-six miners in Plymouth, Nova Scotia in 1992, exposing catastrophic safety failures and ultimately changing Canadian law on corporate criminal liability.

subject: Westsylvania
summary: The fourteenth state that almost was - a 1776 proposal to carve a new commonwealth out of disputed territory west of the Alleghenies, suppressed by Pennsylvania with a treason statute that carried the death penalty.

subject: Wetlands International
summary: From a quiet office in the Dutch heartland, an NGO has spent ninety years counting birds and saving the world's water.

subject: Wetsinge
summary: A pair of Groningen villages where Groot - Big - actually means high, where people have lived continuously on the same earth mound since the third century BC, and where archaeologists once turned up a working oil lamp from the first century BC.

subject: Wetumpka crater
summary: Alabama's only confirmed impact crater, a 4.7-mile-wide scar from a catastrophic collision 83 million years ago that went unrecognized until a geologist noticed something odd in the hills.

subject: Weymouth
summary: A Dorset seaside town where King George III made bathing fashionable, midway along the Jurassic Coast, with the largest fancy-dress New Year's Eve in the country.

subject: Weymouth Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station that has been launching crews into the Channel since 1869, with a lifeboat too large to fit indoors and a date stone carved 1924.

story.title: Weymouth and Portland National Sailing Academy

subject: Weymouth and Portland National Sailing Academy
summary: Where Olympic medals are won and lost - a sailing centre built on a closed naval base, on what experts call some of the finest racing water in the world.

subject: Wezmeh
summary: An archaeological cave in western Iran where a single child's tooth proved that Neanderthals lived in the Zagros Mountains, and where a 9,000-year-old bone fragment revealed a previously unknown human genetic lineage.

subject: Whakapapa skifield
summary: New Zealand's oldest commercial skifield, perched on the slopes of an active volcano, where Edmund Hillary opened the country's first chairlift and skiers sometimes have to dodge volcanic eruptions.

subject: Whatcom Creek
summary: Four miles of falling water that founded Bellingham in 1854 and, on a June afternoon in 1999, became the site of one of the worst pipeline disasters in American history.

subject: Whatcom Trail
summary: In 1858 thousands of gold seekers walked north from Bellingham Bay in open defiance of a British governor; today their route crosses the border as a fence across a farm field.

subject: Wheal Busy
summary: A Cornish copper mine in "the richest square mile on Earth," where one of the first Newcomen engines in the county pumped water, and angry miners later tried to blow it up.

subject: Wheal Jane
summary: When the pumps were switched off at this Cornish tin mine in January 1992, the groundwater rose and turned the Carnon Valley a shocking orange.

subject: Wheal Martyn
summary: An entire Victorian china clay works frozen in place, where settling tanks, an 18-foot waterwheel, and a pan kiln tell the story of how Cornwall turned mud into porcelain.

subject: Wheal Trewavas
summary: Two ruined engine houses cling to the sea cliffs west of Porthleven where Cornish miners worked four copper lodes that ran out under the Atlantic.

subject: Wheal Vor
summary: On the Tregonning hill above Helston, an 18th-century Cornish mine drained its lodes with a coal-hungry Harvey engine and shipped out two million pounds' worth of tin before the water finally beat it.

subject: Where Batavia Governed
summary: Jakarta's Fatahillah Square has been a marketplace, a colonial seat of power, a tramway crossing, and a car-free tourist zone - four centuries of reinvention in a single urban rectangle.

story.title: Where Carlin Took His Last Bow

subject: Where Carlin Took His Last Bow
summary: A performing arts center on the northern edge of Santa Rosa, California, that rose from a bankrupt megachurch, survived the Tubbs Fire, and hosted George Carlin's final recorded performance.

story.title: Where Indonesia Comes to Argue with Its Past

subject: Where Indonesia Comes to Argue with Its Past
summary: Indonesia's founding president wanted a simple grave near Bogor Palace, but his successor buried him in a small East Java city instead -- turning a political slight into the country's most powerful pilgrimage site.

subject: Where Teak Meets Oil
summary: Straddling the Solo River in East Java, Bojonegoro has reinvented itself from a teak-and-tobacco backwater into Indonesia's newest oil frontier, while its Samin people still practice the quiet resistance their founder preached against Dutch colonists.

story.title: Where Three Hundred Thousand Wings Descend

subject: Where Three Hundred Thousand Wings Descend
summary: In the Sacramento Valley, 18,000 acres of wetland that no one can visit shelter one of the largest wintering waterfowl concentrations in North America -- a place that exists precisely because humans agreed to stay out.

story.title: Where Tigers Return and Addicts Heal

subject: Where Tigers Return and Addicts Heal
summary: A 45,000-hectare conservation area on the southern tip of Sumatra where rescued Sumatran tigers breed in the wild, former drug addicts rebuild their lives through forest restoration, and a complete food chain still functions in one of Indonesia's most threatened ecosystems.

subject: Where the Gods Were Smiling
summary: The Parahyangan highlands of West Java - the 'abode of the gods' - have been home to the Sundanese people since the Stone Age, shaped by ancient kingdoms, colonial coffee plantations, and a landscape so striking that legend says it was born from divine laughter.

story.title: Where the Hobbits Grew Small: The Fossils of Mata Menge

subject: Where the Hobbits Grew Small
summary: In the volcanic basin of central Flores, a site called Mata Menge holds the oldest known fossils of Homo floresiensis -- the tiny hominins nicknamed 'hobbits' -- pushing their origins back 700,000 years and rewriting the story of human evolution on an isolated Indonesian island.

subject: Where the Marquees Still Glow
summary: Uptown Oakland rose from parking lots and failed urban renewal schemes to become the East Bay's most vibrant entertainment district, its Art Deco theaters reborn as stages for a new generation.

subject: Where the Rescue Boats Waited
summary: A clapboard boathouse on the sheltered side of Point Reyes spent four decades launching rescue boats into the graveyard of ships that earned the headland its fearsome reputation, and still holds one of its original rescue craft on its launching rails.

story.title: Where the Sheep Rancher Planted Stars

subject: Where the Sheep Rancher Planted Stars
summary: A San Francisco insurance man bought a remote sheep ranch in Mendocino County's Coast Range in 1944 and spent fifty-six years healing its forests, streams, and meadows -- then gave it all to a university so the land could teach what he had learned.

subject: Where the Spice Routes Converged
summary: The Seram Sea, a rocky and tectonically restless body of water between Indonesia's former Spice Islands, was once the crossroads of a global trade network built on nutmeg, cloves, and the empires willing to kill for them.

subject: Where the Streets Are Rivers
summary: Built on a delta at the confluence of the Barito and Martapura rivers, Banjarmasin earned its nickname as the City of a Thousand Rivers -- a place where floating markets predate the sultanate, waterways serve as streets, and the proboscis monkey became an unlikely civic mascot.

subject: Whim Creek copper mine
summary: The Whim Creek copper mine has been worked off and on for 120 years in the Pilbara, powered at one point by diesel engines salvaged from World War One submarines, and troubled in recent years by pollution of the Balla Balla River.

subject: Whisky Galore! (1949 film)
summary: An Ealing Studios comedy based on the true wreck of the SS Politician, filmed on Barra in the Outer Hebrides, where islanders salvaged 50,000 cases of whisky from wartime rationing.

subject: Whisky a Go Go
summary: The legendary Sunset Strip club that invented go-go dancing, launched The Doors, and helped forge the sound of American rock from 1964 onward.

story.title: Whistler: The Olympic Village That Became World's Best

subject: Whistler
summary: The British Columbia resort that went from logging dump to world-class ski destination - where the 2010 Winter Olympics were held, where two mountains offer over 8,000 acres of terrain, and where the pedestrian village that seemed like marketing invention became model for mountain towns worldwide.

subject: Whistler
summary: North America's largest ski resort where Olympic dreams came true - a village built for powder seekers now draws adventurers year-round to its 8,000 acres of terrain.

subject: Whitburn Colliery
summary: A coal mine that drove its shafts out under the North Sea, Whitburn Colliery sustained a pit village for a century before water, geology and economics forced its closure - and the village itself was demolished after it.

subject: Whitburn, Tyne and Wear
summary: A two-row green village on a limestone slope above the North Sea, Whitburn has been a Saxon burial ground, a tithe-paying medieval estate, a fishing hamlet, a coal town and - according to local lore - the place where Lewis Carroll wrote about a Walrus and a Carpenter.

subject: Whitby
summary: The North Yorkshire port where Captain Cook learned to sail, Bram Stoker imagined Dracula's English landing, and goths gather twice a year to claim the streets.

subject: White Cliffs of Dover
summary: Eight miles of chalk, 350 feet high, built from the skeletons of microscopic algae that died one hundred million years ago - the cliffs are the reason Britain has the name Albion and the reason Dunkirk's evacuees wept when they saw them.

subject: White Cliffs, New South Wales
summary: An outback opal town where people live underground to beat the heat, one of cricket history's greatest leg-spinners was born, and a ring of mirrored dishes once made Australia's first commercial solar power.

subject: White Grass Dude Ranch
summary: Jackson Hole's longest-operating dude ranch transformed from a working cattle operation in 1919, survived through fox farming and family drama, and now trains the next generation in preserving Western rustic architecture.

subject: White Ladies Priory
summary: The ruined Augustinian nunnery near Boscobel where Charles II hid for a few terrified hours in September 1651 with the Penderell brothers, on the run after losing his throne.

subject: White Nile
summary: The pale-watered branch of the Nile that rises in Uganda's lakes, squeezes through a seven-metre gorge, and runs north to meet the Blue Nile at Khartoum.

subject: White Rock
summary: A granite boulder dropped by a glacier gave this Semiahmoo Bay beach town its name, its first navigation beacon, and its standing monthly appointment with a paint crew.

story.title: White Sands: The Gypsum Sea Where the Bomb Was Born

subject: White Sands
summary: The New Mexico dunefield of pure white gypsum - where the Trinity test ushered in the atomic age 60 miles north, where the sands are not sand at all, and where the world's largest gypsum desert creates landscapes that look like snow but burn your feet in summer.

subject: White Sands
summary: The gypsum sea in the desert - where 275 square miles of brilliant white dunes shift and undulate in the Tularosa Basin, created by a landlocked lake that evaporated and left behind the world's largest gypsum dune field.

subject: White Sands Missile Range
summary: The largest military installation in the United States, White Sands Missile Range witnessed humanity's first nuclear explosion at Trinity Site in 1945, launched captured German V-2 rockets that began America's space program, and once served as an emergency landing site for the Space Shuttle.

subject: Whitechapel
summary: An East End neighbourhood that has been the home of every wave of London's immigrants - Huguenot, Irish, Jewish, Bangladeshi - and the heart of the East End in popular imagination.

subject: Whitechapel Gallery
summary: A public gallery in the East End that brought Picasso's Guernica, Rothko, and Pop Art to British audiences who could not afford trips to Paris or New York.

subject: Whitechapel Road
summary: A Roman road that became a Jewish high street, a Bangladeshi market, and the cheapest property on the Monopoly board - and still the same artery into the East End it has been for two thousand years.

subject: Whitefish
summary: A railroad town turned mountain resort where the Empire Builder still stops daily and world-class skiing meets the gateway to Glacier National Park.

subject: Whitehaven
summary: A Cumbrian coal town built on Georgian symmetry and undersea pits, raided once by an American captain in 1778 and marked in 2010 by tragedy, Whitehaven has rebuilt itself again and again around the same stubborn harbour.

subject: Whitehaven Lifeboat Station
summary: From a 28-foot oared boat ordered in 1803 to its quiet closure in 1924, Whitehaven's lifeboat station saved 33 lives and lost one of its own to the Solway's contrary tides.

subject: Whitehills Lifeboat Station
summary: For 45 years a small RNLI station on the Moray Firth, born of a 1923 crewing crisis at Banff and Macduff, finally stood down in 1969.

subject: Whitehorse
summary: Whitehorse is the capital of the Yukon. It has spectacular scenery, and easy access to the natural splendor and recreational opportunities around it, such as paddling on the Yukon River and hiking,...

subject: Whitehorse Rapids
summary: The killer rapids that built a city - where Klondike stampeders faced death navigating the Yukon River's most dangerous stretch, prompting the creation of Whitehorse and the White Pass & Yukon Railway.

subject: Whitewater Preserve
summary: Year-round water in the Mojave Desert draws endangered birds, desert bighorn sheep, and mountain lions to a 2,200-acre canyon preserve where a former trout farm has become one of Southern California's most beloved wild places.

subject: Whonnock
summary: A hilly, half-forested community on the Fraser River that exists because a railway surveyor needed a station ten miles from the last one - and that carries, in its name, the one salmon that climbs its creek.

story.title: Wichita: The Air Capital Where Cessnas and Beechcrafts Are Born

subject: Wichita
summary: The Kansas city that builds more airplanes than anywhere in America - where the Chisholm Trail brought cattle, where the aviation industry concentrated, and where the flat prairie became runway for an industry.

subject: Wichita, Kansas
summary: Kansas's largest city earned its 'Air Capital of the World' title by producing an estimated 250,000 aircraft since 1916 -- but its story begins with Wichita Indians, cattle drives, and a poet who found America's vortex on Douglas Avenue.

subject: Wicken Fen
summary: One of Britain's oldest nature reserves and the first land cared for by the National Trust, Wicken Fen is a surviving fragment of the vast wetlands that once defined East Anglia — where sedge has been cut since 1414 and Charles Darwin collected beetles as a young man.

subject: Wicklow
summary: A Viking harbour town named in Old Norse, with a Gaelic name meaning 'church of the toothless one' - county town of Wicklow holds 5,000 years of layered history on Ireland's easternmost mainland point.

subject: Wicklow Gold Rush
summary: For exactly one month in 1795, a thousand Irish prospectors panned the Goldmines River for nuggets weighing several ounces apiece - until British soldiers marched up Croghan Kinsella and claimed the gold for King George III.

subject: Wicklow Mountains
summary: Ireland's largest continuous upland - granite, ice-cut valleys, the monastic city of Glendalough, and the Sally Gap at 498 metres, the country's highest road pass.

subject: Wicomico County, Maryland
summary: Maryland's last Eastern Shore county, carved out of two older ones in 1867, takes its name from an Algonquian phrase meaning 'a place where houses are built.'

subject: Widnes
summary: In 1888 a visiting journalist called Widnes the dirtiest, ugliest and most depressing town in England. The chemical industry built it and almost broke it. The story of how it climbed back out is unfinished.

subject: Wiegboldsbur
summary: A 13th-century law book set this small East Frisian village apart as a place of special protection, and the iron neck collar still bolted to the church wall remembers why.

subject: Wiesmoor
summary: A town built on a peat power plant whose waste heat fed Europe's largest greenhouse — and which then reinvented itself as a flower city with an air-spa designation.

subject: Wietmarschen
summary: A Catholic island in a Protestant district, where the town hall sits in one village and the name lives in another.

subject: Wigston
summary: A Leicestershire town named for a murdered Mercian prince, once known as Wigston Two Spires, where Graham Chapman of Monty Python lived above the police station and a framework knitting museum preserves an industry that defined the East Midlands.

subject: Wigtownshire
summary: The historic county that runs from the Mull of Galloway to the River Cree - 'the Shire' to its Stewartry neighbour, and home to a 4,500-year-old timber circle six times the size of Stonehenge.

subject: Wik-Ngathan language
summary: One of the many Wik languages of the western Cape York coast - a tongue carried by the Wik-Ngathan people, recorded by linguists, and still spoken in the community of Aurukun.

subject: Wilcannia
summary: On a bend of the Baaka, the great river port the paddle-steamers built remains the proud heart of Barkandji country.

subject: Wild Atlantic Way
summary: A 2,500-kilometre scenic touring brand launched in 2014, running from the Inishowen Peninsula in Donegal to Old Head of Kinsale in Cork along Ireland's fractal western coast.

subject: Wild Coast
summary: Three hundred kilometres of untamed Eastern Cape coastline where cliffs plunge into the Indian Ocean, Xhosa villages dot green hills, and the roads remain gloriously, stubbornly unpaved.

subject: Wildebeest Kuil Rock Art Centre
summary: Hundreds of rock engravings on an andesite hill outside Kimberley survived colonial removal, diamond-era disruption, and political upheaval to end up owned by the very San communities whose ancestors may have created them.

subject: Wilderness
summary: A Garden Route village where lakes, lagoons, and the Indian Ocean meet beneath the Outeniqua Mountains, and where an abandoned railway bridge became more famous than the train it carried.

subject: Wildeshausen
summary: A small Lower Saxon town on the Hunte that holds the relics of a Roman martyr, the last preserved urn-field in Europe, and a Pentecost festival running since 1403.

subject: Wildeshausen Geest
summary: A nature park on the sandy Ice Age ridge of northwest Germany, threaded by the Hunte and dotted with the largest concentration of megaliths in the country.

subject: Wildlife of Brazil
summary: Brazil holds the richest biodiversity of any country on Earth, from the heaviest spider to the largest river dolphin to the giant flightless rhea.

subject: Wildwood, New Jersey
summary: A Jersey Shore resort town where Doo-Wop motels glow in neon, rock and roll played its first chords, and a year-round population of 5,000 swells to a quarter million every summer.

subject: Wilgena Station
summary: A South Australian sheep run so vast it once claimed to be the largest fenced flock in the world, wrapped around a near-empty gold-rush town on the Trans-Australian line.

subject: Wilhelmshaven
summary: Built from scratch in 1869 to give Prussia a deep-water naval port, Wilhelmshaven is a city whose entire reason for existing is the sea.

subject: Willa Cather Birthplace
summary: A humble log farmhouse in Virginia's Back Creek Valley where Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Willa Cather was born in 1873 -- the place she left as a child but never stopped writing about.

subject: Willandra Lakes Region
summary: A chain of dry Pleistocene lakebeds in outback NSW that preserves more than 40,000 years of human life - including the world's largest set of ancient human footprints.

subject: Willem Janszoon
summary: The Dutch navigator who, in February 1606, became the first European known to have set foot on Australian soil -- and promptly turned back.

subject: Willemsoord, Den Helder
summary: Napoleon's biggest Dutch shipyard, two centuries later, has traded warships for movie theaters, wet docks for restaurants, and rigging lofts for the town hall.

subject: Willemstad
summary: A Caribbean capital built on Dutch trade and Atlantic slavery, where candy-colored colonial facades line a deepwater harbor that once refined more oil than anywhere on Earth.

subject: William Hillcourt
summary: The Danish-born writer who shaped a generation of American boys — Green Bar Bill spent sixty years teaching Scouts the difference between knowing the outdoors and just walking through it.

subject: William Smith O'Brien
summary: The unionist MP descended from Brian Boru who came home from revolutionary Paris with the first Irish tricolour, led a doomed 1848 rising, and was sentenced to be hanged, drawn, and quartered.

subject: Willow Garage
summary: A Menlo Park robotics lab founded by one of Google's earliest collaborators that created the Robot Operating System, spawned Zipline's drone delivery service, and proved that open-source hardware could accelerate an entire industry.

subject: Willow Glen, San Jose
summary: A former independent city that voted itself out of existence for the sake of functioning sewers, Willow Glen remains one of San Jose's most fiercely proud neighborhoods.

subject: Willow Tearooms
summary: At 217 Sauchiehall Street, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret MacDonald designed Catherine Cranston a tearoom in 1903 - down to the cutlery and the waitresses' uniforms - and called it the Willow.

subject: Willowwood Arboretum
summary: Two bachelor brothers spent fifty years turning a New Jersey farm into one of the most quietly extraordinary plant collections in the eastern United States.

subject: Wilma Dykeman RiverWay Plan
summary: A seventeen-mile greenway along the French Broad and Swannanoa rivers, named for the Appalachian writer whose 1955 book demanded clean water decades before it was popular.

story.title: Wilmington: Where Half of Corporate America Is Legally Headquartered

subject: Wilmington
summary: Delaware's largest city where business-friendly laws have incorporated more than half of Fortune 500 companies, where the du Pont family built a chemical empire and preserved their estates, and where Joe Biden commuted from for 36 years.

subject: Wilmslow
summary: Alan Turing's last home town, where a 2,000-year-old bog body and a generation of pop stars share a stretch of the River Bollin in Cheshire's Golden Triangle.

subject: Wilrijk
summary: They were called Goat Heads by the rich, so they took the insult and built a parade around it. A district of Antwerp where Celtic burials, Roman villas, V1 bombs, Atlas Copco compressors, and a folk giant named Lange Wapper share the same square kilometre.

subject: Wilson Bluff
summary: Where a dead-straight surveyor's line meets the Southern Ocean, the great limestone cliffs of the Nullarbor begin - and a 40-million-year-old seafloor stands on edge.

subject: Wilson Trail
summary: A 78-kilometre footpath threading the full length of Hong Kong from the southern tip of Hong Kong Island to the hills above the Chinese border, named after the penultimate colonial governor and passing through eight country parks on its way.

subject: Wilson, North Carolina
summary: A former tobacco capital where folk-art whirligigs now spin in the wind on the site of old auction warehouses.

subject: Wilton-Fijenoord
summary: For most of the twentieth century a Schiedam shipyard could build a cruiser, a tanker, and a submarine without breathing hard. Then Asian and Eastern European yards learned to do the same work for less, and a seventy-year-old industry quietly ended.

subject: Wiluna, Western Australia
summary: At the edge of the Western Desert, a gold boomtown that swelled to 9,000 and nearly vanished - and the Martu country it sits on, to which the last desert nomads walked home to die among their people.

subject: Wilyakali
summary: The Wilyakali are the Aboriginal people of the Barrier Ranges around Broken Hill, whose connection to this silver country was affirmed by an Australian court in 2023.

subject: Wimbledon Championships
summary: The oldest tennis tournament in the world, played on grass since 1877, where strawberries and cream cost more than the inaugural prize money.

subject: Wind Power in the Netherlands
summary: The country that once drained itself with windmills is trying, four centuries later, to power itself with the same wind, and one of its newest turbines makes more electricity by itself than fifty older ones combined.

subject: Windermere
summary: England's largest lake by length, area, and volume - a long, narrow ribbon of glacial water that has carried steam launches, Romantic poets, water-speed records, refugee children, and ongoing fights over its water quality.

subject: Windhoek
summary: Namibia's highland capital sits at 1,600 meters in the geographic center of the country, where German colonial architecture, African township culture, and the ambitions of a young nation converge under an enormous desert sky.

subject: Windmills in Berlin
summary: Around 1860 some 150 windmills turned on the hills around Berlin. Eight survive inside the city, including one that a film crew burned down in 1921 and volunteers replaced 87 years later.

subject: Windmills in Leeuwarden
summary: The Frisian capital once had at least 130 windmills grinding gunpowder, snuff, chicory, paint, dye, and bark — and pumping vast tracts of polder dry. Today exactly one survives inside the city: the Froskepôlemolen on its small island.

subject: Windorah Solar Farm
summary: Five mirrored dishes once tracked the outback sun above Windorah, a town of roughly a hundred people that had run on diesel alone.

subject: Windover Archeological Site
summary: A Florida pond where a backhoe operator uncovered 168 skeletons with 7,000-year-old preserved brain tissue, rewriting the story of ancient North America.

subject: Windows Refund Day
summary: A 1999 protest where Linux users marched on Microsoft's Foster City office demanding refunds for unwanted Windows licenses, only to find the elevator to the 9th floor had been disabled.

subject: Windpark Noordoostpolder
summary: Eighty-six turbines along a dyke in the IJsselmeer - the largest wind farm in the Netherlands when it opened in 2017, generating enough power for every household in two provinces.

subject: Windscale Piles
summary: The two air-cooled graphite reactors that produced Britain's first atomic bomb material - and whose fatal design choices led, seven years later, to the Windscale fire.

subject: Windy Hill Open Space Preserve
summary: The only bare hilltop on the Peninsula Range -- visible from across the South Bay -- where paragliders launch in winter east winds and the views stretch from San Francisco to Mount Diablo.

subject: Winestead Drain
summary: A slow Holderness river that was once a sea-going waterway, lost its navigation to silt and sluice gates, and now ends in a pumping station that failed during the 2007 floods.

subject: Wing Hing Long & Co. Store
summary: A Chinese-owned general store in the tin-mining town of Tingha survived more than a century, still filled with its counters, ledgers and a working cash-on-a-pulley system - a rare intact monument to the Chinese-Australians who built the New England tin fields.

subject: Wingletang Down
summary: A wind-pruned heath on the southern tip of St Agnes where 43 Bronze Age cairns, a saint's well, the beach where pilgrims still find Venetian beads, and the only British colony of a two-centimetre fern all share a single granite headland.

story.title: Wings Mended: The California Raptor Center

subject: Wings Mended
summary: At the California Raptor Center on the UC Davis campus, injured hawks, owls, and eagles are rehabilitated and released, while non-releasable ambassador birds teach thousands of visitors each week about the lives of raptors.

subject: Winkel van Sinkel
summary: On 9 September 1837, a cast-iron statue being lifted off a barge in central Utrecht broke the city's medieval crane and toppled into the canal. That statue, and three sisters, would soon hold up the facade of the first department store in the Netherlands.

subject: Winnipeg general strike
summary: In the spring of 1919, more than 30,000 workers walked off their jobs in Winnipeg, Manitoba, paralyzing Canada's third-largest city for six weeks in a struggle over collective bargaining that ended in gunfire, mass arrests, and a political legacy that reshaped Canadian democracy.

subject: Winschoten
summary: Of the 493 Jews who lived here when the war began, twenty came home — and the dialect they helped shape still carries Yiddish words on plate lickers' tongues.

subject: Winsor McCay
summary: The visionary cartoonist and animator whose comic strip Little Nemo and animated film Gertie the Dinosaur revolutionized visual storytelling from his Brooklyn home.

subject: Winston-Salem, North Carolina
summary: A North Carolina city of nearly 250,000 built where a Moravian congregation called Salem met a Reconstruction-era tobacco town called Winston.

subject: Winterswijk
summary: A Dutch market town on the German border where Piet Mondriaan grew up, the textile mills built the railways, and the bedrock holds 240 million years of geological history.

subject: Wisbech
summary: Called the Capital of the Fens, Wisbech is a market town on the tidal River Nene whose Georgian architecture, abolitionist heritage, and position at Cambridgeshire's only sea gateway have shaped a town of unusual depth for its size.

subject: Wise County, Virginia
summary: A Virginia coal county that produced George C. Scott, Napoleon Hill, and Ralph Stanley - and holds two of the commonwealth's highest-security prisons.

subject: Wishaw
summary: A Victorian iron-and-coal town in North Lanarkshire that grew out of the Roman road, lost its industry in the late twentieth century, and is now finding what comes next.

subject: Wismar
summary: A brick-Gothic Baltic port that Sweden pawned to Mecklenburg in 1803 and did not finish owning until 1903 - and that played the plague town of Wisborg in the first vampire film.

subject: Wistman's Wood
summary: A 3.5-hectare temperate rainforest of stunted, lichen-cloaked oaks high on Dartmoor - one of Britain's last fragments of its kind, and the haunt of the Wisht Hounds of Devon legend.

subject: Withernsea Lifeboat Station
summary: A coast averaging eight wrecks a year forced the RNLI to plant a lifeboat at Withernsea in 1862, and the town has been hauling people from the North Sea ever since.

subject: Wittemoor Timber Trackway
summary: Tree rings date this Iron Age log road across a Lower Saxon bog to 135 BCE, and the two faceless wooden figures who guarded its stream crossing are among the rarest survivals in northern Europe.

subject: Wittenberg
summary: An Elbe town of printers, painters and professors where a university argument became a continental rupture - and where a medieval slur still sits on the church wall.

subject: Wittmund
summary: A small East Frisian capital where Frisian chieftains, Prussian administrators, and Eurofighter pilots have all left their fingerprints.

subject: Wittmund (district)
summary: A North Sea district whose coat of arms tells a bear legend, and whose 1977 merger lasted just long enough to be ruled unconstitutional.

subject: Witwatersrand
summary: A modest ridge of white-water quartzite hides the richest gold deposit Earth has ever yielded - and it built a city, a currency, and a country's fortunes.

subject: Witwatersrand Gold Rush
summary: The 1886 Witwatersrand Gold Rush created Johannesburg from nothing, drew fortune-seekers from California to Australia, and set in motion the political conflicts that would shape South Africa for the next century.

subject: Wolf Creek ski area
summary: Born from a farmer's rope tow and an old Chevy truck in 1938, Wolf Creek Ski Area quietly became Colorado's snowfall champion, burying its runs under an average of 430 inches every winter.

subject: Wolf Plains Earthworks
summary: A late Adena complex of 30 mounds and circular enclosures on a glacial terrace north of Athens, Ohio - one of the densest concentrations of Adena earthworks anywhere.

subject: Wolfe Creek Crater
summary: The second-best-preserved meteorite impact crater on Earth sits in the Great Sandy Desert, where the Djaru people have long known it as Kandimalal -- the place where the evening star fell.

subject: Wollo Province
summary: The medieval heart of Ethiopia, where Solomonic emperors built rock-hewn churches and where twentieth-century famines killed hundreds of thousands while governments denied they were happening.

subject: Wollogorang Station
summary: A 7,000-square-kilometre cattle run straddling the NT-Queensland border - the Territory's oldest continuously settled station, and a place that has seen its share of trouble.

subject: Wollongong
summary: Australia's steel city, pinned on a narrow shelf between a rainforest escarpment and the Pacific, where a road runs out over the sea itself.

subject: Wolverhampton
summary: A West Midlands city of locks and aerospace, Molineux roars and Northern Soul nights, where Black Country grit meets a surprisingly bold cultural pulse.

subject: Woman Suffrage Procession
summary: On March 3, 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson's inauguration, thousands of women marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in the first large organized political demonstration in Washington, D.C., igniting the final push for the Nineteenth Amendment.

subject: Wong Chuk Kok Tsui (Bluff Head)
summary: The remotest point of Hong Kong's northeastern New Territories, Wong Chuk Kok Tsui — once called Bluff Head by British navigators — is a wild cape that guards the threshold between Tolo Channel and Mirs Bay, and holds some of the oldest rocks in the territory.

subject: Wong Tai Sin District
summary: The only landlocked district in Hong Kong, Wong Tai Sin is a dense Kowloon neighbourhood where public housing towers surround one of the city's most beloved temples, and where an aging but tightly knit community carries the weight of a rapidly changing city.

subject: Woo Bum-kon incident
summary: On a spring night in 1982, a disgraced police officer moved through the rural villages of Uiryeong County, South Korea, killing 56 people before taking his own life.

subject: Woodbine, New Jersey
summary: A tiny Cape May County borough founded in 1891 as a Jewish agricultural colony, Woodbine became a model farming community, a WWII anti-submarine base, and the birthplace of the birth control pill's co-inventor.

subject: Woodford Folk Festival
summary: Every New Year, a regenerated dairy farm north of Brisbane becomes a temporary city of more than a hundred thousand people, ending in a hillside spectacle of fire that burns the old year away.

subject: Woodlands (New Westminster)
summary: For 118 years British Columbia sent its children with disabilities to an institution above the Fraser River; when the last of it came down in 2011, the people who had lived inside were the ones who wanted it gone.

subject: Woodleigh Impact Structure
summary: Beneath a quiet sheep station east of Shark Bay lies the buried scar of one of the largest asteroid impacts ever found in Australia, a crater no one can see from the surface and no one knew was there until a drill bit and a gravity meter gave it away.

subject: Woodrow Wilson Boyhood Home
summary: A brick manse in Augusta, Georgia, where a four-year-old boy heard that Lincoln was elected and there would be war -- the first memory of the child who would become the 28th president.

story.title: Woodstock: Three Days That Became a Generation

subject: Woodstock
summary: The 1969 music festival on Max Yasgur's dairy farm in Bethel, New York drew over 460,000 people, became a free concert by accident, and defined the counterculture of the 1960s.

subject: Woodward's 43
summary: Vancouver imploded a beloved department store and built, on the same block, an argument about who a city is for - with a neon W put back on top.

subject: Wookey Hole
summary: A Somerset village named after its caves, where a Grade II paper mill, a Victorian country house by the architects of Sandringham's stables, and a controversial crazy golf course all crowd together on the slope below the Mendip Hills.

subject: Wookey Hole Caves
summary: A limestone cave system in the Mendip Hills with 25 explored chambers, a stalagmite known as the Witch of Wookey Hole, and a history of British cave diving that began with a homemade respirator in 1935.

subject: Wooleen Station
summary: On a vast, drought-worn pastoral lease in the Murchison outback, two young people made a radical bet: that the way to save degraded land was to take the livestock off it and let the country, and even the dingoes, heal themselves.

subject: Woolgoolga, New South Wales
summary: On a banana-growing stretch of the Coffs Coast, a Punjabi-Sikh community built Australia's first Sikh temple and turned a quiet beach town into a place where bhangra and surf carnivals share the same calendar.

subject: Woolpit
summary: A Suffolk village whose name means pit for trapping wolves, where in the 12th century two children with green skin reportedly emerged from a field, speaking a language no one knew.

subject: Woolsthorpe-by-Colsterworth
summary: A small Lincolnshire hamlet where a young man went home to wait out the plague and quietly invented modern physics.

subject: Woolwich
summary: A small Kentish town that Henry VIII turned into an arsenal, that built the ships, the cannons, and the world's most famous football club, and that is now rediscovering itself after a long decline.

subject: Woomera Prohibited Area
summary: The largest land-based weapons range on Earth, a slab of South Australian desert the size of a country, where rockets reached for space, atomic bombs were tested, and Aboriginal people were pushed off their homelands.

story.title: Worcester: The Second City That Nobody Visits

subject: Worcester
summary: The Massachusetts city in Boston's shadow - where the diners invented American diner culture, where colleges cluster improbably, and where the Heart of the Commonwealth beats quietly.

subject: Worcester (Western Cape)
summary: Ringed by mountains that steal its rain and trap its heat, Worcester thrives as the commercial heart of the Western Cape's interior -- a place where winelands, cycling trails, and spectacular mountain passes converge in a curious rain shadow.

subject: Worcester County, Maryland
summary: Maryland's easternmost county runs from cypress swamp to Atlantic surf, holds the state's only ocean coast, and was once home to the highest proportion of free Black residents in the state.

subject: Workington
summary: Built on phosphorus-free haematite and Bessemer steel, Workington made rails that 'held the world together' — and when coal and steel left, the West Cumbrian port became one of Britain's most famous unemployment blackspots, then a stubbornly improvisational town that keeps remaking itself.

subject: Workington Lifeboat Station
summary: Born out of a single grim morning in 1885 when the schooner Margaret broke up off Mossbay Point, Workington's lifeboat station has run continuously since 1948 and finally received its first brand-new boat in 131 years in 2017.

subject: Worksop
summary: A north-Nottinghamshire market town known as the Gateway to the Dukeries, with an Anglo-Saxon name, a Norman priory still in use, and a long-time identity shaped by coal, malting, timber, and the four great ducal estates that ring its edges.

subject: World Chess Championship 1908
summary: The two best chess players in Germany finally faced each other in Düsseldorf and Munich after sixteen years of avoidance - and the older man blamed his loss on the seaside air.

subject: World Expo 88
summary: For six months in 1988, a derelict stretch of Brisbane riverbank threw a party so good the city refused to let it end.

subject: World's Columbian Exposition
summary: The 1893 Chicago World's Fair that introduced the Ferris wheel, won the war between AC and DC electricity, launched the City Beautiful movement, and drew 27 million visitors to a gleaming white fantasy city that vanished in six months.

subject: World's Largest Ball of Twine
summary: A twenty-thousand-pound sphere of sisal sitting in a gazebo on the main street of Cawker City, Kansas - started by one farmer in 1953, kept growing by his whole town for half a century after he died.

subject: World's Largest Frying Pan
summary: A 1,300-pound, 10-foot-wide frying pan that isn't actually the world's largest -- but is the only giant frying pan that has ever been used to cook food.

subject: World's Largest Gold Pan
summary: The 20-foot gold pan in Burwash Landing, Yukon - built to commemorate the Klondike Gold Rush and located at the site where a gold nugget found in 1903 started one of Canada's last gold stampedes.

subject: Worpswede
summary: A peat-bog village northeast of Bremen where a destitute art student's holiday invitation grew into Germany's most consequential artists' colony.

subject: Worshipful Society of Apothecaries
summary: The London livery company that founded the Chelsea Physic Garden, qualified Britain's first woman doctor, and trained Agatha Christie in poisons before she became a writer.

subject: Worsley
summary: The village where the Industrial Revolution's first canal began, with bright-orange water at Worsley Delph and an underground waterway running deep into the abandoned coal mines.

subject: Wreck Alley
summary: A few miles off Mission Beach, San Diego's Wreck Alley is an underwater graveyard of ships placed here on purpose — a Coast Guard cutter designed to enforce Prohibition, a Canadian destroyer that sank the night before its scheduled scuttling, and a kelp harvester that traveled 800,000 miles before becoming a reef.

subject: Wreck Reefs
summary: A remote chain of Coral Sea reefs named for the night in 1803 when two ships carrying Matthew Flinders broke apart on coral nobody had charted.

subject: Wreck of the Grosvenor
summary: In 1782, the East Indiaman Grosvenor ran aground on the Pondoland coast of South Africa, stranding 150 people in a wilderness hundreds of miles from the nearest European settlement -- a disaster whose survivors, salvagers, and mysteries shaped the region for centuries.

subject: Wreck of the Old 97
summary: A 1903 train derailment near Danville, Virginia, that killed 11 people and inspired one of America's most famous railroad ballads, shaping the birth of country music.

subject: Wrexham
summary: A north-east Welsh city of coal, lager, and football - granted city status in 2022, transformed by Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney's takeover of the football club, and home to the world's oldest international stadium.

subject: Wrightville
summary: A copper-and-gold town of 2,000 that built its own council to rival Cobar, then vanished so completely that a bulldozer finished what the droughts began.

subject: Wroxham
summary: The self-styled Capital of the Broads, where the Edwardian invention of the British boating holiday began.

subject: Wrynose Pass
summary: A single-track road climbs to 1,289 feet over a ridge where Romans marched and three historic counties meet at one stone.

subject: Wu Family Shrines
summary: A second-century Han dynasty funerary complex in Shandong whose stone relief carvings depict Chinese mythology, history, and daily life with a richness that has captivated scholars for nearly two millennia.

subject: Wujal Wujal Aboriginal Shire
