summary: Wujal Wujal — 'many falls' — is a living Kuku Yalanji community beside a sacred waterfall on the Bloomfield River, a place that has carried its people through a mission, a renaming, and the floodwaters of Cyclone Jasper.

subject: Wulai
summary: A mountain town south of Taipei where the Atayal word for 'hot and poisonous' became a name, and the hot springs, waterfalls, and indigenous cuisine became reasons to visit.

subject: Wulai District
summary: The Atayal homeland of Wulai — Ulay in their own language — is New Taipei's largest and most mountainous district, where deep gorges, a thundering waterfall, and enduring indigenous culture define a place that has always belonged to its people first.

subject: Wun Yiu Village
summary: Tucked into the hills above Tai Po, Wun Yiu Village spent five centuries as the New Territories' only significant porcelain-making centre — its kilns declared monuments, its patron-saint temple a surviving testament to Hakka potters who shaped clay into trade.

subject: Wuppertal
summary: In 1950 a young elephant named Tuffi jumped out of Wuppertal's suspended monorail into the river - and somehow survived. It is the second most Wuppertal thing that has ever happened.

subject: Wupperthal
summary: A small Moravian mission village tucked into the Cederberg mountains, known for handmade leather shoes and rooibos tea, still rebuilding after a devastating 2018 fire.

subject: Wurrwurrwuy stone arrangements
summary: On a rocky shelf near Yirrkala, Yolngu people laid out stones to map the ships of their Makassan trading partners - a remarkable Aboriginal historical record, complete down to a vessel's galley and water tank.

subject: Wyandra
summary: A near-empty railway town on the Warrego River, born of steam engines and water tanks, now a quiet outback waypoint of fewer than eighty people between Cunnamulla and Charleville.

subject: Wycliffe Well
summary: A tiny roadhouse on the Stuart Highway that has declared itself Australia's UFO capital, where alien kitsch, 300 beer labels, and some of the clearest night skies on Earth converge in the red dust of the Outback.

subject: Wylam
summary: A small Tyne Valley village that, between 1781 and 1813, produced more of the engineers who invented the railway than any other place on earth.

subject: Wyndham (Western Australia)
summary: The most northerly town on the Western Australian coast — 3,000 kilometres from Perth but only half that from Bali — Wyndham sits at the confluence of five crocodile-infested rivers, sustained by cattle, a port, and the kind of stubborn survival that defines the Kimberley.

subject: Wynwood
summary: A former garment district turned Puerto Rican barrio turned global street art destination, Wynwood's warehouse walls tell the story of Miami's most dramatic neighborhood reinvention.

subject: Wytgaard
summary: A 570-person Catholic village in firmly Protestant Friesland, founded as a hamlet in the seventeenth century, recognized as independent only in 1957 — and still arguing forty years later about whether to spell its own name with an 'i' or a 'y'.

subject: Wytheville, Virginia
summary: A southwestern Virginia town named for the founding father who taught Jefferson the law, birthplace of First Lady Edith Bolling Wilson, and the crossroads where I-77 and I-81 run the same pavement in opposite directions.

subject: Wâlterswâld
summary: A Frisian village that started as a mound called Walthiem, slid south into the peat to mine fuel, and in 2009 quietly took back its old West Frisian name.

subject: Wüste
summary: An Osnabrück district whose name means 'wasteland' - and whose residents joke about wanting quiet apartments in the desert.

subject: Xanadu (Calp)
summary: A dark green cliffside tower near Calpe named for Kublai Khan's pleasure-city, Ricardo Bofill's buildable fragment of a 1960s dream of modular, plug-in architecture.

subject: Xerxes' pontoon bridges
summary: In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes lashed hundreds of warships together across the Hellespont and marched an army into Europe — and into one of antiquity's most famous stories.

subject: Xiadu
summary: The Lower Capital of the ancient state of Yan may have been the largest city on Earth from 400 to 300 BC, a 30 km2 fortress flanked by rivers in the Taihang Mountains whose walls still stand nearly seven meters high.

subject: Xiancantan
summary: Tucked inside Beihai Park, this eighteenth-century altar honors Leizu, the legendary wife of the Yellow Emperor who is credited with teaching humanity the art of silk production.

subject: Xiangtangshan Caves
summary: Thirty-six Buddhist cave temples carved into the limestone cliffs of the Taihang Mountains bear witness to the brief but artistically brilliant Northern Qi dynasty of sixth-century China.

subject: Xiao Qingdao
summary: A tiny island in Qingdao's harbor that gave the city its name and has been renamed by every power that controlled it.

subject: Xiaochangliang
summary: A Paleolithic site in the Nihewan Basin where stone tools dated to 1.36 million years ago rewrite the timeline of human habitation in East Asia, first hinted at by a single flint tool that even its discoverer doubted.

subject: Xiaoshuangqiao
summary: A Bronze Age city on the Suoxu River northwest of Zhengzhou may be the lost Shang capital of Ao -- its sacrificial pits, palace foundations, and mysterious cinnabar-painted symbols bridge the gap between two of China's most important archaeological periods.

subject: Xibaipo
summary: A small village in Hebei Province where Mao Zedong and the Communist Party leadership directed the decisive battles of the Chinese Civil War, Xibaipo is remembered as the place where 'New China came from.'

subject: Xidan
summary: This ancient commercial district in western Beijing is named for a single ornamental archway, houses Beijing's widest hutong, and was once home to the Democracy Wall that launched the Beijing Spring of 1978.

subject: Xidayang Reservoir
summary: A Great Leap Forward-era reservoir in Hebei's Taihang foothills, now linked by canal to its sister reservoir and critical to sustaining northern China's largest freshwater lake.

subject: Ximending
summary: Taipei's oldest entertainment district reinvented itself from a fading theater row into Taiwan's largest pedestrian zone, drawing three million shoppers a month.

subject: Xingang, Chiayi
summary: Xingang Township in Chiayi County is a small town punching far above its size — home to the Fengtian Temple, one of Taiwan's most important Mazu shrines, and the birthplace of the choreographer Lin Hwai-min, whose Cloud Gate Dance Theatre changed what Asian contemporary dance could be.

subject: Xinghai Square
summary: The world's largest city square, built entirely on reclaimed land to mark Dalian's centennial, whose demolished central monument tells a political story the city cannot discuss.

subject: Xinglonggou
summary: Three archaeological sites on a single loess slope in Inner Mongolia trace five thousand years of human development, from the earliest directly dated millet in the archaeological record to Bronze Age farming villages.

subject: Xinglongwa culture
summary: One of China's earliest planned communities, the 8,200-year-old Xinglongwa culture featured row houses, central public buildings, and the country's oldest known defensive ditch, along with jade burial goods and bone flutes.

subject: Xinhua Old Street
summary: A beautifully preserved stretch of Baroque colonial architecture in Tainan's Xinhua District, built in the 1920s and 1930s when the street hummed with the wholesale fruit trade.

subject: Xinhui, Jiangmen
summary: Xinhui is a district of Jiangmen where more than 600,000 people have emigrated over two centuries, where the land itself was built by river silt over nine hundred years, and where the world-renowned dried mandarin orange peel called chenpi has been produced for hundreds of years.

subject: Xinle culture
summary: A 7,500-year-old Neolithic settlement discovered beneath an electrical factory dormitory in Shenyang, the Xinle culture preserves some of the oldest wooden carvings found anywhere in the world.

subject: Xiong'an
summary: China's boldest urban experiment: a city being built from scratch 100 km south of Beijing, designed around 15-minute walkable neighborhoods, wetland restoration, and high-speed rail, with a target population of 5 million by mid-century.

subject: Xishuipo
summary: A Neolithic burial site in Henan where a 6,000-year-old clam-shell mosaic of a dragon flanking a human burial may be the earliest depiction of the Chinese dragon.

subject: Xitou Nature Education Area
summary: A misty mountain forest in Nantou County where ancient trees, bamboo groves, and a high canopy skywalk reveal 2,500 hectares of cool, cloud-shrouded wilderness managed by National Taiwan University.

subject: Xizhimen
summary: Once the gate through which the emperor's drinking water entered Beijing from the Jade Spring Hills, Xizhimen lost its ancient walls in 1969 and reinvented itself as one of the city's busiest transportation hubs.

subject: Xochimilco
summary: The last surviving fragment of the Aztec canal system, Xochimilco's floating gardens and colorful trajinera boats preserve a pre-Columbian landscape within one of the world's largest cities.

story.title: Xochistlahuaca: The Plain of Flowers Where Amuzgo Women Weave the World

subject: Xochistlahuaca
summary: A remote town in Guerrero's mountainous southeast where the Amuzgo people have preserved their language, their traditions, and an extraordinary textile art - hand-woven huipils on backstrap looms, each piece unique, passed from grandmother to granddaughter across centuries.

subject: Xujiayao
summary: A Late Pleistocene site in the Nihewan Basin where fossils of an enigmatic hominin species -- now designated Homo juluensis, the 'Big-headed Human' -- challenge simple narratives of human evolution in East Asia.

subject: Xàbia
summary: A Costa Blanca town where a teardown as easily reveals a Bronze Age farm as a foundation, layering thirty thousand years of history beneath its streets and the shadow of Montgó.

subject: Xàtiva
summary: A Valencian city that has kept its pre-Roman name for millennia, introduced paper to Europe, cradled the Borgias, and still hangs a king's portrait upside down in revenge.

subject: X̱wáýx̱way
summary: The road around Stanley Park was surfaced with the midden of the village it replaced — X̱wáýx̱way, a Coast Salish settlement occupied for more than three thousand years.

subject: YFZ Ranch
summary: A secretive FLDS compound in rural Texas Hill Country that became the site of one of the largest child custody operations in American history.

subject: Yaanga
summary: The largest Tongva village in the Los Angeles basin, home to thousands before Spanish colonization, now buried beneath Union Station.

subject: Yacouba Sawadogo
summary: His neighbors called him a madman for planting trees in dying soil. Decades later, the world called him the man who stopped the desert.

subject: Yaguarón
summary: A plain whitewashed church in a small Paraguayan town hides one of the New World's great surprises: a blazing gold interior carved by Guaraní hands, the masterpiece of Franciscan Barroco-Guaraní.

subject: Yalleroi
summary: A near-vanished locality on the road between Blackall and Jericho, Yalleroi carries an Iningai name meaning 'stony' - and a survey-plan grid for a town that never quite came.

subject: Yam O
summary: A quiet bay on Lantau Island's northeast shore, Yam O once held Hong Kong's only natural timber preservation zone and later became the contested ground where a Disney deal reshaped the map — and renamed the darkness into sunshine.

subject: Yamagata International Documentary Film Festival
summary: A biennial film festival in the mountains of northern Japan that became Asia's most distinguished showcase for documentary cinema, born from the vision of a single filmmaker who died before its third edition.

subject: Yamalia
summary: Russia's northernmost Urals region, where Nenets reindeer herders, Tatar khans' legacy, and Gazprom's gas empire share the frozen Yamal Peninsula along the Arctic Ocean coast.

subject: Yamato Colony
summary: A Japanese immigrant newspaper editor bought 3,200 acres of California farmland and sold it in 40-acre plots to families who turned wind-scoured dirt into one of the Central Valley's most resilient agricultural communities.

story.title: The Ship That Sailed on Magnets

subject: Yamato-1
summary: In June 1992, a 30-meter vessel glided silently through Kobe harbor with no propeller, no jet, and no moving parts in its drive system -- the Yamato-1, the world's first crewed ship propelled by magnetohydrodynamic force, pushing seawater backward using superconducting magnets cooled to near absolute zero.

subject: Yamba, New South Wales
summary: Matthew Flinders sailed past it as worthless; today the headland he dismissed crowns one of the most loved seaside towns in Australia.

subject: Yamen, Guangdong
summary: A quiet coastal town in Xinhui District where the waters of the South China Sea swallowed the last emperor of the Song dynasty in 1279.

subject: Yancey County, North Carolina
summary: A 313-square-mile pocket of the Black Mountains holds Mount Mitchell, five of the ten highest peaks east of the Mississippi, and a county still reckoning with what Hurricane Helene did in September 2024.

subject: Yangbajain Geothermal Field
summary: At over 4,000 meters on the Tibetan Plateau, the largest proven geothermal field in China sends steam columns skyward, powers Lhasa's electrical grid, and heats hot springs that tourists soak in while gazing at the Nyainqentanglha Mountains.

subject: Yangliuqing
summary: A market town on Tianjin's western edge that has specialized for over 400 years in creating nianhua -- vivid woodblock New Year prints depicting children's games and auspicious symbols -- earning it designation as one of China's famous historical and cultural towns.

subject: Yangmingshan
summary: A volcanic national park perched above Taipei — where cherry blossoms share the hillsides with fumaroles, rare aquatic ferns, and the summer residences of presidents — certified in 2020 as the world's first Urban Quiet Park.

subject: Yangon
summary: Where the Shwedagon Pagoda has gleamed gold for 2,500 years, where British colonial architecture decays in tropical humidity, where Myanmar's largest city struggles between military rule and democratic dreams.

subject: Yanshuei District
summary: Once one of Taiwan's five most important maritime towns, Yanshuei is now known for the Beehive Fireworks Festival — a lunar new year tradition born from a cholera epidemic, in which thousands of bottle rockets are fired into a crowd that considers being struck a sign of good luck.

subject: Yaoundé
summary: Cameroon's hilltop capital started as a German ivory trading post in 1889 and grew into a sprawling, francophone city of over three million where street names barely exist and yellow taxis set the rhythm of daily life.

subject: Yapeyú, Corrientes
summary: A small Guaraní mission town on the Uruguay River, birthplace of José de San Martín, the Liberator of half a continent.

subject: Yapunyah waterhole
summary: A rare permanent waterhole in the mulga country of western Queensland, sheltering an endemic turtle and serving as a refuge in one of Earth's most variable river systems.

subject: Yaraka
summary: A speck of a town at the dead end of a vanished railway, where two badly behaved emus once got banned from the pub and made the world pay attention.

subject: Yarchen Gar
summary: Once home to 10,000 Buddhist nuns and monks at 4,000 meters in a remote Kham valley, Yarchen Gar became a target of systematic demolition by Chinese authorities, its residents forced into re-education centers.

subject: Yarloop Workshops
summary: A heritage railway workshop in rural Western Australia that hand-built machinery for 26 timber mills, manufactured wartime armaments, and survived cyclone and bushfire before beginning its resurrection.

subject: Yarluyandi
summary: The Yarluyandi are a living Aboriginal people of the lower Diamantina and western Simpson country, whose ancestors survived the desert by the hand-dug wells called mikiri and whose native title was recognised in 2014.

subject: Yarm
summary: A market town on a meander of the River Tees where the Stockton and Darlington Railway was conceived in a coaching inn, with a Viking helmet and Britain's voted-best high street.

subject: Yarrabubba
summary: A working cattle station in the Western Australian outback that lent its name to one of the oldest known meteorite impacts on Earth - a 2.229-billion-year-old scar whose title is now contested, and which may have helped thaw a frozen world.

subject: Yarrow, British Columbia
summary: A village built on the drained floor of Sumas Lake by Mennonite refugees from the Soviet Union - and a reminder, in November 2021, that the lake never really agreed to leave.

subject: Yasothon
summary: Yasothon is a quiet Isaan province in northeastern Thailand where ancient Khmer ruins, a stupa said to hold the ashes of Buddha's attendant, and a famous rocket festival rooted in rain-summoning tradition define a place the tourist trail has barely touched.

subject: Yassıada
summary: Officially renamed Democracy and Freedom Island in 2013, Yassıada has served the Byzantine and Turkish states alike as a place to confine people the powerful found inconvenient — most infamously as the site of the 1960–61 trials that ended with the execution of Prime Minister Adnan Menderes.

subject: Yasuní-ITT Initiative
summary: Ecuador asked the world to pay $3.6 billion to leave a billion barrels of oil underground. Ten years later, voters finished what the world would not pay for.

subject: Yau Ma Tei
summary: A Kowloon neighbourhood built on reclaimed fishermen's shores, where a 150-year-old Tin Hau Temple presides over jade stalls, night markets, and the lingering memory of typhoon-shelter cuisine.

subject: Yau Ma Tei Fruit Market
summary: A wholesale fruit market in Kowloon's Yau Ma Tei district that has operated continuously since 1913, where lorries still rumble through pre-dawn streets past buildings whose walls carry signboards from before World War II.

subject: Yau Ma Tei Typhoon Shelter
summary: A sheltered harbor built between 1910 and 1915 off the Kowloon coast that protected fishing fleets and became home to a floating community of Boat People for over seven decades, before land reclamation erased its original site and replaced it with residential towers.

subject: Yau Tong
summary: A southeastern Kowloon district that was rural until the 1960s, then transformed by public housing and industrial waterfront, and is now reinventing its harbour edge as a public destination.

subject: Yavuz Sultan Selim Medrese
summary: Built by the master architect Mimar Sinan between 1548 and 1550, the Yavuz Sultan Selim Medrese stands on the very spot where Selim I pitched his tent — a soldier-sultan who asked, before he had won the world, for a place of learning to be built in his name.

subject: Yayoi 2-chōme Site
summary: A small patch of ground on the University of Tokyo campus where a single red-clay jar discovered in 1884 gave its neighborhood's name to an entire era of Japanese civilization -- the Yayoi period -- and then the exact spot of the discovery was lost for nearly a century.

subject: Yazd
summary: An ancient desert city in central Iran where windcatchers pierce the skyline, Zoroastrian fire burns unbroken since 470 AD, and mud-brick architecture earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 2017.

subject: Ybor City
summary: Founded in the 1880s by a Spanish cigar manufacturer, this Tampa neighborhood became America's cigar capital through the labor of Cuban, Spanish, and Italian immigrants, declined to near-abandonment, and reinvented itself as a historic entertainment district.

subject: Ybor City Cigar Factories
summary: The Tampa neighborhood where Cuban, Spanish, and Italian immigrants rolled 700 million cigars a year by hand - while 'lectores' read novels and newspapers aloud to keep workers entertained and politically informed.

subject: Ye (Hebei)
summary: The ancient city of Ye served as capital for six different dynasties over four centuries before being razed twice and forgotten, its ruins yielding nearly 3,000 Buddha statues in a single dig.

subject: Ye Olde Curiosity Shop
summary: A waterfront curiosity shop founded in 1899 that shaped Seattle's identity as totem pole country, supplied world museums with Northwest Coast art, and still displays shrunken heads and mummies after four generations of family ownership.

subject: Yedikule
summary: Named for its famous seven-towered fortress, the Yedikule neighborhood has been feeding Istanbul from its celebrated market gardens for more than fifteen centuries — a deeply rooted place where Byzantine walls, Ottoman bostans, and a living community still share the same ground.

subject: Yee Wo Street
summary: A Causeway Bay thoroughfare whose name traces back to a Qing dynasty trading hong, later renamed by Japanese occupiers, and now one of Hong Kong's most densely trafficked streets — carrying trams, a million pedestrians a day, and the memory of the Umbrella Revolution.

subject: Yehliu
summary: A 1,700-meter cape on Taiwan's northern coast where wind and sea have spent millennia sculpting sandstone into surreal formations, including the iconic Queen's Head that loses a fraction of a centimeter of its neck each year.

subject: Yelizovo
summary: A small Kamchatka city of 40,000 that serves as the sole air gateway to one of the world's most remote volcanic wilderness regions, split between an airport zone and a quiet town where tourists are still a genuine surprise.

subject: Yellow Fever in Buenos Aires
summary: In the autumn of 1871 a mosquito-borne fever killed roughly 14,000 people in Buenos Aires, emptied the city, and split it into a poor south and a wealthy north that endures to this day.

subject: Yellowcraig
summary: A broad East Lothian beach within sight of Fidra Island, the rock that gave Robert Louis Stevenson the shape of Treasure Island.

story.title: Yellowstone: The Supervolcano That Could End Civilization

subject: Yellowstone
summary: Where a volcanic hotspot powers 10,000 geothermal features and holds enough magma to bury the continental US in ash - the world's first national park sits atop a ticking time bomb that last erupted 640,000 years ago.

subject: Yellowstone Caldera
summary: North America's sleeping giant: a supervolcano whose last eruption buried the continent in ash 640,000 years ago, still breathing through geysers and hot springs.

subject: Yemen
summary: An ancient civilization at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, where the Queen of Sheba once ruled and mud-brick skyscrapers rise from the desert -- now enduring a devastating civil war that threatens millennia of irreplaceable heritage.

subject: Yemen Eyalet
summary: An Ottoman province whose conquest cost Istanbul thousands of lives, whose coffee once monopolized a world market, and whose Zaidi tribesmen drove out two separate empires across three centuries.

subject: Yenikapı
summary: When workers broke ground for Istanbul's new metro in 2004, they uncovered one of the most remarkable archaeological sites in Europe: the long-buried Theodosian Harbour, packed with 37 Byzantine shipwrecks and human remains stretching back 8,000 years.

subject: Yenisei
summary: The fifth-longest river system on Earth and the largest flowing into the Arctic Ocean, the Yenisei cleaves Siberia in two across 5,075 kilometers from Mongolia to the Kara Sea.

story.title: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

subject: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts
summary: A multidisciplinary contemporary arts center in two landmark buildings, YBCA celebrates Bay Area diversity through visual art, performance, and film in the heart of Yerba Buena Gardens.

subject: Yerbas Buenas
summary: A sleepy colonial town in Chile's central plain, where whole streets of Spanish-era houses still stand and where the country's war of independence began with a midnight surprise.

subject: Yerpa
summary: Ancient meditation caves in limestone cliffs northeast of Lhasa, where Tibet's kings, saints, and assassins sought solitude across thirteen centuries of unbroken contemplative tradition.

subject: Yevpatoria
summary: A 2,500-year-old Crimean port where Greek colonists, Crimean Tatars, Karaites, and Ottoman traders each left their mark on a single crowded quarter locals call the Small Jerusalem.

subject: Yew Mountains
summary: A ridge of Allegheny peaks in southern West Virginia where five major rivers begin their journeys - the Cherry, the Cranberry, the Williams, the Gauley, and the Greenbrier.

subject: Yeşilköy
summary: Once the resort village of San Stefano where a pivotal peace treaty was signed in 1878, Yeşilköy on Istanbul's western Marmara shore has quietly accumulated centuries of layered history behind its seafront calm.

subject: Yim Tin Tsai (Tai Po District)
summary: A small island in Tolo Harbour, Tai Po District's Yim Tin Tsai carries 4,000 years of human presence — from Late Neolithic settlements to Hakka salt-pan workers to fishing families relocated from their boats to land — connected to the mainland by a road and to a neighbouring island by a tombolo that only appears at low tide.

subject: Yinan tombs
summary: A set of Eastern Han dynasty tombs in Shandong whose 42 carved stone reliefs depict acrobats, cavalry battles, and architectural techniques that may have traveled from ancient West Asia.

subject: Yizhong Street
summary: Yizhong Street in Taichung's North District is the city's premier student shopping zone — a pedestrian street that turns into a night market after dark, surrounded by universities and kept lively by competition that drives prices down.

subject: Yogyakarta
summary: Java's cultural capital still answers to a sultan. Borobudur rises nearby, traditional arts thrive in workshops and theaters, and Indonesia keeps its soul in Yogyakarta.

story.title: Yokohama Chinatown: Japan's Largest Chinese Quarter

subject: Yokohama Chinatown
summary: Established when Yokohama's port opened in 1859, Yokohama Chinatown is Japan's largest Chinatown -- a neighborhood of roughly 250 Chinese-owned shops and restaurants that has survived earthquakes, war, and diplomatic upheaval to become one of the country's most visited urban districts.

story.title: Yokosuka: The City Where Perry Came Ashore

subject: Yokosuka
summary: In 1853, Commodore Perry's Black Ships landed at Kurihama in southern Yokosuka and forced open Japan's doors to the world -- and the city on the Miura Peninsula has been a crossroads of Japanese and American military culture ever since.

story.title: Yokosuka Naval Arsenal: Where a Shogun's Ambition Launched an Empire

subject: Yokosuka Naval Arsenal
summary: A French engineer hired by the Tokugawa shogunate built Japan's first modern shipyard on Tokyo Bay in 1866, and the facility went on to produce battleships, aircraft carriers, and submarines for the Imperial Japanese Navy before American forces seized it in 1945.

subject: Yola
summary: Founded in 1841 as a Fulani emirate capital on the vast plains of northeastern Nigeria, Yola was the first town in the country to have both an airport and electricity -- and the place where explorer Heinrich Barth arrived after crossing the Sahara.

subject: Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area
summary: Where flood control and wildlife restoration coexist: 16,000 acres of managed wetlands, vernal pools, and working ranchland tucked between Sacramento and Davis.

subject: Yonezawa
summary: A quiet mountain town in Yamagata where the ghosts of samurai clans linger in shrine grounds and snow festival lanterns, the beef rivals Kobe, and a sake brewery has been pouring for the same family since 1597.

subject: Yongdingmen
summary: The front gate of Beijing's outer city walls, torn down in the 1950s for road construction and rebuilt in 2005, marking the southern anchor of the capital's ancient central axis.

subject: York
summary: An English cathedral city where Romans, Vikings, and medieval merchants left their bones in the same square mile of cobblestones.

subject: York
summary: The cathedral city at the confluence of the Ouse and Foss, founded by Roman legions in AD 71 and continuously inhabited ever since.

subject: York County, Virginia
summary: Formed 1634 as Charles River Shire, this Tidewater county holds the surrender ground at Yorktown, the Coast Guard training base, and most of Naval Weapons Station Yorktown.

subject: York city walls
summary: Two miles of stone wall - the longest medieval town walls in England - around a city defended by Romans, Vikings, Normans, and Parliamentarians, with traitors' heads once stuck on the gatehouse spikes.

subject: Yorkshire Dales
summary: A network of glaciated Pennine valleys whose name comes from the Old English daed, where dry-stone walls climb every fell and seven rivers carry the rainfall east and west.

subject: Yoshiwara
summary: Established in 1617 by the Tokugawa shogunate, Yoshiwara was Tokyo's licensed pleasure quarter for over three centuries, a place where courtesans set fashion trends for all of Japan while thousands of exploited women lived and died in its walled confines.

subject: Youbou, British Columbia
summary: A Cowichan Lake mill town named for two lumber executives, built by Sikh and settler labour over seven decades, that lost its sawmill in a single January morning and turned the loss into a forest-policy movement.

subject: Youghal
summary: The walled port where Sir Walter Raleigh served as mayor, Cromwell wintered, and a town once stood in for 19th-century New Bedford in John Huston's Moby Dick.

subject: Youghal Lifeboat Station
summary: An Irish lifeboat station that opened in 1839, fell into neglect, was rescued by the RNLI, and won its first gold medal hauling a wreck-bound brig's crew off Whiting Bay by hand.

subject: Youzhou (ancient China)
summary: An ancient Chinese prefecture centered on modern Beijing that survived a thousand years of dynastic warfare, warlord betrayals, and nomadic conquest before disappearing into history.

subject: Yowah
summary: A tiny opal town in outback Queensland where fortune hides inside small ironstone nodules called Yowah nuts, and only one in ten thousand holds fire.

subject: Ypati
summary: Perched on the slopes of Mount Oeta above ancient hot springs that Herodotus mentioned, Ypati — once the city-state of Hypata — was long whispered through Greek folklore as a haunt of witches, and still wears its medieval castle and Byzantine church like a scholar's footnotes on a very long life.

subject: Yr Eifl
summary: Three peaks above the Llyn coast -- the highest at 561 metres -- known to English speakers as The Rivals, though the Welsh name means The Fork. From the central summit on a clear day you can see Ireland, the Isle of Man, and the entire Lake District.

subject: Ysleta Mission
summary: Born from exile after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, Ysleta Mission is Texas's oldest continuously operating parish, where the Tigua people have maintained their faith and traditions for over 340 years.

subject: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo
summary: Forced to march 400 miles south during the 1680 Pueblo Revolt, the Tigua people built a new home in the desert and refused to disappear -- surviving three centuries of governments that alternately ignored, abandoned, and finally recognized them as the southernmost Pueblo tribe.

subject: Yu Shan
summary: Taiwan's highest peak at 3,952 meters once served as Japan's tallest mountain, provided the coded signal for the Pearl Harbor attack, and today appears on the nation's thousand-dollar bill.

subject: Yuai
summary: A small Nuer town in Jonglei State whose name runs through South Sudan's wars like a marker stone - and whose residents have absorbed more displacement than most places absorb history.

subject: Yuanlin
summary: A city named for a woodland that was slowly eaten away, Yuanlin grew from a forest clearing in Qing-dynasty Changhua into central Taiwan's second-largest urban settlement.

subject: Yuba Goldfields
summary: California's largest gold dredge field, where 64 years of industrial mining turned the Yuba River valley into an alien landscape of gravel windrows and turquoise pools that wildlife has quietly reclaimed.

subject: Yubeng
summary: A Tibetan village hidden beneath the sacred peaks of the Meili Snow Mountains, reachable only on foot, where pilgrims and trekkers share trails to glacial lakes, sacred waterfalls, and an unobstructed view of Kawagarbo.

subject: Yuen Long
summary: The name means 'round basin' — a landscape description that still holds, encircled by hills and straddling the line between Hong Kong's ancient village culture and its proximity to the Shenzhen border.

subject: Yuen Long District
summary: Hong Kong's largest alluvial plain shelters 3,500 years of continuous habitation, Tang clan walled villages, international wetlands, and one of the territory's most storied border landscapes.

subject: Yuen Long Kau Hui
summary: The original market town of Yuen Long, founded in 1669 by a Tang clan magistrate after the Qing coastal evacuation, preserves centuries of clan history in its walled villages, temples, and Qing-era shophouses.

subject: Yuexiu Hill
summary: A storied hilltop in the heart of Guangzhou where granite rams, a Ming-dynasty watchtower, and millennia of legend converge inside one of southern China's great urban parks.

subject: Yujing District
summary: In the foothills of eastern Tainan, Yujing carries four centuries of layered names — Tapani, Tamai, Yujing — and a single reputation that has outlasted them all: the mango capital of Taiwan.

subject: Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics
summary: Japan's premier theoretical physics institute, born from a nation's pride in its first Nobel laureate and shaped by the atomic destruction of its sister institution in Hiroshima.

subject: Yulara
summary: A purpose-built resort town in the middle of nowhere, Yulara exists for one reason: to put visitors within reach of Uluru and Kata Tjuta without camping in the sacred park itself.

subject: Yuma Crossing
summary: Two granite outcroppings that narrowed the Colorado River to the only practical ford for a thousand miles in either direction — the strategic chokepoint through which every major movement of people across the American Southwest passed for centuries, from the Spanish expeditions of 1540 through the Gold Rush and beyond.

subject: Yuma Desalting Plant
summary: The largest desalination plant in the United States, built at enormous expense in the 1980s to deliver clean water to Mexico under an international treaty — and then barely operated, while accidentally creating one of the most ecologically significant wetlands in the Sonoran Desert.

subject: Yumeshima
summary: Built from decades of landfill in Osaka Bay, the artificial island of Yumeshima hosted Expo 2025 and is now transforming into Japan's first casino resort district, a manufactured landscape where garbage became grand ambition.

subject: Yungas Road
summary: Bolivia's infamous 'Death Road' -- a narrow, cliff-hugging track carved by prisoners of war in 1930 -- once claimed hundreds of lives a year and now draws thousands of mountain bikers down its 64 kilometers of misty switchbacks.

story.title: Yunomine Onsen: The Seven-Color Bath at the Gate of the Gods

subject: Yunomine Onsen
summary: Tucked in a narrow valley of the Kumano mountains, the world's only UNESCO World Heritage hot spring has been purifying pilgrims for 1,800 years -- and its tiny Tsuboyu bath still changes color seven times a day.

subject: Yuquot
summary: Called 'the birthplace of British Columbia,' this windswept cove on Nootka Island was once home to 1,500 Mowachaht people, then Spain's northernmost colony, then the flashpoint of a crisis that nearly sparked war between European empires -- and today, about six people live there.

subject: Yushan
summary: Taiwan's Jade Mountain soars to 3,952 meters above the island's volcanic heart, carrying three different names from three different peoples and offering a dawn sky that climbers call incomparable.

subject: Yushan Range
summary: The Yushan Range is Taiwan's mightiest mountain spine, carrying 22 peaks above 3,000 meters and crowned by Yushan at 3,952 m — the highest point in Taiwan, East Asia outside the Himalayas and their neighbors, and the axis around which the island's highest landscapes organize themselves.

subject: Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk
summary: The capital of Sakhalin Island has worn three names in 140 years -- a convict settlement, a Japanese colonial capital, and a Soviet city reborn as an oil boomtown at the edge of the Pacific.

subject: Yyteri
summary: Six kilometres of dune and open sand on the Bothnian coast, young enough that the ground the Rolling Stones played on in 1965 had only been dry land for two centuries.

subject: Yzerfontein
summary: A West Coast fishing village of 1,100 people where archaeological digs reveal ancient inhabitants who ate penguins and mole rats but never touched the fish, and where spring wildflowers blanket the dunes from town to the West Coast National Park.

subject: Z Bend
summary: Where the Murchison River doubles back on itself in a sharp zigzag, the gorge wall drops some 150 metres, and abseilers rappel into a kilometre-thick stack of ancient stone.

subject: ZOOM Erlebniswelt Gelsenkirchen
summary: Lions and zebras share the same panorama view, separated only by an invisible moat. The hippos swim in a pond divided from visitors by underwater fencing nobody can see. The zoo's design rule: pretend the cages are not there.

subject: Zaanstreek-Waterland
summary: The flat polders north of Amsterdam look like every postcard cliche about Holland - because this is where most of the cliches came from.

subject: Zacharo
summary: A west-coast town of Elis where long sandy beaches, a sulfurous thermal lake hemmed by pines, and the sweetest tomato in Greece coexist — and where a catastrophic wildfire in 2007 reshaped a community already accustomed to starting over.

subject: Zadar
summary: Croatia's oldest continuously inhabited city, where Venetian walls guard a peninsula holding 34 churches and the Adriatic plays music through a sea organ built into the harbor steps.

subject: Zafar, Yemen
summary: The Himyarite capital at 2,800 meters in the Yemeni highlands once ruled most of Arabia for 250 years; today, 450 farmers work the land where 25,000 people once lived.

subject: Zagros Mountains
summary: A 1,600-kilometer mountain range stretching from Turkey to the Persian Gulf where the Arabian and Eurasian plates still collide, and where humans first cultivated wheat, fermented wine, and built the cities that became civilization.

subject: Zaleski Mound Group
summary: Three Adena culture burial mounds in the small village of Zaleski, Ohio - including the 14-foot Ranger Station Mound near the entrance to Zaleski State Forest, preserved on land later used for federal Depression-era reforestation.

subject: Zaliznyi Port
summary: A sun-baked beach village on the Kherson coast, once a single street facing the sea, whose curious name, the Iron Port, remains an unsolved local puzzle.

subject: Zambezian flooded grasslands
summary: A constellation of vast seasonal wetlands - the Okavango Delta, Kafue Flats, Bangweulu Swamp, and more - scattered across the Zambezi basin, supporting huge numbers of lechwe, waterbirds, and the communities who have fished them for centuries.

subject: Zambia
summary: A squashed-peanut-shaped country where the Zambezi plunges over Victoria Falls, safari camps outnumber cities, and 73 ethnic groups have somehow always managed to get along.

subject: Zambia
summary: A country whose borders were drawn by Cecil Rhodes's mining ambitions, whose rivers drain half a continent, and whose name was taken from the Zambezi on the day of independence in 1964.

subject: Zamboanga City
summary: The sixth-most populous city in the Philippines and the commercial heart of the Zamboanga Peninsula, where Chavacano -- a Spanish creole born from colonial fortress construction -- is still the lingua franca, and where a million people navigate the crosscurrents of Catholic, Muslim, and indigenous traditions.

subject: Zamora (Ecuador)
summary: A small Andean-Amazonian gateway town where three rivers meet, gold built the economy, and the doorstep of one of the world's most biodiverse parks waits a few kilometers away.

subject: Zamora-Chinchipe Province
summary: An Amazonian province where conquistadors were repelled four centuries running, gold runs through the rivers, and the Shuar still hold the high ridges.

subject: Zamzam Refugee Camp
summary: Established in 2004 for survivors of the Darfur genocide, Zamzam grew into a city of half a million displaced people before being overrun in 2025.

subject: Zamzam Well
summary: Twenty meters east of the Ka'ba, a well that Muslim tradition traces to Hagar and Ishmael has been drawn from for at least 1,400 years and probably much longer.

subject: Zanja Madre
summary: Los Angeles's original aqueduct, built in 1781 within weeks of the city's founding, that sustained the pueblo for over a century before being abandoned as the modern water system took over.

subject: Zanzibar
summary: Where the Spice Islands perfumed ocean trade routes, where Stone Town's labyrinth preserves Swahili architecture, where slavery's history haunts paradise beaches.

subject: Zapala
summary: At the geographic heart of Patagonia's Neuquen province, this windswept railhead town launched the first airplane ever to cross the Andes.

subject: Zaporizhzhia
summary: A Ukrainian city whose name means "beyond the rapids," built where a fortress once guarded the frontier and a great dam later forged an industrial giant.

subject: Zaruma
summary: A colonial gold-mining town perched 1,200 meters up in the Andes, named for corn and gold, that has been hollowing itself out from beneath since the conquistadors arrived.

subject: Zaventem
summary: Most Europeans know Zaventem only as the place their plane lands - but the Flemish village beneath Brussels Airport has a thousand-year history that includes an Anthony van Dyck altarpiece still hanging in the parish church.

subject: Zealandia (wildlife sanctuary)
summary: A fenced valley in suburban Wellington where New Zealand is rewinding 800 years of ecological damage, one species at a time.

subject: Zeballos, British Columbia
summary: Named for a Spanish naval officer on an eighteenth-century expedition, Zeballos boomed to 5,000 people during a 1930s gold rush on Vancouver Island's northwest coast, then shrank to 126 residents as gold, iron, and timber each rose and fell in turn.

subject: Zeebrugge Raid
summary: St George's Day 1918: a mile-long Belgian breakwater becomes the stage for seventy-five minutes of point-blank fighting that earned eight Victoria Crosses and changed almost nothing.

subject: Zeedijk
summary: Amsterdam's medieval sea dike has been a street since the Middle Ages; in one human lifetime it has been a respectable promenade, a sailors' bar district, the city's heroin street, and the heart of Chinatown.

subject: Zeewolde
summary: Founded in 1984 on land that was seabed within living memory, Zeewolde is one of the youngest towns in the Netherlands - a planned community built from scratch on the floor of the former Zuiderzee.

subject: Zeila
summary: The ancient Somali port that once held Islam's western gateway into the Horn of Africa, traded frankincense with Rome, and shaped empires that few outside the region now remember.

subject: Zeleia
summary: Homer called it holy, its archers fought for Troy, and centuries later the Persian satraps gathered here to decide how to stop Alexander the Great — yet ancient Zeleia vanished so completely that its site lay forgotten until modern scholars placed it near a Turkish village called Sarıköy.

story.title: Zenko-ji: The Temple That Built a City

subject: Zenkō-ji
summary: A 7th-century Buddhist temple in Nagano harbors a sacred statue that no one -- not even the head priest -- is permitted to see, and the city that grew up around it still revolves around a dark underground corridor where pilgrims grope for a metal key to paradise.

subject: Zentralfriedhof Friedrichsfelde
summary: A municipal cemetery in Lichtenberg that became the burial ground of the German left, where a Politburo decided who was important enough to lie in which row.

subject: Zeyrek
summary: A steep, cobblestoned UNESCO-protected neighborhood in Istanbul's Fatih district, where Ottoman wooden houses cling to a hillside above the Golden Horn and a Byzantine monastery turned mosque still commands the skyline.

subject: Zeyrek Çinili Hamam
summary: Mimar Sinan's 16th-century tiled bathhouse in Istanbul's Zeyrek district lay derelict for decades before a 13-year restoration brought it back — including a museum where fragments of its famous blue-and-white Iznik tiles are displayed alongside the scattered pieces that ended up in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

subject: Zhangjiakou
summary: Beijing's Northern Door -- a city at the junction of the Great Wall and the Mongolian steppe where camel caravans once carried tea to Russia and Olympic skiers now carve through Chongli powder.

subject: Zhaori Hot Spring
summary: One of only three saltwater hot springs in the world, Zhaori on Green Island offers open-air soaking in seawater heated by volcanic activity, with the Pacific surf audible just beyond the pool's edge.

subject: Zhengbin Fishing Port
summary: Built by the Japanese in 1934 as Taiwan's largest fishing port and a copper export hub, Zhengbin has reinvented itself quietly around a row of 16 brightly painted houses that have become one of Keelung's most photographed landmarks.

subject: Zhengyangmen
summary: Beijing's tallest surviving city gate, known colloquially as Qianmen, has guarded the approach to Tiananmen Square since 1419 and marks China's kilometre zero point for all highways.

subject: Zhengzhou Shang City
summary: An ancient walled city dating to 1630 BC lies beneath modern Zhengzhou -- a Bronze Age capital with nearly seven kilometers of rammed-earth fortifications, palace ruins, and workshops that predates the famous Shang site at Anyang by centuries.

subject: Zhenxibao
summary: A remote Atayal village perched at 1,600 meters in Hsinchu County's Jianshih Township, where a grove of towering ancient trees draws hikers into the high mountain forests along the edge of Shei-pa National Park.

subject: Zhili
summary: For five centuries, the administrative region surrounding Beijing bore a name that meant 'directly ruled' -- a designation that made it the political heart of imperial China.

subject: Zhol Village
summary: A village at the foot of the Potala Palace that once housed Tibet's government, its courts, its mint, and a stone pillar bearing the oldest known Tibetan inscriptions.

subject: Zhongdu
summary: The Jin dynasty capital of Zhongdu was a city of nearly one million people before the Mongols reduced it to ash in 1215 -- and then built a new capital just to its northeast.

subject: Zhongguancun
summary: Beijing's technology district grew from a single visionary's trip to Silicon Valley into a hub hosting 12,000 enterprises, birthing Lenovo, and drawing Google, Microsoft, and Intel to build their Chinese headquarters.

subject: Zhongli Incident
summary: In 1977, a small Taiwanese town erupted in fury over election rigging, producing the first mass political protest since the 1940s and igniting the slow burn toward democracy.

subject: Zhongnanhai
summary: The walled compound beside the Forbidden City that has served as China's center of power since 1949, where Mao swam laps and Zhou Enlai refused to renovate.

subject: Zhongshan
summary: Zhongshan is one of the very few cities in China named after a person — the revolutionary Sun Yat-sen, who was born here in 1866 — and it carries that legacy lightly, remaining quieter and greener than its Pearl River Delta neighbors.

subject: Zhongshan (state)
summary: A small but tenacious Warring States kingdom that survived 120 years through shrewd diplomacy, built its own Great Wall, and left behind royal tombs containing the richest artifacts of any 4th-century BC Chinese state.

subject: Zhongshan Square
summary: A 213-meter circular plaza in downtown Dalian that has been Russian, Japanese, and Chinese, and where people now dance on summer evenings among colonial-era architecture.

subject: Zhongxing New Village
summary: Built in the 1950s as Taiwan's planned provincial capital — a garden city carved from Nantou farmland to house a government in waiting — Zhongxing New Village spent six decades as an administrative center before the government it was built for was dissolved.

subject: Zhongyuan
summary: The Central Plains of China -- the Yellow River heartland between Luoyang and Kaifeng that the ancient Huaxia people considered the center of the world and the birthplace of Chinese civilization.

subject: Zhoucun, Zibo
summary: A Shandong textile town whose centuries-old tax-free monument was born from a 17th-century official's cunning wordplay against the Qing emperor.

subject: Zhoukoudian
summary: A small town in Beijing's Fangshan District whose limestone hills and cave formations gave the world Peking Man and reshaped the story of human evolution.

subject: Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage cave system near Beijing where fossils of Homo erectus, up to 700,000 years old, were discovered in the 1920s -- then lost forever during the Japanese invasion.

subject: Zhuhai
summary: Where the Pearl River meets the South China Sea, Zhuhai transformed from a cluster of fishing villages into one of China's cleanest and most livable cities — the city of romance, the city of a hundred islands, and the gateway that connects Macau, Hong Kong, and the Pearl River Delta.

subject: Zhuhai Fisher Girl
summary: Standing on a boulder in Xianglu Bay with a pearl raised to the sky, Zhuhai's Fisher Girl statue encodes a love story, a founding myth, and the ambitions of a city that reinvented itself — carved from granite, completed in 1982 by sculptor Pan He.

subject: Zhuolan
summary: A fruit-growing township in Miaoli County, Taiwan, whose pears, grapes, starfruit, and tangerines define its character — and whose older name, Talan, hints at an indigenous past that predates the orchards.

subject: Zhuolu County
summary: A county in Hebei Province that claims to be the site of the legendary Battle of Zhuolu and the only city founded by the Yellow Emperor, now better known for producing grapes across what may be the largest vineyard in Asia.

subject: Zihuatanejo
summary: A Pacific fishing town on Mexico's Costa Grande whose Nahuatl name may mean 'place of women' -- a reference to the goddess women who guided the sun into the underworld each evening.

subject: Zilverparkkade
summary: Ten architects, ten narrow plots, one Lelystad street that tries to remember what a canal looks like.

subject: Zipaquirá
summary: The Colombian salt-mining town where a cathedral was carved inside the mountain itself, 180 meters below the surface, with nave and crosses and altar all cut from glowing rock salt.

subject: Zittau
summary: Saxony's southeasternmost town, where three countries touch, a painted linen cloth from 1472 survived being cut up for a soldiers' sauna, and one of the largest holes ever dug sits just across the river.

subject: Ziwiye hoard
summary: A treasure trove of gold, silver, and ivory discovered near Saqqez in Iranian Kurdistan in 1947, the Ziwiye hoard captures a moment when Scythian, Assyrian, and Median cultures collided on the Iranian plateau.

subject: Zoetermeer
summary: In 1950 it was a village of 6,392 people growing peat-bog vegetables. In 2023 it was a city of 126,998 with the only indoor ski slope in the Netherlands, the only LDS temple in the country, and the only city hall in Second Life.

subject: Zografou
summary: A steep Athens student suburb sold off in monthly installments a century ago, now home to two of Greece's largest universities on the slopes of Hymettus.

subject: Zomba
summary: Malawi's former capital sits at the foot of a mist-wrapped plateau where waterfalls cascade through forests and the views stretch across the whole of the country's south.

subject: Zona Norte, Tijuana
summary: Zona Norte is Tijuana's red-light district — a few square blocks just south of the US border where legal sex work, bars, and drug activity coexist within a complicated framework of permits, regulation, and urban marginality.

subject: Zonhoven
summary: A small Limburg town whose own name is a misunderstanding it then chose to live inside.

subject: Zons
summary: A medieval Rhine toll fortress so completely walled in that 650 years later you still pay the same town its dues, only now in souvenir money instead of silver Thaler.

subject: Zoological Society of London
summary: Founded in 1826 by Sir Stamford Raffles, this learned society opened London Zoo in 1828, invented the open-air zoo at Whipsnade in 1931, and now runs global conservation programmes.

subject: Zoutkamp
summary: In 1969, the Netherlands closed off Zoutkamp's sea. The fishing village kept its boats, kept its ZK port marks, and kept fishing anyway.

subject: Zuid-Willemsvaart
summary: A 122-kilometer Dutch-Belgian canal dug between 1822 and 1826 to shortcut a difficult stretch of the Meuse, named for King William I, then orphaned by a revolution four years later.

subject: Zuider Ee
summary: A small Frisian river with a four-century argument about where the water should go — and a 21st-century plan to make it navigable again from Dokkum to the sea.

subject: Zuiderduintjes
summary: A tiny Dutch sandbank in the Wadden Sea that has nearly doubled in size since 1995 - and where people are not allowed to set foot.

subject: Zuiderkerk (Enkhuizen)
summary: A 15th-century Gothic hall church built on drowned village ground in Enkhuizen, with vault paintings hidden for centuries and a bell named Salvator that has been ringing since 1509.

subject: Zuidlaren
summary: A Drenthe village on the Hondsrug ridge where, every third Tuesday in October, one of the oldest and largest horse markets in Western Europe still gathers along the streets, descended from medieval livestock fairs that have run here for some eight hundred years.

subject: Zuihōden
summary: The lavish mausoleum of Date Masamune, the 'One-Eyed Dragon' who transformed a fishing village into the great city of Sendai, rises in Momoyama-era splendor from a forested hillside.

story.title: Zuishin-in: The Temple of a Thousand Buried Love Letters

subject: Zuishin-in
summary: A Shingon Buddhist temple in Kyoto's Yamashina district where Japan's most celebrated beauty and poet, Ono no Komachi, is said to have retired -- and where a mound still marks the spot where she buried a thousand love letters from heartbroken courtiers.

subject: Zulu Kingdom
summary: Born from the military genius of one exiled prince, the Zulu Kingdom became the most powerful indigenous state in southern Africa -- only to be shattered by British imperialism and survive as a living cultural force.

subject: Zum schwarzen Ferkel
summary: A Berlin wine shop that Strindberg renamed after a sagging wine sack over the door, and where he, Munch, Przybyszewski and Dagny Juel spent two years making each other into art.

story.title: Zuma Rock: The Gateway Guarded by Guinea Fowls and Spirits

subject: Zuma Rock
summary: A massive Precambrian monolith rising 725 meters above sea level on the road from Suleja to Abuja, featured on Nigeria's 100 naira note, and wrapped in centuries of legend about hidden villages, protective priests, and a deity that demanded black sacrifices.

subject: Zuma, Sudan
summary: Twenty-nine grave mounds rise from the Nile bank near Jebel Barkal, long mistaken for pyramids - the tumuli of el-Zuma mark the burial ground of an elite in the centuries between Kush and Christian Nubia.

subject: Zumaque I
summary: The first petroleum well in Venezuelan territory, drilled to just 135 meters in 1914 near the town of Mene Grande, Zumaque I launched an oil industry that would reshape an entire nation.

subject: Zunbil dynasty
summary: A dynasty that ruled Zabulistan in eastern Afghanistan for over two centuries, blending Buddhist, Hindu, and possibly Zoroastrian traditions while holding off the Arab conquest longer than almost any neighbor.

subject: Zundert
summary: The Dutch town where Vincent van Gogh was born, and where eight million dahlias still bloom every September for the world's largest flower parade.

subject: Zurich
summary: Where Swiss banking met Swiss discretion and money found its home, where the Limmat flows through medieval lanes and the Alps backdrop what is perhaps the world's most efficient city.

subject: Zutphen
summary: A medieval Hanseatic city on the IJssel where books have been chained to their reading desks since the 17th century, and the historic center is so intact it was voted the best in the Netherlands.

subject: Zuytdorp Cliffs
summary: A 150-kilometre wall of limestone named for a Dutch ship that struck it in 1712 — and for the survivors who climbed the cliffs and walked into the unknown.

subject: Zwolle
summary: An Overijssel Hanseatic capital famous for blue-stained fingers, a pepperpot tower, a Canadian who liberated it alone, and the highest cycling rate of any Dutch city its size.

story.title: Zzyzx: The Last Word in American Place Names

subject: Zzyzx
summary: The Mojave Desert settlement named to be last in the alphabet - where a radio preacher built a quack health resort on federal land, invented the name to guarantee uniqueness, and got evicted after 30 years of selling fake cancer cures.

subject: eBay
summary: The San Jose-based online marketplace that began in 1995 when a programmer listed a broken laser pointer and someone actually bought it, proving that the internet could turn anyone's junk into someone else's treasure.

subject: Águas Claras, Federal District
summary: A planned vertical city in Brasília's Federal District, designed by architect Paulo Zimbres and built in three decades from empty cerrado to 135,000 residents.

subject: Águas Emendadas Ecological Station
summary: A six-kilometre strip of boggy grassland on the outskirts of Brasília where water rising a few hundred metres apart sets off toward two different oceans.

subject: Álamos
summary: A silver city in the Sonoran foothills whose colonial mansions financed expeditions to California, fell into ruin for decades, and were rescued by American homebuyers who wandered in and fell in love.

subject: Árran Lule Sámi Centre
summary: In the small village of Drag on the Tysfjord shore, deep above the Arctic Circle, the Árran centre teaches a language spoken by only a few thousand people - and works, year by year, to keep the Lule Sámi culture alive.

subject: Åland
summary: These Swedish-speaking islands belong to Finland, answer to no army, and managed to sell duty-free goods to both sides during World War II - a quirky autonomy born from the League of Nations' first international agreement.

subject: Ånnsjön
summary: A shallow mountain lake in Swedish Jämtland that has drawn people for 7,000 years, from Stone Age fishing camps to an English admiral's family who stayed for sixty years, and now draws birdwatchers to one of Sweden's most important wetlands.

subject: Ærø
summary: A Baltic island of 5,956 people that sent its men to sea for generations and now runs on the world's largest solar heating plant and a battery-powered ferry.

subject: Ærøskøbing
summary: A Danish island town of single-storey houses that survived by staying lived in — and that once forbade its sailors to light a cooking fire aboard ship.

subject: Çamlıca Hill
summary: At 288 metres, Çamlıca is the highest point on Istanbul's Asian side — a hill where a forest of television masts gave way in 2021 to a single elegant tower, and where the entire geography of a city between two seas opens before you.

subject: Çemberlitaş Hamamı
summary: A bathhouse on Istanbul's ancient processional road, built in 1584 as a charitable endowment by Nurbanu Sultan — the powerful head of the Ottoman imperial harem — and long attributed to the great architect Mimar Sinan.

subject: Çengelköy
summary: A quiet residential village on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, beloved for its tea gardens and once world-famous for a small variety of cucumber grown nowhere else in Istanbul — a place where Byzantine emperors named the waterfront and Ottoman admirals built their mansions.

subject: Île d'Orléans
summary: A pastoral island in the St. Lawrence where the Huron word for 'Enchantress' still fits, and where the roots of French-Canadian culture run deeper than anywhere else in North America.

subject: Îles de Los
summary: A ring of volcanic islands off Conakry whose name means 'islands of the idols' - born of a Cretaceous eruption, scarred by the slave trade, and quietly traded between empires.

subject: Óbidos, Pará
summary: At Óbidos the Amazon is squeezed into its narrowest, deepest, fastest channel - the only place on the lower river where the whole flow can be measured at once, which is why the world's figure for the Amazon's discharge is a number taken here.

subject: Óc Eo
summary: A 450-hectare port found from the air in 1942, laid out on canals in the Mekong Delta - where Roman gold, locally struck silver and the oldest spice residues in Southeast Asia came out of the same mud.

subject: Ô Loan Lagoon
summary: A tired bird from a fairy tale, a narrow sand dune separating brackish water from the South China Sea, and blood cockles pulled fresh from the shallows — Ô Loan Lagoon is 15.7 square kilometers of quiet beauty that a Vietnamese film made famous.

subject: Østerild Wind Turbine Test Field
summary: A forest planted to stop drifting sand was cut open in 2010 so Denmark could find out how tall a wind turbine can get — and the world's largest machines have been going up here ever since.

subject: Útila
summary: The smallest of Honduras's Bay Islands, where budget backpackers earn dive certifications by day and follow the music to whichever bar has claimed the night.

subject: Črete
summary: A small Slovenian settlement that once existed in its own right, was renamed by bureaucratic confusion in 1953, and quietly absorbed by its neighbor in 1955.

subject: Đông Ba Market
summary: More than a century old, Đông Ba Market is the beating commercial heart of Huế — burned to the ground in 1885, rebuilt twice by imperial decree, and still drawing crowds before sunrise each morning.

subject: Đất Mũi
summary: At the southern end of Vietnam, the land is still being built: Đất Mũi gains up to eighty metres of new ground a year, and loses some of it back to the sea.

subject: Đầm Dơi
summary: Named for its bats, mapped beside a swamp named for its crows, and isolated by crocodile-haunted channels until living memory — Đầm Dơi is the delta's most literary corner.

subject: Đắk Lắk Province
summary: A highland province named after a freshwater lake, argued over by linguists, contested for four centuries - and in 2025 handed a coastline it had never had.

subject: Đồng Hới
summary: A city on the narrowest waist of Vietnam that has been a frontier fort, a French airbase and a bombing target, and now lives off the largest caves on earth.

subject: İstiklal Avenue
summary: İstiklal Avenue is Beyoğlu's magnificent 1.4-kilometer pedestrian spine — lined with Ottoman architecture, mosques, churches, and the world's second-oldest subway — and the pulsing cultural heart of modern Istanbul.

story.title: Okochi Sanso: The Samurai Star's Secret Garden

subject: Ōkōchi Sansō
summary: A legendary samurai film actor spent thirty years and his entire fortune carving a two-hectare paradise into the slopes of Mount Ogura above Kyoto's famous bamboo grove, and nobody saw it until after he died.

story.title: Omi Kokucho: The Provincial Capital Lost and Found

subject: Ōmi Kokuchō
summary: The ruins of Omi Province's eighth-century government capital -- a double-moated administrative complex of halls, granaries, and corridors -- lay hidden beneath the neighborhoods of Otsu for a thousand years before archaeologists uncovered the first provincial capital ever matched to ancient records.

story.title: Omori Shell Mounds: The Train Window That Launched Japanese Archaeology

subject: Ōmori Shell Mounds
summary: An American zoologist glanced out of a train window near Tokyo in 1877 and spotted ancient shells in a railway cutting -- a chance observation that became the first scientific archaeological excavation in Japanese history and the birthplace of an entire discipline.

subject: Ōnishi Aijirō
summary: Born the youngest child of a rural family in Nara Prefecture, Onishi Aijiro received a divine revelation while serving as a Tenrikyo missionary, founding the Honmichi religion and enduring two lese-majeste arrests for defying imperial authority before his faith outlived the empire itself.

subject: Şarköy District
summary: A wine-growing coastal strip on the Thracian shore of the Sea of Marmara, where Greek-settled fishing villages were exchanged for Macedonian Turkish ones after 1923, and where the vine still outlasts every political rearrangement.

subject: Şile
summary: Şile is Istanbul's Black Sea escape — a resort town of sandy beaches, a white Ottoman lighthouse, an island castle, and a hand-woven cotton cloth that has dressed the region's summers for centuries.

subject: Škocjan Caves
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage cave system in Slovenia where the Reka River vanishes into the earth, carving the largest underground chamber in Europe before reappearing 34 kilometers away near the Adriatic.

subject: ǀXam and ǂKhomani Heartland
summary: South Africa's national motto is written in a language whose last fluent speakers are gone — the words of the ǀXam, whose ancient homeland in the Kalahari is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Chiricahua National Monument
summary: A forest of stone pinnacles born from volcanic fury 25 million years ago, rising from the desert like a fever dream of geological possibility.

story.title: Craters of the Moon National Monument

subject: Craters of the Moon National Monument
summary: Where NASA trained astronauts to walk on volcanic terrain, and where creatures found nowhere else on Earth make their home in lava tubes.

story.title: Devils Tower: The Sacred Stone Hollywood Made Famous

subject: Devils Tower
summary: The Wyoming monolith sacred to over 20 tribes that became America's first national monument - thrust into popular culture by 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind,' now navigating tensions between climbers seeking adventure and Indigenous peoples seeking respect for holy ground.

subject: Devils Tower
summary: The 867-foot volcanic plug rising from the Wyoming prairie - sacred to multiple tribes, America's first national monument, and made famous when aliens landed on it in 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind.'

subject: El Malpais National Monument
summary: A vast volcanic landscape in western New Mexico where 2,000-year-old ice hides inside lava tubes, ancient Pueblo trails cross black basalt flows, and the Manhattan Project once considered detonating the first atomic bomb.

subject: Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument
summary: Thirty-four million years ago, volcanic mudflows buried a redwood forest and sealed an ancient lake, preserving over 1,700 fossil species in one of the richest paleontological deposits on Earth.

subject: Glass House Mountains National Park
summary: A family of jagged volcanic peaks rising from a flat coastal plain north of Brisbane -- a father, a mother, and their children in the Dreaming of the Jinibara and Kabi Kabi peoples, and the eroded cores of volcanoes that died 25 to 27 million years ago.

subject: Hell Gate
summary: Despite its ominous name, Hell Gate actually means 'bright gate' in Dutch. This treacherous tidal strait in the East River wrecked ships for centuries until the Army Corps of Engineers blasted its rocks away in the largest peacetime explosion before the atomic bomb.

subject: Lava Beds National Monument
summary: Nearly 700 caves riddle the landscape of California's volcanic underworld, where ancient lava flows created a labyrinth now harboring bats, ice formations, and echoes of the Modoc War.

subject: Los Pingüinos Natural Monument
summary: On a treeless island in the Strait of Magellan, a hundred and twenty thousand penguins keep one of the great seabird cities on Earth.

subject: McArthur–Burney Falls Memorial State Park
summary: A 129-foot waterfall that President Theodore Roosevelt called the 'Eighth Wonder of the World,' fed by underground springs that pour 100 million gallons daily from million-year-old volcanic rock.

story.title: National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific

subject: National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific
summary: Nestled inside an ancient volcanic crater above Honolulu, the Punchbowl Cemetery holds over 53,000 war dead and bears the names of nearly 29,000 missing across three wars.

subject: Removal of Hell Gate rocks
summary: A seventy-year campaign to blast treacherous underwater reefs from the East River's Hell Gate strait, culminating in the largest planned explosion before the atomic age.

story.title: The Dream That Burned Before Dawn

subject: The Dream That Burned Before Dawn
summary: Jack London spent years designing his perfect home in the Sonoma Valley -- a 26-room mansion of volcanic stone and redwood -- only to watch it burn to ruins a month before he could move in.

subject: 1982 Invasion of the Falkland Islands
summary: Before dawn on 2 April 1982, Argentine commandos and amphibious troops stormed Stanley in Operation Rosario - a few dozen Royal Marines fought a losing battle at Government House that lit the fuse of the Falklands War.

subject: A Sầu Valley
summary: A remote 40-kilometer valley along the Laotian border that served as the main gateway for North Vietnamese supplies and soldiers into South Vietnam — and became one of the war's most contested and costly battlegrounds.

subject: Achill Island Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI station in the shadow of Grace O'Malley's tower house, running an all-weather lifeboat into the same Atlantic the pirate queen once patrolled.

subject: Adventure Island (amusement park)
summary: The family-run amusement park that straddles Southend Pier - a hundred-year evolution from sunken sea-side garden to one of Britain's best-value theme parks, with thirty-six rides and a 22-metre Eurofighter coaster called Rage.

story.title: Afi Mountain: Where the Last Cross River Gorillas Hold On

subject: Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: A wildlife sanctuary in Nigeria's Cross River State sheltering some of Earth's rarest primates - the Cross River gorilla, the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee, and the drill - while 20 million European swallows descend on its western slopes each winter.

subject: Alcatraz Island
summary: The island prison in San Francisco Bay where Al Capone, Machine Gun Kelly, and the Birdman served time - closed in 1963, occupied by Native Americans in 1969, now the most visited attraction in the Bay Area.

story.title: All Saints Anglican Church, Darnley Island

subject: All Saints Anglican Church, Darnley Island
summary: Built in 1919 from burnt coral and basalt on the exact site where the London Missionary Society first landed in 1871, this heritage-listed church on Erub anchors the annual Coming of the Light celebration.

subject: Anderson Valley Brewing Company
summary: A Mendocino County brewery that speaks Boontling on its labels, brews in rescued German copper kettles, and powers it all with the sun.

subject: Andrews Geyser
summary: A railroad-engineered fountain in the McDowell County woods, eighty feet of water powered entirely by gravity and grief.

subject: Archway Islands
summary: Four rock stacks off Wharariki Beach whose sea-carved arches became so iconic they served as the default lock screen on a billion Windows 10 computers.

subject: Ashdown Forest
summary: The Hundred Acre Wood is real - and it is mostly heath. Six thousand acres of open, windswept high ground 30 miles south of London, with the prime minister's house at one corner and Henry VIII's hunting lodge at another.

subject: Assateague Island National Seashore
summary: The hurricane of 1962 destroyed a planned beach resort on Assateague Island. The federal government bought the wreckage and let the wild ponies keep grazing.

subject: Astola Island
summary: Pakistan's largest offshore island, an uninhabited plateau of seven hills rising from the Arabian Sea, where Alexander the Great's sailors once feared to land and where fishermen still pray at a mosque beside the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple.

subject: Atlantis Paradise Island
summary: A 154-acre ocean-themed mega-resort on Paradise Island in the Bahamas, Atlantis weaves the myth of a lost civilization into a sprawling complex of hotel towers, the world's largest open-air marine habitat, and the Caribbean's biggest casino.

subject: Baby Beach, Aruba
summary: Officially called Klein Lagoen, this man-altered lagoon on Aruba's southeastern tip earned its nickname from water so calm that toddlers wade safely -- a sheltered paradise in the shadow of an abandoned oil refinery.

subject: Baiyu Mountain
summary: A 130-meter mountain at the heart of Port Arthur, Baiyu Mountain offers panoramic views of the naval harbor where empires clashed -- and bears a tower built by 3,000 Chinese laborers forced to honor the soldiers who conquered them.

subject: Bald Head Island
summary: A 12,000-acre subtropical island reachable only by ferry, where North Carolina's oldest standing lighthouse, Old Baldy, has watched the Cape Fear River since 1817.

subject: Ballenas Island Light
summary: A white octagonal lighthouse on a privately owned island in the Strait of Georgia, Ballenas Island Light has guided mariners since 1900 through waters named for the whales that once filled them.

subject: Balut Island
summary: A volcanic island at the southern tip of the Philippines where you can see both Polaris and the Southern Cross, shadows vanish at noon twice a year, and local legend says a celestial dragon swallows the sun.

subject: Barnston Island Ferry
summary: A tug shoves a barge across five minutes of Fraser River, free, on demand, because the bridge islanders have asked for since 1916 has never been built.

subject: Bay View Association
summary: A Victorian cottage community on Little Traverse Bay where Methodist camp meetings evolved into one of America's longest-running Chautauqua programs, blending faith, music, and education since 1875.

subject: Bazaruto Island
summary: A barrier island where Pleistocene sand dunes tower over Iron Age trade routes, Bazaruto has been depopulated by slave raids, repopulated by refugees, and stocked with 5,000 crocodiles before becoming a national park.

subject: Beginish Island
summary: A small island in Valentia Harbour with a Viking-era stone house, a runic inscription now in a Cork museum, and basalt columns that echo the Giant's Causeway four hundred kilometers north.

subject: Bengali Language Movement (Barak Valley)
summary: At Silchar railway station on 19 May 1961, eleven people gave their lives defending the right to speak Bengali, transforming a linguistic dispute into a martyrdom that still shapes identity in northeast India.

subject: Bernier Island
summary: On the mainland opposite this island stands a bronze sculpture called 'Don't Look at the Islands' — a memorial to the Aboriginal people sent here in chains a century ago, to an island that is now a sanctuary for animals found nowhere else.

subject: Big Bay Point Light
summary: A haunted lighthouse on Michigan's Upper Peninsula where the first keeper vanished and was found hanging a year later -- now an 18-room bed and breakfast perched on a bluff above Lake Superior.

subject: Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area
summary: A sacred canyon where 12,000 years of human history meet a controversial dam named for the man who fought against it.

subject: Bigwin Island
summary: The largest island on Lake of Bays in Ontario's Muskoka hides Indigenous burial grounds, the ruins of a once-glamorous 350-room resort, a wartime refuge for the Dutch royal family, and a championship golf course with no water hazards.

subject: Bijia Mountain
summary: A small island in the Bohai Sea where a natural tidal causeway appears and vanishes twice daily, connecting the mainland to a mountaintop shrine honoring the god of creation.

subject: Bintan Island
summary: Once feared as Pirate Island for its Malay raiders who seized trading ships in the Strait of Malacca, Bintan is now a resort getaway for Singaporeans -- though its history runs far deeper than its golf courses.

subject: Black Mountain, North Carolina
summary: A Swannanoa Valley town of 8,400 that hosted the most influential experimental college in American art - and survived Hurricane Helene's worst flooding.

subject: Bombay Beach
summary: The post-apocalyptic California town where the Salton Sea retreated and left ruins - abandoned motels, dead fish, and art installations that make the most of the strangest landscape in America.

subject: Bombetoka Bay
summary: Where a great Madagascar river spills blood-red soil into the sea, building a maze of islands so vivid that astronauts photograph it from orbit.

subject: Booby Island Light
summary: The last major lighthouse built along the Queensland coast took decades of lobbying and bureaucratic delay before its Fresnel lens finally lit the western entrance to the Torres Strait in 1890.

subject: Bosumpra Cave
summary: A rock shelter on Ghana's Kwahu Plateau harboring 13,000 years of continuous human history -- from some of the earliest pottery in West Africa to a shrine for the deity of the Pra River.

subject: BottleRock Napa Valley
summary: Where wine country meets rock and roll: Napa Valley's annual Memorial Day festival that nearly collapsed under debt before becoming one of California's premier music events.

subject: Boulders Beach
summary: A small, boulder-sheltered beach near Simon's Town where a colony of African penguins has taken up residence since the 1990s, making it one of the few places in the world where you can swim alongside wild penguins.

subject: Bracken Cave
summary: A sinkhole in the Texas Hill Country where twenty million Mexican free-tailed bats pour out each summer evening in a living tornado visible on weather radar.

subject: Brampton Island
summary: A mountainous island in the Cumberland Group where a famous resort once buzzed with seaplane arrivals and cruise crowds - now a national-park ghost town with empty villas reclaimed by the bush.

subject: Broadhaven Bay
summary: An Atlantic bay where Spanish Armada ships went down, where all five of Ireland's strictly-protected marine mammal species hunt together, and where one fisherman went to jail rather than stop fishing for Shell's pipeline.

subject: Bruce's Beach
summary: A Black couple bought a beachfront lot in Manhattan Beach in 1912, built a resort welcoming Black families turned away elsewhere, and were driven out by eminent domain twelve years later — a century of injustice finally answered when the land was returned to their descendants.
