story.title: Brunei's Green Jewel Across the Bay

subject: Brunei's Green Jewel Across the Bay
summary: Cut off from the rest of Brunei by a wedge of Malaysian territory, Temburong District spent decades as an exclave reachable only by boat or by crossing four international borders -- until a bridge changed everything.

story.title: Bryce Canyon: The Forest of Stone Giants

subject: Bryce Canyon
summary: The Utah amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos rise like frozen flames - formed by freeze-thaw cycles that will eventually destroy them, creating a landscape so improbable the Paiute believed it was a city of people turned to stone.

subject: Bunce Island
summary: A ruined castle on a small river island from which tens of thousands of West Africans were shipped into slavery — and the ancestral homeland of the Gullah people of the American South.

subject: Burgh Island
summary: A tidal island off South Devon where an Art Deco hotel, a 14th-century pub, and Agatha Christie's imagination converge.

subject: Burnaby Mountain
summary: A 370-metre forested ridge above Burrard Inlet carrying a Brutalist university, a conservation area, black bears, and the pipeline that made it a place people were arrested for standing on.

subject: Byriuchyi Island
summary: The Wolf Island, a sandy Azov spit where Scythian coins may have been struck, deer herds roam, and a lighthouse has stood since 1878.

subject: Caher Island
summary: The City of the Saints - an uninhabited Mayo island of seventh-century monastic ruins, an annual August pilgrimage, and an Atlantic swell that breaks without warning.

subject: Caldey Island
summary: A Welsh island monastery where Cistercian monks make perfume from gorse and shortbread for tourists, on ground that has been holy for fifteen centuries.

subject: Camano Island
summary: A quiet Puget Sound island connected by bridge, where Spanish explorers left their name and beaches offer views across Saratoga Passage to the mountains beyond.

subject: Camp Desert Center
summary: Built in weeks in 1942 and closed by 1944, this desert supply depot and hospital sent its 92nd Evacuation Hospital unit on a journey through New Guinea, Leyte, Luzon, and occupied Japan — a medical unit forged in the California heat.

subject: Cana Island Light
summary: A cream-brick lighthouse wrapped in steel armor, still guiding ships through Door County's waters after more than 150 years of storms, ice, and solitude.

subject: Canelobre Cave
summary: Inside a mountain above Busot, a cathedral-tall cavern named for a giant stone candelabra doubles as one of Spain's most extraordinary concert halls.

subject: Cardona Island Light
summary: A petite 1889 Spanish-built lighthouse on a six-acre island off Ponce, still guiding ships with its original French-made lens after more than 130 years of Caribbean storms, wartime blackouts, and automation.

subject: Casa Grande, Mount Isa
summary: A white Spanish-Mission villa on a rise above the mine - the 'big house' of Mount Isa's mine bosses, complete with tennis court, lush gardens, and a suite once redecorated for a queen.

subject: Cavern Mecca
summary: Liverpool's first Beatles museum opened in 1981 across from where the Cavern Club had been buried, run by Liz and Jim Hughes out of love and obstinacy, and almost single-handedly restarted the tourism economy of Mathew Street.

subject: Cenarth Falls
summary: A cascade on the River Teifi that has been a salmon-leap, a mill site, an artist's subject, and the centre of the last surviving tradition of coracle fishing in Wales.

subject: Chalbi Desert
summary: A blinding white salt plain in northern Kenya, the dried bed of a vanished lake, where Gabbra herders cross shimmering mirages to reach the palm-shaded springs of Kalacha.

subject: Channel Islands
summary: The California islands where evolution went its own way - pygmy mammoths, island foxes the size of house cats, and 145 species found nowhere else on Earth, all visible from the Los Angeles skyline yet worlds apart.

subject: Channel Islands
summary: California's Galápagos - where isolation created endemic species found nowhere else on earth, from island foxes the size of house cats to mammoth fossils, all just 20 miles from the Los Angeles sprawl but completely wild.

subject: Cheat Mountain
summary: A 50-mile West Virginia ridge that once held the largest red spruce forest south of Maine, hosted Robert E. Lee's first Civil War offensive, and is now part Monongahela National Forest, part ski resort.

subject: Chengcing Lake
summary: Beneath the surface of this scenic reservoir near Kaohsiung, a Cold War-era tunnel once served as Chiang Kai-shek's nuclear bunker — now repurposed as an aquarium.

story.title: Chermin Island: The Fortress That Swallowed a Sultan

subject: Chermin Island
summary: A five-hectare island choked with jungle, crocodiles, and the ghosts of civil war -- Brunei's most dramatic islet once served as a rebel sultan's palace, his prison, and his grave.

story.title: Chicago: The City That Reversed a River and Rebuilt Itself in Ash

subject: Chicago
summary: The Illinois metropolis that rose from the Great Fire to become America's second city - where engineers reversed a river's flow, where the first skyscraper changed architecture forever, and where the wind that gives it a nickname actually refers to the politicians.

subject: Chicago River
summary: The only river in the world that was made to flow backward -- a feat of engineering so audacious that the American Society of Civil Engineers named it a 'Civil Engineering Monument of the Millennium' in 1999.

subject: Chico Hot Springs
summary: A Montana hot springs resort 30 miles north of Yellowstone where Steve McQueen and Jeff Bridges soaked alongside ranchers in mineral water that emerges from the earth at 113 degrees.

story.title: Chikubu Island: Where Gods Live After Dark

subject: Chikubu Island
summary: A granite island in Lake Biwa that empties of every human being at nightfall -- home to a shrine founded in 420 AD, two National Treasures, and 40,000 cormorants slowly consuming the forest.

subject: China Beach, San Francisco
summary: A hidden cove in San Francisco's Sea Cliff neighborhood, once a campsite for Chinese fishermen, now a pocket beach with Golden Gate views tucked between Lands End and Baker Beach.

subject: Château de Beauregard, Loire Valley
summary: A Loire Valley château whose Portrait Gallery holds 327 paintings spanning three centuries of European power, set above a floor of 5,500 hand-painted Delft tiles depicting an entire army in formation.

subject: Cinnamon Bay Plantation
summary: A 300-acre plantation on St. John where Taino pottery lies beneath Danish sugar mill ruins -- four thousand years of human presence compressed into a few feet of Caribbean soil, now preserved within Virgin Islands National Park.

subject: Clallam Bay, Washington
summary: A steamboat stop that became a mill town, a tanning-extract boomtown, and finally a fishing village of under four hundred people, Clallam Bay sits in the middle of the darkest stretch of the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

subject: Clare Island
summary: Mountain rising out of Clew Bay - Grace O'Malley's island home, with a Spanish Armada wreck, a Cistercian abbey, and one of the most thorough biological surveys in European history.

subject: Clarence River Light
summary: The working lighthouse on Pilot Hill at Yamba has guided ships into the Clarence River since the days of kerosene lamps - and when its handsome Victorian tower was lost, the town built it back by hand.

subject: Clear Water Bay
summary: A bay of startling clarity on Hong Kong's eastern shore, where shark nets guard two beloved beaches, ancient temples watch over the sea, and the former dream factory of Shaw Brothers Studio once lit up the surrounding hills.

story.title: Cleveland: The Mistake by the Lake That Refuses to Give Up

subject: Cleveland
summary: The Ohio city where the river caught fire and the football team broke hearts - where Rockefeller built Standard Oil, where the Rock Hall honors music, and where decades of decline haven't killed stubborn civic pride.

subject: Cockatoo Island
summary: A sandstone island in Sydney Harbour where convicts carved a dry dock by hand, warships slid down the slipways, and campers now pitch tents above the cells.

subject: Cockatoo Island (Western Australia)
summary: A remote island in the Buccaneer Archipelago where BHP built a self-contained mining town, dug iron ore down to sea level, and briefly turned the site into a tourist resort before the ore ran out.

subject: Coquet Island
summary: A small Northumberland island holding a medieval hermit's monastery, a Victorian lighthouse, and Britain's largest colony of the endangered roseate tern.

subject: Corraun Peninsula
summary: The Gaeltacht peninsula reaching from the Mayo mainland toward Achill, dominated by Corraun Hill and connected to the bigger island by the Michael Davitt Bridge.

subject: Cosquer Cave
summary: A prehistoric art gallery hidden 37 meters below the Mediterranean, containing hand stencils and animal paintings up to 27,000 years old, discovered by a diver in 1985 and made public only after three people died in its tunnels.

subject: Cumberland Island
summary: Georgia's largest barrier island holds 4,000 years of human history, feral horses roaming maritime forests, the ruins of a Carnegie estate, and a tiny church where JFK Jr. was secretly married.

subject: Cunda Island
summary: Once the wholly Greek island of Moschonisi, Cunda is now a Turkish Aegean resort whose restored cathedral and whitewashed windmills hold the memory of a community that was lost.

subject: Côn Sơn Island
summary: The largest island in Vietnam's Con Dao archipelago has been known by a dozen names across two millennia -- and has served as pirate base, colonial outpost, political prison, and navigation station.

subject: Davelis Cave
summary: An ancient marble quarry and Byzantine chapel on Mount Penteli, named for a 19th-century brigand and wrapped in some of Greece's most stubborn modern conspiracy lore.

subject: Dawson Island
summary: A storm-lashed island in the Strait of Magellan that twice became a prison: first for the Selkʼnam people uprooted from their land, then for the ministers of a deposed president.

subject: Daydream Island
summary: A kilometre of resort island in the Ngaro sea country of the Whitsundays, where a coral lagoon threads through the buildings and wallabies wander the beach between the swimming pools.

subject: DeTour Reef Light
summary: Standing guard at the gateway to Lake Superior, this Art Deco lighthouse became the first light station ever named to America's most endangered historic places list, then was saved by the community that refused to let it vanish.

story.title: Death Valley: The Hottest Place That Refuses to Be Empty

subject: Death Valley
summary: The California desert that holds the world's hottest recorded temperature - where 49ers named it Death for good reason, where the Timbisha Shoshone call it home, and where extremity itself became the attraction drawing visitors to 134-degree furnace and 282 feet below sea level.

subject: Deep Bay Marine Field Station
summary: Canada's first LEED Platinum university building sits on the edge of Baynes Sound, where scientists are breeding oysters tough enough to survive acidifying oceans.

subject: Departure Bay
summary: Departure Bay has been a coal port, an explosives factory, the site of British Columbia's first telephone, and the place where a dynamite-laden ship exploded so violently it stopped the Nanaimo post office clock.

subject: Desert Queen Mine
summary: A gold mine in Joshua Tree that changed hands through murder, fraud, and court proceedings — and whose ruins document nearly a century of extraction from the Mojave granite.

subject: Desert Studies Center
summary: A California State University field station at Zzyzx where a fraudulent health spa became legitimate science, two fish species found nowhere else on Earth survive in an artificial lake, and researchers from seven campuses study what desert ecosystems are actually doing.

subject: Destruction Island
summary: A 30-acre island off Washington's Olympic coast, named for two 18th-century massacres and home to a lighthouse that has warned mariners since 1892, Destruction Island carries centuries of sorrow and resilience in its very name.

subject: Dharma Drum Mountain
summary: A Chan Buddhist master insisted his monastery follow the contour of the hills rather than reshape them -- and built one of Taiwan's four great Buddhist organizations on a philosophy of environmental and spiritual protection.

subject: Discovery Island (British Columbia)
summary: The island where the Songhees quarantined themselves through the 1862 smallpox epidemic and survived it - now a marine park, a lighthouse, and the last home of a famous lone wolf.

subject: Disney's River Country
summary: The first water park Disney ever built, River Country opened in 1976 as a rustic swimming hole on Bay Lake -- and became the first Disney park to close permanently, sitting abandoned for nearly two decades before demolition made way for a new resort.

subject: Dongji Island
summary: A remote Penghu island where a fisherman pulled a fossilized ivory tusk from the sea, a cargo ship sank and was left where it lay, and a lighthouse has stood since 1911.

subject: Double Island Point Light
summary: A small white lighthouse on a wild Queensland headland, raised at the summit so its beam could reach the ships it was built to save.

subject: Drake Bay
summary: A small off-the-grid Costa Rican town on the Osa Peninsula that serves as the gateway to Corcovado National Park, where the rainforest hermit has the best 1970s rock collection around.

subject: Dresden Elbe Valley
summary: Twenty kilometres of river, meadow and baroque skyline that became a World Heritage Site in 2004 and lost the title in 2009 — the first place in Europe ever struck off the list, over a bridge its own citizens had voted for.

subject: Duchy of the Archipelago
summary: For 350 years a Venetian adventurer and his heirs ruled the Cyclades as a private maritime kingdom, governed from a castle on Naxos that still stands.

subject: Dulas Bay
summary: A small estuary on the northeast coast of Anglesey where three beaches and three offshore islands - one a seal sanctuary with a 19th-century stone food-tower - share a stretch of coastline with the wreck-history of Welsh seafaring.

subject: Eagle Mountain, California
summary: A Kaiser Steel ghost town in the Colorado Desert whose school closed in 1987, whose streets have since appeared in Tenet and Constantine, and whose 2023 sale for $22.5 million to an undisclosed buyer has left its future unresolved.

subject: East Brother Island Light
summary: A Victorian lighthouse perched on a dynamited rock island in San Francisco Bay, now operating as one of America's most unusual bed-and-breakfasts.

subject: East Glacier
summary: A tiny gateway town on the Blackfeet Reservation where the Empire Builder stops daily and the eastern portal to Glacier National Park opens onto the Great Plains.

subject: Eastern Coachella Valley
summary: East of the resort cities and golf courses, the Coachella Valley's four unincorporated communities produce most of the valley's agricultural wealth — and face extreme heat, limited services, and a decades-long struggle for civic recognition.

subject: El Yunque National Forest
summary: The only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest System, where 240 inches of annual rainfall feeds a living cathedral of ancient trees, endemic frogs, and endangered parrots on the slopes of the Sierra de Luquillo.

subject: Ems
summary: Ptolemy mapped it. Tacitus wrote about it. The Romans built a fort at its mouth and got nowhere — the swamps along this 362-kilometer river beat the empire twice.

subject: Entrance Island (British Columbia)
summary: A tiny rock in the Strait of Georgia has been guiding ships into Nanaimo Harbour since 1876, while its lighthouse keepers have been quietly recording ocean temperatures every day since 1936.

subject: Ersha Island
summary: A slender island in the Pearl River that the British called Napier Island and fortified with 35 guns, Ersha today is Guangzhou's quiet cultural district — home to the Guangdong Museum of Art and the Xinghai Concert Hall, divided from the city's noise by the river on both sides.

subject: Fanad Peninsula
summary: A long, narrow peninsula of links courses, sea arches, and a lighthouse built because of a shipwreck whose sole survivor was a parrot.

story.title: Fantasy Fair and Magic Mountain Music Festival

subject: Fantasy Fair and Magic Mountain Music Festival
summary: The first rock festival in American history -- held a week before Monterey Pop and two years before Woodstock -- on a mountainside amphitheater in Marin County.

subject: Fantome Island
summary: A small, uninhabited island in the Palm group, ringed by reef and marked by some 120 graves, where Aboriginal and Islander people were forcibly isolated in a lock hospital and a leprosarium, and where the dead are now threatened by the rising sea.

subject: Federal Correctional Institution, Terminal Island
summary: A federal prison at the entrance to Los Angeles Harbor that has housed some of America's most notorious inmates, from Al Capone to Charles Manson.

subject: Fergus Falls Regional Treatment Center
summary: One of the last Kirkbride Plan asylums built in America, this sprawling 1890 hospital in western Minnesota was designed to heal through architecture itself -- and after more than a century of service, its haunting central tower now hosts artists instead of patients.

subject: Figure Eight Island
summary: A private barrier island reached by the only private bridge across the Intracoastal Waterway in the Southeast, where Civil War blockade runners sank and $13 million homes now sell.

subject: Five Islands Academy
summary: The only secondary school in the Isles of Scilly - and the first federated school in the United Kingdom - educates children across five island sites with a single boarding house, a £13 million campus, and a 28-mile journey home for some students each Friday afternoon.

subject: Fly River
summary: The largest river in the world with no dam anywhere in its catchment is named after a nineteenth-century British survey ship, empties into a hundred-kilometer-wide funnel delta, and is home to a turtle with flippers.

subject: Ford Island
summary: An islet at the center of Pearl Harbor that has been a Hawaiian fertility ritual site, a Spanish deserter's ranch, a sugarcane plantation, an Army airfield, and the epicenter of the December 7, 1941 attack.

subject: Forest City, North Carolina
summary: Once called Burnt Chimney, the Rutherford County mill town now hosts a Facebook data center, the back-to-back champion Forest City Owls collegiate baseball team, and a 13-mile rail trail.

subject: Forest Grove
summary: A quiet college town at the western edge of Portland's sprawl where Pacific University anchors a community and Henry Hagg Lake draws anglers to the Coast Range foothills.

subject: Galiano Island
summary: The gateway to the Gulf Islands stretches 27 kilometers long but barely a kilometer wide, harboring world-class artists, orca-filled waters, and trails leading to spectacular mountain vistas.

subject: Garbh Eilean, Shiant Islands
summary: The rough northern island of the Shiants - a basalt cliff colony of puffins, dolerite columns the height of a tower block, and a vanished community.

subject: Gauley River
summary: A 105-mile West Virginia river whose name may come from French Gaul, whose canyon hosted an 1861 Civil War battle, and whose dam-released rapids draw the world's whitewater paddlers each fall.

story.title: German occupation of the Channel Islands

subject: German occupation of the Channel Islands
summary: The only British soil held by Nazi Germany during the Second World War - 1,775 days of occupation that ended in starvation, after thousands of forced laborers had been worked to death building the Atlantic Wall here.

subject: Gold Reef City
summary: A theme park built on the mine shaft that birthed Johannesburg, where roller coasters plunge toward old workings and the Apartheid Museum stands at the gate.

subject: Gouina Falls
summary: A half-kilometer-wide curtain of the Sénégal River thundering over a ledge in western Mali, nicknamed the Niagara of Mali and now harnessed by a hydroelectric dam.

story.title: Grand Canyon: Two Billion Years in One Glance

subject: Grand Canyon
summary: Edward Abbey called it simply 'the canyon' -- as if no other topographic feature on Earth deserved the name.

subject: Grand Canyon of Crimea
summary: A narrow limestone gorge in the Crimean Mountains where walls plunge more than 300 meters, an icy pool called the Fountain of Youth promises rejuvenation, and a legendary oak once collected the wishes of passersby.

subject: Grandfather Mountain
summary: At nearly 6,000 feet, Grandfather Mountain towers over the Blue Ridge with 16 ecological communities, a mile-high swinging bridge, and winds so fierce they bend the fir trees sideways.

subject: Granville Island
summary: A tidal sandbar dredged into fourteen hectares of industrial land in 1915, abandoned by mid-century, then rebuilt without being demolished — a public market, seven theatres and a working concrete plant sharing one peninsula under the Granville Street Bridge.

subject: Great Falls, Virginia
summary: An unincorporated Fairfax County community of horse farms and mansion estates above the cataract that gave the place its name.

subject: Great Island
summary: Ireland's second-largest island after Achill, connected to the mainland by one 1803 bridge - the place where Titanic last loaded passengers and where killer whales spent the summer of 2001.

subject: Great Keppel Island
summary: Seventeen white beaches and bright fringing reef ring an island the Woppaburra call Wop-Pa, a paradise whose first people were dispossessed and whose resort dream rose and collapsed.

subject: Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge
summary: Fifteen thousand years ago it was the floor of a glacial lake; in 1959, citizens bought it piece by piece to stop the Port Authority from building a jetport — today it shelters 244 species of birds a few miles from the New Jersey suburbs.

subject: Green Island, Hong Kong
summary: Green Island guards the western mouth of Victoria Harbour — a largely uninhabited speck of woodland and granite where lighthouse keepers once marked the way in, pilots still use it as a mandatory reporting point, and rare birds nest undisturbed beside the city's edge.

subject: Green Island, Taiwan
summary: A volcanic island 33 kilometers off Taiwan's east coast that served as a prison for political dissidents during the White Terror era and now draws tourists to its coral reefs, hot springs, and human rights memorial.

subject: Green River (North Carolina)
summary: A dam-released river south of Asheville with a three-mile gorge so steep and technical that one of its rapids is called Go Left and Die; Hurricane Helene rewrote the course in 2024.

subject: Guajará Bay
summary: Three rivers meet here, the gateway by which the Portuguese reached the Amazon in 1616, a bay of mangroves and Tupinambá fishing grounds that now holds a crowded waterfront and 42 offshore islands.

subject: Gualcarque River
summary: A river sacred to the Lenca people of western Honduras, where a fight against a hydroelectric dam cost indigenous activist Berta Caceres her life and ultimately forced international banks to withdraw their funding.

subject: Guaíra Falls
summary: Once the most powerful waterfall on Earth by volume, Guaira Falls -- the Sete Quedas -- was deliberately drowned in 1982 to fill the reservoir behind Itaipu Dam, erasing a natural wonder that will never return.

subject: Gulf Islands
summary: An archipelago in the rain shadow of Vancouver Island where olives ripen, Garry oaks survive on the ground nobody wanted, and not one island is connected to another by a bridge.

subject: Guyandotte River Train Wreck
summary: On New Year's Day 1913, a Chesapeake and Ohio bridge collapsed under a Mikado locomotive crossing the Guyandotte River, killing the engineer and six bridge workers.

subject: Habematolel Pomo
summary: A Northern Pomo tribe that survived massacre, forced relocation, and federal termination rebuilt itself from scratch, reclaimed its land, opened a casino, and became one of Lake County's most significant employers and philanthropists.

subject: Haddington Island (British Columbia)
summary: A small volcanic island in British Columbia's Broughton Strait whose quarried stone built the province's Parliament Buildings, the Hotel Vancouver, and some of the most enduring facades on the West Coast.

subject: Hamilton Island
summary: The largest inhabited island of the Whitsundays runs on golf buggies and jet aircraft, a former grazing lease turned full-scale resort town with its own airport, marina and a August regatta that draws the sailing world.

subject: Harkers Island, North Carolina
summary: The North Carolina island where people still say "hoi toide" instead of "high tide" - home of the Core Sound Waterfowl Museum, an unlikely Latter-day Saints stronghold, and the Earl C. Davis Memorial Bridge.

story.title: Harrison's Cave: The Underground River That Built a Cathedral

subject: Harrison's Cave
summary: Beneath the central uplands of Barbados, an active limestone cave system stretches over a mile long, where running water still sculpts stalactites, stalagmites, and a cavern called the Great Hall that rises fifty feet overhead.

subject: Hatfield Forest
summary: The only intact medieval royal hunting forest in England - 800 ancient trees, fallow deer, and an 18th-century shell house, all within a few miles of Stansted Airport.

subject: Haw River
summary: A 110-mile Piedmont river named in Catawban for the foothills it cuts through - mill-powered, once poisoned, now slowly drinking itself clean.

story.title: Henry Morgan's Raid on Lake Maracaibo

subject: Henry Morgan's raid on Lake Maracaibo
summary: In 1669, English buccaneer Henry Morgan sacked the Spanish towns on Lake Maracaibo, destroyed a pursuing war fleet with a single fireship, and then tricked his way past the fortress guarding the exit -- returning to Jamaica with a fortune and a legend.

story.title: Historic Wintersburg in Huntington Beach, California

subject: Historic Wintersburg in Huntington Beach, California
summary: A National Treasure site where Japanese American pioneers established goldfish farms and a mission church before Executive Order 9066 sent them to internment camps.

subject: Hog Island Light
summary: A 194-foot lighthouse on Virginia's shifting barrier islands that stood for barely half a century before the Atlantic swallowed the ground beneath it -- its massive Fresnel lens the only survivor.

subject: Holkham National Nature Reserve
summary: England's largest national nature reserve, where 50,000 pink-footed geese winter and an Iron Age fort once stood at the end of a tidal spit on the Norfolk coast.

subject: Holy Island, Anglesey
summary: An island off an island, where Neolithic long houses, Bronze Age standing stones, Iron Age hut circles, and the port for Dublin ferries coexist on a landscape so dense with sacred sites that the English named it simply 'Holy.'

subject: Holy Trinity Church, Saibai Island
summary: Built over 19 years from burnt coral, mangrove timber, and Wongai plum by Saibai Islanders and missionaries, this heritage-listed church stands 12 metres from the waterline, looking directly across to New Guinea.

subject: Honeymoon Bay, British Columbia
summary: A Cowichan Lake mill town named for a honeymoon that never happened, built by a lumber company, and emptied when the mill shut down.

subject: Hormuz Island
summary: A 600-million-year-old salt dome island in the Strait of Hormuz, where red ochre beaches, a Portuguese fortress, and 40,000-year-old stone tools converge.

subject: Horn Island
summary: The air gateway to Australia's Torres Strait, Horn Island carries scars from Japanese bombing raids and the quiet persistence of the Kaurareg people who built their village here when no one else would have them.

story.title: Hudson Valley: Where American Art Discovered American Landscape

subject: Hudson Valley
summary: The New York valley where painters created the first distinctly American art movement - where Thomas Cole found the sublime in Catskill scenery, where Frederic Church built an artist's castle at Olana, and where the landscapes that taught Americans to value wilderness still invite contemplation.

subject: Hung Shing Yeh Beach
summary: Lamma Island's most beloved beach sits between a power station and the open sea, drawing swimmers, hikers, and weekenders to a shore that holds, in its sand, a forgotten chapter of Hong Kong's refugee history.

subject: Iimori Mountain
summary: A hillside memorial near Aizuwakamatsu where twenty teenage samurai of the Byakkotai -- the White Tiger Corps -- committed ritual suicide in 1868 after mistakenly believing their castle had fallen, a tragedy compounded by monuments gifted from Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany.

subject: Ikaros (Failaka Island)
summary: The only surviving Greek fortress in the Persian Gulf, built on a Kuwaiti island that Alexander the Great named after Icarus and where a temple to Artemis once protected the local wildlife by sacred decree.

subject: Inishbofin Island
summary: Eight kilometers off the Connemara coast: an island whose name means White Cow, whose seventh-century Saxon monks couldn't get along with their Irish counterparts, whose harbor is guarded by a Cromwellian star fort that doubled as a jail for Catholic priests, and whose airport has never landed a plane.

subject: Iona Island (British Columbia)
summary: A sewage treatment plant at the mouth of the Fraser River, under the approach to Vancouver's airport, is one of the greatest birding sites in Canada -- and you can walk four kilometres out to sea on top of the outfall pipe.

subject: Island Hermitage
summary: The first Theravada Buddhist monastery established by and for Westerners, founded in 1911 on an island in a Sri Lankan lagoon, twice destroyed by world wars, twice rebuilt, and still operating today.

subject: Issaquah Valley Trolley
summary: A heritage streetcar cobbled together from Lisbon trolleys, a failed Colorado resort scheme, and the stubborn optimism of small-town preservationists, the Issaquah Valley Trolley rattled along old freight tracks for two decades before the pandemic silenced it for good.

subject: Jacumba Hot Springs, California
summary: A high-desert town at 2,829 feet near the Mexican border — known for 104°F natural hot springs, a massacre in 1880, a grand hotel that burned in 1983, and the slow unraveling that followed when the interstate bypassed it.

subject: Jerejak Island
summary: A tiny island off Penang that cycled through roles as quarantine station, leper colony, tuberculosis sanatorium, and maximum-security prison before reinventing itself as a resort.

subject: Jiaozhou Bay
summary: The natural harbor that drew German warships in 1897, sparked a student movement that changed China in 1919, and is now spanned by what was once the world's longest bridge over water.

subject: Jordan River, British Columbia
summary: A Spanish chaplain's name, a hydroelectric plant that once housed a thousand workers, a wartime radar post, and a cold-water surf break, all crowded onto one river mouth on Vancouver Island's southwest coast.

subject: KNSM Island
summary: A man-made breakwater that became Amsterdam's busiest steamship terminal, then a squatters' republic, then one of the most ambitious experiments in 1990s European housing.

subject: Karkar Island
summary: An oval volcano in the Bismarck Sea with two nested calderas, 70,000 Lutherans, cacao plantations, and a hospital where rotating German doctors still arrive from abroad.

story.title: Kasugayama Primeval Forest: A Thousand Years Uncut

subject: Kasugayama Primeval Forest
summary: A 250-hectare old-growth forest behind Nara's Kasuga Grand Shrine, protected from logging and hunting since 841 CE by imperial decree, now one of the rarest primeval ecosystems surviving within a major Japanese city.

subject: Kat O (Crooked Island)
summary: Once Hong Kong's gateway to China, Kat O is a Hakka fishing island in Mirs Bay whose crooked shoreline shelters three cannons, a revered Tin Hau temple, and one of the territory's most important marine fish culture zones.

subject: Kawgun Cave
summary: A limestone cave temple in Kayin State where thousands of tiny Buddha statues cover the walls -- placed there over centuries, some by a queen consort fleeing the fall of a kingdom.

subject: Kenting National Forest Recreation Area
summary: A living museum of ancient coral reefs turned jungle, where limestone caves and 300-meter canyon walls reveal Taiwan's deep geological past.

subject: Keys Desert Queen Ranch
summary: Bill Keys arrived in Joshua Tree in 1910 and spent six decades building a ranch, a reputation, and a legal record that included a manslaughter conviction — and a pardon won with help from the author of Perry Mason.

subject: Kharg Island
summary: A small Iranian island in the Persian Gulf where ancient Achaemenid inscriptions, Nabataean-style rock tombs, and Nestorian crosses share the landscape with the ruins of what was once the world's largest offshore oil terminal.

subject: Kitakami River
summary: The largest river in the Tohoku region splits into two mouths, runs dam-free for most of its length, and hosts one of Japan's most celebrated cherry blossom festivals.

subject: Kiyotsu Gorge
summary: One of Japan's three great canyons, where 16-million-year-old volcanic columns rise above emerald water and a 750-meter tunnel ends in a mirrored pool that blurs the line between rock and reflection.

subject: Klamath River
summary: A 263-mile river reborn: after a century of dams, the Klamath witnessed the largest dam removal in American history, and salmon returned within months.

subject: Kowloon Bay
summary: A bay that Hong Kong's most legendary airport carved in two — and is still reinventing itself decades after the last plane departed.

subject: Krishna River
summary: India's third-longest river begins as a trickle from a cow-shaped spout in a temple at Mahabaleshwar and flows 1,400 kilometers east across the Deccan Plateau to the Bay of Bengal, sustaining 80 million people along the way.

story.title: Kuraman Island: The Tiger's Lair of Borneo

subject: Kuraman Island
summary: A small Malaysian island in Brunei Bay that once inspired an Italian novelist's pirate tales, sheltered refugees, and still guards a British lighthouse built at the turn of the twentieth century.

subject: Kure Beach
summary: A narrow strand on Pleasure Island whose century-old fishing pier survived hurricanes, U-boats, and the bromine-from-seawater plant that put it on the map.

subject: Lake Ashi
summary: A volcanic crater lake born from a catastrophic mountain collapse 3,000 years ago, now famous for its reflected views of Mount Fuji, pirate ship cruises, and a lakeside shrine gate rising from the water.

subject: Lake Bled
summary: A glacial lake in Slovenia's Julian Alps with a fairy-tale island church, a thousand-year-old clifftop castle, and hand-built boats whose oarsmen descend from families granted exclusive rights by Maria Theresa in 1740.

story.title: Lake Borobudur: The Vanished Waters That Rewrite History

subject: Lake Borobudur
summary: A century-long scientific debate over whether the world's largest Buddhist temple once sat beside - or even within - an ancient lake, finally resolved by clay sediments, pollen grains, and a volcano named Merapi.

subject: Lake Chelan
summary: America's third-deepest lake stretches 55 miles into the Cascades, accessible by ferry from a sun-drenched resort town to the roadless wilderness of Stehekin.

subject: Lake Crescent Lodge
summary: A 1915 lakeside resort where FDR spent a night that helped create Olympic National Park, surviving demolition plans to become one of the great national park lodges.

subject: Lake Durusu
summary: Lake Durusu — also known as Lake Terkos — sits behind a narrow strip of land from the Black Sea, supplying a fifth of Istanbul's drinking water from a basin that was once a pirates' lair and a Genoese monastery ground.

subject: Lake Edward Sanatorium
summary: A tuberculosis hospital built in the Quebec wilderness in 1904, where there was no road, no electricity, and no telephone -- only a railway, a lake, and the belief that altitude could cure the sick.

subject: Lake Hibara
summary: A volcanic lake born from catastrophe, where the ruins of a submerged Edo-period village and its ghostly torii gate lie beneath the shimmering surface.

subject: Lake Lemuria
summary: A pit dug for salt filled with water, turned an impossible shade of pink, and became a healing resort named after a lost continent.

subject: Lake Manapouri
summary: New Zealand's second-deepest lake, where a Maori legend of grief shaped the name, a hydroelectric power station was carved 200 meters underground, and a national environmental movement was born to keep the waters from rising.

subject: Lake McClure
summary: Named for the engineer who helped blaze the John Muir Trail, this Sierra Nevada reservoir hides a drowned dam beneath its surface and draws hang gliders who ride thermals above its waters 320 days a year.

subject: Lake Murray (California)
summary: A San Diego reservoir that began as an earthen dam in 1894, survived a rainmaker's flood in 1916, and now serves as an aeronautical reporting point for a nearby airport.

subject: Lake Murray (South Carolina)
summary: When the Saluda Dam was completed in 1930, it was the largest earthen dam in the world and created the largest man-made reservoir on Earth - all to flood a German-Swiss farming valley that had been settled since the 1750s.

subject: Lake Mweru
summary: A freshwater lake on the Congo River system where Greek fishermen from the Dodecanese once ran steam-powered boats, Arab traders operated from an island fortress, and the border between two colonial empires was drawn through waters that local kingdoms had controlled for centuries.

subject: Lake Nasser
summary: The vast reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam that gave Egypt its irrigation and electricity - and drowned the homeland of tens of thousands of Nubians whose villages still lie beneath the water.

subject: Lake Pedder
summary: A wild Tasmanian lake with a vast pink-quartz beach was drowned beneath a dam in 1972, and the grief over its loss helped launch the modern environmental movement.

subject: Lake Quinault Lodge
summary: Built in 1926 on the southeast shore of Lake Quinault, this rustic cedar-shingled lodge was designed by Robert Reamer -- the same architect behind Yellowstone's Old Faithful Inn -- and has survived fire, wartime closure, and changing owners to remain one of the Pacific Northwest's great wilderness retreats.

subject: Lambay Island
summary: A privately owned 2.5 km² island five kilometres off the Dublin coast, with 50,000 nesting guillemots, a colony of wild wallabies, and a Lutyens-designed castle.

story.title: Lascaux Cave: The Sistine Chapel of Prehistory

subject: Lascaux Cave
summary: Where four teenagers chasing their dog discovered 17,000-year-old cave paintings so magnificent they're called the Sistine Chapel of Prehistory - now sealed from visitors to preserve them.

subject: Lepida Gorge
summary: A compact gorge on Mount Parnon that hides two waterfalls — 70 meters and 45 meters high — carved from a plateau that feeds Malevi Monastery and empties into the Arcadian landscape below.

subject: Lhasa River
summary: The longest tributary of the Yarlung Tsangpo, a 450-kilometer lifeline that carved Tibet's political and spiritual heartland, where Heinrich Harrer once directed a fleet of yak-skin boats to protect the Dalai Lama's summer palace from floods.

subject: Lian Island
summary: The largest island in Lianyungang and Jiangsu's only AAAA-rated seashore attraction, connected to the mainland by China's longest sea dyke and crowned by a bronze statue of Deng Xiaoping.

subject: Liaodong Peninsula
summary: A contested finger of land jutting into the Yellow Sea, the Liaodong Peninsula has served as a gateway between China, Korea, and the ambitions of empires for over two millennia.

subject: Lindeman Island
summary: A drowned mountain in the southern Whitsundays, Lindeman Island once held Australia's only Club Med - then a cyclone closed it, and the empty resort sat waiting through a decade of broken plans.

subject: Linville Gorge
summary: A practical traveler's view of the 11,786-acre Linville Gorge Wilderness, where the bridge has been washed out for years, the campsites require reservations a month ahead, and the river crossings get you wet.

subject: Liugong Island
summary: A forested island at the mouth of Weihai Bay, Liugong was the birthplace and graveyard of China's first modern navy -- now a museum and memorial to a fleet that changed East Asian history.

subject: Lizard Island
summary: A granite island on the Great Barrier Reef where a stingray-shaped sacred place, Cook's desperate lookout, a luxury resort, and one of Australia's saddest frontier tragedies all share the same shore.

subject: Llovizna Falls
summary: A waterfall on the Caroni River in Venezuela whose very name means drizzle, Llovizna Falls pulses with the rhythms of a dam upstream, roaring back to full glory each time the floodgates open.

subject: Long Beach Naval Shipyard
summary: On Terminal Island, a Navy shipyard lifted battleships out of the water with a captured German crane, refurbished the Iowa-class behemoths that had won the Pacific war, and then closed in 1997 when the Cold War economy came undone.

subject: Long Island, Bahamas
summary: A slender Bahamian island split by the Tropic of Cancer, where a 200-meter-deep blue hole plunges into the earth and Loyalist plantation ruins crumble under tropical overgrowth.

subject: Longqing Gorge
summary: A dramatic canyon north of Beijing where open-top boats glide beneath towering rock walls and winter brings an ice sculpture festival worthy of comparison to Harbin.

subject: Lonquimay (volcano)
summary: On Christmas Day 1988 this Andean stratovolcano tore open a new vent and spent thirteen months building an entirely new cone — which Chileans named Navidad, for the day it was born.

subject: Louisiade Archipelago
summary: A scatter of coral-rimmed islands at Papua New Guinea's southeastern tip, where sailing canoes still cross open ocean and visitors mostly arrive under sail.

subject: Mackinac Island
summary: The island that banned cars - where motorized vehicles have been prohibited since 1898, horse-drawn carriages still provide transport, and time seems frozen in a Victorian resort era of grand hotels and fudge shops.

subject: Malcolm Knapp Research Forest
summary: Fifty-one square kilometres of Coast Mountains rainforest that looks like wilderness and works like a laboratory — and once held a telescope whose mirror was spinning mercury.

subject: Manila Bay
summary: A vast natural harbor on the western coast of Luzon, Manila Bay has served as the Philippines' gateway for centuries -- witness to galleon trade, naval battles, and an ongoing struggle between urbanization and ecology.

subject: Mar Chiquita Lake
summary: South America's largest salt lake, where hundreds of thousands of flamingos turn the water pink and a flooded grand hotel rots on the shore.

subject: Maria Island
summary: A car-free island off Tasmania's east coast where wombats graze among convict ruins, sandstone cliffs run with colour, and a controversial rescue went wrong.

subject: Marmara Islands
summary: Close enough to Istanbul to reach by ferry on a whim, the Marmara Islands offer beaches, ancient marble quarries, and the rare pleasure of a Turkish island destination that has remained almost entirely off the international tourist radar.

subject: Martins Beach
summary: A hidden cove on the San Mateo County coast became the epicenter of California's fiercest battle over public beach access when a Silicon Valley billionaire locked the gate.

subject: Maungawhau / Mount Eden
summary: Auckland's highest natural point is a 196-metre volcanic cone whose 50-metre-deep crater was once believed to house a deity guarding the secrets hidden in the earth.

story.title: Merced Falls: The Town the River Forgot

subject: Merced Falls
summary: A Gold Rush-era mill town on the Merced River that thrived as a gateway to Yosemite, only to be undone twice -- first by a railroad that bypassed it, then by a dam that drowned its namesake rapids.

subject: Mesachie Lake
summary: A Vancouver Island company town whose houses arrived by rail in pieces, whose name means evil in Chinook Jargon, and which survived the mill that built it by more than half a century.

subject: Middle Island, Hong Kong
summary: A small island 100 meters off Hong Kong Island's southern shore, Middle Island belongs to sailors, a temple deity, and anyone willing to catch the sampan ferry.

subject: Mikimoto Pearl Island
summary: A tiny island in Ise Bay where a noodle seller's son cracked the secret of cultured pearls in 1893, upending a global luxury market and building an empire that still dazzles visitors with a Liberty Bell made from 12,250 pearls.

subject: Mission Point (Mackinac Island)
summary: The southeast corner of Mackinac Island where Jesuit missionaries landed in the 1630s, a British fort commander built a doomed summer house on a crumbling cliff, and a succession of missions, colleges, and film studios left layers of reinvention on a single stretch of shore.

subject: Mona Island Tramway
summary: A forgotten 1890s narrow-gauge railway on a remote Caribbean island, built through caves and up cliff faces to construct a lighthouse, then hauled by a stubborn donkey named Macario until automobiles made it obsolete.

story.title: Mona and Monito Islands Nature Reserve

subject: Mona and Monito Islands Nature Reserve
summary: Puerto Rico's largest protected natural area, a pair of remote limestone islands in the Mona Passage where critically endangered iguanas, ancient Taino cave art, and rusting guano-mining ruins share space with the Caribbean's largest hawksbill turtle nesting site.

subject: Monastyrskyi Island
summary: A granite-and-sand island in the middle of the Dnieper where Stone Age hunters left their tools, legend placed a lost Byzantine monastery, and a golden-domed church now anchors Dnipro's favorite park.

subject: Montara State Beach
summary: One of California's cleanest beaches, where the Chiguan people once gathered food, a lighthouse now operates as a hostel, and trails connect the shore to mountain summits.

subject: Montego Bay
summary: Jamaica's second city earned its name from the Spanish word for lard, traded its sugarcane fields for all-inclusive resorts, and now runs the busiest airport in the English-speaking Caribbean.

subject: Montezuma Hot Springs
summary: A cluster of thermal springs near Las Vegas, New Mexico, that inspired indigenous healing traditions, a railroad-era luxury hotel that burned down three times, and folklore linking Billy the Kid and Jesse James to its steaming pools.

subject: Montserrat (mountain)
summary: A serrated mountain of pink conglomerate rock rises from the Catalan lowlands like a row of broken teeth, sheltering a thousand-year-old monastery and inspiring devotion across centuries.

subject: Morongo Valley
summary: A high desert gateway community where movie cowboys, championship mountain bikers, and working-class families share a valley that fire has tested and the canyon next door has made famous.

subject: Mount Agung
summary: Bali's highest peak and holiest mountain, Mount Agung is an active stratovolcano whose catastrophic 1963 eruption killed over 1,500 people yet miraculously spared the island's most sacred temple.

subject: Mount Arrowsmith Biosphere Region
summary: A UNESCO biosphere reserve on Vancouver Island built not around untouched wilderness but around a logged landscape growing back, governed by an unlikely coalition of First Nations, towns, a university and timber companies.

subject: Mount Ashland Ski Area
summary: A community-owned ski area in Southern Oregon where grassroots activism twice saved a mountain from corporate abandonment, creating a nonprofit model that became the world's first STOKE-certified sustainable ski resort.

subject: Mount Aspiring / Tititea
summary: Named twice - once for a Waitaha chief, once by a Victorian surveyor who saw it from afar - this 3,033-metre pyramid stands as the highest peak in New Zealand outside the Mount Cook region.

subject: Mount Bachelor ski area
summary: Oregon's premier ski resort wraps around an active volcano, offering 360-degree skiing from a summit just steps below the crater rim.

subject: Mount Bandai
summary: An active stratovolcano in Fukushima whose 1888 eruption -- the first major natural disaster of modern Japan -- killed 477 people, obliterated the summit, and triggered the Japanese Red Cross's first peacetime relief mission.

subject: Mount Batten
summary: A 24-metre rocky outcrop on a Plymouth peninsula that was a Bronze Age trading port, a Tudor fort, and the RAF station where T. E. Lawrence served out his final years.

subject: Mount Cangyan
summary: A mountain where a temple hall perches on a stone arch bridge spanning a cliff-face gorge, Mount Cangyan blurs the line between natural wonder and human ambition -- and became a star of international cinema.

subject: Mount Cuthbert Township and Smelter
summary: A copper boomtown of a thousand souls that rose and died inside a single decade, leaving the most impressive smelter ruins in North Queensland scattered along a creek in Kalkadoon country.

subject: Mount Damavand
summary: Iran's highest peak and a dormant stratovolcano rising 5,609 meters, Mount Damavand is the prison of a chained dragon in Persian myth and the dome of the world in Persian poetry.

subject: Mount Davidson (California)
summary: San Francisco's highest point wears a 103-foot concrete cross that survived a constitutional lawsuit, a Dirty Harry film shoot, and the theft of an Armenian genocide memorial plaque.

subject: Mount Ecclesia
summary: On a high mesa above Oceanside's San Luis Rey River Valley, the Rosicrucian Fellowship built a spiritual campus in 1911 after a mystical vision — and the federal government later built the city's first post office just to handle their mail.

story.title: Mount Gay Rum: Three Centuries in a Glass

subject: Mount Gay Rum
summary: The world's oldest commercial rum distillery has been producing spirit on Barbados since at least 1703, its history inseparable from the island's sugarcane plantations, parliamentary politics, and deep ties to the sailing world.

subject: Mount Grace Priory
summary: The best-preserved Carthusian charterhouse in England, founded in 1398: a monastery built for silence, where each monk lived alone in a small house with a garden, a latrine, and a hatch through which food arrived without a word.

subject: Mount Guanyin (Dongguan)
summary: A 488-meter forested peak on the Dongguan-Shenzhen border, crowned by a 33-meter seated Guanyin statue and home to China's first ancient tree museum.

subject: Mount Haguro
summary: The smallest and most accessible of Japan's Three Mountains of Dewa, where a 600-year-old five-story pagoda and 2,446 stone steps through ancient cedar forest lead to a shrine that venerates all three sacred peaks.

subject: Mount Hamilton (California)
summary: The highest point in Santa Clara County, home to the first permanently occupied mountaintop observatory in the world, where a piano-maker's fortune built a telescope and a preacher's enthusiasm named a peak.

subject: Mount Hebo Air Force Station
summary: A Cold War radar station perched atop a 3,154-foot Oregon peak where the weather destroyed three giant radomes in six years - and the Air Force kept rebuilding them, because the Soviets weren't going to wait for better conditions.

subject: Mount Heng (Shanxi)
summary: The least visited and least commercialized of China's Five Sacred Mountains, Mount Heng in Shanxi is where Taoist pilgrimage meets genuine wilderness -- and where a temple hangs impossibly from a cliff.

subject: Mount Hombori
summary: Mali's highest point is a flat-topped sandstone fortress rising from the Sahel, its cliff-guarded plateau a green island of life above a parched plain.

subject: Mount Hope, New South Wales
summary: A copper boomtown that twice rose from its own ashes on the Kidman Way, now reduced to a handful of people and one stubborn pub with the only concrete bar in New South Wales.

subject: Mount Isa Mine Early Infrastructure
summary: A lone prospector's 1923 lead find grew into one of Australia's great mines - and its earliest bones survive: a steel headframe on the skyline, a power station with twin black stacks, and a small stone weir that once meant survival.

subject: Mount Ithome
summary: The fortress-mountain that sheltered the Messenians through three centuries of Spartan domination — and became the sacred heart of their liberation.

subject: Mount Khajeh
summary: A flat-topped basalt hill rising from a vanishing lake in eastern Iran, where Zoroastrian prophecy, Sassanid murals, and an Islamic shrine share a single volcanic island.

subject: Mount Kunyu
summary: A sacred mountain range on the Shandong Peninsula where the Quanzhen School of Taoism was founded in the 12th century, still drawing seekers of martial arts and immortality alike.

story.title: Mount Koya: The Living Monastery in the Clouds

subject: Mount Kōya
summary: For over twelve centuries, monks have carried meals twice daily to the mausoleum of Kukai on Mount Koya, honoring the belief that the founder of Shingon Buddhism remains alive in eternal meditation -- a ritual that anchors one of Japan's most extraordinary sacred settlements.

subject: Mount Lehman, Abbotsford
summary: A Fraser Valley farming community that began at a riverboat wharf in the 1870s, moved itself to meet the interurban railway in 1910, and kept its school, church and hall running for well over a century after the town around them dissolved.

subject: Mount Mithridat
summary: The hill at the heart of Kerch, named for a king who defied Rome and died on its slopes, crowned by a grand stone staircase and a memorial to the soldiers of a later war.

subject: Mount Nokogiri (Chiba)
summary: A 329-meter quarry-scarred mountain on the Boso Peninsula where Edo-period stonemasons carved cliffs into jagged teeth, and a master sculptor spent 21 years placing 1,500 stone disciples along the walking paths of a temple founded in 725 AD.

subject: Mount Pieter Botte
summary: A granite tower crowned by a sheer boulder summit, rising from the Daintree rainforest behind Cape Tribulation - to the Kuku Yalanji, the elder and younger sisters in stone.

subject: Mount Pulaski, Illinois
summary: A brick Greek Revival building in Illinois transitioned from a bustling legal hub to a multipurpose utility shed before being restored as a shrine to Abraham Lincoln.

story.title: Mount Rushmore: The Mountain They Carved Into Presidents

subject: Mount Rushmore
summary: The Black Hills memorial where Gutzon Borglum blasted 60-foot faces of Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, and Lincoln into a granite mountainside - celebrating democracy on land taken from the Sioux, unfinished by design or budget depending on who's telling the story.

story.title: Mount Ryozen: Where Tengu Wrestle and Monks Once Prayed

subject: Mount Ryōzen
summary: A sacred basalt peak in northern Fukushima where an ancient Buddhist temple, a doomed medieval castle, and a flat rock said to be a tengu wrestling ring share the same hiking trail through some of Tohoku's finest autumn foliage.

subject: Mount St John Anti-Aircraft Battery
summary: On a low hill west of Townsville's airfield, four concrete gun platforms still face the sky they once defended against Japanese bombers in 1942.

subject: Mount Stewart
summary: A grand National Trust house on Strangford Lough where Castlereagh shaped post-Napoleonic Europe, a Marchioness designed one of Ireland's most extraordinary sub-tropical gardens, and a Marquess once entertained Hitler's ambassador.

subject: Mount Sutro
summary: Originally Mount Parnassus, this 909-foot hill in central San Francisco wears a dense eucalyptus forest planted by Adolph Sutro and carries the city's most recognizable antenna tower.

story.title: Mount Togakushi: The Door the Gods Threw Away

subject: Mount Togakushi
summary: A 1,904-meter peak in Nagano whose name means 'hiding door' -- rooted in the myth of the sun goddess Amaterasu's cave and the stone door hurled across Japan -- Mount Togakushi is sacred ground for Shinto pilgrims, Shugendo practitioners, and the legendary Togakure school of ninja.

subject: Mount Tzouhalem
summary: A mountain above Duncan named first for sunlight, then for the Cowichan Valley's most argued-over man, and topped for sixty years by a cross that someone cut down with a grinder in July 2021.

subject: Mount Vernon Arsenal
summary: A single compound in rural Alabama that served as a munitions factory, a Confederate stronghold, a prison for Geronimo and his Apache followers, and eventually a state psychiatric hospital.

subject: Mount Vernon Trail
summary: Eighteen miles of paved shared-use path along the Virginia bank of the Potomac - from George Washington's house at Mount Vernon to Theodore Roosevelt Island, with airplanes overhead and the Washington Monument across the river.

subject: Mountain Lodge
summary: The summer residence of Hong Kong's governors on Victoria Peak — battered by typhoons, inhabited by eccentrics, demolished after the war, and now a public garden where the masonry platform still marks where power once rested.

subject: Mountain Play Association
summary: A nonprofit that has produced outdoor theater at the Cushing Memorial Amphitheatre on Mount Tamalpais since 1913.

subject: Mudge Island
summary: A Gulf Island of 140 people with no ferry, no bridge, and fibre-optic internet, guarded by a tidal gate where the current runs to nine knots.

subject: Muir Beach, California
summary: A small coastal community and beach on the Pacific Ocean, surrounded by the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.

story.title: The Nanaimo River: Lifeblood of the Coast Salish

subject: Nanaimo River
summary: A 78-kilometer river flowing from the Vancouver Island Ranges to the Strait of Georgia, home to five ancient Coast Salish village sites, North America's first purpose-built bungee jumping bridge, and some of the best steelhead fishing in Canada.

subject: Neah Bay, Washington
summary: The Makah people's ancestral home at the northwestern tip of the contiguous United States, where world-class halibut fishing meets a museum preserving a village frozen in time by a mudslide around 1750.

subject: New Hanover Island
summary: The Lavongai people's volcanic island off northern New Ireland is known for the 1964 election in which its voters wrote in Lyndon Johnson's name - an act of political theater that anthropologists still argue about.

subject: Nicomen Island
summary: A Fraser River island with the mainland's first rural post office, a municipality that existed only on paper, and thirty-five kilometres of dike standing between its farms and the water.

story.title: North Shore Beach and Yacht Club

subject: North Shore Beach and Yacht Club
summary: Albert Frey designed it, Frank Sinatra visited it, and Linkin Park photographed its ruin — the North Shore Beach and Yacht Club traced the Salton Sea's entire arc from glamour to catastrophe in a single building.

subject: North Thormanby Island
summary: A Sunshine Coast island named after a Derby-winning racehorse, joined to its twin by a sand bridge at low tide, and holding one of British Columbia's rarest habitats along its beaches.

subject: North and South Brother Islands (New York City)
summary: Two forbidden islands in New York's East River where Typhoid Mary was quarantined, a steamship disaster killed over a thousand, and nature has slowly reclaimed the ruins of a quarantine hospital.

subject: Nunobiki Falls
summary: One of Japan's three sacred waterfalls hides in plain sight, a fifteen-minute walk from the bullet train station in downtown Kobe -- where tenth-century poets once held verse contests beneath the cascade.

subject: Oak Island (North Carolina)
summary: A 13-mile barrier island at the mouth of the Cape Fear River, guarded by an aviation-warning lighthouse and the dredged-out scar of the Intracoastal Waterway.

subject: Oak Island Light
summary: One of the last lighthouses built in America, the Oak Island Light guards the mouth of the Cape Fear River with a tricolor concrete tower whose black and white bands are not painted on but mixed into the concrete itself.

subject: Omey Island
summary: A tidal island off Connemara you can drive to twice a day across exposed sand - host to a sixth-century monastery, a medieval church the wind buried until 1981, an annual horse race on the beach, and a poet's octagonal retreat that still stands.

subject: Orange Valley Social Institute
summary: In 1897, amid the hat factories and tenement streets of Orange Valley, New Jersey, a settlement house opened its doors — not by its board of directors, but by the workers and families it was built to serve.

subject: Osum Canyon
summary: A 26-kilometer gorge carved over millions of years through southern Albania, where spring snowmelt turns Class II rapids into a corridor of waterfalls and eroded rock formations with names like the Cathedral and the Demon's Door.

story.title: Our Lady of the Sacred Heart Church, Thursday Island

subject: Our Lady of the Sacred Heart Church, Thursday Island
summary: Possibly the oldest surviving building on Thursday Island, this timber church built by French and Italian missionaries features hand-painted trompe l'oeil murals and Gothic arched windows of red, blue, and green glass.

subject: Outlying Islands, Hong Kong
summary: Hong Kong's 263 outlying islands stretch from the airport runways of Lantau to the uninhabited rock stacks of the south, forming a rural counterweight to one of the world's most urbanized coastlines.

subject: Palm Beach, Aruba
summary: Named after a coconut plantation captain's nostalgia for Florida, Palm Beach transformed from Caquetio fishing grounds to Aruba's glittering high-rise hotel strip -- with a Dutch windmill and a bird sanctuary tucked improbably between the resorts.

subject: Palmaria (island)
summary: Liguria's largest island guards the entrance to the Gulf of La Spezia with military ruins, a cave holding 5,000-year-old human burials, and a quarry of rare black marble streaked with gold.

subject: Palmer River Gold Company Dredge
summary: A 350-ton steam dredge, hauled overland by truck and built in the riverbed in 1930, now lies half-buried in the sand of the Palmer River, the earliest surviving steam dredge in Queensland and a monument to a gamble that never paid off.

subject: Pan's Cave (Haidari)
summary: In a wooded hollow near the Daphni Monastery, a small conical cave once smoked with offerings to the goat-god Pan - a shepherd's shrine that outlived the gods it honored.

subject: Panjshir Valley
summary: Afghanistan's Valley of the Five Lions -- a nearly 100-kilometer gorge through the Hindu Kush that has served as a mineral treasure house, a military stronghold, and a symbol of resistance across four decades of war.

subject: Paradise Island
summary: Once called Hog Island, this 685-acre sliver off Nassau's shore was transformed by a supermarket heir with Riviera tastes, traded between moguls like a poker chip, and is now home to the Atlantis resort and a medieval French monastery reassembled stone by stone.

subject: Paraguaná Peninsula
summary: A Caribbean peninsula that was once a separate island, Paraguana is connected to mainland Venezuela by a slender ribbon of sand and houses one of the world's largest oil refinery complexes.

subject: Patos Island Light
summary: A small white tower on the northernmost point of the San Juan Islands, where a lighthouse keeper raised a family of thirteen children and one of them wrote it all down.

subject: Penelakut Island
summary: The island carried a British captain's name for 159 years. In that time it survived a massacre, a naval bombardment, and a residential school its survivors called Alcatraz.

subject: Penn Center (Saint Helena Island, South Carolina)
summary: The first school in the South built for freed people became a secret retreat where Martin Luther King Jr. worked on his 'I Have A Dream' speech -- and it still stands on a Sea Island where Gullah culture lives on.

story.title: Petrified Forest: Where Ancient Trees Turned to Jewels

subject: Petrified Forest
summary: The Arizona landscape where 200-million-year-old logs became stone - crystallized so perfectly that colors blaze through cross-sections, lying scattered across a painted desert that looks like time itself became visible.

story.title: Phillips' Ferry: Where a County Line Met the Current

subject: Phillips' Ferry
summary: A Gold Rush-era ferry crossing on the Merced River where an English immigrant built a livelihood hauling travelers across the water -- until a rival's bridge rendered his business obsolete.

subject: Phong Nha Cave
summary: A vast limestone underworld in central Vietnam where an underground river flows nearly 14 kilometers through cathedral-sized grottoes shaped over 400 million years.

subject: Phú Quý Island
summary: A remote Vietnamese island 100 kilometers offshore in the South China Sea, where 30,000 people live on volcanic rock between a colonial lighthouse and an abandoned military bunker.

subject: Pibor River
summary: A 320-kilometer river that starts at a colonial fort, drains 137,130 square kilometers of the Ethiopian highlands and South Sudanese plains, and carries its own small share of the White Nile into the world.

subject: Pie Island
summary: A mesa-topped island in Lake Superior named for a French meat pie, where silver prospectors, lighthouse keepers, and a 160-year land claim have all left their mark.

subject: Piel Island
summary: Twenty-six acres of grass and shingle in Morecambe Bay where the landlord of the pub is crowned the King of Piel and shipwrecked knights can still demand a bed.

subject: Piers Island
summary: A quiet Gulf Island of golf carts and footpaths that, for three years in the 1930s, held a federal penitentiary built for more than six hundred Doukhobors convicted of protesting without their clothes on.

subject: Playland-Not-At-The-Beach
summary: A volunteer-run museum in a former grocery store kept the spirit of San Francisco's lost amusement park alive for a decade, filling 10,000 square feet with pinball machines, carnival games, and artifacts rescued from the original Playland at the Beach.

subject: Plettenberg Bay
summary: A compact coastal resort on South Africa's Garden Route where whale watching, golden beaches, and proximity to ancient forests make it the region's most beach-focused stop.

subject: Poplar Forest
summary: Thomas Jefferson's octagonal retreat villa in Bedford County, Virginia — a National Historic Landmark built between 1806 and 1826 by enslaved laborers including James Hubbard, with a perfect-cube dining room beneath a skylight.

subject: Porcupine Gorge
summary: Queensland's 'Little Grand Canyon' near Hughenden, where a desert creek has cut more than 100 metres into banded sandstone to reveal 300 million years of Earth's history and the Pyramid rising from its floor.

subject: Powell River, British Columbia
summary: A mainland city reachable only by ferry or floatplane, Powell River built its identity around the world's largest paper mill, then reinvented itself as an arts capital when the mill fell silent.

subject: Priest Island
summary: A small, uninhabited Summer Isle that has sheltered a Celtic hermit, a vanishing stone circle, a writer in exile, and two fugitives who hid for nearly a year before the law caught up.

story.title: Protection Island: Pirate Parks, Floating Pubs, and Gallows Point

subject: Protection Island (Nanaimo)
summary: A small island in Nanaimo Harbour with 350 residents, no paved roads, Canada's only floating pub, parks named after literary pirates, and a history that includes colonial hangings, a dynamite ship explosion that shattered windows across Nanaimo, and a mining disaster that killed sixteen men.

subject: Qi'ao Island
summary: Thirteen kilometres from the center of Zhuhai, Qi'ao Island holds five thousand years of pottery in its bays, seventeen temples in its hills, a Song-dynasty village, and a nine-metre reunion statue on its shore — all wrapped in ninety-percent forest cover.

subject: Qixingtan Beach
summary: The crescent pebble shore north of Hualien carries two names and two histories: the original Qixingtan, erased to build an airport in 1936, and the displaced community that recreated it at a new location and kept the memory alive.

subject: Raine Island Beacon
summary: On a tiny coral cay at the outer edge of the Great Barrier Reef stands a stone tower built by convicts in 1844 — the oldest European structure in tropical Australia, and the lonely guardian of the world's greatest turtle rookery.

subject: Randalls and Wards Islands
summary: Two islands in the East River that were once separate -- home to asylums, hospitals, and potter's fields -- are now a single 530-acre expanse of parkland and public facilities, crossed by the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge and shadowed by the Hell Gate.

subject: Ratargul Swamp Forest
summary: Bangladesh's only freshwater swamp forest, Ratargul transforms twice a year: a submerged emerald cathedral during monsoon season and a muddy, exposed woodland in winter, earning it the local nickname 'the Sundarbans of Sylhet.'

subject: Red Lake shootings
summary: On March 21, 2005, a sixteen-year-old killed nine people and himself at two locations on the Red Lake Indian Reservation in northern Minnesota -- the deadliest school shooting in the United States since Columbine and still the worst in Minnesota history.

subject: Red Rock Island
summary: The only privately owned island in San Francisco Bay, a 5.8-acre uninhabited rock south of the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge where three counties meet.

subject: Repulse Bay
summary: A crescent of sand on Hong Kong Island's southern shore where the name's origin remains genuinely unknown, the hotel became a wartime hospital, and today the address commands some of the world's most extraordinary property prices.

subject: Repulse Bay Beach
summary: Repulse Bay Beach curves along Hong Kong Island's southern shore in a wide crescent of Grade 1-rated water, flanked by a goddess shrine and a famous apartment tower with a hole cut through it to let a dragon pass.

subject: Richmond River
summary: Rising in the Border Ranges and running 237 km past Casino and Lismore to the sea at Ballina, the Richmond River carried red cedar, drowned ships at its mouth, and remains the lifeblood of Bundjalung country.

subject: Richmond River Light
summary: Ballina's oldest surviving building is a squat stone lighthouse that has guided ships across one of the deadliest river mouths in New South Wales for nearly 150 years.

subject: Rikers Island
summary: New York City's notorious 413-acre jail complex, built on landfill and garbage in the East River, where decades of systemic abuse have prompted a historic decision to close the facility.

subject: Rio Vermelho State Forest
summary: A 190,000-hectare state forest in Rondonia that became a pawn in one of Brazil's most tangled conservation battles -- traded between governments, invaded by squatters, and partially drowned by a hydroelectric dam.

subject: River Lea
summary: Forty-two miles of chalk-stream water rising in Bedfordshire and ending in Bow Creek, the River Lea has been Roman ford, Saxon boundary, royal water supply, Victorian factory drain, and Olympic centerpiece.

subject: River Tamar
summary: The 61-mile river that nearly makes Cornwall an island, and that the devil — in Cornish legend — refused to cross.

subject: River Wear
summary: Sixty miles of Pennine water that gave Durham its cathedral, Sunderland its ships, and a Celtic name nobody can quite translate.

subject: Rocky Mount Mills
summary: The second cotton mill built in North Carolina, founded in 1816 with enslaved labor on the Tar River, survived the Civil War, two centuries of industrial change, and its own closure to become a thriving campus of breweries, restaurants, and boutique hotels.

subject: Rodeo Beach
summary: A dark-sand beach in the Marin Headlands where multicolored pebbles of chert, jasper, and agate wash ashore two miles west of the Golden Gate Bridge.

story.title: Round Island Light, Isles of Scilly

subject: Round Island Light, Isles of Scilly
summary: A Victorian lighthouse perched on a granite hump at the northern edge of Scilly, where storm petrels nest and a cat once gave away their secret.

subject: Runaway Bay, Jamaica
summary: A small Jamaican resort town whose name carries the weight of enslaved people's desperate flights to freedom, layered over centuries of colonial conquest, and now ringed by coral reefs where divers explore sunken aircraft known as the Ganja Planes.

subject: Rydal Mount
summary: The hillside house above Ambleside where William Wordsworth lived for 37 years - longer than anywhere else - and where he wrote with a view of two lakes and from a tiny outdoor hut.

subject: Sacramento Valley Station
summary: Sacramento's grand Renaissance Revival train station stands on ground that once held a Chinese immigrant community, a gateway where the transcontinental railroad's origin story meets modern California transit.

subject: Saint Helen's Island
summary: Named by Samuel de Champlain for his wife in 1611, this St. Lawrence River island has served as a seigneury, a military fort, a wartime prison camp, and the centerpiece of Expo 67 -- reshaped by subway excavation soil into the green heart of Montreal's playground.

subject: Saint Macdara's Island
summary: A sixty-acre granite island where local sailors still dip their sails three times in passing, and a tenth-century church has stone roof shingles cut to imitate wooden ones.

subject: Saladi Beach
summary: A 750-metre beach on the Argolic Gulf that briefly became Greece's first nudist resort in 1980, then sparked a confrontation between modernity and provincial tradition that left 160 people out of work and a ten-story hotel standing empty.

subject: Saldanha Bay
summary: A natural harbor named after a Portuguese captain who never actually visited it, Saldanha Bay has served as a refuge for merchant fleets, a battleground between empires, and now South Africa's primary iron ore export terminal.

story.title: Salt Lake City: The Mormon Capital at the Crossroads of the West

subject: Salt Lake City
summary: The city Brigham Young founded in 1847 when he declared 'This is the place,' where the Mormon Temple dominates the skyline, where the Great Salt Lake spreads to the west, and where the greatest snow on Earth falls on the Wasatch.

subject: Salton Sea Beach, California
summary: A small community on the western shore of the Salton Sea where the ruins of mid-century ambition slowly sink into salt-encrusted ground.

subject: Saluda River
summary: A 200-mile river born in the Blue Ridge that powers Lake Murray, threads through textile-mill ruins, and joins the Broad in downtown Columbia to form the Congaree.

story.title: Salvation Mountain: One Man's Painted Sermon in the Desert

subject: Salvation Mountain
summary: The California desert where a man spent 28 years painting a mountain with religious messages - 100,000 gallons of donated paint transformed a dirt hill into America's most surreal folk art monument.

subject: Salvation Mountain
summary: The psychedelic painted mountain built by one man in the California desert over 28 years - 150,000 gallons of paint proclaiming 'God Is Love' on a 50-foot tall folk art monument that the government once tried to condemn as toxic waste.

subject: Salvation Mountain
summary: Leonard Knight spent nearly three decades building a fifty-foot mountain of adobe, tires, and thousands of gallons of paint in the California desert, driven by nothing more than a desire to tell the world that God is love.

subject: San Lorenzo Island (Peru)
summary: Peru's largest island has no fresh water and no permanent residents, yet it has served as a pre-Columbian cemetery, a pirate hideout, a wartime refuge, and a prison for terrorist leaders.

subject: Saturna Island
summary: An aquarium sent a harpooner to East Point in 1964 to kill an orca for a sculpture. The whale survived the shot — and changed what the world believed about killer whales.

subject: Sea Lion Island
summary: The southernmost inhabited speck of the Falklands, where elephant seals battle on the beaches and a quiet memorial marks a wartime loss at sea.

subject: Sebatik Island
summary: A Borneo island split between Indonesia and Malaysia, where a house straddles two countries and the only evidence of a border are concrete piles buried every kilometre.

subject: Second Harvest of Silicon Valley
summary: The largest food bank in the San Francisco Bay Area feeds half a million people a month in the shadow of the world's wealthiest tech companies - and a quarter of its clients have college degrees.

subject: Sedef Island
summary: The mother-of-pearl island east of Büyükada — once a place of patriarchal exile, now a carefully protected private retreat with planted pine forests and a strict two-story building code.

subject: Shillay, Monach Islands
summary: The westernmost island of the Monach group off North Uist - an empty Atlantic outpost with a Stevenson-built red brick lighthouse and a keeper's carving that reads, simply, 'Eternity Oh Eternity.'

subject: Skellig Islands
summary: Two jagged rock pyramids rising from the Atlantic off Kerry's coast, where an ancient monastery, one of the world's largest gannet colonies, and a Star Wars temple coexist on the edge of Europe.

subject: Smith Island (Washington)
summary: A windswept speck in the Strait of Juan de Fuca where a lighthouse once crumbled into the sea and seabirds now outnumber all human visitors combined.

subject: Snowshoe Mountain
summary: A West Virginia ski resort with a backwards layout - the village sits at the top of the mountain instead of the bottom - built on a former logging clearcut that a North Carolina dentist thought might make a good ski hill.

subject: Snowy River
summary: The river Banjo Paterson made into a legend ran wild from Australia's highest peak to the sea, until a nation-building engineering scheme took 99 percent of its water away.

subject: Soko Islands
summary: The Soko Islands — once called the Fishing Net Islands — carry 6,000 years of human presence, from Neolithic stone tools to Tin Hau temple bells, now empty of people but protected as a marine park for Chinese white dolphins.

subject: Sol Duc Hot Springs
summary: A resort in Olympic National Park where geothermally heated pools have drawn visitors since the 1880s, once billed as the most noted pleasure and health resort on the Pacific Coast.

subject: Solentiname Islands
