summary: A remote archipelago of 36 islands in Lake Nicaragua where a poet-priest built a church and an art colony, and where the only way in is by boat from San Carlos.

subject: Sonian Forest
summary: A 4,400-hectare beech cathedral pressed up against the southern edge of Brussels, with trees old enough to have shaded medieval dukes on horseback.

subject: South Georgia Island
summary: A sub-Antarctic fortress of ice and rock where millions of penguins breed, elephant seals brawl on black sand beaches, and Shackleton made his legendary crossing to save his crew.

subject: South Solitary Island Light
summary: The most isolated lighthouse on the New South Wales coast, built of concrete in 1880 on a wind-battered island, where keepers and their children lived behind high stone walls and supplies arrived by crane and basket.

subject: Spanish River derailment
summary: On January 21, 1910, the CPR's Soo Express derailed on a curve approaching the Spanish River bridge near Nairn, Ontario, sending coaches into the frozen river and killing at least 43 passengers in one of Canada's deadliest rail disasters.

subject: Spectacle Reef Light
summary: The most expensive lighthouse ever built on the Great Lakes rises from a reef shaped like eyeglasses, a monument to the engineering ambition that followed shipwreck and disaster in northern Lake Huron.

subject: Spike Island
summary: A 7th-century monastic refuge that became Ireland's Alcatraz, a Treaty Port held by Britain into 1938, and a youth prison that burned in a 1985 riot, before reinventing itself as Europe's leading tourist attraction.

subject: Spreckels Lake
summary: An artificial lake in Golden Gate Park built in 1904 for model boat enthusiasts, Spreckels Lake has hosted miniature yacht races for over a century.

story.title: St Mary's Abbey Ruins, Bardsey Island

subject: St Mary's Abbey Ruins, Bardsey Island
summary: A solitary 12th-century tower stub at the northern tip of Bardsey Island, all that remains of a monastery where 20,000 saints are said to lie.

subject: St Michael's Mount
summary: A tidal island off Cornwall holds a 15th-century chapel, a granite-set heart-shaped stone where a giant supposedly died, and one family — the St Aubyns — who have lived on top of it since 1659.

subject: St. Finian's Bay
summary: A crescent of Atlantic coast on the Iveragh Peninsula where Bronze Age stones, an early Christian saint, a roofless Romanesque church, and modern surfers have all left their marks on the same beach.

subject: St. Helena Island Light
summary: The first Michigan lighthouse to lose its keeper, St. Helena Island Light pioneered the Nobel Prize-winning sun valve technology that would automate lighthouses across the Great Lakes, and was saved from demolition by a volunteer army that turned a vandalized ruin into an award-winning restoration.

subject: St. Joseph Island (Ontario)
summary: Ontario's third-largest Great Lakes island invented the Mackinaw coat, produces 18 percent of the province's maple syrup, and harbors the only surviving Frank Lloyd Wright building in Canada.

subject: St. Michael's Cave
summary: Named after a vision of the archangel in an Italian grotto, this limestone cave network 300 meters up the Rock of Gibraltar has served as Neanderthal shelter, military hospital, and concert hall.

subject: Staten Island Ferry
summary: The fare-free ferry that has carried New Yorkers across the harbor since 1817 offers one of the world's great commutes -- 25 minutes past the Statue of Liberty, free of charge, 24 hours a day.

subject: Stone Mountain of Enlightenment
summary: Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple, a 9th-century monument of 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues that was abandoned, buried under volcanic ash for centuries, and painstakingly restored to become Indonesia's most visited landmark.

subject: Stony Mountain Institution
summary: Canada's oldest operating federal prison has held wrongfully convicted Indigenous chiefs, a legendary bank robber nicknamed 'The Flying Bandit,' and leaders of the Winnipeg General Strike since opening its doors in 1877.

subject: Storms River
summary: A tiny adventure village on the Eastern Cape's Garden Route that serves as the gateway to the Tsitsikamma National Park, where river tubing, canopy tours, and a famous suspension bridge await.

subject: Summersville Lake
summary: West Virginia's largest lake - 2,700 acres of clear water behind a 390-foot rock-fill dam that Lyndon Johnson dedicated, two drowned towns at the bottom, and the only working lighthouse in the state on the rim.

subject: Sumpter Valley Gold Dredge
summary: A haunted industrial leviathan that ate the earth in search of gold, now preserved as a monument to the obsessive dreams of the Blue Mountains.

subject: Swan Islands Nature Reserve
summary: A cluster of barely-there Crimean islets, nowhere higher than a two-story building, where tens of thousands of birds gather each winter.

subject: Tama River
summary: Tokyo's defining river runs from the mountains of Yamanashi to the industrial shore of Haneda Airport, carrying a surprising cargo of wildlife, recreation, and urban reinvention through one of the densest metropolitan areas on Earth.

subject: Taylors Falls, Minnesota
summary: A tiny St. Croix River town of just over 1,000 people, Taylors Falls earned its place in history through a spectacular 1886 log jam, Minnesota's oldest public schoolhouse, and its role as the fictional landing spot for Sweden's most famous literary emigrants.

subject: Tearaght Island
summary: The westernmost island of Ireland - a vertical wedge of rock split by a sea tunnel, crowned by a Victorian lighthouse, and inhabited for 118 years by keepers who had no neighbours west of them this side of Newfoundland.

subject: Tenryū River
summary: Japan's ninth longest river carves through the heart of the Japanese Alps, its turbulent history of floods, shogunate-era ferry crossings, and twentieth-century dam building reshaping both landscape and coastline.

subject: Texada Island
summary: The largest of the Gulf Islands once boasted an opera house, a Chinatown, and J.D. Rockefeller's money -- now its southern half sits virtually deserted, reclaimed by forest.

subject: Tham Lot cave
summary: A 1,666-meter cave system in northwestern Thailand where a river flows through cathedral-sized chambers of stalactites and ancient teakwood coffins rest in the darkness, placed there by the Lawa people thousands of years ago.

subject: The Admiral's Cave
summary: Semarang's oldest Chinese temple traces its origins to Admiral Zheng He, who found a cave in a Javanese hillside six centuries ago and left behind a deputy, a statuette, and a legacy that would survive landslides, landlords, revolution, and political upheaval.

subject: The Brothers Islands, Hong Kong
summary: Two small islands northwest of Hong Kong that were deliberately leveled to clear the flight path for the new international airport — their stone becoming the very ground the airport stands on.

story.title: The Chain That Guards the Island

subject: The Chain That Guards the Island
summary: Pura Pulaki is a Balinese sea temple on the island's northwest coast, one link in a centuries-old chain of sacred sites built to ring Bali in spiritual protection.

story.title: The Farallon Islands: California's Forbidden Rock

subject: The Farallon Islands
summary: The rocky islands 27 miles from San Francisco where no tourists are allowed - home to the largest seabird colony in the continental US, great white sharks that feed on sea lions, and a lighthouse that witnessed the slaughter of millions of seabirds for their eggs.

subject: The Fearless Mountain
summary: A Thai Forest Tradition monastery on 280 acres of California mountainside where monks rise before dawn, eat one meal a day, and practice a 2,500-year-old discipline amid the redwoods of Mendocino County.

subject: The Fifty-Dollar Ghost
summary: A Gold Rush ghost town in Mariposa County that once housed California's first authorized mint, where octagonal fifty-dollar gold slugs were stamped before the operation vanished in three years -- leaving only stone ruins and numismatic legends.

subject: The Forest That Blooms Pink
summary: A 317-acre second-growth forest on the Sonoma coast where wildfire and ecological succession produced groves of native rhododendrons whose pink spring blossoms turn the understory into a cathedral of color.

subject: The Island Diana Chose
summary: Off the north coast of Sumbawa, Moyo Island hides waterfalls in forests thick with butterflies, coral reefs teeming with marine life, and a luxury tent resort that once sheltered a princess seeking solitude.

subject: The Island That Changed Hands
summary: A flat, marshy island in Brunei Bay that has served as a pirate watcher's anchorage, a Japanese naval outpost, an Allied beachhead, and now hosts a multi-billion dollar Chinese petrochemical refinery.

story.title: The Island That Imprisoned a Nation's Greatest Writer

subject: The Island That Imprisoned a Nation's Greatest Writer
summary: Buru, the third largest island in the Maluku archipelago, harbors endemic wildlife found nowhere else on Earth and a dark chapter as Indonesia's most notorious political prison camp.

story.title: The Island of Flowers and Firing Squads

subject: The Island of Flowers and Firing Squads
summary: Nusa Kambangan, an island off Java's southern coast once sought by Javanese princes for its legendary resurrection flower, has spent over a century as Indonesia's most notorious prison island, earning the grim nickname 'Execution Island.'

subject: The Jewel on the Bay
summary: They built the county administration center on reclaimed tidelands, which meant they were building it on mud.

story.title: The Oil Town at the River's Mouth

subject: The Oil Town at the River's Mouth
summary: A fishing village named for the river mouth where it sits became the gateway to Brunei's petroleum fortune, survived Japanese occupation and wartime massacre, and remains the quiet capital of the country's richest district.

subject: The Peninsula Hong Kong
summary: Built in 1928 to be 'the finest hotel east of Suez', The Peninsula Hong Kong has hosted surrendering governors and strafing American pilots — a century of history compressed into one grande dame on the Kowloon waterfront.

subject: The Repulse Bay
summary: A hole in a Hong Kong skyscraper, put there for the dragons — the Repulse Bay building is a luxury residential tower with a feng shui gap through its facade that has made it one of the most photographed buildings in Asia.

subject: The River That Nobody Dammed
summary: The Cosumnes is the last river flowing from the western Sierra Nevada without a major dam, its name a Miwok word meaning 'people of the salmon' -- though the salmon themselves have nearly vanished from its waters.

story.title: The Sign Post Forest: 100,000 Messages from Home

subject: The Sign Post Forest
summary: The Yukon tradition where travelers hang hometown signs on posts - started in 1942 by a homesick soldier, now holding over 100,000 signs from every corner of the world, an accidental monument to everywhere else.

story.title: The Sultan's Island at the River's Mouth

subject: The Sultan's Island at the River's Mouth
summary: Brunei's largest island guards the mouth of the Brunei River, where a sultan once built his palace, a rajah mined coal that turned out to be oil, and proboscis monkeys still swing through protected mangroves.

subject: The Valley
summary: The stadium that supporters built with their own hands in an abandoned chalk pit, then refused to abandon when their club tried to leave.

subject: Thousand Buddha Mountain
summary: A sacred hill southeast of Jinan where 1,400-year-old Buddha carvings share space with matchmaking parents and temple fair food stalls.

subject: Thousand Islands
summary: The archipelago that invented salad dressing - where 1,864 islands dot the St. Lawrence River, Gilded Age millionaires built castle-like summer homes, and the border between Canada and the United States winds through the most scenic stretch of water between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic.

subject: Thursday Island
summary: The administrative capital of the Torres Strait, where you can buy pearls, drink stubbies on a pub deck overlooking aquamarine water, and absolutely cannot swim in the ocean.

subject: Titchwell Marsh
summary: A 171-hectare Norfolk nature reserve where Stone Age blades, First World War hospital bricks, and Second World War tank remains lie in the same mud that avocets nest above — the RSPB's most visited reserve in England.

story.title: Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line: The Highway That Disappears Underwater

subject: Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line
summary: A 23.7-kilometer expressway that dives beneath Tokyo Bay through the fourth-longest underwater tunnel in the world, surfaces on an artificial island with restaurants and shops, then crosses a 4.4-kilometer bridge to the other shore -- cutting a 90-minute commute down to 15.

subject: Tralee Bay
summary: A broad west-Kerry bay scattered with shipwrecks, an oyster fishery, the birthplace of Saint Brendan, and the rebuilt famine emigrant ship Jeanie Johnston - all watched over by the lighthouse on Little Samphire Island.

story.title: Tsiigehtchic: Where Rivers Meet at the Arctic Circle

subject: Tsiigehtchic
summary: The Northwest Territories village where the Arctic Red River joins the Mackenzie - a Gwich'in community of 200 on the Dempster Highway, accessible by ferry or ice bridge depending on whether the river is liquid or solid.

subject: Tsushima Island
summary: Suspended in the strait between Japan and Korea, Tsushima is an island of dense forests, rare wildcats, and a history shaped by its position as the bridge between two civilizations.

subject: Tuzla Island
summary: A low sliver of sand in the middle of the Kerch Strait, torn from a peninsula by a single storm and destined to become the anchor point of a bridge between two shores.

subject: Valley of the Muses
summary: On the eastern slopes of Mount Helicon in Boeotia, the Valley of the Muses was the sacred grove where the Boeotians held the Mouseia festival of poetry and music every four years — a sanctuary whose history stretches from the sixth century BC to late antiquity, and whose hillside theatre once heard the finest poets in Greece compete for glory.

subject: Vashon Island
summary: A bridge-free sanctuary in Puget Sound where giant Pacific octopuses guard underwater gardens and artists have built a bohemian haven just minutes from Seattle.

subject: Victoria Falls, Zimbabwe
summary: A resort town of 35,000 built on the edge of one of the world's great waterfalls, where the railway arrived before the roads did and where over 200 adventure activities now compete with the falls themselves for attention.

subject: Viper Island
summary: A tiny island in the Andaman archipelago that served as Britain's first penal colony for Indian independence fighters, where the chain gang jail earned a reputation so fearsome that inmates named their wardens after venomous snakes.

story.title: Virginia Beach: The Navy Town Where the Boardwalk Never Ends

subject: Virginia Beach
summary: The Virginia resort city that's also a naval stronghold - where the boardwalk stretches three miles, where Navy SEALs train at nearby bases, and where Virginia's largest city spreads across former farmland.

subject: Voidokilia Beach
summary: Shaped like the Greek letter omega, Voidokilia Beach curves in a perfect semicircle below a headland of myths and ruins — Homer's sandy Pylos, Nestor's cave, and a Frankish castle all stacked above one of the most beautiful bays in Greece.

subject: Waglan Island
summary: A tiny rock at the southeastern tip of Hong Kong, home to a lighthouse that has guided ships through these waters since 1893 and survived a world war to become a declared monument.

subject: Waipiʻo Valley
summary: A mile-wide valley carved into the Kohala coast where Hawaiian kings once ruled, waterfalls plunge nearly 2,000 feet, and the gateway to the Underworld lies hidden beneath the black sand.

subject: Waipoua Forest
summary: Home to Tane Mahuta and Te Matua Ngahere, the largest living kauri trees, this Northland forest sanctuary was saved by a 43,000-signature petition delivered to parliament in a wheelbarrow.

subject: Waldron Island
summary: A San Juan island with no ferry, no power grid, no paved roads and no store since 1942 - and a composer working in the building where the store used to be.

story.title: Where the Mangroves Stand Thirty Meters Tall

subject: Where the Mangroves Stand Thirty Meters Tall
summary: Bintuni Bay harbors the second-largest contiguous mangrove forest on Earth, a vast tidal wilderness in West Papua where trees grow to cathedral heights and endangered dolphins navigate channels older than any human settlement.

subject: Whiddy Island
summary: A small, gently-rolling island that has been pirate refuge, naval air station, supertanker terminal, and now a 31-person community sharing the bay with the wreck of a French frigate.

subject: Whitechapel Mount
summary: A vast artificial hill that loomed over 18th-century Whitechapel until it was carted away to make bricks - possibly a Civil War fort, a plague pit, fire rubble, and a rubbish dump all at once.

subject: Whitley Bay
summary: A North Sea seaside town that changed its name to stop people sending its mail to Whitby - home to the Spanish City dome, St Mary's Lighthouse, and a Sam Fender boyhood.

subject: Wonder Valley, California
summary: A High Desert valley east of Twentynine Palms where the federal Small Tract Act of 1938 distributed five-acre homestead parcels, creating a landscape of mostly-abandoned cabins that has attracted artists and desert eccentrics for decades.

subject: World Map at Lake Klejtrup
summary: A Danish farmer found a stone shaped like Jutland, and spent the last twenty-five years of his life building the rest of the world around it.

subject: Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina
summary: A 4.6-mile barrier island where the Lumina Pavilion once glowed under six thousand lights, streetcars ran on a wooden trestle from Wilmington, and a 1923 resort for Black families burned to the ground three years after it opened.

subject: Yerba Buena Island
summary: Once an Ohlone fishing village, then a Civil War fortress, then a naval base where Admiral Nimitz spent his final years -- now San Francisco's newest neighborhood.

subject: Yorke Island (Canada)
summary: A tiny World War II fortress island guarding the 'back door to Vancouver,' where isolation drove soldiers to 'Going Yorkie' and the garrison's only death came not from enemy action but from a water supply run gone wrong.

subject: Yosemite Valley
summary: A seven-mile granite cathedral carved by glaciers and named by a misunderstanding, where a Miwok word meaning 'those who kill' became the name of America's most beloved valley.

subject: Zaleski State Forest
summary: A 28,000-acre Ohio state forest in the unglaciated Allegheny Plateau, wrapping around Lake Hope State Park - whose white oak supplied the wood for Ohio State University's award-winning 2008 library renovation.

subject: Zhifu Island
summary: An islet in the Bohai Sea where China's first emperor searched for the elixir of immortality, now connected to the mainland by a natural sand bridge built over millennia.

subject: 1915 U.S. Open (golf)
summary: Amateur champion Jerome Travers conquered Baltusrol's Old Course in 1915 to win his only U.S. Open, then walked away from competitive golf forever.

subject: 1936 U.S. Open (golf)
summary: Tony Manero, a nervous unknown who nearly failed to qualify, stunned the golf world at Baltusrol in 1936 with the help of a famous friend and a controversial final-round pairing.

subject: 1967 U.S. Open (golf)
summary: Jack Nicklaus shattered the U.S. Open scoring record at Baltusrol in 1967 with a final-round 65, while Arnold Palmer finished second for the fourth time in six years and Ben Hogan played his final major.

subject: 1980 U.S. Open (golf)
summary: Jack Nicklaus silenced doubters at age 40 by setting a U.S. Open scoring record at Baltusrol, winning his fourth title in a four-day duel with Japan's Isao Aoki.

subject: 1993 Cherbourg Incident
summary: For one week in 1993, French trawlermen kidnapped three British naval officers, surrounded a Royal Navy minesweeper, and burned the White Ensign on the quay at Cherbourg.

subject: 1997 Namibia Mid-Air Collision
summary: On a clear September day in 1997, two military aircraft from opposite sides of the world collided over the South Atlantic off Namibia, and all 33 people aboard them were lost.

subject: 2005 PGA Championship
summary: Phil Mickelson won his second major title with a breathtaking flop shot on the final hole at Baltusrol, capping a rain-delayed Monday finish at the 2005 PGA Championship.

subject: 2013-14 Belgian Second Division
summary: Hidden in the back third of the scoring list for Westerlo, a 19-year-old named Leandro Trossard was learning the trade he would later take to Brighton, Arsenal, and the Belgian national team.

subject: 2020 Danish Mink Cull
summary: Denmark ordered every farmed mink in the country killed — some 15 million animals — and then had to admit that the order had no legal basis, ending an industry, a minister's career, and eventually the ground's ability to hold what had been buried in it.

subject: 2025 Tarasin landslide
summary: A mountainside in Darfur gave way at five o'clock on a rainy August evening, and a village called Tarasin was gone.

subject: A Woman's Place Bookstore
summary: One of America's first feminist bookstores opened in Oakland in the early 1970s, growing from a street-corner book table into a movement that would reshape independent publishing before tearing itself apart over the very questions of identity and power it had been founded to confront.

story.title: Abigail Bush: The Woman Who Took the Chair

subject: Abigail Bush
summary: When Abigail Bush became the first woman to preside over a mixed-gender public meeting in America, even her allies doubted she could do it -- then she proved them wrong and changed the convention forever.

subject: Adal Sultanate
summary: Born from the ashes of the Ifat Sultanate, the Adal Empire became the most powerful Muslim state in the Horn of Africa, waging a century-long campaign that nearly conquered Christian Abyssinia.

subject: Aegean Sea
summary: Named for a king who leapt to his death over a misread sail, the Aegean is a sea of two thousand islands, the wine-dark cradle of European civilization, and a contested boundary between two nations.

subject: Afar Triangle
summary: A continent is tearing itself in half in the Afar Triangle - the hottest place year-round on Earth, lowest point in Africa, and the landscape where Lucy walked 3.2 million years ago.

subject: Afuá
summary: An Amazon delta town built on stilts where the streets are wooden planks, the ambulance is a bicycle, and motor vehicles have been shut out since 2002.

subject: Akuntsú language
summary: In a small reserve in the Brazilian Amazon, a handful of survivors keep speaking a language that the people who murdered their families never bothered to learn.

subject: American Cryonics Society
summary: The American Cryonics Society (ACS), also known as the Cryonics Society of America, is a member-run, California-based, 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit

story.title: Angels Landing: The Trail That Tests Your Fear of Heights

subject: Angels Landing
summary: The Zion National Park hike where chain handholds are all that separate you from a 1,500-foot drop - one of America's most dangerous trails and most popular despite the deaths that occur with statistical regularity.

subject: Antrim Hills
summary: A basalt-topped range of rounded summits, moorland and blanket bog stretching from Ballycastle on the north coast down to Larne, with Trostan at its highest point.

subject: Aquariquara Extractive Reserve
summary: A small extractive reserve in Rondonia where rubber tappers harvest latex using traditional methods, facing death threats and plummeting populations as the economics of forest extraction collide with illegal logging.

subject: Aracoma Alma Mine accident
summary: On January 19, 2006, a conveyor-belt fire in a Massey Energy mine near Melville, West Virginia, killed Don Bragg and Ellery Hatfield after smoke poured into an escape route through two missing ventilation walls.

subject: Arroyo Seco Parkway
summary: The oldest freeway in the American West—opened in 1940 along a seasonal river canyon between Los Angeles and Pasadena—is now a narrow, curving relic of an era when roads were still designed for pleasure.

subject: Asphalt Princess
summary: A double-hulled tanker with a history of groundings, fires, and name changes that became the target of an alleged Iranian-backed hijacking in the Gulf of Oman in August 2021.

subject: Asse II mine
summary: A worked-out salt mine in Lower Saxony took 126,000 drums of radioactive waste that were never meant to come back out — and now Germany has to retrieve every one of them.

subject: Atlantic dry forests
summary: A 115,100-square-kilometer ecoregion between Brazil's wet coast and its arid interior - where bottle-trunked trees shelter primates down to their final 260 individuals.

subject: August 2021 Gulf of Oman incident
summary: Armed boarders seized the asphalt tanker Asphalt Princess in the Gulf of Oman on August 3, 2021, ordering it to sail to Iran before abandoning the vessel hours later in one of several maritime confrontations that year.

subject: Aurich (district)
summary: The biggest district in East Frisia, holding three of the East Frisian Islands, the largest Wadden Sea tideland in Germany, and the memory of an oak where free Frisians once held their annual council.

subject: Australia–Indonesia Border
summary: An invisible line across open ocean where the seabed belongs to one nation and the water above it to another — the Australia–Indonesia maritime boundary is one of the strangest borders on Earth.

subject: Ayabaca province
summary: In the Quechua language, aya means both death and immortality - and Ayabaca, a Peruvian province on the Ecuadorian border, is a sanctuary of both, where the longest pilgrimage in South America arrives each October.

subject: Bahr al-Arab
summary: An 800-kilometre river the Arabs call the Sea of the Arabs and the Dinka call the Kiir - a boundary, a tributary, and a line along which two peoples have fought and bargained for centuries.

story.title: Bahr el Ghazal (region of South Sudan)

subject: Bahr el Ghazal (region of South Sudan)
summary: The Sea of Gazelles - a vast floodplain of swamps and ironstone plateaus that British colonial officers called The Bog, and that the Dinka call home.

subject: Bangime
summary: In a handful of villages walled off by the Bandiagara cliffs, 3,500 people speak a language that resembles nothing else on Earth - a linguistic island called Bangime.

subject: Barbary Coast Trail
summary: Marked by 180 bronze medallions embedded in the sidewalk, the 3.8-mile Barbary Coast Trail connects San Francisco's historic sites from the Old Mint to Aquatic Park.

subject: Barbary Coast, San Francisco
summary: San Francisco's notorious Barbary Coast was a nine-block red-light district of dance halls, saloons, jazz clubs, and brothels that thrived from the Gold Rush through the early 20th century.

subject: Batiquitos Lagoon
summary: Over a century of development silted Batiquitos Lagoon nearly shut — reducing it from a tidal estuary supporting dozens of fish species to a stagnant pond supporting five. A 1990s restoration reversed the collapse.

subject: Bear Rocks Preserve
summary: A 477-acre Nature Conservancy preserve on the Allegheny Front, where wind-flagged spruce trees and ice-carved sandstone form one of the most photographed scenes in West Virginia.

subject: Bempton Cliffs
summary: England's only mainland gannet colony, where half a million seabirds nest on white chalk cliffs above the North Sea every spring.

subject: Bimmah Sinkhole
summary: A turquoise pool in Oman's limestone coast that locals believed was created by a falling star, giving it the Arabic name Hawiyyat Najm -- 'the deep well of the star.'

subject: Black Cat Bar
summary: A bohemian bar that became one of San Francisco's first openly queer gathering places, the Black Cat Bar fought a landmark legal battle for the right of gay people to assemble peacefully.

subject: Blue Hole of Santa Rosa
summary: The artesian pool in the New Mexico desert where crystal-clear 62°F water stays the same depth year-round - once a Route 66 swimming hole, now one of America's most popular inland scuba diving destinations.

subject: Bogachiel Peak
summary: A 5,478-foot high point on the Olympic Mountains' High Divide, where a Quileute word for muddy water names the ridge that decides which way the rain will run.

subject: Boho Caves
summary: Beneath a quiet Fermanagh hillside, water-carved limestone passages 325 million years in the making harbor bat colonies and a soil bacterium that may help defeat the world's deadliest superbugs.

subject: Bolshezemelskaya Tundra
summary: A vast subarctic lowland between the Pechora River and the Ural foothills where Izhma Komi reindeer herders navigate a landscape shaped by permafrost, oil deposits, and the long Arctic winter.

story.title: Bonneville Salt Flats: The Fastest Place on Earth

subject: Bonneville Salt Flats
summary: The Utah desert where land speed records go to die - a 40-square-mile salt flat so perfectly flat and featureless that drivers have exceeded 600 mph chasing the sound barrier on a surface that's slowly dissolving.

subject: Borth Lifeboat Station
summary: The small Cardigan Bay station that exists because a veteran of the Arctic convoys could not bear the thought of another twenty minutes between a drowning man and his rescuers.

subject: Brigalow Belt
summary: A near-impenetrable silver-leaved scrub once walled off inland Queensland; in a single century, axes, chains and bulldozers cleared roughly 90 percent of it for cattle and crops.

subject: British Malaya
summary: A patchwork of sultanates, trading posts, and crown colonies stitched together over 170 years, British Malaya transformed the Malay Peninsula from a constellation of feudal kingdoms into the foundation of modern Malaysia.

subject: Caatinga
summary: Brazil's thorn forest covers 912,529 square kilometres of the northeastern interior, holds 26 million people, exists nowhere else on Earth, and has about one percent of itself under full protection.

subject: Caballo Mountains
summary: A geologic time capsule stretching from the Precambrian to the present, the Caballo Mountains preserve nearly half a billion years of Earth's history in New Mexico's arid borderlands.

subject: Cabo Polonio
summary: Uruguay's last off-grid village clings to sand dunes at the edge of the Atlantic, where there are no roads, no electricity, and sea lions outnumber tourists.

subject: Caltrain
summary: The commuter rail line connecting San Francisco to San Jose along a corridor first laid in 1863, carrying Silicon Valley's workforce on a route that predates the technology industry by more than a century.

subject: Cambrian Mountains
summary: Mid-Wales has a backbone of bare green hills called the Desert of Wales, and one of them is the watershed where the Severn and the Wye both begin.

subject: Camden Sound
summary: Home to the world's largest humpback whale population and Western Australia's second-largest marine park, Camden Sound is where the Dambimangari people's saltwater country meets one of the planet's great cetacean nurseries.

subject: Cameron Corner Survey Marker
summary: The surveyed point in the remote outback where New South Wales, Queensland and South Australia meet, marked by a lone post you can stand around with one foot in each state.

subject: Cape Colony
summary: From a Dutch East India Company supply station in 1652 to a British colony that shaped modern South Africa, the Cape Colony's 258-year history is a story of trade, dispossession, migration, and the long consequences of colonialism.

subject: Cape Split
summary: A seven-kilometre basalt headland on the Bay of Fundy where 200-million-year-old volcanic cliffs meet the world's most powerful tidal currents, producing a roar that locals call the Voice of the Moon.

subject: Caribou Wilderness
summary: A volcanic plateau of 23 named lakes and pristine old-growth forest, preserved since 1932 as one of California's original wilderness areas.

subject: Caverna dos Ecos
summary: A cave in central Goiás with no stalactites, no colour and no decoration - just 1,380 metres of mica schist, a 142-metre descent, and a black lake that has been filling with rainwater for longer than anyone knows.

subject: Cerrado
summary: The biologically richest savanna on Earth covers twenty-one percent of Brazil - a fire-born ecosystem of twisted trees and 10,000 plant species now vanishing faster than the Amazon.

subject: Chami
summary: A town conjured out of empty desert in 2012 to control where nomads settle - now Mauritania's gold-rush 'capital of gold,' shadowed by mercury drifting toward a protected coast.

subject: Channel Country
summary: A vast braid of dry riverbeds across the Lake Eyre Basin that, when the rivers finally run, transforms from cracked desert into a green inland sea.

subject: Chapada Limpa Extractive Reserve
summary: A small federal reserve in eastern Maranhão where babassu palm gatherers won a place to live on the advancing edge of Brazil's soybean frontier.

subject: Cherokee Outlet
summary: A vast strip of Indian Territory promised to the Cherokee in perpetuity became the stage for cattle empires, broken treaties, and the largest land run in American history, when over 100,000 settlers raced for claims on September 16, 1893.

subject: Chinese ironclad Pingyuan
summary: The first ironclad warship built in China, Pingyuan fought for the Qing dynasty, was captured by Japan, renamed Heien, and ultimately met its end from a naval mine during the Russo-Japanese War.

subject: Chiquitano dry forests
summary: The world's largest intact tropical dry forest stretches across eastern Bolivia and into Brazil, named for the Chiquitano people whose land rights are bound up with its survival.

subject: Coast Starlight
summary: Amtrak's 35-hour journey down the Pacific coast - from Seattle to Los Angeles through forests, mountains, and a brief glimpse of California's golden shoreline, aboard one of America's most scenic train routes.

subject: Colonial Brazil
summary: Three hundred and twenty-two years of Portuguese colonization - red dye, sugar, gold, and the lives of millions of enslaved people - that shaped the largest country in Latin America.

subject: Comox Sandhills
summary: An ancient dune field near Cape Lazo, buried under a forest that only the poorest soils could allow, and re-mapped three times because the houses built on it kept changing the ground.

subject: Coromandel, Minas Gerais
summary: The largest diamond ever found in Brazil came out of a creek here in 1938 - and in 2025 the second largest came out of another creek eight kilometers away.

subject: Corumbau Marine Extractive Reserve
summary: A 65-kilometer coastal reserve off Bahia where traditional fishers won back their waters - and humpback whales raise calves - in the richest reef zone of the South Atlantic.

subject: Coves dels Hams
summary: A ten-million-year-old cave beneath Mallorca where stalactites curl into fishhooks and Mozart drifts across a candle-lit underground lake.

subject: Cowden family murders
summary: A 1974 Labor Day camping trip in Oregon's Siskiyou Mountains ended in tragedy when an entire family vanished, sparking one of the state's largest search efforts and leaving behind an enduring mystery.

story.title: Crater of Diamonds: The Only Diamond Mine Where You Keep What You Find

subject: Crater of Diamonds
summary: The Arkansas volcanic field where visitors pay admission to dig for diamonds and keep whatever they find - where over 35,000 diamonds have been discovered since 1972, where the largest diamond ever found in America emerged from ordinary-looking dirt, and where geology created the only public diamond mine on Earth.

subject: Crummock Water
summary: A lake whose name simply means 'the crooked one', running for two and a half miles between Mellbreak and the western fells.

subject: Cry of Asencio
summary: On a quiet stream in the Banda Oriental, a hundred men declared a revolution that would give birth to Uruguay.

subject: Darfur
summary: A region the size of mainland Spain, home to the Fur, Masalit, Zaghawa, and many other peoples, whose twenty-first century has been written largely in atrocity, resistance, and refuge.

story.title: Delta do Parnaíba Environmental Protection Area

subject: Delta do Parnaíba Environmental Protection Area
summary: A federally protected delta where three Brazilian states meet the sea - mobile dunes, mangroves, and the only open-ocean river delta in the Americas.

story.title: Denali: The High One That Towers Over a Continent

subject: Denali
summary: The Alaskan peak that is North America's highest - rising 20,310 feet from surrounding terrain that makes it taller in appearance than Everest, where climbers die in sudden storms, and where the Koyukon Athabascan name finally replaced the imposed name of a president who never saw it.

subject: Diamond (1823 ship)
summary: A New York-built packet ship lost on Sarn Badrig reef in 1825 - and the Welsh wreck that was declared to be her, then turned out almost certainly not to be.

subject: Dingo Fence
summary: At 5,614 kilometres, the Dingo Fence is one of the longest structures on Earth, a single line of wire that reshaped an entire continent's ecology to protect its sheep.

subject: Do-Dodonpa
summary: A compressed-air launched roller coaster at Fuji-Q Highland that once held the world record for fastest acceleration, reaching 172 km/h in 1.8 seconds, before a string of broken-bone injuries ended its run permanently in 2024.

subject: Dolomites
summary: Named for a French mineralogist who identified their strange pale rock, the Dolomites glow pink at sunset and hide a century-old war fought in tunnels blasted through their walls.

subject: Donna Nook
summary: A Lincolnshire saltmarsh where 3,000 grey seals give birth each winter, bombs still drop on the targets, and visitors come for the white-furred pups.

subject: Dār Fertit
summary: The lowlands south of Darfur, whose name came to mean 'people legally enslavable' to the sultanates that raided them, remain home to dozens of peoples who share only the experience of being called 'Fertit' by outsiders.

subject: East-Prinovozemelsky field
summary: One of the world's largest undeveloped oil and gas fields sits frozen beneath the South Kara Sea — a geopolitical prize that has attracted BP, ExxonMobil, and the shifting fortunes of international sanctions.

subject: East–West Interconnector
summary: A 500-megawatt high-voltage direct current cable laid across the floor of the Irish Sea, wiring Ireland's grid to Britain's.

subject: Ecuadorian dry forests
summary: A tropical dry forest where one percent of the original cover still stands, guarding cactus, kapok, and seventy-seven endemic birds from final disappearance.

subject: Eden Landing Ecological Reserve
summary: A nature reserve on the eastern shore of San Francisco Bay where former industrial salt ponds are being restored to tidal marsh, creating habitat for endangered species.

subject: Edendale
summary: Before Hollywood became Hollywood, the motion picture industry built its West Coast home in Edendale—a canyon district that is now Echo Park, Silver Lake, and Los Feliz.

story.title: El Corte de Madera Creek Open Space Preserve

subject: El Corte de Madera Creek Open Space Preserve
summary: El Corte de Madera Open Space Preserve, known to locals as Skeggs (after Skeggs Point), is a 2908 acres open space preserve in San Mateo County, Calif

subject: El Djouf
summary: A sea of sand and salt straddling Mali and Mauritania, El Djouf is the great empty heart of the Sahara - and the source of the slab salt that once bought gold.

subject: El Vallecito
summary: A Kumeyaay archaeological site near La Rumorosa in Baja California — with rock art dating to 8000 BCE and a winter solstice phenomenon where sunlight illuminates a painted figure's eyes on December 21 and 22.

subject: Elizabeth Springs
summary: A cluster of ancient artesian mound springs near Boulia, sacred to the Wangkamadla people and home to a tiny fish found nowhere else on Earth, now reduced to a trickle as the Great Artesian Basin is drawn down.

subject: Emirate of Crete
summary: The Andalusian Muslim state that ruled Crete from the 820s to 961, founding the city of Chandax (modern Heraklion) before being destroyed by a Byzantine reconquest that ended in mass enslavement.

subject: Erythraean Sea
summary: The ancient Greek name for a vast maritime region encompassing the Red Sea, Arabian Sea, Persian Gulf, and Indian Ocean, the Erythraean Sea was the stage for one of history's earliest trade route guides -- the Periplus.

subject: Escape Recording Studio
summary: A 140-acre invitation-only recording compound in Pioneertown where Rüfüs Du Sol spent 51 days during a pandemic and emerged with their most celebrated album — and where the desert became the sound.

subject: Esteros de Farrapos
summary: A maze of 24 sedimentary islands and flooded grassland where Uruguay frays into the river that borders Argentina, sheltering maned wolves and more than 200 species of birds.

subject: Ethabuka Reserve
summary: A vast conservation reserve on the Queensland edge of the Simpson Desert, where red dunes, a rare living waterhole, and the floods of the Mulligan River sustain one of Australia's richest desert wildlife communities.

subject: Ewiges Meer
summary: The largest raised-bog lake in Germany, a 91-hectare sheet of dark water sitting on a cushion of peat above the East Frisian Geest, surrounded by a 1,290-hectare nature reserve.

subject: Ewiiaapaayp Band of Kumeyaay Indians
summary: Formerly the Cuyapaipe Community — a 4,102-acre reservation near Mount Laguna with only five enrolled members and no public utilities, where the Kumeyaay people maintain their government on land that is 99% non-arable.

subject: Exide Lead Contamination
summary: For decades, a lead-acid battery smelter in Vernon quietly poisoned the neighborhoods around it. When the full scale of the contamination emerged, it became the largest environmental cleanup of its kind in California history.

subject: Finnmarksvidda
summary: Norway's largest plateau stretches across the Arctic interior of Finnmark, a vast tableland of birch forests, bogs, and glacial lakes where the Sami people have herded reindeer for centuries.

subject: Finocchio's Club
summary: A North Beach nightclub where female impersonators performed for sixty-three years, drawing tourists and locals from the Depression through the dot-com era.

subject: Gamigaya Petroglyphs
summary: Nearly 1,500 rock carvings spanning the 4th to 1st millennia BC cover the slopes of a 3,906-meter peak in the Lesser Caucasus, where ancient peoples recorded their world in stone.

subject: Garamantes
summary: The ancient Saharan civilization of the Fezzan, who mined fossil water through hundreds of kilometers of hand-dug tunnels to build the first cities in a waterless desert.

subject: Gay Games
summary: The international LGBTQ sporting event born in San Francisco in 1982, when Tina Turner performed at the opening ceremonies and 1,350 athletes competed in what was then called the Gay Olympics.

subject: Genovesa
summary: A flooded caldera at the northern edge of the Galapagos, Genovesa Island is a remote seabird city where the air itself seems made of wings.

subject: Geography of Mauritania
summary: Where the Sahara meets the Sahel and the Atlantic, Mauritania is a vast, flat land of shifting dunes, mineral-rich peaks, and the great circular Eye of the Sahara visible from space.

subject: Gran Chaco
summary: South America's vast semiarid heartland, spanning over a million square kilometers across four countries -- a region of quebracho forests, pink fairy armadillos, Mennonite colonies, and the continent's most intense deforestation frontier.

subject: Gran Pajonal
summary: A grassy plateau above the Peruvian Amazon where the Asháninka people defeated Spanish missionaries in 1742 and eventually won back legal title to their land in the 1980s.

subject: Great Artesian Basin
summary: Beneath a fifth of Australia lies the world's largest artesian basin, an underground ocean of ancient water that made life and settlement possible across the dry inland.

subject: Großer Knechtsand
summary: From 1952 to 1957, the British Royal Air Force used this North Sea sandbank as a live bombing range - until the molting shelducks won.

subject: Gruta de Ubajara
summary: A nine-chambered limestone cave in Brazil's smallest national park, reached by a cable car that drops off the edge of the Ibiapaba escarpment in three minutes.

subject: Grès supérieurs Formation
summary: A dull band of red sandstone in southern Laos that has quietly produced a 15-metre sauropod, a fish-eating predator with a sail cut in two, and the first hard proof that dinosaurs walked Indochina.

subject: Guariba-Roosevelt Extractive Reserve
summary: The only state-level extractive reserve in Mato Grosso, where roughly 300 people from a unique traditional community gather nuts and rubber while fending off illegal loggers on what officials call the state's last deforestation frontier.

subject: Gulf of Carpentaria
summary: A vast, shallow sea cut into the top of Australia, where 1,000-kilometre rolling clouds sweep in at dawn, banana prawns fuel a national fishery, and the tide breathes across 300,000 square kilometres of water.

subject: Gulf of Fonseca
summary: Three nations share this Pacific inlet where volcanic islands, mangrove forests, and five centuries of territorial disputes converge at the meeting point of El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua.

subject: Gulflander
summary: The beloved 'Tin Hare' rail-motor that rattles weekly across the Gulf Country on a marooned 1890s railway, a line famously described as running 'from nowhere to nowhere' and connected to no other track in Australia.

subject: Hacker Dojo
summary: Hacker Dojo is a 6,000 sqft community center and hackerspace that is based in Mountain View, California. Predominantly an open working space for softw

subject: Haddon Corner
summary: A lone concrete pillar in the desert marks the exact point where the dead-straight Queensland-South Australia border makes its turn, planted there by surveyors in 1880.

subject: Haida Gwaii
summary: The British Columbia islands where the Haida flourished and evolution went its own way - endemic species, ancient rainforest, and totem poles that crumbled when epidemics killed 90% of the people who carved them.

subject: Hassler Health Farm
summary: A tuberculosis sanatorium in the hills above Redwood City, owned by San Francisco and operating from 1927 to the 1970s -- treating patients in the open air of the Peninsula foothills.

subject: Hengduan Mountains
summary: A massive system of north-south mountain ranges in southwest China where tectonic collision created some of Asia's deepest gorges and the highest peak east of the Himalayas.

subject: Hickory Motor Speedway
summary: A 0.363-mile asphalt short track in Newton, North Carolina - opened on dirt in 1952, paved in 1967, and once promoted by Ned Jarrett - that ran NASCAR's top series for 18 seasons before being left behind.

subject: Hispania Balearica
summary: The Roman province born from a war on pirates, famed for slingers trained since childhood and wheat so rich it fed an empire.

subject: Hispania Carthaginensis
summary: A Roman province carved from Spain by the emperor Diocletian, named for the great enemy Rome once destroyed, and fought over by Alans, Suebi, and Visigoths as the empire collapsed around it.

subject: History of telegraphy in Australia
summary: How 36,000 telegraph poles across 3,000 kilometers of outback connected a remote continent to the rest of the world in 1872.

subject: Holbrook-Palmer Estate
summary: A historic estate in Atherton -- once called Elmwood -- that has been converted into a public park, preserving one of the Peninsula's grand country properties.

subject: Holland
summary: The name foreigners give the Netherlands is really one coastal region of it, sunk below the sea and held up by dikes, which the Dutch government in 2020 officially asked the world to stop using.

story.title: Hollandse Kust Zuid Offshore Wind Farm

subject: Hollandse Kust Zuid Offshore Wind Farm
summary: The 1.5-gigawatt offshore wind farm off Zandvoort that proved you can build at industrial scale in the North Sea without a single euro of subsidy.

subject: Honister Pass
summary: A 1,167-foot pass on the B5289 holds the UK 24-hour rainfall record - 341 millimetres fell here in a single day during Storm Desmond.

subject: Hopewell Rocks
summary: Towering sea stacks on the Bay of Fundy sculpted by the highest tides on Earth, where visitors walk the ocean floor at low tide and watch the same formations disappear beneath 16 metres of water hours later.

subject: Hoye-Crest
summary: The highest point in Maryland at 3,360 feet, sitting along the West Virginia border on Backbone Mountain - reached by a one-mile hike from a West Virginia trailhead.

subject: IJkdijk
summary: At 16:02 on Saturday, 27 September 2008, a hundred-meter test dike in the Dutch province of Groningen collapsed exactly as planned, generating a terabyte of unprecedented data and confirming that dikes can be taught to call for help before they fail.

subject: Ilha dos Lobos
summary: A barely-there speck of rock off the Brazilian coast, less than two meters tall, that serves as a winter haul-out for sea lions and the country's only oceanic wildlife refuge.

subject: Inchiri region
summary: Mauritania's smallest, emptiest region holds a periodic table's worth of buried metal, one city, and barely twenty thousand people clinging to a mineral frontier.

subject: Indigenous Australian Culture
summary: The oldest continuous living cultures on Earth, reaching back more than sixty thousand years - and still here, still speaking, still singing the land.

subject: Indonesia-Malaysia Border
summary: A 1,881-kilometer land boundary through the Borneo interior, plus contested maritime lines across four bodies of water -- where colonial-era treaties, Cold War maps, and international courts have drawn and redrawn the line between two nations.

subject: Ipubi Formation
summary: A thin layer of ancient lake sediment in northeastern Brazil that records the moment an inland sea began swallowing a continent.

subject: Isla de Aves
summary: A sand spit 375 meters long, four meters high, and sometimes entirely underwater during hurricanes -- yet this speck of Caribbean land has been fought over by five nations and gives Venezuela a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone.

subject: Iturralde crater
summary: A perfectly circular 8-kilometer scar hidden in the Bolivian Amazon, possibly carved by a cosmic explosion more powerful than any nuclear weapon ever detonated.

subject: Jamul Indian Village
summary: A federally recognized Kumeyaay tribe with roughly 12,000 years of history in San Diego County, whose people have been managing land, language, and sovereignty against considerable odds for generations.

subject: Japurá–Solimões–Negro moist forests
summary: Nearly 270,000 square kilometers of rainforest between three of the Amazon's greatest rivers, where the water itself comes in two colors and the forest learns to live with both.

subject: Jarai language
summary: A language of sailors and islanders, spoken by farmers on a red basalt plateau more than a hundred kilometres from any coast.

subject: Jehol Biota
summary: An entire ecosystem from 133 to 120 million years ago, preserved with astonishing detail in the rocks of northeastern China -- feathered dinosaurs, the earliest flowers, and the creatures that lived beside them.

subject: Joesjö
summary: A village abandoned by its founders, restarted by one stubborn settler in 1844, and remembered mostly as the birthplace of the greatest male alpine skier who ever raced.

subject: Johnstone Strait
summary: A 110-kilometer channel along Vancouver Island's northeast coast that serves as a major shipping lane, a summer home for 150 orcas, and the site of one of the longest-running whale research programs in the world.

subject: June 2017 Portugal wildfires
summary: On a scorching June afternoon in 2017, wildfires swept through central Portugal with terrifying speed, killing 66 people and exposing the deadly consequences of eucalyptus monoculture in a warming climate.

subject: Keystone Korner
summary: A North Beach jazz club that was one of the most important live recording venues in America from 1970 to 1983.

subject: Kleiner Perkins
summary: The venture capital firm on Sand Hill Road that backed Amazon, Google, and Netscape has shaped Silicon Valley's trajectory since 1972 with bets that turned millions into billions.

subject: Klivazh
summary: Deep beneath a Donbas coal mine, Soviet engineers once detonated a nuclear device to tame the deadly gas in the seams - a Cold War experiment now slowly filling with water and worry.

subject: Knersvlakte
summary: A quartz-strewn plain in the Western Cape whose name mimics the sound of wagon wheels grinding over white stones -- and whose tiny, endemic succulents grow nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Koroit opal field
summary: A remote Queensland opal field with no power and no running water, where prized boulder opal grows in laced webs through hard ironstone.

story.title: La Posta Band of Diegueño Mission Indians

subject: La Posta Band of Diegueño Mission Indians
summary: A Kumeyaay Tiipai band on 3,556 acres near the Mexican border — whose people signed 18 treaties between 1851 and 1852 promising 7.5 million acres, watched those treaties go unratified and buried under a Senate order of secrecy for 53 years, and have governed their small reservation ever since.

subject: La Rumorosa
summary: A Baja California mountain town at 4,193 feet, directly across the border from Jacumba — known for a legendarily dangerous road down to the desert floor, the El Vallecito archaeological site, and a name that translates as 'the murmuring one.'

subject: Lagoa dos Patos
summary: The largest lagoon in Brazil is a brackish inland sea the size of Jamaica, where dolphins, flamingos, and the occasional lost whale share a single narrow door to the Atlantic.

subject: Laguna Colorada
summary: A shallow, hypersaline lake at 4,278 meters on the Bolivian Altiplano, Laguna Colorada glows in shades of crimson and pink thanks to pigmented algae and red sediments, its waters dotted with white borax islands and thousands of flamingos.

subject: Laguna Mountains
summary: The Laguna Mountains rise abruptly from the Sonoran Desert to form the southernmost crest of the Pacific Crest Trail, a sky island where Kumeyaay people lived for millennia above the desert floor.

subject: Lengede
summary: In 1963 a settling pond broke into the iron mine under this Lower Saxon village; eleven men were brought up alive after fourteen days, and twenty-nine were not brought up at all.

subject: Limmen Bight
summary: A vast, shallow curve of the Gulf of Carpentaria where seagrass meadows feed the Northern Territory's largest dugong population, and the Marra people have kept sea country for thousands of years.

subject: Loch Loyal
summary: A four-mile freshwater loch in northern Sutherland, ringed by mountains and home to a thousand greylag geese.

subject: Loch Seaforth
summary: A long, three-elbowed sea loch that draws the boundary between Lewis and Harris and gives its name to two storied Hebridean ships.

subject: Magnetic Hill
summary: The New Brunswick hillside where cars roll uphill against apparent gravity - an optical illusion that's drawn visitors since the 1930s, turned into theme park, and proven that knowing the trick doesn't diminish the experience of watching physics seem to fail.

subject: Manche Chʼol
summary: A Maya people who held out for two centuries against Spanish missionaries, Itza raiders, and epidemic disease in the jungles of eastern Guatemala -- until forced relocation to the cold highlands destroyed them entirely.

subject: Maralinga Tjarutja
summary: The story of an Aboriginal people forcibly removed from their land so the British could detonate atomic bombs on it, and their decades-long fight to return.

subject: Maranoa, Queensland
summary: A vast district of mulga and brigalow in Queensland's south-west, where a river named for duck eggs runs through grazing country older than any map.

subject: Marine World/Africa USA
summary: An animal theme park in the Redwood Shores area of Redwood City that combined marine shows with African wildlife exhibits before relocating to Vallejo.

subject: Marungu highlands
summary: Above the western shore of Lake Tanganyika rises a mountain country where a single small tree frog lives - and nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Mauritania
summary: A land where the Sahara meets the Atlantic, home to the world's longest train, ancient caravan cities, and one of the great bird sanctuaries on Earth.

subject: Mbabaram language
summary: The Aboriginal language of the southern Atherton Tableland, whose word for 'dog' is — by pure chance — 'dog,' and which fell nearly silent before linguists could record what its last speakers carried.

story.title: Medicine Hat: The City Rudyard Kipling Said Had Hell Beneath

subject: Medicine Hat
summary: The Alberta city sitting atop such vast natural gas reserves that Rudyard Kipling declared it 'has all hell for a basement' - where free gas once heated homes, where the name comes from a Blackfoot medicine man's headdress lost crossing the river.

subject: Merina Kingdom
summary: From fortified hilltops on Madagascar's central plateau, the Merina dynasty built a kingdom that unified most of the world's fourth-largest island -- before European ambitions tore it apart.

subject: Meteor Crater
summary: A mining engineer spent 27 years drilling for a meteorite that had already turned to vapor 50,000 years before he arrived.

subject: Minas Basin
summary: An inlet of the Bay of Fundy where tidal currents through a single channel equal the combined flow of every river on Earth, and where Acadian dykes still hold back waters that rise over 16 meters.

subject: Mona's 440 Club
summary: The first lesbian bar to open in San Francisco, operating from 1936 into the 1950s.

subject: Mosquito Coast
summary: The Mosquito Coast -- named not for insects but for the Miskito people -- spent centuries as a contested borderland where indigenous sovereignty, British ambition, and Central American nationalism collided.

subject: Murranji Track
summary: Named after a burrowing frog in the Mudburra language, the Murranji Track earned the names 'ghost road of the drovers' and 'death track' — a 644 km waterless stock route through the Northern Territory that only opened because a Mudburra guide knew where to find water.

subject: Mussel Rock
summary: The San Andreas Fault enters the Pacific Ocean at this eroding sea stack off Daly City, where paragliders ride updrafts above the same geology that shattered San Francisco in 1906.

subject: Narena
summary: A small Malian town in the Mande heartland that takes its name, by local tradition, from a soldier's mother, and that remembers itself as a cradle of the Konaté family.

subject: New Zealand Great Walks
summary: Ten trails chosen by New Zealand's Department of Conservation that span volcanic plateaus, ancient rainforest, coastal beaches, and one river you paddle rather than walk - the country's definitive tramping collection.

subject: Nguồn Language
summary: In the limestone valleys where Vietnam meets Laos, a few thousand people speak a language that outside scholars have spent a century failing to agree about.

subject: Ngäbe-Buglé Comarca
summary: Panama's largest indigenous territory was carved from three provinces in 1997 after decades of political pressure, creating a homeland for the Ngabe and Bugle peoples that stretches from Caribbean rainforest to Pacific grassland.

subject: Niles Cone
summary: An underground aquifer in Alameda County that supplies drinking water to East Bay cities -- an invisible geological feature with enormous practical importance.

subject: North West Coastal Highway
summary: A 1,300-kilometre sealed lifeline that strings together Geraldton, Carnarvon and the Pilbara ports across some of the emptiest, oldest country in Australia.

subject: Northeast Passage
summary: The maritime route that haunted Arctic explorers for centuries now carries tankers and cargo ships along the northern coasts of Norway and Russia, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans through some of the most forbidding waters on Earth.

subject: Northeastern Brazil restingas
summary: A 400-kilometer strip of sand-rooted forest along the Atlantic coast where shrubland, dune systems, and caatinga stitch themselves together.

subject: Northern Annamites rain forests
summary: Forty-seven thousand square kilometres of Laos and Vietnam where fire keeps the pines alive, conifers grow fifty metres tall, and a third of the ground is nominally protected.

subject: Northern Rhodesia
summary: A British protectorate built on dubious treaties and copper wealth, Northern Rhodesia spent six decades under colonial rule before African nationalists broke the Federation and won independence as Zambia in 1964.

subject: Northern Territory
summary: Covering 1.4 million square kilometres with just 246,000 people, Australia's Northern Territory is where the country's oldest cultures, most dramatic landscapes, and outback extremes converge.

subject: Northern Vietnam Lowland Rain Forests
summary: A rainforest with an average elevation of eighty-eight metres, which is another way of saying it grew on the best farmland in Vietnam — and mostly lost.

subject: Nuba Mountains
summary: A green island of inselbergs in Sudan's dry middle, home to fifty distinct Nuba peoples who have survived four decades of being targeted for who they are.

subject: Numto
summary: A sacred lake of the Khanty people in Western Siberia, where a heart-shaped island holds spiritual power and oil companies press at the gates of a protected wilderness.

subject: October 2017 Iberian wildfires
summary: In October 2017, more than 7,900 fires swept across northern Portugal and northwestern Spain in a single week, killing 49 people as Hurricane Ophelia's winds turned arson into catastrophe.

subject: Off-roading in Baja
summary: Where a thousand miles of unforgiving desert, mountain, and marsh became the ultimate proving ground for machines and drivers, the Baja Peninsula has forged motorsports legends since the 1960s.

subject: Offshore wind farm He Dreiht
summary: EnBW won the contract to build this 960-megawatt North Sea wind farm with a bid of exactly zero cents per kilowatt-hour - a number that quietly changed how the offshore wind business works.

subject: Ojos del Salado
summary: The highest volcano on Earth straddles the Chile-Argentina border in air so dry that almost no snow sticks to its summit -- yet a tiny crater lake survives at 6,480 meters, the highest lake of any kind in the world.

subject: Okstindbreen
summary: Norway's eighth-largest mainland glacier lost nearly a third of its area in ten years — a change measured in square kilometres and visible from the Swedish border.

subject: Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary
summary: Over 3,100 square miles of protected Pacific Ocean along Washington's Olympic Peninsula -- one of the largest marine sanctuaries in the United States, stretching 135 miles from Cape Flattery to the Copalis River.

subject: Optimatoi
summary: Once the Byzantine Empire's elite cavalry, the Optimatoi were demoted to muleteers — and then gave their name to the province that stretched across the hills opposite Constantinople.

subject: Oriente (Ecuador)
summary: Nearly half of Ecuador lies east of the Andes in a rainforest region called the Oriente, home to 5 percent of the country's people, most of its petroleum, and nations of indigenous peoples whose ancestral lands have defined their fate.

subject: Orinoco Belt
summary: Stretching 600 kilometers along the southern Orinoco basin, the Orinoco Belt contains the world's largest petroleum deposits, with estimated reserves exceeding those of Saudi Arabia.

subject: Pacheedaht First Nation
summary: The people of the sea foam hold four small reserves at the head of Port San Juan -- and a territory that in 2021 became the most contested forest in Canada.

subject: Pacifica Foundation
summary: The nonprofit that created KPFA in Berkeley, the first listener-supported radio station in the United States.

subject: Papua (province)
summary: In 2022, Indonesia redrew the map and what had been the country's biggest province became three new ones plus a smaller Papua - the northern belt around Jayapura.

subject: Parnaíba Basin
summary: A 600,000-square-kilometer cratonic basin holding 3.4 kilometers of Paleozoic sediment, spanning five states and recording half a billion years of Brazil's tectonic history.

subject: Pendine Sands
summary: Seven miles of hard, flat Welsh beach where Malcolm Campbell and J.G. Parry-Thomas chased the land speed record in the 1920s, and where one of them died trying.

subject: Penyagolosa
summary: The most beloved mountain in the Valencian Community - a solitary 1,813-meter peak long mistaken for the region's highest, crowned with snow and old pilgrim paths.

subject: Pink and White Terraces
summary: Once called the Eighth Wonder of the World, New Zealand's largest silica sinter terraces drew tourists from across the globe before a volcanic eruption buried them in a single night in 1886.

subject: Plantation of Ulster
summary: In 1609, half a million acres of confiscated Gaelic land were handed to English-speaking Protestant settlers - an act of colonisation whose echoes still shape Northern Ireland today.

subject: Port Renfrew
summary: A village of 262 at the end of Vancouver Island's south coast highway, where the Graveyard of the Pacific meets the largest Douglas firs on Earth.

subject: Prirazlomnoye field
summary: Russia's first commercial Arctic offshore oil platform sits alone in the ice-choked Pechora Sea, its name meaning 'at the geological fault' -- an apt description for the fractures it has opened between energy ambition and environmental protest.

subject: Province of Carolina
summary: Eight English noblemen received a charter in 1663 to a strip of North America that stretched, in theory, from the Atlantic to the Pacific - and the philosopher John Locke wrote their constitution.

subject: Province of Georgia
summary: The last of the Thirteen Colonies to join the Revolution, Georgia began as a radical social experiment: a utopian buffer state where slavery was banned and debtors could start over.

subject: Quevedo
summary: A working-class coastal-zone city in central Ecuador known as the Chinatown of the country, where chifa restaurants outnumber tourist brochures.

story.title: Racetrack Playa: Where Rocks Move on Their Own

subject: Racetrack Playa
summary: The Death Valley lakebed where rocks weighing hundreds of pounds leave trails across the mud, apparently moving without human or animal intervention - a mystery that fascinated scientists for decades until cameras finally caught the stones in the act.

subject: Raid on Dunkirk (1800)
summary: A British cutting-out raid on 7 July 1800 captured one French frigate, scattered three others, and proved a handful of experimental weapons mostly useless.

subject: Rancho Canada de Raymundo
summary: A 12,545-acre Mexican land grant given in 1840 to a Baja California native named Raymundo, whose canyon now holds the towns of Woodside, La Honda, and some of the Peninsula's most expensive real estate.

subject: Rancho Guejito
summary: One of California's last intact Mexican land grants — 22,000 acres east of Escondido granted in 1845, burned in 2007, and now growing organic avocados while fending off proposals for 10,000 homes.

subject: Rancho San Dieguito
summary: An 8,824-acre Mexican land grant given to a gambling alcalde in 1845, Rancho San Dieguito passed through debt, death, and a failed eucalyptus scheme before becoming the planned community of Rancho Santa Fe.

subject: Rancho San Gregorio
summary: A massive 17,783-acre coastal land grant from 1839 that stretched from the Santa Cruz Mountain ridgeline to the Pacific Ocean, now divided between San Mateo County farmland and open space.

story.title: Rancho Santa María de los Peñasquitos

subject: Rancho Santa María de los Peñasquitos
summary: The first Mexican land grant issued in what is now San Diego County — granted in 1823 to a presidio commander — this 8,486-acre rancho encompassed a Kumeyaay village site, a stage coach stop, and the only native habitat of the rarest pine tree in America.

subject: Readymix logo geoglyph
summary: A grader driver once carved a company logo two miles wide into the Nullarbor over a holiday weekend, and for nineteen years it held the world record for the largest letters on Earth.

subject: Red Creek Fir
summary: Canada's largest known Douglas-fir stands unprotected in the San Juan Valley, its broken top hinting at a tree that was once even more massive than the giant it remains.

subject: Republic of Acre
summary: A short-lived breakaway republic born from rubber, led three times by three different men, and absorbed into Brazil within four years.

subject: Rhyl Lifeboat Station
summary: Founded 1852 with a defective prize-winning lifeboat that drowned six of its first crew - and rescued by an iron tubular design from a Bala inventor.

subject: Rio Grande do Norte
summary: More than ninety-five per cent of Brazil's salt comes from one dry corner state, where the shortage of rain is the resource rather than the problem.

subject: Rio Roosevelt Ecological Station
summary: One of the most pristine fragments of Amazon rainforest remaining in Mato Grosso, this ecological station has been created, expanded, shrunk, and re-expanded by a decades-long tug-of-war between conservation and colonization.

subject: Roaring Plains West Wilderness
summary: On the highest flat-topped plateau in eastern North America, blizzards rage above 4,000 feet while sphagnum bogs cradle threatened salamanders.

subject: Roca dels Moros
summary: On a rock shelter near El Cogul, a painted circle of women has been dancing for thousands of years, guarding one of Catalonia's oldest and most debated images of human life.

subject: Rockingham Speedway
summary: The Rock — a 0.94-mile oval in the North Carolina Sandhills that hosted NASCAR Cup races for forty years, sat empty for a decade, and refused to stop being a racetrack.

subject: Routeburn Track
summary: A 32 km alpine crossing that links two national parks across the Southern Alps - ancient Maori trail turned Great Walk, rising from beech forest to a saddle at 1,255 metres where kea patrol the ridgeline.

subject: Russian Battleship Ekaterina II
summary: The lead ship of the Imperial Russian Navy's 1880s ironclads was so thoroughly distrusted by her own admirals that when revolution stirred in 1905, they crippled her engines to keep her loyal.

subject: Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve
summary: Home to Borel Hill, the highest named point in San Mateo County, this ridgetop preserve of wildflower meadows and ancient oaks offers some of the finest views on the Peninsula.

subject: SCK CEN
summary: In a former heath at Mol, Belgium has built one of the most ambitious nuclear research centers in Europe, complete with a reactor controlled by a particle accelerator that doesn't yet exist anywhere else on earth.

subject: San Francisco Cable Car System
summary: The world's last manually operated cable car system, a National Historic Landmark that has been pulling passengers up San Francisco's hills since Andrew Hallidie's first run in 1873.

subject: Sandwater
summary: A shallow East Frisian fen lake that has appeared, disappeared, and reappeared over thousands of years — and is now slowly closing itself in with reeds.

subject: Saratoga Passage
summary: An 18-mile waterway between Whidbey and Camano Islands where competing imperial names survive in the place names, salmon runs have vanished, and Dungeness crab still thrive.

subject: Selja Gorges
summary: A hidden desert canyon in southern Tunisia where phosphate railways thread through deep ravines sheltering golden eagles and spotted hyenas.

story.title: Serra da Ibiapaba Environmental Protection Area

subject: Serra da Ibiapaba Environmental Protection Area
summary: A 1.6-million-hectare federal APA stretched across the Piauí-Ceará border, stitching together cerrado, caatinga, and seasonal forest around the red-handed howler's last northeastern redoubts.

subject: Seven Lakes Basin
summary: A glacier-carved bowl at the head of the Sol Duc River holding eight lakes that nobody renamed, reached by a nineteen-mile loop that climbs out of Olympic rainforest onto a ridge facing Mount Olympus.

story.title: Shenandoah: The Skyline Drive Through America's Oldest Mountains

subject: Shenandoah
summary: The Virginia park where 105 miles of mountain driving trace the Blue Ridge - where Skyline Drive follows the crest, where fall color draws millions, and where the Appalachians' ancient geology wears gently into rolling peaks above the Shenandoah Valley that gave the park its name.

subject: Sierra Madre Occidental
summary: Mexico's western mountain spine runs 1,250 kilometers from the Arizona border to central Mexico, sheltering indigenous nations, the deepest canyons in North America, and some of the continent's last old-growth forests.

subject: Smoke Hole Caverns
summary: A West Virginia show cave with the world's largest ribbon stalactite, where Prohibition-era moonshiners once hid their stills underground.

subject: Sol de Mañana
summary: At nearly 4,900 meters in remote southern Bolivia, Sol de Mañana is one of the highest geothermal fields on Earth, where fumaroles, bubbling mud pools, and steam vents erupt from the altiplano floor in an uninhabited volcanic landscape.

subject: Solar eclipse of May 20, 1966
summary: On a May morning in 1966, the Moon nearly swallowed the Sun over the Turkish coast, and the world's eclipse-watchers gathered at Ayvalık to catch a ring of fire that lasted only seconds.

subject: Soom Shale
summary: A thin layer of shale in the Cederberg mountains preserves 440-million-year-old soft tissues with such fidelity that it reverses the usual rules of fossilization.

subject: South China Sea
summary: A 3.5-million-square-kilometer expanse of ocean where ancient trade routes, overlapping territorial claims, and Cold War rivalries converge, the South China Sea carries a third of the world's maritime shipping and remains one of the planet's most contested bodies of water.

subject: Southern Bight
summary: The shallowest, busiest stretch of the North Sea - sea area Thames in the shipping forecast - where four great rivers meet a sand-banked sea floor.

subject: Spider crater
summary: A billion-year-old meteorite impact in the remote Kimberley — invisible from the ground, spectacular from the air, and one of the most visually striking impact structures on Earth.

subject: Strzelecki Creek
summary: A desert creek that is dry most years yet gave its name to an entire desert and one of Australia's most famous outback tracks, an overflow channel that only fills when distant Queensland rains run south.

subject: Stzʼuminus First Nation
summary: The Stz'uminus First Nation reclaimed their Hul'qumi'num name and then helped rename an entire sea, transforming the Strait of Georgia into the Salish Sea.

story.title: Sudbury: Where NASA Trained for the Moon

subject: Sudbury
summary: The Ontario mining city whose meteor-blasted, mining-scarred landscape so resembled the moon that NASA sent Apollo astronauts here to train - now regreened through environmental restoration, transformed from cautionary tale to recovery success.

subject: Sudd
summary: One of the world's largest wetlands, the Sudd is a vast swamp in South Sudan where the White Nile dissolves into channels, lagoons, and floating islands of vegetation -- a barrier that defeated Roman soldiers, Victorian explorers, and a German mega-excavator alike.

subject: Sumas Prairie
summary: Some of the most productive farmland in British Columbia sits on the floor of a lake that was drained a century ago - and that keeps trying to come back.

story.title: Superstition Mountains: Where Gold Kills Everyone Who Finds It

subject: Superstition Mountains
summary: The Arizona wilderness where the Lost Dutchman's Gold Mine has lured treasure hunters for 130 years - most finding nothing, some dying in the attempt, none ever producing the fortune that German immigrant Jacob Waltz supposedly discovered and took to his grave.

subject: Swami's
summary: Named for the Indian spiritual teacher whose ashram watches over it from the bluffs, Swami's is the only right point break in North County San Diego — mentioned in the Beach Boys' 'Surfin' U.S.A.,' surrounded by a marine protected area, and layered with fossils 45 million years old.

subject: São Paulo (state)
summary: The Brazilian state that generates one-third of the national GDP, home to fifteen million people of Italian descent and the largest Japanese population outside Japan.

subject: Taft Point
summary: A mile-high granite ledge in Yosemite where the earth cracks open into fissures dropping straight to the valley floor - named for a president too heavy for the park's horses, and haunted by the last flight of a legendary climber.

subject: Taim Ecological Station
summary: On a thin ribbon of marsh between the ocean and an inland sea, the world's largest rodent ambles across the highway while caimans watch from the reeds.

subject: Tanaru Indigenous Territory
summary: An 8,070-hectare indigenous territory in Rondonia whose sole inhabitant, the last survivor of a massacred people, lived alone in the forest for over 26 years until his death in 2022.

subject: Tanganika-Moero District
summary: A Belgian Congo administrative district that existed from 1912 to 1933, named for two lakes, and dissolved into successor units whose boundaries still shape today's DR Congo provinces.

subject: The Bahamas
summary: An archipelago of more than 3,000 islands where Lucayan, colonial, and modern histories collide across turquoise shallows that have shaped everything from the Age of Exploration to offshore finance.

story.title: The Bermuda Triangle: Where Ships and Planes Vanish

subject: The Bermuda Triangle
summary: Where dozens of ships and aircraft have allegedly disappeared without explanation in a region between Miami, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico - though investigators say the 'mystery' is mostly myth.

story.title: The Chilkoot Trail and the Golden Stairs

subject: The Chilkoot Trail and the Golden Stairs
