subject: Skomvær Lighthouse
summary: Standing at the windswept outer edge of the Lofoten archipelago, Skomvær Lighthouse is a two-million-candela beacon that goes dark each summer because the midnight sun makes it unnecessary.

subject: Sletringen Lighthouse
summary: Scandinavia's tallest lighthouse stands sentinel on the wind-battered western tip of Froya island, its red cast-iron tower dark for only two months each summer when the northern sky never fully dims.

subject: Space Place at Carter Observatory
summary: Perched atop Wellington's Botanic Garden, a 19th-century telescope that once photographed Halley's Comet still shows visitors the southern sky from New Zealand's oldest surviving observatory.

subject: St Bride's Church
summary: The church that gave the world the tiered wedding cake, the parish church of British journalism, and the place where the parents of Virginia Dare were married before they sailed to vanish at Roanoke.

subject: St Helen's Church, Bishopsgate
summary: The largest surviving parish church in the City of London, sometimes called the Westminster Abbey of the City, where Shakespeare worshipped and Robert Hooke is buried.

subject: St Nicholas Cole Abbey
summary: Never an abbey, despite the name, this small Wren church was the first of the City churches to be rebuilt after the Great Fire and the gold-bullion heist scene in The Lavender Hill Mob.

subject: St. James' Church, Antwerp
summary: The unfinished tower never reached the 150 metres planned to humiliate the Cathedral. The interior is the most opulent Baroque in Antwerp - and in the eastern chapel lies the grave of Peter Paul Rubens, painted by his own hand.

story.title: St. Louis: The Gateway City That Opened the West and Then Got Left Behind

subject: St. Louis
summary: The Missouri metropolis where Lewis and Clark launched westward and the Arch now commemorates it - where the Cardinals are religion, where the population has collapsed by two-thirds, and where the Gateway still stands over a city searching for its next act.

subject: St. Paul's Chapel
summary: Manhattan's oldest surviving church has witnessed the birth of a nation, the death of 2,977 people on September 11, and everything in between -- and it has never closed its doors.

subject: Stag Inn, Hastings
summary: Two mummified cats on a wall, a smugglers' bolthole behind a Georgian face, and a 16th-century timber frame still hidden under the plaster.

subject: State Emigrant Refuge and Hospital
summary: Once the largest hospital complex in the world, this forgotten institution on Wards Island was the first stop for hundreds of thousands of sick and destitute immigrants arriving in New York.

subject: Statue of Darth Vader
summary: The Odesa monument where Vladimir Lenin was transformed, cape and helmet and all, into the world's first statue of Darth Vader.

subject: Statue of Graf Vorontsov
summary: The Odesa monument to the governor who built the city, mocked in verse by Pushkin and fought over by every regime since.

subject: Statue of Millicent Fawcett
summary: Parliament Square's first ever statue of a woman, unveiled in 2018 for the centenary of partial women's suffrage - and made by a woman, after a journalist on a jog noticed every other monument in the square was male.

subject: Stockholm Arlanda Airport
summary: Sweden's gateway to the world sits on ancient parish lands, where the name itself plays on the Swedish word for 'to land' - a linguistic joke from the 1950s that stuck.

subject: Stockholm City Hall
summary: The red-brick masterpiece where Nobel laureates dine beneath eighteen million golden mosaic tiles and the Three Crowns of Sweden crown a tower visible across the city.

subject: Strathpeffer Pavilion
summary: A Victorian spa pavilion in the Scottish Highlands that hosted suffragettes, polar explorers, and very nearly the Beatles.

subject: Strathpeffer Railway Station
summary: A Highland Railway branch built because one Victorian laird refused to let a train cross his land, and then refused again when they tried to fix it.

subject: Studio Museum in Harlem
summary: Born in a rented loft in 1968 and reborn in a $160 million building in 2025, the Studio Museum in Harlem has spent nearly six decades as the premier institution for art of the African diaspora.

subject: Sulitjelma Church
summary: The copper town consecrated its graveyard five years before it consecrated its church — and of the 556 people buried in that first ground, half were children under ten.

subject: Sulitjelma Hotel
summary: A mine director's villa that was taken apart on one Arctic fjord, shipped 400 kilometres, rebuilt as the grandest house in a copper town, and has been trying to decide what it is ever since.

subject: Surabaya City Hall
summary: A 1920s municipal building designed by Cosman Citroen in the New Indies Style, where Dutch colonial ambition met tropical reality and produced one of Indonesia's finest examples of climate-conscious modernism.

subject: Susendal Church
summary: When the bishop condemned their 1916 chapel, the farmers of the Susendal valley built its replacement themselves — a log church with an altarpiece about sowing and harvest.

subject: Sydenham Hospital
summary: From 1892 to 1980, Sydenham Hospital served Harlem's Black community -- pioneering in the hiring of African-American doctors, then becoming a flashpoint when New York's fiscal crisis forced it to close.

subject: Taipei Prison
summary: From a Qing-era detention facility to a Japanese colonial prison where Allied airmen were executed in 1945, Taipei Prison carries more than a century of history within its walls — a record of empire, war, and the lives caught between them.

subject: Taitung Children's Story House
summary: A Japanese-era colonial dormitory from 1937 that spent seventy years housing tobacco and liquor company employees before being transformed into one of Taitung's most beloved children's spaces — complete with treehouse, cat trail, and story-filled afternoons.

story.title: Tallinn Museum of Orders of Knighthood

subject: Tallinn Museum of Orders of Knighthood
summary: A small museum on a medieval Tallinn street displaying nearly a thousand orders, decorations, and chivalric badges, including pieces once worn by Peter the Great and Metternich.

subject: Tallinn Town Hall
summary: The oldest town hall in northern Europe, built between 1402 and 1404 and crowned by a weather-vane warrior named Old Thomas who has stood watch since 1530.

subject: Taluksangay Mosque
summary: Built in 1885 by Hadji Abdullah Maas Nuno, this oldest mosque in the Zamboanga Peninsula stands in a village that served as the first center of Islamic propagation in the region, home to the unconquered descendants of the Sama Banguingui seafarers.

subject: Tangeværket Dam
summary: The dam that once carried nearly a quarter of Jutland's electricity now supplies three hundredths of a percent of Denmark's — and Danes have argued for a century about whether to take it down.

subject: Temple Bar
summary: Christopher Wren's only surviving City of London gateway, exiled to a Hertfordshire forest for 125 years and finally returned to stand beside St Paul's Cathedral.

subject: Tenby Town Hall
summary: The neoclassical Pembrokeshire municipal building completed in 1829 that hosted council meetings for over a century - and later gigs by Fleetwood Mac and Super Furry Animals.

subject: Tent House, Mount Isa
summary: A frame of canvas and corrugated iron, this rare survivor is the last of the makeshift homes that sheltered Mount Isa's first miners against the brutal outback heat.

story.title: The Last Stop: Nagoya's Tram & Subway Museum

subject: The Last Stop
summary: A free museum in Nisshin preserves the streetcars and subway cars that once carried 271,000 passengers daily through Nagoya -- a city that chose to bury its transit underground and then built a quiet shrine to what it replaced.

subject: The Mo Sheringham Museum
summary: A Norfolk town's museum, built on top of a sewerage tank, housing four restored lifeboats and the story of a fishing village turned holiday resort.

subject: This Is the Place Monument
summary: At the mouth of Emigration Canyon, where Brigham Young first viewed the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, a massive monument commemorates not just Mormon pioneers but all the explorers and settlers who shaped the American West.

subject: Toowoomba City Hall
summary: A fire cleared the ground, a design called 'Sincerity' won the commission, and a clock shipped from England gave a young city its voice.

subject: Toven Tunnel
summary: Northern Norway's longest road tunnel runs 10,665 metres under a Helgeland mountain to carry about 1,500 vehicles a day - and that arithmetic is the whole argument about roads in a thinly populated country.

subject: Transfiguration Cathedral in Odesa
summary: Odesa's mother church, demolished to rubble in the Soviet era and painstakingly raised again from nothing at the turn of the millennium.

subject: Trinity Church (Manhattan)
summary: The oldest continuously active parish in New York City stands at the corner of Broadway and Wall Street, its churchyard holding Alexander Hamilton and Robert Fulton while its Gothic spire has watched the city grow from a colonial outpost to a financial capital.

subject: Trones Church
summary: A white timber church on the upper Namsen that took ten years to build, and that has spent nearly two centuries being credited to an architect who was born the year after it opened.

subject: Træna Lighthouse
summary: A red cast iron sentinel on a granite perch, Træna Lighthouse has guided vessels through the wild Nordland archipelago since 1877, flashing its solitary white pulse across nearly 23 kilometers of open Norwegian Sea.

subject: Tully Cross
summary: Nine thatched cottages, three Harry Clarke stained-glass windows, and a mussel festival on the Atlantic edge of Connemara.

subject: Tyzenhauz Palace
summary: An 18th-century Vilnius palace built by Lithuania's most ambitious - and ultimately bankrupt - royal treasurer, now a quiet courtyard building hiding a Gothic cellar beneath its floors.

story.title: Uda Matsuyama Castle: The Fortress That Left a Letter

subject: Uda Matsuyama Castle
summary: A Sengoku-era mountain castle in Nara was so thoroughly demolished on shogunal orders in 1615 that even its destroyer complained about the labor -- but the castle town it once protected still stands as a preserved district of traditional buildings.

subject: Underground Hospital, Mount Isa
summary: When Darwin was bombed in 1942, off-duty miners spent two frantic weeks tunneling a fully equipped hospital into a hillside, bracing for an air raid that never came.

subject: Vadstena Castle
summary: A fortress built to defend Stockholm became one of Sweden's finest Renaissance palaces, shaped by every Vasa king yet abandoned by the crown to become a grain barn.

subject: Valentine–Varian House
summary: A 1758 fieldstone farmhouse in the Bronx that survived British occupation, bankruptcy, urbanization, and near-demolition to become the Museum of Bronx History.

subject: Van Cortlandt House
summary: The oldest surviving house in the Bronx, a 1749 Georgian mansion that served as headquarters for both British and American forces during the Revolution and has operated as a museum since 1897.

subject: Vaxholm Fortress
summary: A 16th-century island fortress that guarded Stockholm for 300 years, became a punchline for Prussian generals, and starred as a pirate stronghold in Pippi Longstocking.

subject: Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge
summary: The longest suspension bridge in the Americas took four decades of proposals, false starts, and political maneuvering before it finally opened in 1964 — and it was misspelled for the first 54 years of its existence.

subject: Vestervig Abbey
summary: One of Denmark's oldest religious houses, founded around 1059 near the Limfjord, where a Thuringian missionary's miraculous springs drew pilgrims for centuries.

subject: Viborg Cathedral
summary: Viborg took its own cathedral down to the ground in 1863 and rebuilt it as a nineteenth-century guess at the twelfth — then let Joakim Skovgaard paint every wall.

subject: Villa 31
summary: Wedged between Buenos Aires' grandest avenues and its busiest port, Villa 31 is a neighborhood that built itself over ninety years and refused, again and again, to be erased.

subject: Villa Carlos Paz
summary: Córdoba's busiest resort town announces every hour with a seven-and-a-half-meter cuckoo clock built by German engineers in 1958.

subject: Villa Epecuén
summary: A thriving lakeside spa town vanished beneath ten meters of salt water in 1985, stayed submerged for a quarter century, and rose again as a bleached and silent ghost.

subject: Villa General Belgrano
summary: A Bavarian village in the Argentine sierras, partly built by shipwrecked German sailors and home to the third-largest Oktoberfest on Earth.

subject: Villa Ukika
summary: A cluster of houses by a river on Navarino Island, Villa Ukika is where the Yaghan people - among the world's southernmost - have held on to language, craft, and memory at the end of the Earth.

subject: Villa de Merlo
summary: An Argentine resort town that built its fame on the quality of its air - and on a carob tree older than the conquest.

subject: Villa la Angostura
summary: A pocket-sized alpine village on Lake Nahuel Huapi's shore where mountain bikers share trails with 300-year-old trees and a forest so enchanting it inspired Disney's Bambi.

subject: Visby Cathedral
summary: Built by German traders in the 13th century, this Hanseatic church stands as the sole survivor of medieval Visby's many houses of worship.

subject: Vorontsov Lighthouse
summary: The red-and-white beacon at the end of Odesa's harbor jetty that spells out the city's own initial in flashes of light.

subject: Waltham Abbey
summary: The last English monastery to be dissolved, the believed burial place of Harold Godwinson, and home to 300 years of gunpowder innovation - all in one Essex town on the Greenwich Meridian.

subject: West Gate Bridge
summary: Melbourne's great river crossing carries two hundred thousand vehicles a day above the Yarra, and the memory of thirty-five workers who died building it.

subject: Whaley House
summary: Built in 1857 on the site of a public hanging, the Whaley House served as San Diego's finest home, first commercial theater, county courthouse, and general store — and the Whaley family blamed the ghost of 'Yankee Jim' Robinson for the footsteps they heard at night.

subject: Wolf's Castle
summary: A two-village Pembrokeshire community on the Landsker Line, sitting above a chess opening still played in tournaments today.

subject: Woolworth Building
summary: A five-and-dime magnate's neo-Gothic cathedral of commerce that reigned as the world's tallest building for seventeen years and still dazzles Lower Manhattan with terracotta panels fired in shades of blue, green, sienna, and rose.

subject: Xihua Gate
summary: The western gate of the Forbidden City witnessed imperial flight, rebel assault, and modern political drama across six centuries of Chinese history.

subject: Yankee Stadium (1923)
summary: The original Yankee Stadium, 'The House That Ruth Built,' stood in the Bronx for 85 years, hosted 6,581 regular-season games, three Papal Masses, and the most famous moments in baseball before its demolition in 2010.

story.title: Yuan Dadu City Wall Ruins Park

subject: Yuan Dadu City Wall Ruins Park
summary: A narrow park in Beijing preserving the northern city wall of Khanbaliq, the Mongol capital that Kublai Khan built and Marco Polo described in wonder.

story.title: Yuma: The Sunniest City on Earth Where Outlaws Became School Spirit

subject: Yuma
summary: The Arizona desert city where sunshine is guaranteed 90% of the year - where the Territorial Prison became a high school (mascot: The Criminals), where 90% of America's winter lettuce grows, and where New Year's Eve means dropping a head of iceberg from the water tower.

subject: Zamboanga Cathedral
summary: Three times built and twice destroyed, the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception has served as the seat of faith in Mindanao's oldest Catholic diocese since 1910, its current candle-shaped structure rising from the ashes of World War II and the appetites of termites.

story.title: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa

subject: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa
summary: Carved from 42 derelict grain silos on Cape Town's waterfront, Zeitz MOCAA opened in 2017 as the largest museum of contemporary African art, its cathedral-like interior a testament to both architectural audacity and a continent's artistic coming-of-age.

story.title: Zora Neale Hurston Museum of Fine Arts

subject: Zora Neale Hurston Museum of Fine Arts
summary: A small museum in America's first incorporated Black town honors the writer who made Eatonville immortal in literature and celebrates the African diaspora's artistic legacy.

subject: 1969 People's Park Protest
summary: A muddy lot in Berkeley became the flashpoint for one of America's most violent campus confrontations, where shotguns and tear gas turned a community garden dispute into Bloody Thursday.

subject: 1974 Suez Canal Clearance Operation
summary: After eight years of closure following the Six-Day War, an international military operation involving minesweeping helicopters, deep-sea divers, and 1,700 Egyptian engineers cleared 686,000 landmines to reopen the Suez Canal.

subject: 1990 Guangzhou Baiyun Airport Collisions
summary: On 2 October 1990, a hijacked Boeing 737 collided with two aircraft at Guangzhou Baiyun Airport, killing 128 people in what became the deadliest aviation hijacking before September 11.

subject: 2021 Suez Canal obstruction
summary: For six days in March 2021, a single container ship wedged sideways across the Suez Canal paralyzed 12 percent of global trade, spawned a billion-dollar legal battle, and became the world's most famous meme.

subject: 228 Peace Memorial Park
summary: A Taipei park that began as a colonial showpiece in 1900 became a site of broadcast propaganda, then a memorial to one of Taiwan's darkest chapters: the February 28 Incident of 1947.

subject: 54 University Avenue
summary: A colonial-era villa on Inya Lake in Yangon became the world's most famous house arrest when Aung San Suu Kyi was confined within its walls for nearly fifteen years.

story.title: A King's Canal, Carved in Stone

subject: A King's Canal, Carved in Stone
summary: A fifth-century Sanskrit inscription on an egg-shaped stone records the massive river engineering projects of King Purnawarman, offering the earliest written evidence of hydraulic works in Southeast Asia.

subject: A Sound Garden
summary: A wind-activated sound sculpture on the NOAA campus in Seattle whose twelve steel towers sing with the breeze off Lake Washington, and whose name inspired one of the city's most celebrated rock bands.

story.title: A Wooden Stick in Rohnert Park

subject: A Wooden Stick in Rohnert Park
summary: The 1997 fatal shooting of Kuanchung Kao by a Rohnert Park police officer over a wooden stick became a rallying point for Asian American civil rights and exposed troubling patterns in Sonoma County policing.

subject: Aalborg Air Base
summary: A cement company talked North Jutland into building an airfield in 1938; eighteen months later German paratroopers dropped onto it in one of the first airborne operations ever mounted.

subject: Abel Tasman National Park
summary: New Zealand's smallest national park and perhaps its most beautiful - 22,000 hectares of golden beaches, coastal rainforest, and turquoise bays accessible only by foot, kayak, or water taxi, named for the Dutch explorer who arrived exactly 300 years before its creation.

subject: Aberdare National Park
summary: In Kenya's misty highlands, where bamboo forests hide the rarest bongo antelope on Earth, and colonial-era tree lodges still buzz when elephants appear at the salt lick below.

subject: Aberdeen Country Park
summary: Minutes from one of Asia's most vertical cities, Aberdeen Country Park preserves 4.23 square kilometres of forested hills, ancient volcanic rock, and two quiet reservoirs — a rural pocket that has survived everything Hong Kong's developers could throw at it.

subject: Aberdeen Harbour
summary: Founded in 1136 and still working today, Aberdeen Harbour is the United Kingdom's oldest existing business - and has reinvented itself for every century since.

subject: Aberdeenshire Canal
summary: An eighteen-mile waterway between Aberdeen and Inverurie, designed by John Rennie, opened in 1805, drained in 1854 so that the railway could lay its tracks along the bed.

subject: Aberporth Airport
summary: A former RAF anti-aircraft cooperation station on the Ceredigion cliffs that became the only UK airfield certified for routine flights of large military drones in unsegregated airspace.

subject: Abijatta-Shalla National Park
summary: Twin volcanic lakes born from the same ancient caldera sit side by side in Ethiopia's Great Rift Valley, one shallow and shrinking, the other the deepest in the country, together sheltering over 300 bird species in a landscape under siege.

subject: Abingdon Historic District
summary: A half-mile of Main Street in southwest Virginia preserves 145 contributing buildings, a Greek Revival church, the longest-running professional theater in America, and a hotel built as a private home for nine Preston children.

subject: Abkhazi Garden
summary: An exiled Georgian prince and a woman who survived a Japanese internment camp met again after twenty-four years, married, and spent the rest of their lives building one acre of garden in Victoria.

story.title: Abney Park Cemetery: London's Dissenting Garden of the Dead

subject: Abney Park Cemetery
summary: A pioneering non-denominational garden cemetery in Stoke Newington that became a wild urban woodland, where 200,000 burials share space with nature and the legacy of religious freedom.

subject: Abney Park Chapel
summary: The first nondenominational cemetery chapel in Europe, hidden inside a Victorian arboretum-cemetery in Stoke Newington, built to argue with the Gothic Revival on its own terms.

subject: Abraham Lincoln Memorial Garden
summary: A 100-acre woodland and prairie garden on the shore of Lake Springfield in Springfield, Illinois, designed by Jens Jensen as a living memorial to Abraham Lincoln and stewarded by volunteers and the Abraham Lincoln Memorial Garden Foundation.

subject: Aburi Botanical Gardens
summary: A 64-hectare botanical garden on Ghana's Akuapem Ridge that began as a colonial sanatorium, helped launch the country's cocoa industry, and now fights to preserve plant diversity in West Africa.

subject: Acadia National Park
summary: Where granite mountains meet the Atlantic - Maine's crown jewel where you can catch the first sunrise in America and hike trails carved by ice age glaciers.

story.title: Acadia National Park: Where the Mountains Meet the Sea

subject: Acadia National Park
summary: The first national park east of the Mississippi, where granite peaks shaped by 500 million years of geology rise directly from the Atlantic Ocean on Maine's Mount Desert Island.

subject: Acadia National Park
summary: Where the sun first rises on America - the Maine park where granite mountains meet the Atlantic, created when Gilded Age millionaires donated their summer estates to preserve the first national park east of the Mississippi.

subject: Acadian Village (park)
summary: A living museum in Lafayette, Louisiana, where eleven rescued 19th-century Cajun homes recreate the bayou-side village life of the Acadians who settled the prairies of southwest Louisiana.

subject: Acari National Park
summary: Created in a dramatic last-minute conservation push just days before a presidential impeachment, Acari National Park protects nearly 900,000 hectares of Amazon rainforest where four rivers converge in southern Amazonas.

subject: Action Park
summary: A legendarily dangerous New Jersey amusement park where at least six people died, employees were bribed to test rides, and locals nicknamed it 'Traction Park.'

subject: Addo Elephant National Park
summary: Born from the near-extinction of South Africa's Eastern Cape elephants, Addo grew from a desperate 11-elephant refuge into the world's only Big Seven park, spanning five biomes from mountain valleys to open ocean.

subject: Adelaide–Darwin railway line
summary: The transcontinental railway that took nearly a century to finish, carrying The Ghan across 2,979 km of outback from the southern coast to the tropical north.

subject: Adinkerke Military Cemetery
summary: A quiet field of stones at the end of a fifty-metre grass path, where pilots, labourers, and casualty-clearing dead from two world wars share the same Belgian soil.

story.title: Admiral Makarov National University of Shipbuilding

subject: Admiral Makarov National University of Shipbuilding
summary: The Mykolaiv university that has trained the engineers behind a century of ships, named for an admiral born in the city, and struck by missiles in 2022.

story.title: Agricultural and Technical College of North Carolina Historic District

subject: Agricultural and Technical College of North Carolina Historic District
summary: The historic core of North Carolina A&T - the HBCU that produced the Greensboro Four - sits on ten acres of Colonial Revival brick and Classical Revival stone in west Greensboro.

subject: Agulhas National Park
summary: At the southernmost tip of Africa, where two oceans collide and 2,000 plant species cling to ancient limestone, Agulhas National Park guards one of Earth's richest and most overlooked botanical treasures.

subject: Ai-Ais/Richtersveld Transfrontier Park
summary: A peace park spanning two nations and one of Earth's richest desert flora, where the Nama still herd their goats and where trees are said to be the ancestors, turned to face home.

story.title: Aiguestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park

subject: Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park
summary: Catalonia's only national park, where nearly 200 glacial lakes scatter across the high Pyrenees like shattered mirrors and brown bears still roam the forests.

subject: Air Base Karup
summary: The Luftwaffe chose the emptiest ground in Jutland for its airfield; eighty years later the same runways carry Danish military helicopters and holiday charters to Mallorca.

subject: Airlie Gardens
summary: Sixty-seven acres of azaleas, live oaks, and a chapel made of glass bottles, presided over for decades by the Black folk artist Minnie Evans.

subject: Aizu Matsudaira clan cemetery
summary: Split across two Fukushima locations, these tombs of nine feudal lords tell the story of a clan that defied the shogunate's Buddhist burial decree to honor their dead through Shinto rites for over two centuries.

subject: Akagera National Park
summary: Rwanda's only Big Five reserve, resurrected from near-destruction after the 1994 genocide through one of Africa's most remarkable conservation partnerships.

subject: Aketajawe-Lolobata National Park
summary: A 167,300-hectare national park on Halmahera that protects at least 23 endemic bird species in one of the last great strongholds of Wallacea's vanishing lowland rainforest.

subject: Al Shaheed Park
summary: Kuwait's largest urban park began as a line on a 1952 master plan, waited six decades for construction, and now anchors the nation's cultural identity with one of the world's largest green roofs.

story.title: Al-Andalusian Palatial Complex of San Esteban

subject: Al-Andalusian Palatial Complex of San Esteban
summary: A medieval Islamic quarter of Murcia, uncovered beneath a city garden slated for a car park, that a citizen uprising fought to save.

subject: Al-Baqi Cemetery
summary: Jannat al-Baqi, the principal cemetery of Medina, holds the graves of thousands of the Prophet Muhammad's family and companions beside his mosque.

subject: Alamo Canal
summary: The 14-mile canal that attempted to irrigate California's Imperial Valley — and accidentally created the Salton Sea when its headgates failed and the entire Colorado River flooded the desert for two years.

story.title: Alas Purwo: Where Java Begins and the Surf Never Stops

subject: Alas Purwo
summary: At Java's southeastern tip, a national park named 'first forest' harbors endangered banteng, world-class surf breaks, and the Javanese legend that the earth itself rose from the ocean here.

subject: Albemarle County Courthouse Historic District
summary: An 1803 Federal-style brick courthouse on Charlottesville's Court Square, where Thomas Jefferson and James Madison once worshipped on Sundays and which still anchors 22 contributing historic buildings.

subject: Alberni Pacific Railway
summary: A heritage railway powered by a 1929 Baldwin steam locomotive that spent six years in the repair shop before returning to haul passengers along the Port Alberni waterfront to a historic sawmill.

subject: Albert J. Ellis Airport
summary: The little county airport in Richlands, North Carolina, is the civilian gateway to Camp Lejeune and the Onslow County coast.

subject: Albert Park tunnels
summary: Beneath one of Auckland's most genteel parks lies a forgotten warren of World War II air raid shelters, sealed since 1946 and still waiting for someone to turn the key.

story.title: Albert Whitted Airport: Where Commercial Aviation Was Born

subject: Albert Whitted Airport
summary: The downtown St. Petersburg airport built on the very waterfront where Tony Jannus flew the world's first scheduled commercial airline flight in 1914, and where blimps, Coast Guard seaplanes, and Navy cadets shaped a century of American aviation.

subject: Alberto de Agostini National Park
summary: At the very end of South America, where fjords slice into mountains and glaciers calve directly into the sea, lies a wilderness so remote that the only way in is by ship.

subject: Alberto de Agostini National Park
summary: Where the Andes finally drown in the sea, a roadless wilderness of tidewater glaciers and fjords bears the name of a priest who climbed its mountains in his cassock.

subject: Albufera Natural Park
summary: Spain's largest lagoon is barely a metre deep, ringed by rice paddies that gave the world paella and alive with tens of thousands of migrating birds.

subject: Alderson Broaddus University
summary: The Baptist college on a hilltop above the Tygart Valley invented the four-year physician assistant degree - and closed in 2023 after 152 years.

subject: Aldie Mill Historic District
summary: An early-1800s brick mill in Loudoun County that the same Moore family ran for six generations - powered by two overshot waterwheels on the Little River, with original Oliver Evans machinery patterns inside.

subject: Alerce Costero National Park
summary: In a Chilean coastal ravine grows a tree that may have been alive when the pyramids were new, the centerpiece of a rainforest park named for the giants it protects.

story.title: Alexander Smith Carpet Mills Historic District

subject: Alexander Smith Carpet Mills Historic District
summary: A loom patented in 1877 revolutionized the carpet industry and built a factory complex in Yonkers that, after closing in 1954, has been reborn as a thriving arts district they call 'a little baby SoHo.'

subject: Alford Valley Railway
summary: A narrow gauge heritage railway in the Howe of Alford, running on the old Great North of Scotland branch line that once cut a mile through hard granite.

subject: Algoma Central Railway
summary: A wilderness railway threading through Northern Ontario's roadless Algoma District, born from an industrialist's ambition and kept alive by the sheer beauty of the land it crosses.

subject: Algonquin Provincial Park
summary: Ontario's oldest provincial park sprawls across 7,653 square kilometres of ancient Canadian Shield rock, where loon calls echo off lakes that inspired some of the most iconic paintings in Canadian history.

subject: Alice Lloyd College
summary: A journalist from Cambridge, Massachusetts and a teacher from New York arrived in a Kentucky hollow in 1916 and started a school that today guarantees free tuition to students from 108 Appalachian counties who agree to do 160 hours of work each semester.

subject: Alishan Forest Railway
summary: Built to haul cypress logs down from Taiwan's mountains, this 86-kilometer narrow-gauge railway climbs from sea level to 2,216 meters through Z-shaped switchbacks, 50 tunnels, and 77 wooden bridges -- and has become one of Asia's great train journeys.

story.title: Aliso and Wood Canyons Wilderness Park

subject: Aliso and Wood Canyons Wilderness Park
summary: A wilderness preserve where Ice Age geology meets suburban Orange County, sheltering bobcats, bald eagles, and Miocene fossils within view of five cities.

subject: All Hallows College
summary: The Drumcondra college that exported four thousand Irish priests to the English-speaking world - and that John F Kennedy quietly visited on holiday in 1955.

subject: Allen University
summary: An HBCU founded by AME ministers in 1870 to educate newly freed people, whose Columbia auditorium hosted both Langston Hughes and the strategy meetings that led to Brown v. Board.

subject: Allen University Historic District
summary: A small cluster of red-brick buildings on Harden Street that mark where Black ministers, four years after emancipation, built a university the state's flagship would not admit them to.

subject: Allerton Garden
summary: An 80-acre botanical garden on Kauai's south shore where a father and son transformed a former sugarcane valley into a living gallery of tropical plants, sculpture, and Hollywood film locations.

subject: Alonnisos Marine Park
summary: The Mediterranean's largest marine protected area, born from one German zoologist's observation and a community of fishermen who agreed to give the sea back to its rarest inhabitant.

story.title: Altamiro de Moura Pacheco State Park

subject: Altamiro de Moura Pacheco State Park
summary: A 2,132-hectare reserve of dry forest just north of Goiânia that guards both rare cerrado and the reservoir supplying water to over a million people.

subject: Alum Rock Airport
summary: A vanished early airport in east San Jose established in 1919 by a returning World War I pilot, whose flights produced much of the earliest aerial photography of the Santa Clara Valley's orchard landscape.

subject: Alum Rock Park
summary: California's oldest municipal park, established in 1872 on land that has served the public since San Jose's founding in 1777, with mineral springs, 13 miles of trails, and a canyon full of creek-play opportunities in the Diablo Range foothills.

subject: Amara War Cemetery
summary: A crumbling First World War cemetery on the banks of the Tigris in southern Iraq, where more than 4,600 Commonwealth soldiers lie in graves that have gone largely untended since 1991.

subject: Amazônia National Park
summary: A million-hectare preserve straddling the Tapajos River, where a clear blue-green tributary carves through ancient shield rock halfway between Manaus and Belem.

subject: Ambarawa Railway Museum
summary: A colonial-era railway station turned living museum where century-old German-built steam locomotives still climb the only rack railway ever built in Java.

subject: Amboró National Park
summary: A Bolivian park where giant ferns tower over visitors in rainforest groves, 900 species of bird fill the canopy, and the terrain drops 3,000 meters from cloud forest to tropical lowland within a single protected area.

subject: Amboseli National Park
summary: A 392-square-kilometer Kenyan park where over 900 elephants walk single-file across dusty plains beneath the snow-capped summit of Kilimanjaro, creating one of Africa's most iconic wildlife photographs.

subject: American College of Greece
summary: Founded as a girls' school in Ottoman Smyrna in 1875, this college survived a city's destruction, a forced migration, and a wartime occupation to become the oldest American college in Europe, now on a leafy campus in suburban Athens.

subject: American Museum and Gardens
summary: On a hillside above the Avon valley, a Georgian manor holds the only museum of American decorative arts outside the United States - and a replica of George Washington's Mount Vernon garden.

subject: American University of Afghanistan
summary: Afghanistan's first private university rose from ambition and international support, survived terror attacks, and was ultimately undone not by violence but by the collapse of the state itself.

subject: American Viscose Plant Historic District
summary: On 212 acres along the Roanoke River, a British silk company built what briefly stood as the world's largest rayon mill — a 5,000-worker giant whose chimneys still mark Southeast Roanoke's skyline.

subject: Amoy Gardens
summary: A quiet Kowloon housing estate that became the epicenter of the world's first SARS super-spreader event in 2003, when a flaw in bathroom plumbing spread a novel virus through 19 residential towers.

subject: Ampthill Park
summary: A Bedfordshire country estate where Henry VIII held Katherine of Aragon during the annulment that birthed the English Reformation, where Capability Brown reshaped the grounds, and where, in 1979, a jeweled golden hare was buried as part of the most famous treasure hunt in British publishing history.

subject: Amsterdam Muiderpoort railway station
summary: A 1939 Functionalist station in east Amsterdam that became, three years later, a boarding point for the deportation of Dutch Jews to Westerbork.

subject: Amsterdam University College
summary: A rust-red box in the Science Park where 300 students a year from 65 countries earn one of the only American-style liberal arts honors degrees in the Netherlands.

subject: Amsterdam University Medical Center
summary: Two rival university hospitals, on opposite sides of Amsterdam and on opposite sides of a century-old religious divide, finally merged in 2018 to become one of Europe's largest medical research engines.

subject: An Thoi Naval Base
summary: At the southern tip of Phu Quoc, a fishing town became the base from which America fought a war in fifty-foot aluminium boats originally designed to ferry oil-rig workers.

subject: Anacaona National Park
summary: Named for a Taino queen hanged by Spanish colonizers, this Dominican park protects nearly 600 square kilometers of shifting ecosystems -- from parched lowland scrub to cloud-draped montane forest -- and shelters some of Hispaniola's most endangered reptiles.

subject: Anastasian Wall
summary: A 56-kilometer stone and turf fortification built by the Byzantine Empire across Thrace to defend Constantinople from the west, begun in the late fifth century and visible in fragments in the woodlands west of Istanbul today.

subject: Anchorena National Park
summary: An aristocrat's vision from a hot air balloon became Uruguay's presidential retreat, where exotic deer roam beneath the nation's tallest lighthouse.

subject: Ancol War Cemetery
summary: A Dutch war cemetery in Jakarta where more than 2,000 victims of Japanese occupation lie buried, including resistance fighters executed in a swamp that became sacred ground.

subject: Ancon (archaeological site)
summary: One of the few sites in the Andes with continuous human occupation spanning 10,000 years, from stone-age fishermen to the Inca, crowned by a vast necropolis of pre-Hispanic burials.

subject: Andasibe-Mantadia National Park
summary: In the misted rainforest east of Antananarivo, the indri sings a wail that carries for miles, and the forest answers back.

subject: Anderson Marsh State Historic Park
summary: At the quiet southeast corner of California's largest natural lake, ten thousand years of human history lie buried beneath tule marshes and oak-covered hills that nearly became a budget casualty.

subject: Anderson Regional Airport
summary: Amelia Earhart's 1931 visit to a South Carolina grass field changed the trajectory of the airport that would become KAND, one of upstate South Carolina's busiest general aviation fields.

subject: Andohahela National Park
summary: A UNESCO-listed park in Madagascar's deep south where dripping rainforest, transitional woodland, and bizarre spiny desert collide within a single mountain range, sheltering ring-tailed lemurs and the last wild triangle palms.

subject: Andrew Jackson State Park
summary: Three hundred sixty acres honoring a complicated president - the boy who fought at Hanging Rock, the man who signed the Indian Removal Act, the seventh President of the United States.

subject: Andrew Johnson National Cemetery
summary: A hilltop cemetery in Greeneville, Tennessee, holding the grave of the seventeenth president — bought by Johnson himself in 1852 because, by his own bitter testimony, he wanted to be buried away from his neighbors.

subject: Andringitra National Park
summary: A granite massif in southern Madagascar where snow occasionally falls, the country's coldest temperatures are recorded, and the island's second-highest peak rewards a three-day climb.

story.title: Andromeda Botanic Gardens: Where Flowers Hid a Cold War Secret

subject: Andromeda Botanic Gardens
summary: An eight-acre tropical garden on the rugged east coast of Barbados began as one woman's plant collection and quietly doubled as a U.S. Navy submarine tracking station during the Cold War.

subject: Angkor Archaeological Park
summary: The thousand-year-old temples of the Khmer Empire rise from the Cambodian jungle, including Angkor Wat - the largest religious monument ever built - and the enigmatic stone faces of the Bayon.

subject: Anglesey Airport
summary: A small civilian terminal grafted onto RAF Valley - it ran a subsidised Cardiff service for thirteen years, then COVID and a Welsh Government decision killed the only commercial route to North Wales.

subject: Anglesey Central Railway
summary: A branch line that opened to carry copper ore in 1864, survived its passengers' departure by thirty years, and is still - slowly, against the odds - being reopened.

subject: Ankarafantsika National Park
summary: One of Madagascar's last great stands of dry deciduous forest, where one of the rarest eagles on Earth fishes a crater lake and more than 800 plant species cling to the sandy soil between two rivers.

story.title: Annie's Dell and the Cobblestones That Built San Francisco

subject: Annie's Dell and the Cobblestones That Built San Francisco
summary: A 5,092-acre park in Sonoma County owes its existence to obsidian-quarrying ancestors, cobblestone miners who paved San Francisco, and a philanthropist who twice opened his checkbook to save it from disappearing.

subject: Antietam National Battlefield
summary: America's bloodiest day - where 23,000 men fell in twelve hours on September 17, 1862, in a tactical draw that gave Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation and change the war's purpose.

subject: Antwerpen-Centraal Railway Station
summary: The dome that crowns Antwerp's main station earned it the local nickname spoorwegkathedraal - the railway cathedral - and travelers stepping off the train still look up before they look around.

subject: Aoraki / Mount Cook National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage park sheltering 22 of New Zealand's 23 peaks above 3,000 metres, where glacier-carved valleys meet alpine wilderness in the heart of the Southern Alps.

subject: Aoyama Cemetery
summary: Tokyo's first public cemetery, where seven prime ministers, the inventor of cultured pearls, an Olympic equestrian gold medalist, and a famously loyal Akita dog named Hachiko rest beneath some of the city's finest cherry blossoms.

subject: Aparados da Serra National Park
summary: At the edge of the southern Brazilian plateau, the land simply stops - and the Itaimbezinho canyon opens a 720-meter wound through ancient lava that the rest of the landscape has refused to surrender.

subject: Appalachian Bible College
summary: A small Bible college in the West Virginia hills that grew from a postwar training mission into an accredited college teaching theology - including to maximum-security prisoners.

subject: Appalachian State University
summary: A North Carolina mountain university that started in 1899 as a teachers' school and went on to become the only FCS program to win three straight national football championships - and then beat #5 Michigan in the Big House.

subject: Apple Infinite Loop Campus
summary: For 24 years, this unassuming Cupertino office complex at 1 Infinite Loop was the address where Apple designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad -- before moving to its spaceship campus.

story.title: Appomattox Court House National Historical Park

subject: Appomattox Court House National Historical Park
summary: A preserved 19th-century Virginia village where Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant on April 9, 1865, symbolically ending the American Civil War.

story.title: Appomattox Court House National Historical Park Ruins

subject: Appomattox Court House National Historical Park Ruins
summary: Stone foundations, brick chimneys, and a quiet mill race scattered through the park grounds - the lesser-known archaeological remains of the village where Lee surrendered to Grant in 1865.

subject: Appomattox Historic District
summary: A railroad town that inherited the famous name two miles down the road - 297 contributing buildings, a 1923 depot, and a downtown that grew up after the surrender it is sometimes confused with.

subject: Araguaia National Park
summary: The northern third of the second-largest river island on Earth - where visitors come by boat because there is no bridge and driving is not an option.

subject: Araguaia National Park
summary: Bananal Island floats at the junction of two biomes, and the park that covers its northern 5,577 square kilometers is where rainforest turns to savanna.

subject: Araguaia State Park
summary: A quarter-million hectares of Mato Grosso that becomes a shallow inland sea every year, holding the seam where the cerrado gives way to the Amazon.

subject: Arakurayama Sengen Park
summary: A hillside park in Fujiyoshida where 398 stone steps lead to one of the most photographed views in Japan: a red five-story pagoda framed by cherry blossoms with Mount Fuji rising behind.

subject: Archaeological Site of Terpsithea Square
summary: Beneath a modern Piraeus square lies the perfectly preserved grid of an ancient city — designed by the father of urban planning and frozen in time by a barbarian raid in 267 AD.

subject: Archaeological site of Atapuerca
summary: A railway cutting through the hills near Burgos exposed 1.4 million years of continuous human presence -- including the oldest known evidence of hominid cannibalism and the earliest human face found in Western Europe.

subject: Archaeological site of Carthage
summary: Scattered across a modern Tunisian suburb, the UNESCO-protected ruins of Carthage preserve three thousand years of civilization -- Phoenician, Roman, Christian, and Islamic -- in fragments that require imagination to reassemble.

subject: Arches National Park
summary: Over 2,000 natural stone arches crowd into 76,000 acres of Utah's red rock country, the greatest concentration of such formations on Earth.

subject: Arches National Park
summary: More than 2,000 natural sandstone arches crowd into a single stretch of Utah desert, formed over 300 million years as an ancient salt bed buckled, cracked, and dissolved the stone above it into impossible shapes.

subject: Arches National Park
summary: The Utah park with over 2,000 natural stone arches - more than anywhere else on Earth, including Delicate Arch perched above a red rock bowl, the state's most iconic landmark.

subject: Archipelago National Park
summary: A labyrinth of 2,000 islands rising from the Baltic, where the land itself is still emerging from the sea and white-tailed eagles soar over Stone Age settlement sites.

subject: Arctic–Alpine Botanic Garden
summary: The world's northernmost botanic garden has no gate, no entrance fee, and never closes -- because at 69 degrees north, the sun sometimes never sets.

subject: Ardglass Railway Station
summary: The only Balfour Line ever built in what is now Northern Ireland, a fishing branch from Downpatrick that carried herring north to Belfast for fifty-eight years.

subject: Ards Forest Park
summary: A 480-hectare forest where ringforts, megalithic tombs, a Mass rock, and the bones of a vanished Anglo-Irish estate share the shoreline of Sheephaven Bay.

subject: Arenal Volcano National Park
summary: Home to Costa Rica's most active volcano -- thought dormant until it erupted catastrophically in 1968 -- this national park protects eight of the country's twelve life zones and harbors the endangered resplendent quetzal.

subject: Argentine Military Cemetery
summary: On a windswept rise near Darwin lie the Argentine dead of the Falklands War, and for thirty-five years many of their graves bore no name but a prayer.

subject: Arizona State Prison Complex
summary: A sprawling medium-security prison complex on the Arizona-Mexico border, built in multiple phases since 1986, that now houses over 4,200 incarcerated people just three miles from Mexico.

subject: Arizona State University
summary: From a four-room schoolhouse for training teachers to America's largest public university, ASU's transformation reflects Arizona's own explosive growth.

subject: Arlington Antebellum Home & Gardens
summary: Birmingham's only surviving antebellum mansion, built by enslaved laborers between 1845 and 1850 in a town that no longer exists -- then seized by Union cavalry as a staging point for burning the University of Alabama.

subject: Armenian cemetery in Julfa
summary: Once the world's largest medieval Armenian cemetery, housing up to 10,000 elaborately carved khachkar tombstones, the Julfa cemetery was systematically destroyed between 1998 and 2006 in what has been widely described as an act of cultural genocide.

subject: Arnhem Centraal railway station
summary: A railway station that looks less like a building than a sculpted wave of concrete, finished in 2015 after nearly two decades of construction.

subject: Arnhem Oosterbeek War Cemetery
summary: On the first weekend of every September, Dutch schoolchildren walk among 1,759 white headstones and place flowers, one bouquet for every grave.

subject: Arnsberg Forest Nature Park
summary: A 599-square-kilometer protected landscape of beech, oak and spruce in the Sauerland uplands, set between the Möhne and the Ruhr, with caves, ridge towers, and the Bilstein Caves at Warstein.

subject: Arribes del Duero Natural Park
summary: On the Spanish side of the deepest gorges in Iberia, almond trees bloom where they have no business blooming, sheltered by a microclimate that the river itself created.

subject: Arthur's Pass National Park
summary: Where gold fever punched a road through the Southern Alps in 1865, New Zealand's first South Island national park now draws hikers into terrain beautiful enough to kill the unprepared.

subject: Artlish Caves Provincial Park
summary: Hidden beneath Vancouver Island's old-growth canopy, the Artlish Caves protect the island's last undisturbed karst system with a major river cave, a landscape shaped by water dissolving limestone over millennia.

subject: Arusha National Park
summary: A compact Tanzanian national park where Mount Meru rises above alkaline lakes, colobus monkeys swing through montane forest, and flamingos gather by the thousands.

subject: Asheville Female College
summary: The first institution of higher education in western North Carolina, founded in 1841 - sixty years of educating young women in the antebellum and post-Reconstruction mountains.

subject: Asheville Regional Airport
summary: A Blue Ridge mountain field that has hosted a Concorde, two presidents on Air Force One, and one of the fastest-growing passenger booms in the Southeast.

subject: Asian Pacific Thematic Historic District
summary: San Diego's forgotten Chinatown, where eight blocks of weathered brick buildings preserve the memory of communities that transformed the city.

subject: Assateague State Park
summary: Maryland's only ocean beach state park - two miles of dunes, surf, and grazing wild horses on the north end of Assateague Island.

subject: Assistens Cemetery
summary: A pauper's burial ground of 1760 that became the most fashionable address in the Danish Golden Age — and is now Nørrebro's favourite park, where people sunbathe a few metres from Kierkegaard.

subject: Assumption Harbor's Second Life
summary: Where the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers merge and push toward San Pablo Bay, 447 acres of tidal wetland shelter endangered species and carry the echoes of Spanish explorers who named this cove for a feast day.

subject: Astrebla Downs National Park
summary: A treeless expanse of Mitchell-grass plains in outback Queensland that has become one of the last strongholds of the endangered greater bilby and the tiny carnivorous kowari.

subject: Athens College
summary: A bilingual prep school in the suburb of Psychiko, founded in 1925 by Greeks and American philhellenes, that has educated an improbable share of the country's prime ministers, magnates, and minds.

subject: Atlantic Wall open-air museum
summary: Over sixty bunkers and two miles of trenches survive because a Belgian prince refused to let them be demolished.

subject: Atlas Model Railroad
summary: A Czechoslovak immigrant's garage workshop in Newark became Atlas Model Railroad, the company whose inventions -- flexible track, rail joiners, pre-assembled turnouts -- transformed model railroading from craft into mass-market hobby.

subject: Auckland Harbour Bridge
summary: A bridge built too small and expanded too late, Auckland's 1,020-metre harbour crossing is an engineering icon whose story is really about the cost of thinking short-term.

subject: Audra State Park
summary: A 355-acre West Virginia park where a vanished gristmill's spillway still ripples in the Middle Fork River and a boardwalk runs under an overhanging sandstone cliff.

subject: Augrabies Falls National Park
summary: An 820-square-kilometer park in the Northern Cape where the Orange River plunges 60 meters into a granite gorge the Khoikhoi called 'the place of big noises.'

subject: Aula Magna (Central University of Venezuela)
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage auditorium in Caracas where Alexander Calder's floating acoustic clouds turn sound engineering into art -- and where the artist himself said his favorite work hung.

subject: Australia Zoo
summary: The Sunshine Coast wildlife park that began as a two-acre reptile farm, was made world-famous by Steve Irwin and his crocodiles, and now runs one of the largest wildlife hospitals on Earth -- where 'conservation through exciting education' is still the family creed.

subject: Autonomous University of Baja California
summary: Founded in 1957 in Mexicali, the Autonomous University of Baja California grew into a three-campus institution whose Ensenada branch became Mexico's leading center for oceanographic research — until a 1980 strike turned into riots that tested what university autonomy actually means.

subject: Avebury Manor and Garden
summary: An early-16th-century manor house standing inside Britain's largest stone circle, owned in turn by a marmalade heir, an archaeologist, and a property developer who built a faux torture chamber.

subject: Avery Street Historic District
summary: Parkersburg's first suburb - 109 acres of houses built between 1900 and 1910, with twelve distinct architectural styles often blended in unexpected combinations.

subject: Awash National Park
summary: Ethiopia's oldest national park sits where a dormant volcano meets the Rift Valley floor, harboring hot springs, waterfalls, and over 450 bird species in a landscape the Karayyu Oromo have called home for centuries.

subject: Ayer Itam War Memorial Park
summary: A white obelisk in Penang's Ayer Itam suburb stands over the remains of Sook Ching massacre victims, honoring local Chinese who died resisting Japan and supporting China's war effort.

subject: Ayutthaya Historical Park
summary: The ruins of a city that once rivaled London in size, where Buddha heads grow from tree roots and headless statues guard temples the Burmese burned in 1767.

subject: Ayvalık Islands Nature Park
summary: A scatter of twenty-two islands and countless rocks off Turkey's Aegean coast, the Ayvalık Islands Nature Park carries Greek names, Turkish maps, and a wildness most of its coves have kept to themselves.

subject: Azov-Syvash National Nature Park
summary: A wind-scoured refuge of steppe and salt lagoon where more than a million migrating birds pause each year on their long journeys across two continents.

subject: Aşiyan Asri Cemetery
summary: Tucked between the Bebek and Rumelihisarı neighborhoods on the European shore of the Bosphorus, Aşiyan Asri Cemetery holds the graves of poets, novelists, Ottoman princes and scholars whose words and deeds shaped modern Turkish culture.

story.title: BNI City: The Station That Sold Its Name

subject: BNI City
summary: Indonesia's first corporate-named railway station sits at the center of Jakarta's most ambitious transit hub, where airport express trains, commuter rail, MRT, LRT, and bus rapid transit converge at Dukuh Atas -- a place that keeps absorbing neighboring stations into itself.

subject: BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport
summary: Built on land bought from Friendship Methodist Church in 1946, named first for the church it replaced and now for Baltimore native Thurgood Marshall, BWI sits between two capitals and serves more passengers than either of them most years.

subject: Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery
summary: Beijing's most politically significant burial ground began as a temple for retired eunuchs, where the last abbot negotiated his community's survival before yielding the grounds to revolutionary martyrs.

subject: Babbacombe Cliff Railway
summary: Two counterbalanced wooden cars have shuttled tourists 720 feet down to Oddicombe Beach since 1926, surviving war closures, a 1951 modernisation, and the salt air that eats everything else on the coast.

subject: Babcock State Park
summary: A 4,127-acre New Deal park near the New River Gorge anchored by Glade Creek Grist Mill - one of America's most photographed buildings.

story.title: Babo Airfield: The Last Stop Before the War

subject: Babo Airfield
summary: A Dutch colonial airstrip on the swampy shore of Maccluer Gulf that became a major Japanese air base during World War II, endured relentless Allied bombing, and was never liberated -- its garrison holding out in isolation until the war's end.

subject: Bacanga State Park
summary: A remnant of Amazon rainforest wedged between São Luís's industrial district and its residential sprawl, protecting the reservoir that supplies the city's drinking water - while the city slowly encroaches on the park that sustains it.

subject: Bach Ma National Park
summary: Bach Ma National Park rises from Vietnam's coastal plain to a mist-soaked mountain summit, sheltering some of the country's most extraordinary biodiversity — including the ghostly saola — in forests that survived war and are still healing.

subject: Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex
summary: Four thousand years ago, a Bronze Age civilization flourished in the deserts of Central Asia, building fortified towns, crafting distinctive pottery, and trading with Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley -- then vanished, leaving behind ruins that would not be understood for millennia.

subject: Badlands National Park
summary: A science fiction landscape carved into the South Dakota prairie, where the earth loses an inch of itself each year and ancient fossils emerge from colorful striped walls.

subject: Badlands National Park
summary: Sacred Lakota land, World War II bombing range, and one of the world's richest fossil beds share the same eroded moonscape in South Dakota.

subject: Bafing National Park
summary: A woodland sanctuary on the Bafing River in southern Mali - the only protected refuge for chimpanzees on the Manding Plateau and a haven for some of West Africa's most striking birds.

subject: Bagram Airfield
summary: Built by the Soviets in the 1950s, fought over during decades of Afghan conflict, and expanded into a sprawling American base city before being abandoned in a single night in 2021, Bagram Airfield is a concrete chronicle of superpower ambition in Afghanistan.

subject: Baie de Baly National Park
summary: A remote stretch of Madagascar's northwest coast that is the last wild home of the ploughshare tortoise - widely considered the rarest tortoise on Earth.

subject: Bakossi National Park
summary: A Cameroonian park created not for charismatic megafauna but for plants, after botanists discovered 2,440 species in its highland forests, one in ten of which was new to science.

subject: Balboa Park (San Diego)
summary: Balboa Park is one of the largest urban cultural parks in the United States — 1,200 acres of museums, gardens, and performing arts spaces built on a mesa above downtown San Diego, shaped by a landscape architect who traded trees for a nursery lease and a city that twice used the park to introduce itself to the world.

subject: Bald Rock National Park
summary: A vast granite dome on the New England tableland, second in size only to Uluru, and for thousands of years a place where three nations could meet in peace.

subject: Bale Mountains National Park
summary: An Ethiopian highland park harboring the world's rarest canid -- the Ethiopian wolf -- alongside wild coffee forests, 282 bird species, and one of Earth's highest concentrations of endemic animals.

story.title: Bali Safari and Marine Park: Where Ganesha Watches Over the Savanna

subject: Bali Safari and Marine Park
summary: A forty-hectare safari park in Gianyar where Indonesian, Indian, and African animals roam through landscaped habitat, a nine-meter Ganesha statue guards the entrance to a Balinese theater, and a Hindu temple stands among the enclosures.

story.title: Bali's Gateway Built on Reclaimed Sea

subject: Bali's Gateway Built on Reclaimed Sea
summary: Named for a resistance hero who died fighting the Dutch, Bali's main airport was built on a narrow coastal strip, extended into the ocean, and now handles nearly 24 million passengers a year.

subject: Balinsasayao Twin Lakes Natural Park
summary: Two volcanic crater lakes hidden in the mountains of Negros Oriental, surrounded by ancient dipterocarp forest and home to critically endangered species found nowhere else on earth.

subject: Ballard Avenue Historic District
summary: A stretch of nineteenth-century storefronts in Seattle's Ballard neighborhood where the King of Sweden once read the historic proclamation.

subject: Ballasalla Railway Station
summary: A small Victorian halt on the last surviving steam line in the British Isles, where seasonal trains still pause beside a stone water tower built in 1902.

subject: Ballina Railway Station
summary: An 1873 Mayo railway terminus that saw famine emigrants depart, transported 900 cases of eggs a week to England, was robbed by sledgehammer-wielding burglars in 1906, and survives today as a single-platform terminus and major Irish freight hub.

subject: Ballincollig Regional Park
summary: Where Cork once manufactured the gunpowder that drove the British Empire, families now picnic among 135 acres of ruined mills, canals, and riverside woods.

subject: Balliol College, Oxford
summary: The Oxford college founded as penance for kidnapping a bishop, which has produced four British prime ministers and thirteen Nobel laureates.

subject: Ban Me Thuot East Airfield
summary: Seven names in fifteen years, a week-long last stand behind earthen walls, and now a domestic terminal - the runway southeast of Buôn Ma Thuột has been almost everything a piece of ground can be.

subject: Banc d'Arguin National Park
summary: A vast Saharan shoal where over two million migrant birds spend the winter, where the Imraguen still fish from sail-rigged boats, and where a French frigate's wreck once gave the world its most famous painting of despair.

subject: Band-e Amir National Park
summary: Six lakes of impossible turquoise sit at 2,900 meters in the Hindu Kush, forming Afghanistan's first national park and one of the most strikingly colored landscapes in Central Asia.

subject: Band-e Amir National Park
summary: Afghanistan's first national park protects six startlingly turquoise lakes formed by natural travertine dams in the Hindu Kush, a landscape of rare beauty entangled with the country's contested present.

story.title: Bandai-Asahi National Park: Where Poets, Pilgrims, and Peaks Converge

subject: Bandai-Asahi National Park
summary: Japan's third-largest national park spans three prefectures and three independent mountain systems -- sacred peaks where Yamabushi ascetics have trained for over a thousand years, where Matsuo Basho composed haiku, and where snow lingers into summer on the ridges they call the Tohoku Alps.

subject: Bangil Railway Station
summary: A colonial-era junction where Java's first railway lines forked toward mountains and sea, its abandoned engine shed and turntable still haunted by the ghosts of steam locomotives that once raced the Vlugge Vijf express to Malang in 75 minutes flat.

subject: Bangor University
summary: Founded in 1884 with money raised by Welsh slate quarrymen, Bangor was the first British university to give Welsh academic standing - and its alumni include a Nobel laureate, Danny Boyle, and the title character of 'Bridget Jones's Diary'.

subject: Bani Israel Graveyard
summary: Karachi's only Jewish cemetery holds 5,000 graves in a shrinking plot within the larger Mewa Shah Graveyard -- a quiet testament to the vanished community that once called this city home.

subject: Banning State Park
summary: A ghost town turned state park where the Kettle River carves through Precambrian sandstone, creating Class IV rapids with names like Hell's Gate and Dragon's Tooth -- and where the ruins of a 19th-century quarry slowly dissolve back into the gorge that made them possible.

subject: Baolai Spring Park
summary: In the Kaohsiung mountains along the Laonong River, a hot spring that vanished under Typhoon Morakot in 2009 was painstakingly restored, reopening in 2017 as a park where thermal water at 52°C rises through the forest at 550 meters.

subject: Barber Motorsports Park
summary: A racing circuit in Birmingham called 'The Augusta National of Motorsports,' housing the world's largest motorcycle museum - born from one man's obsession with preserving two-wheeled history.

subject: Barclay Memorial Park
summary: A three-hectare park in Tainan's East District, reclaimed from neglect by 57 volunteers and named for Thomas Barclay, the Scottish missionary who spent sixty years transforming religious and intellectual life in southern Taiwan.

subject: Baritú National Park
summary: Argentina's only fully tropical national park is so remote that the only road in runs through another country, leaving its jaguars and cloud forest nearly untouched.

subject: Barnsdall Art Park
summary: On a hilltop in East Hollywood, an oil heiress commissioned Frank Lloyd Wright's only Los Angeles house and then gave the whole thing to the city—a gift the city took twenty years to decide it actually wanted.

subject: Barra Airport
summary: The only airport in the world where scheduled passenger flights land on a tidal beach, with runways that disappear under the sea twice a day.

subject: Barron Gorge National Park
summary: The gorge where the Barron River throws itself 265 metres off the Atherton Tableland - Din Din to the Djabugay, whose Dreaming carved it and whose people now hold native title over it.

subject: Bartolomeu Dias Museum Complex
summary: A museum complex in Mossel Bay houses a life-size replica of the caravel that brought the first Europeans to southern African shores in 1488, alongside Africa's largest shell collection and the grave of an enslaved person.

subject: Basra War Cemetery
summary: A forgotten military cemetery in Basra holds nearly 5,000 graves from two world wars, its headstones removed, its Cross of Sacrifice gone, its dead left without markers in a city that has moved on around them.

subject: Batchelor Airfield
summary: A quiet general aviation strip south of Darwin that once served as one of the most important Allied air bases in the Pacific War, the ground from which General MacArthur continued his escape from the Philippines.

subject: Bath Abbey Cemetery
summary: A hillside cemetery overlooking Bath was the last cemetery designed by John Claudius Loudon - the man who taught Victorian Britain how to bury its dead.

subject: Battlefield Line Railway
summary: A five-mile heritage line in Leicestershire takes its name from the meadow where the Wars of the Roses ended - and the inaugural train back to Shenton in 1992 was pulled by a tank engine called Richard III.

subject: Battleship Memorial Park
summary: A military history park on Mobile Bay where Alabama's schoolchildren saved a 45,000-ton battleship from the scrapyard with nickels and dimes.

subject: Bazaruto Archipelago National Park
summary: Mozambique's only marine national park protects five islands, the largest dugong population in East Africa, and coral reefs where visibility reaches 40 meters.

subject: Beach Park (water park)
summary: On the dunes of Porto das Dunas, the largest water park in Brazil turned a 135-foot vertical drop into Latin America's most famous scream.

subject: Beacon Hill Park
summary: Victoria's 75-hectare waterfront park, named for two masts that once marked a sunken reef, holding camas meadows the Lekwungen tended for centuries, a 38-metre pole raised by Mungo Martin, and Mile 0 of the Trans-Canada Highway.

subject: Bear Head Lake State Park
summary: A small Minnesota state park near Ely that beat Great Smoky Mountains National Park to win a nationwide popularity contest in 2010 -- thanks to a bear webcam, a dedicated online fanbase, and 5,540 acres of Boundary Waters scenery you can drive to instead of paddle.

subject: Beech Fork State Park
summary: A 1970s recreation area built around an Army Corps flood-control lake where electric trolling motors enforce a particular kind of quiet.

subject: Beechwood Cemetery
summary: Canada's national cemetery holds over 82,000 souls beneath its beech canopy in east Ottawa, from a prime minister and a Nobel laureate to Hockey Hall of Famers and the father of organized ice hockey.

subject: Beihai Park
summary: Immediately northwest of the Forbidden City, Beihai Park has been an imperial garden since the 12th century -- a landscape shaped by Kublai Khan's architects, rebuilt by Ming and Qing emperors, and crowned by a Tibetan-style White Dagoba visible across central Beijing.

subject: Beijing Capital International Airport
summary: When its Terminal 3 opened in 2008, it was the largest man-made structure on Earth by area, a dragon-shaped gateway that transformed Beijing into Asia's busiest aviation hub.

subject: Beijing Daxing International Airport
summary: The starfish that swallowed a city -- Zaha Hadid's 700,000-square-metre terminal building, the world's largest single-structure airport, rose from farmland on the Beijing-Hebei border in just five years and opened six days before the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic.

story.title: Beijing Liao and Jin City Wall Museum

subject: Beijing Liao and Jin City Wall Museum
summary: A museum built directly over the ruins of Beijing's medieval city wall reveals the fortifications that protected the Liao and Jin dynasty capital nearly a thousand years ago.

story.title: Beijing Ming City Wall Ruins Park

subject: Beijing Ming City Wall Ruins Park
summary: A 1.5-kilometer stretch of Beijing's 550-year-old Ming dynasty fortifications, where Boxer Rebellion graffiti carved by foreign soldiers still marks the interior of the Southeast Corner Tower.

subject: Beijing Normal University
summary: China's oldest teacher-training institution has produced two Nobel laureates, hosted the U.S. Olympic Team, and counts a former U.S. Treasury Secretary among its Mandarin students.

subject: Beijing World Park
summary: A 46.7-hectare theme park in southwestern Beijing where visitors walk from the Eiffel Tower to the Pyramids to the Taj Mahal without leaving the city.

subject: Beijing Zoo
summary: China's oldest zoo has survived dynasty collapse, wartime poisonings, and near-total ruin to become a sprawling urban refuge where five million visitors a year stroll through classical Chinese gardens alongside creatures from every continent.

subject: Beijing–Shanghai high-speed railway
summary: The world's longest high-speed line built in a single phase, the 1,318-kilometer Beijing-Shanghai railway cut a journey that once took 44 hours down to just over four.

subject: Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway
summary: China's first entirely Chinese-designed and built railway, engineered by Zhan Tianyou with an ingenious switchback that solved the problem of the Badaling mountains.

subject: Belfast Harbour
summary: The maritime gateway that swallows two-thirds of Northern Ireland's seaborne trade and once launched the Titanic into the world.

subject: Bellarmine College Preparatory
summary: An all-boys Jesuit high school in San Jose whose alumni include governors, tech executives, and athletes, carrying on the Society of Jesus's educational mission since 1851.

subject: Belle Isle Park
summary: A 982-acre island in the Detroit River -- once called Hog Island -- that became the largest city-owned island park in the United States, home to an Olmsted design, an Albert Kahn aquarium, and the only marble lighthouse in America.

subject: Bellefontaine Cemetery
summary: Founded in 1849 during a cholera epidemic that killed 4,000 St. Louisans, this 314-acre cemetery holds William Clark, Adolphus Busch, William S. Burroughs, and a Louis Sullivan masterpiece.

subject: Bellingrath Gardens and Home
summary: A Coca-Cola fortune transformed a humble fishing camp on Alabama's Fowl River into one of the South's most celebrated gardens, where salvaged bricks from a Vanderbilt birthplace built a home among 250,000 azaleas.

subject: Belmont Abbey College
summary: A Catholic liberal arts college founded by Benedictine monks in 1876 on land donated by an Irish priest, anchored by a minor basilica and the only Catholic college in North Carolina.

subject: Belmont Park (San Diego)
summary: Belmont Park opened on July 4, 1925, as Mission Beach Amusement Center — a seaside carnival on San Diego Bay built by sugar baron John D. Spreckels, with a wooden roller coaster that still runs a century later and a saltwater pool that was once the largest in the world.

subject: Belvedere College
summary: The Jesuit boys' school where James Joyce wrote his prefect's reports, where seven Irish Olympians and one Taoiseach learned Latin, and where the abuse of generations of pupils was finally named in 2025.

subject: Benmore Botanic Garden
summary: An avenue of giant sequoias planted in 1863 marks the entrance to a Highland rainforest garden that turned a sugar refiner's fortune into a botanical legacy.

subject: Benson Railroad Historic District
summary: In 1894, Benson was the only point in Arizona served by three independent railroad lines, a transportation crossroads where passengers bound for Tombstone's silver mines stepped off transcontinental trains onto stagecoaches.

subject: Bentonville Battlefield
summary: Three days in March 1865 - the largest Civil War battle ever fought on North Carolina soil and the last major Confederate offensive of the war, ending with a field hospital in the Harper House and the Confederacy nineteen days from surrender.

subject: Berga Naval Base
summary: Sweden's premier naval training facility where generations of sailors have mastered the art of archipelago warfare in the sheltered waters of Hårsfjärden.

subject: Berks Cemetery Extension
summary: A cemetery that grew because of a road — and a memorial that holds the names of more than eleven thousand men who have no grave at all.

subject: Berlin Brandenburg Airport
summary: Two villages moved for it in 2004 and 2005, and it opened in 2020 - nine years late, roughly twice over budget, and into a pandemic.

subject: Berlin Tegel Airport
summary: Built in 90 days by French troops during the Berlin Airlift, Tegel grew into West Berlin's lifeline airport and closed in 2020 after a postwar life shaped by the Cold War.

subject: Berlin Tempelhof Airport
summary: The Nazi-era terminal designed to look like an eagle in flight was built on a cleared concentration camp and worked by forced labour — then became the place that kept West Berlin alive during the airlift.

subject: Berlin Wall
summary: Eight weeks after East Germany's leader promised that nobody intended to build a wall, barbed wire went across Berlin in the dark — and stayed for 28 years.

subject: Bernardo O'Higgins National Park
summary: Chile's largest national park - a trackless wilderness of fjords, glaciers, and the Southern Ice Field, accessible only by boat or helicopter, where the Andes dissolve into channels and ice.

subject: Bethabara Historic District
summary: The Moravian "House of Passage" that was never meant to last, founded in 1753 on land already long inhabited, where archaeologists later read whole foundations out of the dirt.

subject: Betung Kerihun National Park
summary: One of Borneo's largest protected rainforests, where Dayak communities and endangered orangutans share 800,000 hectares of mountain jungle straddling the Indonesia-Malaysia border.

subject: Bia National Park
summary: Ghana's first UNESCO Biosphere Reserve shelters some of the tallest trees and rarest wildlife left in West Africa, in a forest that nearly vanished to farmland.

subject: Bidoup Núi Bà National Park
summary: Named for the two highest peaks of the Langbiang Plateau, Bidoup Núi Bà National Park shelters one of Vietnam's most extraordinary concentrations of rare wildlife and ancient conifers above 2,000 meters.

subject: Bidwell Mansion State Historic Park
summary: A pink-plastered Victorian mansion that hosted generals and movie stars, served as a women's dormitory, and was destroyed by arson in 2024.

subject: Bieszczady National Park
summary: Poland's largest mountainous national park, where depopulated villages crumble beneath primeval beech forests and European bison roam ridges the locals call poloniny.

subject: Big Bend National Park
summary: Where the Rio Grande carves through ancient limestone and the Chisos Mountains rise entirely within park boundaries, Big Bend protects the largest expanse of Chihuahuan Desert in the United States and offers the darkest skies in the contiguous forty-eight.

subject: Big Bend Ranch State Park
summary: Texas longhorns still roam free across the largest state park in Texas, where volcanic canyons become hanging gardens and the night sky is so dark it has earned international protection.

subject: Big Dipper at Camden Park
summary: A 1958 wooden roller coaster in Huntington, West Virginia - the largest and oldest in the state, and one of only three surviving National Amusement Devices coasters anywhere.

subject: Birdsville Airport
