subject: Cooktown Cemetery
summary: A hillside burial ground where a Chinese shrine, a shipwreck heroine, and three thousand gold-rush graves record the most cosmopolitan town in 1870s Australia.

subject: Coorong National Park
summary: A 130-kilometre ribbon of lagoon behind a dune wall, the Coorong is pelican country, Ngarrindjeri country, and the windswept landscape that gave Australia 'Storm Boy.'

subject: Copalis State Airport
summary: The only beach runway in America, Copalis State Airport is a sand strip on Washington's Pacific coast that exists only at low tide -- a place where the ocean decides when you can fly.

subject: Copperbelt University
summary: Zambia's largest public university, born from the need to train the engineers and managers who keep the country's copper-driven economy running.

subject: Coral Over the Sands
summary: The third-largest atoll on Earth hides in the Flores Sea, where the Bonerate people and Bajau sea nomads have sustained a centuries-old partnership of reef and shore.

subject: Corcovado National Park
summary: A Costa Rican rainforest park that National Geographic called 'the most biologically intense place on Earth,' where jaguars, tapirs, and four monkey species share trails with fer-de-lance and bull sharks.

subject: Corinth Canal
summary: The Corinth Canal — a 6.4-kilometre slash through the Isthmus of Corinth, with limestone walls rising 90 metres on both sides — was dreamed of for 2,500 years before anyone actually managed to build it.

subject: Cork Airport
summary: Ireland's second-busiest airport perches on a hilltop above County Cork, where fog still bedevils approaches and a de Havilland Comet once announced the jet age in 1964.

subject: Cork Harbour
summary: One of several natural harbours that claim to be the second-largest in the world - and one that has hosted Napoleonic-era forts, transatlantic emigrant liners, an early American naval base, modern pharmaceutical plants, and the headquarters of the Irish Naval Service all at once.

subject: Cork, Blackrock and Passage Railway
summary: From 1850 to 1932 the CB&PR was Cork's seaside railway, carrying day-trippers to Crosshaven by paddle-steamer connection - and today its old route is the city's most popular linear park.

subject: Cornwall College, Jamaica
summary: The third oldest high school in Cornwall county, where a Presbyterian minister's 1895 petition for 500 pounds of education funding produced a Montego Bay institution that has shaped Jamaican prime ministers, chief justices, and international footballers for over a century.

subject: Cornwall Railway Viaducts
summary: Brunel's solution to crossing Cornwall on a tight budget: 42 wooden viaducts of fan-braced timber on masonry piers, gradually replaced by stone over six decades, with ghostly piers still standing alongside many of their successors.

subject: Corrour railway station
summary: The highest mainline railway station in the United Kingdom, 1,340 feet above sea level on Rannoch Moor, with no public road access and a Trainspotting cameo on its resume.

subject: Cotubanamá National Park
summary: The Dominican Republic's most visited national park, renamed for a Taino chief who was captured and executed by the Spanish in 1504, where sacred caves hold thousands of indigenous pictographs above coral reefs and mangrove coastline.

subject: Courtmacsherry Harbour Lifeboat Station
summary: On the afternoon the Lusitania went down off the Old Head of Kinsale, the lifeboat that rowed eleven nautical miles to reach her came from Courtmacsherry - and arrived at a sea full of bodies.

subject: Covent Garden
summary: A walled monastery garden became London's first modern square, its biggest produce market, its most notorious red-light district, and finally its most theatrical neighbourhood.

subject: Coyote Hills Regional Park
summary: Nearly 978 acres of marsh, grassland, and ancient shell mounds at the edge of San Francisco Bay, where 2,000-year-old Ohlone village sites sit amid some of the best birdwatching in the East Bay.

story.title: Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair National Park

subject: Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair National Park
summary: Tasmania's alpine heart, where a jagged dolerite ridge named for a miner's cradle looms over glacial lakes, ancient pines, and a man's century-old dream of a park for all time.

subject: Crater Historic District
summary: Depression-era stone buildings at 10,000 feet on Haleakala, where Civilian Conservation Corps workers built a visitor center and cabins in a volcanic landscape that made mainland park architecture feel otherworldly.

subject: Crater Lake National Park
summary: The deepest lake in America fills the caldera of a volcano that collapsed 7,700 years ago, its waters so impossibly blue they stunned gold prospectors into naming it Deep Blue Lake on first sight.

subject: Cremorne Gardens, London
summary: The Victorian pleasure ground at the end of the King's Road where Whistler painted fireworks, tightrope walkers crossed the Thames, and Chelsea's respectable neighbours finally got the licence revoked.

subject: Crescent College
summary: Founded by Counter-Reformation Jesuits meeting at night under threat of arrest in 1565 - and still teaching, in a Limerick suburb, 460 years later.

subject: Cripple Creek Historic District
summary: A cowboy's gold discovery in a cattle pasture at 9,500 feet launched the last great Colorado gold rush, building a city of 25,000 that burned to the ground and rose again in brick.

subject: Cristalino II State Park
summary: An Amazon state park whose boundaries have been contested for decades, where biodiversity confronts illegal logging, political maneuvering, and quiet invasion.

subject: Cristalino State Park
summary: A rectangle of surviving Amazon forest on the arc of deforestation, renowned for birdlife and besieged by the agriculture that surrounds it.

subject: Croke Park
summary: Ireland's largest stadium is also the country's most charged piece of ground: site of the Bloody Sunday massacre of 1920, the spiritual home of Gaelic games, and the place where the British anthem was finally allowed to sound in 2007.

subject: Crooked Harbour
summary: Crooked Harbour — Kat O Hoi in Cantonese — is a sheltered inlet at the northeastern edge of Hong Kong's New Territories, enclosed by a scatter of islands and looking north toward the Shenzhen skyline, a world away from the city it is technically part of.

subject: Crooked River Railroad Bridge
summary: A steel arch bridge built in just four months during a railroad war, where trains crossed before workers finished installing half the rivets.

subject: Cross River National Park
summary: Nigeria's last great stand of primary rainforest shelters the critically endangered Cross River gorilla and 78 percent of the country's primate species across 4,000 square kilometers.

subject: Crow Wing State Park
summary: At the confluence of the Mississippi and Crow Wing Rivers, shallow depressions in the earth may be the remains of rifle pits dug during a 1768 Ojibwe ambush -- just one layer of history preserved in a state park that encompasses one of Minnesota's most populous 1850s towns, now vanished.

subject: Crown Hill Cemetery
summary: The third-largest non-governmental cemetery in America, where a U.S. president, Public Enemy Number One, and 1,616 Confederate prisoners rest among 225,000 graves on Indianapolis's highest hill.

story.title: Croydon Station: End of the Line That Floods on Purpose

subject: Croydon Station
summary: The eastern terminus of the last isolated railway still running in Queensland - a line engineered to be drowned by floodwater and put straight back into service, built for a gold rush that faded before the track was even finished.

subject: Crystal Palace Park
summary: The Victorian pleasure ground built around a relocated glass cathedral, dotted with the first life-size dinosaur sculptures ever made, and still trying to recover from the night the Palace burned.

subject: Crystal River Archaeological State Park
summary: A six-mound ceremonial complex on Florida's Gulf Coast where Native Americans buried their dead, traded copper from the Ohio River valley, and carved mysterious stone slabs for 1,600 continuous years - designated a National Historic Landmark in 1990.

story.title: Cueva de las Maravillas National Park

subject: Cueva de las Maravillas National Park
summary: Twenty-five meters beneath the Dominican coastal plain, nearly 500 Taino paintings and engravings cover the walls of a cave that a professor in 1949 renamed the Cave of Wonders for what he saw inside.

subject: Cueva del Guácharo National Park
summary: Venezuela's longest cave shelters thousands of shrieking oilbirds in total darkness, a living ecosystem the Chaima people once considered a gateway to the spirit world.

subject: Cultural Heritage Park
summary: Taichung's Cultural Heritage Park began as a Japanese-era brewery in 1916, spent decades as a state-run production facility, sat abandoned for years, and reopened as a 5.6-hectare arts and heritage park that now hosts exhibitions, performances, and restoration work within its preserved industrial buildings.

subject: Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad
summary: A narrow-gauge steam railroad crossing the Colorado-New Mexico border eleven times as it climbs to the highest point of any narrow-gauge line in North America, saved from abandonment when two states bought it together.

subject: Curraghs Wildlife Park
summary: A small wildlife park in an internationally important Manx wetland, whose escaped wallabies have established a wild population across the Isle of Man.

subject: Currawinya National Park
summary: A vast outback park where a salt lake and a freshwater lake sit side by side, drawing waterbirds in their thousands and sheltering bilbies behind a predator-proof fence.

story.title: Cutting the Orchid in Half: The Proposed Sulawesi Canal

subject: Cutting the Orchid in Half
summary: For over two decades, Indonesian politicians have dreamed of slicing a canal through Sulawesi's narrow neck to connect the Gulf of Tomini with the Makassar Strait -- an 18-kilometer shortcut that could reshape maritime trade across the archipelago.

subject: Cuyahoga Valley National Park
summary: A national park born from a river that once caught fire, where century-old canal towpaths wind through gorges carved by glaciers and nearly one hundred waterfalls tumble over ancient sandstone.

subject: Cuyamaca Rancho State Park
summary: Cuyamaca Rancho State Park — 'the place where it rains' in Kumeyaay — holds 7,000 years of continuous human history, from indigenous villages through Spanish land grants and gold rush boomtowns to the catastrophic 2003 Cedar Fire and its ongoing recovery.

subject: Cypress Hills Interprovincial Park
summary: A forested plateau rising unexpectedly from the Canadian prairie, hosting Montana-like ecosystems at Banff-like elevations where Alberta and Saskatchewan meet.

subject: Cypress Lawn Memorial Park
summary: A rural cemetery in Colma, the 'City of the Silent,' where a Civil War veteran built a final resting place for San Francisco's dead after the city banned burials within its limits.

subject: Cà Mau Gas-Power-Fertilizer Complex
summary: Fuelled by a gas field two countries agreed not to argue over, this 1,500-megawatt complex sits at a river junction on the edge of a peat swamp.

subject: Cát Tiên Archaeological Site
summary: A mysterious Indianized sanctuary hidden in the Vietnamese jungle, home to the largest stone lingam ever found in Southeast Asia — and a civilization that history nearly forgot.

subject: Côn Đảo National Park
summary: Vietnam's most complete marine park protects more water than land — 360 coral species, eleven kinds of seagrass, a dugong nobody can reliably find, and the country's largest sea turtle programme.

subject: Da Lat–Thap Cham railway
summary: An 84-kilometer rack railway that once climbed from the Vietnamese coast to the highland city of Da Lat, built by Swiss and French engineers over three decades and destroyed by decades of war.

subject: Da Nang Air Base
summary: Da Nang Air Base passed through Japanese occupation, French colonial war, and the full arc of American involvement in Vietnam — a single runway that witnessed the first US combat troops to arrive in Southeast Asia and, a decade later, the desperate final hours before the city fell.

subject: Daintree National Park
summary: Where the rainforest meets the reef - a World Heritage park in two halves, Mossman Gorge and Cape Tribulation, and the ancestral country of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji, who in 2021 took it back into their own hands.

subject: Dairy Campus
summary: A working research farm outside Leeuwarden where dairy cows are wired up as data sources for Wageningen University — and where biogas from their own manure now flows into the public gas network.

subject: Dajarra and Selwyn Railway Lines
summary: Narrow-gauge branch lines built to chase copper that ended up creating one of the world's greatest cattle railheads, where drovers from Western Australia loaded more beef than Texas.

subject: Dalian Laodong Park
summary: Dalian's oldest and largest central park has been renamed five times in 125 years, each new name reflecting the power that controlled it.

subject: Dalian Yinshitan Forest National Park
summary: A national park southeast of Dalian where 500-million-year-old silver rock formations rise from primary forests, and visitors can adopt fruit trees.

subject: Daly Waters Airfield
summary: A patch of red dirt deep in the Northern Territory that connected Australia to the world — first as a refuelling stop on the earliest international air routes, then as a wartime bomber base, and finally as a living museum where the original Qantas hangar still stands.

subject: Daniel Pratt Historic District
summary: A 15-block district in Prattville, Alabama preserving the company town built by a New Hampshire industrialist whose cotton gin factory became the largest in the world, where mill cottages, antebellum warehouses, and a cemetery with the earliest grave from 1843 still line Autauga Creek.

subject: Dara Sakor International Airport
summary: Two airlines, one destination, and a runway long enough to raise a decade of questions about what this airport in a Cambodian national park was really built for.

subject: Darién National Park
summary: A vast wilderness bridging two continents, where the Pan-American Highway surrenders to jungle and the harpy eagle still rules the canopy.

subject: Dartington College of Arts
summary: For nearly fifty years a medieval Devon estate housed Britain's most experimental arts college, where students made theatre in lighthouses, fish shops, and Dartmoor prison.

subject: Dartmoor Zoological Park
summary: The 33-acre Devon zoo that inspired *We Bought a Zoo*, where Benjamin Mee's family rebuilt a closed park around a 17th-century house and a recaptured jaguar.

subject: Dartmouth Steam Railway
summary: A 6.7-mile Great Western branch saved from closure in 1972, where steam locomotives still climb out of Paignton, run through a half-mile tunnel, and end at the only railway station that never sees a train.

subject: David Crockett Birthplace State Park
summary: A 105-acre state park along the Nolichucky River in Greene County, Tennessee, marking the August 17, 1786, birthplace of the frontier congressman who became a folk hero by dying at the Alamo.

subject: David Fleay Wildlife Park
summary: The riverside sanctuary where the only man ever to breed a platypus built a life's work out of Australia's strangest and most secretive animals.

subject: Davis & Elkins College
summary: A small Presbyterian liberal arts college built on the estate of two West Virginia railroad senators - and quietly home to the man who taught Pistol Pete to shoot.

subject: De Anza College
summary: De Anza College is a public community college in Cupertino, California, United States. It is part of the Foothill-De Anza Community College District,

subject: De Biesbosch National Park
summary: One of the largest freshwater tidal wetlands left in Northwestern Europe was created by a single catastrophic night in 1421 that drowned villages, killed thousands by tradition, and left a brackish swamp where farmland had been.

subject: De Leon Springs State Park
summary: A 625-acre Florida state park built around an ancient spring where 6,000 years of human history meet 20 million gallons of daily water flow, and visitors cook their own pancakes inside a rebuilt sugar mill.

subject: Dead Horse Point State Park
summary: The view that killed a thousand horses - where Utah's canyon country offers a panorama rivaling the Grand Canyon, cowboys once corralled mustangs on a peninsula of no escape, and the Colorado River snakes 2,000 feet below.

subject: Death Valley National Park
summary: The hottest, driest, lowest place in North America, where extremes of geology and climate create landscapes that seem to belong to another planet.

subject: Deception Pass State Park
summary: Where the tide roars through - Washington's most visited state park, spanning the dramatic waterway between Whidbey and Fidalgo Islands beneath a bridge that has become an icon of the Pacific Northwest.

subject: Deene Park
summary: The Northamptonshire country seat of the Brudenell family for over five centuries, and the home to which Lord Cardigan returned after leading the doomed Charge of the Light Brigade.

subject: Deer Park Monastery
summary: Thích Nhất Hạnh founded Deer Park Monastery in the Escondido hills in 2000 — a 400-acre practice center where 62 monastics and lay practitioners gather weekly to apply the teachings of a Vietnamese Thiền tradition to ordinary life.

subject: Delaware State University
summary: Founded in 1891 as the Delaware College for Colored Students, DSU is the only HBCU to have acquired a historically white college - and the only mid-Atlantic university with a flight school of its own.

subject: Delft University of Technology
summary: A royal academy founded to train colonial civil servants that grew into the Netherlands' most influential engineering school, and accidentally burned down its own architecture faculty.

subject: Delta de l'Ebre Natural Park
summary: A young, flamingo-filled wetland built entirely from river sediment - and now slowly retreating as upstream dams starve it of the earth that made it.

subject: Democracy Wall
summary: For thirteen months in 1978 and 1979, a long brick wall on Xidan Street became the most dangerous public forum in China, where ordinary citizens pasted handwritten demands for democracy.

story.title: Dena: The Zagros Mountains' Longest Spine

subject: Dena National Park and Protected Area
summary: Iran's Dena mountain range stretches 80 kilometers through the Zagros with 49 peaks above 4,000 meters, sheltering leopards, ancient oak forests, and snowmelt rivers in a UNESCO biosphere reserve that straddles two provinces.

subject: Dendera Temple complex
summary: One of the best-preserved temples in Egypt, where a recently cleaned ceiling blazes again in blue and gold and a famous zodiac once mapped the heavens before it was blasted out and shipped to Paris.

subject: Denver International Airport Conspiracies
summary: America's most conspiracy-laden airport - where a murderous blue horse sculpture, apocalyptic murals, mysterious Masonic symbols, and secret underground tunnels have spawned theories about everything from the New World Order to alien bunkers.

subject: Depot Harbour
summary: A ghost town on Georgian Bay where one man's railroad empire rose, boomed, exploded, and left nothing but scattered foundations on Anishinaabe land.

subject: Derreen Garden
summary: A 60-acre sub-tropical garden on the wet, sheltered Beara coast, planted by a Viceroy of India with rhododendrons and tree ferns brought from the other side of the world.

subject: Desembarco del Granma National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where ancient limestone terraces meet revolutionary history - the coastline where Castro's yacht ran aground and a geological record spanning millions of years.

subject: Desengano State Park
summary: A 21,444-hectare refuge where 75-degree slopes protected the last continuous Atlantic Forest in northern Rio de Janeiro - and where the near-extinct muriqui monkey was spotted in 1999.

subject: Desert Center Airport
summary: An airfield built in 1943 to support Patton's desert training has evolved through bomber training, emergency landing designation, and private acquisition to become home to the Chuckwalla Valley Raceway.

subject: Desert Christ Park
summary: During the Cold War atomic scare, an aircraft worker climbed a hillside in Yucca Valley and spent years placing steel-reinforced concrete apostles and a ten-foot figure of Jesus into the desert — a one-man act of prayer set in stone.

story.title: Desert de les Palmes Natural Park

subject: Desert de les Palmes Natural Park
summary: A green Mediterranean mountain park whose misleading name comes not from sand but from monks who called their places of solitude 'holy deserts'.

subject: Desolation Sound Marine Provincial Park
summary: Captain Vancouver named it for what he saw as abandonment and gloom, but the waters he misread have been one of the richest marine environments north of Baja for ten thousand years, a place where Indigenous food systems and yacht tourism now compete for the same sheltered coves.

subject: Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm
summary: An Enlightenment prince spent fifty years turning 142 square kilometres of the Elbe floodplain into a designed landscape - complete with a working artificial volcano, a synagogue and a standing invitation to the public.

subject: Deventer Railway Station
summary: Two rival railway companies once built separate stations on either side of Deventer; the elegant 1914 building that replaced them now sends trains to Berlin, Brussels, and Prague.

subject: Devil's Millhopper Geological State Park
summary: A 120-foot-deep sinkhole on the edge of Gainesville swallows the Florida landscape whole, creating a lush miniature rainforest where three distinct ecosystems stack on top of one another.

subject: Devils Fork State Park
summary: On the South Carolina edge of the Blue Ridge escarpment, Devils Fork opens onto a 7,500-acre lake so deep and so undeveloped that it feels misplaced in the Deep South.

subject: Devrani Jethani Temple Complex
summary: Twin 6th-century temples in Chhattisgarh named for the younger and elder sisters-in-law, one of which guards a monumental statue whose body is composed entirely of animals and human faces.

story.title: Dharma Realm Buddhist University: Where Plato Meets the Lotus Sutra

subject: Dharma Realm Buddhist University
summary: A tiny university inside a former psychiatric hospital turned Buddhist monastery assigns Aristotle alongside the Avatamsaka Sutra, teaches Classical Chinese and Sanskrit, and suspends all classes once a semester so everyone can sit in silent retreat.

subject: Diakopto–Kalavryta Railway
summary: Built by French and Italian engineers between 1889 and 1895 and threading through the sheer limestone walls of the Vouraikos Gorge, the narrow-gauge rack railway from Diakopto to Kalavryta climbs 720 metres in just 22 kilometres — one of the most dramatic rail journeys in Europe.

subject: Diamantina National Park
summary: Half a million hectares of Channel Country where Australia's rarest bird hides in the spinifex and the bilby still digs its burrows in the wild.

subject: Digya National Park
summary: Ghana's oldest protected area and second-largest national park, a 3,743-square-kilometre wilderness on the shores of Lake Volta where forest meets savanna and elephants share the landscape with manatees.

subject: Dinosaur Park Formation
summary: One of the richest dinosaur graveyards on Earth, this Alberta badlands formation has yielded more complete dinosaur skeletons than almost anywhere else, including specimens with preserved soft tissue.

story.title: Dinosaur Provincial Park: The Killing Fields of the Cretaceous

subject: Dinosaur Provincial Park
summary: The Alberta badlands where more dinosaur species have been found than anywhere else on Earth - 44 species from one river valley, so many bones that early collectors shipped them out by the ton and still left plenty behind.

subject: Dinosaur Provincial Park
summary: The richest dinosaur graveyard on earth - where the Red Deer River has exposed 75-million-year-old badlands containing more species of dinosaurs than anywhere else, with 500 skeletons shipped to museums worldwide.

subject: Discovery Park (Seattle)
summary: Seattle's largest park occupies a former Army fort on a Puget Sound peninsula, where 270 bird species share 534 acres with a lighthouse, a grunge music video location, and the occasional cougar.

subject: Dismal Swamp Canal
summary: The oldest continually operating man-made canal in the United States, dug by hand by enslaved laborers through a swamp that George Washington wanted to drain -- and that freedom seekers later used as a path to freedom.

subject: Disneyland Railroad
summary: Walt Disney's childhood dream of running trains became an E-ticket attraction carrying 6.6 million passengers annually around the Happiest Place on Earth.

subject: Dix Park
summary: The 308-acre former site of North Carolina's oldest psychiatric hospital is becoming one of the largest urban parks in the South, with sunflowers, pow wows, and 900 unmarked graves slowly getting their names back.

subject: Djurdjura National Park
summary: The 'Mountain of Mountains' in Kabylie, where Romans named the peaks after iron, Berber language gave them cold, and endangered macaques still inhabit gorges the tectonic forces left shattered.

subject: Dobodura Airfield Complex
summary: Fifteen airstrips carved from New Guinea's coastal plain during World War II - now mostly swallowed by oil palm, but the runways themselves refuse to grow back.

subject: Docklands Light Railway
summary: A driverless toy railway built on a shoestring budget for a derelict bit of east London turned into one of the busiest light-rail networks in Europe, with 38 kilometres of track and almost 98 million passenger journeys a year.

subject: Dolomiti Bellunesi National Park
summary: One of the least-visited corners of the Dolomites protects a UNESCO World Heritage landscape of karst towers, deep canyons, and alpine biodiversity between the Cismon and Piave rivers.

subject: Dominica Botanical Gardens
summary: A colonial-era botanical garden in Roseau, once among the finest in the West Indies, where a baobab tree crushed by Hurricane David in 1979 still lies across a school bus as a monument to the storm's fury.

subject: Domogled-Valea Cernei National Park
summary: A Romanian national park where the Cerna River has carved through four mountain ranges, creating a hidden valley of primeval beech forests, limestone caves, and an endemic black pine found nowhere else on Earth.

subject: Don Det–Don Khon railway
summary: A 7 km narrow-gauge portage railway built by the French across two Mekong River islands in southern Laos, once the only railway in the country and now a haunting relic walked by backpackers.

subject: Don Mueang International Airport
summary: One of the world's oldest operating airports, Don Mueang was declared dead in 2006 when Bangkok opened its gleaming replacement -- then came roaring back as Southeast Asia's largest low-cost carrier hub.

subject: Dongshi Forestry Culture Park
summary: A Cold War-era logging center in Taiwan's mountains, once funded by the U.S. government, burned in a wildfire and was reborn as a 225-hectare cultural park where lotus ponds fill old timber storage basins.

subject: Donington Park
summary: England's first permanent park racing circuit, where Silver Arrows once thundered and Senna delivered the lap of the decade.

subject: Dorob National Park
summary: The final piece of a coastal megapark stretching the entire length of Namibia, where 1.6 million birds gather along a hyper-arid desert coastline and the endangered Damara tern makes its last stand.

subject: Dorotheenstadt Cemetery
summary: Four acres behind a wall on Chausseestraße hold Hegel, Fichte, Brecht, Schinkel and a stone cross for the men hanged in April 1945 — Germany's argument with itself, buried in one place.

subject: Dorrigo National Park
summary: Where the New England plateau breaks away to the coast, a fragment of Gondwana survives as living rainforest, walked first by the Gumbaynggirr and now crossed by a boardwalk that hangs over the escarpment edge.

subject: Dorrigo Steam Railway and Museum
summary: One of the southern hemisphere's largest collections of railway rolling stock sits at the end of a closed mountain branch line in Dorrigo, gathered over decades and, for almost forty years, never quite open to the public.

subject: Doshisha University
summary: A private university in Kyoto born from an act of illegal defiance -- its founder smuggled himself out of isolationist Japan in 1864, earned an American education, then returned to build a Christian school that has shaped Japanese leadership for 150 years.

subject: Douglas Harbour
summary: The first port in the world fitted with radar, defended by a Tower of Refuge on a submerged rock, with a 19th-century breakwater saga that destroyed itself twice.

subject: Douglas Historic District
summary: A mining town's Main Street frozen in early 20th-century splendor, where four churches on one block once made Ripley's Believe It or Not.

subject: Douglas Railway Station
summary: Built in red Ruabon brick on reclaimed marshland, this Victorian terminus once dispatched steam trains to Peel, Ramsey, and Foxdale; today it sends one daily train south to Port Erin.

subject: Doulab Cemetery
summary: A 19th-century Christian cemetery in Tehran where French physicians, Polish war refugees, Armenian artists, and the director of Iran's first feature film all share the same consecrated ground.

subject: Douro International Natural Park
summary: Where the Douro River carves the border between Portugal and Spain, 868 square kilometers of cliff faces and canyon walls shelter one of Europe's most important populations of cliff-nesting raptors.

subject: Dovre National Park
summary: Established in 2003 to stitch together two older national parks, Dovre is a corridor of windswept plateaus where Europe's last truly wild reindeer trace migration routes their ancestors walked since the Ice Age.

subject: Dovrefjell–Sunndalsfjella National Park
summary: Norway's great mountain sanctuary spans three counties and shelters Ice Age reindeer, reintroduced Arctic foxes, and shaggy musk oxen imported from Greenland -- all beneath the 2,286-meter summit of Snohetta.

subject: Downpatrick and County Down Railway
summary: A handful of volunteers in the 1980s rebuilt three miles of disused railway brick by brick, and Ireland's only five-foot-three-inch heritage line still runs steam through the marshes.

subject: Downtown Durham Historic District
summary: Ninety-seven contributing buildings in central Durham trace the story of a tobacco boom town, Black Wall Street, the Royal Ice Cream sit-in, and the long argument over what to remember.

subject: Downtown Historic District, San Jose
summary: A collection of late nineteenth and early twentieth century commercial buildings in downtown San Jose that survived earthquakes, urban renewal, and Silicon Valley's relentless appetite for redevelopment.

subject: Downtown Huntington Historic District
summary: A 112-building National Register district that preserves the commercial heart of a Gilded Age railroad city - including an opera house from 1885 and a 1928 movie palace still in use.

story.title: Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Classical Chinese Garden

subject: Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Classical Chinese Garden
summary: A Ming-style scholar's garden built in Vancouver's Chinatown for Expo 86 - the first Chinese garden constructed outside Asia, and a National Historic Site of Canada.

subject: Drew University
summary: A university born from a railroad tycoon's guilt offering, set on a steamboat magnate's estate in the New Jersey woods, where a Nobel Prize would one day be won.

subject: Droop Mountain Battlefield State Park
summary: West Virginia's first state park, dedicated in 1928 on the mountain where the Civil War effectively ended for the new state - thanks largely to one old Union veteran who would not let his battle be forgotten.

subject: Druid Hill Park
summary: One of the three oldest landscaped public parks in the United States, Druid Hill in Baltimore was the setting for the 1948 protest that ended segregated tennis courts in Maryland.

subject: Dry Tortugas National Park
summary: Seventy miles west of Key West, a cluster of coral islands holds the largest brick fortress in the Western Hemisphere, the least disturbed reefs in the Florida Keys, a $450 million shipwreck, and the cell where a doctor who treated Lincoln's assassin found redemption during a yellow fever epidemic.

subject: Dryandra Woodland National Park
summary: A fragmented mosaic of 17 woodland blocks on Western Australia's ancient Yilgarn plateau, Dryandra shelters over half the world's known numbat population and hides five Noongar archaeological sites among its wandoo groves.

subject: Drysdale River National Park
summary: The largest and least accessible park in the Kimberley, Drysdale River National Park is a wilderness so remote it has no roads, no rangers, and no services — only ancient gorges, plunging waterfalls, and almost 600 species of plants.

subject: Dublin City University
summary: Born in 1975 as a polytechnic experiment on Dublin's quieter northside, DCU has grown into a 20,000-student university whose library is legally entitled to a copy of every book published in Ireland.

subject: Dublin Zoo
summary: Founded in 1830 -- the world's fourth-oldest scientific zoo -- Dublin Zoo bred its first lion cub in 1857, kept its keepers feeding the animals through the 1916 Rising, and now occupies 28 hectares of Phoenix Park beside the President's house.

subject: Dude Chilling Park
summary: An unauthorized park sign bolted up in a Vancouver green space in 2012 was removed, petitioned back, and eventually granted official public art status by the city it was making fun of.

subject: Dudhkundi Airfield
summary: A forest that a king gave to the American Air Force, where the 444th Bombardment Group launched some of the war's longest missions before vanishing into the jungle of West Bengal.

subject: Duhallow ADS Cemetery
summary: Named for an Irish fox hunt, the cemetery grew up around a first-aid post on the road north of Ypres - the place where wounded men were carried, sorted, and sometimes lost.

subject: Duinen van Texel National Park
summary: Forty-three square kilometers of shifting sand, salt marsh, freshwater dune valleys and the largest spoonbill breeding colony in the Netherlands, all of it held in place by marram grass and a botanist who handed it out free with chocolate bars.

subject: Duisburg Inner Harbour
summary: Once the bread basket of the Ruhr, the Innenhafen sat derelict for twenty years before Norman Foster handed it back to the city.

subject: Duisburg Zoo
summary: Koalas in the Ruhrgebiet, fossas from Madagascar, and a busy autobahn that the visitors barely notice.

subject: Duisburg-Hochfeld Railway Bridge
summary: Four bridges have stood on this stretch of the Rhine since 1873 - one with mines in its piers, one bombed twice in a year, one built in six days, and the one still carrying freight to Aachen.

subject: Duke University
summary: Founded as a Methodist and Quaker school in 1838, renamed in 1924 with tobacco fortune, today one of the most selective research universities in the United States.

subject: Dulcie Range National Park
summary: A sandstone plateau rising from the central Australian plain, its cliffs holding more than a hundred rock-art sites where the Akarre Arrernte recorded their world in stone.

subject: Duluth Ship Canal
summary: Duluth citizens dug a canal through Minnesota Point in 1871 so fast that Wisconsin politicians barely had time to file an injunction -- and that act of interstate rivalry created the harbor entrance that still funnels a thousand ships a year beneath the iconic Aerial Lift Bridge.

subject: Dunedin Botanic Garden
summary: New Zealand's oldest botanical garden climbs from a riverside plain up the flank of a volcanic hill spur, housing heritage glasshouses, a Peter Pan statue, and a geological trail through the eruptions that built the city.

subject: Dunedin Chinese Garden
summary: New Zealand's only authentic Chinese garden, prefabricated in Shanghai and reassembled by hand in Dunedin, honours the Cantonese miners who helped build the city during the 1860s gold rush.

subject: Dunedin railway station
summary: Dubbed 'Gingerbread George' for its ornate Flemish Renaissance styling, Dunedin's railway station once handled 100 trains a day and now hosts a farmers market, fashion shows, and the New Zealand Sports Hall of Fame.

subject: Durbin and Greenbrier Valley Railroad
summary: A West Virginia short-line railroad that runs five excursion trains - including a logging Climax and a Shay-driven tour up Cheat Mountain - over track laid for the timber boom a century ago.

subject: Durham Athletic Park
summary: The minor league ballpark north of downtown Durham where Kevin Costner and Tim Robbins filmed Bull Durham in 1987, and where the Bulls played from 1926 to 1994.

subject: Durham Bulls Athletic Park
summary: Durham's downtown 10,000-seat ballpark, opened in 1995 with a 32-foot Blue Monster left-field wall and a snorting bull sign over it, home of the Triple-A Durham Bulls.

subject: Durham University Museum of Archaeology
summary: The second university museum in England open to the public, founded in 1833 and home to internationally important Roman finds and one of the UK's largest collections of post-medieval glass.

subject: Durham University Oriental Museum
summary: Durham University's collection of over 23,500 artefacts from China, Egypt, Korea, India, Japan, and across Asia, with internationally designated Chinese and Egyptian collections.

subject: Dusseldorf Airport
summary: Germany's fourth-busiest airport carries the memory of a fire that killed seventeen people - and the careful rebuilding that followed.

story.title: Dutch Harbor: Where the Deadliest Catch Comes Home

subject: Dutch Harbor
summary: The Alaska port that processes more seafood than any in America - Bering Sea crab boats, factory trawlers, and the deadliest fishing industry on Earth, all operating from a town where sideways rain is called weather.

subject: Dutch Windmill
summary: A century-old windmill that once pumped water to transform San Francisco's sand dunes into one of the world's great urban parks.

subject: Duxford Aerodrome
summary: Eight miles south of Cambridge, a flat piece of Cambridgeshire farmland served as the front line of Britain's air defence in 1940 — and today it is home to the largest aviation museum in Europe.

subject: Dyer Island Nature Reserve Complex
summary: Three small islands off the coast of Gansbaai where 60,000 fur seals, a colony of endangered African penguins, and the great white sharks that patrol the channel between them create one of the most concentrated wildlife spectacles in Africa.

subject: Dykyi Sad Archaeological Site
summary: Beneath a city park in Mykolaiv lie the walls of a Bronze Age port that traded while Troy still stood, and that some believe Homer himself described.

subject: Dytynets Park
summary: A green hill above the Desna where twelve cast-iron cannons guard the thousand-year foundations of Chernihiv, the fortified heart of a city named in the chronicles under the year 907.

subject: Dzanga-Ndoki National Park
summary: Split into two sectors across the southwestern tip of the Central African Republic, this park harbors one of the highest gorilla densities ever recorded and anchors the UNESCO Sangha Trinational.

subject: Dzharylhach National Nature Park
summary: A national park built around the largest island in the Black Sea, prized for its beaches and rare geese, and reduced to ash during the war.

subject: Düren-Neuss railway
summary: A nineteenth-century cross-country line through the Rhineland whose southern half was eaten alive by an open-cast lignite mine.

subject: EMakhosini Ophathe Heritage Park
summary: South Africa's Valley of the Kings, where seven Zulu monarchs are buried and where King Shaka's military genius forged a kingdom that reshaped southern Africa.

subject: Eagle Farm Airport
summary: Brisbane's first airport, where the Southern Cross came home from the Pacific in 1928 and where Allied engineers secretly rebuilt captured Japanese fighters to fly over the city.

subject: Eala Botanical Garden
summary: Founded in 1900 on the banks of the Ruki River near the equator, the Eala Botanical Garden was once among the world's most important tropical gardens before war, neglect, and Zairianisation left it struggling to survive.

subject: Earl Warren College
summary: A house tilts impossibly atop an engineering building while a massive stone bear stands watch over one of UC San Diego's eight undergraduate colleges, where residence halls bear the names of Supreme Court justices.

subject: Earnest Farms Historic District
summary: Four working farms along the Nolichucky River near Chuckey, Tennessee, continuously cultivated by the Earnest family and their successors since the 1770s — and the oldest Methodist congregation in Tennessee.

subject: East Carolina University
summary: A teacher training school chartered to serve eastern North Carolina that grew into the state's fourth-largest university and its only one with medicine, dentistry, and engineering.

story.title: East End Historic District (Charleston, West Virginia)

subject: East End Historic District (Charleston, West Virginia)
summary: The residential neighborhood that grew up around the West Virginia State Capitol - a hundred years of American architectural styles laid out along the Kanawha River.

subject: Eastern Mennonite University
summary: A Harrisonburg university whose Center for Justice and Peacebuilding has trained Nobel Peace laureates, presidents, and 3,000 conflict transformers from 124 countries.

subject: Echo Park
summary: Echo Park's lake and surrounding neighborhood have been at the center of Los Angeles filmmaking, counterculture, and housing politics for more than a century—most recently in a 2021 encampment controversy that divided the city.

subject: Ecola State Park
summary: Where the Lewis and Clark Expedition made its farthest push south along the Oregon Coast, chasing rumors of a beached whale across the headland the Tillamook people had known for centuries.

subject: Edel Land National Park
summary: The wild western arm of Shark Bay — Malgana Country for millennia, the place where the first Europeans met the Australian mainland, and now a national park in the making.

subject: Eden Park
summary: The only stadium on Earth to have hosted both a Rugby World Cup final and a Rugby League World Cup final, Auckland's Eden Park has anchored New Zealand sport since Cornish farmers cleared its stone walls in the 1800s.

subject: Edgewood County Park
summary: A 467-acre preserve in San Mateo County famous for its spectacular spring wildflower displays -- saved from development by activists who fought to protect its rare serpentine grasslands.

subject: Edinburgh Airport
summary: Scotland's busiest airport, born as a World War I defence base in 1916 and now handling over 15 million passengers a year to 152 international destinations.

subject: Edinburgh College of Art
summary: A 1760 drawing academy for textile designers that grew into Scotland's premier art college, where Eduardo Paolozzi sculpted, Basil Spence designed Coventry Cathedral, and Roy Williamson wrote Flower of Scotland.

subject: Edinburgh Napier University
summary: A modern Scottish university built around a 16th-century tower house, the WWI hospital that treated Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon, and the inventor of logarithms whose statue still looks out from his medieval birthplace.

subject: Edinburgh Old Town
summary: The medieval spine that earned the nickname Auld Reekie, where Burke and Hare hunted bodies for the anatomist, John Knox glowers from his cobble, and Arthur's Seat rises from a 340-million-year-old volcano.

subject: Edinburgh Waverley
summary: Tucked into a steep glacial valley between the medieval Old Town and Georgian New Town, Edinburgh Waverley is Scotland's second-busiest station, named for a novelist and forever forbidden from growing upward because it must not block the view of Arthur's Seat.

subject: Edinburgh, Leith and Newhaven Railway
summary: A Victorian railway that hauled passengers up a rope-worked tunnel beneath the New Town and ferried whole trains across the Forth on Thomas Bouch's adjustable ramps to reach Dundee.

subject: Edison's Menlo Park Laboratory
summary: The New Jersey site where Thomas Edison invented the practical light bulb, phonograph, and modern research laboratory itself - the 'invention factory' that changed how innovation happens, now marked by a memorial tower with the world's largest light bulb.

subject: Eduardo Gomes International Airport
summary: Manaus's main airport, briefly called the Supersonic Airport and designed for the Concorde that never quite arrived, built in the rainforest 14 kilometers from a city with no road south.

story.title: Edward Ball Wakulla Springs State Park

subject: Edward Ball Wakulla Springs State Park
summary: A 6,000-acre wildlife sanctuary south of Tallahassee where mastodon bones rest on the floor of one of the world's deepest freshwater springs, and where the Creature from the Black Lagoon first emerged from the depths.

subject: Eemmeerdijk Wind Park
summary: A row of 19 two-bladed NedWind turbines marched along a Flevoland dyke for a quarter century, until a single broken pylon sealed their fate.

subject: Eems Canal
summary: The 26-kilometer canal that promised to make Groningen a seaport, opened in 1876 after a decade of digging and ten million guilders of overruns - and never quite delivered on the dream.

subject: Eemshaven Railway Station
summary: The northernmost train station in the Netherlands - a remote terminus built for ferry passengers heading to a German island.

story.title: Egmont Key: The Island That Refused to Stay Tamed

subject: Egmont Key State Park and National Wildlife Refuge
summary: A barrier island at the mouth of Tampa Bay where a lighthouse keeper once rode out a hurricane in a rowboat, Spanish-American War fortifications crumble into the sand, and gopher tortoises outnumber human visitors on any given day.

subject: Egmont National Park
summary: Now officially Te Papa-Kura-o-Taranaki, this national park forms a near-perfect circle of ancient rainforest around a dormant volcano, its boundary so sharp it is visible from space.

subject: Eindhoven University of Technology
summary: Founded in 1956 to feed Philips its engineers, TU/e grew into a 14,000-student technical university whose alumni and faculty include Edsger Dijkstra, the inventor of the Philishave, and the team that built a Sagrada Familia replica in ice.

subject: Ekenäs Archipelago National Park
summary: A national park that is mostly water, guarding rock islets a Danish pilot's manual already named in 1250 — and an island where convicts dug iron for the Russian crown.

subject: El Cajas National Park
summary: A visitor's guide to Ecuador's high-altitude park of 270 lakes, paper trees, llamas, and the bus that leaves Cuenca for a dollar.

subject: El Cajas National Park
summary: Gateway to the snowy mountains: an Andean paramo of 270 glacial lakes, nineteen endemic plants, and the world's largest hummingbird.

subject: El Cocuy National Park
summary: Home to Colombia's last glaciers and the highest peak of the Eastern Cordillera, El Cocuy is a landscape the U'wa people consider sacred and that climate science says is disappearing within decades.

subject: El Fondo Natural Park
summary: A pair of hand-built irrigation lagoons near Elche became one of the last strongholds on Earth for two of Europe's rarest ducks.

subject: El Imposible National Park
summary: El Salvador's largest national park earned its name from a gorge so treacherous it killed farmers and mules hauling coffee to port -- now it protects 5,000 hectares of endangered tropical forest, thousand-year-old petroglyphs, and species found nowhere else.

subject: El Kala National Park
summary: Algeria's northeastern corner holds a biosphere reserve where cork oak forests meet Mediterranean lagoons, sheltering the last population of the Barbary stag and over 60,000 migratory birds each winter.

subject: El Leoncito National Park
summary: A high Andean park in San Juan province protecting some of the clearest dark skies on Earth, home to two observatories and a vast white plain where the wind drives land-sailors across an ancient lakebed.

subject: El Palmar National Park
summary: These towering yatay palms once carpeted three countries. Ranching and farming erased nearly all of them, and this Argentine park protects one of the last great groves.

subject: El Rey National Park
summary: A former Spanish frontier estate turned national park, where dry Chaco thornland climbs through cloud forest into mountain woods in the span of a single hike.

subject: El Ávila National Park
summary: The forested mountain wall north of Caracas that locals call the city's lungs -- home to 500 bird species, a German doctor's mummification laboratory, and a legend about a flower picker who announces winter's arrival.

subject: El-Kouf National Park
summary: On Libya's northeastern coast, where the green slopes of Jabal al Akhdar meet the Mediterranean, El Kouf National Park shelters a surprising concentration of wildlife in a region better known for conflict than conservation.

subject: Electric Railway Museum
summary: A small heritage railway centre next to Coventry Airport that became Britain's most significant collection of preserved electric multiple units -- the unglamorous workhorses of suburban commuter rail -- before being closed in 2017 and dispersed across the country.

subject: Eleutherian College
summary: A tiny abolitionist school in the Indiana hills that became one of the first colleges in America to educate Black and white students together, and a station on the Underground Railroad.

subject: Elgin and Winter Garden Theatres
summary: The last surviving Edwardian stacked theatres in the world, where one auditorium sits seven storeys above another on Toronto's Yonge Street.

subject: Elizabeth College, Guernsey
summary: A 1563 royal-charter grammar school whose founding year saw three Guernsey women burned for witchcraft, which evacuated to Derbyshire under German occupation, and which counts P.G. Wodehouse among its alumni.

subject: Elk Falls Provincial Park
summary: A waterfall that once thundered with the full force of the Campbell River now shares its flow with three hydroelectric dams, yet Elk Falls Provincial Park still delivers one of Vancouver Island's most dramatic canyon views.

subject: Ellanor C. Lawrence Park
summary: A 640-acre Fairfax County park preserving 8,000 years of human use - a Senate clerk's experimental farm, a Civil War battlefield in the cornfield, and the country estate of the founder of U.S. News & World Report.

subject: Ellis Park Stadium
summary: Built on a Doornfontein quarry, Ellis Park witnessed Mandela hand a rugby trophy to a white captain in 1995 and, six years later, a crowd crush that killed 43.

subject: Elmwood Cemetery (Memphis, Tennessee)
summary: Memphis's oldest active cemetery was established in 1852 when fifty citizens drew its name from a hat, then had to rush-order elm trees from New York because there were none in Tennessee -- and went on to become the final resting place for 75,000 people spanning Civil War generals, yellow fever martyrs, and the man who wrote the definitive history of the war.

subject: Eloy Alfaro International Airport
summary: A coastal airfield that spent a decade hosting U.S. drug-surveillance planes, until Ecuador's president made his point by offering a trade: one base in Manta, one base in Miami.

subject: Els Ports Natural Park
summary: A wild limestone massif on the borders of three regions, sheltering Europe's southernmost beech forests and Spain's largest population of wild goats.

story.title: Emancipation Park: Houston's Sacred Ground of Freedom

subject: Emancipation Park (Houston)
summary: Purchased for $800 by four formerly enslaved men in 1872 to celebrate Juneteenth, Emancipation Park is the oldest park in Houston and Texas -- a place where freedom was not given but bought, brick by brick.

subject: Emas National Park
summary: A UNESCO-protected island of Brazilian cerrado where beetle larvae turn giant termite mounds into glowing green towers, and where 400 bird species share a plateau surrounded on all sides by soybeans.

subject: Embassy Park Presidential Burial Site
summary: Zambia's state burial ground in Lusaka, where each former president's mausoleum carries symbolic details of the life it commemorates - and where one former leader broke the tradition by being buried abroad.

subject: Embry–Riddle Aeronautical University
summary: The world's largest university devoted to aviation and aerospace started in 1926 at a small Cincinnati airfield, trained pilots for World War II alongside a future president, and now sprawls across Daytona Beach with 88 Cessnas on its own ramp.

story.title: Embsay and Bolton Abbey Steam Railway

subject: Embsay and Bolton Abbey Steam Railway
summary: Volunteers patched four miles of a closed Midland Railway line back into life and now run a hundred thousand passengers a year between Embsay and Bolton Abbey behind locomotives older than most of the track they cover.

subject: Emirgan Park
summary: Each spring, Emirgan Park on Istanbul's Bosphorus shore ignites with millions of tulips — a flower that traveled from Central Asia to the Ottoman court, and from the court back to the world.

subject: Emma Prusch Farm Park
summary: A working farm in the middle of San Jose where chickens, goats, and heritage fruit trees preserve the agricultural past of a valley that was once the world's largest fruit-producing region.

subject: Emory and Henry University
summary: The oldest college in Southwest Virginia, founded by Methodists in 1836, where Wiley Hall served as a Confederate hospital, J.E.B. Stuart enrolled as a teenager, and Frank Rowlett cracked the Japanese diplomatic code.

subject: Empire Mine State Historic Park
summary: California's richest gold mine operated for over a century, producing 5.8 million ounces of gold from 367 miles of underground tunnels before becoming a state historic park.

subject: Emsland Railway
summary: The 1854 rail line that became Germany's last home for working steam locomotives, then the test track that almost made magnetic levitation real.

story.title: Engine Number 5 and the Tunnel That Kept Its Secret

subject: Engine Number 5 and the Tunnel That Kept Its Secret
summary: A miniature railroad in Vacaville, California that once shuttled Hollywood stars and a future president from a toy shop to an airport - then spent years sealed inside its own tunnel before a city refused to let it disappear.

subject: English Cemetery, Menorca
summary: A small walled burial ground above Port Mahon where American sailors who died far from home in the early 1800s still lie, once forgotten and now tended each Memorial Day.

subject: Englishman River Falls Provincial Park
summary: A 97-hectare park on Vancouver Island where upper and lower waterfalls carve through a canyon of old-growth Douglas fir, and a grim origin story gives the river its name.

subject: Enschede Airport Twente
summary: An airfield that has been a KLM stop, a Luftwaffe base, an F-104 Starfighter home, a marathon course, and finally an aircraft graveyard where retired airliners come to be taken apart.

subject: Enschede Railway Station
summary: The Dutch and German rails come within thirty centimeters of each other at this station, but they will never touch - a Cold War gap that became permanent.

subject: Erasmus University Rotterdam
summary: A Dutch research university founded by Rotterdam merchants in 1913 to teach commerce - now named for the city's Renaissance humanist son, and ranked among the world's elite for economics and business.

subject: Erie Canal
summary: The audacious 363-mile ditch across New York State that connected the Atlantic to the Great Lakes, made New York City the nation's premier port, and changed the trajectory of American expansion.

subject: Essex Farm Cemetery
summary: 1,204 burials beside the canal-bank dressing station where In Flanders Fields was written - including a 15-year-old private and a sniper-stalking Victoria Cross.

subject: Estadio Luna Park
summary: The 'Cathedral of Boxing' where Argentina crowned champions, mourned Carlos Gardel, and where a young actress named Eva Duarte first met Juan Perón.

subject: Eton College
summary: A 15th-century charity school for seventy poor boys that grew into the most famous boarding school in the world and educated twenty British prime ministers.

subject: Etosha National Park
summary: At the heart of one of Africa's great game reserves lies a salt pan so vast it is visible from space - a shimmering white void that draws elephants, lions and rhinos to its life-giving waterholes.

subject: Eungella National Park
summary: On a cloud-wrapped plateau west of Mackay lies the most reliable place on Earth to watch a wild platypus surface, ringed by a rainforest so long isolated it grew its own species.

subject: Euston railway station
summary: The first inter-city railway terminal in London, whose lost Doric arch became the foundational tragedy of British architectural conservation.

subject: Everglades National Park
summary: The first national park created to protect a fragile ecosystem rather than scenic grandeur - a vast river of grass where alligators engineer the landscape, panthers stalk hardwood hammocks, and the boundary between fresh and salt water decides everything.

subject: Exmoor National Park
summary: Where England's highest sea cliffs meet open moorland grazed by wild ponies and red deer, Exmoor is a landscape shaped by 3,000 years of farming and the persistent rumour of a phantom big cat.

subject: Explore Park
summary: An 1,100-acre living history park on the Blue Ridge Parkway whose Disney-sized ambitions collapsed twice before settling in as Roanoke County's outdoor adventure outpost.

story.title: Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park

subject: Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park
summary: The first marine protected area in the Caribbean, where ospreys are the only creatures allowed to fish and endangered rock iguanas bask on limestone shores that double as a living laboratory for reef recovery.

subject: Eyüp Cemetery
summary: Spread across the hillside above the Golden Horn, the Eyüp Cemetery is one of Istanbul's oldest and most sacred burial grounds — a place where Ottoman sultans, poets, scholars, and commanders sought their final rest near the grave of a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.

story.title: Faculty of Theology, Catholic University of Leuven

subject: Faculty of Theology, Catholic University of Leuven
summary: From its founding in 1834 to its splitting in two in 1968, the Leuven theology faculty quietly shaped twentieth-century Catholic thought - and helped write the Second Vatican Council from the inside.

subject: Fair Park
summary: A Depression-era fairground reborn as the nation's largest surviving Art Deco exposition complex, Fair Park has hosted everything from the Texas Centennial to a Formula One Grand Prix -- and still draws millions each fall for the State Fair of Texas.

story.title: Fairfax Stone Historical Monument State Park

subject: Fairfax Stone Historical Monument State Park
summary: The boundary stone Peter Jefferson placed in 1746, lost to vandals by 1909, replaced in 1957, that still defines where three West Virginia counties meet at the source of the Potomac.

subject: Fairhaven College
summary: Nobody at Fairhaven gets a B. The experimental college on the wooded south edge of Western Washington University has issued narrative evaluations instead of letter grades since 1967.

subject: Fairy Lake Botanical Garden
summary: A vast urban sanctuary in Shenzhen's Luohu District, where a man-made lake, a Buddhist temple, and one of the world's largest cycad collections share a hillside that the city has somehow never swallowed.

subject: Falling Waters State Park
summary: Home to Florida's tallest waterfall -- a 73-foot cascade that drops into a cylindrical sinkhole and vanishes underground into limestone caverns whose destination remains unknown.

subject: False Cape State Park
summary: The state park you can only reach on foot, bicycle, or boat - a barrier peninsula where the wrecks of two centuries built a town that the sea then took back.

subject: Fantasy Gardens
summary: A mock-medieval theme park in suburban Richmond with a Bible-shaped hedge, a miniature railway and a Dutch castle - the castle outlived the park, the premier and the government.

subject: Farina railway station
summary: A railway stop in the outback whose very name - Latin for flour - was a hopeful promise of wheat fields that the dry country never delivered.

subject: Farranfore–Valentia Harbour line
summary: For 67 years a single-track railway ran 39.5 miles along Dingle Bay to the most westerly station in Europe.

subject: Farroupilha Park
summary: Porto Alegre's great central park was once a muddy commons for cattle and garbage, until the city renamed it Fields of Redemption to honor the abolition of slavery.

subject: Father Hennepin State Park
summary: A Minnesota state park on Mille Lacs Lake's southeast shore honors the Franciscan priest who was captured by Dakota warriors in 1680 and became the first European to describe this landscape in print -- though he likely never set foot on the parkland that bears his name.

subject: Fayetteville Historic District (Fayetteville, West Virginia)
summary: 126 contributing buildings ring the Fayette County Courthouse - civil war forts, Greek Revival houses, Art Deco theaters, and the everyday architecture of a coal-era county seat.

subject: Fayetteville Regional Airport
summary: Three nautical miles south of downtown, KFAY moves more soldiers per square foot of terminal than just about any airport its size in America - a regional field whose single most important amenity is the USO inside security.

subject: Fayetteville State University
summary: Seven Black men paid $136 for two lots on Gillespie Street in 1867. From that gift grew the oldest publicly supported school for African American teachers in the South - now an HBCU with more than 7,000 students and a library named for a novelist.

subject: Feldberg Lake District Nature Park
summary: Three hundred and forty square kilometres of ice-age lakes and bog in southeast Mecklenburg, holding Germany's most famous stand of ancient beech and the house where Hans Fallada kept writing after the regime banned him.

subject: Feltville Historic District
summary: A New Jersey ghost town known as the Deserted Village has been abandoned twice, haunted by legend, and revived by murals painted by a Nicaraguan sculptor who never painted anywhere else.

subject: Fengbitou Archaeological Site
summary: On a 9.7-hectare plateau in southern Kaohsiung, the Fengbitou Archaeological Site preserves five thousand years of human habitation, from the earliest cord-marked pottery of Taiwan's Tapenkeng culture to Qing dynasty remains.

story.title: Fenway Park: The Ballpark That Refused to Die

subject: Fenway Park
summary: The oldest active ballpark in Major League Baseball, where the Green Monster, a lone red seat, and a hand-operated scoreboard have defied every attempt at demolition since 1912 -- and where Roger Clemens once mistook the place for a warehouse.

subject: Ferdows Garden
summary: A Qajar-era garden in northern Tehran whose very name traces the ancient Persian word that gave English the concept of paradise -- and now houses Iran's Cinema Museum.

subject: Feriköy Protestant Cemetery
summary: A quiet walled garden in Istanbul's Şişli district holding around 5,000 souls — diplomats, brewers, photographers, linguists — who built the cosmopolitan Ottoman capital and never left.

subject: Ferrum College
summary: A small private Methodist college in the Blue Ridge foothills, founded in 1913 as a mountain mission school for rural Virginia children and still anchored to the Appalachian community that raised it.

subject: Fettes College
summary: Built with a merchant's grief and a son's name, Fettes rises from its Edinburgh grounds like a Loire chateau gone Scottish - a school that produced Tony Blair and Sean Connery's milk route, with a bee on its crest and a long-shadowed history its current pupils inherit.

subject: Ffestiniog Railway
summary: Founded in 1832, the world's oldest surviving railway company still runs Double Fairlie locomotives through Snowdonia on a line built so wagons could roll downhill by gravity all the way to the sea.

subject: Fifth Street Historic District
summary: Eight blocks of Lynchburg's historic African American commercial corridor — taverns from 1800, tobacco factories, Art Deco showrooms, and the church where the community organized — listed on the National Register in 2012.

subject: Fifty Graves in Gold Country
summary: Founded in 1855 by Jewish pioneers who followed the Gold Rush to California's Third City, the Marysville Hebrew Cemetery was abandoned for half a century before a restoration effort reclaimed its stones from the weeds.

subject: Fillmore and Western Railway
summary: The Fillmore and Western Railway ran tourist trains and murder-mystery dinners on a century-old track through the Santa Clara River Valley — and appeared in over 400 films and TV productions before shutting down in 2021.

subject: Fin Garden
summary: Iran's oldest surviving garden, a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Kashan where turquoise-tiled pools, 500-year-old cypress trees, and the bathhouse where a reformist chancellor was assassinated in 1852 converge in a single walled paradise.

subject: Fiordland National Park
summary: New Zealand's largest national park, where glaciers carved steep-sided fiords into the rock during the last ice age, and 8,000 millimeters of annual rainfall now sustain a wilderness so remote that species once thought extinct have been rediscovered.

subject: First Cemetery of Athens
summary: The First Cemetery of Athens, opened in 1837, is Greece's most celebrated necropolis — an outdoor museum of neoclassical sculpture where Nobel laureates, independence heroes, and the sculptor of the heartbreaking 'Sleeping Maiden' lie beneath marble and cypress shade.

story.title: First Creation: Bali's Garden in the Clouds

subject: First Creation
summary: Perched 1,300 meters above sea level on the slopes of Tapak Hill, Indonesia's largest botanic garden holds 21,000 living specimens and a name that means 'first creation' -- a fitting title for the country's first post-independence botanical preserve.

subject: First Nations University of Canada
summary: Canada's only university governed by First Nations people rises from the Regina prairie in a building designed to honor Indigenous traditions.

story.title: First Peoples Buffalo Jump State Park

subject: First Peoples Buffalo Jump State Park
summary: North America's largest buffalo jump, where Indigenous hunters drove bison over sandstone cliffs for over a thousand years.

subject: Fish River Canyon
summary: A 160-kilometer gash in the southern Namibian desert, often ranked second only to the Grand Canyon, carved over hundreds of millions of years by a river that now barely runs.

subject: Fishguard Harbour Railway Station
summary: The last terminus in Britain where you could legally smoke on the platform, built by the Great Western Railway in 1906 for ocean liners that turned out to be too big to dock.

subject: Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge
summary: Cambridge's great equalizer: a college founded in 1869 to give brilliant students who couldn't afford college membership a path to one of the world's finest universities.

subject: Flagler College
summary: A private liberal arts college housed inside a Gilded Age luxury hotel, where students eat breakfast beneath Louis Comfort Tiffany stained glass and attend class in rooms built for railroad tycoon Henry Flagler's wealthiest guests.

subject: Flambards Theme Park
summary: For 48 years a Cornish aero engineer's collection of aircraft, a fifty-shop Victorian village, and a Blitz-era London street co-existed with rollercoasters at the edge of Helston — until the rides started leaving in 2024.

subject: Flamingo International Airport
summary: Bonaire's gateway to the world grew from a 475-meter dirt strip built in 1935 into an international airport capable of handling 747s - its story mirrors the island's own transformation from colonial outpost to diving paradise.

story.title: Flanders Field American Cemetery and Memorial

subject: Flanders Field American Cemetery and Memorial
summary: The only permanent American World War I cemetery in Belgium holds 368 graves arranged beneath a chapel ceiling where doves of peace fly toward a lamp of remembrance.

subject: Florida Caverns State Park
summary: The only Florida state park with air-filled caves open to the public, where limestone formations millions of years old hide beneath the flat Panhandle landscape near Marianna.

subject: Florida Southern College
summary: A small private college in Lakeland, Florida, that holds the world's largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture -- a campus Wright envisioned as a 'child of the sun' rising from a lakeside orange grove.

subject: Flower Garden of Isfahan
summary: A modern botanical garden in Isfahan that weaves together over 400 plant species, Persian carpet-inspired floral designs, and traditional Iranian architecture across 5.5 hectares.

subject: Folgefonna National Park
summary: Three glaciers, 545 square kilometers, and some of the wettest weather in Norway -- a national park where ice and rain have written the landscape for thousands of years.

subject: Font Roja Natural Park
summary: On a shaded mountain flank above Alcoy, one of eastern Spain's last great holm-oak forests survives where the surrounding hills were long ago stripped bare.

subject: Fontys University of Applied Sciences
summary: 44,000 students, three campuses, one Latin word for "source" - the practical engine that feeds Brainport its engineers.

subject: Foothill College
summary: Foothill College is a public community college in Los Altos Hills, California. It is part of the Foothill–De Anza Community College District. It was f

story.title: Ford River Rouge Complex: The Factory That Swallowed a River

subject: Ford River Rouge complex
summary: Henry Ford bought this land in 1915 to build a bird sanctuary. Instead, he built the largest integrated factory on Earth -- a self-contained industrial city that turned raw iron ore into finished automobiles and inspired factory design worldwide.

subject: Forest Lawn Memorial Park
summary: The Glendale cemetery where celebrity burials are so secretive that Michael Jackson's exact location is unknown - featuring full-size replicas of European churches, the world's largest religious painting, and a business model that revolutionized American death.

subject: Forest Lawn Memorial Park (Glendale)
summary: A cemetery like no other — Hubert Eaton's ambitious reimagining of the American burial ground as a place of sweeping lawns, art museums, and joyous Christian optimism, where Humphrey Bogart, Walt Disney, Michael Jackson, and Elizabeth Taylor found their final addresses.

subject: Forest Park (St. Louis)
summary: Larger than Central Park by 500 acres, Forest Park hosted the 1904 World's Fair and Olympics, and today holds five major cultural institutions -- all free to the public.

subject: Forestiere Underground Gardens
summary: A Sicilian immigrant spent forty years hand-digging an underground labyrinth beneath Fresno's hardpan, creating subterranean rooms, passageways, and gardens where citrus trees still bear fruit a century later.

subject: Forillon National Park
summary: Quebec's first national park sits where the Appalachians meet the sea, a place shaped by geological collision, colonial fisheries, wartime fortification, and the displacement of 225 families.

subject: Forrest Airport
summary: Halfway across the Nullarbor, a 1929 airfield with a hangar and a handful of cottages keeps the lights on for anyone crossing the emptiest stretch of Australia.

subject: Forsyth Park
summary: Savannah's iconic thirty-acre park, home to the most photographed fountain in Georgia - cast by the same ironworks that built the Capitol dome - and the backdrop for Forrest Gump, Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil, and 180 years of Southern life.

subject: Fort Apache Historic Park
summary: A tribal historic park where military fort became boarding school became cultural center -- the White Mountain Apache reclaiming a place that tried to erase their identity.

subject: Fort Bayard Historic District
summary: A frontier outpost where Buffalo Soldiers earned the Medal of Honor, then became America's first Army tuberculosis hospital and a World War II POW camp.

subject: Fort Bayard National Cemetery
summary: Six thousand graves mark the final resting place of Buffalo Soldiers, Medal of Honor recipients, and veterans spanning from the Indian Wars to modern times.

subject: Fort Bliss National Cemetery
summary: From Confederate infantry to Chinese aviators, from Medal of Honor recipients to a Harlem Globetrotters legend, Fort Bliss National Cemetery holds over 50,000 graves spanning nearly two centuries of American military history.

subject: Fort Caswell Historic District
summary: A pentagonal brick fortress completed in 1836 to guard the Cape Fear, blown up by its own defenders in 1865, briefly a mineral-water resort, and now a Baptist retreat at the eastern tip of Oak Island.

story.title: Fort De Soto Park: Five Islands, Five Centuries

subject: Fort De Soto Park
summary: A chain of five barrier islands at the mouth of Tampa Bay where Tocobaga people harvested oysters, Spanish-American War mortars still point skyward, a plumber ran a fried mullet lodge, and North Beach was once named America's best.

subject: Fort Ebey State Park
summary: A World War II coastal defense fort turned state park where concrete gun bunkers overlook the Strait of Juan de Fuca and paragliders ride the updrafts off 200-foot bluffs.

subject: Fort Lee Historic Park
summary: A Revolutionary War encampment perched on the Hudson Palisades where George Washington watched his army's fortunes crumble in November 1776.

subject: Fort Macon State Park
summary: From Blackbeard's stomping grounds to Civil War battlefield to one-dollar state park, Fort Macon on North Carolina's Bogue Banks has spent three centuries guarding Beaufort Inlet -- and collecting stories.

subject: Fort Michilimackinac State Park
summary: A reconstructed 18th-century fort where the French fur trade, a lacrosse game that turned into a massacre, and North America's longest-running archaeological dig all converge at the tip of Michigan's mitten.

subject: Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery
summary: A sacred hillside where America's military heroes rest between two waters, their white headstones tracing the contours of Point Loma like silent sentinels.

story.title: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park

subject: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park
summary: Two forts guarding Charleston Harbor bookend nearly a century of American conflict, from the Revolutionary War's spongy palmetto victory to the Civil War's fateful first shots.

subject: Fort Verde State Historic Park
summary: The best-preserved military post from General Crook's 1872-73 Apache campaign stands quietly in Camp Verde, Arizona -- a fort that never had walls and never saw a battle on its grounds.

subject: Fort William Historical Park
summary: A sprawling reconstruction of the North West Company's fur trade headquarters on the Kaministiquia River, Fort William Historical Park re-creates the year 1816 with 42 buildings, working tradesmen, and the cultural crossroads that shaped a continent's commerce.

subject: Fortaleza Airport
summary: Northeastern Brazil's aviation gateway, named for a pioneering Ceará aviator and once a crucial Allied stepping stone across the South Atlantic.

subject: Forth and Clyde Canal
summary: Opened in 1790 to let seagoing ships cross Scotland at its narrowest waist, the canal closed in 1963, reopened for the millennium, and now ends at a turning wheel.

subject: Fossli Provincial Park
summary: A 52-hectare park on Sproat Lake named by a Norwegian immigrant after his home in Eidfjord, Fossli Provincial Park protects a waterfall, a salmon creek, and the ghost of a homestead donated to British Columbia in 1974.

subject: Fota Wildlife Park
summary: A 100-acre Irish zoo where giraffes graze without fences, cheetahs breed for a European programme, and ring-tailed lemurs casually cross your path.

subject: Fourah Bay College
summary: Founded in 1827 on a Freetown hillside, Fourah Bay College is the oldest Western-style university in sub-Saharan Africa — the heart of the city once called the Athens of West Africa.

subject: Fowlmere Airfield
summary: A grass strip southwest of Cambridge that trained First World War cadets, scrambled Spitfires against the Luftwaffe, and now hosts aerobatics — a small airfield with a history far larger than its footprint.

subject: Foxdale Railway
summary: A small narrow gauge branch line built to carry lead ore out of the Manx hills, paired with a single locomotive named Caledonia and a single coach, both of which still run today.

subject: Foyle College
summary: A grammar school older than the city walls that surround its birthplace, Foyle College has educated Derry's young people since 1617, sending its alumni to govern India, settle Western Australia, and fight America's Civil War.

subject: Francois Peron National Park
summary: Where rust-red desert dunes crash straight into white sand and turquoise sea, a former sheep station has become a sanctuary in one of Australia's boldest experiments in bringing back the wild.

subject: Frans Kaisiepo Airport
summary: On a coral runway once carved by forced labor, a small Papuan airport became one of the strangest refueling stops in the history of transpacific aviation.

subject: Fratton Park
summary: Portsmouth's home since 1899 - the only professional English football ground on an island - a creaking, beloved, bomb-marked relic of Victorian football where Pompey beat Cardiff to win the FA Cup in 2008.

story.title: Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park

subject: Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park
summary: Four Civil War battlefields in one park - Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, the Wilderness, and Spotsylvania - protecting more than 8,000 acres where roughly 100,000 men were killed or wounded in eighteen months.

subject: Freedom Monument Sculpture Park
