summary: A 17-acre park on the Alabama River where the Equal Justice Initiative inscribed 122,000 surnames that formerly enslaved people chose for themselves - on a wall 43 feet tall and 155 feet long, in the city where those people were once sold.

subject: Freedom Park
summary: On a Pretoria hilltop, a wall nearly 700 meters long carries the names of the dead from eight conflicts, a national memorial built to remember everyone South Africa lost on the road to democracy.

subject: Freedom Park (Lagos)
summary: Built on the site of a colonial prison where Nigeria's independence heroes were once locked up, Freedom Park transformed a place of confinement into a public space for culture, art, and remembrance.

subject: Freeway Park
summary: A brutalist garden planted on top of an interstate highway, Seattle's Freeway Park turned one of America's ugliest urban scars into a site on the National Register of Historic Places.

story.title: Fresno State: Where Students Make Wine and Horses Live on Campus

subject: Fresno State
summary: A university born as a teacher-training school in 1911 that grew into a 25,000-student campus with its own vineyards, a commercial winery, an equestrian team that stables horses on the grounds, and an alumni roster that includes an astronaut lost on Columbia.

subject: Freycinet National Park
summary: Pink granite peaks, one of the world's most photographed beaches, and a perfect crescent of white sand that owes its lovely name to a grim past.

subject: Friday Harbor
summary: The laid-back capital of San Juan Island where ferries sweep in like clockwork and seaplanes splash down in waters patrolled by orcas.

subject: Friday Harbor Laboratories
summary: The University of Washington marine station where a jellyfish from these waters gave up the green fluorescent protein - and, eventually, a Nobel Prize.

story.title: From Radio Towers to Tribal College: D-Q University

subject: From Radio Towers to Tribal College
summary: Founded in 1971 on a decommissioned Army radio station in Yolo County, D-Q University became one of the first tribal colleges in the United States and the only one in California, before losing its accreditation in 2005.

subject: Fundy National Park
summary: Where the world's highest tides twice daily expose and then swallow an entire ocean floor, Fundy National Park protects 207 square kilometers of rugged coastline, highland forest, and more than 25 waterfalls.

subject: Furman University
summary: South Carolina's oldest private college, founded in 1826 and named for a Baptist pastor who owned slaves, is now a secular liberal arts university with one of the most beautiful campuses in America and a Nobel laureate among its physics graduates.

subject: Furna Feia National Park
summary: Brazil's first national park in Rio Grande do Norte, protecting more than 200 limestone caves and 11 troglobite species previously unknown to science.

story.title: Furnas do Bom Jesus State Park

subject: Furnas do Bom Jesus State Park
summary: A canyon cut into the northeastern edge of São Paulo state, where cerrado and Atlantic Forest meet and coffee country is slowly turning back into wilderness.

subject: Färnebofjärden National Park
summary: A Swedish national park where the Dalälven River spreads across ancient glacial ridges, creating a labyrinth of 200 islands where north and south meet in biological collision.

subject: Galatasaray University
summary: A Turkish university founded by treaty with France in a Bosphorus palace originally built for an Ottoman sultan's brother.

subject: Galathea National Park
summary: A 110-square-kilometer rainforest on Great Nicobar Island -- named for a Danish survey ship, home to coconut crabs and nesting leatherback turtles, and now threatened by a $9 billion development plan.

subject: Gallaudet University
summary: The world's only university designed entirely for deaf and hard-of-hearing students, federally chartered in 1864 by Abraham Lincoln.

subject: Galle Harbour
summary: A natural harbor that connected Sri Lanka to the ancient trading world for two millennia, now home to an underwater museum and the ghosts of Dutch East India Company shipwrecks.

subject: Galway to Clifden Railway
summary: A 48.5-mile single-track line through Connemara built as Famine-era public works in the 1890s, ran direct dining-car expresses from Dublin to Clifden by 1903, and closed in 1935; its bridge was sold to a German scrap company for £10.

subject: Gambir railway station
summary: Jakarta's Gambir Station has carried passengers for over 150 years under three different names and three different nations, its architecture shifting from Dutch neoclassical to Art Deco to a modern elevated terminal with a Javanese joglo silhouette.

subject: Gamble Plantation Historic State Park
summary: The last surviving plantation house on Florida's Gulf Coast stands with two-foot-thick tabby walls in Ellenton, a monument to the sugar empire that enslaved hundreds and the Confederate fugitive who hid there as the war collapsed around him.

subject: Ganjali Khan Complex
summary: A Safavid-era urban masterpiece in the heart of Kerman where a single governor built a square, bathhouse, caravanserai, mint, mosque, and bazaar that still define the city's old quarter four centuries later.

subject: Garamba National Park
summary: One of Africa's oldest parks, on the Congo-South Sudan border, where rangers have died defending elephants and where the northern white rhino made its last wild stand.

subject: Garda Síochána College
summary: Every member of Ireland's national police force passes through one small Tipperary town to become a Garda. The college that trains them is housed in a Victorian-era barracks that has, in turn, held German POWs, IRA volunteers, and the future of Irish policing.

subject: Garden District, New Orleans
summary: Built by wealthy Americans who refused to live alongside Creoles in the French Quarter, New Orleans' Garden District became one of the South's most extravagant neighborhoods -- and an unlikely literary pilgrimage site.

subject: Garden Museum
summary: In a deconsecrated medieval church beside Lambeth Palace, Britain's only garden museum grew up around a single rediscovered tomb.

subject: Garden Route
summary: A 170-kilometer ribbon of coast between the Outeniqua Mountains and the Indian Ocean, the Garden Route is where South Africa compresses ancient forests, lagoons, and human history stretching back 170,000 years into one scenic corridor.

subject: Garden Route National Park
summary: A national park stitched together from three predecessor reserves, protecting 1,210 square kilometers of indigenous forest, dramatic coastline, and the legendary Otter Trail.

subject: Garden Tomb
summary: An ancient rock-cut tomb in a garden outside Jerusalem's Old City walls draws hundreds of thousands of Protestant pilgrims each year to what some believe is the authentic site of Jesus's burial and resurrection.

subject: Garden of Eden, Lucas Kansas
summary: The Kansas backyard filled with bizarre concrete sculptures by a retired Civil War veteran - featuring Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, and elaborate anti-capitalist tableaux, all surrounding his mausoleum where his embalmed body remains on display.

subject: Garden of Serenity
summary: A quiet villa in Tianjin's Japanese concession became the last private refuge of China's final emperor, who named it Jingyuan -- the Garden of Serenity -- during a brief, uneasy exile before his fate was decided for him.

subject: Garden of Surging Waves
summary: A Chinese garden in downtown Astoria, Oregon, honors the immigrant workers who built the canneries, railroads, and jetties that shaped the Columbia River port -- and who were then pushed out by exclusion laws.

subject: Garden of the Gods
summary: The geology lesson that looks like art - where 300-million-year-old red sandstone tilts at 90 degrees against Pikes Peak's backdrop, creating formations so spectacular that the founders deeded it forever free to the public.

subject: Garden of the Gods
summary: Three hundred million years of geology standing on end - where ancient red sandstone fins rise from the Colorado prairie like the ruins of some colossal temple, free to visit every day of the year since 1909.

story.title: Garden of the Gods: Illinois's Hidden Rock Garden

subject: Garden of the Gods
summary: The southern Illinois wilderness that doesn't look like Illinois - sandstone formations, slot canyons, and rock gardens that would be famous in Utah but remain surprisingly unknown in a state most people picture as flat farmland.

story.title: Gardens at 30,000 Feet: Soekarno-Hatta International Airport

subject: Gardens at 30,000 Feet
summary: Jakarta's colossal gateway handles over 54 million passengers a year through terminals where tropical gardens grow between boarding gates and Javanese temple motifs adorn the railings -- an airport designed not merely for transit, but as a statement of Indonesian identity.

subject: Gardens of Monticello
summary: Jefferson's hilltop laboratory in living things, where a president experimented with hundreds of vegetables and exotic seeds gathered from across the world.

subject: Gardens of Versailles
summary: Covering 800 hectares west of the palace, the Gardens of Versailles are Andre Le Notre's masterpiece of French formal design, where the Sun King bent water, stone, and nature itself to serve as metaphors for absolute power.

subject: Gardner-Webb University
summary: A Baptist high school chartered in 1905 above the boiling springs of a small Cleveland County town, now a Division I university with 3,000 students, a granite arch, and Sara McMann's Olympic silver medal in the trophy case.

subject: Garibaldi Provincial Park
summary: Where volcanic peaks pierce glacier-carved valleys and turquoise lakes reflect mountains named for an Italian revolutionary, British Columbia's alpine wilderness delivers raw beauty that rivals any on Earth.

subject: Garuda Wisnu Kencana Cultural Park
summary: A 60-hectare cultural park on Bali's limestone cliffs houses Indonesia's tallest statue, hosts G20 dinners and Iron Maiden concerts, and tells the Hindu myth of a bird who traded servitude for his mother's freedom.

subject: Gas Works Park
summary: The sole remaining coal gasification plant in the United States stands not behind a fence but inside a public park, its rusting towers and machinery preserved as industrial archaeology on a promontory jutting into Seattle's Lake Union.

subject: Gashaka Gumti National Park
summary: Nigeria's largest national park straddles two worlds -- flat savanna woodlands in the north and rugged montane rainforest in the south -- harboring 103 mammal species and the ruins of a German colonial fort atop Gashaka Hill.

subject: Gateway Arch National Park
summary: America's smallest national park holds the nation's tallest monument and the courthouse where the Dred Scott case began, marking the spot where westward expansion truly started.

subject: Gatineau Park
summary: A federal park just minutes from Ottawa that holds the Prime Minister's country retreat, a former PM's estate full of stone ruins, a bright green meromictic lake, and trees nearly 600 years old -- yet it remains the only federal park in Canada without national park protection.

subject: General San Martín Park
summary: A 393-hectare green oasis carved out of the desert after disease and earthquake, where a French landscape architect made trees grow in a place that had almost none.

subject: Gent-Sint-Pieters railway station
summary: The Belle Epoque station that opened weeks before a World's Fair and has been under renovation, on and off, ever since.

subject: Georgetown Loop Railroad
summary: A 19th-century engineering marvel designed to connect silver mines that became, instead, one of Colorado's first tourist attractions.

subject: Georgetown University
summary: The oldest Catholic university in the United States, founded the year George Washington was inaugurated, still teaching foreign service from a hill above the Potomac.

subject: Georgia State Railroad Museum
summary: The most intact antebellum railroad repair complex in America, where an 1853 roundhouse still turns locomotives on its original turntable in the heart of Savannah.

subject: Gettysburg
summary: The Pennsylvania field where 50,000 casualties in three days created America's bloodiest battle and its most persistent ghost stories - where visitors still report phantom soldiers, strange lights, and the unmistakable sounds of battle.

subject: Gettysburg Battlefield
summary: The high water mark of the Confederacy - where 165,000 men fought for three days in 1863, where Pickett's Charge failed across a mile of open ground, and where Lincoln defined what the war meant.

subject: Gezi Park
summary: A small green space near Taksim Square whose planned demolition in 2013 set off weeks of nationwide demonstrations that became one of modern Turkey's most significant episodes of public protest.

subject: Ghent University
summary: Founded by a Dutch king in 1817 to remake the southern provinces, fought over for its language across two world wars, Ghent University now educates more than 44,000 students and remembers where Kekule unraveled benzene.

subject: Ghibli Park
summary: A theme park in Nagakute, Japan, where the animated worlds of Studio Ghibli come to life without a single roller coaster -- just forests, handcrafted buildings, and the quiet magic of Miyazaki's imagination.

subject: Giant's Causeway and Bushmills Railway
summary: A two-mile narrow-gauge revival running across dunes and a golf course - the resurrected ghost of a pioneering electric tramway that ran this coast for sixty-six years until 1949.

subject: Gibraltar Range National Park
summary: A World Heritage corner of the Gondwana Rainforests where granite has weathered into towers and crags, spring sets the heath ablaze with wildflowers, and one of the last rufous scrub-birds still calls.

subject: Gig Harbor
summary: A postcard-perfect harbor town where Scandinavian fishing heritage meets Mount Rainier views and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge delivers visitors to a hidden corner of Puget Sound.

subject: Gilf Kebir National Park
summary: A sandstone plateau the size of a small nation rises from the emptiest corner of the Sahara, hiding caves painted with thousands of figures from a time when this desert held water.

subject: Gir National Park
summary: The last refuge of the Asiatic lion, Gujarat's Gir National Park shelters a population that was once down to a dozen individuals in a landscape of dry teak forest threaded by seven perennial rivers.

subject: Girton College, Cambridge
summary: Founded in 1869 as Cambridge's first women's college — deliberately placed away from the city to avoid controversy — Girton forced the question of whether women belonged at Britain's greatest universities, and answered it definitively.

subject: Giza pyramid complex
summary: The only surviving Wonder of the Ancient World anchors a necropolis where three pharaohs of the Fourth Dynasty built their eternal monuments at the edge of the Western Desert.

subject: Glacier Bay National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where glaciers have retreated 65 miles in two centuries, revealing a living laboratory of ecosystem rebirth.

story.title: Glacier National Park: The Crown of the Continent

subject: Glacier National Park
summary: The Montana park where Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide through scenery that caused it to be called 'the Crown of the Continent' - where glaciers that named the park are melting away, where grizzlies still roam, and where wilderness remains genuinely wild.

story.title: Glacier National Park: Racing to See the Ice Before It Melts

subject: Glacier National Park
summary: The Montana park where 150 glaciers have become 26 and falling - where Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide, where grizzly bears still roam, and where the park's namesake ice may disappear within a generation.

subject: Glacier National Park
summary: Where billion-year-old rock meets ancient ice - Montana's crown of the continent where Going-to-the-Sun Road carves through some of the most dramatic alpine scenery in North America.

subject: Glamorganshire Canal
summary: A twenty-five-mile waterway with fifty locks that carried Welsh iron to the world for a hundred years, then quietly drained away.

subject: Glasgow Airport
summary: Scotland's second-busiest airport, built on a wartime airfield at Abbotsinch, served eight million passengers in 2024 and remains the gateway to the city eight nautical miles east.

subject: Glasgow Prestwick Airport
summary: An airport that the Scottish Government once bought for one pound, that Elvis Presley once briefly stood on, and that the Robert Burns World Federation once tried to rename.

subject: Glasnevin Cemetery
summary: Ireland's national cemetery, founded in 1832 so that Catholics could bury their dead with dignity, holds more than 1.5 million burials including the graves of Daniel O'Connell, Michael Collins, and nearly every major figure in Irish independence.

subject: Glastonbury Cemetery
summary: A Victorian cemetery on Edmund Hill outside Glastonbury, twice nearly demolished, where the occultist Dion Fortune lies among the green burials.

subject: Glendalough State Park
summary: Named after an Irish monastery, this Minnesota state park was once a private game farm where presidents fished and newspaper barons entertained -- donated on Earth Day 1990 and now a haven of prairie lakes, yurts, and quiet solitude.

subject: Glenfinnan Railway Station
summary: A small concrete chalet-style railway station that opened in 1901, sits at the foot of the curving Glenfinnan Viaduct, and became globally famous when the Hogwarts Express crossed its bridge.

subject: Glenmore Forest Park
summary: A surviving fragment of the ancient Caledonian Forest where Norwegian commandos once trained for sabotage missions, Scottish crossbills sing in the canopy, and a small green lochan is said to be the laundry of fairies.

subject: Glenveagh National Park
summary: In wild Donegal, a U-shaped glacial valley holds a mock-medieval castle built by the man who evicted 244 tenants in two days, surrounded by gardens where golden eagles -- hunted to extinction in Ireland by 1912 -- are slowly returning.

subject: Glenville State University
summary: A 150-year-old teachers' school turned regional university in central West Virginia, whose Lady Pioneers won the 2022 NCAA Division II women's basketball championship - and whose more eccentric alumni include the man who coined the term 'men in black.'

subject: Glenwood Cemetery (Houston, Texas)
summary: Houston's 'River Oaks of the dead,' where Republic of Texas presidents, oil barons, and pioneering heart surgeons rest beneath ancient hardwoods on the bluffs above Buffalo Bayou.

subject: Glorieta Pass Battlefield
summary: The site where the Civil War's western ambitions died in a mountain pass, when Union soldiers destroyed a Confederate supply train and ended the South's dream of controlling the American West.

subject: Goblin Valley State Park
summary: Thousands of eerie sandstone hoodoos -- locally called goblins -- populate a remote Utah valley so otherworldly it doubled as an alien planet in Galaxy Quest.

subject: Gola Rainforest National Park
summary: Sierra Leone's largest surviving rainforest, home to pygmy hippos, western chimpanzees, and over 600 butterfly species, was logged for decades before becoming the country's second national park and its first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Golden Ears Provincial Park
summary: With 610,000 annual visitors drawn to its waterfalls, glaciers, and the twin peaks that gave it its name, Golden Ears ranks among British Columbia's most beloved provincial parks.

subject: Golden Gardens Park
summary: A Ballard beach park where bald eagles share the sky with kitesurfers, bonfires burn on summer evenings, and the Olympic Mountains fill the western horizon across Puget Sound.

subject: Golden Gate Cemetery (San Francisco)
summary: A 200-acre potter's field with 29,000 burials that was paved over to become Lincoln Park and the Legion of Honor museum -- San Francisco's dead literally beneath its art.

subject: Golden Gate Highlands National Park
summary: Sandstone cliffs that glow gold at sunset hide the oldest dinosaur embryos ever found, 220-million-year-old fossils nested in a landscape where the Free State's only national park protects beauty first and wildlife second.

subject: Golden Gate National Cemetery
summary: A national cemetery in San Bruno often confused with the Presidio's burial ground, where rows of white headstones honor veterans from the Civil War to the War on Terror.

subject: Golden Gate Park
summary: A 1,017-acre urban park carved from sand dunes, stretching from the Haight to the Pacific, hosting 24 million visitors annually and containing a museum, a Japanese garden, a herd of bison, and a windmill.

subject: Golden Spike National Historical Park
summary: The remote Utah summit where two railroads met on May 10, 1869, completing the first transcontinental railroad and changing America forever.

subject: Goldstream Provincial Park
summary: A small park twenty minutes from downtown Victoria where thousands of salmon return each November to spawn and die, feeding eagles and some of the largest western red cedars in British Columbia.

subject: Golra Sharif Railway Museum
summary: A Victorian-era railway junction turned living museum, Golra Sharif preserves over 150 years of subcontinental rail heritage at the foot of the Margalla Hills.

subject: Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge
summary: Founded in 1348 as the Black Death arrived in England, refounded in 1557 by a physician-scholar who barred Welshmen and the disabled from admission, and now home to fifteen Nobel laureates and a building named for Stephen Hawking — Gonville and Caius is Cambridge in miniature.

subject: Goodison Park
summary: The Grand Old Lady of English football - England's first purpose-built football ground, home to Everton from 1892 to 2025, and from 2025 the largest dedicated women's football stadium in the country.

subject: Gooseberry Falls State Park
summary: Where the Gooseberry River drops over three tiers of billion-year-old lava flows and spills into Lake Superior, a state park preserves CCC-built stone shelters, 18 miles of trails, and a beach where you can still find Lake Superior agates tumbling in the surf.

subject: Gorongosa National Park
summary: Once home to the densest wildlife populations in Africa, Gorongosa National Park lost ninety percent of its large mammals to civil war -- and is now the site of one of the continent's most ambitious ecological restoration projects.

subject: Gosforth Park
summary: A coal-baron's 18th-century pleasure ground that became Newcastle Racecourse - and in 2020 hosted the UK's first socially-distanced concert venue.

subject: Gothenburg Botanical Garden
summary: One of Europe's largest botanical gardens, where a tree extinct in the wild survives and white anemones carpet the spring woodlands.

subject: Gouraya National Park
summary: A UNESCO biosphere reserve on the Mediterranean coast of Algeria where Barbary macaques swing through ancient forests above dramatic cliffs, and 1,655 Berber villagers still live within the park boundaries.

subject: Gowanus Canal
summary: Brooklyn's 1.8-mile canal went from oyster beds to Superfund site -- a waterway so polluted that a minke whale that wandered in died, and a swimmer who braved it called it 'mud, poo, detergent, oil and gasoline.'

subject: Grampians National Park
summary: Victoria's great sandstone range, Gariwerd to its traditional owners, holding the richest concentration of Aboriginal rock art in the south-east of the continent.

subject: Grand Bahama Aux AF Airport
summary: A Cold War missile tracking station on Grand Bahama Island that supported Mercury, Gemini, Apollo, and the Space Shuttle before being handed back to the Bahamas and left to decay.

subject: Grand Canal (Ireland)
summary: 131 kilometres of still water from Dublin to the Shannon, built over half a century to connect cities that mostly preferred not to share, and barely saved from being paved over for a dual-carriageway.

subject: Grand Canal (Venice)
summary: Venice's main artery traces a reverse S through the city, lined with 170 palazzos that chronicle five centuries of merchant ambition and architectural rivalry.

subject: Grand Central Airport (California)
summary: A Glendale airfield where Charles Lindbergh flew the first transcontinental passenger service, Amelia Earhart bought her first plane, Howard Hughes built his record-setting H-1 Racer, and Walt Disney eventually moved in — one of the most storied patches of tarmac in American aviation history.

subject: Grand Teton National Park
summary: Where the Rockies make their most dramatic entrance, rising without foothills from the valley floor in a wall of granite and ice.

subject: Grand Teton National Park
summary: Home to some of the oldest rocks in any American national park and the youngest mountain range in the Rockies, where 2.7-billion-year-old granite towers above a valley still settling into its fault.

subject: Grande Sertão Veredas National Park
summary: A 230,000-hectare Brazilian national park whose founding decree lists, among its legal objectives, the preservation of a landscape described in a novel.

story.title: The Granite Railway: America's First Commercial Railroad

subject: Granite Railway
summary: Built in 1826 to haul stone for the Bunker Hill Monument, the Granite Railway was the first chartered commercial railroad in the United States -- a four-mile line where horses pulled six-ton loads on iron-plated wooden rails, and where a tourist's fatal accident became one of the nation's first railway disasters.

subject: Grantham Canal
summary: A 33-mile Georgian canal that carried coal to Grantham from 1797, was strangled by the railways, and is now being patiently restored by volunteers, lock by lock.

subject: Grasslands National Park
summary: Canada's only protected expanse of mixed-grass prairie, where dinosaur fossils, bison herds, and the refuge of Sitting Bull all share one ancient landscape.

subject: Graveyard of the Pacific
summary: More than 2,000 ships have been lost along a treacherous stretch of Pacific Northwest coastline from Oregon's Tillamook Bay to the northern tip of Vancouver Island -- a graveyard of shifting sandbars, tidal rips, and fog that has claimed vessels and lives for over two centuries.

subject: Grays Harbor
summary: An estuarine bay on Washington's southwest coast where the ice age, the timber industry, and labor radicalism left deep marks on a landscape of mudflats, mill towns, and shifting sandbars.

subject: Grays Harbor Historical Seaport Authority
summary: A small Washington harbor town built a full-scale replica of an 18th-century tall ship and launched a maritime heritage movement that transformed its abandoned industrial waterfront.

subject: Grays Harbor National Wildlife Refuge
summary: A sliver of estuary at the mouth of the Chehalis River that punches far above its weight, hosting half of Grays Harbor's staging shorebirds on just two percent of its intertidal habitat.

subject: Great Australian Bight Marine Park
summary: A vast marine sanctuary off the Nullarbor coast, where southern right whales come to give birth, sea lions haul out on hidden ledges, and a nation once fought off the oil rigs.

story.title: Great Australian Bight Marine Park Whale Sanctuary

subject: Great Australian Bight Marine Park Whale Sanctuary
summary: A narrow strip of protected sea below the Bunda Cliffs, set aside in 1995 to guard the most important nursery on Earth for the southern right whale.

subject: Great Court, Trinity College, Cambridge
summary: The largest enclosed courtyard in Europe, Great Court is also home to one of academia's most absurd annual challenges: running 339 metres before a clock finishes striking noon.

subject: Great Laxey Mine Railway
summary: A pair of impossibly narrow Victorian steam engines hauled lead ore out of a 2,200-foot mine until 1929; today their replicas still run through the Isle of Man's last working railway tunnel.

subject: Great Northern Railway (Mt Isa line)
summary: The 977-kilometre iron thread that hauls Mount Isa's silver, lead, and copper down to the sea at Townsville, built in painstaking stages over half a century to chase one mineral strike after another.

subject: Great Sand Dunes National Park
summary: North America's tallest dunes rise 750 feet against the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in Colorado's San Luis Valley, a surreal desert at 8,200 feet.

subject: Great Seal State Park
summary: The forested Ross County ridges that became the literal model for the Ohio state seal - now an 1,682-acre park preserving the view that early statehood made official.

story.title: Great Smoky Mountains: The Park That Gets More Visitors Than Anywhere

subject: Great Smoky Mountains
summary: The Tennessee-North Carolina park that leads America in visitors - over 12 million annually - where Cherokee heritage meets Appalachian culture, where synchronous fireflies put on June light shows, and where the blue haze that gives the mountains their name comes from the forest itself.

subject: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
summary: The most visited national park in the United States sprawls across the ancient Appalachian ridgeline, where Cherokee named the blue haze that clings to peaks older than the Himalayas.

subject: Great Valley Grasslands State Park
summary: One of the last fragments of native grassland in California's Central Valley, where seasonal flooding still conjures clouds of sandhill cranes and shelters species that have vanished from nearly everywhere else in the San Joaquin watershed.

story.title: The Red Snake: Iran's Forgotten Great Wall

subject: Great Wall of Gorgan
summary: A 195-kilometer defensive wall built by the Sasanian Empire across northeastern Iran - the third longest wall ever constructed, once garrisoned by up to 36,000 soldiers, now largely buried beneath farmland and known to archaeologists as the Red Snake.

subject: Great Wall of Los Angeles
summary: A half-mile mural on the concrete banks of Tujunga Wash in the San Fernando Valley, painted beginning in 1978 by over 400 community youth under artist Judith Baca — one of the longest murals in the world and an alternative history of California told through the eyes of women and minorities.

subject: Great Wall of Qi
summary: China's oldest existing great wall predates its famous northern cousin by centuries, stretching from Jinan across Shandong's mountain ridges to the Yellow Sea at Qingdao.

story.title: Great Western Railway in West Wales

subject: Great Western Railway in West Wales
summary: Brunel's broad-gauge South Wales Railway opened from Swansea to Neyland in 1852, ran on seven-foot track for twenty years, and re-laid the entire West Wales network in a single fortnight in 1872.

subject: Greater Vancouver Zoo
summary: It began in 1970 with one llama in a Fraser Valley field, and has spent the half-century since arguing - sometimes with itself - about what a zoo is for.

story.title: Green Island White Terror Memorial Park

subject: Green Island White Terror Memorial Park
summary: Built on the site where Taiwan imprisoned its political dissidents for nearly four decades, this 32-hectare memorial park preserves a hexagonal prison, a human rights monument, and the memory of those who fought for democracy.

subject: Green Park Estate, Jamaica
summary: A Jamaican sugar plantation whose 1,315 acres and 800 enslaved people built fortunes for absentee English owners, then crumbled into ruins that one eccentric American tried - and failed - to save.

subject: Green Timbers Urban Forest Park
summary: British Columbia's first reforestation plantation went into the ground here in 1930, and the 560-acre forest that grew from it survives inside Surrey only because its neighbours voted, twice, to keep it.

story.title: Green-Wood Cemetery: Brooklyn's City of the Dead

subject: Green-Wood Cemetery
summary: The Victorian cemetery that invented the American way of death - where half a million people are buried in 478 acres of hills and dales that New Yorkers once visited for pleasure, making it the second most popular tourist attraction after Niagara Falls.

subject: Green-Wood Cemetery
summary: The Brooklyn cemetery that was New York's top tourist attraction before Central Park existed - where 600,000 people are buried including Boss Tweed, Leonard Bernstein, and Jean-Michel Basquiat, and wild monk parakeets nest in the Gothic gates.

subject: Greenbank Garden
summary: A 2.5-acre walled garden surrounding a 1763 Georgian house whose construction was paid for, in part, by the transatlantic slave trade - now a National Trust for Scotland property six miles from central Glasgow.

subject: Greenbo Lake State Resort Park
summary: A 3,600-acre park born from a 1948 fishing trip, with a fieldstone lodge named for poet Jesse Stuart and a lake that has produced two state-record largemouth bass.

subject: Greenbrier Valley Airport
summary: A small West Virginia airport with a runway long enough for jets, surviving on subsidized service and stubborn local demand for connections to the resort just down the road.

subject: Greenwich Park
summary: Where east meets west at zero degrees longitude, a hilltop park has shaped how the world keeps time and draws its maps.

subject: Greenwood Gardens
summary: A hidden Italianate jewel in Short Hills, New Jersey, where a real estate auctioneer's dream estate became a sanctuary of ironwork, stone terraces, and rare artistic beauty.

subject: Griffith Park
summary: At 4,310 acres, Griffith Park is the largest municipal park with urban wilderness in the United States — a donated rancho turned urban forest containing the Griffith Observatory, the Los Angeles Zoo, the Hollywood Sign, and more film location days than any other site in Los Angeles.

subject: Groesbeek Canadian War Cemetery
summary: Two thousand three hundred thirty-eight Canadian soldiers rest in Dutch soil here, brought back across an international border so they would not have to sleep in Germany.

subject: Groningen Airport Eelde
summary: A small regional field in Drenthe that, for seventy years, trained the pilots who fly the Netherlands.

subject: Groudle Glen Railway
summary: A Victorian narrow-gauge railway built in 1896 to carry holidaymakers to a clifftop zoo of sea lions and polar bears, restored by volunteers after twenty years of silent undergrowth.

story.title: Grounds of the University of Virginia

subject: Grounds of the University of Virginia
summary: Jefferson's Academical Village, a UNESCO-listed campus laid out like a sentence in brick and column, where students still sleep in rooms his hand drew.

story.title: Gruta da Lagoa Azul State Park

subject: Gruta da Lagoa Azul State Park
summary: A limestone chamber in Mato Grosso holds a pool of impossibly blue water — and has been locked shut for more than two decades because visitors loved it nearly to death.

subject: Grão Mogol State Park
summary: A dry-country park on the northern Espinhaço where streams run year-round through rock gardens, and a stone road laid by enslaved workers still climbs out of the canyon.

subject: Guadalupe Mountains National Park
summary: Rising abruptly from the Chihuahuan Desert floor, the Guadalupe Mountains contain Texas's highest peak and the fossilized remains of an ancient Permian reef - a 250-million-year-old seabed now thrust 8,000 feet into the sky.

subject: Guadeloupe National Park
summary: A UNESCO biosphere reserve on Guadeloupe's volcanic Basse-Terre island where tropical rainforest climbs from mangrove coast to the steaming summit of La Soufriere, the highest peak in the Lesser Antilles.

subject: Guajará-Mirim State Park
summary: A 216,000-hectare state park in Rondônia where an illegal road built by loggers was later legalized by the federal government, splitting the park and severing an ecological corridor.

subject: Guangzhou Martyrs' Memorial Garden
summary: A garden of remembrance in central Guangzhou honoring the thousands of people killed in the suppression of the 1927 Guangzhou Uprising — a place where history is held quietly in stone and greenery.

subject: Guernsey Railway
summary: A three-mile steam tramway that became an electric tram, carried over a million passengers a year at its peak, and was scrapped in 1934 - just six years before the Germans would have used the rails.

subject: Guilford Courthouse National Military Park
summary: A British general won the battle here on March 15, 1781 - and lost his army doing it, setting Cornwallis on the road to Yorktown.

subject: Gulf Islands National Park Reserve
summary: A scattered archipelago of protected islands between Vancouver Island and the mainland, where orcas hunt in tidal rapids, kayakers camp on beaches accessible only by water, and a Mediterranean climate supports prickly pear cactus in Canadian waters.

subject: Gum Wall
summary: What started as a nuisance outside a Seattle improv theater became one of the city's most photographed landmarks: a brick wall coated in millions of pieces of chewed gum beneath Pike Place Market.

subject: Gundabooka National Park
summary: Around the rugged red bulk of Mount Gunderbooka, an outback park guards a sacred mountain and a rock overhang where Ngemba and Paakantyi people painted dancers, animals and creation stories onto stone.

subject: Guy Fawkes River National Park
summary: A vast, gorge-cut wilderness on the edge of the New England Tablelands, home to a famous waterfall, deeply incised river valleys, and the descendants of Australia's wartime cavalry horses.

subject: Gwili Railway
summary: Welsh volunteers spent fifty years rebuilding eight miles of a vanished Beeching line, and now steam trains run again up the Gwili Valley north of Carmarthen.

subject: Gwollu Defence Wall
summary: A mud-brick wall built by the Sissala people in Ghana's Upper West Region stands as one of the world's few surviving monuments to organized resistance against the slave trade.

subject: Gyda National Park
summary: The northernmost national park in Western Siberia, where snow covers the ground for 240 days a year, polar bears share the tundra with genetically distinct reindeer herds, and oil and gas pressure threatens one of the Arctic's most remote protected areas.

subject: Gypsy Hill Park
summary: A 200-acre Staunton park where a Civil War-era brass band has performed every Monday night since the 1850s and the duck pond doubles as the city's living room.

subject: Göztepe Park
summary: A spacious park on Istanbul's Asian shore that commemorates the Turkish Republic's 60th birthday, now home to tulip gardens, a natural pond, and a museum dedicated to the country's most beloved comedic actor.

subject: Gülhane Park
summary: Gülhane Park — the Rosehouse Park — was once the private outer garden of Topkapı Palace; in 1839 it became the birthplace of Ottoman reform, and in 1912 it opened to the public as Istanbul's oldest park.

subject: Hacklebarney State Park
summary: A 978-acre gorge park along the Black River in Morris County whose name might derive from Lenape words, an iron mine foreman's nickname, or a landowner named Barney Hackle.

subject: Hadrian's Wall
summary: Walking the 73 miles of Hadrian's Wall Path takes you from the urban banks of the Tyne to the wild crags of Northumberland and on to the Solway marshes -- a journey through England's most spectacular Roman landscape.

subject: Hadrian's Wall
summary: The Roman Empire's most ambitious frontier work in Britain: 73 miles of stone, turf, ditches, and forts built to control movement between the provinces and the unconquered north.

subject: Hadrian's Wall Path
summary: An 84-mile National Trail tracing the line of the Roman Empire's northern frontier, from the Tyne estuary to the Solway Firth.

subject: Hakusan National Park
summary: One of Japan's Three Holy Mountains shelters a national park where alpine flowers bear the mountain's name and four prefectures meet at a single sacred summit.

subject: Haleakalā National Park
summary: Maui's dormant volcano holds more endangered species than any other U.S. national park and a crater so vast it swallows clouds whole.

subject: Halki Theological School Gardens
summary: On a hilltop seminary closed for over fifty years, scholars rebuilt a Byzantine garden from 12th-century manuscripts — a living archive of faith, symbolism, and resilience on a disputed island in the Sea of Marmara.

subject: Hama-rikyū Gardens
summary: A 250,000-square-meter tidal garden at the mouth of the Sumida River where shoguns once kept an elephant from Vietnam, Ulysses Grant slept for a month, and Tokyo Bay still fills the moat twice a day.

subject: Hamm Railway Bridge
summary: The first solid bridge across the Rhine in Düsseldorf has been built three times, blown up once, and still carries trains where it always did.

subject: Hammerwood Park
summary: The first complete work of the architect who would design the United States Capitol - rescued from collapse in 1982 by a 20-year-old student, restored mostly with visitor entrance fees, and once owned by Led Zeppelin.

subject: Hampden Park
summary: Scotland's national football stadium held the world capacity record for nearly half a century and the European attendance record forever - 149,415 souls watching Scotland v England in 1937.

subject: Hampstead Cemetery
summary: A 26-acre Victorian cemetery in West Hampstead where an estimated 60,000 people are buried — including Joseph Lister, who discovered antiseptic treatment, and Marie Lloyd, who made the music halls sing.

subject: Hampton University
summary: The school where formerly enslaved people learned to read under an oak tree, where Booker T. Washington was a student, and where the Emancipation Proclamation was first read aloud in the Confederate South.

subject: Haneda Airport
summary: Tokyo's original airport, built on reclaimed land in 1931, seized by MacArthur in 1945, and now the fourth-busiest in the world -- with a history of tragedy, reinvention, and a famous photograph of a doomed BOAC 707 taxiing past smoldering wreckage.

subject: Hangar One (Moffett Federal Airfield)
summary: Covering eight acres and once housing the USS Macon airship, this colossal 1930s hangar is one of the world's largest freestanding structures -- now leased by Google.

subject: Hanging Rock State Park
summary: A North Carolina state park in the Sauratown Mountains where the Civilian Conservation Corps built a stone bathhouse on a private resort that the Depression killed.

subject: Hanko Naval Base
summary: Finland went to war rather than lease Hanko to the Soviet Union, lost, and leased it anyway — for twenty months.

subject: Hanze University of Applied Sciences
summary: A 1986 merger that swept up a 1798 art academy, named for a medieval trade league, now teaches 28,000 students in Groningen.

subject: Harbor Defenses of New York
summary: For over three centuries, a ring of forts, batteries, and minefields guarded New York Harbor from enemies who never arrived, making it the most heavily fortified harbor in the United States.

subject: Harbor of Refuge Light
summary: A white conical sentinel standing at the mouth of Delaware Bay, the Harbor of Refuge Light has endured hurricanes, ship strikes, and a century of Atlantic fury from its perch on a breakwater that Congress took 76 years to perfect.

subject: Harbour Island, Bahamas
summary: A tiny Bahamian island where crushed shells of microscopic organisms paint three miles of beach an unmistakable shade of pink.

subject: Hardangervidda National Park
summary: Europe's largest mountain plateau, where wild reindeer herds have drawn hunters for nearly 8,000 years and ancient trails still link Norway's fjord coast to its eastern valleys.

subject: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park
summary: Where two rivers meet, three states touch, and John Brown lit the fuse of the Civil War - 4,000 acres of armory, abolition, and aftermath at the head of the Shenandoah.

subject: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad
summary: The Maryland landscape where Harriet Tubman was born enslaved and later returned 13 times to free 70 others - now a national historical park preserving the waterways, forests, and safe houses of the Underground Railroad.

subject: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad
summary: Moses of her people - where a five-foot-tall woman who escaped slavery returned nineteen times to lead seventy people to freedom through the Eastern Shore marshes she knew better than any pursuer ever could.

story.title: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park

subject: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park
summary: The first national park honoring a Black woman in America, preserving the same Dorchester County marshlands that Harriet Tubman navigated to carry herself and some seventy others from slavery to freedom.

story.title: Harvey Airfield: A Family Airport on the Floodplain

subject: Harvey Airfield
summary: A privately owned, public-use airport in Snohomish, Washington, founded by the Harvey family in 1944 on land that first hosted barnstormers in 1911 - still family-run after eight decades, despite floods, loss, and the encroachment of suburbia.

subject: Haskell Indian Nations University
summary: Founded in 1884 as a federal boarding school with 22 Native American children, Haskell has survived the darkest chapters of American Indian education policy to become a tuition-free tribal university in Lawrence, Kansas, with 12 buildings designated as National Historic Landmarks.

subject: Hastings Park
summary: Granted in 1888 to be kept forever as wilderness, Vancouver's Hastings Park became a racetrack, a fairground, a roller coaster — and in 1942, a holding place for Japanese Canadian families.

subject: Hatley Park National Historic Site
summary: A coal baron's 40-room castle near Victoria that Canada bought in 1940 as a bolt-hole for King George VI, spent half a century as a naval college, and now serves as a university campus and Hollywood's favourite stand-in for Professor Xavier's school.

subject: Hautes-Gorges-de-la-Rivière-Malbaie National Park
summary: Inside a 450-million-year-old meteorite crater in Quebec's Charlevoix region, the Malbaie River has carved some of the tallest rock faces east of the Rockies into the bones of the Canadian Shield.

subject: Hawaii Consolidated Railway
summary: A standard-gauge railroad that served the Big Island's sugarcane coast from 1899 until a 1946 tsunami destroyed the line, leaving behind five steel trestle bridges still standing along the Belt Road.

subject: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park
summary: A place where the Earth is still being born, Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park encompasses two of the world's most remarkable volcanoes and a landscape in constant transformation.

subject: Hawks Nest State Park
summary: A 370-acre state park on the rim of the New River Gorge, sitting directly above the tunnel that became one of the worst industrial disasters in American history.

subject: Haydarpaşa Cemetery
summary: On a hillside on Istanbul's Asian shore, a quiet Commonwealth cemetery holds the graves of British and colonial soldiers who died far from home — most of them not in battle, but of cholera in a military hospital where Florence Nightingale first transformed nursing.

subject: Haydarpaşa Railway Station
summary: For 140 years, Haydarpaşa station was the gate to Asia — the grand European-style terminus where trains left Istanbul bound for Baghdad, Tehran, and Kars — and since 2012 it has stood in a long, uncertain silence, awaiting a future it cannot yet see.

subject: Hazarganji-Chiltan National Park
summary: A 325,000-acre national park in Balochistan whose name means 'of a thousand treasures,' protecting the rare Chiltan ibex on mountain passes once used by Greco-Bactrians, Mongols, and Scythians.

subject: Heart of Dixie Railroad Museum
summary: A heritage railroad museum in Calera, Alabama, where visitors can ride diesel excursion trains over former Louisville and Nashville Railroad track -- and where a 1953 fireless locomotive once ran on nothing but borrowed steam.

subject: Heathrow Airport
summary: Europe's busiest airport, built in 1946 on what had been a small Middlesex airfield, where Concorde used to land and where eighty-three million people still pass through in a year.

subject: Heber Valley Railroad
summary: A heritage railroad that carried the Olympic torch in 2002 after citizens petitioned the state to save it from bankruptcy.

subject: Heinsberg-Lindern Railway
summary: The little branch line that survived demolition, abandonment, and a thirty-three year hiatus to become a lifeline for a district Germany had nearly forgotten.

subject: Hell Hole Gorge National Park
summary: A rugged sandstone gorge in remote southwest Queensland, holding rare permanent water in a dry land - and the memory of a violent chapter of the frontier.

subject: Hell's Gate National Park
summary: One of the few national parks in Kenya where you can walk and cycle among wildlife, Hell's Gate combines towering volcanic cliffs, geothermal steam vents, and flash-flood-carved gorges just 90 kilometers from Nairobi.

subject: Hellingly Hospital Railway
summary: A private electric railway that ran for fifty-six years between a Sussex village station and one of England's largest psychiatric hospitals, carrying coal, supplies, and patients into a community that history would rather forget.

subject: Hellinikon Metropolitan Park
summary: On the site of Athens' old coastal airport, one of Europe's largest urban parks is rising from the concrete — a 263-hectare transformation that is reshaping the city's relationship with the sea.

subject: Hellyer Park Velodrome
summary: A 335-meter cycling track tucked inside a San Jose county park, where Olympic hopefuls once raced and weekend riders still chase each other around banked concrete turns.

subject: Helvetia Village Historic District
summary: Twenty-six buildings of a Swiss-German settlement founded in 1869 high in the West Virginia mountains - log cabins, a Carpenter Gothic church, a cheese house, and a community hall where Fasnacht is still celebrated every winter.

subject: Helvetinjärvi National Park
summary: A Finnish national park named 'Hell's Lake' where a crack in the bedrock plunges 38 meters deep but spans barely two meters wide, splitting ancient forest in the Pirkanmaa wilderness.

subject: Hendrix College
summary: A small Methodist liberal arts college in Conway, Arkansas, that has produced an opera conductor who broke the Metropolitan Opera's gender barrier, a congressman who shaped Medicare, and Navy SEALs -- all from a campus where the most famous social event is a freshman dance-off called Shirttails.

story.title: Hendy Woods: A Dying Man's Promise That Saved a Forest

subject: Hendy Woods
summary: An English blacksmith's deathbed wish to protect two groves of ancient coast redwoods kept the chainsaws at bay for over a century, even as the land changed hands four times and a lumber boom consumed everything around it.

subject: Hengchun Old City Wall
summary: Built between 1875 and 1879 after a series of violent incidents forced the Qing Dynasty to finally take Taiwan's southern tip seriously, Hengchun's walled town is the only place in Taiwan where all four original city gates still stand.

subject: Henri Pittier National Park
summary: Venezuela's first national park, where cloud forests harbor over 580 bird species, nine rivers drain to the Caribbean, and the village of Chuao grows some of the world's finest cacao.

subject: Herbesthal railway station
summary: From 1843 to 1966 it was one of Europe's most important rail frontier stations. Then the border moved, the line was electrified, and Herbesthal became a slow ruin in a Belgian field.

subject: Heriot-Watt University
summary: Founded in 1821 as the world's first mechanics' institute, Heriot-Watt is named for a goldsmith and an inventor and now operates campuses on three continents - the eighth-oldest university in the UK and a deliberate experiment in technical education that began with working-class evening classes.

subject: Herrenhausen Gardens
summary: Sophia of Hanover died in this garden in June 1714, eight weeks before the British throne she was heir to fell vacant - and her son inherited it instead.

subject: Hetman National Nature Park
summary: A ribbon of floodplain forest and forest-steppe that traces the Vorskla River for its entire length across Sumy Oblast, sheltering rare mushrooms and a Cossack-era name.

subject: Hetton colliery railway
summary: An 8-mile private railway opened in 1822 by the Hetton Coal Company, the first railway designed from the start to operate without animal power and George Stephenson's first complete line.

subject: Hexamilion Wall
summary: Built across the Isthmus of Corinth between 408 and 450 AD to bar invaders from the Peloponnese, the Hexamilion — the Six-Mile Wall — was breached, rebuilt, and breached again until the Ottomans made the question moot.

story.title: Hialeah Park: Where Flamingos Watched the Horses Run

subject: Hialeah Park Race Track
summary: An aviation pioneer's greyhound track became one of the most beautiful racecourses in the world, famous for its Renaissance Revival architecture, its resident flamingo flock, and a century of firsts that changed American horse racing.

story.title: Hibiya Park: The Risky Ginkgo and the Riots

subject: Hibiya Park
summary: A 500-year-old ginkgo tree almost derailed the creation of Japan's first Western-style park -- and within two years of opening, the grounds erupted in deadly riots that reshaped the nation's politics.

story.title: Higashiyama Zoo: Where a Gorilla Became a Heartthrob

subject: Higashiyama Zoo and Botanical Gardens
summary: A sprawling 1937 zoo and botanical garden in Nagoya where 469 species roam, the koala logo was drawn by the creator of Dragon Ball, and a silverback gorilla named Shabani became Japan's most unlikely celebrity.

story.title: Highgate Cemetery: Where the Dead Are Never Quite Still

subject: Highgate Cemetery
summary: London's most atmospheric cemetery holds 170,000 burials in 53,000 graves, including Karl Marx and a Gothic western half where Egyptian avenues and crumbling catacombs feel like a Victorian fever dream made real.

story.title: Highland Park Dentzel Carousel and Shelter Building

subject: Highland Park Dentzel Carousel and Shelter Building
summary: The last surviving two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie carousel in the world, spinning in a Mississippi park since 1909 and declared a National Historic Landmark in 1987.

subject: Highland Park Distillery
summary: The world's northernmost single malt Scotch whisky distillery, founded in 1798 by a smuggler-butcher who used a church pulpit to hide his illegal still.

subject: Highland Park Ford Plant
summary: The birthplace of the moving assembly line - where Henry Ford's engineers cut Model T production time from 728 minutes to 93, slashed prices in half, doubled worker wages, and launched an industrial revolution that reshaped the modern world.

subject: Hikkaduwa National Park
summary: One of Sri Lanka's three marine national parks, Hikkaduwa protects a shallow fringing coral reef that harbors 60 coral species and over 170 species of reef fish, yet faces an ongoing tension between tourism and survival.

subject: Hill-Annex Mine State Park
summary: An open-pit iron mine on the Mesabi Range that produced 63 million tons of ore, became a state park, yielded the second dinosaur fossil ever found in Minnesota -- and then closed so mining could resume.

subject: Hills of Eternity Memorial Park
summary: A Jewish cemetery in Colma founded in 1889 by Congregation Sherith Israel, one of four Jewish burial grounds serving San Francisco's historic Jewish community.

subject: Hin Namno National Park
summary: Laos' first natural World Heritage site: a limestone wilderness in Khammouane where an entire river vanishes underground for seven kilometres and comes out the other side of a mountain.

subject: Hingol National Park
summary: Pakistan's largest national park spans 6,100 square kilometers of six distinct ecosystems along the Makran coast, from sphinx-shaped rock formations and bubbling mud volcanoes to pristine beaches ranked among Asia's most beautiful.

story.title: Hirakata Park: The Amusement Park That Outlived Them All

subject: Hirakata Park
summary: Osaka's oldest amusement park began as a chrysanthemum flower exhibition in 1910, survived a wave of closures that wiped out its regional competitors, and was rescued from debt by a hometown celebrity who became its mock 'director' in an inspired marketing campaign.

subject: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park
summary: Built on the open field that the atomic bomb created where Hiroshima's busiest commercial district once stood, this park transforms the absence left by destruction into a landscape of remembrance visited by over a million people each year.

subject: Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden
summary: The cylindrical concrete drum on the National Mall, built around a Latvian immigrant's collection of twentieth-century art and the fortune he made on Canadian uranium.

subject: History Park
summary: An open-air museum in San Jose's Kelley Park where 32 rescued and replicated buildings recreate the look and feel of an early 1900s Santa Clara Valley town.

subject: History of Peiyang University
summary: China's first government-run modern university was founded in Tianjin in 1895, survived invasion, occupation, and exile across wartime China, and lives on today as Tianjin University -- though its original name still echoes across memorial pavilions and alumni gatherings.

story.title: History of San Jose State University

subject: History of San Jose State University
summary: California's oldest public university began as a weekly evening class for 54 women in San Francisco, survived fires and earthquakes, and spawned UCLA along the way.

story.title: History of the Port of Tianjin

subject: History of the Port of Tianjin
summary: The largest man-made port in mainland China traces its origins to canals built by Cao Cao in the Eastern Han dynasty, making it one of the world's longest continuously operating maritime hubs.

story.title: Hitachi Seaside Park: From Bombing Range to Blue Flower Fields

subject: Hitachi Seaside Park
summary: A former World War II airbase turned U.S. military bombing range, now a 190-hectare public park where 4.5 million baby blue-eyes bloom each spring -- transforming a hilltop into what looks like a piece of fallen sky.

subject: Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park
summary: Africa's oldest proclaimed game reserve saved the southern white rhino from extinction and pioneered the wilderness trail concept that changed how humans experience wild places.

subject: Hocking Hills State Park
summary: The Ohio gorge country where waterfalls pour into recess caves carved from 350-million-year-old sandstone - Old Man's Cave, Ash Cave, and Cedar Falls drawing hikers to one of the Midwest's most dramatic hidden landscapes.

subject: Hoge Kempen National Park
summary: Belgium's only national park, raised on the spoil heaps of the closed coal mines of Genk - the country's first attempt to ask what a post-industrial landscape might become.

subject: Hoge Veluwe National Park
summary: A Dutch couple's hunting estate that became a 55-square-kilometer national park, complete with 1,800 free white bicycles and Europe's largest indoor Van Gogh collection.

subject: Hohe Tauern National Park
summary: Austria's largest national park encompasses 266 peaks, 250 glaciers, and the country's highest summit -- a landscape where Bearded Vultures soar again after vanishing from the Alps.

subject: Hoi Ha Wan Marine Park
summary: Tucked into the northern Sai Kung Peninsula, Hoi Ha Wan's sheltered bay has been a marine park since 1996 — protecting some of Hong Kong's richest coral communities in water clear enough to dive in from shore.

subject: Hole-in-the-Wall (Eastern Cape)
summary: A natural arch on the Wild Coast where Xhosa legend says the sea-people punched through a cliff for love, and where a Portuguese ship ran aground four centuries ago.

subject: Hollins University
summary: On the site of an antebellum mineral springs resort, one of America's oldest women's colleges has produced an unlikely concentration of Pulitzer winners and literary legends.

subject: Holly River State Park
summary: The second-largest park in West Virginia's state system, built in the 1930s by 250 WPA workers, with nine original stone-fireplace cabins and a waterfall named for a Shawnee prophet.

subject: Hollywood Cemetery (Richmond, Virginia)
summary: A 135-acre cemetery overlooking the James River holds two U.S. presidents, a Confederate president, 11,000 rebel soldiers, a cast-iron dog standing vigil since 1862, and Richmond's most persistent vampire legend.

subject: Hollywood Forever Cemetery
summary: The only cemetery in Hollywood proper, where Paramount Pictures literally shares a fence with the dead, and where summer nights bring movie screenings projected against mausoleum walls.

subject: Hollywood's Favorite Railroad
summary: A working 19th-century railroad in the Sierra Nevada foothills has doubled as the most filmed train in American cinema, appearing in over 200 productions from High Noon to Back to the Future Part III.

subject: Holosiiv National Nature Park
summary: A genuine wild forest, home to a hundred kinds of bird and forty-four mammals, survives inside the southern edge of a capital city of three million people.

subject: Holy Cross Cemetery (Colma, California)
summary: One of California's oldest and largest Catholic cemeteries, a 300-acre Colma burial ground operated by the Archdiocese of San Francisco since 1887.

subject: Holyhead railway station
summary: The far western terminus of British rail, where Avanti West Coast trains from London Euston roll directly into the Dublin ferry terminal under a Victorian station clock made in Whitchurch.

subject: Holyrood Park
summary: An extinct volcano surrounded by 650 acres of highland wilderness sits in the middle of Edinburgh -- and sheep grazed its slopes until 1975.

subject: Home of Peace Cemetery (Colma, California)
summary: A Jewish cemetery in Colma founded in 1889 that houses the Emanu-El Mausoleum, serving one of San Francisco's oldest and most prominent congregations.

subject: Homerton College, Cambridge
summary: Homerton began as a refuge for Protestant dissenters barred from Oxford and Cambridge, spent a century in London's East End, and arrived in Cambridge in 1894 as an outsider that has never quite forgotten where it came from.

subject: Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park
summary: A Florida wildlife park where crystal-clear springs shelter manatees and once harbored Lu, an honorary citizen hippo who lived to be the oldest in North America.

subject: Hong Kong Cemetery
summary: A hillside cemetery beside the Happy Valley racecourse holds the layered history of colonial Hong Kong — soldiers felled by tropical disease, men who died in the Battle of Hong Kong, and extraordinary individuals whose lives spanned empires.

story.title: Hong Kong Chinese Christian Churches Union Pok Fu Lam Road Cemetery

subject: Hong Kong Chinese Christian Churches Union Pok Fu Lam Road Cemetery
summary: A terraced hillside cemetery founded in 1882 whose headstones read like a who's-who of modern Chinese history — revolutionaries, newspaper founders, department-store dynasties, and Hong Kong's first female doctor all rest here overlooking Sandy Bay.

subject: Hong Kong Dragon Garden
summary: Hidden along Castle Peak Road in the New Territories, Dragon Garden is Hong Kong's largest private garden—a 8-hectare sanctuary of Song, Ming, and Qing dynasty architecture built over twenty years by one man, and nearly lost to developers before being saved.

subject: Hong Kong International Airport
summary: Built on a flattened island in six years at a cost of $60 billion USD, VHHH opened in 1998 and went on to become the world's busiest cargo airport and one of its most important passenger hubs.

subject: Hong Kong Park
summary: Carved from a Victorian-era military barracks in the heart of Central, Hong Kong Park is an 8-hectare oasis of greenhouses, aviaries, and colonial architecture surrounded by some of the densest skyscrapers on earth.

subject: Hong Kong Railway Museum
summary: At the old Tai Po Market station—a 1913 building in indigenous Chinese style that once linked Hong Kong to Canton—seven vintage coaches and three locomotives now wait on tracks that no longer go anywhere, free to enter and open to anyone who wants to sit inside a 1911 third-class compartment.

story.title: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens

subject: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens
summary: Tucked onto the northern slope of Victoria Peak since 1864, the Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens is the city's oldest park — a layered sanctuary where colonial history, rare camellias, and endangered primates coexist on just 5.6 hectares.

subject: Hongmaogang Cultural Park
summary: A memorial park in Siaogang District, Kaohsiung, that preserves the memory of a fishing village displaced to make room for the Port of Kaohsiung's container expansion.

subject: Hooge Crater Cemetery
summary: A cemetery named for an explosion, where the ground itself bears witness to the underground war beneath Flanders.

subject: Hooglede German War Cemetery
summary: A quiet Flemish field where 8,247 German soldiers lie under flat dark stones - a younger, smaller, more austere counterpart to Langemark, watched over by the German War Graves Commission's quiet motto: reconciliation among the graves.

subject: Hopewell Culture National Historical Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in southern Ohio where 2,000-year-old geometric earthworks reveal a civilization of astonishing precision - people who aligned massive structures to solstices, lunar cycles, and a shared architectural vision that stretched across eastern North America.

subject: Horace Williams Airport
summary: A small university-owned airfield north of Chapel Hill, named for a UNC philosophy professor, that operated from the 1930s until 2018 when its single asphalt runway gave way to a solar farm.

subject: Horne Lake Caves Provincial Park
summary: A network of caves on Vancouver Island where the Qualicum First Nation's ancient knowledge met 20th-century discovery, and where vandalism ultimately led to preservation.

subject: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park
summary: A quiet bend in Alabama's Tallapoosa River where the Creek War's bloodiest day unfolded, now preserved as a national military park where nature trails wind through the grounds of a vanished fortress.

subject: Hot Springs National Park
summary: Decades before Yellowstone, Congress set aside the thermal springs of central Arkansas for public use in 1832 -- creating a place where Native American healing traditions, Gilded Age bathhouses, gangster hideouts, and presidential boyhoods would all converge.

subject: Hotham Valley Railway
summary: A volunteer-run heritage railway in Western Australia's Peel region that has kept original government steam locomotives running on their original tracks for over fifty years.

subject: Houdini's Grave at Machpelah Cemetery
summary: The Queens cemetery where Harry Houdini is buried beneath a monument featuring a weeping woman and an exedra he designed himself - where fans still hold séances on Halloween hoping the escape artist will contact them from beyond.

subject: Houtong Coal Mine Ecological Park
summary: Before the cats came — and before the tourists came to see the cats — Houtong was Taiwan's most productive coal mine, where generations of miners descended into sweltering darkness to fuel a nation's growth, a labor and a sacrifice that the Ecological Park now works to honor and remember.

subject: Hovander Homestead Park
summary: A Swedish architect's farmhouse on the Nooksack flood plain near Ferndale, built from timber cured for two years in linseed oil, kept in the family for seven decades, and now a 350-acre county park with the Hovanders' own tools still in the rooms.

subject: Howard University
summary: The Mecca of Black American higher education, federally chartered in 1867, the only HBCU classified as a top-tier research university.

subject: Howard University School of Law
summary: The HBCU law school where Thurgood Marshall trained, Charles Hamilton Houston taught, and the legal strategy for Brown v. Board was built.

subject: Hryshko National Botanical Garden
summary: Every spring the lilacs bloom and Kyiv comes to breathe them in, at a garden where two ancient monasteries stand among thirteen thousand kinds of plant.

subject: Hsinchu Science Park
summary: Modeled on Silicon Valley by a minister who consulted its architect, Hsinchu Science Park became the nerve center of the global semiconductor industry - home to TSMC, UMC, and more than 500 companies that once produced 10% of Taiwan's GDP.

subject: Hua Lamphong railway station
summary: Bangkok's Hua Lamphong station, designed by Italian architect Mario Tamagno and opened in 1916, served as Thailand's central railway hub for over a century before long-distance trains moved to a new terminal in 2023.

subject: Hualien Railway Culture Park
summary: The former headquarters of Taiwan's eastern railway line, built in 1932, has been preserved as a cultural park housing narrow-gauge locomotives and the story of how rail connected Taiwan's remote east coast to the rest of the island.

subject: Huashan 1914 Creative Park
summary: A Japanese-era sake winery that became a government liquor factory, produced Taiwan's most popular cheap spirit, sat abandoned for a decade, was illegally occupied by theater artists, and is now one of Taipei's most important creative spaces.

subject: Huerquehue National Park
summary: In the Mapuche tongue its name means 'the place of the messenger' — a high Andean park of mirror lakes and thousand-year-old monkey puzzle forests above the resort town of Pucon.

subject: Hulne Park
summary: The walled medieval hunting park outside Alnwick Castle, landscaped by Capability Brown and home to a Carmelite priory, a Gothic tower, and a stone friar guarding a cave.

subject: Humboldt University of Berlin
summary: Founded as a model for what a modern research university could be, this Prussian institution shaped science worldwide — and then watched, in 1933, as its own students burned its own library across the street.

subject: Huntington Beach State Park
summary: A 2,500-acre coastal preserve on the South Carolina Grand Strand where birders flock to salt marshes and a Moorish castle stands sentinel over the beach.

subject: Hwange National Park
summary: Zimbabwe's largest national park survives on pumped water in an arid landscape, sustaining over a hundred mammal species around artificial waterholes that become the stage for some of Africa's most dramatic wildlife encounters.

subject: Hyde Park Barracks, Sydney
summary: A convict architect designed it to earn his freedom; it housed transported men, then Irish Famine orphans, and now stands as a UNESCO testament to Australia's penal beginnings.

subject: Hyde Park Corner (Royal Berks) Cemetery
summary: Eighty-seven graves at a Flanders crossroads named after a corner of London — a rugby international, a sixteen-year-old, and a man shot at dawn.

subject: Hyde Park, London
summary: Henry VIII seized this land from Westminster Abbey in 1536 to hunt deer; nearly five centuries later, its 350 acres host duels, Diamond Jubilees, the Rolling Stones, and a hundred-odd thousand people on any given Sunday afternoon.

subject: Hàng Dương Cemetery
summary: Vietnam's great pilgrimage cemetery holds 1,913 graves for a prison island that killed tens of thousands — and nearly two-thirds of the markers carry no name.

subject: Háthayim Marine Provincial Park
summary: A marine park on Cortes Island where a long tidal inlet once named for a drowned Royal Navy officer was renamed to honor the Klahoose word for this place, restoring an identity older than any colonial chart.

subject: Hội An Old Town
summary: Hội An's Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where Cham, Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese influences built and rebuilt a trading port over five centuries — and where 1,068 preserved houses still stand.

subject: Iberá National Park
summary: Argentina's largest protected area, where a clothing company founder's land purchases brought jaguars, giant otters, and macaws back to wetlands that had lost them decades ago.

subject: Ibirapuera Park Conservancy
summary: How a citizen-led nonprofit modeled on Central Park Conservancy fought to professionalize stewardship of South America's most visited park -- and what happened when privatization came knocking.

subject: Ibitipoca State Park
summary: A burst mountain of caramel-colored rivers and quartzite ridges in the Minas Gerais highlands, where 360 degrees of horizon stretch away from a single summit.

subject: Ichetucknee Springs State Park
summary: A crystalline spring-fed river in North Florida where college students discovered tubing in the 1960s, Spanish missionaries built a church in the 1600s, and the aquifer has been pushing water skyward for millennia.

subject: Ichkeul National Park
summary: The last surviving lake in a chain that once stretched across North Africa, where 300,000 migratory birds still gather each winter in a UNESCO World Heritage ecosystem that nearly died.

subject: Idalia National Park
summary: A rugged 144,000-hectare wilderness in the Gowan Range where the yellow-footed rock-wallaby found a foothold, opened by a prince and reachable only by four-wheel drive.

subject: Idora Park
summary: A vanished Victorian trolley park in North Oakland where Charlie Chaplin learned to skate, earthquake refugees found shelter, and cream waffles became legend.

subject: Ihuatzio (archaeological site)
summary: A fortified Purépecha stronghold on the shores of Lake Pátzcuaro, Ihuatzio is the only site in western Mexico with monumental walled causeways built to carry a king.

subject: Ilıca–Palamutluk Railway
summary: A narrow-gauge railway born to move ancient lead ore from the slopes of Mount Ida to the Aegean coast — and briefly beloved by summer bathers seeking the sea.

subject: Imam Khomeini International Airport
summary: Tehran's international gateway, born from pre-revolutionary ambition, shut down by the Revolutionary Guard on opening day, and caught in the crossfire of Iran's struggle between engagement and isolation.

story.title: Imperial College of Engineering: The School That Built Modern Japan

subject: Imperial College of Engineering
summary: A 25-year-old Scotsman sailed to Tokyo in 1873 to run an engineering college that would train the generation of architects, industrialists, and builders who gave Japan its modern infrastructure -- from NEC to Tokyo Station to the National Diet Building.

subject: Independence Park (Jamaica)
summary: Kingston's Independence Park is where Jamaica celebrates itself -- a sprawling sports and cultural complex that has hosted Commonwealth Games, Bob Marley's One Love Peace Concert, and the sprinters who made the island a global track power.

story.title: Indian Grinding Rock State Historic Park

subject: Indian Grinding Rock State Historic Park
summary: The largest collection of bedrock mortars in North America preserves thousands of years of Miwok grinding traditions in California's Sierra Nevada foothills.

subject: Indian Key Historic State Park
summary: A tiny island in the Florida Keys that once served as the county seat of Dade County and the base of a wrecking empire, Indian Key was destroyed in an 1840 Seminole raid and survives today as a ghost town of coral stone foundations.

subject: Indian Rock Park
summary: A volcanic rhyolite outcropping in the Berkeley Hills where Ohlone grinding stones and Depression-era steps share the same ancient rock that launched modern American climbing.

subject: Indian Springs State Park
summary: Thought to be the oldest state park in the United States, Indian Springs has been in continuous public use since 1825 -- its sulfur springs first drew the Creek people as a healing place, then became the centerpiece of a 19th-century resort town, and finally anchored one of Georgia's first state parks.

subject: Indiana Dunes National Park
summary: Indiana's only national park, where towering sand dunes meet the southern shore of Lake Michigan, sheltering over 300 bird species and ecosystems ranging from bogs to prairies within sight of the Chicago skyline.

subject: Indira Gandhi Canal
summary: A 649-kilometer lifeline carved through the Thar Desert, the Indira Gandhi Canal follows the ancient paleochannel of a lost river to bring water where none flowed for millennia.

subject: Inner Harbor
summary: Described by the Urban Land Institute as the model for post-industrial waterfront redevelopment around the world, the Inner Harbor turned Baltimore's abandoned warehouses and rotting piers into the template that more than 100 other cities have since tried to copy.

story.title: Inokashira Park: The Emperor's Gift and the Breakup Curse

subject: Inokashira Park
summary: A gift from the Emperor to the people of Tokyo in 1917, this park in western Tokyo harbors a famous local superstition: couples who ride the boats on its pond are doomed to break up -- yet the swan boats are always full.

subject: Interstate Park
summary: Straddling the Minnesota-Wisconsin border, Interstate Park protects the Dalles of the St. Croix River -- a billion-year-old basalt gorge carved by catastrophic glacial floods, home to the deepest explored pothole in the world and the origin of Wisconsin's entire state park system.

subject: Inwood Hill Park
summary: At the northern tip of Manhattan, a 196-acre park preserves the island's last old-growth forest, glacial potholes, a salt marsh, and the contested legend of where Peter Minuit purchased Manhattan.

subject: Iona National Park
summary: Angola's oldest and largest national park, a 15,150-square-kilometer sweep of shifting dunes, desert plains, and rugged escarpment that connects to Namibia's Skeleton Coast to form one of Africa's great continuous wilderness corridors.

subject: Ipoh railway station
summary: A grand Edwardian Baroque station in the heart of Perak's capital, affectionately called the Taj Mahal of Ipoh, where colonial ambition and wartime perseverance produced one of Malaysia's most striking railway buildings.

subject: Ireland West Airport
summary: Officials said the site was too boggy and too foggy to build an airport - so Monsignor James Horan built one anyway, five years after he decided pilgrims to Knock deserved their own runway.

subject: Irish National War Memorial Gardens
summary: Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and twice bombed by Republican paramilitaries, this memorial to the 49,400 Irish soldiers killed in World War I was not formally dedicated until 1988 -- seventy years after the Armistice.

subject: Iruma Air Base
