summary: A military airfield north of Tokyo that has served three nations across nine decades, from training Imperial Japanese kamikaze pilots to hosting America's Korean War bombers to drawing 200,000 spectators to Japan's premier air show.

subject: Isalo National Park
summary: Madagascar's Colorado - a Jurassic sandstone massif eroded into canyons, ruin-like pinnacles, and hidden palm oases, where ring-tailed lemurs lounge beside cold natural pools.

subject: Ischigualasto Provincial Park
summary: In a desert basin so strange it is called the Valley of the Moon, scientists found some of the oldest dinosaurs that ever lived, frozen in 231-million-year-old rock.

subject: Isla Bastimentos National Marine Park
summary: Panama's first marine park, established in 1988 in the Bocas del Toro archipelago, where strawberry poison-dart frogs, nesting sea turtles, over 80 coral species, and Afro-Caribbean and Ngabe communities share an island landscape of rainforest, mangrove, and Caribbean reef.

subject: Islas Marietas National Park
summary: A cluster of uninhabited volcanic islands off Mexico's Nayarit coast where blue-footed boobies nest above coral reefs, a collapsed crater conceals a secret beach, and the tension between Instagram fame and ecological survival plays out in real time.

subject: Isle Royale National Park
summary: The only U.S. national park that shuts down for winter, Isle Royale is a 45-mile-long wilderness archipelago in Lake Superior where wolves and moose play out nature's longest-running predator-prey study and visitors average four to five days because one is never enough.

subject: Isle of Man Airport
summary: Ronaldsway, the island's main civilian airport, sits on a south-coast site that has yielded Neolithic settlements, a medieval battlefield mass grave, and a wartime naval air station named in Manx for the eagle.

subject: Isle of Man Railway Museum
summary: At the south-western terminus of the Isle of Man Steam Railway in Port Erin, a converted bus garage houses the locomotives, royal saloons and gathered ephemera of the island's vanished narrow-gauge network.

subject: Isle of Mull Railway
summary: For 27 summers, Scotland's first island passenger railway carried visitors from a Hebridean ferry pier to a Victorian castle on a track barely wider than a footpath.

subject: Islote Lobos National Park
summary: On a quiet stretch of the San Matías Gulf, the world's northernmost colony of Magellanic penguins nests among islets that the falling tide stitches back to the mainland.

subject: Ismail Marzuki Park
summary: Jakarta's cultural heart since 1968, Taman Ismail Marzuki is a nine-hectare arts complex built on the site of the city's former zoo, where six theaters, a planetarium, and an art institute keep Indonesian performing and visual arts alive in the middle of one of the world's most congested cities.

subject: Istanbul Railway Museum
summary: Inside the 1890-built Sirkeci Terminal — where the Orient Express made its legendary final stop — a free railway museum preserves 300 artifacts from the age of steam, diplomacy, and transcontinental romance.

story.title: Itami Airport: The International Airport With No International Flights

subject: Itami Airport
summary: Officially called Osaka International Airport until 2025 despite handling only domestic flights, Itami is the closest airport to both Osaka and Kyoto -- a compact urban airfield whose identity crisis, noise lawsuits, and celebrity visitors tell the story of postwar Japanese aviation.

subject: Itapuã State Park
summary: A rocky point where lake meets lagoon, Itapuã survived quarries and illegal beach houses to become the last wild remnant of the landscape that once surrounded Porto Alegre.

subject: Itasca State Park
summary: Minnesota's oldest state park protects the headwaters of the Mississippi River -- the spot where America's mightiest waterway begins as a stream shallow enough to wade across, saved from loggers in 1891 by a single legislative vote.

subject: Itatiaia National Park
summary: Brazil's first national park, established in 1937, holds 250 bird species, Brazil's third-highest peak, and one of the only places in the tropical country where snow occasionally falls.

story.title: Ivory Coast of Sviatoslav National Nature Park

subject: Ivory Coast of Sviatoslav National Nature Park
summary: Where two great rivers meet the Black Sea, freshwater and salt lie side by side across a wild ribbon of sand, pine, and steppe named for a warrior-prince of old.

story.title: Iwatayama Monkey Park: Where the Monkeys Run the Mountain

subject: Iwatayama Monkey Park
summary: Atop a mountain in Kyoto's Arashiyama district, over 120 wild Japanese macaques have turned the tables on the typical zoo -- here, humans climb into a cage to feed the monkeys, not the other way around.

subject: Ixtlán del Rio (archaeological site)
summary: An archaeological site in Nayarit where 2,200-year-old shaft tombs and ceramic figures reveal a western Mexican civilization that worshipped the wind god and buried their dead in vertical wells representing the maternal womb.

subject: JMSDF Yokosuka Naval Base
summary: Japan's principal maritime defense installation, scattered across multiple districts of Yokosuka City, where the Self Defense Fleet commands its forces alongside the US Navy's largest forward-deployed base in the Pacific.

story.title: Jackson's Mill State 4-H Camp Historic District

subject: Jackson's Mill State 4-H Camp Historic District
summary: The first state 4-H camp in America, established in 1921 on the boyhood farm of Stonewall Jackson - thirty-three Craftsman-era buildings, a council circle, and a hundred years of West Virginia summer camp tradition.

subject: Jacqueline Cochran Regional Airport
summary: Built in 1942 to train pilots for Operation Torch — the Allied invasion of North Africa — the airport at Thermal sits 115 feet below sea level in a valley where summer heat can reach 120°F, so flight operations begin at 3am and end at 1pm.

subject: Jakarta Kota Railway Station
summary: Designed by Dutch architect Frans Ghijsels in a style that married art deco with Indonesian tradition, Jakarta Kota Station has served as the gateway to the old colonial capital since 1929 - though the last intercity train departed in January 2025.

subject: Jalapão State Park
summary: A remote cerrado reserve of red dunes, flat-topped plateaus, and a plant whose golden stems have become jewelry across Brazil.

subject: Jamanxim National Park
summary: An 859,000 hectare strict Amazon reserve where mahogany and ipê still grow old, a rare stand of fully protected forest in a region mostly under economic use.

subject: James Cook University
summary: Founded in 1970 and opened by the Queen herself, Australia's leading tropical university built its reputation on the reef, the rainforest and the diseases of the hot world.

subject: James River Park System
summary: Starting with one Boy Scout leader's frustrated permit application in 1965, the James River Park System now wraps over 600 acres of trails, rapids, and islands through the heart of Richmond - the country's only urban Class III-IV whitewater within a major city.

subject: James River and Kanawha Canal
summary: George Washington's grand vision to connect Virginia's coast to the Ohio River by water, a canal that took seventy years to half-build, survived two wars and countless floods, then surrendered its towpath to the very railroads that made it obsolete.

subject: Japanese Cemetery (Colma, California)
summary: A hillside cemetery in Colma that has held the stories of Japanese Americans since 1901, from shipwrecked sailors of the first diplomatic mission to pioneering farmers and community builders.

subject: Japanese Cemetery Park
summary: Southeast Asia's largest Japanese cemetery began as a burial ground for young women who died in destitution in colonial Singapore, and grew to hold the ashes of field marshals, secret agents, literary pioneers, and executed war criminals - a single park containing nearly every chapter of Japan's complicated presence in the region.

subject: Japanese Friendship Garden (San Jose)
summary: A six-acre garden in San Jose modeled after Okayama's Korakuen Garden, where koi sent from Japan in 1966 swim in three interconnected ponds that have survived virus and flood.

subject: Japanese Tea Garden (San Francisco)
summary: The oldest public Japanese garden in America began as a World's Fair attraction in 1894, was nurtured by one family for three generations, and survived their forced internment to become a symbol of reconciliation.

subject: Java's Little Africa
summary: At the northeastern tip of Java, where the Bali Strait narrows and an extinct volcano anchors a ring of savanna, Baluran National Park harbors wild banteng, green peafowl, and the ghost of the Javan tiger.

subject: Jay Cooke State Park
summary: Where 1.9-billion-year-old bedrock meets the swinging bridge that voyageurs never had, Jay Cooke State Park protects the wild gorge of the St. Louis River and the ancient portage route that once connected the Mississippi to the Great Lakes.

subject: Jaú National Park
summary: A UNESCO-protected stretch of untouched Amazon rainforest the size of a small country, reached only by boat through black water from Novo Airão.

subject: Jaú National Park
summary: 2.36 million hectares of Amazonian rainforest - one of the largest protected areas in Brazil and the core of a UNESCO World Heritage Site that spans four conservation units.

story.title: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve

subject: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve
summary: Named for a pirate, spread across six separate sites, and encompassing battlefields, bayous, and Cajun cultural centers, this park tells the tangled story of Louisiana's Mississippi River Delta.

subject: Jean-Drapeau Park
summary: Born from 28 million tons of excavated earth and the ambitions of one relentless mayor, Montreal's island park is a World's Fair ghost town turned year-round playground.

subject: Jeannette Kawas National Park
summary: A Caribbean wetland park on Honduras's northern coast, named for the environmental activist whose murder in 1995 transformed her conservation work into a national cause.

subject: Jebel al-Salayli (archaeological site)
summary: An Early Iron Age copper mining settlement in Oman's mountains, where ancient hut tombs cluster near slag fields and an abandoned mine that once connected this remote valley to the bronze-hungry world.

subject: Jebribillum Bora Park
summary: A preserved bora ground at Burleigh Heads, sacred to the Yugambeh and Kombumerri people, and the site of the first war memorial in Australia dedicated to Indigenous servicemen and women.

subject: Jeddah International Airport (closed 1981)
summary: Before there was King Abdulaziz International, there was Kandara Aerodrome, a sand strip where camels intruded on the runway and pilgrims slept in a city built for them next to the hangars.

subject: Jedediah Island Marine Provincial Park
summary: A 243-hectare Gulf Island saved from private sale by a grassroots campaign that raised four million dollars in six months, Jedediah Island is one of British Columbia's largest island parks.

subject: Jericoacoara National Park
summary: Eighty-nine square kilometres of migrating dune and freshwater lagoon on Ceará's west coast, drawn deliberately around a fishing village that became world-famous.

subject: Jesus College, Cambridge
summary: Founded in 1496 on the ruins of a medieval nunnery, Jesus College Cambridge carries one of the oldest chapels in the university and alumni ranging from Thomas Cranmer to Coleridge to Stormzy.

subject: Jesus College, Oxford
summary: The Oxford college founded in 1571 by Elizabeth I to educate Welsh clergy, which became the academic destination for centuries of ambitious young Welshmen and the alma mater of Lawrence of Arabia.

subject: Jever Air Base
summary: A quiet Friesian airfield where Luftwaffe pilots trained in 1936, RAF squadrons flew Vampires and Hunters through the Cold War, and NATO learned how to fight as a coalition before the engines finally went silent in 2013.

subject: Jewish cemetery of Coro
summary: The oldest Jewish cemetery in continuous use in the Americas began with a father's grief -- a plot of land purchased in 1832 to bury a daughter, which became a lasting testament to the Sephardic community that flourished in Venezuela's oldest colonial city.

subject: Jewry Wall
summary: A surviving 2nd-century Roman wall in Leicester, one of the tallest pieces of civil Roman architecture left in Britain, whose misleading name has nothing to do with Jewish history and whose excavation in the 1930s rewrote local archaeology.

subject: Jewry Wall Museum
summary: A purpose-built 1960s museum facing Leicester's Roman bath ruins, recently reopened in July 2025 after a £16.8 million renovation that pulled it back from years of neglect into one of the city's most ambitious new visitor experiences.

subject: Jianggezhuang Naval Base
summary: China's first submarine base, built into the Yellow Sea coastline east of Qingdao, where nuclear ballistic missile submarines shelter behind breakwaters and inside an underground tunnel.

story.title: Jigokudani Monkey Park: Where Macaques Invented the Spa Day

subject: Jigokudani Monkey Park
summary: In a volcanic valley called Hell, hundreds of wild Japanese macaques soak in steaming hot springs while snow piles on their fur -- the only primates on Earth known to bathe for pleasure.

subject: Jiji Railway Station
summary: A tiny cypress-wood station built in 1933 on Taiwan's longest branch line, Jiji survived threats of closure and a devastating earthquake to become one of the island's most beloved heritage railways.

subject: Jimmy Carter National Historical Park
summary: The small town of Plains, Georgia, preserves the full arc of Jimmy Carter's life -- from a boyhood farm without running water to a Summer White House to his final resting place beside Rosalynn under a willow tree.

subject: Jing-Mei White Terror Memorial Park
summary: A former military detention center in New Taipei City where political prisoners were held and tried during Taiwan's White Terror era, now preserved as a human rights memorial where the stories of those who suffered here are honoured and kept from silence.

subject: Jingshan Park
summary: An artificial hill built from the dirt of the Forbidden City's moats, where a dynasty ended with a suicide and a city's elderly gather to sing opera under imperial pavilions.

subject: Jizera Dark-Sky Park
summary: The world's first cross-border dark-sky preserve, 75 square kilometres of emptied mountain on the Czech-Polish frontier - and it publishes exactly how much light pollution it still has.

subject: Joaquin Miller Park
summary: Five hundred acres of coast redwoods in the Oakland Hills, planted by a nineteenth-century poet who also left behind stone monuments to Moses, Fremont, and the Brownings -- and a waterfall cascade dedicated to California's writers.

subject: Joffre Lakes Provincial Park
summary: Three glacial lakes stacked like turquoise jewels along a mountain trail, each more brilliant than the last, drawing thousands to this Sea-to-Sky gem that now requires advance booking just to enter.

subject: John Dean Provincial Park
summary: The mountain where the W̱SÁNEĆ tied their canoe to survive the flood now carries an air-traffic radar that Victoria calls the big soccer ball, and 174 hectares of a forest type that is 99 percent gone.

subject: John Muir Country Park
summary: Eight miles of East Lothian coastline named for the Dunbar-born naturalist whose ideas, exported to America, helped invent the modern national park.

story.title: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park

subject: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park
summary: America's first undersea park, where a bronze Christ stands with arms raised beneath 25 feet of Atlantic water and the only living coral reef in the continental United States shelters midnight parrotfish, elkhorn coral, and Caribbean reef sharks along the shores of Key Largo.

subject: Johns Hopkins University
summary: Founded in 1876 on the German research university model, Hopkins was the first American institution to combine graduate research training with undergraduate education - the template every modern American university has followed since.

subject: Jonglei Canal
summary: A 360-kilometer ditch meant to drain the Sudd wetlands for Egypt's cotton fields, halted two-thirds of the way in by civil war and a rusting German machine named Sarah.

subject: Jorge Chávez International Airport
summary: Lima's gateway to the world, named after a daring Peruvian aviator who died at 23, has endured terrorism, tragic accidents, and a billion-dollar reinvention.

subject: Joseph D. Grant County Park
summary: At nearly 10,900 acres, the largest park in Santa Clara County preserves a Mexican land grant ranch on the slopes of Mount Hamilton, where Gold Rush-era dry goods money built a cattle empire and 51 miles of trails now thread through oak-studded grasslands.

subject: Joshua Tree National Park
summary: Where two deserts meet among twisted trees and jumbled boulders, creating one of the world's premier destinations for rock climbing and stargazing.

subject: Jostedalsbreen National Park
summary: Home to mainland Europe's largest glacier, this Norwegian national park protects 1,310 square kilometers of ice, rock, and the ruins of farms swallowed by advancing glacial arms.

subject: Jotunheimen National Park
summary: The Home of the Giants: 1,151 square kilometers of Norway's highest mountains, where more than 250 peaks exceed 1,900 meters, Stone Age hunting camps lie beside melting glaciers that are yielding 1,500-year-old Viking arrowheads, and Peer Gynt took his famous fictional reindeer ride along the Besseggen Ridge.

story.title: João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park

subject: João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park
summary: On a sacred two-kilometre beach in Guinea-Bissau, tens of thousands of green turtles haul ashore each year to lay their eggs.

subject: Juan Castro Blanco National Park
summary: Three volcanoes guard a pristine jungle wilderness where rivers are born - Costa Rica's 'Park of Waters' harbors jaguars, quetzals, and 57 mammal species in 14,285 hectares of roadless backcountry.

subject: Juan de Fuca Provincial Park
summary: Three smaller parks were merged in 1996 to protect a stretch of Vancouver Island coastline where a University of Minnesota botanist had built the Pacific Northwest's first marine research station nearly a century earlier.

story.title: Judge C. R. Magney State Park

subject: Judge C. R. Magney State Park
summary: A North Shore state park where half the Brule River vanishes into a rock pothole called the Devil's Kettle -- a geological mystery that stumped scientists for decades and swallowed everything visitors threw in.

subject: Julia-Ann Square Historic District
summary: 116 historic houses on Juliana and Ann Streets in Parkersburg, where Senator Peter Van Winkle built an 1836 residence whose entrance later changed direction to face a different street.

subject: Jungle Railway
summary: Malaysia's 526-kilometer East Coast line cuts through the interior of the peninsula, connecting Tumpat near Kota Bharu to the junction at Gemas through disappearing rainforest, limestone karst, and villages that once had no other link to the outside world.

subject: Junipero Serra County Park
summary: A hillside park where Native American shell mounds, ongoing Stanford archaeological digs, and suburban hiking trails converge above the San Francisco Peninsula.

subject: Junkerdal National Park
summary: A 682-square-kilometre park on the Norwegian-Swedish border where several Arctic plants reach the absolute southern limit of their range, named after a seventeenth-century nobleman who came through it to burn a silver mine.

subject: Juruena National Park
summary: Brazil's third-largest national park spans nearly two million hectares across the border of Amazonas and Mato Grosso, sheltering jaguars, harpy eagles, and 412 bird species in a critical corridor designed to block agricultural expansion into the central Amazon.

subject: Jōshin'etsu-kōgen National Park
summary: A volcanic highland national park straddling three prefectures on Honshu, home to Japan's most active volcano, its largest ski resort, and a scenic alpine highway connecting hot spring towns.

story.title: Kaa-Iya del Gran Chaco National Park

subject: Kaa-Iya del Gran Chaco National Park and Integrated Management Natural Area
summary: Bolivia's largest national park protects the world's biggest remaining tropical dry forest, sheltering over 1,000 jaguars and indigenous communities who co-manage its 34,000 square kilometers.

subject: Kabul University
summary: Afghanistan's oldest university has mirrored every upheaval in its nation's modern history -- from a Turkish-built medical faculty in the 1930s to a Taliban ban on women students in 2022.

subject: Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden
summary: What began in 1956 as a practical effort to help struggling farmers in the New Territories has become one of Hong Kong's most important centers for wildlife rescue, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable living.

subject: Kaeng Krachan National Park
summary: Thailand's largest national park - a 2,915 square kilometer expanse of rainforest on the Tenasserim Range where 461 bird species thrive, elephants are poached by the people paid to protect them, and a UNESCO World Heritage vote passed over the objections of the indigenous Karen who live there.

subject: Kaeng Tana National Park
summary: A compact highland park in northeastern Thailand where the Mun River breaks into its greatest rapids, splitting around ancient boulders and a solitary French colonial-era marker.

subject: Kafue National Park
summary: At 22,400 square kilometers, Zambia's oldest and largest park holds enough water, grass, and wildness for a region of its own.

subject: Kai Tak Sports Park
summary: Rising from the site of Hong Kong's legendary old airport, Kai Tak Sports Park is the city's largest sports venue — a 28-hectare complex with a 50,000-seat retractable-roof stadium that opened in 2025 to immediate global attention.

subject: Kainji National Park
summary: Nigeria's sprawling savanna park unites two game reserves and a man-made lake across 5,341 square kilometers, sheltering lions, elephants, and the submerged memory of a drowned town.

subject: Kaipara Harbour
summary: One of the largest harbours in the world by area, where a treacherous entrance has claimed over a century of shipwrecks and Maori mythology warns that the ocean-going canoe Mahuhu capsized trying to cross the bar.

subject: Kalaupapa National Historical Park
summary: The exile peninsula - where Hawaii banished leprosy patients for a century, where Father Damien gave his life caring for the afflicted, and where the last survivors live out their days in the place that was both prison and home.

subject: Kalbarri National Park
summary: Where the Murchison River cut an 80-kilometre gorge through banded red-and-white sandstone, a glassy platform now floats 100 metres above the drop.

subject: Kalevankangas Cemetery
summary: Tampere's main burial ground holds sixty-six names carved in stone and at least 2,751 people with none - the arithmetic of a civil war, kept in one place.

subject: Kalijodo Park
summary: Built on the ruins of Jakarta's most notorious red-light district, Kalijodo Park traces an arc from colonial-era matchmaking rituals on the Angke River to an international-standard skate park where families now gather on weekends.

subject: Kalkajaka National Park
summary: Kalkajaka — Black Mountain — is a mountain of tumbled black granite near Cooktown, profoundly sacred to the Kuku Yalanji as a home of powerful ancestral beings, and the only place on Earth where three extraordinary creatures live.

subject: Kalka–Shimla Railway
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage narrow-gauge railway that climbs from the plains of Kalka to the Himalayan hill station of Shimla through 103 tunnels, 969 bridges, and 912 curves.

subject: Kaloko-Honokōhau National Historical Park
summary: On a coast ancient Hawaiians called 'lands without water,' ingenious fishponds and aquaculture systems sustained thriving communities for centuries.

subject: Kalundborg Eco-industrial Park
summary: Nobody planned the world's first industrial symbiosis — a Danish port town's factories simply started selling each other their garbage.

subject: Kam Shan Country Park
summary: Just north of Kowloon, Monkey Hill — officially Kam Shan Country Park — is a 3.37 km² pocket of granite forest where macaques descended from 1920s pet releases have formed their own permanent community.

subject: Kamay Botany Bay National Park
summary: The sandstone headlands where Cook stepped ashore in 1770, the Gweagal stood their ground, and two histories of one continent began to collide.

subject: Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Ping River preserving the laterite ruins of a Sukhothai-era fortress city whose temples once displayed Buddhas in all four postures and whose walls guarded the kingdom's southern frontier.

subject: Kanaka Creek Regional Park
summary: A narrow green ribbon along eleven kilometres of salmon creek in Maple Ridge, named for the Hawaiian families who settled its mouth in the 1850s.

subject: Kanger Valley National Park
summary: One of India's densest national parks shelters limestone caves with blind fish, milky waterfalls, and crocodile-filled gorges in the tribal heartland of Bastar.

subject: Kangra Valley Railway
summary: A 164-kilometer narrow-gauge railway threading through the Himalayan foothills from Pathankot to Jogindernagar, built in the 1920s, dismantled for World War II, and restored a decade later.

story.title: Kansai International Airport: The Sinking Island That Refused to Fail

subject: Kansai International Airport
summary: Built on a four-kilometer artificial island in Osaka Bay at a cost exceeding $20 billion, Kansai International Airport has been slowly sinking since the day it opened in 1994 -- and engineers have been fighting back ever since.

subject: Kansas State University
summary: The first land-grant college created under the Morrill Act, Kansas State University has been broadcasting weather forecasts since 1912, televised its second-ever college football game in 1939, and leads all public universities in Rhodes, Marshall, Truman, and Goldwater scholars.

subject: Karacaahmet Cemetery
summary: Seven centuries of Ottoman and Turkish history rest beneath the cypress groves of Üsküdar — the largest cemetery in Turkey by number of interred, a place so dense with trees and shadow that Western visitors have compared it to a dark forest.

subject: Karachi Harbour
summary: From a cluster of 25 huts called Kolachi-jo-Goth to Pakistan's busiest seaport, Karachi Harbour has been shaped by Balochi settlers, Ottoman sailors, Qasimi pirates, and the British East India Company across thirteen centuries.

subject: Karachi Nuclear Power Complex
summary: Pakistan's first nuclear power plant began as a Cold War balancing act between Canada and South Asia, and has evolved over fifty years from a single small reactor to a three-unit complex on the Arabian Sea coast.

story.title: Karet Bivak: Where Jakarta Stacks Its History

subject: Karet Bivak
summary: Jakarta's second-largest cemetery holds 48,000 graves in 16 hectares, where families bury relatives on top of each other to cope with the city's chronic shortage of burial space, and where a controversial government program replaced thousands of gravestones -- sometimes misspelling the names of the dead.

subject: Karijini National Park
summary: In the deep red canyons of Karijini, you are standing on some of the oldest rock on Earth — a fragment of the planet's original crust, preserved for 3.5 billion years in the Pilbara desert.

subject: Karoo Desert National Botanical Garden
summary: At the foot of the Hex River Mountains, one of South Africa's nine national botanical gardens cultivates nearly 3,000 succulent species across 154 hectares, preserving the strange beauty of plants adapted to survive where almost nothing else can.

subject: Karoo National Park
summary: A 750-square-kilometer sanctuary of semi-desert plains and mountain passes just outside Beaufort West, sheltering more tortoise species than any other park on Earth alongside springbok herds, black eagles, and fossils dating back hundreds of millions of years.

subject: Kasanka National Park
summary: A small Zambian park that hosts the largest mammal migration on Earth, when ten million fruit bats descend on a single patch of swamp forest each November.

subject: Katavi National Park
summary: Tanzania's third-largest national park, reachable only by small aircraft, where hundreds of hippos crowd the last pools of the Katuma River each dry season.

subject: Katy Trail State Park
summary: The longest continuous rail trail in the United States stretches 240 miles along the Missouri River, following the route of Lewis and Clark on a crushed limestone path built on an abandoned railroad bed.

subject: Katyn Polish War Cemetery
summary: A cemetery built where the killing took place, opened by the children of those who survived for the fathers who did not.

story.title: Kawashimo: The Town That Kept Its Shape

subject: Kawashimo
summary: On the banks of the Sacramento River, a five-acre block of wooden storefronts built by Japanese immigrants in 1916 still stands exactly as it appeared in period photographs -- a neighborhood emptied by executive order, filled by new arrivals, and never demolished.

story.title: Kearney Park: A Raisin King's Utopia in the Dust

subject: Kearney Park
summary: The 225-acre park west of Fresno began as one man's vision of cooperative farming - an agricultural colony where middle-class families could own land without ruinous debt, built around a ranch headquarters that survives today as a museum.

story.title: Keio University: The School That Taught Japan to Think Differently

subject: Keio University
summary: Founded in 1858 by Fukuzawa Yukichi -- the man on Japan's 10,000-yen note -- Keio is Japan's oldest private university and an institution whose graduates have shaped the country's politics, industry, and culture for more than 160 years.

subject: Kelley Park
summary: A 156-acre San Jose park where a former mayor's farm became a children's zoo, a Japanese garden modeled after one in Okayama, a history museum, and a walnut-orchard disc golf course, all threaded together by Coyote Creek.

subject: Kelly Ingram Park
summary: The four-acre Birmingham park where children faced fire hoses and police dogs in May 1963, producing images that shocked the world and helped pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

story.title: Kembang Kuning: Where the Java Sea Gives Up Its Names

subject: Kembang Kuning
summary: More than five thousand war dead rest in this Surabaya cemetery, anchored by a monument to the 918 Dutch sailors lost in the Battle of the Java Sea -- though only three of them are actually buried here.

subject: Kenai Fjords National Park
summary: Where the Harding Icefield meets the Gulf of Alaska, tidewater glaciers calve into fjords teeming with whales, sea lions, and puffins.

subject: Kennedy Range National Park
summary: A 150-kilometre sandstone mesa rising from the red Gascoyne plains, its sheer eastern wall slashed by gorges that hold cool shade and 20,000 years of human history.

subject: Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39
summary: Originally conceived as the launch site for Apollo's lunar missions, Launch Complex 39 at Kennedy Space Center has served as the departure point for every American astronaut bound for the Moon and every Space Shuttle flight, and now hosts both NASA's Artemis rockets and SpaceX's Falcon fleet.

story.title: Pad 39A: The Most Storied Launch Pad on Earth

subject: Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A
summary: From the Apollo 11 moonshot to the final Space Shuttle flight to SpaceX's Falcon Heavy maiden voyage, Launch Complex 39A has hosted more historic launches than any other pad in the world -- and it is still adding to the list.

subject: Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex
summary: What began as card-table displays in a trailer has become one of America's most visited museums, where real spacecraft and the stories of the people who flew them bring six decades of space exploration to life on Merritt Island.

subject: Kenneth Kaunda International Airport
summary: Zambia's largest airport, renamed in 2011 for the country's founding president and rebuilt with a $360 million Chinese loan, handles three-quarters of the nation's passenger traffic.

story.title: Kensal Green Cemetery: London's First Garden of the Dead

subject: Kensal Green Cemetery
summary: Inspired by Paris's Pere Lachaise, Kensal Green opened in 1833 as the first of London's 'Magnificent Seven' cemeteries -- a place where Grecian architecture, Gothic monuments, and a canalside setting transformed burial from grim necessity into landscaped spectacle.

subject: Kenting National Park
summary: At Taiwan's southernmost tip, Kenting National Park packs coral limestone cliffs, tropical forest, turquoise beaches, and one of the world's great migratory bird corridors into a peninsula the size of a small city.

story.title: Kepulauan Togean: The Islands Where Jellyfish Forgot How to Sting

subject: Kepulauan Togean
summary: In the heart of the Coral Triangle, 56 islands straddle the invisible boundary between Asian and Oceanian life, harboring stingless jellyfish lakes, sea nomad villages, and the greatest coral diversity on Earth.

subject: Kerch Railway Bridge
summary: The longest bridge in the Soviet Union stood for only a single winter before drifting ice tore it apart - a hurried wartime span across the Kerch Strait built on materials left by a retreating enemy.

subject: Kettle Creek Battlefield
summary: On a winter morning in 1779, a force of Georgia and South Carolina militia ambushed 600 Loyalists butchering cattle along Kettle Creek, killing their commander and shattering British hopes of controlling Georgia's interior during the Revolutionary War.

subject: Keweenaw National Historical Park
summary: A national park spread across Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula that preserves 7,000 years of copper mining history, from prehistoric aboriginal miners to the industrial giants whose company towns still stand as living communities.

story.title: Key West Cemetery: I Told You I Was Sick

subject: Key West Cemetery
summary: A 19-acre cemetery at the foot of Solares Hill where 100,000 souls rest on an island of 30,000 living -- with above-ground vaults, Civil War sailors, USS Maine victims, and the driest humor in any graveyard in America.

subject: Keyuan Garden
summary: Completed in 1850 by a retired Qing official who loved poetry, chess, and stone collecting, Keyuan Garden in Dongguan is one of the Four Great Gardens of Guangdong — and the place where Lingnan-style painting, a major school of Chinese art, first took root.

subject: Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park
summary: Africa's first transfrontier park erases the border between Botswana and South Africa across 38,000 square kilometers of red Kalahari dunes, where black-maned lions hunt gemsbok and the silence is so complete it feels like pressure.

subject: Khalid Nabi Cemetery
summary: A mountain ridge cemetery in Iran's Golestan Province where over 600 enigmatic standing stones rise from the grass, drawing pilgrims, archaeologists, and curious tourists to a site tied to a pre-Islamic prophet.

subject: Khao Phra Wihan National Park
summary: Perched on a red sandstone cliff at the Thai-Cambodian frontier, Khao Phra Wihan National Park guards Khmer ruins more than a millennium old — and a border dispute that has never fully cooled.

subject: Khartoum International Airport
summary: Sudan's main international gateway was closed by war for two and a half years after April 2023, reopened in October 2025 under drone attack, and still flies scheduled traffic between Khartoum and Port Sudan.

subject: Khe Gát Airfield
summary: A runway scraped into the limestone of Quảng Bình in seven months, then left empty for three years — because it was only ever meant to be used once.

subject: Kibale Forest National Park
summary: A 795-square-kilometer pocket of equatorial rainforest in western Uganda harbors the highest density of primates on Earth, with 13 species sharing a canopy that has been continuously inhabited for thousands of years.

subject: Kiel Canal
summary: Ninety-eight kilometres of freshwater cut across Schleswig-Holstein carry more ships than any other artificial seaway on Earth — and were dug so a battle fleet would never have to sail past Danish guns.

subject: Kilimanjaro National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site protecting Africa's highest peak and every ecological zone from tropical forest to arctic ice, all within a single national park.

subject: Kilkenny College
summary: Founded in 1538 by an Earl of Ormond, this Church of Ireland school taught Jonathan Swift, George Berkeley, William Congreve, and the surgeon who gave his name to the Colles fracture.

subject: Killarney National Park
summary: Ireland's first national park protects the country's only mainland red deer herd, one of Europe's rarest yew woodlands, and a landscape where Bronze Age copper miners, Guinness heirs, and American millionaires have all left their mark.

subject: Killarney Provincial Park
summary: A wilderness park on Georgian Bay where white quartzite ridges glow against boreal forests, saved from logging by painters who loved it too much to let it vanish.

subject: Killary Harbour
summary: A 16-kilometre glacial inlet often called Ireland's only fjord, where Atlantic seals share the water with mussel rafts, and a famine relief road still traces the southern shore.

subject: Kilmarnock Railway Station
summary: An early survivor of the Scottish railway age, Kilmarnock's station sits beneath a twenty-three-arch viaduct that has dominated the town's skyline since the 1840s.

subject: Kimberley Marine Park
summary: A 74,469-square-kilometre marine park off the northwestern coast of Australia that holds the second-richest demersal fish communities on the continent and serves as a critical highway for humpback whales.

subject: Kinabalu Park
summary: Malaysia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site harbors more than 4,500 species across four climate zones on a mountain that still grows five millimeters every year.

subject: Kinchega National Park
summary: A former vast sheep station on the Darling River at Menindee, where the Menindee Lakes, paddle-steamer history and teeming birdlife now belong to everyone.

subject: King William's College
summary: A Manx boarding school whose 17th-century bequest, royal namesake, and famously brutal Christmas quiz have all made it into the pages of The Guardian.

subject: King's College Chapel, Aberdeen
summary: A medieval chapel crowned by an imperial crown of stone, home to some of the finest 16th-century woodwork in Scotland and a war memorial that names 342 dead without rank or title.

subject: King's College London
summary: Founded in 1829 by Anglicans alarmed at a 'godless college in Gower Street' and now a Russell Group university on the Strand, King's counts 14 Nobel laureates, two Speakers of the Commons, three Oscar winners, and an early-19th-century duel among its origin stories.

subject: King's College, Aberdeen
summary: Bishop Elphinstone founded a university in 1495 to cure ignorance in the north of Scotland - and its crown-topped chapel still rises above Old Aberdeen 531 years later.

subject: King's College, Cambridge
summary: King's College was founded by a king who never finished building it, completed by two later kings with different agendas, and is now known worldwide for a Christmas service that began during wartime with its windows blacked out.

subject: King's College, Hong Kong
summary: A declared monument since 2011, King's College is one of Hong Kong's oldest government schools — its red-brick neo-classical building on Bonham Road has survived war, occupation, and redevelopment to shape generations of the city's leaders.

subject: King's Cross railway accident
summary: On a winter evening in 1945, a heavily loaded express to Leeds slipped to a halt inside Gasworks Tunnel, rolled silently back into King's Cross station - and crushed the carriage carrying Cecil Kimber, the man who built MG.

subject: King's Park, Hong Kong
summary: A hillside district in the heart of Kowloon, King's Park has been layered over by successive eras of Hong Kong history — a British military hospital, cricket and rugby grounds, a Hong Kong Observatory station, and a neighborhood that quietly resisted the commercial redevelopment that erased so much around it.

subject: Kings Mountain National Military Park
summary: On a wooded Carolina ridge in October 1780, frontier riflemen surrounded a Loyalist army, killed its commander on the spot, and turned the Revolution south.

subject: Kinshasa Zoological Garden
summary: Founded in 1933 in the heart of Kinshasa, this zoo has survived colonial rule, independence, two Congo wars, and decades of neglect -- its oldest residents, a pair of crocodiles named Simon and Antoinette, have been there since 1938.

subject: Kintampo Complex
summary: Four thousand years ago, agropastoralists from the drying Sahara settled in central Ghana, creating the Kintampo culture -- West Africa's first settled food-producing society south of the Sahel, whose stone tools, pottery, and oil palm cultivation mark a turning point in the region's prehistory.

subject: Kirk Michael Railway Station
summary: A red sandstone station that once served Glen Wyllin Pleasure Grounds, now home to the village fire brigade and still standing largely as it did when trains last ran.

subject: Kistefos Museum and Sculpture Park
summary: On the banks of the Randselva river in rural Norway, a 19th-century wood pulp mill has been transformed into one of Europe's most striking sculpture parks, crowned by The Twist -- a museum that is also a bridge, designed by Bjarke Ingels Group.

subject: Kit Carson Park
summary: Escondido's largest park — 285 acres named for the scout who fought nearby — contains a 22,000-square-foot skate park, three ponds, a 3,000-seat amphitheater, and the only sculpture garden in the United States by artist Niki de Saint Phalle.

subject: Kitty Coleman Provincial Park
summary: A ten-hectare beach park on the Comox Valley shore, named for a We Wai Kai woman who spent her last years living alone on this sand, selling fish and berries.

story.title: Kiyosumi Garden: A Shipping Magnate's Stone Collection

subject: Kiyosumi Garden
summary: Iwasaki Yataro, the founder of Mitsubishi, used his steamship fleet to haul magnificent boulders from every corner of Japan to build a stroll garden in Tokyo's Fukagawa district -- a garden that would later shelter thousands from the fires of the 1923 earthquake.

subject: Koh Rong Marine National Park
summary: Cambodia's first marine national park protects 524 square kilometres of reef, seagrass and nesting beach — and was declared a year before anyone was hired to patrol it.

subject: Kohima War Cemetery
summary: A hillside cemetery in northeast India marks the site where a tennis court became the stage for one of World War II's most brutal and decisive battles.

subject: Koishikawa Botanical Garden
summary: A living botanical archive dating to 1684, where a shogun's medicinal herb garden evolved into Japan's birthplace of modern botany and still shelters a descendant of Newton's apple tree.

subject: Koli National Park
summary: Finland's most iconic landscape, where painters and composers found the soul of a nation on the shores of Lake Pielinen.

story.title: Komodo National Park: Kingdom of the Dragon

subject: Komodo National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands where the world's largest lizard hunts deer in savanna grasslands, while the surrounding waters harbor some of Earth's richest coral reef ecosystems.

subject: Kon Ka Kinh National Park
summary: Perched on the Kon Tum Plateau of Vietnam's Central Highlands, Kon Ka Kinh National Park shelters one of Southeast Asia's most biodiverse forest ecosystems — where gibbons call from ancient trees and rivers split to feed two different oceans.

subject: Korup National Park
summary: One of Africa's oldest tropical rainforests, Korup National Park in coastal Cameroon covers 1,260 square kilometers of mostly undisturbed forest where 161 mammal species -- including drills, chimpanzees, and red colobus monkeys -- inhabit terrain that nutrient-poor soils have protected from agriculture for millennia.

subject: Kouchibouguac National Park
summary: A national park born from forced displacement, where barrier islands and seal colonies share the coast with a painful human story that changed Canadian conservation law forever.

subject: Kowloon Park
summary: A 13-hectare oasis in the heart of Tsim Sha Tsui — built on the ruins of a British barracks, still guarded by flamingoes and a swimming pool that draws a million visitors a year.

subject: Kowloon Railway Station (KCR) & Clock Tower
summary: The elegant red-brick terminus that once connected Kowloon to Canton survived demolition by the slimmest of margins — only its Clock Tower still stands on the original waterfront site.

subject: Kowloon Walled City Park
summary: Where tens of thousands of people once lived in one of the world's densest urban settlements, a tranquil Qing-dynasty garden now stands — and the layers beneath it still hold the story.

subject: Koygorodsky National Park
summary: One of the last great expanses of virgin southern taiga in Europe, Koygorodsky National Park shelters ancient spruce forests that have never known an axe.

subject: Kranji War Cemetery
summary: On a hillside in northern Singapore, 4,461 Commonwealth war dead rest beneath white headstones, their graves gathered from across the island after World War II ended.

subject: Krefeld Zoo
summary: A small Rhineland zoo that became, on a single New Year's Eve, the site of one of the most haunting accidents in modern European wildlife history.

subject: Krka National Park
summary: A Dalmatian river carves through limestone and living moss to build its own waterfalls, while a 19th-century power plant hidden in the canyon once lit a city before Niagara did the same.

subject: Kromlau Azalea and Rhododendron Park
summary: An eighty-hectare park in Sorbian Upper Lusatia built around a basalt bridge engineered so that its reflection closes the arch into a perfect stone circle.

subject: Kruger National Park
summary: South Africa's flagship safari destination stretches across two million hectares of bushveld - home to the Big Five and accessible enough to explore independently in your own vehicle.

subject: Kuala Lumpur railway station
summary: A masterpiece of Indo-Saracenic architecture completed in 1917, Kuala Lumpur's old railway station once served as the city's transportation heart before becoming a heritage landmark and railway museum.

subject: Kubota Garden
summary: A 20-acre Japanese garden in Seattle's Rainier Beach, born from swampland by a Japanese immigrant who shaped beauty even during internment -- and whose vision outlasted every obstacle.

subject: Kumeyaay Community College
summary: The only American Indian college in California was founded with Sycuan gaming revenue in 2004 — and it exists in part because an ethnohistorian left her archives to a Kumeyaay institution that didn't yet exist.

subject: Kurjenrahka National Park
summary: A national park built around a bog that grew upward until it lost touch with the groundwater, and a boundary stone where the edges of eight parishes once met.

subject: Kursaal Amusement Park
summary: Beneath a great Edwardian dome in Southend-on-Sea, one of the world's first purpose-built amusement parks once roared with rollercoasters, ballroom bands, and a footballing greyhound called Self Starter.

story.title: Kutai: Where the Rainforest Holds the Line

subject: Kutai
summary: Straddling the equator on Borneo's east coast, Kutai National Park shelters one of the world's richest lowland rainforests -- and the scars of everything that has tried to destroy it.

subject: Kutini-Payamu (Iron Range) National Park
summary: Australia's largest lowland tropical rainforest, where New Guinea's wildlife crosses an ancient land bridge into Cape York, on Kuuku Ya'u country.

story.title: The University That Spells Its Own Name Wrong (On Purpose)

subject: Kwansei Gakuin University
summary: Founded by an American Methodist missionary in 1889, Kwansei Gakuin keeps an archaic spelling of 'Kansai' as a badge of honor, houses its campus in Spanish Mission buildings designed by another American, and fields the most dominant college football team in Japanese history.

subject: Kyoto Railway Museum
summary: Japan's largest railway museum spans 31,000 square meters in Kyoto's Shimogyo ward, housing 53 real train cars and a 1914 roundhouse that is itself a designated Important Cultural Property.

subject: Kyoto University
summary: Japan's second-oldest university and a powerhouse of Nobel Prize achievement, Kyoto University was founded in 1897 with war reparations and built its identity on the radical idea of academic freedom.

story.title: Kyu Shiba Rikyu Garden: Built on Reclaimed Sea

subject: Kyū Shiba Rikyū Garden
summary: One of only four surviving Edo-period clan gardens in Tokyo, Kyu Shiba Rikyu was built on land reclaimed from Tokyo Bay in the 1650s -- a samurai estate that passed through shoguns, imperial hands, earthquake fire, and urban encroachment to survive as a quiet oasis hemmed in by skyscrapers.

story.title: Kyu-Furukawa Gardens: Where England Meets Edo in a Single Hillside

subject: Kyū-Furukawa Gardens
summary: A Western mansion and geometric rose garden designed by the 'father of Japanese modern architecture' share a hillside in northern Tokyo with a tranquil Japanese garden whose pond was shaped to trace the character for 'heart.'

story.title: Kyu-Iwasaki-tei Garden: The Mitsubishi Mansion That Almost Disappeared

subject: Kyū-Iwasaki-tei Garden
summary: The 1896 estate of Mitsubishi's third president blends Jacobean England, a Swiss chalet, and Edo-period Japanese design across a 17,000-square-meter property that once held over twenty buildings -- only three of which survived postwar demolition.

subject: Kéran National Park
summary: Once a thriving ecotourism model with elephant herds and South African-built lodges, Oti-Keran National Park in northern Togo was devastated by political upheaval in 1990 -- its wildlife slaughtered, its infrastructure ruined -- and now struggles to recover as a haven for 214 bird species and a link in West Africa's largest transboundary conservation corridor.

subject: Kılıç Ali Pasha Complex
summary: In Tophane, a mosque built on a reef in the Bosphorus by a 16th-century admiral — and completed by an architect in his nineties — stands as one of Mimar Sinan's most personal and improbable masterworks.

subject: Kōkeʻe State Park
summary: A mist-wrapped plateau on Kauai's northwest coast where native koa and ohia forests shelter some of Hawaii's rarest birds, and lookouts peer into valleys once home to thousands of Native Hawaiians.

subject: La Amistad International Park
summary: A binational wilderness straddling the Costa Rica-Panama border, La Amistad protects more than 570,000 hectares of the Talamanca Range -- the largest nature reserve in Central America and a UNESCO World Heritage Site harboring nearly four percent of Earth's terrestrial species.

subject: La Campana (archaeological site)
summary: The largest prehispanic population center in western Mexico, where shaft tombs, storm drains, and a pyramid shaped like a volcano reveal a civilization that thrived for over two thousand years in the Valley of Colima.

subject: La Campana National Park
summary: Charles Darwin climbed its peak in 1834 and never forgot the view; today the park shelters the world's great surviving forest of the Chilean wine palm.

subject: La Colonia de Eden Gardens
summary: A neighborhood in Solana Beach founded by Mexican farmworkers in the 1920s, La Colonia de Eden Gardens has weathered drug violence, community collapse, and slow renewal — a story of resilience anchored by restaurants, neighbors, and stubborn local pride.

subject: La Demajagua National Park
summary: At a ruined sugar mill near Manzanillo, a plantation owner rang a bronze bell, freed his enslaved workers, and ignited Cuba's first war for independence from Spain.

subject: La Fontaine Park
summary: Named not for its famous fountain but for Quebec's first francophone prime minister, this Montreal park grew from a military drill ground into the cultural heart of Le Plateau-Mont-Royal.

subject: La Galgada
summary: A preceramic ceremonial site where the dead were buried flexed and wrapped, a mayor protected it from looters, and an archaeologist realized it was older than he had guessed.

subject: La Garma cave complex
summary: Sealed by a rockslide 16,000 years ago, La Garma's Lower Gallery preserves one of the most pristine Paleolithic living floors ever discovered, complete with cave lion pelts, hand stencils, and mysterious Visigothic burials.

subject: La Grange Historic District (North Carolina)
summary: The Lenoir County tobacco-market town whose railroad-line storefronts and Queen Anne houses tell the rise, brief glory, and slow erosion of a small Carolina market town.

subject: La Jolla Complex
summary: The La Jolla Complex was a prehistoric archaeological culture that occupied the San Diego coast and Baja California from around 8000 BC to AD 500 — shellfish gatherers whose presence was confirmed by two 9,500-year-old skeletons that sparked a decade-long legal battle before being repatriated to the Kumeyaay.

subject: La Malinche National Park
summary: A dormant volcano draped in pine forests where aspiring mountaineers train their legs and lungs before tackling Mexico's higher peaks, La Malinche stands as a gentle giant on the border of Tlaxcala and Puebla.

subject: La Mauricie National Park
summary: One hundred and fifty lakes fill the ancient hills of the southern Canadian Shield, where boreal forest meets deciduous woodland and the ghosts of exclusive hunting clubs linger in converted lodges.

subject: La Ronde (amusement park)
summary: Built as the late-night playground of Expo 67, Montreal's island amusement park outlived the World's Fair by nearly six decades and became Quebec's largest thrill ride destination.

subject: Labuan War Cemetery
summary: The resting place of 3,922 Commonwealth soldiers in Borneo, many of whom survived the Sandakan Death Marches only to perish before liberation.

subject: Lachine Canal
summary: Named for the dream of reaching China, this 14.5-kilometre canal turned Montreal into a port, powered Canada's largest industrial corridor, and then reinvented itself as a National Historic Site.

subject: Ladysmith Harbour
summary: A sheltered Vancouver Island inlet that lost its name to a colonial war on another continent, gained a coal port, and quietly recorded its own water temperature every single day for two decades.

subject: Lagan Canal
summary: A 27-mile Georgian canal that connected Belfast to Lough Neagh, funded by a tax on whiskey, abandoned in 1958, and partly buried under the M1 motorway in 1965.

subject: Lagoa do Peixe National Park
summary: A thread of dunes and shallow water on Brazil's southern coast that serves as a continental crossroads for shorebirds flying between Patagonia and the Arctic, and the only home in Brazil for resident flamingos.

subject: Laguna San Rafael National Park
summary: Where the Northern Patagonian Ice Field meets the Pacific, a massive glacier calves into a turquoise lagoon while 6,000 millimeters of annual precipitation feed one of Earth's most dramatic wilderness areas.

story.title: Laguna de La Restinga National Park

subject: Laguna de La Restinga National Park
summary: A salt-water lagoon on Margarita Island where mangrove channels hide endemic wildlife, oyster-covered roots, and Venezuela's longest beach stretches 15 kilometers along a Caribbean sandbar.

story.title: Lagunas de Chacahua: The Lagoons at the End of the Road

subject: Lagunas de Chacahua National Park
summary: Accessible only by boat across a crocodile-inhabited lagoon, this national park on Oaxaca's Pacific coast covers 132 square kilometers and protects interconnected waterways, ten distinct vegetation types, and a fishing village where bioluminescent waters glow beneath moonless skies.

story.title: Lagunas de Montebello: Fifty-Nine Lakes in Every Color the Earth Can Make

subject: Lagunas de Montebello National Park
summary: A national park on Mexico's southern border with Guatemala where 59 lakes shimmer in colors ranging from aquamarine to deep purple - a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve now fighting to preserve the water chemistry that makes each lake a different shade.

subject: Lahaina Banyan Court Park
summary: A 1.94-acre park built on the ruins of a coral fort, sheltered by the largest banyan tree in Hawaii, where whaling-era cannons once aimed at drunken sailors and the Hawaiian flag was lowered for the last time.

subject: Lahaina Historic District
summary: A National Historic Landmark District that once preserved the character of a 19th-century whaling port and Hawaiian royal capital, Lahaina's historic core suffered catastrophic losses in the 2023 wildfires.

subject: Lahaina, Kaanapali and Pacific Railroad
summary: The Sugar Cane Train once hauled tourists along six miles of historic narrow-gauge track on Maui, crossing a 325-foot curved wooden trestle with views of three islands -- until the 2023 Lahaina wildfire and a 2025 Kaanapali fire destroyed much of what remained.

subject: Lajeado State Park
summary: A cerrado plateau guarding the water supply of Brazil's youngest state capital, where jaguars still walk past ancient cave paintings eighteen kilometers from downtown Palmas.

subject: Lake Bindegolly National Park
summary: A chain of desert lakes near Thargomindah that draws thousands of waterbirds and shelters a gnarled wattle found almost nowhere else.

subject: Lake Bronson State Park
summary: In a Minnesota county with no natural lakes, Depression-era workers built a dam on quicksand to create a reservoir that became so beloved the nearby town renamed itself after the water -- Lake Bronson State Park, now on the National Register of Historic Places.

story.title: Lake Jackson Mounds Archaeological State Park

subject: Lake Jackson Mounds Archaeological State Park
summary: The capital of a pre-Columbian chiefdom on the shores of Lake Jackson in Tallahassee, where seven earthwork mounds once anchored a Fort Walton Culture ceremonial center linked by trade and ritual to distant Mississippian powers across the Southeast.

subject: Lake Malawi National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site protecting the world's most diverse freshwater fish population, where 700 species of cichlid have evolved in a single lake like Darwin's finches beneath the surface.

subject: Lake Nakuru National Park
summary: A fenced sanctuary in Kenya's Rift Valley where two million flamingos turn a saline lake pink, and endangered black rhinos roam among euphorbia forests under the watchful cliffs of Baboon Point.

subject: Lake Newland Conservation Park
summary: A 20-kilometre chain of salt lakes pinned behind a wall of marching dunes, the largest wetland on the Eyre Peninsula and the setting for one of South Australia's most significant Aboriginal songlines.

subject: Lake Superior Provincial Park
summary: Where ancient Canadian Shield rock meets the world's largest freshwater lake, a provincial park preserves the wild coast and deep canyons that inspired the Group of Seven.

subject: Lake Superior Railroad Museum
summary: Housed in Duluth's restored 1892 French Chateauesque train depot, this museum preserves the locomotive that pulled Minnesota's first passenger train in 1862 alongside one of the largest steam engines ever built.

story.title: Lake Vermilion-Soudan Underground Mine State Park

subject: Lake Vermilion-Soudan Underground Mine State Park
summary: Minnesota's oldest, deepest, and richest iron mine descends 2,341 feet into the Precambrian Shield -- and half a mile below the headframe, physicists once hunted for dark matter and neutrinos in the silence between the rock walls.

subject: Lake View Cemetery (Seattle)
summary: Seattle's Pioneer Cemetery holds the founders who built the city, the martial artist who changed cinema, and a monument raised with dollar bills by Japanese American families honoring sons who never came home from war.

subject: Lake Washington Ship Canal
summary: The eight-mile waterway that threads through Seattle connecting Lake Washington to Puget Sound, an engineering feat that reversed a river and reshaped the city's geography.

subject: Lam Tsuen Country Park
summary: Divided by a single road into two distinct mountain ranges, Lam Tsuen Country Park has guarded the green north of Hong Kong's New Territories since 1979 — a landscape of high ridges, working valleys, and peaks that reach above 500 metres just kilometres from the city's edge.

subject: Lamington Black Cemetery
summary: A small African American cemetery in Bedminster Township where 97 known graves, many marked only by plain fieldstones, trace a community's history from enslavement through the Civil War.

subject: Lampang Airfield Complex
summary: A sprawling network of four World War II airfields built by the Imperial Japanese Army in northern Thailand's Lampang province -- once a staging ground for the defense of Burma and the invasion of India, now largely reclaimed by rice paddies and forest.

subject: Lampi Island Marine National Park
summary: Myanmar's first marine national park, where camera traps in the Mergui Archipelago reveal pangolins, slow lorises, and flying squirrels sharing an island with coral reefs and mangroves.

subject: Land's End Airport
summary: Britain's most south-westerly airport has been ferrying passengers across the Atlantic gap to the Isles of Scilly since 1937, in aircraft so small they once landed on a golf course.

subject: Landwehr Canal
summary: Prussia's greatest garden designer cut a ten-kilometre shortcut across Berlin, and the century that followed filled it with everything the city could not keep: a murdered revolutionary, a flooded tunnel, a hijacked pleasure steamer.

subject: Langemark German war cemetery
summary: More than 44,000 German soldiers lie under a small Belgian field at Langemark, including 24,917 in a single mass grave called Kameradengrab - the comrades' grave.

subject: Lanin National Park
summary: An Argentine park crowned by the near-perfect cone of Lanin volcano, sacred to the Mapuche, and carpeted with the monkey-puzzle forests their people have eaten from for centuries.

subject: Lapakahi State Historical Park
summary: The ruins of a 600-year-old Hawaiian fishing village on the arid Kohala coast, where stone walls, salt pans, and canoe sheds still trace the rhythms of an ancient community.

subject: Las Mercedes (archaeological site, Costa Rica)
summary: A gold artifact found during railroad construction in 1871 revealed a 3,000-year-old political capital of the Huetar people - 25 hectares of platforms, causeways, and stone-paved roads on Costa Rica's Caribbean slope.

subject: Lassen Volcanic National Park
summary: The only place in the world where all four volcano types meet, with steaming fumaroles, wolves returning after a century, and possibly the snowiest spot in California.

subject: Lauca National Park
summary: A 1,379-square-kilometer high-altitude wilderness in Chile's far north where emerald lakes mirror volcanic peaks and vicuna herds graze at 4,500 meters.

subject: Laurel Garden Arena
summary: A converted Newark beer hall that became one of New Jersey's most storied boxing and wrestling venues, hosting champions from James J. Braddock to Jersey Joe Walcott before its demolition in the 1950s.

subject: Laurinburg-Maxton Army Air Base
summary: The world's largest glider pilot training base, where young men learned to fly aircraft with no engines, then crash-landed them behind enemy lines from Normandy to Burma.

subject: Lavushi Manda National Park
summary: A 1,500 square-kilometer Zambian park where the last wild black rhino in the country was seen in the 1980s, now run on budgets measured in hundreds of dollars and rebuilt one wire-snare arrest at a time.

subject: Leadville Historic District
summary: A National Historic Landmark District where 67 mines, opera houses, scandal-soaked mansions, and the Old West's most documented Boot Hill cemetery preserve the raw drama of Colorado's silver boom at 10,000 feet.

subject: Leeds Bradford Airport
summary: West Yorkshire's main gateway, opened in 1931 on Yeadon moor and once home to a camouflaged Avro factory that built nearly 700 Lancaster bombers.

story.title: Leeuwarden Achter de Hoven railway station

subject: Leeuwarden Achter de Hoven railway station
summary: For decades the least-used station in the Netherlands - ten passengers a day, no name on the rail map, demolished in 2019.

subject: Leeuwarden Air Base
summary: From Luftwaffe outpost to NATO F-35 hub, the air base on the Frisian flats has been retooled for every fighter generation since 1938.

subject: Legislative Council Complex
summary: Hong Kong's first purpose-built legislature — opened in 2011 on the Tamar waterfront, stormed by protesters in 2019, and now undergoing a contentious expansion — embodies the territory's turbulent political journey.

story.title: Lei Yue Mun Park and Holiday Village

subject: Lei Yue Mun Park and Holiday Village
summary: A 22-hectare former British military fortress on the eastern tip of Hong Kong Island — scene of a brutal night in December 1941, later transformed into a government holiday village where families now stay in the old soldiers' quarters.

subject: Leiden Centraal railway station
summary: Four stations across 180 years on the same patch of land, where Freud once met Mahler and Einstein arrived to argue physics.

subject: Leiden University
summary: The oldest surviving university in the Netherlands, born from a siege in 1575, where helium was first liquefied and where doctoral candidates still sweat their defences in a tiny signed-walled room.

subject: Leiden University Library
summary: Founded with a single donated Bible in 1575, Leiden University Library now safeguards three thousand cuneiform tablets, the world's largest Indonesian collection, and seven entries in the UNESCO Memory of the World Register.

subject: Leimert Park
summary: Leimert Park is a historically Black Los Angeles neighborhood developed in 1928 with a master plan by the Olmsted Brothers. For decades it has served as the cultural center of African American life in the city, home to jazz venues, hip hop open mics, and artists who shaped American culture.

subject: Leipzig University
summary: Founded in 1409 by refugees from Prague, Germany's second-oldest continuously running university - alma mater of Goethe, Nietzsche, Leibniz, and ten Nobel laureates.

subject: Lemmenjoki National Park
summary: Finland's largest national park spans vast Arctic wilderness where gold panners still work river claims first staked over a century ago, reindeer outnumber people, and the Sami name means 'warm river' though the Finnish translation became 'river of love.'

subject: Lemurs' Park
summary: A small botanical garden and lemur sanctuary near Antananarivo where confiscated pet lemurs are rehabilitated for return to the wild, founded by the grandson of Madagascar's first zoo director.

subject: Lennon Wall (Hong Kong)
summary: What began as a staircase covered in Post-it notes near Hong Kong's Central Government Offices became one of the defining images of the 2014 Umbrella Movement — then returned, larger and more defiant, during the 2019 protests against an extradition bill.

subject: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park
summary: Once the rains stop, the lagoons between the dunes lose a metre of depth a month - a national park that spends half the year as a lake district and half as a desert that isn't one.

subject: Leo J. Ryan Memorial Park
summary: A Foster City park honoring Congressman Leo Ryan, the only sitting member of Congress ever assassinated -- killed at the Jonestown airstrip in 1978.

subject: Leofoo Village Theme Park
summary: Half theme park, half safari - Leofoo Village in Hsinchu County began as a wildlife park in 1979 and evolved into Taiwan's most eclectic amusement destination, where Bengal tigers roam a few hundred meters from an inverted roller coaster and an Arabian dark ride.

subject: Leonard J. Buck Garden
summary: A 33-acre rock garden in Far Hills where a geologist and a landscape architect spent decades sculpting a glacial ravine into one of America's premier naturalistic gardens, working entirely without drawings.

subject: Letchworth State Park
summary: The Seneca called it Sehgahunda - the Vale of the Three Falls - and believed the middle waterfall was so beautiful it made the sun stop at midday. A Buffalo industrialist saved it from development and gave it to New York.

subject: Letchworth-Love Mounds Archaeological State Park
summary: Deep in the Florida Panhandle, a 50-foot earthen mound built by the Swift Creek people nearly two millennia ago stands as the tallest prehistoric ceremonial structure in the state.

subject: Letterkenny University Hospital
summary: A Donegal hospital that traces back to an 1844 workhouse, saw Bill Clinton visit Seamus Heaney after a stroke, and was destroyed by flash flooding in July 2013 - then flooded again the following August.

subject: Levashovo Memorial Cemetery
summary: A wooded clearing outside Saint Petersburg holds the unmarked graves of nearly 20,000 victims of Stalin's terror, including 8,000 from the Great Terror alone.

subject: Lewis Ginter Botanical Garden
summary: From Powhatan hunting ground to Patrick Henry's land to bicycle club to baby sanatorium to one of America's top botanical gardens — fifty acres with a complicated arrival.

story.title: Lewis and Clark National Historical Park

subject: Lewis and Clark National Historical Park
summary: A network of sites across Oregon and Washington marking where the Corps of Discovery spent a miserable, rain-soaked winter after crossing a continent - and where America's westward ambition finally touched the Pacific.

subject: Lezama Park
summary: A shaded bluff in old San Telmo where, by tradition, Buenos Aires was first and disastrously founded in 1536, now a beloved park steeped in literature and time.

story.title: Li Po Chun United World College

subject: Li Po Chun United World College
summary: On a hillside above Tolo Harbour, a boarding school where students from over 110 countries share two years of study, service, and the belief that education can be a force for peace.

subject: Liang's Garden
summary: Four generations of the Liang family spent forty years building this classical Lingnan scholar-garden in Foshan — a place that nearly vanished, then was rescued to become one of Guangdong's four celebrated gardens.

subject: Lianhuashan Park
summary: A 150-hectare hilltop park in Shenzhen's Futian district, anchored by a six-meter bronze statue of Deng Xiaoping whose five-year journey from warehouse to hilltop mirrors the complicated story of the city he helped create.

story.title: Liberty Universalist Church and Feasterville Academy Historic District

subject: Liberty Universalist Church and Feasterville Academy Historic District
summary: A Pennsylvania Dunkard family migrated to the Carolina backcountry, drifted toward the radical doctrine that hell was empty, and built the only Universalist church South Carolina would have for generations.

subject: Liberty University
summary: The evangelical Christian university Jerry Falwell Sr. founded in 1971 as Lynchburg Baptist College, now one of the largest private universities in the United States, with about 15,000 residential students and roughly 80,000 online.

subject: Library of Trinity College Dublin
summary: Home to the Book of Kells and the 65-metre Long Room lined with 200,000 ancient volumes, Trinity College's library is Ireland's largest and one of the most celebrated repositories of knowledge in the world.

subject: Liesjärvi National Park
summary: One of Finland's oldest national parks, built around a gravel ridge left by a river that ran underneath a glacier - and a forest ranger's farmstead still worked the way it was in 1910.

subject: Lihué Calel National Park
summary: An island of purple-granite hills rising from the dry La Pampa plain, sheltering ancient rock paintings and a surprising abundance of desert life.

subject: Lijssenthoek Military Cemetery
summary: 10,785 graves at the end of the hospital train line - the largest casualty clearing station cemetery on the Western Front.

story.title: Lille 2 University of Health and Law

subject: Lille 2 University of Health and Law
summary: For 47 years, a French university with 24,000 students taught law, medicine, pharmacy and sport in southern Lille, until a 2018 merger erased its name.

subject: Limahuli Garden and Preserve
summary: Named the best natural botanical garden in America, this Kauai valley preserve shelters ancient taro terraces, plants found nowhere else on Earth, and the mountain Hollywood called Bali Ha'i.

subject: Limmen National Park
summary: A vast Gulf wilderness of sandstone 'lost cities,' barramundi rivers and crocodile-thick water, where archaeologists found one of only three sites on Earth with miniature stencilled rock art.

subject: Lin Family Mansion and Garden
summary: Taiwan's most complete surviving traditional Chinese garden was built by a rice merchant's descendants who turned wealth into a private world of pavilions, ponds, and coded symbolism.

subject: Lincoln Beach amusement park
summary: A segregation-era amusement park on Lake Pontchartrain that gave Black New Orleanians a place to swim, ride, and hear Fats Domino play -- then vanished when the law that created the need for it finally changed.

subject: Lincoln Historic District (Lincoln, New Mexico)
summary: A single dusty street where Billy the Kid escaped the hangman, cattle barons waged war, and the frontier froze in place as America's best-preserved cow town.

subject: Lincoln Homestead and Cemetery
summary: The Virginia farmhouse and family cemetery of Abraham Lincoln's great-grandfather - alongside the grave of Queenie, a woman the Lincolns enslaved.

subject: Lingnan University
summary: A liberal arts university in Hong Kong's Tuen Mun district with roots stretching back to a Christian college founded in Canton in 1888 — dispersed by history, reconstituted by alumni, and still asking what it means to educate the whole person.

subject: Linköping University
summary: Where a retired Cray supercomputer serves as lobby furniture and students study next to Sweden's fastest AI computer, fighter jet research labs, and the world's best 3D dome theater.

subject: Lintianshan Forestry Culture Park
summary: A ghost town reborn as a heritage village, this former Japanese-era logging settlement in Hualien County preserves a century of forestry history through its dormitories, rail tracks, and the silence of mountains that were once stripped bare.

subject: Lion Rock Country Park
summary: The granite ridge that gave Hong Kong its defining symbol — a lion crouching above the city — forms the backbone of a 5.57-square-kilometer country park where mythology, natural history, and urban panoramas converge.

subject: Lippstadt Airfield
summary: A 1936 Luftwaffe airfield where the first fighters of the reborn German Air Force assembled, that absorbed 494 tons of Allied bombs in two raids in 1944, and whose ground has now been almost completely swallowed by suburb and business park.

subject: Litchfield National Park
summary: A 1,500-square-kilometre sanctuary in Australia's Top End where spring-fed waterfalls cascade off a sandstone plateau into clear plunge pools, magnetic termite mounds stand sentinel over the savanna, and the dry season brings visitors from across the continent to swim in water that feels, in the heat, like a gift.

subject: Litchfield National Park
summary: Named for a 19th-century explorer and home to ancient Aboriginal sacred landscapes, Litchfield National Park shelters permanent spring-fed waterfalls, rare bat colonies, magnetic termite mounds, and the haunting sandstone formations of the Lost City.

subject: Little Bighorn Battlefield
summary: Custer's last stand - where Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors annihilated five companies of the 7th Cavalry in 1876, the Native American victory that sealed their defeat.

subject: Little Bighorn Battlefield
summary: Custer's Last Stand - the Montana hillside where Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors annihilated five companies of the 7th Cavalry on June 25, 1876, killing George Armstrong Custer and creating an American legend.

subject: Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument
summary: Where white marble markers and red granite stones stand together on Montana's rolling hills, America remembers its most famous battle and finally honors both sides of the conflict.

subject: Little Qualicum Falls Provincial Park
summary: Where Cameron Lake empties into a rock gorge on central Vancouver Island - 440 hectares of old-growth Douglas-fir protected in 1940, four years before the more famous grove down the road.

subject: Liudui Hakka Cultural Park
summary: A 30-hectare park in Pingtung County celebrating the Hakka communities of southern Taiwan, built on land donated in 2009 from a 1961 tobacco barn estate.

subject: Liuwa Plain National Park
summary: A Zambian grassland where a solitary lioness guarded the plains alone for years, where a king's hunting ground became a national park, and where Africa's second-largest wildebeest migration still thunders across open savanna.

subject: Liverpool John Lennon Airport
summary: Painted on the roof of the terminal, in letters big enough to read from a 737 on approach, is the airport's motto: 'Above us, only sky.' In 2002, Liverpool's airport became the first in the United Kingdom to take the name of a person -- and chose the one whose words run across the building like a benediction.

subject: Liwonde National Park
summary: Malawi's premier wildlife park stretches along the Shire River, where elephants come to drink at dusk and hippos graze the camp lawns after dark.

subject: Llanganates National Park
summary: In the cloud forests and paramos of the Ecuadorian Andes lies one of the most searched-for, and never-found, treasures on Earth - Atahualpa's ransom gold, hidden here nearly five centuries ago.

subject: Llangollen Canal
summary: Forty-six miles of canal that should never have been built where it was - now one of Britain's most popular waterways and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Llangollen Railway
summary: A volunteer-run heritage railway that brought a Beeching-axed line back to life one foot of track at a time, finally reaching Corwen in 2023.

subject: Llanos de Challe National Park
