summary: In one of the driest places on Earth, a rare alignment of rain and seed turns the bare desert floor into a sheet of wildflowers, a phenomenon Chileans call the desierto florido.

subject: Llogara National Park
summary: Where the Ceraunian Mountains plunge toward the Ionian Sea, ancient pines bent into permanent flags by the wind mark the pass that Julius Caesar may have crossed in pursuit of Pompey.

subject: Llullaillaco National Park
summary: Surrounding the second-highest volcano on Earth, this remote Atacama park shelters Inca trails, salt plains at 5,060 meters, herds of vicunas, and a landscape so extreme that even its lowest point rivals the altitude of Lhasa.

subject: Loango National Park
summary: A 1,550-square-kilometer coastal park in Gabon where forest elephants walk on white sand beaches and hippos surf the Atlantic breakers, earning it the nickname 'Africa's Last Eden.'

subject: Loango Slavery Harbour
summary: A UNESCO Tentative World Heritage Site where more than two million enslaved Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas, now an overgrown memorial where mango trees still line the last path the captives walked.

subject: Lobéké National Park
summary: Part of the UNESCO-listed Sangha Trinational, this Cameroonian park protects some of Africa's densest populations of forest elephants and gorillas while fighting an underground trade in African grey parrots.

story.title: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park

subject: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
summary: Scotland's first national park, established in 2002, where the Highland Boundary Fault literally divides the landscape: Lowland green to the south, mountains to the north, with the largest lake in Great Britain stretching between them.

subject: Lochaber Narrow Gauge Railway
summary: The Old Puggy Line: an industrial railway built to drive a 15-mile water tunnel through Highland rock for the aluminium smelter at Fort William.

subject: Lochern National Park
summary: On the Thomson River floodplain west of Longreach, a former grazing run preserves an undisturbed slice of Channel Country - all four Mitchell grasses, and waterholes that pull in the birds.

subject: Lodi Gardens
summary: A 90-acre park in New Delhi where 15th-century royal tombs from the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties rise among manicured lawns, joggers, and picnickers -- the living layered over the dead.

subject: Lofotodden National Park
summary: Norway's youngest national park protects the dramatic southern tip of the Lofoten Wall, where volcanic peaks plunge into white-sand beaches and turquoise Arctic waters on the island of Moskenesøya.

subject: Lombrum Naval Base
summary: A sleepy patrol-boat base on Manus Island has become, quietly and suddenly, one of the most strategically watched pieces of real estate in the Indo-Pacific.

subject: Lommel German war cemetery
summary: More than 39,000 German soldiers lie in 16 hectares of Belgian pine forest - the largest German military cemetery in Western Europe, and a quiet answer to the question of what to do with the dead of an army that should not have come.

subject: Lomsdal–Visten National Park
summary: 1,102 square kilometres of Helgeland running fjord to summit, where rivers vanish into dolomite and reindeer herding is written into the park regulations.

subject: London Zoo
summary: The world's oldest scientific zoo, founded for study and opened to the curious public on the edge of Regent's Park.

subject: Long Harbour (Hong Kong)
summary: A forked sea inlet on Hong Kong's northeastern coast where the last car-free villages in Sai Kung cling to steep shores, connected to the outside world only by small ferries.

subject: Longleat Safari and Adventure Park
summary: A circus showman and a marquess gambled on an idea no one outside Africa had tried: let the lions run free, and let the visitors drive through them.

subject: Longreach Airport
summary: The outback airfield where Qantas built its first operational base, where England-to-Australia record flights touched down, and where American B-17s staged for the Battle of the Coral Sea.

subject: Longtan Lake Park
summary: A Ming dynasty brick quarry that filled with wastewater, redesigned in the 1950s by architect Liang Sicheng into one of Beijing's largest urban parks, complete with dragon boats, moon bridges, and a temple to a heroic Ming general.

subject: Loongana railway station
summary: A near-empty siding on the Nullarbor, Loongana marks one end of the longest dead-straight railway track on Earth.

subject: Lopé National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in central Gabon where 400,000 years of human history meet one of Africa's richest concentrations of wildlife in a landscape shaped by the last ice age.

subject: Lorentz National Park
summary: The largest national park in Southeast Asia climbs from tropical mangroves to equatorial glaciers in a single wild sweep across western New Guinea.

subject: Los Alerces National Park
summary: A pristine sweep of Patagonian forest where alerce trees have been growing since before the pyramids, sheltered between glacier-fed lakes and the Chilean frontier.

subject: Los Arrayanes National Park
summary: On a slender Patagonian peninsula grows one of the world's rare forests of cinnamon-barked myrtle, some trees centuries old, protected by a park created to save them.

subject: Los Cardones National Park
summary: A high-desert national park in northwestern Argentina where forests of giant cardon cacti stand among mountains that still hold dinosaur fossils from a vanished world.

subject: Los Gatos Creek Park
summary: A county park in Campbell, California, where a reshaped natural lake traces its origins to a nineteenth-century Mexican land grant and the Los Gatos Creek Trail connects Silicon Valley suburbs to the foothills of the Santa Cruz Mountains.

subject: Los Glaciares National Park
summary: Argentina's frozen kingdom where forty glaciers flow from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field - including Perito Moreno, one of the few advancing glaciers on Earth, which thunders and calves in explosions of ancient ice.

subject: Los Haitises National Park
summary: On the remote northeast coast of the Dominican Republic, hundreds of limestone mogotes rise from mangrove-fringed waters like a Caribbean version of Ha Long Bay, hiding caves covered in pre-Taino pictographs and sheltering the world's last Ridgway's hawks.

subject: Los Katíos National Park
summary: Colombia's wild sentinel on the Darién border, where the Atrato River floods a forest so fertile that trees grow fifty meters tall and species from two continents collide.

subject: Los Tres Ojos National Park
summary: Three hidden lagoons inside a collapsed limestone cave on the outskirts of Santo Domingo, where the Taino once performed rituals and where Hollywood later filmed dinosaurs.

subject: Lost Gardens of Heligan
summary: A Victorian Cornish garden swallowed by brambles after most of its 22 gardeners died in the First World War, rediscovered under chest-deep weeds in 1990 by Tim Smit and John Willis.

subject: Lost River State Park
summary: A 3,712-acre West Virginia state park, shaped by Civilian Conservation Corps crews around a Lee family cabin, that sits 2.3 miles from the river it is named for.

subject: Lowell National Historical Park
summary: A National Historical Park in Lowell, Massachusetts, preserving America's first planned industrial city, where 5.6 miles of power canals and massive textile mills tell the story of the Industrial Revolution and the immigrant workers who powered it.

subject: Lower Dniester National Nature Park
summary: A vast wetland where the Dniester unravels into reeds and channels before meeting the Black Sea, sheltering tens of thousands of birds within reach of Odesa.

story.title: Lower Saxon Wadden Sea National Park

subject: Lower Saxon Wadden Sea National Park
summary: A 345,800-hectare national park where the sea retreats twice a day to expose the largest unbroken tidal flat system on Earth.

subject: Lu Xun Park (Qingdao)
summary: A seaside park in Qingdao honoring China's most caustic literary voice, where 45 of his poems line a corridor and the Yellow Sea crashes against rugged reefs just steps from pine-shaded paths.

subject: Luambe National Park
summary: A small Zambian park wedged between two famous Luangwa Valley neighbours, written off as a dead zone in the 1990s and now slowly clawing its wildlife back one lodge bed and one anti-poaching patrol at a time.

subject: Lumphini Park
summary: Named after the Buddha's birthplace and donated by a king who died before it was finished, Lumphini Park is Bangkok's first public park -- 57 hectares of green space shared by joggers, swan boats, and 400 monitor lizards.

subject: Luna Park Historic District
summary: Where Charleston's West Side amusement park stood from 1912 to 1923 - now a residential neighborhood of 444 Foursquares, bungalows, Tudor Revivals, and Colonial Revivals.

subject: Luna Park Sydney
summary: Beneath the giant grinning face on Sydney's harbour, an amusement park has spent ninety years balancing delight and disaster.

subject: Luna Park, Berlin
summary: Europe's largest amusement park drew fifty thousand Berliners a day to the shore of the Halensee — and a motorway link road for the 1936 Olympics now runs across the site.

subject: Luna Park, San Jose
summary: A San Jose neighborhood that carries the name of a vanished amusement park built in 1907 to lure streetcar riders to the end of the line.

subject: Lung Fu Shan Country Park
summary: Hong Kong's smallest country park — just 47 hectares pressed between the Mid-Levels and the Peak — where morning walkers, a ruined Victorian artillery battery, and 151 recorded species share a single wooded hillside.

subject: Luodong Forest Railway
summary: For 55 years a narrow-gauge railway hauled timber down from Taiping Mountain to the town of Luodong, earning the affectionate nickname 'Bong Bong Train' before flooding silenced it in 1979.

subject: Luodong Forestry Culture Park
summary: A 16-hectare park in Yilan County, Taiwan, where timber ponds, a bamboo railway station, and Japanese-era forestry buildings preserve the memory of the mountain logging industry that once defined this town.

subject: Luokou Yellow River Railway Bridge
summary: Blown up by warlords, shelled in civil wars, bombed by Nationalists, and threatened by floods -- this German-built railway bridge across the Yellow River has survived everything the twentieth century threw at it.

subject: Luís de Camões Garden
summary: Macau's oldest public park — once the British East India Company's local headquarters and known in Chinese as Phoenix Hill — became a public garden in 1886 and has served as the territory's green lung ever since.

story.title: Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park

subject: Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park
summary: A working cattle ranch, a reconstructed birthplace, and a boyhood home along the Pedernales River preserve the roots of a president who never stopped calling the Texas Hill Country home.

subject: Lüshun railway station
summary: A Russian-style wooden station built to connect Port Arthur to the Chinese Eastern Railway has survived three empires and four changes of rail gauge while keeping its original architectural character.

subject: Ma On Shan Country Park
summary: Twenty-eight square kilometres of volcanic peaks and abandoned iron mines at the centre of the Sai Kung Peninsula, where pangolins still wander and wild rhododendrons cling to ruined slopes.

subject: Maastricht Aachen Airport
summary: A wartime emergency airstrip paved with the rubble of a bombed Dutch town grew into the Netherlands' second-largest cargo hub.

subject: Mabuhay Gardens
summary: The North Beach Filipino supper club turned punk rock venue that became San Francisco's answer to CBGB.

subject: MacMillan Provincial Park
summary: Home to Cathedral Grove, a stand of ancient Douglas fir so magnificent it was shortlisted as one of the Seven Wonders of Canada, preserved thanks to a logging industrialist's unexpected generosity.

subject: Macau Mosque and Cemetery
summary: Macau's only mosque and Muslim cemetery stands as living evidence that South Asian soldiers brought to serve a Portuguese colonial army put down roots that outlasted the empire that brought them here.

subject: Macclesfield Canal
summary: A 26-mile Telford-designed canal opened in 1831, famous for its elegant snake bridges and the Bosley flight of twelve locks.

subject: Machalilla National Park
summary: Ecuador's only coastal national park, home to the 'poor man's Galapagos' and the waved albatross outside the Galapagos themselves.

subject: Machangding Memorial Park
summary: On the bank of the Xindian River in Taipei's Wanhua District, Machangding Memorial Park preserves the memory of an execution ground used during the Japanese colonial era and again during Taiwan's postwar White Terror — a place of deep historical weight now designated a historic site.

subject: Macquarie Harbour
summary: Six times the size of Sydney Harbour and guarded by a passage the convicts named Hell's Gates, this tea-dark fjord is where Tasmania's rivers, mountains, and history all drain to the sea.

subject: Macquarie Harbour Penal Station
summary: On a wooded speck of an island at the bottom of the world, Britain built the prison it sent men to when every other prison had failed to break them.

subject: Madeira-Mamoré Railroad
summary: Known as the 'Devil's Railroad,' this 1907-1912 railway through the Amazon killed thousands of workers and was abandoned after just sixty years of service.

subject: Madidi National Park
summary: One of the most biologically diverse places on Earth, Madidi stretches from Andean glaciers to Amazonian rainforest across nearly two million hectares of Bolivian wilderness.

subject: Magdalen College, Oxford
summary: Oxford's most beautiful college, founded in 1458, where the choir greets May Morning from atop a 144-foot tower and deer still graze in the Grove.

subject: Magdalene College, Cambridge
summary: Home to Samuel Pepys's diaries, a dining hall lit only by candlelight, and the last all-male Oxbridge college to admit women — Magdalene carries its contradictions with a kind of stubborn elegance.

subject: Magee College
summary: A Presbyterian widow's £20,000 bequest, a wartime bunker that hunted U-boats, and a campus that became Derry's bitterest reminder of how Northern Ireland chose its second university.

subject: Magnolia Plantation and Gardens (Charleston, South Carolina)
summary: Fifteen generations of one family, 464 acres along the Ashley River, and gardens that have been growing since 1680 -- Magnolia Plantation is one of the oldest estates in the American South, a place where Barbadian settlers, enslaved West Africans, and the Lowcountry landscape shaped each other for more than three centuries.

subject: Magnuson Park
summary: A 350-acre former naval air station on a Lake Washington peninsula, now Seattle's second-largest park, where submarine fins rise from the grass and wetlands filter the runoff of a century of military and industrial use.

subject: Magong Old City Wall
summary: Built under the Qing Dynasty in 1887–1889 to defend Penghu's harbor capital, the Magong Old City Wall survived colonization and war but lost most of its gates to urban development — leaving only fragments and one restored western entrance to mark where the fortifications once stood.

subject: Maiden Lane, Covent Garden
summary: A short Covent Garden street where Turner was born, Voltaire hid out, and Europe's first recording studio opened.

story.title: Main Building of the University of Hong Kong

subject: Main Building of the University of Hong Kong
summary: The oldest building at HKU, inaugurated in 1912 with donations from a Parsi merchant, became a declared monument and a symbol of learning that survived a century of upheaval.

subject: Main Quad (Stanford University)
summary: Stanford's original heart -- a sandstone quadrangle with Romanesque arcades and a memorial church -- was nearly destroyed in 1906 and rebuilt to become the architectural signature of the West's most influential university.

subject: Main Range National Park
summary: The western wall of the Scenic Rim, where a shield volcano's ancient lava flows hold up the largest rainforest in South East Queensland, sheltering some of Australia's rarest birds on country travelled by Aboriginal people for millennia.

subject: Main Range Railway
summary: Opened in 1867, the railway that clawed its way up the Main Range to Toowoomba was the first to cross Australia's Great Dividing Range, and likely the world's first main-line narrow-gauge line.

subject: Maizuru Castle Park
summary: A hilltop fortress in Kofu where warlords, shoguns, and the Shinsengumi fought for control of the gateway to Tokyo, now a National Historic Site rising from the center of the city Takeda Shingen made habitable.

subject: Makira Natural Park
summary: Madagascar's largest remaining block of rainforest, where seventeen kinds of lemur live in a canopy that holds half the island's plant life.

subject: Makthar (archaeological site)
summary: Perched on a defensible plateau at 900 meters in west-central Tunisia, the ruins of ancient Mactaris span from megalithic burial chambers to Roman baths whose walls still rise twelve meters high.

subject: Malakal Airport
summary: A single 2,000-meter asphalt runway that has been humanitarian lifeline, UN staging base, and the site of three consecutive aviation incidents in early 2024.

subject: Malakoff Diggins State Historic Park
summary: California's largest hydraulic mining scar tells the story of Gold Rush ambition, environmental catastrophe, and one of America's first environmental protection laws.

subject: Malden Historic District
summary: A 95-building historic district along the Kanawha River in West Virginia, preserving the salt-making town where Booker T. Washington spent his childhood.

subject: Malkumba-Coongie Lakes National Park
summary: A desert national park named for the resting place of a Dreaming serpent, co-managed with the Yandruwandha and Yawarrawarrka people who have known this water since long before it was a park.

subject: Mamungari Conservation Park
summary: A UNESCO-listed desert wilderness so remote it went unnamed for decades, now held by its Anangu traditional owners and crossed by a chain of salt lakes along the state border.

subject: Mana Pools National Park
summary: Where the Zambezi's floodplain becomes four great pools each rainy season, one of Africa's least developed national parks draws elephants, hippos, and wild dogs to a UNESCO World Heritage landscape shaped by water and threatened by dams.

subject: Manassas National Battlefield Park
summary: A preserved landscape in northern Virginia where two devastating Civil War battles unfolded, where Stonewall Jackson earned his name, and where the bones of soldiers still surface from the earth.

subject: Manatee Springs State Park
summary: A first-magnitude spring where 9,000 years of human habitation meet an underground labyrinth, and where vultures, manatees, and cave divers share the same dark waters of the Suwannee.

subject: Manbulloo Airfield
summary: A World War II bomber base carved into a Northern Territory cattle station in 1942 — from which B-24 Liberators flew missions over the Dutch East Indies — that is now visible from the air only as a faint scar beneath a mango plantation.

subject: Manchester Ship Canal
summary: Manchester decided it would be a seaport. The city was 40 miles from the sea. Six years and £15 million later, ocean ships were sailing into the heart of an inland industrial city, and Liverpool was furious.

subject: Manchester State Beach
summary: Five miles of windswept Mendocino coastline where the San Andreas Fault slips into the Pacific and driftwood piles become improvised architecture.

subject: Manchester Wall
summary: A sixty-foot granite remnant of a nineteenth-century railroad bridge has become Richmond's most surprising urban climbing gym, hanging over the James River.

subject: Manggarai Railway Station
summary: Built in 1914 on land once known as a slave market, Manggarai Station carried a president to safety during revolution and is now being transformed into Indonesia's largest railway hub.

subject: Manning Provincial Park
summary: Where the Pacific Crest Trail reaches its northern terminus and the Cascade Mountains deliver dry powder snow, this four-season playground bridges wilderness and accessibility.

subject: Manovo-Gounda St. Floris National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Central African Republic that lost 80% of its wildlife to armed poachers and was placed on the danger list after park staff were shot -- a park whose designation now protects little more than an idea of what once lived here.

subject: Manu National Park
summary: A vast vertical wilderness in southeastern Peru where Andean highlands plunge into Amazon lowlands, sheltering more species per hectare than almost anywhere else on Earth.

subject: Manuel Antonio National Park
summary: Costa Rica's smallest national park is also its most visited and possibly its most opinionated -- a place where capuchin monkeys mug tourists for lunch, a former island became a peninsula through sedimentation, and Forbes named it one of the 12 most beautiful parks in the world.

subject: Manx Electric Railway
summary: Trams built in 1893 still rumble along seventeen miles of the Isle of Man coast, the oldest working electric tramway on Earth still using its original cars.

subject: Manx Northern Railway
summary: The Isle of Man's second steam railway, built in 1879 by a town that had been left off the main line and that decided, characteristically, to build its own way back into the network.

subject: Mapinguari National Park
summary: Named for a mythical Amazonian creature, this 1.77-million-hectare park protects one of the Amazon's strangest landscapes: islands of savanna surrounded by endless rainforest.

subject: Mapungubwe National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage park at the confluence of three countries where 210-million-year-old dinosaur fossils, Iron Age archaeology, and 387 bird species share a landscape that took nearly a century of political battles to protect.

subject: Marakele National Park
summary: Named for a Tswana word meaning 'place of sanctuary,' Marakele protects the largest Cape vulture colony on Earth and a remarkable meeting of ecosystems in the ancient Waterberg mountains of Limpopo.

subject: Marcus Garvey Park
summary: A 20-acre outcropping of ancient schist that has served as a Native American lookout, a Revolutionary War battery, and the heart of Harlem's cultural identity since 1840.

subject: Margam Country Park
summary: 850 acres of Welsh history layered on itself - Roman villa beneath, Iron Age camps above, Cistercian abbey in the middle, and 230 fallow deer wandering the lot.

subject: Mariners' Museum and Park
summary: Congressionally designated as America's National Maritime Museum, this Newport News institution guards 32,000 artifacts spanning centuries of seafaring history, from carved figureheads to the recovered remains of the Civil War ironclad USS Monitor.

subject: Marischal College
summary: The second-largest granite building in the world, founded as a rival university in 1593, now serves as Aberdeen's city council headquarters behind a facade of ornately carved pinnacles.

story.title: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings Historic State Park

subject: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings Historic State Park
summary: The rambling Cracker farmstead where a Washington, D.C. transplant wrote herself into the Florida scrub and won the Pulitzer Prize for The Yearling.

subject: Marojejy National Park
summary: A cloud-wreathed massif in northeastern Madagascar, home to the silky sifaka, the snow-white lemur locals call the angel of the forest.

subject: Marshall University
summary: A West Virginia university founded in 1837 that lost 75 people in a 1970 plane crash that killed nearly its entire football team and reshaped a city's identity forever.

story.title: Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park

subject: Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park
summary: Stretching across 35 acres of Atlanta's Sweet Auburn neighborhood, this national park preserves the birthplace, church, and final resting place of Martin Luther King Jr. -- a landscape where the American civil rights movement found its voice.

subject: Mary Baldwin University
summary: A Staunton university founded as a women's seminary in 1842 that runs the only all-female corps of cadets in the world and welcomes 12-year-olds into its early college program.

subject: Mary Immaculate College
summary: A teacher-training college founded by the Sisters of Mercy in 1898, now Limerick's quiet engine of Irish primary education.

subject: Marymoor Park
summary: King County's largest park began as a banker's country estate and a dairy farm named for a child who died too young, and now draws three million visitors a year to its 640 acres of velodrome, concert lawn, off-leash dog fields, and Olmsted-designed grounds in Redmond, Washington.

subject: Maryport Railway Station
summary: A coastal Cumbrian station on the Cumbrian Coast Line whose single bi-directional platform is a relic of nineteenth-century railway politics still showing through every modern timetable.

story.title: Masoala National Park: Madagascar's Largest Wild Shore

subject: Masoala National Park
summary: Madagascar's largest protected area blankets 2,300 square kilometers of rainforest on the remote Masoala Peninsula, where ten lemur species, humpback whales, and the rarest moth on Earth share a landscape accessible only by a three-hour boat journey.

subject: Matadi–Kinshasa Railway
summary: Built between 1890 and 1898 at the cost of thousands of lives, this 366-kilometer railway through the Congolese jungle bypassed the impassable Livingstone Falls and inspired Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness.

subject: Matai'an Wetland Ecological Park
summary: A living wetland at the foot of Mount Masi — named for the Amis community who have fished and farmed it for generations, and now recognized as one of Taiwan's important wetlands.

subject: Matewan Historic District
summary: On May 19, 1920, ten men died on these two streets in a shootout between coal miners, a sympathetic mayor and police chief, and the company detectives sent to break a strike.

subject: Matobo National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site of two-billion-year-old granite domes, ancient rock art, and Africa's densest leopard population, 35 kilometers south of Bulawayo.

subject: Matupiri State Park
summary: A 513,747-hectare Amazon state park where the Mura people retain legal rights to fish, gather, and live on ancestral land within a protected conservation zone.

subject: Matuwa Kurrara Kurrara National Park
summary: On Martu Country at the desert's edge, a former cattle station has become one of Australia's most ambitious rewilding projects, where animals declared locally extinct are being brought home behind a fence built to keep cats and foxes out.

subject: Mauritania Railway
summary: A single steel line crossing 704 km of Sahara, the Mauritania Railway carries one of the longest and heaviest trains on Earth, and travelers ride it for free atop the open ore cars.

subject: Mavinga National Park
summary: A vast Angolan wilderness where landmines from a 27-year civil war still litter roads that once carried wildlife researchers, and where the slow work of ecological recovery anchors Africa's largest transfrontier conservation area.

subject: May 18th National Cemetery
summary: A national cemetery in Gwangju honoring those who died in the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, built after the original burial site was threatened with destruction by the military government.

subject: Maynooth University
summary: Born from a 1795 seminary built so Catholic priests would not have to study revolutionary France, Maynooth University finally opened to lay students in 1966 and now serves over sixteen thousand from a campus split between Georgian quadrangles and modern glass.

subject: Mayotte Marine Natural Park
summary: A double ring of coral wraps an entire French island in the Mozambique Channel, enclosing one of the largest lagoons in the western Indian Ocean.

subject: Mayura Park
summary: A royal water garden in Mataram where peacocks once patrolled for snakes, Dutch soldiers died in an ambush, and Balinese and Sasak history pools around a floating pavilion that has survived three centuries of upheaval.

subject: Mbam Djerem National Park
summary: In central Cameroon, a 4,200-square-kilometer park straddles the boundary where tropical rainforest meets savannah -- a zone so ecologically rich that olive baboons and chimpanzees live within meters of each other.

subject: Mbuji Mayi Airport
summary: The international airport serving one of the world's great diamond cities - where in 2015, eight people on the ground died when a cargo plane could not stop on a wet, crumbling runway.

subject: McClellan-Palomar Airport
summary: Carlsbad's general aviation airport carries two different identifier codes — a quirk that once inspired the name of a Hollywood television company.

subject: McLaughlin Eastshore State Park
summary: A housewife's fight against railroad developers saved 8.5 miles of East Bay shoreline from becoming shopping centers, creating an improbable state park on polluted landfill and reclaimed marshland.

subject: McNee Ranch State Park
summary: A 690-acre ranch on Montara Mountain where endangered plants cling to serpentine soils and clear-day views stretch across the entire San Francisco Bay Area.

subject: Medicine Rocks State Park
summary: Sacred sandstone pillars in eastern Montana where Native Americans sought visions and Theodore Roosevelt found fantastical beauty.

subject: Meerkat National Park
summary: A South African national park created not to protect wildlife from people, but to protect telescopes from radio noise -- and the wildlife came back anyway.

subject: Meiji University Museum
summary: Tucked inside a Tokyo university campus, this free museum displays what may be Japan's only iron maiden, a French guillotine, Edo-period torture devices, and thousands of years of Japanese archaeological finds, all under one roof.

subject: Memorial Park (San Mateo County)
summary: Saved from loggers in 1923 by a school superintendent who fell in love with its old-growth redwoods, Memorial Park has drawn campers to its creekside sites for a century.

subject: Menteng Pulo War Cemetery
summary: One of two Dutch war cemeteries in Jakarta, Menteng Pulo holds 4,300 graves of soldiers and internment camp victims from World War II, with crosses forged from the rails of the Thai-Burma Railway.

subject: Meotyda National Nature Park
summary: A mosaic of spits, salt lakes, and shell islands on the northern shore of the Sea of Azov, named for an ancient people and prized by more than a hundred species of nesting birds.

subject: Mercantour National Park
summary: Where the Alps meet the Mediterranean, Mercantour protects seven valleys, 37,000 Bronze Age petroglyphs, and the wolves that walked back into France on their own.

subject: Merkezefendi Cemetery
summary: A tranquil 16th-century Ottoman cemetery in Zeytinburnu, Istanbul, founded around the tomb of Merkez Efendi — Sufi mystic, scholar, and the man for whom an entire neighborhood is named.

subject: Merry Cemetery
summary: A Romanian cemetery where over 800 hand-carved oak crosses celebrate the dead with colorful paintings, witty poems, and irreverent humor -- turning grief into an open-air folk art museum.

subject: Merton College, Oxford
summary: Founded in 1264 with the first college statutes in Oxford, Merton holds the world's oldest continuously functioning academic library and the room where Tolkien finished The Lord of the Rings.

story.title: Meru Betiri: The Last Forest on Java's Southern Edge

subject: Meru Betiri
summary: On the remote southeastern coast of East Java, a national park protects 580 square kilometers of monsoon rainforest, nesting beaches for four endangered turtle species, and the lingering memory of Java's vanished tiger.

subject: Mesa Verde National Park
summary: The largest archaeological preserve in the United States - over 5,000 sites including 600 cliff dwellings where the Ancestral Puebloans built a civilization into canyon walls, then vanished in the span of a generation.

subject: Messines Ridge British Cemetery
summary: Nearly fifteen hundred soldiers, more than half of them unidentified, on the ground the New Zealanders fought to take in three hours of June 1917.

subject: Metairie Cemetery
summary: Born from one man's revenge against an exclusive jockey club, this former horse racing track became New Orleans' grandest cemetery, where Confederate generals, jazz trumpeters, crime bosses, and literary icons rest beneath elaborate marble monuments.

subject: Methodist College Belfast
summary: A grand Victorian grammar school at the foot of the Malone Road, founded in 1865 by the Methodist Church, known locally as Methody and famous for its rugby, choirs, and the man who split the atom.

subject: Methodist University
summary: A private university in Fayetteville, North Carolina that has grown from a small Methodist college into a Sandhills institution serving soldiers, their families, and a region of 12,000 graduates.

subject: Mexico–United States Border Wall
summary: The barriers dividing Mexico from the United States span nearly 1,100 kilometers — a patchwork of steel, concrete, and wire built over decades of shifting policy, concentrated most densely at San Diego and El Paso.

subject: Mgahinga Gorilla National Park
summary: Uganda's smallest national park sits where three countries and three volcanoes meet, offering gorilla trekking, golden monkeys, and the displaced Batwa people's ancient forest home.

subject: Miaoli Railway Museum
summary: In the heart of Miaoli City, retired steam and diesel locomotives from Taiwan's railway history stand on open ground — machines that once pulled sugar trains, mountain railways, and express services across the island, now preserved as monuments to the age of steam.

subject: Midland Railway War Memorial
summary: Lutyens designed a cenotaph for the 2,833 Midland Railway employees who died in the First World War. The stone soldier on top is lifted high enough that anyone looking up could believe he is theirs.

subject: Midleton College
summary: A school founded in 1696 by William III's discarded mistress has educated, over three centuries, the founder of the Home Rule League, the architect of the Amritsar Massacre, and an Oscar-nominated animator.

subject: Miguasha National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site on Quebec's Gaspe Peninsula preserving 370-million-year-old fossils from the moment fish first crawled toward land.

subject: Mihrişah Sultan Complex
summary: An Ottoman Baroque charitable complex built in the 1790s by the mother of Sultan Selim III, with one of Istanbul's last working soup kitchens still feeding the hungry today.

subject: Mikumi National Park
summary: Tanzania's most accessible major wildlife park, where open Serengeti-like grasslands, 'midget' elephants with small tusks, and abundant tsetse flies create a safari experience that is equal parts thrilling and raw.

subject: Milltown Cemetery
summary: West Belfast's sprawling Catholic burial ground holds 200,000 dead, from ordinary families to hunger strikers, Blitz victims to IRA volunteers, making it an unintended chronicle of the city's most painful century.

subject: Minami Alps National Park
summary: A rugged wilderness of 3,000-meter peaks in central Japan where Mount Kita, the country's second-highest summit, anchors a range so remote that mountaineering is the only way in.

subject: Minkiö railway station
summary: A tiny wooden halt named after a village four kilometres away, which outlived the 750-millimetre railway it was built for and became the working heart of Finland's narrow-gauge preservation movement.

subject: Minkébé National Park
summary: A 7,570-square-kilometer wilderness in northeastern Gabon so remote that it has no permanent human inhabitants, Minkebe shelters one of Africa's largest forest elephant populations beneath a canopy of ancient trees punctuated by isolated granite domes.

subject: Minnekhada Regional Park
summary: Two hundred hectares of marsh, rock knoll and forest on the Pitt River - a birdwatcher's park that found out in October 2022 what a coastal rainforest can do when it dries out.

subject: Mir Castle Complex
summary: A 16th-century Belarusian Gothic and Renaissance castle of the Radziwill family, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Mir Castle stands intact at a small town in western Belarus - despite the wars, abandonments and a Nazi-era ghetto held within its walls.

story.title: Miracle Beach: Where a Starving Man Became a Legend and the Sand Never Stays Still

subject: Miracle Beach Provincial Park
summary: A provincial park on Vancouver Island's east coast named for a We Wai Kai legend of a starving man befriended by the community, where the beach is an ever-shifting intertidal sandbar, coho salmon spawn in Black Creek, and over 125,000 visitors come annually to walk a shoreline that is slowly migrating northward.

subject: Miracle Strip Amusement Park
summary: A beloved Florida panhandle amusement park where you entered a ride by walking through the mouth of a devil, ducking under a giant snowman's legs, or crawling through spider-webbed tunnels - all gone now, replaced by weeds and concrete foundations.

subject: Mirador State Park
summary: The largest state park in Maranhão protects the springs that supply São Luís and twenty other cities, yet it spent most of three decades existing mainly on paper.

subject: Miramar National Cemetery
summary: Opened in 2010 on land that once trained World War I soldiers, Miramar National Cemetery honors veterans of every era — from a Civil War Medal of Honor recipient to Yankees broadcaster Jerry Coleman, who flew combat missions in two wars.

subject: Miri Airport
summary: Sarawak's busiest gateway handles 125 landings a day from jets and jungle hoppers alike -- and maintains its own immigration border with the rest of Malaysia.

subject: Mission Dolores Park
summary: Built on a former Jewish cemetery that sheltered 1,600 earthquake refugee families, Dolores Park is where San Francisco's demographic crossroads gather on sunny weekends by the thousands.

subject: Mission Raceway Park
summary: Three volunteer clubs that once raced on borrowed airport runways ended up sharing one patch of Fraser River floodplain - a dragstrip, a road course and a motocross track behind a single gate.

subject: Mission Railway Bridge
summary: A 1909 swing bridge over the Fraser River that once made cars queue behind trains, still keeps a tender on duty around the clock, and quietly stitches two transcontinental railways into a single one-way system.

subject: Mission Trails Regional Park
summary: Seven thousand acres of open land inside a major American city, where the San Diego River runs past a colonial-era dam and 23 species of bats hunt at dusk.

subject: Mississippi River–Gulf Outlet Canal
summary: A billion-dollar shipping shortcut that barely anyone used, until it funneled Hurricane Katrina's storm surge straight into the heart of New Orleans.

subject: Mitlenatch Island Nature Provincial Park
summary: A tiny island in the Strait of Georgia that hosts the strait's largest seabird colony, the province's biggest garter snakes, and a name that means 'it looks close, but moves away as you approach.'

subject: Mkomazi National Park
summary: A Tanzanian park born from the merger of two game reserves, where black rhinos breed behind fences, African wild dogs roam, and the question of who the land belongs to has never been settled.

subject: Mochima National Park
summary: Venezuela's second marine national park stretches across 32 islands and the entire Caribbean coastline between Puerto La Cruz and Cumana, a realm of turquoise water, fried fish, and oyster sellers with flexible pricing.

subject: Mokala National Park
summary: South Africa's youngest national park, named for the Setswana word for the camel thorn tree, where two ancient biomes collide and endangered species find sanctuary on land reclaimed from diamond prospectors.

story.title: Mole National Park: Ghana's Wild Heart

subject: Mole National Park
summary: Ghana's largest wildlife refuge, where walking safaris bring visitors face-to-face with elephants in the Guinea savanna, and a fifteenth-century mosque guards the park's entrance.

subject: Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park
summary: The world's first underwater sculpture park, where concrete figures cast from Grenadian locals slowly transform into living coral reef beneath Caribbean waters.

subject: Molli Railway
summary: A 900 mm steam railway that runs down the middle of a shopping street in Bad Doberan, with grooved rails set into the pavement and parked cars a forearm's length from the cylinders.

subject: Mols Bjerge National Park
summary: A glacial hill country on the Djursland peninsula, holding more than half of Denmark's wild plant species, a ruined royal castle, and the cobbled causeway a future king of Sweden escaped along.

subject: Monkwearmouth Railway Bridge
summary: An 1879 iron bowstring bridge over the River Wear whose engineer accidentally invented a structural form twenty years before its theory existed.

subject: Monmouthshire and Brecon Canal
summary: An 18th-century industrial canal that became, almost by accident, one of the most tranquil stretches of water in Britain after the iron and coal stopped moving.

subject: Monson Lake State Park
summary: This small Minnesota state park began as a memorial to 13 Swedish American pioneers killed during the Dakota War of 1862 -- a place where grief, memory, and the quiet beauty of prairie lakes have coexisted for over 160 years.

subject: Mont Péko National Park
summary: Established in 1968 around a 997-meter peak in western Ivory Coast, Mont Peko National Park has become a contested landscape where chimpanzee conservation collides with cocoa farming and the aftermath of civil conflict.

subject: Mont-Tremblant National Park
summary: Quebec's oldest provincial park, where over 400 lakes fill the ancient hollows of the Canadian Shield and eastern wolves still hunt by moonlight through forests that blaze crimson every autumn.

subject: Montagne d'Ambre National Park
summary: A cloud-wrapped volcano rises green out of Madagascar's dry north, sheltering crater lakes, waterfalls, and a chameleon small enough to perch on a thumbnail.

subject: Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park
summary: The famous white beach on Galiano Island is not sand — it is three thousand years of crushed clam shell, the edge of one of the longest-occupied village sites on the BC coast.

subject: Montana State University
summary: Montana's largest university began as a consolation prize for losing the state capital, then grew into a research powerhouse with pioneering basketball, world-class dinosaur collections, and a giant whitewashed M on the mountainside.

story.title: Montanhas de Teresópolis Municipal Nature Park

subject: Montanhas de Teresópolis Municipal Nature Park
summary: A 4,397-hectare sanctuary in Rio de Janeiro's mountains where degraded Atlantic Forest is slowly returning, rock climbers scale granite giants named for animals, and a Swiss zoologist's 1891 homestead has become the park headquarters.

subject: Monte Alegre State Park
summary: Sandstone hills above the Amazon floodplain hold caves whose painted walls and buried hearths pushed the human story of the Amazon back to the end of the Ice Age - and started an argument archaeologists have not finished.

subject: Monte Alén National Park
summary: Equatorial Guinea's largest national park shelters 2,000 square kilometers of equatorial rainforest where goliath frogs -- the biggest frogs on Earth -- share the canopy with gorillas, chimpanzees, and forest elephants.

subject: Monte León National Park
summary: On a windswept stretch of Argentine coast, pumas have learned to hunt penguins - the only place on Earth where the two animals meet this way.

subject: Monte Pascoal National Park
summary: The hill Cabral's lookouts sighted on 22 April 1500 stands inside a national park that overlaps Pataxó land, and the park's real history is a long argument over who the forest belongs to.

subject: Montford Area Historic District
summary: A late-Victorian Asheville neighborhood where Biltmore's architect built shingled houses, Zelda Fitzgerald died in a hospital fire, and thirteen thousand Carolinians lie in a hilltop cemetery.

subject: Montjuïc Cemetery
summary: Carved into the rocky slopes of Montjuic hill, Barcelona's largest cemetery holds over a million burials in terraced niches that face the sea -- a city of the dead that mirrors the artistic ambitions of the living city below.

subject: Montreal Botanical Garden
summary: Founded during the Great Depression, this 75-hectare National Historic Site weaves Ming dynasty gardens, Japanese tea ceremonies, and First Nations medicinal plants into one of the world's most important botanical collections.

subject: Monumental Cemetery of Bonaria
summary: Sprawling up the slopes of Bonaria hill atop ancient Punic and Roman burial grounds, Cagliari's monumental cemetery holds 139 years of sculptural artistry -- from an archaeologist buried in a tomb of his own design to marble angels commanding silence.

subject: Moore Farms Botanical Garden
summary: A working family farm in the Pee Dee quietly grew into one of the South's most ambitious private botanical gardens, climbing toward the sky on a borrowed fire tower.

subject: Moorten Botanical Garden and Cactarium
summary: A one-acre family-owned desert garden founded in 1939 by Patricia and Chester 'Cactus Slim' Moorten — one of the original Keystone Cops — who planted 3,000 desert plants from eight global regions and never stopped adding to them.

subject: Morcom Rose Garden
summary: A Depression-era rose garden tucked into an Oakland hillside, designed with Italian grandeur and built not by the famous WPA but by a forgotten New Deal agency.

story.title: Morden Colliery: The Last Headframe Standing

subject: Morden Colliery Historic Provincial Park
summary: A four-hectare provincial park on southern Vancouver Island preserves one of only two surviving coal mine headframe-tipple structures in North America, rescued from collapse by a community group that stabilized it with 16 shipping containers.

subject: Morehouse College
summary: Founded in 1867 in a church basement to educate formerly enslaved men, Morehouse College became the intellectual cradle of the civil rights movement and the nation's largest men's liberal arts college, counting Martin Luther King Jr. among its alumni.

subject: Morgan Park, Duluth, Minnesota
summary: A U.S. Steel company town named for J.P. Morgan that once produced nails intentionally missing a fourth barb as a mark of local pride -- now a Superfund site slowly recovering after nearly seventy years of heavy industry.

subject: Morne Trois Pitons National Park
summary: Dominica's first national park protects 7,000 hectares of volcanic wilderness where boiling lakes, fumaroles, and emerald pools reveal an island still being shaped by the forces that created it.

subject: Morro do Chapéu State Park
summary: A 46,000-hectare state park in Bahia's Chapada Diamantina that has spent half a century being created, forgotten, recreated, almost abolished, and saved again - all while protecting prehistoric cave paintings and 543 springs.

subject: Morrocoy National Park
summary: A Caribbean archipelago of mangrove-fringed cays and white sand beaches where scarlet ibises roost by the thousands, coral reefs shelter endangered sea turtles, and the shore itself is built from Tertiary-period limestone.

subject: Morven Park
summary: A 1,000-acre estate in Virginia's horse country where two governors made their home, Olympic equestrians still compete, and a lockkeeper's love of foxhunting shaped a century of tradition.

subject: Moscoso Park
summary: The oldest municipal park in Vitória, Brazil, built on tidal flats in 1910 and opened in 1912, Moscoso Park has survived a century of fashions - from nineteenth-century gardens to Art Nouveau ruins to modernist architectural interventions - to emerge as a 24,000 square meter pocket of Atlantic Forest green in the middle of a concrete city.

subject: Mouling National Park
summary: Named for the Adi word meaning 'red soil,' Mouling National Park protects 483 square kilometers of nearly roadless eastern Himalayan wilderness where Bengal tigers and red pandas share terrain that rises from tropical forest to snow-dusted peaks.

subject: Mound Cemetery Mound
summary: A surviving Adena-culture burial mound in central Meigs County, Ohio, kept intact because nineteenth-century settlers happened to bury their own dead around it.

subject: Mound Key Archaeological State Park
summary: An island in Estero Bay built entirely by the Calusa people from shells, fish bones, and pottery over two thousand years, believed to be the capital of their kingdom that once stretched across all of Southwest Florida.

subject: Moundville Archaeological Site
summary: Twenty-nine earthen mounds arranged around a central plaza on the Black Warrior River mark the remains of a city that was, for three centuries, the second-largest settlement in North America north of Mexico.

subject: Mount Aspiring National Park
summary: New Zealand's most remote national park stretches across three regions of the South Island, where seven metres of annual rainfall feed rivers so clear you can count the stones on the bottom.

subject: Mount Auburn Cemetery
summary: America's first garden cemetery - where Bostonians invented the rural cemetery movement in 1831, creating a park for the living as much as a resting place for the dead, and changing how Americans think about death.

subject: Mount Augustus National Park
summary: The park guarding Burringurrah - a sandstone ridge nearly eight kilometres long, more than twice the size of Uluru, and one of the loneliest great landmarks in Australia.

subject: Mount Edgcumbe Country Park
summary: An 885-acre Cornish estate where Henry VIII's deer still roam freely, the Beagle weighed anchor for the Galapagos, and an 18th-century folly was built from the stones of bombed churches.

subject: Mount Elgon National Park
summary: An ancient volcano straddling the Uganda-Kenya border where elephants venture deep into lava caves at night to mine salt from the walls, and five vegetation zones climb from tropical rainforest to an alien landscape of giant lobelias on the crater rim.

subject: Mount Elliott Mining Complex
summary: A copper boom rose and fell here in a single generation, leaving a smelter town of 1,500 people to crumble back into the spinifex of north-west Queensland.

subject: Mount Field National Park
summary: An hour from Hobart, Tasmania's oldest national park layers tiered waterfalls, the tallest flowering trees on Earth, and glacier-carved alpine lakes into a single afternoon.

subject: Mount Longonot National Park
summary: A dormant stratovolcano in Kenya's Rift Valley whose crater rim trail offers one of East Africa's most rewarding day hikes -- steep, sun-baked, and crowned with views from Naivasha to the Aberdare Range.

subject: Mount Lowe Railway
summary: A Victorian-era mountain railway that brought tourists by incline and electric trolley to a resort where a searchlight visible on Catalina Island illuminated birthday celebrations across Los Angeles.

subject: Mount Maxwell Provincial Park
summary: The Royal Navy named this Salt Spring Island mountain for an admiral; the neighbours named it for a cattle rancher — and both names won, on a summit guarding Canada's largest Garry oak meadow.

subject: Mount Olive Correctional Complex
summary: West Virginia's only maximum-security prison, built on a Fayette County ridge to replace a crumbling Civil War-era fortress.

subject: Mount Rainier National Park
summary: The Pacific Northwest's guardian peak - a 14,410-foot glacier-cloaked stratovolcano that dominates the horizon from Seattle to Portland, sheltering pristine wilderness beneath its icy crown.

subject: Mount Rinjani National Park
summary: Protecting over 41,000 hectares of volcanic terrain on Lombok, this national park encompasses Indonesia's second-highest volcano, a sacred caldera lake, and forests that shelter species found nowhere else on earth.

subject: Mount Royal Cemetery
summary: On the north slope of Montreal's defining mountain, a terraced Victorian cemetery holds the remains of a fugitive slave, a prime minister, the man who punched Houdini, and the woman who inspired The King and I -- all resting together beneath maple canopy since 1852.

subject: Mount Tamalpais State Park
summary: A California state park featuring the 2,571-foot Mount Tamalpais, the peak that dominates the Marin County skyline.

subject: Mount Washington Cog Railway
summary: The world's first mountain-climbing cog railway has been hauling passengers up New Hampshire's highest peak since 1869, an audacious feat of Victorian engineering that its inventor's contemporaries dismissed as a railway to the moon.

subject: Mountain View Cemetery (Oakland, California)
summary: Frederick Law Olmsted's 226-acre Oakland cemetery where California governors, Bay Area rappers, and the Black Dahlia share a hillside with views of San Francisco.

subject: Mountain View Cemetery (Vancouver)
summary: Vancouver's only cemetery holds more people than most Canadian cities do, and its property lines are a map of how the city grew.

subject: Mountain Zebra National Park
summary: Proclaimed in 1937 to save the Cape mountain zebra from extinction when fewer than a hundred survived, this intimate Karoo-edge park nursed the species back from the brink and still sends its descendants to reserves across South Africa.

subject: Mowbray Park
summary: Sunderland's Victorian park was born of cholera, almost lost to neglect, and resurrected with Alice in Wonderland chess pieces beside a restored boating lake.

subject: Moysalen National Park
summary: One of the few Norwegian national parks that reaches from sea level to alpine summit, Moysalen protects a coastal wilderness on Hinnoya island where white-tailed eagles hunt above undisturbed birch forests.

subject: Mukōjima-Hyakkaen Garden
summary: Tokyo's only surviving Edo-period flower garden began as an antiques dealer's plum orchard in 1804 and survived floods, firebombs, and a proposal to pave it into a baseball stadium.

subject: Mullewa–Meekatharra railway
summary: The narrow-gauge lifeline that hauled the Murchison gold rush out of the desert, then quietly vanished from the map when the trucks took over.

subject: Mullumbimby Hydro-electric Power Station Complex
summary: One of the earliest town hydro schemes in New South Wales, where a creek dammed at Lavertys Gap first lit Mullumbimby in 1925.

subject: Munda Airport
summary: A Japanese deception trick turned this coral runway into the Solomon Islands' busiest wartime airstrip and, decades later, an international airport born from removing its own buried ordnance.

subject: Munga-Thirri National Park
summary: Queensland's vast Simpson Desert park is a place with no roads, no shops, and no walking trails, where the only thing to do is point a 4WD west across a thousand parallel dunes.

subject: Munga-Thirri National Park
summary: Queensland's largest national park protects 10,120 square kilometres of the Simpson Desert, where ancient dunes, a sleeping seed bank, and tens of thousands of years of Wangkangurru and Yarluyandi life all share the same red sand.

subject: Munga-Thirri–Simpson Desert National Park
summary: More than a thousand parallel red dunes, no toilets, no phone signal, and one famous wall of sand called Big Red - the great Simpson crossing through Australia's largest national park.

subject: Munga-Thirri–Simpson Desert National Park
summary: Australia's largest national park - a vast field of parallel red dunes that the Wangkangurru people called home for thousands of years and that the wider world long believed no one could cross.

subject: Mungo National Park
summary: On a dry lakebed in outback New South Wales, eroding dunes called the Walls of China hold some of the oldest evidence of modern human life and ceremony anywhere on Earth.

subject: Murchison Falls National Park
summary: Uganda's largest national park, where the entire River Nile is forced through a seven-meter gap in the rock before plunging 43 meters into a seething cauldron of mist, hippos, and Nile crocodiles.

subject: Murie Ranch Historic District
summary: A cluster of rustic cabins in the shadow of the Tetons where America's wilderness movement found its voice.

story.title: Musashi Imperial Graveyard: Where Tokyo's Emperors Rest Beneath the Trees

subject: Musashi Imperial Graveyard
summary: Hidden in a forest in western Tokyo, this mausoleum complex holds the remains of two emperors and two empresses -- the first imperial burial ground in the capital, marking a break from centuries of tradition that placed Japan's monarchs in Kyoto's soil.

story.title: Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge

subject: Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge
summary: Cambridge's Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology houses spears from Captain Cook's first Pacific voyage, artefacts collected on the Torres Strait expedition, and a choir screen by Inigo Jones that was removed from Winchester Cathedral and never returned.

subject: Muskau Park
summary: Central Europe's largest English landscape garden, built by a prince who divorced his wife to fund it, now cut in two by the German-Polish border and maintained by both countries as a single composition.

subject: Mutawintji National Park
summary: In a place of ancient engravings and ochre hand stencils, Aboriginal people drew a line in the dirt in 1983 and won their country back.

subject: Mycenaean Cemetery of Voudeni
summary: Seven kilometers above Patras, 78 Bronze Age chamber tombs cut into the hillside reveal a thriving Mycenaean community that commanded the Gulf of Patras for five hundred years — and whose buried dead still speak through the vases, weapons, and jewelry they left behind.

subject: Mystetskyi Arsenal
summary: Ukraine's flagship art museum fills a Tsarist cannon workshop built atop a razed convent, where diggers preparing the galleries unearthed the graves of the nuns who once prayed there.

subject: Médanos de Coro National Park
summary: Venezuela's only sand desert - a 91-square-kilometer expanse of shifting dunes up to 40 meters high on the narrow isthmus connecting the Paraguana Peninsula to the mainland, where visitors explore the landscape on imported camels.

subject: Münster Osnabrück Airport
summary: A regional German airport carved from suspicious wartime ground by British soldiers, then thanked with a glider.

subject: Münster-Handorf Airfield
summary: A Luftwaffe airfield that opened in 1935, fell to American P-47s in 1945, briefly hosted Dutch nuclear-tipped Nike missiles in 1960, and is now mostly farmland.

subject: Müritz National Park
summary: Germany's largest land national park was created by a country that had two days left to live, and it protects beech forest old enough to have gone on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

subject: Mũi Cà Mau National Park
summary: A national park at Vietnam's southern tip where the land itself is new — mangroves colonise mud that did not exist last year, building a seawall the delta cannot do without.

subject: NOVI University of Applied Sciences
summary: Born in a 1958 Amsterdam hotel meeting on automatic data processing, NOVI is the oldest Dutch institution dedicated to IT education - and a chess grandmaster helped run it.

subject: NTNU University Museum
summary: Trondheim's university museum traces its roots to an 18th-century scientific society and now holds over a million objects spanning 11,000 years of Central Norwegian history and nature.

subject: Nackeroo Airfield
summary: Deep in the Northern Territory bush, a joint Australian-American engineering team built a fully operational military airfield in just 16 days — named after the legendary World War II scouts known as the Nackeroos.

story.title: Nagoya University: The Last Imperial University That Lit the World Blue

subject: Nagoya University
summary: Founded in 1939 as the last of Japan's nine Imperial Universities, Nagoya University has produced seven Nobel laureates -- including the team that invented the blue LED, a breakthrough that transformed modern lighting and earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

story.title: Nahanni: The Valley of Mystery and Headless Men

subject: Nahanni
summary: The Northwest Territories wilderness where gold seekers lost their heads - literally, decapitated by unknown means - and where waterfalls twice Niagara's height thunder into a river accessible only by floatplane.

subject: Nahuel Huapi National Park
summary: Argentina's oldest national park wraps around an immense glacial lake where Andean peaks meet Patagonian wilderness, offering everything from backcountry trekking to world-class skiing.

subject: Nahuel Huapi National Park
summary: Argentina's first national park began with one man's gift of land and now sprawls across two million acres of Andean lakes, forests, and steppe around a glacial lake said to hide a monster.

subject: Nahuelbuta National Park
summary: A forest of thousand-year-old monkey-puzzle trees crowns the coastal mountains of Araucanía - a marooned island of ancient Chile that should not, by rights, be here at all.

subject: Nairobi National Park
summary: The world's only national park inside a capital city, where rhinos and lions roam the open savanna with Nairobi's glass-and-steel skyline rising directly behind them.

subject: Nakai-Nam Theun National Park
summary: Laos protects 4,270 square kilometres of Annamite wilderness for an animal that no camera has recorded since 2013 - paid for, improbably, by a hydroelectric dam.

subject: Nam Can Naval Base
summary: Unable to build on ground that would not hold, the US Navy anchored thirteen steel barges in the middle of a Cà Mau river and called it a base.

subject: Namaqua National Park
summary: Each spring, one of southern Africa's most austere landscapes erupts into an explosion of wildflowers so vivid that it draws 100,000 visitors a year to this Atlantic-edge park in Namaqualand.

subject: Namib-Naukluft National Park
summary: Africa's largest nature reserve, where 50,000 square kilometers of ancient desert hold towering dunes, a UNESCO World Heritage sand sea, and the Topnaar people who have lived along the Kuiseb River for generations.

story.title: Nanaimo Harbour: Where Coal Built a City on Filled-In Sea

subject: Nanaimo Harbour
summary: A natural harbour on Vancouver Island's east coast where Spanish explorers, Hudson's Bay Company coal traders, and bathtub racers have all left their mark - and where much of downtown Nanaimo stands on ground that was once open water, filled with coal mine tailings.

story.title: Nara Park: Where Sacred Deer Have Owned the Land for a Thousand Years

subject: Nara Park
summary: Over 1,200 wild sika deer roam freely through a 660-hectare cultural landscape of World Heritage temples, ancient shrines, and primeval forest -- and genetic research confirms the Japanese people have been protecting this exact deer population for more than a millennium.

subject: Naracoorte Caves National Park
summary: South Australia's only World Heritage site, where natural pit traps swallowed half a million years of Australia's vanished giants and preserved their bones in stone.

subject: Narita International Airport
summary: Japan's busiest international gateway was born from one of the most bitter infrastructure conflicts in modern history, where farmers, students, and riot police clashed for decades over seized land.

subject: Narrow Gauge Railway Museum
summary: The Tywyn museum that grew up beside the world's first preserved railway, holding more than a thousand fragments of the small-gauge industrial past - including the writing desk of the Reverend who created Thomas the Tank Engine.

story.title: Nascentes do Lago Jari National Park

subject: Nascentes do Lago Jari National Park
summary: An 812,745-hectare national park protecting the headwaters of the Jari River and anchoring an ecological corridor between the Purus and Madeira rivers in the central Amazon.

story.title: Nascentes do Rio Parnaíba National Park

subject: Nascentes do Rio Parnaíba National Park
summary: A remote cerrado wilderness of nearly two million acres where capuchin monkeys use stone tools and the wolves walk on stilts.

subject: National Archives at College Park
summary: The country's largest archival facility, holding most of the federal records from the 20th century onward - including the burned wreckage from the Branch Davidian compound and Adolf Hitler's last will and testament.

subject: National Botanic Garden of Wales
summary: A Foster and Partners glasshouse the size of a football pitch, set in a Georgian water park, on an estate where the mansion melted in 1931 and left puddles of lead on its own walls.

story.title: National College of Art and Design

subject: National College of Art and Design
summary: Ireland's oldest art institution, an unbroken line from a 1746 Dublin drawing school to a contemporary campus in the old Powers Distillery, with Harry Clarke and Michael Healy among the alumni.

subject: National Garden, Athens
summary: A queen's private garden in the heart of Athens, where peacocks once roamed among ancient column drums and a single monkey's bite changed the course of Greek history.

subject: National Heroes Park
summary: Kingston's largest open space began as an 18th-century horse racing track and became Jamaica's most sacred ground -- where the nation buries its heroes and reckons with its own story.

subject: National Maritime College of Ireland
summary: Ireland's only dedicated maritime college, built in 2004 on the doorstep of the naval base at Haulbowline, where students train in helicopter dunkers, 360-degree bridge simulators, and a global wave-energy test lab.

subject: National Park Service
summary: From a 1916 office in the Interior Building to 421 parks, 84 million acres, and 331 million annual visitors - the agency Stephen Mather built has been called America's best idea.

subject: National Railway Museum
summary: On the grounds of York's old North locomotive depot, Britain assembled the world's most consequential railway collection - the trains that invented modern transport and the streamlined machines that set records still unbroken.

subject: National Taiwan University
summary: Founded as an imperial Japanese university in 1928 and transformed after the war into Taiwan's premier institution, NTU has produced four presidents, a Nobel laureate, and the island's largest academic endowment.

subject: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center
summary: On the banks of the Ohio River in Cincinnati, a $110 million museum of conscience houses a two-story slave pen built in 1830 -- the only known surviving rural slave jail -- and challenges visitors to confront the meaning of freedom across three centuries.

subject: National University of Colombia
summary: Seen from the air, Colombia's flagship public university is shaped like an owl - a modernist campus designed in the 1930s by two educators who had just fled Nazi Germany.

subject: National University of Córdoba
summary: The oldest university in Argentina, born of the Jesuits in 1613 - and the place where students in 1918 reinvented the Latin American university.

subject: National Zoological Park (United States)
summary: Frederick Law Olmsted helped lay out the 163-acre zoo as a refuge for vanishing American bison in 1889 - and 136 years later, it draws two million visitors a year to see giant pandas and Asian elephants.

subject: Natur-Park Südgelände
summary: Ninety-five species of bee live on an abandoned Berlin marshalling yard — a forest that grew out of railway ballast after the trains stopped in 1952, saved from redevelopment by the neighbours.

subject: Naval Base Alexishafen
summary: For seven months in 1944, Sek Harbor held two floating drydocks, a flotilla of repair ships, and a PT boat base run by 200 Seabees.

subject: Naval Base Coronado
summary: Consolidated in 1997, Naval Base Coronado is not a single base but a command encompassing eight Navy installations across San Diego County — 57,000 acres, 36,000 personnel, and the operational heart of U.S. Naval Special Warfare.

subject: Naval Base Hollandia
summary: In the spring of 1944, Seabees carved MacArthur's forward headquarters out of a Papuan jungle - and half a million Americans funneled through.

subject: Naval Base Manus
summary: On 10 November 1944 the ammunition ship USS Mount Hood blew up in Seeadler Harbor, killing every man aboard - a single moment of catastrophe at what was otherwise the largest US naval base in the South Pacific.

subject: Naval Base Milne Bay
summary: A twenty-mile protected harbor on New Guinea's eastern tip became one of the US Navy's largest Pacific bases in 1943 - PT boats, seaplanes, destroyers, a 500-bed hospital, and a training center that staged the 1st Marine Division for the jump north.

subject: Naval Base Panama Canal Zone
summary: For eighty years the U.S. Navy ringed the Panama Canal with submarine bases, seaplane stations, dry docks, and fuel depots -- a sprawling network that defended the Western Hemisphere's most strategic waterway.

subject: Naval Base Port Moresby
summary: Built by seventy Seabees in the summer of 1943, a U.S. Navy communications hub at Port Moresby helped run the Pacific War - then closed when the war moved on.

subject: Naval Base Simon's Town
summary: South Africa's largest naval base has operated continuously since 1743, when the Dutch East India Company built a small dockyard on False Bay -- a facility that has served three navies across three centuries.

subject: Naval College
summary: The Irish Naval Service's principal training institution at Haulbowline, where cadets become officers across two years and six terms, and where every Irish sailor's military training begins.

subject: Naval Museum Complex Balaklava
summary: A Cold War submarine base carved into a mountain, built to keep firing after a nuclear war, now open to anyone willing to walk inside.

story.title: Navarro River Redwoods: The Park That Won Its Beach in Court

subject: Navarro River Redwoods
summary: An 11-mile ribbon of second-growth redwood forest follows the Navarro River to the Pacific, where a landmark California Supreme Court case secured public access to its beach after a century of use.

subject: Neath and Tennant Canal
summary: Twenty-two miles of eighteenth-century engineering across the south Wales coalfield, including one self-funded canal built without an Act of Parliament by a man called "that terrible plague Mr. Tennant."

subject: Nebelivka
summary: Beneath a quiet Ukrainian village lie the traces of a settlement of 15,000 people that flourished around 4000 BC, one of the oldest cities humanity ever built.

subject: Nech Sar National Park
summary: Named for the white grass that covers its central plains, this Ethiopian national park fills the land bridge between Lakes Abaya and Chamo, where Burchell's zebras graze above a shoreline crowded with crocodiles and hippos.

subject: Nechkinsky National Park
summary: A protected wilderness in Udmurtia where Iron Age fortifications and Finno-Ugric heritage hide beneath forests that shelter 712 species of vascular plants along the Kama River valley.

subject: Nelson Lakes National Park
summary: Where the Southern Alps begin their march south, two glacial lakes anchor a national park of beech forests, threatened native birds, and alpine terrain that has humbled trampers who underestimate its difficulty.

subject: Neorion Harbour
summary: The oldest harbour of Byzantine Constantinople, the Neorion stood on the Golden Horn for over a millennium — a port of trade, oars, and legend.

subject: Netherlands American Cemetery
summary: Every one of the 8,288 American graves at Margraten has been adopted by a Dutch family. Many of those adoptions have passed down for three generations.

subject: Nevada City Downtown Historic District
summary: A 16-acre time capsule from the Gold Rush era, Nevada City's downtown preserves 70 historic buildings spanning 1852 to 1937 along streets that once hosted California's third-largest city.

subject: Nevado de Toluca National Park
summary: Mexico's fourth-highest peak holds a massive crater with two shallow lakes -- the only volcanic crater in the country reachable by car -- where pre-Hispanic peoples left offerings of copal in the water and the park has shrunk from 54,000 hectares to 17,000.

story.title: Never Come, Never Go: The Railroad That Hauled $200 Million in Gold

subject: Never Come, Never Go
summary: Nicknamed 'Never Come, Never Go' by the locals it served, the Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad ran 22 miles through California's Gold Country for 67 years, carried $200 million in gold without a single robbery attempt, and was once led by the first female railroad president in the world.

subject: New Asia College
summary: Born from the exodus of scholars fleeing Communist China in 1949, New Asia College kept the flame of Chinese classical learning alive in exile and grew into a cornerstone of the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

subject: New College of California
summary: An idealistic Bay Area college founded in 1971 to offer progressive education closed in 2008 after financial mismanagement undid decades of activist scholarship.

subject: New England National Park
summary: On the rim of the Great Escarpment, a World Heritage rainforest of ancient Antarctic beech survives from the age of Gondwana, often wrapped in cloud, with the Tasman Sea glittering far below.

subject: New Mexico State University
summary: New Mexico's oldest university began in a two-room adobe, discovered Pluto, helped launch the space program, and still rings a Victory Bell after every Aggie touchdown.

story.title: New River Gorge National Park and Preserve

subject: New River Gorge National Park and Preserve
summary: America's newest national park protects one of the oldest rivers on the continent, carving the longest and deepest gorge in the Appalachians through a landscape of abandoned coal towns, world-class rock climbing, and extraordinary biodiversity.

subject: New York and Putnam Railroad
summary: A railroad nicknamed 'the Old Put' that ran from the Bronx to Brewster for less than a century, its last customer a cookie factory, its legacy a network of trails through the Hudson Valley.

subject: Newport News/Williamsburg International Airport
summary: Built on a World War II Army camp, briefly America's fastest-growing airport, now a 144,000-passenger regional field facing existential questions.

subject: Newry Canal
summary: Britain's first true summit-level canal, cut through Ulster decades before the Bridgewater made canal-building famous.

subject: Neys Provincial Park
summary: On Lake Superior's north shore, an ancient volcano, a World War II prisoner-of-war camp, a ghost village, and a Group of Seven masterpiece converge in one of Ontario's most layered provincial parks.

subject: Ngong Shuen Chau Naval Base
summary: On Stonecutters Island in Hong Kong Harbour, a PLA naval base layers 150 years of military history — Victorian gun batteries, British curry houses, and a garrison that changed flags without firing a shot.

subject: Nha Trang Air Base
summary: This coastal airfield cycled through four air forces across three decades — French, South Vietnamese, American, and finally North Vietnamese — before a 2016 redevelopment announcement priced it at US$540 million.

subject: Niah National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in Sarawak where a 38,000-year-old skull rewrote the story of human migration through Southeast Asia, and where nest collectors still climb single poles hundreds of feet to cave ceilings by candlelight.

subject: Niavaran Complex
summary: The last home of Iran's final Shah, the Niavaran Palace Complex in northern Tehran preserves the private world of a dynasty that left everything behind when it fled in January 1979.

subject: Nightcap National Park
summary: On the wettest range in New South Wales, a stand of ancient rainforest survived because, in 1979, ordinary people stood in front of the bulldozers and refused to move.

subject: Nikitsky Botanical Garden
summary: One of Europe's oldest botanical gardens, planted in 1812 on a Black Sea slope, where a Swiss-descended botanist gathered the world's plants and generations kept them alive.

story.title: Nikko National Park: Sacred Peaks and Killing Stones

subject: Nikkō National Park
summary: A national park spanning three Japanese prefectures where UNESCO World Heritage shrines share forested mountains with a 97-meter waterfall, a volcanic lake born 20,000 years ago, and a legendary stone said to imprison a nine-tailed fox demon -- which cracked open in 2022.

subject: Niles Canyon Railway
summary: A heritage railway preserving the original transcontinental railroad route through California's rugged Niles Canyon, where Chinese laborers carved the path to connect America's coasts in the 1860s.

subject: Nilpena Ediacara National Park
summary: On a dusty plain of South Australian rangeland lies the richest record on Earth of the first complex animals that ever lived - creatures so strange they gave their name to an entire chapter of geological time.

subject: Ningaloo Marine Park (Commonwealth Waters)
summary: Off the deeper edge of Ningaloo Reef, a federal marine park guards the corridor where the world's largest fish gather each autumn and humpback whales pass on their long migration.

subject: Nitmiluk National Park
summary: Where the Katherine River carved thirteen gorges through ancient sandstone over millions of years, the Jawoyn people's sacred 'place of the cicada dreaming' waits for those willing to paddle its red-walled passages.

subject: Nki National Park
summary: Described as 'the last true wilderness,' this remote Cameroonian park harbors 6,000 gorillas, the region's largest forest clearing, and a nightjar that may exist nowhere else.

subject: Noel Kempff Mercado National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in northeastern Bolivia, Noel Kempff Mercado National Park protects over 1.5 million hectares where the Amazon rainforest meets the cerrado savanna, sheltering jaguars, river dolphins, and an estimated 4,000 plant species.

subject: Nokra Naval Base
summary: For fourteen years a Soviet Navy logistics point operated quietly from a Red Sea island - until it was shelled into evacuation.

subject: Noosa National Park
summary: A headland of rainforest and surf where koalas doze in the gum trees above one of Australia's most famous point breaks.

subject: Norderney Airport
summary: A small island airfield built in 1970 to keep Norderney connected when winter ice shuts down the ferries.
