summary: Hollowed from half a million cubic yards of greenstone, America's underground Pentagon hides inside a Pennsylvania mountain six miles from Camp David, waiting for a doomsday that has arrived exactly once.

subject: Ravenglass and Eskdale Railway
summary: A 7-mile heritage railway threading up Eskdale on track barely wide enough for an adult to straddle, beloved locally as La'al Ratty.

subject: Ream Naval Base
summary: A 190-acre Cambodian naval base on the Gulf of Thailand has become one of the most photographed patches of ground in Southeast Asia - because of what may or may not be moored at its northern pier.

subject: Rebild National Park
summary: Every Fourth of July since 1912, Danish Americans have gathered in this heathland park in northern Jutland for what is believed to be the largest Independence Day celebration held outside the United States.

subject: Recoleta Cemetery, Asuncion
summary: Paraguay's first public cemetery holds presidents, poets, and a controversial Irish first lady whose bones traveled the world before coming to rest here.

subject: Reconstruction Era National Historical Park
summary: The first national park dedicated to Reconstruction tells the story of where freed people first voted, bought land, and sent their children to school -- in the same Lowcountry where some of the first shots of the Civil War were fired.

subject: Red Flag Canal
summary: A 71-kilometer irrigation canal dug entirely by hand through the Taihang Mountains in the 1960s, diverting river water to the drought-stricken fields of Linzhou.

subject: Redwood Valley Railway
summary: A miniature steam railroad built in 1952 by a Western Pacific engineer who planted 800 redwood trees and created a working tribute to narrow-gauge railroading in the Berkeley Hills.

subject: Regent's Park
summary: A Regency-era pleasure garden ringed by John Nash's white stucco terraces, Regent's Park hides London Zoo, a tragic ice disaster, and gardens once known only to royal monks.

subject: Regional Parks Botanic Garden
summary: A 10-acre living museum in the Berkeley Hills where 300 WPA workers built a garden that became the birthplace of the California Native Plant Society.

subject: Reid-Hillview Airport
summary: A general aviation airport born from Depression-era ambition, Reid-Hillview became a lifeline during natural disasters before a lead poisoning crisis sealed its fate and forced a national reckoning with leaded aviation fuel.

subject: Reisa National Park
summary: A river-carved canyon wilderness in Arctic Norway where Sami and Kven traditions meet boreal forests, thundering waterfalls, and ancient rock art.

subject: Remains of Taipei Prison Wall
summary: A surviving section of the wall of the old Taipei Prison, built during Japanese colonial rule and the site where fourteen Allied airmen were executed in 1945, weeks before the end of World War II.

subject: Renmin University of China
summary: Born from a wartime school founded by the Chinese Communist Party in 1937 to train revolutionary cadres, Renmin University evolved into China's leading institution for humanities, social sciences, and law.

subject: Research Triangle Park
summary: The 7,000-acre pine-forest research park founded in 1959 by Governor Luther Hodges that became the largest in the United States - home to IBM, Cisco, GlaxoSmithKline, the NIEHS, and 65,000 workers.

subject: Retezat National Park
summary: Over a hundred glacier lakes, untouched forests, and wolves that still roam freely -- Romania's Retezat National Park is one of the wildest corners left in Europe.

subject: Rhine-Herne Canal
summary: A forty-five-kilometer artery cut straight through the Ruhr coal belt in 1914, with its own specially designed barge - the Rhein-Herne ship - 80 meters long and 9.50 wide, sized to slide through every lock on the run.

subject: Ribble Steam Railway
summary: When Preston Docks closed in 1981, the freight rail network around them fell silent — until a preservation group from Southport moved in and made it home for one of the largest locomotive collections in Britain.

story.title: Richardson Olmsted Complex: The Asylum That Became a Hotel

subject: Richardson Olmsted Complex
summary: A monumental 1870s psychiatric asylum in Buffalo, designed by H.H. Richardson and Frederick Law Olmsted, that spent decades crumbling before its resurrection as a boutique hotel and architecture center.

subject: Richmond National Battlefield Park
summary: Thirteen scattered sites across nearly 3,000 acres around Richmond - hospitals, ironworks, river bluffs, and battlefields - together tell the story of the four years the Confederacy spent trying to defend its capital.

subject: Rideau Canal
summary: The canal built for a war that never came - where British engineers carved 202 km through wilderness in the 1820s to bypass American cannons, creating the longest skating rink in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site that still works.

subject: Riisitunturi National Park
summary: A fell in Finnish Lapland where winter transforms the forest into a surreal gallery of snow-encased trees and sloping bogs cling to hillsides in defiance of gravity.

subject: Rikugi-en Gardens
summary: A 300-year-old Edo-period strolling garden in Tokyo where 88 miniature landscapes recreate scenes from classical waka poetry.

subject: Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park
summary: Queensland's second-largest national park - a vast Cape York wetland of lily lagoons, river systems and immense crocodiles, handed back to its Traditional Owners and jointly cared for as living country.

subject: Rio Abiseo National Park
summary: A World Heritage park in the Peruvian cloud forest so fragile you are not allowed to visit it.

subject: Rio Abiseo National Park
summary: A cloud-forest national park in the Peruvian Andes hiding one of South America's most decorated pre-Columbian ruins - and the monkey that saved it.

subject: Rio Doce State Park
summary: Forty lagoons floating above a river they do not touch, inside Brazil's oldest and largest Atlantic Forest refuge in Minas Gerais.

subject: Rio Novo National Park
summary: A half-million-hectare national park in southern Para where the Serra do Cachimbo plunges into Amazon lowlands, its waterfalls feed contaminated rivers, and conservation collides with illegal gold mining at the edge of Munduruku territory.

subject: Rio Preto State Park
summary: Quartz cliffs, cerrado twisted by wind, rock paintings on ancient walls, and the faint trace of a 1,400-kilometer gold road still running through the hills.

subject: Ripley and the Underground Railroad
summary: The Ohio River town where the Underground Railroad ran in broad daylight - where Reverend John Rankin's hillside house guided freedom seekers across the water, inspiring Harriet Beecher Stowe's 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' and defining what resistance looks like.

subject: Risten–Lakvik Museum Railway
summary: A group of railway enthusiasts outgrew their forest clearing and built a working heritage railway on tracks abandoned for a decade, bringing steam locomotion back to the Swedish countryside.

subject: Ritsurin Garden
summary: A strolling garden in Takamatsu that took five feudal lords over a century to perfect, using the forested slopes of Mt. Shiun as its living backdrop.

subject: Ritter Park
summary: A lumberman's donation became Huntington's green heart - 75 acres of roses, footbridges, and trails along the Ohio River bottomlands.

subject: Riverbanks Zoo
summary: A 170-acre zoo, aquarium, and botanical garden where the Saluda River bends past Columbia, drawing more than 1.3 million visitors a year to bottomland forest, big cats, and a children's water park.

subject: Roanoke College
summary: Founded by Lutheran pastors who hauled their entire school across Virginia in a single covered wagon, Roanoke College is the second-oldest Lutheran college in America - and one of the few Southern schools that stayed open through the Civil War.

subject: Robert College
summary: Founded in 1863 above the Bosphorus by a New York philanthropist and a missionary, Robert College became the oldest continuously operating American school outside the United States — and shaped the political and intellectual lives of two nations.

subject: Robert Louis Stevenson State Park
summary: A California state park honoring the Scottish novelist who honeymooned in an abandoned mine on Mount Saint Helena, where the five-mile summit trail rewards hikers with views stretching 192 miles to Mount Shasta.

subject: Roberts International Airport
summary: Built as a World War II bomber base with the longest runway in Africa, Robertsfield became Pan Am's gateway to the continent, survived two civil wars, served as a Space Shuttle emergency landing site, and emerged with a new terminal in 2019.

subject: Roca dels Bous (archaeological site)
summary: A Neanderthal hunters' lookout above the Segre where some of Europe's last Neanderthals watched the herds, now excavated with pioneering digital archaeology.

story.title: Rochdale College: The 18-Storey Experiment That Swallowed Itself

subject: Rochdale College
summary: North America's largest co-op residence - an 18-storey concrete tower on Bloor Street where 840 residents tried to build a free university, a self-contained society, and a counterculture utopia from 1968 to 1975, until drugs, bikers, and insolvency brought police to weld the doors shut.

subject: Roche Harbor, Washington
summary: A Coast Salish village site turned Royal Marine outpost turned lime company town on San Juan Island - now a resort harbour whose founder lies uphill in an open-air mausoleum of his own limestone.

subject: Rock Creek Cemetery
summary: Washington's oldest cemetery, established as a colonial churchyard in 1719, holds Saint-Gaudens's most haunting sculpture and the bones of a Supreme Court dissenter, an attempted presidential assassin, and Gore Vidal.

subject: Rock Creek Park
summary: The third national park ever established - twice the size of Manhattan's Central Park, threaded through the federal city, and home to a two-story pile of Capitol stones that quietly disappeared in 2022.

subject: Rock Garden of Chandigarh
summary: A government road inspector spent 18 years secretly building a sculpture garden from broken ceramics and urban waste in a protected forest gorge -- and when authorities finally discovered it, the art was too extraordinary to tear down.

subject: Rockhaven Sanitarium Historic District
summary: In 1923, a nurse named Agnes Richards opened a women's psychiatric facility in Glendale's Crescenta Valley that refused to treat patients as inmates — oak trees, citrus groves, and Spanish courtyards instead of locked wards.

subject: Rocky Mountain National Park
summary: The Continental Divide slices through 415 square miles of Colorado's Front Range, where alpine tundra, glacial valleys, and over 60 peaks above 12,000 feet create America's highest national park.

subject: Rodrigues Alves Park
summary: Fifteen hectares of uncut Amazon forest survive inside Belém as a Belle Époque pleasure ground turned botanical garden, marking the boundary the Portuguese Crown drew in 1627.

story.title: Roeding Park: A Family's Gift That Outlasted Everything

subject: Roeding Park
summary: Donated to Fresno in 1903 with a stipulation that the city improve it every year, Roeding Park grew from 70 acres of donated land into a 159-acre complex housing a zoo, two theme parks, and a Japanese War Memorial.

subject: Rogachevo (air base)
summary: A Cold War military air base on Novaya Zemlya, built to intercept SR-71 Blackbirds and stage nuclear bomber flights at the edge of the Arctic.

subject: Rohkunborri National Park
summary: One of Norway's newest national parks protects a vast canyon, Arctic predators, and Sami reindeer herding lands along the Swedish border in Troms county.

subject: Roker Park
summary: For ninety-nine seasons Sunderland AFC played in front of the Roker Roar - the loudest sound in English football - until 1997, when the ground became a housing estate.

subject: Roker Park (park)
summary: A Victorian recreation park opened in 1880 by Sunday School children, with a boating lake, a cast-iron bandstand, and a ravine to the beach.

subject: Rolle Airfield
summary: A small public-use airport in San Luis, Arizona that began as a World War II bomber training field and spent decades serving crop dusters before a 2011 renovation opened it to general aviation.

subject: Ronaldsway Railway Station
summary: A request stop tucked behind an industrial estate that exists for one specific reason: it puts you a short walk from the only commercial airport on the Isle of Man.

subject: Rondane National Park
summary: Norway's oldest national park, established in 1962, protects 963 square kilometers of ancient mountain plateau -- the landscape that inspired Henrik Ibsen's Peer Gynt and sustains one of Europe's last wild reindeer herds.

story.title: Rosario and San Bernardo Corals National Natural Park

subject: Rosario and San Bernardo Corals National Natural Park
summary: Colombia's most visited national park protects the largest coral reef platform in the Colombian Caribbean, spanning 1,200 square kilometers of underwater ecosystems now at the center of the Americas' biggest reef restoration effort.

subject: Rose Garden Palace
summary: A 19th-century mansion in Old Dhaka built by a humiliated landlord to outshine a rival's garden, which later became the birthplace of the Awami League and one of Bangladesh's most ornate surviving buildings.

subject: Rosicrucian Park
summary: A five-acre compound of Egyptian-inspired temples, museums, and gardens in suburban San Jose, Rosicrucian Park has served as the headquarters of the Ancient Mystical Order Rosae Crucis since 1927.

subject: Ross Bay Cemetery
summary: Victoria's seaside Victorian cemetery holds more than 27,000 people, a long row of British Columbia premiers, and the graves of the Anishinaabe-Metis woman whose land it was.

subject: Roundhay Park
summary: Seven hundred acres of Leeds parkland - hunting ground of Norman lords, site of the world's earliest surviving motion picture, and a Victorian gift to a million annual visitors.

story.title: Roxy Theatre and Peters Greek Cafe Complex

subject: Roxy Theatre and Peters Greek Cafe Complex
summary: In a small wheat-and-cattle town in northern New South Wales, three Greek immigrants built a luxurious Art Deco picture palace - then lost it within months, leaving behind one of Australia's last intact Greek cafe-and-cinema complexes.

subject: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
summary: Founded in 1670 to grow medicinal plants, Edinburgh's botanic garden now holds more than 13,000 plant species and is the second-oldest in Britain.

subject: Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney
summary: On the harbour shore where the colony planted its first, failing farm, Australia's oldest scientific institution has grown for more than two centuries.

subject: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
summary: A Victorian glasshouse, a Millennium Seed Bank, and 8.3 million pressed plant specimens. Kew is where the world's botany is catalogued - and increasingly, where it is rescued.

subject: Royal Cemetery at Wat Ratchabophit
summary: A hidden garden of Gothic spires and Khmer prangs on the grounds of a Bangkok temple, where 34 monuments hold the ashes of the Chakri dynasty's most intimate circle.

subject: Royal Deeside Railway
summary: A heritage railway at Milton of Crathes preserving a fragment of the line that once carried Queen Victoria towards Balmoral — restored by volunteers from rust, blackberry, and the ghost of Dr Beeching.

subject: Royal Gorge Route Railroad
summary: A heritage railroad that runs through the Royal Gorge of the Arkansas River, following tracks won in an 1878 railroad war that featured Bat Masterson, Doc Holliday, stone forts, stolen cannons, and a peace treaty signed in Boston.

subject: Royal Military College Saint-Jean
summary: Canada's francophone military college sits on the site of Fort Saint-Jean, where soldiers have trained and garrisoned since 1666 -- making it one of the longest continuously militarized sites in North America.

subject: Royal Natal National Park
summary: Where the Drakensberg's most dramatic face rises three kilometers into African sky, and the Tugela Falls plunge nearly a thousand meters in five cascading steps.

subject: Royal National Park
summary: The second national park ever created, and the first to bear the name, an hour from Sydney where rainforest valleys meet sandstone sea cliffs.

subject: Royal Naval Engineering College
summary: For 115 years, the Royal Navy trained its engineers at Plymouth - first on a wooden hulk, then in a dockside college, finally in a Devon manor house called HMS Thunderer.

subject: Royal Northern College of Music
summary: Manchester's purpose-built conservatoire, born of an 1893 vision by Charles Halle and now training the world's classical musicians on Oxford Road.

subject: Royal Palace Complex of Kandy
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage palace complex that was built, burned, rebuilt, and seized across five centuries -- where the Kandyan Convention ended Sinhalese independence and where the sacred Tooth Relic still draws pilgrims today.

subject: Royal Roads Military College
summary: Canada bought a coal baron's castle for roughly the price of its fence, meant to hide the British royal family in it, and instead spent fifty-five years turning young Canadians into officers on its lawns.

subject: Royal Victoria Park
summary: Opened in 1830 by an eleven-year-old princess seven years before she became queen, the park unfurls beneath the Royal Crescent like a green carpet of Georgian self-confidence.

subject: Ruaha National Park
summary: One of Tanzania's largest national parks, where the Great Ruaha River draws 10,000 elephants, massive lion prides, and endangered wild dogs to a landscape so remote that most safari-goers never find it.

subject: Ruby Gap Nature Park
summary: In 1886 a surveyor scooped a handful of red stones from the bed of the Hale River and sparked Central Australia's first mining rush - until the rubies turned out to be garnets.

subject: Rucker Park
summary: A Harlem basketball court where a teacher's summer tournament for neighborhood kids became the proving ground that shaped NBA style and launched streetball into American culture.

subject: Ruhr University Bochum
summary: The first new university West Germany built after the war - a 14-tower concrete campus designed to look like a fleet of ships moored on a hill above Bochum.

subject: Ruhr Valley Railway
summary: A coal-era railway carved along the banks of the Ruhr River in the 1870s, half-closed by the 1960s, partly reopened as a steam-tourist line in 2005.

subject: Rumbek University
summary: Founded in 2010 on the grounds of Rumbek Secondary School, Rumbek University opened its doors with 500 students in a region where civil war had kept classrooms shuttered for a generation.

subject: Russia's Forgotten Foothold
summary: A 3,393-acre state park on the Sonoma coast preserves the southernmost outpost of Russian colonialism in the Americas, where a multicultural settlement built California's first windmills before the sea otters vanished.

subject: Russian Arctic National Park
summary: Russia's most remote national park spans glaciated Arctic islands and frozen seas — and carries the unusual distinction of being launched partly because its future guardian called it a giant rubbish tip.

subject: Russian Railway Museum
summary: 118 historic locomotives and rail cars - from 1850s steam to nuclear missile trains - in a converted 1850s locomotive shed next to Saint Petersburg's Baltiysky station.

subject: Rutland Railway Museum
summary: A heritage railway preserving the industrial locomotives, wagons, and quarry machinery that once tore ironstone from Rutland's red earth and fed it into Britain's steel mills.

subject: Rwenzori Mountains National Park
summary: Africa's highest mountain range straddles the equator in western Uganda, where glaciers are shrinking fast, giant lobelias grow taller than houses, and a third of the trail is knee-deep mud.

subject: Rye Harbour
summary: A working fishing village built on shingle the sea kept depositing, remembered each November for seventeen lifeboatmen who rowed out into a storm that did not need them.

subject: Ryhope railway station
summary: A vanished Victorian station where every passenger train descending Seaton Bank was ordered to momentarily stop, just to keep drivers in check.

subject: Réunion National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site covering 40 percent of Reunion Island, where an active volcano, three massive calderas, and 900 kilometers of trails make this French national park one of the most geologically dramatic protected areas on Earth.

subject: Río Pilcomayo National Park
summary: A shape-shifting wetland on the Argentina-Paraguay border where flat grasslands flood into temporary lagoons and yellow anacondas glide through the marsh.

subject: SCMaglev and Railway Park
summary: A cathedral of speed in Nagoya where 39 full-size trains trace the arc of Japanese rail innovation from coal-fired steam to magnetic levitation -- including the prototype that once held the world land speed record for rail vehicles.

subject: Sa'dabad Complex
summary: An 80-hectare royal complex in northern Tehran where Qajar and Pahlavi monarchs lived, schemed, and fell -- now a public museum where visitors walk halls that once hosted shahs and presidents alike.

subject: Saadani National Park
summary: Tanzania's only coastal national park, where elephants walk on Indian Ocean beaches and lions hunt within earshot of breaking waves -- born from a village's invitation to protect wildlife, then embroiled in a decades-long land dispute with the very community that started it all.

subject: Sabah State Railway
summary: The only railway on Borneo, a 134-kilometre line born from the tobacco trade in 1896, nearly destroyed in World War II, and still rattling through the jungle on metre-gauge track.

subject: Sacramento's Garden of Stone
summary: Sacramento's oldest cemetery is a Victorian rose garden where Gold Rush governors, Alexander Hamilton's son, and six hundred cholera victims share sixty acres of California history.

subject: Sacred Falls State Park
summary: A waterfall at the end of a steep volcanic gulch on Oahu's North Shore, permanently closed after a 1999 rockfall killed eight hikers -- but still bound up in Hawaiian legend, geological danger, and the irresistible pull of forbidden beauty.

subject: Saguaro National Park
summary: A split national park flanking Tucson that protects the iconic saguaro cactus in two geologically distinct districts, where silent-film westerns first made the towering cactus famous.

subject: Saguenay Fjord National Park
summary: A 105-kilometer glacial fjord slicing through the Canadian Shield, where 350-meter cliffs plunge into waters shared by wolves, peregrine falcons, and four species of whale.

subject: Saguenay-Saint Lawrence Marine Park
summary: Where the cold, deep Saguenay Fjord meets the St. Lawrence River, upwelling currents create one of the richest marine feeding grounds in the Northern Hemisphere, drawing blue whales, belugas, and thirteen species of cetaceans to Quebec's doorstep.

subject: Sai Kung East Country Park
summary: Covering 44.77 square kilometres of Hong Kong's most dramatic coastline, Sai Kung East Country Park hides beaches reachable only on foot, hexagonal volcanic columns rising from the sea, and a reservoir so large it was made by closing off a marine channel.

subject: Sai Wan War Cemetery
summary: On a hillside above Hong Kong's eastern shore, 1,528 soldiers from across the Commonwealth rest beneath white granite headstones — the fallen of a battle that was lost before it began.

subject: Saihanba National Forest Park
summary: A barren desert transformed into 200 square kilometers of forest by three generations of tree planters, earning the United Nations' highest environmental honor.

subject: Saint Anne (wall painting)
summary: A Nubian artist pressed a finger to Saint Anne's lips on the wall of Faras Cathedral - the only known painting in all of Christian iconography to make that gesture.

subject: Saint Croix State Park
summary: Minnesota's largest state park at 33,895 acres preserves 21 miles of St. Croix River shoreline and 164 New Deal-era structures -- the biggest collection of CCC and WPA projects in the state, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1997.

subject: Saint Edward State Park
summary: A 326-acre forested park on Lake Washington where a Catholic seminary built in 1931 sat empty for decades before being transformed into a $57 million luxury hotel, while the surrounding old-growth second-growth forest remains one of the most pristine urban woodlands in the Seattle area.

subject: Saint Louis Cemetery
summary: Three centuries of New Orleans history told in above-ground vaults, where a Voodoo queen, a chess prodigy, a pirate's architect, and a Hollywood actor's pyramid-shaped tomb share a single city block.

subject: Saint Louis University
summary: The oldest university west of the Mississippi River was founded by Jesuits in 1818, built with enslaved labor, and became the first Missouri university to admit African American students in 1944.

subject: Saint Mary's College of California
summary: A small Catholic college tucked into a Moraga valley where students read Euclid instead of solving problem sets, Australian basketball stars learn to play like Gaels, and a museum holds the largest collection of California landscape painter William Keith's work.

subject: Saint Patrick's Seminary and University
summary: A Roman Catholic seminary in Menlo Park founded in 1898 that has formed more than 2,000 priests, including two cardinals, surviving institutional upheaval to remain a cornerstone of Western U.S. Catholic education.

story.title: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Botanic Gardens

subject: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Botanic Gardens
summary: The oldest botanic garden in the Western Hemisphere, founded in 1765 on a military garrison's requisitioned land, where Captain Bligh delivered breadfruit from Tahiti after surviving the most famous mutiny in naval history.

subject: Saint-Louis University, Brussels
summary: Across the road from Brussels's Botanical Garden stands a Catholic university that began as a small philosophy department and, 160 years later, dissolved itself into its larger sister to keep a Catholic voice alive in the capital.

subject: Sajama National Park
summary: Bolivia's oldest national park, founded in 1939, where the country's highest peak towers over silent altiplano plains that reward hikers with solitude and meditation.

subject: Sakhalin Railway
summary: An isolated island railway that began as a Japanese narrow-gauge colonial line, ran Soviet-built diesels on imported Japanese railcars, and was finally converted to Russian broad gauge more than a century after its first tracks were laid.

subject: Saky Air Base
summary: A Crimean airfield where an American president once landed for the Yalta Conference, later home to the only Soviet mockup deck for training carrier pilots on dry land.

subject: Salamis Naval Base
summary: The principal base of the Hellenic Navy, occupying the northeastern tip of Salamis Island — the very strait where the Greeks defeated Persia in 480 BC — and employing around 10,000 personnel.

subject: Salekhard–Igarka Railway
summary: Built by Gulag prisoners across the Arctic permafrost, Stalin's Transpolar Railway consumed billions of rubles and tens of thousands of lives before being abandoned within months of his death.

subject: Salem College
summary: The oldest continuously operating women's educational institution in the United States, founded in 1772 by Moravian women and still graduating women in the same Old Salem buildings.

subject: Salem University
summary: Founded by Seventh Day Baptists in 1888, briefly Japanese in the 1990s, now Singaporean-owned and online-first - Salem University has reinvented itself more times than any other small college in West Virginia.

subject: Salisbury National Cemetery
summary: Born from a Confederate prison where Union soldiers played baseball before overcrowding turned the camp into a mass grave, Salisbury National Cemetery carries one of the Civil War's most haunting stories.

subject: Salisbury University
summary: A teachers' college founded in 1925 has become the Eastern Shore's research engine, with a lacrosse program that has won more Division III titles than almost anyone.

subject: Sallandse Heuvelrug National Park
summary: A 75-meter ridge of glacial leftovers in central Overijssel - and the last place in the Netherlands where the black grouse still dances at dawn.

story.title: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve

subject: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve
summary: On a bay where Taino people played ball games for centuries before Columbus arrived, St. Croix preserves the only site where a Columbus expedition set foot on what is now U.S. territory -- and the place where indigenous people first fought back.

subject: Saltwell Park
summary: Gateshead's beloved Victorian park, anchored by a Gothic mansion built for a stained-glass master and reborn through a decade-long restoration.

subject: Salvador Bahia Airport
summary: Brazil's oldest airport still serving commercial traffic - an ex-WWII South Atlantic ferry base turned modern hub, tucked between sand dunes, native vegetation, and a bamboo-lined access road.

subject: Sam McDonald County Park
summary: Named for a beloved African American park ranger and Stanford employee, this 867-acre redwood park between La Honda and Loma Mar offers ridgeline views to the Pacific Ocean.

subject: Samothrace temple complex
summary: The Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace ran a mystery cult open to slaves and free, women and men, Greeks and barbarians alike, and counted Philip II of Macedon among its initiates.

subject: Samuel P. Taylor State Park
summary: A Gold Rush prospector turned paper mill pioneer built California's first recreational campground in a redwood canyon that still shelters old-growth trees and spawning coho salmon.

subject: San Carlos Airport
summary: A general aviation airport on the San Francisco Peninsula whose airport code SQL predates the database language by years, sitting next to Oracle headquarters in one of tech history's better coincidences.

subject: San Diego Botanic Garden
summary: What began as a private Encinitas estate in 1957 has grown into a 37-acre botanical garden with more than 5,000 plant species — including the largest public bamboo collection in North America and a grove of cork oaks that visitors walk through like a California dream of the Mediterranean.

subject: San Felipe International Airport
summary: San Felipe's international airport carries the big name but sees only general aviation traffic, its commercial aspirations frustrated by distance and a changing airline landscape.

story.title: San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park

subject: San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park
summary: A national park on the San Francisco waterfront preserving a fleet of historic vessels, including an 1886 square-rigger and a World War II submarine, at the Hyde Street Pier.

subject: San Francisco National Cemetery
summary: Nestled in the Presidio with views of the Golden Gate Bridge, this cemetery holds veterans from every American conflict since the Civil War -- including Union soldiers who never left California.

subject: San Germán Historic District
summary: A 36-acre district of colonial and Victorian architecture in one of Puerto Rico's oldest towns, where the poet who rewrote the national anthem once lived and American cavalry once marched through streets strewn with flowers.

subject: San Guillermo National Park
summary: In the high, wind-scoured Andes of western Argentina, a protected wilderness shelters the largest herds of vicuña and guanaco in the country, watched over by pumas and condors.

subject: San Jacinto Battlefield
summary: Eighteen minutes that created Texas - where Sam Houston's army crushed Santa Anna's forces on April 21, 1836, in a battle so brief and decisive that it won Texas independence before dinner.

subject: San Jose International Airport
summary: Silicon Valley's commercial airport, where a teenager once survived a five-hour stowaway flight in a wheel well, a hijacker was shot on the jetway, and the city's skyline was literally shaped by the need to keep flight paths clear.

subject: San Jose State University
summary: The oldest public university in the western United States, born as a modest evening teaching school in 1857 San Francisco and now a sprawling 154-acre campus in downtown San Jose that produced Olympic sprinters, civil rights icons, and Silicon Valley's workforce.

subject: San Jose Steam Railroad Museum
summary: A museum that has been searching for a home since 1992, with a disassembled 19th-century roundhouse in storage and three historic locomotives waiting for a building to call their own.

story.title: San Juan Island National Historical Park

subject: San Juan Island National Historical Park
summary: Two army camps at opposite ends of an island, kept there for twelve years by a boundary dispute that began with a pig in a potato patch and ended with a German emperor.

story.title: San Lorenzo Marine Archipelago National Park

subject: San Lorenzo Marine Archipelago National Park
summary: A marine national park in the Gulf of California where 95 percent of the world's Heermann's gulls and elegant terns nest on rocky islands surrounded by whale-filled waters.

subject: San Lucas Island National Park
summary: A former island prison in Costa Rica's Gulf of Nicoya where graffiti still peels from cell walls and howler monkeys now roam the grounds, San Lucas became the country's 30th national park in 2020.

story.title: San Marcos de Apalache Historic State Park

subject: San Marcos de Apalache Historic State Park
summary: Where the Wakulla and St. Marks rivers meet, the ruins of a Spanish fort tell a 350-year story of empires won and lost at one of the most fought-over points in Florida.

story.title: San Pasqual Battlefield State Historic Park

subject: San Pasqual Battlefield State Historic Park
summary: A 50-acre California state park in the San Pasqual Valley honoring the bloodiest battle of the Mexican-American War in California — where Californio lancers routed General Kearny's exhausted American forces on December 6, 1846.

subject: San Pedro Cemetery Museum
summary: Medellin's 'White City' of Carrara marble mausoleums, founded by the elite in 1842, where Colombia's presidents, poets, and painters rest beneath Italian sculptures -- and where concerts still echo on full-moon nights.

subject: San Pedro Valley County Park
summary: A valley park in Pacifica where steelhead trout spawn in suburban creeks, Brooks Falls cascades 175 feet in three tiers, and trails lead to Montara Mountain's summit views.

subject: Sanaa International Airport
summary: Yemen's primary international airport, struck repeatedly by Saudi and Israeli airstrikes since 2015, whose 3,200-meter runway is shared with Al-Dailami Air Base and whose commercial flights have been measured in the handful over the past decade.

subject: Sanchez Adobe Park
summary: The finest example of Mexican-era architecture in San Mateo County, an adobe that has served as a rancho residence, a hotel, a Prohibition speakeasy, and an artichoke farm before becoming a museum.

subject: Sanctuary Wood Cemetery
summary: A First World War cemetery beside a wood where, more than a century later, the original trenches still wind through the trees.

subject: Sandakan Japanese Cemetery
summary: On a hill above Sandakan, weathered headstones mark the graves of Japanese women who were trafficked to Borneo and died far from home -- their feet buried pointing toward the country that abandoned them.

subject: Sandakan Memorial Park
summary: Built on the grounds of a World War II prisoner-of-war camp where 2,500 Allied soldiers were held, Sandakan Memorial Park marks the starting point of the death marches to Ranau.

subject: Sandwich Harbour
summary: A remote bay on Namibia's Atlantic coast where towering sand dunes meet the ocean directly, once a whaling port and guano scheme, now a Ramsar wetland teeming with birdlife inside the Namib-Naukluft National Park.

subject: Sandy Island Marine Provincial Park
summary: Thirty hectares of sand, fir and tidal flat off the tip of Denman Island - an island you can walk to, if you read the tide table correctly.

subject: Sangay National Park
summary: A UNESCO-listed Andean park built around three named volcanoes, including one whose center literally blew out, leaving nine peaks in a horseshoe around a sulfur-yellow crater lake.

subject: Santa Clara University
summary: California's oldest operating university grew from an 18th-century Spanish mission into a Jesuit institution that has produced governors, tech pioneers, and an NBA MVP.

story.title: Santa Maria Magdalena de Pazzis Cemetery

subject: Santa María Magdalena de Pazzis Cemetery
summary: A colonial-era cemetery on the Atlantic cliffs below El Morro, where the waves carry an unbroken vigil for five centuries of Puerto Rican poets, revolutionaries, musicians, and soldiers.

subject: Santa Monica Airport
summary: Santa Monica Airport, known as Clover Field, opened in 1923 and became one of the most historically significant airfields in America — the origin point of the first round-the-world flight, the birthplace of the DC series of airliners, and a site of Hollywood camouflage during World War II.

subject: Santa Rosa National Park
summary: Costa Rica's first national park protects 49,515 hectares of tropical dry forest, battlefield history, and Pacific beaches where thousands of olive ridley sea turtles come ashore in mass nesting events called arribadas.

subject: Santa Teresa National Park
summary: A coastal park run by the Uruguayan Army, where two million trees were planted to keep the dunes from burying a colonial fort, and where 12 km of beach meet a forest that should not exist.

subject: Santarém-Maestro Wilson Fonseca Airport
summary: The airport serving Santarém is named for a local composer, was opened by the Air Force in 1977, and sits almost exactly midway between Manaus and Belém.

subject: Santiago General Cemetery
summary: Latin America's largest cemetery, where Chile's presidents, poets, and the names of the disappeared share the same shaded avenues.

subject: Santon Railway Station
summary: The last station on the Isle of Man Railway still housed in its original 1874 building, once a holding pen for the line's lost property and now a sleepy halt with palm trees.

subject: Sarek National Park
summary: Sweden's wildest national park has no trails and no huts, just glaciers, river deltas, and the same mountain silence the Sami have known for millennia.

subject: Sarmiento Park
summary: Córdoba's grand green heart was the first Argentine commission of the French designer who would go on to landscape half the nation.

subject: Sault Ste. Marie Canal
summary: Canada's answer to an American snub, this 1895 canal on the St. Marys River was once the world's largest and first electrically operated lock -- and houses the only emergency swing dam ever used in a real crisis.

subject: Savanna Portage State Park
summary: A swampy trail through the Minnesota northwoods once served as the critical link between the Mississippi River and Lake Superior -- the hinge point where two continental watersheds nearly touch, and where voyageurs, fur traders, and Native Americans hauled their canoes across the divide for centuries.

story.title: SCAD: The Art School That Saved a City's Buildings

subject: Savannah College of Art and Design
summary: An art school that started in 1978 with 71 students and one renovated armory, then quietly became Savannah's largest historic preservation force - rescuing over 60 derelict buildings and turning a fading Southern city into a campus without walls.

subject: Sawit Seberang Factory Railway
summary: A narrow-gauge plantation railway in North Sumatra that hauled palm fruit for nearly a century, the Sawit Seberang line traced the arc of colonial industry, postcolonial nationalization, and the slow victory of trucks over rails.

subject: Saxion University of Applied Sciences
summary: Erasmus walked these Deventer streets as a student in the 15th century - and the institution that traces its roots back to that schoolhouse now teaches 27,000 students across three eastern Dutch campuses.

subject: Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine) Park
summary: A small island off Nanaimo that has been a Snuneymuxw fishing ground, a coal mine, a sandstone quarry for the San Francisco Mint, a Japanese-Canadian herring saltery, a CPR resort, and finally a provincial marine park.

subject: Scenic Railway, Dreamland Margate
summary: Opened in 1920 at Dreamland Margate, this Grade II*-listed wooden roller coaster was the oldest still running in the UK and one of only eight scenic railways left in the world - until a derailment in 2024 finally retired it.

subject: Schiermonnikoog National Park
summary: The first Dutch national park to draw its borders out into the sea covers 72 square kilometers of dunes, salt marsh, tidal flats, and the only landscape in the Netherlands still allowed to move.

subject: Schiphol Airport
summary: One of Europe's busiest airports sits on the bed of a drained lake, named for the ships that used to sink in it.

subject: Schiphol Airport station
summary: Six tracks under the airport, twelve escalators up to the concourse, and a train every few minutes to Amsterdam, Brussels and Paris. The country runs on this connection.

subject: Schleswig-Holstein Wadden Sea National Park
summary: Germany's largest national park is a sea that empties twice a day - 4,400 square kilometres of tidal flat, salt marsh and sandbank that feeds ten million migrating birds and hosts the only mass moult of its kind on Earth.

subject: Schoen Lake Provincial Park
summary: A remote park on northern Vancouver Island that protects old-growth forests critical to black-tailed deer survival and harbors the island's tallest waterfall.

subject: Scioto Trail State Park
summary: A 218-acre Ohio state park nestled inside a much larger state forest, with a hermit's cave, a replica frontier church, and the kind of mixed oak-hemlock hills that wrap around Caldwell Lake.

subject: Sea Lion Rocks railway station
summary: Once the terminus of a Victorian railway that ferried tourists to a clifftop zoo of sea lions and polar bears, this Manx station fell silent for half a century before volunteers rebuilt it from postcards.

subject: Secret Harbor School
summary: A boarding school for troubled teenagers on an island with no phone line to the mainland, remembered now mainly through court records and escape attempts.

subject: Seeadler Harbor
summary: The deep protected anchorage at Seeadler Harbor made Manus Island a strategic prize in three eras - German colonial, Japanese occupation, and American wartime - and the wrecks on its seafloor still mark the day it held more Navy ships than almost any harbor on Earth.

subject: Sellafield Railway Station
summary: A small Cumbrian Coast Line station whose unusual freight role has, for decades, made it one of Britain's most quietly important rail hubs.

subject: Selwyn College, Cambridge
summary: Selwyn College was founded in 1882 to honour a bishop who rowed in the first Boat Race, served as New Zealand's first bishop, and carried a Maori staff that is now in the college chapel.

story.title: Seminole Canyon State Park and Historic Site

subject: Seminole Canyon State Park and Historic Site
summary: Deep in the canyons of the Lower Pecos, ancient peoples left behind some of the oldest rock art in North America -- paintings of shamans, panthers, and shape-shifting figures dating back 8,000 years to a time when mammoths still roamed these lands.

subject: Seram's Last Wilderness
summary: On the island the Maluku people call the Mother Island, a national park protects the deepest cave in Indonesia, the tallest peak in the Moluccas, and the last stronghold of the salmon-crested cockatoo.

subject: Serengeti National Park
summary: The 'endless plains' of northern Tanzania host the greatest wildlife spectacle on Earth - nearly two million wildebeest and zebras following ancient routes across an ecosystem that has remained essentially unchanged for a million years.

subject: Serra Azul State Park
summary: Brazil's geodetic center sits inside this Mato Grosso state park, where paragliders launch from sandstone escarpments above the Araguaia and the Bororo called the place Kieguereiral, the Place of Birds.

subject: Serra Dourada State Park
summary: A 56-kilometre stone ridge in western Goiás that shelters the paper-barked state tree of Goiás, thousands of springs, and a park whose boundaries nobody has ever fully settled.

subject: Serra Geral National Park
summary: A Brazilian national park split in two by the great escarpment, guarding the cathedral-scale walls of Fortaleza canyon and a tangle of cloud forest and grassland endemics.

subject: Serra Mariola Natural Park
summary: A limestone massif steeped in the scent of more than two hundred aromatic and medicinal plants, rising to Montcabrer's 1,389 metres where the Baetic mountains fray into the Valencian interior.

subject: Serra Nova State Park
summary: A 498-square-kilometer state park straddling the divide between Brazil's two great river basins - the São Francisco and the Jequitinhonha - in the Espinhaço Mountains of northern Minas Gerais.

subject: Serra Ricardo Franco State Park
summary: A besieged 158,621-hectare state park on the Brazil-Bolivia border where Mato Grosso's highest waterfall plunges 248 meters off a plateau that politicians have repeatedly tried to shrink for soybean farming.

subject: Serra da Bodoquena National Park
summary: A Brazilian national park where crystal-clear rivers carve through limestone canyons, sinkholes teem with macaws, and the cerrado savanna harbors jaguars and pumas at the edge of the Pantanal.

subject: Serra da Canastra National Park
summary: The tableland where the São Francisco River begins, falls 186 metres off an escarpment, and shares its grasslands with maned wolves, a nearly extinct duck, and the best cheese in Brazil.

subject: Serra da Capivara National Park
summary: In the thorn-scrub canyons of southeastern Piaui, painted figures dance across sandstone walls in one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric art anywhere on Earth.

subject: Serra da Cutia National Park
summary: A 283,500-hectare Amazon stronghold in western Rondonia, created in 2001 to shield rainforest from the cattle ranchers and illegal loggers devouring the state around it.

subject: Serra das Lontras National Park
summary: A 113-square-kilometer pocket of Atlantic Rainforest high above southern Bahia's coastline, home to 330 bird species - 16 of them globally threatened - and one of the last strongholds of the golden-headed lion tamarin.

subject: Serra de Montsant Natural Park
summary: A limestone massif the Catalans named the Holy Mountain, where a medieval shepherd's dream of a stairway to God gave rise to the Iberian Peninsula's first Carthusian monastery and to the vineyards that became the Priorat.

subject: Serra do Conduru State Park
summary: A 93-square-kilometer state park in southern Bahia's cacao coast where 456 tree species can stand in a single hectare - one of the highest tree diversity counts ever recorded on Earth.

subject: Serra do Gandarela National Park
summary: The national park that Belo Horizonte's drinking water depended on - created in 2014 after years of argument over iron ore mining.

subject: Serra do Mar State Park
summary: A dense Atlantic Forest park spanning 332,000 hectares along the São Paulo coast, where serious trekkers find waterfalls, sweeping coastal views, and trails through one of the most biodiverse forests on Earth.

subject: Serra do Mar State Park
summary: Brazil's largest Atlantic Forest protected area, where 332,000 hectares of ancient escarpment forest shelter half the biome's mammal species, protect São Paulo's water supply, and connect conservation corridors from Rio de Janeiro to Paraná.

subject: Serra do Pardo National Park
summary: A young national park born in 2005 from expropriated cattle ranches, guarding one of the Amazon's most fought-over patches of forest between the Xingu and the Tapajos.

subject: Serra do Rola-Moça State Park
summary: A state park where the drinking water for part of Belo Horizonte rises out of six protected springs - and where Alpine tundra sits improbably in Brazil.

subject: Serra dos Martírios/Andorinhas State Park
summary: Ancient rock carvings, Cold War guerrillas, and a House of Stone where devotees walk 30 kilometers to celebrate the Divine Holy Spirit - all within one Para state park.

subject: Serra dos Órgãos National Park
summary: Brazil's third national park, protecting the granite pipe-organ peaks an hour's drive from Rio de Janeiro - including the 1,692-meter finger pointing at the sky.

subject: Sete Cidades National Park
summary: A small Piauí national park where eroded rock has been sorted into seven numbered "cities" — created for its prehistoric paintings, visited for its stone.

subject: Seton Hall University
summary: Founded in 1856, Seton Hall is the oldest diocesan university in the United States — a Catholic institution in South Orange, New Jersey that has grown from a small college into a multi-campus research university, shaped by tragedy, ambition, and a motto that means 'at whatever risk, yet go forward.'

subject: Seward Park (Seattle)
summary: A forested peninsula jutting into Lake Washington that shelters one of Seattle's last old-growth groves, a colony of feral parrots, nesting bald eagles, and a Japanese stone lantern given in gratitude after the 1923 earthquake.

story.title: Sha Chau and Lung Kwu Chau Marine Park

subject: Sha Chau and Lung Kwu Chau Marine Park
summary: A 1,200-hectare marine sanctuary off Hong Kong's western coast where the Pearl River meets the sea — and where the rare Chinese white dolphin still finds refuge.

subject: Sha Tin Airfield
summary: A forgotten military airfield that once lined the Shing Mun River, Sha Tin Airfield was erased by a typhoon in 1962 and buried under a new town — but it was also the site of Hong Kong's very first powered flight, in 1911.

subject: Shalamar Gardens, Lahore
summary: A Mughal paradise garden completed in 1642, the Shalamar Gardens in Lahore descend across three terraces in a geometric cascade of fountains, pavilions, and water channels designed to evoke the Islamic vision of heaven.

subject: Sham Shui Po Park
summary: Beneath the fountains and tai chi courts of Sham Shui Po Park lie the bones of a POW camp, a Vietnamese refugee centre, and decades of Hong Kong history compressed into a few hectares of reclaimed land.

subject: Shamsi Airfield
summary: A desert airstrip leased to Emirati sheikhs for hunting rare birds became the CIA's secret drone base in Pakistan's war on terror -- until a friendly-fire incident shut it down.

subject: Shannon Airport
summary: Built on drained bog in the 1930s, Shannon became the world's first duty-free airport, an early gateway between Europe and America, and even a backup landing site for the Space Shuttle.

subject: Shantar Islands National Park
summary: Fifteen uninhabited islands in the Sea of Okhotsk shelter bowhead whales, Steller's sea eagles, and the world's largest owl behind eight months of annual ice.

subject: Shanwang National Geological Park
summary: A 13-square-kilometer park in Shandong Province where 17-million-year-old fossils are preserved in diatomite with such clarity that insect wing veins and animal hair remain visible.

subject: Shark Bay Marine Park
summary: Beneath the turquoise shallows of this World Heritage bay lies the largest seagrass meadow on Earth, feeding one of the planet's biggest populations of dugongs.

subject: Sharya Forest Museum Railway
summary: A narrow-gauge museum railway in Kostroma Oblast preserves the locomotives and rolling stock that once hauled timber through Russia's vast boreal forests.

subject: Shaw University
summary: Founded in 1865, Shaw University is the oldest HBCU to offer courses in the South, the birthplace of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and a campus where charred beams and historic halls tell the story of Black education's determined rise.

subject: Shazdeh Garden
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Persian garden that defies the surrounding desert with cascading fountains and terraced greenery, fed by ancient qanat channels from the snowmelt of Jupar Mountain.

subject: Shei-Pa National Park
summary: Taiwan's fifth national park shelters the island's second-highest peak, ancient forests drenched in 4,000mm of annual rainfall, and the last wild population of Formosan landlocked salmon.

subject: Shek Kong Airfield
summary: Tucked into the Kam Tin valley beneath the New Territories' highest peak, Shek Kong Airfield has served as a British colonial base, a wartime runway, a Vietnamese refugee detention centre, and now the sole People's Liberation Army Air Force base in Hong Kong.

subject: Shek O Country Park
summary: A 701-hectare wedge of green at the southeastern end of Hong Kong Island, Shek O Country Park holds the Dragon's Back — once named the best urban hiking trail in Asia — and enough biodiversity that a new spider species was discovered here as recently as 2019.

subject: Shenandoah National Park
summary: A 105-mile ridge of billion-year-old rock turned national park, where Skyline Drive runs the spine and over 450 families were displaced to make the wilderness America wanted.

subject: Shenandoah National Park
summary: Virginia's Shenandoah National Park was carved from more than 5,000 privately owned parcels in the Blue Ridge Mountains -- a creation story tangled with ambition, displacement, and billion-year-old rock.

subject: Shenandoah National Park
summary: The park they emptied to create - where 500 mountain families were displaced in the 1930s to make a wilderness within a day's drive of the capital, and where the forest has reclaimed farms, orchards, and memories.

subject: Shenandoah Plaza National Historic District
summary: The historic core of Moffett Field -- including the iconic Hangar One, built in 1933 for the USS Macon dirigible -- forms a National Register district spanning 62 acres of aviation history.

subject: Sheng Hsing Railway Station
summary: Shengxing Station — a wooden railway station completed in 1905 without a single nail — sat at the highest point on Taiwan's main north-south railway for most of the 20th century before being retired, preserved, and eventually revived for steam train excursions.

subject: Sherwood Forest Railway
summary: A one-mile light railway, built by enthusiasts on the dry beds of a Duke's irrigation system, with two steam locomotives named Smokey Joe and Pet.

subject: Shields Date Gardens
summary: Since 1924, Shields Date Gardens in Indio has been presenting 'The Romance and Sex Life of the Date' in a small on-site theater — a film created around 1950, updated in 2007, still running — while selling date varieties that Floyd Shields bred himself and that remain exclusive to Shields to this day.

subject: Shifen Railway Station
summary: At Shifen, trains pass through an open-air street market a few meters from the stalls, and every day tourists light sky lanterns that drift up above the tracks and over the green mountains of Pingxi.

subject: Shimofusa Air Base
summary: A Japanese naval air base born from a commandeered golf course in the final months of World War II, now training the next generation of maritime patrol aviators.

subject: Shin Railway Viaduct
summary: A single 230-foot iron span over the Kyle of Sutherland, opened in 1868 and still carrying every train that runs between Inverness and the far north.

subject: Shing Mun Country Park
summary: A 14-square-kilometre refuge in the central New Territories where wolfram mines, a wartime clearcut, and a decades-long reforestation effort have layered history onto a landscape that now conceals pangolins and a camellia named after a governor.

subject: Shoal Harbour Migratory Bird Sanctuary
summary: A 1931 federal bird sanctuary on the Saanich Peninsula that also happens to be a working harbour full of marinas — 146 hectares of mudflat and eelgrass sustaining more than forty species through the winter.

story.title: Shockoe Hill Burying Ground Historic District

subject: Shockoe Hill Burying Ground Historic District
summary: A single hilltop in Richmond holds an almshouse, two hospitals, the city gallows, a powder magazine, and three burial grounds - one of them likely the largest enslaved-people's cemetery in America.

subject: Shockoe Hill Cemetery
summary: Chief Justice John Marshall is buried here. So is the Union spy who ran a network out of Confederate Richmond. So are the people Edgar Allan Poe loved.

subject: Shoushan Zoo
summary: Kaohsiung's municipal zoo on Monkey Mountain, founded in 1978, which overcame a crisis of neglect and a NT$150 million renovation to become a diverse collection spanning Africa's savannas to Taiwan's own endemic wildlife.

subject: Si Thep Historical Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in Thailand's Phetchabun province preserving an ancient city-state that thrived for a millennium, from Dvaravati through the Khmer period, before falling silent as Ayutthaya rose to power.

subject: Sia Boey Urban Archaeological Park
summary: Malaysia's first urban archaeological park, where a forgotten canal basin and 19th-century market hall were rescued from demolition and transformed into a green space that anchors George Town's UNESCO heritage identity.

subject: Sibalom Natural Park
summary: One of the last remaining lowland rainforests on Panay Island, this 5,500-hectare park shelters the endangered Rafflesia speciosa and feeds the water supply of five municipalities.

subject: Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge
summary: Founded in 1596 on the site of a medieval Franciscan friary, Sidney Sussex is where Oliver Cromwell studied in 1616 — and where part of him was secretly buried in 1960.

subject: Sierra Leone National Railway Museum
summary: In a Freetown workshop where displaced families once sheltered, a lost collection of narrow-gauge steam locomotives survived war and rumor - including the royal coach built for a queen and one of the most powerful engines ever to run on tracks just two and a half feet apart.

subject: Sierra de Bahoruco National Park
summary: A Dominican Republic national park where 30 of Hispaniola's 32 endemic bird species shelter across biomes ranging from dry coastal scrub to cloud-draped mountain rainforest, all above a collapsed cave system called the Caribbean's Grand Canyon.

story.title: Sierra de las Quijadas National Park

subject: Sierra de las Quijadas National Park
summary: Red sandstone canyons in western Argentina that hide the bones of a Cretaceous flying creature with a thousand teeth.

subject: Sierra de Órganos National Park
summary: A compact national park in Zacatecas where volcanic rock formations resembling organ pipes rise above arid scrubland, doubling as a wildlife refuge and a backdrop for dozens of Hollywood westerns.

subject: Silliman University
summary: Founded in 1901 with a ten-thousand-dollar gift from a retired New York businessman, Silliman University became the first Protestant and first American university in Asia -- and it still defines the character of Dumaguete today.

subject: Simien National Park
summary: A trekker's view of Ethiopia's flagship mountain park, where a 40-kilometer ridge walk takes visitors past gelada troops, the walia ibex cliffs, the 4,553-meter summit of Ras Dashen, and community lodges that require only a good sleeping bag for the sub-zero nights.

subject: Similajau National Park
summary: Where Borneo's rainforest meets the South China Sea, Similajau protects a narrow coastal strip where dolphins, crocodiles, hornbills, and sea turtles share 90 square kilometers of beach, mangrove, and ancient dipterocarp forest.

subject: Simmons Army Airfield
summary: The Army's helicopter heartland in North Carolina, where the 82nd Aviation Regiment and special operations aviators have launched from Fort Bragg into every American war since Korea.

subject: Simon Fraser University
summary: A university designed and built in eighteen months on the summit of a rainforest mountain - one enormous interlocking concrete building that has been quietly reinventing itself ever since.

subject: Simon Mwansa Kapwepwe International Airport
summary: Zambia's newest major airport opened in 2021 beside the site where UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold died in 1961 - and five months before it officially opened, an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 737 accidentally landed on its unopened runway.

subject: Simón Bolívar Park
summary: Bogotá's green center - a system of parks larger than Central Park where popes have led Mass and Metallica has played to 100,000 people.

subject: Sindh Madressatul Islam University
summary: Founded in 1885 by Hassan Ali Effendi, this Karachi institution educated Pakistan's founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah and has grown from a colonial-era school into a full university situated on Karachi's Wall Street.

subject: Sintung Sugar Factory Culture Park
summary: A bombed-out sugar refinery in Dulan Village, Taiwan, reborn as a driftwood-and-pebble arts hub where indigenous creativity meets Pacific coastline.

subject: Sirkeci Railway Station
summary: The golden-domed terminal where the Orient Express ended its legendary journey from Paris — 3,094 kilometres of European rail, terminating on the Golden Horn shore.

subject: Sissinghurst Castle Garden
summary: The garden Vita Sackville-West and Harold Nicolson created together at a ruined Kentish manor - now the most visited garden in England.

subject: Skuleskogen National Park
summary: A primeval forest on Sweden's High Coast where the land is still rising from the sea, mountains wear caps of ancient vegetation, and a legend of forest brigands inspired one of Sweden's most celebrated novels.

subject: Skye Marble Railway
summary: A four-mile narrow gauge industrial railway operated for just two years on the Isle of Skye, hauling polished marble blocks bound for Antwerp before the company collapsed.

story.title: Skyline Trail (Cape Breton Highlands National Park)

subject: Skyline Trail (Cape Breton Highlands National Park)
summary: Cape Breton's most famous hiking trail delivers sweeping ocean views from a clifftop boardwalk, but it also carries a darker distinction: the site of the first documented fatal coyote attack on an adult in North America.

subject: Sleeping Giant Provincial Park
summary: A 244-square-kilometre park on the Sibley Peninsula where billion-year-old diabase cliffs form the profile of a reclining figure, voted the number one wonder in a 2007 CBC competition.

subject: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery
summary: The New York cemetery where Washington Irving invented the Headless Horseman and is now buried beside his creation - along with Andrew Carnegie, William Rockefeller, and generations of Astors and Vanderbilts in one of America's most storied graveyards.

subject: Sligo Airport
summary: On a sand peninsula less than two kilometres long, Sligo Airport still launches Coast Guard rescues - 24 hours a day, 365 days a year - even though the last scheduled passenger flight left in 2011.

subject: Sligo Mac Diarmada Railway Station
summary: In January 1923 the station building burned to the ground during the Civil War; one of seven engines sent down to the quay smashed through a concrete wall and ended up in the harbour.

subject: Smith Reynolds Airport
summary: An airfield named for a tobacco heir who died at twenty under circumstances North Carolina has argued about for nearly a century.

subject: Smuggler Cove Marine Provincial Park
summary: A sheltered all-weather anchorage on the Sunshine Coast named for a Confederate veteran turned people-smuggler, where boardwalks now wind through sensitive wetland ecology to hidden bays and rock cliffs.

subject: Snaefell Mountain Railway
summary: The British Isles' only electric mountain railway, opened in 1895, still hauls Victorian wooden tramcars up a five-mile gradient to the highest point on the Isle of Man.

subject: Snaefell Summit railway station
summary: A small stone building at the top of the Isle of Man, with no piped water, the highest tram-served cafe in the British Isles, and a marketing slogan that promises seven kingdoms at a glance.

subject: Snowdon Mountain Railway
summary: Britain's only public rack-and-pinion railway pushes single carriages up the flanks of Snowdon, the highest peak in Wales, using Swiss-inspired technology that has operated for over a century in some of the harshest weather conditions in the country.

subject: Snowdonia National Park
summary: Wales's mountain heartland -- officially renamed Eryri in 2022 -- where the last Welsh princes held out against English kings, slate quarries scarred the valleys, and Snowdon trained Edmund Hillary for Everest.

subject: Sofiyivka Park
summary: A Polish count spent a fortune carving a mythological landscape of waterfalls and grottoes into a Ukrainian ravine, all as a birthday gift for the woman he loved.

subject: Solo Balapan Railway Station
summary: One of Indonesia's oldest major railway stations, built on a Javanese prince's horse-racing grounds in 1870, where a beloved campursari ballad turned a train platform into a national symbol of heartbreak and departure.

subject: Songshan Airport
summary: Built as a Japanese military airfield in 1936, Taipei's downtown airport launched bombing raids against China, survived American B-24 attacks, and now sits in the heart of a metropolis that cannot decide whether to keep it or tear it down.

subject: Songshan Cultural and Creative Park
summary: A 1937 Japanese-era tobacco factory that once employed 1,200 workers now houses design museums, art exhibitions, a 24-hour bookstore, and a Baroque garden with a fountain surrounded by sculptures of bathing women.

subject: Sonoma Coast State Park
summary: Seventeen miles of California coastline where mammoths once scratched their backs on sea stacks, the San Andreas Fault runs parallel to the shore, and the land itself erodes up to three feet per year into the Pacific.

subject: Sooke Harbour House
summary: A doctorate in political economics, an Italian food movement, and a small inn at the end of a gravel spit road made one of Canada's most celebrated restaurants.

subject: Sooke Potholes Regional Park
summary: Meltwater and trapped boulders spent thousands of years drilling round swimming holes into the bedrock of the Sooke River — and a failed 1980s resort left its concrete skeleton in the trees above them.

subject: Sophia University
summary: Japan's first Catholic university, born from a dream that Saint Francis Xavier carried to Japan in 1549 and three Jesuit priests finally realized 354 years later in central Tokyo.

subject: Soto Cano Air Base
summary: A Honduran military base south of Comayagua that has served as America's strategic foothold in Central America since 1980, operating on a handshake agreement and housing the only permanent U.S. military presence between Texas and Colombia.

subject: Soulangh Cultural Park
summary: Built as the Jiali Sugar Factory in 1906 during Japanese rule, the Soulangh Cultural Park transformed its 14 former warehouses into an arts complex celebrating Tainan folk art and the heritage of the Siraya people.

subject: South Devon Railway sea wall
summary: Isambard Kingdom Brunel laid a railway along four miles of open Devon coastline in 1846, and the sea has been trying to take it back ever since.

subject: South Luangwa National Park
summary: A 9,050-square-kilometer wildlife sanctuary in eastern Zambia where leopard density ranks among the highest on Earth, endemic subspecies roam the floodplains, and night safaris reveal a world most national parks keep hidden.

subject: South Pacific Coast Railroad
summary: A narrow-gauge steam railroad built by silver barons and strawberry farmers that carved eight tunnels through the Santa Cruz Mountains before becoming a casualty of the 1906 earthquake.

subject: South Penghu Marine National Park
summary: Taiwan's ninth national park protects a cluster of volcanic islands where abandoned villages crumble beside columnar basalt cliffs and 254 species of fish patrol some of the healthiest coral reefs in the archipelago.

story.title: South West Rocks Pilot Station Complex

subject: South West Rocks Pilot Station Complex
summary: A flood that tore a new mouth in the Macleay River forced a whole pilot station to pick up and move, leaving behind one of only two intact maritime pilot precincts in New South Wales.

subject: Southern Cardamom National Park
summary: A 4,104-square-kilometre park built partly for a tiger that no longer exists in Cambodia, and funded by carbon credits that displaced the people already living there.

subject: Southern Fuegian Railway
summary: The cheerful tourist train at the end of the world was built by prisoners, in the cold, to haul the wood and stone that built the jail that held them.

subject: Southern National Motorsports Park
summary: The Lucama short track that almost died in 2009, sold at auction for $650,000, and came back to host the richest Late Model Stock race in history.

subject: Southern Virginia University
summary: A Latter-day Saint-values college on a Blue Ridge campus that was once a girls' school, then a junior college, and has spent the last decade trying to reckon with what is carved on its older buildings.

subject: Southwest National Park
summary: Tasmania's largest national park has exactly one road, fewer than a hundred wild orange-bellied parrots on Earth, and a wilderness so trackless you can only reach most of it on foot, by boat, or by light plane.

subject: Soviet War Memorial (Treptower Park)
summary: Ten hectares of Berlin park where about seven thousand Red Army soldiers are buried, beneath a twelve-metre bronze soldier that Germany is treaty-bound to maintain.

subject: Spanish–American War Memorial (Arlington National Cemetery)
summary: Of the 2,910 Americans who died in the ten-week Spanish-American War, just 345 fell in combat - the rest died of disease. Arlington's granite column with a bronze eagle remembers all of them, and is the reason their bodies came home in the first place.

subject: Spartanburg Downtown Memorial Airport
summary: South Carolina's first commercial airport, opened in 1927 with Charles Lindbergh on hand to cut the ribbon months after his Atlantic crossing - now a thriving general aviation field on the edge of downtown Spartanburg.

subject: Spelman College
summary: The oldest private historically Black liberal arts institution for women, Spelman College was born from $100 and 11 students in a church basement in 1881, rising to become the nation's top-ranked HBCU.

subject: Sperenberg Airfield
summary: A secret Soviet air base hidden in the Brandenburg pines, with a town of 5,000 attached, a daily train to Moscow, and one very famous last passenger.

subject: Spipiyus Provincial Park
summary: A rugged mountain park on the Sechelt Peninsula where old-growth forest shelters the threatened marbled murrelet and a historic fire lookout tower commands views from Vancouver Island to the Strait of Georgia.

subject: Sproat Lake Provincial Park
summary: Ancient petroglyphs, the world's largest firefighting flying boats, and a lake named for a colonial entrepreneur -- Sproat Lake Provincial Park packs layers of history into 39 hectares on Vancouver Island's Highway 4.

subject: Spruce Railroad Trail
summary: A World War I railroad built to harvest spruce for warplanes arrived a year too late for the war, but its abandoned grade along the sapphire shores of Lake Crescent became one of the Olympic Peninsula's most beloved trails.

subject: Spurn Point military railway
summary: The standard-gauge military railway that once ran down a shifting sand spit - and the wind-driven 'sailing bogies' that local residents rode along its rails.

subject: Sriwijaya Kingdom Archaeological Park
summary: An archaeological park in Palembang preserves the ghostly outline of ancient canals and artificial islands that may trace back to the powerful Srivijaya empire, though the jungle and the river have erased almost everything else.

subject: St Flannan's College
summary: A neo-Gothic Ennis secondary school that began as a private academy in 1846, became a hub of Irish republican sentiment, and produced a future President of Ireland.

subject: St Helena Island National Park
summary: An island the Quandamooka people called Noogoon became colonial Queensland's high-security prison, branded 'the hell hole of the Pacific' yet run as a near self-sufficient farm.

subject: St James' Park
summary: The gallows it was named for closed in 1844; the football that replaced them has been played on the same patch of Newcastle ground ever since.

subject: St James's Park
summary: Henry VIII drained a marsh here to hunt deer; Charles II opened it to the public and used it to entertain mistresses; a Russian ambassador sent pelicans in 1664 that still live here today.

subject: St John's College, Cambridge
summary: The second wealthiest college in Oxbridge, founded in 1511 by the Tudor matriarch Lady Margaret Beaufort, where the D-Day landings were partly planned, where William Wordsworth and William Wilberforce studied, and where the Bridge of Sighs spans the Cam.

subject: St John's Railway Station
summary: Railwaymen called it the Manx Crewe - a junction of three companies, three platforms, an unofficial daily race to Peel, and a station master who cycled to his signal box well into the 1960s.

subject: St Kieran's College
summary: Founded in 1782 the moment the penal laws relaxed, Kilkenny's diocesan college became the most successful hurling school in Ireland - and the alma mater of Ralph Fiennes and Tomm Moore.

subject: St Mary Magdalene's Church, Battlefield
summary: A church built over what is probably the mass grave of the Battle of Shrewsbury, where chaplains chanted daily masses for the souls of soldiers killed in 1403.

story.title: St Mary's Airport, Isles of Scilly

subject: St Mary's Airport, Isles of Scilly
summary: Before there was a runway, the de Havilland Dragons landed on a golf course - and the only way off the islands was at the captain's pleasure.

subject: St Michael's College, Enniskillen
summary: The Catholic boys' grammar school at Drumclay has produced All-Ireland Hogan Cup winners and well-known alumni, and is also reckoning publicly with decades of clerical abuse uncovered in a 2025 trial.

subject: St Munchin's College
summary: A diocesan school founded in 1796 that turned into a Munster rugby nursery and a Cranberry's drumming ground.

subject: St Pancras Railway Station
summary: The Victorian cathedral of the railways saved from demolition by John Betjeman and the Furious Mrs Fawcett, now the London terminus for Eurostar trains to Paris, Brussels, and Amsterdam.

subject: St Patrick's College, Maghera
summary: A co-educational Catholic comprehensive in a small Ulster town whose Gaelic football team has won six All-Ireland Hogan Cups - more than any other school in the country.

subject: St Patrick's College, Tuam
summary: The Tuam boys' school whose first building was burned to the ground the night after the Christian Brothers were evicted - and whose great rivalry with St Jarlath's defined Connacht schoolboy football for forty years.

subject: St Patrick's Pontifical University, Maynooth
summary: Founded in 1795 to keep Catholic priests away from the dangerous ideas of revolutionary France, the Royal College of St Patrick became the largest seminary in the world and now grants degrees in canon law, philosophy and theology under a charter from Pope Leo XIII.

subject: St Stanislaus College
summary: A Jesuit school in a bog became 'the Bog'—where Francis Browne photographed the Titanic, Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote his last bleak retreat notes, and Evie Hone's stained glass briefly glowed.

subject: St. Cloud State University
summary: Founded in 1869 as a teacher-training school in a renovated hotel, St. Cloud State became the unlikely cradle of a Division I hockey powerhouse -- coached by the man who led the 1980 Miracle on Ice -- and a five-time NCAA wrestling champion, even as enrollment plunged by nearly half in a decade.

story.title: St. Ignatius Greek Orthodox Cemetery, Kadıköy

subject: St. Ignatius Greek Orthodox Cemetery, Kadıköy
summary: On the Asian shore of Istanbul, a ten-acre Greek Orthodox cemetery founded in 1895 holds the remains of a community whose ancient roots in Chalcedon — and whose painful twentieth-century diminishment — are written in marble across its grounds.

subject: St. Michael's Catholic Cemetery
summary: Hong Kong's oldest Catholic cemetery, tucked behind the Happy Valley Racecourse, where bishops, missionaries, and a golden age film star rest side by side.

subject: St. Peter's Mission Church and Cemetery
summary: A frontier mission in Montana where Jesuit priests, Ursuline nuns, a Metis revolutionary, and an African American woman known as 'Stagecoach Mary' crossed paths in one of the West's most colorful religious outposts.

subject: Staaken Garden City
summary: Germany stopped building in 1914 — except here, where a 29-year-old architect assembled 793 homes for munitions workers out of five house types and made them look like a town that had stood for centuries.

subject: Stahnsdorf South-Western Cemetery
summary: A 206-hectare pine forest holding 120,000 graves, a Norwegian-style stave church, the war dead of two foreign armies, and the grave from which someone stole F. W. Murnau's skull in 2015.

subject: Stamp River Provincial Park
summary: Half a million salmon climb its fish ladder each year, black bears gather on its banks, and the river itself carries the name of a Victorian sawmill pioneer -- Stamp River Provincial Park is where Vancouver Island's industrial past meets its wild present.

subject: Stanford Research Park
summary: The world's first university research park, born from Stanford's postwar financial desperation, became the incubator for Hewlett-Packard, Xerox PARC, Facebook, and the culture of Silicon Valley itself.

subject: Stanford University
summary: Built on a horse ranch by grieving parents, Stanford University sits on 8,180 acres of undeveloped peninsula land and has become one of the most influential institutions on Earth.

subject: Stanford University Libraries
summary: Nearly 12 million items across 24 libraries, a bookplate showing Jane Stanford offering jewels to Athena, and the story of how Stanford almost -- but didn't -- become home to the Reagan Presidential Library.

subject: Stanford University Medical Center
summary: A Level I trauma center ranked among the top 10 hospitals in America, with a rooftop helicopter pad and a history that began with a children's convalescent home in 1911.

subject: Stanford University School of Medicine
