summary: A 19th-century examination board that grew into the federation of 17 self-governing colleges Hitler reportedly chose as his London headquarters in the event of invasion.

subject: University of Lubumbashi
summary: One of the largest universities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, UNILU was the site of a 1990 massacre of student protesters that helped end Western support for Mobutu's regime.

subject: University of Manitoba
summary: Western Canada's first university, founded in 1877, produced more Rhodes Scholars than any other institution west of Ontario and counts Marshall McLuhan among its student newspaper alumni.

subject: University of Maryland
summary: Founded in 1856 as the Maryland Agricultural College on land bought by Charles Benedict Calvert, the flagship campus now spreads across 1,250 acres of arboretum, federal partnerships, and the largest academic mall in the United States.

subject: University of Maryland Eastern Shore
summary: An HBCU on Maryland's Lower Eastern Shore that began in a converted farmhouse with nine students - and now sends bowlers to NCAA finals and sprinters to the Olympics.

subject: University of Maryland, Baltimore
summary: Founded in 1807, UMB is a downtown campus of professional schools whose graduates include Edgar Allan Poe's neighbors, two governors, and the world's most powerful wine critic.

subject: University of Maryland, Baltimore County
summary: Founded in 1966 on land taken from a psychiatric hospital, UMBC became the first public Maryland university open to all races - and under Freeman Hrabowski's thirty-year presidency, a national model for producing Black scientists and engineers.

subject: University of Missouri
summary: The first public university west of the Mississippi River, founded in 1839, Mizzou pioneered the world's first journalism school, claims to have invented homecoming, operates the nation's sole source of medical isotopes, and has produced alumni from Sam Walton to Tennessee Williams.

subject: University of North Carolina Wilmington
summary: What began in September 1947 as a junior college for returning World War II veterans, with 238 students meeting in the basement of an old high school, is now a 19,000-student research university - the fastest-growing campus in the UNC system.

story.title: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

subject: University of North Carolina at Charlotte
summary: From night classes in a downtown high school to a thousand-acre research campus, UNC Charlotte grew up alongside the city that finally got the university it had wanted for sixty years.

story.title: University of North Carolina at Greensboro

subject: University of North Carolina at Greensboro
summary: North Carolina's first public university for women opened in 1892 in a single Greensboro building. It now anchors a Spartan campus, an art museum, and a writing program that has counted Nobel laureates among its visiting faculty.

story.title: University of North Carolina at Pembroke

subject: University of North Carolina at Pembroke
summary: Founded in 1887 by the North Carolina legislature to train Lumbee teachers, UNC Pembroke is the only historically Native American institution in the state's university system.

subject: University of North Dakota
summary: Founded six years before North Dakota was even a state, UND has produced the first female NASA technical employee, a pioneer Arctic aviator, an NBA coaching legend, and the nation's first unmanned aircraft degree program -- all from a campus that once connected to downtown Grand Forks by horse-drawn carriage.

subject: University of Oklahoma
summary: Founded in 1890 before Oklahoma was even a state, OU planted trees before it built buildings, pioneered civil rights law at its library, coined an architectural style called 'Cherokee Gothic,' and became a sports powerhouse with 45 national championships.

subject: University of Oxford
summary: The English-speaking world's oldest university, scattered across central Oxford in 43 colleges and halls, where teaching has continued without interruption since at least 1096.

subject: University of Pikeville
summary: A small Presbyterian college on a hillside in coal country that quietly became one of the three medical schools in Kentucky.

subject: University of Reading
summary: A red brick university in Berkshire where the weather of tomorrow gets calculated today and Samuel Beckett's archive sits next door to a working dairy farm.

subject: University of Richmond
summary: The university adopted a spider as its mascot, and in 1969 received what was then the largest single gift in American higher education — $50 million from a single alumnus.

subject: University of South Carolina
summary: Founded in 1801, built by enslaved labor, briefly the most progressive university in the South during Reconstruction, then resegregated for 86 years until three students integrated it in 1963.

subject: University of Southern California
summary: California's oldest private research university, founded in 1880, with the world's most influential film school, a historic campus near downtown Los Angeles, and 326 Olympic medals.

subject: University of Southern Mississippi
summary: A university born as a humble teachers' college in 1910, Southern Miss grew into Mississippi's research powerhouse -- surviving hurricanes, controversies, and a $500 fine for picking its roses.

subject: University of St Andrews
summary: Scotland's oldest university, founded in 1413 on a windswept Fife headland, where students wear scarlet gowns, jump cobblestones to dodge curses, and once included a future king and queen.

subject: University of Tehran
summary: Iran's oldest and most prestigious university carries the nickname 'Mother University' -- and the weight of nearly a century as the country's most politically charged campus, where revolutions have been sparked and Friday prayers held on the same grounds.

story.title: University of Texas at El Paso

subject: University of Texas at El Paso
summary: A fire destroyed the original mining school in 1916 -- and a dean's wife found inspiration in National Geographic photos of Bhutanese monasteries. Today UTEP's Himalayan-style campus overlooks the Rio Grande, bearing witness to the 1966 basketball championship that shattered college sports' color barrier.

story.title: The University of Tokyo: The Red Gate and the Nation It Built

subject: University of Tokyo
summary: Japan's first modern university -- founded in 1877 on a feudal lord's estate -- has produced 17 prime ministers, 20 Nobel laureates, the founder of Toyota, the creator of judo, and the team that launched the country's first satellite.

subject: University of Tulsa
summary: Born as the Presbyterian School for Indian Girls in 1882, the University of Tulsa evolved from a frontier mission school in Indian Territory into a research university that manages the world's largest collection of American Western art and houses the archives of both Woody Guthrie and Bob Dylan.

subject: University of Turku
summary: Born from national pride and citizen donations in 1920, Finland's first Finnish-language university rose from the ashes of what fire and politics had taken away nearly a century before.

subject: University of Twente
summary: A 1961 Dutch technical university built on an American campus model that has spun out more than a thousand companies, including the one that invented Bluetooth.

subject: University of Victoria
summary: A college that met in a coal baron's castle, died once, came back twice, and now runs the world's largest transgender archive and a cable on the floor of the Pacific.

subject: University of Virginia Health System
summary: From a single professor recruited by Jefferson to one of the South's largest academic medical centers - and a place that integrated its wards only in 1960.

story.title: University of Virginia School of Medicine

subject: University of Virginia School of Medicine
summary: America's tenth-oldest medical school, founded by Jefferson with one imported professor, has produced two Nobel laureates, the man who solved yellow fever, and a research culture that connects the brain to the immune system.

story.title: University of Wales Trinity Saint David

subject: University of Wales Trinity Saint David
summary: A multi-campus Welsh university built around Lampeter's 1828 royal charter - the oldest in Wales - and the 1848 teacher training college at Carmarthen, with newer campuses in Swansea, Cardiff, London, and Birmingham.

subject: University of Washington
summary: Founded in 1861 when Seattle was barely a town, the University of Washington grew from a ten-acre claim into one of the world's premier research universities, its cherry-lined Quad and lakeside stadium defining the intellectual heart of the Pacific Northwest.

subject: University of Winnipeg
summary: Born from the 1938 merger of two nineteenth-century colleges, the University of Winnipeg anchors the city's downtown and offers the world's only master's degree in Development Practice focused on Indigenous Development.

subject: University of Yangon
summary: Myanmar's oldest and most prestigious university, where the country's independence movement was born and where students have repeatedly risked their lives to challenge authoritarian rule.

subject: University of Zambia
summary: Zambia's oldest and largest university, UNZA opened in 1966 with Kenneth Kaunda as its first chancellor and later hosted Nelson Mandela's first university speech after his release from prison.

subject: University of ancient Taxila
summary: Centuries before Nalanda, the scholars of Taxila created one of history's first centers of higher learning -- a loose federation of teachers where students studied everything from Sanskrit grammar to surgery.

subject: University of the Bahamas
summary: A college born from four merged institutions in 1974 spent four decades becoming the Bahamas' national university, with research stations stretching from Nassau to coral reefs and cave systems on San Salvador Island.

subject: University of Évora
summary: Portugal's second-oldest university, founded by the Jesuits in 1559, shut down by the Marquis of Pombal with cavalry troops in 1759, and reopened nearly two centuries later in the same Renaissance cloister.

subject: Upemba National Park
summary: At its 1939 creation the largest national park in Africa, covering 17,730 square kilometers of Congolese wetlands, grasslands, and mountain forest, Upemba preserves the Upemba Depression's lakes where 1,800 species of plant and animal still live.

subject: Upper Nile University
summary: Founded in 1991, then scattered by war and reassembled in peace - a university on the banks of the White Nile that embodies South Sudan's struggle to build institutions amid conflict.

subject: Uppsala University
summary: The oldest university in Scandinavia, where Linnaeus tended his garden, Celsius measured temperature, and five centuries of scholars shaped Swedish culture and science.

subject: Upsala College
summary: A Swedish-American Lutheran college that opened in a Brooklyn church in 1893, migrated across New Jersey for a century, and closed in 1995 -- but left behind one of America's most legendary freeform radio stations.

subject: Urho Kekkonen National Park
summary: Finland's second-largest national park sprawls across Lapland's fells and wild forests along the Russian border, where Father Christmas reportedly rests between appearances and temperatures can plunge to minus fifty degrees.

subject: Ussangoda National Park
summary: A windswept plateau of rust-red earth on Sri Lanka's southern coast where iron-rich soils, ancient legends of Ravana's flying chariot, and sea turtles nesting on empty beaches converge in one of the island's youngest and most enigmatic national parks.

subject: Utrecht University
summary: Founded in 1636 with a Latin poem written by a woman, Utrecht University grew into one of Europe's most consequential research institutions - the university where Descartes argued, Eleanor Roosevelt received an honorary degree, and twelve Nobel laureates were shaped.

subject: Utría National Natural Park
summary: A pristine Colombian Pacific cove where humpback whales give birth in warm shallow waters, surrounded by one of the most biodiverse rainforests on Earth.

subject: Vale of Rheidol Railway
summary: The narrow gauge steam line that British Rail kept running for twenty years after it had given up on steam everywhere else - because nobody had quite the heart to close it.

subject: Valle Nuevo National Park
summary: A frost-bitten plateau in the heart of the Caribbean where glacial history, cloud forests, and political memory converge above 2,200 meters in the Dominican Republic's Cordillera Central.

story.title: Vallejo's Sonoma: Where California Changed Hands

subject: Vallejo's Sonoma
summary: Six historic sites clustered around a single plaza tell the story of how one man shaped Northern California's passage from Spanish mission to Mexican pueblo to American city.

subject: Van Cortlandt Park
summary: New York City's third-largest park, a 1,146-acre expanse in the Bronx that contains the nation's oldest public golf course, a 17,000-year-old forest, and the scars of Robert Moses's highway ambitions.

subject: Van Starkenborgh Canal
summary: In the depths of the Depression, 1,300 unemployed men dug the Van Starkenborgh Canal across Groningen province by hand. A century later, Queen Wilhelmina's plaque still sits at the lock, and the canal is being rebuilt to take four layers of stacked containers.

subject: Vancouver International Airport
summary: Canada's second-busiest airport, built on a Fraser River sandbar, where a five-tonne Haida canoe sits in the departures hall and floatplanes still carry the mail to villages with no roads.

subject: Vancouver Island University
summary: A Nanaimo university that heats its buildings with water from the flooded coal mine beneath it, began in a converted hospital, and eventually let go of the name of an explorer who never came here.

subject: Vassununga State Park
summary: A São Paulo forest park where a 600-year-old jequitibá-rosa called The Patriarch stands 40 meters tall in a scrap of cerrado spared by the coffee barons.

subject: Vauxhall Gardens
summary: London's great Georgian pleasure garden - rococo, scandalous, gas-lit and gone - whose name still means 'railway station' in Russian.

subject: Veluwezoom National Park
summary: Glaciers pushed up these hills 150,000 years ago and never quite finished the job, leaving the Netherlands' first national park and the closest thing the country has to a mountain.

subject: Venice Canal Historic District
summary: The six remaining canals of Abbott Kinney's 1905 vision of a California Venice, now a National Historic Landmark threading through one of Los Angeles's most beloved neighborhoods.

subject: Ver-o-Peso Complex
summary: Named for a colonial weighing house, Belém's great riverside market is 35,000 square meters of working commerce - fish, açaí, herbs and medicine - run by vendors who once faced down the engineers who wanted to bury it.

subject: Veun Sai-Siem Pang National Park
summary: A Cambodian forest counted not by sight but by sound, where an estimated 389 groups of a gibbon species unknown to science before 2010 sing over the noise of chainsaws.

subject: Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park
summary: Chile's oldest national park, where a perfect volcano stands over a turquoise lake and meltwater roars through black lava in the heart of the Valdivian rainforest.

subject: Vicksburg National Military Park
summary: Preserving the site of the 47-day siege that split the Confederacy in two, Vicksburg National Military Park holds 1,325 monuments along the bluffs where Union and Confederate forces fought for control of the Mississippi River.

subject: Victoria Boulevard Historic District
summary: Hampton's streetcar suburb where oyster wealth built Queen Anne mansions and Hampton Institute students helped raise the American Foursquares.

subject: Victoria Harbour
summary: A working harbour that begins with cruise ships on the open strait and ends, kilometres inland, as a tidal channel eighteen metres wide - and an estuary hiding inside a capital city.

subject: Victoria Harbour
summary: Victoria Harbour is the deep, sheltered waterway between Hong Kong Island and Kowloon that made the colony possible, shaped the skyline, and remains the most contested body of water in Asia.

subject: Victoria International Airport
summary: A 1939 grass strip on the Saanich Peninsula that trained Royal Air Force pilots, hosted flying boats on Patricia Bay, and now shelters a maritime helicopter squadron in a heliport named after a castle in Sussex.

subject: Victoria Park (Hong Kong)
summary: Hong Kong's most-visited public park — built on reclaimed seafloor in Causeway Bay, home to a statue that survived a wartime journey to Japan, and a gathering place for candlelight vigils, flower shows, and pro-democracy marches.

subject: Victoria Peak Garden
summary: Where the Governor of Hong Kong once retreated to a hilltop summer residence, a small Victorian garden now offers the closest publicly accessible view toward the summit — and a rare stillness above the city's noise.

subject: Vila Velha State Park
summary: In southern Brazil's Parana state, 340-million-year-old sandstone formations carved by wind and rain into towers, goblets, and castle-like ruins give Vila Velha its name: the Old Village, a city built by geology rather than human hands.

subject: Villa Borghese gardens
summary: Rome's third-largest public park began as a cardinal's party villa in 1605, holds six museums, a Shakespeare replica theater, and a colony of Mediterranean snails accidentally shipped to England on a stolen balustrade.

subject: Village Historique Acadien Provincial Park
summary: A living-history village on the marshes of northeastern New Brunswick where more than forty historic buildings and costumed interpreters recreate nearly two centuries of Acadian life after the great deportation.

subject: Villarrica National Park
summary: A Chilean park where one of the world's few permanently active lava lakes glows above ancient monkey-puzzle forests and a canyon of red-decked hot springs.

subject: Vilnius University
summary: Founded in 1579 as a Jesuit academy, closed by a tsar after a failed uprising, and reborn three times - Lithuania's oldest university and one of Eastern Europe's most consequential.

subject: Vilnius University Library
summary: Lithuania's oldest academic library - older than the university it serves - holding 5.4 million items including a first edition of Copernicus and frescoes painted by a Smuglewicz.

subject: Virachey National Park
summary: At 3,325 square kilometers, Virachey is one of Southeast Asia's largest and least-explored protected areas — a roadless wilderness of evergreen forest, high grasslands, and wild rivers on Cambodia's mountainous border with Laos and Vietnam.

subject: Viretta Park
summary: A quiet Seattle pocket park on the shore of Lake Washington became an unlikely pilgrimage site after Kurt Cobain was found dead next door, its weathered benches layered with decades of graffiti tributes from grieving fans.

subject: Virginia Commonwealth University
summary: An 11-seed Cinderella basketball team, a 1920s Moorish theater built by Shriners, and a downtown campus woven into the Fan: VCU is Richmond's biggest, weirdest university.

subject: Virginia Intermont College
summary: A women's college that opened in 1884, won three straight NAIA cross-country titles in the 2000s, closed in 2014 after 130 years, and burned to the ground a decade later on a December morning.

subject: Virginia-Maryland College of Veterinary Medicine
summary: A two-state veterinary college born of an interstate compact - and one of only a handful in the country shared by two land-grant universities and built around a curriculum of large animals, small animals, and Hokie Stone.

subject: Virunga National Park
summary: Africa's oldest national park -- a 7,800 square kilometer UNESCO World Heritage Site in the DR Congo where rangers risk their lives to protect mountain gorillas, active volcanoes, and the continent's most biodiverse landscapes.

subject: Visby City Wall
summary: The strongest and best-preserved medieval defensive wall in Scandinavia has encircled this Hanseatic town for over 700 years.

story.title: Vizcaya: The Harvester Fortune's Tropical Palace

subject: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens
summary: A farm machinery heir spent $15 million building an Italian Renaissance villa on Biscayne Bay, complete with seventy rooms of European antiques -- some of whose originals sank with the Titanic -- and gardens that transplanted Tuscany into the subtropics.

subject: Vjosa Wild River National Park
summary: Europe's first Wild River National Park protects 270 kilometers of the Vjosa and its tributaries as a free-flowing ecosystem, sheltering over 1,100 species including the critically endangered Balkan lynx.

subject: Vlissingen Naval Base
summary: Three centuries of Dutch warships started life on this stretch of Schelde waterfront, including the first dry dock in the Netherlands and the shipbuilder that still launches naval vessels today.

subject: Vlissingen Railway Station
summary: Once the Dutch end of the London-to-Berlin express line, now the second-westernmost station in the Netherlands, rebuilt in neo-baroque after a 1944 bombing.

subject: Volcan Baru National Park
summary: Panama's highest point is a dormant stratovolcano where, on a clear morning, you can see both the Pacific and the Caribbean from a single summit -- if the 13.5-kilometer climb doesn't stop you first.

subject: Volcanoes National Park
summary: Rwanda's volcanic sanctuary where mountain gorillas survive in misty bamboo forests, and the legacy of Dian Fossey still shapes every trek into the Virungas.

subject: Volkel Air Base
summary: A Dutch fighter base that has hosted Luftwaffe night fighters, RAF Tempests, and - for more than sixty years - American nuclear bombs the Dutch government refused to admit existed.

subject: Volunteer Park (Seattle)
summary: Designed by the Olmsted Brothers atop Capitol Hill, this Seattle park has cycled through four names, once served as a cemetery, and now holds an Art Deco museum, a Victorian greenhouse, and a sculpture locals call "The Doughnut."

subject: Volunteer Park Conservatory
summary: A Victorian glass greenhouse modeled on London's Crystal Palace has stood on Capitol Hill since 1912, housing 3,426 glass panes, five living plant worlds, and a Jade Tree grown from a cutting taken over a century ago.

subject: Voyageurs National Park
summary: Minnesota's only national park is also its most unusual -- a 218,000-acre labyrinth of interconnected lakes and boreal forest where the primary mode of transportation is water, the bedrock is up to three billion years old, and a gold rush once built an entire city on an island in Rainy Lake.

subject: Vũ Quang National Park
summary: A skull bought from a hunter in these Hà Tĩnh hills in May 1992 turned out to belong to an animal science had never recorded — and the mountain above had already hidden a rebel army for a decade.

subject: W. H. Bramble Airport
summary: Montserrat's international airport, named after the island's first Chief Minister, was swallowed by the Soufriere Hills eruption in 1997 -- severing a tiny Caribbean nation's lifeline to the world.

subject: Wadi El Gemal National Park
summary: The Valley of the Camels stretches from Red Sea mangroves to mountains that once held the only emeralds the ancient world knew.

subject: Wadi Seidna Air Base
summary: The Sudanese Air Force's main northern base, born as a World War II ferrying field and reborn in April 2023 as the last way out of Khartoum for the world's foreign nationals.

subject: Wageningen University & Research
summary: A small university in a small Dutch town that has, year after year, ranked as the best agriculture and forestry institution in the world - and helped make the Netherlands the second-largest food exporter on Earth.

subject: Wai-iti Dark Sky Park
summary: New Zealand's first International Dark Sky Park, a 135-hectare reserve near Wakefield where astronomers measured skies dark enough to rate Bortle 1 -- and then watched light pollution rise 150 percent in three years.

subject: Waimea Canyon State Park
summary: Ten miles long and 3,000 feet deep, Kauai's Waimea Canyon was carved by rainfall, river, and volcanic collapse into layers of basalt that have weathered from black to vivid red over millions of years.

subject: Wake Forest University
summary: A Baptist college founded on a Wake County plantation in 1834, transplanted to tobacco money in Winston-Salem in 1956, where the Demon Deacons now live.

story.title: Walkway Over the Hudson: The Abandoned Bridge That Became a Sky Park

subject: Walkway Over the Hudson
summary: The New York railroad bridge that burned in 1974 and sat abandoned for 35 years - now the world's longest elevated pedestrian bridge, offering views of the Hudson Valley from 212 feet above the river.

subject: Wall Drug
summary: The South Dakota drugstore that saved itself during the Depression by offering free ice water - now a 76,000 square foot roadside attraction with a giant dinosaur, a fake Mount Rushmore, and signs advertising it from as far away as Antarctica.

subject: Wall House II
summary: A house designed in 1973, abandoned for decades, and finally built in Groningen the year its architect died - a posthumous masterpiece in primary colors.

subject: Wall Street Mill
summary: The last intact gold-crushing mill in Joshua Tree is also the site of a killing — and the place where Bill Keys left a stone marker so plainspoken it became a monument.

subject: Wallace Island Marine Provincial Park
summary: A long, thin Gulf Island reachable only by boat, once a resort run by the photographer who discovered Marilyn Monroe, with a coal ship's bones on the reef at its southern tip.

subject: Wangerooge Island Railway
summary: A narrow-gauge railway from the ferry pier to the village has carried almost everything that arrives on Wangerooge since 1897.

subject: Wards Airfield
summary: The busiest airfield in the Southern Hemisphere in 1943 is now an avenue of government offices - but a concrete slab above it still bears a Fifth Air Force insignia.

subject: Warta Mouth National Park
summary: Poland's youngest national park protects a river valley nobody got around to straightening — 80 square kilometres of floodplain that turns into a lake every spring and back into pasture every summer.

subject: Waseda University
summary: Founded by a samurai-scholar prime minister in 1882, Waseda University has produced nine Japanese prime ministers, the co-founder of Sony, the novelist Haruki Murakami, and the diplomat who saved thousands of Jews during the Holocaust -- all from a campus whose clock tower stands exactly 125 shaku tall, honoring the founder's eccentric theory about the natural human lifespan.

subject: Washington Airport
summary: For fourteen years, planes landed on the patch of Virginia mud now occupied by the Pentagon's south parking lot - with a burning garbage dump on one side, an amusement park's roller coaster on the other, and pilots forced to dodge both.

story.title: Washington Maritime National Wildlife Refuge Complex

subject: Washington Maritime National Wildlife Refuge Complex
summary: Hundreds of rocky islets along Washington's outer coast, set aside by Theodore Roosevelt in 1907, shelter over a million seabirds and a growing population of sea otters in one of the wildest stretches of American coastline.

subject: Washington Park Arboretum
summary: A 230-acre living museum in the heart of Seattle where Duwamish portage routes, a former horse racing track turned azalea promenade, and one of America's most authentic Japanese gardens share space with freeway ghosts.

subject: Washington Rock State Park
summary: A 52-acre state park on the first Watchung ridge in Green Brook, New Jersey, where George Washington monitored British troop movements in 1777 from a vantage point that still offers a 30-mile panorama to New York City.

subject: Washington Slagbaai National Park
summary: The first nature reserve in the former Netherlands Antilles, built on the ruins of two plantations -- one named for the slaughter of thousands of goats -- where flamingos now wade through salt pans that hurricanes reclaimed from industry.

subject: Washington University in St. Louis
summary: Founded in 1853 by civic leaders worried about the lack of higher education in the Midwest, WashU's Collegiate Gothic campus hosted the 1904 Olympics and has been the venue for four presidential debates.

subject: Washington and Lee University
summary: A 1749 Lexington college kept alive by George Washington's gift of canal stock, presided over after the Civil War by Robert E. Lee, and still arguing in the present tense about whose name it carries.

subject: Washpool National Park
summary: A World Heritage remnant of the ancient Gondwana forests, holding the largest stand of coachwood rainforest left on Earth - saved from the chainsaw and now alive with lyrebirds.

subject: Wasur National Park
summary: Called the 'Serengeti of Papua,' this vast wetland in Indonesia's South Papua province shelters birds-of-paradise, cassowaries, and crocodiles while four indigenous communities continue ancient ways of life within its borders.

subject: Watarrka National Park
summary: Home to Kings Canyon and its vertiginous 300-meter cliffs, Watarrka National Park shelters a hidden oasis called the Garden of Eden in the heart of Australia's Red Centre.

subject: Waterberg Plateau Park
summary: A sheer-sided sandstone tabletop rising from the Namibian bushveld, Waterberg shelters rhino, vultures, and rare antelope above ground where a nation once made its last stand.

subject: Waterford Airport
summary: Ireland's smallest regional airport, kept alive through closures, comebacks, and a tragedy that changed how the country rescues its sailors.

story.title: Waterton-Glacier: The World's First International Peace Park

subject: Waterton-Glacier
summary: The park where Canada and the United States decided the border shouldn't matter - Rotary Clubs started it in 1932, and the ecosystem that ignores the line has been protected as one ever since.

subject: Watoga State Park
summary: West Virginia's largest state park, named for a Cherokee word meaning starry waters, built by Depression-era young men and certified today as one of the darkest skies in the eastern United States.

subject: Watters Smith Memorial State Park
summary: A 532-acre Harrison County state park preserving the 1796 homestead of a New Jersey settler who walked west to the western Virginia hills - now also a mountain-biking destination with twelve miles of single-track.

subject: Way Kambas National Park
summary: A last refuge in southern Sumatra where Sumatran rhinos, elephants, and tigers cling to survival amid regenerating rainforest, guarded by anti-poaching patrols and a sanctuary closed to the public.

story.title: Weaverville Joss House State Historic Park

subject: Weaverville Joss House State Historic Park
summary: California's oldest Chinese temple still stands in a small mountain town, a testament to the immigrant workers who built the West and the advocate who saved their sacred space.

subject: Wedgwood Memorial College
summary: For half a century, a residential college in a Staffordshire village taught weekend courses in Esperanto, art history, and literature - until the council closed it, leaving the language behind to carry on.

subject: Weequahic Park
summary: An Olmsted Brothers-designed park in Newark's South Ward where Lenape boundary markers, a racing oval that once hosted President Grant, Philip Roth's literary landscapes, and the world's longest rubberized trail share 311 acres of storied ground.

subject: Weerribben-Wieden National Park
summary: The largest peat bog in northwestern Europe — and a landscape almost entirely made by people digging it apart for fuel.

subject: Weißensee Cemetery
summary: Forty-two hectares and nearly 116,000 graves in north-east Berlin: the largest preserved Jewish cemetery in Europe by area, which came through the Nazi years essentially untouched and is still burying its dead.

subject: Welford National Park
summary: Where red dunes meet Mitchell-grass plains and the Barcoo River, a single park holds three of outback Queensland's great ecosystems - and the memory of who walked them first.

subject: Welford Road Cemetery
summary: Leicester's main Victorian cemetery, where Thomas Cook lies a short walk from a Napoleonic veteran, and where a controversial council policy in the 2000s laid a thousand headstones flat.

subject: Wellington Harbour
summary: A harbour born from the thrashing of mythic taniwha, shaped by earthquakes and war, and still teeming with dolphins, orca, and the restless wind that defines New Zealand's capital.

subject: Wells Harbour
summary: A tidal harbour with over 600 years of maritime history, where navigating the shifting channel across the sand bar remains as much an art as it ever was.

subject: Wells Harbour Railway
summary: A beloved 10¼-inch gauge railway that carried holidaymakers between Wells-next-the-Sea and the Holkham pinewoods for 45 years before closing in 2021.

subject: Welsh Highland Heritage Railway
summary: Born in 1961 from a small group of railway enthusiasts (and a few disgruntled volunteers), the WHHR preserves the original Welsh Highland Railway with the only surviving locomotive from that lost line.

subject: Welsh Memorial Park, Ypres
summary: Ninety-six years after the Armistice, Wales finally built a national memorial to its war dead - on the Belgian ridge where the poet Hedd Wyn was killed.

subject: Welsh Mountain Zoo
summary: A hillside zoo above Colwyn Bay where snow leopards, chimpanzees and Welsh mountain goats share thirty-seven acres of woodland, started in 1963 by one enthusiastic naturalist.

subject: Wembley Park
summary: A north London district that began as a landscape architect's country estate and became the home of a failed Eiffel Tower, a stadium, and an entire decade's worth of Olympic events.

subject: Wessem-Nederweert Canal
summary: Seventeen kilometres of straight water dug between 1925 and 1928 to carry Limburg coal toward Tilburg - the unglamorous backbone canal whose Panheel Lock saves 60 per cent of its water in summer.

subject: West Coast Fossil Park
summary: A former phosphate mine on South Africa's west coast that unearthed one of the world's richest collections of five-million-year-old fossils, preserving over 300 animal species from a vanished coastal ecosystem.

subject: West Coast National Park
summary: A park where migratory birds from three continents converge on a single turquoise lagoon, and spring wildflowers transform the coastal scrub into one of South Africa's most extraordinary natural spectacles.

subject: West Coast Wilderness Railway
summary: A restored Abt rack railway that grips the rails by its teeth to haul travellers through the King River rainforest, retracing the only line that once connected Queenstown to the rest of the world.

subject: West Norwood Cemetery
summary: Forty acres of Victorian Gothic cemetery in south London where Mrs Beeton, Sir Henry Tate, and the founder of Reuters were laid to rest under oaks older than the cemetery itself.

subject: West Somerset Railway
summary: Britain's longest independent heritage railway, where steam still hauls chocolate-and-cream carriages along 22 miles of Somerset coast and Quantock foothills.

subject: West Virginia State University
summary: A 1891 land-grant HBCU founded on land donated by the mixed-race daughter of an interracial Virginia couple - whose alumni include Katherine Johnson, Earl Lloyd, and Antoine Fuqua.

story.title: West Virginia University Institute of Technology

subject: West Virginia University Institute of Technology
summary: An engineering college born in 1895 to serve the coalfields, packed up in 2017 and moved 30 miles down the road - leaving an Appalachian river town with empty classrooms and a National Register Old Main.

subject: West Virginia Wesleyan College
summary: A 1,055-student Methodist-affiliated liberal arts college in Buckhannon, West Virginia, founded in 1890, whose graduates include the actor who played Lurch, a leading cell biologist, and the football coach who built the Philadelphia Eagles into champions.

subject: Western Area Peninsula National Park
summary: The rainforest above Freetown - water source, bird haven, and refuge for rescued chimpanzees.

subject: Western Pacific Railroad Museum
summary: Where visitors can climb into the cab of a real locomotive and run it themselves, at a museum preserving one of America's most complete railroad collections.

subject: Western Wall
summary: The last remnant of Herod's Temple Mount expansion, where two thousand years of Jewish longing are pressed into the cracks between ancient limestone blocks.

subject: Western Washington University
summary: The northernmost university in the contiguous United States keeps Noguchis and Serras out on the lawn, and opened the country's first college devoted to environmental science in 1969.

subject: Westland Tai Poutini National Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage park where glaciers grind through temperate rainforest to within reach of the sea, and 11 meters of annual rainfall feed one of Earth's most compressed ecological gradients.

subject: Westwood Motorsport Park
summary: Canada's first purpose-built road course was carved into a Coquitlam mountainside by a volunteer car club in 1959; after thirty-one years of Formula Atlantic and Trans-Am, it was paved over for a golf course and a subdivision.

subject: Weymouth Harbour Tramway
summary: A heavy mainline railway that ran through the streets of Weymouth for 155 years, with railwaymen walking ahead waving flags to clear parked cars from the tracks.

subject: Whanganui National Park
summary: A national park shaped more by human settlement than by wilderness, where a concrete bridge leads to farms that vanished and a marae stands on contested ancestral ground.

story.title: What San Diego Looked Like Before It Became San Diego

subject: What San Diego Looked Like Before It Became San Diego
summary: Richard Henry Dana Jr. was nineteen years old when he first saw Old Town San Diego from the deck of a hide-trading vessel in 1835.

subject: Whatcom Falls Park
summary: The creek that built Bellingham still falls through 241 acres of city forest - past a children's fishing pond, a cliff-jumping swimming hole, and a stretch of woods that has never fully recovered from 1999.

subject: Wheeler Army Airfield
summary: A National Historic Landmark on central Oahu where Amelia Earhart once landed, Japanese bombers struck minutes before Pearl Harbor, and Spanish Colonial Revival homes still line garden-city loops designed to reject the industrial bleakness of company towns.

subject: Wheelus Air Base
summary: Once the largest American military installation outside the United States, this Libyan air base served Italian, German, British, American, and Soviet forces before becoming Tripoli's international airport.

subject: Where Brunei Meets the Sea
summary: The headquarters of the Royal Brunei Navy sits on a stretch of coast that has served naval powers since the Japanese occupation, guarding the mouth of the Brunei River where it empties into the South China Sea.

story.title: Where Gold Seekers Crossed and the River Kept Flowing

subject: Where Gold Seekers Crossed and the River Kept Flowing
summary: South Yuba River State Park protects 22 miles of wild Sierra canyon, the longest wooden covered bridge in the world, and swimming holes that have drawn visitors since the Gold Rush.

story.title: Where World Leaders Go for a Morning Walk

subject: Where World Leaders Go for a Morning Walk
summary: Brunei's sultan has a habit of inviting visiting heads of state to his favorite park for an early stroll -- and each one plants a tree before leaving.

subject: Where the Peacocks Once Stood
summary: The Port of Merak, named for the green peafowl that once roamed Java's northwestern tip, is a seaport rebuilt from total destruction by Krakatoa's 1883 tsunami -- now the chokepoint where Java's 150 million people connect to Sumatra across the Sunda Strait.

story.title: Where the Rocks Remember the Sea

subject: Where the Rocks Remember the Sea
summary: A stretch of Sonoma coast where honeycomb sandstone tells a story forty million years old, the Kashaya Pomo harvested salt with abalone chisels, and California's first underwater park protects a world beneath the waves.

story.title: Where the Valley Came to Grind

subject: Where the Valley Came to Grind
summary: Before Napa Valley was famous for wine, it was famous for flour -- and one waterwheel-powered mill built from redwood and Douglas fir was the reason settlers gathered here at all.

subject: White Desert National Park
summary: A surreal field of wind-carved white chalk towers in Egypt's Western Desert, where the seabed of an ancient ocean has been sculpted into mushrooms, animals, and impossible shapes.

subject: White Sands National Park
summary: The world's largest gypsum dunefield, a surreal white desert in southern New Mexico that holds the oldest human footprints in North America and is completely surrounded by a military missile range.

subject: Whitney Plantation Historic District
summary: Once a sprawling sugar plantation worked by enslaved people for over a century, Whitney Plantation became America's first museum dedicated exclusively to the history of slavery.

subject: Wicklow Mountains National Park
summary: Just south of Dublin, 205 square kilometres of blanket bog, oak woodland, and granite uplands preserve a landscape where monks once hid from Viking raiders and lead miners tunnelled through mountains.

subject: Wildcat Canyon Regional Park
summary: A nearly 2,800-acre stretch of canyon and ridgeline above Richmond where Cold War missile silos gave way to grazing cattle and hiking trails with sweeping Bay Area views.

subject: Wildwoods Shore Resort Historic District
summary: The largest concentration of mid-century Doo Wop motels in the world, where plastic palm trees, neon, and Tiki dreams survive against the condo tide.

subject: Willandra National Park
summary: A grand 1918 woolshed-and-homestead complex marooned in the saltbush plains west of Hillston, where one of Australia's great Merino studs once ran sheep by the hundred thousand.

story.title: William B. Ide Adobe State Historic Park

subject: William B. Ide Adobe State Historic Park
summary: This California state park honors the only president of the short-lived California Republic, though the adobe building that bears his name was never actually his home, a delightful irony that the state decided to embrace.

subject: William B. Umstead State Park
summary: 5,442 acres of farmland too tired to grow cotton, bought by the New Deal in 1934 and turned by the Civilian Conservation Corps into a forest that sits between the runway lights and downtown Raleigh.

subject: William O'Brien State Park
summary: A lumber baron bought up cut-over pinelands along the St. Croix River for his personal estate; twenty years after his death, his daughter gave them to Minnesota, creating the state's first park within reach of the Twin Cities and one of its five most visited.

subject: Willow River State Park
summary: Trilobite fossils in the gorge walls date back 600 million years, but this Wisconsin state park near Hudson owes its existence to a German immigrant who built hydroelectric dams on the Willow River in the 1890s -- and the power company that eventually sold the land to the state.

subject: Wiluna Railway Line
summary: The branch line that ran the rails as far from Perth as they ever went - out to the desert town of Wiluna, where the Canning Stock Route ended and the cattle finally caught a train.

subject: Wind Cave National Park
summary: A breathing cave beneath untouched prairie, where 95% of the world's boxwork formations hide in passages that have never known water.

subject: Winnipeg Railway Museum
summary: Housed inside the active Union Station on disused platforms and tracks, the Winnipeg Railway Museum shelters the Countess of Dufferin -- the first locomotive to reach the Canadian prairies -- along with vintage railcars and model layouts that chart how steel rails built a city and connected a nation.

subject: Winter Harbour
summary: Vancouver Island's westernmost settlement has dwindled from a bustling fishing hub where 200 boats crowded the harbour to a community of just two permanent residents -- yet its sheltered cove, wild surf beaches, and stubborn general store keep drawing people to the edge of the map.

subject: Winthrop University
summary: Founded in 1886 with $1,500 from a Boston philanthropist to train white women teachers, Winthrop became Rock Hill's anchor institution - the only public university in South Carolina with all arts programs accredited, and now the only Division I school offering cornhole scholarships.

story.title: Wisconsin Dells: The Water Park Capital of the World

subject: Wisconsin Dells
summary: The Wisconsin Dells that went from geological wonder to tourist trap - where spectacular sandstone gorges became irrelevant compared to the indoor water parks, go-kart tracks, and haunted houses that now define America's kitschiest destination.

subject: Witjira National Park
summary: On the western lip of the Simpson Desert, a vast park guards a chain of warm springs that have sustained Aboriginal life for tens of thousands of years.

subject: Wittenborg University of Applied Sciences
summary: A Dutch business school that began in 1987 teaching banking to ex-soldiers in Deventer and now teaches international management in English to students from 97 countries.

subject: Wollumbin National Park
summary: The small but extraordinary national park wrapped around the sacred peak of Wollumbin - a refuge for threatened wildlife, a fragment of ancient Gondwana rainforest, and the place where a famous summit climb was set aside out of respect for its Bundjalung custodians.

subject: Wolverton Railway Works
summary: The Victorian railway works that built locomotives, fed two new towns, made Horsa gliders for D-Day, and still services Britain's trains 187 years after it opened.

subject: Woodland Park (Seattle)
summary: A 91-acre urban park in Seattle that evolved from a lumber baron's private estate into a beloved public green space, bisected by a highway and haunted by a presidential ghost story.

subject: Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx, New York)
summary: A 400-acre National Historic Landmark cemetery in the Bronx where Miles Davis, Herman Melville, Duke Ellington, Bat Masterson, and Madam C.J. Walker rest among the most eclectic collection of notables in American ground.

subject: Woodlawn Memorial Park
summary: Established in 1905 as the Masonic Burial Ground, Woodlawn Memorial Park in Colma is one of seventeen cemeteries in the town that houses more dead than living residents.

subject: Woodward Park
summary: Born from a businessman's bequest and shaped by decades of community ambition, Fresno's largest park holds a Japanese garden built with boulders from a sister city, a cross-country course that hosts state championships, and a music festival that brought Snoop Dogg to the San Joaquin Valley.

subject: Work People's College
summary: A Finnish Lutheran school in a Duluth suburb was taken over by socialists in 1907 and became a radical labor college aligned with the Industrial Workers of the World -- educating miners, loggers, and dockworkers for 34 years.

subject: Wrecks of Saint-Pierre harbor
summary: Nearly 400 ships were destroyed in minutes when Mount Pelee's pyroclastic surge swept through Saint-Pierre's harbor on May 8, 1902, killing over 500 sailors and creating one of the Caribbean's most haunting underwater graveyards.

subject: Wright Brothers Park (Montgomery, Alabama)
summary: A small Montgomery park overlooking the Alabama River where a full-scale Wright Flyer replica marks the spot where Orville Wright opened the nation's first civilian flight school in 1910.

subject: Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where 9,000 years of Indigenous rock art adorns sandstone cliffs along the Milk River, sacred to the Blackfoot people.

subject: Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park
summary: Ancient sandstone deposited 84 million years ago along an inland sea now bears 9,000 years of Indigenous rock art, the largest concentration on the Great Plains.

subject: Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park
summary: The Alberta badlands where the Milk River carved hoodoos from sandstone and Indigenous peoples carved stories into rock - the largest concentration of rock art on the North American Plains, sacred to the Blackfoot for millennia.

subject: Wude Airfield
summary: A forgotten World War II military airfield on Penghu Island's southwestern tip, built by Imperial Japan in 1937 and bombed by the U.S. Army Air Forces in 1944, now locked behind a military garrison and all but erased from public memory.

story.title: Wufeng Lin Family Mansion and Garden

subject: Wufeng Lin Family Mansion and Garden
summary: One of Taiwan's grandest family compounds spans nearly two centuries of architecture, from a thatched farmhouse built in 1837 to ornate halls that hosted operas for a devoted son's elderly mother.

subject: Wutaishan National Park
summary: A practical guide to visiting China's most sacred Buddhist mountain, where five flat terraces shelter over 53 monasteries, vegetarian noodle shops line the pilgrimage town, and minibuses ferry visitors to peaks above 3,000 meters.

subject: Xiaolin Village Memorial Park
summary: A memorial park in Jiasian District, Kaohsiung, built on the site where a landslide triggered by Typhoon Morakot on August 9, 2009 buried Xiaolin Village, killing more than 400 people — many of them Taivoan indigenous residents.

subject: Xinghai Park
summary: A beach park on Dalian's southern coast that began as a Japanese colonial resort called Star Beach and remains one of the city's most popular seaside escapes.

subject: Xingu Indigenous Park
summary: A 26,420 square kilometer island of forest protected in 1961 for the sixteen indigenous peoples who live there, the first territory of its kind in the world.

subject: Yala National Park
summary: Sri Lanka's most visited national park holds the highest leopard density on Earth -- nearly 100 cats prowling 979 square kilometers of monsoon forest, thorn scrub, and coastal lagoons.

subject: Yangmingshan National Park
summary: Taipei's volcanic backyard, renamed by Chiang Kai-shek after his favorite philosopher, is a place where sulfur vents hiss through fumaroles, milky lakes steam at 40 degrees, and septuagenarian hikers outpace visitors half their age on basalt-paved trails.

subject: Yarmouk Military Industrial Complex
summary: Sudan's main state munitions factory, inaugurated 1996, hit by an alleged Israeli airstrike in 2012, and site of the "Yarmouk massacre" airstrike of June 2023 that killed five children among seventeen dead in the ongoing civil war.

subject: Yasuni National Park
summary: The most biodiverse place on Earth, where 100,000 insect species and the Waorani people share a park that survived a national referendum on its future.

subject: Yasuní National Park
summary: Between two Amazonian rivers lies a rainforest so biodiverse that a single hectare holds as many insect species as all of North America combined.

subject: Ybycuí National Park
summary: A forested Paraguayan park of waterfalls and clear pools that hides the rusted bones of La Rosada, one of South America's first ironworks, burned in the War of the Triple Alliance.

subject: Yeager Airport
summary: Charleston's clifftop airport, named for the West Virginia farmboy who broke the sound barrier - where pilots land on a runway carved from a flattened mountain and stopped by EMAS crushable concrete at both ends.

story.title: Yellowstone: The First National Park on Earth

subject: Yellowstone
summary: The Wyoming preserve where Old Faithful erupts on schedule, where grizzlies roam freely, and where a supervolcano slumbers beneath hot springs and geysers - the world's first national park, established in 1872 to protect wonders that early visitors thought no one would believe.

subject: Yellowstone National Cemetery
summary: Born from a grassroots campaign by Montana veterans who built their own cemetery to federal standards, then convinced the government to adopt it.

subject: Yellowstone National Park
summary: The world's first national park, where half of Earth's geothermal features bubble and steam above a supervolcano that could reshape continents.

subject: Yellowstone National Park
summary: The world's first national park sits atop a supervolcano that has shaped not just its own spectacular landscape but the global conservation movement itself.

subject: Yenching University
summary: A Christian university in Beijing that merged East and West, built on a Qing prince's royal gardens, and partnered with Harvard before being dissolved by Cold War politics.

subject: Yerba Buena Gardens
summary: Two blocks of public parks in SoMa featuring a Martin Luther King Jr. memorial, a children's creativity museum, and a waterfall that anchors San Francisco's cultural south-of-Market renaissance.

subject: Yokoamichō Park
summary: A small park in Sumida, Tokyo that holds the ashes of over 160,000 people killed in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and the World War II firebombing of Tokyo, making it one of the most solemn memorial sites in Japan.

subject: Yokohama War Cemetery
summary: The only Commonwealth War Graves Commission site in Japan holds the remains of over 1,500 Allied soldiers who died as prisoners of war or during the occupation, along with a cremation memorial sheltering the ashes of 335 more.

subject: Yokota Air Base
summary: A joint U.S.-Japanese air base in Western Tokyo that has served as America's front door to the Pacific since 1945, hosting everything from Korean War combat missions to earthquake relief operations.

subject: York Museum Gardens
summary: Ten acres beside the River Ouse where Roman walls, Gothic abbey ruins, and Victorian science cohabit in a single botanic garden.

subject: Yorkshire Dales National Park
summary: A 2,178-square-kilometre stitchwork of green valleys, dry-stone walls, and dark skies across the Pennines, designated in 1954 and now famous for limestone, sheep, and James Herriot.

subject: Yosemite National Park
summary: America's first scenic preserve - where granite cliffs rise 3,000 feet from the valley floor, waterfalls tumble from impossible heights, and giant sequoias have stood for millennia.

subject: Yosemite National Park
summary: Nearly 1,200 square miles of granite, glaciers, and giant sequoias in the Sierra Nevada, where Abraham Lincoln signed the first land preservation act in history and where the very idea of a national park was born.

subject: Yosemite Village Historic District
summary: A cluster of rustic buildings on the floor of Yosemite Valley where a publisher's apple orchard, an Army superintendent's residence, and Ansel Adams' first studio tell the story of how America learned to manage its most spectacular landscapes.

story.title: Yoshino-Kumano National Park: Cherry Blossoms, Sacred Water, and Ancient Stone

subject: Yoshino-Kumano National Park
summary: Japan's most spiritually layered national park stretches across three prefectures in disconnected fragments -- from a mountain draped in 30,000 cherry trees to a 133-meter sacred waterfall to gorges carved through volcanic rock by rivers that have never stopped praying.

subject: Yoyogi Park
summary: From Japan's first powered flight to a U.S. military housing complex to the 1964 Olympics, Yoyogi Park has reinvented itself with every generation -- and now belongs to Sunday rockabillies and cosplayers.

subject: Ypoá National Park
summary: Paraguay's largest lake anchors a vast, road-poor wilderness of marsh and grassland where more than 200 bird species thrive and rheas run across the plains.

subject: Ypres Town Cemetery and Extension
summary: Belgian civilians and Commonwealth soldiers share a single cemetery on the edge of Ypres - and somewhere among the rows lies Queen Victoria's grandson, killed at twenty-three.

subject: Ysselsteyn German War Cemetery
summary: 31,598 German graves in a Dutch field - including SS officers, conscripted teenagers, Anne Frank's betrayer, and thousands of men who never wanted to be there.

subject: Yuchi Naval Base
summary: Home port of China's first aircraft carrier Liaoning, this sprawling naval base south of Qingdao underwent massive expansion starting in 2012 and anchors the PLAN's North Sea Fleet.

subject: Yuen Po Street Bird Garden
summary: Tucked between Mong Kok's high-rises, Hong Kong's famous bird market preserves a living tradition of songbird culture that stretches back to the Qing dynasty — where elderly men still carry caged birds on morning walks and handmade bamboo cages sell alongside the chirping of hundreds of birds.

subject: Yuma International Airport
summary: A joint civil-military airport where Amelia Earhart once nosed into the sand, where President Coolidge signed the enabling legislation in 1928, and where Boeing tests its widebody jets because the desert provides conditions no other location can replicate.

subject: Yunlong Park
summary: An urban park in Xuzhou built on a former cemetery, where a Tang dynasty pavilion, a Han dynasty burial mound, and 1.7 million annual visitors share ground named for the Cloud Dragon.

subject: Yuraygir National Park
summary: Sixty-five kilometres of beaches, heath and headlands with almost nothing built on them - the longest stretch of undeveloped coastline left in New South Wales, walked end to end by emus and hikers alike.

subject: Yushan National Park
summary: Taiwan's largest, highest, and least accessible national park spans 103,121 hectares of the Central Mountain Range, harboring more than thirty peaks above 3,000 meters and the Bunun people who have called these mountains home for three centuries.

subject: Yuyuantan Park
summary: A Beijing park with an imperial lake created by the Qianlong Emperor that nearly vanished before being revived, now famous across China for its cherry blossoms each spring.

subject: Yıldız Park
summary: The wooded former palace grounds above the Bosphorus — once sealed for the sultan's exclusive use, now Istanbul's beloved hilltop retreat of pavilions, porcelain, and panoramic water views.

subject: Zahamena National Park
summary: A roadless World Heritage rainforest on Madagascar's eastern escarpment, where some of the rarest raptors on Earth still hunt unseen.

subject: Zahedan railway station
summary: Where two nations' rail gauges collide at the edge of Iran's southeastern desert, Zahedan Railway Station marks the endpoint of a line born from imperial strategy, abandoned, revived by war, and rebuilt across some of the most punishing terrain in Central Asia.

subject: Zahir-od-dowleh cemetery
summary: A small cemetery in northern Tehran where Iran's greatest poets, musicians, and artists are buried beneath the tree where a Sufi leader once sat -- the country's unofficial cultural pantheon.

subject: Zakouma National Park
summary: A 3,000-square-kilometer park in southern Chad where 95% of the elephants were poached in eight years, then a nonprofit took over management and the herds began to recover -- now home to possibly the largest single elephant herd in Africa.

subject: Zalissia National Nature Park
summary: An old-growth pine forest near Kyiv that has spent decades as a guarded retreat for senior officials - a national park that has never quite become a park you can visit.

subject: Zhalan Cemetery
summary: The oldest Christian cemetery in China, where Matteo Ricci and eighty-seven other Jesuits lie buried, their tombstones surviving vandals, rebels, and Red Guards through sheer luck and one quick-thinking party official.

subject: Zhang Garden
summary: A Tianjin mansion that sheltered both the first president of the Republic of China and the last emperor of the Qing Dynasty before being demolished and rebuilt as a Japanese garrison.

subject: Zhengzhou railway station
summary: Called 'the heart of China's railway network,' Zhengzhou's central station has stood at the junction of two major rail lines since 1904, surviving war, flood, and revolution to become one of the busiest transit hubs in the country.

subject: Zhongshan Park (Beijing)
summary: A former imperial altar where Ming and Qing emperors prayed for bountiful harvests now serves as a public park at the very heart of Beijing's power center.

story.title: Zillebeke Churchyard Commonwealth War Graves Commission Cemetery

subject: Zillebeke Churchyard Commonwealth War Graves Commission Cemetery
summary: In a Flemish village churchyard lie a handful of British officers killed in autumn 1914 - so many of them titled that the place became known as 'the aristocrats' cemetery.'

subject: Zincirlikuyu Cemetery
summary: Istanbul's great modern cemetery on Büyükdere Avenue, where prime ministers, novelists, footballers, and folk singers rest side by side — a gathering place for the full range of Turkish public life in the 20th century.

subject: Zion National Park
summary: Utah's first national park, where sheer sandstone cliffs rise 2,000 feet from the Virgin River in a landscape early settlers could only call Zion.

subject: Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex
summary: The most beautiful coal mine in the world - a 1932 Bauhaus-influenced industrial cathedral in Essen that closed in 1986 and rose again as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, museum, and design landmark.

subject: Zombitse-Vohibasia National Park
summary: A fragmented national park straddling Madagascar's Route Nationale 7 where the island's western and southern ecological domains collide, harbouring a lemur that exists in no other protected area on Earth and an orchid found only within its boundaries.

subject: Zorgvlied
summary: An English garden cemetery on the Amstel where Dutch celebrities are buried under increasingly theatrical monuments, including a nightclub owner forever raising a glass of beer.

subject: Zoro Garden Nudist Colony
summary: The 'nudist colony' at the 1935 California Pacific International Exposition in Balboa Park was staffed by hired performers rather than actual nudists — and the San Diego Braille Club protested it anyway.

subject: Zuid-Kennemerland National Park
summary: A 38-square-kilometer ribbon of dunes between Haarlem and the sea, where European bison graze, songbirds nest in sea buckthorn, and the woods remember a girl with red hair.

subject: Zuidbroek railway station
summary: A nineteenth-century Dutch country station whose 1865 building once anchored three different railway lines, lost two of them, and now houses the Noord-Nederlands Trein and Tram Museum while still selling tickets to Groningen.

subject: Zuoying Naval Base
summary: Taiwan's largest naval installation, where a billion-dollar expansion program shares a coastline with villages preserving the mainland Chinese culture of 1949 exiles.

subject: Zwolle railway station
summary: A 19th-century junction that quietly became the spine of train travel in the northern Netherlands, then had to be rebuilt to keep up with itself.

subject: Zōshigaya Cemetery
summary: A 10-hectare public cemetery in Tokyo where Japan's greatest novelist lies buried in the same ground he chose as a fictional graveyard, alongside castaways, war criminals, and the country's first female physician.

subject: iSimangaliso Wetland Park
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage wetland on South Africa's east coast where 800 hippos, 1,200 crocodiles, nesting sea turtles, and coral reefs share a single shoreline named for a miracle.

subject: Ånderdalen National Park
summary: On the wild island of Senja, a primeval pine forest hides trees that were saplings when the Black Death swept through Norway.

subject: Øvre Dividal National Park
summary: Norway's second-driest valley harbors all four of the country's large predators in a 750 square kilometer expanse of tundra, birch forest, and glacial erratics above the Arctic Circle.

subject: Øvre Pasvik National Park
summary: Norway's easternmost national park, where ancient Siberian taiga meets three national borders and Scots pines older than the Viking Age still stand.

subject: Şişli Armenian Cemetery
summary: A place of memory for Istanbul's Armenian community — a burial ground established in the 1860s that holds the poets, musicians, painters, patriarchs, and ordinary lives of a people who made this city their home across centuries.

subject: Şişli Greek Orthodox Cemetery
summary: Founded in 1859, this 52-acre burial ground holds roughly 85,000 people of the Orthodox Christian communities of Istanbul — Greeks, Russians, Serbians, Bulgarians, and others — and the chapel built in their memory in 1888.

subject: ʻAkaka Falls State Park
summary: A 442-foot waterfall named for a Hawaiian chief plunges into a gorge where a magical stone is said to summon rain, and a tiny shrimp has evolved to climb the falls.

subject: 27-29 Fountain Alley
summary: The only surviving late Victorian commercial building on one of San Jose's oldest streets, listed on the National Register since 1982 as a remnant of the city's nineteenth-century commercial district.

subject: 921 Earthquake Museum of Taiwan
summary: Built around the ruins of a school destroyed in Taiwan's deadliest modern earthquake, the 921 Earthquake Museum is a place of memory, grief, and hard-won knowledge about living on an active fault.

subject: Aachen Town Hall
summary: A Gothic city hall raised on the walls of Charlemagne's lost palace, where coronation banquets once fed the new kings of the Germans and the Charlemagne Prize is awarded each year.

subject: Aalborg Historical Museum
summary: One of Denmark's earliest provincial museums, where a perfectly preserved Renaissance room and Viking-age excavations tell a thousand years of North Jutland history.

subject: Abbey of Saint Bertin
summary: For a thousand years, monks in Saint-Omer copied the night sky onto parchment and chronicled the kings of France - until the Revolution turned their abbey into a quarry.

subject: Abbey of Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte
summary: A Benedictine abbey founded in 1067 in Normandy was sold off as a quarry in the French Revolution - and rebuilt half a century later by an elderly nun who appealed to a queen for help.

story.title: Abbey of St Mary, St Dogmaels

subject: Abbey of St Mary, St Dogmaels
summary: On the south bank of the River Teifi where it meets the sea, the ruined walls of a Tironensian abbey preserve eight centuries of Welsh, Norman, and Tudor history — and a single stone that unlocked the lost alphabet of the Celts.

subject: Abbeymahon Abbey
summary: A ruined Cistercian abbey on the Argideen estuary - unusual among Cistercian foundations for standing beside salt water rather than fresh.

story.title: Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Folk Art Museum

subject: Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Folk Art Museum
summary: The world's oldest continuously operated museum of American folk art, built around the collection of a Rockefeller who took anonymous portraits and weathervanes seriously.

subject: Aberystwyth Castle
summary: An Edwardian fortress on the Welsh coast that served as Owain Glyndwr's seat of government, housed a Civil War-era royal mint, and was slighted by Cromwell.

subject: Adrichem Castle
summary: A 13th-century castle near Beverwijk whose first owner helped murder a count, whose stones now lie beneath a campground, and whose ghost is said to be a swan.

story.title: Aekuni Shrine: Guardian of the Northeast

subject: Aekuni Shrine
summary: The highest-ranking shrine of ancient Iga Province has survived imperial records, ninja warfare, and Oda Nobunaga's fire -- standing for over a millennium at the foot of Mount Nangu as spiritual protector of ninja country.

subject: Aghadoe Cathedral
summary: A ruined Romanesque cathedral overlooking the Lakes of Killarney - and the unmarked grave of roughly 2,000 famine victims buried in its grounds between 1846 and 1849.

subject: Aghalard Castle
summary: A ruined fifteenth-century tower house south of Castlebar, built by Scottish mercenaries who took service with a Norman Irish family and held it for four centuries.

subject: Agnes Keith House
summary: An American writer's hilltop home in Sandakan, destroyed by war and rebuilt on the ruins of someone else's house, is now a museum with a reputation for ghosts that predates its most famous occupant.

subject: Ahmed III Mosque, Acrocorinth
summary: High on the fortress of Acrocorinth, a small Ottoman mosque — crumbling but still standing — embodies five centuries of Greek, Venetian, and Ottoman struggle for the heights above Corinth.

subject: Aichi Museum of Flight
summary: A hangar-turned-museum beside Nagoya Airfield where Japan's first postwar passenger plane and a reconstructed Zero fighter sit just 300 meters from an active runway.

subject: Airlie Castle
summary: A medieval Ogilvy stronghold above the meeting of the Isla and Melgund, burned by the Earl of Argyll in 1640 and rebuilt as a mansion that still stands on its ruins.

subject: Aizuwakamatsu Castle
summary: A castle that changed hands between warlords, survived a devastating earthquake, endured a month-long artillery bombardment during Japan's civil war, was demolished, used as a velodrome, and finally rebuilt as the symbol of an entire city.

subject: Ak-Saray Palace
summary: The ruined portal of Timur's grandest palace still towers 38 meters above Shahrisabz -- a fragment of ambition so massive that its vault once spanned 22 meters, built by a conqueror trying to upstage his own capital of Samarkand.

subject: Akyū ruins
summary: Japan's largest stone circle and a Jomon settlement occupied for thousands of years lie hidden beneath a highway, deliberately buried to preserve them from the very road built on top.

subject: Al-Zaytuna Mosque
summary: The oldest mosque in Tunis, Al-Zaytuna has served as both house of prayer and university for over a millennium, its columns salvaged from the ruins of Carthage and its schools drawing scholars from across the Islamic world.

subject: Alabama State Capitol
summary: A Greek Revival monument on Goat Hill where the Confederacy was born, the civil rights movement marched, and a formerly enslaved bridge builder served in the legislature he helped construct.

subject: Albert Hall Music Hall
summary: One of Hull's first music halls, born from a Victorian merchant's speculation, demolished in 2016 after a century-and-a-half slide from variety stage to bingo hall to ruin.

subject: Alcázar of Seville
summary: A palace begun as an Islamic citadel in the 10th century, rebuilt by a Christian king using Muslim craftsmen in the 14th, and still serving as a royal residence today -- the oldest in continuous use in Europe.

subject: Allington Castle
summary: A Kentish riverside castle demolished by Henry II, rebuilt by Edward I's licence, lost to the Crown after the Wyatt rebellion, and saved from ruin by a polar explorer's wife.

story.title: Amagasaki Castle: The Fortress That Disappeared and Came Back

subject: Amagasaki Castle
summary: Built in 1617 at the strategic delta where two rivers met Osaka Bay, Amagasaki Castle served as the seat of power for a feudal domain until the Meiji Restoration, when its buildings were auctioned off and carted away -- only for a local entrepreneur to fund the reconstruction of its tower keep four centuries later.

subject: American Civil War Museum
summary: Spanning three sites across Virginia, this museum holds 500 original Confederate battle flags, the provisional Confederate Constitution, and artifacts from figures like Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson -- all rooted in a collection that Richmond's society ladies began rescuing in 1894.

subject: American Falls Dam
summary: A dam that drowned a town and then had to be replaced entirely when its concrete began to crumble from within.

subject: Anadoluhisarı (Fortress)
summary: The oldest surviving Ottoman structure in Istanbul, the Anadoluhisarı fortress was built by Sultan Bayezid I in 1393–1394 to begin strangling Constantinople — and it stands today on the narrowest point of the Bosphorus, surrounded by wooden waterside mansions, as picturesque as it is historically charged.

subject: Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall
summary: A marble throne hall built by Italian architects for a Thai king, which became the unlikely headquarters of the revolution that ended absolute monarchy in Siam.

subject: Ancient theater of Sabratha
summary: The largest Roman theater in Africa, buried under sand for centuries, was painstakingly reassembled column by column in the 1930s and now faces threats from coastal erosion, political instability, and time.

subject: Aoba Castle
summary: The hilltop seat of Date Masamune, the One-Eyed Dragon, has been burned, bombed, and shaken by earthquakes across four centuries -- yet its stone walls and an equestrian statue still command the Sendai skyline.

subject: Appleby Castle
summary: Overlooking the River Eden in Westmorland, Appleby Castle survived Scottish invasion, Civil War slighting, and centuries of family drama -- held together by Lady Anne Clifford's fierce determination to rebuild what war had broken.

subject: Aqueduct of Segovia
summary: A Roman engineering marvel of 167 granite arches, built without mortar around the first century AD, that carried water to Segovia for nearly two thousand years -- the last drop flowing in 1973.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Amphipolis
summary: On a quiet hill above the Strymon River, a small Greek museum holds the gold and stone of an Athenian colony, the coinage of Alexander's father, and the contested treasures of a tomb that Alexander himself may have ordered built.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Ancient Corinth
summary: Built in the shadow of a 2,500-year-old temple, the Archaeological Museum of Ancient Corinth houses the recovered life of a city that the Romans destroyed, rebuilt, and made the capital of their province of Achaea.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Andros
summary: Founded in 1981 in the neoclassical capital of Andros, this compact museum houses artifacts spanning from Mycenaean times to the Roman period — and the graceful Hermes of Andros, a Roman copy of a lost Praxiteles-school original.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Delos
summary: On a tiny, treeless island that ancient Greeks believed was the birthplace of Apollo, a small museum guards the marble that survived twenty-five centuries of wind, salt, and looting.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Eretria
summary: A small museum beside the ruins of one of Greece's great early city-states, holding everything from a wax-modeled hero wrestling an Amazon to a necklace that crossed the sea from Cyprus three thousand years ago.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Messenia
summary: Built on the ruins of Kalamata's old market hall, the Archaeological Museum of Messenia preserves millennia of Messenian history — from Mycenaean warriors to Byzantine monks — after the 1742 Benakeion museum it replaced was destroyed in the 1986 earthquake.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Mystras
summary: Set inside the medieval metropolitan complex of Mystras, this small Byzantine museum holds the material memory of a city — fragments of carved stone, gilded frescoes, and a mysterious mummified figure — that was once the last flowering of a thousand-year empire.

subject: Archaeological Museum of Nicopolis
summary: Housed 5 km north of Preveza amid the ruins of Augustus's City of Victory, the Archaeological Museum of Nicopolis preserves two thousand years of Epirote history — including the last surviving bronze ram from Mark Antony's defeated fleet.

subject: Archaeology Museum of Catalonia
summary: Housed in a fair pavilion that was meant to be demolished, this five-site museum guards Catalonia's deepest past, from cave-dwellers to Greek colonists.

subject: Archcliffe Fort
summary: A 14th-century watchtower turned Tudor fort turned Victorian gun battery turned mostly demolished ruin - now run by a homeless charity that operates a furniture workshop in the surviving bastions above Shakespeare Beach.

subject: Ardrossan Castle
summary: A ruined moated keep on a hill above the Firth of Clyde, with vaults still called Wallace's Larder and a ghost that walks on stormy nights.

subject: Ardvreck Castle
summary: A ruined tower house on Loch Assynt where a Royalist general was handed over to his enemies in 1650 and a clan war ended the castle's working life in 1672.

subject: Arena Fonte Nova
summary: Salvador's horseshoe stadium rose from the rubble of a collapse that killed seven fans - and became a venue for World Cup, Olympics, and everything in between.

subject: Arles Amphitheatre
summary: A two-tiered Roman amphitheatre from 90 AD that became a medieval fortress with 200 houses inside, was painted by Van Gogh, and now hosts bullfights and concerts as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Armenian Church, Dhaka
summary: A 1781 church in Old Dhaka built by Armenian merchants who traded jute and leather, now maintained by a small staff for a congregation that no longer exists, its graveyard of 350 tombstones chronicling centuries of a diaspora community that once thrived in Bengal.

story.title: Armenian Genocide Memorial Church, Der Zor

subject: Armenian Genocide Memorial Church, Der Zor
summary: A memorial church and museum in the Syrian desert marking the endpoint of the Armenian death marches, consecrated in 1991 and destroyed in 2014.

subject: Armory Square Hospital
summary: A Civil War hospital on the National Mall where the gravest Union casualties received care -- and where Walt Whitman found the suffering that transformed American poetry.

subject: Astley Castle
summary: Three women linked to this ruined Warwickshire manor became Queen of England. Five centuries later, the house burned down. The architects who rebuilt it inside its own ruins won the Stirling Prize.

subject: Athcarne Castle
summary: A ruined Elizabethan tower house outside Duleek where King James II is said to have slept the night before losing the Battle of the Boyne.

subject: Avoncroft Museum of Historic Buildings
summary: England's first open-air museum, where thirty rescued buildings - from a 15th-century merchant's house to a 1946 prefab and a working windmill - have been reassembled in a Worcestershire field.

subject: Awatovi Ruins
summary: A Hopi pueblo on Antelope Mesa destroyed by its own people in 1700, whose vivid kiva murals survived centuries underground before a Harvard expedition unearthed them in the 1930s.

subject: Aydon Castle
summary: A Suffolk merchant's vanity manor built in 1296, fortified just in time for the Scottish wars to ruin its owner and his finances forever.

subject: Ayuwang Pagoda
summary: Named for the Indian emperor who spread Buddhism across Asia, the Ayuwang Pagoda in Shanxi has been destroyed and rebuilt three times, its current Tibetan-style form a gift from Mongol rulers who favored a different school of the faith.
