summary: The last survivor of the Three Treasures of Tai Hom Village, this modest granite house in Diamond Hill is all that remains of a squatter community that once thrived where a metro depot now stands.

subject: Storkow Castle
summary: A Brandenburg marsh castle that has been a frontier fort, a bishop's Renaissance residence, a torture chamber, a Hitler Youth training castle and a town hall, burned down twice, and now explains the surrounding lakes to visitors.

subject: Strata Florida Abbey
summary: A ruined Cistercian abbey in the Welsh uplands that served as the cultural and political heart of medieval Wales, burying 11 princes and producing the nation's greatest chronicle.

subject: Strome Castle
summary: A ruined fifteenth-century stronghold on the shore of Loch Carron, demolished and blown up by the victorious Clan Mackenzie in 1602 after one of the bitterest clan feuds in West Highland history.

subject: Sturdivant Hall
summary: A Greek Revival mansion in Selma, Alabama, built with Italian marble in the 1850s, haunted by the ghost story of a banker who was killed trying to escape a Reconstruction-era prison.

subject: Sugamo Prison
summary: A Tokyo prison built in 1895 that held political dissidents, Soviet spies, and Japan's most senior war criminals before being demolished and replaced by what was then the tallest skyscraper in Asia.

subject: Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II Museum
summary: A colonial-era building on the banks of the Musi River in Palembang that has cycled through identities -- royal palace, British demolition site, Dutch residency, Japanese headquarters, army base, and now a museum honoring the sultan whose palace once stood here.

story.title: Sun Moon Lake Wen Wu Temple

subject: Sun Moon Lake Wen Wu Temple
summary: Perched above Sun Moon Lake in the Chinese palace style, the Wen Wu Temple unites the God of Literature with the Martial Gods in a three-hall complex born from two drowned shrines and rebuilt through three eras of Taiwanese history.

subject: Sun Temple (Sogamoso)
summary: A sacred Muisca temple destroyed by Spanish treasure hunters in 1537, painstakingly reconstructed centuries later on its original site, where sunlight still strikes the central pillar each December solstice.

subject: Sunbeam Theatre
summary: Hong Kong's last dedicated Cantonese opera house, born from Shanghai exile and saved three times from demolition, closed in 2025 after more than five decades on King's Road.

subject: Sunderland Power Station
summary: The coal-fired power station that lit Sunderland for seventy-five years before being demolished, its cooling tower felled in February 1979 above the River Wear.

subject: Sunderland Synagogue
summary: The Grade II listed former Orthodox synagogue on Ryhope Road, last designed work of architect Marcus Glass, dissolved in 2006 after 145 years of Wearside Jewish life.

subject: Sunderland Town Hall
summary: The Italianate Fawcett Street town hall opened in 1890 and demolished in 1971, whose bells still sit in 'secure storage' awaiting a future the city has yet to decide.

subject: Supraśl Orthodox Monastery
summary: An Orthodox monastery founded in 1498 in northeastern Poland - destroyed by retreating Germans in 1944, slowly rebuilt, and home to one of the oldest Slavic literary manuscripts in the world.

subject: Sutro Baths Ruins
summary: The San Francisco swimming palace that could hold 10,000 bathers in seven heated saltwater pools - built by a visionary millionaire in 1896, abandoned for decades, destroyed by fire in 1966, and now a haunting oceanside ruin.

subject: Sutton Valence Castle
summary: A ruined 12th-century Kentish keep that watched the road to the south coast, passed through the great medieval families of Marshal, de Montfort, and Valence, and crumbled into ivy-covered fragments by the time Edward Hasted came to describe it.

subject: Swansea Castle
summary: A medieval castle in the centre of a Welsh city that has spent the last seven hundred years being a workhouse, a bottle factory, a newspaper office, and a place where Dylan Thomas wrote his first reviews.

subject: Syon Abbey
summary: Henry V's vow, England's wealthiest monastery, and one community of Bridgettine nuns whose journey from a Thames bank in 1415 to Lisbon to Devon ended in 2011 with three elderly sisters and a 600-year unbroken chain.

story.title: Soma Nakamura Castle: The Fortress That Never Fought

subject: Sōma Nakamura Castle
summary: A Japanese castle designed with its strongest defenses facing the wrong enemy, whose three-story tower was destroyed not by war but by a lightning bolt -- and which surrendered without a shot in the only conflict that ever reached its gates.

subject: Tahtakuşlar Ethnography Museum
summary: A private museum on the slopes of Mount Ida, founded by a retired schoolteacher to preserve the living culture of the Tahtacı Turkmen — a distinct Alevi community whose traditions, textiles, and ways of life are documented here with rare care.

subject: Takaoka Castle
summary: A castle designed by a Christian samurai in exile, built for beauty over defense, used for only a few years, and now one of Japan's beloved cherry blossom parks.

subject: Takatō Castle
summary: A ruined Sengoku-era castle in Nagano Prefecture whose grounds hold 1,500 cherry trees of a unique pink variety found nowhere else, making it one of Japan's three most celebrated cherry blossom sites alongside Hirosaki Castle and Mount Yoshino.

subject: Takayama Castle
summary: A mountaintop fortress built in 1588 by the warlord who conquered Hida Province, deliberately demolished a century later by the Tokugawa shogunate, leaving only scattered stone walls and a magistrate's office that became the only surviving jin'ya in Japan.

subject: Takeda Castle
summary: Called the 'Machu Picchu of Japan,' the ruins of Takeda Castle perch 353 meters above sea level on a mountaintop that regularly rises above the morning clouds, leaving its stone walls floating in a white sea.

subject: Takeda Shrine
summary: A Shinto shrine in Kofu built on the ruins of a warlord's fortress, where the spirit of Takeda Shingen -- the Tiger of Kai -- is venerated alongside a Kamakura-era sword that traveled as a bridal gift between clans.

story.title: Takiyama Castle: The Fortress That Fooled 20,000 Soldiers

subject: Takiyama Castle (Tokyo)
summary: A hilltop castle on a ridge above the Tama River, built by a regional clan in 1521, became the staging ground for a warlord's conquest of Musashi Province -- and survived a siege by 20,000 troops because the entire attack was a feint.

subject: Tallahassee Museum
summary: A 52-acre open-air museum nestled between two lakes in Florida's capital, where black bears roam wooded enclosures, an 1880s farmstead comes to life, and a Napoleonic princess's plantation house tells the tangled story of Old Florida.

subject: Talley Abbey
summary: The only Premonstratensian monastery ever founded in Wales, Talley Abbey sits between two lakes in a remote Carmarthenshire valley -- its ruinous tower still rising above a village built largely from its own stones.

subject: Tamreswari Temple
summary: A copper-roofed tribal temple near Sadiya in Assam, where the fierce goddess Kecaikhati was worshipped by non-Brahmin Deori priests for centuries before floods swallowed the ruins.

subject: Tamworth Castle
summary: One of England's best-preserved motte-and-bailey castles, where Mercian kings, Norman conquerors, and Civil War soldiers have all left their mark over a thousand years.

subject: Tanais Archaeological Reserve Museum
summary: At the edge of the Don delta stands Russia's first archaeological open-air reserve, built around a Greek trading city that guarded the far frontier of the ancient world.

subject: Tartu Cathedral
summary: The roofless red-brick ruins of one of medieval Eastern Europe's largest cathedrals, perched on the hill above Tartu where Estonia's pagans once held their last stronghold.

subject: Tateyama Castle
summary: A castle built to guard Edo Bay by a nearly independent warlord, destroyed by the Tokugawa, and resurrected four centuries later as a museum devoted to one of Japan's greatest epic novels.

subject: Tautra Abbey
summary: A Cistercian monastery founded in 1207 on an island in the Trondheimsfjord, dissolved during the Reformation, and reborn in 1999 as Norway's first permanent Cistercian community in nearly five centuries.

subject: Taynal Mosque
summary: A Mamluk mosque in Tripoli with Corinthian columns, black-and-white marble floors, and twin spiral staircases, the Taynal Mosque may stand atop the ruins of a Roman temple to Zeus.

subject: Temple of Anahita, Kangavar
summary: A monumental stone platform in western Iran whose true identity remains one of Persian archaeology's great debates: temple to a water goddess, Sasanian palace, or something older still.

subject: Temple of Awwam
summary: The largest temple complex in ancient South Arabia, where pilgrims journeyed for over a millennium to worship the god Almaqah, sleep in oracle chambers for prophetic dreams, and purify themselves in alabaster water channels.

subject: Temple of Bel
summary: Dedicated in AD 32 to a triad of Mesopotamian gods, the Temple of Bel survived conversion to church, mosque, and fortified citadel before ISIS destroyed its cella in August 2015 -- but thousands of tourist photographs are now fueling its digital and physical reconstruction.

subject: Temple of Hera, Olympia
summary: Built around 580 BC, the Temple of Hera at Olympia is the oldest temple at the sanctuary — a building that began with wooden columns, accumulated stone replacements across ten centuries, stored the treasures of Greek civilization, and today is where the Olympic flame is kindled before every modern Games.

subject: Temple of Isis (Pompeii)
summary: A small Egyptian temple inside a Roman city, rebuilt by a freedman father for his six-year-old son, frozen in time by Vesuvius, and rediscovered in 1764 -- where it inspired a thirteen-year-old Mozart to compose The Magic Flute.

subject: Temple of Isthmia
summary: The Poseidon temple where the Isthmian Games were held, one of the four great Panhellenic festivals, on the narrow neck of land between the Aegean and the Gulf of Corinth.

subject: Temple of Literature, Hanoi
summary: Vietnam's first national university, founded in 1076 within a Confucian temple, where 82 stone turtles still carry the names of 1,307 doctoral graduates.

subject: Temple of Mercury (Puy de Dôme)
summary: A massive Gallo-Roman temple to Mercury crowns the summit of an extinct volcano in central France, blending Celtic and Mediterranean traditions at 1,435 meters above sea level.

subject: Temple of Sangri
summary: An almost-square Late Archaic marble temple to Demeter on rural Naxos, with the oldest known marble roof in ancient architecture and 1,600 surviving fragments.

subject: Temple of Zeus, Cyrene
summary: One of the largest Greek temples ever built stands in the Libyan desert -- a 2,500-year-old monument to Zeus that was destroyed, rebuilt, smashed by Christians, toppled by earthquake, and painstakingly reassembled by archaeologists.

subject: Ten Duinen Abbey
summary: A Cistercian abbey that ran the medieval Flemish wool trade from a vast complex in the dunes - until the sea won and buried it.

subject: Tenby Museum and Art Gallery
summary: The oldest independent museum in Wales, founded in 1878 inside the ruins of a Norman castle, with a collection ranging from prehistoric flints to paintings by Gwen and Augustus John.

subject: Terre Haute House
summary: A hotel that was the first in the world to have electric lights in every room was sold for a dollar and demolished by a wrecking ball.

subject: The Beatles Statue
summary: Andy Edwards's larger-than-life bronze of the four Beatles walking together at Pier Head, unveiled on 4 December 2015 on the 50th anniversary of their final Liverpool concert - with hidden details from Paul's camera to John's acorns from outside the Dakota.

subject: The Breakers (hotel)
summary: A Palm Beach luxury hotel that has burned down twice, served as a World War II army hospital, and survived a century of hurricanes -- yet remains one of America's most prestigious resorts, modeled after the Villa Medici in Rome.

story.title: The Courthouse Fresno Couldn't Stop Replacing

subject: The Courthouse Fresno Couldn't Stop Replacing
summary: Fresno's courthouse has been torn down and rebuilt so many times that the cycle itself has become the story -- a concrete monument to the city's restless relationship with its own architecture.

subject: The Fort That Gold Destroyed
summary: John Sutter built a fortified colony in the Central Valley using Indigenous forced labor and named it New Helvetia -- then watched the Gold Rush he inadvertently triggered tear it apart, seeding the city of Sacramento in its ruins.

story.title: The Fortress That Swallowed a Hilltop

subject: The Fortress That Swallowed a Hilltop
summary: A 16th-century fortress crowns a steep hill above Baubau, its 2,740-meter stone perimeter enclosing an entire world of gates, bastions, mosques, and royal tombs from the Buton Sultanate.

story.title: The Ghost Fort Beneath the Mosque

subject: The Ghost Fort Beneath the Mosque
summary: A Dutch colonial fortress in Jakarta passed through lives as a tavern, a country house, and a hospital before becoming an obsolete citadel -- then vanished entirely when Indonesia demolished it to build the largest mosque in Southeast Asia.

subject: The Reach Gallery Museum
summary: Abbotsford's public gallery and regional archive, holding the photographic record of a valley that drained a lake in 1924 and watched it come back in 2021.

subject: The Ruins
summary: A sugar baron's Italian-inspired mansion in Talisay, Negros Occidental, burned for three days during World War II yet still stands as a monument to love and resilience.

subject: The Savannah Theatre
summary: Opened in 1818 with a William Jay facade, battered by a hurricane, gutted by two fires, and rebuilt in Art Deco, the Savannah Theatre is one of America's oldest continually operating theaters.

subject: The Stanley Hotel
summary: The Colorado mountain hotel where a dying inventor sought a cure, and where Stephen King dreamed up The Shining.

subject: Tin Hau Temple, Causeway Bay
summary: A temple to the Goddess of the Sea that was built on the Hong Kong waterfront in 1747, now stands inland — a measure of how completely land reclamation has changed the shape of the island around it.

subject: Tintagel Castle
summary: A ruined medieval castle on the Cornish coast where archaeology keeps uncovering a far older and more remarkable story than the Arthurian legend that draws 200,000 visitors a year.

subject: Togariishi Museum of Jōmon Archaeology
summary: Home to two National Treasures -- the sensuous Jomon Venus and the enigmatic Masked Goddess -- this museum in Chino, Nagano sits on the ruins of the first complete Jomon settlement ever confirmed in Japan.

subject: Toklu Dede Mosque
summary: A single surviving wall in a residential side street near Istanbul's Blachernae walls holds the ghost of a Byzantine church that outlasted an empire and was mostly demolished in 1929.

subject: Tomb of Cyrus the Great
summary: A small stone chamber atop six stepped platforms at Pasargadae has outlasted every empire that tried to claim it -- from the Achaemenids who built it to the Magi who guarded it to the conqueror who wept at its looting.

subject: Top Gun House
summary: A Folk Victorian beach cottage built in 1888 in Oceanside survived nearly being demolished for a hotel, appeared in the 1986 film Top Gun, and now houses a pie shop with a replica of Tom Cruise's motorcycle out front.

subject: Torna Fort
summary: The first fort captured by a sixteen-year-old Shivaji in 1646, launching the Maratha Empire from a mountaintop where buried treasure funded the construction of an entire kingdom.

subject: Tower of Jewels (PPIE)
summary: A 435-foot tower covered in 100,000 faceted glass jewels that sparkled in the sun and glowed under spotlights -- then was demolished when the 1915 world's fair ended.

subject: Toyota Municipal Museum of Art
summary: A $122 million art museum designed by the architect who later redesigned MoMA in New York, perched on a hillside above the ruins of a feudal castle in a city better known for manufacturing cars than collecting Klimts.

subject: Trakai Island Castle
summary: The 14th-century red-brick island castle on Lake Galve where Vytautas the Great died - controversially restored under Soviet rule, now a Lithuanian national symbol.

subject: Tristernagh Abbey
summary: A 12th-century Augustinian priory on Lough Iron, demolished in 1783 in an act that the topographers of the time called 'an outrage' and which locals believed brought a curse on the family responsible.

subject: Trumpan Church
summary: A ruined 13th-century church on Skye's Waternish peninsula where MacDonalds locked MacLeod worshippers inside and set the building ablaze in 1578 -- one atrocity in a cycle of clan violence that consumed the Hebrides.

subject: Tryon Palace
summary: North Carolina's colonial capitol, built in 1770 for Governor William Tryon, burned in 1798, and faithfully reconstructed in the 1950s, anchors the historic waterfront of New Bern with three centuries of garden history.

subject: Tsuruga Red Brick Warehouse
summary: A pair of 1905 petroleum warehouses built by Standard Oil of New York on the shores of Tsuruga Port, now reborn as a restaurant and a diorama museum celebrating the city's golden age as a gateway between Japan and the world.

story.title: Tsurugaoka Castle: Seven Centuries of Betrayal and Cherry Blossoms

subject: Tsurugaoka Castle
summary: A flatland castle in northern Japan changed hands through assassination, battlefield conquest, and shogunal decree across seven centuries before being demolished -- only to find a second life as one of Japan's most celebrated cherry blossom parks.

subject: Tung Lung Fort
summary: A Qing-era coastal fortress built in the 1720s to guard against pirates and watch over one of Hong Kong's key sea lanes — now a declared monument on a clifftop above the South China Sea.

subject: Turnberry Castle
summary: On a cliff above the Firth of Clyde lie the broken vaults of the castle where Robert the Bruce probably grew up - and which Bruce himself ordered destroyed rather than let it fall to the English again.

subject: Tønsberg Fortress
summary: The ruins of Norway's largest medieval castle crown a hilltop in what is believed to be the country's oldest town, where Viking kings were proclaimed and the last sovereign of an independent Norway drew his final breath.

subject: Tŵr Mawr Lighthouse
summary: The 1846 lighthouse on Ynys Llanddwyn off the southwest tip of Anglesey - 'the Great Tower', marking the western approach to the Menai Strait until it handed off the job to its smaller neighbour Twr Bach in 1975.

story.title: United States Astronaut Hall of Fame

subject: United States Astronaut Hall of Fame
summary: Inside the Heroes & Legends building at Kennedy Space Center, the world's largest collection of astronaut memorabilia surrounds visitors with the actual spacecraft and spacesuits that carried Americans beyond the atmosphere.

subject: Urquhart Castle
summary: On a headland jutting into Loch Ness, the ruins of Urquhart Castle have witnessed Pictish saints, Scottish wars of independence, clan raids, and deliberate destruction -- blown up in 1692 to keep it from the Jacobites.

subject: Uspenski Cathedral
summary: Built of bricks salvaged from a fortress destroyed in the Crimean War, the red-brick Uspenski Cathedral on Helsinki's Katajanokka peninsula is the largest Eastern Orthodox church in Western Europe.

subject: Uzunköprü Bridge
summary: A 174-arch Ottoman stone bridge across the Ergene river, claimed as the longest in the world, still carrying traffic almost six centuries after it opened.

subject: Valide Mosque, Mytilene
summary: Four centuries old and now half in ruins, the Valide Mosque is the oldest surviving Ottoman house of worship on Lesbos, a stone witness to the island's layered past.

subject: Verkhnii Saltiv Museum-Reserve
summary: Above a bend of the Siverskyi Donets lie the ramparts and catacomb cemeteries of a vanished people, the archaeological fingerprint of the Khazars who once ruled this land.

subject: Victor Emmanuel II Monument
summary: Romans call it the 'wedding cake' or the 'typewriter' -- a colossal white marble monument to Italian unification that took fifty years to complete, demolished a medieval neighborhood to make room, and remains one of the most divisive buildings in a city that has been arguing about architecture for two thousand years.

subject: Victoria Bridge (Montreal)
summary: When it opened in 1859, the Victoria Bridge was the longest in the world -- a wrought-iron tube shipped across the Atlantic, built by 3,040 workers over five brutal Canadian winters to tame the St. Lawrence River.

subject: Villa Aurora
summary: Villa Aurora at 520 Paseo Miramar in Pacific Palisades was built in 1928, saved from demolition in the 1990s by German artists, and has been an artists' residence since 1995 — on the same hillside where Lion Feuchtwanger once entertained Brecht, Mann, and Chaplin in exile.

subject: Villa Kerylos
summary: A French archaeologist so admired ancient Greece that he built a full-scale replica of a nobleman's villa from 2nd-century Delos on the tip of a rocky point overlooking the Mediterranean.

subject: Vilnius Belarusian Museum
summary: A Belarusian national museum founded in interwar Polish-era Vilna, dismembered by the Soviets in 1945, and quietly reborn in 2001 by exiles still trying to recover what was lost.

subject: Votive Temple of Maipú
summary: A 91-meter basilica rising over the field where Chile won its independence in 1818, built to honor a promise its liberator made on the eve of battle.

subject: Walden Abbey
summary: A 12th-century monastery founded by a rebel earl, dissolved by Henry VIII, and replaced by one of the greatest Jacobean houses in England - Audley End.

subject: Walnut Tree Viaduct
summary: Two brick pillars beside the A470 are all that remain of a steel-girder viaduct that once carried coal trains 120 feet above the Taff valley - built in under a year, demolished after sixty-eight years, and never quite forgiven by the people who watched it come down.

subject: Waltham Abbey Royal Gunpowder Mills
summary: For more than 300 years the British state made things that exploded here - from black powder for Trafalgar to the RDX inside the Dam Busters' bouncing bomb - in a riverside maze of canals and timber sheds now reclaimed by herons.

subject: Wan Chai Pier
summary: Three generations of pier, nearly a century of ferry crossings, and a coastline that kept moving northward — Wan Chai Pier is a small structure that tells a large story about how Hong Kong has remade itself.

subject: Wardour Castle
summary: A hexagonal English castle, unique in Britain and modeled on French chateaux, blown apart in 1644 during the Civil War and left as one of the country's most photogenic ruins.

subject: Wari-Bateshwar ruins
summary: Buried beneath Bangladeshi farmland, the Wari-Bateshwar ruins reveal an Iron Age fortified city with paved roads, a Buddhist temple, and the oldest punch-marked silver coins on the Indian subcontinent, possibly the ancient trading post 'Sounagora' described by Ptolemy.

subject: Warner Grand Theatre
summary: The last surviving Art Deco movie palace from Warner Bros.' 1930s Los Angeles trio, saved from demolition by community activists and now a cultural landmark in San Pedro.

subject: Warsaw Ghetto Museum
summary: A museum under construction in the former Bersohn and Bauman Children's Hospital — one of the few buildings from the Warsaw Ghetto still standing — dedicated to the lives, not just the deaths, of Warsaw's Jews.

subject: Washington Old Hall
summary: Eight centuries before George Washington was born in Virginia, his ancestors took their name from this small sandstone manor in the north of England.

subject: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
summary: A 17th-century Khmer-style temple on the Chao Phraya River that was built as a king's tribute to his mother, survived Burmese destruction, and now stands as Ayutthaya's most recognizable ruin.

subject: Waterloo Bridge
summary: London's best-loved Thames crossing was built largely by women during World War II, painted obsessively by Monet, and served as the stage for a Cold War assassination.

subject: Waverley Abbey
summary: England's first Cistercian abbey, founded in 1128 on the floodplain of the River Wey, whose 500-year-old yew tree still stands amid ruins beloved of film crews.

subject: Waytemore Castle
summary: A Norman motte beside the River Stort, white-painted to dominate the Saxon town, demolished by King John in a quarrel with the Pope, later a prison.

subject: Weiyuan Fort
summary: Built in 1835 to guard the Pearl River's narrowest passage, Weiyuan Fort is a Qing-era coastal fortress whose ruined cannons still face the strait they failed to hold.

subject: Wentworth Castle
summary: A Grade I listed South Yorkshire country house built in two architectural campaigns by feuding earls, praised by Horace Walpole as a paragon of architectural taste, and now home to Northern College.

subject: Werwolf (Wehrmacht Headquarters)
summary: In a pine forest north of Vinnytsia lie broken slabs of concrete, all that remains of the easternmost field headquarters Hitler ever used, and of the thousands who were killed to build and hide it.

subject: West Virginia State Capitol
summary: The 292-foot Cass Gilbert masterwork rising on the south bank of the Kanawha River, designed by the same architect who shaped the U.S. Supreme Court - and West Virginia's third try at a capitol after two of them burned down.

subject: Weymouth Pavilion
summary: A seafront theatre that has burned down once, housed 800 Moroccan soldiers and No. 4 Commando in wartime, and been saved from demolition by a petition.

subject: Whalley Abbey
summary: The Cistercian abbey that took a century to build, then became a country house, and now serves as a diocesan retreat alongside its surviving ruins.

subject: Whatcom Museum
summary: A Victorian city hall copied from a Michigan courthouse, a logging photographer's glass plates, and a wall built to hold daylight - three buildings that carry Bellingham's memory.

subject: White City Stadium
summary: Built in ten months for the 1908 Olympics, White City Stadium hosted everything from greyhound derbies to World Cup matches before vanishing under BBC office blocks.

subject: White House State Ballroom
summary: An 89,000 square-foot addition that replaced the East Wing in 2025 - privately funded, fast-tracked, and the most contested change to the White House complex since Truman's reconstruction.

subject: White Monastery
summary: Near Sohag stands the great fortress-like church of Saint Shenoute, built of white limestone in the shape of a pharaonic temple and still living after sixteen centuries.

subject: Wideford Hill Chambered Cairn
summary: A Neolithic tomb on a steep west-facing hillside above Kirkwall, entered today through a hatch in the roof and a metal ladder descending into solid Orkney darkness.

subject: Wigmore Castle
summary: The Mortimers built an empire from this ridge above Herefordshire; today their castle stands half-buried in its own debris, one of the few major British ruins never tidied up by the Victorians.

subject: Wil-Cox Bridge
summary: A seven-arch concrete bridge that has spanned the Yadkin River since 1924, replaced a toll bridge from 1818, was nearly demolished in 2009, and now carries pedestrians where General Stoneman once tried to burn a railroad.

subject: Wingfield Castle
summary: Wingfield Castle held a royal prisoner from Agincourt for twenty-five years, housed a Duke of Suffolk who married Geoffrey Chaucer's granddaughter, and was once considered for purchase by both Elton John and Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols.

subject: Winnipeg Art Gallery
summary: Home to the world's largest collection of Inuit art -- over 13,000 works -- and a permanent collection exceeding 24,000 pieces, the Winnipeg Art Gallery traces its origins to a hotel art room that burned down in 1899.

subject: Woburn Abbey
summary: A Cistercian monastery turned stately home that was saved from ruin by a duke who opened it to the public to pay off 14 million dollars in death duties.

subject: Woodstock Palace
summary: The vanished royal hunting palace where Henry II kept his mistress, the Black Prince was born, and the future Elizabeth I scratched verses on a window with a diamond.

subject: Wren Building
summary: The oldest college building in the United States, burned three times, hit by a tornado, rebuilt five times on the same 1695 walls - and still holding classes at the College of William & Mary in Williamsburg.

subject: Wupatki National Monument
summary: The ruins of a thriving 12th-century pueblo community in the Arizona high desert, built from red Moenkopi sandstone after a volcanic eruption made the barren land surprisingly fertile.

subject: Xingguo Temple (Jinan)
summary: A Buddhist temple in Jinan that has been destroyed, rebuilt, and renamed across five dynasties since its founding in the sixth century.

subject: Yaa Asantewaa Museum
summary: A museum in Besease, Ghana, honoring the queen mother who rallied an army of 5,000 against the British Empire in 1900 -- and whose legacy outlasted the fire that gutted its walls.

subject: Yester Castle
summary: A ruined East Lothian castle whose subterranean Goblin Hall, built before 1267, was reputedly raised by a thirteenth-century warlock with an army of hobgoblins.

subject: Yoros Castle
summary: Perched above the Black Sea mouth of the Bosphorus, Yoros Castle has served Phoenicians, Byzantines, Genoese, and Ottomans — each empire leaving its mark on the same commanding hill.

subject: Zaraka Monastery
summary: The Cistercian monks who built Zaraka around 1225 were the only Western religious order to construct their own abbey on Greek soil — a fact that makes its ruined Gothic arches beside Lake Stymphalia all the more improbable.

subject: Zeze Castle
summary: Built by Tokugawa Ieyasu's orders days after the Battle of Sekigahara to control Japan's most important highway, this lakeside fortress on Lake Biwa was dismantled after the Meiji Restoration -- but its gates survived, scattered across shrines where they stand as National Important Cultural Properties.

subject: Zhenhai Tower
summary: Built in 1380 to suppress a dynastic prophecy, Guangzhou's Zhenhai Tower has been destroyed and rebuilt five times — and still stands on Yuexiu Hill as the city's oldest surviving monument and home of the Guangzhou Museum.

subject: Zibad Castle
summary: A ruined Sasanian fortress in eastern Iran where the last emperor of pre-Islamic Persia may have taken his final refuge before the empire collapsed in 651 CE.

subject: Zoodochos Pigi Church, Dervenosalesi
summary: A Byzantine church that is really the surviving porch of a vanished monastery, its lost sanctuary echoed in the marble floors of nearby Hosios Loukas.

subject: Zuiderzee Museum
summary: An open-air museum preserving the maritime culture of a sea that no longer exists, featuring entire buildings transported across the Netherlands and a boat that once sailed to the Black Sea as a honeymoon vessel - and later for British intelligence.

subject: Zülfaris Synagogue
summary: A Sephardic synagogue in Karaköy whose name means 'bridal curls' in Persian — it served Istanbul's Jewish community for over 300 years before becoming home to the Jewish Museum of Turkey, commemorating five centuries of Sephardic life in the Ottoman world.

subject: 's-Hertogenbosch
summary: The North Brabant capital - Den Bosch to its residents - is a Gothic cathedral, a hidden underground river, the hometown of Hieronymus Bosch, and a giant chocolate-covered cream puff.

subject: 1 July Police Stabbing
summary: On the 24th anniversary of Hong Kong's handover, a 50-year-old man stabbed a police officer outside a Causeway Bay department store, then fatally stabbed himself — an act that exposed the depth of Hong Kong's unresolved political wounds.

subject: 10 Admiral Grove
summary: A two-up two-down terraced house in Toxteth where Richard Starkey lived for twenty years before he became Ringo Starr; the front door opens onto a Liverpool street that still bears his music's first audience.

subject: 10050 Cielo Drive
summary: A Benedict Canyon house where Sharon Tate and four others were murdered by the Manson Family in August 1969 — one of the most notorious crime scenes in American history.

subject: 11 Downing Street
summary: The Chancellor of the Exchequer's official residence next door to Number 10 - and, for most prime ministers since 1997, secretly their actual home.

subject: 126 Artist-run Gallery
summary: A Galway artist-run gallery founded in a living room in 2005, named after the house number, that built an international reputation while moving locations five times.

subject: 14 Henrietta Street
summary: One Dublin Georgian townhouse, four lord lieutenants, seventeen tenement flats, and one hundred people - the same walls held them all.

subject: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue
summary: A modest Bronx apartment building where a teenager's back-to-school party in 1973 launched a musical revolution that would reshape global culture.

subject: 1733 slave insurrection on St. John
summary: On November 23, 1733, one hundred and fifty enslaved Akwamu people seized Fort Fredericksvaern on St. John and held most of the island for nearly nine months -- one of the earliest and longest acts of organized resistance to slavery in the Americas.

subject: 1891 New Orleans lynchings
summary: The largest single mass lynching in American history unfolded at the Orleans Parish Prison in 1891 when a mob murdered eleven Italian immigrants, triggering an international crisis and introducing the word 'Mafia' into the American vocabulary.

subject: 1918 Vancouver General Strike
summary: British Columbia's first general strike lasted twenty-four hours, began at the funeral of a shot coal miner, and ended with veterans storming a union hall on Dunsmuir Street.

subject: 1921-1928 Newport, Kentucky steel strike
summary: A seven-year standoff between steelworkers and mill owners in Newport, Kentucky, brought tanks into residential streets, machine gun fire into neighborhoods, and Samuel Gompers himself to a packed theater on the banks of the Licking River.

subject: 1929 Barcelona International Exposition
summary: Barcelona's second World's Fair transformed the hill of Montjuic into a cultural landscape of fountains, palaces, and avant-garde architecture, including Mies van der Rohe's legendary pavilion.

subject: 1947 Yogyakarta Dakota Incident
summary: A Red Cross mercy flight chartered from India and cleared by both British and Dutch authorities was shot down by Dutch fighter planes on approach to Yogyakarta in 1947, killing eight of nine people aboard -- including two Indonesian air force founders now honored as national heroes.

subject: 1957 Pacoima Mid-Air Collision
summary: Two aircraft collided at 25,000 feet over the San Fernando Valley on a January morning in 1957, and the wreckage fell onto a school playground—killing eight people. Ritchie Valens, absent that day at his grandfather's funeral, was haunted by the crash for the rest of his short life.

subject: 1958 NFL Championship Game
summary: The 'Greatest Game Ever Played' at Yankee Stadium, where the Baltimore Colts defeated the New York Giants in the first sudden-death overtime in NFL history and launched professional football into the American mainstream.

subject: 1965 Hendek Bus Accident
summary: On the D-100 highway near Hendek in the early hours of 11 August 1965, twenty-five people died when a passenger bus struck a broken-down nitric acid truck — and a roadside memorial holds their memory today.

subject: 1967 Hong Kong Riots
summary: What began as a factory labor dispute in May 1967 escalated into eight months of bombings, street battles, and fifty-one deaths — a crisis that forced British colonial Hong Kong to confront what it was, and what it needed to become.

subject: 1970 Omani coup d'état
summary: A British-orchestrated palace coup in Salalah replaced an isolationist sultan with his Sandhurst-educated son, transforming Oman from a country with one hospital and 10 km of paved roads into a modern state within a single decade.

subject: 1985 Sudanese coup d'état
summary: The coup that deposed Nimeiry came not from tanks but from doctors, lawyers, and university professors calling a general strike - then the army joined in.

subject: 1989 Jonesborough Ambush
summary: On a hilltop south of Jonesborough in March 1989, two senior RUC officers returning from a cross-border police meeting were killed in the highest-ranking police deaths of the Troubles.

subject: 1993 Storm of the Century
summary: On March 12, 1993, a cyclonic superstorm formed over the Gulf of Mexico and stretched from Honduras to Canada, killing over 300 people, knocking out power to 10 million households, and closing every airport from Halifax to Tampa in what became the benchmark for modern winter storm forecasting.

subject: 1996 Belgian Air Force Hercules accident
summary: A flock of starlings brought down a military transport at Eindhoven Airport, killing 34 young Dutch Army musicians in a disaster compounded by fatal delays.

subject: 1st Canadian Tunnelling Company
summary: Canadian miners who waged war underground in the darkness beneath Flanders, building the largest mine of the Battle of Messines and earning a Victoria Cross at the war's end.

subject: 20 Forthlin Road
summary: Paul and Mike McCartney's childhood home in Allerton, where the first Lennon-McCartney songs were written; the National Trust has owned the council house since 1995 and calls it "the birthplace of the Beatles".

subject: 2001 Biggin Hill Airshow disasters
summary: A weekend of warbird displays at the Battle of Britain's most famous airfield ended with two crashes in two days, three pilots killed, and an airshow that never quite recovered.

subject: 2003 Angola Boeing 727 disappearance
summary: A Boeing 727 that had sat idle for fourteen months at Luanda's airport taxied to a runway without clearance, took off into the sunset with no lights and no radio contact, and vanished over the Atlantic Ocean, never to be found.

subject: 2003 Derrybrien Landslide
summary: On Halloween 2003, the side of an Irish hill liquefied and slid downhill, dragging a wind farm with it and embarrassing a nation that thought it was building the future.

subject: 2003 La Paz riots
summary: In February 2003, a tax hike demanded by the IMF triggered a police mutiny and two days of armed combat in the heart of La Paz that left thirty-one dead and drove the president from his own palace.

subject: 2003 Tuen Mun Road Bus Accident
summary: On the morning of July 10, 2003, a double-decker bus plunged 35 meters from a viaduct on Tuen Mun Road, killing 21 people in the deadliest road traffic accident in Hong Kong's history.

subject: 2004 Summer Olympics opening ceremony
summary: On the night the Games came home to Athens, a flooded stadium floor became a pool of Greek memory, and a comet of fire drew the Olympic rings on the water.

subject: 2009 Summer Deaflympics
summary: Taipei hosted the 21st Summer Deaflympics in September 2009, building a new stadium, welcoming athletes from 80 nations, and closing with a banquet of beef noodles and mango shaved ice instead of the usual fireworks.

subject: 2009 USS Port Royal grounding
summary: A guided missile cruiser ran aground on a coral reef off Honolulu in full view of airport traffic, causing $40 million in ship damage and destroying acres of reef habitat.

story.title: 2010 IIHF World Championship: The Miracle at Mannheim and 77,803 in Gelsenkirchen

subject: 2010 IIHF World Championship
summary: Germany opened its 2010 world championship in a football stadium in front of 77,803 fans, the biggest crowd ever to watch a hockey game. Sixteen days later in Cologne, the Czech Republic beat Russia 2-1 in the final. In between, the host nation made a quarterfinal called the Miracle at Mannheim.

subject: 2010 Penang dragon boat tragedy
summary: On a January morning in 2010, a school dragon boat training session in the Penang Strait ended in catastrophe when strong currents swept the vessel into a tugboat, killing six young paddlers and exposing systemic failures in student safety oversight.

subject: 2014 Sundarbans oil spill
summary: When an oil tanker sank in the Shela River, 350,000 liters of furnace oil spread through the waterways of a UNESCO World Heritage mangrove forest, threatening rare dolphins and exposing the Sundarbans' vulnerability.

subject: 2015 Sousse attacks
summary: On a June afternoon in 2015, a gunman disguised as a tourist killed 38 people at a Tunisian beach resort, devastating families across three continents and shaking a young democracy's fragile stability.

subject: 2015 Women's European Volleyball Championship
summary: Russia took a 19th European title in a Rotterdam arena packed with Dutch fans hoping to watch their own team win the final - and Tatiana Kosheleva became MVP for the second straight tournament.

subject: 2016 Jakarta attacks
summary: On January 14, 2016, a coordinated assault of suicide bombs and gunfire near Jakarta's Sarinah shopping mall killed eight people and brought ISIS-directed violence to the heart of Indonesia's capital for the first time.

subject: 2017 Tehran attacks
summary: On June 7, 2017, coordinated ISIL attacks struck Iran's parliament and Khomeini's mausoleum in Tehran, killing 17 people and wounding 52 in the first major terrorist assault on the Iranian capital.

subject: 2019 Townsville flood
summary: In early 2019, a monsoon that would not move drowned Townsville, forced the Ross River Dam's gates wide open, and left thousands of families to rebuild from the mud.

subject: 2021 Hualien Train Derailment
summary: On April 2, 2021, a construction truck rolled onto the tracks near Qingshui Tunnel in eastern Taiwan, derailing a Taroko Express train and killing 49 people in Taiwan's deadliest rail disaster in decades.

subject: 2021 Ypres Rally
summary: In August 2021, the World Rally Championship's premier drivers raced flat-out over the narrow farm lanes and battlefield ridges around Ieper, on a course that ran past cemeteries, mine craters and the Menin Gate.

subject: 2024 Shenzhen Stabbing
summary: On 18 September 2024, a ten-year-old Japanese boy was fatally stabbed near his school in Shenzhen; he died the following day. This is a record of what happened, and of the grief and humanity that followed.

subject: 2025 Wrexham National Eisteddfod
summary: Wales's largest cultural festival came to a farm field in Isycoed for one week in August 2025 - 6,000 competitors, 150,000 visitors, and one chair shaped like the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct.

subject: 23 de Enero
summary: A Caracas parish named for the date a dictator fell, where Le Corbusier-inspired tower blocks became a crucible of Venezuelan revolution and resistance.

subject: 24 Sussex Drive
summary: Canada's most famous address sits empty and crumbling on the banks of the Ottawa River, a limestone house that once hosted prime ministers now infested with rodents and stripped of asbestos.

subject: 3. Liga
summary: Germany's third division of professional football, where 27,500 fans can pack a stadium and a single bankruptcy can erase a season - the league of giants in exile.

subject: 369th Regiment Armory
summary: Built for the Harlem Hellfighters, the first all-Black National Guard unit in New York State, this Art Deco armory on Fifth Avenue has served as a military home, homeless shelter, community center, and living monument since the 1920s.

subject: 42nd G7 summit
summary: The 2016 G7 summit on tiny Kashiko Island in Mie Prefecture became a stage for last acts: the final summit for Obama, Cameron, Hollande, and Renzi, held at a venue hand-picked by Prime Minister Abe for its proximity to Japan's holiest shrine.
The world's most famous house number is a perfume - born when French troops numbered every door in Cologne and a Carthusian monk's wedding gift recipe found its way to the building they marked 4711.

subject: 555 California Street
summary: San Francisco's fourth-tallest building, a dark red granite tower that served as Bank of America's world headquarters and whose polished black granite sculpture locals call 'Banker's Heart.'

subject: 555 Edgecombe Avenue
summary: Known as 'The Triple Nickel,' this Washington Heights apartment building became a National Historic Landmark as the home of Paul Robeson, Count Basie, Coleman Hawkins, and dozens of other African American luminaries who made it the most celebrated address in uptown Manhattan.

subject: 710 Ashbury Street
summary: The Victorian house where the Grateful Dead lived communally from 1966 to 1968 - ground zero for the Summer of Love, where the band was famously arrested, and where a psychedelic revolution briefly had a home address.

story.title: A $40 Million Medieval Fantasy in Wine Country

subject: A $40 Million Medieval Fantasy in Wine Country
summary: A fourth-generation Italian-American winemaker spent 15 years and $40 million building an authentically constructed medieval castle in the Napa Valley -- complete with a moat, a drawbridge, and a torture chamber.

story.title: A Thousand Doors and the Ghosts Behind Them

subject: A Thousand Doors and the Ghosts Behind Them
summary: Semarang's iconic Lawang Sewu - Javanese for 'a thousand doors' - served as a colonial railway headquarters, a Japanese wartime dungeon, a battlefield, and Indonesia's most famous haunted house before its restoration as a heritage museum.

subject: A. P. Carter Store
summary: The 1945 country store A.P. Carter built after he stopped recording - now the Carter Family Museum.

subject: A. P. Hill Boyhood Home
summary: A three-story Italianate brick townhouse in Culpeper, Virginia, where Confederate General Ambrose Powell Hill grew up - built by a Revolutionary War general and later expanded into the building that still stands on Main Street.

subject: AKI Academy for Art & Design
summary: Founded in 1946 by textile manufacturers to train fabric designers, this Enschede art school became known as the most rebellious academy in the Netherlands.

subject: ARA Presidente Sarmiento
summary: The last intact cruising training ship of the 1890s, a full-rigged frigate that circled the globe six times and now rests as a museum in the heart of Puerto Madero.

story.title: Aachen: Charlemagne's Capital at Europe's Crossroads

subject: Aachen
summary: Where Charlemagne built his empire's heart, crowning thirty German kings in a cathedral that still holds his bones, at the precise point where Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands converge.

subject: Aalholm
summary: Lolland's oldest castle spent seven centuries collecting kings, countesses and rebuilds - and then became famous for a shed full of veteran cars that sold off in a single August afternoon.

subject: Aarhus Air Raid
summary: On 31 October 1944 the Danish resistance asked Britain to bomb the building where its own people were being interrogated — and twenty-five Mosquitoes flew from Norfolk to do it.

subject: Abadía del Niño Dios
summary: The first Benedictine monastery in the Spanish-speaking Americas, where monks near the Paraná River have prayed, taught, and distilled a 73-herb liqueur from a secret formula for over a century.

subject: Abbeyside, Dungarvan
summary: A Waterford townland that produced one of Ireland's two Nobel laureates in physics - and watched its 17th-century tower house collapse one January morning in 1916.

subject: Abe Lenstra Stadion
summary: The stadium in Heerenveen carries the name of a Frisian striker who scored 700 goals across 730 matches, and who died the night before the first international ever played in his own park.

story.title: Abeno Harukas: Osaka's Tower That Clears the Sky

subject: Abeno Harukas
summary: Standing 300 meters tall in Osaka's Abeno-ku ward, Abeno Harukas held the title of Japan's tallest building from 2014 to 2023, its name drawn from an archaic Japanese word meaning 'to brighten, to clear up.'

subject: Abercastle
summary: A tiny northwest-facing fishing harbour on the Pembrokeshire coast, Abercastle was the landing point for the first solo west-east Atlantic crossing in 1876 - and sits beneath a 5,000-year-old dolmen that local legend says was placed by Samson's little finger.

subject: Aberdeen Reservoirs
summary: Twin reservoirs tucked into Hong Kong Island's southern hills — born from a paper factory's private water supply, declared monuments for their colonial-era stonework, and now the centrepiece of one of Hong Kong's earliest country parks.

subject: Abolitionist Place
summary: A short stretch of Duffield Street in downtown Brooklyn carries the name Abolitionist Place, marking where the Truesdell family sheltered freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad and where a community fought to save the last surviving house from demolition.

subject: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
summary: A neoclassical marble temple in rural Kentucky enshrines a log cabin that almost certainly is not the one Lincoln was born in. The architectural irony is the point.

subject: Abram's Delight
summary: The oldest house in Winchester, Virginia, built in 1754 by Quaker settlers from Ireland - acquired with a cow, a calf, and a piece of red cloth.

subject: Absalom Jones
summary: Born enslaved near Milford, Delaware in 1746, he bought his wife's freedom before his own, walked out of a segregated church, and became the first Black priest in the Episcopal Church.

subject: Abuyama Kofun
summary: A 7th-century burial mound on Mount Abu where earthquake scientists accidentally uncovered a mummified nobleman in 1934 -- then the government ordered the tomb sealed shut because the body might be too important to study.

subject: Acadamh na hOllscolaíochta Gaeilge
summary: The only Irish university where you can graduate entirely through the Irish language — a deliberate act of linguistic survival founded in 2004.

subject: Academia Sinica
summary: Founded in Nanjing in 1928 and transplanted to Taiwan during the Chinese Civil War, Academia Sinica is the island's national academy, home to Nobel laureates, a forest park, and an earth god temple.

subject: Academie Minerva
summary: An art school that began in 1798 by teaching painters and ship captains side by side, and quietly shaped two centuries of Dutch art from a wedge of the country most outsiders never visit.

subject: Academy of Athens
summary: A gleaming marble temple on a busy Athens avenue, the modern Academy borrows the name of Plato's school and the look of the ancient gods to honour the life of the mind.

subject: Academy of Music
summary: The 1905 Beaux-Arts theatre on Main Street where Sarah Bernhardt, Anna Pavlova, and Paderewski performed, now one of Virginia's only surviving legitimate theaters from the turn of the twentieth century.

subject: Achillbeg
summary: Little Achill - an abandoned island off the southern tip of its bigger sister, with a 1965 lighthouse, a featherweight world champion's plaque, and a Gaeltacht silence.

subject: Achilleion (Corfu)
summary: A grieving empress built a palace on Corfu dedicated to Achilles, then a German kaiser bought it and replaced her poet's statue with a warrior's, and then James Bond played baccarat in it.

subject: Achiltibuie
summary: A scattered coastal community on the Coigach peninsula whose Gaelic name - the field of the yellow-haired boy - has held longer than most empires, and whose smokehouse, mountain and Iron Age broch still draw the few who come.

subject: Achmeatoren
summary: A 115-meter office tower that has shed its granite cladding three times without ever hitting a passerby — and that the Dutch Air Force tried to block from being built at all.

subject: Action of 14/15 February 1918
summary: A night raid by eight German destroyers shattered the British anti-submarine barrage in the Strait of Dover - and the British, hearing the guns, mistook them for an air raid on Dover.

subject: Acueducto de los Milagros
summary: Thirty-eight pillars of alternating granite and red brick rise 25 meters above Merida, the ruins of a Roman aqueduct so improbable in its survival that locals named it the Aqueduct of the Miracles.

subject: Adare Friary
summary: Augustinian friars built it in 1316, Tudor monarchs emptied it, and Church of Ireland children now learn maths in what used to be the refectory - the Adare Friary has had three lives in three different Irelands.

story.title: Adashino Nenbutsu-ji: The Temple of Eight Thousand Nameless Dead

subject: Adashino Nenbutsu-ji
summary: A Kyoto hillside temple where eight thousand stone statues -- collected from ancient open-air burial grounds -- sit in silent rows, lit by candlelight each August in one of Japan's most haunting memorial ceremonies.

subject: Admiralty Arch
summary: The grand ceremonial gateway between Trafalgar Square and The Mall was built as a memorial to Queen Victoria — and its creator, King Edward VII, died before seeing it finished.

subject: Admiralty Arch, Holyhead
summary: A triumphal arch on Salt Island, built in 1824 to commemorate the August 1821 visit of George IV -- the king arrived by yacht, was stranded by bad weather, and made history by boarding the world's first Royal Mail steam packet to Ireland.

subject: Aegina
summary: The triangular island that minted Europe's first coins, raised a temple rivaling the Parthenon, briefly served as the first capital of liberated Greece, and today perfumes the Saronic Gulf with the scent of roasting pistachios.

subject: Affric-Beauly hydro-electric power scheme
summary: Britain's only double-arched dam, the largest dam ever built by the Hydro Board, and a power station with crow-stepped gables and Borland fish lifts—the Affric-Beauly scheme threaded power generation through three of the most scenic glens in the Highlands.

subject: Agia Lavra
summary: Built in 961 AD on the slopes of Mount Chelmos, the monastery of Agia Lavra is revered as the symbolic birthplace of modern Greece — the place where Bishop Germanos of Patras raised the flag of revolution on 25 March 1821.

subject: Agia Theodoti
summary: A quiet bay on the far side of Ios, where a five-century-old church sits on the bones of an ancient temple and a road only reached the sea in 1998.

subject: Agnews Developmental Center
summary: A former psychiatric hospital in Santa Clara whose main building collapsed in the 1906 earthquake killing over 100 patients and staff, later becoming a developmental center before closing in 2009.

subject: Ahsan Manzil
summary: A pink palace on the banks of the Buriganga River that served as the seat of the Nawabs of Dhaka, survived tornadoes and earthquakes, fell into ruin as a slum, and was reborn as a museum preserving Old Dhaka's grandest architectural statement.

subject: Ahu A ʻUmi Heiau
summary: A 16th-century Hawaiian temple built on the remote high plateau between Mauna Loa and Hualalai, where King Umi moved the seat of government from Waipio Valley to the heart of the island.

subject: Aillebrack
summary: On the western tip of the Errismore peninsula sits a townland of 122 souls, a holy well named for seven daughters, and a memorial to American airmen who never made it home.

subject: AirTrain Newark
summary: Newark Airport's monorail people mover, plagued by breakdowns since it opened in 1996, is being replaced by a $3.5 billion cable-driven system expected to open in 2030.

subject: Ajax 5-1 Liverpool (1966)
summary: The night a 19-year-old Johan Cruyff and a fog-shrouded Amsterdam stadium handed Liverpool its worst European defeat and announced Total Football to the world.

subject: Akasaka Estate
summary: A hidden compound of six imperial residences in the heart of Tokyo, where the Tokugawa shoguns once kept their grandest Edo mansion and where Japan's Imperial Family still lives behind walls the public never enters.

subject: Akibayama Kofun Cluster
summary: Six ancient burial mounds on a Kanagawa hilltop preserve 1,700 years of ritual, trade, and political hierarchy from the dawn of Japan's tumulus age.

subject: Al-Attarine Madrasa
summary: A 14th-century theological school in Fez whose intimate courtyard packs three layers of decorative mastery -- zellij tilework, carved stucco, and cedar wood -- into one of the finest spaces the Marinid dynasty ever built.

subject: Al-Qasr al-Sagir
summary: A Muslim pleasure palace in Murcia that housed a rebel king, then Christian monarchs, and for over six centuries has been home to cloistered nuns.

story.title: Alabama Department of Archives and History

subject: Alabama Department of Archives and History
summary: The nation's first publicly funded state archives agency, born in an Alabama Capitol cloakroom in 1901 and now housed behind bronze doors depicting eight scenes from state history.

subject: Alabama Shakespeare Festival
summary: One of the world's ten largest Shakespeare festivals, born from a disastrous debut before a single critic in an Alabama high school auditorium and saved by a $21.5 million gift.

subject: Alameda Mole
summary: A vanished transit pier that once pushed rail lines across the East Bay mud flats into deep water, connecting Alameda to San Francisco by ferry from 1878 until the Bay Bridge made it obsolete.

subject: Alamo Mission
summary: A Spanish mission that became a fortress, a grocery store, a bat colony, and finally a UNESCO World Heritage Site -- saved from demolition by two women who fought each other almost as fiercely as they fought to preserve it.

subject: Alamut
summary: A remote mountain valley in Iran's Alborz range where Hassan-i Sabbah built an impregnable fortress in 1090 CE and founded the Order of Assassins, shaping two centuries of Middle Eastern history from a castle perched on a 200-meter rock.

subject: Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition
summary: The 1909 world's fair that transformed a forested university campus into Seattle's grandest stage, drew 3.7 million visitors, and planted the architectural bones that still define the University of Washington today.

subject: Alauna (Maryport)
summary: A Roman fort on a hill above the River Ellen that has yielded more inscribed altars than any other site in Britain, and whose Roman name comes from a single line in a sixth-century geography.

subject: Albrechtsburg
summary: Saxony's rulers built a castle on the Meissen rock that was meant to be lived in rather than defended — then divided their inheritance before it was finished, and hardly anyone ever moved in.

subject: Albrook Air Force Station
summary: A U.S. Air Force base beside the Panama Canal that spent sixty-five years defending the waterway, then became a civilian airport and shopping mall.

story.title: Alcatraz: The Escape That May Have Worked

subject: Alcatraz
summary: The 1962 prison break from America's most inescapable penitentiary - where three men vanished through ventilation shafts and paddled into San Francisco Bay, never to be seen again, leaving investigators uncertain whether they escaped or drowned.

story.title: Alcatraz: The Rock That Couldn't Hold Them All

subject: Alcatraz
summary: Where the federal government built an 'escape-proof' prison in San Francisco Bay that held America's most dangerous criminals - until 36 men tried to escape and three vanished without a trace.

subject: Alcatraz Wharf
summary: The gateway to America's most infamous prison, where every prisoner, guard, and supply shipment passed for nearly a century.

subject: Alcazaba of Almería
summary: A thousand-year-old citadel where Moorish walls, a Christian castle, and Hollywood film sets have coexisted on a hilltop overlooking the Mediterranean.

subject: Alcazaba of Málaga
summary: One of the best-preserved Moorish fortifications in Spain, this 11th-century palatial citadel rises above Malaga's port with double walls, five gates, and the ruins of a Roman theatre at its feet.

subject: Alexander von Humboldt
summary: A floating lighthouse that spent eighty years going nowhere, learned to sail at the age of eighty-two, rounded Cape Horn at a hundred - and now sits dismasted on a Bremen quay.

subject: Alexandria Arachosia
summary: Beneath modern Kandahar lies one of Alexander the Great's forgotten cities, founded around 330 BC on the ruins of an ancient Persian fortress at the crossroads of empires.

subject: Alexandrovskiye Trade Rows
summary: A row of shops in Taganrog built to look like an ancient temple - and the very place a young Anton Chekhov learned to hate the family business.

subject: Algo Centre Mall
summary: A shopping mall in Elliot Lake, Ontario, whose rooftop parking deck collapsed on June 23, 2012, killing two people and exposing decades of engineering negligence, falsified safety reports, and a community's dangerous dependence on a single building.

subject: Ali Qapu (Tabriz)
summary: A lost Safavid palace in Tabriz whose name meant 'Grand Gate' -- rebuilt by the Qajars with mirror-decorated walls and a cruciform music hall, then demolished in the 1940s to make room for government offices.

subject: Aliʻiōlani Hale
summary: Designed as a palace but built as a government building, Aliʻiōlani Hale witnessed the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy and now houses the state Supreme Court beneath the watchful gaze of a golden Kamehameha.

subject: Allandale Station
summary: Half a million hectares of gibber plain and dry riverbed near Oodnadatta, where a few thousand cattle range across country bigger than many small nations and an abandoned railway bridge still spans the Neales River.

subject: Allied Arts Guild
summary: Founded in 1928 among Spanish Colonial gardens in Menlo Park, this artists' complex has quietly supported Lucile Packard Children's Hospital for nearly a century.

subject: Almendres Cromlech
summary: The largest group of structured menhirs on the Iberian Peninsula, older than Stonehenge by two thousand years, arranged across a Portuguese hillside in alignments that track the moon and mark the winter solstice.

subject: Aloalo
summary: The carved funerary posts of the Mahafaly people of southwestern Madagascar, where the word for the sculpture means 'messenger' - a wooden intermediary meant to carry the dead into the community of ancestors.

subject: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol
summary: In March 2016, a Google AI defeated one of Go's greatest players in a Seoul hotel room, crossing a threshold that experts believed was a decade away and redefining the boundary between human and machine intelligence.

subject: Alte Feste
summary: Windhoek's oldest building is a German colonial fort that never fired a shot in battle — and is now slated to become a museum of the very colonialism it once embodied.

subject: Alte Tonhalle
summary: Mendelssohn premiered Paulus here. Brahms played. Mahler's Eighth filled it with a thousand performers. Then the bombs came, and a department store rose on the ashes.

subject: Althorp
summary: Five hundred years of the Spencer family, one of the great private libraries of Europe, a Tudor manor wrapped in Georgian tiles, and a small island lake where the Princess of Wales rests.

subject: Alto Biobío
summary: High in the Andean headwaters of Chile's great river, the Pehuenche people still gather pine nuts beneath ancient araucarias - and still remember the valley a dam took from them.

subject: Altıkulaç Sarcophagus
summary: Discovered in 1998 in a tumulus near Çan in northwestern Turkey, the Altıkulaç Sarcophagus is a painted Greco-Persian stone coffin from around 400–375 BC that depicts its occupant — a young warrior-dynast who survived a catastrophic fall — hunting and fighting in the manner of Persian royal iconography.

subject: Alupka
summary: A small Black Sea resort named for a fox, where a British-designed castle briefly made it more fashionable than Yalta itself.

subject: Alushta
summary: A relaxed Black Sea resort on Crimea's southern shore, guarded for fifteen centuries by the crumbling stones of a fortress the Byzantines raised against the mountains.

subject: Amalienborg
summary: Four identical rococo palaces built for four noble families around an octagonal square — and the home the Danish royal family moved into only because their own palace burned down.

subject: Amanohashidate
summary: A pine-covered sandbar stretching across Miyazu Bay that the Japanese have called one of their country's three most beautiful views for over three centuries, and that mythology says was once a bridge to heaven.

subject: Amarapura
summary: A former Burmese capital whose palace was dismantled and carried away by elephant, Amarapura endures as a place of silk looms, bronze foundries, and the world's longest teak footbridge.

subject: Amba Geshen
summary: A flat-topped mountain in northern Ethiopia where emperors once imprisoned their own brothers and sons, a fortress whose legend reached Milton and Coleridge.

subject: American Legation, Tangier
summary: The first American public property outside the United States and the only U.S. National Historic Landmark on foreign soil -- a Moorish building in Tangier's medina that has served as a diplomatic post, a spy headquarters, and a museum for over two centuries.

subject: American Shakespeare Center
summary: A Staunton theater company that built the world's only working recreation of Shakespeare's indoor Blackfriars Playhouse - and stages plays the way the Elizabethans actually did, with the house lights on.

subject: Amharclann Ghaoth Dobhair
summary: The small Gaeltacht theatre in Derrybeg where Enya, Moya Brennan, and the future members of Clannad and Altan first stepped onto a stage.

subject: Amsterdam Centraal Station
summary: A Neo-Renaissance cathedral of rail, balanced on 8,687 wooden piles and three artificial islands in the IJ, where 192,000 passengers a day pass through the most-visited national monument in the Netherlands.

subject: Amsterdam Wooden Drydock I
summary: Europe's first modern floating dry dock, a wooden raft engineered to lift 1,000-ton ships out of Amsterdam's marshy harbor in 1842.

subject: Amsterdam Wooden Drydock II
summary: A patent, a deadline, and a 49-metre wooden box in the Westerdok - the second floating dry dock Amsterdam ever built, opened on 30 September 1844 by lifting a three-masted West Africa trader out of the water.

subject: Ancient Greece
summary: From a scatter of rocky peninsulas and island harbors, the ancient Greeks built the civilization that gave the Western world democracy, philosophy, theatre, and the very idea of history itself.

subject: Ancient Siam
summary: A 320-hectare outdoor museum shaped like the map of Thailand, where 116 replicas of the kingdom's lost and surviving monuments are positioned in their real-world geographic locations, built by a man who started out designing a golf course.

subject: Ancol Dreamland
summary: Jakarta's sprawling waterfront playground began as mosquito-infested swampland that President Sukarno envisioned as Southeast Asia's largest integrated resort - a 552-hectare dreamscape of theme parks, beaches, and casinos turned family fun.

subject: Ancud
summary: The northern gateway to Chiloé was once the Spanish crown's last fortress in Chile, where the empire's flag in the country came down for the final time in 1826.

subject: Andøya Space
summary: From a field called The Ox Pasture on a windswept Arctic island, Norway has been launching rockets since 1962 -- and is now building Europe's first continental orbital spaceport.

subject: Anna Hyatt Huntington
summary: An American sculptor whose Joan of Arc was the first New York monument to a historical woman, and who - with her husband Archer - built Brookgreen Gardens into America's largest outdoor sculpture park.

subject: Anna Ranch Heritage Center
summary: A restored 1910s ranch house in Waimea preserves the legacy of Anna Lindsey Perry-Fiske, a woman who ran her own cattle ranch in Hawaii for over fifty years when the industry was almost exclusively male.

subject: Anrakuju-in
summary: A Buddhist temple in southern Kyoto where two emperors lie entombed in pagodas, the last remnants of a vast imperial villa that once served as the nerve center of Japan's cloistered government.

subject: Ansi City
summary: A Goguryeo fortress in present-day Liaoning whose defiant stand against the Tang emperor in 645 CE became one of East Asia's most celebrated military legends.

subject: Antenor Kore
summary: Smashed by Persian invaders, buried by reverent Athenians, and dug up in pieces two and a half thousand years later, this marble maiden is one of the grandest survivors of Archaic Greek sculpture.

story.title: Antietam: The Day America Lost 23,000 Men

subject: Antietam
summary: The Maryland battlefield where the bloodiest single day in American military history unfolded on September 17, 1862 - where cornfields became killing grounds, where Burnside's Bridge became a slaughter, and where Lincoln found enough victory to change the war's meaning forever.

subject: Antoine's
summary: The oldest family-run restaurant in the United States, where Oysters Rockefeller was invented in 1840s New Orleans and where Prohibition-era diners smuggled cocktails through the ladies' restroom.

subject: Anuradhapura kingdom
summary: For nearly 1,400 years, a single kingdom ruled Sri Lanka from the banks of a stream called Kolon -- building colossal stupas, engineering vast irrigation networks, and surviving wave after wave of invasion until the Cholas finally brought the curtain down in 1017.

subject: Aokigahara
summary: A dense forest growing on 30 square kilometers of hardened lava from Mount Fuji's 864 CE eruption, where exposed tree roots twist across bare rock, ice-filled caves draw school groups, and an eerie silence has given rise to centuries of ghost stories.

subject: Apollo-Soyuz
summary: The first international crewed space mission saw American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts dock their spacecraft and shake hands in orbit, turning Cold War rivals into partners two hundred miles above Earth.

subject: Appomattox Iron Works
summary: A nine-building Federal-style foundry complex at 28 Old Street in Petersburg that cast iron for 73 years and stands as one of the most intact industrial sites of its era on the National Register.

subject: AquaDom
summary: For nineteen years a glass elevator carried visitors up through a million litres of seawater in a Berlin hotel lobby — until one freezing December morning when the tank let go.

subject: Arai-juku
summary: The thirty-first station on the Tokaido road, where Edo-period travelers boarded boats to cross Lake Hamana and daimyo processions made their grandest water crossings.

story.title: Arashiyama: Where the Moon Crosses the Bridge

subject: Arashiyama
summary: Kyoto's western mountain retreat -- where Heian-era aristocrats built their villas, an emperor named a bridge for the moon, monkeys rule a mountaintop, and a bamboo forest makes sounds the government declared a national treasure.

subject: Arboretum Oleksandriya
summary: Ukraine's second-largest park, laid out for a countess along the Ros River, hides colonnades, a golden Chinese bridge, and artful ruins among its ancient trees.

subject: Arboretum d'Antsokay
summary: A 40-hectare botanical garden near Toliara where a Swiss conservationist spent decades rescuing Madagascar's most threatened plants from slash-and-burn deforestation, and where an elephant bird egg sits in a small museum surrounded by 900 species found almost nowhere else.

subject: Arbroath
summary: A former royal burgh of 23,902 souls on the Angus coast, built around an abbey, a harbour, a smokehouse industry, and a fish-shaped sense of itself.

subject: Arc Institute
summary: Arc Institute is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit biomedical research organization based in Palo Alto, California. It was co-founded by Stanford University bioch

subject: Arc de Triomf
summary: A triumphal arch of rust-red brick that celebrates no battle, built to welcome the world to Barcelona's 1888 fair.

story.title: Arc de Triomphe: The Monument Napoleon Never Saw Finished

subject: Arc de Triomphe
summary: Commissioned after Austerlitz and completed thirty years later under a different king, the Arc de Triomphe stands at the center of twelve radiating avenues, sheltering the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath its vault.

subject: Arcadia
summary: Odesa's most famous seaside resort borrows its name from a Greek land of shepherds and idyll, a stretch of Black Sea coast that has meant leisure for over a century.

subject: Arch of Septimius Severus (Leptis Magna)
summary: Buried for centuries beneath Libyan sand, this four-way triumphal arch was raised in AD 203 by Rome's first African-born emperor at the crossroads of his hometown -- and painstakingly reassembled by archaeologists after its rediscovery in 1928.

subject: Arch of Triumph (Pyongyang)
summary: Deliberately built eleven meters taller than Paris's Arc de Triomphe, Pyongyang's Arch of Triumph is a 60-meter monument made of 25,500 blocks of white granite -- one for each day of Kim Il Sung's life at the time of its unveiling.

subject: Arch of the Philaeni
summary: A Fascist triumphal arch built in 1937 on the Libyan coast to celebrate imperial ambition, the Arch of the Philaeni stood for barely three decades before Gaddafi demolished it as a symbol of colonial oppression.

subject: Ardabil
summary: Birthplace of the Safavid dynasty, home to a UNESCO-listed shrine and the world's most famous carpet, where a dormant volcano watches over five thousand years of history.

subject: Ardchattan Priory
summary: A 1230 priory on Loch Etive where Robert the Bruce held Scotland's last Gaelic-speaking parliament, yew trees may have furnished longbows for Bannockburn, and monks' gardens still bloom eight centuries on.

subject: Ardfinnan Woollen Mills
summary: From sheep to suit, all under one roof - the Tipperary mill that clothed Eamon de Valera at the League of Nations and patented a waterproof motoring cloth.

subject: Ardoileán
summary: An uninhabited island off the Connemara coast where early Christian hermits built stone beehive cells, an Irish poet spent thirty years restoring the ruins, and the asking price in 2019 was 1.25 million euros - sheep and gulls included.

subject: Ardtornish
summary: A Highland estate in Morvern, Scotland, where a Victorian mansion built by a London distiller now anchors gardens, hydropower, and one of Europe's few silica sand mines.

subject: Arg of Tabriz
summary: A 14th-century citadel in Tabriz whose builders tried to surpass the legendary vault of Ctesiphon -- the roof collapsed during construction, and seven centuries of wars, fires, and misguided renovations have left only a single wall standing.

subject: Arg, Kabul
summary: Kabul's 83-acre presidential palace has witnessed every Afghan power transition since 1880 -- coronations, coups, assassinations, and the Taliban's return.

subject: Argentine Declaration of Independence
summary: On July 9, 1816, thirty-three deputies gathered in a borrowed house in Tucuman to sever the last legal ties between Spain's South American colonies and the Crown of Castile, creating a new nation in a single afternoon's vote.

subject: Argos
summary: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, spreading across a broad plain beneath the ancient citadel of Larissa, where the mythic and the mundane have coexisted for three thousand years.

subject: Arguin
summary: A small, reef-ringed island off Mauritania where Europe built its first fortress outside its own continent - and from which, by 1455, some 800 enslaved West Africans were shipped to Portugal every year.

subject: Ariau Towers
summary: The abandoned treetop hotel that once hosted celebrities twenty meters above the Amazon floor, now stripped for scrap in the canopy.

subject: Arirang Mass Games
summary: Over 100,000 performers transform a Pyongyang stadium into a living mosaic of political devotion -- a Guinness World Record spectacle named for a folk song about a couple torn apart, just like Korea itself.

subject: Arktikum
summary: A 172-meter glass corridor stretching northward from Rovaniemi serves as the Gateway to the Arctic, housing a museum and science centre that burrows below the frozen earth like the animals it celebrates.

subject: Arle, Großheide
summary: A 12th-century East Frisian provostship whose tuff-stone church and lost castle tower trace the slow shift of power among coastal noble families.

subject: Arlington Cinema 'N' Drafthouse
summary: An Art Deco movie theater opened on Columbia Pike in 1940 - desegregated in 1963 after Dorothy Hamm's lawsuit, converted to a dine-in drafthouse in 1985, and now a stage for the country's top touring comics.

subject: Arlington Ridge, Virginia
summary: A high ridge overlooking the Pentagon - first Confederate land seized by the Union in May 1861, photographed by every news outlet after September 11, 2001, and home to Allison's Little Tea House where Eleanor Roosevelt used to lunch.

subject: Armenian Catholic Archeparchy of Istanbul
summary: The Armenian Catholic Archeparchy of Istanbul has kept faith with a small, resilient community — in 2008 numbering around 3,650 — that maintains a distinct liturgical tradition bridging Rome and the ancient Armenian Church.

subject: Army and Navy Academy
summary: Colonel Thomas A. Davis opened a military boarding school in Pacific Beach in 1910, moved it to Carlsbad in 1936, and created an institution that shaped students ranging from a Hollywood gunslinger to a NASCAR driver.

subject: Art Institute of Chicago
summary: Born from the ashes of the Great Fire and housed in a building made for the 1893 World's Fair, the Art Institute of Chicago guards nearly 300,000 works spanning 5,000 years - including Nighthawks, American Gothic, and the finest Impressionist collection outside France.

subject: Arthur Dobbs
summary: An Irish surveyor-general who built Dublin's Parliament House, hunted the Northwest Passage from a desk in Ulster, governed colonial North Carolina for a decade, and wrote the first scientific description of the Venus flytrap.

subject: Arthur M. Sackler Gallery
summary: A Smithsonian museum of Asian art - 96 percent of it underground beneath the Enid A. Haupt Garden, opened in 1987 with funding from a Japanese prime minister, the U.S. Congress, and a pharmaceutical fortune that would later become very public.

subject: Arti et Amicitiae
summary: For Art and Friendship — a Dutch artists' society founded in 1839 whose Rokin clubhouse still hosts exhibitions in a glass-roofed hall designed for natural light.

subject: Artà
summary: A hilltop church wrapped inside a fortress, a knee-high palm that has fed a craft for centuries, and 25 kilometers of coast the tourist boom never reached — Artà is the Mallorca that stayed itself.

subject: Asclepieion of Athens
summary: An ancient sanctuary-hospital on the Acropolis slope, where the sick slept beside a sacred spring hoping the healing god would visit them in their dreams.

story.title: Ashikaga Gakko: Japan's Oldest School and the Books That Survived Warlords

subject: Ashikaga Gakkō
