summary: Founded around 839 in what is now Tochigi Prefecture, the Ashikaga Gakko is Japan's oldest academic institution -- a school that survived fire, looting by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and the end of Confucianism's dominance, only to be restored to its Edo-period form in the 1980s.

subject: Ashkenaz
summary: A Berkeley world music and dance hall founded in 1973 by activist David Nadel, whose murder in 1996 transformed the venue from one man's vision into a community-owned nonprofit that still fills its 5,000-square-foot dance floor every week.

subject: Askut
summary: An island fortress on the Nubian frontier where Egyptian soldiers married Nubian women and the archaeology tells their story through pottery, graves, and cookpots.

subject: Aspen, Colorado
summary: A former silver mining boomtown turned global luxury resort, Aspen sits in the Roaring Fork Valley where $9.5 million median home prices coexist with deed-restricted worker housing and world-class skiing.

subject: Assateague Light
summary: A 142-foot red-and-white candy-striped tower built in 1867 at the southern tip of Assateague Island - and the island has grown five miles past it since.

subject: Assen
summary: The capital of Drenthe began as a relocated nunnery built to atone for a bishop's death, and grew into a quiet provincial seat famous for two unrelated things: the Cathedral of Motorcycle Racing, and a sixteen-year-old girl pulled from a peat bog.

story.title: The Astoria Column: 525 Feet of History Wrapped Around Concrete

subject: Astoria Column
summary: A 125-foot tower on Coxcomb Hill in Astoria, Oregon, modeled after Trajan's Column in Rome, its spiral frieze depicting 14 key events in Oregon's early history - financed by a railroad magnate and the great-grandson of John Jacob Astor.

subject: Astrodome
summary: The world's first domed stadium invented AstroTurf, hosted Muhammad Ali and Billie Jean King, sheltered Hurricane Katrina refugees, and now sits empty as Houston tries to decide what to do with its Eighth Wonder.

subject: Astypalaia
summary: A butterfly-shaped Dodecanese island where a Venetian castle crowns the whitewashed Chora and the world's largest infant cemetery rests beneath the hills.

story.title: Asuka Mizuochi Site: Japan's Oldest Known Clock Tower

subject: Asuka Mizuochi Site
summary: In 660 AD, a Japanese prince built a water clock tower on the banks of the Asuka River -- a sophisticated timekeeping device whose ruins, hidden for over a millennium, revealed trumpet-shaped copper pipes and a black lacquered receiving box that once marked the hours for an empire.

story.title: Asuka-dera: Where Buddhism First Took Root in Japan

subject: Asuka-dera
summary: Japan's first full temple complex, built on a sixth-century battlefield vow, houses a bronze Great Buddha that spent two hundred years sitting in the open air after its hall burned down.

subject: Atacama Large Millimeter Array
summary: Sixty-six radio telescopes on a 5,000-meter plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert form the most expensive ground-based telescope ever built, capable of imaging forming planets, colliding galaxies, and the shadow of a black hole.

subject: Athena Cinema
summary: A continuously operating movie theater on Athens, Ohio's main street since 1915 - now owned by Ohio University and staffed almost entirely by students.

subject: Athena Parthenos
summary: Phidias's lost cult statue of Athena once towered nearly twelve meters inside the Parthenon, plated in a ton of gold and carved from ivory, a treasury you could worship.

subject: Athens
summary: Where democracy was invented beneath the Acropolis, where Socrates asked questions that got him killed, where Western philosophy began in the agora.

subject: Athens Conservatoire
summary: Greece's oldest performing-arts school, founded in 1871, where a teenage Maria Callas and a young Dimitri Mitropoulos trained, now housed in the country's great unfinished Bauhaus masterpiece.

subject: Athens Epidaurus Festival
summary: Every summer, audiences climb into a 2,000-year-old theatre to watch the oldest plays in the Western tradition performed where they were meant to be heard.

subject: Athens Lunatic Asylum
summary: A massive Kirkbride Plan asylum in southeastern Ohio that housed 1,800 patients at its peak, now reborn as Ohio University's 'The Ridges' mixed-use campus.

subject: Athens Towers
summary: A 103-metre modernist landmark in Ampelokipi, Athens Tower 1 has been the tallest building in Greece for more than half a century.

story.title: Athletics at the 1896 Summer Olympics – Men's 100 Metres

subject: Athletics at the 1896 Summer Olympics
summary: On 6 April 1896, at the Panathenaic Stadium in Athens, the very first race of the modern Olympic era was run — a 100-metre sprint that produced a winner nobody expected and a finish nobody could separate.

story.title: Atlanta: The City Too Busy to Hate

subject: Atlanta
summary: The Phoenix of the South that burned to the ground in 1864 and rose to become the headquarters of Coca-Cola and CNN, the birthplace of Martin Luther King Jr., and the busiest airport on Earth.

story.title: Atlantic City Boardwalk: The First and the Fallen

subject: Atlantic City Boardwalk
summary: The New Jersey shore where America invented the boardwalk, Miss America, and saltwater taffy - a 19th-century resort that rose, fell, gambled its way to a partial resurrection, and still defines seaside kitsch.

subject: Atlantic City Boardwalk
summary: The world's first boardwalk, built in 1870 as a temporary summer fix for hotel owners tired of sand on their carpets, and still the longest and busiest boardwalk in the world.

subject: Atlantic City Convention Center
summary: A half-million-square-foot convention center with a bronze statue of Bert Parks that sings 'There She Is' when you put your head in the crown.

subject: Atlantis (Barquentine)
summary: A Hamburg lightship built to stand still for seventy years now sails the Mediterranean and Baltic under three masts of canvas.

story.title: Atria Institute on Gender Equality and Women's History

subject: Atria Institute on Gender Equality and Women's History
summary: An Amsterdam library where Dutch feminists hid their archive from the Nazis - some of it only came home in 2003.

story.title: Attempted Theft of George Washington's Skull

subject: Attempted theft of George Washington's skull
summary: In 1830, a fired gardener broke into the crumbling Mount Vernon crypt to steal the skull of George Washington, grabbed the wrong one, and inadvertently triggered the construction of the secure tomb that stands today.

subject: Attempts to escape Oflag IV-C
summary: Hermann Göring called Colditz Castle escape-proof; its own guards ended up curating a museum of the forged papers, duplicate keys and bed-sheet ropes that proved him wrong.

subject: Attymass
summary: A small Mayo parish that gave the world Father Patrick Peyton - the "Rosary Priest" who built the Family Rosary Crusade into an international movement - and a stone cottage now standing in the Irish Hunger Memorial in lower Manhattan.

story.title: Auberge Le Saint-Gabriel: North America's First Licensed Inn

subject: Auberge Le Saint-Gabriel
summary: Built as a soldier's house in 1688 and granted the first liquor licence under British rule in 1754, Auberge Le Saint-Gabriel in Old Montreal has survived three centuries of owners, fires, and reinventions to become one of the oldest continuously operating establishments on the continent.

subject: Audubon Ballroom
summary: A lavish 1912 theater in Washington Heights, built by the founder of Fox Film and decorated with terra-cotta foxes in his honor, became the site of Malcolm X's assassination in 1965.

story.title: Augusta Arsenal: From Fever Refuge to College Campus

subject: Augusta Arsenal
summary: A military arsenal established in 1816 on the Savannah River, relocated to a plantation estate to escape deadly fevers, transformed into the Confederacy's munitions powerhouse, and eventually reborn as a university campus.

subject: Augusteum, Oldenburg
summary: Oldenburg built a Florentine palace to show off a Grand Ducal art collection; then in 1919 the abdicated Grand Duke fled to Holland with the best paintings, and the curators have been buying them back ever since.

subject: Aung San Suu Kyi
summary: The house on University Avenue in Yangon where Aung San Suu Kyi spent nearly fifteen years under house arrest became one of the most potent symbols of nonviolent resistance in modern history.

story.title: Auschwitz: The Site of Industrialized Murder

subject: Auschwitz
summary: Where Nazi Germany murdered over 1.1 million people in gas chambers between 1940 and 1945, creating the largest and deadliest concentration camp in history - now preserved as humanity's most solemn memorial.

story.title: Austin: The City That Made Weird a Battle Cry

subject: Austin
summary: The Texas capital where 'Keep Austin Weird' became a rallying cry against homogenization - where bats pour from a bridge at sunset, where Leslie ran for mayor in a thong, and where the live music capital fights to remember what made it worth saving.

story.title: Austin: The Live Music Capital That Keeps Itself Weird

subject: Austin
summary: The Texas capital where a million and a half bats emerge nightly from Congress Avenue Bridge, where South by Southwest transformed from a small music festival into a global phenomenon, and where 'Keep Austin Weird' became both slogan and prayer.

subject: Autostadt
summary: Volkswagen's park beside its Wolfsburg factory, where two 60-metre glass towers hold new cars in the air until their owners arrive to collect them.

subject: Avenida 9 de Julio
summary: A boulevard so wide it can take three green lights to cross on foot - around 110 meters of asphalt long claimed to be the widest avenue in the world, with the Obelisco rising from its heart.

subject: Avenida de Mayo
summary: A slice of Paris and Madrid in the heart of Buenos Aires - a grand boulevard linking the presidential palace to Congress, lined with Art Nouveau domes, a Dante-coded skyscraper, and Argentina's oldest café.

subject: Aviodrome
summary: The Dutch national aviation museum at Lelystad Airport, where a Boeing 747 once traveled by canal barge and a 1928 airport terminal stands rebuilt from scratch.

subject: Awe Hydro-Electric Scheme
summary: To build the UK's first major pumped-storage power station, engineers carved a cavern the size of a cathedral inside Ben Cruachan - and discovered, mid-excavation, that the granite was wrong.

subject: Azougui
summary: A ruined desert fortress on Mauritania's Adrar Plateau, Azougui was the first capital of the Almoravids, the Saharan movement that went on to rule from Ghana to Spain.

subject: Aztec Brewing Company
summary: Founded in Mexicali during Prohibition by San Diego businessmen who needed to be somewhere legal, Aztec Brewing Company is the only brewery in history to move from Mexico to the United States.

subject: Baalbek
summary: Home to the largest Roman temple complex ever built, Baalbek in Lebanon's Beqaa Valley contains stones so massive that engineers still debate how ancient builders moved them, and ruins so magnificent that UNESCO called them among the finest examples of Imperial Roman architecture.

subject: Bab al-Azizia
summary: Gaddafi's fortified compound in Tripoli -- equal parts military base, personal palace, and political theater -- endured bombings, a coup attempt, and a civil war before the people it was built to control tore it apart.

subject: Bad Bentheim
summary: A castle of honey-colored sandstone stands on a hill so visible from the surrounding plain that medieval travelers could see it from miles away - and the stone itself shipped out to build Amsterdam's Royal Palace.

subject: Badagry
summary: Founded in the fifteenth century on a lagoon off the Gulf of Guinea, Badagry became one of West Africa's most significant slave ports before reinventing itself as the site of Nigeria's first church, first school, and first encounter with Christianity.

story.title: Badlands: The Land Too Poor to Farm, Too Beautiful to Ignore

subject: Badlands
summary: The South Dakota landscape where 75 million years of geological history lie exposed in eroded spires and striped formations - a terrain French trappers called 'bad lands to cross,' now a national park revealing ancient seas, vanished forests, and species that no longer exist.

subject: Baimai Springs
summary: A cluster of artesian karst springs in Shandong that inspired one of China's greatest poets and still bubbles up through the courtyard of an ancient temple.

subject: Bala Hissar, Peshawar
summary: A fortress on a high mound in Peshawar that has been fought over by Buddhists, Mughals, Afghans, Marathas, Sikhs, and the British -- and still serves as a military headquarters today.

subject: Balay Negrense
summary: The first museum in Negros Occidental preserves the ancestral home of a French-descended sugar baron, a window into the opulent world of the Philippine sugar industry's golden age.

subject: Balclutha (1886)
summary: A steel-hulled full-rigged ship that rounded Cape Horn seventeen times, the Balclutha is one of the finest preserved sailing ships in America — temporarily berthed at Mare Island while her San Francisco berth at Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.

subject: Baliqiao
summary: Eight li from the old imperial boundary of Beijing, a marble bridge once marked the point where emperors changed out of their robes for travel -- and where, in 1860, an Anglo-French army shattered China's defenses and opened the road to the capital.

subject: Ballabeg, Lonan
summary: When workers built the Manx Electric Railway through this Laxey Bay hamlet in 1894, they unearthed an ancient Celtic chapel and a graveyard of triple-stacked lintel graves.

subject: Ballast Point Whaling Station
summary: Built in 1858 on the tip of Point Loma, the Ballast Point Whaling Station processed California gray whales until petroleum made whale oil obsolete — then became a fort, then a lighthouse, then a submarine base.

subject: Ballinskelligs
summary: An Irish-speaking township at the edge of the Atlantic, where a sixteenth-century pirate castle, a transatlantic telegraph cable, and an artists' colony all left their marks on the same small bay.

subject: Bally's Atlantic City
summary: The casino that sits at Park Place and the Boardwalk - the two squares on the Monopoly board - built on the rubble of the demolished Marlborough-Blenheim Hotel.

subject: Ballycotton Lifeboat Station
summary: Patrick Sliney and his crew spent 49 hours at sea in a hurricane to save the eight men of the Daunt Rock lightship - one of the most decorated rescues in the history of the lifeboat service.

subject: Ballyfin
summary: A 600-acre Laois demesne with a thirty-acre lake, an Alhambra-inspired floor, and a 1820s neo-classical mansion that took nine years to restore - longer than to build.

subject: Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art
summary: A converted 1950s flour mill on the south bank of the Tyne that became one of Europe's largest contemporary art galleries, with no permanent collection and a deliberate refusal to settle.

subject: Bamfield Marine Sciences Centre
summary: A world-class marine research station housed in the concrete ruins of a Victorian-era telegraph cable station on Barkley Sound.

subject: Banda Neira
summary: The administrative heart of the Banda Islands has served as a spice trading hub, a colonial stronghold, a political prison for Indonesian independence leaders, and today an improbable tropical getaway where crumbling forts overlook some of the clearest water in the world.

subject: Banganarti
summary: A medieval Nubian pilgrim church where 1,000 graffiti inscriptions on the walls record the prayers of Christian travelers across seven centuries.

subject: Bankalar Caddesi
summary: A single short street in Istanbul's Galata quarter once housed the Ottoman Central Bank, the stock exchange, and the grandest financial institutions of a dying empire — and Henri Cartier-Bresson photographed its staircase.

story.title: Banshu Kiyomizu-dera: The Other Clear Water Temple

subject: Banshū Kiyomizu-dera
summary: Overshadowed by its famous Kyoto namesake, this Tendai temple in the hills of Hyogo Prefecture holds National Important Cultural Properties from the Nara and Heian periods and a founding legend involving a flying monk from India.

subject: Barbican Estate
summary: Two thousand flats stacked into one of London's most uncompromising brutalist landscapes, built on a Roman fort, a medieval Jewish cemetery, and a Blitz-flattened ward.

subject: Barcelona Royal Shipyard
summary: Seven centuries of Gothic arches sheltered the galleys of the Aragonese armada, including the flagship that fought at Lepanto, before becoming Barcelona's maritime museum.

subject: Barclodiad y Gawres
summary: A 5,000-year-old passage tomb on Anglesey's wild south-west coast, decorated with the same spirals and zigzags that mark Ireland's Boyne Valley graves across the water.

subject: Bareq
summary: A fertile governorate in Asir where the last pre-Islamic market once stood - now a winter resort of 500 villages and 60,000 speakers of its own Arabic dialect.

subject: Bargebur
summary: A 500-resident quarter of Norden in East Frisia that exists because seventeenth-century townspeople refused to let the Reformed Christians build a church inside their walls.

subject: Barkly Tableland
summary: A treeless sea of golden grass the size of a small nation, where two sealed highways cross some of the loneliest and best cattle country in Australia.

subject: Barnwell Priory
summary: Founded in 1092 because a sheriff's wife made a vow during a serious illness and recovered, Barnwell Priory grew to house 30 Augustinian canons on the eastern edge of Cambridge — and may have quietly helped a new university find its feet.

subject: Barony of Akova
summary: One of the twelve great Frankish baronies of the Morea, Akova — whose very castle name meant 'kill-Greek' — presided over the Arcadian highlands for a century before dynastic chaos delivered it to the Byzantines.

subject: Barony of Karytaina
summary: The Barony of Karytaina was the most strategically vital Frankish fiefdom in medieval Greece — a mountainous domain in Arcadia that controlled the gateway to the entire central Peloponnese.

subject: Barony of Passavant
summary: A French knight named John de Nully built a fortress in the mountains guarding the entrance to the wild Mani Peninsula shortly after 1220, gave it a name that echoes a battle cry — 'passe avant,' go forward — and created the last and most strategically peculiar of the twelve Frankish baronies of the Principality of Achaea.

subject: Barpa Langass
summary: A five-thousand-year-old chambered cairn on North Uist, still standing on the slope of Ben Langass with two massive roof slabs and one chamber you can still crawl into.

subject: Barra
summary: A thirteen-mile coastal loop, a castle in a bay, a beach that doubles as a runway, and around twelve hundred people who keep Gaelic alive at the southern tip of the Outer Hebrides.

subject: Barra
summary: An island of Vikings, pirates, and beach-landed aircraft, where a 2,500 BC pottery beaker turned up under a road and the MacNeil clan still leases its medieval castle to the nation for one pound and a bottle of whisky a year.

subject: Bartholomew Ledges Wreck
summary: Spanish lead ingots, silver coins struck between 1474 and 1555, and a stolen English church bell rest together on the floor of St Mary's Sound - the riddle of a ship that may have sailed with the second Armada.

story.title: Barton Academy: Alabama's First Public School and Its Long Second Act

subject: Barton Academy
summary: A Greek Revival masterpiece on Government Street in Mobile that opened in 1839 as Alabama's first public school, nearly fell to neglect, and was restored with $14 million to reopen in 2021.

subject: Basketmakers' Kiosk
summary: The only surviving pavilion from a vanished row of Ottoman pleasure palaces, the Basketmakers' Kiosk stands at the tip of the Golden Horn — named for the Roma basketmakers who once sold their wares in its shadow.

subject: Basking Ridge white oak
summary: For more than 600 years, a white oak in the churchyard of the Presbyterian Church in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, witnessed the Great Awakening, the American Revolution, and the march of centuries before dying quietly in 2016.

subject: Bass Rock
summary: A 340-million-year-old volcanic plug in the Firth of Forth, home to the world's largest northern gannet colony and once a notorious Covenanter prison.

subject: Bass Strait
summary: The shallow, storm-battered channel between Tasmania and mainland Australia has swallowed hundreds of ships, drowned an ancient land bridge, and become one of the country's richest energy basins.

subject: Bassae
summary: The Temple of Apollo Epikourios at Bassae — designed by Iktinos, architect of the Parthenon, and built at 1,131 meters in the Arcadian mountains — became the first Greek site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986, and is now sheltered under a vast protective tent.

subject: Bastei
summary: A sandstone bastion above the Elbe where a butcher sold brandy before anyone built a bridge, and where seven stone arches have carried walkers over a forty-metre ravine since 1851.

subject: Baths of Zeuxippus
summary: Between the Hippodrome and Hagia Sophia, the Baths of Zeuxippus once displayed over eighty marble statues of Homer, Plato, and Julius Caesar — a gallery of the ancient world's greatest minds, open to any citizen who could pay the modest entrance fee.

subject: Battery Chamberlin
summary: A coastal artillery battery in the Presidio with a restored disappearing gun that once guarded the Golden Gate, Battery Chamberlin demonstrates Endicott-era coastal defense technology at the edge of the Pacific.

subject: Battlebox
summary: A bomb-proof bunker buried under Singapore's Fort Canning Hill where the British decision to surrender to the Japanese was made on 15 February 1942, lost for decades, and rediscovered by a journalist in 1988.

subject: Battles of Latrun (1948)
summary: Five failed Israeli assaults on a Jordanian-held fortress between May and July 1948 became one of the most contested chapters of Israel's founding myth, marked by the desperate improvisation of the Burma Road that saved besieged Jerusalem.

subject: Battles of Wenden (1577–1578)
summary: Across two years of besieging, sacking, and recapturing the same Latvian fortress, the long Livonian War tipped against Ivan the Terrible — and a small Swedish-Polish-Lithuanian force at Wenden in October 1578 marked the moment the tide turned.

subject: Bauhaus
summary: A German art school that lasted fourteen years, moved three cities, was shut down by its own faculty in 1933 - and rearranged how the twentieth century looked.

subject: Bauhaus Dessau
summary: Gropius put a three-storey glass wall where a facade should be, the building ran hot in summer and cold in winter, and modern architecture never went back.

subject: Baumwollspinnerei Ermen & Engels
summary: A cotton mill on the Agger river where Friedrich Engels learned the family business - and where the contradictions of industrial Europe were close enough to touch.

subject: Bautzen II
summary: The only prison in East Germany run directly by the Stasi, where the state held the people whose offence was disagreement - preserved since 1993 exactly as it was, and free to walk into.

subject: Bayezid II Hamam
summary: Built as part of Sultan Bayezid II's imperial complex between 1500 and 1505, this great bathhouse on the old Byzantine road through Istanbul is now a museum of Turkish bath culture—and still shows the bones of Byzantine churches beneath its floors.

subject: Beaconsfield Station Sheep Wash
summary: The ruins of an 1890s steam-powered sheep wash near Ilfracombe, where outback graziers tried to industrialize an ancient task before the technology rendered itself obsolete.

subject: Beaufort Historic Site
summary: Nine 18th- and 19th-century buildings in Beaufort, North Carolina that include the home of a Confederate spy, the oldest wood-framed courthouse in the state, and a jail that held prisoners until 1954.

subject: Beauly Priory
summary: The Valliscaulian monks who founded Beauly Priory around 1230 gave it a French name meaning 'beautiful place' -- and John Keats, visiting six centuries later, found skulls in its ruins and turned them into poetry.

subject: Bebelplatz
summary: An eighteenth-century Berlin square ringed by opera house, cathedral and library, whose most important feature is an empty white room buried under the cobblestones.

subject: Beehive (New Zealand)
summary: Wellington's iconic circular parliament building, designed by a Scottish architect and shaped like a traditional woven skep, houses New Zealand's executive government behind copper-clad walls and wedge-shaped rooms.

subject: Beidaihe, Qinhuangdao
summary: China's 'smoke-filled room' -- the seaside resort where Communist Party leaders have retreated each summer to plot strategy, write poetry, and occasionally flee for their lives.

subject: Beijing Guozijian
summary: For six centuries, China's highest-ranking scholars walked through the Glazed Archway of the Beijing Guozijian -- the Imperial Academy where emperors themselves lectured on the Confucian classics, and which is now the ancestor of Peking University.

subject: Belgrano, Buenos Aires
summary: A leafy, upper-middle-class barrio in northern Buenos Aires that was briefly the capital of Argentina in 1880, where English-style mansions, a compact Chinatown, museums, and a round church share streets named for the man who designed the national flag.

subject: Bellacorick
summary: A bog townland in north Mayo with a Musical Bridge that a seventeenth-century prophet said would never be finished, Ireland's first commercial wind farm, and the demolished chimney of a peat power station that was once the area's biggest landmark.

subject: Belle Grove Plantation (Middletown, Virginia)
summary: Thomas Jefferson shaped its design, James Madison honeymooned on its grounds, a Civil War general died within its walls, and for more than two centuries the limestone manor house in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley has quietly witnessed American history.

subject: Belle Isle (Richmond, Virginia)
summary: A 54-acre island in the James River that has been Powhatan homeland, colonial fishery, nail factory, Civil War prison camp for 30,000 Union soldiers, hydroelectric plant, and urban nature park -- all within sight of Richmond's skyline.

subject: Bellevue
summary: Seattle's tech-powered sibling across Lake Washington, where the world's largest floating bridge delivers commuters to a skyline that didn't exist a generation ago.

subject: Bellows Air Force Station
summary: A former World War II airfield on Oahu's windward coast that traded its runways for beachfront cabins, becoming an unlikely military recreation area where a hidden Japanese cemetery and ongoing Hawaiian land restoration quietly complicate the palm-tree scenery.

story.title: The Belvedere: A General's Trophy Case Turned Art Shrine

subject: Belvedere, Vienna
summary: Built as a summer residence for Prince Eugene of Savoy, the military genius who broke Ottoman power at Vienna, the Belvedere's two Baroque palaces now house Gustav Klimt's 'The Kiss' and one of Europe's finest art collections.

subject: Belém
summary: The metropolis at the mouth of the Amazon: a 1616 Portuguese fort that grew rich on rubber, feeds Brazil's largest religious procession, and hosted the first climate summit ever held in the rainforest.

subject: Bema of Phaidros
summary: A Roman stage front in the world's oldest theater, carved with the life of the wine god and reassembled from older marble that no longer fit.

subject: Ben Nevis
summary: The highest mountain in the British Isles is not a peak at all but a ruined volcano, its summit a stony plateau where the remains of a Victorian observatory still stand in cloud and wind.

subject: Bendegó Meteorite
summary: A 5,360-kilogram block of iron that fell in the Bahian sertão, defeated an ox cart in 1785, crossed the caatinga on relaid rails over 277 days, and walked out of the 2018 National Museum fire without serious damage.

subject: Bendlerblock
summary: A Berlin office block where German officers ran the 20 July 1944 plot against Hitler, were shot in its courtyard the same night, and are now remembered in the building where they died.

subject: Benelux
summary: Three exiled governments signed the agreement that became the Benelux in a London townhouse in 1944, while their countries were still occupied — building a customs union for a peace that didn't yet exist.

subject: Beng Mealea
summary: Forty kilometres east of Angkor stands a temple with Angkor Wat's own floor plan and none of its restoration - a collapsed, root-bound ruin that stayed closed to the world until the mines came out of the ground in 2003.

subject: Benguela
summary: Founded by the Portuguese in 1617 and connected to Africa's copper heartland by a famous railway, Benguela spent centuries as Angola's gateway to the interior before civil war severed its lifeline and left it rebuilding from the coast inward.

story.title: Benicia Arsenal: From Camels to Canvas

subject: Benicia Arsenal
summary: For over a century, the Benicia Arsenal armed every American war from the Civil War to Korea -- and once stabled camels for the U.S. Army. Today, its sandstone buildings house artists instead of ammunition.

subject: Benissa
summary: One of the oldest towns on the Costa Blanca, where a Neo-Gothic church too grand for its size crowns a preserved medieval centre 254 metres above a coast of hidden coves.

subject: Bentley Priory
summary: A Sir John Soane country house that hosted Pitt and Wellington, sheltered the dying Queen Adelaide, then became the nerve centre from which Hugh Dowding directed the Battle of Britain.

story.title: Bento Gonçalves, Rio Grande do Sul

subject: Bento Gonçalves, Rio Grande do Sul
summary: A wooden cross at a lonely crossroads gave this place its first name; today its hillsides hold the vineyards that made it the wine capital of Brazil.

subject: Beomeosa
summary: A 1,300-year-old Buddhist temple on Busan's Mount Geumjeongsan, named for a golden fish from heaven and renowned as one of Korea's three great southeastern temples.

subject: Berenice Troglodytica
summary: An ancient Red Sea port that began as a harbor for war elephants and became Rome's gateway to the riches of India.

subject: Bergen
summary: Where Hanseatic wooden warehouses line the wharf and rain falls 270 days a year, where Norway's gateway to the fjords has traded for a millennium.

subject: Berkeley Plantation
summary: A Virginia plantation on the James River where settlers held Thanksgiving two years before Plymouth, two presidents were born, Taps was first played, and a Confederate cannonball still sits embedded in the guest house wall.

subject: Berlin Anhalter Bahnhof
summary: Once Continental Europe's largest railway terminus and Berlin's gateway to Rome, Vienna and Athens, the Anhalter Bahnhof was demolished in three days in 1960, leaving a fragment of façade standing alone in an empty square.

subject: Berlin Conference
summary: From November 1884 to February 1885, fourteen governments met at a building on Wilhelmstrasse to set the rules for the partition of Africa. No African was invited, and the one African ruler who asked to attend was refused.

subject: Berlin Victory Column
summary: A monument to three Prussian wars that the Nazis made taller, the French wanted demolished, and Berliners eventually turned into a meeting point for the Love Parade and the Pride march.

subject: Berliner Ensemble
summary: Brecht's greatest hit premiered in this theatre in 1928. He did not get the keys to it for another twenty-six years.

subject: Beverley Minster
summary: A Gothic masterpiece built on the bones of an 8th-century saint, larger than a third of England's cathedrals, that survived the Dissolution by demoting itself to parish church and then nearly fell down on its own.

subject: Beverly Hills Oil Field
summary: Below the manicured lawns and designer storefronts of Beverly Hills lies one of California's richest urban oil fields, discovered in 1900 and still producing today from four hidden 'drilling islands' — including one on the grounds of Beverly Hills High School.

subject: Bexley Station
summary: A working sheep station north of Longreach whose history is written in extremes: fire, flood, a homestead full of snakes, and the steady grind of producing wool on the outback plains.

subject: Beyazıt Square
summary: Officially named Freedom Square, Beyazıt is Istanbul's oldest public plaza — the site of the Byzantine Forum of Theodosius, flanked by an Ottoman imperial mosque, a grand university gate, and centuries of contested history.

subject: Bhismaknagar
summary: A vast medieval fortress hidden in the forests of Arunachal Pradesh, Bhismaknagar was the capital of the Chutia Kingdom and remains one of northeastern India's most significant archaeological sites.

subject: Bibi Ka Maqbara
summary: The Taj Mahal's lesser-known twin in the Deccan - a mausoleum built on a shoestring budget by the son of the man who helped build the Taj, for the wife of an emperor who forbade extravagance.

subject: Bibliotheca Rosenthaliana
summary: How a Hanover rabbi's private library survived being offered to Bismarck, the Nazi looting machine, and the bureaucratic indifference of two centuries.

subject: Big Air Shougang
summary: The world's first permanent big air venue rises from the ruins of a shuttered steel mill in western Beijing, its Olympic ski ramp framed by decommissioned cooling towers in one of sport's most surreal backdrops.

subject: Big Ben
summary: A bell that cracked twice, a tower that leans, and a clock that is corrected by adding pennies to the pendulum.

subject: Big Hole
summary: A 463-meter-wide pit in the South African veld where 50,000 miners once dug for diamonds by hand, leaving behind a scar so vast it became the country's most famous monument to obsession.

subject: Bilbao (Mesoamerican site)
summary: Hidden beneath sugarcane fields on Guatemala's Pacific coastal plain, Bilbao was a major center of the Cotzumalhuapa culture where ballgame rituals, monumental sculpture, and Mexican-influenced art thrived in the shadow of one of the world's most active volcanoes.

subject: Bilderberg Meeting
summary: An annual private conference of around 150 European and North American leaders, born in 1954 at a quiet Dutch hotel west of Arnhem and named for the woods around it.

subject: Biltmore Estate
summary: America's largest privately owned house, a 250-room French Renaissance chateau built by George Vanderbilt in the North Carolina mountains, which once sheltered priceless art from the National Gallery during World War II.

subject: Binham Priory
summary: Founded by a Norman lord in 1091, Binham Priory contains England's earliest example of Gothic bar tracery — predating Westminster Abbey by a decade — and a history that English Heritage describes as 'almost continuous scandal.'

subject: Binnenhof
summary: The oldest parliament building in the world still in use began as a 13th-century hunting lodge - and twice in its eight centuries, it was nearly demolished by its own government.

subject: Biomuseo
summary: Frank Gehry's first building in Latin America sits at the mouth of the Panama Canal, telling the story of how a narrow strip of land changed the biology of two continents.

story.title: Bird Girl: The Statue That Became an Accidental Icon

subject: Bird Girl
summary: A small bronze sculpture spent decades unnoticed in a Savannah cemetery before a single photograph turned it into one of the most recognizable images in American publishing.

subject: Birmingham Civil Rights District
summary: Six blocks in downtown Birmingham where children marched, fire hoses turned, a church was bombed, and the conscience of a nation was forced awake - now preserved as a National Monument.

story.title: Birth of the New World: The Statue Nobody Wanted

subject: Birth of the New World
summary: A 360-foot bronze Columbus statue rejected by five American cities wandered for 25 years before landing on Puerto Rico's coast - where it became both the tallest sculpture in the Western Hemisphere and a lightning rod for debate over whose history deserves a monument.

subject: Birthplace of Anton Chekhov
summary: One of the giants of world literature entered life in a whitewashed cottage smaller than many living rooms - and Taganrog has kept it exactly so.

subject: Birthplace of Simón Bolívar
summary: A seventeenth-century colonial house in Caracas where Latin America's great liberator was born in 1783, now a museum covered in heroic murals by painter Tito Salas.

subject: Bishop Rock
summary: A 49-metre granite tower on the world's smallest island with a building - the lighthouse the Atlantic tried to shake apart, twice.

subject: Bishopscourt, Isle of Man
summary: A castellated palace where the Bishops of Sodor and Man lived for centuries, Bishopscourt now sits at the sixteenth milestone of the TT course - sacred ground turned racing landmark.

subject: Björklinge runestones
summary: Five Viking Age memorial stones stand at a Swedish church, including one raised by a grieving mother for her son who died in Hedeby, the great Danish trading center that would soon be abandoned to war.

subject: Black Heath
summary: A Virginia coal estate whose mines heated the White House, killed dozens of enslaved workers, made the Heth family rich, and ultimately swallowed the mansion that sat above them.

subject: Blackall, Queensland
summary: On the Barcoo River, where a gun shearer set a record that still stands and a stump on the school grounds marks the edge of the known world, Blackall is the heart of Queensland's wool country.

subject: Blackpool
summary: A Lancashire seaside resort built on a peat-stained pool, the wakes weeks, the world's second-oldest tramway, and an enduring talent for refusing to take itself too seriously.

subject: Blairgowrie and Rattray
summary: A twin burgh at the foot of the Grampians, the soft-fruit capital of Scotland and the southern gateway to the Cairngorms Snow Road.

subject: Blarney Stone
summary: A block of Carboniferous limestone set into Blarney Castle's battlements in 1446 that supposedly grants the gift of eloquent speech to anyone who kisses it.

subject: Blaue Balje
summary: A North Sea tidal channel whose moving floor swallowed the East Pier of Wangerooge, and where the pier's wooden stumps still surface at low tide.

subject: Blockhouse No. 1
summary: The oldest structure originally built within Central Park, this War of 1812 fort sits on a rocky outcrop in the North Woods, a forgotten defensive post turned picturesque ruin whose commemorative plaques keep getting stolen.

subject: Blood Road
summary: A road in Nordland built by Yugoslav, Polish, and Soviet prisoners of war under German occupation from 1942 to 1945, named for a cross painted in a slain prisoner's blood by his brother.

subject: Bloomingdale Insane Asylum
summary: The asylum that stood where Columbia University now rises was once the only facility for mentally ill patients in New York State, a place of elegant gardens and therapeutic farming that an undercover journalist exposed for holding sane people against their will.

subject: Bloomsbury
summary: The intellectual heart of London - a grid of Georgian squares laid out by the Dukes of Bedford, home to the British Museum, University College London, and the writers who gave their name to the Bloomsbury Group.

subject: Blue Oak Ranch Reserve
summary: A 3,260-acre University of California natural reserve in the hills above San Jose, protecting blue oak woodland and grassland ecosystems used for ecological research at the edge of the Diablo Range.

subject: Bluestonehenge
summary: An invisible second henge a mile from Stonehenge, discovered in 2009 at the end of the avenue where the River Avon meets the processional route, possibly a cremation gateway between worlds.

story.title: Bockscar: The B-29 That Dropped the Last Atomic Bomb

subject: Bockscar
summary: The Boeing B-29 Superfortress that dropped the Fat Man atomic bomb on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945, now stands silently in a Dayton museum - a pun-named airplane that flew the most consequential mission of the twentieth century on borrowed fuel and borrowed time.

subject: Boconnoc
summary: A 96-soul Cornish parish where a diamond bought an estate, a fire claimed a mansion, and ancient oaks shelter one of Europe's most important lichen colonies.

subject: Bodai-ji
summary: Perched 395 meters up on the south slope of Mount Tokozan near Sanda, this Shingon temple served as a 14-year retreat for the cloistered Emperor Kazan, who followed a mysterious light to its door around 992 AD.

subject: Bodega Catena Zapata
summary: A Mayan-style stone pyramid rises from the Mendoza vineyards, built by the family that bet Argentine Malbec could be world-class - and proved it by planting grapes higher than almost anyone thought possible.

subject: Bodrum
summary: Where Turkey's St. Tropez meets ancient Halicarnassus, where the Mausoleum once amazed and yachts now anchor, where Aegean glamour finds Turkish expression.

subject: Boeing Field
summary: Seattle's original commercial airport, built in 1928 from Duwamish River dredge material, evolved from a barnstorming airstrip into a critical hub for Boeing test flights, cargo operations, and the Museum of Flight.

subject: Bogdan Saray
summary: A tiny Byzantine chapel buried in the Fatih hillside held the diplomatic secrets of the Moldavian princes who used it as their Istanbul embassy church for centuries.

subject: Bohai Sea
summary: China's inland sea, a shallow gulf that has served as the maritime gateway to Beijing for millennia, witnessing imperial trade, decisive naval battles, and an ambitious plan for the world's longest undersea tunnel.

subject: Bokor Hill Station
summary: A French colonial pleasure resort built on a Cambodian mountaintop at enormous cost in Cambodian lives, abandoned twice, held by the Khmer Rouge into the 1990s, and now rebuilt as a casino resort.

subject: Boké
summary: A river port in Lower Guinea where a colonial-era fort, once a slave-trading stronghold, now houses a museum that confronts the dark history of the Rio Nunez.

subject: Boland's Mills
summary: A flour mill where Eamon de Valera raised the rebel flag during the 1916 Easter Rising is now a Google campus with affordable housing for nurses and teachers -- Dublin's docklands in a single address.

subject: Bolivarian National Intelligence Service
summary: Venezuela's secret police force, SEBIN, operates from a repurposed modernist landmark and an underground prison known as 'The Tomb,' enforcing political control through surveillance, intimidation, and documented torture.

subject: Bolton Priory
summary: Augustinian canons have worshipped at Bolton Priory since 1154, and worship continues today in the surviving nave -- one of England's most beautiful examples of a monastic church that outlived the Dissolution.

subject: Bombardment of Qui Nhơn
summary: A chance encounter in 1861 — an American warship searching for missing sailors, a Vietnamese fort with guns at the ready — set off a brief but violent collision on the coast of central Vietnam.

subject: Bonnie and Clyde Ambush Site
summary: Where the outlaws died - the Louisiana backroad where lawmen riddled Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow with 130 bullets on May 23, 1934, ending their crime spree and creating Depression-era legends.

subject: Booker T. Washington Community Center
summary: An Art Deco brick high school in Staunton that served Black students through the Jim Crow era and became one of the few public meeting places African Americans could call their own.

subject: Booloominbah
summary: A vast Gothic mansion built for a pastoral dynasty in the 1880s, crowned by Australia's grandest domestic stained-glass window, and given away to found the nation's first regional university.

subject: Bop City
summary: The after-hours jazz club in a Victorian house that didn't open until 2 AM, where Dizzy Gillespie, Billie Holiday, and Charlie Parker played for a San Francisco that was just learning to swing.

subject: Bopiliao Historic Block
summary: One of Taipei's oldest commercial streets preserves over two centuries of layered architecture -- Qing Dynasty shophouses, Japanese-era plazas, and postwar neglect -- saved from demolition by an elementary school and a gangster movie.

subject: Borgia Apartments
summary: Hidden within the Vatican's Apostolic Palace, the Borgia Apartments preserve frescoes commissioned by one of history's most notorious popes, rooms so tainted by his legacy that his successor refused to set foot in them for centuries.

subject: Borgring
summary: A Viking ring fortress found near Køge in 2014 because it was missing from the map — and still argued over.

subject: Borneo Orangutan Survival
summary: The world's largest primate rescue operation teaches orphaned orangutans how to be wild again, one forest school lesson at a time.

story.title: Borobudur: The Temple That Slept Under Volcanic Ash for 1,000 Years

subject: Borobudur
summary: Where Buddhist pilgrims built the world's largest Buddhist temple in 9th-century Java - then abandoned it to volcanic ash and jungle, only to have it rediscovered by British colonizers in 1814.

subject: Borough Market
summary: London's oldest food market has been selling provisions on the south bank since at least the 12th century — and Parliament had to abolish it in 1754 because it was blocking traffic on London Bridge.

subject: Borremose
summary: A Himmerland bog that held both an Iron Age fortress and three people who were put into the water and never came out.

subject: Bou Inania Madrasa
summary: The only madrasa in Morocco that also functioned as a congregational mosque, built in the 1350s by a Marinid sultan at the peak of his dynasty's artistic achievement -- complete with an elaborate water clock that no one has managed to make work again.

subject: Bouleuterion of Ancient Olympia
summary: Inside the sacred precinct of Olympia, the Bouleuterion was the chamber where every Olympic athlete swore a sacred oath before a fearsome statue of Zeus — the moment where sport became covenant.

subject: Boulevard of Sabana Grande
summary: Once called the Royal Street, Caracas's pedestrian boulevard through Sabana Grande shelters Latin America's most important ornithological collection, modernist architecture, and public sculpture beneath its canopy of trees.

subject: Bourtange moor
summary: Once a 3,000-square-kilometer bog straddling the Dutch-German border — the largest in northwest Europe — drained over four centuries for fuel, farmland, and military advantage, with a handful of preserved Iron Age corpses and one star-shaped fortress to remind us what it used to be.

subject: Bowser, British Columbia
summary: A small Vancouver Island highway community named for a one-year premier, best remembered for the 1930s hotel dog who carried beer to tables and made change.

subject: Boydell Shakespeare Gallery
summary: A Pall Mall gallery that tried to forge a national school of English painting through Shakespeare, bankrupted its founder, and gave the architectural world the Ammonite Order.

subject: Bozo language
summary: The tonal Mande tongue of the Niger's renowned fisher-people, whose name means 'house of straw' and whose dialects map the bends of the Inner Delta.

subject: Bradda Head
summary: A 382-foot headland above Port Erin where a Liverpool safe-maker's friends built him a memorial tower shaped like a key and lock, paying back his quiet philanthropy in stone.

subject: Braddan
summary: An elongated Manx parish named for an Irish saint of voyagers, stretching from uninhabited mountains to the original Fairy Bridge.

subject: Brancaster
summary: A Roman fort, a tidal golf course, a shipwreck used by the RAF for target practice, and a stretch of north Norfolk coast where the British space programme was once nearly born.

subject: Brandenburg Euthanasia Centre
summary: In a converted shed behind a disused prison in Brandenburg an der Havel, 9,772 disabled and mentally ill people were murdered in nine months of 1940 — the first purpose-built gas chamber in Germany, and the place where the method was worked out.

subject: Brandtaucher
summary: Wilhelm Bauer's 1850 submarine sank on its acceptance trial in Kiel harbour; the three men trapped inside escaped by deliberately flooding the hull, and the boat now sits in a Dresden museum.

subject: Brantwood
summary: John Ruskin's last home above Coniston Water, a Grade II*-listed house full of his books, his shells, and the wallpaper he designed himself.

subject: Brauron
summary: Every four years, young Athenian girls put on saffron robes at this quiet coastal sanctuary on the eastern shore of Attica and became, for a time, bears — initiates of Artemis, learning what it meant to cross the threshold into womanhood in ancient Greece.

subject: Brauroneion
summary: A small, oddly shaped sanctuary on the Acropolis where Athenian mothers draped clothing over a wooden goddess and young girls once played the bear.

subject: Bray, County Wicklow
summary: James Joyce, Arthur Conan Doyle, Sheridan Le Fanu, Sinead O'Connor and the Olympic boxer Katie Taylor all lived in this Victorian seaside resort on the southern edge of the Pale, where Ireland's oldest railway terminated in 1854 and Ireland's oldest film studio opened in 1958.

subject: Brazilian National Congress
summary: Oscar Niemeyer's twin domes and twin towers - the most iconic building in Brazil's planned capital, and the nation's legislative heart.

subject: Breakers station
summary: A vanished beach resort and rail stop on Washington's Long Beach Peninsula where the 'social center of the summer season' burned, rebuilt, and burned its way through the early 1900s.

subject: Brennan & Geraghtys Store
summary: A Maryborough grocery that closed its doors in 1972 with a century of stock still on the shelves, now a museum of more than 100,000 things nobody threw away.

subject: Brick Academy
summary: A Federal-style schoolhouse in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, the Brick Academy educated future governors, senators, and vice presidential candidates before Princeton even had its current name.

subject: Brick Lane Market
summary: Brick Lane Market grew from a 17th-century farmers' market into a sprawling weekend institution housed inside a Victorian brewery — one of the few places in London where you can buy antique books, Korean tacos, and handmade jewelry on the same Sunday morning.

subject: Bridgetown Priory
summary: Among the most extensive monastic ruins in Ireland, where the Awbeg meets the Blackwater - dissolved by Henry VIII, briefly Edmund Spenser's, and once home to a woman who lived in a tomb with two cats.

subject: Bridlington Priory
summary: The nave of a vanished Augustinian priory survives as a parish church whose last prior was hanged at Tyburn for the Pilgrimage of Grace.

subject: Bridlington Spa
summary: An Art Deco ballroom and Edwardian theatre on the Yorkshire coast that burned down twice, was rebuilt in 52 days, and hosted Oasis's last indoor show.

subject: Brighton Bathing Boxes
summary: A row of candy-colored Victorian beach huts on Port Phillip Bay, where a wooden shed with no power or water can cost as much as a house.

subject: Brisbane Powerhouse
summary: A brick power station that once drove Brisbane's trams now drives its arts scene, with the old machine scars and graffiti left deliberately on the walls.

subject: Bristol Motor Speedway
summary: The Last Great Colosseum - a half-mile concrete bowl in Tennessee that seats 146,000 fans and produces some of the loudest, most violent racing in NASCAR.

subject: Bristol Old Vic
summary: The oldest continually-operating theatre in the English-speaking world, opened in 1766 with a prologue by David Garrick, training ground for Peter O'Toole, Daniel Day-Lewis and Jeremy Irons.

subject: British Film Institute
summary: On the south bank of the Thames sits the world's largest film archive, a brutalist cinema that became a temple for cinephiles, and the slowly-digitising memory of British television.

subject: British Mission in Lhasa
summary: From 1936 to 1950, a small British outpost at Dekyi Lingka in Lhasa served as the unlikely nerve center of Western engagement with Tibet -- securing Everest expedition permits, founding a doomed English school, and witnessing the end of Tibetan independence.

subject: Broad Street, Birmingham
summary: From John Baskerville's eighteenth-century printing house to the Rum Runner nightclub where Duran Duran rehearsed, one Birmingham street keeps reinventing itself.

subject: Broadcroft Quarry
summary: A working Portland stone quarry that supplies London building sites and Commonwealth War Graves headstones, with seven hectares of its old workings now home to a rare butterfly that needs bare earth to survive.

subject: Broadstairs
summary: Dickens wrote David Copperfield in a clifftop house here and called the parish church a petrified haystack.

subject: Brockhole
summary: A Manchester silk merchant's lakeside summer house that became the UK's first national park visitor centre and remains the gateway to Windermere by water.

subject: Broken Circle/Spiral Hill
summary: Robert Smithson's only large earthwork outside the United States sits in a sand quarry near Emmen. He built it in 1971, a year after completing Spiral Jetty in Utah, and asked the Dutch to keep it forever. They have.

subject: Bruce P. Crandall
summary: A University of Washington alumnus and helicopter pilot who flew unarmed into a killing zone during the Battle of Ia Drang in 1965, evacuating over 70 wounded soldiers across more than a dozen flights, earning the Medal of Honor forty-two years later.

subject: Brussels
summary: Where the European Union makes its headquarters and Belgium struggles to stay united, where Art Nouveau flourished and French fries were actually invented, where compromise is the only constant.

subject: Bruunshåb Gamle Papfabrik
summary: A water-powered mill south of Viborg that has been making cardboard on the same machinery since 1920 - first as a factory, and since 1986 as a museum that never stopped production.

subject: Bryan-Bell Farm
summary: A 19th-century plantation near Pollocksville, North Carolina, with a Classical Revival main house and 25 surviving outbuildings that read like a textbook of Southern farm life.

subject: Bryn Celli Ddu
summary: Anglesey's most famous Neolithic tomb - aligned to the midsummer sunrise, built on the site of an older henge, and still in use for solstice ceremonies five thousand years after it was raised.

subject: Bryn Gwyn Stones
summary: Two surviving uprights from what was once a full Neolithic stone circle on Anglesey - the tallest standing stones in Wales, with six of their original companions torn down in the 18th century by treasure-hunters.

subject: Buachaille Etive Mòr
summary: The Great Herdsman of Etive: a pyramid-shaped mountain at the head of Glen Etive whose north-east face is perhaps the most photographed in Scotland.

subject: Bubrah
summary: A 9th-century Buddhist temple whose very name means 'ruins' -- rebuilt after twelve centuries of neglect to guard the southern gate of Java's great Sewu mandala.

subject: Buck's of Woodside
summary: This eccentric Woodside restaurant, decorated with a Statue of Liberty replica and cowboy memorabilia, is where more Silicon Valley deals have been negotiated over pancakes than in any boardroom.

story.title: Buddhist Monuments in the Horyuji Area: The Oldest Wooden Buildings on Earth

subject: Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area
summary: A collection of 48 wooden temple buildings in Nara Prefecture, some dating to the early 7th century, that became Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993 -- the oldest surviving wooden structures anywhere in the world.

subject: Buhen
summary: An Egyptian fortress rebuilt by pharaoh Senusret III, captured by Kushites, recaptured by Egyptians, and finally drowned by the Aswan High Dam.

subject: Bukkō-ji
summary: A medieval Japanese temple whose founder outpreached his own parent organization, built a network of branch temples across western Japan, and was murdered by bandits at the height of his success -- only for his life's work to be absorbed by the very institution he had outshone.

subject: Bulgarian Exarchate
summary: When the Ottoman Empire issued a decree creating an autonomous Bulgarian Orthodox church in 1870, it set off a chain of events that helped forge a modern Bulgarian national identity — and triggered a schism that would last 75 years.

subject: Bulguksa
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage temple on the slopes of Mount Tohamsan housing six National Treasures, including stone pagodas over thirteen centuries old and one of the world's earliest woodblock prints.

subject: Bulla Regia
summary: The Romans of ancient Bulla Regia solved North Africa's brutal heat by building underground, creating subterranean houses with polychrome mosaics so fine they are unsurpassed anywhere on the continent.

subject: Bullenhuser Damm
summary: A bombed-out Hamburg schoolhouse where twenty Jewish children were murdered in April 1945 to hide the evidence of Nazi medical experiments, and where a rose garden now keeps their names.

subject: Bundaberg Rum
summary: Born from a sugar mill's waste problem, Bundaberg's dark rum became one of Australia's most stubbornly loved icons, fronted by a polar bear in the subtropics.

subject: Bunscoill Ghaelgagh
summary: When UNESCO declared the Manx language extinct in 2009, the children of a small primary school in St John's wrote back to ask, politely, what language they were writing in.

subject: Burano
summary: A lagoon island where fishermen's wives invented a lace industry, where every house blazes in government-regulated color, and where Leonardo da Vinci once came shopping.

subject: Buried Alive in Summer
summary: On a July afternoon in 1976, three wealthy young men hijacked a school bus in Chowchilla, California, abducting the driver and 26 children and burying them alive in a quarry -- a crime so brazen and bizarre it reshaped American understanding of childhood trauma.

subject: Burlington Arcade
summary: Built in 1818 to stop people throwing oyster shells over a garden wall — or so the story goes — Burlington Arcade became the world's first modern shopping mall and is still policed by uniformed Beadles enforcing conduct rules written two centuries ago.

subject: Burrator Reservoir
summary: An 1898 granite-faced dam on the southern edge of Dartmoor that still supplies Plymouth's drinking water, photographed in Spielberg's War Horse and beloved of cyclists and fishermen.

subject: Burrell Collection
summary: A shipping magnate's lifelong magpie eye filled a single Glasgow museum with nine thousand objects, from Assyrian sculpture to Degas pastels.

subject: Burry Port
summary: The Carmarthenshire harbour where Amelia Earhart's seaplane Friendship splashed down on 18 June 1928, making her the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air - even though she did not fly the plane herself.

subject: Butrint
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in southern Albania where Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Venetian, and Ottoman ruins stack atop one another on a forested hill above a lagoon.

subject: Butt of Lewis
summary: The northernmost headland of Lewis - claimed to be one of the windiest places in the United Kingdom, marked by a red-brick lighthouse and a natural arch called the Eye of the Butt.

subject: Buttermere
summary: A two-kilometre lake ringed by fells, where Norse legend, Norman war, and a young woman's life all converged at the Fish Inn.

subject: Byodo-In (Hawaii)
summary: A concrete replica of a 900-year-old Japanese temple, built in a Hawaiian valley in 1968 to honor a century of Japanese immigration.

subject: Bytown
summary: Before it became Canada's capital, Ottawa was Bytown -- a rough canal-building camp on the Ottawa River where Irish labourers lived in shanties, timber barons clashed in open warfare, and a lieutenant colonel's joke of a name stuck for nearly thirty years.

subject: Byōdō-in
summary: The only surviving building from the Fujiwara Regent era, Byodo-in's Phoenix Hall was built in 1053 as a vision of paradise on earth -- and nearly a thousand years later, it graces Japan's 10-yen coin and appeared on the 10,000-yen banknote until a 2024 redesign.

subject: Bà Nà Hills
summary: A mountain resort 1,500 meters above Da Nang where French colonists once escaped the coastal heat — and where, since 2013, a cable car longer than five kilometers carries visitors to a hilltop that the Cham once considered sacred.

subject: Büyük Valide Han
summary: Built in 1651 by Kösem Sultan, the largest caravanserai in Istanbul once housed 3,000 merchants in three courtyards, with a Shi'a mosque at its center and a Byzantine tower at its edge.

subject: Büyük Yeni Han
summary: Built for Sultan Mustafa III in 1764, the Büyük Yeni Han is Istanbul's second-largest surviving caravanserai — a grand commercial palace that once hummed with foreign merchants, non-Muslim moneychangers, and the daily negotiations of empire.

subject: CBC Monkstown
summary: The Christian Brothers college that was the first school ever to perform at the Abbey Theatre - the only CBS in Ireland that paid for its boys to play rugby instead of Gaelic football.

subject: CFB Esquimalt
summary: Canada's Pacific naval base began as three wooden hospital huts built for Crimean War casualties who never arrived - and grew into a 41-square-kilometre establishment employing nearly 8,000 people.

subject: Cabedelo
summary: A sandspit eighteen kilometres long and three wide at the mouth of the Paraíba, guarded by a 1580s fortress, working Brazil's closest port to Europe, and stopping every evening for Ravel.

subject: Cabo Froward
summary: The continent of the Americas ends here, on a wind-hammered headland where a 24-meter steel cross marks the last solid ground before the sea takes over.

subject: Cabo da Roca
summary: The westernmost point of mainland Europe, where the Sintra Mountains plunge into the Atlantic and a 1772 lighthouse marks the edge of the Eurasian continent.

subject: Cadillac Ranch
summary: The Texas art installation where ten Cadillacs are buried nose-down in a pasture along Route 66 - covered in decades of spray-paint graffiti, changing daily as visitors add their own marks to the evolving sculpture.

subject: Cadiz Dunes Wilderness
summary: A congressional wilderness area established in 1994 within the Mojave Trails National Monument, where wind-blown sand from the Cadiz dry lake has built dunes across the Cadiz Valley between the Calumet and Old Woman Mountains.

subject: Caer y Twr
summary: An Iron Age hillfort on the summit of Holyhead Mountain -- the highest point on Anglesey -- whose later use included a Roman tower watching the Irish Sea for raiders, and whose foundations of two-thousand-year-old huts still nestle on the slope below.

subject: Caernarfon Mithraeum
summary: A small Roman temple to the bull-slaying god Mithras, discovered by accident under a sewer trench in 1958 - the western frontier outpost of one of the strangest cults of the Roman Empire.

subject: Caesars Atlantic City
summary: The second East Coast casino to open after legalization, built inside a Howard Johnson's Motor Hotel and now wrapped in Roman columns and statues of emperors.

subject: Caesars Superdome
summary: The largest fixed domed structure in the world, where a governor demanded something 'bigger' than the Astrodome and got a stadium that has hosted eight Super Bowls, survived Hurricane Katrina, and once had someone build a scale model entirely out of pennies.

subject: Cafe Batavia
summary: An 1830s colonial building on Jakarta's historic Fatahillah Square has lived as a governor's office, a warehouse, a pilgrim booking agency, and finally a celebrated restaurant where Newsweek once crowned the bar the world's best.

subject: Caferağa Medrese
summary: A 1559 theological college designed by Mimar Sinan in the shadow of Hagia Sophia, now reborn as a living workshop where Istanbul's traditional crafts — calligraphy, ceramics, jewelry — are still made by hand.

subject: Caffe Trieste
summary: The first espresso coffeehouse on the West Coast, Caffe Trieste has served North Beach's artists, writers, and Italian families since 1956.

story.title: Cahaba: Alabama's Capital That Drowned and Disappeared

subject: Cahaba, Alabama
summary: Alabama's first permanent state capital rose at the confluence of two rivers, thrived on cotton wealth, survived a Civil War prison camp, and then simply vanished -- swallowed by floods, abandonment, and time.

subject: Caherdorgan North
summary: An early medieval stone fort overlooking Smerwick Harbour, where five corbelled drystone huts and a ruined chancellor's house mark a layered ecclesiastical landscape.

subject: Cahuilla Band of Indians
summary: A federally recognized Cahuilla tribe who relocated to the Anza Valley in 1875, whose 18,884-acre reservation includes a casino opened in 1996, and whose origin story begins with brothers Mukat and Tamaoit shaping the world.

subject: CaixaForum Madrid
summary: A decommissioned 1900s power station transformed by Herzog and de Meuron into a cultural center that appears to float above the street, topped by a living wall of 15,000 plants.

subject: Cala d'Hort
summary: A modest western Ibiza beach facing the great rock of Es Vedrà, saved from a resort development when one in seven islanders marched in the 'Battle of Cala d'Hort'.

subject: Calabar Carnival
summary: Billed as Africa's biggest street party, the Calabar Carnival transforms the capital of Cross River State every December into a month-long explosion of color, music, and fierce band competition.

subject: Calandbrug
summary: The vertical lift bridge that connected two halves of the world's largest port, until the wind started bullying its ships.

subject: Caldas Novas
summary: The world's largest hydro-thermal resort, where 86 wells pump water from a 600-meter quartzite column beneath the Serra de Caldas plateau in Goias.

subject: Calgary, Mull
summary: A hamlet on Mull's northwest coast whose pale crescent beach and stone pier gave a name to a Canadian metropolis of 1.7 million.

subject: California Institute of Integral Studies
summary: The graduate school where Alan Watts taught, Jack Kerouac hung out, and the founders of Esalen cut their teeth -- all in the name of integrating Eastern and Western philosophy.

subject: California Institute of the Arts
summary: Walt Disney's most unconventional legacy: a radical art school in Santa Clarita that produced the animators, filmmakers, and artists who reshaped American popular culture.

subject: California Jazz Conservatory
summary: The only independent conservatory in America devoted solely to jazz was born in an 1880s house on Shattuck Avenue, where a cafe doubled as a concert hall and a 60-year-old poet laureate enrolled to learn piano.

subject: California Midwinter International Exposition of 1894
summary: San Francisco's answer to Chicago's World's Fair: a six-month spectacle in Golden Gate Park designed to lure freezing Easterners west with sunshine and spectacle.

subject: California Science Center
summary: The California Science Center in Exposition Park, the West Coast's largest hands-on science museum, traces its origins to 1912 and now houses Space Shuttle Endeavour — soon to be displayed vertically in a $425 million building that broke ground in 2022.

subject: Callander
summary: The eastern gateway to Scotland's first national park, where the Lowlands collide with the Highland Boundary Fault and the streets remember Rob Roy.

subject: Callanish II
summary: A satellite stone circle a short walk from the famous main site at Callanish, where Neolithic builders raised standing stones around a burial cairn nearly five thousand years ago.

subject: Callanish IV
summary: A small, never-excavated stone circle on Lewis - a satellite of the famous Callanish Stones, with a cairn at its heart and the peat keeping its secrets.

subject: Callanish Stones
summary: On the Isle of Lewis, a cruciform arrangement of standing stones erected around 2750 BC -- older than Stonehenge -- has outlasted the people who raised them, the peat that buried them, and the centuries that forgot them.

subject: Callanish VIII
summary: Four standing stones arranged in a deliberate semicircle on a cliff edge of Great Bernera, looking across the strait at Lewis - probably the only Neolithic monument in Britain shaped this way.

subject: Callanish X
summary: A ring of seventeen standing stones that mostly stood for only a few centuries before collapsing onto a ridge above the Callanish moor - a Neolithic structural failure that lay buried in peat for thousands of years.

subject: Caloundra Lighthouses
summary: Two lighthouses, seventy years apart, standing side by side on a Sunshine Coast hilltop -- a corrugated-iron tower from 1896 that was carted away, nearly lost, and dramatically rescued, beside the 1968 concrete tower that briefly replaced it and outlived its own usefulness.

story.title: Calumet Air Force Station: Cold War Eyes on the Keweenaw

subject: Calumet Air Force Station
summary: A Cold War radar station perched on Michigan's remote Keweenaw Peninsula spent nearly four decades scanning the skies for Soviet bombers before closing in 1988 -- and was allegedly saved from an earlier shutdown by being the only station to detect a simulated air incursion.

subject: Calumet, Michigan
summary: A former copper boomtown on Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula where grand sandstone churches and a 1,200-seat opera house still stand over miles of empty mine shafts, haunted by the memory of a Christmas Eve tragedy that killed 73 people.

subject: Camino de Santiago
summary: For over a thousand years, pilgrims have walked to the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, making the Camino de Santiago one of only three great pilgrimages of Christendom.

subject: Camminghaslot
summary: A path of white seashells marks the floor plan of a castle that ruled a free island for four centuries before being dismantled for being too expensive to keep.

subject: Camp Boiro
summary: A memorial to the thousands of Guineans imprisoned, starved, and killed at Conakry's most notorious detention camp under Sékou Touré's regime.

subject: Camp Callan
summary: During World War II, the coastal bluffs of Torrey Pines trained 65,000 soldiers to aim anti-aircraft guns at targets they hoped never to see in real life — then became a golf course and a university.

subject: Camp Douglas
summary: Chicago's Civil War prison camp, sometimes called 'the North's Andersonville,' where thousands of Confederate prisoners endured disease, bitter cold, and a death rate of roughly seventeen percent on muddy prairie ground that is now covered by condominiums.

subject: Camp Lawton (Georgia)
summary: Built in 1864 as a 42-acre replacement for the notorious Andersonville prison, Camp Lawton became the largest military prison in the world -- then was abandoned in six weeks as Sherman's army advanced, leaving its horrors buried until archaeologists followed a prisoner's watercolor paintings to rediscover the stockade in 2010.

subject: Camp Lemonnier
summary: A former French Foreign Legion post next to Djibouti's airport became the largest U.S. military base in Africa - and the nerve centre of a drone war that reshaped the Horn of Africa.

subject: Camp Morton
summary: A Civil War prisoner-of-war camp in Indianapolis where cattle stalls became prison barracks, a humane commandant earned the gratitude of his Confederate captives, and 1,700 men never returned home.

subject: Campo Grande
summary: The gateway to the Pantanal and an unlikely foodie capital of central Brazil, where Japanese Okinawan noodle soup meets Paraguayan polka on the brown-soil plateau.

subject: Campo de Cahuenga
summary: In a small adobe near Cahuenga Pass in 1847, a treaty was signed that ended the American conquest of California—and that the state spent decades trying to remember, and then to preserve, before losing the original building entirely.

subject: Camposanto Monumentale
summary: Pisa's Camposanto was built around a shipload of sacred soil from Golgotha and filled with frescoes spanning more area than the Sistine Chapel -- until a single bomb fragment in 1944 set it all on fire.

subject: Canadian Forces Station Ladner
summary: A delta bog filled with hay became a flying school, a bomber university, a Cold War listening post, and finally one of Canada's busiest general aviation airports.

subject: Candi Kalasan
summary: Java's oldest dated Buddhist temple, built in 778 CE to house a towering bronze goddess who has long since vanished, leaving behind walls that once gleamed with diamond plaster.

subject: Candi Sukuh
summary: A pyramid temple on Mount Lawu where fifteenth-century Javanese sculptors carved explicit fertility imagery and mystical kris-forging scenes into the last Hindu sanctuary built before Islam swept Java.

subject: Candida Casa
summary: The White House at Whithorn - Scotland's first Christian church, built by St Ninian in 397 AD while Roman legions still occupied Britain.

subject: Cango Caves
summary: South Africa's most famous subterranean system, where Precambrian limestone has been sculpted into over four kilometers of chambers first used by Stone Age peoples and rediscovered in 1780 by a farmer lowered into a hall the size of a football field.

subject: Cantor Arts Center
summary: Cantor Arts Center (officially Iris and B. Gerald Cantor Center for Visual Arts at Stanford University, previously the Stanford University Museum of A

subject: Cap Trinité
summary: A colossal three-tiered cliff rising over 350 metres from the Saguenay Fjord, Cap Trinite bears both a 9-metre statue hauled up its face in 1881 and an Innu origin story written in stone.

subject: Cap de Cavalleria Ecomuseum
summary: On Menorca's wild northern cape, a small museum hands you the whole windswept landscape as its true collection.

subject: Cap de Formentor
summary: Mallorca's northernmost cliff, where locals say the winds come to meet, guarded by a lighthouse that could only be reached by boat or mule.

subject: Cap de la Nau
summary: The easternmost point of the Valencian Community, a limestone Cape of the Ship pointing toward Formentera, crowned by a lighthouse and undercut by a sea cave reachable only by boat.

subject: Cape Beale Light
summary: An active manned lighthouse guarding the entrance to Barkley Sound since 1874, where keeper's wife Minnie Paterson braved a storm in 1906 to rescue the crew of the wrecked barque Coloma.

subject: Cape Byron Light
summary: Australia's most powerful lighthouse, an eight-ton French lens turning on a bath of mercury at the easternmost edge of the continent, on a headland the Arakwal people call Walgun, the Shoulder.

subject: Cape Capricorn Light
summary: On the very line that names the tropics, a small concrete tower on a wild island headland has guided ships toward the Fitzroy for a century and a half.

subject: Cape Charles Air Force Station
summary: A Cold War radar station and the Coast Artillery fort that came before it, now reclaimed by the marshes of the Eastern Shore of Virginia National Wildlife Refuge.

subject: Cape Cleveland Light
summary: A small timber-and-iron lighthouse from 1879 still marks the rugged headland that guards the way into Townsville's Cleveland Bay.

subject: Cape Collinson
summary: At the easternmost point of Hong Kong Island, a cape named after a Royal Engineers surveyor guards a lighthouse, an ancient rock carving, and a cluster of cemeteries holding the dead of wars fought half a world away.

subject: Cape Cornwall Mine
summary: A failed tin mine whose chimney was kept as a navigation mark, whose ore floors became greenhouses, and whose ruins were bought for the nation by Heinz baked beans.

subject: Cape Eluanbi
summary: The southernmost point of Taiwan's main island, where Paiwan people named the cape after a sail, a fortified lighthouse survived wars and bombardment, and 26 species of terrestrial crabs make it the most biologically diverse land-crab location on Earth.

subject: Cape Fonar
summary: The easternmost point of Crimea takes its name from the fires that have burned here for millennia to guide ships, a wild rocky headland where seabirds wheel and a lighthouse still keeps the ancient promise of light.

subject: Cape Foulwind
summary: Named by James Cook after his ship was blown offshore in 1770, this windswept West Coast headland shelters a fur seal colony, a historic lighthouse, and the ruins of a cement works that once employed 200 people.

subject: Cape Horn
summary: At the storm-lashed southern tip of the Americas, where the Atlantic and Pacific collide, a single dark headland has become both a sailor's ultimate trophy and a memorial to the countless dead.

subject: Cape Inubō
summary: A Pacific headland at Chiba's eastern tip where a legendary dog howled for seven days, a 150-year-old lighthouse holds one of the world's most powerful Fresnel lenses, and three wave-battered rocks became the most recognized film logo in Japanese cinema.

subject: Cape Lookout Coast Guard Station
summary: Built in 1916 to rescue mariners from the deadly shoals reaching ten miles into the Atlantic, the cupola-topped station is now home to college students studying dolphins and sea turtles instead.

subject: Cape May
summary: America's first seaside resort, rebuilt after an 1878 fire into one of the largest collections of Victorian houses anywhere in the country.

subject: Cape Meares
summary: A steep Oregon headland named for a British explorer, where an old-growth Sitka spruce with a 50-foot circumference grows in the shape of an octopus, and a ghost resort lies buried beneath the beach sand to the north.

subject: Cape Meares Light
summary: An iron-plated lighthouse on Oregon's coast that served Tillamook Bay for 73 years, survived decades of salt air and storms, and then fell to two drunk vandals with guns who shattered its irreplaceable 1888 Fresnel lens.

subject: Cape Moreton Light
summary: Queensland's oldest lighthouse, a sandstone tower raised by convict hands in 1857 to turn ships away from the very rocks that sank the Aarhus.

subject: Cape Sant Antoni, Spain
summary: The closest point on mainland Spain to Ibiza, a 170-metre limestone cape where the Montgo meets the sea, layered with chapel, watchtower, and lighthouse and ringed by a marine reserve.

subject: Cape Sounion
summary: At the southernmost tip of Attica, where the Aegean wraps around a limestone headland on three sides, the Temple of Poseidon has watched fleets come and go for 2,500 years — including the one that won at Salamis, and the one carrying Lord Byron.

subject: Cape St. George Light
summary: Three times built, twice toppled by hurricanes, and finally swallowed by the Gulf of Mexico in 2005, the Cape St. George lighthouse was salvaged brick by brick and reconstructed by island volunteers who refused to let it vanish.

subject: Cape Wrath Trail
