summary: Britain's hardest long-distance walk: 200 miles of unmarked Highland wilderness from Fort William to a windswept lighthouse.

subject: Cape d'Or
summary: Named 'Cape of Gold' by French explorers who mistook its copper for precious metal, this Bay of Fundy headland has drawn Mi'kmaq toolmakers, colonial miners, and lighthouse keepers to its basalt cliffs for millennia.

subject: Capel Lligwy
summary: A roofless 12th-century chapel above Lligwy Bay, with a 16th-century burial vault that a fox once dug into - and a fox-rumour that found human bones still inside.

subject: Capela Dourada
summary: Recife's Golden Chapel, built by wealthy Franciscan lay brothers from 1696, is a room where almost no surface was left unglided - and where an anonymous devotee once scratched the faces off the villains in two of its paintings.

subject: Capilla del Cristo
summary: A tiny chapel at the dead end of one of Old San Juan's most photographed streets, built on a legend of a horseback miracle that may never have happened the way anyone remembers it.

subject: Capitulation of Stettin
summary: In October 1806, eight hundred French hussars and two field guns talked a fortress of 5,300 Prussian soldiers and 281 cannon into surrendering without a shot - the most notorious of the collapses that followed Jena.

story.title: Captain Tony's Saloon: The Bar Hemingway Left Behind

subject: Captain Tony's Saloon
summary: The building at 428 Greene Street in Key West has been an icehouse, a morgue, a telegraph station, a cigar factory, a bordello, a speakeasy, Hemingway's favorite bar, and Jimmy Buffett's first stage -- and it is still pouring drinks.

story.title: Captain Vancouver Landing Site on Maui

subject: Captain Vancouver landing site on Maui
summary: A weathered totem pole monument on Maui's south shore marks the spot where Captain George Vancouver reportedly landed in the 1790s, bringing the first cattle to Hawaii and forging a relationship with Kamehameha I that would help shape the kingdom's future.

subject: Capture of Grenada (1779)
summary: A daring French night assault up Hospital Hill seized one of Britain's richest Caribbean colonies in hours - then the victorious admiral's arrogance turned triumph into lasting bitterness.

subject: Capture of Muscat (1552)
summary: When the Ottoman fleet under the legendary cartographer Piri Reis besieged Portuguese Muscat for 18 days in 1552, shattering the fort and taking 60 defenders captive in a contest for control of the Indian Ocean.

subject: Caracol
summary: Hidden in the jungles of western Belize, Caracol was a Maya superpower that defeated mighty Tikal, housed up to 180,000 people, and built a sky-palace that remains the tallest structure in the country.

subject: Carhenge
summary: The Nebraska farmer who built a full-scale replica of Stonehenge using 38 vintage automobiles - spray-painted gray, buried trunk-first, and arranged precisely to match the mysterious British original.

story.title: Carhenge: Stonehenge, But Make It American

subject: Carhenge
summary: The Nebraska roadside attraction where 39 vintage cars replicate Stonehenge - spray-painted gray, buried trunk-down in a prairie field, proving that American folk art responds to ancient mysteries with V8 engines and a total commitment to the bit.

subject: Carhenge
summary: The Nebraska monument built from 38 vintage automobiles arranged exactly like Stonehenge - created by Jim Reinders in 1987 as a memorial to his father and now surrounded by a sculpture garden of car art.

story.title: Carlsbad Caverns: The Underground Cathedral of a Million Bats

subject: Carlsbad Caverns
summary: The New Mexico caves where 400,000 bats spiral from the earth at sunset - where a 16-year-old cowboy followed the flight into darkness and discovered a cathedral beneath the desert, where formations took millions of years to grow, and where the descent still feels like entering another world.

subject: Carnton
summary: A Tennessee plantation house that became a blood-soaked field hospital during the Battle of Franklin, where four Confederate generals' bodies were laid on the back porch and one woman devoted 41 years to tending the dead.

subject: Carolands
summary: A 98-room Gilded Age chateau in Hillsborough designed by France's foremost architect, built by a Pullman heiress, and haunted by abandonment, murder, and a century of near-demolition.

subject: Carolina-Duke Rivalry
summary: Eight miles separate the two campuses; almost a century of basketball games connects them in the most charged rivalry in American college sports.

subject: Carrawburgh
summary: A Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall whose name may mean 'badger holes' and whose most famous discovery was a cave-like temple to a Persian mystery god.

subject: Carreglwyd
summary: A Welsh country house that has belonged to the same descendants for nearly six centuries - and whose family archive is the oldest in northwest Wales.

subject: Carrie Furnaces
summary: The surviving blast furnaces of Pittsburgh's Homestead Steel Works - where two 92-foot iron giants stand amid industrial ruins, monuments to the steel industry that built America and the labor battles that defined it.

subject: Carrollton bus collision
summary: The deadliest drunk driving disaster in American history, a 1988 head-on collision on Interstate 71 that killed 27 people on a church youth group bus and transformed the nation's drunk driving laws.

subject: Carthaginian II
summary: Built in 1920 at the Krupp shipyard in Kiel from steel intended for U-boats, the Carthaginian II served as Lahaina's whaling museum ship for three decades before being deliberately sunk in 2005 to become one of the world's top-rated wreck diving sites.

subject: Cartmel Priory
summary: Saved from Henry VIII's demolition crews by a technicality, Cartmel Priory survives as a medieval church with a tower set at a 45-degree angle and misericords carved with the face of the Green Man.

subject: Cartoixa d'Escaladei
summary: Spain's first Carthusian monastery took its name from a shepherd's vision of angels on a stairway to heaven, planted the vines that became Priorat wine, and burned to ruin in two days in 1835.

subject: Casa Batlló
summary: Gaudí's 'House of Bones' on the Passeig de Gràcia, where a dead dragon sprawls across the roof and no straight line survives.

subject: Casa Loma
summary: A Gothic Revival castle in the heart of Toronto, built by a financier who dreamed too big and lost it all within a decade.

story.title: Casa Na Bolom: House of the Jaguar

subject: Casa Na Bolom
summary: A neoclassical seminary in San Cristobal de las Casas transformed by a Danish archaeologist and a Swiss-German photographer into a museum, hotel, and living bridge between the Lacandon Maya and the outside world - still operating decades after both founders died.

subject: Casa Real de Iloilo
summary: The first provincial capitol building in the Philippines, where a governor was inaugurated by William Howard Taft, another governor was assassinated, and the walls have survived fire, war, and a century of political reinvention.

subject: Casa Rosada
summary: Argentina's presidential palace is painted pink, the story goes, to blend the red and white of two warring factions, and its balcony and walls have absorbed the country's most turbulent history.

subject: Casa da Junta
summary: Porto Alegre's last surviving building from the 1700s has been shuttered by war, dictatorship, and political upheaval more times than almost any structure in Brazil.

subject: Casa de Cultura Mario Quintana
summary: A grand hotel that once hosted presidents fell into decline, and its most famous resident was a poet who paid rent on apartment 217 long after the luxury had faded.

subject: Casa de Ferro
summary: A prefabricated iron mansion shipped from Belgium to tropical Maputo in 1892 - and abandoned almost immediately because the sun-baked metal made it impossible to live in.

subject: Casa de Isla Negra
summary: Pablo Neruda built a house that pretends to be a ship on a stretch of Chilean coast that pretends to be an island, and filled it with the wreckage of a lifetime spent loving the sea.

subject: Casa de Tableta
summary: Casa de Tableta, now known as the Alpine Inn, and formerly known as Rossotti's Saloon and Zott's, was built c.1851 in Portola Valley, California at th

subject: Casa de Tucumán
summary: The colonial house where Argentina declared independence in 1816 nearly crumbled into oblivion before a single photograph saved it, enabling a reconstruction that made it the nation's most sacred civic monument.

subject: Casa de les Punxes
summary: A spiked medieval castle dropped into Barcelona's modern grid, built for three sisters and carved with a defiant plea for Catalan freedom.

subject: Casa del Arte
summary: Step through the doors of this hexagonal museum in Concepción and a 300-square-meter mural of the whole Latin American epic rises around you.

subject: Casapueblo
summary: A white, hand-sculpted citadel on the Uruguayan cliffs that one artist spent 36 years building without a single plan, modeled on the mud nest of a small bird.

subject: Casbah of Algiers
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage citadel that has served as Phoenician trading post, Ottoman capital, colonial backdrop, and revolutionary stronghold -- Algiers' ancient medina tells 3,000 years of Mediterranean history in its steep, winding streets.

subject: Caserma Ermanno Carlotto
summary: An Italian military barracks in Tianjin named for a lieutenant killed during the Boxer Rebellion, which housed 600 marines, hosted a visit from the last Chinese emperor, became a last-stand fortress against Japanese forces in 1943, and still serves China's armed police today.

subject: Casma–Sechin culture
summary: A Peruvian coastal civilization whose 5,600-year-old frieze at Sechin Bajo is the oldest known monumental architecture in the Americas, with sites including a fortress and a 2,300-year-old solar observatory.

subject: Castanhão Ecological Station
summary: Created in environmental compensation for the largest public dam in Brazil, this strictly protected reserve shelters the dry-country caatinga vegetation that the reservoir itself partly submerged.

subject: Castel Sant'Angelo
summary: A Roman emperor's mausoleum that became a papal fortress, a prison for heretics and charlatans, and the stage for opera's most famous suicide leap.

subject: Castell Malgwyn
summary: A West End banker bought a Welsh estate to control a tinplate works, closed a public road through it, and built the country house and bridges that still bear his name.

subject: Castell Nadolig
summary: An Iron Age hillfort in Ceredigion known as the 'Christmas Castle', where a farmer in 1829 unearthed two bronze divination spoons now held by the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.

subject: Castellers de Vilafranca
summary: The green-shirted human-tower builders of Vilafranca del Penedès raise the tallest and hardest castells ever attempted, topped always by a small child who scales the whole structure and lifts a hand.

subject: Castelão (Ceará)
summary: The "Big Castle" of Fortaleza was the first stadium finished for the 2014 World Cup - a fifty-year-old arena that once drew 120,000 people to hear a pope.

subject: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas
summary: The largest Spanish colonial fortress in the Americas, where a one-eyed, one-armed, one-legged admiral defeated the greatest naval armada assembled since the Spanish Armada -- and where the tunnels built by enslaved Africans still echo beneath the hill of San Lazaro.

subject: Castillo San Felipe del Morro
summary: For nearly five centuries, this six-level fortress on a rocky headland has guarded the entrance to San Juan Bay -- surviving attacks by Drake, the Dutch, the British, and the U.S. Navy, and outlasting the empire that built it.

subject: Castillo de San Julián
summary: A brooding fort on the hill above Cartagena's harbor mouth grew for nearly two centuries around a single tower left behind by British invaders in 1706.

subject: Castillo de San Marcos
summary: The oldest masonry fort in the continental United States, built from shellstone that swallowed cannonballs whole, never taken by force in over 300 years, and witness to everything from colonial sieges to Seminole escapes to the civil rights movement.

story.title: Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro

subject: Castillo de los Tres Reyes Del Morro
summary: A 16th-century Spanish fortress guarding the entrance to Havana harbor, where the dramatic 1762 British siege and the nightly cannon firing ceremony echo centuries of colonial conflict over Cuba's strategic riches.

subject: Castledillon, County Kildare
summary: A hermit's name, a vanished tower house, a soldier's lonesome ballad - the Liffey-side parish of Castledillon hides a thousand years of half-erased history beneath its quiet fields.

subject: Castlegate, Aberdeen
summary: The castle gates the square was named for were torn down in 1308 - but the name stuck, the gallows stayed for centuries, and a unicorn still circles the cross when the moon is full.

subject: Castletown, Isle of Man
summary: The former Manx capital, dominated by a thirteenth-century Viking castle, served by parliament for centuries before losing that role to Douglas in 1869.

subject: Castletroy
summary: The Black Castle that gives the place its name has been a ruin since Cromwell's cannon - but Castletroy itself, once farmland, is now Limerick's university quarter.

subject: Catedral Alta Patagonia
summary: South America's largest ski area, named for granite spires that resemble a Gothic cathedral, dropping skiers more than a kilometer toward the blue of Lake Nahuel Huapi.

subject: Catharina Ziekenhuis
summary: Founded in 1843 by seven Tilburg sisters, Eindhoven's Catharina Hospital is now the Netherlands' largest heart and vascular center - and a quiet pipeline of medical firsts, from a 2004 ovarian cancer discovery to a 2022 bypass without a saw.

subject: Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur d'Alger
summary: A modernist Roman Catholic cathedral built in Algiers in 1956 to replace a mosque that had been converted into a church -- a building whose very existence traces the tangled religious history of colonial Algeria.

subject: Cavalcante
summary: The northern gateway to the Chapada dos Veadeiros, and the entrance to Kalunga quilombola country.

subject: Caves of Nerja
summary: A five-kilometer cave system near Malaga that holds the world's largest known stalagmite column, possibly the oldest cave paintings ever discovered, and an underground concert hall.

subject: Cedar Avenue of Nikkō
summary: Some 13,000 cryptomeria trees, planted starting in 1625 as a living offering to the deified shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, line three roads converging on Nikko -- the longest tree-lined avenue in the world, and the only Japanese cultural property designated as both a Special Historic Site and a Special Natural Monument.

subject: Cedar Key Light
summary: A lighthouse on Seahorse Key that witnessed revolutions, wars, and imprisonment before becoming the oldest standing light on Florida's Gulf Coast -- and a college dormitory.

subject: Cementerio Presbítero Matías Maestro
summary: Lima's first civil cemetery, inaugurated in 1808, is an open-air museum of neoclassical sculpture and Peruvian history, housing 766 mausoleums, the tombs of dozens of presidents, and a Crypt of Heroes honoring the fallen of the War of the Pacific.

subject: Centennial Exposition
summary: America's first world's fair, held in Philadelphia's Fairmount Park in 1876, drew nearly 10 million visitors to witness the nation's industrial coming-of-age -- from Alexander Graham Bell's telephone to the towering arm of the Statue of Liberty.

story.title: Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences

subject: Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences
summary: The Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS) is an interdisciplinary research institution at Stanford University. Established with

story.title: Center for Studies of the Holocaust and Religious Minorities

subject: Center for Studies of the Holocaust and Religious Minorities
summary: Norway's Holocaust research center operates from Villa Grande, the former residence of Vidkun Quisling, transforming a collaborator's mansion into a place of remembrance and accountability.

subject: Central Academy of Drama
summary: The school that trained Gong Li, Zhang Ziyi, and generations of China's finest actors traces its roots to a wartime arts academy in the caves of Yan'an.

subject: Central Academy of Fine Arts
summary: China's most prestigious art school gave the world the Goddess of Democracy statue, trained generations of painters and sculptors, and guards a collection of over 2,000 Ming dynasty scroll paintings.

subject: Central Bookstore
summary: Taichung's Central Bookstore opened in 1927 as a meeting place for democracy advocates under Japanese colonial rule, survived decades of transformation and closure, and was restored and reopened in 2020 as a living monument to Taiwan's literary and political history.

subject: Central Market, Hong Kong
summary: A Bauhaus gem that began as colonial Hong Kong's first market bazaar in 1842 and survived demolitions, Japanese occupation, and decades of neglect to reopen as a vibrant public hub in 2021.

subject: Central Plaza, Hong Kong
summary: For four years Central Plaza was the tallest building in Asia — a triangular reinforced concrete tower that turned harbour-reclaimed land into 374 metres of glass and steel, and put a neon clock on top to tell the time in colours.

subject: Central Restaurante
summary: The world's top-ranked restaurant, where Peruvian chef Virgilio Martinez Veliz transforms obscure indigenous ingredients from Peru's coast, highlands, and Amazon into a dining experience that maps an entire country's biodiversity.

subject: Centro Cultural Gabriela Mistral
summary: A cultural center built by volunteers in 275 days, seized by a dictatorship, gutted by fire, and reborn as a place of art - the GAM holds half a century of Chilean history in one building.

subject: Centro Financiero Confinanzas
summary: An unfinished 45-story skyscraper in Caracas that became the world's tallest squat, housing over 2,500 people in a vertical improvised community before its evacuation in 2015.

subject: Cerro Castor
summary: At 54 degrees south, on the slopes of a Fuegian mountain, sits the most southerly ski resort on the planet, where the season runs long, the moon can light your descent, and the next stop is Antarctica.

subject: Cerro Catedral (Uruguay)
summary: At 513.66 meters, Uruguay's highest point is a hill you can walk up, named for rock formations that someone once thought resembled a cathedral.

subject: Cerro Dominador Solar Thermal Plant
summary: Latin America's first concentrated solar power plant rises from the Atacama Desert, its 252-meter tower surrounded by thousands of sun-tracking mirrors that store energy in molten salt to generate electricity long after dark.

subject: Cerro Negro
summary: Central America's youngest volcano first tore open a Nicaraguan hillside in 1850 and has erupted at least 23 times since, building a stark black cinder cone that adventurers now ride down on wooden boards.

subject: Chabahar Port
summary: Iran's only oceanic port, called the 'Golden Gate' to landlocked Central Asia, where ancient Sasanian trade routes meet modern geopolitical chess between India, China, and the United States.

subject: Chabot Space and Science Center
summary: Born from a 19th-century observatory donated by a hydraulic mining magnate, Chabot Space and Science Center has spent over 140 years giving the people of Oakland a window to the stars.

subject: Chagpori
summary: A sacred hill in Lhasa whose medical college taught Tibetan medicine for over 260 years before Chinese artillery reduced it to rubble in 1959.

subject: Chak Chak, Yazd
summary: Perched beneath a desert cliff in central Iran, Chak Chak is the holiest mountain shrine of Zoroastrianism, where an ever-dripping spring recalls the legend of a fleeing princess and the mountain that sheltered her.

subject: Chalcis
summary: On the narrowest strait in Greece, the sea reverses itself several times a day, a riddle that reputedly defeated Aristotle and still draws crowds to the bridge at Chalkida.

subject: Chamber of Deputies (Brazil)
summary: The lower house of Brazil's National Congress - 513 deputies elected by proportional representation, meeting inside Oscar Niemeyer's concrete bowl on Brasília's Monumental Axis.

subject: Chamber of Representatives (Belgium)
summary: Belgium's lower house meets in a green hemicycle inside a neoclassical palace — and the math of its 150 seats explains why Belgian governments are always coalitions.

subject: Changdeokgung
summary: Seoul's best-preserved royal palace was built as a secondary residence but became the preferred home of Joseon kings for centuries, earning UNESCO World Heritage status for its harmony with the natural landscape.

subject: Chaonei No. 81
summary: A crumbling French Baroque mansion in the middle of modern Beijing became the capital's most famous haunted house, inspiring a blockbuster horror film and drawing hundreds of thrill-seekers a day.

subject: Chapelle du Rosaire de Vence
summary: Henri Matisse, aging and ill, poured his last creative energy into a tiny Dominican chapel in Vence -- designing everything from the stained glass to the priests' vestments, calling it his masterpiece.

subject: Chappaquiddick
summary: The bridge that ended a dynasty - where Senator Ted Kennedy's car plunged into a tidal channel in 1969, killing his passenger Mary Jo Kopechne and destroying his chances of ever becoming president.

subject: Charioteer of Delphi
summary: Cast around 470 BC and buried by an earthquake in 373 BC, the Charioteer of Delphi is a life-size bronze figure of serene, almost uncanny presence — one of the finest surviving bronzes of the ancient world, now displayed at the Delphi Archaeological Museum.

subject: Charles Dickens
summary: A twelve-year-old labelling shoe polish in a Covent Garden warehouse — and the novelist he became because of it.

story.title: Charleston: The Holy City That Fired the First Shot

subject: Charleston
summary: The South Carolina port where the Civil War began at Fort Sumter - where antebellum architecture survived because Sherman didn't reach it, where slave markets supplied the plantations, and where the weight of history makes every cobblestone politically charged.

subject: Charleston Farmhouse
summary: In 1916, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant moved to a Sussex farmhouse and proceeded, over the next fifty years, to paint every surface they could reach - turning Charleston into a country meeting place for the Bloomsbury Group and a working monument to a particular kind of English unconventionality.

subject: Charlotte Motor Speedway
summary: Built in eleven chaotic months in 1960, the speedway nearly went bankrupt before its first race; today it hosts the Coca-Cola 600, NASCAR's longest event and a Memorial Day weekend tradition.

subject: Chase Center
summary: The Warriors' waterfront arena that brought professional basketball back to San Francisco after a half-century across the bay -- and ignited a gentrification debate in the process.

story.title: The Chase Vault: Barbados's Coffins That Refused to Stay Put

subject: Chase Vault
summary: A sealed marble burial vault at Christ Church Parish Church in Barbados became the Caribbean's most enduring ghost story when, according to legend, heavy lead coffins were found rearranged every time the door was opened.

subject: Chaukhandi tombs
summary: Centuries of sandstone carving produced an Islamic necropolis near Karachi whose pyramid-shaped graves bear horsemen, jewelry, and geometric designs found nowhere else in the Muslim world.

subject: Chef Chu's
summary: Chef Chu's is a Chinese-American restaurant in Los Altos, California, owned by chef Lawrence Chu. It opened in 1970 and has been operating since, and

subject: Chek Lap Kok
summary: A small island inhabited since the Neolithic was leveled and expanded into one of the world's busiest airports — but the finger-sized frogs, the granite temple, and twenty families who once called it home were carefully moved first.

subject: Chekhov Gymnasium
summary: The oldest school in southern Russia kept a jail cell for misbehaving boys - and its most famous inmate grew up to write The Cherry Orchard.

subject: Chellah
summary: A walled necropolis in Rabat where Roman columns stand beside Marinid mausoleums and storks nest atop a ruined medieval minaret, layering two thousand years of civilization in a single garden.

subject: Chelsea Flower Show
summary: Five days in May at the Royal Hospital Chelsea, where a gold medal can change a career and a garden can be made of Plasticine.

subject: Chemische Fabrik Kalk
summary: For 135 years, a chemicals giant defined the skyline of right-bank Cologne with chimneys, soda ash, and the smell of sulfur. Now its grounds hold a shopping mall, a police headquarters, and a single surviving water tower.

subject: Cheomseongdae
summary: The oldest surviving astronomical observatory in Asia, built during the reign of Queen Seondeok in seventh-century Gyeongju, encodes the Korean calendar in its stonework.

subject: Cheong Wa Dae
summary: The Blue House served as South Korea's presidential compound for over seven decades, its blue-tiled roof becoming one of Seoul's most recognizable and politically charged landmarks.

subject: Chepstow
summary: On a clifftop above the tidal Wye, the oldest surviving stone castle in Britain has guarded the border between Wales and England for nearly a thousand years.

subject: Chequers
summary: The British prime minister's country retreat, a Tudor manor in the Chiltern Hills given to the nation in 1921 - and named for a medieval usher of the King's Exchequer.

subject: Cherbourg Maritime Station
summary: An Art Deco palace built for ocean liners and emigrants - and the building through which Titanic's last passengers walked before sailing.

subject: Cherbourg-en-Cotentin
summary: A working Norman port at the top of the Cotentin Peninsula - half ferry terminal, half film set, with a harbour the size of a small sea.

subject: Chernihiv Collegium
summary: The Baroque school in the heart of Chernihiv once called the 'Chernigov Athens,' where Cossack-era students learned Latin, rhetoric, and philosophy beneath a soaring bell tower.

subject: Chernobyl Reactors 5 and 6
summary: Two nuclear reactors that were never finished, frozen in half-built silence beside the world's most infamous power plant, their cranes still standing where workers dropped their tools in 1986.

subject: Cherokee Heritage Center
summary: Built by hand using ancient methods on the site of the old Cherokee Seminary, this living museum near Tahlequah preserves Cherokee culture from the 1830s Trail of Tears through centuries of tradition.

subject: Cherry Hill Plantation
summary: A mid-nineteenth-century North Carolina plantation house where ninety enslaved people lived in fourteen cabins, now hosting classical concerts in a room their labor built.

subject: Chester Racecourse
summary: The Roodee, where horses have run since 1539, where the Romans once moored their ships, and where local legend says a statue of the Virgin Mary stood trial for murder.

subject: Cheung Sha Wan
summary: Where a Han dynasty tomb lurks beneath Kowloon apartment towers, and 588 unexploded Japanese shells surfaced in a residential street in 2006 — Cheung Sha Wan has been quietly burying its past under successive waves of reclamation.

subject: Chez Panisse
summary: A Berkeley restaurant that rewired American dining by insisting on one radical idea: food should taste like where it comes from.

subject: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus
summary: A Victorian Gothic railway station in Mumbai that took ten years to build, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, survived a terrorist attack, and still moves millions of commuters through its 18 platforms every day.

subject: Chibok schoolgirls kidnapping
summary: On the night of April 14, 2014, Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from a secondary school in Chibok, Nigeria -- a mass kidnapping that ignited a global movement, exposed the limits of government protection, and left families waiting years for daughters who may never come home.

story.title: Chichen Itza: The Mayan City That Conquered Time

subject: Chichen Itza
summary: The Yucatan ruins where twice a year the pyramid casts a serpent shadow at equinox - a feat of astronomical engineering by a civilization that tracked Venus with precision, sacrificed to cenotes, and built monuments that have lasted a millennium.

story.title: Chichén Itzá: The Pyramid That Screams

subject: Chichén Itzá
summary: Where the Maya built a pyramid that creates a snake-shadow at equinox and produces a chirping echo designed to mimic their sacred bird - engineering acoustic magic into stone a thousand years ago.

subject: Chicken Ranch Rancheria
summary: On fewer than three acres in the Sierra Nevada foothills, the Me-Wuk people built a sovereign nation that survived termination-era federal policy and now operates a casino resort an hour from Yosemite.

subject: Chien-Cheng Circle
summary: A humble fish pond became northern Taiwan's most beloved night market, then a bomb shelter, then a restaurant maze — and finally a quiet public plaza carrying the ghost of a hundred years of Taipei street life.

story.title: Chikurin-ji: The Bamboo Grove Temple and the Grave of a Monk Who Built Japan

subject: Chikurin-ji
summary: Nestled on the eastern slopes of Mount Ikoma, Chikurin-ji is a small Ritsu Buddhist temple holding the grave of Gyoki, the eighth-century monk who helped construct the Great Buddha of Todai-ji and whose social works earned him a reputation as an incarnation of Manjusri.

subject: Chin Pao San
summary: On a hillside above the East China Sea near Jinshan, this private cemetery is also a sculpture garden — and the most visited resting place belongs to Teresa Teng, whose memorial includes a keyboard embedded in the ground that visitors play with their feet.

subject: China World Trade Center
summary: Beijing's largest building complex began filling tenants before it even officially opened, marking the spot where China's economic ambitions met the world.

possibleMolenMatches.title: China World Trade Center Tower III

subject: China Zun
summary: Shaped like an ancient wine vessel and tall enough to see into the political heart of China, Beijing's tallest skyscraper became a symbol of ambition that proved a little too revealing.

subject: Chinatown, Vancouver
summary: Canada's largest Chinatown, built by people the country taxed for arriving and then barred outright, and now reckoning with quieter streets and a museum that reclaimed the date of the exclusion.

subject: Chinese Historical Society of America
summary: The oldest and largest organization devoted to documenting Chinese American history, CHSA operates a museum in a landmark Julia Morgan-designed building in Chinatown.

subject: Chinese submarine Changcheng 237
summary: A Cold War-era diesel submarine that spent two decades patrolling the Yellow Sea before being decommissioned and placed on permanent display at the Qingdao Naval Museum.

subject: Chinese submarine Changzheng 1
summary: China's first nuclear-powered submarine, built in secret without Soviet help, now rests as a museum ship at Qingdao after being stripped of its reactor in a painstaking denuclearization process.

subject: Chinqua Penn Plantation
summary: An English-style manor outside Reidsville built in the 1920s on a Penn-family tobacco fortune, opened to the public for decades, and ultimately broken apart in a two-day Greensboro auction after a tobacco entrepreneur's bankruptcy.

story.title: Chinreisha: The Shrine That Honors the Enemy

subject: Chinreisha
summary: Hidden behind a steel fence within the Yasukuni Shrine precinct, a small wooden shrine called the Chinreisha does what its famous neighbor will not -- it enshrines the spirits of all war dead, including Japan's former enemies.

subject: Chinyingi
summary: A Capuchin mission on the west bank of the Zambezi where an untrained Italian friar built a suspension bridge so that no one else would drown trying to cross the river.

subject: Chipata
summary: The eastern gateway between Zambia and Malawi, a former colonial capital where overlanders pause before heading into the wild Luangwa valley.

subject: Chlemoutsi
summary: Built between 1220 and 1223 with funds seized from the Church, Chlemoutsi is the finest surviving Frankish castle in Greece — a hexagonal hilltop fortress that watched princes, Byzantine despots, and Ottoman pashas come and go while it stood largely unchanged.

story.title: Chongryon: North Korea's Shadow Embassy in Tokyo

subject: Chongryon
summary: Headquartered in Chiyoda, Tokyo, Chongryon has served as North Korea's de facto embassy in Japan since 1955, operating a parallel society of schools, banks, and businesses for Zainichi Koreans while entangled in espionage allegations and Cold War politics.

subject: Chouinard Art Institute
summary: A Los Angeles art school that trained the animators of Hollywood's golden age—and the school that Walt Disney saved, then transformed into something entirely new.

subject: Choum
summary: A scatter of wooden shacks in the empty Sahara, Choum exists for one reason: it is where the legendary Iron Ore Train stops, the desert gateway to Mauritania's Adrar.

subject: Chris Jorgensen
summary: A Norwegian orphan who sketched his way into San Francisco's art academy at fourteen, married a Ghirardelli chocolate heiress, and built Yosemite Valley's first museum - a living room stuffed with water buffalo horns and beer steins.

story.title: Christ the Redeemer of the Andes

subject: Christ the Redeemer of the Andes
summary: Two nations stood on the brink of war until a bronze Christ was hauled up a mountain pass by mule and raised on the border itself - a monument cast, by some accounts, from the very cannons that might have been turned against each other.

subject: Christoffelpark
summary: Curacao's largest national park wraps around the island's highest peak, hiding rare orchids that bloom on ten-foot cacti, white-tailed deer found nowhere else in the Caribbean, and the plantation ruins of three centuries of colonial agriculture.

subject: Chun Quoit
summary: A 4,400-year-old Neolithic dolmen with a mushroom-shaped capstone, the only quoit in West Penwith still standing exactly as the builders set it.

subject: Chungking Mansions
summary: A 17-storey labyrinth on Nathan Road where people from at least 120 nationalities converge — traders, refugees, backpackers, and long-term residents — making this aging building one of the most genuinely globalized places on Earth.

subject: Chushka Spit
summary: An eighteen-kilometer arm of sand reaching into the Kerch Strait, carrying a lighthouse, a railway, and a busy port, and once the anchor of a doomed wartime bridge.

subject: Chwarszczany
summary: A Polish duke handed a thousand hides of borderland to the Knights Templar in 1232; the granite chapel they raised on a low rise above the Myśla is still standing, and still a parish church.

subject: Ché Cafe
summary: In a former Marine Corps mess hall on the UC San Diego campus, a student cooperative has hosted punk shows and radical politics since 1980 — surviving eviction attempts, budget crises, and decades of institutional pressure by simply refusing to leave.

story.title: Chuguji: The Nunnery with the Smile That Rivals the Mona Lisa

subject: Chūgū-ji
summary: A 7th-century nunnery adjacent to Horyuji founded by Prince Shotoku, housing a camphor-wood Miroku Bosatsu statue whose enigmatic half-smile has been compared to the Mona Lisa and a fragmentary embroidery that is Japan's oldest surviving textile artwork.

subject: Chūson-ji
summary: A gold-covered Buddhist temple in rural Iwate Prefecture that shelters the mummified remains of three medieval warlords beneath its altars, built by a man who lost everything in war and resolved to create a paradise on Earth.

story.title: Chuzen-ji: The Temple That Floated Back from the Deep

subject: Chūzen-ji
summary: On the shore of Japan's highest natural lake, a Buddhist temple houses a sacred statue carved from a living tree in 784 CE -- a statue that survived being washed into the lake by a typhoon and was found floating, largely intact, more than a thousand years after it was carved.

subject: Chūō Shinkansen
summary: Japan is boring a 286-kilometer tunnel through the Alps so a magnetically levitating train can connect Tokyo to Nagoya in 40 minutes -- if a dispute over river water, a stubborn governor, and nine trillion yen don't stop it first.

subject: Cidade Velha (Belém)
summary: Belém's oldest quarter, grown from a straw-roofed fort raised in 1616 to hold the Amazon for Portugal, and refaced three centuries later in tile bought with rubber money.

subject: Circular Mound Altar
summary: Within Beijing's Temple of Heaven complex, the Circular Mound Altar is a three-tiered marble platform where emperors spoke to the heavens -- and where the architecture itself is built on the sacred mathematics of the number nine.

story.title: Circus Maximus: 150,000 Voices in a Valley

subject: Circus Maximus
summary: The largest stadium in ancient Rome - 621 meters long, capable of holding over 150,000 spectators - the Circus Maximus hosted chariot races, religious festivals, and public spectacles for over a millennium in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine Hills.

subject: Cistern of Aetius
summary: For fifteen hundred years, the vast open-air reservoir that Aetius built to water Constantinople has been successively a Roman cistern, an Ottoman vegetable garden, and a working football stadium — the same rectangular depression wearing different civilizations like rings on a trunk.

story.title: City of Paris Dry Goods Co.

subject: City of Paris Dry Goods Co.
summary: A Gold Rush-era department store that sailed into San Francisco as a ship full of French merchandise, survived until 1972, and left behind only a rotunda and a stained-glass dome now inside Neiman Marcus.

subject: Ciudad Mitad del Mundo
summary: A 30-meter monument marking the equator north of Quito, built to commemorate an eighteenth-century French expedition - except the equator actually runs 240 meters further north.

subject: Ciudad Vieja, Montevideo
summary: On a peninsula at the mouth of the bay, Montevideo began as a walled Spanish fort and grew into a quarter where colonial stone, Art Deco towers, and the smell of grilling meat all share the same narrow streets.

subject: Clacton-on-Sea
summary: An Essex seaside resort founded in 1871 around a pier, famous for the world's oldest known wooden spear, Mods and Rockers riots, and Butlin's at its mid-century peak.

subject: Clara Barton National Historic Site
summary: The 38-room Glen Echo home of Clara Barton, founder of the American Red Cross, built partly from lumber salvaged from disaster relief buildings after the Johnstown Flood of 1889.

subject: Clare Priory
summary: Established in 1248 as the first house of the Augustinian Friars in England, suppressed by Henry VIII in 1538, and reclaimed by the Augustinians in 1953 - Clare Priory has been a religious house for most of the last eight centuries.

subject: Claridge's
summary: Claridge's has been London's most rarefied hotel since Empress Eugenie entertained Queen Victoria there in 1860 — and in the 1940s its suite 212 was briefly ceded to Yugoslavia so a crown prince could be born on technically Yugoslav soil.

subject: Clark's Tree
summary: A bronze sculpture on Washington's coast marks the spot where William Clark carved his name into a pine tree in 1805, staking America's claim to the Pacific -- and where the sculpture itself nearly sank on its own epic journey downriver.

subject: Classical Greece
summary: In barely two centuries — from the Persian Wars to the death of Alexander — the Classical Greeks invented the Parthenon, Athenian democracy, Western theatre, and systematic philosophy, while waging almost continuous war among themselves.

story.title: Clatsop Spit: The Graveyard's Front Door

subject: Clatsop Spit
summary: A vast sand spit at the mouth of the Columbia River where 8,500 years of sediment built a landscape that has swallowed ships whole -- the northern gateway to what sailors called the Graveyard of the Pacific.

subject: Clay Center (Charleston, West Virginia)
summary: A 240,000-square-foot cultural complex in downtown Charleston that combines a science museum, an art museum, a planetarium, and a 1,883-seat concert hall under one roof.

subject: Clef Club
summary: Founded in 1910 by James Reese Europe, the Clef Club was a musicians' society, labor exchange, and concert hall in Harlem that brought a 125-piece orchestra of Black American musicians to Carnegie Hall.

subject: Cleitor
summary: Nestled in an enclosed upland valley in northern Arcadia, ancient Cleitor was famous across the Greek world for two peculiarities: a fountain whose water permanently removed the drinker's desire for wine, and fish in the river Aroanius that were said to sing like thrushes.

subject: Clipper Mountains
summary: An eastern Mojave range where the peak drops in sharp cliffs to the desert floor, 40 to 50 desert bighorn sheep maintain a herd, Castle Dome is visible from Route 66, and spring brings sheets of yellow brittlebush blooms across the alluvial fans.

subject: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass
summary: A 1342 white marble gateway at the Great Wall's Juyong Pass bears Buddhist texts in six scripts, a monument to the Yuan dynasty's multilingual empire.

subject: Clouth Gummiwerke
summary: A Cologne rubber factory that built the first Zeppelin's gas envelope, laid the first submarine telegraph cable from Emden to New York, and invented the Cologne Egg, a rail bearing that quiets tram tracks in cities worldwide.

subject: Club Fugazi
summary: Home to Beach Blanket Babylon for over 40 years, Club Fugazi is a North Beach performance venue that has hosted Italian cultural events and musical theater since 1913.

subject: Clube do Choro de Brasília
summary: A music club that started as a planetarium cloakroom and became the venue Paul McCartney chose for his most intimate South American show.

subject: Clyde Arc
summary: The bridge Glasgow calls the Squinty: a steel-arched road crossing of the Clyde, opened in 2006, that crosses the river at a deliberate angle and has the personality to match.

subject: Cobquecura
summary: On a wild stretch of the Chilean coast, the ocean has carved a cathedral out of solid rock, and a colony of sea lions has claimed the islets just offshore as their own.

subject: Cobra Mist
summary: A Cold War over-the-horizon radar built on the Suffolk shingle to watch Soviet airspace, defeated by mysterious noise and shut down in 1973 after only months of operation.

subject: Cockington Court
summary: A Saxon-era Devon manor where a young Agatha Christie performed amateur theatricals before becoming the world's bestselling novelist.

subject: Codorníu Winery
summary: Founded in 1551 and declared a National Monument in 1976, Codorniu is the oldest producer of cava in Spain, its Modernista cellars designed by Josep Puig i Cadafalch rising from the vineyards of the Alt Penedes.

subject: Colditz Cock
summary: British officers built a two-man glider in the attic above Colditz Castle's chapel, planning to launch it off the roof with a bathtub full of concrete — and it never flew until strangers rebuilt it half a century later.

subject: Colegio Nacional de Monserrat
summary: A Jesuit boarding school founded in 1687 that has tested and taught Córdoba's young people for over three centuries, and only admitted its first 44 girls in 1998.

subject: Colegio del Uruguay
summary: The school a caudillo built in 1849 to be free, public, and secular, the first of its kind in Argentina and the classroom that produced three presidents.

subject: Coleraine Academical Institution
summary: A 70-acre grammar school that produced four Olympic medallists, two Open Championship golfers, the actor James Nesbitt, and the architect of the Pompidou Centre.

subject: Collegium Trilingue
summary: In 1517, a circle of Renaissance humanists led by Erasmus founded a small college in Leuven where students could study Latin, Greek, and Hebrew for free. It changed how Europe read the Bible.

subject: Coloane
summary: Macau's quieter, southernmost island holds a pirate battle turned local holiday, bones of martyred Jesuit priests, a chapel built in 1928, and a cobblestone square that still manages to face the sea despite everything the Cotai Strip has built around it.

subject: Cologne Charterhouse
summary: A monastery of vow-bound silent monks who built one of medieval Europe's largest libraries, lost it twice, and whose church now serves Cologne's Protestant congregation - an unlikely 700-year afterlife for a place founded in 1334.

subject: Cologne Opera
summary: A modernist 1957 opera house whose stage hosted Maria Callas and a jazz concert that became the best-selling solo piano record in history - now sealed behind a renovation that started in 2010 and is still not finished.

subject: Cologne hostage crisis
summary: On a July morning in 1995, twenty-five people boarded a sightseeing bus at the cathedral square. Seven hours later, two of them were dead - the driver Raimund Geuer, twenty-six years old, and a second passenger - along with the gunman himself.

subject: Colonial Williamsburg
summary: The restored capital - where Rockefeller money recreated the eighteenth-century Virginia capital, creating America's first and largest living history museum and shaping how Americans imagine their colonial past.

subject: Colonsay
summary: An eight-mile Hebridean island of about 120 people, with a pit full of 8,000-year-old hazelnut shells, the world's smallest island brewery, and a population of black bees protected by Scottish law from interbreeding with any other honey bee.

subject: Colossi of Memnon
summary: Two 18-metre quartzite giants of Amenhotep III guard a vanished temple on the Theban plain, one of which famously sang at dawn until Roman repairs silenced it.

subject: Colson Track
summary: A 336-kilometre line of wheel ruts through the Simpson Desert carries the name of the bushman who, in 1936, became the first European to cross these dunes, guided across by an Aboriginal man named Peter Ains.

subject: Columbia Air Center
summary: The first licensed Black-owned and operated airport in America rose from a fallow farm field along Maryland's Patuxent River in 1940, training generations of African American aviators before racism closed its gates in 1962.

subject: Column of Justinian
summary: The lost colossus of the Augustaeum — a 70-meter column crowned by a colossal bronze emperor that stood between Hagia Sophia and the Great Palace until the earthquake of 1509 brought it down.

subject: Column of Leo
summary: A vanished 5th-century Roman column in Constantinople whose fragments lie scattered in the Topkapi Palace courtyards — and whose crowning statue may have washed up on a beach in southern Italy.

subject: Column of the Goths
summary: The oldest surviving Roman monument in Istanbul — an 18.5-meter marble column in Gülhane Park that predates Constantinople itself, raised to mark a Roman victory over Gothic invaders in the 3rd or 4th century.

subject: Coláiste Iognáid
summary: A Jesuit secondary school in Galway founded in 1645, bilingual in Irish and English, the alma mater of Olympic rower Aifric Keogh - and of William Joyce, 'Lord Haw-Haw'.

subject: Commando Basic Training Centre
summary: The wartime training base at Achnacarry Castle in Lochaber, where over 25,000 commandos learned an intense new kind of warfare, widely regarded as the birthplace of modern special forces.

subject: Company rule in Rhodesia
summary: For over three decades, a private corporation governed a territory larger than France -- raising armies, making laws, and carving a colony from the African interior without ever answering to an elected parliament.

subject: Computerspielemuseum
summary: On a socialist showcase boulevard in Friedrichshain, the world's first permanent museum of video game culture keeps 25,000 games playable — including one that shocks you when you lose.

subject: Concatedral de San Nicolás, Alicante
summary: Alicante's co-cathedral, a severe Herrerian shell crowned by a 45-meter blue dome and hiding one of Spanish Baroque's loveliest chapels inside.

subject: Concertgebouw, Amsterdam
summary: A neoclassical concert hall in Amsterdam where the dust is never cleaned because removing it would change the legendary acoustics.

subject: Conciergerie
summary: A medieval royal palace turned revolutionary prison, where Marie Antoinette spent her final days and 2,781 prisoners passed through on their way to the guillotine.

subject: Condor Field
summary: A Mojave Desert airfield that served as a civil airport, a World War II Army glider school, a Navy auxiliary station, and eventually a Marine Corps expeditionary runway — a piece of ground worked by every branch of the American military over four decades.

subject: Confederation Centre of the Arts
summary: Canada's national memorial to the Fathers of Confederation doubles as a cultural powerhouse in Charlottetown, home to a Guinness World Record-holding musical and a permanent art collection of over 17,000 works.

subject: Confitería del Molino
summary: An Art Nouveau coffeehouse facing the Argentine Congress, its windmill-crowned turret dark for a quarter-century before craftsmen coaxed it back to life.

subject: Congregation Emanu-El (Victoria, British Columbia)
summary: Built in 1863 by gold-rush immigrants, Victoria's Congregation Emanu-El is the oldest synagogue building still in use as a synagogue in Canada and on the west coast of North America.

subject: Congregation Shearith Israel
summary: The oldest Jewish congregation in the United States, founded in 1654 by twenty-three refugees from Dutch Brazil, whose Neoclassical synagogue on Central Park West anchors nearly four centuries of American Jewish history.

subject: Conishead Priory
summary: A Gothic Revival country house on the Furness peninsula whose lives have included Augustinian canons, Victorian spa-goers, recovering coal miners, wartime wounded, and Buddhist monks.

subject: Connemara Heritage and History Centre
summary: An open-air museum near Clifden built around the remains of one family's pre-Famine farm - a working homestead, reconstructed Iron Age structures, and the first Pit Stop on Season 12 of The Amazing Race.

subject: Conquest of Coron (1685)
summary: In August 1685, a Venetian siege of the Ottoman fortress at Koroni ended with the massacre of approximately 1,500 people — soldiers and civilians alike — after a cannon accidentally fired during surrender negotiations, triggering a slaughter that no one had ordered.

subject: Conradh na Gaeilge
summary: The Gaelic League, founded in Dublin in 1893 by a Church of Ireland rector's son when only 3.5% of Irish children were being raised as Irish speakers - the organisation that revived a language.

subject: Conservatory of Flowers
summary: The oldest building in Golden Gate Park and the oldest wooden municipal conservatory in the United States, a Victorian greenhouse whose dome has sheltered rare plants since 1879.

subject: Constitution Hill, Johannesburg
summary: A hilltop fort-turned-prison that once held Gandhi, Mandela, and thousands of apartheid-era detainees now houses South Africa's Constitutional Court, its bricks literally built from the demolished walls of the old jail.

subject: Constitutional Convention (United States)
summary: In the sweltering summer of 1787, fifty-five delegates gathered behind nailed-shut windows in Philadelphia's Pennsylvania State House to secretly debate, argue, and ultimately draft the Constitution of the United States.

story.title: Consulate General of the United States, Karachi

subject: Consulate General of the United States, Karachi
summary: The largest U.S. consulate in the world, the Karachi diplomatic compound has survived shootings, truck bombs, and a foiled liquid explosives attack -- a fortress reflecting the complicated alliance between Pakistan and America.

subject: Control Yuan
summary: A watchdog branch of government born from imperial China's censor tradition and Sun Yat-sen's five-power theory, housed in a Japanese colonial-era building that has outlasted the constitutional framework it was designed to serve.

subject: Convento de la Popa
summary: Perched on the highest hill in Cartagena, a 1607 Augustinian convent whose founding legend involves a friar, a vision of the Virgin Mary, and a goat flung from a cliff -- and whose later history placed Simon Bolivar in its windows as cannonballs sailed past his head.

subject: Conwy
summary: One of Europe's best-preserved walled medieval towns, home to a thirteenth-century castle, a Telford suspension bridge, a Stephenson tubular railway bridge - and the smallest house in Great Britain.

subject: Conwy Lifeboat Station
summary: An RNLI inshore lifeboat station in the shadow of Conwy Castle, born in 1966 from a national push to put fast small boats where the leisure traffic had grown.

subject: Cooktown
summary: A frontier port at the mouth of the Endeavour River where Cook's 48-day landing, a wild gold rush, and thousands of years of Guugu Yimithirr country all meet - the gateway to the wilderness of Cape York.

subject: Copinsay
summary: An Orkney island that emptied in 1958, became a bird reserve in 1972, and still holds the bones of a community in its abandoned farmhouse and schoolhouse.

story.title: Cora Hartshorn Arboretum and Bird Sanctuary

subject: Cora Hartshorn Arboretum and Bird Sanctuary
summary: A 16.5-acre woodland sanctuary in Short Hills, New Jersey, where 275-year-old tulip trees tower over trails designed by Cora Hartshorn herself, and a Stone House built from local quarry rock serves as a nature education center.

story.title: Coronation of Charles III and Camilla

subject: Coronation of Charles III and Camilla
summary: On 6 May 2023, Westminster Abbey hosted the first British coronation in 70 years — scaled down from 1953, watched by two billion people, and held under one of the wettest spring skies London could provide.

subject: Coronation of Vajiralongkorn
summary: The 2019 coronation of King Vajiralongkorn at the Grand Palace was Thailand's first royal coronation in 69 years and the first ever broadcast live on television and streamed online.

subject: Corregidor
summary: A tadpole-shaped island at the mouth of Manila Bay where Spanish galleons once anchored, American and Filipino soldiers held out for months against Japanese bombardment, and a sunlit memorial now marks the exact moment of surrender.

subject: Corsican Republic
summary: Fourteen years before the American Revolution, a Corsican general named Pasquale Paoli created a republic with a written constitution, a university, and female suffrage -- and inspired revolutionaries from Philadelphia to Paris.

subject: Cosco Busan Oil Spill
summary: A fog-blinded container ship struck the Bay Bridge in 2007, spilling 53,000 gallons of heavy fuel oil into San Francisco Bay and killing nearly 7,000 birds.

subject: Costa Teguise
summary: Born from dynamite blasting through volcanic rock in the 1970s, this Canary Islands resort transformed barren lava fields into a sun-seeker's haven where artist Cesar Manrique's vision still shapes the streetscape.

subject: Cotehele
summary: One of Britain's least-altered Tudor houses, built by Sir Richard Edgcumbe in thanksgiving for surviving Richard III's pursuit - rambling granite walls above the River Tamar, a working mill, a medieval dovecote, and a 250-tree orchard of West Country apples.

subject: Council of Hieria
summary: In 754, Emperor Constantine V assembled 338 bishops in a Bosphorus-shore palace to settle Christianity's most explosive question: whether sacred images were holy or heretical — and the council they held was later declared null by its own church.

subject: Council of State (Greece)
summary: Greece's supreme administrative court, born of a French model, abolished twice in its first three decades, and now the body that decides whether the nation's laws are constitutional, seated in a grand neoclassical building in central Athens.

story.title: County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos

subject: County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos
summary: For nearly three centuries, a succession of Italian dynasties — pirate-admiral, Roman noble house, and Neapolitan merchant clan — ruled these sun-drenched Greek islands at the crossroads of East and West.

subject: Court Farm, Pembrey
summary: An overgrown but structurally sound 16th-century manor house in Pembrey, once a navigational marker on shipping charts of the Burry Inlet and one of the last medieval houses in Carmarthenshire.

subject: Cova des Coloms
summary: Menorcans call this vast limestone chamber the Cathedral, a natural hall where Talaiotic islanders laid their dead more than two thousand years ago.

subject: Coventry Colliery
summary: A Warwickshire deep mine that worked the local coal seams for 74 years before closing in 1991, now a Prologis distribution park where the only obvious clue is a road called Winding House Lane.

subject: Coventry Ordnance Works
summary: A 60-acre Stoney Stanton Road factory that armed Royal Navy battleships and the Western Front, became a founding piece of English Electric, and now makes car parts for American Axle.

subject: Cragside
summary: The first house in the world lit by hydroelectric power - built by Victorian arms-magnate William Armstrong on a Northumberland hillside, with seven million trees, the tallest Scots pine in Britain, and a tonne of mechanical engineering hidden in its plumbing.

subject: Craters of the Moon (geothermal site)
summary: A geothermal landscape north of Taupō where human interference accidentally awakened a field of steam vents, mud pools, and eruption craters that now shifts and collapses faster than the boardwalks built to cross it.

subject: Creighton Mine
summary: Born from a meteorite impact 1.85 billion years ago, Creighton Mine descends more than two kilometres into the Sudbury Basin -- deep enough to house the world's cleanest underground physics laboratory and an automated greenhouse that grows 100,000 pine trees.

subject: Crimea
summary: A diamond of land in the Black Sea where Greek ruins, cave cities, tsars' palaces, and cliffside vineyards stack up along a warm Mediterranean coast.

subject: Crimean Khanate
summary: For three centuries a Genghisid dynasty ruled the Black Sea steppe from a palace at Bakhchysarai, shaping the fate of Poland, Russia, and the Ottoman world before Catherine the Great erased it from the map.

subject: Crissy Field
summary: A former Army airfield on the San Francisco waterfront, transformed from a hazardous waste dump back into the tidal marsh that existed before the military arrived.

subject: Cristo de la Concordia
summary: A colossal Christ statue atop a Bolivian hill that was deliberately designed to be taller than Rio's famous Redeemer -- with the extra 44 centimeters cheekily explained as Jesus living 'a little past' his 33rd year.

subject: Crown Colony of Sarawak
summary: For seventeen years between the White Rajahs and Malaysian statehood, Sarawak endured a contested colonial interlude marked by assassination, infrastructure building, and the slow emergence of a modern state from a private kingdom.

subject: Crypt of Civilization
summary: Sealed in a converted swimming pool beneath a Georgia university in 1940, this room-sized time capsule is addressed to the people of 8113 AD -- and contains everything from a bottle of Budweiser to the voice of Adolf Hitler.

subject: Cueva de los Tayos
summary: An Ecuadorian cave famous for its oilbirds, for the pseudoscientific 'Metal Library' hoax, and for the 1976 expedition that somehow convinced Neil Armstrong to squeeze into its depths.

subject: Cuiabá
summary: A state capital founded in 1719 after bandeirantes found gold, whose name means 'arrow-fishing' in Bororo and whose obelisk once marked the geographical center of South America.

subject: Cullera
summary: A single castle-crowned mountain breaks the flat Valencian coastline where the Xúquer River finally reaches the sea, above fifteen kilometres of beach.

subject: Cultural Center of the Republic
summary: Paraguay's old Cabildo building, which has served as a colonial seat of power, the national congress, and now a cultural center, holds Jesuit wood carvings, Agustín Barrios's guitar, and the library named for Augusto Roa Bastos.

subject: Curicó
summary: The capital of Chilean wine country, where sixty Canary palms shade a historic square, a world-record cake once rose, and a monument honors the Mapuche leader who fought and died nearby.

subject: Custer Creek train wreck
summary: Montana's deadliest rail disaster, when a flash flood collapsed a bridge beneath the Olympian in the dark of a June night in 1938.

subject: Cyzicus
summary: Once one of the wealthiest cities in the ancient world, Cyzicus commanded the Sea of Marmara from its tombolo peninsula, minted gold coins that circulated across the Mediterranean, and raised a temple to Hadrian so colossal that its columns dwarfed even those at Baalbek — before earthquake and plunder reduced it to silence.

subject: DESY
summary: A campus of low halls in western Hamburg sitting on kilometres of buried accelerator tunnel, where the gluon was found, the ribosome was decoded, and X-ray lasers were invented.

subject: DIII-D
summary: In a building on the General Atomics campus north of La Jolla, a magnetic chamber heats plasma to temperatures ten times hotter than the sun's core — and has been doing so for research purposes since the late 1980s.

subject: Da Lat Station
summary: A 1938 Art Deco railway station in the Vietnamese highlands that survived a war, a dismantled railway, and decades of silence to become one of Vietnam's most beloved architectural landmarks.

subject: Dahlonega, Georgia
summary: The Cherokee word means 'yellow,' and the hills delivered on the name -- Dahlonega was the site of America's first significant gold rush, a decade before California, and the phrase 'Thar's gold in them thar hills' was born on its courthouse steps.

story.title: The White Finger Pointing at the Sky

subject: Dai Heiwa Kinen Tō
summary: Rising 180 meters above the suburbs of southern Osaka, the Dai Heiwa Kinen To is a massive white cenotaph tower built in 1970 by the Church of Perfect Liberty -- a memorial to every war victim in human history, regardless of nation, race, or creed, and a landmark so enormous yet so seldom discussed that locals call it one of Osaka's best-kept secrets.

story.title: Daian-ji: The Temple That Followed the Capital

subject: Daian-ji
summary: Founded by Emperor Jomei in 639 as Japan's first official temple, Daian-ji was relocated and renamed at least four times across a century of capital shifts before reaching Nara, where it became one of the Seven Great Temples -- and then slowly faded into a fragment of its former self.

subject: Daigo Fukuryū Maru
summary: A Japanese tuna fishing boat whose 23 crew members were contaminated by nuclear fallout from the Castle Bravo hydrogen bomb test at Bikini Atoll in 1954, sparking Japan's anti-nuclear movement and inspiring the original Godzilla film.

story.title: Daigo-ji: The Cream of Buddhist Thought

subject: Daigo-ji
summary: A thousand-year-old Buddhist temple complex sprawling across 6.6 million square meters of Mount Daigo, where the oldest wooden building in Kyoto still stands beside a pagoda that has survived earthquakes, civil wars, and typhoons since 951 AD.

subject: Daikaku-ji
summary: An imperial palace turned Shingon Buddhist temple in western Kyoto, where emperors ruled from behind monastery walls and a 1,200-year-old pond still hosts moon-viewing parties in the style of the Heian court.

story.title: Daikandai-ji: The Grand Temple That Burned Before It Was Finished

subject: Daikandai-ji
summary: The ruins of what was once the largest Buddhist temple of the Asuka period, with a presumed nine-story pagoda and a Main Hall stretching 45 meters long -- destroyed by fire while its gate and corridors were still under construction.

subject: Daisen-in
summary: A 500-year-old Zen sub-temple in Kyoto whose narrow rock garden compresses an entire human life -- from turbulent youth to serene old age -- into a strip of raked gravel barely wider than a hallway.

subject: Daitoku-ji
summary: One of Kyoto's largest Zen temple complexes, where a wooden statue in a gate once so offended a warlord that it led to a tea master's ritual suicide -- and where a gate called 'Higurashimon' earned its name because visitors forget the sun is setting while gazing at it.

subject: Daizen-ji
summary: Japan's 'Grape Temple' -- a Shingon Buddhist sanctuary in Yamanashi where an eighth-century monk's vision of the Medicine Buddha holding grapes launched Japanese viticulture, and whose 1290 main hall remains the oldest building in the prefecture.

subject: Daku Balay
summary: Bacolod's art deco Boat House, designed by a sugar planter who never left the Philippines, built to tower over a rival's home, and commandeered as the Japanese seat of power during World War II.

subject: Dalian PX protest
summary: A rare successful citizen protest in China forced the relocation of a toxic chemical factory from Dalian after a typhoon exposed the danger it posed to millions.

subject: Daliburgh
summary: A crofting township in South Uist where the Co-op, the chip shop, and the annual Gaelic music school all share the same junction.

subject: Damghan
summary: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on the Iranian plateau, Damghan has 7,000 years of layered history including Iran's oldest mosque, Assassin mountain fortresses, and the birthplace of a Qajar shah.

subject: Danevirke
summary: Northern Europe's largest archaeological monument: a chain of ramparts thrown across the neck of Jutland over a thousand years, abandoned without a fight in 1864, and saved from destruction in 1944 by one archaeologist with a telephone.

subject: Dar al-Fonun
summary: Iran's first modern university, founded in 1851 by a grand vizier who was executed just weeks after its doors opened, trained the nation's first generation of Western-educated engineers, doctors, and military officers.

subject: Dar al-Manasir
summary: The Nile's S-bend at the Fourth Cataract created a network of fourteen inhabited islands. A dam drowned them and dispersed the people who called them home.

subject: Dartmoor Tin Mining
summary: For two thousand years the granite of Dartmoor gave up its tin to streamworkers, beamworks, and deep shafts - and the miners gave themselves their own parliament to govern it all.

story.title: Daruma-ji: The Temple Built on an Empty Tomb

subject: Daruma-ji
summary: A Zen temple in Nara Prefecture stands over a tomb that was sealed for a starving man in 613 AD, only to be found empty days later -- a mystery that has drawn pilgrims and scholars for over a thousand years.

subject: Daugavpils Ghetto
summary: A 19th-century fortress on the south bank of the Daugava River, converted in 1941 into a holding pen for the Jewish community of Latgale before they were taken to the Pogulanka forest.

subject: Daulis
summary: A near-impregnable citadel high on the Parnassus heights, ancient Daulis was where myth set the terrible story of Tereus, Procne, and Philomela — and where real armies repeatedly failed to dislodge its inhabitants.

subject: David Grant USAF Medical Center
summary: The Air Force's largest medical center in the continental United States, born as a 125-bed wartime hospital and forged by every American conflict since World War II into a half-million-patient institution on a hill above Travis Air Force Base.

subject: David Livingstone
summary: The Scottish mill-boy missionary explorer whose African servants carried his body 1,500 miles to the coast - and whose legacy is the complicated one of humanitarian work tangled with imperial expansion.

subject: Davidstow Circuit
summary: A wartime RAF airfield on Bodmin Moor that became Cornwall's only Formula One racing circuit for four foggy summers between 1952 and 1955, then quietly disappeared.

subject: Daybreak Star Cultural Center
summary: Born from a 1970 occupation of surplus military land, this Native American cultural center in Discovery Park stands as a monument to urban indigenous activism.

story.title: Dayr-e Gachin: The Mother of Iranian Caravanserais

subject: Dayr-e Gachin
summary: A fortress-like caravanserai standing alone in the heart of Iran's Kavir desert, built by Sasanian kings and rebuilt across empires, earning its reputation as the mother of all Iranian roadside shelters.

subject: De Grolsch Veste
summary: FC Twente's home stadium - a fortress named for a brewery, scarred by a 2011 roof collapse that killed two construction workers, and rebuilt with a monument standing where they fell.

subject: De Hoop, Stiens
summary: A Frisian grain mill called The Hope, demolished in 1922, brought back to life in the 1970s and 1990s with two million guilders, computer-controlled valves, and a stubborn refusal to let an empty stone base stay empty.

subject: De Huinsermolen
summary: Five windmills started draining the Huinserpolder in 1828. A year later a single new mill took over the job — and almost two centuries on, it is still moving the water that keeps the polder dry.

subject: De Marssumermolen
summary: Most polder mills only pump one direction. De Marssumermolen, built in 1903 with two crown wheels and two Archimedes screws, can drain the polder, flood it, or just stir the water in a closed circuit — and was the first mill in Friesland used to teach new millers their craft.

subject: De Olde Molen
summary: A 19th-century Dutch windmill disassembled in Groningen, shipped across the Atlantic, and reassembled in Aruba -- where it now turns the wrong way.

subject: De Oude Meerdijk
summary: On 5 August 1992, FC Barcelona came to a small Dutch provincial stadium to test new floodlights at halftime of a friendly. Three decades later, the same lights flash for goal celebrations at FC Emmen home games.

subject: De Poll
summary: A heath kept deliberately empty as a defense against raiders became a flax-merchant's estate, then a banker's villa, then a golf course, then briefly the command post for a hostage crisis.

subject: De Steenhuistermolen, Stiens
summary: A short, squat polder mill near Stiens that survived a storm, a windpump, and an electric motor - and is now kept in reserve, just in case the wind is ever needed again.

subject: De Zwaluw, Burdaard
summary: The Swallow still grinds flour every day in Burdaard - a five-storey stage mill that replaced its predecessor and then quietly outlived almost every working windmill north of it.

subject: DeJarnette Sanitarium
summary: A Georgian-Revival psychiatric hospital in Staunton, Virginia, founded by a eugenicist whose advocacy for forced sterilization Nazi Germany openly admired.

subject: Deakin, Western Australia
summary: At the last siding before the South Australian border, a copper plug set in a concrete obelisk decides exactly where one Australian state ends and the next begins.

subject: Death of Edgar Allan Poe
summary: On October 3, 1849, America's master of mystery was found delirious in a Baltimore tavern wearing someone else's clothes -- and his own death became the greatest unsolved puzzle he never wrote.

subject: Death of Elisa Lam
summary: In February 2013, Canadian tourist Elisa Lam was found dead in a rooftop water tank at downtown Los Angeles's Cecil Hotel, three weeks after elevator security footage of her last known moments went viral.

subject: Death of Rebecca Zahau
summary: On July 13, 2011, Rebecca Mawii Zahau — a Burmese-American woman — was found hanging at her boyfriend's Coronado beach house, her hands and feet bound. Authorities ruled it suicide. A civil jury disagreed.

subject: Death of Sandra Bland
summary: A routine traffic stop on University Drive in Prairie View, Texas escalated into an arrest, a jail cell death, a national movement, and a state law that now bears Sandra Bland's name.

subject: Debre Maryam Qorqor
summary: A rock-hewn church carved into the Tigray cliffs, reached only by a 45-minute climb, where 13th-century frescoes depict the Virgin Mary with Christ in utero.

story.title: The Nerve Center of the Wabash

subject: Decatur station (Illinois)
summary: A story of the Decatur station's transition from a railroad headquarters to a sanctuary for antiques.

subject: Deception Pass
summary: A strait named after the mistake it caused, where eight-knot tides boil under a 1935 steel bridge and more than three million visitors a year come to watch the water.

subject: Deekshabhoomi
summary: The ground where hundreds of thousands of people renounced the caste system in a single day, and where the largest hollow stupa in the world now marks what one man set in motion.

subject: Del Mar Skate Ranch
summary: For nine years in the late 1970s and 1980s, a skatepark in a Del Mar parking lot was one of the most influential pieces of concrete in the history of skateboarding — and Tony Hawk, Rodney Mullen, and Danny Way all skated there before it was demolished for a hotel.

subject: Deltapark Neeltje Jans
summary: A theme park built on a man-made island that exists only because engineers needed somewhere to stand while building a barrier that holds back the North Sea.

subject: Dendra
summary: A Mycenaean cemetery near Midea in the Argolid that yielded Europe's oldest known bronze armor — a complete articulated panoply sealed in a chamber tomb since the 15th century BCE.

story.title: Denver: The Mile High City Where Gold Ran Out and Weed Got Legal

subject: Denver
summary: The Colorado capital built on gold rushes that busted and thin air that athletes covet - where the airport conspiracy theories are actually intentional, where Coors built an empire, and where cannabis became a billion-dollar legitimate industry.

subject: Department of San Martín
summary: Where the eastern Andes dissolve into the upper Amazon, a rainforest department named for a liberator shelters jungle cities, cloud-forest ruins, and one of Peru's rarest monkeys.

subject: Der Aa-kerk
summary: On a quiet morning in April 1710 the tower of this Groningen church collapsed for no apparent reason, killing two people and destroying the Schnitger organ inside. They rebuilt it. And then they brought in another Schnitger.

subject: Derge Parkhang
summary: A printing temple in Kham that has preserved Tibetan literature for nearly three centuries using the same hand-carved woodblocks and cinnabar ink techniques since its founding in 1729.

subject: Derzhprom
summary: The Soviet Union's first skyscraper, a Constructivist colossus of concrete towers and sky-bridges that rose over Kharkiv in 1928 and survived a world war before a 2024 bomb.

subject: Desamparados station
summary: Lima's Beaux-Arts railway station, built in 1912 as the terminus of one of the world's highest railways, now houses Peru's national literature museum while still running occasional trains to the Andean highlands.

subject: Deshengmen
summary: Beijing's Gate of Virtuous Triumph once sent armies to war and welcomed them home, and its surviving archery tower now stands as an island of Ming dynasty stone in a sea of modern traffic.

subject: Destrehan Plantation
summary: The oldest documented plantation house in the lower Mississippi Valley survived Spanish rule, slave revolts, an oil refinery, and treasure hunters to stand as a haunting witness to Louisiana's tangled past.

story.title: Detroit: The City That Motorized America and Then Broke Down

subject: Detroit
summary: The Michigan metropolis that put the world on wheels and then watched those wheels drive away - where Henry Ford invented mass production, where Motown invented soul, and where the ruins of American industry stand as monuments to what was.

subject: Devil's Slide
summary: A landslide-prone coastal promontory between Pacifica and Montara that devoured highways for decades, hid World War II bunkers, and finally surrendered to a tunnel that turned the old road into a trail.

subject: Devipuram
summary: A temple complex near Visakhapatnam built in the shape of a sacred geometric diagram, founded by a nuclear physicist who left his career to follow visions of the Divine Mother.

subject: Dewa Sanzan
summary: Three sacred peaks in northern Japan where Shugendo mountain ascetics have trained for over 1,400 years, and where the holiest shrine guards a secret that pilgrims are forbidden to reveal.

subject: Dialogue in the Dark
summary: In a Speicherstadt warehouse, blind and partially sighted guides lead sighted visitors through a world with the lights switched off - and the usual hierarchy of competence quietly inverted.

story.title: Diamond Interchange: How a Simple Idea Reshapes Towns Like Julich

subject: Diamond Interchange
summary: Look down at the autobahn at Julich and you see a strange object: two roundabouts on either side of the bridge, connected by ramps. It is a turbo dumbbell, one variation in a family of interchanges all descended from the humblest highway shape of all, the diamond.

subject: Diergaarde Blijdorp
summary: The Rotterdam zoo that escaped a Nazi firebombing by moving house three years early - and has been planning, building, and outlasting trouble ever since.

subject: Din Dryfol
summary: A 5,000-year-old Neolithic chambered tomb on Anglesey - built in three successive phases over centuries, with one fallen capstone and a three-metre portal stone still standing watch in the field.

subject: Dinorwic Quarry
summary: Seven hundred acres of stepped purple galleries, once the second-largest slate quarry in the world - now a museum, a film set, and the visible roof of one of Europe's most powerful hydroelectric stations.

subject: Diocese of Canterbury
summary: Founded in 597 by Augustine of Canterbury, the Diocese of Canterbury is the oldest see in the Church of England - the place from which Christianity spread across the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

subject: Diocese of Charlotte
summary: The Catholic diocese covering 46 western North Carolina counties grew from fewer than 700 Catholics in 1868 to over 530,000 today - centered on Charlotte's Cathedral of Saint Patrick.

subject: Diocese of Hong Kong
summary: The Catholic Diocese of Hong Kong, established as a prefecture apostolic in 1841 to care for Irish soldiers, has grown into a church of nearly 400,000 faithful navigating the fault lines between Rome, Beijing, and Hong Kong's own political identity.

subject: Diocese of Osnabrück
summary: The oldest see Charlemagne ever founded - and the only one that for 150 years rotated, by treaty, between a Catholic bishop and a Lutheran prince of the British royal house.

subject: Diocese of Raleigh
summary: From 350 Catholics in 1860 to half a million today, the Diocese of Raleigh has spent 150 years building eastern North Carolina's Catholic life across 54 counties.

subject: Diocese of Richmond
