summary: Established in 1820 in a colony that had outlawed Catholic practice a century earlier, the Diocese of Richmond now serves over 226,000 Catholics across central and southern Virginia from its seat at Sacred Heart Cathedral.

subject: Diocese of Sodor and Man
summary: The Church of England diocese that the Reverend W. Awdry borrowed when he invented the fictional Island of Sodor for Thomas the Tank Engine.

subject: Diocese of the Isles
summary: A medieval bishopric stretching from the Isle of Man to the Outer Hebrides, governed for centuries from a small Norse-built cathedral on a rocky islet off Peel.

subject: Dipsea Trail
summary: A 7.5-mile trail from Mill Valley to Stinson Beach that hosts America's oldest invitational trail race, running since 1905.

subject: Dipylon
summary: The largest gate of the ancient world, where the great Panathenaic procession began and one of the oldest texts in the Greek alphabet was scratched onto a wine jug.

story.title: Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations

subject: Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations
summary: Inside a Brussels building that never sleeps, the EU's humanitarian arm tracks earthquakes, evacuates citizens, and funds aid in more than 80 countries.

subject: Discovery Place
summary: Charlotte's hands-on science museum traces its lineage to a 1946 schoolteacher's collection - and now anchors a network including an IMAX dome and three sister sites.

subject: Doai Station
summary: Japan's deepest railway station, where catching a northbound train means descending 486 steps into a tunnel 70 meters underground -- earning it the nickname 'Japan's Number One Mole Station.'

subject: Doberan Minster
summary: An order that forbade ornament built, in a Mecklenburg swamp, the most completely furnished medieval church interior in northern Germany - and almost all of it is still there.

subject: Doleib Hill
summary: A Presbyterian mission on the Sobat River that became one of the most important schools for the Shilluk people, twice shuttered by civil war, and a site where the headmaster of the girls' school was killed in 1965 for the crime of teaching.

subject: Domaine de Marie
summary: Inaugurated in 1942 atop a Da Lat hill, the Domaine de Marie convent blends seventeenth-century French architecture with Vietnamese highland life — and has operated as a working religious community, school, and kindergarten ever since.

subject: Dome of the Rock
summary: The golden-domed octagonal shrine on Jerusalem's Temple Mount is the oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture, built in 691-692 CE atop one of the most contested sacred sites on Earth.

subject: Doncaster Minster
summary: Sir George Gilbert Scott's Victorian rebuild after the 1853 fire is the most cathedral-like parish church the prolific Gothic Revival architect ever designed.

subject: Donegal Town
summary: The 'fort of the foreigners' was once the capital of a Gaelic kingdom, lost its castle to the English in 1607, and 410 years later was named the world's coolest destination by National Geographic.

subject: Donner Pass
summary: A mountain notch in the northern Sierra Nevada became California's gateway, witness to pioneer tragedy, railroad triumph, and some of the heaviest snowfall in the contiguous United States.

subject: Donoughmore
summary: A rural Cork parish that produced two American bishops, three Titanic passengers, a bronze relic-shrine now in the National Museum, and an Earl named for it who never actually lived there.

subject: Doon Hill
summary: An extinct volcano's throat now rises 67 metres above the Errismore peninsula, with the ruins of Bunowen Castle - confiscated from the O'Flahertys by Cromwell - at its feet.

subject: Doonshean
summary: A windswept townland east of Dingle where a sea stack shaped like a foal stands offshore and a promontory fort guards the cliffs.

subject: Doopsgezinde kerk, Haarlem
summary: A 17th-century Mennonite hidden church in Haarlem, entered through inconspicuous doors that conceal a quiet sanctuary built by people who learned to worship out of sight.

subject: Doppelkirche Schwarzrheindorf
summary: A twelfth-century archbishop built himself a private chapel with two churches stacked inside one building - one for the nobility, one for everyone else - and decorated both with frescos that have survived eight hundred and seventy years.

subject: Dos Palmas Kidnappings
summary: On May 27, 2001, Abu Sayyaf militants seized twenty hostages from a luxury resort on Honda Bay, Palawan, triggering a year-long crisis that drew American military forces into the southern Philippines.

subject: Douglas Head
summary: Manx fishermen, RNLI gunners, radar engineers, and the makers of Waking Ned all left their fingerprints on this rocky promontory south of Douglas harbour.

subject: Douglas Lifeboat Station
summary: On the Manx pier where Sir William Hillary launched into a storm with six broken ribs, the RNLI's founding station still keeps a lifeboat ready at Battery Pier.

subject: Dover Air Force Base
summary: The busiest military air freight terminal in the Department of Defense, Dover AFB has served as America's gateway for airlift operations and as the solemn port through which fallen service members return home.

subject: Dover Priory
summary: The fairest church in that quarter of Kent vanished into housing and a railway yard - but its 12th-century refectory still serves Dover College, and the Dover Bible still rests in a Cambridge library, the last fragments of a lost world.

subject: Dovzhenko Film Studios
summary: Kyiv's great film studio shot its very first movie at night, because by day the crews were still building the walls around them.

subject: Downpatrick
summary: A drumlin above the River Quoile holds a cathedral, a granite slab, and the traditional grave of Saint Patrick - one of Ireland's oldest towns built on top of all of it.

subject: Drachenfels (Siebengebirge)
summary: The hill where Siegfried killed the dragon, where Lord Byron wrote a stanza, and where Cologne Cathedral's stone came from.

subject: Dragoon Springs Stage Station Site
summary: A stone fortress in the Arizona desert where six graves tell the intertwined story of frontier massacre, Civil War combat, and the final chapter of the Apache Wars.

subject: Drommedaris
summary: A stone harbour gate built in 1540 that has been, in turn, a fort, a prison, a gunpowder store, a telegraph office, and a student bar - and still rings the hour, every quarter, day and night.

subject: Drumlane
summary: An Augustinian monastery founded in the 6th century by Saint Columba in the drumlin country of west Cavan, ruined by Viking raiders, rebuilt in stone, burned in clan wars, dissolved by Henry VIII — and home to one of the last surviving round towers in the Diocese of Kilmore.

subject: Dry Tortugas
summary: America's most remote national park and its strangest prison - where Fort Jefferson rises from a tiny island 70 miles from Key West, built to guard the Gulf but best known for holding Dr. Samuel Mudd, who set John Wilkes Booth's broken leg.

subject: Du Toitskloof Pass
summary: Named for a seventeenth-century Huguenot refugee, Du Toitskloof Pass was carved from an animal track through the Western Cape mountains during World War II and served as the main route between Paarl and Worcester until a tunnel replaced it in 1988.

subject: Dubh Artach
summary: A 145-foot Stevenson lighthouse balanced on a black basalt skerry 15 miles offshore in the open Atlantic, built between 1867 and 1872 in conditions so brutal that 92-foot waves regularly broke against its base - and the future writer Robert Louis Stevenson watched his father do it.

subject: Duchy of Athens
summary: For 250 years a French knight and his Catalan and Florentine successors ruled Athens from the Acropolis, and the Parthenon said Mass as a Catholic cathedral.

subject: Dudinka
summary: The world's only port that evacuates its cranes every spring, Dudinka has served as the Arctic gateway to Norilsk since 1667.

subject: Duitse Huis
summary: Founded in 1348 as a Teutonic Knights monastery, this Utrecht complex hosted Charles V and the Order of the Golden Fleece in 1546 - and seven centuries later still belongs to the same order, now turned charity.

subject: Duluth Depot
summary: A French Norman-style railroad palace built in 1892 from local granite and sandstone, the Duluth Union Depot once served seven railroads hauling iron ore and passengers along Lake Superior's shores -- and after narrowly escaping demolition in the 1970s, it reinvented itself as a thriving arts and heritage center.

subject: Dulwich Picture Gallery
summary: England's oldest public art gallery, designed by Sir John Soane for a collection commissioned by a vanished Polish king, and home to the most frequently stolen painting in history.

subject: Dumbarton
summary: The fort of the Britons stood on an ancient volcanic plug, capital of a lost kingdom and birthplace of a Formula 1 world champion and David Byrne.

subject: Dun Bharabhat, Great Bernera
summary: An Iron Age semi-broch built on an islet in a small loch on Great Bernera, reached by a 30-metre causeway and preserved because there was no easy way to steal its stones.

subject: Dun Carloway
summary: An Iron Age broch on the west coast of Lewis where walls still stand nine metres tall after two thousand years, and where a clan feud once ended with a man climbing the stones using two daggers.

subject: Dun Telve
summary: One of the two best-preserved Iron Age brochs anywhere on mainland Scotland, a 2,000-year-old drystone tower still standing 10 metres tall on the bank of a small Highland burn.

subject: Dun Troddan
summary: An Iron Age broch standing four hundred and seventy metres east of its sister tower Dun Telve, still tall enough at the start of the eighteenth century to be sketched as the most intact broch in Scotland.

subject: Dundee Contemporary Arts
summary: Opened in 1999 in a converted Nethergate garage, DCA is a two-gallery, two-cinema, print-studio art centre that helped reinvent Dundee's cultural quarter and was nominated Art Fund Museum of the Year in 2024.

subject: Dunfermline
summary: The ancient capital of Scotland, burial place of Robert the Bruce and birthplace of Andrew Carnegie, where royal patronage built an abbey and a steelmaker's fortune built the world's first Carnegie library.

subject: Dunfermline
summary: Once the working capital of Scotland and the burial place of Robert the Bruce, Dunfermline was reborn as the birthplace of Andrew Carnegie and the site of the world's first Carnegie library.

subject: Duoliang Station
summary: A former Taiwan Railway station in Taimali Township that closed due to low ridership in 2006, then became one of Taiwan's most visited destinations — its empty platform perched above the Pacific, looking out over what many consider the island's most beautiful stretch of coastline.

subject: Duvillaun
summary: A cluster of seven black islands off the Mullet Peninsula where storm petrels nest in the ruins of abandoned cottages, and a six-foot stone slab carved with a crucifixion has stood for 1,300 years.

subject: Dwarfie Stane
summary: Britain's only known Neolithic rock-cut tomb - a chamber and two side cells hollowed out of a single block of Old Red Sandstone on the island of Hoy.

subject: Dynamic Earth (Edinburgh)
summary: Built on the site of an old brewery where James Hutton once formulated the principles of modern geology, Dynamic Earth tells the story of the planet from its fiery origin to its uncertain future.

subject: Dáil Éireann
summary: Ireland's parliament traces an unbroken line back to a clandestine 1919 meeting of 27 rebels in the Mansion House -- an assembly the British Empire considered illegal and which only Soviet Russia recognised.

subject: Dōjō-ji
summary: A 1,300-year-old Buddhist temple in Wakayama whose legend of a woman scorned -- transformed into a serpent who melted a bronze bell to kill the monk hiding inside -- has haunted Japanese theater for a millennium.

subject: ENIAC
summary: Built in secret at the University of Pennsylvania during World War II, ENIAC was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer -- a 30-ton machine of 18,000 vacuum tubes that ushered in the computing age.

subject: Eaglehawk Neck
summary: A strip of land barely thirty metres wide once held back an entire prison peninsula, guarded by a line of chained, snarling dogs.

subject: Earls Cove, British Columbia
summary: A two-berth ferry terminal at the mouth of the deepest fjord on the British Columbia coast, and the hinge that holds the roadless Sunshine Coast together.

subject: Easington Catchment Area
summary: A cluster of North Sea gas fields named for Greek and Roman gods, a turbojet inventor and a Georgian chemist, all piping their gas back to one Yorkshire terminal.

subject: Eassie Stone
summary: A mid-8th-century Pictish cross-slab sheltered inside a ruined church in Angus, the Eassie Stone bears angels, warriors, hunting scenes, and symbols that place it among the finest examples of early medieval Scottish sculpture.

subject: Eastern Biniac naveta
summary: A Bronze Age tomb near the heart of Menorca that spent centuries as a cattle shed, its ancient dead long since scoured away.

subject: Eastern Isles
summary: Twelve uninhabited islets off the south-east of St Martin's, where a Roman shrine, Bronze Age cairns, and a sea stack named Hanjague hold four thousand years of human absence and presence.

subject: Eastern Netherlands
summary: Forget the windmills and tulips for a moment - the Netherlands has a quiet eastern quarter of Hanseatic riverports, heath deserts, Van Gogh paintings in a hidden museum, and a language the rest of the country does not fully speak.

subject: Eastern Qing tombs
summary: Five emperors, fifteen empresses, and 136 concubines lie buried across 80 square kilometers of mountain-ringed landscape at the Eastern Qing Tombs, China's largest and most complete imperial mausoleum complex.

subject: Ebbw Vale Steelworks
summary: From a population of 120 farmers in 1790 to the largest steel mill in Europe by the 1930s, Ebbw Vale's rise and fall is the South Wales story in one valley.

subject: Eberswalde Hoard
summary: Germany's greatest prehistoric gold find came out of a brass factory yard in 1913, vanished from Berlin in 1945, and has been in Moscow ever since.

subject: Ed-Deir, Petra
summary: Carved into a sandstone cliff in the mid-first century AD, Petra's Monastery stands 47 meters high with a facade nearly as wide -- a Nabataean monument that blends Hellenistic grandeur with Mesopotamian austerity, reached only by climbing 800 ancient steps.

subject: Edfu
summary: Home to the most completely preserved temple in Egypt - a Ptolemaic monument to the falcon-god Horus that desert sand buried, and then protected, for two thousand years.

subject: Edgar Thomson Steel Works
summary: The last integrated steel mill standing in Pittsburgh's Mon Valley - still pouring molten steel on a site where British soldiers fell in 1755, Whiskey Rebels rallied in 1794, and Andrew Carnegie launched the empire that made America a steel superpower.

subject: Edible Schoolyard
summary: What began as a chef's experiment in a vacant school lot has grown into a network of over 6,200 kitchen-garden programs worldwide, redefining what counts as a classroom.

subject: Edificio del Seguro Obrero
summary: An elegant Art Deco tower a few steps from Chile's presidential palace - and the site where 59 young men were executed by police in 1938 after they had already surrendered.

subject: Edifício Itália
summary: A 46-story monument to Italian immigrant ambition in the heart of São Paulo, where Queen Elizabeth II once stood speechless before an endless skyline.

subject: Edinburgh South
summary: The Victorian villa belt that absorbed students and visitors, where Robert Louis Stevenson summered at Swanston, the world's first kidney transplant was performed, and a Neolithic megalith stands in a suburban driveway.

subject: Edison, Washington
summary: A Skagit flats hamlet of 240 people, named for America's most famous capitalist inventor, that spent a decade as the national headquarters of a socialist utopia - and that later sent Edward R. Murrow off to high school.

subject: Edith Macefield
summary: The Ballard woman who turned down $750,000 to sell her tiny house, forcing developers to build a commercial complex around it.

subject: Education in Northern Ireland
summary: A schooling system that still tests every eleven-year-old for grammar-school selection, still teaches Protestant and Catholic children mostly in separate classrooms, and is slowly trying to change both of those things.

subject: Edward Stratemeyer
summary: The man behind Nancy Drew, the Hardy Boys, and Tom Swift ran a fiction factory from Newark that sold over 500 million books - yet most readers never learned his name.

story.title: Eigen-ji: The Temple of the Hidden Buddha

subject: Eigen-ji
summary: The head temple of an entire branch of Rinzai Zen Buddhism, founded by a poet-monk in 1361, keeps its principal image locked behind closed doors -- revealed to worshippers only once every quarter century.

subject: Eightercua
summary: Four standing stones in a Kerry field, aligned east to west, hold a story older than the pyramids and a queen who never reached her kingdom.

subject: Eihei-ji
summary: A 13th-century Zen monastery deep in Fukui's cedar forests where more than two hundred monks still rise before dawn to train in the austere traditions of Soto Zen Buddhism.

story.title: Eiho-ji: Seven Centuries of Zen Among the Maples

subject: Eihō-ji
summary: A Kamakura-era Zen temple in Tajimi, Gifu Prefecture, where two National Treasure buildings and a garden designed by the legendary monk Muso Soseki have drawn seekers of stillness for over seven hundred years.

subject: Eilean Donan
summary: Where three sea lochs converge in the western Highlands, a castle rebuilt from its own ruins has become the most photographed fortress in Scotland -- a Mackenzie and MacRae stronghold whose history stretches from Viking raids to Hollywood films.

subject: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
summary: A 1919 opera house where Carlos Gardel once recorded, now lined floor to ceiling with books - and crowned the most beautiful bookstore in the world.

subject: El Celler de Can Roca
summary: Three brothers turned their parents' roadside restaurant near Girona into a temple of Catalan gastronomy, twice ranked the best in the world, where dessert can arrive as a cloud of perfume.

subject: El Cortez (San Diego)
summary: When the El Cortez Hotel opened in 1927, it was the tallest building in San Diego. It hosted presidents and movie stars, installed the first outdoor glass elevator in the country, was stripped of its historic interiors by a televangelist, and nearly met the wrecking ball — before becoming condominiums and a registered landmark.

subject: El Escorial
summary: Philip II built El Escorial as monastery, palace, library, mausoleum, and school -- a single granite complex in the Sierra de Guadarrama that served simultaneously as the center of a global empire and a retreat for a king obsessed with death.

subject: El Infiernito
summary: Spanish conquistadors called this Muisca astronomical observatory 'Little Hell' -- but the 109 pink sandstone monoliths aligned to track solstices and equinoxes reveal a civilization that read the sky with remarkable precision.

subject: El Museo del Barrio
summary: Born from a community's demand that its children learn their own culture, El Museo del Barrio grew from a public school classroom in East Harlem into the oldest Latino art museum in the United States.

subject: El Paraíso stampede
summary: A tear gas canister detonated during a high school prom party in Caracas killed at least 19 young people in June 2018, exposing Venezuela's crisis of weapons proliferation and failing emergency services.

subject: Elbow Cay
summary: A five-mile Bahamian cay where Loyalist settlers built a lighthouse that outlasted the strongest Atlantic hurricane on record, and where residents still rely on VHF radios instead of telephones.

subject: Elephant Tea Rooms
summary: A polychrome Hindu Gothic and Venetian Gothic tea merchant's building in central Sunderland, complete with faience elephants standing on bracketed shelves between its gables.

subject: Elephanta Caves
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage island temple complex in Mumbai Harbor where sixth-century sculptors carved an 18-foot three-faced Shiva from living rock, creating one of the masterpieces of Indian art.

subject: Elephantine
summary: A Nile island at Egypt's ancient southern border, where archaeologists found the letters of a Jewish garrison that worshipped Yahweh in its own temple 2,500 years ago.

subject: Eleusinion
summary: On the north slope of the Acropolis stood the Athens shrine where the secret objects of the Eleusinian Mysteries were guarded before the great procession set out for Eleusis.

subject: Elgin, Moray
summary: A medieval royal burgh in northeast Scotland whose 13th-century cathedral was called the Lantern of the North — burned by the Wolf of Badenoch, stripped by Reformers, and ruined into one of the country's most beautiful Gothic skeletons.

subject: Elland Road
summary: Home of Leeds United since 1919, Elland Road is a 37,645-capacity football cathedral at the foot of Beeston Hill that Alex Ferguson once called the most intimidating venue in Europe.

subject: Ellora Caves
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain temples were carved side by side from the same basalt cliff over four centuries, including the Kailash Temple -- the largest monolithic rock excavation on Earth.

subject: Ely, Cambridgeshire
summary: Rising out of the flat fenland like a ship with stone sails, Ely is one of England's smallest cities — anchored by an extraordinary medieval cathedral, shaped by centuries of fen life, and home to a school that may have educated Edward the Confessor.

subject: Elçi Han
summary: A long-vanished caravanserai in the heart of old Istanbul, the Elçi Han — the Ambassadors' Inn — once lodged foreign envoys on the very ground where Constantine built one of Rome's great forums.

subject: Embarcadero Plaza
summary: A San Francisco plaza whose roaring fountain was designed to drown out a freeway, whose namesake was stripped for displacing minorities, and where Bono was fined for spray-painting a sculpture.

subject: Emerald Triangle (Southeast Asia)
summary: Where Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand converge at the Dangrek Range, the Emerald Triangle marks a tripoint that has passed through armed conflict and emerged as a symbol of regional cooperation — though it took until 1993 to build a pavilion where soldiers once fought.

subject: Emeryville Mudflat Sculptures
summary: For 35 years, anonymous artists built ever-changing sculptures from driftwood and debris on the Emeryville mudflats, creating the Bay Area's strangest drive-in art gallery -- visible only to I-80 commuters -- before ecological restoration reclaimed the shoreline.

subject: Emil Siepmann
summary: The elder of the two Siepmann brothers, whose shovel-and-shovel-fork factory in Warstein grew into one of Germany's largest drop-forge concerns and whose name a Westphalian street still carries.

subject: Eminönü
summary: Where the Golden Horn meets the Bosphorus, Eminönü has been Istanbul's beating commercial heart for two and a half millennia — a waterfront of ferries, spice stalls, mosque domes, and two million daily visitors.

subject: Emperors Yan and Huang
summary: Two colossal stone faces -- each with 3-meter eyes and 8-meter noses -- gaze from a mountainside above the Yellow River near Zhengzhou, a 106-meter monument to China's mythical founding emperors that took 20 years to build.

subject: Emporio, Chios
summary: On a quiet bay in southern Chios, layers of ruins record eight thousand years of people choosing the same harbor, the same spring, the same hill.

subject: Emporium Capwell
summary: The Bay Area department store chain that merged two Gold Rush-era retailers and anchored Market Street for a century before the mall era swept it away.

subject: Enaghbeg
summary: A 401-acre Mayo townland whose history is told through court cases between brothers, a Neolithic portal tomb in a field, and a bone-setter who lived to 106 without ever seeing a train.

subject: Endeavour Hydrothermal Vents
summary: Two kilometers beneath the Pacific, over 800 chimneys of mineral-rich superheated water tower above the seafloor on the Juan de Fuca Ridge -- home to 12 species found nowhere else on Earth and the organism that holds the record for the upper temperature limit of life.

subject: Engaku-ji
summary: Founded in 1282 to honor both sides of the Mongol invasion, Kamakura's second-ranked Zen temple shelters two National Treasures and seven centuries of unbroken meditation practice.

subject: Engels-Haus
summary: The Wuppertal house where the boy who would write the Communist Manifesto grew up - and a traffic light that still wears his face.

story.title: Engineer's Office of the Former Pumping Station

subject: Engineer's Office of the Former Pumping Station
summary: A stubborn red-brick survivor at 344 Shanghai Street in Yau Ma Tei — the only remnant of Hong Kong's oldest pumping station, built in 1895, which nearly vanished beneath a 36-storey tower before its forgotten identity was rediscovered.

subject: English National Opera
summary: A Victorian philanthropist's evening of opera excerpts in a Lambeth music hall became, over a century, one of London's two great opera companies.

subject: Enichi-ji
summary: A 9th-century temple in Fukushima's Aizu highlands that once commanded 3,500 sub-temples and fielded armies in the Genpei War, only to be razed by Date Masamune and later dismantled by government decree -- its ruins now a National Historic Site whispering of vanished power.

subject: Enola Gay
summary: The Boeing B-29 that dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima sits fully restored in a Virginia hangar, still carrying the weight of the moment that split history in two.

subject: Enryaku-ji
summary: A 1,200-year-old Tendai Buddhist monastery on Mount Hiei that once commanded an army of warrior monks, was burned to the ground by warlord Oda Nobunaga in 1571, and remains the training ground for marathon monks who run the equivalent of the Earth's circumference in seven years.

subject: Entsū-in (Matsushima)
summary: A Zen temple in Matsushima where a seventeenth-century mausoleum hides playing-card symbols and roses among its golden interior, evidence of the Date clan's fascination with the Christian West.

subject: Epidaurus
summary: On the Argolid coast, Epidaurus was the ancient world's most celebrated healing sanctuary — where the sick slept in a sacred hall awaiting divine dreams, and where a theatre built for 14,000 people still hosts performances today.

subject: Erasmus MC
summary: The largest teaching hospital in the Netherlands - born in a nineteenth-century corner building, destroyed by the Luftwaffe in 1940, rebuilt across the river, and now ranked first in Europe for clinical medicine.

subject: Eresburg
summary: The largest known Saxon refuge castle, on a flat-topped hill above the Diemel - taken by Charlemagne in 772 in the campaign that destroyed the Irminsul and began thirty years of war.

subject: Erin-ji
summary: A Zen temple where a defiant monk spoke his last words in flames, where a warlord's grave lies beneath garden stones, and where a 14th-century landscape design became the blueprint for Kyoto's most famous gardens.

subject: Erraid
summary: A tidal islet off Mull where the Stevensons quarried lighthouse stone and Robert Louis Stevenson stranded his fictional hero, Davie Balfour, for one hundred hours of cold limpets and pure folly.

subject: Errington, British Columbia
summary: A Vancouver Island farming community named after a line in a Walter Scott ballad, built around a hall the neighbours paid for themselves.

subject: Ershawan Battery
summary: Known as the Tenable Gate of the Sea, this Keelung battery endured bombardment by both French and Japanese warships and served as the command post of Taiwan's first governor.

subject: Es Vedrà
summary: A 413-metre pyramid of limestone off Ibiza's west coast that geology calls ordinary and legend calls magnetic — home to sirens, a goddess, a visionary friar, and a modern cult following.

subject: Eski Dürbe
summary: A silent domed tomb in Bakhchysarai keeps a secret nobody has solved: no one knows who lies inside, or even for certain when it was built.

subject: Eski Saray
summary: The Old Palace was Mehmed the Conqueror's first great residence after he took Constantinople in 1453, but it was gradually sidelined to become a gilded retirement home for displaced women of the imperial household — until a catastrophic fire in 1687 killed its last royal resident and left nothing standing.

subject: Espace Léopold
summary: A glass-domed parliament the Belgians nicknamed after a cheese, hosting a chamber that legally sits empty three weeks out of four because its real home is 435 kilometres away.

story.title: Espaço Cultural José Lins do Rego

subject: Espaço Cultural José Lins do Rego
summary: Sérgio Bernardes wrapped a planetarium, a comics library, two theatres and a novelist's sewing machine under a single steel roof called the White Wing.

subject: Essen Hauptbahnhof
summary: A railway station built on iron because the coal mines below kept moving the ground.

subject: Essen Minster
summary: A thousand-year cathedral that grew up around a women's abbey, with the oldest Madonna in the West sleeping in its side chapel.

subject: Estación Mapocho
summary: A grand Beaux-Arts train station built for Chile's centennial, saved from demolition and reborn as one of Santiago's great cultural halls.

subject: Estadio Centenario
summary: The only stadium FIFA has ever named a Historical Monument of World Football, built in nine frantic months to host the first World Cup final in 1930.

subject: Estadio Monumental
summary: South America's largest stadium, where Argentina lifted its first World Cup in 1978 under a dictatorship - and where the world's biggest acts still come to play.

subject: Estação das Docas
summary: Three iron warehouses built to load rubber, reopened in 2000 as Belém's waterfront cultural complex - with the dissolved ruins of a 1665 fort serving as its amphitheatre.

subject: Estádio Nacional Mané Garrincha
summary: A $900 million stadium built for seven World Cup matches, named after the crooked-legged Brazilian winger who won two World Cups despite scoliosis, polio, and one leg shorter than the other.

subject: Estádio Presidente Vargas (Ceará)
summary: Fortaleza's historic downtown stadium, known as the PV - grass pitch, 1941 vintage, and home to the fiercest local rivalries in Ceará football.

subject: Ether Dome
summary: A domed amphitheater inside Massachusetts General Hospital where, on October 16, 1846, a dentist silenced the screams of surgery forever -- and where a 2,500-year-old Egyptian mummy watched it happen.

subject: Etruria Works
summary: Josiah Wedgwood's purpose-built ceramics factory on the Trent and Mersey Canal, opened in 1769 and named for an ancient Italian civilization Wedgwood believed (mistakenly) had made the painted vases he was copying.

subject: Eucla, Western Australia
summary: Once a telegraph hub of a hundred people, Eucla now watches the desert slowly bury and unbury the ruins of the station that gave it life.

subject: Eugene O'Neill National Historic Site
summary: Tucked in the hills above Danville, California, Tao House is where America's only Nobel Prize-winning playwright wrote his greatest works -- and where his restless life finally found stillness.

subject: Eureka (ferryboat)
summary: The largest wooden passenger ferry ever built, now preserved at Hyde Street Pier -- one of only two surviving vessels with a walking beam engine.

subject: EuroBasket 1995
summary: In an Athens arena in the summer of 1995, a basketball final became a window onto a continent coming apart, where a single player scored 41 points and a championship was decided amid a tournament-wide refusal to play.

subject: EuroBasket Women 2025
summary: The 40th Women's European Basketball Championship came to Piraeus in 2025, where a record-breaking crowd of 10,503 fans packed the Peace and Friendship Stadium for Greece's do-or-die battle against Turkey.

subject: Euronext Amsterdam
summary: The world's first modern stock exchange, born in 1602 when Dutch merchants invented the idea of selling shares in a single voyage to a crowd of strangers.

subject: Europa Point
summary: The southernmost tip of Gibraltar where a 19th-century lighthouse, a mosque gifted by Saudi Arabia, and a 15th-century Catholic shrine stand within steps of each other, marking the boundary between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.

subject: European Air Transport Command
summary: From a single office building on a Dutch airbase, seven European nations pool the cargo planes that move their armies.

subject: European Medicines Agency
summary: How a single Brexit vote forced 900 EU regulators to pack up a London office and move every drug approval for a continent of 450 million people to a new building in Amsterdam.

subject: European Schools
summary: Eight years after World War II, the first European School opened in Luxembourg with a radical premise: teach the children of former enemies in each other's languages, side by side.

subject: Europol
summary: Europol cannot arrest anyone. It is the European Union's central intelligence hub for serious cross-border crime, and that limitation is precisely what makes it work.

subject: Eurovision Song Contest 1994
summary: Ireland won its third Eurovision in a row at the Point Theatre on 30 April 1994 -- but everyone remembers the seven-minute interval act instead. Riverdance made its debut that night and never sat down again.

subject: Eurovision Song Contest 2006
summary: When Finland's monster-costumed heavy metal band Lordi won Eurovision 2006 at the Olympic Indoor Hall in Athens — Finland's first win in 45 years of competing — the contest had never heard anything quite like it.

subject: Eurovision Young Musicians 2016
summary: On a September evening in 2016, eleven teenagers played classical music in the shadow of Cologne Cathedral - and a Polish saxophonist walked away with the trophy.

subject: Evenburg
summary: A neo-Gothic moated castle near Leer that started as a colonel's gift to his wife - and started, more practically, as a way to pay off his gambling debts.

subject: Ewald Colliery
summary: The fortress-like Malakow tower of Shaft 1 has its name painted on the wrong side - facing away from the road that was supposed to make it famous. The pit closed in 2001. The tower still glares the wrong way.

subject: Ex-Voto of Daochos
summary: A nine-figure marble monument dedicated at Delphi around 336–332 BCE by the Thessalian ruler Daochos II, including the famous statue of the pankratiast Agias attributed to the workshop of Lysippus.

subject: Exchange Square (Hong Kong)
summary: The three-tower complex in Central that has housed the Hong Kong Stock Exchange since the 1980s — built during a financial high tide, financed through a crisis, and adorned with sculptures by Henry Moore and Elisabeth Frink.

story.title: Expo '70: When Japan Invited the World to the Future

subject: Expo '70
summary: The first world's fair ever held in Asia drew 64 million visitors to the Senri Hills outside Osaka in 1970, showcasing Moon rocks, the first IMAX film, a spherical concert hall, and an avant-garde Tower of the Sun that still stands today.

subject: Eyemouth
summary: A Berwickshire fishing port whose narrow vennels, sixteenth-century artillery fort, and the catastrophic 1881 disaster still shape the rhythm of every harbour morning.

subject: Eyre Telegraph Station
summary: An 1897 limestone telegraph station, marooned in the dunes for fifty years, reborn as Australia's first bird observatory.

subject: FAME Studios
summary: A tiny recording studio in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, where a self-taught fiddler named Rick Hall forged the most improbable hit factory in American music, launching Aretha Franklin into greatness and proving that soul has no zip code.

subject: FH Aachen
summary: Germany's top-ranked university of applied sciences in engineering and informatics, with a bridging program that pulls about 300 international students through a boarding-school campus in Geilenkirchen each year.

subject: FaSinPat
summary: When the owner locked them out, the ceramics workers of Neuquén did not go home. They restarted the factory themselves and named it 'Factory Without Bosses.'

subject: Fairmont San Francisco
summary: The luxury hotel atop Nob Hill that was nearly finished when the 1906 earthquake struck, introduced America's first concierge service, and served as the backdrop for the TV series Hotel.

subject: Fajr International Film Festival
summary: Held every February in Tehran since 1983, the Fajr Film Festival is Iran's premier cinematic event -- equal parts cultural showcase, political theater, and defiant assertion that Iranian cinema matters on the world stage.

subject: Falkland, Fife
summary: A former royal burgh at the foot of the Lomond Hills in Fife, home to Scotland's earliest French-Renaissance palace, the world's oldest real tennis court still in use, and Johnny Cash's distant ancestry.

subject: Fallas
summary: Every March, Valencia spends a year of craft and satire building towering sculptures, then burns them all in a single roaring night — the UNESCO-listed festival of Fallas.

subject: Fallmore
summary: The Gaeltacht townland at the southern tip of the Mullet Peninsula, home to a 1,400-year-old church, the legend of Saint Deirbhile, and a notable instance of post-Famine land clearance that reshaped how this corner of Mayo was farmed.

subject: Falstad concentration camp
summary: A Norwegian boys' school transformed into one of the most brutal Nazi prison camps in Scandinavia, where the surrounding forest became a killing ground for political prisoners and prisoners of war.

subject: Fanad
summary: The Donegal peninsula whose name simply means sloping ground, where Scottish mercenaries built a sixteenth-century castle and the lighthouse keeper's cottages still take guests.

subject: Fantasy of Flight
summary: One man's obsessive love of vintage aircraft built the world's largest private collection and a museum in central Florida that refuses to die quietly.

subject: Fashoda Incident
summary: In 1898, a French captain with 120 men and a small Shilluk audience raised the tricolor at a ruined Egyptian fort on the White Nile - and nearly started a war between Europe's two great colonial empires, on land whose actual inhabitants the diplomats barely noticed.

subject: Fayetteville Arsenal
summary: Built by the federal government in 1838, seized peacefully by Confederate troops in 1861, and burned to the ground by Sherman in 1865 - the Fayetteville Arsenal lasted twenty-seven years, then existed only as ruins.

subject: Federal Chancellery (Bonn)
summary: The low brown box where West German chancellors governed from 1976 to 1999, mocked as a savings bank and yet a working monument to the deliberately modest Bonn Republic.

subject: Federal District (Brazil)
summary: Brazil's smallest federal unit, carved from Goias in 1960 to house a brand-new capital, designed by Lucio Costa in the shape of an airplane and built by 30,000 workers in 41 months.

subject: Federal Senate (Brazil)
summary: The upper house of Brazil's National Congress, created in 1824 as a life-term aristocratic body modeled on the House of Lords, now 81 senators serving eight-year terms beneath Niemeyer's inverted dome.

subject: Fehmarn Belt Fixed Link
summary: Eighty-nine concrete boxes, each the length of two football pitches, are being sunk one by one into a trench across the Baltic to build the world's longest immersed tunnel.

subject: Felix Nussbaum Haus
summary: Daniel Libeskind aimed three walls of this Osnabrück museum at the cities where Felix Nussbaum learned to paint, and the fourth at the camp where he was murdered.

subject: Felixstowe
summary: The largest container port in the United Kingdom, where 2.4 kilometres of quay handle the deepest-draughted ships afloat - and also the resort that invented the British beach hut.

subject: Fermilab
summary: A national particle physics laboratory near Chicago where bison graze above buried accelerator rings, Wilson Hall rises like a cathedral, and scientists hunt for the ghost-like neutrino and forces beyond the Standard Model.

subject: Fernsehturm Berlin
summary: East Germany built a 365-metre tower to prove what socialism could do, and the sun turned its steel sphere into a shining cross that Berliners named the Pope's Revenge.

subject: Festival Internacional Cervantino
summary: Born from university students performing short plays by Miguel de Cervantes in Guanajuato's plazas, the Festival Internacional Cervantino has grown into Latin America's most important international arts festival, drawing performers from the Bolshoi Ballet to Joan Baez.

subject: Festspiele Balver Höhle
summary: Since 1947 the cathedral-sized mouth of the Balver Höhle, the largest open-mouth cave-theater in Europe, has hosted Bach, Brecht, Carmina Burana, Irish folk bands, and a generation of children's plays performed under a hundred-million-year-old limestone roof.

story.title: Fillmore East: The Church of Rock and Roll

subject: Fillmore East
summary: A former Yiddish theater on Second Avenue where Bill Graham staged three years of legendary rock concerts that produced more classic live albums than any other venue in history.

subject: Fillmore West
summary: Bill Graham's legendary rock venue at Market and South Van Ness that burned bright from 1968 to 1971, where psychedelic rock found its cathedral in a former swing-era dance hall.

subject: Finca Los Alamos
summary: A frontier fort became a poets' retreat, where Borges walked the gardens and a labyrinth shaped like an open book now spells his name in mirror writing.

subject: Finchale Priory
summary: The ruins of a 13th-century Benedictine priory beside the River Wear, founded on the hermitage where Godric of Finchale lived for fifty years as a solitary religious.

story.title: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco

subject: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco
summary: The largest public arts institution in San Francisco, uniting the de Young Museum in Golden Gate Park and the Legion of Honor in Lincoln Park under one administration.

subject: Fingal Head Light
summary: A small 1872 lighthouse stands above the hexagonal basalt columns of a miniature Giant's Causeway - the last bones of an ancient volcano, on country the Bundjalung call Booninybah.

subject: Finlayson industrial area
summary: The cotton mill that made Tampere was the largest industrial complex in the Nordic countries for seventy years, and in one record year a thousand of its workers were children.

subject: Finnieston Crane
summary: A 175-foot cantilever crane that once hoisted 30,000 locomotives onto Clyde-bound ships and now stands as Glasgow's quiet monument to its shipbuilding past.

subject: Fisher Poets Gathering
summary: Every February, commercial fishermen gather in Astoria, Oregon to read poetry, sing songs, and tell tales born on the water -- a celebration that started with a handful of friends in a pub in 1998 and has grown into a nationally recognized literary event.

subject: Fishguard and Goodwick
summary: Twin Welsh harbour towns wrapped around a sheltered bay, with rocks 460 million years old, a Neolithic burial line above the ferry terminal, and a Dylan Thomas location set still standing on the quayside.

subject: Five Dragon Pool
summary: Legend says a Tang dynasty general's house sank beneath torrential rains to create this spring-fed pool -- Jinan's deepest artesian waters, guarded by the memory of five dragons.

subject: Flags from Macha
summary: Two silk flags hidden behind a portrait of Saint Teresa in a Bolivian chapel in 1813 survived seventy-two years of obscurity to become Argentina's oldest surviving national banners.

subject: Flensburger Brauerei
summary: Germany's northernmost big brewery built a national identity out of one sound: the plopp of a swing-top bottle opening.

subject: Flint Lifeboat Station
summary: In the shadow of Flint Castle, an RNLI inshore lifeboat has stood ready on the Dee estuary since 1966, crewed by volunteers who know the tidal sands better than anyone alive.

subject: Floating Clouds (artwork)
summary: Alexander Calder's massive sculptural installation inside Caracas's Aula Magna began as pure art but accidentally solved the concert hall's catastrophic acoustics, creating one of the finest-sounding venues in the world.

subject: Florence Court
summary: An 18th-century Fermanagh house named for an English woman in Devon, devastated by a 1955 fire, and home to a single yew tree that is the parent of nearly every Irish Yew on Earth.

subject: Florence Stockade
summary: A hastily built Confederate prison camp in South Carolina where men already broken by Andersonville were sent to die in even worse conditions during the final winter of the Civil War.

subject: Florham
summary: A Gilded Age mansion named by blending two first names, designed by the architects of Penn Station, landscaped by the designer of Central Park, wired by Thomas Edison — and now a New Jersey university campus.

subject: Flowerdew Hundred Plantation
summary: One of Virginia's earliest surviving plantations, where the first windmill in British America turned, Grant's engineers built the longest pontoon bridge in history across the James River, and a bald cypress tree helped rediscover its exact location 122 years later.

subject: Forbidden City
summary: The world's largest surviving imperial palace complex, home to 24 emperors across 500 years, now guards one of China's greatest treasure collections behind walls that once sealed an entire civilization's power from ordinary eyes.

subject: Forever Marilyn
summary: Seward Johnson's 26-foot, 34,000-pound stainless steel sculpture of Marilyn Monroe — the skirt-blowing moment from *The Seven Year Itch* rendered at monumental scale — has traveled from Chicago to Palm Springs to New Jersey to Australia, becoming as nomadic as Monroe herself was restless.

subject: Fork Union Military Academy
summary: A Baptist minister's school for nineteen boys in rural Virginia grew into one of America's premier military academies, producing NFL stars, Medal of Honor recipients, and the founder of Under Armour.

subject: Formentera
summary: The smallest and southernmost of the Balearics has no airport, no high-rises, and beaches so clear the sea reads like glass.

subject: Former British Consulate at Takao
summary: Taiwan's oldest surviving Western building sits on a hilltop above Kaohsiung Harbor, a red-brick reminder of the century when the British Empire forced open the ports of Qing-era Formosa.

story.title: Former Japanese Navy Fongshan Communication Center

subject: Former Japanese Navy Fongshan Communication Center
summary: Built in 1919 as the Imperial Japanese Navy's first radio station in Taiwan, this Kaohsiung compound spent the next century cycling through identities: civilian transmitter, wartime intelligence post, political interrogation facility, military prison, and finally a cultural heritage site.

subject: Formosa Boulevard Metro Station
summary: Deep beneath a Kaohsiung intersection, the world's largest glass artwork transforms a transit hub into a cathedral of light, commemorating the 1979 pro-democracy protest that gave the station its name.

subject: Formosa Ha Tinh Steel
summary: Vietnam's largest industrial investment, and the source of the worst environmental disaster the country has ever recorded — a steel mill whose real ledger is written in fish, prison terms and funerals.

subject: Formosan Aboriginal Culture Village
summary: Part amusement park, part living museum, this hillside complex in central Taiwan preserves the architecture and traditions of nine indigenous tribal communities alongside roller coasters and a Gothic clock tower.

subject: Fortaleza de Santa Teresa
summary: A pentagonal stone fortress begun by the Portuguese in 1762 and seized by the Spanish within months, guarding the only dry road through Uruguay's coastal marshes.

subject: Forte Príncipe da Beira
summary: A vast star-shaped fortress raised deep in the Amazon to mark the edge of an empire, where a kilometer of stone walls still stands guard over a remote river.

subject: Forte dos Reis Magos
summary: The star-shaped fort on the Potengi sandbar is older than Natal itself — begun on Epiphany 1598, finished in stone by a royal engineer, and Dutch for twenty-one years.

subject: Fortifications of Bangkok
summary: Centuries of forts and walls that shaped Bangkok from a river outpost into a fortified capital -- built for a Burmese invasion that never came, now reduced to four forts and a ghost gate's memory.

subject: Fortifications of Kotor
summary: Climbing 280 meters from the bay to the castle of San Giovanni, Kotor's fortifications compress Illyrian, Byzantine, Venetian, and Austrian military architecture into 4.5 kilometers of walls that are Montenegro's only cultural World Heritage Site.

subject: Fortifications of Mycenae
summary: The great limestone walls of the Mycenaean citadel — built with stones so massive that later Greeks could only explain them as the work of the mythical Cyclopes — still stand after more than three thousand years.

subject: Fortsberg
summary: A hilltop fort on St. John built by enslaved labor in 1717, seized by enslaved Akwamu warriors in the 1733 revolt -- the first major slave uprising in the colonial Caribbean -- and rebuilt by the Danes who crushed it.

subject: Forty-seven rōnin
summary: Japan's most celebrated tale of samurai loyalty began with an insult in a castle corridor and ended with forty-seven graves at Sengaku-ji temple in Tokyo's Minato ward, where incense still burns for men who chose honor over life more than three centuries ago.

subject: Fortín Solano
summary: The last colonial fortress Spain ever built in Venezuela, perched on a jungle hilltop where Bolívar hanged a war criminal from its flagpole and twentieth-century rebels made their final stand.

subject: Fortín de San Gerónimo
summary: A small 18th-century fort at the mouth of San Juan's Condado Lagoon that helped repel a massive British invasion in 1797 and has survived centuries of bombardment, neglect, and modern development battles.

subject: Fotomuseum Den Haag
summary: The Dutch museum that grew so much photography it had to leave its parent museum and open next door.

subject: Fotomuseum aan het Vrijthof
summary: The building once housed the governors of the Spanish Netherlands and a smuggler-printer who slipped banned French books past the border. Since 2019 it shows only photography.

subject: Francis Crick Institute
summary: Europe's largest biomedical research centre, where Queen Elizabeth II sequenced a director's genome on opening day — a building dedicated to questions science has not yet answered.

subject: Franklin Barbecue
summary: An Austin trailer-turned-restaurant where the line starts before dawn, the brisket sells out every single day, and the pitmaster became the first barbecue chef ever to win a James Beard Award.

subject: Franklin and Armfield Office
summary: A quiet brick building on Duke Street in Alexandria once housed the largest slave trading firm in America, where at least 5,000 enslaved people were trafficked before being shipped to the Deep South.

subject: Franziskaner-Klosterkirche
summary: A roofless Gothic brick shell on Klosterstraße is one of the oldest structures in Berlin — a Franciscan church that outlived the Reformation, seven centuries of renovation, and one air raid too many.

subject: Fraserburgh
summary: Locals call it the Broch - a fishing port at Scotland's far northeast corner where the silver darlings once made millionaires and where the lighthouse dynasty began.

subject: Fraserburgh
summary: Once Scotland's herring capital and now Europe's biggest shellfish port, Fraserburgh - the Broch - has been remaking itself at the windswept corner of Aberdeenshire for five centuries.

subject: Frauenkirche, Dresden
summary: Bombed flat in 1945, rebuilt stone by numbered stone between 1994 and 2005, the Church of Our Lady is now Dresden's most visited symbol of reconciliation.

story.title: Frederick A. and Sophia Bagg Bonanza Farm

subject: Frederick A. and Sophia Bagg Bonanza Farm
summary: A foreman and a cook at someone else's farm built one of the great agricultural empires of the Northern Plains -- a 'bonanza farm' run like a factory, now preserved as one of the finest surviving examples of industrial-scale prairie agriculture and a National Historic Landmark.

subject: Fremont Rocket
summary: A Cold War-era aircraft tail boom transformed into a neon-adorned rocket sculpture, standing guard over Seattle's self-proclaimed 'Center of the Universe.'

subject: French Colonial Aviation in Africa
summary: Across the Sahara, faint white stone circles scratched into the desert mark where French airmen once landed - the navigation marks of an age that flew the sands before radar, and an instrument of empire as much as a feat of nerve.

subject: French Equatorial Africa
summary: France's equatorial federation governed nearly an eighth of Africa from Brazzaville for half a century, mirroring the Congo Free State's rubber atrocities before becoming the unlikely headquarters of the Free French resistance.

subject: Frick Collection
summary: A steel baron who said 'I can make money, I cannot make pictures' left his Fifth Avenue mansion and its Vermeers, Rembrandts, and Goyas to the public -- but his daughter spent decades fighting to keep the collection exactly as he left it.

subject: Frijsenborg
summary: A Jutland estate that once counted forty-two parish churches among its holdings, rebuilt in the 1860s by Denmark's prime minister into the most lavishly appointed private house in the country.

subject: Fringe Club
summary: A Victorian cold-storage depot turned into Hong Kong's most beloved independent arts space, where the rooms that once chilled milk and fur coats now host jazz, theatre, and the work of emerging artists.

story.title: From Aluminum to Ammunition to Aviation Fuel

subject: From Aluminum to Ammunition to Aviation Fuel
summary: A California factory that produced aluminum for warplanes, steel cartridge cases for Korea, and mortar shells for Vietnam is now being transformed into a sustainable aviation fuel plant, completing a strange industrial circle.

subject: Fu Guohao Incident
summary: On August 13, 2019, journalist Fu Guohao was detained, searched, beaten, and zip-tied by protesters at Hong Kong International Airport during the height of the 2019 protests — an incident broadcast live that reverberated on both sides of a widening divide.

subject: Fuerte Bulnes
summary: A log-and-sod fort raised in 1843 to plant Chile's flag on the Strait of Magellan, built within sight of the ruins of a Spanish colony where 300 settlers once starved.

subject: Fuerte San Miguel (Uruguay)
summary: A Portuguese-built star fort that changed hands between empires, fell into ruin, and was rebuilt stone by stone - now standing on its hill above the wetlands as a National Monument of Uruguay.

subject: Fuji-Q Highland
summary: An amusement park at the foot of Mount Fuji that has made a habit of building world-record-breaking roller coasters -- including the steepest, the tallest, and the fastest-accelerating -- all with Japan's most famous volcano as their backdrop.

story.title: Fujii-dera: The Temple with More Than a Thousand Arms

subject: Fujii-dera
summary: A Buddhist temple in Osaka Prefecture guards Japan's oldest Thousand-Armed Kannon statue -- the only one known to actually have more than a thousand arms, with 1,041 limbs fanning out in a golden circle behind a figure sculpted in the 8th century using dry lacquer technique from mainland Asia.

subject: Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha
summary: The head shrine of 1,300 Sengen shrines across Japan, whose sacred grounds extend from downtown Fujinomiya all the way to the summit of Mount Fuji -- a claim of divine real estate that has held for over twelve centuries.

subject: Fulham
summary: A loop of West London on the north bank of the Thames where the Bishops of London held court for thirteen hundred years, where Fulham FC plays at Craven Cottage, and where the Hurlingham Club still governs world polo.

subject: Fundacion Yannick y Ben Jakober
summary: On a hillside above Alcudia, an Egyptian architect's whitewashed house guards a cistern full of watching children painted centuries ago.

subject: Fundació Joan Miró
summary: Joan Miro built his museum not as a shrine to his own work but as a greenhouse for young artists, and his architect friend designed it so the Mediterranean light could do half the curating.

story.title: Fundació Pilar i Joan Miró in Mallorca

subject: Fundació Pilar i Joan Miró in Mallorca
summary: The Palma museum built around the studios where Joan Miró spent his last decades, walls still bearing his sketches.

subject: Fung Ying Seen Koon
summary: Founded in 1929 on a Fanling hillside, Fung Ying Seen Koon is a working Taoist temple complex named for mythical fairy islands — a place of incense, immortals, vegetarian food, and an unexpected television channel.

story.title: Fushimi Inari-taisha: Ten Thousand Gates to the Fox God

subject: Fushimi Inari-taisha
summary: The head shrine of Inari, the deity of rice and commerce, where roughly 10,000 vermilion torii gates donated by Japanese businesses form tunnels up a sacred mountain -- and where Nintendo's Shigeru Miyamoto found inspiration for Star Fox.

subject: Fusion Festival
summary: Seventy thousand people spend a long June week practising what the organisers call Holiday Communism, on a Mecklenburg airfield the Luftwaffe built and the Soviet air force left behind.

subject: Fuxingmen
summary: A gate whose very name -- 'Revival' -- traces the arc of Beijing's transformation from walled imperial capital to modern metropolis.

subject: Fyrkat
summary: A Viking ring fortress near Hobro that stood for barely a decade, and the grave of a woman buried with henbane seeds, a metal wand, and bronze bowls from Central Asia.

subject: Gajapati Empire
summary: The Gajapati Empire, whose name means 'Lords of the Elephants,' ruled from Odisha across much of eastern India for over a century, building temples, patronizing art, and waging wars that shaped the subcontinent's medieval history.

subject: Galata
summary: The medieval Genoese trading colony on the wrong side of the Golden Horn, with a tower at the top and bankers at the bottom.

subject: Galilee (ship)
summary: A fast brigantine that ran packets to Tahiti before being converted into a floating magnetic observatory that charted the Earth's magnetic field across the Pacific.

subject: Gallarus Oratory
summary: A small drystone chapel shaped like an upturned boat that has stood without mortar on the Dingle Peninsula for roughly a thousand years - and is still completely watertight.

subject: Galleria Borghese
summary: A cardinal's private pleasure villa on the edge of 17th-century Rome became one of the world's greatest art museums, holding six Caravaggios, Bernini's most dynamic sculptures, and a Canova that scandalized Napoleon's family.

subject: Gallerie dell'Accademia
summary: Venice's supreme art museum occupies a medieval charity house, a Palladian convent, and a Gothic church, holding Venetian masterpieces from Bellini to Titian -- and Leonardo's Vitruvian Man, which almost no one is allowed to see.

story.title: Galloping Gertie: The Bridge That Danced Itself to Death

subject: Galloping Gertie
summary: Where a new suspension bridge began swaying so wildly in 40-mph winds that it tore itself apart in 1940, becoming history's most famous engineering failure - and the most-filmed bridge collapse ever.

subject: Gansen-ji
summary: A 13th-century hydrangea-draped temple in Kyoto Prefecture where stone pagodas, Kamakura-era carvings, and Tokugawa patronage converge in a quiet corner of the Kansai pilgrimage circuit.

subject: Gao
summary: A traveler's Gao: blocks of Saharan salt in the river markets, tailors at work along the road to the Tomb of Askia, and the long routes in and out of one of the Sahel's most remote cities.

subject: Gatecrasher One
summary: For a brief, brilliant decade, a converted Victorian warehouse on Matilda Street was the loudest, neon-lit heart of British trance music - until the night it burned.

subject: Gateshead
summary: Newcastle's working-class twin on the south bank of the Tyne, transformed by Baltic, the Millennium Bridge and the Angel from post-industrial backwater into the cultural quarter of the North East.

subject: Gavin Maxwell
summary: The Scottish naturalist who wrote Ring of Bright Water, raised otters at Sandaig on the Sound of Sleat, and ended his days at the Kyleakin lighthouse on Eilean Bàn.

subject: Gedeo Cultural Landscape
summary: A UNESCO landscape on Ethiopia's Rift escarpment where the Gedeo people farm coffee and enset beneath a forest canopy, tend sacred groves, and live among thousands of ancient standing stones.

subject: Gedikpaşa Tiyatrosu
summary: The Gedikpaşa Theatre, active from 1866 to 1884 in Istanbul, was the first stage where Muslim Turkish actors performed plays — a brief, radical experiment that helped invent modern Ottoman theatre.

story.title: Gedong Songo: Nine Temples on a Volcanic Hillside

subject: Gedong Songo
summary: Nine Hindu temples from the 8th or 9th century dot a volcanic hillside near Semarang, representing some of the oldest Hindu architecture in Java and a mystery about how Indian temple-building traditions reached Southeast Asia.

story.title: Gedung Setan: The Devil's House That Became a Refuge

subject: Gedung Setan
summary: A crumbling Dutch colonial mansion in Surabaya has sheltered Chinese-Indonesian families through two waves of political persecution, earning the name 'Devil's House' from the darkness its residents endured.

subject: Geibikei
summary: A two-kilometer gorge in Iwate Prefecture where limestone cliffs tower 124 meters overhead and visitors glide through on flat-bottomed boats propelled by a pole, the boatman singing traditional songs on the return journey.

subject: General Archive of the Indies
summary: Inside a Renaissance building designed by the architect of the Escorial, nine kilometers of shelving hold 80 million pages documenting Spain's empire -- including Columbus's journal and Cervantes' job application.

subject: Generalife
summary: The summer palace and gardens of Granada's Nasrid rulers, where water channels, courtyards, and a celebrated staircase with flowing handrails create an earthly approximation of paradise.

subject: Gennadiy Borisov
summary: From a hand-built observatory on a Crimean hilltop, an amateur astronomer spotted the first comet ever confirmed to come from beyond our solar system - and it now bears his name.

story.title: Genoa: Le Strade Nuove and the Palazzi dei Rolli

subject: Genoa
summary: When the Republic of Genoa needed to house visiting kings and popes, it turned its aristocrats' private palaces into a public lodging system -- chosen by lottery.

subject: Geographic Center of Taiwan
summary: Atop Tiger Head Mountain near Puli, a layered monument marks the precise geographic heart of Taiwan — a pilgrimage site where three distinct histories converge on a single point.

subject: George Flavel
summary: An Irish immigrant who became one of Oregon's first millionaires by mastering the deadliest river bar on the Pacific coast, Captain George Flavel built a fortune -- and a mansion -- by guiding ships across the Columbia.

subject: George Stephenson's Birthplace
summary: A modest stone cottage above the Tyne where, in 1781, the man who would invent the modern railway was born into a single shared room.

subject: George W. Bush Presidential Center
summary: The second-largest presidential library in the United States sits on the campus of Southern Methodist University in Dallas -- a LEED Platinum complex where over 500 million dollars in fundraising, a contentious site selection battle, and 900 native Texas trees converge to house the legacy of the 43rd president.

subject: Georgia Guidestones
summary: A mysterious granite monument commissioned under a pseudonym stood in rural Georgia for 42 years, inscribed with ten guidelines for humanity in eight languages, before a bombing destroyed it in 2022.

subject: Gerdkuh
summary: The Nizari Ismaili fortress of Gerdkuh endured one of the longest sieges in medieval history, holding out against the Mongol Empire for seventeen years before finally falling -- the last major Assassin stronghold to surrender.

subject: German Archaeological Institute at Athens
summary: The man who dug up Troy paid for this building, and the institute it houses has been excavating Greece, from Olympia to the Kerameikos, for a century and a half.

subject: German Bight
summary: A shipping forecast area on BBC Radio 4, a UNESCO mudflat, an oil rig, and one of Germany's busiest seaways - all at the same southeast corner of the North Sea.

subject: German Diabetes Center
summary: On the Heinrich Heine University campus in Dusseldorf, researchers comb through data on 65 million Germans to redraw the map of what diabetes actually is.

subject: German submarine U-8 (1935)
summary: A training U-boat that never sank a ship, but whose existence broke a treaty - and whose end came at the bottom of a Wilhelmshaven lock.

subject: Geronimo Surrender Site
summary: A cairn of stones on a windswept Arizona bluff marks where Geronimo surrendered in 1886, ending four decades of Apache resistance.

subject: Ghirardelli Square
summary: A landmark public square at the foot of Russian Hill where a chocolate factory became one of America's first adaptive reuse retail developments.

story.title: Gifu Great Buddha: The Giant Built from Bamboo, Scripture, and Thirty-Eight Years of Faith

subject: Gifu Great Buddha
summary: Standing 13.63 meters tall inside the wooden hall of Shōhō-ji temple, the Gifu Great Buddha is Japan's largest lacquered Buddha -- built over 38 years on a skeleton of ginkgo wood and bamboo, wrapped in Buddhist scriptures, then sealed in lacquer and gold leaf.

subject: Giralda
summary: Seville's iconic tower began as a 12th-century Almohad minaret, survived a devastating earthquake, and was crowned with a Renaissance belfry -- then inspired replicas from New York to Moscow.

subject: Girvan
summary: A burgh on the Carrick coast where Romans pitched camps, Robert the Bruce held court, and a distillery now ships chocolate down to York for Kit Kats.

subject: Gisborough Priory
summary: A single soaring gable wall - all that survived the Reformation of one of Yorkshire's wealthiest Augustinian houses - stands at the foot of the North York Moors, an early monument to the Romantic taste that learned to love a ruin.

subject: Gla
summary: The largest Mycenaean citadel by area ever built — roughly ten times the size of the citadels of Mycenae or Tiryns — rose on a rocky island in Lake Copais around 1300 BC, and its purpose remains debated to this day.

subject: Glasmuseet Ebeltoft
summary: A museum in a Danish customs house whose collection is allowed to change its mind — artists may swap their old work for something better.

subject: Glasnevin
summary: A 6th-century monastery, a Battle of Clontarf casualty, the place that became known as 'the dead centre of Dublin' for its enormous cemetery -- and the home of Ireland's national botanic gardens, where the cause of the Great Famine was first identified.

subject: Glencastle
summary: A wooded glen that opens after miles of barren moor into the 'Gates of Erris,' guarded by an unexcavated mythological fort whose keeper, the warrior Domhnall, once charged tolls at this very gateway to the Mullet Peninsula.

subject: Glencullen, County Mayo
summary: A north Mayo glen where a small mountain lake once slid down its own hillside, where an 1860s hedge teacher governed his school well despite being judged a poor instructor, and where booleying cattle once climbed each summer from the Mullet.

subject: Glendalough
summary: In a glacial valley where two lakes meet, a sixth-century monk founded a monastery that survived Viking raids, supplied timber for longships, and drew pilgrims whose gatherings became so riotous the authorities tried to ban them.

subject: Glendoe Hydro Scheme
summary: High in the Monadhliath Mountains above Loch Ness, the United Kingdom's deepest-drop hydropower scheme generates enough electricity to light Glasgow neighbourhoods—after a celebrated 2009 opening, a collapsing tunnel, and a decade-long legal fight.

subject: Glengyle Station
summary: A Channel Country cattle run where floodwater takes three months to cross a single paddock, and where the Cattle King once lost ten thousand head to drought.

subject: Glenormiston Station
summary: A 6,920-square-kilometre cattle run at the top of the Channel Country, where a 38-kilogram meteorite once fell, floodwaters once stranded the homestead for a week, and the Georgina River still decides who eats.

subject: Glensanda
summary: On a roadless stretch of the Morvern peninsula, a mountain has been hollowed out from the inside to ship six million tons of granite a year through a one-mile tunnel beneath it.

subject: Glensheen Historic Estate
summary: A 39-room Jacobean mansion on Lake Superior's shore, built by an iron ore magnate's fortune and haunted by one of Minnesota's most infamous double murders.

subject: Glin North
summary: A National Monument site on the slopes below Scragg mountain consisting of a stone-walled cashel, an inner stone fort and the remains of beehive huts - one of which still has a stone-paved path leading to its entrance.

subject: Glinsk Hermitage
summary: Beekeepers found a holy icon in the branches of a tall pine, and where it hung, a monastery grew that would outlast tsars, revolutions, and decades of persecution.

subject: Global TransPark
summary: A bold bet to reinvent eastern North Carolina's economy by building a massive air-cargo industrial complex on a quiet rural jetport.

subject: Globe Works
summary: Possibly the world's first purpose-built cutlery factory, the Globe Works has survived bombings, arson, and a 1970 council vote to bulldoze it for a motorway.

subject: Globe of Gottorf
summary: A duke built a hollow copper world three metres across, sat twelve people inside it, and turned the night sky around them with a waterwheel — the first planetarium you could walk into.

subject: Glyndebourne Festival Opera
summary: John Christie built an opera house in his Sussex back garden in 1934 because he wanted to hear Mozart properly - and ninety years later the festival he founded still runs without state subsidy, still expects black tie, and still breaks for a ninety-minute picnic dinner on the lawn.

subject: Glynllifon
summary: A 102-room neoclassical mansion at the heart of a Welsh estate that has been by turns a princely seat, an agricultural college, a luxury hotel, and a battleground for receivers.

subject: Gobabeb
summary: A research station at the intersection of three desert ecosystems where scientists have studied arid-land survival for over sixty years, harvesting fog for water and building with river clay.

subject: Goddess of Democracy (Hong Kong)
summary: The Goddess of Democracy statue at CUHK stood as the only replica of the Tiananmen original on Chinese soil — and its contested history mirrors the broader story of Hong Kong's struggle to hold memory alive.

subject: Godesburg
summary: A volcanic cone that has been a pagan height, an archbishop's strongbox, a ruin, a romantic souvenir, and finally a hotel.

subject: Godolphin Estate
summary: A 550-acre National Trust estate built on Cornish tin, Godolphin holds the remnant of a Tudor mansion, four hundred recorded archaeological features from Bronze Age to Victorian, and one of the strangest annual rents in English history - a quart of beer and a snail.

subject: Golconda
summary: A fortress whose name became synonymous with unimaginable wealth, where the Hope Diamond and the Koh-i-Noor were once traded and a handclap at the gate echoes a kilometer away.

subject: Golden Madonna of Essen
summary: Carved around 980 from a single poplar trunk and sheathed in gold leaf, the Golden Madonna is the oldest free-standing sculpture of any kind north of the Alps - and likely a piece of imperial political theater.

subject: Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone
summary: A 3,000-hectare enclave on the Lao bank of the Mekong where a Hong Kong-registered company built a casino empire under a 99-year lease, creating a de facto Chinese colony that the U.S. Treasury has sanctioned for drug trafficking and money laundering.

subject: Golden spike
summary: The 17.6-karat ceremonial spike that completed America's first transcontinental railroad, now displayed at Stanford University's Cantor Arts Center.

subject: Goldin Finance 117
summary: Certified by Guinness as the world's tallest unoccupied building, this 597-meter supertall skyscraper in Tianjin stands as a monument to ambition outpacing reality -- topped out in 2015, abandoned months later, and now slated for completion in 2027.

subject: Googleplex
summary: Google's sprawling Mountain View headquarters occupies the site of a former Silicon Graphics campus, complete with dinosaur skeleton, volleyball courts, and the colorful Android lawn statues.

subject: Gora Qabaristan, Karachi
summary: Karachi's only operational Christian cemetery has served as a burial ground since at least 1843, holding 300,000 registered burials in space meant for 3,000 graves, alongside a Polish refugee memorial and a 43-meter cross.

subject: Gordonstoun
summary: Founded in 1934 by a German-Jewish educator who had just fled the Nazis, Gordonstoun became the school that taught two generations of British royalty - and one famous reluctant student called it Colditz in kilts.

story.title: Goshikizuka Kofun: The Keyhole Tomb That Watched the Strait

subject: Goshikizuka (Sentsubo) Kofun
summary: The largest burial mound in Hyogo Prefecture -- a 194-meter keyhole-shaped tomb overlooking the Akashi Strait -- was the first kofun in Japan restored to its original appearance, covered in 2.23 million riverbed stones.

subject: Grace Darling
summary: At 22, a Northumberland lighthouse keeper's daughter rowed out into a storm with her father to save nine survivors of the SS Forfarshire - and became Victorian Britain's most famous heroine, almost against her will.

subject: Gran Torre Costanera
summary: At 300 metres, the tallest building in South America, a glass tower rising over Santiago with the snow line of the Andes for a backdrop.

subject: Grand Duchy of Oldenburg
summary: From a small Lower Saxon court came the rulers of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Greece, Russia, and through Prince Philip the consorts of the United Kingdom; the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg was the smallest royal house with the longest reach in Europe.

subject: Grand Indonesia
summary: A sprawling Jakarta mall that once recreated Rockefeller Center inside a tropical atrium, Grand Indonesia has spent two decades chasing spectacle -- building the only Waltzing Waters fountain in Indonesia, hosting one of the world's largest ScreenX cinemas, and slowly dismantling its own themed districts to make room for more shops.

subject: Grand Lisboa
summary: At 261 metres, the Grand Lisboa is Macau's tallest building and most recognizable landmark — a 47-floor lotus-and-egg structure housing 800 gaming tables, a three-Michelin-star restaurant, and a 218-carat diamond on permanent display.

subject: Grange-over-Sands
summary: A Victorian seaside resort on the north shore of Morecambe Bay whose famous sands have refused to behave for over a century.

subject: Grassy Hill Light
summary: A tiny corrugated-iron lighthouse crowns the hill James Cook climbed in 1770 to find a way out of the reef that had nearly destroyed him.

subject: Grave Circle A, Mycenae
summary: The ring of six royal shaft graves inside Mycenae's citadel walls where Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 unearthed a trove of Mycenaean gold — including the golden death mask he called the Mask of Agamemnon.

subject: Gravensteen
summary: A medieval fortress that served as castle, court, prison, and cotton mill before becoming Ghent's most imposing museum.

subject: Gravesend Blockhouse
summary: Henry VIII's brick-and-stone river gate, built when invasion seemed certain and demolished long after the threat had passed.

story.title: Great Banda: The Island That Fought Back

subject: Great Banda
summary: The largest of the Banda Islands bears the scars of colonial violence and volcanic upheaval, its clifftop ruins and nutmeg groves testifying to a history in which an entire people were nearly erased for the sake of a spice.

subject: Great Cumbrae
summary: A small island in the Firth of Clyde where Glaswegians have gone 'Doon the Watter' for generations, with painted rocks, a tiny cathedral, and roads quiet enough to circle by bike.

subject: Great Glen Way
summary: A 73-mile trail from Fort William to Inverness that walks the length of the Highlands without ever climbing a real mountain.

subject: Great Mull Air Mystery
summary: On Christmas Eve 1975, a pilot took off from Glenforsa Airfield on a moonless night and was never seen again; his body turned up on a hillside four months later, with no plane and no explanation.

subject: Great Ocean Road
summary: Carved by hand by 3,000 returned soldiers as a memorial to the dead of World War I, the Great Ocean Road is the largest war memorial on Earth and one of its most beautiful drives.

subject: Great Sphinx of Giza
summary: The largest monolithic statue in the ancient world, carved from the living bedrock of the Giza Plateau, has guarded Egypt's necropolis for over four thousand years -- losing its nose, its beard, and its paint, but never its mystery.

subject: Great Train Robbery (1963)
summary: On a Buckinghamshire railway bridge in August 1963, a gang stopped a Royal Mail train and stole more money than anyone had ever taken in a British robbery. They also beat the train's driver, a man whose name the headlines forgot.

subject: Great Yarmouth
summary: A medieval herring port on a Norfolk sandspit, owing the Crown 100 herring baked in 24 pasties each year, bombed by Zeppelins, beloved by Dickens, and home to a Nelson monument built before his column in London.

subject: Greek Cruiser Georgios Averof
summary: The armoured cruiser Georgios Averof dominated the Aegean in the Balkan Wars, survived two world wars, escaped Nazi capture when her crew cut through a harbour boom with axes, and now rests as a museum ship at Palaio Faliro — the last armoured cruiser still afloat.

subject: Greek and Roman Mythology
