summary: Greek and Roman mythology is not a museum exhibit — it is alive in the landscape of Greece itself, from the Acropolis of Athena to the cave of the Cyclops to the strait where Odysseus heard the sirens. Standing in this country, the myths become geography.

subject: Green Bank
summary: The 13,000-square-mile zone in West Virginia where WiFi is illegal, cell phones don't work, and microwave ovens are banned - all to protect a radio telescope listening for signals from the edge of the universe.

subject: Green Vault
summary: Augustus the Strong's mirrored treasure chambers in Dresden Castle, the 2019 axe raid that emptied three jewel sets, and what came back three years later.

subject: Greenway Estate
summary: Agatha Christie called it her dream house - and she set three murders here.

subject: Greetsiel
summary: An East Frisian fishing harbor where twin windmills, 28 shrimp cutters, and the largest ship-in-a-bottle museum in Europe crowd around a 14th-century sluice.

subject: Greyfriars Kirk
summary: Built on the grounds of an abandoned Franciscan friary, Greyfriars Kirk is where the National Covenant was signed in 1638, where Cromwell's troops stabled their horses, where a 1718 gunpowder explosion blew out the tower, and where the Church of Scotland's first post-Reformation organ played in defiance of three centuries of austerity.

subject: Greyfriars, Lincoln
summary: The oldest surviving Franciscan friary church in England, built within a decade of the order's arrival from Italy and lived in by men who owned nothing.

subject: Grianan of Aileach
summary: A circular stone ring fort 244 metres above the Inishowen peninsula, royal seat of the northern Ui Neill, sacked by a Munster king in 1101, rebuilt in the 19th century from imagined Kerry blueprints.

subject: Groombridge Place
summary: A moated manor house where Christopher Wren helped a friend rebuild, John Evelyn planted the pines, a French duke was held prisoner after Agincourt, and Sherlock Holmes solved the Valley of Fear.

subject: Groot Constantia
summary: South Africa's oldest wine estate, granted to a Dutch governor in 1685 and built with enslaved labor, now a museum that confronts both its beauty and its past.

subject: Groote Kerk, Cape Town
summary: South Africa's oldest place of Christian worship began with a lay preacher in a fort in 1652 and has survived four centuries of colonial upheaval, a shrinking congregation, and a pulpit carved from Indian teak that remains its masterpiece.

subject: Groote Kerk, Galle
summary: A Dutch Reformed church inside Galle Fort, born from one man's decades-long prayer for a daughter and built at the fort's highest point on the foundations of a Portuguese convent.

subject: Groote Schuur
summary: From Dutch grain barn to Cecil Rhodes's mansion to the room where Mandela and De Klerk began dismantling apartheid - one estate that held the keys to South African history.

subject: Gross Barmen
summary: A Namibian hot springs resort whose peaceful thermal waters mask a violent colonial past of Rhenish missionaries driven out and resettled seven times by war between the Herero and Nama peoples.

subject: Grosvenor Square
summary: Mayfair's grandest garden square has housed John Adams, Dwight Eisenhower, the American Embassy, and Oscar Wilde — a 300-year experiment in what it means to be at the centre of power.

subject: Grote Kerk, Haarlem
summary: The 15th-century Gothic church on Haarlem's market square holds a 1738 organ that Mozart played at age ten, and the bones of Frans Hals beneath its stone floor.

subject: Grote or Andreaskerk (Hattem)
summary: The Gothic church of Hattem grew up around an older tower, and the older tower won.

subject: Grote or Jacobijnerkerk
summary: Leeuwarden's oldest building holds a royal crypt and one of the Netherlands' most celebrated baroque organs, both tying a Frisian church to the future of the Dutch monarchy.

subject: Grote or Sint-Jacobskerk (The Hague)
summary: The Hague's medieval church where Dutch kings are baptised, with a 93-meter six-sided tower and stained glass that survived a Holy Roman Emperor's restoration.

subject: Growthfund
summary: Greece's sovereign wealth fund, headquartered in central Athens, quietly part-owns the airport you land at, the canal at Corinth, the national power company, and the ports along the coast.

subject: Großes Schauspielhaus
summary: A failed market hall became a circus, then Max Reinhardt's Theatre of the Five Thousand under a ceiling of hanging plaster stalactites — and finally died because a hospital next door lowered the water table and rotted its oak piles.

subject: Guangzhou Circle
summary: A 138-meter ring-shaped skyscraper on the Pearl River that evokes a jade bi-disc, an ancient Chinese royal symbol — designed by an Italian architect using the logic of Renaissance geometry and Fengshui.

subject: Guarapari
summary: A beach resort on the Espírito Santo coast whose population triples in summer, whose sands are naturally radioactive, and whose quarries now host dance parties.

subject: Gubeikou
summary: An ancient chokepoint where the Great Wall crosses the mountains between Northeast China and Beijing, Gubeikou has served as a strategic gateway for armies, traders, and emperors for more than two thousand years.

subject: Gulf of Georgia Cannery
summary: They called it the Monster Cannery: 2.5 million cans of salmon in a single 1897 season, packed by a workforce of First Nations, Chinese, Japanese and European hands, in a building on the Fraser that outlived the industry that built it.

subject: Gunung Gangsir
summary: A thousand-year-old Hindu temple in East Java whose name recalls a treasure hunter who tunneled into its ruins, Gunung Gangsir is the only known temple on the island to blend Central and East Javanese architectural styles in red brick.

subject: Guogang Shell Fossils
summary: A coastal cliff near Houlong preserves half a million years of Pleistocene seafloor in cross-section — 135 species of shellfish frozen in shale where an ancient sea once covered what is now Taiwan's western lowlands.

subject: Gusto Shipyard
summary: The Dutch shipbuilder that gave the world the first jackup oil rig outside America and the first single-buoy mooring - then was shut down in 1978 under circumstances that still smell wrong.

subject: Gwanghwamun
summary: The main gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace has been destroyed and rebuilt so many times that its very survival has become a symbol of Korean resilience.

subject: Gyeongbokgung
summary: Seoul's first and grandest royal palace has been burned, abandoned, systematically dismantled by colonial occupiers, and rebuilt across six centuries -- a cycle of destruction and renewal that mirrors Korea itself.

subject: Gytheio
summary: Sparta's ancient sea-gate — where legend says Paris and Helen began their fateful voyage — Gytheio has been coveted, burned, rebuilt, and reborn across three thousand years of Laconian history.

subject: Gänseliesel
summary: A small bronze goose girl in Göttingen's market square, rejected by the jury, chosen by the townspeople, and kissed by every new doctor of the university - a practice the police once banned and the courts upheld.

story.title: Göbekli Tepe: The Temple Built Before Agriculture

subject: Göbekli Tepe
summary: Where hunter-gatherers built massive stone temples 11,500 years ago - 6,000 years before Stonehenge, before pottery, before farming - rewriting everything we thought we knew about civilization.

subject: Güell Pavilions
summary: Behind a wrought-iron dragon gate in Pedralbes, Gaudí's earliest work for the Güell family turned a stable and a riding ring into a lesson in brick, myth, and light.

subject: H. J. Lovink Pumping Station
summary: A farmer and a fisherman shake hands across a dyke on the wall of this modernist pumping station - the first national monument ever designated in the Flevopolder.

subject: H401
summary: A canal house on the Amsterdam Herengracht that sheltered Jewish youth during the Nazi occupation, now a foundation grappling with the contested legacy of the circle that hid there.

subject: HMNB Devonport
summary: Western Europe's largest naval base, where Britain's nuclear submarines come for refit and one wall of a 1696 officers' terrace remains the oldest building in any Royal Dockyard.

subject: HMQS Gayundah
summary: A colonial Queensland gunboat that once aimed her gun at Parliament now rusts on the Redcliffe foreshore, a hull you can walk out to at low tide.

subject: Haarlemmermeer
summary: An inland sea that drowned villages and elected princes was pumped dry by steam in 1852, and Schiphol Airport now sits on its floor.

subject: Hackney Empire
summary: The theatre The Guardian called London's most beautiful launched as a music hall in 1901 — where Charlie Chaplin and Marie Lloyd once performed, and where the Rolling Stones announced their comeback album in 2023.

subject: Hagia Irene
summary: Older than the Hagia Sophia and the only major Byzantine church in Istanbul never converted to a mosque, Hagia Irene served as a janissary armory for centuries before becoming the concert hall it is today.

subject: Hagia Sophia
summary: Cathedral, mosque, museum, mosque again: for nearly fifteen centuries the great domed building above the Bosphorus has reshaped what humans believed architecture could do, and what worship could feel like.

subject: Hagia Sophia Hurrem Sultan Bathhouse
summary: Squeezed between Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque, this 1556 double hamam — designed by Mimar Sinan for Hürrem Sultan on the ruins of a Byzantine bath complex — is one of the most elegantly engineered charitable buildings in the Ottoman world.

subject: Hague Congress (1872)
summary: In five days at a Hague theatre, Karl Marx engineered the expulsion of Mikhail Bakunin and split the international workers' movement into two warring traditions that still argue today.

subject: Haji Ali Dargah
summary: A 15th-century Sufi shrine perched on an islet in the Arabian Sea, reachable only at low tide via a narrow causeway that the ocean swallows twice a day.

subject: Halbmondlager
summary: Germany's first mosque was built inside a First World War prison camp, part of an attempt to turn 30,000 captured Muslim, Sikh and Hindu soldiers against the empires that had conscripted them.

subject: Halifax Minster
summary: A 15th-century parish church with Jacobean box pews, a Snetzler organ, and the grave of diarist Anne Lister.

subject: Hamadan
summary: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, Hamadan was the capital of the Median Empire before Persia existed - a place where Avicenna completed his greatest works, where the Tomb of Esther draws Jewish pilgrims, and where a bear cub once began a journey that would make him a corporal in the Polish army.

subject: Hamm (Westfalen) Hauptbahnhof
summary: A Westphalian railway hub whose marshalling yard was once among Europe's largest - 10,000 wagons a day - and whose Jugendstil station hall, half-flattened by RAF Bomber Command, won a Europa Nostra Award for its restoration.

subject: Hang En
summary: Vietnamese named this cave after the birds that nest in it - a tunnel 1,645 meters straight through a mountain, with its own river, its own jungle, its own beach and its own weather.

subject: Hanna City Air Force Station
summary: A Cold War radar station designed to monitor the skies was repurposed into a correctional facility where its towers watched the ground.

subject: Hansa Tonstudio
summary: A chamber-music hall built by a property owners' association in 1913 ended up 150 metres from the Berlin Wall, and became the room where David Bowie sang "Heroes".

subject: Harderwijk
summary: A Hanseatic port that lost its sea — and kept its walls, its gate, and the strange honor of having handed Linnaeus a doctorate.

subject: Hargrave Military Academy
summary: Founded in 1909 in Chatham, Virginia, this Baptist-affiliated military boarding school became, improbably, a feeder pipeline to NCAA Division I basketball and the NBA — 26 alumni and counting.

subject: Harishchandragad
summary: An ancient hill fort in Maharashtra's Sahyadri range where microlithic remnants, 6th-century temples, and a cliff that produces circular rainbows share a plateau that has drawn pilgrims, sages, and trekkers for over a thousand years.

subject: Harland & Wolff
summary: The Belfast shipyard that built the Titanic, was bombed by the Luftwaffe, expelled its Catholic workers, and is still on the lough - now Spanish-owned and building barges and Navy supply ships.

subject: Harrah's Reno
summary: The birthplace of America's largest casino empire stands silent now, its towers awaiting transformation into apartments after 83 years of neon-lit history.

story.title: Harriet Tubman Byway: The Routes That Led to Freedom

subject: Harriet Tubman Byway
summary: The Maryland landscape where Harriet Tubman was enslaved and from which she escaped - where she returned thirteen times to guide others north, where the Underground Railroad was network not tunnel, and where the marshes and forests hid those running for their lives toward freedom.

subject: Harrods
summary: The Knightsbridge department store that grew from a single-room grocer's into a million-square-foot palace of consumption, and whose long history holds a great deal more than gilt and marble.

story.title: Harry S. Truman National Historic Site

subject: Harry S. Truman National Historic Site
summary: The 33rd president never owned a home until after leaving the White House -- this National Historic Site preserves the Independence house where Harry and Bess Truman lived from their 1919 wedding until his death in 1972.

subject: Harry's Walls
summary: The unfinished bastions of a Tudor artillery fort on St Mary's, abandoned in 1554 mid-construction and named for the wrong king.

story.title: Hartford: The Insurance Capital Where Mark Twain Lived

subject: Hartford
summary: Connecticut's capital where America's oldest newspaper still publishes, where Mark Twain wrote his greatest works in a Gothic mansion, and where the insurance industry built a skyline of corporate towers along the Connecticut River.

subject: Hase-dera
summary: A 7th-century temple in Nara Prefecture that has burned and risen from its ashes ten times, Hase-dera shelters Japan's largest wooden statue -- a 31-foot, eleven-headed Kannon -- and draws pilgrims up 399 stone steps lined with 700 Chinese peonies each spring.

subject: Hase-dera (Kamakura)
summary: A hilltop Buddhist temple in Kamakura housing one of Japan's largest wooden statues -- an eleven-headed golden Kannon carved, according to legend, from a single camphor log in 721 AD.

subject: Hashihaka Kofun
summary: The 'Chopstick Grave' in Nara Prefecture may be the tomb of the legendary Queen Himiko -- or a princess who killed herself with a chopstick. Either way, this keyhole-shaped burial mound from the 3rd century marks the dawn of Japan's Kofun period and the birth of the Yamato state.

story.title: Hashino: The Samurai Who Read a Dutch Textbook and Forged Modern Japan

subject: Hashino iron mining and smelting site
summary: In 1857, a samurai-engineer named Oshima Takato built Japan's first successful western-style blast furnace in a remote Iwate mountain valley, using a design copied from a Dutch engineering manual -- launching the iron industry that would transform a feudal nation into an industrial power.

subject: Hat Lek
summary: The southernmost gate on the 817-kilometre Thai-Cambodian frontier: a handful of shacks, a wall of money changers, and a barrier whose opening is now a political question.

subject: Hat Works
summary: A 200-foot brick chimney still rises over Stockport, marking the seven-storey fireproof mill that became the UK's only museum dedicated to hats.

subject: Hatakeyama Shigeyasu's grave
summary: A beautifully crafted 3.45-meter stone pagoda in Kamakura marks the traditional grave of a samurai who died fighting off an entire army -- while suffering an asthma attack.

subject: Hattem
summary: Hattem packs Hanseatic walls, a vanished castle called the Fat Merlon, and the painters of Dutch country light into a few quiet streets above the IJssel.

subject: Haulbowline
summary: An island home of the world's first yacht club in 1720, headquarters of the Irish Naval Service today, and for sixty years one of Ireland's worst toxic-industrial sites - now reborn as a public park.

subject: Haus Vaterland
summary: A Weimar pleasure palace on Potsdamer Platz that sold the whole world in one building, taken from its Jewish operators by the Nazis, bombed out, burned out, and finally scrapped for 600 tonnes of steel.

subject: Haus am Horn
summary: The first building anywhere put up on Bauhaus principles - a one-storey show house in Weimar, built in four months in 1923 while the currency around it dissolved.

subject: Hawaii hotspot
summary: A plume of magma rising from deep in Earth's mantle has been building volcanoes for at least 80 million years, leaving a 6,200-kilometer trail of seamounts, atolls, and islands across the Pacific -- with the Big Island of Hawaii as its latest creation.

subject: Hawkins County, Tennessee
summary: A 500-square-mile slice of upper East Tennessee where the future King of the French paid a visit in 1797 and where the oldest brick house west of the Appalachians still keeps watch over Big Creek.

subject: Hawks Nest, West Virginia
summary: A cliff on Gauley Mountain where the New River bends 585 feet below, a railroad ran the hawks off in the 1870s, and an industrial tunnel killed hundreds of workers in the 1930s.

subject: Hayes Plantation
summary: A five-part Palladian villa east of Edenton built by enslaved labor, and the unacknowledged Black families - Forten, Grimke, Wood - whose lives ran through it.

subject: Haytor
summary: A Dartmoor granite tor whose stone built London Bridge - now sitting in the Arizona desert - and whose handrail offended a Victorian doctor.

subject: Headlands Center for the Arts
summary: An artist-in-residence program housed in former military buildings in the Marin Headlands, where creative work happens inside decommissioned barracks overlooking the Pacific.

subject: Hec Edmundson
summary: An Idaho farm boy who became the first Olympian from his state, Hec Edmundson brought his track speed to basketball and invented the fast break, coaching at the University of Washington for nearly three decades in a pavilion that now bears his name.

subject: Hedonism Resorts
summary: Jamaica's most notorious all-inclusive resort, where a government-built beachside hotel reinvented itself as an adults-only playground on 22 acres of Negril's white sand coastline.

subject: Heerlen
summary: A Roman crossroads that became Dutch coal country, lost its industry, and rebuilt itself around a glass palace.

subject: Heers, Netherlands
summary: A tiny Veldhoven hamlet whose nearby woods hold Bronze Age burial mounds, a Roman watchtower, and a 175 AD terracotta sculpture of Diana the huntress.

subject: Hehuanshan
summary: Taiwan's most accessible high peak offers 360-degree views from 3,416 meters, designated dark skies for stargazing, and the ruins of an abandoned ski lift from the martial law era -- all reached by the highest road on the island.

story.title: Heichinrou: The Restaurant That Survived Earthquakes, Air Raids, and Iron Chef

subject: Heichinrou
summary: Founded in 1884 in Yokohama Chinatown, Heichinrou was Japan's oldest operating Chinese restaurant -- surviving the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake and World War II air raids before its grand chef defeated Iron Chef Chen Kenichi on national television, only for the restaurant to finally succumb to bankruptcy in 2022.

subject: Heiligendamm
summary: Continental Europe's oldest seaside resort, founded in 1793 because a duke's doctor read a magazine article asking why Germany had no place to bathe in the sea.

subject: Heineken Experience
summary: The 1867 brewery where Gerard Heineken started a Dutch beer empire is now a four-storey tourist attraction in the heart of Amsterdam.

subject: Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum
summary: The world's biggest computer museum began as a heap of anniversary presents its founder did not want to throw away - and opened ten years after he died.

subject: HelleniQ Energy
summary: Greece's largest oil company grew from a single 1958 refinery near Athens into a regional giant, and now wrestles publicly with where its crude comes from.

subject: Hellenic Military Academy
summary: The Hellenic Military Academy — the Evelpidon — was founded in 1828 by Greece's first governor, Ioannis Kapodistrias, making it the oldest institution of higher education in the country and the school that has trained the Greek Army's officers through every conflict of modern Greek history.

subject: Hellespontine Phrygia
summary: The Persian satrapy that guarded the gateway between Europe and Asia for two centuries — until Alexander came and rewrote the rules.

subject: Hellfire Caves
summary: A quarter-mile of chalk tunnels dug into a Buckinghamshire hillside in the 1750s, scandalous meeting place of Sir Francis Dashwood's notorious gentlemen's club, sat three hundred feet below the church Dashwood built to crown the same hill.

subject: Helmstedt–Marienborn border crossing
summary: Checkpoint Alpha: the busiest gate in the inner German border, thirty-five hectares of floodlit control halls staffed by a thousand people, built to inspect the shortest road to West Berlin.

subject: Hembrug
summary: A vanished railway bridge across the North Sea Canal, a state munitions factory that ran for three centuries, and two swimmers who saved both from German demolition in September 1944.

subject: Heraion of Perachora
summary: Perched at the very tip of the Perachora peninsula across from Corinth, the Heraion is one of the oldest sanctuaries of Hera in Greece — a place where mythology, maritime prayer, and the origins of Greek temple architecture converge on a dramatic cove above the Corinthian Gulf.

subject: Hercules (1907 ship)
summary: A 1907 ocean-going steam tug preserved at Hyde Street Pier -- one of the most powerful tugs of her era, built to tow log rafts along the Pacific Coast.

subject: Hereke Carpet
summary: Made for Ottoman sultans and given to kings, the Hereke carpet represents the apex of Turkish weaving — silk on silk, with up to 10,000 knots per square decimeter, knotted at a small factory on the Gulf of İzmit.

subject: Heritage Square (Fayetteville, North Carolina)
summary: Three buildings - a 1797 Federal-period townhouse, a freestanding 1818 Regency ballroom, and an 1804 Georgian house - preserved on a single downtown block by the Woman's Club of Fayetteville since 1945.

subject: Hermannsdenkmal
summary: A sculptor spent thirty-seven years and his own fortune on a colossal statue nobody would fund, on a hill where the battle it commemorates almost certainly never happened.

subject: Hermes and the Infant Dionysus
summary: Discovered in 1877 in the ruins of the Temple of Hera at Olympia, this marble sculpture of the god Hermes cradling the infant Dionysus has sparked one of art history's fiercest debates: is it a genuine fourth-century BC original, possibly by Praxiteles himself, or something else entirely?

subject: Heroes' Acre (Namibia)
summary: Built into barren hills south of Windhoek by a North Korean construction firm, Namibia's national war memorial honors liberation fighters with cenotaphs, mausoleums, and a statue of the Unknown Soldier that bears a striking resemblance to the country's founding president.

subject: Herveys Range Heritage Tea Rooms
summary: A split-log inn from 1865, once a wayside stop for bullock teams and Cobb & Co coaches on the long haul to the goldfields, now pours Devonshire tea and the strangest coffee in Queensland.

subject: Hetman's Capital
summary: On the site of a Cossack capital burned in a single morning, Ukraine has rebuilt the only surviving hetman's palace and gathered the memory of a vanished statehood.

subject: Hida Kokubun-ji
summary: One of the last surviving provincial temples ordered built by Emperor Shomu in 741, anchored by a 1,250-year-old ginkgo tree and a pagoda rebuilt four times across twelve centuries.

subject: Hida Minzoku Mura Folk Village
summary: An open-air museum of over 30 relocated farmhouses where steeply thatched gassho-zukuri roofs, built to shed heavy mountain snow, preserve centuries of mountain life in the Japanese Alps.

subject: Hieria
summary: At the headland now known as Fenerbahçe, on the Asian shore where the Bosphorus meets the Sea of Marmara, the Byzantine emperor Justinian I built an imperial palace in the sixth century — a retreat above the waters where two continents meet.

story.title: Higashi Hongan-ji: The Temple That Burned Four Times and Was Raised by Human Hair

subject: Higashi Hongan-ji
summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu split a Buddhist sect in half to weaken it, creating this temple in 1602 -- and after four devastating fires, female devotees cut their hair and braided it into ropes strong enough to hoist the massive timbers of the largest wooden building in Kyoto.

subject: High Street, Hong Kong
summary: A quiet one-way street in Sai Ying Pun, High Street is best known for the haunting neoclassical building at its western end — a former mental hospital that stood derelict for decades and became one of Hong Kong's most enduring ghost stories.

subject: Highbridge Skirmish
summary: The first engagement of the 1745 Jacobite rising, where eleven Highlanders and a piper bluffed eighty-five Royal Scots into surrender on a bridge over the River Spean.

subject: Hiidenlinna
summary: A self-taught woodcarver built himself a three-storey stone castle on a lake in Somerniemi, made it one of Southwest Finland's most visited sites, and then spent five years looking for someone to inherit it.

subject: Hill o' Many Stanes
summary: Around 200 low standing stones fan out across a Caithness hillside in rows that may, or may not, have once tracked the moon.

story.title: Hills and Dales Estate: Where Seventy Years of Love Built a Garden

subject: Hills and Dales Estate
summary: A textile magnate's Italian villa set within pre-Civil War gardens that one nineteenth-century visitor described as a 'bewildering paradise' -- where the soil is ordinary LaGrange, Georgia clay, but seventy years of devotion made extraordinary things grow.

subject: Himeji
summary: Home to Japan's most magnificent surviving castle, Himeji has guarded the western edge of the Kansai plain for over four centuries.

subject: Hindu Gymkhana, Karachi
summary: Once spanning 47,000 square yards as Karachi's first Mughal-Revival public building, the Hindu Gymkhana has shrunk to just 4,500 square yards, its story a microcosm of Partition's long aftermath.

subject: Hine-no-shō
summary: A medieval Japanese feudal estate stretching from the coast of Osaka Bay to the Izumi Mountains, whose shrines, temples, irrigation ponds, and castle ruins survive as a remarkably intact landscape -- fourteen sites collectively designated a National Historic Site.

subject: Hippie Hill
summary: The gentle slope in Golden Gate Park between the Conservatory of Flowers and Haight Street where the Summer of Love gathered, and where San Francisco still comes to drum, smoke, and sprawl in the grass.

story.title: Hiraga Gennai: The Man Who Wrote About Farting and Built Japan's First Electrostatic Generator

subject: Hiraga Gennai
summary: An Edo-period ronin who was simultaneously a pharmacologist, mining prospector, pottery maker, satirical novelist, painter, and inventor -- best remembered for building Japan's first electrostatic generator and writing a philosophical treatise on flatulence.

subject: Hirsholmene
summary: A scatter of low islets off Frederikshavn where you may sail close but not land — forty-five hectares of gull colony, a 1640s church, and a community that finally ended in the spring of 2024.

subject: Historic Center of São Paulo
summary: Where Jesuit missionaries planted a school in 1554 and a megacity grew around it, São Paulo's historic center holds five centuries of ambition, decay, and reinvention in a few square kilometers.

subject: Historic Filipinotown
summary: Officially designated in 2002, Historic Filipinotown in Los Angeles contains the nation's largest Filipino-American mural, its first park dedicated to Filipino historical figures, and a memorial to 250,000 soldiers who fought for the United States.

subject: Historic Flight Foundation
summary: An aviation museum that collected and flew rare warbirds from the golden age of flight, the Historic Flight Foundation soared at Paine Field and Felts Field before a fraud lawsuit grounded it permanently.

subject: Historic Jamestown
summary: The actual archaeological site where England's 1607 James Fort once stood -- not a replica, not a recreation, but the ground itself, where William Kelso's team proved everyone wrong by finding a fort the river was supposed to have swallowed centuries ago.

story.title: Seventeen Monuments, Eleven Centuries: Kyoto's UNESCO World Heritage

subject: Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)
summary: The one decision that saved Kyoto from atomic destruction also preserved seventeen temples, shrines, and a castle spanning eleven centuries -- now collectively recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site containing 38 National Treasures.

story.title: Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara: Eight Sites, Thirteen Centuries

subject: Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara
summary: Eight places in the old capital Nara -- five Buddhist temples, one Shinto shrine, an imperial palace, and a primeval forest where hunting has been forbidden since 841 -- together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site holding 26 National Treasures and 53 Important Cultural Properties.

subject: History of Jamestown, Virginia (1607–1699)
summary: Ninety-two years of survival, reinvention, and transformation -- the full arc of Jamestown from desperate fort in 1607 to abandoned capital in 1699, tracing how a commercial venture became a colony, a colony became a society, and a society outgrew the swamp that birthed it.

subject: History of Limerick
summary: From a Viking fortress in 922 to the Treaty of the Broken Stone in 1691 to the modern multinational hub - Limerick's history is twelve centuries of negotiating with bigger powers and surviving them.

subject: Ho Tung Lau
summary: Ho Tung Lau began as a holiday mansion on the Sha Tin shore named after England's Lake Windermere — then became an army camp, a college campus, a ferry pier, and finally a name attached to an MTR maintenance depot in a landscape its founders would not recognise.

subject: Hochschule Niederrhein
summary: A university born from looms and spinning frames, where Germany's textile capital still teaches the world how cloth gets made.

story.title: The Hofburg: Seven Centuries in One Address

subject: Hofburg
summary: From a medieval fortress built by Bohemian kings to the seat of the Austrian president, the Hofburg has been continuously occupied by the rulers of Austria for over seven hundred years - a palace that grew wing by wing as empires rose and fell around it.

subject: Hofburg, Innsbruck
summary: A Habsburg palace built from medieval fortifications in the heart of Innsbruck, ranking alongside its Viennese siblings as one of Austria's three most important cultural buildings.

subject: Hogueras de Alicante
summary: Every June, Alicante spends a year building towering satirical monuments in wood and cork, then burns them all in a single ecstatic night of fire.

subject: Hoh Rainforest
summary: The wettest forest in the contiguous United States, where 129 inches of annual rain feed Sitka spruce that tower 300 feet and moss drapes every surface in emerald green.

subject: Hoh people
summary: The Chalat people have lived along the Hoh River for millennia, building a civilization around cedar, salmon, and a rainforest that receives 140 inches of rain per year.

subject: Hohenlychen Sanatorium
summary: A children's tuberculosis hospital in the Uckermark pines became an SS clinic whose director ordered the surgical mutilation of women prisoners at Ravensbrück, eleven kilometres west.

story.title: Hokke-ji: The Empress's Nunnery and Its Eleven-Faced Goddess

subject: Hokke-ji
summary: Founded by Empress Komyo on the site of her father's mansion, Hokke-ji became the head nunnery of all Japan -- burned in battle, shattered by earthquakes, abandoned, and revived across thirteen centuries, all while guarding a National Treasure statue carved from a single piece of kaya wood.

subject: Hokki-ji
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage temple in Ikaruga holds Japan's oldest and largest three-story pagoda -- a National Treasure completed in 706 AD that was once completely dismantled and reassembled by modern restorers who burned dates into the new timber.

subject: Hole of Horcum
summary: A 400-foot-deep amphitheatre carved into the North York Moors by springs, slow water, and - if local legend is to be trusted - an enraged giant.

subject: Hollywood Bowl
summary: America's most famous outdoor amphitheater, carved into a natural hillside called Daisy Dell, where the Beatles, the Doors, and Bugs Bunny have all performed.

subject: Hollywood Road
summary: Hong Kong's oldest completed road winds through antique empires, a temple built before the colony had streets, and a police compound that became a cultural landmark.

subject: Holter Burg
summary: A ruined hilltop castle near Osnabrück that produced an Archbishop of Cologne, an Essen prince-abbess, and three bishops of Münster - all from a single small family seat.

subject: Holy Land Experience
summary: A Christian theme park in Orlando that recreated first-century Jerusalem, the Holy Land Experience drew millions of visitors before closing in 2020, its replica temples and colosseum demolished to make way for a hospital campus.

story.title: Home of Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site

subject: Home of Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site
summary: Springwood, the Hyde Park estate where FDR was born, governed from, and chose to be buried, served as America's Summer White House for twelve transformative years.

subject: Home of the Good Shepherd
summary: A 1906 Catholic school for girls deemed 'wayward' by society became one of Seattle's most unlikely cultural hubs, its chapel now hosting experimental music and its old swimming pool reborn as a community garden.

subject: Homomonument
summary: Three pink granite triangles set into a canal-side pavement, the world's first monument to gay and lesbian people persecuted for who they loved.

subject: Hong Kong Coliseum
summary: The Hong Kong Coliseum — the inverted pyramid on Hung Hom Bay — has been Hong Kong's premier indoor concert venue since 1983, hosting everyone from David Bowie to Cantopop legends in a building whose distinctive silhouette is as recognizable as any in Kowloon.

subject: Hong Kong Garrison
summary: The People's Liberation Army force that took up residence in Hong Kong at midnight on 1 July 1997 — occupying the same barracks the British Army had left hours before.

story.title: Hongan-ji Nagoya Betsuin: The Temple Where Hokusai Painted a Giant

subject: Hongan-ji Nagoya Betsuin
summary: A Buddhist temple in central Nagoya with over five centuries of history, where Hokusai once painted a Daruma on a sheet of paper the size of a house, and whose wooden bell tower survived the firebombing that destroyed the rest.

subject: Honorary decrees for the Samians
summary: On a marble slab in the Acropolis Museum, two goddesses clasp hands above the text of an ancient treaty, recording the moment Athens repaid the one ally that never abandoned it.

subject: Hooglandse Kerk
summary: The Gothic giant of Leiden, dedicated to Saint Pancras, holding the tomb of the mayor who refused to surrender.

subject: Hope Street, Liverpool
summary: Liverpool's most celebrated street runs for half a mile between two cathedrals - the Anglican at one end, the Catholic at the other - past theatres, the Philharmonic, two universities, and the pub John Lennon and Stuart Sutcliffe used to drink in.

subject: Hope Waddell Training Institution
summary: Founded by Scottish missionaries in 1895 at the urging of Mary Slessor, this Calabar school became West Africa's largest vocational training institution and may have introduced soccer to Nigeria.

subject: Hopewell Centre
summary: A 222-metre circular tower in Wan Chai, Hopewell Centre was Hong Kong's tallest building when it opened in 1980, featured a revolving restaurant that locals insisted on calling by the wrong number, and had a rooftop pool built because neighbors said the building looked like a cigarette.

subject: Hornøya (Finnmark)
summary: Norway's easternmost point is a treeless, 0.4-square-kilometer island in the Barents Sea where a lone lighthouse stands watch and hundreds of thousands of seabirds make their home.

subject: Horse Racing in Ireland
summary: Two North Cork men made a four-and-a-half mile bet between two church steeples in 1752, and accidentally invented an entire branch of horse racing.

subject: Hosios Loukas
summary: A radiant 11th-century Byzantine monastery on the slopes of Mount Helicon near Distomo, Hosios Loukas holds the best-preserved mosaic complex of the Macedonian Renaissance and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990.

subject: Hostynnyi Dvir
summary: For two centuries this neoclassical trade hall has anchored Kyiv's old merchant quarter, its name meaning both a house of goods and a house of welcome, and its fate fought over to this day.

subject: Hotak dynasty
summary: The Afghan Pashtun dynasty that overthrew the mighty Safavid Empire in 1722, seized the Persian throne, then destroyed itself through palace coups and massacres in less than three decades.

subject: Hougoumont
summary: A walled Belgian farmhouse where, by Wellington's own account, the success of Waterloo turned on the closing of a single gate.

subject: Houthi–Saudi Arabian conflict
summary: Since 2015, a cross-border war has run along the Saudi-Yemeni frontier - Saudi air strikes into Houthi-held Yemen, Houthi missiles and drones deep into the Kingdom - and the civilians on both sides have paid for every escalation.

subject: How Hill
summary: An Edwardian house on a low Norfolk hill above the River Ant, surrounded by windpumps and reedbeds - a former architect's retreat now teaching new generations to read the Broads.

story.title: How a Gathering of Fans Became the Center of Everything

subject: How a Gathering of Fans Became the Center of Everything
summary: In 1970, a small group of San Diego comic book enthusiasts organized a one-day event at the U.S. Grant Hotel to celebrate the medium they loved.

subject: Howard Air Force Base
summary: Carved from jungle 460 meters from the Pacific, Howard Air Force Base spent half a century as America's southernmost jet-capable airfield before becoming Panama's newest international airport.

subject: Howard Smith Wharves
summary: Depression-era wharves under the Story Bridge, dug with air-raid shelters during the war and left derelict for decades, are now Brisbane's favourite riverfront.

subject: Howden Minster
summary: A vast medieval church in the Vale of York with a roofless choir, an unfinished octagonal chapter house, and a 135-foot tower that took two bishops' bequests to complete.

subject: Hoylake Lifeboat Station
summary: Established in 1803 by the Liverpool Dock Trustees, Hoylake claims a lifeboat heritage older than the RNLI itself.

subject: Huanggutun incident
summary: The 1928 assassination of warlord Zhang Zuolin by a bomb planted on a railway bridge outside Shenyang, an act that backfired on its Japanese plotters and delayed the invasion of Manchuria by three years.

subject: Hugo Siepmann
summary: Known to his workers as Schippen-Hugo, the younger Siepmann brother turned a small Westphalian forge into Germany's second-largest drop-steel foundry and became one of the wealthiest men in the Sauerland.

subject: Huilo-Huilo Biological Reserve
summary: A private rainforest reserve in southern Chile where a moss-covered hotel shaped like a volcano pours a waterfall from its peak, and a once-logged landscape now shelters returning huemul deer and the tiny Darwin's frog.

subject: Hull History Centre
summary: A purpose-built archive that united Hull's university and council collections under one roof, holding Philip Larkin's papers, the 1299 royal charter, and 225,000 catalogued documents.

subject: Hull Minster
summary: The largest parish church in England by floor area, where William Wilberforce was baptised in 1759 and where Luftwaffe bombs spared some of the finest medieval brickwork in the country.

subject: Hulne Priory
summary: A 1240 Carmelite friary in Northumberland - reputedly chosen for resembling Mount Carmel - with substantial ruins, a fifteenth-century pele tower, and a Hollywood second life.

subject: Humen
summary: The Humen — Tiger Gate — is the narrow Pearl River strait where China met the outside world for centuries: the sole maritime gateway to Canton, the site of Lin Zexu's opium destruction in 1839, and the flashpoint where the First Opium War began.

subject: Humphreys Peak
summary: Arizona's highest point - a dormant volcano that once stood 15,000 feet tall before a catastrophic collapse reshaped it, now home to subarctic tundra, a ski resort, and 360-degree views stretching to the Grand Canyon.

subject: Hunstanton
summary: England's only east-coast seaside resort that faces west — its striped cliffs of red chalk and white limestone setting a backdrop for sunsets over The Wash, while P.G. Wodehouse once plotted Bertie Wooster's misadventures in its gardens.

subject: Huáscar (ironclad)
summary: Three commanders died on her deck, two Chilean and one Peruvian, and both nations still honor her; the Huáscar floats at Talcahuano as a shrine to the courage of the men who fought her.

subject: Hwangnyongsa
summary: Once home to the tallest wooden structure in the world, Hwangnyongsa -- the Imperial Dragon Temple -- now survives only as massive foundation stones scattered across a field in Gyeongju, a monument to both Silla ambition and Mongol destruction.

subject: Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array
summary: A radio telescope in South Africa's Karoo desert built from wood and PVC pipes, listening for whispers from the first stars that ever shone.

subject: Hyper-Kamiokande
summary: Buried 600 meters beneath a mountain in central Japan, the world's largest neutrino detector is taking shape -- a cathedral-sized water tank designed to catch the faintest whispers of the universe's most elusive particles.

subject: Hypogeum of Torre del Ram
summary: A Bronze Age tomb near Ciutadella, later emptied to shelter cattle, still guards three ships carved into its walls that no one can quite explain.

subject: Hyōgo-ku, Kobe
summary: The ward whose name means 'weapons warehouse' has served as Japan's gateway to the Inland Sea since the 8th century, briefly held the nation's capital in 1180, and bore the heaviest toll of Kobe's wartime bombing.

subject: Hämeenkatu
summary: A kilometre of cobblestone from the railway station to the park, once widened for traffic and now handed back to trams, buses and people on foot.

subject: Hämeensilta
summary: Tampere's central bridge was demolished and rebuilt in 2018, then dressed again in its own 1929 granite and its four bronze giants, so that nothing appeared to change.

subject: Hörnum
summary: The southern tip of Sylt was uninhabitable for centuries because the dunes kept burying the houses. Only after a ship company built a pier in 1901 did anyone bother to stay.

subject: Hørdum stone
summary: A Viking Age picture stone in a Thy church porch, showing the moment Thor hooked the Midgard Serpent - and the giant beside him reaching for the line with a blade.

story.title: Hogon-ji: The Temple Built by an Emperor's Dream

subject: Hōgon-ji
summary: A 1,300-year-old Buddhist temple on a tiny island in Lake Biwa, founded after Emperor Shomu dreamed that Amaterasu commanded him to build it -- home to National Treasures relocated from Toyotomi Hideyoshi's mausoleum and a corridor built from the wood of his warship.

subject: Hōkō-ji (Kyoto)
summary: A Kyoto temple built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi to house a Great Buddha rivaling Nara's -- destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly over four centuries, its giant bell once served as a political pretext for the war that ended the Toyotomi dynasty.

story.title: Honen-in: Where Kyoto's Intellectuals Rest Among the Camellias

subject: Hōnen-in
summary: A moss-draped temple tucked just off Kyoto's Philosopher's Path, where the graves of Japan's greatest literary minds lie beneath camellia trees and visitors walk between sculpted sand mounds that purify them before they even reach the gate.

subject: Hōrai-ji
summary: A 1,300-year-old mountain temple reached by climbing 1,425 stone steps, where an ascetic once carved gods from living trees and the Eurasian scops owl still calls from ancient forest canopy.

story.title: Horinji: The Temple That Rose from Lightning

subject: Hōrin-ji (Nara)
summary: A seventh-century Buddhist temple in Ikaruga, Nara, Horinji preserves some of Japan's oldest wooden statues and a three-story pagoda rebuilt after lightning struck in 1944 -- its reconstruction powered by a novelist's pen and the coins of ordinary citizens.

subject: Hồ Thủy Tiên
summary: A water park that opened half-finished in 2004, closed within months, spent two decades as one of Southeast Asia's most photographed ruins, and finally reopened as a community park in 2025 — its graffitied dragon still watching over the lake.

subject: Hồng Lĩnh Mountains
summary: A ridge of ninety-nine peaks above the Lam River, named for phoenixes that never landed, holding a pagoda older than its famous namesake and the hunting ground of Vietnam's greatest poet.

subject: INS Kursura
summary: A Cold War-era submarine that patrolled the Arabian Sea during the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War now sits on a beach in Visakhapatnam, the first submarine museum in South Asia.

subject: ITC Enschede
summary: A former Dutch prime minister founded a school to teach the world how to make maps - and 75 years later it has trained more than 19,000 people from 170 countries.

subject: Iberê Camargo Foundation
summary: On the bank of the Guaíba, a Pritzker laureate carved a museum of white concrete from an old quarry, wrapping its galleries in ramps that loop out toward the water and back into the dark.

subject: Ibini Ukpabi
summary: The oracle shrine of the Aro Confederacy in southeastern Nigeria, known to the British as the Long Juju, served as a court of divine justice whose guilty verdicts secretly fed the transatlantic slave trade for generations.

subject: Idarado Mine
summary: A five-mile tunnel bored straight through the San Juan Mountains connected two mining towns and became Colorado's second-largest mine before economics brought it all crashing down.

subject: Iga Idunganran
summary: The palace of the Oba of Lagos stands on the exact spot where a 15th-century nobleman once grew pepper, its Yoruba name translating to 'the palace built on a pepper farm.'

story.title: Iga Kokubun-ji: The Temple That Vanished Twice

subject: Iga Kokubun-ji
summary: An eighth-century Buddhist temple ordered by an emperor to heal Japan after a devastating smallpox epidemic -- its stones were stolen for a castle, its memory was lost for centuries, and its ruins were destroyed again in 1944 to build an airfield for the Imperial Japanese Navy.

story.title: Iglesia de San Francisco, Santiago de Chile

subject: Iglesia de San Francisco, Santiago de Chile
summary: The oldest surviving building in Santiago, a Franciscan church that has outlasted roughly fifteen major earthquakes since the 1600s.

subject: Iglesia de San Pedro Claver, Cartagena
summary: The church where a Spanish Jesuit who declared himself 'the slave of the slaves forever' spent forty years boarding incoming slave ships to nurse, comfort, and baptize the hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans forced through Cartagena's port.

subject: Iglesia de la Matriz
summary: Valparaíso's oldest church, burned by Francis Drake, leveled by earthquakes, and rebuilt four times on the same patch of ground at the foot of Cerro Santo Domingo.

subject: Ignacio Escudero District
summary: The hill with its top cut off stands as a monument to two origin stories and a flood that pushed a people toward higher ground.

story.title: Ikegami Honmon-ji: Where Nichiren Drew His Last Breath

subject: Ikegami Honmon-ji
summary: A 750-year-old temple marking the site where the Buddhist priest Nichiren died in 1282, featuring a 1608 pagoda that survived centuries of earthquakes but not the firebombing of 1945 -- and an annual lantern procession that draws tens of thousands through the streets of south Tokyo.

subject: Ikon Gallery
summary: Founded in a glass kiosk in a Birmingham shopping centre by four art-school graduates who wanted to bring contemporary art to people who never went to galleries, now housed in a Victorian school.

subject: Ile Maroia Laji
summary: A Candomblé terreiro in Salvador whose lineage reaches back to Yoruba princesses captured in 1789 and carried across the Atlantic, where they built a house for the orixás that still stands.

subject: Ilha de Itamaracá
summary: Sixty-six square kilometres of Atlantic forest and reef-sheltered beach off Pernambuco, holding the first sugar mill in Portuguese America, one of the earliest Jewish congregations in the hemisphere, and the dance that fishermen's wives invented waiting on the sand.

subject: Ilha do Marajó
summary: A river island the size of Switzerland at the mouth of the Amazon, where a sophisticated mound-building society flourished for centuries before Europeans arrived, and where police now patrol the flooded grasslands on water buffalo.

subject: Ilha do Mel
summary: A car-free Brazilian island where 95% of the land is protected wilderness, ancient shell middens mark 6,000 years of human presence, and a Scottish-built lighthouse still guides ships into Paranaguá Bay.

subject: Ilkley
summary: A Roman fort, a Victorian water cure, and an unlikely place where Charles Darwin sat out the publication of On the Origin of Species.

subject: Illa del Rei
summary: A small island in the channel into Port Mahon that has been a king's landing place, a 6th-century basilica, a British naval hospital nicknamed Bloody Island, and now a restored art gallery.

subject: Illaunloughan
summary: A third-of-an-acre island in the Portmagee Channel held an 8th-century monastery whose shrine was decorated with scallop shells, as though pointing the way to Santiago.

subject: Illauntannig Monastic Site
summary: An early medieval Irish monastery on a small Atlantic island - two oratories, three beehive huts, a stone cross, all enclosed by a circular drystone wall and still standing after fifteen centuries.

subject: Imai Foundation
summary: In a 1920s pavilion on the Düsseldorf Rhine, an institute is racing to save the early decades of video art before the tapes themselves dissolve.

subject: Imakumano Kannon-ji
summary: A Kyoto temple founded on a vision of light, where an emperor's headache cure became centuries of devotion along Japan's oldest pilgrimage route.

subject: Imamzadeh Yahya
summary: A Mongol-era mausoleum in Varamin whose exquisite lusterware tiles were systematically looted across two waves in the 19th century and now reside in at least 30 museums worldwide, while local worshippers have transformed the stripped interior into a living shrine adorned with fairy lights and handwritten signs.

story.title: The Emperor's Tomb That Bureaucracy Forgot

subject: Imashirozuka Kofun
summary: A massive keyhole-shaped burial mound in Takatsuki, Osaka -- almost certainly the tomb of sixth-century Emperor Keitai -- sits open to the public because Japan's Imperial Household Agency already assigned the emperor to a different grave and refuses to reconsider.

subject: Imjingak
summary: A park on the banks of the Imjin River where 1.2 million visitors a year come to confront the Korean War's unfinished legacy -- through memorials, a bullet-riddled locomotive, and a bridge that once carried prisoners home.

subject: Imperial Crypt
summary: Beneath a modest Capuchin church on Vienna's Neuer Markt, 145 members of the Habsburg dynasty lie in metal sarcophagi spanning four centuries of European power.

story.title: The Imperial Household Agency: Keepers of Japan's Oldest Dynasty

subject: Imperial Household Agency
summary: Hidden inside the grounds of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo, a secretive government agency has managed the affairs of the world's oldest hereditary monarchy for over a thousand years -- and guards more than 740 ancient tombs it refuses to let anyone excavate.

subject: Inauguration of Willem-Alexander
summary: On 30 April 2013, after his mother signed away the throne in the Royal Palace, Willem-Alexander walked across Dam Square to the Nieuwe Kerk and became the first Dutch king in 123 years.

subject: Inca Trail to Machu Picchu
summary: A four-day trek along ancient Inca roads that climbs over 4,200 meters through cloud forest and alpine tundra before arriving at the Sun Gate of Machu Picchu -- one of the most regulated hiking trails on Earth.

subject: Inch, County Kerry
summary: A five-kilometre sand spit reaching into Dingle Bay, where the Atlantic, a thirteenth-century church, and David Lean's Ryan's Daughter all share the strand.

subject: Inchcolm
summary: Known as 'the Iona of the East', Inchcolm is a small island in the Firth of Forth whose Augustinian abbey - the best-preserved cloister in Scotland - has survived hermits, English raiders, Reformation iconoclasts, and two World Wars of coastal artillery batteries.

subject: Inchgarvie
summary: A tiny rock in the Firth of Forth that has been a fortress, a plague colony, a prison, and the cantilever foundation that holds up Scotland's most iconic bridge.

subject: Indianola, Texas
summary: Once Texas's second-largest port, Indianola was erased from the map by two catastrophic hurricanes in 1875 and 1886 -- its courthouse now lies underwater in Matagorda Bay.

subject: Ingapirca
summary: The largest Inca ruins in Ecuador survived because the Inca who built them chose alliance over conquest.

subject: Inhotim
summary: A Brazilian mining magnate turned his hillside ranch into the largest open-air contemporary art museum in Latin America, then lost control of it in a debt crisis. The art stayed.

subject: Inishmore
summary: Ireland's second-largest offshore island holds a Bronze Age cliff fortress that George Petrie called the most magnificent barbaric monument in Europe.

subject: Inishnabro
summary: An uninhabited Blasket island with cathedral-shaped sea cliffs once nearly became Ireland's spaceport, in a 1973 proposal the Irish government dismissed as bordering on disbelief.

subject: Inishturk
summary: Wild Boar Island - a community of around fifty-six people fifteen kilometres off the Mayo coast, home to Ireland's smallest primary school and one of its most stubborn island traditions.

story.title: Initial Point of Boundary Between U.S. and Mexico

subject: Initial Point of Boundary Between U.S. and Mexico
summary: Monument No. 258 marks the western terminus of the U.S.–Mexico border where it meets the Pacific Ocean — a concrete obelisk that has been rebuilt, disputed, and visited by millions, standing 60 meters from the sea.

subject: Inner Hebrides
summary: A scattered archipelago off Scotland's west coast where Skye's mountains, Iona's ancient abbey, and the basalt cathedral of Fingal's Cave reward those who slow down.

subject: Inner Niger Delta
summary: Where the Niger River unclenches into a 400-kilometer maze of lakes and grass, a desert grows a sea each year - and a million cattle wait for the signal to cross.

subject: Institut Valencià d'Art Modern
summary: Spain's first museum of modern art, opened in 1989 around a collection of iron sculpture — and built atop a rediscovered stretch of Valencia's medieval wall.

subject: Institut für Sexualwissenschaft
summary: Magnus Hirschfeld's Berlin institute was the world's first sexology research centre and the world's first trans clinic — until students hauled its library into the street and burned it in May 1933.

story.title: Institute for Chemistry and Biology of the Marine Environment

subject: Institute for Chemistry and Biology of the Marine Environment
summary: Lower Saxony's only university-based marine research institute - studying how the carbon, nutrients, and microbes of the Wadden Sea actually work.

subject: Institute for Contemporary Art, Richmond
summary: Steven Holl designed it to look like a musical instrument and Richmond opened it in 2018 at the corner of Broad and Belvidere - VCU's Institute for Contemporary Art is a non-collecting museum whose zinc and glass exterior was one of Architectural Digest's most anticipated buildings of its year.

subject: Instituto Nacional Mejía
summary: A Quito high school founded in 1897 by a president who would be murdered for liberalism, where poets, generals, and presidents learned to write sentences they would later live by.

story.title: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia

subject: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia
summary: For twenty-four years, in an unremarkable office building in The Hague, witnesses from Bosnia, Croatia, Kosovo, and Serbia stood up and told the world what had happened to them. The tribunal that listened indicted 161 people and changed international law.

subject: International Olympic Academy
summary: Established in 1961 near the ruins of ancient Olympia, the International Olympic Academy was founded to do what Pierre de Coubertin feared might not happen: keep the philosophy of Olympism alive long after the politics and spectacle of modern sport threatened to obscure it.

subject: Intuit Dome
summary: Intuit Dome is the home arena of the NBA's Los Angeles Clippers, opened in August 2024 in Inglewood, California. The $2 billion venue seats 18,000, features the world's largest halo scoreboard at 38,375 square feet, and will host basketball events at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

subject: Invasion of Minorca (1781)
summary: A Franco-Spanish army laid siege to Fort St. Philip for five months, but it was scurvy, not cannon fire, that finally forced the British garrison to surrender Menorca.

subject: Inverness Royal Academy
summary: Dominican friars opened a school in Inverness in 1223, the burgh continued one through 1668, and an Enlightenment academy followed in 1792—producing James Macpherson, Josephine Tey, Alistair MacLean, and forensic anthropologist Sue Black.

subject: Iona
summary: The cradle of Celtic Christianity in Scotland, where Columba founded his monastery in 563, the Book of Kells may have been begun, and Scottish kings from Kenneth I to Macbeth are said to lie buried.

subject: Ipswich Docks
summary: The Suffolk wet dock that opened in 1842 as the largest enclosed dock in the United Kingdom, fed coprolite fertiliser to British agriculture, and was reborn as a waterfront of apartments and yacht moorings.

subject: Ipswich Waterfront
summary: One of England's oldest continuously occupied ports, where Anglo-Saxon traders unloaded Rhineland pottery on the same quay where yachts now moor in front of Suffolk's tallest building.

story.title: Ira F. Brilliant Center for Beethoven Studies

subject: Ira F. Brilliant Center for Beethoven Studies
summary: North America's only institution devoted entirely to Beethoven, housed on the fifth floor of a San Jose university library, where visitors can touch a fortepiano and examine a lock of the composer's hair.

subject: Iran Mall
summary: One of the world's largest shopping complexes sits beside an artificial lake in northwest Tehran, blending ancient bazaar traditions with a Guinness World Record for concrete pouring -- and once transformed overnight into a 3,000-bed hospital.

subject: Iran hostage crisis
summary: The 444-day seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran that redefined American foreign policy and helped bring down a presidency.

subject: Irish Famine (1879)
summary: Three decades after Black '47, the potato failed again in the west of Ireland - and a generation that remembered the last Famine reacted in terror and in organisation, helping launch the Land War and the Marian shrine at Knock.

subject: Iron Lion of Cangzhou
summary: Cast in a single mold in 953 AD, the Sea-suppressing Howler is China's largest and oldest surviving cast-iron sculpture -- a 40-tonne lion that once carried a Buddhist bodhisattva on its back and, according to legend, silenced a flood-causing dragon.

subject: Iron Mike
summary: Originally a sailor's term for a gyrocompass that holds a steady course, Iron Mike became the unofficial name of a half-dozen military monuments - the most famous of which stands sixteen feet tall at Fort Bragg, dedicated to every paratrooper who ever jumped.

story.title: Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences

subject: Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences
summary: Cambridge's international center for mathematical research, where Andrew Wiles famously proved Fermat's Last Theorem in 1993, named for the university's most illustrious alumnus.

subject: Isanapura
summary: Chinese court historians wrote down a great hall at the heart of a Khmer capital in the 630s; thirteen centuries later, archaeologists dug into a grid traced from the air and found a terrace seventy metres long.

subject: Isfahan
summary: Once the capital of the Safavid Persian Empire, Isfahan earned the Persian proverb 'Isfahan is half the world' through centuries of architectural splendor, from its UNESCO-listed public square to its vaulted bazaar and Armenian cathedral.

subject: Ishibutai Kofun
summary: Japan's largest megalithic tomb sits stripped bare in the Asuka countryside -- its earthen covering deliberately removed as punishment for the powerful Soga clan, exposing 2,300 tons of granite that have drawn pilgrims and puzzled visitors for over a thousand years.

subject: Ishiyama-dera
summary: The temple where Murasaki Shikibu began writing the world's first novel, built around a statue that mysteriously fused to a boulder in eighth-century Japan.

subject: Isis Downs Woolshed
summary: The only semicircular, prefabricated-steel shearing shed in Australia - 52 stands fanned around a single great pillar, its steel shipped from England to rise like a tin amphitheatre on the empty Barcoo plains.

subject: Isla Gorgona
summary: A Colombian Pacific island that was a maximum-security prison, then a national park, and now belongs to snakes, sharks, and humpback whales.

subject: Isla Grosa
summary: A tiny volcanic island off La Manga that has been a ship-killing reef, a Phoenician graveyard, a pirate refuge, a navy dive school, and now one of Europe's most important seabird sanctuaries.

subject: Isla de Lobos
summary: A rocky island off Punta del Este crowded with a quarter-million sea lions and crowned by the tallest lighthouse in South America.

subject: Isla de los Estados
summary: A storm-battered island off the tip of Tierra del Fuego whose lonely lighthouse gave Jules Verne the most famous beacon in literature.

subject: Isle Brevelle
summary: Known as the 'Joyous Coast,' this 18,000-acre community between the Cane River and Bayou Brevelle in Louisiana is considered the birthplace of Creole culture -- founded by the son of a French trader and a Caddo woman, built by a man born into slavery who traveled to France and returned to construct a church.

subject: Isle Martin
summary: An uninhabited island at the head of Loch Broom that has been, in turn, a Celtic monastery, a herring station that predated Ullapool, a working flour mill, and a community-owned bird sanctuary.

subject: Isle of Ewe
summary: A small Scottish island where a single extended family - the Grants - have lived for over a century, and where the children's commute to school used to be 26 miles a day.

subject: Isle of Man
summary: A self-governing island in the middle of the Irish Sea, ruled in legend by a sea god and in fact by the world's oldest continuously sitting parliament.

subject: Isle of Man
summary: A Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea where a Norse-era parliament still sits, the symbol is three running legs, and the national flower is a poisonous weed.

subject: Isle of May
summary: A small basalt island in the outer Firth of Forth that hosts 200,000 nesting seabirds, an 1816 Stevenson lighthouse, and a 13th-century priory.

subject: Isle of Mull
summary: The second-largest island in the Inner Hebrides, where colourful Tobermory, ancient Duart Castle, and the sacred island of Iona create one of Scotland's most layered landscapes.

subject: Isova
summary: In a field in the western Peloponnese stand the walls of Notre Dame at Isova — a pure Gothic abbey built by Frankish crusaders in the 13th century, burned by Turkish mercenaries in 1263, and left to the elements ever since.

story.title: Israeli Infiltration of an Iranian Nuclear Archive

subject: Israeli infiltration of an Iranian nuclear archive
summary: On one night in January 2018, fewer than 24 Mossad agents broke into an unmarked Tehran warehouse, cut open six of 32 safes in six and a half hours, and carried out 100,000 documents detailing Iran's secret nuclear weapons program -- evidence that would help end a landmark international agreement.

story.title: Istana Darul Hana: The Palace That Survived a Rebellion

subject: Istana Darul Hana
summary: Brunei's former royal residence on a hilltop in Bandar Seri Begawan witnessed an abdication, a revolt, and the education of a future sultan within its walls.

subject: Istana Negara (Jakarta)
summary: Built as a private mansion in 1796 by a Dutch colonial official, Istana Negara became the governor-general's residence, survived British occupation and Japanese capitulation, and now serves as Indonesia's ceremonial State Palace -- a single building that has witnessed every regime change in the nation's history.

story.title: Istana Nurul Iman: The Palace of Light and Excess

subject: Istana Nurul Iman
summary: The world's largest residential palace, with 1,788 rooms and air-conditioned stables for 200 polo ponies, sits on the banks of the Brunei River -- a monument to oil wealth designed by a Filipino architect who trained as a pianist.

subject: Istanbul 4th Vakıf Han
summary: A stone office block in Sirkeci designed in 1911 and still unfinished when French troops used it as barracks in 1920 — the Istanbul 4th Vakıf Han has lived through two world wars, the fall of an empire, and a century of changing tenants before becoming a luxury hotel.

subject: Istanbul Archaeology Museums
summary: Three museums beside Topkapı Palace housing the world's oldest known peace treaty, the Alexander Sarcophagus, and a million artifacts pulled from the breadth of an empire.

subject: Istanbul Modern
summary: Turkey's first museum of modern and contemporary art, Istanbul Modern opened in a converted customs warehouse in 2004 and reopened in a landmark Renzo Piano building on the Galataport waterfront in 2023.

subject: Istanbul to Izmir
summary: The 500–700 km corridor between Istanbul and Izmir is one of Turkey's most layered journeys — ancient Troy, Gallipoli battlefields, Pergamon's acropolis, and the olive-scented Gulf of Edremit all fall between two of the world's great cities.

subject: Istanbul's Rural Outskirts
summary: Beyond Istanbul's famous skyline, three vast districts — Silivri, Çatalca, and Arnavutköy — stretch into Thrace where Byzantine heritage, Black Sea beaches, and Europe's busiest new airport share the same horizon.

subject: Isted Lion
summary: A Danish victory monument that stood in Flensburg for twenty months, spent 147 years being carried between Berlin and Copenhagen, and came home in 2011.

subject: Isthmus of Chignecto
summary: A narrow strip of marsh and ridge barely 24 kilometers wide connects Nova Scotia to the rest of North America, and for four centuries every empire, army, and engineer who encountered it tried to cross it, control it, or cut through it.

subject: Isthmus of Perekop
summary: A narrow neck of land that is the only overland gateway to Crimea, so fiercely contested that its very name means the Trench.

story.title: Isui-en: Nara's Garden of Borrowed Mountains

subject: Isui-en
summary: Nara's only strolling garden dissolves the boundary between cultivated beauty and wild landscape, using the ancient technique of shakkei to pull distant temple roofs and forested hills into its intimate frame.

subject: Ithomi, Messenia
summary: A modern Greek municipal unit that takes its name from the ancient fortress-mountain at its heart — and quietly contains, within its boundaries, the ruins of one of antiquity's most defiant cities.

subject: Itsukushima
summary: On an island so sacred that trees cannot be felled and no one was traditionally permitted to die there, a vermillion torii gate appears to float on the sea at high tide.

subject: Itumbiara
summary: Where the Paranaíba splits two Brazilian states, a 2,082-megawatt hydroelectric lake made this Goiás gateway the country's second-best peacock bass hunting ground.

subject: Iwashimizu Hachimangū
summary: A hilltop Shinto shrine near Kyoto that has guarded the supernatural southwestern flank of the imperial capital for nearly 1,200 years, with ten buildings designated as National Treasures.

subject: Izumo-taisha
summary: Japan's oldest and most mythologically significant Shinto shrine, where all eight million gods are believed to gather each October to decide matters of love and fate, guarded by a sacred straw rope weighing five tons.

subject: Jackson Barracks
summary: A military post on the Mississippi where future Civil War generals once shared quarters, survived Confederate occupation and twenty feet of floodwater, and still stands as Louisiana's National Guard headquarters.

subject: Jade Spring Hill
summary: Once the source of the imperial palace's drinking water and now one of the most restricted residential compounds in China, Jade Spring Hill embodies Beijing's layered relationship with power.

subject: Jagdschloss Grunewald
summary: Berlin's oldest surviving palace is a moated hunting box on a forest lake — the building that named the Grunewald, and the road to it that became the Kurfürstendamm.

subject: Jahrtausendturm
summary: Sixty metres of leaning laminated timber on the east bank of the Elbe, built for a garden show and kept — a science museum you climb chronologically, with a Foucault pendulum hanging down the middle of it.

subject: Jakarta Fair
summary: From colonial-era night markets in the shadow of Merdeka Square to a month-long spectacle on an abandoned airport, Jakarta Fair has reinvented itself across three eras while remaining the capital's most boisterous annual celebration.

subject: Jalan M.H. Thamrin
summary: Named for a national hero who never saw it built, Jakarta's Thamrin Avenue evolved from a muddy lane beside a demolished Armenian church into Indonesia's most politically charged boulevard, where Sukarno staged his vision of a modern nation and ordinary Jakartans still reclaim the asphalt every Sunday morning.

subject: Jalan Malioboro
summary: Yogyakarta's famous seven-hundred-meter boulevard runs on a cosmological axis between the sultan's palace and Mount Merapi, threading through a century of Chinese merchants, Dutch colonial hotels, street artists, and lesehan restaurants.

subject: Jam Gadang
summary: A Dutch-built clock tower in the heart of Bukittinggi whose roof has changed shape with each regime -- from round colonial cupola to Japanese pagoda to the horn-curved Minangkabau silhouette it wears today.

subject: James McGill
summary: A Glasgow metalworker's son paddled canoes into the Canadian wilderness, built a fur-trading fortune, and left behind a bequest that would seed not just one university but several across an entire nation.

subject: James Plaintain
summary: A Jamaican-born pirate spent his plunder building a private kingdom on the northeast coast of Madagascar - then crowned himself its king and went to war with his neighbors.

subject: Jane Austen Centre
summary: Bath knew Jane Austen, and Jane Austen rather disliked Bath - which has not stopped a Gay Street townhouse from becoming the world's premier Austen pilgrimage site.

subject: Janet Smith case
summary: A 22-year-old Scottish nursemaid died in a Shaughnessy mansion in 1924; the investigation that followed destroyed the evidence, produced a racist bill, and sent an innocent man into a torture cellar.

story.title: The Japan Sumo Association: Sacred Sport, Street Brawl Origins

subject: Japan Sumo Association
summary: The governing body of professional sumo operates from Tokyo's Ryogoku Kokugikan arena, where retired wrestlers run a sport that began as Shinto harvest rituals, survived a 1648 street-fighting ban, and has weathered scandals from organized crime to match-fixing.

subject: Japanese icebreaker Fuji (AGB-5001)
summary: A bright orange icebreaker that spent 18 years smashing through Antarctic pack ice now sits quietly at Nagoya Port, its bridge still set for a heading south and mannequins still playing checkers below decks.

subject: Japanese occupation of Gyeongbokgung
summary: On a July morning in 1894, Japanese troops stormed Gyeongbokgung Palace, seized the Korean king, and installed a puppet government -- an act that triggered the First Sino-Japanese War.

subject: Jaru Biological Reserve
summary: A strict nature reserve in Rondonia that has grown from its 1961 origins into a 346,000-hectare fortress against deforestation, sheltering jaguars, giant otters, and over 500 bird species in one of the Amazon's least-known interfluvial regions.

subject: Jawne
summary: Cologne's only Jewish secondary school taught English and modern Hebrew through the 1930s to prepare its children to leave - and saved 130 of them before time ran out.

subject: Jaú
summary: Named for a greedy catfish, Jaú once shipped more coffee than any station on earth; today it turns out up to 120,000 pairs of women's shoes a day and plays a sport it invented in a school gym.

story.title: Jesuit Block and Estancias of Córdoba

subject: Jesuit Block and Estancias of Córdoba
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage ensemble where the oldest university in Argentina and five rural estates reveal how the Jesuits built an empire of learning on the labor of the unfree.

story.title: Trinidad and Jesús: Paraguay's Unfinished Cathedrals in the Forest

subject: Jesuit Missions of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue
summary: Two Jesuit mission ruins in Paraguay's Itapúa Department -- one the largest of all 30 reductions, the other an ambitious church left unfinished when the Jesuits were expelled in 1767 -- stand as UNESCO World Heritage testimony to a 150-year experiment in communal society.

subject: Jesuset del Miracle
summary: A beloved Alcoy procession honors a statue said to have pointed out a 1568 theft — a tender tradition rooted in a foreigner's confession and a brutal public execution.

subject: Jiji, Nantou
summary: Taiwan's smallest township by area carries one of its most resonant histories — a camphor boomtown, an earthquake epicenter, and now a slow-tourism destination where the old railway station still runs.

subject: Jikō-in
summary: A 17th-century Zen temple in Nara Prefecture built by the founder of one of Japan's most influential tea ceremony schools, where borrowed scenery turns the entire Nara Basin into a garden.

story.title: Jingo-ji: The Temple Where You Throw Away Your Bad Luck

subject: Jingo-ji
summary: A 1,200-year-old Shingon Buddhist temple perched on Mount Takao in Kyoto, Jingo-ji guards sixteen National Treasures, the legacy of the monk Kukai, and a cliff where visitors hurl clay plates into the valley to cast off misfortune.

subject: Jirón de la Unión
summary: Lima's most storied pedestrian street runs eleven blocks from the presidential palace to the grand hotels, carrying five centuries of Peruvian history underfoot.

subject: Jogyesa
summary: Seoul's chief Buddhist temple has survived the fall of dynasties, colonial suppression, and modern power struggles, sheltering Korean Seon Buddhism for over six centuries.

subject: Johannesburg Central Police Station
summary: The blue building once known as John Vorster Square housed apartheid's Security Branch on its top floors, where detainees were tortured and several died in custody that the state called suicide.

subject: Johannisthal Air Field
summary: Germany's first commercial airfield opened three weeks after the world's first, taught the country to fly, spent forty years behind a fence, and is now a nature reserve surrounded by laboratories.

subject: John Baskeyfield
summary: A 21-year-old butcher from Stoke-on-Trent who held a road junction in Oosterbeek alone after his anti-tank crew was killed, awarded a posthumous Victoria Cross, and never found.

story.title: John Dillinger: Indianapolis's Most Wanted Son

subject: John Dillinger
summary: Born on Cooper Street in Indianapolis in 1903, John Dillinger became Depression-era America's most notorious bank robber, escaped from an 'escape-proof' jail with what may have been a carved wooden gun, and was gunned down outside a Chicago movie theater at age 31 - all while inadvertently creating the modern FBI.

subject: John Dudley, 1st Duke of Northumberland
summary: The man who tried to put Lady Jane Grey on the English throne in July 1553, ruled England as regent for Edward VI, lost everything in a matter of weeks, and was executed on Tower Hill on 22 August 1553.

subject: John Wilkes Booth
summary: The farm in rural Northern Virginia where America's most infamous assassin met his end, twelve days after shooting Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre.

subject: John the Russian
summary: A young soldier captured into slavery in Ottoman Cappadocia refused to abandon his faith - and three centuries later, his shrine on a Greek island still draws pilgrims by the thousand.

subject: Johnstown Flood
summary: On May 31, 1889, the South Fork Dam collapsed and sent 14.55 million cubic meters of water barreling into a narrow Pennsylvania valley at a flow rate matching the Mississippi River -- killing 2,208 people in 57 minutes and changing American law forever.

subject: Jokhang
summary: The spiritual heart of Lhasa and Tibet's most sacred Buddhist temple, built around 640 CE to house a statue brought from Nepal and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Jokioinen
summary: Finland's largest estate was broken into fifteen hundred farms here, and what the state kept it turned into an instrument: the country's plant breeding, its weather record, and now its largest Buddhist shrine.

subject: Jondaryan Woolshed
summary: A 300-foot timber cathedral to wool on the Darling Downs, where 52 shearers once worked shoulder to shoulder and a single union ban helped set Australian Labor in motion.

subject: Jonglei State
summary: South Sudan's largest state by area, where the White Nile meets vast floodplains, ethnic communities compete for dwindling resources, and the rusting hulk of an abandoned mega-canal stands as a monument to ambitions that outran reality.

subject: Jongmyo
