subject: Oban
summary: The gateway to the Hebrides, where ferries fan out to a dozen islands, trains arrive on one of Britain's most scenic railway lines, and the seafood shack by the pier serves lunch with a side of marauding seagulls.

subject: Object 100
summary: Hidden in the mountains above Balaklava, a Cold War fortress buried anti-ship missiles under enough concrete to survive a nuclear strike, its launchers rising from the rock only to fire.

subject: Obras Sociais Irmã Dulce
summary: The charitable foundation built by Saint Dulce of the Poor in Salvador, Bahia, which grew from a chicken yard clinic in 1949 into Brazil's largest fully public-care hospital complex with more than a thousand beds.

subject: Occupation of Alcatraz
summary: When 89 Native Americans claimed the abandoned federal prison in 1969, they offered to buy it for the same price the government had offered their ancestors: 47 cents per acre.

subject: Ockenburg
summary: A small auxiliary airfield on the southwest edge of The Hague, captured and recaptured in 72 hours during the German airborne assault of May 1940.

subject: Ocotillo Wells, California
summary: A desert community that has hosted Juan Bautista de Anza's colonial expedition, an F-35B crash, and a classic science fiction film, and that serves as the gateway to one of California's largest off-highway vehicle parks.

subject: Odeon of Agrippa
summary: A Roman concert hall in the heart of the Athenian Agora that grew too ambitious, collapsed under its own roof, and left a row of stone Giants to mark its grave.

subject: Odeon of Herodes Atticus
summary: A grieving husband built this great stone theatre below the Acropolis for his dead wife - and nearly two thousand years later, the music has never stopped.

subject: Odeon of Pericles
summary: Athens built its first concert hall from the masts of beaten Persian warships - a roofed music hall shaped like the tent of the king they had defeated.

subject: Odin Teatret
summary: A company founded by people who had failed their drama-school auditions, rehearsing in an Oslo air-raid shelter, has spent sixty years in a west Jutland farmhouse changing what the world thinks actor training is.

subject: Odinstårnet
summary: Europe's second-tallest tower stood over Odense for nine years, until Danish Nazi collaborators blew it up at dawn.

story.title: Ohio State Reformatory: Where Redemption Found a Second Act

subject: Ohio State Reformatory
summary: A castle-like prison in Mansfield, Ohio, built to inspire spiritual rebirth in young offenders, closed under federal order for inhumane conditions, then found immortality as the filming location for The Shawshank Redemption.

subject: Oireachtas (Irish Free State)
summary: For fifteen turbulent years between 1922 and 1937, this parliament invented modern Ireland one amendment at a time.

story.title: Okunoin: Japan's Largest Cemetery and a Monk Who Never Died

subject: Okunoin
summary: Beneath a canopy of thousand-year-old cryptomeria trees on Mount Koya, over 200,000 graves line the path to the mausoleum of Kukai, where monks still deliver daily meals to a man they believe entered eternal meditation in 835 AD.

subject: Old Alabama Town
summary: Six blocks of restored 19th-century buildings in downtown Montgomery where General Lafayette once slept in a tavern, a cotton gin still turns, and a fourteen-foot-ceilinged Italianate townhouse shows how antebellum Alabama kept cool before air conditioning.

subject: Old Andado
summary: On the western edge of the Simpson Desert stands a corrugated-iron homestead frozen in time, kept as a living museum by a woman who refused to let her home die.

subject: Old Bailey Street
summary: Named for London's most famous criminal court, this steep Central street ran from the colony's first prison to its cultural heart — carrying punishment, education, bombs, and eventually cocktail bars in its short descent.

subject: Old City of Luoyang
summary: A 75-square-kilometer archaeological site east of modern Luoyang preserving the ruins of multiple imperial capitals, from the Han dynasty through the Northern Wei to the Sui, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Silk Road corridor.

subject: Old Dairy Farm Depot
summary: A Victorian cold-storage warehouse built in 1892 now shelters two of Hong Kong's most distinctive institutions — the Foreign Correspondents' Club and the Hong Kong Fringe Club — in the heart of Central.

subject: Old Kandahar
summary: A ruined citadel in southern Afghanistan where Greek inscriptions from Emperor Ashoka sit alongside fortifications fought over by Macedonians, Mughals, and Afghans across twenty-three centuries of continuous strategic importance.

story.title: Old Sanctuary of Our Lady of Caravaggio

subject: Old Sanctuary of Our Lady of Caravaggio
summary: Italian immigrants carried a devotion across the ocean in 1876, and the little stone chapel they raised for it became one of Brazil's great pilgrimage sites.

subject: Old Tai Po Police Station
summary: Built in 1899 on a hill above Tai Po as the New Territories' first police headquarters, this colonial station survived over a century to become a UNESCO-recognised heritage landmark and sustainable living campus.

subject: Old Trafford
summary: Manchester United's home for 115 years — the Theatre of Dreams, the Munich memorial, the largest club ground in England, soon to be replaced by a 100,000-seat successor on the same site.

subject: Oldenburg Hauptbahnhof
summary: The Art Nouveau main station that replaced one of the most romantic railway buildings in Germany, built with a private hall reserved for a Grand Duke who would lose his throne three years later.

subject: Older Parthenon
summary: The first Parthenon was still under construction when the Persians razed Athens in 480 BC; its column drums were built into the Acropolis wall as a memorial that became a foundation.

subject: Olumo Rock
summary: Rising 137 meters above Abeokuta, Olumo Rock served as a fortress for the Egba people during 19th-century wars, a sacred site in Yoruba religion, and an archaeological trove with stone tools dating back 1.5 million years.

subject: Olympia London
summary: An 1885 iron-and-glass exhibition hall in West Kensington that has hosted Jimi Hendrix, Mosley's blackshirts, a chess Olympiad, and a Hatsune Miku concert.

subject: Olympic Green
summary: Beijing's Olympic Park, home to the Bird's Nest Stadium, the Water Cube, and the 246.8-meter Olympic Tower, served as the centerpiece for both the 2008 Summer and 2022 Winter Olympics.

subject: Ombalantu Baobab Tree
summary: An 800-year-old baobab in northern Namibia, hollow enough to hold thirty-five people, has been a chapel, a post office, a home, and a hiding place across eight centuries of human history.

subject: Omnisport Apeldoorn
summary: An indoor velodrome whose wooden cycling track kept splintering, whose central infield converts into a 6,500-seat volleyball arena, and which has hosted three UCI Track World Championships and a Giro d'Italia opening time trial.

subject: Onassis Stegi
summary: On Syngrou Avenue in Athens, the Onassis Stegi is a 18,000-square-metre cultural centre endowed by the Onassis Foundation — a building wrapped in marble that has become one of the most active and politically engaged arts venues in southern Europe.

subject: Onbashira
summary: Every six years, men ride 12-ton fir logs down a mountainside in Japan's most dangerous festival, a tradition over 1,200 years old at Suwa Grand Shrine.

story.title: One World Trade Center: 1,776 Feet of Defiance

subject: One World Trade Center
summary: The tallest building in the Western Hemisphere rises to exactly 1,776 feet -- a height chosen to echo the year of American independence -- from the same sixteen acres of Lower Manhattan where the original Twin Towers stood until the morning of September 11, 2001.

possibleMolenMatches.title: One World Trade Center, New York

subject: Onizuka Center for International Astronomy
summary: Halfway up Mauna Kea, a modest complex of dormitories and a visitor station serves as the acclimatization waypoint for astronomers heading to the summit and the gateway for anyone who wants to see the Hawaiian sky at its clearest.

subject: Onze Lieve Vrouwetoren
summary: A 98-metre Gothic tower in Amersfoort that lost its church, kept its bells, and quietly became the origin point of every map in the Netherlands.

subject: Opera San Jose
summary: An opera company that gives its resident artists free apartments and a stage inside a restored 1927 vaudeville theater, bringing the European repertory model to Silicon Valley.

subject: Opera Village Africa
summary: A dying German director dreamed of building an opera house in the African savanna - and instead his collaborators built a school, a clinic, and a community.

subject: Operation Carthage
summary: On 21 March 1945 the RAF destroyed the Gestapo's Copenhagen headquarters at rooftop height - and, a mile and a half short of the target, a Catholic girls' school.

subject: Operation Gold
summary: The KGB knew about the Berlin spy tunnel before the first shovel went in, and let the Americans dig anyway.

subject: Operation Harling
summary: On the night of 25 November 1942, British commandos and Greek resistance fighters blew up the Gorgopotamos railway viaduct in occupied Greece — one of the first major acts of sabotage in Axis-occupied Europe.

subject: Operation Infinite Reach
summary: On August 20, 1998, American cruise missiles destroyed a Khartoum pharmaceutical factory, and twenty-seven years later the evidence for why remains contested.

subject: Operation Ramrod 16
summary: Twelve Lockheed Ventura bombers took off from Norfolk on the afternoon of 3 May 1943 to bomb a power station near Amsterdam. By the time the last one was shot down, eleven had been destroyed and a New Zealand squadron leader was floating to earth in a parachute, alone above the polder.

subject: Operation Rhino
summary: A high-profile 2001 airfield seizure in Afghanistan's desert that yielded no intelligence but produced the war's first propaganda footage -- and cost two Rangers their lives in a helicopter crash across the border.

subject: Operation Storm-333
summary: On December 27, 1979, Soviet special forces stormed a fortified palace on a hilltop in Kabul and assassinated Afghanistan's leader -- igniting a war that would last a decade and reshape the world.

subject: Operation Washing
summary: In June 1943, a small SOE team descended an impassable gorge in central Greece and destroyed the Asopos viaduct — a feat of wartime sabotage that exceeded even the celebrated Gorgopotamos raid.

subject: Opryland USA
summary: Nashville's beloved music-themed amusement park drew 2.5 million visitors a year at its peak, only to be demolished in 1997 and replaced by a shopping mall -- a decision its own company's CEO later called 'the dumbest thing I've ever seen.'

subject: Oranje Locks
summary: The 1872 lock complex east of Amsterdam where 120,000 vessels a year cross a Dutch engineering improvisation that began with a king laying a cornerstone at the bottom of a pit.

subject: Orchomenus (Boeotia)
summary: Homer ranked it with Egyptian Thebes for its wealth — and the great beehive tomb of the Minyans, a Byzantine church built from its ancient stones, and the plain where Philip II conquered Greece all remain to explain why.

subject: Orford Ness
summary: Europe's largest vegetated shingle spit, where Britain quietly invented radar in 1935 and later tested the trigger mechanisms for atomic bombs inside concrete pagodas designed to channel the blast upward.

subject: Organ Mountains
summary: Granite spires named for pipe organ resemblance rise nearly 9,000 feet above the Chihuahuan Desert, harboring 870 plant species, endemic primroses, and climbing routes that challenged Fort Bliss soldiers in the 1950s.

story.title: Organ in the Aa-kerk in Groningen

subject: Organ in the Aa-kerk in Groningen
summary: Schnitger built two organs for Groningen. One was destroyed when the tower fell on it in 1710; the other has 90 percent pure tin facade pipes and was moved here in 1815 as a royal gift.

story.title: Organ of St. Ludgeri in Norden

subject: Organ of St. Ludgeri in Norden
summary: Arp Schnitger broke his own rules to build this organ - splitting it across two parts of the church and writing the result into musical history.

story.title: Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons

subject: Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons
summary: The intergovernmental body that has overseen the destruction of declared chemical weapons stockpiles since 1997, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013, and has its semicircular headquarters in The Hague.

subject: Orkesta Runestones
summary: A collection of 11th-century runestones at a Swedish church memorialize Ulf of Borresta, a Viking who returned home three times carrying Danegeld from England under commanders including Canute the Great.

story.title: Oroncota: The Fortress Plateau Between Empires

subject: Oroncota
summary: On a triangular plateau above the Pilcomayo River in southeastern Bolivia, the ruins of Oroncota mark the contested frontier where the Yampara, Inca, Guarani, and Spanish each fought for control of the eastern Andes.

subject: Orton Plantation
summary: A 1735 plantation house on the Cape Fear River that survived Native American attacks, a Civil War hospital conversion, and 19 years of abandonment before becoming Hollywood's favorite Southern mansion.

story.title: Osaka Arsenal: The Weapons Factory Inside a Castle

subject: Osaka Arsenal
summary: For 75 years, the grounds of Osaka Castle housed one of Imperial Japan's largest weapons factories -- born from a murdered reformer's vision, fed by five wars, and obliterated in a single air raid the day before Japan surrendered.

subject: Osaka International Peace Center
summary: A peace museum near Osaka Castle whose identity was transformed by political pressure -- originally confronting Japan's wartime actions, now focused primarily on the devastation Osaka itself suffered.

subject: Ottoman conquest of Lesbos
summary: In September 1462, Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror crossed from the ruins of Troy to take Lesbos, ending a century of Genoese rule and emptying Mytilene of much of its people.

subject: Oud Herlaer
summary: The medieval castle that gave its name to a whole lordship is gone, demolished in 1737. What remains is a farm, a recently re-dug moat, and a plan to turn the site into a Kroller-Muller of the south.

subject: Our Lady of Caysasay
summary: A tiny wooden statue pulled from a Philippine river in 1603 sparked the country's first recorded Marian apparitions, survived a catastrophic volcanic eruption, and remains a living center of devotion four centuries later.

subject: Our Lady of Tinos
summary: Panagia Evangelistria — the Church of Our Lady of Tinos — is Greece's most important Orthodox pilgrimage site, built around a miraculous icon of the Annunciation found in 1823.

subject: Our Lady of the Isles
summary: A Catholic priest nicknamed Father Rocket commissioned a granite Madonna to defend South Uist against a missile base; the statue and the missile range still share the same hill.

subject: Outside Lands (festival)
summary: A three-day music festival in Golden Gate Park that combines headlining rock acts with wine, craft beer, and California cuisine in the foggy western reaches of San Francisco.

subject: Ozymandias on the Plains
summary: The giant concrete legs and broken face rising from an Amarillo ranch - a replica of Shelley's famous ruined statue, built as art about impermanence and abandoned to slow decay on the Texas plains.

subject: PK Porthcurno
summary: In a granite tunnel cut by tin miners during the Blitz, the museum that tells the story of how Britain wired the world.

subject: PMQ (Hong Kong)
summary: On a corner of Hollywood Road where Sun Yat-sen once studied, two seven-storey blocks of former police housing now house a hundred design studios, making PMQ one of Hong Kong's most unlikely creative transformations.

subject: PSV Eindhoven
summary: Founded in 1913 to give Philips workers something to do on Sundays, PSV grew into one of Dutch football's big three, won a European treble in 1988, and became a finishing school for some of the best forwards on the planet.

story.title: PT PAL Indonesia: The Shipyard That Arms an Archipelago

subject: PT PAL Indonesia
summary: From a Dutch colonial dry dock to a state-owned enterprise building submarines and frigates for navies across three continents, Surabaya's PT PAL shipyard is where Indonesia's maritime ambitions take physical form.

subject: Pachena Point Light
summary: An octagonal wooden lighthouse on Vancouver Island that guided mariners through the Graveyard of the Pacific for over a century before losing its keepers in 2024.

subject: Pacific National Exhibition
summary: Vancouver's fair has run at Hastings Park since 1910 - through the year its livestock barns were used to hold Japanese Canadian families, and on into a century of building and unbuilding.

subject: Packard Automotive Plant
summary: Once the most modern automobile factory in the world, employing 40,000 craftsmen who built luxury cars and P-51 Mustang engines, the 3.5-million-square-foot Packard Plant became the planet's largest industrial ruin before Detroit finally brought it down in 2024.

subject: Padstow
summary: A Cornish fishing port that bought a Welsh saint, lost a monastery to Vikings, and is now half-jokingly called Padstein after the chef who took the high street.

subject: Paigah Tombs
summary: Hidden among Hyderabad's concrete houses, a 200-year-old necropolis of marble latticework and stucco artistry marks where the Nizam's most powerful nobles -- wealthier than most maharajahs -- chose to rest.

subject: Paikkari Croft
summary: A tailor's log cottage beside a lake in Sammatti, where Elias Lönnrot was born in 1802 — and which became a national shrine three years after his death, because the Kalevala had to have come from somewhere.

subject: Paikuli inscription
summary: A bilingual victory monument from 293 AD where the Sasanian emperor Narseh carved his claim to power in both Parthian and Middle Persian on the walls of a tower in Iraqi Kurdistan.

subject: Paksong
summary: Perched at 1,300 metres on the Bolaven Plateau in southern Laos, Paksong is where the country's best coffee grows — cool, quiet, and largely off the radar of the travellers passing through Pakse below.

subject: Palacio Baburizza
summary: An Art Nouveau mansion on Cerro Alegre, built for one fortune and inherited by another, where a Croatian nitrate magnate left Valparaíso his collection of European paintings.

subject: Palacio Barolo
summary: A 100-meter skyscraper built as a three-dimensional reading of Dante's Divine Comedy, with hell in the basement, heaven at the top, and a lighthouse meant to greet ships from across the river.

subject: Palacio Federal Legislativo
summary: Caracas's neoclassical Capitolio, built in the 1870s on the site of a demolished convent, houses Venezuela's handwritten Declaration of Independence beneath a dome painted with the battle that won it.

subject: Palacio Salvo
summary: Montevideo's improbable Dante-inspired tower, once the tallest building in South America, rising over the corner where La Cumparsita was first played.

subject: Palacio de Aguas Corrientes
summary: Behind a fairy-tale facade of 300,000 imported English tiles, this lavish Buenos Aires palace was never a palace at all, but a giant disguised water tank.

subject: Palacio de Aguirre
summary: A mining magnate turned a fortune dug from the hills into a corner palace of glazed tile, ceramic bees, and painted ceilings, one of the jewels of Cartagena's Art Nouveau age.

subject: Palacio de Carondelet
summary: Simón Bolívar named this Quito palace after the man who rebuilt it - and centuries later its bronze fittings would be quietly swapped for gold-sprayed lead.

story.title: Palacio de la Real Audiencia de Santiago

subject: Palacio de la Real Audiencia de Santiago
summary: Spain built this palace to house its colonial courts, but within years of its completion Chileans had repurposed it to declare their independence inside the very walls meant to enforce the king's law.

subject: Palacio de las Garzas
summary: Panama's presidential palace, where live herons roam a marble courtyard and bullet holes from a 1951 coup still mark the colonial facade.

story.title: Palacio de los Capitanes Generales, Antigua Guatemala

subject: Palacio de los Capitanes Generales, Antigua Guatemala
summary: The seat of Spanish colonial power for over two centuries, the Captain General's Palace on Antigua Guatemala's Central Square has been built, damaged by earthquakes, stripped for parts, abandoned, rebuilt, and declared a World Heritage Site -- a building whose survival is as improbable as the empire it once administered.

subject: Palaestra at Olympia
summary: The colonnaded wrestling school at Olympia was where the most dangerous combat athletes of the ancient world trained in the dust — a nearly perfect square where boxing, wrestling, and the no-holds-barred pancration were practiced under the same roof as philosophy.

subject: Palais Garnier
summary: A 35-year-old unknown architect won the competition to design what became the most famous opera house in the world, only to see political upheaval nearly kill his masterpiece before it was finished.

subject: Palais Schaumburg
summary: A cloth merchant's neoclassical villa that became the first home of the German Federal Chancellery in 1949 — Adenauer's office, Brandt's negotiating room, and the garden where Helmut Schmidt's chancellorship effectively ended.

subject: Palais de Marbre
summary: A palace built for a central banker, seized by a dictator, and now a memorial to political assassination, the Marble Palace traces the arc of Congolese power through its own walls.

subject: Palais-Royal
summary: Built for a cardinal, inherited by kings, and transformed into the world's first shopping mall, the Palais-Royal has reinvented itself across four centuries of Parisian life.

subject: Palau Güell
summary: Gaudí's first great commission, a Raval mansion with a starlit indoor dome and a rooftop where his signature broken-tile mosaic was born.

subject: Palau Reial Major
summary: The royal palace of medieval Barcelona, whose great Gothic hall is where, by tradition, the Catholic Monarchs received Columbus home from the New World.

subject: Palau de la Música Catalana
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage concert hall built for a choral society at the heart of Catalonia's cultural rebirth, where stained glass, mosaic, and sculpture transform the act of listening into something close to synesthesia.

subject: Paleis voor Volksvlijt
summary: Amsterdam's iron-and-glass Crystal Palace stood on the Frederiksplein for 65 years until a single April night in 1929 erased it forever.

subject: Paliki
summary: The Paliki peninsula forms the western lobe of Cephalonia — a land of red-sand beaches, cliff monasteries, and ancient ruins that one modern theory proposes was once the island Homer called Ithaca, home of Odysseus.

subject: Palácio da Alvorada
summary: The first building constructed in Brazil's new capital - Niemeyer's Palace of Dawn sits on a peninsula in Lake Paranoá and has housed every Brazilian president since Kubitschek.

subject: Palácio de Friburgo
summary: The most monumental building in seventeenth-century Brazil had a lighthouse in one tower and an observatory in the other - and was pulled down so completely that it now survives only as engravings, a floor plan, and a computer model.

subject: Palácio do Planalto
summary: The flared columns lifting the roof slab of Brazil's presidential workplace became such a recognizable symbol that Brazilians call the entire executive branch by the building's name.

subject: Pampas Grande
summary: A mountain parish where San Jerónimo's statue kept walking home, and where a thousand people still farm the Cordillera Negra at 3,690 meters.

subject: Pampus
summary: An artificial-island sea fort in the IJmeer near Amsterdam, built 1887 to 1895, whose name gave Dutch a phrase for being knocked flat - and which never fired its guns in anger.

subject: Panagia Chrysopigi
summary: The Panagia Chrysopigi — the Golden-Spring Virgin — stands on a narrow rock spur jutting into the sea on Sifnos's southeast coast, connected to the island by a bridge, patron saint of the island since 1964.

subject: Panagia Ekatontapiliani
summary: A Byzantine church complex in Parikia on Paros dating to 326 AD, legendarily founded by Saint Helena on her pilgrimage to the Holy Land and revered as one of the oldest and most significant early-Christian churches still standing in Greece.

subject: Panagia Gremniotissa
summary: Perched 150 metres above sea level on the cliff edge of Ios Chora, the white chapel of the Virgin Mary of the Cliff arrived on the island — according to legend — by raft from Crete, and built itself where it chose to stay.

subject: Panagia Kanala
summary: The monastery above Kanala bay on Kythnos holds an icon of the Virgin Mary that fishermen are said to have found floating in the waters between two islands — and which the Virgin herself, appearing in their sleep, directed them to enshrine on this particular hillside.

subject: Panagia Krina, Chios
summary: A jewel-box Byzantine church hidden in the orchards of central Chios, built by aristocrats of the imperial court and modeled on the great monastery nearby.

subject: Panagia Vlacherna, Arta
summary: The Panagia Vlacherna near Arta is a Byzantine monastery church that served as the burial place of the Komnenos Doukas dynasty of Epirus — a building whose layers of stone and fresco span more than a millennium.

subject: Pandharpur Wari
summary: An 800-year-old Hindu pilgrimage in which a million devotees walk 250 kilometers across Maharashtra carrying saints' sacred sandals in palanquins, converging on the Vithoba Temple at Pandharpur.

subject: Panepistimiou Street
summary: A 1.2-kilometre boulevard in central Athens lined with the marble-and-gold 'Athenian Trilogy' - the Academy, University, and National Library that two Danish brothers built to dress the new Greek capital in the costume of its ancient self.

subject: Pangu Plaza
summary: Shaped like a dragon and built for the 2008 Olympics, this five-building complex near the Bird's Nest became a symbol of Beijing's ambitions before its tallest tower was seized and auctioned for $734 million.

subject: Pant-y-Saer Burial Chamber
summary: A Neolithic dolmen near Benllech where excavators found the bones of fifty-six people - including nine newborns - laid over generations beneath a single capstone.

subject: Panthéon
summary: Built as a church, seized by the Revolution, and transformed into a secular temple for France's greatest citizens, the Panthéon has swung between God and the Republic for over two centuries.

subject: Paparoa Track
summary: New Zealand's newest Great Walk was born from tragedy, threading across the Paparoa Range as a living memorial to 29 miners lost in the Pike River disaster.

subject: Paper Dome
summary: A church built from 58 cardboard tubes survived two earthquakes in two countries, traveling from Kobe to rural Taiwan as a symbol of shared resilience.

subject: Pappy & Harriet's
summary: A western movie set turned BBQ restaurant in Pioneertown where Paul McCartney and Robert Plant have performed on the same stage that once served as a backdrop for Roy Rogers — and where Anthony Bourdain once ate ribs.

subject: Paradiso (Amsterdam)
summary: Pink Floyd played a former church in Amsterdam in May 1968. Fifty-seven years later the stained glass is still there, and so is the noise.

subject: Paraiba do Sul
summary: A 1,137-kilometer river that drains industrial southeast Brazil, home to 100 native fish species, carrying both factory waste and the country's aircraft manufacturing past.

subject: Paramonga
summary: The massive stepped fortress the Chimú built at the southern edge of their empire, painted with pumas and once visited by Pizarro's men on their way to loot Pachacamac.

subject: Paramount Arts Center
summary: A 1931 Rapp and Rapp movie palace that survived the Depression, hosted Billy Ray Cyrus's Achy Breaky Heart video, and still claims a friendly ghost named Joe.

subject: Parchin
summary: Iran's most scrutinized military complex sits 30 km southeast of Tehran -- a munitions factory founded in 1935 by the grandfather of eBay's Pierre Omidyar, now at the center of decades of nuclear controversy and mysterious explosions.

subject: Parnngurr Community
summary: A Martu community in the heart of the Western Desert, born when families walked back to their country and planted a windmill in the path of a uranium mine.

subject: Parque Rodó
summary: Montevideo's seaside pleasure park pairs a little lakeside castle and an old amusement park with the memory of the writer whose name it carries.

subject: Parque del Buen Retiro, Madrid
summary: Once the private pleasure garden of Spanish kings, Madrid's Retiro Park is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site where you can row past a monument to Alfonso XII, visit the only public statue of Satan, and step inside a crystal palace built for Philippine orchids.

subject: Parthenon
summary: The most famous building in classical antiquity uses optical illusions, contains a 1687 explosion at its core, and remains the subject of an ongoing diplomatic dispute over half its sculpture.

subject: Pasadena Playhouse
summary: George Bernard Shaw called Pasadena the 'Athens of the West' because of this theater — the State Theatre of California and a training ground for some of Hollywood's most celebrated names.

subject: Paso Internacional Los Libertadores
summary: The busiest land crossing between Chile and Argentina threads the high Andes through a single tunnel - and when winter slams it shut, thousands can be trapped on the wrong side of the mountains in hours.

subject: Passage of Humaitá
summary: On a single February night in 1868, an armored Brazilian squadron ran a gauntlet of cannon at the fortress called the Gibraltar of South America - a feat seasoned naval officers had judged nearly impossible.

subject: Passaleão Incident
summary: In August 1849, a confrontational Portuguese governor was assassinated outside Macau's Barrier Gate by men seeking a posted reward, triggering a battle that a thirty-six-man charge won against impossible odds — then ending in catastrophe when the Portuguese punitive fleet destroyed itself by accident.

subject: Pat Sin Leng
summary: Eight peaks, eight immortal gods, and a small pavilion built for five people who died on a school hike — the Pat Sin Leng ridge carries both mythology and memory across its Hong Kong skyline.

story.title: Pawon: The Jewel Between Two Giants

subject: Pawon
summary: Historians call it 'the jewel of Javanese temple architecture' - a small, exquisite Buddhist shrine positioned on the exact line between Mendut and Borobudur, where pilgrims purified their minds before ascending to enlightenment.

subject: Païta
summary: A commune in the suburbs of Nouméa, New Caledonia, home to the territory's international airport and to petroglyphs possibly carved 3,000 years ago by the Pacific's earliest Lapita settlers.

subject: Peaks of Otter
summary: Thomas Jefferson thought these three Blue Ridge summits were the tallest mountains in North America - and Virginia sent their stones to the Washington Monument before anyone realized he was wrong.

subject: Pearl Brewing Company
summary: A San Antonio brewery that changed its name four times, bought a candy company to psychologically torment a rival, survived Prohibition under a woman CEO, and after 118 years of brewing became a boutique hotel named after her.

subject: Peasant Movement Training Institute
summary: A 14th-century Confucian temple in Guangzhou that became, in the 1920s, the training ground where the Kuomintang and Communist Party jointly prepared organizers to mobilize China's rural population.

subject: Peckforton Hills
summary: A 250-million-year-old sandstone ridge runs across the Cheshire plain, holding the source of two rivers, a real castle and a fake one, and an Ascension Day procession that climbs to the summit at sunset.

subject: Pedion tou Areos
summary: One of Athens's largest parks, named the Field of Ares for the god of war and laid out in the 1930s as a green memorial to the heroes of the 1821 revolution, its avenues lined with the marble busts of the men who won Greek independence.

subject: Peel
summary: A small Manx fishing port with a ruined castle on a tidal islet, the best beach on the island, and the unmistakable smell of curing kippers in the harbour air.

subject: Pemberton
summary: Beyond Whistler where the Sea to Sky Highway ends and the Lil'wat Nation's traditional territory offers hot springs, peaks, and the kind of adventure that draws those seeking wilder country.

subject: Pembroke, North Carolina
summary: The seat of the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina, the largest tribe east of the Mississippi and now a federally recognized nation after a century of advocacy, and home to a university founded in 1887 to train Lumbee teachers.

subject: Pen-y-Pass
summary: Where the road over Llanberis Pass tops out at 359 metres, the Pyg and Miners' Tracks set out for Snowdon - and a hotel down the road once trained the men who summited Everest.

subject: Penarth Fawr
summary: The oak-timbered hall built around 1480 for Hywel ap Madog -- the westernmost surviving spere truss in Wales, restored to medieval form in 1936, and now Cadw's quietest treasure on the Llyn Peninsula.

story.title: Penataran: Where Rama Walks in Stone

subject: Penataran
summary: The largest Hindu temple complex in East Java, built over three centuries beneath a deadly volcano, where the Ramayana epic unfolds in carved stone reliefs that link Javanese kingship to divine narrative.

subject: Penghu
summary: Ninety wind-scoured volcanic islands in the Taiwan Strait where basalt columns meet turquoise sea, Dutch forts crumbled four centuries ago, and the Pescadores guard the gateway to Taiwan as they have since the Song Dynasty.

subject: Penghu Air Raids
summary: From October 1944 to August 1945, Allied bombers systematically pounded Japanese naval and air installations on the Penghu Islands, turning a fortress that had guarded the Taiwan Strait for decades into rubble.

subject: Penghu Refugee Camp
summary: For eleven years, a converted military base on a windswept Penghu island sheltered Vietnamese boat people who had risked everything to cross the South China Sea -- a chapter Taiwan has only recently begun to remember.

subject: Penyberth
summary: The site of the 1936 Tan yn Llyn arson protest, where three Welsh nationalists burned a newly built RAF bombing school and surrendered, a defining moment for modern Welsh nationalism.

subject: Perili Köşk
summary: The nine-story red brick tower that locals called the 'Haunted Mansion' stood half-finished on the European shore of the Bosphorus for decades before it was restored and transformed into the headquarters of Borusan Holding and the Borusan Contemporary art museum.

subject: Permanente Quarry
summary: Henry Kaiser bought this limestone quarry in 1939 to supply 5.5 million barrels of cement for Shasta Dam, creating a scar in the hillside that is now one of Silicon Valley's most visible landmarks.

subject: Perryfield Quarry
summary: A working stone quarry that has supplied the masonry of Westminster Abbey and Waterloo Bridge, with butterflies thriving in the cuts that have been retired.

story.title: Persepolis: Visiting the Throne of Jamshid

subject: Persepolis
summary: Sixty kilometers northeast of Shiraz, the ruins of Persepolis rise from the Marvdasht plain -- the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC and still standing twenty-three centuries later.

story.title: Persepolis: The Empire That Burned in a Single Night

subject: Persepolis
summary: The ceremonial capital of the largest empire the ancient world had known stood for two centuries on a stone terrace in southern Iran before Alexander the Great burned it to the ground in 330 BC -- and its ruins still reshape our understanding of the ancient world.

story.title: Peter Iredale: The Shipwreck That Stayed

subject: Peter Iredale
summary: A four-masted steel barque that ran aground on the Oregon coast in 1906 and never left - her rusted skeleton still rises from the sand at Fort Stevens State Park, the most accessible shipwreck in the Graveyard of the Pacific and a monument to the Columbia River Bar's lethal indifference to human schedules.

subject: Peterhead
summary: Founded in 1593 on land that belonged to monks, bombed twenty-eight times by Luftwaffe pilots looking for Scotland, home to a notorious prison and the UK's busiest fishing port.

subject: Peterhouse, Cambridge
summary: Peterhouse is the oldest college in Cambridge, has alumni who discovered hydrogen, invented the computer, created electromagnetic theory, and built the jet engine — and spent the 1980s as the setting for a legendary ideological civil war among its fellows.

subject: Petersberg (Siebengebirge)
summary: A mountain hotel above the Rhine that became the working address of postwar West German diplomacy.

story.title: Petersfriedhof: Where Salzburg Buries Its Own

subject: Petersfriedhof Salzburg
summary: One of the oldest cemeteries in Austria, nestled at the foot of the Festungsberg since around 700 AD, with catacombs possibly dating to the Early Christian era, graves of Mozart's sister and Haydn's brother, and a chapel dedicated to the assassinated Thomas Becket of Canterbury.

subject: Petersglocke
summary: Cologne Cathedral's bourdon bell, 24 tons of bronze cast during the Weimar hyperinflation, has been silenced by cracks and a falling clapper twice in its first century — and still rings on the great occasions.

subject: Petit Trianon
summary: A small neoclassical château built for a royal mistress and later given to Marie Antoinette, the Petit Trianon became the queen's private refuge from Versailles -- and a lightning rod for the resentment that helped ignite the Revolution.

subject: Petronius (oil platform)
summary: A 2,100-foot compliant tower in the Gulf of Mexico -- taller than most skyscrapers, yet designed to sway with the sea -- that lost an entire module to the ocean floor during construction and still became one of the world's most productive deepwater platforms.

subject: Peñol de Cerquín
summary: A mountaintop Lenca fortress in southern Honduras where the indigenous leader Lempira made his last stand against the Spanish conquest -- and was killed during a parley by a hidden gunman.

subject: Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm
summary: Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm carries 1,300 years of history in its name: a Sanskrit epithet for a Hindu god, filtered through the Cham kingdom, transliterated into Vietnamese, paired with words meaning 'Cham Tower' — and the towers are still there.

subject: Philadelphion
summary: A vanished Byzantine square at the heart of ancient Constantinople, the Philadelphion — 'place of brotherly love' — was named for a statue group commemorating an imperial reunion that probably never happened, and is now best known for sculptures that ended up in Venice.

subject: Philopatium
summary: The Philopatium was a Byzantine imperial retreat outside Constantinople's walls — a cypress-shaded hunting park, sacred spring, and palace complex beloved by Justinian and Theodora that hosted crusader royalty, imperial weddings, and one empress's house arrest before vanishing entirely.

subject: Phleger Estate
summary: A former tuberculosis sanitarium turned national parkland on the San Francisco Peninsula, where second-growth redwoods now tower over the ruins of a health farm and the land once walked by the Portola expedition.

subject: Phnom Chisor
summary: An eleventh-century Khmer temple called the Mountain of the Sun, reached by six hundred unshaded steps, looking out over the delta where Cambodian civilisation began.

subject: Phoenixonian Institute
summary: California's first African American secondary school, founded in San Jose in 1861 by the son of a Philadelphia abolitionist, offered classical education to Black students from across the West Coast during an era when most were denied any education at all.

story.title: Phra Pathom Chedi: The Stupa That Swallowed a Stupa

subject: Phra Pathommachedi
summary: Thailand's tallest stupa -- 120 meters of golden tile over an ancient ruin that King Mongkut discovered as a wandering monk and later encased inside an entirely new monument.

subject: Phra That Dum
summary: One brick Khmer tower survives out of three on a shared laterite platform just outside Sakon Nakhon, its northern lintel still carrying Vishnu asleep on the cosmic ocean.

subject: Phra That Narai Cheng Weng
summary: A thousand-year-old Khmer sandstone stupa on the plain west of Sakon Nakhon, which local tradition credits entirely to women who built it in a night-long race against the men on the mountain.

subject: Phu Quoc
summary: Vietnam's largest island sits fifteen kilometres off Cambodia, holds a prison museum, the world's most protected fish sauce, and a construction boom rebuilding it from the sand up.

subject: Phylakopi
summary: Phylakopi on the northern coast of Milos was one of the great cities of the Bronze Age Aegean, continuously inhabited for over a thousand years and the site where obsidian trade, Minoan frescoes, Mycenaean conquest, and an extraordinary shrine all converged.

subject: Piazza dei Miracoli
summary: The walled 'Square of Miracles' in Pisa gathers a cathedral, baptistery, bell tower, and cemetery into one of the most celebrated architectural ensembles in the world -- a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

subject: Pibor
summary: Pibor Post began its life in 1912 as a British colonial fort on the Pibor River, and today serves as the small, flood-isolated headquarters of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area in Murle country.

subject: Picayune Rancheria of Chukchansi Indians
summary: A federally recognized tribe whose 12,000-year presence in the Sierra Nevada foothills survived colonization, erasure, and a modern civil war over casino wealth that split families and silenced some of the last speakers of an ancient language.

subject: Pichilemu
summary: A faded Belle Époque resort on Chile's Pacific coast found a second life as the country's surfing capital, where left-breaking waves can rise ten meters at Punta de Lobos.

subject: Pidurangala Rock
summary: The granite outcrop where King Kashyapa relocated five hundred monks to make room for his fortress at Sigiriya, leaving behind a reclining Buddha, ancient stupas, and what may be the finest view of the Lion Rock from any angle.

subject: Pillar of Shame
summary: Danish artist Jens Galschiøt's eight-metre copper sculpture of 50 twisted bodies stood for 24 years at the University of Hong Kong as a memorial to those killed in the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre — until it was removed in the night of 22–23 December 2021.

story.title: Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo

subject: Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo
summary: São Paulo's oldest art museum began in 1905 with just 26 paintings in an unfinished building — its exposed brick facade was never meant to stay that way, but after 120 years, it has become the institution's most recognizable feature.

subject: Pine Islet Light
summary: The last working kerosene lighthouse in the world burns a steady flame at the Mackay marina, rescued from a remote islet by volunteers who refused to let it go dark.

subject: Pinewood Battery
summary: A crumbling hilltop fortress above Hong Kong Island, Pinewood Battery guarded the harbour for four decades before a single devastating Japanese raid ended its role in one morning.

subject: Piney Grove at Southall's Plantation
summary: A log corn crib that became a store that became a house - the rare Tidewater Virginia building that wore three lives in two centuries.

subject: Ping Shan Heritage Trail
summary: A 1-kilometre walk through Yuen Long's Tang clan villages encounters Hong Kong's only ancient pagoda, a 700-year-old ancestral hall, a well that once served two villages, and the quiet persistence of a lineage that has lived in the New Territories for nearly a millennium.

subject: Pioneer Yosemite History Center
summary: A collection of relocated historic buildings in Wawona where visitors cross a covered bridge built by Yosemite's first guardian to step into the park's pioneer past.

subject: Pirámide de Mayo
summary: Argentina's oldest national monument, raised in 1811 to mark the first year of independence, survived a century of demolition threats and now anchors the circle the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo have walked since 1977.

subject: Pitlochry
summary: A Victorian Highland resort built on Queen Victoria's enthusiasm, the arrival of the railway, and a stubborn local refusal to let the twentieth century spoil what the nineteenth had created.

subject: Place Royale, Brussels
summary: Brussels' Place Royale has spent its entire existence arguing about which statue belongs in the middle of it - and on 21 July 1831 a new king took his oath of office on its front steps.

subject: Plainfield Armory
summary: Built in 1931 as home to Headquarters Company of the 44th Division, the Plainfield Armory is a compact Flemish bond brick building that spent decades in limbo before a 2013 sale finally ended its long wait.

subject: Plas yn Rhiw
summary: A small Jacobean manor on the Llyn Peninsula that three sisters bought in 1939 and slowly restored - now the only organic National Trust garden in Wales.

subject: Platja d'en Bossa
summary: Ibiza's longest beach, where a failed exhibition hall became the legendary club Space and the island's after-hours party was born almost by accident.

subject: Platonic Academy
summary: Every university, every academy, every academic on Earth owes a debt to a quiet olive grove north of Athens, where Plato bought a garden and began to teach.

subject: Plaza Sotomayor
summary: Valparaíso's grand civic square, built over reclaimed sea, where a monument and a hidden crypt hold the bones of the sailors who died at the Battle of Iquique.

subject: Plaza de Mayo
summary: The symbolic heart of Argentina, where the nation was founded, governed, celebrated, bombed, and mourned, and where the Mothers of the disappeared have circled the May Pyramid for nearly half a century.

subject: Plaza de Toros de Ronda
summary: One of Spain's oldest all-stone bullrings, built in 1785 for the Royal Riding School that helped define modern bullfighting, where three generations of the Romero family shaped the spectacle.

subject: Plaza de la Independencia
summary: Quito's central square began as packed dirt around a water source; 400 years later it holds the monument to the First Cry of Independence.

subject: Plaça de Sant Felip Neri
summary: A quiet Gothic Quarter square whose shrapnel-scarred church walls record a 1938 bombing that killed 42 people, most of them children, and the lie later told to hide it.

subject: Plen-an-gwary
summary: A medieval Cornish playing place: a circular outdoor theatre where mystery plays in the Cornish language drew crowds so loud that one of them once frightened an entire Spanish raiding party back into the sea.

subject: Pleuron (Aetolia)
summary: Ancient Pleuron, twice-built in Aetolia, sailed ships to Troy in Homer's Iliad, hosted the mythic wars of Oeneus and Meleager, and left behind walls of thirty-one towers and a theater whose cavea still faces the Missolonghi lagoon.

subject: Plevna, Tampere
summary: A windowless Tampere weaving hall named for a Bulgarian siege became the first building in the Nordic countries lit by electric bulbs — and is now a ten-screen cinema and a brewery.

subject: Plymouth Hoe
summary: The clifftop promenade where Drake supposedly finished his bowls, where giants were carved into the turf, and where the upper third of the Eddystone Lighthouse now stands re-erected stone by stone.

story.title: Plymouth Rock: America's Most Disappointing Landmark

subject: Plymouth Rock
summary: The Massachusetts boulder where the Pilgrims allegedly first stepped - identified 121 years after the fact, broken by attempted moves, carved with the wrong date, and now protected in a monument because America needed an origin story.

subject: Pnyx
summary: On a rocky hillside west of the Acropolis, a single carved step of stone marks the spot where ordinary Athenians invented the radical idea of ruling themselves.

subject: Po Lin Teahouse Poisoning Incident
summary: A plate of vegetarian fried kway teow at a department store restaurant in Taipei killed six people and hospitalized dozens in March 2024, exposing Taiwan to a toxin so rare it had no Mandarin name.

subject: Po Toi
summary: Hong Kong's southernmost island, where Bronze Age rock carvings share the clifftops with an abandoned mansion known as the Haunted House, a Tin Hau temple renovated in 1893, and the dramatic finale of a John le Carré spy novel.

subject: Poble Espanyol
summary: An open-air museum on Montjuic where 117 full-scale replicas of buildings from across Spain reveal that there is no single 'Spanish' architecture -- only a glorious patchwork of regional identities.

subject: Pobull Fhinn
summary: An oval Bronze Age stone circle on the south slope of Ben Langass, named for the legendary Gaelic hero Fingal - "Fingal's People" silhouetted against the lochs.

subject: Pocahontas Times Print Shop
summary: A 21-by-75-foot wooden building in Marlinton that has housed a weekly West Virginia newspaper since 1900 - the same paper that has been publishing continuously since 1882.

subject: Poechos Reservoir
summary: A billion cubic meters of water sit behind a rock-filled dam in northern Peru, the centerpiece of a nation's bet that engineering could outrun drought.

story.title: Point Adams Light: The Lighthouse the River Outgrew

subject: Point Adams Light
summary: A vanished lighthouse near the mouth of the Columbia River that guided ships for just twenty-four years before the construction of a south jetty and the arrival of a lightship made it obsolete - designed by the architect who would go on to help design the Library of Congress.

story.title: Point Calimere Wildlife and Bird Sanctuary

subject: Point Calimere Wildlife and Bird Sanctuary
summary: Where the Palk Strait meets the Bay of Bengal, over 100,000 migratory birds descend each October on a landscape of salt marshes, mangroves, and dry evergreen forest -- one of India's great avian spectacles, watched over by blackbuck and a thousand-year-old Chola lighthouse.

subject: Point Charles Light
summary: A wrought-iron lighthouse shipped in crates from Birmingham in 1891, Charles Point Lighthouse has guided ships into Darwin Harbour for more than a century — surviving Cyclone Tracy, outlasting Radio Australia's broadcast masts, and still operating today on solar power.

subject: Point Cloates
summary: A low headland on the Ningaloo coast that early mariners doubted even existed, later home to Western Australia's first modern shore whaling station and a lighthouse now standing in ruins.

subject: Point Hueneme Light
summary: An Art Deco lighthouse guarding the entrance to the Santa Barbara Channel, where a luxury liner met its end.

subject: Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station
summary: Atlantic Canada's only nuclear power plant sits on the Bay of Fundy shore, a CANDU reactor whose troubled refurbishment became the most expensive lesson in Canadian nuclear history.

subject: Point Lookout Light
summary: A lighthouse at the confluence of the Potomac River and Chesapeake Bay whose nearly two centuries of service encompassed a daughter keeper, a Civil War prison camp that killed thousands, and a long fight for preservation.

subject: Point of Ayr Lifeboat Station
summary: The RNLI replacement for the old Gronant station - built beside the lighthouse keepers' cottages in 1894 and closed in 1923 when steam ended the age of stranded sailing ships.

subject: Point of Honor
summary: An 1815 Federal-style brick mansion above the James River, named for the dueling ground beneath it, built by Patrick Henry's physician and later home to the Langhorne family — ancestors of the original Gibson Girl and Nancy Astor.

subject: Pok Fu Lam Reservoir
summary: Hong Kong's first reservoir was born from epidemic desperation and a Royal Engineers clerk's idea — a Victorian dam in a green valley that still stands declared as a monument more than 160 years later.

subject: Poker Flat Research Range
summary: The world's largest land-based rocket range and the only university-owned rocket facility in the United States - where scientists launch sounding rockets into the aurora borealis from the Alaskan wilderness.

subject: Polo Grounds
summary: The bathtub-shaped stadium in Coogan's Hollow hosted some of the most iconic moments in American sports history before falling to the wrecking ball in 1964, its light poles still standing in Arizona.

story.title: Polonnaruwa Vatadage: The Circular Shrine That Two Kings Claimed

subject: Polonnaruwa Vatadage
summary: The best-preserved vatadage in Sri Lanka, this circular relic house in ancient Polonnaruwa features two stone platforms of extraordinary carving, four seated Buddhas facing the cardinal directions, and an authorship dispute between two medieval kings.

subject: Polynesian Cultural Center
summary: A 42-acre living museum on Oahu's North Shore where college students from across the Pacific perform the dances and crafts of their home islands to pay their way through school.

subject: Ponce de Leon Inlet Light
summary: Florida's tallest lighthouse at 175 feet, the Ponce de Leon Inlet Light survived Seminole attacks, the drowning of its chief engineer, and decades of abandonment before being restored as a National Historic Landmark.

subject: Ponta da Madeira
summary: Three locomotives, 330 wagons and 892 kilometers of track end here - at the iron-ore terminal that moves more cargo than any other port in Brazil.

subject: Ponto-chō
summary: A single narrow alley running parallel to the Kamo River in Kyoto, Ponto-cho has been home to geisha, kabuki, and riverside dining since the seventeenth century -- and it all began with a landfill and a Portuguese word for bridge.

subject: Pools of ʻOheʻo
summary: Tiered freshwater pools cascading through a volcanic gulch in Haleakalā National Park, misnamed the 'Seven Sacred Pools' by a hotel owner in the 1940s -- neither seven in number nor sacred to Hawaiian culture.

subject: Pope Field
summary: One of the Air Force's oldest installations, named for a Jenny pilot drowned in the Cape Fear in 1919 - the airfield that puts the Air in Airborne.

subject: Popular Center of Remembrance
summary: A police building in Rosario that hid one of Argentina's largest secret detention centers is now kept open by the families of the disappeared, so the country cannot forget.

subject: Port Arthur
summary: On a quiet bay at the bottom of the world, the ruins of Australia's most feared convict prison stand among English gardens and the names of the dead.

subject: Port Moresby
summary: The capital of Papua New Guinea, known in Tok Pisin as Pot Mosbi - a Motu-Koitabu coastline that became the gateway to a nation of 800 languages.

subject: Port San Juan
summary: A deep Pacific inlet on Vancouver Island carved along two fault lines, home of the Pacheedaht First Nation and the southern gate to the Graveyard of the Pacific.

subject: Port St Mary
summary: A herring port that became a Victorian resort, a lifeboat station with 130 years of saves, and a memorial to a ship that went down in two minutes off Dunkirk.

subject: Port St Mary Lifeboat Station
summary: The all-weather RNLI station on Lime Street that has guarded the south coast of the Isle of Man since 1896, kept afloat by a Birmingham developer's bequest and a Manx brewery family's gratitude.

subject: Porta Coeli (Puerto Rico)
summary: One of the oldest surviving church structures in the Western Hemisphere, this 17th-century Dominican chapel in San Germán now houses Puerto Rico's first museum of religious art.

subject: Portals of the Past
summary: A marble doorway that once led into a Nob Hill mansion now stands at the edge of a Golden Gate Park lake, framing nothing but sky and water -- San Francisco's most poetic earthquake memorial.

subject: Portas do Cerco
summary: The Barrier Gate at the northern tip of the Macau Peninsula has been a contested threshold for over four centuries — built by the Ming dynasty to contain Macau, rebuilt by Portugal after blood was spilled there, and nicknamed 'Far Eastern Checkpoint Charlie' during the Cold War.

subject: Porth Hellick Down
summary: The largest surviving cluster of Bronze Age entrance graves in the world, on a small heath on the south coast of St Mary's, including a tomb that an antiquarian named simply The Great Tomb.

subject: Porthdinllaen
summary: The Llyn hamlet that almost became Britain's gateway to Ireland in 1810, where you can only arrive on foot, and where the Ty Coch Inn -- voted one of the best beach pubs in the world -- sits at the centre of two dozen cottages owned by the National Trust.

subject: Portillo
summary: A canary-yellow hotel marooned beside a frozen Andean lake, Portillo is South America's oldest ski resort and the only place in the Southern Hemisphere ever to host the World Ski Championships.

subject: Portinatx
summary: The quiet, pine-fringed bay at Ibiza's northern tip, home to the tallest lighthouse in the Balearics and a stubborn Hollywood legend.

subject: Portobello, Edinburgh
summary: A Royal Navy sailor named his Scottish cottage for a Caribbean battle, and an entire seaside resort grew from that act of nostalgia.

subject: Portree
summary: The capital of Skye, built around a Thomas Telford pier on a cliff-fringed harbour, with archaeological traces of human occupation reaching back 4,500 years.

subject: Portrush
summary: A seaside resort on a mile-long peninsula called Ramore Head, where the Atlantic does most of the talking, the trains have been arriving for 170 years, and the Open Championship has come home twice this decade.

subject: Portuguese Mozambique
summary: For nearly five centuries Portugal claimed this stretch of the East African coast, building an empire on trade, forced labor, and the fiction that an African colony could be made Portuguese.

subject: Posición Yuste
summary: A country house hidden in the pines near Petrer became the last seat of the Spanish Republic, where a cornered government spent its final days trying not to win the war but to save lives.

subject: Potsdamer Platz
summary: Once the busiest intersection in Europe, then a weed-covered no man's land, then the largest building site on the continent — all on the same few hectares of Berlin.

subject: Powerscourt Estate
summary: A 13th-century castle transformed into a Palladian mansion, surrounded by gardens modeled on Versailles, burned to a shell in 1974, and rebuilt -- Powerscourt's story mirrors the turbulent arc of the Anglo-Irish estate itself.

subject: Praia de Iracema
summary: Fortaleza renamed its fish beach after a character in a novel, then built a port, an unfinished British pier and a bohemian quarter on it - and watched the sea take the sand back.

subject: Praia do Forte
summary: A Bahian beach named for a fortified house that took seventy-three years to build, anchored an estate the size of a tenth of Brazil, and now stands in ruins above a sea-turtle sanctuary.

subject: Prambanan
summary: Southeast Asia's largest Hindu temple compound, where 240 stone structures once rose from the Javanese plain as a dynasty's answer to Buddhist Borobudur.

subject: Praça do Comércio
summary: Lisbon's grand waterfront square, once the site of a royal palace destroyed by the 1755 earthquake, rebuilt as the monumental gateway through which Portugal's wealth flowed.

subject: Preah Vihear
summary: Preah Vihear is a Khmer Hindu temple built on a 525-meter cliff on the Cambodia-Thailand border — a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Southeast Asia's most contested pieces of sacred geography, where ancient stone and modern sovereignty have collided for decades.

subject: Preseli Mountains
summary: A modest Pembrokeshire mountain range whose blue-grey stones were quarried 5,000 years ago and somehow transported 180 miles across southern Britain to become the inner ring of Stonehenge.

subject: Presidio La Bahía
summary: A Spanish fortress that changed hands six times across three revolutions, witnessed the deadliest massacre of the Texas Revolution, and still stands on the San Antonio River after nearly three centuries.

subject: Presidio San Agustín del Tucsón
summary: The birthplace of Tucson, where an Irish mercenary serving Spain founded a fortress that would survive Apache wars, Mexican independence, Confederate occupation, and urban development before archaeologists resurrected its story.

subject: Presidio Santa Cruz de Terrenate
summary: An Irish-born colonel built this Spanish fortress in 1775, but relentless Apache attacks and crushing hardship forced its abandonment in just five years, leaving behind one of the best-preserved presidio ruins in the American Southwest.

subject: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: The only national park required by Congress to pay for itself, this former Spanish fortress has served three nations across 250 years before becoming home to Lucasfilm and the Internet Archive.

subject: Presidio of Santa Barbara
summary: The last military outpost built by Spain in the New World, now a state historic park containing the second oldest surviving building in California.

subject: Princess Louisa Inlet
summary: A 6-kilometer fjord hidden behind tidal rapids on BC's Sunshine Coast, where an aviation tycoon's failed Hollywood resort became a youth camp and glacial walls rise thousands of feet from water deep enough to swallow a skyscraper.

subject: Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanage
summary: Europe's largest wooden building was born as a luxury hotel, became a Greek Orthodox orphanage that sheltered 5,800 children, was seized by the Turkish state, and now stands as both a monument to loss and a possible new chapter.

subject: Prinsenhof, Ghent
summary: Charles V was born here in 1500, in a palace of 300 rooms with lions in the gardens. Only a gateway remains.

story.title: Priory of St. Thomas near Stafford

subject: Priory of St. Thomas near Stafford
summary: An Augustinian house so wealthy it became England's richest priory of its order, founded for a saint freshly martyred at Canterbury and buried under the stones of a working farm.

subject: Prittlewell Royal Anglo-Saxon Burial
summary: In 2003, between an Aldi supermarket and a pub called The Saxon King, archaeologists uncovered an undisturbed seventh-century chamber tomb - the most spectacular Anglo-Saxon burial discovered in sixty years.

subject: Prospect Bluff Historic Sites
summary: A National Historic Landmark on the Apalachicola River where a British fort, a free Black maroon community, and three successive American forts rose and fell between 1814 and 1863.

story.title: Providence: Where Religious Freedom Began and WaterFire Burns

subject: Providence
summary: Rhode Island's capital where Roger Williams founded America's first colony with true religious freedom, where Brown University anchors College Hill, where Federal Hill serves little Italy's best, and where bonfires float down the river on summer nights.

subject: Pucará de Tilcara
summary: A pre-Inca hilltop fortress whose stone walls have watched over the Quebrada de Humahuaca for a thousand years, and whose modern story is a reckoning with who gets to tell it.

subject: Pudding Shop
summary: The Lale Restaurant in Sultanahmet — universally known as the Pudding Shop — became the legendary halfway point of the 1960s–70s hippie trail, where travelers swapped notes, posted messages, and ate cheap pudding in the shadow of the Blue Mosque.

subject: Pueblo Bonito
summary: The largest great house in Chaco Canyon, Pueblo Bonito was the center of the Ancestral Puebloan world for nearly three centuries, an 800-room complex whose alignment to solar and lunar cycles reveals a civilization of extraordinary sophistication.

subject: Puerto Bories
summary: A vast British-built meat freezer on a Patagonian fjord once shipped a quarter-million sheep a year to Europe; today it is a luxury hotel that kept its machines.

subject: Puerto Madryn
summary: Where the Welsh first landed in 1865 and where southern right whales now glide past the beach, Puerto Madryn is Patagonia's gateway to Peninsula Valdes.

subject: Puerto Princesa
summary: Named for a Spanish princess and built on a hilltop plateau overlooking Palawan's eastern coast, Puerto Princesa grew from a colonial outpost into the Philippines' eco-tourism capital and gateway to one of the New Seven Wonders of Nature.

subject: Puget Sound Navigation Company
summary: The Black Ball Line ruled cross-sound traffic for half a century, then shut itself down to win a fare dispute - and accidentally handed Washington its state ferry system.

subject: Puig Major
summary: Mallorca's highest peak is crowned by a military radar dome and closed to the public, and it once relayed the news that Apollo 11 had landed safely on the Moon.

subject: Pukara of La Compañía
summary: On a hilltop near Rancagua stand the ruins of the southernmost fortress of the Inca Empire - the very edge of a realm that once stretched the length of a continent.

subject: Pulchri Studio
summary: Founded in 1847 by painters who wanted to escape state-mandated neoclassicism, Pulchri Studio became the institutional home of the Hague School and is still painting at the same Lange Voorhout address.

subject: Puna Geothermal Venture
summary: On the Big Island's volcanic east side, a geothermal power plant taps 640-degree fluids from Kilauea's rift zone -- and in 2018, the lava came to collect, burying wells and forcing a dramatic race to cap boreholes before magma reached them.

subject: Puncak Jaya
summary: The tallest island peak on Earth, a limestone pyramid the Amungme call Peak of the White Arrow, with equatorial glaciers that may outlive none of us.

subject: Punta Carretas
summary: An affluent seaside barrio at Montevideo's southern tip, where the country's most notorious prison became a shopping mall.

subject: Pura Dasar Buana Gelgel
summary: A royal temple in Bali's former capital of Gelgel, Pura Dasar Buana honors the celibate Brahmin Mpu Ghana and carries over a thousand years of unbroken Hindu devotion through its shrines and festivals.

story.title: Pura Griya Sakti: The Priest's Grandson and the Temple on the Hill

subject: Pura Griya Sakti
summary: A 17th-century Brahman temple in Bali's highlands founded by the grandson of the legendary priest Nirartha, built on a hilly outcrop where a banyan tree dwarfs the inner shrine.

subject: Pura Kehen
summary: The royal temple of the Bangli Kingdom, Pura Kehen has guarded the god of fire since the ninth century, where oath-breakers once faced divine curses and serpent-wrapped vessels held the power of Agni.

subject: Pura Lingsar
summary: A 300-year-old temple complex on Lombok where Hindus and Muslims pray side by side, then pelt each other with rice cakes in a joyful annual ritual meant to bring rain - a living monument to the kind of interfaith coexistence that most of the world only theorizes about.

story.title: Pura Penataran Sasih: The Temple of the Fallen Moon

subject: Pura Penataran Sasih
summary: A Balinese temple guards the largest single-cast bronze drum in the world, a 2,300-year-old relic that legend says fell from the sky as a shattered moon.

story.title: Pura Taman Ayun: The Garden That Floats on Sacred Water

subject: Pura Taman Ayun
summary: Bali's second-largest temple rises from a broad moat in the heart of a vanished kingdom, its waters feeding the ancient irrigation system UNESCO recognized as a masterpiece of cooperative agriculture.

story.title: Pura Taman Saraswati: The Sculptor Who Fled a King

subject: Pura Taman Saraswati
summary: A temple built by an artist who was already married when Krakatoa erupted, designed for the Hindu goddess of learning, its lotus pond now the most photographed water feature in Ubud.

subject: Pura Ulun Danu Batur
summary: A 17th-century Balinese temple complex of 285 shrines dedicated to the goddess of Lake Batur, rebuilt on the caldera rim after lava destroyed its original site -- twice -- and now part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape.

subject: Purefoy-Dunn Plantation
summary: A Greek Revival house near Wake Forest whose first builder helped found a college and whose second owner enslaved twenty-four people to work the surrounding 500 acres.

subject: Pusading
summary: Perched at the summit of Mount Wutai's temple valley, Pusading is reached by climbing 108 stone steps -- one for each worry a pilgrim must leave behind to see the true capacity of Buddha.

subject: Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site
summary: The last great Hawaiian temple, built on the orders of Kamehameha the Great to fulfill a prophecy that would unite the islands, still stands on a hill overlooking Kawaihae Bay -- and visitors are forbidden to enter because bones may still lie within its walls.

subject: Pyre of Heracles
summary: High on Mount Oeta in central Greece, the ruins of a 3rd-century BCE Doric temple mark the spot where myth says Heracles built his own funeral pyre and ascended to the gods — and where archaeologists found evidence suggesting the ritual preceded the story.

subject: Páirc Uí Chaoimh
summary: Cork's great GAA stadium - 45,000 seats on the south bank of the Lee, where hurling, football, Springsteen, U2, Oasis and Ed Sheeran all draw crowds in their tens of thousands.

subject: Qasr Ibrim
summary: The lone survivor of Lower Nubia: a clifftop citadel that became an island, where the desert preserved 3,000 years of words other floods erased.

subject: Qidong Street Japanese Houses
summary: A rare, largely intact cluster of Japanese colonial-era wooden dormitories in central Taipei, now home to the Taiwan Literature Base and its writers-in-residence program.

subject: Qingshui Cliff
summary: Taiwan's highest sea cliff rises 2,408 meters straight from the Pacific Ocean - a wall of marble and gneiss where two tectonic plates collide, the Suhua Highway clings to its face, and even frogs cannot cross.

subject: Qom
summary: One of the holiest cities in Shia Islam, Qom draws twenty million pilgrims a year to the shrine of Fatima bint Musa while anchoring Iran's most powerful center of religious scholarship.

subject: Quamby
summary: A name meaning 'rest a while', a pub built as a 1860s customs house, and a 1934 shooting: the whole outback condensed into one hotel on the Burke Developmental Road.

subject: Quarterbridge, Isle of Man
summary: A junction outside Douglas where a stone mason's bridge from 1809 became, a century later, the first slow corner of the world's oldest motorcycle race.

subject: Queen Califia's Magical Circle
summary: The last major work of artist Niki de Saint Phalle, an outdoor sculpture garden in Escondido that summons a legendary warrior queen through mosaic, myth, and 400 feet of serpentine wall.

subject: Queen Elizabeth 2
summary: Cunard's flagship for nearly four decades, the QE2 carried 2.5 million passengers across the Atlantic, hauled troops to the Falklands, and now serves dinner in Dubai as a floating hotel.

subject: Queen's Staircase
summary: Carved from solid limestone by six hundred enslaved people in a single year, Nassau's Queen's Staircase rises 102 feet through a tropical canyon to a hilltop fort that never saw battle.

subject: Queensferry Crossing
summary: Scotland's third Forth bridge, opened in 2017, rises in three slender cable-stayed towers beside two Victorian and mid-century predecessors.

subject: Queensland National Bank, Charleville
summary: A timber bank built in 1888 for the colony's own homegrown bank, complete with marble fireplaces and a manager's quarters, now keeps Charleville's history as the Historic House Museum.

subject: Queenstown Winter Festival
summary: A grassroots winter party that grew from a quiet-season pub idea in 1975 into the Southern Hemisphere's biggest winter celebration, before unsustainable costs ended it in 2023.

story.title: Quincy Smelter: The Last Copper Furnace Standing

subject: Quincy Smelter
summary: The only surviving early 20th-century copper smelter in the United States sits on the shore of the Keweenaw Waterway, a monument to Michigan's copper boom that outlasted its own usefulness by decades.

subject: Quinta de Olivos
summary: Argentina's presidents live on a riverside estate that was once an apiary, an equestrian playground, and a mansion its owner nicknamed his birdcage.

subject: Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino
summary: On this 22-hectare hacienda near Santa Marta, Simon Bolivar -- liberator of six nations -- spent his final days in a borrowed shirt, issuing one last plea for Colombian unity before dying of tuberculosis at age 47.

subject: Qumran
summary: The desert ruins where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found sit on a barren marl plateau above the lowest place on Earth, hiding centuries of sectarian life and one of archaeology's greatest discoveries.

subject: Quobba
summary: On Australia's westernmost sheep station, the ocean fires plumes of seawater through the cliffs, a blunt sign warns that king waves kill, and a quiet cairn marks the country's worst naval loss.

subject: Qutb Shahi tombs
summary: A royal necropolis near Golconda Fort in Hyderabad where seven of the eight Qutb Shahi sultans lie entombed beneath domes that once gleamed with blue and green tiles, blending Persian and Indian architecture in one of the Deccan's most concentrated displays of Indo-Islamic art.

subject: RAAF Base Scherger
summary: A full-scale military airfield carved out of the Cape York scrub near Weipa, staffed in peacetime by just four people and waiting, runway lights dark, for the day it is needed.

subject: RAAF Base Townsville
summary: Born as a quiet aerodrome in 1940, Garbutt became one of the great Allied air hubs of the Pacific war and remains an active RAAF base today.

subject: RAF Andreas
summary: A 500-acre fighter and gunnery training station on the Isle of Man's flat northern plain, where Australian Spitfire pilots, air gunners bound for Lancasters, and the truncated tower of a 19th-century church all share the same wartime story.

subject: RAF Bircham Newton
summary: A Norfolk airfield that opened in the First World War ready to bomb Berlin — but the Armistice came first — then spent the Second World War hunting submarines over the North Sea before fading into quiet farmland.

subject: RAF Bodorgan
summary: A small wartime satellite airfield on the Meyrick estate in southwest Anglesey, briefly busy with anti-aircraft cooperation flights between 1940 and 1945, then quietly returned to farmland.

subject: RAF Bottisham
summary: From this Cambridgeshire airfield in 1944, American P-51 Mustangs of the 361st Fighter Group escorted bombers deep into Germany. Today the runway outline survives as a long thick row of trees.

subject: RAF Boulmer
summary: A Northumberland coastal RAF station that began life as a fake airfield with canvas Hurricanes and grew into the underground nerve centre of British air defence.

subject: RAF Burtonwood
summary: By 1945 it was the largest airfield in Europe, home to 18,000 American servicemen who paid their rent in tobacco. Now it's mostly demolished, with bunker scars still visible from the M62.

subject: RAF Carew Cheriton
summary: A Welsh airfield that started as a 1915 airship station hunting U-boats with hydrogen-filled blimps, became a Coastal Command base in WWII, and is now a restored heritage site beside a go-kart track.

subject: RAF Charterhall
summary: A Berwickshire training airfield nicknamed Slaughterhall, where Battle of Britain pilot Richard Hillary died in 1943 and Jim Clark and Jackie Stewart later raced on the redundant runways.

subject: RAF Coningsby
summary: The home of Britain's Quick Reaction Alert south — three Typhoon squadrons on permanent readiness — and of the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, including one of only two airworthy Lancasters in the world.

subject: RAF Cottesmore
summary: A Rutland airfield that opened with Wellesleys in 1938, dropped American paratroops on Normandy in 1944, trained Tornado crews from three nations and finally trained Harrier pilots before the army moved in.

subject: RAF Debach
summary: The last Eighth Air Force heavy bomber base to become operational, where the runways crumbled under B-24s and the control tower is now a restored 493rd Bomb Group museum.

subject: RAF Defford
summary: A wartime airfield in the Worcestershire flood plain where civilian scientists test-flew the radar systems that turned the tide of the Battle of the Atlantic.

subject: RAF Downham Market
summary: A Norfolk satellite airfield that grew from a Marham overflow into a Pathfinder base, then vanished beneath farmland and a bypass.

subject: RAF Drem
summary: The East Lothian airfield where the second German bomber of the Second World War was shot down, where night-landing lights were invented, and where an air marshal once saw the future through a hole in the clouds.

subject: RAF Dundonald
summary: A short-lived Ayrshire airfield that trained commandos for D-Day, briefly entered Rudolf Hess conspiracy theories, and has since faded back into farmland and a business park.

subject: RAF East Fortune
summary: The East Lothian airfield from which the British airship R34 launched the first east-west aerial crossing of the Atlantic, and where night fighter crews trained at terrible cost during the Second World War.

subject: RAF Eastchurch
summary: The Kent airfield where the first British pilot officially flew in Britain, Winston Churchill learned to handle the controls, and the founding cohort of the Royal Naval Air Service was trained - now a working prison whose internal roads still bear the names of the Wrights, the Shorts and Charles Rolls.

subject: RAF Elvington
summary: The only British airfield used in WWII by the Free French Heavy Bomber squadrons, later a Cold War land-speed record venue.

subject: RAF Eye
summary: A Suffolk bomber base built late in the war, home to the 490th Bombardment Group's B-17 'Alice Blue Gown' (67 missions), and now the site of the world's first poultry-litter power plant.

subject: RAF Feltwell
summary: A 1930s Norfolk RAF airfield that became a Cold War nuclear missile base, then a US space-surveillance site - and was overflown by mysterious drones in November 2024.

subject: RAF Finningley
summary: The South Yorkshire bomber base that hosted Vulcans, Victors and Valiants through the Cold War, became Doncaster Sheffield Airport, and now sits silent again.

subject: RAF Fylingdales
summary: The truncated pyramid on a North Yorkshire moor that has, since 1963, watched the skies for the four minutes that would end everything.

subject: RAF Haverfordwest
summary: A wartime Coastal Command training airfield carved out of Pembrokeshire farmland, RAF Haverfordwest trained crews to hunt U-boats, fly photo reconnaissance, and survive the Atlantic war - then quietly became a general aviation airport.
