story.title: Site of the First National Congress of the Kuomintang

subject: Site of the First National Congress of the Kuomintang
summary: A clock tower on Wenming Road in Guangzhou hosted ten days in January 1924 that rewired Chinese politics — when the Kuomintang, reorganized by Sun Yat-sen, admitted Communist Party members and forged an alliance that would shape the century to come.

subject: Six Bells Colliery
summary: The South Wales coal mine where 45 miners died one morning in June 1960, and the 20-metre steel sculpture that now stands watch over the empty land where they worked.

subject: Six Flags New Orleans
summary: An abandoned theme park that stood frozen in time for nearly two decades after Hurricane Katrina, becoming one of America's most haunting modern ruins.

subject: Sizewell
summary: A Suffolk fishing hamlet where, in September 1941, two Dutch brothers paddled ashore in a collapsible canoe after fifty-six hours at sea, and where Britain's nuclear future is now being built right beside the cottage that the Engelandvaarders memorial stands behind.

subject: Skagen Odde
summary: Denmark ends in a finger of sand where two seas collide head-on — a spit that buried a medieval church, taught a generation of painters about light, and is still growing northeast toward Sweden.

subject: Skellig Michael
summary: A twin-pinnacled Atlantic crag where sixth-century monks built a monastery so remote that it survived intact for over a millennium -- and later became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

subject: Skerryvore
summary: Alan Stevenson's hyperbolic-curved granite tower, rising 156 feet from a reef eleven miles southwest of Tiree, is the tallest lighthouse in Scotland - and the one Robert Louis Stevenson, the engineer's nephew, called the noblest of all extant deep-sea lights.

subject: Skiringssal
summary: Buried beneath a farm called Huseby in Vestfold, Norway, lie the remains of a Viking chieftain's great hall that once commanded one of Scandinavia's earliest trading towns.

subject: Skokholm
summary: A small red-sandstone island off Pembrokeshire that became Britain's first bird observatory in 1933 and home to 11,000 puffins.

subject: Skull Hill, Malaysia
summary: A volcanic hilltop near Semporna, Sabah, where 3,000-year-old pottery shards litter the slopes -- the remains of Southeast Asia's largest Neolithic pottery factory and evidence of one of the world's longest prehistoric sea trade networks.

subject: Skye
summary: The largest of the Inner Hebrides, a rugged mountainous island linked to the Scottish mainland by a once-controversial bridge, where Gaelic is still spoken by nearly a third of the population.

subject: Slane Festival
summary: Since 1981, the natural amphitheatre at Slane Castle has hosted Bowie, Dylan, the Stones, Springsteen, Queen, Madonna, U2, and Eminem - one rock concert in a green Meath field, every August or so.

subject: Slave Lodge, Cape Town
summary: Built in 1679 to confine up to 500 enslaved people for the Dutch East India Company, this building has been reinvented as government offices, a supreme court, and finally a museum -- but its walls remember what they were built for.

subject: Slieve Donard
summary: At 850 metres, the highest mountain in Northern Ireland holds the highest passage tomb in Britain and Ireland - and stories of a saint who never died but waits inside the rock.

story.title: Sloss Furnaces: Where Iron Met Fire and Art Rose from the Ashes

subject: Sloss Furnaces
summary: Birmingham's Sloss Furnaces ran for nearly ninety years turning Alabama ore into pig iron, then became the only blast furnace in America preserved as a museum -- a rusted cathedral where metalworkers now sculpt art among the ghosts of industry.

subject: Slănic mine
summary: Three centuries of salt extraction carved an underground world beneath the Romanian hills -- 14 cathedral-sized chambers totaling 2.9 million cubic meters, now a tourist attraction where the air stays 12 degrees Celsius year-round and visitors play ping-pong in rooms sculpted from pure rock salt.

subject: Smithfield Plantation (Fredericksburg, Virginia)
summary: An 1822 plantation house turned Union field hospital turned country club - and the ground where 24-year-old artillery officer John Pelham brought a single battery to a stop in the path of an entire Union flank.

subject: Snaefell
summary: Six kingdoms on a clear day, a 150-mph wind on a bad one, and a slender concrete obelisk in between marking the highest point on the Isle of Man.

subject: Snoqualmie
summary: Home to a 268-foot waterfall sacred to the Snoqualmie people, the world's first underground power plant, and over 1.5 million visitors per year seeking the Pacific Northwest's most accessible natural wonder.

subject: Snyder Academy
summary: A prep school in Elizabeth, New Jersey founded in 1767, where Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr studied under the same headmaster — though not at the same time — decades before one killed the other in a duel.

story.title: Soga no Umako: The Man Who Brought Buddhism to Japan

subject: Soga no Umako
summary: The most powerful courtier of 6th-century Japan defeated his rivals in battle, married his daughters into the imperial family, championed Buddhism against fierce opposition, and may lie buried beneath the largest exposed stone tomb in the country.

subject: Soho Square
summary: A 1670s garden square that has hosted a king's statue, a circumnavigating naturalist's scientific salon, an animation studio that won an Oscar, and a memorial bench for a singer who loved the place.

subject: Solar Ark
summary: A 315-meter-wide ark-shaped solar facility in central Japan, born from a product recall turned into a monument of corporate accountability, now facing demolition after two decades of clean energy production.

subject: Soldier Field
summary: Opened in 1924 with Neoclassical Doric columns and a capacity exceeding 100,000, Soldier Field is the oldest and smallest stadium in the NFL -- and the only one to have its National Historic Landmark status revoked after a controversial renovation critics called 'a spaceship landing on a Roman temple.'

subject: Soleb
summary: On a sandstone column at the southernmost temple Amenhotep III ever built, three hieroglyphs may preserve the earliest known mention of Yahweh.

subject: Solway Firth
summary: An inlet of treacherous mudflats and quicksand that carves the border between England and Scotland, the Solway Firth gave its name from an Old Norse word for a pillar, drowned a Covenanter named Margaret Wilson in 1685, and now hosts wind turbines where iron-ore trains once crossed on a five-thousand-foot viaduct.

subject: Somerset Graves Site
summary: A small, heritage-listed cemetery on Cape York holds the graves of frontier settlers, pearl divers from Japan, and a monument to a failed explorer -- a compressed history of colonial ambition, Indigenous dispossession, and the hazardous pearling trade.

subject: Son Bou
summary: Behind Menorca's longest beach lie the ruins of a fifth-century church and a hidden wetland alive with birds, all sharing a single stretch of southern shore.

subject: Sonnenburg concentration camp
summary: A prison at Słońsk was condemned as unfit in 1930 and reopened as a concentration camp in 1933 for exactly that reason; on the night of 30 January 1945, days ahead of the Red Army, its guards shot 819 prisoners against a wall.

subject: Sonnenstein Euthanasia Centre
summary: On a hill above Pirna, a hospital with a reputation for humane psychiatry was turned into a killing centre where 13,720 disabled and mentally ill people were murdered — and where the staff who did it were trained before being sent east to the extermination camps.

subject: Sonsorol
summary: One of Palau's most remote states, Sonsorol was first sighted by Europeans aboard Magellan's Trinidad in 1522 and today sustains a population of 40 on islands where children must travel 300 kilometers to attend high school.

subject: Sound City Studios
summary: A former Vox instrument factory in Van Nuys became one of rock music's most sacred recording spaces — home to Fleetwood Mac's Rumours, Nirvana's Nevermind, and a Neve console that Dave Grohl called irreplaceable.

subject: South China Mall
summary: Built on former farmland in Dongguan and opened in 2005, South China Mall was designed to be the world's largest shopping mall — then stood famously near-empty for years, became a symbol of overreach, and has since slowly, improbably, come back to life.

subject: South Jersey
summary: Seven counties of pine barrens, Quaker villages, casino towers, and almost-statehood - the half of New Jersey that looks toward Philadelphia and has spent two centuries quietly going its own way.

subject: South Stack
summary: A 1809 lighthouse on a tiny sea stack reached by 400 steps and an aluminium bridge, with 8,000 nesting seabirds screaming on the cliffs above.

subject: South Stoa II (Athens)
summary: Built from the recycled bones of an older Athenian building, South Stoa II closed the south side of the Agora's grand new courtyard - and may have been where Athenian juries sat in judgment.

subject: South Sudan
summary: The world's youngest country was born in 2011 after decades of civil war, carrying both the scars of over a million lives lost and the fierce hope of more than sixty ethnic groups building something new.

subject: Southern Ireland (1921–1922)
summary: A country that never quite existed: 26 counties given a parliament that met once with four members, while everyone else was busy being a republic instead.

subject: Southport
summary: A planned Victorian resort on the Lancashire coast, knit together by railways, dunes, golf, and Red Rum, whose exercise on the beach made the National's three-time winner.

subject: Southport, North Carolina
summary: Founded as Smithville in 1792 around an 18th-century fort and renamed Southport to sell ships on a promise that never quite arrived, this Cape Fear waterfront has instead become a film set, a Fourth of July spectacle, and the warmest place in North Carolina.

subject: Southwell Minster
summary: A Norman cathedral with twin pyramid spires, three twelfth-century arches, and the most celebrated naturalistic foliate stone carvings in medieval Europe.

subject: Sovereign Hill
summary: An open-air museum near Ballarat where costumed townsfolk, working mines and real gold panning rebuild the wild first decade of the world's richest shallow gold rush.

subject: Soviet Submarine B-39
summary: Built in 1967 as the Soviet Navy's largest non-nuclear submarine, B-39 spent the Cold War stalking American warships across the Pacific — and ended her days as a museum exhibit on San Diego's waterfront, before rust claimed her in 2022.

subject: Soviet destroyer Rekordny
summary: A Soviet destroyer that served two navies and two names before becoming a museum ship at Qingdao, where she was visited by both Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping.

subject: Soviet destroyer Reshitelny (1940)
summary: A Soviet destroyer built from Italian plans, shipped across Siberia by rail, sold to China, and now preserved as a museum ship in Shandong -- a Cold War artifact with an improbable journey.

subject: Soviet destroyer Retivy
summary: Built in Ukraine, assembled in Siberia, and now a museum ship in Dalian, the Gnevny-class destroyer Retivy traces a journey across the entire breadth of the Soviet Union and into the 21st century.

subject: Soviet submarine K-21
summary: A World War II Soviet cruiser submarine now preserved as a museum ship in Severomorsk, K-21 is best remembered for its audacious -- if unsuccessful -- torpedo attack on the German battleship Tirpitz in July 1942.

subject: Soğukçeşme Sokağı
summary: Tucked between Hagia Sophia and the Topkapı Palace walls, this pedestrian lane of restored Ottoman wooden houses is one of Istanbul's most photographed streets — and the birthplace of a Turkish president.

subject: Space Research Corporation
summary: On the Quebec-Vermont border, a brilliant artillery engineer tried to shoot satellites into orbit with a giant cannon - then sold his gun technology to apartheid South Africa, went to prison, and was murdered in Brussels.

subject: Space Shuttle Enterprise
summary: The space shuttle that never went to space now sits on the deck of an aircraft carrier in Manhattan, a monument to the era when America built its first reusable spacecraft -- and named it after a fictional starship.

subject: Spaceport 1
summary: On a windswept headland of North Uist, a controversial new spaceport is rising in a place better known for corn crakes and prehistoric standing stones.

subject: Spanish Steps
summary: A monumental stairway of 135 travertine steps connects the French church above to the Spanish embassy below, born from over a century of diplomatic argument and now protected by fines for anyone who dares sit down.

story.title: Spanish colonization attempt of the Strait of Magellan

subject: Spanish colonization attempt of the Strait of Magellan
summary: Spain tried to lock the door at the bottom of the world, and roughly three hundred colonists paid for the attempt with their lives at a place sailors would name Port Famine.

subject: Spata Training Centre
summary: AEK Athens' sprawling 144-acre training complex near Athens International Airport — one of the most modern football facilities in the Balkans, crowned since 2022 by the Serafidio mini-stadium.

subject: Spean Praptos
summary: A twelfth-century laterite bridge that carried the road from Angkor for eight hundred years, until modern trucks finally got too heavy for it.

subject: Special Tribunal for Lebanon
summary: For fifteen years, a quiet building in suburban Leidschendam tried to answer a question Lebanon could not answer itself: who killed Rafic Hariri and the twenty-one people who happened to be near him on Saint Valentine's Day, 2005.

subject: Speight's
summary: Dunedin's iconic brewery, founded in 1876 by three men who left Scotland's Wellpark Brewery to build what became New Zealand's largest, still operates from its original Rattray Street site.

subject: Sphinx of Naxos
summary: Carved from a single block of Naxian marble and set atop a 10-metre Ionic column beside Apollo's temple at Delphi, the Sphinx of Naxos was one of the most audacious gifts any Greek island ever offered to the god.

subject: Spiekeroog
summary: An East Frisian island where bicycles are discouraged, the church holds a Virgin Mary portrait rescued from a Spanish Armada wreck, and a horse-drawn tram still runs on rails along the beach.

subject: Splendid China (Florida)
summary: A $100 million Chinese government-owned theme park in central Florida that featured 60 miniature replicas of Chinese landmarks, drew protests from Tibetan activists, lost $9 million a year, and was eventually bulldozed to build a Margaritaville resort.

subject: St Agnes, Isles of Scilly
summary: The southernmost inhabited place in the United Kingdom - a 366-acre island with a Viking labyrinth, an 18th-century lighthouse and a playing field that may be a mass grave.

subject: St Andrews Sarcophagus
summary: An eighth-century Pictish stone coffin found by gravediggers in 1833, carved with David tearing a lion's jaws - the finest surviving sculpture of the Picts.

subject: St Bartholomew-the-Great
summary: Founded in 1123 after a dream at the Vatican, St Bartholomew-the-Great in Smithfield is London's oldest surviving church fabric — where Benjamin Franklin once typeset books, William Hogarth was baptised, and a ghost still reportedly appears on the morning of July 1st.

subject: St Botolph's Priory
summary: The first Augustinian house in England, founded around 1093 in Colchester, ruined by Civil War cannon and standing today as one of Europe's most striking Norman skeletons.

subject: St Clement Danes
summary: St Clement Danes on the Strand was built by Christopher Wren in 1682, gutted by the Luftwaffe in 1941, and resurrected in 1958 as the central church of the Royal Air Force — its Welsh slate floor inscribed with the badges of over 800 RAF units.

subject: St Germans Priory
summary: The former cathedral of Cornwall for 116 years, an Anglo-Saxon see briefly fixed here in 926 AD - now a large Norman parish church with a Burne-Jones east window and a Rysbrack monument under the north tower.

subject: St James' Priory
summary: Bristol's oldest building - a Norman priory from 1129 that survived the Dissolution by becoming a parish church, and survived the twentieth century through a Lottery-funded resurrection.

subject: St Katharine Docks
summary: Immediately beside the Tower of London, a working dock that displaced 11,300 people, survived the Blitz, and reinvented itself as London's most elegant marina.

subject: St Levan
summary: A Cornish coastal parish where Bertrand Russell once lived, Rowena Cade carved a theatre out of a cliff, and an endemic flower grows nowhere else in the world.

subject: St Magnus the Martyr
summary: T. S. Eliot called the interior "inexplicable splendour of Ionian white and gold." For six hundred years it was the gateway to London.

subject: St Margaret's, Westminster
summary: The parish church of the House of Commons, dwarfed between Westminster Abbey and Big Ben - where Pepys, Churchill, and Mountbatten were married, William Caxton was buried, and a Victorian restorer once thought he'd found doors covered in human skin.

subject: St Mary-le-Bow
summary: The church whose bells define who is truly a Londoner—a survivor of tornado, fire, and Blitz, rebuilt by Wren after the Great Fire, whose name literally means 'the church of the arches.'

subject: St Michael's Isle
summary: A tidal islet off the Langness Peninsula carrying a 12th-century chapel, a Civil War fort, and the memory of two great battles for the Isle of Man.

subject: St Osyth's Priory
summary: An Augustinian abbey built around the arm bone of a martyred Saxon princess, converted into a country house under Henry VIII, plundered in the Civil War, and still standing in chequered flint and limestone today.

subject: St Patrick's Isle
summary: A tidal islet off the west coast of the Isle of Man holds Bronze Age foundations, an Irish round tower, a ruined cathedral, and the seat of a bishopric that once ran from Iona to Arran.

subject: St. Andrews Presbyterian Kirk
summary: Founded by fifty-five Scottish settlers in 1798, Nassau's oldest Presbyterian church spent two centuries building schools, launching missions across the Bahamas, and quietly anchoring a community far from the Highlands.

subject: St. Ann's Academy (Victoria, British Columbia)
summary: The oldest part of this Victoria landmark is not part of the school at all - it is a cathedral that was picked up and moved.

subject: St. Augustine Light
summary: Florida's first lighthouse site, where beacons have burned since 1565, survived Civil War sabotage and rifle fire, and is now home to a maritime museum whose archaeologists have pulled Revolutionary War shipwrecks from the seafloor.

subject: St. Elisabeth Gasthuis, Haarlem
summary: A Haarlem hospital that nursed the sick for four uninterrupted centuries, in buildings reclaimed from a monastery, decorated by Frans Hals, and named for a 13th-century princess who hid bread in her cloak.

subject: St. Eloy's Hospice
summary: In 1440 the blacksmiths of Utrecht bought a building to look after their own widows and elderly. Almost six centuries later, the same guild is still in residence - and they still play 18th-century kolf in the courtyard.

subject: St. Louis Union Station
summary: Once the world's largest and busiest train station, this is where Harry Truman grinned behind the 'Dewey Defeats Truman' headline -- now reinvented as a hotel and entertainment complex with a 1-million-gallon aquarium.

subject: St. Manchan's Oratory
summary: A boat-shaped stone oratory and an ogham stone fifteen centuries old sit together on a slope above Dingle, the bright church of An Teampall Geal.

subject: St. Maria im Kapitol
summary: Two wooden doors carved around 1065 have hung in the same church for nearly nine centuries, built on the foundations of a Roman temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva.

subject: St. Roch (ship)
summary: A 104-foot RCMP schooner built in North Vancouver crossed the Northwest Passage in both directions, became the first vessel to circumnavigate North America, and now sits in dry dock a few kilometres from the yard that built her.

subject: Stade des Martyrs
summary: Kinshasa's 80,000-seat stadium, named for four ministers publicly hanged on Pentecost 1966, has served as arena, prison, concert hall, and symbol of the DRC's turbulent persistence.

subject: Staffin
summary: A Gaelic-speaking crofting community on northeast Skye whose tide-washed shore holds 170-million-year-old dinosaur footprints and a war memorial that remembers American airmen.

subject: Stalag VIII-A
summary: In a freezing wooden hut at a German prison camp on the Neisse, four captured Frenchmen premiered Messiaen's Quartet for the End of Time to an audience of fellow prisoners and their guards.

subject: Stalag X-B
summary: A POW camp on the edge of a Lower Saxon bog where western prisoners got Red Cross parcels and Soviet prisoners got nothing, and where nobody counted the dead.

subject: Stanley Internment Camp
summary: For 44 months from January 1942 to August 1945, about 2,800 civilian men, women, and children — among them Hong Kong's Governor, its Chief Justice, and 286 children under sixteen — were held in a makeshift camp on the grounds of St. Stephen's College and Stanley Prison.

subject: Stari Most
summary: A 16th-century Ottoman bridge whose architect reportedly prepared for his own funeral on the day the scaffolding was removed, destroyed by shelling in 1993 and painstakingly rebuilt with its own stones pulled from the river.

subject: Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center
summary: Renzo Piano's sweeping $861 million complex on Faliro Bay — an artificial hill housing the National Library and the National Opera under a vast solar canopy — is both a gift from one of the world's great shipping fortunes and Athens's boldest architectural statement in generations.

subject: Steep Holm
summary: A limestone island in the Bristol Channel that has been a Roman watchtower, a 6th-century saint's refuge, a Victorian fort, and a wartime gun emplacement - and is now the only place in Britain where wild peonies grow.

subject: Steinfurter Bagno
summary: A Westphalian count built a 125-hectare pleasure park with 105 follies on it - a Chinese palace, an Egyptian temple, an Arion ship - then watched Napoleon's tax collectors tear most of it down.

subject: Stekenjokk
summary: A treeless plateau on the Norway border that holds Sweden's wind record, swallowed a copper mine for twelve years, and lets the country's highest road cross it only four months a year.

subject: Stepney
summary: The Mother Church of the East End, the Whitechapel Bell Foundry, and a thousand years of arrivals, departures, and the people who stayed.

subject: Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center
summary: A Hungarian refugee who once built model planes from matchsticks grew up to fund the hangar where the Space Shuttle Discovery, the Enola Gay, and an SR-71 Blackbird all live under one roof.

subject: Stevns Klint
summary: A seventeen-kilometre Danish chalk cliff where a five-centimetre band of clay records the worst day in the history of animal life - and where the Cold War drilled a fortress into the rock above it.

subject: Stoa of Attalos
summary: A 2,100-year-old shopping arcade, rebuilt whole in the 1950s, that now houses the museum of Athenian democracy.

subject: Stoa of Eumenes
summary: A king of Pergamon shipped a marble shelter to Athens so theatergoers could escape the rain on the Acropolis slope.

subject: Stoa of the Athenians
summary: The colonnade Athens built at Delphi around 478 BC displayed the ropes that had held together Xerxes' pontoon bridge across the Hellespont — turning the war's most unglamorous trophy into the most pointed possible statement about Persian ambition undone.

subject: Stockholm
summary: A capital built on fourteen islands where medieval streets meet cutting-edge innovation, hosting Nobel ceremonies in gilded halls while its metro stations double as the world's longest art gallery.

subject: Stockholm Central Station
summary: Sweden's busiest railway station harnesses the body heat of 200,000 daily visitors while showcasing century-old landscape paintings that capture the nation's soul.

subject: Stone Brewing Co.
summary: What started in a San Marcos strip mall in 1996 became the ninth-largest craft brewery in the United States — known for aggressive hop-forward beers, a combative marketing persona, and the Arrogant Bastard Ale that 'put San Diego on the craft brew map.'

subject: Stone Nullah Lane
summary: A one-way street in Wan Chai where a stream once ran openly down the middle, Stone Nullah Lane preserves layers of Hong Kong's history in a Blue House whose cast-iron balconies are said to recall New Orleans, and a Taoist temple built from granite in 1863.

subject: Stonehaven
summary: Where Scotland's Highland Boundary Fault meets the North Sea — a small fishing port with a 16th-century tolbooth, a heated open-air saltwater pool, fireball-swinging Hogmanay revellers, and Dunnottar Castle on the cliffs.

story.title: The Storming of the Bastille: The Day the Old Regime Fell

subject: Storming of the Bastille
summary: On July 14, 1789, a Parisian mob stormed a medieval fortress-prison holding just seven inmates, transforming a largely symbolic target into the most powerful emblem of the French Revolution.

subject: Stormont Estate
summary: The hilltop estate east of Belfast where a Greek-classical parliament building has spent nearly a century at the center of Northern Ireland's politics.

subject: Storyeum
summary: Vancouver spent more than CA$22 million digging a 104,000-square-foot theatre under Gastown to perform the history of British Columbia — and closed it 28 months after opening night.

subject: Stover, Teigngrace
summary: A Georgian Devon estate built on a fortune made in India, whose owner's tramway hauled Dartmoor granite to ships bound for London Bridge.

subject: Strahan
summary: Once the poor relation to the booming mining cities behind it, this little port on Macquarie Harbour outlived them all to become the gateway to Tasmania's wild west coast.

subject: Strait of Juan de Fuca
summary: Named for a Greek navigator sailing under the Spanish flag who may or may not have actually found it, this 96-mile channel between Vancouver Island and the Olympic Peninsula is the Salish Sea's turbulent gateway to the Pacific.

subject: Straits of Mackinac
summary: The narrow waterway connecting Lake Michigan and Lake Huron, the Straits of Mackinac have served for centuries as a strategic chokepoint where empires, engineering, and ecology collide -- from French forts to the Mackinac Bridge to an aging oil pipeline on the lakebed.

subject: Strandhill
summary: Surfers in wetsuits stride past the closed-down airport every morning to a beach where you're warned not to swim - and from there, at low tide, a road appears across the sands to Coney Island.

subject: Strangford
summary: Vikings named it for the strong current that still runs past its front door - and a string of monks, saints and tower-house builders have all left marks within walking distance.

subject: Strangways Springs
summary: Where Arabana ancestral snakes once camped, water rises from the desert - and the ruins of a telegraph station mark where the modern world arrived.

subject: Stratford Station
summary: Britain's seventh busiest railway station, serving more rail lines than almost anywhere else in the country—a multi-level interchange that grew from a single platform opened in 1839 into one of London's great transport hubs.

subject: Striezelmarkt
summary: The oldest Christmas market of its kind began in 1434 as a single day of meat sales to break the Advent fast — and grew into 240 stands, three million visitors, and a fourteen-metre candle pyramid built by people whose ancestors carved because the mines closed.

subject: Strofades
summary: Two remote specks of rock in the southern Ionian Sea hold a fortress-monastery older than the Ottoman Empire, a myth about winged monsters, and the story of the last monk who refused to leave.

story.title: Structure of the Common Security and Defence Policy

subject: Structure of the Common Security and Defence Policy
summary: The EU's defence architecture is mostly invisible - acronyms layered on acronyms in offices around Brussels - but a small headquarters established in 2017 finally gave Europe its first permanent military command for joint missions.

subject: Stuart Highway
summary: A 2,720-kilometre ribbon of asphalt slicing through the empty heart of Australia, the Stuart Highway traces the route of explorer John McDouall Stuart from tropical Darwin to the Southern Ocean gateway of Port Augusta.

subject: Su'ao Cold Spring
summary: Taiwan's only carbonated cold spring, discovered in 1928, where you can bathe in naturally fizzing 22°C water that once fed the island's first soda factory.

subject: Sublime Porte
summary: A gate became a government, and a government became a phrase: the Sublime Porte was once the seat of the Ottoman Grand Vizier and the term by which the entire empire spoke to the world.

subject: Sueno's Stone
summary: Scotland's tallest surviving Pictish cross-slab, a 6.5-metre pillar of yellow sandstone near Forres whose carved battle scenes depict a victory nobody can definitively identify, by a people who left no written history.

subject: Suicide of Tyler Clementi
summary: In September 2010, an 18-year-old Rutgers freshman jumped from the George Washington Bridge after his roommate broadcast his private life -- a death that transformed the national conversation about cyberbullying and LGBTQ youth.

story.title: Sukiyabashi Jiro: Ten Seats, One Lifetime

subject: Sukiyabashi Jiro
summary: In a basement beneath a Ginza office building, a man who began his apprenticeship at age seven built the first sushi restaurant ever awarded three Michelin stars -- then lost them because he refused to let strangers walk in off the street.

subject: Sully Historic Site
summary: A Virginia plantation estate saved from the bulldozers of Dulles Airport, Sully tells the tangled saga of the Lee family through debt, tragedy, and endurance.

subject: Sumas–Huntingdon Border Crossing
summary: A 24-hour port of entry on the 49th parallel where customs once ran out of a farmhouse, smugglers ran opium and people, and a 714-ton customs house was moved rather than demolished.

subject: Sumba
summary: An Indonesian island the size of Jamaica where megalithic tombs share the landscape with hand-woven ikat textiles, endemic parrots, and a mythology that remembers a stone bridge to neighboring Flores.

story.title: Sumiyoshi Taisha: Where the Gods Set Sail

subject: Sumiyoshi-taisha
summary: The head shrine of over 2,000 Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, founded in the 3rd century to enshrine sea gods and a warrior empress -- and once the departure point for Japan's earliest diplomatic voyages along the Silk Road.

subject: Summer Isles
summary: An archipelago off Achiltibuie where a financier owns the islands, the post office no longer prints its famous stamps, and the cafe closed for good.

subject: Sunderland Barracks
summary: Hastily built in 1794 to defend the coal trade from a French invasion that never came, the barracks housed Wearside soldiers for nearly 140 years before being swept away by a dock.

subject: Sunderland Minster
summary: A thousand-year-old church on the south bank of the Wear, redesignated a minster in 1998 - the second post-Reformation minster in England - and rededicated in 2007 to Benedict Biscop, the saint who built the church up the river in 674.

subject: Sunflower Square
summary: The main public square of Palmas - Brazil's youngest state capital - claims one of the largest square areas in the world and holds the geodesic center of the country inside its executive palace.

subject: Sunflower Student Movement
summary: In March 2014, Taiwanese students stormed and occupied the Legislative Yuan for 24 days to block a trade pact with China -- the first citizen occupation of Taiwan's parliament in its history, sparked by sunflowers and fueled by fears of Beijing's economic leverage.

subject: Sunland Baobab
summary: For two decades a Limpopo farm had a fully stocked pub inside a living tree, until the thousand-year-old baobab that housed it began, quietly and catastrophically, to fall apart.

subject: Sunnylands
summary: Walter and Leonore Annenberg's 200-acre Rancho Mirage estate earned the nickname 'Camp David of the West' for hosting world leaders from seven presidencies — and the Impressionist art collection that once hung on its walls, including Picassos, Van Goghs, and Monets, now lives at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

subject: Sunshine 60
summary: A 60-story skyscraper in Ikebukuro that was the tallest building in Asia when it opened in 1978, built directly on the site of Sugamo Prison where seven convicted war criminals including former Prime Minister Hideki Tojo were hanged in 1948.

subject: Super-Kamiokande
summary: A cathedral-sized tank of ultrapure water buried a kilometer underground in the Japanese Alps, Super-Kamiokande proved that neutrinos have mass -- a discovery that earned a Nobel Prize and rewrote the Standard Model of physics.

story.title: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia

subject: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
summary: In 2018, the West Virginia House of Delegates impeached every member of the state's highest court at once - the most extraordinary judicial reckoning in modern American history.

story.title: Supreme Court of the United States

subject: Supreme Court of the United States
summary: For 146 years the highest court in the country had no building of its own - it borrowed rooms in the Capitol and met in private houses - until Cass Gilbert's marble temple opened in 1935 and gave the Supreme Court the architectural authority its decisions had been claiming since Marbury v. Madison.

story.title: Surawana: The Temple That Reads Like a Compass

subject: Surawana
summary: A partially ruined Majapahit-era Hindu temple in East Java whose directional relief carvings map sacred and profane narratives onto the cardinal points, encoding a 14th-century Javanese worldview into stone.

subject: Surfing Madonna
summary: On an April afternoon in 2011, two men dressed as construction workers quietly installed a 10-foot mosaic of the Virgen de Guadalupe on a rail bridge in Encinitas — and created one of California's most beloved pieces of guerrilla public art.

subject: Sutro Baths
summary: Once the world's largest indoor swimming establishment, the Sutro Baths now survive only as haunting concrete ruins where the Pacific surges through the skeleton of Adolph Sutro's aquatic palace.

subject: Suvarnadurg
summary: A sea fort off India's Konkan coast where Maratha admirals built warships and defied European colonial powers for over a century.

subject: Suwa-taisha
summary: One of Japan's oldest shrine complexes, Suwa-taisha sprawls across four sites around Lake Suwa, where a defeated god became a war deity and an eight-year-old boy became a living incarnation of the divine.

subject: Swallow's Nest
summary: A tiny Neo-Gothic castle perched on a sheer cliff above the Black Sea, so improbable it looks less like architecture than a fairy tale someone forgot to wake up from.

subject: Swedish Institute at Athens
summary: Tucked beside the New Acropolis Museum, the Swedish Institute at Athens has spent nearly eight decades excavating the deep past of Greece — from Mycenaean chamber tombs to a Bauhaus guesthouse in a tobacco port.

subject: Sweetwater Saloon
summary: For thirty years, this tiny Mill Valley bar was the place where Jerry Garcia, Bonnie Raitt, and Carlos Santana showed up on Monday open-mic nights just to play.

story.title: Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation

subject: Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation
summary: From a bingo palace opened in 1983 to the U.S. Grant Hotel, an expanded resort casino, and co-ownership of an MLS soccer team — the Sycuan Band's economic trajectory is one of the more remarkable stories in California tribal history.

subject: Sydney Cricket Ground
summary: More than a stadium, the SCG is a hundred and fifty years of Australian sporting memory pressed into a few acres of Bulli soil at Moore Park.

subject: São Simão, Goiás
summary: A Goiás river port where a 1957 bridge washout is still called Judgement Day, and a reservoir twice the size of Guanabara Bay now holds the carnival crowds.

subject: Säppi
summary: A Bothnian Sea lighthouse island where Mediterranean wild sheep have grazed since 1949, Highland cattle mow the shore meadows each summer, and Finland's second-oldest bird observatory works out of the keeper's house.

subject: Sé, Macau
summary: The Sé parish is the historic heart of Macau, where Portuguese colonial architecture, China's financial institutions, casino towers, and centuries of layered civic life share the same few square kilometers on the tip of the peninsula.

subject: Séminaire de Québec
summary: A 1663 seminary founded by the first bishop of New France that grew to birth Canada's oldest French-language university and shaped centuries of Quebec's intellectual life.

subject: Süleymaniye Hamam
summary: Mimar Sinan built this bathhouse in 1557 as part of his great mosque complex on Istanbul's third hill — a place where the metalworkers from nearby foundries once came to wash, and where the architect himself is said to have bathed for three decades.

subject: Sōji-ji (Osaka)
summary: A ninth-century Buddhist temple in Ibaraki born from a legend of turtle-borne rescue, Soji-ji is the 22nd stop on the ancient Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage and the birthplace of Japan's ceremonial knife art.

story.title: T. G. Richards and Company Store

subject: T. G. Richards and Company Store
summary: Washington's oldest brick building arrived by ship from San Francisco - 100,000 bricks and 73 barrels of lime, delivered to a gold-rush boomtown in 1858.

subject: TSMC
summary: Founded in 1987 with Taiwanese government backing and Philips technology, TSMC invented the dedicated semiconductor foundry model and became the world's most critical chipmaker - manufacturing processors for Apple, Nvidia, and most of the global technology industry.

subject: TT Circuit Assen
summary: The only race track on the planet that has hosted Grand Prix motorcycling nearly every year since the world championship was invented in 1949 - missing only 2020 to a pandemic - which is why motorcyclists call it the Cathedral of Speed.

subject: Tado Taisha
summary: A Shinto grand shrine in Mie Prefecture where young men ride horses up a steep hill and over a wall each May to divine the harvest, continuing a ritual over a thousand years old.

subject: Tahtakale Hamam
summary: Built within years of the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, the Tahtakale Hamam near the Grand Bazaar may be the oldest surviving bathhouse in Istanbul — a 15th-century monument that survived earthquakes and fire only to spend decades as a frozen-food warehouse before its restoration.

subject: Tai Long Wan, Sai Kung
summary: A three-kilometre bay on Hong Kong's wild eastern coast, where Cretaceous volcanic cliffs meet surf-swept beaches, ancient villages hold centuries of memory, and a chapel closed in 1988 still opens its doors when one of its faithful dies.

subject: Tai Po Lookout
summary: Built by a British engineer in the early twentieth century, this colonial hilltop residence overlooking Tolo Harbour has served as a private home, a wartime torture site, and a care facility for AIDS patients — and is now a private residence again.

subject: Tai Tam Byewash Reservoir
summary: A 1904 concrete dam in Tai Tam Country Park built to capture overflow from an overstretched reservoir above — an engineering solution whose graceful stonework is now a declared monument.

subject: Tai-an
summary: The only surviving tea house built by the legendary tea master Sen no Rikyu, this two-tatami room at Myoki-an temple distills the radical philosophy that even warlords must bow to enter.

subject: Taichung City Second Market
summary: Built in 1917 for Taichung's Japanese colonial residents, the Second Market still hums with vendors and steam and the smell of ba-wan — a century-old market hall that outlasted every regime that shaped it.

subject: Taichung Shiyakusho
summary: Built in 1911 as a Japanese municipal hall, the Taichung Shiyakusho is a three-storey Baroque survivor that now houses Café 1911 on its ground floor and an art centre above — the name of its colonial past worn lightly into its present identity.

story.title: Taima-dera: The Temple Between Two Worlds

subject: Taima-dera
summary: A 7th-century Buddhist temple at the western edge of the Nara Basin that guards Japan's only surviving pair of original twin pagodas, the oldest stone lantern in the country, and a legendary mandala said to depict the Buddhist paradise -- all built on the burial grounds of an ancient clan beneath a mountain the Japanese regarded as the gateway to the afterlife.

subject: Taipa
summary: Once two separate islands known by names like Dragon Ring and Chicken's Neck, Taipa became a firecracker-manufacturing hub, then a casino resort corridor, and is now one of the most rapidly transformed pieces of land in the Pearl River delta.

subject: Taipei 101
summary: The world's tallest building from 2004 to 2009, this 508-meter bamboo-stalk tower was the first skyscraper to exceed half a kilometer, holds the world's largest tuned mass damper, and survived a deadly construction crane collapse and a typhoon-prone location on the Pacific Ring of Fire.

subject: Taj Mahal
summary: A mausoleum of white marble rising beside the Yamuna River - Emperor Shah Jahan's monument to love and loss, and the most recognizable building on Earth.

subject: Takadachi Gikeidō
summary: A hilltop chapel in Hiraizumi where Japan's most celebrated tragic hero, Minamoto no Yoshitsune, made his last stand in 1189 -- and where Matsuo Basho composed one of the most famous haiku ever written.

subject: Takarazuka Revue
summary: Japan's all-female musical theater troupe, where women play every role -- prince and princess alike -- in lavish Broadway-style spectacles that draw two million fans a year and helped shape the entire tradition of manga for girls.

subject: Takht-e Soleymān
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site where a Zoroastrian fire temple, a Mongol palace, and folk legends of King Solomon share a volcanic hilltop above a bottomless spring pond in northwestern Iran.

subject: Takkoku-no-Iwaya
summary: A cliff-face Buddhist temple in Hiraizumi modeled after Kyoto's Kiyomizu-dera, built into a cave where Emishi warriors once fortified themselves against the imperial armies of the 9th century.

subject: Taksim Military Barracks
summary: The Halil Pasha Artillery Barracks once overlooked Taksim Square; demolished in 1940 to make way for a park, the plan to rebuild them as a shopping mall in 2013 triggered the Gezi Park protests — one of Turkey's largest episodes of civil unrest in modern times.

subject: Taku Forts
summary: Coastal fortifications at the Hai River estuary that were attacked four times in forty years by Western and Japanese forces, earning the youngest-ever Victoria Cross recipient and becoming a national symbol of China's resistance to foreign invasion.

subject: Talisker
summary: Samuel Johnson called it a place beyond all that I have seen from which the gay and the jovial seem utterly excluded; the distillery five miles away borrowed the name and the rest is whisky history.

subject: Talladega Superspeedway
summary: NASCAR's longest and most anarchic oval, a 3,000-acre cathedral of speed in eastern Alabama where driver boycotts, alleged curses, and multi-car pileups have been part of the show since 1969.

story.title: Tama New Town: The Planned City Where Raccoon Dogs Fought Back (In Film, at Least)

subject: Tama New Town
summary: Japan's largest housing development was built in the Tama Hills west of Tokyo to house 200,000 people in orderly neighborhoods -- and became famous worldwide as the setting for Studio Ghibli's Pom Poko, where shapeshifting tanuki wage a doomed battle against suburban expansion.

subject: Tamsui Customs Wharf
summary: Taiwan's only surviving Qing Dynasty pier, where the treaty-port era opened the Tamsui River to foreign trade in 1862 — a 150-meter stone wharf that has outlasted three empires.

subject: Tanbar Station
summary: A cattle station the size of a small country, strung along Cooper Creek in the Channel Country, where a single flood can fatten the herd or cut the homestead off for weeks.

story.title: Tancredo Neves Pantheon of the Fatherland and Freedom

subject: Tancredo Neves Pantheon of the Fatherland and Freedom
summary: A Niemeyer-designed cenotaph shaped like a dove, built in grief for the first civilian president-elect after twenty years of military rule - a man who died of a bowel obstruction the night before his inauguration.

subject: Tanforan Racetrack
summary: From thoroughbred racing to Japanese American internment to a shopping mall, Tanforan Racetrack's transformations mirror a century of California history.

subject: Tang Lung Chau
summary: A small uninhabited islet off Ma Wan in Hong Kong's western approaches, Tang Lung Chau is home to a pre-war lighthouse declared a monument in 2000 — a skeletal steel tower that has guided ships through the Kap Shui Mun channel since 1912.

subject: Tangshan
summary: The cradle of Chinese industrialization -- birthplace of the nation's first standard-gauge railway, first steam locomotive, and first cement factory -- rebuilt entirely after a devastating 1976 earthquake.

subject: Tarfala research station
summary: A remote Stockholm University outpost in the Arctic mountains holds the world's longest continuous glacier monitoring record -- and Sweden's wind speed record.

subject: Tarikhaneh
summary: One of the oldest mosques in Iran was built on the ruins of a Zoroastrian fire temple, using construction techniques borrowed from Sasanian palaces -- a building where three civilizations meet in brick and mortar.

subject: Tashirojima
summary: A tiny Japanese island where cats outnumber the roughly 100 remaining human residents, complete with a cat shrine, cat-shaped cottages, and a strict no-dogs policy.

subject: Tate Britain
summary: On the Thames at Millbank, the world's most comprehensive collection of British art - built on the site of a Victorian prison, paid for by a sugar refiner, and home to the entire painted output of J. M. W. Turner.

subject: Tate Liverpool
summary: Britain's national modern art gallery in a converted 1846 Albert Dock warehouse - James Stirling's 1988 transformation of cast iron and red brick into the Tate's first outpost beyond London, and the catalyst for Liverpool's waterfront cultural revival.

subject: Tate St Ives
summary: On the site of an old gasworks above Porthmeor beach stands a curved white gallery that brought St Ives' century of modernist painters home and won Museum of the Year in 2018.

subject: Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route
summary: A 37-kilometer sightseeing corridor through the Japanese Alps that stitches together cable cars, trolleybuses, ropeways, and a walk between 20-meter-high snow walls -- all built on infrastructure carved out during the construction of Japan's tallest dam.

subject: Tavistock Square
summary: A Bloomsbury square that holds memorials to three of the twentieth century's defining tragedies—Hiroshima, conscientious objection, and the 7/7 bombings—and a Gandhi statue at its centre.

subject: Taxila
summary: One of South Asia's oldest cities, Taxila was a crossroads of empires for two thousand years -- from Persian satraps to Greek conquerors, Mauryan emperors to Kushan Buddhists -- each leaving ruins atop the last.

subject: Taytay, Palawan
summary: A former kingdom and colonial capital on northern Palawan, where a 17th-century Spanish fort still guards the shores where Magellan's crew once took a king hostage.

subject: Tazumal
summary: El Salvador's tallest pyramid rises 24 meters from a site whose name means 'pyramid where the victims were burned' -- a pre-Columbian crossroads linking the Maya, Teotihuacan, and the Pipil across more than a thousand years of continuous occupation.

subject: Taşkışla
summary: A grand 19th-century stone complex near Taksim Square, Taşkışla was built by a British architect for the Ottoman military, briefly housed French wounded from the Crimean War, and now anchors Istanbul Technical University's architecture faculty.

subject: Te Papa
summary: New Zealand's national museum sits on reclaimed land at the edge of Wellington Harbour, a 36,000 square-metre 'container of treasures' that holds everything from a 495-kilogram colossal squid to the diary of a Gallipoli captain.

subject: Teampull na Trionaid
summary: The ruined 13th-century Augustinian nunnery at Carinish - said to have been a college of learning, perhaps even the first university - founded by Somerled's daughter and rebuilt by his great-granddaughter.

subject: Teapot Dome
summary: The scandal that defined corruption - the Wyoming oil field whose secret leasing in 1922 sent a cabinet secretary to prison and made 'Teapot Dome' synonymous with government graft for generations.

subject: Teatre Principal de Maó
summary: Spain's oldest opera house sits not in Madrid or Barcelona but in a small Menorcan port, a horseshoe of gilded boxes that has staged bel canto since 1829.

subject: Teatro Arthur Azevedo
summary: By 1989 the only original part left of Brazil's second-oldest theatre was its front wall - so São Luís knocked down the rest and built 1817 again from the drawings.

subject: Teatro General San Martín
summary: A modernist landmark on Buenos Aires' theater street, the San Martín stacks three stages over thirteen floors - and once hosted the chess match that crowned Bobby Fischer's path to the world title.

subject: Teatro La Perla
summary: Inaugurated in 1864, this neoclassical theater in Ponce is the largest and most historic in the Spanish-speaking Caribbean -- and the place where Puerto Rico first saw a movie.

subject: Teatro Nacional Cervantes
summary: A Spanish actress poured her fortune into a baroque dream theater in Buenos Aires - lost it within five years, and watched it become the national stage of Argentina.

subject: Teatro Nacional de El Salvador
summary: Twelve architects from five countries competed for the commission, and the French entry named 'Melpomene' -- after the muse of tragedy -- won Central America's oldest and grandest theater.

subject: Teatro Puerto Rico
summary: A 2,300-seat theater in the South Bronx that became the cultural heart of New York's Puerto Rican community from the 1940s to the 1960s -- launching Jose Feliciano and hosting stars from across Latin America.

story.title: Teatro del Libertador General San Martín

subject: Teatro del Libertador General San Martín
summary: An opera house shipped piece by piece from Europe, opened the year its architect died, and renamed every time Argentina's politics turned over.

subject: Ted Swales
summary: A South African rugby player turned RAF Pathfinder master bomber, whose Victoria Cross was earned on the same night he received his Distinguished Flying Cross - and whose grave at Leopoldsburg is the reason the story sits over Belgian Limburg.

subject: Tehran Conference
summary: The first meeting of the Big Three -- Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill -- took place inside the Soviet Embassy in Tehran in late 1943, producing the decision to launch D-Day and reshaping the postwar world.

story.title: Tekigai-so: The Villa Where Japan Chose War

subject: Tekigai-sō
summary: A quiet wooden villa in suburban Tokyo where Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe hosted the meetings that pulled Japan into the Tripartite Pact, watched his peace efforts collapse, and ultimately took his own life with potassium cyanide rather than face a war crimes tribunal.

story.title: Tekijuku: The Tiny School That Modernized Japan

subject: Tekijuku
summary: In a modest Osaka townhouse, physician Ogata Koan taught Western medicine through Dutch textbooks to roughly a thousand students -- alumni who would go on to found universities, build armies, and drag Japan into the modern age.

subject: Telekom Center Athens
summary: Four steel pillars 35 meters tall hold up Greece's largest indoor arena, where Olympic gymnasts soared, Eurovision crowned a winner, and Panathinaikos chases European basketball glory.

subject: Telesterion
summary: The great initiation hall at Eleusis where, for nearly a thousand years, thousands of initiates gathered in darkness each autumn for the Eleusinian Mysteries — rites so sacred that no ancient source ever betrayed their secret.

subject: Television City
summary: The CBS studio complex built in 1952 on the site of a baseball stadium, where The Price Is Right ran for 51 uninterrupted seasons and American television was made for seven decades.

subject: Telfair Academy
summary: A young English architect's 1818 Regency mansion became the oldest public art museum in the American South, guarding Savannah's artistic heritage for nearly 140 years.

subject: Telluride
summary: The box canyon they turned into a ski resort - where Butch Cassidy robbed his first bank in 1889, Victorian mining buildings survived because no one could afford to tear them down, and Hollywood discovered Colorado's most beautiful dead end.

subject: Temuco
summary: The capital of Araucanía began as a frontier fort, grew into the marketplace of Mapuche country, and shaped the boy who became Pablo Neruda.

subject: Tena, Ecuador
summary: A bronze statue of the indigenous leader who led the 1578 uprising against Spain greets you at the entrance to Ecuador's jungle-rafting capital.

subject: Tenampúa
summary: A Lenca mountaintop fortress and ceremonial center in central Honduras, with 250 structures hidden beneath pine forests, where bullet casings from a 1924 civil war mingle with obsidian arrowheads from centuries before.

subject: Tengenenge
summary: A failing tobacco farm turned into the most influential stone sculpture community in Africa, Tengenenge gave Zimbabwe's Shona sculptors a place to work with the hard serpentine of the Great Dyke.

subject: Tenkyōkaku
summary: A French Renaissance villa on the shores of Lake Inawashiro, designed by an imperial prince and named by a future emperor after a Tang dynasty poem calling the lake a 'mirror of heaven.'

subject: Tepe Giyan
summary: A necropolis in the Zagros highlands where 123 graves and seven millennia of pottery reveal the deep roots of civilization in western Iran.

subject: Tepe-Kermen
summary: A flat-topped Crimean butte honeycombed with more than 230 hand-cut caves, crowned by a Byzantine cave church where a carved inscription still names the man who dug a tomb.

subject: Terrorism Confinement Center
summary: Latin America's largest prison sits at the base of a volcano in rural El Salvador, holding tens of thousands of alleged gang members in conditions that have drawn both international praise and accusations of systemic torture.

subject: Tete, Mozambique
summary: A Swahili trading post turned Portuguese colonial outpost turned coal-boom provincial capital, Tete sits 260 miles up the Zambezi and holds two of the four bridges that cross the river in Mozambique.

subject: Teufelsberg
summary: A hill made out of the wreckage of Berlin, piled over a Nazi college the Allies could not blow up, topped by an American listening post and now covered in graffiti.

subject: Thaba Bosiu
summary: A flat-topped sandstone plateau in Lesotho that became the birthplace of the Basotho nation when King Moshoeshoe I turned it into an impregnable fortress during the devastating Mfecane wars of the 1820s.

subject: The American Adventure (Epcot)
summary: Benjamin Franklin and Mark Twain, born nearly a century apart, share a stage at Epcot to narrate America's story through Audio-Animatronic theater inside a Colonial building that hides five stories behind an illusion of two and a half.

subject: The Big Blue
summary: A small white chapel on a cliff in Amorgos became a place of pilgrimage - not for a saint, but for a 1988 film about men who loved the deep more than they loved the surface.

subject: The Bighorn Medicine Wheel
summary: The mysterious stone circle on a Wyoming mountaintop - 80 feet across, built by unknown people 500 to 800 years ago, aligned with sunrise on summer solstice and still used for ceremonies by tribes who consider it sacred ground.

subject: The Biltmore Los Angeles
summary: Opened in 1923 as the largest hotel west of Chicago, the Biltmore hosted the founding of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, eight Oscar ceremonies, and more than a century of Los Angeles power.

subject: The Black Dog of Newgate
summary: A 1596 London ghost story written by an inmate of Newgate Prison about a spectral hound said to haunt the gaol after starving prisoners ate a fellow inmate during a famine in the reign of Henry III.

story.title: The Blond King's Ashes: Savage Trading Post

subject: The Blond King's Ashes
summary: A Gold Rush trader's log cabin on the Merced River became the unlikely spark for the first European American expedition into Yosemite Valley -- a story of ambition, war, and the collision of worlds at the gateway to the Sierra Nevada.

subject: The Boat That Carried Trains
summary: For fifty-one years, the world's largest ferry shuttled entire trains across the Carquinez Strait, making the transcontinental railroad work by solving the problem no bridge could yet span.

subject: The Bowl (Douglas)
summary: A Douglas stadium named for King George V, nicknamed the Bernabowl by hopeful locals, and the unlikely home pitch of an Isle of Man football club playing in the English league system.

subject: The Breakers
summary: A 70-room Renaissance Revival palazzo perched on Newport's cliffs, The Breakers stands as the supreme monument to Gilded Age excess -- and the complicated family saga of the Vanderbilts who built, inherited, and ultimately gave it away.

subject: The Broad
summary: The contemporary art museum opened in 2015 by Eli and Edythe Broad, offering free general admission to one of the finest collections of postwar and contemporary art in the United States.

subject: The Brown Derby
summary: The Brown Derby restaurant chain, whose Hollywood location opened on Valentine's Day 1929, was the definitive gathering place for the film industry's golden age — the reported birthplace of the Cobb salad and the Shirley Temple cocktail, and the setting of an iconic I Love Lucy episode.

story.title: The Cadaver Synod: The Trial of a Dead Pope

subject: The Cadaver Synod
summary: Where Pope Stephen VI exhumed the corpse of Pope Formosus in 897 AD, dressed it in papal vestments, and put it on trial for crimes against the church - then had the body thrown in the Tiber.

story.title: The Cloisters: Medieval Europe on a Manhattan Hilltop

subject: The Cloisters
summary: A museum built from the stones of five dismantled French and Catalan monasteries, reassembled on a hilltop in northern Manhattan to house one of the world's finest collections of medieval art.

story.title: The Coconut Port That Built a Capital

subject: The Coconut Port That Built a Capital
summary: Jakarta's oldest harbor has been a pepper trading post for Hindu kings, a contested prize between Portuguese and Islamic forces, the gateway of the Dutch East India Company, and the cradle of a megacity - and today it still operates, crowded with the wooden pinisi schooners that carry freight across the Indonesian archipelago.

story.title: The Defenestration of Prague: The Thrown Men Who Started a Thirty Years' War

subject: The Defenestration of Prague
summary: Where Protestant nobles threw two Catholic governors and their secretary out of a castle window in 1618, sparking a religious war that killed 8 million people.

subject: The Dirty Duck
summary: The Waterside pub whose walls are plastered with signed photographs of RSC actors and which carries two licensed names -- The Dirty Duck and The Black Swan -- one given to it by American GIs in World War II, the other dating back to 1776.

subject: The Don CeSar
summary: A lovestruck real estate developer poured his heartbreak into a pink Moorish palace on the Gulf Coast, and the Jazz Age playground he built has survived bankruptcy, war, and abandonment to remain one of Florida's most iconic landmarks.

subject: The Dorchester
summary: The hotel that opened in 1931 on Park Lane with a Lace Ball, became London's safest building in the Blitz, sold to the Sultan of Brunei in 1985, and has been simultaneously glamorous and controversial ever since.

subject: The Eagle, Cambridge
summary: Watson and Crick walked into this Cambridge pub for lunch on 28 February 1953 and announced they had discovered the structure of DNA. The pub still pours a beer called Eagle's DNA.

subject: The Emporium
summary: A Late Victorian department store that lasted only six months became a telephone exchange, a grocery store, an antiques shop, and one of the most enduring buildings in Gold Country.

subject: The Entebbe Raid
summary: In July 1976, Israeli commandos flew 2,500 miles in the dark to free hostages held in an abandoned terminal at Entebbe, in one of the most audacious rescues ever attempted.

subject: The Finnish Dormitory in Taichung
summary: For nearly three decades, a brick building on the campus of Morrison Academy in Taichung served as home for the children of Finnish missionaries — and later became the subject of a painful reckoning with abuse.

story.title: The Flannan Isles Mystery: The Lighthouse Keepers Who Vanished

subject: The Flannan Isles Mystery
summary: Where three lighthouse keepers disappeared from a remote Scottish island in December 1900, leaving behind an untouched meal and a mystery that has never been solved.

subject: The Gettysburg Electric Map
summary: The giant illuminated battle map that explained Gettysburg to millions of visitors for 50 years - now retired to a museum, replaced by digital technology but remembered fondly by generations who first understood the battle through its blinking lights.

subject: The Geysers
summary: The world's largest geothermal field has been harnessed for 12,000 years -- first by Native Americans who bathed in its steam, then by a resort that hosted presidents, and now by 18 power plants drawing energy from a magma chamber four miles underground.

subject: The Glen, Cork
summary: A glacial valley on Cork's northside that has hosted a Victorian fertilizer factory, an 1850s railway tunnel, an IRA escape route, a sand martin colony, and Ireland's first publicly owned ski slope.

story.title: The Great Stink: When London's Smell Shut Down Parliament

subject: The Great Stink
summary: Where the Thames became so polluted in the summer of 1858 that the smell forced Parliament to flee, finally convincing the government to build a modern sewer system.

subject: The Great Thunderstorm
summary: On a Sunday afternoon in 1638, a ball of fire tore through a Dartmoor church packed with three hundred worshippers, killing four and leaving a legend that endures four centuries later.

subject: The Greenbrier Bunker
summary: The luxury West Virginia resort that hid a 112,000-square-foot nuclear bunker beneath its new wing for 30 years - designed to shelter Congress during atomic war while guests above played golf.

story.title: The Hague Academy of International Law

subject: The Hague Academy of International Law
summary: Tobias Asser used part of his Nobel Peace Prize money to fund a summer school for international law. A century later, lectures are still held in the same rooms beneath the same stained-glass dome.

subject: The Hekatompedon
summary: Before the Parthenon there was another temple on the same spot - the Hekatompedon, the 'hundred-footer' - and almost everything we know about it has been pieced together from scattered fragments and a century of scholarly argument.

story.title: The Henry Ford: Where Edison's Last Breath Shares a Room with Rosa Parks' Bus

subject: The Henry Ford
summary: America's largest indoor-outdoor museum complex holds the chair Lincoln was shot in, the bus Rosa Parks refused to leave, Thomas Edison's last breath sealed in a test tube, and nearly one hundred historic buildings transported whole from across the country.

subject: The Hermitage (Nashville, Tennessee)
summary: Andrew Jackson's plantation east of Nashville -- the fourth-most-visited presidential home in America -- preserves not just the mansion of the seventh president but the layered stories of the enslaved people who built and sustained it for four decades.

subject: The History of Mexico (mural)
summary: Diego Rivera spent six years painting an entire nation's story across three walls of the National Palace stairwell - a mural so large that some panels measure 70 meters wide, turning conquest, revolution, and utopian dreams into pigment that still provokes arguments nearly a century later.

story.title: The Hungarian Who Planted California's Dreams

subject: The Hungarian Who Planted California's Dreams
summary: Founded in 1857 by a Hungarian aristocrat who fled revolution, Buena Vista Winery survives as one of California's oldest wineries, its hand-dug caves and press house still standing on the original Sonoma grounds.

subject: The Jabberwock
summary: A Berkeley coffeehouse that lived only six years but incubated the Free Speech Movement's soundtrack and hatched Country Joe and the Fish.

subject: The KEE to Bala
summary: A lakeside dance hall in Muskoka cottage country that has been reinventing itself since 1930, passing through the eras of big bands, rock and roll, and corporate concerts without ever losing its wooden-floored charm.

subject: The Kelpies
summary: Two 30-metre steel horse heads at the eastern gateway of the Forth and Clyde Canal, completed by Andy Scott in 2013 - among Scotland's largest and most photographed sculptures.

story.title: The Kensington Runestone: Minnesota's Viking Hoax

subject: The Kensington Runestone
summary: The 200-pound slab covered with runic inscriptions that a Swedish immigrant found in 1898 - claiming Vikings reached Minnesota in 1362, supported by true believers, debunked by linguists, and still displayed in a museum that really wants it to be real.

subject: The Last Stop West
summary: Oakland's Western Pacific Depot was the final stop of the original California Zephyr -- a grand Mission Revival terminal that outlived its railroad, became Oakland's first designated landmark, and reinvented itself as a restaurant while the tracks it once served vanished beneath new streets.

subject: The Leadmill
summary: Forty-five years of British music history pressed into one old flour mill in Sheffield - and the final song, on the final night in June 2025, was Frank Sinatra singing 'My Way'.

subject: The Leonardo
summary: At 234 metres, the Leonardo is the tallest building in South Africa, a glass spire over the richest square mile on the continent.

subject: The Lizard
summary: A peninsula whose name has nothing to do with lizards, whose rock came from the floor of an ancient ocean, and where Marconi first proved a radio signal could cross the Atlantic.

subject: The Mall Athens
summary: Greece's first modern shopping mall rose on land meant to house Olympic journalists, becoming both a retail landmark and one of the country's most notorious construction scandals.

story.title: The Maze: The Last Wilderness in the Lower 48

subject: The Maze
summary: The Utah canyon system so remote that rescue may be impossible - where 30 miles of dirt road lead to the trailhead, where canyons within canyons confuse all navigation, and where the isolation that Edward Abbey celebrated remains as complete as anywhere in the contiguous United States.

subject: The Mengo Crisis
summary: In May 1966, soldiers stormed the palace of the Kabaka of Buganda on Mengo Hill - and the king escaped over the wall in a rainstorm, into exile and into legend.

subject: The Meux Home
summary: A Confederate surgeon's Victorian mansion survived more than a century in Fresno without alteration, its gas-lit fixtures and conical turret preserving a vanished era of Central Valley ambition.

subject: The Mills, Hong Kong
summary: A Tsuen Wan textile factory that produced 30 million pounds of cotton yarn annually at its peak, then reinvented itself as a cultural and innovation hub while deliberately preserving the green oil stains and iron-frame windows that remember what it was.

subject: The Model, Sligo
summary: A Victorian schoolhouse on The Mall in Sligo now holds Ireland's most important Jack Yeats collection - begun when one Sligo librarian borrowed five paintings for a summer school in 1959.

story.title: The Moon of Pejeng: A Fallen Wheel from the Chariot of the Sky

subject: The Moon of Pejeng
summary: The largest single-cast bronze kettle drum in the world sits in a Balinese temple, where villagers have guarded it for over two thousand years -- ever since, legend says, a thief's sacrilege silenced its glow.

subject: The Murray, Hong Kong
summary: A 27-storey government office block completed in 1969 on Cotton Tree Drive in Central — once the tallest government building in Hong Kong — was auctioned, converted, and reopened in 2018 as a luxury hotel whose distinctive sun-shielding window design earned an energy efficiency award a quarter-century before the renovation.

subject: The Naze
summary: An eroding Essex headland topped by an 18th-century brick tower, the Naze loses about two metres of cliff a year to the North Sea while drawing migrating birds and erosion-curious schoolchildren in equal numbers.

story.title: The Northern Lights: The Sky Show That Vikings Thought Was Bridge to the Gods

subject: The Northern Lights
summary: Where solar particles collide with Earth's atmosphere to create dancing curtains of green, purple, and red light - a phenomenon that has inspired myths from the Vikings' Bifröst bridge to modern Instagram pilgrimages to Iceland.

subject: The Nunnery, Douglas
summary: A medieval Manx priory turned Gothic Revival mansion turned university campus, with a Scottish king once asleep within its walls.

subject: The Old Adobe
summary: Napa's oldest building -- an 1845 adobe house built by a Californio soldier whose children grew up speaking the Patwin language -- survived neglect, bad renovations, and an earthquake to become a Mexican restaurant.

subject: The Old Vic
summary: A 1,000-seat producing theatre at Waterloo opened in 1818, transformed by Lilian Baylis into the cradle of English Shakespearean acting, and the temporary home of the National Theatre until 1976.

story.title: The Only Home She Ever Owned

subject: The Only Home She Ever Owned
summary: At 248 Mill Street in Grass Valley stands a replica of the cottage where Lola Montez -- Irish-born dancer, countess, mistress of a king, and one of the most scandalous women of the nineteenth century -- briefly tried to live a quiet life.

story.title: The Paris of Java's Finest Promenade

subject: The Paris of Java's Finest Promenade
summary: A narrow carriage path built to reach a Dutch coffee warehouse became colonial Indonesia's most glamorous shopping street, earning Bandung the nickname Parijs van Java and leaving behind one of Southeast Asia's finest collections of Art Deco architecture.

subject: The Pilgrimage That Drowned
summary: For centuries, Balinese pilgrims waded through mangroves and sailed colorful outrigger boats to reach this island temple - until a bridge and land reclamation erased the sea crossing forever.

story.title: The Pirate Who Claimed California for England

subject: The Pirate Who Claimed California for England
summary: In 1579, Sir Francis Drake landed at Point Reyes and claimed the entire Pacific coast north of Mexico for Queen Elizabeth I -- a bold act of geopolitical theater that shaped English expansion across North America for centuries.

subject: The Printworks (Manchester)
summary: Once Europe's largest newspaper printing house, now Manchester's neon-lit entertainment complex - reborn from rubble after the 1996 IRA bombing.

story.title: The Red Shop That Outlived Its Owners

subject: The Red Shop That Outlived Its Owners
summary: Built in 1730 along Jakarta's main canal, Toko Merah has served as a merchant's mansion, a governor's family residence, a colonial bank, and a state enterprise office - three centuries of ownership changes painted in a single persistent shade of red.

story.title: The Rice Goddess and the Dutchmen with Strings

subject: The Rice Goddess and the Dutchmen with Strings
summary: A 15th-century Balinese temple dedicated to the rice goddess Dewi Sri, Pura Beji Sangsit is a masterwork of northern Balinese stone carving where every surface erupts with botanical detail and where colonial-era sculptors hid two Dutch musicians among the sacred guardians.

story.title: The Riverboat That Refused to Die

subject: The Riverboat That Refused to Die
summary: A paddle steamer born in a Scottish shipyard, pressed into wartime service, sunk in San Francisco Bay, and resurrected as a floating hotel on Sacramento's waterfront.

subject: The Rivonia Trial
summary: In a Pretoria courtroom in 1964, Nelson Mandela told the apartheid state he was prepared to die - and helped found a democracy from the dock.

subject: The Rockpile
summary: A solitary limestone pinnacle rising 790 feet from a Vietnamese river valley, The Rockpile was one of the most dramatic — and strategically vital — outposts of the American war along the DMZ, a fortress that could only be reached by helicopter and could see all the way to the South China Sea.

subject: The Roosevelt New Orleans
summary: A New Orleans landmark since 1893, this hotel has survived fire, hurricanes, and identity crises -- hosting Huey Long's secret headquarters, giving birth to the Sazerac Bar, and inspiring a bestselling novel along the way.

subject: The Royal Cache
summary: A hidden tomb in the Deir el-Bahari cliffs where ancient priests secretly reburied dozens of looted pharaohs, kept secret again for a decade by a family quietly selling antiquities until 1881.

story.title: The Scribble Den Where America Learned to Love Its Wilderness

subject: The Scribble Den Where America Learned to Love Its Wilderness
summary: The Martinez mansion where John Muir wrote the words that launched the American conservation movement, surrounded by the orchards and oak woodlands he tended between expeditions.

subject: The Second City
summary: The comedy theater on Wells Street that turned improvisation into an art form and launched the careers of John Belushi, Bill Murray, Tina Fey, and generations of performers who reshaped American comedy.

subject: The Shard
summary: The tallest building in Western Europe, sketched by Renzo Piano on the back of a restaurant menu and built from 11,000 panes of angled glass to look like a spire emerging from the Thames.

subject: The Ship That Wasn't There
summary: Built in secret inside a floating barge, the Sea Shadow was the U.S. Navy's Cold War experiment in making warships invisible to radar -- a ship so classified it only moved at night.

subject: The Sign He Was Carrying
summary: On May 12, 1998, Indonesian soldiers opened fire on students at Trisakti University in Jakarta, killing four unarmed demonstrators and igniting the uprising that ended Suharto's 31-year rule.

subject: The Six-Year-Old Next Door
summary: At 238 Mill Street in Grass Valley, a boarding house for Cornish miners produced one of America's greatest entertainers -- a girl who learned to dance from the most scandalous woman in California.

subject: The Speewah
summary: Australia's mythical outback station where the frying pan requires a motorbike to cross and the legendary Crooked Mick could kick crocodiles to the moon, the Speewah is the tall tale that mapped the national character.

subject: The Strand, Townsville
summary: Townsville's 2.2-kilometre beachfront promenade - rock pool, century-old figs, stinger nets, and a glowing sculpture that reads the temperature of the reef.

subject: The Submarine in the City
summary: A Cold War submarine built from captured German blueprints now sits landlocked in downtown Surabaya, a monument to Indonesia's earliest years of naval ambition.

subject: The Tech Interactive
summary: A mango-and-azure science museum born from Silicon Valley's conscience, where visitors build robots, solve climate puzzles, and discover that the valley's real innovation has always been people.

subject: The Venetian Macao
summary: Built on reclaimed land in Macau's Cotai Strip, The Venetian Macao is simultaneously the world's largest casino and Asia's largest single-structure hotel — a 39-story monument to spectacle that opened in 2007 and has never stopped demanding attention.

subject: The View from The Shard
summary: The highest public viewing platform in London, 800 feet above the Thames at the top of Western Europe's tallest building, where on a clear day you can see 40 miles in every direction.

story.title: The Village at the Cliff's Edge

subject: The Village at the Cliff's Edge
summary: Kampung Naga, a Sundanese hamlet of 113 buildings tucked into a river valley in West Java, has preserved its ancestral way of life for centuries by following a strict code of taboos that governs everything from house construction to the refusal of electricity.

subject: Theodor-Fliedner-Gymnasium
summary: A Düsseldorf high school descended from a deaconess training institute - and one of the largest Protestant schools in modern Germany.

subject: Theodoros Kolokotronis
summary: The bronze figure of Theodoros Kolokotronis on horseback outside Athens's Old Parliament is the face of the Greek War of Independence — a mountain bandit turned commander-in-chief who broke an Ottoman army, survived imprisonment by his own government, and died as a national hero.

subject: Third Council of Constantinople
summary: In a domed hall inside Constantinople's imperial palace in 680–681, bishops from across Christendom settled a century-old debate about the nature of Christ — and one desperate priest tried to prove his case by raising a corpse.

subject: Third and Townsend Depot
summary: For most of the 20th century, the Third and Townsend Depot served as San Francisco's main train station, the northern terminus of Southern Pacific's Peninsula Commute line.

story.title: Thirteen Weeks on the Parade Deck

subject: Thirteen Weeks on the Parade Deck
summary: The building that greets new arrivals at the Marine Corps Recruit Depot in San Diego was designed to impress — to signal, from the first moment, that this is a place that takes itself seriously.

subject: Tholos of Delphi
summary: The most photographed building at Delphi, a circular Doric temple in the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, with three columns reerected in 1938 against the cliffs of Mount Parnassus.

subject: Thomas Edison Birthplace
summary: The small brick house in Milan, Ohio where America's most prolific inventor was born in 1847 - preserved as a museum filled with original Edison family artifacts and early incandescent bulbs from the man who lit the world.

subject: Thomas Mooney
