summary: Convicted of the 1916 Preparedness Day Bombing on falsified evidence, labor activist Thomas Mooney spent 22 years in prison before a governor finally pardoned him.

subject: Thomastown, County Kilkenny
summary: Founded by an Anglo-Norman mercenary from Wales at a strategic River Nore crossing, Thomastown gave its name to a Texan empresario and a philosopher who became the namesake of a Californian university.

subject: Thorpeness
summary: Glencairn Stuart Ogilvie's private fantasy resort from 1910, where a water tower was clad in wood to look like a five-storey house perched in the sky and a boating lake was laid out from J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan.

subject: Thotlakonda
summary: A 2,000-year-old Buddhist monastery on a coastal hilltop near Visakhapatnam, discovered by accident during a Navy aerial survey, where Roman coins and ancient cisterns reveal a forgotten waypoint on the maritime Silk Road.

subject: Three Days Inside Mako Brimob
summary: In May 2018, convicted terrorists seized a prison block at Indonesia's elite Mobile Brigade headquarters in Depok, killing five police officers and triggering a three-day standoff that exposed the dangers of housing extremist inmates together.

story.title: Three Sharp Peaks of Hong Kong

subject: Three Sharp Peaks of Hong Kong
summary: Castle Peak, Sharp Peak, and High Junk Peak form Hong Kong's unofficial mountaineering benchmark — three summits scattered across the territory that serious hikers chase as a collective rite of passage.

subject: Thurles
summary: Birthplace of the Gaelic Athletic Association and spiritual home of Munster hurling, where a single hotel room changed the shape of Irish sport.

subject: Tiananmen
summary: The Gate of Heavenly Peace has been burned, rebuilt, secretly reconstructed, and hung with the portraits of revolutionaries and dictators, yet its vermilion facade remains China's most recognizable national symbol.

subject: Tibet (1912–1951)
summary: The four decades when Tibet functioned as a de facto independent state, building its own army, issuing its own stamps, and navigating the collapse of the Qing dynasty before annexation by the People's Republic of China.

subject: Tightwad Hill
summary: A dirt pile left over from the 1923 construction of Cal's Memorial Stadium became the most beloved freeloader's perch in college football, complete with its own cannon, its own governors, and a legal battle to preserve the right to watch without paying.

story.title: Tikal: The Lost Maya City That Rose Above the Jungle

subject: Tikal
summary: Where a Maya metropolis of 100,000 people built pyramid-temples that still pierce the jungle canopy - abandoned around 900 AD and not rediscovered until 1848, when explorers heard howler monkeys screaming from the ruins.

subject: Tiled Kiosk
summary: Built in 1472 by Mehmed II as a pleasure pavilion on the edge of Topkapı Palace, the Tiled Kiosk is Istanbul's oldest surviving non-religious Ottoman structure — a dazzling fusion of Central Asian, Persian, and Byzantine decorative traditions.

subject: Tillamook Rock Light
summary: A deactivated lighthouse perched on a tiny basalt rock 1.2 miles off the Oregon coast, so battered by storms that keepers called it Terrible Tilly -- and so remote it later became a repository for cremated remains.

subject: Timeline of Cologne
summary: Two thousand years on the Rhine: aqueducts in the year 80, Hanseatic trade in 1201, four hundred years of unfinished cathedral, and a million-person rebuild after 1945.

subject: Tinença de Benifassà
summary: A cluster of seven small mountain villages around a medieval monastery, once a self-governing comarca, now a quiet, protected wilderness of forest, honey, and slowly emptying stone hamlets.

story.title: Tirta Empul: Where the God Struck the Earth

subject: Tirta Empul
summary: A thousand-year-old Balinese temple built around a spring that legend says was created by a god's staff, where pilgrims still line up under thirty sacred spouts to wash away what the visible world cannot reach.

story.title: Tirta Gangga: A King Who Built Heaven in Water

subject: Tirta Gangga
summary: A Balinese king built a water palace so beautiful that he worked in the mud alongside his laborers to finish it -- then a volcano destroyed it, and the people rebuilt it stone by stone.

subject: Tiryns
summary: A Mycenaean citadel of walls so massive the ancient Greeks could only explain them by attributing their construction to Cyclopes — the legendary birthplace of Heracles, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and one of the most formidable Bronze Age fortresses in the ancient world.

subject: Titanic Belfast
summary: Standing 126 feet tall -- the exact height of Titanic's hull -- this angular museum of 3,000 aluminium shards sits on the very slipway where the ship was built, and has drawn over 800,000 visitors a year to become Northern Ireland's most visited attraction.

story.title: Titanic Wreck Site: Where the Unsinkable Ship Rests

subject: Titanic Wreck Site
summary: Where the 'unsinkable' ship lies split in two on the Atlantic seabed, 12,500 feet down, a monument to hubris and tragedy that took 73 years to find.

subject: TivoliVredenburg
summary: Five concert halls stacked into a single building in Utrecht, each tuned to a different genre - an acoustic experiment that almost broke its own budget.

subject: Tjaskers in Friesland
summary: Imagine a windmill that fits in the corner of a meadow — four sails, an Archimedes screw, a single tilted post. Thirteen of them still turn in Friesland, the smallest functional drainage windmills in the world.

subject: Tobacco Road
summary: Four universities, twenty-five miles, twelve men's basketball national titles. Why one stretch of central North Carolina became college sport's most concentrated rivalry.

story.title: Toki Messe: The Tallest Building on the Sea of Japan

subject: Toki Messe
summary: Named for the crested ibis that symbolizes Niigata Prefecture, this 140-meter convention tower rises at the mouth of the Shinano River where it meets the Sea of Japan, offering free panoramic views from its 31st-floor observatory that stretch to Sado Island on clear days.

story.title: Tokiwa-so: The Apartment That Invented Modern Manga

subject: Tokiwa-sō
summary: A cramped, bathless wooden apartment building in Toshima, Tokyo, where Osamu Tezuka, Fujiko Fujio, Shotaro Ishinomori, and a generation of young artists lived side by side in the 1950s, inventing the collaborative manga production system still used in Japan today -- now rebuilt as a museum complete with replica mold.

subject: Tokyo Big Sight
summary: Japan's largest convention center sits on the Tokyo Bay waterfront with a Conference Tower made of four inverted pyramids sheathed in glass and titanium, a building so architecturally bizarre that it has become one of Tokyo's most recognizable silhouettes.

subject: Tokyo DisneySea
summary: The world's most acclaimed theme park -- born from a failed California waterfront concept, built for 335 billion yen on Tokyo Bay's reclaimed shoreline, and organized not around a fairy-tale castle but around a smoldering volcano and eight nautical 'ports of call.'

story.title: Tokyo Second Army Arsenal: From Gunpowder to Physics

subject: Tokyo Second Army Arsenal
summary: A Belgian grinding wheel purchased by a shogunate engineer in 1865 still stands as a monument at the site of Japan's first explosives factory -- a place that evolved from feudal lord's estate to Imperial Army arsenal to physics research campus to protected National Historic Site.

subject: Tollund Man
summary: A face from the fifth century BC, so calm and so intact that the men who dug him out of a Jutland bog in 1950 called the police instead of the museum.

subject: Tomogashima
summary: A cluster of four uninhabited islands in the Kitan Strait where crumbling Meiji-era gun batteries, swallowed by subtropical vegetation, have earned comparisons to the floating ruins of a Studio Ghibli film.

subject: Toombeola
summary: Once a Dominican abbey, then a martyred friar's last desperate swim across the Owenmore River, now eighteen people in a Connemara townland with the abbey ruins still standing.

subject: Torcello
summary: The nearly deserted island where Venice was born -- once home to perhaps 20,000 people, now inhabited by just ten, its Byzantine cathedral still standing among the marshes.

subject: Toren van Goedereede
summary: A 39.5-meter brick tower that began as a parish church, served three and a half centuries as one of the oldest lighthouses in the Netherlands, and now plays a 50-bell carillon over the polders.

subject: Torentje van Drienerlo
summary: On a quiet pond at the University of Twente, the top of a church spire pokes above the water - a 1979 artwork by a Fluxus prankster who once carpeted a gallery floor in peanut butter.

subject: Toringkerk
summary: A church in Paarl whose 1875 founding is inseparable from the birth of the Afrikaans language movement, its tower a monument to the congregation that sheltered the Society of Real Afrikaners.

subject: Torre Monumental
summary: A British gift to Argentina that lost its name to a war, Buenos Aires' English clock tower keeps Westminster time over the port it has watched for more than a century.

subject: Torre dels Escipions
summary: A Roman funerary tower outside Tarragona carries the name of the Scipio brothers, though the mourning figures carved on it are really a Phrygian god, and the men it honors remain unknown.

subject: Tossal dels Tres Reis
summary: A 1,350-metre limestone summit where the borders of three medieval kingdoms once met, marked by a simple cairn and remembered in a legend of three kings who climbed it to survey their lands.

subject: Touat
summary: A 160-kilometer chain of Saharan oases in central Algeria, Touat turned a waterless desert into a green ribbon of date palms through the foggara, an ancient gravity-fed water tunnel, and stood for centuries as a crossroads of trans-Saharan trade, faith, and tragedy.

subject: Tour Paradis
summary: The tallest building in Wallonia rises 136 meters over Liège like an upended iron - a tax office that won an architecture fight, then arrived just in time for everyone to start working from home.

subject: Tout Quarry
summary: A working stone quarry until 1982, now a sculpture park where Antony Gormley's Still Falling tumbles forever down a rock face on the Isle of Portland.

subject: Toyokawa Inari
summary: A Buddhist temple with a Shinto torii gate at its entrance, Toyokawa Inari embodies centuries of religious fusion where fox spirits, demon goddesses, and the promise of worldly prosperity weave together into one of Japan's most fascinating sacred sites.

subject: Trader Vic's
summary: A one-legged bartender borrowed five hundred dollars in 1934 to open a small bar in Oakland, then built it into the tiki restaurant empire that spawned the Mai Tai, inspired Trader Joe's, and put a werewolf in a Warren Zevon song.

subject: Traigh Mhor
summary: The only airport runway in the world washed twice a day by the tide, and the cockle bed that feeds it, on the north end of Barra in the Outer Hebrides.

subject: Transbay Tube
summary: Born from an eccentric emperor's 1872 proclamation, the Transbay Tube became one of the most audacious feats of underwater engineering in American history -- a 3.6-mile rail tunnel assembled in 57 sections and sunk to the bottom of San Francisco Bay.

subject: Transport
summary: Victor 'Transport' Maghakian, the son of Armenian immigrants, fought wounded through seven Pacific campaigns, earned the Navy Cross and over two dozen decorations, and returned to Fresno so broken that he was sixty percent disabled -- but not before raising the flag on Tinian.

subject: Tree of Knowledge
summary: The ghost gum outside Barcaldine's railway station where striking shearers gathered in 1891, poisoned by an unknown hand in 2006, and now preserved inside a soaring timber memorial.

subject: Trefignath
summary: A Neolithic burial chamber on a low rocky knoll on Holy Island - built and rebuilt over 1,500 years, with three successive tombs preserved under one long cairn.

subject: Trelleborg (Slagelse)
summary: A motocross club wanted to race on the ramparts. The excavation that followed uncovered the best-preserved Viking ring fortress in Denmark - and gave an entire class of monuments its name.

subject: Tren a las Nubes
summary: The Train to the Clouds climbs to 4,220 meters across the Andes of northwest Argentina, crossing the soaring La Polvorilla viaduct on one of the highest railways on Earth.

subject: Trerice
summary: An Elizabethan manor where Cornish swallows still grace the heraldry, and a twenty-foot oak refectory table waits in a room it can never leave.

subject: Tresco Priory
summary: A thousand-year-old Benedictine monastery whose ruins now stand among subtropical flowers in the Tresco Abbey Gardens.

subject: Tresco, Isles of Scilly
summary: A car-free privately leased island where medieval priory ruins, Tudor castles, and a subtropical garden share two square miles of granite and dune at the western edge of England.

subject: Trieste II (Bathyscaphe)
summary: The U.S. Navy's deep submergence vehicle that located the wreck of USS Thresher, recovered a spy satellite capsule from 16,000 feet below the Pacific, and now rests as a museum ship in Keyport, Washington.

subject: Trindade, Goiás
summary: The site of the world's only basilica dedicated to God the Father, founded on an 1840 clay medallion found in a farmer's field, where every July 230 ox carts and a million pilgrims form one of Brazil's largest religious festivals.

subject: Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius
summary: Russia's most important monastery, founded in 1337 by St. Sergius of Radonezh, has survived Tatar raids, Polish sieges, Soviet closure, and nearly seven centuries of Russian history.

subject: Trinity plantation
summary: A colonial Jamaican sugar plantation where over 1,000 enslaved people labored, a mile-long aqueduct fed the refinery, and a 1760 rebellion revealed the limits of control in Bayly's Vale.

subject: Triple Crossing
summary: One of only two places in North America where three railroad lines cross at different levels at the same point, Richmond's Triple Crossing is a century-old engineering marvel built layer by layer as rival railroads competed for dominance along the James River.

subject: Troldkirken
summary: A 50-metre Neolithic long dolmen outside Sønderholm, ringed by 47 standing stones, that the locals explained as the work of trolls with poor aim.

subject: Trolleybuses in Valparaíso
summary: Valparaíso's electric trolleybuses, running since 1952, included the oldest such vehicles still in daily service anywhere on Earth, and Chile declared them a national monument.

subject: Trudelturm
summary: A twenty-metre tower at Adlershof where the wind blows straight up, built in the 1930s so that model aircraft could be made to spin indoors and filmed doing it.

subject: Trumpington Bed Burial
summary: In 2011, archaeologists excavating a future housing development on the edge of Cambridge unearthed something extraordinary: a teenage girl from seventh-century Germany, buried on a wooden bed, wearing a gold and garnet cross that could only have belonged to someone close to royalty.

subject: Tränenpalast
summary: A glass pavilion at Friedrichstrasse station processed westbound crossings out of East Berlin for twenty-seven years, and Berliners named it for what happened on the pavement outside.

subject: Tsang Tai Uk
summary: Begun in 1847 by a Hakka granite merchant who wanted a fortress his clan could live in, Tsang Tai Uk is one of Hong Kong's best-preserved walled villages — a rectangular stronghold that outlasted the empire that made it necessary.

subject: Tsarskoye Selo
summary: Twenty-four kilometers south of Saint Petersburg, the Romanov summer estate of Tsarskoye Selo holds the Catherine Palace, the Alexander Palace, and the long shadow of an empire's end.

subject: Tsing Lung Tau
summary: A quiet coastal enclave on the southwest New Territories shore where a Tin Hau temple predating 1889 still stands, and a stretch of Dragon Beach was reclaimed for a road widening in 2006.

subject: Tsing Yi
summary: An island named after a fish, once the site of nudist beaches and stilt-house fishing villages, Tsing Yi has been so completely remade by reclamation, tunnels, bridges, and industrial development that it now serves as a critical infrastructure hub for one of the world's busiest ports — while its granite hills remain stubbornly green.

subject: Tsitongambarika
summary: The last great low-altitude rainforest in southern Madagascar, a ridge of ridges north of Fort-Dauphin where species new to science still turn up and where the forest and the people who depend on it are running out of time.

subject: Tsukiji Hongan-ji
summary: A Japanese Buddhist temple that looks like it belongs in India -- designed by an architect obsessed with tracing Buddhism back to its roots, rebuilt in reinforced concrete after the 1923 earthquake leveled its wooden predecessor.

subject: Tsukuba Space Center
summary: Japan's nerve center for space operations, where a 50-meter H-II rocket greets visitors at the gate and mission controllers guide the Kibo laboratory module orbiting 400 kilometers overhead.

story.title: Tsurugaoka Hachimangu: Where Shinto and Shogunate Collide

subject: Tsurugaoka Hachimangū
summary: Kamakura's most important Shinto shrine began as a warrior clan's prayer for divine favor in 1063, survived an assassination that ended a dynasty, lost half its buildings to a government decree separating Buddhism from Shinto, and watched its legendary ginkgo tree topple in 2010 after nearly a thousand years.

subject: Tswaing crater
summary: A meteorite the size of a house slammed into the African bushveld 220,000 years ago, gouging a crater whose salty lake humans have visited for a thousand centuries.

subject: Tu Hwnt i'r Bont
summary: A fifteenth-century stone farmhouse turned courthouse turned tearoom, smothered in Boston ivy beside the bridge across the Conwy at Llanrwst.

subject: Tuborg Bottle
summary: A 26-metre beer bottle on the Copenhagen coast road, built in 1888 as an advertisement, fitted with a water-powered lift, and still standing long after the brewery behind it moved away.

subject: Tucuruí transmission line
summary: To put the Amazon's northern cities on Brazil's power grid, engineers strung four cables across 2,148 metres of open river between two steel towers nearly as tall as the Eiffel Tower - and then ran into a problem no tower could solve.

subject: Tulbagh
summary: Earthquake-shattered in 1969 and painstakingly rebuilt, Tulbagh's Church Street now holds the largest concentration of National Monuments on a single street in South Africa -- 32 buildings that survived by being reconstructed.

subject: Tulum
summary: Where Maya temples meet Caribbean waves - the only major ruins built directly on the sea, now surrounded by wellness retreats, cenote swimming, and the Riviera Maya's most photogenic beach.

subject: Tumubao
summary: The ship-shaped fortress where a Ming emperor was captured by Mongol cavalry in 1449, changing the course of Chinese military history.

subject: Tung Chung Battery
summary: Built in 1817 to guard a Lantau bay from pirates, this Qing-era artillery battery now faces Hong Kong International Airport instead of open water — a monument caught between two eras.

subject: Tung Lung Chau
summary: A small uninhabited island off the Clear Water Bay Peninsula where a Qing-era fortress, Hong Kong's largest prehistoric rock carving, and some of the territory's best sport climbing share the same two square kilometres.

subject: Tunis
summary: Where Tunisia's capital bridges African and Mediterranean worlds, where Carthage's ruins remember Punic glory, where the Arab Spring began and complicated democracy continues.

subject: Tuolumne Grove
summary: A small grove of giant sequoias near Crane Flat in Yosemite, home to the first tunnel tree ever carved - a burned-out giant through which stagecoaches once passed.

subject: Tupã, São Paulo
summary: Named for a thunder god and founded on ground cleared by a violent frontier, Tupã holds Brazil's great museum of Kaingang memory, a century-old Latvian colony, and the country's biggest peanut harvest.

subject: Turkmenistan
summary: One of the most isolated nations on Earth, Turkmenistan is a land of white marble cities, ancient Silk Road ruins, a desert crater that has burned for over fifty years, and a cult of personality that makes even seasoned travelers do a double take.

story.title: Moton Field: Where They Fought Two Wars

subject: Tuskegee Airmen National Historic Site
summary: The Alabama airfield where African-American pilots trained during WWII, fighting fascism abroad and racism at home, now preserved as a National Historic Site.

subject: Tuy Hòa
summary: Cradled between the sea and two sentinel mountains — one of them crowned with a Champa tower — Tuy Hòa has been a crossroads of Central Vietnam for centuries, recently reorganized by national reform but rooted in its own distinct identity.

subject: Ty Newydd
summary: The last house of David Lloyd George -- the Welsh radical who led Britain through the Great War -- is now where Wales sends its writers to learn their craft. He died in the library in 1945. Forty-five years later, the words began.

subject: Tyndall National Institute
summary: Inside a converted Cork brewery on the River Lee, more than six hundred researchers from fifty-two nations chase the physics of light and the limits of the very small.

subject: Tyntesfield
summary: A Victorian Gothic Revival country house built on guano, rescued from auction by the National Trust in 2002, and now home to ten species of British bat.

subject: Tyrolean Terrace Colony
summary: Eight Swiss-style chalets perched on the cliffs above La Jolla's sea caves from 1911 to 1975 — possibly the unlikely origin point of the American motor hotel.

subject: Tân Cảnh Base Camp
summary: The fall of Tân Cảnh in April 1972 — T-54 tanks at the gate, a command structure shattered by anti-tank missiles, and John Paul Vann landing under fire — was the moment the PAVN opened the road to Kon Tum.

subject: Tân Ấp station
summary: A small stop on Vietnam's north–south line that was once meant to be the gateway to Laos — and where, for a while, freight bound for the border finished its journey hanging from a cable.

subject: Tō-ji
summary: One of only three Buddhist temples permitted in Japan's new capital in 796, Tō-ji endured fire, earthquake, and centuries of political upheaval to become a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its 55-meter pagoda still the tallest wooden tower in Japan.

subject: Tō-no-Hetsuri
summary: A 200-meter wall of tower-shaped cliffs carved from 28-million-year-old rock by a river with the patience to sculpt stone into pagodas.

subject: Tōdai-ji
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage temple in Nara housing the world's largest bronze Buddha, built by an emperor who mobilized 2.6 million people and nearly bankrupted 8th-century Japan in the process.

subject: Tōfuku-ji
summary: One of Kyoto's five great Zen temples, Tofuku-ji holds Japan's oldest temple gate, gardens by modernist master Mirei Shigemori, and a 700-year-old shipwreck mystery linking it to the shores of Korea.

subject: Tōkei-ji
summary: For over 600 years, women fleeing abusive marriages ran to this Kamakura nunnery where three years of religious service earned them legal freedom -- a right so powerful that the temple's couriers did not have to bow before passing feudal lords.

subject: Tōshōdai-ji
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage temple in Nara founded by a blind Chinese monk who failed five times to cross the sea before finally bringing formal Buddhist precepts to Japan.

subject: UCCA Center for Contemporary Art
summary: Inside a former Cold War munitions factory designed by East German Bauhaus successors, Beijing's leading contemporary art institution navigates the space between creative freedom and political reality in one of the world's most censored countries.

subject: UH88
summary: The telescope that proved Mauna Kea could host world-class astronomy, the University of Hawaii's 88-inch reflector was the mountain's first major instrument and one of the first professional telescopes controlled by a computer.

subject: Ubud
summary: Where Bali's cultural heart beats in rice terraces and temple ceremonies, where Elizabeth Gilbert found herself, where yoga studios multiply beside ancient traditions.

subject: Ucheldre Centre
summary: A Holyhead arts centre housed in a 1936 convent chapel saved from demolition by local volunteers - now exhibiting Kyffin Williams and showing films under its Romanesque arches.

subject: Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves
summary: Two hills on the outskirts of Bhubaneswar hold 33 rock-cut caves carved for Jain monks in the 1st century BCE - among them a tiger whose mouth is a doorway, a queen's double-storied palace, and an inscription that remains the single most important historical document of ancient Kalinga.

story.title: Ueno Toshogu: The Golden Shrine That Survived Everything

subject: Ueno Tōshō-gū
summary: A gold-leaf Shinto shrine built in 1627 to honor Japan's most powerful shogun has survived civil war, earthquakes, firebombings, and nearly four centuries of Tokyo's relentless reinvention -- all without being rebuilt.

subject: Ulmarra
summary: A whole 19th-century river port frozen in time on the Clarence - National Trust-classified in its entirety, where antique shops fill old butter factories and a 1906 pub leans out over the water.

subject: Ulupō Heiau State Historic Site
summary: A massive stone platform on the edge of Kawai Nui Marsh in Kailua, Ulupo Heiau is an ancient Hawaiian temple whose walls rise thirty feet high, built with stones transported from miles away, and whose origins are attributed in legend to the menehune.

subject: Underground works
summary: From Cold War bunkers to medieval catacombs, Japan's flood cathedrals to Coober Pedy's dugout homes, humanity has been building downward for millennia -- and these subterranean spaces are now a growing category of travel.

subject: Union Buildings
summary: Herbert Baker's sandstone seat of South African government crowns the highest hill in Pretoria, and its amphitheatre is where Nelson Mandela was sworn in as the country's first democratically elected president.

story.title: Union Station Toronto: The Cathedral of Canadian Rail

subject: Union Station (Toronto)
summary: Where the Prince of Wales once quipped 'you build your train stations like we build our cathedrals' - Toronto's Union Station has served as Canada's busiest transportation hub since 1927, moving 72 million passengers a year through a Great Hall of Tennessee marble and Missouri stone.

subject: United Indians of All Tribes
summary: A foundation born from the 1970 occupation of Fort Lawton that secured 20 acres in Seattle's Discovery Park, built the Daybreak Star Cultural Center, and now serves one of the most diverse urban Native American communities in the country.

story.title: United States Army Border Air Patrol

subject: United States Army Border Air Patrol
summary: After World War I, the Army deployed 67 aircraft and nearly 600 personnel to patrol the US-Mexico border against Pancho Villa's threat — and two pilots who got lost over Baja California survived 17 days in the desert only to be murdered by fishermen before rescue arrived.

story.title: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops

subject: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
summary: Founded in 1917 to support Catholic chaplains during World War I, the conference of American bishops became, a century later, the institution that had to confront one of the largest clergy abuse scandals in the church's history and pay roughly four billion dollars in settlements.

story.title: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit

subject: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
summary: The largest and most frequently reversed federal appellate court in the nation, the Ninth Circuit covers nine western states and two Pacific territories from its headquarters in San Francisco.

story.title: United States National Radio Quiet Zone

subject: United States National Radio Quiet Zone
summary: A 13,000-square-mile federal zone across three states where radio transmissions are restricted to protect a giant radio telescope and a Navy intelligence station - and where, as of late 2024, Starlink finally works almost everywhere.

subject: Unité d'Habitation of Berlin
summary: Le Corbusier designed this seventeen-storey concrete block above the Grunewald, lost an argument with Berlin's building authorities over twenty-four centimetres, and struck the finished building from his own catalogue of works.

subject: Universal Esperanto Association
summary: On a quiet street in Rotterdam, a building serves as the world capital of a language nobody was born speaking and everybody could, in theory, learn.

subject: Universidad del Rosario (Colombia)
summary: Colombia's oldest university, founded in 1653 in colonial Bogotá, whose graduates include at least 28 presidents and whose cloister is printed on the 200-peso banknote.

subject: Unkervatnet
summary: A deep, nine-kilometre lake in Hattfjelldal fished through the ice in winter and open water in summer, sitting on one of the few roads that cross the mountains into Sweden.

subject: Unterburg trolleybus turntable
summary: In a narrow river valley below a medieval castle in Solingen sits a steel disc that spent fifty years rotating trolleybuses end-for-end — the last surviving turntable of its kind anywhere in the world.

subject: Uppsala
summary: Sweden's ancient spiritual and intellectual capital, where pagan temples gave way to a Gothic cathedral, Viking kings to university scholars, and centuries of history line the banks of the Fyris River.

subject: Uronarti
summary: A triangular Egyptian fortress still stands on a Nubian island in the Nile, its mud brick walls conforming to ancient rock nearly 4,000 years after they were raised.

subject: Ushiku Daibutsu
summary: A 120-meter bronze Buddha rising from the rice paddies of Ibaraki Prefecture -- three times the height of the Statue of Liberty and, for 15 years, the tallest statue on Earth.

subject: Usina del Arte
summary: A brick powerhouse disguised as a Florentine palace once fed electricity to Buenos Aires; abandoned and nearly lost, it now fills the same halls with symphonies.

subject: Usina do Gasômetro
summary: A coal-fired power plant that everyone wanted to demolish became the place where Porto Alegre gathers to watch the sun drop into the Guaíba.

subject: Utrecht Archives
summary: A thousand-year-old abbey rebuilt as a courthouse rebuilt as the regional archive - 200 kilometers of records, all stored on the foundations of a medieval monastery.

subject: Utsunoya Pass
summary: The only surviving stretch of the original Heian-period Tokaido highway, a mountain pass where warring generals marched their armies, Heian poets listened for bush warblers, and Japan's first toll tunnel was blasted through solid rock in 1876.

subject: V&A Dundee
summary: Kengo Kuma's first UK building — a cliff-edged museum of 780 tonnes of pre-cast concrete that opened on the Tay in 2018 as Scotland's first design museum.

subject: Valentin submarine pens
summary: A submarine factory on the Weser built in twenty months by forced labourers from across occupied Europe; around 1,600 of them died, and not one U-boat was ever finished inside it.

subject: Valiasr Street
summary: The longest street in the Middle East stretches 18 kilometers through Tehran, rising nearly 500 meters in elevation from the railway station to Tajrish Square -- a boulevard whose plane trees are slowly dying along with a century of history.

subject: Valldemossa Charterhouse
summary: A royal palace turned Carthusian monastery where Chopin spent one bitter, brilliant winter composing his Preludes.

subject: Valle Crucis Episcopal Mission
summary: A short-lived Episcopal monastery in the North Carolina mountains that scandalized 1840s America by practicing confession and ordained one of the first Black ministers from the rural South.

subject: Valmet Automotive
summary: One assembly hall on the Bothnian coast has built Saabs, Talbots, Ladas, Opels, Porsches, Fiskers and Mercedes for other people's badges, and is now building armoured vehicles and buses.

subject: Valtetsi (village)
summary: Perched at 1,050 meters in the mountains west of Tripoli, Valtetsi served as Kolokotronis's headquarters before the siege of Tripolitsa in 1821 — and has been marked by history, hard and glorious, ever since.

subject: Van Harinxmakanaal
summary: A 37.5-kilometer Frisian canal from the North Sea at Harlingen to Leeuwarden — widened and straightened in 1951, kept at sea level by a single seventeenth-century lock, and quietly serving since 2002 as a highway for the returning Eurasian otter.

subject: Vancouver
summary: The 'other Vancouver' where the Hudson's Bay Company established its Pacific Northwest headquarters and the Columbia River separates Washington from Oregon.

subject: Vancouver
summary: Where mountains meet the sea and half the population was born elsewhere, Vancouver ranks among the world's most livable cities while serving as Canada's gateway to Asia.

subject: Vancouver Film Studios
summary: Thirty acres of East Vancouver light industry - a mattress factory, a bakery, an elevator test tower, a Costco parking lot - bought up building by building and turned into the largest studio complex in Canada.

subject: Vaphio
summary: A Mycenaean tholos tomb on the Eurotas riverbank near Sparta yielded two extraordinary gold cups depicting the capture of wild bulls — objects so exquisite that scholars still debate whether they were made in Crete or on the Greek mainland.

subject: Vargas Swamp Lancers
summary: Colombia's largest monument immortalizes fifteen horsemen whose desperate charge through a swamp turned the tide of South American independence.

subject: Varginha
summary: A coffee-trading capital in southern Minas Gerais with a disc-shaped water tower downtown and a legend that still sells tickets thirty years later.

story.title: Varosha: The Ghost Resort of Cyprus

subject: Varosha
summary: Where a luxurious Mediterranean resort was abandoned overnight during the 1974 Turkish invasion of Cyprus and has remained frozen in time behind barbed wire ever since, its hotels crumbling while awaiting a political solution.

subject: Vasaloppet
summary: The world's oldest and largest cross-country ski race traces a fugitive king's legendary escape across 90 kilometers of Swedish wilderness.

subject: Vat Phou
summary: A ruined Khmer-Hindu temple complex in southern Laos that has served as a place of worship since prehistoric times, shaped by empires and sacred geography over two millennia.

subject: Vatersay
summary: The southernmost and westernmost inhabited island of the Outer Hebrides, where the Vatersay Raiders defied an absentee landlady to reclaim crofting land and where the Annie Jane disaster of 1853 still lies buried under a cairn above West Bay.

subject: Vatican Museums
summary: Seventy thousand artworks spanning five millennia, housed in a palace complex where Renaissance popes competed to amass the most spectacular collection on Earth.

subject: Veere
summary: For 258 years, this tiny Walcheren port was Scotland's only Continental Staple - the official, treaty-protected gateway for all Scottish trade with mainland Europe.

subject: Vefsn Municipality
summary: An English timber company, a wartime prison camp, a South Sami name and Norway's warmest northern day all belong to one Nordland valley that has been cut apart and stitched back together for two centuries.

subject: Venezuelan Declaration of Independence
summary: The document that made Venezuela the first Spanish American republic, drafted in a Caracas chapel and voted into existence on July 5, 1811.

subject: Ventspils
summary: A Hanseatic trading port that built ships for colonial expeditions to Africa and the Caribbean, survived plague and war, became the USSR's top crude oil export terminal, and now welcomes visitors with colorful cow sculptures.

subject: Ver-o-Peso
summary: Belem's iconic open-air market on the shores of Guajara Bay, widely called the largest street market in Latin America, with an 1,197-square-meter iron pavilion inaugurated in 1901.

story.title: Versailles: The Palace That Bankrupted France

subject: Versailles
summary: Where Louis XIV built the most extravagant palace in European history to imprison his nobles in ceremony and etiquette - spending so lavishly that it helped trigger the revolution that would destroy the monarchy.

story.title: Victoria: The British Columbia Capital More British Than Britain

subject: Victoria
summary: The island capital cultivating English garden charm - where afternoon tea is served in an Empress hotel, where the parliament buildings glow at night, and where the mild Pacific climate created Canada's retirement destination.

subject: Victoria Rooms
summary: A Greek Revival assembly hall named for a queen on her birthday - Jenny Lind, Dickens, suffragettes, Pink Floyd, and now the University of Bristol's music department.

subject: Vikingskipet
summary: Norway's iconic inverted-hull speed skating arena in Hamar, built for the 1994 Winter Olympics, where Johann Olav Koss won three golds and Dan Jansen finally got his.

subject: Vilanculos
summary: Gateway to the Bazaruto Archipelago, Vilanculos is Mozambique's barefoot-luxury capital of water sports, where dhow sails catch the Indian Ocean wind and black marlin patrol the shallows.

story.title: Village of Columbus and Camp Furlong

subject: Village of Columbus and Camp Furlong
summary: The only place in the continental United States attacked by a foreign army in the 20th century, where Pancho Villa's 1916 raid launched America toward World War I.

story.title: Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania

subject: Villages with fortified churches in Transylvania
summary: Seven Transylvanian villages, selected from over 150 surviving fortified church sites, form a UNESCO World Heritage ensemble that preserves the medieval Saxon and Szekely tradition of turning houses of worship into strongholds against Ottoman and Tatar raids.

subject: Villavicencio
summary: Where the Andes finally end and the Llanos Orientales open into a horizon-to-horizon grassland, Villavicencio is Colombia's gateway to cowboy country.

subject: Vilna Ghetto
summary: The two-year prison that ended six centuries of Jewish Vilna - and the poets, librarians, and partisans who fought to save what they could from the fire.

subject: Vindolanda
summary: A Roman fort where waterlogged soil preserved some of the oldest handwritten documents in Britain -- personal letters, shopping lists, and a birthday invitation from the edge of empire.

subject: Virginia Military Institute
summary: America's oldest state-supported military college, founded in 1839 to guard a Lexington arsenal, shaped by the Civil War and a bloody afternoon at New Market, and still reckoning with what it carries.

subject: Virginia Tech
summary: A land-grant university built around Hokie Stone, the Corps of Cadets, and Ut Prosim - That I May Serve - that has shaped southwestern Virginia since 1872 and that carries the memory of April 16, 2007 in 32 stones on the Drillfield.

subject: Vischpoort
summary: The last surviving gate of Harderwijk's medieval walls, the Vischpoort guarded a Zuiderzee harbor for six centuries and lit ships home for nearly a hundred years.

subject: Visquard
summary: A perfect circle of medieval houses, 450 metres across, with a church at the centre - and a brief uprising of armed villagers against Emden's hungry workers in 1919.

subject: Vlissingen Navy Drydock
summary: An English engineer's 1697 design for the oldest dry dock in the Netherlands, abandoned for nearly a century, then resurrected as Dok van Perry.

subject: Voetboogdoelen, Amsterdam
summary: A 16th-century crossbow guild's banquet hall that gave Amsterdam one of the great peace paintings of the Dutch Golden Age, then was demolished in 1816 and replaced by a church, then a library, on the same spot beside the Singel.

story.title: Plant Vogtle: America's Nuclear Gamble in the Georgia Pines

subject: Vogtle Electric Generating Plant
summary: The largest nuclear power plant in the United States, where a $34 billion construction saga spanning decades, bankruptcies, and redesigns finally brought the first new American reactors online since the Three Mile Island era.

story.title: Von Karman Institute for Fluid Dynamics

subject: Von Karman Institute for Fluid Dynamics
summary: A Cold War handshake between NATO and a Hungarian-born aerodynamicist turned a Belgian airfield laboratory into one of Europe's premier hypersonic research centers.

subject: Vondelkerk
summary: Pierre Cuypers's 1880 octagonal church on the edge of Vondelpark - twice gutted by fire, twice declared worth rebuilding.

subject: Voorst
summary: A scatter of villages along the IJssel between Apeldoorn and Deventer, where Saint Lebuinus built a chapel in 768 and an Encyclopedia man was born in 1817.

subject: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
summary: Founded in 1880 by a Calvinist preacher who became prime minister, funded for decades by 10,000 women going door to door with green collecting boxes, today a major research university whose name still means 'Free.'

subject: Vrouwenhuis
summary: A 17th-century Zwolle house turned women's almshouse, where a will preserved an entire 1700s art collection intact as a time capsule.

subject: Väinö Linna Square
summary: A cotton-mill courtyard in Tampere named for the fitter who worked there and went on to write Finland's most argued-over novel.

subject: Värmland
summary: A Swedish borderland where Nobel laureates, ironmasters, and cross-country ski champions emerged from forests of pine and folklore.

subject: Waag (Alkmaar)
summary: A 14th-century chapel turned weigh-house turned cheese stage, with 47 bells, a clockwork trumpeter, and a Latin motto carved across its Renaissance face.

subject: Wadi Halfa
summary: Once Nubia's great trading gateway between Egypt and Sudan, Wadi Halfa has been a crossroads for pilgrims, steamers, soldiers, and railways - and finally, for a reservoir that swallowed its older self.

subject: Wadi Hayl
summary: A seasonal watercourse in the Hajar Mountains of Fujairah where ancient petroglyphs, an Umm Al Nar tomb, and a 1932 fort mark a wadi that was once a three-hour donkey ride from the coast.

subject: Wageningen
summary: In a Dutch hotel called The World, German generals signed the surrender that ended five years of occupation in the Netherlands.

story.title: Wakamiya Oji: The Sacred Road Built for an Unborn Son

subject: Wakamiya Ōji
summary: Kamakura's main avenue doubles as the sacred approach to its greatest shrine -- a 1.8-kilometer boulevard built in 1182 as a prayer for the safe birth of a shogun's heir, lined with cherry trees on a raised path engineered with forced perspective, and named one of Japan's hundred finest streets.

story.title: Wakura Onsen: Twelve Centuries of Healing Water on Nanao Bay

subject: Wakura Onsen
summary: A 1,200-year-old hot spring resort on the shores of Nanao Bay, Wakura Onsen was discovered -- legend says -- when a fisherman watched an injured heron heal itself in warm seawater, and has drawn travelers to the Noto Peninsula ever since.

subject: Walkway over the Hudson
summary: A railroad bridge that nearly became scrap metal was reborn as the world's longest elevated pedestrian bridge, drawing nearly 600,000 visitors a year to walk 212 feet above the Hudson River.

subject: Walls of Constantinople
summary: For a thousand years, the Theodosian walls — triple-layered, moat-fronted, tower-studded — kept Constantinople alive when every strategic logic said it should have fallen; then, on the morning of 29 May 1453, a postern gate was left open.

subject: Walter Reed Army Medical Center
summary: Named for the Army physician who proved yellow fever was carried by mosquitoes, the rose-brick Georgian Revival hospital on Georgia Avenue treated American soldiers for 102 years - from the Spanish-American War to the Iraq War - before closing in 2011 to merge with the Bethesda naval hospital.

story.title: Walter Reed National Military Medical Center

subject: Walter Reed National Military Medical Center
summary: The hospital where John Kennedy's autopsy was performed, where Reagan was treated for cancer, and where Trump was admitted for COVID - the Bethesda tower whose cornerstone Franklin Roosevelt himself laid on Armistice Day, 1940, is where Presidents have been treated for eighty-five years.

subject: Walter Sully Emporium
summary: Broken Hill's first post office and longest-running shop — a stone emporium from the silver-rush days that now holds the oldest regional art gallery in New South Wales.

subject: Wannsee Conference
summary: On 20 January 1942, fifteen officials met for ninety minutes in a lakeside villa southwest of Berlin to coordinate the murder of Europe's Jews; the villa is now a memorial.

subject: Wapping
summary: Where pirates were hanged in public at Execution Dock, England's first river police force was founded, and Rupert Murdoch's 'Fortress Wapping' triggered one of Britain's defining industrial disputes.

subject: Warangesda Aboriginal Mission
summary: On Wiradjuri country beside the Murrumbidgee, a mission named house of mercy became a place where Aboriginal children were taken from their families, and where the Stolen Generations began.

subject: Warburg Institute
summary: A library rescued from the Nazis in 1933, rebuilt in London, and dedicated to understanding how the ancient world never really ended—how classical images, myths, and ideas kept shaping European culture long after Rome fell.

subject: Warkworth Hermitage
summary: A medieval chapel carved directly into a sandstone cliff above the River Coquet, reached only by boat, with a fourteenth-century altar and a tomb effigy still in place.

subject: Warm Mineral Springs (spring)
summary: Florida's only warm mineral spring -- a 30,000-year-old sinkhole where divers found 10,000-year-old human bones with preserved brain matter, a 360-degree Fountain of Youth mural gathers dust inside a sealed Cyclorama, and the warm sulfurous water still draws bathers today.

subject: Warm Springs Pools
summary: The oldest European-style spa structure in the United States - an octagonal 1761 men's bath house and a 22-sided 1836 ladies' house, fed by a 98-degree mineral spring that has been flowing for as long as anyone has measured.

story.title: Warner Bros. Studio Tour Tokyo: Where an Amusement Park Became a Wizarding World

subject: Warner Bros. Studio Tour Tokyo
summary: Built on the grounds of a beloved 94-year-old amusement park in northwest Tokyo, the world's largest indoor Harry Potter attraction opened in 2023 -- a walk-through journey into filmmaking magic where even the train station got a Hogwarts makeover.

subject: Warsteiner
summary: Germany's largest privately owned brewery, founded in 1753 when a Westphalian farmer named Antonius Cramer paid one thaler and nineteen guilders in tax on the beer he had brewed at home.

subject: Wartburg
summary: A Thuringian ridge-top castle that sheltered a saint, hid Martin Luther while he rewrote the German language, and hosted the bonfire that frightened the German Confederation into censorship.

subject: Washington Marriott Marquis
summary: It took fifteen years of political fights, three mayors, two competing site proposals, a Supreme Court case, eminent domain, and 520 million dollars in public financing to build the 1,175-room headquarters hotel for Washington's convention center.

subject: Washington Place
summary: A Greek Revival palace in Honolulu where a sea captain's widow waited for a husband who never returned, a queen was arrested during the overthrow of her kingdom, and thirteen governors made their home.

subject: Washington, Baltimore and Annapolis Trail
summary: An 11.7-mile rail trail on the bones of an electric commuter railway that ran from 1908 to 1935 - finally united across the Patuxent River by a bridge that took twenty-five years to build.

subject: Washougal
summary: Where the Washougal River meets the Columbia and summer brings motocross, swimming holes, and the gateway to the Gorge's Washington shore.

story.title: Water Tribunal of the plain of Valencia

subject: Water Tribunal of the plain of Valencia
summary: Every Thursday at noon, farmers in black smocks gather at a cathedral doorway in Valencia to settle water disputes by voice alone - a court with no paperwork that may be the oldest in the world.

subject: Waterford Crystal
summary: Founded in 1783 by two Quaker brothers, Waterford Crystal made the chandeliers for Westminster Abbey and the New Year's Eve ball for Times Square -- and almost did not survive the Great Recession.

subject: Waterloo-Tor
summary: Osnabrück's triumphal arch to Waterloo - a memorial nobody calls by its real name.

subject: Waternish
summary: A twelve-kilometre peninsula in Skye's northwest where clan feuds, ancient burial grounds, and Scotland's oldest inn share the same windswept coast.

subject: Watersnoodmuseum
summary: A museum built inside the four concrete caissons that finally plugged the last broken dyke in 1953 — and that now hold the names of every person the flood took.

subject: Waugoshance Light
summary: The first lighthouse on the Great Lakes to replace a lightship, Waugoshance Light guarded one of the most treacherous passages in the Straits of Mackinac for six decades before abandonment, Navy bombing practice, and rising waters left it a crumbling ruin that preservation efforts could not save.

subject: Wave Organ
summary: Built from tombstones and PVC pipes on a spit of land at the Marina, this sculpture lets you hear the San Francisco Bay breathe.

subject: Wawona
summary: A tiny community inside Yosemite National Park where Galen Clark built a way station, the Washburn brothers raised a Victorian hotel, and barely a hundred people still live among the meadows and sequoias.

subject: Weardale
summary: The dale that gave the word 'fluorescence' to the English language - a Pennine valley where lead, silver, and ultraviolet-glowing fluorite made fortunes and a chapel of Methodism endures.

subject: Weinhaus Rheingold
summary: Fourteen halls, four thousand seats and its own power station beside Potsdamer Platz — the most lavish restaurant imperial Berlin ever built, and one of the worst investments anybody made there.

subject: Well of Barhout
summary: A 112-meter-deep sinkhole in eastern Yemen that locals call a prison for jinn, unexplored until a team of Omani cavers rappelled to the bottom in 2021 and found waterfalls, cave pearls, and an entire hidden ecosystem.

subject: Wenlock Priory
summary: The Shropshire ruins where Saint Milburga's bones were rediscovered in 1101, and where a Cluniac fountain still survives a thousand years later.

subject: Wereldmuseum Leiden
summary: Europe's first ethnographic museum, founded in 1837 around a German doctor's smuggled Japanese collection - and now slowly sending much of itself back home.

subject: Wesel Station
summary: A railway station built of wood and timber because the Prussian War Ministry insisted it must be possible to dismantle within a single day.

subject: West End
summary: K Street's lobbyists meet Foggy Bottom's universities meet the Kennedys' Watergate scandal - the small slice of Washington that holds the White House, the World Bank, the Kennedy Center, and the densest population of squirrels ever recorded.

subject: West Highland Line
summary: Scotland's 'Iron Road to the Isles,' a railway from Glasgow to Fort William and Mallaig that floats on bog, tunnels through history, and remains a lifeline for communities no road can easily reach.

subject: West Kordofan
summary: A Sudanese state created, abolished, and recreated - West Kordofan's geography of oil, cattle, and ethnic mixing has made it a central theater of both the 2005 peace agreement and the current civil war.

story.title: West Point: The Academy That Trained Both Sides

subject: West Point
summary: The Hudson River fortress where America trains its Army officers - where Grant learned alongside Lee, where Benedict Arnold tried to betray the Revolution, and where 'Duty, Honor, Country' has shaped leaders who fought each other and every enemy since.

subject: West Virginia Hot Dog Festival
summary: Each summer in Huntington, the state's beloved chili-slaw-mustard hot dog gets its own festival - and raises money for the local children's hospital.

subject: West Virginia Ordnance Works
summary: An 8,323-acre World War II TNT plant outside Point Pleasant whose contaminated remains became a Superfund site, a wildlife refuge, an airport, and the supposed home of Mothman.

subject: Wester Suikerraffinaderij
summary: An Amsterdam sugar refinery that processed 150,000 tonnes a year at its peak and laid off its last 250 workers on 1 November 1965, leaving behind a square named Suikerplein.

subject: Westerdijk Institute
summary: In a quiet building in Utrecht's science park lives the largest collection of fungi on Earth — and the legacy of the first woman ever made a full professor in the Netherlands.

subject: Westerkerk
summary: Amsterdam's tallest church tower kept time over Anne Frank's hiding place, and somewhere on the floor below, in an unmarked pauper's grave, lies Rembrandt.

subject: Western Chalukya Empire
summary: A Kannada dynasty that seized power from the Rashtrakutas in 973 CE and ruled the western Deccan for two centuries, leaving behind some of South India's finest temple architecture at their capital of Kalyani, today's Basavakalyan in Karnataka.

story.title: Western District Public Cargo Working Area

subject: Western District Public Cargo Working Area
summary: A working cargo pier on Hong Kong's Sai Wan waterfront that became an unlikely phenomenon: the Instagram Pier, where photographers line up at sunset to photograph reflections so perfect the water looks like a mirror of the sky.

subject: Western Pipe and Steel Company
summary: From pipe manufacturing to building World War II Liberty ships, Western Pipe and Steel helped construct the Grand Coulee Dam and the wartime fleet from its San Francisco Bay shipyard.

subject: Western Qing tombs
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage necropolis 140 km southwest of Beijing where four Qing emperors rest -- founded by a ruler who may have refused to be buried near the father he allegedly betrayed.

subject: Westin St. Francis
summary: Surviving the 1906 earthquake, hosting presidents, and witnessing the Fatty Arbuckle scandal, the St. Francis Hotel has anchored Union Square since 1904.

subject: Wewelsburg
summary: A Renaissance castle in Westphalia that Heinrich Himmler leased for one Reichsmark a year and rebuilt with concentration camp labour - and around which a great deal of postwar mythology has been invented.

subject: Wheal Coates
summary: A ruined engine house clings to the Cornish cliff at St Agnes, where 140 tin miners once worked shafts that ran six hundred feet down and out under the Atlantic.

subject: Where Brunei Met the World
summary: For centuries, Brunei's fortunes arrived and departed through a single wharf on the Brunei River -- a gateway that hosted Spanish invaders, floating markets, royal pilgrimages, and a queen before the modern world rendered it obsolete.

subject: Where Vineyards Became a Canvas
summary: A Yale-educated journalist turned Napa Valley grape grower spent half a century collecting Bay Area art, then traded his vineyards for a 217-acre sculpture park that nearly lost its collection to a controversial deaccessioning plan.

story.title: Where a Sultan Was Crowned and a Constitution Was Born

subject: Where a Sultan Was Crowned and a Constitution Was Born
summary: A modest white building on Jalan James Pearce witnessed two of the most consequential moments in Brunei's modern history: the crowning of its 28th Sultan and the signing of its first constitution.

subject: Where the Linens Became Legends
summary: A stone building that once cleaned clothes with French steam now serves nine-course meals that have shaped American fine dining -- and the journey between those two identities tells the story of Napa Valley itself.

subject: White Dacha
summary: The white, asymmetrical house Anton Chekhov built above Yalta in the last years of his life, where he planted a garden, kept tame cranes, and wrote some of his greatest work.

subject: White Grass Ski Touring Center
summary: A defunct downhill ski area turned into one of America's steepest and oldest cross-country touring centers, on a high Allegheny valley that holds snow for half the year.

subject: White Horse Stone
summary: A solitary sarsen stone above the River Medway in Kent that absorbed the folklore of a destroyed sibling, became the centrepiece of an Anglo-Saxon battle legend, and is now both a scheduled monument and a contested site of modern Pagan ritual.

subject: White Shoal Light (Michigan)
summary: The only barber-pole-striped lighthouse in the United States, White Shoal Light has guarded a treacherous Lake Michigan shoal since 1910 and become so iconic that it graces Michigan's 'Save Our Lights' license plate.

subject: Whitefish Point Light
summary: The oldest operating lighthouse on Lake Superior stands sentinel over the Graveyard of the Great Lakes, where the Edmund Fitzgerald and countless other vessels met their end.

subject: Whithorn
summary: The royal burgh where Saint Ninian built Scotland's first recorded Christian church around 397 CE, and where a 1926-born poet and a Standard Oil co-founder also count as natives.

subject: Whithorn Priory
summary: The Premonstratensian cathedral that became Scotland's wealthiest see, drew kings and queens on pilgrimage, and ended with its last Catholic prior in prison for saying Mass.

subject: Wick
summary: A herring port at the far northeast corner of Scotland, where Norse names cling to the cliffs and the world's shortest street pretends to be a building.

subject: Wijnsermolen, Wyns
summary: When the miller Sierksma retired in 1967, the Wijnsermolen had no replacement — so two members of the local water board's polder committee climbed in and ran the mill themselves, by hand, for the next eight years.

subject: Wilcannia Athenaeum
summary: A grand sandstone temple of learning, raised in a frontier river port that believed it was destined for greatness.

subject: Wilhelm Gustav Friedrich Wardenburg
summary: A pastor's son who fought for Austria, then Russia, then his own tiny duchy, came home to build Oldenburg's army from nothing, and left his collected artefacts to the museum that still has them.

subject: Willem de Kooning Academy
summary: The Rotterdam art school that produced one of America's greatest abstract expressionists waited until he was dead a year before putting his name on the door.

subject: William Creek
summary: A pub, an airstrip, and a permanent population of six, marooned at the heart of the world's largest cattle station.

subject: William Head Institution
summary: A headland southwest of Victoria that held quarantined immigrants for 75 years, hid tens of thousands of Chinese labourers during the First World War, and is now a prison with a public theatre season.

subject: Willkomm-Höft
summary: At a bend in the Lower Elbe, every ship large enough gets its flag dipped and its national anthem played - a courtesy performed since 1952 by a restaurant and five volunteer captains.

subject: Willow Run
summary: The Michigan factory where Henry Ford's assembly line genius was turned to war, producing one B-24 Liberator bomber every 63 minutes at the peak of World War II production.

subject: Wilpena Pound
summary: A vast natural amphitheatre of folded mountains in the Flinders Ranges, sacred to the Adnyamathanha as Ikara, where two creation serpents lie in the rock.

subject: Wilshire Grand Center
summary: The tallest building in the United States west of Chicago, completed in 2017 with a concrete foundation pour that set a world record and a rooftop bar floating 73 stories above downtown Los Angeles.

subject: Wimbledon Common
summary: Eleven hundred acres of London heathland holding an Iron Age hill fort, a windmill where Baden-Powell wrote Scouting for Boys, and Thomas Cromwell's birthplace.

subject: Windlust, Burum
summary: On Easter Sunday 2012, six teenagers burned down a 255-year-old Dutch windmill. Two years later, Burum rebuilt it from the ground up.

story.title: Windmills in the Isle of Man

subject: Windmills in the Isle of Man
summary: A handful of stumps, a converted tower with a glass roof, and a building set in a tree - what remains of an island industry the wind quietly took back.

subject: Window of the World
summary: A 48-hectare theme park in Shenzhen where 130 of the world's most famous monuments stand together — the Eiffel Tower, the Pyramids, Machu Picchu, and dozens more — drawing over 3 million visitors a year.

subject: Windows on the World
summary: The legendary restaurant atop the World Trade Center's North Tower, where New York itself was the main course - until September 11, 2001.

story.title: Windsor Station: The Fortress That Outlived Its Railroad

subject: Windsor Station (Montreal)
summary: Bruce Price's Romanesque Revival masterpiece served as the Canadian Pacific Railway's headquarters for over a century, survived a plan to replace it with a 60-storey tower designed by the architects of the World Trade Center, and endures today as a National Historic Site -- severed from the rail network by the Bell Centre hockey arena.

subject: Wing Lung Wai
summary: Founded by the Tang Clan in the 1400s and walled against bandits during the Qing dynasty, Wing Lung Wai in Kam Tin is one of Hong Kong's quietly enduring fortified villages — its gate once moved for feng shui, its moat long filled, its ancestral hall still standing.

subject: Winterland Ballroom
summary: An ice rink turned rock cathedral, the Winterland hosted The Last Waltz, the Sex Pistols' final concert, and a Grateful Dead closing night that lasted until dawn -- before apartments replaced it all.

subject: Woerden
summary: A Roman fort sat where the cheese market now runs, and the layers between them tell the story of the Low Countries.

subject: Wonderhouse
summary: A dying man's defiant masterpiece in central Florida - an 18-room concrete mansion stuffed with secret gadgets, rainbow prisms, rooftop bathtubs, and enough ingenuity to get its builder arrested as a suspected spy.

subject: Wooden churches of Maramureș
summary: Nearly a hundred timber churches with impossibly tall spires rise from the valleys of northern Romania -- built because the authorities forbade the Orthodox faithful from building in stone.

subject: Woodhenge
summary: Discovered from the air in 1926, Woodhenge is a Neolithic timber circle within the Stonehenge World Heritage Site whose wooden posts may have represented the realm of the living, complementing Stonehenge's stone domain of the dead.

story.title: Woodrow Wilson Boyhood Home (Columbia, South Carolina)

subject: Woodrow Wilson Boyhood Home (Columbia, South Carolina)
summary: The only house Woodrow Wilson's parents ever owned, now reinterpreted as the Museum of the Reconstruction Era - one of the few in the country dedicated to that period.

subject: Woodside Store
summary: A Gold Rush-era general store that doubled as a post office, bank, saloon, and dentist's office, run by the same man for 55 years -- and supposedly still haunted by his dog.

subject: Woodspring Priory
summary: An Augustinian priory in North Somerset where canons drained salt marshes, sold their property to escape Henry VIII, and left behind a 13th-century church now rented out as holiday accommodation.

subject: Woolwich Common
summary: A grazing common turned mortar testing ground turned nuclear weapons laboratory turned dog-walking park, fronted by the longest building façade in London.

subject: Woolwich Dockyard
summary: The Mother Dock of all England, where Henry VIII's Great Harry was launched, Darwin's Beagle was built, and 800 men drowned with the Royal George - now a stretch of preserved slipways and a fight over an apartment block.

subject: Worksop Priory
summary: An Augustinian priory founded in 1103 whose nave survived the dissolution to become Worksop's parish church, home to a 13th-century Lady Chapel, an early medieval bestiary now in New York, and a coronation duty that still binds the parish to the British monarch.

subject: World Clock (Alexanderplatz)
summary: A state that would not let its citizens leave built a ten-metre monument to every time zone on Earth — and left twenty cities off it for political reasons.

story.title: Wormsloe: Georgia's Oldest Plantation and the Oak-Lined Road That Guards Its Secrets

subject: Wormsloe Historic Site
summary: On the Isle of Hope southeast of Savannah, over 400 live oaks form a mile-and-a-half cathedral of Spanish moss leading to the tabby ruins of Noble Jones's 1739 fortified house -- the oldest standing structure in Savannah and the seed from which colonial Georgia grew.

story.title: Worshipful Company of Stationers and Newspaper Makers

subject: Worshipful Company of Stationers and Newspaper Makers
summary: The London guild that invented the word copyright, controlled what England read for 150 years, and still meets in a Grade I hall behind St Paul's.

subject: Wulai Hot Spring
summary: At the confluence of two mountain rivers in Atayal territory south of Taipei, the Wulai Hot Spring rises clear and scalding from the Xueshan Range — water the Atayal have known and named for far longer than any resort has stood beside it.

subject: Wushantou Reservoir
summary: Built between 1920 and 1930 under engineer Yoichi Hatta, the Wushantou Reservoir transformed the parched Chianan Plain into Taiwan's rice bowl — and remains the world's sole surviving dam built with the semi-hydraulic fill technique.

subject: Xiluo
summary: A Yunlin township whose name traces back to the indigenous Babuza people, famous for its long bridge over the Zhuoshui River and its role as Taiwan's vegetable heartland.

subject: Xinhuamen
summary: Once a pavilion built for moonlit reflections on an imperial lake, Xinhua Gate was transformed into the symbolic entrance to Chinese state power.

subject: Xiyang Lou
summary: The ruins of European baroque palaces built by Jesuit missionaries for the Qianlong Emperor, the Xiyang Lou are the most visible remnants of the Old Summer Palace and a haunting symbol of cultural collision.

subject: Xueshan Range
summary: Taiwan's Snow Mountain Range packs 54 peaks above 3,000 meters into northern Taiwan, crowned by Xueshan at 3,886 m — a landscape of razor ridges, alpine meadows, and a mountain road tunnel that transformed island life.

subject: X̱á:ytem
summary: A boulder above the Fraser at Hatzic is, in Stó:lō account, three leaders turned to stone - and when archaeologists dug beneath it in 1990 they found a house floor five thousand years old.

subject: Yad Vashem
summary: Israel's official Holocaust memorial, where a concrete prism cut into a Jerusalem hillside holds the names, stories, and fragments of six million lives.

story.title: Yakushi-ji: The Temple That Moved With an Empire

subject: Yakushi-ji
summary: Commissioned in 680 as a prayer for healing, this UNESCO World Heritage temple in Nara has been dismantled, relocated, burned, and rebuilt across thirteen centuries -- yet its sole surviving original structure, the East Pagoda, still stands as one of the finest examples of Nara-period architecture in Japan.

subject: Yalta
summary: A Black Sea resort of pebble beaches, cliffside follies, and czarist palaces, where emperors once convalesced, three Allied leaders once redrew a map, and mass tourism still fills the promenade each summer.

subject: Yalta Conference
summary: For eight days in February 1945, three exhausted leaders gathered in a seaside palace and redrew the map of a continent, shaping the world that would follow the deadliest war in history.

story.title: Yamadera: A Thousand Steps Into Silence

subject: Yama-dera
summary: A Buddhist temple clinging to a forested mountainside in Yamagata where over a thousand stone steps lead pilgrims past a flame that has burned since the ninth century, and where Matsuo Basho heard cicadas sinking into rock.

subject: Yamashina Mido
summary: A fortified Buddhist temple that doubled as a castle, Yamashina Hongan-ji was the stronghold of warrior monks who defied samurai rule until its fiery destruction in 1532.

subject: Yanmen Pass
summary: First of the Nine Passes under Heaven, Yanmen Pass controlled the gateway between central China and the Eurasian Steppe for over two millennia -- a choke point where armies clashed from the Han dynasty through World War II.

subject: Yau Ma Tei Police Station
summary: A 1922 Kowloon police station that closed in 2016 after nearly a century of service, leaving behind a semi-circular portico, a permanently locked side gate rumored to bring misfortune, and a small shrine in the compound to appease the spirits of the flyover next door.

subject: Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem
summary: A pub carved into the sandstone below Nottingham Castle, claiming a 1189 origin and a piece of Britain's longest-running argument about which inn is the oldest.

subject: Yellow Mama
summary: Built by a British inmate serving 60 years for theft, painted with leftover highway-line paint, and stored in a prison attic since 2002, Alabama's electric chair carried out its grim work for 75 years under a nickname no one planned.

subject: Yeni-Kale
summary: An Ottoman fortress designed to lock the Kerch Strait against the Russian navy, betrayed in the end by its single unsolvable weakness: it had no water of its own.

subject: Yenidze
summary: Dresden forbade anything that looked like a factory near its baroque centre, so a cigarette manufacturer built his chimney as a minaret and put a stained-glass dome on the roof.

subject: Yim Tin Tsai (Sai Kung District)
summary: A 24-hectare Hakka island in Port Shelter, Sai Kung, where the only salt pans in Hong Kong were revived after decades of abandonment alongside an 1890 Italian Romanesque chapel that earned two UNESCO heritage awards.

subject: Yinxu
summary: The ruins of the last Shang dynasty capital near Anyang hold 150,000 oracle bones -- the earliest known Chinese writing -- and rewrote the timeline of Chinese civilization when rediscovered in 1899.

subject: Yirrkala
summary: The small Yolngu community on the Gove Peninsula whose 1963 bark petitions to Federal Parliament launched the modern Australian land-rights movement, and whose artists, musicians and teachers carry Yolngu law forward to the world.

subject: Ynys Llanddwyn
summary: A tidal island off Anglesey's southwest coast where a 5th-century Welsh saint of lovers, a slim white lighthouse, and rocks 600 million years old all share the same windswept stretch of sand.

subject: Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation
summary: A Patwin tribe that transformed 185 acres in the California Coast Range from a nearly dissolved rancheria into a self-sustaining nation with a casino resort, olive groves, and vineyards.

story.title: Yokohama Archives of History: Where Japan Met the World

subject: Yokohama Archives of History
summary: Housed in the former British Consulate building near the spot where Commodore Perry signed the Convention of Kanagawa in 1854, the Yokohama Archives of History preserves the diplomatic papers, newspapers, and personal accounts of Japan's dramatic opening to the West.

subject: Yolo Causeway
summary: The I-80 bridge that carries 100,000 daily commuters over a floodplain, shelters a quarter-million bats, and lends its name to a college football trophy made from its own concrete.

subject: Yoshi's
summary: A Japanese restaurant in Berkeley that stumbled into becoming one of the West Coast's most important jazz clubs, launching live albums and hosting legends from Oscar Peterson to Esperanza Spalding.

subject: Yoshimi Hundred Caves
summary: A hillside riddled with 219 ancient burial caves in Saitama Prefecture that sparked one of Japan's first great archaeological debates and later became an improvised wartime aircraft factory.

subject: Yoshizaki-gobō
summary: The ruins of a 15th-century Buddhist temple in Fukui Prefecture where an exiled monk launched a religious revolution that toppled feudal lords.

subject: Young Vic
summary: A theatre built from a former butcher's shop and a wartime bombsite, originally meant to last five years, that became one of London's most adventurous stages.

subject: Ypey Mole, Ryptsjerk
summary: Built in 1858, set on fire by children in November 1970, saved by the local fire brigade, moved across Friesland in 1981, and still pumping water — Ypey Mole has survived almost everything a Dutch windmill can be asked to survive.

subject: Ysbyty Ifan
summary: Two hundred residents, one medieval bridge over the Afon Conwy, and a name that translates as 'John's Hospital' - a Knights Hospitaller refuge for pilgrims since the late medieval period.

subject: Yser Towers
summary: A peace monument dynamited in revenge, rebuilt in defiance, and still stirring controversy nearly a century later.

subject: Yuen Yuen Institute
summary: A rare temple complex in Tsuen Wan that holds Taoism, Buddhism, and Confucianism under one roof — and under a replica of Beijing's Temple of Heaven.

subject: Yuli
summary: Yuli is a quiet farming township at the center of Taiwan's East Rift Valley, flanked by mountains on two sides and known for a historic indigenous trail, local noodles, and the gateway to Yushan National Park.

subject: Yung Kee
summary: The Central Hong Kong restaurant that in 1968 became the only Chinese entry in Fortune magazine's Top 15 Restaurants in the World — built on roast goose, wartime survival, and a founder who started at a street stall.

subject: Yungaba Immigration Centre
summary: For more than a century, the first Australian roof over a new arrival's head at Kangaroo Point was a building whose name means "place of sunshine."

subject: Yungang Grottoes
summary: One of China's three great Buddhist cave temple complexes, where 51,000 Buddha statues carved into sandstone cliffs in the 5th century represent the fusion of Central Asian and Chinese artistic traditions.

subject: Yushan Weather Station
summary: Perched atop Yushan's Northern Peak at 3,858 meters, the Yushan weather station is the highest building in Taiwan and the highest weather station in Northeast Asia — a place where meteorologists have monitored the island's most extreme conditions since 1943, and where, in 2021, station workers built a secret cafe from recycled crates.

subject: Yushima Seidō
summary: A Confucian temple in Tokyo's Bunkyo ward that served as the intellectual engine of the Tokugawa shogunate, housing Japan's most important academy and spawning the institutions that would become the University of Tokyo, the Tokyo National Museum, and the National Diet Library.

subject: Yushima Tenmangū
summary: A 1,500-year-old Shinto shrine in Tokyo where students still come to pray for exam success, hanging thousands of wooden wish tablets beneath plum trees that bloom just as university results arrive.

subject: Yūshūkan
summary: Japan's oldest military museum, housed within the grounds of the controversial Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, displays a Zero fighter, a locomotive from the Death Railway, and letters from kamikaze pilots -- while presenting an account of World War II that has drawn sharp international criticism for historical revisionism.

subject: Zaculeu
summary: A Maya fortress-capital in the western Guatemalan highlands whose name means 'white earth' -- where the last Mam king surrendered to the Spanish after a siege so brutal that survivors were found eating the dead.

subject: Zavora
summary: A Mozambican beach where a 1910 lighthouse still flashes every ten seconds, a pipefish species exists nowhere else on Earth, and the wreck trail of a German pocket battleship's raiding sortie lies just offshore.

subject: Zeppelin Mooring Mast, Recife
summary: A nineteen-metre steel stub in a Recife park is the last zeppelin mooring tower left standing anywhere, and for eight years it was the point where transatlantic air travel first touched the Americas.

subject: Zhengding County
summary: An ancient religious capital of northern China where four pagodas from different dynasties still punctuate the skyline, and where the founding temple of Rinzai Zen Buddhism draws Japanese pilgrims a thousand years after its establishment.

subject: Zhunan
summary: Zhunan is a coastal township on Taiwan's northwest shore where a sea goddess temple anchors a community that has always looked both inland toward the mountains and outward toward the water.

subject: Zhuoying Spring
summary: An artesian karst spring in the heart of Jinan whose waters have been used as a public swimming pool, a battlefield wash station, and a royal palace garden.

subject: Zuid, Antwerp
summary: The Spanish demolished their fortress in 1874 and a Haussmann-inspired grid rose in its place. They called it Le Petit Paris, then watched it decline for thirty years - until galleries, museums, and a new Palace of Justice gave the Zuid back its swagger.

subject: Zuiderhofje
summary: A 1640 almshouse in Haarlem founded by a Mennonite widow who built her charity to outlast every schism, every shunning, and every meddling church board for nearly four centuries.

subject: Zuiderkerk
summary: The first church in Amsterdam built from scratch for Protestant worship - Hendrick de Keyser's 1611 Renaissance spire, painted by Monet, mourned by Rembrandt, and turned into a morgue during the hunger winter of 1944.

subject: Zuidpoldermolen, Edam
summary: A thatched octagonal windmill on the edge of Edam, built in the 1620s to pump a drowned landscape dry - and to remind anyone who looks at it that this part of the Netherlands is engineered, not given.

subject: Zuigan-ji
summary: A Zen temple whose founding legend collapses under archaeological evidence, whose conversion from one Buddhist sect to another required armed force, and whose rebuilding by a one-eyed warlord may have concealed a hidden fortress.

story.title: Zuiryuji: Toyama's Zen Masterpiece in Copper and Cypress

subject: Zuiryū-ji (Toyama)
summary: Built over twenty years to honor a fallen lord, Zuiryuji temple in Takaoka is the only National Treasure in Toyama Prefecture -- a perfectly symmetrical Zen compound where copper-roofed halls, a painting by Sesshu, and 300 meters of covered corridors preserve the ambitions of the Maeda clan.

subject: Zwaanendael Colony
summary: A piece of tin changed American history. In 1631, a Dutch colony of 28 settlers built a palisaded fort near present-day Lewes, Delaware, naming it Zwaanendael -- 'swan valley' -- only to be destroyed within a year over a misunderstanding about a stolen coat of arms.

subject: Zwinger (Dresden)
summary: Augustus the Strong's late-baroque pleasure palace in Dresden, built for orange trees and royal weddings, bombed nearly to dust in 1945, and patiently put back together stone by stone.

subject: Zzyzx, California
