summary: A place name invented in 1944 to be the last word in the English language, attached to a fraudulent health resort on federal land, which was eventually evicted and replaced by legitimate science — but the name, absurd as it is, has stuck.

story.title: Zojoji: The Shoguns' Temple in Tokyo Tower's Shadow

subject: Zōjō-ji
summary: A 600-year-old Pure Land Buddhist temple in central Tokyo where six Tokugawa shoguns are buried, standing in quiet defiance beside the steel lattice of Tokyo Tower.

subject: c-base
summary: Berlin's television tower is not a television tower. It is the antenna of a space station that crashed here 4.5 billion years ago, and the people digging it out have been at it since 1995.

subject: Ålum Runestones
summary: Four Viking Age memorials stand at Ålum church, and one of them carries a line about grief that a thousand years has not dulled.

subject: Çeşme
summary: A Genoese castle, hot springs bubbling up through the sea, and beaches at the very tip of Turkey, ten kilometers from Greece: the peninsula resort of Çeşme.

subject: Çiçek Pasajı
summary: The Flower Passage off İstiklal Avenue has been a theatre, an Ottoman banker's showpiece, and a refuge for impoverished Russian nobles — each reinvention leaving its mark on the most atmospheric arcade in Istanbul.

subject: Église Notre-Dame de Calais
summary: The only church in France built in the English Perpendicular style, where a young Charles de Gaulle married Yvonne Vendroux in 1921.

subject: Đình Lạc Giao
summary: Eleven lowland households built a communal house on the basalt plateau in 1928, and it has been a shrine, a massacre memorial and a seat of government ever since.

subject: Ōkunoshima
summary: A small island in Japan's Inland Sea known today as 'Rabbit Island' for its hundreds of free-roaming rabbits, but hiding a dark secret as the former site of a clandestine chemical weapons factory that produced over six kilotons of poison gas.

subject: Ōminesan-ji
summary: A 7th-century mountain temple perched near the summit of Sanjōgatake, where Shugendō ascetic monks still lean over cliff edges on ropes and climb chains bolted into rock faces -- all in pursuit of spiritual awakening.

story.title: Ono-ji: The Cliff Face That Watches the River

subject: Ōno-ji
summary: A Buddhist temple in the mountains of Nara Prefecture guards one of Japan's most remarkable magaibutsu -- a 13.8-meter Miroku Bosatsu carved into a riverside cliff face in 1207 by a stonemason from Song China, witnessed at its consecration by a cloistered emperor.

subject: Ōsaki Hachimangū
summary: A National Treasure shrine built by Date Masamune in 1607, where Kyoto's finest craftsmen created one of the oldest surviving examples of gongen-zukuri architecture.

subject: Ōta Tenjinyama Kofun
summary: The largest keyhole-shaped burial mound in eastern Japan, this 210-meter tumulus in Gunma Prefecture has guarded the mystery of an unknown 5th-century ruler for over 1,500 years -- a ruler whose stone sarcophagus links the remote Kanto plains to the powerful Yamato kingdom hundreds of miles to the west.

story.title: Otori Taisha: Where the White Heron Landed

subject: Ōtori taisha
summary: An ancient Shinto shrine in Sakai, Osaka, marks the legendary spot where the spirit of the folk hero Yamato Takeru -- transformed into a white heron -- made its final landing before ascending to heaven.

subject: ʻImiloa Astronomy Center
summary: A place where Polynesian wayfinding and modern telescope science share the same sky, housed under three titanium cones that mirror the volcanoes of Hawaii Island.

story.title: After the Fire, the Collection Grew

subject: After the Fire, the Collection Grew
summary: On February 22, 1978, someone set fire to the building that housed the San Diego Aerospace Museum.

story.title: Alcatraz: The Rock That Held America's Worst (And Some Who Weren't)

subject: Alcatraz
summary: The San Francisco Bay island prison that held Al Capone and the Birdman - where escape was officially impossible though three men may have proven otherwise, where Native Americans occupied the island for 19 months, and where 1.4 million tourists now visit what was once the nation's most feared penitentiary.

subject: Amgueddfa Cymru
summary: Wales's national museum service runs seven sites, attracts nearly two million visitors a year, charges no admission anywhere, and contains the first open-air museum in the United Kingdom.

subject: Arson and a Second Act
summary: The Old Globe Theatre in Balboa Park was built in 1935 as a temporary structure for a world's fair, and it was so obviously worth keeping that when the fair ended, San Diego kept it.

subject: Banging on the Ballroom Door
summary: Three activists stormed a closed-door legislative meeting at Jakarta's Fairmont Hotel to protest a military law revision they feared would return Indonesia's armed forces to their authoritarian-era dual role in civilian life.

subject: Blood on the Foundation Stones
summary: The first Dutch fort in the Banda Islands was built on Portuguese ruins, over Bandanese resistance, and its construction cost an admiral his life.

story.title: Bombay Beach: The Salton Sea's Post-Apocalyptic Resort

subject: Bombay Beach
summary: The California beach town that died when its sea turned toxic - where the Riviera of the desert became a landscape of abandoned trailers, dead fish, and art installations that celebrate rather than mourn the decay.

subject: Built on Ashes
summary: Designed to echo a royal palace that was burned to the ground, Bali's oldest museum preserves the island's art and history inside walls modeled on the very kingdom the Dutch destroyed.

subject: California's First Curtain Call
summary: Before California had a constitution, it had a theater -- a canvas-covered shack on the Sacramento waterfront where Gold Rush miners paid two dollars to forget the mud.

subject: California's Underground Treasury
summary: The only California state park without any land holds over 13,000 minerals and the largest crystalline gold nugget found during the Gold Rush, a collection that traveled from San Francisco's Ferry Building to a county fairground in the Sierra foothills.

story.title: Candi Kidal: The Temple That Inspired a Nation's Emblem

subject: Candi Kidal
summary: A 13th-century Singhasari mortuary temple in East Java whose Garuda reliefs telling a story of a son rescuing his enslaved mother became the philosophical basis for Indonesia's national emblem.

story.title: Canopy of Light: The Manetti Shrem Museum of Art

subject: Canopy of Light
summary: A perforated aluminum canopy inspired by surrounding farm fields shelters the Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis, housing nearly 6,000 works and honoring a faculty that helped define Funk art, conceptual art, and video art in the 1960s and 70s.

subject: Clandestine Churches
summary: Hidden churches built inside houses, warehouses, and barns across the Dutch Republic - the architectural compromise that let Catholics, Lutherans, and Mennonites worship in a Calvinist state.

subject: Crossing the Uncrossable Strait
summary: For decades, the Carquinez Strait was considered unbridgeable -- a deep, wind-raked channel that forced travelers onto ferries or a hundred-mile detour through the Central Valley.

subject: Cube Houses
summary: Piet Blom tilted a house onto its corner and asked people to live inside it, which they have been doing in Rotterdam since 1984.

subject: Cyrus
summary: A Michelin-starred Wine Country restaurant that closed, declared itself finished, and then returned in a former prune-packing plant -- reinvented as a 20-course culinary journey through four dining rooms ending in a hidden dessert chamber with a chocolate waterfall.

story.title: Every Name This Stage Has Known

subject: Every Name This Stage Has Known
summary: A 1911 vaudeville house in Petaluma has reinvented itself through five names and a century of changing entertainment, landing on the National Register while booking everyone from Carlos Santana to Snoop Dogg.

subject: Exposure
summary: On a Dutch dike facing the IJsselmeer, a 26-meter steel man crouches looking at the water - Antony Gormley's largest figure, built from more than 5,000 steel pieces and 14,000 bolts.

subject: Faces in the Glass
summary: A community gift that became Yuba City's memory vault, the Sutter County Museum preserves everything from Nisenan artifacts to rescued glass plate negatives that nearly vanished when a building came down.

subject: Fat and Thin
summary: A bronze tableau on a Taganrog side street freezes the exact moment a friendship curdles into cringing deference, straight from a Chekhov short story.

subject: Forty Acres of Memory
summary: California's Capitol is both a working seat of government and an open-air museum where a Moon Tree grows beside Civil War saplings and 155 memorials chronicle a state's turbulent, layered history.

story.title: Four Corners: The Only Place in America Where Four States Meet

subject: Four Corners
summary: The quadripoint where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah touch - a surveying decision from 1868 that created America's only four-state intersection and a tourist trap where visitors pay to stand in four places at once.

story.title: From Churchill's Shadow to the Sultan's Gold

subject: From Churchill's Shadow to the Sultan's Gold
summary: Brunei's Royal Regalia Museum began life as the world's only memorial to Winston Churchill, commissioned by an admiring sultan -- before being transformed into a gleaming showcase of monarchical splendor.

subject: From Residency to Memory
summary: A 1938 colonial residence in Kuala Belait that once housed British administrators now preserves the cultural heritage and oil industry history of Brunei's most resource-rich district.

story.title: Galen's Hospice: The Cabin That Kept Watch Over the Giants

subject: Galen's Hospice
summary: A small log cabin in Yosemite's Mariposa Grove, rebuilt three times on the same spot since 1864, that traces the arc from frontier shelter to conservation landmark.

story.title: Gold from the Sky Over Gold Country

subject: Gold from the Sky Over Gold Country
summary: In April 2012, a minivan-sized asteroid entered Earth's atmosphere at record speed and scattered fragments of some of the oldest material in the solar system across the same California foothills where the Gold Rush began.

subject: Island of a Thousand Temples
summary: Bali's puras are open-air Hindu temples built in three sacred zones, arranged along axes from mountain summit to sea, forming a spiritual architecture that maps the entire island into a cosmos of stone, offerings, and ritual.

story.title: Jalesveva Jayamahe: Surabaya's Sentinel of the Sea

subject: Jalesveva Jayamahe
summary: A 60-meter bronze naval officer stands guard over Surabaya's waterfront, sword drawn, gaze fixed on the Java Sea -- Indonesia's declaration in steel and stone that its glory lies on the water.

story.title: Karnak: The Temple Built by 30 Pharaohs Over 2,000 Years

subject: Karnak
summary: Where every pharaoh for 2,000 years added to a single temple complex, creating the largest religious building ever constructed - 200 acres of pylons, obelisks, and hypostyle halls that dwarfed medieval cathedrals.

story.title: Kertha Gosa: Where Justice Looked Up

subject: Kertha Gosa
summary: Bali's eighteenth-century court of justice is covered in ceiling paintings that depict the torments of hell and the rewards of heaven, a visual sermon that once loomed over every defendant awaiting judgment.

subject: Kgosi Mampuru II Correctional Centre
summary: The Pretoria prison where the apartheid state hanged scores of liberation fighters now bears the name of a Pedi king executed on its gallows in 1883.

subject: Le Papillon
summary: A former Iranian Army officer turned a remodeled coffee shop on a San Jose strip-mall corner into one of the Bay Area's most celebrated French restaurants.

subject: Mamelon
summary: A modest hillock outside Sevastopol so fiercely contested in the Crimean War that its French nickname entered a Gilbert and Sullivan patter song as shorthand for military expertise.

story.title: Montauk: Where Long Island Ends at the Atlantic

subject: Montauk
summary: The New York peninsula where the oldest lighthouse in the state guards the end of the island - where George Washington authorized the beacon in 1792, where the Hamptons glamour gives way to working fishing village, and where land finally surrenders to the ocean that rolls to Europe.

story.title: Mount Rushmore: The Shrine That Scandalized Sacred Land

subject: Mount Rushmore
summary: The South Dakota granite where four presidents' faces gaze across stolen Lakota territory - where dynamite carved a democratic monument on land the treaty of 1868 promised would remain Indigenous forever, and where America's most famous sculpture asks uncomfortable questions about whose faces belong on whose mountains.

story.title: Neon and Nostalgia at the Flamingo

subject: Neon and Nostalgia at the Flamingo
summary: A mid-century modern resort on Highway 12 became Sonoma County's living room -- its neon sign tower still glowing decades after the Golden Deed Ball drew 900 guests in evening wear.

story.title: Nghệ An – Xô Viết Nghệ Tĩnh Museum

subject: Nghệ An
summary: Built on the ground of the colonial prison that held its subject, this Vinh museum keeps the drums, presses and prisoner files of the 1930 peasant uprising that French aircraft bombed from the air.

story.title: Ninety Years at the White Horse

subject: Ninety Years at the White Horse
summary: Opened in 1933 on Telegraph Avenue near the Oakland-Berkeley border, the White Horse Inn has endured police raids, political protests, cultural revolutions, and nine decades of changing times to become one of the oldest continuously operating gay bars in the United States.

story.title: Ninety-Nine Names in Steel and Stone

subject: Ninety-Nine Names in Steel and Stone
summary: Surabaya's Al-Akbar Mosque survived a financial crisis mid-construction to become Indonesia's second-largest mosque, its 99-meter minaret encoding divine names in concrete and altitude.

story.title: Ninety-Nine Names in the Sky Over Samarinda

subject: Ninety-Nine Names in the Sky Over Samarinda
summary: Rising from a former sawmill site on the banks of the Mahakam River, the Samarinda Islamic Center Mosque encodes Islamic numerology into every dimension of its architecture, from its 99-meter tower to its 33-step staircase.

subject: Not a Distant Memory
summary: Tucked beside Sutter's Fort in midtown Sacramento, this small museum insists on a truth that California often forgets: the state's Native peoples are not history -- they are here.

story.title: Olana: The Persian Castle a Painter Built to Frame the Hudson

subject: Olana
summary: The New York hilltop where America's most famous landscape painter built a Persian fantasy castle - designed so every window framed a perfect composition, including the view that made him famous.

story.title: One Billion Barrels of Black Gold

subject: One Billion Barrels of Black Gold
summary: A concrete arch on Seria Beach marks the exact spot where Brunei's oil story began and the moment it reached a staggering milestone -- one billion barrels pumped from a single coastal field.

story.title: Port Chicago: The Explosion That Desegregated a Navy

subject: Port Chicago
summary: On a July night in 1944, a catastrophic ammunition explosion killed 320 men at a California naval magazine -- and the aftermath forced the U.S. Navy to confront the racism that put them there.

story.title: Puri Saren Agung: The Palace Where Medicine Became a Kingdom

subject: Puri Saren Agung
summary: A royal palace in Bali's cultural heart, built where a wandering priest sensed healing energy in the river confluence, its stone carvings shaped by an artist who may have lived 116 years.

story.title: Raúl Uranga – Carlos Sylvestre Begnis Subfluvial Tunnel

subject: Raúl Uranga
summary: An engineering gamble that buried a highway beneath the Paraná River, finally stitching together two Argentine provinces that the water had kept apart for centuries.

subject: Red Market (Macau)
summary: Built in 1936 from the red bricks that gave it its name, Macau's Almirante Lacerda Municipal Market is a symmetrical Art Deco landmark where fresh seafood arrives twice daily and the city's daily rhythms have remained unchanged for ninety years.

subject: Remember the Alhambra
summary: A Moorish palace of cinema that Sacramento demolished for a supermarket, sparking a preservation movement that still carries its name as a battle cry.

subject: Sacramento's Only Star
summary: A husband-and-wife team built Sacramento's first and only Michelin-starred restaurant from a small storefront on Marconi Avenue, turning a city better known for politics than cuisine into a farm-to-fork destination.

subject: Seven Hundred and Ninety-Nine Pillars
summary: Surabaya's oldest Catholic church stands on a foundation of 799 wooden pillars driven deep into unstable ground, its European bricks scarred by independence and its faith unbroken across three centuries.

story.title: Seven Million Specimens: The Bohart Museum of Entomology

subject: Seven Million Specimens
summary: Tucked inside the UC Davis campus, the Bohart Museum of Entomology houses seven million insect specimens, making it the seventh largest collection in North America and a quietly extraordinary archive of arthropod life.

story.title: Seven Years of Fever and Flag

subject: Seven Years of Fever and Flag
summary: In 1828 the Dutch planted a flag on Triton Bay to claim all of western New Guinea - then watched malaria, isolation, and resistance destroy the settlement they built to hold it.

subject: Shadows on Sacred Ground
summary: Jakarta's Wayang Museum keeps Indonesia's ancient shadow puppet tradition alive in a building that has been a Dutch church, a colonial warehouse, and the burial site of one of Asia's most controversial colonial governors.

subject: Swannanoa
summary: An Italian Renaissance Revival villa perched above Rockfish Gap, built in 1912 by a Richmond millionaire as a marble-and-Tiffany love letter to his wife.

subject: The Adobe Where Generals Drank
summary: Sonoma's Blue Wing Inn began as a mission overseer's residence, became a Gold Rush hotel where future presidents and Civil War generals gambled, and has spent nearly two centuries refusing to disappear.

subject: The Ahwahnee
summary: A grand hotel built of granite and steel in the heart of Yosemite Valley, where Ansel Adams once climbed the dining room pillars as a jester, Stanley Kubrick found his Overlook Hotel, and a company tried to trademark the name of a national park.

story.title: The Art Circle That Outlasted Its Empire

subject: The Art Circle That Outlasted Its Empire
summary: Built in 1914 as the cultural centerpiece of colonial Batavia's finest residential quarter, the Kunstkring Art Gallery was Indonesia's first reinforced-concrete building -- and after a century of neglect, looting, and reinvention, it still displays art on its upper floor.

story.title: The Banker Who Quit the Gold Rush

subject: The Banker Who Quit the Gold Rush
summary: A 22-year-old from New York came to Sacramento chasing gold, saw that miners needed a bank more than California needed another prospector, and built an empire that outlasted the rush itself.

subject: The Bell That Remembers
summary: A 45-meter monument shaped like a Hindu priest's prayer bell rises from the heart of Denpasar, its architecture encoding Indonesia's independence date while its dioramas preserve the fierce resistance of a people who chose death over surrender.

story.title: The Brick Vault of Chinese Camp

subject: The Brick Vault of Chinese Camp
summary: A fireproof brick building from 1849 still stands at the corner of Main Street and Solinsky Alley in Chinese Camp, a Gold Rush settlement where Wells Fargo once shipped gold under iron shutters while wooden towns burned around it.

story.title: The Brothers Who Built Sacramento's Stage

subject: The Brothers Who Built Sacramento's Stage
summary: Born from a Hollywood actor's belief that live theatre should reach every child in Northern California, B Street Theatre grew from a touring van into Sacramento's most celebrated performing arts institution.

story.title: The Burning of Washington: When the British Torched the White House

subject: The Burning of Washington
summary: Where British troops marched into Washington D.C. in 1814, ate President Madison's dinner, and burned the White House, Capitol, and Treasury - the only time a foreign power has captured the American capital.

subject: The Cattleman's Victorian
summary: A German immigrant who owned 69,000 acres of cattle ranch hired Sacramento's finest architect to build a mansion for his family of ten -- and it outlasted nearly every grand home in the neighborhood.

subject: The Chimney of Labuan
summary: A 32-meter brick tower built from 23,000 unplastered British bricks stands in the jungle of northern Labuan, and after more than a century, nobody can agree on what it was actually for.

story.title: The Collector Who Could Not Stop

subject: The Collector Who Could Not Stop
summary: Born from a German immigrant's obsessive habit of photographing colonial Surabaya, the Mpu Tantular Museum has survived Japanese occupation, looting, and four relocations to become East Java's state museum of history and culture.

subject: The Doors of Thunder
summary: Built by Java's nine Muslim saints in the 15th century, the Demak Great Mosque fuses Hindu-Buddhist architecture with Islamic purpose, its carved "thunder doors" guarding one of the oldest mosques in Indonesia.

story.title: The End of the Line: Sacramento's Pony Express Terminal

subject: The End of the Line
summary: An unremarkable brick building at 2nd and J Streets that spent eighteen months as the most important address in the American West, where Pony Express riders completed their 1,800-mile journey from Missouri.

subject: The Floating Colossus of Surabaya
summary: A massive floating dry dock built in Amsterdam, towed halfway around the world through the Suez Canal, and stationed in Surabaya for four decades of service to the Dutch East Indies and Indonesia.

subject: The Fresno Met
summary: Born from civic ambition and $5.5 million in community fundraising, Fresno's Met brought Sue the T. rex and Georgia O'Keeffe to the San Joaquin Valley -- then a $28 million renovation became the debt that killed it.

story.title: The Glory Hole: Monticello Dam and the Drain That Swallows a Lake

subject: The Glory Hole
summary: A 304-foot concrete arch dam in Napa County whose hypnotic morning-glory spillway has become an internet sensation - and claimed at least one life.

subject: The Golden Domes of Depok
summary: One woman's vision produced a mosque with gold-plated domes, Italian chandeliers, and Turkish marble in the suburbs of Jakarta -- a landmark visible from miles away and one of Southeast Asia's largest.

story.title: The Governor Who Arrived by Rowboat

subject: The Governor Who Arrived by Rowboat
summary: Sacramento's Stanford Mansion -- raised twelve feet to escape floods, expanded from a cottage to a palace, and reborn from orphanage to statehouse -- has survived every reinvention California has thrown at it.

story.title: The Grand Old Lady of Canada Hill

subject: The Grand Old Lady of Canada Hill
summary: On a hilltop above Miri, a 30-meter wooden derrick marks the spot where a Swiss geologist's hunch transformed a fishing village of twenty houses into the birthplace of Malaysia's oil industry.

story.title: The Greenbrier: A Mayor's Mansion in Merced

subject: The Greenbrier
summary: A Queen Anne Victorian at 356 W. 21st Street in Merced, California, built for a Civil War major turned mayor, whose ornate tower and seven-sided bay have watched the house transform from family home to sanitarium to guest house over more than a century.

subject: The Helena May
summary: Built in 1916 with philanthropic donations, the Helena May at 35 Garden Road in Central Hong Kong began as a sanctuary for single women in a frontier city and has survived occupation, requisition, and a century of change to remain a private club housing the largest private English-language library in Hong Kong.

subject: The Hole in the Head
summary: A fishing village's six-year fight against Pacific Gas & Electric's plan to build a nuclear reactor on the San Andreas Fault gave birth to America's anti-nuclear movement and left behind a water-filled pit locals call 'The Hole in the Head.'

story.title: The Horse Pentagon: UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine

subject: The Horse Pentagon
summary: The largest veterinary school in the United States treats more than 50,000 animals per year, pioneered the discovery of feline immunodeficiency virus, and spent decades fighting for buildings worthy of its world-leading research.

story.title: The Iron Wanderer: A Floating Dock's Sixty-Year Odyssey

subject: The Iron Wanderer
summary: Built in Amsterdam in the 1860s and shipped in pieces to the Dutch East Indies, the Onrust Dock of 3,000 tons spent over six decades being towed between naval bases across the Indonesian archipelago -- a restless workhorse of empire that outlived the fleet it was built to serve.

story.title: The Johnstown Flood: The Dam That Killed 2,209 People

subject: The Johnstown Flood
summary: The Pennsylvania disaster that happened because rich men wanted a fishing club - when the South Fork Dam collapsed in 1889, sending a wall of water into a valley of steel workers who never had a chance, the first great American man-made catastrophe.

subject: The Judge's Gallery
summary: How a Sacramento judge and his wife built a private art collection that outgrew the Metropolitan Museum of Art -- then gave it all away.

story.title: The Last Congregation: Surabaya's Vanished Synagogue

subject: The Last Congregation
summary: For decades the only synagogue in Indonesia, Beth Shalom served a dwindling community of Iraqi Jewish emigres in Surabaya until its controversial demolition in 2013 erased the physical trace of a faith that once threaded quietly through the archipelago.

story.title: The Letter E and the End of Empire

subject: The Letter E and the End of Empire
summary: Brunei's oldest government building was shaped like a letter of the English alphabet in tribute to a foreign queen -- and then became the seat of the nation's own sovereign power.

story.title: The Lodge That Outlasted the Gold

subject: The Lodge That Outlasted the Gold
summary: Built by Italian stonemasons during the California Gold Rush, this tiny building in a near-ghost town has served as a photo studio, a jewelry shop, a saloon, and - since 1875 - a Masonic lodge that still meets today.

story.title: The Lodge That Outlived Its Namesake's Legacy

subject: The Lodge That Outlived Its Namesake's Legacy
summary: A Tudor Revival granite lodge built in Yosemite in 1903 to honor a Sierra Club founder, where Ansel Adams once worked as summer custodian and whose name was stripped in 2016 when the man it memorialized turned out to have championed white supremacy.

subject: The Longest Span
summary: The world's longest single-span wooden covered bridge has stood over the South Yuba River since 1862, a relic of the freight roads that fed the Comstock silver rush.

subject: The Man Breaking His Chains
summary: Rising 36 meters above a former Dutch colonial parade ground in Central Jakarta, the West Irian Liberation Monument captures in bronze the moment Indonesia declared its colonial past finally over.

subject: The Marquee That Fell
summary: A Sacramento theatre born in vaudeville, scarred by tragedy, and reborn as a cultural nerve center where cult films, French cinema, and punk rock share the same stage.

story.title: The Marquee That Refused to Go Dark

subject: The Marquee That Refused to Go Dark
summary: Sacramento's oldest continuously running movie theater has survived the death of the picture palace era, a three-screen conversion, corporate ownership, and the streaming revolution -- and still draws audiences to a 1938 Streamline Moderne gem on Broadway.

subject: The Media Tycoon's Hilltop Folly
summary: A Dutch press baron nearly bankrupted himself building an Art Deco masterpiece on a Bandung hilltop, lived in it for mere months before dying in a plane crash, and left behind a building whose motto -- 'I isolate myself and live' -- proved more prophetic than he could have imagined.

subject: The Mural Under the Paint
summary: Napa's Uptown Theatre opened in 1937 as an Art Deco movie palace, was carved into a four-screen multiplex, closed in 2000, then was resurrected with Francis Ford Coppola's help — and a Greco-Roman ceiling mural that nobody knew was there.

story.title: The Night Keith Richards Nearly Died

subject: The Night Keith Richards Nearly Died
summary: Built in 1926 to honor Sacramento County's war dead, this brick auditorium became a legendary rock venue where Keith Richards was nearly electrocuted and every major act of the 1960s played.

story.title: The Perfection of Smoke: Surabaya's House of Sampoerna

subject: The Perfection of Smoke
summary: A Dutch orphanage turned clove cigarette empire, where hundreds of women still hand-roll kretek on the same floors where a Chinese immigrant built Indonesia's most iconic tobacco brand.

story.title: The Printer Who Broke the Internet

subject: The Printer Who Broke the Internet
summary: A small museum in Old Sacramento, housed in a replica of the city's 1854 city hall, became a social media phenomenon when a volunteer printer's demonstrations went viral with over a billion YouTube views.

subject: The Red Bricks of Gedangan
summary: Semarang's first Catholic church survived a collapsed tower, a Japanese occupation, and the end of colonialism itself, transforming from a Dutch outpost into the spiritual center of a Javanese congregation.

story.title: The Scholar's Gift: Palopo Old Mosque

subject: The Scholar's Gift
summary: Built in 1604 by a West Sumatran scholar who converted a king, the Palopo Old Mosque stands as the oldest trace of Islam in South Sulawesi and a monument to the Kingdom of Luwu's spiritual transformation.

subject: The Shuttered Armory
summary: California's official military museum rose, earned three governors' endorsements, and then closed its doors amid bureaucratic infighting -- a Sacramento story of honor, memory, and institutional failure.

story.title: The Stage Where Twain Told Jokes and Motley Crue Plugged In

subject: The Stage Where Twain Told Jokes and Motley Crue Plugged In
summary: California's oldest existing theater building has hosted Mark Twain, Motley Crue, and everything in between since opening night in 1865, surviving fire, economic collapse, and a pandemic along the way.

subject: The Star Pylon's Shadow
summary: Fresno's Tower Theatre borrowed its iconic spire from the 1939 New York World's Fair, gave a neighborhood its name, and survived debt, closure, and a half-century of reinvention to become the cultural anchor of the Tower District.

subject: The Sultan's Mirror
summary: Brunei's largest national museum, opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1972, houses Islamic treasures from the Sultan's personal collection and traces a sultanate's identity from archaeological ruin to oil-fueled modernity.

subject: The Sultans' Rest
summary: Along the Brunei River, past the stilted homes of Kampong Ayer, the Royal Mausoleum quietly holds the remains of the monarchs who shaped one of Southeast Asia's oldest surviving dynasties.

story.title: The Tasting That Shook the Wine World

subject: The Tasting That Shook the Wine World
summary: A small Napa Valley winery at the foot of Mount Saint Helena humbled the French establishment in a blind tasting that rewrote the rules of winemaking forever.

subject: The Town Beneath the Water
summary: An earthfill dam on the Mokelumne River that drowned a Gold Rush town to deliver flood control and drinking water to the East Bay, while harboring the world's largest artificial salmon spawning channel at its base.

subject: The Valley's Attic
summary: A small museum in Yountville preserves the quirky, dangerous, and deeply personal history of Napa Valley -- from radioactive children's toys to military working dogs.

subject: The Vault Beneath the Columns
summary: A Neo-Renaissance bank building designed by a celebrated Amsterdam architect became Surabaya's window into two centuries of Indonesian monetary history.

story.title: The Wooden Raft That Lifted a Navy

subject: The Wooden Raft That Lifted a Navy
summary: The first floating dry dock in the Dutch East Indies was a wooden raft modeled on an American design, shipped in pieces from the Netherlands to Surabaya in the 1840s, where it served the colonial navy for over three decades.

story.title: Thirteen Thousand Voices from the Deep

subject: Thirteen Thousand Voices from the Deep
summary: A museum shaped like a ship guards thirteen thousand artifacts pulled from a Ming-era wreck discovered by accident on the seafloor off Brunei's coast.

story.title: Thirty Kilometers to Rejoin a Country

subject: Thirty Kilometers to Rejoin a Country
summary: Southeast Asia's longest bridge at 30 kilometers, this US$1.2 billion structure across Brunei Bay reconnects a nation that was split in two when a British-backed rajah seized the land between its halves in 1890.

subject: Thirty Villages Under Water
summary: Indonesia's controversial Jatigede Dam took over fifty years from first proposal to impoundment, displacing 70,000 people and flooding 30 villages to irrigate West Java's farmland and generate 110 megawatts of hydroelectric power.

subject: Thirty-Two Miles Along the River
summary: One of the longest paved bike trails in America follows the American River from Sacramento to Folsom Lake, retracing a route that fur trappers walked, Victorian cyclists pedaled, and five million people now use every year.

story.title: Three Hundred Steps Down to the Light

subject: Three Hundred Steps Down to the Light
summary: Perched on the windiest, foggiest headland on the Pacific coast, the Point Reyes Lighthouse required a fifteen-year land dispute before it could be built, three hundred steps carved into a cliff to reach it, and a first-order Fresnel lens to cut through weather that routinely defeated everything else.

story.title: Tugu Pahlawan: The Inverted Nail That Honors a City's Defiance

subject: Tugu Pahlawan
summary: Surabaya's Heroes Monument rises 41 meters over the site of Indonesia's bloodiest independence battle, its shape inspired by Sukarno's belief that the human spirit outlasts any human form.

subject: Twenty-Nine Domes of Gold
summary: Brunei's largest mosque encodes the sultanate's dynasty into every surface, from 29 golden domes honoring 29 rulers to a mihrab plated in 24-carat gold.

story.title: USP Atwater: From Runways to Cell Blocks

subject: USP Atwater
summary: A high-security federal penitentiary built on the grounds of a decommissioned Cold War air base in the Central Valley, where the violent realities of American incarceration have played out in incidents that forced national reckoning with prison safety.

story.title: Utqiagvik and the Whale Bone Arch

subject: Utqiagvik and the Whale Bone Arch
summary: The northernmost town in America where Inupiat hunters still take bowhead whales each spring - the skulls and bones of centuries of hunts scattered across the tundra, framing the Arctic Ocean and the ice that defines everything here.

subject: Walk In and Help Yourselves
summary: A Victorian mountain resort in southern Yosemite that grew from a homesteader's open-door policy into the largest intact hotel complex of its era in any American national park -- where presidents slept, a painter captured the light, and the name itself holds a botanical secret.

subject: Where Batavia Buries Its Dead
summary: A former Dutch colonial cemetery opened during a disease outbreak in 1795, Museum Taman Prasasti holds the graves of colonial administrators, a British governor's wife, and an Indonesian student activist who died on a volcano.

story.title: Where Fever and Fortune Share a Floor

subject: Where Fever and Fortune Share a Floor
summary: Housed in Placer County's first hospital, the Gold Country Museum in Auburn lets visitors pan for gold, walk through a replica mine tunnel, and reckon with the fever -- both medical and mineral -- that built the Sierra foothills.

subject: Where Incense Meets Incantation
summary: In a Betawi village on the outskirts of Jakarta, a Catholic parish preserves indigenous rituals alongside the Eucharist -- stirring dodol for seven hours, blessing rice harvests, and praying the Our Father in a language the Vatican never anticipated.

story.title: Where Indonesia Was Written Into Existence

subject: Where Indonesia Was Written Into Existence
summary: An Art Deco building in Central Jakarta where, on the night of August 16, 1945, Sukarno sat at a round table and handwrote the proclamation that would sever Indonesia from 350 years of colonial rule -- now preserved as a museum with the original rooms frozen in time.

subject: Where Java Learned to Pray
summary: Built in 1421 by one of Java's nine legendary Muslim saints, the Ampel Mosque stands as East Java's oldest and holiest, its founder's simple grave still drawing pilgrims six centuries later.

story.title: Where Sousa Played and Sullivan Sang

subject: Where Sousa Played and Sullivan Sang
summary: The Napa Valley Opera House, an Italianate gem designed by the architects of the Carson Mansion, has survived earthquakes, decades of abandonment, and the death of vaudeville to become one of California's most storied live music venues.

story.title: Where Spice Met Sea: Jakarta's Maritime Museum

subject: Where Spice Met Sea
summary: Inside the former Dutch East India Company warehouses at Sunda Kelapa harbor, Indonesia's Maritime Museum preserves centuries of seafaring tradition, from Bugis schooners to ancient Majapahit vessels carved in stone at Borobudur.

story.title: Where Three Worlds Meet: The Great Mosque of Sumenep

subject: Where Three Worlds Meet
summary: An 18th-century mosque on the island of Madura where Chinese, Javanese, and Dutch architectural traditions converge in a single extraordinary complex, designed by a Chinese architect for a Madurese duke.

story.title: Where a Field Trip Changed Everything

subject: Where a Field Trip Changed Everything
summary: Born from one boy's childhood visit to a grass airstrip in Sonoma wine country, the North Bay Air Museum preserves flying warbirds and vintage biplanes at the same airport that sparked its founder's lifelong obsession with flight.

story.title: Where an Empire's Memory Lives in Clay and Stone

subject: Where an Empire's Memory Lives in Clay and Stone
summary: The Trowulan Museum houses the largest collection of Majapahit relics in Indonesia, preserving artifacts from a civilization that once ruled an archipelago from its red-brick capital in East Java.

story.title: Where the Komodo Dragon Got Its Name

subject: Where the Komodo Dragon Got Its Name
summary: A colonial-era zoology museum in Bogor holds one of Southeast Asia's largest specimen collections -- and the desk where the world's largest lizard was first described by science.

subject: Where the Water Village Remembers
summary: Funded by oil money and opened in 1988, this Brunei museum preserves the ingenuity of Kampong Ayer -- the world's oldest water village -- where houses on stilts, goldsmithing, and boat-building sustained a civilization for over a thousand years.

subject: Woolaroc
summary: The Oklahoma oil baron's retreat that became one of the world's strangest museums - where the Spirit of St. Louis rival aircraft, massive Western art collection, and Frank Phillips's obsessions collide in a wildlife preserve named for woods, lakes, and rocks.

subject: 12 June 2019 Hong Kong Protest
summary: On June 12, 2019, tens of thousands of people occupied the streets around Hong Kong's government headquarters to stop a vote on an extradition bill — the day that transformed a protest movement into a prolonged confrontation.

story.title: The 1596 Keicho-Fushimi Earthquake: Five Days, Three Quakes, and Hideyoshi's Rage

subject: 1596 Keichō–Fushimi earthquake
summary: In September 1596, three powerful earthquakes ripped across Japan's Median Tectonic Line in just five days, killing over 1,200 people in the Kansai region, demolishing Toyotomi Hideyoshi's beloved Fushimi Castle, and destroying the Great Buddha of Kyoto -- which Hideyoshi reportedly punished by shooting an arrow into its cracked face.

subject: 1754 Hōreki River incident
summary: A tale of political cruelty disguised as public works: the Tokugawa shogunate ordered distant Satsuma samurai to tame three flooding rivers near Nagoya, then sabotaged the project until 85 men were dead.

subject: 2 Willow Road
summary: Architect Erno Goldfinger demolished cottages to build his modernist family home in Hampstead - and his angriest neighbour, Ian Fleming, took revenge by naming a Bond villain after him.

subject: 2009-10 Eerste Divisie
summary: The season a 120-year-old Dutch club ran out of money in January and simply ceased to exist - mid-table, mid-fixture, mid-history.

subject: 2018 Laos Dam Collapse
summary: On 23 July 2018, Saddle Dam D of the Xe-Pian Xe-Namnoy hydroelectric project failed in Attapeu Province, Laos, sending floodwaters through six villages and displacing more than 6,600 people.

subject: 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests
summary: The largest demonstrations in Hong Kong's history erupted in 2019 over an extradition bill and grew into a sustained, leaderless movement for democratic freedoms, reshaping the city's politics for years to come.

subject: 2021 Lagos high-rise collapse
summary: A 21-storey luxury tower that was only approved for 15 floors collapsed in Lagos's Ikoyi neighborhood in 2021, killing 42 people including the developer who built it.

subject: 2025 Israeli attacks in Yemen
summary: Through 2025, Israeli aircraft and warships struck Yemen more than fifteen times - bombing airports, ports, power plants, and a gathering of senior Houthi officials that killed the Houthi prime minister.

subject: 416 Fire
summary: Embers from a coal-burning steam locomotive on the historic Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad ignited one of the largest wildfires in Colorado history, devastating the tourism economy of the San Juan Mountains.

subject: A.G. Gaston Motel
summary: The Birmingham motel where Martin Luther King Jr. and the SCLC planned Project C from Room 30 -- the 'war room' of the 1963 civil rights campaign -- before white supremacist bombers blew a hole beneath it.

subject: Abbeville, South Carolina
summary: A small Old 96 District town that holds the strange distinction of being where the Confederacy was first proposed and last dissolved.

subject: Air Mobility Command Museum
summary: An aviation museum at Dover AFB that began as a B-17 restoration project in 1978 and now holds a complete set of every major Lockheed military airlifter from World War II forward.

subject: Al-Khiday
summary: Along the White Nile near Khartoum, an Italian road project revealed a cemetery where hunters, farmers, and Meroitic Sudanese had buried their dead across more than eight thousand years.

subject: Almere
summary: Almere is the Netherlands' newest city, built on land that was open sea within living memory, and the eighth largest city in the country.

subject: Almudena Cathedral
summary: Madrid's cathedral took over a century to build, surviving a civil war and three architectural reinventions before finally being consecrated in 1993.

subject: Alotau
summary: The provincial capital of Milne Bay - a small, walkable town at the foot of the bay where the kids call out DimDim, the market has crabs on most days but not Sunday, and the only road back to Port Moresby was never built.

subject: Alta Hydroelectric Power Station
summary: Norway's tallest dam became the nation's most contentious infrastructure project, pitting state energy ambitions against Sami indigenous rights and inspiring the plot of Frozen II.

subject: Amalgamated Housing Cooperative
summary: A socialist labor union's 1927 experiment in cooperative housing became the blueprint for affordable living in New York City, surviving the Great Depression and earning praise from Franklin D. Roosevelt.

subject: American University
summary: A federally chartered Methodist university in northwest Washington whose hilltop grounds once held the country's chemical weapons program - and whose 1963 commencement gave John F. Kennedy the stage to call for nuclear disarmament.

subject: Amsterdam Airport Schiphol
summary: Europe's third-busiest airport sits on the floor of a vanished lake, three meters below sea level, where Dutch engineers turned a 19th-century drainage project into one of the world's great hubs.

subject: Amsterdam Zuid Station
summary: A 1978 commuter platform that has quietly overtaken Centraal as Amsterdam's busiest gateway, anchoring the country's largest infrastructure project.

subject: Anacostia Community Museum
summary: The first federally funded community museum in America, born in a 1967 storefront across the river from the National Mall to bring the Smithsonian to a neighborhood the Smithsonian had largely ignored.

subject: Angel of the North
summary: Antony Gormley's 20-metre rust-coloured steel angel rises from a former colliery hill above Gateshead, its 54-metre wings angled forward in what the sculptor calls 'a sense of embrace.'

subject: Anglesey Abbey
summary: Northeast of Cambridge in the village of Lode, Anglesey Abbey began as a medieval priory, became a country house, and finally the obsessive life's project of one collector — a man who transformed 98 acres of flat Cambridgeshire farmland into one of England's most atmospheric gardens.

subject: Appalachian Trail
summary: Nearly 2,200 miles of white-blazed footpath from Georgia to Maine, dreamed up by a grieving forester in 1921 and now walked by three million people a year.

subject: Ardtornish Castle
summary: From this promontory on the Sound of Mull, the Lords of the Isles launched galley fleets, signed charters in Gaelic and Latin, and secretly offered to divide Scotland with the King of England.

subject: Art & Project
summary: An Amsterdam gallery that ran out of a parental living room and helped redefine European conceptual art through a mail-order magazine printed in editions of 800.

subject: Atlantic City Rail Terminal
summary: The end of the Gambler's Express line - a 1989 train terminal built underneath the convention center to deliver Philadelphia gamblers directly to the boardwalk.

subject: Atlantic Shores Offshore Wind South
summary: A cancelled offshore wind project that would have put 200 turbines about eight miles off the New Jersey coast - formally abandoned in June 2025 after Shell walked away with a billion-dollar write-off and the Trump administration froze permitting.

story.title: Attempts to Build a Canal Across Nicaragua

subject: Attempts to Build a Canal Across Nicaragua
summary: For nearly five centuries, dreamers and empires have tried to carve a shipping canal through Nicaragua's narrow waist, only to see the project slip away to Panama every time.

story.title: Augusta Canal: The Waterway That Refused to Die

subject: Augusta Canal
summary: The only canal in the United States still in continuous use for its original purposes of providing power, transport, and municipal water -- a 180-year-old waterway that survived the Civil War, nearly became a superhighway, and reinvented itself as a National Heritage Area.

subject: Ballaghaderreen Branch Line
summary: A small Irish railway branch built in 1874, kept running by a steam locomotive numbered 574 on the day it closed in February 1963, and now proposed as a community greenway through the bog country between Lough Gara and Ballaghaderreen.

subject: Ballajá Barracks
summary: The last great construction project of the Spanish Crown in the Americas now houses a museum of the continent's shared heritage, a dance school, and a living green roof.

subject: Ballyglass
summary: A small Mayo village built around a hotel that became a Garda barracks because the railway never came, and a Neolithic house uncovered in 1970 that turned out to be one of the oldest in Ireland or Britain.

story.title: Bandelier National Monument: Where Cliff Dwellers Met the Atomic Age

subject: Bandelier National Monument
summary: A volcanic landscape on the Pajarito Plateau where Ancestral Puebloans carved homes from soft tuff cliffs 800 years ago, and where CCC workers and Manhattan Project scientists later left their own marks on the canyon.

subject: Banzai Pipeline
summary: The most famous and deadly surf break on Earth was named after a construction project visible from the road, breaks over a reef full of underwater lava spires, and did not host an elite women's competition until 2020.

subject: Baram Dam
summary: A proposed mega-dam on Sarawak's Baram River that would have displaced up to 20,000 indigenous people -- until Kenyah, Kayan, and Penan communities blockaded the construction site for over a year and won.

subject: Basileiades
summary: Founded in Piraeus in 1859, the Basileiades machine works built Greece's industrial revolution from the waterfront — steamships, boilers, bridges, and even a locomotive named the Greek Lady — before war and economics finally brought it down.

subject: Batoque Extractive Reserve
summary: A small coastal reserve in Ceará where fishermen and subsistence farmers won a decade-long fight against a massive hotel project - and secured the legal right to keep living on the land their grandparents settled.

subject: Battle of Fort Beauséjour
summary: The 1755 siege on the Isthmus of Chignecto that ended French military presence in mainland Acadia, sealed the fate of the Acadian people, and triggered the largest forced deportation in North American colonial history.

subject: Battle of Sellasia
summary: In the summer of 222 BC, on two fortified hills at the northern gateway to Laconia, the reforming Spartan king Cleomenes III fought his last battle — and lost not just the engagement but his city, his throne, and the social revolution he had tried to build.

subject: Battle of Tripoli (2011)
summary: Codenamed Operation Mermaid Dawn, the rebel assault on Tripoli in August 2011 began with a call from a mosque loudspeaker during Ramadan and ended with the fall of Gaddafi's four-decade regime.

subject: Beith
summary: A North Ayrshire hill town that smuggled tea, made fine furniture for the QE2, and gave the world Henry Faulds, the man whose unanswered letters first proposed using fingerprints to identify criminals.

subject: Belo Monte Dam
summary: The world's fifth-largest hydroelectric project, built over three decades of indigenous resistance on the Xingu River the Juruna call 'house of God.'

subject: Berlaymont Building
summary: Building the cross-shaped headquarters of the European Commission took eight years. Stripping the asbestos out of it, then putting it back together, took thirteen.

subject: Berlin International Film Festival
summary: An American occupation officer proposed a film festival for a half-city that had been under blockade three years earlier — and it has been arguing with itself in public ever since.

subject: Bernardino Jalandoni Museum
summary: A bright pink heritage house in Silay City became Negros Occidental's first National Historical Landmark, saved from demolition by residents who refused to let a road widening project erase their history.

subject: Bhakra Dam
summary: A colossal concrete gravity dam on the Sutlej River in Himachal Pradesh, Bhakra Dam was independent India's defining infrastructure project and remains the second tallest dam in Asia.

subject: Bigfoot Trail
summary: A 360-mile unofficial hiking trail through the Klamath Mountains, designed to celebrate one of Earth's most diverse temperate coniferous forests with 32 conifer species along the route.

story.title: Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project Area

subject: Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project Area of Relevant Ecological Interest
summary: A 3,288-hectare research area 80 kilometers north of Manaus where biologists have watched isolated patches of rainforest for over four decades.

subject: Birkenhead Dock Disaster
summary: Just after midnight in a blinding snowstorm on 6 March 1909, a coffer dam gave way and fourteen navvies died with the Vittoria Dock only hours from completion.

subject: Birmingham Civil Rights National Monument
summary: Five city blocks in downtown Birmingham where children marched into fire hoses, a church was bombed, and a motel sheltered the revolution -- designated a U.S. National Monument in 2017 to preserve the ground where the civil rights movement reached its breaking point.

subject: Bishop Auckland
summary: The market town the Prince Bishops of Durham chose over their cathedral seat - a coal town in decline being remade by an investor's £200 million bet on tourism.

subject: Black Swan Project
summary: In 2007 a Florida treasure-hunting company flew seventeen tons of silver and gold coins out of Gibraltar in unmarked crates. Five years and a Supreme Court refusal later, two C-130s flew them back to Spain. The case rewrote the rules of underwater treasure hunting.

subject: Blackburn
summary: The weaving capital of the world in the nineteenth century, post-industrial Lancashire town in the twentieth, and a £200 million revitalisation project in the twenty-first.

subject: Blenheim Palace
summary: Built as a grateful nation's reward for the Duke of Marlborough's victory over the French in 1704, Blenheim Palace became instead a monument to architectural ambition, political scandal, and the birthplace of Winston Churchill.

subject: Bogibeel Bridge
summary: India's longest rail-cum-road bridge took 21 years from foundation to inauguration, a saga of bureaucratic delays and cost overruns that produced a strategic lifeline across the Brahmaputra.

subject: Bohai Strait tunnel project
summary: A proposed 123-kilometer undersea tunnel would connect Dalian to Yantai beneath the Bohai Strait, creating a crossing longer than the Seikan and Channel Tunnels combined, at an estimated cost of 300 billion yuan.

subject: Bohorodytska Fortress
summary: A turtle-shaped fort of earth and timber where the Dnieper meets the Samara, built to project Moscow's power over the free-roaming Cossacks, now a field of buried treasure and revived Cossack festivals.

subject: Bombing of Braunschweig (15 October 1944)
summary: The firestorm that took ninety percent of Henry the Lion's medieval city in forty minutes — and the hose full of holes that walked 23,000 people out of it.

subject: Bonanza Spring
summary: The largest freshwater spring system in the Mojave Desert, flowing at ten gallons per minute through a half-mile of cottonwoods and cattails in the Clipper Mountains foothills — a biological island threatened by a proposed aquifer pumping project that would remove billions of gallons from the system that feeds it.

subject: Bone Valley
summary: Central Florida's Bone Valley holds the largest phosphate deposits in the United States, fueling a 140-year mining industry that feeds the world's crops while leaving behind radioactive waste stacks, poisoned rivers, and a landscape perpetually torn open and stitched back together.

subject: Boston Manor House
summary: A Jacobean house in west London, built by a widow in 1622, with a trompe l'oeil balustrade and a single ghost.

subject: British Columbia Parliament Buildings
summary: A 25-year-old immigrant entered the design competition under a false name, won it, and gave Victoria the domed legislature that still defines its harbour.

subject: Broadfield House Glass Museum
summary: The Kingswinford farmhouse-turned-museum that held the Stourbridge region's glass collections from 1980 until 2015, when the story moved on.

subject: Brougham Hall
summary: A country house that survived a Norman conquest, an aristocratic gambler, and a wartime secret weapons program, and is now being rebuilt by volunteers.

subject: Brunswick Nuclear Generating Station
summary: Two General Electric boiling water reactors that share a parking lot with the unfinished foundation of a cooling tower that was never built, and a five-mile canal that pipes warm water under the Intracoastal Waterway out to the Atlantic.

subject: Buffalo Bill Dam
summary: When completed in 1910, this concrete arch spanning a narrow canyon of Pre-Cambrian granite was the tallest dam in the world, and engineers came back in the 1990s to add 25 feet more.

subject: Buku-Larrnggay Mulka Centre
summary: The Yolngu-run art centre at Yirrkala, one of Australia's most celebrated, where bark painting carries ancestral law, the historic church panels are kept, and the Mulka Project guards a digital archive of a living culture.

subject: Cache River National Wildlife Refuge
summary: A 69,000-acre Arkansas refuge protecting the largest remaining tract of bottomland hardwood forest in the United States, where duck hunters saved a river from Army engineers and a four-second video once reignited hope for an extinct woodpecker.

subject: Cachoeira dos Patos Dam
summary: A proposed 528 MW hydroelectric dam on the Jamanxim River, halted since 2013 because the Federal Public Ministry noticed the indigenous people were never consulted.

subject: Cahora Bassa (HVDC)
summary: Two 1,420-kilometer parallel power lines named Zeus and Apollo, the first HVDC scheme in Africa and the first in the world to operate above 500 kilovolts - and the first victim of the Mozambican civil war.

story.title: Calf Canyon/Hermits Peak Fire: When the Government Started New Mexico's Worst Wildfire

subject: Calf Canyon/Hermits Peak Fire
summary: A routine prescribed burn spiraled into the largest wildfire in New Mexico history, destroying over 900 structures and centuries-old Hispanic communities in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

subject: Camden Lock
summary: Camden Lock was built to solve a water management problem on the Regent's Canal — and the building constructed in 1815 for the lock's experimental predecessor is now a Starbucks.

subject: Canal du Midi
summary: A 240-kilometer canal connecting the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, dreamed up by a salt-tax collector and built by 12,000 workers in the seventeenth century, now a UNESCO World Heritage waterway shaded by plane trees.

subject: Canberra
summary: Australia's capital was drawn on paper before it was built on ground - a city dreamed up by two architects in Chicago and laid out across Ngunnawal country.

subject: Cape Henry Lighthouses
summary: A pair of lighthouses at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay where the first federal construction project under the Constitution still stands beside its iron successor, built from the same sandstone as the White House.

subject: Capp Street Project
summary: America's first artist residency dedicated solely to installation and conceptual art, born in a David Ireland-designed house on a Mission District side street.

subject: Capture of Chernobyl
summary: On the first day of the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, Russian troops seized the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone and held roughly 300 plant staff and National Guard soldiers under armed occupation for thirty-five days, while Ukrainian operators kept the world's most damaged nuclear site safe.

subject: Capture of the Bahamas (1782)
summary: A rogue Spanish governor defied orders to seize Nassau without firing a shot during the American Revolution, only to be imprisoned for his own success.

subject: Carolwood Pacific Railroad
summary: Walt Disney built a 2,615-foot miniature railroad in his Holmby Hills backyard in 1950—the obsessive, joyful experiment that seeded the idea for Disneyland.

subject: Carpow Roman Fort
summary: A thirty-acre Roman legionary fortress at the confluence of the Tay and the Earn, built to support the emperor Septimius Severus's invasion of Caledonia.

subject: Carrownagappul Bog
summary: Once carved up by turf-cutters and crisscrossed with drainage trenches, this 486-hectare raised bog north of Mountbellew was nursed back to life by a project called The Living Bog - and now sequesters carbon while the red grouse return.

subject: Castle of Guimarães
summary: Built by a widowed countess in the 10th century to protect monks from Vikings and Moors, the Castle of Guimaraes became the birthplace of Portugal's first king and the cradle of a nation.

subject: Causeway Bay Typhoon Shelter
summary: Hong Kong's first typhoon shelter, born from the catastrophic 1906 storm that killed 15,000 people — a 17-hectare refuge of calm water tucked beside Victoria Harbour that still protects boats where the bay once was.

subject: Cavendish Square
summary: A Marylebone garden square begun in 1717 by an earl who ran out of money, Cavendish Square has accumulated three centuries of remarkable residents, a Jacob Epstein sculpture unveiled without telling the nuns who commissioned it that the artist was Jewish, and a car park shaped like a DNA double helix.

subject: Celtic Array
summary: A proposed offshore wind farm of up to 5.4 gigawatts in the Irish Sea, cancelled in 2014 when its foundations proved too expensive to build.

story.title: Central Police Station (Hong Kong) / Tai Kwun

subject: Central Police Station (Hong Kong) / Tai Kwun
summary: The compound at the eastern end of Hollywood Road served Hong Kong as police headquarters, prison, and magistracy for over 150 years before architects Herzog & de Meuron transformed it into Tai Kwun — the city's largest heritage revitalisation project.

subject: Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica
summary: A modest brick building in the Amsterdam Science Park is where a Dutch programmer wrote the language now running half the internet, and where the Dutch internet itself first plugged in.

subject: Chad–Cameroon Petroleum Development and Pipeline Project
summary: A 1,070-kilometer oil pipeline built from landlocked Chad to the Cameroonian coast was supposed to be a model for how resource extraction could reduce poverty in Africa - instead, it became a case study in how promises made by governments and corporations unravel.

subject: Charlotte Douglas International Airport
summary: A Depression-era WPA project that grew into American Airlines' fortress hub, where 50 million passengers a year pass beneath an original 1936 hangar still standing on the field.

subject: Chavez Ravine
summary: Three Mexican-American communities were displaced from Chavez Ravine for public housing that was never built—then the land was handed to the Brooklyn Dodgers. The resulting stadium opened in 1962.

subject: Cheow Lan Lake
summary: A vast artificial lake in Thailand's Khao Sok National Park where drowned forests still breach the surface and 1,364 animals were rescued by helicopter as the waters rose.

subject: Chicago Tunnel Company
summary: A secret narrow-gauge freight railroad tunneled beneath downtown Chicago starting in 1899, initially disguised as a telephone cable project -- it delivered coal, hauled away ashes, and even provided air conditioning to theaters before the river broke through and flooded the entire Loop in 1992.

subject: Chinese aircraft carrier Liaoning
summary: Born as a Soviet hull in Ukraine, sold as a casino project, towed halfway around the world, and reborn as China's first operational aircraft carrier.

subject: Christ Church Cathedral (Victoria, British Columbia)
summary: Anglican cathedral of the Diocese of British Columbia - a third building on ground that has seen a fire, a famous schism, a stonemason's robin, and a central tower that was designed but never built.

subject: Christ the King (Almada)
summary: A 110-meter monument on the south bank of the Tagus, built as Portugal's act of gratitude for being spared from World War II, inspired by Rio's Christ the Redeemer.

subject: Château d'Azay-le-Rideau
summary: A Renaissance jewel set on an island in the Indre River, built by a treasurer's wife and left forever unfinished when her husband fled royal justice.

subject: Cincinnati Subway
summary: The largest abandoned subway tunnel system in the United States lies beneath Cincinnati's streets, a century-old transit project killed by inflation, political feuds, and the automobile, with tracks never laid and trains never run.

subject: Clinton Power Station
summary: A story of a nuclear facility that survived economic struggles and threats of closure to power the modern data era.

subject: Clock Tower of Guayaquil
summary: An English clock bought in 1842 that has outlived four towers, survived one architect's death mid-project, escaped a fire scare, and finally - 89 years after it reached Ecuador - found a permanent home in Guayaquil's Moorish Tower.

subject: Cláudio Santoro National Theater
summary: A concrete pyramid that has spent much of its life closed — and whose most famous surface is not a stage but a wall designed to be performed on by the sun.

subject: Coastal Fortifications of Colonial Chile
summary: To guard the back door of its empire against the Dutch and the British, Spain built a chain of forts down the Chilean coast, an expensive shield against an invasion that mostly never came.

subject: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind
summary: The largest U.S. offshore wind project under construction - 176 turbines, over $11 billion, and a Danish-American partnership that has become a political flashpoint.

subject: Columbia Center
summary: Seattle's tallest skyscraper, a 76-story tower born from a legal loophole that redefined the city's skyline and sparked a building-height revolution.

subject: Confluence Project
summary: Maya Lin's series of landscape artworks along the Columbia River -- where the architect of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial turned 15,000 acres of Pacific Northwest terrain into a meditation on what Lewis and Clark's journals recorded and what they left out.

subject: Conquest of madina Laqant
summary: The slow 13th-century fall of Muslim Alicante, where the last emir of Valencia made a final stand by the sea, buying time to evacuate his people before Christian rule emptied the medina.

subject: Construction of Rockefeller Center
summary: How John D. Rockefeller Jr. turned a failed opera house scheme and a Depression-era gamble into the most ambitious private construction project in modern history, raising 14 buildings on 22 acres of Midtown Manhattan.

subject: Crazy Horse Memorial
summary: A monument seven decades in the making, carved into sacred Lakota land by three generations of one family, honoring a warrior who refused to be photographed in life.

subject: Curtea de Argeș Cathedral
summary: A 16th-century cathedral whose twisted cupolas defy geometry, whose founding legend involves a wife sealed alive in the walls, and whose crypt holds the bones of Romania's kings.

subject: Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport
summary: The remnant of America's most ambitious airport project - planned as a 39-square-mile supersonic jetport in the Everglades, halted by environmental protests after a single 10,500-foot runway was built, then repurposed for pilot training, car racing, and controversy.

subject: Daming Lake
summary: Jinan's largest lake has been drawing poets for 1,500 years, though it also witnessed a Mongol execution, a warlord's vanity project, and a civil war general's desperate escape.

subject: Damodar River
summary: Once called the Sorrow of Bengal for its catastrophic floods, the Damodar River became independent India's first great taming project -- modeled on America's Tennessee Valley Authority and transforming a valley of grief into the industrial engine known as the Ruhr of India.

subject: Deception Pass Bridge
summary: Two green steel spans thrown 180 feet above one of the fastest tidal channels in Puget Sound - a 1935 New Deal project that replaced a ferry you summoned by hitting a saw with a mallet.

story.title: Densho: The Japanese American Legacy Project

subject: Densho
summary: A Seattle nonprofit racing against time to record the voices of Japanese Americans incarcerated during World War II, preserving nearly two thousand hours of testimony so that over 120,000 silenced stories are never forgotten.

subject: DigiPen Institute of Technology
summary: A small Redmond university whose student projects became some of the most influential video games ever made -- including the prototype that became Valve's Portal.

subject: Dirk Hartog Island
summary: Western Australia's largest island carries layers of history from Dutch pewter plates to a 20,000-sheep station, and is now the site of an ambitious project to restore its ecology to the way it was in 1616.

subject: Djerbahood
summary: In the summer of 2014, 150 street artists from 30 countries descended on the ancient village of Erriadh on the island of Djerba and transformed its whitewashed walls into one of the world's largest open-air street art museums.

subject: Dominga
summary: A $2.5 billion iron and copper mining and port project on Chile's desert coast that has become the country's defining clash between development and the protection of the Humboldt penguin islands.

subject: Dongping Lake
summary: The last surviving fragment of the legendary Eight Hundred Li Liangshan Marsh from Water Margin, now serving as a reservoir for China's colossal South-North Water Transfer Project.

subject: Duncansby Head
summary: The northeasternmost corner of mainland Britain, where pyramid sea stacks rise from a roiling Pentland Firth and a Stevenson lighthouse marks the end of the road.

subject: Dung Quất Refinery
summary: Vietnam's first oil refinery took two decades, three continents of investors, and $3 billion to build — a saga that mirrors the country's turbulent emergence as an industrial nation.

subject: Döda fallet
summary: A Swedish waterfall that died in a single night when an amateur canal project accidentally drained an entire lake in four hours, reshaping the landscape forever.

subject: Eads Bridge
summary: When steamboat interests demanded bridge spans so grand that no known construction technique could build them, self-taught engineer James Eads pioneered the use of structural steel, set the deepest underwater foundations ever attempted, and proved the bridge safe by parading an elephant across the Mississippi.

subject: East Point Lighthouse
summary: Built in 1867 at Prince Edward Island's easternmost tip, this octagonal wooden tower earned the nickname 'Canada's Confederation Lighthouse' and has been moved twice to keep pace with shifting coastlines and corrected charts.

subject: Eden (2016 TV Series)
summary: Channel 4's ambitious 2016 reality experiment dropped 23 strangers in a remote corner of Scotland for a year, then cancelled the show without telling them - and the wilderness location, Cul na Croise on Ardnamurchan, became the unwitting backdrop of one of British TV's strangest experiments.

subject: Eden Project
summary: A botanical cathedral built inside a worked-out china clay pit, where the largest indoor rainforest in the world sits beneath honeycombed geodesic domes once mistaken for Magrathea.

subject: El Helicoide
summary: A futuristic pyramid-shaped mall from the 1950s that was never completed and instead became one of Venezuela's most notorious political prisons before its closure in 2026.

subject: El Salvador mine
summary: A copper mine in Chile's Atacama Desert earned the name 'The Savior' when it rescued a mining company's production — then became a flashpoint for nationalization, labor rights, and the question of who profits from the earth's riches.

subject: Ennerdale Water
summary: The most westerly lake in the Lake District, ringed by Great Gable and its fellow giants, where a young Bill Clinton once proposed and a mysterious carnivore killed hundreds of sheep.

subject: Ennis
summary: The county town of Clare grew from a 13th-century Franciscan friary into a market town whose narrow medieval streets still curve around the meandering River Fergus.

subject: Estonian Open Air Museum
summary: Seventy-two hectares of rescued Estonian rural buildings, from a 1670s Swedish chapel to a Soviet kolkhoz apartment block, reassembled on the Baltic shore at Rocca al Mare.

subject: Exploratorium
summary: A hands-on science museum founded by a Manhattan Project physicist who was blacklisted, became a cattle rancher, and then reinvented how the world teaches science.

subject: Federal Triangle
summary: Seventy acres of neoclassical limestone built on top of Murder Bay's bordellos in the 1930s, the largest single construction project in Depression-era America.

subject: Firck Palace
summary: A Baltic German baron's neoclassical villa on the highest of nine hills in Talsi, Latvia, now home to the Talsi Regional Museum and a century of regional memory.

subject: First Horizon Coliseum
summary: The Greensboro Coliseum opened in 1959 as a war memorial - and ended up hosting the ACC tournament 26 times, Elvis twice, and one of the strangest two-year NHL stops in league history.

subject: First Transcontinental Railroad
summary: Built in six years across 1,900 miles of plains, deserts, and mountains, America's first transcontinental railroad was the Moon landing of the 1860s - a project so audacious that Lincoln compared it to being remembered for a century.

subject: Fly Geyser
summary: An accidental wonder where a 1964 well drilling mistake created a constantly growing alien landscape of brilliant green and red mineral cones, now owned by the Burning Man Project.

subject: Fordlândia
summary: Henry Ford's 1928 plan to export American civilization to the Amazon and grow his own rubber collapsed within six years, the victim of bad soil, worker resistance, and tree blight.

subject: Forres
summary: A former royal burgh on the Moray coast with Neolithic roots, Pictish stones, and a population that grew from 2,844 in 1841 to over 12,000 today.

subject: Fort Morgan (Alabama)
summary: A pentagonal bastion fort at the tip of Mobile Point that survived the War of 1812, anchored the most famous naval battle of the Civil War, and kept reinventing itself through four more conflicts before Alabama finally claimed it.

story.title: Freaknik: Atlanta's Spring Break That Swallowed a City

subject: Freaknik
summary: What started as a 150-person picnic for homesick college students in 1982 became a 250,000-person street festival that gridlocked Atlanta, generated $20 million in economic impact, and left a cultural imprint from Tom Wolfe novels to Beyonce lyrics.

subject: Fredericksburg Academy
summary: An independent pre-K through 12 school in Fredericksburg, Virginia, where every graduating senior must apprentice with a master in their chosen field for thirty hours before presenting an Exhibit project.

subject: Fuxue Confucian Temple
summary: Built in the 1070s, converted into a primary school under Mao, and raised 1.5 meters during a millennial restoration project -- Jinan's Confucian Temple refuses to stay buried.

subject: Fábrica Argentina de Aviones
summary: The oldest aircraft factory in Latin America, founded in Córdoba in 1927, where exiled European designers helped Argentina build one of the first jet fighters outside the world's great powers.

subject: Galata Bridge
summary: Five bridges across the Golden Horn, a rejected Leonardo da Vinci design, and a railing lined with fishermen.

subject: Garinish Island (County Kerry)
summary: A private island in Kenmare Bay where a Victorian earl planted tree ferns and a Swiss financier still tends what survived the Irish Civil War.

subject: Gateway Arch
summary: A 630-foot weighted catenary of stainless steel that took a rigged election, a father's misidentified letter, and civil rights protests on its own scaffolding to bring into existence.

subject: Gateway Pacific Terminal
summary: A $500 million coal export terminal proposed at Cherry Point was stopped in 2016 by a sentence written into a treaty in 1855 — and by the Lummi Nation that has fished this shoreline since long before either.

subject: General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge
summary: Spanning 8.7 kilometers across the outlet of Lake Maracaibo, this cable-stayed concrete bridge designed by Riccardo Morandi has connected western Venezuela to the rest of the country since 1962.

subject: Gila Wilderness
summary: Before wilderness had a legal definition, before any land in the world carried that protected designation, Aldo Leopold looked at these remote New Mexico mountains and saw something worth saving forever.

subject: Girvan Lifeboat Station
summary: Girvan's RNLI station has guarded the Firth of Clyde for more than a century and a half - a relationship between a fishing town, an insurance broker's bequest, and a stream of small acts of human kindness.

subject: Glasgow Science Centre
summary: A titanium-clad science centre on the south bank of the Clyde, the millennium project that turned a derelict garden festival site into Pacific Quay's media and learning quarter.

subject: Gode Wind Farm
summary: Three Orsted wind farms north-west of Norderney — 120 turbines that grew bigger and quieter through the decade it took to finish them, ending in 2025 with one of the largest single rotors at sea.

story.title: Golden Gate Bridge: The Impossible Span

subject: Golden Gate Bridge
summary: The San Francisco bridge that engineers said couldn't be built - where treacherous currents, savage winds, and earthquake risk made the project seem suicidal until Joseph Strauss proved otherwise in 1937.

subject: Govan
summary: Once the fifth-largest burgh in Scotland and the world's busiest shipbuilding district, Govan now holds the carved stones of a forgotten kingdom and the unfinished project of post-industrial reinvention.

subject: Governor's Palace (Williamsburg, Virginia)
summary: The Royal Governor's residence in colonial Virginia, lived in by Patrick Henry and Thomas Jefferson, burned in 1781 while serving as a hospital for wounded soldiers, and reconstructed in the 1930s.

subject: Graceland
summary: Elvis Presley's Memphis mansion was named for a woman called Grace who never lived there, almost went bankrupt after the King's death, and draws over 650,000 visitors annually to a house that critics call tacky and fans treat as a pilgrimage shrine.

subject: Granada Cathedral
summary: A cathedral that took 181 years to build, where a revolutionary Renaissance architect created a circular chapel inside a five-nave structure atop the site of Granada's main mosque.

subject: Grandfather Falls
summary: Wisconsin's highest waterfall, where voyageurs named the rapids after a grandfather bull, an 80-million-board-foot log jam once choked the river, and a 1938 hydroelectric project now harnesses the full 89-foot drop.

subject: Great Falls Park
summary: Eight hundred acres on the Virginia bank of the Potomac where the river drops seventy-six feet through Mather Gorge and George Washington's first American canal still remembers him.

subject: Great Man-Made River
summary: The world's largest irrigation project, a 2,820-kilometer Libyan pipeline network drawing ice-age fossil water from beneath the Sahara to the coastal cities.

subject: Great Wall of China
summary: Not one wall but many, built across two millennia by dynasties that rose and fell while the stones endured.

subject: Green Bank Observatory
