summary: A West Virginia radio observatory at the center of a 13,000-square-mile zone where cell phones and microwave ovens are illegal - all to keep the world's largest steerable telescope listening to the universe.

subject: Green Mountain Reservoir
summary: A mountain lake born of political compromise, where Colorado's Western Slope kept its water rights and gained a recreational gem.

subject: Greensboro massacre
summary: On a November morning in 1979, a caravan of Klansmen and neo-Nazis drove into a Greensboro housing project and opened fire on anti-Klan marchers, killing five -- all of it captured on television cameras.

subject: Grossglockner High Alpine Road
summary: Austria's highest paved mountain pass road, born from Depression-era unemployment and built by 3,200 workers who carved numbered hairpin curves to 2,504 meters across the Alpine divide.

subject: Growian
summary: The world's largest wind turbine ran for 420 hours before being scrapped — and some of the people who built it had wanted exactly that outcome from the start.

subject: Gualala River
summary: A 40-mile coastal river born along the San Andreas Fault whose Pomo name means 'where the waters meet' -- and whose waters once nearly got towed in giant bags to San Diego.

subject: Gustav Ludwig Hertz
summary: The German Nobel laureate who proved the quantization of atomic energy, was wounded fighting in Fritz Haber's chlorine gas unit, and was driven from his university chair for being a quarter Jewish before defecting to the Soviet atomic project.

subject: Gwadar
summary: A Pakistani port city that was part of Oman until 1958, now designated capital of South Balochistan and the center of China's most ambitious overseas infrastructure project.

subject: Gyaros
summary: A barren Cycladic island that served as a place of Roman exile, then endured a darker chapter as a prison camp for thousands of Greek political prisoners in the twentieth century.

subject: HMS Conqueror (1855)
summary: A mighty 101-gun Royal Navy warship that survived the Crimean War only to be undone by a navigation error in the Bahamas, HMS Conqueror now rests in shallow Caribbean waters as an underwater museum.

subject: Habitat 67
summary: A student's radical thesis project became one of the 20th century's most daring experiments in urban housing, stacking 354 prefabricated concrete boxes into a hillside village on the banks of the Saint Lawrence River.

subject: Haga Palace Ruins
summary: The monumental foundation of a palace that was never built, a testament to one king's grandiose vision cut short by an assassin's bullet.

subject: Hall Caine Airport
summary: A short-lived 1930s airfield on the Isle of Man's northern plain that briefly out-foged its rival before vanishing into farmland.

subject: Hallandsås Tunnel
summary: A railway tunnel that became Sweden's most troubled infrastructure project—23 years of scandal, poisoning, and perseverance before finally connecting Scandinavia.

subject: Hampstead Heath
summary: London's ancient heath — 320 hectares of hills, ponds, and woodland that humans have been defending from development since 986 AD, most recently from a plan to run the Underground through it.

story.title: Hanford: The Secret City That Built the Bomb

subject: Hanford
summary: The Washington desert site where the Manhattan Project produced plutonium for the Nagasaki bomb - where 50,000 workers built a secret city in months, where the Columbia River cooled the reactors, and where the most contaminated site in North America awaits cleanup that will take decades.

subject: Hanford Site
summary: Where they made the bomb - the Washington desert facility that produced plutonium for the atomic bombs, and now the most contaminated site in the Western Hemisphere.

subject: Hanhikivi Nuclear Power Plant
summary: A Finnish nuclear power plant that was never built -- killed by geopolitics when Russia's invasion of Ukraine ended a fifteen-year partnership with Rosatom.

subject: Harbour of Eleutherios
summary: Beneath a busy Istanbul neighborhood lies one of antiquity's great harbours — and the accidental discovery that rewrote the city's entire early history.

subject: Hard Rock (Exercise)
summary: The 1982 British civil defence exercise that was cancelled before it began - because nineteen county councils, the Greater London Council, and several Labour-run authorities simply refused to take part.

subject: Hardy Memorial Tower
summary: An eleven-story bell tower on the San Diego State campus where Depression-era murals lay hidden behind ceiling tiles for decades, waiting to be rediscovered.

subject: Haseki Sultan Complex
summary: The first imperial commission Mimar Sinan ever received came not from the sultan himself but from his remarkable wife — and the complex she built tells the story of a woman who changed the Ottoman court forever.

subject: Hatgyi Dam
summary: A controversial planned hydropower dam on Myanmar's Salween River, where a multinational energy project collides with ethnic conflict, environmental fragility, and the rights of indigenous communities in Karen State.

subject: Helgeland Museum
summary: One museum spread across eighteen municipalities of coast, island and inland valley, run from an office on a street that the town once planned to bulldoze for parking.

subject: Hellenic Maritime Museum
summary: Beside the sheltered waters of Zea Harbour in Piraeus, the Hellenic Maritime Museum tells three thousand years of Greek seafaring — from ancient oared warships to the submarine Papanikolis — through more than 2,500 objects and a naval library of 17,000 volumes.

subject: Henrichenburg Boat Lift
summary: Five upside-down wells, each forty meters deep, hold the lift on cylindrical floats. A coal barge weighing a thousand tonnes rises fourteen meters in two and a half minutes, powered by a motor barely larger than a household furnace.

subject: Het Bildt
summary: A patch of land lifted from the sea in 1505, settled by Dutch labourers from South Holland, where their descendants still speak a language no one else in the world speaks.

subject: HidroAysén
summary: The largest energy project in Chilean history would have dammed two of Patagonia's wildest rivers, until a movement under the banner Patagonia Sin Represas stopped it cold.

subject: High Speed 2
summary: Britain's most expensive infrastructure project, a high-speed railway from London to Birmingham whose northern branches to Manchester and Leeds were cancelled in 2023, and which has been bored through the Chilterns one carefully-spread cubic metre at a time.

story.title: Hinkley Point C nuclear power station

subject: Hinkley Point C nuclear power station
summary: On a windswept stretch of the Somerset coast rises the most expensive object ever built by humans, a generation-defining bet on Britain's energy future.

subject: Holy Trinity Church, Cork
summary: The lacy Gothic spire on the River Lee that Father Theobald Mathew - the priest who persuaded half of Ireland to give up drink - laid down on his birthday and waited a lifetime to see finished.

subject: Honnō-ji Incident
summary: On a June morning in 1582, the warlord closest to unifying Japan woke to the sound of his own army surrounding his temple -- sent not by an enemy, but by his trusted general Akechi Mitsuhide, in a betrayal whose motive remains history's most debated mystery.

subject: Hoosac Tunnel
summary: A railroad tunnel through western Massachusetts that took 24 years to build, cost ten times its estimate, killed 135 workers, and pioneered the technologies that would define modern tunneling.

subject: Hotel Tammer
summary: Tampere's grand hotel was finished for the city's 150th birthday in 1929 — then the lake steamer Kuru went down and the celebrations were cancelled.

subject: Huemul Project
summary: On a tiny island in a Patagonian lake, an Austrian outsider convinced Argentina's president he had cracked fusion power. The hoax fooled a nation, jolted the world's physicists into action, and left only ruins.

subject: Humboldt Forum
summary: Berlin's most expensive cultural project rebuilt the facade of a vanished Prussian palace to house ethnographic collections — and immediately ran into a question it cannot avoid: should the things inside go home?

subject: Hunters View
summary: A Hunters Point housing project undergoing redevelopment from deteriorating public housing into mixed-income homes, testing San Francisco's promises to its most vulnerable communities.

subject: Hằng Nga Guesthouse
summary: Known worldwide as the 'Crazy House,' this five-storey expressionist building in Da Lat was designed by Vietnamese architect Đặng Việt Nga as a personal project — then opened to paying tourists in 1990 to help cover the debt it had accumulated.

subject: Ichthys gas field
summary: A US$37-billion liquefied natural gas project in the Timor Sea, the largest overseas investment ever undertaken by a Japanese company, connected to Darwin by the longest subsea pipeline in the Southern Hemisphere.

subject: Imperial Valley Geothermal Project
summary: Eleven geothermal power stations tapping superheated brine beneath the Imperial Valley make this the second largest geothermal field in the United States — and the potential source of enough lithium to transform America's electric vehicle supply chain.

subject: Indonesia in 363 Acres
summary: Conceived by Indonesia's first lady as a nation-building project and inaugurated in 1975, Taman Mini Indonesia Indah compresses the world's largest archipelago into a single park -- complete with a lake shaped like the islands, 15 museums, and pavilions representing every province.

subject: International Church of Cannabis
summary: A 113-year-old Denver church transformed into a kaleidoscopic temple where cannabis is sacrament and the Golden Rule is the only doctrine.

subject: International Finance Centre (Hong Kong)
summary: Two towers rising above Victoria Harbour define Hong Kong's skyline and embody the city's improbable reinvention as a global financial capital — built through economic crisis, completed during SARS, and instantly iconic.

subject: International Flight Training Center, Kalamata
summary: Greece spent two decades trying to build a world-class pilot training center before finally opening the International Flight Training Center at Kalamata Air Base in 2021 — a €1.375 billion partnership with Israeli defense firm Elbit Systems that now trains Greek, German, and allied NATO pilots.

subject: Inveraray Jail
summary: A small Highland prison whose cells held debtors, women, and children alongside violent offenders, now a museum that asks visitors to look at what we used to do to one another.

subject: Inverness Cathedral
summary: The first new Protestant cathedral built in Britain since the Reformation, Inverness Cathedral was designed for twin spires that were never completed -- the funding ran out, leaving the towers flat-topped and the architect's vision permanently unfinished.

subject: Ipanema Park
summary: A steel town in the Rio Doce valley hired Brazil's greatest landscape architect to design its urban park. The project took decades to finish and twelve thousand trees to become what it is.

story.title: Isiboro Secure National Park and Indigenous Territory

subject: Isiboro Sécure National Park and Indigenous Territory
summary: A Bolivian park and indigenous territory where three native peoples, a government highway project, coca farmers, and oil concessions collide in one of Latin America's most contested conservation battles.

subject: Isle of Man TT
summary: Since 1907, the world's most uncompromising motorcycle race has unfolded each spring on the closed roads of a small island in the Irish Sea.

subject: Istanbul Canal
summary: Turkey's most controversial infrastructure project — a proposed 45-kilometer artificial waterway through European Istanbul — has been proposed, debated, partially begun, and fiercely opposed since its modern announcement in 2011.

subject: Italian Empire
summary: Italy's late, troubled, and comparatively brief colonial project (1882-1960), built in the Horn of Africa, Libya, and the Mediterranean and largely undone by World War II.

subject: Itatiaia
summary: A mountain municipality at the foot of Brazil's oldest national park, home to a century-old Finnish colony and a town that grew along the gold roads from Minas Gerais to the coast.

subject: Ituango Dam
summary: Colombia's largest hydroelectric project became an engineering emergency when landslides sealed its diversion tunnels in 2018, threatening 25,000 people downstream and reshaping the debate over mega-dams in Latin America.

subject: Jamrud Fort
summary: A Sikh fortress built in 54 days at the mouth of the Khyber Pass, where a general's last stand sealed both his legend and the pass's contested fate.

subject: Jatobá Hydroelectric Power Plant
summary: A 2,338-megawatt dam planned on the Tapajós river that would flood Munduruku homeland and river-dwelling communities - suspended since 2017 but never formally canceled.

subject: Jewish quarter of Inca
summary: In a Mallorcan market town, a medieval Jewish community fought for decades over the walls meant to contain it — a call that flourished briefly before the fires of 1391.

subject: Jiroft culture
summary: A proposed Bronze Age civilization in southeastern Iran whose chlorite vessels, undeciphered inscriptions, and sprawling urban ruins have sparked fierce debate over whether an unknown culture once bridged Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.

subject: John Hart Dam
summary: Built on dangerously unstable ground and rebuilt for over a billion dollars, the John Hart Dam on Vancouver Island is a story of engineering ambition, seismic anxiety, and the largest hydroelectric modernization project in British Columbia in decades.

subject: John McLaren Park
summary: San Francisco's third-largest park, where an unbuilt freeway, Jerry Garcia's childhood, and the city's last native grasslands converge on some of its steepest hills.

story.title: K. I. Sawyer Air Force Base

subject: K. I. Sawyer Air Force Base
summary: A decommissioned Cold War air base in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, built over blueberry fields by a road commissioner's dream, home to B-52 bombers for three decades, and now a quiet community still reckoning with the silence the jets left behind.

subject: Kabukichō
summary: Tokyo's neon-drenched entertainment district was named for a kabuki theater that was never built, and has spent eight decades reinventing itself between shadow and spectacle.

subject: Kader Toy Factory fire
summary: The 1993 Kader Toy Factory fire in Nakhon Pathom Province killed 188 workers and injured 469, making it the deadliest industrial factory fire in history -- worse than the Triangle Shirtwaist fire yet far less remembered.

subject: Kahnawake
summary: A Mohawk community on the Saint Lawrence whose people walked steel beams over Manhattan, stood defiant during the Oka Crisis, and produced Canada's first Indigenous symphony conductor.

subject: Kalahari Meerkat Project
summary: A research reserve in the South African Kalahari where decades of patient study turned wild meerkats into the best-documented mammals on Earth - and TV stars.

subject: Kallak mine
summary: A proposed iron ore mine in Swedish Lapland has become a flashpoint between industrial ambition and Sami indigenous rights, drawing protests from local reindeer herders to Greta Thunberg.

subject: Kaohsiung Music Center
summary: A sweeping harborfront complex at the mouth of the Love River, designed by a Spanish architecture team and opened in 2021, that puts Kaohsiung at the center of Asia's pop music industry with an open-air auditorium for 10,000 and a waterfront park planted with over a thousand trees.

subject: Katanga Province
summary: The Congolese province whose uranium built the first atomic bombs, whose secession nearly broke the country, and whose mineral wealth has never made its people rich.

subject: Kent Island (California)
summary: A small Marin County island where a 1960s hotel and marina development was defeated by conservationists.

subject: Kiautschou Governor's Hall
summary: A grand German colonial government building in Qingdao that served five occupying powers in four decades before becoming the city's town hall for the People's Republic.

subject: Kilchurn Castle
summary: A ruined Campbell stronghold on Loch Awe that served as both clan fortress and government barracks across three centuries of Highland power struggles.

subject: Kinkasan Lighthouse
summary: A Meiji-era lighthouse on the sacred island of Kinkasan, designed by the Scottish engineer who built Japan's entire modern lighthouse system -- destroyed by the U.S. Navy in 1945, rebuilt within months, and still guiding ships today.

subject: Kirkbride Plan
summary: A 19th-century architectural philosophy that tried to cure mental illness through building design, leaving behind haunting bat-winged asylums across America.

subject: Klamath Project
summary: One of America's first federal irrigation projects, where drained wetlands feed both farms and fierce water wars that pit salmon against settlers.

subject: Kolwezi tailings project
summary: A copper-and-cobalt reclamation effort on a Congolese valley filled with seventy years of mine waste, where a billion-dollar dispute reshaped a town's fortunes.

subject: Krishna Temple, Islamabad
summary: Islamabad's first Hindu temple, approved after decades of effort but still unbuilt, has become a flashpoint for Pakistan's struggle between constitutional minority rights and religious extremism.

subject: Ksiaz Castle
summary: Poland's third-largest castle perches above the Pelcznica gorge, with 400 rooms above and a still-mysterious Nazi tunnel complex carved by forced labor below.

subject: LWD Basket
summary: A Leeuwarden basketball club that lost a cup final to a virus, lost its licence to a balance sheet, and rose again in 2023 in blue and yellow as LWD Basket, named after the city's airport code.

subject: La Chureca
summary: For decades, hundreds of families in Managua lived and worked inside Central America's largest open-air landfill, building a community from what the rest of the city threw away — until an international development project began transforming the site.

subject: La Orchila Island
summary: A Caribbean island named for the lichen that once covered it, La Orchila has served as a guano mine, a presidential retreat, a political prison, and a proposed base for Russian strategic bombers.

subject: La Quemada
summary: An archaeological fortress in Zacatecas that may be the legendary 'Seven Caves' of Aztec migration -- a hilltop citadel that thrived for nine centuries before burning to the ground.

subject: Lagdo Reservoir
summary: A Chinese-built dam in northern Cameroon whose periodic water releases have flooded Nigerian cities, displaced tens of thousands, and ignited a decades-long transboundary dispute over a downstream dam that was promised but never built.

subject: Laguna Diversion Dam
summary: The first dam ever built on the Colorado River — completed in 1909, it ended the era of steamboat travel on the lower river, created Mittry Lake, and was decorated with swastikas that carried no Nazi meaning, only the ancient symbol of good fortune that most of the world had not yet learned to see differently.

subject: Lam Chau
summary: A small granite island west of Chek Lap Kok that ceased to exist in the 1990s, flattened and absorbed into the land reclamation project that built Hong Kong International Airport.

subject: Leeuwarden Middelsee railway station
summary: Planned for 2018, then 2020, then later - a still-unbuilt station in the south of Leeuwarden whose name commemorates a vanished sea.

subject: Lelystad Airport
summary: A finished terminal, a paved 2,700-metre runway, and a decade of political deadlock have made Lelystad the airport that cannot quite open.

subject: Lewa Wildlife Conservancy
summary: A former cattle ranch turned UNESCO-listed sanctuary in the shadow of Mount Kenya, home to the world's largest population of Grevy's zebra - and the place a future king proposed.

subject: Lille Vildmose
summary: Northwest Europe's largest surviving raised bog, drained for two centuries and mined for peat, is now the ground under Denmark's only wild moose.

subject: Lion Rock Tunnel
summary: Hong Kong's first major road tunnel, bored through a granite ridgeline in 1967 as a byproduct of a water-supply scheme, and now the busiest non-harbour road crossing in the city.

subject: Little Saigon, San Jose
summary: Home to more Vietnamese residents than any city outside Vietnam, San Jose's Little Saigon is a neighborhood whose very name was won through protests, hunger strikes, and a community that refused to compromise on identity.

subject: Lochaber Hydroelectric Scheme
summary: An interwar engineering project that bores 18 miles of tunnel through the Highlands to power an aluminium smelter at Fort William, drawing water from the Spey and Spean catchments.

subject: Lok Ma Chau Loop
summary: A 0.97 km² riverside parcel transferred from mainland China to Hong Kong in 2017 — created by accident when river-straightening engineering work moved the border, leaving a loop of land that spent years in jurisdictional limbo before becoming the proposed site of a cross-border technology park.

subject: London Docklands
summary: Once the world's largest port, London's Docklands collapsed in a decade, sat derelict for another, and then became the most dramatic urban regeneration project in British history — producing Canary Wharf's skyline, one of Europe's biggest internet hubs, and some of the starkest inequality visible from any city street.

story.title: Los Alamos: The Secret City That Changed the World

subject: Los Alamos, New Mexico
summary: Perched on a remote mesa in the Jemez Mountains, the town that began as a boys' ranch school became the birthplace of the atomic bomb and remains one of the most scientifically concentrated communities on Earth.

subject: Love Canal
summary: The neighborhood that poisoned America - where 21,000 tons of toxic chemicals buried beneath a suburban housing development caused birth defects, illness, and the birth of the environmental justice movement.

subject: Lower Se San 2 Dam
summary: Cambodia's largest hydropower project flooded three villages and moved nearly five thousand people, most of them Indigenous. More than 180 families refused to go.

subject: Lower Zambezi National Park
summary: A Zambian national park that began life as the president's private hunting ground, now shares a UNESCO-listed floodplain with Zimbabwe's Mana Pools and fights a live court battle over a copper mine proposed inside its boundaries.

subject: Lunar Orbiter Image Recovery Project
summary: In an abandoned McDonald's near NASA Ames, volunteers rescued the highest-resolution images of the Moon ever taken from 1960s tape drives that were destined for the scrap heap.

story.title: Luray Caverns: The Cave Where Rocks Make Music

subject: Luray Caverns
summary: The Virginia cave system where an engineer spent three years wiring stalactites to create the world's largest musical instrument - covering 3.5 acres, producing eerie tones when rubber mallets strike ancient rock formations in a subterranean concert hall.

story.title: Lviv Theatre of Opera and Ballet

subject: Lviv Theatre of Opera and Ballet
summary: Built atop a buried river on what was then Europe's first reinforced concrete foundation, the Lviv Opera has outlasted the architect who designed it, the empires that claimed it, and the rumors that it was sinking.

subject: MIPS Technologies
summary: Stanford's RISC processor project became a company that powered everything from game consoles to routers before abandoning its own architecture for the open-source RISC-V standard.

subject: Mabilafu
summary: A Temne village on the Rokel River where four families have shared the land for generations, until a foreign biofuel project rewrote the rules.

subject: Mackinac Bridge
summary: A suspension bridge 70 years in the making, the Mackinac Bridge finally stitched Michigan's two peninsulas together in 1957 -- and its design was born from the spectacular collapse of another bridge 17 years earlier.

subject: Magdeburg Water Bridge
summary: Construction began in 1905 and finished in 2003: a canal carried across the Elbe on 918 metres of steel and concrete, so that barges bound for Berlin never have to touch the river below.

subject: Marincello
summary: A failed 1960s development that would have covered the Marin Headlands with a planned city of 30,000 people.

subject: Marjah
summary: An American-engineered irrigation project turned Cold War showcase turned opium capital turned battleground -- Marjah's identity has been remade by outsiders for seventy years.

subject: Marpole Midden
summary: c̓əsnaʔəm, an ancient Musqueam village and burial ground near the mouth of the Fraser River, occupied for four thousand years, excavated by outsiders for a century, and finally returned to the Musqueam by 2018.

subject: Mbandaka
summary: Founded by Henry Morton Stanley just four kilometers from the equator, Mbandaka was once planned as the capital of the Congo Free State and later became the birthplace of Habitat for Humanity's first project.

subject: Merowe Dam
summary: Africa's largest contemporary hydropower project, inaugurated in 2009 after displacing 55,000 to 70,000 Manasir, Hamadab, and Amri villagers whose date palms and river-farming lives were buried beneath a 174-kilometer-long reservoir.

subject: Metrocentre
summary: When it opened in 1986 on the site of a demolished power station, Metrocentre had over 210 shops, an enclosed funfair, and a Roman Forum, and for a moment was Europe's largest shopping centre.

story.title: Minato Mirai 21: Yokohama's Port of the Future

subject: Minato Mirai 21
summary: Built on the bones of a Mitsubishi shipyard and a rail classification yard, Yokohama's Minato Mirai 21 district transformed derelict waterfront into Japan's most ambitious urban renewal project -- a glittering business district where 79,000 people work beneath the country's third-tallest skyscraper.

subject: Mogadishu Lighthouse
summary: A crumbling Italian colonial lighthouse on Mogadishu's waterfront, once a vital navigation aid and now the centerpiece of a UNESCO-led heritage restoration project.

subject: Moldavian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic
summary: A republic invented as a political weapon, drawn on the Dniester in 1924 to lay claim to land across the river, ruled from Tiraspol until it vanished in 1940.

subject: Monroe Correctional Complex
summary: Washington state's largest prison, the Monroe Correctional Complex has operated on the same site since 1910, evolving from a single reformatory into a sprawling multi-unit facility that holds over 3,100 people.

subject: Montreal Laboratory
summary: Hidden inside a borrowed university building, a team of French, British, and Canadian scientists quietly designed some of the world's first nuclear reactors during World War II -- a secret chapter of the Manhattan Project that reshaped atomic history and nearly tore three allied nations apart.

subject: Morecambe
summary: Once Bradford-on-Sea and home to Eric Morecambe himself, the town is rewriting a long story of seaside decline with the Midland Hotel restored and Eden Project Morecambe on the way.

subject: Morlais
summary: A 240 MW tidal energy demonstration zone off Holy Island - the largest consented tidal scheme of its kind anywhere - led by a Welsh social enterprise rather than a multinational utility.

subject: Mount Coffee Hydropower Project
summary: A hydroelectric dam on Liberia's Saint Paul River, destroyed by civil war in 1990, was rebuilt over 25 years to more than double the nation's power-generating capacity.

story.title: Mount Rushmore: The Mountain They Carved Into Presidents

subject: Mount Rushmore
summary: The South Dakota granite carved into four presidential faces - a monument conceived to boost tourism, sculpted by a man with Klan connections, on land sacred to the Lakota, using dynamite to remove 450,000 tons of rock that still lies in rubble below.

subject: Mountain View Adobe
summary: Built in 1934 as a New Deal Civil Works Administration project on land the city bought for ten dollars in 1929, the Historic Adobe Building on Moffett Boulevard has served as pump station, reservoir site, and multi-purpose community building.

subject: Museo Picasso Málaga
summary: Housed in a 16th-century palace built atop Phoenician ruins and a Roman fish-sauce factory, this museum returned Picasso's art to the city of his birth fifty years after the idea was first proposed.

subject: Museu Picasso
summary: The world's first museum dedicated to Pablo Picasso occupies five medieval palaces on a single Barcelona street, tracing the young artist's formative years in a city he chose over his birthplace.

subject: Museum Nord, Narvik
summary: Housed in Narvik's original 1902 railway headquarters, this industrial heritage museum tells the story of how Swedish iron ore built an Arctic town from nothing.

story.title: Museum of the Great Western Railway

subject: Museum of the Great Western Railway
summary: Inside one of the largest railway works the world has ever seen, a museum tells the story of Brunel's broad-gauge dream, three locomotives a week, and the women who built boilers in 1943.

subject: Naegi Castle
summary: A mountain castle with distinctive red clay walls, Naegi Castle served the Toyama clan for twelve generations through some of the most dramatic episodes of Japan's feudal era, from Oda Nobunaga's wars against the Takeda to the Battle of Sekigahara.

subject: Nansi Lake
summary: Northern China's largest freshwater lake is actually four lakes in one, shaped across centuries by Yellow River floods, Grand Canal engineering, and now serving as a critical reservoir for the South-North Water Diversion Project.

subject: National Art Schools (Cuba)
summary: Born from a round of golf between Castro and Che Guevara, Cuba's National Art Schools became one of the revolution's greatest architectural achievements -- then were abandoned to the jungle for decades.

subject: National Coach Museum
summary: The most visited museum in Portugal houses a dazzling collection of royal horse-drawn vehicles spanning four centuries, displayed across a historic riding school and a striking modernist pavilion.

story.title: National Museum of African American History and Culture

subject: National Museum of African American History and Culture
summary: African American Union veterans first proposed this museum in 1915 - 101 years before David Adjaye's bronze corona on the Mall finally opened in 2016 to tell the whole story.

subject: National War Memorial (Canada)
summary: A granite arch in the heart of Ottawa where 22 bronze figures march forever toward duty, honoring every Canadian who has served in every conflict past and future.

subject: Navy Island, Jamaica
summary: A 64-acre island off Port Antonio that passed from a colonial governor to the Royal Navy to Errol Flynn to a doomed resort venture before Jamaica's government finally closed it to development entirely.

subject: Never Forgotten National Memorial
summary: A proposed 24-metre war memorial statue for Cape Breton's Green Cove that ignited a national debate over patriotism, landscape, and the limits of commemoration before being cancelled in 2016.

subject: New Westminster
summary: British Columbia's first mainland capital burned to the ground in a single night in 1898, and the city that rebuilt itself on the Fraser has been quietly reinventing its name ever since.

subject: Nghi Sơn Refinery
summary: Vietnam's second oil refinery — nine billion dollars, four owners on two continents, and a village levelled to make the ground flat enough to build on.

subject: Ngong Ping 360
summary: A 5.7-kilometer gondola ride across Tung Chung Bay to the plateau above — and the troubled, tenacious story of how Hong Kong built a cable car that took years, criminal charges, and a typhoon to finally get right.

subject: Niels Bohr Institute
summary: The Copenhagen institute where quantum mechanics was argued into its modern shape, where hafnium was discovered, and from which its founder escaped occupied Denmark in the bomb bay of a Mosquito.

subject: Nieuwe Toren, Kampen
summary: A 17th-century Kampen bell tower whose 48 Hemony bells still mark the hours, and whose lantern was designed for a building it never reached.

subject: Norfolk Tank Museum
summary: A private collector's passion project turned registered charity, the Norfolk Tank Museum houses around 30 armoured vehicles in the Norfolk countryside — including a replica of a First World War tank built for television that retraced a real tank's final journey to France.

subject: North Fork Sol Duc Shelter
summary: A fourteen-by-ten log lean-to built around 1932, one of roughly eighteen survivors from a network of ninety Forest Service trail shelters that opened the Olympic interior and then were mostly torn down.

subject: North Point Estate
summary: Completed in 1957 and hailed as one of Asia's most impressive housing schemes, North Point Estate gave 1,956 families a harbour-front home — then was quietly demolished and replaced with hotels and parking.

subject: Northeast Ecological Corridor
summary: A nearly 3,000-acre stretch of Puerto Rico's northeast coast that community activists fought for decades to protect from mega-resort development, saving critical nesting habitat for endangered leatherback sea turtles.

subject: Oak Ridge National Laboratory
summary: Born from the Manhattan Project's wartime secrecy, Oak Ridge National Laboratory grew from a plutonium production site into the largest science and energy lab in the U.S. Department of Energy system, home to world-leading supercomputers and neutron research.

subject: Ocean Wind 1
summary: An offshore wind farm that was supposed to power half a million New Jersey homes - and which was cancelled in 2023 after eight years of planning, leaving 75,525 acres of leased ocean empty.

subject: Oceanside Pier
summary: The Oceanside Pier has been rebuilt six times since 1888 — battered by storms, rebuilt by stubborn optimism, and as of 2024, partially damaged by fire — yet it remains the defining landmark of California's North County coast.

story.title: Oistins: Where a Drunkard's Name Became a Nation's Treaty

subject: Oistins
summary: A fishing village on the south coast of Barbados where a 1652 treaty secured the island's autonomy, a Cold War-era supergun project operated nearby, and Friday night fish fries became a beloved island tradition.

subject: Old Mission Dam
summary: Built in 1803 by mission labor to redirect the San Diego River, this stone dam was the first major irrigation project on the Pacific coast of the United States — and it still stands.

subject: Olivenhain Dam
summary: California's first roller-compacted concrete dam was built near Escondido without sitting on any river — its reservoir filled entirely by pumps and pipes as part of San Diego's emergency water storage system.

subject: Oosterscheldekering
summary: Nine kilometres of concrete pillars and sixty-two movable steel doors that decided, after a decade of debate, that an estuary was worth keeping alive.

subject: Oosterweel Link
summary: The road that took thirty years to start: a multi-billion-euro tunnel project to finally close Antwerp's R1 Ring Road, after referendums, citizen revolts, name changes, and three Flemish governments.

subject: Orange–Fish River Tunnel
summary: Blasted through 82.8 kilometers of rock beneath the Karoo, the Orange-Fish River Tunnel is the longest continuous enclosed aqueduct in the southern hemisphere -- and it cost 51 workers their lives to build.

story.title: Osaka Science Museum: Where Japan's First Planetarium Met Its First Nobel Prize

subject: Osaka Science Museum
summary: The Osaka Science Museum sits on the Nakanoshima island where physicist Hideki Yukawa developed the meson theory that won Japan's first Nobel Prize, and where Japan's very first planetarium projected stars onto a dome in 1937.

story.title: Our Lady of the Rosary Church, Lavras

subject: Our Lady of the Rosary Church, Lavras
summary: The oldest surviving building in Lavras, this Baroque-Rococo church was nearly demolished for a social club in 1940 before locals fought to save it.

subject: Ouse Washes
summary: A 32-kilometer strip of managed floodplain between two parallel artificial rivers in the East Anglian Fens, the Ouse Washes host one of England's most important wetland habitats — drawn from deliberate 17th-century engineering and holding international significance for wintering wildfowl.

subject: Oxford University Press
summary: The world's largest university press, where a forty-four-year dictionary project, a flawed first edition of Alice in Wonderland, and four hundred years of printing privilege all live on Walton Street.

story.title: Ozark Riverways: America's First Protected Wild Rivers

subject: Ozark Riverways
summary: The Missouri spring-fed rivers where America first decided some waterways shouldn't have dams - the Current and Jacks Fork flowing clear through Ozark hills, protected since 1964 as the country's first national scenic riverway.

subject: Padma Bridge
summary: Bangladesh's most ambitious infrastructure project, the 6.15 km Padma Bridge crosses the mighty Padma River to connect the country's impoverished southwest to the capital - built entirely with domestic funds after a World Bank corruption scandal nearly killed the dream.

subject: Palm Springs Aerial Tramway
summary: The world's largest rotating aerial tramway climbs from the Sonoran Desert floor to the alpine wilderness of Mount San Jacinto in ten minutes, rising nearly six thousand feet through five distinct life zones — a journey that Francis Crocker dreamed up in 1935 and everyone else called impossible.

subject: Panama Canal expansion project
summary: Completed in 2016 after nearly a decade of construction, the Third Set of Locks doubled the canal's capacity and opened the waterway to a new generation of massive cargo ships.

subject: Pedro Carbo Canton
summary: Named for a nineteenth-century Guayaquileño statesman who died in exile, Pedro Carbo Canton covers a thousand square kilometers of dry tropical forest, farmland, and seasonal rivers.

subject: Peninnis Head
summary: The southernmost point of St Mary's, a tangle of weathered Hercynian granite cairns and rare lichens that ends in a lighthouse and a rock climber's project called Rock Hard Peninnis.

subject: Penrith Castle
summary: A 15th-century red sandstone fortress that was Richard III's northern base, now reduced to ruined walls beside a Cumbrian railway station.

subject: Permanent Court of International Justice
summary: The first true world court, attached to the League of Nations, which sat at the Peace Palace in The Hague from 1922 to 1946 and laid the practical foundation for today's International Court of Justice.

subject: Ping Yuen
summary: Chinatown's first public housing project, whose name means 'Tranquil Gardens' -- a complex that has served the community since the 1950s.

subject: Pisgah Astronomical Research Institute
summary: A former NASA Apollo tracking station turned NSA spy base turned public observatory, hidden in the dark forests near Balsam Grove.

subject: Polar Line
summary: An incomplete railway in northern Norway, built by the Wehrmacht during World War II using forced labor, stretching from Fauske toward Narvik through some of the most rugged terrain in Scandinavia.

subject: Polavaram Project
summary: India's most ambitious dam project, decades in the making, promises to transform Andhra Pradesh's Godavari delta while displacing hundreds of thousands and redrawing state borders.

subject: Port Erin
summary: A south-west Manx seaside village with a sandy bay, a failed Victorian breakwater under its waters, and a long association with marine biology and motor racing.

subject: Port of Belém
summary: The engineers who designed Belém's modern port wanted to bury its old marketplace under landfill; the traders stopped them, and the port grew up around the dock it failed to erase.

subject: Presidential Palace, Hanoi
summary: A mustard-yellow colonial palace where Ho Chi Minh famously refused to live, choosing a modest stilt house on its grounds instead.

subject: Presidential Palace, Naypyidaw
summary: A moat-encircled 100-room palace built to legitimize military rule, the Presidential Palace in Naypyidaw embodies the grandiose ambitions and turbulent politics of modern Myanmar.

subject: Princess Amalia Wind Farm
summary: The 2008 wind farm off IJmuiden, named for a newborn crown princess, that broke the financial mold for offshore wind and outlasted the turbines it was built with.

subject: Project Carryall
summary: A 1963 proposal to blast an interstate highway pass through California's Bristol Mountains using 22 nuclear bombs — a plan that promised 'occasional rock missiles' up to 4,000 feet high, a dust cloud 100 miles wide, and a four-day closure of everything nearby.

story.title: Project HARP: The Space Gun of Barbados

subject: Project HARP
summary: On the eastern coast of Barbados, a rusting 120-foot cannon points skyward -- the remains of a Cold War program that tried to shoot objects into orbit and set a world altitude record that still stands.

subject: Project One (San Francisco)
summary: A 1970s technological commune in a South of Market warehouse where artists, hackers, and community radio pioneers shared space and built the infrastructure for San Francisco's digital counterculture.

subject: Puerto Nariño
summary: A car-free town of 2,000 at the edge of the Amazon, where 95% of residents are Ticuna, Cocama or Yagua, and the streets have never heard an engine.

subject: Purissima, California
summary: A ghost town on the San Mateo County coast that was supposed to be the big town but was always harder to get to.

subject: Putuo Zongcheng Temple
summary: A massive Qing-era replica of Tibet's Potala Palace, built in the hills of Hebei to celebrate an emperor's birthday and project imperial power across a multicultural empire.

subject: Puyehue-Cordón Caulle
summary: A coalesced complex of Chilean volcanoes whose 2011 eruption sent ash around the entire Southern Hemisphere, grounding flights from Bariloche to Melbourne.

subject: Pwllheli Railway Station
summary: The northern terminus of the Cambrian Coast line, opened in 1867, scaled back from a busy GWR junction to a single-platform halt where the rails simply stop.

subject: Queen Victoria Hospital
summary: The small Sussex hospital where Archibald McIndoe rebuilt the faces of burned airmen during the Second World War - founding the Guinea Pig Club, transforming plastic surgery, and remaking the town around them.

subject: Quinta Monroy
summary: A radical half-a-house housing project in Iquique, Chile, where architect Alejandro Aravena gave 93 families the bones of a home and let them finish the rest.

subject: RAF Cark
summary: A wartime RAF training station between Cark and Flookburgh that began as a fighter base, became a pilot school, and now spends its days launching parachutists over Morecambe Bay.

subject: Race Rocks Ecological Reserve
summary: Eleven islets in the Strait of Juan de Fuca where the tide runs like a river, a granite lighthouse from 1860 stands, and a student science project turned into a protected area.

story.title: Race Rocks Tidal Power Demonstration Project

subject: Race Rocks Tidal Power Demonstration Project
summary: North America's first in-stream tidal generator spun beneath a granite lighthouse in one of the fiercest tidal races on the coast — and the same water that powered it ground its bearings apart.

subject: Raceway Venray
summary: The only NASCAR-style banked oval in the Netherlands - born from a parish motocross fundraiser, demolished as illegal, and rebuilt half a kilometre away.

subject: Raid on Manila
summary: In January 1798, two British frigates sailed into Manila Bay flying French colors, tricked Spanish officers into boarding for dinner, captured gunboats without a shot fired, and sailed away -- one of the most audacious deceptions of the French Revolutionary Wars.

subject: Rainbow Bridge (Tokyo)
summary: A 798-meter suspension bridge spanning Tokyo Bay between Shibaura Pier and the Odaiba waterfront, where white towers, solar-powered tri-color lights, and views of Mount Fuji on clear days transformed an infrastructure project into the city's most photogenic landmark.

subject: Ramona Gardens
summary: Built in the early 1940s as modern public housing for working families in Boyle Heights, Ramona Gardens became home to generations of Chicano families — and to an extraordinary collection of murals that turned the walls of a housing project into outdoor art galleries.

subject: Randolph Air Force Base
summary: The 'West Point of the Air' -- a perfectly circular military base designed by a motor pool dispatch officer, built as the largest Army construction project since the Panama Canal, and named after a man who died while serving on the committee to name it.

subject: Red River Floodway
summary: Mocked as 'Duff's Ditch' when proposed, the Red River Floodway moved more earth than the Suez Canal and has since prevented billions of dollars in flood damage to Winnipeg.

subject: Remains of the 13 Levels
summary: A terraced smelter built into a Taiwanese hillside in 1933, nicknamed the 'Potala Palace of Mountain Mines,' where Allied POWs once labored and artists now project light onto the ruins during the Moon Festival.

subject: Rhodesia (region)
summary: A colonial territory named after Cecil Rhodes by the company he founded, split by a river into what would become Zambia and Zimbabwe - a name imposed in the 1890s and largely abandoned by 1980, along with the political project it described.

subject: Ridderzaal
summary: A 13th-century Gothic banqueting hall in central The Hague whose timber ceiling looks like an upturned ship, whose carved heads watch politicians for lies, and whose floor has seen the founding of the European project and the negotiated end of an empire.

subject: Rincon Center
summary: The former Rincon Annex Post Office, with its controversial New Deal murals depicting California's history without flinching, was reborn as a mixed-use center in San Francisco's South of Market.

subject: Rocky Point, Montana (ghost town)
summary: Where buffalo trails became outlaw hideouts: a Missouri River ghost town that served steamboats, sheltered rustlers, and vanished beneath a dam that was never built.

subject: Roscrea Castle
summary: A 13th-century Norman castle in the heart of Roscrea, County Tipperary, where a Georgian house was nearly demolished to build a bacon factory.

subject: Rossport
summary: A Gaeltacht village on the north Mayo coast where five farmers went to prison in 2005 rather than yield their land to a Shell pipeline, and where an English conman once spent a £4,000 legacy on stolen horses.

subject: Rotterdam Ahoy
summary: An indoor arena designed to look like a ship that became a Covid field hospital, then turned around and hosted Eurovision a year later.

subject: Roy Hill Mine
summary: Australia's richest woman bet ten billion dollars and a private railway that her father's iron empire could be reborn in the red dirt of the Chichester Range.

subject: Royal Air Force Museum Midlands
summary: The Shropshire half of the Royal Air Force Museum: V-bombers, the surviving TSR-2, the world's only Boulton Paul Defiant, all free to walk among.

subject: Royal Courts of Justice
summary: George Edmund Street's Gothic Revival masterpiece on the Strand has dispensed England's highest civil justice since 1882 — and killed its architect before he ever saw it open.

subject: Royal Whanganui Opera House
summary: New Zealand's last surviving Victorian theatre, born from a borough councillor's ambition and an architect who died the day his foundation stone was laid.

subject: SMS Iltis (1878)
summary: Named for the polecat, this small German gunboat spent sixteen years patrolling East Asian waters -- chasing pirates, planting flags, rescuing shipwrecked soldiers -- before a typhoon broke her in half off the Shandong coast.

subject: SS John Witherspoon
summary: A Liberty ship named for a Founding Father, sunk on her maiden voyage in the Arctic during the catastrophic Convoy PQ-17.

subject: Sacré-Cœur, Paris
summary: Born from national humiliation, built on contested ground, and still sparking political fury more than a century later, the white basilica crowning Montmartre is the most argued-about church in France.

subject: Sai Cinza Indigenous Territory
summary: Home to the Munduruku people along the upper Tapajos, this 126,000-hectare territory in Para became a flashpoint in Brazil's dam wars when a proposed hydroelectric project threatened to flood indigenous land the constitution forbids relocating.

subject: Sai Kung Peninsula
summary: The Sai Kung Peninsula juts into the South China Sea as Hong Kong's wildest and least urbanized terrain — a volcanic landscape of pirate history, hexagonal rock columns, coral reefs, and trails that take you somewhere that feels nothing like a city of seven million people.

subject: Saigon Governor's Palace
summary: A ruinously expensive neo-Baroque palace built on waterlogged ground in 1860s Saigon to project French imperial power, only to sink, crack, get bombed, and finally be demolished a century later.

subject: Saint Isaac's Cathedral
summary: Forty years to build, 112 monolithic granite columns weighing more than 100 tons each, and three lives - cathedral, Soviet Museum of Atheism, museum-with-occasional-services - in two centuries.

subject: Sakhalin-II
summary: A massive oil and gas project off Sakhalin Island where endangered gray whales feed, Sakhalin-II became a flashpoint for geopolitics, environmental activism, and Russia's reassertion of control over its energy resources.

subject: Salem Memorial Ballpark
summary: The minor league park where Salem voters approved their own ballpark by an 85 percent margin - and where, on a 15-inning opening night, the Avalanche won in front of a standing-room-only crowd with the Blue Ridge as the backdrop.

story.title: Samboja Lestari: Planting a Forest from Scratch

subject: Samboja Lestari
summary: On 2,000 hectares of land so degraded that coal seams spontaneously caught fire, a controversial project has regrown a forest, returned orangutans to the wild, and changed the local weather.

subject: Sambor Wildlife Sanctuary
summary: Fifty thousand hectares of Mekong forest and riverbank in Kratie province, protected by a single sub-decree in 2018 - on the same stretch of river where the largest dam ever proposed for the lower mainstream is still drawn on paper.

story.title: San Antonio: The Alamo City Where Texas Identity Was Forged

subject: San Antonio
summary: The Texas city where 189 defenders died becoming legend - where the River Walk turns a flood control project into tourist attraction, where the missions still stand from Spanish colonial days, and where Tex-Mex cuisine originated.

story.title: San Antonio River Walk: The Drainage Ditch That Became Texas's Soul

subject: San Antonio River Walk
summary: The Texas waterway that was almost paved over for a parking lot until civic imagination saved it - where mariachi music echoes off limestone walls, where barges cruise beneath towering cypress, and where a flood-control project became America's second-most-visited attraction.

subject: San Bruno Mountain State Park
summary: The park that pioneered America's first habitat conservation plan protects endangered butterflies and Bay Area views on a ridge developers nearly buried under houses.

subject: San Jose de Buenavista
summary: The capital of Antique province on Panay Island, San Jose de Buenavista earned its name -- Spanish for 'good view' -- when colonial administrators fled a swampy, earthquake-prone capital for higher ground.

subject: San Vicente Dam
summary: Between 2009 and 2014, engineers raised San Vicente Dam by 117 feet — the largest dam raise in American history — transforming a Depression-era water project into San Diego's biggest reservoir.

subject: Sand Engine
summary: A 21.5-million-cubic-meter hook of sand off the South Holland coast, deposited in one giant pulse and left to the sea to redistribute over twenty years.

subject: Sangarius Bridge
summary: Justinian's 430-meter limestone bridge, completed in 562 CE in Anatolia, has carried traffic across a shifting river plain for nearly fifteen centuries.

subject: Santa Ana de Velasco
summary: The smallest and most authentic of the Chiquitos missions, its church was raised by the indigenous community itself after the Jesuits were gone.

subject: Sarmizegetusa Regia
summary: The mountaintop capital of the Dacian kingdom held running water, astronomical sanctuaries, and a name so potent that Rome's conquerors borrowed it for their own replacement city 40 kilometers away.

subject: Sawré Muybu Indigenous Territory
summary: The Munduruku-named Daje Kapap Eipi, a sacred homeland on the Tapajos River where the Munduruku stopped Brazil's largest proposed Amazon dam through self-demarcation.

subject: Scolpaig Tower
summary: A Georgian folly built around 1830 on an Iron Age dun in a North Uist loch - architecture as famine relief, ruin as bird sanctuary.

subject: Scottish Parliament Building
summary: A bold, controversial architectural statement at the foot of Edinburgh's Royal Mile, the Scottish Parliament Building became one of the most debated structures in British history before winning the Stirling Prize.

subject: Seelbach Hotel
summary: Two Bavarian brothers built Louisville's grandest hotel just in time for the 1905 Kentucky Derby, creating a place that would host presidents, shelter gangsters, inspire F. Scott Fitzgerald, and survive bankruptcy to anchor an entire district.

subject: Sepilok Orangutan Rehabilitation Centre
summary: The world's first official orangutan rehabilitation project, opened in 1964 in Borneo's virgin rainforest, has returned orphaned orangutans to the wild for six decades.

subject: Serra d'Irta Natural Park
summary: A rare stretch of undeveloped Costa del Azahar coast, where a mountain range drops in cliffs and coves straight into a protected sea.

subject: Seton Castle
summary: Robert Adam's final Scottish project, a castellated Georgian mansion built from the stones of the demolished Seton Palace - the very palace where Mary, Queen of Scots had taken refuge after the murder of her husband.

subject: Shannon Hydroelectric Scheme
summary: Ireland's young Free State staked a fifth of its annual budget on a single dam, and Ardnacrusha electrified a nation.

subject: Shannon-Erne Waterway
summary: A 63-kilometre canal with sixteen locks linking the Shannon and the Erne - failed in 1860, abandoned by 1869, reopened as a cross-border peace project in May 1994.

subject: Shrewsbury Flower Show
summary: The world's longest-running flower show, founded in Shrewsbury in 1875 and held in the Quarry Park until financial pressures cancelled the 2025 and 2026 editions.

subject: Siadar Wave Power Station
summary: A four-megawatt wave farm planned for the Atlantic edge of Lewis, approved with fanfare in 2009 and quietly cancelled four years later.

subject: Sites Reservoir
summary: A decades-old dream to bank California's floodwater is finally breaking ground in the Sacramento Valley, promising to reshape how the state survives drought.

subject: South Amazon Ecotones Ecological Corridor
summary: A proposed 761,000 square kilometer corridor of linked reserves and indigenous territories where the rainforest bleeds into savanna - one of the most threatened stretches of the Amazon basin.

subject: South Kasai
summary: Born from ethnic violence and diamond wealth during the Congo Crisis, South Kasai's brief existence as a secessionist state left behind massacres, a deposed leader, and a renamed city.

subject: South Ronaldsay
summary: The southernmost Orkney Island, connected to Mainland by causeways the Italian POWs who built them weren't supposed to be building, and home to a small town named for an English saint by way of a Norse earl.

subject: Soviet Cruiser Mikhail Kutuzov
summary: One of the last big-gun cruisers the Soviet Navy ever built now sits at a quay in Novorossiysk, a 210-meter relic of the Cold War that visitors can walk from bow to stern.

subject: Soviet cruiser Murmansk (1955)
summary: A Cold War-era Soviet light cruiser that ended its days as a rusting shipwreck off a Norwegian fishing village, too far gone to tow and too toxic to ignore.

subject: Space Center Houston
summary: The only place on Earth where you can touch a Moon rock, walk inside a Space Shuttle, and stand beneath a Saturn V rocket assembled from stages that were meant to fly to the Moon but never did.

subject: Sparta
summary: For three centuries, the city-state of Sparta shaped the ancient Greek world through military discipline, a rigid social order built on enslaved labor, and a system of total formation — the agoge — that turned its citizens into the most feared soldiers in Greece.

subject: Spruce 1
summary: A proposed mountaintop-removal coal mine in West Virginia that became the most contested permit in American mining history before the EPA killed it in 2011.

subject: St Austell
summary: A Methodist tin-town turned into Cornwall's china clay capital, where white tips still rise like minor Alps and the Eden Project blooms inside an exhausted pit.

subject: Stanford Mausoleum
summary: A sphinx-guarded tomb where Stanford University's founding family rests -- and where sophomores throw one of the campus's wildest Halloween parties each year.

subject: Stanford University Arboretum
summary: Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted to showcase 'all the trees and wood plants of the world,' Stanford's arboretum was instead partly sold off for a shopping mall -- though Jane Stanford had declared it should be 'sacredly preserved from mutilation.'

subject: Stanford University School of Engineering
summary: From a student-built electric railroad in 1894 to the 1969 occupation of the Applied Electronics Lab, Stanford Engineering has been at the center of both innovation and controversy.

subject: State of Kanawha
summary: The name West Virginia almost had - a proposed Indigenous name for the new state rejected by a 30-14 vote at the 1861 Wheeling Constitutional Convention.

subject: Statue of Bruce Lee, Mostar
summary: In a city still healing from ethnic war, a youth group chose a kung fu movie star as the one figure everyone could agree on -- and placed his bronze likeness in a park.

subject: Strathcona, Vancouver
summary: Vancouver's oldest residential neighbourhood was condemned, partly bulldozed, and then saved by the people who lived in it - a rescue the city has been quietly undoing ever since.

subject: Stung Sen Dam
summary: A 38-metre dam proposed for the biggest of the Tonle Sap's tributaries, whose official file answers the three most important questions with the words "not available."

subject: Stung Treng Dam
summary: A proposed eleven-kilometre wall across the Mekong mainstream that has changed hands, been shelved, and been quietly restudied for nearly two decades without a single cubic metre being poured.

subject: Stånga Church
summary: A medieval church on Gotland harboring monumental Gothic sculptures that were never meant to be where they stand today, remnants of an ambitious building project abandoned seven centuries ago.

story.title: The Submarine Boat Company: Newark's Wartime Shipyard That Never Built a Submarine

subject: Submarine Boat Company
summary: Despite its name, the Submarine Boat Company never built a single submarine -- instead, this Newark shipyard employed 25,000 workers at its peak and launched 150 cargo ships during World War I, assembling prefabricated hulls at a speed that helped sustain the Allied supply chain across the Atlantic.

subject: Sulukule
summary: For nearly a thousand years, the Romani community of Sulukule kept the music alive against Istanbul's ancient land walls — until a 2000s demolition project erased the neighborhood and scattered its people.

subject: Sunda Strait Bridge
summary: A decades-long dream to span the 27-kilometer Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra with one of the world's longest bridges -- a megaproject that has been proposed, debated, championed, and shelved since the 1960s.

subject: Swartz Bay ferry terminal
summary: Vancouver Island's front door to the mainland and the Gulf Islands - a five-berth ferry terminal at the end of Highway 17 that a premier proposed seventy years before anyone built it.

subject: São José do Rio Preto
summary: The northwest São Paulo city that eliminated its last favela, treats 100% of its sewage, and plants trees on 97.78% of its streets.

subject: Taikoo Dockyard
summary: For seven decades, the Taikoo Dockyard and Engineering Company built some of the largest ships in the British world at Quarry Bay — where a shopping mall and MTR station now stand.

subject: Taipei Dome
summary: A 40,000-seat domed stadium in Taipei's Xinyi District that took over a decade of political battles to complete, then immediately began breaking attendance records for baseball, basketball, and concerts.

subject: Tamarack Resort
summary: Idaho's phoenix resort that rose from bankruptcy to become a four-season destination on the shores of Lake Cascade.

story.title: Tanjung Perak: Gateway to the Eastern Archipelago

subject: Tanjung Perak
summary: Before Tanjung Perak, Surabaya's ships unloaded into barges on the Madura Strait and hauled cargo up the Kalimas River by hand -- a century of dredging, construction, and reinvention transformed a colonial-era project into Indonesia's second-busiest port.

subject: Tapajós hydroelectric complex
summary: A proposed chain of five Amazon dams that promised ten gigawatts of power and a soy-barge highway, defeated by Munduruku resistance and a constitutional prohibition on flooding indigenous land.

subject: Tar Hollow State Forest
summary: Ohio's third-largest state forest at 16,120 acres, born from a Depression-era federal project that moved subsistence farmers off marginal Appalachian land - a forest grown back from a failure of farming.

subject: Tate Modern
summary: The world's most visited modern art museum, housed in a decommissioned brick power station across the Thames from St Paul's Cathedral, where Olafur Eliasson once put a sun inside a turbine hall.

subject: Taxco
summary: A colonial hillside town in Guerrero where an American architect revived a dying silver mining tradition and turned it into a global jewelry capital, its Baroque church nearly bankrupting the man who built it.

subject: Temperance Flat Dam
summary: A proposed 665-foot dam on the San Joaquin River that would be California's second tallest - if it weren't shelved indefinitely due to staggering costs, environmental objections, and the stubborn math of water economics.

subject: The American College, Leuven
summary: For 154 years a small Catholic seminary in a Belgian university town trained European priests for service in the United States and American priests for advanced study in Leuven - until quietly closing in 2011 for lack of students.

subject: The Bay Lights
summary: 25,000 LEDs turned the Bay Bridge into the world's largest light sculpture -- a Burning Man-inspired artwork that cost $8 million and used $30 of electricity per day.

story.title: The Bridge Built for a Lake That Never Came

subject: The Bridge Built for a Lake That Never Came
summary: California's tallest bridge soars 730 feet above the North Fork American River -- built for a dam that was never completed, it stands as an accidental monument to plans gone sideways and a canyon left wild.

story.title: The Busway That Tamed the Gridlock

subject: The Busway That Tamed the Gridlock
summary: Modeled on Bogota's TransMilenio and launched in 2004 when Jakarta could not afford a subway, TransJakarta grew into the longest bus rapid transit system on Earth -- 251 kilometers of dedicated lanes carrying over a million passengers daily through one of the world's most congested cities.

subject: The Cenotaph, Penang
summary: Built in 1929, bombed in 1945, and rebuilt in 1948, Penang's war memorial on the Esplanade has been destroyed and resurrected, each version a measure of what the community was willing to sacrifice to honor its dead.

subject: The Curve Over the Canyon
summary: A 1,400-foot bridge sweeps in a graceful arc across the Tuolumne River canyon, a young engineer's first major project that foreshadowed a career spent keeping California's bridges standing through earthquakes.

story.title: The Dam That California Could Never Finish -- Or Forget

subject: The Dam That California Could Never Finish -- Or Forget
summary: A 680-foot concrete arch dam that was half-built when an earthquake fifty miles away stopped everything -- leaving behind a billion-dollar hole, the tallest bridge in California, and a debate that refuses to die.

subject: The Dam That Drew Blood
summary: When soldiers opened fire on villagers protesting a dam project on Madura Island in 1993, four people died - and the dam they tried to stop took another two decades to finish.

subject: The Empty Library
summary: Micha Ullman's memorial on Bebelplatz is a white room of empty shelves sunk beneath the cobblestones, sized for the twenty thousand books the Nazis burned above it on 10 May 1933.

story.title: The Fence That Ran to the Sea

subject: The Fence That Ran to the Sea
summary: For two weeks in September 1976, a white nylon fence stretched 24.5 miles across the hills of Sonoma and Marin counties and into the Pacific Ocean -- the most ambitious land art project America had ever seen.

story.title: The Great Wall: The Monument Built on Bones

subject: The Great Wall
summary: Where Chinese dynasties built over 13,000 miles of walls across two millennia, at the cost of perhaps a million lives - creating humanity's largest construction project and most powerful symbol of endurance.

subject: The Greenbrier
summary: Beneath the manicured grounds of one of America's oldest luxury resorts lies a Cold War bunker built to shelter Congress from nuclear annihilation -- a secret that stayed hidden for three decades inside a West Virginia mountain hotel that has hosted 28 presidents since 1778.

subject: The Greenbrier Bunker
summary: Congress's secret hideout - the massive Cold War bunker hidden beneath a luxury West Virginia resort, designed to shelter the entire U.S. Congress during nuclear war and kept secret for thirty years.

subject: The Lake They Almost Nuked
summary: Eastman Lake in the Sierra Nevada foothills exists because the U.S. government decided not to detonate a nuclear bomb to build its dam, choosing conventional construction for Buchanan Dam instead.

subject: The Million-Hectare Mistake
summary: Indonesia's Mega Rice Project turned one million hectares of ancient peat swamp into a carbon bomb that still burns today.

subject: The Peak Lookout
summary: Perched at Victoria Gap near the summit of Victoria Peak, The Peak Lookout is a Grade II Historic Building that has been, in sequence, an engineers' workshop, a sedan chair shelter, a suspected Japanese army police station, and — since 1947 — a restaurant with a terrace overlooking the South China Sea.

story.title: The Redwood Retreat Where Power Relaxes

subject: The Redwood Retreat Where Power Relaxes
summary: Hidden among ancient redwoods near the Russian River, a private campground has hosted presidents, physicists, and captains of industry since 1878, including a meeting that helped launch the Manhattan Project.

subject: Theatro Municipal (São Paulo)
summary: A Parisian-inspired opera house born of coffee wealth, where a baritone's refusal to sing one opera launched opening night with another, and where a week-long artistic rebellion in 1922 remade Brazilian culture forever.

subject: Thirty Meter Telescope protests
summary: A proposed telescope became the focal point for decades of tension between astronomical ambition and Native Hawaiian sovereignty, drawing global attention to the question of who decides what happens on sacred land.

subject: Tom Lantos Tunnels
summary: Twin tunnels bored through Montara Mountain that took 55 years of political battles, one Caltrans scandal, and a 76-percent voter mandate to finally bypass the infamous Devil's Slide.

subject: Treaty of Hadiach
summary: In 1658 a treaty signed in a Ukrainian town proposed a commonwealth of three equal nations; historians call its failure one of the great what-ifs of Eastern Europe.

subject: Tropical Islands Resort
summary: A hangar built for an airship that was never finished now holds a rainforest, a beach and 8,200 swimmers a day, in the pine country south of Berlin.

subject: Tsavo Man-Eaters
summary: In 1898, two maneless male lions terrorized railway workers at the Tsavo River bridge in Kenya, killing dozens of people over nine months before being hunted down by the project's chief engineer.

subject: Tucuruí Dam
summary: The first large hydroelectric dam built in the Brazilian Amazon powers millions of people — and displaced tens of thousands more, including Indigenous communities whose fisheries went under the water.

subject: Tummel Hydro-Electric Power Scheme
summary: A network of nine power stations, ten dams, and miles of tunnels that turned the Tummel Valley into a postwar engineering project, built largely by Donegal Tunnel Tigers and German and Italian former prisoners of war.

subject: UK Holocaust Memorial
summary: A proposed national memorial in a small park beside Parliament - and a decade of arguments about how Britain should remember.

subject: Udawalawe National Park
summary: A Sri Lankan wildlife sanctuary born from a reservoir project that displaced both farmers and elephants, now home to one of Asia's most visible wild elephant populations and the world's largest orphaned elephant release program.

subject: Uganda National Mosque
summary: East Africa's largest mosque, where roughly 300 steps up the minaret deliver the finest panorama of Kampala's legendary hills.

subject: Ulawun
summary: One of only sixteen Decade Volcanoes on Earth, Ulawun rises 2,334 meters above New Britain with near-constant activity and thousands of people living in its shadow.

subject: Ungdomshuset
summary: The house where Clara Zetkin proposed International Women's Day was sold by Copenhagen for 2.6 million kroner, occupied by autonomists for twenty-five years, taken by helicopter in 2007, and demolished within a week.

subject: Union Street, Aberdeen
summary: A mile of grey granite that nearly bankrupted Aberdeen to build, crossing a buried river on a bridge that held a world record, now part-pedestrianised and half-empty.

subject: Unisphere
summary: Built in 110 days from 700,000 pounds of stainless steel, the world's largest globe was proposed as a symbol of peace and simultaneously derided as the most uninspired design anyone had ever seen — and it has outlasted every other relic of the 1964 World's Fair.

subject: United States Army Aviation Museum
summary: Home to the world's largest collection of military helicopters, the United States Army Aviation Museum at Fort Rucker traces the arc of rotary-wing flight from a Wright brothers replica to a stealth helicopter that never saw combat.

subject: University of Concepción
summary: A bell tower copied from Berkeley rises over the only university campus in Chile protected as a national monument, raised by a city that wanted to learn without going to Santiago.

subject: Université libre de Bruxelles
summary: Conceived in 1834 as a Masonic counterweight to Catholic Leuven, the Universite libre de Bruxelles has produced five Nobel Prize winners, two Fields Medalists, the inventor of the Big Bang theory's modern form, and the engineer who designed the Atlas rocket.

subject: Valparaíso de Goiás
summary: Named for a Chilean engineer's hometown, this city grew from a 1979 housing project into one of the densest satellites of Brasília.

subject: Vietnamese Women's Museum
summary: A Hanoi museum founded by a former guerrilla commander that tells the story of Vietnamese women -- from rice paddies to battlefields -- through 40,000 artifacts.

subject: Villa El Chocón
summary: Built to house the workers of Argentina's 'work of the century,' this engineered company town outlived its dam's construction and reinvented itself as the Valley of the Dinosaurs.

subject: Vĩnh Tế Canal
summary: Eighty thousand Vietnamese and Khmer labourers cut eighty-seven kilometres of straight water across the frontier - and the canal carries the name of the woman who sat with their families.

subject: W. M. Keck Observatory
summary: Two telescopes with segmented mirrors solved an engineering problem thought impossible, then spent three decades rewriting humanity's understanding of the universe from atop a Hawaiian volcano.

subject: Wangkuai Reservoir
summary: A massive Great Leap Forward-era reservoir in Hebei that controls nearly 4,000 square kilometers of watershed and now channels water to sustain the ecologically vital Baiyangdian Lake.

subject: Washington National Cathedral
summary: An 83-year Gothic construction project that became the nation's spiritual stage, hosting presidential funerals, harboring a Darth Vader gargoyle, and sheltering the ashes of Helen Keller.

story.title: Waterton-Glacier: The World's First International Peace Park

subject: Waterton-Glacier
summary: The place where Canada and the United States decided their border should celebrate friendship rather than division - creating the world's first International Peace Park in 1932, when the idea of peaceful borders between nations still seemed worth celebrating.

subject: Weardale Railway
summary: An 18-mile heritage line from Bishop Auckland to Stanhope - born in 1842 to carry limestone, kept alive across four owners, and now run by the Auckland Project.

story.title: Wendover: Where the Atomic Bomb Crew Trained in Secret

subject: Wendover
summary: The Utah desert airfield where the 509th Composite Group practiced dropping dummy atomic bombs in absolute secrecy - so isolated that the government was certain no one would notice the unusual aircraft, the strange ordnance, or the men who would change history.

subject: West Kowloon Cultural District
summary: Built on 40 hectares of reclaimed Kowloon waterfront, the West Kowloon Cultural District spent nearly 20 years in planning controversy before emerging as one of Asia's most ambitious concentrations of museums, theatres, and public space.

subject: Westgate, Queensland
summary: A town that exists only on paper, surveyed beside a Queensland railway line, populated for a single census, and never built.

story.title: Where a Soccer Field Became a Cathedral of Faith

subject: Where a Soccer Field Became a Cathedral of Faith
summary: Built on a colonial-era soccer pitch in the first years of Indonesian independence, the Grand Mosque of Makassar grew from a modest community project into one of Southeast Asia's largest mosques, visited by presidents and cherished as a symbol of Makassar's identity.

story.title: Where the Iron Horse Came to Rest

subject: Where the Iron Horse Came to Rest
summary: Sacramento's 244-acre railyard -- once the western terminus of the transcontinental railroad and the biggest rail facility west of the Mississippi -- is being reborn as the city's most ambitious urban development project.

subject: Whitburn Lifeboat Station
summary: From 1818 to 1918, an unassuming boathouse at the south end of Whitburn launched volunteer crews into the North Sea to save the lives of strangers - 107 of them by one boat alone.

subject: White House (Rock Hill, South Carolina)
summary: A one-room cottage built in 1837 grew into an eighteen-room house, sheltered Civil War refugees, and stood at the center of one woman's losing fight to keep Rock Hill an unincorporated village.

story.title: Willie Smits: The Dutchman Who Regrew a Rainforest

subject: Willie Smits
summary: A Dutch microbiologist who grew up hungry on a farm in the Netherlands became an Indonesian citizen, founded the world's largest orangutan conservation organization, and proved that a dead forest could be brought back to life.

subject: Wiluna uranium mine
summary: The first uranium project ever fully approved in Western Australia - and more than a decade later, still a mine that exists only on paper, contested on Aboriginal country south of Wiluna.

subject: Wing Lee Street
summary: A narrow Sheung Wan street lined with 1960s tenement blocks that was scheduled for demolition until a film shot there won an award at the 2010 Berlin Film Festival — and the bulldozers never came.

subject: Wittenoom, Western Australia
summary: Wittenoom is Australia's most dangerous ghost town — a former asbestos mining settlement where more than 2,000 of its 20,000 former residents have died of asbestos-related diseases, and where the land itself cannot safely be cleaned.

subject: Woodhouse Colliery
summary: A proposed undersea coking-coal mine off Whitehaven became Britain's most contested planning fight, pitting the promise of 500 well-paid jobs against the country's net-zero commitments before being withdrawn in 2025.

subject: Wudaokou
summary: Named after a now-vanished railway crossing and dubbed the 'Center of the Universe' for its sky-high real estate prices, this Beijing student neighborhood thrives on the energy of a dozen surrounding universities.

subject: Wybalenna Aboriginal Establishment
summary: On a low rise above Bass Strait stand the ruins of a place where a colonial government promised the surviving Tasmanian Aboriginal people safety, and delivered instead a graveyard.

subject: Wylfa Newydd nuclear power station
summary: A 2,700 MW nuclear power station that was planned, partly designed, approved by the regulator, and then abandoned without a single piece of concrete poured — an emblem of British nuclear ambitions in the 2010s and their collapse.

subject: X-100 (house)
summary: An experimental all-steel house built by Eichler Homes in 1956 to prove that the future of American housing could be prefabricated, modernist, and affordable -- and named after a spaceship.

subject: Yamal LNG
summary: A $27 billion liquefied natural gas project above the Arctic Circle that produces 16.5 million tonnes per year, ships gas through ice on purpose-built tankers, and supplies roughly one-seventh of the European Union's LNG imports despite sanctions and geopolitical tensions.

subject: Yamal project
summary: Beneath the frozen tundra of the Yamal Peninsula lies nearly 22 trillion cubic meters of natural gas -- a reserve so vast that Russia built railways, bridges, pipelines, and an Arctic seaport across permafrost to extract it.

subject: Yamdrok Hydropower Station
summary: A controversial hydroelectric plant that taps a sacred Tibetan lake through tunnels bored into the mountainside, built over the objections of the Panchen Lama and haunted by the question of whether it will drain the very waters it was designed to preserve.

subject: Yedikule Gasworks
summary: Istanbul's first gasworks, built in the Ottoman era and completed in 1880, lit hundreds of street lamps across the historic peninsula for more than a century before falling silent in 1993 — its brick furnace halls now awaiting the reinvention that architects and the city have long been planning.

subject: Yeelirrie uranium project
summary: One of Australia's largest undeveloped uranium deposits, Yeelirrie has sat unmined for fifty years, held back by collapsing markets, tiny groundwater creatures, and the enduring resistance of the Tjiwarl traditional owners.

subject: Yellowtail Dam
summary: A 525-foot concrete arch dam named for the man who fought hardest against it, dividing a tribe and transforming a river.

subject: Yolo Bypass
summary: California's 59,000-acre engineered floodplain that protects Sacramento by deliberately flooding itself, then doubles as farmland, fish nursery, and wildlife haven.

subject: Yuen Long New Town
summary: Hong Kong's most remote new town took three decades to fully connect to the rest of the city — a slow-burn transformation that turned a traditional market town into a major regional centre only after a rail line finally arrived in 2003.

subject: Yuendumu
summary: Yuendumu, a Warlpiri community on the edge of the Tanami Desert, launched one of Australia's most celebrated Aboriginal art movements when five elders painted their school's doors in 1982 — and has been defying expectations ever since.

subject: Zug, Western Sahara
summary: A remote outpost in the disputed far south of Western Sahara, where a sand sea meets a contested border and a small town's hospital became a project of long-distance solidarity.

subject: Zuiderzee Works
summary: The audacious engineering project that dammed an arm of the North Sea and created an entire Dutch province from water - recognized as one of the Seven Wonders of the Modern World.
